The ambulance was responding after a footballer broke his leg in three places in a game on Saturday in Omagh. Omagh Hospitals player Mark O'Sullivan was badly hurt 40 minutes into the match against Glebe United. The team's manager Paul McCabe has urged the council to install a path or road so vehicles can get to the pitch. The Fermanagh and Western League match was taking place off Retreat Close near the Tyrone County Hospital. Mr McCabe said people get to the pitches after crossing about 100 yards of "marshland". "People could end up having a life-threatening problem like a heart attack and an ambulance may not be able to reach them," he said. "He (Mark) was in serious pain. Even when we were waiting for the ambulance, we were saying that the ambulance was bound to get struck in the grass. "We were on standby to help the ambulance if it got stuck again on its way out but there was no issue. It probably went over the same tracks as when it came in." He added: "We've been asking for a road, a path, some gravel even just to make sure you can get to the pitch. "It's not the maintenance men, they do what they can. "But it's not the last time somebody is going to get injured on a football pitch down there and the ambulance won't be able to get to it." Mr McCabe said the player was taken to Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry.

Mr Annan told the Financial Times (FT) that President Uhuru Kenyatta and his deputy William Ruto should not have remained free during their trials. The ICC dropped charges of crimes against humanity against both men but said witnesses had been intimidated. The cases related to violence after disputed elections in 2007. Some 1,500 people were killed and 600,00 forced from their homes as ethnic clashes spread around the country. Both men denied the charges and accused the ICC of unfairly targeting African leaders. Kenya says it will withdraw from the ICC. Africa Live: BBC news updates from the continent Mr Annan, who was appointed by the African Union to mediate Kenya's post-election crisis of 2007-08, accused the Kenyan government of using state resources to undermine the ICC. "The president and vice-president were the ones in the dock and so they put lots of efforts and resources into fighting the case," he said. The former UN secretary general told the FT that Africans should seek justice abroad if they could not get it domestically. He also rejected accusations that the ICC was biased against Africa, saying: "Slobodan Milosevic and others convicted of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia had been tried in The Hague before the ICC was established." The African Union has been critical of the ICC with member states on the continent threatening to withdraw from the court. Mr Annan also praised the recent conviction of Hissene Habre, the former president of Chad, who was tried in an African Union-backed court in Senegal.

Officers came across the injured 27-year-old woman in Main St, Kildysart, at about 19:30 local time on Wednesday and called for emergency medical help. Police also became aware there was an injured man at a house in the street. The pair later died at the scene. Police said they are not looking for anyone else over the double fatality. The dead man, who was 44, had been found in a "serious condition" in the house. Police tried to help both of the injured but they were pronounced dead by a local doctor and their bodies remain at scene. A Garda (police) spokesman said the area has been sealed off for a technical examination and the state pathologist has been contacted. "Gardai at this stage can confirm that they are not looking for a third party in relation to this incident," the spokesman added. He appealed to anyone who had been in Kildysart village, particularly Main St between 18:00 and 19:30 local time, to contact officers.

Saturday was the hottest day of the year so far, with the mercury peaking at 30.2C (86.36F) in Teddington, south-west London, the Met Office said. Forecaster Charles Powell said Sunday and Monday would be the same. He said there would be a lot of "dry, sunny, warm, humid weather with high UV, high pollen". The high temperatures are due to warm, humid air originating from the tropical Atlantic, with the south and south-east of England and Greater London predicted to experience highs of 32C (89.6F) on Sunday and 33C (91.4F) on Monday, about 10C (18F) above the usual average for this time of year. However, some northern parts of Scotland saw some rain on Sunday and were due to have more on Monday. The Met Office said "a wedge of really hot air" would blow over from France on Thursday, with temperatures in eastern and southern England predicted to climb as high as 34C. The strength of the UV in some spots has been recorded as being as high as that in Cyprus and Gibraltar. "All throughout this period we will have some pretty mild uncomfortable nights - a lot of places in the mid to high teens for night-time temperatures," Mr Powell said. The weather is expected to remain dry in the lead-up to the Glastonbury Festival next weekend with a 20% chance of "isolated showers" on Wednesday and Thursday. "It is mainly going to be dry, looking at the whole event," the Met Office said. "Wednesday, Thursday and Friday look dry with good spells of sunshine. However, the Met Office predicts "cooler and fresher" temperatures on Saturday and Sunday with a mixture of sunny spells and showers. Public Health England (PHE) has issued a heat health warning. Spokesman Dr Thomas Waite said: "For some people, such as older people, those with underlying health conditions and those with young children, the summer heat can bring real health risks. "That's why we're urging everyone to keep an eye on those you know who may be at risk this summer."

The Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) senior player selection policy (SPSP) means only three players who play outside Wales can be picked. Hadley thinks Taulupe Faletau, George North and Jamie Roberts will be the three wildcards. "They'll leave Rhys Priestland out," said ex-dual-code international Hadley. He feels the presence in Wales of Ospreys rivals Dan Biggar and Sam Davies plus Scarlets' Rhys Patchell and Gareth Anscombe leaves Priestland facing the end of his Test career. "With the other outside halves in the pecking order at the moment you would probably think that was the end of it," Hadley said. "You've got Sam Davies, Dan Biggar, Rhys Patchell - who is going to play a fair bit at 10 - and you've got Gareth Anscombe. "Unless one of the others gets injured and cannot be picked then there's a possibility he [Priestland] becomes the third wildcard choice then." Priestland, who joined Bath from Scarlets after the 2015 World Cup, announced in October 2015 that he was taking an 18-month break from playing for Wales. But the 48-times capped player reversed his decision two months later and featured in all five games of the 2016 Six Nations and went on the summer tour to New Zealand. Priestland is affected by a player selection policy is aimed at ensuring more players play their domestic rugby in Wales. The WRU has revealed its seven-man list for the first time. Three wildcard selections are available for each Wales campaign during 2016-17. Lock Dominic Day, flanker Nicky Thomas and scrum-half Rhodri Williams are the others affected while Bath lock Luke Charteris is exempt from the rule and free for selection. The SPSP does not affect players who signed contracts with clubs outside Wales before the policy was introduced, such as Toulon's Leigh Halfpenny and Exeter's Tomas Francis. "I just think the whole rule is ridiculous," Hadley told BBC Radio Wales Sport. "They should just scrap it and (the coach) should be able to pick whatever players he wants to pick. "For Wales you want to be playing your best players, whether they're playing in Wales or not "You want to try and keep them in Wales if you can, but if you can't then surely you want them still playing for Wales."

The Israeli's contract is shortly to expire and at the Africa Cup of Nations, where Ghana finished fourth, he said there would be no renewal. Grant said he had met with Ghana FA president Kwesi Nyantakyi and informed him "the time is right for me to move on to a new challenge". He led Ghana to the Nations Cup final in 2015 and the semi-finals this year. While he was unable to end Ghana's more than 30-year wait for a fifth title - beaten on penalties in the final against Ivory Coast two years ago and losing to Cameroon in the last-four this time - Grant has once again made them contenders. When he took the role in November 2014, Ghana were still reeling from a turbulent World Cup campaign in Brazil, where they failed to win a single match against a backdrop of off-field issues. "I've hugely enjoyed my time in Ghana taking over after the disastrous 2014 World Cup campaign and rebuilding the squad to reach the final in the African Cup of Nations for only the second time in 23 years, and also the semi-final of this year's competition," he said. "And the passion and loyalty of the supporters is something I'll always remember."

The FTSE 100 share index had already been trading lower, but dropped further as the pound strengthened, and was down 106.72 points at 7,220.38 by the close. For multinational firms on the FTSE 100, a stronger pound means profits earned overseas are worth less when they are converted back into sterling. Sterling soared back above the $1.23 mark following Mrs May's speech. The pound had already been trading higher, but took off during the speech and throughout the afternoon to close up nearly 2.9% against the dollar, or three and a half cents, at $1.2392 for the day as a whole. Against the euro, the pound was up 1.83% at 1.157 euros. On the stock market, shares in Rolls-Royce jumped nearly 7% before losing some of the gains to 694.50p after the engineering firm agreed to pay £671m to settle bribery and corruption cases with UK and US authorities. British American Tobacco (BAT) shares slipped 3.83% to £45.80 after the company said it had agreed a deal to take control of US rival Reynolds, The $49.4bn (£40bn) deal will see BAT buy the 57.8% stake in Reynolds that it does not already own. STockbrokers Hargreaves Lansdown closed up 4%, making it the second best riser of the top 100. Bakery chain Greggs saw its shares rise 1.2% to £10.13 after it said full-year profits were set to beat expectations following "strong" Christmas sales. Like-for-like sales grew 6.4% in the final three months of the year, and were up 4.2% in the year as a whole.

Henry Lynch II's luck ran out when his tutor, who had been working extremely late, surprised him - and an accomplice - when he came back to his office. It happened at about 02:00 on Wednesday, a university spokesman said. Fellow student Troy Kiphuth has also been charged. The duo will go before a judge next month. According to Jay Blanton, the university spokesman, Mr Lynch, a 21 year-old biosystems engineering student, had entered the campus building ceiling ducts, crawled through them and dropped into his statistics instructor's room. It is not clear how he had accessed the air ducts in the first place. He had then opened the door to Mr Kiphuth, and both had proceeded to look for the paper while keeping the door blocked. Meanwhile the teacher, John Cain, was on his way back down the corridor after a meal. When he tried to open his office door and couldn't, Mr Cain shouted that he would call the police, upon which the men opened the door and ran out. Later, Mr Lynch confessed - and told the police that he had tried to get the test earlier that day, too, but couldn't find it. The air duct method had worked for him before. He has confessed to stealing an exam earlier in the semester, but said he had not shared it with other students, Mr Blanton said. The matter has been referred to the university's internal discipline system. "Cheating and theft of this kind is very serious in an academic institution," the university spokesman said.

Coleman, 46, guided Wales to the semi-final of Euro 2016 - the side's first major tournament in 58 years. He got the honour at a ceremony at the city's Guildhall on Thursday. Coleman told BBC Wales it was "important" that he is still surrounded by the people he was brought up with in Swansea. "The things that were instilled in me from a young age - you hold onto the good things - and they have certainly stood me in good stead," he added. "I'm so proud of the achievements of this Welsh team, so proud to be associated with it, and to be a Welshman." Lord Mayor David Hopkins said: "Chris is a proud Swansea boy and a terrific ambassador for the city, so he's thoroughly deserving of being offered the highest honour we can confer." Other people to be given the freedom of the city include Prince Charles and President Jimmy Carter, as well as footballers John Charles and Mel Nurse. Following the ceremony, a celebration was held at Brangwyn Hall, which included a performance by James Dean Bradfield of the Manic Street Preachers. Mr Hopkins added: "Chris took over the Wales football manager's job in extremely difficult circumstances following the death of his close friend Gary Speed, but his achievements ever since mean the nation has truly taken him to their hearts. "Nobody will ever forget what his Welsh team did at the Euro 2016 championships in France this summer. It was a magical time for Welsh football, with Chris leading his men to the semi-finals and setting the tournament alight with a series of inspired performances."

Jacques Rudolph (17) fell early, but Kettleborough (81) and Colin Ingram (30) added 71 for the second wicket. Kettleborough put on a further 66 with Donald (91 not out) before being caught off the bowling of David Payne. Chris Cooke also contributed with a quickfire 65, as rain brought about an early close with Glamorgan on 315-4. The visitors' score could have been even higher were it not for bad weather, as rain saw 19 overs lost. Donald's half-century was the third of the 18-year-old's career in first-class cricket, and surpassed his previous best of 67 to end the day on 91. Glamorgan batsman James Kettleborough told BBC Wales Sport: "It was very satisfying to get some runs though it would have been nice to go on and get to three figures. "It was tricky this morning with a bit of dampness around and they bowled well but we got through and it got a bit easier as the day went on. "Aneurin Donald and Chris Cooke played really well and made it our day, it would be brilliant for Aneurin (to become Glamorgan's youngest Championship centurion), so fingers crossed he goes on and gets a big one."

Janina Gehlau, 26, from Dusseldorf, died in October 2014 when the lorry turned left at Ludgate Circus, pulling her under its wheels. A jury at the Old Bailey found him not guilty after an hour's deliberation. Gehlau's mother said she hoped her daughter's death would make people "think twice before cycling in London". Vincent Doyle, 45, failed to spot the German postgraduate in the cycle lane, despite overtaking her 200 metres before the junction, where he waited for 23 seconds at a red light. Had his mirrors been correctly positioned, he would have had her in his sights for three to five seconds before his wheels clipped hers, sending her underneath the vehicle, the court heard. Mr Doyle said he always made safety checks and had looked in his mirrors "five or six times" before the green light. He told jurors that he never saw Mrs Gehlau waving her arms or heard her shouting before she fell under the lorry. He felt a "bump" and looked in his mirror to see her head sticking out, he said. Mr Doyle described how he held her hand and pleaded with her to "hold on". "I was taking her pulse, chatting to her all the time. I was holding her hand telling her'Please hang on'. We were chatting away. And then she died. She died just as the ambulance got there." On how the accident had affected him, he said: "I had a nervous breakdown last year. I was in psychiatric hospital for eight months." In a statement, her mother Andrea Tasic said: "We are devastated by the verdict and do not feel that we have got justice for Janina. "I miss her so much. She had a great future ahead of her and it was erased in a moment. "I told her I thought the roads were too dangerous when I visited her, but she was an experienced cyclist and told me not to worry, she said it would be fine. "My only hope is that this makes people think twice before cycling in London."

It rejected an appeal by David Chaytor, Elliot Morley and Jim Devine that their cases should be heard by Parliament, not the courts. The three men, who all deny theft by false accounting, will face separate trials at Southwark Crown Court. The Supreme Court said the reasons for rejecting the appeal would be given at a later date. But the decision upholds a ruling by the Court of Appeal in July that the three were not protected by parliamentary privilege - an ancient right protecting MPs from legal action arising from proceedings in Parliament - in relation to their expenses claims. Former Bury North MP Mr Chaytor, 61, of Todmorden, West Yorkshire; former Scunthorpe MP Mr Morley, 58, of Winterton, north Lincolnshire; and former Livingston MP Mr Devine, 57, of Bathgate, West Lothian, are all on unconditional bail and face separate trials. The first, Mr Morley's trial, is expected to begin on 22 November. In the Supreme Court hearing last month, Nigel Pleming QC, representing two of the men, told a panel of nine Supreme Court Justices that their appeal was "not, and never has been, an attempt to take them above or outside the law". He argued important issues of principle were raised by the case and the allegations had to be "dealt with by the correct law, the law of Parliament" - arguing that only Parliament could question and impugn statements made in Parliament. He argued that the expenses scheme was created and is administered by Parliament for Parliamentarians: "The administration of the scheme is also entirely a matter for the House of Commons - this extends not only to its creation but to its regulation and enforcement." But in a brief hearing on Wednesday, Supreme Court President Lord Phillips said: "Each of these appeals is dismissed. The reasons will be given later." In July the Court of Appeal ruled that parliamentary immunity or privilege had never been attached to allegations MPs had committed "crimes of dishonesty". All three men were barred by their party from standing again as Labour MPs at the general election. The charges against them followed a nine-month police investigation triggered after details of all MPs' expenses claims were leaked to a national newspaper.

The 17-year-old says she would sit in her bedroom crying and her brother would ask why she was so grumpy. "I was the one person that got an opportunity first," she says. "I was told,'They're just jealous' but that doesn't make me feel any better. It still hurts, they're still doing it." She says because she felt she couldn't tell anyone what was happening at the time, her mood was put down to being a teenager. "I just felt like,'Yeah I am a teenager,' but actually there's something really, really wrong and not being able to reach out," she explains. "I remember being sat on the train right next to my mum and scrolling through messages and messages and messages. "My heart just dropped and you get that lump in your throat and you're trying not to cry." The bullying finally stopped when she deleted her online profiles and left school. Maisie, who plays Arya Stark in Game of Thrones, says that isn't the answer in most cases, but she says she did it because her career was really beginning to take-off. "Don't say anything or post anything on the internet that you wouldn't say or do in person," she says. "I thought that the popular girls at school meant that the whole world hated me. "I've now got one best friend from school and we both decided to leave that popularity contest behind." You can hear more from Maisie on Radio 1 Stories: Anti-Social Media on Tuesday night at 21:00 GMT. Radio 1 has linked up with YouthNet to host an hour of live advice on how to deal with online bullying between 10-11pm every night (Mon-Thurs) and there's help at BBC Advice. Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube

It is the third time the island have played in the fourth tier of the global tournament, having been relegated on their previous two appearances. Jersey won Division Five in May, having made the World Twenty20 global qualifiers in 2015. "We think we've got a young squad with a lot of experience and we're really confident," said coach Neil MacRae. "It's a huge tournament because we have the potential to play the highest level we've ever played at if we get promoted." The island side, who have been an international cricket nation since 2005, finished in the bottom two in both the 2008 Division Four event in Tanzania and the 2014 tournament in Singapore. But they go into the 2016 event following a third World Cricket League tournament win in four, having won the World League Five final in May. "We're really excited, we've come off a great effort in division five earlier in the summer and a big win against Oman in the final, who are our first opponents in the USA," MacRae told BBC Radio Jersey. "Two years ago in Singapore it was a tough week for us, but I thought that the players did exceptionally well in tough conditions out there. "We now go out there off the back of winning World Cricket League Five again and a squad which is two years more experienced, so we're really looking forward to the challenge." The sites are three of 56 across the UK that will be sold as part of a long-term strategy to reduce costs and improve efficiency. The sites are in County Down - Abercorn Barracks, Ballykinler; Kinnegar Logistics Base, Holywood; and Volunteer Gliding School at Newtownards Airfield. The move was announced by Sir Michael Fallon, the defence secretary. Sir Michael said it would deliver better value for money and release enough land to build 55,000 homes. It is estimated that about Â£140m will be saved over the next decade by selling off the sites, which Sir Michael said would be reinvested in creating "areas of military expertise" in locations across the country. However, Strangford MP Jim Shannon described the moves as "backwards" and "illogical". The MoD previously said it is considering knocking down the 200 houses at Abercorn Barracks. "It would be a rather backwards step because I think they should be retaining the accommodation for use as social housing," he said. He added that it appeared that the Kinnegar base would move to Palace Barracks nearby and it was "unconfirmed" as to whether any jobs would be lost because of the move. He said the decision to sell two hangars at Newtownards Airfield was an "unbelievable step". "There is no potential for housing to be built at this site. The decision hasn't been thought out clearly, particularly as we recently got funding for the air cadets."

Several websites offering fatwas have recently been blocked, following a decree by King Abdullah. The decree was seen as an attempt to reduce controversial fatwas issued by minor or ultra-conservative clerics. Some of these have been a serious embarrassment to the Saudi authorities. The Saudi newspaper, Arab News, said Islam Today had closed its fatwa pages in order to avoid closure of the website by the authorities. The decree restricts the right to issue fatwas - usually translated as religious edicts, but sometimes carrying the status merely of advice - to members of an officially approved council of Islamic scholars. King Abdullah is known to favour reform, but he has faced opposition from conservative clerics and some members of the Saudi ruling family allied with the religious establishment. Ultra-conservative clerics have sometimes used fatwas to publicly oppose what they see as attempts to Westernise their society. There have also been a number of controversial fatwas that have embarrassed Saudi reformers. In one such instance, clerics suggested that the Saudi prohibition on mixing of the sexes could be overcome if a man were symbolically to become a woman's child by sucking on her breast or drinking her breast milk. In other cases, more liberal interpretations of Islam sparked counter-fatwas by conservatives, leading to what some commentators have described as fatwa chaos. Islam Today gave no explanation for why it had closed its fatwa section. As of 1300 GMT on Thursday, the closure applied only to the website's more popular Arabic-language section and it was still possible to access the smaller fatwa archive in English. Salman al-Awdah himself was once a controversial figure, a hardline cleric who was imprisoned in the 1990s for inciting opposition to the Saudi government. He has since reinvented himself as a moderate figure and has become one of Saudi Arabia's most influential religious figures, with a wide following through the media although he has remained outside the government-backed religious establishment.

The US company is in the process of finalising a purchase of a controlling interest in Formula 1. The FIA's approval was the final regulatory hurdle before the sale, which will see Liberty take over from investment group CVC Capital Partners. The FIA believed its partnership with Liberty will "ensure the continued success and development" of F1. Liberty is expected to complete its takeover of the sport within the next few weeks. It bought just over 18% of the shares in Delta Topco, the holding company of the F1 Group, in September. Liberty announced before Christmas that it had cleared all regulatory hurdles and had the necessary approvals for the purchase. And on Tuesday in Colorado, the company's shareholders approved the buy-out. Its purchase of its second tranche of shares, to take its holding to 35.3%, is due to be completed within the next few weeks. Liberty has said it wants to protect F1's historic European races, establish new races in the USA and Latin America and grow the sport through the exploitation of digital media.

Under a deal with Ukraine's M.V. Cargo, the money will be used to build a grain terminal on the Black Sea that will boost agricultural exports. The terminal will allow Ukrainian farmers to export an additional five million tons of grain. Overseas companies have been reluctant to invest in Ukraine because of its ongoing struggle with Russia. Ukraine has been fighting pro-Russian separatists in the eastern part of the country and working to root out corruption that has made investors nervous. Prime Minister, Arseniy Yatsenyuk, said the deal was a first step in getting foreign investors to see the country as a "truly reliable and good place for making investments". "Ukraine is already one of the world's great agricultural producers, but it should be an agricultural superpower," said US ambassador to Ukraine, Geoffrey Pyatt. The new terminal is scheduled to be completed by the spring of 2018. Ukraine expects to export a record 37 million tons of grain between July 2015 and June 2016. Cargill is the largest privately held company in the US.

Pakistan's Akmal, 25, the second Foxes overseas T20 Blast player, scored 133 T20 runs in four matches this season. Ireland international O'Brien, 31, will be available for both the T20 Blast and the One-Day Cup. "We saw the positive influence Umar and Kevin had on the club this year," said Leicestershire chief executive Wasim Khan. "They are both match-winners." He continued: "They showed their ability by both having an immediate impact with Kevin batting beautifully in his first game at Lancashire and Umar playing our best innings of the tournament at Nottinghamshire on his debut." "I know our members and supporters enjoyed watching them play and we are excited to welcome both players back to Grace Road."

Several schools around the 5,450m (17,900 foot) volcano were closed as a precaution, and evacuation shelters have been prepared. The National Disaster Prevention Centre (Cenapred) raised the alert to "yellow stage three" - the third-highest level. The volcano lies around 70km (40 miles) from Mexico City, and is visible from the capital on a clear day. "We can hear the roar of the volcano, sometimes we can feel its force," Concepcion Perez from the town of Xalitzintla in Puebla State, 12km (seven miles) from the volcano told the French news agency Agence France-Presse. Cenapred officials said the alert could remain for weeks or months until the volcano's activity diminished. Popocatepetl - which means "Smoking Mountain" in the indigenous Nahuatl language - is Mexico's second-highest peak. In 2000 a major eruption forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people from nearby communities.

Nel, 30, had been included in head coach Vern Cotter's 37-man squad for the upcoming championship. However, a scan revealed that the Edinburgh tight-head damaged an intervertebral disc in his neck during a Challenge Cup tie against Harlequins. The Scots open their campaign at home to Ireland on 4 February before travelling to France eight days later. Nel, who has won 15 caps, will be assessed to decide whether he requires corrective surgery, Scottish Rugby said. This year's championship will be head coach Vern Cotter's last in charge of the national side before he takes charge of Montpellier. Last year, Scotland finished fourth in the championship after victories against Italy and France. In November's autumn Tests, the Scots beat Argentina and Georgia after a narrow defeat by Australia. South Africa-born Nel joined Edinburgh in 2012 and qualifies to play for Scotland on residency rules. French Top 14 sides Toulon and Clermont Auvergne are reportedly interested in signing him, though Edinburgh say they have had "positive conversations" about keeping him in the Scottish capital. BBC Scotland's Tom English This is devastating news. Vern Cotter hinted that all was far from well with Nel earlier in the week, but the confirmation that he is now out injured again after less than half an hour of his comeback game is cruel on the player and cruel on Scotland too. Nel is a world-class tight-head and was, until this latest injury, one of Scotland's very few guaranteed Lions for the summer tour to New Zealand. With so much uncertainty around a serious neck problem - particularly serious for a prop forward - you have to consider him a major doubt for the Lions. For Nel, it's a catastrophe on two different fronts. Scotland played well in the autumn without him, but there's no question that they are a better team when he's around. He brings experience and solidity to the scrum and carries hard in the loose. Hopefully his recovery will go well. He'll be a big miss. Speculation rose about his whereabouts after a consortium of banks and creditors approached the Supreme Court over $1.4bn (Â£980m) in unpaid debts. They demanded that his passport be impounded, and a $75m (Â£53m) severance pay he was to receive from Diageo be blocked and used to repay them. The payout was blocked, but it emerged that Mr Mallya had already left India. The issue caused an uproar in India with opposition MPs accusing the government of allowing the flamboyant businessman to leave the country. But Mr Mallya insisted that he "did not flee from India", and also criticised his "media trial" over the issue. Media reports say Mr Mallya is currently living in London. Opposition MPs have demanded that the government should bring him back to face the law. Mr Mallya, who is a household name in India, sold a large chunk of United Spirits, which he inherited from his father, to Diageo in April 2014. He was to receive the $75m payout as settlement after being ousted from the firm in February. Mr Mallya, once dubbed by Indian media as "India's Richard Branson" and the "King of Good Times" for his lavish lifestyle also owns a stake in the Formula One team Force India.

The former Dundee United front man, who has also played for Albion Rovers and Montrose, joins the Bannsiders from the Candystripes until January. "Jordan gives us another option up top and provides a bit more competition for places," said Coleraine Oran Kearney. "He holds the ball and can go in behind defences and runs the channels well. He can also finish too and has a lot of experience despite only being 21." Allan started off in Dundee United's academy, going out on loan to Albion Rovers during the 2013-14 season, before joining Scottish League One team Morton in July 2014. He made eight appearances for the club during the 2014-15 season for the club before moving to League Two side Montrose in January 2015. Allan went on to play a part as Montrose survived dropping out of the league by beating Highland Football League side Brora Rangers. The striker left Montrose after the season's end in July 2015 and joined Derry last December.
sampled: Africa's Elephants in Crisis: Historic Census Reveals Alarming Decline A groundbreaking aerial census spanning 18 African countries has revealed a devastating decline in elephant populations. The comprehensive survey, stretching from Mali in West Africa to South Africa, uncovered that 30% of the continent's elephants have vanished in just seven years. According to Elephants Without Borders, approximately 30,000 elephants are lost annually, with 144,000 killed since 2007. The primary threat is poaching—the illegal hunting of elephants for their valuable ivory tusks, which command enormous prices on the black market. Tanzania, Mozambique, Angola, and Cameroon have emerged as the hardest-hit regions. Meanwhile, Botswana holds the largest elephant population with 130,451 individuals, though poachers are increasingly targeting this sanctuary. The current population stands at roughly 380,000 elephants across the surveyed nations, but experts warn that hundreds more have likely died since the count concluded. This alarming trend highlights the urgent need for stronger anti-poaching measures and international cooperation to protect Africa's iconic elephants before more irreplaceable populations disappear forever.

Flying Disc Federation Granted Official IOC Recognition The International Olympic Committee has granted full recognition to the World Flying Disc Federation (WFDF), marking a significant achievement for disc-based sports worldwide. The WFDF, which governs activities including Ultimate Frisbee, Disc Golf, and Freestyle, expressed being "honoured and humbled" by the historic decision announced at an IOC session in Kuala Lumpur on Sunday. "This is an incredible milestone in the 30-year history of WFDF," the organization stated, adding that the recognition "will give a further boost to our efforts to increasing the presence of Flying Disc sports in all countries and on all continents." Disc-based games are currently played by thousands of athletes across 58 countries. Ultimate, the most popular variant, originated in the United States during the 1960s and is played as a non-contact, mixed-team sport on field or indoor pitches. Uniquely, Ultimate operates without referees, instead relying on principles of "sportsmanship and fair play" according to WFDF guidelines.

US Economy Hits Speed Bump with Weakest Growth in Two Years The US economy experienced a significant deceleration in early 2016, with growth slowing to its weakest pace in two years. This sharp downturn marked a dramatic departure from the 1.4% expansion recorded in the final quarter of 2015, catching many economists off guard with its severity. ## Multiple Factors Behind the Slowdown The economic stumble has been attributed to several interconnected factors. Declining domestic demand combined with a strengthening dollar has considerably hampered export performance. Perhaps most notably, American consumers—whose spending accounts for over two-thirds of the economy—have tightened their purse strings, with consumption growth slowing from 2.4% to just 1.9%. This consumer caution has created a ripple effect throughout the business sector. With shoppers purchasing less, companies have grown reluctant to replenish inventories, leading to a dramatic 5.9% drop in business investment—the steepest quarterly decline since the 2009 financial crisis. ## Energy Sector Takes Major Hit The oil industry has been particularly hard-hit, with exploration activities plummeting by a record 86% as companies slashed spending in response to tumbling oil prices. While cheaper fuel has provided consumers with additional disposable income, it has simultaneously devastated profits for oil-dependent businesses. ## Mixed Signals Ahead Despite these concerning economic indicators, the labour market has shown resilience, with unemployment dipping below 5% in January. The Federal Reserve acknowledged this paradox, noting improved employment conditions despite apparent economic slowing. While many forecasters anticipate a rebound, analysts like Chris Williamson of Markit remain cautious, warning that survey data suggests only modest recovery extending into the second quarter, with weakness spreading from manufacturing to services sectors.

Historic Yorkshire Mill Reopens as Green Energy Hub The Greenholme Mill station in Burley, Wharfdale, has been officially opened by MP Philip Davies, marking a significant milestone in sustainable energy production. The £700,000 facility will generate 14,000 megawatt hours of electricity annually, with power sold directly to the National Grid. CO2Sense, a Yorkshire Forward subsidiary, contributed £200,000 and technical expertise to the project.

Markets Dip Amid North Korea Tensions and Disney Streaming News US stock markets experienced modest declines on Thursday as geopolitical tensions escalated between Washington and Pyongyang. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.17% to 22,048.7, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.04% to 2,474.02 and the Nasdaq declined 0.28% to 6,352.3. The market jitters followed North Korea's threat to strike the US military base in Guam, responding to President Trump's warning of "fire and fury" against the regime. Trump continued his aggressive rhetoric on Twitter, highlighting America's nuclear capabilities, though Secretary of State Rex Tillerson attempted to calm concerns, stating no imminent threat existed. Despite opening lower, stocks recovered throughout the day, maintaining positions near recent record highs. Walt Disney significantly impacted the market, dropping nearly 4% after announcing plans to launch proprietary ESPN and Disney streaming services while terminating its Netflix distribution agreement in 2019. Netflix shares fell approximately 1.5% following the news.

Tim Cook Shows Political Prowess in Apple Tax Battle In the wake of the European Commission's bombshell ruling on Apple's tax arrangements, CEO Tim Cook has demonstrated he's more than just a tech executive—he's a savvy political operator navigating treacherous waters between European regulators, the Irish government, and American interests. Cook's response to charges that Apple received illegal state aid from Ireland was a masterclass in political positioning. Speaking to Irish media, he deployed a carefully calibrated strategy that touched on emotion, loyalty, and economic pragmatism. The personal element came first, with Cook expressing outrage at accusations so "contrary to our values"—positioning Apple not as a tax avoider but as a company wronged by mischaracterization. This was followed by a deliberate appeal to Irish solidarity, invoking 37 years of partnership "through thick and thin." He even recalled a 1998 near-closure of Apple's Cork facility, which he claimed was saved after recognizing the exceptional quality of Irish employees—a not-so-subtle reminder of Apple's importance to Ireland's economy. Cook's repeated insistence that "Apple hasn't done anything wrong and the Irish government hasn't done anything wrong" attempted to cement a united front against European Commissioner Margrethe Vestager's ruling. Simultaneously, he threw American politicians a bone by promising to repatriate "several billion dollars" to the US, acknowledging the sentiment back home that if anyone deserves Apple's tax dollars, it's Washington, not Dublin. However, Cook's performance, skillful though it was, obscured some inconvenient truths. His claim that Apple pays a 26% tax rate globally is misleading. This calculation includes US taxes at 35%—taxes that are merely deferred, not actually paid. These payments remain suspended indefinitely, awaiting either lower US tax rates or a special repatriation amnesty. The entire Irish structure exists precisely to avoid that 35% rate. Cook's assertion that Apple had no "sweetheart deal"—that anyone could have parked money untaxed in Ireland—is technically true but practically absurd. As the article aptly notes, it's like saying any pub team could win the FA Cup. Without elite tax lawyers—the Pogbas and Ibrahimovics of the financial world—such arrangements remain theoretical possibilities rather than practical realities. Margrethe Vestager has wielded her considerable powers as Competition Commissioner boldly, taking on one of the world's most powerful corporations. But in Tim Cook, she faces a formidable adversary who understands that this battle will be won not just in courtrooms but in the court of public opinion, where political skill matters as much as legal arguments. The clash between these two heavyweights promises to reshape the landscape of international corporate taxation.

Leg Power May Hold Key to Healthy Brain Aging, Study Suggests A groundbreaking study from King's College London has identified leg power as a potentially important marker for brain health in aging adults, suggesting that lower body strength could indicate whether someone is getting sufficient exercise to maintain cognitive function. The research, published in the journal Gerontology, tracked more than 150 pairs of twin sisters aged 43 to 73 over a decade-long period. Scientists measured leg power at the study's outset using modified gym equipment that assessed both speed and power during leg extension exercises. Brain function was evaluated through computerized tasks testing memory and mental processing skills at the beginning and end of the study. The findings revealed a striking pattern: twins with greater leg power at the study's start maintained better cognitive function and experienced fewer age-related brain changes after 10 years. This correlation persisted even after researchers accounted for other known dementia risk factors, including heart health and lifestyle variables. Lead researcher Dr. Claire Steves emphasized the significance of the results: "When it came to cognitive ageing, leg strength was the strongest factor that had an impact in our study. We think leg strength is a marker of the kind of physical activity that is good for your brain." The researchers believe exercise releases beneficial chemicals in the body that may protect and boost elderly brains. However, they acknowledge that more research is needed to definitively prove this connection and to determine whether improved memory test scores actually translate into reduced dementia risk. Dr. Doug Brown, director of research at Alzheimer's Society, noted that the findings contribute to mounting evidence linking physical activity with brain health. "However, we still don't fully understand how this relationship works and how we can maximise the benefit," he cautioned. Dr. Simon Ridley from Alzheimer's Research UK added that the research highlights the importance of incorporating strength training alongside aerobic exercise in dementia prevention strategies. Experts emphasize that while the connection between leg strength and brain health is promising, it remains difficult to separate leg power from other lifestyle factors that may influence cognitive aging. The study did not specifically examine dementia diagnosis rates, leaving questions about practical applications for prevention.

Fatal Helicopter Crash Prompts Safety Inspections A Super Puma 225 helicopter crashed near Turoey island off Bergen, Norway, while returning from an oil field, killing all 13 people aboard, including 41-year-old Iain Stuart from Laurencekirk, Aberdeenshire. An interim report from Norway's Air Accident Investigation Board indicates the most probable cause was a fatigue fracture in the helicopter's gearbox, leading to the main rotor detaching mid-flight. Following the tragedy, the European Aviation Safety Authority has mandated one-off gearbox inspections for all EC225 and L2 aircraft operators. A full investigation into the crash circumstances continues as authorities work to prevent similar incidents.

Russian Internet Pioneer Fined for Syria Blog Post Calling for Country's Destruction Anton Nosik, a prominent Russian internet entrepreneur and blogger, has been found guilty of inciting racial hatred and fined 500,000 roubles (approximately £6,000 or $8,000), though he managed to avoid imprisonment. The case revolved around a controversial 2015 blog post Nosik published on LiveJournal titled "Wipe Syria off the Face of the Earth." In the post, he expressed support for those bombing Syria during the ongoing conflict. Judge Yevgeni Naydenov ruled that "Nosik's actions sought to incite enmity and hatred towards Syrians, a group of people based on ethnic and geographic characteristics." Nosik defended his position, stating: "My opinion on this issue is that my statements do not contain any extremist views..... I positively do not see any extremism in the fact that I will not feel sorry for the Syrian state." The verdict has sparked debate across Russia, with critics accusing the government of applying double standards while others have condemned Nosik's controversial statements. The former journalist is widely regarded as an internet pioneer in Russia, having been instrumental in developing several popular websites. This case exemplifies a growing trend in Russia where bloggers and social media users face prosecution for online content. Article 282 of Russia's criminal code, which addresses extremism, is frequently invoked in such cases. Recent prosecutions have targeted individuals who were once accused of actually inciting violence, but now often involve critics of Kremlin policies, particularly regarding Russia's involvement in Ukraine. Previous cases under this law have included a 23-year-old Muslim woman from Pervouralsk who was convicted of extremism in 2015 for calling New Year's Eve celebrations "pagan." Unlike Nosik, several defendants in similar cases have received substantial prison sentences of up to five years. The case highlights concerns about freedom of expression and the interpretation of extremism laws in Russia's increasingly controlled online environment.

Nadal Suffers Consecutive Semi-Final Defeat in Brazil Rafael Nadal's struggles continued as the 14-time Grand Slam champion was upset by world number 45 Pablo Cuevas in the Brazil Open semi-finals. The top seed won a tight first-set tiebreak and saved two set points in the second before falling 6-7 (6) 7-6 (3) 6-4 to the Uruguayan. "I lost an opportunity," Nadal admitted. "I have to accept it and keep working to try to change the dynamic." Cuevas will face unseeded compatriot Guido Pella in Sunday's final. Pella defeated Austrian fifth seed Dominic Thiem 6-1 6-4, the same player who knocked out Nadal at the Argentina Open semi-finals last week. The consecutive last-four exits extend a disappointing start to the season for the 29-year-old Spaniard, who suffered a first-round loss to Fernando Verdasco at the Australian Open. "I didn't win a title, so it wasn't a positive two tournaments," Nadal reflected. "I just have to look forward."

Brothers who taught in Wales schools sentenced for indecent images Two brothers who worked as teachers in Wales have been sentenced after admitting to possessing indecent images of children. Robyn Wheldon-Williams, 39, a chemistry teacher from Caernarfon who previously presented a science programme on S4C and held a world record for bubble-making, admitted having 1,399 indecent images and movies. His brother Dyfan Wheldon Williams, 43, who taught in Blaenau Ffestiniog, admitted possessing 40 indecent images of children and extreme images. Judge Peter Heywood at Caernarfon Crown Court said the pair from Bontnewydd had been living a "Jekyll and Hyde existence". Both men have been suspended from their teaching positions and must attend an internet sexual offending programme.

House Encased in Ice as Winter Storm Hits Eastern US A house near Lake Ontario has been completely covered in thick ice following a severe winter storm that battered the northeastern United States. The strong winds and low temperatures caused water from Lake Ontario to blow over the house and then freeze. It is part of a winter storm that is expected to bring blizzard-like conditions from New York City to Boston this week. More than half a metre of snow is expected in some areas. The mayor of New York has called on people to stay indoors to stay safe.

Revolutionary Laser System Allows Firefighters to See Through Flames and Smoke Italian researchers have developed groundbreaking technology that could transform firefighting operations by enabling rescuers to see through dense smoke and flames to locate trapped victims. The innovative imaging system, created by scientists at the Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche (CNR) Istituto Nazionale di Ottica in Italy, uses an infrared laser to penetrate areas obscured by fire and smoke. The laser beam reflects off objects and people within burning rooms, and the data is then decoded by an imager to generate detailed 3D models of everything inside. Lead researcher Pietro Ferraro explained that current infrared cameras used by firefighters have significant limitations. "IR cameras cannot'see' objects or humans behind flames because of the need for a zoom lens that concentrates the rays on the sensor to form the image," he said. The new technology overcomes these limitations by bypassing the need for traditional lenses, which can be blinded by intense flames. "It became clear to us that we had in our hands a technology that could be exploited by emergency responders and firefighters at a fire scene," Ferraro added. Remarkably, the system can detect moving victims. "Perhaps most importantly, we demonstrated for the first time that a holographic recording of a live person can be achieved even while the body is moving," Ferraro noted. Beyond firefighting, the technology could potentially monitor breathing and cardiac activity. The research team's next priority is developing a more portable version of the system. The findings have been published in the journal Optics Express.

Historic Renovation Begins at Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre **JERUSALEM** - After centuries of delays caused by inter-denominational rivalry, a major renovation project has commenced at one of Christianity's holiest sites: the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The ambitious restoration aims to reinforce and preserve the sacred structure, with particular focus on the Edicule - the ancient chamber housing what Christians believe is Jesus's tomb. According to tradition, this shrine marks the spot where Jesus's body was anointed, wrapped in cloth and buried following his crucifixion. In an unprecedented display of cooperation, clerics from the Greek Orthodox, Roman Catholic and Armenian churches have set aside their longstanding differences to undertake the essential repairs. The three denominations, which jointly administer different sections of the church, have historically maintained tense relations. A 2008 dispute between Greek Orthodox and Armenian monks infamously escalated into a physical altercation. However, urgent necessity has fostered collaboration. Last year, Israel's antiquities authority declared the structure unsafe, prompting Israeli police to temporarily close the church. "We equally decided the required renovation was necessary to be done, so we agreed upon it," explained Samuel Aghoyan, the senior Armenian church official. The last major restoration occurred in 1810 following a devastating fire. Scientific coordinator Antonia Moropoulou notes that while the tomb remains stable, it has become warped after prolonged exposure to water, humidity and candle smoke. The structure also requires earthquake-proofing measures. The $3.3 million (£2.3m) project, funded jointly by the three denominations with an additional personal contribution from Jordan's King Abdullah, is expected to take eight to twelve months. Church officials have assured visitors that pilgrims will maintain access throughout the renovation period. King Abdullah's involvement reflects Jordan's continuing role in protecting Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem's Old City, which it controlled until the 1967 Arab-Israeli war.

Australians Better Off Buying Than Renting, Says Central Bank Economist Australians would be financially better off purchasing a home rather than renting, despite soaring property prices in major cities, according to Reserve Bank of Australia economist Peter Tulip. Mr Tulip told a Queensland conference on Wednesday that low interest rates have created the best conditions in three decades for buying property over renting, local media reported. His comments come as housing affordability remains a critical issue across Australia, with property prices in capital cities increasingly out of reach for many residents. Sydney's residential market has seen particularly dramatic rises, with some analysts warning of a potential market correction. The economist's research, based on bond price changes, suggests mortgage rates will remain at historically low levels for at least another decade. The Reserve Bank maintained Australia's official cash rate at a record-low 2% this week. According to Mr Tulip's preliminary findings, the economics of homeownership versus renting have shifted significantly over the past year. Twelve months ago, rental costs were comparable to regular mortgage repayments. "What has changed since then is that real long-term interest rates have fallen substantially," Mr Tulip told Fairfax Media. "That fall made housing more attractive relative to renting, despite the increase in prices." His research calculated that the annual cost of owning a home purchased in April would likely be 2.7% of its value, compared to 3.9% for renting the same property. However, separate data from Domain Group showed rental costs continue climbing in nearly all Australian capital cities. Sydney's median weekly house rent reached A$530 ($393, £256), rising 1.9% over the quarter. Property prices have surged dramatically over the past year, with Sydney house prices jumping 16.2%, Melbourne rising 10.2%, and other capital cities averaging 9.8% growth, according to Fairfax Media.

British Swimming Names Strong Squad for World Championships British Swimming has announced a well-balanced team for the upcoming World Championships, with 22-year-old Adam Peaty set to defend his 100m breaststroke title when competition begins on 14 July. The world record holder leads a squad featuring several Rio 2016 Olympic medallists, including Jazz Carlin, James Guy, Stephen Milne, Siobhan-Marie O'Connor, Duncan Scott, and Chris Walker-Hebborn. "It's a good balance between youth and senior," said British Swimming head coach Bill Furniss, following the team's selection at last week's British Swimming Championships in Sheffield. The 29-strong squad comprises 14 men and 15 women, blending experienced campaigners with emerging talent. Notable inclusions are Ben Proud, Max Litchfield, and rising stars Freya Anderson and Abbie Wood. The championships will test Britain's swimming depth as they prepare for future international competitions.

Solange Knowles Marries in All-White New Orleans Ceremony Solange Knowles celebrated her wedding to Alan Ferguson in a stunning all-white ceremony in New Orleans over the weekend. The bride and groom made a memorable entrance, arriving at their venue on matching white bicycles. The strict colour scheme of white and ivory extended throughout the celebration, with the couple and nearly all guests adhering to the elegant palette. Family members in attendance included the bride's mother, Tina Knowles, her 10-year-old son Daniel, and niece Blue Ivy. Sister Beyoncé was also present to celebrate the occasion. The wedding comes months after footage of Solange arguing with brother-in-law Jay Z in a New York lift went viral in May. The family has since released a statement saying they've "moved forward as a united family." Speaking to Vogue magazine, Solange explained: "Everyone I worked with on the wedding are friends who I love. Everything was a labour of love." The weekend celebrations began Friday evening when the couple hosted approximately 50 friends for a private cinema screening at the Indywood movie theatre. Even DJ Questlove, drummer for The Roots, maintained the white theme by spinning exclusively white vinyl records.

Award-Winning Designer to Create Riverside Garden for Hepworth Wakefield Renowned garden designer Mr Stuart-Smith has been commissioned to create a 65,000 square foot riverside garden at the Hepworth Gallery in Wakefield. The designer, who has won eight gold medals at the prestigious Chelsea Flower Show, expressed his delight at securing the project. "Public commissions like these are scarce in the UK," Mr Stuart-Smith said. The gallery has launched a £2.2 million fundraising campaign to finance the ambitious garden development, which will transform the 6,000 square metre riverside space into a significant public attraction for West Yorkshire.

Parents Rally Behind Dorset Hospital Services Under Review Dozens of parents have launched a social media campaign to protect vital children's services at Dorset County Hospital in Dorchester. The hospital is currently reviewing several departments, including maternity services, the special care baby unit (SCBU), and Kingfisher children's ward. Dorset Clinical Commissioning Group said it was examining ways to reorganise health services for the future. In response, concerned parents have flooded the "Save the SCBU, Kingfisher and Maternity at DCH" Facebook page with heartfelt photographs. The images show children who were born prematurely and youngsters who received treatment at the hospital, demonstrating the unit's importance to local families. Parents are strongly opposed to potential changes, fearing the loss of crucial healthcare services for children in their community.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic undergoes knee surgery after ligament injury Manchester United striker Zlatan Ibrahimovic has successfully undergone surgery on his knee following cruciate ligament damage sustained during the Europa League victory against Anderlecht on 20 April. The 35-year-old former Sweden international expressed gratitude to supporters for their encouragement throughout the ordeal. His representative, Mino Raiola, confirmed the operation was successful and assured fans that Ibrahimovic would make a complete recovery, dismissing concerns that the injury could end his playing career. The forward, who has been United's leading scorer with 28 goals this campaign, will now commence his rehabilitation programme in Pittsburgh. Ibrahimovic arrived at Old Trafford last summer on a one-year contract from Paris St-Germain, though his future remains uncertain as he has not yet signed an extension with the Premier League club.

Divorce Court Rules Mother Must Seek Work as Maintenance Cut Upheld A High Court judge's decision to slash the maintenance payments of a Suffolk mother has been upheld by the Court of Appeal, establishing that divorced parents should seek employment once their children reach school age. Ian Wright, 59, who operates an equine hospital in Newmarket, successfully challenged the £75,000 annual maintenance and school fees he was ordered to pay his ex-wife Tracey Wright, 51, following their divorce in 2008. The Appeal Court has now rejected Mrs Wright's attempt to overturn that reduction. The couple's 11-year marriage ended with the sale of their £1.3 million, seven-bedroom Suffolk home, with proceeds divided between them. Mrs Wright received a £450,000 mortgage-free property in Wickhambrook, Newmarket, complete with stabling facilities for her horse and their daughters' ponies. A former riding instructor who chose not to return to work after the divorce, Mrs Wright argued that caring for the couple's 10-year-old daughter restricted her ability to earn. Their older daughter attends boarding school. Mr Wright contended it was unreasonable to expect him to financially support his ex-wife indefinitely, particularly beyond his retirement, whilst she remained unemployed. Judge Lynn Roberts, in last year's High Court ruling, stated: "Mrs Wright has made no effort whatsoever to seek work or to update her skills. I am satisfied that she has worked on the basis that she would be supported for life." Mrs Wright's barrister, Mark Johnston, warned the ruling would cause "a plummeting in the standard of living" for the youngest child, arguing that childcare responsibilities inherently limited his client's earning capacity. However, Lord Justice Pitchford upheld the decision, emphasising the importance of Mrs Wright becoming self-sufficient. "There is a general expectation that, once children are in Year Two, mothers can begin part-time work and make a financial contribution," he ruled. The judge confirmed the maintenance order was never intended as lifelong income and dismissed the appeal.

US Hero Spencer Stone Stabbed in Sacramento Street Attack An American serviceman celebrated for stopping a terror attack on a French train is recovering in hospital after being stabbed multiple times in California. US Air Force Staff Sergeant Spencer Stone, 25, was attacked in the early hours of Thursday morning on a Sacramento street corner following an argument that escalated into violence, according to police reports. An Air Force official confirmed to the BBC that Mr Stone is currently in stable condition at a local hospital. Investigators initially treated the incident as a homicide, as they did not expect him to survive the attack. Mr Stone gained international recognition in August when he and two other Americans helped thwart a terror attack aboard a French train. The trio confronted a gunman carrying a Kalashnikov rifle, automatic pistol with ammunition clips, and a box cutter knife. Working with other passengers, they subdued the attacker by throwing him to the floor and removing his weapons. During that August incident, Mr Stone was slashed by the attacker and required surgery to reattach part of his hand. The three Americans—Mr Stone, Alek Skarlatos, and Anthony Sadler—were honored by French President Francois Hollande and received a hero's welcome upon returning to the United States. They subsequently received awards from Defense Secretary Ashton Carter and met President Barack Obama at the White House. Mr Skarlatos responded to Thursday's attack on social media, tweeting: "Everybody send prayers out to the Stone family today."

Glasgow Prestwick Airport Appoints New Board Members to Drive Turnaround Glasgow Prestwick Airport has announced the appointment of four new non-executive directors as part of efforts to transform the struggling facility into a profitable enterprise. The new board members bring significant experience from various sectors. Gordon Arthur, former communications chief of the Glasgow 2014 Commonwealth Games, joins alongside Bob Goldfield, the former chief executive of the Port of Dover. Also appointed are Jayne Maclennan, a group director at transport giant FirstGroup, and Ken Dalton, a former senior executive at professional and technical services firm Aecom Technology Corporation. The Scottish government acquired the airport for just £1 in 2013 amid concerns it would be forced to close. Since then, it has been operated under public ownership "on a commercial basis." Airport chairman Andrew Miller expressed optimism about the facility's prospects: "I firmly believe the airport has a bright future and it's my team's priority to see it return to profitability and become a strategic anchor for economic growth in Ayrshire and Scotland." Scottish Infrastructure Secretary Keith Brown welcomed the appointments, stating: "We know there is real potential for growth at Glasgow Prestwick Airport, but it will take strong leadership and vision to drive this improvement." The airport faces significant challenges ahead. Under its previous owners, Infratil, it recorded a pre-tax loss of £9.77m in its final full year. Last year, then Deputy First Minister Nicola Sturgeon cautioned there was "no quick fix solution for Prestwick" and acknowledged the airport may not achieve profitability for several years. The new appointments represent the latest step in the airport's transformation strategy.

Man Who Met Victim on Dating Site Jailed for Minimum 23 Years for Murder A man who strangled a woman he met on a dating website before attacking another woman while on the run has been sentenced to life in prison with a minimum term of 23 years. Miles Donnelly, 35, from Paddington, admitted to strangling Usha Patel, 44, at her home in Cricklewood, north-west London, in October 2015. The single mother shared the property with her five-year-old son. ## The Attack The Old Bailey heard that Donnelly and Ms Patel had met on a dating site seven months before the fatal incident on 7 October. After she invited him to her home and put her son to bed, the pair undressed before Donnelly launched his attack in what was described as a "drunken rage". Ms Patel suffered a horrific ordeal, being stabbed 13 times with a large bread knife, punched repeatedly in the head, and strangled. Her body was discovered the following morning by her father, who had arrived to take her grandson to school. The young boy told his grandfather: "Mummy's not well". The prosecution revealed that the five-year-old continues to suffer nightmares and repeatedly asks family members when his mother will return. ## Second Attack Following the murder, Donnelly fled to the west London home of Rosie Ferrigno, 43, where he concealed himself from police for 36 hours. During this time, he claimed to be sexually frustrated and made unwanted advances toward Ms Ferrigno. When she refused, he assaulted her with a stool that had a nail protruding from it, striking her on the back of the head. On 11 October, Donnelly contacted police himself, revealing his location and ending the manhunt. ## Sentencing Prosecutor Simon Denison QC told the court that despite the pair exchanging "I love you" text messages on the day of the murder, Donnelly would have known he was a "significant and serious danger to women" and was "driven by compulsions to drink, take cocaine and have sex". Judge Rebecca Poulet QC described the killing as "a particularly ferocious and violent attack" on "an extremely vulnerable woman" who was "clearly anxious to meet a new partner". "She paid for this invitation with her life," the judge said. Donnelly received an additional 18-month sentence for assaulting Ms Ferrigno, to run concurrently with his life term.

Government Plan to Revive England's Hen Harriers Under Fire as Nesting Numbers Remain Low A government initiative aimed at boosting hen harrier populations across England's moorlands is facing criticism after conservationists reported only a handful of nesting attempts this year, raising questions about the effectiveness of the collaborative effort. The action plan, launched in January by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) with support from organizations including the RSPB and the Moorland Association, was designed to reverse the fortunes of the "persecuted" birds. The initiative followed the 2015 disappearance of five male hen harriers from sites in Lancashire and Cumbria, which led to the collapse of multiple nests. The RSPB has indicated that "human interference" may be contributing to the lack of nesting success, pointing to several troubling incidents this year. In April, video footage emerged apparently showing an armed man using a decoy bird to lure a hen harrier in the Derbyshire Peak District. The following month, a man was filmed setting illegal pole traps on the Mossdale estate near Hawes, North Yorkshire. Hen harriers had been observed in both areas. These incidents have prompted Raptor Persecution UK, a conservation group, to declare the plan ineffective and call for the RSPB to withdraw its support. A spokeswoman stated: "There has been clear evidence that illegal raptor persecution is continuing. The RSPB should withdraw its support of the Hen Harrier Action Plan and join the increasing call for a ban on driven grouse shooting." The conflict stems from hen harriers' predation of grouse on moors used for shooting, a longstanding tension the action plan hoped to resolve through partnership. However, Martin Harper, the RSPB's conservation director, defended the organization's continued involvement, saying it was too "premature to change tack" and expressing hope for progress by season's end. Amanda Anderson, director of the Moorland Association, reaffirmed her organization's commitment to hen harrier breeding success, stating: "We have joined voices with conservationists to condemn all wildlife crime and will continue to do so."

Steve Bruce Confirms England Manager Talks as Hull Boss Among Candidates Hull City manager Steve Bruce has confirmed he has been interviewed for the England manager's position, describing it as "the prime job that any Englishman could ever want to have." The 55-year-old is among the leading candidates to replace Roy Hodgson, who resigned following England's shock elimination by Iceland at Euro 2016. Sunderland boss Sam Allardyce has also been interviewed and is currently the bookmakers' favourite for the role. Bruce told Sky Sports he was "highly flattered" to be considered, adding: "I put my case across and let's hope it was successful." However, Hull City released a statement confirming Bruce held "informal discussions" with the Football Association but insisted there had been "no official approach" to the club. The former Manchester United captain, who was never capped by England during his playing career, acknowledged the competition, saying he was up against "a big pal of mine" in Allardyce. He emphasized that whoever takes the job must address England's mental fragility in major tournaments, with players appearing "afraid" during crucial matches. England's recent tournament record has been disappointing, with elimination at the last-16 stage of Euro 2016 and failure to progress beyond the group stages at the 2014 World Cup. Bournemouth manager Eddie Howe and USA coach Jurgen Klinsmann have also been linked with the vacancy. Both Hull and Sunderland are pressing the FA to make a swift appointment. FA chief executive Martin Glenn is leading a selection panel that includes technical director Dan Ashworth and board member David Gill. Bruce successfully guided Hull back to the Premier League last season, though uncertainty surrounds his position amid ongoing takeover talks at the KC Stadium.

New Zealand Court Orders Return of Kim Dotcom's Seized Assets A New Zealand court has ruled that assets seized from internet entrepreneur Kim Dotcom must be returned, dealing a blow to authorities who have held the property for two years. The Auckland court declined police requests to extend the holding period for the assets, which include more than 15 luxury vehicles seized during a dramatic 2014 raid on Mr Dotcom's mansion. Among the collection is a distinctive pink 1959 Cadillac. US authorities accuse the German-born businessman of "massive scale" copyright infringement through his file-sharing website Megaupload. Several major film and music publishers have also filed lawsuits, alleging he encouraged illegal uploads of copyrighted material and profited from the operation. Mr Dotcom and his associates deny all charges. Since the raid, Mr Dotcom has remained defiant, launching a new file storage service called Mega and even establishing his own political party. He announced the court decision on Twitter, stating he and his wife Mona would recover their New Zealand assets unless authorities appeal within 14 days. "The NZ asset ruling is HUGE," Mr Dotcom tweeted, adding that his legal team has filed a case in Hong Kong against Megaupload's seizure. An extradition hearing is scheduled for July. If extradited and convicted, Mr Dotcom faces up to 20 years in prison.

Geraint Thomas Wins Paris-Nice After Contador Takes Final Stage Alberto Contador won the final stage of Paris-Nice in a time of four hours, 24 minutes and 47 seconds. Team Sky's Geraint Thomas, 29, finished 28 seconds behind to secure overall victory, while previous leader Tony Martin drifted out of contention. Ion Izagirre finished second overall, 19 seconds behind Thomas, with Contador third, a further seven seconds back. The Welshman's triumph marks a significant achievement in the prestigious "Race to the Sun," demonstrating his consistency throughout the week-long stage race despite pressure from Spain's Contador on the demanding final stage.

Athens Struggles with Mountains of Rubbish as Municipal Workers Strike Tourist areas of Athens were among those worst affected by a mounting refuse crisis as municipal workers staged protests over job security concerns. Problems were also reported in the northern city of Thessaloniki and the island of Corfu. Protesters marched on the interior ministry in the centre of Athens as a 24-hour strike took hold. They fear up to 10,000 workers could lose their jobs as their contracts end. At one point on Thursday, protesters set fire to rubbish outside the interior ministry and threw paint at the building. Riot police fired tear gas to stop the building being stormed, reports said. For days, members of the municipal workers' union have blocked refuse lorries from entering the main depots as the dispute escalates, leaving some street pavements an obstacle course for pedestrians. Driving through Athens' central neighbourhoods this morning you cannot miss the piles of rubbish in every corner. Pedestrians hold their noses as they pass the barricades of waste and at times cross to the opposite pavement. The situation is worse near businesses like restaurants which have big waste loads every day. Greeks have known bin strikes in the past and try to keep their waste indoors for as long as possible. But a heatwave is on its way and a weekend stroll will be far from idyllic for Athenians and tourists alike. The temperature in Athens on Thursday was 32C and is expected to climb in the coming days. Authorities have urged residents and businesses not to put out their rubbish. The problem facing the government is that its attempt to renew the contracts of temporary municipal workers has been rejected by the courts as unconstitutional. Interior Minister Panos Skourletis has promised the unions to find a solution, offering to provide 2,500 of the threatened workers with permanent posts.

Ferret Becomes First to Receive Pacemaker at Kansas State University Surgeons at Kansas State University have achieved a veterinary milestone by successfully implanting a pacemaker in a four-year-old ferret named Zelda, marking the first time they have performed such a procedure on this species. Zelda was admitted to the Veterinary Health Center in Manhattan, Kansas, shortly after Christmas, suffering from a third-degree heart block that caused a dangerously low heartbeat and severe lack of energy. Without treatment, her condition could have significantly shortened her lifespan. Before proceeding with surgery, veterinarians conducted extensive tests to determine if Zelda was a suitable candidate for the device. Due to her small size and narrow veins, a specially ordered pacemaker was required. The procedure proved successful, and Zelda was released just two days after surgery. The university's veterinary college reports she is now expected to live a normal ferret life, spanning approximately ten years with her new device regulating her heart rhythm.

**Munster Cruise to Comprehensive Victory Over Treviso in Pro12 Clash** Munster delivered an emphatic performance at a freezing Stadio Comunale di Monigo, running in seven tries to defeat Benetton Treviso 47-3 in their Guinness Pro12 encounter on Saturday. Andrew Conway led the try-scoring charge with a brace, while Ronan O'Mahony also crossed twice for the Irish province. Robin Copeland, Darren O'Shea and substitute Alex Wootton completed the comprehensive victory, with man-of-the-match Tyler Bleyendaal orchestrating proceedings brilliantly from fly-half. The hosts made a promising start when former Leinster fly-half Ian McKinley kicked an early penalty in the eighth minute to give Treviso a 3-0 lead. However, that would prove to be the Italian side's only score of the afternoon as Munster's dominant display took over. Bleyendaal responded with a penalty on the quarter-hour mark before Munster's forward power began to tell. A terrific five-metre scrum in the 20th minute saw the visitors march Treviso back over their own line, allowing number eight Copeland to touch down. Bleyendaal added the conversion to make it 10-3. The New Zealand fly-half continued to pull the strings, producing a perfectly weighted chip through that created panic in the Treviso defence. O'Mahony applied pressure on the cover, and Conway reacted quickest to pounce on the loose ball for an unconverted try. After Darren Sweetnam thwarted Michael Tagicakibau from a dangerous McKinley cross-field kick, Munster produced the try of the match in the 34th minute. Starting from inside their own half, Bleyendaal's deft kick pass found O'Mahony at full tilt, and the winger linked superbly with the supporting Conway, who sped along the left touchline for a classy seven-pointer that gave Munster a commanding 22-3 half-time lead. The second half continued in similar fashion, with O'Shea scoring his first Pro12 try barely two minutes after the restart. The lock charged onto a Bleyendaal pass and proved unstoppable from close range, with the fly-half threading the difficult conversion through the posts. Treviso, missing numerous players through international call-ups and injuries, continued to struggle at set-piece time and could not penetrate a resolute Munster defence, which featured an impressive debut from young centre Sam Arnold. O'Mahony grabbed his second try in the 64th minute after an initial maul had been held up, dotting down in the corner. Wootton, the Ireland Sevens international, made an immediate impact off the bench, rounding his man for the second time to notch a well-deserved try, converted by substitute Ian Keatley. Munster's seventh and final try came when Copeland used lineout ball to break to the blindside and feed O'Mahony for another crisp finish, capping a thoroughly professional performance in difficult conditions. The victory consolidates Munster's position in the Pro12 table as they continue their push for playoff qualification, while Treviso remain rooted to the bottom of the standings. **Munster 47-3 Treviso**
