Tilbury Pioneer Academy will be the first school to participate in the scheme, with a parent volunteer having completed a week of training to take on the role. However, the plan has raised concerns among teaching unions. Jerry Glazier, national executive member of the National Union of Teachers in Essex, described it as "unusual and innovative" but warned of potential consequences. "Teachers are there to teach and maintain positive relations with parents and I'm pretty certain most teachers would not want to put themselves into situations of potential conflict," Mr Glazier said. He suggested that educating parents would be preferable and criticised the scheme as "masking the bigger problem of cuts to local authorities." Thurrock Council currently employs only six full-time traffic wardens to cover 50 schools across the borough. Council leader John Kent defended the initiative, saying dangerous parking outside schools was a persistent problem reported by teachers, parents and residents. "There are teachers and head teachers who try to marshal the traffic already and what they've said to us is that if they have the authority to issue a ticket, it's another weapon in their armoury," Mr Kent explained. He emphasised that issuing tickets would be a last resort, with the focus on encouraging behavioural change through dialogue. "I would be delighted if we never issue a single ticket," he added.

Prison Kitchen Knife Killer Given Life Sentence for Second Murder A prisoner who fatally stabbed a fellow inmate with a kitchen knife while preparing meals at Dartmoor Prison has been handed a life sentence with a minimum term of 33 years. William Tolcher, 51, from Liverpool, killed Alex Cusworth in the prison kitchen last November using a 10-inch knife he had been given to chop vegetables. Tolcher was already serving a life sentence, 15 years into his term, for murdering a woman in Newquay in 1996. Plymouth Crown Court heard that the two men did not speak before the attack at the Category C prison, where inmates and staff collaborate to prepare 650 meals three times daily. Prosecutors suggested Mr Cusworth, 37, originally from Stafford, may have said something earlier that caused offence. He suffered internal bleeding from the stabbing and died in hospital. Despite denying murder, Tolcher was found guilty by a jury. At sentencing, Mr Justice James Dingemans described him as "extremely dangerous" and suggested he may never be considered fit for parole, adding: "You are a person who is a complete stranger to the truth." The victim's adoptive mother, Ann Edgeller, a former Mayor of Stafford, delivered an emotional statement describing her son as "a very vulnerable young man with mental health issues" who had been failed "by every establishment in the country." His "biggest desire was to live a normal life," she said, adding: "Alex, I am very, very sorry. I was not there to protect you when you needed it the most." A Ministry of Justice spokesman stated: "We will not tolerate violence in prisons and work closely with the police and Crown Prosecution Service to prosecute those involved and always push for the harshest penalty."

Sony Pictures Threatens Twitter Over Leaked Information Sony Pictures Entertainment has escalated its fight against the distribution of stolen information from last year's devastating cyber-attack by threatening legal action against Twitter if the social media platform doesn't shut down accounts sharing leaked data. David Boies, the film company's high-profile lawyer, sent a letter to Twitter demanding the removal of accounts disseminating information obtained during the November hack. According to documents published by US website Motherboard, the letter specifically identifies Val Broeksmit, who operates the Twitter account @BikiniRobotArmy and regularly posts screenshots of stolen Sony emails. The legal warning extends beyond this single account. Boies' letter insists that Twitter must "comply with all future requests with regard to any other account holder seeking to disseminate the Stolen Information via Twitter." In an explicit threat, the letter states: "If Twitter does not comply with this request, and the Stolen Information continues to be disseminated by Twitter in any manner, SPE will have no choice but to hold Twitter responsible for any damage or loss arising from such use or dissemination by Twitter." This represents Sony's latest attempt to contain the fallout from the November cyber-attack, which the US government attributed to North Korea, though the country has denied involvement. The breach resulted in unreleased films, corporate financial information, and embarrassing private emails between executives and Hollywood figures being leaked online. Sony has already warned several American news outlets about publishing information from the stolen emails. The company was also forced to cancel the Christmas release of "The Interview," a comedy about assassinating North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, which many believe triggered the attack. The situation intensified this week when North Korea's entire internet infrastructure went down on Tuesday. While the US had promised a "proportional response" to the Sony hack, officials refused to comment on any American involvement in the outages.

Injured Indian Police Horse Shaktiman Shows Remarkable Recovery After Assault DEHRADUN, India - A police horse in northern India is showing signs of remarkable recovery after undergoing major surgery following an alleged assault by a state legislator that sparked national outrage. Shaktiman, a police horse serving in the city of Dehradun, Uttarakhand, was forced to have a leg amputated after allegedly being beaten with a stick during a protest rally. The incident led to the arrest of Ganesh Joshi, a legislator from Uttarakhand, though he was later released on bail and has denied the assault charges. According to Rakesh Nautiyal, the veterinary officer overseeing Shaktiman's care, the horse is now standing and "improving day-by-day." "The positive approach of the animal has amazed me," Nautiyal told the BBC. "Even after undergoing a major surgery Shaktiman is displaying normal behaviour. He is eating well, which is a good sign." The recovery effort has attracted international attention and support. A special shoe called an "ice boot" is being brought from the United States to help reduce weight on the amputated limb. "Through the ice boot we will be able to take precautionary measures to keep the hind leg safe," a senior veterinarian explained. Shaktiman has become the center of attention in Dehradun, where he is housed at police quarters with round-the-clock care. Despite the fact that he will never resume official police duties, local authorities are sparing no expense for his treatment. Leading the rehabilitation efforts is Jamie Vaughn, a US animal welfare advocate who runs the Maya Foundation in Bhutan. Fondly called "chachi" (aunt) by Dehradun police officers, Vaughn has used her extensive network to fund most of Shaktiman's post-operative care. Under her coordination, Shaktiman now enjoys specially designed accommodation complete with a tin shed, water-cooled fans, mosquito netting, and fluorescent lighting. The horse receives daily massages, fresh bedding every two days, and bandage changes twice weekly. "A lot of people are concerned about the horse and are providing help," Vaughn told the BBC. "The horse is adjusting to the new prosthetic leg. But the road to recovery is still long and needs patience."

Bolivia Battles First Locust Plague as Insects Threaten Crops Bolivia is confronting an unprecedented locust invasion that President Evo Morales says is the first in the country's history, prompting urgent cooperation with neighbouring Argentina to combat the spreading infestation. The locusts, first detected in January, have already consumed over 1,000 hectares in Santa Cruz province. In response, the Bolivian government has established a specialized unit to address the crisis and has sought assistance from Argentina, which has dealt with locust plagues since the 1920s. Authorities and local farmers are preparing to fumigate up to 17,000 hectares to prevent further spread and protect the nation's food security. Agricultural producers are working urgently to locate locust eggs and nymphs to control the plague at its earliest stages. Currently, the affected area represents just a fraction of the 100,000 hectares of grain cultivation in Santa Cruz. Bolivia maintains self-sufficiency in grain production, though officials remain vigilant about potential threats to supply. The locust outbreak follows a severe drought that caused water rationing and disputes over water resources throughout the country. The crisis has renewed calls from Santa Cruz producers—representing one of Bolivia's wealthiest regions—for government approval of genetically-modified seeds, which they argue would create crops more resistant to plagues and extreme climate conditions. Experts warn that swift action is essential to prevent the infestation from escalating into a full-scale agricultural disaster.

**Macau: Asia's Gaming Hub with Portuguese Roots** Macau, a former Portuguese colony located on a small peninsula and two islands off China's southern coast, has transformed itself into one of the world's premier gambling destinations, rivaling and even surpassing Las Vegas in gaming revenues. The special administrative region, situated near Hong Kong, has built its modern economy primarily around tourism and casino gambling. The gaming industry experienced explosive growth after 2002, when Stanley Ho's decades-long monopoly ended, opening the market to foreign casino companies. Major international operators invested billions, replacing traditional gambling establishments with lavish "mega-casinos" featuring integrated hotel and entertainment complexes. By 2006, Macau's casino revenues exceeded those of Las Vegas, marking a significant milestone for the territory. The gambling mecca has attracted thousands of visitors, particularly from mainland China and Hong Kong, seeking gaming opportunities unavailable elsewhere in the region. However, economic challenges emerged in 2014 when annual gaming revenue declined for the first time in twelve years. Analysts attributed this downturn partly to Beijing's anti-corruption campaign, which discouraged mainland officials and businesspeople from conspicuous gambling. The development raised concerns about Macau's heavy reliance on a single industry. Chief Executive Dr. Fernando Chui responded by pledging to diversify the local economy, addressing concerns from Beijing about the territory's economic vulnerability. Macau reverted to Chinese sovereignty in 1999 after four centuries of Portuguese rule. Under the "one country, two systems" framework similar to Hong Kong's arrangement, Beijing promised to preserve Western-style freedoms for fifty years. Despite this autonomy, Macau's pro-democracy movement remains notably weaker than Hong Kong's. A 2009 state security law passed with minimal opposition, contrasting sharply with Hong Kong's 2003 mass protests against similar legislation. In 2014, activists attempted an unofficial referendum on democratic reforms, but security forces disrupted the vote. Only 9,000 participants cast ballots, with 89% supporting universal suffrage by 2019. Portuguese seafarers first established settlements in the 1500s, initially prospering through regional trade. When commerce declined in subsequent centuries, licensed gambling—introduced in the mid-1800s—revitalized Macau's economy, setting the stage for its current status as Asia's gambling capital.

Guernsey Honours Islanders Who Resisted Nazi Occupation A memorial plaque has been unveiled in Guernsey to commemorate islanders who died after resisting German occupation during World War II. Bailiff Sir Richard Collas unveiled the plaque near the Liberation Monument at North Beach, St Peter Port. At least eight islanders perished in prisons, detention camps, or from ill-treatment following their imprisonment for resistance activities. The plaque is "dedicated to the memory of all Islanders who committed acts of protest, defiance and resistance" and names seven individuals: Charles Machon, Percy Miller, Marie Ozanne, Joseph Gillingham, Sidney Ashcroft, Louis Symes, and John Ingrouille. An eighth person died, but their family requested their details remain private. Members of the wartime generation and relatives of the deceased laid wreaths during the ceremony. Jean Harris, whose father Joseph Gillingham was involved in the Guernsey Underground News Service (GUNS), attended the event. GUNS was a clandestine network that secretly monitored BBC broadcasts on hidden or homemade radios, transcribed the news, and distributed it among islanders. Mrs Harris and her husband Alan were instrumental in organizing the memorial. The plaque was funded entirely through public donations, with support from the Guernsey Deportees Association, and installed by the Culture and Leisure Department. The memorial ensures that these acts of courage and sacrifice will not be forgotten.

Coronation Street Actress Loses Role After Age Deception Katie Redford has lost her role on Coronation Street after producers discovered she had misrepresented her age during the audition process. The actress was set to play the 14-year-old granddaughter of Gail McIntyre later this year, with producers believing she was 19 years old. However, it has emerged that Katie is actually 25. Last week, ITV issued a press release announcing Katie had secured the role, which she described as a "dream come true." Her agent, Joanne McLintock, told Newsbeat: "It wasn't [Katie's] idea to audition as a 19-year-old. People in the industry do it regularly and she sort of went along with what we said." McLintock expressed regret over the situation, saying: "I'm feeling really stressed and so sorry for Katie. It's her first real job and she's a star in the making - she's a very talented young actress." The agent confirmed she had spoken with casting directors who expressed disappointment. Katie was unavailable for comment, and producers are believed to already have a replacement in mind.

Judy Huth Files Lawsuit Alleging Bill Cosby Molested Her as Minor at Playboy Mansion A woman has filed a lawsuit alleging that comedian Bill Cosby molested her at the Playboy mansion in Los Angeles when she was 15 years old in 1974. Judy Huth's civil suit claims she and a 16-year-old friend met Cosby on a film set before being invited to his tennis club. According to the lawsuit, the teenagers were given alcohol at the club before being taken to the Playboy mansion, where Ms Huth alleges she was forced to perform a sexual act against her will. The lawsuit states that Cosby instructed the teenagers to lie about their ages and claim they were 19 if questioned. Ms Huth is seeking unspecified damages for "psychological damage and mental anguish" resulting from the alleged incident. Cosby's lawyer had no immediate comment on the accusation. The 77-year-old entertainer has faced a mounting wave of allegations in recent months, with more than a dozen women accusing him of drugging and sexually assaulting them. Cosby has not been criminally charged in connection with any of these allegations, which his legal team has dismissed as "discredited" and "defamatory." This lawsuit marks the first public allegation that Cosby assaulted someone who was underage, according to the Associated Press. In 2005, another woman who accused Cosby of sexual assault brought a lawsuit that was ultimately settled out of court. The filing comes one day after Cosby resigned from Temple University's board of trustees in Philadelphia. Several major broadcasters, including NBC and Netflix, have also cancelled or postponed projects involving the comedian amid the growing scandal.

Ugandan Soldiers Jailed for Fuel Theft in Somalia The African Union has announced that nine Ugandan soldiers serving with its peacekeeping mission in Somalia have been sentenced to prison terms ranging from one to three years by a military court. The soldiers, including two majors, were convicted of selling fuel belonging to the AU Mission in Somalia (Amisom) to civilians in Mogadishu. They were arrested during a sting operation in June and were among 18 soldiers initially charged with the offense. In a historic first, the Ugandan military court convened in Somalia rather than repatriating the accused for trial. The decision to hold proceedings locally was intended to demonstrate accountability to Somali citizens and show that Amisom forces are subject to justice for their actions. "The prosecution has proved all the accusations of pursuing personal interest and endangering operational efficiency beyond reasonable doubt," stated Uganda's Brig Gen Dick Olum, who presided over the case. Three of the convicted soldiers received additional punishment, being "dismissed with disgrace from the army" and stripped of their military benefits. Uganda is the largest contributor to the 22,000-strong Amisom force, which has been deployed in Somalia for nine years alongside government forces to combat al-Shabab Islamist militants. The convictions come amid ongoing concerns about troop welfare. In June, reports revealed that deployment allowances from the European Union were being withheld due to accounting discrepancies, despite these payments significantly exceeding the soldiers' regular government salaries.

Welsh Climber Mike Hopkins Safe After Nepal Earthquake Strikes Everest Mike Hopkins, a 56-year-old Welsh mountaineer attempting to become the oldest Welsh person to summit Mount Everest, has confirmed he is safe following the devastating earthquake that hit Nepal. Mr Hopkins had reached Camp 1 when the 7.8 magnitude tremor struck on 25 April. He was able to contact his wife to reassure her of his safety. The earthquake claimed more than 2,300 lives across Nepal, with 17 fatalities occurring around Everest's base camp. Mr Hopkins was climbing with a group of nine other climbers and Sherpas on the mountain's north side. In response to the disaster, a team of seven firefighters from South Wales and Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Services flew to Nepal to support rescue operations.

Historic Royal Wedding Crown Faces Export Unless UK Buyer Found A diamond crown designed by Prince Albert for his 1840 wedding to Queen Victoria risks leaving Britain unless a domestic buyer matches its £5 million price tag. The 11.5cm piece, featuring 11 sapphires set in gold, is considered one of the most significant jewels from Queen Victoria's reign by experts who are urging it remain in the UK. An international buyer could potentially purchase and export the historically important crown, prompting concerns from heritage specialists about losing this crucial piece of British royal history to overseas collectors.

Petition Calls for London Independence After Brexit Vote A petition demanding London become independent from the UK and remain in the European Union has gained significant traction following the Brexit referendum result. The petition's organiser James O'Malley, said the capital was "a world city" which should "remain at the heart of Europe". Nearly 60% of people in the capital backed the Remain campaign, in stark contrast to most of the country. The LSE's director said the vote showed how "radically different" London is. Prof Tony Travers said London's economy and politics "look so different" to the rest of the country and it was up to the mayor to decide whether to argue for more power. "Maybe moving more decision making to cities and councils could be a solution to the differences within the country," he said. Following the result, Sadiq Khan said it was "crucial that London has a voice at the table during those renegotiations" with the EU. "We will continue to look outwards and trade and engage with the entire world, including the European Union," he said. The petition, which suggests the mayor could become "President Sadiq", has already been signed by more than 27,000 people. Mr O'Malley said he was a "big EU fan" and was "fed up watching the results" when he set up the page on change.org. He said he was "astonished" the petition had taken off but suggested it showed he had "clearly touched a nerve" with others who "like me want to live in an international city". One person who commented on the page said he felt "morally, culturally and historically closer to Paris, Brussels and Rome than I do to Sunderland". Another wrote: "We need to break free of the dead weight." A second petition calling for London to remain part of the EU has been signed by more 7,500 people.

Iraq Denies Air Strike Caused Mass Civilian Deaths in Mosul Iraq's military has strongly rejected claims that a coalition air strike was responsible for mass civilian casualties in western Mosul, instead blaming explosive booby-traps planted by the so-called Islamic State (IS). The United States announced on Saturday that it was launching an investigation into an air strike conducted on 17 March "at the location corresponding to allegations of civilian casualties." Meanwhile, the Iraqi government's offensive to liberate western Mosul from IS continued on Sunday, with helicopter gunships actively engaged in operations. "Ignore reports Iraq forces have paused Mosul offensive," the BBC's Jeremy Bowen tweeted from the city. "It continues. Have seen gunships firing and heard much activity in the last few hours." Reports have suggested that the disputed air strike killed more than 100 people in the Jadideh neighbourhood, though details remain unclear and the exact date is uncertain. Some accounts claim more than 200 bodies were recovered from a collapsed building. However, the Iraqi military issued a detailed rebuttal on its Facebook page, naming al-Resala neighbourhood rather than Jadideh as the location in question. According to the statement, coalition forces conducted an air strike at 08:25 local time on 17 March at the request of Iraqi forces. Iraqi military experts subsequently inspected a house "reportedly targeted by an air strike and they found out that the house was completely destroyed and there was no sign that it was destroyed by a strike." The statement continues: "A huge detonated booby-trapped vehicle was found near the house. Some 61 dead bodies were pulled from under the rubble." The military claims eyewitnesses described IS using houses rigged with explosives and containing families as firing positions against security forces. In its Saturday statement, US Central Command confirmed that "an initial review of strike data" indicated a strike was conducted in western Mosul on 17 March at the location in question. The coalition stated it "takes all allegations of civilian casualties seriously and a formal Civilian Casualty Credibility Assessment has been opened to determine the facts surrounding the strike." The battle is currently focused on the Old City as Iraqi forces work to expel IS from western Mosul. The jihadists were driven from eastern Mosul in January following a months-long offensive.

Man Convicted of Murder After Fatal Stabbing in Greenock Flat Dispute A 38-year-old man has been found guilty of murder after fatally stabbing a 23-year-old neighbor during a confrontation over noise complaints at a block of flats in Greenock, Inverclyde. Thomas Sellar was convicted at the High Court in Edinburgh of murdering Jamie Walsh on 10 September 2015. The incident occurred at 123 Wren Road in Greenock, where both men lived in the same building. The court heard that Mr Walsh had recently moved into a flat below Sellar's, which was being rented by the victim's friend. In the days before the fatal incident, Sellar had repeatedly complained about noise coming from the downstairs flat. ## Claims of Self-Defence Rejected During the trial, Sellar maintained he had acted in self-defence, claiming he feared for his life. He told the court he had gone to the downstairs flat on the night of the incident to ask residents to reduce the noise level. According to Sellar's account, a group of youths took exception to his request and attacked him, chasing him back to his own flat. Sellar claimed he grabbed a knife to protect himself during the confrontation. "They chased me down. I couldn't breathe. I never intended to kill him. I never intended for anything like this to happen," he told the jury. However, the prosecution argued that Mr Walsh was unarmed during the confrontation. Christopher Walsh, the victim's brother, testified that Jamie had done nothing wrong and that Sellar had attacked him unprovoked. ## Allegations of Fabricated Evidence The court also heard allegations that Sellar had stabbed himself after the incident in an attempt to evade justice. Christopher Walsh told jurors that Sellar claimed to have been stabbed first by Jamie and displayed a wound he alleged was inflicted during the fight. "He was trying to get a defence," Christopher Walsh said, explaining his brother never had a knife. Sellar denied stabbing himself but the jury rejected his claims of self-defence and returned a guilty verdict. Following the conviction, it emerged that Sellar had six previous convictions for offences involving knives. He was returned to custody and now faces a mandatory life sentence, with sentencing deferred to a later date.

Newborn Baby Found in County Durham Street Named Jack by Hospital Staff A newborn baby boy discovered abandoned in a County Durham street has been named Jack by hospital staff caring for him. The infant, less than 12 hours old, was found at approximately 04:50 BST at Emerson Court in Horden, near Peterlee. He was immediately taken to the University Hospital of North Tees in Stockton for medical care. Durham Police confirmed at a press conference that the baby's mother has since come forward. She has undergone a medical examination and will be interviewed by officers, who are working alongside the county council's children's services unit. The baby was discovered by a pet dog during an early morning walk. Mary Cartwright, mayor of Peterlee, witnessed the emergency response whilst returning from Newcastle Airport. "I saw the policeman with a bundle in his arms and I could see the baby's head and it was in a blanket," she said. "He ran across the road and round to the side of the ambulance and the crew took the baby." Ms Cartwright added: "There was nobody around and then there was this baby and I knew something wasn't quite right." Police have confirmed that baby Jack is "fit and well" despite his ordeal. Initial reports incorrectly stated the child had been found on nearby Fourth Street.

Steve Bruce Appointed Hull City Manager After Month-Long Search Hull City have appointed Steve Bruce as their new manager following a month without a boss after the dismissal of Nick Barmby. The 51-year-old former Manchester United captain has signed a three-year deal with the Championship club and is determined to restore Premier League football to the KC Stadium. Bruce said: "I'm looking to bring back the Premier League days if we possibly can, that's the reason I'm sitting here, for the challenge of it. There were a few weeks of talks and negotiations and I'm now relishing the challenge of getting the club back to where it wants to be." The Tigers had been without a manager since sacking Barmby last month. The former Hull midfielder was removed from his position after less than six months in charge following controversial comments he made to the media. Bruce arrives at the KC Stadium with extensive managerial experience, having previously led Wigan Athletic and Birmingham City in the Premier League. He has been out of football since being dismissed by Sunderland in November 2011 after a disappointing start to the 2011/12 season. The former defender enjoyed a glittering playing career, winning three Premier League titles with Manchester United before transitioning into management with Sheffield United in 1998. However, he moved to Huddersfield Town after just one year. His managerial journey continued with brief spells at Wigan and Crystal Palace before a successful period at Birmingham City, where he secured promotion to the Premier League in his first season. He returned to Wigan in November 2007, replacing Chris Hutchings and guiding them to safety with a 14th-place finish, followed by 11th position in his only full season. Niall Quinn appointed Bruce as Sunderland manager for the 2009/10 campaign, where he achieved 13th and 10th-place finishes in his first two seasons. However, he was relieved of his duties after the Black Cats managed just two wins in their first 13 matches of the 2011/12 season. Former Hull midfielder Bryan Hughes, who played alongside and under Bruce at Birmingham, told BBC Radio Humberside: "I think it's a fantastic appointment, I really do. He's shown what his capabilities are as a manager and he's done it at the top level as well as getting promotion from this division." Hughes added: "When I played under him he just gave everyone a belief that they could do well and he's great to work with. I think Hull have done really well to get him. It's a real coup." Bruce has gained promotion from the Championship twice in his managerial career, helping Birmingham achieve promotion in both 2002 and 2007. His son Alex, recently released by Leeds United, expressed his support on Twitter: "Pleased to see Dad back in work with Hull City. Big challenge for him and I know he's looking forward to it, I'm sure he'll be a success!" Hull City, relegated from the Premier League in 2010, finished eighth in the Championship last season, seven points adrift of the play-off positions.

Pop star Olly Murs sympathises with Zayn Malik over stage anxiety Singer Olly Murs has expressed sympathy for former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who has cancelled several live performances due to severe anxiety. "It is definitely one of my worst fears and my heart goes out to Zayn," Murs told BBC News. The star befriended One Direction through the X Factor, where they were runners-up in consecutive years. He said Malik's anxiety had only surfaced since he had become a solo artist earlier this year. "I feel for him, because he did seven or eight worldwide tours and he always had friends around him," said Murs. "Now, he has that daunting anxiety [of] having to come out on stage without those other guys around." So far this year, Malik has cancelled appearances at the Autism Rocks Arena in Dubai and the Summertime Ball in Wembley Stadium. "Unfortunately my anxiety that has haunted me throughout the last few months around live performances has gotten the better of me," Malik told fans after pulling out of the latter gig. "I know those who suffer anxiety will understand and I hope those who don't can empathise with my situation." ## Building confidence Murs said that the sheer scale of the concerts could be the root of Malik's fears. "He's got to start at theatres or smaller shows where he can build that confidence again. Once Zayn gets out there and starts performing, he'll be great," he said. "It's just that initial thing of getting over the line. But fingers crossed he does get to perform that album at some point." Malik is not the only pop star to suffer anxiety. Selena Gomez recently cancelled the remaining dates of her world tour, citing the anxiety and depression that are side effects of Lupus, the auto-immune disease from which she suffers. Justin Bieber also said his touring schedule was leaving him "mentally and emotionally exhausted to the point of depression". He subsequently cancelled "meet and greet" sessions with fans before and after his shows. "You have to put your heart out to those guys for coming out and being honest," said Murs. "You've got to remember they're young and the pressure is massive. "People have paid for their tickets and they want you to entertain them. It can take its weight on you." The singer admitted he had also experienced "difficult" nights on tour, but they paled in significance compared to Malik and Gomez. "I'm not going to moan about it because these are our jobs. That's what we get paid to do," he said, indicating a poster in his management company's office that reads: "No whining". "Whining and whinging..... you shouldn't," he added, discussing his own shows. "You should just get on with it." Follow us on Twitter @BBCNewsEnts, on Instagram at bbcnewsents, or if you have a story suggestion email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk.

Comet Electronics Chain Unlikely to Find Buyer, Says Retail Boss The struggling electronics retailer Comet is "very unlikely" to be sold as a going concern, according to John Roberts, the founder and chief executive of rival firm Appliances Online. Mr Roberts has submitted an offer worth "millions" of pounds for Comet's brand name and website, but believes the chain will not survive beyond Christmas in its current form. Administrator Deloitte, which was appointed at the beginning of this month, announced plans to close a further 125 stores starting in January if a buyer cannot be found. This would leave just 70 stores operating from the original 236-strong chain. The move puts more than 3,000 additional jobs at risk, on top of the 1,000 redundancies already made from Comet's total workforce of 6,611 employees. Deloitte said it is in discussions with a small number of potential buyers and is seeking to sell the business as a whole rather than breaking it up. Joint administrator Chris Farrington said: "Should any acceptable offers be received for stores, we will delay the closure process. Unfortunately, in the absence of a firm offer for the whole of the business, it has become necessary to begin making plans in case a sale is not concluded." Reports earlier this week suggested entrepreneur Clive Coombes was in talks with Deloitte about purchasing 180 Comet stores, but no firm offer has materialised. Mr Roberts, whose Bolton-based company competes with Comet in the white goods market, explained why he believes a rescue is unlikely. He said 85% of Comet's white goods business involved delivery, yet the company "no longer has any delivery network" following cutbacks. "It's a business that relied on high volumes, and closing stores was undermining vital economies of scale," he said. "Costs spiral when you close stores, and the business is massively cash hungry. It's very, very unlikely that a white knight will emerge for these operational reasons." Mr Roberts confirmed he made an initial offer for Comet's stock when administrators were appointed, which was rejected. His company is now interested in acquiring the brand and website, which he said would allow Appliances Online to "compete against ourselves" rather than face a new competitor. He said he would reposition Comet to focus more on customer service if his bid succeeds. If Deloitte cannot find a buyer for the entire business, it will have to sell off individual assets including store leases, remaining stock, and the brand name separately. Comet has struggled to cope with declining consumer spending since the 2008 financial crisis and joins a growing list of High Street retailers that have collapsed during the economic downturn.

Swindon Fined £15,000 for Player Confrontation with Officials Swindon Town have been handed a £15,000 fine following a confrontation with match officials during the 67th minute of their County Ground fixture against Millwall, who received a £5,000 penalty. Sporting director Seamus Brady acknowledged the club's responsibility to improve player discipline. "We just have to educate the players a bit more on that respect for the referee," he told BBC Wiltshire. Brady emphasized the need for behavioral improvements, stating: "We're trying to educate them a little bit and just let them know that we have had a couple of instances in the past and that's what we need to be careful about moving forward."

Horse Owner Denies Mistreatment Claims as RSPCA Investigates Merseyside Property The owner of horses allegedly found in poor conditions on Merseyside land has defended his treatment of the animals, whilst the RSPCA continues its investigation into welfare concerns. John Davey, founder and managing director of Davey's Chemists and a racehorse breeder, insisted the horses were "in good order" and said he was fully co-operating with the charity following complaints about animals kept on land in Tarbock Green, Knowsley. Local resident Amanda Woods, who discovered the horses on Sunday, painted a starkly different picture, describing the animals as being in "horrific condition". She reported finding a dead foal in a barn on Coney Lane and said other horses appeared "very thin" with poorly maintained hooves. A foal was also discovered entangled in electric fence tape, though Mr Davey stated the power to the fence was switched off. He thanked the "Good Samaritans" who alerted him to the trapped animal and confirmed arrangements were being made to remove the deceased foal. Mrs Woods described the barn conditions as having a "repulsive" smell and said mares in the field were emaciated with overgrown feet. She has called for the horses to be removed from Mr Davey's care, launching a petition that has attracted more than 4,000 signatures. Mr Davey acknowledged that one horse had sustained a forehead injury but said it was receiving veterinary treatment with prescribed cream. He also revealed that concerned residents had moved a mare and foal to different stables "to give them a chance to come right." The RSPCA confirmed it was investigating animal welfare concerns regarding horses in stables and on land in Knowsley. An inspector requested attendance from an experienced equine veterinarian and has visited the site daily to ensure welfare recommendations are being implemented. "We are unable to comment further as this is an ongoing investigation," the RSPCA stated. "We want to reassure the public we are doing all we can to help these horses and their welfare is very important to us."

West Africa Ebola Outbreak Worsens as Cases Surge by 20% The World Health Organization (WHO) has reported a dramatic escalation in the West African Ebola outbreak, with 68 deaths recorded since June 23rd alone. The total number of cases has climbed from 635 to 759 during the same period, representing a concerning 20% increase. This outbreak marks the largest in history in terms of cases, deaths, and geographical spread, affecting Guinea, Sierra Leone, and Liberia. The haemorrhagic fever, which has no known cure, spreads through contact with bodily fluids of infected individuals or animals, including urine, sweat, and blood. The epicenter remains Guinea's southern Guekedou region, where the outbreak was first identified in February. The escalating crisis has prompted an emergency meeting of health ministers from 11 West African nations in Ghana on Wednesday and Thursday. The WHO has emphasized the need for "drastic action," stating that "containment of this outbreak requires a strong response in the countries and especially along their shared border areas." Regional governments are taking increasingly stern measures. Liberian President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf announced Monday that anyone hiding suspected Ebola patients will face prosecution, noting that some patients have been kept in homes and churches rather than receiving proper medical care. Sierra Leone issued similar warnings last week after patients fled hospitals. Health workers report facing significant resistance throughout the region, with some even experiencing attacks while attempting to provide care. In response, Liberia's health ministry has established treatment centres and launched comprehensive public service campaigns. These initiatives include training health professionals in proper use of protective equipment and mandating that hospitals cannot refuse patients displaying Ebola symptoms. The international community watches anxiously as West African nations struggle to contain this unprecedented health emergency.

Glamorgan Edge Past Surrey in Thrilling T20 Clash at The Oval Glamorgan secured a narrow victory over Surrey in a pulsating T20 encounter at The Oval, successfully defending 181-6 despite a stirring late fightback from the hosts. Aneurin Donald was the architect of Glamorgan's competitive total, smashing a career-best 76 off just 40 balls. The Welsh side's innings was built on a blistering 95-run partnership between Donald and Colin Ingram (42), who struck three sixes including one that cleared the ground entirely. The pair added their runs in just 8.3 overs before Surrey fought back with three quick wickets. Surrey's bowling response was measured, with returning hero Rikki Clarke, back after a nine-year absence, claiming 1-23, while Tom Curran chipped in with 2-25 from four economical overs. In reply, Surrey started brightly through Aaron Finch (33) and Mark Stoneman (34), maintaining their aggressive approach despite losing regular wickets. Tom Curran's explosive 51 off 27 balls brought the equation down to 17 needed off the final over, then nine off four balls, but Michael Hogan held his nerve to seal victory for Glamorgan. Marchant de Lange's 3-29 proved crucial in restricting Surrey before a crowd of 20,000.

**Campaign Website Claims Police Lost Murder Victim's Diary** A campaign group supporting convicted murderer Michael Ross has launched a website alleging that police lost a diary belonging to his victim, Shamsuddin Mahmood. Ross was convicted in 2008 of murdering the 26-year-old Bangladeshi waiter at the Mumataz restaurant in Kirkwall, Orkney. The former Black Watch sniper, who was 15 at the time, shot Mr Mahmood in the head in front of a room full of diners, including families with children. He was sentenced to a minimum of 25 years in prison. The Justice 4 Michael Ross group has consistently campaigned for his conviction to be overturned, citing what they claim is insufficient evidence presented at trial. In 2014, Ross's attempt to have his case re-examined was rejected by the Scottish Criminal Cases Review Commission, which ruled there was inadequate evidence to support claims of a miscarriage of justice. Police Scotland has declined to comment on the allegations made on the campaign website.

Two Matalan Workers Found Dead in Cardiff; Man Charged with Murder A 20-year-old man has been charged with the murder of two Matalan employees found dead outside the Cardiff city centre store. Zoe Morgan, 21, and Lee Simmons, 33, were discovered close to the Queen Street store at approximately 05:50 BST on Wednesday morning. South Wales Police arrested Andrew Saunders, 20, from Castleton, within an hour of the bodies being found. He is scheduled to appear at Cardiff Magistrates' Court on Friday morning. In an emotional tribute, Miss Morgan's family described her as a "beautiful daughter, sister, granddaughter and auntie who had a heart of gold and would do anything for anybody." "She was taken away from us tragically, too soon, and has left a massive hole in our lives that will never be filled. Zoe will always be in our hearts forever and always. We are all broken hearted," their statement continued. Detective Superintendent Ceri Hughes of South Wales Police said: "What happened to Zoe and Lee is an absolute tragedy. Their families are devastated. Our thoughts remain with them. This has shocked the community of Cardiff." She appealed for witnesses to come forward and confirmed that support would be offered to anyone traumatised by what they saw. Miss Morgan, from Llandaff North, was a former University of South Wales fashion student who worked as a visual merchandiser at the store. Mr Simmons, from Grangetown, was employed as a sales assistant. The couple had been in a relationship since July. Matalan staff attended a tearful meeting on Thursday, with former colleagues later viewing the numerous floral tributes left at the scene. The store remained closed for a second day on Thursday but will reopen on Friday. The discovery led to the closure of part of Queen Street for several hours on Wednesday, with some shops remaining shut until police investigations concluded and the street reopened at approximately 12:50.

Carers Urged to See GPs as New Support Service Launches in Leicestershire A leading health official is urging the thousands of unpaid carers in Leicestershire to visit their GPs, warning that many are neglecting their own health while looking after loved ones. Professor Mayur Lakhani, Chair of West Leicestershire Clinical Commissioning Group, made the appeal as the new Carer Health and Wellbeing Service was launched during National Carers Week. The initiative, run jointly by the NHS and county council, aims to support an estimated 70,000 carers across the region. "Visiting the GP unlocks the doors for a carer," said Prof Lakhani. "Once we've identified them, they get an assessment of their need that could be a health check, a flu jab but also they get an assessment of their financial situation." The emotional and physical toll of caring was highlighted by Linda Lee, 70, who cares for her husband of 50 years who has Parkinson's disease. Mrs Lee described how the caring role has transformed their relationship. "I'm not his wife anymore, I'm my carer," she said. "Instead of doing the nice wifey things for him, I'm having to wash him, I have to clean his teeth, I have to cut his food up because he chokes on it." Mrs Lee revealed the couple now sleep in separate rooms, adding: "We've lost that lovely closeness - he was my one and only and I was his one and only and we've had a wonderful, loving marriage." She said she used to cry herself to sleep before seeking help from her GP. "It has been very difficult. Life has been horrendous. I've lost so much, he's lost so much." Charles Huddlestone, manager of Leicester Carers Centre, who himself cares for his autistic son and wife Gill following her spinal injury, described the new service as "vital." "We've found some carers completely ignoring their own needs," he explained. "We're very good at ignoring our own pain."

Welsh Actor and Entertainer Howell Evans Dies Surrounded by Family Veteran Welsh actor, comedian and singer Howell Evans has passed away peacefully at home with his family by his side on Tuesday, his agents have confirmed. Born in Maesteg, south Wales, Evans enjoyed a remarkable career spanning over seven decades in entertainment, appearing in numerous beloved television programmes including Coronation Street, Casualty, Open All Hours, Holby City, and the children's series The Story of Tracy Beaker. His agents, Cardiff-based Emptage Hallett, paid tribute to their client, stating: "His warmth, positivity and sense of humour made him a joy to work with. His love of life and brilliant sense of humour was inspirational. Howell was a hugely talented actor, a consummate professional and a lovely human being." Evans began his entertainment career at just 16 years old as an impressionist, touring war zones to entertain troops. It was during these tours that he met his future wife, Pat Kane, a dancer in a troupe entertaining servicemen. After serving three years in the RAF, Evans joined the Carroll Lewis Discovery Show in 1949, billed as "the star from the services". He and Pat formed a successful comedy double act, performing together for many years across music hall, variety, revue and pantomime. Their son Warwick accompanied them on tour until school age and later followed his parents into acting. Evans' extensive television credits included Welsh favourites How Green Was My Valley and Satellite City, classic series Z Cars and Softly, Softly, and he played memorable roles such as Grandpa Jack in Tracy Beaker and Mr Bolder in The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby. His film work included The Ipcress File and An Englishman That Went Up a Hill But Came Down a Mountain. He is survived by his wife Pat Kane and son Warwick Evans.

Biker Dies in A5 Crash as Van Driver Held A motorcyclist has died following a collision on the A5 at Cerrigydrudion, Conwy county, on Sunday evening at approximately 19:10 BST. North Wales Police confirmed a 46-year-old driver of a VW Transporter van remains in custody, arrested on suspicion of causing death by careless driving. The incident marked the second fatal motorcycle crash in the area that day, though police confirmed the accidents were unrelated. The other fatality occurred near Betws-y-Coed. Investigations into both incidents continue.

Bus Use in England Falls to Lowest Level in a Decade Bus passenger numbers in England have fallen to their lowest level in a decade, official statistics have revealed, with concerns mounting over congestion and reduced subsidies. Passengers made 119 million fewer journeys in 2015-16 than the year before, a fall of 2.6%. The total number of bus journeys in England dropped to 4.5 billion, the lowest figure recorded since 2006. London, traditionally a stronghold for bus travel, was not immune to the decline. The capital recorded its first drop in bus use since 2012, with journeys down 3% to 2.29 billion. Transport for London (TfL) has attributed this to increased congestion slowing services across the city. ## Congestion and Subsidies Blamed Campaigners have pointed to worsening traffic congestion as a major factor behind the decline. Research by the Campaign for Better Transport (CBT) found that buses in London are now moving only marginally faster than the average adult walking pace. "The news that bus use is falling in London is worrying, but as buses are now moving only marginally faster through the city than the average adult can walk, it's hardly surprising," said Lianna Etkind, public transport campaigner at the CBT. "Congestion is bringing London to a standstill and needs to be urgently tackled." The Department for Transport (DfT) said the drop in bus mileage was "largely due" to a fall in services subsidised by local councils. CBT research revealed that subsidies for bus routes have been reduced by £78 million since 2010, leading to service cuts, particularly in rural areas. Bus fares increased by 1.8% during the period, which the DfT said was "similar" to other price rises in line with the 1.6% Retail Price Index of inflation. ## Future Outlook TfL remains optimistic about reversing the trend. Gareth Powell, TfL's Director of Strategy for Surface Transport, acknowledged the "small reduction" but said bus network reliability has now stabilised. He cited the completion of major road projects and introduction of the new "Hopper" fare as measures expected to boost passenger numbers. A DfT spokesman emphasized continued government support, stating: "We provide some £250 million a year to support bus services in England and about £1 billion is spent annually to give nearly 10 million older and disabled people in England off-peak bus travel."

Dettori Forced to Miss Irish Champion Stakes After Race Time Change Frankie Dettori's plans to ride in both the St Leger at Doncaster and the Irish Champion Stakes at Leopardstown on Saturday have been dashed after race officials brought forward the Irish race. The Italian jockey had hoped to compete in the world's oldest Classic at Doncaster on Saturday (15:45 BST) and then fly by helicopter to Leopardstown to partner Golden Horn. But the Irish race has been brought forward 65 minutes to 17:45 because of concerns over the ground. Dettori's agent Ray Cochrane said there was not enough time to ride in both. "Frankie had rides in the first four races at Doncaster, the last one being in the Leger and then we were going to shoot over to Ireland and be there in good time," he said. "Now they've changed it by bringing it forward there's no point thinking of trying to do both." William Buick will come in for the ride on Bondi Beach, trained by Aidan O'Brien. The Irish Champion Stakes is being billed as "the race of the season" with Derby winner Golden Horn and Guineas victor Gleneagles finally set to clash after their planned showdown at York was scuppered by the weather. However, trainer O'Brien has said he does not want to run Gleneagles on soft ground, and Irish officials have moved the race forward because they were concerned the ground could become churned up later on as rain is forecast on Friday night. The race will be held on an outside track on fresh ground, which has not been used so far this season.

Victim of Southampton Attack Speaks Out as Police Hunt Two Brothers A woman who suffered life-changing injuries in a brutal assault in Southampton has spoken publicly about the devastating impact the attack has had on her life. Carla Whitlock, 37, was attacked in Guildhall Square, Southampton, on Friday night, leaving her with severe facial injuries and partial blindness. Hampshire Constabulary is urgently seeking two brothers from London in connection with the assault. Officers have raided properties in the Medway area of Kent in their efforts to trace Billy Midmore, 22, and Geoffrey Midmore, 26. Despite these efforts, the suspects remain at large. Speaking about her injuries, Ms Whitlock described the ongoing pain she is experiencing. "It's painful. My eyes are swollen at the moment. It's going to get more painful before it gets better. It just feels like someone is stabbing me in the eyeball all the time," she said. The attack has left Ms Whitlock with significant vision loss. "I can pretty much see everything out of my left eye but I cannot see anything out of my right eye," she explained. "It has changed my life completely. I'm coping with it as best as I can." Ms Whitlock praised staff at the nearby Turtle Bay restaurant who provided crucial first aid following the assault, which occurred at approximately 9pm on Friday. "The efforts that they went to is why I've got sight in my left eye now," she said. Detective Inspector Will Whale warned the Midmore brothers that "there is no hiding place." He revealed that CCTV footage captured the pair at a McDonald's in the Swathling area of Southampton on Monday, appearing "relaxed, confident and smirking." "The victim is now out of hospital, but her injuries are life-changing and horrific," Det Insp Whale said. "So far the public has been fantastic in coming forward with information to help us, but we need you to help us find these men who we believe were involved in this horrendous attack." Billy Midmore is described as white, stocky, 5ft 8in tall, with blue eyes, a scar on his left arm, and a London accent. Geoffrey Midmore is white, stocky, 5ft 1in tall, with green eyes, a scar on his right cheek, and a tattoo on his hand. Police are also investigating whether Ms Whitlock had previously reported concerns for her safety.

CIA Director's Personal Email Account Allegedly Hacked by High School Student A teenager claiming to be angry about US foreign policy has allegedly hacked into CIA Director John Brennan's personal email account, according to reports from the New York Post. The anonymous hacker, described as "a stoner high-school student," told the newspaper he discovered sensitive work-related files, including Mr. Brennan's application for top security clearance. The teenager posted evidence of the alleged breach on Twitter, including what appeared to be contact lists, phone call records from a former CIA deputy director, and documents containing names, telephone numbers, email addresses, and social security numbers. The CIA has acknowledged awareness of the situation but has not confirmed whether the hack actually occurred. "We are aware of the reports that have surfaced on social media and have referred the matter to the appropriate authorities," the agency said in a statement. The alleged hacker also claims to have accessed an email account belonging to Homeland Security Secretary Jeh Johnson. This incident comes at a particularly sensitive time, as the use of private email by senior US officials has become a significant political issue. The controversy gained prominence after revelations that presidential candidate Hillary Clinton used a personal email server during her tenure as secretary of state. Investigations into the alleged breach are currently underway.

Murray Prioritizes Baby's Birth Over Australian Open Final Andy Murray has revealed he would withdraw from the Australian Open final if it clashed with the birth of his first child, stating family takes priority over his quest for a maiden Melbourne title. The British tennis star's wife Kim is expecting their baby in the second week of February, just days after the Australian Open concludes at the end of January. Despite being a four-time losing finalist at the tournament, including last year's defeat to Novak Djokovic, Murray insists the decision is straightforward. "It would be disappointing if I was to get to that position, not being able to play the final," Murray said. "But I'd be way more disappointed winning the Australian Open and missing the birth of the child." The world number two plans to take the entire month of February off to be with Kim and their newborn. While acknowledging the potential dilemma if the baby arrives early, Murray confirmed that after discussions with his wife, "it was an easy decision to make" to prioritize his family. However, he remains hopeful that such a situation won't materialize. Murray was speaking to Eurosport following his convincing 6-2, 6-2 victory over France's Kenny De Schepper in his opening Hopman Cup match in Perth. "'It was good, I played well today. I got off to a quick start and that settled me down a bit, and I played some good stuff," he said. The British number one briefly appeared uncomfortable in the second set, holding his right hip, but dismissed fitness concerns. "It's just a little sore, but I was able to move around well," Murray added.

Chiefs Dominate Lions with 38 Unanswered Points in Record-Breaking Wembley Performance LONDON - The Kansas City Chiefs produced a stunning turnaround at Wembley Stadium on Sunday, scoring 38 consecutive points to crush the Detroit Lions in what became their most emphatic victory of the season, despite conceding on the game's opening drive. Quarterback Alex Smith orchestrated a masterful performance, throwing two touchdown passes and adding a rushing touchdown of his own as the Chiefs equalled the New England Patriots' record for the most points scored by an NFL team at Wembley, matching the Patriots' 45-7 victory over the St Louis Rams in 2012. The contest served as the third and final NFL International Series game at Wembley in 2015, following the New York Jets' 27-14 win over the Miami Dolphins and the Jacksonville Jaguars' 34-31 victory against the Buffalo Bills, both played in October. The Lions, who made the playoffs last season but now hold a dismal 1-7 record, appeared to gain an early advantage after arriving in London several days before their opponents. That strategy seemed to pay immediate dividends when Matt Prater opened the scoring with a 35-yard field goal. However, the Chiefs responded emphatically. De'Anthony Thomas scored on a 10-yard run to ignite what would become a dominant performance before 83,624 spectators. Smith then took control, exploiting gaps in the Detroit defense with ruthless efficiency. After a career-best 49-yard rushing effort, he capped the drive with a 12-yard touchdown run. The floodgates truly opened when Lions quarterback Matthew Stafford threw two interceptions, leading to a Cairo Santos field goal and a Charcandrick West touchdown. By halftime, Kansas City had established a commanding 24-3 lead. The second half brought no respite for Detroit. Smith connected with Travis Kelce in the end zone, before Jeremy Maclin—returning from concussion protocol after missing the previous week's victory over Pittsburgh—became the fifth Chiefs player to find the end zone. Stafford managed a consolation touchdown pass to Lance Moore for his third score of the season, but Spencer Ware answered immediately with his first NFL touchdown, restoring the 35-point margin. "It was about putting four quarters together and we did that today," said Smith afterward. "I was especially pleased with the second half when we stayed focused despite having a big lead. We had dug a little hole for ourselves earlier in the season, but the last two weeks have been good for us." The victory represents Kansas City's second consecutive win following a five-game losing streak, offering renewed hope as they enter the season's second half.

Two Men Convicted of Murder After Fatal House Fire in Gainsborough Two men have been found guilty of murdering a 24-year-old man who died in a house fire in Gainsborough, Lincolnshire. Martynas Kupstys, 26, and Andrus Giedraitis, 30, had both denied the murder of Ivans Zdanovics, who perished in the blaze at his rented terraced home on Etherington Street in January last year. Lincoln Crown Court heard that Mr Zdanovics's body was discovered by a friend in an upstairs bedroom. Fire investigators found five separate seats of fire in the downstairs area of the property. A post-mortem examination revealed Mr Zdanovics died from smoke inhalation after drinking with the two defendants earlier that evening. During the five-week trial, prosecutor James House QC outlined how Kupstys admitted starting multiple fires at the house but claimed he only intended to damage the property, not to kill or seriously harm Mr Zdanovics. Kupstys, of Aegir Close, Gainsborough, told the jury he believed the house was empty and said he felt humiliated by Mr Zdanovics over a failed cannabis delivery. Giedraitis, of Riseholme Road, Gainsborough, denied being present when the fires were started. The jury convicted Kupstys on Monday and Giedraitis on Tuesday. The case attracted additional attention when the Ministry of Justice launched an investigation in August after Kupstys was mistakenly released from HMP Lincoln while awaiting court transport. Media reports indicated he attempted to alert prison officers to their error but was still escorted out. He reportedly waited at a bus stop for three hours while police searched for him. Both men are scheduled to be sentenced on Thursday.

Prison Service Lorry Damaged After Hitting Historic Bridge in Banbridge A Prison Service lorry had its roof torn off after striking a 19th Century stone bridge in Banbridge, County Down, with the driver continuing for 10 miles without realizing the extent of the damage. The incident occurred on 27 November when the vehicle passed under the Cut, a historic low bridge known for catching out drivers of high-sided vehicles. A Prison Service spokesperson confirmed that one of its vehicles "was involved in a road traffic incident at Banbridge" and that no other vehicles were involved and no one was injured. The incident is currently under investigation. Police shared a photograph of the damaged lorry on social media on 28 November, describing the driver's decision to continue as "not the smartest move." The vehicle reportedly traveled on to Portadown before the damage was discovered. Officers joked that "only the fire service are qualified to make your motor a convertible by the roadside, but you really don't want that to happen." Adding to concerns, a second lorry struck the same bridge the following day, prompting police to issue warnings to drivers of high-sided vehicles about knowing their vehicle dimensions before passing under low bridges. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) emphasized the serious safety implications of bridge strikes, particularly those involving railway bridges. Officers reminded motorists to immediately contact Northern Ireland Railways (NIR) using numbers displayed under bridges if a collision occurs, warning that "there's no way of telling what structural damage could be caused by a bridge strike, and those trains aren't light." Bridge strikes have become an increasing problem across Ireland this year, with Irish Rail launching a high-profile campaign in the Republic to address the issue.

Wales Major Trauma Centre: Cardiff and Swansea Make Their Cases Cardiff and Vale University Health Board is making a strong pitch to host Wales' first major trauma centre, emphasizing their capabilities across multiple specialisms. Dr Graham Shortland, the health board's medical director, said their case spans from "world class" paediatrics to neurosurgery, with particular enthusiasm for securing the major trauma centre designation. "We are very much up for this," Dr Shortland said. "We have a significant number of committed senior clinicians and managers to deliver a coordinated service in Cardiff." He highlighted neurosurgery as crucial, requiring rapidly available surgeons who can make swift decisions, including determining when surgery isn't necessary. This expertise must be supported by radiology and high-care bed facilities. Dr Shortland acknowledged potential challenges, stating Cardiff would maintain high-quality routine orthopaedic operations whilst managing the risk to elective surgery as the trauma unit becomes operational. Meanwhile, Swansea is also presenting its case for the centre, with decision-makers examining how Bristol's Major Trauma Centre operates as a model.
