Campbell made 37 appearances for the Magpies in all competitions last season, scoring eight goals. The 22-year-old, who can play up front or on the wing, started his career at Newcastle, before moving to League Two side County in July 2015. "He has a lot of pace and has a lot of the qualities that we have been looking for," said manager Jim Bentley. Meanwhile, midfielder Aaron Wildig, 25, has signed a new two-year contract with the Shrimps, while forward Kevin Ellison, 38, midfielder Alex Kenyon, 24, and midfielder Andy Fleming, 29, have all agreed new one-year deals.

New Plastic £5 Notes Enter Circulation in UK The Bank of England has introduced new polymer £5 banknotes, marking a significant change in British currency. These innovative notes are slightly smaller than traditional paper versions and incorporate advanced security features designed to prevent counterfeiting. According to the Bank of England, the plastic banknotes offer several advantages: they're cleaner, more secure, and significantly more durable than their paper predecessors. Existing paper £5 notes remain legal tender and can still be used for transactions, but they will gradually be phased out as they're deposited into banks. The UK joins over 30 countries worldwide that have already adopted polymer currency technology, including Scotland, Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. The transition to plastic currency will continue with new polymer £10 notes scheduled for summer 2017, followed by £20 notes in 2020.

DUP-Tory Deal: £1bn Windfall Dominates Northern Ireland Headlines Northern Ireland's newspapers have given extensive coverage to the controversial confidence-and-supply agreement between the Conservative Party and the Democratic Unionist Party, with front pages dominated by the £1bn financial package secured for the region. The Irish News features a striking political cartoon depicting Prime Minister Theresa May up a ladder shaking a "money tree" while DUP leader Arlene Foster gleefully collects falling cash in her dress. The paper dedicates its first eight pages to analyzing the deal and its implications for the stalled Stormont power-sharing talks. According to the Irish News, if the current political negotiations fail to restore devolved government, the additional funding will be administered through a "co-ordination committee" involving the DUP and Conservatives, effectively excluding Sinn Féin from any influence over how the money is spent. Political analyst John Manley compares Mrs Foster to "the cat who got the cream" in his assessment of the deal. The paper's editorial acknowledges that political pressure has now intensified on Sinn Féin to return to the executive, though it notes the party will not want to appear to be "dancing to the DUP's tune." ## Unionist Papers Celebrate Historic Agreement The News Letter celebrates with the headline "One billion smiles," featuring a photograph of DUP MPs Nigel Dodds and Sir Jeffrey Donaldson alongside Mrs Foster and a more reserved-looking Mrs May. The paper describes the agreement as "historic," drawing comparisons to Irish nationalist leader John Redmond holding the balance of power at Westminster over a century ago. The News Letter also reports on warnings from TUV leader Jim Allister that an Irish language act would be "a vehicle to hollow out our Britishness." Mr Allister suggested the DUP might be prepared to compromise on the contentious language issue to secure the return of the Northern Ireland executive. ## Pressure Mounts on Sinn Féin The Belfast Telegraph makes its position clear with the headline "£1bn reasons to bring back Stormont now." Like its counterparts, the paper devotes eight pages to the story, with multiple articles and comment pieces emphasizing the renewed pressure on Sinn Féin to restore power-sharing. In other news, the Belfast Telegraph reports exclusively on a significant split within the republican political party Saoradh, with up to 23 members reportedly resigning in support of a high-profile republican who has been expelled from the organization. Meanwhile, the Northern Ireland edition of the Daily Mirror runs with "Now we've got money to burn," making a pointed reference to both the new funding and the Renewable Heat Incentive scandal that has plagued Mrs Foster's leadership.

Officers Face Misconduct Probe Over Man's Broken Neck During Arrest Four police officers remain on active duty while facing potential gross misconduct charges following an investigation into an arrest that left a young man paralyzed with a broken neck. Julian Cole, then a 23-year-old student, suffered catastrophic spinal injuries outside Elements nightclub in Bedford in May 2013. The incident has been the subject of a lengthy investigation by the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC). After examining the circumstances surrounding the arrest, the IPCC has concluded there may be a case to answer for gross misconduct and has referred the matter to prosecutors. Bedfordshire Police confirmed that four officers involved in the incident remain on active duty, while a fifth has since retired from the force. The investigation findings indicate four officers could face charges relating to honesty and integrity, while one officer could face misconduct proceedings for use of force, though this is not believed to be directly linked to Julian's spinal injury. The IPCC described the inquiry as "complex and lengthy," involving examination of over 900 documents, witness interviews, multiple medical expert opinions, CCTV analysis, and forensic examination. The Crown Prosecution Service will now determine whether criminal charges should be brought against any of the officers. Julian's mother, Claudia Cole, told BBC News the announcement was "welcome" but noted the investigation had taken far too long. "It has been the hardest three years waiting for the IPCC investigation to conclude," she said. "Julian is still alive, but it cannot be said that he is really living." The case has profoundly changed Julian's life. Once an energetic and athletic young man passionate about football and Arsenal FC, he now requires round-the-clock care and is completely dependent on nursing staff and his devoted parents for all his daily needs. The exact circumstances of how Julian sustained his injuries remain unclear and may never be known with complete certainty. However, under new rules, any misconduct hearings will be open to the public, providing greater transparency in what has become a deeply serious case requiring public scrutiny. The family continues to seek answers about what happened that night outside the Bedford nightclub, moving one step closer to understanding the truth behind the incident that changed their lives forever.

**Supreme Court Rejects News Group Appeal in Sheridan Defamation Case** The Supreme Court has dismissed an attempt by News Group to overturn a defamation case won by former MSP Tommy Sheridan against the now defunct News of The World in 2006. News Group, the paper's owner, sought to have the original ruling "struck down" following Mr Sheridan's 2010 conviction for perjury. However, the Supreme Court ruled they had failed to "raise an arguable point of law of general public importance". The decision follows a hearing at the Court of Session in Edinburgh last year, where News Group attempted to obtain permission to have the original trial rerun. That application was rejected in November. The company subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court, which has now also declined to hear the case, upholding the Edinburgh judgement. In a statement, the court explained: "The Court ordered that permission to appeal be refused because the application does not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance, which ought to be considered at this time, bearing in mind that the case has already been the subject of judicial decision and reviewed on appeal". The judgement finally concludes an 11-year legal saga that began when the newspaper published articles about Mr Sheridan's private life. The former Scottish Socialist Party leader and Glasgow MSP was awarded compensation after winning the defamation trial in 2006, though it is understood he was not paid the money at that time. In 2010, Mr Sheridan was found guilty of perjury for giving false evidence during the earlier case and was jailed for three years. He was released from prison after serving just over a year of his sentence.

Wales Forwards: Lydiate Returns to Training as Williams Makes Comeback Wales forwards coach Robin McBryde has delivered positive news regarding key players' fitness ahead of the Six Nations, confirming that Osprey Dan Lydiate has returned to training following a neck injury, while Liam Williams successfully completed 60 minutes for the Scarlets last weekend. "Everything's good with Liam and Dan Lydiate has joined back in," McBryde told reporters. Williams featured in the opening hour of Scarlets' defeat at Connacht on Sunday, marking his first appearance since sustaining a foot injury during Wales' 15-6 loss to Australia on 10 October. Lydiate, meanwhile, has been sidelined since being forced off during Ospreys' New Year's Day victory over Newport Gwent Dragons. His return to training represents a significant boost for Wales' back-row options. McBryde expressed satisfaction with Williams' comeback performance, noting: "Things went as well as they could for Liam. He definitely won one collision (when Connacht wing Matt Healy was forced off through injury) and he was pretty secure under the high ball." While acknowledging the difficult circumstances of Williams' return, McBryde added: "He's come through unscathed so whether he's fit enough to start an 80 minutes - he's certainly fit enough to play some part." Lydiate isn't the only Wales back-rower facing a shortage of recent match action. Captain Sam Warburton has featured just once for Cardiff Blues in the past two months - against Calvisano on 22 January - due to an ankle problem. However, McBryde suggested Warburton requires minimal game time to return to peak condition: "Sam Warburton doesn't need a lot of match time and he's straight back up there." Regarding Lydiate's readiness, McBryde explained: "It's a discussion to be had with Dan. The one thing we are seeing in a positive light is that Dan is taking part in our training sessions which are quite intense, and he's come through those scenarios okay, though it's not the same as a game." Warburton did not feature for Cardiff Blues against Edinburgh despite previously indicating he wanted more playing time following his comeback. "Warren just held him back," McBryde explained, citing squad management difficulties after losing French and English-based players during the week. Wales are scheduled to announce their team to face Ireland at 1100 GMT on Wednesday, 3 February.

Lord Bilimoria Champions "Good Immigration" as Government Faces Criticism As net migration figures are set to be released this week, the immigration debate in Britain has reached fever pitch, with critics lining up to attack current government policy. However, one prominent voice is bucking the trend – Lord Karan Bilimoria, the newly installed Chancellor of the University of Birmingham, who insists there is such a thing as "good immigration". The Indian-born founder of the Cobra Beer empire has launched a passionate defence of international students, warning that Britain will pay a heavy price for its latest immigration clampdown. In a hard-hitting interview with the Mail on Sunday, Lord Bilimoria accused Prime Minister David Cameron of making a "big mistake" by setting "unattainable" immigration targets – a policy from which Home Secretary Theresa May has admitted the government has been "blown off course". Lord Bilimoria pointed to alarming statistics that illustrate the impact of tougher visa rules: "The number of international students to Britain fell for the first time last year. And the number from India have collapsed by over 20%." He criticised the government's approach as counterproductive, arguing that whilst they claim to have lost control of illegal immigration – challenging Home Secretary Theresa May to say how many illegal immigrants there actually are – they are instead targeting legitimate students who contribute significantly to Britain's economy and universities. The financial stakes are considerable. The University of Birmingham's 4,500 international students bring in nearly £60 million in fees annually. Neighbouring Warwick University, the other Russell Group institution in the Midlands, reports that its 5,000-plus international students generate nearly £90 million – money that is reinvested to benefit British students. "The government may say Britain is open for business but they're sending out a message that's not so welcoming," Warwick University stated. Lord Bilimoria has called for a complete policy reversal, advocating for new targets to increase international student numbers. He noted that France plans to double its number of students from India by 2020, suggesting Britain is falling behind in the global competition for talent. This week, Lord Bilimoria accompanied his vice chancellor and universities minister Greg Clark on a visit to India, presumably to repair some of the damage done by current policy. Four months into his role as chancellor, Lord Bilimoria appears determined to be more than a ceremonial figurehead, using his platform to advocate forcefully for what he terms "good immigration". The debate continues on Sunday Politics in the Midlands at 11:00 GMT on BBC One.

New Welsh-Medium School Plans Move Forward Despite Setback Plans for a new Welsh-medium secondary school in Newport will proceed despite a setback over its proposed location. The school, intended to open on the site of Duffryn High School, was refused planning permission due to flooding concerns. However, council officials remain committed to launching the facility this autumn. At a meeting attended by approximately 100 parents at Newport's Civic Centre on Friday, James Harris, the council's head of education, announced alternative arrangements. The school will temporarily operate at Ysgol Bro Teyrnon in Shaftesbury for up to two years while authorities continue searching for a permanent site. Elin Maher, chair of the new school's governing body, also revealed that governors have recommended naming the institution Ysgol Gyfun Gwent Iscoed.

Machynlleth Town Council Criticised for Handling April Jones Appeal Funds Machynlleth Town Council has been heavily criticised by auditors for accepting and banking £71,663 in public donations intended for the April Jones fund without having the legal authority to do so. The damning report by auditor BDO stated that the council should have refused money offered by members of the public following the five-year-old's disappearance in October 2012. Y Plas, the council's base in Machynlleth, became a focal point during the extensive search operation, with many people wanting to contribute financially. "The council had no power to collect this money or to establish a bank account for its retention," the report stated. "When people came into the office and gave them money they should not have accepted the money." April's disappearance triggered the largest search operation in UK police history. Mark Bridger was convicted of her murder in May 2013 and received a whole life sentence. The judge described him as a "pathological liar" and "a paedophile". Beyond the handling of donation funds, the audit report highlighted significant concerns about the council's overall governance and financial management. The council failed to complete annual accounting statements and submit returns on time for six consecutive years. The report also revealed that the former clerk's poor record-keeping resulted in £5,073 in unclaimed VAT - representing 2% of the council's entire annual budget. However, auditors noted that the new clerk has been working to strengthen internal controls and update the accounts. The council has scheduled a meeting for 24 August to discuss implementing the report's recommendations and addressing the identified deficiencies.

Kenyan Governor to Face Court as Political Blame Game Intensifies Over Coastal Attacks **NAIROBI** - Issa Timamy, the governor of Lamu County, is scheduled to appear in court on Thursday amid escalating tensions following a series of deadly attacks in the coastal region. President Uhuru Kenyatta has controversially attributed the violence to "local political networks," rejecting claims by Somali Islamist group al-Shabab that they were responsible for the assaults. The president's dismissal centers on the ethnic targeting of victims, with most casualties being Kikuyus—the president's own ethnic group—and non-Muslims specifically singled out for execution. Governor Timamy, a member of the United Democratic Front (UDF), an affiliate of President Kenyatta's governing Jubilee coalition, now faces legal scrutiny. Opposition parties have strongly criticized the president's explanation, with opposition leader Raila Odinga demanding dialogue to address what he calls catastrophic security failings. Authorities announced Wednesday the arrest of 13 alleged separatists from the Mombasa Republican Council (MRC), a coastal separatist organization. The interior ministry claims those detained were planning "ethnic cleansing" attacks in the region. The violence began on June 15 in Mpeketoni, when gunmen attacked residents watching a World Cup football match. Follow-up assaults occurred the next day in nearby villages. On Tuesday, five more people were killed in Witu, approximately 15 kilometers from Mpeketoni. In response to the ongoing threat, the Kenyan government has issued advisories recommending citizens watch World Cup matches at home rather than gathering in bars or public venues, highlighting the persistent security concerns gripping the coastal region.

Northern Ireland Police Warn of Dormant Ransomware Threat Following Global Cyber-Attack The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) has issued an urgent warning that the ransomware virus responsible for Friday's massive global cyber-attack may already be lurking in computer systems across Northern Ireland, lying dormant and waiting to activate. The warning comes in the wake of a devastating cyber-attack that affected more than 200,000 victims across 150 countries. The malicious ransomware locked users' files and demanded payment to restore access, threatening to destroy data if victims refused to comply. Detective Chief Inspector Douglas Grant, who leads the PSNI's cyber crime unit, emphasized that while there is currently no evidence the virus has infiltrated Northern Ireland's computer networks, this does not guarantee the region hasn't been targeted. "Thankfully we haven't experienced any of this current strain, but we must be vigilant because it could come to Northern Ireland at any point and it could have infections in our systems at the moment that just haven't activated," Det Ch Insp Grant stated. The PSNI is working closely with national and international law enforcement agencies to minimize risks to local computer networks. The force has called upon public and private sector organizations to take immediate action to protect their systems and reduce vulnerability. Authorities are encouraging businesses and industries to join the local Cyber Information Sharing Partnership (CISP) to receive the latest threat intelligence and mitigation information to bolster their cyber security defenses. The PSNI's cyber crime centre continues to participate actively in the national coordinated response to the attack. Additional guidance is available through the National Cyber Security Centre, which has issued specific protective measures for companies to implement. Police warn that organizations and individuals in Northern Ireland face daily targeting by cyber criminals attempting to steal data or commit fraud and blackmail. According to the PSNI, a large-scale attack on Northern Ireland is not a question of if, but when. Anyone who believes they may have fallen victim to a cyber-attack is urged to contact the PSNI immediately.

Ancient Footprints on Welsh Beach Prove 7,000 Years Old, Not Bronze Age Mysterious footprints discovered on a Gower beach have been revealed to be thousands of years older than originally believed, according to new research from Cardiff University. The ancient tracks, found at Port Eynon in 2014, were initially estimated to date from the Bronze Age. However, radiocarbon dating has now shown they are actually approximately 7,000 years old – making them 3,000 years more ancient than first thought. Rhiannon Philp, an archaeology PhD student at Cardiff University's School of History, Archaeology and Religion, believes the prints may have been left by a Mesolithic hunting party. The footprints, belonging to both adults and children, were preserved in what was once freshwater marshland. "These'frozen' footprints give us a fleeting glance of a group of adults and children travelling together seven millennia ago," Ms Philp explained. Adding to the intrigue, wild animal tracks – possibly from deer and wild boar – were found moving in the same direction, suggesting the group may have been tracking prey through the boggy landscape. Post-Ice Age human footprints are exceptionally rare in the UK, with only nine recorded tidal sites, most located in Wales. Ms Philp emphasised the importance of documenting such fragile evidence, particularly given the threats posed by climate change. The landscape where these ancient travellers once walked has long since been claimed by the sea.

Bristol City Boss Lee Johnson Rejects Birmingham's "Derisory" Bid for Key Players Bristol City manager Lee Johnson has strongly dismissed Birmingham City's joint bid for defender Aden Flint and left-back Joe Bryan, describing the offer as "derisory" on 2 August. The Championship club rejected the approach from Birmingham, with Johnson making it clear that neither individual nor combined offers met the club's valuation of the two players. "Neither solo bid met our requirements or the figure we felt was acceptable," Johnson told BBC Radio Bristol. "We're in a strong position. We don't want to lose quality players but, if we do, it would be at the right price." According to BBC Radio Bristol sources, the joint bid for the pair totalled approximately £4 million, a figure Bristol City considered insufficient for two key squad members. The transfer speculation has already had an impact on team selection. Flint, 28, appeared as a late substitute in Saturday's season-opening 3-1 victory over Barnsley but was notably absent from Tuesday's EFL Cup win against Plymouth Argyle. Johnson confirmed the decision followed a private conversation with the defender, formerly of Swindon Town. "Aden knocked on the door. We had a good conversation. We've got a lot of respect for each other," the 36-year-old manager explained. "After that conversation, which I won't reveal because it's private between player and coach, I felt it was better for the team to leave him out. The result and the team come first." Johnson was careful to emphasize that Flint's omission didn't necessarily signal his departure, adding: "It doesn't mean that Aden's going, or the door is closed on Aden at all." The situation adds extra spice to Saturday's fixture, when Bristol City travel to St Andrew's to face Harry Redknapp's Birmingham in their second Championship match of the 2017-18 season. Despite the ongoing transfer tensions, Johnson maintained a diplomatic stance regarding the former Tottenham manager, confirming he would still be happy to share a post-match drink if invited. "I've spoken to Harry on three or four occasions since venting my frustration with the current circumstances in the transfer market," Johnson said. "Harry is a top, top manager. He's also very good with young managers. I always love listening to his stories." In other transfer news, Johnson confirmed that Swedish striker Gustav Engvall, 21, will depart on loan again before the Swedish transfer window closes on Friday. The forward, who joined in 2016, spent the end of last season at Djurgarden IF and will return to Sweden to gain regular playing time.

Barry Island Pleasure Park Keys Handed to New Owner The keys to Barry Island Pleasure Park were officially handed over to new owner Henry Danter on Monday, marking the beginning of a new chapter for the beloved Welsh seaside attraction. The handover follows extended negotiations with former owners Hilco, and Mr Danter is wasting no time in revitalizing the site. The experienced fairground operator, who brings 50 years of industry expertise and currently runs Treasure Island fairground in Stourport-on-Severn, Worcestershire, has ambitious plans to restore the park's former glory. "It's taken a long time to get to this point," Mr Danter said. "But we promised the people of Barry we would have it up and running for Easter." He plans to mobilize large vehicles immediately to clear the site, with the goal of operating a small fair by Friday. While Mr Danter paid a deposit "quite a long time ago," the deal was delayed pending Hilco receiving planning permission for nearby residential flats. The new owner envisions investing up to £20 million in the fairground's regeneration, including constructing an arcade to make it a year-round destination. Finance Wales and Barclays are backing the project. Beth Cousins, deputy fund manager at Finance Wales, expressed confidence in the venture: "Henry and his family have a strong heritage in the fairground industry. We're confident that their passion and experience will put the pleasure park back on the map." The park has struggled since Butlins holiday camp closed 18 years ago. Hilco has been contacted for comment.

Partick Thistle's Archibald Shows No Sympathy to Former Club Dundee United Partick Thistle manager Alan Archibald insists there will be no sentiment when his side faces former club Dundee United in a crucial Scottish Premiership clash at Firhill on Tuesday evening. Eighth-placed Thistle host bottom club United at Firhill on Tuesday evening, with the Tangerines able to move to within two points of Kilmarnock with a victory. Despite United's remarkable fight against relegation, Archibald remains focused on his own team's objectives. "All the media are enjoying United's comeback story but we've got something to fight for as well," said Archibald. "We've got that incentive to get into the top six." The stakes are high for Thistle, who sit just two points behind sixth-placed Dundee following their goalless draw with Kilmarnock on Saturday. United, meanwhile, boosted their survival hopes with a victory over St Johnstone. Archibald, who spent four years as a centre-back at Tannadice, dismissed any notion of sympathy towards his former employers. "It could be us and I don't think anybody would feel sorry for us," he said. "I said if they can get within touching distance then they'll give themselves a chance and they've done that." The match features an intriguing subplot, with United having already approached Thistle midfielder Steven Lawless about a summer move. Inverness Caledonian Thistle have also expressed interest in the 24-year-old, but Archibald has no reservations about selecting him. "Not at all, Stevie's our player," the Jags boss stated. "Since January, Stevie's actually got better so we've got no concerns at all about playing him." Pitch conditions may also prove decisive, with Firhill's surface having struggled during wet weather this season. However, both managers expect the game to proceed, with United boss Mixu Paatelainen acknowledging conditions will "play a role" but insisting his team will adapt accordingly.

Scottish Football Legend Alex Young Dies Alex Young, the legendary Scottish footballer celebrated for his elegant style and dubbed "The Golden Vision," has passed away. The striker's remarkable career spanned notable clubs across British football during the late 1950s and 1960s. Born in Loanhead, Young began his professional journey with Hearts from 1955-1960, where his prolific goal-scoring helped secure the Scottish league title in 1958. His impressive performances earned him a transfer to Everton, where he truly made his mark. At Everton, Young became an icon, making 273 appearances and scoring 87 goals. He helped the Merseyside club win both the First Division title and the FA Cup. His graceful playing style earned him the nickname "The Golden Vision," coined by Northern Ireland defender Danny Blanchflower. Young's influence extended beyond the pitch. His impact on Evertonians was so profound that Ken Loach directed a 1968 play celebrating him. A 2001 testimonial drew over 20,000 fans to Goodison Park. Internationally, Young represented Scotland eight times, scoring five goals. After playing for Glentoran and Stockport County, he later managed Glentoran before returning to Edinburgh to run his family's upholstery business.

Sprint Buys Stake in Jay Z's Music Streaming Service Tidal Sprint has agreed to purchase a 33% stake in Tidal, the music streaming service owned by rapper and entrepreneur Jay Z, in a deal valued at approximately $200m (£162m). Jay Z acquired Tidal three years ago for $56m from Norwegian company Aspiro, positioning it as an artist-friendly alternative to dominant players like Spotify and Apple Music. The service distinguishes itself by offering musicians greater control over their content and how it's distributed. The streaming platform boasts an impressive ownership structure, with equity held by some of music's biggest names including Beyoncé, Madonna, Rihanna, Daft Punk, and Kanye West. These artists form a star-studded board of directors and are expected to retain their stakes following Sprint's investment. The deal represents a strategic move by Sprint, owned by Japan's Softbank, to enhance its content offerings in an increasingly competitive mobile market. Sprint customers will gain access to exclusive Tidal content as part of the agreement. Despite its celebrity backing and catalogue of 42 million songs across 52 countries, Tidal remains significantly smaller than industry leaders Spotify and Apple Music. The substantial investment from Sprint could provide crucial resources for Tidal to expand its subscriber base and compete more effectively in the rapidly growing music streaming sector. The partnership signals growing convergence between telecommunications and entertainment industries as companies seek competitive advantages through exclusive content.

Scottish Personal Insolvencies Rise 38.9% in Quarter but Remain Below Last Year Personal insolvencies in Scotland rose sharply during the summer months, new figures have revealed, though they remain significantly lower than the same period in 2014. Data published by Accountant in Bankruptcy (AiB) showed that personal insolvencies increased by 38.9% to 2,230 between July and September. Despite this quarterly rise, the total was still more than 25% lower than the figure recorded in the same period last year. The Scottish government emphasized that the longer-term trend shows people seeking debt relief continues to decline, offering a more positive outlook on the nation's financial health. The insolvency figures encompass both traditional bankruptcies and protected trust deeds (PTDs), which allow individuals to repay their debts under structured agreements. During the quarter, 965 people were declared bankrupt - a 27.5% increase compared to the previous three months. AiB attributed this rise to figures "returning to a normal level" following recent changes to bankruptcy and debt advice legislation. The number of people opting for PTDs showed an even more dramatic increase, rising 49% to 1,265. PTDs, which are similar to individual voluntary agreements (IVAs) used in England and Wales, have become more attractive to debtors following recent legal changes. The duration of these agreements has been reduced from five years to four years - bringing them in line with bankruptcy periods. This means individuals using PTDs no longer face an additional year of repayments. In contrast to personal insolvencies, corporate failures declined. The number of companies becoming insolvent or entering receivership dropped by 8.6% compared to the previous quarter, falling to 180. Business minister Fergus Ewing welcomed the longer-term trends, stating: "The longer term trend of people falling into financial difficulty and seeking debt relief continues to be a declining one, which will be welcomed by everyone who wishes to see Scotland prosper. Fewer businesses becoming insolvent also means more people can remain in work, which is good news for industry and provides further evidence that Scotland's economy goes from strength to strength." Alistair Dickson from accountants RSM noted that while the downward trend is encouraging, the quarterly increase must be considered against economic challenges facing sectors such as oil and gas, and steel manufacturing.

Medieval Wall Discovery Preserved Beneath Leicester Development Site Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of a medieval wall during a survey conducted ahead of a £50 million student accommodation development on Fairfax Street in Leicester. Richard Buckley, co-director of University of Leicester Archaeological Services and project lead, explained that the wall served a commercial purpose rather than a defensive one. It was designed to ensure that outside traders "paid the relevant tolls" when entering the area. The discovered remains are now being carefully recorded before being covered up and preserved underground. Mr Buckley indicated that the foundations of the planned development might need to be adjusted "slightly" to help protect the historic structure. He noted that while one section—the east-west stretch—contains "nice bit of super-structure surviving" beneath the tarmac, the north-south section has suffered significant damage. The site reflects Leicester's complex urban history, with evidence of multiple developments layered from the 20th and 19th centuries. "It is a sort of horrific mess," Buckley remarked, adding that one building appeared to have been bombed.

Russia Moves to Decriminalise Domestic Violence Russia's parliament has overwhelmingly backed controversial legislation that would decriminalise some forms of domestic violence, sparking outrage among human rights activists and abuse victims' advocates. The State Duma voted 368 to one on Wednesday in favour of the bill, which has been dubbed the "slapping law" by Russian media outlets. The proposed legislation would reclassify first-time assaults causing less serious injuries as administrative offences rather than criminal ones. MP Yelena Mizulina, a supporter of the bill, defended the measure by arguing that people should not be imprisoned and branded as criminals "for a slap". The legislation applies to both spousal abuse and parents' treatment of their children. According to Olga Batalina, one of the bill's authors, the law concerns violent actions that cause injuries not requiring hospital treatment or forcing the victim to take sick leave from work. Under the proposal, first offences would be punished with fines or community service rather than criminal prosecution. However, subsequent incidents could still result in criminal charges and potential jail terms. The push for decriminalisation emerged in response to amendments made to Russia's criminal code in July, which made beating a family member a criminal offence. Conservative lawmakers have argued that current penalties do not align with traditional Russian values. Mizulina told the Moscow Times that penalties should not "contradict the system of social values that society holds on to," adding that "in Russian traditional family culture parent-child relationships are built on the authority of the parents' power..... The laws should support that family tradition." However, the proposed changes have drawn fierce criticism from domestic violence experts and activists who warn it will undermine efforts to address what they describe as an endemic problem in Russian society. Olga Bobrova, a journalist at Novaya Gazeta, argues that violence not leaving visible marks can still "transform her life into a living hell." She has previously written that "domestic violence is a normal way of life" in Russia. Outside the Duma, activists distributed flyers featuring stories of abuse victims, while campaigner Alena Popova's petition calling for comprehensive domestic violence legislation has garnered 175,000 signatures. Olga Yurkova, executive director of the "Sisters" sexual assault referral centre, warned that decriminalisation would "set loose" people accustomed to resolving problems violently. "A huge number of women tolerate domestic violence but do not bring it out to the public. The decriminalisation will worsen the situation," she told Novaya Gazeta. Official statistics on domestic violence in Russia remain limited, but regional studies paint a disturbing picture. Estimates suggest approximately 600,000 Russian women face physical and verbal abuse at home, with 14,000 dying annually from injuries inflicted by husbands or partners—nearly 40 deaths per day. According to the ANNA National Centre for the Prevention of Violence, the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs reported in 2008 that violence occurs in one in four families, with two-thirds of homicides attributed to household or domestic motives. Alcohol is widely considered a major contributing factor. Critics fear the new legislation will further silence victims and embolden abusers in a country where domestic violence already remains largely hidden from public view.

Montana Congressman-elect Greg Gianforte Sentenced for Assault on Guardian Reporter Montana congressman-elect Greg Gianforte, 56, has been sentenced after pleading guilty to assaulting a journalist from the UK's Guardian newspaper on the eve of his election last month. The Republican politician initially faced four days in jail, but the penalty was ultimately reduced by the presiding judge. Gallatin County Justice Court Judge Rick West handed down a 180-day deferred jail sentence to Gianforte, who is expected to be sworn into office later this month. As part of his sentence, Gianforte was ordered to pay $385 (£304), complete 40 hours of community service, and attend 20 hours of anger management counseling. The incident occurred when Guardian reporter Ben Jacobs approached Gianforte to ask whether he supported the Republican healthcare plan. According to Fox News reporter Alicia Acuna, who witnessed the attack, Gianforte "grabbed Jacobs by the neck with both hands and slammed him into the ground" before beginning to punch the reporter. Initially, Gianforte's spokesperson claimed the incident was "aggressive behaviour from a liberal journalist," and the politician alleged that Jacobs had grabbed his wrist, pulling them both to the ground. However, in his formal apology, Gianforte acknowledged his actions and took full responsibility. As part of a settlement agreement, Jacobs agreed not to sue Gianforte on the condition that he write a letter of apology and donate $50,000 (£39,500) to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Following the sentencing, Jacobs released a statement expressing concern about the increasing prevalence of such incidents in political discourse. "While I have no doubt that actions like these were an aberration for Congressman-elect Gianforte personally, I worry that, in the context of our political debate, they have become increasingly common," he said. "This needs to stop." Despite the assault charge, Gianforte won the special congressional election in Montana just hours after being charged. The multimillionaire technology executive and Christian conservative defeated Democrat Rob Quist to fill an empty seat in the House of Representatives. In his victory speech, Gianforte said he had "learned a lesson" and was "sorry." President Donald Trump praised the election victory during an official trip to Italy, calling it a "great win in Montana."

Historic Nelson Letter From HMS Victory Expected to Fetch Up to £30,000 at Auction A rare letter written by Admiral Lord Nelson aboard HMS Victory is set to go under the hammer this weekend, with experts estimating it could fetch between £20,000 and £30,000. The three-page letter, dated 28 April 1804, was penned during a crucial period when Nelson was attempting to lure the French and Spanish fleet out of Toulon for battle. Addressed to Captain Frank Sotheron of HMS Excellent, the correspondence reveals Nelson's strategic reliance on smaller vessels as reconnaissance ships. In the letter, Nelson instructs Captain Sotheron to monitor French movements, stating: "In the event of their sailing..... you will use every effort to communicate the same to me as early as possible." Auctioneer Charles Hanson noted that the document demonstrates how Nelson depended on these vessels to "inform him should the French fleet leave the safety of the harbour." Although Nelson pursued the French fleet to the West Indies following this letter, he would not engage them in battle until October 1805 at Trafalgar. That historic encounter, where Nelson famously signalled "England expects that every man will do his duty," resulted in a decisive victory over the Franco-Spanish fleet but cost the admiral his life when he was mortally wounded aboard Victory. Mr Hanson described Trafalgar as "renowned for the tactical skill employed by Nelson and for his courage in leading the first column of British vessels into the attack." The letter will be auctioned at Hansons in Etwall, Derbyshire, on Saturday.

Two Men Jailed Over Manchester Nightclub Stabbing Death Two men have been sentenced for their roles in the fatal stabbing of Clarence Edwards outside a Manchester nightclub. The 26-year-old was found outside the RBase club on Charles Street in Manchester's city centre in the early hours of 4 January and later died in hospital from a chest wound. At Manchester Crown Court, Earl Atta Rooms, 27, from Rusholme, admitted manslaughter and violent disorder. He was sentenced to seven years in prison. Dwayne Henry, 34, also from Rusholme, was convicted of violent disorder and received a three-year jail term. Police said Mr Edwards had been inside the nightclub when a dispute erupted with Rooms and Henry. The confrontation continued outside where a fight broke out, resulting in Mr Edwards being fatally stabbed in the chest. Detective Chief Inspector Ian Crewe said: "This is another sad case where a night out ended in tragedy. Violence destroys lives and there is no place for it on our streets. "Clarence's family have spent the last 10 months trying to come to terms with what happened on that dreadful night. I hope now that they can start to look forward to the future." Four other men charged in connection with Mr Edwards's death were either cleared or had charges dropped.

Australia Beat New Zealand to Win Women's Rugby Sevens Gold Australia claimed Olympic gold in the women's rugby sevens, defeating defending champions New Zealand in a thrilling final at Rio 2016. The Australians outscored the Black Ferns four tries to three, capitalizing significantly when New Zealand's star player Portia Woodman received a sin bin, scoring two tries during her absence. In the bronze medal match, Great Britain's women fell short against Canada, losing 33-10. Despite the disappointment, captain Emily Scarratt remained philosophical: "If we've inspired any girls to take up rugby, we've done our job." Britain, who had lost their semi-final 25-7 to New Zealand earlier on Monday, found themselves trailing 26-5 at half-time. Canada exploited Scarratt's yellow card for a deliberate knock-on, dominating the physical contest and controlling the breakdown throughout. Although Jasmine Joyce and Danielle Waterman crossed for consolation tries, third-seeded Canada's superior performance secured the medal. The men's rugby sevens competition begins Tuesday at 15:00 BST with Australia facing France, followed by GB's opening match against Kenya.

Japanese Supermarket Owner Pays $10,800 for 30 Premium Grapes A supermarket owner from western Japan walked away with 30 grapes, each worth about $360. They were the first Ruby Romans - a super sweet grape variety grown in Ishikawa prefecture - of the season. "We will display them at our store before giving our customers a sample taste," Takamaru Konishi said. The Japanese are often willing to pay top-dollar for premium samples of fruit, sometimes with the intention of giving them as gifts to people perceived to be of higher status - for example, their boss at work. A single apple can cost up to $3. And melons are sometimes sold for the equivalent price of a vintage wine. Last year a pair of melons sold under the hammer for more than $12,000. "I am so happy and I am honoured," Mr Konishi said. "These are truly Ruby Roman gems."

Bus Driver Banned from Buses Pending Trial Alan Halliday, 56, from Beeswing, appeared in court denying charges of sexually assaulting a teenager on a bus route between Dumfries and Castle Douglas on Sunday night. The accused denies taking hold of the girl's hands, touching her inappropriately in the groin area, making sexual remarks, and repeatedly asking questions of a sexual nature. A sheriff has imposed an interim ban prohibiting Halliday from travelling by bus until the case is resolved. A trial has been scheduled for May.

Wells Fargo Reaches Settlement Over Unauthorized Accounts Scandal Wells Fargo has reached a settlement in a class action lawsuit stemming from a massive scandal involving unauthorized customer accounts, marking another chapter in America's efforts to address misconduct at its biggest bank. The settlement, which still requires court approval, follows a $185 million fine imposed on Wells Fargo in September of last year. The penalty came after authorities discovered the bank had illegally opened approximately two million accounts without customer authorization. The scandal led to the resignation of Chief Executive John Stumpf. The class action lawsuit was originally filed in May 2015 by Shahriar Jabbari and Kaylee Heffelfinger at the district court in Northern District of California. According to Wells Fargo's statement, the settlement will cover "all persons who claim that Wells Fargo opened an account in their name without consent, enrolled them in a product or service without consent, or submitted an application for a product or service in their name without consent." Tim Sloan, the bank's new president and chief executive, described the agreement as "another step in our journey to make things right with customers and rebuild trust." He emphasized that the settlement provides "an additional option" for customers affected by the sales practices issue. The original fine was imposed by the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau after investigators found that bank employees illegally signed up customers for unwanted accounts to meet aggressive sales targets. Wells Fargo expects Tuesday's settlement to resolve claims in 11 other pending class action lawsuits.

FIFA to Consider Expanding World Cup to 48 Teams as Bidding Rules Announced FIFA has announced that confederations who hosted the previous two World Cups will be barred from bidding for the 2026 tournament, ruling out Europe and Asia following their staging of the 2018 and 2022 competitions respectively. The announcement comes as world football's governing body considers a significant expansion of the tournament, potentially increasing participation from 32 teams to either 40 or 48 nations. The proposals will be presented at FIFA's next council meeting on 9 January 2017. "The feeling amongst the council is rather positive towards expansion," said FIFA president Gianni Infantino, speaking at a council meeting in Zurich, Switzerland. Infantino, who assumed the FIFA presidency in February, made expanding the World Cup one of his key election promises, initially proposing an increase to 40 teams. However, the 46-year-old Italian has recently suggested a more ambitious expansion to 48 countries. Under one proposed format, 32 teams would participate in a preliminary knockout round in the host nation, with winners joining 16 seeded teams in the group stages. FIFA is considering four different options for the 2026 tournament structure. The expansion plans have drawn criticism from some quarters, with concerns raised about the potential impact on the quality of football at the finals. Former England striker and Match of the Day presenter Gary Lineker expressed his reservations on social media, urging Infantino to "do the right things for the game rather than stuff to get re-elected." "Come on Mr Infantino! You have a mandate to look after football's best interests, not your own. Do not destroy the World Cup! Please," Lineker wrote. However, Infantino defended the proposals, arguing that expansion would actually improve quality rather than diminish it. "When a team qualifies for the tournament the whole country is in football euphoria," he said. "More youngsters want to play the game, companies want to get involved in sponsorship and the benefits to football as a whole are immense. "In a 48-team format, the quality would be higher because the 32 teams would have a play-off. The quality would improve and not decrease in any way." Meanwhile, FIFA secretary general Fatma Samoura, the first female appointed to the role, revealed she has implemented cost-saving measures since taking office in May. "In four days in changing hotels, we saved £99,500," Samoura told BBC Sport. "No more limousines are available - we are carpooling." She added that FIFA had recently become the first sporting institution to sign a climate change agreement with the United Nations in New York. The 2018 World Cup will be held in Russia, with Qatar hosting the 2022 competition.

Air France to Unveil Major Restructuring Plan Amid Labor Disputes Air France is set to present a comprehensive cost-cutting plan on Monday following a board meeting where directors unanimously agreed to pursue an alternative restructuring strategy. The airline has declined to confirm specific numbers regarding potential job cuts, though union sources have leaked details to news agencies. The sources suggest the restructuring could involve significant workforce reductions, along with the retirement of five long-haul aircraft next summer and nine additional planes in 2017. The French carrier has been struggling with profitability, hampered by ongoing strikes from pilots protesting the expansion of its budget subsidiary, Transavia. Additionally, Air France faces mounting pressure from low-cost competitors and rapidly growing Middle Eastern airlines. In a statement released after the board meeting, Air France explained that the restructuring had become necessary due to the "impossibility of reaching an agreement to implement productivity measures" with its workforce. The company emphasized that these changes are essential to "restore long-term profitability" and "accelerate its recovery." The plan will be formally presented to the Works Council on Monday for review. One union official noted that while these points were shared with the board, "no vote has been taken" on the specific measures. Air France merged with Dutch carrier KLM in 2004 to form the Air France-KLM group.

Victor Valdes Deal with Besiktas Collapses as Goalkeeper's Future Remains Uncertain Victor Valdes's proposed move to Turkish side Besiktas has fallen through after the club allegedly attempted to alter the terms of an already agreed deal, according to sources close to the 33-year-old goalkeeper. The Spain international, who has no future at Manchester United following a falling out with manager Louis van Gaal, has now withdrawn from the transfer. Valdes joined United on an 18-month contract in January after leaving Barcelona, but was excluded from this season's squad after reportedly refusing to play in an Under-21 match. With the transfer window closing on Tuesday in England and Scotland, and Monday in most European countries, Valdes faces an uncertain immediate future. Meanwhile, Manchester United's David De Gea remains in limbo as Real Madrid have yet to submit a formal bid for the 24-year-old goalkeeper. The Spanish giants are reportedly unwilling to meet United's demands for a world-record fee for a goalkeeper, which would exceed the £32.6 million Juventus paid for Gianluigi Buffon in 2001. Van Gaal has confirmed he will not select De Gea until the transfer window closes.

Thailand Warned Over Using Ex-Prisoners on Fishing Boats Human rights groups have warned Thailand against using former prisoners to work on fishing boats, expressing concerns about exploitation and prisoners' rights. In a letter to Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha, advocacy organizations argued that the project would not address the fundamental problems plaguing the fishing industry and posed serious threats to prisoners' rights. Thailand ranks as the world's third-largest seafood exporter, with an industry employing more than 300,000 people. The fishing sector has been experiencing severe labour shortages, largely filled by illegal migrants from neighbouring countries who frequently face ill-treatment. This manpower deficit has contributed to human trafficking in the region. "Simply replacing vulnerable migrant workers with released prisoners will not solve the abusive working conditions and many other problems present in the Thai fishing industry," the letter states. Last December, Thailand's labour ministry announced plans to send consenting prisoners with less than a year remaining on their sentences to work on fishing vessels. However, on Wednesday, the ministry clarified that it was not dispatching current inmates but rather implementing a pilot scheme to help ex-prisoners find employment whilst addressing labour shortages and combating human trafficking. According to the ministry, more than 170 former prisoners are now working on fishing boats in Samut Sakhon province, west of Bangkok. The warning comes as Thailand attempts to improve its human trafficking record before a US deadline. Last June, the US State Department downgraded Thailand to the lowest status for failing to fully comply with minimum standards for eliminating trafficking. Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha has acknowledged that some Thai authorities have been complicit in smuggling people and forcing them into the fishing industry.

UKIP Selects New Candidate After MEP Expelled Over Expenses Scandal UKIP has announced a new parliamentary candidate for Folkestone and Hythe following the expulsion of South East MEP Janice Atkinson over allegations involving falsified expense claims. Harriet Yeo, former chairwoman of Labour's national executive committee, will now represent the party in the Kent constituency. In her first statement, Ms Yeo emphasized that the region needed representation that would "put the people first." "We don't have that at the moment," she said. "The Conservatives take us for granted, the Labour Party ignore us and it's about time that we had a voice that this part of the country needs." The leadership change follows a disciplinary hearing that resulted in Ms Atkinson and her assistant, Christine Hewitt, being expelled from UKIP. Both have 14 days to appeal the decision. The scandal emerged after The Sun newspaper published a secret recording appearing to show Ms Hewitt requesting an inflated invoice from a restaurant manager in Margate, Kent. In the recording, Ms Hewitt is heard saying: "The idea is we overcharge them slightly, because that's the way we repatriate it." When the manager suggests a figure of £3,150, Ms Hewitt responds: "Oh God yeah, that's more than enough." It remains unclear whether Ms Atkinson was aware of or authorized her staff member's apparent actions. Following her expulsion, Ms Atkinson expressed her disappointment but stated she would continue her work. "I was elected to represent the constituents of the South East of England and I will continue to work tirelessly on their behalf and for the best interests of our country," she said. Ms Atkinson was initially suspended on Friday following the investigation.

Iran Displays Russian S-300 Missiles at Military Parade Iran has publicly showcased components of Russia's advanced S-300 missile defense system for the first time, marking a significant milestone in the controversial arms deal between the two nations. Pictures released by the semi-official ISNA news agency showed S-300 missile tubes and radar equipment during a military parade in southern Tehran. Iran insists the system is necessary to defend itself, but the US and Israel have criticised the sale. The controversial contract got the go-ahead after last year's deal to lift international sanctions on Iran. Six world powers led by the US agreed in July to lift the sanctions which had locked down much of Iran's economy for years, in exchange for limits on Tehran's nuclear programme. The missile parts went on display as President Hassan Rouhani pledged to defend Muslim countries against "terrorism and Israel" while insisting that his country's neighbours should not feel threatened. Speaking during the National Army Day parade he praised Iran's role in assisting Syrian and Iraqi forces curtail advances made by the so-called Islamic State group. "If tomorrow your capitals face danger from terrorism or Zionism, the power that will give you a positive answer is the Islamic Republic of Iran," the president said. The $800m (£562m) missile contract, signed in 2007, was frozen by Russia in 2010 because of international sanctions against Iran. President Vladimir Putin unfroze it a year ago. The S-300, made by Rostec, can be used against multiple targets including jets, or to shoot down other missiles. The advanced system flies at five times the speed of sound and has a range of 400km (249 miles), according to Russia's Tass news agency.

Police Appeal for Missing Woman and Boy Last Seen in Town Centre Police have launched an appeal to trace a 54-year-old woman and a young boy who have been missing for several days. Sandra Element and Aiden Hoggard were last seen at approximately 08:45 on Monday, 8 May, in Main Street. The pair were not reported missing until 14:00 on Friday afternoon. Ms Element is described as approximately 5ft 5in tall with a slim build and brown hair. She was wearing black clothing when last seen. Aiden is about 4ft tall with a slim build, pale complexion, and was carrying a black rucksack. Inspector Jane Nicolson said: "We are looking to trace Sandra and Aiden to ensure they are safe and well. It may be that they have left the area by using public transport and we just want to make sure they are ok." Police believe the pair may have travelled away from the local area using public transport and are appealing for any information regarding their whereabouts.

Charity Collection Box Stolen in "Despicable" Theft A chained donation box for the Guide Dogs For The Blind Association has been stolen from a Dorset gift shop. The box was taken from the Pug and Puffin Gift Shop on Broad Street in Lyme Regis between Sunday night and Monday morning. Police have not confirmed how much money was inside at the time of the theft. Authorities are describing the incident as a "despicable act." PC Sean Cannon said: "We don't know the motive for the theft, so if the box was taken as a prank, we would ask those responsible to hand the box in to police."

Pacquiao Faces Perjury Investigation Over Undisclosed Shoulder Injury Manny Pacquiao is facing serious legal consequences after the Nevada Athletic Commission (NAC) accused the Filipino boxing champion of failing to disclose a shoulder injury on a pre-fight questionnaire before his highly anticipated bout with Floyd Mayweather. The 36-year-old boxer now faces potential perjury charges that could result in a jail sentence of between one and four years, plus a fine of up to $5,000 (£3,305) if found guilty. Two lawsuits have been filed in Nevada, with claimants alleging Pacquiao defrauded ticket buyers, television viewers, and gamblers by not revealing his injury before the fight. The legal action came just hours after the NAC's accusations emerged. ## Conflicting Accounts Pacquiao has maintained he was transparent about his shoulder problem and had agreed to a treatment plan. The fighter blamed his points defeat to Mayweather on the injury, stating it prevented him from using his right hand effectively during the bout. A joint statement from Team Pacquiao and his promoters, Top Rank, claimed the United States Anti-Doping Agency (Usada) had been notified about the injury during training camp and on fight night. According to the statement, a Usada doctor approved the use of a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medication, but the NAC refused it because they were "unaware" of the shoulder injury. "This was disappointing since Team Pacquiao had disclosed the injury and treatment to Usada, who approved the treatments and Manny had listed the medication on his pre-fight medical form," the statement read. ## NAC's Position While the NAC acknowledges that Pacquiao wasn't "obligated" to disclose the injury, executive director Bob Bennett emphasized the issue wasn't just about incomplete paperwork. "It's not just the fact he didn't fill out the question completely, it's that he wasn't honest," Bennett said. He added that two hours before the fight, Pacquiao's camp requested a painkiller injection, putting officials "in a very precarious position." The questionnaire Pacquiao signed specifically asked about injuries to shoulders, elbows, or hands requiring evaluation. The legal disclaimer clearly states the signatory "swears, under penalty of perjury, that the above information is true and correct." ## Medical Prognosis Surgeon Neal ElAttrache confirmed Pacquiao has a "significant tear" in his rotator cuff, likely sidelining him for nine to twelve months. Mayweather won the four-belt unification bout by unanimous decision at the MGM Grand Garden Arena, extending his unbeaten professional record to 48 fights. The 38-year-old American has insisted he will retire after one more fight in September, making a rematch unlikely.

Vanessa-Mae Ban Overturned by Court of Arbitration for Sport Violinist Vanessa-Mae has had her skiing ban overturned, clearing her path to compete in future Winter Olympics. The 36-year-old Thailand skier was suspended by the International Ski Federation (FIS) in November after results were manipulated to help her qualify for the Sochi Winter Olympics. But the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) said there was no direct evidence to implicate her in the fixing. However her 67th-place finish in the giant slalom will not stand because the qualifying events were "so defective". The Cas panel said "a number of irregularities" occurred in the "organisation and management" of the four races which raised Vanessa-Mae's racer status. Five officials involved in the qualifying event were banned by the FIS. Vanessa-Mae, a British citizen, competed in Sochi for her father's native country under the name Vanessa Vanakorn. She can now try to qualify for the 2018 Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea.

Rome Metro Accident: Woman Dragged Along Platform After Bag Caught in Train Door A woman was left in intensive care after being dragged along a Rome metro platform when her bag became trapped in closing train doors, according to CCTV footage that has emerged of the incident. Natalya Garkovich, 43, was boarding a train at Rome's Termini station when she changed her mind at the last minute and attempted to exit the carriage. As she backed out, her bag became caught in the closing doors, trapping her as the train began to move. The footage shows fellow passengers on the platform desperately trying to free Ms Garkovich, but they were unable to release her before the train started pulling away. Local media report that Ms Garkovich, believed to be a Belarusian national, suffered broken bones in the incident but has since been moved out of intensive care and her condition has improved. The incident has raised serious questions about safety systems on Rome's metro network. Reports indicate that passengers aboard the train pulled multiple emergency levers in an attempt to halt the train's advance, but none of the emergency braking systems responded. The CCTV footage also captured train driver Gianluca Tonelli eating while the train was at the platform. However, Mr Tonelli has defended his actions, insisting he followed proper protocol. "I know that I was wrong and I am devastated by what happened to that woman," Mr Tonelli told Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. "But in the video it can also be seen that I looked twice in the mirror, I was not reckless." According to reports, Mr Tonelli was unaware of the accident until he pulled into the next station. It is believed Ms Garkovich was not dragged into the tunnel. Carlo Rienzi, president of consumer rights group Codacons, argued that the failure of both the door sensors and emergency braking systems meant the driver could not be held fully responsible. "The emergency systems on board must function properly," Mr Rienzi said in a statement. "Therefore we consider it outrageous and offensive to say the train driver is entirely responsible, when you should thoroughly investigate the Rome subway security systems and their proper operation." Stefano Bottoni, national secretary of trade union Sul, called for additional safety measures, suggesting that cockpit cameras might prevent similar accidents in future. The incident remains under investigation.

Warburton Admits He May Not Be Ready for First Lions Test Despite Captaincy British and Irish Lions tour captain Sam Warburton has admitted he may not be ready to feature in the first Test against New Zealand, despite recovering from injury to lead the side in their midweek fixture against the Highlanders on Tuesday. The Wales open-side flanker has been sidelined with an ankle injury but has returned to captain the Lions in Dunedin. However, with intense competition for back-row positions, Warburton acknowledges his current form may not guarantee him a starting spot in the crucial opening Test. "If I play Tuesday and I still feel I'm a bit undercut, then I might not be ready for that first Test," Warburton said candidly. "Maybe that would be the situation, or maybe I could have a blinder on Tuesday and feel absolutely fine so we'll see how it goes really." The Lions face three matches before the first Test against the All Blacks on 24 June at Eden Park, where coach Warren Gatland will finalise his selection from the 41-strong squad. Gatland faces an embarrassment of riches in the back-row, with options including Warburton's Wales teammates Justin Tipuric, Taulupe Faletau and Ross Moriarty, Ireland's CJ Stander, Peter O'Mahony and Sean O'Brien, and England lock Maro Itoje, who has also played in the position. The 28-year-old Cardiff Blues player missed the final six weeks of the domestic season with a knee injury and admits he needs more game time to reach his peak performance level. "I definitely need more games. I definitely admit that and I knew that coming into the tour," Warburton explained. "I've learned from experience that it takes me at least two games and then the third game I'll probably be playing some good rugby but Gats knew that." Despite holding the prestigious position of tour captain, Warburton maintains a realistic view of his Test prospects. "I've received this role as tour captain and I know there's every chance that I might not even get involved in that first Test because there's every other player," he said. "I see it as I'm tour captain, and if I've made the Test then that would be a bonus for me." Warburton is renowned for his expertise at the breakdown, specialising in winning turnovers and protecting possession. He acknowledges that this will be crucial to his selection hopes. "When I play well and I am match-fit, I am aggressive in the tackle; I'll contribute a handful of good carries, and you become a lineout option," said Warburton. "More importantly, which hasn't really been a factor in the last three games, is turnovers. My one specialist element is the contact area. I guess I have to deliver in that area on Tuesday. That's my role of expertise."

Welsh Funding Deal Lacks Certainty, Says Finance Minister Jane Hutt Welsh Finance Minister Jane Hutt has criticized the coalition government's funding offer, telling BBC Sunday Politics Wales that the deal fails to provide adequate certainty for public spending in Wales. Mrs Hutt's comments echoed those of First Minister Carwyn Jones, who previously stated that promises of fair funding were lacking in crucial detail. Prime Minister David Cameron recently pledged to protect the Welsh budget through a "funding floor" mechanism, a measure Welsh ministers have long sought. However, the specific amount will remain unknown until after the general election, when the next UK government spending review takes place. The proposal would shift Wales away from complete reliance on annual Treasury grants, with the Welsh government instead raising some revenue through devolved taxes. Mr Cameron argues this funding floor—designed to prevent the Barnett formula from squeezing Wales's budget—removes any justification for delaying a referendum on income tax-varying powers. However, Mrs Hutt expressed frustration that the coalition had not provided more comprehensive details about the funding floor's terms. "They took us for granted and they can't do that," she said. "This is not about being told at the last minute'We'll give you this, you do that'. That is not about an agreement. That is not about a respect agenda," the finance minister added. Mrs Hutt indicated that the Welsh government could support tax devolution, but only with proper guarantees. "If we get that reassurance, that clarity we can sign up to it, then of course you could consider beginning to make a start in terms of considering tax devolution," she stated.

Toy Dog Astronaut Reaches Edge of Space in School Science Project A toy dog named Sam has completed a remarkable journey to the edge of space after being launched by helium balloon from a Morecambe hotel. Attached to a special camera and sent skywards by a helium balloon, he reached an altitude of 15.5 miles (25km). Sam left mission control - the Midland Hotel - as part of a school science initiative on Tuesday. It was the climax of a project by Morecambe Bay Primary School which joined forces with the hotel and SenditintoSpace.com. Trudi Wilkinson, business manager of the school, said: "It was brilliant - we loved it." Children tracked Sam using images and other data in a project that has helped them learn more about space exploration. The cuddly cosmonaut's ascent was charted using GPS tracking equipment and specialist cameras. It is understood his flight was not too "ruff".

Syrian Air Strikes Kill at Least 25 in Aleppo After Brief Lull At least 25 people, including children, have been killed in renewed air strikes on rebel-held areas of eastern Aleppo, monitoring groups report. The bombardment follows a temporary lull called by the Syrian government, partly to allow civilians to leave rebel areas in the east of the city. It has come under intense aerial attack since a ceasefire brokered by the US and Russia collapsed last month. The air strikes came as Russian President Vladimir Putin cancelled a planned visit to France. He had been due to meet French President Francois Hollande later this month but pulled out after Paris said talks would be confined to Syria, French presidential sources said. On Monday, Mr Hollande suggested Russian officials could face war crimes charges over the bombardment of Aleppo. On Tuesday UK Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson told the UK parliament Russia was in danger of becoming a pariah nation because of its involvement in Syria. Moscow has repeatedly denied attacking civilians, and says it targets terrorist groups in Syria. ## Heavy Casualties Reported The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that at least 25 civilians were killed in Tuesday's air strikes and considerable damage was inflicted on several areas. The observatory said Russian war planes had dropped so-called "bunker busters" and other bombs, with children thought to be among the dead. Footage shared by activists showed lifeless bodies of toddlers wrapped in sheets, with their parents distraught beside them. Some of the most intense attacks have come in the Bustan al-Qasr and Fardos neighbourhoods near the citadel, which sits near the front line with the government-held west. Aid organisation Medecins Sans Frontieres said on Tuesday there were now only 11 working ambulances left in the city because five had been hit by bombs and another eight were missing essential spare parts. Meanwhile, Syrian state media reported rebel attacks on government-held western Aleppo, in which it said four people were killed and 14 injured. ## Diplomatic Efforts Stalled Diplomatic efforts to revive the ceasefire have so far come to nothing. The UN has warned that eastern Aleppo, where an estimated 275,000 people still live, could face "total destruction" in the space of two months. Last week, Russia vetoed a UN Security Council resolution drafted by France calling for an end to the bombing in Aleppo.

Student Motorcyclist Dies in Collision Near Welshpool A university student from Tamworth has died following a motorcycle collision in Powys while returning from a day trip with her boyfriend. Melanie Lakin, from Glascote, was killed in the crash on the A458 between Llanfair Caereinion and Welshpool on Sunday afternoon. The 19-year-old had been enjoying a picnic at Bala lake with her boyfriend, with the couple travelling on separate motorbikes. The incident occurred at approximately 4:30 PM and has been voluntarily referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) by Dyfed-Powys Police due to a police vehicle being in the vicinity at the time. According to police reports, a marked police motorcyclist was conducting routine vehicle checks in the area, resulting in several cars stopped in a line of traffic. Initial investigations indicate Ms Lakin's motorcycle collided with one of the stationary vehicles in the queue. In a heartfelt tribute, Ms Lakin's family described her as "a keen motorcyclist who loved life, people, nature and animals especially her cats Hector and Cleo." She had just completed her first year studying diagnostic radiography at Birmingham City University and was enthusiastic about pursuing a career in the NHS. Her family highlighted her creative passions, noting her "keen eye and appreciation for photography, music and art," which she often combined by photographing bands and musicians at music festivals. Ms Lakin is survived by her mother Pam, father Nigel, brother Jody, his partner Elena, boyfriend Oliver, and numerous friends and colleagues who knew and loved her.

**Wales Updates Alcohol Guidelines After 20 Years** Wales' chief medical officer Dr Ruth Hussey has joined her UK colleagues in updating 20-year-old alcohol consumption guidelines, warning against several common drinking habits. One key recommendation advises people not to "save up" their 14 weekly units of alcohol to consume on just one or two days. The guidelines also challenge the popular belief that one or two glasses of red wine can protect against heart disease, stating this benefit is "less significant" than previously thought. The proposed changes are currently subject to a UK-wide consultation running until April. The guidelines recommend several measures to reduce health risks associated with alcohol consumption. The Change4Life Wales alcohol campaign is already encouraging people to have at least two alcohol-free days a week. Dr Hussey said the updated guidelines "draw on the latest evidence on how different levels of drinking affect health risks for individuals" and help people "make informed decisions about their drinking". The announcement comes as the Welsh government launched a three-year strategy to tackle substance and alcohol abuse, particularly targeting "risky drinking behaviour" among those under 24 and older people. Hospital admissions in Wales for over-50s with alcohol issues have risen for three consecutive years. The Department of Health is leading the consultation, with Mark Bellis, director of policy at Public Health Wales, involved in developing the guidelines.

Sir Christopher Bland, Former BBC Chairman, Dies After Battle with Cancer Sir Christopher Bland, the former chairman of the BBC board of governors and a distinguished figure in British broadcasting and business, has died peacefully at home after a three-year battle with cancer. Sir Christopher was chairman of the BBC board of governors between 1996 and 2001. He also held a number of senior roles in business, including chairman of BT, and was head of the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC). His son, Archie, said: "He was as sweet and gentle and wise as he was tough and bold and brave." BBC director general Tony Hall said: "Sir Christopher Bland was an outstanding chairman of the BBC. He was a great communicator who both understood the creativity of broadcasting as well as the business of it. "He was hugely admired and will be greatly missed." In a statement, Sir Christopher's family said he had died peacefully at home, having defied cancer for three years. The statement continued: "He relished every day of his life, and to those that loved him he is irreplaceable. We're enormously proud of everything he achieved, from steering the BBC through tough times to his late flowering as a novelist, and we'll miss him more than we can say." Sir Christopher, who also spent time as head of London Weekend Television (LWT), spoke out in support of the BBC on a number of occasions after he left the corporation. Two years ago, he criticised the government for transferring the funding of free licence fees for the over-75s to the BBC, saying it was "the worst form of dodgy Whitehall accounting". In 2008, when Jonathan Ross and Russell Brand were suspended from the BBC for leaving lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs's phone, Sir Christopher said "the meal that those who are not natural lovers of the BBC have made out of it all is excessive". After leaving the BBC, he became chairman of BT, turning the company around at a time when its senior management had come under sustained criticism from investors. Between 2004 and 2011 he was chairman of the RSC, overseeing a £112m re-development of the company's home in Stratford-upon-Avon. On artistic director Michael Boyd's departure, he said: "If the RSC is in good shape now, it is in large part due to the expert, passionate and playful chairmanship of Sir Christopher Bland." Archie Bland reported his father's death on Twitter, ending his message with the words, "God I'll miss him". BBC News presenter Huw Edwards offered his sympathy, writing that "at the BBC many of us remember him as an exemplary chairman". Master of Selwyn College, Cambridge, and former head of BBC News and BBC Sport Roger Mosey said: "[He] was the best BBC chairman in recent times. Tough, independent, wise and fair."
