Despite the mounting pressure, Martinez insists the Toffees will maintain their stance before Monday's transfer deadline. "Sometimes money can't buy everything and that is going to be a very strong statement at Everton," Martinez said. "This is not a moment when we can use any money to get us stronger." Stones demonstrated his professionalism by playing the entire 120 minutes in Everton's 5-3 extra-time League Cup victory over Barnsley on Wednesday. "John, for a young man under massive pressure, was terrific," Martinez praised. The Spanish manager has criticized Chelsea boss Jose Mourinho's public pursuit of the defender and expressed confidence in chairman Bill Kenwright's resolve. "We have a chairman who will do the right thing for the club and for the team," Martinez said. "He will not be easily influenced in taking the money and accepting things which will clearly make our team weaker." Stones, who joined from Barnsley for £3m in February 2013, has four years remaining on his contract after signing an extension last August. Martinez emphasized the club's commitment to protecting the young defender and ensuring he can focus on his football.

Australian Man Jailed for Minimum 22 Years for Murdering Northern Ireland Woman An Australian man has been sentenced to at least 22 years in prison for the brutal murder of his estranged wife, a woman originally from Northern Ireland. Christopher Cullen repeatedly stabbed 39-year-old Victoria Comrie Cullen and cut her throat during a frenzied attack at Taren Point in Sydney in January 2014. The victim was originally from Bangor, County Down. Cullen had denied the murder charge, claiming he acted in self-defence, but was found guilty last month following a trial. He received a 30-year sentence and must serve a minimum of 22 years before becoming eligible for parole. During sentencing, the judge described the killing as a "frenzied and brutal attack," saying it was difficult, if not impossible, to imagine the terror Ms Cullen experienced in her final moments, according to ABC Australia. The court heard during the trial that Ms Cullen had been a victim of domestic abuse and had taken out an Apprehended Violence Order (AVO) against her estranged husband. Several months before her death, Cullen had threatened to kill her and ordered her from their home after accusing her of having an affair. On the night of the murder, Ms Cullen's body was discovered kneeling face down on grass at a fishing club. Her ex-husband was arrested nearby. The sentencing judge said Cullen "callously decided to kill the deceased for his own selfish and personal reasons" and had shown no remorse. He added that the death was "another example of the extremely prevalent violence perpetrated by men in our society against women to whom they are married or with whom they share a relationship of domestic intimacy." The judge noted that "this malignant cycle of domestic violence is given publicity and media attention without corresponding or equivalent success in its prevention." Friends and colleagues of Ms Cullen wept in court as the sentence was delivered.

New Zealand WWI Monuments Granted Protected Status in England Two historic monuments commemorating New Zealand troops' contributions during World War One have been granted protected status in England, ensuring their preservation for future generations. The Bulford Kiwi, a massive 130-meter-tall (420-foot) figure carved into chalk on Bulford Hill near Stonehenge, has been designated a scheduled monument by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The landmark was created by New Zealand soldiers stationed at the site during the war and serves as a lasting tribute to their presence in England and their achievements on the battlefield. The designation comes on the advice of Historic England, which also recommended protection for a second monument at Cannock Chase in Staffordshire. The Terrain Model of Messines is a detailed scale model of the Belgian battlefield where New Zealand forces played a crucial role during the Battle of Messines in June 1917. The terrain model, constructed by German prisoners of war using soil, concrete, bricks and pebbles, was originally a popular tourist attraction following the war's conclusion. However, it subsequently fell into neglect and was eventually lost. After recent excavation work rediscovered the model, it has been covered over again to prevent damage and erosion whilst maintaining its protected status. Roger Bowdler from Historic England emphasized the monuments' significance: "These two monuments pay tribute to the bravery of New Zealand's fighting forces in the First World War and we are delighted that they are now being protected for the future." He noted that the Bulford Kiwi was carved by the soldiers themselves at war's end, whilst the Messines model represents the meticulous planning that enabled one of the war's most successful attacks—the taking of Messines ridge. "One hundred years on, it is right to remember New Zealand's valour," Bowdler added. Sir Jerry Mateparae, New Zealand High Commissioner to the UK, welcomed the protection, stating: "The special connections that were forged 100 years ago, with communities in the UK where New Zealanders trained, are still strong today and it's moving to see these sites protected for generations to come."

Former Chinese Oil Executive Jiang Jiemin Stands Trial for Corruption BEIJING — Jiang Jiemin, the former head of China's largest state-owned oil company, has been formally charged with bribery and abuse of power, marking another significant development in China's sweeping anti-corruption campaign, state news agency Xinhua reported. The charges stem from Mr. Jiang's tenure at the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC), where he held various high-level positions between 2004 and 2013. He was arrested in 2013, just months after leaving CNPC to assume what was supposed to be the pinnacle of his career. According to a statement posted on the microblog account of the Hanjiang Intermediate People's Court in Hubei province, Mr. Jiang faces accusations of "accepting bribes and large amounts of assets of unclear provenance, and misusing his authority as an employee of a state-owned company." In a subsequent court statement, Mr. Jiang reportedly pleaded guilty to all charges. He was quoted as acknowledging that he had "caused great losses to the country's assets" and "damaged the management and development of the country's oil and gas fields." Prosecutors allege that Mr. Jiang exploited his influential positions within CNPC—the parent company of PetroChina, Asia's largest oil producer—to facilitate promotions and grant access to lucrative projects in exchange for bribes. Xinhua reported that prosecutors claim Mr. Jiang and his family possessed assets that "clearly far outstripped" their legitimate income as of August 2013, and that he was "unable to give the sources" for the additional wealth. Mr. Jiang's career trajectory at CNPC was impressive, rising through the company's ranks during the late 1990s and 2000s to eventually become chairman. In April 2013, he left the oil giant to assume a Cabinet-level position as head of the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission, which oversees all of China's state-owned enterprises. However, his time in that prestigious role was short-lived. Just five months after his appointment, Mr. Jiang was dismissed and accused of corruption. The trial is expected to conclude within a few days, consistent with similar high-profile cases in China. CNPC has emerged as one of the primary targets of President Xi Jinping's extensive anti-corruption initiative, launched in 2012, which has resulted in the detention of thousands of government officials. President Xi has repeatedly emphasized that rampant corruption poses an existential threat to the Communist Party's hold on power. Mr. Jiang is reportedly a protégé of Zhou Yongkang, the former domestic security chief and one of the most senior officials to face corruption charges. Mr. Zhou, who once sat on China's highest decision-making body, the Politburo Standing Committee, has been charged with bribery, abuse of power, and intentional disclosure of state secrets.

Labour's Owen Smith Calls for Unity as Crisis Talks Continue Labour MP Owen Smith has pledged to do "anything" to serve his party while urging members to allow more time for crisis talks aimed at resolving the leadership turmoil engulfing the Labour Party. Mr Smith, who recently resigned from the shadow cabinet, has been in discussions with Unite union leader Len McCluskey and Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn to "explore what I can do" to heal the deep rifts that have emerged within the party. He described the talks as "productive" and said they needed more time over the weekend to reach a resolution. The intervention comes as the Labour Party faces its most serious crisis in recent memory. Mr Corbyn's authority has been severely undermined after he lost a no-confidence vote among Labour MPs by 172 votes to 40, and suffered the mass resignation of shadow cabinet members, including Mr Smith himself. In a statement released on Wednesday, Mr Smith expressed alarm at the possibility of the party splitting apart. "Over the last week, I have been contacted by hundreds of Labour members and MPs deeply worried that the Labour Party is truly in danger of splitting apart," he said. "I share those fears and call on everyone in our movement to do all we can to avert such a disastrous outcome." Mr Smith said he had "spoke directly" with Mr McCluskey and Mr Corbyn to discuss ways forward. He revealed that Mr McCluskey, representing the trades unions, had informed him that talks between Mr Corbyn and deputy leader Tom Watson had been productive and requested additional time this weekend to make further progress. "Jeremy has also reassured me that he is engaging in talks with an open mind," Mr Smith added. He called on all colleagues to give the talks "every chance to succeed" and to prioritize restoring unity in order to "defeat our only true enemy, the Tories." Despite the overwhelming no-confidence vote and mass resignations from his frontbench team, Mr Corbyn has steadfastly refused to step down. Both Mr Smith and former shadow business secretary Angela Eagle have been reportedly considering launching formal challenges to his leadership position. The coming days will be crucial in determining whether the party can find a way forward or faces an unprecedented split.

Blind Author Trish Vickers Dies Hours Before Seeing Published Novel A blind author with terminal cancer has died just hours before her first novel arrived in print, despite a publisher's extraordinary efforts to rush the book to completion. Trish Vickers, 64, from Charmouth, Dorset, passed away on Thursday morning, two hours before copies of "Grannifer's Legacy" reached her home. The novel had been published in just two weeks, rather than the usual six months, after the author made a public appeal for help. Ms Vickers, who lost her sight 11 years ago, spent six years writing the book by hand without using a computer or Braille. She devised an ingenious system using rubber bands and a clipboard to guide her pen across the pages. However, she was unaware that her pen had run out of ink for 26 pages. Forensic experts from Dorset Police came to her aid, recreating the missing text by analysing the indentations left on the paper. Simon West, editor at Dorset-based publisher Magic Oxygen, worked tirelessly to complete the project. "As soon as we met Trish we fell in love with her, but we soon realised that her condition was deteriorating and we needed to act fast," he said. "I'm absolutely elated we published the book within two weeks, and devastated that [Trish] was so cruelly taken before she could see the book." The novel tells the story of Jennifer, who discovers a book written by her great-grandmother. It will be officially launched at an awards ceremony in Lyme Regis, with part of the profits donated to South West Talking Newspapers.

French Unemployment Rises Despite Hollande's Promise France's unemployment figures have dealt a blow to President Francois Hollande's pledge to reverse joblessness by the end of 2013, with 10,200 additional people joining unemployment rolls in December. The French unemployment rate now stands at 11.1%, having increased by 5.7% throughout 2013, with a 0.3% rise in December alone. Speaking in Ankara, Turkey, ahead of the official figures' release, Mr Hollande acknowledged: "Stabilisation, which we have achieved, is not enough." The president, whose approval ratings have plummeted to record lows, had made reducing unemployment a cornerstone priority last year. While the Labour Ministry pointed to some progress—with 177,800 people becoming unemployed in 2013 compared to 283,800 in 2012—economists remain skeptical about a genuine recovery. Eric Heyer from think tank OFCE noted that most improvements stemmed from state-sponsored jobs rather than organic economic growth. He warned that Hollande's proposed tax breaks wouldn't materialize until at least 2016, eliminating prospects for rapid labour market improvement. "For the private sector to create jobs, you need growth stronger than 1%, whereas the government sees growth of 0.9% this year," Heyer explained. Earlier this month, President Hollande announced tax incentives for companies committing to hire more workers. He also pledged to eliminate 30 billion euros ($41 billion, £25 billion) in company charges for family benefits by 2017, contingent upon businesses accepting hiring targets and domestic investment commitments. The persistent unemployment challenge continues to undermine Hollande's presidency as France struggles to jumpstart economic growth.

Barcelona's preparations for El Clasico hit a stumbling block as they were held to a 1-1 draw by third-tier side Hercules in their Copa del Rey last-32 first leg clash. David Mainz gave the Segunda Division B underdogs a shock lead in the second half, slotting home from close range to stun the visiting Catalan giants. However, teenager Carles Alena rescued Barcelona with a well-taken equalizer, drilling in from outside the box to level the tie. The Spanish champions were without their fearsome attacking trio of Lionel Messi, Luis Suarez and Neymar for the trip to Alicante. The result continues a worrying trend for Luis Enrique's side, who have now drawn their last three domestic matches following league stalemates against Malaga and Real Sociedad. Barcelona will hope to secure passage in the second leg at the Nou Camp on 21 December, but their immediate focus turns to Saturday's crucial El Clasico against Real Madrid. The champions sit six points behind league leaders Real Madrid ahead of the 15:15 GMT kick-off at the Nou Camp.

Download Festival: Police Hail Crime Reduction After Using Facial Recognition Technology Leicestershire Police have reported a significant drop in crime at this year's Download Festival, where facial recognition technology was deployed for the first time at a UK outdoor event. The force recorded just 60 crimes at the three-day rock festival, representing a 35% reduction compared to 2014 figures. This marks the third consecutive year of declining crime rates, bringing offences to a five-year low at the event held at Donington Park from 12-14 June. The facial recognition system was used to identify known criminals among the crowds, though the measure drew criticism from civil liberties campaigners. Big Brother Watch described the technology's deployment as "worrying". Detective Inspector Matt Ditcher of Leicestershire Police defended the approach: "Crime at Download has always been low but this year has been really exceptional. When you consider that 80,000 people flood into Leicestershire over five days, almost doubling the size of its population, it is incredible that so few crimes have been reported to us." Most reported offences involved theft from cars and tents. The force attributed the success partly to a new cashless payment system introduced at the festival, reducing the need for attendees to carry money. Police said the facial recognition technology provided an "efficient and effective way" of spotting known offenders in crowds. A full report on the trial's results will be published. The festival was headlined by rock acts Kiss, Muse and Slipknot.

Robber Brian Martin Jailed After Knifepoint Raid on Ann Gloag's Daughter A man who held a knife to the throat of businesswoman Ann Gloag's daughter during a terrifying robbery has admitted stealing £200,000 worth of jewellery from her Perthshire home. Brian Martin, 58, dramatically interrupted proceedings at the High Court in Edinburgh to change his plea from not guilty to guilty and apologise directly to his victim, Sarah Gloag. The court heard how Martin and an accomplice burst into Mrs Gloag's property in January while she was doing DIY work. Mrs Gloag told the court she noticed two men at her front door and opened it, asking: "Can I help you? Are you lost?" Martin immediately produced a knife and forced his way inside with a second man. He held the blade to Mrs Gloag's throat and ordered her to get on the ground before tying her up with tape. The attackers demanded to know the location of her safe. Mrs Gloag's husband, Sundeep Salins, was also restrained during the terrifying ordeal. Martin took Mr Salins upstairs before returning with a supermarket bag containing the stolen items, which included jewellery worth £200,000 and £4,000 in cash. Before leaving, Martin issued a chilling threat, warning Mrs Gloag not to contact police. "He said'don't press the panic alarms and don't use the phone. Give us 20 minutes and then you can call whoever you want,'" she told the court. He also threatened to return and stab her if she raised the alarm. After the robbers fled, Mrs Gloag and her husband managed to free themselves. Her mother, Ann Gloag, coincidentally phoned the house about another matter. Mr Salins answered and told the prominent businesswoman: "Ann - can I call you back. We've just been robbed." Ann Gloag, one of Scotland's best-known entrepreneurs and co-founder of the Stagecoach transport empire, immediately contacted police, who arrived at the property within six minutes. In an extraordinary courtroom scene, Martin - sitting in the dock just feet away from Mrs Gloag - shouted across an apology after hearing her evidence. "I'm sorry Mrs Gloag. Please accept my heartfelt apologies - you and your family shouldn't have to go through this," he said. He then addressed temporary judge Paul Arthurson QC, saying: "Your honour - I wish to change my plea from not guilty to guilty." As she left court, Mrs Gloag looked to Martin and said: "Thank you." Martin pleaded guilty to assaulting both Mr Salins and Mrs Gloag while "face masked" and holding a knife, detaining them against their will and robbing them. He told the court he could not remember who his accomplice was. A second accused, Christopher McMultan, 40, denies all charges brought against him by prosecutors. His trial is due to continue on Thursday. Martin has also admitted separate charges of assaulting and robbing David Gilfoyle and Joanne Miles at another property in Muthill, Perthshire, in January.

Welsh Government's Top Civil Servant Sir Derek Jones to Step Down Sir Derek Jones, the Permanent Secretary of the Welsh Government since October 2012, has announced his intention to step down at the end of the year. In an email to staff, Sir Derek revealed his plans to depart after ensuring "a new first minister and cabinet hit the ground running" following the upcoming Assembly elections. The Welsh Government confirmed that arrangements for appointing his successor would be finalised "in due course". Reflecting on the transition period ahead, Sir Derek wrote: "Although we'll continue to be busy, I hope the next few weeks will give us all the opportunity to find time for a bit of reflection on the huge amount that's been achieved and what we can do to prepare for the all-consuming early months of the new Assembly term." He explained his timing, stating: "By that time we will have helped a new First Minister and Cabinet to hit the ground running and the new Programme for Government will be well under way. There will also be sufficient time for a competition to appoint my successor." Sir Derek promised to provide staff with further details about the transition in the coming months.

Mageean Narrowly Misses Rio Standard Despite Setting New Northern Ireland Record Ciara Mageean continued her impressive return to form by shaving 0.05 seconds off her Northern Ireland record at the Rieti meeting on Sunday, clocking 4:06.49 in the 1500 metres. However, the Portaferry athlete's time fell just 0.49 seconds short of the Rio Olympic qualifying standard as she finished fifth. Ethiopian Gudaf Tsegay claimed victory in 4:05.17, narrowly ahead of Canadian Fiona Benson who recorded 4:05.24. Benson had also pipped Mageean to first place in Tuesday's race in Rovereto, where the 23-year-old initially set her national record. Ethiopian-born runners Mimi Belete and Axumawit Embaye also finished ahead of the Northern Irish athlete, while Kenya's recent World Championships representative Viola Lagat placed sixth behind Mageean. The County Down runner chose to skip the recent World Championships in Beijing as she continues her comeback from a challenging injury period. After winning world junior 1500m silver in 2010, Mageean's Olympic hopes were dashed by a foot injury that prevented her competing at London 2012. Another foot problem forced her to miss this year's European Indoor Championships in March. Despite the setbacks, Mageean's recent performances suggest she is well-positioned to secure Olympic qualification for Rio, having only returned to major competition late in the current outdoor season.

Milwaukee Mother Shot in Back by Toddler Son on Highway A Milwaukee mother was fatally shot by her two-year-old son after he found a loaded gun in the car she was driving, her father confirmed. Patrice Price, 26, had been driving a car belonging to her security guard boyfriend who had left his gun in the car, her father Andre said. Milwaukee police said she was shot once in the back while driving on Highway 175 on Tuesday morning. Mr Price said his daughter had been driving her sons, aged one and two. He said she also had an older daughter aged seven or eight, and described Patrice as "hardworking". "Now I don't have her no more. My chest has been hurting," Mr Price said. There have been a number of incidents in the US of toddlers getting hold of loaded guns and accidently firing them. Last month, a four-year-old boy in Florida shot his mother, Jamie Gilt, in similar circumstances. A gun slid from underneath the front seat of the car to the back, and he unbuckled himself to get it. Ms Gilt survived the shooting.

Ireland Begin ICC Intercontinental Cup Campaign with Test Cricket Ambitions Ireland's new head coach John Bracewell has emphasised the crucial importance of the ICC Intercontinental Cup as his team begins their campaign to become a Test-playing nation. The 2015-17 edition of the competition kicks off on Tuesday with added significance, as it now offers a direct pathway to Test cricket status. Ireland, the reigning champions, will be among four Associate nations from the recent ICC Cricket World Cup 2015 competing in the opening round of four-day matches, whilst Scotland hosts Afghanistan in another fixture. "It's a very important game as we take a first step towards our aim of being a Test playing nation," said Bracewell. "That opportunity was one of the main reasons I took on the job of coach." The tournament format sees eight teams compete in a round-robin competition, with the winner earning the right to face the 10th-ranked Test nation (as of 31 December 2017) in a four-match ICC Test Challenge during 2018. Should the Associate Member prevail in this home-and-away series, they would become the 11th Test nation. Ireland enter the competition with an impressive pedigree, having won the trophy on four previous occasions - 2005, 2006-7, 2007-8 and 2011-13. This marks their seventh consecutive appearance since the competition's inception in 2004, during which they have compiled a remarkable record of 20 wins, just two losses and 10 draws from 32 matches. The former New Zealand off-spinner described the enhanced incentive as "incredibly exciting for the team and the country as we look to write new chapters in our cricketing history". "The team has a fantastic record in the competition having won it four times and we'd like nothing better than to make it five wins," Bracewell added. Ireland have selected a full-strength squad for the opening match, including the return of Tim Murtagh, who proved his fitness playing for Middlesex's 2nd XI last week and will feature in an Ireland line-up for the first time in 13 months. The competition also features former winners Afghanistan, along with Hong Kong, Namibia, Netherlands, Papua New Guinea, 2004 champions Scotland and the United Arab Emirates.

Smaller Broadband Providers Outshine Industry Giants in Customer Satisfaction Survey Britain's three largest broadband providers have received dismal customer satisfaction ratings, all scoring below 50% in a recent Which? survey, highlighting widespread dissatisfaction with mainstream internet services. In stark contrast, smaller providers including John Lewis Broadband, Plusnet, Utility Warehouse and Zen Internet achieved impressive scores exceeding 70%, demonstrating that size doesn't guarantee quality service. Most providers received three-star ratings for broadband speed, though TalkTalk customers proved least satisfied, awarding their provider just two stars for connection speeds. Richard Lloyd, executive director of Which?, stated: "Smaller suppliers are leaving larger rivals in their wake when it comes to the service they provide so we need to see the big players up their game." The consumer campaign group is actively challenging current advertising regulations, which permit providers to promote broadband speeds that only 10% of customers actually experience, calling for greater transparency in speed claims.

Yellow Fever Outbreak in Angola Raises Global Health Concerns LUANDA, Angola - A devastating yellow fever outbreak in Angola has claimed 277 lives since December, prompting international health experts to warn of a potential global health emergency, according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO). The mosquito-borne viral disease has sparked concerns about vaccine shortages and the possibility of the epidemic spreading to other continents. Nearly six million people have been vaccinated in Angola, which has a population of 24.3 million, but the WHO reported in April that emergency vaccine stockpiles had been depleted. The virus has already crossed borders, spreading to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kenya, and China. BBC Africa's health correspondent Anne Soy explained that the six-month production time for vaccines creates significant delays in responding to large-scale outbreaks like Angola's current crisis. In an article published in the Journal of the American Medical Association titled "A Yellow Fever Epidemic, A New Global Health Emergency?", Georgetown University professors Daniel Lucey and Lawrence Gostin warned that insufficient vaccine supplies could trigger a health security crisis if the disease spreads further across Africa, Asia, and the Americas. Notably, Asia has never experienced a yellow fever epidemic. The professors urged the WHO to "urgently convene an emergency committee to mobilise funds, co-ordinate an international response, and spearhead a surge in vaccine production." Yellow fever causes bleeding, jaundice, and kidney failure in infected individuals. It spreads through mosquitoes, primarily the Aedes aegypti species, which also transmits the Zika virus. The disease is endemic in tropical regions of Africa and South America. While vaccination can prevent infection, there is currently no specific drug treatment available for those already infected, making prevention through vaccination critical to containing the outbreak.

Schmidt Confident Ireland Will Rise to Challenge in Series Decider Ireland coach Joe Schmidt has expressed his complete confidence in his significantly reshuffled team ahead of Saturday's crucial Test series decider against South Africa, despite a rollercoaster tour that has seen his squad come agonizingly close to a historic achievement. The New Zealander has been forced to make six personnel changes and one positional switch to his starting XV as Ireland prepare for their 17th and final game of an exhausting season. The alterations come after a dramatic series that saw Ireland claim their first ever away win over the Springboks in the opening Test, only to surrender a commanding 16-point lead in last week's second Test at Ellis Park, missing out on what would have been a landmark series victory. "I'm utterly confident they'll make me and themselves proud," Schmidt declared, backing his revamped lineup to deliver when it matters most. The Ireland coach faces significant challenges with the absence of key players. Jared Payne has been ruled out with a calf injury, while Robbie Henshaw departed the tour early with a knee problem. The loss of both established centres represents a considerable blow to Ireland's backline structure. However, Schmidt has been able to welcome back several important figures. Keith Earls, Mike Ross, and Jordi Murphy have all been recalled to the starting XV, while CJ Stander returns after serving a one-match suspension. Connacht's Tiernan O'Halloran will make his first start in Payne's absence, and Ulster pair Stuart Olding and Luke Marshall will form an untested centre partnership. Despite the disruption and the toll of a grueling season, Schmidt remains unwavering in his belief in his players. "I've no doubt that they'll be no different than it has been in the last two Tests," he said. "Yes, it's been a long season, people are tired and that's going to maybe detract from people being at their optimum. But, at the same time, I don't think too many people will detect that because what they don't have in fresh reserves of energy, they'll make up for in the full commitment they make to doing the job that they do." The match takes on added significance given speculation about Schmidt's future. He has indicated he will decide whether to remain as Ireland coach until the 2019 Rugby World Cup after the tour's completion, with his current contract set to expire in the summer of 2017. South Africa, buoyed by their thrilling 32-26 comeback victory last weekend, have made two changes to their lineup, bringing in Ruan Combrinck and Warren Whiteley for Lwazi Mvovo and the injured Duane Vermeulen as they seek to clinch the series.

Brexit-Themed Phishing Attacks Surge Following Referendum Cybersecurity experts are warning internet users about a dramatic spike in phishing attacks exploiting Brexit-related anxiety, with scammers using subject lines like "Brexit causes historic market drop" to lure victims. James Chappell, co-founder of London-based cybersecurity firm Digital Shadows, told the Telegraph that there has been a sharp increase in such attacks since polling day. Security experts are advising users not to click on links or attachments in suspicious emails referencing Brexit. According to Symantec's threat intelligence researchers, spam emails using Brexit in the subject line have increased by a staggering 392% following the referendum results. A Symantec spokeswoman told the BBC that blocked emails on behalf of customers surged from 81,323 between June 9-23 to 399,892 between June 24 and July 5. Phishing attacks typically involve fraudulent messages that trick users into clicking malicious links or downloading files that install malware or redirect to harmful websites. Psychologist Dr Aaron Balick explained the attacks' effectiveness: "These people are quite smartly riding on an assumption that Brexit has made a huge chunk of the population anxious and insecure. They're more vulnerable in that situation to grabbing on to something that offers them reassurances." Security experts urge caution when handling unexpected Brexit-related emails.

YouTube Star Stampy Warns Young Fans About Screen Time Before Bed Popular YouTube gaming star Stampy, whose channel boasts over seven million subscribers, is speaking out about the importance of taking breaks from screens, especially before bedtime. The content creator, known for his gaming videos, admits that his own work habits sometimes interfere with his sleep. "The big problem for me is generally whenever I'm looking at a screen I'm doing something that is very engaged," he tells Newsround. "I'm either playing something, editing or writing. You need some time to tune down and relax before you try and go to sleep." Stampy has noticed firsthand how excessive screen time affects his rest. "I know that the light that screens give out can sometimes trick the brain into thinking that it's still daytime but it isn't," he explains. "I think that being very switched on and actively thinking just before bed is a bad idea." His comments come as Newsround's latest special programme, Is Tech Taking Over?, challenges children to survive three days with minimal technology while their classmates have unlimited access. To combat screen fatigue, Stampy has developed his own strategies. He uses his love of tea as a reminder to take breaks, and also suggests talking to someone or playing with pets. "At least an hour before bed just try not to look at a screen and not do anything too active mentally," he advises young viewers.

Millwall defender Mahlon Romeo will serve a three-match ban after the Football Association upheld his red card from the League One play-off quarter-final victory over Gillingham. The 20-year-old right-back was dismissed following a challenge on Brennan Dickenson during Sunday's 2-1 win, and Millwall's appeal against wrongful dismissal was rejected by the FA. Romeo's suspension means he will miss both legs of Millwall's semi-final against Bradford City, with the first leg on Sunday and the return at The Den on 20 May. If the Lions progress to the League One play-off final at Wembley on 29 May, Romeo will also be absent. Should Neil Harris' side be eliminated by Bradford, Romeo will miss the opening match of next season.

Maldives Presidential Election: Nasheed Faces Run-off After Delayed Vote The Maldives finally held a long-delayed presidential election run-off on Saturday, with former President Mohamed Nasheed seeking to reclaim power amid mounting international pressure. Mr Nasheed secured nearly 47% of votes in the first round earlier this month, falling just short of the 50% threshold required for outright victory. He now faces runner-up Abdulla Yameen, who requested additional time to campaign before the second round. The election process has been plagued by controversy and delays. A September 7 vote was annulled by the Supreme Court following allegations of irregularities from candidate Gasim Ibrahim, despite international observers declaring it free and fair. The court subsequently imposed new electoral guidelines. A scheduled October 19 re-run was blocked by police after Mr Yameen and Mr Gasim refused to approve the voter register, claiming the court's guidelines had not been satisfied. Elections Commission official Aishath Reema reported strong voter enthusiasm on Saturday, with many citizens queuing before polling stations opened at the 475 designated booths. The political drama intensified when outgoing President Mohamed Waheed—who assumed office after Nasheed's forced resignation in 2012—departed for Hong Kong on Thursday for his wife's medical appointment. His spokesman assured the public that Waheed remained in contact. The prolonged political instability has alarmed international observers. EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton issued a stern warning on Thursday, stating the bloc was "ready to consider appropriate measures" if the run-off failed to proceed successfully, underscoring the global community's concern over the Maldives' democratic crisis.

Cumbria Police Face £9.5m Funding Cut Under New Grant Proposals Cumbria Police could lose more than £9.5 million under changes being considered for the allocation of key government grants, prompting urgent appeals to the Home Office. Police and Crime Commissioner Richard Rhodes has called on the Home Office to treat Cumbria as a special case, citing the county's unique challenges. He argued that its vast size, difficult geography, and large number of tourists result in significantly higher vehicle and communication costs compared to urban areas. Mr Rhodes criticised the proposed funding formula as "flawed in methodology," stating: "We are being penalised for our rurality. Cumbria has the same number of bars as other areas, but because there are twice as many hectares in the county it attracts only half the funding under the proposals." He emphasised the particular difficulties of policing a rural area like the Lake District, where technology and vehicles are more expensive and require greater numbers of personnel to cover the terrain. "We have put a robust case forward to the Home Office and would ask that our points are considered with the relevance that they deserve," Mr Rhodes added. Policing minister Mike Penning acknowledged that plans were being refined following feedback from the public and police chiefs, with a final decision expected next month.

Stuart Baggs Death: Apprentice Star Died from Asthma, Say Police The body of Stuart Baggs, former contestant on BBC's The Apprentice, was discovered at his Isle of Man home on 30 July. Police have confirmed the 27-year-old entrepreneur died from natural causes related to his long-term asthma condition. Inspector Iain MacMillan stated: "Mr Baggs had suffered from asthma for many years and died as a result of his condition." The coroner has been informed that no suspicious circumstances surrounded his death. Inspector McKillop paid tribute to the young businessman, saying: "From the reaction we have encountered during our enquiries, it is clear that this is a tragic and premature loss of such a hardworking and visionary young man. We extend our thoughts to the family at this sad time and on their behalf I would request that they are now left in peace to grieve." Plymouth-born Baggs had lived in the Isle of Man for most of his life, where he successfully ran a telecommunications company. In 2010, at just 21 years old, he became the youngest ever candidate to appear on The Apprentice, making it to the semi-final before being fired. He became known for memorable catchphrases including "Everything I touch turns to sold" and his signature line, "I'm Stuart Baggs the brand." Police discovered his body after being called to his residence on Central Promenade in Douglas at 09:00 BST last Thursday.

Retired Teacher Denies Historical Child Abuse Charges at Nottinghamshire School A 90-year-old retired teacher has denied allegations of historical child abuse dating back nearly six decades at a Nottinghamshire school. Dennis Young, of Burton Stone Lane, York, is facing seven charges of indecently assaulting a child under 14 while teaching at Skegby Hall near Mansfield in the 1950s. Nottingham Crown Court heard the alleged abuse began when the pupil was just 10 years old. In a police video interview shown to the jury, the complainant said he was threatened with being sent to a borstal if he spoke out about the abuse. He also claimed that when he reported the incidents to the school's headmaster, he was dismissed and told "not to be a silly boy". When asked why he had waited so long to report the allegations, the man said: "To get it off my chest, I'm ashamed, I feel guilty as though it's my fault." The trial continues.

DVLA Speeds Up Licence Removal Process After Campaign by Bereaved Mother The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) has introduced streamlined procedures allowing police to quickly request the removal of driving licences following a determined campaign by Jackie McCord, whose teenage daughter was killed by an elderly driver who had failed a police eye test. The changes, implemented nearly two years after 16-year-old Cassie McCord's death, mean police officers can now telephone or email requests for licence revocation, replacing a cumbersome system that required written letters or faxes and could take several days. Cassie, an aspiring lawyer from Colchester, was struck by 87-year-old Colin Horsfall whilst walking on a pavement on her way to college in February 2011. Just three days before the fatal collision, Mr Horsfall had failed a police eye test after driving into the exit of a petrol station. Despite his obvious visual impairment, he refused to surrender his licence voluntarily, and police were still attempting to have it revoked through official channels when the tragedy occurred. The incident sparked Mrs McCord to launch a petition calling for what became known as "Cassie's Law" – proposed legislation that would grant police direct powers to immediately confiscate licences from dangerous drivers. The petition garnered more than 45,000 signatures and brought national attention to gaps in road safety procedures. While the DVLA changes stop short of giving police the authority to physically remove licences, Mrs McCord expressed satisfaction with the outcome. "I am confident this is a really good solution," she said. "The fact the Department for Transport has listened to someone like me who has no power is amazing. Next week it will be two years since Cassie died. The timing could not be better." Under the new email system, licence removal could now be completed in minutes rather than days, potentially preventing similar tragedies. Road Safety Minister Stephen Hammond acknowledged Mrs McCord's efforts, stating: "We have every sympathy with Mrs McCord and would like to thank her for her valuable work in raising awareness of this issue. The DVLA and the police have worked closely to greatly streamline the process for revoking a licence when the police identify that a driver's eyesight is inadequate." Alan Jones from the Police Federation's roads policing division welcomed the changes, saying: "It seems absolute nonsense a police officer who knows someone has defective eyesight has not been able to do anything." He confirmed that whilst officers won't directly suspend licences, acting as a "conduit" to the DVLA represents significant progress. The decision whether to revoke licences on medical grounds remains with the DVLA, but the accelerated notification process addresses the critical delays that contributed to Cassie's death.

**Swansea Monitor Chadli as Sigurdsson Saga Continues** Swansea City are keeping tabs on West Bromwich Albion's Nacer Chadli as uncertainty surrounds Gylfi Sigurdsson's future at the Liberty Stadium. The Swans had targeted the Belgium international last year before he joined West Brom from Tottenham. Baggies manager Tony Pulis dismissed speculation linking Chadli with a move away after a reported argument between the two earlier this summer. But Swansea continue to monitor the 28-year-old, particularly as their midfielder Gylfi Sigurdsson remains a prime target for Everton. The Toffees have had a £40m offer rejected for the Icelander, who is valued at £50m. Should the move go through, Swansea head coach Paul Clement would be eager to use those funds to strengthen his squad. The Swans were interested in Las Palmas playmaker Jonathan Viera, though the Spanish club's asking price of around £25m was deemed too high.

Man Found Dead Outside Derby Flat Died from Stab Wounds Richard Bernard, 51, was discovered outside his flat in Trocadero Court, Derby, on Tuesday night after suffering fatal stab wounds. Detective Chief Inspector Dave Cox of Derbyshire Police said investigators believe Mr Bernard was attacked inside his home before collapsing outside, where he died. Two people, a man and woman, were arrested in connection with the death but have since been released on bail. Police have not disclosed what specific offences they were arrested for. A post-mortem examination confirmed Mr Bernard died from stab wounds. His family, including mother Nita, sister Claire and brother Andrew, released a statement saying: "We are devastated to hear the tragic news about Richard." Derbyshire Police are appealing for witnesses or anyone with information to come forward.

Salmon Fry Numbers Plummet to Critical Lows in Welsh Rivers Natural Resources Wales (NRW) has reported alarmingly low numbers of salmon fry in three major Welsh rivers, marking an unprecedented decline in fish populations. The Usk, Towy and Clwyd rivers have seen juvenile salmon numbers drop to critically-low levels, according to surveys conducted this year. These waterways had previously maintained consistent fry populations, making the sudden decline particularly concerning for environmental officials. In contrast, the Tawe, Glaslyn and Wye rivers continue to show normal fry levels. ## Survey Findings Paint Worrying Picture The survey results reveal the severity of the situation. In the Tywi catchment, salmon were completely absent from 31 of 37 monitored sites. The Usk fared little better, with eight of 13 sites recording no salmon fry whatsoever, whilst the remaining five sites showed very-low numbers. The Clwyd catchment presented the most alarming findings, recording not only zero salmon fry but also its worst trout fry numbers in recorded history. Peter Gough, NRW principal fisheries advisor, described the findings as "unprecedented in Wales in 30 years of monitoring." "These initial survey results are clearly very concerning, especially as our salmon and sea trout stocks already face serious challenges," he said. Mr Gough warned that the decline threatens both river biodiversity and the local economy, particularly the angling and tourism sectors. The cause remains unknown, though NRW is investigating several possibilities including extreme winter river flows, high water temperatures, and potentially disease or parasites, though the latter is considered unlikely. Officials have pledged to continue investigations and implement measures to support spawning efforts this winter.

Kurdish Forces Recapture Strategic Mount Zartak from Islamic State Kurdish forces have recaptured Mount Zartak, a strategic peak overlooking the plain leading to Mosul, in a significant victory against Islamic State militants. The mountain, which fell to IS last month during a lightning assault on Iraqi Kurdistan, was retaken in a fierce battle that resulted in more than 30 IS fighters killed, according to Kurdish sources. US air strikes played a crucial role in the operation, with Kurdish forces acknowledging they made a "big difference" in the outcome. Mount Zartak's elevated position provides commanding views across the Nineveh plain toward Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city, which IS seized in June. Kurdish peshmerga fighters now control the high ground, placing nearby IS-held villages within range of their weapons. Gene Aziz Oweisi, commander of the Kurdish elite commandos who led the assault, emphasized the victory's broader significance. "For the Iraqis it's important too because it's a step towards taking back Mosul," he told the BBC. However, Kurdish forces have stressed they do not intend to recapture Mosul independently, as it is predominantly a Sunni Arab city. The recapture comes amid ongoing efforts to push back IS, which has seized vast territories across Iraq and Syria, declaring a "caliphate" over the land it controls. Last week, Iraqi media reported that senior IS commander Abu Alaa al-Iraqi was killed in an air strike on Mosul, though this remains unconfirmed. The United Nations and human rights organizations have documented numerous IS atrocities, including mass killings of ethnic and religious minorities throughout the region.

Mozart Hair Lock Valued at £10,000 Ahead of Sotheby's Auction Sotheby's auction house has placed a £10,000 estimate on a lock of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's hair, dating from the year of his death in 1791, ahead of Thursday's sale in London. The precious keepsake has been preserved in a gilt locket and boasts impressive provenance. It was originally passed from Mozart's widow Constanze to German conductor Karl Anschutz before being acquired by English composer Arthur Sommervell. Also featured in the sale are a lock of Ludwig van Beethoven's hair and a printed invitation to his 1827 funeral, collectively estimated at £2,000. All lots will be publicly displayed in central London until Wednesday. The practice of taking hair locks as keepsakes from deceased composers was common during this era. Mozart, who died after composing masterpieces including The Magic Flute and The Marriage of Figaro, remains highly collectible. In 2002, another Mozart hair lock fetched £38,240 at auction—double its pre-sale estimate.

Meerkat Live-Streaming App Shut Down by Developers The live-streaming app Meerkat, which generated significant buzz at last year's SXSW festival in Austin, Texas, has been pulled from app stores by its creator, Life on Air. The company has shifted focus to Houseparty, a group video chat application that enables friends to communicate in real-time through private conversations rather than public broadcasts. Life on Air co-founder Ben Rubin revealed the decision to change direction was made six months after Meerkat's initial launch. "Our mission remains to connect people in the most human way possible while physically apart," Rubin explained. "Not only do we believe that Houseparty is a better manifestation of that vision, but also the market has told us that too." Houseparty, which has been under development for ten months, allows users to create and join virtual "rooms" accommodating up to eight participants. The app has reportedly already attracted nearly one million users, signaling strong market acceptance of the pivot toward more intimate, private group interactions over public broadcasting.

Man Charged After 51 Turtles Found Taped to His Legs at US-Canada Border A Michigan man faces federal smuggling charges after Canadian border guards discovered 51 turtles strapped to his body during an attempted crossing from Detroit to Windsor, Ontario. Kai Xu, 26, was apprehended following an investigation that began when a postal worker in Detroit contacted the US Fish and Wildlife Service about a suspicious package marked "live fish keep cool" that was being held for pickup. On August 5, wildlife investigators conducted surveillance of Mr Xu after he crossed into the United States from Ontario to collect the parcel. According to the federal criminal complaint, officers watched as he retrieved the package, transferred its contents into a bag, and then disappeared between two large trucks for approximately 10 minutes. "As he did so [an investigator] noticed irregularly shaped bulges under Xu's sweat pants on both his legs," authorities documented in their report. When Mr Xu attempted to return to Canada through the Detroit-Windsor tunnel, Canadian border guards conducted a thorough search of both his vehicle and person. The inspection revealed 41 turtles taped to his legs and an additional 10 concealed between his legs. The reptiles were identified as North American species, including Eastern box turtles, Red-eared sliders, and Diamondback Terrapins, all protected under international wildlife trafficking regulations. Mr Xu has been charged with smuggling goods from the United States and trading in specimens contrary to international conventions on endangered species. He was released on bond Thursday and has not yet entered a plea. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in federal prison. The confiscated turtles have been turned over to the US Fish and Wildlife Service.

Expert Approves Child Interview Methods in Liam Fee Murder Trial A child psychology expert has told a court that interviews with two young boys allegedly mistreated by accused murderers Rachel and Nyomi Fee were conducted appropriately. Dr Gary MacPherson was asked to review video recordings of interviews with the children at the centre of the case against the two women. The pair deny murdering two-year-old Liam Fee on 22 March 2014 at a house near Glenrothes, Fife, instead blaming his death on another child in their care. Dr MacPherson concluded the interviews complied with official guidelines for questioning children. Social worker Charlie Finlay, one of the interviewers, defended his methods during cross-examination by Nyomi Fee's lawyer Mark Stewart, stating: "I am satisfied we conducted the interview in a professional and attentive manner." The women, both originally from Ryton, Tyne and Wear, also face allegations of neglecting Liam and abusing two other children over a two-year period. They deny all charges. The trial at the High Court in Livingston continues.

Laverty Confirmed for Milwaukee Aprilia Team Return to World Superbikes Eugene Laverty's highly anticipated return to the World Superbike Championship has been officially confirmed, with the Northern Irish rider joining the Milwaukee Aprilia team for the upcoming season. The Toomebridge man revealed last month his decision to return to the Superbike series following two seasons competing in MotoGP. On Thursday, the Milwaukee Aprilia team announcement confirmed Laverty will race alongside Lorenzo Savadori, the 2015 World Superstock champion. Laverty brings impressive credentials to his comeback, having secured 10 race wins during his previous World Superbike stint and finishing second overall in the championship standings. "I'm excited to return to Superbike with Aprilia and the RSV4, a bike with which I took 10 wins and second place overall in the championship," said Laverty. "I hope to be able to pick up where I left off with those results, thanks to the support of Aprilia and a fantastic team like Shaun Muir's. Everything is in place for us to be competitive straight away." The Milwaukee team will benefit from full factory support and technical assistance from Aprilia Racing throughout the season. Romano Albesiano, Aprilia Racing's manager, emphasized the partnership's significance. "Shaun Muir's team, after making a good name for themselves in the British championship, wants to get to the top of a world category," Albesiano explained. "Our agreement includes, in addition to providing bikes and materials, support from Aprilia Racing personnel to manage and develop the RSV4." Laverty's switch from MotoGP came after facing the prospect of riding an uncompetitive GP15 bike for the Aspar Ducati team in 2017.

Senate Passes Keystone XL Pipeline Bill Despite Veto Threat The US Senate has approved legislation to authorize construction of the controversial Keystone XL pipeline, voting 62-36 after weeks of intense debate and numerous amendment votes. The decision comes after the House of Representatives had already passed the measure, but faces an almost certain veto from President Barack Obama. The proposed 875-mile (1,400km) pipeline would transport tar sands oil from Alberta, Canada, to Nebraska, where it would connect with existing infrastructure running to refineries in Texas. The project has become a flashpoint in American politics, dividing lawmakers along partisan lines. White House spokesman Josh Earnest reiterated that President Obama would veto the legislation, arguing it would undermine a "well-established" review process for such projects. Overriding a presidential veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers of Congress, a threshold supporters may struggle to reach. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell hailed the bill as "an important accomplishment for the country," citing State Department estimates that the project could create up to 42,000 jobs with "little to no impact on the environment." He expressed hope the president would reconsider his position. However, Democratic Senator Barbara Boxer sharply criticized the legislation as "a disgrace," lamenting that Democratic efforts to improve the bill were rejected. The debate has exposed deep divisions over energy policy and environmental priorities. Republicans and project supporters emphasize job creation and energy infrastructure development, while many Democrats and environmental groups warn the pipeline would increase carbon emissions and exacerbate climate change. During the amendment process, lawmakers added provisions on energy efficiency and included language acknowledging that climate change is not a hoax. President Obama has previously questioned the pipeline's benefits, noting it would primarily serve Canadian oil companies and would have minimal impact on already declining gasoline prices. The State Department, which must weigh in because the pipeline crosses an international border, issued a report last February raising no major environmental concerns. However, the final recommendation has been delayed due to ongoing legal challenges in Nebraska. A decision is expected within weeks. The pipeline would carry approximately 830,000 barrels of heavy crude daily from Alberta's oil fields, with the southern section already completed last year.

Exam Paper Replaced After Potential Security Breach Ahead of Scottish Highers Tens of thousands of students across Scotland preparing to sit their Higher English examination on Thursday have been affected by an emergency paper replacement, after exam authorities identified a potential security breach. The Scottish Qualifications Authority (SQA) took the unprecedented step of distributing a completely new version of one of the two Higher English exam papers to schools and exam centres last week, in what officials described as a "precautionary measure." The BBC understands that concerns were raised that some of the questions on the original paper may have been leaked, prompting the swift action to protect the integrity of the examination. ## SQA Response An SQA spokesman confirmed the situation, stating: "We identified a potential issue with one of the Higher English question papers. The appropriate adjustments were made and a new paper was distributed to centres. Our Chief Invigilators have been informed." The exam body sought to reassure students and parents that the replacement would not disadvantage candidates. "We always create more content than is needed for each examination. All content, including that which is selected for the final exam, goes through the same rigorous quality checks," the spokesman explained. He added: "Robust procedures are in place to ensure the integrity of our qualifications - and we took swift and appropriate precautionary action to ensure candidates would not be affected and are able to sit the examination as intended." The SQA stressed that candidates should not feel anxious about the last-minute change. ## Security Protocols Exam papers are subject to extremely tight security measures. After printing, they are distributed to schools and exam centres with strict instructions to store them securely until shortly before each examination begins. The EIS teaching union supported the decision to replace the paper. A spokesman said: "Where there is doubt over an element of an examination paper, the sensible option is to replace that section of the paper. The most important consideration is that no pupil is unfairly advantaged or disadvantaged, so that the exam can deliver a fair measure of each pupil's level of attainment." However, the union called for a thorough investigation, adding: "Clearly, there will have to be a thorough investigation into the circumstances that led to this situation, but the most important issue in the short term is to ensure that any issues with the paper are rectified." ## Context and Background The SQA declined to specify exactly how much of the exam paper required changing. Exam papers typically undergo careful scrutiny to ensure they contain an appropriate range of questions with varying levels of difficulty. Last year's Higher Maths examination highlighted the importance of proper calibration when the paper proved significantly harder than anticipated, resulting in the pass mark being reduced to just 35%. Unlike subjects with definitive right or wrong answers, Higher English assessments evaluate candidates' skills and understanding through their responses. If a paper proves easier or harder than intended, grade boundaries can be adjusted to ensure fair outcomes. This year's examination diet begins on Wednesday and represents a significant milestone, being the first year when only the new-look Highers are available. These revised qualifications were redesigned to align with the qualifications that replaced Standard Grades two years ago. Last year, both revamped and traditional-style Highers were offered simultaneously.

Thongchai Jaidee Takes Lead at Turkish Airlines Open After Stunning Third Round Thailand's Thongchai Jaidee surged into the lead at the Turkish Airlines Open with a superb seven-under-par 65 on Saturday, positioning himself strongly for what would be his eighth European Tour title. The 46-year-old veteran produced a blistering start, birdieing five of his opening eight holes to reach 15 under par for the tournament. His only blemish came with a dropped shot on the final hole, but it wasn't enough to diminish an otherwise dominant performance. Halfway leader Lucas Bjerregaard of Denmark, still seeking his maiden European Tour victory, slipped back after posting a two-under 70. He shares second place on 13 under alongside Spain's Sergio Garcia and South Korea's Byeong Hun An. Three Englishmen—Ross Fisher, Paul Casey, and Ian Poulter—are firmly in contention at 12 under. Fisher, who lost in a playoff at this event last year, highlighted his five-under 67 with a spectacular chip-in from heavy rough at the par-three 17th for one of his six birdies. Australian Marcus Fraser made a dramatic move, jumping nine places to joint-11th after a spectacular back nine of 29, crowned by holing his second shot from 231 yards for eagle at the 18th. Danny Willett, second in the Race to Dubai standings, struggled to a 70 and sits tied for 27th. The tournament took on added significance as players and caddies wore black ribbons to honor victims of the Paris attacks, which claimed at least 127 lives. The seven French competitors in the field wore black clothing as a mark of respect at this penultimate event of the season.

Post Office Computer System "Not Fit for Purpose" for Some Branches, Report Claims More than 150 sub-postmasters have come forward claiming they were wrongly prosecuted or forced to repay money due to problems with the Post Office's computer system, according to a confidential report seen by BBC News. The report, commissioned by the Post Office and conducted by investigators Second Sight, concluded that the Horizon transactions processing system was "not fit for purpose" in some branches. However, the Post Office has maintained there is "no evidence" of systemic computer issues. The controversy centres on the Horizon system, introduced in 1995 to process transactions across the Post Office network. Sub-postmasters - who run smaller post offices but are not directly employed by the Post Office - are contractually responsible for any deficits at their branches. Following the system's introduction, numerous sub-postmasters reported discrepancies between money from bank machines, lottery terminals, and tax disc sales and the figures shown on their computers. The report criticised investigators for failing to identify the root causes of these errors, instead accusing sub-postmasters of theft or false accounting. Jo Hamilton, who previously ran a sub-post office in South Warnborough, Hampshire, told the BBC last year that the system had generated a £36,000 deficit at her branch. Sarah Burgess Boyd from Newcastle-upon-Tyne said she lost her life savings repaying an incorrect shortfall. The Second Sight report identified several problems, including inadequate training for those without IT skills, outdated equipment, and complications caused by power cuts and communication issues. An interim report was published last year. While the vast majority of the 11,500 sub post offices have operated without problems, the Post Office is now in mediation with those claiming unfair treatment. In a statement, the Post Office said: "Although we will not comment on the contents of any confidential documents, after two years of investigation it remains the case that there is absolutely no evidence of any systemic issues with the computer system which is used by over 78,000 people across our 11,500 branches and which successfully processes over six million transactions every day."

Heathrow Unveils £16bn Vision for Airport Expansion Heathrow Airport has revealed ambitious new designs for its proposed expansion, which architects Grimshaw describe "as setting a new standard for the future of aviation". The comprehensive plans include the construction of a third runway and convenient access to the new Crossrail link, representing a £16bn privately funded infrastructure investment. The airport is locked in competition with Gatwick for government permission to expand capacity in the south east of England. A decision on whether to approve an extra runway for Gatwick or Heathrow has been delayed until "at least October". Architecture firm Grimshaw designed the new plan after being selected from a shortlist of four of the UK's top architects. Partner Andrew Thomas said: "We look forward to developing a design that provides an authentic and uniquely British sense of place. Our concept will deliver an outstanding passenger experience by building upon the airport's rich history." A promotional video fly-through shows innovative features including indoor trees and expansive glass roofs revealing large expanses of sky above check-in areas. Heathrow boss John Holland-Kaye emphasized the economic benefits: "At a time of uncertainty, a £16bn privately funded infrastructure investment will create jobs and growth across the UK." However, Gatwick Airport continues advocating for its own second runway proposal, arguing it would cause less environmental damage. Chief executive Stewart Wingate said: "The enormous pollution - both noise and air quality - that Heathrow inflicts on hundreds of thousands of people, if not millions - it's this issue that politicians are going to have to grapple with. "If you look at Gatwick, we have a tiny fraction of the environmental impact of Heathrow, yet you get all of the same economic benefits, all of the same connections to short-haul and long-haul destinations, all at a cheaper price."

Republic of Ireland Name 39-Man Squad for Crucial World Cup Qualifiers Republic of Ireland manager Martin O'Neill has announced an extended 39-man squad for the upcoming crucial World Cup qualifying matches against Georgia and Serbia in September. The squad features several notable inclusions, including uncapped striker Sean Maguire, who earned his call-up following an impressive 20-goal season with Cork City in the Irish Premier Division before securing a move to Preston North End. The forward, who has represented Ireland at underage levels through to U21s, will be hoping to make his senior international debut. O'Neill has also included two other uncapped players: Matt Doherty of Wolverhampton Wanderers and Reading's Liam Kelly. Additionally, Preston defender Greg Cunningham receives a recall after his last appearance for the national team in 2013. The Republic face a pivotal period in their qualification campaign, currently sitting level on points with Group D leaders Serbia. They will host Serbia in Dublin on 5 September, just three days after traveling to Georgia for an away fixture. Speaking about the importance of the upcoming matches, O'Neill emphasized the critical nature of the fixtures: "These two matches will make ferocious inroads into the make up of the group - goal difference is pretty important too. We need to remain unbeaten if we can and probably need to win at least three out of the four games." The extended squad sees the return of several key players who missed previous friendlies against Mexico, Uruguay and Austria, including Newcastle goalkeeper Rob Elliot, Reading's Paul McShane, Ciaran Clark, James McCarthy, Stephen Quinn, David Meyler, Shane Long and Kevin Doyle. With the qualification race heating up, O'Neill has cast his net wide, selecting players from clubs across England's football pyramid and beyond, giving himself maximum options as Ireland look to secure their place at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

BBC Journalists to Vote on Strike Action Over 1% Pay Offer Members of the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) at the BBC will vote on potential industrial action following what the union describes as an inadequate pay offer from the corporation. The ballot, scheduled to run from 20 June to 11 July, comes after the BBC proposed a 1% pay increase tied to a minimum of £390, whilst freezing pay entirely for staff earning more than £50,000. NUJ general secretary Michelle Stanistreet criticised the "huge differential" between journalist salaries and senior management pay packages. She proposed capping executive salaries at £150,000, which the union calculates would free up £20 million for programming and journalism. "The union has argued for a genuine alternative to the excessive payments to managers and the waste in the corporation," Ms Stanistreet said. "There are structural changes that can be made that would result in fair pay and free up cash for programming. This would be to the benefit of the staff and licence payers." Currently, director general Tony Hall and managing director Anne Bulford each earn £450,000 annually – three times the proposed cap. The NUJ stated its members felt "betrayed" by Lord Hall, who defended the modest pay offer by saying it was vital to demonstrate the BBC "gets austerity." A BBC spokeswoman expressed surprise at the ballot announcement, noting that discussions with unions were ongoing. "The 1% pay increase we have offered is in line with the public sector. It is structured to benefit our lowest paid staff and excludes senior managers," she said, adding that the licence fee settlement meant the corporation was "constrained financially." This dispute follows similar tensions last year when BBC journalists threatened strike action over a £600 flat-rate offer, ultimately settling for an improved deal of £800 or 1%, whichever was higher. The ballot results will determine whether the BBC faces its first major industrial action in years.

Germany's Brendel and Vandrey Retain Canoe Sprint Title Media playback is not supported on this device. Germany's Sebastian Brendel and Jan Vandrey successfully defended their canoe sprint title, crossing the finish line in 3:43.912. The Brazilian duo of Erlon de Souza Silva and Isaquias Queiroz dos Santos held the early lead but were overtaken in the final 250 metres, finishing less than a second behind the German champions. Ukraine's Dmytro Ianchuk and Taras Mishchick claimed bronze. The victory contributes to Germany's impressive medal haul, placing them fourth overall with 15 gold medals, two ahead of Russia. For more sports coverage, subscribe to the BBC Sport newsletter for curated news, features and video content.

Turkey Blocks Social Media Sites Over Images of Prosecutor Hostage Crisis Turkey has temporarily blocked access to Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube after the social media platforms shared images of a prosecutor being held at gunpoint during a hostage crisis at an Istanbul courthouse. The blocks on Facebook and Twitter were later lifted after they both complied with government demands. Talks with YouTube are continuing. Two gunmen, reportedly from a far-left group, took prosecutor Mehmet Selim Kiraz hostage at an Istanbul courthouse last week. All three died during a police rescue bid. Turkish officials described the images of the prosecutor as "anti-government propaganda" and moved swiftly to prevent their distribution. Before imposing the blocks on the websites, Turkish authorities had already moved to stop newspapers from printing the images. The newspapers were accused by the government of disseminating "terrorist propaganda" for the DHKP-C group that was reportedly behind the attack on the courthouse. The DHKP-C is considered a terrorist group by Turkey, the European Union and the United States. Mr Kiraz was apparently taken hostage because he headed an investigation into the 2013 death of a boy during anti-government protests. The pictures showing attackers holding a gun to his head were being widely shared on social media, prompting authorities to act. "The wife and children of prosecutor Kiraz have been deeply upset. The images are everywhere," a senior Turkish official told the Reuters news agency. In total, 166 websites which shared the images were blocked by court order. Millions of social media users tried to access their favourite platforms but with no success. However, the block did not stop people from attempting to communicate. Newspapers and individuals alike shared guidelines on how to circumvent the ban. The hashtag #TwitterisblockedinTurkey became the number one trending topic worldwide. Facebook was subject to the same block but restrictions were lifted after it removed the images before the expiration of a deadline imposed by the court. Twitter reacted more slowly and access to the messaging system was blocked for several hours on Monday. YouTube published the text of the court ruling on its website saying an "administration measure" had been enacted by Turkey's telecoms authority, adding it was seeking ways to restore access. This is not the first time that Turkish authorities have imposed blocks on social media sites and networks. The Turkish government has a complicated relationship with social media platforms. In the run-up to local elections in March 2014, blocks were imposed after recordings circulated allegedly revealing corruption among senior officials. The then prime minister, now President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, described Twitter as a menace to society. Figures provided by Twitter revealed that Turkey filed more requests to remove content from the social network than any other nation between July and December 2014. With general elections scheduled for 7 June and tensions running high, many people fear similar bans on social platforms could follow.

Cardinal Pell Admits He "Should Have Done More" About Paedophile Priest Cardinal George Pell has admitted he "should have done more" after learning of allegations against a paedophile priest in 1974, during his testimony to an Australian Royal Commission investigating institutional responses to child sexual abuse. The cardinal told the commission, which is conducting hearings in Rome, that a student at St Patrick's College in Ballarat informed him that Brother Edward Dowlan was "misbehaving with boys" in 1974. However, Cardinal Pell said the information was "casually mentioned" and claimed the boy did not explicitly ask him to take action. Dowlan, who has since changed his name to Ted Bales, was jailed last year for abusing boys throughout the 1970s and 1980s. Cardinal Pell is giving evidence via video link from Rome after being excused from returning to Australia due to a heart condition. ## Survivors Confront Cardinal's Testimony A group of abuse survivors and their supporters have traveled to Rome to face Australia's most senior Catholic as he testifies. Among them is Peter Blenkiron, who was abused by Brother Dowlan and spoke shortly after the cardinal's admission. "That's me in 1973, six months before I went to St Patrick's," Mr Blenkiron said, pointing to a photograph on his T-shirt. "If action would've been taken, that little boy wouldn't have gone through what he went through." Cardinal Pell described it as a "disastrous coincidence" that five paedophiles came to be at the same school and parish in Ballarat during the 1970s. This characterization angered abuse survivor Stephen Wood, who has previously disclosed being bashed and molested starting from age 11. "Coincidence my foot, it was clearly systemic," he said. ## Bribery Allegations Denied The cardinal also denied allegations that he attempted to bribe the nephew of notorious paedophile priest Gerald Ridsdale. David Ridsdale, who was abused by his uncle, has claimed that Cardinal Pell offered him money to "keep quiet." The inquiry heard that David Ridsdale initially avoided involving police because he feared his grandmother would discover his uncle's actions. On the eve of Cardinal Pell's final day of testimony, David Ridsdale expressed hope that the group's request to meet with Pope Francis would be approved. "Most likely we will meet with Cardinal Pell and we have a good chance of a Papal meeting on Friday," he said. "We want an understanding and an acknowledgment this is a global systemic problem." Cardinal Pell released a statement offering to meet victims in small groups without lawyers or media present, and said he would be "happy to assist with requests to meet Pope Francis."

Passenger Restrained on British Airways Flight to Boston A British Airways flight from London to Boston was met by police on Tuesday after a female passenger was restrained by crew members during the flight. An airline spokesman told the BBC that reports of a passenger trying to access the cockpit were incorrect and they were not particularly concerned. Police met the plane upon landing at Boston's Logan Airport on Tuesday. The 30-year-old woman was restrained by the crew during the flight, the FAA said. The six-and-half-hour Flight BA 213 originated from London's Heathrow Airport. British Airways officials said they believe the woman was intoxicated and they did not believe the incident was related to terrorism. "We do not tolerate abusive behaviour," a statement said. Earlier on Tuesday, four passengers were removed from a Baltimore to Chicago flight because of "suspicious behaviour". The incidents come as authorities have been put on heightened alert after devastating gun and suicide attacks killed at least 129 people in Paris.

Russia Denies US Claims of Supplying Taliban in Afghanistan Russia has firmly denied American allegations that it is supplying weapons to the Taliban in Afghanistan, dismissing the claims as "absolutely false" and designed to cover up US failures in the region. The denial came after General Curtis Scaparrotti, Nato's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, told US lawmakers in Washington on Thursday that Moscow was "perhaps" supplying the extremist group. However, he provided no evidence to support the serious allegation. Zamir Kabulov, the Kremlin's special envoy in Afghanistan, responded swiftly on Friday, telling RIA Novosti state news agency that the accusations were fabrications. "These fabrications are designed, as we have repeatedly underlined, to justify the failure of the US military and politicians in the Afghan campaign. There is no other explanation," he said. The allegations represent a significant point of tension in an already complicated relationship between Russia and the Taliban. Russia officially considers the Taliban a terrorist organisation and historically backed the Northern Alliance against the group during Afghanistan's civil war in the 1990s.
