I came through as a player and started as an academy coach and I have ended up as director of rugby. But I have had to prove myself on the way. It's been a great eight or nine years and hopefully that will continue for another five."

Visa delays threaten Llangollen International Music Eisteddfod performers The renowned Llangollen International Music Eisteddfod is facing significant challenges after being inadvertently excluded from a crucial Home Office list of permit-free festivals, causing severe delays in visa processing for international performers. The administrative oversight means competitors must undergo lengthier visa application procedures, with several participants from China, Algeria, Tanzania and Ivory Coast already facing rejection. Over 100 dancers and musicians from multiple countries remain uncertain about their participation in this year's festival, scheduled for 7 July. Clwyd South MP Susan Elan Jones has intervened, writing directly to the home secretary requesting urgent government assistance. She confirmed that Home Office officials have acknowledged the error in correspondence with eisteddfod organisers. Merle Hunt, the eisteddfod's competitors liaison officer, explained that inclusion on the permit-free list is vital as it "confirms they're coming for bona fide reasons," streamlining the visa process considerably. The annual celebration, first established in Llangollen in 1947, traditionally welcomes performers from approximately 50 nations. Currently awaiting visa decisions are two groups from India, five from Morocco, 14 dancers from Ghana and five from Nepal, among others. The Home Office has been approached for comment on the matter.

Rare Welsh Whisky Bottles Fetch Over £14,000 at Auction Two exceptionally rare bottles of Welsh whisky have sold for a combined total of more than £14,000 at a Carmarthen auction house, far exceeding expectations. The bottles from the historic Welsh Whisky Distillery Company were auctioned by Peter Francis Auctioneers, selling for £7,300 and £7,200 respectively to private collectors. Both bottles date back to approximately 1900. Auctioneer Charles Hampshire expressed delight at the results: "We're thrilled that a lot of people got involved in it - the sale has done exceptionally well." The bottles had been estimated to fetch around £3,000 each, but Mr Hampshire acknowledged the difficulty in valuation, noting "it was almost impossible to put a figure on it because there's nothing to compare it to." The Welsh Whisky Distillery Company operated in Frongoch, Bala, Gwynedd, from its founding in 1889 until closure in the early 20th Century. The distillery site later served as a World War One prison camp and, more notably, an internment camp following the Easter Rising in Ireland. These particular bottles were purchased by a Fishguard wine merchant in the 1960s for just £5 each, having been in the original family's possession since 1914. Only a handful of these bottles are known to exist today, with examples on display at Penderyn Distillery and Cardiff's St Fagans National History Museum. Another was previously auctioned in Cardiff in 2001. Mr Hampshire revealed that one bottle will return to Wales near the original distillery location, calling it "a nice finish, particularly for one of them."

Wales Coach Gatland Challenges North to Reach Full Potential Despite Impressive Career Northampton Saint George North will be 23 years and 138 days old when he takes the field at Dublin's Aviva Stadium, carrying the weight of immense expectations alongside his impressive rugby resume. With 22 international tries and three Lions Test appearances already to his name, the Welsh wing has achieved more than most players accomplish in an entire career. Yet Wales coach Warren Gatland believes North's best rugby still lies ahead. "I think he's got the ability to be a lot better than he is," Gatland stated candidly. "He's had 50 caps which is fantastic but I think there's still a lot of improvement. And probably in the last 12 months he hasn't played as well as we would have liked, he's aware of that and we've been working hard on his game." North's upcoming appearance marks his return after a five-month absence due to concussion recovery. His last outing in a Wales jersey showcased his undeniable talent—a hat-trick against Italy in the 2015 Six Nations. He also impressed during the 2013 British and Irish Lions tour to Australia, scoring twice in the Test series. Despite these highlights, Gatland has identified areas requiring improvement, particularly North's tendency to drift out of matches. "Players of that ability need to get their hands on the ball," the coach explained. "He probably went through a couple of campaigns where his touches weren't enough, and he made some defensive errors." Gatland, who first selected North for international duty as an 18-year-old against South Africa in 2010, remains deeply impressed by his protégé's achievements. "What he has achieved in the game at such a young age is exceptional," he acknowledged. "I remember seeing him as an 18-year-old playing for the Scarlets and saying'look we have to cap him as soon as possible because there's a freakish talent there'." Looking forward, Gatland hasn't ruled out positional changes, suggesting North could eventually excel at centre, hinting at even greater versatility in the young player's future.

Church of England Appoints Eighth Female Bishop for Sherborne Diocese The Church of England has announced Archdeacon Gorham as the new Bishop of Sherborne, becoming the eighth female bishop in the denomination's history. The Bishop of Sherborne serves within the Diocese of Salisbury, primarily overseeing parishes throughout Dorset. Archdeacon Gorham expressed gratitude for her time serving the church in Buckinghamshire and working in the Diocese of Oxford, calling it "a real privilege." She succeeds the Right Reverend Graham Kings, who departed the position in July. Looking ahead, Archdeacon Gorham said: "I now look forward to getting to know the people and places of Dorset, an area I have loved since childhood holidays." The Bishop of Salisbury, the Right Reverend Nicholas Holtam, praised the appointment, stating that Archdeacon Gorham "emerged as the right person for this post from a company of excellent men and women considered equally." The consecration ceremony will take place on 24 February at Westminster Abbey, marking another milestone for women's leadership in the Church of England.

Historic Wedgwood Vase Campaign Receives Major Boost as Deadline Extended A campaign to save an historic Wedgwood vase for Stoke-on-Trent has received a significant boost with a £90,000 grant from Art Fund, extending the fundraising deadline. The First Day's Vase, created on the opening day of Josiah Wedgwood's Etruria factory in the 18th Century, had been on long-term loan to The Potteries Museum & Art Gallery. However, its owner withdrew the piece and sold it to an overseas buyer at auction last year, prompting urgent action from the city council. The Friends of the Potteries Museum & Art Gallery are leading efforts to raise £482,500 to purchase the vase and secure its permanent display in the city. The campaign has already gathered momentum, with £83,000 raised including a £60,000 grant from Arts Council England. Art Fund's £90,000 contribution has proved crucial, enabling an extension of the original Tuesday deadline to 14 July. This follows a temporary export ban placed on the vase by the government in December, which has also been extended. The vase holds exceptional historical significance as one of only four surviving pieces made by Wedgwood on Etruria's first day of operation. The Victoria and Albert Museum owns two of the other vases, whilst the fourth remains with the Wedgwood family. Campaigners continue their efforts to keep this important piece of local heritage in Stoke-on-Trent.

US Spy Allegations Rock Brazil and Mexico as NSA Surveillance Exposed Brazil and Mexico are demanding answers following explosive allegations that the United States National Security Agency (NSA) spied on their presidents' communications, according to reports broadcast on Brazilian television. Rio-based American journalist Glenn Greenwald made the startling revelations during a programme on TV Globo on Sunday evening, citing secret documents obtained from former US intelligence contractor Edward Snowden. The claims have sparked diplomatic tensions and raised serious questions about US surveillance activities in Latin America. According to the report, the NSA not only intercepted communications between aides of Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff but also deployed sophisticated programmes to monitor all internet content accessed by the president herself. The allegations suggest extensive and intrusive surveillance of Brazil's highest office. Mr Greenwald, who writes for the British Guardian newspaper, told the Fantastico news programme that classified documents revealed systematic spying on Brazilian government communications. The report also alleges that Mexican President Enrique Pena Nieto was targeted by US intelligence, with his emails reportedly being read even before his election in July 2012, according to documents dating from June of that year. Brazil's response was swift, with US Ambassador to Brazil Thomas Shannon summoned briefly to the Brazilian foreign ministry to explain the allegations. The ambassador declined to speak to reporters following the meeting, and the foreign ministry has yet to issue an official statement. Brazilian Justice Minister Jose Eduardo Cardozo expressed strong concern over the allegations, stating: "If these facts prove to be true, it would be unacceptable and could be called an attack on our country's sovereignty." President Rousseff's office confirmed she was meeting with top ministers to discuss the situation. A spokesman for the Mexican foreign ministry acknowledged seeing the report but offered no immediate comment. The BBC's Julia Carneiro in Sao Paulo suggests the suspected motivation for the alleged surveillance relates to Brazil's significant economic influence and substantial commercial interests at stake. The revelations come as Mr Greenwald continues to publish stories based on documents leaked by Edward Snowden, who was granted temporary asylum in Russia after exposing secret US and UK surveillance programmes. Mr Greenwald was the first journalist to publish Snowden's leaked documents on 6 June. The case has already generated international controversy, particularly following the nine-hour detention of Mr Greenwald's partner, David Miranda, at London's Heathrow Airport last month. Mr Greenwald condemned the detention as "bullying" and an attempt at "intimidation" against those working on the NSA revelations. The British government defended the detention, stating police were right to act when they believed someone possessed "highly sensitive stolen information."

Alton Towers Crash Victim Shares Hopeful Photo After Amputation Leah Washington, a 17-year-old from Barnsley, South Yorkshire, has shared an uplifting photograph with friends on Facebook following the devastating Alton Towers Smiler rollercoaster crash that resulted in the amputation of her left leg. The teenager was seated on the front row when the ride collided with an empty carriage on 2 June, leaving 16 passengers trapped for up to four-and-a-half hours. In addition to losing her leg above the knee, Miss Washington also suffered a fractured hand. Her recent photograph, showing herself surrounded by 15 supporters, received hundreds of likes from well-wishers on social media. Miss Washington was one of five people seriously injured in the accident. Fellow front-row passenger Vicky Balch from Lancashire had her right leg amputated below the knee after undergoing seven rounds of surgery. The teenager attended the theme park with her 18-year-old boyfriend Joe Pugh, who sustained shattered knees and hand injuries. Merlin Entertainment Group, Alton Towers' parent company, has confirmed that all 16 passengers will receive compensation. Legal representatives for eight victims revealed that interim payments were distributed in late June to support rehabilitation efforts.

Why do people willingly pay for pain? Study examines Tough Mudder phenomenon Cardiff University academics have investigated why millions voluntarily subject themselves to the grueling Tough Mudder obstacle course, despite its deliberately painful design and serious injury risks. The extreme endurance event, which features obstacles including electric wires delivering 10,000-volt shocks, has attracted 2.5 million participants worldwide—even though injuries have ranged from strokes and heart attacks to fatalities. Dr. Rebecca Scott of Cardiff Business School highlighted a striking paradox: "Consumers spend billions of dollars every year on pain relief, while exhausting and painful experiences such as obstacle races and ultra-marathons are gaining in popularity." The international research collaboration, involving Cardiff, Singapore's Nanyang Business School, and France's Kedge Business School, uncovered several motivations behind this trend. Researchers found that pain helps office workers combat physical inactivity and allows participants to "rediscover the nature of their body." Additionally, the study revealed that pain "facilitates escape" from modern life pressures, providing "temporary relief from the burdens of self-awareness." Professor Bernard Cova of Kedge Business School explained: "Electric shocks and ice-cold water may be painful but they also allow participants to escape from the demands and anxieties of modern life." He added that these experiences help people create "the story of a fulfilled life spent exploring the limits of the body," with marks and wounds serving as tangible reminders of achievement.

South Sudan Hold Sudan to Draw, Move Closer to Quarter-Finals South Sudan's defensive tactics paid dividends as they held on for a point against their northern neighbors Sudan in the CECAFA Cup on Wednesday. After beating Djibouti 2-0 in their opening Group C game on Monday, the result puts South Sudan in a strong position to qualify for the quarter-finals of the tournament. "We are happy that we have picked a point against a strong Sudan side," said South Sudan's goalkeeper Juma Ginaro after the game. "We now wait to face Malawi in our last group game." The draw leaves Sudan in third place behind their southern neighbors with just a single point so far, after they lost 2-1 to Malawi in their first match. Guest team Malawi top the group and have already qualified for the last eight after brushing aside Djibouti 3-0. Yaboh Idriss Moussa missed several chances for Djibouti before Gerald Phiri converted a penalty for Malawi, with John Banda and Chiukepo Msowoya securing the victory. In other Wednesday fixtures, defending champions Kenya and Burundi settled for a 1-1 draw, while hosts Ethiopia recovered from their opening loss to Rwanda by beating Somalia 2-0 in front of a capacity crowd.

Fatal Stabbing at Dublin Flat Complex Under Investigation A man has died following a stabbing at the Oliver Bond flat complex in Dublin 8 on Sunday morning, police have confirmed. The victim was initially transported to St James's Hospital for emergency treatment but succumbed to his injuries. A post-mortem examination is scheduled for later Sunday to determine the exact cause of death. The incident is part of a violent weekend in Dublin. Separately, a man remains in critical condition after being stabbed at a bonfire on Dromheath Drive, Mulhuddart, on Saturday night. In another attack on Sunday morning, a man was hospitalized in serious condition following a stabbing on Templeview Avenue, Clarehall. Two additional men sustained minor injuries in that incident. Police investigations are ongoing.

UK Government Confirms Driverless Lorry Trials Following Budget Announcement The government has officially confirmed that "lorry platooning" trials will proceed on UK motorways, following speculation earlier in March about tests on a quiet stretch of the M6 in Cumbria. The innovative scheme involves convoys of heavy goods vehicles travelling in formation, with only the lead lorry requiring a driver. The announcement, made in Wednesday's Budget, forms part of the government's ambition to establish the UK as "a global centre for excellence in connected and autonomous vehicles". Additionally, the government revealed plans for driverless car trials on British roads by 2017, joining companies like Ford and Google who have been testing autonomous vehicles, primarily in California. However, the proposals have attracted criticism from motoring experts. Edmund King, president of the AA, raised concerns about the UK's motorway infrastructure. "The problem with the UK motorway network is that we have more entrances and exits of our motorways than any other motorways in Europe or indeed the world," he stated. King questioned how a 44-tonne, 10-lorry platoon would operate practically, noting that "other vehicles need to get past the platoon to enter or exit the road." The Budget also included various other technology-related initiatives as the government pushes forward with its autonomous vehicle strategy.

Youth Reoffending Falls to Lowest Level in 15 Years, New Report Shows A comprehensive report on criminal reconviction rates has revealed encouraging trends, with reoffending among young offenders dropping significantly over the past decade. The study shows that a third of criminals under 21 went on to commit further offences in 2012-13, representing a 9.4% decrease from peak levels recorded in 1997-98. Among 21 to 25-year-olds, there was an even more dramatic fall of 28% in reconviction rates over the past ten years. The overall reconviction rate has fallen by one percentage point for 2012-13, with the report noting: "Between 2003-04 and 2012-13, the reconviction rate has fallen by 4.1 percentage points from 32.7 to 28.6, and the average number of reconvictions has fallen by 18% from 0.62 to 0.51." The data revealed that people convicted of dishonesty crimes were most likely to reoffend, while those who committed sexual offences had the lowest reconviction rates. These reductions coincide with falling crime numbers recorded by police since 2004-05. However, the report highlighted concerning patterns in short-term imprisonment effectiveness. People imprisoned for three months or less had a 60% reconviction rate, compared to just 10.1% for those serving more than four years. Those given drug treatment and testing orders (DTTOs) showed the highest average number of reconvictions. "Those that commit relatively low-level crimes but in high volumes are more likely to be reconvicted, and are more likely to get short custodial sentences," the report explained. Offenders under 21 had the highest reconviction rate at 33% in 2012-13. Men were more likely to reoffend than women, and just under a third of people given community payback orders went on to commit further offences.

Trump Opens DC Hotel as Celebrity Chef Campaigns Against Him Donald Trump mixed business with politics Wednesday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for his Trump International Hotel in Washington DC, but one name was conspicuously absent from the glittering affair – celebrity chef Jose Andres, who was instead campaigning for Hillary Clinton in Florida. Andres, who originally agreed to open a flagship restaurant at the luxury hotel, pulled out of the project after Trump's controversial comments about Mexican immigrants during the campaign. Speaking from Florida, the Spanish-American chef was unequivocal: "We're not supposed to mention him until he apologises to every Latino..... every Mexican and every person he has insulted." The opening of the hotel marks the 32nd campaign event Trump has held at one of his own properties, according to NBC's count, with Trump Tower in New York leading the tally at 13 events. The blending of business interests with presidential politics has raised eyebrows among ethics watchdogs throughout the campaign. Despite the controversy, Trump has seen modest improvements in recent polling. Gallup reports gains among Republican-leaning voters, while Bloomberg shows the Republican nominee making ground in the crucial swing state of Florida, though he still faces an uphill battle to the White House. Meanwhile, Hillary Clinton marked her 69th birthday on the campaign trail, but made sure the occasion didn't pass unnoticed. She tweeted in the morning: "Happy birthday to this future president" – a confident message that appeared to resonate with supporters. The Democratic nominee enjoyed multiple celebrations throughout the day. She was serenaded on stage, received doughnuts dipped in tequila and beer from a radio host, and revealed on Twitter that her "birthday surprise" was an Adele concert. In jovial spirits, Clinton even proposed "a big national dance" to bring the country together after Election Day. Not all campaign news was celebratory, however. Trump's running mate Mike Pence took to Twitter to announce that Maverick, his beagle of 13 years, had died. In other developments, the New York Times released five hours of previously unreleased interviews with Trump, offering new insights into the Republican nominee's thinking. The paper's editor, Dean Baquet, told BBC's Newsnight that Trump had fundamentally changed their publication. "We've literally never seen anything like him..... he's a comic book figure," Baquet said. "Donald Trump has changed us, we're different as a result." He noted that the newspaper had been forced to use the word "liar" in a headline for the first time. The Clinton campaign also made waves on social media, responding to a viral meme suggesting her debate outfits – in red, white, and blue – were tributes to Death Row Records figures Tupac, Suge Knight, and Snoop Dogg. Looking ahead, Clinton will campaign in North Carolina alongside First Lady Michelle Obama, while running mate Tim Kaine heads to Ohio. Trump is also targeting Ohio, with Pence scheduled for rallies in Nebraska and Iowa as both campaigns intensify their final push for the White House.

AC/DC Guitarist Malcolm Young Diagnosed with Dementia Malcolm Young, the legendary rhythm guitarist and co-founder of rock band AC/DC, has been diagnosed with dementia, his family has confirmed. The announcement comes after it was revealed last week that the 61-year-old musician would not be returning to the band following a break earlier this year due to an unspecified illness. "Malcolm is suffering from dementia and the family thanks you for respecting their privacy," his family told People magazine. The diagnosis confirms earlier rumours about Young's condition. According to reports from the Sydney Morning Herald, Young has been moved into full-time care at a nursing home in Sydney. A family friend revealed the severity of his condition, stating that the guitarist can no longer remember how to play AC/DC songs. "If you were in the room with [Young] and walked out, then came back in one minute later, he wouldn't remember who you are. He has a complete loss of short-term memory," an unnamed source said. Despite this setback, AC/DC will continue. The band announced that "due to the nature of Malcolm's condition," Young will not feature on their upcoming album, Rock or Bust, scheduled for release in December. His nephew, Stevie Young, will replace him on rhythm guitar for both the new recordings and the planned world tour next year. Scottish-born brothers Malcolm and Angus Young formed AC/DC in 1973, with the Australian band selling over 200 million albums worldwide, including their biggest hit, 1980's Back in Black.

Ex-Rotherham Mayor Barry Dodson Faces Historical Sex Assault Trial A former mayor of Rotherham is on trial accused of sexually assaulting a 13-year-old girl nearly three decades ago. Barry Dodson, 67, is alleged to have assaulted the girl at Boston Castle in 1987. Sheffield Crown Court heard she came forward after Mr Dodson became the town's mayor in June 2014. Mr Dodson, of Cranworth Road, Rotherham, denies one charge of indecent assault. In police interviews played to the jury, the woman said she wanted people to know "what sort of man he was." The victim, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told officers her "life had been ruined" and she "couldn't live with it any longer". Mr Dobson stood down from the role following the allegations and also resigned from the Labour Party, which he has represented in Rotherham East since 2000. The trial continues.

Nick Clegg Loses Sheffield Hallam Seat in Major Election Upset In one of the most stunning results of Thursday's general election, Nick Clegg has lost his Sheffield Hallam constituency to Labour's Jared O'Mara, ending the former deputy prime minister's 12-year tenure representing the area. Mr Clegg, who had held the seat since 2005 with a majority of 2,353 in the 2015 election, was defeated by first-time MP Mr O'Mara in what represents a significant personal blow to the former Liberal Democrat leader. The loss comes as exit polls suggest the Liberal Democrats will secure 14 seats overall - an improvement on the eight seats won in 2015, but still far below their historical strength. Mr Clegg led the party into coalition government with the Conservatives in 2010, becoming deputy prime minister to David Cameron when the Lib Dems held 57 seats. That arrangement proved electorally disastrous, with the party's representation collapsing to just eight MPs in 2015. With Thursday's election producing another hung parliament and the Conservatives emerging as the largest party without a majority, senior Liberal Democrat figures have been quick to rule out any repeat of the coalition arrangement. The party's press office tweeted emphatically that there would be "no coalition" and "no deals." Former leader Sir Menzies Campbell told the BBC he would be "astonished" if current leader Tim Farron joined with the Tories for a second coalition or formed a "progressive alliance" with Labour. He explained the harsh lessons learned from the previous coalition: "The major party gets the credit for everything that is done and the junior party takes the blame for the things people don't like." Sir Menzies argued that Theresa May's commitment to a hard Brexit made any alliance impossible, saying Mr Farron "could not take the party with him, nor any of the over 100,000 membership" in supporting such a position. However, he was equally critical of Jeremy Corbyn's Brexit approach, which he said "frankly almost defies definition." Former Lib Dem leader Paddy Ashdown observed that Britain "is more polarised than ever in my lifetime" and declared it "REALLY time now for the centre to get its act together." He also told ITV News that Mrs May had "lost all credibility" during the election campaign. Baroness Lynne Featherstone warned on Sky News: "If the exit poll is right we'll have a government of chaos." The Liberal Democrats had campaigned heavily on attracting Remain voters, pledging a second referendum on the Brexit deal, continued single market membership, a penny income tax rise to fund the NHS, and cannabis legalisation.

McKibbin Wins by Two Strokes at Palm Beach Gardens Tom McKibbin secured victory at Palm Beach Gardens, finishing two under par to win by two strokes. The young golfer from Newtownabbey received congratulations from Rory McIlroy, 2012 Honda Classic champion, who tweeted: "Well done Tom. Great to see all your hard work paying off." McKibbin previously won the World Kids Championship at Pinehurst, North Carolina in August, demonstrating his continued success in junior golf.

Kiddisave Customers Left Without Prams Despite Paying Hundreds Dozens of customers who paid for baby equipment from Kiddisave have been left empty-handed after the company ceased trading, leaving families devastated just weeks before Christmas. Kay Possard, of WP Mayfield insolvency practitioners, confirmed she expected to be formally appointed as liquidator at a directors' meeting scheduled for 3 December. The firm has remained unavailable for comment regarding the situation. Among those affected is Chloe Khan, 27, from Dudley, who paid an £878 deposit towards goods totalling £1,756, including a double buggy for twins she is expecting within the next fortnight. The mother of an 18-month-old son said she has received nothing and feels "devastated" by the situation. Miss Khan explained that when she placed her deposit in late October, the company agreed to allow her a month to pay the balance. However, after just two weeks, they contacted her requesting immediate collection, claiming the items were obstructing new stock and risked damage. "[When I said I didn't have the money] the phone went quiet, they just went'OK' and put the phone down," she recalled. Now facing the imminent arrival of her twins, Miss Khan finds herself with "no money and no pram." "I think so many have been affected, it's disgusting," she added, highlighting the widespread impact on vulnerable families.

Welsh Farmer Convicted in Landmark DNA Case Over Stolen Sheep A Welsh farmer has been convicted of sheep theft in a groundbreaking case that used DNA testing to prove his guilt, marking the first time such evidence has been employed in Wales for livestock crime. Andrew Thomas, 39, from Garnant, pleaded guilty at Swansea Crown Court after DNA tests revealed that lambs born to stolen ewes had been fathered by rams belonging to the victim, Alan Price of Derwydd near Llandybie. The case began when approximately 50 sheep were stolen from Mr Price's land in Carmarthenshire. Two weeks later, Thomas attempted to sell 18 sheep at Llanybydder market, but mart officials and local farmers grew suspicious after noticing the animals' earmarks had been tampered with. Judge Geraint Walters praised the farming community for pulling together "to defeat those who seek to deceive it." He sentenced Thomas to eight months imprisonment, suspended for two years, and ordered him to pay £1,000 compensation. The judge told Thomas he had "caused a great deal of hurt" by stealing from those he worked alongside, warning it would be "a long time before they forgave him." Dyfed-Powys Police confirmed this landmark prosecution demonstrates the force's commitment to tackling rural crime using cutting-edge forensic techniques.

Warrington Wolves' Ben Currie Faces Nine-Month Injury Layoff After ACL Tear Warrington Wolves forward Ben Currie is facing up to nine months on the sidelines after suffering a severe knee injury during Friday's Super League match against Wigan Warriors. The 22-year-old tore his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) off the bone while scoring a try in Warrington's 35-28 home defeat. He was immediately sent to London for surgical repair, which will involve grafting the ligament back onto the bone. Wolves head coach Tony Smith confirmed the devastating news: "Our worst fears have come to fruition. He's torn his ACL off the bone. The minimum recovery would be six months but I reckon he will be close to nine months. It's a big blow for the young man." The injury is particularly disappointing timing for Currie, whose impressive form this season had him widely tipped for England selection in the upcoming Four Nations tournament.

Pig on M62 Causes Hour-Long Closure Near Leeds A seven-week-old piglet brought traffic to a standstill on the M62 motorway after escaping from a moving vehicle on Tuesday evening. Highways England reported the unusual incident occurred between junctions 28 and 29, south of Leeds, at approximately 19:00 BST near Tingley. Both carriageways were closed at 19:20 while authorities worked to recover the wandering animal. The West Yorkshire Police Dogs unit was deployed to assist in capturing the porcine escapee. The operation resulted in significant disruption, with a 3.5-mile queue forming eastbound and a 1.8-mile tailback westbound. After more than an hour of closure, the motorway reopened at around 20:30 BST. West Yorkshire Police Road Policing Unit later confirmed via Twitter that the piglet had been safely reunited with its owner.

Top IS Aide Reportedly Killed in Iraq Air Strike Iraq's defence ministry has announced the death of a senior aide to Islamic State leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi in an air strike on Mosul, though the claim remains unconfirmed. The development comes as IS fighters reportedly kidnapped 40 men from a northern Iraqi town. According to Iraqiya TV, defence officials confirmed that Abu Alaa al-Iraqi, head of the IS military council in Tal Afar, was killed in the air strike. Initial reports on social media had suggested al-Baghdadi himself was the target of a separate strike on Mosul, but the defence ministry later clarified that intelligence indicated a senior aide was killed instead. The strikes come amid ongoing military operations against IS positions that began in August when US forces started conducting air strikes after the group seized several northern Iraqi cities. It remains unclear whether the latest strikes were carried out by US or Iraqi forces. In a separate incident on Thursday, residents of Hawija in Kirkuk province reported that IS fighters kidnapped dozens of men, forcing them into vehicles before driving away. The motive for the abductions remains unclear, particularly since IS had taken control of the Sunni town last month without resistance. Locals reported that IS militants had retreated from the village on Wednesday, and residents subsequently set fire to a flag left behind by the group. The Islamic State has taken control of vast territories across Iraq and Syria in recent months. Amnesty International has accused the group of "systematic ethnic cleansing," including mass killings of ethnic and religious minorities. Human Rights Watch has also reported discovering new sites of mass killings in Tikrit. The situation escalated further when President Barack Obama vowed to destroy IS following the release of a video showing the beheading of American journalist Steven Sotloff. The group has carried out multiple beheadings, including that of US journalist James Foley and several Kurdish fighters. Iraqi security forces, supported by Kurdish and Shia fighters, have recently launched offensives against IS-controlled towns. While they have successfully pushed IS out of several areas, the group maintains control over large swathes of territory across the region.

Circuit of Wales: Economy Secretary Demands Progress on Ebbw Vale Racing Project **Welsh Government minister Ken Skates has issued an ultimatum to developers behind the troubled Circuit of Wales motorsport project, demanding they provide proof of private investment within two weeks.** The Economy Secretary has told the Heads of the Valleys Development Company (HOVDC) that they must make "faster progress" with the ambitious scheme planned for Ebbw Vale. The proposed motorsport and technology hub is claimed to have the potential to create up to 6,000 jobs in the area. A spokesman for the Circuit of Wales said the company welcomed Mr Skates' "desire for a speedy resolution." The project has been mired in uncertainty over funding arrangements. In July 2016, Mr Skates informed the firm it would need to secure at least 50% of the project's budget and underwriting from private sources before the Welsh Government would consider supporting it. On Wednesday, the Economy Secretary expressed his concerns to Assembly Members about the long-running saga. "The project has been publicly debated for many years" without sufficient private finance being found, he said. "The people of Ebbw Vale deserve to know if this project is going ahead and crucially if so when," Mr Skates added. The minister's frustration is evident in his latest statement. "I am keen to avoid more opportunity costs associated with a project that does not have a final date," he said. "I have therefore written to the Heads of Valleys Development Company today asking them to make faster progress on this project and asking for evidence to be provided to me of named investor term sheets within the next two weeks." The Circuit of Wales initially requested the Welsh Government underwrite the entire £400 million-plus project with taxpayer funds. Ministers rejected this approach and suggested they might potentially underwrite half the costs, but only if substantial private investment could be demonstrated. BBC Wales business correspondent Brian Meechan described the move as "very significant," noting it represents "the latest sign of growing frustration from the Welsh Government about how this company has been approaching this project." Sources suggest ministers still haven't received concrete information about the identity of investors or confirmation that funding is in place, despite the company bringing in a merchant bank to secure additional investment. The development's backers claim it could attract 750,000 visitors annually and inject approximately £50m into the Welsh economy each year. While insurers Aviva have been named as likely financial backers, negotiations with government over risk-sharing have continued. Earlier this year, HOVDC announced Extreme Sports Company as a new business partner for the venture.

Homes Evacuated After Suspicious Device Found in Northern Ireland Approximately 20 houses in Gelvin Gardens were evacuated on Sunday evening following the discovery of a suspicious object, believed to be a pipe bomb. The evacuation began at 17:00 GMT, with residents permitted to return to their homes four hours later. Army bomb disposal experts are currently examining the device. Police have stated that the incident is not believed to be sectarian in nature and is not connected to recent attacks elsewhere in Northern Ireland. SDLP MLA Gerard Diver condemned the incident as "disgusting" and "repugnant," emphasizing that the device posed severe danger to local residents. "Clearly, whoever put this device (there) had no regard for the safety and well being of the people of Gelvin Gardens," Mr Diver said. "These are lethal devices that could kill people very easily or maim people." Community worker Geraldine Doherty described the palpable anger among residents during the alert. "You have to condemn attacks like this at all times," she stated.

Head Teachers Reject Grammar School Expansion Plans The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) has formally backed moves to reject the government's proposed expansion of grammar schools, citing a lack of evidence that selective education improves social mobility for disadvantaged children. At their annual conference in Telford, delegates heard strong criticism of Conservative plans to increase the number of grammar schools across England, with speakers warning that the policy would add further pressure to an already strained education system. Prime Minister Theresa May has consistently defended grammar schools, arguing they provide valuable opportunities for bright children from poorer backgrounds to access high-quality education. However, this stance faces opposition from Labour, the Liberal Democrats, and now the nation's head teachers. The NAHT argues that investment in early-years education represents a far more effective approach to closing the achievement gap between rich and poor pupils. According to the union, by the time children complete primary school, the educational advantages enjoyed by wealthier students have already become firmly established. Robert Campbell, proposing the motion at the conference, criticized the government's approach: "The government is fixated with delivering a policy for the few at the expense of the many." However, the practical mechanisms through which head teachers might actively oppose the planned expansion remain unclear. ## A "Perfect Storm" Facing Secondary Schools The union used the conference platform to warn of what it describes as a "perfect storm" of challenges confronting secondary schools this summer, which could have "dire consequences for pupils and standards." These pressures include the implementation of a new secondary examination system, ongoing difficulties with teacher recruitment and retention, and projected real-term cuts of £3bn to school budgets by 2020. NAHT General Secretary Russell Hobby expressed frustration that concerns from head teachers, teachers, and parents about school funding were being ignored by ministers. He announced the union's intention to make education funding a key general election issue. "We need to make sure that all our parliamentary constituencies are asking questions on school funding," Mr. Hobby said. ## Schools Filling Public Service Gaps Conference delegates highlighted how schools are increasingly being required to compensate for underfunded public services as local government finances become progressively stretched. Past NAHT president Kim Johnson revealed that schools in Medway were being asked to part-fund police officers working in schools despite lacking adequate resources. He disclosed that his special school, Bradfields Academy, was spending £200,000 from its £6m budget on social care and health support—including two social workers, three therapists, and counsellors—services that should be provided by frontline public agencies. The government maintains that schools are receiving record levels of funding.

Jordanian Security Forces Kill Three Suspects in Raid After Deadly Karak Attack Jordanian security forces have killed three people in a raid on a house in the northern city of Irbid, according to official sources. The operation targeted suspected militants believed to be hiding in the residence, security sources confirmed. A security official told the state-run Petra news agency that Tuesday's raid was not connected to Sunday's deadly shootings in the historic city of Karak that claimed 10 lives. The Islamic State (IS) jihadist group has claimed responsibility for Sunday's attack. A statement distributed Tuesday through the Telegram messaging app stated that "four soldiers of the caliphate" had targeted Jordanian security forces and citizens of countries participating in the US-led coalition fighting IS in neighboring Iraq and Syria. Jordanian authorities have not verified the attackers' identities or confirmed any IS affiliation, referring to them only as "terrorist outlaws." Sunday's violence began when police responded to reports of a fire in Qatraneh village, approximately 32 kilometers east of Karak. Officers came under fire from the house, with two wounded before the assailants escaped toward Karak castle, a popular tourist destination overlooking the town. Interior Minister Salameh Hammad said tourists were inside the castle during the incident but denied they were held hostage, explaining they took shelter during the hours-long standoff between gunmen and security forces. Minister Hammad revealed that five or six explosive belts were recovered from the attackers, suggesting additional targets may have been planned. "I don't think the target was only Karak castle," he stated. "Maybe there were more targets, but Allah helped us discover this cell before more attacks took place." The assault killed seven Jordanian security personnel, two local civilians, and Canadian tourist Linda Vatcher, a 62-year-old retired teacher from Newfoundland visiting her son Chris, who was among 34 people injured. Jordan remains a key partner in international efforts against Islamic State militants in the region.

Scottish Business Leaders Demand Voice in New Powers Debate The chief executive of Scottish Chambers of Commerce has called for businesses to have a central role in shaping Scotland's constitutional future, warning that tax changes could have far-reaching consequences for the economy. Liz Cameron acknowledged that 2014 had brought "great advances" for Scottish business but expressed concern that many recommendations from the Smith Commission, particularly regarding taxation powers, carried significant implications for the commercial sector. "Scottish businesses have been extraordinarily patient over a protracted period that has seen political attention dominated by constitutional politics," Ms Cameron said in her New Year message. "While the political battle raged, little attention was paid to the daily endeavours and achievements of business." She criticised the referendum campaign period, claiming that "lip service was paid to the business sector" and insisted this approach must change going forward. Ms Cameron emphasised the urgency of securing "clarity, resolution and speed" on Smith Commission recommendations concerning additional powers for the Scottish Parliament. She stressed that Scotland needs not only to create more businesses but to "grow our medium-sized businesses into tomorrow's corporate giants." Highlighting the crucial link between business prosperity and social progress, she warned: "Truly, without a thriving business sector, our chances of economic and social improvement are slim indeed." The business leader called for "full and extensive consultation" with businesses and business organisations as Smith Commission proposals advance toward legislation. She particularly cautioned that taxation changes must not "prejudice the ability of Scottish companies to attract skills and talent from across the UK and overseas as well as within Scotland." Ms Cameron insisted it was "vitally important" that business voices are not just heard but listened to during this critical phase of constitutional change.

Justin Thomas Sets PGA Tour Records at Sony Open Justin Thomas continued his extraordinary form at the Sony Open in Hawaii, carding a third-round 65 to establish a new 54-hole scoring record on the PGA Tour. The 23-year-old American has been rewriting the record books for three consecutive days at Waialae Country Club. After opening with a remarkable 59 on Thursday - becoming the youngest player to break 60 on the PGA Tour - Thomas followed up with a 64 on Friday, setting the lowest 36-hole total in tour history. On Saturday, Thomas extended his commanding lead with another impressive round. Starting five shots clear, he played cautiously through the front nine, making eight consecutive pars before finally recording his first birdie at the par-five ninth hole. He added further birdies at the 10th, 14th, 16th and 18th holes to complete a bogey-free 65. His three-round total of 188 (22 under par) matches the 54-hole record previously set by Steve Stricker at the 2010 John Deere Classic. Two-time major champion Zach Johnson sits in second place after matching Thomas's 65, while England's Justin Rose is part of a group on 14 under par. Scotland's Russell Knox and American Kevin Kisner, who narrowly missed a 59 after failing to convert a nine-foot eagle putt on the final hole, are one shot further back. Thomas needs a final round of 65 or better to break the all-time 72-hole PGA Tour record of 254.

North Devon Families Told to Remove Tributes from Cemetery Graves North Devon Council has sparked controversy after ordering families to remove personal tributes from graves at Bear Street cemetery in Barnstaple, with some relatives accusing the authority of acting like "dictators." The council said people were breaking cemetery rules by spreading photographs, messages, lights and other items along the length of graves, making it difficult to maintain the grounds and reopen burial plots for relatives. Families have been given a 90-day deadline to remove the items. While some have complied, 27 families have yet to clear the graves. Peter Hull, who has been told to remove flowers from his brother-in-law's grave, expressed frustration at the decision. "For my wife it's very upsetting, for me it is more annoying that a council do not want to listen," he said. "We live in a world of democracy but they're making me feel like they're dictators." North Devon Council insisted it had tried to deal "sympathetically and tactfully" with affected families. Mark Drummond, representing the authority, explained that most graves were designed for two burials. He said the tributes made it "almost impossible to be able to get a digger in to actually reopen the grave" when needed for additional family burials.

Google Street View Captures Pembrokeshire Coast Path The Pembrokeshire Coast Path has been captured on Google Street View, offering virtual access to one of Wales' most scenic routes. The route covers 186 miles (299 km) from Amroth to St Dogmaels and passes cliff tops, beaches and estuaries. It took 28 days between April and June 2016 to film after Google loaned the authority a backpack-mounted camera. Rights of way manager Anthony Richards said it "shows the national park at its absolute best". People can access the route on their mobile phone, computer or tablet. In total, Google plans to make 15 national trails available on street view.

School Meals Investigation After Gluten Found in "Free-From" Products A county council has launched an investigation after discovering gluten in shepherd's pie and beef bolognese meals that were labeled as gluten-free and served to schoolchildren. The authority's nutritionists identified the contamination during routine ingredient monitoring of food supplied to schools across the county. The gluten was traced to a gravy powder used in both dishes. Twenty pupils registered with gluten intolerance or coeliac disease could have been affected, though the council confirmed no children have reported adverse reactions. Councillor Andrew Grant stated: "Our nutritionists regularly monitor the ingredients used by our suppliers in the food we provide and it was as a result of these checks that we picked up the discrepancy between the labelling and the actual ingredients." He added: "While the quantity of gluten a child may have consumed is quite small, it is nevertheless completely unacceptable for a child with allergies to be exposed to this risk." The council has requested a full investigation into how the mislabeling occurred and believes the issue is limited to these two specific meals. Gluten, a wheat protein, triggers an auto-immune response in intolerant individuals, causing inflammation and damage to the small intestine's lining, which impairs nutrient absorption. The condition requires strict dietary management to prevent health complications.

Nobel Prize Winner John Nash and Wife Alicia Killed in New Jersey Taxi Crash John Nash, the brilliant mathematician whose life story inspired the Oscar-winning film "A Beautiful Mind," has died alongside his wife Alicia in a taxi accident in New Jersey. Nash was 86, and his wife was 82. The couple were killed when their taxi crashed on Saturday, according to police reports. Authorities stated that both John and Alicia Nash were ejected from the vehicle during the accident, with media reports suggesting they may not have been wearing seatbelts at the time. The taxi driver and a passenger in another vehicle involved in the crash also sustained injuries. Nash was internationally renowned for his groundbreaking work in game theory, which earned him the Nobel Prize for Economics in 1994. His life, marked by both extraordinary mathematical achievements and a devastating battle with schizophrenia, became the subject of the acclaimed 2001 film "A Beautiful Mind," starring Russell Crowe. Crowe expressed his shock and sadness on Twitter, writing: "Stunned..... My heart goes out to John & Alicia & family. An amazing partnership. Beautiful minds, beautiful hearts." Director Ron Howard also paid tribute to the "brilliant" mathematician and his "remarkable" wife. Born in Bluefield, West Virginia, Nash began his academic career in Pittsburgh before moving to Princeton University. His recommendation letter famously contained just one sentence: "This man is a genius." He married Alicia Larde in 1957, shortly after publishing some of his most important works in game theory—the mathematical study of decision-making and strategic interaction. However, Nash's life took a difficult turn when he developed severe schizophrenia. "I was disturbed in this way for a very long period of time, like 25 years," Nash said in an interview on the Nobel Prize website. Alicia had him committed for psychiatric care on several occasions, and the couple divorced in 1962. Despite the divorce, the two remained close. As Nash's condition gradually improved during the 1980s, their relationship strengthened, and they remarried in 2001. Together, they became prominent advocates for mental health awareness. Nash's contributions to mathematics continued to be recognized until his final days. Just this week, he received the Abel Prize, another prestigious honour in mathematics. Christopher Eisgruber, President of Princeton University, said he was "stunned and saddened" by the news. "John's remarkable achievements inspired generations of mathematicians, economists and scientists who were influenced by his brilliant, groundbreaking work in game theory," he stated. Nash's famous Nash Equilibrium has been applied across numerous fields, including computing, evolutionary biology, artificial intelligence, and studies of economic corruption, cementing his legacy as one of the most influential mathematicians of the modern era.

Abortion Case: Charges Dropped After Warnings Issued to Belfast Pair Charges have been withdrawn against two people in a high-profile abortion case after they received formal warnings last week. A judge imposed reporting restrictions preventing identification of a 21-year-old woman involved in the case, citing a significantly elevated suicide risk associated with any media coverage. The woman had been charged with using poison to procure her own abortion. The alleged offence centred on the administration of Mifepristone and Misoprostol, drugs commonly used for medical abortions. Her co-defendant, aged 22, faced charges of supplying a poison with intent to procure a miscarriage. The incidents allegedly occurred in Belfast during 2015. Unlike the rest of the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland has never adopted the 1967 Abortion Act. Current legislation permits terminations only when a woman's life or long-term health faces serious risk. Defence lawyers presented the woman as vulnerable and immature, highlighting three previous self-harm episodes. A consultant forensic psychiatrist's assessment warned that prosecution and media attention would substantially increase suicide risk. The judge granted anonymity to protect the woman's right to life under human rights legislation. Prosecutors confirmed they re-evaluated the case following expert medical testimony. Both defendants received formal cautions on 13 January, effectively concluding the proceedings without trial. The case has reignited debate about Northern Ireland's restrictive abortion laws.

NHS Introduces Nursing Apprenticeships as Alternative Route to Degree The NHS is launching a new apprenticeship scheme that will allow up to 1,000 staff members to train as nurses without attending university through the conventional route, Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt has announced. Starting in September 2017, the nursing degree apprenticeship programme will provide an alternative pathway into the profession, working alongside the nursing associate role that was introduced a year earlier. Both initiatives are designed to offer more flexible entry routes into nursing across England. The announcement comes at a time when the government is planning significant changes to nursing education funding. Currently, student nurses receive bursaries ranging from £4,500 to £5,500 for those living in London, plus an additional £1,000 annual grant throughout their course, with tuition fees fully covered. However, ministers intend to scrap these bursaries in September 2017, introducing university fees to align health staff training with other students. Some NHS financial support will remain available for expenses such as travel costs during placements. Under the new apprenticeship scheme, trainees will typically receive funding from the NHS trust employing them. Participants can join at various stages depending on their existing qualifications and experience, and crucially, they can continue working while learning. The training pathway usually takes five years to complete and results in a full nursing degree. This differs from the nursing associate route, where trainees also receive paid training while working but would need additional qualifications to become registered nurses. The apprenticeship scheme therefore offers a direct route to full nurse registration. The Royal College of Nursing welcomed the expansion of training opportunities but urged caution. Chief executive Janet Davies said: "Nursing has progressed over many years, we must be careful to learn from the lessons of the past when student nurses were often seen as nursing on the cheap. We must be careful we do not create a two-tier system which reduces equality of opportunity." She emphasised the importance of attracting people from all ages and diverse backgrounds into the profession whilst ensuring new courses meet educational standards. Mr Hunt defended the initiative, saying: "Nurses are the lifeblood of our NHS, but the routes to a nursing degree currently shut out some of the most caring, compassionate staff in our country. Not everyone wants to take time off to study full time at university, so by creating hundreds of new apprentice nurses, we can help healthcare assistants and others reach their potential as a fully trained nurse." Chief nursing officer Professor Jane Cummings added that the programme offers "a new, exciting route into nursing that is open to more people whether they are working within the NHS already or would like to pursue a career in nursing."

Protestors Disrupt James Bulger Memorial Event at Liverpool Hotel A charity event in memory of James Bulger was disrupted by protestors who broke windows and kicked doors at Liverpool's Titanic Hotel on Friday night. The incident occurred during an event hosted by Liverpool mayor Joe Anderson, when approximately 40 members of Love Activists staged a demonstration understood to be targeting the mayor rather than the memorial occasion. Stuart Fergus, married to James's mother Denise, condemned the protestors as "vile" and described how one member used a rolled-up banner bearing James's image as a battering ram. The disturbance left Mrs Fergus in tears as security staff worked to remove the group from the building. "We heard them say'get Joe out' and that was when we realised what it was all about," Mr Fergus said. "But this wasn't a political night. There was nothing political about it at all, so we are surprised." He praised the people of Merseyside for their continued support of the family, adding: "Denise adores the people of Merseyside, who have always stood by her and helped her in James's name." Merseyside Police confirmed that about 12 members of the group entered the hotel's reception area, causing damage to several items. A spokeswoman for Love Activists claimed the protest was peaceful and alleged that security staff assaulted group members. She insisted they were unaware the event was connected to James Bulger. "As far as we are concerned, both prior to the event and at the event itself, there was no indication that the event was anything to do with James Bulger," she said. "Of course we would not want to offend the name of James Bulger." When asked about apologising to the family, the spokeswoman said: "We regret any upset caused."

Mike Leigh to Direct Film About 1819 Peterloo Massacre British director Mike Leigh is set to helm a film about the Peterloo Massacre, a pivotal moment in British history when government forces violently dispersed a peaceful pro-democracy gathering in Manchester in 1819. The incident saw approximately 15 people killed and hundreds injured when troops charged into a crowd of 60,000 who had assembled to demand political reform. Leigh told Screen International the project holds "personal resonance" for him as a native of Manchester and Salford. The film, reportedly Leigh's biggest-budget production to date, is scheduled to shoot in 2017. The director will reunite with cinematographer Dick Pope, who earned an Oscar nomination for their previous collaboration on Mr Turner. That 2014 biographical drama garnered four Academy Award nominations and has grossed over £6.4 million in the UK alone, despite Leigh and star Timothy Spall missing out on hoped-for wins. Leigh emphasized the Peterloo Massacre's "universal political significance," noting that the historic event was a defining moment in British political history and led to the founding of the Guardian newspaper. Currently, Leigh is rehearsing with the English National Opera for their production of Gilbert and Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance, opening May 9th. He previously explored the famous duo in his 1999 film Topsy-Turvy.

NI Water Customers Face Service Interruptions Due to Industrial Action Customers across Northern Ireland are facing the prospect of significant water supply interruptions as industrial action by trade unions continues to affect NI Water services. The disruption is being caused by ongoing industrial action by three trade unions - Nipsa, Unite and GMB - whose members voted last month for a work-to-rule and withdrawal of on-call services and overtime. Regional Development Minister Danny Kennedy met with union representatives on Wednesday in an attempt to resolve the dispute. However, he made it clear that any resolution would have to be within the Northern Ireland Executive's current pay and pensions policy. NI Water chief executive Sara Venning expressed regret on Friday that the industrial action was preventing customers from receiving an "essential public service". She said she believed the proposals in the latest offer presented to the unions "could be acceptable" and appealed for measures to be put in place to protect public drinking water while the proposals were being considered. "We are working round the clock from an operational perspective to minimise the impact on customers," Ms Venning said. "We have been talking to the unions almost daily. We are working late into the night to try and find a proposal and a common ground that would enable the unions to withdraw and to suspend this action." Since Wednesday's meeting, NI Water said "intensive negotiations" had been ongoing. The company has made a third formal offer to unions "which includes movement on pension issues as well as the potential for a two-year pay settlement". While this offer is being considered, NI Water sought a re-instatement of the Christmas arrangement to protect public health and critical customers, but this request was declined. "The result of this is that customers across Northern Ireland now face the prospect of supply interruptions on a scale greater than those which affected Fermanagh and Tyrone during the week," the company said in a statement. NI Water emphasised that while it had sought to end the dispute by putting forward numerous proposals, "the key demand from unions that pension reform be deferred is not something that NI Water management have in their power to deliver." The company said the major incident regime which has been in place since before Christmas would continue over the weekend. This regime has largely allowed services to be maintained across the province, but without the emergency cover that has been withdrawn, customers will suffer. "Unfortunately the extent and exact location is something which we cannot predict in advance," the company warned. Where customers are off supply for more than 24 hours, NI Water said it will seek to provide alternative water supplies, though the company acknowledged that its ability to provide these alternatives will also be impacted by the ongoing industrial action.

Chibok Schoolgirl Rescued by Nigerian Troops After Boko Haram Abduction A 15-year-old Nigerian schoolgirl has been rescued by government troops after being abducted by Boko Haram militants, according to presidential spokesman Femi Adesina. While the girl attended the same school in Chibok as the 276 girls kidnapped in 2014, she was taken in a separate incident. The teenager was found by security forces as she attempted to escape from her captors in north-eastern Nigeria, where the militant group has been waging an eight-year insurgency aimed at establishing an Islamic caliphate. Three years after the mass abduction that shocked the world, 113 of the original Chibok girls remain in Boko Haram captivity. However, 103 have been released, including 82 freed earlier this month in a prisoner exchange involving five Boko Haram commanders. These 82 girls met with President Muhammadu Buhari on 7 May and are expected to reunite with their families this week. President Buhari has stated that the government remains "in constant touch through negotiations, through local intelligence, to secure the release of the remaining girls and other abducted persons unharmed." Aid organisations emphasize that while the Chibok case received international attention, thousands of others abducted by Boko Haram have received little media coverage or support. The conflict has killed more than 30,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands, according to government figures. Aid agencies are now warning of potential famine in the region, as residents have been unable to farm for several years.

Church Break-in: Vandals Urinate in Holy Water at Northampton Catholic Church Would-be thieves who broke into a Northampton Catholic church caused extensive damage and desecrated holy water by urinating in it, police have confirmed. The perpetrators smashed through a window at St Mary's Roman Catholic Church on Bridge Street before using fire extinguishers to break down internal doors during Thursday's break-in. Father Marc Lyden-Smith expressed shock at the discovery, saying he found it "incredible" that anyone could commit such an act. A police officer detected the contamination of the holy water stoup during the investigation. Despite the vandalism, nothing was reported stolen from the church. Cleaning volunteers discovered the damage Thursday morning. The holy water stoup, typically positioned near the church entrance for Catholics to make the sign of the cross upon entering, has since been cleaned. Father Lyden-Smith responded philosophically to the incident: "It is disappointing but it is the year of mercy and we have to keep that in our thoughts."

Guernsey Honors Canadian Military Hero Gen Isaac Brock on 200th Anniversary A series of commemorative events were held in Guernsey, Channel Islands, marking the 200th anniversary of the death of General Sir Isaac Brock, the celebrated "Hero of Upper Canada." The day's ceremonies began at 08:45 BST when Colonel Paul Keddy, the Canadian Defence Attache, raised the Canadian flag on the memorial mast, honoring the military commander born on this British island. General Brock earned his legendary status in 1812 when he led a combined force of British, Canadian and First Nation troops to victory against an invading American army during the War of 1812. He was killed at the Battle of Queenston Heights in Ontario on October 13, 1812. A formal parade followed the flag-raising ceremony, featuring veterans and standard bearers from local emergency services, armed forces groups, and volunteer and charity organizations. The procession marched from the memorial mast to Boots, which now occupies the site of Sir Isaac's former family home. Wreaths were solemnly laid outside the shop before participants continued to the Town Church for a commemoration service. A 15-gun salute was fired precisely at midday Guernsey time, corresponding exactly to 07:00 Canadian time—marking 200 years to the moment when General Brock fell in battle. Plans to unveil a specially commissioned bust were postponed due to the sculptor's illness. The Brock Memorial Foundation, established by one of the general's descendants, aims to "provide support for projects that celebrate the legacy of Sir Isaac Brock," including plans to erect identical statues in both Guernsey and Canada. Richard Collas, the Bailiff of Guernsey, shared a letter from Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, who wrote: "His leadership and bravery at the Battle of Queenston Heights earned him iconic status as the'Hero of Upper Canada.' Though he died in defence of the colony, his sacrifice was not in vain. Brock's thwarting of the American assault was a key victory in the War of 1812 and a step towards forging a strong and united Canada."

Paramount Pulls Out of Planned Kent Theme Park Resort A major theme park development near Dartford has lost its headline partner after Paramount Pictures withdrew from the ambitious project. The London Resort Company Holdings (LRCH) confirmed it has ended its agreement with the Hollywood studio, though the company insists the massive entertainment complex will still proceed as planned. The resort, set for the Swanscombe Peninsula, is envisioned to be twice the size of London's Olympic Park. Plans include 5,000 hotel rooms, a water park, and more than 50 rides and attractions across a 900-acre brownfield site. Originally, attractions were to be based on Paramount's extensive catalogue of films and television programmes. However, chief executive Humphrey Percy said the split actually provides greater flexibility. "What it means is we won't have the name Paramount above the door," Percy explained. "We are not looking for a new studio." He emphasized that the Paramount deal had restricted the park from collaborating with other entertainment companies. "It just gives us the freedom to work with other partners," Percy said. LRCH plans to submit its planning application in November, with the park scheduled to open in 2022 pending government approval of a Development Consent Order. Despite losing its flagship brand, Percy stressed: "We are committed to going ahead - nothing has changed on that score."

DX Group Acquires City Link Assets for £1.125m Following Courier Firm's Collapse DX Group has announced the acquisition of assets from the collapsed courier company City Link for £1.125 million, purchasing scanners, cages, and certain intellectual property rights from the failed business. The deal comes as administrators continue to wind down City Link's operations following its dramatic collapse over the Christmas period. DX, which floated on the London Stock Exchange's Alternative Investment Market (AIM) last year with a valuation of £175 million, is led by former City Link managing director Petar Cvetkovic, who left the courier firm in 2009. Commenting on the acquisition, Mr Cvetkovic expressed sympathy for those affected by City Link's failure. "It is very sad that City Link has been unable to continue as a going concern, particularly for its employees and contractors," he said. "The administrators are now proceeding with an orderly sale of assets and we have made a limited investment to acquire certain assets." The DX chief executive added that his company was committed to helping former City Link staff, stating: "We are also doing all we can to provide opportunities for former City Link employees and contractors and to offer solutions to customers who may need a new carrier." City Link's administrators announced 2,356 job losses on New Year's Eve after rejecting a last-minute rescue bid from an unnamed consortium, which "offered no money up front and significantly undervalued the assets to be acquired." The Coventry-based company, founded in 1969 and employing 2,727 people, had suffered sustained losses. It was acquired by Better Capital for £1 in April 2013, with the investment firm subsequently injecting £40 million. However, administrators Ernst & Young concluded this investment proved insufficient to save the business. Business Secretary Vince Cable confirmed government support measures were in place to assist affected workers in finding new employment.

Delhi Brings Back Odd-Even Car Scheme to Combat Pollution Delhi has reintroduced its controversial odd-even car rationing scheme in a bid to tackle the Indian capital's severe air pollution crisis. Private cars with even and odd number plates will only be allowed on alternate days from 15 to 30 April, Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal announced. The scheme means vehicles with registration numbers ending in odd digits can drive on odd-numbered dates, while even-numbered plates are permitted on even dates. This marks the second phase of the experimental program, following a fortnight-long trial from 1 January that took more than a third of the city's three million private cars off the road, significantly easing traffic congestion. However, it remains unclear whether the initiative actually helped reduce pollution levels. The local government has described this second phase as "decisive" in determining the scheme's effectiveness as a pollution control measure and whether it should be implemented monthly going forward. The scheme will be enforced by 2,000 traffic personnel, 580 enforcement officials, and more than 5,000 civil defence volunteers. Violators face fines of 2,000 rupees (£21; $30), and a special task force has been appointed to investigate complaints. As with the January trial, emergency vehicles including ambulances, police cars, fire engines, and taxis are exempt. Single women drivers and two-wheelers are also allowed daily access. While January's trial successfully reduced traffic congestion, its impact on air pollution remains disputed. Authorities claimed a "more than 50% drop in air pollution primarily caused by vehicular traffic," but the state-run System of Air Quality Weather Forecasting and Research showed PM 2.5 particulate levels hovering between "very poor" and "severe," well above WHO safe limits. Delhi faces mounting pollution challenges with 8.5 million vehicles on its roads and approximately 1,400 new cars added daily to the capital's already congested streets.

Lincoln Christmas Market Makes Just £4,000 Profit After £100,000 Loss Lincoln's Christmas Market generated a meagre profit of just £4,000 in 2013, prompting concerns about its financial viability following a £100,000 loss the previous year. The City of Lincoln Council has attributed the disappointing figures to a significant decline in coach parties and reduced stallholder numbers. Coach visits dropped dramatically from 438 in 2012 to just 314 last Christmas, while the number of stalls fell from 243 to 199. The unavailability of parts of Lincoln Castle also impacted the event. Despite the financial challenges, the council insists the market's future remains secure. However, it has proposed a controversial 12% increase in pitch fees, raising the maximum charge to £1,411. Council leader Ric Metcalfe defended the decision, arguing that stallholders making "a significant amount of money" should contribute more towards running costs. "Given there are very significant overhead costs falling on the council primarily but other public authorities as well, it's only fair that those businesses should share the infrastructure costs of maintaining the event," he said. The proposed increase has drawn criticism from local business leaders. Linda Wardale, chairman of the Bailgate Traders' Group, warned that traders may struggle to afford the higher fees. "There will not be the variety of stalls there and it could be a potential flop," she cautioned. The 2012 market was heavily criticised after organisers introduced a controversial one-way system to manage overcrowding. A council report now acknowledges that "a fundamental review of the business plan is required" to ensure the event's sustainability.

National Theatre Makes Rare Move into Film Production with London Road The National Theatre has ventured into film production for the first time with London Road, though artistic director Rufus Norris insists this doesn't signal a permanent shift in the institution's focus. "We're not opening up a film slate because that's not what we're given public money to do," Norris told the BBC. "We are a theatre, but occasionally things come up where you think,'Why not? Let's give it a go.'" The NT acquired the film rights to the musical London Road last year, marking its first foray into production. While there have been successful adaptations of NT plays previously—including Amadeus, The Madness of King George, The History Boys and War Horse—the theatre had no financial or creative stake in those films. The theatre has been expanding its reach through live cinema broadcasts of shows including Macbeth, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, Frankenstein and The Audience, but producing a standalone film represents new territory. Norris admitted making a feature film was "not something that we set out to do," though he's eager to "see how it goes in the next few weeks and months." While the theatre won't open a full-time film division, he added: "I wouldn't be surprised if another little idea popped up sooner or later. I would never say we'd never do it again." Norris directed both the stage and screen versions of London Road, which documents the arrest of Steve Wright, an Ipswich man convicted of murdering five sex workers in 2008. The production uses real dialogue from rural townsfolk whose lives were disrupted when they discovered a serial killer had been living in their community. The cast includes Olivia Colman, Anita Dobson and Tom Hardy, who had a "get-out clause" written into his contract over concerns about his singing ability. "He said from the beginning,'I'm going to keep the back door open until the last minute, so you've got to have a Plan B,'" Norris revealed. "But there was no Plan B. I knew that Tom wouldn't give up."

Lukashenko: Leaders Ate Omelettes During Marathon Minsk Peace Talks Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko has revealed details about the grueling 16-hour peace negotiations that produced a ceasefire agreement for eastern Ukraine on Thursday. Speaking to Belarus news agency Belta, Lukashenko described how world leaders sustained themselves during the marathon talks in Minsk. "They ate omelettes, cheese, dairy produce, drank several buckets of coffee," he said, adding that his role was "to provide the ammunition on time." The Belarusian leader emphasized that only Belarusian and Russian products were served—a pointed reference to Russia's ban on EU food imports imposed in response to Western sanctions over the Ukraine conflict. The talks brought together Russian President Vladimir Putin, French President Francois Hollande, German Chancellor Angela Merkel, and Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko. Their expert advisers "slept in shifts - in order to keep clear heads," Lukashenko noted. Lukashenko, often called "Europe's last dictator," has ruled Belarus in authoritarian style since 1994, maintaining tight state control and suppressing dissent in the former Soviet republic.

Lions Tours Must Continue Despite Club Concerns, Says Gavin Hastings The British and Irish Lions remains the pinnacle of rugby despite mounting pressure from club owners, according to former captain Gavin Hastings, who has called for stakeholders to prioritize the historic touring tradition over domestic interests. Hastings, speaking to BBC 5 live, delivered a pointed message to Premiership club owners who have expressed dissatisfaction with the current Lions model: "You have to say'guys, the Lions is bigger than your clubs'. Let's look at what's best for British and Irish rugby - that's the Lions."
