The debate over the Lions' future has intensified, with plans to shorten tours from 2021 onwards amid concerns from club rugby directors. The current New Zealand tour has particularly highlighted tensions, with the squad arriving just three days after the domestic season concluded and before embarking on a 10-game itinerary that some club directors have labelled "ludicrous." Hastings, who captained the 1993 Lions tour of New Zealand and led the side to victory in the second Test in Wellington, witnessed history repeat itself on Saturday. The former Scotland full-back was in attendance at the Westpac Stadium to watch the current Lions square the series with a 24-21 victory - ending his 24-year reign as the last Lions captain to defeat the All Blacks in a Test match. "That final whistle will be a moment that will live with everyone who was there for a very long time," said Hastings, who described himself as "delighted" to share the distinction. "We are all supporters. To share in that joy of victory was amazing, and it will show the Lions has to stay." Despite the ever-growing popularity of the Lions brand, the future of the tours hangs in the balance. While some parties advocate for condensed schedules, Lions organisers maintain that anything shorter than the current format would prove damaging. Hastings acknowledges the ongoing dispute but insists a compromise must be reached. "It just goes on and on," he said. "For people who have been with the Lions and are as passionate as I am, we feel there is no debate - the Lions should continue."

West Way Shopping Development Unveils Video Plans Developer Doric Properties has released a "walk-through" video showcasing proposed plans for the West Way shopping area in Botley, following a request from North Hinksey Parish Council. The development, submitted to Vale of White Horse District Council in December 2013, features restaurants, a hotel, and student accommodation. Proponents claim the project will generate 600 construction jobs and 480 permanent positions once operational. However, the plans have faced opposition from residents concerned about the development's size relative to the site. Critics have also raised issues regarding potential increases in traffic and congestion in the area. The district council continues to review the application.

Smart Meters Will Save Consumers Little Money, MPs Warn The government's ambitious smart meter rollout programme will deliver only modest savings on household energy bills, a parliamentary committee has warned. The Science and Technology Committee said ministers must make a stronger case for the wider benefits of the technology, including creating a more efficient energy grid and reducing pollution, rather than focusing primarily on cost savings for consumers. The government has pledged that every home and business in the country will be offered a smart meter by the end of 2020, requiring the installation of 53 million meters across more than 30 million premises over the next four years. Smart meters automatically measure gas and electricity consumption and send readings directly to energy suppliers, eliminating the need for manual meter readings. However, the massive installation programme has encountered significant problems. The committee highlighted that the communication system linking meters to suppliers has been delayed. More significantly, there is an "unresolved" issue with early meters installed during the initial rollout phase losing their smart functionality when customers switch energy suppliers. Interim committee chairwoman Tania Mathias criticised the government's handling of the problem. "The government has known for years that early smart meters can lose their smartness if the customer switches supplier," she said. "Ministers merely have an'ambition' to fix this by 2020. Taxpayers will be unimpressed with this situation, and timely action is needed." Ms Mathias emphasised that consumers need personalised advice on maximising the benefits of smart meters. "The'smartness' comes from what customers can do with them - fit and forget would be a wasted opportunity," she said. The committee also called on the government to reassure customers about cybersecurity concerns surrounding the technology. A spokeswoman for the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy defended the programme, stating: "Smart meters will bring Britain's energy infrastructure into the 21st century - as the committee has made clear." Sacha Deshmukh, chief executive of Smart Energy GB, which is managing the rollout campaign, highlighted "the transformative effect smart meters will have, not only on how we buy and use energy as individual consumers, but on Britain's energy infrastructure as a whole."

Primark Opens 16 New Stores as Owner AB Foods Reports Strong Performance Associated British Foods (AB Foods) has announced the opening of 16 new Primark outlets across the UK, Europe and the United States last year, as the discount fashion retailer continues its expansion despite economic uncertainties. The company predicts total sales for Primark will increase by 11% in the six months to March 4, with no evidence that UK consumers are cutting back on spending. Finance director John Bason emphasized the resilience of the British consumer, stating: "The consumer in the UK has got more disposable income this year than they had a year ago - fact." Primark's UK operations are performing particularly well, with like-for-like sales expected to rise by 2% for the six-month period, though remaining flat for the overall business. The chain plans to open additional stores in London, Belgium, Spain and the US over the coming three months. However, AB Foods cautioned that the weakened pound could put pressure on Primark's profit margins. The retailer, which accounts for approximately half of the group's profits, faces increased costs as sterling has fallen 16% against the US dollar and 10% against the euro since last June's EU referendum, making imports more expensive. Industry analysts suggest Primark's competitive pricing offers some protection, but the retailer faces growing competition. Kate Ormrod, senior analyst at GlobalData, warned: "Ensuring product ranges remain fashionable and relevant will be imperative to retain appeal. This is particularly important as emerging players such as boohoo.com and Missguided continue to encroach on Primark's fast fashion USP." Beyond Primark, AB Foods' other divisions are performing strongly. Twinings tea and Ovaltine reported revenues well ahead of last year, with Twinings gaining market share in the US, Australia, France and the UK. Ovaltine showed good growth in Vietnam and Brazil. The company's sugar business also benefited from higher prices and increased African production. AB Foods expects "excellent progress" in group profits, with its full-year outlook unchanged. Shares traded flat at £26.09 in afternoon London trading, though they have declined more than 20% over the past year.

Cardiff Student Jailed for Planning to Join Islamic State in Syria A Cardiff college student who saved £3,000 to travel to Syria and join Islamic State has been sentenced to more than three years in a young offenders' institution after admitting preparation of terrorist acts. The Old Bailey heard the only reason 19-year-old Syed Choudhury did not go was because he could not find someone to travel with. The Cardiff and Vale College student admitted to engaging in conduct in preparation of terrorist acts. He will serve three years, four months at a young offenders' institution. Originally from Bradford, Choudhury was living with his aunt in Cardiff. The court heard he had been radicalised by people he regarded as elders after he left home to study in Cardiff. ## Chilling Custody Rant His extreme views were revealed when he ranted to officers about Sharia law, saying he wanted to be the one to bring it to the UK while in custody. "The bluntness of what you said on that occasion is chilling. It reveals your dangerousness," Judge Peter Rook QC said. "However I do accept you are immature. You are impressionable to indoctrination. "You now say'I'm lucky I came to prison, I'm lucky I got stopped'. "You have shown some awareness of how misguided your earlier extremist position was." ## Gaza Protest Brought Attention The court heard how in July 2014, Choudhury took part in a demonstration in Cardiff protesting about the conflict in Gaza. He carried a banner proclaiming his support for Islamic State which brought him to the attention of anti-terrorism officers. Prosecutor Sarah Whitehouse QC said in the weeks following the demonstration, Choudhury accessed websites about travelling to Syria and another one that was entitled "10 reasons to join ISIS". Ms Whitehouse said he also downloaded images that showed his active interest in extremism and had conversations on social media about travelling to Turkey and Syria to fight. ## £3,000 Saved for Jihadi Travel Choudhury was arrested last December and during interview he repeatedly said he supported IS and that he would be happy to kill non-believers under Islamic State rule. The court also heard throughout 2014 he was downloading extremist ideology and had saved £3,000 working in a fast food restaurant to fund his jihadi travel. He was due to go on trial on Wednesday at the Old Bailey, but changed his plea after the jury had been sworn in. Abdul Iqbal QC, defending, said the evidence showed Choudhury's enthusiasm to travel to Turkey or Syria, but said that Choudhury had not got further than making inquiries. "There are no direct links with anyone in the area of Turkey or Syria who could assist him," he said. "Naivety, immaturity and lack of insight are the hallmarks of his character," Mr Iqbal said. Choudhury was vulnerable and was targeted by older individuals in the Cardiff area who indoctrinated him in extremist views, he added. ## Police Statement Following the sentence, South Wales Police Assistant Chief Constable Nikki Holland said: "Cardiff is a multi-cultural city and local policing teams, together with partner agencies, work hard to ensure that the people who live there can do so in a safe and peaceful environment. "It is therefore vital that those who wish to support violent and murderous actions against others are identified both through rigorous policing and the support of communities who can report suspicious actions and behaviour."

MPs Clash Over Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon Funding Concerns A heated exchange erupted in Westminster as MPs debated the future of the Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon project, with politicians crossing party lines over concerns about government commitment to the groundbreaking renewable energy scheme. Conservative MP Craig Williams accused Labour colleagues of jeopardizing the project by publicly questioning the government's dedication, claiming their comments were "shaking" potential investors during crucial price negotiations. The dispute arose during a Westminster Hall debate on Tuesday following the Autumn Statement, when Neath Labour MP Christina Rees expressed concern that the "vital" lagoon received no mention in Chancellor George Osborne's Spending Review. "In light of the landmark agreement reached in Paris this last weekend, we know that projects like the tidal lagoon are essential if this country is to meet its international obligations to combat climate change," Ms Rees said, referring to the recent UN climate change conference. Cardiff North Conservative Mr Williams sharply intervened, warning: "Investors around the world are being shaken by what you and mainly members of the Labour party are saying about the tidal lagoon at a very critical point when we're negotiating the strike price. You are endangering lagoons, not just Swansea." Ms Rees firmly rejected the accusation, responding: "We're not giving the uncertainty - the government are." The £1bn Swansea Bay project has faced delays, with Tidal Lagoon Power announcing in October that construction would be postponed until 2017 while negotiations continue with UK government ministers over energy pricing. Ms Rees emphasized the project's importance to south Wales, highlighting potential investment and up to 1,900 construction jobs. "It will be a travesty if the UK government were to fail to deliver this opportunity," she concluded.

Everton Sign Striker Oumar Niasse from Lokomotiv Moscow Everton have completed the signing of Senegalese striker Oumar Niasse from Russian side Lokomotiv Moscow on a four-and-a-half-year contract. The 25-year-old forward has been in impressive form this season, netting 13 goals in 23 appearances for the Russian club before making the move to Goodison Park. Everton manager Roberto Martinez expressed his satisfaction with the acquisition: "We're delighted as Oumar is a player we've been following for a long time. He brings a real hunger and desire to be successful into what is already a strong squad." The signing comes after Everton's attempts to secure their primary target, Dynamo Kiev's Andriy Yarmolenko, proved unsuccessful. The move also follows recent departures, with Steven Naismith joining Norwich and Aiden McGeady moving to Sheffield Wednesday on loan. Niasse revealed he had been monitoring Everton since October after learning of their interest. "I was interested to see how they play. If you see players who are aged 20 or 21 and see them perform like that, you know you have a good coach," the striker said. The transfer represents Everton's efforts to strengthen their attacking options for the remainder of the season.

Philippines' Duterte Threatens to Drop US Arms Deal Over Human Rights Concerns Philippines President Rodrigo Duterte said Monday he would seek alternative weapons suppliers after a US senator moved to block a rifle sale over human rights concerns related to his controversial drug war. According to Reuters, a US senator had planned to block the arms purchase over concerns about human rights violations. The decision came as thousands have been killed as part of Mr Duterte's bloody crackdown on drugs since he took office. In a televised speech on Monday, Mr Duterte said: "We will not insist on buying expensive arms from the United States. We don't need them. We will just have to look for another source that is cheaper and maybe as durable and as good as those made in the place we are ordering them." The Philippine leader, who once promised to kill 100,000 criminals, has consistently brushed off criticism from the UN, which said the killings could be crimes under international law, as well as from the US and numerous human rights bodies. Last week, Mr Duterte accused his American counterparts of "rude" treatment and said he could alternatively source rifles from Russia or China. "Look at these monkeys, the 26,000 firearms we wanted to buy, they don't want to sell. These American fools," he said. The US State Department declined to comment on the sale of rifles to the Philippines, but spokesman John Kirby said Mr Duterte's rhetoric was "inexplicably at odds" with US-Philippine relations. Philippine police chief Ronald dela Rosa supported the president's position, saying the US had lost out on the rifle sale.

Historic Fareham School Faces Closure After a Century **Wykeham House School in Fareham could close at the end of the Autumn term after being open for 100 years.** The independent school, which was founded in 1913 as a girls' school, announced it is facing closure due to mounting financial pressures affecting both its boys' and girls' sites. In a statement, the school confirmed: "Due to increasing financial pressure, Wykeham House School in Fareham is facing the prospect of closure at the end of the Autumn term." The Board of Trustees has assured families that the school will continue operating until at least the end of term. Staff are actively working with parents to help secure alternative school placements for affected pupils. The announcement affects both the boys' and girls' schools, which operate on separate sites with independent teaching but function under the same organizational structure. "Although they are on separate sites and are taught separately, they are part of the same organisation so this news applies to both sites," the statement added. The potential closure marks the end of an era for the century-old institution.

UK's Syrian Refugee Programme to Cost Nearly £1.2bn Over Five Years The UK government's plan to resettle 20,000 Syrian refugees over five years will cost approximately £1.2 billion, ministers have revealed, raising concerns about transparency and funding. Syrian refugee minister Richard Harrington estimated the figure would be £589m. Home Affairs Committee chairman Keith Vaz said the cost was "huge". The UK has already accepted more than 1,000 Syrian refugees, as part of the government's Vulnerable Persons Relocation (VPR) scheme. The figures came to light in a written response to a parliamentary question from Labour's Coventry MP Jim Cunningham. Mr Harrington's reply confirmed that the first year of the VPR scheme will be paid for through the UK's overseas aid budget, and that the government had already allocated £129m to help local authorities with costs for the remaining years. But it is unclear where the remainder of the money will come from. Mr Harrington said the scheme would cost approximately £1.2 billion over its five-year duration, though the precise breakdown of annual costs was not provided. Mr Vaz said he had written to the prime minister for clarification. "This is a huge figure," he added. "As the Home Office refuses to provide regular updates on the numbers being resettled, or where they are being placed, there is an unacceptable lack of transparency in the use of these significant funds." So far 1,194 Syrians have been resettled in the UK under the scheme, including 605 under-18s, according to government figures. Local authorities can volunteer to take part in the VPR scheme and as of the beginning of December, 55 had signed up. The government has previously signalled that the refugees getting resettled in the UK will be taken from established refugee camps. Syria has been embroiled in a bloody armed conflict for nearly five years. More than 250,000 Syrians have been killed, and 11 million displaced from their homes - more than four million have already left the country. Earlier in the year, the prime minister was criticised by a group of 27 charities - including Oxfam and Amnesty International - which said the UK should take a "proportionate" share of refugees.

New Tolkien Book'Beren and Lúthien' Published on Anniversary A new book by JRR Tolkien, edited by his son Christopher, has been published, featuring a deeply personal story inspired by the author's experiences in World War One. Beren and Lúthien has been described as a "very personal story" that the Oxford professor thought up after returning from the Battle of the Somme. It was edited by his son Christopher Tolkien and contains versions of a tale that became part of The Silmarillion. The book features illustrations by Alan Lee, who won an Academy Award for his work on Peter Jackson's film trilogy. More on this and other stories from across the south of England. It is being published on Thursday by HarperCollins on the 10th anniversary of the last Middle Earth book, The Children of Húrin. Tolkien specialist John Garth, who wrote Tolkien And The Great War, said the Hobbit author used his writing like an "exorcism" of the horrors he witnessed in World War One. He said: "When he came back from the trenches, with trench fever, he spent the winter [of 1916-1917] convalescing. "He'd lost two of his dearest friends on the Somme and you can imagine he must have been inside as much of a wreck as he was physically." Mr Garth said on a walk in an East Yorkshire wood Tolkien's wife Edith danced in a glade filled with white flowers, which became the key scene in Beren and Lúthien. He said: "Mr Tolkien felt the kind of joy he must have felt at times he would never feel again." The names Beren and Lúthien are carved on the gravestone Tolkien and his wife share in Wolvercote cemetery in Oxford. The story is about the fate of lovers Beren and Lúthien, a mortal man and an immortal elf who together try to steal from the greatest of all evil beings, Melkor. For the new book Christopher Tolkien, now aged 92, has kept his father's story in the original form in which it was written and has also shown how the narrative changed to become part of The Silmarillion. Published in 1954, The Lord of the Rings was the sequel to The Hobbit and is one of the most successful novels ever written, having sold more than 150 million copies. The film adaptation, released from 2001 to 2003, is one of the highest-grossing series of all time, with the final movie also winning 11 Academy Awards, tied for the most ever with Ben Hur. NI Finance Minister Considers Corporation Tax Cut Below Republic's Rate Northern Ireland's Finance Minister has indicated the region may need to slash corporation tax below the Republic of Ireland's 12.5% rate in response to UK government plans. The Executive has sought the devolution of tax powers for years. It is committed to matching the Republic of Ireland's 12.5% rate by 2018. But Mr Ó Muilleoir said they may need to consider reducing it below that. The UK corporation tax rate is currently at 20%. However, the Chancellor, George Osborne, is now pointing to a rate "below 15%" to attract businesses when the UK leaves the EU. Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show on Tuesday, Máirtín Ó Muilleoir, said: "I think he has put a horse and carriage through our policy." The minister explained that Northern Ireland's strategy relied on two key factors: differentiating from the British rate and matching the southern rate. "We know, especially in north America, that Ireland is viewed very favourably and actually they view Ireland as one island, they are not big on borders," he said. "And if we had have been able to say, the tax rate is the same across the island, I think that would have been compelling, that's no longer true." Mr Ó Muilleoir confirmed that "unless we go for an different strategy and reduce it ever further, and that will need to be considered."

Ukraine Releases Intercepted Calls After Airliner Shot Down The Ukrainian Security Service has released what it claims are intercepted phone conversations between pro-Russian separatists discussing the downing of a civilian aircraft, posting the audio recordings on YouTube within hours of the crash. The BBC cannot independently verify the authenticity of these recordings. In the first conversation, a voice identified as separatist leader Igor Bezler reportedly tells Russian military intelligence Colonel Vasily Geranin that "the group of the Miner has just shot down a plane" near Yenakiyevo. When asked about pilots, Bezler responds that personnel have "gone to search for and photograph the plane," adding that "it's smoking." The exchange allegedly took place approximately 30 minutes after the incident. A second recording features voices identified as "The Greek" and a "Major" discussing the downed aircraft. The Major states that "the Chernukhino lads shot down the plane" from a roadblock manned by Cossacks. He describes the aircraft falling apart in mid-air near the Pertropavlovskaya coal mine, with debris scattering across residential areas. Most significantly, the Major concludes: "Basically it was 100% a civilian aircraft." When asked about the debris field, he reports finding "civilian things, medical bits and bobs, towels, toilet paper" but "nothing at all" in terms of weaponry. He mentions discovering documents belonging to "an Indonesian student from Thompson University." A third conversation allegedly involves a fighter reporting the crash near Grabovo, stating: "There are lots of corpses of women and children." The speaker notes confusion about the aircraft's identity, mentioning that while Ukrainian television reported it as a military AN-26 transport plane, the wreckage bore Malaysia Airlines markings. In the final exchange, a voice identified as Cossack commander Nikolai Kozitsyn responds to the civilian aircraft revelation by suggesting: "That means they were carrying spies. They shouldn't be flying. There is a war going on." The Ukrainian Security Service's rapid release of these recordings represents an attempt to shape the narrative surrounding the tragedy. However, the authenticity and context of the conversations remain unverified. BBC Monitoring, which reports and analyses news from global media sources, continues to follow developments in this story.

Greybull Capital in Talks to Acquire Tata Steel's Long Products Division Greybull Capital has signed a letter of intent to pursue a deal that could secure the future of thousands of steel industry jobs across the UK and Northern France, it has been announced. The investment firm is in negotiations to acquire Tata Steel's Long Products Europe division, which includes key mills in Teesside and Northern France, along with other strategic facilities. However, Tata Steel cautioned that it was "too early to give any certainty about the potential outcome of these discussions". The potential acquisition has been cautiously welcomed by steel unions following a devastating period of job losses across the industry. Roy Rickhuss, general secretary of the Community steelworkers' union, said: "We welcome the interest from Greybull in giving Long Products a future outside Tata Steel. Of course, the devil will be in the detail of the deal and we will be seeking further discussions with both Tata Steel and Greybull to fully understand their intentions and the implications for steelworkers." The UK steel sector has been severely impacted by cheap Chinese imports and collapsing prices, leading to waves of redundancies. In October, Tata Steel announced nearly 1,200 job cuts in Scunthorpe and Lanarkshire alone. The proposed deal encompasses Tata Steel UK's Scunthorpe steelworks, mills in Teesside and Northern France, Scottish facilities at Dalzell and Clydebridge, an engineering workshop in Workington, a design consultancy in York, and associated distribution facilities. Approximately 4,700 employees work in Long Products Europe, part of Tata Steel Europe's 30,000-strong workforce, including 17,000 in the UK. Greybull Capital specializes in long-term investments in struggling businesses. The firm acquired a majority stake in budget airline Monarch in October 2014, investing £125 million while staff accepted 700 redundancies and pay cuts of up to 30% to save the Luton-based carrier. Sources indicate Greybull would likely require backing from both unions and the UK government before proceeding. Detailed negotiations are expected to begin after Christmas and could take approximately three months to complete.

Inquest Opened into Death of Guernsey Woman Sarah Groves in Kashmir An inquest has been opened into the death of 24-year-old Sarah Groves from Guernsey, who died on a houseboat in Srinagar, Kashmir, on 6 April. Judge Philip Robey opened and adjourned the inquest at Guernsey magistrate's court while Indian police continue their investigations into the suspected murder. ## Suspect Held in Custody Richard De Wit, a Dutch national, was arrested on the day of Miss Groves' death and remains in custody in Srinagar on suspicion of murder. Inspector Mazir Ahmed confirmed that De Wit is awaiting trial and is expected to be charged with murder. ## Victim's Journey to India The inquest heard that Miss Groves had travelled alone to India on 15 November without a fixed itinerary. Four of her relatives, including her father Victor Groves, attended the court hearing. While in the southern state of Goa, she met Samir Ahmad. In February, the pair travelled together to Konakhan near Srinagar in Kashmir, where she lived on a houseboat belonging to his family. Her family had expressed concerns about this move, as the Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) website described the Kashmir region as a "no-go area." ## Family Notified of Death At approximately 05:30 BST on 6 April, Victor Groves received a call from Indian police informing him of his daughter's murder. He immediately contacted Guernsey Police, who, with assistance from the FCO, confirmed the tragic news. ## Forensic Examinations Miss Groves' body has undergone two post-mortem examinations. The first was conducted in India before her body was repatriated to Guernsey on 13 April. The second examination was carried out by Home Office pathologist Dr Amanda Jeffrey. Judge Robey has agreed to release Miss Groves' body to her family, though a full forensic pathology report is still awaited. ## Memorial Service Planned A memorial service will be held at St James Concert Hall in St Peter Port on 8 June. Miss Groves' family have announced that "the event will be informal, open to anyone and everyone who knew or knew of Sarah and bright colours are the order of the day."

South Korea Accuses North of Sending Spy Drones After Joint Investigation South Korean and US experts have concluded that three unmanned drones discovered in South Korea earlier this year originated from North Korea, according to officials in Seoul. Ministry spokesman Kim Min-seok announced on Thursday that the finding represents "clear military provocation" by Pyongyang. North Korea had previously denied any ownership of the unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), which were recovered from different locations across South Korea between March and April. "By analysing the data, the joint investigation team has secured the smoking gun - clear, scientific evidence that all three UAVs originated from North Korea," Mr Kim stated. He emphasized that the drones were "programmed to fly over" sensitive military facilities, constituting a new military threat requiring a robust response. South Korean Vice-Defence Minister Baek Seung-joo characterized the drones as rudimentary in design but warned of potential dangers. "However, there is always the possibility that the North might use them for attacks after arming them with high explosives, considering its irrational and reckless tendency for provocative acts," he told journalists. One drone found in Paju, near the demilitarised zone separating the two nations, reportedly carried a camera that captured images of military installations and South Korea's presidential compound. The discovery follows preliminary investigations last month that initially pointed to North Korean origins. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in armistice rather than a peace treaty. North Korea continues to face international sanctions over its nuclear weapons programme.

Deadly Illicit Alcohol Claims Dozens of Lives in Kenya At least dozens of Kenyans have died and many others have been blinded since Sunday after consuming illegal homemade alcohol across four counties, officials reported. The deaths occurred in Embu, Kitui, Limuru and Kiambu counties. Authorities believe the toxic brew contained methanol, a dangerous substance often added to strengthen the drink's potency. Officials suspect the contaminated liquor originated from the same distributor or batch. Consumption of homemade alcohol, locally known as "changaa" or "kumi kumi", remains widespread in Kenya where many residents cannot afford commercially produced, standardised alcohol. This tragedy echoes a similar incident in 2005 when over 45 people died from methanol-laced illegal alcohol. In response to recurring poisonings, Kenya's government passed legislation in 2010 to regulate traditional brewing by legalising production whilst requiring commercial bottling and sales only at licensed premises. However, the informal brewing industry continues to thrive despite these regulatory efforts.

S4C Urged to Include Automatic English Subtitles on Welsh Language Programmes A former S4C commissioner has called for the Welsh language broadcaster to introduce automatic English subtitles on all programmes to make them more accessible to non-Welsh speakers. Tweli Griffiths told BBC Radio Cymru's Post Cyntaf that the move would be inclusive and could attract more viewers to the channel. He said the proposal has been prompted by the "continuing decline in the number of Welsh speakers" and argued it was time to adopt new approaches. Mr Griffiths, who spent two years as a commissioner for factual language programming at S4C, called on the broadcaster to follow the example of TG4, the Gaelic language channel, where English subtitles appear automatically on screen for all programmes. He said Welsh speakers needed to "adopt measures that will attract more people who don't speak the language to show an interest and be entertained by it." Mr Griffiths added: "In Ireland, there is a different philosophy. It's not just a channel for Irish speakers. It is for the whole population. That's the kind of message we need to get across here in Wales." In response, Rachel Evans, S4C deputy director for content and broadcasting, said the idea was "interesting" but the broadcaster had not received feedback suggesting viewers wanted automatic subtitles. She said: "We haven't received feedback that the audience want to see automatic subtitles on screen, and we have no plans at the moment to introduce them." Ms Evans added that subtitles were available for 78.05% of S4C programmes during 2014-15.

2015 Set to Become One of Warmest Years on Record, WMO Reports Even more striking is the fact that if this occurs, then fourteen out of fifteen of the warmest years on record will have occurred since the turn of the century. However, while record-breaking warmth is consistent with the general trend of global warming, it's not always the case that each year is warmer than the previous one. There are temporary ups and downs that ride on top of the overall warming trend. It's quite possible for a few years to elapse before the next record year, and the warming can speed up or slow down for runs of years, as happened for example in the slowdown of warming since the end of the last century. So what makes one year warmer or colder than its predecessor? The answer to this depends on a number of factors. Large volcanic eruptions can cause a temporary dip in temperatures for a few years due to reflection of sunlight by the resulting atmospheric particles. This happened following the eruption of Mt Pinatubo in 1991, for example. Fluctuations in the ocean can also cause temporary ups and downs, and the massive heat release during an El Niño event in the tropics can temporarily raise global temperatures, such as occurred in 1998. This year, the tropical ocean has indeed warmed up in both the Pacific and the Atlantic, but both of these ocean basins have also been very warm in northern latitudes, compounding the effect on global temperature. While the oceans exhibit record warmth, it is the average temperature over land regions and in the Arctic that has risen most. It is worth noting that this is consistent with predictions from computer models of climate change, which have suggested for many years that warming over land, and over the Arctic, will outstrip the increase in global average temperature as climate change progresses. The WMO report highlights a number of record-breaking weather events around the world, underscoring the continuing impact of climate change on global weather patterns and temperatures.

Nicola Sturgeon Writes to Donald Trump Emphasising Shared Values Scotland's First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has written to US President-elect Donald Trump congratulating him on his election victory while emphasising the importance of shared values including equality, tolerance and diversity. In the letter, Ms Sturgeon stressed the historic bonds between Scotland and the United States, noting how Scottish thinkers and people of Scottish descent helped shape America into the global power it is today. She highlighted that the USA represents Scotland's most important international export market and source of inward investment. The SNP leader, who had publicly backed Hillary Clinton during the presidential campaign, acknowledged the divisive nature of the election but said she was encouraged by Mr Trump's victory speech pledge to be "a President for all of America" and to work towards unifying the country. "Our nations share fundamental values of equality, tolerance, diversity and human rights for all regardless of race, faith, gender or sexual orientation, and I hope we will see these values flourish during your Presidency," Ms Sturgeon wrote in the letter. Despite her diplomatic tone, the First Minister has previously said she will engage "positively and constructively" with the new president whilst refusing to "maintain a diplomatic silence" in the face of what she described as "abhorrent comments". The relationship between Ms Sturgeon and Mr Trump has been strained in recent years. Last year, she stripped the property tycoon of his role as a business ambassador for Scotland following his controversial suggestion that Muslims should be banned from entering the United States. However, Ms Sturgeon's approach to dealing with the president-elect has attracted criticism from within her own party. Former SNP MSP Chic Brodie, who has met Mr Trump on several occasions, told BBC's Good Morning Scotland programme that he believed the First Minister had not handled the situation particularly well. Mr Brodie suggested Ms Sturgeon should have raised her concerns directly with Mr Trump when he visited his Trump Turnberry golf resort in Scotland earlier this year, rather than what he described as "sniping from the sidelines". "You can't complain about President Obama getting involved in the independence campaign and in turn get involved in a vastly different election campaign than we are normally used to," Mr Brodie said. "I think it would have been better to have turned up and tried to have that conversation." Despite the criticism and past tensions, Ms Sturgeon concluded her letter by wishing Mr Trump success as he prepares to assume the responsibilities of office and in the years ahead, expressing hope that the close ties between Scotland and the United States can be strengthened during his presidency.

Manchester Gorton By-Election in Doubt After General Election Announcement Manchester's returning officer is seeking clarification following Theresa May's announcement of a snap general election, which has thrown the Manchester Gorton by-election into uncertainty. The by-election poll was scheduled for 4 May - the day after parliament is set to be dissolved. This would potentially create the anomaly of a newly-elected MP without a parliament to sit in. Returning Officer for Manchester Joanne Roney OBE said: "We are seeking advice in discussion with the Government and Electoral Commission and will confirm arrangements for the Manchester Gorton constituency as soon as possible." The Electoral Commission confirmed that the general election decision would not affect the metro mayor elections in Liverpool City Region and Greater Manchester on 4 May, as these dates were "set in law". However, the BBC understands the snap poll means the Gorton by-election is unlikely to take place. Cabinet member David Davis, Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union, said on Sky News the by-election would be cancelled, while the Leader of the House David Lidington told the Commons the decision on whether to hold the poll is one for the returning officer in Manchester. Mr Lidington said parliament was likely to be dissolved on 2 or 3 May. The House of Commons votes on Wednesday whether to approve the election. The by-election was caused by the death of long-serving Labour MP Sir Gerald Kaufman in February.

Djokovic and Federer Drawn Together for ATP World Tour Finals World number one Novak Djokovic and seven-time Wimbledon champion Roger Federer have been placed in the same group for the upcoming ATP World Tour Finals. The Serbian star and Swiss maestro will compete alongside Tomas Berdych and Kei Nishikori in their group. The tournament, which begins on 15 November, follows a round-robin format with the top two players from each group advancing to the semi-finals. Djokovic enters the competition in dominant form, having secured his 10th title of the year in Paris last week. The defending champion will be seeking his fourth consecutive World Tour Finals title. In the doubles competition, Jamie Murray and John Peers face a challenging draw against 16-time Grand Slam champions Mike and Bob Bryan. ATP chief executive Chris Kermode announced that the prestigious tournament will remain at London's O2 Arena until at least 2018.

Fish Pass to Help Salmon Spawn in Shropshire River The Severn Rivers Trust is set to construct a fish pass at the Mill Street weir on the River Teme in Ludlow, opening up vital spawning grounds for Atlantic salmon and other fish species. Currently, salmon can only navigate the weir during exceptionally high water flows, severely limiting their access to upstream habitats. The new pass will also benefit trout, bullhead, eel, grayling and dace populations. The project will utilize a Larinier design, featuring a series of baffles or plates arranged on a gentler slope than the existing weir, allowing fish to swim upstream more easily. Once completed, the pass will provide access to an additional 85 kilometres (53 miles) of river habitat above the weir. Chief executive Tony Bostock described the initiative as "a fantastic opportunity to greatly increase all fish species throughout the Teme catchment." The project has been funded by Sita Trust through the Landfill Communities Fund.

Deadly Bomb Blast Kills Dozens Near Recaptured Nigerian Town A roadside bomb explosion has killed at least 30 people near the town of Mubi in northeastern Nigeria, according to local officials. The blast occurred in Marabar-Mubi, approximately 30 kilometers west of Mubi, close to the Cameroonian border. A spokesman for the governor of Adamawa state confirmed that the majority of victims were civilians, though five soldiers were among the dead. Earlier reports had suggested the death toll could be as high as 35. Witnesses described seeing several buses engulfed in flames following the explosion. The attack comes just days after Mubi was recaptured from Boko Haram, the Islamist extremist group that has seized control of numerous towns across the region. The Nigerian military, supported by local vigilante groups and hunters, successfully drove the militants from Mubi this week after the town fell under their control last month. Authorities have imposed a 24-hour curfew in the affected area as security forces work to restore order. The blast represents the latest in a series of devastating attacks by Boko Haram, which has intensified its campaign of violence in recent months. Just two days earlier, at least 78 people were killed in a twin suicide bombing in Maiduguri, the capital of Borno state. Last week, the group killed nearly 100 people in separate attacks, with some victims having their throats slit while others drowned in Lake Chad. Boko Haram gained international notoriety in April when it kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from Chibok, sparking worldwide condemnation. The group, designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and other Western nations, was founded in Maiduguri in 2002 but has since expanded its operations throughout northeastern Nigeria.

Essex Police Officers Face Misconduct Hearing Over Travelodge Incident Two Essex police officers are facing a misconduct hearing after allegedly refusing to leave a Norwich Travelodge and being "rude and aggressive" to staff following a colleague's hen party. PCs Jason Munns and Luke Salmon, both based in Colchester, had been drinking since 14:30 BST in June 2016 when the incident occurred at the hotel. The hearing was told the officers became "noisy and rowdy" and "verbally abusive" towards the night receptionist, who subsequently asked them to leave. When four police officers were called to the scene, PCs Munns and Salmon are accused of being "obstructive" and pretending to be asleep when officers attempted to speak with them at their hotel room door. The pair allegedly refused to depart, stating they "knew the law and were police officers." The misconduct hearing heard that seven police colleagues attended the hen party, with one being sick during the evening and another admitting their recollections were "hazy at best." PC Munns is also accused of instructing PC Salmon to tell the night manager to "do one." However, his solicitor denied the actions constituted aggression, insisting his client did not intend to be threatening or intimidating. The solicitor added that PC Munns recognised his behaviour amounted to misconduct and was "ashamed of himself." The panel heard the situation was eventually resolved after PC Munns identified himself as a police officer. All parties shook hands before the officers left approximately 40 minutes after police arrived. Both officers are accused of conduct breaching standards of professional behaviour. The hearing continues.

**Bianca Walkden Becomes Britain's Heavyweight Taekwondo World Champion** Britain's Bianca Walkden has made history by claiming the world heavyweight taekwondo title, becoming only the second British woman to achieve this feat after Sarah Stevenson. The 23-year-old Liverpudlian secured the title in the +73kg category with victory over France's Gwladys Epangue, 31, in Chelyabinsk, Russia. Last year, Walkden won +73kg gold in the European Championships in Baku but this is her first medal at world level. "I'm the new heavyweight champion of the world and honestly, I'm so happy," she said. "It's unbelievable." Walkden, who trains in Manchester and is nicknamed "Queen B," has overcome two serious knee injuries in the last four years, making her victory even more remarkable. "To have had my knee troubles and to come back like this, it is such an emotional win," she said. "It just shows it's all about your head and your heart as well." Her housemate, London 2012 Olympic gold medallist Jade Jones, was eliminated in the quarter-finals of the -57kg division.

Welsh Runner Completes Grueling Death Valley Ultra-Marathon Rhys Jenkins, 27, has accomplished an extraordinary feat by running the equivalent of 10 marathons across California's Death Valley in just over four days. The Welsh athlete completed 270 miles in 107 hours, falling short of his 96-hour target that would have secured a Guinness World Record for the fastest double crossing on foot. Despite missing the record, Jenkins persevered through extreme conditions, with temperatures soaring to 56.7C in the desert terrain typically inhabited only by venomous snakes and scorpions. Jenkins began the challenge alongside his brother Scott, 34, who unfortunately couldn't complete the full distance due to injury. "Scott is obviously devastated," said his girlfriend Abby Fleming. Both men survived on roughly seven hours of sleep throughout the ordeal and have raised over £5,000 toward their £10,000 fundraising target. The brothers made history as the first siblings and first Welsh people to run Death Valley.

A6 Upgrade Near Castledawson Faces Opposition Despite Seamus Heaney Connection Work on a major upgrade to the A6 near Castledawson is set to begin later this month, but the £160m project has sparked controversy over its route through an area closely associated with Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney. The scheme will create a new stretch of dual carriageway close to the former home of the renowned poet. Infrastructure Minister Chris Hazzard has defended the chosen route as "the best available" for improving the main Belfast to Londonderry road, which becomes gridlocked during rush hour and has been in need of improvement for over a decade. However, the project faces opposition on multiple fronts. Environmentalists have raised concerns about the impact on important habitat for overwintering swans near Lough Beg, close to Toomebridge. A legal challenge appears imminent, with contractors already beginning exploratory work this week. Stephen Rea, the actor who co-founded the Field Day Theatre Company with Heaney in 1980, has questioned the necessity of the route. "Does it have to go exactly through there?" Rea asked. "Do you have to choose a place that has been dignified by the greatest poet we've ever had?" He contrasted the preservation of Heaney's landscape with the promotion of Game of Thrones filming locations, arguing that the poet's legacy deserves greater respect. "This is a great poet, we need to preserve his landscape," he said. Minister Hazzard acknowledged that any route through the area would cross "Heaney country and environmentally sensitive areas," but insisted the project was "fitting." The current route was selected following a public inquiry a decade ago, which concluded that alternative routes would cause greater disruption and require purchasing more homes. Environmentalists plan to challenge the route through judicial review, arguing that the environmental data supporting the decision is outdated and may not have been collected according to current regulations.

Irish Actor Frank Kelly Dies at Age 77 Veteran Irish actor Frank Kelly, best known for his role as Father Jack Hackett in the beloved sitcom Father Ted, has passed away at the age of 77. The actor's death comes exactly 18 years to the day after his Father Ted co-star Dermot Morgan died on February 28, 1998. Kelly's six-decade career spanned stage and screen, with more recent appearances including roles in the soap opera Emmerdale and the feature film Mrs Brown's Boys D'Movie. Despite revealing last November that he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease, the determined actor had stated his intention to continue working. The Irish entertainment legend had faced several health challenges in recent years, including bowel cancer, from which he received the all-clear in 2011, skin cancer treatment last year, and heart problems. News of Kelly's passing prompted an outpouring of tributes from colleagues and fans. Graham Linehan, writer of Father Ted, tweeted: "Just hearing from various sources that Frank Kelly has passed away. Terribly sad news. Thanks for everything Frank." Co-writer Arthur Mathews called him a "comedy legend," adding: "So thrilled we had him in Father Ted." Co-star Ardal O'Hanlon, who played Father Dougal McGuire, described Kelly as "a gentleman" and "an all-round talent, an institution in Irish entertainment." He revealed they had shared lunch at Christmas when Kelly was "in his usual feisty form." Mrs Brown's Boys star Brendan O'Carroll, speaking from Australia, said: "Such a lovely man and a joy to work with." Irish President Michael D. Higgins paid tribute to Kelly as "a friend" and "a distinguished actor who made such a wide and valued contribution both on the stage and in film," adding, "He will forever be remembered for his roles." Kelly is survived by his wife of 51 years, Bairbre, their seven children, and 17 grandchildren.

Civil Partnerships in England and Wales Drop 85% Since Same-Sex Marriage Introduced The number of civil partnerships formed in England and Wales has plummeted dramatically following the introduction of same-sex marriage, new figures reveal. There were 861 civil partnerships formed in 2015 compared with 1,683 the year before. Civil partnerships have declined by 85% since 2013, a result of the introduction of marriage for same-sex couples in 2014. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said dissolutions of civil partnerships had risen as more couples swapped them for marriages. The figures for 2015 showed two thirds (66%) of civil partnerships were between men, and almost half (48%) of people forming a partnership were aged 50 and over. Dissolved partnerships increased 14% on 2014 to 1,211. Elizabeth McLaren of the ONS said: "Civil partnerships have fallen sharply since the introduction of marriages for same-sex couples in March 2014. On the other hand, civil partnership dissolutions have increased due to the rising number of civil partnerships that were formed since they were introduced in December 2005." London was the most popular place to form a civil partnership with 294 of the total. The figures also showed that in the North East, Yorkshire and The Humber and Wales more partnerships were formed between women than men.

Russian Gulag Museum Perm-36 Taken Over by Authorities A historic Gulag museum in Russia's Ural mountains has been taken over by local authorities in what critics are calling a politically motivated move to downplay Stalin-era repressions. Perm-36, the only surviving Soviet labour camp with buildings dating back to the Stalinist terror, has been managed by a non-governmental organization that is now disbanding following disputes with Perm regional officials. "Of course it's a political move," Viktor Shmyrov, a representative of the previous management group, told the BBC. He explained that local authorities have installed their own appointees who have "totally changed the content" of the museum. "Now it's a museum about the camp system, but not about political prisoners. They don't talk about the repressions or about Stalin," Mr Shmyrov said. The takeover marks a significant shift in how one of Russia's most important historical sites commemorates the millions of Soviet citizens who were sent to labour camps or executed during Joseph Stalin's rule. The worst repressions occurred during the 1930s under the notorious Gulag system. The conflict between the museum's operators and local authorities began in 2013, triggering protests by thousands of people. Last year, Perm authorities cut off the site's water and electricity, citing unpaid bills. The sprawling complex covers 14,000 square meters and includes more than 20 buildings. According to Mr Shmyrov, up to 3,000 political prisoners were housed there under Stalin, and approximately 1,000 during Leonid Brezhnev's leadership in the 1970s. Many prisoners were Ukrainian and Baltic nationalists—groups that are currently vilified in Russian state media. The camp was closed in 1988 and transformed into a museum in 1996. Mr Shmyrov suggested the takeover reflects broader political trends in Russia rather than simply rehabilitating Stalin's image. "We are already seeing the creation of a Stalinist-type state—enormous power is concentrated in the hands of one man," he said, referring to President Vladimir Putin. The museum's fate comes amid surveys indicating that many Russians now regard Stalin as a hero. Portraits of the Soviet dictator, once taboo after the full scale of his crimes was revealed, have become increasingly common since the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991. "The political system is returning to totalitarianism," Mr Shmyrov warned, though he noted that under Putin, "there is no need now for repressions—the people have become obedient."

Northants build strong lead as Newton hits century against Derbyshire Starting on 153-6, the visitors added just 23 more runs to trail by 42 as Ben Sanderson finished with 5-52. Max Holden and Newton (108) made 92 for the first wicket, and Newton added 133 alongside Alex Wakely (79). Tony Palladino removed Holden and Newton for the visitors, before another McKerr wicket left it 247-4 at stumps. Derbyshire were a man light with Luis Reece spending Friday night in hospital after complaining of breathing difficulties on day one, but the club say he is "feeling much better in himself". Newton, who has also scored four half-centuries this season, recorded the 12th first-class ton of his career to help his side to a healthy 289-run advantage.

Snow and Ice Warnings Cover Most of UK as Winter Weather Hits The Met Office escalated weather warnings on Friday, upgrading to a yellow "be aware" alert covering most of Britain as snow and icy conditions gripped the nation. In Scotland, Aberdeenshire bore the brunt of heavy snowfall, forcing closure of the A93 between Braemar and Spittal of Glenshee and the A939 from Cockbridge to Tommintoul. Traffic Scotland issued warnings about treacherous driving conditions as the weather deteriorated. North Yorkshire Police confirmed via social media that snow was "falling and settling" across their region, whilst snowfall also reached Wales and southern England. Even Eastbourne in East Sussex experienced flurries, with Beachy Head's downland receiving a light dusting on Saturday morning. Meteorologists cautioned about dangerous icy patches forming on untreated surfaces and potential blizzards in upland regions where gale-force winds combined with snow. Though significant snowfall wasn't anticipated for Saturday night, ice remained a concern for Sunday morning following overnight frost. Looking ahead, the Met Office forecast Sunday would bring another cold but sunny day with coastal showers continuing throughout. A spokesman offered some relief: "It will still be cold tomorrow but perhaps not as cold as it feels on Saturday because the winds will be just that little bit lighter."

Body of Missing Diver Andy Moll Found Off Dorset Coast The body of a missing diver has been recovered off the Dorset coast, police have confirmed. Andy Moll, 59, from North Curry near Taunton, was part of a three-man team exploring a dive vessel six miles south of Swanage on Sunday, 24 May, when he failed to surface. Dorset Police said his body was recovered near the wreck site on Friday night. A large search operation covering approximately 10 nautical miles was launched immediately after the incident. The Maritime and Coastguard Agency called off the six-hour search at 23:00 BST that Sunday evening. Mr Moll, a father-of-four, was an experienced diving instructor trainer who also served nationally with the British Sub-Aqua Club.

Irish Health Authority Investigates Potential Drug Contamination The Health Products Regulatory Authority has announced an investigation after a contaminant was discovered during testing procedures by a pharmaceutical manufacturer. The authority stressed that the issue was identified in a test product - not an actual medicine - and crucially, no test products were administered to patients. According to RTÉ, the contamination was detected in only a single unit, and officials noted this doesn't necessarily indicate the medicine itself has been compromised. The Health Service Executive has proactively contacted affected patients through their hospitals, offering expedited appointments for assessment and reassurance. Authorities confirmed that none of the potentially affected medications were distributed to Northern Ireland healthcare facilities. The investigation continues as officials work to determine the full extent and implications of the contamination.

Warrington Wolves Edge Past Huddersfield Giants in Six-Lead-Change Thriller Warrington Wolves secured a dramatic 32-28 victory over bottom-placed Huddersfield Giants in a see-saw Super League encounter at the Halliwell Jones Stadium. The Wolves established an early 16-14 half-time advantage through tries from Stefan Ratchford, Ben Currie and Ben Westwood. Huddersfield responded with Gene Ormsby grabbing a brace alongside Aaron Murphy's effort to keep the visitors in contention. The lead changed hands six times throughout the afternoon in humid, overcast conditions. Nathan Mason put the Giants ahead after the interval, but Warrington struck back immediately through Chris Sandow and Ryan Atkins to establish a 28-20 cushion. Ormsby, facing his former club, completed his hat-trick before Craig Huby's try restored Huddersfield's lead. However, Daryl Clarke's late try proved decisive, settling the contest in Warrington's favour. The match lacked intensity with bottom-placed Huddersfield already resigned to competing in the Qualifiers. Warrington's momentum suffered when full-back Ratchford departed with injury midway through the first half, having helped his side to a 10-0 lead. The defeat means new Huddersfield coach Rick Stone is still searching for his first victory. The Giants now have a two-week break before beginning their Qualifiers campaign. Warrington turn their attention to next Saturday's Challenge Cup semi-final against Wakefield before commencing their Super 8s fixtures.

Wales Bans Smoking in Cars with Children, £50 Fine from October Wales will introduce a £50 fixed penalty for smoking in vehicles carrying children from October, following approval by Assembly Members in the latest crackdown on second-hand smoke harm. The ban extends existing legislation from 2007 that prohibited smoking in public service and work vehicles. From October, anyone smoking in a private vehicle with passengers under 18 will face enforcement action. Health Minister Mark Drakeford emphasised the serious risks posed to young people. "Smoke posed'a real and substantial threat to children's health'," he said. "Children cannot escape from the toxic chemicals contained in second-hand smoke when travelling in cars." Mr Drakeford noted that children often have no choice about their travel arrangements and may feel unable to challenge adults who smoke. He stressed that success would be measured by changing behaviours and attitudes rather than enforcement numbers. Unlike existing smoke-free regulations enforced by local authorities, police will be responsible for tackling offenders in private vehicles. The Welsh legislation follows similar measures already approved for England, where a comparable ban on smoking in cars carrying children has been introduced. The new rules aim to protect vulnerable young passengers from the dangers of passive smoking in enclosed spaces.

Police Officer Accused of Voyeurism Offences Appears in Court A police constable from Blackburn has appeared in court charged with multiple voyeurism offences. PC Jayson Lobo, 46, is accused of 18 counts of sexual spying allegedly committed over a three-and-a-half-year period between December 2011 and May 2015. The former Commonwealth Games runner appeared at Liverpool Crown Court and was granted bail. His trial is scheduled to begin on 16 January. The Preston-based response officer has been suspended from duty following his arrest in December. Voyeurism is legally defined as observing individuals engaged in private activities without their consent for the purpose of sexual gratification.

Global Shares Surge on Fed Rate Rise Speculation Shares around the world have been boosted by hopes that the US Federal Reserve will push back rate rises following weak US jobs data last week. London's benchmark FTSE 100 index closed up 128.31 points, or 1.88%, at 6,961.77, reflecting the positive sentiment sweeping global markets. Oil-related shares saw big gains following a sharp rise in the price of crude on Monday. BG Group rose 6.7% while Premier Oil jumped 13%. However, the rise in oil costs hit shares in airlines, with British Airways owner IAG down 1.2%. Shares in Royal Mail rose 1.3% to 448p following news that Dutch parcels delivery firm TNT Express had agreed to be bought by US firm FedEx. The takeover has raised speculation that there could be more deals in the sector. On the currency markets, the pound was boosted by a strong survey of the UK's services sector. The latest Markit/CIPS services purchasing managers' index (PMI) recorded an eight-month high of 58.9 last month. The pound rose 0.13% against the dollar to $1.4849, while against the euro it climbed 0.48% to €1.3693.

Birmingham School Tackles Child Obesity with Weekly Food Boxes A Birmingham primary school has launched an innovative scheme to combat rising childhood obesity rates by providing families with affordable, healthy meal boxes. Hillstone Primary in Shard End is offering food boxes designed to feed a family of four for a week, assembled by school catering manager Matthew Knight. The scheme comes amid growing concerns about obesity levels in the area, which are significantly above average. Head teacher Gillian Sparrow explained the initiative's origins: "We are concerned about childhood obesity, as many schools are, so we wanted to encourage healthy eating in the community." The boxes, priced at £22, contain ingredients for five nutritious meals including cottage pie, chicken pie and chicken burritos. The school purchases extra ingredients and sells them directly to parents at cost, with approximately 15 families participating so far. "It's going well and growing," Ms Sparrow said, adding that the scheme aims to "transform the children's eating habits" whilst helping families save money. The initiative addresses a pressing regional issue. Across the West Midlands, one in four pupils are overweight or obese when starting primary school, rising to one in three by the time they leave. The school hopes the programme will encourage lasting changes in family eating habits throughout the community.

Climate Change Shows Similar Impact on Bird Populations Across Continents, Landmark Study Reveals For the first time, researchers have demonstrated that climate change is having a comparable and significant impact on bird populations in large, geographically distant regions of the world. The groundbreaking study, published in the journal Science, utilized sophisticated population-predicting models combined with three decades of field data collected by thousands of dedicated bird-watching volunteers. The research team, led by scientists from Durham University, developed advanced models that connected each bird species' habitat requirements to long-term climate patterns. By analyzing annual climate records spanning from 1980 to 2010, these models successfully predicted where specific species had experienced improvements or declines in suitable climate conditions. "We then had this amazing data set collected by thousands of volunteers over decades - where people have gone out and counted birds across different countries in Europe and the United States," explained lead researcher Dr. Stephen Willis. "We can use that to see to what extent our predictions match what people are finding on the ground." The study reveals that while individual species face different outlooks depending on their specific habitat requirements, the overall trends across the United States and Europe are remarkably similar. Rising temperatures in the UK, for instance, have enabled some species to expand their range and grow their populations, while simultaneously making the region less hospitable for others. The research consistently shows that populations are increasing in species predicted to benefit from climate change, while declining in those expected to be negatively affected. "One important thing is that we're looking at the most common birds," said Dr. Willis. "These birds are doing a lot of good in the countryside - eating crop pests and helping our ecosystems work. So we need to understand how they'll respond." The findings illustrate how climate change is gradually remapping avian habitats across two continents. In Europe, species such as the wren have been expanding into northern areas as winters become milder, but declining in southern countries. Similarly, the American robin has decreased in some southern US states while increasing further north. "This is really the first time anyone's ever looked at changes in climate across two really extensive parts of the world," said Dr. Willis. "So we're getting an idea that [the impacts of] climate change on wildlife are more far-reaching than individual countries." David Noble from the British Trust for Ornithology, a co-author of the study, emphasized the importance of the extensive volunteer-generated data. "The similarities in results between the two continents, despite very big differences in their landscapes, geographic barriers and patterns of vegetation, are compelling evidence for the climate change effects," he stated. The study, conducted in partnership with the RSPB and United States Geological Survey (USGS), demonstrates the powerful contribution of citizen science to understanding global environmental changes.

Shop Front Smashed After Car Crash on Birmingham's Pershore Road Both sides of the busy Pershore Road in Birmingham were sealed off following the incident near First Avenue just after 07:00 BST, said West Midlands Police. A man and woman were checked by paramedics but nobody was seriously injured in the collision. Street bollards were damaged and the shop front window was smashed during the incident. The road has since reopened to traffic.

Wick Airport Runway to be Upgraded for Potential Nuclear Material Transport The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (NDA) is funding significant improvement work to enhance the runway at Wick John O'Groats Airport in the Scottish Highlands, potentially to facilitate the transport of nuclear material from the nearby Dounreay site. The airport upgrades come as the UK and US governments agreed last month on a material exchange deal. Under the agreement, the UK would send highly enriched uranium (HEU) currently stored at Dounreay to the United States in return for a type of uranium used in the diagnosis of cancer. Wick John O'Groats Airport is located approximately 30 miles (48km) from the Dounreay nuclear site, which is currently undergoing decommissioning. The NDA has confirmed that air transport is among several options being considered for moving the HEU, though officials stress that no final decisions have been taken. "The protection of the public and personnel is of paramount importance at all times," an NDA spokeswoman said. "For those reasons we are unable to disclose information about the transport arrangements that could jeopardise the security of this material." She added that the proposed exchange would see HEU sent to the US "in return for material to be used in the production of medical isotopes for Europe." ## Runway Refurbishment Details A spokesman for Wick John O'Groats Airport, which is operated by Highlands and Islands Airport Limited, confirmed that refurbishment work will begin later this month. The project aims to "enhance its operational capability and, in particular, its ability to accommodate larger aircraft." The majority of construction work will be carried out overnight to minimize disruption, with completion expected by August. The NDA noted that radioactive material from the civil nuclear industry has been transported by plane previously, and that funding the airport improvements secures "the option of moving material by air on a range of aircraft." ## Dounreay Decommissioning Programme The Dounreay nuclear power complex is currently being decommissioned and the site cleaned up. Most radioactive materials, including fuel, are being relocated to other facilities such as Sellafield in Cumbria for reprocessing or storage. These shipments are typically made by rail. However, nuclear material transport has not always proceeded smoothly. Over four years, 150 tonnes of waste were transported from Dounreay to Belgium by sea in 21 shipments. In October 2014, a fire broke out on the MV Parida while it was transporting cemented radioactive waste in the Outer Moray Firth. The vessel began drifting after the fire started in a funnel, though the blaze was quickly extinguished. As a precautionary measure, 52 workers were evacuated by helicopter from the nearby Beatrice oil platform. The cargo ship was subsequently towed to Invergordon for repairs before completing its journey to Antwerp. The NDA stated at the time that both the ship and its cargo had been categorised at the lowest level of safety concern.

Man Sought After Vandalism Attack at Glasgow Cafe Police are appealing for witnesses following a brazen vandalism incident at Cube Café on Garscube Road in Glasgow. The attack occurred around 17:00 on Tuesday when a man broke into the closed premises. According to police reports, the suspect smashed the external CCTV system before forcing open the security shutter and causing damage to the cafe's interior. Despite the break-in, nothing was reported stolen. The suspect is described as a white male of medium build, approximately 5ft 6in to 5ft 8in tall, and in his mid-40s. He was wearing light-coloured jeans and a blue jacket at the time of the incident. Detective Constable Fiona Fraser emphasized the timing of the attack, noting it occurred during the busy evening commute. "Many passing motorists may well have seen or heard the disturbance as they travelled towards Maryhill or down towards Cowcaddens during that busy period," she said. Police are urging anyone with information to come forward.

Google Trekker Maps Historic North Downs Way Trail The historic North Downs Way, stretching from Farnham in the Surrey Hills to Dover's coastline in Kent, is being digitally mapped using Google Trekker technology - the off-road counterpart to Google Streetview. Around 15 volunteer walkers have been traversing the trail equipped with specialized 15-angle-lens cameras, similar to technology previously deployed at iconic locations like the Grand Canyon and the Taj Mahal. Peter Morris, the North Downs Way trail manager, spearheaded the project to showcase the protected landscapes of the Surrey Hills and Kent Downs to virtual visitors. The camera system is operated via a handheld device, allowing walkers to control image capture and monitor quality, ensuring lenses remain clear of water, dirt, and debris. However, the 23kg camera equipment presents significant challenges. "Walking uphill is fine as long as you can lean forward," Morris explained. "The problems are when you're trying to get over a stile or through a gate which has an overhanging tree, so you're trying to duck and climb with 23kg on your back." The weight dramatically affects balance and mobility, particularly when navigating obstacles along the route. "This all throws out your centre of gravity," Morris added. "So walking uphill is fine but getting over objects is a little bit more problematic." Much of the North Downs Way follows routes believed to be original medieval pilgrim paths connecting Winchester and Canterbury cathedrals. The complete imagery is expected to be available online by year's end. Following this success, the South Downs Way - running from Beachy Head in East Sussex to Winchester in Hampshire - is scheduled for mapping beginning this autumn.

Police Scotland Admits Unlawful Surveillance of Journalist Without Court Approval Police Scotland has acknowledged conducting surveillance operations without obtaining the required judicial authorization, a senior officer has revealed. Assistant Chief Constable Ruaraidh Nicolson told Holyrood's justice committee that an officer had misunderstood recent changes to regulations governing the interception of communications. He explained that the force had been concerned that leaked information regarding a murder investigation could jeopardize future court proceedings. The breach came to light when the Interception of Communications Commissioner reported in November that Police Scotland had obtained communications data without judicial approval on five separate occasions. Investigative journalist Eamon O'Connor has stated he believes his communications were intercepted by Police Scotland's Counter Corruption Unit in an effort to identify his sources within the force. O'Connor had been investigating the police inquiry into the 2005 murder of Emma Caldwell. During his appearance before the committee, Mr. Nicolson confirmed the Counter Corruption Unit had been requested by "someone external" to determine how sensitive material had entered the public domain. He acknowledged that while there was awareness of new rules requiring judicial approval for communications interception, details of the regulatory changes had not reached the "single point of contact" within the unit. Mr. Nicolson characterized the failure to obtain proper authorization as a "misinterpretation issue." He also revealed that powers to intercept communications had been utilized on seven additional occasions involving journalists, though he maintained these cases concerned journalists' sources rather than the journalists themselves. The justice committee had sought to question four officers directly involved—Det Supt David Donaldson, Det Insp Joanne Grant, Det Supt Brenda Smith, and Ch Supt Clark Cuzen. However, Police Scotland cited "critical legal issues" that prevented their appearance, offering Mr. Nicolson instead. Committee members expressed disappointment that the four officers were unavailable and that not all 16 questions submitted to Police Scotland had been answered. The breach is currently under investigation by both an Investigatory Powers Tribunal and HM Inspector of Constabulary in Scotland.

McKay's Eight-Wicket Haul Not Enough as Leicestershire Claim Thrilling Victory Paceman Clint McKay's outstanding bowling performance of 4-37, giving him match figures of 8-84, couldn't prevent Leicestershire from securing a nail-biting four-wicket victory over Essex. Essex resumed on 22-1 but struggled throughout, being dismissed for just 133 in their second innings. Morning play was disrupted by a lengthy stoppage for bad light, during which three wickets fell. Tom Westley top-scored with 25, falling lbw to Rob Taylor immediately after lunch. Essex's collapse saw their final five wickets tumble for a mere 32 runs. Chasing 159 from 33 overs, Leicestershire's victory looked assured as opener Angus Robson (56 off 75 balls) recorded his second half-century of the match, partnering with Mark Cosgrove (38) in a 53-run stand. However, both departed within four overs, causing late jitters. Neil Dexter eventually sealed the win with two crucial runs at the start of the penultimate over, leaving just 11 balls remaining as Leicestershire finished on 159-6, claiming their second victory of the summer.

EU to Contact Spain Over British Woman's Stolen Baby Case The European Parliament has agreed to intervene in the case of a British woman who believes her baby was stolen in Spain over two decades ago. Ruth Appleby was told her daughter died after she gave birth in 1992 but later learnt thousands of Spanish babies were taken and given up for adoption. Mrs Appleby, from North Yorkshire, had appealed to the EU over the lack of progress in her case. The EU Committee on Petitions said it would contact the Spanish government. A spokeswoman for the Parliament said: "The petition will be referred to the committee's new working group on children's rights. They also decided to send a letter to the Spanish authorities in order to encourage them to take the next steps." Mrs Appleby, from Catterick Garrison, gave birth by Caesarean section at a hospital in La Coruna in northern Spain but the following day was told that the child had died. "I never got to see my baby. We asked many times but we were never allowed to see her," she said. When her daughter's remains were exhumed for cremation in 2010, Mrs Appleby said the skeleton she saw in the coffin appeared to be of a much older infant. The following year she heard about the scandal of Spain's'Niños robados' (stolen children) and immediately thought there were similarities with her own daughter's case. "It just started all sorts of doubts," she said. "For 19 years we believed that she had suddenly been taken ill and inexplicably died. It leaves a huge vacuum." In 2012, she contacted the police in England who referred her case to the Spanish authorities, but she was unhappy with their handling of the case and petitioned the European Parliament. Her petition was heard alongside similar ones from Spanish nationals.
