The problem has escalated dramatically since the first reported laser attack on an aircraft in 2004, which saw over 200 incidents by 2008. Recent years have witnessed a substantial increase in such attacks, with similar incidents targeting train and bus drivers. Steve Landells, flight safety specialist at the British Airline Pilots Association, welcomed the announcement: "Any move to give the police and authorities more powers to tackle this real and growing threat to flight safety is a good thing." The urgency of the issue was highlighted in February 2016 when a New York-bound aircraft was forced to return to Heathrow Airport after a laser beam struck the cockpit, causing a medical issue for one pilot. This incident prompted calls from both the British Airline Pilots Association and Civil Aviation Authority to classify laser pointers as offensive weapons. The Department for Transport confirmed that details of the new powers and penalties will be outlined in forthcoming legislation.

Eugene Laverty Finishes Tenth at Czech Republic MotoGP Northern Ireland's Eugene Laverty secured a tenth-place finish at the Czech Republic MotoGP in Brno on Sunday. The Aspar Ducati rider from Toomebridge has moved on to 63 points and lies 11th in the 2016 standings. Laverty has scored points in 10 of the 11 rounds this season with a best finish of fourth in Argentina in April. Britain's Cal Crutchlow took his maiden MotoGP win with Valentino Rossi second and Marc Marquez of Spain in third. Crutchlow's hard tyres suited the testing conditions in Brno and he worked his way from 10th on the grid to take the lead with seven laps to go. He is the first Briton to win an elite-class GP since Barry Sheene in 1981. Laverty crashed out on the final corner of the last lap while in 11th place in the previous round in Austria. The next race is the British GP at Silverstone on 4 September.

**Antonsson Joins Rovers on Loan Deal** Marcus Antonsson has completed a loan move to Rovers after struggling to make an impact at Leeds United. The 26-year-old Swedish striker joined Leeds from Kalmar in June 2016 but managed just three goals in 21 appearances. Rovers have secured special dispensation allowing Antonsson to feature in the EFL Cup, EFL Trophy and FA Cup during his loan spell. The forward could make his debut on Saturday when Rovers face Doncaster in League One action. For more transfer news, visit our dedicated transfers page.

Obama: US-Led Coalition Making Progress Against Islamic State President Barack Obama has delivered a strong message about progress in the fight against the Islamic State group, speaking at the Pentagon after a National Security Council meeting. November saw more airstrikes launched against the group than in any previous month, he said. He said the US had killed a number of its leaders and attacked oil facilities it relies on for cash. He has been seeking to reassure the public following an attack in California at the hands of militants. Fourteen people were shot dead by a radicalised Muslim couple, weeks after the killing of 130 people by Islamist gunmen in Paris. On Thursday he will visit the National Counterterrorism Center in Virginia, where he is also expected to speak. The National Security Council (NSC) held a rare outside-of-the-White House meeting at the Pentagon ahead of Mr Obama's remarks. The marquee visits come about a week after Mr Obama gave a major televised address to reassure the public of his strategy and to warn against anti-Muslim sentiment in the US. In recent weeks, US fears of a terror attack have swelled, with about 70% of Americans saying the risk of an attack in the US is at least somewhat high. Just before the Thanksgiving holiday in November, Mr Obama delivered a speech saying that there was no "specific or credible" threat of a terrorist attack in the US.

Mock Firearms Incident Exercise Held at Royal Shakespeare Company A major multi-agency emergency exercise was conducted at the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) in Stratford-upon-Avon to test response capabilities to a simulated firearms incident. Exercise Titus, which had been planned for three months, involved personnel from Warwickshire Fire Service, Warwickshire and West Mercia police forces, and West Midlands Ambulance Service. Police emphasized the operation was "not in response to any threat" and remained contained within the RSC grounds. RSC executive director Catherine Mallyon explained the theatre regularly updates its major incident procedures and trains staff for various scenarios, from severe weather to technology failures. "Having the chance to take part in this multi-agency exercise allows us to observe and ask questions about the appropriate management of serious incidents, which will help us with our own future planning," Mallyon said. The exercise provided valuable experience for emergency services and RSC staff in coordinating responses to potential security threats.

Cyclists Stage Rush-Hour Protest at Bank Junction After Latest London Deaths Cyclists brought central London to a standstill during Wednesday morning's rush hour in protest over road safety, following two cycling deaths in just two days. The 15-minute protest from 08:30 BST brought traffic to a halt on all six arms of Bank junction. Ying Tao, 26, died in a collision with a lorry while she was cycling to work at PricewaterhouseCoopers on Monday. The London Cycling Campaign (LCC) is calling for segregated space for cyclists on London's roads. The campaign group, which organised the demonstration, also wants the removal of dangerous lorries from streets. A minute's silence was also held in memory of Ms Tao and 60-year-old Clifton James, who was killed in a collision with a car in Harrow, north west London on Sunday. Neil Hampson, a partner at PricewaterhouseCooper, said the company was "shocked" by the news of their employee's death and sent their condolences to her family. "Ying was a bright and popular colleague with a promising career in front of her," he said. "She excelled at everything she did, with a passion for life, for work and for the friendships she made. "It is a tragedy that a wonderful young woman should lose her life at such an age." During Prime Minister's Questions, David Cameron said a lot had been done to try to make cycling safer in London and money had been invested in cycling lanes. However, he added: "The number of fatalities is still very high and extremely depressing [that] young lives [are] being snuffed out in this way." Of the eight fatalities on the capital's roads this year, seven have involved heavy goods vehicles.

Turkish President Erdogan Supporters Charged Over Washington Brawl Two supporters of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have been charged with assault following a violent brawl outside the Turkish ambassador's residence in Washington last month. Eyup Yildirim of New Jersey and Sinan Narin of Virginia face charges in connection with what police described as a "brutal attack on peaceful protesters" during President Erdogan's visit to the United States. The incident occurred while Mr Erdogan was in a car parked nearby, where he witnessed the violence unfold. According to a detailed New York Times investigation, both men had travelled to Washington specifically to support the Turkish president, though their formal connection to his security detail remains unclear. Video footage captured men in suits pushing past police officers to kick and punch demonstrators. The clash resulted in injuries to eleven people, with nine requiring hospital treatment. The charges bring the total number of people charged to four. The US government has lodged a formal complaint with Turkey, confirming involvement by Turkish security guards. However, the Turkish Embassy maintains that protesters provoked Turkish-Americans who were present to greet their president, claiming their actions were in self-defence.

Northern Ireland Teacher Describes Stockholm Terror Attack Scene A science teacher from Northern Ireland has described the chaotic scenes he witnessed during a suspected terror attack in Stockholm that has left at least four people dead. Dr. Jonathan Lappin, from Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, was having coffee with a colleague across from the affected area when the incident unfolded on Friday afternoon. What began as seemingly innocent excitement quickly descended into mass panic. "I thought they were chasing a celebrity," Dr. Lappin told the BBC, describing how he initially saw people running with their phones out. "People started to mass panic, and run into the coffee shop and crowd the back of it." The confusion in the café was immediate, with conflicting messages from staff telling customers not to worry while others fled. Moments later, police arrived on scene, shouting at people to evacuate the area. After waiting several minutes, Dr. Lappin and his colleague decided to leave. Upon stepping outside, they immediately "could smell the burning and the smoke," though the full extent of what had happened remained unclear. "I jumped to the conclusion that it must be a terrorist attack and wanted out of there, so we started to run as fast as we could down the street," Dr. Lappin said. He praised the swift response of Swedish authorities, noting that riot police with shields and helicopters arrived promptly. However, the size of Stockholm created additional challenges. "It's such a spread out city, there's a lot of confusion," he explained, with much of the area now in lockdown. Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven has stated that all evidence points toward an act of terrorism. Police have confirmed one arrest has been made in connection with the attack.

Manslaughter Trial Over Thomas Orchard Police Custody Death Halted A manslaughter trial involving three custody staff has been stopped after 11 weeks, with the judge announcing his intention to order a retrial. Thomas Orchard, 32, who had schizophrenia, died in October 2012 after being arrested in Exeter. Custody sergeant Jan Kingshott, 44, and civilian detention officers Simon Tansley, 38, and Michael Marsden, 55, were on trial for manslaughter at Bristol Crown Court. Mr Justice King told the jury of seven men and four women: "I have decided this trial cannot continue. I appreciate this may be a disappointment to you given the number of weeks you have sat. Given there may be a re-trial we cannot say anymore." Mr Orchard suffered a heart attack at Heavitree Road Police Station and died later in hospital. Julian Evans, representing the Crown, confirmed the prosecution intended to pursue a retrial. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) stated it would await the retrial decision before addressing "disciplinary matters." Tom Milsom, associate commissioner of the IPCC, said: "I appreciate the trial has been a difficult experience for everybody involved, in particular Mr Orchard's family who have listened with dignity and strength to painful details about his tragic and untimely death." The IPCC emphasized it had conducted a thorough investigation leading to the Crown Prosecution Service bringing these prosecutions.

Murray Faces Potential Federer Showdown as Australian Open Draw Revealed Andy Murray will begin his first Grand Slam tournament as world number one with the tantalizing prospect of facing Roger Federer in the quarter-finals of the Australian Open. The British star, seeking his fourth Grand Slam title and first in Melbourne after five previous final appearances, was drawn in the same quarter as the Swiss maestro. However, Murray's path through the early rounds appears manageable, with all British men facing opening opponents ranked outside the world's top 50. The Scot's potential route to a Federer clash could see him face Japan's Kei Nishikori before the quarter-finals, offering a chance to avenge his US Open quarter-final defeat last year. Yet Federer, now seeded 17th after six months recovering from injury, stands in Nishikori's section and could prevent that rematch. The 17-time Grand Slam champion's return to competitive tennis adds significant intrigue to the men's draw. Defending champion Novak Djokovic opens his campaign for a record seventh Australian Open title against Spain's Fernando Verdasco, who famously knocked out Rafael Nadal in last year's opening round before falling to Djokovic at the recent Qatar Open. Nadal, seeded ninth, begins against Germany's Florian Mayer with a potential quarter-final meeting against Canada's Milos Raonic on the horizon. In the women's draw, Britain's number 10 Johanna Konta faces Belgium's Kirsten Flipkens, a former Wimbledon semi-finalist, in what promises to be a challenging opener. Konta, fresh from a dominant 6-2 6-2 victory over Eugenie Bouchard at Thursday's Sydney International, finds herself in the same quarter as Slovakia's Dominika Cibulkova and American legend Serena Williams. Williams, chasing a 23rd Grand Slam title, opens against Switzerland's Belinda Bencic, while defending champion and world number one Angelique Kerber faces Ukraine's Lesia Tsurenko. Kerber aims for her third Grand Slam triumph following her maiden US Open victory last year. British women Heather Watson and Naomi Broady face seeded Australian opponents, though Watson may find encouragement in Sam Stosur's historically poor home record.

Labour Loses Key Dudley Seat by Three Votes in West Midlands Elections Labour suffered a narrow defeat in Dudley's Wollaston and Stourbridge Town ward, losing to the Conservatives by just three votes in Thursday's local elections. Despite this setback, Labour maintained control of major councils across Birmingham, Wolverhampton, and Sandwell. The party's grip on Sandwell strengthened considerably, with Labour now holding 71 seats compared to just one UKIP councillor after sweeping all contested seats. In Birmingham, Labour increased its majority on the City Council, whilst Wolverhampton saw an unusual incident where an administrative error resulted in two Conservative candidates appearing on the same ballot paper, effectively splitting the Tory vote. Pete Lowe, Dudley Labour group leader, expressed disappointment over the narrow loss: "On the whole we are disappointed that we lost the crucial last seat, and just by three votes." Conservative Patrick Harley countered: "To take four gains, three from Labour, I would say is exceptional." In Walsall, Labour gained one seat, bringing their total to 28 on the 60-seat council. The Liberal Democrats retained their two wards in Short Heath and Willenhall North, while Conservatives held 25 seats with support from three UKIP and two independent councillors. Labour's Sean Coughlan indicated potential coalition talks with the Liberal Democrats, stating: "There is a positive chance that we'll be running this council with their support." The Conservatives retained control in Solihull, completing a mixed picture across the West Midlands region.

Kell Brook to Defend IBF Welterweight Title Against Errol Spence Jr in Sheffield British boxer Kell Brook will defend his IBF welterweight title against American challenger Errol Spence Jr in his hometown of Sheffield this May, with Sheffield United's Bramall Lane stadium emerging as a potential venue for the bout. Promoter Eddie Hearn confirmed via Twitter that terms for the highly anticipated fight have been agreed between both camps. Brook, 30, will be making his return to the ring following his defeat to middleweight champion Gennady Golovkin in September. The Sheffield fighter suffered a broken eye socket during that fifth-round stoppage, which required surgery. It marked Brook's first professional loss in 37 fights. After the ambitious move up two weight divisions to challenge Golovkin, Brook has chosen to return to welterweight to face his mandatory challenger Spence, 27. Brook won the IBF belt by defeating Shawn Porter in August 2014 and has successfully defended it three times against Jo Jo Dan, Frankie Gavin, and Kevin Bizier. Spence brings an impressive unbeaten record of 21 fights, with 18 victories coming by knockout.

Gilmour loses Scottish Open final to Malaysia's Goh Scotland's Kirsty Gilmour was beaten by Malaysia's Goh Jin Wei in the Scottish Open badminton final in Glasgow. Second-seed Gilmour, 21, had eased past Denmark's fourth seed Line Kjaersfeldt in the semi-finals but lost 21-15 21-18 in the 44-minute final. Goh had come through qualifying and won seven matches on the way to her first senior title. "I'm a little disappointed not to come away with a win," said Gilmour. "I thought I played well. She was very solid and I made some poor decisions at some crucial points." The Commonwealth silver medallist from Hamilton was appearing in her first final since retaining her Swedish Masters title in January.

Have Your Say: BBC Interactive Debate Show Ahead of General Election As the UK prepares for the General Election on 8 June, the BBC is inviting voters to shape an innovative interactive debate programme that will air on Facebook. Westminster's decisions affect every aspect of daily life - from employment and education to healthcare and immigration. Now, ahead of polling day, the BBC wants to ensure voters' concerns take centre stage in the democratic conversation. The broadcaster is asking people to submit their most pressing political questions and issues. Whether concerns relate to NHS staffing levels, Brexit uncertainties, taxation, or immigration policy, all submissions will help shape the debate's direction. On Wednesday 7 June at 7.30pm, the BBC will live-stream an interactive show exploring these submitted concerns. The programme will feature voters from across the West of England, with audiences able to engage with the studio presenter and live attendees through social media and video calling. The initiative particularly targets young adults across Bristol, Gloucestershire, Somerset and Wiltshire, encouraging them to send their messages to those seeking power and ensure their voices are heard before election day.

Bromyard Celebrates Rich Motoring Heritage with Inaugural Festival of Speed Hundreds of car enthusiasts gathered in Bromyard this weekend for the town's first Festival of Speed, celebrating its significant contributions to British automotive history. The Herefordshire market town has deep roots in the motor industry, having been home to the chairmen of Austin, Bean and Morgan motor companies. Notably, parts for the iconic Morgan three-wheelers were manufactured locally, establishing Bromyard's place in motoring heritage. Approximately 120 vintage and historic vehicles paraded through the town streets, with the star attraction being a Sunbeam Bluebird. This legendary car was driven by Sir Malcolm Campbell to set a world speed record in 1924, exceeding 140 mph. Organisers highlighted that automotive engineering in Bromyard began with the Pettifer family, who manufactured chassis components for Morgan Three Wheelers from 1910, before Morgan established its Malvern factories. For the inaugural festival, Morgan Motor Company was featured prominently, recognizing its special association with the area. Founded by HFS Morgan in 1909, the company began producing three-wheelers in 1910 and remains the UK's last privately owned motor manufacturer. "The town and its immediate locality has been linked to the British motor industry since the birth of the motor car," organizers stated, promising this celebration of Bromyard's automotive legacy will become an annual tradition. The company continues its reputation for hand-built small sports cars today.

Broad Suffers Broken Nose But Expected to Play in Fifth Test England fast bowler Stuart Broad suffered a broken nose during the fourth Test against India but is expected to be fit for the series finale at The Oval. The injury occurred when Broad, after hitting successive sixes off an Indian bowler, attempted a third aggressive shot but top-edged the ball. It struck him between the grille and peak of his helmet during England's first innings. The 28-year-old Nottinghamshire player immediately retired hurt and received stitches before being sent for X-rays after tea. The scans confirmed a fracture, though Broad wasn't required to bowl again as England secured a comprehensive innings and 54-run victory. Despite the injury, Broad remained in good spirits, tweeting a photo Sunday morning: "Little bit sore this morning but not too bad! Doc did a great job with the stitches. On to The Oval! (With a mask)." England declared on 367, establishing a 215-run lead, before dismissing India for just 161 in their second innings. Broad had been instrumental in the victory, taking 6-25 on the opening day as India collapsed to 152. Chris Woakes partnered James Anderson with the new ball in Broad's absence during India's second innings. The England medical team will continue treating Broad throughout the week ahead of Friday's fifth Test.

Visit Britain Delegation Tours Hull Ahead of UK City of Culture 2017 A delegation from Visit Britain has toured museums and local attractions in Hull as the city prepares to host the year-long UK City of Culture arts festival in 2017. Garry Taylor from Hull City Council emphasized the visit's significance, describing it as "incredibly important" for promoting the city internationally. "Visit Britain are incredibly influential," he said. "The role they play internationally in changing perceptions, them experiencing Hull first hand is incredibly important." Taylor noted the delegation's positive reaction, saying "the conversations we're having, it's not the place that they were expecting it to be." Hull is currently undergoing a £25 million revamp in preparation for the festival. The transformation includes repaving streets and installing new lighting to showcase the city's landmark buildings. Additionally, over £15 million is being invested in refurbishing the New Theatre and the Ferens Art Gallery.

Carnivorous Plant Found to Selectively Devour Invasive Asian Hornets in France A botanical garden director in western France has made a remarkable discovery that could help combat the invasive Asian hornet population threatening European beehives. Romaric Perrocheau, head of the botanical garden in Nantes, recently found a stem of the carnivorous pitcher plant Sarracenia completely filled with dead Asian hornets. What makes this discovery particularly extraordinary is the plant's apparent selectivity – it devours Asian hornets whilst leaving European hornets, bees, and wasps unharmed. "Sarracenia had invented a very selective trap" for the aggressive Asian hornets, Mr Perrocheau told AFP news agency. The insects are lured by the plant's nectar and pheromones on its tubular leaves. Once a hornet crawls inside the rim, it easily slips and plunges into the pitcher, where it is digested by the plant's juices. Interestingly, this appears to be a European adaptation, as Asian hornets do not exist in Sarracenia's native Massachusetts in the eastern United States. The plant grows easily in Europe and poses no threat to native flora. Mr Perrocheau and an entomologist now plan to study the contents of 200 pitchers, hoping to identify the chemical secret behind their attraction for Asian hornets specifically. Asian hornets, catalogued as Vespa velutina nigrithorax, pose a significant threat to honeybees across France, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Germany, and Belgium. First spotted in France in 2004, their native habitat is China's Shanghai region. In some cases, hornet stings have proven fatal to humans due to allergic reactions. Each Sarracenia plant possesses up to 15 pitchers and can attract as many as 50 hornets. However, with typical hornet nests housing 4,000 insects, the plants alone cannot solve the problem entirely. The Independent reported in April that Asian hornets had not yet reached the UK, though plans exist to destroy any nests should they cross the English Channel. These nests prove notoriously difficult to locate and destroy, often hidden high in trees or underground hollows.

Adlington backs Peaty to handle Olympic pressure after European test Retired two-time Olympic champion Rebecca Adlington believes the European Championships, which begin in London on Monday, will provide the perfect preparation for Adam Peaty ahead of the Rio Olympics. The 21-year-old breaststroke sensation from Derby captured three world titles in 2015 and has established himself as Britain's brightest swimming prospect. "He's the hot favourite who everyone wants to beat," said Adlington. "At the Europeans everyone will be looking at him and hopefully facing up to all of that pressure and experiencing the atmosphere will make the Olympics a little easier." Peaty has demonstrated exceptional early-season form, claiming victory in the 100m breaststroke at the British Olympic trials last month and subsequently climbing to the top of the world rankings in the event. The swimmer is part of a 26-strong squad selected for this summer's Olympic Games in Rio, all of whom will compete together at the London Europeans as part of their final preparations. Adlington, speaking to BBC Sport, praised the improved depth within British Swimming: "The strength in depth is a great thing for British Swimming because everyone is really pushing each other on. "Traditionally GB swimmers haven't been able to swim fast in the heats and then again in the finals as we lacked the depth and didn't need to do that at trials. We were being caught out at big events, but now we're starting to see that consistency." She highlighted Peaty as an exemplar of this consistency: "Adam does it all the time - he's a born racer - but there are others too and that's great for Britain's prospects at the Europeans and Olympics." While British men dominated the 2015 World Championships, with Peaty, James Guy and the 4x200m freestyle relay team all claiming gold medals, Adlington believes the GB women can make significant impact in 2016. "Fran Halsall and Hannah Miley have so much experience but I think both Jazz Carlin and Siobhan-Marie O'Connor have great chances too," she said. "Jazz has had illnesses but is really coming into her own, whilst I think Siobhan is at the right age to push forward and get to the stage Adam [Peaty] is at. They have done it at the Worlds [with bronze medals each] and now they will want to make their mark at the Europeans and Olympics."

Britain's Katie Ormerod Claims Maiden Big Air World Cup Victory in Moscow British snowboarder Katie Ormerod secured her first World Cup big air victory in brutal conditions in Moscow, edging out Austria's Anna Gasser in extreme -29C temperatures. The 19-year-old from Yorkshire scored 153.75 points, narrowly defeating World Cup leader Gasser who finished with 153.50. The judges counted the two best runs from three attempts. This marks Ormerod's third World Cup podium finish this season, ahead of big air's historic Winter Olympics debut at PyeongChang 2018. "It was by far the coldest and some of the toughest conditions I've ever had to compete in but an amazing place," Ormerod said. "I'm stoked to be on the podium with some awesome riders, Anna Gasser and Klaudia Medlova." Media playback is not supported on this device.

Scottish Economy Shows Further Signs of Slowdown as Business Activity Contracts Scotland's private sector experienced a contraction in business activity during September, according to the latest Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) report from the Bank of Scotland, adding to concerns about the country's economic performance. The bank's PMI fell from 50.8 in August to 49.0 in September, dropping below the critical 50 threshold that separates economic expansion from contraction. The report revealed that new business declined "at a marginal pace" while backlogs of work also fell. Particularly concerning was the continuation of declining export orders, which have now fallen for eight consecutive months. Manufacturing firms bore the brunt of the downturn, reporting a sharp fall in new orders from both domestic and international markets. This led to deterioration in production across the sector. The service sector also experienced contraction in activity during September, despite a modest rise in incoming new business, though this increase was the weakest recorded in seven months. However, there were some positive indicators within the report. Workforce numbers expanded "at an accelerated rate," with the service sector leading employment growth. Manufacturing companies also registered modest increases in staffing levels, suggesting businesses remain cautiously optimistic about future prospects. Price pressures presented a mixed picture. Service sector companies reported higher input costs, while manufacturing firms experienced sharp reductions in prices. Overall, input prices softened, and output prices fell again during the month. Bank of Scotland chief economist Donald MacRae commented: "September's PMI showed a broad-based decline in economic activity across both service and manufacturing sectors. The slowdown in the Scottish economy identified in summer has taken further hold in the month of September but employment intentions suggest a return to moderate growth in coming months." The PMI data follows national statistics released last week showing Scotland's economic growth slowed to just 0.1% in the second quarter of 2024, down from 0.4% in the previous quarter. This compares unfavourably with the UK economy as a whole, which expanded by 0.7% during the same period. The figures raise questions about Scotland's economic trajectory as businesses face continued challenges from weak demand and uncertain export markets.

Hundreds Attend Funeral of Arthur Jones After Crete Tragedy More than 300 mourners gathered at St Mary's Church in Denbigh to pay their final respects to Arthur Jones, the 73-year-old keen motorcyclist whose disappearance in Crete captured national attention. The church was filled to capacity, with hundreds more listening to the service outside. In a fitting tribute to his passion for motorcycling, Mr Jones's coffin was carried in a hearse mounted on a motorcycle side-car, whilst his own Army-style motorcycle and side-car were parked prominently at the church entrance. Over 100 bikers, many wearing their leathers, attended the service to honour their fellow enthusiast. Mr Jones vanished on 19 June, just two days after arriving in Crete. His disappearance sparked a massive search effort, with a Facebook campaign titled "Find Arthur" attracting support from more than 3,000 people. Prime Minister David Cameron pledged to do "everything he can" to assist in locating Mr Jones. Tragically, his body was discovered on 3 August near the Chania resort where he had been staying. An inquest into his death was adjourned on Monday. The Reverend Jonathan Smith, Rector of Denbigh, described Mr Jones as a popular community figure known for his charity work and dedication to the annual Remembrance Day parade. A former soldier, Mr Jones had trained more than 7,000 Army cadets throughout his life. His son Jeff, who travelled to Crete to search for his father, led the tributes. Mr Jones is survived by three daughters and eight grandchildren.

Elderly People Targeted in Third of Fraud Cases, Charity Warns Over-65s are being disproportionately targeted by fraudsters, making up more than a third of all fraud referrals to a leading victims' charity despite representing less than a fifth of the population, new figures reveal. Victim Support received 39,272 fraud referrals in England and Wales in the year to September, with people aged 65 and over accounting for 35% of cases. This is nearly double their 18% share of the population. Even more concerning, those aged 75 and over represented 22% of victims despite making up just 8% of the population, the analysis showed. Lucy Hastings, director of Victim Support, described the targeting of older people as "disturbing and despicable." She warned that many other cases were likely going unreported. "We need to take away the stigma, so that victims of fraud have the confidence to report it, knowing that they are not alone and will be taken seriously," she said. Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, said elderly people could be scammed through multiple channels – on the doorstep, by phone, online or by post. "Figures like this aren't surprising to us as time and time again we're seeing stats that highlight this horrible problem and as scams become more sophisticated the risks they pose to older people are growing," she said. "To most of us it's unbelievable that anyone would target an older person to defraud them but unfortunately it happens and we know that older people can be especially vulnerable if they are lonely and isolated or suffer with dementia." ## Real-life victims speak out Pat Bottomley from Hull lost her entire £8,500 life savings after falling victim to fraudsters impersonating police officers. The 76-year-old widow received a call from a fake officer claiming a teenager with her son's name had been arrested in possession of her bank card. "The police officer assured me he was genuine and needed my assistance," Pat recalled. "He even gave me the name and phone number of a real policeman, which I looked up - so I thought he was being honest." A second fraudster then convinced her to transfer money into a savings account, supposedly to help catch international criminals. She only realised it was a scam when her son returned home. "I was totally drawn in and I felt absolutely gutted," Mrs Bottomley said. "The experience made me totally lose my confidence. I felt very stupid. It wasn't about the money - it was about how I was made to feel. I didn't want to answer the phone to anyone or go out anymore." ## Growing problem Last month, fraudsters posing as bank staff tricked 65-year-old Nargess Sadjady from west London into handing over her £12,000 savings. In March, Cormac McGuckin, 29, from County Londonderry, was sentenced to 20 months in prison after stealing more than £17,000 from a pensioner to pay gambling and wedding debts. He had befriended the elderly man and persuaded him to write blank cheques. Concerns have also been raised about the vulnerability of those approaching retirement under new pension rules, which make it easier to access money in pension pots. The Financial Conduct Authority has warned that con-artists have been keen to take advantage of the change.

Two Arrested After Fatal Crash Involving Spanish Workers in Tutbury A fatal collision occurred on Tutbury Road in Tutbury shortly before 07:00 GMT, involving a minibus transporting Spanish nationals to their workplace in the area. Two men have been arrested in connection with the incident. A man in his 40s from Quinta das Pedras, Portugal, and another in his 20s from Appleby Magna, Leicestershire, face accusations of causing death by careless driving. Six people sustained injuries in the crash. One victim remains in critical condition at Queen's Medical Centre in Nottingham, according to Staffordshire Police. A police spokesman confirmed: "We have interpreters helping us and our officers are currently liaising with the relevant embassies to keep their families fully informed." The A511 was temporarily closed following the incident but reopened at 12:15 GMT.

Trump Calls House Healthcare Bill "Mean" After Previously Praising It President Donald Trump has described the Republican healthcare bill passed by the House of Representatives as "mean," urging senators to craft more generous legislation, according to reports. Mr Trump had called the House bill a "great plan" when it passed by four votes but it was heavily criticised and was unlikely to get through the Senate. Mr Trump told 13 senators at a lunch that their version should be "kind". Repealing the Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare, was a key Trump poll pledge. Sources present at the White House lunch meeting told Politico that Mr Trump said senators needed to "pass a bill that Republicans are able to more easily defend". "That may be adding additional money into it," he reportedly said. Mr Trump's remarks on the "mean" House bill are in stark contrast to his previous public position. Although the bill gave Mr Trump his first legislative win, it was criticised by both Democrats and Senate Republicans. It was passed before being fully assessed - and a later assessment from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office concluded some 23 million people would lose health insurance over the next decade. One Republican Senator, Bob Corker, said at the time the bill had "zero" chance in the Senate. Instead, Senators decided to "start fresh" on drafting their own legislation. That new bill is being crafted in private by the Senate's Republicans. The 13 senators invited to lunch at the White House were a mix of conservative and moderate Republicans. One attendee, Finance Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch, told Reuters news agency that there still was a lot of work to do before legislation can be unveiled. "The total bill hasn't been resolved," he said. While Mr Trump's Republican party has a majority in both the House and Senate, his margin in the Senate is considerably smaller - just three Republicans voting against the bill would prevent it from passing. Sources at the meeting told Politico that Republicans "risk getting savaged in the 2018 midterms" if they failed to repeal Obamacare, after campaigning against it for seven years. During his election campaign, Mr Trump consistently criticised President Obama's healthcare policy, vowing to "repeal and replace" the legislation. The president first attempted to push through a bill in March, but withdrew it at the last minute when House Speaker Paul Ryan told him he would not have the minimum 215 votes needed. The debacle was seen as a major defeat for the new president, who blamed Democrats for not supporting his bill. The failure led to a new version of the bill allowing states to opt out of several of its provisions, and allow higher premiums for some patients.

Indian School Warden Suspended After Forcing Students to Strip During Menstruation Inspection A female warden at Kasturba Gandhi Girls Residential School in Uttar Pradesh, northern India, has been suspended following allegations that she forced students to strip naked during an inspection to identify which girl had started menstruating. The incident came to light after parents lodged complaints with school authorities. Surekha Tomar, the accused warden, initially defended her actions to Indian television channels, claiming she was acting in the students' best interests. "I thought a 10-year-old might feel scared or ashamed to tell me if they had started their period so I wanted to find out. I am like their guardian. If I ask them something like this or check them, I have not committed a crime," Tomar told reporters, explaining that she discovered blood on a bathroom door and wanted to determine if a child had begun menstruating for the first time. However, the warden later changed her statement entirely, claiming the incident was fabricated by colleagues who wanted her removed from her position. Multiple students have corroborated the allegations, describing a humiliating ordeal. "Ma'am wanted to investigate. She asked us to strip. She wanted to check if one of us had started our period," one student told reporters. "She told two of our schoolmates to check and said if you don't tell us I will beat you. She said if you don't have shame I don't either." Parents expressed outrage upon learning of the incident. One father said he left his job immediately to retrieve his daughter from the school. "I called my girl and she said it is true, and that she was also asked to strip. The warden should be jailed," he stated. Other teachers at the school have condemned the incident and called for strict action if the allegations are proven true. The investigation continues as authorities examine the claims.

Four Teams Compete for £40m Thames Bridge Design Four design teams have been shortlisted to create a new £40 million cycle and pedestrian bridge linking Nine Elms to Pimlico across the River Thames in south London. The proposals were selected from 74 entries in a competition run by Wandsworth Council, which hopes the bridge will boost economic growth in the Nine Elms area. The shortlisted teams are Buro Happold, Bystrup Architecture Design and Engineering, and Ove Arup & Partners, who have submitted two separate proposals. The winning design must meet several challenging criteria. The bridge needs to accommodate two-way movement of cyclists and pedestrians during peak times whilst being high enough to allow large boats to pass underneath. However, it cannot be too steep for users to comfortably climb. Ravi Govindia, leader of Wandsworth Council, said: "There is still a long way to go but these teams have given us real hope that a solution can be found to the complex challenges involved in creating a new pedestrian and cycle link across this stretch of the river." However, Westminster City Council has expressed reservations about the project. Councillor Heather Acton, cabinet member for sustainability, said local Pimlico residents have raised concerns about the proposed location. "Westminster is not against connecting the two banks of the Thames for pedestrians and cyclists, in fact we are very enthusiastic," she said. "The location, however, needs far more careful thought, in terms of connectivity and also with regard to cost to the taxpayer." She suggested a preferable alternative would be adding a pedestrian-cyclist bridge alongside the existing rail bridge connecting Battersea to Victoria Station. Residents have been invited to comment on the designs, and their feedback will be considered before a winner is announced later this year.

Mel Gibson Planning Sequel to The Passion of the Christ Mel Gibson is reportedly planning a sequel to his controversial 2004 biblical epic, The Passion of the Christ, focusing on the resurrection of Jesus. Screenwriter Randall Wallace revealed to the Hollywood Reporter that he is currently working on a script for the follow-up film. "I always wanted to tell this story," Wallace explained. "The Passion is the beginning and there's a lot more story to tell." The collaboration emerged from discussions between Wallace and Gibson while working on their forthcoming film Hacksaw Ridge. Gibson has not yet publicly commented on the Passion sequel. The original Passion of the Christ became a phenomenal commercial success, earning $612 million worldwide and claiming the title of most successful independent film of all time. However, the film sparked significant controversy when it was released 12 years ago. Scripted entirely in Latin and Aramaic, Gibson's graphic depiction of Christ's final hours drew widespread criticism from Jewish groups who condemned it as anti-Semitic. Gibson's own reputation was further damaged in 2006 when he was arrested for drink-driving and subsequently accused of making anti-Semitic remarks. Despite the controversy, Wallace emphasized strong support from the Christian community for a sequel. "The evangelical community considers The Passion the biggest movie ever out of Hollywood, and they kept telling us that they think a sequel will be even bigger," he said. Wallace, who recently directed the faith-based drama Heaven is for Real, declined to discuss financing details, stating: "It's too early to talk money. This is a huge and sacred subject." Meanwhile, Hacksaw Ridge marks Gibson's return to directing since 2006's Apocalypto, starring Andrew Garfield as Medal of Honor recipient Desmond Doss.

Major Internet Companies Stage'Internet Slowdown' Protest Over Net Neutrality Rules Dozens of major internet companies are preparing to stage a coordinated protest on Wednesday against proposed Federal Communications Commission regulations that they fear could fundamentally alter how the internet operates, potentially forcing content providers to pay extra fees for fast access to consumers. The protest, dubbed "Internet Slowdown," will see participating websites displaying a spinning wheel icon—the familiar symbol of slow loading speeds that frustrates internet users worldwide. However, the sites themselves will continue to function normally, with the icon serving as a symbolic reminder of what could happen if net neutrality protections are weakened. Netflix, the streaming video giant, signaled its participation by posting an animation of the loading wheel on its US Twitter account Monday. The company urged other firms to join the campaign, with the icon linking to information about how users can take action to defend net neutrality principles. According to Free Press, one of the protest organizers, participants include some of the internet's most popular platforms: Reddit, Mozilla, Kickstarter, Upworthy, Automattic (which operates WordPress), Digg, Vimeo, Boing Boing, Thunderclap, Urban Dictionary, Foursquare, and Cheezburger. The American Civil Liberties Union has also confirmed its participation. Twitter, while supporting the cause, said it would participate "in other ways" rather than adding a banner to its homepage, though a spokesman declined to provide specific details about the form its protest would take. The controversy stems from FCC proposals introduced following a January ruling by the US Court of Appeals that found broadband providers were not obligated to treat all internet traffic equally. The FCC's new rules would require telecom providers to ensure users have access to internet service that is "sufficiently robust, fast and effectively usable." However, critics argue the proposals contain a critical flaw: while providers would be banned from blocking legal content, they would be allowed to charge for "prioritized" data delivery. This has raised concerns about the creation of internet "fast lanes" where companies that can afford to pay receive better service, potentially disadvantaging smaller competitors and startups. "The cause of net neutrality is important to us as a business. It's important to our visitors, and it's important for our democracy. We're proud to take part in the Internet Slowdown and encourage others to join with us," said Erik Martin, general manager of Reddit. Paul Sieminski, general counsel of Automattic, emphasized the broader implications: "The free and open internet has been central to the economy and to global free expression. Everyone has to step up now and do everything they can to protect it." More than 100 technology companies, including Microsoft, Google, Facebook, and Twitter, have already written to the FCC expressing their concerns. In their letter, they warned that the proposed rules "would enable phone and cable internet service providers to discriminate both technically and financially against internet companies and to impose new tolls on them." Craig Aaron, president of the Free Press Action Fund, framed the issue as a David versus Goliath battle: "We need our leaders to stand up to the cabal of cable and phone giants that have called the shots in Washington for too long." The companies concluded their letter with a stark warning: "This represents a grave threat to the internet."

Man Banned from Football Matches After Racist and Disability Abuse A football fan has been banned from attending matches for three years after admitting to racist and disability-related abuse at two separate games at Glasgow's Ibrox stadium. John Brown, 25, from Motherwell, targeted Cowdenbeath player Kudus Oyenuga with racist gestures on 28 March as the footballer celebrated scoring a goal. Glasgow Sheriff Court heard that Brown "made monkey gestures using his arms and directed them towards the Cowdenbeath football player." Police officers at the stadium immediately arrested him for the offence. Brown committed a second offence on 3 October during a match against Falkirk. When the visiting team scored an equaliser, he shouted abuse towards Falkirk's away supporters and made offensive gestures specifically directed at fans in the disabled section. In addition to the three-year football banning order, Brown was handed a community payback order requiring him to complete 70 hours of unpaid work. Stephen Ferguson, football liaison prosecutor for the west of Scotland, condemned Brown's actions as "utterly reprehensible." He stated: "There is absolutely no place in modern Scotland for individuals who commit crimes motivated by prejudice towards a person's race or disability." Ferguson emphasised that police and prosecutors take such offences extremely seriously and remain committed to bringing offenders to justice.

Cyclist Celebrates Victory One Lap Too Early at Giro d'Italia A premature celebration left Slovenian cyclist Luka Pibernik red-faced during stage five of the Giro d'Italia on Wednesday, as he mistakenly thought he had won the race in Messina. Pibernik punched the air in triumph as he crossed what he believed was the finish line. However, the route looped back for another lap, and his celebration turned to embarrassment as the peloton swept past him moments later. Colombia's Fernando Gaviria actually claimed the stage victory, finishing the 159km route from Pescara in 3 hours, 40 minutes and 11 seconds. This was Gaviria's second stage win of this year's race, having also triumphed on Sunday's stage three. Italy's Jakub Mareczko finished second, with Ireland's Sam Bennett taking third place. Pibernik eventually crossed the genuine finish line in 148th position, 20 seconds behind the winner. In the overall standings, Luxembourg's Bob Jungels retained the pink jersey as race leader. Welsh cyclist Geraint Thomas of Team Sky remains in second place, just six seconds behind, while fellow Briton Adam Yates sits third, 10 seconds off the pace. Yates shares his time with defending champion Vincenzo Nibali and 2014 winner Nairo Quintana, setting up an intriguing battle for the podium positions. Thursday's sixth stage presents a challenging 217km ride from Reggio Calabria to Terme Luigiane, featuring both category-three and category-four climbs that could shake up the general classification.

South Korea Heads to Polls as Moon Jae-in Leads Presidential Race South Koreans are voting today in a presidential election that comes at a critical time for the nation, facing economic challenges and escalating tensions with North Korea. Left-leaning candidate Moon Jae-in enters election day as the clear front-runner, with centrist Ahn Cheol-soo his nearest challenger. The vote takes place against the backdrop of unprecedented political upheaval following the impeachment of former President Park Geun-hye. On the final day of campaigning, Mr. Moon called for an "overwhelming victory," arguing it would help heal the national divide caused by Ms. Park's downfall and impeachment. Meanwhile, Mr. Ahn, campaigning in swing states, expressed confidence he could still secure victory. The election follows the dramatic removal of Park Geun-hye in March, who became the first South Korean president to be impeached. She is currently standing trial on charges of bribery and abuse of power, though she denies wrongdoing and has repeatedly apologized. **North Korea Policy a Key Divider** Mr. Moon, who narrowly lost to Ms. Park in 2012, proposes a markedly different approach to North Korea than his conservative predecessor. While Ms. Park cut almost all ties with Pyongyang, Mr. Moon advocates for increased contact and dialogue. He has criticized previous conservative administrations for failing to stop North Korea's weapons development and favors a two-track approach combining increased dialogue with sanctions to encourage change. BBC Korea correspondent Stephen Evans notes this approach could create tensions with Washington, particularly if US President Donald Trump pursues a harder line against North Korea, especially following any potential nuclear tests. **Domestic Issues Drive Voters** Beyond foreign policy, domestic concerns feature prominently in voters' minds. All candidates have promised to protect South Korea's fragile economic recovery—the fourth largest in Asia—and tackle stubbornly high youth unemployment. Candidates are also pledging to reform the family-run conglomerates, or chaebols, that dominate the domestic economy and address perceptions of elitism in political society. Observers expect high turnout, boosted by younger voters. Polls close at 20:00 local time (11:00 GMT), with results expected soon after.

**Warnock Demands Desire as Cardiff Face Championship Leaders Brighton** Cardiff City manager Neil Warnock has warned he will not tolerate players lacking commitment when his side travels to face Championship leaders Brighton on Friday. After his team again conceded late to draw at Brentford on Boxing Day, Warnock accused some of his players of lacking "desire" and vowed to make changes for the crucial encounter. "I can't pick anyone who is going to drift in that game because Brighton are a good side," said Warnock, clearly frustrated by his team's recent performances. The Bluebirds boss has been particularly disappointed by his side's inability to see out games when in winning positions. At Brentford, Cardiff appeared to have secured all three points when Kenneth Zohore scored in the 89th minute, only for Sullay Kaikai to grab his second goal in added time to level the match. It was a familiar pattern for Cardiff, who had similarly surrendered a late lead in their previous fixture against Barnsley in the Welsh capital. Now they face a Brighton side sitting top of the Championship following their victory over QPR, which was aided by Newcastle's defeat to Sheffield Wednesday. "We have to stand up and be counted. It's good to be going down there. They are as good a team in the league as there is," Warnock acknowledged. The manager may be forced into changes regardless, with midfielder Peter Whittingham—who scored from the penalty spot at Brentford—doubtful after being substituted at half-time with a hamstring problem. "He felt a little bit tight and he'd been booked as well so we thought we would be careful," Warnock explained.

Sainsbury's Apologises for Seeking Unpaid Artist to Refurbish Store Canteen Supermarket giant Sainsbury's has issued an apology after facing a social media backlash over an advertisement seeking an unpaid artist to redecorate a staff canteen. The store in Camden Road took out an advert for "an ambitious artist" to "voluntarily refurbish" the facility. The company was shamed on social media by people who pointed out the successful supermarket chain should pay its way. Artist Conor Collins attacked the supermarket's attempt to hire someone for free and suggested the store deducted some money from its bosses' salaries to "pay someone to do work for you so that the concept of'starving artist' wouldn't have to be a thing." He wrote on Twitter: "Dear Sainsbury's, I am looking for a company worth £150,000,000 to feed all of my artist friends in Manchester." Other social media users expressed similar outrage. One tweet read: "@Sainsbury's Awful. You can afford to pay an artist their worth." Another said: "So @sainsburys let me get this straight. You turnover £26bn yet want an artist to voluntarily decorate your canteen?" A spokesman for the company said the advert was an "error of judgement". Sainsbury's told the BBC it was discussing the matter with the store in Camden, adding: "It is not our policy to hire volunteers and we are sorry for this error of judgement."

Former Flint Emergency Managers Charged in Water Crisis Two former state-appointed emergency managers and two city employees face felony charges for their roles in the Flint water crisis that exposed thousands of residents to lead-contaminated drinking water. Michigan Attorney General Bill Schuette announced charges Tuesday against Darnell Earley and Gerald Ambrose, who served as emergency managers during the critical period when Flint's water supply became dangerously contaminated with lead in 2014. Mr. Earley and Mr. Ambrose each face charges of false pretenses, conspiracy to commit false pretenses, misconduct in office, and willful neglect of duty in office. The charges carry a combined maximum sentence of 46 years in prison. "The tragedy that we know of as the Flint water crisis did not occur by accident," Mr. Schuette said at a press conference. "Flint was a casualty of arrogance, disdain and failure of management, an absence of accountability." Also charged were two former city employees: Howard Croft, a public works superintendent, and Daugherty Johnson, a utilities manager. Both face conspiracy charges for allegedly operating a water treatment plant that was not properly equipped to treat water from the Flint River. They face up to 40 years in prison. Mr. Johnson's attorney, Edwar Zeineh, told the Associated Press his client will plead not guilty. The other defendants and their lawyers could not immediately be reached for comment. The water crisis began in April 2014 when Mr. Earley, serving as emergency manager, decided to switch the city's water source from Lake Huron to the Flint River as a cost-saving measure. The acidic river water corroded aging pipes throughout the city, causing lead to leach into the drinking water supply. Tests later revealed high levels of lead in blood samples from children in the majority African-American city of approximately 100,000 residents. Lead exposure can cause serious developmental problems in children and other health complications. Flint switched back to its previous water system in October 2015. Federal regulators now say filtered tap water is safe to drink, though they still recommend bottled water for young children and pregnant women. The charges bring the total number of people facing criminal counts related to the investigation to 13. Previous charges have been filed against state regulators, health officials, and environmental workers accused of concealing data about elevated lead levels in children's blood. The announcement comes one day after a Reuters report identified nearly 3,000 areas nationwide with lead poisoning rates twice as high as Flint's during the peak of its crisis, highlighting the scope of lead contamination problems across the United States.

**Blackburn's Jordan Rhodes Set for Middlesbrough Talks** Blackburn Rovers have granted permission for striker Jordan Rhodes to discuss a potential move to Middlesbrough. The 25-year-old Scotland international, who joined Rovers from Huddersfield for £8m in 2012, has been prolific at Ewood Park with 83 goals in 169 appearances, including 11 this season. "The player has expressed his desire to talk to the Teesside club and will travel for discussions," Blackburn confirmed in a statement.

Doll's House Listed on Rightmove Attracts Genuine Buyer Interest in Charity Fundraiser A miniature Georgian doll's house has been listed on property website Rightmove in an unusual fundraising effort for a Warwickshire hospice charity, prompting at least one potential buyer to request a viewing of what they believed was a real property. The 75cm (30in) high toy house belongs to Shipston Home Nursing, a hospice charity supporting terminally-ill patients in south Warwickshire. The charity is hoping to raise funds through the sale to continue its vital care services. The listing was placed on Rightmove "as a joke" by Peter Clarke Estate Agents, which is supporting the charity's fundraising efforts, according to the Warwick Courier. However, the elaborate description and professional photographs proved convincing enough to confuse at least one prospective homebuyer. The property is described on the website as a "classic Georgian house" featuring four bedrooms, a drawing room, and "potential for further accommodation" in a "quiet location situated in a popular village in south Warwickshire." The listing highlights traditional features including a fireplace, an Aga, exposed wood floors, and "charming period features." It notes that "a unique feature of the property is the roof and front elevations swing open to reveal beautiful accommodation set on three floors and it is part furnished." Sally Coombs, branch manager at Peter Clarke Estate Agents, recounted the confusion: "We put it on Rightmove as a joke but we actually had somebody who wanted to view it, thinking it was a proper house. We said to the caller that if they looked at it properly, they would see it was a doll's house." Rebecca Mawle, the hospice's fundraising co-ordinator, explained that the house was created as a "labour of love" by a charity supporter. The charity is accepting bids until 7 September and hopes offers will be "as high as possible." "It's beautifully made," Ms Mawle said, adding that she found the buyer confusion "hilarious." "Looking at it on the pictures, it really does look like a charming property." Rightmove's housing expert, Miles Shipside, acknowledged the unusual listing: "We wouldn't normally allow listings like this but as it's captured the attention of so many and it's for the agent's local charity, we've let it stay on Rightmove to help them get as many offers as possible."

Hannah Mills Eyes Tokyo Gold in New Olympic Sailing Class Media playback is not supported on this device Britain's Olympic sailing champion Hannah Mills is embarking on an exciting new challenge as she aims to become the nation's most successful female Olympic sailor. The 29-year-old Welsh athlete, who claimed gold at the Rio Olympics and silver in London alongside Saskia Clark in the 470 dinghy class, is switching to the 49er FX skiff for the Tokyo Games. With Clark's retirement following Rio, Mills has chosen to pursue this demanding new discipline. "The FX to me just presents such a new and exciting shift. Every day I go sailing I'm scared, I'm excited, I'm laughing so much," Mills explained enthusiastically. After a decade competing in the 470 class, Mills felt the need for a fresh challenge to rekindle her passion for the sport. "For me it was about finding the love of sailing again. It's an amazing sport, I love the 470 and the racing is awesome," she said. "But having done something for ten years, at some point in time I think you have to step away. And I didn't want to step away and not sail." The 49er FX, which made its Olympic debut in Rio, presents a significant challenge for the decorated sailor. However, Mills remains realistic about her prospects. "It's a big challenge, that's for sure. I'm not deluded that I'm stepping into the FX and everything will be rosy. But I think that challenge is really positive for me," she acknowledged. "Obviously it is all about winning a gold medal in Tokyo," Mills added. "To me right now I'm fully committed to the FX and I'm going to be giving that as good a shot as I can."

Carli Lloyd Hat-Trick Fires USA to World Cup Glory Carli Lloyd scored a stunning hat-trick, including a remarkable long-range strike, as the United States defeated Japan 5-2 to win the Women's World Cup final in Vancouver. The 32-year-old midfielder netted three times within the opening 16 minutes, with her third goal - a spectacular shot from the halfway line - becoming one of the most memorable moments in World Cup history. "I did it once in training but very rarely do you wind up and hit it like that," said Lloyd, who had suffered penalty heartbreak in the 2011 final defeat to Japan. "You train and train and train and I dreamed of scoring a shot like that." Lloyd opened the scoring after just three minutes before doubling the lead two minutes later. After Lauren Holiday's volley made it 3-0, the Houston Dash player completed her hat-trick with an audacious strike that beat Japanese goalkeeper Ayumi Kaihori from distance. Tobin Heath added a fifth goal as the USA became the first nation to win the tournament three times, adding to their 1991 and 1999 triumphs. "When you're feeling good mentally and physically, those plays are instinctive," Lloyd explained. The midfielder, who had scored in each of her side's previous three matches, revealed she uses visualization techniques as part of her preparation. "I was at home with my headphones on but I was on the field and I was running and doing sprints," she said. "I completely zoned out and dreamed of playing in a World Cup final and scoring four goals. It sounds funny but that's what it is all about. I feel like I blacked out for the first 30 minutes of the game. It was crazy." Despite trailing 4-0 after 16 minutes, Japan showed resilience by pulling two goals back through Yuki Ogimi and a Julie Johnston own goal before Heath's strike sealed victory for the Americans. Lloyd's hat-trick brought her tournament total to six goals, matching Germany's Celia Sasic for the Golden Boot. "I've had people believe in me," she said. "Fitness was definitely an issue for me but I've turned that into a strength and the mental side of the game is a huge thing. I'm just really proud of everyone. It's a surreal moment, we made history." The victory came under English-born coach Jill Ellis, who took charge just 14 months ago following Tom Sermanni's dismissal. The 48-year-old, born in Portsmouth, defended her team's journey despite criticism during the build-up and group stages. "I told the players they had to continue to believe in the process," Ellis said. "There have been some growing pains but it's not vindication, it just feels really good and I could not be more proud of the players and the staff because I knew they had it in them."

Hallam Amos Returns from Injury in Time for Six Nations Consideration Dragons wing Hallam Amos has returned from a shoulder injury at what could prove to be a crucial time for his international ambitions, with Wales head coach Warren Gatland set to name his Six Nations squad on Tuesday. The 21-year-old medical student, who sustained the injury during Wales' memorable World Cup victory over England in October, marked his comeback with a try after just 50 seconds in Dragons' 31-18 European Challenge Cup Pool Two victory over Castres. "I've come back at a good time. There are exciting matches coming in the next few weeks," Amos told BBC Wales Sport, though he remained cautious about his international prospects. "I'm not sure, it's a tough one because I'm only just back from injury and there are other boys playing really well at the moment," he said. "I haven't thought too much about it, I just wanted to get back on the pitch with the Dragons, and whatever happens, happens." Amos, who has five international caps, faces stiff competition for a place in Gatland's squad. He will be vying for selection alongside established names like Northampton's George North and Cardiff Blues' Alex Cuthbert, with the Ospreys' Eli Walker and Blues' Tom James also in contention. The wing returned to action ahead of schedule, having originally targeted a return around this time but managing to come back a couple of weeks early. His first touch could hardly have gone better, finishing off a move involving Sarel Pretorius and Jason Tovey. "You think about it the night before and that's exactly what you want," Amos said. "In rugby you will pick up injuries, though it's been tough watching the boys. But I can't ask for much more than that with my first touch back after three months." Amos will now focus on helping Dragons secure a home quarter-final in the Challenge Cup when they face Sale Sharks away on Thursday.

Northern Ireland Politicians Divided on Brexit Vote Following High Court Ruling Political tensions have intensified in Northern Ireland following a landmark High Court ruling in London that determined the UK government cannot trigger Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty without parliamentary approval. The ruling means MPs must vote before formal exit negotiations with the European Union can begin, sparking contrasting responses from Northern Ireland's political parties. The Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) has pledged to vote against triggering Article 50 when the matter comes before parliament. SDLP representative Mr Durkan, speaking on the Sunday Politics programme, emphasized his party's commitment to reflecting the wishes of Northern Ireland voters. "If we get to a situation where parliament will be voting on the terms, I want to make one thing clear, we will be voting against Article 50 because that is our position and that is the position that the people of Northern Ireland have voted for," Mr Durkan stated. In contrast, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) plans to leverage their parliamentary position differently. DUP MP Nigel Dodds indicated his party would work to secure favorable terms for Northern Ireland during the Brexit process, stating he expects "a deal which is in the mutual interests of the Irish Republic, of the other member EU states, of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland." The division reflects Northern Ireland's unique position on Brexit. While the overall UK electorate voted to leave the EU, 56% of Northern Ireland voters opted to remain, creating ongoing political friction. Prime Minister Theresa May had argued that the referendum result and existing ministerial powers eliminated the need for a parliamentary vote, but campaigners successfully challenged this position as unconstitutional. The Westminster government plans to appeal Thursday's ruling at the Supreme Court, with a further hearing expected next month.

Stonehenge Bluestones May Have Been Chosen for Their Musical Properties A groundbreaking study has revealed that the ancient bluestones of Stonehenge may have been selected for their unique acoustic qualities, offering a fascinating new perspective on one of archaeology's greatest mysteries. Researchers from London's Royal College of Art have discovered that rocks in the Preseli Hills of Pembrokeshire possess remarkable sonic properties, ringing like bells when struck. The investigation, part of the Landscape and Perception Project, aimed to understand what "Stone Age eyes and ears" would have experienced in a prehistoric landscape. "It hasn't been considered until now that sound might have been a factor," said Paul Devereux, the project's principal investigator. The team tested thousands of stones along the Carn Menyn ridge and found an unusually high proportion produced clear, resonant tones when struck. "The percentage of the rocks on the Carn Menyn ridge are ringing rocks, they ring just like a bell," Mr Devereux explained. "And there's lots of different tones, you could play a tune. In fact, we have had percussionists who have played proper percussion pieces off the rocks." Since the 1920s, archaeologists have known that Stonehenge's bluestones were transported 199 miles (320 km) from Mynydd Preseli to Wiltshire, but the reason for selecting these particular stones has remained elusive. The monument, constructed between 3,000 BC and 1,600 BC, has puzzled researchers for generations. "There had to be something special about these rocks," Mr Devereux said. "Why else would they take them from here all the way to Stonehenge?" Prof Tim Darvill, who has conducted hundreds of excavations at Stonehenge, supports the theory that prehistoric peoples had different relationships with stone than modern society. "We don't know of course that they moved them because they rang but ringing rocks are a prominent part of many cultures," he noted. "You can almost see them as a pre-historic glockenspiel, if you like and you could knock them and hear these tunes," Prof Darvill added. "And soundscapes of pre-history are something we're really just beginning to explore." This discovery opens new avenues for understanding how ancient peoples interacted with their environment and selected materials for sacred monuments.

Bristol bridge approval'begins new era' for UK masonry arch construction A pedestrian and cyclist bridge approved for construction over Bridge Valley Road in Bristol marks a significant milestone in British engineering, according to experts. The bridge will complete a missing link in the circular route around the Downs, addressing longstanding safety concerns at what has been described as a "busy and dangerous junction". Dr Adrienn Tomor, from the University of the West of England, who proposed the scheme alongside the Friends of the Downs and Avon Gorge group (FODAG), expressed her delight at the approval. "This is the first time thatadelical stone bridge has been approved for construction during the past 100 years," she said. Dr Tomor believes the project "represents a new era for masonry arch bridge construction in the UK and Europe" and will "provide great improvements for pedestrians and cyclists". Before construction can begin, planning conditions must be finalised and an independent charity established to oversee fundraising efforts. Jack Penrose from FODAG welcomed the city council's decision, stating: "It'll be infinitely safer than what's on offer at the moment."

Derby County Edge Nottingham Forest in Hard-Fought East Midlands Derby Martin Olsson's late strike was enough to secure a 1-0 victory for Derby County over Nottingham Forest in an East Midlands derby that was long on effort but desperately short on quality at the iPro Stadium. The Swedish defender curled home a superb 79th-minute effort past Dorus de Vries to settle a tense encounter that had promised much but delivered little in terms of genuine goalmouth action until that decisive moment. Forest, under the interim stewardship of Paul Williams, had actually enjoyed the better of a scrappy first half, their high-tempo pressing game causing the Rams all sorts of problems in the opening exchanges. The visitors' energetic approach forced numerous errors from the hosts, leaving the home supporters increasingly frustrated as their side struggled to find any rhythm. However, the introduction of Derby's new football adviser Harry Redknapp's influence at half-time proved pivotal. The experienced coach had trudged down from his seat in the directors' box towards the dressing room at the interval, and whatever words of wisdom he and head coach Darren Wassall imparted clearly had the desired effect. Derby emerged a transformed side after the break, finally beginning to assert themselves in midfield and looking far more threatening in attack. Tom Ince started to cause problems with his pace and trickery, producing a couple of surging runs and a fierce low strike that De Vries dealt with comfortably – remarkably, it was the first effort on target in the match. The breakthrough eventually arrived eleven minutes from time when Ince turned provider, slipping a pass to Olsson who demonstrated excellent technique to curl a first-time shot beyond the helpless De Vries and into the net. The reality was that this derby match, while full of committed tackles, passion and intensity, offered precious little in the way of genuine quality or entertainment. Bone-crunching challenges, blocked shots, misplaced passes and a succession of free-kicks dominated proceedings, but clear-cut chances remained conspicuous by their absence. Forest had looked relatively comfortable for long periods and managed a couple of speculative long-range efforts, but they too were disappointingly toothless in the final third and had no answer once Olsson had broken the deadlock. The victory ensures Derby remain firmly in the promotion race, staying fifth in the Championship table. For Forest, the search for goals continues to be their Achilles heel. Derby head coach Darren Wassall was quick to praise Redknapp's contribution: "I wanted Harry in the dressing room before the game, at half-time and at full-time. His input is just as much as anyone else's and I welcome that because if he can improve us in our promotion push by three or four per cent we will be delighted." Forest's Williams remained philosophical despite the defeat: "For the majority of the game I was very pleased with how the players performed. The pressure is on me now as to how we are going to create and score goals."

Netflix Identifies Popcorn Time as Major Piracy Threat Netflix has publicly acknowledged a growing concern over illegal streaming services, specifically calling out Popcorn Time as a significant competitor in a recent letter to shareholders. The streaming giant's admission highlights how digital piracy continues to challenge legitimate subscription services. Popcorn Time operates as an application that streams films and television programmes using torrent technology. The app has gained substantial traction, particularly in the United Kingdom, where it has been installed on hundreds of thousands of computers, according to TorrentFreak, a website specializing in copyright and privacy news. The founder of TorrentFreak, identified only as "Ernesto," explains that Popcorn Time poses a unique threat because "its easy-to-use user interface appeals to a mainstream audience." This accessibility makes it particularly dangerous for legitimate streaming services, as it lowers the technical barrier that typically prevents casual users from engaging with piracy. Despite its user-friendly design, Popcorn Time remains entirely illegal. Copyright holders have repeatedly attempted to shut down the service, with major movie studios successfully pressuring the original developers to close their project. However, because the application's code is open source, it was quickly revived by other developers, allowing the service to persist and grow. Ernesto reports that Popcorn Time now boasts millions of users worldwide. This claim is supported by Google search data cited by Netflix, which shows a dramatic increase in searches for the app in the Netherlands. Netflix described these findings as "sobering," underscoring the scale of the piracy challenge. In response to such threats, Netflix has been investing heavily in original content production, including high-profile series like House of Cards starring Kevin Spacey. The company also identified other legitimate competitors in their shareholder letter, including HBO Go, Hulu, and Amazon Prime. The piracy problem is compounded by geographical content restrictions. Some Netflix subscribers attempt to use workarounds to access the US version of the service, which offers a different content library. While Netflix is working to close these loopholes, they remain unresolved. Popcorn Time maintains an advantage over legitimate services by operating without rights agreements with studios and producers, allowing them to offer unrestricted content regardless of users' locations. This fundamental difference continues to make piracy an attractive, albeit illegal, option for many viewers worldwide.

German Teen Gets Six Years for IS-Ordered Knife Attack on Police A German court has sentenced a teenage girl to six years in youth detention for stabbing a police officer in what prosecutors say was an attack ordered and supervised by the Islamic State group. Safia S, who was 15 at the time of the incident, stabbed and seriously wounded a police officer in the neck at Hanover's central station on 26 February last year. The Celle regional court convicted her of attempted murder and helping a terrorist organisation, as well as grievous bodily harm. The German Moroccan teenager had previously travelled to Istanbul with the intention of joining IS in Syria, but was brought back by her mother. Despite returning to Germany, she maintained contact with the jihadist group via the internet. Judge cited phone messages as evidence that the attack was carried out in support of IS. In one text to an acquaintance after the November 2015 Paris attacks, she wrote: "Allah bless our lions who carried out an operation in Paris yesterday."
