Blogger Anton Hodza welcomed the ban as a "fantastic opportunity" for Ukrainian start-ups to fill the void, whilst another commentator joked that authorities should brace for riots from disgruntled schoolchildren and pensioners. However, IT expert Artur Orujaliev condemned the move as censorship, and journalist Oksana Romanyuk from Reporters Without Borders argued that the economic justifications were actually sanctions against ordinary Ukrainians. Popular VK news community Tipichnyy Kiev, which has 695,000 subscribers, offered practical guidance to readers, suggesting mirror sites on Facebook, Twitter and Instagram, and assistance with proxy servers. The sanctions extend beyond social media, affecting cyber-security firm Kaspersky Lab, Doctor Web, airline Aeroflot, television companies including NTV and RT, and news agency Ria Novosti. The row has even impacted cultural events, with Russia's Eurovision contestant Julia Samoilova barred from travelling to Kiev due to prior performances in Crimea. Ukraine's sanctions list has grown steadily, now encompassing over 1,200 individuals. Since Russian troops annexed Crimea following President Yanukovych's 2014 removal, conflict in eastern Ukraine has claimed approximately 10,000 lives. Despite a tentative ceasefire, violations persist, with 13 deaths reported last month. Both the European Union and United States have imposed sanctions on Russian entities linked to the conflict, prompting retaliatory measures from Moscow.

Ireland Women's Rugby: Paula Fitzpatrick to Captain Side Against Scotland in Six Nations Opener Paula Fitzpatrick will lead Ireland Women into their Six Nations opener against Scotland on Friday after regular captain Niamh Briggs was ruled out through injury. The number eight will take on the captaincy role for the crucial Broadway Stadium clash, with coach Tom Tierney making several changes to his squad ahead of the tournament. Hooker Leah Lyons will earn just her second cap for Ireland, joining props Lindsay Peat and Ailis Egan in the front row. The experienced Marie-Louise Reilly partners St Mary's College player Orla Fitzsimons at lock, whilst the back-row sees flankers Ciara Griffin and Claire Molloy pack down alongside captain Fitzpatrick. Uncapped scrum-half Ali Hughes will partner the experienced Nora Stapleton at half-back, marking her debut in the green jersey. Behind the scrum, Sene Naoupu, Jenny Murphy, Alison Miller, Niamh Kavanagh and Mairead Coyne complete the starting XV. The replacements bench features significant depth, with Ulster prop Ilse Van Staden joining fellow uncapped players Ciara O'Connor, Jennie Finlay and Eimear Considine. Another Ulster representative, Claire McLaughlin, is also named among the substitutes. Despite Ireland being strong favourites against a Scottish side that failed to qualify for next year's World Cup, coach Tierney has warned his players against complacency. "The first game of the Six Nations is always a big challenge, as it's very difficult to know what the opposition are going to throw at you," said Tierney. "Scotland in front of their home crowd will be looking to give their fans something to get excited about, so it's really important that we go into the game fully focused." Following Friday's encounter, Ireland face a busy schedule with Italy in L'Aquila nine days later, before hosting France at Donnybrook on 26 February. They then travel to Cardiff to face Wales on 11 March before completing their campaign with a home fixture against England on 16 March.

Malta: A Journey Through Modern History from Colony to EU Member Malta's modern history represents a remarkable transformation from British crown colony to independent republic and European Union member state, marked by pivotal moments of conflict, political upheaval, and strategic realignment. ## Colonial Era and World War II Heroism Malta became a crown colony of the British Empire in 1814, establishing a relationship that would define the island nation for over a century. This connection proved crucial during World War II, when Malta's strategic Mediterranean location made it a vital Allied base and a primary target for Axis forces. The German and Italian air forces subjected Malta to relentless bombing campaigns, testing the resilience of its population. In recognition of extraordinary civilian courage during these attacks, King George VI awarded the entire colony the George Cross in 1942, Britain's highest civilian decoration for heroism—a honor that remains part of Malta's national flag today. ## Path to Independence Malta's journey toward self-governance proved circuitous. Self-government was first granted in 1947, only to be revoked in 1959 before being restored in 1962. Full independence finally arrived in 1964, launching a new chapter in Maltese history. Under the Nationalist Party from 1964-71, Malta pursued pro-Western alignment. However, the 1971 election of Dom Mintoff's Malta Labour Party dramatically shifted the nation's trajectory toward non-alignment, cultivating special relationships with Libya and Communist states. Malta became a republic in 1974, and the closure of British military bases in 1979 symbolically ended the colonial era. ## Political Oscillation and European Integration Malta's political landscape witnessed significant oscillation between parties with contrasting visions. After Mintoff's resignation in 1984, the Nationalist Party's 1987 victory under Eddie Fenech Adami signaled a pivot toward European integration. Malta's diplomatic significance was highlighted when it hosted the historic 1989 summit between Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev and US President George Bush. The nation submitted its EU membership application in 1990, though this ambition was temporarily shelved when the Labour Party returned to power in 1996. The Nationalist Party's 1998 return revived EU aspirations. In December 2002, Malta received formal invitation to join the EU, confirmed by a March 2003 referendum where 53% voted yes. Malta officially joined the EU in May 2004 as one of ten new member states. ## Contemporary Challenges Lawrence Gonzi succeeded Adami as prime minister in 2004, overseeing Malta's euro adoption in January 2008. The 2008 elections saw the Nationalist Party retain power by a narrow margin. Malta's predominantly Catholic identity was celebrated through papal visits in 2001 and 2009. In 2011, parliament legalized divorce following a referendum, ending Malta's status as Europe's only country banning the practice. The 2012 financial crisis brought economic concerns, with credit downgrades and IMF warnings about contagion risks. Labour returned to power in March 2013 elections. That August, Malta faced international criticism when refusing docking rights to a tanker carrying rescued African migrants, highlighting ongoing Mediterranean migration challenges. Malta's history demonstrates remarkable adaptability, navigating between great powers while forging its distinct identity in modern Europe.

Venezuela's Currency Change Sparks Creative Response Online Venezuela has announced that its 100-bolivar banknotes will cease to be legal tender, giving citizens just a limited window to deposit or exchange them for new currency. While a 10-day grace period will allow people to exchange the bills at the central bank, concerns are mounting over the logistics of the transition. With six billion 100-bolivar notes currently in circulation, many Venezuelans fear that overcrowded banks and lengthy queues will prevent them from exchanging their money in time. Social media users have responded with a mixture of anxiety and dark humor. Twitter user @RPolicial shared imaginative scenarios about what the bank visit might entail. Others proposed creative alternative uses for the soon-to-be-worthless bills, with suggestions ranging from the practical to the satirical. The most popular idea was using the notes as toilet paper, addressing the chronic shortage of basic goods plaguing Venezuela. Satirical website La Patilla jokingly recommended using them as Christmas tree decorations that could be set on fire instead of candles. Some suggested the bills would be perfect for playing Monopoly. Several Venezuelans compared the tight deadline to the horror film "Saw" (known in Spanish as "Juegos Macabros"), where victims must solve deadly puzzles against the clock to survive.

Lancashire Fracking Protests: Campaign Group Plans "Escalated Action" at Drilling Site Protesters opposing fracking operations in Lancashire have vowed to intensify their direct action campaign, drawing criticism from business leaders who have compared their tactics to those of "animal rights extremists". Campaign group Reclaim The Power has announced two weeks of "escalated action" aimed at disrupting companies working at the Preston New Road site near Little Plumpton, where energy firm Cuadrilla has been authorized to extract shale gas. Protests have been ongoing since drilling operations commenced in January, with activists employing tactics including "slow walking, roadside protests and lock-ons" to hamper site access. Lancashire Police reported that 59 people were arrested between 27 January and 17 March, with 47 subsequently charged. The North and Western Lancashire Chamber of Commerce (NWLCC) has coordinated a letter to MPs and councillors expressing concern about the impact on businesses. The organization said firms have endured "weeks of harassment and intimidation," citing a St Annes concrete supplier that withdrew from the project after being "blockaded by an intimidating group of activists wearing hoods and masks". NWLCC chief executive Babs Murphy said over 800 businesses wanted to supply the site and "deserve the chance [to] without fearing that they will be targeted". The letter has been backed by various business groups including the East Lancashire Chamber of Commerce and the GMB union. Reclaim The Power dismissed the letter as "yet another attempt by pro-fracking groups to falsely attack people who oppose them, and to distract from the fact that the industry doesn't have public backing". Lancashire Police said it aims to "ensure a balance between the rights of people to lawfully protest [and] the rights of the wider public, including local businesses, to go about their lawful activities". The government approved Cuadrilla's fracking plans in October 2016.

Birmingham International Marathon Returns After 32-Year Absence Birmingham is set to welcome back a full-distance marathon in October 2017, organisers announced, reviving a tradition that ended more than three decades ago. The Birmingham International Marathon and accompanying half marathon will follow in the footsteps of the historic People's Marathon, which captured the nation's imagination between 1980 and 1985. The new event has been developed by the Great Run company, which already organises the successful Great Birmingham 10K and Great Birmingham Run, working in partnership with Birmingham City Council. A provisional route has been mapped out, starting at the Alexander Stadium and culminating on Broad Street. Organisers plan to incorporate themed miles along the course that will showcase Birmingham's rich cultural diversity and multicultural heritage. Birmingham holds a special place in British marathon history. When elite runner John Walker launched the People's Marathon on 11 May 1980, it pioneered the concept of open-to-all marathon racing. Athletics Weekly recognised its significance at the time, predicting it would be remembered as "the event which triggered off the mass long-distance running movement in this country." Mark Hollinshead, chief executive of the Great Run Company, expressed ambitions for the marathon to serve as trials for the 2018 Commonwealth Games. "Not only will this be a great event for British elite runners, we will also aim to attract runners of all abilities from the UK and beyond," he said. Steve Hollingworth from Birmingham City Council emphasised the health benefits: "It will encourage more residents to become physically active and have access to a full complement of running events in the city."

North West 200 Receives £200,000 Safety Boost Following Fatal Crashes Communities Minister Paul Givan has announced a substantial funding package aimed at enhancing safety measures at Northern Ireland's North West 200 motorcycle road race, following a tragic history of fatal accidents on the circuit. The minister confirmed that the money will enable the promoting Coleraine Club "to purchase equipment to help improve the safety of the course for competitors and spectators." This announcement comes in the wake of Malachi Mitchell-Thomas's death in a crash at the event in May of this year. Tragically, he was the fifth rider to lose his life in nine years at the north coast race. Robert Dunlop, Mark Young, Mark Buckley and Simon Andrews have also died due to racing incidents on the nine-mile course over the past decade. Beyond fatalities, a number of other serious accidents have taken place, including an incident involving several riders and a spectator at the Mill Road roundabout section of the course in 2015, and a collision between Ryan Farquhar and Dan Cooper at Black Hill this year. The funding will be allocated to purchase more safety bales, kerb protectors and pole protectors, as well as introducing a new warning light system and make improvements to the paddock area. "It is important that we do what we can to make the races a safe and memorable experience for everyone and this funding will contribute to that," said Givan. "Much of the equipment being purchased will be available to other event organisers so this is not just an investment that will benefit the North West 200." The minister emphasized road racing's importance to Northern Ireland, noting it "makes a significant contribution to tourism and to marketing Northern Ireland as a venue to come to for major international sporting events." Race Director Mervyn Whyte welcomed the financial injection, stating it will help his team "make significant improvements to the Triangle course." Givan indicated this represents "the first of a number of safety investment announcements" for local races.

**Share Your Olympic Spirit with England's Big Picture** The BBC is calling on photography enthusiasts across England to submit their Olympics-inspired pictures for this week's #EnglandsBigPicture theme. Whether you've captured local sporting events, Olympic celebrations, or creative interpretations of the Games, the BBC wants to see your images. Submissions can be made through multiple platforms to make sharing as easy as possible. **How to Submit** Contributors can email pictures to england@bbc.co.uk, post them on the BBC England Facebook page, or tweet them to @BBCEngland. Instagram users should utilize the hashtag #englandsbigpicture when sharing their images. Those interested in browsing previous submissions can view the archive on the England's Big Picture Pinterest board. **Submission Guidelines** When submitting photographs, contributors must include all relevant information about the image. The BBC has indicated a preference for recently taken photographs, particularly those captured within the past week. **Important Terms** By submitting pictures, contributors agree to the BBC's Terms and Conditions, granting the broadcaster a royalty-free, non-exclusive licence to publish the material across any media platform worldwide. However, photographers retain full copyright ownership of their work, and credited names will appear alongside published images. The BBC reserves the right to select which images are featured and may edit accompanying comments. The broadcaster emphasizes that contributors should never put themselves or others at risk or break any laws whilst gathering photographs. Not all submissions are guaranteed publication, but all Olympic-themed entries are welcome for consideration.

Moorland Fire in Stalybridge Brought Under Control Firefighters have successfully tackled a major moorland fire in Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, that broke out on Thursday evening. The blaze started on moorland off Brushes Road at approximately 18:15 BST on Thursday and spread rapidly across the grassland, covering an area of roughly 0.5km square, equivalent to 124 acres. Witnesses reported seeing huge amounts of ash filling the sky as the fire intensified. Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service worked through the night to contain the flames and protect nearby properties from the advancing fire. Residents in the surrounding area were advised to keep their doors and windows closed to prevent smoke from entering their homes and were urged not to travel in the immediate vicinity. Fire crews successfully brought the blaze under control by approximately 09:00 on Friday morning. The cause of the fire remains unknown and is likely to be investigated.

Wigan Warriors Re-sign Thomas Leuluai on Long-term Deal Thomas Leuluai is returning to Wigan Warriors on a deal that will see the 31-year-old utility player finish his playing career before transitioning into a coaching position with the Super League club. The New Zealand international previously enjoyed a successful six-year spell with Wigan, capturing the Grand Final trophy in 2010 and the Challenge Cup the following year. "When I knew Wigan were interested, it was a no-brainer," Leuluai explained. "With my wife being from Wigan and us having a new-born baby, I thought for my family it would be better for us to be back in England." The experienced playmaker added: "I've got a lot of close friends at Wigan and I really love the club and its history."

Giant Water Slide Cancelled Hours Before Ramsgate Festival Event A giant water slide attraction at the Ramsgate Festival was cancelled at the last minute on Sunday, leaving thousands of participants disappointed after the supplier pulled out late Saturday night. Adam Faulkner, director of Bloon, the company contracted to provide the inflatable slide, stated that full payment had not been received for the service. According to the company's terms and conditions, no credit terms had been agreed upon, and they could not proceed without complete payment. However, festival spokeswoman Lorraine Williams disputed this account, explaining that half the payment had already been made and that pre-payment of the remaining balance had never been mentioned in their agreement. "We are devastated," Williams said. "This money could have been immediately transferred but we have not been able to contact them since they sent that email last night." The cancellation came as a major blow to the festival organisers and the town. "This is a disaster for us," Williams added. "The point of the Ramsgate Slide was to bring joy and fun into the town. It was something different to draw attention to our fantastic harbour and seafront." More than 5,000 people had entered a draw for the opportunity to use the giant inflatable chute, with 180 winners selected, including 40 children. The festival has promised all selected participants they will be given another opportunity to experience the slide at a future date. "This is our commitment to the town," Williams said, while Bloon maintains the outstanding balance remains unpaid.

**Shrewsbury Town's Aristote Nsiala Wins Red Card Appeal** Shrewsbury Town defender Aristote Nsiala has successfully overturned his red card after being sent off just six days into his League One career with the club. The 24-year-old, who recently joined from Hartlepool, was dismissed during Saturday's 1-1 draw at Swindon Town following a challenge on striker Luke Norris. The incident initially resulted in a four-match ban from the Football Association, but that suspension has now been rescinded following an appeal. Nsiala is now available for selection and could make his home debut when Shrewsbury face Bradford City on Saturday. The timing is particularly significant as Town find themselves outside the League One relegation zone for the first time in four months. Manager Paul Hurst expressed his satisfaction with the outcome. "I'm pleased for myself and the club and I'm particularly pleased for Toto," he said. "He was delighted when the message was passed on. It would have been a long time training with no game to look forward to when you've just arrived at a club." This marks the second time this season that Shrewsbury has successfully appealed a red card, having received eight dismissals overall. Hurst defended the tackle, stating the video footage clearly showed Nsiala won the ball.

Turkey Gay Pride: Scuffles Break Out After Istanbul and Ankara Marches Banned Several dozen activists gathered in defiance of a ban on gay pride events in Turkey, leading to confrontations with police and the reported destruction of a gay rights banner by at least one individual. Turkish authorities prohibited both the Ankara march and Istanbul Pride, scheduled for June 26, citing the need to "safeguard security and public order." Istanbul Pride, which has taken place annually since 2003, joins a growing list of curtailed LGBT events in the country. While homosexuality remains legal in Turkey—distinguishing it from many Arab nations—experts note that homophobia continues to be pervasive throughout Turkish society. The ban comes amid heightened tensions in Istanbul, where suspected Islamists attacked patrons at a record store Friday evening. The victims were targeted for consuming alcohol and listening to music during Ramadan, Islam's holy month. Police dispersed a subsequent protest against that attack on Saturday. Last year's Istanbul Pride ended violently when police deployed water cannon and tear gas against participants. This year's prohibition means anyone attempting to march faces potential intervention by security forces. Organizers condemned the ban as a "flagrant violation of the constitution and the law," arguing that city authorities are failing to protect citizens' fundamental rights. They announced plans to pursue legal challenges. Security throughout Istanbul remains elevated following recent bombings attributed to Islamic State militants and Kurdish separatists. The ultra-nationalist Alperen Hearths youth group called potential participants "immoral" and threatened to physically prevent any march from proceeding. The prohibitions represent a significant setback for LGBT rights in Turkey, raising concerns about the country's commitment to protecting minority communities.

British Sikh Man Freed After Portugal Rejects India Extradition Case A British Sikh man detained in Portugal while Indian authorities sought his extradition over alleged involvement in murder and terrorism has been released and is returning home to the West Midlands. Paramjeet Singh Saini, from Smethwick, was arrested in Portugal in December while on holiday with his family. Indian authorities had been seeking his extradition in connection with the 2009 murder of Sikh politician Rulda Singh and bomb attacks in India in 2010. John Spellar, the Labour MP for Warley, announced on Tuesday that Mr Saini's lawyer confirmed the Portuguese government had rejected India's extradition request. "I understand he is on his way home," Mr Spellar said. The father-of-four came to the UK approximately 13 years ago and was granted refugee status until 2023, along with his family. Indian authorities allege he was a leading member of Babbar Khalsa International, a Sikh separatist group banned in the UK under anti-terrorism legislation. Mr Saini was previously arrested in 2010 by West Midlands Police as part of a joint investigation with Indian authorities, but was later released without charge. Mr Spellar had questioned the legality of Mr Saini's December arrest, arguing he was protected under the European Convention and criticizing the Indian government for attempting to "grab" someone whilst on holiday. Speaking about the release, Mr Spellar said: "This is obviously tremendous news, wonderful for his family, his wife and his four children here in Smethwick and also very good news for the Sikh community who've been campaigning for justice for him." Mr Saini's family have maintained that his detention was politically motivated and violated his human rights.

Family Marks 20 Years Since Kevin Mcleod's Death with Renewed Call for Justice The family of Kevin Mcleod, whose body was discovered in Wick harbour in February 1997, are marking the 20th anniversary of his death with a renewed determination to uncover the truth about what happened to the 24-year-old. Although authorities initially treated Mr Mcleod's death as accidental, his family have never accepted this conclusion and firmly believe he was murdered. Police Scotland has now agreed to assess information relating to his death, offering a glimmer of hope to his long-campaigning relatives. Speaking on the 20th anniversary, Kevin's mother June Mcleod told BBC Scotland: "Every day is a sad day - for 20 years." She revealed that if the current review "turns up nothing new," the family would continue their fight for justice. Mrs Mcleod, along with her husband Hugh and Kevin's uncle Allan, have spent two decades campaigning for a criminal investigation. They have consistently rejected the official explanation that Kevin entered the harbour waters after tripping on an ornamental street bollard during a night out. "Kevin was given a kicking by someone or some people," Mrs Mcleod said. "Kevin was kicked to death. It is terrible for me to say that as I am his mother." The family believes there are people in Wick who know who is responsible for Kevin's death but have remained silent. The Mcleods secured the fresh assessment after participating in a radio phone-in with Police Scotland's chief constable Phil Gormley. Hugh Mcleod emphasised their commitment, stating simply: "We are fighting for justice." The case has been marred by criticism of the original investigation conducted by Northern Constabulary. In 2007, the Police Complaints Commissioner for Scotland accused the force of "institutional arrogance" in handling complaints from Kevin's parents. The then chief constable, Ian Latimer, was ordered to apologise in person to the family, which he did. The Mcleods have also criticised a fatal accident inquiry held into the death, saying it "raised more questions than answers." Mr Mcleod's father expressed hope that the new review would examine all documents and evidence concerning his son's death. Gail Ross, MSP for Caithness, Sutherland and Ross, said the Mcleod family had "been through hell" and deserved a thorough investigation of what happened the night Kevin died.

Stephen Ferris: Ireland Can Prove Critics Wrong and Defend Six Nations Title Former Ireland flanker Stephen Ferris has dismissed Lawrence Dallaglio's prediction that Ireland will finish fourth in the Six Nations, insisting the reigning champions remain firmly in contention for a third consecutive title. Dallaglio's forecast has raised eyebrows given Ireland's back-to-back championship victories, and Ferris believes such predictions are premature. "You definitely cannot write off Ireland," the Ulster legend stated. "If they can stay injury free, the Irish will be in with a shout." The former British and Irish Lion is confident that Joe Schmidt's squad will not be affected by their disappointing World Cup campaign, where they exited at the quarter-final stage. "There will not be any hangover from the World Cup. Joe Schmidt will want to move on. It is all about the Six Nations now and winning the championship." **The Importance of Momentum** Ferris emphasized the crucial nature of the opening fixture, drawing on painful personal experience from Ireland's 2012 campaign. "It is all about winning your first match and gaining momentum," he explained. "I remember Ireland's first match in 2012 was against Wales. I was given a controversial yellow card and Leigh Halfpenny won the match with the penalty. We should have won that match, but it was Wales who went on to complete the Grand Slam." The consequences of that opening defeat illustrated how quickly fortunes can change in the championship. "If you start with a win, you can build on that. But lose, and people start to question the coach, the captain, the performance - and the pressure just builds." **Selection Debates** While Ferris anticipates Johnny Sexton will start at fly-half, he believes Ulster's Paddy Jackson is currently in superior form. However, he acknowledged Sexton's value: "Johnny puts a lot of pressure on himself, but his big-game mentality is important." Concerns remain over Sexton's recent head injury and limited game time for Leinster. Ferris strongly advocated for Ulster centre Stuart McCloskey's inclusion, highlighting impressive statistics. "If you look at his stats he is perhaps the best centre in Europe. Most carries, line breaks and turnovers. So why shouldn't he be playing?" The 35-cap international also backed CJ Stander for his Ireland debut, describing the Munster number eight as "an outstanding back row" who has been "single-handedly winning games for Munster." **Backing Best as Captain** Ferris expressed full confidence in new captain Rory Best, dismissing concerns about the added responsibility affecting his form. "There are plenty of experienced heads around him, such as Jamie Heaslip, Johnny Sexton and Rob Kearney. Rory was pretty much a second captain to Paul O'Connell anyway. He will just get on with the job." **Championship Prediction** Looking ahead to the tournament, Ferris backed Eddie Jones as the right appointment for England, praising his experience and relaxed demeanor. However, his money is on Ireland retaining their crown. "I am going for Ireland, and we'll take it from there," Ferris concluded. "Joe Schmidt always seems to get a good squad out on the pitch and they work hard for him."

Boredom and Drugs Fuel Violence at Shropshire Prison, Report Finds A damning report from HM Inspectorate of Prisons has revealed that boredom, drugs, and alcohol are driving poor behaviour at HMP Stoke Heath near Market Drayton in Shropshire. The category C "closed" prison, which houses 745 inmates including 40 young offenders, was found to have high levels of violence and "some concerning finds of weapons". Prisoners at such facilities are not trusted in open prison conditions but are considered unlikely to attempt escape. The inspection uncovered serious operational failings, including one foreign national prisoner being detained solely on immigration grounds despite completing his sentence two years earlier. Inspectors found that 40% of inmates – those unemployed, working part-time, or in domestic roles – were "milling about aimlessly on the wings during the working day". The report stated: "Many prisoners were under-occupied and boredom contributed to poor behaviour." The facility holds a high proportion of prisoners with domestic violence convictions, yet no programmes were in place to address this behaviour – a significant gap in rehabilitation efforts. Chief Inspector of Prisons Nick Hardwick emphasised that the prison's priorities should include "a focus on tackling violence, keeping men fully occupied and doing more to reduce the risks that they will reoffend after release". Michael Spurr, chief executive of the National Offender Management Service, acknowledged the findings, saying: "The Governor and his staff have worked hard to make real improvements at the same time as managing significant change." He confirmed the prison would develop an enhanced strategy to tackle and reduce prisoner violence based on the report's recommendations.

Ireland's Best Ready to Lead as O'Connell Ruled Out of World Cup Ireland will face Argentina in their Rugby World Cup quarter-final without the influential Paul O'Connell, but veteran hooker Rory Best insists the team must rally together to fill the leadership void left by their stricken captain. O'Connell will miss the rest of the tournament after having surgery on a hamstring injury sustained in the 24-9 win over France last weekend. Best said: "While Paul will be a loss, everyone has to step up. It's important guys stand up and lead by example. They're not going to have their hand held by Paulie's leadership this week." Along with Jamie Heaslip, who will captain the Irish against Argentina, Best will be one of those expected to lead from the front against a formidable Argentine pack. The Ulster hooker said that Ireland - seeking to reach their first World Cup semi-final - would cover every angle for the game against the Pumas in Cardiff, with Jerome Garces in charge - the same referee as against Italy two weeks ago. "This is knock-out rugby and the chance to make history," said Best. "Against Italy there were a lot of things we could have done better - we probably weren't as prepared for that scrum. From our point of view, probably what we've learned in hindsight is that we need to prepare for every eventuality." "We didn't then and for us it's about making sure that we do everything we can. The referees are doing a good job; our responsibility is to make sure we take it out of their hands by preparing properly, and making sure we execute the plan as accurately as we can." Argentina's unorthodox "Bajada" scrummaging method has caught several sides cold during the World Cup, the locks unusually binding on the props' hips in a bid to pin all the pressure through the opposing hooker. Ireland's number two knows full well the Pumas will try to pin him in at the set-piece, but insisted Joe Schmidt's side have been hard at work devising strategies this week with scrum coach Greg Feek. "We've got to make sure we have the tools to try to combat that," Best said. "Traditionally everyone talks about Argentina and the scrum and it's probably only in the last couple of years they've got that back again. It's a big weapon for them. We know they're going to come after us because that's what they do no matter who they are playing." "We need to be able to make sure that doesn't become a factor that makes us lose the game. Myself, Mike Ross and Cian Healy, last weekend was our 30th cap starting together, so we're used to each other. And for us it's about making sure our technique is good and correct and that we trust what's worked for us for a large part of those 30 Tests."

Japanese Woman Dies After Cat Bite Transmits Rare Tick-Borne Virus A Japanese woman in her 50s has died from a rare tick-borne virus ten days after being bitten by a sick cat, in what may be the world's first animal-to-human transmission case of the disease. The woman contracted Severe Fever with Thrombocytopenia Syndrome (SFTS) while attempting to help an apparently ill cat. With no tick bite detected on her body, doctors believe the virus was transmitted directly from the infected feline. "No reports on animal-to-human transmission cases have been made so far," a Japanese health ministry official told AFP. "It's still not confirmed the virus came from the cat, but it's possible that it is the first case." SFTS is a relatively new infectious disease emerging in China, Korea and Japan, with fatality rates reaching up to 30%. The virus particularly affects people over 50, and first appeared in Japan in 2013. The health ministry has warned people to exercise caution when handling animals in poor physical condition, though officials stressed such cases remain rare. Globally, tick-borne diseases like Lyme disease remain significant health concerns, potentially causing severe illness or death without proper treatment.

Small Electrical Fire Breaks Out at Manchester United's Old Trafford Stadium A small electrical fire broke out in the lift motor room of Old Trafford's Sir Bobby Charlton stand early this morning at approximately 07:00 GMT. Eyewitness Sarah Louise Feeney reported on Twitter: "Fire at Old Trafford in South Stand..... Fire alarm going off since 7am and smoke!!!" Firefighters responded promptly and remained on scene for approximately 90 minutes to contain the blaze. Manchester United confirmed there were no injuries and minimal damage resulted from the incident. The club stated the electrical fire was "identified quickly" and "dealt with quickly and effectively" by attending fire services. The isolated incident caused no disruption to stadium operations.

Teenage Pedestrian Seriously Injured in A720 Collision Near Edinburgh Police Scotland are investigating after a teenage pedestrian sustained serious injuries in a collision on the A720 near the Dreghorn junction on Saturday evening. Emergency services were called to the scene shortly before 17:00, where the teenager was struck by a blue Skoda Citigo travelling westbound. The victim was immediately transported to Edinburgh Royal Infirmary for treatment. The road remained closed until approximately 03:00 on Sunday morning whilst officers conducted a thorough investigation of the scene. Sergeant Andy Gibb of Police Scotland appealed for witnesses, stating: "We're currently working to establish the full circumstances surrounding this collision and are asking anyone who may have witnessed this, or who has any other information which can help with our inquiries, to come forward."

Labour Candidate Apologises for'Sour-Faced Ladies' Tweet About Loose Women Labour's candidate in the Stoke-on-Trent Central by-election has apologised after old tweets emerged in which he made derogatory comments about women on television programmes. Gareth Snell described panellists on ITV's Loose Women as "squabbling sour-faced ladies", according to the Guido Fawkes political website. He also made disparaging remarks about broadcaster Janet Street-Porter and a female contestant on BBC's The Apprentice. In a statement responding to the revelations, Mr Snell expressed regret for the social media posts. "They were from years ago when I was tweeting along with TV programmes but nevertheless, I shouldn't have tweeted those comments and I apologise for the offence they have caused," he said. UKIP, whose leader Paul Nuttall is mounting a strong challenge in the constituency, condemned the comments as "distasteful" and suggested they demonstrated a lack of maturity from the Labour candidate. The by-election was triggered following the resignation of former Labour MP Tristram Hunt in January, who left Parliament to become director of the Victoria and Albert Museum. Meanwhile, Mr Nuttall has strongly denied accusations that he lied about being present at the Hillsborough disaster in 1989, calling the allegations "an absolute disgrace". The UKIP leader, then aged 12, says he attended the FA Cup semi-final at Sheffield Wednesday's stadium where 96 Liverpool fans tragically lost their lives. "I've never been so personally insulted in my life," Mr Nuttall said.

Enid Blyton Letter Discovery in Second-Hand Book Leaves Buyer'Amazed' A woman browsing through second-hand books has made an unexpected discovery - a letter apparently signed by beloved children's author Enid Blyton. Jacqueline Ralph found the note tucked inside a copy of Silas Marner, by George Eliot, which she purchased in the Cinema Bookshop in Hay-on-Wye. Ms Ralph, from Lichfield, Staffordshire, told the Hereford Times she was "amazed" by the find. The letter, addressed to someone named Mary, reads: "Dear Mary, my warm congratulations on winning one of my prizes. You did very well and you deserve a prize. I am very pleased to send it. Well done! Love from Enid Blyton." Ms Ralph said she found the note attached to the inside cover of the book. "When I opened it up I couldn't believe what I saw," she said. "Enid Blyton's signature is so recognisable from growing up reading the Famous Five books." However, experts have suggested the letter was probably a generic copy that was sent to the writer's fans. They noted that the recipient's name appeared to be in different ink and handwriting. Chris Albury, auctioneer and senior valuer at Dominic Winter Auctioneers, said: "It has the'smell' of a pre-printed facsimile with just the word'Mary' inked in." Sarah Lawrance, collection and exhibitions director at Seven Stories, the National Centre for Children's Books, agreed: "Enid probably dispatched so many prizes that she wrote the certificates in bulk and had some help with personalising them." Despite being a mass-produced item, the discovery remains a charming glimpse into Blyton's connection with her young readers.

Woman Calls US Police to Report Devon Car Crash in Cortana Mix-Up A woman attempting to report a car crash near Muddiford, Devon on Monday found herself speaking to police officers across the Atlantic after using Windows' digital assistant Cortana to find the emergency number. The Ilfracombe resident asked Cortana for the police contact number and was inadvertently connected to Barnstable Police Department in Massachusetts, USA. The call lasted two and a half minutes before American officer Mark McWilliams realised the caller was phoning from England. "I haven't stopped laughing," said the woman, who has chosen to remain anonymous. "The more I hear it the more I laugh." Paul MacDonald, Chief of Police for Barnstable, Massachusetts, commented: "It's not unusual for us to have tourists or guests from England but this is the first time someone called from England to report a motor vehicle crash." Ironically, Barnstable, Massachusetts is twinned with the north Devon town where the incident occurred.

Peter Odemwingie Confident of Helping Rotherham United Escape Relegation Peter Odemwingie has expressed his confidence in helping Rotherham United climb out of the Championship relegation zone after joining the struggling club on a short-term deal. The 35-year-old Nigerian striker, who became a free agent after departing Stoke City in the summer, signed with the Millers on Monday, choosing the Championship opportunity over a potential move to League One side Bolton Wanderers. "I was close to signing for Bolton but the Championship is a higher league and it's a good league for me. I didn't need to think for long about the move," Odemwingie told BBC Radio Sheffield. The experienced forward has agreed to a short-term contract with the possibility of an extension. "It's a short-term deal but if things go well then we can talk about a longer deal closer to Christmas," he explained. Odemwingie arrives at a club in crisis, with Rotherham sitting eight points adrift of safety following the recent appointment of Kenny Jackett as manager after Alan Stubbs' dismissal. However, the former West Brom and Cardiff striker remains optimistic about the challenge ahead. "I know it's a difficult situation but I've been in these positions before and done quite well and I think they bring out the best in me," he said. Drawing on his experience from last season with Bristol City in the Championship, Odemwingie believes the Millers can mount a survival bid. "It's a huge task but you expect teams around you to have a dip in form as well," he added. "November and December are always big months in English football."

Primary School Pupils Learn Meditation to Build Emotional Resilience Primary six and seven pupils at Bunscoil an Lúir have been learning meditation and breathing exercises on a regular basis as part of an innovative wellbeing programme. The depression charity, Aware, is behind the initiative, which aims to help children develop emotional resilience and fight the effects of stress through mindfulness techniques. ## Learning to Slow Down In lessons at Bunscoil an Luir, pupils are taught to relax, moderate their breathing, and concentrate by taking things a little more slowly. An external mindfulness tutor appointed by Aware leads the sessions, which appear to be having a positive impact both inside and outside the classroom. Eleven-year-old Brídín Ni Mhurchú said she had learned how to relax and not become anxious about things like homework. "I take a deep breath in and then out and just don't think about anything else," she explained. Ten-year-old Lonan Mac Domhnaill said mindfulness helps him keep his temper in difficult situations. "I learn how to calm down whenever I'm stressed and don't get into a tantrum and get angry," he said. Eleven-year-old Amber McGinnis Mallon uses the techniques she has learned in class to relax at home. "Say if I'm angry at my brothers I would go to my room," she said. "Then I hear the birds outside instead." ## Teacher Conversion Even their initially sceptical teacher, Ciarán Catney, has been won over by the classes. "We're giving the children the tools to deal with stress," he said. "When we started I thought I was getting time to correct some books or get some plans ready. But when I was sitting doing different activities and things with the children, I was learning that I didn't realise how stressed out I could be at times as well. So I was de-stressing myself." ## Expanding the Programme The chief executive of Aware, Siobhan Donaghy, said she hoped to be able to offer similar classes in other schools across Northern Ireland. "It would help children to reduce stress, and to cope with things that happen in life," she said. "Younger and younger children nowadays are suffering from stress, many from anxiety and some from depression." Addressing concerns that it is not a school's role to teach mindfulness, Ms Donaghy said: "We believe that emotional education for young people is so incredibly important as they try to make their way through life. These children are going to move into secondary school soon, where they're going to face all sorts of pressures. They need the techniques and tools to deal with that."

Bolt Wins Comfortably in Ostrava Despite Slow Start **Media playback is not supported on this device** Usain Bolt cruised to victory in his first European race of the year, despite getting off to a sluggish start in Ostrava. The Jamaican sprinting legend finished well clear of Barbados' Ramon Gittens, who trailed by 0.23 seconds in second place. The 29-year-old's previous 100m outing this season saw him clock 10.05 seconds at the Cayman Islands Invitational Meet, after which he required treatment for a tight hamstring. Bolt has been relatively inactive since his triple gold medal haul at the Beijing World Championships last August, where he dominated the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay events. Looking ahead to Rio, the world record holder has set his sights on breaking his own 200m world record at this summer's Olympic Games.

Police Hunt Duo After Early Morning Robbery in Edinburgh Police are appealing for witnesses following a violent robbery in Edinburgh that left a man in his 20s requiring hospital treatment. The victim was attacked at approximately 03:00 on Saturday in Craigour Avenue, near its junction with Moredun Park Road. He was assaulted from behind and forced to the ground before two suspects stole his mobile phone and wallet. Following the attack, the victim made his own way to the nearby Royal Infirmary, where he received treatment for facial injuries. Police are searching for two suspects. The male is described as white, approximately 20-25 years old, between 5'1" and 5'5" tall, with a slim build and dirty blond hair. His female accomplice was between 5'1" and 5'3" tall, slim with shoulder-length dark hair, and was wearing blue jeans. Detective Constable Gavin Watson said: "Our inquiries are at an early stage however anyone who was in the Craigour area around 3am on Saturday, April 9, and who saw anything suspicious should contact police immediately. Similarly anyone who recognises the description of the suspects or who can assist in locating them should also come forward."

Italian Navy Locates Wreckage of Migrant Boat in Mediterranean's Deadliest Disaster The Italian navy announced Wednesday that it has discovered a sunken migrant vessel lying 375 meters (1,230 feet) beneath the Mediterranean Sea, three weeks after what the United Nations has deemed the deadliest maritime disaster in the region's history. The 25-meter blue boat was found on the seabed, matching descriptions of the three-deck vessel that sank near the Libyan coast. Sicilian prosecutors, currently investigating the tragedy, must now determine whether the wreckage will be raised for further examination. The catastrophe claimed hundreds of lives when the overcrowded boat collided with a merchant ship. Of the estimated passengers aboard, only 28 survived—including four children—while rescuers recovered just 24 bodies at the scene. Italian investigators reveal that migrants paid between $700 and $7,000 for passage, enduring up to a month of captivity on a Libyan farm before departure. During this period, prosecutors say migrants suffered abuse, with reports of deaths resulting from violence and exhaustion. Two men, including the boat's Tunisian captain and a crew member, face investigation on multiple charges, including suspected culpable homicide and illegal confinement. This tragedy highlights a broader humanitarian crisis. The UN reports that 60,000 people have attempted to cross the Mediterranean this year, with nearly 1,800 losing their lives. The crisis continues unabated. On Wednesday evening, 100 migrants reached Sicily after being rescued from a boat that had drifted near the island for 12 days, the final two without food or water. The discovery of the wreckage may provide crucial evidence as authorities work to prevent future disasters.

Police Search House in Caroline Graham Murder Investigation Police have begun searching a house in Portadown as part of their investigation into the murder of Caroline Graham, who disappeared more than 25 years ago. Caroline Graham was 19 and living with her boyfriend at Hanover Street, in Portadown, County Armagh, when she disappeared in March 1989. A murder inquiry was launched in August 2012 after police said they had a number of new lines of inquiry. Monday's search has been taking place at the house in Hanover Street. The search is being conducted with the consent of the current owner who, police believe, has no knowledge of the events of 1989. Officers have carried out a number of searches in the Portadown area over the years, but Caroline's body has not been found. The officer leading the investigation, Detective Chief Inspector Peter Montgomery, said: "It is more than 25 years since Caroline was last seen and almost two years since the most recent phase of investigative activity resumed. "Despite all the hurdles posed by the passage of time, I still believe that a form of closure is possible for Caroline and her family. "Our appeals for information have been productive. In general, people have been very helpful. "We are now at a point where it is appropriate to once again begin a planned search operation, primarily to locate Caroline's remains, but also as an important part of the overall investigation into her murder." He said Caroline had been for a night out in Banbridge with a girlfriend and had stayed part of the night in a hostel in Portadown, but was gone in the morning. Ch Insp Montgomery said police have information that she returned to Hanover Street to get some clothes. She has not been seen since. "I believe she was murdered some time later and that her remains are somewhere in Portadown," he said. "All our enquiries lead us to believe there is more than one person who knows exactly where Caroline is buried. "We need them to come forward and tell us exactly what they know. "Whoever is responsible for Caroline's murder may have spoken to people and they may know exactly what has happened to Caroline." The detective added that two men, possibly off-duty soldiers, who gave Caroline a lift in a black Ford XR3i on the night before she disappeared had yet to come forward. He said the men are not being treated as suspects, but need to come forward.

Stonework Falls from St Magnus Cathedral Ahead of Major Ceremony A section of sandstone surrounding a stained glass window high in the south transept of St Magnus Cathedral fell approximately 70 feet to the ground overnight between Saturday and Sunday. The incident comes just days before the cathedral is scheduled to host commemorations for the Battle of Jutland on Tuesday. The event is expected to draw numerous dignitaries, including the Duke of Edinburgh and Prime Minister David Cameron. Cathedral officials are assessing the damage ahead of the important ceremony.

US States Sue Drugmakers Over Alleged Price-Fixing Conspiracy Twenty US states have filed a civil lawsuit against six major pharmaceutical companies, alleging they conspired to artificially inflate prices of generic drugs including the antibiotic doxycycline and diabetes medication glyburide. The defendants named in the case include US-based Mylan, Heritage Pharmaceuticals, Teva Pharmaceutical USA, and Citron Pharma, alongside India's Aurobindo Pharma and Australia's Mayne Pharmaceuticals. Mylan, Teva, and Aurobindo have denied the allegations. Heritage Pharmaceuticals has been identified as the "principal architect" of the alleged conspiracy. The civil action follows criminal charges filed Wednesday by the US Department of Justice against two former Heritage executives for price-fixing. Heritage stated it is cooperating fully with investigators and has filed its own complaint against the former executives. The lawsuit follows a two-year investigation led by Connecticut Attorney General George Jepsen's office, which alleges company representatives colluded at steak dinners and "girls nights out" to coordinate price increases. Jepsen told Reuters the lawsuit represents just "the tip of the iceberg," describing price fixing in the generic drug industry as "widespread and pervasive" and involving "many other drugs and a number of other companies." The financial impact has been significant for consumers. According to one Democratic senator, the price of 500 doxycycline tablets skyrocketed from $20 to $1,849 in merely seven months. Mayne Pharmaceuticals confirmed its involvement in the case, with its shares plummeting 22% following the announcement. While not commenting on the specific allegations, the company stated the proceedings would "not have a material impact on its future earnings." Citron Pharma has not yet issued a statement regarding the allegations.

Convictions in Mumbai Train Blasts **Mumbai, India** - Twelve men accused of waging war against the nation, conspiracy and murder in connection with the devastating 2006 Mumbai train bombings have been convicted, while one man was acquitted, a court ruled Friday. The serial bombings on 11 July 2006 killed 189 people and injured more than 800 in one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in India's history. The attack was blamed on Islamic militants backed by Pakistan, an allegation that Pakistan has consistently denied. Sentencing is expected to be pronounced on Monday after judge Yatin D Shinde hears arguments from prosecutors and defence lawyers. The guilty face either the death penalty or life imprisonment. "Justice has been done for the people of Mumbai. I will ask for the strictest punishment when I argue for their sentences," public prosecutor Raja Thakre told reporters outside the courtroom. During the attack, seven blasts ripped through trains during the evening rush hour. The bombs were packed into seven pressure cookers and placed in bags. The coordinated explosions were detonated within 15 minutes of each other. The blasts took place in the areas of Matunga, Khar, Mahim, Jogeshwari, Borivali and Mira Road, with most occurring on moving trains and two at stations. The bombs appeared to have specifically targeted first-class compartments as commuters were returning home from the city's financial district. More than 200 witnesses were examined during the eight-year-long trial, which concluded in August last year. Prosecutors say the attack was planned by Pakistan's intelligence agency ISI and carried out by operatives of Pakistan-based militant group Lashkar-e-Taiba with help from the Students' Islamic Movement of India, a banned Indian group. Pakistan has rejected these allegations, maintaining that India has provided no concrete evidence of Pakistani involvement in the attacks. Mumbai's suburban train system is one of the busiest in the world, carrying more than eight million commuters daily.

Welsh'Super-Dairy' Fined £36,000 for Severe Stream Pollution A large-scale dairy operation in Carmarthenshire has been hit with a substantial fine after severe sewage pollution left a local brook "80 to 90% covered in sewage fungus", Llanelli Magistrates' Court heard. Cwrt Malle Ltd, which operates a controversial "super-dairy" housing 1,900 cows, admitted to six environmental regulation breaches that occurred between December 2015 and September 2016. The farm is run by owners Howell and Susan Richards. Natural Resources Wales discovered the foaming, discoloured effluent in Fernhill Brook near two farms operated by the company. Tests revealed shocking pollution levels, with Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) readings of 5,178 – dramatically exceeding the EU's safe level of three. Prosecutor John Tarrant told the court that while the contamination levels were exceptionally high, no fish deaths or long-term environmental damage had been confirmed. However, the stream displayed clear signs of severe pollution, with strong odours and extensive foam coverage. The court heard the pollution originated from an overflowing "slurry lagoon" containing animal waste. Defence solicitor Aled Owen attributed the incident to extraordinary weather conditions, noting it was "the highest rainfall recorded in 100 years." "This is a very well run and modern farm," Owen argued in mitigation. However, this was not the farm's first offence. Cwrt Malle had previously received a £5,000 fine for similar environmental breaches in 2013. Five offences occurred at the main Cwrt Malle site, with one additional breach at Wernolau Farm in January 2016. The company must pay the £36,000 fine plus £8,500 in prosecution costs.

Salford Gang Violence: Multiple Feuds Spark Wave of Shootings Following Massey Murder The death of Paul Massey, a 55-year-old father of five known as "Salford's Mr Big", has ignited concerns about escalating gang violence across Greater Manchester, with police now tracking multiple feuds and numerous shootings across the region. Mr Massey, who had a previous conviction for stabbing and was under investigation by the regional organised crime squad for money laundering allegations, was shot dead outside his home. The security boss had attempted to enter mainstream politics in 2012, running for mayor of Salford with a pledge to eliminate drugs from the city's streets. His prescient words from a 1998 BBC documentary, which was never broadcast, now carry chilling significance: "The only reason that's kept me alive today is because the person who fires that shot knows that they've got to fly the flag and handle the pressure after it..... and they won't be able to handle the pressure." The day after the murder on 27 July, Greater Manchester Police and Crime Commissioner Tony Lloyd issued a public warning against retaliation. "Clearly no-one wants to see any further retaliation," he told the Manchester Evening News. "The right answer for this is for people to come forward and help the police to arrest those who are responsible - because that's what will put a stop to guns in Salford." Greater Manchester Police were sufficiently concerned about potential violence at Mr Massey's August funeral that they deployed armed response units and Superintendent Mark Kenny made a direct appeal to criminal gangs "not take action into their own hands" during the service. Since the killing, GMP have identified two shootings directly linked to Mr Massey's death, believed to be connected to a feud between rival gangs in Swinton and central Salford. On 12 August, a 33-year-old man was shot in the hip in Weaste. Most recently, a 29-year-old mother and her seven-year-old son were shot on their doorstep in Eccles on Monday. Complicating matters further, police confirmed on Saturday that three shootings in Salford and Bolton are part of a separate, "escalating" gang rivalry between organised crime groups in Little Hulton, a feud dating back a year that has generated at least six shootings. Detective Chief Superintendent Russ Jackson stated there was currently nothing linking the Little Hulton feud with the Massey-related shootings, though police believe both conflicts may have generated a series of "low-level shootings" that have gone unreported. The multiple, overlapping feuds present a significant challenge for law enforcement seeking to restore order to Salford's streets.

Kayaker Dies After Search Off Scottish Coast Emergency services were called out to search for Jerzy Florkowski, from Lancashire, at about 20:30 on Tuesday. He had been reported as "overdue" having left Burnmouth earlier in the day. He was found in the water close to the town and brought to the shore but died a short time later after attempts to revive him had failed. Insp John Scott said: "This is a tragic set of circumstances and our thoughts are with Jerzy's family as they come to terms with their loss."

Swansea Manager Francesco Guidolin Criticises Ki Sung-yueng's Attitude After Substitution Swansea City manager Francesco Guidolin has criticised midfielder Ki Sung-yueng following his reaction to being substituted during their Premier League defeat at Southampton. The South Korea international appeared unhappy and notably refused to shake Guidolin's hand when he was replaced in the second half at St Mary's. "This is not a good attitude. I have to speak with him," said Guidolin following the match. The incident comes just a week after the Italian manager apologised to Neil Taylor for substituting him during Swansea's 2-2 draw with Chelsea. Despite the setback dropping Swansea to 15th in the Premier League table, Guidolin denied that players were unhappy with his management style. "I respect all people, all my players because the relationship is the most important thing for me," he explained. "In this league, in this squad I've found good, good guys. Good players - no problem for relationships." While acknowledging Ki's disappointment, Guidolin added: "I can understand, but it's not a good situation." The manager expressed concern about his side's inability to create sufficient goal-scoring opportunities as they face a challenging week ahead. Swansea will host Premier League leaders Manchester City twice at the Liberty Stadium - first in Wednesday's EFL Cup third round, then in Saturday's league fixture, before welcoming Liverpool. Guidolin has promised squad rotation for the midweek cup tie, confirming Taylor will feature. "It's impossible to play three games with the same line-up," he said.

Hillsborough Inquests: Police'Lost Control' Before Disaster, Court Hears A retired police officer has told the Hillsborough inquests that control room staff "had basically lost control" on the day 96 Liverpool fans died in the 1989 stadium disaster. Retired PC Trevor Bichard, one of five officers in the control room, was giving evidence at the new inquests. He also told the jury no-one inside the box was monitoring the central pens where the crush took place. Ninety-six fans died following the crush at the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. Mr Bichard told the jury that after 15:00 BST on the day of the disaster, 15 April 1989, police radios were not working and "we had basically lost control". "It was clear that we weren't controlling what was happening," he said. "The instruction had gone out to open the gates. Another message had come in about opening another gate. The situation had created a life of its own." He told the inquests he began to receive radio messages about the volume of people outside the gates at the Leppings Lane end of the Sheffield stadium at 14:30. He turned one of the cameras to look at the crowd outside and estimated there were about 3,000 people there, the jury heard. Mr Bichard, who retired after reaching the rank of chief inspector, said he focused completely on events taking place outside the turnstiles at Leppings Lane, not on the terraces. He said one of the cameras, camera number five, which was overlooking the Leppings Lane terraces, was "iffy" and having "whiteouts". He said he was surprised when he overheard a "unique" order by Supt Roger Marshall to open exit gate C at the Leppings Lane end to relieve the crush outside, the jury heard. Mr Bichard said the instruction was "insistent and desperate" and his voice was "very distressed". He said there was "no discussion" about where fans would go, and that he had "no idea" why he did not question where fans would go once it was opened. The gate was opened at 14:52. "People would come in, choose where they wanted to stand and gradually it would fill out," he said. "Central pens always fill first and then it moves outwards," Mr Bichard told the inquests. He said that the concern was about the people outside. "Leppings Lane was left in these particular type of circumstances to find its own level," he said. Mr Bichard also told the jury of a brief discussion, lasting only seconds between 14:30 and 14:45, in which senior officers talked about delaying the kick-off. "I would describe it as Sgt [Michael] Goddard saying'The policy is that we don't delay the kick off if the fans have chosen to come late, if there's a road accident' and [Supt] Bernard Murray saying to [Ch Sup] David Duckenfield'Yes, that's right'," he said. The inquests continue.

UK Winter Weather Brings Minor Disruptions Despite Snow Warnings The UK has experienced better-than-expected winter conditions despite Met Office warnings, with only minimal disruption to schools and transport services across the affected regions. While the Met Office had issued alerts for rain turning to snow as weather systems moved eastward across the country, the actual impact proved less severe than anticipated. Snow was largely confined to higher ground in Wales, though the forecaster continues to warn of ongoing risks from snow and ice on Friday, which could create difficult driving conditions and potential disruptions. According to official weather warnings, Wales received between 2-4cm of snow on lower ground, with 5-10cm accumulating on higher elevations. Ice remains a concern on untreated surfaces throughout the region. Several roads experienced challenging conditions, with authorities urging caution on the A465 Heads of the Valleys Road between Brynmawr and Ebbw Vale roundabouts due to snow accumulation. The Rhigos mountain road saw hazardous driving conditions, while Colonel Road at Heol-Y-Felin in Betws, Ammanford, Carmarthenshire was temporarily closed. Dyfed-Powys Police have issued appeals for responsible parking around the Storey Arms area near Brecon this weekend, anticipating high visitor numbers for the Fan Dance endurance event at Pen y Fan. The force referenced last January's significant problems when snowfall over the Brecon Beacons, combined with two pre-planned events, caused major traffic issues on the A470. Sergeant Owen Dillion of the roads policing unit recalled that illegally parked vehicles created substantial difficulties for emergency services responding to a three-vehicle crash and forced pedestrians into the roadway. "Last January, we issued fines to over 100 vehicles parked illegally in one weekend. We really hope not to do the same this year," he stated. Despite the warnings and localized problems, the overall impact has been manageable, with only a small number of schools forced to turn pupils away and minor transport disruptions reported.

GB Bobsleigh Coach Anderson Steps Back from Day-to-Day Duties GB Bobsleigh coach Gary Anderson has announced he is stepping back from his day-to-day responsibilities, though he will remain in his role with a focus on preparing for next year's Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. Anderson's decision follows a turbulent period for the sport, coming weeks after BBC Sport reported that another senior GB Bobsleigh official was accused of making racist comments amid complaints over a "toxic atmosphere". Earlier this month, GB Bobsleigh had £48,198 of UK Sport funding cut. However, Anderson's decision is not linked to either situation. He cited personal health concerns requiring "urgent attention" and "pressing family commitments" as reasons for his reduced involvement. "Being successful in South Korea is our main performance aim and I remain fully committed to ensuring that is the case," Anderson said. "I will be kept abreast of all performance matters and will still be in attendance at numerous summer training sessions, with some of my wider responsibilities designated to other members of my coaching team." The British Bobsleigh and Skeleton Association confirmed it was "fully supportive" of Anderson's decision.

Rotherham United 3-0 Bradford City Kieran Agard's turn and shot opened the scoring for the Millers in what proved to be a comfortable victory over their Yorkshire rivals. Bradford thought they had levelled shortly after the opener but James Hanson's header was ruled out for a foul. Alex Revell then turned home a Michael O'Connor free-kick to double the hosts' lead before Agard added his second with a close-range looping header. Rotherham boss Steve Evans told BBC Radio Sheffield: "The performance levels have continued where they have been for a number of weeks. "It was a thoroughly professional performance, it could have been more and perhaps should have been more. "The training ground work that these have put in for the last three or four days, long days for them, has been worthwhile. "Alex is a super player. If he scored goals he would be playing at the top of the Championship. He destroyed their back two."

Eurozone Economic Growth Slows to 0.3% in Second Quarter The eurozone economy experienced modest growth of 0.3% in the second quarter of 2015, according to preliminary figures released by Eurostat, marking a slight deceleration from the 0.4% expansion recorded in the first three months of the year. The European Union's statistics agency also reported that inflation across the 19-nation currency bloc remained at 0.2% in July, unchanged from June, underscoring persistent concerns about weak price pressures in the region. Economic performance varied significantly among member states. Germany, Europe's largest economy, accelerated to 0.4% growth from 0.3% in the previous quarter, while Italy's expansion slowed to 0.2% from 0.3%. France's economy stagnated completely, recording zero growth between April and June, though first-quarter figures were revised upward from 0.6% to 0.7%. French Finance Minister Michel Sapin remained optimistic, insisting the country was still on course to achieve the government's 1% annual growth target. He pointed to robust export performance, which increased 1.7% during the quarter, though household consumption slowed dramatically from 0.9% to just 0.1%. Finland continued to struggle, contracting 0.4% after a 0.1% decline in the first quarter. In contrast, Greece delivered a positive surprise with 0.8% growth, significantly exceeding expectations. Across the broader 28-member EU, GDP growth held steady at 0.4%. Inflation pressures remained subdued throughout the bloc, with eleven member states experiencing deflation in July. Cyprus recorded the steepest price decline at -2.4%, while Malta reported the highest inflation rate at 1.2%. The weaker euro continued to support export growth, particularly benefiting Germany's trade-dependent economy.

Thames Water Apologises as Thousands Face Christmas Day Without Water Thames Water has issued an apology to customers in the TW and W postcode areas after a pump failure at its Hampton facility left thousands without water on Christmas Day. The water company confirmed that engineers had successfully restarted the affected pumps, but warned that water pressure was "still rebuilding" across the region. The disruption affected residents preparing Christmas dinners and hosting family gatherings during one of the most important days of the year. The water problems were not isolated to London. In the north-west of England, United Utilities customers in Stockport's SK6 postcode area experienced similar issues due to a leak on Derby Way at the junction of Derby Street. The company reported that repairs were taking longer than expected, with engineers still working at the site. Meanwhile, in Bolton, a burst water main on Baysdale Avenue has since been repaired. Juan Xu, a Twickenham resident, described the escalating situation. Initially dismissing the lack of water as a minor issue, she and her husband discovered the extent of the problem when they encountered long queues for bottled water at a nearby petrol station whilst shopping for their planned family barbecue. "I can't believe this is happening in London," she said, adding that they were considering booking into a hotel as their 10 expected guests might not be able to stay. Social media platforms were flooded with complaints from frustrated residents. Emma Ling tweeted: "There is no running water in Twickenham on Christmas Day, can't cook Christmas dinner. Merry Christmas to you all. Bah humbug." Emma Pound expressed similar frustration, whilst John Soones acknowledged the difficulty for engineers working on Christmas Day to resolve the crisis. The incidents highlight the vulnerability of water infrastructure during peak usage periods and the significant impact such failures have on customers during major holidays.

Burnley goalkeeper Conor Mitchell has signed a new contract with the Premier League club. The 21-year-old joined Burnley's academy in 2012 on a youth scholarship before turning professional two years later. Mitchell, a Northern Ireland Under-21 international, has gained experience through loan spells at Bradford Park Avenue and Sheffield FC. He made his first-team debut in a pre-season friendly against Bradford City last year.

China Secures Major Diplomatic Victory as 50 Nations Sign AIIB Agreement Delegates from 50 countries gathered at Beijing's Great Hall of the People on Monday to sign the founding articles of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), marking a significant diplomatic triumph for China and reshaping the global financial landscape. The historic signing ceremony saw representatives determine each member's shareholding and the bank's initial capital structure. Notable founding members include the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, and South Korea, with Australia becoming the first country to sign the articles of association creating the AIIB's legal framework. The most conspicuous absences were Japan and the United States, both of which have actively opposed the institution. The US has publicly questioned the governance standards at the new bank, viewing it as a vehicle for spreading Chinese "soft power." Washington had attempted to persuade its allies to refrain from joining, but those efforts ultimately proved unsuccessful. The AIIB, initially created in October by 21 countries under Chinese leadership, will finance Asian energy, transport, and infrastructure projects. Seven additional countries are expected to sign by year's end, bringing the total membership to 57 nations from Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America. ## Economic and Strategic Implications Beyond diplomatic significance, the AIIB serves crucial economic objectives for Beijing. As China seeks to redirect its engineering capabilities abroad, the bank provides a mechanism to finance infrastructure development throughout Asia. "Answer - lend the region the money to pay Chinese companies to build a 21st Century Asia according to a Beijing master plan and with Chinese influence at its core," explained one analyst. The BBC's Martin Patience notes this is one of several institutions China has established to advance its economic agenda, driven largely by frustration over its limited influence in established global financial institutions like the World Bank. ## Financial Structure The AIIB will commence operations with authorized capital of $50 billion (£31.8 billion), eventually expanding to $100 billion. According to China's Finance Ministry, Beijing will hold the largest stake at 30.34%, translating to 26.06% of voting rights within the multilateral institution. India will serve as the second-largest shareholder with a projected 10-15% stake, while Russia and Germany will occupy the third and fourth positions respectively. ## Shifting Global Power Dynamics One British official candidly observed: "If an alien landed on earth they would be puzzled by its international financial institutions as China is grossly underrepresented." Many observers suggest the AIIB's rapid development might not have occurred had the US successfully reformed existing institutions to accommodate China's growing economic clout. After three decades of remarkable growth, China's representation in international financial institutions no longer reflects global economic realities. Under President Xi Jinping, this initiative demonstrates China's determination to assert itself as a major power on the world stage. Chinese Finance Minister Lou Jiwei expressed confidence on Monday that the AIIB could begin functioning before year's end, according to Reuters.

Horse Rider Thrown After Chinook Helicopter Flyover in Bradford-on-Avon A staff member at a Wiltshire riding stable was injured when a military Chinook helicopter caused her horse to panic during a training exercise. Vicky Fielding, 20, suffered bruising after being thrown from her horse at Hudds Farm in Bradford-on-Avon when the aircraft flew overhead last Friday. "She panicked straight away and there was nothing I could do," Ms Fielding said. "I'll be anxious if I hear another Chinook coming over." Bernice Marshallsay, the yard's owner, said whilst she was aware of military exercises in the area, the stable received no advance warning about the low-flying aircraft. "We get no information at all and I've complained to the MoD on at least two other occasions and it still keeps happening," she said. "Somebody's going to be seriously injured before something's done about this." A Ministry of Defence spokesman said it was raising aircrews' awareness of horse riders and doing all it can to minimise disturbance to the public whilst crews train for operational duty.

Manchester City Close to Signing Claudio Bravo as Joe Hart's Future Remains Uncertain Manchester City are on the verge of completing the signing of Barcelona goalkeeper Claudio Bravo, with the Chile international having arrived in Manchester on Tuesday afternoon to finalise the deal. City manager Pep Guardiola, while refusing to officially confirm the transfer, acknowledged the widespread reports when he said: "I cannot deny what everyone knows. The deal is not complete. After I will answer about a player who at the moment is not our player." The imminent arrival of Bravo has cast further doubt over the future of England's number one goalkeeper Joe Hart, who has not featured for City this season despite being fit and available. However, in what could be seen as a lifeline for the 29-year-old, Guardiola confirmed that Hart will start Wednesday's Champions League qualifier second leg against Steaua Bucharest at the Etihad Stadium. Barcelona have reportedly given Bravo, 33, permission to leave the Nou Camp, paving the way for his move to the Premier League champions. The goalkeeper's expertise with the ball at his feet aligns perfectly with Guardiola's tactical philosophy, which demands a'sweeper-keeper' capable of initiating attacks from the back.
