Halfpenny, who represented the Blues 87 times between 2008 and 2014 before his move to France, would likely be offered a national dual contract (NDC) should he opt to return to Wales. Under this arrangement, the Welsh Rugby Union would fund 60% of his salary, with the region covering the remaining 40%. In exchange, the player's workload would be carefully managed to prioritize his availability and fitness for Wales. Wilson believes this structured approach to player management represents a significant selling point, particularly given Halfpenny's injury history. The full-back missed the recent Rugby World Cup due to fitness concerns, making the prospect of careful load management increasingly attractive. "The design of the central contract is to get our best players playing and staying in Wales, and therefore the management of those players has to be a huge selling point," Wilson explained. "Between us and the strong relationship with the Welsh Rugby Union, the player gets the management he wants to peak and perform for Wales." However, the Blues face stiff competition for Halfpenny's signature. The Scarlets have publicly expressed interest in the British and Irish Lion, while Premiership side Wasps have been strongly linked with a move. Both the Scarlets and Wasps are likely to compete in next season's Champions Cup, whereas the Blues are set for the second-tier Challenge Cup. Despite these challenges, the Blues hold a significant advantage. Under the binding agreement between the WRU and Welsh regions, Cardiff Blues have first refusal on Halfpenny as the region that originally developed him. "If Leigh does make a decision he wants to come back to Wales, I'd like to think Cardiff Blues would be high on his list of considerations," said Wilson. "A calibre of player like Leigh Halfpenny will have many options, whether that's regions, clubs over the bridge, clubs in France." Wilson confirmed the club is in negotiations with several players as they build their squad for next season.

Bank of England Economist Admits Forecasting Failures in Rare Candid Confession In an unusually frank admission, Andrew Haldane, the Bank of England's chief economist, has acknowledged that criticisms of economic forecasting failures are justified. Speaking about predictions that missed the mark both before the 2008 financial crisis and regarding Brexit's immediate aftermath, Mr Haldane conceded the critiques were "a fair cop", adding that the economics profession now faces a crisis of confidence. Mr Haldane drew a striking comparison between economists' failure to anticipate the devastating impact of Lehman Brothers' 2008 collapse and Michael Fish's infamous 1987 weather forecast, when the BBC meteorologist dismissed warnings of a hurricane hours before severe storms battered south-east England. He dubbed it the profession's "Michael Fish moment". While his comments addressed economists broadly rather than specifically the Bank of England, Mr Haldane maintained support for the Bank's November forecast predicting a "material" slowdown and significant inflation rise in 2017-2018. The Bank correctly anticipated sterling's post-Brexit devaluation, but significantly underestimated consumer confidence resilience. The admission highlights ongoing challenges in economic modelling, particularly when accounting for unexpected "shock" events. Models underestimated the financial crisis's severity whilst overestimating Brexit's short-term impact, failing to anticipate dynamic policy responses like the Bank's interest rate cuts to historic lows. Mr Haldane suggested economists should emulate meteorologists, who now employ vastly more data to understand weather patterns. However, he acknowledged a fundamental difference: meteorology is pure science, whilst economics ultimately studies human behaviour—attempting to predict what millions or billions of individuals might do under specific circumstances. This distinction makes economic forecasting inherently imprecise and challenging. As consumers, businesses, and policymakers respond unpredictably to changing conditions, even sophisticated models struggle to capture the complexity of human decision-making across entire economies. The rare public acknowledgement of professional limitations represents an important moment of transparency from one of Britain's most influential economic voices.

Three More Arrested Over Leeds Halloween Bike Chaos Three more people have been arrested in connection with a Halloween motorcycle ride-out that brought chaos to Leeds city centre, police have confirmed. About 50 bikers caused mayhem on 31 October when they brought a major route into Leeds to a standstill and rode dangerously through the city centre. Two men, aged 27, and one man, aged 23, have been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to cause public nuisance. Nine men and a woman who were previously arrested remain on police bail. Meanwhile, Leeds City Council has been granted a five-year extension to its county court injunction banning similar events. The injunction allowed officers to stop ride-outs planned to take place before Christmas and on New Year's Eve, police said. Labour councillor Debra Coupar, executive member for communities at Leeds City Council, said the injunction allowed the authority to "take action against people behaving irresponsibly", but would "not affect people who ride in groups in a law-abiding and sensible fashion". The order bans more than one motor vehicle meeting in a public place in the Leeds district to drive anti-socially. It also forbids people from promoting or organising any such meet-ups. In October, witnesses posted videos online showing bikers in convoy, with some pulling wheelies and others riding on the pavement. The scene was described as "utter chaos" by one passer-by and compared with the Mel Gibson film Mad Max.

Ulster Farmers Split on Brexit as Union Warns of Uncertainty The Ulster Farmer's Union has revealed deep divisions within farming families over the EU referendum, with its president Ian Marshall telling MPs that there are "husbands and wives who are completely opposed on this". Speaking to a parliamentary inquiry examining referendum issues, Mr Marshall described the debate as "head versus heart" for many farmers, who are weighing the need for European market access against concerns about loss of identity. Despite these divisions, the union maintains that in the "absence of a compelling case" for leaving, continued EU membership remains the better option for Northern Ireland's agricultural sector. Mr Marshall, alongside chief executive Wesley Aston, emphasized that farming currently fails to deliver profits, with the industry heavily dependent on subsidies for survival. They stressed that Northern Ireland's 30,000 farmers require "information, guarantees and assurances to come to an informed decision". The officials revealed significant financial figures, stating that farmers received £266 million in direct subsidy support in 2013/14, with an additional £83 million supporting the wider rural economy. During questioning, DUP MP Ian Paisley highlighted ongoing frustrations with the Common Agricultural Policy's complexity, claiming farmers had complained about it throughout his 18 years as an elected representative. He insisted the UK government would continue financial support post-Brexit. However, Mr Aston outlined that any new UK arrangement would require continued subsidies and reduced red tape. The union officials expressed doubts about whether Westminster would match EU subsidy levels. Mr Marshall warned that without guarantees, they would have "huge concerns" about any potential new UK scheme, highlighting the uncertainty facing the farming community ahead of the referendum.

Police Hunt for Missing Prisoner Simon Brown Police Scotland has launched an urgent search for Simon Brown, a 45-year-old prisoner who failed to return to HMP Castle Huntly near Dundee yesterday evening. Brown was reported missing at 17:00 after not returning to the open prison. He is described as 5ft 11in tall, bald, of slight build with brown eyes, and walks with a distinctive stoop and limp. He was last spotted in Dundee's King Street area wearing a black jacket, black trousers and a white T-shirt. Brown was carrying a black and grey holdall featuring a white Puma emblem. Police Scotland has warned the public not to approach Brown and urged anyone with information to contact them immediately.

Somalia and North Korea Top Corruption Index as African Powerhouses Show No Progress Transparency International (TI) has released its annual corruption index, placing Somalia at the top of the list of the world's most corrupt countries, sharing the dubious distinction with North Korea. The global watchdog expressed concern that it has seen no improvement in African powerhouses Nigeria and South Africa, despite their economic significance on the continent. The annual index evaluates factors including the prevalence of bribery and the perception that government officials escape punishment for corruption. According to TI, the countries perceived to be most corrupt typically share common characteristics: ongoing conflict, weak institutions such as police and courts, and a lack of independent media. Somalia has struggled without an effective central government since long-serving ruler Siad Barre was overthrown in 1991. North Korea, one of the world's most secretive societies, shared the spot of most corrupt nation with Somalia. In contrast, the "cleanest" countries—Denmark, Finland, and Sweden—demonstrate transparency in public spending and maintain judicial systems that don't differentiate between rich and poor, the report states. Despite the grim overall picture, TI identified pockets of hope. Ghana was highlighted positively, where activists "worked hard to drive out the corrupt," despite being recently rocked by an undercover film showing judges allegedly taking bribes. Senegal emerged as one of the biggest improvers this year, following the government's introduction of a series of anti-corruption laws. The index underscores the continuing global challenge of corruption, particularly affecting nations already struggling with instability and weak governance structures.

Long-Lost Spider Species Rediscovered After Century of Absence A rare spider species believed extinct in Britain has been spotted for the first time in over a century at a Dorset nature reserve. Hypsosinga heri was on the verge of being removed from the official list of British species when RSPB volunteers made the remarkable discovery at Radipole Lake Nature Reserve in Weymouth. Two female spiders were found among flowers during a routine butterfly survey. The species had not been seen since sightings at Wicken Fen near Ely, Cambridgeshire, in 1898 and 1912. The volunteers photographed "a very small, brightly-coloured spider on flowers," which was later verified by the British Arachnological Society. Since the initial discovery several months ago, additional females have been observed at the nearby Lodmoor reserve. However, RSPB volunteer Allan Neilson noted a puzzling absence: "Which begs the question, where are the males?" The rediscovery offers hope for the species' survival in Britain.

**Scarlets prop Rob Evans facing December return from wrist surgery** Wales and Scarlets prop Rob Evans will not return to action until December as he continues his recovery from wrist surgery, the region has confirmed. The 24-year-old has not played since Wales' summer tour to New Zealand in June and has missed the entire season so far. "We're not expecting to see Rob back until December," a Scarlets spokesperson said. Evans has been competing with Cardiff Blues' Gethin Jenkins for Wales' starting loosehead position since the 2015 World Cup. Scarlets head coach Wayne Pivac previously indicated Evans might return near the autumn internationals in August.

Irish Language Campaign Exceeds Targets as 13,000 Sign Up A campaign to promote Irish language fluency has vastly exceeded its original goals, organisers announced on Saturday as they marked the initiative's fourth anniversary. The Líofa campaign, which translates as "fluent" in Irish, was launched by Minister of Culture, Arts and Leisure, Carál Ní Chuilín, in September 2011. Its initial target was to get 1,000 people to sign up and commit to learning and speaking Irish by 2015. On Saturday, Ms Ní Chuilín revealed that more than 13,000 people have now registered for Líofa, exceeding the original target thirteenfold. The campaign organisers have set an ambitious new goal to enrol 20,000 people on Irish language courses by 2020. "Irish is a language for everyone and when I launched Líofa in 2011 I never imagined that I would have to revise the target so many times," Ms Ní Chuilín said in a statement. "People from all walks of life have availed of the opportunity to sign up to learn the language." To celebrate the anniversary, the minister announced that a series of free intensive Irish language courses will be held at various venues across Northern Ireland on Saturday. "The courses are free and are accessible to all and every support will be given to participants both on this course and beyond as they endeavour to improve on their language skills," she added. The announcement comes despite research showing significant disparities in Irish fluency across the island. Last month, a report by the Republic of Ireland's Economic and Social Research Institute found that 11% of respondents in the Republic could conduct most conversations in Irish, compared to just 2% in Northern Ireland.

Two Men Arrested Over Fatal Shooting of Eddie Hutch in Dublin Irish police have arrested two men in connection with the fatal shooting of Eddie Hutch Senior in Dublin last month. Mr Hutch Snr, 59, was killed at his flat in Poplar Row, North Strand, in the north inner city on 8 February. Police believe it may have been in reprisal for a fatal shooting at a boxing match weigh-in days earlier. RTÉ reports that the men can be detained for up to seven days. They were arrested in the Dublin area and are being held at Mountjoy Garda Station and Bridewell Garda Station. Mr Hutch Snr was the uncle of Gary Hutch who was shot dead in Spain in September of last year. He was also the brother of Gerry Hutch, a notorious criminal in Dublin in the late 1980s and 1990s, who was nicknamed the Monk.

Paralympic Champion David Smith Faces Fourth Surgery on Spinal Tumour Paralympic gold medallist David Smith is preparing for his fourth operation on a life-threatening spinal tumour, scheduled for 1 March, as he continues his courageous battle with the condition that has forced him to put his sporting ambitions on hold. The 37-year-old from Aviemore, who won rowing gold at the London 2012 Paralympics, had been training to represent Great Britain in Para-cycling at the Rio Games. However, the aggressive growth of the tumour has made further surgery unavoidable. Smith revealed that the tumour causes him constant pain but has also given him an unexpected purpose - inspiring others facing severe illnesses. "It is a love-hate relationship," he told BBC Radio Scotland's The Stephen Jardine Programme. "In a lot of ways it's changed who I am as a person." The athlete described receiving an emotional email from a family whose son has cystic fibrosis, saying: "Please never give up because our family is holding it together on your strength." Such messages have helped Smith maintain perspective on his situation. "I can't be angry at my situation if my efforts give hope to others," he said. Despite his health challenges, Smith attempted to delay surgery last September in hopes of competing in Rio. However, earlier this month he acknowledged the tumour had grown dangerously large - threatening to crush his spinal cord and potentially stop his breathing. A cycling accident that caused the tumour to bleed added further urgency to the need for surgery. Smith credits sport with providing the mental and physical strength to cope with his condition. Remarkably, just seven months after his last surgery in June last year, he cycled up France's Mont Ventoux three times in one day. The determined athlete has already mapped out a timeline for his return to cycling following the operation.

Six More Come Forward Following Footballer's Abuse Revelations Six people have contacted Cheshire Police following revelations by former professional footballer Andy Woodward about sexual abuse he suffered as a youth player. Mr Woodward, who played for Bury and Sheffield United, was abused by convicted paedophile Barry Bennell whilst at Crewe Alexandra between the ages of 11 and 15. Bennell, a former football coach, was jailed for nine years in 1998 after admitting sexual offences against six boys. Cheshire Police confirmed they are contacting the six individuals who have come forward, though it remains unclear whether they are potential victims or witnesses. The force stated no one else is currently under investigation. Mr Woodward recently waived his legal right to anonymity to raise awareness about abuse in football, believing there were more victims of Bennell and other abusers within the sport. Since going public, he said he has been "speechless" at the overwhelming support from fans and former players, and has encouraged other victims to come forward. Acting Detective Sergeant Ben Hilton of Cheshire Police's Public Protection Unit stated: "We take all reports of sexual abuse extremely seriously and are currently in the process of making contact with the six people."

Top Gear Nominated for National Television Award Despite Clarkson Controversy The BBC's Top Gear has secured a nomination at the National Television Awards despite the controversial departure of its former host Jeremy Clarkson earlier this year. Clarkson was sacked from the show in March following a fracas with a producer and has since signed to present a new car show on Amazon Prime. His last series with Top Gear is nominated in the factual entertainment category, but faces stiff competition from last year's winner Gogglebox and Big Blue Live. Viewers have until 18 October to cast their votes, with several categories being shortlisted ahead of the ceremony scheduled for 20 January 2016. This year introduces several changes to the awards format. Viewers are being asked to choose their TV moment of the year, with suggestions on the NTA website including memorable scenes such as Poldark star Aidan Turner's topless scything and the shocking betrayal of Game of Thrones' Jon Snow. Four new categories have been added to the awards, including best international, best new drama, live magazine show, and a new TV presenter category that pits factual show presenters against their entertainment counterparts. The competition features several well-known presenting duos vying for recognition, including This Morning's Philip Schofield and Holly Willoughby, and Pointless hosts Alexander Armstrong and Richard Osman. Real-life couples are also competing, with husband and wife presenters Vernon Kay and Tess Daly alongside Rochelle and Marvin Humes on the longlist. The international category showcases streaming services' growing influence, with Amazon Prime's Transparent and Netflix's Orange Is The New Black and House Of Cards nominated alongside Channel 5's Gotham and BBC Three's Family Guy. In the new drama category, nominations span from costume drama Poldark to Suranne Jones' Doctor Foster and Channel 4's sci-fi series Humans. Adventurer Bear Grylls receives double recognition in the Challenge Show category for both ITV's Mission Survive and Channel 4's The Island, competing against favourites including The Great British Bake Off, The Apprentice, and MasterChef. The awards ceremony will be broadcast live from the O2 Arena on ITV, hosted by Dermot O'Leary, who himself is nominated in the TV presenter category.

Donaldson Strike Keeps Birmingham's Play-off Hopes Alive Clayton Donaldson's clinical finish earned Birmingham City a crucial 1-0 victory over struggling Bolton Wanderers, keeping their Championship play-off ambitions firmly on track. The striker tucked away a low cross from Diego Fabbrini at the near post to claim his seventh goal of the season, securing three precious points that lift Blues to within three points of the coveted play-off positions. The victory ended a concerning run that had seen Birmingham fail to win in their previous three outings. For Bolton, the struggles continue both on and off the pitch. Despite avoiding a winding-up order on Monday after agreeing to a £7.5m takeover, the Trotters remain rooted in second-from-bottom position, their survival hopes looking increasingly bleak. Former Bolton striker Dean Holdsworth, who heads the consortium set to take control at the Macron Stadium, was once again present in the stands to witness another disappointing performance from his future charges. The home side's attacking impotence was compounded by the absence of top scorer Gary Madine, who was controversially left out by manager Neil Lennon for disciplinary reasons. Birmingham hardly dominated proceedings but made their moment of quality count when Donaldson expertly flicked home Fabbrini's delivery. The former Watford midfielder, making his first start for Blues, provided the creative spark that had been missing from an otherwise tepid encounter. The visitors nearly doubled their advantage late on when substitute David Cotterill was thwarted by Bolton goalkeeper Paul Rachubka, who was making his first league start for the club. Bolton boss Neil Lennon was frank about his side's limitations: "What we need to do is get the embargo lifted and get some players in to bolster the squad. It's wafer thin at the moment. We do need a bit of strength in depth, it's something we've lacked for a while." Regarding the Madine situation, Lennon remained tight-lipped about specifics but firm in his stance: "You have to set certain standards as a manager. There are some things which you can't tolerate and you have to put a marker down. It's up to Gary, the ball is in his court." Birmingham manager Gary Rowett was satisfied with the result, acknowledging: "You always felt this was a really pivotal game. We're not a free-scoring team, we didn't use the ball well enough but the one bit of quality in the game we ended up scoring from. We're still very much in the mix, something that, after 32 games, everyone at the club would have been really pleased with."

Welsh School Celebrates 70 Years Since Historic Opening Ysgol Gymraeg Dewi Sant, a Welsh-medium school in Llanelli, has celebrated its 70th anniversary with special commemorations at the site where it all began. The school was originally established at Seion Chapel in Llanelli in 1947, opening its doors with just 34 pupils and two teachers. Since those modest beginnings, it has flourished into a thriving institution now educating 450 children at its current location. To mark the milestone, the school hosted a special assembly and Eisteddfod, including the unveiling of a commemorative plaque. Distinguished guests included Maureen Williams, who holds the unique distinction of being both one of the school's first pupils and a former teacher. Current head teacher Ann Clwyd Davies described the occasion as "a very emotional morning," noting that pupils are "very proud" of their school's heritage. She acknowledged the "huge battle during the 40s" that established Welsh-medium education. Looking ahead, Ms Davies confirmed discussions with Carmarthenshire council regarding a new school building.

Geraint Thomas Claims Thrilling Stage Two Victory at Tirreno-Adriatico Britain's Geraint Thomas secured a dramatic solo victory on stage two of the Tirreno-Adriatico cycling race, attacking in the closing kilometres to claim his first win of the season. The Team Sky rider made his decisive move with approximately 5km remaining of the 228km stage, holding off a charging peloton to cross the line nine seconds clear in Pomarance, Italy. Dutch rider Tom Dumoulin finished second, with Slovakia's Peter Sagan taking third place. The victory provided some redemption for Thomas and Team Sky following a disappointing performance in the opening stage team time trial. However, the time lost on that first day means the 30-year-old Welshman faces an uphill battle to challenge for the overall title. Belgium's Greg van Avermaet of BMC Racing currently leads the general classification, with teammates Rohan Dennis and Tejay van Garderen occupying second and third positions respectively. The BMC squad's dominance in the opening team time trial has given them a significant advantage heading into the remaining stages. Thomas's attacking ride demonstrated his excellent form ahead of the spring classics season, though his focus will likely shift from overall victory to hunting further stage wins as the race progresses through central Italy towards the Adriatic coast.

Brentford Stadium Plans Modified as Community Facilities Moved Outside Brentford Football Club has revised its new stadium plans, relocating the Community Sports Trust facilities from inside the venue to an adjacent site. The Bees have announced construction will commence in 2018, with completion targeted for late 2019 or early 2020. Club officials insist the changes won't compromise the stadium's overall quality. The amendments will be presented to the London Borough of Hounslow Planning Committee on 24 August, with formal submissions to the council scheduled for early September. The modification represents a significant shift in the original design but maintains the club's commitment to community engagement.

Two Teenage Boys Arrested in Australia on Terror-Related Charges **SYDNEY** - Two 16-year-old boys have been arrested and charged with terrorism-related offences after allegedly planning an imminent attack inspired by the Islamic State group, Australian police announced. The teenagers were apprehended by a counter-terrorism team in a laneway behind a Muslim prayer hall. According to authorities, they were carrying two bayonet-style knives purchased on the day of their arrest, along with handwritten notes pledging allegiance to IS. "We will be alleging this attack was inspired by Islamic State," said New South Wales Police Deputy Commissioner Catherine Burn at a news conference. "We don't have any specific information of a particular target where we will allege that there was going to be an imminent attack." The Australian Broadcasting Corp reported that one of the arrested boys is the son of a convicted terrorist, though police declined to comment on this claim. The pair did not appear in Parramatta Children's Court and did not apply for bail, which was formally refused. The arrests were part of an ongoing counter-terrorism operation. Australian Federal Police Deputy Commissioner Mike Phelan emphasized public safety concerns, stating: "Anybody who says they've got the silver bullet to youth radicalisation, please tell me all about it." The incident follows the arrest of a 22-year-old man charged with committing a terrorist act last month in southwest Sydney. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull warned in September that the threat of terror attacks in Australia was "real" following IS calls to target prominent Australian locations.

Medieval Seawall Breach Leaves Gower Coastal Path Cut Off for Three Years A picturesque section of the Wales Coastal Path near Llanmadoc in north Gower remains impassable three years after winter storms breached a centuries-old seawall, flooding the area and cutting off a beloved local walking route. The 2014 storms damaged the medieval seawall at Cwm Ivy, allowing seawater to inundate what was previously grassland rich with flowers and wildlife. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) has since ruled that restoring the original coastal path is not feasible, despite mounting pressure from local residents and walking groups. Local resident Randolph Jenkins, whose family has lived in the area since 1923, expressed frustration at the loss. "Three years ago this marshland was grassland, full of flowers and wildlife. The wall has been here for centuries," he said. "There are so many people who support re-connecting the path - from local walking and rambling groups to the local assembly member." Following the breach, NRW created a diversion through nearby Cwm Ivy woods to maintain the Wales Coastal Path's continuity. However, locals argue this has spoiled a popular circular walk and diminished the area's appeal. The impact extends beyond recreation. Café owner Sian Griffiths reported decreased footfall for her business, noting: "There was a lot of places you could go for a walk. That has all gone now." NRW has proposed alternatives to Swansea council, which owns the path, including constructing a new route away from the marshland or building a wooden or rope bridge. Hywel Manley of NRW confirmed: "The council is responsible for the public footpath, and we have suggested alternatives." Swansea council stated it is working with multiple organizations to resolve the ongoing issue.

Vintage Uniforms Mark Belfast Somme Parade Bands led a procession of men and women, many dressed in vintage military uniforms and carrying replica weapons, through Belfast to commemorate the Battle of the Somme. The parade was organised by the 36th Ulster Division Memorial Association, with a wreath-laying ceremony held at Belfast City Hall. Ch Supt Nigel Grimshaw praised the "large scale police operation with community safety at its core" and thanked those involved in planning the event. "The efforts made by community representatives and event organisers show a real willingness to achieve resolutions," he said. He expressed hope that the successful parade would "create a positive platform for dealing with sensitive parades throughout the coming months."

Smart Motorway Plan Could Cost Up to £70m for Belfast Routes A proposal to convert hard shoulders into traffic lanes on Belfast's main motorways could cost between £60m and £70m, according to consultants' estimates. Transport NI commissioned experts to examine solutions for "recurrent traffic congestion at peak times" on the region's busiest roads. The resulting report recommends transforming sections of the M1 and M2 into "smart motorways", similar to schemes already operating in England. The plans would see the hard shoulder converted into permanent traffic lanes on the M1 between Stockman's Lane and Blaris, and on the M2 between York Street and Greencastle, in both directions. A BBC-obtained summary indicates the concept-stage proposal is considered "value for money", though concerns exist that it might encourage increased car use over public transport. The Freight Transport Association, representing haulage companies, has said the initiative deserves "given serious consideration" as a potential solution to Belfast's mounting traffic problems.

Two Teenagers Deny Murder Charges in Rhyl Death Case Two teenagers have pleaded not guilty to murdering Amarjeet Singh-Bhakar, 37, who died following a disturbance on Prince Edward Avenue in Rhyl on 30 April. The youths, aged 15 and 16, appeared at Mold Crown Court and also denied charges of wounding with intent and violent disorder. Their identities are protected by law due to their ages. A trial has been scheduled for 3 October, with both defendants remanded in custody until then.

Scottish Labour Must Elect Leader "For Long Haul" After Election Devastation, Says Lamont Former Scottish Labour leader Johann Lamont has said the party must appoint a leader for the long term if it is to recover from its catastrophic general election defeat in Scotland. In her first broadcast interview since resigning, Ms Lamont said the scale of the party's election defeat was worse than anyone "possibly imagined". The party must now elect a leader "for the long haul" to recover, she said. Ms Lamont also praised the SNP and its leader Nicola Sturgeon for running a campaign that "got everything right". The SNP won 56 out of 59 seats in Scotland in last month's general election. Labour was left with just one MP in Scotland, after losing 40 seats, including those of Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy, and shadow foreign secretary Douglas Alexander. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Johann Lamont, who led Scottish Labour from 2011 to 2014, said: "Even those of us who were preparing for the worst possible defeat couldn't possibly have imagined what happened. "We couldn't have predicted it, but we need to analyse it if we're going to survive. "The instinct of the Labour Party is if there's a problem, change the leader, then sit back, fold your arms and wait to be disappointed because they're sure it's not going to deliver. "We can't do that this time. We need to elect a leader not on a short term contract, but a long term appointment for the long haul. There is no quick fix to this, there are not any ploys, not any gimmicks, that will get us through the next period." She said it "defies logic" that Labour MPs of the "highest calibre" lost their seats, but said the SNP "took all before them". "That therefore means people were putting faith not just in individual candidates, but putting faith in a message that was coming to them from the SNP." She said the SNP had provided "a lesson in how to run a campaign", and leader Nicola Sturgeon had been "completely in control". "It seems to me they got everything right, and Nicola Sturgeon has become a politician over many years. She was the most experienced person on the podium during the leaders' debate, and that shone out." Ms Lamont added that she felt some comments about the new SNP MPs had been "disrespectful". "Some of the commentary around some of them choosing to take their oath in Gaelic I found personally offensive as a Gael," she said. "They are a mixed bunch like any bunch of people, but the fact of the matter is they are significantly representing Scotland's interests." Ms Lamont, who is MSP for Glasgow Pollok, resigned as Scottish Labour leader last October accusing Westminster colleagues of treating Scotland like a "branch office". "The recovery [of Labour] in Scotland which matters to the whole of the United Kingdom must be shaped in Scotland itself," she said. Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy has announced he will tender his resignation later this month having tabled a plan to reform the party. Deputy leader Kezia Dugdale has confirmed she will stand for the leadership.

New Law Bans Wheel Clamping on Private Land in England and Wales A new law coming into effect makes it a criminal offence to clamp or tow away vehicles parked on private land in England and Wales, in a move designed to protect motorists from rogue operators. The Protection of Freedoms Act introduces the ban, which could save drivers an estimated £55 million annually in clamping charges. However, the legislation does not extend to Northern Ireland, while Scotland has already prohibited the practice since 1992. Under the new regulations, private landowners retain some powers through strengthened ticketing provisions. Unpaid parking charges can now be claimed from the registered keeper of the vehicle, not just the driver who parked it. This change addresses a previous loophole that made it difficult for landowners to pursue payment. The government has also established an independent appeals service, funded by the British Parking Association (BPA), allowing motorists to challenge parking charges issued on private land by companies enrolled in the BPA's approved operator scheme. Lord Taylor of Holbeach, the Home Office minister responsible for the clamping law changes, welcomed the reforms: "This common-sense ban will give motorists the protection they deserve against rogue wheel-clamping and towing companies. It will save motorists £55m each year in clamping charges and finally penalise the real criminals - the corrupt firms themselves." Local Transport Minister Norman Baker added: "These new parking arrangements deliver a fairer legal framework for motorists and landowners, while getting rid of the indiscriminate clamping and towing by private companies for good." Despite the reforms, both the AA and BPA have expressed reservations, arguing the measures don't provide adequate protection against unscrupulous parking operators. A BPA spokesperson highlighted concerns about little-known by-laws that grant certain landowners, including some railway stations, airports, and port authorities, exemptions allowing them to manage parking on their own terms. BPA chief executive Patrick Troy acknowledged the significance of the changes whilst noting their limitations: "The Protection of Freedoms Act ushers in perhaps the most significant shake-up of the private parking industry ever seen in this country. However, the regulations do not yet go far enough. An independent appeals service which is not binding on all operators is likely to be a recipe for confusion among motorists." The AA has also raised concerns that rogue operators may now shift to issuing bogus parking tickets on private land, potentially creating new problems for drivers despite the clamping ban.

Chile's Lower House Approves Limited Abortion Rights Bill Chile's Chamber of Deputies has approved a bill that would allow abortion under three specific circumstances, marking a significant shift in the country's restrictive reproductive laws. The draft, which was submitted by Michelle Bachelet's government, needs Senate approval to become law. Despite being predominantly Catholic, Chile allowed abortion until 1989. But the practice was banned by General Augusto Pinochet in one of the last acts of his military government. "Incredible, the motion is passed," said the leader of the Chamber of Deputies, Marco Antonio Nunez. Opinion polls say most Chileans approve the change. The proposal was approved by 66 to 44 votes. The government, which tabled the bill 14 months ago, managed to get the support of some members of the conservative Christian Democrats. "This is an historic day. We see the political will to let women make their own decisions," said lawmaker Karol Cariola of the Communist Party, which is part of Ms Bachelet's governing coalition. However, opposition remains strong. "This is a setback for protection of the unborn," said Claudia Nogueira of conservative Independent Democratic Union party. Chile is one of seven Latin American countries where there is still a total ban on abortion. The others are El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua and Surinam. Only Cuba, Guyana, Puerto Rico and Uruguay allow abortions in cases other than rape, incest or threats to a woman's health. In Mexico, only Mexico City has legalised abortion, during the first 12 weeks.

Massive Manhunt Underway for Escaped Rape Suspect in Japan Japanese authorities have launched an extensive search operation involving more than 4,000 police officers for 20-year-old Yuta Sugimoto, who escaped custody during a visit to prosecutors' office in Kawasaki. Sugimoto, suspected of participating in a gang rape and robbery of a woman on January 2nd, managed to flee after requesting his restraints be loosened during a toilet break while meeting with his lawyer. He successfully evaded his guards and remains at large. The escape has sparked concern among local residents, with schools issuing warnings for children not to travel alone. Police have deployed substantial resources, including 850 vehicles, sniffer dogs, helicopters, and boats to track down the fugitive. Authorities are treating the manhunt as a high priority given the serious nature of the allegations and public safety concerns in the Kawasaki area.

Search Planned for Missing Suffolk Woman Sylvia Stuart A search is set to be organized for a missing Suffolk woman whose husband was found dead near their home earlier this month. Sylvia and Peter Stuart, aged 69 and 75, were reported missing on Friday 3 June. Mr Stuart's body was discovered near their home in Weybread, Suffolk, later that day. Ali Qazimaj, 42, of Tilbury, is wanted over the murder and disappearance. A group is due to set off from The Bell in Wortwell later. Suffolk Police are aware of the search taking place. Wortwell is near Harleston in Norfolk and about five miles from Weybread. It is an area of fields, hamlets and the River Waveney, which forms the county border. On Friday, police searched fields near the couple's home in Mill Lane. Police believe Mr Qazimaj boarded a ferry from Dover to Calais on 4 June, the day after Mr Stuart was found dead. His car was found on a terraced street within sight of the ferry terminal. Any connection he may have to the Stuarts is not known. The couple's son-in-law Steve Paxman, 61 and from Leicester, was arrested on 5 June in connection with Mr Stuart's death, and released on police bail until 3 August.

End of an Era: Last VCR Manufacturer Ceases Production After 33 Years Funai Electric, the last remaining manufacturer of VHS-playing VCRs, is ending production after 33 years, marking the final chapter for a once-revolutionary technology. The Japanese company, which has been producing VCRs most recently in China for Sanyo, sold just 750,000 units last year—a dramatic decline from its peak of 15 million units annually. The decision comes as sourcing necessary parts has become increasingly difficult. VCRs were introduced in the 1970s and revolutionized home entertainment, but were eventually superseded by DVD technology. The writing was on the wall years ago: UK retailer Dixons phased out VCR sales 12 years ago due to DVD popularity, and Sony discontinued Betamax video cassettes last year. Unlike vinyl records, which have experienced a remarkable renaissance among audiophiles and collectors, experts don't anticipate similar nostalgia for VHS formats. "I don't see VCR becoming like vinyl," said Tania Loeffler, an analyst at IHS Technology. "The quality on VHS is not something I think anyone would want to go back to." However, Loeffler acknowledged that niche markets, particularly those focused on archival purposes, will likely mourn the loss of VCR availability for accessing historical VHS content. The end of VCR production closes a significant chapter in consumer electronics history.

Road collapses into giant sinkhole in California A massive sinkhole has opened up in a street in California, USA, swallowing part of the road surface. The street in Madera began slowly collapsing into an underground sewage line below. Police officers spotted a dip forming in the road and quickly cordoned off the area to protect residents and motorists. The Madera Police Department estimates the hole measures approximately 15 to 20 feet deep. Officials believe recent storms may be responsible, with rainwater soaking into the ground and eroding the topsoil beneath the road surface. The police department captured dramatic video footage showing the extent of the collapse, which has left a significant crater in the residential street.

How to Communicate Better with Deaf Children Two deaf children who are fluent in both English and British Sign Language have shared helpful tips on communicating with them effectively. Despite their language skills, they explain there are simple things people can do to make understanding easier. The children's advice was captured in a video produced by Hannah Gelbart.

Newcastle Falcons Rugby Player Denies Rape Allegations at Crown Court A professional rugby player for Premiership team Newcastle Falcons has told a court that nothing he did with a woman was "against her will," as he faces multiple sexual assault charges. Zach Kibirige, 21, is accused of subjecting a woman to a series of sexual offences at her home in November. He denies four counts of rape, attempted rape, sexual assault and another serious sexual assault allegedly committed over approximately an hour. Beginning the defence case at Newcastle Crown Court, the player's barrister Nicholas Lumley QC asked directly whether Mr Kibirige had raped the complainant. The 5ft 10ins tall defendant, who has represented England Under-17s and Under-20s, replied: "Absolutely not." When asked if he had gone to the woman's flat with the intention to rape her, the Middlesbrough-born player, who was raised in Yarm, Teesside, answered: "No." Mr Kibirige told the court he has never been sent off during his rugby career and has no previous convictions, cautions or police reprimands. At the time of the alleged incident, he was not playing for the Falcons as he was recovering from an ankle injury. The court heard that Mr Kibirige and the complainant had initially matched on Tinder before exchanging WhatsApp messages. He said he met her at her home for the first time on the night in question, claiming he was sober when he arrived. He told jurors they began watching a film in her bedroom. Earlier in the trial, the complainant alleged that Mr Kibirige gripped her throat before raping her. The trial continues.

Cyclist Wins Damages After Pothole Crash Left Him With Severe Head Injury Alan Curtis, 57, from Bushey in Hertfordshire, suffered a "severe head injury" in the crash on The Drive, Rickmansworth, in 2009. He sued Hertfordshire County Council for failing to fix the pothole, which he said was a "real source of danger". The council said it was "disappointed" the High Court had ruled in Mr Curtis's favour. Mr Curtis, a charity fundraising director, was cycling with two friends when a "defect" in the road surface caused him to lose control, fall from his bike and hit his head. Kevin O'Sullivan, from Levenes solicitors, said Mr Curtis had experienced "pain, suffering and loss of amenity". "Potholes tend to cause [cyclists] more serious injuries than accidents involving motor vehicles and this is a classic example," he said. The claim stated the pothole could be seen on a Google Street View image from October 2008, but the council failed to note it and order its repair during a scheduled inspection the following March. Mr Curtis fractured his skull and damaged his brainstem, which led to "significant deafness", the claim stated. His left arm was also broken. Mr Curtis, who had been wearing a safety helmet, was given emergency treatment at Watford General Hospital. A report from neuropsychologist Dr Yvonne McCulloch said "cognitive impairments" caused by the brain injury had hampered Mr Curtis in the workplace since the accident. He has since switched to a similar, but less stressful, job which has meant a loss of earnings.

Thailand-Australia World Cup Qualifier: Fans Told to Wear Mourning Colors Football associations in Thailand and Australia have instructed fans to wear black, grey, or white clothing for an upcoming World Cup qualifier match, in respect of Thailand's period of national mourning. The match, scheduled for November 15, comes as Thailand observes a year-long mourning period following the death of King Bhumibol Adulyadej last week. The 88-year-old monarch reigned for 70 years and was regarded by many Thais as semi-divine, making him the world's longest-reigning monarch. The Football Association of Thailand initially attempted to postpone the fixture, but Australian officials requested the game proceed as scheduled. Football Federation Australia has announced strict restrictions for the match. Banners, flags, and megaphones will be banned from the stadium, and "joyful activities" are strictly prohibited both inside and around the venue. The king's death has deeply affected Thailand, with much of the nation expressing profound grief. Crown Prince Maha Vajiralongkorn has been named successor but has requested a delay in the formal succession process. Thailand maintains strict lese-majeste laws protecting senior royal family members, with public discussion of succession potentially resulting in lengthy prison sentences.

Mountain Weather Service Warns of Closure Risk Over Funding Dispute The Mountain Weather Information Service (MWIS) has warned it could be forced to close if it loses crucial support from sportscotland, potentially putting the safety of climbers and walkers at risk. The non-profit forecasting service said it would stop producing forecasts at the end of this year if funding is not continued. However, sportscotland has dismissed the safety warning as "disappointing and misleading." The Scottish government sporting body said it remains committed to providing reliable, authoritative mountain weather forecasts and confirmed investment in MWIS would continue until the end of 2023. Sportscotland said it has been involved in collaborative discussions for over a year with the Met Office and MWIS about building a "resilient and development-focused mountain weather forecast provision for Scotland." In a statement, sportscotland said: "Our priority is to ensure there is a sustainable mountain forecast for Scotland through the provision of reliable, authoritative forecasts, which are relevant to outdoor activities and enable forecast users to make informed judgements about their chosen activities. This is precisely what we will deliver and we will ensure there is a continuity of this service." Geoff Monk, Galloway-based lead forecaster at MWIS, expressed concern about the situation: "The funding withdrawal by sportscotland, following their previous decision to collaborate with MWIS, was a real shock and jeopardises the safety of those who use the mountains every day." He added: "All we want is for MWIS to continue to provide a consistent, quality service so that mountain users can enjoy the mountains safely, fully aware of what the weather will throw at them." Both organisations said they remain open to further discussions to resolve the dispute. MWIS is calling on sportscotland to return to the negotiating table and commit to continued funding to secure the service's long-term future.

Dortmund Cruise Past Lotte to Set Up Bayern Semi-Final Borussia Dortmund secured their place in the German Cup semi-finals with a convincing second-half performance against third-division Lotte. After a goalless first half, American teenager Christian Pulisic broke the deadlock, slotting home Ousmane Dembele's pass. Andre Schurrle doubled the advantage, converting from close range, before captain Marcel Schmelzer sealed the victory with a late free-kick. Dortmund, seeking their first cup triumph since 2012, will now face holders Bayern Munich on 25 or 26 April. "We took a bit of time to get into the game, but we didn't make any major mistakes before half-time," Schmelzer said. "Then we put in a very good performance in the second half." The fixture had been postponed from 3 March due to heavy snowfall.

Nigerian Court Sentences Nine to Death for Blasphemy in Kano KANO, Nigeria - A Sharia court in northern Nigeria has sentenced nine Muslims to death by hanging after they pleaded guilty to blasphemy charges, according to the head of Kano's religious police. Aminu Ibrahim Daurawa told the BBC that the trial was conducted swiftly and in secret following violent protests that resulted in part of the courthouse being burned down last month. It remains unclear whether the convicted individuals plan to appeal the sentence. The alleged blasphemy occurred during a religious gathering held in honor of Sheikh Ibrahim Niasse, the Senegalese founder of the Tijaniya sect, which commands a substantial following throughout West Africa. The nine defendants - eight men and one woman - were accused of stating that "Niasse was bigger than Prophet Muhammad," comments that sparked immediate unrest in the predominantly Muslim city. The controversial remarks triggered violent reactions, with an angry mob burning the venue to the ground. The nine individuals were subsequently arrested to prevent further violence. "There has been consensus among Muslim scholars that insulting the prophet carries a death sentence," Mr. Daurawa explained to BBC Hausa service. "We quickly put them on trial to avoid bloodshed because people were very angry and trying to take law into their hands." When news of the verdict emerged, celebrations reportedly broke out in some areas of Kano, according to BBC Kano reporter Yusuf Yakasai. The Tijaniya sect, founded in Algeria in 1784, is the largest Sufi order in Islam, with followers spanning north and west Africa, South Africa, Indonesia, and beyond. Sheikh Ibrahim Niasse is credited with reviving the sect in the 20th century, and his shrine attracts pilgrims from across the continent. The convicted individuals belonged to the Haqiqa (Realist) faction of the movement. In Kano and several other northern Nigerian states, Islamic Sharia courts operate alongside secular judicial systems, a development that followed the country's return to civilian rule in 1999. This case marks the first time a death sentence has been handed down for blasphemy in northern Nigeria. While death sentences have been issued for other offenses such as adultery under Sharia law, none have been carried out to date.

Mindfulness Therapy as Effective as Anti-Depressants for Depression Relapse Prevention Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy could offer a viable alternative to long-term anti-depressant medication for people at risk of depression relapse, according to a major new study. Scientists tested the therapy against anti-depressant pills for people at risk of relapse and found it worked just as well. The therapy trains people to focus their minds and understand that negative thoughts may come and go. In England and Wales doctors are already encouraged to offer it. Patients who have had recurrent clinical depression are often prescribed long-term anti-depressant drugs to help prevent further episodes. And experts stress that drug therapy is still essential for many. In this study, UK scientists enrolled 212 people who were at risk of further depression on a course of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) while carefully reducing their medication. Patients took part in group sessions where they learned guided meditation and mindfulness skills. The therapy aimed to help people focus on the present, recognise any early warning signs of depression and respond to them in ways that did not trigger further reoccurrences. Researchers compared these results to 212 people who continued to take a full course of medication over two years. By the end of the study, a similar proportion of people had relapsed in both groups. And many in the MBCT group had been tapered off their medication. Scientists say these findings suggest MBCT could provide a much-needed alternative for people who cannot or do not wish to take long-term drugs. In their report, they conclude it "may be a new choice for millions of people with recurrent depression on repeat prescriptions." Nigel Reed, who took part in the study, added: "Mindfulness gives me a set of skills which I use to keep well in the long term. Rather than relying on the continuing use of anti-depressants, mindfulness puts me in charge, allowing me to take control of my own future, to spot when I am at risk and to make the changes I need to stay well." Providing an independent comment on the study, Dr Gwen Adshead, of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said: "These findings are important from the point of view of people living with depression who are trying to engage in their own recovery. And it provides evidence that MBCT is an intervention that primary care physicians should take seriously as an option." But he cautioned the research does not suggest MBCT is useful for all types of depression; nor that it should replace anti-depressant treatment for people with severe disorders who have needed hospital treatment or are suicidal. And experts caution patients should only reduce their anti-depressant medication under medical supervision. Prof Eduard Vieta, Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Barcelona, Spain, said there needed to be more studies to establish how effective MBCT might be. Researchers say their next step is to tease out what the active ingredient in mindfulness therapy might be, and to check it compares favourably to other group-based approaches.

Tracey Ullman Returns to BBC One with Mixed Reviews for New Sketch Show Tracey Ullman has made her long-awaited return to British television with her new sketch show on BBC One, receiving a range of responses from critics who praised her versatility while questioning whether the format felt fresh enough for 2016. The show, which aired on Monday evening, featured the 56-year-old comedian's impressions of Dame Judi Dench as a kleptomaniac and German Chancellor Angela Merkel reimagined as a "sex bomb". Among the original characters were Karen, a drugs mule readjusting to contemporary society after spending 28 years in a Thai prison, and Sally Preston, a topless feminist Member of Parliament. The Times reviewer Alex Hardy was largely positive, declaring the sketch show delivered "mostly hits". She wrote: "Someone confiscate her passport. It's as if a prodigal daughter - last seen mucking about with French, Saunders and pop producers in the mid-1980s - has returned to the UK from 30 gap years in America and wrapped herself instantly round British hearts and funnybones." Veronica Lee of The Arts Desk highlighted Ullman's ability to maintain her perspective on British culture despite her decades in America. "Last night's opener didn't just have some of her pitch-perfect impressions, but also her keen-eyed observations of British life today. Clearly her long sojourn in the States hasn't blurred her view, nor made it more rosy about dear old Blighty." Lee particularly praised Ullman's portrayal of the shoplifting Dame Judi Dench and Dame Maggie Smith recording an audition tape for Star Wars as standout moments. The Independent's Sally Newall said Ullman was "on fine fighting form", noting that "the duds were few and far between". She expressed excitement about upcoming sketches targeting the royal family, mentioning photographs of Ullman dressed as Camilla Parker Bowles and Carole Middleton. However, not all reviews were glowing. The Telegraph's Michael Hogan described the show as "hit and miss", comparing it to a cross between Victoria Wood and Little Britain. While he found the darker, more surreal material successful, he felt the gentler sketches fell flat. Nevertheless, he concluded: "She might be 56 and rich enough to never need work again, but Ullman's lost none of her youthful bite. Welcome home." The Guardian's Sam Wollaston was less convinced, calling the show "unashamedly same-old" and criticising it as "not brave or funny enough, like a step backwards from Little Britain, 10 years after Little Britain." Comedy website Chortle's Steve Bennett questioned whether the show justified its existence beyond Ullman's star power, suggesting it didn't feel like a classic. Ullman last appeared on BBC television in the early 1980s with A Kick up the Eighties and Three of a Kind, before relocating to America where she created The Tracey Ullman Show for Fox, winning multiple Emmy and Golden Globe awards. That programme notably gave birth to The Simpsons, which began as short animated segments.

Price Comparison Websites Win Consumer Trust Despite Flaws, Regulator Finds Price comparison websites have earned high levels of trust and satisfaction from British consumers, despite some significant shortcomings in how they operate, according to new research by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). The regulator launched a comprehensive study of digital comparison tools (DCTs) last September to examine how these increasingly popular services could be improved for consumers. The interim findings, released today, suggest that no full-scale market investigation is currently needed. "Overall DCT users think these tools work well, making it easier to make informed choices and save money," the CMA said in its update. "Although DCTs are still a relatively new way of purchasing, the survey indicates that consumers are generally confident in the way they use them, and many use more than one site." The study, which will deliver its final report at the end of September this year, aims to better understand how people use price comparison websites, apps and switching services across multiple sectors of the economy. Beyond energy, the research encompasses insurance, banking, phone and broadband services, and airline flights. A central component of the research has been a survey of 4,000 consumers, complemented by a mystery shopping project and a comprehensive review of the comparison websites themselves. The findings reveal widespread adoption, with 85% of internet users having used a DCT at some point, and most reporting they use multiple sites to shop around. However, the research uncovered some concerning gaps in consumer understanding. Only 11% of respondents believed they had been shown all possible deals available in the market. This suggests many comparison sites fail to make clear they might not cover the entire market—a significant flaw in transparency. Despite this apparent limitation, customer satisfaction remains remarkably high, with 90% of users saying they were happy with the DCTs they had used. Many reported making better purchasing decisions as a result of using these services. The CMA has identified several potential problems with the price comparison industry that may lead to recommendations for improvement later this year, though specific details were not disclosed in the interim update. The regulator believes these digital tools could offer even greater benefits to consumers than they currently do, suggesting room for significant improvement in how they operate. The launch of the CMA's study last year was met with some surprise from consumer groups and small energy suppliers. Critics pointed out that just months earlier, in June 2016, a full-scale CMA inquiry into the UK's energy market had controversially decided that price comparison websites should no longer be required to show deals on which they did not earn a commission—a decision some viewed as "turning the clock back" on consumer protection.

University of Bristol Scientists Launch Big Tick Project to Combat Rising Lyme Disease Cases Scientists at the University of Bristol have launched an ambitious campaign to better understand infection levels in ticks and how diseases can be transmitted to humans through their pets. The Big Tick Project is specifically targeting dog owners to raise awareness about the dangers of tick-borne diseases, particularly Lyme disease. When infected ticks bite dogs, they can subsequently spread the bacterial infection to their human owners. Public Health England estimates there are approximately 3,000 new cases of Lyme disease in England and Wales annually, though some Lyme disease charities suggest the actual figure could be as high as 15,000 cases per year. While Lyme disease can often be managed effectively with early detection, it can cause chronic pain and severe fatigue if left untreated, making prevention and awareness crucial. Project leader Professor Richard Wall explained that tick numbers and related ailments have increased significantly over the past decade. "Data from all types of practices ranging from urban to rural locations will help advance the understanding of the level of diseases and pathogens ticks carry in the UK," he said. According to Professor Wall, tick distribution has expanded by 17% nationally over the last ten years, with tick numbers increasing in 73% of surveyed locations, highlighting the growing urgency of this public health concern.

China's Trade Data Shows Continued Weakness in Global Demand China's export performance showed marginal improvement in July, though the figures remained disappointing and point to continued weakness in global economic activity. Exports fell by 4.4% compared to a year earlier, which was a slight improvement over June's 4.8% drop but still worse than analysts had been expecting. Imports were also weaker than estimated, down by 12.5%. As China is a crucial driver of the worldwide economy, the data is seen as a snapshot of the global outlook. The country's exports have fallen for 12 out of the past 13 months. Global uncertainty ranging from low commodity prices to the EU debt crisis and the UK leaving the bloc continues to mute economic activity around the world. The figures do "not bode well for the state of global demand, given that Chinese exports benefited from a weaker currency," Louis Kuijs of Oxford Economics wrote in a note. "Looking forward, we expect the trade data to remain lacklustre in the coming months, given our outlook of subdued momentum in global trade and China's domestic demand." In US dollar denominated terms, exports fell to $184.7bn (£141bn) while imports dropped to $132.4bn. This leaves the country with a trade surplus of $52.31bn for the month of July. The sluggish domestic demand indicates that Beijing's efforts to boost consumption to spur growth have yet to take effect. The fresh data, though, comes on the heels of better-than-expected economic growth in the second quarter. Gross domestic product expanded by 6.7% in the three months to June compared to a year earlier.

Former Army Serviceman's Job Reinstated After Citizenship Application Refused A former soldier who lost his job after being refused UK citizenship has been allowed to return to work while his case is reviewed by the Home Office. Sam Cataki, 36, from Neyland, Pembrokeshire, was dismissed from his position at Milford Haven Port Authority on Wednesday following the rejection of his visa application. The Fijian national, who served in the British Army for 12 years, has now had his job reinstated following public outcry and political intervention. A petition supporting Mr Cataki has gathered nearly 30,000 signatures, highlighting widespread community backing for the father of two young children, aged one and five. Stephen Crabb, MP for Preseli Pembrokeshire, said he had received assurances from the UK government that Mr Cataki's application was being handled "with urgency." The MP has been assisting Mr Cataki since 2014 and recently raised his case with Immigration Minister Brandon Lewis. Mr Cataki, who left the Army in 2013, believes his citizenship application was rejected due to three penalty points on his driving licence. He had been working at Milford Haven for two years before his dismissal. Despite his job being reinstated, Mr Cataki remains anxious about the final decision. "I am really hopeful now the job has been re-instated, but the thing is we still do not know if they are going to reject it," he said. The situation has also put his wife Seini's visa status at risk. The couple has spent nearly £6,000 on visa applications for both of them. "If it wasn't for the media attention and the help of Stephen Crabb I would have just lost my job, that would be it," Mr Cataki added. Mr Crabb welcomed the development, saying: "This is positive news for Sam, his family and the people of Neyland who have shown strong support for Sam. Hopefully the whole matter will be resolved very shortly."

Barclays to Pay $13.75m Over Unsuitable Fund Switching Practices The US Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (Finra) has ordered Barclays Capital to pay more than $10 million in compensation to affected customers, along with a $3.75 million fine, following revelations of inadequate supervision of mutual fund switching practices. The settlement, which includes a censure but no admission of wrongdoing by Barclays, addresses failings that occurred between January 2010 and June 2015. During this period, the bank failed to properly supervise procedures that resulted in numerous customers swapping one mutual fund for another. According to Finra, more than 6,100 fund switches took place over the five-year period, with customers losing a total of $8.63 million. In many cases, the benefits of switching funds were undermined by transaction costs, and most customers were not adequately warned about these expenses before proceeding. The regulator found particularly troubling practices between March and August 2014, when Barclays processed 1,723 fund transactions—39% of those reviewed—that were inconsistent with customers' stated investment objectives, risk tolerance, or existing investment portfolios. This fine arrives two months after Barclays appointed James "Jes" Staley, a former JP Morgan senior executive, as chief executive. Mr. Staley has indicated a renewed focus on investment banking while simultaneously cutting costs and divesting non-core assets. The penalty adds to Barclays' recent regulatory troubles. In November, the bank was fined £72 million in the UK for failing to conduct proper due diligence on wealthy clients. The Financial Conduct Authority found that Barclays had arranged £1.88 billion worth of deals for high-net-worth clients in 2011 and 2012 without conducting appropriate checks on those who should have been considered politically high-risk individuals.

Alliance Party Leader Praises Colleagues at Belfast Conference Alliance Party leader David Ford addressed his party's annual conference in Belfast on Saturday, using the occasion to pay tribute to departing colleagues and outline his political future following his decision not to seek reappointment as justice minister. Mr Ford, who has held the justice portfolio since policing and justice powers were devolved to Stormont in 2010, confirmed he will step down from the ministerial role after May's Assembly elections, though he intends to seek re-election as an MLA. During his speech, the Alliance leader offered warm praise for his deputy, Naomi Long, describing her tenure as the party's "lone voice in the House of Commons." Despite losing her Westminster seat for East Belfast, Mr Ford emphasized that Ms Long had made a significant impact and expressed hope she would join him at Stormont. "After the flag protests, the insults, the threats, the violence, Naomi added 4,000 votes to what we were told was the high water mark of 2010," Mr Ford said. He attributed her defeat to what he characterized as "a cynical five-party pact" that barely secured 50% of votes in the traditionally unionist constituency. Mr Ford also recognized the contributions of Judith Cochrane, Anna Lo, and Kieran McCarthy, all of whom will not contest the May elections. Turning to broader political issues, the Alliance leader challenged other Stormont parties to accelerate efforts toward building a united community, criticizing what he termed their "delay, fudge and waffle." He distributed his criticism evenly, labeling Sinn Féin "economic illiterates" whilst accusing the DUP of subterfuge regarding abortion policy. Mr Ford concluded by positioning Alliance as "the only party working for everyone," committed to transforming society and building a united community across Northern Ireland's traditional divides.

Indian Teen Dies After Onlookers Film Instead of Help at Accident Scene A 17-year-old boy has died in India after bystanders recorded him on their mobile phones rather than providing assistance following a road accident, local media reported. Anwar Ali was fatally injured when his bicycle collided with a bus in Karnataka state's Koppal district. According to reports, people gathered around the scene to take pictures and videos of the bleeding teenager but failed to offer any help. The teen was eventually taken to hospital approximately half an hour after the collision. However, he succumbed to his injuries, having bled to death. Medical professionals stated that Ali could have survived if he had received prompt medical attention. The tragic incident has reignited debate about the widespread reluctance among Indians to assist road accident victims. India recorded 146,133 road deaths in 2015, making it one of the world's deadliest countries for traffic accidents. Safety campaigner Piyush Tewari explained that the problem stems from systemic issues rather than lack of compassion. "The foremost reason is intimidation by police," he told the BBC. "Oftentimes if you assist someone the police will assume you're helping that person out of guilt." Other deterrents include fears of being falsely implicated in the accident, becoming entangled in prolonged legal proceedings as a witness, or being pressured to pay hospital fees. While India's Supreme Court ruled last year that "good Samaritans" would be protected from harassment, and Karnataka has passed similar legislation, correspondents note that many citizens remain unaware of these protections and distrust police compliance. The case highlights ongoing challenges in encouraging public assistance at accident scenes across India.

Italy's Six Nations campaign has been dealt another blow with the news that centre Michele Campagnaro will miss Saturday's match against Wales in Cardiff through injury. The Exeter Chiefs player has been a consistent presence for the Azzurri this tournament, starting all of Italy's 2016 Six Nations matches and previously scoring two tries when the team visited Cardiff in 2014. Zebre centre Giulio Bisegni, 23, who has earned just two caps, has been called up as his replacement. The 23-year-old will be hoping to make an impression in what is a challenging situation for the Italian side. Italy's injury crisis deepened after their defeat to Ireland, with fly-half Edoardo Padovani, prop Lorenzo Cittadini and lock George Biagi all ruled out. This forces coach Jacques Brunel to make at least four changes to his lineup. There is some positive news with Racing92 prop Martin Castrogiovanni, 34, returning from suspension, while Perpignan fly-half Tommy Allen and uncapped duo Jacopo Sarto and Tommaso Castello join the 28-man squad.

G7 Summit: Merkel Pushes Climate Action and Security Talks **KRUEN, Germany** - German Chancellor Angela Merkel is pressing fellow G7 leaders to commit to ambitious climate goals during the two-day summit at the luxurious Schloss Elmau hotel in the Bavarian Alps. The German leader is seeking agreement from the group's members - the United States, United Kingdom, Japan, France, Canada and Italy - to limit global temperature increases to within 2 degrees Celsius of pre-industrial levels. Additionally, Merkel is urging G7 nations to contribute to a fund designed to help poor countries most severely impacted by climate change. The climate and energy discussions dominated Monday's first working session, as Merkel attempts to build momentum ahead of the crucial United Nations climate summit scheduled for Paris this December. Beyond environmental concerns, the summit has also addressed international security threats. Leaders were joined by Iraqi Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi, Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari, and Tunisian President Beji Caid Essebsi for discussions on combating radical extremism from groups including Islamic State and Boko Haram. British Prime Minister David Cameron announced Sunday that the UK would deploy an additional 125 military trainers to Iraq, calling IS "the biggest threat" facing G7 leaders. The militant group continues to occupy significant territories across Iraq and Syria despite ongoing US-led airstrikes. Meanwhile, Nigeria faces its own battle against Boko Haram, which has conducted attacks since 2009 in its campaign to establish an Islamic state in the region. The picturesque alpine setting provides a dramatic backdrop for discussions on these pressing global challenges, as world leaders work to forge consensus on both environmental sustainability and international security.

Hope Powell Joins FA as Coach Educator for Men's Professional Game Hope Powell, England's most decorated women's football figure, has taken on a groundbreaking role as coach educator within the men's professional game. The 49-year-old, who became the first woman to achieve the Uefa Pro Licence in 2003, brings extensive experience having scored 35 goals in 65 England caps and managed the women's national team from 1998 to 2013, including leading Great Britain at the 2012 Olympics. "I am keen to help develop the next generation of coaches in this country," Powell said. "It's a great opportunity to work within the men's professional game." She hopes to inspire future female coaches entering the field.

Lost Exmoor Writer's Manuscript Discovered After 45 Years The Exmoor Society has unveiled its newly organized archive after uncovering remarkable historical treasures during a two-year relocation project. The society's collection of books, maps, letters and photographs was previously stored in two disorganized and inaccessible old storerooms. However, during the move to new premises in Dulverton from the Parish Rooms, staff made an extraordinary discovery: a lost manuscript by renowned Exmoor writer Hope Bourne, missing for 45 years. Archivist Dr Helen Blackman revealed additional finds, including several slide collections documenting six decades of landscape changes across the moor and material related to Exmoor's establishment as a national park. "All of this helps us gain a more complete picture of Exmoor's landscape, people and heritage," Dr Blackman said. The archive, now based on Dulverton High Street, will be officially opened by Graeme Bonham-Carter. His father, Victor Bonham-Carter, served as society president for over 30 years and authored numerous books about Exmoor. Victor was also a distant relative of British actress Helena Bonham-Carter.

England Beat Ireland 2-1 to Reach EuroHockey Semi-Finals England staged a dramatic second-half comeback to defeat Ireland 2-1 in a crucial EuroHockey Championships pool match in Amsterdam, securing their place in the semi-finals. Ireland, needing only a draw to progress, took an early lead through Matthew Nelson, who deflected in a penalty corner in the 13th minute. The 10th-ranked side appeared set to cause an upset against their higher-ranked opponents. However, England turned the match around after the break. David Goodfield equalized just one minute into the third quarter, firing home from close range past Irish goalkeeper David Harte. The decisive moment came when Ireland's Shane O'Donoghue received a 10-minute sin bin for an elbow. England capitalized on their numerical advantage as centre-forward Sam Ward tapped in from close range to complete the comeback. The victory sees England finish as runners-up in Pool B behind Germany, who defeated Poland 7-3. England will now face hosts Netherlands in Friday's semi-final, while Germany meet Belgium. This result reverses the outcome of the teams' last EuroHockey meeting in London two years ago, when Ireland won 4-2 in the bronze medal play-off. England's women's team also advanced to the semi-finals, where they face the Netherlands on Thursday at 19:00 BST after finishing top of their pool.

Celebrated Zimbabwean Writer Chenjerai Hove Dies in Exile Renowned Zimbabwean author and poet Chenjerai Hove has died while living in exile, according to his wife Tekla Hove. The exact cause of death remains unclear, though he had been suffering from liver problems and had fallen ill three weeks prior to his passing. Mr Hove, widely regarded as one of the leading figures in post-colonial African literature, died with his wife and sister by his side - marking the first time they had been together since 2001, when he left Zimbabwe. The celebrated writer went into self-imposed exile in 2001 after facing harassment from authorities due to his outspoken criticism of President Robert Mugabe's government.
