Despite his deteriorating health in recent weeks, friend and colleague Helge Lunde, executive director of the International Cities of Refuge Network, said Mr Hove remained "bright and clear until the end." Mr Lunde described the late writer as "a great writer, novelist, poet and playwright," but emphasized that "first and foremost he was a freedom fighter, fighting for human rights in his country." Mr Hove's literary achievements were exceptional, with his work drawing deeply from Shona oral traditions. His novel "Bones" is particularly celebrated for its powerful allegories and imagery rooted in his native language and culture. He demonstrated remarkable command of both English and Shona throughout his career. Among his four novels was "Masimba Avanhu" (Is This the People's Power?), which examined the situation of women in Zimbabwe. This work, combined with his political criticism, brought him to the attention of authorities, according to the International Writers Project at Brown University. Throughout his exile, Mr Hove continued writing, producing numerous poems that frequently explored themes of separation. He also contributed plays and proverbs to the BBC and remained committed to his role as a social commentator. Speaking to BBC's Focus on Africa radio programme last year, Mr Hove articulated his sense of duty: "As a citizen, as an African, as a Zimbabwean..... to look at our lives and at whether our leaders are enhancing our dignity or taking it away." His literary excellence was recognized through numerous prestigious awards, including the Zimbabwe Writing Award in 1987, the Noma Award for Publishing in Africa in 1989, and a German-Afrika Award for freedom of expression in 2001. After Zimbabwe's independence in 1980, Mr Hove emerged as one of the country's most important literary voices, mentoring new talent alongside other celebrated writers such as Charles Mungoshi and Dambudzo Marechera. The family is currently hoping to fly Mr Hove's body back to Zimbabwe for burial, though funeral arrangements have not yet been finalized. His death in exile raises poignant questions about Zimbabwe's treatment of its greatest artistic talents.

Jamaica international Garath McCleary has signed a new contract with Reading until the summer of 2019. The 29-year-old winger's previous deal was due to expire at the end of the season. McCleary joined the Royals from Nottingham Forest on a free transfer in May 2012 and has made over 200 appearances for the club. "I'm very happy Garath has signed a new deal," Reading manager Jaap Stam said. "He's been a very important player for us this season." McCleary has scored eight goals in 23 Championship appearances this campaign.

Protesters Call for Closure of Aberthaw Power Station Environmental campaigners have staged a protest at Aberthaw Power Station in the Vale of Glamorgan, demanding its closure and the creation of more renewable energy jobs in the area. The demonstration comes after the European Court of Justice ruled in September that the coal-fired station had been emitting illegal levels of air pollution, highlighting growing concerns about its environmental impact. In response to the court's findings, plant operators RWE announced they would invest £5 million in new technology designed to "significantly lower" emissions of toxic nitrogen oxides from the facility. A company spokesman also confirmed the station would reduce its generation levels this year to ensure continued operation within its Environmental Permit whilst remaining competitive. However, environmental activists dismissed these measures as insufficient. Alyson Austin from the United Valleys Action Group criticized the investment, saying: "This is a sticking plaster for a severed arm, it's just not good enough." Ms Austin argued that the station's closure was inevitable and called for proactive planning: "We need to put something positive in place of Aberthaw. Renewable energy could provide thousands of jobs." She urged that workers at the station should be "re-skilled" now to facilitate the transition to cleaner energy. The protest brought together multiple environmental organizations, including Reclaim the Power, Bristol Rising Tide, and the Coal Action Network. RWE defended the station's continued operation, emphasizing its importance for energy security. A spokesman stated that the combination of reduced operating hours and lower emissions would allow Aberthaw to "provide security of electricity supply for Wales and beyond into the 2020s." The company highlighted that UK generation margins had reached record lows multiple times during the winter, prompting warnings from National Grid. They described Aberthaw as "an important bridge to the UK's vision of a renewable future" and crucial for balancing renewable technologies. The spokesman acknowledged the situation was "regrettably a challenging time" for the more than 200 employees as staff structures undergo updates.

Man Jailed for Brutal Rape and Sexual Assault in Guildford A man has been sentenced to 18 years for a horrific attack on an 18-year-old woman in Guildford, Surrey. Avan Mogridge, 32, of Church Street, Stamford, Lincolnshire, was convicted at Guildford Crown Court of dragging his victim into a wooded area off Parkway on the morning of October 22, 2016. He was found guilty of two counts of rape, two counts of sexual assault, and one count of making a threat to kill. He will remain on the sex offenders register for life. The young woman was on her way to work when she was attacked at approximately 06:15 GMT. Mogridge pulled her into woodland adjacent to the pavement, where he held her down, threatened her life, and subjected her to a prolonged sexual assault lasting around an hour. The attack was interrupted when two members of the public discovered the assault in progress. They immediately intervened and contacted police, leading to Mogridge's arrest at the scene. In a victim impact statement read to the court, the survivor described the devastating effect the attack had on her life: "I used to be a bubbly and confident girl and enthusiastic about life and living it. I had dreams for my future. I am now traumatised, scared, drained and frightened. One day in October, because of one person, my life turned upside down and my dreams disappeared." Detective Constable Tim Faltermeyer of Surrey Police praised the victim's courage throughout the judicial process and expressed gratitude to the couple who intervened. "This was a horrifying and traumatising hour-long attack on an innocent young woman," he said, adding that the case demonstrates how seriously Surrey Police treats sexual assault reports. Mogridge will serve 14 years in custody followed by four years on licence.

Stalker Michael Lane Jailed for Murder of Shana Grice After Police Failures A man who murdered his ex-girlfriend after police fined her for wasting their time when she reported his stalking has been jailed for life. Shana Grice, 19, was found with her throat cut in the smoke-filled bedroom of her Brighton flat in August 2016. Michael Lane, 27, had placed a tracker device on her car during a campaign of harassment, his trial heard. Sentencing Lane, Mr Justice Green said he would serve a minimum of 25 years. The judge also criticised police over their contact with Miss Grice. Lewes Crown Court was told Miss Grice had contacted police several times about Lane's unwanted attention. The jury heard that after making one complaint to Sussex Police about Lane, Miss Grice was issued with a fixed penalty notice for wasting police time because she did not disclose she had been in a relationship with him. Mr Justice Green, criticising Sussex Police, said: "You jumped to conclusions. In other words, she was treated as the wrongdoer and having committed a criminal offence, and Michael Lane was treated as the victim. "There was seemingly no appreciation on the part of those investigating that a young woman in a sexual relationship with a man could at one and the same time be vulnerable and at risk of serious harm," he said. "The police jumped to conclusions and Shana was stereotyped." He said that after penalising Miss Grice for time-wasting, police then treated all further complaints by her with "scepticism". The judge said another consequence was that Lane felt police would not act if he continued his "obsessive stalking". Miss Grice's mother, Sharon Grice, said Lane had been harassing, stalking and pressuring her daughter for more than a year. In a statement following Lane's sentencing, she and Miss Grice's father Richard Green said their daughter would have still been alive if Sussex Police had acted on her complaints. They said: "Shana had complained to the Sussex Police about his stalking her over five times but this was treated as being of low risk and she was given a fine for wasting police time." They described Lane as a "dangerous and obsessive man" who had shown "arrogance and cowardice" by pleading not guilty and blaming others for his actions. "He compounded this by relying on the wholly inadequate police assessment of risk to Shana to suggest he was no danger to her. "We firmly believe Shana would be alive today if Sussex Police had acted to protect Shana on the many occasions she complained about Lane, rather than issue her with a fine for wasting police time." The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) has begun an investigation.

Syrian Jets Strike Kurdish Positions in Hassakeh City, Sparking Tensions Syrian government warplanes have conducted air strikes against Kurdish security forces in the northeastern city of Hassakeh, marking a rare escalation between two parties that have largely avoided direct confrontation throughout Syria's five-year conflict. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights reported that Kurdish security forces had been targeted in the strikes. The Syrian military has not commented on the incident, but sources said the Kurds had seized government buildings in Hassakeh and the nearby city of Qamishli. Both sides were later reported to have agreed to a ceasefire, though tensions remain high. However, the Kurdish Democratic Union Party's Popular Protection Units (YPG) militia said it would "not be silent" over what it called an act of flagrant aggression, warning that "every hand spattered with the blood of our people will be held to account." Kurds made up between 7% and 10% of Syria's population of 24.5 million before the uprising against President Bashar al-Assad began five years ago. Although they were denied basic rights and suffered decades of political suppression by the Arab-led state, most Kurds avoided taking sides when protests swept the country in 2011. When government forces withdrew from Kurdish areas to concentrate on fighting rebels elsewhere in mid-2012, Kurdish militias swiftly took control, led by the YPG. The Kurds later established autonomous administrations but allowed the government to retain footholds in Hassakeh and Qamishli. Both sides have largely avoided clashes over the past four years, with the government focusing on fighting rebel groups and the Kurds battling so-called Islamic State. However, tensions have increased recently following the Kurds' unilateral declaration in March of a new federal region—a move rejected by both the government and opposition forces. The latest clashes reportedly erupted in Hassakeh on Tuesday and spread to several locations around the city by Wednesday. A YPG spokesman said the air strikes hit Kurdish districts and positions of the Asayish, Kurdish security personnel. "There are martyrs and wounded," Redur Xelil told Reuters. The YPG has emerged as a major fighting force in northern Syria over the past two years, becoming a key ally of the US-led coalition against Islamic State, complicating the delicate balance of power in the region.

Rail Electrification Costs Could Double Due to Network Rail Failures, MPs Warn Network Rail's severe planning and budgetary failures have caused significant delays to the Great Western Main Line electrification project and could see costs double, according to a damning report by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC). The estimated cost of the ambitious electrification scheme increased dramatically between 2014 and 2015, rising from £1.6bn to £2.8bn - and that figure does not even include the planned extension to Swansea. Network Rail has acknowledged the problems and said changes have now been implemented to control costs. The line from London to Oxford and Bristol Parkway was originally scheduled to be electrified in 2016, with the extension to Cardiff due in 2017 and Swansea in 2018. However, the project has faced repeated setbacks. In June, UK Ministers "paused" the Midland Main Line and TransPennine route electrification schemes due to spiralling costs, though they maintained that the Great Western Main Line scheme remained "a top priority". Despite this assurance, the Public Accounts Committee heard in October that there was now no firm completion date and costs could reach £2.8bn. The PAC report criticised the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), the industry regulator which calculated the original £1.6bn estimate, saying it had not been robust enough in scrutinising Network Rail's plans or ensuring the organisation addressed known risks. The MPs warned that the delays will put public money at risk, as the Department for Transport will have to pay up to £400,000 per day to rent new trains that cannot be used until the line is electrified. Committee chair Meg Hillier delivered a stinging verdict: "Network Rail has lost its grip on managing large infrastructure projects. The result is a twofold blow to taxpayers: delays in the delivery of promised improvements and a vastly bigger bill for delivering them." Plaid Cymru MP Jonathan Edwards expressed "real concern that spiralling costs for compensation to the train operator will compromise when the scheme will be finished". He called for an end to the "profit-for-dividend model, which sees the shareholders of a private company benefiting from the inevitable disruption to a public infrastructure scheme". An ORR spokesman acknowledged that escalating costs and delays were "unacceptable" and agreed a review of its role was "appropriate" following changes to Network Rail's ownership and finances. "We need to learn the lessons," he said. Network Rail admitted the industry had been "overly ambitious" about what could be achieved with available funding. A spokesman said: "Our understanding of how best to plan and deliver major new electrification schemes was not good enough." The organisation has now made "significant changes" to how it plans and delivers investment programmes, ensuring schemes progress only once reliable cost estimates can be established. Network Rail noted that electrifying the Great Western Main Line was "extremely complex" on an operational railway, with efforts to minimise disruption to line-side neighbours increasing costs.

O'Dowda Excited for International Duty Despite Oxford United's Crucial Run-In Oxford United's Callum O'Dowda will join the Republic of Ireland Under-21 squad for crucial qualifiers against Italy and Slovenia, following his impressive two-goal performance against Barnet on Saturday. The 20-year-old winger acknowledged the timing of his international call-up, stating: "It's the third time I've gone away after scoring. But I'll be fully buzzing when I come back for the run-in." The Oxford-born player was named runner-up for Republic Under-21 player of the year on Sunday, finishing behind Preston midfielder Alan Browne. O'Dowda credits international football with enhancing his development. "I spoke to the manager (Michael Appleton) when I last went and he said it's only going to benefit my game," he explained. "Being with a different manager and a different team broadens your experience. There's a lot more one-touch passing involved in international football and there's a real structure of play in terms of approaching the game." The midfielder will miss Oxford's crucial fixtures before returning for their final push.

KKK Group to Hold Rally at Historic Gettysburg Battlefield A white supremacist organization will hold a controversial event on October 5 at the historic Gettysburg battlefield in Pennsylvania, where one of the Civil War's bloodiest battles took place in July 1863. Park officials announced they are legally required to permit the gathering under US freedom of speech protections, despite the site's profound historical significance. The Battle of Gettysburg resulted in as many as 50,000 soldiers being killed or wounded during three days of fierce fighting. The battlefield holds particular importance in American history as the location where President Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address in November 1863. During the cemetery dedication ceremony, Lincoln delivered what would become one of the most famous speeches in American history, envisioning "a new birth of freedom" emerging from the conflict between northern free states and southern slave-holding states. The Ku Klux Klan, formed after the Civil War, has a notorious history of violence and is recognizable by its white-hooded ceremonial attire. Richard Preston, leader of the Confederate White Knights of the Ku Klux Klan, described his organization to local media as "white separatist," stating their goals include removing President Barack Obama from office and implementing stricter immigration policies. "This is about America for Americans," Preston said. "The only thing we want is our country back." The group previously conducted a membership rally at Maryland's Antietam battlefield earlier this month, another Civil War site known for being the war's deadliest single-day battle. In an official statement, the National Park Service explained their obligation: "As custodians of land owned by the American people, the National Park Service has a responsibility to make that land available for exercising [free speech] rights." Park officials confirmed they would work to protect park resources and ensure other visitors are not negatively impacted by the event.

Welsh GPs Await Government Decision on Recruitment Incentives General practitioners and health planners across Wales are anxiously awaiting the Welsh government's response to their appeals for support in addressing recruitment challenges in struggling areas. However, senior medical figures have expressed reservations about the effectiveness of financial incentives as a solution. Professor John Bligh, head of Cardiff University's school of medicine, warned that such incentives have produced "variable results" in practice. The recruitment crisis has become increasingly acute, with Hywel Dda University Health Board recently taking direct control of two GP practices after they failed to find replacements for retiring doctors. Catherine Davies, the health board's executive director for primary care, emphasised that career development opportunities were more important than financial inducements. "It's about offering career development. We want to attract the brightest, the best, the most driven," Ms Davies said. "While it is a helpful tool to have, it's by no means the golden bullet answer." Professor Bligh echoed these sentiments, stating: "I would much rather doctors chose to work in an area because that's where they wanted to work, as opposed to having a debt reduction scheme or some similar process." The statistics paint a concerning picture. Whilst GP numbers in Wales have increased by 10% over the past decade to 2,006, the ageing population and mounting workload pressures are taking their toll. Dr Paul Myers, representing the Royal College of General Practitioners in Wales, noted that many experienced GPs "can't wait to finish." The British Medical Association estimates Wales requires at least 200 trainee GPs annually to maintain adequate staffing levels. Yet the current quota of 136 training positions frequently goes unfilled. Dr Ruth Hussey, chief medical officer for Wales, acknowledged recruitment difficulties in certain areas. A comprehensive primary care workforce plan, addressing sustainability challenges and potential solutions, will be published later this month. The issue will be examined further on Eye on Wales, BBC Radio Wales, Sunday 5 July at 12:30 BST.

Manor F1 Team Bolsters Technical Leadership with Pat Fry Appointment Manor F1 team has appointed Pat Fry as their new engineering consultant in a significant move to strengthen their technical capabilities for the 2016 season. Fry, 51, was dismissed from his position as Ferrari's engineering director following a disappointing winless 2014 campaign. He joins former Ferrari chief designer Nikolas Tombazis, who faced a similar fate, at the ambitious backmarker team. The recruitment represents the latest development in Manor's comprehensive restructuring program as they attempt to climb up the Formula 1 grid. Fry brings extensive experience, having previously worked for Benetton and McLaren during his distinguished career. He reunites with former McLaren colleague Dave Ryan, who joined Manor as racing director in November. Ryan has been rebuilding his F1 career after leaving McLaren in 2009 following his involvement in the controversial "lie-gate" incident at the Australian Grand Prix. Manor has made significant technical partnerships for 2016, securing deals to use Mercedes power units and Williams' rear-end components. Ryan expressed his enthusiasm about the appointment: "We are extremely fortunate to have Pat on board to help us hit the ground running with our exciting new technical package." The team aims to demonstrate improved performance at the Barcelona tests before the season-opening Australian Grand Prix on 20 March.

Cyclist Forced Off M5 Motorway Given Conditional Discharge A cyclist who rode on the M5 motorway has been given a conditional discharge after appearing at Exeter Magistrates' Court. Balin Hobbs, 52, was cycling on the hard shoulder of the M5 when police intercepted him and forced him from the road into a service station near Cullompton, Devon. He pleaded guilty to riding a pedal cycle on a motorway and resisting arrest. The court imposed a 12-month conditional discharge and ordered Hobbs to pay a £20 victim surcharge. ## Three-Day Journey From London In a remarkable demonstration of his commitment, Hobbs cycled to Devon from London to attend the court hearing because it was against his spiritual beliefs to be driven in petrol or diesel vehicles. The journey took him three days, and he slept on the courtroom steps the night before his appearance. The incident occurred on the afternoon of April 29 when Hobbs was heading towards Bristol on his bicycle. Police caught up with him on the M5, but he overtook the police car before officers forced him from the road two miles later at Junction 28, where he entered a service station. The court heard that Hobbs wrestled with officers during his arrest as he was placed into a police van. "You are putting me in shackles for no reason," he protested. ## Defendant Represents Himself Hobbs, whose address was given as Hennock, Devon, but who is currently living in London, represented himself in court. He admitted being on the motorway, stating: "I was definitely on the M5 on my bike." However, he claimed police had "intimidated, harassed and harangued" him, explaining: "I did not intend to cycle on the M5 but I had to try and find my way to Bristol and then London." Hobbs, who had no previous convictions, mounted his bike following the hearing to begin his journey back to London.

Nepal Bomb Blast Kills Two Near Government Offices At least two people were killed and six others injured in a bomb explosion outside the Nepal Oil Corporation offices, officials confirmed on Wednesday. The blast occurred at 1:25pm local time (0740 GMT) in an area near government buildings and the district court. Nepal police spokesman Binod Singh told Agence France Presse that authorities have cordoned off the site and deployed a special investigative team to gather evidence. A little-known militant organisation calling itself the Unified National Liberation Front has claimed responsibility for the attack. A person identifying as the group's spokesman told BBC Nepali that the organization fights for indigenous communities' rights. The spokesman cited the government's failure to address corruption and rising fuel prices as motives behind the bombing. There has been no official comment from the Nepali government regarding the incident or the group's claims. Security forces continue to investigate the attack whilst maintaining a strong presence in the affected area.

German Man Arrested After Fatal Knife Attack at Bavarian Train Station A knife attack at a train station in Bavaria has left one person dead and several others injured, including one victim in a life-threatening condition, German authorities confirmed Tuesday. The incident occurred shortly before 05:00 local time (03:00 GMT) on Tuesday morning at Grafing station, located approximately 40 kilometers east of Munich. A 27-year-old German man attacked four people before being overpowered and arrested by police. While some witnesses reported hearing the suspect shout "Allahu akbar" ("God is great" in Arabic) during the attack, authorities have emphasized they have found no evidence of an Islamist motive. Oliver Platzer, spokesman for Bavaria state's interior ministry, told AFP news agency that "we have found the man had psychological and drug problems." The suspect, identified as a German national apparently from the Hessen area of central Germany, attacked one victim on a train and others at various locations around the station, including outside the building. Footage from the scene showed bloody footprints on both a train and the station platform. Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann described the incident as a "terrible attack" and stated there were no indications the man was from a migrant background. He added, "So far there are no findings that are relevant for state security," though police initially said a political motive had not been ruled out. Grafing's mayor, Angelika Obermayr, expressed shock at the violence. "The idea that people get on an S-Bahn train on a beautiful morning or do their paper round and then become victims of a maniac is terrible," she said. The investigation continues, with one platform at Grafing station cordoned off and commuter train services experiencing delays.

UK Government Announces Alan Turing Institute for Big Data Research The British government has unveiled plans to establish the Alan Turing Institute, a major research facility dedicated to advancing big data analytics and algorithm research. The institute, named after the legendary World War Two code-breaker, will receive £42 million in government funding over five years. Chancellor George Osborne announced the initiative during his Budget speech in the House of Commons, emphasizing Britain's ambition to become a global leader in data science. "I am determined that our country is going to out-compete, out-smart and out-do the rest of the world," he declared. The institute will focus on developing new methods for collecting, organizing, and analyzing large datasets—capabilities that have become increasingly crucial in the modern economy. According to the government, big data applications can help businesses improve manufacturing processes, refine marketing strategies, and deliver more efficient services to customers. Universities and other interested organizations will be invited to submit bids for the funding to establish and operate the facility. The competitive process aims to ensure the institute benefits from the strongest possible academic and research partnerships. The timing of the announcement is particularly poignant, coming just months after Alan Turing received a posthumous royal pardon in December 2013. Turing, who lived in Osborne's constituency, made groundbreaking contributions to the Allied victory in World War Two through his work at Bletchley Park, where he helped crack the German Enigma code. Tragically, Turing's life was cut short following his 1952 conviction for "gross indecency" after having a relationship with a 19-year-old man. He was chemically castrated as punishment and stripped of his security clearance, ending his vital code-breaking work. The conviction reflected the discriminatory laws of the era that criminalized homosexuality. In his Budget speech, Chancellor Osborne paid tribute to Turing's legacy: "Alan Turing did more than almost any other single person to win the war, and was persecuted for his sexuality by the country he helped save. I am delighted that he has finally received a posthumous royal pardon." While welcoming the initiative, the think tank Policy Exchange suggested that government itself should make greater use of big data technologies in public services.

Northern Ireland's Changing Landscape: How Peace Transformed the Physical Scars of the Troubles BBC News NI examines the dramatic physical transformations across Northern Ireland's landscape that mirror the region's journey from conflict to peace, through photographs of key landmarks from the Troubles era. During the height of the Troubles, the simple act of shopping in Belfast city centre required passing through military-style security checkpoints. Royal Avenue, one of Belfast's premier shopping streets, was accessible only through security gates where police routinely searched bags for explosives. Today, those imposing barriers have been completely removed, allowing shoppers to move freely through the bustling commercial district. The rural landscape of County Armagh once bristled with sangars – fortified observation posts that formed a crucial part of the British Army's defensive strategy. These structures were designed to control both the landscape and movement of people across Northern Ireland. One such installation, known as Watchtower Golf Five Zero or Borucki Sangar in Crossmaglen, was named after Private James R Borucki of 3 Para, who was killed by a remote-controlled bomb concealed in a bicycle. The security infrastructure began to disappear rapidly following the IRA's decommissioning of weapons in 2005. Within weeks, demolition work commenced on watchtowers and military bases throughout the region. By August 2007, the British army's emergency operation in Northern Ireland officially ended, marking a significant milestone in the peace process. Perhaps no structure symbolizes the Troubles more powerfully than the Maze prison. Constructed on a former airfield in the early 1970s, this sprawling complex housed paramilitary prisoners from both sides of the conflict. Demolition began in 2006, and nearly all the notorious H-blocks have since been razed. While controversial proposals to convert the site into a peace centre remain shelved, the location now serves as home to the Ulster Aviation Society and hosts the Balmoral Show, a cornerstone event in Northern Ireland's agricultural calendar. In Derry's Bogside area, the iconic slogan "You are now entering Free Derry," painted on a gable wall in 1969, remains standing – though it's now the sole remnant of an entire row of terraced houses. The so-called normalisation process has seen numerous Army barracks and police stations demolished, including the prominent Andersonstown facility in west Belfast, which was torn down in 2005. The border between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland once meant lengthy queues and rigorous identity checks at what was termed the "hard border." Those delays are now largely a memory. Street art has also evolved with the times. While hundreds of murals painted by Republicans and Loyalists during the Troubles still exist, new artwork celebrating contemporary life has emerged. One notable transformation saw a UFF mural replaced with a colourful patchwork quilt featuring words about women and their roles in families and communities. The most visible remaining legacy of division are the "peace walls" – permanent barriers erected in the 1970s to separate Catholic and Protestant neighbourhoods in Belfast. The Crumlin Road wall became the first to be removed, and Northern Ireland's power-sharing government has committed to dismantling all peace walls by 2023, representing perhaps the final physical chapter in the region's journey toward reconciliation.

Two Sam Mitchells: The Strangers Who Became Internet Famous What started as a curious Facebook friend request has blossomed into one of 2017's most heartwarming internet stories, capturing global attention and proving that sometimes the best connections happen by pure chance. It all began when Sam Mitchell, a 19-year-old plasterer from Tasmania, Australia, decided to reach out to a complete stranger on social media. The reason? They shared not just a first name, but a full name, including middle names. "You may be wondering why I have sent you a friend request. I had to because we share the same name. Middle name as well. Good day sir," the Australian Sam wrote to his British namesake. The 22-year-old London backpacker responded quickly with surprising news: "Yeah, and what is stranger is that I've just moved from the UK to Australia." What happened next became the stuff of internet legend. Four hours after that initial exchange, Australian Sam and his friends, fueled by enthusiasm and beer, pooled their money together to purchase a plane ticket for British Sam to fly from Victoria to Tasmania for New Year's Eve, departing the very next morning. "The idea of flying him down got tossed about," Australian Sam told the BBC. "The more beers we had, the better the idea became." After collecting their new friend from Launceston Airport, the group organized the "Sam Mitchell Olympics," featuring competitions including a sack race using laundry buckets, taste-testing challenges, and beer pong. The festivities culminated at a bar where the two Sams rang in 2017 with a kiss at midnight. "It was strictly platonic, but it was very nice for me knowing that he had chosen to kiss me at midnight, instead of his girlfriend who he has been with for four years," British Sam joked. The story quickly went viral, with media outlets and websites around the world celebrating the unlikely friendship. Pedestrian called it "The games. The drinks. The mateship. The pash," while Mashable described it as an "extremely cute bromance." Techly declared it "a story for the digital age." British Sam reflected on the phenomenon: "It seems to be a story that everyone is really enjoying amongst all the bad news over the past year." Before parting ways, the friends made a promise to stay connected. They've even discussed organizing an international "Sam Mitchell Olympics" by next New Year's Eve, bringing together Sam Mitchells from around the world. "We'll definitely have a drink and a few laughs at some point," British Sam said.

Berlin Attack Suspect's Movements Under Investigation as Dutch SIM Card Discovered Police are investigating the movements of Anis Amri, the Berlin attack suspect, after discovering an unused Dutch SIM card in his backpack, according to French and Italian media reports. Initially, authorities indicated there were "signs" Amri had visited the Netherlands following the Berlin attack, though these could not be definitively confirmed. The Tunisian national was shot dead by police in Milan early Friday morning. The SIM card was reportedly issued between 20-22 December in one of three Dutch cities: Breda, Zwolle, or Nijmegen. German police searched a refugee centre in Emmerich, near the Dutch border at Nijmegen, shortly after the attack. Investigators are examining whether Amri travelled to Amsterdam before proceeding to Lyon, France, and ultimately Italy. CCTV footage captured him at Lyon-Part-Dieu station before he boarded a train towards Milan. Police have reconstructed his journey from Lyon to Turin, then Milan, where he took a coach to Sesto San Giovanni, a north-eastern suburb. However, how he travelled from Berlin to Lyon remains unclear. The fact that Amri was able to travel across Europe despite being subject to a European arrest warrant has raised significant security concerns. Investigators are also working to determine whether the 24-year-old had accomplices. A video has emerged showing Amri pledging allegiance to the leader of Islamic State (IS).

Cancer Patient's Dance Video Goes Viral, Inspiring Millions A heartwarming video of a cancer patient dancing during chemotherapy has captured the hearts of more than two million viewers on Facebook and Instagram within just two days of being posted. Ana-Alecia Ayala, undergoing treatment at the Baylor T Boone Pickens Cancer Hospital in Dallas, Texas, was filmed performing the popular internet dance craze "TZ Anthem" alongside her "chemo buddy" Danielle Andrus. The upbeat video shows both women smiling and laughing while Ana-Alecia remains connected to her intravenous chemotherapy lines. "Who says cancer and chemo have to get you down? We'll have the last laugh!" Ana-Alecia proclaimed on her Instagram page, emphasizing her belief that "dancing and laughter" are the best medicine. The inspiring video has generated an overwhelming response from viewers worldwide. Thousands of positive comments have flooded her social media posts, with many using the word "beautiful" to describe both Ana-Alecia and her message. "Love your video and your positive attitude. Such an inspiration. Praying for you!" commented Valerie Faulkner Bentley on Facebook. Laura Swiatovy Roy-Gures added, "Keep on dancing beautiful girl. Praying for you. Thank you for inspiring others. Sharing with my Facebook friend that has breast cancer. She needs this." Ana-Alecia was diagnosed with a rare uterine tumour in December 2015. According to her gofundme page, she has since undergone two surgeries and begun chemotherapy treatment. Speaking to local news channel KVUE, Ana-Alecia explained her motivation for sharing the video. "I want to inspire others not to look at cancer as a death sentence," she said. "I also want to encourage cancer patients' loved ones to step out of their comfort zones and be silly, have a dance party, be present in the moment and have a great time." Her message of positivity continues to resonate with audiences worldwide, offering hope and inspiration to others facing similar battles.

Northern Ireland Records One of Lowest Road Death Tolls in 80 Years Northern Ireland has recorded one of its lowest road death tolls in eight decades, according to PSNI Superintendent David Moore, though officials stress that any loss of life on the roads remains unacceptable. Speaking about the 2013 figures, Superintendent Moore emphasized that while the numbers represent significant progress, "one death is one too many." The statistics show 58 people lost their lives on Northern Ireland's roads during the year. Environment Minister Mark H Durkan highlighted the critical importance of further reducing road deaths and serious injuries. "It only takes one bad choice to ruin a life. We all share the road, so we all share the responsibility to prevent these collisions," he said. Minister Durkan announced the government's ambitious new target of zero road deaths, urging all road users to "commit to sharing the road to zero." This aligns with the Road to Zero safety campaign, launched in April 2013, which focuses on portraying the human impact of road deaths by highlighting the devastating effect on bereaved families. Subject to executive approval, a Road Traffic Amendment Bill is planned for introduction in 2014. The legislation would introduce tougher measures against drink-driving and address the disproportionately high number of young people killed on the roads. The 2013 statistics reveal that 24 victims were drivers, 12 were passengers, 10 were motorcyclists, seven were pedestrians, and three were cyclists. Tragically, two children died on Northern Ireland's roads last year, down from five in 2012. Superintendent Moore delivered a straightforward message about road safety: "If everyone slowed down, did not drive after drinking or taking drugs, wore a seatbelt and drove with greater care and attention, then more people would live. It really is that simple." Since records began in 1931, 14,626 people have died on Northern Ireland's roads, with 75,070 suffering serious injuries since 1971. Road deaths peaked in 1972 with 372 fatalities, while 2012 saw the lowest number on record.

British Gymnasts Shine at European Championships with Multiple Medal Haul British gymnasts delivered a stellar performance at the European Championships in Romania, with Ellie Downie and Courtney Tulloch leading a remarkable medal rush for the team. Courtney Tulloch, 21, made history by securing Britain's first major international rings medal with an impressive silver finish. The young gymnast scored 15.066, holding off Turkey's Ibrahim Colak who finished fifth, while Olympic champion Eleftherios Petrounias of Greece claimed gold, finishing just 0.367 points ahead of Tulloch. Ukraine's Igor Radivilov rounded out the podium with bronze. Seventeen-year-old Ellie Downie continued her exceptional championship run, claiming her third medal in as many finals. The teenager tied for bronze on the uneven bars alongside Germany's Eli Seitz, with Belgium's Nina Derwael taking gold and Russia's Elena Eremina earning silver. "The bars bronze was just so unexpected," Downie told BBC Sport, dedicating her performance to her older sister Becky. "If Becky had gone through her routine I'm sure she would've knocked me into fourth." Earlier on Saturday, Downie had also secured silver in the vault final with an average score of 14.350 from her two vaults. Despite leading for most of the competition, she was overtaken by the final competitor, France's Coline Devillard, with Hungary's Boglarka Devai claiming bronze. "I was really happy with the vault - I was in first until the last girl and she fully deserved it," Downie said graciously. "Her vaults were definitely tidier than mine." However, the championships brought disappointment for Becky Downie, 25, who was defending her uneven bars title. The older Downie sister fell during her routine and required medical attention, casting doubt on her participation in Sunday's beam final. Claudia Fragapane stands ready to replace her should she withdraw. The medal success comes on the back of Friday's historic achievement, when Ellie Downie became the first British gymnast to win all-around gold at a major international championship. She will compete in both beam and floor finals on Sunday. The impressive results continue a strong showing from Britain's largely inexperienced men's team, which contains no Rio Olympics competitors, following James Hall's all-around bronze on Friday.

Mental Health Trust Deaths Rise Sparks Investigation Concerns Norfolk & Suffolk Foundation Trust (NSFT) has been criticised for not doing enough to understand why patient deaths have risen dramatically, following an independent investigation. The trust recorded 157 deaths in 2015-16, a significant increase from 88 deaths in 2012-13. The figures also showed 105 deaths in 2013-14. Verita, commissioned by NSFT to investigate the rise, found that whilst the trust's investigation process meets national requirements, there is insufficient analysis to establish the underlying causes of these deaths. The investigation revealed several areas requiring improvement. Internal reports into each death lacked consistency, support for bereaved families needed enhancement, and there was inadequate evidence that the trust's board had discussed each unexpected death thoroughly. However, the report cautioned that data collection was not standardised across the UK, meaning "limited means for making meaningful comparisons" about death rates between different trusts. Michael Scott, NSFT chief executive, emphasised patient safety as paramount, stating: "One avoidable death is one too many - that is why we commissioned this investigation." He confirmed that recommendations were "already, or will be, acted upon." A separate report by NHS England's Nursing and Quality Directorate offered some reassurance, concluding that since April 2015, NSFT had reported deaths appropriately under the NHS Serious Incident framework and "investigated in a timely and appropriate manner." The trust was originally commissioned the investigation after statistics showed it had a higher number of deaths than other mental health trusts in the UK. NSFT was placed in special measures by the Care Quality Commission in February 2015.

Teenager Stabbed to Death in Hoxton Estate Attack Police have launched a murder investigation after a teenage boy was stabbed to death in east London following what witnesses described as a chase through a housing estate. The Metropolitan Police were called to reports of an assault at approximately 23:15 BST on Friday evening in the St John's Estate on Pitfield Street, Hoxton. The victim, believed to be 17 years old, was pronounced dead at the scene by paramedics despite emergency treatment. A 40-year-old witness, who asked to remain anonymous, described seeing the fatal attack unfold from her flat window. "There was a big chase," she told reporters. "They ran through the estate, some on bikes, some on foot. By the end of it when he died there were about 15 people around him." Officers believe they have identified the victim and are currently working to inform his next of kin. Detective Chief Inspector Andy Partridge appealed for witnesses to come forward. "A young man has lost his life in a brutal manner and I am appealing to anyone who was in the area last night and witnessed this attack to come forward and speak to police," he said. A post-mortem examination will be scheduled in due course. Local residents have left candles and flowers near the estate in tribute to the victim. This tragedy marks the second fatal teenage stabbing in London within 48 hours. On Thursday, Shaquan Mario Fearon died from a stab wound following a fight at a block of flats in Brockley, south-east London.

Second Walker Dies on Ben Nevis Route in Same Week A 51-year-old man from the Aberdeen area has died after falling on the Carn Mor Dearg Arete, a challenging ridge route to Ben Nevis, Scotland's highest mountain. The walker was tackling the popular but demanding route, often chosen by experienced mountaineers as an alternative approach to the summit, when the fatal incident occurred on Friday morning. His two companions raised the alarm, and the Lochaber Mountain Rescue Team recovered his body. He was airlifted to Fort William hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Mountain rescue team leader John Stevenson reported that conditions were good at the time and the group had been properly equipped. Tragically, this marks the second fatality in the area within days. On Tuesday, the body of Ian Bell, 60, from Hertfordshire, was discovered on Carn Mor Dearg after being reported missing the previous day. The Lochaber team has recently reported dealing with an "exceptional amount" of call-outs in recent months, highlighting the increased pressure on mountain rescue services.

Football clubs pay tribute to Daniel Wilkinson Football clubs across Yorkshire and beyond are preparing to honour Daniel Wilkinson, the former Hull City youth player who tragically died following a medical emergency during a match. The 24-year-old collapsed while playing for non-league side Shaw Lane on Monday and later passed away in hospital. Shaw Lane officials are currently in discussions with Wilkinson's family and teammates to determine appropriate memorial arrangements. Brighouse Town, Shaw Lane's opponents at the time of the incident, have postponed their scheduled Saturday fixture against Colne FC as a mark of respect. Several clubs have already paid tribute. Harrogate AFC, where Wilkinson previously played on loan, held a minute's silence before their match against Stalybridge Celtic on Tuesday. Hull City, where Wilkinson was part of the successful 2010 Youth Alliance North East Conference championship-winning squad, has invited supporters at the KCOM Stadium to observe a minute's silence this weekend. The silence will be conducted under the direction of referee Roger East's whistle. The Evo-Stik Northern Premier League has requested all fixtures this week include a minute's silence in Wilkinson's memory. Following his time at Hull, Wilkinson's career included stints at North Ferriby United, Scarborough Athletic, Harrogate Town, Goole Town, and Rushall Olympic before joining Shaw Lane this summer.

England striker Harry Kane has withdrawn from the squad for Tuesday's friendly against Spain at Wembley to continue his recovery from an ankle injury with Tottenham. The 23-year-old has played just 73 minutes for Spurs since damaging his ankle against Sunderland on 18 September. He was an unused substitute for England's World Cup qualifying win over Scotland on Friday. "The sessions we're going to do aren't what Harry needs at this time," said interim England boss Gareth Southgate. "It was never really my intention to start him in a game and I think it's important that he gets a different training programme to what we're going to follow over the next couple of days." England have not called up a replacement for Kane, leaving Daniel Sturridge, Jamie Vardy, Marcus Rashford, Wayne Rooney and Theo Walcott as striker options. Spain's visit to Wembley is the fourth and final fixture Southgate was given responsibility for, but with England still top of their 2018 World Cup qualifying group, he is heavy favourite to get the job on a full-time basis. Kane, who scored his third league goal of the season on his return from injury in the north London derby against Arsenal, will be available for Spurs' fixture against West Ham on Saturday. Subscribe to the BBC Sport newsletter to get our pick of news, features and video sent to your inbox.

Jersey Could Print More Banknotes to Boost Government Returns The States of Jersey is considering increasing its banknote issuance limit from £100m to allow greater investment opportunities and boost government returns. Russell Crowe, head of the States' treasury and investment management unit, explained that Jersey currently sells locally issued banknotes to high street banks in exchange for UK pounds. The proposed increase would enable the government to invest more sterling, significantly improving returns "from almost nothing". Draft legislation is scheduled for presentation to the States in January, though Mr Crowe indicated this could be brought forward if Christmas shopping season demand increases substantially. Currency circulation is expected to rise from £83m to approximately £98m during the festive period. Robert Kirkby from the Jersey Chamber of Commerce expressed surprise at continued cash usage in today's digital age. He noted it would be "interesting to see the impact" of younger "digital natives" on consumer spending habits in the coming year, suggesting traditional cash usage may decline as technology-savvy generations mature.

Girl, 6, Bitten by Police Dog During Chase in Manchester A six-year-old girl suffered multiple bite wounds after being attacked by a police dog during a pursuit in Newton Heath, Manchester, on Tuesday evening. Phoebe Malone was playing outside with friends when she was bitten by the dog as officers chased a suspect who had fled from a stolen vehicle that crashed into a wall on Blackstone Walk. Her mother, Sarah Malone, described the traumatic incident that occurred at approximately 19:55 BST. "My son saw what happened from the window and shouted:'Mum, Phoebe's been bitten by a police dog,'" she said. Mrs Malone rushed outside to find her daughter surrounded by police officers. "She was just sat on the chair and there was loads of police around her and she was just shaking," she recalled. "They asked me if I could get her in the house because she's cold, we need to get her warm." The youngster sustained ten wounds, with two described as very deep. "They said if it was two inches more, it could have gone for her arteries, so it was serious," Mrs Malone explained. Phoebe was taken to hospital and kept overnight for observation. Mrs Malone expressed her shock at the incident, saying: "I just can't believe it's happened to a little girl, let alone my daughter." She criticised the police decision to release the dog in an area where children were playing and called for a review of dog handler training procedures. Greater Manchester Police confirmed the incident occurred during pursuit of a driver who abandoned a stolen Fiat Punto following the crash. A spokesman said: "A police dog was deployed to pursue the offender and during the chase a six-year-old girl was unfortunately bitten." While police described the injuries as "not believed to be serious," the incident has been automatically referred to the force's Professional Standards Branch for investigation. GMP has launched an internal review into the circumstances surrounding the attack.

Ronnie O'Sullivan Critical of Form Despite Recent Success Five-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan has downplayed his recent tournament victories, claiming he has been "overachieving" despite winning his sixth Masters in January and his fourth Welsh Open title in February. The snooker star made the surprising admission following his 4-3 defeat to world number 31 Michael Holt at Venue Cymru on Tuesday in the opening round of the World Grand Prix. "I know I won the Welsh Open and the Masters but, the Masters, I only won it because everyone played pretty abysmal against me," O'Sullivan told BBC Radio Wales. "Winning two tournaments was a bit too much return for how I've been playing." The 42-year-old was gracious in defeat, praising his opponent's performance. "Well done to Michael. He played a good match and deserved his win. He played better on the day," O'Sullivan said. However, he remained critical of his own form, stating: "I wasn't really on form. I was pleased with how I stuck in there and tried to turn it around but my game just wasn't strong enough." O'Sullivan suggested he has been "papering over the cracks" and acknowledged significant work is needed before the World Championship in Sheffield. "For me to do well at Sheffield, I'm going to need to find some consistency. I need to do some work between now and when Sheffield starts." Holt, who produced breaks of 119 and 88 to secure victory, was delighted with his performance. "It's great to beat him. He's the best player," Holt said. "It's up there with one of my best wins." Holt will face either Liang Wenbo or Graeme Dott in Thursday's second round.

Boy, 12, Dies from Asthma After Hospital Discharge Failures A 12-year-old boy died from an asthma attack just five days after being discharged from a London hospital where doctors failed to recognise the severity of his chronic condition, an inquest has concluded. Michael Uriely was taken to the Royal Free Hospital in London twice within 24 hours in August 2015, but medical staff failed to diagnose his condition as chronic asthma despite clear warning signs. Coroner Dr Shirley Radcliffe stated that had Michael been given a high dose of steroids during his hospital stay, "it's unlikely he would have died." The tragedy began on 18 August when Michael's parents brought him to hospital following a violent coughing and vomiting episode that left him struggling to breathe. He was released by 8pm that evening, but suffered another severe attack in the early hours and was rushed back to A&E. Although he was kept overnight during the second admission, doctors failed to connect the two visits or recognise the seriousness of his condition. Two internal investigations also failed to identify his chronic asthma. Michael was discharged the following day and died from an acute asthma attack on 25 August. Dr Radcliffe told Westminster Coroner's Court that "alarm bells should have begun to ring" when Michael was admitted twice within 24 hours. She said a "totally inadequate" medical history was obtained and staff missed a crucial opportunity to recognise the severity of his condition. "The history and signs were there to be seen and understood, but sadly it wasn't recognised and he was discharged essentially on the same treatment he had been on," the coroner said. Following the tragedy, the Royal Free Hospital appointed two specialist respiratory clinicians, opened a dedicated asthma clinic, and introduced a new strategy for treating children with asthma. Michael's parents, Ayelet and Roy Uriely, described their son as "an extraordinary boy, both in personality and intelligence" who had been diagnosed with asthma at age two and began learning chess aged three. He "doted on his younger twin sisters, who adored him." The inquest heard that since Michael's death, seven other children in London have died from asthma.

Olympic Silver Medallist Becky James Retires from Cycling to Pursue Baking Career **Media playback is not supported on this device** Welsh cycling star Becky James has announced her retirement from professional cycling at the age of 25, revealing plans to transform her cake-making hobby into a full-time baking business. The double world champion and Olympic silver medallist made the surprise announcement on Wednesday, 17 August, explaining that the decision crystallized just two weeks earlier. "I thought'this is what I want to do' and it just clicked," James said. "I came to the decision it was the right thing for me to do and I'm feeling very excited." James's cycling career reached its pinnacle in 2013 when she won world sprint and keirin titles, followed by silver medals in the same events at the 2016 Rio Olympics. Her Olympic success was particularly remarkable given she had endured a two-year battle with knee injuries and illness, during which she "gave up" her life for a year to concentrate on qualification. Speaking on BBC Radio Wales' Good Morning Wales programme, the Abergavenny athlete revealed she had spent a year-long break after Rio contemplating her future. "It's been up and down," she explained. "I was on such a high after the Olympics, and then you have a massive dip and it's really hard to get out of that rut." **Media playback is not supported on this device** James acknowledged experiencing the "post-Olympic blues" that many elite athletes face after major competitions. "People say you have the post-Olympic blues and I definitely had that, but then I came out of that dip and I was half training and trying to figure out what to do," she said. The announcement comes less than a month after James indicated she was looking forward to returning to competitive action. However, she insists the timing feels right and she harbours no regrets about her career. "I kind of gave up my life the year before Rio because I wanted to give it everything," James reflected. "So I gave up my life, I shipped off my dog Lola to George (boyfriend, rugby player George North) and committed everything just to get to Rio." Looking back on her achievements, James expressed contentment with her legacy. "I'm so happy with everything I've achieved in my career. I didn't feel like I was desperate to carry on to the next Olympics, I'm so chuffed with what I've done." The decision to retire stemmed from James's realization that her heart was no longer fully committed to cycling. "If it wasn't what I wanted to do I knew in my heart I wouldn't achieve what I'd want to," she explained. "I couldn't do anything half-hearted - if I didn't really want to do it I knew I wouldn't achieve my goals and be the best I could be." **Find out how to get into cycling with our special guide.**

Arsenal Chief Gazidis Defends Transfer Strategy Despite Fan Criticism Arsenal chief executive Ivan Gazidis has defended the club's cautious approach to the transfer market, insisting they cannot compete financially with wealthier rivals. The club have made one major signing this summer, buying Granit Xhaka from Borussia Monchengladbach for £35m. "We can't afford to outgun competitors that have far more money. We have to be very careful, very selective," Gazidis told the New York Times. The 51-year-old reiterated his support for manager Arsene Wenger, denying it is based on a "sense of nostalgia". Wenger has overseen 20 consecutive top-four finishes in the Premier League, but the last of his three league titles came in 2004. Some supporters protested at the end of last season, calling for a change in manager. The Frenchman insisted that the club would "add what we missed" during the transfer window to close the 10-point gap to champions Leicester, but his pursuit of France forward Alexandre Lacazette has been frustrated with Lyon turning down a £29.3m offer. Arsenal were the only club in Europe's top five leagues not to buy an outfield player in last season's summer transfer window. Goalkeeper Petr Cech, signed for £10m, was the only arrival, despite the club having almost £200m in cash reserves. But Gazidis - who spoke of "an escalation in our financial firepower" in 2013 - claims that the Premier League's large and relatively evenly-shared television deal means money is less decisive than it was. "The constraints within the Premier League are less and less about pure finances. More relatively important become things like how well you identify players, how well you develop players, what kind of sports science you have, your analytics, your psychology," he added. "All of these support areas around what we do increasingly become bigger differentiators."

Brexit Uncertainty Persists Despite Rising Business Optimism A survey by accountancy firm Deloitte has revealed a notable uptick in business confidence among finance directors, though Brexit concerns continue to dominate corporate thinking. The fourth-quarter survey of 119 finance directors found that 27% were more optimistic about business prospects, up from just 16% in the third quarter. The improvement has been attributed to better-than-expected GDP growth figures. However, the research showed that two-thirds of respondents remain anxious about Brexit's potential impact on their operations. Before the referendum, chief financial officers identified Brexit as their most significant business risk. Confidence plummeted to levels not seen since the global financial crisis immediately after the vote, prompting companies to curtail investment and spending. "Since then the UK has proved more resilient than expected and talk of the UK falling into recession has abated," the Deloitte report noted. Despite this resilience, most finance bosses anticipate continued economic uncertainty. Nearly half plan to adopt defensive measures, including spending cuts and building cash reserves. Approximately 48% expect slowdowns in hiring and merger and acquisition activity over the coming year.

Osteopath Struck Off After Illegally Parking in Disabled Space During Court Hearing An osteopath who brazenly parked in a disabled bay while admitting to blue badge fraud has been struck off the professional register. Nigel Graham, 56, from Southbourne, was appearing at Southampton magistrates' court in June 2015 to plead guilty to parking offences when BBC cameras captured him committing another violation outside the very same courthouse. His illegally-parked vehicle received a parking ticket, which remained attached to the windscreen as the car was driven away. Inside the courtroom, Graham admitted to five counts of false representation to avoid parking fines across Southampton, Bournemouth and Christchurch, plus one count of illegally using a disabled person's blue badge. The badge belonged to his deceased mother and had been fraudulently applied for after her death. The magistrate described his actions as "despicable dishonest offences committed over a long period of time with no regard to bona fide blue badge holders." Graham received a suspended jail sentence and 120 hours of community service. In May, the General Osteopathic Council ruled that Graham's conduct was fundamentally incompatible with professional practice. The council noted that he "continued to obfuscate" during their hearing and demonstrated "no insight into the seriousness of his criminality." The "degree and persistence" of his dishonesty led to his removal from the osteopathic register, effectively ending his career in the profession.

Man Convicted of Murdering Derby Student After "Fit" Comment A man has been found guilty of murdering a 22-year-old student who was stabbed in the heart following a trivial comment about a woman's appearance in Derby city centre. Haris Mohammed was convicted at Nottingham Crown Court of killing Tom Webb on 19 January after one of Mr Webb's friends remarked that a young woman was "fit". The jury rejected Mohammed's claims that he acted in self-defence after Mr Webb allegedly swung a bottle at him. The trial heard that Mr Webb had been with two friends buying food and drink from Tesco in St Peter's Street when one of them made the comment about a passing woman being attractive. One of Mohammed's friends overheard the remark and informed him about it. Mohammed, who had been in a nearby McDonald's, then decided to pursue Mr Webb's group as part of what prosecutor Michael Auty QC described as "an angry mob". "Haris Mohammed had no need to become involved at all," Mr Auty told the court. "Neither he nor anyone else was in any danger. And yet he led others off in pursuit of Thomas Webb. He wanted confrontation. He wanted to demonstrate his power." The prosecutor emphasised that Mr Webb was "entirely innocent" and Mohammed had no reason to attack him. "Haris Mohammed could have walked away at any time. He could have stayed in McDonald's," he said. Mohammed used a butterfly knife with a blade approximately seven centimetres long to stab Mr Webb. The weapon was later recovered from within a McDonald's cup found in a raised planter where Mohammed had been in the immediate aftermath of the killing. Outside court, Mr Webb's mother Rachel paid an emotional tribute to her son. "Tom was everything to me," she said. "I have no mother, I have no father, I have no other children, no husband or partner. Tom was my entire family and I'll miss him, but I have his memory." When asked about Mohammed, she said simply: "I feel for his family." Detective Chief Inspector Dave Cox, who led the investigation, said: "Not only is a family grieving for the loss of a young man, another family will now be grieving for a teenager who will undoubtedly spend a long time behind bars." Mohammed will be sentenced on 29 July.

Wycombe Wanderers have completed the signing of former Bristol City defender Liam Fontaine on a permanent deal. The 31-year-old spent a decade at Ashton Gate, amassing 247 league appearances before moving to Aberdeen in 2014. After joining Wycombe last summer, he was loaned to Eastleigh in November. The League Two club have also secured Huddersfield Town defender Will Boyle, 21, on a free transfer, with the youngster signing an 18-month contract at Adams Park.

Tourist Convoy Ambushed in Afghanistan, Multiple Westerners Injured A group of twelve Western tourists travelling through Afghanistan came under attack when their convoy was ambushed by Taliban militants, Afghan officials confirmed to the BBC on Thursday. The tourists, comprising eight British nationals, three American citizens, and one German, were being escorted by Afghan army personnel en route to Herat city when attackers struck using small arms fire and an improvised explosive device in the Chesht-e-Sharif district. Jailani Farhad, spokesman for Herat's governor, confirmed the attack details, though it remains unclear exactly who sustained injuries. Several tourists reportedly suffered light wounds and are receiving treatment. The German foreign ministry has stated that its citizen was unharmed in the assault. A Taliban spokesman claimed responsibility for the ambush, highlighting the persistent dangers on Afghanistan's main roadways where militant attacks and kidnappings by the insurgent group remain frequent. Afghan interior ministry spokesman Sediq Sediqqi told Tolo news that the group had been travelling from Bamiyan to Herat via Ghor province. The tourists are currently being held at an Italian military hospital in Herat city, with plans for evacuation to Kabul. Security reinforcements have been deployed to the attack site. Despite the ongoing insurgency and warnings from Western governments against non-essential travel, Afghanistan continues to attract small numbers of adventure tourists annually. Bamiyan province, known for its ancient cultural sites and natural landscapes, remains particularly popular with foreign visitors organized through specialized adventure tourism companies.

Gilbert Stages Dramatic Comeback to Defeat Carter at UK Championship World number 21 David Gilbert produced a remarkable recovery to defeat two-time World Championship runner-up Ali Carter 6-5 in a thrilling encounter at the UK Championship. The Derby player found himself trailing 3-0 in what looked set to be an early exit from the tournament. However, Gilbert turned the match around with an impressive display of scoring, including a half-century and two century breaks, followed by another 50 to establish a 5-3 advantage. "It was looking like it would be an early bath," admitted the 35-year-old Gilbert. "But I got a bit lucky going in at 3-1 down and then I actually started playing really well. I started off and was useless. Maybe I was too chilled." The decisive frame proved to be a tense affair, with Carter missing several opportunities early on. Gilbert capitalised on his opponent's errors, clearing to the black in what he described as "probably the best clearance I have ever made." Gilbert, who has already secured £15,000 for his best UK Championship run, will face either Ding Junhui or Jamie Jones in the last 16. "I was a bit lucky, but I will take it. It's a big win for me," Gilbert said. "Happy days."

Millions of Energy Customers Could Save Hundreds by Switching Tariffs More than 1.7 million Npower customers could save as much as £261 annually simply by switching to a different tariff with the same supplier, according to new figures released by energy regulator Ofgem. The data reveals the extent to which British households are overpaying for their energy. As many as 6.6 million British Gas customers could save £129 a year by moving to cheaper deals, though British Gas disputes this figure, claiming that recent price changes mean the actual saving is now £43. The figures also expose a troubling trend: the vast majority of customers with some suppliers remain on expensive standard variable tariffs. SSE has the highest proportion, with 91% of its customers on standard variable tariffs, compared to just 9% at First Utility. Across the UK as a whole, 66% of households remain on standard tariffs, which are typically more expensive than fixed-rate deals. This has sparked controversy within the industry and drawn criticism from consumer advocates. However, Npower has challenged the £261 savings claim, arguing that fixed-price deals are usually limited to a certain number of customers. Once the quota is reached, the deal is withdrawn, meaning many customers may not actually be able to access the advertised savings. The revelations come after business and energy secretary Greg Clark met with energy suppliers last month amid claims that companies were profiteering from customers on standard variable tariffs. While the industry has denied these accusations, three of the biggest suppliers have frozen their tariffs through winter in response to public pressure. "Millions of people across Britain continue to pay too much for their energy," said Mr Clark. "The measures announced today are a positive step to help more people benefit from increased choice and competition." Citizens Advice welcomed the comparison table but called for energy companies to do more proactively. "We'd like to see energy companies do more off their own back to help customers who are on a low income, like moving them to a cheaper deal," said Gillian Guy, chief executive of Citizens Advice. Meanwhile, the Competition and Markets Authority has confirmed plans to assist the 10 million households that have remained on standard tariffs for more than three years. From next year, suppliers must inform Ofgem which customers haven't switched tariffs. With customer consent, they will receive details of better deals to encourage switching.

FTSE 100 Slips as Rolls-Royce Tumbles on Heavy Losses London's benchmark FTSE 100 index closed marginally lower on Thursday, dropping 10.36 points, or 0.14%, to finish at 7,286.56. Travel firm Tui led the gainers, surging 5.27% after reporting narrowed first-quarter losses. The company's performance was driven by robust UK bookings, which jumped 10% in volume compared to the previous year. RBS and Capita also posted solid gains. However, Rolls-Royce suffered the steepest decline, plummeting 3.99% after announcing a massive pre-tax loss of £4.6bn. The aerospace giant was weighed down by costs from a bribery settlement and currency-related contracts impacted by sterling's depreciation following the Brexit referendum. In currency markets, the pound weakened 0.49% against the dollar to $1.2464 and fell 0.25% versus the euro to 1.1790 euros.

Court of Appeal Dismisses Challenge to £85 Car Park Overstay Charge A motorist who challenged an £85 parking fine for overstaying a two-hour limit has lost his case at the Court of Appeal, in a decision that could have significant implications for private parking enforcement across the UK. Barry Beavis, 48, from Chelmsford, received the charge letter from car park operator ParkingEye after exceeding the time limit at a facility in Chelmsford in April 2013. He refused to pay, arguing the charge was excessive and unfair. The case progressed through the courts after Mr Beavis received a court summons and saw the charge increase to £150. Last May, Cambridge County Court ruled the £85 charge was lawful and did not breach the Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations. Mr Beavis subsequently appealed the county court decision, but three Court of Appeal judges unanimously dismissed his challenge. They concluded the amount charged "is not extravagant or unconscionable". ParkingEye defended the charges as "a commercially-justified deterrent" necessary to discourage motorists from over-staying at the site, which is located close to the railway station and law courts. Following the judgment, Mr Beavis expressed his frustration, stating: "I am absolutely furious that they have not upheld the law as it stands but have created new law." He is now considering taking his case to the Supreme Court, the highest court in the land. Prof Stephen Glaister, director of the RAC Foundation, called the outcome "deeply frustrating" for the motorist. However, the British Parking Association welcomed the court's decision, saying it "provided clarity on the use of contract law for parking on private land". The association stated it would not expect members to increase charges following the judgment, noting that "only a small minority of motorists fall foul of such conditions". The ruling confirms that current private parking charges are considered lawful and reasonable under existing regulations.

Fox Hunting Debate Reignites in House of Lords A heated debate over fox hunting has erupted in the House of Lords, with prominent figures clashing over animal welfare and the future of the controversial ban. Lord Mancroft, chairman of the Council of Hunting Associations, sparked controversy by claiming that hunting organizations are "the only two organisations clearly which have any interest in the welfare of the animals concerned." He made the remark during a Lords debate on the fox hunting ban, which the government has now shelved for at least two years. The Hunting Act, introduced by Tony Blair's Labour government in 2004, prohibits the use of dogs to hunt foxes and wild mammals in England and Wales. The law has remained a contentious issue, dividing politicians and the public alike. Labour's Baroness Jones strongly opposed any attempts to overturn the ban, calling fox hunting "cruel, inhumane and ineffective." She noted that Prime Minister Theresa May's support for hunting during the election campaign had proved "massively unpopular on the doorstep." Lord Mancroft defended his position by arguing that Baroness Jones showed "absolutely no interest in the welfare of the quarry species who were supposedly the object of this Act." He claimed that populations of both foxes and hares have declined since the hunting ban was implemented. Before the general election, a leaked email from Lord Mancroft suggested that Mrs. May's poll lead represented "the chance we have been waiting for" to overturn the ban. However, following the Conservatives' loss of their Commons majority, the government confirmed it would not bring forward a vote during this Parliamentary session. Government spokeswoman Baroness Vere acknowledged the passionate views on both sides. She shared her experience of attending her first hunt earlier this year, expressing amazement at the diversity of participants "from all walks of life." Labour peer Baroness Mallalieu, president of the Countryside Alliance, criticized current legal fox control methods, including snaring and night shooting. She urged the government to develop "a method which is stable, which is acceptable on both sides of the argument and which puts animal welfare at the forefront." Baroness Vere responded that no control methods were "without difficulty," adding that the entire framework of wildlife legislation would be reviewed once Britain leaves the EU and regains control of such laws.

Rangers striker Martyn Waghorn targets Scottish Cup semi-final return Rangers striker Martyn Waghorn is targeting a return to action in next month's Scottish Cup semi-final against Celtic after making progress in his recovery from a knee injury. The 26-year-old has been sidelined since mid-February but remains hopeful of featuring in the crucial Old Firm clash at Hampden Park. "I'll push myself but I have to be cautious too," Waghorn told Rangers' website. "If everything goes well then there is a chance I could be involved against Celtic but that is just if everything goes spot-on." The former Wigan Athletic forward has been in prolific form this season, netting 28 goals for the Scottish Championship leaders, including four in the cup competition. His last appearance came in the fifth-round replay victory over Kilmarnock, where he scored a penalty before sustaining the injury. "The last six or so weeks have been tough, playing Dundee in the cup game and then knowing we have Celtic coming up - hopefully I can get fit and in contention for that," he added. Waghorn emphasized the importance of being fully fit before returning to action. "I have to be 100 per cent ready - I want to push myself but I don't want to push myself too far in case we get further on in the competition or rule myself out of the latter stages of the season. "I'm a little bit ahead of schedule. It is going well but I don't want to say it is going great until I can go outside because I haven't tested it as much, we'll know more in the next week to 10 days about whether I am ready to come back."
