Lincoln City Edge Closer to National League Title Despite Red Card Drama Lincoln City moved three points clear at the top of the National League with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over relegation-threatened Chester FC in a dramatic encounter marred by two red cards and touchline confrontations. Harry Anderson emerged as the unlikely hero, scoring just six minutes after replacing the injured Lee Angol. The substitute pounced on a hard, low cross from the left that broke fortuitously, slotting home from close range to secure three precious points for Danny Cowley's side. The victory gives Lincoln breathing space over second-placed Tranmere Rovers, who suffered a home defeat to Forest Green, but it came at a cost. The Imps were forced to play the final 15 minutes with ten men after substitute Alan Power was shown a straight red card for a late challenge on Chester captain Luke George, remarkably just three minutes after entering the fray. The drama intensified during seven minutes of added time when Chester's Kane Richards received his marching orders for a late tackle on Bradley Wood. The incident sparked an angry confrontation between both benches, highlighting the tension of a match with huge implications at both ends of the table. Chester, desperately needing points to secure their National League status, proved stubborn opponents and could count themselves unfortunate not to take something from the match. Before Anderson's decisive strike, the visitors created several promising opportunities. Wade Joyce and James Alabi both unleashed powerful drives that sailed narrowly over the crossbar, while Richards found himself clean through on goal only to be thwarted by a superb recovery tackle from Sean Raggett. Lincoln's attacking threat in the first half came primarily through Nathan Arnold and Elliott Whitehouse, though both fired over from promising positions. Paul Farman was relatively untroubled until the break, but the second half proved far more challenging for the Lincoln goalkeeper. After the interval, Chester pressed hard for an equalizer. Alabi's low left-footed effort was cleared off the line, and the visitors felt aggrieved when appeals for a penalty were waved away after Richards went down under Alex Woodyard's challenge. Farman produced the save of the match to deny Elliott Durrell's spectacular long-range drive, clawing the ball away brilliantly. The match saw numerous bookings, with Luke Waterfall, Alex Woodyard, and Paul Farman cautioned for Lincoln, while Ryan Lloyd, Elliott Durrell, and Lucas Dawson went into the referee's notebook for Chester. Despite the challenging circumstances, Lincoln's resilience ensures they maintain pole position in the race for automatic promotion with the finish line now firmly in sight.

HMRC Seeks NHS Records Access to Identify Scottish Taxpayers HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is seeking access to NHS records as it struggles to identify taxpayers eligible for Scotland's new income tax regime, prompting Labour to demand both governments take control of the situation. The tax collection agency has admitted that preparations for implementing the Scottish Rate of Income Tax (SRIT) have "proved more complex than was initially anticipated," leading to an increased risk rating for the project. However, HMRC maintains the initiative remains "on track for successful delivery." From April 2016, the Scottish Parliament will gain the power to set income tax rates for the first time in its history. The new system will only apply to those who spend most of the tax year resident in Scotland, requiring HMRC to accurately identify Scottish taxpayers from among the wider UK population. In a letter to the Commons public accounts committee dated 16 January, HMRC's tax assurance commissioner Edward Troup acknowledged the challenges facing the project. The agency has raised concerns that some individuals may attempt to dodge tax by falsifying their main residence when rates differ between Scotland and the rest of the UK. To combat this potential abuse and improve accuracy, HMRC wants to cross-reference its data with NHS records. The Scottish government is currently consulting on whether to grant this access, with the consultation period running until 25 February. No decision has yet been taken on the matter. Shadow Scottish Secretary Margaret Curran criticised both governments' handling of the situation, stating: "This letter confirms what Scottish Labour has been saying all along - that HMRC and the Scottish government are struggling to identify all Scottish taxpayers. Both our governments need to get a serious grip of this." The Scottish government has distanced itself from responsibility, stating that administering the tax is a matter for the UK government and HMRC. Despite the challenges, there has been some positive news regarding costs. HMRC has revised downwards its estimated expenditure for setting up the new tax from £40-45 million to £35-40 million. As an alternative data source, HMRC has also suggested using the electoral register to identify Scottish residents. The agency noted that voter registration is particularly high following last year's independence referendum. However, this proposal may prove controversial, as the Scottish government previously strongly objected when local authorities suggested using electoral data to pursue poll tax arrears. Mr Troup emphasised the agency's thorough approach, stating: "We need to be sure that we have thoroughly explored all the available options for improving the accuracy of information we hold." A Scottish government spokesman confirmed: "A consultation is ongoing as to whether HMRC should be allowed administrative data to assist their identification of where people should pay tax."

Trouble at Prison Near Doncaster Quelled Overnight A disturbance involving a "small number" of inmates on one wing at a Category C prison near Doncaster has been brought under control overnight, the Prison Service confirmed. One prisoner sustained injuries during the incident but did not require hospital treatment. No staff members were harmed. The facility, which houses approximately 1,000 inmates, was found to have "high" levels of violence during HM Inspectorate of Prisons' latest inspection in February. Notable inmates reportedly include former England footballer Adam Johnson, who is serving a six-year sentence for grooming and engaging in sexual activity with a 15-year-old girl.

Hanson Academy Sends Hundreds of Students Home Over Uniform Policy Hanson Academy has sent home more than 240 pupils over three days as head teacher Elizabeth Churton's strict uniform policy crackdown continues. The Bradford school turned away 152 students on Tuesday, followed by 63 on Wednesday and 33 on Thursday during the ongoing enforcement campaign. The controversial policy has sparked a divided response from parents on the school's Facebook page. Students are being sent home for various uniform infractions, including wearing hoop earrings, having two or more earrings per ear, or sporting patterned trousers. The rules also prohibit unnatural hair colours and ban students from wearing jumpers, jackets or coats indoors. Strict regulations also apply to footwear. Single parent Diane Hickey said her 13-year-old daughter was sent home twice – on both Tuesday and Wednesday – for wearing black pumps, shoes the girl has worn to school for the past two years. "I'm not buying her a new pair of shoes. I'm a single parent. I can't afford a new pair of shoes," Miss Hickey said. "I don't think it's fair she's been sent home twice. She's embarrassed we can't afford new footwear." Miss Hickey added: "I think it's ridiculous. I am keeping her home today because what's the point in making her walk to school if she's going to be sent home?" In a statement, Mrs Churton defended the policy, explaining that students with uniform issues that could be resolved were sent home to rectify them, with parents contacted. "As forewarned, some students were sent home for this reason," she said. "They were sent home to change and the majority rectified this immediately and returned to school ready to learn." The principal emphasized that rules are an important part of preparing students for "adult life."

Harper Lee Secures Future of To Kill a Mockingbird Play in Monroeville The beloved stage adaptation of To Kill a Mockingbird will continue to be performed in its spiritual home of Monroeville, Alabama, after author Harper Lee intervened to save the production. The announcement comes after Dramatic Publishing, the licensing firm that previously controlled the performance rights, chose not to extend its agreement for the production. Lee responded by establishing the Mockingbird Company, which will take over producing the play starting in 2016, with proceeds benefiting local communities. Dramatic Publishing expressed its support on Facebook, stating it was "thrilled" with the arrangement. "We are also happy to announce that the play will be performed by Mockingbird Players, who have acted this American classic so well for so long," the company wrote. "We believe that this is the best way (from the stage) to celebrate Ms Lee's masterpiece throughout the greater Monroeville area." The decision has been warmly welcomed by the community. A Facebook campaign called Save Monroeville's To Kill a Mockingbird play had been actively lobbying for the production's continuation. Supporter Johnny Johnson commented: "Thank you Miss Harper Lee, you have made Monroe County proud," while Meagan McDonald added: "Thank you for working towards an agreement!! What a blessing for Monroeville!!" The Monroe County Heritage Museum has staged the show for years, though its relationship with Lee has been complicated. In 2013, the 88-year-old author sued the museum over unauthorised merchandise sales, following the museum's opposition to her federal trademark application. That dispute has since been resolved. Current performances are completely sold out through next month, driven partly by anticipation surrounding Lee's upcoming second novel, Go Set a Watchman. The book, written in the 1950s but shelved on editorial advice, will be published on 14 July, marking Lee's first release since the 1960s. To Kill a Mockingbird, published in July 1960, has sold over 40 million copies worldwide, won the Pulitzer Prize, and inspired an Oscar-winning film starring Gregory Peck. The novel's exploration of race, class, and innocence continues to resonate with audiences globally.

Ofcom Investigates Britain's Got Talent Over Dog-Swap Controversy Broadcasting regulator Ofcom has launched an investigation into ITV's Britain's Got Talent after receiving 1,150 complaints about the show's finale. The controversy centres on dog trainer Jules O'Dwyer, who used a second dog called Chase to perform a tightrope walk because her Border Collie, Matisse, was afraid of heights. The switch was not made clear to viewers during the broadcast. ITV boss Peter Fincham subsequently admitted the programme should have been transparent about using a different dog. "We've opened an investigation to determine whether viewers of ITV's Britain's Got Talent final, who may have paid money to vote, were misled about the competition," an Ofcom spokesman confirmed. O'Dwyer and Matisse narrowly won the final, watched by 13 million people, securing a £250,000 prize and a Royal Variety Performance spot.

ICC Chairman Shashank Manohar Resigns After Less Than a Year Shashank Manohar has resigned as chairman of the International Cricket Council (ICC) after less than a year in the role. The 59-year-old was elected as the body's first independent chairman on a two-year term in May last year. Manohar, a two-time president of the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI), said the decision was because of personal reasons. "I hope the ICC achieves greater heights in future," the Indian added. The ICC confirmed it had received Manohar's resignation on Wednesday, adding that it would "assess the situation" before making any further announcements. Manohar had previously sought to reduce the power of England, Australia and India - the so-called Big Three - on the ICC's decision-making executive committee. Speaking in February 2016, he stated: "No member of the ICC is bigger than the other." A final decision on a new governance structure was due to be taken at a meeting in April.

Rare European Wolf Cubs Filmed Playing at Highland Wildlife Park Adorable European Wolf cubs, born just four weeks ago, have been captured on camera playing at the Highland Wildlife Park in a heartwarming display that has delighted staff and conservationists alike. The arrival of the cubs came as an unexpected surprise to zookeepers, as their parents successfully bred only two months after arriving at the facility. Staff had anticipated the pair would not breed until next year at the earliest, as part of the carefully managed European breeding programme. The mother, Aurora, was born at the Highland Wildlife Park in 2013, while the male, Loki, was born in 2012 in the Netherlands. Despite being first-time parents, the pair have adapted remarkably well to their new roles. Keeper Kellie Ross, who cares for the wolves, described the magical moment she witnessed the cubs playing. "We have set up cameras with motion sensors and I was down changing the memory card," she explained. "I was lucky enough to be there at the same time the cubs were out playing." Ross expressed feeling privileged that the parents trusted staff enough to allow the siblings to remain outside the den while she was nearby. "It is lovely to see them playing like normal puppies. It really is something special," she said. Bradley Yule, the zoo's network manager, emphasized the significance of the birth. "This is an important event in the role of our zoo and these pups will enhance the population," he stated. "They will also serve as ambassadors to help reduce the pressure on wild environments where these wolves come from." The cubs, which have yet to be named, represent hope for the conservation of European Wolves. Loki has been observed feeding and sharing food with Aurora, who continues to carefully rear her young in their den.

Carlisle United Sign Former Chelsea Youth Player Isaiah Wright Carlisle United have completed the signing of 20-year-old defender Isaiah Wright on a short-term contract, following his departure from Chelsea after a decade with the Premier League club. Wright, who joined Chelsea's academy at the age of 10, signed his first professional deal with the Blues in 2013. However, persistent injuries significantly impeded his progression into the first team, with the full-back's appearances limited to youth team, reserve, and under-21 fixtures. "It's very exciting for me, it's been a long journey since I left Chelsea," Wright told BBC Radio Cumbria. "I'm excited and in love with the fans and the club already." The Waltham Forest-born player has been on trial at Brunton Park for some time and is joined by Alexander McQueen, who has also returned to the club on a short-term deal. Reflecting on leaving Chelsea, Wright admitted: "It was quite upsetting because it was a big part of my life for so long. That said, I was also ready to take the next step and start pushing for first-team football because that's my end goal."

Parents Reunited with Daughter After False Abuse Allegations Seek to Move On Craig Stillwell and Carla Andrews are determined to rebuild their lives after a harrowing ordeal that saw their daughter Effie removed from their care for nearly eight months over false allegations of child abuse. The Aylesbury couple, both 23, were accused of causing grievous bodily harm to their infant daughter after she collapsed last August at five months old. Mr Stillwell was arrested at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, and Effie was immediately placed into foster care while Buckinghamshire County Council pursued a case in family court to secure permanent local authority care. For months, the devastated parents were limited to seeing their daughter just three times weekly for 90-minute supervised visits at a contact centre. However, the council's case collapsed when medical experts discovered Effie suffered from Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV, a rare genetic condition that causes易 bruising and can mimic signs of physical abuse. Despite being cleared and having Effie returned to their care, the couple say they have not received an apology from the council. They report that social workers have visited their home twice since their daughter's return, causing ongoing distress. "I want to move on with Effie without having any more interference," said Miss Andrews. "I want to shut the door and tell them to leave us alone to get on with our lives because we have proved our innocence." Mr Stillwell echoed his partner's frustration, expressing their desire to simply resume normal family life. Buckinghamshire County Council declined to comment on the specific case but stated that social care decisions "draw evidence from multiple sources" and follow proper assessment procedures. The family now hopes to put this traumatic chapter behind them and focus on Effie's ongoing medical needs.

Police Investigate "Body in Boot" Report That Turned Out to Be Dog Duvet A Norfolk man received an unexpected visit from police after a concerned member of the public mistook a duvet in his car boot for a wrapped body. Chris Richmond, 30, was going about his daily business at a petrol station in Fakenham, Norfolk, when another customer spotted what they believed to be suspicious circumstances. The distressed witness contacted police, reporting they had seen what appeared to be a body wrapped in a duvet in the boot of Mr Richmond's Land Rover Freelander. Officers attended Mr Richmond's home near Wells-next-the-Sea to investigate the report. Upon inspection, they quickly discovered the "body" was actually bedding for his pet dogs that he keeps in the vehicle. Mr Richmond, who had been filling cans for his strimmer and refuelling his car at the station, said his boot had been open throughout his visit. He recalled that another vehicle had pulled in behind him during the incident. "The police officer did say himself it was a bit of an odd call," Mr Richmond told the Eastern Daily Press. "I'm not criticising them for doing their job. If I was daft enough to go out with a dead body in my car in the middle of the day, they could have got a good lead." While initially annoyed by the questioning, Mr Richmond has since come to appreciate the humorous side of the misunderstanding. Norfolk Police confirmed they received the call at 13:55 BST regarding suspicious circumstances. After visiting the registered owner's address and examining the dog bed in the boot, officers determined no further action was necessary. The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of public vigilance, even when suspicions prove unfounded.

Florida Woman Uses Scent Preservation Kit to Help Find Missing Relative A Florida woman's forward-thinking preparation paid off when she used a two-and-a-half-year-old scent sample to help locate a missing family member, according to the Citrus County Sheriff's Office. The anonymous woman had stored the scent using a specialist preservation kit back in January 2015. These kits can preserve a person's unique scent for up to seven years, making them valuable tools in missing person investigations. Scent preservation works by rubbing a pad on a person's underarm and sealing it in a sterile jar. Police dogs can then smell the sample before beginning their search. Manufacturers claim these kits are more effective than using clothing because they contain pure scent, uncontaminated by environmental odors or smells from other people. Dogs possess a far superior sense of smell compared to humans, and trained police dogs can detect drugs, locate people, and even find corpses. Various police forces worldwide, including those in China and Germany, maintain databases of scent samples from suspects and crime scenes. However, the technique has critics. A 2006 study in New South Wales, Australia, found that only 25 percent of people identified by sniffer dogs actually carried drugs when searched. Despite these concerns, the Florida case ended successfully. The missing person was located, and the helpful police dog celebrated with a well-deserved ice cream, the Sheriff's Office announced on Facebook.

Man in Critical Condition After Dumfries Assault Police are investigating a serious assault in Dumfries after a man sustained critical head injuries early Saturday morning. Officers were called to Queensberry Street at approximately 01:15 on Saturday. The victim was initially taken to Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary before being transferred to the Western General Infirmary in Edinburgh, where he remains in critical condition with a head injury. Detective Chief Inspector Colin Burnie said: "Our investigation is ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding this incident and officers are currently carrying out door-to-door inquiries and studying CCTV footage to gather more information on this incident and whoever is responsible."

Crusaders Cruise Into Irish Cup Semi-Final with Comfortable Victory Over Carrick Crusaders booked their place in the Irish Cup semi-final with a dominant 3-0 victory over Carrick Rangers, with Paul Heatley starring in a man-of-the-match performance at Seaview. The Crues will face Glenavon in the last four at Windsor Park on 2 April, setting up what promises to be an intriguing encounter. Heatley opened the scoring in spectacular fashion, finding the net with a looping header over debutant goalkeeper Ryan Morrell in the 16th minute after the ball was deflected into his path from Jordan Forsythe's left-foot cross. He then turned provider on 33 minutes, delivering a low cross from the right which Colin O'Carroll tapped home from six yards out for the second. Heatley completed his impressive display eight minutes after the break with a cool right-foot finish that slid past Morrell and went in off the post to make it 3-0. Carrick's afternoon went from bad to worse as they had Aaron Smyth and Brian McCaul dismissed. Smyth received a straight red card for fouling Heatley, denying him a clear goalscoring opportunity to complete his hat-trick. Midfielder McCaul was shown a second yellow card to compound a disappointing day for the struggling Premiership side. Crusaders manager Stephen Baxter was respectful of their semi-final opponents: "The last time we met Glenavon in a semi-final, we lost, so we will hope to reverse that this time around. They are a fabulous team who defend well and have goal threats all over the park. It will be a great occasion for everyone, played on a beautiful surface."

Brexit: Northern Ireland businesses face "enormous paperwork" if UK leaves customs union A leading European law expert has warned that Northern Ireland businesses could face "an enormous amount of paperwork" depending on the UK's decision on customs union membership after Brexit. Professor Michael Dougan made the remarks as the UK prepares to decide whether to remain in the EU customs union following its departure from the European Union. Staying in the union would prevent the UK from negotiating independent trade agreements, but leaving would subject goods moving between the UK and EU to customs procedures and likely tariffs. The decision carries particular significance for Northern Ireland, as departure from the customs union would transform the Irish border into a customs frontier, potentially creating substantial challenges for cross-border trade. ## Customs enforcement inevitable Speaking to the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee, Professor Dougan, an expert at the University of Liverpool, stated that some form of customs enforcement would be unavoidable. Beyond tariffs, he emphasized that customs borders involve "regulatory enforcement" covering product standards and other requirements. "There does have to be a frontier, it does have to involve checks and does have to involve pre and post border formalities," he told the committee. Dr Stephanie Reynolds, also from the University of Liverpool, explained that EU customs controls rely on an "electronic risk management system" identifying "high risk" cargo before border arrival. Modern customs operations have increasingly moved toward paperless systems, with most declarations filed electronically. She noted that Authorised Economic Operator status provides expedited access to simplified procedures and allows some shipments to be'fast-tracked.' Most cargo inspections now use "non-intrusive methods" such as x-rays. ## Nordic model examined The experts cited the Norway-Sweden border as an example of a "well-managed, fully co-operative" frontier, despite Sweden's customs union membership and Norway's non-membership. BBC Northern Ireland has visited the main Nordic crossing to assess traffic and business impacts and explore potential lessons for Northern Ireland. Reports on the subject are being broadcast across all BBC platforms, including The View on BBC One Northern Ireland at 22:45 GMT Thursday.

Scottish Film-maker Champions Wild Swimming in Cold Highland Waters A passionate film-maker and photographer is inspiring others to embrace wild swimming in Scotland's icy waters through his captivating documentaries and social media presence. Calum Maclean, based in Inverness, has built a following by documenting his adventures swimming in rivers, lochs and seas across Scotland. His work, shared online and through BBC The Social, showcases the raw beauty and exhilaration of cold-water swimming in some of the country's most spectacular locations. His dedication to exploring new swimming spots is now the focus of a television series on BBC Alba, the Gaelic language channel. "Into the Water" (Dhan Uisge) features Mr Maclean at stunning locations throughout the Highlands, islands and Argyll, including the dramatic waters of Loch Maree in Torridon, the remote beaches of Sanna in Ardnamurchan, and a challenging swim between Seil and the island of Luing. Safety remains paramount for the experienced swimmer. Before attempting difficult sea swims, he carefully researches tides and currents, and consults with local boatmen about water conditions. "I never jump straight into cold water - so always acclimatise for a minute first," he explains. "It's the first 90 seconds that take your body to get used to it, to help avoid cold water shock." His pre-swim routine involves thorough assessment: checking water depth and temperature, identifying underwater hazards like rocks or branches, planning exit points, and evaluating currents or rip tides. Though he sometimes swims alone, he stresses his experience and knowing personal limits, always exiting before feeling dangerously cold. Despite the challenges, Mr Maclean emphasises that Scotland offers many locations suitable for novice wild swimmers. He attributes wild swimming's growing popularity to its addictive nature: "You go once and then you've just got to go again." The activity has experienced a significant boom, with groups forming on social media worldwide to share information about natural swimming pools and organise group swims. Mr Maclean believes this surge reflects people's desire for connection with nature and the unique thrill that wild swimming provides.

Brazilian Man Dies After Cow Falls Through Roof Onto His Bed A Brazilian man has died after being crushed by a cow that fell through his roof while he was sleeping. The one-tonne cow was grazing on a hill behind the small house, in the town of Caratinga, when it stepped onto the asbestos roof, which collapsed under its weight. Joao Maria de Souza, 45, was lying in bed when the animal fell on him. He was taken to hospital and died the day after, reportedly of internal bleeding. Mr Souza was conscious and appeared to be in a good condition, but he had to wait too long to be seen by a doctor, relatives said. Local media says this is the third such incident in the region in the past three years. There were no casualties in the two previous incidents. In the first occasion, there was no one inside the house when the cow fell through the roof. In the second incident, a baby and a small child were sleeping next to the spot where the animal fell, in what was described at time as a miraculous escape. Caratinga is in a hilly area of Minas Gerais, a Brazilian state traditionally known as a cattle raising and dairy producing region.

Uganda Election: Museveni Leads with 61% as Observers Criticize Poll Conditions Uganda's long-time President Yoweri Museveni appears headed for victory in the country's presidential election, with more than 80% of ballots counted showing him securing 61% of the vote. His main challenger, Kizza Besigye, trails with 34% and is currently under house arrest. Full results are expected within hours. The election has drawn sharp criticism from European Union observers, who highlighted significant concerns about the electoral process. EU Chief Observer Eduard Kukan acknowledged that "voters actively participated in the campaign events and expressed a remarkable determination while waiting for the long hours on the election day to cast their ballots." However, he noted that "the National Resistance Movement's domination of the political landscape distorted the fairness of the campaign," pointing to an "intimidating atmosphere" created by the governing party. The voting process has been marred by sporadic violence, opposition allegations of electoral fraud, and government-imposed blocks on social media sites and messaging apps. Mr. Besigye was arrested on Friday on suspicion of planning to publish his own results, which would violate electoral laws. Kampala police chief Andrew Felix Kaweesi stated authorities would detain him until official results are announced. This marks the fourth electoral contest between the former allies, who once fought together as guerrilla fighters, with Mr. Besigye serving as Mr. Museveni's personal doctor. President Museveni, who seized power in 1986, is credited with restoring stability to Uganda but faces growing criticism for increasingly authoritarian tendencies. Former Prime Minister Amama Mbabazi is in distant third place and is also reportedly under house arrest.

**Music Festival Celebrates Milestone 10th Anniversary in Wester Ross** A popular music festival in Wester Ross marked its 10th anniversary over the weekend with sold-out performances on Friday and Saturday. Approximately 2,500 revellers attended each day to enjoy headline acts including Utah Saints, Twin Atlantic, Shed Seven, and The Undertones, alongside Alabama 3, Public Service Broadcasting, and Hunter and the Bear. In a testament to the event's popularity, this year's festival sold out before any performers were even announced, highlighting its strong reputation among music fans in the Scottish Highlands community.

Trump and Clinton Debate: Rivals Find One Nice Thing to Say In an unusually tense television debate on 10 October 2016, US presidential rivals Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton broke protocol by refusing to shake hands at the start. The frosty encounter saw heated arguments over multiple issues, notably Mr Trump's controversial remarks about women. Despite the hostile atmosphere throughout, both candidates managed to find something positive about their opponent when prompted. Mrs Clinton praised Mr Trump's children, whilst he acknowledged her determination and refusal to quit. The debate highlighted the deeply strained relationship between the two presidential hopefuls.

South Korean Ferry Captain Lee Joon-seok Sentenced to Life in Prison for Sewol Disaster GWANGJU, South Korea — A South Korean appeals court on Tuesday sentenced the captain of the sunken ferry Sewol to life in prison, overturning his previous 36-year jail term and significantly increasing his punishment for one of the country's worst maritime disasters. Lee Joon-seok, now nearly 70 years old, was at the helm when the ferry capsized and sank in April 2014, killing more than 300 people, most of them high school students on a field trip. While he had been found guilty of gross negligence in November and sentenced to 36 years in prison, the appeals court determined his actions warranted the harshest possible punishment short of execution. The judge at the Gwangju High Court delivered a scathing verdict, comparing Lee's decision to abandon the sinking vessel to a doctor deserting sick and dying patients in a hospital. The captain's actions, the judge said, left passengers trapped on his ship "in a state of fatal and indescribable suffering." Prosecutors had argued for the death penalty, telling the court that Lee deserved the ultimate punishment for abandoning his passengers. They emphasized that his actions led to the deaths of 250 high school students and "inflicted an incurable injury on their parents," according to Yonhap news agency. Despite the life sentence, families of the victims protested outside the court, demanding even harsher punishment. "He should have received death penalty. Imprisonment for life? They want to give life sentence to a person so that he can peacefully die when he is old?" asked Jeon Myung-sun, whose son Jeon Chan-ho died in the disaster, according to the Associated Press. Lee had been captured on video and in photographs leaving the ship while passengers remained trapped inside the sinking vessel. While he apologized for abandoning passengers, he argued that he never intended to sacrifice their lives and claimed he was "confused" during the incident. The appeals court also handed down revised sentences to 14 other crew members, ranging from 18 months to 12 years in prison. These sentences were actually lighter than their previous jail terms of five to 30 years. Judge Jeon Il-ho explained that the new sentences took into account that the crew members were following orders from the captain. "We drew a distinction between the captain Lee Joon-seok who has a grave responsibility and crew members who took orders from the captain," Reuters quoted the judge as saying. "And we considered health conditions of the crew members and actions they took in the rescue operation as well as how they boarded the ferry Sewol." The Sewol disaster, which occurred on April 16, 2014, triggered widespread mourning across South Korea and became one of the worst maritime disasters in the country's modern history. Investigations revealed the tragedy was caused by a combination of factors including illegal redesigns of the vessel, overloading of cargo, the inexperience of the crew member steering the ship, and lax government safety regulations. President Park Geun-hye has vowed to implement reforms and agreed to demands from grieving relatives to salvage the ferry. Nine bodies remain missing from the disaster. The tragedy continues to resonate in South Korean society. Over the weekend, thousands of protesters peacefully demonstrated in Seoul against the government's handling of the disaster, following clashes with riot police at another protest that left dozens injured.

Labour Leadership Race Intensifies as Corbyn Leads Polls Amid Party Tensions The Labour Party leadership contest has erupted into open warfare, with left-wing candidate Jeremy Corbyn calling for politics to be conducted in a "comradely and friendly" manner amid escalating attacks from party grandees and rival candidates. The controversy intensified after former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn joined Tony Blair in warning against a Corbyn victory, declaring that Labour would have a "death wish" if it shifted leftward. Fellow leadership candidate Liz Kendall went further, describing a potential Corbyn win as a "disaster" for the party. The stark warnings came after a YouGov poll for The Times placed Mr Corbyn significantly ahead in the leadership race, with 43% of first preference votes, compared to Andy Burnham on 26%, Yvette Cooper on 20%, and Ms Kendall trailing in fourth place with just 11%. The prospect of a Corbyn victory has sent shockwaves through the party establishment. Labour donor John Mills told The Guardian that Mr Corbyn's election could trigger an "SDP-style split" – referencing the 1981 breakaway that formed the Social Democratic Party – and predicted that wealthy donors would withdraw their financial support. Mr Mills, who has donated to Ms Kendall's campaign, suggested that "some of the major donors" would be "less likely to give" if Mr Corbyn won, raising questions about the party's financial viability under his leadership. Responding to the barrage of criticism, Mr Corbyn struck a conciliatory tone, telling the BBC: "I think politics should be conducted on a comradely and friendly basis, and if people disagree with each other then say what they disagree on, and let's keep these silly remarks to themselves." Ms Kendall firmly rejected suggestions that she should withdraw from the race to consolidate opposition to Mr Corbyn. "I'll be fighting for what I believe in until the very end," she declared, arguing that "turning back to the politics of the 1980s and losing elections does nothing to help the people" Labour wants to support. The controversy follows comments from former Prime Minister Tony Blair, who warned that Labour would not win from a "traditional leftist platform" and suggested that those with Mr Corbyn's politics should "get a transplant." One of Mr Blair's former advisers even described MPs who nominated Mr Corbyn to ensure a broad debate, but don't support him, as "morons." However, not all Labour figures agree with the attacks on Mr Corbyn. Former deputy prime minister Lord Prescott criticized Mr Blair for "abusing" Corbyn supporters and urged the party to "calm down." Mr Milburn emphasized that Labour could only win the next election by occupying the centre ground, warning that any leftward lurch would be fatal for the party's electoral prospects. Despite leading in the YouGov poll among party members, a subsequent Ipsos Mori survey of the general public showed Mr Burnham ahead, with 27% saying he would make a good prime minister, compared to 22% for Ms Cooper, 17% for Mr Corbyn, and 16% for Ms Kendall. As the leadership contest continues, the deep divisions within Labour over its future direction show no signs of healing, with establishment figures increasingly alarmed at Mr Corbyn's unexpected surge in popularity among party members.

Vettel Set to Test Modified'Halo Two' Safety Device at Austrian Grand Prix Sebastian Vettel is expected to trial the latest version of Formula One's controversial cockpit protection system during Friday's opening practice session, as the sport continues its push to enhance driver safety. The four-time world champion will complete at least one lap with the'Halo Two' device fitted to his car, giving engineers and officials their first on-track look at the modified design. The system, intended to shield drivers from impacts with large airborne debris, represents an evolution of the original halo concept tested in March. While the visual changes may be subtle, significant modifications have been made to both materials and dimensions. Most notably, the new iteration uses titanium rather than steel construction, offering improved strength-to-weight ratios. However, the FIA has indicated this may not represent the final material specification when the device becomes mandatory in 2017. Beyond performance testing, the governing body's medical team will assess how the halo affects driver extraction procedures in emergency situations—a crucial consideration for race safety protocols. The FIA has informed teams that cockpit protection will form part of next year's sweeping regulation changes, designed to make cars faster and more visually striking. However, officials continue refining the final design to optimize the balance between safety benefits, driver visibility, and cockpit access. The halo's development comes after Red Bull's alternative'aeroscreen' concept failed mandatory impact tests, which simulate a wheel striking the device at 250km/h. Though the FIA hoped to continue aeroscreen development for potential 2018 introduction, Red Bull has suspended work to focus resources on their 2017 challenger.

New Welsh Plant Species Named After Sir David Attenborough A newly discovered plant species found in the Brecon Beacons has been named in honour of Sir David Attenborough. The Attenborough Hawkweed belongs to the daisy family and is believed to have evolved in the Welsh mountains since the last ice age. These plants are close relatives of dandelions, sharing similar-looking flowers. Sir David expressed his delight at the tribute, saying he was "thrilled" by the honour. "Bestowing a name on a new species is surely one of the greatest of biological compliments and I am truly grateful," he said. Dr Tim Rich, the plant taxonomist who made the discovery and named the species, described finding it as "a really exciting moment and something that you dream of as a naturalist." He explained his choice: "I decided to name this special little plant found in the mountains of the Brecon Beacons after David Attenborough as he inspired me to study ecology when I was 17."

Indian Court Orders Fresh Investigation Into Mohammad Akhlaq Lynching Case A court in northern India has ordered a fresh investigation into the 2015 killing of Mohammad Akhlaq, who was beaten to death by a mob over allegations of storing beef in his home. Mohammad Akhlaq was beaten to death by a group of men in Dadri in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh. Eighteen people are on trial for his murder. The slaughter of cows, considered sacred by Hindus, is banned in many Indian states. The court in Gautam Buddh Nagar, near the Indian capital, Delhi, gave the order after hearing a petition filed by one of Mr Akhlaq's neighbours. Mohammad Danish, Mr Akhlaq's son, said he "hoped a fresh investigation will bring out the truth". "I am hoping for a fair probe. The real facts will be revealed then," he told the CNN-IBN news channel. A lab test cited widely in the aftermath of the killing in September had said that the meat allegedly found in his refrigerator was mutton and not beef. However, a new lab report, revealed in June by the lawyers of 18 people on trial for his murder, said that the meat in question was, in fact, beef. Later, it was also revealed that the meat was never in his house, but found inside a bin near his home. Although police have said that the type of meat is irrelevant to the murder case, the defence team has been using the new test results to demand the release of the 18 suspects on the grounds that they were "provoked" into attacking Mr Akhlaq. Uttar Pradesh is one of the 10 Indian states where the slaughter of cow, calf, bull and bullock is completely banned. However, the slaughter of buffaloes and the sale and consumption of its meat is permitted.

Russia Names 68 Athletes for Rio Olympics Despite Doping Ban Russia has named 68 track and field athletes it hopes will compete at the Rio Olympics, despite the country's athletics federation remaining suspended over doping allegations. Athletics' governing body first imposed the ban in November following allegations of widespread state-sponsored doping in the country. The Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) and its athletes last week appealed against the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas). A final decision is due by 21 July. The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) has said a handful of Russian athletes could compete in Rio as "neutral athletes". To do so, they must meet a number of criteria, including being repeatedly tested outside their homeland. Russian doping whistleblower Yuliya Stepanova has been cleared to run and was described as a "symbol" for clean competitors. The All-Russian Athletics Federation (Araf) on Tuesday published a list of the 68 athletes it said had met its criteria for taking part in the Olympics, which start on 5 August. Two-time Olympic pole vault champion Yelena Isinbayeva and London 2012 high jump gold medallist Ivan Ukhov are included. Araf said each of its athletes has "sent an individual request to the Olympic Games" to be checked by the IAAF, as "Araf is not now a member". It said it had also appealed about the "overall legality of adding extra criteria for the participation of sportsmen competing at the Olympics". The International Olympic Committee's deadline to achieve qualifying criteria for the Games is 11 July, though the ROC says that would be extended should Cas rule in favour of its athletes.

**Humpback Whale Spotted Off Norfolk Coast for Third Consecutive Year** Whale watchers have been treated to a spectacular sight after spotting what is believed to be the same humpback whale returning to Norfolk waters for the third year running. The mammal was observed approximately 2.5 miles (4km) off Winterton, accompanied by gannets feeding on herrings - the whale's preferred food source in the area. Norfolk cetacean recorder Carl Chapman spent one-and-a-half hours observing the creature, though he was unable to get close enough to confirm its identity through its unique undertail pattern. Despite this, he remains optimistic about the sighting. "I was ecstatic to see the whale off the Norfolk coast," Mr Chapman said. "However, because it's turned up at the same time as it has done in the two previous consecutive years, it's probably the same returning individual making use of the same food source." Lucy Babey from charity ORCA confirmed the whale was visible for five to six hours and was regularly fluking - lifting its tail out of the water. She noted that humpback whales are more commonly seen on the European side of the North Sea rather than UK waters. The Sea Watch Foundation reported additional sightings along the Norfolk coast at Sheringham, Hemsby and Horsey Gap. Minke whales were also spotted from Trimingham, Mundesley and Happisburgh, suggesting rich marine activity in the region.

Northants Release Scotland Captain Coetzer and Paceman Chambers Northamptonshire have released Scotland captain Kyle Coetzer and pace bowler Maurice Chambers from their playing staff. Coetzer, 31, joined Northants in 2011 and was instrumental in helping the county win the FLt20 trophy in 2013. However, the opener struggled for form this season, playing just four Championship matches with a disappointing batting average of 5.29, despite representing Scotland at the World Cup earlier this year. Chambers, 28, moved from Essex in 2013 but managed only five Championship appearances in 2015, unable to establish himself as a regular in the side. Northants head coach David Ripley praised both departing players. "Kyle has been a model professional during his time here," Ripley said. "He deals with success and failure in equal measure, a very valuable thing in a cricket dressing room." Regarding Chambers, Ripley added: "After a slow start in 2014, Maurice has put in a big effort this year but has been unable to get past our other seam bowlers."

Government Should Take Over Tata Steel Pension Fund, Says Sir Vince Cable Sir Vince Cable has suggested the UK government should consider taking control of Tata Steel's pension fund rather than nationalising the company itself, describing it as a more practical solution to the crisis. The former Business Secretary made his comments following Tata Steel's announcement on Tuesday that it plans to sell its struggling UK operations. He identified the pension fund's substantial liabilities as a "massive deterrent" preventing potential buyers from acquiring the business. "It would be more sensible if they were to take ownership of the pension fund rather than run the company which governments aren't very good at," Sir Vince told BBC Radio Wales. "This could be a way that the government could provide a real game-changer, and change the economics of it substantially." Sir Vince criticised the UK government's response to the crisis, claiming ministers were unprepared for Tata's announcement in Mumbai. He also called the government's opposition to increased EU tariffs on Chinese steel "bizarre". Business Secretary Sajid Javid is scheduled to meet with Port Talbot steelworkers on Friday to reassure them the government is "on their side". The UK government maintains it is doing everything possible to support the industry.

Choppers the Chimp, Star of Iconic PG Tips Adverts, Dies at 48 Choppers, the chimpanzee who charmed television audiences as Ada in the famous PG Tips tea advertisements, has died at the age of 48 at Twycross Zoo. The "much-loved" ape was put to sleep on Wednesday after showing signs of heart and liver failure, the Leicestershire zoo announced. Her passing marks the end of an era for one of Britain's most recognizable animal television personalities. Choppers was among several chimps trained by Twycross Zoo who appeared in the beloved PG Tips commercials that entertained viewers from the 1950s onwards. Dressed in human clothing and lip-syncing to the voices of celebrated actors including Peter Sellers and Bob Monkhouse, the apes became household names. The chimpanzees also made memorable appearances on popular children's programmes such as Tiswas and Blue Peter, with their chaotic tea parties delighting the British public. However, the zoo's relationship with these advertising campaigns has since been acknowledged as problematic. In 2014, Twycross told the BBC that using apes on television had been wrong, noting that Choppers was "mixed up" as a result of her performing career. After approximately 30 years, the zoo ended its agreement to provide apes for advertising, though chimpanzees from abroad continued appearing in tea adverts until 2003. Choppers' journey began in Liberia, where she was rescued from poachers as a baby by a British couple in 1973. They brought her to Twycross for care, but her life in television had lasting damaging effects on her natural behaviour. Only in her later years did Choppers begin to exhibit typical chimpanzee behaviour. Following the death of her companion Louis—who played Mr Shifter in the PG Tips adverts—in July 2013, keepers introduced Choppers to the zoo's larger chimpanzee group. Dr Charlotte Macdonald, director of life sciences at the zoo, said the integration proved successful. "She loved grooming the other chimps and even the keepers, she was very friendly and sociable," Dr Macdonald explained. "She integrated well into the larger group and acted as a peacemaker, she wanted to be everyone's friend. "We are very upset and she will be sadly missed."

**Denly Century Anchors Kent Recovery Against Sussex** Former England batsman Joe Denly led Kent's fightback with a resilient century on day one against Sussex. The 31-year-old struck 16 boundaries during his 119-run knock, steadying the innings after early setbacks. Vernon Philander (2-42) and Jofra Archer reduced Kent to a precarious 115-4, but Denly anchored the recovery alongside Darren Stevens (44) and Will Gidman (42). His patient 208-ball innings frustrated Sussex's attack throughout the day. Joe Weatherley contributed 33 as Kent rebuilt their position. David Wiese claimed 3-54, removing James Harris late in the day, but Adam Rouse remained unbeaten on 32 at stumps. Philander eventually dismissed Denly lbw, but the damage was done as Kent reached a respectable total after the opening day's play.

One Direction's Zayn Malik Quits Twitter Over Abuse One Direction star Zayn Malik has deleted his Twitter account, citing the daily abuse and negativity he received on the social networking site. The 19-year-old singer from Bradford, West Yorkshire, posted two farewell messages before abandoning his account, which had attracted more than five million followers. "The reason I don't tweet as much as I use to, is because I'm sick of all the useless opinions and hate that I get daily goodbye twitter," he wrote. Malik directed fans to contact him through the official One Direction account instead, saying: "Fans that have something to say can tweet me on the one direction account." The departure follows a growing trend of celebrities leaving Twitter due to online harassment. American rapper Nicki Minaj briefly quit in April following a dispute with a fan who leaked portions of her album, though she returned within days. Blue Peter presenter Helen Skelton recently deleted her account, admitting she couldn't handle the negative feedback. Singer Miley Cyrus and actress Demi Lovato have also taken extended breaks from the platform. Twitter allows users 30 days to reactivate deactivated accounts. The remaining One Direction members - Niall Horan, Liam Payne, Harry Styles and Louis Tomlinson - continue to maintain active Twitter profiles. The group, who finished third on The X Factor in 2010, have since achieved international success.

Search Called Off for Man Reported Clinging to Rocks at St David's Head A major search operation has been suspended after emergency services failed to locate a man reportedly seen clinging to rocks at St David's Head in Pembrokeshire. The search, launched on Saturday, involved lifeboat crews, coastguard teams and police. It concluded on Sunday evening with no plans to resume unless new information emerges. Searchers discovered a coat believed to belong to the missing man, containing money but no identification documents. Dyfed-Powys Police are urgently appealing for information to identify the man and contact his family. He is described as white European, approximately 60 years old, of lean build with a long face, short hair and distinctive white eyebrows. He was wearing a dark rucksack, dark blue or black trousers, and a dark blue long-sleeved shirt or jumper. Based on his accent, police believe he was not from the UK. Authorities are asking anyone with information to come forward immediately.

Girl's Hair Trapped in Lanzarote Hotel Pool Filter for Two Minutes A young girl from Leeds fell unconscious after her hair became trapped in a swimming pool filter at a holiday resort in Lanzarote, leaving her underwater for more than two minutes. Darcey Morgan was pulled to safety by fellow holidaymakers at the H10 Rubicon Palace in Playa Blanca during a family holiday in April. Her mother, Alex Morgan, described the incident as "terrifying" and said her daughter turned blue before losing consciousness. The 32-year-old mother was staying at the resort with her husband Gareth, 35, and their three children when the accident occurred. Darcey received CPR by the poolside before being rushed to hospital in Arrecife, where she was kept overnight for observation. "It took over two minutes to get her hair free, by which time she was unconscious. She was blue," Mrs Morgan said. "There are no words for what I was feeling. It's every parent's worst nightmare." Darcey lost four clumps of hair in the incident but has since made a full recovery. Mrs Morgan said she reported the incident to hotel management but claimed they "did nothing" in response. "The swimming pool was not closed, the waterfall and the filter remained on," she said. Following the accident, Mrs Morgan said other guests came forward to report they had previously raised concerns about the filter with staff. She claimed one boy had his swimming trunks sucked into the device just two days before Darcey's ordeal. However, First Choice said it had received no other reports regarding the filter and confirmed the device had been switched off immediately after being informed of the incident. Mrs Morgan shared her experience on Facebook to raise awareness of potential dangers at swimming pools. The post has been shared more than 100,000 times and attracted over 11,000 comments. "Myself and Gareth don't want any other parents or family members to go through what we experienced that day," she wrote. "We will never get over what happened that day, but if this post can raise some awareness, save someone's life, then we will be happy." A spokesperson for First Choice said the company had launched a "full and thorough investigation" and had taken "immediate action" to resolve the issue. They confirmed they had been in contact with the Morgan family to update them on the steps taken. "We continue to ensure that the health and safety of all of our holidaymakers is our top priority," the spokesperson added.

KPMG Under Investigation Over Rolls-Royce Bribery Scandal The Financial Reporting Council has launched an investigation into KPMG's auditing of Rolls-Royce, raising fundamental questions about the effectiveness of corporate financial oversight following one of Britain's most significant corruption scandals. Earlier this year, Rolls-Royce paid £671 million in fines, including £498 million to the Serious Fraud Office, and issued an apology after being found guilty of paying millions in bribes to middlemen over decades to secure lucrative orders. The engineering giant's long-standing auditor, KPMG, had been examining the company's accounts for 26 years, yet apparently failed to detect the widespread illegal activity. KPMG has stated it is cooperating with the investigation and remains "confident in the quality" of its work. However, critics are asking how a detailed professional audit could miss such systematic and recurring corruption. The case has reignited debate about the fundamental purpose and effectiveness of corporate auditing. The Rolls-Royce scandal, along with previous high-profile failures at Enron, WorldCom, Tesco, and during the financial crisis, highlights structural problems at the heart of auditing and financial oversight. The first issue is that auditors are neither police nor regulators. They cannot simply seize whatever documents they wish. Instead, they largely must work with information the company chooses to provide. This makes it relatively easy for a determined company to mislead its auditors—a defence frequently offered by audit firms when questioned about failures. The second problem concerns the commercial relationship between auditors and their clients. Auditors are contractors paid by the very companies they examine. The "Big Four" accounting firms—PwC, KPMG, EY, and Deloitte—audit over 90% of major company accounts. They compete for this lucrative business, creating inherent incentives to maintain favour with those who employ and pay them. KPMG audited Rolls-Royce for 26 years, earning tens of millions of pounds and inevitably developing close relationships. Similarly, PwC audited Tesco for 32 years before agreeing not to seek reappointment following that company's accounting scandal. Such long associations hardly provide ideal conditions for maintaining tough, arms-length scrutiny. While outright corruption remains rare, unconscious bias favouring a client paying substantial fees over decades is difficult to avoid. Recent regulatory changes require large public companies in the FTSE 350 to tender their auditing contracts every ten years, though they need only change auditors every twenty years. Critics argue this still allows excessive coziness to develop. Auditors do face penalties occasionally. The record fine in the United States is $8 million, whilst in the UK it stands at £3 million. These sums are minuscule compared to fines levied on misbehaving companies and relative to the enormous size of major accounting firms. The fundamental problem remains: major accountancy firms have historically enjoyed substantial rewards whilst facing relatively little risk, raising questions about whether current structures can deliver the independent oversight investors and the public require.

Council to Survey Sites for Grimsby Town FC's New Stadium North East Lincolnshire Council has agreed to conduct a comprehensive survey to identify suitable locations for Grimsby Town FC's proposed new stadium and leisure complex. The decision follows extensive discussions about the potential benefits such a development could bring to the local area. The football club's preferred location is a 22.7-hectare parcel of council-owned land situated between Peaks Parkway and Weelsby Avenue. While the authority confirmed that more than three potential sites are under consideration, it has declined to reveal specific locations at this stage. The council plans to examine sites across the entire North East Lincolnshire area, with findings to be published in a comprehensive report expected later this summer. Council Leader Ray Oxby emphasised the broader community benefits: "It's clear that a thriving local football club makes sense - it's good for business, creates a lasting legacy and provides a catalyst to boost to the borough's general wellbeing." The independent land survey was first agreed upon in 2012, though no planning application has yet been submitted for the development.

Surrey Pair Burns and Henriques Recovering After Horrific On-Field Collision Surrey cricketers Rory Burns and Moises Henriques are recovering following a sickening collision during their T20 Blast match against Sussex on 14 June that left both players requiring hospital treatment. The incident occurred when both team-mates attempted to take the same catch, resulting in a heavy impact that abandoned the match. Australian all-rounder Henriques, 28, suffered the more serious injuries, breaking his jaw in three places, while opening batsman Burns, 24, needed stitches for cuts near his left eye. "I literally don't remember any of the collision," Burns told BBC London 94.9. "The first thing I remember is waking up. The Sussex physio was holding my neck and the paramedic was over my face." Burns recalled diving for the ball but has no memory of the actual impact. "I remember the whole game and then waking up and seeing the paramedics," he said. Both players were taken from the field by ambulance, with Burns praising the "fantastic" emergency staff. The headaches have since subsided, and he expressed gratitude for the support from director of cricket Alec Stewart and his teammates. "He came off slightly worse, with his jaw and his teeth, but he's on the mend and that's the important thing," Burns said of Henriques. "I don't think we'll be forgetting each other for a while. I'm looking forward to having a beer with him when he's fully recovered."

Prison Drug Problem'Threatens to Overwhelm' HMP Ranby A damning report has revealed that the widespread availability of so-called "legal highs" at a Nottinghamshire prison is threatening to overwhelm its healthcare services. The HM Inspectorate of Prisons found that New Psychoactive Substances (NPS) pose a significant challenge at HMP Ranby, which houses approximately 1,000 male inmates. These substances are chemically designed to mimic already-banned drugs. Deputy Chief Inspector Martin Lomas said the jail faces the urgent task of "destabilising the supply of NPS which threatens to overwhelm it." The report also raised serious concerns about six suicides occurring within just 17 months at the facility. In response, the National Offender Management Service acknowledged the severity of the situation. Chief Executive Michael Spurr confirmed that since the inspection in September, the prison population has been reduced by 120 inmates whilst staff numbers have increased. "NPS remains a real concern in prisons," Spurr stated, adding that a new testing regime would be implemented across the country from April. He emphasised that authorities would work closely with police to disrupt supply chains and take "robust action" against those supplying or using NPS in prisons. Despite these challenges, inspectors noted some positive developments, including fewer prisoners reporting feelings of being unsafe or victimised, though these figures remained significantly higher than comparable prisons. The inspections were conducted between late August and early September 2015.

Inverness West Link Road Plans Face Opposition Despite Official Backing Planning officials have recommended approval for two controversial applications related to Inverness's West Link road project, designed to ease traffic congestion across the city. However, the proposals face strong opposition from local campaigners who argue the new road will destroy valuable green space. The south planning applications committee is set to consider both applications, which include the West Link itself and a secondary project involving relocating Torvean Golf Course, developing a new sports hub and parkland at Torvean, and extending Kilvean Cemetery. The development has divided local residents over balancing infrastructure needs with environmental preservation.

Comic Relief 2017 Faces Ofcom Complaints Over Content The BBC's Comic Relief fundraising show has attracted complaints to media regulator Ofcom, with viewers taking issue with content broadcast before the watershed. Ofcom has received 151 complaints about the Comic Relief 2017 broadcast and is now considering whether to launch a formal investigation into the charity event. Most complaints centred on the content of Friday's show rather than technical issues. Language used before the watershed by Steve Coogan, a game of Innuendo Bingo, and a sketch by comedy duo Vic Reeves and Bob Mortimer have come in for particular criticism. One of the most controversial moments saw Reeves and Mortimer interview TV presenter Susanna Reid, with Reeves apparently brandishing a prosthetic penis from under a kilt. Reid later tweeted: "Well. That was an experience" - complete with a red-faced emoji. She added that she "wasn't looking" when Reeves sat with his legs open while asking innuendo-laden questions about whether or not she had seen new film Kong. Another moment that sparked social media complaints was comic Russell Brand swearing live on air after a technical glitch. Some viewers also complained about sound problems, though Ofcom confirmed most complaints related to content rather than technical difficulties. Despite the controversy, the evening featured several popular segments. Highlights included a 12-minute "sequel" to Love Actually, showing what the characters - played by stars including Keira Knightley and Andrew Lincoln - had been doing since the original film. Take That joined James Corden for Carpool Karaoke, Ed Balls reprised his Strictly Come Dancing routine to Gangnam Style, and there were previews of Mrs Brown's new chat show and the second series of Peter Kay's Car Share. Press reviews were less favourable, describing the show as "dreadful and unfunny," with the Love Actually special accused of having "lousy jokes" and "texted-in performances." Ofcom said: "We will assess these complaints before deciding whether or not to investigate." The BBC declined to say how many people had complained directly to the corporation. A BBC spokesperson defended the broadcast: "The Red Nose Day 2017 broadcast was a live studio environment enjoyed by a peak audience of 7.6 million which raised over £73m. This will go a huge way to help improve the lives of many people both here in the UK and in some of the world's poorest countries."

Malaysia PM Calls Myanmar Violence Against Rohingya Muslims "Genocide" Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak has described the treatment of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar as "genocide", urging the international community to take action against what he called systematic persecution. Mr Razak made the comments in an opening statement to members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) gathering in Kuala Lumpur. The OIC is made up of 57 countries with large or majority-Muslim populations. It is holding the emergency session to discuss what it says is a humanitarian crisis faced by the Myanmar minority. Approximately 65,000 Rohingyas have fled Myanmar's Rakhine state since Burmese soldiers began intensive counter-terrorism operations there in October. Describing the situation as "a cause of great and immediate concern", Mr Najib said: "Far too many people have lost their lives in Myanmar. Many have suffered appalling deaths, and those that have lived through the atrocities have witnessed or endured unspeakable cruelty. That in itself is a reason why we cannot keep silent." The situation also threatens to create "a new home for terrorist groups", he said, as "militant elements could infiltrate and possibly radicalise this oppressed community". ## What is the OIC? Formerly known as the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, the 57-member organisation is largely made up of majority-Muslim countries. It was established in 1969 in the wake of an arson attack by an Australian Christian on the al-Aqsa mosque in Jerusalem. Its aims include the promotion of co-operation among member states, safeguarding Islamic holy places and working towards eradicating racial discrimination and colonialism. But despite its size, numerous committees and stated scope, it has limited resources at its own disposal. ## What is happening in Rakhine state? After lethal attacks in October on security forces in Maungdaw district in Myanmar (also called Burma), the authorities launched a counter-insurgency operation that critics claim has involved widespread killings, rape and the destruction of Rohingya villages. The government of Myanmar has denied the accusations and has suggested Rohingya burned their own homes down to attract international attention. It has also prevented NGOs and international media, including the BBC, from entering the region to investigate the claims. In his speech, Mr Najib called on the Burmese government to allow humanitarian aid in. The country's leader Aung San Suu Kyi has previously asked for "space" from the international community to deal with the issue. After a trip to Rakhine state, former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan also said he would not describe the violence against the Rohingya as "genocide". But John McKissick, a senior official in the UN's refugee agency, told the BBC in November that Myanmar is seeking the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim minority from its territory. ## Who are the Rohingya? The estimated one million Muslim Rohingya are seen by many in mainly Buddhist Myanmar as illegal migrants from Bangladesh. They are denied citizenship by the government despite many having lived there for generations. Communal violence in Rakhine state in 2012 left scores dead and displaced more than 100,000 people. They face widespread discrimination and mistreatment.

El Salvador Gang Truce Leads to Sharp Drop in Murders El Salvador has witnessed a dramatic decline in violent crime following a historic truce between the country's most feared street gangs, according to police figures released this week. Authorities reported that killings have fallen nearly 24% overall this year, with May murders plummeting by more than 50% compared to the same period last year. Justice and Public Security Minister David Munguia Payes credited the gang ceasefire, stating it "has had an important effect on the drop in violence." The unprecedented peace deal between Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) and Barrio 18, two gangs notorious for ruthless violence, was brokered by the Catholic Church. The agreement came after gang leaders were transferred from maximum security facilities to prisons with more relaxed conditions. President Mauricio Funes emphasized that his government did not directly negotiate with the gangs but merely facilitated the accord. On 19 June, imprisoned gang members held ceremonies marking the first 100 days of the truce. Gang leaders signaled willingness to make the pact permanent. "We want a definitive ceasefire," gang leader Oscar Armando Reyes told the Associated Press, though he stressed the government must provide concrete job proposals. El Salvador's gangs originated from immigrant street gangs in the United States and have evolved into powerful trans-national criminal organizations with thousands of members. The successful truce has captured attention in neighboring Honduras and Guatemala, countries also plagued by high murder rates and gang violence.

Norway Accuses Fitness Tracker Companies of Breaking Data Privacy Laws Norway's Consumer Council (NCC) has filed a formal complaint against four major fitness tracker manufacturers, accusing them of violating local data protection laws. The consumer watchdog said Fitbit, Jawbone, Garmin and Mio had all failed to comply with Norwegian regulations governing how companies handle consumer information. According to the NCC, the firms collected excessive amounts of personal data without adequately informing users about who could access it or how long it would be retained. The complaint has now been submitted to Norway's data protection authority for investigation. Finn Myrstad, director of digital services at the NCC, criticized the companies for operating under "asymmetrical and obscure terms" that forced users to surrender personal information in exchange for using the fitness tracking devices. "We fear that this information can be exploited for direct marketing and price-discrimination purposes, and that basic privacy principles are being neglected," Mr Myrstad said in a statement. The allegations emerged from a detailed research project conducted by the council examining the terms and conditions employed by the four wristband manufacturers. The investigation found that users had minimal access to information about what data was collected, who viewed it, and how it was utilized. "It is important that we don't give up basic rights in order to use the products and services of the future," Mr Myrstad emphasized. In response to the complaint, Jawbone issued a statement saying it was reviewing the NCC report. The company insisted it only shares user data with explicit permission, such as when integrating with third-party applications. A Jawbone spokesman described the company as a "custodian" of user data, noting that users can download their information and request deletion at any time. The BBC has contacted all four companies for comment.

Portsmouth's Spinnaker Tower to be Painted Blue and Gold After Red Design Backlash Portsmouth City Council has revised its controversial plans to rebrand the iconic Spinnaker Tower following a public outcry that saw more than 10,000 residents sign a petition against the original colour scheme. The landmark tower will now be painted blue and gold instead of red and white, after the council's initial design sparked fury among local residents who objected to the use of Southampton Football Club's colours on one of Portsmouth's most recognisable structures. The rebranding is part of a £3.5 million sponsorship deal with airline Emirates, announced earlier this month. The tower will be renamed the Emirates Spinnaker Tower, with the new livery set to be in place in time for the America's Cup World Series sailing event in July. More than 100 litres of red paint that had already been purchased for the original scheme will now be donated to charities and community organisations across Hampshire, the council confirmed. ## A City Divided The revised blue and gold design reflects Portsmouth's traditional colours, matching those of the city and its football team. Blue has long been associated with Portsmouth, making the new scheme more palatable to local residents. Donna Jones, leader of Portsmouth City Council, defended the decision and the subsequent U-turn. "We have listened to the public and created a new blue, gold and white design that is in keeping with suggestions from residents," she said. "This gives us a unique opportunity to promote Portsmouth around the world." Ms Jones emphasised that the financial terms of the Emirates deal remained unchanged despite the design revision. She stressed the importance of the funding for the cash-strapped council: "We wouldn't have to do any of this if we weren't so desperately short of money. We have a primary school places crisis at the moment - this money is going towards building new classrooms." ## Opposition Criticism However, the Liberal Democrat opposition has criticised the council's handling of the entire affair. Councillor Ben Dowling said the saga had made Portsmouth the "laughing stock of the country." "It's good that the new design isn't red but we still have some fairly serious questions about the process that has taken place," Mr Dowling said. "Most Portsmouth people are asking'why didn't we just get asked in the first place?' - someone surely would have pointed out that red wasn't the best idea." ## Moving Forward Sir Tim Clark, President of Emirates, acknowledged the public feedback: "We listened to the feedback and worked with the council to adapt the designs in order to create something that Portsmouth residents will be proud of." An application for advertising consent has been posted on Portsmouth City Council's website, though it currently faces 13 objections. Several objectors have complained about the lack of detailed visual representations accompanying the application, making it difficult to assess the full impact of the proposed changes. The branding will remain in place for five years, until June 2022, if approved at a planning committee meeting scheduled for 7 July. The 560-foot tower, which opened in 2005, is owned by the council but operated by a private company.

Te'o Commits to Worcester Warriors Despite Injury-Hit Season Ben Te'o has pledged his commitment to Worcester Warriors for next season, dismissing speculation about his future despite an injury-disrupted campaign at Sixways. The New Zealand-born rugby league convert, 30, has played infrequently this season after joining from Irish side Leinster in the summer of 2016. He has suffered two separate concussion injuries, added to his England calls. "It's been a little bit disjointed but I want to finish the season strongly," Te'o told BBC Hereford & Worcester. "I am definitely here for next season. I am flying the Worcester flag. "I know guys like Tom Wood, Dylan Hartley and Matt Mullan were at Worcester previously. Unfortunately, they felt the need to leave. But, fingers crossed, it's not going to be the case in the future. "I haven't even thought about it. If there are people out there thinking that (he is leaving), that's not the case." Te'o, who was signed in December 2015 by then Warriors boss Dean Ryan on a one-season contract, has played in more international games for England this season (eight) than Premiership matches for Worcester (six). He has scored four tries in his eight appearances for Worcester in all competitions, plus two Six Nations tries for England against France and Italy. And, having been recalled for Friday's game at Sale, Te'o wants to be part of completing the job of ensuring safety for Warriors, who are nine points above bottom club Bristol with just four matches left. **Positional Preference** Te'o, who has made six of his seven starts for Worcester at inside centre, said: "I see myself in the long term as a 12 because of the way I am built and what I am good at. "A lot of things I am good at suits a 12 but I have also played a lot of 13. People like to talk about the two positions as a lot different but they are quite similar. We often play both roles." **Mills Future Uncertain** Warriors' options in the number 12 shirt next season may hinge on where they opt to play Ryan Mills, boss Gary Gold having stated that the 24-year-old's preferred role is also at inside centre. "Ryan is predominantly a 12 and wants to play 12," said Gold. "We want him at the club and want him to stay. "It means we need to go out and find someone to replace him as a 10 or have another back-up as a 10."
