If Mills were to leave when his contract expires at the end of the season, one option could be 66-times capped South Africa international Morne Steyn, who plays for French club Stade Francais. "He would be one of the players we would look at," said Gold. "We are in the market for a world-class 10 and he would certainly be somebody we would look at. "My understanding is he is under contract. It's a position we haven't denied we are looking at."

Former GP Andrew Johnson receives additional jail time for historical sex abuse A former GP from Bawtry, South Yorkshire, has had his prison sentence increased by 30 months after admitting to further sexual offences against patients. Andrew Johnson, 64, targeted women and girls, some as young as 12 years old. The 30-month increase to his sentence brings his total jail term to more than 14 years. He pleaded guilty on Monday to 12 counts of indecent assault against eight patients between 1978 and 1997 at GP surgeries in Doncaster. Two of Johnson's victims were under 16 at the time of the abuse, and his youngest was 12. In July 2014, Johnson was sentenced to 11 years and eight months for numerous sexual assaults against his patients. Following that trial at Sheffield Crown Court, further victims came forward to report sexual offences. Det Chf Insp Steve Whittaker said: "Johnson completely and utterly abused his position. On his own admission, he was unable to remember precisely how many victims he had abused." Johnson was struck off by the General Medical Council prior to the start of the police investigation in 2010.

Halloween 2023: Your Photos and Trick-or-Treating Tips **BBC readers have been sharing their Halloween preparations, costume ideas, and etiquette advice for the spooky season. Here's a selection of your creative pumpkin carvings, costumes, and top tips for trick-or-treating.** The Halloween spirit is alive and well, as demonstrated by Emily's adorable five-month-old kitten Ivy, photographed in anticipation of the festivities. "She's hoping to get lots of treats," Emily told us. Samuel Williamson documented his pumpkin carving competition with partner Charlie Millard, tweeting a picture of them hard at work. "My pumpkin is on the left and my partner is still working on hers," he said. The finished results, photographed with lights off, were impressively spooky – though Samuel's creation appeared to have the edge in scariness. Edinburgh resident Alexandra Choa showcased impressive artistic talent with an intricately carved pumpkin, while Jen Davidson's "small pretty pumpkin" sat alongside two other lanterns carved by her children, Cameron and Kiera. The preparations extended beyond pumpkins. Jenny Powell captured a ghoulish cloth creature attempting to frighten her daughters, who responded with mock horror. Face painting featured prominently, with Amandeep Dhami's particularly frightening efforts likely to "scare more than just the faint hearted." Even pets joined the celebrations, with Valerie's photograph of Poppy the dog dressed as a canine pumpkin proving particularly popular. ## Trick-or-Treating Etiquette Alongside the festive photos, readers shared valuable advice for Halloween night. The most common suggestion was to only visit decorated houses. Liam Flanagan-Todd offered clear guidance: "#Halloween etiquette- no pumpkin by the door means do not knock" – advice echoed by numerous other contributors. Kelly Marie had an unconventional tip for homeowners wanting to discourage visitors: offer healthy treats, suggesting this might ensure you're "left in peace the following year." Twitter user @Sweckles confirmed this strategy's effectiveness from personal experience. For those preferring to opt out of trick-or-treating entirely, readers suggested various approaches. Laura Claire switches off her doorbell, while Sarah admitted to hiding. Other creative solutions included turning off lights and pretending not to be home. However, Colin offered a different perspective, reminding everyone of the occasion's spirit of fun. BBC_HaveYourSay thanks everyone who contributed their Halloween pictures and tips, wishing all readers a happy Halloween. *When sending pictures or accounts, please ensure you don't endanger yourself or others, take unnecessary risks, or infringe any laws.*

Viral Appeal Leads to Overwhelming Support for Down's Syndrome Football Team A Londonderry-based football team for young people with Down's syndrome has been inundated with offers of support after a social media plea went viral, featuring Republic of Ireland winger James McClean. The Oxford Bulls, established with help from the Foyle Down's Syndrome Trust, were struggling to find opponents when manager Kevin Morrison made an appeal on social media. McClean responded by getting in touch and visiting the team, with a video of his visit spreading rapidly across social platforms. "The response had been so good the team could play every week for two years," said a delighted Mr Morrison. "Our first competitive match will now take place in Sion Mills on 24 April." The impact on the young players has been profound. Seamus Breslin, parent of one player, said his son "finishes school on a Friday and then plans his whole weekend around football. He absolutely loves it." John Morris, another parent, described how his son had become a local celebrity since McClean's visit, with people taking pictures of him in shops. "With James McClean coming down, they've become famous," he said. "The exposure has been unbelievable. Manchester City, Liverpool FC and UEFA have even been in contact." One mother praised the club for giving her 10-year-old son confidence and helping him make friends. "They've been treated like heroes and we couldn't believe the story was even in French Canadian papers," she said. The Foyle Down's Syndrome Trust provides various activities for young people and adults with the condition.

Asda Reports Sales Decline Despite Market Share Gains Asda, the UK supermarket chain owned by US retail giant Wal-Mart, has reported a 1.6% decline in like-for-like sales during the third quarter, marking a reversal from the 0.6% growth recorded in the previous quarter. Despite the drop in sales at stores open for more than a year compared with the previous three months, chief executive Andy Clarke expressed satisfaction with the company's performance, noting that Asda continues to gain market share in challenging conditions. "A year ago we took clear action to address the changes in our market and implement a five year strategy to redefine value retailing. That is a long term strategy that won't be delivered overnight," Mr Clarke said. He emphasised that whilst the company's focus on value for money and online shopping expansion was proving successful, market conditions remained extremely difficult. "The last quarter has seen a shockwave go through our industry and others are starting to respond to the challenges they face. I expect that we will see another tough quarter and I'm under no illusions that the battle continues to rage." Asda, which competes with Sainsbury's for the position of Britain's second-largest supermarket behind market leader Tesco, took aim at competitors' promotional tactics during a press briefing. Chief merchandising officer Barry Williams criticised rival supermarkets' heavy use of vouchers, describing several Morrisons promotions as akin to "quantitative easing" and "desperate measures." "You can win a quarter with a voucher..... We're not immune from the turbulence, but we judge our performance over a much longer period of three to five years," Mr Williams said, adding he had never seen as many money-off vouchers in his 25-year career. The comments came shortly after Sainsbury's announced £150m in price cuts as part of its new customer strategy. Mr Clarke dismissed this as "a drop in the ocean," claiming Asda's price advantage over Sainsbury's already exceeds double digits. He also asserted that Asda's Everyday Low Prices strategy is narrowing the gap with discount retailers, stating: "We are pulling away from the other three. There are very clear winners and losers in our market."

Aldershot Town Cruise to Emphatic 6-0 Victory Over Guiseley Aldershot Town recorded their biggest league victory since December 2013 with a commanding 6-0 demolition of Guiseley at the EBB Stadium on Saturday. The Shots dominated proceedings from the opening whistle and came agonisingly close to breaking the deadlock in the 14th minute when Bobby-Joe Taylor headed home from a James Rowe cross, only for the effort to be ruled out for offside. However, the home side's persistence paid off just six minutes later when Matt McClure curled a beautiful effort into the far post to give Aldershot a deserved lead. The striker's shot clipped the inside of the upright before nestling into the net, sending the home supporters into raptures. Guiseley briefly threatened when they had a goal disallowed, but any hopes of a comeback were swiftly extinguished as Aldershot turned on the style. Callum Reynolds doubled the advantage before Jim Kellerman added a third to put the contest beyond doubt. The hosts weren't finished there, though, as Shamir Fenelon grabbed a fourth goal before the interval to cap off a remarkable first-half performance that left the visitors shellshocked. The second period continued in similar fashion, with James Rowe adding his name to the scoresheet with a thunderous 20-yard drive into the bottom corner. McClure then completed the rout with his second goal of the afternoon, rounding off the comprehensive 6-0 victory. The match saw several bookings, with Guiseley's John Rooney and Robert Atkinson shown yellow cards in the first half, whilst Connor Brown and Aldershot's Will De Havilland joined them in the referee's notebook after the break. Both managers made changes throughout the contest, with Guiseley introducing Callum McFadzean, Reece Thompson, and Kayode Odejayi in search of a consolation, whilst Aldershot brought on Scott Rendell, Jake Gallagher, and Nick Arnold. The emphatic victory will provide a significant boost to Aldershot's confidence as they continue their league campaign.

Thai Activist Charged with Lese-Majeste for Sharing BBC Profile of New King Thai activist Jatupat Boonpattararaksa has been detained and charged with insulting the monarchy after sharing a BBC Thai profile of the new king on Facebook, marking the first lese-majeste charge since King Maha Vajiralongkorn's ascension to the throne. The 64-year-old monarch officially became king on Thursday, nearly two months after his father's death. Mr Jatupat, known for his involvement in anti-government protests, was arrested in Chaiyaphum province in north-eastern Thailand, with charges filed in Khon Kaen city. Under Thailand's strict royal defamation law, the activist faces up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Human rights organizations have criticized the military-backed government for allegedly weaponizing lese-majeste legislation to suppress political opposition. King Vajiralongkorn succeeded his father, the widely revered King Bhumibol Adulyadej, who died on October 13 at age 88 after reigning for seven decades. The case highlights ongoing tensions surrounding free speech and royal criticism in Thailand's current political climate.

**Barnsley Striker Joins Barrow After Grimsby Loan Spell** A 25-year-old Barnsley striker has completed a move away from Oakwell after struggling for first-team opportunities. The forward spent the first half of the season on loan at Grimsby Town, making 12 appearances but failing to find the net. Since joining Barnsley from FC Halifax a year ago, he has yet to make a starting appearance for the club. Meanwhile, Barrow have parted ways with 28-year-old winger Andy Haworth by mutual consent, who has subsequently signed for Macclesfield Town.

Judge Criticises Fertility Clinic Over Legal Parent Forms Error A fertility clinic has been sharply criticised by a High Court judge after paperwork errors left a woman fighting in court to be recognised as the legal parent of her own children. The case involved a same-sex couple who underwent fertility treatment at IVF Hammersmith Limited. One of the women gave birth to twins after the treatment. But her partner, who was the biological mother, had to go to court to be declared a legal parent - because the wrong forms were filled in at the clinic. The case is among 15 similar ones brought to the High Court. The president of the Family Division, Sir James Munby, said the clinic's lawyers had been "grossly insensitive" in their handling of the case. He granted the woman - identified only as X - a declaration that she was a legal parent of the twins in February. Giving his reasons for Wednesday's judgement, he said the women had been left "shocked and angry" when the clinic's error came to light. Sir James said the women had paid more than £15,000 for their treatment with IVF Hammersmith Limited. He described how the clinic's solicitors sent a "crass and insensitive" letter to the women, offering them £1,000 in compensation. Sir James said in his ruling: "The offer of money, whatever the amount, was merely adding insult to injury. "If an offer of financial compensation was appropriate at all, the idea that £1,000 began to approach a realistic figure was so wide of the mark as to be not merely insulting but almost offensively so. "If ever there was a situation calling for empathy, understanding, humanity, compassion and, dare one say it, common decency, never mind sincere and unqualified apology, it is surely this." The clinic's director had expressed regret in a witness statement and said there were now procedures to try and avoid any repeat of the situation. Sir James described this as a "mealy-mouthed observation". This case is among eight, involving a number of clinics, which have been resolved at the High Court, after the UK's fertility regulator identified the form-filling errors. A further seven cases are still awaiting a final court hearing. It is thought as many as 85 couples could be affected in total. A spokeswoman for IVF Hammersmith said: "We understand the stress the process and hearing has caused and we are sorry for this. "We would like to reiterate that we have learned from this case. "To safeguard all other patients receiving donor sperm, since 2013 we have introduced witnessing to the process, run dedicated staff training and operated continuous audits."

Road Closure After Motorbike Crash on Anglesey The A4080 in Llanfaelog remains closed following a motorbike incident that occurred shortly after 10:00 GMT on Friday. The motorcyclist has been transported to Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor for treatment. No other injuries were reported in the incident. Police are appealing for witnesses and are particularly keen to speak with drivers or passengers from two vehicles that were in the vicinity at the time of the crash, as they may have vital information. Motorists are advised to check if the closure is affecting their journey.

Apple iPhone 7: Petition Launched to Keep Headphone Socket **A petition calling on Apple to retain the standard headphone socket on its forthcoming iPhone 7 has attracted more than 200,000 signatures.** Online reports suggest Apple plans to omit the 3.5mm socket to make the iPhone 7 thinner and more waterproof, with more room for the battery. The Fast Company reported it would rely on the Lightning cable port, currently used for charging, for sound output. Others suggest Apple will ship the iPhone 7 with wireless headphones. The Sum of Us, a website "fighting for people over profits", which organised the petition, said: "Not only will this force iPhone users to dole out additional cash to replace their hi-fi headphones, it will singlehandedly create mountains of electronic waste that likely won't get recycled." Tech website The Verge said: "Removing [the] headphone [socket] from phones is something that no-one is asking for and has serious drawbacks including poor compatibility and accessibility, [and] DRM [digital rights management] audio [ie with built-in copyright enforcement]." ## Public Reaction Mixed Many complained on Twitter that removing the socket would render expensive headphones useless. Some complained having to use the Lightning port would mean "no music while charging". One tweeted: "I am OK with Apple removing the headphone [socket] as long as they bundle Lightning EarBuds with the iPhone 7." Others said that they would not be upgrading. But not everyone is convinced that losing the jack is a bad idea. John Gruber, who writes the technology blog Daring Fireball and is regarded as an authority on all things Apple, makes the point that losing the jack would make more room for a larger battery. "Removing the analogue headphone jack is inevitable. This is what makes Apple different. They will initiate a painful transition for a long-term gain," he writes. "In five years we'll look at analogue headphone jacks the way we look at all the other legacy ports we've abandoned." ## Apple's Audio Strategy Apple introduced support for headphones over its Lightning cable in 2014. In the same year, it paid $3bn (£2bn) for the acquisition of headphone maker Beats. And the Mac Rumours website suggests Apple could be preparing bespoke headphones for the phone. It noted that a trademark application had been filed for the term "AirPods" in October last year. And while Apple was not directly linked to these applications, the site said, "the pattern of filings is consistent with Apple's usual strategy". If the rumours prove true, it will not be the first time Apple has abandoned what it sees as outdated technology. In 1998 it released the iMac G3 without a floppy disk, leaving many questioning the wisdom of the move. But, just more than a decade later, Sony - a pioneer of the floppy disk - announced it was killing off the storage device.

Hamilton Critical of Own Form Despite Victory at UK Championship Nottingham-born snooker player Anthony Hamilton delivered a scathing assessment of his own performance despite advancing to the last 64 of the UK Championship with a hard-fought 6-5 victory over Craig Steadman. The 43-year-old, who once reached number 10 in the world rankings, showed little optimism about his chances ahead of his Saturday evening clash with former world champion Graeme Dott. "It was rubbish - seriously. I can't play any worse," Hamilton told BBC Sport after his opening-round success. "It was a good attitude but rubbish snooker. I am rubbish now a lot of the time." Hamilton, who turned professional in 1991, enjoyed a distinguished career that included five years in the world's top 16. He reached two ranking event finals and competed in four World Championship quarter-finals, with his last appearance in the last eight coming in 2007. However, recent years have been challenging for the veteran player. Plagued by a persistent neck injury, Hamilton had slipped to number 50 in the world rankings by the time the York tournament began. Despite praising the quality of the tables at the venue, Hamilton lamented his declining form. "The tables are gorgeous," he said. "A few years ago I would have been making 80 every poke, now I am making eight every poke. I am getting old basically. It's no fun but it's better than working." Interestingly, Hamilton suggested that facing a top-class opponent like Dott might actually work in his favour. "I will probably play better against a top player," he explained. "They go for their shots, force the issue and if they miss they are in position so the chances come easier. You get fewer chances but the chances are better. I might be able to glean some old school form." He added: "Graeme might be a bit too clever for me now I am old and rubbish. But if I play well then I have a chance, it's simple." Hamilton's match against Steadman was complicated by an unusual incident before play began. The Muswell Hill resident was docked a frame for being late after waiting in the wrong location. "I came out of the dressing room and saw some players standing around waiting and just joined them," Hamilton explained. "My lot were over the other side, but obviously I didn't know that. I was only there a couple of minutes. By the time I got there I was late so I got docked a frame." Despite accepting responsibility, Hamilton suggested there had been insufficient information about the dual assembly points. However, he recovered from the setback, noting: "I got over it straight away and that was the only time I played well."

Government Suffers Defeat on Constituency Boundary Review The coalition government has suffered a significant defeat in the House of Lords over plans to redraw parliamentary constituency boundaries, with Liberal Democrat ministers breaking ranks to vote against their Conservative partners for the first time. The House of Lords approved a cross-party amendment to delay the review of parliamentary constituencies until 2018, effectively pushing the changes beyond the next general election. The amendment passed with a substantial majority of 69 votes, marking a dramatic rupture in the coalition partnership. Prime Minister David Cameron now faces a critical decision on whether to attempt to overturn the Lords vote when the legislation returns to the House of Commons. However, with Deputy Prime Minister Nick Clegg having instructed Liberal Democrat MPs to oppose the boundary changes, the prospects for a Conservative victory appear slim. At the heart of the dispute is the Conservative plan to reduce the number of MPs from 650 to 600, including a reduction from 40 to 30 seats in Wales, where constituencies typically have smaller electorates. Political analysts have suggested the review could deliver approximately 20 additional seats to the Conservatives, potentially proving crucial to their chances of winning the next general election. Conservative MP Glyn Davies, who observed the Lords debate, acknowledged the vote would "really put cat among pigeons." He questioned on Twitter whether the government would attempt to reverse the amendment, noting that the 69-vote majority would embolden opposition in the Commons. Speculation has emerged that David Cameron might seek support from smaller Westminster parties. However, the Scottish National Party quickly dismissed such prospects, stating: "There have been no discussions and no deal will be done on the boundary review." The SNP also criticised what they described as "fall-out and petty score-settling between the Tories and Lib Dems," suggesting the entire process may have been "a waste of time and waste of money." Plaid Cymru, whose three MPs form a joint parliamentary party with the SNP's six representatives, appeared equally reluctant to negotiate unless the UK government offers substantial devolution of powers from Westminster to Cardiff Bay. Even with such concessions, the parliamentary arithmetic appears unfavourable for the Conservatives. The political uncertainty has prompted the Conservative Party to select candidates for 2015 based on existing constituency boundaries rather than the proposed new ones. Downing Street confirmed the government would attempt to overturn the Lords vote in the Commons. A spokesman said: "The PM remains of the view that we should have fewer MPs to cut the cost of politics, and more equal size constituencies so that people's votes have more equal weight." However, Nick Clegg's comments suggest the prime minister faces an uphill battle. The Deputy Prime Minister told the BBC: "We are leaving the boundary changes on the statute book but we are saying that we should miss a beat and do it in the next parliament not this one."

Bosworth Sets British Record Despite Stomach Issues in Olympic Race Walk British race walker Tom Bosworth finished sixth in the Olympic 20km race walk despite battling illness, but celebrated breaking the national record by a significant margin. China's Wang Zhen claimed gold in a time of one hour, 19 minutes and 14 seconds, improving on his bronze medal from London 2012. His compatriot Cai Zelin took silver, also bettering his fourth-place finish from four years ago. Australia's Dane Bird-Smith rounded out the podium with bronze. Bosworth had positioned himself among the race leaders during the opening hour before Wang and Cai pulled away in the final stages. Despite the challenging circumstances, the British athlete remained philosophical about his performance. "I can't be disappointed with sixth place at the Olympics but I could have done better as I had a dodgy stomach last night and that affected me a little bit," said Bosworth. He added: "To break the British Record by such a margin and at the Olympics is a dream come true. It was just an amazing experience. I'm so happy I cannot put it into words." The performance marks a career highlight for Bosworth despite the physical difficulties he faced during the competition.

Studio in Talks to Adapt Brexit Campaign Book for Television An unnamed Hollywood studio is reportedly in negotiations to adapt "The Bad Boys of Brexit" into a television series, with Benedict Cumberbatch rumored to play Nigel Farage, the former UKIP leader and prominent Brexit campaigner. The potential six-part adaptation is based on former UKIP donor Arron Banks's book, which chronicles the chaotic journey of Mr Farage's Brexit campaign. According to the Sunday Times, talks between the studio and Mr Banks are scheduled to take place next month in Los Angeles. Mr Farage, speaking to BBC News, confirmed he was not directly involved in the project but joked about the casting speculation: "I have to play myself, obviously." However, he suggested the adaptation's appeal extends beyond Brexit itself, noting that interest has been generated because the story is "linked directly to Mr Trump's presidency itself." The connection to American politics appears to be a key selling point. Mr Farage appeared alongside then-candidate Donald Trump on the campaign trail last year, with Trump expressing hopes of replicating Brexit's upset of the political establishment. Since then, Mr Farage has become a frequent visitor to the United States, working as a Fox News contributor and maintaining close ties with the Trump administration. He was notably the first British politician to meet Trump after his inauguration and has dined with the president at his Washington DC hotel. "As an idea it [Brexit] has taken America by storm," Mr Farage told BBC News, adding that he is often "accosted in the street" by Americans wanting to discuss the topic. Publisher Biteback describes the book as a tale that lurches "from comedy to crisis (often several times a day)" during the EU referendum campaign. Biteback boss Iain Dale told the Daily Mail there is a "real appetite for this kind of thing" in America, citing the success of political dramas like House of Cards. The script has reportedly been written from the perspective of Gerry Gunster, an American pollster who advised Mr Banks's Leave.EU campaign. Andy Wigmore, a close associate of Mr Banks, revealed they were approached about the adaptation just before Christmas while visiting Trump in New York, initially thinking it was a "joke" before realizing it was "very serious." Mr Farage has ruled out a fourth bid for UKIP leadership.

Cardiff City Manager Neil Warnock Plans Squad Overhaul Ahead of New Season Cardiff City manager Neil Warnock has confirmed that several players will be departing the Championship club before the start of the upcoming season as he looks to streamline his squad. The Welsh side has already seen the exits of midfielder Peter Whittingham, striker Rickie Lambert, and young prospect Emyr Huws. Now, wingers Craig Noone and Anthony Pilkington, along with left-back Declan John, are reportedly among those who could be leaving Cardiff City Stadium. "There's players who won't be here at the start of the season," Warnock stated. "Fans might guess without me telling them really. I don't envisage going with more than about 21 or 22 players this year." The manager's comments came after Cardiff's pre-season friendly against Welsh League Division One side Taffs Well, which also served as a charity event. Pilkington scored the winner in the match, while four new signings made their debuts for the Bluebirds. Winger Nathaniel Mendez-Laing, goalkeeper Neil Etheridge, striker Danny Ward, and midfielder Loic Damour all featured against Taffs Well. "Thanks to all the fans because it was a super night," Warnock said. "I was pleased with our lads' attitude and it was a great night all round."

MPs Reject Calls to Postpone EU Referendum Date The House of Commons has decisively rejected a motion to delay the EU referendum, despite a cross-party appeal from representatives of devolved administrations who warned the June date would interfere with regional elections. The motion was defeated by 286 votes to 70 on Tuesday, following an impassioned debate in which MPs from Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales expressed concerns about the timing of the referendum. The DUP's deputy leader, Nigel Dodds, led the calls for postponement, urging the government to respect the wishes of the devolved administrations. "It needs to be treated with the respect it deserves," he told the Commons. "We hear a lot about the respect agenda and about taking on board the views of the administrations in the devolved countries of the UK and this now needs to be put into practice." The first ministers of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales have all written jointly to Prime Minister David Cameron expressing opposition to a late June referendum date. Nicola Sturgeon, Carwyn Jones and Arlene Foster warned that holding the vote so soon after devolved elections would "confuse" the process and make it difficult for them to campaign effectively. However, Mr Cameron has maintained his position that voters will be capable of distinguishing between the different polls. During the debate, Mr Dodds emphasised that the European debate should "not impinge on other elections due to take place this year, including to the Scottish Parliament as well as the Welsh and Northern Ireland Assemblies." Independent MP Lady Sylvia Hermon, despite supporting the UK's continued EU membership, backed the call for delay. She urged the prime minister to confirm he would visit Northern Ireland to campaign, but only after the Assembly elections. The UUP's Danny Kinahan used a Doctor Who analogy to illustrate his concerns about the uncertainty surrounding the referendum. "It's like we're trying to make a decision and all those that want to leave are charging into the Tardis," he said, adding that he wanted "the electorate to know what they are voting for." The SDLP's Margaret Ritchie argued that a period of purdah from March to June would be undemocratic, as "it prevents ministers, it prevents MPs and it prevents members of devolved administrations from properly representing their constituents." Despite these concerns, the government has pressed ahead with its proposed referendum date.

Syrian Surgeon Struggles with Language Test to Resume Medical Career in UK A Syrian surgeon who fled his homeland and was granted asylum in the UK is unable to practice medicine because he cannot pass the required English language test, despite Wales facing a significant shortage of doctors. Hussam arrived in the UK in 2014 using a fake passport, escaping a country torn apart by civil war. While he has been granted asylum and safety, his professional life remains in limbo. Before he can register with the General Medical Council (GMC) and apply for positions as a surgeon, he must achieve an 80% mark on a specialized English language examination. Despite taking the test five times, Hussam has been unable to reach the required threshold. His brother Shadi, also a qualified doctor from Syria, faces the same predicament, having failed the test on five occasions as well. The brothers have now opened a currency exchange shop on City Road to support themselves financially. "I didn't come here because I wanted a better life. I was forced to come here to find a life," Hussam explained. "I used to be a surgeon and suddenly my life has been changed..... I was forced to leave." Shadi argues that the language requirements are unreasonably demanding: "To reach this level we need to have a very high level of English language. Even the native speakers can't reach this level." The situation is particularly frustrating given that the British Medical Association has reported Wales is short of 400 doctors, highlighting the cruel irony of qualified medical professionals being unable to fill desperately needed positions. Hussam's decision to flee Syria came after several of his colleagues disappeared following arrests by government forces. He believes they were taken to Saydnaya prison, a facility that Amnesty International has accused of executing up to 50 people daily without proper trials. "It's a nightmare. I don't know yet if they are alive or not," he said, adding that he feared it was only a matter of time before authorities came for him. Upon arriving in Cardiff, Hussam learned English through the refugee charity Oasis and subsequently worked for the organization, helping other refugees navigate housing and asylum claims. However, two-and-a-half years later, his dream of returning to medicine remains unfulfilled. "Before I came here I thought it would be a few months and I would get the language and be able to communicate with people and be at a hospital. But after two-and-a-half years I'm still dreaming about it," he said. The longing for his former profession is so strong that Hussam regularly visits the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, standing outside the accident and emergency department. "I come here quite often, I miss being a doctor," he admitted. Despite the setbacks and occasional doubts about whether leaving Syria was the right decision, Hussam maintains hope: "One day you will see me here wearing the uniform and you can say,'hello Dr Hussam'." Hussam's story is featured in the BBC Wales documentary "Strangers in a strange land."

Doctors Urged to Monitor Colleagues Over Antibiotic Prescriptions in Fight Against Drug Resistance Doctors should monitor each other's prescribing habits and resist pressure from demanding patients as part of urgent new measures to tackle the growing crisis of antimicrobial resistance, according to draft guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE). The proposals come after years of failed policies to reduce antibiotic use, with prescription rates rising by 6% between 2010 and 2013. Alarmingly, experts estimate that half of all antibiotic prescriptions during this period were "inappropriate," despite repeated warnings about the catastrophic threat posed by drug-resistant infections. Prof Mike Baker, director of the centre for clinical practice at NICE, acknowledged the severity of the situation. "Antibiotic use has gone up and up and up each year despite a number of initiatives to damp down on their use," he said. "We have to turn this tanker around." The guidelines, which establish best practice for the NHS, introduce several controversial recommendations, including the concept of peer pressure among medical professionals. "Health professionals should question the practices of colleagues when they are not in line with local and national guidelines," Prof Baker told the BBC News website. "I think peer pressure has to be a part of any strategy to reduce antimicrobial use." The draft rules also address the difficult issue of patient expectations, urging doctors to become more comfortable refusing requests for antibiotics. "Patient pressure is a real problem and it puts GPs under pressure, and they can be afraid of not prescribing antibiotics even when they know it's wrong," Prof Baker explained. Under the proposed guidelines, doctors would spend more time explaining to patients why antibiotics are unsuitable for many conditions. The recommendations also encourage wider use of "watchful waiting" strategies, where antibiotics are only prescribed if a patient's condition fails to improve naturally. However, Prof Baker stressed that the approach required careful judgment. "These ideas were not a'blunt instrument' and doctors needed to'walk a tightrope,'" he warned, noting that withholding antibiotics inappropriately could lead to serious complications such as sepsis in some cases. The stakes could not be higher. Without effective antibiotics, routine surgeries, chemotherapy treatments, and organ transplants become impossibly dangerous. The rise of resistant bacteria threatens to strip doctors of one of their most powerful weapons against infection, potentially returning medicine to a pre-antibiotic era. England's chief medical officer, Prof Dame Sally Davies, welcomed the initiative. "Preserving the effectiveness of the antibiotics we have is absolutely crucial and everybody, including patients, has a role to play," she said, encouraging prescribers to participate in the consultation process. Dr Maureen Baker, chairwoman of the Royal College of GPs, supported the team approach outlined in the guidelines. "Antibiotics have served us well in treating infections for over 60 years, but as a society we have become too dependent on them and they are now seen as a'catch-all' for every illness and infection," she said. The Royal College emphasized that GPs, practice teams, and pharmacists must work together to discuss alternatives with patients seeking antibiotics for minor illnesses, most of which resolve naturally over time. The consultation on these draft guidelines represents a crucial step in addressing one of the most serious threats to modern healthcare.

Michael Jones, 46, must serve 25 years for killing his son Adrian. The boy's step-mother, Heather Jones, 31, has already been jailed for the same crime. A Kansas father has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for the killing of his seven-year-old son, Adrian Jones, a case that has shocked the state and spurred calls for stronger child protection laws. Michael Jones received the sentence after officials detailed the horrific abuse Adrian endured in the final year of his life. Heather Jones, Adrian’s stepmother, is already serving time for her role in the crime. Adrian’s remains were discovered in November 2015 in a barn on a property rented by the Jones family. Authorities believe the boy died months earlier from starvation. Investigators initially went to the home after receiving reports of domestic abuse. While the couple awaited trial, their landlord found photos and videos on their computer that meticulously documented the abuse Adrian suffered. During sentencing, Detective Stuart Littlefield struggled to contain his emotions as he described what he called the worst crime he had witnessed in his 23-year career. “Imagine the screams of a 7-year-old boy,” he said, recounting the abuse and its aftermath. The case has prompted legislative action. State Representative Louis Ruiz has introduced “Adrian’s Act,” a bill that would require family members or other household residents to report suspected abuse to authorities. Under current Kansas law, only mandated reporters—such as healthcare workers, teachers, social workers, and law enforcement officers—are legally obligated to report. Adrian’s grandmother, Judy Conway, praised the proposal, saying, “If you witness child abuse, I don’t care if you’re a mandated reporter or not, we should report these things.” Lawmakers will now consider whether to expand reporting requirements in hopes of preventing similar tragedies.

Talks between Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil on forming a minority government resume today, after both sides described Friday’s discussions as constructive. Fianna Fáil leader Micheál Martin said his party would facilitate a government but will not sign up to a formal programme, adding that “understandings” would be offered, though he did not specify whether they would be written. The stance comes despite Fianna Fáil having campaigned against the outgoing Fine Gael administration in the recent election. February’s poll left no party with a majority: Fine Gael won 50 seats, Fianna Fáil 44, Sinn Féin 23 and Labour seven. With the Dáil unable to elect a leader on three previous votes, pressure is mounting on the main parties to bridge differences and end the impasse.

Stephen Anthony Hough, 58, was due to go on trial at Mold Crown Court, but proceedings were adjourned after delays on Monday. Mr Justice Lewis has set a new date of 26 June. Hough, of Maes y Dre, Flint, denies the murder of 15-year-old Janet Commins in January 1976 and has pleaded not guilty to charges of rape and a further sexual offence. Miss Commins’ body was found under a hedge in a school playing field in Flint. The judge was told one reason for the adjournment was the unavailability of prosecuting barrister Elwern Evans QC, who had spent the previous night in hospital. Senior officers are to speak to Miss Commins’ mother to explain the postponement. The case, which revisits a killing that shocked the Flint community four decades ago, will return to Mold Crown Court on the rescheduled date.

Emma Baum, 22, was found dead with head injuries in the garden of her Llwyndu Road home in Penygroes, near Caernarfon, on 18 July. David Nicholas Davies, of Clynnog, appeared at Mold Crown Court on Tuesday and was remanded in custody. A provisional trial is scheduled for November at Caernarfon Crown Court. Police continue investigation, and residents have expressed shock at the incident.

A Norwich police sergeant has taken to social media to give residents a candid look at night-time policing in the city centre. Sgt Mark Shepherd, of the Norwich South Safer Neighbourhood Team, shared photographs and updates on Twitter throughout his weekend shift, highlighting the realities of late-night incidents and the importance of public engagement. Figures released by police earlier this year indicate that more than half of violent crime in Norwich occurs between 21:00 and 06:00. Posting from after 22:00 on Saturday until after 05:00 on Sunday, Shepherd used the hashtag “#SelfiesWithCops” as he documented call-outs and offered safety messages. One tweet described “a few assaults coming in now. Also collapsed drunks,” and urged people to “#DrinkResponsibly #KnowYourLimits #AlcoholHarm Think, how will you get home?” Shepherd said the approach aims to humanise officers and build trust: “This hopefully shows we are human. People love the fact they are getting put on social media. Engagement is really important and we regularly get asked for photos. This takes it a small step further.” The posts drew supportive responses from users, with one writing, “great sport Mark, loving the picture. You even look like you were enjoying it!” A Norfolk Police spokesperson said social media plays a positive role in policing, helping inform the public about incidents and providing another way for officers to keep in touch with residents.

London Fire Brigade has urged the public to think twice before dialling 999 after a steady rise in callouts to free people stuck in everyday objects, costing taxpayers at least £377,000. The brigade says each incident costs around £290 to attend. Crews were called to 416 incidents in 2010–11, 441 in 2011–12 and 453 in 2012–13. Firefighters say many could be avoided with greater care. The most frequent mishaps involved handcuffs, prompting 79 callouts since 2010. Other emergencies included men with their genitals trapped in a toaster and a vacuum cleaner. “Some of the incidents our firefighters are called out to could be prevented with a little common sense,” said Third Officer Dave Brown. “I don’t know whether it’s the Fifty Shades effect, but incidents involving items like handcuffs seem to have gone up.” The brigade advises anyone using handcuffs to keep keys within reach and to consider alternatives before calling 999. Children were also frequent patients: 18 had heads stuck in potties or toilet seats, and 17 got fingers caught in toys, including one with a piece of Lego on his finger and another with a tambourine over his head. The service urged Londoners to use common sense, read instructions, and seek further non-emergency advice before tying up valuable 999 resources.

Macedonian soldiers erected a new fence along the country’s southern border with Greece on Saturday in an effort to manage the surge of migrants moving through the Balkans, prompting clashes on the Greek side. Dozens of migrants, stranded after neighboring countries tightened entry rules, threw stones as the barrier went up. Aid groups said some 20 migrants were treated for head injuries and breathing problems. Macedonia’s interior ministry reported that 18 police officers were injured, two of whom were hospitalized. Reports suggest Macedonian police briefly crossed into Greek territory and fired stun grenades to disperse rioters, as tensions flared near the official crossing at Idomeni. Footage from the scene showed groups chanting “Open, open” before the confrontations broke out. According to the Associated Press, roughly 250 people were involved in the clashes, with as many as 800 migrants stranded on the Greek side. Macedonia stressed it is not closing the border entirely. A government spokesman said the newly erected fence is intended to redirect people to designated crossing points. Those crossings, however, are now limited to refugees from Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan, mirroring new restrictions imposed by Slovenia, Croatia, and Serbia. Migrants from other countries—including Iran, Morocco, and Pakistan—are being refused entry, triggering growing protests. On Thursday, hundreds of people from Morocco, Algeria, and Pakistan tore down a section of barbed wire, and others have engaged in extreme demonstrations, including sewing their mouths shut. In a separate incident on Saturday, a Moroccan man denied entry into Macedonia suffered severe burns after climbing onto a train carriage and touching a live wire, as frustration and desperation mounted among those blocked from continuing their journey. “I have been here for 10 days with my two sons,” said Fatemeh, an Iranian woman stranded at the border. “We have decided to return to Athens and see what we will do.” The International Organization for Migration (IOM) estimates that 105,000 migrants passed through Macedonia after arriving in Greece this month alone. From 1 January to 25 November, 721,217 migrants reached Greece, including 217,936 in October, compared with 34,442 in all of 2014. Between January and October, 388,130 Syrians arrived, and throughout 2015 close to 720,000 people—mainly from Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan—have come to Greece, with most then moving north through Macedonia toward destinations such as Germany and Scandinavia. A note on terminology: The BBC uses the term “migrant” to refer to all people on the move who have yet to complete the legal process of claiming asylum. This includes those fleeing conflict who are likely to be granted refugee status, as well as people seeking jobs and better lives, whom authorities may classify as economic migrants.

Former Burundian army chief Col Jean Bikomagu was gunned down as he drove through the gates of his home in Bujumbura, a family member told AFP. His daughter was badly injured in the attack. Authorities have not named suspects, but the killing adds to a wave of violence that has swept Burundi since President Pierre Nkurunziza sought and won a controversial third term. Burundi’s 1993–2005 civil war was fought along ethnic lines, with mostly Hutu rebels battling the politically dominant Tutsi minority. Bikomagu led the Tutsi-dominated armed forces during the conflict, while Nkurunziza belonged to a Hutu rebel movement. A peace deal paved the way for Nkurunziza’s election in 2005. His bid for a third term in July sparked months of unrest, with opposition parties and many voters calling it unconstitutional. The turmoil has forced more than 100,000 people to flee this year to neighboring countries.

The waterway was completely restored by volunteers after falling into decline and was officially reopened by the Queen on 8 August 1990. It was originally opened in 1810, but gradually fell into decline after the Great Western Railway was built. Volunteers will re-enact the reopening at the Caen Hill lock flight, which is a Scheduled Ancient Monument later. The 87-mile waterway links the River Thames at Reading to the River Avon in Bath. The last time the complete length was navigable, before it was restored, was in 1950, when a stoppage at Burghfield near Reading made the canal impassable. Major structures along its route also include the Dundas and Avoncliff aqueducts and Bruce Tunnel. Richard Parry, chief executive of the Canal and River Trust, said: "It's all down to the volunteers and the incredible amount of work they did that [the canal] is here. "The Kennet and Avon Canal really does enrich the lives of everyone around it, and this is a great opportunity to celebrate it and the achievement of those who restored it." Rob Dean, chairman of the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust, said: "Restoration of the Kennet and Avon has proved a huge success for our community. "The volunteers who led the restoration from the 50s to the 90s have given us a great legacy which we're pleased to help care for and improve." The success of the canal restoration spurred on the other restorations across the country. Volunteers are set to re-enact the 1990 reopening of the Kennet and Avon Canal at the Caen Hill lock flight, marking a milestone for a waterway that was brought back from decline through decades of community effort. First opened in 1810, the 87-mile canal links the River Thames at Reading with the River Avon in Bath. Its fortunes waned after the advent of the Great Western Railway, and by 1950 a stoppage at Burghfield near Reading had rendered the full length impassable. A volunteer-led restoration followed, culminating in a ceremony on 8 August 1990 when the Queen reopened the route. “It’s all down to the volunteers and the incredible amount of work they did that [the canal] is here,” said Richard Parry, chief executive of the Canal and River Trust. “The Kennet and Avon Canal really does enrich the lives of everyone around it, and this is a great opportunity to celebrate it and the achievement of those who restored it.” Rob Dean, chairman of the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust, added: “Restoration of the Kennet and Avon has proved a huge success for our community. The volunteers who led the restoration from the 50s to the 90s have given us a great legacy which we’re pleased to help care for and improve.” Major landmarks along the route include the Dundas and Avoncliff aqueducts and the Bruce Tunnel. The canal’s revival is credited with inspiring further restoration projects across the country.

Think Like a Man Too tops slow box office as Jersey Boys underwhelms; Maleficent crosses $500m worldwide Kevin Hart’s Las Vegas ensemble comedy Think Like a Man Too led a sluggish North American box office, debuting with an estimated $30 million (£17.6m) and narrowly edging 22 Jump Street, which collected $29 million (£17m) in its second weekend. The modest frame saw holdovers dominate as audiences split among sequels and summer tentpoles. DreamWorks Animation’s How to Train Your Dragon 2 slipped to third with $25.3 million (£14.8m), ensuring the weekend’s top three titles were all sequels. Despite a mere 22% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, Think Like a Man Too drew loyal fans, proving critical pans could not dent its appeal. “This success is all about Kevin Hart,” said Paul Dergarabedian, senior analyst at box-office tracker Rentrak. “He’s a bona fide movie star. He’s versatile, he’s so well liked and he’s super funny. Talking about what actors are bankable and consistent, he’s right there in that group.” The comedian has now headlined three films this year to open north of $25 million, following January’s Ride Along and February’s About Last Night. Clint Eastwood’s Jersey Boys, a screen adaptation of the Tony Award-winning musical about Frankie Valli and the Four Seasons, opened to a muted $13.5 million (£7.9m). Featuring a largely unfamiliar cast aside from Christopher Walken, the film earned mixed reviews and a 55% Rotten Tomatoes score. Time’s Richard Corliss called it “a turgid botch,” while USA Today’s Claudia Puig wrote that what was “blandly charming on stage” feels “contrived, cheesy and cliched” on screen. Nearly three-quarters of Jersey Boys’ opening audience was over the age of 50, a demographic that tends to avoid opening-weekend rushes, giving the studio hope for steadier play in coming weeks. The stage show, which won the Tony for best musical in 2006 and has played across the globe including London’s West End, remains a potent brand with older moviegoers. Rounding out the top five, Angelina Jolie’s live-action fairy tale Maleficent continued its robust international run, surpassing $500 million (£293m) worldwide. That makes it Jolie’s highest-grossing live-action film to date on an unadjusted basis, eclipsing her previous mark with 2005’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith, which finished with $478.2 million. Overall, the frame reflected a slower summer corridor, with studios eyeing upcoming releases to re-energize the market and broaden appeal well beyond sequel-driven fare. Family fare remained a steady draw.

The U.S. Department of Justice has accused activist investor ValueAct Capital of failing to fully disclose the extent of its stakes and influence in Halliburton and Baker Hughes while the oilfield services rivals pursued a $35 billion merger announced in 2014. ValueAct purchased about $2.5 billion worth of shares in the two companies after the deal was unveiled, becoming one of their largest shareholders during an ongoing antitrust review. “ValueAct’s substantial stock purchases made it one of the largest shareholders of two competitors in the midst of our antitrust review of the companies’ proposed merger, and ValueAct used its position to influence decision-making at both companies,” Assistant Attorney General Bill Baer said. The Justice Department alleges the firm leveraged access to executives to influence the outcome of the transaction and did not fully disclose its role. ValueAct denied the accusations, saying, “We fundamentally disagree with the Department of Justice’s allegations in this case.” The Halliburton-Baker Hughes merger, initially slated to close by the end of last year, remains delayed amid antitrust scrutiny.

Two men have been charged with the murder of Neel Croos, 26, who died from a head injury after a fight on Holborn Way, Mitcham, on 23 November. Gowrishanth Loganathan, 21, of Cambridge Road, Mitcham, and Mohanran Parimalanathan, 22, of Stafford Road, Wallington, will appear at Wimbledon Magistrates’ Court. Both face a charge of violent disorder, while Mr Parimalanathan is accused of possessing an offensive weapon. Three other men have previously been charged with Mr Croos’s murder. A 23-year-old arrested on 17 December on suspicion of murder has been bailed until January. Five men detained in connection with the incident have been released with no further action.

A Welsh farmer has warned of the severe distress livestock suffer when chased by dogs, likening it to “running after a heavily pregnant woman with a motor car.” Gareth Wyn Jones, of Llanfairfechan, issued the stark comparison as new figures show more than 300 dogs have been shot by landowners in England and Wales over the past five years. The data was obtained through a Freedom of Information request by the BBC. Under current law, farmers are permitted to shoot dogs that pose an immediate threat to animals, but they must notify police within 48 hours. Jones told BBC 5 Live that public awareness remains dangerously low about the risks of walking dogs near livestock, especially during vulnerable periods such as lambing. “I don’t think farmers take it lightly on shooting people’s dogs. It has to come to the final straw,” he said. Jones recounted a personal incident in which repeated lamb losses led him to take action. “I’ve had to do it and it’s not a nice situation to be in. We’d lost a few lambs night after night and this dog was getting let out of the house very early in the morning.” Calling for greater responsibility, Jones said owners must keep dogs under control at all times. “[Dogs] are natural born killers. That’s what their jobs are; they are to herd or to hunt. People must understand that it’s their responsibility to take control, put their dogs on the lead, not leave them out at all times. We’ve got to drum this into them.”

Farrell fires Saracens past Leicester as Tuilagi limps off in bruising Premiership clash Saracens edged a gripping encounter at Welford Road, defeating Leicester Tigers 16-12 in a match defined by ferocious defenses, costly missed kicks and high-profile injuries watched closely by England head coach Eddie Jones. Owen Farrell was the difference, trading first-half penalties with Tigers fly-half Owen Williams before adding a third after the break and then scoring and converting the game’s only try to secure a vital away win. With the sides locked at 6-6 at halftime, the opening period offered little daylight between two of the Premiership’s heavyweights. Farrell and Williams were flawless from the tee early on, capitalizing on infringements in a tense, tactical battle. The match’s tone shifted when Manu Tuilagi, recalled to England’s training camp only a day earlier, was forced off with an apparent right knee injury after landing awkwardly in a tackle, curtailing his comeback to a brief cameo and prompting concern for both club and country. Saracens suffered their own setback when winger Chris Ashton, making his first start in 15 weeks following suspension for biting, departed after a clash of heads with Leicester center Jack Roberts. Yet the visitors struck decisively soon after. A loose pass from Ben Youngs was mishandled by Williams, allowing Brad Barritt to pounce before Farrell threw a deft dummy and accelerated clear to finish under the posts, adding the conversion for a seven-point swing. Leicester remained in the hunt and ultimately claimed a losing bonus point thanks to Williams’ two second-half penalties, but pressure in the closing stages went unrewarded. Two missed kicks from Williams proved pivotal as Saracens absorbed late Tigers attacks and closed out the result to move within a single point of leaders Wasps at the top of the Premiership table. Despite the defeat—only their second in 15 home games across all competitions—Leicester took heart from a powerful forward display. Director of rugby Richard Cockerill praised his pack and defensive effort, insisting the performance offered belief for the run-in. “It was tight, we played very well, they played well. We defended outstandingly well and our set-piece was dominant,” he said. “Saracens’ pack don’t get dominated very often but we dominated their pack today. Our boys were fantastic. There are a lot of positives. I know we are five points from the top four but we were playing the best side in Europe last season. If we can play like that away we will win more than we lose and we will keep in the mix.” Saracens director of rugby Mark McCall admitted it was far from a complete performance but lauded his side’s resolve. “We are chuffed to bits to come here and win where they have not lost this season,” he said. “Not everything in our game was perfect, far from it. But what was tremendous was the fight we had and the effort we showed all the way through the game. We had to win without a platform because our scrum today was poor. To get a result without a scrum is tough.” Referee: JP Doyle. For the latest rugby union news follow @bbcrugbyunion on Twitter.

An ebonised wooden desk clock linked to Winston Churchill’s wartime Whitehall complex drew limited interest at auction on Friday, despite a £400–£600 estimate. The clock, stamped “PM” on the back and gifted in 1945 to George Rance, a clerk and custodian of the complex beneath Whitehall in London, had been described as having “fantastic provenance” by auctioneers Stride & Son of Chichester, West Sussex. Peter Parker of the auction house said he was “very disappointed” by the outcome. Ahead of the sale, Conservative MP Sir Nicholas Soames, Churchill’s grandson, said he could imagine the clock on his grandfather’s desk, underscoring its evocative historical association.

Republic of Ireland’s preparations for Friday’s World Cup qualifier against Wales have suffered another setback after a Newcastle United forward withdrew with a calf problem and returned to his club for treatment. The latest blow adds to a mounting list of absences for manager Martin O’Neill, who has already lost Wes Hoolahan, Shane Duffy, Ciaran Clark and Harry Arter, while Burnley winger Robbie Brady is suspended. Everton’s James McCarthy is being monitored for a hamstring issue that kept him out of his club’s win over Hull City on Saturday, leaving his participation at the Aviva Stadium in doubt. “He’ll just take it on a day-to-day basis,” O’Neill said on Monday. “He thinks that he might be able to make it — that would be great if he can. If he doesn’t, well, we’ll just have to do without him.” There were further concerns on Tuesday as Southampton striker Shane Long, Everton full-back and captain Seamus Coleman, and Aberdeen midfielder Johnny Hayes sat out the morning training session as a precaution. O’Neill will hope the trio can train later in the week as he weighs up his options. Despite the disruption, Ireland remain in a strong position in Group D, unbeaten and top with 10 points from four games. Chris Coleman’s Wales, semi-finalists at Euro 2016, sit third, four points back, and arrive in Dublin needing a result to reignite their campaign. O’Neill is expected to lean on senior figures such as goalkeeper Darren Randolph, defender John O’Shea, midfielders Glenn Whelan, Jeff Hendrick and James McClean, and forwards Jonathan Walters and Kevin Doyle as Ireland look to maintain momentum in a pivotal qualifier.

The Cobblers finished this season as League Two champions under Wilder Northampton Town’s title-winning season has been followed by uncertainty over the future of manager Chris Wilder, who confirmed he is considering his next move after leading the club to promotion. “My relationship with the chairman and the fans is going to make this a very difficult decision, but I do feel at this stage of my career it is one I need to explore,” said Wilder, 48. Under Wilder, Northampton surged 13 points clear of second-placed Oxford United, powered by a remarkable 24-game unbeaten run. Their success came despite significant off-field turmoil, including financial uncertainty linked to £10.25m in outstanding loan repayments to the local council and a winding-up petition from HM Revenue & Customs. BBC Radio Northampton will host a Monday Night Sport phone-in from 18:00-19:00 BST to discuss Wilder’s potential departure and what it could mean for the club. Elsewhere, Charlton Athletic have confirmed the resignation of manager Jose Riga following the Addicks’ relegation to League One. The Belgian returned to The Valley in January after the sacking of Karel Fraeye but was unable to halt the slide into the third tier. Charlton supporters staged protests on Saturday against owner Roland Duchatelet as the team fell to a 3-0 home defeat to Championship winners Burnley, underscoring ongoing tensions at the club.

Gir Sanctuary’s Most Photographed Lion, Ram, Dies at 15 Ram, one of Gir Sanctuary’s most iconic Asiatic lions, died on Saturday at approximately 15 years of age, officials in Gujarat confirmed. Forest staff described him as “beautiful” and “flamboyant,” and many regarded him as the reserve’s “most photographed lion,” a testament to his striking presence and long reign over the forest. Deputy Conservator of Forests Ram Ratan Nala told the BBC that a post-mortem was conducted to determine the cause of death. “He died from natural causes. He was cremated in the presence of government and local village officials,” Nala said. The loss resonated across nearby communities, where Ram was beloved. According to Nala, many forest staff members fasted for a day in mourning. Gir Sanctuary, in western Gujarat, is the world’s only habitat for Asiatic lions and now supports a population of more than 500. Ram and his brother Shyam formed a dominant coalition that ruled parts of Gir for years, fathering numerous cubs and building a large pride. “Ram along with his brother Shyam ruled over Gir for many years and the two fathered many cubs over the years,” said Sandeep Kumar, Nala’s predecessor. “At one point, the duo had about two dozen cubs in their pride.” The forest staff named the brothers Ram and Shyam—popular Indian names and also the title of a hit Bollywood film—reflecting their cultural resonance. Kumar noted the difference between lions and tigers in territorial behavior: while male tigers are solitary and defend territories alone, male lions often form coalitions, typically with a relative, to jointly protect their range. “But every kingdom must come to an end,” Kumar added. With Ram gone and Shyam aging, the coalition’s hold is likely to weaken, opening the territory to younger male lions. For those who knew him, Ram’s death marks the close of a memorable chapter in Gir’s conservation story.

An auction in Leominster has spotlighted the enduring fascination with the Kray twins, featuring personal items linked to the notorious East End gangsters. Among the lots were photographs of the brothers, orders of service from their funerals, and original artworks produced while they were in prison. One landscape painting sold for £2,000, while individual letters—mainly from Reggie Kray—went for between £10 and £50 each. The items were collected by Laurie O’Leary, who grew up with the Krays and later wrote a book about their lives. Toby Service of Brightwells Auctioneers said the letters offer rare insight into the twins’ thoughts behind bars, calling the sale “rather interesting, rather different” for the Herefordshire countryside—yet consistently popular. The Krays were jailed for life in 1969, with a recommended sentence of 30 years, for two separate murders in London. Ronnie Kray died aged 61 at Wexham Park Hospital, Berkshire, in 1995 after a heart attack, while Reggie Kray died from cancer at 66 at the Town House Hotel in Norwich in 2000. The auction reflects ongoing public interest in the brothers’ criminal legacy and personal stories.

Scotland’s prison estate for women is set for reform as the Scottish Prison Service (SPS) develops plans for a smaller, refurbished prison for around 80 women at the Cornton Vale site, alongside new community-based custody units. The shift follows the 2015 decision to abandon a large women’s prison in Inverclyde, with ministers aiming to keep women closer to families and local support services while addressing complex needs. About 110 prisoners were moved from Cornton Vale in Stirling to HMP Polmont near Falkirk last August to facilitate redevelopment. On Tuesday, Justice Secretary Michael Matheson will start demolition works at the prison and publish a paper outlining “challenges and priorities” for criminal and civil justice in Scotland. A Scottish government spokesman said: “This week will mark another key milestone towards the transformation of how the prison service, and other public services, work together to deal with women in custody.”

Kushner Companies Cancels China Investor Events Amid EB-5 Backlash Kushner Companies has canceled investor presentations planned for the southern Chinese cities of Shenzhen and Guangzhou following criticism over promotional remarks referencing the company’s ties to the White House. The developer had been scheduled to pitch real estate opportunities over the weekend, but controversy erupted after Nicole Meyer Kushner, Jared Kushner’s sister, invoked her brother’s name while courting investors for a New Jersey project. Critics accused the firm of playing up its political connections to attract funding. Kushner Companies said Meyer’s comments were misconstrued and issued an apology. Promotional materials for the events had listed Meyer, a principal at the company, and Laurent Morali, the firm’s president. On Thursday, spokesman James Yolles said in a statement: “No one from Kushner Companies will be in China this weekend.” Meyer’s remarks were made while encouraging potential backers to invest $500,000 (£386,500) through the EB-5 immigrant investor program, which offers a pathway to a U.S. green card for foreign nationals whose investment helps create jobs. The EB-5 program is popular among wealthy Chinese investors, but it has long faced criticism as a vehicle for cheap financing for property developers and for potential abuses that exploit immigration incentives. The episode comes amid broader scrutiny of the company’s business dealings. In March, Kushner Companies ended talks with Chinese conglomerate Anbang Insurance over a proposed major redevelopment in New York City, a potential agreement that had raised conflict-of-interest concerns. Jared Kushner, a senior adviser to President Donald Trump, has said he stepped away from the operations of his family’s business. However, government ethics filings indicate he and his wife, Ivanka Trump, continue to benefit from their stake in Kushner Companies, keeping the firm under persistent public and regulatory scrutiny.

Police closed Ballyrobin Road in Aldergrove after a collision involving a pedestrian shortly before 16:40 GMT on Saturday. The Northern Ireland Ambulance Service said the pedestrian was taken to the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast. Ballyrobin Road is closed from the airport to the Tully Road roundabout, with diversions in place. Motorists heading to the airport are advised to allow extra time for their journey. No further details were immediately available.

Fastest of his era: England great Frank ‘Typhoon’ Tyson dies Frank “Typhoon” Tyson, the Lancashire-born fast bowler celebrated for his blistering pace and decisive role in England’s Ashes triumph of 1954-55, has died. Though his Test career spanned less than five years, Tyson left an indelible mark: in 17 Tests he captured 76 wickets at a remarkable average of 18.56. Tyson shone brightest during England’s 1954-55 Ashes series in Australia. Selected ahead of fellow quick Fred Trueman, he took 28 wickets across five Tests, including an electrifying 7-27 in the second innings at Melbourne. In the annals of Ashes bowling performances, that haul has only been surpassed by two England greats: spinner Jim Laker, with match figures of 9-37 and 10-53 at Old Trafford in 1956, and paceman Stuart Broad, whose 8-15 at Trent Bridge ranks among the most devastating spells. After retiring at the age of 30, Tyson had amassed 767 first-class wickets. He later emigrated to Australia, where he forged a successful second act as a coach, commentator, and writer, shaping generations of cricketers and enriching the game’s narrative with insight and authority. Despite injuries and a relatively brief international career, Tyson was widely hailed as the fastest bowler of his era by Australian legends Sir Donald Bradman and Richie Benaud, as well as his great rival Trueman. Former Australia batsman Dean Jones wrote: “Sad to hear that Frank Tyson has passed away. Ex Vic coach. I was his student for a few of his books. Terrific cricketer. Terrific bloke.”

David Gauke, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, signalled a saver-focused approach to pension reform, saying a review of pension taxation would keep savers firmly in mind. “We need to ensure it is effective in terms of encouraging saving, and it is going in the right place,” he told BBC2’s Daily Politics Show. His remarks come ahead of the Budget on 16 March, when the Chancellor, George Osborne, is expected to unveil the findings of a Treasury inquiry into pension taxation. Gauke’s comments are likely to be seen as encouraging by those who favour keeping the current structure under which pensions are taxed when money is taken out, rather than at the point of contribution. One option considered by the Treasury was to make pension saving more like Individual Savings Accounts (Isas), which are taxed on the way in but grow tax-free thereafter. Supporters of the existing system argue that immediate tax relief on contributions is a stronger incentive for people to put money aside for retirement. Ministers are also weighing a significant change to the way tax relief is granted on pension contributions: replacing the current variable relief with a single flat rate. At present, basic-rate taxpayers receive 20% relief, higher-rate taxpayers receive 40%, and those paying the additional rate receive 45%. Under a flat-rate system, relief could be set somewhere between 25% and 33%, according to suggestions circulating in Westminster. While millions of higher earners would lose out under such a reform, basic-rate taxpayers would stand to gain. “Nobody wants to punish anybody,” Gauke said. “But it is, of course, right that we look – in a careful and consultative way – at the way pension tax relief works.” The impact on savers would depend heavily on the rate chosen. For example, a higher-rate taxpayer making a £10,000 pension contribution currently receives £4,000 in tax relief. Under a 25% flat rate, that relief would fall to £2,500, a loss of £1,500. Conversely, a basic-rate taxpayer contributing the same amount would gain £500 compared with the current system. The higher the flat rate set, the more savers would benefit overall, but the greater the cost to the public finances. Some experts believe any change could take effect immediately on Budget day, to prevent a surge of last-minute contributions by higher earners that could cost the Treasury up to £6bn. “Any higher earners who are looking at paying into a pension, should think seriously about doing so before 16 March,” said Tom McPhail, pensions expert at Hargreaves Lansdowne. “Conversely, for basic rate taxpayers, it may make sense to wait until after that date.”

The White House is launching a new Office of American Innovation led by senior adviser Jared Kushner, aiming to streamline government operations and import private-sector efficiency into federal agencies, according to a report in the Washington Post. Described by the paper as a “SWAT team” composed of former private-sector executives, the unit is expected to wield broad authority to reform government procedures and overhaul how services are delivered to citizens. “Our hope is that we can achieve successes and efficiencies for our customers, who are the citizens,” Kushner told the Washington Post, adding that “the government should be run like a great American company.” Technology and data will be central to the effort, with Apple CEO Tim Cook and Microsoft founder Bill Gates among those said to be working with the White House as outside advisers. In a statement to the Post, President Trump framed the initiative as a cornerstone of his campaign promises to shake up Washington. “Government stagnation has hindered our ability to properly function, often creating widespread congestion and leading to cost overruns and delays,” he said. The new office, he added, will allow him to apply his “ahead of schedule, under budget mentality” to the federal government. Kushner, 36, a property investor and media executive married to the president’s daughter Ivanka Trump, already plays a prominent role in the administration, advising the president on foreign relations and personnel decisions. Top White House strategist Steve Bannon is expected to have no formal role in the new group, despite his earlier calls for the “deconstruction of the administrative state” that drew significant attention and debate. The move comes days after congressional Republicans failed to advance their healthcare overhaul, a setback that has prompted the White House to shift focus to tax reform. GOP leaders pulled the bill before a vote when it became clear they lacked the necessary support, with members of the conservative Freedom Caucus among those opposing the measure on grounds that it didn’t roll back enough Affordable Care Act regulations. The BBC’s Anthony Zurcher noted the misstep may have dented President Trump’s dealmaker image and left party leadership looking weakened amid internal divisions.

Ruth Madoff says she and her husband Bernie Madoff attempted suicide on Christmas Eve 2008, taking a “bunch of pills” as their world collapsed in the wake of his Ponzi scheme, she told CBS’s 60 Minutes. “I don’t know whose idea it was, but we decided to kill ourselves because it was so horrendous what was happening,” she said. Ruth Madoff said she avoided alcohol for fear of vomiting and believed the pills included the sedative Ambien and possibly Klonopin, a medication used to treat seizures and panic disorders. “We took pills and woke up the next day..... It was impulsive and I am glad we woke up,” she added, describing the decision as an extension of “the whole depression” enveloping the couple. Bernie Madoff is serving a 150-year prison sentence after his 2009 conviction for orchestrating a fraud that ran since the early 1990s and wiped out the savings of thousands of investors. CBS said the full interview, airing October 30, will include previously undisclosed revelations about the Madoff family’s life after the scandal, offering new details on how they coped with the fallout and the public outrage that followed.

For the first time, couples in Scotland who have children from previous relationships will be eligible for IVF treatment on the NHS, under changes announced by the Scottish government. Ministers said the move, designed to widen access and better reflect modern family circumstances, could come into effect from September. The policy shift follows recommendations from the National Infertility Group, which advised extending eligibility to couples who already have a child living in their home. Alongside the broader eligibility, the government is exploring increasing the number of funded IVF cycles for women from two to three, in an effort to raise the chances of a successful pregnancy. Talks with Scotland’s health boards will take place on the feasibility of offering three cycles from April 2017. Officials said the proposals aim to improve outcomes and reduce the need for repeat referrals, while ensuring services remain fair and sustainable across the country. Infertility affects around one in seven couples, and about 2% of births in the UK now result from fertility treatment. Scotland’s health service has already met national targets to see eligible couples within a year and to provide two rounds of treatment. Ministers say the latest steps build on that progress and reflect a commitment to equitable access for those struggling to conceive. Public Health Minister Aileen Campbell said she hoped widening access would help more couples who face the distress of infertility. “Scotland already leads the way on IVF access and rights in the UK, and these changes will ensure Scotland’s provision is as fair and generous as possible,” she said. However, Ms Campbell confirmed the government will not accept a recommendation to remove eligibility for couples where the woman is aged between 40 and 42.
