Current criteria in this area will remain, with women in that age range eligible for one cycle of treatment if they meet certain additional conditions. The National Infertility Group noted that successful outcomes for women aged 40 to 42 are generally “very poor.” Professor Adam Balen, chairman of the British Fertility Society, welcomed the announcement as “great news for people in Scotland planning a family who have fertility problems.” He said infertility can have a “devastating effect” on people’s lives, and argued IVF is cost-effective, offering childless couples the chance to form much-wanted families. The society highlighted a “gulf” between IVF funding in Scotland and England, citing a continuing “postcode lottery” south of the border. Further details will be confirmed following discussions with health boards, with the first changes expected to begin from September.

The Teesside Collective said their proposed Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) network should cut the area's annual carbon emissions by a quarter by 2024. They also believe the scheme could support 5,900 jobs and lead to 15m tonnes of carbon dioxide being stored a year by the 2030s. Environmentalists welcomed the move. Steel producer SSI UK, fertiliser producer GrowHow, polyester resin producer Lotte Chemical UK and hydrogen producer BOC are the four anchor companies behind the plan along with Tees Valley Unlimited. Carbon dioxide, generated through the burning of fossil fuels, would be turned into a liquid and then pumped by a pipeline and stored 1.2m (2km) beneath the sea. Stuart Haszeldean, Professor of Carbon Capture and Storage at the University of Edinburgh, said the liquid carbon can be stored safely for tens of thousands of years. He said: "It's crucial because in the UK we have a law that says we will emit 80% less carbon dioxide by 2050. "Teesside is one of the biggest industrial sites in Europe so it's good they are leading on this." Simon Bowens, North East campaigner for Friends of the Earth told BBC Tees: "The carbon capture proposals are really welcomed. "It is very difficult for these companies to decarbonise at the rate we need them to, CCS is the most likely solution to be able to do that effectively." The Teesside Collective has unveiled plans for a Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) network that it says could cut Teesside’s carbon emissions by a quarter by 2024. Under the proposal, carbon dioxide produced by energy-intensive manufacturers would be captured, compressed into a liquid, and transported by pipeline for permanent storage about 2km beneath the seabed. By the 2030s, the group estimates the network could securely store up to 15 million tonnes of CO2 each year and sustain around 5,900 jobs across the cluster and its supply chain. The initiative aims to protect industry and attract investment. Steelmaker SSI UK, fertiliser producer GrowHow, polyester resin producer Lotte Chemical UK and hydrogen producer BOC have signed on as anchor participants, working with local economic partnership Tees Valley Unlimited to advance the scheme. Stuart Haszeldean, Professor of Carbon Capture and Storage at the University of Edinburgh, said the technology offers safe, long-duration storage. “The liquid carbon can be stored safely for tens of thousands of years,” he said, adding that UK law requires 80% lower CO2 emissions by 2050 and praising Teesside’s leadership as one of Europe’s largest industrial sites. Environmental groups welcomed the move. Simon Bowens, North East campaigner for Friends of the Earth, told BBC Tees: “The carbon capture proposals are really welcomed. For these companies, CCS is the most likely way to decarbonise at the pace needed.”

A shortlist has been unveiled for a major literary award that recognises “books being written and published exploring the role of medicine in our lives and our literature.” Open to both fiction and non-fiction, the prize carries a £30,000 award for the winner, to be announced at a ceremony on 25 April. The judging panel is chaired by broadcaster Joan Bakewell and includes cancer biology professor Frances Balkwill alongside writers Damian Barr, Tessa Hadley and Sathnam Sanghera. Amy Liptrot’s The Outrun is among the contenders, a critically praised memoir charting her struggle with alcoholism and recovery on the windswept island of Orkney. It is joined on the shortlist by Cathy Rentzenbrink’s bestselling The Last Act of Love, which movingly recounts the aftermath of an accident that left her brother in an eight-year coma. Fiction is represented by Alex Pheby’s Playthings, a novel inspired by a real case of schizophrenia, and Sarah Moss’s Signs for Lost Children, which follows the life and work of a pioneering doctor confronting the medical and social challenges of her time. From the world of medical science and narrative nonfiction, neurologist Suzanne O’Sullivan’s It’s All in Your Head offers an exploration of psychosomatic illness, examining the complex interplay between mind and body. Rounding out the list is Steve Silberman’s Neurotribes, a landmark work about autism that won the 2015 Samuel Johnson Prize. Last year’s winner was Marion Coutts’ The Iceberg, a searing memoir by the widow of a man who died of a brain tumour. This year’s shortlist continues the prize’s tradition of highlighting compelling, humane writing that illuminates the many ways medicine shapes personal lives and public understanding.

TUC says Brexit would cut average earnings by £38 a week by 2030; Reality Check: plausible if growth forecasts prove right, but figures are uncertain The Trades Union Congress (TUC) has claimed that leaving the European Union would reduce average weekly earnings in the UK by £38 by 2030. The union body bases its estimate on existing forecasts suggesting the economy would grow more slowly outside the EU, and argues that weaker GDP growth would feed directly through to pay. In its report, the TUC aggregates projections from several prominent institutions. It takes the predicted falls in GDP for 2030 from the OECD, the UK Treasury, and the Centre for Economic Performance at the London School of Economics, alongside a separate outlook on wages from the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR). Averaging these, the TUC arrives at a 5.6% reduction compared with remaining in the EU. The TUC then assumes that a 5.6% fall in GDP would translate to a 5.6% decline in average earnings relative to the current official baseline. Average weekly earnings stand at £492 today. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) currently expects them to rise by £220 a week by 2030 if current trends continue. Under the TUC’s Brexit scenario, that rise would be £182, creating a gap of £38 a week. Reality Check’s verdict is that while the exact numbers are highly uncertain, the broad logic holds: if the UK economy grows more slowly than it otherwise would, wages are likely to be lower than they otherwise would be. Most mainstream economic models suggest that leaving the EU would dent growth, though the scale and duration of any impact remain contested. Economic modelling involves many assumptions, and long-term projections are inherently imprecise. The link between GDP and wages is, in general, a reasonable one. NIESR’s separate analysis suggests real wages could be hit even harder than overall output, as a weaker pound would raise the cost of imported goods and push up inflation, eroding pay in real terms. The TUC itself acknowledges uncertainty, but contends it is “not contentious to project a material further downward impact on living standards following Brexit.” The overall takeaway: if you accept forecasts of slower economic growth after leaving the EU, it is consistent to expect lower average earnings—though the specific figure of £38 a week should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

They say the missile, launched off the east coast, flew about 800km (500 miles) and fell into the water. North Korea has not commented on the report. A US defence spokesperson later said a second missile was launched. US President Barack Obama earlier imposed new sanctions on Pyongyang, after its recent "illicit" nuclear test and satellite launch. His executive order freezes North Korean government property in the United States. It bans US exports to - or investment in - North Korea and also greatly expands powers to blacklist anyone, including non-Americans, dealing with North Korea. The 6 January nuclear test and 7 February satellite launch were violations of existing UN sanctions. South Korea's Yonhap news agency also cited unnamed sources saying a second missile was detected but it may have disintegrated in mid-air. They appeared to be medium-range Rodong missiles fired from road-mobile launch vehicles. With a maximum range of 1,300km, the Rodong would have the capability to reach all of South Korea and parts of Japan. Lt Col Michelle Baldanza, from the US defence press office said after the latest launch: "We call on North Korea to refrain from actions that further raise tensions in the region." Amid the heightened tensions, the North sentenced a US student to 15 years hard labour on Wednesday for "severe crimes" against the state. The US demanded North Korea immediately release Otto Warmbier, 21, who was arrested for trying to steal a propaganda sign from a hotel while on a visit in January. The US and South Korea are also holding their biggest annual military drills this month, which routinely generate tension. But this year North Korea threatened to launch a "pre-emptive nuclear strike of justice" against the US and South Korea.

Malaysian Authorities Seize Malay-Language Bibles in ‘Allah’ Dispute; Two Briefly Detained Malaysian authorities seized copies of Malay-language Bibles from the Malaysian Bible Society (MBS) in Selangor, near Kuala Lumpur, amid an escalating dispute over the use of the word “Allah.” Bible Society officials told Reuters that two of their members were briefly detained following the raid, which they said was linked to a state law prohibiting non-Muslims from using certain words, including “Allah,” to describe God. The seizure comes after an October appeals court ruling that non-Muslims may not use the term “Allah,” arguing it must be exclusive to Islam to prevent public disorder. That decision overturned a 2009 High Court ruling permitting the Catholic weekly The Herald to use “Allah” in its Malay-language edition to refer to the Christian God. The earlier dispute sparked tensions nationwide, with churches and mosques attacked in the aftermath, highlighting the sensitivity of religious identity in Malaysia. “We were told that we were under investigation for breaking a Selangor state law banning non-Muslims from using the word ‘Allah’,” MBS Chairman Lee Min Choon said, adding that the society has long distributed Malay-language Bibles for Christian communities that worship and read scripture in Malay. The United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the main party in Prime Minister Najib Razak’s ruling coalition, said its Selangor members would protest at churches across the state on Sunday over what it called unauthorized use of “Allah.” Deputy Prime Minister and UMNO deputy president Muhyiddin Yassin defended enforcement actions, saying, “There are laws in Selangor and there was a decree by His Royal Highness the Sultan. So what they are doing is carrying out the Sultan’s decree. They are not doing anything against the law.” The Council of Churches of Malaysia said it was “alarmed” by the raid and urged the federal government to uphold religious freedoms guaranteed in the Federal Constitution. Christian leaders argue they have used “Allah” for centuries in Malay-language worship and translations, noting the term entered Malay from Arabic and is commonly used by people of different faiths to refer to God. Critics accuse the government of tacitly condoning Bible seizures to deflect anger among poor Malay Muslims over subsidy cuts expected to raise electricity, petrol, and sugar prices. Although Najib’s coalition retained power in May elections, it recorded its worst performance in more than 50 years, underscoring growing discontent. Malay Muslims constitute nearly two-thirds of Malaysia’s population, alongside significant Hindu and Christian communities. With legal interpretations and state decrees varying, the “Allah” issue continues to test Malaysia’s multi-faith balance and constitutional protections.

Beeston Businesses Host Street Party as Roads Close for Nottingham Tram Extension Chilwell Road and High Road in Beeston have been closed to traffic to allow construction of an extension to Nottingham’s tram network. City officials said a total closure will speed up work and limit disruption, and a compensation package for affected firms is in place. In response, traders are planning a community street party on 30 March to remind customers they remain open. Organisers aim to treat the closure as “temporary pedestrianisation,” with street entertainment, face-painting and an outdoor stage for bands. Julie Cameron, owner of Cameron House, a gift and furnishings shop, said some of the roughly 80 businesses affected have already left, but many are determined to stay. “It’s an opportunity to get local people and visitors from Nottingham to see how fabulous the businesses are and that we are still open,” she said, adding that traders are sharing directions and car park information. Councillor Jane Urquhart said a single, permanent closure was chosen over rolling restrictions to provide certainty. She said the council has worked closely with retailers and created new parking spaces nearby to help. The £570m project will link Nottingham city centre with Beeston and Chilwell and is scheduled for completion in 2015. The roads closed on Monday to accelerate construction and reduce overall disruption.

Thousands of federal inmates are being released under new sentencing rules aimed at reducing long jail terms for non-violent drug offenders, in what officials describe as the largest one-time liberation in U.S. history. Many of the prisoners left federal custody on Friday, with the remainder expected to be released by Tuesday. About 3,400 of those affected were already in community confinement, including halfway houses, and are now transitioning further back into society under supervision. Another roughly 1,700 are not U.S. citizens and may be transferred to immigration authorities for potential deportation. The Department of Justice did not respond to a BBC inquiry about how those cases will be handled. The releases mark the first wave under changes approved by the U.S. Sentencing Commission, which made earlier guideline reductions for drug offenses retroactive. On average, eligible inmates are seeing their sentences cut by about two years. Up to 46,000 of the approximately 100,000 federal drug prisoners could ultimately qualify for reduced terms through the policy shift. The changes continue a broader push by the Obama administration and Congress to recalibrate punishments for non-violent offenses, particularly drug crimes. The effort accelerated in 2013 when then–Attorney General Eric Holder instructed prosecutors to avoid seeking mandatory minimums for certain low-level drug cases. Many lawmakers in both parties now argue that decades of mandatory sentencing contributed to mass incarceration without commensurate public safety gains. The scale of the challenge is substantial. There are about 208,000 people in federal prisons, nearly half for drug offenses. The population is disproportionately minority: 37% are Black and 34% are Hispanic. The financial burden is heavy as well; incarceration cost the U.S. an estimated $80 billion in 2010. Advocates say the current releases are a crucial step toward fairness and fiscal responsibility, while acknowledging that successful reentry—stable housing, employment, and treatment—will determine long-term outcomes. Critics warn that rapid releases could strain local services and pose public safety risks. The United States holds almost a quarter of the world’s prison population, with roughly one in every 99 Americans behind bars, underscoring the stakes of ongoing criminal justice reform.

Pogba strikes as Juventus come from behind to beat AC Milan; Inter climb to fourth AC Milan took an early lead when Alex headed in from Mario Balotelli’s corner, but Juventus rallied to claim a 2-1 victory in a tense Serie A clash. Mario Mandzukic levelled soon after, stroking a composed finish into the bottom corner following a perfectly weighted return pass from Alvaro Morata. Balotelli briefly thought he had restored Milan’s advantage, only for his close-range effort to be ruled out for handball. Paul Pogba clipped the post with a free-kick before delivering the decisive moment. The France international chested down Claudio Marchisio’s corner at the far post and hammered a shot into the turf, with the bounce carrying the ball across goal and in, sealing the points for the leaders. Recalled to Milan’s starting XI, Balotelli endured a mixed night. He registered the assist for Alex’s opener and forced Gianluigi Buffon into a sharp first-half save with a curling free-kick, but was booked for punching the ball into the net after Buffon produced a superb double save. The striker was substituted with 13 minutes remaining as Milan sought an equaliser that never arrived. The defeat leaves Milan in sixth place, while Juventus remain clear at the summit; their lead could be trimmed to six points if second-placed Napoli beat bottom club Verona on Sunday. Elsewhere in Serie A, Mauro Icardi’s second-half strike lifted Inter Milan to fourth with a 1-0 win at next-to-bottom Frosinone, who finished with 10 men after defender Leonardo Blanchard was sent off late. Carpi stay outside the relegation zone on goal difference after a 1-0 defeat at Chievo, and Genoa earned a valuable 1-0 victory away at Sassuolo.

Four people have been sentenced for a racially aggravated incident at Bristol’s Jamia Mosque in Totterdown, where a group shouted racial abuse at a worshipper and tied a St George’s flag to the mosque’s fence. The incident took place on 17 January and was described in court as a targeted act intended to intimidate and distress members of the local Muslim community. At Bristol Crown Court, Kevin Crehan, 34, of Knowle, was jailed for 12 months, while Mark Bennett, 48, of Patchway, received a nine-month prison sentence. Both men admitted religiously aggravated public order offences. Two women also pleaded guilty to religiously aggravated public order offences: Alison Bennett, 46, the wife of Mark Bennett, was handed a six-month sentence suspended for two years, and Angelina Swales, 31, of Brislington, received a four-month sentence suspended for two years. All four defendants were given restraining orders prohibiting them from going within 100 metres of any mosque in England or Wales for the next 10 years. The orders are intended to protect worshippers and deter further harassment or intimidation of faith communities. Inspector Nigel Colston of Avon and Somerset Police praised the solidarity shown by local residents following the incident. “The way local people came together with overwhelming support for the mosque made me proud to be associated with Bristol,” he said. “There can never be any excuse for hate crime in any shape or form and this criminality will not be tolerated. All of our communities have the right to live and worship peacefully without fear of being targeted for their race or religion.”

Swindon Town have begun a swift restructuring after relegation to League Two, parting company with head coach Luke Williams on 5 May. Owner Lee Power, long known for hands-on involvement in transfers, said the club will pivot to a clearer managerial model, granting the new boss control over a defined budget. Power previously experimented with a director of football setup, appointing friend Tim Sherwood in November, but the former Tottenham manager has stepped back following a poor run in which Swindon won just seven of 31 matches since his arrival. The Robins aim to appoint Williams’ successor within eight days as they seek stability ahead of the new campaign. Partick Thistle manager Alan Archibald is among those linked to the vacancy at the County Ground, alongside Mansfield’s Steve Evans and ex-QPR boss Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink. The change signals a move away from owner-led recruitment as Swindon try to rebuild and regain momentum.

Fulham midfielder Jozabed has struggled for time since arriving from Rayo Vallecano for an undisclosed fee in August 2016, making just eight appearances. The 26-year-old’s last outing for the Cottagers was as a substitute in a 2-1 defeat to QPR on 1 October. He joined Celta Vigo on loan in January, scoring twice in 28 appearances in all competitions. Charlie Hodgson has announced he will retire from playing at the end of the season and move into a new role at Saracens, closing a distinguished career as the Premiership’s all-time record points scorer. The 35-year-old joined Saracens from Sale Sharks in 2011 and has amassed nearly 2,500 points in 239 Premiership appearances to date. He earned 38 England caps before stepping away from international rugby in 2012. “It was a very tough call to make, as being a rugby player is the only thing I’ve ever known,” Hodgson said. “In one sense my career seems to have lasted a lifetime and in another sense it’s just flown by. It was a difficult decision to make, but my body is now telling me that it’s probably the right thing to do. I’ve been presented with an amazing opportunity to be here at Saracens in a different capacity, and it’s an opportunity I felt that I just couldn’t turn down.” Hodgson won the Premiership title with Sale in 2006 and lifted the trophy again last season as Saracens defeated Bath in May. On his England debut in 2001, he scored 44 points against Romania—a record that still stands as the most by any England player in a Test match. The Yorkshireman has made 77 Premiership appearances for Saracens but has started just once this season. “It’s great for the club to provide our players with a pathway into a different career,” said Saracens director of rugby Mark McCall. “As a guy with such rugby knowledge and intelligence, Charlie is tailor-made for the role and he will prove to be a huge asset for the club going forward.”

Merseyside Police’s Protecting Vulnerable People Unit arrested 14 men after coordinated visits to addresses across Wirral, Liverpool, St Helens, Sefton and North Wales on Thursday. The suspects were detained on suspicion of offences including serious assault, rape, sexual assault and harassment. Police said the operation was to show victims that reports of abuse will be taken seriously. Det Supt Chris Green said arrests covered alleged behaviour “such as choking a woman in front of her children, coercing a partner into non-consensual sex, sending threatening text messages to an ex-girlfriend, and even the attempted robbery of a relative.” He added such incidents often form part of a wider pattern of abusive, controlling behaviour endured for years. Investigations are ongoing.

Haseeb Hameed says he is determined to learn from a difficult spell and rebuild his form with Lancashire as he targets a return to the England setup. The 20-year-old opener, who impressed with 82 on his Test debut against India in November 2016, was omitted from England’s recent series against South Africa after struggling for runs early in the domestic season. “The last few months haven’t gone the way I would have liked but that happens,” Hameed told BBC Radio Manchester. “It’s about learning from these experiences, not just completely forget about them, and making sure I keep developing. Sometimes you actually learn more from instances like this.” Hameed was denied the chance to push for a confidence-boosting century when rain washed out Lancashire’s County Championship match against Hampshire at the Ageas Bowl. His unbeaten 77, however, marked his first fifty in first-class cricket this summer and offered a timely reminder of his potential. “England is the aim and to try to take each game as it comes – whoever that is for, which is Lancashire right now,” he said. “I will try and perform to the best of my ability for Lancashire and if I can do that then, hopefully, further honours can come again.” Reflecting on the scrutiny that accompanies a downturn in form, Hameed added: “If you have a difficult period, there’s lots of different things that people think is the reason why. It could be a number of reasons but I’m just looking at putting that to one side now and hopefully approach the second half of the season for myself.” England begin a three-Test series against West Indies on 17 August, starting with a historic day-night match at Edgbaston. With competition for top-order places intensifying, Hameed will look to build on his latest innings and make a strong case for future selection.

Rock music was found to be particularly distracting for men. A study by researchers at Imperial College London and the Royal College of Music suggests that rock music can hamper men’s concentration and accuracy during complex tasks, while women’s performance remains largely unaffected. Published in the Medical Journal of Australia, the research explores how different sound environments influence task performance, with potential implications for both everyday study habits and professional settings such as operating theatres. In a playful but controlled experiment, the team used the classic Operation board game as a proxy for fine motor control and focus. A total of 350 participants attempted to extract pieces with tweezers without triggering the game’s buzzer, while listening via headphones to either Mozart, rock tracks by AC/DC, or recordings of typical operating theatre background noise. The findings were strikingly gendered. Women’s performance did not significantly change across the different soundscapes, suggesting they maintained consistent levels of speed and accuracy regardless of music type or ambient operating room noise. Men, however, were slower and made more mistakes when listening to rock music. The researchers observed a modest improvement for men during Mozart, but this was closely tied to individual musical preferences; once the effect of liking classical music was accounted for, the apparent advantage disappeared. Lead author Dr. Daisy Fancourt described the use of the Operation game as “tongue in cheek,” but emphasized that the study forms part of broader research examining how music can alter performance in real-world environments. The team is particularly interested in whether background music in professional settings could affect the speed, precision, and teamwork of people engaged in demanding tasks, including surgical teams. While the study does not provide a definitive explanation for the gender differences observed, the authors suggest men may be more susceptible to auditory stress—where loud or discordant music disrupts perception and concentration. The results also touch on familiar domestic debates over whether teenagers should listen to music while studying. “This study suggests that for men who are operating or playing a board game, rock music may be a bad idea,” said Dr. Fancourt, noting that thoughtful choices about sound environments could be beneficial in both homes and workplaces.

The 1988 African Footballer of the Year has been in Gabon where the African Under-17 Championship ends today with Ghana playing Mali in the final. He told the BBC that based on the quality of football displayed in Gabon, there is cause for optimism, not pessimism, regarding the future. Kalusha Bwalya, the former president of the Football Association of Zambia and a member of the Confederation of African Football’s executive committee, praised the high standard of play throughout the tournament, which was relocated from Madagascar at the last minute to Gabon, a country without recognised junior football structures. “The standard has been very high and the four teams going to the World Cup have all played very well,” he said, pointing to Ghana, Mali, Niger and Guinea as evidence of the continent’s depth at youth level. Bwalya highlighted the leading performances of Ghana and Guinea, and lauded Niger for defying expectations to qualify for their first ever youth World Cup. “There’s no doubt in my mind that the future of African football is very bright,” he said. “Ghana and Guinea set the tempo for the tournament while Niger defied all odds to qualify for their first ever youth World Cup and that’s a great achievement.” Africa’s representatives will head to India for the FIFA U-17 World Cup, which kicks off on 6 October, with impressive pedigree. Ghana, who face Mali in today’s final, are two-time world champions at this level (1995 and 1999) and have twice finished as runners-up. Mali, beaten finalists in 2015, will be making their fifth appearance on the global stage. Guinea reached the semi-finals in 1985, while Niger are celebrating their historic first qualification for a FIFA tournament. “Don’t forget that Africa has done very well in the under-17 tournaments [seven titles] and I think all these teams are good for the quarter-finals and more,” Bwalya added. He singled out the quality of the Malian side and Ghana’s sharpness: “This Malian team is good as the team that got to the final last time around and Ghana are looking really sharp.” “I’m confident these teams will uphold our reputation as Africans in the junior tournaments,” he said, predicting that all four African teams will pose serious problems for their opponents in India.

Tottenham Hotspur defender Connor Ogilvie, 19, who can operate at left-back or centre-back, has yet to make a first-team appearance for Spurs and played 16 U21 Premier League games last season, joining on a one-month youth loan. Goalkeeper Chris Kettings, 22, formerly of Manchester City and Blackpool, has moved on a one-month loan. Find all football transfers on the dedicated page.

Paddy Lowe returns to Williams in senior leadership role with board seat and stake Paddy Lowe has rejoined Williams in a wide-ranging leadership position that places him in charge of the engineering operations across the entire company, including the Formula 1 team and its Williams Advanced Engineering commercial division. The 54-year-old, who left Mercedes in January, began work on Thursday and will also join the Williams board of directors while taking an undisclosed shareholding in the business. Lowe’s move to Williams had been widely anticipated since December, but finalising the deal took longer than expected. One of the most respected technical figures in Formula 1, Lowe served as executive director (technical) at Mercedes from 2013 and played a central role in the team’s dominance, overseeing three consecutive drivers’ and constructors’ title doubles from 2014 to 2016. His departure from Mercedes followed a difference of opinion with team boss Toto Wolff over the outfit’s future direction, after which Lowe was placed on gardening leave over the winter. Mercedes has since appointed James Allison as technical director. Allison, who left Ferrari last year, takes a differently titled role to Lowe’s former position. For Lowe, the Williams appointment marks a return to his roots and a full-circle moment in a distinguished career. He began his Formula 1 journey with Williams in 1987 and was instrumental in developing the groundbreaking active suspension system that underpinned the dominant FW14B, with which Nigel Mansell won the 1992 world championship, and its successor, the FW15C, which carried Alain Prost to the 1993 title. Lowe moved to McLaren in 1993, rising to technical director before joining Mercedes two decades later. “I’ve always had a deep respect for Williams – my first team in Formula 1,” Lowe said. “It is a huge honour to return in this leadership position and to have the opportunity to become a shareholder. I am extremely motivated to play my part in bringing success back to the team.” Deputy team principal Claire Williams hailed the appointment as transformative. “Having someone of Paddy’s calibre and engineering competence is not only a morale boost for everyone at Williams, but I know it will also significantly support our efforts to return this team back to the front of the grid. Our ambitions at Williams are unwavering; we want to win races and championships. In Paddy we believe we have just that, as well as a leader who will drive change. This is a game changer for us.” Williams heads into the new season seeking to rebound after slipping from third to fifth in last year’s constructors’ standings. Lowe’s arrival adds seasoned championship-winning experience to the team’s technical leadership as it targets a return to the sharp end of the grid.

With less than a month to go until the UK general election on 7 May, party leaders intensified campaigning across Scotland with contrasting pitches on jobs, the economy and social security. Scottish Conservative leader Ruth Davidson, touring the south of Scotland, argued rural communities need a better deal and more decision-making power, accusing the SNP government in Edinburgh of being overly centralising. “We’ve been the only party to argue that more power should pass to our great rural areas,” she said. “We want to help create dynamic rural towns and villages across rural Scotland which attract young people and give them the chance of a great career and a good life.” Davidson framed the Conservatives as champions of devolving authority and opportunity to smaller communities, linking local empowerment to retaining young talent and building sustainable rural economies. In Glasgow, Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy launched Labour’s “workplace manifesto,” casting his party as the guarantor of a “fair economy.” He pledged a higher minimum wage and the extension of the living wage into low-paid private sector jobs. Murphy also drew sharp contrasts on zero-hours contracts, attacking both Conservatives and the SNP. “David Cameron admits he couldn’t live on a zero-hours contract but his solution is to rebrand them,” he said. “The SNP are no better than the Tories. For all their promise of being bold, they want to consult on zero-hours contracts — Labour will ban them, and give workers the right to a regular contract after 12 weeks of regular work.” Labour’s message sought to put workplace security and pay at the centre of Scotland’s election debate. Speaking in Aberdeen, Liberal Democrat Treasury Chief Secretary Danny Alexander said his party’s role in coalition with the Conservatives had underpinned economic stability after the recession. He cited warnings from figures in the UK financial industry that a Labour government could cost the economy more than £10bn a year and add at least £800 annually to average household mortgage bills if interest rates rose. “The markets are showing their concern. I believe they are right to do so,” Alexander said. “An unstable government, unable to take serious decisions, pulled sharply to left or right, with Alex Salmond or Nigel Farage, would cost us all dear. It would jam the brakes on the economic recovery.” The Liberal Democrats’ pitch centred on steady governance and safeguarding the recovery. Elsewhere, SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon set out plans to increase support for carers, promising that SNP MPs would push to raise the carers allowance to the level of jobseekers allowance — from £62 per week to £73. The party says the change would deliver up to £600 extra per year for more than 100,000 unpaid carers in Scotland. “Carers are often reliant solely on the social security system for their income because they have to take time out of work to look after others — the same social security system which is under a relentless and sustained attack by this Tory-led government,” Sturgeon said. The flurry of announcements underscores Scotland’s central battleground themes: rural opportunity, workers’ rights, economic stability and welfare support, as parties vie to shape the post-election landscape.

Mark Carriline, executive director for children, young people and culture at Bury Council, has resigned after a disciplinary panel found him guilty of serious misconduct and recommended dismissal without notice. The recommendation, made by the council’s HR panel last month, was due to go to a full council meeting, but Carriline quit first. Carriline oversaw children’s services, education and cultural programmes in the borough. The misconduct finding related to reports about former councillor Simon Carter, who later admitted in court to making indecent images of children. Carter, who represented Tottington ward from 2012, received a three-year community sentence at Bolton Crown Court in October 2015. In a statement, Bury Council said Carriline’s resignation takes effect immediately and that no payment has been made on his departure except for outstanding holidays. Carriline was understood by the BBC to be earning more than £100,000 a year. The council added that Karen Dolton will continue in the statutory role of interim director of children’s services. Carriline’s departure comes weeks after the resignation of chief executive Mike Owen, marking another high-profile exit from the authority.

Hamilton Academical face a mounting injury list ahead of their Scottish Cup meeting with Dunfermline Athletic, even as defender Scott McMann returns to the squad after illness. The Premiership side remain without several key players, with midfielder Ali Crawford likely to miss out again through injury and Gramoz Kurtaj set for a late fitness test following an ankle problem. Georgios Sarris continues his recovery following knee surgery, while fellow defender Jesus Garcia Tena and midfielders Greg Docherty and Darren Lyon are also sidelined. Dunfermline, sitting sixth in the Scottish Championship, have their own concerns, with defenders Ben Richards-Everton and Ryan Williamson still unavailable. Hamilton, second bottom of the Premiership, are seeking a morale-boosting cup run to lift spirits, but the absences mean manager Martin Canning will have selection decisions to make as he balances experience and recent arrivals. Pars manager Allan Johnston believes the pressure lies with the top-flight visitors. “The pressure is all on Hamilton as the Premiership club to go and win the game,” he told the club website. “They probably don’t deserve to be in the position they are just now. They have put in a lot of good performances this season and maybe not got the rewards they deserved at times. Hamilton have a lot of quality going forward and are well established in the Premiership now. “We know that it is going to be a hard tie and we are going to have to play a lot better than last week, probably at our best, to get a result. With the players that we have got, we are capable of causing any team a problem, especially going forward. It is a chance for our boys to go and compete against a Premiership club. The last time we got into the quarter-finals was 2009, so it would be a great achievement. When you look at the clubs that are likely going to be left, it is a magnificent chance to get through to progress further in the cup.” Accies defender Blair Adams is relishing his first taste of the competition. “I played on Saturday and had 60 minutes on Tuesday, so I have settled in quick and am just hoping to start on Saturday as well and get a good run in the team,” he said. “Of course I have heard of Dunfermline, but I can’t say that I know much about them. But we won’t be taking them lightly. Everyone wants a good cup run, and it’s a good opportunity to reach the quarter-finals.” Both clubs will see Saturday’s tie as a chance to build momentum and secure a place in the last eight, with Dunfermline chasing a notable upset and Hamilton hoping their quality can show despite a threadbare squad.

Community leaders said despite talks with police, it was better to shut to “avoid any confrontation” during the Wales Portugal match Several Portuguese-run businesses in Wrexham will close early this evening as a precaution ahead of the Wales versus Portugal match, amid concerns about potential tensions following the EU referendum. Two cafés, a restaurant and a shop are expected to shut at about 18:00 BST, with owners citing a number of reasons for the decision, not solely fear of disorder. Iolanda Banu Viegas, chair of the Portuguese-speaking community group in Wrexham, said proprietors had discussed security measures with police before opting to close for the evening. “They all spoke to police about security measures but they all decided that to avoid any confrontation it was better to just close down,” she said. “There is definitely a fear. It’s sad because of the sense that we want to be able to celebrate together. We have all been cheering for Wales until this match—and our children who were born here all want Wales to win.” Viegas said some Portuguese residents had previously experienced vandalism during football matches, including smashed windows and damaged cars. While she stressed there had been no physical violence linked to the referendum result, she reported an uptick in verbal abuse. “It’s something I’ve heard from Portuguese people across England and Wales,” she added. Saith Seren, the Wrexham Welsh centre, has invited the local Portuguese community to watch the match there, hoping to provide a welcoming and inclusive environment. Marc Jones, chair of Saith Seren, acknowledged that “a tiny minority” has been behind recent issues and said the invitation aimed to defuse anxiety. “I know anecdotally there has been tension post the referendum,” he said. “But obviously there have been some concerns, and it’s a precaution from their point of view. They want to avoid anything that antagonises anyone. It’s a shame. They have been here for a long time, they are very well-established and integrated.” Jones said the venue would offer a warm reception. “I have invited Iolanda and anyone else who wants to come to the Saith Seren this evening—they will get a very warm and robust welcome. I’m sure there will be a lot of banter and singing,” he said. North Wales Police said they have not seen an increase in reported hate crimes or community tensions since the referendum. Police and Crime Commissioner Arfon Jones condemned hate offences, calling them “shameful and appalling” and stressing they will not be tolerated. Assistant Chief Constable Richard Debicki urged anyone targeted by abuse to come forward. “I would like to reassure all of our communities across North Wales that we will do everything that we can to protect them from this kind of crime. Please do not suffer in silence. If you are concerned or have fallen victim to any sort of abuse or harm motivated by hatred, then contact us,” he said.

Merseyside Police are treating the death of Anita Stevenson, 39, as unexplained after her body was discovered on Saturday on land bordering Poole Lane and Old Court House Lane in Bromborough, Wirral. Stevenson, originally from Bradford, West Yorkshire, was last seen at her home in Tranmere on 18 October. Officers previously released CCTV images from the day she disappeared as friends and relatives joined efforts to find her. Her brother, Jake Stevenson, paid tribute on Facebook, calling it “soul destroying” that he cannot give her “one last hug.” He described Anita as “an amazing sister, daughter and, more than anything, the best mother anyone could have wished for,” adding: “Rest in peace for all the positivity and joy you’ve brought into everyone else’s lives. I love you more than words can even describe.” A 41-year-old man from Birkenhead was arrested earlier on suspicion of murder and has since been released. Police have not yet disclosed the results of a post-mortem examination and say inquiries are ongoing. Anyone with information that could assist detectives is urged to contact Merseyside Police or Crimestoppers anonymously, in confidence.

The amended rule comes into effect at the end of 2020 World Rugby has approved a significant reform to international eligibility, extending the residency qualification period for players from 36 to 60 months. The change, ratified at the governing body’s council meeting in Kyoto, Japan, is designed to ensure that players have a genuine, close, credible and established link with the nation they represent. “This is an historic moment for the sport,” said World Rugby vice-chairman Agustin Pichot. “National team representation is the reward for devoting your career, your rugby life, to your nation and these amendments will ensure that the international arena is full of players devoted to their nation, who got there on merit.” World Rugby chairman Bill Beaumont described the reform as “an important and necessary step to protecting the integrity and credibility of international rugby.” Raising the residency period to five years is widely viewed as a measure that could help protect smaller unions, particularly the Pacific Island nations, by discouraging players from switching allegiance after relatively short stints overseas. The issue has been thrown into sharp relief by recent selections: last autumn, England capped Fiji-born Nathan Hughes and Semesa Rokoduguni after both qualified on the three-year residency rule. England head coach Eddie Jones has also included Sale’s Auckland-born Denny Solomona in his training squad, with the former rugby league winger set to become eligible for England in August under the existing regulations. Some nations have already taken unilateral steps to limit reliance on foreign-born players. France has declared it will only select players who hold a French passport, a move intended to reinforce the national team’s identity and reduce dependence on overseas talent. The Kyoto meeting delivered further governance changes. Argentina and Japan, reflecting their growing influence and contributions to the global game, have been granted expanded voting rights and will now hold three votes each on the World Rugby Council with immediate effect. In addition, French Rugby Federation president Bernard Laporte has been elected to the World Rugby Executive Committee. Reaction within the sport has acknowledged both the practicality and the principle behind the residency reform. Former England and British and Irish Lions centre Jeremy Guscott said the practice of recruiting “project players” to qualify on residency “hasn’t been particularly in the spirit of rugby,” while noting that unions were operating within the laws. He suggested the longer qualification could stem the flow of Pacific Island and South African players moving abroad, or at least encourage earlier commitments, and hoped it would strengthen domestic competitions. “It is a long time for someone to commit to a new country and perform well enough over that time to make an international squad so I think five years is fair,” Guscott added. The amended rule will take effect at the end of 2020, giving unions, players and pathways time to adjust to a landscape that places national connection at the heart of international selection.

Travis Head, 22, to replace New Zealand’s Kane Williamson from 18 July and play in all three formats Yorkshire have signed Australia’s Travis Head as their overseas player from 18 July, with the 22-year-old set to feature across all three formats after taking over from New Zealand captain Kane Williamson. Head, who has appeared in two Twenty20 internationals for Australia, will reunite with Yorkshire coach Jason Gillespie, having previously worked with him at the Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League. “I can’t wait to get over to England and play for Yorkshire, the best side in the English game,” Head said. “To work alongside Dizzy (Jason Gillespie) is also an added attraction. He was brilliant for the Strikers and I have heard so many positive things about what he is doing with the team at Yorkshire. To play across all formats is important to me and playing in English conditions will be a good challenge.” Head enjoyed a strong recent Big Bash campaign, scoring 299 runs in nine innings at an average of 42.71 as the Strikers reached the semi-finals. Although not selected for Australia’s upcoming World Twenty20 squad, he is set to further his experience in the Indian Premier League with Royal Challengers Bangalore before arriving at Headingley. Gillespie welcomed the move, highlighting Head’s versatility. “The fact that he can adapt to all formats is beneficial to us,” the former Australia fast bowler said. “He will add something different to the squad with his aggressive batting style and his ability with the ball as a genuine spinner.”

A stark first-hand account from a senior nurse at Cardiff’s University Hospital of Wales has laid bare the intense pressures confronting emergency care, detailing incidents in which patients endured long waits and acute distress during a recent Sunday night shift. The nurse’s written testimony, pinned to a notice board and shared with the Western Mail, was also presented at a high-level meeting of emergency unit staff and hospital managers, prompting renewed scrutiny of staffing and demand across the service. In the account, the nurse described a woman miscarrying after waiting more than two hours to be assessed, a suicidal patient locking herself in the toilets, and another patient suffering a suspected heart attack in the waiting area. She wrote that she had been forced to make decisions “that put patients at risk and put the staff under extreme pressure,” capturing the strain felt on the front line as teams attempted to manage a surge in attendance and complexity. Adam Cairns, chief executive of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, said staff had been encouraged to share their experiences at a weekly forum, and called the nurse’s account “compelling.” “I recognise the pressures our fantastic staff, including the nurse, are dealing with,” he told BBC Wales. “It’s relentless, it’s been extremely tough. One of the reasons we’ve asked for these sort of stories to be produced is so we can circle our wagons, we can together talk about what we can do to keep responding to the pressures we’re encountering.” Cairns said the emergency unit had seen more people arriving by ambulance with increasingly complex illnesses. While capacity has been expanded, he added the hospital is currently unable to staff any additional areas. Therapy staff volunteered to come in last weekend to help relieve pressures, which he suggested have eased slightly in the past couple of days. “It’s a very difficult winter,” he said. “We’ve had a lot of flu in our community and it’s come earlier than it normally would. We’re holding up, patients are getting treatment, we’re looking after them and we’ll continue to do so.” Tina Donnelly, director of the Royal College of Nursing in Wales, described the nurse’s account as “absolutely shocking” and “worrying.” She said it offered a blow-by-blow illustration of how complex and challenging emergency care had become, and argued the issues highlighted stem from staffing levels not being at their optimum to safely manage such demand. At First Minister’s Questions, Carwyn Jones said the nurse’s testimony reflected the “great pressures” faced by many hospitals, noting that strain on A&E was at its highest level in five years. While he cautioned that some people should not attend A&E for minor issues, he pointed to other drivers, including a new strain of flu, behind recent problems. Deputy health minister Vaughan Gething said the situation was not unique to Wales, praising staff who he said had “worked tirelessly, often in difficult situations,” to deliver urgent and emergency care with compassion and high standards.

Portaferry swimmer Sycerika McMahon announces retirement after decorated career Northern Irish swimmer Sycerika McMahon has announced her retirement, closing a distinguished career that saw her rise from European junior champion to Olympic athlete and senior medallist. The Portaferry native won two European junior gold medals in 2010 and 2011 before stepping seamlessly into senior ranks, claiming 50m breaststroke silver at the European Championships in Hungary in 2012 and adding a European short course bronze later that year. She also represented Ireland at the London Olympics in 2012. “This was an unexpected and difficult choice,” McMahon said on Tuesday. “It is not easy to give up something that you have done your whole life. My sport took me to some unimaginable highs and it’s been an honour for me to represent my country all over the world. I will always cherish the unforgettable memories I have from my career, as well as the friendships I made along the way.” McMahon set a host of Irish records across multiple events and distances, but acknowledged in her retirement announcement that she felt “I was capable of a lot more.” Despite her early success, she has struggled for form in recent seasons. She went into the 2014 Commonwealth Games with hopes of challenging for medals but found Glasgow difficult, and she missed out on qualification for the Rio Olympics in 2016. “Regardless, I would like to say a huge thank you to everyone who has been involved in helping me reach my goals over the years,” she added. “I wouldn’t have been able to live out my dream as an Olympian or take up a scholarship in the USA without you all.” McMahon departs the sport as one of Ireland’s most accomplished swimmers of her generation, leaving a legacy of records, resilience, and inspiration for aspiring athletes.

Noren carded a two-under-par 70 to finish on 14 under, while Hatton, who went round in 69, earned a place at next week's Open Championship. Nicolas Colsaerts, Matteo Manassero and Danny Lee tied for third on 12 under. Scotland's Richie Ramsay, whose closing round of 67 earned him a share of sixth with England's Andy Sullivan, will also compete at Royal Troon. Compatriot Russell Knox also shot a 67 to finish 10th on nine under. Four Open spots were available for players who had not yet qualified. Alex Noren sealed his fifth European Tour title with a composed final-round performance at Castle Stuart, overcoming blustery conditions and a charging pack. The Swede, who turns 34 on Tuesday, began Sunday with a two-shot lead and maintained his advantage with a crucial birdie at the par-four 15th, ultimately posting a two-under 70 to win on 14 under. Tyrrell Hatton closed with a 69, birdieing the last to apply late pressure and secure one of the coveted Open Championship berths at Royal Troon. Noren’s victory was particularly sweet given his history at the venue. “I had a really sour finish in 2012,” he recalled. “I missed out from four feet to get in a play-off. Now it feels just so happy it is over. It feels amazing. It is by far the biggest win in my career against a great field of players. I probably can't believe it still.” With multiple contenders posting birdies around him, Noren admitted the final round tested his resolve. “It was pretty tough out there to see those guys making a few birdies, so many players just behind me that is always tough. I doubted myself so many times through this round and, when you get on top, it doesn't feel real. Hopefully soon it does.” Behind the top two, Belgian Nicolas Colsaerts produced a brilliant 66 to join Italy’s Matteo Manassero and New Zealand’s Danny Lee in a tie for third at 12 under. The low round secured Colsaerts’ spot at the Open alongside Manassero and Hatton, while Scotland’s Richie Ramsay earned the fourth place available to non-qualified players after his 67 lifted him into a share of sixth with Andy Sullivan. “It's a big deal for everyone, it's the Open,” said Colsaerts. “I knew coming down the stretch, it was kind of looking like I needed a four on the last to make sure. I was able to do it today, which feels really, really good.” US-based Russell Knox finished 10th at nine under and took positives from his closing 67. “I battled as hard as I could. This was really the only good putting round I had. Today was a great day, building confidence into next week.” Ramsay was buoyed by his form heading to Troon. “I played to win today, which is a great feeling when you're in that position - home pride, great golf course, striking it well. I putted well, which helped, but to be honest I had a sea of chances out there. I feel like I could have been five under on the back nine.”

An exhibition in New Delhi confronts the spaces where sexual violence occurs through The Rape in India Project, a crowd‐sourced archive of photographs mapping locations of reported assaults. Co‐founded by photographer Poulomi Basu, the initiative seeks to spark dialogue and challenge assumptions about safety by highlighting the unsettling banality of sites—streets, homes, parks, workplaces—where women have been raped. Conceived by PROOF: Media for Social Justice, the show is on view at the India Habitat Centre until 23 December, inviting visitors to reflect on how environment, community and policy intersect. Organizers say the project aims to destigmatize conversations about rape, encourage reporting and accountability, and mobilize civic engagement. Submissions continue online, building a living record that underscores the scale and urgency of the crisis.

The BBC Sports Personality of the Year will be revealed on 18 December at Birmingham’s Genting Arena, with tickets now on sale. The public can vote for their favourite by phone and online during the live show, presented by Gary Lineker, Clare Balding and Gabby Logan. Coverage begins at 18:40 GMT on BBC One, with additional programming on BBC Radio 5 Live and the BBC Sport website. Andy Murray won the award last year and in 2013, either side of Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton’s triumph. The 10 contenders for the Young Sports Personality of the Year were also announced on Friday, and the top three will be revealed during Blue Peter on 8 December. "This is an unparalleled era to be competing under the Union Jack," said BBC chief sports writer Tom Fordyce, reflecting on the depth of British achievement. "Sports Personality of the Year? Good luck with whittling it down to the shortlist, let alone choosing your winner." The shortlist reflects standout British performances.

Rachel Taylor, 54, of Southport, has been jailed for 16 months after admitting a series of frauds against singer Miss Ferguson, who finished second in a TV talent show in 2010. At Liverpool Crown Court, Judge David Aubrey QC said Taylor betrayed the performer’s trust and had “sought to exercise unscrupulous control” over her finances. Taylor pleaded guilty to making false representation by claiming to be a qualified accountant and to retaining £21,000, including funds intended for a trust for Ferguson’s daughter. The court heard she became involved in the singer’s financial affairs while purporting to manage them. Ferguson attended the hearing and read a victim impact statement, saying: “As a result of what happened I trust nobody and question everybody. My heart is broken.” She added that Taylor’s “crimes go deeper than money,” alleging the defendant became obsessed with her family and attempted to “rob everything that I had worked hard for.” Taylor’s husband, Raymond Taylor, 62, was also sentenced after previously admitting charging the singer for services as a solicitor despite not being qualified. He further admitted applying for a £32,000 student grant to which he was not entitled. He received a five-month term.

Former Wales back-row Andy Powell, 35, has taken a coaching role at Brecon RFC in National League Division One East. Powell retired in October 2016 after helping Merthyr win Welsh Premiership promotion after joining in 2015. The ex-Newport, Cardiff Blues, Newport Gwent Dragons, Scarlets, Leicester, Sale, Wasps and Béziers forward won 23 Wales caps and toured as an uncapped Lion to South Africa in 2009. "Can't wait to get started," he tweeted.

Two months after its planned reopening, a midwife-led birth unit has resumed services after staffing pressures forced a merger with a labour ward. In October, 28 vacancies left the service short-handed, prompting leaders to combine the units as an “essential but non-sustainable” measure. Charge midwife Andrea Lawrie told BBC Scotland safety was never compromised and defended the delay. “The delay was, I feel, the correct decision. It was around safety,” she said. Lawrie said recruitment over recent months has brought in a cohort of newly qualified midwives, and managers opted to keep the birth unit closed until the team’s skill mix was balanced. “We didn’t feel it was the right thing to open the birth unit to have all those newly qualified midwives,” she added, noting time was needed for them to settle and gain experience. The unit has reopened.

Simon Bennett, 44, has admitted the manslaughter of Elliot Handley on the grounds of diminished responsibility. Mr Handley, from Eastleigh, Hampshire, was found at a property in The Grove, Dorchester, on 26 May. Appearing at Winchester Crown Court, Bennett, of The Grove, was detained under the Mental Health Act following sentencing on Monday. A post-mortem examination concluded Mr Handley had suffered multiple blunt force injuries to the head. Dorset Police said the scene was forensically examined over three days and several items believed to have been used in the attack were seized, including a claw hammer, a heavy metallic object and a bottle. Senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Neil Devoto said: “Our thoughts today are with Elliot’s family who are being supported by family liaison officers.” Police thanked the local community for its cooperation during the investigation.

The event requires funding from Northern Ireland's government but is at risk after the collapse of Stormont. Louise Martin, the federation's president, had set Thursday as the deadline to release funding. Northern Ireland is due to be handed the event next month at the closing ceremony of the 2017 games. Stormont collapsed in January and a deadline to restore the devolved institutions passed on Thursday. Talks between Northern Ireland's political parties will now continue until Monday. The Commonwealth Games Federation said it has been encouraged by political support but "empathises with the administration's current circumstances". Sources have told the BBC that the federation will monitor political developments over the weekend before a decision is taken on the games' future. The business case for funding the games has been with the Department of the Economy, but was not approved by former DUP economy minister Simon Hamilton so was not brought to the executive table. The department said the games were not "value for money", but the BBC understands that ministers could still have approved the project if it had been discussed, and backed, by the executive. All five main political parties attended a meeting with games officials in Belfast last Tuesday to try to find a way forward. About 1,000 young athletes are due to take part in the games, which would have been a landmark event for Northern Ireland's centenary year. Sports stars like Carl Frampton, Michael Conlon, Jessica Ennis-Hill, Beth Tweddle and Louis Smith have all taken part in previous events. Northern Ireland’s bid to host the next edition faces a critical juncture as the absence of a sitting executive complicates funding decisions. The CGF’s deadline, set by president Louise Martin, coincided with the latest failed effort to restore power-sharing at Stormont, intensifying uncertainty. While officials say they remain encouraged by cross-party support, the impasse has prevented formal approval of the business case. Further talks are due to continue into Monday, with the federation expected to review progress before ruling on the event’s future. Organisers and political leaders argue the games would showcase Northern Ireland internationally during its centenary year, bringing economic and social benefits and inspiring a new generation of athletes. However, the Department of the Economy’s value-for-money concerns have stalled the process. Despite those reservations, sources suggest the executive could still have endorsed the project had it been tabled, underscoring the importance of a functioning government for major event commitments. Last week’s meeting in Belfast, attended by all five main parties and games officials, sought to salvage the bid and outline alternative funding pathways. Around 1,000 young competitors are expected to participate, with the event’s pedigree highlighted by past involvement from figures such as Carl Frampton, Michael Conlon, Jessica Ennis-Hill, Beth Tweddle and Louis Smith. As the CGF monitors developments, the weekend will be pivotal in determining whether Northern Ireland secures hosting rights or the opportunity is deferred.

Meath community mourns Lorna Carty, mother-of-two killed in Sousse beach attack The County Meath community gathered to mourn Lorna Carty, a mother-of-two in her 50s who was among 38 people murdered at the beach resort of Sousse, Tunisia, on 26 June. At the Church of the Assumption in Robinstown, Fr Noel Horneck told mourners the community was in shock, paying tribute to Carty’s commitment to the local GAA club in Dunderry. “Friends, neighbours, colleagues, and the local GAA club here in Dunderry to which she was so committed, so often giving her nursing aid to players when injured — she was a club nurse — that’s probably the best way of describing Lorna’s involvement,” he said. “Her goodness and kindness will always be remembered and appreciated and spoken of.” Members of Meath’s Senior GAA team and her local club formed a guard of honour. Addressing the family, Fr Horneck added: “Our mourning as friends, neighbours, colleagues, club and parish is nothing compared to your loss.” The tragedy also claimed the lives of Laurence (Larry) and Martina Hayes from County Westmeath. Their funerals took place in Athlone on Friday, poignantly coinciding with their only daughter Sinead’s 30th birthday. Across the UK, a minute’s silence was held on Friday to remember the 30 British victims of the attack. The final five bodies of British nationals were being flown back to the UK on Saturday. Other victims included two Germans, a Belgian, a Portuguese and a Russian.

Haru Nomura of Japan won by four shots in punishing winds at Lake Merced in Daly City on Sunday, as none of the top 10 after the third round broke par with gusts reaching 40 mph. Catriona Matthew, 46, finished tied for 13th, 10 strokes back, after five bogeys and a double bogey at the par-four 16th; her lone birdie came at the eighth. World No. 1 Lydia Ko opened with a four-bogey outward 40 and closed with a three-over 75 to share sixth with American Lexi Thompson. England’s Jodi Ewart Shadoff tied for 27th following a final-round 76. Michelle Wie withdrew on the back nine after 15 holes due to neck spasms, capping a grueling final day on the LPGA tour.

UK-Registered Yacht Seized off Martinique as 250kg of Cocaine Found; Two Jersey Men Arrested French customs officers boarded the UK-registered yacht SY Hygeia of Halsa off the island of Martinique, seizing 250kg of cocaine and arresting two men from Jersey, aged 42 and 57. The vessel had begun a transatlantic crossing when authorities intervened after a joint investigation involving British and French police and the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA). The detainees face prosecution by French authorities. Hank Cole, the NCA’s head of international operations, said: “We have no doubt that without this intervention the drugs would have ended up on the streets of the UK where, after being cut, they would have had a potential value of £30-40 million. Our investigation into the organised crime network involved in this attempt continues.” Detective Superintendent Neil Thompson said the seizure would prevent harm. “It is clear that the drugs recovered would have been distributed throughout the streets of London, generating further criminality and fuelling gang activity. If you deal in drugs in any scale we will find you, we will arrest you, and you will face the consequences of your actions.” The operation follows a similar haul intercepted by the Irish Naval Service in September, based on intelligence supplied by the NCA earlier this year.

Teenage student dies after meningitis diagnosis; hospital says initial symptoms were not typical A 16-year-old Bristol student has died two days after being readmitted to hospital with meningitis, prompting an internal review and plans for a coroner’s inquest. Isabel “Izzy” Gentry, a pupil at St Brendan’s Sixth Form College, began feeling unwell last Wednesday while revising for her AS exams and was taken by ambulance to Bristol Royal Infirmary (BRI). After initial treatment and a five-hour observation period in the accident and emergency department, she was discharged home. University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust, which runs BRI, said Izzy appeared to improve during her time in hospital and was advised to seek further medical attention if her symptoms returned. She was readmitted later the same day and, on reassessment, doctors identified symptoms “typical” of meningitis. Despite treatment, she died two days later. Deborah Lee, chief operating officer for the trust, said an initial investigation into the circumstances of Izzy’s death had not found shortcomings in the care provided during her first presentation. “Izzy’s symptoms were not typical of meningitis at the time of first presentation and we believe that both the assessment and treatment were appropriate,” she said. “Sadly, we cannot bring Izzy back but will do our very best to see if there is any learning for ourselves or others that could prevent such a tragedy happening again.” The trust added that it believes the assessment and treatment were “appropriate” given the initial clinical picture, and that staff acted in line with guidance by advising further medical attention if symptoms recurred. Friends and classmates have paid tribute to Izzy on social media, describing her as warm, funny and full of life. “Absolutely devastated to hear of the sudden passing of Izzy Gentry. One of the nicest, funniest girls I’ll ever meet,” wrote Ben Flinton. Chloe Hughes said her friend was “taken way too soon,” adding: “God really does take the best ones, rest in peace you gorgeous girl.” Eryn O’Connell remembered Izzy as “one of the most bubbly souls” whose energy “brought so much life to us all.” Avon Coroner’s Court confirmed that an inquest into the teenager’s death is likely to be opened and adjourned next week. Further details will be released in due course.

At least 21 cars in Festing Road and Salisbury Road in Southsea were targeted overnight. It is thought a blade was used to puncture holes in the tyres. The damage has left many victims unable to travel for Christmas and is set to cost some hundreds of pounds in repairs. Police described it as a random attack and are appealing for witnesses. Sgt Alan Cameron from Hampshire Police said: "Whoever is responsible for this mindless act of damage has not only impacted financially on their victims at an expensive time of year but may have also stopped some of them being able to travel to visit loved ones over this festive period." Police are investigating after at least 21 cars on Festing Road and Salisbury Road in Southsea had their tyres punctured overnight, in what officers believe was a random attack using a blade. The damage has left many residents unable to travel for Christmas and facing repair bills running into hundreds of pounds. Hampshire Police are appealing for witnesses and any footage that could help identify the culprit. Sgt Alan Cameron said: “Whoever is responsible for this mindless act of damage has not only impacted financially on their victims at an expensive time of year but may have also stopped some of them being able to travel to visit loved ones over this festive period.”

Members of the Fire Brigades Union (FBU) voted 90% in favour of action, short of a strike, amid a row over North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service’s plan to introduce smaller Tactical Response Vehicles (TRVs) that carry two crew instead of the usual four. NYFRS described the ballot result as “disappointing and saddening” following a decision approved in December 2015 to replace six fire engines at six of the county’s 38 stations, a move intended to save £1.5m a year. The FBU argues the new vehicles are “totally inadequate to meet the needs of firefighters,” warning that reduced staffing could slow response times and compromise safety. “These proposals are not only a cut in the level of service the taxpayers pay for. They pose a danger to the public and firefighters alike. It is an utter disgrace,” said Steve Howley, North Yorkshire FBU secretary. In a statement, NYFRS insisted the changes are evidence-based, citing risk assessments and impact analyses conducted over the last three years that suggest no significant adverse effect on public service or staff safety. The service said it had extensively consulted the union for two and a half years on introducing TRVs, but claimed the FBU was unwilling to accept new ways of working.

Darren Moorhouse, 49, died after an attack at Athol Close in Halifax on Wednesday, West Yorkshire Police said. A post-mortem found he died from a stab wound to the chest. Christopher Churchill, 33, of Athol Close, Halifax, and Dale Dwyer, 25, of Alma Street, Buxton, Derbyshire, were charged on Saturday and are due to appear at Bradford Magistrates’ Court. A 31-year-old woman arrested on Wednesday evening has been released without charge. Police appeal for information as inquiries progress.

Search crews have intensified efforts around Blackrock Lighthouse, about 10 miles off the coast, after a signal from the Irish Coastguard Rescue 116 helicopter was detected last Wednesday. The aircraft had lost contact and crashed in the early hours of Tuesday. The immediate priority is to recover the bodies of chief pilot Mark Duffy and winchmen Paul Ormsby and Ciarán Smith, who remain missing. They were among four crew on board Rescue 116. The fourth crew member, Captain Dara Fitzpatrick, was recovered from the sea within hours of the crash; her funeral took place on Saturday. For much of the week, heavy Atlantic swells prevented search teams from safely approaching the crash site. On Sunday, improved conditions allowed crews to get close to Blackrock Lighthouse for the first time since the middle of last week. Local vessels conducted extensive sonar scanning to map the undersea terrain, surveying depth, access routes, and potential obstacles. The aim is to give divers a detailed understanding of the local geography before they begin operations in challenging waters. All of the mapping data was collated overnight and will be presented to the agencies coordinating the search on Monday. Teams remain hopeful the missing crew will be located in the wreckage of the helicopter once divers are able to reach the site. Captain Fitzpatrick, the most senior pilot with CHC—the company contracted to provide search and rescue services in the Republic of Ireland—was remembered by hundreds of mourners at St Patrick’s Church in Glencullen, County Dublin. Members of the Irish Coast Guard formed a guard of honour, and a coastguard helicopter performed a fly-past in tribute. Fitzpatrick was the mother of a young son, and tributes praised her professionalism, courage, and dedication to public service. Officials caution that conditions remain changeable, but say the detailed seabed mapping has significantly advanced preparations for the next phase of the recovery mission. Families and colleagues continue to await news with solemn hope.

Images include prisoners taking part in a snowball fight during World War One and a tunnel which may have been dug as part of an escape attempt. The pictures have been shared by the great nephew of Captain Eli Bowers, who was among the camp's guards. They "add to our understanding of the history of the camp", said island historian Ian Ronayne. The site at Les Blanches Banques housed nearly 2,000 men from the German armed forces from 1915-1917. A remarkable set of six photographs taken by Captain Eli Bowers of the Royal Jersey Militia between late 1916 and early 1917 has surfaced, illuminating daily life and security at the First World War prisoner of war camp on Jersey’s dunes. The images, discovered in a family home by Bowers’s great nephew, Helier Falle, depict scenes ranging from prisoners engaged in a snowball fight to what appears to be a tunnel that may have been dug during an escape attempt. “Rather than leave them sitting in a drawer for nobody to see, I thought they should be shared,” said Falle, who added that although he had seen similar photographs auctioned, “it wouldn’t feel right to profit from them.” Island historian Ian Ronayne, a WW1 blogger for Jersey Heritage, said the collection adds valuable detail to the record of Les Blanches Banques, which held nearly 2,000 members of the German armed forces from 1915 to 1917. He noted that several images show tunnel structures that might be linked to documented attempts to flee the camp. “If the images related to one of these incidents it would be a fantastic find,” he said. Dr Brian K Feltman of Georgia Southern University highlighted the snowball fight as an evocative glimpse of prisoners “breaking the monotony of camp life,” suggesting it could reflect efforts to stave off “barbed wire disease,” a form of depression associated with “the boredom and regulations” of captivity. Another photograph shows two layers of fencing—“barbed wire on the inside..... and then an electrified fence”—a configuration Dr Heather Jones of the London School of Economics described as rare. “I have not come across an electric fence being used for a UK home front prisoner of war camp before,” she said. Together, the images offer a humanizing and historically significant window into wartime confinement, discipline, and resilience on Jersey.

Dunlop led throughout and won by 13.3 seconds from Peter Hickman for his second victory of the week, and his third in the blue riband event. The triumph sees the 28-year-old move into fourth place in the all-time solo winners' list. The race was run over four laps after initially being red-flagged for an incident involving Ian Hutchinson. Sixteen-time winner Hutchinson was taken by helicopter to Noble's Hospital after sustaining a broken femur in a crash at the 27th Milestone. Michael Dunlop had equalled the late Mike Hailwood’s tally of 14 wins by taking victory in the Supersport race earlier in the week, and he returned to the Mountain Course to deliver another commanding performance in the Senior TT. On the restart, an opening lap of 132.29mph gave the Northern Irishman a 4.2-second lead over Hickman, and he stretched the advantage by five seconds with a blistering second circuit at 132.90mph. “Today we have made the impossible possible on a brand new bike,” said the Bennetts Suzuki rider, referencing the GSX-R1000. “It was hard work and I was trying to go as easy on the bike as I could. The bike never missed a beat and everyone remembers who won the Senior.” Dunlop previously won the showpiece finale in 2014 and 2016.
