Hickman, who had been battling for the lead with Hutchinson when the initial race was halted, sealed his fifth podium from five starts this week, further underlining a breakthrough run after never previously finishing in the top three at the TT. Kawasaki’s Dean Harrison finished 10 seconds adrift of the Lincolnshire rider in third, replicating his result from Sunday’s Superbike race. James Hillier, Michael Rutter and Josh Brookes completed the top six. Manxman Conor Cummins ended eighth, while his Padgett’s Honda teammate Bruce Anstey retired at Bedstead Corner on the second lap as he contended for a rostrum. The victory capped a standout week for Dunlop and reinforced his status among the TT’s modern greats.

Ciaran Thomas Morris has admitted possessing a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence and affray following an incident in Cynwyd, near Corwen, that prompted an armed police response in March. Appearing via video link at Mold Crown Court on Friday, Morris pleaded guilty to possessing an air pistol with intent to cause fear of violence to a police officer and to affray between 24 and 27 March. He was remanded in custody ahead of sentencing on 5 May. Armed officers and negotiators were deployed during the incident. Prosecutor Emmalyne Downing said the Crown would not proceed with counts of threatening to kill a police officer or damaging a police car. Defending, Simon Mills stressed the air pistol was not a prohibited weapon requiring a licence. Judge Philip Hughes warned Morris to expect a custodial sentence.

Bicester Community Hospital, a 12-bed facility, has opened with a first aid unit plus x-ray and physiotherapy suites after a September delay to resolve issues. Oxford Health NHS Foundation Trust COO Yvonne Taylor said the site provides a modern, safe environment for patients. Adjacent land has planning permission for 14 homes, integrating health and housing. An official opening ceremony is scheduled for next year.

Andrew Robertson reflects on rise from youth ranks, welcomes culture in Scotland squad, and urges unity at struggling Dundee United Scotland international Andrew Robertson has reflected on his rapid ascent from the youth ranks to the national team and offered words of encouragement to his former club Dundee United during an appearance on BBC Radio Scotland’s Sportsound. The 21-year-old full-back charted a path that began in Celtic’s academy before a pivotal spell at Queen’s Park set up his move to Dundee United in 2013. Within a year he had broken into the Scotland squad for his senior international debut, and his performances in the Premiership earned a transfer to Hull City in a £2.85m deal. Speaking about life with Scotland, Robertson highlighted the energy and inclusivity he felt upon joining the national setup, praising the positive environment fostered by the coaching staff. “His enthusiasm always comes across to the boys,” he said of the manager. “He’s one of those people who can easily pass on his enthusiasm to all the players.” Robertson reserved special mention for the leadership shown by Scott Brown during his time as national team captain. “They were all brilliant. [Celtic’s] Scott Brown was up here [in Scotland] and he was the captain. He spoke to us and made us feel welcome. That was us into training and you could just look forward to it. He really put any nerves that we had to ease. The squad was really welcoming. When you see new boys coming in, we’re all not scared to chat to them and make them feel welcome into the squad and I think that’s the most important thing.” Turning to Dundee United, Robertson admitted it was hard to watch his former side struggle near the foot of the table after seasons spent competing at the top end. “When you look at the league table and you see them bottom, it is tough to look at, especially with how well our team did when I was there and even the season after, they were always up trying to fight for Europe,” he said. He urged patience with youth players and called for strong voices in the dressing room, adding: “I think they do need a few leaders and I know there is a few there like [John] Rankin and [Sean] Dillon. I’d probably try my best to get the boys all pulling together and hopefully they can get a couple of results put together and start climbing that table.” His advice to youngsters mirrored his own journey: “Listen to your coaches. If you get a chance then take it..... whenever you get a chance, you’ve just got to take it with both hands.”

Media playback is not supported on this device Pastor Maldonado’s afternoon at the Chinese Grand Prix encapsulated the combustible mix of speed and error that has defined his Formula 1 career, sparking a familiar debate over whether the Venezuelan’s reputation as the sport’s perennial firebrand is deserved. The 30-year-old Lotus driver looked set for a tidy points finish before his race began to unravel mid-distance. An apparent brake problem saw Maldonado overshoot the pit-lane entrance, a costly mistake that dropped him down the order. Attempting to recover, he lost control and spun soon after rejoining, erasing any immediate hope of salvaging his earlier progress. What followed was the day’s most compelling on-track duel, a hard-fought, wheel-to-wheel scrap with McLaren’s Jenson Button over 13th place. Maldonado initially gained the upper hand through sharp race craft and brave positioning. But the battle ended abruptly when Button missed his braking point at Turn One and collected both cars, eliminating them from contention. The 2009 world champion later took to social media to apologise, tweeting an apology to Maldonado “for getting a little over excited,” acknowledging his role in the collision. As is often the case with Maldonado, the incidents triggered a torrent of criticism online. Twitter users dubbed him “shocking,” “awful,” and “the gift that keeps on giving,” while a tongue-in-cheek website that tracks whether he has crashed on any given day again circulated widely. The sharp tone is amplified by Maldonado’s status as one of F1’s best-known pay drivers, bringing an estimated £30m a year to Lotus via sponsorship from Venezuelan state oil company PDVSA—making him an easy target for ridicule when things go wrong. Yet the question persists: is Maldonado really as bad as his reputation suggests? His raw pace has never been in doubt. He famously won the 2012 Spanish Grand Prix from pole position in a Williams that was nowhere near the class of the field that season, a stunning outlier that showcased his peak performance potential. In his rookie year, he held his own in qualifying against veteran Rubens Barrichello, an 11-time grand prix winner with 322 starts, underlining that Maldonado’s speed is real. The problem, as it always has been, is consistency and a tendency to crash. The weeks following his Barcelona triumph brought a string of collisions, including three penalties in one weekend at Spa, and nine races passed before he scored points again. If any season captured Maldonado’s yin and yang, it was 2012: flashes of brilliance offset by costly errors. China offered a similar narrative arc. For the first 34 laps, Maldonado drove impressively at the front of a lively midfield battle between Lotus, Sauber, and Toro Rosso, even leading team-mate Romain Grosjean. He then overcooked his pit entry and ran wide, and later spun while trying to recoup the lost time. Though blameless for the clash with Button, his prior exchange with the Briton highlighted precision and bravery under pressure. In a largely uneventful grand prix, Maldonado’s rollercoaster provided genuine drama. For a sport often accused of lacking personality and excitement, there is something to be said for a driver who, for better or worse, never blends into the background.

A civil breach-of-privacy case involving a woman who says she was secretly filmed while relieving herself among sand dunes near Donald Trump’s Menie golf resort is set to be heard in April at Edinburgh Sheriff Court. Rohan Beyts, 62, a retired social worker, said she “had to answer the call of nature” after a beach walk last April and later discovered men had been filming her. She was reported to the procurator fiscal at the time, but no criminal action was taken. Her solicitor, Mike Dailly, confirmed attempts to have the civil claim dismissed have failed, clearing the way for a three-day hearing next year. Beyts told BBC Scotland she is “glad” the case is proceeding, noting April will mark a year since the incident. “When I discovered men had been filming me I felt really uncomfortable — mortified,” she said. “It’s ironic they said my act was disgusting, but you hear about Donald Trump’s claims about women. I know which I think are disgusting.” A spokeswoman for Trump International said: “Our position on Rohan Beyts’ claim remains unchanged and the matter is now in the hands of our lawyers.” The Menie course, developed by Trump International Golf Club Scotland and opened in July 2012 after lengthy opposition from local residents and environmentalists, recorded a loss of just under £1.1m in 2015. The resort has drawn controversy.

East Overcliff Drive in Bournemouth was shut on 26 April as engineers assessed a cliff face after a landslip sent rubble cascading from the 30m (100ft) East Cliff near the Jon Egging Memorial two days earlier. Bournemouth Borough Council said cordons along promenade on both sides of the site will remain in place while surveys and monitoring continue. Initial inspections have found no further movement, but the authority warned that additional road closures on East Overcliff Drive will be required during clearance and safety works. The slip partially submerged the East Cliff Lift, an Edwardian funicular railway, and destroyed a public toilet block at the foot of the cliffs. The Jon Egging Memorial has also moved closer to the cliff edge. Cracks were observed on the promenade the day before the fall, prompting the council to close the area as a precaution. Work to remove debris is due to begin shortly, with teams continuing to monitor the cliff to protect the public and infrastructure.

Having renewed his commitment to reducing immigration in the Conservative manifesto, the prime minister now faces the challenge of reversing a stubborn trend. The government signalled its intent with a photocall at the scene of an immigration raid on Tuesday, highlighting a new law designed to hit illegal migrant workers in the pocket and deter abuse of the system. Ministers say enforcement will be paired with efforts to curb legal migration, which they acknowledge is where the numbers are most affected. Downing Street argues the plan hinges on better-trained Britons, expanded apprenticeships and tighter EU welfare rules to reduce incentives for movement. The prime minister’s decision to chair a cross-government taskforce is intended to concentrate minds in Whitehall and sharpen delivery across departments. Yet officials and industry warn that crackdowns, legislation and declarations may not translate into lower net migration. The UK cannot dictate how many EU citizens arrive, nor how many Britons depart, under free movement rules. Business groups worry that by targeting the immigration they can influence—legal migration from outside the EU—ministers risk making it harder to recruit the skilled workers needed to fill gaps and drive growth. No statute can change the economic pull: there are more jobs and often better pay in Britain than in many countries, and migrants will continue to come. The stakes are high. Conservatives are acutely aware there could be a heavy political price if they head into a second election having conspicuously failed to deliver on their ambition.

A 65-year-old woman from Northampton drowned after being swept into rough seas during a coastal break in Moelfre, a coroner has concluded. Toni Robinson, who had recently retired after running an award-winning restaurant and pub for 22 years, was found in the water by an angler last October. A lifeboat reached the scene within minutes and crew performed CPR, but she was pronounced dead on arrival at a hospital in Bangor. At an inquest in Caernarfon, Coroner Dewi Pritchard Jones recorded a conclusion of accidental death. Evidence from a lifeboat crew member described a heavy swell of up to 3m (10ft), with waves breaking over the rocks, creating conditions in which “if someone had fallen in the sea it would not be easy to get out.” Pathologist Dr Mark Lord said Mrs Robinson died from drowning. He told the hearing that injuries to her hands and fingernails were consistent with attempts to climb out against the rocks. The coroner noted there were no witnesses to the moment she entered the water, but offered a cautious hypothesis. “My guess — you can’t put it any stronger — based on weak evidence, is that the dog probably fell into the sea and she tried to recover it and fell in herself,” he said. “She tried to get out but failed because of the rocky nature of the coastline and she drowned.” Mrs Robinson had been on a break with her husband at the time.

Welsh Government Puts Betsi Cadwaladr Health Board into Special Measures Amid Trust Crisis The Welsh government has placed Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board into special measures, citing a profound loss of public trust and a breakdown in the relationship between the board and its communities as central reasons for intervening. The move coincides with the publication of a previously unseen report by former Welsh NHS chief executive Ann Lloyd, which ministers say helped inform their decision. The Lloyd report paints a stark picture of a dysfunctional organisation requiring a “mammoth” effort to turn around, detailing concerns about a rigid and bullying culture identified by the board’s chairman. First Minister Mark Drakeford said the report was pivotal and led officials to advise immediate special measures. He acknowledged being aware of findings presented to the Betsi board in March but emphasised that he had sought to follow the established formal intervention process. While the report has provided justification for the government’s action, it also heightens the pressure on ministers to deliver rapid, visible improvements. Central to the intervention is a renewed focus on listening to patients, staff and communities, and rebuilding confidence in the health board’s leadership and services. The new management structure installed under special measures is expected to report back in the autumn, creating a critical window to demonstrate progress. That timeline intersects with the run-up to the assembly election, binding the Welsh government’s fortunes to the health board’s performance, particularly for Labour candidates in north Wales. Ministers will hope to present evidence of stabilised services and a clearer path to reform. However, the challenge will be ensuring that any positive message cuts through public perceptions shaped by recent failures and controversy. For now, the emphasis is on repairing relationships, strengthening governance and ensuring safe, reliable care. The autumn assessment will offer the clearest test yet of whether special measures—and a commitment to listening—can restore trust in Betsi Cadwaladr and underpin a sustainable turnaround.

Matthew Rhys will step into the role of Fitzwilliam Darcy in a new television adaptation of P.D. James’s Death Comes to Pemberley, the crime sequel that revisits the world of Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice. The drama places Elizabeth Bennet, Mr Darcy and George Wickham at the heart of a murder mystery set six years after the events of Austen’s novel. Anna Maxwell Martin has been cast as Elizabeth Bennet, with Matthew Goode portraying the rakish Wickham. Rhys, currently starring in the U.S. series The Americans, acknowledged inevitable comparisons with Colin Firth’s 1995 portrayal. “Exciting as it is, one of the challenges of a part such as Darcy are the comparisons that will be drawn to those who’ve institutionalised him in the past,” he said. “The beauty of Pemberley is that it is an entirely new and different Darcy six years on. And also, I don’t have to appear from a lake in a white shirt and breeches,” he added, referencing the scene from the BBC classic. Death Comes to Pemberley finds Elizabeth and Darcy settled at their Derbyshire estate, parents to two young sons and preparing for the annual ball when events turn their lives upside down. Juliette Towhidi, co-writer of Calendar Girls, has adapted James’s international bestseller for the screen. Filming is due to begin in June on location in Yorkshire.

Zamalek’s board convened after Sunday’s 3-2 defeat to El-Gaish and announced the club would not complete this season’s competition, escalating tensions over refereeing in the Egyptian league. The board will reconvene on Monday to review the decision. The Egyptian Football Association (EFA) said it has received no official notification from Zamalek and defended the standard of officiating. Zamalek’s pre-match request to replace assigned referee Mahmoud Al Banna was rejected. During the game, Al Banna sent off Zamalek defender Ali Gabr after four minutes and awarded El-Gaish two penalties, the first immediately after the red card and the second 10 minutes into the second half. Under league regulations, withdrawal would carry severe sanctions: Zamalek could be relegated directly to the fourth tier of Egyptian football. The standoff leaves one of Egypt’s most successful clubs facing a pivotal decision.

An inquest in Northampton has concluded that racing driver Justin Wilson died following an incident during the ABC Supply 500 at Pocono Raceway in Pennsylvania last August. Wilson, 37, a father of two competing for Andretti Autosport, was struck by flying debris and succumbed to his injuries the following day. The hearing heard that race leader Sage Karam crashed into a barrier at 200mph on lap 179 of 200, scattering debris across the track. As Wilson approached the scene, a large, heavy component from Karam’s car flew and struck him on the helmet, rendering him unconscious. He was extracted from his car, transported to hospital, underwent surgery and was placed on life support, which was switched off the next day. Coroner Anne Pember read a statement from Wilson’s father, Keith, who described the sequence as a “freak accident.” “[Karam] was unhurt but debris from his car flew high into the air and a large, heavy piece hit Justin on the head as he approached the scene of the accident,” the statement said. Mrs Pember recorded a verdict of accidental death. “Justin was a kind, caring and loving son who is sadly missed by all of his family and friends,” his father added. Sheffield-born Wilson, who divided his time between Northampton and Colorado, previously raced in Formula 1 with Minardi and Jaguar before enjoying greater success in Champ Car, finishing runner-up in 2006 and 2007. He moved to IndyCar in 2008 following the Champ Car–IRL merger. Wilson finished second at Mid-Ohio on 2 August, his first podium since 2013, and his final victory came at the Firestone 550 at Texas Motor Speedway in June 2012. About 500 people attended his funeral in Paulerspury, Northamptonshire, in September.

Lionel Messi became La Liga’s all-time leading scorer, surpassing Telmo Zarra’s 251-goal mark held since 1955, by netting a hat-trick in Barcelona’s 5-1 win over Sevilla. The 27-year-old now has 253 league goals. Barcelona coach Luis Enrique hailed Messi’s feat, calling him “a unique player” and predicting the new benchmark will be “unreachable for anyone else.” Enrique also noted that Zarra’s tally came “in an age when there were more forwards than defenders.” Among active players, Real Madrid’s Cristiano Ronaldo is the closest pursuer with 197 La Liga goals, though he is two years older than the Argentina forward, underscoring Messi’s astonishing pace.

The University of Brighton’s presence in Hastings faces an uncertain future as the institution’s board of governors considers a review that could lead to the closure of its three sites in the town. The board is due to meet on Tuesday, with an announcement expected on Wednesday. Students and local leaders warned that shutting the Hastings campus would have far-reaching consequences for the community. “It would be a massive loss to Hastings, the uncertainty is a huge worry,” said student Sophie Hewitt. Fellow student Alice Naylor said many at the campus are mature students with children. “Not having a university in Hastings would mean that some people wouldn’t be able to access a university at all,” she said. The university said it has struggled to recruit sufficient numbers to make the campus sustainable. “One of the biggest drivers of student choice is location,” a spokesperson said, noting that Hastings competes with Brighton and other regional and national campuses. The university added that any changes would be carefully considered and that partners, staff and students would be fully involved in the process. The Hastings campus opened 13 years ago and has benefited from significant investment, including £12m of public funding and £14m from the university for development and operations. The institution also highlighted its broader role in the town’s regeneration, citing its sponsorship of nine academy schools alongside higher education provision. Local representatives vowed to oppose any closure. “The whole community—elected politicians, business leaders and heads of schools—are all absolutely united that we will fight to keep the university here,” said Amber Rudd, the Conservative MP for Hastings and Rye. “We will be making a strong case for why it’s such a great place to live and work.” The outcome of the board’s review will be closely watched by students, staff and residents concerned about the future of higher education and skills in Hastings.

PC Gareth Francis, 28, has died following an assault in Edgeley, Stockport, in the early hours of Sunday, Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said. The off-duty officer was walking home along Castle Street at about 01:20 GMT after a night out with friends when he was attacked. He was taken to Stepping Hill Hospital with a head injury and died a short time later. Two men, aged 20 and 21 and both from Stockport, have been arrested on suspicion of murder and remain in custody for questioning. Detectives believe PC Francis was dropped off by a taxi in Edgeley after socialising in Manchester city centre and was assaulted minutes later. Chief Superintendent Chris Sykes said PC Francis joined GMP in 2007 and was serving at West Didsbury Police Station. “Gareth was a dedicated police officer with six years’ experience and he will be greatly missed by his colleagues,” he said. “However, the loss will be even greater for Gareth’s family and I would like to reassure them that we have a team of detectives working round-the-clock now to establish exactly what happened this morning. Gareth’s colleagues on the South Manchester Division have been dealt a terrible blow by today’s news and welfare is being provided to any members of staff affected by this tragedy.” In a statement released through the force, his family paid tribute to “a gorgeous son” who brought “love and laughter” to their lives. A post-mortem examination will take place later to determine the cause of death. GMP said the investigation is ongoing and further updates will be provided as inquiries continue.

A 25-year-old driver narrowly escaped serious injury after his car was struck by a commuter train on Wednesday night, police said. The man mistakenly turned onto railway tracks, became stuck while trying to reverse, and abandoned the vehicle moments before the train hit. The collision pushed the wreckage about 15 metres along the line and triggered lengthy delays for evening commuters. None of the 13 passengers on board the train was hurt, and services eventually resumed after crews cleared the scene and inspected the track. A local resident told ABC News the location can be confusing at night, describing how drivers can misread the approach. “His GPS has turned him left onto the railway lines,” the resident said of the latest mishap. “It looks a lot like a road at night.” Police are investigating the circumstances and said they would review signage and lighting in the area, while renewing warnings for motorists to remain alert and avoid blindly following navigation prompts. GPS misdirection has been blamed for a string of incidents in Australia and abroad. In 2012, police in Mildura, Victoria, publicly cautioned drivers after satnav systems erroneously directed several motorists into a remote national park rather than the town itself. A group of Japanese tourists famously drove a rental car into the Pacific Ocean in 2012, following GPS instructions toward North Stradbroke Island. Similar mistakes have made headlines worldwide. In March 2015, Belgian tourists endured an almost 1,200km detour when a bus driver’s GPS took them to La Plagne in the Pyrenees rather than La Plagne in the Tarentaise Valley. In June 2013, a US motorist in Belmont drove onto rail tracks and into the path of an oncoming train. And in January 2013, a Belgian woman who set out to pick up a friend in Brussels ended up in Zagreb, Croatia, after relying on GPS guidance. Other cases include a group nearly driving off a cliff on a scenic route between Bryce Canyon and the Grand Canyon in May 2008, and a man who crossed into Canada instead of Pennsylvania in October 2006. Authorities urge drivers to use common sense, heed road signs, and confirm routes before turning onto unfamiliar paths.

They are accused of killing hundreds of Bosnian men and boys in a single day at a warehouse near Srebrenica. Serbian prosecutors have filed charges against eight former members of a Bosnian Serb special police unit over the mass killing of prisoners at a warehouse in the village of Kravica, marking the first time a Serbian court has brought a case related to the Srebrenica massacre. The move represents a significant shift in accountability for crimes committed during the 1995 slaughter, in which approximately 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were murdered by Bosnian Serb forces. According to the prosecutor’s statement, the victims were herded into a warehouse in Kravica, near Srebrenica, where they were subjected to an all-night assault using machine guns and grenades. The eight men charged were members of the special police unit operating in the area at the time, and the case centers on the killing of hundreds of detainees in a single day. Among those charged is the unit’s commander, Nedeljko Milidragovic, also known as Nedjo the Butcher. Prosecutors allege he gave the order for the killings and declared that “nobody should get out alive.” Milidragovic already faces genocide charges in Bosnia but had been living freely in Serbia due to the absence of an extradition treaty between the two countries, according to BBC correspondent Guy De Launey in Belgrade. That changed in March, when Milidragovic and seven other suspects were detained following cooperation between Serbia’s war crimes court in Belgrade and its counterpart in Sarajevo. Announcing the charges, Serbian Prosecutor Vladimir Vukcevic said they were “a message that there will be no impunity for war crimes and that the victims will not be forgotten.” If convicted, the defendants face a maximum sentence of 20 years. Previous prosecutions related to Srebrenica have been conducted by authorities in Bosnia and by the UN’s International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague. Fourteen people have been convicted by the ICTY in connection with the massacre, and former Bosnian Serb army chief Ratko Mladic and former political leader Radovan Karadzic have faced trials there over crimes linked to Srebrenica. Both the ICTY and the International Court of Justice have ruled that the killings constitute genocide. The Srebrenica massacre occurred amid the violent breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, as Serbia backed Bosnian Serb forces against the Muslim-led Bosnian government. In July 1995, Bosnian Serb troops overran Srebrenica, a designated UN safe haven, rounding up men and boys who were then killed and buried in mass graves across eastern Bosnia. The new Serbian case is seen as an important step toward broader regional accountability for the atrocity.

The Scottish government has launched an independent expert review of substitute drug therapies, including methadone, as part of its national strategy to tackle substance misuse. The move underscores a renewed emphasis on recovery from addiction, shifting away from policies that focused primarily on stabilising lives through long-term reliance on alternatives to heroin. Chaired by the chief medical officer, Sir Harry Burns, the review will draw on independent expertise from the Scottish Drugs Strategy Delivery Commission. Its remit is to consider objectively the role of opiate replacement therapy (ORT) in treatment, with the aim of ensuring doctors can offer a full range of proven interventions, including methadone, in ways that promote sustained recovery. Methadone has been central to successive governments’ drug treatment strategies since the 1980s, but it has faced increasing criticism as a “one-size-fits-all” approach to a complex and multifaceted problem. Many recovering users say they feel “parked” on methadone for years without access to further therapy or support to help them move on. A number of other medications can be prescribed to help people overcome dependence, among them buprenorphine (Subutex), buprenorphine combined with naloxone (Suboxone), diamorphine (pharmaceutical heroin), and dihydrocodeine. Despite these options, methadone remains the most commonly used, with an estimated 24,507 patients currently receiving it on prescription in Scotland. “We know that opiate replacement therapies stabilise the lives of people seeking to address their drug addictions,” Sir Harry said. “This group brings together great expertise, and its work will give us a clearer picture of how these therapies are being used across Scotland.” The government’s policy, The Road to Recovery, introduced in 2008, aims to ensure that service users are eventually free from dependence on any drug, including methadone. Community Safety Minister Roseanna Cunningham said ORT has saved thousands of lives in Scotland, but stressed it must not be seen as the sole route to recovery. “However, the Scottish government is clear that prescribed drug treatment is not, and cannot be, the only treatment option available on the pathway to recovery,” she said. “People have a right to a full range of treatment and support options and to decide in consultation with professionals what is best for them.” Officials said that between April 2011 and March 2012, prescribed drug treatment—including methadone—accounted for less than 20% of treatment options started. The expert group will consult with all political parties before making recommendations to ministers and the Scottish Parliament, with a report expected in spring 2013. The initiative has been welcomed by frontline workers. David Liddell, director of the Scottish Drugs Forum, said: “It is unfortunate that methadone seems to have become something of a political football. The numbers on methadone have been used as a sign that the strategy is not working. This analysis is simplistic when a more measured and sophisticated debate could make a useful contribution.” He added that politicians must think more deeply about why people turn to drugs and how society can respond effectively. Supporters say the review offers an opportunity to refocus services on long-term recovery, balancing harm reduction with comprehensive, person-centred care. Critics hope it will address concerns about entrenched prescribing and open access to wider therapeutic support, including psychosocial interventions, tailored to individual needs.

Police are investigating an incident on Toberdoney Road in Liscolman, near Bushmills, shortly after 16:00 GMT today. A boy was taken to Causeway Hospital and later transferred to Belfast’s Royal Victoria Hospital. A man in his 70s has been arrested. Officers have appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Although the Queen’s birthday falls on 21 April, official celebrations took place over the weekend, following long-standing practice to seek better weather for national events. Councils received around 60 applications to close streets for community parties, coinciding with the 2016 Big Lunch on Sunday. The Big Lunch, launched by the Eden Project, encourages neighbours across the UK to share a meal together each June. Street festivities and picnics marked the milestone, with residents embracing the opportunity to celebrate locally and strengthen community ties.

Polish President Andrzej Duda has marked the anniversary of the Kielce pogrom, honoring the 42 victims. At a ceremony in the city on Monday, Duda laid flowers on graves, accompanied by Poland’s Chief Rabbi Michael Schudrich this week. The massacre took place on 4 July 1946 in Kielce, about 150km south of Warsaw, when communist police, soldiers and a mob attacked a Jewish centre at 7 Planty Street. Most of the victims were Holocaust survivors who had returned after the war. The violence was sparked by a false claim from a Christian boy, Henryk Blaszczyk, who told his family he had been kidnapped by Jews. Before the war, Poland was home to Europe’s largest Jewish community, and Kielce itself had around 24,000 Jewish residents. Only about 200 returned after the Nazi occupation. In the weeks following the pogrom, more than a quarter of Poland’s surviving Jews fled the country, accelerating an exodus already under way. Twelve perpetrators were put on trial and nine were sentenced to death. “It was the army and police who first opened fire on the Jewish residents of Kielce,” Duda said, placing responsibility on the then communist authorities. “In a free, sovereign, independent Poland there is no room for any prejudice, there is no room for racism, there is no room for xenophobia, there is no room for anti-Semitism.”

Peter Moore, 28, from Bonhill, West Dunbartonshire, has been jailed for the murder of his younger brother, Derek Moore, 25, following a fatal stabbing at their mother’s flat in Glasgow’s Govan area on 3 January. At the High Court in Glasgow, Moore was given a life sentence and told he must serve a minimum of 18-and-a-half years before he can apply for parole. Jailing him, judge Lady Wolffe said: “You stand convicted of the murder of your own brother in the house of your mother. In convicting you the jury rejected your defence of self defence.” She noted that although Derek Moore was initially the aggressor by punching his brother, Peter Moore escalated the confrontation by using a knife while Derek lay on the ground. The court heard that Derek Moore suffered a devastating array of injuries during the attack. He was stabbed four times, with the fatal wound to his abdomen causing massive internal bleeding. In total, 75 injuries were recorded, including around 70 wounds described as defensive, indicating a struggle to ward off blows. Evidence presented during the trial included a trail of blood leading from the flat to the common close, which prosecutors said was consistent with Derek Moore having been dragged out of the home and onto a downstairs landing. Lady Wolffe told Peter Moore: “You left him there to die. This was a prolonged and vicious attack. The crime of murder is a most egregious crime. You have doubly punished your family.” The trial also heard that the brothers had a history of violent altercations. On a previous occasion, Derek Moore broke Peter Moore’s jaw during a fight that took place in front of a six-year-old boy. The child was also present at the early stages of the fatal fight before being taken away by his mother. Peter Moore’s partner, Ashley Picken, 24, told the court how she awoke to the sound of the brothers arguing and fighting. She described looking into the hallway and seeing Peter standing over Derek with a knife in his hand, “hitting Derek” in the legs and the side of his body, while Derek lay on his back. When asked about Derek’s demeanour earlier that night, she replied: “He was angry.” In a statement to police after the incident, Peter Moore said: “When we fight, we fight for hours. I can’t remember arguing with him. He’s pure evil when he’s been drinking. He started it.” He added: “I said I wasn’t going to fight with him again.” Moore, who has a number of previous convictions, including for violence, did not give evidence during the trial. The jury found him guilty of murder, leading to the sentence imposed by Lady Wolffe. The case has left the family with profound loss and devastation.

StepChange urges ban on unsolicited sales of high-cost credit as survey highlights aggressive cold calling Debt charity StepChange has called for a ban on the unsolicited marketing of high-cost credit and fee-charging debt management services, warning that cold calls are pushing financially vulnerable people deeper into hardship. The charity says products such as payday loans and paid-for debt advice should not be sold via unsolicited calls, citing survey findings that a third of its clients receive more than five marketing calls a week. StepChange estimates that buying such services after cold calls added an average of £1,052 to the existing debts of its clients. “The problem is particularly serious among the most financially vulnerable in our society,” said Mike O’Connor, chief executive of StepChange. “When someone is already in financial difficulty, they may be at their lowest ebb and feel they have no option but to make quick decisions through desperation, which can bring devastating consequences. “Before taking out any financial product, people need to know whether it is right for them, work out if they can afford it and shop around for the best deal, but unsolicited phone calls can take these key decisions away from them. It is not a good way to sell credit or financial services and it is certainly not a good way to buy them.” The call for tighter marketing rules comes amid wider debate over the cost of short-term borrowing. Consumer group Which? has suggested that, in some cases, taking an unarranged overdraft from a bank can be more expensive than a payday loan. It calculated that borrowing £100 for 28 days from a payday lender would incur a maximum charge of £22.40, compared with up to £90 for an unarranged overdraft. Banks argue that unarranged overdrafts should be a last resort and say cheaper alternatives are available. The payday lending industry disputed StepChange’s findings. Russell Hamblin-Boone, chief executive of the Consumer Finance Association (CFA), which represents some payday lenders, said: “This small survey by StepChange is misinformed and draws the wrong conclusions. Cold calling is carried out by unscrupulous firms who purchase people’s data, not lenders. The sector is regulated and CFA members do not cold call, do not lend to people who cannot afford credit and ensure all lending is responsible. Regulations exist to protect borrowers and there is no need to further restrict how lenders market to their customers.”

Ofsted has rejected claims of inspector misconduct after two North East free schools were rated inadequate in November, prompting formal complaints from their leaders and a full investigation by the watchdog. Sunderland’s Grindon Hall Christian School and Durham Free School both challenged the conduct of inspectors, alleging inappropriate and hostile questioning of pupils. Grindon Hall principal Chris Gray said inspectors asked leading questions about homosexuality, race and other faiths, describing the approach as “hostile” and “inappropriate.” In a statement, Ofsted said initial interviews with the three inspectors who visited the schools found no evidence of improper behavior and noted that the concerns were not raised during the inspections themselves. “We have undertaken a detailed examination of the evidence base, interviewed each of the three inspectors who carried out the inspection and have held a separate meeting between the principal and Ofsted’s North East regional director in respect of these allegations,” the watchdog said. “To date, we have found no evidence to indicate that inspectors failed to act with care and sensitivity and to ask age-appropriate questions when they spoke to pupils, as they are trained to do.” Durham Free School complained that inspectors’ conclusion that “pupils were not being prepared for modern British life” relied on an interview with a single student. Ofsted disputed that characterization, saying “in reaching their conclusions about the effectiveness of the school’s work inspectors considered a wide range of evidence. Discussions with students formed just a part of the evidence.” In their reports, inspectors criticized both schools for failing to tackle “prejudice-based bullying” and the use of racist or homophobic language by students. Leaders at both schools said they did not recognize Ofsted’s portrayal. Ofsted added that it visited two other North East schools in November and neither raised concerns about inspectors’ conduct. Following the publication of the reports, Education Secretary Nicky Morgan announced she was terminating funding for Durham Free School, which currently has 94 pupils. Ofsted said it will continue its investigation into the allegations, acknowledging their seriousness while maintaining that no issues were raised during the visits.

Welsh Steel Union Leaders and Management Unite as Tata Warns of Fight for Survival A rare show of solidarity has emerged in Wales as union leaders and local officials vowed not to “roll over or waive the white flag” in defense of the country’s steel industry, even as Tata Steel’s latest job losses underscore a precarious future. While a task force moves quickly to support the hundreds of workers now facing redundancy, those remaining in the plants at Port Talbot and Llanwern confront a deeper uncertainty that may be decided far beyond Wales. Speaking with unusual frankness for a major manufacturing executive, Stuart Wilkie, who oversees the Port Talbot and Llanwern sites, warned that attention should not rest solely on the 750 jobs set to be cut. Instead, he said, the remaining 3,500 jobs are in a fight for survival. His message was stark: Tata’s continued backing for a loss-making operation depends on “swift” action from the European Union to level the playing field against cheap imports—particularly Chinese steel undermining global prices. The critical question, according to Wilkie, is how long “swift” will take, and whether it will arrive in time. An informal timeframe of 18 months has been floated by some as the window for a turnaround, but no definitive deadline has been offered. That ambiguity fed tensions at a news conference following a high-level meeting, where Welsh economy minister Edwina Hart pushed back against suggestions of a doomed outlook, accusing sections of the media of being too negative. Tata, for its part, has not taken issue with recent coverage; the company’s own assessment—embodied in Wilkie’s “fight for survival” line—has set a sober tone that has reverberated throughout the week. Business leaders and politicians across Wales have voiced mounting concern. Welsh MPs used a Westminster debate to highlight the fundamental challenge posed by cheap Chinese steel, arguing that depressed global prices are squeezing UK producers to the brink. The EU has signaled action against unfair imports, but industry figures say timing is pivotal: delays could render any measures too late to prevent irreversible damage. Despite the bleak backdrop, some cling to signs of long-term commitment by Tata. Significant recent investment at Port Talbot and Llanwern, including money sunk into a blast furnace with a 15 to 20-year lifespan, suggests the company is not eager to walk away. That reality fuels cautious optimism that, with the right trade remedies and energy cost support, a path to viability remains open. Perhaps the most striking element of the current crisis is the unusually tight bond between unions and management. In a departure from past industrial disputes, union leaders have not publicly criticized Tata’s executives for the cuts. Instead, their ire is directed toward the UK Conservative government, which they accuse of failing to move decisively to protect strategic manufacturing and to defend domestic producers against dumped imports. As the task force gears up to support those immediately affected, the fate of the thousands who remain employed appears increasingly tethered to decisions made in Brussels and London. For Welsh steel, the next few months may determine whether solidarity and recent investment can hold the line against global pressures—or whether the battle for survival becomes a fight too far.

Drone filming of alleged liaison in Oklahoma City leads to prison sentence, ignites privacy concerns An Oklahoma City woman has been sentenced to a year in state prison after footage captured by a drone showed an alleged liaison in a parked vehicle, a case that has stirred debate over privacy and the use of drones for citizen-led investigations. According to court documents seen by the BBC, Amanda Zolicoffer was convicted of a misdemeanour and received a one-year sentence. The case against her alleged client, who was arrested in December and subsequently released, remains pending. The video was provided to Oklahoma City police by Brian Bates, a local figure who has spent two decades documenting what he describes as street-level and forced prostitution and human trafficking. “I’m sort of known in the Oklahoma City area,” Bates told the BBC. “For the last 20 years I’ve used a video camera to document street-level and forced prostitution, and human trafficking.” He said he used a drone on this occasion last August because he felt safer and it allowed him to obtain “very good footage.” Bates, who runs a website publishing videos of alleged sex workers and their clients, acknowledged his reputation. “I am openly referred to as a video vigilante, I don’t really shy away from that,” he said. However, he emphasized that drone use is not routine for him, noting this was the only time he has deployed one to film such an encounter and adding that he is generally reluctant due to safety concerns. In this instance, he said, the two individuals were inside a vehicle and the incident occurred away from members of the public. He cautioned others against using drones to document suspected criminal activity. “I’d certainly caution other people who may be tempted to use drones to maybe fight drug activity or prostitution or gangs in their neighbourhood,” Bates said. “If one thing goes wrong, you will probably be the person facing criminal charges or civil liability.” Civil liberties advocates warn that drones raise complex privacy issues. “People operating drones have to think about whether there is a reasonable expectation of privacy when they are filming,” said Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group. “Filming in public spaces [for example] is very different from filming someone’s private property.” Killock added that while drone technology is distinctive, “the technologies may be different but the ethics are fundamentally the same,” likening the concerns to those associated with traditional photography.

Mexico’s decision to extradite Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzmán to the United States has been delayed after a court ruling opened the door to appeals. The government agreed in May to transfer the Sinaloa cartel leader after Washington assured he would not face the death penalty. The ruling means extradition could be months or even years away. Guzmán, who faces murder and drug trafficking charges in the U.S., is being held in a maximum-security prison near the border. He was recaptured in January after six months on the run following a tunnel escape from custody, his second breakout after spending 13 years at large following a prior escape. One appeal argues statutes of limitations have expired on some counts, his lawyer José Refugio Rodríguez told the Associated Press. The defense contends several accusations lack direct evidence.

Health organisations in Cornwall that pooled resources to tackle delayed discharges have instead seen a sharp rise in bed blocking, prompting apologies from local leaders and criticism from campaigners. A report prepared for Cornwall Council shows that from July to September, hospitals in the county lost a total of 3,815 bed days because patients ready to leave could not be discharged due to problems arranging social care packages. That compares with 2,255 lost bed days during the same period in 2014. Bed blocking occurs when patients who are clinically ready to be discharged, for example to a care home, remain in hospital because appropriate care placements or support are not available. The initiative, introduced under the government’s Better Care Fund, encouraged Cornwall Council and NHS Kernow to pool resources to ensure care packages were in place for people leaving hospital. Despite receiving £44.5 million from the scheme, launched nationally in April 2015, the county has faced increasing delays. Graham Webster, vice-chairman of campaign group Health Initiative Cornwall, said the situation “has only got worse,” warning the new approach could turn out to be “useless.” He added: “The Better Care Fund was meant to take the bull by the horns and resolve this situation. We are blocking numerous beds with patients that don’t need to be there.” Patients have felt the impact. Iona Hevican from Newquay had her hysterectomy cancelled at the last minute last January due to bed shortages at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. “Ordinary people are being pushed away. It was awful to have to fight to get into your own hospital,” she said. In a joint statement, Cornwall Council, NHS Kernow and local health providers apologised to those affected and said patients are discharged “as soon as clinically appropriate.” Dr Iain Chorlton, chairman at NHS Kernow, said he was “confident that patient experience and outcomes will further improve” as the organisations work to streamline discharge processes and expand community support. The Department of Health said it is up to local organisations to spend Better Care Fund money effectively, underscoring the need for coordinated planning between health and social care to reduce delays and free up hospital capacity for planned procedures and emergency care.

Message in a bottle sent by Swedish children in 1992 washes up in Panama, reuniting old friends A message in a bottle cast into the sea by two Swedish siblings and their childhood friend in 1992 has resurfaced more than two decades later in Panama, sparking a cross-continental search for the man who found it. Erik and Lina Runestam, along with their friend Christoffer Höglström, dropped the letter into the water at Hunnebostrand, Sweden, during the summer of 1992. Speaking to Newsbeat, Erik said his memory is “a bit blurry” because he had “just turned six that summer,” but he still recalls the thrill of sending the message. Wanting to give it an “old school” look, the children burned the edges of the paper and penned a dramatic note claiming they were stranded on a desert island and “in desperate need of help.” Their father advised them to wait for an offshore wind in hopes the bottle might drift as far as England. “It would have travelled north of Denmark, through the English Channel to cross the Atlantic,” Erik said. “Our hopes weren’t that high to even get to England.” In November 2014, the bottle was found by Leonard Pearson at Playa del Dragos in Bocas del Toro, Panama. In a reply dated 6 November 2014, Pearson wrote: “Bueno dias. I have found this message in a bottle at Playa del Dragos, Bocas del Toro. I used Google Translate, and it seems the message is in Swedish? I hope that the address is correct and that this letter reaches the kids who sent the message.” Erik and Christoffer, who had not spoken for a decade, reconnected when Christoffer sent Erik a photo of Pearson’s reply alongside the original note. “I really want to tell Leonard that it has reached us and we’re no longer kids,” Erik said. “But he didn’t post a return address so we’re trying to find him.” Anyone with information about Leonard Pearson is encouraged to get in touch. Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

Colombia formalizes medical marijuana regulation, Santos touts health benefits while pledging crackdown on illegal drugs Colombia has formally regulated the cultivation, production, and use of medical marijuana, President Juan Manuel Santos announced Tuesday, calling the move a step that places the country “at the forefront...in the use of natural resources to fight disease.” Santos stressed that authorities will continue to combat illegal drug production and trafficking. The decree resolves a legal grey area. A 1986 law permitted manufacture, export, sale, and medical and scientific use of cannabis, but the industry lacked formal oversight. Under the new framework, anyone seeking to grow marijuana for medical purposes must obtain a licence from the National Narcotics Council, establishing clear controls over cultivation and distribution. Medical marijuana is used to alleviate symptoms associated with conditions such as Crohn’s disease, epilepsy, HIV, and chemotherapy-induced nausea. Santos, who has admitted smoking cannabis in Kansas in the 1970s, has argued that legalisation can remove production from criminal networks. Several Latin American countries have decriminalised or legalised use, and U.S. states including Colorado, Oregon, and Washington permit recreational markets. Uruguay fully legalised production, sale, and recreational use in 2013. Colombia remains scarred by decades of drug-related violence and is still among the world’s leading producers of cocaine, alongside Peru.

Bill May and Christina Jones made history at the World Aquatics Championships in Kazan, claiming gold in the duet technical synchronized swimming final in the first world-level event to allow male competitors. The American pair scored 88.5108 points to finish ahead of pre-event favorites Russia, with Italy taking bronze. “I can’t believe that this moment has finally happened,” May, 36, told BBC Sport. “This is the future of synchronised swimming because we’ve seen such strong calibre male athletes here and I really think it’s going to help the sport grow.” Jones, 27, said earlier this month that simply reaching the final would be one of the best days of her life. Both May and Jones are full-time performers with Cirque du Soleil in the United States. May previously retired more than a decade ago, frustrated by the lack of international opportunities for male synchronized swimmers. The pair returned to competition late last year after Fina, swimming’s global governing body, approved men’s participation in mixed duet events for the first time. “It’s an event people can relate to, like ballroom dancing,” Jones said. “I think that the strength and power of a man is the perfect balance to a woman’s qualities.” While mixed duet synchronized swimming is not currently part of the Olympic program, the International Olympic Committee has signaled interest in expanding mixed-gender disciplines, raising hopes for inclusion at the Tokyo 2020 Games. “We want to be there, it’s our dream and we want in,” May added. Elsewhere on day two in Kazan, China secured gold in the men’s synchronized 10m platform final. Mexico took silver ahead of host nation Russia, while Britain’s young duo James Denny and Matty Lee placed ninth in their first world final together.

Krisztián Gyöngyi, a Hungarian rhino specialist, was killed in Rwanda’s Akagera National Park while tracking animals, African Parks said. The conservation NGO did not immediately release details of the incident publicly. Gyöngyi, who had more than five years’ experience, played a key role in efforts to reintroduce eastern black rhinos to Rwanda, African Parks CEO Peter Fearnhead said, calling his death “very tragic” and a “huge loss.” Eastern black rhinos had been extinct in Rwanda for roughly a decade, with the last confirmed sighting in Akagera recorded in 2007 after numbers plummeted due to widescale poaching. In May, African Parks successfully translocated 20 rhinos from South Africa back to Akagera following strengthened security measures in the reserve, marking a milestone for the species’ return. In the 1970s, Akagera hosted more than 50 black rhinos, but their decline mirrored the broader crisis facing rhinos across Africa. Gyöngyi’s death underscores both the dangers of frontline conservation and the urgency of protecting the newly reintroduced population. African Parks said his contributions were instrumental to restoring the species in Rwanda and vowed to continue the work he helped lead.

Notts County owner Ray Trew has reopened dialogue with local businessman Alan Hardy as he continues efforts to sell the League Two club, after putting it on the market following “foul and mindless abuse” directed at his family. Hardy, chief executive of the Paragon group and owner of the Nottinghamshire Golf and Country Club, has previously tabled two written, cash offers to buy the Magpies. The latest approach, made by one of Trew’s advisers, “came out of the blue”, according to BBC Radio Nottingham’s Notts County correspondent Colin Slater. Trew, who met prospective buyers from the United States and China in March, has yet to conclude a deal. Slater said Hardy has not responded to the fresh overtures and is expected first to seek clarity on Notts County’s current financial position. Trew acquired the club from Peter Trembling in 2010, taking on more than £1.5m in debt accrued during five turbulent months under the Middle Eastern consortium Munto Finance. While the club’s off-field future remains uncertain, on the pitch Notts County sit 12th in League Two, one point outside the play-off places. Hardy was at Meadow Lane on Saturday to watch Notts draw with Crewe, while Trew was away on other business. Any agreement would end a protracted sale process and could provide stability ahead of the season’s run-in, though significant due diligence is expected before talks progress.

George Michael has cancelled nine Australian concerts on his Symphonica tour, saying the decision “breaks my heart” as he prepares to seek treatment following ongoing health challenges. In a statement on his website, the ex-Wham singer confirmed he will complete his scheduled UK dates in October before undergoing therapy for trauma stemming from the life-threatening pneumonia he suffered last winter. Michael spent a month in a Vienna hospital and said he was warned by doctors he would experience post-traumatic effects. “I have tried in vain to work my way through the trauma that the doctors who saved my life warned me I would experience,” he wrote. “They recommended complete rest and the type of post-traumatic counselling which is available in cases like mine but I’m afraid I believed (wrongly) that making music and getting out there to perform for the audiences that bring me such joy would be therapy enough in itself.” The nine cancelled shows were scheduled in Perth, Adelaide, Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and the Hunter Valley. Michael noted he has “enjoyed” recent performances across Europe but admitted he “seriously underestimated how difficult this year would be.” Symphonica resumed this autumn after the tour was halted in November last year, just hours before a planned Vienna performance, when Michael became ill. He had completed 46 of the original 65 dates before contracting pneumonia. The singer said he would focus on recovery after his UK commitments, thanking fans for their understanding as he prioritises his health.

The US Open draw has delivered an early blockbuster and several tantalizing possibilities across both singles fields, with former champion Maria Sharapova set to face second seed Simona Halep in the first round and a potential quarter-final rematch between Britain’s Johanna Konta and Halep looming if the Romanian advances. Konta, who begins her campaign against an opponent ranked 77 in the world, could again meet Halep at the last-eight stage as she did at Wimbledon, though the Romanian’s opening assignment against Sharapova is one of the headline matches of the tournament. Sharapova, a five-time Grand Slam winner and former US Open champion, will play at a major for the first time since the 2016 Australian Open, where she produced the positive drugs test that led to a 15-month suspension. The US Open is the first Slam to award her a wildcard into the main draw since her return. While injuries have limited her to just one match in the past three and a half months, the Russian carries a flawless 6-0 record against Halep, including victory in the 2014 French Open final. The matchup is widely expected to be scheduled under the lights in prime time during the opening two evenings, underscoring Sharapova’s ongoing box-office appeal. In the men’s draw, Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal are seeded to meet in the semi-finals, an eagerly anticipated showdown between the sport’s two biggest names who have never faced each other at the US Open. Third seed Federer opens against American youngster Frances Tiafoe, while newly crowned world number one Nadal starts against Serbia’s Dusan Lajovic, ranked 84. Andy Murray, who has not played a match since his Wimbledon quarter-final due to a troublesome hip and has since surrendered the top ranking to Nadal, is set to test himself against American Tennys Sandgren in round one. Sandgren, 26, made his Grand Slam debut at Roland Garros this year, losing in the first round. The first seed Murray is scheduled to meet would be Diego Schwartzman in the third round, with David Ferrer, Lucas Pouille and Jo-Wilfried Tsonga among the potential obstacles deeper into the tournament. The absence of defending champion Stan Wawrinka, who beat Novak Djokovic in last year’s final, and Djokovic himself simplifies the path for Nadal, Federer and Murray, although fitness and form questions remain: Federer has been managing a back issue, Murray’s match readiness is uncertain, and Nadal has yet to hit peak hard-court form this summer. Britain’s Kyle Edmund opens against Dutch veteran Robin Haase, while Heather Watson will try to snap a run of six straight first-round losses at Flushing Meadows when she meets France’s Alize Cornet. In the women’s field, defending champion Angelique Kerber of Germany faces Japan’s Naomi Osaka in a dangerous opener for the top half, and Wimbledon champion and world number three Garbine Muguruza begins against American Varvara Lepchenko. Top seed Karolina Pliskova takes on Poland’s Magda Linette as she launches her campaign for a maiden major title. With marquee names returning, notable absences, and compelling storylines across the board, the first week in New York promises drama from the very first night.

Unison has accused the council of slowing an independent inquiry into the closure of Awel Deg care home, saying social care expert Tony Garthwaite has been unable to finish his report because key questions remain unanswered. Awel Deg was shut in February 2014 following the suspension of 11 members of staff and concerns about standards of care, with 40 employees made redundant. In May 2014, the council said the facility would reopen as a specialist dementia home in spring 2015. However, a council spokesman said on Wednesday that any reopening cannot proceed until Mr Garthwaite completes his investigation. Unison said the delay is unacceptable and has written to the council to press for progress. “It is very disappointing,” said Jeff Baker, Unison’s regional organiser. “Unison understands that Mr Garthwaite cannot complete his report because the council has not taken steps to provide answers to key matters that Mr Garthwaite has put forward.” The council said it was aware of Unison’s concerns and insisted it is cooperating with the investigation. “The council is working with Tony Garthwaite to ensure that he has access to all the relevant information that he requires in order that he can complete his investigation,” the spokesman said. No revised timescale for the report or any reopening has been given.

title: Jamie Taggart, from the Linn Botanic Gardens at Cove on the Rosneath peninsula, was on a plant hunting expedition near the border with China. Scottish botanist Jamie Taggart, 41, has been missing in northern Vietnam since setting out alone on a plant-hunting trip near the Chinese border. His father, Dr Jim Taggart, said it would take “very freak circumstances” for his son to be found alive, but urged anyone with knowledge of the case to come forward, insisting “someone, somewhere must know something.” Taggart, a retained firefighter associated with Linn Botanic Gardens, was travelling by hired motorbike taxis and was familiar with the region, having visited two years earlier. His rucksack and passport were discovered at his guest house in the mountain town of Sapa, heightening concerns about his fate. Dr Taggart suggested potential witnesses may be reluctant to speak because they “should not have been there” or fear “getting involved with local police.” He appealed to people with family or friends in the area to share any information or rumours that might shed light on the disappearance. “It is very hard to disappear absolutely, completely,” he said, while acknowledging it is most likely his son slipped on a hillside and suffered fatal injuries. Residents of Cove and Kilcreggan have raised thousands of pounds to support search efforts. Vietnamese authorities, local guides and volunteers have scoured steep ravines and dense forest without success.

Ashwin Daudia, 50, of Lyme Road, Leicester, is due to appear at Leicester Magistrates’ Court on Thursday accused of killing 46-year-old Kiran Daudia. Mrs Daudia was discovered by a member of the public Tuesday in Cromer Street, Leicester. In a statement, her family described her as a “much-loved mum, daughter, sister and auntie,” adding: “She will be deeply missed by us all.” Police inquiries continue.

A pod of dolphins provided an unexpected escort as Larne RNLI towed a 30-ft yacht to safety after its propeller became fouled in fishing nets during a passage from Bangor to Scotland. The marine visitors were captured on camera during the tow. Conditions were fair but there was too little wind to sail without engine power, and the two people on board requested assistance. A fisheries protection vessel was first to reach the scene and alerted the lifeboat, which launched and secured a tow back to port. Speaking after the call-out, Roy McMullan of Larne RNLI urged sea-goers to "respect the water." "Sailing and motor-boating are popular pastimes particularly at this time of year," he said. "We would encourage sailors to always wear a lifejacket and always have a means for calling or signalling for help, and ensure everyone onboard knows how to use it."

At about 05:00 BST, a Mercedes B220 sports car collided with a stationary minibus taxi on Goosemore Lane at the junction with Kirkwood Avenue in Erdington before knocking down a pedestrian in his 40s, police said. Galaxy Cars confirmed the victim was one of their drivers, who was on his way home after finishing his shift. It is believed he was behind the parked minibus at the time of the crash. He died at the scene. A 49-year-old woman and two 17-year-old boys were arrested at the scene on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and are assisting with inquiries. Specialist officers are supporting the man’s family. Galaxy Cars said they were “devastated” to lose a “well-known and well-loved” colleague. The minibus taxi was parked at the time of the collision. Police have cordoned off the area while investigations continue.

Man in Northern Ireland seriously ill with infection linked to heart surgery equipment; Belfast Trust warns 2,000 patients A man in Northern Ireland is seriously ill in hospital with a rare bacterial infection linked to medical equipment used during open-heart surgery, his family has revealed. The patient underwent heart surgery in 2014 and several months later developed symptoms associated with mycobacterium chimaera, becoming increasingly unwell. In January, doctors confirmed the infection, which is now the subject of a UK-wide investigation. His case is one of 28 known across the UK, according to the family, who said he was told he was the 27th person to be diagnosed. Fifteen people have died in connection with the infection. The family has asked for their identity to be protected but said they want the public to understand the seriousness of the illness. On Monday, the Belfast Health and Social Care Trust wrote to around 2,000 patients who have had open-heart surgery since 2013, advising them of a potential—but low—risk. However, the family said they were shocked to read a report on the BBC News website stating that no cases had been identified in Northern Ireland. That report followed a briefing from the Belfast Trust in which it said it was not aware of any cases having presented locally. It has since emerged that the man is being treated in Northern Ireland, raising questions about communication around the issue. The UK-wide investigation is examining links between mycobacterium chimaera and medical equipment used during cardiac procedures, with health authorities advising patients to be aware of symptoms and seek medical advice if concerned.

England are poised for timely injury boosts as they continue their defence of the Six Nations title, with head coach Eddie Jones hopeful of welcoming back prop Mako Vunipola and wing Anthony Watson for the visit of Italy to Twickenham on 26 February. Number eight Billy Vunipola could also return in time for the final-round trip to Dublin on 18 March, a match that could decide the championship. “Mako has a big chance. He will play for Saracens next weekend and if he gets through that game we will bring him into camp for the Italy week,” Jones said, confirming the loosehead is close to action after being sidelined by a knee issue in December. Watson, who suffered a hamstring injury last month, is also nearing full fitness. “Watson ran at 95% on Friday so we are confident he will be able to play against Italy. It will be great to have him back and we will probably use him,” Jones added. Billy Vunipola, out since sustaining knee ligament damage against Argentina in November, is targeting the Ireland clash. “Billy might get back for Ireland. He’d be pretty useful off the bench at 150kg,” Jones quipped. England, defending champions and winners of their opening two fixtures, host Italy at 15:00 GMT and are strong favourites to extend their record 16-Test winning streak and maintain momentum in pursuit of back-to-back Grand Slams. Captain Dylan Hartley, withdrawn after 46 minutes in Saturday’s 21-16 win over Wales in Cardiff, downplayed the timing of his substitution and praised England’s depth and leadership across the squad. Hartley has been replaced in each of Jones’ 15 matches in charge and made his briefest appearance yet against Wales, but insisted the change was part of the plan. “I don’t think it was too early. I talked to Eddie and he said I captained the side brilliantly this week,” the 30-year-old hooker said. “There is a reason we have these finishers who come on and do their job for the team, as much as I do mine. I came off the field and the team handled itself brilliantly — there is so much experience out there and these guys have good heads on them so the team runs itself.” With reinforcements set to return, England’s bench strength and rotation policy appear central to Jones’s approach as the campaign enters its middle rounds.

Germany carried out its largest evacuation for an unexploded bomb since the end of World War Two on Christmas Day, after a 1.8‐tonne British device, believed to date to a 1944 air raid that destroyed the old town, was uncovered during construction on Tuesday. Authorities chose December 25 for the operation, saying the holiday would disrupt fewer people than a normal working day. As the evacuation began, Augsburg mayor Kurt Gribl urged residents in a video to ensure relatives and neighbors had places to stay outside the security zone and to “look out for one another.” Officials anticipated most affected residents could stay with friends or family, and opened schools and sports halls as shelters for those in need. Most Germans mark Christmas on December 24, easing the logistics on the day itself. German police later announced the bomb had been made safe, allowing the city to begin returning to normal. Unexploded wartime ordnance is still frequently found across Germany, often during building work, prompting precautionary evacuations.

Keates has already made changes to the National League club's squad since succeeding Gary Mills in October 2016. Wrexham manager Dean Keates says the club’s stature and passionate support can help attract players, even as they compete with the greater financial power of National League rivals. The 38-year-old, who took charge in October following Gary Mills’ departure, acknowledged the realities of the market after Saturday’s 1-0 defeat to promotion-chasing Tranmere Rovers, a result that leaves Wrexham 10th in the table. “You’re going to be competing and we can’t match them money wise,” Keates said. “If we’re up against Tranmere or Forest Green it might come down to finances with players – that’s the be all and end all. But we have a big football club with passionate support. We can encourage players to come here by the fact we can offer an unbelievable stadium to play in.” Tranmere have publicly boosted their budget this season, raising £30,000 through crowdfunding in February to fund new signings as they push for a return to the English Football League. Keates highlighted the difference, noting: “There’s some big budgets and that’s one of the big budgets. They pay a lot of money and for their changes they had two strikers off and two strikers on.” Wrexham have responded with their own initiative, launching a Build the Budget fund earlier this year to support Keates’ plans for next season. The manager insists the club’s ambitions remain clear. “The size of this football club, it shouldn’t be sat in mid table. I know what the expectations are and what the fans want,” he said, adding that he will continue reshaping the squad to meet those demands.

Versatile 21-year-old defender Davies has been signed in time to be included in the squad for Monday’s game at Shrewsbury. The Preston North End player has made two appearances this season, in EFL Cup ties against Bournemouth and Newcastle. Since first joining the Lilywhites in 2013, he has gained experience on loan with York City, Tranmere Rovers, Southport and Newport County. Find all the latest football transfers on our dedicated page.

Monarch Airlines says a flight bound for Dalaman, Turkey, made an unscheduled landing at Sofia Airport around 17:40 BST after an onboard incident. Police met the aircraft and removed six passengers before the plane continued its journey. The carrier declined to confirm reports the individuals were drunk. Monarch later said the flight is believed to have arrived at Dalaman as scheduled, without further incident.

Auditors have criticised Derby City Council for a series of governance failings in its taxi licensing, warning of a culture of “holding back bad news” and raising concerns that licences were issued to individuals with convictions including hate crime. The Labour-led authority says it has tightened rules and is undertaking a comprehensive review. Grant Thornton, the council’s external auditor, reported that between 2012 and 2015 some council members lobbied on behalf of individual drivers. A subsequent internal review found “poor decisions” were made in granting licences to applicants with criminal records, with offences cited including hate crime, harassment, intimidation and making improper comments to young females. While acknowledging “positive action” by the council over the past 12 months, the auditor said further steps may be needed to ensure robust governance and restore confidence in the licensing process. Chief executive Paul Robinson said a full overhaul of the taxi licensing system is under way. “We have significantly tightened the rules around how people get taxi licences,” he said, outlining plans for a transparent points-based assessment with set criteria. Robinson stressed that the auditor’s concerns relate to governance rather than public safety, adding that drivers who were licensed had “paid their debt back to society.” Council leader Ranjit Banwait said many of the issues highlighted occurred some time ago and that a governance action plan has already delivered numerous improvements. The audit report will be referred to the full council for debate within the next month. Residents can find more on this story and other Derbyshire news via local updates as the council’s reforms progress.

Qatari poet Mohammed al-Ajami has had his prison sentence reduced to 15 years, his lawyer said, as the country’s Supreme Court prepares to deliver a final ruling within the next 30 days. Al-Ajami, also known as Mohammed Ibn al-Dheeb, was convicted over poems deemed critical of Qatar’s leadership and broader authoritarianism in the Arab world, in a case that has drawn sustained condemnation from human rights groups. Advocacy organizations say al-Ajami’s trial was marred by irregularities, including court sessions held in secret, and argue his conviction violates international standards for freedom of expression. The case initially centered on a poem he wrote in 2010 that criticized the then-emir, Sheikh Hamad al-Thani. Activists, however, contend the authorities were particularly angered by a separate piece, Tunisian Jasmine, which al-Ajami recited and posted online in January 2011 at the height of regional uprisings. In that poem, he voiced solidarity with Tunisia’s revolution, declaring, “We are all Tunisia in the face of the repressive elite,” and denounced “all Arab governments” as “indiscriminate thieves.” The verses resonated widely online as protests swept parts of the Middle East and North Africa, even as Qatar itself avoided the large-scale unrest seen elsewhere. Al-Ajami, a father of four, has acknowledged writing the poems but maintains they were neither offensive nor seditious. He has argued that the 2010 recital criticizing the emir took place privately at his home, challenging the basis for charges of incitement. As he was led from a recent hearing, he shouted, “There is no law for this,” according to Reuters. Freedom of expression is tightly controlled in Qatar, where political dissent is limited and defamation of the emir is criminalized. The country’s human rights record has long drawn scrutiny from international campaigners and remains a sensitive issue in its relations with the United States, which maintains a major military presence in the Gulf state. The looming Supreme Court decision will be closely watched by activists and diplomats alike.

From April 2018, the total amount of dividends that company directors and shareholders can receive tax-free will fall from £5,000 to £2,000.
