Chancellor Philip Hammond has confirmed the reduction in the dividend allowance as part of his Budget, describing it as a move to “address the unfairness” created by what he called “an extremely generous tax break for investors with substantial share portfolios.” The measure is the Budget’s largest single revenue-raiser and is forecast to bring in an increasing amount for the Treasury, reaching £930m in 2021-22. The £5,000 dividend allowance was announced by former chancellor George Osborne in 2015. Mr Hammond said around half of those affected by the cut are directors and shareholders of private companies. Many small traders have structured their businesses as limited companies and remunerate themselves through a combination of salary and dividends, a strategy that will now carry a higher tax cost. From April 2018, a basic-rate taxpayer receiving £5,000 in dividends will pay an additional £225 in tax compared with the current rules. A higher-rate taxpayer in the same position will pay an extra £975. The government argues the change will reduce incentives for individuals to incorporate for tax reasons, bringing the treatment of earned income and investment income closer into line. Business groups warned the move could dampen investment and growth among smaller firms. Mike Cherry, national chairman of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said: “Many of our members, including those on modest incomes, will now see a significant rise in their tax liabilities. FSB is concerned about the increased uncertainty this may cause across the business community. We would now like clarity over how this fits in to the publication of the government’s Business Tax Roadmap, which prioritised the importance of creating a stable and certain tax environment for small firms.” The FSB labelled the cut “a further disincentive for businesses to invest and grow.” Self-employed representatives also voiced concern. Chris Bryce, chief executive of IPSE, which represents self-employed workers, said: “The reduction in dividend tax allowance, whether you work as a sole trader or through a limited company [will mean] you will be facing higher bills. The chancellor shouldn’t forget that growth in self-employment has driven our labour market in recent years and punitive rises in tax will make many people have second thoughts about striking out on their own.” The change will also affect savers with significant shareholdings held outside Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs). According to the Treasury, savers account for around half of the 2.2 million people impacted by the cut, and will lose an average of about £320 a year. Among those affected, 1.4 million basic-rate taxpayers will lose an average £200, 725,000 higher-rate taxpayers will lose £440 on average, and 124,000 additional-rate taxpayers will lose about £890. Experts said some investors can mitigate the impact by making greater use of tax-efficient wrappers. “Investors should make the most of their ISA and pension allowances, to protect as much of their wealth as possible from the taxman,” said Laith Khalaf, senior analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown.

Cleaner cleared of attempted murder after hammer attack ruled self-defence A Glasgow High Court jury has cleared a Clydebank woman of attempting to murder a pensioner after accepting she struck him with a hammer in self-defence during a confrontation at his flat. Gillian Lavery, 43, was found not guilty after jurors deliberated for just half an hour over the incident on 16 February 2016 at the home of Tom Winter. The court heard Ms Lavery had been cleaning Mr Winter’s flat and had known him for several years. During the trial, the jury was told that Ms Lavery and Mr Winter had previously had a sexual relationship, with Mr Winter saying they had been intimate three or four times. He told the court he believed Ms Lavery was visiting that day for sex, but claimed he told her to leave when she said she was expecting a friend. Mr Winter said he walked out ahead of her when he was suddenly attacked from behind and repeatedly struck with a hammer. Photographs shown to the court depicted the OAP with bruising to his head, face, arms and legs following the incident. Under cross-examination, Mr Winter admitted he had also been expecting a “mystery woman” to arrive that day. He told the jury: “Gillian said she was bringing someone up..... if the mystery woman did not turn up, I would have sex with Gillian with her consent.” Ms Lavery gave a different account of events, telling the court she had agreed to visit because a woman called Sarah was due to come to Mr Winter’s flat and she could help make the visitor “feel comfortable.” She said tensions rose when the woman failed to appear, and that Mr Winter became angry and demanded sex, telling her: “I have already taken my tablet..... his Viagra,” and, “You are not going anywhere. She is not here, so you are doing it.” Ms Lavery said she attempted to flee but was struck with a walking stick. She told the court a hammer fell from a table during the struggle and that she used it to “get him off me” before managing to escape. The jury accepted Ms Lavery’s assertion that she acted in self-defence and returned a not guilty verdict on the charge of attempted murder. No further charges were brought. The case highlighted conflicting accounts about the nature of the pair’s relationship and the events leading up to the altercation, but jurors concluded the force used by Ms Lavery was a response to a perceived imminent threat. Neither party gave statements outside court following the verdict.

No injuries have been reported, and some migrants have now been allowed to return to the camp. Police still investigate whether the fire was deliberate, but an aid worker says it started after a food dispute. There are some 5,600 refugees currently in Lesbos, according to the UN, but the island only has capacity for 3,600. The fire destroyed 30% of the camp, according to Aris Vlashopoulos, an aid worker with the Swiss charity SAO. "People are returning to the camp now as I can see. But the biggest number of the refugees are already on the streets, sleeping outside," he added. According to Greek state news agency ANA, a brawl started on Monday after a rumour that refugees would be deported to Turkey en masse. Many on the island are afraid of being returned to Turkey or their home countries, correspondents say. The situation on Lesbos is exacerbated as many refugees land there and are held on the island until their asylum claim is fully processed. Those granted asylum are permitted to journey to the Greek mainland, while others are turned back. The procedure is part of the EU-Turkey deal brokered in March, in which the EU pledged to work towards visa-free travel for Turkish citizens to Europe's Schengen zone in exchange for Ankara's assistance in curbing migrants crossing to the Greek islands. Authorities continued to assess damage on Tuesday as residents and aid groups sought temporary shelter for those displaced. Police are examining witness accounts and footage to determine whether the blaze was sparked intentionally or spread amid the unrest. The incident highlights the strain on overcrowded facilities and the tensions fueled by uncertainty over asylum outcomes, with fears of deportation intensifying anxiety among camp residents.

Olympique Lyonnais have ended their pursuit of free agent Emmanuel Adebayor after talks with head coach Bruno Genesio failed to produce an agreement, the Ligue 1 club announced on Saturday. Adebayor, unattached since his contract with Crystal Palace expired at the end of last season, had held discussions with Lyon this week, but a deal did not materialise. In a statement, the seven-time French champions cited several factors behind the decision. The club said the striker “delayed his arrival in Lyon” on Friday and noted he would not be eligible for the first phase of the Uefa Champions League. Lyon also highlighted Adebayor’s desire to represent Togo at the Africa Cup of Nations at the start of 2017, a commitment that “would have led to an absence of one to two months.” The imminent returns to fitness of attacking duo Mathieu Valbuena and Nabil Fekir have further strengthened Lyon’s forward options during Alexandre Lacazette’s injury layoff, reducing the urgency to add a veteran striker. Adebayor’s professional career began in France with Metz in 2001 before a move to Monaco in August 2003. He rose to prominence after joining Arsenal in 2006, scoring 62 goals in 142 appearances and tallying 97 Premier League goals across spells with Arsenal, Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur. In January 2011, he joined Real Madrid on loan and helped Jose Mourinho’s side win the Copa del Rey in the 2010/11 season. Adebayor returned to London with Tottenham, netting 41 times in 106 games over four years at White Hart Lane, before being released in September 2015. He signed for Crystal Palace in January 2016, where he scored once in seven league appearances prior to his summer departure. Internationally, Adebayor remains Togo’s most influential football figure despite a sometimes difficult relationship with the national federation and coaches. He led Togo to their historic debut at the 2006 Fifa World Cup in Germany and has 29 goals in 63 caps. With Lyon choosing not to proceed, Adebayor continues to evaluate his options as he seeks the next chapter of a distinguished career.

Net income rose to $5.43bn (Â£3.76bn) in the three months to the end of December against $4.93bn a year earlier. The bank cut costs by 7.4% to $14.26bn in the quarter. Legal expenses fell by almost 50% to $644m from $1.1bn. Salaries fell 2.4% to $6.69bn as the bank shed around 7,000 staff to 234,598, from 241,359 a year earlier. JPMorgan Chase reported a rise in fourth-quarter profit as aggressive cost-cutting and sharply lower legal bills offset a challenging operating environment marked by pressure from falling oil prices and concerns about slowing growth in China. Net income increased to $5.43bn in the three months to 31 December from $4.93bn a year earlier, while total net revenue edged up about 1% to $23.75bn, topping analysts’ expectations. “We had a good quarter as 2015 came to a close,” chief executive Jamie Dimon said in a statement. “The businesses generated strong loan growth and credit quality, except for some stress in energy. The consumer business continues to gather deposits, outpacing the industry,” he added. “Markets were somewhat quieter, and we saw the impact reflected in the results of our trading and asset management businesses.” Noninterest expenses fell 7.4% to $14.26bn, helped by a near-halving of legal costs to $644m from $1.1bn, and a 2.4% decline in salaries to $6.69bn as headcount dropped by about 7,000 to 234,598. Provisions for credit losses rose 49% to $1.25bn, reflecting strains tied to the energy sector. By business line, profit from investment banking surged 80% to $1.75bn even as revenue declined 4%, while the consumer banking unit reported a 10% rise in profit to $2.41bn. US banks broadly have faced a difficult year amid weak credit markets that discouraged risk-taking, while ongoing legal charges and higher capital requirements continued to weigh on costs. JPMorgan is the first of the major US banks to report fourth-quarter earnings. Citigroup and Wells Fargo are due to report on Friday.

Police granted more time to question suspect as body of Sian O’Callaghan found; search for second body continues Magistrates sitting in Swindon have granted Wiltshire Police an extension to continue questioning a 47-year-old man arrested in connection with the disappearance and death of Sian O’Callaghan. The extension allows officers to hold the suspect until early on Monday morning. The man, named locally as taxi driver Christopher Halliwell, was detained at an Asda supermarket in Swindon’s Orbital Centre on Thursday and remains in custody at Gablecross Police Station. Miss O’Callaghan, 22, from Swindon, was last seen leaving the Suju nightclub at 02:52 GMT on Saturday, 19 March, intending to walk the half-mile back to the flat she shared with her boyfriend in Westmorland Road. A signal from her mobile phone was later picked up near Savernake Forest, and her boyfriend sent her a text at 03:24 GMT that night. Following the arrest on 24 March, police said the suspect took detectives, including Det Supt Steve Fulcher of Wiltshire Police, to a site near White Horse Hill, Uffington in Oxfordshire, about 15 miles (24km) from Swindon, where a body believed to be Miss O’Callaghan’s was discovered in a shallow grave. On Friday, officers were granted an initial additional 24 hours to question the man, and a further extension was approved on Saturday morning. As part of the ongoing investigation, searches have expanded to Gloucestershire amid concerns there may be a second victim. Det Supt Fulcher said officers were searching near Eastleach for the body of an adult. “Wiltshire only has one outstanding missing adult and that’s from several years ago,” he noted, without identifying the individual. Police have been using mechanical diggers to excavate a corner of a field near the Oxfordshire-Gloucestershire border as part of the search. Det Ch Insp Sean Memory, who is leading the search near Eastleach, said officers had received “relatively specific” information from the man being held in connection with Miss O’Callaghan’s death, but no remains had yet been found. “We were given some indication of where there might be a find. Of course, it isn’t as simple as that,” he said. Investigators continue to examine several sites connected to the suspect, including a property in Ashbury Avenue in Swindon. Meanwhile, a Wiltshire Police spokeswoman confirmed that floral tributes placed outside the Suju nightclub by friends and well-wishers would be moved from the doorway because the venue plans to open on Saturday night. Miss O’Callaghan’s family has agreed to the tributes being relocated. Police have appealed for the public to remain vigilant and to come forward with any information that could assist in the investigation as officers continue their searches and questioning over the weekend.

Glasgow City Council has withdrawn proposals to alter public holidays after members of the GMB union voted in favor of industrial action in protest. The union warned the changes would have hit low-paid staff, particularly those who regularly receive enhanced payments for working holidays, with average losses estimated at around £500 a year. The holiday changes were originally tabled in March as part of efforts to plug budget gaps. However, the council said it has since made “significant” progress toward achieving £130 million in savings, allowing it to scrap the plan. Martin Rhodes, the council’s executive member for personnel, said the authority was confronting “the greatest budget cuts in its history from the Scottish government,” but praised staff for delivering reforms and efficiencies to protect frontline services. “As a result, we are now in a position to withdraw proposals to make alterations to public holidays,” he said. “This progress on budget savings will also allow the council to improve some elements of frontline services further in the near future.” GMB Scotland welcomed the reversal. Benny Rankin, a GMB Scotland officer, said: “We are pleased the council has listened to the concerns of our members and climbed down from its imposition plan, which could have plunged thousands of low paid workers into the ranks of the working poor. Our campaign of resistance has protected our members’ interests, but there can be no doubt that the swingeing cuts to local government funding means the road ahead will be tough for all local government workers across Scotland.” Rankin urged councils to engage constructively with unions to find alternatives to austerity. “GMB Scotland is calling on all our councils to engage positively with trade unions and their members and work with us to find alternatives to an austerity agenda that is punishing working people and their communities,” he added.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) sent unencrypted DVDs, showing named victims talking openly, to the National Crime Agency but they were not received. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) said the force was “cavalier in its attitude to this data.” GMP claimed the discs “were sent in accordance with national guidance”. The DVDs, which were sent by recorded delivery to the Serious Crime Analysis Section (SCAS) of the NCA in 2015, have never been found. An ICO investigation concluded the force breached data protection law by failing to keep highly sensitive personal information secure and not having appropriate measures to prevent accidental loss. The watchdog found GMP had been sending unencrypted DVDs by recorded delivery to SCAS since 2009, a practice that only ceased after the 2015 security breach. “The information GMP was responsible for was highly sensitive and the distress that would be caused if it was lost should have been obvious,” said Sally Anne Poole from the ICO. “Yet GMP was cavalier in its attitude to this data and it showed scant regard for the consequences that could arise by failing to keep the information secure.” The force has a previous history of data security failings. In 2012, it was fined after an unencrypted memory stick containing sensitive information was stolen during a burglary at a detective’s home. Assistant Chief Constable Rob Potts said GMP “immediately reviewed our own procedures” following the incident and that “postal delivery is no longer used by GMP for sensitive information,” while national guidance has also been amended. He added that the three individuals featured in the lost videos were notified straight away, have been kept updated throughout the investigation, and provided with support. The ICO’s findings highlight persistent risks in handling highly sensitive data and the importance of robust safeguards to protect victims and uphold public trust.

“Kwesi Appiah should qualify Ghana to Afcon 2019 and win it,” Ghana FA vice-president George Afriyie declared at Appiah’s unveiling in Accra on Tuesday, setting a bold mandate for the returning Black Stars coach. “That is the target given to him and we all hope he will be able to do that,” Afriyie added, as Ghana seeks to end a 34-year wait for continental glory. The Black Stars have not lifted the Africa Cup of Nations since defeating Libya on penalties in Tripoli in 1982. Appiah, a former international defender, has signed a two-year contract to replace Israeli coach Avram Grant, marking his second stint at the helm after guiding Ghana to the 2014 World Cup. Since his previous tenure, the 56-year-old has been in charge of Sudanese club Al Khartoum. Ghana begin their 2019 Afcon qualifying campaign next month with a home fixture against Ethiopia. Appiah, reflecting on the turbulence of the 2014 World Cup—where a bonus row overshadowed Ghana’s campaign—promised to learn from past mistakes. “I’ve learnt a lot; there were so many mistakes I believe I made and I won’t repeat them,” he said. Despite a precarious start to 2018 World Cup qualifying, Appiah insisted Ghana’s hopes remain intact. The Black Stars have taken just one point from their first two matches and trail Group E leaders Egypt by five points, but the coach maintained belief in a turnaround. Appiah also signaled openness to recalling midfielders Sulley Muntari and Kevin-Prince Boateng if their club performances merit selection. Boateng, currently with Spanish side Las Palmas, and Muntari, based in Italy with Pescara, were suspended indefinitely in 2014. Muntari was sidelined for an unprovoked physical attack on a Ghana FA official, while Boateng was expelled for verbally abusing Appiah during the ill-fated World Cup campaign. “If they are doing well, why not? I’ll always want the best for Ghana,” Appiah said, underscoring his willingness to prioritize form and harmony as he embarks on a new chapter with the national team.

Inquest opens into 1994 disappearance of Arlene Arkinson as PII dispute looms A long-delayed inquest into the disappearance of Arlene Arkinson, the 15-year-old who vanished after a school disco in County Donegal in 1994, opened in Belfast on Monday, hearing stark accounts of a bright but vulnerable teenager failed by those around her. Arkinson was last seen getting into a car driven by Robert Howard, a man later convicted of other serious offences. Howard was acquitted of Arkinson’s murder in 2005 and died in prison last year aged 71. Jurors in his 2005 trial were not told he was already serving a life sentence for the 2001 rape and murder of English schoolgirl Hannah Williams. At the opening of the inquest, the coroner’s court was told Arkinson came from a troubled background. Her mother died when she was 11, her father struggled with alcohol addiction, and she had gone missing several times prior to her disappearance. The court heard that in 1993 her brother-in-law, Seamus McGale, was convicted and jailed for sexually abusing her; he was released 10 days before Arkinson went missing. A barrister for the coroner’s service told the court that on the night she disappeared, Arkinson confided to friends that she was pregnant and that “the father was a person closely connected, but not a member of the Arkinson family.” The inquest heard she was a “bright but vulnerable” girl who had been sexually abused in her younger years. Howard, with a long record of sexual assaults and rape, was described to the court as an “extremely dangerous man” who posed a serious threat to vulnerable girls. However, the court was also told he was “not the only person who had wronged her or to whom she was vulnerable,” underscoring the complex and sensitive nature of the investigation into her disappearance. The coroner has yet to rule on information that police do not want made public, as that evidence has not been presented. The disclosure issue follows last week’s decision by the Northern Ireland Office (NIO) to approve a request from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) to withhold certain documents linked to the case. Northern Ireland Office Minister Ben Wallace approved a Public Interest Immunity (PII) application, which can be used to prevent disclosure of state documents when it is believed that releasing them could harm the public interest, including matters related to national security or the protection of police informers. The coroner will make the final determination on whether the PII application will be granted. The hearing at Belfast’s Laganside Courts is proceeding without a jury. Arkinson’s sister, Kathleen, is scheduled to deliver a personal statement to the inquest.

Gloucester-born Wayne Russell, 34, has completed a year-long charity running challenge, covering the equivalent of about 200 marathons since starting on 6 September last year. He finished the journey in Greenwich at about 15:45 BST, crossing the line to a large crowd of friends, family and well-wishers. The effort has raised about £28,600 for the Superhero Foundation, which helps families in need of medical treatments. “I’m absolutely overwhelmed, to be honest,” Russell said. “Having spent the best part of the last year alone, running into such an incredible reception was mind-blowing.” He explained the challenge was inspired by the death of his sister, who died aged 35 and “dedicated her life to charity.” “I want to thank every single person that donated, shared and supported me and my run,” he added. “We’ve raised more than £25,000 for an incredible cause, and I just can’t imagine a more perfect end. I just hope I’ve made my family proud. I wish my sister could have seen this.” Funds raised will support the Superhero Foundation’s work assisting families with vital medical treatments.

Gerry Flynn, 57, has been named locally as the victim of a single-vehicle crash at Duncrew, Castleblayney, County Monaghan, on Sunday. Mr Flynn, who owned and operated a pharmacy in Falcarragh, County Donegal, died after the car he was driving left the road at about 16:00. A passenger was uninjured. Gardaí have appealed for witnesses, urging anyone with information to contact Castleblayney Garda Station.

Chiba Zoo Culls Crossbred Snow Monkeys After DNA Tests Confirm Rhesus Mix Takagoyama Nature Zoo in Chiba culled snow monkeys after DNA testing showed they were crossbred with rhesus macaques, a non-indigenous species banned under Japanese law. Local officials said the animals had to be killed to protect the native environment, citing fears the hybrids could escape and reproduce in the wild. Japan prohibits the possession and transport of invasive species, including crossbreeds, under rules enforced by the Office for Alien Species Management. An official from the environment ministry division told local media the culling was unavoidable. The zoo’s operator held a memorial service for the monkeys’ souls at a nearby Buddhist temple. Japanese macaques, commonly known as snow monkeys, are native to Japan and are among the country’s major tourist attractions. Junkichi Mima, a spokesman for WWF Japan, said invasive species cause problems because they mix with indigenous animals and threaten the natural environment. Authorities and conservationists say strict enforcement is needed to prevent ecological disruption and protect Japan’s native wildlife.

FDA Moves to Regulate E-Cigarettes Nationwide as California Raises Tobacco Age to 21 The Food and Drug Administration on Wednesday issued long-awaited rules bringing electronic cigarettes and several other tobacco products under federal oversight, a move officials said is designed to protect young people as use of vaping devices soars. For the first time, manufacturers of e-cigarettes will be required to submit their products to the agency for review. The regulations also extend to cigars, pipe tobacco and hookah tobacco. E-cigarettes—battery-operated devices that turn flavored nicotine liquid into an inhalable vapor—lack the tar and many of the chemicals found in combustible tobacco, and are widely used by smokers trying to quit. But the nicotine they deliver is addictive. In a statement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Sylvia Burwell called the announcement “an important step in the fight for a tobacco-free generation.” “It will help us catch up with changes in the marketplace, put into place rules that protect our kids and give adults information they need to make informed decisions,” she said. The FDA cited a recent survey showing e-cigarette use among high school students rose from 1.5% in 2011 to 16% in 2015, with hookah tobacco use also increasing significantly. The new rules, which take effect in 90 days, will require retailers to ask buyers for proof of age, ban sales of the products in vending machines, and prohibit free samples. Public health advocates welcomed the move. “Ending the tobacco epidemic is more urgent than ever, and can only happen if the FDA acts aggressively and broadly to protect all Americans from all tobacco products,” said Harold Wimmer, president of the American Lung Association. In a parallel push, California Gov. Jerry Brown signed five bills tightening tobacco restrictions statewide. The measures regulate e-cigarettes, expand funding for anti-smoking programs, and raise the legal age to purchase tobacco from 18 to 21, except for active military personnel. Electronic cigarettes, like traditional cigarettes, will be banned in public spaces across the state.

Colombia tops global internal displacement list for fourth year as worldwide numbers climb Colombia has again recorded the world’s largest population of internally displaced people, the fourth consecutive year it tops the list, according to the Norwegian Refugee Council’s Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC). The annual report says the global tally of people forced to flee within their own borders rose over the past year, driven largely by Syria’s war, while sub-Saharan Africa accounts for roughly one-third of all cases. IDMC Director Kate Halff warned internal displacement will keep accelerating without lasting, comprehensive peace and political solutions. “Governments are responsible for finding long-term solutions for their displaced citizens,” she said, urging much stronger protection, assistance, and pathways to sustainable return or resettlement. In Colombia, the IDMC estimates between 4.9 million and 5.5 million people remain displaced by decades of internal armed conflict. Around 230,000 Colombians fled their homes in 2012 alone. The figure is provisional because the government did not release official data for the year, and it likely understates the scale of the crisis by excluding families uprooted by violence linked to criminal and drug-trafficking gangs. Violence by such groups has surged, with President Juan Manuel Santos identifying the expansion of criminal networks as one of Colombia’s most pressing security threats. Police figures released Sunday suggest the country’s largest criminal organization, Los Urabeños, now boasts more members than the National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrillas. Authorities estimate Los Urabeños have more than 2,000 operatives active in major cities such as Medellín and across rural corridors, where they are involved in drug and arms trafficking and extortion. Both the Colombian Red Cross and the IDMC have cautioned that victims of criminal gangs often do not receive the same official recognition and assistance as those targeted by the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) or the ELN, complicating efforts to track displacement and deliver aid. Colombia has endured nearly five decades of conflict pitting left-wing insurgents and right-wing paramilitaries against each other and state forces. Government envoys and Farc representatives are currently negotiating in Havana in search of a peace accord, while Bogotá has launched a land restitution program to return property seized during the conflict to rightful owners—measures that advocates say are vital to ending displacement and preventing new cycles of flight.

Japan’s Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Yuko Obuchi and Justice Minister Midori Matsushima resigned on Monday following allegations of financial impropriety and election law violations, dealing a major setback to Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s effort to bring more women into the highest levels of government. Abe, who reshuffled his cabinet last month to include five women, said he took responsibility for appointing both ministers and pledged to name their replacements within a day. Both Obuchi, 40, and Matsushima, 58, are members of the governing conservative Liberal Democratic Party. Obuchi, widely viewed as a rising star and even a potential future prime minister, faced claims that staff in her political support groups misused thousands of dollars in campaign funds and other donations. She has not acknowledged personal wrongdoing. At a televised press conference, Obuchi said she was stepping down to prevent her issues from disrupting policy. “We cannot let economic policy and energy policy stagnate..... because of my problems,” she said, adding, “I take seriously the impact I have caused.” She apologized for being unable to contribute fully to Abe’s key goals, including economic recovery and “a society where women shine.” Hours after Obuchi’s announcement, Abe confirmed Matsushima’s resignation. According to NHK, Matsushima had distributed paper fans bearing her image and policy messages at a festival in her constituency. The opposition Democratic Party filed a criminal complaint against her on Friday, alleging an apparent violation of election law and rules governing political funds, and demanded her resignation. The episode intensified scrutiny of Abe’s newly appointed female ministers. Correspondents say the twin resignations are a sharp blow to Abe’s agenda and could rekindle memories of his first term as prime minister in 2006–2007, when a series of ministerial scandals culminated in his own resignation for health reasons after just one year. The BBC’s Japan correspondent Rupert Wingfield-Hayes noted that Abe’s troubles may not be over: Eriko Yamatani, minister in charge of the North Korean abduction issue, has been photographed with members of an ultra-nationalist group accused of hate speech against Japan’s ethnic Korean community, raising further questions about the cabinet’s stability and vetting.

The announcement follows the handing over to Mongolian officials on Monday of a 70-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus bataar at a ceremony in New York. The latest group includes two more Tyrannosaurus bataars, six Oviraptors and several Gallimimuses. The Mongolian government has announced its intention to open a dinosaur museum to display the skeletons. U.S. authorities announced the repatriation of an additional cache of dinosaur skeletons to Mongolia, following Monday’s handover in New York of a 70-million-year-old Tyrannosaurus bataar. The latest group slated for return includes two more T. bataars, six Oviraptors and several Gallimimuses. Mongolian officials said the government plans to open a dedicated dinosaur museum to publicly display the recovered specimens. “The recovery of this treasure trove of dinosaur fossils is the latest significant step in returning missing pieces of the Mongolian people’s history that were literally dug out from under them,” U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara said. James T. Hayes, a U.S. customs official, added: “We simply cannot allow the greed of a few looters and schemers to trump the cultural interests of an entire nation..... We look forward to returning these fossils to their rightful owner – the government of Mongolia.” The repatriation follows a U.S. investigation into fossils smuggled into the country between 2010 and 2012, in violation of Mongolian law banning fossil exports. A Florida fossils dealer admitted smuggling the Tyrannosaurus bataar bones returned on Monday; the skeleton sold at auction for more than $1m (£643,000). Officials said the actions reflect a broader crackdown on illicit trafficking of cultural heritage.

Carlisle United have bolstered their attack with the signings of Jamie Devitt and Reggie Lambe. Devitt, 25, a former Hull City young player of the year, agrees a two-year deal after 18 months at Morecambe’s Globe Arena. He made 98 appearances for the Shrimps, scoring 12, including seven last season — his best return since 2009. The Irish midfielder held talks with Crewe Alexandra boss Steve Davis, who hoped to make him his second summer signing, but chose Brunton Park. Head of recruitment Lee Dykes said Devitt was among the most effective players Carlisle faced. Lambe, also 25, joins on a one-year contract after rejecting a new deal at Mansfield Town. He moved to the Stags in September 2014 following spells in Canada and Sweden, and made 73 appearances. Carlisle head of recruitment Lee Dykes said Lambe turned down more lucrative offers to come to Cumbria, and praised his versatility: a wide player who can cut inside, go down the line, and use both feet. Dykes added that Devitt impressed against Carlisle last season, noting he was involved in three of the four goals Morecambe scored. “People like Reggie can unlock doors for you in difficult situations,” Dykes said.

City of Edinburgh Council has switched on a free public WiFi network providing blanket outdoor coverage across the city centre, following a 10-year contract signed in March to expand connectivity and improve mobile reception. The service, delivered by intechnologyWiFi and branded EdiFreeWiFi, replaces the traditional hotspot model with continuous access in busy streets and public spaces. The network goes live ahead of Edinburgh’s festive celebrations, which are expected to attract nearly one million people. The council has published an online map of EdiFreeWiFi coverage across central Edinburgh. Officials say the rollout is central to plans to grow the capital’s economy by encouraging people to spend more time in the city centre and supporting local businesses. Councillor Frank Ross, the council’s digital champion, said the launch means “everyone will be able to get free outdoor access to the latest information on their favourite apps and websites while they are out and about over the festive season and beyond.” Ross added that providing reliable, free connectivity for millions of residents and visitors each year would help ensure they have easy access to the information they need.

Dywedodd: "Ni wedi bod wrthi ers sawl blwyddyn yn trio cael y broses wedi ei gweithredu, mae hwn yn rhan o'n cynllun I ehangu addysg Gymraeg drwy'r sir." Mae Mr Jones yn derbyn bod rhai o'r rheini yn gwrthod newid: "Maen nhw'n hapus gyda'r sefyllfa fel mae ar hyn o bryd. Ond beth ydym ni am ei sicrhau yw bod mwy o gyfleoedd gyda'n plant ni I fod yn ddwyieithog, a bod ganddynt fwy o gyfleoedd yn y byd gwaith." Dywed y gwrthwynebwyr eu bod yn ystyried cymryd camau cyfreithiol pe bai'r cyngor yn bwrw ymlaen gyda'u cynlluniau. Maen nhw'n dweud nad ydyn nhw'n wrth-Gymraeg, ond y byddai'r newid yn golygu y byddai'n rhaid I blant sy'n dymuno addysg cyfrwng Saesneg deithio o'r pentref I ysgolion cyfagos. Mae Julia Rees wedi penderfynu symud ei phlant o'r ysgol, ac mae hi'n gwrthwynebu'r newid: "Ni eisiau ein plant I siarad Cymraeg ond ni eisiau dewis pa ffrwd maen nhw'n cael mynd iddo." Fe wnaeth grŵp o rieni sy'n ffafrio'r newid anfon llythyr at y cyngor gan ddatgan: "Yn dilyn cyfrifiad 2011, ni allwn bellach anwybyddu sefyllfa fregus yr iaith Gymraeg yn ein cymunedau a thrwy greu Ysgol Gymunedol Gymraeg yn Llangennech, gallwn gyda'n gilydd ddechrau ar y broses o unwaith eto greu pentref Cymraeg ei iaith yn Llangennech. Y pwynt pwysicaf I ystyried yn ystod y cyfarfod ddydd Mercher yw addysg ein plant ac felly rydym ni'n gofyn I chi'n garedig iawn I gofio effaith hirdymor y newid hwn ar y plant." Ar hyn o bryd, mae Ysgol Llangennech ar ddau safle ar wahân, un I blant yr adran fabanod, a'r llall I'r adran iau. Dan y cynllun, byddai un ysgol 3-11 oed cyfrwng Cymraeg yn cael ei sefydlu. Trwy bleidlais glir y cyngor, mae’r cam nesaf yn canolbwyntio ar weithredu’r newid, er y gallai trafodaethau pellach a heriau cyfreithiol gan rai rhieni olygu bod y broses yn parhau I ddenu dadlau ac archwiliad. Roedd y naill garfan o rieni a’r llall yn cytuno mai lles addysgol a dyfodol ieithyddol y plant sy’n ganolog, ond maent yn anghytuno ar y ffordd orau i’w sicrhau.

A suspected case of acute poisoning at the Time Warp electronic music festival in Buenos Aires left young attendees in distress and forced organizers to cancel the event’s second night. Alberto Crescenti, head of the city’s emergency services, said the victims, aged 21 to 25, were taken ill during a private party in the Costa Salguero complex that “had gone out of control.” “We’ll see what substances they took,” he added, noting that emergency crews were called when on-site private ambulances could no longer cope. One participant told local TV channel TN, “We couldn’t stay inside, we couldn’t breathe. It was too hot and there were too many people.” Time Warp, launched in Germany in 1994 and in Buenos Aires for the third consecutive year, featured DJs Chris Liebing, Barem and Deep Mariano. Authorities are investigating conditions at the venue.

Statue Unveiled in Orkney Honours Explorer Dr John Rae on Bicentenary A new statue on Stromness harbour front has been unveiled to honour Dr John Rae, the Orkney-born explorer whose feats in the Canadian Arctic helped complete the Northwest Passage but whose reputation was clouded by Victorian controversy. The commemoration coincides with a series of events across Orkney this weekend marking the 200th anniversary of Rae’s birth in 1813. Born on the island and trained as a doctor, Rae joined the Hudson’s Bay Company, initially to provide medical care for its fur-trading posts in Canada. His exceptional stamina and skill in traveling long distances on foot soon propelled him into exploration and surveying, and he mapped vast stretches of previously uncharted territory. In the late 1840s, while searching for traces of Sir John Franklin’s ill-fated 1845 expedition, Rae discovered the final link in the Northwest Passage. His landmark achievement was overshadowed after he relayed to the British Admiralty eyewitness accounts from Inuit communities describing how Franklin’s last surviving crew resorted to cannibalism in a desperate bid to stay alive. When the information reached the press, Franklin’s widow, Lady Jane Franklin, and her ally, the writer Charles Dickens, publicly attacked Rae for accepting Indigenous testimony, damaging his standing in Britain. Rae died in 1893, relatively little known in his homeland despite his Arctic accomplishments. The new statue, created by Orkney artist Ian Scott, was funded by a donation from businessman Alan Twatt, a Stromness native now a successful potato merchant in Aberdeenshire. Twatt said he wanted to see Rae receive the recognition he deserves, praising the explorer’s “incredible achievements.” Organisers say the bicentenary programme aims to restore Rae’s place in polar history and highlight the vital role of Indigenous knowledge in Arctic exploration.

The paperless system was introduced at Addenbrooke's and Rosie hospitals in Cambridge in October. Monitor has opened an investigation into Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust over financial concerns and the rollout of its eHospital system. The trust, which runs Addenbrooke’s and the Rosie hospitals, said it is working with Monitor and “doing everything possible to improve our financial position whilst ensuring safe care for our patients.” Monitor managing director Stephen Hay said the probe would also examine “how the trust handled the introduction of a new IT system.” In October, the trust became the first in the UK to deploy Epic’s eHospital platform, used in the United States. Nurses access and update patient records via 500 iPod Touch devices and use barcode scanning for tasks such as measuring blood pressure. However, in December senior hospital consultants warned the rollout had been “fraught with problems.” Monitor previously took regulatory action over the trust’s finances between 2013 and July 2014. The trust forecasts a deficit but says patient safety remains its priority as it works to stabilise performance.

An 80-year-old former officers’ mess at Duxford, Cambridgeshire, is set for a sensitive conversion after South Cambridgeshire District Council approved plans to bring the Grade II-listed building back into public use. Owned by Imperial War Museum (IWM) Duxford, the site last served the military in 1961 and in recent years has been used for museum storage across the road. The scheme, led by developer Mantle, will create a new courtyard featuring a “visual history” of the building’s RAF life and the people who lived and worked there. IWM said many historic features will be retained, including sash windows, cast iron radiators, original door labelling and a number of the internal spaces that reflect its past function. “This will give the building a new lease of life,” said Alan Stoneman, IWM’s interim director. “It will be wonderful to see the officers’ mess renovated in a style that embeds its history into its modern-day use. It will be an inspirational setting for its users.” Guy Baker of Mantle said the company, experienced in regenerating historic sites, “will be respecting the human stories associated with the space.” Work is expected to begin early next year, with museum and developer promising restoration.

Two men have been charged after assaults in Kirkcaldy just after midnight on Tuesday. Incidents occurred on Canmore Road and at North Street bus station. Victims, aged 22 and 38, suffered head and body injuries. The accused, both 21, are due to appear at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court on Wednesday. Police have appealed for witnesses and those with CCTV or dashcam footage to contact officers.

Munster overturned a second-half deficit with a late surge to defeat Cardiff Blues at the Arms Park, climbing to second in the Pro12 and denting the hosts’ push for a top-six finish. The visitors trailed at half-time after two Steve Shingler penalties put the Blues three points up, but rallied after the break as Francis Saili and replacement Conor Oliver crossed, with Rory Scannell adding a key drop goal. Cardiff had seized control shortly after the interval despite adversity. Centre Willis Halaholo was sin-binned for a high tackle on Andrew Conway just after the restart, yet wing Aled Summerhill struck moments later with the game’s opening try to extend the home side’s advantage. It was a timely contribution from Summerhill on a day when Wales retained Blues duo Kristian Dacey and Alex Cuthbert for Six Nations duty, prompting veteran hooker Matthew Rees to start and shoulder leadership up front. Munster, captained by Billy Holland, absorbed Cardiff’s pressure and gradually turned the contest. Saili’s finish reignited the visitors before Scannell coolly slotted a drop goal to narrow the gap. With the Munster pack forcing territory and errors, Oliver then crossed late to settle the outcome, completing a composed comeback steered by half-backs Ian Keatley and Duncan Williams. For the Blues, Gareth Anscombe marshalled play alongside captain Lloyd Williams, while Nick Williams and Josh Navidi delivered graft in the back row. However, Cardiff could not close out the game, and the loss leaves them eighth, their hopes of a top-six berth and European qualification taking a blow. Munster’s victory lifts them to second, a point behind the Ospreys, with Leinster still to face the Scarlets on Saturday. Referee Mike Adamson oversaw proceedings with TMO Jim Yuille assisting. The result underlines Munster’s resilience and depth, with impact off the bench proving decisive, while Cardiff are left to rue missed opportunities in a match they led for long spells.

Harlequins withstood a stirring late surge from Worcester Warriors to claim a 24-20 Premiership victory at Sixways, climbing to third in the table after a match that swung dramatically in the final half-hour. Charlie Walker set the tone inside three minutes, exchanging passes with Ross Chisholm to finish smartly for the visitors. Worcester briefly steadied when George Lowe was sin-binned for coming in at the side of a ruck, but Tom Heathcote could only trim the deficit with a penalty. Quins pressed again through their set-piece, and flanker Luke Wallace powered over from a well-executed line-out drive. Nick Evans converted to pass 1,500 Premiership points, underlining a milestone on a night that seemed to be heading firmly Harlequins’ way. The Londoners took a 17-3 lead into the interval, their control and accuracy reflected in territory and scoreboard alike. Soon after the restart, Danny Care’s sharp grubber along the turf was gathered expertly by Walker, who slid in for his second try to extend the advantage to 24-3. At that point there was little sign of the remarkable response to come. As the rain and mud deepened, Worcester’s pack began to assert themselves, and Harlequins’ discipline frayed. Back-rower Marco Mama was driven over to ignite the fightback, and when Jamie Roberts was shown a yellow card, Warriors capitalised immediately with a penalty try. Ryan Mills added the conversion to bring the hosts within nine points. With momentum and belief surging, captain Phil Dowson finished in the corner to set up a tense finale at 24-20. Worcester pressed relentlessly, their forwards punching holes and their backs probing for space, but Harlequins’ defence held firm in the closing stages, absorbing pressure and clearing their lines when it mattered most. Despite running in 17 unanswered points, Warriors were unable to overturn the 21-point deficit, though they did secure a losing bonus point. The result extends Worcester’s long winless run against Harlequins, which dates back to a 15-9 victory at the Stoop in February 2005. For Quins, Care’s leadership, Walker’s clinical finishing and a resolute rearguard under duress were enough to bank an important away win, even as yellow cards for Lowe and Roberts reflected a dip in discipline that made the contest far more dramatic than it appeared early on. Worcester’s resilience and set-piece resurgence will offer encouragement, but Harlequins depart Sixways with the spoils, their top-four ambitions reinforced by a hard-fought triumph.

The Met Office has downgraded its weather warning to yellow, but strong winds are still expected across Londonderry and Antrim following a day of disruption driven by the remnants of Hurricane Katia. On Monday, gusts peaked at 75mph (120km/h) in Castlederg, contributing to widespread travel problems and hazardous driving conditions. The Foyle Bridge in Londonderry was closed to high-sided vehicles and a 40mph speed limit was imposed for smaller vehicles and cars. Ferries were cancelled, trains delayed and motorists urged to take extra care. Maritime services remain disrupted into Tuesday. P&O has cancelled its Fastcraft service, though its conventional Larne–Cairnryan ferry continues to operate. Stena Line services from Belfast are running, but the operator has warned that delays and further cancellations remain possible depending on conditions. Passengers are advised to check before travelling; further information is available via the ferry check service on 08705 755 755. The Rathlin Island ferry was suspended on Monday, and Stena Line sailings between Belfast and Stranraer were cancelled until at least 1900 BST that evening. All P&O fast-craft sailings on Monday were also cancelled, though conventional P&O services ran as normal. There was also an incident on the north coast linked to the high winds: a catering marquee being used on the set of the series Game of Thrones was ripped into the air near the Carrick-a-Rede Rope Bridge. It is understood one person was taken to hospital with back injuries. The Met Office said the remains of Hurricane Katia moved across the UK on Monday, bringing very windy weather. “There remains some uncertainty about its track and intensity, though with increasing indications that Scotland and Northern Ireland are most likely to bear the brunt the warning has been upgraded to amber here. The public should be aware of the risk of disruption to transport and of the possibility of damage to trees and structures,” it said. That warning has now been reduced to yellow for Tuesday, which is expected to be brighter and less windy, with gusts typically around 50mph and up to 60mph along the north coast.

The 20-year-old is set to have a scan on a shoulder problem this week. Sussex face a wait over a 20-year-old player as a shoulder problem is assessed by scan this week. Seamer Mustafizur Rahman has featured twice in the T20 Blast for the Hove side, taking 4-23 in a win over Essex before returning 0-31 in defeat to Surrey. The left-armer could be available for the knockout stages of both the Blast and the One-Day Cup if Sussex qualify. Sussex sit sixth in their T20 Blast group with one match remaining, level on points with fourth-placed Essex, and are bottom of their One-Day Cup group after one win in five.

A £780,000 upgrade will introduce four new exhibitions exploring the castle’s history, the town and former monarchs. Funded by the EU Regional Development Fund, the project forms part of wider waterfront regeneration. As one of Wales’ leading visitor attractions, the castle will unveil new features aimed at enriching the visitor experience.

Developers behind the Leale’s Yard regeneration in St Sampson have been asked to reduce proposed retail space by 20% after planners warned the scheme could harm St Peter Port’s retail sector. The Co-op and Leales Yard Limited submitted plans more than a year ago for homes, shops and parking, but last month the planning department issued its verdict, demanding changes before permission can be granted. Following talks, several options have been outlined and are being considered by the developers. In an open letter, they expressed frustration at the setback and warned the project could be at risk if delays or reductions are required. Officials say revisions should rebalance retail provision while supporting housing and infrastructure goals.

A simple blood test already used to diagnose heart attacks could help identify people at risk long before they develop symptoms, researchers say. Scientists from the Universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow report that measuring troponin—a protein released when heart muscle is damaged—may offer a more precise way to assess heart risk than relying on blood pressure and cholesterol levels alone. The study, funded by the British Heart Foundation and published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, followed 3,300 men with high cholesterol but no history of heart disease. Researchers found that men with higher troponin levels were significantly more likely to have a heart attack or die from heart disease over the next 15 years. Crucially, those identified as high risk and treated with preventive therapy, such as statins, not only reduced their risk but also saw their troponin levels fall. “Troponin is almost like a barometer of heart health. If it creeps up, that’s bad and your risk of heart problems increases. If it goes down, that’s good,” said Professor David Newby, one of the study’s authors. “It also appears to predict who benefits from statins and opens a door to a whole new way of testing.” He added that troponin could complement established measures like blood pressure, cholesterol, and smoking status to build a more comprehensive risk profile. Professor Nicholas Mills, who led the research, said the approach could help uncover “silent” heart disease in people who appear healthy. “Troponin testing will help doctors to identify apparently healthy individuals who have silent heart disease so we can target preventive treatments to those who are likely to benefit most,” he said. Troponin tests are widely used in hospitals to confirm recent heart attacks in both men and women. The researchers believe the same test can be applied in routine risk assessments to prevent such events, although their current findings are based on men. They plan further research to confirm that the strategy is effective in women as well. Dr Tim Chico, a cardiologist at the University of Sheffield, welcomed the findings but stressed that prevention remains paramount. “The problem with heart disease is that it remains very difficult to detect the early signs in people without symptoms, so these findings may provide a way to help identify people at risk,” he said. “Nevertheless, the best way to treat heart disease is to prevent it in the first place, and this is why a healthy diet, regular physical activity, not smoking, and maintaining a healthy weight and blood pressure is so important.”

Vlogger Becky Sheeran hit by fake Facebook profile impersonating late grandmother Nottinghamshire vlogger Becky Sheeran says she was targeted by a fake Facebook account posing as her late grandmother, a hoax she fears may have been an attempt to extort money. The 28-year-old, whose TalkBeckyTalk YouTube channel has more than 150,000 subscribers, said she received a friend request on Sunday from an account using the name and photos of her grandmother, Nina Sheeran, who died in January. The profile also reached out to her sister, other relatives and friends of her grandmother. Before her death, Nina Sheeran used Facebook regularly, making the impersonation particularly upsetting for the family. “It brings all these emotions up of somebody that’s not here any more,” Ms Sheeran said. “You always wish you could see that person again and to suddenly see their name again..... it’s really distressing.” She added that she had reported the account to Facebook and wanted the person behind it to be “brought to justice.” “It’s good to suspend an account but it’s not teaching someone a lesson – no-one has been held accountable,” she said. Facebook said it was investigating and had removed a fake profile that had been contacting Ms Sheeran. Nottinghamshire Police said the case was a matter for Facebook. Ms Sheeran has previously been targeted by online trolls, including after the death of her father. Facebook urges users to report impostor profiles by using the “Report” feature on the suspicious account or through its Help Center. People affected are advised to warn friends and family and review privacy settings.

Lilly-May Page-Bowden suffered a cardiac arrest as she left Willow Bank School in Woodley, Berkshire, in 2014, and the first paramedics at the scene did not use a defibrillator, an inquest at Reading Coroner’s Court heard. Peter Bedford, senior coroner for Berkshire, concluded Lilly-May died of natural causes after a post-mortem found she had an undiagnosed genetic heart condition. However, he said she probably would have survived if South Central Ambulance Service (SCAS) staff had defibrillated her in time, adding that this “neglect” contributed to her death. The inquest was told the first paramedic on scene felt she had not received adequate training. Evidence indicated the paramedic failed to recognise that Lilly-May had a shockable rhythm and did not deliver appropriate treatment with a defibrillator, contrary to nationally recognised paediatric resuscitation protocols. In a statement read outside court, the family’s solicitor said: “We are concerned that a paramedic was unable to properly understand nationally-recognised resuscitation protocols for the treatment of cardiac arrest in children. The paramedic failed to recognise that Lilly-May had a shockable rhythm and failed to deliver appropriate treatment with a defibrillator. We now also know that if Lilly-May had been defibrillated within 15 minutes of her collapse, she would have survived and still be with us.” The family added they had lost Lilly-May “far too early” and hoped “a child does not die again for want of defibrillation.” Deirdre Thompson, director of patient care for SCAS, said the trust had “undertaken a detailed investigation” following the death. “We accept the findings of the coroner today and offer our sincere apologies to Lilly-May’s family,” she said.

Leipzig, founded in 2009 with backing from drinks firm Red Bull, will play in the group stage after a 4-1 win at Hertha Berlin on Saturday guaranteed a top-three finish in the Bundesliga. RB Leipzig clinched a historic Champions League berth with a comprehensive 4-1 victory at Hertha Berlin, a result that ensures the club cannot finish below third place with two games remaining. The achievement caps a remarkable rise for the team bankrolled by Austrian energy drink giant Red Bull, who propelled the club from the lower leagues to the Bundesliga last season after four promotions in seven campaigns. “At the start of the season, we just talked about being worry-free from relegation,” said sporting director Ralf Rangnick. “I am simply proud.” Leipzig sit second, 10 points behind champions Bayern Munich, and have already surpassed expectations in their first top-flight season. Their ascent has sparked debate across German football, with Leipzig frequently labelled “Germany’s most hated club” by opposition supporters who have protested against its commercial structure. Rangnick, who previously managed Hoffenheim, Schalke and Hannover, acknowledged that competing in Europe will demand deeper resources. “When we play in the Champions League, we’ll have to strengthen the squad,” he said. “Whether three or four new additions will be enough, I do not know. Perhaps we’ll need five or six and we need more quality across the board.” Saturday’s victory marked Leipzig’s 20th win in 32 league matches. German forwards Timo Werner and Davie Selke each scored twice, underlining the team’s attacking prowess. Twenty-year-old midfielder Oliver Burke, signed for around £13m last August, was an unused substitute.

Devon and Cornwall Police are appealing for information about 15-year-old Arthur Heeler-Frood from Axminster, who failed to arrive at school on 6 September and has not been seen since. His mother, Caroline, said she and his father, Jeremy, are missing him “terribly,” urging: “We don’t know that you are safe or what situation you’re in. I don’t think you realise how hard it is for us. Please make contact.” Supt Sam de Reya appealed to businesses, including restaurateurs, hoteliers and café owners, who may have employed a young man or provided accommodation in the last four to five weeks. Arthur is described as white, 5ft 4ins tall, of slight build, with short, light brown hair that may be cropped or shaven. Anyone with information is urged to contact Devon and Cornwall Police. The family is asking the public to help bring Arthur home safely.

Police were called to Hanging Rock at Blackheath in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, on Tuesday afternoon, local time, after a man struck a ledge while rope swinging from the cliff. The rock formation, nicknamed “the death swing,” is popular with tourists and thrill-seekers. Local media identified the victim as 31-year-old Sydney circus performer Toby Benham, a rock climber and BASE jumper. Police said rescuers brought him to an anchor point on the cliff face, where medical teams attempted to stabilize him before he was pronounced dead. Rope swinging involves leaping from a cliff while attached to a rope to arc like a pendulum beneath an overhang. Reports said Benham previously had a mishap there when his foot was caught in his parachute during a jump. Authorities are investigating the circumstances and have urged caution there.

Portsmouth builder steps in to rescue Clanfield couple after botched £13k kitchen job A Hampshire couple left with an uninhabitable home after a tradesman vanished mid-project have had their kitchen rebuilt by a local builder who heard their story on the radio. Malcolm Arnott, 70, ordered a new kitchen as a birthday present for his wife Carolyn at their home in Clanfield, paying more than £13,000 to a local tradesman who disappeared after completing only part of the work. The unfinished job left gaping holes, exposed wiring and a bathroom floor so damaged “you could actually near enough see the footings,” according to builder Ernie Etah of Epic Construction in Portsmouth. “It was atrocious,” Mr Etah said. “It was a fire hazard there — very unsafe, uninhabitable. In the bathroom there was a massive hole that you could actually near enough see the footings in — we expected rats to start coming in there.” Mr Etah, who suffered temporary paralysis after a serious accident, said his own experience motivated him to help after he heard the couple’s plight on BBC Radio Solent in November. He and his team carried out the necessary work to make the property safe and restore the kitchen. Mr Arnott, who lives in a nursing home after being paralysed by cancer of the spine, said his 60-year-old wife, who has heart problems, remained at the couple’s home while the situation unfolded. He described Mr Etah’s intervention as “epic.” “It’s more than you can dream of — far, far more than I expected,” he said. “In this day and age, when it’s dog eat dog, to find a company like this is just amazing.” The original tradesman has not returned to complete the job and remains uncontactable.

The 28-year-old and rowing partner Grainger, a 2012 gold medallist, compete in the women's double sculls heats at the European Championships. Victoria Thornley says she is confident of securing a place at the Rio Olympics as she lines up alongside Katherine Grainger at the European Championships in Brandenburg, Germany, which begin on Friday. Thornley, 28, from Wrexham, believes Grainger’s vast Olympic experience will be pivotal as the pair contest the women’s double sculls heats. “With it being Katherine’s fifth Olympics there’s no-one else you’d want sat behind you,” Thornley said. “She knows how to handle pressure so well.” Grainger won gold in the double sculls at London 2012 with Anna Watkins, following three consecutive Olympic silver medals, and returned to the sport in September 2014 after a two-year sabbatical. Her comeback has reunited her with the top level of international competition, this time partnering Thornley as the British duo target a spot on the Olympic start line in Rio. “I haven’t won an Olympic medal and haven’t had that feeling of being on an Olympic podium,” Thornley added. “That, of course, is what I wake up to do every day and to achieve. That brings strengths into the boat from different sides.” While excitement builds in an Olympic year, Thornley stressed the importance of staying grounded. “Obviously it’s exciting, in Olympic year, to be selected for the first race of the year,” she said. “But there’s a long way to go in terms of sessions to do and days of training to do. Every day I’m waking up and making sure I’m improving every single day. Yes, we’re looking to Rio but there’s a lot of things to put in place before then. It’s about keeping the focus on the here and now.”

TUV SUD to invest £11.1m in East Kilbride flow measurement centre German engineering firm TUV SUD will invest £11.1m in a new Centre for Excellence for Flow Measurement and Fluid Mechanics at its site in East Kilbride, following a £4.9m research and development grant from Scottish Enterprise. The £16m subsea development centre is designed to help maximise economic recovery from wells by advancing the measurement of liquid flow under high pressure—capabilities the Scottish government says will position Scotland as a world leader. The announcement was made during a visit by Economy Secretary Keith Brown to the Scottish Enterprise Technology Park, where construction of the facility will take place over the next two years. The project is set to create at least 17 new jobs and safeguard 82 existing roles. Brown said the investment reflects the international standing of Scotland’s oil and gas sector and signals a bright future for the industry and its supply chain, supported by innovation. The centre aims to support companies operating in challenging offshore environments, improving accuracy, efficiency, and safety in subsea operations while strengthening collaboration between industry and research partners.

Following a post-mortem examination, a man has been charged over the death of Richard Stroud, 46, from Guildford, who was assaulted in Josephs Road on Saturday and died the next day. Matthew Boyd, 32, of Waverley Road, Plumstead, London, faces murder and two counts of assault. Two men injured were treated in hospital. Boyd has been remanded in custody to appear at Guildford Crown Court on 1 April.

Four people have been arrested after a man was found with a stab wound and died at the scene in Shepshed, Leicestershire. The victim, believed to be in his 40s and from Oxfordshire, was discovered in a silver Ford Fiesta off Gelders Hall Road at an industrial estate on Thursday evening, after police were initially called to a road traffic collision. He has not yet been formally identified. Three men, aged 53, 20 and 17, and a woman, 53, were arrested on suspicion of offences linked to the death. A 22-year-old man arrested earlier has since been released. Detectives are appealing for sightings of the victim’s silver Ford Focus in the Shepshed area on Thursday evening, and of two males seen running from the industrial estate. The pair were seen to turn right out of the entrance before turning right again back into the estate. Enquiries are ongoing.

Continuing NHS Healthcare can cover all the care costs of people with complex ongoing illnesses Health Minister Mark Drakeford has pledged that claims for Continuing NHS Healthcare (CHC) in Wales will be handled promptly, following criticism over a backlog of cases. The Welsh Government has set a new deadline of 1 October for people to register claims for costs incurred between 1 August 2013 and 30 September 2014. CHC provides fully funded care for adults with complex, ongoing health needs. For those deemed eligible, the NHS meets all assessed care needs, including nursing home fees of up to £40,000 a year. The support is not means-tested and is available to anyone aged 18 or over who meets the clinical criteria. Local health boards are responsible for assessing eligibility, ruling on claims and paying any refunds due. More than £50m in wrongly paid care home fees and interest has already been returned to families in Wales, often after lengthy delays. Mr Drakeford said health boards will offer free advice to individuals who wish to make a claim and will complete the necessary paperwork on their behalf. “These claims will be managed in a robust and timely manner,” he said. “We are also working with health boards to ensure staff get it right first time to minimise the number of people who are unnecessarily paying for continuing healthcare.” People wishing to register a claim should contact their local health board before the October deadline.

title: The failure was the latest in a series for Hamilton, who is 23 points behind team-mate Nico Rosberg with five races to go and 125 points still available. "We have so many engines for eight drivers and mine are the only ones failing," said the Briton. "Someone has to give me some answers because it is just not acceptable." Lewis Hamilton’s hopes of reclaiming the Formula 1 championship lead suffered a crushing blow in Malaysia when his Mercedes engine failed while he was comfortably out front, handing victory to Daniel Ricciardo and a Red Bull one-two over Max Verstappen. The setback leaves Hamilton 23 points adrift of team-mate Nico Rosberg with five races remaining and 125 points still on the table. A visibly dejected Hamilton questioned why reliability issues seem to be hitting him hardest. “We have so many engines for eight drivers and mine are the only ones failing,” he said. “Someone has to give me some answers because it is just not acceptable. To be fighting for the championship and only my engines are failing just doesn’t sit right with me. There have been many decisive races but this is definitely one of those. Something or someone doesn’t want me to win this year but I won’t give up. I will keep pushing.” Asked to clarify his comment about “someone,” Hamilton added: “A higher power. It feels right now as if the man above or a higher power is intervening a little bit. But I feel I have been blessed with so many opportunities. So I have to be grateful for those. While this does not feel great, I have to remain grateful.” Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff expressed sympathy and urged perspective. “It’s clear he is super-frustrated. He has been really unfortunate this year. He is losing many points but the championship is not over yet,” Wolff said. “I am so gutted for Lewis. He was in control of that race. Not good.” Hamilton’s season has been a rollercoaster. He fell 43 points behind Rosberg after the first four races, hampered by two identical engine failures in qualifying in China and Russia that forced starts down the grid. He responded with six wins in the next seven grands prix to take a 19-point lead into the summer break. Rosberg then won in Belgium, where Hamilton started from the back following engine changes to replace earlier failures, and a poor getaway from pole in Italy left Hamilton second behind the German. Rosberg dominated in Singapore, with Hamilton third, to retake an eight-point advantage. Malaysia offered Hamilton a chance to swing momentum back his way—until his engine let go. Hamilton will seek redemption next Sunday at the Japanese Grand Prix. “I’m just going to try to recollect myself and get myself together for the next race and try to perform as I did this weekend,” he said.

A 15th gold of the Games has put Team GB second in the table, with 38 medals in total by the end of the weekend. And it wasn’t just Team GB that did well — super sprinter Usain Bolt claimed a record third 100m title, cementing his status as one of the greatest Olympians of all time. It was a blockbuster weekend in Rio, with British athletes delivering across the board. Gymnast Max Whitlock made history with two gold medals, shining in the men’s floor and pommel horse finals. Mo Farah thrilled fans with a dramatic victory in the men’s 10,000m, recovering from a stumble to storm home for gold. Jessica Ennis-Hill added a proud silver in the heptathlon, continuing her remarkable Olympic journey. On the water, sailor Giles Scott secured the Finn class gold with a race to spare, and there were more medals in cycling, rowing and swimming to keep the momentum going. Fans shared their favourite moments with us. “I love BOLT, he is amazing!” said Bianca, 11, from London. Nawar, 12, also in London, said: “I have watched the athletics that Mo Farah has won in, the swimming, the gymnastics, the cycling, the rowing and many more, but Newsround has kept me updated with all the top Olympic stories.” Cara, 12, from County Wicklow in Ireland, told us: “My favourite moment of Rio 2016 was when Jessica Ennis-Hill won her silver medal as she is my true athletic idol. I actually woke up at 2:45 am to watch her 800m.” Cadence and Madison from the UK said their highlight was seeing their dad — a GB coach — on TV, and how happy he was when GB won golds. Sarah, 9, from Liverpool, loved Max Whitlock’s double gold, while Akshita, 10, from Milton Keynes, cheered Mo Farah’s 10,000m win. Ben from Cornwall picked Giles Scott’s dominant Finn performance.
