Valentine’s Day returns on February 14, bringing a global celebration of affection expressed through cards, flowers, chocolates, and heartfelt messages. This year also highlights a charming leap-year tradition: in some cultures, women are encouraged to propose marriage to their partners, a custom said to date back centuries and observed every four years. The day’s name is tied to St Valentine, though his true identity remains shrouded in legend. The most popular account centers on a Roman priest in the third century AD who defied Emperor Claudius II’s ban on marriage, imposed under the belief that single men made better soldiers. Valentine quietly arranged weddings in secret, was discovered, and imprisoned. While awaiting execution, he reportedly fell in love with the jailer’s daughter; on February 14, he is said to have sent her a note signed “from your Valentine,” a phrase that endures in modern love letters. Valentine’s Day may also trace its roots to the ancient Roman festival of Lupercalia, held in mid-February to mark the onset of spring. As part of the festivities, boys reportedly drew girls’ names from a box, pairing up as couples for the duration—sometimes leading to marriage. As Christianity spread, the Church sought to recast Lupercalia into a Christian observance, aligning it with the commemoration of St Valentine. Over time, his name became synonymous with expressing love. Today, the holiday is embraced in diverse ways around the world—through intimate dinners, public proposals, charitable acts, and digital declarations of affection. Whether inspired by legend, tradition, or simple sentiment, Valentine’s Day continues to offer a moment to celebrate love in all its forms.

A 13-year-old youth footballer, Ethan Houghton from Dunstable, died alongside his mother and younger brother in a multi-vehicle crash on the A34 on Wednesday. Ethan, who played for Dunstable Football Club’s under-14s, was travelling with his mum Tracy Houghton, 45, and his brother Joshua, 11, when the collision occurred between Chieveley and East Ilsley at about 17:10 BST. An 11-year-old girl was also in the car. Thames Valley Police said a further 12 people were injured. Dunstable Football Club said it was devastated by the loss and would pay tribute at its next first-team home match. “The club is deeply shocked,” said the club’s Simon Reilly. “He was a very popular lad who will be sorely missed.” Players will wear black armbands during the Emirates FA Cup preliminary round tie against Chesham United on 20 August. A photo of Ethan will feature on the front of the match programme, and the under-14 team will accompany the first team onto the pitch. Police confirmed a 30-year-old man from Andover, who was driving one of the lorries involved, was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and has been bailed until 5 October. Officers declined to comment on reports that Ms Houghton’s partner was travelling behind in a separate car at the time. Thames Valley Police said inquiries into the crash are ongoing. The force has not released further details about the circumstances of the collision but confirmed multiple vehicles were involved.

VJ Day - 15 August 1945 - followed the destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki by atomic bombs An 83-year-old Nagasaki survivor living in Belfast has recalled the horror of the atomic bombing as events take place this weekend to mark Victory over Japan (VJ) Day. Nobuko Pollock, who has made north Belfast her home for more than 50 years after marrying a local man, survived the August 9, 1945 attack that killed tens of thousands. Her brother, who was closer to the blast, did not return home. “I was 13 when the bomb dropped,” Mrs Pollock said. “I didn’t know much about it. My brother didn’t come home that night. We didn’t know if he was dead, and they went to search for him. He was just lying dead on the road, like he was sleeping. There were so many dead people and we had to cremate him on the road.” Reflecting on the anniversary, she added: “I still want to know why they dropped the bomb. I saw so many injured people coming back from Nagasaki, and you saw the suffering of the women and children—some people have never forgiven them.” A series of commemorative events will honour the sacrifices of UK service personnel who fought and died in the war against Japan. The Japanese government announced its surrender on 14 August 1945, with the following day celebrated as VJ Day across the Allied nations. The formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945 in Tokyo Bay aboard the American battleship USS Missouri, bringing World War Two to its official end. Organisers say the commemorations aim to remember the fallen, acknowledge the survivors’ enduring pain, and educate younger generations about the war’s final chapter.

Paul Trollope has been appointed to take charge of Cardiff City’s first team as the Championship club reshapes its leadership, with Russell Slade moving into a newly created head of football role. Trollope, 43, a former Wales midfielder who joined Slade’s coaching staff in February 2015, said he is targeting the play-offs and, ultimately, promotion as he brings his own ideas and style to the team. “We have to be ambitious and create a belief within the club,” Trollope said after his elevation. “The target is the play-offs and hopefully promotion. There are areas that need addressing within the team and we will be looking to add quality and also the right people. Every coach has their own philosophies and way of doing things. I have clear ideas of what I want. I will bring my own style to that. I had no reservations; it is a good club with a good fan base. Anyone who knows me will know that.” Cardiff missed out on the Championship play-offs after winning just once in their final seven games, finishing eighth. Slade, removed as manager at the end of the season, will oversee scouting and broader football operations in his new capacity. The club confirmed Trollope, who assumes day-to-day control of the first team, will not report to his predecessor as part of the restructured hierarchy. Malaysian owner Vincent Tan backed the appointment and signalled a desire for more attractive football alongside a return to the top flight. “I believe Paul will improve the team in several areas. In particular, I hope he will lead the team to play an attractive style of football that Cardiff City fans love,” Tan said. “We hope that under Paul’s leadership, Cardiff City will return to the Premier League. He has our full support.” Trollope brings significant experience, having managed Bristol Rovers for five years and served as first-team coach at Birmingham City and Norwich City before joining Cardiff midway through the 2014-15 campaign. The former Derby County and Fulham player is also part of Chris Coleman’s Wales coaching staff and confirmed he will continue in that role at this summer’s European Championship in France, saying he does not see it as a hindrance to Cardiff’s pre-season preparations. He added he will review the viability of remaining with Wales after the tournament. Trollope emphasized collaboration with the club’s recruitment department to identify targets early and said pre-season planning is already under way. Slade had been in charge at Cardiff City Stadium since October 2014, arriving from Leyton Orient to replace Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. His final match as manager was a 1-1 draw with Birmingham on the last day of the season.

Bradford University Pioneers Animal Motion Capture to Transform Film, Games, and Veterinary Teaching Researchers at the University of Bradford have adapted motion capture technology to record animal movement, a breakthrough they say can dramatically improve the realism and efficiency of animated creatures on screen while advancing veterinary education. The team presented its work at the British Science Festival and is already collaborating with major film studios and the gaming industry. Traditionally, motion capture focuses on humans, leaving animals to be crafted directly by animators. That process is time-consuming and prone to biomechanical inaccuracies that can nudge viewers into the “uncanny valley,” where subtle errors distract from the story. By capturing and embedding authentic animal biomechanics into animation software, Bradford’s approach promises more convincing movement with less manual effort. Motion capture systems place infrared LED cameras around a space and track reflective markers attached to a subject. While the technology itself is established, the Bradford group is applying it in a novel way. “We thought, humans have been done a lot — but animals have not. It seemed like a very obvious thing to do,” said Karl Abson, lecturer in Biomechanical Animation and Motion Capture, in an interview with BBC News. The team has already attached markers to a horse to capture a range of movements. Those data sets allow animators to start from a biomechanically grounded performance, reducing build time and improving realism. As newer camera systems come to market, costs are falling, making comprehensive animal motion capture more accessible. Abson underscored the cost-benefit for filmmakers by contrasting current techniques with high-profile productions. “In Avatar six years ago, they placed one or two markers on the animal to track its position. If you’re paying for the motion capture system you might as well fully utilise it, rather than tracking the position and then getting an animator to do all the work,” he said. Beyond contemporary species, the method could inform lifelike renderings of extinct animals and mythical creatures such as dragons and flying horses, grounding fantasy in plausible movement. Abson is already working with British, American, and Russian film studios, as well as gaming giant Electronic Arts. The project’s roots lie in veterinary science, where the system serves as a teaching aid. By collecting precise movement data rather than relying solely on observation, instructors and clinicians can achieve more accurate diagnoses of conditions such as horse lameness. The dual impact — elevating screen realism and enhancing clinical insight — suggests animal motion capture could become a standard tool across entertainment and education.

The trio are alleged to have used an elaborate scheme involving text messages and computer software to help beat opponents at Khanty-Mansiysk. The French Chess Federation has launched disciplinary proceedings against three members of its national team over suspected cheating during the tournament in Khanty-Mansiysk, Russia. Federation head Laurent Verat described the accusations as the first case of its kind, saying that while chess has faced prior suspicions, the sport has rarely produced concrete evidence. The players at the center of the probe—international grand master Sebastien Feller, 19, Cyril Marzolo, and team captain Arnaud Hauchard—have all denied any wrongdoing. According to the federation’s account, the alleged scheme unfolded while Feller was at the board. Marzolo reportedly followed the game’s progress online, using computer software to identify optimal moves. He then sent the recommended move by coded text message to Hauchard, who was said to relay the information inside the hall by strategically choosing where to sit. Each table corresponded to a pre-arranged square on the chessboard, creating a covert signaling system. French media have characterized this final step as the most delicate part of the operation. The strategy was allegedly uncovered by federation vice president Joanna Pomian, who noticed a text message on the phone of one of the players during a match and alerted officials. In the wake of the discovery, Feller and Marzolo face suspensions and have vowed to appeal, while Hauchard risks a lifetime ban as a coach and selector. The case is being examined by the federation’s disciplinary bodies, with potential implications for broader anti-cheating measures. Verat told AFP that “there have already been suspicions of cheating in chess, even involving strong players in the past, but there has never been proof of cheating.” Feller’s lawyer, Charles Morel, said his client will fight the charges, telling Europe 1 radio that Feller is confident he will be cleared and that the allegations undermine years of dedicated training.

David Cameron announced on Monday the UK would accept up to 20,000 people from camps surrounding Syria with priority given to vulnerable children. First Minister Carwyn Jones will hold a Wales summit on the refugee crisis next week. The WRC is happy to take its share, but it wants it to happen more quickly. Hannah Wharf, policy manager for the WRC, said: “We welcome the UK government’s commitment and this rapid change in political and social support for the resettlement and relocation of refugees from Syria. But 20,000 over five years isn’t fast enough and we can’t wait until 2020 for this to happen. This needs to happen in the next year or so.” Wharf noted Wales currently receives about 8% of refugees who seek asylum across the UK and said Wales stands ready to take its proportion under the new scheme. “We don’t know the details of how that will pan out with this new scheme unfolding but we do know that Wales is ready to take its fair share of 8% of 20,000 – that’s just about 1,600 refugees to be taken across Wales,” she said. Local authorities in Wales have indicated they are willing to “play their part” in welcoming refugees, while asking for assistance to meet associated costs. According to Wharf, councils have been holding “ongoing conversations across Wales about how best to support people who come into local communities,” and there is “a huge surge of support.” The Welsh government has said funding should come from Westminster, arguing the matter is not devolved. Carwyn Jones’s summit aims to coordinate efforts across Wales as the UK finalises plans for resettlement from the region’s camps.

A popular Highland dance festival is set to return to the shores of Loch Ness with a renewed focus on safety and wellbeing for all attendees. Groove Loch Ness will take place in a field near Dores, south of Inverness, where about 3,000 people are expected to gather for a night of electronic music featuring headliners Patrick Topping, Skream, Julio Bashmore, Theo Kottis and a DJ set from Faithless. Local DJs will also join the bill, showcasing homegrown talent alongside international acts. Ahead of the event, organisers are working closely with Police Scotland and NHS Highland to ensure the festival is enjoyable and safe. Dougie Brown, of Groove Loch Ness, said: “We are looking forward to welcoming everyone to the third outing of Groove Loch Ness to enjoy world class DJs, local talent and much more. We continue to work closely with police and partner agencies, anyone found in possession of controlled drugs will be refused entry or ejected from the event. We have welcomed an incredible audience over the previous two events and hope that all our Groovers have a fantastic 2017 festival.” Police Scotland said officers would have a visible presence and that a proactive operation targeting illegal drugs would be in place. Event commander Ch Insp Colin Gough said: “Our focus is always to keep people safe while preventing public disorder and anti-social behaviour in order to make the festival enjoyable for all who attend. A proactive drugs operation will be in place to ensure the event is held safely and officers will take a robust approach against an activity of this kind. Drugs have the potential to ruin lives, let alone weekends, and they are not worth the risk.” He added: “If sensible advice from partner agencies is followed then it will help make Groove 2017 a memorable and safe experience for everyone involved.” NHS Highland has issued health guidance for revellers, urging responsible drinking and the avoidance of drugs. Eve MacLeod said a welfare tent would be set up on site to offer assistance. “Finally, keep an eye on your friends. If you notice someone becoming ill, especially through alcohol or drugs, get help straight away. Never leave your friends if they are unwell. Welfare staff and stewards are there to help you. Have a brilliant time at Groove, make it one to remember for all the best reasons.”

“Prices would go up if we leave the EU,” David Cameron warned on 22 May, arguing that Brexit would push up the cost of everyday shopping. The claim, repeated during an interview on Peston on Sunday, draws on new analysis from the Treasury, which forecasts a weaker pound if the UK leaves the European Union. The Treasury says it reviewed several external studies and concluded that Brexit would lead to a 12% fall in the value of sterling. A broad range of economists, including members of the Economists for Brexit group, agree that the exchange rate would likely drop following a vote to leave, though they differ on the wider economic consequences. BBC Reality Check’s verdict is that there is a clear consensus that Brexit would weaken the pound, and that this would feed through into higher prices over time. While the precise impact is difficult to quantify at this stage, Reality Check notes that the referendum campaign itself has already been a contributing factor in sterling’s recent weakness. A weaker pound raises the cost of imports, which can eventually lift consumer prices. The Treasury examined how this exchange-rate effect could influence typical household spending, using a detailed formula to estimate the pass-through from currency movements into shop prices. According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), an average two-adult, two-child household spends £81.40 a week on food and non-alcoholic drinks and £38.20 a week on clothing and footwear. Based on those spending patterns, the Treasury estimates that by 2018 the average household would pay about £120 more per year for food and drink, and almost £100 more per year for clothing and footwear. The department stresses that its analysis covers a two-year period: the impact on import costs would appear relatively quickly after a depreciation, but the full effect on consumer prices would take time to work through supply chains. Cameron’s warning underscores a central fault line in the EU referendum debate. While many economists expect a weaker pound to raise shop prices, the ultimate scale and timing of any increase remain uncertain, dependent on market reactions, trade responses, and how retailers choose to manage costs and margins.

‘Second Skin’ Polymer Film Mimics Youthful Skin, Shows Promise for Drug Delivery and Sun Protection A lab-made “second skin” that tightens under-eye bags and boosts skin elasticity has shown encouraging results in early tests, according to research published in Nature Materials. Developed by scientists at Harvard Medical School and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the transparent, breathable coating is being explored as a cosmetic product, with longer-term potential to deliver medicines and provide sun protection. The prototype is a polysiloxane polymer assembled from silicone and oxygen-based molecules. Once applied as a topical formula, it dries to form an ultra-thin, flexible film designed to emulate the look and mechanical properties of youthful skin. In small trials involving a handful of volunteers, the team applied the material to under-eye bags, forearms, and legs. The coated skin appeared smoother and firmer to the naked eye, and performed better in a standard “recoil” test, in which pinched skin is released to see how quickly it returns to its original position. Skin naturally loses elasticity and firmness with age, but areas treated with the polymer rebounded more quickly than untreated areas, the researchers reported. Beyond cosmetic effects, the film acts as a moisture barrier while remaining permeable enough for comfort, suggesting a role as a protective layer on the skin. The team says the coating is essentially invisible when worn, can be left on all day without irritation in their initial studies, and can withstand sweat and rain. However, they emphasize that larger studies are needed to confirm safety and performance across diverse skin types and conditions, and regulatory approval would be required before any medical claims could be made. The researchers have founded a spin-off company and hold patents on the technology. Early commercialization efforts are focused on cosmetic applications, but the group is also exploring how the film could be used to deliver active ingredients, including medications and sunscreen agents, in a controlled manner. Dr Tamara Griffiths of the British Association of Dermatologists, who was not involved in the work, said under-eye bags are commonly caused by the protrusion of fat pockets associated with aging. While the condition is natural, many people find it undesirable and some pursue surgical options. “The results with the polymer film appear to be comparable to surgery, without the associated risks,” she said. “Further research is needed, but this is a novel and very promising approach to a common problem.” Prof Robert Langer of MIT, who led the work, noted the challenges in designing a comfortable, effective “second skin.” “It has to have the right optical properties, otherwise it won’t look good, and it has to have the right mechanical properties, otherwise it won’t have the right strength and it won’t perform correctly,” he said. “We are extremely excited about the opportunities presented by this work and look forward to further developing these materials to better treat patients who suffer from a variety of skin conditions.”

The former Ireland international succeeds Matt O'Connor, who left the job after the Irish province's disappointing campaign last season. Leinster have appointed Leo Cullen as head coach, confirming the former captain will lead the province following Matt O’Connor’s departure in May. Cullen, 37, served as forwards coach during the final year of O’Connor’s tenure and was installed as interim head coach after the Australian’s exit. A stalwart of the province, Cullen won 32 caps for Ireland and captained Leinster to three Heineken Cup triumphs, cementing his reputation as one of the club’s greatest leaders. Leinster chief executive Mick Dawson hailed Cullen’s credentials, noting his 220 appearances place him second only to Gordon D’Arcy in senior outings for the province. “His status as a player is beyond question,” Dawson said. “He was an outstanding captain and leader on the pitch. Over the last 12 months or so in his capacity with the forwards and indeed over the pre-season as interim head coach, Leo has continued to impress everyone at Leinster with his tactical and strategic direction.” The coaching ticket around Cullen also takes shape: Kurt McQuilkin’s short-term arrangement as defence coach has been extended for two years, while John Fogarty remains scrum coach. Girvan Dempsey will continue as backs coach until the end of the World Cup, after which skills and kicking coach Richie Murphy will return from his duties with Ireland. Cullen’s first game in charge will be Friday’s pre-season friendly against Ulster at Kingspan Stadium, with his competitive debut coming away to Edinburgh in the Pro12 on 4 September.

Azerbaijan’s Defence Ministry is facing allegations that it published a doctored photograph from Moscow’s Victory Day parade, after an image on the ministry’s website appeared to obscure the flag of an Armenian unit marching behind Azerbaijani troops. A live broadcast of the event showed both contingents walking one after the other, each carrying national flags, as they took part in commemorations marking the 70th anniversary of the end of World War Two in Europe. The parade in Red Square featured foreign military formations arranged according to the Russian alphabet, including units from Armenia and Azerbaijan—two former Soviet republics whose relations have long been strained. Azerbaijani military expert Uzeyir Jafarov told BBC Azeri he was convinced the image had been Photoshopped. “According to sources in the ministry, they did not expect the military units of Armenia and Azerbaijan to march one after another. During rehearsals they were in different parts of the area,” he said. Further scrutiny from media outlets added to the controversy. Armenia’s state news agency Armenpress observed that the facade of Moscow’s State Historical Museum appeared altered in the ministry’s version of the photo, while a contributor to Russia’s Regnum news agency noted that one of the building’s windows seemed to have vanished. Azerbaijan’s Defence Ministry has declined to comment on the reports. The question of whether the photograph was edited has been widely discussed on social media in both countries, where the symbolism of the parade carries significant weight. Relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan have been tense since the 1990s conflict and the ongoing dispute over Nagorno-Karabakh, a landlocked region within Azerbaijan with an ethnic Armenian majority. The incident highlights how a celebratory event intended to honor a shared wartime legacy can reignite sensitivities and underscores the growing scrutiny of official imagery in an era of digital manipulation.

US charges Harlem Suarez with attempting to use a weapon of mass destruction in Key West plot The U.S. Justice Department said Harlem Suarez, also known as Almlak Benitez, has been charged with attempting to use a weapon of mass destruction after allegedly planning to bury a nail-filled bomb on a Key West beach and detonate it with a mobile phone. Prosecutors say Suarez was inspired by the Islamic State group. According to the FBI, Suarez recorded a video in May declaring, “We will destroy America and divide it into two.” Officials said he first drew the agency’s attention in April after posting extremist messages on Facebook. Suarez was arrested Monday in a sting operation after purchasing what he believed was an explosive device from an undercover FBI agent; the device was inert. The case comes amid a series of recent arrests of young men in the United States suspected of plotting attacks in the name of the Islamic State group. Authorities continue to investigate whether Suarez had any direct ties to militants or acted alone, as federal agencies step up efforts to disrupt suspected plots inspired by extremist propaganda.

Singaporean teenager Amos Yee, 16, was sentenced to four weeks in jail on Tuesday for posting online content that authorities said offended religious feelings and was obscene, following a case that has stirred debate over free speech in the city-state. Yee, who pleaded not guilty, will appeal both his conviction and sentence, his lawyer said. The sentence dates from 2 June, allowing Yee’s immediate release because he has already spent 50 days in remand. District Judge Jasvender Kaur described the offences as “not serious in nature but not trivial either.” Yee posted a video titled “Lee Kuan Yew is Finally Dead!” on 23 March, days after the death of Singapore’s founding prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, amid nationwide mourning. In the video, Yee compared Lee to Jesus Christ and disparaged both. He later published an obscene cartoon depicting Lee and former UK Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, apparently referencing their close political relationship. Authorities arrested Yee after at least 30 people filed police reports. Prosecutors charged Yee with distributing obscene images and wounding religious or racial feelings; a third count of harassment was later dropped. Singapore has strict laws against hate speech, particularly involving race and religion, and Yee faced a maximum of three years’ imprisonment for the religious offence and up to three months for distributing obscene material. The case has drawn criticism from human rights groups and ignited public debate over censorship, the limits of satire, and the treatment of young online critics. Yee’s supporters argue his posts were provocative but protected expression, while others contend they were offensive and unlawful under Singapore’s standards.

The Night Manager, The Crown and Planet Earth II among big winners at Bafta Television Craft Awards The Night Manager led a strong field at the Bafta Television Craft Awards, taking home prizes for editing and sound as the ceremony celebrated the behind-the-scenes talent that powers British television. The BBC espionage thriller’s technical triumphs came amid a mixed showing in the Bafta TV nominations, where only Tom Hollander was recognized for best supporting actor—an unexpected outcome given the series’ success at the Golden Globes, where Tom Hiddleston, Olivia Colman and Hugh Laurie all won acting prizes, and its Emmy win for director Susanne Bier. Netflix’s The Crown, which leads this year’s Bafta TV nominations, also secured two craft awards. The lavish drama charting the early reign of Queen Elizabeth II was honored for costume design and for special, visual and graphic effects, underscoring its reputation for meticulous period detail and technical polish. Sir David Attenborough’s Planet Earth II converted two of its nine nominations, winning the factual photography award for its Cities episode—triumphing over three other installments from the same series—and the factual sound category, reflecting the landmark nature series’ technical ambition and immersive production. Channel 4’s National Treasure, starring Robbie Coltrane as a comedian accused of historic sex crimes, was recognized for direction and original music. Happy Valley creator Sally Wainwright collected the writing award, marking her third Bafta in that category and fifth overall, while Mum writer Stefan Golaszewski won best comedy writing, ahead of nominees Phoebe Waller-Bridge (Fleabag), Julia Davis (Camping), and Steve Coogan with Neil and Rob Gibbons (Alan Partridge’s Scissored Isle). BBC One’s War and Peace, nominated in five categories, took home the production design award. Single-award winners also included Black Mirror for make-up and hair design, Hillsborough for factual editing, Rillington Place for photography and lighting, and Ant & Dec’s Saturday Night Takeaway for multi-camera direction. The Bafta Special Award for outstanding contribution to the industry went to veteran prop master Bobby Warans, honored for a career spanning nearly 100 of the UK’s most popular television programs over four decades, including The Morecambe and Wise Show, The Two Ronnies, Strictly Come Dancing, Absolutely Fabulous and Ant & Dec’s Saturday Night Takeaway. The results highlight a year in which UK television’s craft disciplines—editing, sound, design and writing—took center stage alongside high-profile hits.

Heroic bystanders rescued a baby after a pram plunged into a river near Victoria Street on Friday, with police praising their quick actions for averting a tragedy. The child’s grandmother had been walking along the river when the pram she was pushing fell into the water. James Williams and Andy Hill immediately jumped in, while Mickey Bramall ran to fetch a life buoy and then provided first aid. West Mercia Police said the men’s quick thinking and swift response were crucial. “We heard an almighty scream and shriek, turned around and saw the pram had gone over the edge,” said Mr Williams. “We instantly turned around and myself and Andy jumped straight into the river and Mickey went to get the life buoy.” Mr Hill said he was “really panicking” but did “what any parent would do” in that situation. Mr Williams said it was a struggle to remove the baby from the pushchair because she was strapped in, but they managed to get her to safety. The youngster was taken by ambulance to Royal Shrewsbury Hospital and has since made a full recovery. Mr Williams said the hundreds of messages of praise they received were reward in themselves. The baby’s mother told BBC Midlands Today it was difficult to put into words how grateful she was. Det Insp Paul Mathison described the men as “incredibly heroic.”

Archaeopteryx had pennaceous (quill-like) feathers all over its body, not only its wings, a new fossil - only the 11th of the creature found - reveals. These "trousers" were probably used for display, say scientists from Germany, writing in Nature journal. Their discovery adds weight to the theory that feathers originally evolved for purposes other than flight. Archaeopteryx caused a major stir when the first fossil was unearthed in Germany in 1861 - just two years after Charles Darwin published On The Origin of Species. With the claws and teeth of a dinosaur, but the feathers of a bird, it was clearly a transitional form - apparent proof of Darwin's theory. Its German name "Urvogel" means "first bird". And though earlier bird-like dinosaurs have been unearthed since, many scientists still believe Archaeopteryx was the first capable of "flight" as we know it today. The 11th fossil specimen was announced in 2011 and is remarkably well preserved, with detailed impressions of feathers all over its skeleton. The feathers are long and symmetrical on its upper leg and shorter lower down. Previous specimens had shown some evidence of feathered hind legs but this "completes the picture", according to Dr Oliver Rauhut and colleagues at the Bavarian State Collection for Palaeontology and Geology. These "trousers", as he describes them, may have been used for display, camouflage, insulation, brooding and manoeuvring while on the ground. They were not primarily designed for flight but might have helped steady the bird during landing, similar to the hindlimb feathers of hawks, eagles and other modern raptors. The wing feathers of the new specimen show robust shafts - further evidence that the "first bird" really could fly. Recent studies assuming limited flight ability in Archaeopteryx "might be in error owing to the poorer preservation quality of the feathers," said Dr Rauhut. "I'm pretty sure it could fly. Though of course there is still a debate about how well it could fly," he told BBC News. The trousers are also a new clue to the mystery of how flight evolved in modern birds. Traditionally it was thought that feathers and flight evolved hand in hand. But the wide variation of plumages in early birds and feathered dinosaurs suggests that feathers first arose for a different purpose, said Dr Rauhut. "Given the great diversity of pennaceous feathers found within different body regions and across the phylogeny, it seems plausible that the evolution of this feather type (especially in the wing, hindlimbs and tail) was primarily driven by display functions," he wrote in Nature. Only later were these feathers recruited for flight - which may have arisen many times in parallel in different feathered species, he said. The new Archaeopteryx fossil underscores the complex, multifaceted journey from dinosaur to bird, reinforcing the view that modern birds are the living legacy of their dinosaur ancestors and that the origins of flight were likely as diverse as the feathers themselves.

It reported net profit of $28m (£18.8m), against a loss of $148m a year earlier. It was the second quarter running the company had posted a surprise profit. However, revenue slid to $660m from $793m, below analysts' expectations. For the year, Blackberry reported that its loss had narrowed to $304m. "Our focus this past year was on getting our financial house in order while creating a multi-year growth strategy and investing in our product portfolio. We now have a very good handle on our margins and our product roadmaps have been well received," chief executive John Chen said in a statement. "The second half of our turnaround focuses on stabilisation of revenue with sustainable profitability and cash generation." The firm reported a positive cash flow of $76m, compared with a cash burn of $784m a year previously. "Blackberry continues to do a good job controlling operating expenses and eliminating its cash burn during its business transition, but the total revenue was still a big miss and we still have concerns about the demand side of the equation," said Morningstar analyst Brian Colello. Mo Farah has confirmed he will run the 3,000m at the Glasgow Indoor Grand Prix on 20 February, and says the race is likely to be his only indoor appearance of 2016. The World Indoor Championships take place in Portland, Oregon, from 17–20 March, but the Briton, 32, plans to focus his efforts on the outdoor season. “The 3,000m in Glasgow is likely to be my only indoor race of 2016 and I want to make it a good one,” Farah said. “It will give a good indication of how my training is going and will hopefully set me up for a successful outdoor season.” The double Olympic champion has been based in Portland since joining Alberto Salazar’s Nike Oregon Project training group in early 2011. He missed the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow because of injury, and will open his 2016 campaign in Scotland at the Great Edinburgh International Cross Country on 9 January. Farah, who has won seven global long-distance titles, retained his 5,000m and 10,000m world crowns in August and is targeting a defence of both titles at the Rio Olympics in August. He has not competed in Glasgow since 2012 and has not raced at World or European Indoor Championships since that year. “I haven’t competed in Glasgow since 2012 and it will be great to be back,” he added. “The Scottish crowd love athletics and I’m sure they will give great support to the athletes.”

The rail regulator has approved FirstGroup’s plan to run new open access services between London, the north-east of England and Edinburgh from 2021, setting up direct competition on the East Coast Main Line and prompting concern from the incumbent operator. Under a 10-year deal, FirstGroup will operate five trains a day in each direction, calling at Stevenage, Newcastle and Morpeth, with a single class of carriage and average fares of less than £25. The Office of Rail and Road (ORR) said the additional trains would give passengers more choice and increase frequencies to under-served towns and cities. “Our decision has been informed by extensive analysis, formal industry hearings and detailed engagement with all parties,” said John Larkinson, the ORR’s director of railway markets and economics. “We have carefully weighed up the potential passenger benefits and the financial impacts on existing operators and the government, as we are required to do by law.” FirstGroup chief executive Tim O’Toole said the services would be positioned as a low-cost, high-frequency alternative. “Our brand new trains will be cheaper than other rail services, greener than the plane, quicker than the coach and will get passengers from London to Edinburgh earlier than they can arrive now, and all for an average fare for less than £25,” he said. Stagecoach Group, which owns 90% of Virgin Trains East Coast (VTEC), criticised the move. VTEC currently holds the franchise to run services on the East Coast route until at least March 2023. Stagecoach warned that the decision would harm its revenues and questioned the impact on taxpayers. “Open access competition with an established franchise was not in the interests of passengers or taxpayers,” said Stagecoach chief executive Martin Griffiths, adding the company would review the ruling in detail and “consider its options.” Alongside the approval for FirstGroup, VTEC was granted permission to increase its own services on the main line between Edinburgh and London and on its branches, with changes taking effect from May 2019 at the earliest and by May 2021. The franchise operator also plans to boost links to Bradford, Lincoln, Harrogate and Middlesbrough, as pressure mounts to improve capacity and connectivity on one of the country’s busiest rail corridors.

Body of 41-year-old found in river days after speaking to media in Myanmar’s Rakhine Authorities in Myanmar’s Rakhine state say they are investigating the death of a 41-year-old man whose body was found floating in a river on Friday, days after he spoke to journalists about attacks on security forces and alleged army repression in the region. His family raised concerns on Wednesday, according to local reports, after he participated in a rare, tightly controlled media tour and discussed sensitive events with Burmese reporters. Police said the circumstances of his death remain under investigation. The area has been under lockdown for more than two months, imposed after militants attacked border posts in October, killing nine police officers. Troops moved in to secure the remote region bordering Bangladesh, and authorities say they are conducting counter-terrorism operations aimed at dismantling armed networks. During the media tour, the man reportedly told journalists that local villagers had been involved in attacks on security forces and described abuses by the army, the BBC has learned. His death comes amid intensifying scrutiny of the military’s conduct in Rakhine, home to Myanmar’s Muslim Rohingya minority. Rights groups, including Amnesty International, have accused security forces of widespread abuses—among them rape, murder, and torture—during sweeping raids that followed the October attacks. Myanmar’s military has denied the allegations, saying its operations target militants and are conducted within the law. The crisis has displaced tens of thousands, with many Rohingya fleeing across the border into Bangladesh. The estimated one million Rohingya in Myanmar are widely viewed by many in the predominantly Buddhist country as illegal migrants from Bangladesh and are denied citizenship despite generations of residence. Communal violence in 2012 left scores dead and forced more than 100,000—mostly Rohingya—into squalid camps where many still live. Hundreds of thousands of undocumented Rohingya are also believed to be in Bangladesh after decades of flight from persecution and instability in Myanmar.

Sale Sharks edged Leicester Tigers in a weather-hit Premiership thriller in Greater Manchester, with Danny Cipriani’s dazzling late solo try proving the difference after a dramatic ten-minute suspension for a thunderstorm. The fly-half, set to rejoin Wasps in the summer, was influential with the boot throughout and then underlined his class with ball in hand, weaving through weary defenders to finish in the corner and secure a hard-fought home victory. Sale struck first through flanker Cameron Neild, who crashed over amid swirling wind and rain, before Nev Edwards added a second well-worked try as the Sharks capitalised on Leicester’s handling errors. The Tigers, who welcomed back England trio Dan Cole, Ben Youngs and Manu Tuilagi following the Six Nations, looked unsettled for long spells of the opening period. Nonetheless, Tommy Bell’s reply kept them in touch, and the sides turned around with Sale leading 17-13 at half-time after a bruising, scrappy exchange shaped by the conditions. The weather took centre stage early in the second half, when referee Tom Foley halted play for safety reasons as fork lightning split the sky and torrential rain lashed the AJ Bell Stadium. The pause did little to dampen the spectacle once the players returned, however, and Leicester found renewed energy, pressing hard for the score that would tilt the contest their way. Vereniki Goneva, typically powerful and elusive, burst through to level matters at 20-20, igniting hopes of a late turnaround for the visitors. But the decisive moment belonged to Cipriani, who spotted a half-gap, arced into space, and finished with supreme control near the corner flag. It capped a performance that blended tactical control off the tee with the kind of attacking flair that has long defined his game. With Leicester camped on Sale’s line in the final minutes, the Sharks’ defence held firm, repelling multiple phases to deny the Tigers a draw. The conditions had a say before the interval as well, with heavy showers and gusting winds compounding a slippery surface and making both handling and kicking hazardous. Sale’s second try carried a hint of controversy, as replays appeared to show Sam James close to, if not over, the touchline when he gathered in the build-up to Edwards’ finish. The officials allowed it to stand, and that margin would prove valuable in a contest where territory and accuracy were at a premium. Afterwards, Sale director of rugby Steve Diamond praised Cipriani’s commitment despite his impending departure. “Danny will be replaced and we have replaced him already. The announcement will be made in the next week or so. Danny sees his future elsewhere and it has been written about for months now, so good on him,” Diamond said. “The good thing was that we had a sit down and he wants to get us as high up in the league as he can. You saw in his performance today that he doesn’t look like a lad who wants to leave.” Leicester counterpart Richard Cockerill accepted the decision to suspend play, while lamenting its oddity in a contact sport. “The television match official decided it was a health-and-safety risk, which is a bit bizarre really in a contact sport. But I suppose it was a sensible thing to do and Sale played well and took their opportunities,” he said. “We’ll take the point and we live to fight another day, but I think that takes our top-two ambitions out of the equation and you’re fighting for top four.” Sale’s victory extends their formidable unbeaten home run beyond 11 months, while Leicester, despite the return of their international stars, left ruing missed chances at the death in a compelling, weather-scarred encounter.

The team found patients who were given electrical stimulation alongside rehabilitation sessions fared better than people given rehab alone. Volunteers who had the electrical treatment saw greater improvements when moving their arms, and some found it easier to do everyday tasks. Charities welcomed the early results. A small clinical study has reported promising benefits from pairing rehabilitation with transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for stroke survivors experiencing lingering arm and hand movement difficulties. Published in the Journal of Science Translational Medicine, the trial involved 24 participants who had suffered strokes at least six months prior and continued to struggle with upper-limb function. All volunteers underwent nine sessions of intensive rehabilitation focused on encouraging movement in their affected limbs. For the first 20 minutes of each session, 11 participants received additional therapy using tDCS, in which electrodes were placed on the scalp above the stroke-affected brain region and a low electrical current was applied. The remaining participants received a sham procedure—just a few seconds of electrical stimulation before the device was switched off. Researchers reported that every patient showed some improvement, but the greatest gains were seen in those who received sustained electrical stimulation. Notably, these improvements persisted three months after the therapy had ended. Some individuals found everyday tasks easier, such as feeding themselves, while others demonstrated better lifting, grasping, and reaching abilities. The extent of improvement varied across participants, influenced in part by the severity of their original stroke. Brain scans added further insight, revealing increased activity in movement-related regions among the group receiving electrical stimulation. This suggests the therapy may help re-engage neural circuits involved in motor control. Jan, one of the study volunteers, described the experience and the impact: “I have definitely improved and benefited. People who haven’t seen me say ‘Wow – you can move better now.’” She added, “The stimulation didn’t hurt – more like a mild tingle or a static electric shock right on top of my head. The worst part was that my head itched afterwards!” Lead researcher Prof Johansen-Berg said she was encouraged by the results and hypothesized that tDCS may enhance the brain’s capacity to re-wire after a stroke. However, she emphasized that larger, more comprehensive trials are needed to confirm benefits, assess variability, and weigh costs before considering widespread adoption in clinical settings. Charities welcomed the findings. Shamim Quadir of the Stroke Association called the study an important step toward bigger trials, noting, “Stroke is one of the largest causes of disability and more than half of stroke survivors are left dependent on others for help with everyday activities. It is crucial that we find alternative ways to help improve the recovery rates from this devastating condition.”

Exeter Chiefs have signed Australia international back Turner, who can operate on the wing or at centre, with the Wallaby set to link up with his new teammates this week. The 28-year-old becomes the third Australia international to commit to Exeter in recent months, following forward Dave Dennis and prop Greg Holmes, who are due to arrive at Sandy Park in the summer. Turner joins from Toulon, where he scored four tries in seven appearances this season after moving to the French club as World Cup cover. He has been capped 15 times by the Wallabies and previously featured in Super Rugby for the Sydney-based Waratahs and the Queensland Reds before heading to France last summer. “We’ve tracked him for some time now and, once we knew he had finished his time with Toulon, we started the process of having a real good look at him,” said Exeter head coach Rob Baxter. “Immediately you could see he was a very good rugby player and having really looked at his game, we believe he can really add something to us in terms of our back three options. “Now he’s here, we will look to ease him gently following his flight over and then as the week progresses, gradually introduce him into full training with the squad.” Baxter highlighted Turner’s versatility as a key asset for the club as they navigate domestic and European campaigns. “The fact he can play in numerous positions is a big thing, just because at times I’ve felt this season we have been a little bit exposed in certain areas,” he added. “I just feel if we are that little bit thicker and little stronger in certain areas, it will help us in the long term. “People will know that we are a club who like to bring through quality young players, but at the same time some of them you would say are relatively inexperienced when it comes to the Premiership and to Europe. Therefore it’s important that we have a good balance in terms of our squad make-up.”

Fleetwood Town midfielder Grant has signed a new contract until 2019 after an ever-present League One season. The 26-year-old, who joined from Blackpool in July 2015 following a brief loan spell, has featured in every league game this campaign, scoring seven goals to boost Uwe Rosler’s side into third place. “The manager was a massive part of the decision. I’ve enjoyed the style that he wants to play,” said Grant. “I’m happy to be a part of what we’re creating here.” Grant began his career at Accrington Stanley and has also played for Scunthorpe, Rochdale and Blackpool, with a loan at Shrewsbury. With eight matches remaining, Fleetwood have lost one of their last 21 league fixtures and sit four points shy of an automatic promotion spot currently held by Bolton.

An 18-year-old from Barry died four days after a serious assault on Sunday, 8 March, at Trecco Bay caravan park in Porthcawl, Bridgend county. On Tuesday, David James Braddon, 26, from Caerphilly, appeared at Cardiff Crown Court and admitted carrying out the attack. He will be sentenced on 3 June. Det Ch Insp Kath Pritchard of South Wales Police said: “This was a brutal attack on a teenage boy which has left his family and friends devastated by the incident, and brought shock and sadness to both the visitors of Trecco Bay and also the community of Barry.” “We know incidents like this can cause a great deal of concern and anxiety. The community support has undoubtedly helped us to bring the person responsible for Conner’s murder to justice.” Following the fatal attack in March, his family paid tribute to the former Ysgol Bro Morgannwg pupil as “a unique, caring and compassionate young man with a warm, infectious smile complete with a cheeky wink”.

Cameron and Tusk Extend EU Talks as ‘Emergency Brake’ Nears Breakthrough David Cameron and European Council President Donald Tusk have agreed to extend talks by 24 hours on the UK’s proposed renegotiation of its European Union membership, delaying the publication of a draft deal but raising hopes of a breakthrough on welfare reform. The pair met for a working dinner at Downing Street on Sunday, with Mr Cameron later describing it on Twitter as a “good meeting” and confirming that Mr Tusk would hold off releasing the text to allow further progress. An early agreement had been expected to be put before EU leaders on Monday, paving the way for a package to be finalised at the European Council summit on 18 and 19 February. Securing a deal this month would enable Mr Cameron to call the promised referendum on the UK’s EU membership before the summer holidays. According to an EU source, Mr Tusk’s negotiating team remained at Downing Street after the dinner to continue discussions. After the agreed 24-hour extension, officials will assess whether sufficient consensus has been reached to table a draft agreement for member states’ consideration. Central to the talks is Mr Cameron’s drive to curb the pull factors for EU migration into the UK. His original plan sought to deny in-work benefits to EU migrants until they had been resident for four years, including access to tax credits that supplement the income of low-paid workers. He argued the restrictions would help reduce high levels of immigration. In recent weeks, attention has shifted to an alternative mechanism: an “emergency brake” on in-work welfare payments to EU migrants, designed to be triggered swiftly after a referendum in which the UK votes to remain. EU officials have indicated the brake could be used for up to four years, but only if the UK can demonstrate that public services are under excessive strain. Under current proposals, the measure could be imposed within three months of an application, subject to the agreement of other EU states. A Downing Street spokesman described the Sunday dinner as a “productive working dinner,” noting that “progress has been made in the past 48 hours, but we are not there yet.” He highlighted that the European Commission had tabled a text stating the UK meets the criteria for triggering the emergency brake on in-work benefits, calling it a “significant breakthrough” that would allow the prime minister to deliver on his pledge to restrict such benefits for four years. However, officials cautioned that other elements of the renegotiation still require resolution. BBC political correspondent Carole Walker reported that Mr Cameron and Mr Tusk agreed more time was needed to address outstanding issues, including economic governance protections for non-eurozone members and measures to tackle the abuse of free movement. The government has previously signalled its preference for a swift referendum following a February deal, with guidance and timelines set to be clarified once the draft agreement is tabled and reviewed by EU leaders.

Police have confirmed that a palm print discovered on a getaway van linked to the Kingsmills massacre belongs to a 59-year-old man who was arrested in Newry earlier this year. The man, detained as part of the reopened investigation in May, was later released pending a report to the Public Prosecution Service. At the Kingsmills inquest on Friday, officers clarified that they believe the print is his, after previously stating only that the arrest was “in connection” with the forensic find. The inquest was adjourned, with the coroner telling families he hopes to learn soon whether prosecutors will bring charges against the man and how any decision will affect the inquest’s progress. A lawyer representing some of the relatives had sought greater clarity from police regarding the forensic evidence and its implications. The Kingsmills massacre occurred in January 1976, when 10 Protestant workmen were shot dead by an IRA gang after their mini-bus was stopped near the County Armagh village of Kingsmills. The victims were returning home from a textile factory when they were ambushed. An 11th man, Alan Black, survived despite severe injuries. A Catholic man who was also on the bus was ordered to leave before the shootings. Police reopened their inquiry in May following the discovery of the palm print, shortly after the inquest into the killings was launched. That inquest followed a 13-year campaign by victims’ relatives seeking answers and accountability for one of the Troubles’ most notorious atrocities. Authorities said further updates would be provided as the investigation continues.

Net sales rose to $35.75bn, which was about $200m short of Wall Street predictions. That was enough to send shares tumbling more than 13% in after-hours trading in New York. Annual net profit of $596m also missed estimates as operating expenses jumped almost 18%. However, profits for the three months to 31 December more than doubled to a record $482m (£335m). It was the third consecutive quarter that Amazon has reported a profit and the first time it has done so since 2012. Sales for the full year were up 20% to $107bn - the first time the total has exceeded $100bn. Amazon also reported a 51% increase in its global Prime membership, which costs $99 a year and offers access to its video streaming service as well as free shipping. Analysts think it has about 50 million members, but the exact number is not revealed. Before the results were released, Amazon shares had risen almost 9% on Thursday and have more than doubled in the past 12 months. Investors were also paying attention to Amazon Web Services, the company's cloud computing business. The unit has been a bright spot for growth since Amazon began reporting figures separately at the start of the 2015 financial year. Fourth quarter sales rose almost 70% to $2.4bn, but that was down from 78% in the previous three months. Amazon’s mixed report underscores the company’s expanding scale and improving profitability alongside rising costs and slightly softer-than-expected topline momentum. While AWS and Prime continue to drive growth and deepen customer engagement, the market’s reaction highlights sensitivity to revenue targets and margin pressures. Executives said they remain focused on investing in infrastructure, content, and services to support long-term growth.

Nicola Sturgeon has been named the top influencer in a new list highlighting women whose ideas and actions shape public life across politics, fashion, journalism, business and entertainment. The judging panel described the Scottish National Party leader as “the woman of the moment,” placing her ahead of American Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour and actor, director and humanitarian ambassador Angelina Jolie. The top 10 also features Guardian editor Kath Viner, Downing Street policy unit director Camilla Cavendish, and chart-topping singer-songwriter Sia. Caitlyn Jenner appears on the list for “the part she has played in bringing the experience of being a trans woman to a global audience,” underscoring the organisers’ focus on women who exert broad cultural and political influence. The organisers said the aim was to identify figures who have an “exceptionally large impact” on people’s lives through their ability to influence others, whether from positions of formal authority or through soft power behind the scenes. Journalist and broadcaster Emma Barnett, who chaired the judging panel, said: “Those who influence usually have the ear of the traditionally powerful – but are one step removed. Sometimes, as in the case of Nicola Sturgeon, they will be both the power broker and the influencer.” Barnett added that many of the women selected operate as key voices shaping the decisions of the most powerful, citing Cavendish “whispering policy suggestions into David Cameron’s ear” and Sia “deciding what tunes Beyoncé and Rihanna belt out on their next respective albums.” She said Sturgeon commands “huge power” as SNP leader and “wields a huge amount of influence right now because of the state of both the UK union and the European one.” With Britain approaching an in-out referendum on European Union membership, Barnett said how Sturgeon chooses to use her political capital “could have potentially huge ramifications for this country,” calling her “the woman of the moment in terms of influence and hard power.”

UKIP’s Nicholas McQueen and the Green Party’s John Foster have called Tower Hamlets’ executive mayoral system “totally anti-democratic,” arguing it concentrates too much power in a single office and risks corruption and mismanagement. Speaking during a BBC London 94.9 hustings ahead of the borough’s re-election, the candidates said recent events had underscored the need for change, following the removal of former mayor Lutfur Rahman after he was found guilty of election fraud. Ten candidates are standing in the upcoming vote for Mayor of Tower Hamlets on 11 June. Frontrunners include Labour’s John Biggs and Independent Rabina Khan, who is supported by Rahman. Neither expressed support for scrapping the current governance model, but both stressed the need for greater transparency if elected. McQueen told the debate the executive mayoral role had “caused us so much trouble here and given us a bad image,” adding: “To get rid of the role, first you have to become the role. I think people now want rid of this executive mayoral role. We want the councillors to have the power back with committees.” Foster echoed the concerns, saying: “I think the mayoral system is totally anti-democratic and putting too much power in the hands of one person. It’s opening the door for corruption and it’s opening the door for mismanagement.” Tower Hamlets adopted the executive mayor model in 2010 after a local referendum, and is one of four London boroughs to operate the system, alongside Hackney, Newham and Lewisham. Executive mayors wield greater control over budgets and services than councils using the leader-and-cabinet structure. Supporters argue the post is more accountable because the officeholder is directly elected by voters. The contest comes amid calls for both reform and renewal in the borough’s political culture. The full list of candidates has been published for the 11 June poll, with the result expected to set the tone for future governance in Tower Hamlets.

Robinson urges ‘maturity’ in Maze row, warns against ‘punishing’ Northern Ireland Northern Ireland First Minister Peter Robinson has called for “maturity” in handling the dispute over plans for a peace centre at the former Maze prison site, insisting the wider redevelopment should proceed despite political tensions. Speaking during a visit to the Driver and Vehicle Agency in Coleraine, County Londonderry, on Wednesday, Mr Robinson said there was “no reason why the wider development of the site cannot go ahead” and argued the project could deliver significant employment. “What politician is going to say we could have created 5,000 jobs and then didn’t?” he asked. He described it as “cruel” for Sinn Féin to “punish the people of Northern Ireland” by blocking broader work at the Maze because of disagreement over the peace centre. Mr Robinson halted plans for the centre over the summer, a move that has heightened tensions between his Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and Sinn Féin. On Monday, Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness said there could be no progress on the wider Maze development unless it was based on previous agreements that included the peace centre. Addressing his relationship with Mr McGuinness, Mr Robinson sought to downplay the strain. “When you look at what’s going on in the coalition government at Westminster, things here are sweetness and light in comparison,” he said. He added that Northern Ireland was faring better than other parts of the world, citing the United States, where the federal government has been shut down. However, former Sinn Féin publicity director Danny Morrison warned that disagreements over the Maze and other issues were putting the peace process on “a slippery slope.” Speaking on Radio Ulster’s Nolan Show, he said some leaders were “sleepwalking us into a situation where they don’t appreciate how dangerous this is,” and cautioned that many within nationalist and republican communities feared unionists were not treating the process seriously. “I think we’re on a slippery slope as to whether or not a political arrangement can work in the north,” he said. The Maze site, long seen as a symbolic and sensitive location, remains a litmus test for cooperation within the power-sharing Executive amid competing visions for reconciliation and economic development.

McNeill skippered the club to the European Cup in 1967 in a career spanning a record 790 appearances, and yielding 31 major honours. Celtic have unveiled a statue of Billy McNeill at the beginning of The Celtic Way, celebrating the club’s greatest captain and one of its most enduring icons. Cast in bronze and mounted on a granite base, the statue honours McNeill’s leadership of the Lisbon Lions to the European Cup in 1967, a landmark achievement in Scottish football history, and commemorates his extraordinary career of 790 appearances and 31 major honours. The plinth is engraved on all four sides with McNeill’s achievements as both player and manager, the names of the players who brought the European Cup to Celtic, and a quote from legendary manager Jock Stein. As a player, McNeill’s haul included nine league championships, seven Scottish Cups, six League Cups and the European Cup. He later returned as manager to add four league titles, three Scottish Cups and a League Cup, reinforcing his influence across generations. “To now think that I will be honoured alongside such great men as Brother Walfrid and Jock Stein really does fill me with great pride,” McNeill said at the unveiling. “To be recognised in this way, by the club I love, is truly humbling.” Celtic chief executive Peter Lawwell paid tribute to McNeill’s stature within the club and the wider game. “I have had the honour and privilege of knowing Billy for many years now, and while there is sometimes caution offered in wanting to meet your heroes, in Billy’s case he is everything you would ever expect from Celtic’s greatest ever captain, and so much more,” he said. “Billy’s statue will stand at the beginning of The Celtic Way, proud and imposing – just as Billy was as a player – to welcome visitors to our stadium, and I am delighted to be part of this very special occasion today. I know that Billy, Liz and their family feel honoured by the decision to erect this statue, but as every Celtic supporter would testify, the honour has been ours in enjoying Billy’s lifetime of devoted service to our club.” Among the large crowd of supporters and former teammates was Bertie Auld, another of the famed Lisbon Lions. He addressed those gathered, including the present first-team squad. “Billy was a magnificent captain,” Auld said. “More than that, he was a magnificent man. He wasn’t just a centre back, he was a goal-scorer as well. When I was at Birmingham there were clubs every week wanting to sign him but he was Celtic through and through. He, and every single one of us did, loved speaking about the history of Celtic. Look at Billy when he was manager, he still had that passion.” Current manager Ronny Deila and his players were also in attendance. Speaking to BBC Scotland after the undraping, Deila reflected on the moment: “It was very special; it was almost too much for me. So I’m very happy to have been there, it’s a great thing for a great man and a legend in the club. You talk about his performances but you also talk about what he is as a man and his values and that’s so important. It shows how much this club means for the people and what’s been achieved here before. We are very lucky to be here.” The statue stands as a lasting tribute to a figure whose leadership, loyalty and success helped define Celtic’s identity, linking past glories to the present and inspiring future generations.

Posthumous Helen Rollason Award honours Hillsborough campaigner Anne Williams Hillsborough campaigner Anne Williams has been honoured with the BBC’s Helen Rollason Award, recognising her extraordinary strength and determination in the face of adversity. The award, presented posthumously, was accepted on her behalf by her daughter Sara, son Michael, and brother Danny, who paid tribute to the mother-of-three’s decades-long fight for justice following the death of her son Kevin in the 1989 football tragedy. “My mum embodied the very reason this award was created – strength, determination and passion,” said Sara. “Her tireless campaigning was driven by the love she had for her son Kevin and her dedication to seeking a new inquest. If anyone triumphed over adversity, it’s my mum.” Anne Williams, who had been suffering from cancer, died aged 60 just days after the annual Hillsborough memorial service at Liverpool’s Anfield stadium. Kevin, 15, was one of 96 Liverpool supporters who lost their lives at the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Sheffield Wednesday’s Hillsborough ground on 15 April 1989. For more than 20 years, Williams challenged the original inquest verdict of accidental death, delivered in 1991. That inquest heard evidence that Kevin and 94 other victims were dead by 15:15 BST, a determination she never accepted. Refusing to collect Kevin’s death certificate from the coroner, she set about independently gathering evidence, tracking down witnesses across the country. One witness suggested Kevin had uttered the word “mum” at about 16:00 BST, a detail Williams believed contradicted the official timeline and warranted further scrutiny. Her efforts, alongside those of other bereaved families and campaigners, helped prompt the establishment of the Hillsborough Independent Panel. Its report, published in September 2012, revealed extensive failings and led to the High Court quashing the original inquest verdicts in December that year. New inquests for all who died were ordered, with the hearings due to begin the following spring. Despite being terminally ill, Williams travelled to the High Court to witness the historic ruling, telling supporters she was “never going to give up”. The Helen Rollason Award is named after the respected BBC presenter, who died in 1999 aged 43 after a battle with cancer, and is awarded for outstanding achievement in the face of adversity. Previous recipients include Paralympian Martine Wright (2012), Grand National-winning jockey Bob Champion (2011), Formula One team boss Sir Frank Williams (2010), marathon fundraiser Major Phil Packer (2009), broadcaster Alastair Hignell (2008), Paralympic athlete Oscar Pistorius (2007), snooker player Paul Hunter (2006), footballer Geoff Thomas (2005), charity fundraiser Kirsty Howard (2004), boxer Michael Watson (2003), amateur endurance runner Jane Tomlinson (2002), sailor Ellen MacArthur (2001), Paralympian Tanni Grey-Thompson (2000), and racehorse trainer Jenny Pitman (1999). Anne Williams, who lived in Chester, became a symbol of persistence and courage for the Hillsborough families and supporters nationwide. Her legacy endures in the continued pursuit of truth and accountability, and in the new inquests her campaigning helped to secure.

Close call on Severn as high tides flood homes across West Country; Environment Agency warns of further surges Several homes were flooded across parts of Gloucestershire, Bristol and Somerset on Friday as a powerful tidal surge pushed up the River Severn and into coastal communities, but officials say the region narrowly avoided far worse damage. The Environment Agency said water levels came within inches of overtopping significant flood defences along the Severn, calling the episode “a very close shave.” More high tides are expected on Friday evening and Saturday morning, and three severe flood warnings remain in force in Gloucestershire. Communities including Minsterworth, Maisemore, Elmore and Newnham experienced flooding and disruption as the Severn Bore swept upstream. Dave Throup of the Environment Agency said locals “haven’t seen anything like this since 1999,” describing an unusual combination of high tide and surge that rapidly lifted river levels. “The [water] was within a few inches of overtopping some significant defences,” he said. Gloucestershire Police urged sightseers to stay away from the river and warned motorists that conditions could change quickly. River Severn expert Chris Witts said the bore wave itself was “fairly small,” a result of the large amount of fresh water coming downriver. “The tide had to push against that and had to overcome the bore — it’s reversed the flow and is looking quite spectacular, and that flow’s fast,” he said. Rest centres opened in Tewkesbury and the Forest of Dean, with centres in Stroud and Gloucester placed on standby. The Severn Bore occurs when a large tidal surge pushes sea water up the Severn Estuary and can travel as far upstream as Gloucester. In Bristol, flooding partially blocked the A4 Portway beneath the Clifton Suspension Bridge, while Cattle Market Road and Cumberland Road were also affected, causing delays for morning commuters. A temporary flood barrier was deployed for the first time to protect homes on Avon Crescent. Further west, debris was cleared from roads in Weston-super-Mare and Clevedon after earlier high tides. In Somerset, callers reported hailstones “bigger than the size of two pence pieces,” and several homes near Porlock Weir were flooded. The Environment Agency said Somerset avoided widespread flooding because winds were not as strong as forecast. Saturday’s League Two fixture between Bristol Rovers and Crawley Town at Broadfield Stadium was called off due to a waterlogged pitch. Officials urge residents to heed warnings as levels are monitored.

The Care Quality Commission has found nurse staffing levels “continued to be a problem” at Mid Yorkshire Hospitals NHS Trust, with Pinderfields Hospital, Pontefract Hospital, and Dewsbury and District Hospital each rated “requires improvement” following an inspection in June. The watchdog said the trust had made progress since its previous visit but warned that further action was needed to ensure patients consistently receive good quality care. Overall, the trust’s services were rated “good” for being caring, but “requires improvement” for being effective, responsive and well led. Maternity services, services for children and young people, and outpatients and diagnostics at all three hospitals were rated “good.” A previous inspection last year found staffing in some areas was a “significant concern.” Prof Sir Mike Richards, the CQC’s chief inspector of hospitals, said: “When we inspected the hospitals, we saw that the trust had made some clear improvements to improve the safety and quality of services since our previous inspection. However there is still work for the trust to do to ensure that people using its services consistently receive good quality care and treatment.” He added: “The trust must continue to tackle staff shortages and ensure patients receive the care they need.” In response, the trust said it had recruited an extra 100 nurses since the June inspection and is planning a £1.2m recruitment drive starting in the new year. Jules Preston, trust chairman, said: “Of course we would like to see the Trust performing to the very highest standards in all that we do but set against financial constraints and increasing demand we have made demonstrable achievements. Rome wasn’t built in a day and we still have much to learn from the CQC’s findings, but I do believe the changes we have made since the inspection mean we are now providing a safe service.” The CQC said it will continue to monitor the trust’s progress against its recommendations.

The University of South Wales will launch a new cyber security initiative at its Newport campus in October to tackle a growing skills shortage. Backed by Welsh Government funding, computer forensics and computer security undergraduates will partner with businesses to identify and solve real-world cyber challenges. The programme responds to forecasts that 4.5 million specialists will be needed worldwide by 2019, as companies spend as much as £16m annually to protect themselves online. If successful, the pilot will be developed into a full-time cyber security degree. Vice Chancellor Prof Julie Lydon called cyber crime “one of the four major national security threats,” underscoring the urgency of building expertise.

The details are contained in the 2010 accounts of William Ewart Properties William Ewart Properties has reported a sharp decline in its net asset value and an operating loss for 2010, reflecting what its directors describe as persistently challenging market conditions. The company’s net asset value fell to £105m at the end of 2010, down from £211m a year earlier, while it posted an operating loss of £4.5m. Despite the deteriorating headline figures, the directors said the business remains cash generative and continues to meet all loan obligations. They added that the company is actively pursuing opportunities to refinance or repay borrowings and has successfully done so in several cases since the year end. That activity is believed to include the sale of the shopping centre above London’s Victoria Station for almost £92m in September 2011. William Ewart’s portfolio spans retail and office assets across the UK and Germany, including shop units on Donegall Place in Belfast city centre, shopping centres in England, Scotland and Wales, and a substantial German portfolio. The accounts also disclose that certain bank loans have been transferred to another provider, although the identity of the new lender has not been specified. A subsidiary, WEP Gyle, which owns and operates the Gyle Shopping Centre in Edinburgh, reported that loans totaling £245m have likewise been transferred to another provider. Those facilities were originally advanced by the former Anglo Irish Bank, which has undergone significant restructuring following the financial crisis. William Ewart sits within a wider group controlled by a company called Brunswick No1, which has yet to file its 2010 results. The business is owned by Frank Boyd and Andrew Creighton, who are among Northern Ireland’s wealthiest individuals. Earlier this year, Mr Boyd’s family enterprise, Killultagh Estates, reported a £22m loss for 2010 and confirmed that some of its borrowings had been moved into the Irish government’s National Asset Management Agency (Nama), underlining the pressure facing property investors across the region.

A 10-year-old boy suffered a severe burn across his neck after riding into a rope that had been tied between a gate and school railings near Alderman Blaxill School in Colchester on Thursday afternoon. Essex Police said they are treating the incident as assault and appealed for witnesses to come forward. Michael-Ryan Mansfield was left shaken and in pain following the collision. His mother, Kimberley Brand, from the Shrub End area, said the injuries could have been far worse. “He was very shaken. He is quite little and the rope threw him backwards,” she said. “At first I thought he’d been in a fight. He came in sobbing his heart out.
