I saw his neck and it has got worse since it happened.” She added that Michael-Ryan, a pupil at Gosbecks Primary School who has two younger sisters, remains in significant discomfort. PC Esther Butcher condemned the act, calling it “complete stupidity” that could have caused far more serious harm. “Whoever is responsible may have thought this was simply a childish prank, but we are taking this matter seriously and treating it as assault,” she said. Ms Brand urged those responsible never to repeat such a prank. Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident or has information to contact Essex Police.

Residents in parts of mid Wales have raised concerns about patchy mobile reception, with some reporting long delays in services such as text messaging and mobile internet access. Wayne Evans, from Newtown in Powys, said his mobile service has deteriorated sharply in recent months. “It’s very frustrating,” he said. “It takes four to five hours before a text message will come through. It takes an hour to get through to Twitter on the internet. It’s just appalling really.” Montgomeryshire Assembly Member Russell George, who chairs the Senedd’s cross‐party group on digital communications, said he has been contacted by numerous frustrated residents and is calling a meeting of mobile operators serving the area. He urged a concerted effort to tackle rural not‐spots. “In recent years, we’ve heard a lot about the launch of new 4G services and network‐sharing agreements between operators, meant to improve coverage and speeds,” Mr George said. “But the reality in some rural areas is that mobile coverage has actually got worse. I believe that mandatory roaming and compulsory sharing of mobile infrastructure are the two most practical solutions to resolve this issue.” Mr George said he hopes to meet the main providers in November to press for immediate steps and a clearer timetable. Elinor Williams, Ofcom’s regulatory affairs manager for Wales, said the current disruption is linked to “mast rationalisation” as operators consolidate infrastructure. Companies have agreed to share sites and are switching off some masts while they test which deliver the strongest signals and serve the largest number of people. “They are working out which ones are the most powerful, which services the greatest population and, therefore, which ones are the most profitable to them,” she said. “It’s a programme of hit and miss at the moment, I think. In time it will settle down.”

Samia Shahid, a 28-year-old beautician from Bradford, died last month in northern Punjab in a case authorities are investigating as a suspected “honour killing.” Her ex-husband, Chaudhry Muhammad Shakeel, has been arrested on suspicion of murder and has now told investigators he strangled Ms Shahid with a scarf, according to BBC Pakistan correspondent Shaimaa Khalil. Police said Ms Shahid’s father, Chaudhry Mohammad Shahid, has been detained as an accessory to murder. Both men appeared in a Pakistani court on Saturday and were remanded in custody for four days. Police had previously denied reports that Mr Shakeel had confessed when he and Mr Shahid were first arrested and brought to court. Ms Shahid’s relatives initially claimed she died of a heart attack, but her husband, Syed Mukhtar Kazim, has maintained she was killed. A post-mortem examination has since confirmed she died as a result of strangulation, police said. Mr Kazim, Ms Shahid’s second husband, believes she was killed because her family disapproved of their marriage. In his reported confession, Mr Shakeel—who is also Ms Shahid’s cousin—said he demanded she leave her second husband and remarry him, which she refused. Ms Shahid had filed for divorce from Mr Shakeel and later married Mr Kazim in the UK. The case has drawn significant attention in both Pakistan and the UK, with calls for a thorough investigation and justice for Ms Shahid. Authorities continue to examine the circumstances surrounding her death.

Republic of Ireland winger Aiden McGeady, 30, has made 32 Premier League appearances for Everton and previously scored 31 league goals in 185 games for Celtic before a move to Spartak Moscow. He spent last season on loan with Championship side Sheffield Wednesday, netting once in 13 matches. Preston North End have signed Belgian right-back Marnick Vermijl, 24, on a three-year contract after he made 32 appearances on loan for the club last term. Defender Alex Baptiste, 30, joined Middlesbrough in 2015 but suffered a double leg fracture before featuring and finished last season on loan at League One Sheffield United. Follow football transfers on our dedicated page.

Ofcom review could impose price cap on Royal Mail as competition wanes Ofcom has launched a wide‐ranging review of Royal Mail’s universal postal service that could lead to a price cap on the operator, as the regulator examines whether deliveries can be provided efficiently and on a financially sustainable basis across the UK. The universal service requires Royal Mail to deliver to every address in the country at a uniform price. The move comes amid concern over declining competition in both letters and parcels. The collapse of Whistl’s national letter delivery service, formerly known as TNT, has left Royal Mail without a nationwide rival in that market, while parcels competitor City Link has also folded in recent months. Ofcom said it will look at Royal Mail’s position in parcels and assess whether the company has the ability to set wholesale prices in a way that might harm competition. In outlining the scope of the inquiry, the regulator said it could roll back some of the commercial flexibility granted to Royal Mail in 2012, which included latitude to raise prices. Ofcom first signalled the review last month and said its work would focus on safeguarding consumers while ensuring the viability of the UK‐wide service. Royal Mail’s shares closed down 3.5%, or 18.5p, at 508.5p on the news, valuing the company at about £5bn. Despite the drop, the stock remains around 14% higher than at the time of the company’s flotation in October 2013. In May, Royal Mail reported pre‐tax profits of £400m for the year to 29 March, down from £1.66bn the previous year. The company said it would participate fully in Ofcom’s review and called for regulatory stability. “We will be highlighting the need for a consistent approach to regulation. Ofcom’s existing framework, put in place in 2012, was to have provided certainty for seven years,” it said, adding that it had used its commercial freedoms “in a responsible and appropriate manner” to support the universal service amid significant market change. Ofcom expects to conclude the review next year.

Birmingham’s Barclaycard Arena to Host Great Britain v Japan in 2016 Davis Cup First Round The 9,000-seater Barclaycard Arena, formerly known as the National Indoor Arena (NIA), will host Great Britain’s Davis Cup first-round tie against Japan from 4-6 March. The event marks Birmingham’s seventh time staging a Davis Cup tie and could see Britain compete as defending champions for the first time since 1937, depending on the outcome of next week’s final against Belgium in Ghent. Birmingham has a rich Davis Cup history, with the arena previously witnessing memorable occasions including the dramatic 3-2 defeat to the United States in 1999 featuring Tim Henman and Greg Rusedski. Since then, five further ties have been held at the NIA, most recently a 4-1 victory over The Netherlands in 2007. “We are delighted to be heading to Birmingham for the first round of our 2016 Davis Cup campaign,” said captain Leon Smith. “It is a city with a great sporting history that has hosted some incredible Davis Cup ties in the past. Japan will be a tough contest but I'm sure the Birmingham fans will get right behind us and make as much noise as they can.” British number one Andy Murray has indicated he hopes to play regardless of the Ghent result, despite the tie’s proximity to the scheduled birth of his first child in February. Should Murray feature, fans could see an enticing showdown with last year’s US Open finalist Kei Nishikori, currently ranked world number eight. The tie will be the first meeting between Great Britain and Japan in the Davis Cup since 1931. The winners will advance to face either Kazakhstan or Serbia in the quarter-finals.

Durham Cathedral’s ambitious LEGO replica reached a milestone when the 200,000th brick was placed by South Korean student Chang Soo Lee. Visiting with classmates as part of a collaborative venture organised by Northumbria University, Lee said he was surprised to learn his contribution was so significant. In recognition, he received a commemorative medal and called the project “awesome,” adding that he can’t wait to see the finished model. Launched in July 2013, the fundraising initiative invites the public to donate £1 for each brick, with proceeds supporting Open Treasure, a programme to enhance public access to the cathedral’s historic collections. With 300,000 bricks required to complete the miniature, only 100,000 remain, and the cathedral hopes the latest milestone will inspire more visitors and supporters to take part. “We invite everyone to help us complete the model and celebrate the opening of the cathedral’s new exhibition spaces later this year,” said Gaye Kirby, Durham Cathedral’s head of development. When finished, the LEGO model will measure 12ft 6in (3.84m) long, 5ft (1.53m) wide and 5ft 6in (1.7m) high. The cathedral encourages visitors to buy a brick and follow the build.

Durham’s lower order hauled their side to 301, turning 274-8 into a competitive total as Barry McCarthy (39) and Paul Coughlin (73 not out) extended their ninth-wicket stand to 90 before the visitors were dismissed. Derbyshire, who held a 67-run first-innings advantage, stumbled to 31-3 in their reply but were rescued by Alex Hughes’ unbeaten 108, bowled out for 214. That set Durham 282 to win, and they made a solid start, reaching 36-0 at stumps with Michael Richardson unbeaten on 29. Derbyshire were left ruing the morning session, when Durham recovered from 205-8. Only three Derbyshire batters reached double figures in the second innings, with Luis Reece adding 37 and first-innings centurion Matt Critchley 28.

Former Everton prospect George Green, 22, left Oldham Athletic by mutual consent in November, months into a two-year deal signed last summer. The ex-England Under-18 international moved from Bradford City to Goodison Park aged 15 for a reported £2m. Speaking to his new club’s website, Green said: “I’ve got Football League experience under my belt already, but I want to play at a higher level than League One.” For updates, visit our dedicated transfer page.

Northampton officer given final written warning after spraying colleague during briefing A Northamptonshire Police constable has been found guilty of misconduct after accidentally discharging incapacitant spray into a colleague’s forehead during a team briefing he was leading. PC Greg Taylor, 37, was issued a final written warning that will remain on his file for 18 months. He was cleared of gross misconduct. The incident happened on 22 June at Campbell Square police station in Northampton, where Taylor was acting as a sergeant. Prosecuting solicitor David Ring told a disciplinary panel there had been a stand-off between Taylor and another officer in the team, who cannot be named. “He (PC Taylor) said if he did not stop talking he would spray him,” Mr Ring said, describing how the second officer challenged Taylor. “In an element of bravado, he dared him to spray him and he took off his glasses to give him a clear shot. PC Taylor removed the cap and depressed the plunger in short bursts. It hit him in the forehead. Everyone in the room thought it was extremely funny.” Taylor told the hearing he had not intended to fire the spray, which is typically used to incapacitate suspects, and accepted he had been “stupid.” He added: “I hate to use the word banter but there is a culture of wit and mockery.” Assistant Chief Constable Rachel Swann, who chaired the panel, ruled that Taylor’s conduct amounted to misconduct. She said he had been “irresponsible and foolish” but had not breached standards of honesty. The panel said his actions “fell well below” those expected of a police officer. The final written warning means any further misconduct within the next 18 months could lead to more severe disciplinary action.

Fraud cases in the UK rose by 25% last year compared with 2013, driven largely by a surge in identity theft, according to new figures from fraud prevention service Cifas. Identity fraud accounted for 41% of all recorded incidents, with hotspots identified in London, Leicester, Birmingham, Manchester, Leeds and Glasgow. Cifas's annual Fraudscape report, compiled from data submitted by its member organizations, warns that digitally savvy young adults are increasingly being targeted. Often applying for financial products for the first time, many are vulnerable to criminals who impersonate them to open new accounts or take out loans, siphoning off funds before the fraud is detected. These new-account schemes have overtaken traditional account-takeover scams as security on existing accounts has improved. "The frauds we are recording point to increasingly sophisticated, predatory and organised criminals. This is crime at an industrial scale," said Simon Dukes, chief executive of Cifas. The report also found men were 1.7 times more likely than women to have their identities stolen. Nick Mothershaw, director at credit reference agency Experian, said the findings underscore the persistent risk to lenders and customers as more applications move across multiple channels, including online and mobile. Concerns about enforcement capacity are growing. In October, Commander Steve Head of the City of London Police told the BBC that there are not enough officers dedicated to tackling fraud. A subsequent BBC investigation found specialist fraud units have been outstripped by a rising caseload.

The trust angered farmers when it paid £200,000 above guide price for the land at Thorneythwaite Farm in Borrowdale. The broadcaster said the higher bid made it impossible for local farmers "critical to the preservation" of the Lake District "to get a look in". The National Trust said it was the best way to secure the landscape's future. Thorneythwaite Farm’s private owner put the property up for auction in two lots, with a guide price of £750,000 for the land and £800,000 for the farmhouse and buildings. The National Trust offered £950,000 for the land alone, a move that drew criticism from farming groups and local advocates who hoped the farm would remain a working enterprise. The Herdwick Sheep Breeders Association wrote on X, formerly Twitter: “Another farm lost. Hopes that the farm could be taken on by a new young fell farmer have been dashed.” Broadcaster and author Melvyn Bragg echoed the frustration in a letter to The Times, accusing the Trust of outbidding local farmers. “The National Trust..... behaved very badly. It put in a bid which was way above that which was reasonable for the land, thus making it impossible for local farmers to get a look in. It was a nasty piece of work. Had a billionaire bullied his way into this disgraceful purchase there would have been a deserved outcry,” he wrote. The National Trust defended the decision, saying it prioritized the land purchase to safeguard the area’s ecological and cultural value. The charity said it did not have funds to buy both lots and offered the higher price to avoid the risk of being gazumped—particularly if the auctioneer chose to package the land and buildings together at a price beyond its reach. While acknowledging that local preference was for a single buyer to run the farm, the Trust said its bid was the most viable way to ensure the long-term protection of the Borrowdale landscape.

Bristol City head coach Lee Johnson says the club has rejected a “derisory” £4m offer, understood to be from Birmingham City, and insists defenders Aden Flint and Joe Bryan will only leave on the club’s terms. “His head has definitely been turned,” Johnson admitted of Flint, 28, who joined from Swindon Town in 2013. “We don’t have to do anything that we do not feel is right for Bristol City.” Johnson revealed the bid arrived on Tuesday and became public “one minute later,” a leak he called “very disappointing.” He stressed City’s strong financial position under Financial Fair Play means they are under no pressure to sell. “Nothing needs to be forced upon us by anybody,” he said. “We’re trying to bring players in and not lose our best players.” Flint has scored 29 goals in 200 appearances for the Robins, while Bryan, 23, a product of the club’s academy, has featured 181 times since his 2012 debut. Both, Johnson noted, are on “good, strong, healthy-length” contracts. “If anybody is to go, it will be on our terms because we have a good owner,” Johnson added, reiterating that City’s valuation of their assets must be met before any departures are considered. Meanwhile, Bailey Wright has been named club captain for the new season, highlighting Johnson’s focus on continuity and leadership as City seek to build on last year’s progress. The head coach’s firm stance underscores Bristol City’s resolve to protect key players and maintain momentum as the transfer window intensifies and Championship rivals test their resistance.

Bury have signed 33-year-old former Blackburn trainee Danns following a successful pre-season trial. The experienced player, who has represented 10 clubs including Leicester City, Crystal Palace and Birmingham City, becomes the League One side’s ninth new arrival of the summer as the Shakers prepare for a second consecutive campaign in the third tier. Find all the latest football transfers on our dedicated page.

Authorities have arrested several senior members of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints in raids across Utah and South Dakota, alleging a scheme to siphon money from Utah’s food assistance program. Police said suspects were taken into custody in Hildale and Salt Lake City, Utah, and in Custer County, South Dakota. Among those detained is Lyle Jeffs, brother of imprisoned sect leader Warren Jeffs, and believed to oversee daily operations. “This indictment is not about religion. This indictment is about fraud,” U.S. Attorney John Huber said, accusing a network in the Hildale–Colorado City community of conspiring to defraud a program meant to help low-income families buy food. The FLDS, an offshoot of the mainstream Mormon church, is thought to count up to 10,000 adherents. The group split from The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints more than a century ago after the LDS church renounced polygamy. In 2011, Warren Jeffs received a life sentence for sexually assaulting two underage followers he took as brides. The defendants are expected to appear in court in the coming days. Prosecutors emphasized the case targets alleged financial crimes, not religious practice.

title: A copy of the ceasefire deal, seen by the BBC, says the main entrances to the camp in Damascus will be opened and basic services will be restored. About 18,000 people have been besieged since last July. Rights groups say more than 100 people have starved to death. Syria has been engulfed in a bloody conflict between government and rebel forces over the past three years. The ceasefire is said to include the Syrian regime, rebel groups based in Yarmouk and many Palestinian factions, Sana news agency reports. It is not clear when the truce will begin. Previous truces have been broken. Both food and medicine are in scarce supply in Yarmouk and large parts of the suburb lie in utter ruin, the BBC's chief international correspondent Lyse Doucet reports. For the last two weeks, United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) has been unable to distribute food because of continued clashes and shelling, our correspondent adds. Yarmouk has become a symbol of suffering in Syria. This once vibrant Palestinian community has been targeted by a punishing government siege, and rivalry among numerous Syrian and Palestinian armed groups. We saw, on the two occasions this year we managed to enter the besieged area, how desperate conditions are. Nearly 18,000 people are struggling to survive, without basic necessities, under constant shelling and sniper fire. On our last visit in May, Syrian military officers told us they expected to reach an agreement soon. UN officials also spoke of possible positive change. It's taken weeks longer than expected. But the document I've seen sets out a complicated deal. If all the parties to this conflict stick to their agreement to keep this southern gateway to Damascus both neutral and peaceful, it will be a major achievement, and rare good news for the long suffering people of Yarmouk. UNRWA spokesman Chris Gunness said the agency had received "credible information about an agreement signed yesterday between Syrian authorities and armed opposition groups inside Yarmouk". "We would welcome any durable and binding agreement that achieves a cessation of hostilities, full humanitarian access and an end to the suffering of civilians in Yarmouk and all of Syria," he added. The camp, first built for Palestinians fleeing the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, became the focus of heavy fighting in late 2012 when armed opposition groups moved in. Government forces cut off the rebel-held camp in July 2013, trapping the refugees and some Syrians.

In a speech in Colorado, the Fed's number two policymaker was upbeat about the economy's recovery and prospects. “We are close to our targets,” Vice Chair Stanley Fischer said on Sunday, adding that jobs growth had been “remarkably resilient.” He did not mention interest rates, but the remarks are likely to fuel debate about when they may rise. Fischer said this year’s pace of jobs growth, although slower than in 2015, was “more than enough” for the labour market to continue to improve. Speaking at a conference in Aspen, he noted that inflation outside of food and energy prices was “within hailing distance” of 2 percent, the Federal Reserve’s target. He noted the U.S. has weathered shocks in recent years, including the Greek debt crisis, a stronger dollar and bouts of market turbulence. “Yet, even amid these shocks, the labour market continued to improve,” Fischer said, calling the return to near-full employment a “remarkable, and perhaps under-appreciated,” post-crisis achievement. One major concern, however, is the slowdown in U.S. productivity growth observed over the past few years. If that weakness persists, Fischer warned, it could curtail job creation and wage gains, complicating efforts to sustain momentum and ultimately limiting the pace at which living standards can rise. Although Fischer avoided commenting on the precise path for interest rates, expectations have been building that the Fed could raise rates again this year as long as growth remains on track and inflation continues to firm. Fischer said he expects U.S. growth “to pick up in coming quarters,” reinforcing views that the expansion retains underlying strength. Markets will scrutinize upcoming data on employment and inflation to gauge the timing of any move. The Fed’s dual mandate—maximum employment and price stability—has guided officials as they balance steady job gains against still-moderate price pressures in the months ahead. His remarks come ahead of a closely watched speech by Fed Chair Janet Yellen on Friday, when she is expected to offer guidance on monetary policy. Economists said Fischer was unlikely to stake out a position that could be contradicted within days. “It would be quite an event if Fischer went out so close to Yellen’s speech,” former Fed Board economist Roberto Perli told Bloomberg.

The script in the site targeted visitors using the anonymising web browser Tor and sent information about their computers to a server in France. A hidden tracking program embedded in an illicit website has sparked alarm among privacy advocates after it targeted Tor users and exfiltrated device information to a mysterious server in France. The code, which exploited a security flaw in Tor, may have been crafted by a law enforcement agency, raising fears that similar techniques could be applied across other sites to identify law-abiding people who rely on anonymizing tools. The Tor Project has pushed an update that disables the tracker, and the underlying vulnerability has been patched. Tor, which routes traffic through a network of relays to mask users’ identities and is widely used to access the so-called dark web, is based on Mozilla’s Firefox browser. The exploit leveraged a bug affecting both Tor and Firefox, enabling the hidden site to collect data that could deanonymize visitors. Technology outlet Motherboard reported online posts discussing the discovery of the tracking code on a child sex abuse website, with one user describing it as a “network investigative technique” (NIT) commonly used by law enforcement to identify people browsing anonymously. The specific website was shut down on 15 November. The party behind the tracking code has not been publicly identified. However, a security researcher told Ars Technica that a majority of the code closely matched a script the FBI deployed in 2013 to unmask Tor users. Daniel Veditz, security lead at Firefox-maker Mozilla, wrote in a blog: “The exploit in this case works in essentially the same way as the ‘network investigative technique’ used by [the] FBI to deanonymise Tor users. This similarity has led to speculation that this exploit was created by FBI or another law enforcement agency. As of now, we do not know whether this is the case.” Veditz warned that if a government did develop and deploy the exploit, its public release means “it can now be used by anyone to attack Firefox users,” underscoring how targeted government hacking can threaten the broader web. Both Firefox and Tor have issued patches, and users are urged to update immediately to mitigate the risk.

Wholesale costs of both fuels have risen significantly Wholesale costs for petrol and diesel have climbed sharply in recent weeks, a trend partly attributed to an agreement by Opec oil-producing nations to cut output. Despite this upward pressure, fuel prices in Northern Ireland appear to be rising more slowly than in other parts of the UK, with industry observers pointing to strong local competition as a key factor. Data gathered by breakdown-cover provider the RAC showed that Northern Ireland recorded the lowest average pump prices in the UK during December. By the end of the month, the average cost of unleaded petrol stood at 117.23p per litre and diesel at 119.63p, according to the RAC. Those figures reflected average monthly increases of 2.99p for petrol and 3.07p for diesel. In Northern Ireland, however, the rise over the same period was smaller: petrol up by 1.9p and diesel up by 2.71p. RAC fuel spokesman Simon Williams said healthy competition in Northern Ireland had helped to contain prices. “Northern Ireland is the cheapest place to buy fuel and does well month-on-month in our figures because of the competition here,” he told BBC News NI. “There are proportionally more fuel retailers and more fuel distributors here than in the rest of the UK – that’s kept the prices down so far.” Williams cautioned that the trajectory of prices remains uncertain. “It is incredibly difficult to predict how much prices will be affected in the future,” he said, noting that wholesale movements, currency shifts and global supply dynamics can feed through to the pump at different speeds. Finding the best local deal can be challenging for motorists, given the variation between forecourts. Price-comparison service PetrolPrices.com said Cookstown was the cheapest town to fill up in over the past week, with average unleaded at 112.7p per litre. The most expensive petrol price they recorded was more than 7p higher per litre, underscoring the spread between the lowest and highest-priced stations. “These price differences make a huge difference when added up over the year and the spread, or difference between the most expensive and cheapest fuel, is evident in every town and city across Northern Ireland as well as the entire UK,” said Jason Lloyd, Managing Director of PetrolPrices.com. “That means that there are cheaper alternatives in every town – so it’s about monitoring prices yourself, or using a service like ours to make sure you are getting the best deal in your area.” BBC News NI asked readers to share the cheapest prices they had seen at the pump, and none reported a lower price than 112.7p per litre.

Russell Knox will set off at 15:12 BST on Thursday, aiming to improve on last year’s missed cut in his Masters debut. The 31-year-old Scot, ranked No 23 in the world, has two PGA Tour wins and in 2015 became the first Scot to capture a World Golf Championship. Fellow Scot and 1988 Masters champion Sandy Lyle plays alongside English amateur Scott Gregory and Sean O’Hair. Defending champion Danny Willett begins his title defence with Matt Kuchar and Australian amateur Curtis Luck. Northern Ireland’s Rory McIlroy is paired with Spain’s Jon Rahm and Japan’s Hideto Tanihara at 18:41, while world No 1 Dustin Johnson headlines the final group at 19:03 with two-time winner Bubba Watson and Jimmy Walker. Knox and Lyle are Scotland’s only representatives in a field that features a record 11 Englishmen.

Three arrested after clash outside Railway pub leaves man with serious head injuries Three men were arrested after a clash outside the Railway pub in East Street, Southend, that reportedly involved about 15 people and left one man with serious head injuries. Essex Police said officers were called at around 19:20 GMT on Saturday. A man in his 40s from Suffolk was found on the ground with head injuries and taken to the Royal London Hospital. A 33-year-old man from Southend and a 23-year-old man from Westcliff were arrested on suspicion of causing grievous bodily harm. A 47-year-old man from Cambridge was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage in relation to damage to the pub door. The pub is less than a mile from Roots Hall stadium, where Southend United and Cambridge United had earlier drawn 0-0. Police said East Street was likely to remain closed for most of Sunday to allow investigations to continue. Officers urged anyone who witnessed the incident or has footage to contact Essex Police. Enquiries are ongoing.

Police are investigating after a lorry overturned on the London-bound M4 near Reading on Wednesday, between junctions 12 and 11, killing its driver, a 49-year-old man from Essex, at the scene. The crash damaged the central reservation and carriageway, with repair work carried out overnight. The closure caused tailbacks, leaving some motorists stranded in vehicles for up to seven hours. Officers are urging anyone who witnessed the collision to contact police.

At least 38 troops were killed in Aleppo when a tunnel bomb destroyed a building used by Syrian government forces, a UK-based monitoring group said Friday. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights (SOHR) said the explosion occurred on Thursday and revised an initial death toll of 14 upward after more bodies were recovered. The rebel faction Thuwwar al‐Sham claimed responsibility, posting video that shows its fighters planting explosives in a tunnel beneath the position before a blast sends a cloud of rubble and ash. The footage could not be independently verified. Aleppo remains split between opposition-held eastern districts and government-controlled western neighborhoods. Hundreds of thousands of civilians in the east were largely cut off earlier this month as government forces, backed by Russian air strikes, tightened their grip on supply routes and escalated bombardments. The city has been divided for four years, with both sides deploying tunnel bombs in an urban war. There was no immediate comment from Syrian state media on the blast or the reported casualty toll.

GL Assessment is investigating a possible breach of security in Plymouth after allegations that some children saw the 11-plus English paper before taking the exam. The test provider said it has extensive security measures to prevent leaks but is treating the claims seriously and reviewing what happened. Parents reported hearing from pupils that they recognised questions on the paper. “It’s a big shame that we can’t now relax because we were looking forward to it being all over and done with. What will happen? Will we have to retake? Will there be a delay in the results? It will have an impact on us going forward,” said Louise Higgins. Another parent, Caroline Tall, added: “At first I thought it was just a rumour, but to think it could be true is very concerning to me.” Hundreds of pupils sit the exam each year to compete for places at the city’s three grammar schools. Plymouth City Council said it is working with GL Assessment to explore whether there were any irregularities with the English paper. A spokesperson for GL Assessment said the potential for a leak is remote, but suggestions of a breach are taken seriously and updates follow.

Glamorgan stalwart Mark Wallace has announced his retirement from professional cricket at the age of 35, drawing the curtain on an 18-year first-team career with the Welsh county. Wallace, who captained Glamorgan from 2013 to 2015 and played 264 first-class games, leaves a legacy defined by durability, leadership and record-breaking performances behind the stumps and with the bat. He became the first wicketkeeper for Glamorgan to score more than 1,000 first-class runs in a season and was long celebrated as one of the county’s most reliable performers. An Abergavenny product, Wallace made his debut for Glamorgan in 1999 against Somerset at Taunton and, at 17 years and 287 days, became the club’s youngest wicketkeeper to appear in a County Championship match. Over the course of his career, he helped Glamorgan secure the National League one-day title in 2004, surpassed Eifion Jones’ record for the highest aggregate of runs by a specialist wicketkeeper in 2012, and passed the landmark of 10,000 first-class runs three years later. His resilience was underscored by a remarkable streak of 230 consecutive Championship appearances between 2001 and 2015. Wallace also represented England Under-19s, reinforcing his standing as a player of national promise early in his career. “I’ve been extremely fortunate to have been able to represent the club for so long and I walk away with a heavy heart,” Wallace said. “I’m hugely thankful to the club for the opportunities they’ve given me. I would like to thank the supporters for enduring some of my performances and to my family and friends for their unwavering support.” Despite signing a contract extension last year to keep him at Sophia Gardens until the end of the 2017 summer, Wallace has opted to hang up his gloves a year early. Elected as Professional Cricketers’ Association (PCA) chairman in December 2012, he will now take up a permanent PCA role as Player Development Manager, supporting cricketers in the South West and Wales. “I’m delighted to be able to start the next chapter of my life,” he added. Glamorgan chief executive Hugh Morris paid tribute to Wallace’s contribution. “Mark has been an integral part of Glamorgan for almost two decades. He will be long remembered for his skill with bat and gloves, his leadership qualities, as a role model in the dressing room and as an ambassador for the club. Mark can look back on an outstanding professional career with great pride and it is excellent news that he will continue to contribute to the game of cricket in his new role at the PCA.”

Police appeal after boy attacked and robbed in Thatcham Police are appealing for information after a boy was attacked and robbed while riding a scooter in Thatcham, Berkshire. Officers said the victim was scooting along Station Road with another boy when they were approached by a man on a bike. The offender elbowed the victim, causing him to fall into bushes, before kicking him and stealing his mobile phone. Thames Valley Police described it as a “nasty unprovoked attack” that has left the boy “scared to leave his home.” The stolen phone was later recovered in Horne Road, the force added. The suspect is described as white, around 5ft 8ins (1.72m), aged in his 20s or early 30s, well built, with pale skin and dark circles under his eyes. He had short brown curly hair and big bushy eyebrows. He was wearing a black bandana with red stars covering his nose, a black hooded Adidas top, dark jogging bottoms with white stripes down each side that were ripped at the knees, and black Nike trainers with blue soles. Det Con Claire Midwinter said: “This may have appeared to be youngsters messing around, we urge anyone to call us if they have any information which would help us identify a suspect for this nasty unprovoked attack.” Police are urging anyone with information to contact Thames Valley Police.

Stephen Flynn said it was "beyond disappointing" that no progress had yet been made Stephen Flynn has criticised Aberdeen City Council over what he described as a lack of accountability following revelations that baby and adult ashes were mixed at Hazlehead Crematorium and returned to the relatives of adults, while parents of infants were told there were no ashes. Flynn said months had passed since the “true, and horrific, extent” of the issue became clear, and although practices have changed and steps to compensate families have been taken, “we have yet to see any proper level of accountability within the council and that, quite frankly, is beyond disappointing.” The director responsible for the department running Hazlehead Crematorium, Pete Leonard, did not attend the council meeting in August 2016 at which his department’s conduct was discussed. He has not returned to work since and remains on sick leave. In response to Flynn’s call for clarity, Angela Scott, chief executive of Aberdeen City Council, told the chamber: “Just to remind the chamber, in the proceeding months action has been taken against the crematoria manager resulting in his dismissal following an investigation. The chamber will recall that I instructed a management review. That has concluded. The chamber will be aware that the director has advised that he's on a period of sick leave. That's the current position as it stands.” The scandal in Aberdeen first came to light in 2013 when BBC Scotland revealed that no ashes had been offered to families of infants cremated in the city over a five-year period. It followed similar findings at Mortonhall crematorium in Edinburgh, where baby ashes had been secretly buried for decades. An independent report by Dame Elish Angiolini later described the practices as “abhorrent,” prompting widespread calls for reform, transparency, and accountability across Scotland’s crematoria services.

More than two-thirds of 220 websites surveyed failed to comply with key consumer protection laws, including cancellation rights and providing refunds when due, according to a new report by Scottish trading standards officers. The survey, carried out by officials from 22 Scottish local authority areas, examined sites selling a wide range of consumer goods across the UK and found what they described as “worryingly high” levels of non-compliance. The project, organised by the Society of Chief Officers of Trading Standards in Scotland (SCOTSS), revealed that more than 50% of the randomly selected sites did not provide a full refund when required. In addition, more than one in four retailers illegally deducted the original delivery charge from money refunded, while 43% failed to inform consumers of their right to cancel. One in five added unexpected surcharges onto prices late in the buying process. SCOTSS chairman Colin Baxter said: “These are worryingly high levels of non-compliance. These legal requirements are important for a variety of reasons: to protect online buyers, to ensure fairness and a level playing field for reputable retailers, and to ensure the smooth working of the internet marketplace. Since the early days of e-commerce, trading standards officers have worked hard with significant success to ensure that internet sellers are complying with the law. However, with the continuing expansion of e-commerce in the UK, new entrants are joining the market every day, many of them small micro-businesses with little experience of consumer law.” He added: “It is a battle for law enforcement to keep up.” The investigation combined online inspections with “test purchases” to analyse how customers are treated in practice. Officers cancelled purchases within the statutory seven-day period to verify whether website operators honoured their obligations, including full refunds and clear cancellation processes. Where non-compliance was identified, cases were followed up by officers either contacting the retailer directly or referring matters to the trading standards service in the area where the company is based. SCOTSS said the findings underline the need for continued enforcement, guidance, and education for online sellers, especially smaller businesses entering the marketplace. The organisation urged retailers to familiarise themselves with consumer protection rules to avoid enforcement action and to ensure trust and fairness for shoppers.

Boat skipper Nick Davies of Gairloch-based Hebridean Whale Cruises says humpback whales have been putting on a show in the Hebrides, with repeated sightings over the past five weeks. Davies captured photographs off Tuimpan Head on Lewis and reported additional encounters with minke whales and hundreds of dolphins around Lewis and near Skye. He believes the visits by the great whales are becoming more frequent in these waters. Marine charity Whale and Dolphin Conservation notes humpbacks are famed for their dramatic breaches, delighting wildlife watchers and boosting local eco-tourism.

Kell Brook, the 28-year-old IBF welterweight champion from Sheffield, is in a stable condition after being stabbed in his left leg while on holiday in Tenerife, his promoters Matchroom have said. No arrests have been made. A spokeswoman for Spain’s Guardia Civil said the incident occurred at Golf del Sur in San Miguel de Abona, and that Brook “lost a lot of blood.” Brook’s parents have travelled to Spain to be at his bedside. Brook captured the IBF title last month with a points victory over Shawn Porter in California, extending his unbeaten professional record to 33 fights. He had been lined up for a clash with Amir Khan, expected on 6 December. His long-time trainer Dominic Ingle told BBC Look North: “We’ve been through a lot together, me and Kell, and receiving the news this morning hit me in the pit of my stomach. I think he’s stable. We don’t know the extent of his injuries, but knowing Kell, he’ll try to make that date if he can.” It is the second time Brook has been stabbed, following an incident in Sheffield in 2007. Spanish police are continuing their investigation.

Bayern Munich advanced to the cup semi-finals with a 3-0 win, sparked after three minutes when Robert Lewandowski chipped in Franck Ribery’s pass. Thiago Alcantara doubled the lead with a header from Lewandowski’s cross before the Polish striker tapped in a third. The visitors finished with 10 men after Holger Badstuber received a second yellow for a foul on Javi Martinez. Borussia Monchengladbach also booked a semi-final spot, edging Hamburg 2-1.

The draft National Park Partnership Plan 2018–2023 aims to widen the park’s social, environmental, cultural and economic benefits, with a 12-week public consultation open until 3 July. The plan sets out three priorities—conservation and land management, visitor experience, and rural development—designed to protect the landscape while supporting thriving communities and a high-quality experience for all. A central focus is attracting and retaining more skilled working-age and young people, alongside encouraging people of all abilities and backgrounds to enjoy the outdoors. The park’s new convener, James Stuart, said: “The national park is a truly special place and this plan proposes how we, along with a wide range of other organisations, can work together over five years to look after, enhance and make the most of it. By working collaboratively with all of our partners we can achieve a much greater impact.” Chief executive Gordon Watson said work is already underway to provide young people with opportunities to gain skills and experience to support future employment. “We want to build on that by working closely with our partners to broaden that range of opportunities, whether through training, volunteering, modern apprenticeships and employment, so that young people growing up in the national park aren’t missing out on the opportunities that those living in more urban areas have access to,” he said. He added that measures to address the lack of affordable housing and efforts to protect and enhance local services and infrastructure will help ensure a bright future for young people living and working within the park. The draft plan emphasizes joint working with communities, businesses and public bodies to deliver practical actions that both safeguard natural heritage and strengthen the park’s long-term resilience. The consultation seeks views from residents, visitors, stakeholders and partners to help shape final priorities for implementation.

Police have launched a murder investigation after a man's body was found at a property on Broombeg View around 20:30 GMT on Thursday. Formal identification is pending. A 33-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder. Det Ch Insp Gareth Talbot said the inquiry is at an early stage and urged anyone with information about this “heinous crime” to come forward. Authorities are appealing for witnesses.

Swiss Right Surges as SVP Wins 65 Seats, Shifting Lower House Balance Switzerland’s rightward tilt sharpened after the Swiss People’s Party (SVP) captured 65 of 200 seats in the National Council, a gain of 11, in elections that analysts say were shaped by Europe’s migrant crisis. While Switzerland has admitted far fewer asylum seekers than Germany, commentators argue the continent-wide debate energized the SVP’s hard line on immigration and the European Union. The right-wing liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) also advanced, finishing third, reinforcing a bloc that Swiss media dubbed a “Rechtsrutsch” — a slide to the right. Together, the SVP, FDP and several smaller right-leaning factions can now command a majority in the lower house. The upper house, the 46-seat Council of States, has not mirrored that shift; many cantons require second-round runoffs, leaving its final composition undecided. The SVP, already the largest party after winning 26.6% in 2011, extended its lead while the leftist Social Democratic Party (SP) slipped to second with 44 seats, two fewer than before. “The vote was clear. The people are worried about mass migration to Europe,” SVP leader Toni Brunner said after polls closed. The party spearheaded the 2014 referendum to introduce immigration quotas, which passed but conflicts with the EU’s freedom of movement — a principle Switzerland previously agreed to respect under a web of bilateral accords. Brussels and Bern face a January 2017 deadline to reconcile the quota mandate with existing agreements; failing that, the Swiss government is obliged to implement the referendum’s provisions, risking a broader rupture in EU-Swiss ties. Switzerland has pledged to participate in the EU’s controversial plan to relocate 120,000 refugees from Italy and Greece, though it remains unclear how many it will accept. The SVP’s strengthened hand could reshape the seven-member federal government, whose composition is decided by parliament in December. The party is pushing for the three largest parties to hold two seats each. At present, the SVP occupies one seat. Notable SVP newcomers include Magdalena Martullo-Blocher, daughter of the party’s influential vice-president Christoph Blocher. A billionaire industrialist and former cabinet member (2004–2007), Mr Blocher helped turn the SVP into Switzerland’s best-funded party and was instrumental in the country’s rejection of European Economic Area membership — a step seen as a pathway toward joining the EU. Roger Köppel, a prominent commentator and editor-in-chief of Die Weltwoche magazine, also won a seat for the SVP in Zurich, underscoring the party’s growing profile across media and politics.

Sheffield Wednesday sign Barnsley striker Sam Winnall; debut set for Huddersfield Sheffield Wednesday have completed the signing of Barnsley striker Sam Winnall, with the 25-year-old available to make his debut when Huddersfield Town visit on Saturday. Winnall joined Barnsley from Scunthorpe in July 2014 and would have been out of contract in the summer. He scored 48 goals in 116 appearances for the Tykes, including 11 in 22 Championship matches this season. Posting on Twitter, Winnall said he “can’t wait to get started and help this club back up to where it belongs!” Wednesday sit sixth in the Championship, 10 points off the automatic promotion places, while Barnsley are eighth. Winnall was instrumental in Barnsley’s double success last season, lifting the Johnstone’s Paint Trophy and winning the League One play-off final at Wembley. In a farewell message to supporters, he said he would “never forget the memories we shared.” In a separate development, Barnsley announced that chief executive Linton Brown has left the club.

Maersk Oil will cut workforce by 10-12%, bringing 2015 job losses to about 1,250, as it pursues a 20% operating cost reduction by end-2016 amid prolonged low oil prices. In the UK, redundancies are tied to the retirement of the Janice installation, located 150 miles southeast of Aberdeen, and modifications to offshore rotation schedules. The company will also scale back operations in Qatar and Norway, at its Copenhagen headquarters, and in Kazakhstan, following an extensive internal review of business activities. Chief executive Jakob Thomasen acknowledged the human impact of the restructuring, saying: “These are difficult decisions and my immediate concern is for the welfare of those affected.” The moves reflect ongoing pressure on upstream operators to streamline portfolios and reduce expenditures as the oil downturn endures.

SSE has spent £750,000 on the unit at Contin in Easter Ross, as part of its historic responsibility to keep the Conon River system stocked with fish. Hydro schemes built in the area 60 years ago, and now operated by SSE, destroyed important spawning beds in upriver tributaries, prompting a long-term effort to restore salmon populations. To replace the lost spawning habitat, a hatchery has been operating for about 50 years under the oversight of the Cromarty Firth Fishery Board. Simon McKelvey, who is in charge of the hatchery project, said salmon play a crucial role in healthy river ecosystems and that the facility enables the Conon River to continue supporting the species. “At every stage we are trying to mimic what the salmon would be doing naturally,” he said. The hatchery’s work focuses on replicating the salmon life cycle. Egg-laden female fish are caught in traps and “stripped” of their eggs, which are then artificially fertilised. In February, a high proportion of the fertilised eggs are taken from the hatchery and placed in holes dug into the riverbed, where they are left to incubate in conditions similar to natural spawning sites. Alastair Stephen, a biologist at SSE, said the programme aims to bridge a critical gap created by historic infrastructure. “We are effectively filling in one part of the life cycle. We are trying to minimise the impact we are having on the genetic make-up of the fish stocks,” he said. “We catch as many of the fish as we can in the traps we have and strip the fish, in hopefully as natural a way as possible, before putting the fish back in as eggs or fry.” Mr Stephen added that safeguarding salmon on the Conon River is not only a legal obligation for the company, but a moral responsibility.

A typed letter signed by Muhammad Ali on “Muhammad Ali in South Africa” stationery has been sold at auction in Devizes, Wiltshire. Dated to 1993, the document was offered by Henry Aldridge & Son and purchased by a collector in the United States. The auction house had guided the item at £6,000 to £8,000. Typed by the personal assistant to the general manager of the Elangeni Hotel in Durban—where the former world heavyweight champion stayed during his visit—the letter includes an explanation for why Ali’s name was initially typed incorrectly. The personal assistant, who consigned the piece, detailed the error within the document, adding to its provenance and anecdotal interest. “It’s fair to say Mohammad Ali was the greatest sportsman of all time and Nelson Mandela was one of the greatest figures of the last century,” said auctioneer Andrew Aldridge. He described the letter as a “truly iconic cross collectable,” likely to appeal to collectors of Ali memorabilia as well as those focused on Nelson Mandela, apartheid-era history, political ephemera, and iconic cultural artifacts. Ali’s brief trip to South Africa in April 1993 forms a poignant backdrop to the letter. He arrived shortly after the assassination of Chris Hani on 10 April, a moment that pushed the country to the brink of widespread unrest. Hani, the chief of staff of Umkhonto We Sizwe—the armed wing of the African National Congress—was a fierce opponent of the apartheid regime and was murdered by a far-right extremist outside his home in Boksburg. “Against that backdrop Ali arrived in South Africa at a time when the country stood on the edge of a precipice with civil war a possibility,” Aldridge said. Ali attended Hani’s farewell at FNB Stadium in Johannesburg on 19 April 1993, where crowds greeted him with chants of “Ali! Ali!” Aldridge added that Nelson Mandela kept a photograph of himself with Ali on his desk and, in later years, regarded an autographed copy of Ali’s biography as his favorite book—underscoring the mutual admiration between two of the 20th century’s most resonant figures.

Former RAF pilot Andy Hill has been interviewed under caution by police in connection with the 2015 crash involving a vintage Hawker Hunter jet, according to documents filed by Sussex Police in a High Court application to access investigative material. Hill, 52, was spoken to by officers in December after recovering from critical injuries sustained when his aircraft broke into four pieces and struck people on the A27 during a display on 22 August 2015. Sussex Police confirmed a man had been notified he is under investigation for possible endangerment pursuant to Article 138 of the Air Navigation Order 2009 and manslaughter by gross negligence. As part of its inquiry, the force is seeking permission to review evidence held by the Air Accident Investigation Branch (AAIB), including cockpit recorders from the Hawker Hunter and other footage captured at the time of the accident. Hill was taken to the Royal Sussex County Hospital in Brighton following the crash and placed in a medically induced coma before being transferred to a specialist hospital. BBC Sussex reported in December that the pilot voluntarily attended an appointment at a police station in Hertfordshire, where he was interviewed under caution but not arrested. The pace and communication of the investigation have prompted criticism from local representatives. Tim Loughton, Conservative MP for East Worthing and Shoreham, said the families of those affected had been left waiting too long for answers and should not have learned about the manslaughter inquiry through media reports. “I am most concerned that it has taken so long to get to this point,” he said. “The families need some sort of closure; to find out about this in the press is hugely insensitive and I really feel for them.” Detective Chief Inspector Paul Rymarz, who is leading the investigation, rejected suggestions that families had been kept in the dark. He said it was “completely incorrect” to claim they were informed only via the media. “Throughout, we have kept all of the victims’ families up-to-date with the progress of the investigation as we seek to provide answers as to what happened on that dreadful day,” Rymarz said. “They were advised some months ago of the content of the legal appeal and that the man had been notified in December that he is being investigated for possible endangerment pursuant to Article 138 Air Navigation Order 2009 and also manslaughter by gross negligence.” The High Court bid to access AAIB material forms part of the ongoing effort by Sussex Police to establish a full account of the circumstances surrounding the crash.

Armagh manager Kieran McGeeney has been hit with a minimum 12-week suspension by the GAA’s Central Competitions Control Committee (CCCC) following an incident involving linesman Joe McQuillan. The sanction, arising from a contentious league game, was imposed after the CCCC reviewed referee Niall Cullen’s match report. McGeeney’s initial appeal has been rejected, though he still has two further avenues to contest the decision. As it stands, McGeeney will be barred from patrolling the sideline when Armagh face Down in their Ulster Senior Football Championship opener on 4 June. The ban is also likely to apply to Armagh’s subsequent championship fixture, which will either be an Ulster semi-final or their first All-Ireland qualifier, depending on results. The ill-tempered match in question saw three players sent off: Antrim’s Conor Murray and Stephen Beatty, and Armagh’s Stephen Sheridan. Murray has received a two-game suspension for his red card, while a further investigation into the game led to an additional ban for Antrim’s Matt Fitzpatrick. McGeeney, who captained Armagh to All-Ireland glory in 2002, is believed to have breached GAA regulations forbidding minor physical interference, threatening or abusive conduct, or the use of threatening language towards match officials, including referees, umpires, linesmen, or sideline officials. Such violations carry a minimum penalty of 12 weeks. Armagh defeated Antrim at the Athletic Grounds on 25 March, but their push for promotion to Division Two ended in heartbreak after a last-gasp defeat to Tipperary. The suspension adds further uncertainty to Armagh’s championship campaign as the county awaits the outcome of McGeeney’s remaining appeals.

Mystery Piglet Found Nestled in Mustang Stable in Suffolk A mystery piglet discovered nestled among straw used by mustangs has left a Suffolk stable owner baffled as to how it arrived there. Martine Lettau, who runs stables in Tuddenham St Mary, said she found the tiny animal “rustling and squeaking” in a stable on Monday morning, with no sign of its mother nearby. “Mustangs are quite renowned for seeing off predators,” Ms Lettau said, suggesting the foals may have played a role in the piglet’s unlikely rescue. “The only thing I can imagine is that a fox carried the piglet off when it was born, carried it over a mile here and happened to come through the paddock. The foals might have then chased the fox off and the piglet got herded into the stable.” She added that when the piglet squealed, several mustangs approached from the paddock. “They came over to see what I was doing to it, so they must have taken ownership,” she said. Ms Lettau took the piglet to a neighbouring pig farm in the Mildenhall area. The farm’s manager, who did not wish to be identified, said the animal was only a day old and had been placed with a sow to begin weaning. However, he expressed doubt over the fox abduction theory. “I think it would be highly unlikely for a fox to carry a piglet for a mile, let alone for it to have no mark or injury as a result,” he said. “If the piglet’s temperature dropped by even a couple of degrees it would not have survived.” While the piglet’s origins remain unclear, both the stables and the farm say the animal is now warm, feeding, and appears to be in good health. An appeal for local information has not yet yielded any leads on where it was born.

In a statement, club employees say they are “hugely concerned” by the “lack of communication” from the O’s hierarchy as Leyton Orient face a critical week on and off the pitch. Bottom of League Two, the East London side could see their 112-year Football League stay end with relegation on Saturday, compounding financial uncertainty and mounting operational strain. Staff have appealed to the club’s directors to “communicate the situation and provide us with an update regarding our pay,” noting that a formal grievance was lodged in line with internal policies but “to this date it remains unacknowledged with no indication as to when, or if, we are to be paid.” Employees are due their April wages in nine days’ time. Orient were recently the subject of a winding-up petition from HM Revenue & Customs over unpaid taxes. While those debts have now been settled, the club still owes money to four other creditors. The club also avoided an immediate winding-up order last month, with owner Francesco Becchetti granted until 12 June to clear outstanding liabilities or sell the club. “With debts continuing to mount and us as staff not being paid our contractual wage, it raises questions as to whether the directors are on course to meet this arrangement,” the statement continued. Despite the uncertainty, staff say they have maintained their duties, “rallying behind the team in their bid to preserve Leyton Orient’s proud English Football League association.” The situation underscores deepening concerns about governance and financial stability at Brisbane Road, with staff and supporters seeking clarity as the season’s final fixtures approach and the club’s future hangs in the balance.

Tony Pulis says West Bromwich Albion are pushing to add reinforcements before the transfer window closes at 23:00 GMT on Tuesday, but a tight market and budget constraints make deals difficult. The Baggies have already signed midfielder Jake Livermore from Hull City in a £10m move, and Pulis admitted he has missed out on several targets, with players choosing rivals such as West Ham and Everton. “There is such a small pool that we are fishing in..... We’re moving forward, but it will take time. We have a budget and we’ve got to make sure the players are right. We’re desperate to bring players in,” he said. West Brom sit eighth in the Premier League but were knocked out of the FA Cup by Championship side Derby County. The club sold striker Saido Berahino to Stoke City for £12m earlier this month. Albion visit Middlesbrough on Tuesday night (19:45 GMT) as the deadline approaches.

Justin Gatlin was booed by sections of the crowd at London Stadium before and after winning the men’s 100m at the World Championships, and again during the medal presentation, as the American sprinter’s controversial past resurfaced amid his return to the pinnacle of the sport. Gatlin, 35, clocked 9.92 seconds to edge compatriot Christian Coleman, with Jamaican icon Usain Bolt finishing third in what was the final individual 100m race of his storied career before retirement. Bolt, 30, was unable to secure a 20th global gold, adding to the poignancy and tension of the evening. Gatlin’s victory drew a mixed response from the athletics community, with International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) president Lord Sebastian Coe saying the result was “not the perfect script” for the sport. “I’m not eulogistic that someone who has served two bans has walked off with one of our glittering prizes,” Coe told BBC Radio 5 live’s Sportsweek, underscoring longstanding concerns about doping and the message such comebacks send to fans and athletes. Gatlin’s father, Willie, defended his son’s character and perseverance, saying he was not “upset” by the jeers. “I know what kind of son I raised, what kind of character he has,” he said. “He served his ban and he worked his heart out doing what he could. He worked to come back, and he worked his way back to championship form.” He added that booing was “disrespectful to the sport,” arguing that Gatlin’s performance created “a memory that is going to be in people’s minds a long time.” Gatlin’s history with doping is well documented. In 2001, while still in college, he received a two-year suspension for a banned amphetamine, which he successfully argued was due to prescribed medication for attention deficit disorder; he was allowed to return to competition after one year. In 2006, following his 100m and 200m double at the 2005 World Championships in Helsinki, he tested positive for testosterone. He accepted an eight-year ban that avoided a potential lifetime sanction in exchange for cooperation with anti-doping authorities; the suspension was later reduced to four years on appeal. Willie Gatlin said his son is focused on mentoring the next generation. “For the youngsters coming up, he is trying to help to tutor and help to be good, clean athletes,” he said. “He is trying to teach good character and good sportsmanship. I don’t think he has regrets; it is a lesson learned.” Toni Minichiello, former coach of Britain’s Olympic heptathlon champion Jessica Ennis-Hill, said fans have the right to express their views but stressed that the sport’s governance should also be scrutinized. “It’s not his fault in any way, shape or form,” Minichiello said. “It’s the fault of the federations and WADA [the World Anti-Doping Agency] for putting the rules down in such a way that allows him to return. Really, if you want to boo somebody, boo WADA, boo the federations.” Gatlin’s win closes a chapter in the 100m as Bolt bows out, and it reignites debate over redemption, regulation, and how athletics balances second chances with its quest for credibility.

Lynch rescues point for Huddersfield as dominant hosts held by Birmingham Huddersfield Town were left to rue missed chances after a dominant display at the John Smith’s Stadium yielded only a 1-1 draw with Birmingham City. The hosts racked up 18 shots, enjoyed 65% possession and forced 15 corners to Birmingham’s two, yet needed a late equaliser from defender Lynch to cancel out David Cotterill’s superb free-kick. City goalkeeper Tomas Kuszczak was outstanding, setting the tone early by brilliantly clawing away an Emyr Huws header and later denying Karim Matmour’s overhead kick in stoppage time. Buoyed by a 2-0 win at Blackburn last week and a midweek draw at Rotherham, Huddersfield started brightly, with Nahki Wells dragging an effort wide. Birmingham captain Michael Morrison almost diverted into his own net, and Joe Lolley went close before Cotterill struck. The Wales international, who scored the only goal in this fixture last season with another expertly-struck set-piece, put the visitors ahead from 25 yards, his curling effort beyond the reach of a helpless Joel Coleman and appearing to have settled the contest. But Huddersfield’s pressure eventually told. With around 10 to 15 minutes remaining, Lynch took control of a loose, wayward effort in the area, prodding home his second goal of the season to earn a deserved point for David Wagner’s side. Town could have snatched victory late on. Wells was inches from turning in a teasing cross, while Matmour’s acrobatic attempt drew a sensational save from Kuszczak, epitomising the Polish custodian’s excellence on a night where Birmingham had to dig deep. Despite the performance, Huddersfield’s end-of-season form remains patchy, with just three wins in their last 11 matches. Sitting 16th in the Championship, their status is secure, but Wagner lamented his side’s wastefulness. “We had problems with our finishing and we need to do better,” he said. “Our shots were not good enough and a lot were blocked or went wide. We did not make their goalkeeper work hard enough. I am disappointed with the result but when you come back with 10 or 15 minutes left you can be satisfied. In the last 10 or 15 minutes everybody can see our fitness was good and we were stronger than our opponent. We have shown a good fighting attitude.” Birmingham, ninth and in the top 10 all season, again let an advantage slip after squandering a two-goal lead to Preston in midweek—a lapse that prompted manager Gary Rowett to be “pretty tough” on his players for a “lack of desire.” Assistant manager Kevin Summerfield reflected: “It was a game where we needed to dig in and we looked to play on the counter attack but we did not have enough legs or quality. It was a set-piece that opened the door for us and Cotterill produced a great free-kick but that’s what he does. We still have an awful lot to play for and we want to win games.”

Sunderland have completed the signing of France-born defender Lamine Koné on a four-and-a-half-year deal, bolstering Sam Allardyce’s defence. The 26-year-old arrives after a pursuit that appeared to collapse on 8 January, when Allardyce said negotiations had broken down. “He is big and strong, attributes you need to play in central defence in the Premier League,” the Sunderland manager told the club’s website. “Strengthening our defensive options was a priority for us and Lamine is a player that has impressed me when I’ve seen him play. His arrival will give us competition for places in a key position.” Koné becomes the Black Cats’ fourth January addition, following goalkeeper Steve Harper, striker Dame N’Doye and defender Jan Kirchhoff. Sunderland sit 19th in the Premier League, four points from safety with 15 matches remaining, as they attempt to secure top-flight survival. Allardyce’s side host second-placed Manchester City in their next league fixture on 2 February.

Sam Allardyce says Crystal Palace’s Premier League survival has helped draw a line under the turmoil that ended his brief spell as England manager. The 62-year-old began the season in charge of the national team, but his reign lasted just 67 days after a newspaper sting in which he appeared to offer advice on how to “get around” player transfer rules. He took over at Palace in December and has since guided the club away from relegation. “It's been great being back in football,” Allardyce said. “I've worked hard with the backroom and support staff and the owners, and we've pulled it together in a short time. That puts the past in the past. I look to the future, because you can't affect the past.” Palace’s turnaround followed a rocky start under Allardyce. By mid-February, a little over six weeks into his tenure at Selhurst Park, the side sat 19th after back-to-back defeats: 4-0 at home to Sunderland and 1-0 at Stoke. Four straight wins, including a 2-1 triumph at Chelsea, propelled them clear of trouble, and their top-flight status was sealed with last weekend’s emphatic 4-0 victory over Hull City. The resurgence lifted Palace well clear of the drop zone.

The luge, which translates as'sled', sees competitors travelling feet-first down an icy track at up to 85mph — with only a helmet for protection. The high-speed winter sport marries nerve with finesse as athletes lie supine on a streamlined pod and navigate twisting, banked ice tracks by the smallest of movements. The luge sled is a moulded fibreglass pod shaped to the rider’s contours. It sits atop two metal runners, known as steels, which curve upward at the tips and connect to front-mounted “kufens” used to steer. Doubles sleds feature longer steels and kufens to accommodate two athletes. There are no brakes. To scrub speed, a slider must drag their feet along the ice while applying subtle pressure to the kufens — a skill that requires both precision and poise. Despite its intimidating image, luge offers a host of physical benefits. The confined cockpit rewards fine motor control, building agility, balance and coordination through minute weight shifts. As speeds rise and G-forces build, strength and conditioning become essential to withstand the demands of the sport. For aspiring British sliders, a first step now exists closer to home. Manchester’s Chill Factor-e hosts a dedicated 60-metre luge facility, far removed from the Olympic experience but ideal for beginners to sample the sensation. Progression beyond that introduction, however, generally means travelling abroad to access full-length tracks and coaching. Britain’s most recent Olympic luger, AJ Rosen, was born in the United States and continues to train there. Luge traces its roots to early sledding contests in Scandinavia and the birth of skeleton and bobsleigh in Switzerland, particularly around St Moritz. According to Team GB, an Australian student, George Robertson, won what is reputed to be the world’s first international sled race in 1883 on a four-kilometre stretch of Swiss road, signalling the sport’s competitive potential. The sport made its Olympic debut in 1964, when East Germany’s Thomas Kohler claimed the first gold medal. While equipment and venues have evolved, the Olympic programme has remained largely unchanged, and modern luge now runs on the same courses as bobsleigh. Inspired to give luge a try, or already a keen enthusiast? Share your experience by tweeting @bbcgetinspired or emailing getinspired@bbc.co.uk. For more ideas, explore our full list of activity guides.

Neil Lennon made a low-key return to Windsor Park on Thursday, attending Northern Ireland’s international friendly against Norway—his first visit to the ground since quitting international football. Lennon, who was booed by home fans in one of his final appearances there in 2001, said those days were behind him. “Those days are long gone,” he noted. “It’s completely incidental now. I haven’t actually been here at Windsor Park but I’ve done my coaching badges through the IFA. And I’ve been in Belfast the last consecutive years three or four times, on really good courses. I’ve learned a lot, which has stood me in good stead for what I’m doing now.” The Lurgan native attended to watch Northern Ireland’s Celtic contingent, Pat McCourt and Niall McGinn, as well as Celtic’s Norwegian defender Thomas Rogne. Norway defeated Northern Ireland 3-0. Lennon’s presence underscored improving relations and his ongoing professional ties with the Irish Football Association.

A Daf lorry in a convoy bound for the Brockloch wind farm at Carsphairn left the roadway at about 22:45 on Monday on the A713 Castle Douglas to Ayr road, just north of Parton. No injuries were reported, but the route is expected to remain closed for a considerable time. Police Scotland said heavy lifting equipment is required to recover the vehicle and its load. Insp Campbell Moffat confirmed the road is “fully closed at present” and will stay shut until recovery is complete. A full diversion has been implemented around the scene, and motorists are urged to avoid the area where possible. An investigation into the circumstances is under way.

The US-backed coalition of mostly Arab states began air strikes a year ago in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government. A Saudi military spokesman said that the coalition would continue to provide air support to Yemeni forces. The announcement came as the death toll from a strike on a market this week doubled to more than 100. Witnesses said at least two missiles hit the busy market in the Mustaba district of Hajja province, north of the capital Sanaa, an area controlled by the Shia Houthi rebels. Video footage purportedly of the aftermath of the strike showed what appeared to be the bodies of several children. A UN official said 22 children were among those killed. In January, a UN panel found that coalition air strikes had targeted civilians in Yemen and assessed that some attacks might constitute crimes against humanity. The Houthi rebels are fighting forces loyal to exiled President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. The fighting has killed more than 6,200 civilians, displaced millions and pushed the Arab world's poorest country to the brink of famine. Practising medicine under fire in Yemen A young girl and a city struggling for life Yemen crisis: Who is fighting whom? Saudi military spokesman Brigadier General Ahmed al-Asiri told the Associated Press that the coalition would continue to provide air support to Yemeni forces battling the Houthis. "The aim of the coalition is to create a strong cohesive government with a strong national army and security forces that can combat terrorism and impose law and order across the country," Mr al-Asiri said. Only "small" teams of coalition troops would remain on the ground to "equip, train, and advise" Yemeni forces, which are gradually replacing coalition forces, he said. The attack on the market in Hajja province was the second deadliest in Yemen since the Saudi-led air strikes began, after an air strike hit a wedding party in September, killing at least 131 people. Mr Al-Asiri said the coalition was investigating the attack, arguing that Tuesday's airstrikes targeted a "gathering area" for Houthi fighters, located about 10km (6 miles) away from the market. UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon condemned the strike. He said: "Attacks directed against civilians and civilian objects, including populated markets, are strictly prohibited." On Wednesday, Jamie McGoldrick, the UN's humanitarian chief in Yemen, said none of the warring parties in Yemen were fulfilling their obligations to protect civilians or facilitate humanitarian assistance. The war has left Yemen fragmented and facing a humanitarian crisis. Militants from the so-called Islamic State group have also taken advantage of the chaos to wage a series of deadly attacks across the country.

Leeds Rhinos delivered a blistering second-half performance to overwhelm Catalans Dragons in West Yorkshire, lifting the mood around Headingley after a chastening derby defeat to Castleford and silencing talk of upheaval. The hosts led 14-4 at the interval courtesy of tries from Adam Cuthbertson and Matt Parcell, with Brayden Wiliame replying for the visitors. After the break it became one-way traffic as Leeds’ attack caught fire, piling on further scores through Jimmy Keinhorst, Cuthbertson again, Rob Burrow, Danny McGuire and Liam Sutcliffe. Julian Bousquet’s late effort was little more than consolation on a night when Catalans were second-best in every department. Parcell was the catalyst throughout, his sharp darts from dummy-half repeatedly shredding the Dragons’ ruck defence and creating quick-ball situations that Leeds exploited with ruthless efficiency. Even the disruption of two sin-binnings for Leeds—Cuthbertson and Keinhorst both spending time in the bin—failed to stem the flow; at one stage down to 11 men, the Rhinos still found ways to maintain momentum and pressure. The emphatic win arrives at a delicate moment for the club. A heavy loss to local rivals Castleford in their previous outing prompted chief executive Gary Hetherington to write to supporters, acknowledging that a coaching change could not be ruled out if standards remained below expectations. Against Catalans, however, Brian McDermott’s side showed the ambition and fluency he has long urged, snapping a three-game losing streak against the Perpignan outfit and reigniting belief within the camp. Catalans entered the contest with a solid recent defensive record, having conceded just 40 points across their past three games, but they were torched by Leeds’ variety and pace.
