To compound their troubles, winger Jodie Broughton departed injured, and the Dragons struggled to regain composure during the Rhinos’ purple patches. McDermott, buoyed by the response, said he believes his team can win the Grand Final, adding that the group handled a “really difficult night” with resolve and unity, even when severely outnumbered. He praised the willingness to back a more expressive attacking philosophy, acknowledging that Leeds’ risk-taking approach can occasionally misfire but insisting that, on nights like this, it shows its worth. The coach also noted he has been a harsh critic of the offense this year, and that the display marked a welcome shift toward the standards the squad sets internally. Catalans head coach Laurent Frayssinous did not hide his frustration, pointing to his side’s attitude as the root cause of the defeat. He said Leeds simply wanted it more across the park and hinted the warning signs were present defensively during the first half. Referee James Child oversaw proceedings, with Leeds’ senior trio of McGuire, Burrow and Sutcliffe among several standouts in a morale-boosting win that resets the Rhinos’ trajectory.

Four fire engines and a command support unit were dispatched to a blaze at Technotots Nursery on the Wester Gourdie Industrial Estate at 06:30. Firefighters in breathing apparatus used hose reels to bring the fire under control within an hour. Crews remained on scene to ventilate the building and damp down. Police assisted at the incident and urged motorists to avoid the area.

After a two-year upgrade, CERN’s Large Hadron Collider is restarting, promising higher-energy proton collisions to probe fundamental physics. The 16-mile-long accelerator, buried 100 metres underground on the French-Swiss border, previously enabled the discovery of the Higgs boson. Scientists now aim to illuminate mysteries such as dark matter and the nature of the early universe. Teams have completed extensive safety checks, reactivated detectors including ATLAS and CMS, and begun circulating first beams. Full-power collisions are expected soon, possibly this spring, launching a new phase for the world’s biggest scientific experiment.

UK house price growth accelerates to 6.5% as mortgage approvals hit five-year high UK house prices are rising at an annual rate of 6.5%, up from 5.8% a month earlier, according to Nationwide Building Society, which said the average home now costs £174,566—the highest level since April 2008. On a monthly basis, prices rose by 0.6% in November, easing from a sharp 1% gain in October. Despite the recent acceleration, Nationwide stressed that values remain below their pre-crisis peak. “Prices are still around 6% below the all-time high recorded in late 2007,” said Robert Gardner, Nationwide’s chief economist. He attributed the improvement to a better outlook in the jobs market and “a brighter economic outlook, which has helped to bolster sentiment.” Separate Bank of England data underscored the momentum in housing activity, showing mortgage approvals climbed to 67,701 in October, up from 66,891 in September and the highest tally since February 2008. Even so, approvals remain well below pre-crisis norms, when more than 90,000 mortgages were typically arranged each month. While Nationwide’s figures point to brisk gains, other measures suggest more moderate growth. The Land Registry reported annual price inflation of 3.4% in England and Wales this week, while the Office for National Statistics estimated a 3.8% rise. Methodological differences help explain the gap: Nationwide’s index is based largely on mortgage approvals, capturing market shifts earlier, whereas the Land Registry reflects completed sales and is subject to a time lag. The outlook for 2014 is complicated by changes to the Bank of England’s Funding for Lending Scheme (FLS). From January, the FLS will be focused on business lending and no longer support household mortgages, prompting debate over whether the housing market will cool. Some economists warn the shift could act as a brake by nudging up borrowing costs and tempering demand. Others argue the impact will be limited. “House prices look set to see further strong increases over the coming months despite the Bank of England ending Funding for Lending support for mortgage lending,” said Howard Archer, chief UK economist at IHS Global Insight, who maintains his forecast for an 8% rise in house prices next year. Nationwide’s Gardner also expects only a “fairly modest impact” from the FLS change, noting that the scheme is just one factor behind historically low mortgage rates. He cited the Bank’s quantitative easing policy as instrumental in keeping funding costs down, a process that will continue. Introduced to stimulate credit, the FLS has allowed banks and building societies to borrow cheaply provided they lend to households and businesses. Its refocusing toward corporate credit aims to channel support to the real economy while addressing concerns about overheating in parts of the housing market.

People were paying 89p more for a 750ml bottle of water and £1.50 more for an A4 refill pad at one hospital in Wakefield than at a store in Leeds. Following pressure from Dewsbury MP Paula Sherriff, WH Smith has pledged to bring its hospital store prices into line with those on the high street, after evidence showed patients and visitors in Wakefield were paying significantly more for everyday items. The discrepancy — including a 750ml bottle of water costing 89p more and an A4 refill pad priced £1.50 higher than at a Leeds branch — prompted Sherriff to call the practice “fundamentally wrong” and demand immediate changes. After meeting the Labour MP, the retailer said it would match stationery prices and cut food and drink costs in hospital outlets. “We had a productive meeting with Paula Sherriff MP and showed that most products are the same price in our hospital and high street stores,” a spokesman said. “We will ensure High Street stationery promotions are available in hospital stores and monitor average selling prices to keep them aligned.” Sherriff welcomed the commitment, calling it “a better deal for patients.” She said the company had agreed to set up a monitoring process so prices are “constantly checked” and kept within a 1–2% difference between hospital and high street outlets. The issue of hospital pricing gained attention in August when a BBC investigation found Marks & Spencer charging different prices in hospital and high street stores. M&S said hospital prices “could be a little higher” due to longer opening hours and the convenience of on-site locations. Sherriff said she hoped M&S would now “offer something similar” to WH Smith’s approach. Retail expert Clare Rayner said WH Smith’s move “sets a precedent” and warned that if other retailers fail to follow, they risk being seen to exploit a captive audience. The BBC inquiry was conducted by BBC Radio Leeds reporter Liam Smedley.

Mattel is unveiling a revamped lineup of Ken dolls featuring a broader range of skin tones and contemporary hairstyles — including a man bun and cornrows — in a move that continues the company’s push to modernize its iconic Barbie brand. The update follows an earlier expansion of the Barbie range at the start of 2016, a period when Barbie sales fell 13% in the first quarter, marking a second consecutive quarter of declines for the doll franchise. “By continuing to expand our product line, we are redefining what a Barbie or Ken doll looks like to this generation,” said Lisa McKnight, general manager of Barbie. “Evolving Ken was a natural evolution for the brand and allows girls to further personalise the role they want him to play in Barbie’s world.” Mattel, one of the world’s largest toy companies, underscored that Barbie “has always reflected the times,” and described modernising Ken as the next step in delivering more diverse products to consumers. The strategy appears to be gaining traction. Barbie sales rose across the first nine months of 2016, buoyed by refreshed marketing and new doll launches. The updated Ken dolls will be available through various national retailers in the UK, offering shoppers expanded choices that align with the brand’s broader focus on inclusivity and contemporary style. Ken, full name Ken Carson, was introduced in 1961 as Barbie’s boyfriend. According to the dolls’ fictional backstory, the pair met on the set of their first television commercial in 1961, with Ken traditionally standing half an inch taller than Barbie. Early versions of Ken featured molded plastic hair in blond or brown and were sold wearing red swimming trunks and cork sandals. Over the decades, Ken has been marketed in roughly 40 occupations and has modelled numerous fashions, including 1993’s much-discussed Magic Earring Ken. Mattel’s marketing has occasionally played up the duo’s relationship: Ken and Barbie “broke up” on Valentine’s Day 2004 before reuniting on Valentine’s Day 2011. They have never officially married, a Mattel spokeswoman noted, though “dream wedding” sets have been sold. She added that the messaging remains kid-focused rather than overly romantic and declined to disclose the company’s spending on market research and manufacturing for the new Ken range.

Hyundai Motor Group has elevated German designer Peter Schreyer to president of Kia, making him the brand’s first foreign chief as the group moves to unify and strengthen its global design strategy. Schreyer, appointed three weeks ago, will streamline the design operation and deepen synergies between Hyundai and Kia, aiming to sharpen brand identities and shorten development cycles. Woong-Chul Yang, Hyundai’s vice chairman, called the move “imperative to secure long-term competitiveness” and to “enhance our brand value.” He added that Schreyer “brings a wealth of experience in design from the global auto industry and has a deep understanding of the Hyundai Motor Group,” qualities he said would help position Hyundai and Kia as leading global automakers. Schreyer spent a decade at Volkswagen Group, serving as head of design at both Audi and Volkswagen, and is widely credited with elevating Audi’s modern design language. Kia, acquired by Hyundai in 1998 during the Asian financial crisis, has been expanding faster than Hyundai in the US and Europe. Together, Hyundai-Kia sold 7.12 million vehicles worldwide last year, up 8% from 2011.

The attack in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province is the first to be claimed by the Saudi branch of IS, which was formally established last November. The claim was posted on Twitter with an image of the bomber by an account that is a reliable source on the group. IS has previously threatened to attack Shia Muslims in Saudi Arabia. A powerful blast ripped through the Imam Ali mosque in the village of al-Qadeeh, in Qatif governorate, during Friday prayers, killing at least 21 people and injuring more than 80, Saudi officials said. Witnesses described a huge explosion as worshippers gathered for the weekly service, sending shattered glass and debris across the prayer hall and leaving many victims lying wounded as others scrambled for safety. Saudi Health Minister Khalid al-Falih told state television that the death toll stood at 21, with more than 80 people receiving treatment for injuries of varying severity. A doctor at a nearby hospital said some of the wounded were in critical condition and undergoing emergency procedures as medical teams worked through the afternoon. The Saudi interior ministry said the attacker detonated a suicide belt inside the mosque. “Security authorities will spare no effort in the pursuit of all those involved in this terrorist crime,” a spokesman said in a statement carried by the state news agency SPA. Authorities cordoned off the area and launched an immediate investigation, while additional security units were deployed across the Eastern Province to reassure residents and prevent further incidents. The Islamic State group quickly claimed responsibility, saying “the soldiers of the Caliphate” carried out the attack and vowing “dark days ahead” for Saudi Arabia’s Shia community. The group identified the bomber as Abu Amer al-Najdi and circulated an image of him on social media. In a separate online statement, IS said it was behind a similar attack on a Shia mosque in neighboring Yemen on Friday that injured about a dozen people. The bombing marks the first attack publicly claimed by the Saudi branch of IS since it announced its formal establishment last November. The group, which espouses an extreme Sunni ideology, has repeatedly threatened Saudi Arabia and has urged its followers to target Shia Muslims. In November, an audio recording purportedly from IS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi called on supporters inside the kingdom to strike Shia sites. Saudi officials say more than 2,000 Saudis are believed to have joined IS in Syria and Iraq, with hundreds having returned home. In recent months, security forces have mounted a broad crackdown, arresting hundreds of suspects linked to extremist cells, and warning of plots aimed at destabilizing the kingdom. Saudi Arabia’s Shia minority, largely concentrated in the Eastern Province, has long sought greater rights and protections. Community leaders and activists have voiced concern about inflammatory rhetoric from hardline Sunni clerics who label Shias as “not real Muslims,” sentiments mirrored in IS propaganda. Friday’s attack is likely to heighten sectarian tensions and deepen fears among Shia residents about their safety. The bombing comes as Saudi Arabia leads a coalition of Arab states in an air campaign against Shia Houthi rebels in Yemen, a conflict that has sharpened regional sectarian divides. As investigations continue, Saudi authorities have pledged to strengthen security around places of worship and bring those responsible for the al-Qadeeh attack to justice.

Aleppo offensive intensifies as IS battles rebels near Turkish border, displacing 30,000; peace talks resume in Geneva Syrian government forces, backed by Russian troops and allied militias, intensified their assault on rebel-held districts of Aleppo on Thursday, targeting vital supply lines and key routes out of the opposition-controlled areas. Activist networks reported heavy bombardment from warplanes, helicopter gunships, and artillery across the city, with the fiercest clashes unfolding to the north of Aleppo along a strategic corridor that has been central to the rebels’ logistics. The push on Aleppo, which has entered its third week, is backed by Russian air strikes, personnel from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, and fighters from Lebanon’s Hezbollah movement. The coordinated offensive has tightened pressure on opposition factions as international diplomats reconvene in Geneva for UN-backed peace talks aimed at advancing a political transition after years of war. Further north, the self-styled Islamic State group sought to regain momentum by seizing several villages near the Turkish border. The renewed fighting has driven a surge of displacement, with Human Rights Watch estimating that at least 30,000 people fled their homes in a 48-hour period. The rights group accused Turkish border guards of opening fire on those attempting to cross into Turkey to seek safety and urged Ankara to allow civilians to enter. It described families forced to dig ditches to hide from IS militants and other armed groups as frontline lines shifted. The spike in violence has alarmed international stakeholders who helped broker a nationwide cessation of hostilities that took effect on 27 February. A senior US administration official warned that all parties must uphold their commitments “to refrain from any further destabilising actions,” while European Union foreign policy chief Federica Mogherini called for the “respect, consolidation, and expansion” of the fragile truce. Russian President Vladimir Putin, a key ally of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, said he was closely monitoring developments around Aleppo and expressed hope that the Geneva talks would produce a new constitution and pave the way for early elections. The Syrian government delegation is due to arrive in Geneva on Friday, maintaining that Assad’s fate is non-negotiable, a stance that dimmed prospects for compromise. Earlier, the main Syrian opposition group signaled readiness to negotiate with government figures not implicated in killings, but ruled out any talks with Assad himself. UN special envoy Staffan de Mistura, mediating the Geneva process, urged both sides to take concrete steps toward a political transition, referencing a December UN Security Council resolution that envisions the formation of a transitional government, drafting of a new constitution, and elections. He emphasized the imperative of extending the cessation of hostilities and ensuring humanitarian aid reaches all parts of the country. As the Geneva talks resume, the escalating battles in and around Aleppo and the mass displacement near the Turkish border underscore the fragile reality on the ground, threatening to overshadow diplomatic efforts and further complicate the path to a negotiated peace.

Asos sales jump 30% in four months to June; shares hit two-year high on upbeat outlook Online fashion retailer Asos reported a 30% surge in sales for the four months to June, lifting its shares 3.7% to a two-year high after issuing a bullish trading update. Chief executive Nick Beighton said the company now expects full-year sales growth at the upper end of its guided 20-25% range and expressed confidence in hitting pre-tax profit targets. Beighton added that the recent slide in sterling following the UK’s vote to leave the European Union should deliver a medium-term benefit, making UK-based retailers more competitive in overseas markets. The pound has fallen to around $1.30 from nearly $1.50 before the 23 June vote. Total sales reached £500.5 million for the period, up from £386 million a year earlier, as the number of active customers rose 24% to 12 million. Growth was broad-based, with UK sales up 28% to £203 million and international sales rising 31% to £297 million, underscoring the brand’s strong appeal across markets. Asos also confirmed the closure of its Chinese business, first announced in April, a move it said will free up £2 million for investment elsewhere and remove a drag on earnings. Founded in 2000, Asos was an early pioneer in online fashion retailing but has faced intensifying competition from High Street chains expanding online, as well as domestic and European e-commerce rivals. The latest figures, however, suggest the company’s strategy and global reach continue to gain traction despite a challenging retail landscape.

The rebel al-Nusra Front said the man conducted the bombing on their behalf. It was one of four attacks carried out in the northern city of Idlib that day. It is thought to be the first suicide attack by a US citizen in the conflict. A US citizen is believed to have carried out a suicide bombing in Syria’s Idlib, the al-Nusra Front claimed, marking what is thought to be the first such attack by an American in the country’s civil war. The militant Islamist group, which has pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda, said the attacker drove a truck packed with explosives as part of four coordinated strikes in the northern city on Sunday. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said dozens of Syrian government soldiers were killed in the bombings, according to AFP. US State Department spokeswoman Jen Psaki confirmed a US national was involved, adding that the individual was believed to be Moner Mohammad Abu-Salha. Psaki said Washington remains concerned about the movement of foreign fighters in and out of Syria. The Quilliam Foundation has been cited as a source in identifying the bomber. Syria’s conflict, which erupted in 2011, has devastated entire neighborhoods and displaced civilians on a massive scale. More than 100,000 people have been killed, and nearly three million have fled the country amid the battle between forces loyal to President Bashar al-Assad and armed groups seeking his ouster.

Burns will face Michele di Rocco for the vacant WBA light-welterweight belt in Glasgow on 28 May. Former two-weight world champion Ricky Burns will bid to make Scottish boxing history when he meets Italy’s Michele di Rocco for the vacant WBA light-welterweight title at the SSE Hydro in Glasgow on 28 May. Burns’ manager, Morrison, says victory would elevate the Coatbridge fighter into the company of the nation’s greats. “You’re talking about Ken Buchanan, Jim Watt and Walter McGowan,” he said. “For Ricky to win at three different weights would put him up there with them – true greats.” Burns first announced himself on the world stage in 2010, dethroning Puerto Rican Roman Martinez to claim the WBO super-featherweight crown. A year later he captured the interim WBO lightweight title by defeating Australia’s Michael Katsidis, beginning a run that would include four successful defences. His momentum stalled in March 2014 when he lost his belt to American Terence Crawford, but the 32-year-old—who turns 33 next month—now has an opportunity to reach the summit again. “He wants to show the world how good he is,” Morrison added. “He’s hungry for a third world title. The move to super lightweight was the only option to get him a shot, but he’s shown in the past how versatile he is in making weights, so I think it’s good for him.” Home advantage could prove crucial against Di Rocco, who is unbeaten in nearly nine years. “Ricky loves fighting in front of his own fans,” said Morrison. “The noise and atmosphere really lift him. Di Rocco is a good fighter, but he’ll be up against the crowd and an inspired Ricky Burns.”

Vettel tests latest halo at British GP, urges “further running” as Horner warns against rushing 2017 rollout Sebastian Vettel trialled the latest version of Formula 1’s proposed halo head-protection device during Friday practice at the British Grand Prix, offering cautious feedback as debate intensifies over its planned introduction in 2017. While the FIA is pushing to bring the halo in next season, formal approval is still pending and several leading figures, including Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, have questioned the timing and design. FIA F1 director Charlie Whiting has told teams in technical meetings to expect the halo to be mandated in 2017, prompting constructors to design their new cars to accommodate it. However, the device must clear a three-stage approval pathway: first through the strategy group comprising leading teams, the FIA and F1 commercial boss Bernie Ecclestone; then the F1 Commission, which includes all teams, sponsors, circuits, tyre suppliers, plus the FIA and Ecclestone; and finally the FIA World Council. Sources have told BBC Sport that, alongside Horner, Ecclestone, Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff and Williams deputy team principal Claire Williams harbour reservations about the halo, which is intended to protect drivers from impacts with large flying objects. Horner said: “I am not a big fan of the halo and the limitations it has. It is an inelegant solution to the problem it is trying to deal with. I would prefer there to be more research time taken to do the job properly rather than rushing something through that may have other consequences. I certainly wouldn’t vote in favour of it.” Vettel, a director of the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association, which broadly supports increased head protection and wants a solution deployed as soon as possible, ran the device for a single lap and reported mixed impressions. “Forward visibility was fine,” the four-time world champion said. “But it was quite a bit on top of you, (even if) you are not looking at the sky all the time. It needs some further running. I know the decision is up fairly soon. I don’t know what the results are on the actual research. It is clear what it is made for and what it is supposed to do, but we just need to make sure we introduce something safer in all circumstances and we don’t have any compromises.” The FIA has promised teams a decision on the halo by the end of July, underscoring the urgency as 2017 car designs progress. Red Bull had proposed an alternative concept, the “aeroscreen,” but it failed FIA tests, including an assessment that fires a wheel at the device at 250km/h (155mph). Following the setback, Red Bull has halted aeroscreen development to focus resources on its 2017 challenger, with major regulation changes set to bring wider cars and target lap time reductions of about four seconds. As the approval process unfolds, teams must balance safety ambitions with operational and aesthetic concerns, leaving the sport poised for a pivotal decision on the future of cockpit protection.

Parents in Britain are spending more time reading with their children than in previous years, but stress and tiredness remain significant barriers, according to a new poll commissioned by the publisher Pearson and the reading charity Booktrust. The survey, conducted by pollsters Opinion Matters, found that parents devoted an average of one hour and 26 minutes a week to reading with their children in 2011, up from one hour and 18 minutes in 2009. For most families, shared reading is a cherished routine: 71% of parents said reading with their child is one of the highlights of their day. Yet the study also revealed that many struggle to keep the habit going. Eighteen percent of the more than 1,000 parents surveyed reported feeling too stressed to read together, and tiredness emerged as a common obstacle. Two-fifths (41%) said a child’s fatigue often undermined the enjoyment of reading time, while 30% cited their own tiredness as a problem. More than a third (36%) said they were too tired to spend longer reading. Despite these difficulties, daily reading appears to be robust, particularly among families with younger children. Sixty percent of parents and carers of children aged four to six reported reading daily for fun, averaging 46 books per child per year. Just over half (51%) said they also read daily for school or educational purposes. The importance of being read to in childhood also resonated strongly: 64% of parents described it as a treasured memory from their own early years. The poll suggests that daily reading rates may have increased across generations. Only 23% of today’s parents reported being read to daily as children, compared with 60% who say they now read for pleasure with their own child every day. Traditional books remain the preferred medium for young readers, with 86% of respondents saying their child likes to be read to from a book rather than an e-reader or laptop. The survey also canvassed the views of 207 teachers of four- to six-year-olds in England and Northern Ireland, who reported clear differences between pupils who are read to at home and those who are not. Nearly three-quarters (72%) said children who regularly enjoy shared book time with parents demonstrate more developed language skills and more advanced reading levels. Thirty percent observed that these children tend to be the first to answer questions in class. An overwhelming 98% of teachers expressed concern that reading for pleasure does not occur often enough in some homes. The findings come as Booktrust and Pearson continue to sponsor the Booktime programme, which this year will provide 1.38 million free books to reception-age children in England. Viv Bird, chief executive of Booktrust, welcomed the gains but urged continued focus. “It is good news that parents are spending more time reading to their children,” she said. “But I think that parents are pretty busy people and the stress of daily life can get in the way of reading with a child. So we’ve got to keep reinforcing the message.” Peter Hughes, head of corporate responsibility at Pearson, underscored the long-term benefits. “A passion for reading is one of the greatest gifts we can give. Good reading skills are the basic cornerstone that helps all of us progress throughout our lives. Books inform, educate, but also inspire. Good reading starts early.”

Ireland have reshaped their backline for Saturday’s Women’s Six Nations clash with Wales at Cardiff Arms Park, with wingers Hannah Miller and Hannah Tyrrell coming in and centre Sene Naoupu returning, while Kim Flood switches from the wing to full-back. Naoupu replaces Claire McLaughlin, who injured an ankle during training. Miller, Tyrrell and Naoupu were on Ireland Sevens duty in Las Vegas when Tom Tierney’s side defeated France in Dublin last month. Ireland have won their opening three games and trail leaders England on points difference, keeping the title race finely balanced heading into Cardiff. Tierney said: “The squad has been developing nicely over the course of the Championship, and while it was great to get the win against France in the last game, we haven’t dwelled on that and have firmly turned our attention to the challenge the Welsh will give us. We are expecting Wales to be very much up for this game and there is set to be a big crowd in the Cardiff Arms Park on Saturday. With that in mind, it will be important that the players stay fully focused on their jobs and that we go out on Saturday ready to perform. We’d also encourage any Ireland fans that are in town for the men’s game on Friday evening and are still in Cardiff on Saturday to come to the game and give the team their support.” Ireland team: K Flood; H Tyrrell, J Murphy, S Naoupu, A Miller; N Stapleton, M Healy; L Peat, L Lyons, A Egan, S Spence, ML Reilly, C Griffin, C Molloy, P Fitzpatrick. Replacements: C O’Connor, I Van Staden, R O’Reilly, C Cooney, N Fryday, L Muldoon, N Caughey, M Coyne.

First Minister calls for calm amid row over Welsh-medium shift at Ysgol Llangennech Carmarthenshire council’s January vote to end the English stream at Ysgol Llangennech, near Llanelli, has sparked a heated political row. A Labour councillor branded the move “segregation,” while a Welsh-medium education campaigner suggested parents who oppose the change could “cross the border.” At First Minister’s Questions, Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood claimed some Labour members had worked with UKIP to undermine the policy, which she argued aligns with the Welsh Government’s aim of promoting the Welsh language. The First Minister, Mr Jones, said he disagreed with some of the comments made by politicians and urged restraint. “I’ve seen those comments and I think it’s hugely important now that calm prevails, and the toxicity we last saw some years ago is now reduced,” he told the Senedd. He added that it was for the Plaid Cymru-run Carmarthenshire administration to explain its decisions in Llangennech. Mr Jones reiterated the Welsh Government’s commitment to its “quest” to reach one million Welsh speakers, saying the debate should focus on constructive steps to expand Welsh-medium education while maintaining community cohesion.

Madrid authorities have classified Tuesday’s tie at the Santiago Bernabéu as “high risk” and will reinforce security, the city government said Friday. The measures follow UEFA’s directive to tighten protection at European fixtures after the 11 April attack on the Borussia Dortmund team bus. Around 4,000 Atlético Madrid supporters are expected at Real Madrid’s 80,000-capacity stadium, far more than the few hundred who typically travel to away games in Spain. Police presence on 2 May will exceed levels seen at Real’s last European home match against Bayern Munich, when riot officers clashed with visiting fans at half-time. There were also violent confrontations before Atlético’s quarter-final home tie involving police and Leicester City supporters.

Thirty-nine football fans were killed when a crush against a stadium wall that later collapsed unfolded moments before the 1985 European Cup final between Liverpool and Juventus in Brussels. The Heysel Stadium disaster, triggered when a surge by Liverpool supporters forced Juventus fans toward a fragile boundary, was marked with memorial events. At Liverpool’s Anfield stadium, tributes centered on the Heysel Memorial in the Centenary Stand. Former Reds captain Phil Neal, who led the team on the night of the tragedy, laid a wreath, and the stand will remain open for the rest of the day to allow supporters to pay respects. Representatives from Liverpool, including club ambassador Ian Rush — who also played for Juventus — travelled to Turin, where a special Mass was held at the Chiesa della Gran Madre di Dio. In Brussels, the site of the disaster, now renamed the King Baudouin Stadium, hosted a ceremony that included the laying of wreaths. Families of those who died released balloons in remembrance of their loved ones, while club officials and local authorities joined in moments of silence. The aftermath of Heysel reshaped European football. Following a five-month trial, 14 Liverpool fans were convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to three years in prison. A Belgian inquiry recommended that responsibility should also be shared by the police and football authorities, citing failures in crowd control and stadium management. English clubs were barred from European competition for five years, with Liverpool serving an additional year, a sanction that underscored the lasting impact of events at Heysel on the sport and its safety standards.

Norwich City supporter Ashley Howell has told how a case of mistaken identity involving the club’s identical twins, Josh and Jacob Murphy, led to an unexpected betting windfall — and a gesture of goodwill from bookmaker Paddy Power. Ahead of Saturday’s fixture against Burton Albion, Mr Howell intended to place a £10 wager on Jacob Murphy to score, tempted by what he thought were attractive odds. “I thought, I’ll put a tenner on that,” he said. “Then when I looked back I realised I had put the money on Josh Murphy accidentally.” When the match was settled, the confusion deepened. Paddy Power processed a payout on Josh Murphy, mirroring the mix‐up. Howell kept quiet at first, but said his conscience prompted him to contact the firm on Sunday to explain the error. “They said due to the fact I had been so honest they’ve let me keep the winnings anyway.” Paddy Power spokesman Lewis Davey said the company understood how the slip could happen. “We all make honest mistakes, the confusion is quite easy to make,” he said, praising Howell’s honesty in coming forward.

Airbus slams Poland’s cancellation of Caracal helicopter deal as diplomatic row escalates Airbus has sharply criticized Poland’s abrupt decision to abandon a planned purchase of 50 Caracal military helicopters, deepening a diplomatic rift with France and casting uncertainty over future defense cooperation between Warsaw and Paris. The European aerospace company’s chief executive, Tom Enders, said the firm had been “misled for months” by the Polish government and would seek compensation after talks collapsed last week. “We wanted to invest in Poland big time,” Enders said, adding that the government had “slammed the door on us” following lengthy negotiations on an industrial offset package tied to the deal. Airbus Helicopters won a tender in April 2015 to supply the Polish armed forces with the multi-role Caracal, designed and developed at the company’s headquarters in France. The contract’s finalization hinged on an offset agreement, a common practice in the defense and aerospace sectors in which the supplier commits to investment and technology transfers in the purchasing country. Relations deteriorated after Poland’s right-wing government under Prime Minister Beata Szydlo took office in October last year. Warsaw terminated the negotiations last week, asserting that the proposed contract did not meet Poland’s economic and security interests. The decision triggered an immediate backlash in France. President Francois Hollande cancelled a planned visit to Warsaw and warned that Paris would review other strands of defense cooperation. A separate trip by French Defense Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian was also called off. Polish officials have blamed Airbus for the breakdown. Defense Minister Antoni Macierewicz said the company “did not make a satisfactory offer in the last phase of talks,” claiming Airbus failed to respond adequately to Poland’s position on offsets. “This is why negotiations on the contract stopped,” he told reporters. Airbus rejected those assertions in an open letter to Prime Minister Szydlo published Tuesday. The company said its investment package “would have generated more value in Poland than the revenues that would have been generated for Airbus Helicopters through the helicopter supply contract.” It detailed plans to build a full assembly line in the central city of Lodz, mirroring capabilities at its Marignane facility in southern France, and to establish a parts factory. The Lodz operation, Airbus said, would have been 90% owned by the Polish government and, together with the parts facility, was expected to create 3,800 jobs. “We have an impression that we have been misled for months by the current Polish government,” Enders said, noting the company had invested “a huge amount of efforts and money in recent years trusting that we were in a fair and professionally-conducted competition.” He added: “We will of course seek remedies.” With both sides entrenched, the episode threatens to leave a lasting mark on Franco-Polish relations and on Poland’s defense modernization plans, even as Airbus prepares potential legal steps to recover costs from the collapsed deal.

Police probe series of attacks in Cardiff student area; two arrests, links unconfirmed South Wales Police are investigating a series of reported attacks in central Cardiff, an area with a high student population, and say it is too early to determine whether the incidents are connected. Officers received the latest report of an attack on a 19-year-old woman at Gorsedd Gardens at 04:30 BST on Thursday. The incident follows two earlier reports: one near the Cardiff Civic Centre in the early hours of Sunday, and another on Cathays Terrace in the early hours of Tuesday. A 40-year-old man from Riverside has been taken to Cardiff Bay police station for questioning, while a 22-year-old man from Cardiff, arrested earlier on Thursday, remains in custody. Detectives stressed that inquiries are ongoing and that no definitive link between the incidents has yet been established. Chief Superintendent Belinda Davies said the force has "zero tolerance towards anyone who commits these appalling crimes," adding: "Crimes like this are never the victim's fault, but I would like to take this opportunity to remind everyone to follow basic safety advice so they keep themselves and their friends safe." The first attack occurred close to the main Cardiff University buildings, as thousands of students returned to the city for the start of the new academic year. A Cardiff University spokesman said the security team had visited student residences during freshers' week to discuss personal safety and that the university is in consultation with its Students' Union to consider further measures. "We encourage anyone affected by these events to speak to someone in Student Support," he added. Extra police patrols are continuing in the area to reassure residents. On Wednesday, South Wales Police advised people to walk in pairs at night and stay in well-lit areas.

The ban on travel to the United States by people from a list of mainly Muslim countries has caused widespread political protest. While it is being discussed at top government level, it is also impacting individuals. Milad Korkis has lived in Northern Ireland for three years. He is married to Holly, an American, and both work with a Christian charity. They were due to visit Holly's family in Pennsylvania in April. “My travel document says that I am from Syria,” Mr Korkis said. “I called the US Consulate here and our friends in the States and they explained the executive order and it says I can’t travel to the States and if I get there I’ll be deported.” Holly Korkis said she hopes the measure is temporary. “I know that there’s processes of safety and there’s so much going on,” she said. “But my hope is that it will get better and we’ll be able to see family,” she said. The couple said the tickets they bought may not be refundable, adding financial strain to the uncertainty. “As a Christian myself, I’m banned from going to the States,” Mr Korkis said. “It does affect, not just Muslims, but also Christians in the Middle East.” The policy, debated at the highest levels of government, has sparked demonstrations and legal challenges across the United States. Protests have been held at airports and city squares. Mr Korkis said friends in the U.S. had urged them to wait for clarity before attempting to travel. Holly added that family ties are central to their lives and work. “We just want a system that works well so people can be safe and still see their loved ones,” she said.

James Salter, acclaimed American novelist and former US fighter pilot, died on Friday at a gym near his New York state home, his publisher said. Revered by peers but rarely a commercial powerhouse, Salter won the admiration of celebrated authors including Philip Roth and Joseph Heller, even as he struggled to convert critical acclaim into sustained sales. Salter’s literary career began with The Hunters, published in 1956 amid his service in the Korean War. He flew combat missions alongside future astronaut Buzz Aldrin, who later became the second man to walk on the moon. Salter’s fiction explored masculine themes—conflict, desire, and honor—drawing frequent comparisons to Ernest Hemingway. Speaking to the BBC in 2013, he reflected on how war shaped his sensibility: “Having been to war satisfies a certain classical definition of manhood. To have seen war is some kind of pillar of manhood, and I felt that at the time.” The Hunters was adapted into a Hollywood film in 1958 starring Robert Mitchum, but Salter’s subsequent five novels brought him far less mainstream attention. He continued to earn ardent praise from fellow writers and critics. In 1975, novelist Richard Ford wrote, “It is an article of faith among readers of fiction that James Salter writes American sentences better than anybody writing today.” After a long hiatus, Salter returned with his final novel, All That Is, published two years ago at age 87. It marked his first novel in nearly 30 years and briefly reached The New York Times best-seller list. It may have fallen short of the popular success he craved, as the BBC’s Nick Bryant observed, but the enduring adulation secured Salter’s reputation as a writer’s writer, almost without peer.

In a letter to the transport secretary, the London councils and Greenpeace said judicial review proceedings will begin if the government fails to comply. The group said expansion plans were "unlawful" and a "fair and lawful consultation" had not been carried out. The government said it would "strongly defend any challenge". A coalition of London councils and Greenpeace has warned the government it faces legal action over airport expansion plans, arguing the proposals breach air quality and noise obligations and were advanced without proper public consultation. In a 33-page letter to the transport secretary, Hillingdon, Richmond, Wandsworth and Windsor and Maidenhead Councils, together with Greenpeace and a Hillingdon resident, set out what they described as a “comprehensive legal challenge” to the decision-making process. They claim the government’s approach to air quality and noise is unlawful and that a correct consultation exercise was not carried out “prior to issuing its decision”. The group says it will begin judicial review proceedings if the government fails to address the alleged deficiencies. Responding, a Department for Transport spokesperson said the expansion “can be delivered in line with our obligations on air quality,” adding: “We are confident that our process for decision-making is robust and will strongly defend any challenge.” London mayor Sadiq Khan has directed Transport for London to provide “expert advice and assistance” to the councils in preparation for potential court proceedings.

Swindon Town have handed Liverpool loanee Lawrence Vigouroux a second chance after the 21-year-old goalkeeper was briefly sent back to Anfield for paying a £50 club fine with 5,000 coins following a late arrival to training. Vigouroux, on a season-long loan, had faced disciplinary action for the stunt but returned to Wiltshire this week, attending Tuesday night’s 2-2 draw with Doncaster Rovers and rejoining the squad amid strong backing from teammates and staff. Manager Mark Cooper said the player has shown genuine remorse. “Lawrence is going to come back. He is very humble and very apologetic,” Cooper told BBC Wiltshire. “He knows the way he behaved was wrong and he has been in the changing room after the game and apologised to the players. He asked them if they wanted him back and they all said yes.” Vigouroux also issued a public apology on social media on Wednesday, saying he wants to move on from the incident and is grateful for another opportunity. Cooper praised the youngster’s talent while stressing the need to learn from the episode. “Lawrence is an exceptional young goalkeeper and it’s important he learns from this little mishap and it will benefit his career going forward,” he added. “It did happen and I thought it was brilliant banter, but in the context it was the wrong way to go about it. We are giving him a second chance and I’m sure he will be grateful.” Vigouroux has made nine appearances for Swindon with one clean sheet and could come into contention for Saturday’s League One trip to Blackpool.

Monaghan have suffered a significant blow ahead of their Ulster Championship opener, with manager Malachy O’Rourke confirming that key player Hughes will be sidelined for 12 weeks after tearing medial knee ligaments. The 30-year-old sustained the injury at the weekend while lining out for his club Scotstown, and scans on Wednesday verified the damage. Ulster champions in 2013 and 2015, Monaghan begin their campaign against Fermanagh on Saturday 20 May, and Hughes faces a race to feature. Speaking to the Irish News, he said he could require surgery if the injury does not respond within the next four weeks, a scenario that would end his season. “It’s not the cruciate so I suppose that’s kind of a bonus,” he said. “At the minute I don’t need surgery..... I’ve just to look after it and hopefully it’ll heal well.”

YMCA scales back Great Yarmouth housing plan, eyes smaller hostel The YMCA has abandoned plans to convert the former Two Bears Hotel in Great Yarmouth into 23 flats and a community centre, citing financial risk amid uncertainty over government welfare reform. The charity had secured permission for the redevelopment in December but now intends to pursue a smaller hostel elsewhere in the town. Tim Sweeting of the YMCA said the Two Bears scheme required a lengthy lease to be viable, but the level of risk was too high given unclear future funding. “We needed to take on a very long lease in order to make it work and unfortunately the financial risk, considering the uncertainty over welfare reform, was just too much for us,” he said. “[The new centre] will have the accommodation, but we won’t have the ability to create the community space that we wanted to.” The YMCA is now looking to develop accommodation at the former GPO exchange building on Hall Quay, recently vacated by another charity. Mike Younger of James Aldridge Chartered Surveyors, which worked on the Two Bears project, said the deteriorating hotel may now have to be demolished.

The sudden change of policy comes after days of economic chaos. After days of economic chaos in Venezuela, President Nicolás Maduro announced in a national broadcast that international sabotage prevented the arrival of new 500-bolivar notes in time, exacerbating turmoil that followed the government’s decision to scrap the 100-bolivar note. The abrupt move left millions scrambling to hand in or swap old notes, with long queues at banks and processing centers. Thousands of shops closed because of a nationwide cash shortage, and the public was forced to rely on credit cards or bank transfers. In a country where electronic payment infrastructure is uneven and power cuts are common, many were left unable to buy food or basic goods, deepening anger and frustration. Unrest flared in multiple cities. According to the Associated Press, skirmishes broke out in six urban centers on Friday, leading to 32 people taken into custody and at least one injury. In Maracaibo, incidents of looting were brought under control after police fired tear gas to disperse crowds, authorities said. The government has defended the withdrawal of the 100-bolivar note as a necessary step to combat smuggling and organized crime. Maduro argues that criminal networks have been hoarding Venezuelan currency abroad as part of what he has long described as an “economic war” against his administration. He claimed gangs hold more than 300 billion bolívares, largely in 100-bolivar notes, stored in “entire warehouses” in the Colombian cities of Cucuta, Cartagena, Maicao and Bucaramanga. By withdrawing the 100-bolivar bills and blocking them from re-entering the country, authorities say they aim to render those hoarded notes worthless. Central bank data indicate there are more than six billion 100-bolivar banknotes in circulation, accounting for almost half of Venezuela’s currency, underscoring the scale and potential disruption of the move. Economic experts warn the policy is unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to Venezuela’s chronic economic and political crises, which include runaway inflation, shortages, and a prolonged recession. Opposition leaders contend the initiative highlights mismanagement by Maduro and argue he must be removed to restore stability. Correction 10 January 2017: This article has been amended to clarify where police used tear gas and the circumstances in which it was fired.

Teachers have been offered a pay rise of just over 1%, according to the National Association of Schoolmasters Union of Women Teachers (NASUWT), which says any increase must beat inflation. The union has rejected a 1.37% deal, arguing it comes with strings attached and does not address pay erosion since 2010. NASUWT has written to Education Minister John O’Dowd outlining its reasons. “Since 2010, inflation has risen by 15%, yet teachers’ pay has risen by 2%,” said the NASUWT’s Justin McCamphill. “An offer of 1.37%, which does have strings attached to it, is nowhere near enough to address the real cuts in teachers’ pay. “The education system is currently undergoing radical change, and teachers are subject to continuing and increasing pressure. “Year-on-year, teachers continue to deliver high standards of education but their commitment and dedication should not be taken for granted.” The Department of Education said pay talks are continuing and accused the union of breaching a confidentiality agreement, adding it would be inappropriate to comment further as negotiations have not reached a conclusion.

Saving Christmas Sweeps Razzies as 35th Golden Raspberry Awards Skewer Hollywood’s Worst Kirk Cameron’s faith-themed film Saving Christmas dominated Saturday night’s 35th Golden Raspberry Awards, taking home four “wins” at the tongue-in-cheek ceremony that revels in cinematic misfires. Staged a short walk from the venue for Sunday’s Academy Awards, the Razzies crowned Saving Christmas worst picture, while Cameron was named worst actor. The film also earned worst screenplay and worst screen combo, the latter cheekily cited as “Kirk Cameron and his ego.” “This is a vanity project that Kirk Cameron put together,” Razzie founder John Wilson told BBC Radio 5 live after the show. “It’s about on the level of a super 8 movie from when I was a kid. It has no cinematic value at all.” Wilson noted the film’s ignominious status as the number one worst movie of all time on IMDb, and one of only two releases last year to score a zero on Rotten Tomatoes. Marketing for the film embraced the mantra “Put Christ back in Christmas.” Cameron Diaz was named worst actress for a double helping of broad comedy, The Other Woman and Sex Tape. The worst supporting actress award went to Megan Fox for the reboot of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. Michael Bay’s Transformers: Age of Extinction led the nominations with seven but ultimately collected just two trophies, worst director for Bay and worst supporting actor for Kelsey Grammer. Annie was cited as worst remake, rip-off or sequel. In a nod to turnaround stories, the Razzies introduced a new Razzie Redeemer award, honoring a past target who delivered strong work over the last year. Ben Affleck won in an online public vote, recognized for his journey from the much-panned Gigli to the Oscar-winning Argo and the Oscar-nominated Gone Girl. His award was announced by real-life nun and veteran film critic Sister Rose Pacatte, who told the audience: “We Catholic nuns are all about redemption.” Razzie winners, who rarely attend, receive a $4.79 gold-spray-painted trophy. This year’s irreverent ceremony, held at Hollywood’s Montalban Theatre, welcomed paying members of the public for the first time. The regular awards were decided by 757 voting Razzie members in the United States and abroad.

The future of the Teesside steel plant, which paused production on 18 September due to a global drop in the price of steel, remains unclear. The plant employs about 2,000 people and unions and MPs had called on the company to make sure they were paid. SSI said this month's pay roll is being processed. The payment was made possible through a tax relief given to SSI by the government. Business Minister Anna Soubry said: "I am very pleased that action we have taken has allowed the company to ensure workers got paid today. I made it clear that workers getting paid was a priority and government officials have worked very hard to help the company so they could achieve this. It will be some relief for workers and their families at this difficult and uncertain time." A task force has been set up to support the workforce and liaise with SSI. Amanda Skelton, chief executive of Redcar and Cleveland Borough Council and chairman of the task force said: "The aim of the group is to ensure that following any announcements about the future of SSI, the impact on the workers, local businesses and the wider community is reduced as far as possible by delivering a programme of tailored support." While salaries have been secured for now, the long-term outlook for the plant remains in doubt amid continued pressure on global steel prices. Officials say the task force will coordinate assistance and prepare contingency plans, as unions and local leaders continue to press for clarity on the company’s next steps.

As the shortlist for world football’s top individual prize is unveiled, Manchester City trio Sergio Aguero, Kevin De Bruyne and Yaya Toure are among five Premier League stars nominated, while last year’s winner Cristiano Ronaldo of Real Madrid and Barcelona icon Lionel Messi remain favourites. Wales forward Gareth Bale is the only British player to make the list, highlighting how rare British recognition has become. That scarcity makes the roll call of British Ballon d’Or winners all the more special. Sir Stanley Matthews set the standard in 1956, becoming the first ever recipient of the award. One of England’s greatest footballers, Matthews dazzled for Blackpool for 14 years and earned nicknames such as “The Wizard of the Dribble” and “The Magician” for his exquisite close control. Remarkably, he continued at the top level until the age of 50, a career longevity that remains almost unheard of. Scotland’s Denis Law joined the elite in 1964 and remains the only Scottish player to have lifted the trophy. A prolific striker famed for his sharp instincts and acrobatic finishes, Law spent 11 memorable years at Manchester United, netting 237 goals in 404 appearances for the Red Devils. His haul of 46 competitive goals in a single season is still a club record. Two years later, Sir Bobby Charlton claimed the 1966 Ballon d’Or, the same year he inspired England to their historic World Cup triumph. Universally respected as one of the greatest midfielders of all time, Charlton played virtually his entire club career at Manchester United and is still the club’s all-time leading scorer. His association with United endures; he sits on the board of directors and remains a towering figure at Old Trafford. Northern Ireland’s George Best won the award in 1968, the only player from his nation to do so. Best burst onto the scene at 17 with Manchester United in 1963 and went on to become a global icon, scoring 179 goals in 470 appearances over the next 11 years. His blend of flair, pace and finishing made him a phenomenon. England’s Kevin Keegan stands alone as the only British player to win the Ballon d’Or twice, in 1978 and 1979. A dynamic forward for Liverpool and Germany’s Hamburg, Keegan was dubbed by the media “the first superstar English player.” After hanging up his boots, he managed Newcastle United, Fulham, Manchester City and the England national team. The most recent British winner is Michael Owen, who captured the prize in 2001. The former Liverpool prodigy starred for Real Madrid, Newcastle United, Manchester United and Stoke City, as well as England. He scored 118 Premier League goals in 216 appearances for Liverpool and is widely regarded as one of the club’s greatest strikers. Today, he is a regular football pundit. With Bale leading the British challenge and a strong Premier League contingent in contention, all eyes now turn to the ceremony to see if anyone can dethrone Ronaldo and Messi’s era of dominance.

Government ministers are preparing to curb the House of Lords’ ability to impede secondary legislation after a string of defeats in the upper chamber, culminating in the high-profile rebuff of the chancellor’s now-abandoned tax credit cuts. Since the general election, the government has lost 23 votes in the Lords on issues ranging from pub companies and childcare to criminal court charges, electoral registration, city devolution, charities, and psychoactive substances. The tax credits showdown, in which peers sent a key Statutory Instrument (SI) back to the Commons, has prompted a concerted response. According to a report in The Times, and pending a statement expected in the Lords later today, ministers plan to limit peers to a single power of delay on SIs, enabling the Lords to send measures back to the Commons once for reconsideration but not to block them outright. The move closely mirrors what peers actually did over tax credits: they rejected a fatal motion to kill the measure and instead insisted the Commons think again. The government’s proposed change would formalize that practice while removing any lingering ambiguity over the Lords’ capacity to wield a veto. SIs—secondary legislation made under powers granted by existing Acts—are a crucial but often under-scrutinized part of the legislative machinery. Some must be debated in both houses, some are debated only if challenged, and some can be voted on without debate. Their impact can be substantial. For example, a recent SI on fracking in national parks, made under Section 50 of the Infrastructure Act amending the 1998 Petroleum Act, bypassed a full Commons debate, was examined in a Delegated Legislation Committee, and received just over an hour’s discussion in the Lords’ Moses Room on November 24. That episode underscored how significant SIs can be—and why the tax credit changes, viewed by many as “hyper-important,” drew such intense scrutiny. Critics of the tax credit approach argued that the reforms were too far-reaching for secondary legislation and warranted a full bill. Most peers see the power to strike down SIs as a blunt instrument and favour a mechanism to prompt Commons reconsideration without creating constitutional standoffs. The government’s preferred path, associated with Conservative peer Lord Strathclyde, is to amend the 1946 Statutory Instruments Act to codify the Lords’ revising role. That proposal is thought to have some support across the upper chamber, making a showdown—such as invoking the Parliament Act—unlikely. Even so, constitutional experts warn that altering the delicate conventions governing Lords–Commons relations can have unpredictable consequences. As one veteran maxim warns, once you open the constitutional Pandora’s box, you cannot be sure what Trojan horses might jump out. The government’s statement later today will set the tone for how far it intends to go.

Bowditch Sets Unwanted WGC Record at Doral, Still Banks $48,000; Adam Scott Triumphs Australia’s Steven Bowditch endured a historically rough week at Doral, carding rounds of 81, 80, 80 and a closing 12-over-par 84 to finish 37 over par at the WGC event — the highest total ever recorded at a World Golf Championships tournament. Despite finishing 65th, Bowditch still collected $48,000 (£33,700), quipping afterward: “I shot 37 over par and still made a paycheck. All’s not that bad.” He completed his final round in just two hours and 12 minutes, playing alone over the weekend after Brandt Snedeker withdrew with a rib injury. Bowditch, ranked 78th in the world, earned his spot via ranking in the no-cut, limited-field tournament. His final round featured two triple bogeys. The last player to post four rounds in the 80s at a top-level event was Mike Dunaway at the 1983 Las Vegas Pro-Celebrity Classic. At the top of the leaderboard, Adam Scott won by one shot on 12 under, holding off Bubba Watson to claim the title.

UK Nuclear Lab to Turn Sellafield Plutonium into Long-Life Space Batteries for ESA Chemists at Britain’s National Nuclear Laboratory (NNL) plan to transform a portion of Sellafield’s large civil plutonium stockpile into radioisotope batteries capable of powering European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft for decades. The initiative, which could generate new skilled jobs and significant multi-million-pound export revenues, aims to establish a European source of Radioactive Power Sources (RPS) for long-duration missions. ESA funded a £1 million pilot project in 2009 to assess the cost and practicality of securing an indigenous supply of material for RPS. These ultra-long-life batteries do not propel spacecraft; rather, they provide reliable electrical power to scientific instruments far from the Sun or in harsh environments where solar energy is insufficient, underpinning ESA’s deep space exploration plans. “We’re more than half way through the £1m pilot proving the viability of being able to extract the isotope from the civil plutonium stockpiles,” said Tim Tinsley, programme manager for NNL. “We have a quantity of this plutonium at our labs at the Sellafield site and a team of highly experienced chemists are ‘proving’ the chemical flow-sheet for the process.” ESA’s current RPSs rely on plutonium-238, available only from Russia and the United States and largely produced in military reactors. Global supplies are constrained and could run short around 2018, threatening future missions. The isotope targeted at Sellafield—americium-241—can be extracted from aged civil plutonium and offers a more accessible, Europe-based alternative. If successful, it could support ESA projects and open an export market to countries currently dependent on plutonium-238. “Technically, there are no barriers to the success of the project; it would be down to funding and politics within Europe and they are already tightly constrained,” Tinsley said. “ESA needs this fuel source for their space road-map—they cannot do it without it and we at NNL are doing everything we can to make that a success.” Beyond space, americium-241 batteries could power devices in remote or inaccessible locations on Earth, such as deep-sea sensors or instruments installed deep underground in oil wells, where maintenance is impractical and a 20- to 30-year power supply is required. ESA is expected to decide in November whether to continue funding. If ratified, NNL anticipates a steady ramp-up of jobs from 2014, leading to full-scale production around 2020, positioning the UK as a key supplier in a strategically important high-technology niche.

An average of 1,870 people contract meningitis B each year in the UK, and one in 10 of them die, according to figures highlighted as a pioneering vaccine moves closer to approval. The 4CMenB jab, developed by Swiss pharmaceutical firm Novartis and branded as Bexsero, has been recommended for approval by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). The charity Meningitis UK has described the development as the biggest leap forward in the field in three decades and is urging the government to prioritise its inclusion in the routine immunisation schedule. Meningitis B is the most common form of bacterial meningitis in the UK, causing inflammation of the brain and spinal cord. Children under five are most at risk, and about a quarter of survivors suffer life-altering after-effects, including brain damage, hearing loss, or limb loss. The complexity of the disease, driven by many different strains, has long frustrated efforts to develop an effective vaccine. Novartis says it has taken 20 years to reach this point. The EMA’s recommendation is typically endorsed by the European Commission within two to three months. If that timetable holds, Bexsero is expected to receive its UK licence early next year. It has been recommended for use in children aged two months and older, a key demographic given the heightened vulnerability of infants and toddlers. Studies indicate the jab is likely to be effective against about 73% of the different variations of meningitis B. Meningitis UK has called the EMA decision a landmark moment in the fight against meningitis. The charity’s founder, Steve Dayman, whose baby son died of meningitis and septicaemia in 1982, said it is vital the vaccine is introduced into the UK immunisation schedule as soon as possible. “It will save countless lives and prevent many people enduring the suffering caused by this devastating disease,” he said. “We will be campaigning hard to make the government introduce it.” Andrin Oswald, head of vaccines at Novartis, welcomed the EMA’s recommendation, saying the vaccine represents a major advance against a historically challenging disease target. He noted the scale of the breakthrough in the context of previous efforts, which have succeeded against other strains but not meningitis B. A vaccine against the less common meningitis C has been administered since 1999 and is routinely given to babies in their first year, leading to a dramatic fall in cases among people under 20. The decision on whether to introduce Bexsero into the UK schedule will be made by the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation, which advises the government on vaccine policy. If approved, health campaigners expect the rollout to have a significant impact on rates of severe illness and death among young children.

Britain’s slopestyle hopes received a timely boost as Bristol-born snowboarder Jones claimed second place at the season’s opening World Cup, scoring 87 points behind American Jamie Anderson’s winning 97.45 in challenging fog. The 33-year-old, a three-time X Games gold medallist, said the conditions made the result especially satisfying. “I was so relieved to stay on my feet and make it past qualifications,” she said. “Putting down my run in the finals in such harsh conditions and finishing second has put a huge smile on my face.” Slopestyle—where riders navigate a course featuring rails and jumps and are judged on difficulty and execution—will make its Olympic debut at Sochi next February, positioning Britain as genuine medal contenders in both ski and snowboard disciplines. Alongside Jones, fellow snowboarder Billy Morgan has already stood on a World Cup podium, achieving the feat in Sierra Nevada last season. His chance to build on that form this week was curtailed when the final in New Zealand was cancelled due to fog. On the ski side, freestyle star James Woods, currently ranked world number one, competes later this week and is considered a leading British contender. Meanwhile, Katie Summerhayes is recovering well after a second operation on her cruciate knee ligament and is expected to be fit for Russia, bolstering a strong and increasingly confident British slopestyle squad.

Police are investigating a work-related death after a 51-year-old man was pronounced dead at Victoria Mills on Victoria Lane in Golcar, near Huddersfield, at about 02:10 GMT. Ambulance and fire crews attended. The Health and Safety Executive has been notified and is assisting the ongoing inquiry.

Rob Roussel, senior project manager, says bioremediation is breaking down oil into carbon dioxide and water at a quarry in the Vale, where waste was dumped after the 1967 Torrey Canyon spill. The weather-dependent process is progressing well and, he hopes, will be completed by the end of next month. The 974ft (297m) supertanker Torrey Canyon was carrying 100,000 tons of crude when it struck rocks off the UK’s south-west coast, unleashing one of Europe’s worst marine pollution disasters. Miles of Cornish shoreline were coated in brown sludge, with contamination stretching from Hartland Point in North Devon to the Channel Islands and the coast of Normandy.

Edinburgh Airport handled nearly 1.1 million passengers in June, marking its second busiest month on record and the second consecutive month in which the hub welcomed more than one million travelers. Glasgow Airport also saw strong growth, recording more than 905,000 passengers, an annual increase of 14.2%. In contrast, Aberdeen Airport experienced a decline, with just under 324,000 passengers in June, down 5.7% year-on-year. Edinburgh’s surge was driven by gains across both domestic and international markets. Domestic traffic rose 9.9% to nearly 476,000 passengers, bolstered by increased services to London operated by Ryanair, Flybe and BA Cityflyer. International volumes climbed 11.1% to just under 623,000, supported by expanded EasyJet schedules to Paris, Amsterdam, Milan, Nice, Berlin and Madrid, alongside additional Ryanair flights to Dublin, Rome and Barcelona. “We had an incredibly busy month in June with more passengers travelling through than ever before,” said Gordon Dewar, chief executive of Edinburgh Airport. “As the summer properly gets underway we’re anticipating our passenger numbers will continue to grow as people head off on the holidays.” Glasgow’s performance mirrored the broader summer travel uptick. International traffic rose by 15.6%, while domestic passenger numbers were up 12.2%. The airport attributed the domestic rise to significant increases in demand for services to London, with additional growth coming from regional routes such as Belfast and Bristol. “June has always been a busy month at the airport with the arrival of the school holidays, but this year we were busier than ever as we continue to enjoy unprecedented levels of growth in our passenger numbers,” said Amanda McMillan, managing director of Glasgow Airport. Aberdeen’s downturn reflects ongoing pressures in the oil and gas sector, which continue to dampen demand for travel in the region. Helicopter traffic fell 7.6% compared to June 2014, while fixed-wing traffic declined 5.4%. “We have seen a reduction in traffic across both fixed wing and helicopter traffic last month compared with the same month last year as the oil and gas sector continues in its cost efficiency drive and the impacts are felt across the region,” said Aberdeen Airport managing director Carol Benzie. She noted that June 2014 had been a record period for the airport, providing a high benchmark for comparison.

Jurors at Sheffield Crown Court have heard harrowing testimony from a woman who says she was abused and assaulted from the age of 11 while in local authority care. Over a period spanning a decade, five men and two women are facing more than 60 charges, including rape and false imprisonment. All seven defendants deny the allegations. The woman, now 36, told the court that despite seeking help, she felt ignored by those responsible for her welfare and protection. Under questioning by prosecutor Michelle Colborne QC, the witness described attempting to report what was happening to a detective. She told the jury: “He used to come to houses where we were. He used to have sex with girls and he used to take drugs from people and pass them on to Ash.” The court has heard that two of the defendants, Arshid Hussain and Qurban Ali, were known as “Mad Ash” and “Blind Ash” respectively, though the witness did not specify which individual she was referring to in her account. Asked when these events occurred, she replied: “It was while I was still in care.” She added that after she disclosed what was happening, “He wrote it down in his book.” The woman said she received no help while living in children’s homes. When asked if there was anyone in the care system she felt she could trust, she replied, “No.” She claimed staff at the home were concerned only with “sitting at the end of the night and writing reports up — that was it,” emphasizing her sense of isolation and a lack of meaningful support during the period in question. The defendants include Arshid Hussain, 40, of High Street, East Cowick, Goole, who faces 30 charges, among them five counts of rape; Qurban Ali, 53, of Clough Road, Rotherham, who faces four charges including rape and conspiracy to rape; Majid Bostan, 37, of Ledsham Road, Rotherham, who faces one charge of indecent assault; and Sajid Bostan, 38, of Broom Avenue, Rotherham, who faces seven charges, including four counts of rape. Basharat Hussain, 39, of no fixed abode, faces 15 charges including two counts of rape. Karen MacGregor, 58, of Barnsley Road, Wath, South Yorkshire, faces four charges, including conspiracy to rape, while Shelley Davies, 40, of Wainwright Road, Kimberworth Park, Rotherham, faces three charges, including conspiracy to rape. The trial continues.

Hitachi has unveiled plans for what it says will be the world’s fastest lift, set to debut in the Guangzhou CTF Financial Centre in southern China. The ultra-high-speed elevator is designed to whisk passengers from the first to the 95th floor in just 43 seconds, a feat the company claims will redefine vertical transportation. The 530-metre skyscraper is scheduled for completion in 2016, with Hitachi promising a “comfortable ride” even at peak speeds. If performance matches the specifications, the lift will surpass the current world record held by Taipei 101 in Taiwan. The Taipei 101 elevators travel at up to 60.6 km/h, moving passengers from the fifth to the 89th floor in 37 seconds — a rate of 1,010 metres per minute. Other high-speed systems include Japan’s Yokohama Landmark Tower at 750 metres per minute, Dubai’s Burj Khalifa at 600 metres per minute, and London’s Shard, the tallest building in Western Europe, at 360 metres per minute. Comfort and safety at such speeds pose significant engineering challenges. Hitachi says the new lift will prevent ear blockages by artificially modulating air pressure within the cabin, mitigating discomfort during rapid altitude changes. Dr Gina Barney, a lift technology expert, told the BBC that protecting passengers from pressure-related ear pain remains one of the most significant obstacles for high-speed elevator travel. To ensure a smooth ride, Hitachi’s design includes guiding rollers that adapt to minute warping caused by wind pressure on the tower, maintaining stability at high velocities. The system will also feature brakes capable of withstanding extreme heat, designed to engage in the unlikely event of a malfunction. In total, the Guangzhou CTF Financial Centre will house 95 lifts, including two operating at ultra-high speed and 28 “double-decker” units to improve capacity and efficiency. The mixed-use skyscraper will combine office, hotel, and residential space, underscoring the growing demand for advanced vertical transport solutions in mega-tall buildings. If Hitachi’s elevator meets its targets, it will comfortably top the global charts, marking a new benchmark in skyscraper engineering.

Eubank was set to make a second defence of his title on 22 October in Cardiff. Chris Eubank Jr has withdrawn from his scheduled title defence after suffering an injury during a sparring session, his team announced. The 27-year-old was reportedly hurt on Thursday while working with a 14-stone opponent, and the injury has been verified by a British Boxing Board of Control doctor. A new date for the bout has not yet been confirmed. Unbeaten challenger Tommy Langford could still box for the title on the original 22 October date against a different opponent, with promoter Frank Warren expected to issue a statement outlining alternative plans. Responding on social media, Langford, also 27, said he was “extremely disappointed” and labelled Eubank Jr a “time-waster.” Eubank Jr’s team, however, framed the setback as a “blessing in disguise,” arguing there is a “vast chasm” between their fighter and recent domestic contenders in terms of ability, speed, strength, accuracy and skill. They indicated that the injury may prompt Eubank Jr’s management to step aside from the British Championship and pivot toward “high-calibre world competition.” The development arrives amid continued scrutiny of Eubank Jr’s domestic campaign, which included his March title win over Nick Blackwell. In that fight, his father and trainer Chris Eubank Sr instructed him mid-bout to avoid targeting Blackwell’s head; the contest was ultimately stopped, and Blackwell later suffered a bleed on his skull, was placed in an induced coma, and has since retired from the sport. Eubank Jr had been expected to vacate his belt before the Langford fight was arranged, with a world title shot against Gennady Golovkin previously rumoured to be near. Those plans were overtaken when Briton Kell Brook was named as Golovkin’s opponent. Brook moved up two weight divisions for the September 10 bout and was stopped in five rounds. With the Cardiff date approaching, attention now turns to Warren’s announcement and whether Langford will meet a new opponent as the British scene awaits clarity on Eubank Jr’s recovery and future direction.

The Harry Potter author tweeted a photo of herself in the Scottish Resistance garment, in response to the group's own April Fool joke. JK Rowling responded to an April Fool’s prank by posting a selfie in a Scottish Resistance outfit, after the group circulated a doctored image claiming she had joined. Founder James Scott shared the photoshopped picture on Facebook with the caption: “Breaking News: JK Rowling has joined the Scottish Resistance and has started her new book The Fall of the House of Westmonster.” BuzzFeed’s Jamie Ross flagged the gag on Twitter, prompting the Edinburgh-based author to play along. “They needn’t have used photoshop, though,” she wrote, posting her own tongue-in-cheek selfie. By Friday afternoon it had been retweeted more than 300 times, drawing a mix of amusement and political point-scoring. Rowling was a prominent pro-union voice during Scotland’s 2014 independence referendum and frequently faced online opposition from nationalist activists, including the Scottish Resistance.
