The group has staged attention-grabbing protests, notably in January 2015 against Uddingston confectioner Tunnock’s, after the brand promoted its “great British teacake” on London Underground posters. The exchange added levity to Scotland’s constitutional debate while underscoring Rowling’s enduring visibility—and the Scottish Resistance’s flair for attention-grabbing stunts. No formal membership was implied.

Paul Olney, 35, was found dead at a property after police were called to Denham Close, Wivenhoe, at 15:50 BST on Monday. Richard Waterhouse, 30, of Golden Noble Hill in Colchester, appeared at Colchester Magistrates’ Court and was remanded in custody; he is due to appear at Chelmsford Crown Court on Thursday. A 37-year-old man arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 21 July.

title: It comes after the observation pod broke down three times in five days. About 200 people were stuck for more than an hour at ground level. British Airways, which runs the attraction, apologised and said those who had made bookings would be offered a refund or a chance to rebook. It said the incidents happened after automatic brakes were triggered. A spokeswoman said a load imbalance led to a breakdown on Thursday. She said: "When the pod was near full capacity this triggered the default safety mode and the brakes were automatically applied." Further problems occurred on Sunday when one of the sensors around the pod docking stations at ground level became loose, she said. She said a false reading sent to the control system put the pod once more into safety mode by activating the brakes. "We have a highly qualified engineering team on site during all operating hours and we are confident that these same issues will not happen again," she said. And she said final checks would be run on Tuesday night and an announcement would be made on Wednesday morning about plans for reopening. She said: "We would like to assure our customers that their safety and comfort is our number one priority and apologise again for any inconvenience caused." In one incident, visitors were trapped in the viewing pod for two hours - with no proper toilet facilities. And 180 passengers were left stuck in mid-air for two hours on Thursday evening. The i360 pod was carrying a private party, including a heavily pregnant woman, who boarded the pod at about 17:00 BST. The tower - branded the world's thinnest tall building - offers views of up to 26 miles of Sussex coastline and opened on 4 August. The 531ft (161m) viewing tower stands on the site once occupied by the entrance to Brighton's ruined West Pier. Visitors ascend 450ft (137m) in a 360-degree curved-glass pod.

Authorities in Beled Hawa, a Somali border town neighboring Kenya, have introduced strict caps on wedding expenditures in a bid to curb rising costs and social pressures that officials say are discouraging marriage. Commissioner Mohamud Hayd Osman told the BBC Somali service that receptions in hotels will no longer be permitted and hosts may slaughter no more than three goats to feed guests. New spending limits set by the local administration include a maximum of $600 (approximately £500) on furnishings for the couple’s new home and a bride price capped at $150. It is common for a groom’s family to spend around $5,000 on a wedding, according to the BBC Somali service’s Bashir Mohamed—covering the bride price, reception, outfits and jewelry, as well as new furniture. “Islamic teachings indicated that getting married should be cheap,” Commissioner Osman said, explaining that the decision followed a meeting of officials seeking to understand why 150 children had recently been born out of wedlock in the town. “Young women were refusing to get married unless a fortune was spent on wedding gold and household furnishings,” he added. Osman said the measures were prompted by broader economic strain in Beled Hawa, including drought and unemployment, which have pushed some residents to leave. High wedding costs were cited as an additional burden limiting family formation. “A young woman must be supported to get married to the young man she chooses..... so the community can grow,” he said. The commissioner argued that $600 should suffice to purchase essentials—such as a double bed, table, chairs, crockery and cutlery—while maintaining modest celebrations. Traditionally, Somali wedding festivities last seven days, but officials hope the new rules will refocus ceremonies on simplicity and accessibility rather than costly displays.

Cardiff council has chosen its Marland House and NCP car park site for the city’s new bus station, part of the Central Square regeneration. The current station will close in June 2015, with temporary stops set up elsewhere to maintain services. Final approval, for a scheme due to be completed in 2017, will be sought from the cabinet on Monday. The hub aligns with plans for BBC Wales to relocate from Llandaff to new headquarters at Central Square in 2018. Ramesh Patel, cabinet member for planning and sustainability, said the project will transform how public transport is delivered in Cardiff and is on schedule. Contingency arrangements will be in place by the time of the June 2015 closure. The authority says the location offers connectivity and supports city-centre redevelopment.

Nato will deploy around 4,000 additional troops to Eastern Europe in a move described as a preventive step aimed at deterring conflict rather than provoking it, Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said during a meeting in Brussels. Despite heightened tensions with Moscow, Stoltenberg emphasized that the alliance does not view Russia as presenting an imminent threat, but stressed that Nato must ground any pursuit of improved relations in credible collective defense and deterrence. Relations between Russia and the West are widely considered to be at their lowest point since the Cold War. The United States and European Union imposed sanctions on Russia following its 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the conflict in Syria has further exacerbated tensions. Western powers have accused Russia of committing war crimes through its bombardment of opposition-held areas in support of the Syrian government—allegations the Kremlin denies. Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Russia harbors aggressive designs in Europe as “ridiculous,” arguing that the West is seeking to undermine Russia and encircle it. The deployment forms part of a broader strategy to reassure Nato’s eastern members, particularly the Baltic states and Poland, amid concerns about Russia’s intentions and military posture. Four multinational battalions, each comprising approximately 1,000 troops, will be stationed in Poland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania early next year. The units will be led respectively by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Germany, reflecting a collective effort to reinforce Nato’s northern and south-eastern flanks with visible, symbolic deterrence. According to Nato, Russia has roughly 330,000 troops positioned near its western border, a buildup that the alliance views in the context of Moscow’s actions in Ukraine and what Stoltenberg described as the use of nuclear rhetoric to intimidate European nations. While the alliance remains wary of escalating tensions into a full-blown arms race, it insists that its posture is defensive and measured. BBC defence correspondent Jonathan Marcus noted that Russia, in many respects a relatively weak country, is governed by leaders with a pronounced sense of encirclement, fueling a more assertive approach that alarms neighboring states like the Baltics, Poland, Romania, and Bulgaria. In a recent episode underscoring the strain, plans for Russian warships to refuel at a Spanish port were cancelled after Nato allies raised concerns that the vessels might be used to intensify bombing in Syria. Stoltenberg reiterated that Nato seeks “a more co-operative and constructive relationship” with Russia, but underscored that such engagement must rest on “collective defence – deterrence,” signaling the alliance’s determination to prevent miscalculation and reassure its members.

SportPesa to End Kenyan Sports Sponsorships After New 35% Betting Tax Nairobi — SportPesa, one of East Africa’s largest gambling firms, says it will end all sports sponsorships in Kenya following the government’s decision to impose a 35% tax on betting revenues, a move the company says will severely disrupt its operations and the wider sports ecosystem. Chief executive Ronald Karauri said the tax increase would negatively affect the company’s business and warned it could push betting underground rather than protecting young people. He told the BBC that regulation, not punitive taxation, was the better approach to addressing concerns about minors’ exposure to betting. Karauri added that SportPesa would formally notify affected clubs and organizations in the coming days of its decision to withdraw support. The uniform tax was introduced by parliament—initially proposed at 50% before being revised down to 35%—and later signed into law by the president. Officials said the levy is intended to deter minors from gambling amid growing concerns over the impact of betting on young people. Parents and religious leaders have urged authorities to act, citing the ease with which young men can place wagers through mobile phone apps on local and international football matches. Kenya has emerged as the biggest gambling market in sub-Saharan Africa, with a recent survey indicating that three-quarters of 17- to 35-year-olds have placed a bet. The rapid growth of mobile money and ubiquitous smartphone use has fueled the boom. The decision by SportPesa deals a significant blow to Kenyan sport. The company sponsors two of the country’s most popular football clubs, Gor Mahia and AFC Leopards, as well as the Kenyan Premier League and the Kenya Football Federation. It is also a major backer of rugby and boxing domestically, and earlier this year funded a training trip for the national football team to England, where it played a friendly against then-Premier League side Hull City. Kenyan Premier League chief executive Jack Oguda called the development devastating and urged the government to find a solution to the standoff, saying SportPesa had been “uplifting football in the country.” A joint statement from the Association of Gaming Operators–Kenya warned that the higher tax could force many businesses in the industry to close, leading to job losses and ripple effects across sectors such as hotels, banks, and telecommunications. SportPesa said its international sponsorships will not be affected. The company currently sponsors English clubs Everton and Hull City, and supports teams in Tanzania’s top flight, agreements Karauri confirmed will continue despite the changes at home.

The Metropolitan Police Service said a 54-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of actual bodily harm following an incident at a convenience store in Camden. A 14-year-old boy was also arrested at the scene on suspicion of possession of cannabis and taken to a central London police station for questioning alongside the 54-year-old. In a statement posted on his website, Mr Joyce said he had asked for police to be called after he “detained a youth.” He confirmed he spoke to officers at the store on Friday 17 October and that the matter has been referred to the Crown Prosecution Service. Mr Joyce added that officers told him the CPS and the Met Police press office would be informed “because of my identity.” He said he would make no further comment for now, emphasizing that “no alcohol was involved” and that he is not in the habit of summoning police if he believes he is in the wrong. A Met Police spokesman said inquiries are ongoing. No further details have been released about the circumstances of the incident or the individuals involved.

Writing on the Brexit Central website, he called for an urgent review of the Joint Ministerial Committee (JMC) of leaders from across the UK. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has urged an overhaul of the Joint Ministerial Committee, arguing that the existing forum for UK and devolved governments is not fit for purpose as Brexit reshapes constitutional responsibilities. Writing on the pro-Brexit platform Brexit Central, Mr Davies said better ways were needed “to engage as a United Kingdom,” warning that the transfer of powers from Brussels would make reform unavoidable. First Minister Carwyn Jones is among those who have voiced deep frustration with the JMC process. Earlier in June, Mr Jones proposed replacing the JMC with a more powerful UK Council of Ministers, designed to settle disputes and “reinvent and strengthen” the UK’s governance after leaving the European Union. The JMC, which brings together ministers from Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland with their UK government counterparts, was revived in October for the first time since 2014. At that meeting, Prime Minister Theresa May described the forum as “the start of a new grown-up relationship between the devolved administrations and the UK government.” However, critics across the devolved nations say the committee has not delivered on that promise, with meetings perceived as infrequent and lacking in genuine joint decision-making. Mr Davies said the views of the devolved administrations must be properly heard. “This is not the 1950s,” he wrote. “We need to establish better ways to engage as a United Kingdom, the need for which will soon become clear once additional powers are returned to the UK from Brussels.” He added that the Brexit vote was driven in part by a sense of distance from Brussels among voters, and cautioned that Westminster must not repeat that mistake. With the prospect of new UK-wide frameworks for farming, regeneration and research, he argued, it is vital to have structures that give people in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland a bigger stake in decision-making. “That means a better voice for the devolved nations,” he said. The UK government’s Cabinet Office, which oversees how the JMC operates, has been asked to comment on Mr Davies’s proposals. His intervention comes amid tensions with UK ministers over a potential Conservative agreement with the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) at Westminster. On Wednesday, he warned that “any potential incentives considered for one nation in securing that majority must also be considered for Wales.” Welsh Secretary Alun Cairns rejected Mr Davies’s stance as “simplistic.” Speaking on BBC Wales’s The Wales Report, Mr Cairns said: “Wales now gets £120 for every £100 spent in England. We’ve also introduced the funding floor. These issues don’t exist in Northern Ireland as they are. And, certainly, the devolution settlement and the responsibilities are very different as well. So it’s far too easy to try to make simplistic comparison when it’s much more complicated than that.”

Engineers on the Thameslink Programme uncovered the former ticket hall and platforms of Southwark Park station, a long-lost stop that served passengers from 1902 to 1915 before shutting for good. The discovery was made during construction of the Bermondsey Dive Under, a major element of the £6.5bn upgrade rebuilding railway lines from New Cross Gate through London Bridge to Blackfriars and St Pancras. Located on a viaduct above Rotherhithe New Road, Southwark Park was one of several stations in the area, including nearby Spa Road. Both closed amid competition from trams and buses and the onset of World War One, leaving only traces of their existence along the Victorian railway structures. Project manager Greg Thornett said: “We uncovered the footings for the former platforms while we were preparing the top of the viaduct for new track and we are now working up in the roof space of the former ticket hall to fill in the old skylights, ready to carry the final track alignment. Much of the existing stretch of viaduct will be replaced by the ramps into and out of the new dive under, but the arch that used to house the old booking hall will remain.” The Bermondsey Dive Under will see two Victorian viaducts partially demolished and rebuilt, enabling trains from south east London and Kent to pass beneath a new route carrying Thameslink services from Croydon. The find offers a rare glimpse into the area’s transport heritage as modern infrastructure is laid in its place.

An overnight search is under way off the Isle of Whithorn after an empty boat was spotted drifting near a reef around 23:00. A man had been seen aboard earlier and is understood to be from Lancashire. A coastguard helicopter and lifeboats from Kirkcudbright and Port William are involved, with crews continuing to scour the area.

Jaap Stam has been appointed Reading manager on a two-year contract, becoming the Championship club’s first non-British or Irish boss. The 43-year-old former Netherlands defender, capped 67 times by his country, takes over from Brian McDermott, whose second spell in charge lasted just six months. Stam worked as a coach at Ajax last season and had been widely tipped to succeed McDermott. “Reading are very ambitious like I am and want to get back to the Premier League,” Stam said as he was unveiled at a press conference on Monday. “Hopefully we can have a good partnership and get there. Everyone knows that teams in the Championship are very competitive. It’s not going to be easy, but we’ll work very hard.” Stam’s move to Berkshire marks his first role in management after an illustrious playing career that included three seasons at Manchester United, where he was part of the 1998-99 treble-winning side, as well as spells at Lazio, AC Milan and Ajax. He becomes the latest high-profile former player to step into the dugout in England’s second tier. Dutch duo Andries Ulderink and Said Bakkati will join Stam’s coaching staff, having worked with him at Ajax, while first-team coaches Steven Reid and Dave Beasant will remain in their positions. Reading chairman Sir John Madejski, who sat alongside Stam during his introduction, acknowledged mixed feelings over McDermott’s departure in May. McDermott led the Royals to promotion to the Premier League in 2011-12, but won only nine of 30 games during his second spell as the club finished 17th last season. “I wish that Brian had been given a bit longer,” Madejski said. “But the shareholders decided it was time for a change. I respect the shareholders’ decision, although I didn’t agree with the decision that Brian shouldn’t have stayed longer. That’s in the past now, so we have to move forward. I wish Jaap every success for the future and I really do mean that.” Before accepting the role, Stam said he consulted fellow countrymen Southampton boss Ronald Koeman and former Chelsea manager Guus Hiddink. “It’s very important to speak to people who have been working at the top level as well as in the UK to ask them for advice about the way to go,” he explained. Stam’s priority will be to shape a competitive squad and reignite Reading’s push for promotion, with the club targeting a swift return to the top flight.

Motocross rider Thomas Brown died following a crash at a privately run event next to Low Hardwick Farm, near Sedgefield, County Durham, on Sunday. The 27-year-old, from Barnard Castle, worked on his family’s farm and had competed in motocross since the age of eight, Durham Police said. Brown was airlifted to hospital in Middlesbrough but was pronounced dead shortly before arrival. His family said they are “devastated.” In a separate incident at the track the same day, a woman in her 30s from the Sedgefield area was injured and remains in hospital; her injuries are not thought to be life-threatening. Police closed the event, which drew about 100 participants and 300 spectators, on safety grounds following the crashes. Organisers have yet to comment, and inquiries into the circumstances are ongoing.

Several of the UK’s biggest water suppliers have been criticised for sending debt-chasing letters that look as though they come from independent collection agencies but are, in fact, issued by the companies themselves. The practice, revealed by BBC Radio 4’s You and Yours, mirrors tactics previously identified in the banking sector, among energy providers and at payday lender Wonga. Twelve large water firms told the programme they had used the approach, and five said they are still doing so or may continue in future. Typically, the letters carry the name of a debt collection business prominently at the top, while any relationship to the water company is disclosed only in small print — and in some cases, not at all. Yorkshire Water has written to customers in arrears under the brand Rockford Debt Collections Ltd. Following regulatory scrutiny, its stationery has been revised: the Rockford name remains prominent, but a note at the bottom now states the link to Yorkshire Water. Ofgem, which has reviewed similar tactics by energy suppliers, described layouts that foreground a collection agency brand with minimal disclosure of the parent company as “unacceptable.” The water regulator Ofwat has told water companies the same principles apply to them, warning that customers must not be misled or frightened into paying. Ofwat said it still has concerns about two firms’ practices, but declined to name them. Yorkshire Water said it has “temporarily changed” its approach but defended the use of an internally branded collection arm. “Any customer who receives a letter from Rockford would already have received three letters from Yorkshire Water urging them to get in touch, as well as a text,” a spokesperson said. Other suppliers, including Northumbrian Water, Affinity Water and Welsh Water, have stopped sending such letters this year. Thames Water, the UK’s largest domestic supplier, continues with the strategy. Its letters, headed County Wide Collections, now state in three places that the brand is part of the Thames Water group; previously, no such link was made. “We try hard to engage with our customers in arrears. This is a long process, but our open and transparent letters do increase in severity,” a Thames Water spokesperson said, adding that the internally branded agency approach has proven “effective and cost-efficient” at the final stage. Consumer advocates urged firms to pursue debts without resorting to intimidation. “We’re not saying don’t pursue debt,” said Gillian Guy, chief executive of Citizens Advice. “Clearly companies are entitled to do that, but we are saying that they really ought to do that honestly and with some sensitivity. These letters are about increasing the level of aggression to get payment, and they’re made on the assumption that people won’t pay rather than that many can’t.” Campaigners are calling for clearer rules and enforcement to ensure vulnerable customers are treated fairly, while regulators continue to monitor compliance.

Leigh Griffiths shook off a mini goal drought with a decisive brace to hand Celtic a vital win at Motherwell, stretching the champions’ lead at the top of the Scottish Premiership to eight points. The 25-year-old striker, who had failed to score in four previous outings, including Scotland’s friendly victory over Denmark, missed a first-half penalty at Fir Park before finding the net twice in a gritty 2-1 victory. Griffiths opened the scoring, only for Scott McDonald to level and raise the prospect of another frustrating afternoon for Celtic’s leading marksman. Motherwell goalkeeper Connor Ripley produced several impressive saves but was undone when Griffiths’ driven effort squirmed through his legs to restore Celtic’s advantage. The result increases daylight between Celtic and second-placed Aberdeen, who were beaten at Hearts on Friday. “There’s been talk of me hitting a barren spell and a few reporters giving me a bit of stick,” said Griffiths. “My all-round game’s about scoring goals; if I’m not scoring I’m disappointed. When Motherwell pegged us back, I thought it was going to be one of those afternoons. The goalie was terrific and it’s unfortunate he’s made a mistake for my goal.” Griffiths was booked for removing his shirt after his first strike, a celebration he admitted was fueled by pent-up frustration. “There was so much anger in that celebration, partly because I set such high standards for myself, and a lot of belief as well,” he added. “The last three weeks haven’t been good enough by my own standards, especially Wednesday night against Dundee. My first touch wasn’t good enough, and I was criticised, rightly so.” Celtic’s win, driven by Griffiths’ rediscovered scoring touch, leaves the champions firmly in control of the title race.

Castleford Tigers head coach Daryl Powell has signed a new long-term deal to remain with the Super League club through the 2020 season. The 51-year-old took charge at Wheldon Road in May 2013 and led the Tigers to the 2014 Challenge Cup final, revitalizing the side’s fortunes. Chief executive Steve Gill hailed the extension as “a massive boost,” telling BBC Radio Leeds Powell was “probably one of the best signings the club’s made.” Gill added Powell always wanted to coach Castleford and hopes he will finish his career there, praising his hands-on, honest approach and the players’ respect.

The company believes that any further claims related to the spill will "not have a material impact". BP says it has drawn a line under remaining liabilities from the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster, asserting that any additional claims are unlikely to be material. The oil giant’s chief financial officer, Brian Gilvary, said the company has made progress resolving outstanding cases and can now estimate all obligations linked to the incident, giving investors more clarity on future costs. The Deepwater Horizon drilling rig exploded on 20 April 2010 in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers and triggering an oil spill, the worst environmental crisis in US history. In the years since, BP has paid tens of billions of dollars in fines, compensation and legal fees, and reshaped its business to survive the aftermath. Last year, chief executive Bob Dudley called the catastrophe a “near-death experience” that shook BP “to its core,” prompting a sweeping reorganisation. “Sometimes it takes a near-death experience to radically change a company,” he said, noting a “forced focusing” on essential activities. To help fund liabilities, BP has sold more than £30bn ($45bn) in assets. In October last year, BP agreed a $20bn (£13.2bn) settlement with the US government, the largest resolution the government has reached with a single company. Gilvary said BP has a clear plan to manage remaining costs and that the latest estimates should provide certainty for shareholders. While litigation continues, BP maintains that any further claims will not have a material impact on the company.

Michael Doyle will rejoin Coventry City in July after leading Portsmouth to the League Two title, citing family considerations and the absence of a formal offer. Doyle told BBC Radio Solent that, despite manager Paul Cook saying he was part of Portsmouth’s plans for next season, no new deal was put on the table. “It’s one of those things in football,” he said. “Coventry came in and wanted to get it done.” “We’ve just achieved something special here at Portsmouth,” “But we’ll never know about a new deal as we didn’t get into that situation.” Based in the Midlands, Doyle’s family location played a significant role in his decision to return to Coventry, where he made more than 300 appearances between 2003 and 2011. “I spoke to the manager at the start of the week, but then Coventry expressed an interest.” “I just thought, what’s best for me and my family at this time? It was time to probably move on and family comes first. What’s meant to be is what’s meant to be.” Doyle said conversations with Mark Robins, keen to complete the move quickly, convinced him. “I thought it was right to go with a manager who wants me.”

Anthony Barrett, 56, has built a replica of the Sam Maguire Cup - the trophy traditionally presented to Ireland's Gaelic football champions each year. His trophy is, however, built from stone. But Anthony is a farmer, not a stone mason by trade, nor is he trained in the skills of dry stone walling. An Omagh native, Barrett discovered an unlikely passion for dry stone walling after his family acquired a farm near Newtowncunningham in County Donegal. Dry stone walling, the age-old practice of building without mortar, is a familiar sight across Ireland’s countryside. Barrett said the Donegal land he has farmed since 1979 revealed a bounty of material that set his imagination in motion. “It was very, very gravelley ground on the farm. There were a lot of stones on it,” he told the BBC. “I started, about 10 years, ago building walls. There used to be a driving range on the farm and that’s why I built the walls. It was just a hobby, I had no experience at all.” His farm sits on land once occupied by the manor house of the Earl of Wicklow, and Barrett repurposed stones from the historic site into new creations. Several years on, his handiwork has grown beyond walls: dotted across the fields are a huge castle and two round towers, each assembled with patience and care. Despite their scale, Barrett is modest about his craftsmanship, noting a trained mason “would not consider it good.” His latest work, however, has captured hearts and headlines: a stone homage to Irish football, a replica of the Sam Maguire Cup. The original trophy, awarded annually to the All-Ireland senior Gaelic football champions, is one of the most revered symbols in Irish sport. Barrett’s version stands alone in a field, 12 feet wide and built over three months. “It took a bit of time. I could only build an inch or so each day. If I had put on more stone at the same time I was afraid of it collapsing,” he explained. “It’s my wee treat,” he added, “because of my love of football and the fact my daughter plays with the Tyrone minor ladies.” Unlike his other stone features, the towering cup and the castle are reinforced with steel and cement due to their sheer size. While the structures have attracted attention from passers-by and the media, Barrett remains disarmingly self-effacing. Asked whether he keeps photos of his creations, he replied: “Aw, no. I’m much better with a stone, than a camera or phone.” In a corner of Donegal, a farmer’s quiet fascination has turned field stones into landmarks, blending tradition, sport, and personal pride into a landscape all his own.

Media playback is not supported on this device Former England international Luke Robinson has announced his retirement from rugby league on medical advice, drawing a close to a distinguished career that included spells with Wigan, Castleford, Salford and Huddersfield Giants. Robinson, who made his Super League debut at just 17 and has been with Huddersfield since 2008, said specialists warned that continuing to train and play would jeopardise his long-term mobility following recent surgery. “You never want to hear those sorts of words and it does shock you,” Robinson said. “But after a few days the message sinks in and you have to do what’s right for yourself and your family.” The Halifax-born playmaker added that his immediate focus is rehabilitation, but he hopes to remain with the Giants in another role. “I have come to regard this as my club and it’s the only one I want to be at. I want to put something back into them and the local community that has been so supportive of my time here.” Huddersfield managing director Richard Thewlis paid tribute to Robinson’s impact and confirmed the club would continue to support him. “This is a very sad day for all concerned. He has been an absolutely key figure in our rise from cellar dwellers to play-off regulars,” Thewlis said.

Bob Dylan will release his 36th studio album on 2 February, unveiling a collection of 10 songs he pointedly calls “uncovers” rather than covers. “I don’t see myself as covering these songs in any way,” Dylan said of the project. “They’ve been covered enough. Buried, as a matter of fact. What me and my band are basically doing is uncovering them. Lifting them out of the grave and bringing them into the light of day.” The album revisits standards closely associated with Frank Sinatra, including I’m A Fool To Want You, The Night We Called It A Day and Irving Berlin’s What’ll I Do, alongside Nat King Cole’s Autumn Leaves and Some Enchanted Evening from Rodgers and Hammerstein’s South Pacific. Produced by Jack Frost, a name long used by Dylan for his studio work, the record strips back the lush, big-band and orchestral arrangements that defined many of these songs and reframes them for a lean five-piece ensemble. Dylan emphasized the raw, live nature of the sessions. “I’ve wanted to do something like this for a long time but was never brave enough to approach 30‐piece complicated arrangements and refine them down for a five‐piece band,” he said. “That’s the key to all these performances. We knew these songs extremely well. It was all done live. Maybe one or two takes. No overdubbing. No vocal booths. No headphones. No separate tracking, and, for the most part, mixed as it was recorded.” Columbia Records chairman Rob Stringer praised the approach, saying Dylan has infused “new life and contemporary relevance into the songs.” He noted the absence of “strings, obvious horns, background vocals or other such devices often found on albums that feature standard ballads.” The release marks Dylan’s first new music since 2012’s critically acclaimed Tempest. His last five albums have reached new heights of commercial success, and 2009’s Together Through Life became his first to debut at number one in both the US and the UK. With more than 125 million records sold worldwide and multiple Grammy wins, Dylan’s latest venture revisits timeless material with a stark, intimate urgency.

Mohammed Rehman, 25, from Reading, told a London court he was “truly and deeply sorry for everything” and expressed remorse that his wife was “locked away like an animal,” as he and Sana Ahmed Khan, 24, deny preparing acts of terrorism. The Old Bailey heard allegations that Mr Rehman amassed chemicals capable of creating a large bomb. He also denies possessing an article for terrorist purposes. The trial continues. Jurors were told the couple concealed the fact they had married in an Islamic ceremony from Ms Khan’s relatives, who did not approve of her choice of husband. Mr Rehman, who the court heard had taken drugs and was previously divorced, described Ms Khan, an aspiring teacher, as a “precious diamond.” In a letter sent in June to Ms Khan’s mother, Saleen Ahmed Khan, he wrote: “The minute I laid eyes on her, there was nothing more that I could desire from life than to be with her forever.” In the letter, Mr Rehman told Mrs Khan that her daughter had been “dragged into this with me,” insisting she was “completely innocent” and had been “undermined” by their association. He continued: “Had I wished to take your daughter away from you, I would have ran away with her, but I’m not one to take a family apart. I’m truly and deeply sorry for everything and I’m also really sorry if this letter only adds to your pain.” He added: “They could give me a life sentence and I couldn’t care less, but they’ve taken the most beloved and precious thing from me and locked her away like an animal.” Previously, the jury heard a “Jihadi John-style” hunting knife and dangerous chemicals believed suitable for a large bomb were found at Mr Rehman’s home on Radstock Road. Both defendants deny the charges, and proceedings at the Old Bailey are ongoing.

Matthew McSheffery, 29, from Sutton Coldfield, died after being found unconscious at the Individual Bar on Trinity Street in Hanley around 01:00 BST on Saturday. Emergency services responded and he was taken to hospital, where he later died. Staffordshire Police said the death is being treated as unexplained and urged witnesses or anyone with information to come forward. Seven people were arrested on suspicion of affray in connection with an incident at the club and have been released on bail pending further enquiries. In a statement on Facebook, the venue said Mr McSheffery was not involved in any confrontation and that it is fully supporting the ongoing police investigation. The club thanked police and ambulance crews for their swift response and offered condolences to Mr McSheffery’s family and friends.

Sahid Conteh, aged 14, leaves Sierra Leone to begin a four-year sports scholarship in California Sierra Leonean teenager Sahid Conteh is set to leave for the United States to begin a four-year sports scholarship at Dunn School near Santa Barbara, marking a significant milestone for the foundation that identified his talent. Conteh, 14, was selected from a pool of 100 youngsters scouted across 60 locations, reflecting the breadth of the programme’s outreach and its commitment to nurturing potential both on and off the pitch. The foundation, created by Bellamy after visiting Sierra Leone in 2007 while he was a player at Liverpool, has steadily expanded its impact across youth football and education. Chief executive officer Tim Kellow said the initiative aims to scout footballing and academic potential in boys aged 10 and 11, feeding into a football academy that offers five-year scholarships to children aged 11 to 13. Last year, three boys trained with Cardiff City, and this summer two more spent time at Liverpool FC’s academy. Since its formation, the foundation has helped establish the country’s youth football league structure, now involving around 2,400 youngsters—both boys and girls—across some 70 clubs. Bellamy last visited Sierra Leone in 2011, during which he met and trained with Sahid over a 10-day visit. “Sahid is a wonderfully polite and mature and well-rounded boy who has taken to the training and education and life skills so well. We think he is ready,” said Kellow. Conteh expressed his excitement about the opportunity ahead. “I am very excited to be going to America. I am looking forward to meeting new people, playing football and getting a good education,” he said. In January, the foundation also supported a project enabling disadvantaged young people in Cardiff to volunteer in Africa. Ten Cardiff youngsters spent two weeks in Sierra Leone, leading workshops on sexual health, nutrition, skills and football alongside local children. The foundation’s USA co-ordinator, Kelsey Sullivan, will accompany Sahid to California and help him settle into daily life at Dunn School.

The government will make the report public after holding talks with major political parties on 6 January, a senior federal minister said. India’s federal Home Minister P Chidambaram has said the government will publish the Srikrishna Committee’s report on Telangana after consultations with eight recognised political parties from Andhra Pradesh on 6 January. “That is the only way in a democracy and those who respect democracy must also respect the process of democracy,” Mr Chidambaram said, urging stakeholders to engage through dialogue. The report, prepared by a panel headed by former chief justice of the Supreme Court of India BN Srikrishna, was submitted to Mr Chidambaram on Thursday. The committee was set up in February to examine the demand to carve out Telangana as a separate state from Andhra Pradesh, a contentious issue that has sparked sustained political and street-level agitation. While the final decision to create a new state rests with India’s parliament, the Andhra Pradesh assembly must first pass a resolution approving the formation of Telangana, a step that underscores the need for broad political consensus. Correspondents say there are deep divisions within and across parties over the issue. The Congress party, which leads the national government and also holds power in Andhra Pradesh, announced in December last year that Telangana would be formed, but later said more talks were required, prompting criticism and renewed protests. The government has appealed for calm ahead of the report’s publication, fearing fresh unrest. Andhra Pradesh has witnessed demonstrations both for and against statehood, and tensions rose last year after a student died by suicide in support of Telangana. Opponents remain particularly concerned about the future of Hyderabad, the state’s economic hub and home to many major information technology and pharmaceutical firms, which is expected to become the capital of a new Telangana. The upcoming talks aim to chart a path forward amid competing regional and political interests.

Warm temperatures are being experienced widely across Scotland, but so far they are still below the Scottish May record of 30.9C of five years ago. By 14:00 on Thursday, Aboyne in Aberdeenshire reached 27.2C, with Inverness and Aviemore at 25C, and Edinburgh and Glasgow at 24C. BBC Scotland Weather said 27-28C was likely to be Thursday’s peak, compared with typical May averages of 13-16C. Forecasters expect the warmth to persist into Friday, when temperatures could climb as high as 29C. The top May temperature was recorded at Inverailort in the Highlands. This month has delivered warm, dry conditions, a shift from April, which was mostly cold and wet with some snowfall. May is traditionally regarded as one of Scotland’s best months for settled, fine weather, bringing longer spells of sunshine before summer sets in. Warm, dry weather has dominated.

Christine Sugarhood, 66, from West Sussex, died after suffering a heart attack while pulling her husband, Norman, from the sea at the resort of Paphos in Cyprus, local police said. A second British man, aged 61, who tried to save Mrs Sugarhood and provided first aid, also died from a heart attack, according to police in Paphos. The incident took place on Tuesday in the Yeroskipou area, a stretch of coast known for strong currents. Friends and neighbours in Lindfield, near Haywards Heath, where the couple had lived for more than a decade, paid tribute to Mrs Sugarhood. Neighbour Pam Barber said Mr and Mrs Sugarhood were close to their family and grandchildren. “They had family, grandchildren, and they were quite involved with them,” she said. “Her husband is older and I’m not sure how he’s going to manage as I don’t think he’s very well.” Another neighbour, who asked not to be named, described Mrs Sugarhood as “a delightful person” and called the loss “an absolute tragedy.” Mr and Mrs Sugarhood were active members of Lindfield Bowling Club. Match secretary Mick O’Donnell said he believed the couple were in Paphos with other club members, though it was unclear whether they had travelled for a bowling event. “We were shocked to hear that Christine had passed away, and our thoughts are obviously with her husband and family,” he said. “Christine was a popular and very active member in all aspects of the club and she will be greatly missed.” The UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office confirmed that two British nationals had died in Cyprus and said it was providing consular assistance to the families at this difficult time.

Richard Kell, 71, from Abingdon, Oxfordshire, has died following injuries sustained when he hit a tree during RideLondon on 31 July. He was airlifted to hospital and died on 23 August, organisers said, offering condolences to his family and friends. Kell is the second participant to die in this year’s event; Robin Chard, 48, from Bicester, suffered a cardiac arrest during the ride. James Choulaton of the Outdoor Traders cycling club, which Kell belonged to, described him as a passionate, one-of-a-kind cyclist who will be sorely missed. RideLondon is a mass-participation cycling festival, created as part of the London 2012 legacy, featuring closed-road rides for amateurs and professional races across London and Essex.

Halifax reached Wembley for the first time in the club’s history, defeating seventh-tier Nantwich Town 6-4 on aggregate in the FA Trophy semi-finals. Jordan Burrow scored both goals in Saturday’s second leg, a 2-2 draw at The Shay witnessed by 3,009 fans, sealing the Shaymen’s place in the showpiece. Grimsby Town also advanced, with Padraig Amond netting twice in a 2-1 win over Bognor Regis at Blundell Park to complete a 3-1 aggregate victory. The FA Vase final will feature Hereford against Morpeth Town. Hereford overcame Salisbury 2-1 in their second leg to progress 3-1 overall, while Morpeth’s Luke Carr struck an injury-time winner to edge Bowers & Pitsea 4-3 on aggregate. Both finals will be played the same day.

The Supreme Court has agreed to hear the petition on Tuesday. India’s Supreme Court will on Tuesday hear a clutch of petitions challenging the government’s decision to lift a 2014 ban on Jallikattu, the traditional bull-taming sport practiced during the annual January festival. The order, issued last Friday, paves the way for events to resume this month after a year-long halt, and has ignited a fresh clash between animal welfare advocates and supporters who say the sport is integral to regional culture. In 2014, the Supreme Court prohibited the use of bulls in public performances, finding that Jallikattu “severely harmed” the animals and violated the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act. The ban followed sustained objections from animal rights activists and the Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI). On Monday, AWBI, several animal rights groups, and activists filed six petitions urging the court to quash the government’s new order, calling Jallikattu a “cruel sport.” “We have petitioned the Supreme Court to immediately quash the government order,” Gauri Maulekhi of People for Animals told the BBC, describing the move as “against every law and ethic” and a “politically-motivated, people-pleasing exercise.” Jallikattu involves releasing bulls from pens as men attempt to grab prizes tied to the animals’ horns by clinging to the hump for 15-20 metres or three jumps. Over the years, scores of participants have been gored or trampled to death, and hundreds of competitors and spectators have been mauled or injured, prompting persistent safety and welfare concerns. The ban has faced strong criticism from political parties and cultural groups in the state, who argue Jallikattu is a more than 2,000-year-old tradition and among the oldest sports still practiced. With no events held last year, organizers and enthusiasts had anticipated a revival this festival season. Tuesday’s hearing will determine whether the government’s order stands and whether the contests can proceed.

Melinda Korosi, 33, suffered fatal head and neck injuries in Carlisle in September in an attack described by prosecutor Andrew Thomas QC as “exceptional in its brutality.” Neighbours reported hearing screams from the Hungarian woman’s Orton Road home. Miklos Verebes, 29, of no fixed address and also from Hungary, denies murder and three counts of rape. Carlisle Crown Court heard officers when they arrived found Verebes beside Korosi’s body with blood on him. The trial continues.

Police were called to Pitt Lane in Bideford just after 06:00 GMT on Christmas Eve to a man with serious head injuries. The 64-year-old was taken to Derriford Hospital in Plymouth but died on Boxing Day. Detectives say it is not clear how he was injured and death is being treated as unexplained. Officers appealing for witnesses and anyone in Pitt Lane in the early hours of Christmas Eve to come forward.

Cardiff Devils seized a first-leg advantage in the Challenge Cup semi-final, overcoming Belfast Giants after a 2-2 deadlock. The hosts struck through Trevor Hendrikx and Ryan Russell, while Belfast answered via James Desmarais and David Rutherford. Kris Beech added a third for the Giants, but Cardiff powered ahead as Guillaume Doucet, Leigh Salters and Joey Haddad found the net, leaving the Devils in pole position for the return leg. The second leg takes place at the SSE Arena, Belfast, on Tuesday, 23 February, with the final in Sheffield on 6 March. Cardiff are defending champions, having beaten Sheffield last year; Belfast’s last Cup triumph was in 2009.

Lochaber Mountain Rescue Team has reached its 100th call-out of the year earlier than usual, after being deployed across Lochaber. The milestone came Friday when volunteers assisted a walker with a dislocated shoulder on the West Highland Way. The team handled two further incidents over the weekend, including an overdue hillwalker. Members resumed searching on Monday morning for a man reported missing after failing to return from Ben Nevis on Sunday. The operation was stood down when he turned up safe at a nearby campsite. The team typically attends 70 to 100 incidents annually, highlighting rising demand.

The Intellectual Property Office (IPO) has raised an objection to the New College of the Humanities’ attempt to trademark its name, leaving the private Bloomsbury institution’s application unresolved ahead of its planned first intake this autumn. The college, founded by philosopher Anthony Grayling, submitted its proposal in May to protect how its title could be used and to prevent other organisations from adopting it for other purposes. While the IPO has examined the application, it has not formally refused it; instead, the office says the filing faces an “objection to registration,” with the objection issued by the IPO itself. The New College of the Humanities said it will reapply and expressed confidence in securing approval. “We will reapply to trademark our name in due course and we expect a reapplication to be successful,” the college said, noting that it sought protection “before it launched and before it had been used.” The IPO has not disclosed the grounds for its objection. Concerns about the institution’s chosen name were first raised by New College, Oxford, one of the university’s oldest colleges, which feared potential confusion. In response, New College, Oxford submitted its own trademark application in July to protect its long-established title. The Oxford college’s filing was accepted and registered in December. Despite submitting earlier, the New College of the Humanities’ application remains under objection. The naming dispute underscores broader controversy surrounding the London college, which plans to charge £18,000 per year for its degree courses—double the maximum fee cap at publicly funded universities. Announced during a febrile period over tuition fee reforms, the price point provoked strong criticism from student leaders and some academics, who questioned affordability and the implications for access. The college has argued that its model, built around intensive teaching and small seminars, justifies the higher fee. The New College of the Humanities has also faced scrutiny over its use of the term “university college.” Government officials previously challenged this description because the institution has not been granted university college status and does not possess its own degree-awarding powers. Students will instead receive degrees as external candidates of the University of London. Despite this, the college’s website currently describes the institution as a “university college,” which it defends as a generic term indicating the provision of university-level education rather than a claim to formal status. In an effort to broaden access, the college says it will offer reduced fees for some academically outstanding applicants in its first cohort. These merit-based “exhibition places” would charge £7,200 per year, significantly below the headline fee. As the trademark application returns to the IPO, the outcome may help resolve lingering questions about branding and identity for a new entrant seeking to position itself among the UK’s higher education institutions.

E-learning specialist Learning Pool has secured investment from Carlyle Cardinal Ireland (CCI), marking the fund’s first deal in Northern Ireland and setting the stage for accelerated growth. Founded in 2006, Learning Pool employs 80 people and counts the NHS and Capita among its customers. The company said the funding will be used to grow its team and develop new products, supporting its expansion in a UK e-learning market estimated at £675 million. While the size of the deal has not been disclosed, it is understood to be a seven-figure sum. CCI typically invests between €5 million (£4 million) and €50 million (£40 million) in small and medium-sized Irish firms with strong growth potential. Its portfolio includes well-known names such as Lily O’Brien’s chocolates and Payzone. Learning Pool’s existing management team, led by chief executive Paul McElvaney, will remain in place and has committed additional investment as shareholders. McElvaney, who founded the business and was the majority shareholder, said the backing will allow the firm to “fast track” its growth and deliver products more quickly. Jonathan Cosgrave, managing director at the Carlyle Group, said Learning Pool is well positioned to expand its share of the UK e-learning market, adding that CCI had been impressed by the company’s “entrepreneurial leadership team.” John Dolan, managing director at Cardinal Capital Group, noted that the e-learning sector is growing at over 10% per year and said Learning Pool is “ideally placed to meet this demand,” reflecting strong confidence in the firm’s trajectory.

Ronald Koeman launched a scathing assessment of his Everton side after a 2-1 defeat to Leicester City ended their FA Cup campaign and, with it, his hopes of lifting silverware in his first season at Goodison Park. The Dutchman insisted the exit was self-inflicted and warned that significant improvements are needed in the January window to meet the club’s ambitions. “I know what is needed to change,” the 53-year-old said after the loss, which saw Romelu Lukaku’s opener swiftly overturned by two goals from Leicester substitute Ahmed Musa. “If everybody opened his eyes maybe we will get further in our improvement – because that is what this team needs.” Everton showcased new £11m signing Ademola Lookman to the home crowd before kick-off, but Koeman admitted the squad requires more than one addition. Talks continue with Manchester United over midfielder Morgan Schneiderlin, a player Koeman worked with at Southampton, though negotiations have dragged. “I have [the changes] in mind and the board knows because we speak together about what we and the team needs and that is the job of Steve Walsh,” Koeman said, referencing the club’s director of football. “I hope everybody realises what the team needs to get results that are the expectation of this football club.” Koeman refused to blame luck for the defeat, instead condemning a lapse in concentration that allowed Leicester back into the tie almost immediately after Everton took the lead. “It is not bad luck. We did it ourselves and it was just unbelievable how we dropped back,” he said. “It was a lack of concentration at 1-0. I just can’t see how they score the goal to make it 1-1. No pressing on the ball, a pass inside Seamus Coleman and Musa is faster – three defenders for us and it is 1-1. If you play like we did at 1-0 you ask for goals against. That is not the way you need to play at 1-0.” The manager also highlighted the performance of teenager Tom Davies as both a positive and a stark reminder of the team’s shortcomings. “The fact Tom Davies was one of the best players says enough,” he said. With a Premier League fixture against Manchester City looming, Koeman issued a stark warning. Citing City’s 5-0 FA Cup demolition of West Ham, he added: “If we play like the last 30 minutes it can be the same result as against West Ham.”

Brazil’s federal police have secured a new pay deal that averts further industrial action ahead of the World Cup, with agents set to receive a 12% salary increase from July and a further 3.8% rise in January. The agreement follows nationwide strikes earlier this year that union officials say drew an estimated 250,000 agents, underscoring discontent over pay and career prospects as the country prepared to host the tournament, which kicks off on 12 June. Fenapef, the trade union representing federal officers, welcomed the offer and said it had suspended planned strike action “before, during and after the Cup and before the general election” on 5 October 2014. Union president Jones Borges Leal said the government also agreed to establish a working group to address officers’ career progression, a central union demand. The salary adjustments will also apply to typists and forensic teams, officials said. Brazil’s federal police conduct criminal investigations and fight drug trafficking and terrorism, and are responsible for security at the nation’s borders and airports. The government has reinforced security across all 12 host cities, with up to 20,000 security personnel to be deployed in Rio de Janeiro to safeguard the World Cup final on 13 July. The pay deal comes amid a broader wave of labor unrest. Last month, state police forces in at least 14 states struck over pay, and teachers and civil servants have also staged stoppages. Authorities are determined to avoid a repeat of the mass demonstrations during last year’s Confederations Cup, when more than a million people protested against corruption and what they saw as excessive World Cup spending, with many rallies descending into violence.

Anthem said it will acquire smaller rival Cigna for $54bn (£35bn) in a deal that would create the largest health insurer in the United States, intensifying a wave of consolidation sweeping the industry. The agreement, one of the biggest in the sector’s history, follows Aetna’s recently announced $37bn purchase of Humana. If both transactions clear regulatory review, the five largest U.S. health insurers would be consolidated into three dominant players: the combined Anthem-Cigna, UnitedHealth, and the merged Aetna-Humana. Analysts say the deals are being driven by mounting pressure to reduce costs and adapt to a more consumer-focused marketplace. “The landscape has changed completely. Firms are now competing to be the ‘Amazon’ of the healthcare sector. It’s a much more consumer-orientated landscape,” said Forrester analyst Alex Cullen, who cited “huge pressure” on insurers to become more efficient. Much of the upheaval stems from the Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare. The 2010 law expanded access to coverage and introduced rules that reshaped insurer economics, including a ban on denying coverage to people with pre-existing conditions and a requirement that young adults can stay on their parents’ plans until age 26. It also created online marketplaces that allow individuals to compare plans and prices, introducing retail-like transparency that has intensified competition and squeezed margins. By joining forces, Anthem and Cigna aim to combine their customer bases and technology platforms, expand their geographic reach, and strengthen their hand in negotiations with hospitals, physicians, and pharmaceutical companies. Proponents argue that larger scale will enable insurers to extract better prices from drugmakers and providers, helping to curb overall medical inflation. But consumer advocates and some policymakers warn that fewer competitors could ultimately lead to higher premiums and narrower networks. “The business motives are relatively obvious, but we don’t know yet if it’s good for consumers,” Cullen said. Healthcare spending remains a central concern for the U.S. economy. In 2013, the nation spent $2.5 trillion on health care—17.4% of GDP—according to official figures. Per capita spending climbed from $4,129 in 2000 to $7,826 in 2013, underscoring the stakes as regulators scrutinize whether the industry’s biggest-ever tie-ups will deliver promised efficiencies without undermining competition.

A criminal gang that posed as police officers to swindle elderly victims out of their life savings has been jailed at the Old Bailey, after detectives uncovered links between the proceeds and travel from the UK to Syria. Investigators fear some of those who travelled may have had connections to so-called Islamic State. Gang leader Makzhumi Abukar was sentenced to seven years and four months in prison, alongside several accomplices, including former X Factor contestant Nathan Fagan-Gayle. Police said the group’s victims ranged in age from their 70s to their 90s, with the oldest aged 94, and some were defrauded of as much as £130,000. The average age of those targeted was 83. Passing sentence, Judge Anuja Dhir said none of the convicted men had shown genuine remorse and told them their crimes would have a “devastating and lasting impact” on the victims. She praised detectives from Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorism command for their work in bringing the gang to justice, noting the courage of those who came forward to testify. “I was struck by their dignity and their courage when giving evidence about a matter that was so obviously painful for them to relive,” she said. The defendants will serve half their sentences before being eligible for release on licence. The scam, carried out across southern England, saw gang members telephone elderly people and claim to be police officers investigating suspected fraud at the victims’ banks. The callers instructed victims to withdraw cash or transfer funds to accounts for supposed “safe keeping,” and in some cases arranged for “couriers” — gang members posing as police staff — to collect money directly from victims’ homes. Many were manipulated into lying to family, friends and bank staff about their actions, further isolating them and concealing the fraud. World War Two veteran Kenneth Whitaker, who fought at the Battle of Arnhem, was 93 at the time he was targeted. He said he felt “dumb and stupid” after losing £113,000. Barbara Davidson, 86, lost £14,000 she had intended to use to visit relatives in South Africa, and now fears she will never see them again. The Metropolitan Police said around 140 frauds and attempted frauds were identified during the inquiry, and warned the true figure may be higher as some victims were too embarrassed to report what had happened. Officers found 16 telephone lines used by the group, which made 5,695 calls to 3,774 different numbers. Fagan-Gayle received £20,000 from the scam and went on a spending spree. Commander Dean Haydon, head of the Met’s counter-terrorism command, welcomed the sentences. “They callously and systematically defrauded elderly people of their life savings,” he said. “Had we not arrested them and put them before the courts, the group may have gone on to defraud many more victims across the UK.” Police continue to urge the public to be vigilant and to verify the identity of anyone claiming to be from law enforcement or a bank.

But along with the traditional wind farms and solar panels, scientists have also been adding some fun and creativity into the mix with these unusual designs. As countries race to cut carbon emissions and secure cleaner energy, a new generation of projects is redefining what renewable infrastructure can look like. From floating wind turbines to panda-shaped solar arrays, engineers and designers are blending utility with imagination to expand the reach and appeal of green power. Off the northeast coast of Scotland, the world’s first full-scale floating wind farm is taking shape. The project, known as Hywind, is a trial based in Peterhead that aims to unlock wind resources in waters too deep for conventional bottom-fixed turbines. By anchoring turbines to floating foundations, developers can capture stronger, steadier winds far offshore. If performance meets expectations, Hywind is projected to produce enough electricity to power around 20,000 homes, offering a glimpse of how deep-water wind could complement existing onshore and nearshore installations. In China, creativity is front and center at a solar farm in Datong that departs from the standard grid of panels. Designers arranged the array to form the outline of the country’s national animal, the Giant Panda, turning a power plant into a symbol of conservation and innovation. Covering an area about the size of two football pitches, the project’s backers say that once fully completed it will generate enough energy to supply roughly 16,400 homes, while also serving as a playful landmark to engage the public. Not all imaginative ideas make it off the drawing board. In 2015, Dutch renewable energy company Qurrent floated plans for what it called the world’s first sustainable theme park, powered entirely by wind. The concept envisioned rides drawing electricity from turbines—and even rides built into the turbines themselves, including a spiraling water slide around a tower and a “turbine blade booster” attraction. The designs were part of a study to test feasibility, and the company says it currently has no plans to build the park, though the proposal sparked widespread interest. In Singapore, a man-made forest of “supertrees” has become a striking emblem of urban sustainability. The 18 towering structures in Bay South Garden are equipped with solar panels that generate electricity for lighting and to power air vents. Acting as vertical gardens, they host a variety of plants that help cool the city by providing shade. Their distinctive shape also collects rainwater, which is filtered and released back into the environment. Further south, Australian firm Carnegie Wave Energy has developed wave power technology that operates entirely underwater. By placing devices below the surface, the system is less exposed to storm damage and remains invisible from the shore. It converts wave motion into electricity much like other tidal plants, but its submerged design minimizes impacts on beachgoers and reduces environmental disruption. Together, these projects highlight how innovation in form and function can broaden renewable energy’s reach—making it more resilient, more accessible, and, at times, more delightful to behold.

The Government will unveil its comprehensive spending review on Wednesday, with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) among the departments expected to face budget cuts, raising concerns across the UK sporting landscape. UK Sport, which funds elite Olympic and Paralympic athletes, currently receives about £45m annually from the DCMS. Any significant reduction, officials warn, could have long-term consequences for Britain’s competitive standing on the world stage. “We’ve obviously done a bit of contingency planning,” said Carr of UK Sport. “But we also live in the real world.” Carr stressed that while any immediate cuts would be unlikely to derail preparations for the Rio 2016 Olympic and Paralympic Games, the impact would be felt in the cycle beyond. He said UK Sport had presented its case to the Treasury, highlighting the tangible and intangible returns from investment in elite sport. “We believe we provide heroes and heroines that enhance the mood of the nation,” Carr added. “Who can forget that magic Saturday in the middle of the London Games when we won those medals on the track?” He noted that one of the enduring outcomes of London 2012 has been the UK’s “unsurpassed reputation” for staging world-class events, pointing to the recent World Gymnastics Championships in Glasgow as an example. “Gymnast after gymnast told me it was the best ever. We can do that. I think our bids and the way we present those championships stand on their merits.” Carr also acknowledged that UK Sport’s “aspiration” for British athletes to surpass London’s medal haul in Rio—65 medals at the Olympics—is ambitious and may not be fully reflected in the official target range to be announced before the Games open on 5 August. “We have an aspirational goal to win more medals in Rio than any other country has done in the Games after they have hosted one,” he said. “That would be 66 medals at the Olympics, 121 at the Paralympics. That’s a tough goal. Next June and July we’ll be in a position to publicly give a medal range: a low level where we’d be disappointed and a high level where we would be very pleased.” Tim Hollingsworth, chief executive of the British Paralympic Association, emphasized that funding is the “underpinning force to our success.” He described sport as “spectacular value for money when it is spent in the right way,” generating national pride and delivering broader societal benefits. “Our Paralympians, in particular, can teach people as well as enjoying the sport,” he said. “You can then get a situation where people will watch the Paralympics and then think differently about disability, challenge their perceptions. There are all kinds of societal benefits, we just need to show it.”

The announcement came as the Edinburgh-based challenger bank saw underlying profit rise by nearly 5%, to £65m. Total income was up more than 5% to £274m in the year to 12 March. Sainsbury’s Bank said it will launch new mortgage products in 2017, unveiling the plan alongside an interim results update that highlighted broad-based growth across lending and insurance. The bank performed strongly in the personal loans market, with 15% year-on-year growth in advances to new customers. Its portfolio of insurance products also continued to perform well, resulting in new business growth of more than 10% year-on-year. Sales of new home insurance policies increased by more than 25%. In the interim results statement, Sainsbury’s said: “Given the bank’s strong trading performance and the trust people have in the Sainsbury’s brand, we have decided to launch new mortgage products in 2017. We believe these products will complement our existing financial services portfolio and we expect customers to respond well.” The bank added that it was “making good progress” in moving towards “a new, more flexible” banking IT platform, and forecast total transition costs to be “at the top of the £340m to £380m range.” Meanwhile, Edinburgh-based Virgin Money reported a sharp rise in gross mortgage lending, which climbed year-on-year by 30% in the first quarter to a record £2.1bn, giving the bank a market share of 3.4%. The bank said residential gross mortgage lending increased by 35%, while buy-to-let lending was up by 17%. Credit card balances surpassed £1.8bn at the end of the quarter, up from £1.6bn as at 31 December. Virgin Money said it was looking towards an “accelerated target” of £3bn of credit card “outstandings” by the end of 2017. Chief executive Jayne-Anne Gadhia said: “I am delighted to report it has been another excellent quarter for Virgin Money. We had a record start to the year for mortgages and our savings franchise continues to flourish with a strong inflow of cash ISAs. I am particularly pleased with the performance of the credit card business which continues to exceed expectations one year on since launching to the public.” The twin updates underline the momentum among UK challenger banks, with Sainsbury’s expanding into mortgages to complement its financial services offering and Virgin Money consolidating gains in home loans and cards.

Dauda punishes Collin error as Hearts edge Aberdeen; Dons fall short of last season’s points tally Hearts secured a narrow 1-0 win over Aberdeen at Pittodrie, capitalising on a costly goalkeeping error to record their third victory of the year against Derek McInnes’ side. Nigerian forward Abiola Dauda struck the decisive goal after Adam Collin spilled a routine Alim Ozturk free-kick, leaving the Dons unable to recover despite bossing long spells of possession. The result confirms Aberdeen, Premiership runners-up for a second consecutive season, cannot match last term’s 75-point haul. It also underscores the contrasting fortunes of the clubs in 2016, with Robbie Neilson’s Hearts continuing to frustrate the Dons in both league and cup. Aberdeen began with urgency and bite, the kind of intensity McInnes felt had been missing in their earlier defeats at Tynecastle. Niall McGinn and Jonny Hayes repeatedly stretched the visitors out wide, but the hosts lacked a cutting edge in the box. With strikers Adam Rooney and Simon Church sidelined, midfielder Kenny McLean led the line and toiled gamely without a clear sight of goal. Crosses fizzed across the face of Jack Hamilton’s penalty area as Aberdeen dominated territory and the ball, yet clear chances proved scarce. McGinn’s first-half free-kick from a central position dipped too late to trouble the young Hearts goalkeeper. Hearts, sluggish and short of tempo in the early exchanges, offered little until the 34th minute when they finally pieced together a fluent move. The ball broke to Prince Buaben, who bent a measured 25-yard effort towards the left post, drawing a full-stretch save from Collin. The game’s turning point arrived after the interval. Ozturk’s set-piece from distance should have been routine, but Collin failed to gather cleanly, and Dauda reacted quickest to sweep home the rebound. From there, Hearts sat compact, protected Hamilton diligently, and limited Aberdeen to half-chances and hopeful deliveries. Despite sustained pressure, the Dons could not find a leveller and were left to rue the lapse that decided a tight contest with precious few opportunities. With both clubs set to begin Europa League qualifying in just seven weeks—nearly a fortnight before the Euro 2016 final in France—the focus now shifts to recharging quickly and addressing thin attacking options before the demanding early start to next season. Hearts, meanwhile, leave with a statement win to cap an assured third-place campaign.

Qantas has pledged to compensate passengers for all reasonable losses incurred during its weekend fleet grounding, following a request from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). The airline temporarily halted all flights on Saturday amid an industrial dispute, leaving almost 70,000 travellers stranded. Operations resumed on Monday after a court ordered a permanent end to the dispute, clearing the way for services to restart. “Qantas agrees to, and accepts, the ACCC’s request that it compensate passengers for all reasonable losses incurred as a direct result of the grounding,” the airline said in a statement. “Qantas has always intended to ensure that disrupted customers incur no financial loss.” The carrier said it has already offered refunds, rebooking options and compensation for expenses incurred by travellers, and will announce further measures as an apology to affected customers. Earlier, the ACCC said it had asked Qantas for a report detailing the claims received and the redress provided. “It is squarely in the airline’s camp to make good,” ACCC chair Rod Sims said. “If you have incurred additional expenses as a result of the grounding, the ACCC is of the view that Qantas should compensate you for all your reasonable losses.” The regulator’s stance underscores consumer protections following the unprecedented shutdown.

Taoiseach Enda Kenny has signalled that the Government is considering establishing a dedicated security and intelligence unit in the wake of the Manchester bombing, telling the Dáil that options are being examined. Responding to questions from Fianna Fáil leader Micheál Martin, the Taoiseach said he has convened a meeting for Thursday morning bringing together officials from Defence, Justice, Transport and Health to review Ireland’s security posture and coordination. “I was very impressed with the immediate response of the first responders in Manchester to the tragedy,” Mr Kenny said. “There is an issue here as to whether we should have a security and intelligence unit, separate from the way the structure currently operates, and we will reflect on that. It’s important for the Government to be able to give assurance to people that everything humanly possible is done to protect innocent people and the citizens of our country.” He pledged to update the House as deliberations progress, stressing the need to “get it right.” The Gardaí confirmed they are liaising closely with UK security and law-enforcement counterparts. Officials say no specific threat.

Everyone is living longer but rich people's lives are extending faster, the City University London study says People in the UK are living longer than in previous generations, but the pace of improvement is not equal across society, with wealthier groups pulling ahead in recent decades, according to new research from City University London. The study, led by Professor Les Mayhew of Cass Business School, finds that while life expectancy rose steadily through the 20th Century, recent gains have widened lifespan inequalities, especially among men. Using data from the Human Mortality Database, researchers examined the distribution of adult deaths by comparing the youngest 10% with the oldest 5%. From 1870 to 1939, the gap between early and late deaths narrowed. “Everyone benefited from improvements in clean drinking water, better housing, higher incomes and better health,” Prof Mayhew said, emphasising the broad public health advances that uplifted all social groups. After 1950, life expectancy continued to rise; however, the study notes that inequalities persisted rather than diminishing further. In the 1990s, a marked reversal occurred: disparities in when people die widened for the first time since the late 1870s. This shift was particularly pronounced for men, with the distribution of male deaths showing greater divergence between those dying earlier in adulthood and those living into very old age. Commenting on the findings, Prof Mayhew said: “This is partly due to some men now living to exceptionally old ages and in many cases equalling women — but at the other end of the distribution there has been a lack of progress.” The researchers attribute the widening gap largely to lifestyle factors. “Many of the big gains from public health improvements are in the past and personal choices are now much more important,” the report states. Men in lower socio-economic groups are more likely to smoke, drink heavily, and engage in riskier activities at certain stages of life, according to the study. The authors argue that lack of wealth is not directly responsible for the difference in outcomes; rather, the poorest groups are more vulnerable to the cumulative effects of decades of unhealthy behaviours and income inequality, while wealthier, better-educated individuals tend to find it easier to adopt healthier habits. The negative health impacts of smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, poor diet, and physical inactivity are described as disproportionately affecting the poorest in society. The report calls for policies and programmes that encourage healthier lifestyles and help counter pressures arising from advertising, community norms, and peer influences. Baroness Sally Greengross, chief executive of the International Longevity Centre, described the figures as “particularly worrying” and urged immediate action. “Preventing inequalities in ill health and disability must be a priority for policy action,” she said. A Department of Health spokeswoman said the government aims to ensure everyone has the opportunity to live a long and healthy life, highlighting economic measures as part of the solution. “The number of workless households is at a record low and we know that economic security can provide the foundation for better physical and mental health. We have shown that we are willing to take tough action to protect the public’s health,” she said.
