Worcestershire have bolstered their bowling ranks with the signing of South Africa seamer Kyle Abbott on a short-term deal, pending visa approval and clearance from Cricket South Africa. The 28-year-old is set to be available from early July through late September, covering a key stretch of the county season across all formats. Abbott brings international pedigree and proven county know-how. He has represented the Proteas in three Tests, 20 one-day internationals and 14 Twenty20 internationals, and previously impressed in England with Hampshire in 2014 and Middlesex in 2015. During his Hampshire stint, Abbott played a pivotal role in their promotion push, taking 36 wickets in nine Championship matches as the club returned to Division One. “I enjoyed my previous time in county cricket and hope I can play my part in helping Worcestershire get back into Division One,” Abbott said. “They came close to staying up last season and have a good squad of young players who are only going to get better. Hopefully I can play my part in terms of taking wickets and passing on any advice, and also making an impact in white-ball cricket.” Worcestershire were relegated to Division Two in 2015, but director of cricket Steve Rhodes believes Abbott’s experience and versatility will be invaluable at New Road. “It’s very exciting to welcome Kyle on board,” Rhodes said. “He’ll pass on some excellent experience to our younger bowlers and we know he is the type of person that has the right character for our dressing room. He’s not just a Test match bowler. He’s a one-day bowler and has also got good T20 skills – he’ll potentially be playing in all three formats.” Abbott’s signing underlines Worcestershire’s intent to mount a strong promotion challenge while strengthening their white-ball options.

A series of violent crimes in an underpass linking Station Road and Oasis Leisure Centre has renewed calls for a safer crossing, and Swindon Borough Council says a bid to government is needed for a £10m pedestrian bridge. The underpass, which runs beneath the railway line, has been the scene of incidents. Last June a man was stabbed to death, earlier this week a woman was sexually assaulted, and last year there was an attempted robbery and an assault on a woman. “We want to put a pedestrian bridge across the rail line to connect North Star with the town centre, but getting it built is linked to the wider regeneration of that area,” a council spokesman said. “The cost of building a bridge will be in excess of £10m, so we will need to put in a bid to central government for the money and show the wider benefits it will bring. We won’t get funding for that amount simply because a bridge would be safer for users than an underpass — we have to show other reasons as well.” North Swindon’s Conservative MP, Justin Tomlinson, backed the move, saying: “This should be a thing of the past. As part of the town centre regeneration we would be better off having a pedestrian bridge with visibility and access.”

VW’s electric ID Buzz rekindles Kombi spirit, launches in 2022 without factory camper option Volkswagen’s iconic microbus is poised for a modern comeback, with the all-electric ID Buzz making its debut in January and slated to hit roads in 2022. VW says it has been inundated with pleas to “please build this car,” and plans to sell the new van in North America, Europe and China, alongside a dedicated cargo variant. The launch taps decades of nostalgia for the Kombi, also known as the Bulli in Germany, which first went into production in 1950. Originally conceived as a utilitarian, jack-of-all-trades van, it became synonymous with counterculture road trips and camping. Factory-built campers were never part of VW’s own lineup. The movement began in 1950 when engineering firm Westfalia-Werke, responding to a request from a British Army officer, created the first “Camping Box” to transform a VW van into a mobile home. Westfalia subsequently became VW’s designated subcontractor for camper conversions. While the ID Buzz will launch without a factory camper configuration, its design invites customization. The microbus features a hand-wave-activated sliding door and electric motors at both ends, opening up a generous, flat-floored interior—attributes that enthusiasts say are ideal for bespoke touring conversions. Westfalia-Werke, now Westfalia Mobile and owned by Daimler-Chrysler, continues to convert vans, including VWs. Whether VW and Westfalia rekindle their historic partnership remains unclear, but the aftermarket community that turned countless Kombis into homes-on-wheels suggests a new generation of DIY “hippy vans” is plausible. The ID Buzz also marks a symbolic bookend to the original era of VW microbuses. The last classic Kombi, or VW T2, rolled off a Brazilian production line in 2013, when tightening local safety rules made further adaptations unviable. With an electric drivetrain and modern tech, VW aims to blend heritage with future-focused mobility. For now, fans eager to relive Kombi culture may simply dust off the arc welding gear and start planning their builds.

A father from Aylesbury has praised hospital staff as “amazing” after his fiancée collapsed at home while heavily pregnant and underwent an emergency Caesarean section. In May, 38-year-old Nicola Lansdown suffered a bleed on the brain just two days before she was due to have an induced labour. She was rushed to the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, where doctors delivered the couple’s daughter, Lexi, before placing Ms Lansdown in an induced coma. Subsequent tests revealed a brain tumour. Nicola spent two days in a neurological ward and then four weeks in a medically induced coma while doctors worked to stabilise her condition. Now out of intensive care, she can speak up to 100 words and has regained some feeling on her right side. Her rehabilitation is due to begin next week. Her partner, 38-year-old Kevin Smees, said he was overwhelmed by the care the family received and has started fundraising for the hospital charity in gratitude. “I can’t thank them enough,” he said. “I owe them everything. I can’t stop thinking how great these people are..... they really know their stuff, so I feel I just want to give something back. What they did over there was absolutely amazing.” Mr Smees described the support he has received since launching his appeal as humbling. “I thought if I could get £500 I’d be happy, but the generosity of friends, family and some people completely anonymous..... it just shows what kind people there are out there. I’m amazed really. I’m very shocked and stunned and very appreciative of everything that people have done.” He called baby Lexi a “very good little girl.” “She’s had the odd moment like babies do, but in general I can’t complain at all,” he said. “From what was a bad situation..... to where Nicola is today, it’s an absolute miracle. That’s the only way I can describe it.” Sarah Vaccari, from Oxford Radcliffe Hospitals Charitable Funds, said it was “wonderful” to meet the family and thanked Mr Smees for his extraordinary efforts. “We are incredibly grateful to Kevin and his family for thinking of the hospital charity. To know that he somehow found the time to raise this money whilst caring for a newborn and looking after his very ill fiancée is simply inspiring. We thank him wholeheartedly.”

Survey finds nearly half of Welsh parents use childcare, most rely on unpaid help from family and friends New figures from Statistics Wales show that 49% of parents with children up to age 14 use childcare, and among those users, 77% said their child was looked after by family or friends for free. The findings, published Thursday in the National Survey for Wales 2014-15 Childcare report, highlight the extent to which informal networks underpin care provision across the country. The report details how frequently informal carers step in: 51% of care provided by family or friends amounted to between one and 10 hours a week, 32% covered 10 to 30 hours, and 6% said relatives or friends looked after their child for at least 30 hours weekly. While such arrangements help parents bridge gaps, charities warn they are often a necessity rather than a preference. Joy Kent, chief executive of Chwarae Teg, which supports women in work, said parents lean on family because it is “accessible and affordable.” She added: “In the conversations that we have with women, childcare comes up as the number one barrier in terms of their engagement with work. They do rely heavily on informal support networks and it’s not necessarily out of choice.” Kent warned that the pressure is particularly acute for older women. “There is also an issue with older women being in a position where they are looking after older members of the family as well as their grandchildren. They are a sandwich generation who have had to change their lifestyle and expectations as a result of this.” Lynne Hill, policy director at Children in Wales, called the statistics “quite worrying.” She said: “It’s a challenging time for parents trying to maintain a work/life balance. I understand that childcare is expensive. It’s because people are providing a quality product in a quality setting.” But the expense, she noted, forces families to make difficult decisions about how to “make ends meet,” particularly during the summer holidays, when demand spikes. “For many it is family and friends that provide back up childcare,” she said, adding that parents of children with disabilities face additional obstacles finding suitable care. Affordability and availability remain persistent concerns across the survey. Overall, 46% of parents reported finding it difficult to afford childcare, rising to 52% among those with children aged three or four. Separately, 40% of parents with a child aged five to 14 said they struggled to secure childcare during school holidays. Responding to the report, the Welsh Government said it recognised the importance of accessible, affordable childcare for working families. “This is why we have committed to offer working parents 30 hours a week of free early education and childcare for three and four year olds,” a spokesman said. “Work is already under way with local authorities, parents and providers to develop and deliver the offer and the first pilot schemes will be rolled out in September 2017.” The findings intensify debate over supporting parents and expanding affordable, high-quality childcare across Wales right now.

Australian opener Chris Rogers produced a monumental unbeaten 241 to power Middlesex to a record fourth-innings victory at Lord’s over Yorkshire, in a chase that rewrote the county’s books and left their opponents reflecting on a rare and bruising defeat. Rogers struck 37 boundaries and shared an unbroken fourth-wicket stand of 145 with Neil Dexter, who finished 72 not out, as Middlesex surged past their previous highest successful fourth-innings pursuit at Lord’s of 366-5, set against Sussex in 1926. While the total fell short of Middlesex’s overall club record fourth-innings chase of 502-6 achieved at Nottinghamshire at Trent Bridge in 1925, it was the highest winning fourth-innings score the club has compiled at Lord’s and the third-highest chase ever completed on the ground. It was only the third time Yorkshire have conceded over 400 runs in a fourth innings and lost: in 2009, Somerset chased 479-6 at Taunton, and three years earlier Hampshire won by five wickets with 404-5 at Headingley. Rogers also etched his name into individual history by registering the Championship’s 11th fourth-innings double-century, matching the 241 not out made by fellow Australian Justin Langer against Kent in 1999. It was the 36-year-old left-hander’s 67th first-class hundred, a landmark that lifted his career average to exactly 50. Beginning the final morning with Middlesex 230-1, Rogers survived a huge lbw appeal from Ryan Sidebottom and later edged Jack Brooks through the slips, but otherwise he was in complete command as Yorkshire’s attack laboured fruitlessly to dislodge him. It was a testing first outing as Championship captain for England’s Joe Root, who led Yorkshire with county skipper Andrew Gale having dropped himself. Sidebottom did strike early by trapping Dawid Malan lbw for 35, and Kane Williamson’s off-spin accounted for Eoin Morgan for 27, briefly offering Yorkshire hope of a breakthrough. But Dexter joined Rogers to close out the chase with authority, finishing the match in style by striking Williamson for two fours and a six in the space of four deliveries. Rogers hailed the collective effort as he spoke to BBC London 94.9. “It’s been a great day. Hopefully, the club can go from strength to strength from that. In a fourth innings, to play like that and win, doesn’t happen every day. To get over the line is something to be very proud of. But the other guys deserve a lot of credit too. They came out and played very well and took the pressure off me. It was almost a perfect run chase. We’ve been criticised for our batting, so that can be an excellent step for us.” Yorkshire coach Jason Gillespie paid tribute to Rogers’ masterwork. “It was a fantastic knock. Sometimes you have to take your hat off to the opposition. We gave it our best, but it just didn’t quite work in the second innings with the ball. You can’t rest on your laurels, you need to make sure your skills are right each and every over.” BBC London 94.9’s Kevin Hand summed up the scale of the achievement: Middlesex completed their highest chase at Lord’s, the third highest at the ground and the third highest in their history. Rogers’ 241 was just four runs shy of equalling the highest individual score in a successful fourth-innings chase, and the result ranks among the greatest in the county’s 150-year story.

UEFA has charged Celtic over crowd trouble during the 1-1 draw with Manchester City at the Etihad Stadium last December. It is the 10th time in five years the Scottish Premiership side have faced action from European football’s governing body for fans’ behavior. The result left Celtic bottom of their group. The club has yet to comment on the latest fine.

It comes after environmental campaigners said the issue was causing a public health crisis. Scotland’s air quality is under renewed scrutiny as the Scottish Parliament’s Environment, Climate Change and Land Reform Committee launches an inquiry into toxic air, following warnings from campaigners and fresh evidence of widespread pollution. A January report by Friends of the Earth Scotland found that some of the country’s most polluted streets regularly breached the European limit for nitrogen dioxide (NO2), a harmful gas produced largely by vehicle engines. Recent evidence also suggests air pollution may contribute to as many as 15,000 early deaths in Scotland each year. The European Ambient Air Quality directive sets the annual limit for NO2 at 40 micrograms per cubic metre. According to the report, the top three Scottish streets most polluted with NO2 in 2016 were Hope Street in Glasgow, St John’s Road in Edinburgh and Wellington Road in Aberdeen. NO2 has been linked to respiratory disease and is especially dangerous for vulnerable groups. Graeme Dey, convener of the committee, said Scotland must take air quality seriously to meet its ambitious environmental and public health targets. “Not only can poor air quality impact our natural environment and wildlife, but it is also bad for our own health and is especially harmful for the young, elderly and people who already have heart and lung conditions,” he said. “In fact, recent evidence suggests air pollution may be a contributory factor to 15,000 early deaths in Scotland each year. As part of our new inquiry, the committee wants to hear whether Scotland is doing all that it can to tackle toxic gases and how this fits into the overall plans to cut pollution within the UK and EU.” Dr Richard Dixon, director of Friends of the Earth Scotland, welcomed the inquiry, describing the “national disgrace” of air pollution as causing thousands of deaths and imposing a billion pound cost on the economy. “Air pollution endangers the most vulnerable in our society — the young, the elderly and those with existing health problems,” he said. “Toxic air has been linked with heart attacks, strokes, cancers, and even mothers giving birth to babies prematurely and with reduced birth weights. Tackling air pollution by getting cars off the roads will deliver huge co-benefits in terms of reducing climate emissions.” Transport recently became the single biggest source of greenhouse gases in Scotland, with figures still stuck around 1990 levels. The committee is inviting evidence from the public, experts and industry on how best to curb pollution and comply with domestic and European standards.

Pentagon officials are downplaying concerns after a report cited by the Washington Post said numerous U.S. weapons designs were compromised in cyber intrusions, including systems for combat aircraft, naval vessels and missile defenses. The findings stem from a Pentagon advisory paper and follow a public Defense Science Board (DSB) report in January that warned the United States remains unprepared for a full-scale cyber attack. According to the Washington Post, the compromised designs include advanced Patriot missile systems known as PAC-3, the Army’s Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad), and the Navy’s Aegis ballistic-missile defense system. Aircraft and ship programs were also cited, among them the F/A-18 fighter jet, the V-22 Osprey, the Black Hawk helicopter, the Navy’s new Littoral Combat Ship, and the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter, the most expensive weapons system ever built. The reports do not detail the extent of the theft, but correspondents note that access to such designs could offer insights useful to an adversary in a future conflict. The Washington Post’s revelations come as Australia disclosed that Chinese hackers stole floor plans for the new headquarters of its domestic intelligence agency, underscoring the global reach of cyber espionage. In a statement, U.S. defense department spokesman George Little said the Pentagon maintains “full confidence in our weapons platforms.” He added, “The Department of Defense takes the threat of cyber espionage and cyber security very seriously, which is why we have taken a number of steps to increase funding to strengthen our capabilities. Suggestions that cyber intrusions have somehow led to the erosion of our capabilities or technological edge are incorrect.” The Defense Science Board did not respond to requests for comment from the BBC. The Pentagon did not say whether additional specific programs were under review as part of its cybersecurity efforts.

Heavy rainfall has triggered flooding across the Dominican Republic, forcing thousands to seek refuge with friends and relatives after rivers burst their banks. Authorities say more than 4,000 homes have been inundated and at least 50 have been destroyed. President Danilo Medina expanded a state of emergency from four to eight provinces as rescue operations intensified. The military saved 13 stranded residents in Los Naranjos, in the country’s northeast. Forecasters warn that downpours will continue on Tuesday, though the weather front is expected to shift away from the worst-hit areas later in the day. Additional rainfall is likely over the weekend, raising concerns of flooding. Communities along rivers and on hillsides have been urged to remain vigilant for flash floods and landslides. The disaster comes less than two months after Hurricane Matthew battered the island of Hispaniola, shared by the Dominican Republic and Haiti, compounding recovery efforts.

White House: 5.6 Million Fingerprints Stolen in OPM Breach, Far Exceeding Initial Estimate The White House has confirmed that more than 5.6 million fingerprint records were stolen in the massive cyberattack on the Office of Personnel Management (OPM), a sharp increase from the initial estimate of 1.1 million. The OPM, which serves as the personnel office for the U.S. government, maintains records on approximately 21.5 million current and former federal employees and contractors. The breach, discovered in April, resulted in the theft of a wide range of sensitive data, including Social Security numbers, names, addresses, health and financial information, security clearance details, and biometric identifiers. While the extent of the fingerprint theft is greater than first believed, OPM officials sought to temper concerns, saying the potential for abuse of fingerprint data is currently limited. However, they acknowledged that the risk could grow as technology evolves and biometric authentication becomes more prevalent across government and commercial systems. To address the threat, an inter-agency working group with specialized expertise has been convened to analyze how fingerprint data could be misused now and in the future. The task force includes representatives from the FBI, the Pentagon, and the Department of Homeland Security. OPM said it will soon launch a large-scale effort to notify all individuals whose information was compromised. Security experts emphasized the unique challenges posed by biometric breaches. “The biggest concern about biometrics since day one has been revocation,” said Ken Munro of Pen Test Partners. “It is easy to get a new password, pin or credit card after a breach but it's rather harder to get new fingers.” The announcement comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping begins a state visit to the United States, with cybersecurity expected to be a key topic in talks with President Barack Obama. U.S. officials and security researchers have long suspected China’s involvement in the OPM intrusion, an allegation Beijing has consistently denied. As investigations continue, the federal government is grappling with the long-term implications of losing immutable biometric data and reinforcing defenses against future attacks.

Best found guilty of instructing jockey Paul John not to let two horses run to their full ability, prompting the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) to acknowledge a significant “fairness” issue in its disciplinary process. The authority admitted it used solicitor Matthew Lohn as chairman of its disciplinary panel while he was simultaneously being paid by the regulator to advise on other matters, a dual role that was not disclosed at the time. A BHA spokesman said the organization takes full responsibility and apologized for the non-disclosure, which created an appearance of bias and necessitated a rehearing. “While there was no suggestion of any actual bias in this case, the BHA now accepts that it was an error not to disclose details of Mr Lohn’s other paid work,” the spokesman said. Best has denied any wrongdoing. The case, centered on instructions given to jockey Paul John not to let two horses run as fast as possible, remains a flashpoint for debate over integrity and transparency in racing’s disciplinary structures. BHA Chief Executive Nick Rust said the authority would make a full statement once proceedings are concluded. He emphasized that although BHA disciplinary panels are not judicial bodies, their processes “must not only be fair, but, particularly relevant in this case, be seen to be fair.”

England all-rounder Ben Stokes has accepted a charge for breaching the International Cricket Council’s code of conduct after making an “inappropriate comment” picked up by the stump microphone during the second Test against West Indies at Headingley. The incident occurred in the 101st over of the tourists’ first innings after Stokes was edged to the boundary by Shai Hope. Stokes, 26, received one demerit point for the offence, taking his tally to three and leaving him one point away from a suspension. Under ICC regulations, four or more demerit points within a 24-month period convert into suspension points, triggering a ban. An ICC statement confirmed Stokes’ current total and detailed the timeline of his previous sanctions. His earlier demerit points were recorded on 30 October 2016 and 26 November 2016. In line with the two-year rolling window, the first will be removed from his record on 30 October 2018, with the second expiring on 26 November 2018. Saturday’s charge was brought by on-field umpires Chris Gaffaney and S Ravi, along with third umpire Marais Erasmus and fourth official Nick Cook. England won the opening Test of the three-match series by an innings and 209 runs. However, West Indies will resume the third day of the second Test on Sunday with a 71-run lead and five first-innings wickets in hand.

ITV has removed Pakistan-born actor Marc Anwar, 45, from Coronation Street with immediate effect after screenshots from his private Twitter account showed racially offensive remarks about Indian people and calls for Pakistani actors to stop working in India. The posts, first reported by the Sunday Mirror, appeared after the Indian army said it had killed a militant in a gunfight in the disputed region of Kashmir, claimed by both India and Pakistan. Anwar joined the long-running ITV soap in February 2014 as Sharif Nazir, a member of the first Muslim family on the famed cobbled street. In a statement, ITV said: “We are deeply shocked by the entirely unacceptable, racially offensive comments made on Twitter by Marc Anwar. We have talked to Marc and, as a consequence of his comments, he will not be returning to Coronation Street with immediate effect.” The broadcaster said episodes featuring Anwar already filmed will still be shown, but his presence will be minimized while producers work to write the character out. Anwar has appeared in Captain Phillips and The 51st State. Coronation Street has aired on ITV since 1960. The controversy underscores ongoing tensions around Kashmir and the sensitivities surrounding cross-border cultural work between India and Pakistan.

The government will refit an RAF Voyager A330 air-to-air refuelling aircraft at a cost of about £10m so it can double as transport for senior ministers and members of the Royal Family, officials have confirmed. Ministers say the move will cut annual costs by around £775,000 compared with chartering flights, while ensuring the aircraft remains available in its primary role as an air tanker when not in use for passenger transport. A government source said the Prime Minister’s flights, currently using either Royal Squadron planes or long-haul charters, cost on average £6,700 per flying hour. By contrast, the refitted RAF Voyager would cost around £2,000 per hour. The aircraft would be equipped to meet security and communications requirements associated with transporting ministers and the Royal Family, and continue serving refuelling duties when required. Full details are expected in Monday’s Strategic Defence and Security Review, part of broader efforts to squeeze savings from defence and across Whitehall. Most government departments are facing budget reductions of at least 25% over the next four years as the Treasury prepares to set out the spending review. The SNP’s Stewart Hosie called for “absolute transparency” over the project to ensure “the best deal is made on behalf of the tax-payer.” He added: “This announcement comes just a week before the spending review when we can expect to hear of more cuts from the Tories, which are already hitting people hard.” There is no definitive timeline for the aircraft to come into service, though officials indicated it could be available as early as next year, subject to the completion of modifications and certification. A government spokesperson said: “As part of the government’s defence review, we have been looking at ways to make better use of the RAF fleet to transport senior ministers and consequently deliver savings for taxpayers. We have decided to adapt one of our existing Voyager aircraft so that, in addition to its primary air tanking role, it can transport Ministers and it will also be available for the Royal family to use.” The move follows earlier debates over prime ministerial travel. Gordon Brown scrapped plans drawn up under Tony Blair to acquire two private jets, proposals that were nicknamed “Blair Force One” in reference to the US president’s aircraft.

Emyvale prospect Darren McAllister, a former Minor star, struck inside the opening minute to set Monaghan on their way to a tight 1-13 to 0-15 victory over Fermanagh at Clones. The lightning finish past keeper Chris Snow gave the hosts an early cushion, but Fermanagh, powered by Tomás Corrigan’s dead-ball kicking, clawed back and led midway through the second half. Corrigan finished with nine frees as the visitors punished Monaghan indiscipline, while points from Daryl McCusker, Pádraig McCusker, Eoin Donnelly and substitutes Conall Corrigan and Darragh Teague kept Fermanagh in the hunt. Monaghan, however, found answers down the stretch. Thomas Kerr top-scored from play with 0-4, Micheál Bannigan added 0-3 including a free, and the Hughes brothers, Darren and Kieran, chipped in 0-2 apiece to tilt the contest back their way. Rory Beggan marshalled a disciplined Monaghan defence, while late introductions Niall McAdam and Stephen Carey helped close it out. Despite Fermanagh’s spirited surge, the goal ultimately proved decisive as the hosts shaded a compelling opener. In the section’s other fixture, St Mary’s edged Antrim by 2-16 to 3-12, sealing a narrow one-point win. The result leaves Monaghan well placed in Section B after the opening round.

Worcester Warriors’ resurgence has gathered pace with a run of four straight Premiership victories and five wins in their last six matches, a sequence that has lifted them 16 points clear of bottom club London Irish and all but secured their top-flight status for next season. Former Ireland international lock Donncha O’Callaghan, 37, says the turnaround has been driven by a sharpened defensive edge and the demanding standards set by the club’s coaching staff. “I love working with him,” O’Callaghan said of defence coach “Crossy.” “It’s tough but you get challenged. Crossy does an awful lot of work with guys individually as well as a group.” O’Callaghan, who joined Warriors at Sixways last summer, believes the meticulous approach has empowered players to improve and execute under pressure. “Crossy looks at you and, even at 37, he sees you as someone who can learn and improve in the type of defence he wants you to play,” he told BBC Hereford & Worcester. “It gives you massive energy when the coaches give you a play or pattern out on the pitch and you do and get a result out of it. Everyone grows a bit.” That growth has been evident in Dean Ryan’s side over the past six weeks, with Worcester now able to shift focus from survival to climbing the table. With only four matches remaining, Warriors are aiming to reel in Bath, Gloucester and Sale, all hovering just ahead of them. “We’re now looking at a process—how we can put into practice what we’re saying in the week,” O’Callaghan added. “Results have fallen out the back—before we were all worried about getting the result and not about how we do it. There’s a maturity in the squad now and the coaches have done a fantastic job.” There has been movement within the squad as well. Fellow lock Darren O’Shea, who has largely been displaced by O’Callaghan this season, will return to his former club Munster at the end of the campaign. O’Shea signed for Worcester in May 2014 and played a key role in their 2014/15 Championship and British & Irish Cup-winning season. Meanwhile, centre Max Stelling has been named in England’s squad for the HSBC World Rugby Sevens Series event in Hong Kong from 8–10 April, a selection that underscores the individual progress being made at Sixways alongside the team’s collective improvement.

Martin Trollope-Bellew surprised colleagues by proposing to fellow Conservative Rosemary Woolley during his final speech as authority chairman in the council chamber. Ms Woolley said she was caught unawares and did not answer immediately, pausing for a few minutes before saying yes. The couple, together for more than 12 years, reflected on the moment. Trollope-Bellew said he felt the chamber was an appropriate time and place to ask, marking the close of his tenure. His bride-to-be called it ‘definitely a shock’ and joked she delayed her reply not to appear too keen, adding she thought he ought to wait before she answered.

Rafael Nadal reclaimed the Monte Carlo Masters title with a gritty 7-5 5-7 6-0 victory over Gael Monfils, sealing his 68th win from 100 ATP World Tour finals and drawing level with Novak Djokovic on a record-equaling 28 Masters crowns. The triumph, achieved in two hours and 46 minutes, also marked the Spaniard’s ninth success at the event and extended his unmatched streak of winning at least one clay-court title in each of the past 13 years. Nadal, 29, had navigated a demanding route to the final, beating Andy Murray in the semifinals, and found himself pushed again by 13th seed Monfils, who earned the backing of the Monte Carlo Country Club crowd. The Frenchman saved a set point before a costly double fault gifted Nadal the opening set. The second set turned into a test of nerve and endurance, featuring five breaks of serve as Monfils edged the former world number one to level the match. From there, Nadal surged. He tightened his grip on the rallies, broke early and repeatedly, and raced into a 5-0 lead in the decider, closing out the match with a forehand winner on championship point. Across a match littered with chances, the pair conceded 34 break points; Nadal converted eight of his 21 opportunities while Monfils took five from 13. For Monfils, 29, it was a third Masters final defeat after a strong season that included a runner-up finish in Rotterdam. Yet he made Nadal earn every point, drawing roars of approval with his athletic shot-making and refusal to let the contest slip without a fight. Nadal, who last won a Masters title in Madrid two years ago and lost the 2013 Monte Carlo final to Djokovic, called this triumph “so special.” He added: “I had a tough season last year, but I’ve had better preparation this year—even with a tough start to the season. It’s great to win a Masters title again. I hope this week will help me a lot.” The Spaniard withdrew from last month’s Miami Open with a virus but appears reinvigorated as the clay swing gathers pace. With Monte Carlo secured, Nadal’s focus turns to next month’s French Open, where he will aim for an unprecedented 10th title at Roland Garros.

Three civilians engaged in mine-clearance work have been kidnapped near Kibumba, about 19 km north of Goma in eastern DR Congo, the UN said. The trio are believed to be two Congolese and a Zimbabwean, and went missing Thursday afternoon, BBC correspondent Maud Jullien reported. Locals say their vehicle was found abandoned with the engine running. It is unclear who seized them or where they are held. Residents say the Congolese army’s presence has been reduced in recent weeks, and insecurity has risen. Government officials report incursions by Rwandan soldiers, an allegation Rwanda denies. The claims cannot be independently verified. The abductions come amid volatility in North Kivu, where multiple armed groups operate along the Rwanda border. Rwanda has twice sent troops into DR Congo and was a key player in conflict that killed up to six million people. In 2013, the UN mission in DR Congo (Monusco) worked with the army to flush out M23 rebels. A planned operation against the FDLR earlier this year was halted after a dispute over two Congolese generals accused of human rights abuses. Monusco, one of the world’s largest UN missions with more than 20,000 personnel, says it is seeking information on the missing civilians as mine-clearance efforts continue in a region scarred by years of fighting. Local leaders urged the abductors to release them and called for patrols to protect aid workers. Mine-clearance teams are vital to opening roads and farms contaminated by unexploded ordnance.

Thousands of head teachers across southern England have written to their MPs warning that schools face job losses and cuts to subjects unless the government urgently clarifies how much money will be available in the coming years. The group of about 4,000 heads, representing 17 local authorities, says current levels of funding are “unsustainable” and that uncertainty over future budgets is hampering planning and risking the quality of education. The heads’ intervention comes amid questions over a Conservative manifesto commitment to provide an extra £1bn per year for schools. That pledge depended on ending universal free school meals for infants, a proposal ministers now say they are “reflecting” on, with revised plans yet to be set out. The Department for Education has not presented an alternative funding plan, prompting heads to call for immediate “clarity” to prevent further strain on school budgets. In a joint letter to MPs, the heads warn they could be forced into “the unwanted position of having to ask parents for regular financial contributions in order to prop up our devastated budgets.” They say they have been pressing for a decision on funding for two years but “unfortunately schools continue to wait in vain for improved funding.” The signatories include schools in areas with many Conservative MPs, spanning Brighton, Cambridgeshire, Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, East Sussex, Essex, Hertfordshire, Norfolk, Northamptonshire, Oxfordshire, Peterborough, Suffolk, Surrey, Thurrock, West Sussex and Wokingham. They argue that without a clear settlement, schools will have to cut staff and scale back subject choices to balance their books. Head teachers are also seeking confirmation on whether the manifesto’s extra money is “still on the table” and specifics on minimum per-pupil funding levels. They want a clear timetable for implementing the long-planned National Funding Formula, which is intended to make allocations fairer by reducing the wide disparities between schools and regions. Adding to the pressure, unions and campaigners have intensified calls to lift the public sector pay cap, which could increase teachers’ salaries. The independent pay review body for teachers is expected to publish its recommendations in the summer. Any pay rise above current assumptions, if accepted, would need to be funded, as staff costs account for the largest share of school spending. Jules White, a West Sussex head teacher who coordinated the letter, said a pay increase for teachers would be welcomed by schools but must not be unfunded. “Our campaign is focused on adequate funding..... to ensure that there are enough teachers, support staff and equipment in every school,” he said. “It’s no good just awarding a pay increase if this squeezes school budgets and overall resources still further.” Responding to the growing pressure, a Department for Education spokeswoman said the government remained committed to increasing overall funding and to reforming how it is distributed. “The core schools budget has been protected in real terms since 2010 and is set to rise from £41bn in 2017-18 to over £42bn in 2019-20 with increasing pupil numbers,” she said. The department has consulted on a national funding formula and received more than 25,000 responses. “We are analysing in detail and will respond in due course,” she added. Head teachers say assurances and a firm schedule are needed quickly so schools can set budgets, plan staffing and protect the breadth of their curriculum for the next academic years.

title: Delaney, an ex-London Irish player, returned in 2012 and had spells as forwards coach and interim head coach before taking the role in 2015. However, changes have been made to the rugby department following relegation from the Premiership last season. London Irish have confirmed Glenn Delaney’s departure as they reshape their rugby department after Premiership relegation. The former Exiles player rejoined in 2012, served as forwards coach and interim head coach, and took charge in 2015. His exit comes amid broader coaching changes at the club. Chief executive Bob Casey said relegation had inevitably led to changes: "Glenn has been a great servant to London Irish. We will all miss him and wish him and his family well." Delaney said: "It is unfortunate my time at London Irish has ended. The players and staff have been magnificent to work with and I am sure they will serve the club well." Meanwhile, Samoa back-row Ofisa Treviranus has signed a two-year extension. The 32-year-old has made 85 appearances for the Exiles since joining in 2011 and captained his country at the 2015 Rugby World Cup.

Dozens of migrants stranded a distance from the French Riviera’s resorts have staged a sit-in after being blocked at the Franco-Italian border last week, with some launching a hunger strike and camping at Ventimiglia’s railway station. French authorities say responsibility lies with Italy to house the group and process asylum claims, as the migrants arrived by boat onto Italian shores. Most in the Ventimiglia group are from Sudan, Libya and Eritrea. The standoff highlights the strain of the Mediterranean migration crisis on frontline states Italy, Greece and Malta, as unprecedented numbers continue to depart Libya. People-smuggling gangs, exploiting Libya’s war and chaos, are dispatching packed, unseaworthy vessels toward Europe, overwhelming coastal rescue and reception facilities and stretching communities. EU interior ministers will meet in Luxembourg on Tuesday to discuss the crisis, with Italy and other Mediterranean countries urging partners to share the burden of registering and hosting asylum seekers. Although France and Italy are part of the Schengen zone, where border checks are minimal, states can temporarily toughen controls in exceptional circumstances, including an unexpected migrant influx. The standoff is testing EU solidarity and coordination amid humanitarian pressures.

Brentford midfielder Alan Judge faces an agonizing spell on the sidelines and is likely to miss Euro 2016 after suffering a serious leg injury during Saturday’s 3-1 win at Ipswich Town. The 27-year-old, who made his Republic of Ireland debut in March, was hurt following a second-minute challenge by Ipswich’s Luke Hyam, who was booked for the tackle and later sent off for a second yellow card in first-half stoppage time. Hyam issued an apology via Ipswich’s club website, expressing remorse and acknowledging his own reaction compounded the situation. “I’d like to contact him in a day or so and give him my best and say how sorry I am,” Hyam said. “I feel distraught over it. It was distressing to see and definitely affected me. My head had gone. I know the Brentford lads were getting into me but I should never have reacted the way I did to get sent off. I’ve been out injured for a year myself and the last thing I want to see is a fellow pro getting injured like that.” Judge, who joined Brentford in 2014 and has scored 14 goals in all competitions this season, posted a picture from his hospital bed on Sunday and vowed to return stronger. “This is football, things like this happen,” he wrote. “I will be back stronger and much better than I have been before. I will achieve my dream one way or the other — nothing will hold me back.” Brentford confirmed Judge has been transferred to a London hospital to be managed by a leading lower limb consultant. “The nature of his management and long-term prognosis cannot be speculated on at this time,” a club statement read. “However, it should be stated that a full recovery is not in question.” On the pitch, Brentford’s 3-1 victory marked their first ever win at Portman Road and their first over Ipswich since 1955.

South Africa's Sundowns hosted the first leg in Pretoria as the top-ranked clubs entered the competition at the last-32 stage. The hosts set off to a blistering start, going 2-0 up inside the first six minutes, before KCCA's second half strike. KCCA FC's coach Mike Mutebi, who had warned his opponents that his players could cause a shock, could not have predicted a worse start for his side. Soumahoro Bangaly put Sundowns in front after just 2 minutes with Brazilian Ricardo Nascimento making it 2-0 to the South Africans just four minutes later. However, the Ugandans frustrated the hosts, and their resilience was rewarded in the second half. KCCA's goal came from in-form Geoffrey Sserunkuma in the 68th minute which could prove to be vital ahead of the return leg next weekend. Elsewhere on Saturday, record eight-time African champions Al Ahly of Egypt edged South African league leaders Bidvest Wits 1-0 in Cairo. Centre-back Ahmed Hegazy, fresh from starring in Egypt’s run to the Africa Cup of Nations final last month, headed the winner on 57 minutes to give the Red Devils a narrow advantage to take to Johannesburg. Former African title-holders Esperance of Tunisia and Wydad Casablanca of Morocco also capitalized on home advantage to build first-leg leads. In Rades, Ferjani Sassi opened the scoring for Esperance against Horoya of Guinea, only for Burkinabe forward Yacouba Mando to level before half-time. Sassi restored Esperance’s lead after the break and Fakhreddine Ben Youssef added a third with 15 minutes remaining to seal a 3-1 cushion. In Rabat, Liberian striker William Jebor struck late to hand Wydad Casablanca a 1-0 win over Mounana of Gabon. The visitors played with 10 men after David Massamba was sent off just before half-time, yet Wydad, semi-finalists last season, were wasteful and missed several clear chances to extend their lead. Completing a strong day for North African sides, 2015 Champions League runners-up USM Alger of Algeria defeated Rail Kadiogo of Burkina Faso 2-0 in Algiers. The return legs are scheduled for next weekend, with slender margins setting up a series of finely poised deciders. Fixtures and results are available via the CAF’s official channels.

Plans to reinstate the historic Scott’s Square and Horner’s Square in Hull have been submitted by Wykeland Beal with Hull City Council. Councillor Steven Bayes said the scheme could “put the area on the map as one of Hull’s cultural gems.” The application proposes four rebuilt commercial units on Humber Street, suitable for retail, restaurants or cafés, supporting the revived squares. Horner’s Square dates to the mid-1800s, while records show Scott’s Square was created around 1757 by builder Joseph Scott. If approved, the project aims to restore heritage and boost business.

Philosophy-style classroom discussions are giving a measurable lift to pupils’ attainment, particularly for those from disadvantaged backgrounds, according to a large trial across 48 UK primary schools. More than 3,000 children in Years 4 and 5 (aged nine and ten) took part in hour-long Philosophy for Children (P4C) sessions and, on average, made two months’ additional progress in reading and maths over the course of a year compared with peers not on the programme. For disadvantaged pupils, gains were even greater and extended to writing. The study, commissioned by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) and conducted by researchers at Durham University’s School of Education, examined whether structured dialogue that encourages questioning, reasoning and argument-building could translate into improved academic outcomes. Among pupils eligible for free school meals, reading scores improved by an average of four months, maths by three months and writing by two months. Lead researcher Professor Stephen Gorard said the results indicate that philosophy sessions can positively influence core attainment and appear to be especially effective for those facing the greatest barriers. He added that robust evidence of what works is vital to help headteachers make the best use of pupil premium funding, which is intended to raise the achievement of children from lower-income families. The findings are significant because many interventions designed to help disadvantaged pupils catch up often benefit their better-off peers even more, making it harder to close the attainment gap. In contrast, P4C appears to deliver a stronger impact for pupils from poorer backgrounds, potentially helping to narrow disparities. At an estimated cost of around £30 per pupil, the programme could offer schools a cost-effective way to deploy limited resources, the report suggests. Beyond test scores, teachers involved in the trial also reported gains in pupils’ confidence, patience and self-esteem, as well as improvements in classroom talk and listening skills. A typical P4C lesson sees pupils and teachers sit in a circle to explore a stimulus—such as a short video or a newspaper article—that raises a big idea or ethical dilemma. After a brief period of silent reflection, children discuss their questions in pairs or small groups before returning to a whole-class dialogue. Topics can be challenging and thought-provoking; for example, whether a healthy heart should be donated to someone who has not looked after their own health. The EEF said the results underscore the value of evidence-led approaches and offer schools a promising option as they consider how best to support disadvantaged learners.

Five councillors have defected to UKIP on West Norfolk and King’s Lynn Borough Council, delivering a symbolic boost to the party ahead of May’s local and general elections while leaving the Conservatives with a substantial majority. The recruits — June Leamon, Stephanie Smeaton, Michael Pitcher, Michael Langwade and Paul Foster — joined sitting UKIP councillor Ashley Collins, who was elected in 2013 and had been the party’s sole representative on the 62-seat authority. UKIP leader Nigel Farage hailed the move, saying: “These individuals have realised the old parties have forsaken the interests of the British people.” Four of the five — all except Ms Leamon — were previously Conservative councillors before becoming independents. Their switch, UKIP says, represents the largest single defection to the party on any local authority, and comes on the heels of recent defections in North Norfolk, Great Yarmouth, and two on Tendring District Council in Essex. Explaining his decision, Mr Foster criticised the government’s immigration record and the burden he said it places on local infrastructure. “The home secretary admitted the government were not going to hit their immigration targets,” he said. “This year 260,000 migrants have come into the country requiring six and a half towns the size of King’s Lynn to accommodate them. We do not think the hard working tax payers should be made to pay for infrastructure because of Conservative mistakes at national and local level.” While the new UKIP councillors say they support the party’s stance on immigration and Europe, they also cited local grievances including the volume of new housing being approved in the borough. Their criticisms extended to Conservative council leader Nick Daubney, whom they accused of poor leadership. Local defections often reflect personal and leadership disputes as much as policy differences, and several of the councillors indicated dissatisfaction with the direction of the Conservative group. Mr Daubney rejected the criticisms and questioned the motives of those who left. He said the four former Conservatives frequently opposed his administration’s policies and were “quite bitter” after being passed over for promotion. “We’re not running scared, because they’ve been independent and I expected they would declare themselves for UKIP,” he said. “The Conservatives need to be much clearer about our policies to control immigration and UKIP need to be more honest about what they stand for in overall council strategy.” UKIP argues the shift shows momentum is building at grassroots level. The party says more than 70 local councillors nationwide have joined its ranks, and that many defectors are now choosing to sit under the UKIP banner rather than remain as independents. With less than five months until the general election, the new members are expected to bolster UKIP’s campaign capacity on the ground. Opposition parties predicted electoral consequences. Clive Joyce, borough councillor and chairman of the North West Norfolk Labour Party, said: “There’s now a strong probability it will split the Conservative vote and cause considerable damage in next year’s elections.” All 62 council seats are up for election on the same day as the general election in May.

Falkirk manager Peter Houston has urged his side to seize a pivotal opportunity in the race for second place in the Scottish Championship as they prepare to face Hibernian at Easter Road on Tuesday. A win would move the Bairns nine points clear of their nearest rivals, tightening their grip on the position that brings significant play-off advantages and, potentially, a shorter route to the Premiership. Houston believes securing second is crucial for a club with modest resources, particularly given the demanding nature of the Championship play-offs and the current form of rivals Raith Rovers. Rovers, in fourth place, have won seven of their last 10 league matches and, in Houston’s view, are the team to avoid in the first stage of the post-season. “Raith Rovers are a very difficult team to play against and whose confidence is sky high after their recent results,” Houston told BBC Scotland. “It would be a huge benefit for a club with the resources we have to finish in second place. A freshness to players is really, really important and two mentally and physically tough fixtures against Raith Rovers would be better avoided.” Reflecting on previous play-off experiences, Houston recalled a conversation with former Falkirk midfielder Will Vaulks about the 2014 campaign. “I spoke to Will Vaulks, who was here when Falkirk played Queen of the South in 2014 in a third and fourth-place play-off over two games and won. Then they went into the Hamilton Accies fixture and Will said that even in the first leg their legs were starting to fall off them. They had a small squad and they had been having to reach a peak all the time.” While admitting it was a “pleasant surprise” to see Hibs lose to relegated Alloa Athletic on Saturday, Houston expects a fierce response from the Edinburgh side at home. Falkirk have drawn twice and lost once against Hibs this season, and the manager anticipates a match with cup-tie intensity. “One thing Hibs will be is up for the game, because they have disappointed themselves and their supporters probably by losing at Alloa,” he said. “It makes them much more dangerous to us in many ways, because they will be desperate to avenge what was a poor performance and who better to take it out on than their rivals for that second spot. I think Hibs will come out with all guns blazing. It will be more like a cup tie than a normal league match between two teams trying to get that second place.” Falkirk’s momentum was bolstered at the weekend when Blair Alston scored a last-minute winner against St Mirren, taking his tally to 11 goals for the season. The 24-year-old midfielder is out of contract in the summer and has attracted interest, including an approach from St Johnstone, but Houston remains hopeful of keeping him. “The St Johnstone thing has not been followed up,” Houston explained. “I’ve heard there was interest from a couple of other Premiership teams. But, having asked Blair as recently as last week if anything was happening, he said that not a thing had happened. I’d like him to still be available for me next season. It’s a long shot because he’s sort of got it in his head that he’d like to play in the higher division. We might still be able to give him that. What comes with promotion is being able to budget a little bit higher.”

About 3,500 protesters marched through Berlin’s Friedrichshain district on Saturday, in what police described as the most violent demonstration in five years. The rally, initially peaceful, escalated as some masked participants hurled missiles, prompting officers to fire tear gas. Shop windows were shattered, police cars were damaged, and 86 people were arrested. Authorities deployed roughly 1,800 officers and reported helicopters circling overhead as tensions flared around Rigaer Strasse 94, a block of flats at the center of a long-running standoff. Since June, police units have monitored the building day and night amid moves to evict squatters, who refuse to leave and frame their occupation as a left-wing stand against gentrification and rising rents. Friedrichshain has rapidly gentrified in recent years, sharpening conflicts over housing and affordability. While clashes unfolded, some residents, many in housing collectives, signaled solidarity by beating spoons against pots. The confrontation highlights divide over urban transformation and housing politics in the city.

In the 1960s, they found two gigantic dinosaur arms underground. For decades, scientists have wondered what kind of beast they belonged to. Now, two near-complete skeletons discovered in Mongolia have solved the mystery and revealed a creature stranger than anyone imagined. Researchers say the dinosaur, Deinocheirus mirificus—whose name means “unusual, horrible hands”—was a massive, slow-moving giant with a duck-like beak, a humped sail on its back, and enormous, hoofed feet. “It turned out to be one of the weirdest dinosaurs, it’s weird beyond our imagination,” said lead researcher Yuong-Nam Lee of South Korea’s Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources. For half a century, only the colossal forearms were known: each measured about 2.4 meters (8 feet) and ended in three huge claws. The new skeletons show the animal grew to roughly 11 meters (36 feet) long and weighed around six tonnes. Its elongated head and broad beak point to specialized feeding, while its short, stumpy legs and vast, hoof-like toes suggest an adaptation to marshy wetlands, helping it avoid sinking in soft ground. Analysis of stomach contents indicates a varied diet of plants and fish, painting a picture of a lumbering omnivore foraging in freshwater habitats. The team believes the extraordinary arms, once the only clue to its identity, were likely used for digging and gathering herbaceous vegetation. “We did not know their function before,” Dr. Lee said, “but the long forearms with giant claws may have been used for digging and gathering herbaceous plants in freshwater habitats.” The findings transform Deinocheirus from a cryptic set of limbs into one of the most bizarre and captivating dinosaurs ever discovered.

Executive director Zak Brown has credited Ron Dennis with initiating his move to McLaren, even as the long-time team boss departs day-to-day operations. Speaking at his first official engagement for McLaren during the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Brown said Dennis was instrumental in bringing him to Woking. “Ron at the end of the day is the one who recruited me,” Brown said. “The last couple of years he left the door open. He turned up the volume in pursuit of me. I wouldn’t be talking to you right now if it wasn’t for him.” Dennis, who remains chairman and chief executive of McLaren for now, has been placed on gardening leave until his contract ends in mid-January. After that date, his involvement will be limited to his status as a 25% shareholder and board member, with no active role in running the company. The leadership reshuffle follows a period of commercial and competitive challenges for McLaren, including the failure to secure a title sponsor over the past three years, a factor cited among the reasons for Dennis’s exit from day-to-day control. Brown, who left his position as boss of sports marketing agency JMI in September, said he chose McLaren over an opportunity with new Formula 1 owners Liberty Media, who are taking over the commercial rights of the sport. A lifelong McLaren fan, Brown framed his mission clearly: “to be part of a team that gets back to winning world championships.” He outlined a three-fold focus—attract more fans, grow sponsorship, and raise the funding needed to succeed—to underpin McLaren’s return to the front. Renowned as one of Formula 1’s leading dealmakers, Brown emphasized his commercial background while detailing how he will work alongside chief operating officer Jonathan Neale, who brings technical expertise. Together, he said, they are “jointly responsible for the collective efforts of running the F1 both commercial and motorsports operations.” Brown added: “I have more of a commercial background. Jonathan has a technical background. The two of us are working very closely together on the phone and we report to the executive committee, which is made up of Sheikh Mohammed and Mansour Ojjeh.” Brown’s position places him senior to McLaren Racing’s new chief executive Jost Capito, who joined in September from Volkswagen Motorsport. While there have been reports of friction between Capito and racing director Eric Boullier, Brown was cautious about drawing conclusions. “I have not started yet,” he said. “I don’t know what I don’t know. Jonathan is much closer to the technical side so we are going to be sitting down and working out what’s the best way for McLaren to get into the winners’ circle.” As for timelines, Brown admitted there is no simple answer. He said he has “no idea” how long it will take McLaren to return to winning ways, adding only: “I just hope it is sooner rather than later.”

A 33-year-old woman died after being struck by a vehicle on the A90 near Nigg Way at 19:10 on Saturday. Police said she had been walking on the southbound carriageway and was pronounced dead at the scene. The driver and passengers were uninjured. The road was closed for six hours for investigations. Officers are appealing for witnesses and dashcam footage to contact Police Scotland.

Leukaemia patient urges ethnic minorities to join stem cell register after life-saving transplant from mother A 24-year-old student from Walthamstow, London, is urging people from Asian and other ethnic minority backgrounds to join stem cell donor registers after a life-saving transplant from her mother. Vithiya Alphons was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia just days after returning for her final year of study and needed an urgent stem cell transplant. The search for a donor proved challenging because relatively few South Asian people are on donor registers. With no suitable unrelated match found, doctors proceeded with a transplant using her mother’s cells, which were only a 50% match. The procedure took place in May. Alphons said her recovery has been “a very tough journey,” but added, “I am now getting better,” expressing gratitude to everyone who supported her. “I was very lucky that my mum was fit and healthy and able to be a donor,” she said. “There are a lot of people who will not have that option and will only be able to rely on an unrelated donor.” The charity Anthony Nolan led the search for a suitable match, while Alphons’s family launched a social media campaign to boost registrations. Although a full match was not found in time, thousands of people signed up to the donor register in the weeks that followed. Ann O’Leary, head of register development at Anthony Nolan, said: “Vithiya’s appeal raised huge awareness of the need for more Asian and ethnic minority donors to join the stem cell register. And it is remarkable that Vithiya continues to raise awareness of this need, despite being in the early stages of recovery. She has remained positive throughout her illness and is a true inspiration to us all.”

It will tell drivers when lights are due to turn green and when they will not make it before a light turns red. Audi has introduced new vehicle-to-infrastructure technology designed to take the stress out of waiting at traffic lights by displaying real-time countdowns and advisories inside the car. The Volkswagen-owned manufacturer said the system, which it describes as “V-to-I,” is now available in A4 models built after 1 June and will be rolled out to select Q7 models next year. The capability relies on safety and other operational data being wirelessly transmitted between traffic signals and vehicles over the cloud. While the company hopes the technology will ultimately contribute to fewer crashes and less congestion on roads, Audi emphasized it is being positioned as a comfort and convenience feature rather than a dedicated safety aid. “This is designed not as a safety feature, but a comfort and convenience feature,” said Pom Malhotra, general manager of Audi’s connected vehicles division. At the heart of the system is an in-car display that shows a countdown until a red light turns green. Audi says that knowing exactly how long the wait will be can reduce driver anxiety and help encourage attention as the light is about to change. The feature also alerts drivers when they are unlikely to make it through an approaching signal before it turns red, prompting them to begin braking in good time and avoid unnecessary acceleration. Future applications could extend the technology’s usefulness beyond simple countdowns. According to Reuters, Audi is exploring linking traffic signal data to a vehicle’s navigation and stop-start functions to optimize routes and engine idling. Executives also said traffic signals could eventually advise the car to maintain a certain speed to harmonize with the flow of lights, potentially creating “green waves” that smooth traffic through urban corridors. Audi plans to deploy the system in five to seven U.S. cities this year, adding locations one at a time, though it declined to name which city will be first. The rollout depends on local infrastructure and cooperation from traffic management authorities, which vary widely by region. In the UK, experts say the concept is promising but will require significant investment to be viable. David Bailey, professor of industry at Aston University, said Audi has pioneered traffic light recognition and is building on that foundation. “It could bring benefits in easing journey time. For example, if you are driving through a city at a quiet time of day with little other traffic, the lights could switch to let you through,” he told the BBC. “We would need to see a substantial investment in infrastructure here in the UK to make such technologies workable. Longer term, though, we are looking at the development of connected and autonomous cars that will communicate with each other and the infrastructure around them.”

A 37-year-old inmate was attacked at HMP Ranby near Retford on Monday and died in hospital the following day. Nottinghamshire Police said four men, aged 22 to 39, are being questioned in connection with the incident. The victim has not yet been formally identified, and a post-mortem examination will be conducted to establish cause of death.

"It would end Olympic boxing as we know it," said Price, who has held British and Commonwealth heavyweight titles during his time as a professional. The Merseyside fighter, 32, added that the proposal to introduce professionals in time for Rio 2016 was "far-fetched". "Qualifying has become so complicated, I don't see how it can work." British heavyweight David Price has warned that a fast-tracked move to admit fully licensed professionals into the Rio 2016 boxing tournament risks upending the sport’s traditional Olympic model. Price, who rose through the amateur ranks before turning professional, cautioned that any change should be phased in gradually rather than rushed through months before the Games. His comments follow a bold push from Dr Ching-Kuo Wu, president of world governing body AIBA, who said he wants to abolish rules preventing fighters with 15 or more paid bouts from competing at the Olympics. The proposal must be approved by AIBA’s executive committee, but Wu signaled urgency: "We want something to change..... not after four years, but now." Price noted that amateur boxing has already evolved significantly, with the lines between amateur and professional blurring in competitions such as World Series Boxing and AIBA Pro. The traditional amateur code—now branded Olympic-style—has adopted elements closer to the professional game, intensifying debate over who should be eligible for the sport’s biggest multisport stage. Reaction among leading fighters is sharply divided. IBF super-bantamweight world champion Carl Frampton argued that the shift is logical: "The amateurs at the moment are pretty much professionals. The established governing bodies are entitled to say: ‘If you guys are fighting as pros, why can’t our pro boxers enter the Olympics?’ They have a justified point." Others voiced strong opposition. English flyweight champion Charlie Edwards called the proposal "a bit of a joke," adding, "The likes of Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao aren’t going to fight for peanuts." Light-welterweight Josh Taylor, the 2014 Commonwealth Games champion, said it would be "so unfair" on long-serving GB squad hopefuls who have targeted the Olympics. Scott Fitzgerald, the 2014 Commonwealth welterweight champion, warned: "It could spell the end of amateur boxing. If this goes through, why would anyone stay amateur?" With qualifying already complex and time running short before Rio, the sport faces a pivotal decision on whether to open its Olympic gates to the professional ranks—or preserve a distinctive amateur tradition.

Stoke Gifford Parish Council voted to become the first in the world to charge Parkrun a fee for use of its grounds Stoke Gifford Parish Council has voted to become the first authority in the world to charge Parkrun for use of its grounds, prompting the closure of the popular Little Stoke event. Hundreds of runners take part in two free, timed 5k runs organised by Parkrun UK in Little Stoke Park on Saturdays, but organisers said the new levy meant the end of the event, as Parkrun does not pay for access to public spaces. At a meeting on Tuesday, councillors voted 6–4 to introduce a fee to cover “wear and tear,” arguing it is unfair for non-running residents to fund the upkeep of paths. The council said it has received hundreds of abusive emails since the decision. The move has drawn widespread criticism. The local Labour group called it a “mean-spirited decision” and a “health tax.” Double Olympic champion Dame Kelly Holmes tweeted: “Have I missed the whole reason parkruns exist and are free? Parish council decision is a disgrace.” Marathon world-record holder Paula Radcliffe said she was “totally against this decision,” while sports minister Tracey Crouch said it ran “contrary to government sports strategy” and created a “barrier to participation.” TV personality Ben Fogle also condemned the vote.

The IMF also has strong warnings about what a Brexit would do to the economy, and the Reality Check team will look forward to evaluating those next month, when the IMF gives the full detail of its forecasts. But it is worth bearing in mind the IMF describes itself as an organisation "working to foster global monetary cooperation". It is hardly surprising a potential Brexit would not be its cup of tea. It actually cited two reasons for the currency's weakness, saying between August 2015 and February 2016 "the British pound depreciated by 7%, driven by expectations of a later normalisation of monetary policy in the United Kingdom and concerns about a potential exit from the European Union". The point about the "later normalisation of monetary policy" means as a result of the general weakness of the economy, the expected date of the first rise in interest rates from the Bank of England was delayed. The IMF is presumably comparing the pound with a selection of currencies. Between the beginning of August and the end of February, the pound actually fell about 11% against the US dollar and 10% against the euro. How much of this was due to the referendum and how much was down to other factors? Well, the referendum date was not confirmed until 20 February, but it was widely expected to be announced. There was a pretty sharp fall in the value of the pound around the time of the announcement, as you can see from the graphs, although that particular dip was relatively short-lived. So, how much of the pound's fall was down to uncertainty surrounding a potential Brexit as opposed to factors such as interest rate expectations? As we have discussed before, predicting uncertainty cannot be seen as a controversial forecast, and it is generally accepted markets do not like uncertainty. So it is fair to say some of the fall in the pound has been due to the potential for Brexit - it is a factor that has been cited regularly in analysts' reports. The Office for Budget Responsibility cited some of the banks predicting weakness for the pound. But given the result of the referendum will have implications for the economy for decades to come, a bit of weakness in the pound ahead of the vote should not be seen as too worrying a factor. In particular, a weak pound is not a bad thing for everyone - it is good news for many exporters in the UK. Reality Check verdict: The referendum debate is likely to be one of the factors weakening the pound, but things like delayed interest rate rises are also responsible. Former world champion Raymond van Barneveld advanced at the PDC World Championship and will face No.21 seed Alan Norris next after progressing as the No.12 seed. Australia’s No.17 seed Simon Whitlock swept Germany’s Dragutin Horvat 3-0 to book a meeting with Darren Webster. Earlier, Northern Ireland’s Brendan Dolan, seeded 23rd, defeated Dutchman Christian Kist 3-1 and will meet the winner of Jelle Klaasen versus Jeffrey de Graaf in round two. Horvat had edged Boris Koltsov of Russia 2-1 to earn his first-round tie with Whitlock. Several seeds progressed as momentum built this week.

The scam claimed to come from Google Docs, a service that allows people to share and edit documents online. Google has moved quickly to shut down a deceptive email campaign that masqueraded as a Google Docs invitation and tricked some users into granting hackers access to their accounts. The company said it stopped the attack “within approximately one hour,” including through “removing fake pages and applications.” In an updated statement, Google added: “While contact information was accessed and used by the campaign, our investigations show that no other data was exposed. There’s no further action users need to take regarding this event; users who want to review third party apps connected to their account can visit Google Security Checkup.” During the attack, recipients received an invitation to edit a Google Doc with the subject line indicating a contact “has shared a document on Google Docs with you.” The message also copied the email address hhhhh@mailinator[.]com; Mailinator, a free email service provider, denied any involvement. Those who clicked the “Open in Docs” button were directed to a legitimate Google-hosted page and prompted to allow a seemingly real service, labeled “Google Docs,” to access their email account data. By granting permission, users unwittingly gave the attackers potential access to their email accounts, contacts, and online documents. The malware then propagated by emailing everyone in the victim’s contacts list. “This is a very serious situation for anybody who is infected because the victims have their accounts controlled by a malicious party,” said Justin Cappos, a cyber security professor at NYU, speaking to Reuters. According to PC World, the operation was more sophisticated than typical phishing attempts, which generally rely on tricking people into handing over usernames and passwords by posing as reputable companies. In this case, the perpetrators built a third-party app that leveraged Google’s own processes to gain account access, bypassing the need to steal login credentials directly. The notorious Russian hacking group Fancy Bear has been accused of using similar techniques, although one security expert cast doubt on their involvement in this incident. “I don’t believe they are behind this..... because this is way too widespread,” Jaime Blasco, chief scientist at security provider AlienVault, told PC World. Google said the spam campaign affected “fewer than 0.1%” of Gmail users, which would equate to about one million people. The incident echoes past high-profile phishing episodes, including a case last year in which an American man pleaded guilty to stealing celebrities’ nude photographs by hacking their iCloud and Gmail accounts, and a 2013 campaign that Google said targeted thousands of Iranian users ahead of the country’s presidential election.

Andrew RT Davies, the Welsh Conservative leader who campaigned for Leave in the EU referendum, has questioned whether the Welsh Government should continue to administer funds that replace European programmes, arguing that Westminster could instead distribute the money directly to Wales. Wales currently receives £1.8bn in European Structural Funds during the 2014-2020 programme, with the cash administered by Welsh Government departments. Farmers also benefited from £240m through the Common Agricultural Policy’s single payment scheme in 2014 alone. With the UK set to leave the EU, Davies said new arrangements should be explored to ensure communities reliant on this funding have confidence the money will keep flowing. “It is vital that Wales’ interests are protected and secured, and communities which have had this money spent are given the confidence that the money will continue irrespective of whether it comes from the Treasury in London or Welsh Government,” he told a press conference. “That money could, could come directly from Westminster. Why should the Welsh Government handle the money?” Davies suggested that once the Wales Bill is passed and negotiations with the EU progress, alternative models could be considered for delivering funding, rather than relying on routes developed since devolution in 1999. “I’m just saying that as a possible negotiating position that needs to be considered,” he said. His comments come amid wider debate about safeguarding EU-derived funding for Welsh projects, with analysis highlighting pleas to make the funding secure as the UK reshapes its arrangements post-Brexit. On national politics, Davies said there is no need for a general election following the referendum. “The current government in Westminster was only elected 14 months ago, this referendum was a key part of the manifesto, so it was understood that this referendum was coming,” he said. “I see no need because of the referendum result of last Thursday that is a requirement to have a general election.” He added it was important that whoever becomes prime minister on 2 September “can empathise with the views that were expressed at the ballot.” Davies also argued there are “vested interests” seeking to make Brexit fail, claiming “the establishment were on the Remain side.” On immigration, he described himself as “a supporter of the free movement of people,” saying it enriches communities and helps economically, but stressed that a British government will determine policy in future. He predicted the approach would be “somewhere in the middle.”

Halifax says UK house price inflation held steady at 9.2% in the year to May, the lowest annual rate since last autumn, and expects a further slowdown in the months ahead as affordability pressures mount. The lender reported that prices rose 0.6% in May, while values in the three months to the end of May were 1.4% higher than in the previous quarter. The average UK house price now stands at £213,472.
