The figures follow a record-breaking surge in transactions in March, as buyers rushed to complete purchases before stamp duty changes took effect on 1 April. Earlier this week, economics consultancy Capital Economics said house price inflation had likely peaked, pointing to easing momentum after the spring spike. “Low interest rates, increasing employment and rising real earnings continue to support housing demand. The strength of demand, combined with very low supply, is causing house prices to rise at a brisk pace in quarterly and annual terms,” said Martin Ellis, Halifax’s housing economist. However, he cautioned that “increasing affordability issues, caused by a sustained period of higher-than-earnings house price growth, should curb housing demand and result in some slowdown in house price growth as the year progresses.” While tight supply and supportive borrowing costs have underpinned prices, Halifax’s outlook suggests the market may cool as stretched affordability increasingly weighs on buyers, particularly first-time purchasers.

Misdelivered FedEx Box Labeled ‘Patient Tumor’ Stuns Bristol Man; Package Redirected to Royal Free Hospital A Bristol environmental consultant says he was shocked to receive a FedEx parcel marked “patient tumor – specimen enclosed” that was intended for the Royal Free Hospital in London. James Potten, 37, of Cotham, Bristol, said the package arrived from an address in California and appeared to have been mixed up with an expected delivery of a Kindle. “When I opened it I had quite a shock,” he said. “My name was on the outside, but the contents weren’t what I expected. I haven’t opened the sealed box, which says exempt patient tissue, as it doesn’t belong to me.” Potten said FedEx contacted him on Thursday to say it had attempted delivery while he was out. After he called the company, the driver returned to his house. He noticed the tracking code on the item shared the same first five and last three numbers as his order, but it was not his Kindle. “I’ve been trying to get FedEx to collect it as it is potentially a sample that needs to be tested and sent back with some urgency. I don’t know where my Kindle is, but if it is at the Royal Free I’d be happy to do an exchange,” he said. The Royal Free Hospital said it was aware that a package intended for one of its institutions had been delivered to an address in Bristol. “If [we were] the intended recipient, we will await answers from the delivery company as to how this mistake was made,” a spokesperson said. FedEx said it “regretted the error” and would consider future changes to its processes. A FedEx spokeswoman said on Sunday the company had retrieved the package and was “delivering it to the correct address today.”

Pope Francis has underscored the rights of indigenous communities to defend “their ancestral relationship to the earth,” as tensions rise over the Dakota Access Pipeline (DAPL) in the United States. Speaking Wednesday at the Indigenous Peoples Forum in Rome, the pontiff said development must be balanced with “the protection of the particular characteristics of indigenous peoples and their territories,” adding that “the right to prior and informed consent should always prevail.” He argued that only by honoring this principle is it possible to secure “peaceful co-operation between governing authorities and indigenous peoples, overcoming confrontation and conflict.” The Pope did not specifically name the Standing Rock Sioux and Cheyenne River Sioux tribes, who have led opposition to the pipeline in North Dakota, but his remarks echo the concerns at the heart of their months-long protest. Thousands of demonstrators have descended on the area, establishing camps along the final stretch of the planned 1,172-mile (1,886km) route. Opponents contend the project threatens to contaminate drinking water and damage sacred burial sites. The dispute has sharpened after Joey Mahmoud, executive vice president of Texas-based Energy Transfer Partners, told Congress that the protest movement “induced individuals to break into and shut down pump stations on four operational pipelines.” He added: “Had these actions been undertaken by foreign nationals, they could only be described as acts of terrorism.” Regulatory decisions have seesawed. The Obama administration denied a key land permit, but President Donald Trump has pushed to advance the $3.8bn (£3bn) oil pipeline. A judge recently rejected the two tribes’ plea for a temporary stay after the U.S. Army gave the project permission to proceed. Part of the route lies on U.S. Army-controlled territory. As the administration presses forward and opponents dig in, the Pope’s appeal for consent and dialogue sets a moral marker likely to resonate beyond North Dakota, spotlighting broader questions of indigenous rights, environmental protection, and the terms of modern development.

A Cardiff coroner has concluded that the death of Ceri Ann Sullivan, 21, from Cyncoed, was accidental after she lost control of her Renault Clio on the A48 near St Mellons and collided with an oncoming car on 24 May 2014. Cardiff Coroner’s Court heard that Sullivan, a mother of one, sustained massive head injuries in the collision and was pronounced dead at the University Hospital of Wales. Rodney Jones, who was driving a Ford Mondeo in the opposite direction, told the inquest he saw the Clio “twitch” as it rounded a bend before it “violently went into a slide.” “As it came round the bend its rear came outwards towards the other lane—it seemed to twitch,” Mr Jones said. “It righted itself for a split second and I thought she’d gained control and then it violently went into a slide. The car skidded sideways and came at me—I was unable to avoid a collision.” His vehicle struck the passenger side of the Clio “head-on.” South Wales Police collision investigator Wayne Evans said the carriageway was damp at the time, but he did not consider surface conditions to be a factor. He noted the Clio’s front tyres were below the legal tread depth; however, he did not believe the defects caused the crash. Investigators found no evidence Sullivan was speeding or using her mobile phone. A post-mortem found no alcohol in Sullivan’s system. Pathologists found traces of prior cannabis use, with no evidence of impairment. Coroner Andrew Barkley recorded a conclusion of accidental death, saying: “Why she lost control will never be known.”

How does the £500m add up? Most of the new money is directed at Northern Ireland-specific priorities, with a substantial slice earmarked for security. A total of £188m is set aside for security-related spending, including an unconditional £160m for the PSNI over the next five years to combat dissident republicans and other paramilitaries. A further £25m could be released if the executive provides matched funding from its own resources. Another £3m will cover the cost of establishing a new monitoring and implementation body. Alongside security, “shared future” cross-community initiatives will receive an additional £60m over five years. Part of this funding is intended to support projects aimed at removing Belfast’s “peace walls,” a longstanding physical manifestation of division. There is also £125m for the Social Security Agency (SSA) to tackle fraud and error. However, this is where the headline total becomes less certain. The package assumes that investing in the SSA will enable it to detect up to £300m of additional fraud and error over the next five years, with Stormont permitted to retain half of any recovered funds. In the last financial year, the SSA identified losses of £17.4m from official error, £9.3m from customer error and £25.2m from customer fraud — a total of £51.9m. Hitting the new target would require more than doubling annual detection levels. While politicians are confident this is achievable, falling short would leave the financial package under pressure. Complicating the arithmetic further, the DUP and Sinn Féin have agreed to fund measures mitigating the impact of welfare reform. Those mitigations will remove £585m from departmental budgets — exceeding the gains anticipated from the current package. The result is a plan that leans on ambitious assumptions about fraud detection and savings, even as departments face significant additional costs to soften welfare changes.

The Playpen site was located on the Tor network which is used to anonymise web-browsing activity A federal child exploitation case tied to the notorious Playpen website is poised to be dismissed after the FBI declined to reveal how it pierced the anonymity of the Tor network during a sweeping investigation. In a filing on Friday, federal prosecutor Annette Hayes said the government was “deprived of the evidence needed to establish defendant Jay Michaud’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt” because it remains unwilling to disclose discovery related to the FBI’s deployment of a “network investigative technique” (NIT). Assistant public defender Colin Fieman told the BBC a dismissal order is expected “within the next day or two.” Playpen operated on Tor, a system that conceals users’ locations by routing traffic through a chain of computers and encrypting data. The FBI has acknowledged it used NITs to identify visitors, but it has refused to detail the technology in court, citing security and investigative concerns. That stance has triggered a legal clash over due process and transparency, with defense attorneys arguing defendants cannot meaningfully challenge evidence they cannot scrutinize. The Michaud case is one of many arising from the Playpen probe. In December, Assistant Attorney General Leslie Caldwell said the investigation resulted in more than 200 active prosecutions and the identification or rescue of at least 49 American children who were being sexually abused. In January, Michael Fluckiger was sentenced to 20 years in prison for running the site. After arresting site administrators, the FBI continued to operate Playpen for 13 days to gather evidence on users, a tactic that has fueled debate over law enforcement’s role in temporarily sustaining illegal platforms to ensnare suspects. The pending dismissal underscores the tension between protecting investigative methods and meeting evidentiary standards in court, a balance that could shape future cybercrime and privacy cases involving anonymizing technologies like Tor.

State Department Reopens Email Review After FBI Declines Charges Against Clinton Hillary Clinton, the likely Democratic presidential nominee, learned this week that she will not face criminal charges over her use of a private email server while serving as secretary of state. FBI Director James Comey announced that although Clinton sent and received sensitive material through the system, investigators found no evidence of intentional misconduct and therefore would not recommend prosecution. With the criminal inquiry closed, the State Department is reopening its internal review into possible mishandling of classified information. The renewed administrative review will cover not only Clinton but also several of her former senior aides, all of whom have since left the department. State Department spokesman John Kirby said the agency will proceed “as expeditiously as possible,” but will not set artificial deadlines. Former officials can still face administrative sanctions, ranging from counseling and formal reprimands to the revocation of security clearances. While the most severe consequence—loss of security clearance—would be difficult to apply to Clinton if she is elected president, the process could have tangible implications for any aides hoping to serve in a future Clinton administration. Revoked or limited clearances could prevent them from taking positions that require access to sensitive information. Even lesser sanctions, such as official letters of reprimand, would likely be seized upon by Republican opponents as evidence of poor judgment and become a persistent campaign issue. Clinton’s campaign had signaled relief after Comey’s announcement, saying it was glad the matter had been resolved. The State Department’s decision ensures, however, that the email controversy will remain in the public eye for an indeterminate period. Republican critics have argued the FBI’s decision shows Clinton is “above the law,” a charge Comey pushed back against during testimony before a House committee on Thursday. He reiterated that “no reasonable prosecutor” would bring charges based on the evidence, while noting that Clinton and her staff were “extremely careless” in handling classified information. Clinton served as secretary of state until early 2013. She is expected to be officially nominated as the Democratic Party’s presidential candidate later this month. The State Department’s review will determine whether any administrative rules were violated and what sanctions, if any, are warranted. Officials have not provided a timetable for completion.

Mark Rutte is set to lead a centre-right minority coalition with the Christian Democrats (CDA), backed by Geert Wilders’ Freedom Party (PVV), which will remain outside the government. The VVD and CDA together hold 52 of 150 seats and will rely on the PVV’s 24 MPs to pass legislation. The support arrangement keeps the PVV outside cabinet posts while giving it leverage over key proposals. The coalition agenda includes a ban on the full Islamic veil, curbs on immigration, more police officers and €18bn in budget cuts by 2015, about $24bn and £15bn. The deal has angered some CDA lawmakers who oppose working with Wilders, a polarising figure. Wilders went on trial in Amsterdam this week on charges of inciting hatred over his film Fitna. The 2008 work juxtaposes passages from the Koran with images of the 9/11 attacks, in which 3,000 people were killed, and has drawn condemnation from Muslim groups and rights advocates. The Netherlands has been governed by a caretaker cabinet since February, when a CDA-led coalition under former prime minister Jan Peter Balkenende collapsed in a dispute over the military mission in Afghanistan. In June’s election, the PVV surged to become the third-largest party, reshaping coalition arithmetic and paving the way for Rutte’s bid to form a government.

An American surged into a share of the lead at six under after making five straight birdies from the 10th at Old Westbury, New York, in the first event of the PGA Tour’s FedEx Cup Playoffs. He joins Dustin Johnson (69), Rickie Fowler (66) and Jhonattan Vegas (65), with Matt Kuchar (64) and Bubba Watson (68) one back. Rory McIlroy improved on his opening 73 with a 68 to sit at one over. England’s Justin Rose posted a second straight 68 to reach four under alongside first-round leader Russell Henley (72) and Spain’s Jon Rahm (68). Fellow Englishman Paul Casey is three under after 68. Play resumes this weekend as the field chases early playoff momentum.

Pat Cummins ruled out of Bangladesh Tests with back injury; Faulkner called up Australia fast bowler Pat Cummins has been ruled out of the upcoming Test tour of Bangladesh after scans revealed the early stages of a back injury. The 22-year-old felt discomfort during the fifth one-day international against England in September and, while no return date has been set, he hopes to be fit for the World T20 in India in March. All-rounder James Faulkner, 25, has been drafted into the squad as Cummins’ replacement. The first Test in Chittagong begins on 9 October. “This is really unfortunate for Pat and I know how disappointed he will be,” said chairman of selectors Rod Marsh. “He is a young bowler with a bright future and we were really pleased with how he bowled in the UK.” Cummins has endured a stop-start international career since making his solitary Test appearance in 2011. He impressed in the recent ODI series in England, regularly topping 96mph (154kph) and claiming 12 wickets in five matches. However, his progress has repeatedly been hampered by injuries, including a back problem that sidelined him between 2012 and 2014. Dominic Thornely, a member of Cummins’s management team, told the Sydney Morning Herald the paceman was keeping perspective. “He was disappointed but said, ‘It’s part of the game. I bowl 150km per hour; it’s going to happen.’ As I said to him, I saw Brett Lee in a full-blown body cast when he was only 18 and he ended up taking 310 wickets and he was rattled by injuries. I told Pat, ‘You’re only young. Brett retired when he was 38.’” Australia’s squad is: Steven Smith (capt), Adam Voges (vice-capt), Cameron Bancroft, Joe Burns, James Faulkner, Andrew Fekete, Usman Khawaja, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Marsh, Shaun Marsh, Glenn Maxwell, Peter Nevill (wk), Stephen O’Keefe, Peter Siddle, Mitchell Starc.

The jawbone is 2.8 million years old: 450,000 years older than researchers believed human beings first lived. A fossilized jawbone discovered in Ethiopia has pushed back the earliest known evidence of human lineage by roughly 450,000 years, reshaping timelines of our evolution. Dated to about 2.8 million years old, the specimen predates the previously oldest known human bones, which were estimated at 2.35 million years. Ethiopia, long regarded as a cradle of human evolution, has again yielded a find with profound implications for understanding how our species emerged. Prof Brian Villmoare of the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, who led the study, said the jaw shows a clear connection between our own kind and apes. The fossil was found in the same region where “Lucy,” a 3.2 million-year-old ape-like ancestor, was unearthed in 1974. Notably, the new jawbone has much smaller back teeth than Lucy’s, a feature researchers highlight as one of the defining traits of early humans. However, some scientists urge caution. Prof Chris Stringer of London’s Natural History Museum said that although the jawbone is an important discovery, by itself it cannot establish how human the creature was. “These new studies leave us with an even more complex picture of early humans than we thought,” he said. “They challenge us to consider the very definition of what it is to be human. Are we defined by our small teeth and jaws, our large brain, our long legs, tool-making, or some combination of these traits?”

SRC director David Lonsdale has warned that rising inflation and council tax increases are likely to squeeze household budgets this year, putting pressure on consumer spending and the wider retail sector. In a New Year message outlining the challenges ahead, he said retailers continue to grapple with a hotchpotch of government-imposed cost pressures and called for a more coherent approach to policy-making to help the industry thrive. “In many respects our economy lives or dies by what happens to consumer spending,” Mr Lonsdale said. “That’s why policy-makers should be concerned about the formidable challenges for Scottish retail in the year ahead. Rising inflation and council taxes are likely to put a strain on disposable incomes.” He added that households would be relieved by the Scottish government’s decision not to increase income tax rates, an area where the Scottish Retail Consortium (SRC) and ministers are firmly aligned. A Scottish government spokesman insisted the administration has already taken significant steps to support retailers and the broader economy. “The Scottish government is doing everything within our powers to support our economy and we welcome the recent uplift in retail sales in Scotland,” he said. As part of the budget, ministers announced a package to reduce business rates, including an expansion of the Small Business Bonus Scheme, which has already saved firms more than £1bn in total. From 2017, the scheme will lift 100,000 properties out of rates entirely. In addition, 8,000 business properties will no longer pay the Large Business Supplement, and the overall business rates poundage—the core tax rate applied to the rateable value of business properties—will be cut by 3.7% to 46.6p. Mr Lonsdale welcomed support to date but argued that more could be done to reduce overheads faced by SRC members. He highlighted the apprenticeship levy, which begins to bite in early 2017 for larger employers, as another cost pressure on firms already managing tight margins. “This reinforces the need for government at every level to work more effectively with the retail industry to help it keep down the cost of living for consumers and to help it thrive and prosper,” he said. “A more coherent approach towards policy-making in the year ahead is certainly required.” Looking ahead, Mr Lonsdale said he hoped 2017 would bring greater clarity on the implications of Brexit for Scottish retailers and supply chains. He also voiced support for the Barclay review of business rates, urging that it lead to reductions that boost retailers’ confidence and help revitalise Scotland’s high streets.

Ryan Brunt will miss at least six months after tests on Monday confirmed the Plymouth Argyle forward suffered a serious knee injury in last week’s 1-0 defeat at Barnet. The 22-year-old former Bristol Rovers striker had warned on social media that the problem was “not looking too promising.” Brunt previously damaged the cruciate ligament in his other knee in 2011 and underwent further knee surgery in 2014. The setback comes as his contract is due to expire this summer. Brunt had just broken into Argyle’s first team, starting five straight matches and scoring three goals before being sidelined.

Ex-Team Sky medic Dr Richard Freeman, who received the package on behalf of the team in 2011, will not appear before the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee because of ill health. Ex-British Cycling coach Simon Cope, who couriered the package, will attend. UK Anti-Doping chief Nicole Sapstead is also set to attend on Wednesday. A spokesperson for the select committee said it will offer Freeman "the option of supplying written evidence and may call him to appear when he's well enough". The hearing had already been postponed by a week after Sapstead asked for more time because of a development into UK Anti-Doping (Ukad's) own investigation into the package. This content will not work on your device, please check Javascript and cookies are enabled or update your browser The Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee will proceed with its inquiry into the contents and delivery of a medical package to Team Sky at the 2011 Criterium du Dauphine, despite the absence of former team doctor Richard Freeman due to ill health. Former British Cycling coach Simon Cope, who transported the package, will give evidence, alongside UK Anti-Doping chief executive Nicole Sapstead. In December, Team Sky principal Sir Dave Brailsford told MPs the package contained Fluimucil, an over-the-counter decongestant. Team Sky has said it is confident Ukad will find no evidence of wrongdoing. The committee previously delayed the session by a week after Sapstead sought additional time, citing a development in Ukad’s ongoing investigation. Sir Bradley Wiggins and Brailsford have faced scrutiny since hackers released details of Wiggins’ therapeutic use exemptions (TUEs), which permitted the use of otherwise banned substances to treat medical conditions. Wiggins’ TUEs were approved by British authorities and cycling’s world governing body, the UCI. There is no suggestion that Wiggins, 36, or Team Sky broke any rules. Brailsford has insisted Team Sky can be trusted “100%,” while acknowledging “regrettable” questions over Wiggins’ medical records and the 2011 delivery. The committee said Freeman will be offered the opportunity to submit written evidence and could be called to appear when fit. Wiggins is a five-time Olympic gold medallist and, in 2012, became the first Briton to win the Tour de France.

Bus company TM Travel has begun fitting its vehicles with “anti-surf” devices following the publication of footage showing two men clinging to the back of a moving bus on Greenland Road in Darnall, Sheffield. Deputy general manager Paul Hopkinson said the products are being installed on routes and vehicles where there is a high risk of this kind of behaviour. He warned that, while the stunt may seem like fun, those attempting it risk falling and face a very high chance of being struck by other traffic. The video, shared by Sheffield Online, prompted the company to act to improve passenger and public safety.

A young boy has died after a mirror reportedly fell in a Hugo Boss store at the Bicester Outlet shopping village in Pingle Drive, Oxfordshire. The incident occurred at about 20:30 BST on Tuesday. He was taken to hospital following the incident and later died at the John Radcliffe Hospital in Oxford, authorities said. Thames Valley Police has launched an investigation and is appealing for witnesses. Investigating officer Det Insp Steve Duffy said: “Our thoughts are with the family at this time.” He added: “We are currently investigating the circumstances of this boy’s death and we would ask anyone who was in the Hugo Boss store at around that time on Tuesday to please contact us as a matter of urgency.” Hugo Boss confirmed the store has been closed until further notice. In a statement, the designer retailer said: “Everyone at Hugo Boss is devastated by this tragic accident and we would like to extend our deepest condolences and sympathies to his family. Hugo Boss will assist the authorities in any way with an investigation into the accident.” A company spokesman declined to provide details about the mirror’s size or how it fell, including whether it fell from height. The Health and Safety Executive said it is not involved in the inquiry, noting that health and safety enforcement in shops falls under the remit of local authority environmental health departments. Police enquiries are ongoing.

The verdict comes in an official report by the Care Inspectorate which is conducting a series of reviews on services across the country. Inspectors have expressed confidence that children’s services in North Lanarkshire are improving outcomes for local young people, following a visit to Scotland’s fourth largest local authority between October and November last year. The joint inspection assessed how well the council and its partners support children and families, with particular focus on the impact services are having on health, safety and wellbeing. The review examined provision delivered by North Lanarkshire Council alongside key partners, including Police Scotland, Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, NHS Lanarkshire and the Children’s Reporter. As part of their evidence gathering, inspectors met almost 100 children, their families and care staff to understand the standard of care being received and the difference it is making in daily life. The report covered young people under 18, and those up to 21 and beyond if they have been looked after. Across nine key quality indicators deemed essential to improving the lives of young people, the inspection awarded six “very good” ratings and three “good” ratings. Inspectors and partners agreed one area for improvement: ensuring consistency of practice across agencies in responding to child protection issues. This priority had already been identified by the council and its partners, and work is under way to strengthen a coordinated approach. The report also highlighted examples of effective practice, notably a partnership with Motherwell Football Club Community Trust. Harnessing the influence of the club and the power of sport, the Trust delivers programmes addressing sexual health, smoking, alcohol and substance misuse. Initiatives feature first-team footballers and coaches from Motherwell FC as role models, with sessions held at the SPFL club’s Fir Park Stadium. The Care Inspectorate’s findings form part of its ongoing national programme reviewing children’s services across Scotland.

Roger Christian, the Oscar-winning filmmaker celebrated for his work on Star Wars: A New Hope and the short film The Bottom Dollar, is returning to Scotland to expand his cult classic Black Angel into a feature-length movie. The original Black Angel, a 25-minute Arthurian tale about a knight—played by Tony Vogel—who rescues a princess on his way home from the Crusades, was commissioned by Star Wars creator George Lucas and famously screened ahead of Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back in cinemas across Europe, Asia, and Australia in 1980. Made on a shoestring budget of £25,000, the short was filmed across striking Scottish locations, including Steall Falls in Glen Nevis, Loch Eck in Argyll, the swimming pool at Dunoon Riverside Health Club, and the ruin of Bernera Barracks, an 18th Century red coats base in Glenelg. After its initial run, the film’s prints disappeared and were long believed lost, until a studio archivist rediscovered them in 2012. Last year, Black Angel received its first public screenings in Scotland in 34 years, reigniting interest in Christian’s long-planned expansion of the story. Christian now intends to shoot the new feature in many of the landscapes that helped define the original’s mythic tone. Proposed locations include Eilean Donan Castle, Glencoe, and the Isle of Skye. “I have to return to Scotland, it is a major part of Black Angel,” he said. “I need Eileen Donan Castle as it was such a mystical and mythological element of Black Angel. A truly romantic vision that is an essential element of the film. I wanted to film in Glencoe originally, so am determined to film there this time. Maybe Skye, it’s fascinating and quite appropriate for Black Angel.” To help fund the production, Christian has launched a 45-day Indiegogo campaign to raise £66,000. While the story’s heart lies in Scotland, the production will also make use of studio facilities abroad. “Sadly I need studios for sets, so have to go to Hungary where existing sets and studios exist and tax credits make it financially viable,” he explained. “Also, the film starts in the desert so we will be in Morocco for that.” Filming could begin as early as September, with an enticing cast already attached. John Rhys-Davies, the Welsh star known for his roles in The Lord of the Rings and Indiana Jones, and Dutch actor Rutger Hauer, best known for Blade Runner, are set to join the production. Christian, who also contributed to Return of the Jedi and The Phantom Menace, says the timing is ideal, citing the successes of Game of Thrones and The Lord of the Rings in drawing massive audiences to epic, mythic storytelling. “Black Angel is exactly for that audience,” he said, describing it as “a legend full of drama, romance and action as a lone warrior with the help of a renegade princess and guided by an ancient sorcerer tackle the evil Black Angel and his army of undead.”

An inquest has raised concerns about the escalation of care at Gloucestershire Hospitals after a Cheltenham man died following surgery in 2016. Steven Amos, 57, died seven days after undergoing a gastrectomy reconstruction, with the coroner warning that delays in senior medical review and transfer to theatre may have reduced his chances of survival. The inquest, held in March, heard that Mr Amos’s condition deteriorated at about 01:00 BST on Monday 16 May. He was first assessed by a junior doctor at 03:15 but was not examined by a senior doctor until 08:00. An emergency operation took place at 14:00, and Mr Amos died the following evening. Following the hearing, Gloucestershire coroner Katy Skerrett wrote to Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, which runs Cheltenham General Hospital and Gloucestershire Royal Hospital. In her letter, seen by the BBC, Ms Skerrett said she was “concerned whether there is appropriate escalation of care given to a patient who acutely deteriorates during the night shifts over the weekend period.” She added: “It is likely that if Steven had been taken to theatre sooner..... his chances of survival following the emergency operation would have been increased. In my opinion there is a risk that future deaths will occur unless action is taken.” In response, the trust’s chief executive, Deborah Lee, said the organisation had “robust processes in place for investigating incidents that give rise to concern,” and that it is “committed to making any changes in practice required to help us improve care for future patients” where standards fall short. “We continue to be vigilant about quality of care, with a low threshold for investigating concerns,” Ms Lee said. “We have provided assurance to the coroner, Ms Skerrett, that we are confident we have processes in place to ensure our junior clinicians are able to effectively escalate concerns about patients who deteriorate during the night.” She added that the trust uses “an established pathway of escalating clinical concerns that is considered standard practice and is used routinely to ensure patients receive the appropriate level of care, day or night.” Ensuring patients receive “safe, effective, high quality care remains our top priority,” she said. The coroner’s concerns centre on overnight and weekend care escalation, a known pressure point in hospitals, and the trust says it will continue reviewing practices to maintain patient safety.

North Tyneside Council will transform a 32-acre (13-hectare) shipyard into a hub for renewable energy, advanced engineering and offshore industries, with the authority expecting around 1,000 new jobs when the site is complete. Elected mayor Norma Redfearn said the site is “very much open for business,” highlighting infrastructure, a development partner, and fresh funding to unlock more space for investment. Money secured by the North East Local Enterprise Partnership will be used to fill a redundant wet berth, creating new plots for potential occupiers. The project forms part of a £100m investment package involving development funds, the local authority and private sector backers. Council leaders say the redevelopment will attract local employers and supply-chain activity, positioning North Tyneside as a key base for the fast-growing offshore and clean-tech sectors while revitalising an industrial area.

High Court judges have rejected Kenneth Noye’s latest bid to overturn his murder conviction for the 1996 road-rage killing of Stephen Cameron, ruling there is no doubt the 21-year-old was deliberately stabbed and that the attack was not self-defence. Noye, 63, was jailed for life at the Old Bailey in 2000 after he fatally stabbed Mr Cameron during a confrontation on an M25 slip road at Swanley, Kent. He fled to Spain after the killing but was extradited in 1998 to face trial. Two previous appeals, in 2001 and 2004, were unsuccessful. In the latest challenge, Noye’s lawyers argued that two key witnesses whose evidence underpinned the prosecution case at trial had since been discredited and that his conviction was therefore unsafe. Sitting with Mr Justice Henriques and Mr Justice Davis, Lord Judge dismissed the arguments, describing the stabbing as a gross over-reaction in a fight with an unarmed man, almost certainly because the appellant was losing it. “There was no self-defence,” Lord Judge said in his judgment on Tuesday. “Mr Cameron was deliberately stabbed.” Mr Cameron’s mother, Toni Cameron, welcomed the ruling as long-awaited vindication but said it could not repair the loss suffered by her family. “We’re happy we’ve got justice for Stephen, but it doesn’t take away the fact that I’ve lost my son,” she told BBC Radio Kent. “Every day I think of Stephen. It hurts because of the life we’ve lost. No grandchildren, no wedding. He was starting his own business that week.” She added: “We always had a happy family life with Stephen..... it’s such a great loss to all of us. At the end of the day he left my son to die in the gutter.” Mr Cameron was stabbed in front of his fiancée, Danielle Cable, who later entered witness protection. Noye denied murder at trial, claiming he acted in self-defence. Tuesday’s decision leaves his life sentence intact.

Laura Muir’s bid to contest both the 1500m and 5,000m at this summer’s World Championships in London remains on track despite recent concerns over a foot injury, according to her coach Andy Young. The 24-year-old Scot missed two weeks of training this month after a stress fracture in her second metatarsal was detected, but Young says she has returned to training and is already running at a “world-class pace.” British Athletics performance director Neil Black said on Monday that Muir had “a 1%” chance of attempting the middle- and long-distance double in London, remarks that sparked alarm among fans and observers. Muir, the double European Indoor champion, swiftly played down the fears, tweeting: “Reports of my demise have been greatly exaggerated.” Young suggested Black’s comments were made without full information. “He was perhaps caught off guard and did not have all the information to hand,” Young told BBC Sport. “Perhaps he had forgotten she ran one of the fastest times for the 5,000m in the world this year, had the qualifying time and subsequently broke all these records. Once he said it, it was out there. There was a bit of panic that she had a bigger problem than it was. But it has not been that big of a deal, she has not been in pain or limping.” Muir qualified for the 1500m by winning last season’s Diamond League event and secured the 5,000m standard by breaking the British indoor record in January. Young emphasized that, with more than a month to go before the championships, the team will remain cautious with her recovery but sees no reason she cannot target both events. “She is looking good for the 1500m and 5,000m. She has got the qualifying times and is keen to do both,” he said. The stress fracture occurred “weeks if not months” ago and was identified by a scan on 1 June after Muir reported tightness on the top of her foot. She resumed training on 16 June. “Her times are ones that the majority of international athletes would be happy with at the peak of their season, not the first 10 days or so back in training,” Young added. “She seems back to normal. She described her pain as a 0.25 out of 10 this morning and that was after being at the track last night. She seems quite happy again.” Muir, who finished seventh in the 1500m at the Rio Olympics, will skip this weekend’s British Athletics Trials as a precaution. Young says she will race three Diamond League meetings next month and will attempt to break Zola Budd’s 32-year-old British mile record at the Anniversary Games on 9 July.

Ambulance equipment thefts across Scotland trigger outrage; 31 incidents recorded Figures uncovered by the Scottish Conservatives reveal that ambulance vehicles across Scotland have been targeted in 31 separate theft incidents over the past three years, with items including laptops, response kits, radios, phones, and paperwork taken. The Scottish Ambulance Service (SAS) stressed that no patient information was stored on the stolen phones and said the laptops were encrypted. The service added that the paperwork thefts had been reported to the Information Commissioner for Scotland. Among the incidents detailed, equipment was stolen from a special operations response division vehicle in 2012/13, while ambulances at the Scottish Ambulance Service academy in Glasgow were also targeted. The revelations have sparked anger and concern over the security of ambulance vehicles and the impact on frontline emergency responders. Conservative chief whip John Lamont condemned the thefts, saying: “The idea of thieves targeting ambulances while paramedics attempt to save lives is sickening. People will be disgusted that this has occurred so many times across Scotland over the last three years. There may well be questions for the ambulance service about security of vehicles, but paramedics can hardly be expected to worry about break-ins while patients’ lives are at risk.” He added: “Clearly the contents of ambulances make for appealing rummaging among some crooks. But anyone caught thieving from these vehicles is the lowest of the low, and must be treated as such by the law if and when they are caught.” A Scottish government spokeswoman highlighted the scale of the service’s work: “As the front line of NHS services in Scotland, our Ambulance Service respond to 700,000 calls per year, around 500,000 of which receive an emergency response. Delivering patient care is the absolute priority of ambulance crews and it is despicable that mindless thieves capitalise on these situations to steal equipment. Not only is the equipment on board vital to the ambulance crews but it could also be potentially dangerous in the wrong hands.”

Emergency response after incident at Bwlch Pen Barras near Ruthin Emergency services attended an incident at Bwlch Pen Barras, just below the Moel Famau beauty spot car park, shortly before midday Thursday. Two Welsh Air Ambulances, firefighters and a mountain rescue team responded. A woman was airlifted to a specialist trauma hospital in Stoke-on-Trent. Motorists in the area are advised to check for travel updates and possible disruption.

A Kyiv court has convicted Yevgeny Yerofeyev and Alexander Alexandrov, who were captured in eastern Ukraine last May, of waging an “aggressive war” against Ukraine, committing a terrorist act, and using weapons to provoke an armed conflict, Interfax reported. The pair had denied the charges. Russia continues to deny sending troops to the region, insisting the men were volunteers who had left active service. The verdict comes amid a fragile ceasefire between Ukrainian forces and pro-Russian separatists. Moscow, according to state media, said it would do everything in its power to bring the two men home. The case has been marked by controversy. In the run-up to the trial, Yuriy Hrabovsky, a lawyer for one of the defendants, was found dead after being kidnapped and brutally beaten, prompting concerns about due process and the safety of legal representatives. Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko has proposed swapping Yerofeyev and Alexandrov for Nadiya Savchenko, a Ukrainian military pilot convicted by a Russian court last month over the deaths of two Russian journalists. Savchenko, captured by separatists in 2015 and accused of directing artillery fire, has become a symbol of resistance in Ukraine. Her trial was widely condemned, and her lawyers say her health has deteriorated after she launched a hunger strike to protest her treatment. Last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow is in contact with Kyiv regarding the issue, raising hopes of a possible exchange.

Afghanistan capped a high-octane Twenty20 contest with a 28-run win over Ireland after piling up a formidable 233-8 in Greater Noida. The visitors, who had already secured the series, rode blistering knocks from Mohammad Nabi and Mohammad Shahzad to set a target that ultimately proved beyond Ireland despite a spirited chase. Afghanistan’s innings ran at a blistering 11.65 an over, anchored by Nabi’s explosive 89 and Shahzad’s 72 at the top. Ireland’s Kevin O’Brien was the pick of the bowlers, claiming 4-45 to check the momentum at crucial junctures, but the depth of Afghanistan’s hitting kept the scoreboard racing throughout the 20 overs. Ireland, who won the toss and chose to bowl, launched a fearless reply. Paul Stirling and Stuart Thompson powered a whirlwind opening stand of 65 off just 26 balls, giving the chase real impetus. Thompson bludgeoned five sixes in a 43 off 18 deliveries, while Stirling added 49. Middle-order anchor Gary Wilson battled to a fine 59 to keep Ireland in contention, but wickets fell regularly and the chase ended at 205 all out in 19.2 overs. Afghanistan’s attack held its nerve under pressure. Leg-spinner Rashid Khan was the standout with 3-28, striking at key moments. He was backed by Amir Hamza and Karim Janat, who took two wickets apiece to stall Ireland’s surges. “It was a fantastic game of cricket to have both teams score over 200, so credit to the ground staff and to how the teams played,” Ireland captain William Porterfield said. “It’s been a deserved series win for Afghanistan but there hasn’t been that much between the teams really, just five balls either way. You know in these games it’s going to come down to the last over or so. I was pleased with the way we kept coming and kept fighting to the end.” The sides will remain at the same venue for five one-day internationals and an Intercontinental Cup match.

The Welsh rower's time of 14 minutes 28.4 seconds over two 1900m singles races ensured a repeat of her trials win in November. Welsh sculler Vicky Thornley has strengthened her case for Olympic selection with a commanding performance in the latest GB trials, clocking a combined 14 minutes 28.4 seconds across two 1900m singles races to repeat her November victory. The 28-year-old’s display keeps her at the top of the squad’s singles rankings as the Rio 2016 build-up intensifies. Thornley, who won the women’s single scull 5km trials in Boston, Lincolnshire in November, has long been tipped for Brazil. Five-time Olympic champion Sir Steve Redgrave said then he was sure Thornley would go to Rio. Thornley makes no secret of her ambitions: “I want to win an Olympic medal, preferably gold,” she said. While her singles form is emphatic, uncertainty remains around her place in the double sculls. Thornley has been competing alongside Scotland’s Katherine Grainger, having previously raced in the women’s eight at London 2012. The pair are regarded as two of GB’s fastest individual scullers, but their combination has faced scrutiny after finishing sixth at the World Championships in Aiguebelette this year. Helen Glover and Heather Stanning, who delivered Team GB’s first gold in London 2012, will continue in the pair for Rio, leaving selectors to weigh up the optimal boat combinations elsewhere. Thornley believes consistent results can help sway those decisions. “I will want to be in the boat with the best chance of winning a medal,” she said. “I was really pleased with the weekend. I won the trial in November so wanted to keep myself at the top of the team in the singles results. I did that and had a good margin over the second place.” “Fundamentally it comes down to what the coaches feel they want to prioritise,” she added. “But the better results you have, the more sway you might have over the decisions that are made.”

Petition to Cancel Trump State Visit Tops One Million: How UK State Visits Work and Past Controversies More than a million people have signed a petition calling for US President Donald Trump’s proposed state visit to the United Kingdom to be cancelled, underscoring public unease over extending the highest level of diplomatic hospitality so early in his presidency. No date has been set for the visit, which was announced during Prime Minister Theresa May’s trip to Washington last week. Asked why an invitation was issued so soon after Mr Trump took office, a spokesperson for Mrs May said there is no set timeframe for when a president may be offered a state visit. State visits are the most formal category of international visits to the UK, typically limited to two per year. They are designed to cement strategic relationships and showcase Britain’s ties with key partners. Guests receive full ceremonial honours: a formal welcome with a guard of honour, carriage procession, and a state banquet hosted by the Queen at Buckingham Palace or Windsor Castle. The programme usually includes meetings with the prime minister and other senior officials, cultural engagements, and visits to national institutions. While the Queen formally issues the invitation, the decision is taken on the advice of the government, with the Foreign Office and No 10 weighing diplomatic, economic and security considerations. Public discontent around controversial guests is not new. In recent years, protesters have focused on leaders from countries criticised for human rights abuses. Despite outcry, past visits have gone ahead. In October 2015, President Xi Jinping’s state visit prompted demonstrations over China’s human rights record and its rule in Tibet. Campaigners accused authorities of harassing, imprisoning and torturing activists and their families, and rights groups cited persecution for religious beliefs, discrimination against ethnic minorities, tight media restrictions, limited access to foreign publications and broadcasts, and use of the death penalty. Critics also linked UK steel job losses to Chinese steel being sold cheaply on global markets. In October 2007, Saudi Arabia’s King Abdullah was greeted by protesters condemning the kingdom’s human rights record and urging the reopening of a corruption inquiry into a major arms deal. Demonstrators shouted “shame on you” as the royal procession passed along The Mall. In November 2005, Chinese President Hu Jintao’s visit drew protests over human rights, Taiwan, and Tibet, including booing during events at Guildhall. Two years earlier, in November 2003, an estimated 100,000 people marched in London against President George W. Bush’s visit, opposing the US-led war in Iraq; an effigy of Mr Bush was toppled in Trafalgar Square. Earlier decades brought their own controversies: in October 1971, veterans and former prisoners of war protested Emperor Hirohito of Japan over wartime atrocities; and among other contentious guests were Romania’s Nicolae Ceaușescu (1978), Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe (1994), and Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak (1991). Despite protests, successive governments have maintained that state visits serve the national interest.

Louis Zamperini, the Olympian and World War Two survivor whose extraordinary life inspired millions, died peacefully on Wednesday following a 40-day battle with pneumonia, his family announced. “His indomitable courage and fighting spirit were never more apparent than in these last days,” they said in a statement, honoring a man whose resilience became emblematic of perseverance against impossible odds. Zamperini’s story captivated readers in Laura Hillenbrand’s 2010 bestseller Unbroken and is the subject of a forthcoming film adaptation. The film’s director, Angelina Jolie, called his passing “a loss impossible to describe,” adding, “We are all so grateful for how enriched our lives are for having known him. We will miss him terribly.” Born in 1917 in New York state to an Italian-immigrant father, Zamperini discovered distance running as a boy and rose quickly through the ranks at his high school and the University of Southern California. At 19, he represented the United States at the 1936 Berlin Olympics and finished eighth in the 5,000 meters. He stunned spectators by sprinting a final lap in 59 seconds, a performance that earned him a handshake from Adolf Hitler and hinted at the grit that would later define his life. Zamperini left competitive running to enlist in the U.S. Army in 1941, months before the attack on Pearl Harbor. Serving as a bombardier, he was searching for a downed aircraft when his own crew’s plane crashed into the Pacific. Eight of the 11 men on board were killed. He and the remaining survivors drifted for 47 days, struggling to endure with almost no supplies. “We had rations of concentrated chocolate aboard, but during a storm the first night it all went overboard,” he recalled in a 1988 interview. “All we had left was three pints of water in cans.” They caught fish and sharks, and collected rainwater to survive. Eventually captured by a Japanese patrol, Zamperini spent two harrowing years in prison camps. He endured weeks of solitary confinement on Kwajalein, where he was told he would be executed, and later was held in an unregistered POW camp near Yokohama. He was singled out by a brutal guard he came to call “The Bird,” and endured “constant beatings, punishments and torture, especially when bombers came over.” He refused to broadcast propaganda messages in exchange for better conditions, even as the U.S. military declared him killed in action. After the war, Zamperini returned home, married, and became a devout Christian following an encounter with evangelist Billy Graham. He continued to inspire, running a leg of the torch relay at the 1998 Winter Olympics in Japan. In May, he was named grand marshal of the 2015 Rose Parade in California. Unbroken, the book that brought his story to a new generation, will reach even wider audiences when the film adaptation opens in U.S. theaters in December.

German high court overturns convictions over judge’s phone use during trial Germany’s Federal Court of Justice (BGH) has overturned the convictions of two men in a Frankfurt stabbing case after finding the presiding judge repeatedly checked a mobile phone during witness testimony. Defense lawyers filed a motion alleging bias when the judge was seen using the device; subsequent findings showed he looked at the phone several times over 10 minutes and sent two texts to a babysitter because the hearing ran late. The BGH said such conduct violated judicial duty to concentrate fully on proceedings and undermined the appearance of impartiality, ordering a retrial. BGH Judge Thomas Fischer stated that mobile phones "do not belong in the courtroom" - for onlookers, lawyers, and judges alike - and emphasized that judges must remain focused at all times. The judge involved was not identified. The decision underscores stricter expectations for courtroom decorum and the protection of fair-trial rights in Germany.

Michigan’s Schwandt family welcomed its newest member on Wednesday morning in Grand Rapids, continuing a remarkable streak: another baby boy. Jay and Kateri Schwandt, both 40, maintained their tradition of not learning the baby’s sex before birth. “I was thinking, ‘If this is a girl, I don’t know what my reaction is going to be,’” Jay said moments after his son arrived. The couple’s boys span more than two decades, starting with Tyler, 22, followed by Zach, 19, Drew, 18, Brandon, 16, Tommy, 13, Vinnie, 12, Calvin, 10, Gabe, 8, Wesley, 6, Charlie, 5, Luke, 3, and Tucker, 21 months. “There’s a lot of commotion, a lot of chaos, but there’s also a lot of love,” Kateri said. The family is now working on choosing yet another boy’s name, with the older brothers weighing in—though no consensus has emerged. Kateri, who grew up in a family of 14 children, was herself the 13th child. She noted the coincidence that their 13th child was born on the 13th day of the month—a detail not lost on the family. The Grand Rapids Press reported that several TV production companies have approached the Schwandts about a potential reality show, reflecting widespread curiosity about their uniquely large, all-boy household. Mother and baby are doing well and resting in the hospital. Asked whether a 14th boy could someday join the brood, Jay replied, “You never say never.” Does having children of one sex affect the chances of future births being the same sex? Experts say each pregnancy is essentially independent. In most populations, the odds remain close to a slight male majority at birth (about 51% boys to 49% girls). While family clusters of same-sex children can happen, prior births do not reliably influence the sex of future babies. Minor factors—such as parental ages and environmental influences—have been studied, but no consistent, decisive effect has been established.

Irwin Lipkin, 77, pleaded guilty of helping to hide the fraud from US regulators by falsifying documents. His six-month sentence marks the end of a six-year prosecution saga. A total of 15 people have been convicted for their parts in the Ponzi - pyramid - scheme orchestrated by Madoff that defrauded investors out of billions of dollars. Madoff's fraud emerged in 2008. What was thought to be a fund worth $68bn turned out to be all but worthless having been paid as fake profit or stolen by Madoff and his associates. Madoff pleaded guilty to fraud and was sentenced to 150 years in prison. The judge rejected the defence case that Lipkin should not be jailed because of his failing health, and that he did not know the full extent of Madoff's scheme. Prosecutor David Abramowicz told the court in New York: Madoff "didn't do it alone because he couldn't do it alone. He needed the help of people like Mr Lipkin". Lipkin was hired as one of Madoff's first employees in the 1960s. He apologised to the court, "and to everybody else who may have been hurt by the things that I've done".

Cavan eased past Carlow 2-13 to 0-12 in the All-Ireland SFC qualifiers, responding smartly to last weekend’s Ulster semi-final replay loss to Tyrone. The Breffni men struck early when Kevin ‘Ginger’ Keating fisted to the net in the third minute after Martin Mackey’s incisive pass. Gearoid McKiernan (3), Dara McVeety, Mackey and Killian Clarke added points to open a 1-6 to 0-5 interval lead. Mackey capped a flowing move with Cavan’s second goal after the break, though the winners soon had to cope with 14 men when McVeety was sent off. They maintained control, stretching clear through points from Keating, Seanie Johnston (3), Tom Hayes and McKiernan. Carlow battled to the end, with second-half scores from Robbie Molloy, Darragh O’Brien, Chris Blake, Daniel St Ledger and John Murphy, but never seriously threatened a comeback. Cavan advance to Monday’s third-round draw. Elsewhere: Derry 1-14 1-11 Meath; Limerick 0-10 2-12 Cork; Mayo 2-14 1-12 Fermanagh; Kildare 1-22 2-14 Offaly; Monaghan 1-13 2-13 Longford.

The Mercedes drivers, with Rosberg 23 points ahead in their championship battle, were 0.323 seconds quicker than Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen. Red Bull's Max Verstappen beat Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel to third. Jenson Button struggled for McLaren, in 16th, eight places and 0.413secs behind team-mate Fernando Alonso. Mercedes set the pace in Friday practice at Suzuka, with Nico Rosberg fastest in both sessions as the world championship leader continued to press his advantage over team-mate Lewis Hamilton. Rosberg’s edge narrowed slightly in the afternoon as clouds rolled in over the legendary figure-of-eight circuit, but the silver cars remained the benchmark, ending the day a clear 0.323 seconds ahead of Kimi Raikkonen’s Ferrari. Hamilton, who has five races left to overturn his 23-point deficit, had hoped to begin the Japanese Grand Prix weekend in the dominant form he showed in Malaysia, where he was on course for a comfortable win until a late engine failure. The Briton sounded satisfied with his day’s work despite trailing Rosberg: “It’s been a really good day with no problems on the car which is great. But there’s still some work to be done overnight in order to find more pace. Hopefully we’ll be going into Sunday in good shape.” Behind Mercedes, Red Bull looked increasingly threatening. Max Verstappen edged Sebastian Vettel for third on the timesheets, and race-simulation runs in second practice indicated the Milton Keynes team could push Mercedes in the race as well. On the soft tyres expected to feature in at least the opening stint, Verstappen and Daniel Ricciardo matched Hamilton’s average lap times. Ricciardo, last Sunday’s Malaysia winner, ended only 12th after his qualifying simulation was cut short by a virtual safety car, triggered when Esteban Gutierrez’s Haas stopped on track. Ferrari’s true pace remained harder to gauge due to off-set tyre strategies during long runs. Raikkonen’s headline lap came with a new front wing introduced for Japan, hinting the Scuderia could be in the mix. However, the Finn reported a lack of front grip on his race run, suggesting set-up work remains. Vettel, pipped by Verstappen in the afternoon, kept within touching distance but will seek improvements overnight to mount a stronger challenge. Force India emerged as comfortably the fourth-quickest team, reinforcing their strong recent form. McLaren showed promise with Fernando Alonso in eighth, indicating at least one car could reach Q3, while Jenson Button endured a difficult day. The 2009 world champion complained of poor balance and said the car felt no different from the morning session, ending 16th and 0.413 seconds slower than Alonso. Second practice was largely incident-free, with no major crashes. Renault’s Kevin Magnussen, Williams’ Felipe Massa and Sauber’s Felipe Nasr all ran wide at various points but rejoined without damage. Weather remains a wildcard: earlier forecasts predicted rain overnight and into qualifying, but confidence has waned, and Suzuka’s coastal microclimate could yet spring surprises. Rain would likely enhance Red Bull’s hopes of disrupting Mercedes’ grip on the front row.

The victim, who is in his 70s, remains critically ill after being cut several times and beaten by a gang of men. The incident happened while he was in bed at his home at Clogharevan Park at about 02:40 BST on Monday. Police believe a sum of money was stolen and have renewed their appeal. Det Insp David Henderson described the attack as "vile and terrifying". He said the man was attacked with a "sharp implement, possibly a hook" and that police wanted to "identify the callous criminals responsible and bring them to justice". "The man sustained multiple serious stab wounds and remains in a critical condition in hospital," he added. "We have heard from several witnesses who were in the area at the time and we are grateful for their help, however we are keen to speak to others who have not yet come forward. We know from CCTV that there were several vehicles travelling on the McShanes Road at around the time the three men made their escape from the gentleman's home. I would like to appeal specifically to any motorist who was travelling on that stretch of road between 1.30am and 3.30am and who may have seen the three men or anything else that could be useful to investigators." The man was taken to Daisy Hill Hospital in Newry before being transferred to the Royal Victoria Hospital in Belfast, where he remained in a critical condition on Wednesday. Detectives are treating the incident as an aggravated burglary and have urged anyone with information, including drivers who may have dashcam footage, to come forward. Officers said there have been several helpful witness accounts but believe others in the area at the time may hold vital clues to the perpetrators’ movements. No arrests have yet been reported. Police have reiterated that even seemingly minor details from the early morning timeframe on McShanes Road could assist the investigation.

Pollution in Picknall Brook kills over 1,500 fish; River Dove ecology unaffected, says Environment Agency The Environment Agency has confirmed a significant fish kill in Picknall Brook, Uttoxeter, tracing the incident to an agricultural source. While the brook feeds into the River Dove, officials said there has been no visible impact on the river’s ecology. “Our initial assessment is that over 1,500 fish have died in the brook, mainly bullheads and minnows, although we are still assessing the impact,” spokesperson Susan Bowen said. She added that the pollution pulse has passed and dissipated, water quality has returned to normal, and the agency will look at ways to help the brook’s ecology recover. The Environment Agency said it is still considering its enforcement response and cannot provide further details while investigations continue. It is also reviewing measures to prevent a recurrence. Staffordshire County Councillor for Uttoxeter, David Brookes, called it “an unfortunate incident,” and urged caution in the immediate aftermath. “I understand the pollution has now gone but I would suggest livestock are kept away from the brook for the time being,” he said.

Ordnance Survey has revealed Britain’s most-walked locations, with Snowdon’s summit area topping the list. The national mapping agency said 3,779 of nearly 400,000 subscriber-downloaded routes over the past year passed through the peak’s square kilometre. Two nearby hotspots also featured prominently: the Pyg Track ranked seventh and Pen y Pass 12th. Pen y Fan in the Brecon Beacons, Powys, placed 11th. Overall, the Lake District and Peak District dominated, claiming 16 of the top 20 spots. OS compiled the list by dividing Britain into 1km squares and counting how many downloaded routes passed through each.

Cardiff sous chef jailed after setting sleeping man’s hair on fire with aerosol flame A 23-year-old Cardiff man, Davey Paxton, was given an immediate prison sentence after admitting assault causing actual bodily harm at Cardiff Crown Court. The court heard Paxton used an aerosol deodorant and a lighter to ignite the hair of 20-year-old Connor Gammer, who was asleep at a friend’s flat following a night of drinking. Prosecutor John Warren said Gammer woke “terrified” to find his hair alight. Paxton, originally from Kilgetty in Pembrokeshire, had crept into the bedroom to carry out the drunken stunt. When Gammer ran shouting into the kitchen, a row broke out and Paxton punched him in the face. Gammer tried to go back to bed, but Paxton returned minutes later and sent another jet of flame toward his head, again setting his hair on fire. Warren told the court that Gammer’s hair was burnt away on the left side and he suffered burn wounds to his ear and the side of his neck. He received burn lotion and was advised he might need a skin graft to repair damaged skin. The court heard the two men knew each other but were not friends. Paxton, a sous chef who had recently moved to Cardiff to start work at the Pilot restaurant in Penarth, pleaded guilty to assault occasioning actual bodily harm. Aubrey Samson, defending, said Paxton was “disappointed” by his behaviour and had hoped to make a fresh start after accumulating 24 convictions in his hometown. Sentencing him on Tuesday, Judge Thomas Crowther told Paxton: “You used a flamethrower on a man who was fast asleep. The public would be horrified if I didn’t give you an immediate prison sentence.” Paxton was taken into custody following the hearing. Gammer continues to recover from his injuries.

Gemma Whyley, 28, helped coach the Welsh Paracheer Unified Freestyle Pom team to a historic gold at the ICU Cheerleading Championships in Orlando, Florida. With a quarter of athletes having physical disabilities, the inclusive team delivered a routine that secured Wales’ first-ever cheerleading title. “Winning Wales’ first gold was a dream come true,” Whyley said, noting an intense build-up from January. “All the hard work paid off in the end. It’s something we’ll all remember for the rest of our lives.”

Geoffrey Boycott’s bid to stand for election at Yorkshire’s upcoming annual general meeting has sparked a public split among club figures, with chairman Steve Denison urging members not to back the former president. Denison, who has called for stability, asked supporters to vote against Boycott at the AGM on 26 March. Former Yorkshire and England captain Michael Vaughan weighed in on social media, appealing to Boycott to withdraw. “Come on Geoffrey..... Back down. This is doing nothing for our great club,” Vaughan tweeted, later adding: “Let the experts on finance deal with it..... not cricket experts.” Boycott, 75, a BBC Test Match Special summariser and prolific former opener who made 414 first-class appearances for Yorkshire between 1962 and 1986, served as club president from 2012 to 2014 and informally acts as an overseas ambassador. He has voiced deep concern over the county’s debt, reportedly exceeding £20m. Speaking to BBC Look North, he said: “I’m not trying to create any trouble. If you carry on with the debt as it is, there won’t be a club in existence as it’s a recipe for bankruptcy. The debt’s gone from £5m in 2002 to £24m in 12 years, so the businessmen on the board haven’t done a very good job have they?” Despite those fears, Yorkshire recently announced an after-tax profit of £368,000 for 2015, its first since 2009, a result the club hopes signals improving financial health. The debate underscores a broader tension between cricketing legends and current administrators over how best to secure Yorkshire’s future, with members set to decide at the AGM amid calls for fiscal expertise and continuity.

Lord Justice Weir has sharply criticised a wave of anonymity requests emerging in Northern Ireland’s legacy inquests, describing many as “a lot of dross” and warning that such applications are causing unnecessary delays. His comments came on the second day of a two-week review into 56 legacy cases, which collectively involve 95 deaths from some of the most controversial incidents during the Troubles and where inquests have yet to be heard. The judge’s remarks followed an indication that a former soldier, expected to give evidence in the inquest into the 1973 murder of Daniel Carson, might seek anonymity. Carson, a 29-year-old Catholic, was shot dead by the Ulster Volunteer Force in the Shankill area of Belfast in November 1973. No one has ever been charged over the killing. The soldier in question was among the first to arrive at the scene, and lawyers for Carson’s family want to question him about an eyewitness claim that she told soldiers who the gunman was. “Why on earth would he want anonymity?” Lord Justice Weir asked in court. A barrister representing the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said he could not comment as he did not have full details of the potential application. Weir went on to say the legal system was being weighed down by “completely futile applications,” adding: “I often think that if people did not cry wolf so often, you might be more prepared to listen to them when the wolf actually arrives.” He stressed that while there are genuine and appropriate circumstances for anonymity, the volume of requests was contributing to lengthy and avoidable delays. The judge suggested the MoD was often the source of such applications. “Ordinary people living in England don’t go to bed at night thinking about anonymity and screening,” he said. “The idea has to come from somewhere, and to my mind it comes all too frequently and inappropriately.” The review aims to streamline the path to inquests and address long-standing concerns of bereaved families seeking answers. The court is expected to examine procedural issues and outstanding evidential matters across the legacy caseload over the coming days.

Sacha Dench, dubbed the “human swan,” is nearing the end of her epic migration-inspired journey by powered paraglider. Starting in Russia in September, the conservationist has followed the route of migrating swans across Europe, arriving in the UK last week. On Monday she plans to fly across Kent, then switch to a boat through central London, where powered flights are restricted, before resuming her route up the Thames Valley to Slimbridge in Gloucestershire. Slimbridge, the swans’ traditional wintering ground and home of the Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust, will mark the final leg of Dench’s awareness-raising expedition.

Jaguar Land Rover revenue climbs 12.8% to £21.87bn as FX pressures dent early-year profits Jaguar Land Rover, the luxury carmaker owned by India’s Tata Motors, reported annual revenue of £21.87bn, up 12.8%, after a tough start to the year was offset by strong performance in the preceding nine months. In the first three months of 2015, sales rose 8.9%, but pre-tax profit dropped 31.3% as foreign currency costs weighed on margins. The company sold 470,523 vehicles to wholesale buyers and recorded 462,209 retail sales over the year. It spent £3.15bn on capital expenditure and research and development, underscoring plans to broaden its product range and manufacturing footprint. “Jaguar Land Rover has delivered five years of solid financial results, enabling us to invest in our long-term future,” said chief executive Ralf Speth. Rising annual profits at Jaguar Land Rover helped scale back losses elsewhere in its parent company. Pre-tax losses at Tata Motors’ standalone unit, largely its Indian business, widened to 39.7bn rupees in the year to March from 10bn rupees a year earlier. Even so, Tata Motors reported a 15% rise in pre-tax profit to 217bn rupees, compared with 188.7bn rupees, while a 76bn-rupee tax charge shaved net profit by 0.3% to 140bn rupees. The results reflect currency headwinds and ongoing investment across the group.

Kumar Sangakkara marked his County Championship debut for Surrey with a masterful unbeaten century as the visitors closed on 363-3 against Glamorgan in Cardiff, while Kevin Pietersen’s bid to reignite his England Test career began with a brief innings of 19. Coming in at 111-2 after an opening stand of 104 between Rory Burns and Zafar Ansari, Pietersen struck four boundaries but was dismissed when he pushed at Craig Meschede and edged to Colin Ingram at first slip. It was the South Africa-born batsman’s first Championship appearance since he made an unbeaten 177 against Yorkshire in June 2013, and his first competitive four-day outing since the 2013-14 Ashes. With recent changes at the England and Wales Cricket Board, including the departure of managing director Paul Downton, the 34-year-old has made no secret of his desire to return to the Test arena this summer. Pietersen survived a top-edged hook off Graeme Wagg before Meschede, who had spoken before the match about relishing big moments, found the outside edge. “My first first-class wicket was Sachin Tendulkar, so it’s nice to add him [Pietersen] to my numbers. He’ll be my number two!” Meschede told BBC Wales Sport. “It’s nice to get a big scalp to my name and he had a lot to prove today. I’m sure he’ll bounce back, but hopefully not in this game. It’s been a tough day on a pretty flat wicket, Kumar is a fantastic player and a world-class cricketer but as a youngster I can learn a lot from it. We’ve got to hit our lengths, bowl to our fields and pick up a few wickets – then we need to get our mindset right and bat big.” That proved to be Glamorgan’s final success of the day as left-handers Sangakkara and Steven Davies took control in ideal batting conditions. Sangakkara, elegant and authoritative, reached three figures with a boundary off Andy Carter and finished unbeaten on 112, while wicketkeeper-batsman Davies was equally assured in registering 109 not out, his 17th first-class century, five overs before the close. The pair added an unbroken 213, collecting 30 boundaries between them, with Sangakkara also lofting spinner Dean Cosker for a six as the home attack toiled. Surrey’s strong platform had been set by Burns’ composed 50 and Ansari’s fluent 48, the latter falling lbw to Carter to open the door for Pietersen’s entrance. But once Meschede removed the former England batsman, Sangakkara and Davies made sure there would be no further inroads. “Kevin missed out here but I’ve no doubt in my mind he will get the runs he needs to play for England again,” Davies said. “He’s been great at Surrey. I’ve never had any problems with him, and he looked great last week on a tough wicket at Oxford. Sangakkara was unbelievable. He’s a hero of mine and to play alongside him is a great honour. To get that partnership with him was a special day for me.”

China said Tuesday it will soon complete land reclamation on features in the disputed Spratly Islands, signaling the next phase of construction in the South China Sea as tensions with the United States and rival claimants rise. The foreign ministry, referring to the area by its Chinese name, the Nansha islands, did not provide a timeline or specify which of the seven reefs currently being transformed would be finished “soon.” Once reclamation ends, Beijing said it will begin building facilities to “fulfil the relevant functions,” describing the projects as serving defense, maritime search and rescue, disaster relief and scientific research. Washington and countries with competing claims in the area maintain China is creating artificial islands for use as military bases, a charge Beijing rejects. China claims most of the South China Sea, and last year accelerated its island-building, prompting the United States in May to call for an “immediate and lasting halt” to reclamation in disputed waters. Recent U.S. operations and Chinese patrols near the Spratlys have heightened risks of miscalculation as both sides assert their positions.

Police were called to Woodvale Drive on Sunday at about 07:30 GMT after multiple men were injured, including stab wounds and assault-related injuries. The incident is believed to have occurred both inside a house and out on the street. Two men have been arrested and are being questioned on suspicion of attempted murder.

SS Great Britain Trust Collection awarded Arts Council designated status The SS Great Britain Trust Collection has been added to Arts Council England’s roll call of designated collections, an accolade reserved for “unique collections of national and international importance.” It is one of four new additions to a list that now numbers more than 140 collections across the country. Phil Gibby of Arts Council England said the recognition “highlights the extraordinary wealth of the South West’s cultural heritage,” noting the collection’s breadth and its contribution to understanding maritime history and engineering innovation. Built by engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel and launched in 1843, the pioneering ocean liner SS Great Britain revolutionised transatlantic travel. Over its lifetime, the steamship is estimated to have travelled a million miles at sea and circumnavigated the globe 32 times. Since 1970, it has been docked in Bristol, where it was originally constructed, and transformed into a major visitor attraction. The ship sits alongside the Brunel Institute, which provides public access to archives and resources that illuminate Victorian maritime technology, the history of 19th Century emigration, and Brunel’s engineering legacy. “This is a great and important accolade for the SS Great Britain Trust Collections,” said Matthew Tanner, chief executive of the SS Great Britain Trust. “I am extremely proud to care for a nationally-designated collection and also of the entire team who look after it and ensure it is accessible for everybody, every day.”

Promoted Premiership side London Irish have bolstered their pack with three signings: Fiji international prop Manasa Saulo, 28, from Toulon; Samoa lock Filo Paulo, 29, after his stint with Benetton Treviso; and Australia flanker Jake Schatz, 26, from the Melbourne Rebels. Saulo will tour with Fiji this summer. The arrivals take Irish’s tally to 10 recruits since securing promotion from the Championship.

His family say the 75-year-old is able to sit up in bed, adding that while he is "by no means out of the woods there is room for cautious optimism." England and Tottenham legend Jimmy Greaves is showing encouraging signs in hospital, his family said, as the 75-year-old continues to receive treatment. In a statement issued on Tuesday, his wife Irene said: “Jimmy is having to do what he is told and understands the seriousness of what has happened. He’s in the best hands.” Greaves previously suffered a minor stroke in 2012. One of English football’s most prolific forwards, Greaves holds Tottenham’s club record with 220 league goals scored between 1961 and 1970. He remains fourth on England’s all-time scoring list, with 44 goals in 57 appearances, behind Sir Bobby Charlton, Gary Lineker and Wayne Rooney. Before his Spurs heroics, he struck a then-club record 124 league goals for Chelsea from 1957 to 1961, and also had spells with AC Milan and West Ham. Greaves was part of England’s 1966 World Cup-winning squad, though he originally missed out on a medal after being injured during the group stage.
