Beyond his playing career, he became a household name on television in the 1980s as a pundit on ITV, most notably alongside Ian St John on the popular Saint and Greavsie show, which ran from 1985 to 1992.

Armagh, Banbridge and Craigavon Borough Council has reprinted promotional material for a July outdoor performance of Charles Dickens’ Great Expectations after a misplaced apostrophe slipped into an advert, incurring an estimated £1,200 in costs, the BBC understands. A council spokesperson said correcting the error was “the right thing to do” because the event celebrates a “literary giant.” The free production was supported by a campaign across boards, sheets, leaflets, flyers, posters and window vinyls. “Unfortunately, due simply to human error, a misplaced apostrophe was not picked up,” the spokesperson added. Itemised costs include £140 to amend 48 sheets, £95 for delivering additional leaflets, £295 to reprint advertising boards, £332 on flyers and posters, and £290 for a window vinyl. The incident places the council among many organisations ensnared by the rogue apostrophe. In February last year, Tesco apologised after two grammatical gaffes appeared on a two-pack of baby clothing. And in April, the BBC highlighted a self-styled “grammar vigilante” in Bristol who roams at night, correcting street signs and shop fronts bearing errant punctuation. Despite the slip, the council says its priority remains ensuring strong public awareness and attendance at the free cultural event.

Only the driver remains in hospital after coach overturns near Stroud Only the driver is still being treated for shoulder and rib injuries after a coach carrying families overturned into a ditch near Stroud, a spokesman for the Confederation of Passenger Transport (CPT) said. The crash happened just before 10:00 BST close to junction 13 of the motorway. The coach, operated by Stourbridge-based Prospect Coaches and chartered by the charity Action for Children, had been taking a group from a children’s centre in Sandwell on a day trip to the beach at Weston-super-Mare. Christopher Nice of the CPT, which represents UK bus and coach operators, said all passengers were discharged from hospital on Tuesday night and the coach company arranged for them to be transferred back to West Bromwich. He added that the driver, who suffered shoulder and rib injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening, remains in hospital. Action for Children said there were 25 children on board, aged between 11 months and eight years, among 53 people in total. Gloucestershire Police said five adults and one child were injured. The southbound carriageway of the motorway was closed for several hours while emergency services responded and recovery work took place. Mr Nice said the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency will examine the coach “to see if there were any problems,” and confirmed the driver is due to be interviewed as part of efforts to establish how the vehicle left the road and overturned. Passenger Barinder Kaur, who was travelling with her two children, described a frightening scene as the coach veered off the carriageway. “People started screaming. The coach started to shake then it just turned over. My eyes were closed. I hit something and when I opened my eyes there was broken glass and blood everywhere,” she said. A Gloucestershire Police spokesperson said inquiries into the cause are continuing.

Consent Workshops Made Compulsory Across Oxbridge Colleges Amid Calls to Tackle ‘Rape Culture’ A woman who says she was raped at Oxford University after a drinking game has welcomed the rollout of compulsory consent workshops across Oxford and Cambridge colleges, calling them “long overdue.” The woman, who wishes to be known as Maria Marcello, wrote on her blog that she was assaulted as she lay passed out on her bed after drinking. “Obviously it won’t stop rape altogether, but it’s a huge step in the right direction,” she said. “It’s crucial they’re compulsory or the people who need to go won’t go, but they’re also important to reduce victim-blaming attitudes in colleges — we want to not only combat rape itself, but also rape culture.” She added that she hopes Oxbridge will lead the way and that similar sessions will be offered at other universities and schools. The workshops, which will take place in small groups of about 10, are compulsory in 22 of the 30 Oxford colleges running them. In Cambridge, 20 out of the university’s 31 colleges will hold workshops marked as a compulsory part of freshers’ week. Oxford University Student Union vice president and organiser Anna Bradshaw said the initiative aims “to break the culture of silence.” She advocated for a focus on “enthusiastic consent,” adding: “A more healthy culture of enthusiastic consent we think would be about looking for the consent, making sure that you have got it, feeling sure of it, then you don’t get into these murky questions of, ‘was she too drunk? Or maybe she was just about OK?’” Linda Darrall of Thames Valley Victim Support welcomed the courses, emphasizing: “It is important that people understand no means no.” The push comes amid growing concern about student safety. A National Union of Students survey published last month suggested that one in four students is groped or harassed while at university, underscoring calls for clearer education on consent and a stronger institutional response to sexual misconduct.

Media playback is not supported on this device Cricket Scotland chief executive Malcolm Cannon says the prospect of Scotland securing full ICC membership and, with it, the chance to play Test cricket is “possibly on the cards” after encouraging signals from the game’s global governing body. Cannon, who succeeded Roddy Smith in September 2015, revealed his renewed optimism stems from discussions during an ICC conference hosted by Cricket Scotland in June. “I won’t give a timescale, but I’ll give a lot of hope,” he said. “I would put Scotland at the vanguard of these opportunities just now, so I’m not promising anything – but I do think it is possibly on the cards.” “From the whispers, this was the most positive and encouraging noises that have been heard from the ICC about potential full membership and potential Test cricket or multi-day cricket for minor nations,” Cannon told BBC Scotland, indicating a shift in tone toward emerging nations seeking a pathway to the longest format. While Test ambitions grow, Cricket Scotland’s nearer-term target is to elevate both the senior men’s and women’s teams into the top 12 of the ICC one-day international rankings by 2019. The men currently sit 13th, having seen the first match of a two-game ODI series against Afghanistan at The Grange abandoned due to rain on Monday. Head coach Grant Bradburn’s side entered that series on the back of a watershed moment at the World T20 in March, where Scotland claimed their first victory at a major global tournament in 21 attempts by defeating Hong Kong. The breakthrough buoyed the squad and administrators alike, yet Cannon remains measured about its significance. “We mustn’t lose sight of the fact that it’s taken 21 times to do it,” he cautioned. “We’ve still to cause a major upset on the world stage and I think we’ve got to keep on believing in ourselves and proving that we can compete with the best of them.” Cannon’s message blends ambition with realism: sustained progress and consistency will be essential if Scotland are to turn promise into a permanent place among cricket’s elite.

Burkina Faso, which means "land of honest men", has significant reserves of gold, but the country has faced domestic and external concern over the state of its economy and human rights. A former French colony, Burkina Faso gained independence as Upper Volta in 1960 and later adopted its current name in 1984. Despite its mineral wealth and strategic position in West Africa, the nation has struggled to translate resources into broad-based development, amid recurring political upheavals and persistent security threats that have strained state institutions and social services. Political turbulence has shaped much of Burkina Faso’s modern history. After a series of coups that followed independence, Capt Thomas Sankara seized power in 1983 and embarked on radical left-wing reforms aimed at self-sufficiency, anti-corruption, and social equality. His rule ended in 1987 when he was ousted and killed by Blaise Compaore, who introduced limited democratic reforms in 1990 but remained in power for 27 years. Mounting frustration over efforts to extend his tenure culminated in massive protests in 2014 that forced Compaore to step aside, paving the way for a transitional administration. The transition faced serious tests. In September 2015, troops allied to the ousted president attempted a coup, which acting President Michel Kafando and loyalist forces ultimately repelled. Stabilization efforts cleared the way for elections that November, when Roch Marc Christian Kabore, a French-educated banker who had served as prime minister and speaker of parliament under Compaore, won the presidency. Kabore, a long-time ally who had broken with Compaore in 2014 over plans to alter the constitution, cast himself as a social democrat. He pledged to tackle youth unemployment, strengthen education and healthcare, and provide free health care for children under six. Security challenges intensified soon after. In 2016, Islamist militants attacked a hotel and a café frequented by the French military and other expatriates in the capital, killing 29 people. The assault highlighted the spillover of regional extremism into Burkina Faso, compounding pressures on a country already navigating fragile institutions and economic constraints. Burkina Faso’s demographics and social indicators underscore the urgency of reform. With a population of about 17.4 million and an area of 274,200 square kilometers, the country is multilingual—French and numerous indigenous languages are widely spoken—and religiously diverse, with indigenous beliefs, Islam, and Christianity all present. Life expectancy stands at roughly 55 years for men and 57 for women. The economy relies significantly on gold and agriculture, and uses the CFA franc (Communaute Financiere Africaine). Past controversies have included a 2000 agreement to establish a UN-run mechanism to monitor weapons imports following allegations of illicit arms transfers to regional conflicts, as well as bouts of unrest, including a 2011 mutiny. From independence to the present, Burkina Faso’s trajectory reflects the tension between popular aspirations for accountable governance and the persistent headwinds of insecurity and underdevelopment. The country’s leadership has vowed reforms, but sustaining progress amid economic and human rights concerns remains a formidable challenge.

Ofcom is proposing to cut the price that BT’s infrastructure arm, Openreach, can charge operators for its popular superfast broadband service, a move the regulator says should lead to cheaper bills for consumers. Openreach operates the wires and cables that power the UK’s broadband network, leasing lines to BT’s rivals such as Sky and TalkTalk. Under the proposals, the wholesale price for 40 Mbit/second broadband would fall from £88.80 a year to £66.28 next year and £52.77 by 2020. “We would expect much of this reduction to be passed through by retail providers to their customers, resulting in lower bills,” Ofcom said. The regulator will not cap prices for even faster broadband services, aiming to spur network investment by encouraging operators to build their own lines in competition with Openreach. Ofcom is also planning new service quality rules to speed up installations and repairs. Openreach would be required to complete 93% of fault repairs within two working days, up from 80% currently, and install 95% of connections on the date agreed with telecoms providers, compared with 90% today. Jonathan Oxley, Ofcom’s competition group director, said: “Our plans are designed to encourage long-term investment in future ultrafast, full-fibre networks, while promoting competition and protecting consumers from high prices.” The proposals arrive days after Ofcom issued BT with a record £42m fine over delays by Openreach in installing high-speed lines. In a separate measure intended to bolster competition, Ofcom has forced BT to legally separate Openreach into a distinct business. The regulator’s package seeks to balance lower prices and better service now with incentives for industry to invest in next-generation broadband infrastructure.

Scrum-half Sarel Pretorius raced 80 metres for the opening try after Dorian Jones had kicked two penalties, setting the tone for a composed Newport Gwent Dragons performance at Rodney Parade. Jones added two more shots at goal to stretch the lead before capping his night with a solo, shorter-range dash to the line shortly after the break, rewarding the home side’s control in territory and tempo. Pau struggled to turn pressure into points, with Dragons’ pack, led by Taulupe Faletau and Lewis Evans, disrupting at the breakdown and holding firm in the set piece against a front row featuring Euan Murray and Chris King. Adam Hughes and Ashton Hewitt threatened out wide, while Sarel Pretorius’s pace and support lines repeatedly unsettled the visitors’ defence. The result gives Dragons valuable momentum ahead of the return fixture in Pau next Saturday, though head coach staff face a concern over wing Tom Prydie, who was helped off in the second half and will undergo assessment. Referee Craig Maxwell-Keys oversaw proceedings, assisted by touch judges Steve Lee and Robin Goodliffe, with Andy Blyth acting as citing commissioner. Dragons will aim to replicate their composure away from home to complete the double.

English Heritage has unveiled new staircases and viewing platforms in Leicester’s Building at Kenilworth Castle, Warwickshire, opening up Queen Elizabeth I’s former private chambers to visitors. The installation allows people to climb 18m (60ft) to the queen’s bedroom and take in views over the castle grounds and woodland. Private chambers were created in the tower for the queen’s visits. “Leicester’s Building was one of the most spectacular works of architecture in Elizabethan England, a soaring tower expressly built to win the queen’s hand in marriage,” said Jeremy Ashbee, head curator at English Heritage. “Visitors can now get right up to the top of this building and get a real sense of the luxury and views she enjoyed.” Elizabeth I granted Kenilworth Castle to her favourite, Robert Dudley, in 1563; the following year he was created Earl of Leicester. Dudley, who shared her passion for riding and dancing, spent a fortune transforming the castle and laid out a garden to impress her. Despite four royal visits, including a 19-day stay in 1575, he failed to secure her hand in marriage. After the English Civil War ended in 1651, Leicester’s Building fell into ruin. The new access offers a glimpse into its storied past.

A body found near the Bridge of Sourden in the Rothes area has been identified as 85-year-old Kathleen Edward from nearby Aberlour, police have confirmed. A second body recovered in the same vicinity was later identified as 77-year-old Rosemary Laing, who had been reported missing from her home in Rothes. Police Scotland said it is understood the deaths are being treated as unrelated. Chief Inspector Stewart Mackie thanked the local community and partner agencies for their support during the searches. “I would like to take this opportunity to thank the public for their help and information in relation to the searches for both ladies. The support from the public for both of these sad cases has been very much appreciated,” he said. “I would also like to express our gratitude for the assistance we’ve received from the coastguard and members of the Braemar mountain rescue team.” Ms Edward was last seen on Monday and reported missing from the Broomfield Square area of Aberlour on Tuesday afternoon. Ms Laing was last spoken to on Tuesday evening and reported missing the following day.

Anastasija Sevastova battled past Maria Sharapova 5-7, 6-4, 6-2 to reach the US Open quarter-finals in New York, setting up a last-eight meeting with American Sloane Stephens. The 16th seed from Latvia, 27, absorbed Sharapova’s first-strike power and gradually turned the match with elastic defence, clever changes of pace, and acute angles that repeatedly drew errors from the former champion. Sevastova, 5ft 5in, said afterward that persistence was decisive. “The first set was very close, it could have gone either way,” she said. “She played unbelievable throughout the first and second set and I just kept fighting, running every ball, and just stayed there.” Sharapova, ranked 146th and competing in just her second event since May after injuries and her April return from a doping ban, had been granted a wildcard into the main draw. Despite limited match practice, the 2006 US Open winner announced her return in style with a first-round upset of world number two Simona Halep, then followed with wins over Timea Babos and Sofia Kenin to reach the last 16. Against Sevastova, she started brightly, edging a tight opening set after the Latvian hauled back a 4-1 deficit. Two thunderous forehands sealed it for Sharapova in the 12th game, but the momentum had already begun to shift. Sevastova earned the lone break of the second set at 2-1, a passage that featured two deft lobs in a single rally and forced Sharapova into a desperate left-handed retrieval at the net. From there, Sevastova managed the scoreboard with poise to level the match. A six-minute bathroom break by Sharapova before the decider did little to halt Sevastova’s surge. The Latvian raced ahead 3-0 and, though Sharapova’s grit surfaced to narrow the gap to 3-2, the five-time major winner could not sustain her level. Sevastova closed strongly, mixing drop shots and slice backhands to draw Sharapova forward and out of rhythm, and converted her fourth match point after two hours and 17 minutes when a big first serve forced a wide return. Sharapova finished with 42 winners but 51 unforced errors as she pressed to hit through Sevastova’s defenses. In the deciding set her forehand misfired alarmingly, yielding 18 unforced errors against just four winners. “Sevastova carved out a hard-earned victory with some mighty defence, and clever use of the drop shot and slice to drag Sharapova into the net,” observed BBC Sport tennis correspondent Russell Fuller. “The Russian was outstanding in patches, but lost her way completely in the deciding set.” Sevastova will face Stephens in the quarter-finals after the American defeated Julia Goerges earlier. For Sharapova, the run to the fourth round is projected to lift her back into the top 100 and offered signs of progress after an injury-disrupted summer, even as a lack of match sharpness ultimately told. More broadly, the result highlighted the tour’s depth: a current top-20 player calmly finishing against a five-time major champion who, despite her aura, has competed in only five events in 19 months.

The two sergeants from Croydon, south London, are on restricted duties pending the outcome of the inquiry Two Metropolitan Police sergeants from Croydon have been placed on restricted duties while an inquiry examines allegations about their response to a fatal stabbing in 2014. The claims emerged during an ongoing misconduct investigation, the Met said. Andrew Else, 52, was stabbed more than 200 times during an incident on Selsdon Park Road, Croydon, in April 2014. Paranoid schizophrenic Ephraim Norman, 24 at the time, admitted manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility in February. He was ordered to be detained indefinitely at the maximum-security Broadmoor Hospital. The Metropolitan Police said officers were at the scene within seven minutes of the emergency call. A file relating to the conduct of the two sergeants has been referred to the Crown Prosecution Service for consideration. The officers have not been suspended but remain on restricted duties pending the outcome of the inquiry. Det Ch Supt Alaric Bonthron, from the Directorate of Professional Services, which is leading the investigation, said: “The suggestion that any police officer has in some way failed to do their duty and respond properly to any call for a response must be fully and properly investigated. If any officer has failed in their duty it is only right that they are held to account. Everyday in London police officers work hard to keep the public safe. Allegations such as these trouble us all.”

AIBA president Ching-Kuo Wu has vowed disciplinary action against Irish boxer Michael Conlan after the bantamweight fighter made an obscene gesture toward officials and delivered a profanity-filled interview following his unanimous-decision loss to Russia’s Vladimir Nikitin at the Rio 2016 Olympics. “He immediately showed his finger to the referee-judges. Disciplinary action will follow, you can’t humiliate in public our judges,” Wu said, adding that the International Olympic Committee deemed Conlan’s outburst “totally unacceptable.” “He put himself in a difficult position, I can tell you,” Wu noted. Conlan, a Belfast native, claimed he had been “robbed” and “cheated” after the quarter-final bout, amplifying scrutiny of judging at the Games. In response to mounting criticism, AIBA sent home several referees and judges amid a string of debated verdicts, including the heavyweight final in which Russia’s Evgeny Tishchenko was awarded victory over Kazakhstan’s Vassiliy Levit. Wu, who was ringside for that fight, defended the outcome. “I felt in my mind, nothing wrong [about the decision]. Nothing wrong. But the next day, suddenly it becomes a very controversial issue. It was really surprising,” he said. Facing accusations of corruption against AIBA, Wu issued a forceful denial and challenged critics to substantiate their claims. “People accusing AIBA of corruption, please give me the evidence. I have no mercy to those [corrupt] people. I hate manipulation, corruption,” he said, suggesting legal action may be pursued against individuals who publicly allege wrongdoing without proof. Wu emphasized that AIBA applies strict oversight to officiating and has acted decisively in Rio. “We always assign the evaluators of the referees and judges to watch for fair play. If they find certain referees and judges not meeting expectations, or if some mistake is made, then immediately we interview them. The [suspension usually] runs three days. This time, we sent them home. Our policy is zero tolerance. I want perfect. The best,” he said. In the wake of the Conlan bout and broader concerns about scoring, Wu said the organization will undertake a comprehensive review of its system ahead of Tokyo 2020. “Since that happened [the Conlan fight], we want to totally review our [scoring] system and how to improve. It will be transparent. We will continue to work to make it in a more perfect condition,” he promised.

Two 18-year-old men from Wednesfield have been arrested on suspicion of wounding and violent disorder over the assault on Nic Cruwys in Littles Lane, Wolverhampton, following the Wolves v Watford Championship match. West Midlands Police said both suspects have been released on bail. A total of 11 people have now been detained as part of the investigation. Cruwys, 44, from Hemel Hempstead, remains in a specialist care ward with critical head injuries. Officers continue to appeal for witnesses and footage to aid inquiries.

Edmund advances to third round as Konta progresses; Murray, Evans and Broady set for Thursday Britain’s Kyle Edmund continued his impressive run with a straight-sets victory over American Ernesto Escobedo, winning 7-5 6-4 6-4 to reach the last 32. The 21-year-old Yorkshireman, ranked 84th in the world, backed up his first-round upset of 13th seed Richard Gasquet and will face American 20th seed John Isner next. In humid, energy-sapping conditions, both Edmund and world No. 201 Escobedo struggled to find their first serves, producing a contest packed with long, bruising rallies. Edmund absorbed early pressure to edge the opening set and, despite letting six break points slip by in the second, stayed composed. Some brilliant defense earned him a seventh opportunity, prompting Escobedo to smash his racquet, and Edmund converted to establish a two-set lead after around 90 minutes. The third set brought more resistance from Escobedo, with Edmund denied repeatedly on break points. It was the Briton’s sixth chance of the set—and 16th of the match—when he finally made the breakthrough, before confidently serving out to seal a deserved win. “I’m very pleased, a lot of good things today,” Edmund told Eurosport. “I thought I played a much cleaner match, a lot of things went better for me against Gasquet. This was about toughing out more longer rallies, I made a few more errors, but you can’t be too tough on yourself. I thought every set I stayed tough, and when it counted towards the end I got the break.” Meanwhile, Briton Johanna Konta overcame Bulgaria’s Tsvetana Pironkova 6-2 5-7 6-2 to move into the third round. Compatriots Andy Murray, Dan Evans and Naomi Broady are scheduled to play their second-round matches on Thursday, as British interest remains strong heading into the latter stages.

Scottish new car registrations fell 17.5% in April as buyers rushed to beat new VED rules New car sales in Scotland dropped sharply in April, with registrations down 17.5% year-on-year to 12,059, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). The slide mirrors a broader cooling across the UK, where April sales were off by nearly 20% compared with the same month last year, following a record-breaking March. Industry leaders say the decline was anticipated as consumers accelerated purchases to avoid higher Vehicle Excise Duty (VED) rates that came into force on 1 April. Under the new regime, all newly registered cars—apart from those with zero emissions—are subject to an annual flat rate charge, replacing the previous system that was more closely tied to carbon dioxide output. The change prompted a surge of registrations in March as buyers sought to minimize future tax liabilities, leaving a void in April. Despite last month’s fall, Scottish sales remain resilient, up around 1% over the first four months of the year compared with 2016. Performance varied widely by region. Dumfries and Galloway was the worst affected area, with registrations plunging by more than 42% year-on-year in April, highlighting the uneven impact of shifting consumer sentiment and tax policy across local markets. Scottish Motor Trade Association (SMTA) chief executive Sandy Burgess said: “With the strong March and the added incentive of beating the new rules on Vehicle Excise Duty coming into play on 1 April there was always going to be something of an ‘emergency stop’ in the results. The tail-off was evident across our dealers showrooms and even online inquiry levels have softened.” He added that speculation over a potential scrappage scheme for older, less efficient diesel cars may have contributed to a “double whammy” in demand. “Ironically of course an introduction of such a scheme may well serve to bring a degree of ignition to the new car market,” Burgess said. Looking ahead, Burgess noted retailers hold “fantastic levels of outstanding pre-owned vehicles” and reported a reassuring “business as usual” message for motorists considering a change, as the market adjusts to the new VED landscape.

Kerry Boyd, 20, has left her role as Kent Youth Commissioner after pausing public engagements in June while reports of a relationship were investigated. Boyd, who took a gap year from her education and business studies to serve full-time from 2014, was appointed by Kent’s police and crime commissioner (PCC) Ann Barnes in March, succeeding Paris Brown, who resigned following controversy over past Twitter posts. A spokeswoman for PCC Ann Barnes said there were no plans to replace Boyd at present, adding that Mrs Barnes is “still thinking about ways to engage with young people.” The youth commissioner post, created by Mrs Barnes, is not a statutory role and many other counties do not have youth commissioners. In a blog post, Mrs Barnes praised Boyd’s contribution and character: “I hope that Kerry has enjoyed her time with us – there have been tough times, certainly, but 20-year-old Kerry has risen to the challenge and we shall miss her dry sense of humour and quick wit. She has been a great advocate for my office and given up numerous evenings and weekends as she has travelled far and wide to get the widest views possible.” Boyd, a former London 2012 Olympic Torch-bearer from Margate, paused public duties in June after reports surfaced of a relationship with former county councillor and youth leader Robert Burgess, who is believed to have acted as a referee for the £15,000-a-year role. Burgess told BBC Radio Kent at the time that he and Boyd had been “good friends.” The PCC’s office said it will continue to explore alternative routes to ensure young people’s voices are heard across Kent, despite the decision not to immediately appoint a successor.

Paul Hill, 42, has been jailed for six months at the High Court in Edinburgh for recklessly discharging a firearm and failing to appear for trial after a 1996 incident outside a pub in Killin, Perthshire. Hill, who had fled Scotland and spent years living in England, Ireland and the Channel Islands, surrendered to authorities last year, bringing an end to nearly three decades evading arrest. The court heard that the incident unfolded after Hill spent an evening with his parents, sister and a friend at the Falls of Dochart Inn in Killin. An altercation began between Hill’s father and another man, and a witness, Crichton Davies, told Hill to go home. Davies described Hill as “really wound up.” A struggle ensued during which Hill produced a small handgun and fired a shot into the air. As Davies tried to wrest the weapon from his grasp, Hill fired a second shot upwards. The firearm was never recovered. Hill handed himself in to police the day after the shooting and was initially charged with attempted murder. He was released on bail but failed to appear for trial in February 1997 and subsequently fled, remaining at large for many years before turning himself in last year. He admitted struggling with Mr Davies and recklessly discharging the gun, as well as failing to attend court and absconding to avoid detection and arrest. Defence counsel Brian McConnachie QC told the court the shooting was “a one-off, impetuous, reckless act which had never been repeated.” He said that, shortly before Hill’s original trial date, the Dunblane school massacre had occurred, in which gunman Thomas Hamilton murdered 16 children and a teacher before killing himself. McConnachie said Hill’s former solicitor “somewhat unwisely” suggested Hill could be made an example of because of the prevailing climate following Dunblane, contributing to his decision to flee. Sentencing Hill, Judge Lord Ericht acknowledged the offence of conviction was “much less serious” than the original charge but stressed the gravity of firing a weapon in public. “Nonetheless, the discharge of a firearm is a serious matter,” he said. “You have also defied the authority of the court by failing to attend for trial and evaded arrest since then.” Hill, of Killin, Perthshire, will serve six months in prison for the offences arising from the 1996 incident and his prolonged failure to face justice.

Ethiopia’s Oromia Ruling Party Drops Addis Ababa Expansion Plan After Protests and Deadly Clashes Demonstrations by members of Ethiopia’s Oromo community have prompted the ruling party in the Oromia region to drop a controversial “master plan” to expand Addis Ababa into surrounding areas. Human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, estimate that at least 140 people were killed by security forces during the protests, which began in November and intensified amid fears that Oromo farmers could be displaced. The government disputes the death toll, calling it an overestimate. Abiy Berhane of Ethiopia’s London embassy told the BBC that authorities had tried to avoid confrontation and that the protests were hijacked by people intent on provoking violence. The Oromo People’s Democratic Organisation (OPDO) decided to abandon the plan after three days of discussions with local communities, state broadcaster EBC reported. OPDO, together with the Addis Ababa city authority, would have overseen implementation. Officials had maintained that the plan would be carried out only after broad consensus following in-depth consultations. However, a leading online campaigner said on Facebook that Oromo activists have dismissed the reversal as too little, too late, reflecting deep mistrust after months of unrest and reported crackdowns. The master plan was designed to integrate areas adjacent to the capital into Addis Ababa’s rapidly expanding economy, but it triggered strong resistance in Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest region, which completely surrounds the city. Anger over the capital’s proposed expansion dates back to 2014 and builds on long-standing complaints among the Oromo that they have been excluded from political and economic power. At the 2007 census, the Oromo were Ethiopia’s largest ethnic group, with about 25 million people out of a total population of nearly 74 million. Observers say the decision to halt the plan may ease immediate tensions, but they also note calls for independent investigations into protest-related deaths and detentions. Activists continue to demand accountability and broader reforms, while the government says it remains committed to consultation on any future development initiatives.

Joseph Mathunjwa, president of the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union (AMCU), says the union has accepted a wage deal that would end a five-month strike across South Africa’s platinum belt, with members to return Wednesday. The stoppage, which began on 23 January when more than 70,000 workers downed tools to demand higher pay and benefits, has disrupted about 45% of global platinum supply and contributed to South Africa’s first-quarter economic contraction. Anglo American Platinum, Impala Platinum and Lonmin have not commented. Management is due to meet AMCU on Tuesday, when the deal is expected to be signed. Addressing a stadium packed with workers who have gone unpaid for five months, Mathunjwa said the companies had "agreed to the bulk of our demands," prompting chants of "sign, sign, sign" from the crowd. The agreement is expected to lift entry-level pay toward 12,500 rand (£694) per month over the next three years, with increases varying by seniority. The companies have reported combined lost earnings of 23.8bn rand (£1.3bn; $2.2bn) during the strike, which has sharply curtailed production in the world’s top exporter of platinum. South Africa holds around 80% of known global reserves of the metal, widely used in catalytic converters to reduce automotive emissions. Despite the prolonged disruption, stockpiles have largely kept markets supplied. The South African rand strengthened almost 1% to 10.5575 per US dollar, its firmest level since 9 June, as investors welcomed signs of a resolution that could restore output and ease pressure on the economy.

Phil Dollman, the 32-year-old former Newport Gwent Dragon, has been called into Wales’ squad to replace injured Rhun Williams. The Exeter Chiefs full-back is set to play in Saturday’s Premiership final against Wasps after their last-gasp win over Saracens. Dollman’s selection leaves Dan Evans out of contention and sets up competition with Gareth Anscombe and Sam Davies for the full-back starting jersey.

Horatio Chapple, 17, from Salisbury, was on an adventure holiday in August 2011 with the British Schools Exploring Society (BSES) when he died. The court was told the pain suffered by the bear would have influenced its behaviour and increased its stress. An inquest has heard harrowing details of the polar bear attack that killed Eton schoolboy Horatio Chapple during a British Schools Exploring Society expedition in the Norwegian Arctic territory of Svalbard. Chapple, 17, was asleep in his tent when a polar bear entered the camp, dragged him from the tent, and inflicted fatal injuries to his head and upper body. Four others were seriously hurt before the animal was shot dead by one of the group leaders. The injured included expedition leaders Michael Reid, 29, from Plymouth, and Andrew Ruck, 27, from Brighton and now living in Edinburgh, as well as trip members Patrick Flinders, 17, from Jersey, and Scott Bennell-Smith, 16, from Cornwall. The attack occurred in the early hours, when the group was camped on a glacier, and has prompted sustained scrutiny of expedition safety protocols in polar bear habitats. Evidence presented to the court detailed the bear’s poor condition. A post-mortem examination found worn-down teeth, a cavity, swollen and reddened gums, and periodontitis affecting several teeth. Tests estimated the bear’s age at around 24, with experts noting that the fatality rate for Svalbard polar bears is high after 15 years, very high after 20 years, and that it is rare for a polar bear to reach 25. An independent report prepared by High Court judge Sir David Steel for BSES concluded the animal was “seriously underweight,” weighing about 250 kg (551 lbs) compared with a typical 400 kg (882 lbs). The court was told the pain and stress caused by the bear’s dental disease likely influenced its behaviour. Sir David’s report criticised the expedition’s reliance on a tripwire alarm system to warn of a bear’s presence and recommended that a dedicated “bear watch” become standard practice for expeditions in Svalbard. It also called for a rigorous upgrade of rifle training. BSES executive director Lieutenant General Peter Pearson, from Chepstow, Monmouthshire, said the organisation had adopted all the report’s recommendations. He noted that polar bear-specific measures had not been implemented because BSES has not returned to areas occupied by polar bears since the 2011 attack. Pearson defended the competence of the expedition leaders, Mr Ruck and Mr Reid. The inquest continues.

title: She tumbled backwards over her cape as she sang Living For Love, her new single. Madonna suffered a dramatic tumble during a live performance of her new single, Living For Love, after a dancer in goat horns tugged at her ruby-lined cape. Video and photos show the 56-year-old star falling backwards and landing with a loud thwack, prompting a brief, stunned silence in the venue, according to Newsbeat reporters positioned metres away. She quickly recovered, though momentarily tangled in the cloak, and pushed through to finish the song. The slip was instantly the talk of Twitter, with “Madonna” and #shefellover trending worldwide. Fans shared concern and praise for her professionalism in carrying on. Later, Madonna reassured followers on Instagram: “My beautiful cape was tied too tight! But nothing can stop me and love really lifted me up! Thanks for your good wishes! I’m fine!” There is a clear pause in the vocals during the fall, underscoring that she was singing live. For updates and behind-the-scenes coverage, follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

Cardiff gears up for world football’s biggest club game as Champions League final heads to Principality Stadium on 3 June Cardiff will host world football’s biggest club game on 3 June, when the UEFA Champions League final comes to the Principality Stadium, and Wales’s first minister Carwyn Jones says preparations, while challenging, are progressing well. Speaking to BBC Wales, Mr Jones called the occasion “a great showcase for Wales,” adding that authorities are working intensively to ensure the city is ready for the influx of supporters. Thousands of fans are expected to pour into the Welsh capital for the final, which follows closely on the women’s UEFA Champions League final at Cardiff City Stadium on 1 June. The 100-day countdown to the women’s showpiece was marked on Tuesday with a choir flash mob in central Cardiff, where the trophy was unveiled to kick off celebrations. Mr Jones said the scale and unpredictability of the men’s final add complexity to planning. “This is the biggest [event Cardiff has hosted] to my mind, no question about that,” he said. “It’s the sheer numbers of people, the sheer size of the event and the fact that we don’t know who’s going to be in the final so we don’t know where the fans are going to come from.” Welsh international Gareth Bale starred in last year’s decider, helping Real Madrid defeat city rivals Atlético at Milan’s San Siro, but the first minister noted that this year’s finalists remain unknown. He said planners are liaising with all relevant authorities and organisations to deliver a safe, seamless experience. “Cardiff is the smallest city to have hosted the event. It’s always challenging, of course, but we’ll get there and we’ll be offering a fantastic welcome to all who come to our capital city,” he added.

Noel Thomas, from Gaerwen, on Anglesey, is among those joining forces against their former employer. Anglesey county councillor Noel Thomas, a former sub-postmaster, is joining a group of ex-Post Office workers preparing legal action over alleged faults in the Horizon computer system. Thomas was jailed for nine months in 2006 after admitting false accounting totalling £48,000. He maintains he was driven to falsify records after experiencing unexplained discrepancies, claiming a glitch in Horizon added thousands of non-existent pounds to his accounts. The Post Office has denied his claim. Tens of other sub-postmasters have reported similar issues, alleging money disappeared from branch accounts due to software faults in Horizon, which records transactions at hundreds of Post Offices and sub-Post Offices across the UK. They say there is no alternative but to begin civil proceedings to uncover the cause of the discrepancies and seek redress. Earlier this year, the BBC’s Panorama programme alleged the existence of a document suggesting the Post Office did not believe Thomas was guilty of theft. Thomas said he hopes that document will be made public during the civil action. A Post Office spokesperson said the organisation had not been informed of any impending court case. Previously, the Post Office stated it could not comment on individual cases due to confidentiality, and that financial loss combined with false accounting is often sufficient evidence to support a theft charge.

High Cross House in Dartington, Devon, will close to the public after the National Trust activated a pull-out clause in its lease, citing insufficient visitor numbers to make the site financially sustainable. The charity took on a 10-year lease in January 2012, but the landmark attracted 21,000 visitors in its first year—11,000 fewer than the 32,000 the Trust says were needed to break even. Dartington Hall Trust, the property’s owner, said there are no current plans to reopen the house for now. The decision effectively ends the National Trust’s management of the property. “Whilst it is disappointing that High Cross House is now closing to the public, we continue to welcome people to the Dartington Hall Estate,” said Vaughan Lindsay, chief executive of Dartington Hall Trust. He added the owner is still exploring options for the building’s future use. Designed in 1932 by Swiss-American architect William Lescaze, High Cross House is widely regarded as one of the UK’s finest examples of modernist architecture.

Uncapped full-back Phil Dollman, 32, scored Exeter’s second try in the Premiership final at Twickenham but limped off early in the second half with a knee injury. Dollman had been called up by Wales midweek to replace injured Cardiff Blues teenager Rhun Williams for June’s two-Test tour against Tonga and Samoa. He learned of his selection while preparing for the showcase. Wales prop Tomas Francis featured as a second-half replacement as Exeter edged Wasps in extra time to claim their first Premiership title. Dollman’s injury could threaten his availability for the summer tour.

Massaro and Willstrop reach World Series Finals after late-night semis Massaro, the defending champion, booked her place in Saturday’s World Series Finals title match after a late-night victory over Egypt’s Nouran Gohar, prevailing 12-14, 12-10, 11-7. The 33-year-old Briton will face Egyptian world number one Nour El Sherbini after a schedule pushed deep into the night because of Ramadan. “It’s a tough situation for us both,” Massaro said of the midnight finish. “It’s really late and even though you get up late and do everything you can to recover, your body clock says that you should be in bed and not warming up for a squash match.” In the men’s draw, world number six James Willstrop upset top-ranked Karim Abdel Gawad of Egypt 14-12, 11-6 to reach his first World Series Finals championship match in a 17-year professional career. He will meet Egypt’s Mohamed El Shorbagy in Saturday’s final. “I’m 33, I’ve had time out like a few of us have, but I’m not taking it for granted that I’ll be able to get back to where I was when I was 29, it’s not that simple,” said the Yorkshireman. The World Series Finals serve as the season-ending championship for both the men’s and women’s professional tours.

British diver Jack Laugher, 21, has been awarded an MBE for services to diving, alongside his synchro partner Chris Mears. The pair captured Olympic gold in the men’s synchronised 3m springboard in Rio, before Laugher added a silver in the individual 3m springboard six days later. Their honours cap a breakthrough year for British diving. Paralympic rower Laurence Whiteley is also appointed MBE for services to rowing after winning gold in the mixed trunk and arm double sculls with teammate Lauren Rowles in Rio. The 25-year-old Northallerton athlete waited two years to find a suitable partner, and the duo signalled potential with silver at their first major competition, the 2015 World Championships. Countertenor Iestyn Davies, from York, receives an MBE for services to music. A former Cambridge chorister under music director George Guest, Davies has performed with companies including English National Opera, Welsh National Opera and New York City Opera.

St Helens head coach Keiron Cunningham says he is approaching Thursday’s Super League play-off semi-final at Warrington with calm confidence after growing into the role in his second season in charge. The 39-year-old, who spent his entire playing career with the Saints before joining the coaching staff, admitted he felt anxious at times last year but now trusts his preparation and his squad’s ability to deliver. “I don’t get anxious, I wouldn’t know what the emotion is,” the former hooker told BBC Radio Merseyside. “When I was a player I just used to get angry so I could get out and play and have an influence on a game. Sometimes I was anxious last year, a little bit and worried about things – but this year I don’t have any anxiety towards games.” The former Wales international said experience and belief within the group have brought a more relaxed, focused mindset. St Helens, who finished fourth, head to Warrington aiming to book a place in the Grand Final. “I know as a club, me as a coach and my players are desperate to get out there on Thursday and it can’t come quick enough,” Cunningham added.

Samantha Barks Lands Éponine in Les Misérables Film After Surprise Onstage Announcement Samantha Barks has been cast as Éponine in the forthcoming film adaptation of Les Misérables, following a surprise announcement delivered onstage at Manchester’s Palace Theatre. Moments after Barks finished performing as Nancy in Oliver!, producer Cameron Mackintosh appeared before the curtain to reveal that the 21-year-old Isle of Man native will join a star-studded cast that includes Hugh Jackman and Russell Crowe. Describing the news as the “happiest moment,” Barks said it was “still sinking in” and “the biggest surprise of my life.” Mackintosh, who previously cast Barks as Éponine in a theatre production of the musical, told the audience he had searched in Hollywood, on New York’s Broadway and across London’s West End to find the right actress. He added that director Tom Hooper had chosen Barks to reprise the role on the big screen. The announcement comes after reports that singer Taylor Swift was in line to play the tragic Éponine, one of the central characters in Victor Hugo’s 19th-century tale of love, loss and revolution in France. The film, slated for a December release, will also feature Anne Hathaway and Amanda Seyfried, the latter known for her role in the film version of Mamma Mia! Mackintosh hailed Barks’s ascent as “so rare” in the industry. “This is a real rags-to-riches story — a 17-year-old who had done nothing when she started out on I’d Do Anything on the BBC,” he said. Barks reached the final of the 2008 talent show, which invited the public to choose an unknown actress to play Nancy in a new production of Lionel Bart’s Oliver! She finished third behind winner Jodie Prenger, but ultimately secured the coveted role in 2011 — a breakthrough that has now led to her biggest screen opportunity yet. Filming is now underway.

Wales international Rhys Webb remains sidelined as he continues his recovery from a foot injury sustained during a World Cup warm-up match against Italy in September. The 27-year-old has not played since the setback, and while he has returned to training, he is still short of the match fitness required for selection. Wales begin their Six Nations campaign with an away fixture against Ireland in Dublin on Sunday, 7 February. Ospreys will also be without back-row Tyler Ardron for approximately eight weeks after the Canada international underwent knee surgery in October, following an injury picked up at the World Cup. The dual absence is a significant blow for the region as they navigate a crucial phase of the season. Chris Towers, Ospreys’ medical performance manager, said Webb’s rehabilitation is progressing well but emphasized the need to reach the right physical standards before a return. “His recovery is going well and we’re now concentrating on getting him to the physical level he needs to be in order to perform as we want,” Towers said. “He has begun running again, started doing some skills work, and the focus is on getting him available for selection at the end of February, which would be five months post-op.” Webb, capped 16 times by Wales, recently renewed his national dual contract with Ospreys and the Welsh Rugby Union, turning down offers from elsewhere to remain with the region where he made his debut in 2007.

President Donald Trump has expressed strong support for his senior adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner amid reports that Kushner discussed establishing a secret communications channel with Russia’s ambassador during the presidential transition. In a statement to the New York Times, Mr Trump praised Kushner’s performance and character but did not directly address the specific allegations that have intensified scrutiny around the aide’s contacts with Moscow. The New York Times and The Washington Post reported that Kushner sought to use Russian diplomatic facilities to conduct conversations beyond the reach of U.S. monitoring in December, weeks before Mr Trump took office. At the time, Kushner, who is married to the president’s eldest daughter, Ivanka Trump, was a private citizen. The reports emerged as Kushner was said to be under scrutiny in the FBI’s investigation into alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election. U.S. media outlets have cited officials saying investigators believe Kushner possesses information relevant to the probe, though he is not necessarily suspected of wrongdoing. “Jared is doing a great job for the country. I have total confidence in him,” Mr Trump said in his statement. “He is respected by virtually everyone and is working on programs that will save our country billions of dollars. In addition to that, and perhaps more importantly, he is a very good person.” Senior administration officials moved to downplay the significance of the allegations without confirming their accuracy. Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly told ABC News on Sunday that establishing back channels with foreign governments is “normal” and “acceptable.” He said such communications can be beneficial, especially with entities “not particularly friendly to us,” provided the information is shared within the government. National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster echoed that sentiment, saying generally that the United States maintains back-channel communication with a number of countries. Neither official directly addressed the reported use of Russian facilities to avoid U.S. surveillance or the specific timing of Kushner’s contacts. The president’s remarks came as he reportedly met with attorneys at the White House on Sunday, a sign of the growing legal focus on the Russia matter inside the administration. Mr Trump also took to Twitter to condemn what he described as fabricated leaks and anonymous sourcing, accusing the “fake news media” of making up stories. “Whenever you see the words ‘sources say’ in the fake news media, and they don’t mention names it is very possible that those sources don’t exist,” he wrote, declaring “#FakeNews is the enemy!” The reports about Kushner add to a series of revelations about contacts between Trump associates and Russian officials that have fueled questions about the campaign’s interactions with Moscow and the conduct of the transition. The ongoing FBI inquiry remains a central challenge for the White House as it seeks to advance its agenda while confronting mounting scrutiny over Russia-related issues.

Standard Chartered will cut up to a quarter of its senior managers as chief executive Bill Winters pushes through a sweeping cost reduction and restructuring after years of rapid expansion across its footprint. In a memo to staff, Winters said roles at director level and above will be reduced, leaving the bank with up to 25% fewer senior staff. About 4,000 bankers are in the grades affected. The lender employs roughly 88,000 people worldwide, up from around 44,000 in 2005, and sources told the BBC that some positions created during its post-crisis growth are no longer needed. The bank said it had previously disclosed that further personnel changes were coming and that it had already moved to reduce management layers. Winters, who took over from former chief executive Peter Sands in June, has pledged to simplify Standard Chartered with a new leadership team and a simpler organisational structure. In recent months the group has shed businesses in Hong Kong, China and Korea, booking a $219m gain and strengthening its capital position. It has also hired Mark Smith from Asia-focused rival HSBC as chief risk officer. Winters has cut the dividend to help shore up the bank’s capital base, a buffer against unexpected financial shocks, and has not ruled out raising additional capital if needed. The measures aim to streamline operations and restore performance at the emerging-markets-focused lender.

Ben Youngs says a renewed sense of freedom and belief under England head coach Eddie Jones and Leicester Tigers boss Aaron Mauger has helped him rediscover his best form. The 26-year-old scrum-half played a key role in England’s Six Nations Grand Slam, and as Leicester prepare for Sunday’s Champions Cup quarter-final against Stade Francais at Welford Road, Youngs told BBC Radio 5 live he feels invigorated on both fronts. “With Mauge and Eddie, I feel I can play like I did when I first came on the scene for Leicester, when I didn’t fear what might happen if it went wrong,” he said. “It’s a new lease of life — I’ve been given confidence by both coaches to express myself,” Youngs added. “It’s given me a new motivation, and I feel I’m being challenged and tested every day.” Following England’s group-stage exit at last year’s World Cup, the 57-cap international was one of several senior players whose places came under scrutiny. Youngs, who toured with the British and Irish Lions in 2013, admitted he needed to convince Jones of his worth. “To start with he was probably testing me out a little bit,” he said. “But I feel like I’ve got a very good relationship with Eddie. He instils a huge amount of belief both within the squad and individually, and I really enjoy being coached by him.” Youngs featured in all five of England’s Six Nations matches but began the Grand Slam decider against France in Paris on the bench, with Danny Care preferred to start. His second-half impact proved telling. “When [Jones] told me [I wasn’t starting], he said I was going to come off the bench and win us the Grand Slam. I thought, ‘I quite like the sound of that!’” Youngs said. “At that point I said to Eddie it’s just about winning the Grand Slam. Of course I want to start every game, but so does Danny, so that naturally isn’t going to happen. I was just happy that I could come on and really help the team. The plan paid off, so credit to him.” At club level, Youngs believes his decision to recently sign a new contract with Leicester has already been vindicated. “Definitely,” he said. “I really think whatever happens this year, I feel like we are only just touching the surface under Mauge. Next season we have Matt Toomua coming in, JP Pietersen coming in. The best is yet to come.” Listen to live commentary of Leicester Tigers versus Stade Francais on BBC Radio 5 live on Sunday at 13:45.

Prof Calvin Jones has cautioned that expectations around the South Wales Metro risk outpacing reality, warning that the first tangible benefits may be felt in Cardiff before reaching the valleys. The Welsh Government continues to describe the Metro as “transformational” and hopes first services will be running by 2023, but Jones, of Cardiff Business School, told BBC’s Sunday Politics Wales the project is a minimum 15- to 20-year endeavour and will develop incrementally rather than delivering instant, sweeping change. Initial work will focus on upgrading existing Valleys lines, with costs estimated at around £734m up to 2023 as part of a wider, billion-pound scheme. The Metro promises better trains, faster buses, and light rail or tram services linking Cardiff and communities across the south Wales valleys. Ministers are aiming to submit funding applications by mid-2017, with construction slated to begin in 2019 and completion targeted for the end of 2022, paving the way for early operations the following year. The financing package outlined to date includes £125m from UK government sources and £369m from the Welsh budget. First Minister Carwyn Jones travelled to the European Commission in Brussels this week seeking an additional £110m in EU support for the project, and a Welsh Government spokesman said the response from those meetings had been “encouraging.” Economy Secretary Ken Skates said the administration hopes to “have diggers in the ground towards the end of this decade,” stressing that the Metro will connect isolated communities and should primarily serve the valleys. “By 2023 we hope to have Metro services up and running,” Skates said, adding that the scheme is designed to improve daily life and opportunity for residents across the region. Local business owners share that optimism. Geraint Corkrey, who runs the Navigation pub and cafe in Treharris, Merthyr Tydfil county borough, said a Metro stop could draw visitors into the village, boosting the local economy and providing a much-needed uplift for the area. Yet Jones reiterated that early gains could cluster in the capital. “The first places to benefit from the Metro may indeed be in Cardiff,” he said. “The problem with that is people in Treharris don’t want to wait too long.” Balancing the promise of a “shiny” Metro with the realities of long-term, incremental construction will be critical to maintaining public confidence as the timeline unfolds. Officials say the integrated network will reduce congestion and cut journey times.

IS Claims Seizure of US Gear in Nangarhar; Pentagon Denies Troop Capture IS-affiliated media on Sunday published photos purporting to show U.S. military equipment and identification recovered after clashes in Afghanistan’s Nangarhar province, raising questions about a recent operation near the Pakistan border. The images, released by the Amaq news agency, include ID cards for Specialist Ryan Larson alongside a portable rocket launcher, radio, grenades and other items not commonly issued to Afghan forces. Amaq did not specify when the photos were taken or how the kit was seized. U.S. officials acknowledged a loss of equipment but rejected claims that American troops were captured. “We are still working to determine if all of the equipment in the pictures was lost during recent operations or at some other time in the past,” Brigadier General Charles Cleveland told the BBC. Earlier, U.S. military spokesman Commander Ron Flesvig said Specialist Larson had been “attached to a unit conducting a partnered [operation] with Afghan forces,” adding, “The loss of personal identification is unfortunate.” There remains uncertainty, including why U.S. troops left quickly and whether Islamic State’s local strength was underestimated. The U.S.-based Founderscode.com website said IS fighters seized the items after repelling a joint U.S.-Afghan assault involving tanks and heavy air cover, and reported that an American flag was among the materials. Islamic State has consolidated a presence in parts of eastern Afghanistan in recent years. Last month, the group claimed responsibility for a suicide attack on a protest march in Kabul that killed 80 people and wounded 230; Afghan intelligence officials say the bombers were dispatched from Nangarhar. IS had not previously acknowledged assaults in the capital. The Taliban and IS have been locked in frequent battles since January 2015, with Taliban special units seeking to blunt IS expansion. Afghan and U.S. officials also warn that IS recruiters target Afghan fighters. Investigations into the Nangarhar incident are ongoing.

Here are five things you should know, so you're switched on about the news..... Nintendo’s new Switch aims to bridge the gap between handheld and home gaming, launching as a hybrid system priced at £279.99. At its core is a portable, tablet-style screen that slots into a TV dock for living-room play, then lifts out to go on the move. On either side sit detachable Joy-Con controllers that slide off and can be used separately, including motion controls reminiscent of the Wii. While the base package includes the console, dock and one set of Joy-Cons, accessories such as extra controllers and spare docks will add to the cost. At launch, headline games include The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Just Dance 2017, with more titles promised through the year. Some fans have voiced concerns about a relatively lean day-one lineup, but Nintendo says it is pacing releases for the long term, rather than front-loading its catalogue. The Switch arrives with high expectations after the Wii U struggled to compete with Sony’s PlayStation 4 and Microsoft’s Xbox One. This time, it faces fresh pressure from Sony’s PS4 Pro, released in November, and Microsoft’s high-powered Project Scorpio, due later this year. Nintendo is betting that the Switch’s flexibility—play on the TV, then pick up and go—will set it apart and win back players across both portable and home console markets.

Oxford University’s Wildlife Conservation Research Unit (WildCRU), which had been studying lions including Cecil before the animal was shot dead in Zimbabwe, has defended its research independence after receiving a $20,000 donation from the Dallas Safari Club. The hunting organization says it “absolutely” supports sustainable trophy hunting and “abhors poaching,” but declined further comment. Prof David Macdonald, director of WildCRU, said the unit’s work remains impartial regardless of funding sources. “We simply do our work,” he said. “There is no risk of any donor affecting our results—we report our results regardless of whether they state any particular point of view or not.” Cecil, a popular tourist draw in Hwange National Park, was killed by Minnesota dentist Walter Palmer, sparking global outrage and renewed scrutiny of trophy hunting. Zimbabwean authorities are seeking Palmer’s extradition. The donation has drawn criticism from some conservation advocates. Chris Macsween, a trustee of LionAid, called it “unfortunate” that research organizations accept sponsorship from pro-hunting groups, likening it to tobacco-funded science. “This is equivalent to a tobacco company accepting research from their stable of scientists to say that smoking is not damaging to health,” he said. In a statement posted after Cecil’s death, the Dallas Safari Club argued that “lawful, ethical, vigilant hunters play an important role in public acceptance of sustainable hunting as a vital tool for modern wildlife conservation and management.” Public support for WildCRU’s work surged, with donations for Cecil surpassing £550,000. Ty Warner, the founder of Beanie Babies, pledged further funding, with profits from a Cecil Beanie Baby designated for WildCRU. Prof Macdonald said the unit will channel the funds into lion conservation in Hwange and across neighboring landscapes. “We will devote ourselves, supported by the incredible generosity of these donations, to working for the conservation of lions in Hwange and, with this marvellous support, the surrounding landscapes in adjoining countries,” he said.

British volunteer shot in arm while fighting Islamic State with Kurdish YPG in Syria A 22-year-old man from Bournemouth who travelled to Syria to fight alongside Kurdish forces has described being shot on the frontline during an operation against Islamic State. Jac Holmes left the UK in January to join the People’s Protection Units (YPG), the main Kurdish force in northern Syria, and spoke to BBC South from the conflict zone about his injury and ongoing involvement. “Me and my group were trying to advance, and then I literally just got shot in the arm,” Mr Holmes said. “It was a bit of a surprise – obviously I’ve never been shot before. My arm suddenly felt a bit strange and then there was blood everywhere.” He said he spent time recovering in a Kurdish hospital before returning to the frontlines, where he is staying in an abandoned village with other Kurdish and western fighters. Mr Holmes said his interest in the region began in 2011, when he started following Kurdish social media accounts and those of western volunteers fighting with Kurdish units. After leaving the UK in January, he crossed into Syria from Iraq to join the YPG in its campaign against Islamic State (IS) fighters. “They [IS] are a horrendous terrorist organisation, they enslave, pillage – they think they’re justified under their version of Islam,” he said. “Anyone of a sane mind can see there is nothing religious or righteous about it. I can’t get over why anyone would actually join a group like Isis.” Authorities and counter-terrorism experts in the UK have repeatedly warned against travelling to Syria. David Knowles, of Hampshire Constabulary’s Prevent team, cautioned that volunteers risk breaking the law both in the UK and in Syria. “They could well be committing offences in the UK by fighting overseas and they may well be committing offences in Syria,” he said. “The Syrian government passed a law two years ago to say anybody fighting in their country would be imprisoned for up to 10 years.” He added that fighters face the danger of being imprisoned, killed, or captured, tortured and executed by IS. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) maintains that British citizens should not travel to any part of Syria, even for humanitarian reasons, warning that returning volunteers could face arrest. The FCO says the safest and most effective way to help is to donate to reputable charities operating in the region. Terrorism expert Dr Anthony Richards, of the University of East London, suggested a distinction could be drawn between those fighting for and those fighting against Islamic State. “It is very unlikely that those fighting against Isis upon their return are likely to present a domestic threat to the security of the United Kingdom,” he said. “So my feeling is that the British government perspective is that they will take a pragmatic approach to this.”

Reading have signed 25-year-old forward Mendes on a two-year deal at the Madejski Stadium, becoming the Royals’ third addition. The former Le Havre attacker netted nine goals in 24 league starts during the 2015-16 season. Manager Jaap Stam said Mendes can operate centrally as a striker or in wider forward roles, offering flexibility to the squad as Reading build for the new season. Find all the latest football transfers on our dedicated page.

Teenager Jason McGovern from Tydavnet, County Monaghan, has died following two separate assaults in Omagh, County Tyrone, prompting a cross-border investigation led by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) with support from An Garda Síochána. The 19-year-old was found dead at a friend’s house in Mullan village near Emyvale on Monday, after travelling home in the early hours. A post-mortem examination determined his death was due to a head injury sustained during the initial assault. Police said Mr McGovern had travelled by taxi with a group of friends to Omagh on Sunday night and visited two pubs during the evening. The group became separated and shortly before 2am, Mr McGovern and a friend were outside the Terrace Bar on John Street where they encountered a group of about five men. A verbal exchange reportedly took place, after which “punches were thrown and Mr McGovern was struck several times in the head and upper body,” according to the PSNI. Mr McGovern and his friend then moved down Kevlin Road towards a taxi waiting at the Weigh Inn. They were followed by at least three members of the original group. At the Cunningham Terrace car park, Mr McGovern was confronted by a man from the group and struck once more in the face, causing him to collapse. Two middle-aged men, who police say were not involved in either incident, helped him into the taxi along with his friend. The Monaghan group returned home, and Mr McGovern went to bed. He was discovered dead at around noon on New Year’s Eve. Detectives are now appealing for witnesses, particularly taxi drivers and motorists who were at Cunningham Terrace car park around the time of the second assault, and for the two men who assisted Mr McGovern into the taxi, to contact police. “We want to make it clear that these two men had nothing to do with the assault,” said Detective Chief Inspector Richard Harkness. A local priest who knew Mr McGovern described him as “a very caring and affable young man.” Canon Macartan McQuaid said the teenager’s family is struggling to cope with the loss and appealed for anyone with information to come forward to help provide answers in the investigation.

Two boys who cannot be named for legal reasons are on trial at Chester Crown Court accused of murdering Lee Briggs in St Marie’s Park, Widnes, Cheshire, last May. Jurors heard that the pair, now aged 16 and 15, travelled from Liverpool to deal cocaine and heroin and allegedly armed themselves during a confrontation with Mr Briggs, 43. Prosecutor Gordon Cole QC said one youth waved a machete while the other delivered a single stab to Mr Briggs’s chest, a wound later identified by a post-mortem as the cause of death. Mr Cole told the court the killing was witnessed by Nicola Riley, who had gone to buy drugs from the boys. She said she heard Mr Briggs demand “give me the bits,” which she understood to mean money and drugs, while he threatened them with a knife, at one point holding it to the younger boy’s throat. According to the prosecution, the defendants knew where weapons were hidden around the park in case of a violent confrontation and reacted by arming themselves. Paramedics and police treated Mr Briggs at the scene before he was taken to hospital, where he later died. The court heard the teenagers fled the area after the attack, returning to Liverpool in a taxi, and were subsequently captured on CCTV appearing to re-enact the stabbing. Both boys deny murder. The jury was told they admit being in the park to deal drugs but contest the prosecution’s account of the fatal encounter. The trial continues at Chester Crown Court.

The Lawn Tennis Association has launched its Tennis for Kids initiative, enlisting Andy Murray and Great Britain’s Davis Cup-winning team to front a video encouraging youngsters to fall in love with the sport. Former British No.1 Annabel Croft hailed the programme as an accessible entry point for children who are new to tennis, and a welcoming experience for families, noting that parents are invited to join the final session. LTA chief executive Michael Downey said the campaign was conceived in the wake of Britain’s momentous 2015 Davis Cup triumph, with the goal of inspiring the next generation and fostering a lifelong passion for tennis. By spotlighting national champions and trusted voices, the LTA hopes to translate recent success into grassroots participation, building skills, confidence and community engagement across the country. The video-led drive underscores the sport’s inclusivity and aims to make tennis a fun option for kids and their parents, with guidance available for those interested in getting started.

Former world number one Djokovic, 30, will not play again in 2017 because of an elbow injury Novak Djokovic will sit out the remainder of the 2017 season after an elbow injury forced him to retire from his Wimbledon quarter-final against Tomas Berdych on 12 July. The 30-year-old Serbian, a 12-time Grand Slam champion and former world number one, has opted to take an extended break to fully recover, drawing support from former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash, who believes the layoff could be a crucial reset. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Cash said the time away might help Djokovic “mentally refresh, get his enthusiasm back, and start back again strongly.” He added: “We all know how tough and athletic he is, we want to see that again.” Cash suggested Djokovic’s issue resembles “tennis elbow,” noting there is “literally no cure for it, it just takes time, usually about a year or so, to fix it.” He argued the hiatus could ultimately prove beneficial. “It is probably just what the doctor ordered, to take time off. After so many unbelievable years, 2017 has been poor for him.” Djokovic’s season has been marked by inconsistency and setbacks. In January, he suffered a shock second-round defeat to world number 117 Denis Istomin at the Australian Open, where he was the defending champion. In June, he lost his French Open crown after falling to Dominic Thiem in the quarter-finals. There were glimpses of his best, notably winning the Aegon International at Eastbourne in early July—his 68th career title and his first since January—but at Wimbledon he was forced to quit mid-match due to the elbow problem. Cash cautioned against expecting a swift return to dominance akin to Roger Federer’s comeback from a knee injury in 2016. “It will take time for him to get his intensity back,” he said. “It won’t be like Roger Federer, who was winning Grand Slams straight out of the blocks after he came back, but some time next year he will be playing well again.” Reflecting on Djokovic’s strengths, Cash said: “He was just that bit fitter, that bit more flexible, that bit more mentally tough. He has probably lost two of those three major qualities, but he will be very sensible and make sure he is ready when he does come back. I do think he will be competitive again.”

Man remanded over Ladywood shooting of Kenichi Phillips Kenichi Phillips was fatally shot while sitting in a car in Ladywood, Birmingham, on 17 March. West Midlands Police said Dean Silvera, 37, of Perry Barr, has been remanded in custody to appear at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court on Thursday. It follows last month’s charging of a 17-year-old boy with murder in connection with the case. A 22-year-old man arrested on suspicion of murder the day after the shooting remains on bail as inquiries continue. Police urged witnesses to contact local investigators.

Just 1.3% of school leavers went into work place training programmes, such as apprenticeships, last year. Only 1.3% of young people leaving school at 16 in Wales entered workplace training schemes such as apprenticeships at the end of the last academic year, sparking warnings of a “national disgrace” over missed opportunities to lift children out of poverty. The figure, drawn from a Careers Wales survey, is down from 1.6% in 2012. Prof David Egan, of the Cardiff School of Education and Social Policy and chair of a national child poverty conference held near Cardiff, said the findings pointed to a “national crisis” in careers advice and progression routes for young people, particularly those from the most deprived communities. “I do think that is a disgrace, that we’re not providing, not encouraging, not enabling our young people, particularly those perhaps from the most disadvantaged backgrounds, to have those kinds of routes forward,” he said. “We do not have an appropriate careers service that can give independent and impartial advice to young people in Wales.” Anti-poverty campaigners at the conference called for new targets for schools and for inspections to assess whether they encourage apprenticeships on the same footing as academic degrees. They argue that, in the absence of robust guidance and parity of esteem, many young people are steered towards limited options that fail to match their aspirations, abilities or local labour market needs. According to the latest figures, there is approximately one careers adviser for every six schools in Wales, equating to around one adviser for 4,500 pupils. Prof Egan said that shortfall is especially damaging in deprived areas, where children are more likely to rely on impartial advice about routes into apprenticeships, further education and higher education—support they may not receive from families or within their communities. An estimated 200,000 children live in poverty in Wales, roughly one in three. Prof Egan warned that without stronger guidance and expanded training pathways, many will miss out on the chance to secure stable, reasonably paid employment. “In the end it will be through getting reasonably paid employment that they will have the chance of moving out of poverty, and moving their families out of poverty,” he said. The Welsh Government said increasing the number of young people taking up apprenticeships is central to its policy commitment to deliver at least 100,000 high-quality apprenticeships during this Assembly term.
