A Welsh Government spokeswoman said investment in apprenticeships has risen from £96m to £111.5m for 2017-18, bringing total investment in apprenticeships and traineeships next year to more than £126m. “We are working closely with Careers Wales and the National Training Federation on an action plan to increase the number of young people taking up apprenticeships and working with schools to improve the focus on apprenticeships and increase career advice capacity,” she added. Careers Wales, a minister-funded service tasked with providing impartial careers support, has been working with schools, employers and training providers to raise awareness of vocational routes. Campaigners say sustained investment, strengthened inspection criteria and greater visibility of apprenticeships alongside academic pathways will be crucial to reversing the decline and ensuring young people can access meaningful, well-paid work.

BBC Radio 1 presenter Fearne Cotton has announced she is leaving the station after a decade on air and is expecting her second child. The DJ shared the news on her official website, calling time on “an incredible decade” at Radio 1 and revealing that she and her husband, Jesse Wood, are delighted to be expanding their family. The couple, who married in 2014, already have a son, Rex. Cotton, 33, currently fronts Radio 1’s mid-morning show, a flagship slot known for its Live Lounge sessions featuring high-profile musicians. She will present her final programme on Friday 22 May, with Radio 1’s Big Weekend serving as her last event for the station. “After much time and careful thought I have decided to leave Radio 1 after ten amazing years,” she wrote, thanking colleagues and listeners for their support. Reflecting on her time at the station, Cotton said she had loved helping break new artists and watching world-class live performances, adding that she will depart “with the best memories and many great friends.” Looking ahead, she said it was “time for a new chapter” focused on family and new adventures. “Jesse and I are very happy to announce we are having another baby,” she wrote, saying she felt “extremely blessed and happy that Rex will be a big brother.” Clara Amfo, currently host of the Official Chart Show, will take over Cotton’s mid-morning slot. Ben Cooper, controller of BBC Radio 1 and 1Xtra, praised Amfo and congratulated Cotton on her news. “All of us at Radio 1 are delighted for Fearne and Jesse and wish them all the best for the future. It’s fantastic news,” he told Newsbeat, describing Amfo as “brilliant” with “warmth, enthusiasm and friendliness on air,” and “really slick as a presenter.” Cotton joined Radio 1 in 2005 and became one of its most familiar voices, interviewing major artists and curating memorable Live Lounge performances that helped cement the show’s reputation for intimate, stripped-back sessions. Her influence extended beyond daily playlists, with listeners often discovering new acts through her programme. As she prepares to sign off, Cotton thanked Radio 1 for being “such a great home” and paid tribute to the audience who had “been on this journey” with her. “It’s such a kick to know you heard a band on my show first, or that the songs I’ve played have helped you through the day,” she wrote. “Here’s to family and new adventures.”

Newport Gwent Dragons have confirmed they will seek new ownership and fresh investment, a move backed by the Welsh Rugby Union and designed to usher in a new chapter for the region. Joint-owners Newport RFC would also transfer their shares as part of the process. “This is an important decision that will enable a new chapter to be written,” said Dragons chief executive Stuart Davies. “I am excited by the potential we have and the prospects that this moment brings, and the search can begin in earnest now for the people who wish to take a place at Welsh rugby’s top table and embark on what could be a great adventure.” The Dragons are the only Welsh region partially owned by the WRU. A WRU spokesman told BBC Wales that the union and the region “are joined up on this,” signalling alignment on the strategy to attract new investors. On the field, the Dragons have endured a difficult era, finishing as the lowest Welsh region in eight of the past 12 Pro12 seasons, while struggling to attract marquee signings or retain top Wales internationals. The desire for new capital and expertise is aimed at improving competitiveness and long-term sustainability. The current board comprises chairman Martyn Hazell and seven directors, including major contributor Tony Brown and Newport RFC chairman Will Godfrey. They will remain in place until new owners or investors are found. “The time is right to hand over the reins and in the process hopefully secure our prosperity and competitiveness,” Hazell said. The proposed changes will not affect the ownership of Rodney Parade, which will continue to be held by Newport RFC. Newport County AFC also remain tenants at the venue under a ten-year lease agreement. “Newport RFC understand and support the aspirations of the Dragons and will assist in helping them achieve their aim,” Godfrey said, reiterating the club’s commitment to a smooth transition.

St Mirren have signed 20-year-old forward Ross Caldwell after a successful pre-season trial. Caldwell, who debuted for Hibernian in 2011, made 19 appearances in 2012/13, scoring twice, but fell out of favour under Terry Butcher last term and went on loan to Alloa, netting two goals. "We hope that we develop him into the player that we believe he can be," said manager Tommy Craig. The striker expressed his delight at joining the Buddies: "I am delighted to have joined St Mirren. Having been at the club for a couple of weeks I have enjoyed every minute and already feel part of the set up. I now want to repay the faith shown in me by Tommy, Gary [Teale] and Jim [Goodwin] in the season ahead."

Ross Moriarty has been retained at number eight for Wales’ Six Nations clash with Scotland at Murrayfield on Saturday, rewarded for a commanding display in the 21-16 defeat to England on 11 February. British and Irish Lion Taulupe Faletau, fit again after injury, remains among the replacements as interim head coach Rob Howley backs Moriarty to continue his form in a fiercely contested back-row selection. “If I play as well as I know I can, I will give coaches less reason to not let me be in the team,” said the Gloucester forward, who was a standout with his aggressive carrying and tackling against England. “[The England game] was probably the best I have ever felt in a Test match, and the best game I have played. It’s confidence, and things going my way.” Howley acknowledged Faletau’s pedigree but insisted Moriarty’s performances merit the starting shirt, adding that the competition will sharpen both players. Moriarty will again pack down alongside captain Sam Warburton and Justin Tipuric, forming a balanced trio as Wales chase a 10th successive win over Scotland, a streak dating back to 2007. “I think it [Wales’ winning run v Scotland] puts more pressure on us, because if you lose it then we will look a lot worse than anyone else,” Moriarty said. “We don’t want to be the team that falls short. Hopefully, we will be bringing our best game. We have trained hard for it this week.” A former England Under-20 international, Moriarty relished the physical battle against familiar faces at the Principality Stadium. “Even when you are playing for your local team, you put a big hit in and all your mates go a bit crazy. It’s always a good laugh,” he said. “That’s the way I felt against England. Obviously, a lot more of my friends were behind me, and to have people enjoying what I was doing always feels good.” Wales will look to convert their momentum into points at Murrayfield, with Moriarty’s energy and edge central to Howley’s game plan.

Remi Garde has questioned the commitment of his Aston Villa squad as the club remain seven points adrift at the bottom of the Premier League after just three league wins all season. Eleven days after a 6-0 home defeat by Liverpool—their heaviest at Villa Park in 81 years—the manager warned that some players are failing to meet basic standards in training and on matchdays. "I don't see the commitment from all the players every day in training sessions," Garde said ahead of Saturday’s trip to Stoke City (15:00 GMT). "Sometimes it's about fighting and commitment. It's the first thing professional players should have on the pitch. How can you be confident if you're not fighting?" The former Lyon boss, appointed in November and unable to make additions during the January window, acknowledged he lacks selection options. “If I had the choice of other players I would like to select, I would like to — but I don't have the possibility,” the 49-year-old added. Meanwhile, Garde said he held face-to-face talks with Joleon Lescott after the defender posted a picture of an expensive car on social media an hour after the Liverpool defeat. The post drew criticism from supporters. Lescott apologised, saying the message was sent accidentally from his pocket. “He told me the same thing he told the press: it was an accident. I have no reason not to believe Joleon,” Garde said, while adding he expected better judgement from an experienced player. Villa, who have struggled throughout the campaign, face a crucial test at the Britannia Stadium as they attempt to spark a revival and keep their hopes of top-flight survival alive.

A remarkable glimpse of Britain’s prehistoric past has emerged off the Norfolk coast, where divers have uncovered a newly exposed section of a submerged forest believed to be part of Doggerland, the ancient land bridge that once connected Great Britain to continental Europe after the last Ice Age. Dawn Watson and Rob Spray, volunteer divers with the marine conservation project Seasearch, made the discovery about 30 metres (100 feet) offshore from Cley at a depth of around 9 metres (30 feet). The forest was first revealed when thousands of tonnes of sand shifted during the powerful 2013 storm surge, peeling back layers that had long concealed ancient tree remains on the seabed. Watson initially found the submerged forest bed last year, describing to BBC Inside Out how they had come across “an enormous wave of black stuff,” which she later realised were the flattened remains of an oak woodland. On a subsequent visit, the pair located a Victorian anchor lying atop the ancient bed. During their latest dive, they found a newly uncovered stretch nearby. “They say there’s a veneer of sand down there, but the word ‘veneer’ really doesn’t do it justice,” said Spray. “We dived and came across an area where it looked as if the sea bed was black. If you had a big broom it looked as if you could have swept it away, to reveal a flat black floor under thick sand. You get the impression it might stretch for tens of metres, but you could only see for five to six metres anyway. It was a lovely surprise but it’s very hard to get a complete scope or handle on it.” Watson said the fresh exposure had rapidly attracted marine life. “Thousands of sea animals had swarmed in on it, creating excellent photographic opportunities,” she said. The divers noted that they approached the site from an unusual angle and could easily have missed the subtle transition where the sand layer thins to reveal the dark substrate beneath. “We really would have assumed that it would have been covered over again,” Spray added. The pair hope to continue surveying the area with further dives to better understand the extent and condition of the prehistoric forest bed. “We’ll continue to survey the prehistoric forest bed but, as amateurs, resources are always limited,” Spray said. “But it’s a fine example of how citizen scientists often lead the way where ever-shrinking government resources may never reach.” Doggerland’s inhabitants are thought to have endured centuries of rising seas before abandoning the low-lying landscape. The remaining communities were ultimately wiped out by a catastrophic five-metre tsunami around 8,200 years ago, leaving remnants of their environment preserved beneath the North Sea’s shifting sands.

Britain’s Met Office has issued a yellow rain warning until 02:00 Friday, with scattered thunderstorms possible. While many areas may avoid storms, any that develop could bring intense downpours, sudden flooding of roads and properties, and travel disruption. Forecasters also warn of lightning and hail. People are advised to monitor updates and allow extra time for journeys.

Work to overhaul the rugby pitch will begin in October, the first major renovation since undersoil heating was installed in 1963. Opened in 1890, the ground’s playing surface will be dug out to 18in (450mm), with completion due in December. The upgrade is intended to prepare the venue to host matches at the 2013 Rugby League World Cup and to broaden its appeal for other fixtures and events. The stadium complex also hosts Yorkshire County Cricket Club and rugby union side Leeds Carnegie, underscoring its multi-sport role. Rugby posts currently concreted in place will be replaced with a removable system to improve flexibility for different codes. Leeds Rhinos chief executive Gary Hetherington said the project represents a “considerable investment” that would help attract more events to the stadium. Head groundsman Jason Booth said the club had considered an artificial surface but opted for reinforced grass. In recognition of the ground’s significance to supporters, club chaplain the Reverend Steve Mitchell will lead a pre-works remembrance service on the pitch for those whose ashes were scattered there.

Snap Inc. shares soared on Thursday after making their Wall Street debut, closing 44% higher at $24.48 and valuing the parent of Snapchat at roughly $28bn. The company raised $3.4bn in the offering, marking the richest U.S. technology listing since Facebook’s in 2012. The momentum carried into Friday as the stock traded even higher intraday, before enthusiasm began to cool amid a wave of cautious commentary from Wall Street. By Monday, the debate over whether Snap can emulate Facebook’s trajectory intensified, sending the shares down $3.32 to close at $23.77. Analysts questioned whether the company can expand beyond its core base of younger users and how it will fare in international markets where competition among social media platforms remains fierce. According to Bloomberg data, five of the seven analysts initiating coverage advised investors to sell the stock, with none recommending a buy. Needham’s Laura Martin rated Snap “underperform,” likening the shares to a lottery ticket and underscoring the risks tied to the company’s path to profitability and user growth. History also suggests caution for investors chasing hot tech IPOs. A Reuters analysis found that globally, most of the 25 largest technology offerings have struggled in their first year, with 16 posting significant declines from their debut-day closing prices. The pattern has often favored investors who wait rather than rushing to buy immediately after a listing, as early exuberance can give way to reassessments of fundamentals. Snap faced additional headwinds on Monday when a group representing major U.S. institutional investors urged index providers S&P Dow Jones Indices and MSCI to bar companies that issue non-voting shares—like Snap—from inclusion in their benchmarks. Both index firms said they are reviewing Snap’s eligibility. Inclusion in widely tracked indexes such as the S&P 500 can be a powerful catalyst, forcing index fund managers to buy the stock and prompting other investors who measure performance against those benchmarks to follow suit. Conversely, exclusion could limit demand from passive investors. The broader market tone was subdued, with Wall Street closing lower for the second time in the past three sessions. Bank stocks gave back a portion of recent gains, while mining and chemical shares fell after China trimmed its economic growth forecast. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.2% to 20,954, the S&P 500 lost 0.3% to 2,375, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.4% to 5,849. “We think there’s a reasonable chance at the end of the year we’ll be a little bit lower than we are right now,” said Scott Wren, equity strategist at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Among individual movers, General Motors dropped 0.8% after disclosing a $4.5bn charge—primarily pension expenses—tied to the sale of Opel and Vauxhall to Peugeot. Delta Air Lines fell 2.6% after guiding profits to the low end of expectations, adding to the day’s risk-off tone.

Welsh landmarks lit for Remembrance as Legion urges support for younger veterans Dozens of Welsh landmarks have been illuminated ahead of Remembrance Sunday on 13 November, as the Royal British Legion launches events and calls for greater recognition of younger veterans and serving personnel. Llandaff Cathedral in Cardiff is among more than 30 sites lit up, along with all Cadw locations. Conwy Castle, St Mary’s Cathedral in Wrexham, Aberystwyth Castle and its war memorial, the Senedd, and Cardiff City Hall are among those glowing in red. The illuminations continue until Remembrance Sunday, complementing services, parades and fundraising nationwide. “It’s important to remember there’s a new generation that needs your support,” said Antony Metcalfe, urging people not to link the poppy only with older Second World War veterans. The tribute also marks the centenary of the Somme and honours the 38th (Welsh) Division, with about 4,000 men killed or injured at Mametz Wood in the First World War.

Phase two of a review into Scotland’s enterprise and skills agencies has recommended retaining the independent boards of Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE), Scottish Enterprise and other bodies, while creating a new national strategic board to oversee and coordinate their activities. The proposal follows a political row sparked last year when the first phase suggested a national board to direct the agencies, raising concerns that HIE’s own board could be wound up. The newly published report has been welcomed by Economy Secretary Keith Brown and Kate Forbes, the SNP MSP for Skye, Lochaber and Badenoch. However, Shetland and Orkney Liberal Democrat MSPs Tavish Scott and Liam McArthur warned that, despite the retention of individual boards, “control from the centre” was still being proposed. HIE supports businesses and communities across Shetland, Orkney, the Western Isles, the Highlands, Argyll and Moray. It originated as the Highlands and Islands Development Board 50 years ago and became HIE in 1990. In January, MSPs voted to demand that the Scottish government allow HIE to retain its own board. Responding at the time, Mr Brown said HIE would “continue to be locally based, managed and directed” under his plans. Phase two of the governance review was chaired by HIE’s chairman, Professor Lorne Crerar. In the report published this week, Prof Crerar recommends establishing a national strategic board while confirming that HIE, Scottish Enterprise and other agencies should keep their individual boards. Mr Brown said he welcomed Prof Crerar’s “detailed report which sets out a number of options for the potential scope, structures and functions for a new statutory board for our enterprise and skills agencies.” He added: “We thank Prof Crerar for taking the time to speak to each of the four agencies, their chairs and a number of experts, with these discussions forming the basis of his recommendations. We will now consider the detail and make a statement to parliament on our next steps in the next few weeks.” The economy secretary said the government remains committed to the review and will continue to listen to stakeholders’ views. “It is essential that we do not lose sight of our aim of giving our businesses and individuals the right access and support to national services which will help to boost Scotland’s economy and deliver our ambition of Scotland ranking among the top quartile of OECD countries in terms of productivity, equality, wellbeing and sustainability,” he said. In a joint statement, Mr Scott and Mr McArthur said: “This report confirms everything a centralising government wants. This means absolute control by ministers of Highlands and Islands Enterprise. Lorne Crerar should have simply done what he was asked and produced a justification for the HIE board abolition. His proposal is even worse. This is control from the centre. A delivery board that will do exactly what it is told by ministers.” The Scottish government is expected to set out its next steps to parliament in the coming weeks.

Sandwood Primary School in Penilee has introduced tighter rules on how parents and carers contact teachers after a rise in aggressive behaviour towards staff. In a letter sent to families, the head teacher said the changes were implemented “with regret” but stressed she would not allow staff to face shouting, offensive language or any other inappropriate conduct, nor for pupils to witness such incidents. The school reported a growing number of cases where family members shouted at staff or used offensive language. Under the new procedures, parents and carers are asked to make appointments to discuss concerns rather than approaching teachers at the school gate. The head teacher warned that anyone breaking the rules would receive a written warning and that persistent breaches “could result in not being allowed within the grounds of the school.” While emphasising that the school remains “more than happy to speak with parents/carers,” the letter noted that an open-door approach has become harder to maintain as the school roll increases and senior staff face additional commitments. As a result, appointments are now required to ensure matters are handled appropriately and without disruption to the school day. Glasgow City Council said problems were caused by a minority of parents and backed the school’s stance. A council spokeswoman said the school roll has grown significantly in recent years and the head teacher has redesigned the playground layout to ease congestion at home time and help the school run smoothly. She added that inappropriate behaviour towards staff is unacceptable, will not be tolerated, and that action will be taken to set a positive example for children and young people. The council stressed it has no intention of preventing parents from greeting teachers, but said the school gate is not the right place to discuss a child’s progress. Parents who wish to raise specific issues are encouraged to make an appointment. The council also highlighted its duty of care to protect staff from aggressive or inappropriate behaviour.

Torquay United secured a composed 2-0 victory over York City at Plainmoor, powered by a clinical first-half brace from 26-year-old striker Nathan Blissett. He opened his account for the season in the sixth minute, heading in Dan Sparkes’ precise cross from four yards. Sparkes was involved again ahead of the half-hour, meeting Aman Verma’s delivery and nodding back across goal, where Blissett arrived to volley beyond the goalkeeper from close range. The former Kidderminster striker almost completed his hat-trick five minutes before the interval, but Matt Fry cleared his goal-bound effort off the line. Torquay’s early work had already put them in control, and although York emerged with greater intent after the break, the Gulls’ well-organised back four protected the advantage, restricting the visitors to half-chances and set pieces. Both managers turned to their benches in the second half. Torquay introduced Chay Scrivens for Sparkes, Sam Chaney for Joe Ward and Brett Williams for Jamie Reid. York brought on Justin Johnson for Scott Fenwick, Tyler Walton for Yan Klukowski and Kaine Felix for Aidan Connolly. The contest also saw cautions for Richard Brodie of York and Courtney Richards of Torquay. With the job effectively done before half-time, the hosts saw out the closing stages without alarm to claim the points. Blissett’s brace proved decisive, and despite late pressure York rarely forced a clear opening. Full time: Torquay United 2, York City 0. Report supplied by the Press Association.

Conservative Margo Stewart narrowly topped the poll in the Huntly, Strathbogie and Howe of Alford ward, edging SNP candidate Gwyneth Petrie by 36 votes. Stewart secured 1,469 votes to Petrie’s 1,433, in a contest triggered by the death of SNP councillor Joanna Strathdee and the resignation of Liberal Democrat Alastair Ross for health reasons. Turnout was 34.5%. Liberal Democrat Daniel Millican finished third with 928 votes, followed by Labour’s Sarah Flavell on 196 and Scottish Libertarian Party candidate Derek Scott with 20. The result reflects a tightly fought race in the north-east ward.

Balliol College, Oxford have been crowned University Challenge champions after defeating Wolfson College, Cambridge 190 to 140 in Monday night’s BBC Two final. The series became a social media sensation thanks in large part to Wolfson’s captain, Eric Monkman, whose fierce focus and encyclopaedic breadth earned him a legion of admirers and the label "people’s champion." The finale drew strong ratings and lively debate online among quiz devotees. Host Jeremy Paxman praised both teams, calling Wolfson "entertaining" and telling them there was "no shame in being runners-up," while congratulating Balliol on a composed, clinical display. The trophy presentation, only the second to be staged outside the show’s studio in its 55-year history, featured a message from Professor Stephen Hawking, who saluted the competitors’ intellect and wit. "I have said in the past that it is not clear whether intelligence has any long-term survival value - bacteria multiply and flourish without it," Hawking said. "But it is one of the most admirable qualities, especially when displayed by such young minds. Many congratulations to both teams but especially to Balliol College Oxford on becoming series champions on University Challenge, a programme I have long enjoyed." Captained by Joey Goldman, Balliol sealed Oxford’s first title after three consecutive victories for Cambridge colleges, and celebrated with a traditional toast of port. Their win owed much to quick buzzing and breadth across subjects, from classical antiquity and philosophy to earth science and modern thought. Monkman, 29, from Canada, had previously scored 120 of Wolfson’s 170 points in a single match, fueling the #Monkmania hashtag as viewers cheered his high-octane performances. But in the final, Balliol’s balance and speed proved decisive. Among the topics Balliol fielded successfully were: Alexandria; Neoplatonism; Immanuel Kant; and the Mohorovicic discontinuity. Answers: 1. Alexandria 2. Neoplatonism 3. Immanuel Kant 4. Moho

Dyfed-Powys Police Told to Improve Ethical Culture After Nationwide Inspection Dyfed-Powys Police must do more to embed an ethical culture and ensure fair handling of complaints and misconduct, according to findings from Her Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary (HMIC) following inspections of all 43 forces in England and Wales. HM Inspector Wendy Williams said the force “had not done enough to develop an ethical culture, to incorporate the code of ethics into policy or practice, or to ensure complaints and misconduct cases were free of bias.” As a result, HMIC judged Dyfed-Powys to “require improvement” under the legitimacy pillar, which examines how fairly and ethically forces treat the public and their own staff. The force’s police and crime commissioner, Christopher Salmon, said action was needed. “Dyfed-Powys needs to do more to develop an open and questioning culture. I want to see more progress on this,” he said. “I have made clear to the chief constable that, as this report states, he has more to do.” Despite the concerns, HMIC rated Dyfed-Powys as good in its use of stop-and-search and Taser deployment. The other three Welsh forces were rated good overall, with South Wales Police and Gwent Police receiving outstanding marks for public engagement. “Overall this is a very pleasing report,” said South Wales Police Assistant Chief Constable Richard Lewis. “What it shows is we are listening to and working together with our communities, which is central to everything we do.” HMIC’s inspection programme assesses forces on effectiveness, efficiency and legitimacy, with the latest findings highlighting variations in how forces build trust, uphold ethical standards, and maintain fair, transparent practices across England and Wales.

Police in Cologne investigating the crimes are focussing on people of North African origin, they say. German authorities are under intense scrutiny after mass sexual assaults and robberies on New Year’s Eve in Cologne and other cities shocked the country and ignited a fierce debate over immigration and public safety. Police handling of the events has been sharply criticised, and Chancellor Angela Merkel’s immigration policy has come under renewed pressure amid figures showing around 1.1 million asylum seekers arrived in Germany in 2015. Tensions flared over the weekend. On Saturday, riot police used water cannon to disperse anti-migrant protesters in central Cologne. On Sunday evening, apparent reprisal attacks were reported: a group of around 20 people assaulted six Pakistanis in the city centre, leaving two requiring hospital treatment, while in a separate incident five people attacked a Syrian man, who did not need hospital care. Justice Minister Heiko Maas said he was convinced the New Year’s Eve attacks were pre-arranged and called for a comprehensive investigation into whether similar crimes in other cities were connected. “If such a horde gathers in order to commit crimes, that appears in some form to be planned,” he told Bild newspaper. “Nobody can tell me that this was not co-ordinated or prepared.” Authorities and witnesses say roughly 1,000 people, mostly men, congregated at Cologne’s central train station on 31 December before breaking into smaller groups that molested and robbed women. Victims described chaotic scenes as dozens of assaults and thefts unfolded with little apparent response from police around the station area. Reports of similar attacks emerged in Hamburg and Stuttgart the same night. In Bielefeld, hundreds of men tried to force their way into nightclubs, Die Welt reported, and police said several women alleged sexual assault. The fallout has already claimed a senior police official. On Friday, Cologne’s police chief Wolfgang Albers was suspended amid accusations he withheld information about the origin of suspects and mishandled communication in the aftermath. Investigations into the Cologne attacks continue, with police saying they are focusing on suspects of North African origin while appealing for witnesses and video evidence. Officials have vowed transparency and a thorough accounting of failures, as community leaders urge calm and warn against vigilantism. The debate over Germany’s migration policy has intensified, balancing public security concerns with the rights and integration of asylum seekers.

Wastewater tests show sustained Class A drug use in Middlesbrough and Stockton, say Teesside University academics A study by academics at Teesside University has detected sustained use of a Class A drug in the Teesside towns of Middlesbrough and Stockton through analysis of domestic wastewater, indicating consistent consumption patterns across the week and spikes at weekends. Researchers stressed there is no risk to the public from the trace amounts detected, which are diluted and treated in accordance with regulatory standards, but said the findings provide an objective picture of local drug trends. Dr Gillian Taylor, senior lecturer in forensic and analytical science, said the ongoing project is shedding light on community-level drug use. “The results are very interesting because they tell us the trends of drug abuse across the Middlesbrough central and Stockton areas,” she said. “The high levels that we are seeing are comparable with other European cities. Middlesbrough, for example, is up to four times smaller than many of the major European cities that have also been tested in this way and yet the results are exactly the same. We have focused on cocaine, but can also see heroin and cannabis markers within the wastewater.” Forensic science student Emma Peacock, part of the research team, explained that the methodology involves extracting and measuring drug residues from wastewater samples taken in both areas. “The concentrations found told us that there is fairly consistent usage in Middlesbrough central and usage that spiked on a weekend in Stockton,” she said. Measured per 1,000 people, the Stockton samples ranged from 379mg on Mondays to 1,307mg on Fridays, indicating a marked rise toward the end of the week. In Middlesbrough, usage fluctuated between 508mg and 707mg per 1,000 people throughout the week, suggesting steady levels rather than a pronounced weekend surge. Comparable studies in other European cities recorded average daily usage of 191mg per 1,000 people in Berlin, 234mg in Paris, and 461mg in Barcelona, placing Teesside’s readings at the higher end of the spectrum. A spokesman for Northumbrian Water, which treats wastewater across the North East, emphasised that the traces detected pose no public health risk. “This is wastewater which is discharged to consent levels set by the Environment Agency and it goes back into the natural environment such as rivers and estuaries where it is diluted,” he said. “The traces we are talking about here are absolutely inconsequential and literally a drop in the ocean.” Cleveland Police said it is “aware and interested” in the study. A spokesman added: “Officers in our community drugs enforcement team are aware of the research and will take an interest in the findings as and when it is finalised.” Researchers hope the data will help authorities build a more reliable picture of drug use and identify potential hot-spots, informing targeted prevention and enforcement strategies.

Edinburgh City climbed above Clyde after a 2-1 victory over Forfar Athletic, while Clyde were edged 1-0 by Arbroath, leaving City only five points clear of bottom Cowdenbeath. James Lister had put Forfar ahead five minutes before half-time, but former Celtic, Hibernian and Scotland striker Derek Riordan levelled and Lewis Allan sealed the points for City. Cowdenbeath earned their first win in eight matches in Gary Locke’s first game in charge, beating Berwick Rangers 3-1. Robbie Buchanan and Brian Ross put the hosts in command before Kriss Renton added a third; Greg Rutherford netted a consolation for Berwick. Annan Athletic moved up to third by leapfrogging visitors Elgin City with a 1-0 win, David McKenna converting a 20th-minute penalty as the sides swapped places in the table. The results reshaped the mid-table picture across the division. Elsewhere, Stirling Albion jumped above Montrose into fifth courtesy of a 3-1 success. Darren Smith, Ross Kavanagh and Connor McLaren were on target for Albion, with Kerr Hay pulling one back for Montrose.

Central Bedfordshire Council said it would serve an enforcement notice on Syed Raza Shah, after a planning inspector rejected his appeal. Mr Shah, the owner of a property in Barton-le-Clay, Bedfordshire, had originally been granted permission to expand his home by 45%. The council says the extension went far beyond that, increasing the size by 165%. Following the latest decision, he will be instructed to reduce the house to the scale previously approved. Planning inspector Bridget Campbell concluded the seven-bedroom building “harms the landscape character of the area,” dismissing Mr Shah’s appeal and clearing the way for enforcement action. Councillor Nigel Young, the council’s executive member for regeneration, welcomed the ruling, calling it the latest step in a long-running dispute. He said the outcome “reflects the concerns of the council and local residents” and “defends our green belt from inappropriate and unlawful development.” Local estate agent Ken Ravey, from Country Properties in Barton-le-Clay, described the expanded house as “Hollywood come to Barton” and said it was difficult to value. “I sold the five bedroom house set in four acres next door about five years ago for £1.25m – this house has seven bedrooms and is set in 1.5 acres,” he said. “If it were down the road in Harpenden, yes it could be worth £5m – but this is Barton-le-Clay.” In May 2013, an inspector granted retrospective planning permission for the property, named Random House, but the council challenged that decision. It argued Mr Shah’s alterations amounted to a “new dwelling” and constituted “inappropriate development” within an area of outstanding natural beauty. Mr Shah has not yet commented on the inspector’s latest ruling.

His family's Stellar International Art Foundation owns more than 600 rare works of art by artists including Picasso, Renoir and Andy Warhol. He has been photographed receiving a business award from Theresa May and his family has given more than £1.6m to the Liberal Democrats. The 67-year-old is now an adviser to Lib Dem party leader Tim Farron. Sudhir Choudhrie, a prominent businessman and political donor whose family runs a global empire spanning hotels, healthcare and aviation, is facing fresh scrutiny after an investigation by BBC Panorama and The Guardian suggested he is one of the world’s biggest arms dealers. Leaked documents from the Choudhrie family’s Swiss bank, Clariden Leu, indicate that companies linked to the family were paid almost €100m by Russian arms firms in a single 12‐month period. Between October 2007 and October 2008, Belinea Services Ltd, a company owned by the family, received €39.2m. Another family company, Cottage Consultants Ltd, was paid €32.8m in the same period, while Carter Consultants Inc received €23m. According to the leaked files, one of the Russian arms firms making the payments “makes cruise missiles.” The documents show that Clariden Leu’s compliance office in Singapore raised anti‐money laundering alerts related to the family’s accounts, which were then reviewed by the bank’s risk management team. It is not clear what action, if any, the bank ultimately took. The bank’s report described the payments from the arms companies as “incoming funds from clients offset business.” Offset payments are sometimes part of defense contracts, with arms companies committing to invest in the purchasing country as a condition of the sale. However, anti‐corruption campaigners warn that offsets can also be used to funnel bribes to intermediaries and officials under the guise of legitimate commercial arrangements. In the leaked documents, Clariden Leu characterizes the Choudhrie family as “very wealthy with an overall fortune of approx $2bn.” Sudhir Choudhrie declined to comment on the allegations. Lawyers acting for his son, Bhanu Choudhrie, stated that he had no knowledge of the Clariden Leu documents and has not breached any money‐laundering rules in any of his business dealings. They also argued that questions about offset payments were too vague, saying, “You have not given the dates or amounts of the alleged payments or the basis on which you say they were ‘suspicious’ or made in relation to Russian arms deals. The business of Cottage Consultants was conducted in a lawful and proper manner.” In 2014, Sudhir and Bhanu Choudhrie were arrested as part of a Serious Fraud Office investigation into Rolls‐Royce. Both were released without charge. BBC Panorama’s program, How Rolls‐Royce Bribed Its Way Around The World, airs on BBC One at 20:30 and will be available on BBC iPlayer. The revelations raise difficult questions for political parties and institutions connected to the family, even as the Choudhries maintain that their businesses are lawful and that they have complied with all relevant regulations.

Nestlé is exploring a sale of its U.S. confectionery business, which includes Butterfinger, BabyRuth, 100Grand, SkinnyCow and Raisinets, citing underperformance after calling the unit "disappointing". The potential divestment, excluding the Toll House baking line, would represent about 3% of Nestlé’s U.S. sales. The unit generates annual revenue of 900 million Swiss francs (£723m). Nestlé said it remains committed to expanding its leading global confectionery portfolio, particularly the KitKat brand, as it refocuses its U.S. operations on higher-growth categories.

Leah McCourt, 23, from Saintfield, has been crowned amateur world featherweight champion in Las Vegas. McCourt defeated Germany’s Julia Dorney by technical knockout in the final, adding the world title to the European Open crown she won last year. Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster’s Good Morning Ulster, she described MMA as “the most extreme way to test your body in combat,” and said phone calls with her daughter, Isabella, “kept me motivated.” A black belt in judo, McCourt initially came up through that discipline before switching to Muay Thai after Isabella’s birth, eventually embracing MMA’s blend of judo, boxing, wrestling and jujitsu. “It is so mentally tough because you could be coming out against a boxer, or somebody who does wrestling,” she said, highlighting the sport’s technical demands and strategic complexity. Her victory follows a gruelling recovery from major knee surgery in February. Determined to make the 65-kilo featherweight limit, she said she dieted strictly and took salt baths to cut weight in the lead-up to the competition. While acknowledging that “to the untrained eye, it does just look like you’re going in and fighting,” McCourt called MMA “the most realistic, lifelike way of a fight.” Now Northern Ireland’s latest world champion, McCourt hopes her success will inspire more women to enter the sport. “It’s a really fast growing sport, but there’s still not much profile for women, but I’m hoping to change that,” she said.

Missing corn snake Jemima rescued from Leighton Buzzard flat after three months A 3ft (1m) corn snake named Jemima has been reunited with her owner after a tricky early-morning rescue from inside the wall of a flat in Leighton Buzzard, Bedfordshire. The RSPCA was called at about 04:00 BST on Thursday after the snake was spotted in a property. Kate Wright, from the charity, said the operation required moving a household machine to reach Jemima. When the snake bolted into a cavity, rescuers carefully removed sections of skirting board before managing to secure the animal. Wright described Jemima as a “healthy-looking” adult and then went door-to-door in the building to locate the owner. She eventually found Colin Millar, a neighbour who said the pet had been missing since Easter. “Jemima went missing at Easter and I’d pretty much given up on ever finding her. I looked everywhere I could think of,” Mr Millar said. “It is remarkable that Jemima has managed to survive and be returned reasonably healthy. She must have been insulated in the walls of the building. We’re so pleased she’s home.” Corn snakes are non-venomous, native to parts of North America, and can grow up to 6ft (1.8m). Authorities said Jemima likely stayed warm inside the insulated wall during her absence.

A Northwich mother has described an “abusive” confrontation on a flight to Manchester, saying a fellow passenger shouted “shut that child up” as her eight-year-old daughter cried. Nicola Colenso said her daughter, Yasmin, has Sturge-Weber syndrome, a rare neurological condition affecting the skin, brain and eyes. In a Facebook post shared nearly 100,000 times, Ms Colenso said the incident occurred on a flight from Ibiza, where she was travelling with her partner Rick Murray and Yasmin’s three siblings. She said the outburst “didn’t help” her daughter’s anxiety and that she tried to explain Yasmin’s condition “very politely,” suggesting the woman speak to staff about moving seats. The passenger allegedly replied that she was “sick of the noise” and demanded Ms Colenso “just shut her up.” Ms Colenso added that Yasmin became “seriously unwell” later that day and was taken to hospital by ambulance. The post has sparked a strong reaction online, with many offering support to the family.

Italian banking giant UniCredit has disclosed a major cyber incident in which personal data and account numbers may have been stolen, marking the largest breach of its kind reported by an Italian bank to date. The lender said account passwords were not compromised, preventing hackers from initiating unauthorized transactions. UniCredit attributed the breaches to an unnamed third-party provider, noting two separate incidents: one believed to have occurred between September and October 2016, and a second spanning June and this month. The bank said it has launched an internal audit and notified all relevant authorities. It also shared a dedicated telephone number via Twitter for international customers to check if they were affected. Following the announcement, UniCredit shares fell about 1 percent. Other Italian banks, including Intesa Sanpaolo, Banco BPM, and UBI, reported no signs of similar attacks. The incident comes as the European Union prepares to implement stricter data protection rules. Under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), taking effect in May next year, banks face fines of up to 4 percent of annual turnover if they suffer a data breach and fail to report it within hours of discovery. UniCredit’s response underscores growing scrutiny of third-party providers and highlights the escalating stakes for financial institutions amid rising cyber threats and tighter regulatory expectations.

Marko Arnautovic played 45 minutes in Stoke City’s 1-0 pre-season win over Neuchatel Xamax on Monday, but limped off at half-time as manager Mark Hughes rotated his entire team. The 28-year-old forward joined the Potters from Werder Bremen for £2m in 2013 and penned a new four-year contract in 2016. An Austria international with 62 caps, Arnautovic has scored 26 goals in 145 appearances for Stoke, including seven in 35 outings in the 2016-17 season.

Federal review finds widespread flaws in FBI hair analysis; dozens of capital cases affected A new report from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) has identified “irregularities” in the FBI’s microscopic hair analysis unit, concluding that flawed forensic testimony or reporting was used in at least 60 capital punishment cases. According to the Washington Post, which first reported the findings, 14 defendants were either executed or died in prison in cases that relied, in part, on such evidence. The OIG’s review, prompted by a 2012 Washington Post investigation that found three men were wrongly placed at violent crime scenes by FBI hair examiners, raises the prospect of hundreds of unsafe convictions nationwide. The report criticizes “the use of scientifically unsupportable analysis and overstated testimony by FBI lab examiners in criminal prosecutions,” underscoring long-standing concerns about the reliability of microscopic hair comparison. In a statement, the FBI acknowledged “errors made in statements by FBI examiners regarding microscopic hair analysis in the context of testimony or laboratory reports,” adding that “such statements are no longer being made by the FBI.” The Bureau said it is “committed to ensuring that affected defendants are notified of past errors and that justice is done in every instance.” The Washington Post, citing data compiled by the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers and the Innocence Project, reported that 26 of 28 examiners in the hair comparison unit overstated forensic matches in ways favoring prosecutors in more than 95% of the 268 trials reviewed so far. The extent of the problem suggests a far-reaching impact across state and federal prosecutions over several decades. Campaign groups, including the NACDL and the Innocence Project, are expected to release a detailed report soon outlining specific cases and errors that could trigger hundreds of appeals. More information on the affected cases is anticipated as defense organizations and prosecutors review trial records and notify defendants.

Exeter City have extended the stay of 36-year-old former Republic of Ireland international Morrison, who will now remain at St James Park until after Christmas. He had initially agreed a short-term deal until the end of August. Morrison has featured as a substitute in four of Exeter’s seven matches this season. He first joined the club on non-contract terms last year before signing a permanent deal in January. In April, he told BBC Sport he would only prolong his 17-year career with Exeter.

Darren Pidgeon, 29, required skin grafts to repair third degree burns to his face and body. Basildon Crown Court has heard there was “no obvious reason” for an alleged acid attack on Mr Pidgeon in Thundersley, Essex, in June 2014. Two people, Ashley Russell, 30, of Basildon, and Christina Storey, 32, of Rayleigh, are on trial and each denies throwing a corrosive liquid. Ms Storey also denies aiding and abetting an offender. Opening the case, prosecutor Greg Unwin told the jury that Mr Pidgeon had stopped at traffic lights when he noticed a red Rover, said to be driven by Ms Storey, pull alongside. As he pulled away, the Rover moved in front of him, although it was not a “near miss,” Mr Unwin said. Mr Pidgeon then drove into Kingsmere, a residential cul-de-sac, to turn around. As he went to reverse, another car pulled in behind, blocking his exit. “He was essentially trapped, blocked in by this other vehicle,” Mr Unwin said. “The prosecution say this is the same car.” A passenger from the red Rover allegedly got out, ran to Mr Pidgeon’s driver-side door—where the window was down—and asked, “Have you got a problem?” It is alleged that Mr Russell then sprayed a corrosive liquid into Mr Pidgeon’s face and punched him in the head. “Darren Pidgeon was in excruciating agony, his eye was watering, some of the substance had gone into one ear,” Mr Unwin said. “He was confused and disorientated. Mr Pidgeon has no idea why he was attacked.” As the liquid burned into his face, arm, and side, Mr Pidgeon screamed in pain. Residents provided water to help him wash his eyes, and emergency services arrived moments later. Tests later showed the substance had a pH level of one, indicating “extreme acid.” Mr Pidgeon underwent treatment for severe burns and required skin grafts. Both defendants deny the allegations. The court has heard no clear motive, and the prosecution maintains the attack was unprovoked. The trial continues.

He told Radio 4's Today that Philip Hammond, Mr Osborne's successor, should change tack and raise public spending Former Greek finance minister Yanis Varoufakis has urged Chancellor Philip Hammond to abandon austerity and increase public investment, arguing that Britain’s economy needs a decisive shift toward spending. Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme ahead of next week’s Conservative Party conference in Birmingham, Varoufakis said Hammond “will spend more” and should “change tack” from the approach pursued by his predecessor, George Osborne. Varoufakis claimed that each round of cuts under Osborne had led to missed budget targets and further postponements, suggesting the policy had become self-defeating. “Every time he cut, he had to push back his targets,” he said. Hammond is expected to set out his fiscal plans at the conference, amid calls from some economists for looser policy to support growth and investment. The outspoken former minister, in London for the Institute of Directors’ annual conference, drew mixed reactions online. His criticism of Osborne prompted a wave of tweets, with barbed comments including “Kettle ‘particularly inept at not being black’, says Pot” and “Takes one to know one,” highlighting the polarised view of Varoufakis since his combative tenure during Greece’s debt crisis. Varoufakis said he has spoken “frequently” with Labour’s shadow chancellor, John McDonnell. McDonnell this week outlined Labour’s economic platform, featuring a £250bn infrastructure plan and a £10-an-hour minimum wage. “I have spoken to John McDonnell many times,” Varoufakis said. “And we agree that the one thing Britain needs is investment.” He argued that an estimated £900bn is “trapped doing nothing” within City financial institutions and should be mobilised to finance productive projects. Turning to Europe, Varoufakis predicted an eventual split into two economic blocs—one centred on Germany in the north and another in the south—and warned of deeper instability. He backed recent criticisms by the International Monetary Fund of European creditor demands on Greece, noting the IMF’s assessment that targets for large primary budget surpluses are unrealistic without further debt relief. “My country is in a debt trap and it needs a much smaller budget surplus target if it is ever to escape,” he said. Varoufakis added that he expects the eurozone to “implode” eventually, citing strains in the German and Italian banking systems as significant threats to the bloc’s stability. Hammond’s forthcoming statement will be closely watched for signs of a post-austerity turn and how the government plans to deploy public spending to support the UK economy.

Bristol City have signed 26-year-old experienced Schalke goalkeeper Fabian Giefer to bolster competition between the posts. Giefer has made just one appearance for the Bundesliga side this season, featuring in a Europa League tie against Red Bull Salzburg in December. The former Bayer Leverkusen prospect joined Schalke from Fortuna Düsseldorf in the summer of 2014. "Fabian has come in to compete for the number one jersey," said City head coach Lee Johnson. "He's certainly got a good pedigree, having played in the Bundesliga, and we hope he has a successful spell with us." Meanwhile, City have sold keeper Richard O'Donnell to Rotherham United for an undisclosed fee.

Jamieson's two-under-par 70 leaves him alongside Italy's Francesco Molinari and Belgium's Thomas Pieters, one shot ahead of Germany's Maximilian Kieffer. England's Lee Westwood and Sweden's Henrik Stenson are two shots back. Olympic champion Justin Rose scored an eagle on the par five 18th to salvage his round and finish two over. Two other Englishmen, Graeme Storm and Oliver Fisher, are on four under after carding a 72 and a 70 respectively. Andrew Johnston is on three under after his 68, alongside Tyrell Hatton and Ross Fisher, while Danny Willett and Ian Poulter are at one over. On another sweltering day at Wentworth, players battled gusts up to 20mph that turned the course into a stern test. Scott Jamieson recovered impressively from a jittery bogey-par-double bogey stretch with a blistering run of six birdies in seven holes either side of the turn, vaulting himself into a share of the lead heading into the weekend. “It’s a tough stretch of the golf course, especially the way the wind was blowing today,” said the 33-year-old. “The last thing you need to do in that situation is panic. Just try and take a wee minute to yourself and start again. I’m not in any of the majors this year so this is as big as it gets. This is the pinnacle of my season.” With the leaderboard tightly bunched and conditions likely to remain testing, Wentworth is set for a compelling weekend. Form players Molinari and Pieters will press, while seasoned contenders Westwood and Stenson lurk within striking distance, and Rose seeks momentum after his late eagle.

Jack Laugher underlined his world-class form by qualifying second for the men’s 3m springboard final at the World Aquatics Championships in Budapest, posting 498.75 points across six dives. Only China’s Yuan Cao outscored the Briton, leading the semi-final with 517.45, to set up a compelling showdown on Thursday. Laugher will be joined in the decider by team-mate Ross Haslam, giving Great Britain two chances at a podium in one of the marquee events of the week. Laugher, 22, from Harrogate, arrived in Hungary as the Rio 2016 Olympic champion in the synchronised 3m and the individual silver medallist. He finished fourth with Chris Mears in Saturday’s synchro final and is now aiming to improve on the individual bronze he won at the last World Championships in Kazan in 2015. With a strong semi-final score and the confidence of a seasoned contender, he appears well placed to challenge the Chinese contingent for top honours. His girlfriend Lois Toulson and Matty Lee, who claimed mixed 10m platform silver on Saturday, remain Britain’s only diving medallists in Budapest so far. “Lois did a cracking job with the silver alongside Matty and it’s our best result so far,” Laugher told BBC Sport. “After the synchro I’m a bit gutted, but individual has been my strongest event this year and hopefully with a score like that today, in the final I’ll be able to do something magical.” Haslam, 18, is making his World Championship debut and believes his outing in the non-Olympic 1m springboard over the weekend laid the groundwork for his composed 3m showing. “If you’d have told me at the start of the year I’d be in a world final now, I’d have said ‘keep joking’ so it’s amazing,” he said. “The 1m really helped take away the nerves when I was getting out there today and in the final I just have to do my best and keep it consistent.” Thursday’s programme will also see the start of the women’s individual 3m event, with Grace Reid and Katherine Torrance—fifth together in Monday’s synchronised final—both set to compete. BBC Sport diving commentator Bob Ballard said Laugher’s progression was expected, while Haslam’s second final of the week is an added bonus after making the 1m final on day one. Ballard noted Haslam’s consistency despite a fifth-round stumble and suggested that if Laugher nails his high-tariff 3.9 dive, gold could be within reach.

Solicitor John Owen, 79, has admitted stealing money from a client’s estate after being appointed executor of his will, pleading guilty to 17 counts of theft and false accounting at Newport Crown Court. Judge Tom Crowther QC condemned the offences as a breach of trust “of the grossest sort” and said a custodial sentence is likely at sentencing on 17 October. Prosecutor Janet McDonald told the court that the deceased, John Williams, had been a long-standing client of Owen, who was made executor of his estate. She said Owen would submit bills for legal work, charge them to the estate, and then take the money without carrying out any work. Funds were subsequently withdrawn from the law firm’s account, and the court was told no one knows where the money has gone after it vanished from Owen’s practice in Llandeilo. The offences date back to 2003 and came to light after a Solicitors Regulation Authority investigation. Owen was arrested in 2011 after the watchdog said it had “reason to suspect dishonesty.” He resigned as coroner, a post he had held for 25 years. Defence barrister Leah Pollard said Owen is a man of previous good character and is currently receiving treatment for prostate cancer. Owen, of Llandeilo, was released on bail pending sentence. Judge Crowther reiterated the seriousness of the case, warning that imprisonment is probable.

Fire broke out at St Dominic’s Primary on Petersburn Road, Airdrie, shortly after Thursday lessons ended. North Lanarkshire Council said no pupils were inside and firefighters remain on scene tackling the blaze. Damage is believed to be extensive, and the school is unlikely to open on Friday. The council thanked crews and said contingency plans for pupils and staff are prepared, with parents to be updated.

Wind turbines alone provided enough electricity to supply 95% of Scottish homes Scotland’s wind sector delivered a powerful month in May, generating enough electricity to meet 95% of the monthly needs of the nation’s households, according to WWF Scotland’s analysis of renewables data from WeatherEnergy. Wind farms supplied 863,495 MWh to the National Grid, an increase of almost 20% on May 2016, when output reached 692,896 MWh. The data show that on 11 of the 31 days in May, wind power generated enough electricity to supply 100% or more of Scottish homes. Across all consumers—households, business, and industry—Scotland used 1,857,566 MWh over the month, with wind providing the equivalent of 46% of total electricity demand. The standout day was 15 May, when turbines produced enough power to meet 190% of household demand or 99% of Scotland’s total electricity needs. “Despite the disappointment of last week’s announcement that President Trump is to pull the US out of the Paris Agreement, the global energy revolution is unstoppable and continues at pace here in Scotland,” said Dr Sam Gardner, acting director of WWF Scotland. “May proved to be another great month for renewables with the wind sector meeting 95% of the electricity needs of Scotland’s households. On one day in particular, 15 May, output from turbines generated enough electricity to power 190% of homes or 99% of Scotland’s total electricity demand. Month after month, renewables play a vital role in cutting carbon emissions and powering the Scottish economy.” Solar energy also had a standout month. Homes with solar photovoltaic panels generated more than 100% of average household electricity needs in Aberdeen, Dumfries, Dundee, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Inverness, and Lerwick. Lerwick in the Shetland Islands recorded the highest relative output, producing the equivalent of 114% of an average household’s electricity consumption, followed closely by Dundee at 112%. “Thanks to a super sunny month, solar was on sizzling form and could have met more than 100% of household electricity demand in towns and cities across Scotland,” Dr Gardner added. Sunshine also boosted solar thermal performance. In Aberdeen, Dumfries, Dundee, Lerwick, Perth, Edinburgh, Glasgow, Inverness, and Stirling, solar hot water panels generated more than 90% of an average household’s hot water needs. “Scotland again managed to pump out clean power by the bucket load during May,” said Karen Robinson of WeatherEnergy. “While people might not be too surprised to learn solar power output was up in May, they might be surprised to discover that wind power output was also pretty impressive.” Across the UK, solar panels set a record on 26 May, when the National Grid reported an 8.5 GWh peak over a half-hour from midday—nearly a quarter of total demand at that time.

City Council to Remove Resident’s DIY Yellow Lines Amid Road Safety Protest A longtime resident’s grassroots effort to curb hazardous parking on an increasingly busy Holloway Road has ignited a debate over safety and civic action. Russell Taylor, who has intermittently painted yellow lines along the street for the past two decades, says the unofficial markings are necessary to stop cars from parking dangerously. “It’s a major contribution to road safety,” he told the BBC, describing his efforts as a protest against what he sees as the council’s failure to act. Taylor, who moved to Holloway Road in 1979, said the area has transformed as it has become more middle class and gentrified, bringing a surge in car ownership and traffic. He described frequent instances of vehicles parking on blind corners and both sides of the narrow street, sometimes preventing fire lorries and rubbish collection vehicles from turning around. “More recently we have had the additional problem of drivers going far too fast down our narrow street,” he added. With official measures slow to arrive, Taylor said the only practical tool at hand was a can of yellow paint stored in his garage. His personal campaign has drawn thousands of online comments since local media highlighted the story on Monday, reflecting a broader community concern over road safety and access. The city council, however, says the lines are illegal and will be removed. A spokesman, Richard MacLean, told Stuff New Zealand the council is aware of the parking problem and plans to discuss solutions with residents and councillors shortly. Among the measures under consideration are “no stopping” restrictions later this year. Despite declaring the DIY markings unlawful, MacLean indicated it was unlikely Taylor would face punishment for his long-running campaign. “Given the glorious and healthy history of civic activism in Holloway Road, we would rather not pick an unnecessary fight with the locals,” he said, signaling a preference for collaboration as formal changes are weighed.

Welsh First Minister Carwyn Jones has condemned suggestions that EU nationals living in the UK could be used as leverage in Brexit negotiations, telling the Senedd it was “utterly wrong” to treat people as “bargaining chips.” Speaking during First Minister’s Questions, Mr Jones said: “It makes them sound like hostages. They are not hostages. They are welcome in Wales,” and confirmed he has written to Home Secretary Theresa May calling for immediate clarity and reassurance on the status of EU citizens in the UK. His comments followed a question from Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood, who urged the Welsh Government to provide firm guarantees to those from other EU nations living and working in Wales. The issue has surged to the forefront of the Conservative leadership contest, after Ms May suggested last weekend that the status of existing EU residents could form part of Brexit negotiations. In contrast, leadership contenders Andrea Leadsom and Stephen Crabb both argued that EU citizens already in the UK should not be treated as “bargaining chips,” pledging to protect their rights. During an urgent Senedd session on the treatment of EU citizens, Plaid Cymru’s Simon Thomas highlighted the scale of the issue in Wales, noting that 67,000 people from EU countries live in Wales, including around 500 doctors working in the health service. “We can’t afford to lose these people,” he said. “They are part of our families, part of our communities and part of contemporary Wales. It is disgraceful that these people are treated in the way that they have been in the past week.” Cardiff Central Labour AM Jenny Rathbone reported spending part of Monday morning removing a racist slogan from a constituent’s front door, warning such incidents were “not isolated.” Mr Jones said Wales values EU citizens’ contributions and reiterated calls for the UK Government to guarantee their rights without delay.

Ireland edged France 13-10 in a tense Women’s Six Nations clash at Donnybrook, with hooker Leah Lyons’ 50th-minute try proving decisive on a blustery evening in Dublin. Tom Tierney’s side, missing three first-choice backs through Sevens commitments, showed resilience to reclaim the lead and hold off a late French push, moving level on points with England at the top of the table, though the English remain ahead on points difference. Ireland began with intent, controlling territory and tempo far better than in their wins over Scotland and Italy, but initially lacked the finishing touch. Fly-half Nora Stapleton struck an upright with a 10th-minute penalty before making amends shortly after when France were penalised for an illegal pull, her kick the only score of a tight first half. France hit back immediately after the interval, moving the ball wide to send centre Caroline Ladagnous over in the corner. Full-back Jessy Tremouliere added the conversion for a 7-3 lead, briefly turning the momentum. Ireland’s response was emphatic: a powerful driving maul from a line-out rumbled over, with Lyons grounding to restore the advantage. Stapleton’s conversion made it 10-7. As the contest tightened, Stapleton and Tremouliere traded late penalties, preserving Ireland’s three-point cushion to the final whistle. It was a notable victory given the absence of backs Alison Miller, Hannah Tyrrell and Sene Naoupu, all on Sevens duty, and underlined the depth and discipline within Tierney’s squad. Ireland travel to Cardiff to face Wales on 11 March, before returning to Donnybrook six days later for a potential title-decider against England that could shape the championship’s outcome.

Leicester Tigers powered past Sale Sharks to close in on a Premiership play-off berth, surging beyond 40 points in a comprehensive home victory in front of their highest crowd of the season. With nearly 24,000 supporters packed into Welford Road, the hosts shook off a recent three-game losing run against Sale to deliver an assertive, all-court performance that puts them on the brink of a top-four finish for the 13th successive year. Sale struck first when captain Rob Webber finished from a line-out move, but Leicester responded with intent. Freddie Burns, heading to Bath at the end of the season, was instrumental throughout and began his 19-point haul with an early penalty after Josh Charnley was shown a yellow card for taking Adam Thompstone in the air. Burns then crossed for a try, and Graham Kitchener followed suit as Tigers turned the early deficit into a 20-10 lead at the interval. After the break, Leicester’s momentum grew, with Owen Williams, Jack Roberts and replacement hooker George McGuigan all going over to stretch the advantage. Sale’s Bryn Evans provided a late consolation, but the visitors were ultimately outgunned as the Tigers’ physicality and accuracy around the breakdown suffocated any hopes of a comeback. The result tightens Leicester’s grip on a semi-final spot. Their place will be confirmed if Bath fail to beat Gloucester on Sunday, and Matt O’Connor’s side can guarantee a top-four finish with just two points in their final outing at Worcester, regardless of Bath’s remaining fixtures. It was the second time this season Leicester have topped 40 points in the Premiership, a timely statement as the business end approaches. The occasion also carried personal milestones, with Thompstone and try-scoring lock Kitchener both making their 100th starts for the club. Tigers’ performance matched the celebratory mood, particularly in a first half where they capitalised on Sale’s early indiscipline and injuries. The Sharks lost lock Andrei Ostrikov in the warm-up, and prop Ross Harrison departed midway through the opening period, prompting a debut for 20-year-old Portugal international Diogo Ferreira. Leicester head coach Matt O’Connor praised his squad’s resilience and craft in a display that reignited the Welford Road faithful. “Tigers in the semi-final? There will be some clubs looking over their shoulders,” O’Connor said. “Fair credit to the lads, they have worked hard to nail that detail and it was really pleasing to hear the crowd almost happy again. We misfired a bit in the first half and we were a bit slow in the second half to get going, but I am pleased with the result.” Reflecting on Burns, O’Connor added: “He can play, he’s a good lad. He has been good for the group. He works hard and he has been a fantastic character to have around.” Sale director of rugby Steve Diamond admitted his side’s inconsistency proved costly. “It was a reflection of our season. We are good in parts and then we undo ourselves,” he said. “We built the first 25-30 minutes and we were taking line-out off them and then we gave the ball away. After the first 10 or 15 minutes of the second half we could not get in the game. They were more physical and they were dominant around the tackle area. They tackled people past the ruck and didn’t get pulled for it, which is what they are good at.” With confidence restored and momentum building, Leicester now turn to Worcester knowing that a controlled, professional performance will secure their passage to the semi-finals.

Wigan Warriors kept their top-four pursuit on track with a grinding victory over Huddersfield Giants, prevailing in filthy conditions thanks to disciplined defence and the steady boot of Sam Powell. The Challenge Cup finalists showed just enough composure in a low-scoring contest to edge away in the second half, before Sam Tomkins’ last-second score put the seal on a bruising night. Huddersfield struck first when Jermaine McGillvary finished smartly in the corner, but Anthony Gelling hit back to level for Wigan. Liam Farrell then powered over to give the hosts the lead, a slender advantage that felt significant given the wet, error-inducing conditions and the ferocious goal-line work from both sides. After the break, the game became a war of attrition, with both teams coughing up promising possession. Wigan’s bench made a telling difference, notably Powell, who came on to orchestrate territory and add two crucial penalty goals that stretched the gap to eight. The Giants mounted pressure late on but were repeatedly repelled by Wigan’s scrambling defence, and Tomkins’ dart at the death added gloss and frustration in equal measure for the visitors, who simply ran out of time. Only points difference separated the teams before kick-off, lending the clash the feel of a shootout to stay in touch with the play-off places. The defeat leaves Huddersfield eighth, five points adrift of fourth-placed Wakefield, and with so many teams in the mix, the path back into contention looks narrow. Wigan head coach Shaun Wane praised his side’s steel: “Our defence was miles better. You have to remember Huddersfield have been flying, beating teams and scoring lots of points. They have some great attacking players in their team, so to defend that way was great. They were difficult conditions. Our attack at times was good, the score could have easily been 30 points if Joe Burgess had caught the ball a few times. It’s been a really tough week for everybody and it will be another one this week.” Giants boss Rick Stone admitted his side were second best on the night: “I think the opposition were a bit better to be honest. They were a bit hungrier and keener. We had our chances..... We threw enough bullets at them, but they defended pretty well on their goal line and they were a little bit more intense than us and had more desire in their carries and defence.” Referee: Phil Bentham.

BAE Systems says investigators have identified custom malware used in the $81 million (£56m) theft from Bangladesh Bank in February, according to Reuters. The finding comes as SWIFT releases a software update to improve customer security and reiterates that its core network and messaging services were not compromised. The hackers were reportedly able to penetrate the central bank’s systems via a cheap internet router that lacked a firewall, gaining the foothold needed to access its SWIFT environment and issue forged transfer orders. Their attempt to siphon nearly $1 billion (£690m) was foiled when a misspelling in one instruction drew attention, but $81 million had already moved through accounts linked to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In a blog post, BAE described components of the attack toolkit it believes were deployed inside the bank, saying the malware was designed to manipulate local records and cover the attackers’ tracks as fraudulent payment messages were sent. The tools appear to target SWIFT’s Alliance Access software, widely used by banks to interface with the messaging network, according to BAE. BAE noted the intrusion would rely on compromising local systems, not SWIFT’s central infrastructure. SWIFT—the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, used by more than 11,000 banks and institutions—said the malware has no impact on its network or core messaging services. “We understand that the malware is designed to hide the traces of fraudulent payments from customers’ local database applications and can only be installed on users’ local systems by attackers that have successfully identified and exploited weaknesses in their local security,” the cooperative said. To assist customers, SWIFT has issued a software update intended to enhance security and help spot inconsistencies in local database records, spokeswoman Natasha Deteran told Reuters. The incident has intensified scrutiny of cybersecurity at financial institutions, underscoring how relatively basic network weaknesses can enable high-value fraud and how attackers strive to erase evidence within compromised environments. Authorities in Bangladesh and the United States continue to probe the breach and trace the money flows.

Guardiola denies imminent retirement, clarifies Manchester City ‘behind’ comments Pep Guardiola has moved to cool speculation about an early retirement, insisting he has no plans to step away from management any time soon and is fully committed to Manchester City. Speaking ahead of Friday’s FA Cup third-round tie at West Ham, the 45-year-old said remarks made in a television interview that aired last weekend were misinterpreted. “Maybe it was inappropriate to say I’m starting to say goodbye to my career,” Guardiola said. “I’m not thinking that I’m going to retire.” He explained that while he does not see himself coaching into his 60s, any departure from the touchline is years away. “I said in the interview that I won’t be a trainer when I’m 60. But I’m 45. I’m not going to retire in two or three years,” he continued. “I’m not going to train at 60 because I want to do something else in my life. I started playing football young and my career was on the pitch. I want to do something else in my life, but in the next three or four or five or six or seven years.” Guardiola, who took charge at City in the summer following trophy-laden spells at Barcelona and Bayern Munich, emphasized his contentment in England. “I love my job and I’m in the perfect place to do my job especially here in England.” City, currently fourth in the Premier League, edged Burnley 2-1 on Monday, after which Guardiola gave an awkward post-match interview. Newspaper reports the following day suggested he had claimed Manchester City were a decade behind local rivals Manchester United, prompting him to clarify his comments on the club’s stature. “When I said to compare the titles with Liverpool, Manchester United, Barcelona and Real Madrid, we are behind. If people don’t understand that, I’m sorry,” he said. “In the last five or six years Manchester City achieved more targets and got better and grew the most. It is one of the best clubs in the world by far. But in terms of just the titles, winning the Champions League, we are behind other clubs in the last 20 years.” Guardiola stressed that City’s ambitions remain undimmed. “I never said this club is below the other ones. Of course we are going to fight until the end of the season for all the titles.”

Researchers have demonstrated a low-cost 3D printing approach to chemical synthesis, using a £1,250 system to create a range of organic compounds and inorganic clusters, including building blocks used in some cancer treatments. The team says the technique could eventually enable on-demand, customised medicines, with pharmaceutical companies adopting the method within five years and the public gaining access within two decades. “We are showing that you can take chemical constituents, pass them through a printer and create what is effectively a chemical synthesiser,” researcher Mark Symes told the BBC. “In the future you could buy common chemicals, slot them into something that 3D prints, press a button to mix the ingredients and filter them through the architecture, and at the bottom you would get out your prescription drug.” The process relies on a robotically controlled syringe that deposits a gel-based “ink,” into which chemicals and catalysts are mixed.
