Instead of filling traditional glassware and moving liquids between flasks, the printer fabricates bespoke reaction chambers—what the team calls “reactionware”—so that the container and its chemistry are designed together. “We are mixing the concept of the glassware and the chemicals together in the 3D printer,” said Prof Lee Cronin, who conceived the approach. He likened the design to a layer cake: reactive components are printed in a programmed sequence, and a liquid reagent added at the top triggers a cascade of reactions through successive layers until the final product emerges. To date, the researchers have used bathroom sealant to form their printed reactors, and the resulting substances are not suitable for human consumption. The next step, they say, is to switch to biocompatible materials and reproduce medicines already available in pharmacies, while collaborating with engineers to increase print speed and resolution. If the platform matures, doctors and patients could download pre-set “recipes,” modifying them to adjust dosage or drug combinations to individual needs. “This would not only place traditionally expensive chemical engineering technology within reach of typical laboratories and small commercial enterprises, but also could revolutionise access to healthcare and the chemical sciences in general in the developing world,” the team wrote in a paper in Nature Chemistry. The researchers emphasise that rigorous testing and regulation would be essential before any patient use, but argue the approach could transform how and where medicines are made. The team predicts pharmaceutical firms will be early adopters before the technology eventually trickles down to clinics and, later, homes.

CMA investigates Live Nation’s takeover of Isle of Wight Festival The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has opened an inquiry into Live Nation’s move to become the majority shareholder of the Isle of Wight Festival, announced in March. The regulator said it is examining whether the deal could result in a “substantial lessening of competition” in the live music and festivals market, and has asked Live Nation and the festival to operate independently until any merger is approved. Live Nation, which has declined to comment, acquired the controlling stake via LN-Gaiety, its UK joint venture with music mogul Denis Desmond’s Gaiety Investments. Announcing the plan last month, Desmond hailed it as “fantastic” to add the event to a portfolio of more than 85 festivals worldwide, including Reading, Leeds, Wireless and T in the Park. Isle of Wight Festival founder John Giddings welcomed the partnership, saying it would enable the event to tap into Live Nation’s scale and talent pool, promising to bring more acts and a better experience to UK audiences. The CMA said it has not yet set a date for consultation submissions or a decision on the case. Live Nation has been on an acquisition drive, completing eight major deals globally in 2016, with the Isle of Wight Festival marking its sixth purchase so far this year. The company’s growing footprint has drawn scrutiny from regulators and rivals concerned about market concentration in ticketing, promotion and festival operations. The festival, which is expected to attract about 42,000 fans this June, had faced uncertainty in October when organisers warned it could be cancelled unless fee changes were agreed with Solo Promoters Ltd. The event went ahead, later confirming Sir Rod Stewart as headliner, with DJ David Guetta, indie-pop group Bastille and singer-songwriter George Ezra among other acts. Revived by Giddings in 2002 after a 32-year hiatus, the Isle of Wight Festival first launched in 1968 and is famed for Jimi Hendrix’s historic headline performance in 1970.

He said he had requested federal resources to help local police fight the drug cartels. Mr Corral's comments come four days after the murder of a local journalist, Miroslava Breach, in Chihuahua City. Ms Breach had reported extensively on the links between organised crime and politicians in the state. She was shot in her car on Thursday outside her house in Chihuahua City, becoming the third journalist killed in Mexico this month. One of her children, who was in the vehicle, was not hurt. Mr Corral said there had been "significant progress" in the investigation since Sunday. Police have released a surveillance camera image of one of the men suspected of shooting her. But no arrest warrants have been issued so far. Mr Corral said that Chihuahua will not be able to combat the powerful criminal organisations operating in the state without federal help. "The Federal Government is notably absent in the fight against violence in Chihuahua, even though 75% of the murders that happen here are in the remit of the federal authorities," he told La Jornada newspaper. Ms Breach worked for La Jornada and a regional newspaper, Norte de Juarez. The gunmen left a note at the crime scene that read: "For being a loud-mouth." On Friday and Saturday, dozens of her colleagues and other demonstrators took part in protests calling for justice and demanding a thorough investigation. The Committee to Protect Journalists says 38 journalists have been killed in Mexico since 1992.

Rescuers have spent days digging through a massive landslide that engulfed the village of Cambray near Guatemala’s capital, reporting grim conditions as some homes reached are filled with water and the smell of decomposing bodies spreads across the site. The disaster struck on Thursday when tons of rain-saturated soil slid off a mountain, burying dozens of houses. Bulldozers were brought in to speed up the operation, but no survivors were found over the weekend. Authorities say around 30 people have been rescued so far, while burials began for those recovered from the debris. Alejandro Maldonado, head of Guatemala’s disaster agency, told the BBC that communities had been warned the area was high risk and should have been cleared by local authorities. “We have here a very steep hillside of over 35% inclination which is very high risk for the community and should have been avoided,” he said. “Other factors are the river that runs at the base is eroding the support for the hill, it is very sandy material and we also have several illegal sewage discharges which weakened further the hillside causing collapse.” Rescue officials said they were following international protocols that recommend 72 hours of search and rescue, a period that ended Sunday night. However, spokesmen emphasized teams were prepared to continue efforts to recover victims despite diminishing chances of finding survivors. Condolences have poured in from abroad, including messages from Pope Francis and the presidents of Mexico and Spain to families of the missing. While Guatemala has experienced larger landslides, officials noted those events typically occurred in remote rural areas, resulting in fewer casualties. The Cambray disaster, striking a community close to the capital, has underscored the country’s vulnerability to extreme weather and the urgent need for improved land-use planning and enforcement.

Rocky the spaniel drafted to sniff out protected newts on Norwich bypass route A two-year-old sniffer spaniel has been brought in to help ecologists ensure no great crested newts remain along the route of the planned Norwich Northern Distributor Road. Rocky, a specially trained detection dog, will work for a week along the 12-mile (20km) corridor north of the city, where Natural England is overseeing the safe relocation of protected species before construction begins. With spring temperatures bringing amphibians out of hibernation, teams have installed more than 7km (4.3 miles) of amphibian fencing across three areas of the route. The barriers channel newts and other wildlife into bucket traps that are checked daily by ecologists. Any animals found are carefully transferred to suitable habitats away from the development site. So far, more than 340 great crested newts have been relocated, alongside 450 smooth newts, about 850 toads, and 90 frogs. Crews have also encountered an assortment of reptiles and mammals, including a baby hedgehog, during the operation. The effort is part of strict measures to protect species afforded legal safeguards and to reduce ecological impacts associated with the project. Rocky’s handler, trainer Aran Clyne of Wagtail UK, said it takes several months to prepare a dog to detect wildlife in the field. “It’s all about building an association between the newt smell and Rocky’s reward, the tennis ball,” he explained. “Whenever he finds a newt, he gets his ball.” Once Rocky identifies a location, ecologists move any remaining animals by hand to secure areas nearby. This will be Rocky’s first assignment involving newt conservation; he has previously been deployed to sniff out bats, another protected species, at sites earmarked for new windfarms. Norfolk County Council, which commissioned the canine checks, said the approach is a fast and cost-effective way of confirming that cleared areas are free of lingering amphibians. “Using a sniffer dog is a quick, efficient and cost-effective way of carrying out final checks of cleared areas,” the authority said. “Without a trained sniffer dog all suitable areas would have to be laboriously searched by hand by ecologists.” The final sweeps aim to ensure wildlife is safeguarded before construction progresses on the bypass.

Bomb Hoax Triggers Inspection and Temporary Closure at Warsaw Modlin; 48-Year-Old Arrested Polish police arrested a 48-year-old man after tracing an anonymous bomb threat to his home, following a call that claimed an explosive device was aboard a Ryanair flight due to depart Warsaw Modlin Airport for Oslo on Thursday morning. The aircraft, which had arrived earlier from Oslo and was scheduled to return at 08:40 local time, was held on the ground while security teams conducted a thorough inspection. As a precaution, airport authorities closed Modlin to inbound arrivals during the sweep, Ryanair said in a statement. Officials determined the call was a hoax and expected the search to confirm no threat, allowing the aircraft to be released and the airport to reopen shortly. The flight had not yet boarded when the alert was received. “This was an irresponsible prank,” police spokesman Mariusz Mrozek told broadcaster TVN24, urging the public to recognise the serious consequences of false alarms. Ryanair apologised to affected customers and said security authorities ordered an immediate inspection and temporarily closed the airport to inbound arrivals. Police said the investigation is ongoing, and the suspect could face charges related to making a false bomb threat and disrupting transport operations. Modlin is a smaller auxiliary airport serving Warsaw and is used exclusively by Ryanair.

Rimantas Karvelis, 56, has died after being struck by a black Vauxhall Astra that failed to stop on London Road shortly before 18:45 BST on 24 October, Kent Police said. He was taken to a London hospital with serious injuries and died on 3 November. Mr Karvelis’s family paid tribute, describing him as a “magnificent dad” and “an amazing person.” He had been on a one-month holiday, visiting one of his two sons who is in hospital in Dartford. His other son, Audrius Karvelis, who travelled back from the United States, said: “I can’t believe he’s gone, my magnificent dad, who came here to visit my brother and encourage him to fight Guillain-Barre syndrome at Darenth Valley Hospital. Our life has changed irrevocably — we are shocked and deeply saddened. He was an amazing person, a real example to others.” The Vauxhall Astra was later found abandoned in Grange Road. Kent Police said three people have been arrested in connection with the incident and released on bail as investigations continue.

Venezuela’s presidential race intensified on the eve of the vote as massive rival rallies underscored a polarized nation preparing to choose a successor to the late Hugo Chávez on 14 April. In Caracas, hundreds of thousands of red-shirted supporters of acting president Nicolás Maduro packed the city’s main avenues, signaling enduring loyalty to the socialist project Chávez championed during his 14 years in office. Maduro, handpicked by Chávez as his political heir, described himself as a son of the late leader and vowed to continue the “socialist revolution” if elected. Meanwhile, opposition candidate Henrique Capriles drew another large crowd in the northern city of Acarigua, delivering a final appeal centered on economic revival, anti-corruption measures, and improved public security. “I ask you for the opportunity to show that I can indeed govern and make things right,” the 40-year-old lawyer and politician told supporters, promising to revive the economy within a year and stressing that his team is already preparing first steps. Capriles has said he will not dismantle Chávez-era social programs, but plans to root out official corruption while fostering free-market policies to spur growth and tackle crime. Capriles has often cited the Brazilian model under former President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose administration combined economic expansion with poverty reduction. Yet Lula recently released a video backing Maduro, highlighting the regional left’s support for continuity in Caracas. Opinion polls suggest Maduro holds a strong lead over his rival. With emotions running high and competing visions for Venezuela’s future on display, Sunday’s vote will test whether the country opts for continuity under Chávez’s chosen successor or a shift toward market-oriented reforms under Capriles.

Brazil’s Alison Cerutti and Bruno Schmidt, the reigning world champions, claimed Olympic gold on Copacabana Beach, coming from behind in both sets to beat Italy’s Paolo Nicolai and Daniele Lupo 21-19, 21-17. Spurred by a partisan midnight crowd, the hosts overturned an 11-7 deficit in the second set, with the 6ft 8in Cerutti’s towering blocks and Schmidt’s scrambling defence driving a surge back to 14-14 before the pair calmly converted match point amid thunderous roars. The win delivers Brazil’s fifth gold of these Games and their first men’s beach volleyball title in 12 years, underscoring a tradition of excellence that has produced multiple Olympic podiums since the sport joined the programme in Atlanta in 1996. It also brings redemption for Cerutti, a silver medallist in 2012, now champion alongside long-time partner Schmidt. Earlier, the Netherlands secured bronze—their first Olympic medal in the event—by edging Russia’s Konstantin Semenov and Viacheslav Krasilnikov 23-21, 22-20. Alexander Brouwer and Robert Meeuwsen prevailed in a tight, serve-and-block battle played before a half-full stadium, setting the stage for the hosts’ late-night finale. Brazil’s men add to the women’s silver won on Thursday, capping a triumphant home Games for the country’s beach volleyball programme.

Since taking over in 2011, Hansen has a win ratio of 91%, and guided the All Blacks to World Cup success in 2015. New Zealand Rugby Union chief executive Steve Tew has left the door open for Steve Hansen to remain as All Blacks head coach beyond the 2019 World Cup, praising the extraordinary record of the man who has overseen one of the most dominant eras in international rugby. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 live, Tew lauded Hansen’s achievements and suggested the NZRU would seriously consider an extension if the coach wished to continue. “I doubt his record will ever be mirrored, and long may it continue,” Tew said. Hansen, who is contracted through to the end of the next World Cup in Japan in two years’ time, is widely expected to step down after the tournament. Since moving into the top job from his role as assistant to Sir Graham Henry, he has amassed a remarkable 91% win ratio and guided New Zealand to the 2015 World Cup title, while also maintaining the team’s status as the sport’s benchmark. Yet Tew emphasized that any decision is not set in stone, indicating the union’s openness to Hansen staying on if the circumstances align. “Steve has gone from strength to strength,” said Tew, who was appointed in 2011. “If Steve had an appetite to keep going, and was sure he had the group of people around him and the players were motivated by that, then it’s obviously something we would very seriously consider.” While names such as Vern Cotter, Joe Schmidt and Warren Gatland have been touted as potential successors, Tew cautioned that it is not a foregone conclusion that Hansen will vacate the role after Japan. Should Hansen depart, Tew signaled that promoting from within remains an appealing pathway for the NZRU, mirroring the progression that saw Hansen succeed Henry. He singled out current assistant coach Ian Foster as a prime candidate. “Don’t overlook Ian Foster in this country,” Tew said. “He is sitting in a very successful environment and making an enormous contribution. We certainly want to have that option, and Ian is definitely one of those options we want to have ready and appropriately skilled and experienced.” Tew also underscored the NZRU’s ongoing engagement with New Zealand coaches operating abroad, noting the depth of the coaching talent pool and the professional game’s draw for former players. “We produce a lot of coaches, and in this professional era there is a strong drive from ex-players to stay in the game,” he said. “We can’t actually offer all of them jobs, so some of them going overseas is beneficial, but we are very keen to keep them connected and very keen to keep them back when the time is right.” Despite the All Blacks’ sustained success, Tew warned against complacency, pointing to the volatile nature of elite rugby. “People are currently questioning where Australian rugby is at — I won’t join that debate — but it was only 2015 when they won the Rugby Championship and reached a World Cup final,” he said. “Things can change very, very quickly. We won’t take anything for granted and we won’t get complacent, but we certainly won’t be giving anyone a break, because we don’t think that’s the right thing to do either.”

UK manufacturing staged a surprisingly strong rebound in August as the closely watched Markit/CIPS purchasing managers’ index (PMI) rose to 53.3 from 48.3 in July, signaling a return to expansion after a sharp post-referendum downturn. A reading above 50 denotes growth. The survey suggests the slump that immediately followed June’s Brexit vote was shorter-lived than feared, with a weaker pound helping to revive export demand but also stoking inflationary pressures. IHS Markit said the month-on-month rise was the joint largest in the survey’s 25-year history. Rob Dobson, senior economist at IHS Markit, said the data pointed to “a solid rebound in the performance of the UK manufacturing sector from the steep downturn that followed the EU referendum.” He noted that the domestic market improved “especially for consumer products,” while the depreciation of sterling “drove higher inflows of new business from the US, Europe, Scandinavia, Middle East and Asia.” The pound’s decline since the vote—down more than 10% against both the US dollar and the euro—has lowered the price of British goods for overseas buyers, helping to lift export orders. But the weaker currency has also increased the cost of imported components and raw materials. Dobson warned that inflation was “raising its ugly head,” adding that the rates of increase in input prices and output charges “both hit five-year highs,” with manufacturers citing the impact of sterling on import costs. Financial markets cheered the PMI surprise. Following the release, sterling jumped about 1% against the dollar to $1.33, before easing slightly, and was up 0.6% against the euro at just under €1.19. The upbeat manufacturing snapshot echoed last week’s CBI survey, which reported the fastest growth in export orders for two years. The August bounce-back contrasts sharply with July’s PMI, which slid below the 50 threshold and was initially taken as an early sign of a looming downturn. That weakness was among the pieces of evidence that helped prompt the Bank of England to cut interest rates to a record low of 0.25% in early August and to launch additional stimulus measures to bolster the economy. However, the improving run of data may complicate the case for further monetary easing. Laith Khalaf of Hargreaves Lansdown said the figures suggest “companies and consumers alike are carrying on with business as usual now the referendum is disappearing into the rear view mirror.” While acknowledging uncertainty remains as the UK negotiates its exit from the EU, he added that the “gathering pile of robust economic data might start to dissuade policymakers from any further monetary easing.” Investors will look next to the services PMI due next week, a broader gauge of economic momentum given the sector’s dominant share of UK output.

Surrey town centre shut as crews tackle industrial estate blaze; probe ongoing A Surrey town’s centre was closed for several hours on Monday as emergency teams battled a major fire at the Renshaw Industrial Estate in Mill Mead, with crews remaining on scene into Tuesday while investigations continue. Part of the High Street was still shut on Tuesday morning, though Surrey Police later tweeted that the road had reopened. Firefighters stayed overnight to damp down hotspots and maintained a “watching brief,” according to Surrey’s Assistant Chief Fire Officer Steve Owen-Hughes, who said crews were still in attendance more than 24 hours after the blaze began. “At the moment the cause isn’t known and it’s going to be quite difficult until we can get closer in to determine the actual place where the fire started and possibly the cause as well,” he said. A structural engineer was at the scene to assess the safety of affected buildings before investigators move in. Owen-Hughes said a number of businesses in one unit on the industrial estate had been completely destroyed. Repairs have been carried out to gas and electricity supplies and the telephone network, allowing the focus to shift to the industrial unit where the fire is believed to have started. “As soon as it’s safe to do so, we’ll allow businesses to get back in there and keep on trading,” he added. Authorities urged people to follow updated travel advice as normal access to the area is gradually restored.

Andy Burnham will call for tougher government action to protect children and tackle obesity, urging mandatory limits on the fat, salt and sugar content of food and a clearer approach to labelling. In a speech setting out Labour’s public health agenda, he will criticise the current government’s reliance on voluntary agreements with industry, arguing that binding rules are needed to make meaningful progress. While the levels of fat, salt and sugar in many products have been reduced in recent years, Burnham will say that too many people still consume above recommended amounts. He is expected to argue that setting mandatory maximum limits would provide a level playing field for manufacturers and ensure healthier options become the default. The proposal is likely to be the most closely watched element of his remarks, given industry sensitivities and the broader debate over the role of regulation. Burnham will also push for clearer food labelling, calling for a traffic light-based system that gives consumers simple, front-of-pack colour coding alongside nutritional information. A version of this system is already in use, but he will contend that it needs to be more consistent and easier to understand. He will acknowledge the challenge of delivering mandatory labelling, noting that EU-level agreement has historically been required and that industry opposition has complicated progress. On tobacco, Burnham will pledge support for plain cigarette packaging, following a government consultation that concluded ministers were “minded” to introduce the measure but stopped short of a firm commitment. He will further argue for targeted action on high-strength, cheap alcohol, with options such as pricing and bottle size controls under consideration to curb harm. “Labour has traditionally led the way on public health and this new approach will chart a new course towards a healthy nation in the 21st century,” Burnham will say. “Children need better protection from the pressures of modern living and the harm caused by alcohol, sugar and smoke, and Labour will not flinch from taking the action needed to provide it.” Professor John Ashton, president of the Faculty of Public Health, said the steps outlined were in line with the organisation’s priorities. “We need an honest discussion about whether we can still have a world-class health system without government intervening, where only it can, to improve and protect our health,” he said. The Conservatives defended their record, insisting “real progress” has been made under the current government. A party spokesman said: “Labour are naive to think that just banning particular types of food will support people to make informed choices. The public deserve better.” Recent data suggests childhood obesity rates may be levelling off, but 15% of under-15s are still obese, underlining the scale of the challenge.

Police are investigating a fatal crash near Kinfauns Castle at 15:10 on Tuesday involving a white Mercedes Sprinter van and a heavy tractor articulated lorry. The van’s 36-year-old male driver was pronounced dead at the scene. Officers have appealed for witnesses with information to come forward to local police.

James Hilton, 25, of Aberdeen, has been jailed for four years and two months for a fatal crash on the A920 between Dufftown and Huntly in 2015, killing 81-year-old great‐grandfather Patrick Pirie. Hilton was trying to catch up with a friend travelling in another car when his vehicle collided with a car carrying Mr Pirie, a retired farmer. Mr Pirie died in hospital from his injuries. Sentencing at the High Court in Edinburgh, Judge Lord Woolman said: “This is a tragic case for everyone involved. Mr Pirie was a retired farmer aged 81. He was married with four grown children. Your crime casts a terrible shadow over them. The harm caused by an offence that causes a person’s death is immeasurable. My duty is to discourage others from such irresponsible conduct. I must also mark the gravity of what happened.” Hilton was also banned from driving for nine years and until he passes a fresh test. Defence counsel Tony Lenehan said Hilton had shown “genuine remorse.” Mr Pirie had been travelling home from a farmers’ mart in Huntly when the collision happened.

title: Self is shortlisted for the first time for Umbrella, about an epidemic of encephalitis lethargica after World War I which killed almost a million people. Previous winner Mantel is nominated for Bring Up the Bodies, the second book in her fictional Thomas Cromwell trilogy. Bookies William Hill said it would be the closest finish ever. Its most recent odds for Mantel are 6/4, making her the narrow favourite over Self at 2/1. But Ladbrokes place Self as the favourite at 6/4, ahead of Mantel at 9/4. The Man Booker Prize race is shaping up to be one of the tightest in years, with Will Self and Hilary Mantel leading a richly varied shortlist. Self, shortlisted for the first time, is recognised for Umbrella, a daring modernist novel centred on an outbreak of encephalitis lethargica in the aftermath of World War I, a disease that killed nearly a million people. Mantel, a previous winner, returns with Bring Up the Bodies, the second instalment in her acclaimed Thomas Cromwell trilogy. Bookmakers are split on the likely winner. William Hill has Mantel as a narrow favourite at 6/4, ahead of Self at 2/1, calling it “the closest finish ever.” Ladbrokes, however, tips Self at 6/4, placing Mantel at 9/4. The divergence underscores a field with no clear frontrunner and strong support for multiple contenders. The shortlist also features Indian poet Jeet Thayil with his debut novel Narcopolis, and Malaysia-born Tan Twan Eng for The Garden of Evening Mists, set in the mountains of central Malaya amid the political upheaval of the 1950s. Alison Moore’s The Lighthouse follows a middle-aged man to Germany on a walking holiday after his marriage collapses, only for the journey to unearth painful memories. Deborah Levy’s Swimming Home, her first novel in more than a decade, reached publication through the backing of supporters and friends via subscription after traditional publishers initially turned it down. “This has been an exhilarating year for fiction. The strongest I would say for more than a decade,” said Sir Peter Stothard, chair of the judges, highlighting the breadth of ambition and stylistic range on the list. Sales momentum is already reflecting public interest. Amazon reports Mantel’s Bring Up the Bodies as the best-selling shortlisted title on its site since the announcement on 11 September, accounting for 36% of shortlist sales, followed by Moore’s The Lighthouse at 20%. Self’s Umbrella currently trails with 8%. Winning the Man Booker can dramatically boost sales: every winner since 1996 has grossed more than £1m. Yann Martel’s Life of Pi (2002) made just under £10m, Mantel’s Wolf Hall earned £5.4m, and last year’s winner, Julian Barnes’s The Sense of an Ending, has sold 300,000 copies to date. If Mantel triumphs again, she would become the first living British writer to win the prize twice. The winner will be announced on Tuesday evening at the Guildhall in central London.

Trial Opens in Rennes Over 2005 Electrocution Deaths in Clichy-sous-Bois A decade after the deaths of teenagers Bouna Traoré, 15, and Zyed Benna, 17, a court in Rennes has begun hearing a case that will determine whether two police officers, Sébastien Gaillemin and Stéphanie Klein, failed to help the boys when they were in mortal danger. The teenagers were electrocuted on 27 October 2005 after fleeing police and entering an EDF power substation in Clichy-sous-Bois, a Paris suburb. A third youth, Muhittin Altun, survived with severe burns and is expected to attend the five-day trial alongside relatives of the victims. The case has moved slowly through France’s legal system, becoming a symbol of the fraught relationship between police and residents in the country’s disadvantaged “banlieues.” In 2012, France’s highest court overturned a ruling that had dropped the charge of “failure to assist a person in danger,” paving the way for this week’s proceedings. Police were initially called after a neighbor reported a group of boys crossing a building site. As the chase unfolded, three of the youths entered the substation. Prosecutors say the officers knew the teenagers were at risk and did not intervene. Central to the case is a radio message attributed to Gaillemin, 41 at the time, in which he reportedly told colleagues he expected the boys to leave the substation but added, “If they enter the site there’s not much hope they’ll make it alive.” The defense argues that Gaillemin’s words were hypothetical and that the officers did not see the youths enter the facility. “Speaking hypothetically is very different from witnessing them going in,” said their lawyer, Daniel Merchat, on French television. The deaths of Traoré and Benna ignited 21 days of rioting across France, prompting the first state of emergency in more than two decades. Clichy-sous-Bois and similar suburbs have long been viewed as flashpoints for social unrest, and in January, following attacks in Paris that left 17 people dead, Prime Minister Manuel Valls described a “territorial, social and ethnic apartheid” in France’s ghettos. Siyakha Traoré, Bouna’s elder brother, said the family had waited years for the trial. “According to the day and my mood, I’m either optimistic..... or not,” he told French media. If convicted of failing to help individuals in danger, Gaillemin and Klein face up to five years in prison and fines of up to €75,000.

The so-called "English votes for English laws" measures have been announced in response to devolution. Commons Leader Chris Grayling said the change would bring "real fairness to our constitutional arrangements". But former Tory Welsh Secretary David Jones said decisions on some services in England would affect Wales. The UK government has outlined plans to give English MPs — and in some cases both English and Welsh MPs — a veto over Westminster legislation that applies to matters devolved to administrations elsewhere in the UK. Under proposals set out in Parliament on Thursday, all MPs will continue to vote at every key stage of bills, preserving the overall role of the House of Commons, while introducing an additional consent mechanism for England-only or England-and-Wales-only provisions. Chris Grayling argued the approach addresses long-standing concerns raised by devolution, saying it ensures English decisions “cannot simply be imposed on the English against their wishes.” He insisted the change preserves the United Kingdom-wide role of MPs and the integrity of the Commons’ legislative process. However, David Jones, MP for Clwyd West, warned of complex cross-border implications, particularly for communities in north Wales “heavily reliant upon services provided in England, most particularly health services.” He said people were “already disadvantaged by the defective devolution settlement put in place by the party opposite,” and sought assurances they would not be further disadvantaged. Grayling responded that Welsh MPs would retain a vote and a voice on health issues in England, while maintaining that English consent should be respected. Newport West Labour MP Paul Flynn called for a constitutional convention to consider establishing a federal UK, accusing the government of “staggering and stumbling with these ad hoc steps..... that will lead to the certain break up of the United Kingdom.” Answering a question from Plaid Cymru’s Hywel Williams, Grayling said only a “relatively small” number of England-only committees would be required, with most Commons committees continuing to include MPs from across the UK. Supporters say the plan balances fairness with unity; critics warn it risks complicating governance and straining the union.

She lured her victim to a quiet area at the Hampshire school by promising her a gift before stabbing her in the chest, Winchester Crown Court heard. The attacker, who cannot be named for legal reasons but was then aged 14, was influenced by an interest in murderers. She had also plotted to kill her mother and brother, her trial was told. The defendant will be sentenced at a later date and the judge has ordered a pre-sentence psychiatric report. Jurors were told the girl arrived at school on 25 April wearing a bandana and with her mouth cut to resemble the Joker from the Batman film The Dark Knight. Prosecutor James Newton-Price said she approached her 15-year-old friend and told her she had a present, urging: “Close your eyes and put your hands out.” The victim briefly opened her eyes and saw her friend lunge forward with a knife. The court heard the victim stepped back as the blade pierced her blazer and shirt. Despite being stabbed near the heart, she suffered only a superficial puncture wound and was able to seek help. The attacker later sent a message saying she did not care “if they blamed it on The Joker or Columbine, they didn’t inspire me, they motivated me,” the jury was told. In police interviews read to the court, the defendant described basing a fashion GCSE project on US serial killers Ted Bundy and Richard “Nightcrawler” Ramirez, which she considered “cool and edgy.” She had researched the 1999 Columbine High School massacre and the 2011 killings carried out by Anders Breivik in Norway to gain “more insight into their whole case,” the court heard. In the early hours before the assault, she looked up the position of the heart and the fatality of stab wounds. The girl admitted compiling a “kill list” of potential victims, including fellow pupils as well as her mother and brother. She told the court that plans for a wider school attack were “not serious” and that she did not understand her own motives. She said she felt compelled to harm her friend, adding: “A very big part of me was disgusted at what I was thinking. I didn’t feel very much in control of what I was doing. I didn’t want to, I felt I had to, I felt that within myself.” Jurors previously heard that the defendant bore a grudge against the victim, believing she had set up fake Instagram and Tumblr accounts in her name. At the start of the trial, the girl pleaded guilty to possessing a bladed article on school premises and to unlawful wounding. She told the court she carried out the stabbing because “I had a driving force to hurt someone. I was scared of losing face. I intended to stab her.” She denied intending to kill or to cause serious harm. The judge has requested a psychiatric assessment before sentencing. No date has yet been set. The defendant remains subject to reporting restrictions due to her age.

He gave the order at a swearing-in ceremony for the new service commanders he appointed last month. Nigeria’s President Muhammadu Buhari has directed newly appointed military chiefs to intensify operations against Boko Haram, renewing his pledge to confront the Islamist insurgency “head on.” Issuing the directive at their swearing-in, Buhari said the commanders must deepen cooperation with neighboring Chad, Cameroon, and Niger and would receive the resources needed to deliver results. Since Boko Haram launched its campaign in northern Nigeria in 2009, at least 17,000 people have been killed, according to Amnesty International. While the group has been driven from many of its former strongholds, it continues to mount deadly raids and bombings. Security analysts note a rise in suicide attacks since Buhari took office in May, alongside an uptick in cross-border assaults on communities in neighboring countries. In Cameroon’s Far North region on Wednesday, suspected Boko Haram fighters reportedly killed five villagers and a soldier in Lame, near Fotokol. Local sources said the militants slipped into the area quietly using horses and bicycles, torched homes and schools, and fled before senior army officers arrived, underscoring the group’s continued ability to strike and retreat swiftly. Buhari, a former army general, has made a revitalized multinational force of about 8,700 troops central to his strategy. He stressed that the campaign must be conducted within the law, urging the armed forces to protect civilians and respect the rights of combatants even as they press the offensive. The call comes amid longstanding concerns among international partners over human rights violations; the United States has withheld certain arms sales to Nigeria in the past on such grounds. Two of the president’s key appointees, Maj Gen Tukur Yusuf Buratai and National Security Adviser Maj Gen Babagana Monguno, hail from Borno state, the epicenter of the conflict. Observers say their local knowledge could sharpen intelligence and operational planning as Nigeria seeks to reclaim rural areas and secure urban centers. With regional coordination deepening and Abuja promising new equipment and support, the government hopes to reverse recent gains by the militants. The challenge will be sustaining momentum while safeguarding civilians and rebuilding trust in communities battered by years of violence.

An anonymous bidder has purchased a pair of boxing gloves linked to Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier’s 1971 “Fight of the Century” at an auction in Cleveland, US. The bout, held amid intense social and political debate, ended with Frazier defeating Ali by unanimous decision to become the undisputed world heavyweight champion. Ali, who had earlier been stripped of his title for refusing induction into the US Army during the Vietnam War, later beat Frazier in their 1974 and 1975 rematches, bolstering his legacy as the greatest boxer of all time. The same auction house previously sold gloves from Ali’s first world title fight for $836,500 USD.

Tributes have been paid to Suzanne Goodall, the visionary founder of Ty Hafan, who inspired the creation of one of Wales’s first children’s hospices. Goodall, from Beddau, Pontypridd, launched the hospice in Sully, near Penarth in the Vale of Glamorgan, in 1999 after 11 years of tireless fundraising. She was awarded an MBE in 2004 for her services to children and families, officially retiring in 2011 but remaining closely connected to the charity she helped build. A spokesperson for Ty Hafan described Goodall as a “true inspiration to staff and families,” adding that “her dedication and commitment meant that hundreds of families across Wales have been given a light in the dark while facing the realities of caring for a child with a life-limiting condition.” The charity provides specialist one-to-one care and outreach services to life-limited children and their families across Wales. Goodall conceived the idea for Ty Hafan after hearing a friend’s experiences volunteering in a children’s hospice in Yorkshire, and discovering there were no equivalent facilities in Wales. “Suzanne’s endless motivation to continue providing the best possible care and support to these families never wavered and she has remained a much-loved and highly respected figure throughout the charity,” the spokesperson said. “We are all deeply saddened by today’s news and will greatly miss Suzanne’s warmth and determination. Every one of us at the charity will honour her legacy by continuing to do all we can to support families who need us.”

Calls to protect Irish Sea habitats intensify as fishermen warn of economic pain Conservationists and fishermen are at odds over whether two ecologically rich areas in the Irish Sea should be granted marine conservation zone (MCZ) status, amid a government review that could reshape protections and livelihoods. The Wildlife Trust has urged the UK government to designate Slieve na Griddle and South Rigg—located midway between Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man—as protected zones, warning that excluding them puts vulnerable sea life at risk. The Northern Ireland Fish Producers’ Association counters that the proposed sites are prime fishing grounds and that stricter rules would harm an industry that supports coastal communities. In January, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which has responsibility for the two offshore sites, did not include Slieve na Griddle and South Rigg among dedicated MCZs, arguing protection could have a “significant impact on Northern Ireland’s fishing sector.” The department plans to review that decision in the coming months as part of a wider consultation on new marine protections. Of nine MCZs proposed for the Irish Sea, two—Fylde and Cumbria Coast, off England—have already been approved. MCZ status can restrict destructive activities such as dredging and trawling, measures proponents say are crucial to restoring habitats and safeguarding species. The Wildlife Trust highlights the presence of Dublin Bay prawns (nephrops) and ocean quahogs—long-lived clams that can survive for more than 500 years—as evidence of the sites’ ecological value. Emily Baxter, of the trust, said fisheries should recognise that well-managed MCZs can benefit both nature and the industry. “We’re not saying they would be banned outright from fishing in marine conservation zones,” she said. “But if we do want to conserve the special species, then it would make sense to restrict access. Supporting sustainable fisheries, instead of encouraging overfishing and habitat destruction, would increase fish landings, generate more income and create more jobs in the sector. If these areas are allowed to recover, there will be more of them (nephrops) and they can grow bigger.” Dick James, head of the Northern Ireland Fish Producers’ Association, warned that designating Slieve na Griddle and South Rigg would cause real hardship. “Eight thousand tonnes of nephrops are trawled from the Irish Sea each year; it’s a £20m industry,” he said. “We’ve offered alternatives which don’t leave us entirely clear of the issue, but the areas they’ve picked are the most intensely fished areas in the Irish Sea. In some of the areas we’ve put forward, the fisheries are not as intense. We’re basically hoping that common sense will prevail and that there are alternatives, more diverse than the areas they’ve proposed in the first instance.” The push for new protections comes amid a decade-long effort to expand marine conservation across UK waters. In 2013, 127 zones were initially proposed following two years of negotiations among fishermen, conservationists and other sea users. To date, 27 have been designated, and the government is seeking public views on a further 23. The consultation is due to close on 24 April.

Günther Oettinger, the incoming EU commissioner for the digital economy and society, has come under heavy criticism for remarks suggesting that celebrities whose intimate images were leaked bore some responsibility for the breach. Speaking at a meeting in Brussels on Monday, Oettinger said he was being “semi-serious” before questioning public reactions to the leaks and implying that those who took such photos should not expect protection. “The fact that recently there have been an increasing number of public lamentations about nude photos of celebrities who took selfies—I just can’t believe it,” he said. “If someone is dumb enough as a celebrity to take a nude photo of themselves and put it online, they surely can’t expect us to protect them. I mean, stupidity is something you can not—or only partly—save people from.” His comments referred to the leak of intimate images of more than 80 women, including actress Jennifer Lawrence and singer Rihanna. The images first appeared on the 4Chan message board and are believed to have been obtained by accessing private cloud storage accounts, not publicly posted content. Julia Reda, a Member of the European Parliament representing the Pirate Party, sharply condemned Oettinger’s remarks. “The statement is unbelievable,” she said, adding in a blog post that “the person applying to be in charge of shoring up trust in the internet so that Europeans do more business online, just blamed people whose personal data was accessed and spread without authorisation.” She continued: “He placed the moral blame for that crime squarely on the victims rather than the perpetrators.” Reda also posted a video of the exchange on YouTube. When approached by the BBC to clarify his remarks, Oettinger said: “Everybody has a right to privacy. The EU Commission wants to make cloud computing safer.” Asked whether he would apologise for, or expand on, his comments, his spokeswoman responded: “No.” Critics contend that Oettinger’s framing overlooks the core issue of criminal intrusion into private accounts and risks normalising victim-blaming in cases of data theft. They argue the images were kept private and were stolen, not voluntarily shared “online,” as his phrasing suggested. Reda questioned whether Oettinger is suited to oversee the bloc’s digital agenda for the next five years. “By making a mockery of what he should recognize as a serious problem and by doing it in this aloof and insulting tone, Günther Oettinger is seriously calling into question whether he is qualified for the job of shaping our digital society for the next five years,” she said. German magazine Der Spiegel added to the backlash, writing that Oettinger’s comments showed he had “no clue about current events and issues at the core of his new resort.” Oettinger is set to take up the commissioner post in November.

Sabah Bourdras recorded a video of herself encouraging her pupils to repeat "Arabic is the world's richest language..... This year I'll speak Arabic and express myself only in Arabic." A classroom video posted by Algerian teacher Sabah Bourdras has ignited a nationwide debate over language and identity, underscoring enduring sensitivities in a country shaped by its colonial past. In the clip, widely shared on social media, Bourdras asks her pupils to pledge they will speak and express themselves only in Arabic this year, calling it “the world’s richest language.” The Algerian government has since announced she will face disciplinary action, saying the video breached students’ privacy and was recorded without parents’ permission. Language has long been a fault line in Algeria, a former French colony where the official languages are Arabic and Berber. In schools, most children are taught only in Arabic for the first four years, with French introduced later. Yet French remains widely spoken in daily life, administration, media and commerce, a reality that many older Algerians resent, referring to French as “the language of the occupiers.” Others, however, say they feel more comfortable and precise expressing themselves in French than in Arabic, reflecting a complex linguistic landscape and layered identities. Education Minister Nouria Benghebrit said Bourdras would be questioned over the video’s compliance with privacy and consent rules. Benghebrit, who earned her PhD in France and often speaks French on television, has been a lightning rod in debates over language policy. Critics have accused her of “waging a war” on Arabic during her tenure. Earlier this year, media reports suggested the ministry was considering removing diacritics—the symbols that indicate vocalisation and are essential to clarifying meaning—from Arabic syllabuses as part of education reforms. Linguists criticized the proposal, arguing the signs are fundamental to learning and comprehension. Press reports also claimed the ministry planned to reduce classroom hours dedicated to Arabic and scrap “citizenship education,” prompting further controversy. Benghebrit has faced additional scrutiny after a massive leak of exam papers, despite new measures designed to curb cheating. Nevertheless, she maintains pockets of support. One social media page described her as a “true Algerian without complex,” praising her modernizing agenda. The response to Bourdras, meanwhile, has been swift and largely supportive online. On Twitter, @zohor4m1d wrote: “What this noble teacher is going through reflects the worst image of our psychological defeat and our shameful submission to occupation.” Another user, @OmOb_2, said: “The French did not like the fact that Bourdras insisted on speaking in proper Arabic.” Teachers across the country have posted photos and videos from their own classrooms in solidarity. Beyond social media, imams in the north-eastern city of Skikida reportedly used Friday prayer sermons to back Bourdras, urging worshippers to resist what they called the government’s attempts at “Frenchification.” The outpouring highlights the enduring power of language in Algeria’s public life and the way cultural debates can quickly become political. While some embrace bilingualism as a pragmatic asset, the messages of support for Bourdras suggest a broader contest over what defines a “true Algerian”—and whether that identity should be anchored first and foremost in Arabic. As officials weigh disciplinary steps, the conversation shows no sign of abating, reflecting the deep roots and real-world implications of Algeria’s linguistic choices.

Glen Kirton, the Football Association’s press chief in 1989, has told the Hillsborough inquests that the match commander, Chief Superintendent David Duckenfield, said inside the police control box that a gate had been forced and an in-rush of Liverpool supporters had caused casualties. Kirton’s account, given in a witness statement in 1989 and reiterated at the Warrington hearings, sheds light on how an early narrative about the disaster took hold as events unfolded. At an earlier hearing, the jury heard that Mr Duckenfield had in fact given an order at 14:52 GMT to open an exit gate at Hillsborough. Ninety-six people died as a result of the crush at Sheffield Wednesday’s stadium on 15 April 1989, during the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. In his 1989 statement, Kirton said: “Chief Superintendent Duckenfield told us the gate had been forced and an in-rush of Liverpool supporters had caused casualties.” Reports suggesting fans had broken in were widely carried by the media for much of the day, the inquests heard, until a press conference on the evening of the disaster. Jurors were told that South Yorkshire Police’s chief constable, Peter Wright, later told journalists that “a gate had been opened by police.” Kirton said he went to the police control box as the crisis developed, accompanied by FA chief executive Graham Kelly and Sheffield Wednesday secretary Graham Mackrell, because they believed that was where the most accurate information could be obtained and where they could determine whether the match would continue. “Because we thought that was the place where we could get the most accurate information about what was happening and also be able to ascertain whether the match was going to continue or not,” he said. He described a conversation between Mr Kelly and Mr Duckenfield in the control box, during which the match commander pointed to CCTV monitors and said there had been “a break-in.” Under questioning from John Beggs QC, counsel for Mr Duckenfield, Kirton accepted that the police commander did not identify a specific gate at that time. Kirton told the jury that it was not until the evening press conference that “it became apparent” a gate had not been forced, though he was earlier aware that some fans believed the gate had been opened by the police. He also recounted a discussion with Mr Mackrell at about 14:40 GMT regarding the possibility of delaying kick-off, saying Mackrell told him there were still many fans outside—his recollection was “around 20,000,” a figure he found high for that time. Kirton said he asked whether the police were likely to request a delay, and was told they did not like to do so because of potential problems dispersing spectators after the final whistle. Jonathan Laidlaw QC, representing the FA, questioned Kirton about a former police inspector’s claim that the ground was a “death trap” and that the FA was playing “Russian roulette” with fans’ lives. Kirton rejected that characterisation, saying he could not think anyone would have regarded the stadium as a death trap and that he saw no justification for suggesting the FA risked supporter safety. The inquests in Warrington continue on Thursday.

Uber is facing a landmark legal challenge in the UK over the employment status and working conditions of its drivers, brought by law firm Leigh Day on behalf of the GMB union. The case argues that Uber does not currently ensure its drivers are paid at least the minimum wage or receive paid holiday, and that the company denies drivers rights normally afforded to employees by classifying them as “partners.” Uber operates a car hire smartphone app that connects passengers to drivers and covers London and more than 300 cities worldwide. Using the app, passengers can request to be picked up from any location within those areas. Passengers pay Uber for the journey, and the company then passes on a percentage of that payment to the driver. Leigh Day’s lawyers claim that Uber’s contract terms breach UK employment law and that the firm’s practices raise serious health and safety concerns. They allege Uber does not ensure its drivers take rest breaks or adhere to a maximum number of hours per week. The lawyers argue this creates a substantial risk to all road users, particularly given that, according to Uber’s chief executive, there will be 42,000 Uber drivers in London in 2016. The law firm added there had been reports of drivers being suspended or deactivated by Uber after making complaints about unlawful treatment, without being given any opportunity to challenge the claims. Leigh Day says the law requires that workers should not be denied the right to work for raising such issues, and that any retaliation for bringing concerns forward would be unlawful. If successful, the legal action could result in substantial payouts for drivers, including compensation for past failures by the company to make appropriate payments to what the lawyers argue are Uber’s workers. Nigel Mackay, a lawyer in the employment team at Leigh Day, said: “Uber not only pays the drivers but it also effectively controls how much passengers are charged and requires drivers to follow particular routes. As well as this, it uses a ratings system to assess drivers’ performance. We believe that it’s clear from the way Uber operates that it owes the same responsibilities towards its drivers as any other employer does to its workers. In particular, its drivers should not be denied the right to minimum wage and paid leave.” The case is the first of its kind to be brought against the San Francisco-based firm in the UK, although Uber has faced legal action elsewhere around the world. Last week, taxi drivers in Toronto, Canada’s largest city, initiated legal proceedings against Uber. They are seeking C$400 million (£198 million) in damages and an injunction to stop the taxi-booking app from operating in the province of Ontario. The action alleges that services such as UberX and UberXL have created an “enormous marketplace” for illegal transportation in the city. In London, taxi drivers have staged a number of protests over Uber’s operations and last month launched a campaign to highlight their struggle with the company. Meanwhile, France has seen riots in response to UberPop, a subsidiary of Uber that allows unlicensed and untrained drivers to offer journeys to potential customers in their own cars.

Claire Hatch, 27, from Southampton, was on the gravity swing at Hangloose Adventures while she was on holiday in Cornwall. She said: "It was only me being yanked backwards that saved me from being very seriously hurt, or worse." A woman from Southampton has described a “terrifying” incident on a giant swing at Hangloose Adventures, based at the Eden Project in Cornwall, in which a rope reportedly wrapped around her neck. Claire Hatch, 27, was two days into her holiday and riding the Gravity swing with her nine-year-old son when a rope used to start the swing was left dangling, her partner said. Richard Dawkins, 47, who filmed the incident, said the rope “wrapped around her throat,” adding: “It could have been fatal. We just want to know that everything has been done to prevent it happening again.” Ms Hatch was treated for a rope burn at the Royal Cornwall Hospital near Truro and released the same day. Posting on her Facebook page, she urged improvements: “I would really like to point out that the safety checks and on site medical facilities need to be better.” Hangloose Adventures Ltd apologised for “the distress caused to Claire Hatch as a result of the regrettable recent accident on Gravity the giant swing where she received a rope burn to her neck.” The company said that, following the incident, it has reviewed “the design of the swing’s release mechanism, our standard operating procedures and our staff training.” The Eden Project, which hosts the attraction but does not operate it, said the swing is run by a separate company and that it was “upset to learn about the accident.” It added that it was in contact with the operator. Ms Hatch said that being “yanked backwards” prevented more serious injury, and hopes measures now taken will ensure the incident is not repeated.

St Mirren claimed a deserved 3-1 win over Falkirk after a spirited fightback in Paisley, overturning an early setback and capitalising on a second-half red card to secure all three points. Falkirk struck first inside two minutes. Craig Samson parried a driven effort from Rory Loy, but Nathan Austin reacted quickest to sweep home the rebound from close range, giving the visitors a dream start. The Buddies regrouped and gradually wrestled control of the midfield, with Stephen McGinn prominent in breaking up play and setting a tempo that pushed Falkirk back. The hosts’ pressure told before the interval when Stelios Demetriou levelled with a crisp low drive, finding the bottom corner after St Mirren worked an opening down the right. Demetriou continued to be a lively outlet, and his pace and direct running caused problems for the Falkirk defence throughout. St Mirren made a perfect start to the second half, surging ahead within a minute of the restart. Cammy Smith pounced inside the area, capitalising on hesitant defending to turn the ball in and tilt the momentum firmly in the Buddies’ favour. Falkirk tried to respond with set-piece pressure, but Lee Miller’s header from the centre of the box flashed wide of the left post as their best chance went begging. The game pivoted decisively just past the hour when Aaron Muirhead was sent off for violent conduct following an elbow on Demetriou on the right wing. Reduced to ten men, Falkirk reshuffled, introducing Luca Gasparotto for Austin to shore up the back line. Gasparotto was soon booked for a heavy challenge as St Mirren pressed, while Myles Hippolyte’s frustration showed with a series of fouls that handed the hosts territory and free-kick opportunities. Gavin Reilly then made the points safe for St Mirren, finishing clinically to extend the lead and cap a well-worked move. The Buddies kept their foot on the gas, with Lewis Morgan testing the visitors’ goalkeeper from distance—one curling effort bound for the top-left corner was palmed away—while Jordan Kirkpatrick, on for John Sutton, fired just wide from outside the box. Ross Stewart replaced Reilly late on and was denied from close range as Falkirk scrambled to prevent further damage. Jack Baird also went close, sending a header over the bar from a corner. Falkirk continued to seek a lifeline via set pieces in the closing stages, with Miller earning free kicks in the attacking half. However, St Mirren’s back line, marshalled by Gary Irvine and the tireless McGinn, held firm. The Buddies managed the game efficiently, winning key fouls to slow play and maintaining control in midfield. Despite an Ian McShane handball adding brief intrigue, St Mirren saw out the match with few alarms. The result reflects St Mirren’s balance of resilience and ruthlessness after an early setback, while Falkirk’s bright start faded amid indiscipline and missed chances. With Demetriou influential, Smith sharp, and Reilly decisive, the Buddies’ 3-1 victory was fully merited.

A woman has been detained in connection with the death A woman has been detained in connection with the death of a young boy in Alva after police were called to concerns for the child’s welfare on Friday morning. Officers attended an address on Carnaughton Place at about 08:50, where the boy was found with what police described as a “significant” injury to his body. He was pronounced dead at the scene by the Scottish Ambulance Service. It is understood the detained woman, aged 32, is the child’s mother. A report has been prepared for the procurator fiscal. Police said another child, believed to be the boy’s sister, is safe and well. The family is said by neighbours to have moved into the area only recently. A number of streets remain cordoned off while inquiries continue into the full circumstances of the incident. Local police commander Chief Inspector Stephen Sneddon appealed for calm and cooperation, stressing there is no wider threat to the community. “This is a quiet area and I would emphasise that this is a very unusual incident which poses no risk to others,” Ch Insp Sneddon said. “Police officers will be carrying out various enquiries in the area and I would ask the public to continue to give us the full support they have shown so far, to allow us to conclude these investigations as soon as possible and allow the area to return to normal.” Floral tributes have been laid along with teddy bears outside the house, and a number of candles have been lit by locals in remembrance of the boy. Anne Blair, who delivered flowers from the local bowling club, said: “I’m so sorry to hear about the youngster’s death. Why in this day and age? There is just no logic to it.” David Gibson, a local postal worker, said the boy had waved to him a few times during his deliveries. “People are flabbergasted,” he said, reflecting the shock felt across the tight-knit community. Police confirmed the Alva inquiry began only hours after an apparently unrelated incident in Falkirk, where a woman’s body was found, prompting a separate murder investigation. Forth Valley police commander Chief Superintendent Davie Flynn said both incidents are being treated as critical, but officers are not seeking anyone else in connection with either case at this time. “Officers today launched two significant investigations in Falkirk and Alva, which are being treated as critical incidents,” Ch Supt Flynn said. “I would like to stress that in both cases individuals have been detained by police and we are not looking for anyone else in connection with them. “I have been able to draw on resources from across Police Scotland to support our activity around these incidents. We work closely with our communities in the Forth Valley and will continue to provide reassurance to the public in Falkirk and Alva.” Ochil MSP Keith Brown expressed his condolences and urged residents to support officers as they work to establish what happened. “I am shocked and saddened to learn of this tragic event, and having represented the community of Alva for over 16 years, I know the community will share these feelings,” he said. “It is now important to allow the police and other emergency services to do their job and carry out a full investigation into the situation. I would encourage the local community to continue to support this process.” Police said inquiries are ongoing. No further details about the boy or the detained woman have been released.

Hull FC moved up to second in the Super League table after turning an early deficit into a commanding home victory over Widnes Vikings, with Albert Kelly crossing twice and Marc Sneyd orchestrating the attack in a clinical second-half surge. Widnes struck first inside four minutes when Aaron Heremaia sold a dummy to slice through the Hull defence and touch down, with Lloyd White adding the conversion. The visitors’ bright opening was swiftly extinguished as Hull hit back with precision. Sneyd’s pinpoint cross-field kick was plucked from the air by Mahe Fonua, who offloaded for Kelly to crash over. Fonua then dived in for his first try of the season following neat work from Kelly, ensuring the hosts turned around 14-6 ahead at the break. Hull seized total control shortly after the restart, piling on two tries in three minutes to break the contest open. Danny Houghton was first to react to a teasing Sneyd kick-through, grounding the ball to extend the advantage. Moments later, Mark Minichiello burst down the left edge and released Jamie Shaul to finish, with Sneyd on target from the tee to capitalise on the momentum. Two minutes later, Minichiello was held up just short, but Kelly showed his strength and guile to power over after a smart dummy, and Sneyd again nailed the conversion to cap a devastating spell. White crossed late for Widnes and converted his own try with eight minutes remaining, but it proved scant consolation for the visitors, who have now lost four of their opening five matches. While Widnes managed to contain Hull for spells, the hosts’ incisiveness with ball in hand and superior game management told as the contest wore on. The win lifts Hull level on points with leaders Castleford, who travel to Salford on Sunday, and represents a timely statement as Lee Radford’s side look to build early-season momentum. The head coach praised the composure and fluency of his team’s response after half-time. “First and foremost I’m pleased with the result. How we started the second half went a long way towards dictating the scoreline,” Radford said. “I’m pleased with the way we went about our business. There was some fluency in what we did, which I said would come. It sets us up nicely for the fixture next week. Wigan at Wigan is a tough fixture and it’s one we’re looking forward to.” Widnes boss Denis Betts lamented his side’s lapses. “We keep giving sides 18 points by rolling over in patches in the game. We are making it easy for sides,” he said. “We were up against a side running pretty hot with threats from all over the field, but I felt we handled them well for big patches. We went toe to toe with them in the first half, which shows we’re not far off, but then we hit a patch and look like a side that doesn’t know what it’s doing.”

Exeter Chiefs underlined their Premiership title credentials with a composed second-half display to see off Worcester Warriors, overcoming tricky conditions and a spirited showing from the visitors. Fresh from booking a European Champions Cup quarter-final spot, Rob Baxter’s side started with the confidence of a team in form, striking early and ultimately outscoring the Warriors three tries to none to secure a hard-earned win. The Chiefs opened with a flowing move that showcased their trademark width and precision. The ball was spun quickly to the left wing where James Short, enjoying a standout season, crossed for his eighth try of the campaign. Short’s influence continued as Exeter doubled their tally from a well-executed line-out. Breaking through the initial defensive screen, Short found scrum-half Will Chudley, who drew the last defender and sent Ian Whitten in to finish with ease. Despite Exeter’s early dominance, Worcester kept the scoreboard ticking through the reliable boot of Scotland fly-half Tom Heathcote. In difficult underfoot conditions that made attacking rhythm hard to sustain, Heathcote remained unflustered, landing four penalties before the interval to bring the Warriors level at 12-12 at half-time. His accuracy—five from six overall—ensured the visitors stayed in contention even as Exeter threatened with ball in hand. Heathcote nudged Worcester ahead briefly after the restart, but the Premiership’s leading try-scorers (34 in their first 10 games) reasserted control through their powerful pack. Number eight Thomas Waldrom, a constant menace around the fringes, powered over at the tail of a driving maul to swing momentum back Exeter’s way. Don Armand then added the decisive flourish, finishing wide on the right after beating two defenders with a strong hand-off to put daylight between the teams and end Worcester’s resistance. For Worcester, the result extended a troubling sequence to 11 straight defeats in all competitions, increasing the stakes ahead of next Sunday’s trip to relegation rivals London Irish, who sit four points below them. Yet director of rugby Dean Ryan was encouraged by aspects of his team’s display, as the Warriors matched Exeter’s structure for long stretches and showed resilience in the face of sustained pressure. “To be fair, they just saw things a little bit faster than us,” Ryan said. “Our general structure was about the same pace as theirs, but they had two or three players who could step things up and hurt us. We are pretty happy with the level we are playing at. We look like we are enjoying our rugby. The whole season is not defined next weekend. London Irish are at home and the pressure is on them. We’ve talked about how well we’ve played against Leicester, Exeter and Harlequins. We have to see if we can do something against a side who are not necessarily performing at those levels and see where we are.” Baxter acknowledged Worcester’s doggedness, stressing the importance of tempo and accuracy. “If you don’t get a lot of things right against Worcester, they stay in the fight,” he said. “When we got tempo and accuracy into the game, we looked good..... In the second half, things didn’t go to hand for them and their mistakes counted against them, and we were able to capitalise and gain some momentum.” Exeter’s mix of sharp finishing and forward power proved decisive, reinforcing their upward trajectory in the Premiership race.

England wing Jonny May faces an anxious wait after suffering a significant knee injury in Gloucester’s Premiership draw with Harlequins on Sunday. The 25-year-old limped off and will undergo surgery, with a clearer prognosis expected after he sees a specialist on Tuesday, according to Gloucester director of rugby David Humphreys. “It’s a huge blow for Jonny at this stage of the season, but knowing him he’ll leave no stone unturned in his recovery,” Humphreys said. The setback threatens May’s participation in England’s Six Nations campaign, which begins under head coach Eddie Jones against Scotland on 6 February. Jones has already been deprived of centre Henry Slade, back-row Dave Ewers and prop Kieran Brookes through injury, compounding selection challenges as he assembles his first squad. Gloucester have not provided a timeline for May’s return.

TPG and Fosun to acquire Cirque du Soleil; founder Guy Laliberté retains minority stake Cirque du Soleil has agreed to sell a controlling stake to U.S. private equity firm TPG Capital LP and China’s Fosun Capital Group, with founder Guy Laliberté retaining a minority interest. Quebec pension fund giant Caisse de Depot et Placement will also acquire a minority stake, the Montreal-based entertainment company said. “After 30 years building the Cirque du Soleil brand, we have now found the right partners in TPG, Fosun and the Caisse to take Cirque du Soleil forward to the next stage in its evolution as a company founded on the conviction that the arts and business, together, can contribute to making a better world,” Laliberté said in a statement. Founded in 1984, Cirque grew from a troupe of stilt-walkers and street performers — the Le Club des Talons Hauts (the High Heels Club) — created to mark the 450th anniversary of Jacques Cartier’s 1534 arrival in Canada. The company has since become a global phenomenon, staging performances for more than 160 million people across 48 countries. It operates 18 shows worldwide, a mix of touring productions and long-running residencies in Las Vegas, and generates roughly $1 billion (£600 million) in annual revenue. Cirque employs about 5,000 people and is renowned for its blend of acrobatics, avant‐garde costumes and choreography. The new ownership is expected to accelerate expansion, particularly in China, where Cirque has sought to grow its presence. The company’s rapid rise has not been without setbacks: efforts to broaden operations led to layoffs in 2012, and in 2013 U.S. regulators fined the company after an acrobat died during a live Las Vegas performance. Fosun Capital Group is owned by Chinese conglomerate Fosun International Ltd. Terms were not disclosed.

Queens of the Stone Age have paused work on their next album, with bassist Michael “Mikey Shoes” Shuman confirming the band is taking a break after an intense period of activity. Speaking to Gigwise, Shuman said that while the group had been eager to dive into a follow-up, they decided stepping back was the right move for now. “We were eager because we were in a good spot, having fun and the record had done really well,” he explained. “But we decided to take a break because we had been going so hard for so long, and we really worked on that record for a long time.” The decision comes after frontman Josh Homme suggested last year that new songs were ready and that the band hoped to hit the studio as soon as possible. Fans will remember there was a six-year gap between 2007’s Era Vulgaris and the band’s 2013 comeback,...Like Clockwork. Shuman stressed that the current pause isn’t about internal strife but about pacing. “It’s not like we’re sick of each other and don’t want to do it,” he said. “It’s just better to step back for a second and come back once the world has had a little bit of a break from you.” He also reassured fans that fresh Queens of the Stone Age material is still on the horizon. “There will be future stuff with Queens, we’re just taking a break since we had a long, long two years of touring. We’ll take a break to do other stuff.” For Shuman, that “other stuff” is Mini Mansions, the trio he co-founded, which becomes his immediate focus. Mini Mansions have been touring with Royal Blood, and their new single, Vertigo, features Arctic Monkeys’ Alex Turner. “Mini Mansions is my focus right now,” Shuman said. “I think music and working with different people is the kind of process where you gain things along the way. Whether it’s a big band, a small band, a different production or crew — you learn something from everybody, well I do.” He added that Queens of the Stone Age encourage that creative freedom. “It’s a very open family and everyone is free to do what they want and bring different aspects about what they do to the table.” Mini Mansions’ new album, The Great Pretenders, is out on Monday.

Almost 2,000 people will lose their jobs when Michelin and JTI Gallaher close within the next two years. Liam Neeson, who is originally from Ballymena, has lent his voice to the campaign. A message from the Hollywood actor was played to the crowd on a big screen on Saturday. He told them "this is the start of the fight back". Other speakers at the event asked for politicians at Stormont to take note that they want manufacturing jobs brought back to Ballymena. One 17-year-old told the crowd she had no option but to leave her home town in search of work. "Stormont aren't recognising us as a town worthy of investment," Shealyn Caulfield said. "They need to get off their backsides and put some energy and put some hope and life back into a town that we love so much. "We look towards our politicians and our leaders to care for us, but all they're doing right now is covering their tracks from the past and fighting about it and they're so engrossed in it." The rally was organised by the Unite union. The union's Irish regional secretary Jimmy Kelly said thousands of well-paid and well-organised jobs were being lost and that a community spirit had developed within the workforce at the two factories. "What we didn't want to do was this day next year talk about how terrible it is," he said. "Young activists here in Ballymena wanted to do something, wanted to fight back, wanted to declare to politicians that they've got to get the investment and build a future here." Last November, it was announced that the Michelin tyre factory in the town would close in 2018 with the loss of 860 jobs. It was the second major jobs blow to the town in just over a year. In October 2014, cigarette maker JTI Gallaher announced it would be shutting its plant in the town with the loss of 800 jobs. Redundancies there are expected to begin in May 2016 and the factory will shut down completely in 2017.

Hull KR chief Jamie Peacock makes shock playing comeback amid injury crisis Jamie Peacock is set for a remarkable return to the field after retiring at the end of last season, stepping back into playing duties to help injury-hit Hull KR. The 38-year-old, who ended his glittering career after helping Leeds Rhinos complete a historic treble, has been serving as head of rugby at the Lightstream Stadium. However, a mounting injury list has prompted the former England and Great Britain prop to lace up his boots again. “Although my family don’t quite understand it, this feels like the right decision,” Peacock told the club’s website. “The time has come for me to put my boots on again.
