Physically, it may take me some time to get back up to speed, but I’ve been preparing as best I can and mentally I’m in a good place.” Peacock, a multiple Super League, Challenge Cup and World Club Challenge winner and the 2003 Man of Steel, could make his comeback against London Broncos on Sunday. He will continue his off-field responsibilities alongside playing, as Hull KR fight to secure their Super League status. Rovers currently sit fourth in the Qualifiers, with only the top three guaranteed a place in next season’s top flight. “I understand my decision will be a big talking point but as far as I’m concerned I’m just focusing on training as hard as I can and getting back out there on the field as quickly as possible,” he said. “With the loss of three more players to injury against Leigh on Saturday and Maurice Blair returning home to Australia temporarily this week, we are now down to the bare bones in terms of the squad.” Peacock revealed salary cap constraints prevented late reinforcements before the deadline, leading the club to explore internal options. He had been registered with the RFL as a Hull KR player “in case of emergency,” paving the way for his dramatic return.

Francie Molloy, MP for Mid Ulster, said police visited his home on Saturday morning and warned of an "imminent threat to his life". On Saturday around 2am, police warned of an imminent threat to the life of Mid Ulster MP Francie Molloy, citing intelligence of a possible attack by a loyalist paramilitary organisation on him or his home. Molloy said he was surprised and concerned but affirmed his commitment to representing all sides of the community and insisted he would not be deterred. He suggested the threat may be linked to events in recent weeks. Sinn Féin colleague Mickey Brady, who has also received death threats, urged anyone with information to contact police so those seeking to drag society backwards can be brought to justice. Police are understood to be conducting inquiries and have advised security precautions. Local representatives condemned intimidation and called for calm, stressing the importance of democratic politics and the rule of law. No arrests have been reported.

Lafayette police said they responded to a call from the Grand Theatre at about 19:30 local time (01:30 GMT) after reports of shots fired during a screening of the film Trainwreck. The ambulance service told reporters two people were killed, including the gunman. Witnesses said the shooting began about 20 minutes into the movie. “We heard a loud pop we thought was a firecracker,” Katie Domingue told local newspaper The Advertiser, adding that the gunman, described as “an older white man,” fired about six shots. Lafayette is a city of about 120,000 people, located roughly 55 miles (90 km) southwest of Baton Rouge. Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal said he was on his way to the scene, tweeting: “Please say a prayer for the victims at Grand Theatre and their families.”

Former Anglo Irish Bank executives John Bowe and Willie McAteer have been jailed for their roles in a scheme that misled depositors, lenders and investors by artificially inflating the bank’s corporate deposits. McAteer was sentenced to three-and-a-half years in prison, while Bowe received a two-year term. Denis Casey, the former chief executive of Irish Life & Permanent, was sentenced to two years and nine months for his part in the conspiracy. The case centered on so-called circular transactions. In 2008, Anglo loaned €7.2bn (£6bn) to Irish Life & Permanent, which then placed the same sum back with Anglo. The transfers were recorded on Anglo’s year-end balance sheet as customer deposits rather than as an inter-bank loan, boosting a metric used by markets and consumers to gauge a bank’s health. Prosecutors described the accounting as a dishonest scheme intended to mislead anyone reading the accounts. Sentencing the men, the judge said the defendants had, “by means that could be termed dishonest, deceitful and corrupt,” manufactured €7.2bn in deposits through “obvious sham transactions.” The judge added: “The public is entitled to rely on the probity of blue chip firms. If we can’t rely on the probity of these banks we lose all hope or trust in institutions.” Anglo Irish Bank was rescued by the Irish government in 2009. The bailout cost taxpayers about €30bn (£23bn).

Pupils create memorial magazine after fatal bus attack on Birmingham teenager Pupils from two Birmingham primary schools have created and sold a memorial magazine to help them process their grief following the fatal attack on Christina, who was assaulted on a bus on Hagley Road in March while travelling to Leasowes High School in Halesowen. Children at St Patrick’s Catholic Primary School in Ladywood and its sister school, St Edmund’s Catholic Primary School—where Christina had been a pupil—were encouraged to produce a publication celebrating “youth and children’s young experiences.” The project was designed to give classmates and younger pupils a constructive outlet for their sorrow. Lorraine Sergeant, a mentor at St Patrick’s, said the initiative helped children “channel their memories [of Christina] in a positive way.” She added: “Even though this was a very sad event, this was a way to show the children that it was not wrong to talk about someone who’s gone.” Ms Sergeant said the schools chose the magazine format because of the number of children affected by Christina’s murder, noting that it provided a gentle route into conversations about loss. “It has helped them come to terms with it—during any counselling with any children who have suffered a bereavement we encourage them to think about the cycle of life,” she said. Parents have been invited to refer their children for additional counselling sessions if needed. Alongside the magazine project, pupils at Christina’s former schools have paid tribute through fundraising and messages on social media. Sales of the magazine raised £95. At the request of Christina’s family, the money will fund an annual sports trophy recognising outstanding achievement. The award will be presented each July for 16 years—the number of years Christina lived—honouring her memory and love of sport while giving future pupils a lasting, positive legacy.

The Old City of Sanaa, a World Heritage site, was hit in a raid on Friday morning that killed five people, residents and medics said. Locals reported that the strike destroyed three houses in the oldest part of Yemen’s capital and marked the first direct hit on the historic district since a Saudi-led coalition began bombing Houthi rebels in late March. The coalition has denied responsibility. Brig Gen Ahmed al-Assiri, spokesperson for the Saudi-led forces, told AFP: “For sure we did not conduct any operation inside [the] city.” The strike comes amid intensifying battles across Yemen as coalition aircraft and allied forces target Houthi positions in an effort Riyadh says is aimed at restoring President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi to power and pushing back the Iran-aligned movement. Unesco Director-General Irina Bokova said she was “profoundly distressed” by the reported destruction and warned it would “only exacerbate the humanitarian situation.” “This heritage bears the soul of the Yemeni people, it is a symbol of a millennial history of knowledge and it belongs to all humankind,” she said, urging all parties to respect international conventions and protect Yemen’s cultural treasures. President Hadi fled to Saudi Arabia in March after being placed under effective house arrest by Houthi rebels who seized control of Sanaa. According to the UN, more than 2,200 people have been killed and about 10,000 injured since the coalition’s campaign began, with millions facing shortages of food, fuel, and medical supplies. The raid follows a pattern of damage to Yemen’s heritage: at the end of May, the ancient city of Marib was bombed, and a week earlier the National Museum in Dhamar—housing some 12,500 artefacts—was completely destroyed, Unesco said.

Abdul Hadi Arwani, 48, a cleric believed to be a critic of Syria’s President Bashar al-Assad, was found shot dead in his car in Wembley, London, on 7 April. Police charged Leslie Cooper, 36, from Brent, with murder on 14 April. A 61-year-old man initially held on suspicion of murder was arrested on terrorism offences. Scotland Yard said a woman was detained in Brent Wednesday as inquiries continue.

China busts fake jellyfish syndicates as tests find high aluminium levels Police in eastern China have dismantled syndicates producing and selling artificial jellyfish made from industrial chemicals, warning of serious health risks after tests showed aluminium levels up to eight times the national limit. Authorities estimate the groups earned more than 170,000 yuan (about £18,100; $26,100) in a year of production. Huzhou municipal police in Zhejiang province, which led the investigation, said the probe began with a small workshop run by a man identified as Mr Yuan, who was selling the fake product at a local farmer’s market. Mr Yuan directed detectives to a larger operation in Changzhou, Jiangsu province, run by a man identified as Mr Jia, whom he said had taught him how to manufacture the imitation jellyfish. Several suspects, including Mr Jia, were detained in late April; authorities made the case public late last week. According to an official release on Huzhou police’s WeChat account, Mr Yuan told investigators he produced the artificial jellyfish by mixing alginic acid, ammonium alum and calcium chloride anhydrous. Officers said laboratory checks found “excessive levels” of aluminium in the resulting product—up to 800mg per kilogram—exceeding China’s legal limit by a factor of eight. The food and drug safety branch of Huzhou police warned that chronic exposure to high aluminium levels could damage bones and nerves and impair memory, advising pregnant women, children and older adults to avoid consuming any suspect jellyfish products. Police urged consumers to purchase only from reputable vendors and to be alert to telltale signs of counterfeits. Jellyfish is widely regarded as a delicacy in China, especially along the southern and eastern coasts, where it is commonly sliced and served chilled as a salad with various dressings. It is prized for its texture and is often marketed as a source of collagen. Demand typically rises in the summer months, putting pressure on supplies. Local media, including Zhejiang’s Metropolitan Express, have reported on jellyfish aquaculture in the region. Fish farmers say it takes around 40 days to raise half a kilogram of jellyfish, with wholesale prices of about 30–40 yuan. By contrast, the cost of producing artificial jellyfish can be roughly half that amount and requires far less time, creating a strong incentive for fraud. Huzhou police issued guidance to help consumers distinguish fake from real. Artificial jellyfish tends to be tasteless, lacks any smell, is tough to tear and has a texture similar to sellotape. Genuine jellyfish typically has a fishy smell and is yellowish with natural color variations. The latest case follows earlier crackdowns. In November 2014, Huzhou police detained three people for selling fake jellyfish made from a similar chemical mixture. In October 2013, police in Hunan province dismantled another operation that produced an estimated 40 tonnes; the ringleader received a six-month jail sentence. Authorities say inspections will be stepped up as the investigation continues.

Drummonds Mill in Manningham was ravaged by fire on Thursday, forcing demolition after the building partially collapsed. The blaze, which began in the basement at 11:30 GMT, drew more than 100 firefighters as crews fought to contain the inferno and protect surrounding properties. West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue said investigators have been unable to determine the cause because demolition has limited access to key areas of the site. Crews remain on Lumb Lane, and the road will stay closed until Wednesday. Crews are still at Lumb Lane making the site safe. Martin Speed, Bradford district commander, said demolition is “very intricate” and must proceed step by step. “The two gable ends are still standing but could collapse, so it’s essential the area remains cordoned,” he added. Nearby homes were evacuated, with residents removed from about 100 properties on Lumb Lane, Manningham Lane and Grosvenor Road. Investigators plan to return once demolition is complete.

PC Richard Whitham, 36, was sentenced at Leeds Magistrates’ Court after being found guilty of two counts of common assault stemming from an off-duty incident in Sheffield on 22 February earlier this year. He was off duty at the time of the assaults. Whitham, of Woodfield Road, Sheffield, served at Moss Way Police Station in the city and was dismissed from South Yorkshire Police following his conviction. Det Supt Terry Mann, from the force’s professional standards department, said South Yorkshire Police treats those in its ranks suspected of wrongdoing in exactly the same way as any other member of the public, adding that such accountability is vital to restoring public confidence in the service.

Senior judges in Belfast have rejected an appeal by Barry McCarney, 35, against his convictions for the murder of toddler Millie Martin and related offences, ruling that his trial was fair and properly conducted. McCarney had challenged verdicts finding him guilty of killing the two-year-old, subjecting her to sexual assault, and inflicting grievous bodily harm. He also criticised the handling of “no case to answer” applications and alleged failures in the judge’s directions to the jury. Delivering the Court of Appeal’s decision on Friday, Lord Justice Higgins said: “We do not consider that any of the matters relied upon by the applicant rendered his trial for the murder of Millie Martin to have been unfair.” Sitting with Lord Justice Coghlin and Mr Justice Horner, he described the trial judge as “scrupulous” in ensuring fairness. The court noted that McCarney declined to give evidence in his own defence, unlike his co-accused, Millie’s mother, Rachael Martin. McCarney was ordered to serve a minimum 25 years as part of a life sentence imposed for Millie’s murder. The toddler died in December 2009 after being admitted to hospital in Enniskillen, County Fermanagh, with severe injuries, including fractured ribs, extensive bruising, and a burnt finger. McCarney, formerly of Trillick, County Tyrone, had begun a relationship with Rachael Martin and moved into the family home in Enniskillen months before Millie’s death. While McCarney was convicted of murder, no verdict was entered on a separate count of causing the death of a child. Rachael Martin was acquitted of charges alleging she allowed her daughter’s death and cruelty through wilful neglect. McCarney appeared by video-link from prison for Friday’s hearing as his appeal was dismissed. He is now expected to pursue a separate bid to have the length of his sentence reduced.

US lifts $100 cap on Cuban rum and cigars as Obama accelerates normalization The United States has lifted a longstanding $100 (£82) spending cap on Cuban rum and cigars, allowing most American visitors to bring home up to 100 cigars and several bottles of rum. The move, announced through an administrative order by President Barack Obama, marks another significant step in the effort to normalize relations with Cuba after 53 years of estrangement and enables the White House to implement changes without the approval of the Republican-controlled Congress. Officials and analysts say the decision is designed to cement commercial and cultural ties before Obama leaves office in January. Among the latest measures, the administration also scrapped a restriction that forced cargo ships to wait at least 180 days before docking at U.S. ports after visiting Cuba, a barrier that had long complicated logistics and limited trade flows between the countries. While a range of technical adjustments were included in the package, the rum and cigar changes are expected to deliver the biggest immediate benefit to Cuba’s economy. With premium cigars fetching high prices, Havana could see hundreds of millions of dollars in additional annual revenue as record numbers of U.S. travelers purchase more goods to take home. The easing comes amid a broader thaw that has seen diplomatic relations formally restored in July 2015 and direct commercial travel resuming between the two countries. Obama made a historic visit to Havana in March, underscoring his administration’s view that engagement is the best way to encourage change. “Challenges remain—and very real differences between our governments persist on issues of democracy and human rights—but I believe that engagement is the best way to address those differences and make progress on behalf of our interests and values,” the president said in a statement. More than 160,000 Americans visited Cuba in 2015, a figure that could double this year as travel options expand and restrictions ease. Recent crossings by sea and air have been described as emotional by many Cuban-Americans, reflecting the deep personal ties and long separations that have defined the diaspora’s experience. Despite the momentum, Cuba continues to press for a full end to the U.S. economic embargo. Its delegation plans to present a resolution at the United Nations General Assembly by month’s end, which is widely expected to win overwhelming support. Obama cannot lift the embargo without congressional action, but he has steadily weakened its impact through executive authority over the past two years, reshaping the bilateral landscape in ways that may prove difficult to reverse.

Two men rescued near Loch Muick amid blizzard; helicopter grounded Two men believed to be in their 30s were reported overdue after visiting Loch Muick in Aberdeenshire. Four mountain rescue teams—Braemar, Aberdeen, Tayside and Police Scotland—were deployed to the area, alongside a Coastguard helicopter. The aircraft was forced to return to its base in Inverness due to high winds and poor visibility amid driving snow, officials said. Rescuers described conditions on the ground as “challenging,” with visibility reduced to around 10 metres. The men were located at about 04:30 near Broad Cairn and are being walked to safety, according to Police Scotland. Inspector Matt Smith, leader of the Police Scotland Mountain Rescue Team, told BBC Scotland the pair were “probably not as well-equipped as they might have been,” adding: “It is full winter up there.” Braemar Mountain Rescue later posted on social media: “Overnight callout to rescue 2 males from near Broad Cairn. Incredible team effort in very challenging conditions..... Small reminder if heading out into the mountains, please be prepared and have the relevant skill base.” No injuries were immediately reported. Rescuers urged hillwalkers to check forecasts, carry winter gear and ensure they have the skills for severe conditions.

William Burns, 56, and Alexander Porter, 48, deny assaulting Russell Findlay to the danger of his life at his Glasgow home on 23 December 2015 by throwing sulphuric acid in his face. At the High Court in Glasgow, Burns took the witness stand and rejected the central allegation, insisting he did not throw acid at the journalist. He told jurors: “Mr Findlay is incapable of telling the truth about anything.” Burns admitted he went to Mr Findlay’s home posing as a postman, but said his intention was to “beat him up,” not to use a weapon or chemicals. He denied carrying a knife or a glass jar containing sulphuric acid, adding: “I’ve never used a knife. I’ve boxed all my life. I use my hands to fight.” At the time of the incident, Mr Findlay was the investigations editor at the Scottish Sun. Burns said he was angered by a phone call the night before, during which he claimed Mr Findlay threatened to show Burns’s wife a photograph of him with another woman. Burns testified that Mr Findlay wanted to speak to him about Darryl Fitch, who had lived next door to Burns 25 years earlier and was found murdered in the River Gryffe at Bridge of Weir. He told his defence counsel, Thomas Ross, that he refused to help and it was then Mr Findlay mentioned the photograph. Asked by Mr Ross if he had any intention of visiting Mr Findlay before that call, Burns replied: “No, no intention whatsoever.” He said he already knew what Mr Findlay looked like and had seen him driving in Glasgow’s West End, memorising his registration number because he was annoyed about an article the journalist had written about him. Burns told the court he went to the West End to look for Mr Findlay’s car and found it on the fourth street he walked along. Burns claimed that after he knocked and forced his way inside, he was attacked in the hallway by Mr Findlay and a “mystery man.” He said he was knocked unconscious by the unidentified man and stabbed under the chin by Mr Findlay, injuries that required four stitches. “The worst mistake I ever made was telling that man I was coming to his door,” he said. “I think they were waiting for me.” Mr Findlay earlier told the jury that Burns said, “Wee Jamie sends his regards” when asked who had sent him. Burns denied using those words, saying: “I came from Ferguslie Park — that’s not words I would use.” He further suggested that Mr Findlay may have put a corrosive substance on his own face. Burns also denied that Porter was his getaway driver. Both Burns and Porter were earlier cleared of attempting to murder Ross Sherlock, 35, who was shot outside St Helen’s Primary School in Bishopbriggs on 24 September 2015. The jury returned not-guilty verdicts on that separate allegation. The current trial, before judge Lord Matthews, continues. Prosecutors allege the pair targeted Mr Findlay at his home and threw sulphuric acid at him, causing life-endangering injuries. The defence contests the claims, and the jury has yet to reach a verdict.

Jocelyn Elliott, 76, was released over the weekend after three weeks in captivity in West Africa, while her husband Ken Elliott, 81, remains a hostage. The couple, long-time aid workers who have provided services in the northern Burkina Faso town of Djibo since the 1970s, were abducted by militants who reportedly said the kidnapping was intended to secure the release of imprisoned fighters. Mrs Elliott arrived in Burkina Faso’s capital, Ouagadougou, on Monday, where she met President Roch Marc Christian Kabore. “I really hope to be with my husband soon so that we can again go to Djibo and continue our work there,” she told journalists. Expressing relief at being reunited with her “Burkina family,” she thanked the governments of Niger, Burkina Faso and Australia for their efforts, but declined to give details about her captivity or the circumstances of her release. Officials said the aid worker was freed in neighbouring Niger after jihadists from al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) stated they did not want “to make women involved in the war.” Niger acted as a mediator to secure her release, according to authorities. The couple were kidnapped in Djibo, near Burkina Faso’s border with Mali, on the same day as a deadly attack on a hotel in Ouagadougou, an assault also claimed by AQIM. Burkina Faso’s Foreign Minister, Alpha Barry, told AFP that no ransom had been paid and no conditions were imposed for Mrs Elliott’s release. He said efforts to free Mr Elliott were continuing. In the wake of the abductions, local residents in Djibo launched a social media campaign calling for the couple’s release, highlighting the community’s deep appreciation for their decades of service and their hope for a swift reunion.

The European Union has pledged 17.4m euros to a planned single-lane cable bridge linking County Louth in the Republic of Ireland with County Down in Northern Ireland. The 660-metre crossing, which has secured planning permission from authorities on both sides of the border, could open by 2015 if schedules are met. Democratic Unionist Party leader Mr Robinson welcomed progress and insisted that available funding must back top-ranked infrastructure priorities. “We have money available for infrastructure projects and the case was made, very strongly, that these have to be to the infrastructure projects that come out at the top of the list and not what some people were able to choose that weren’t even on it,” he said. Mr Robinson also rejected allegations from South Down MP Margaret Ritchie, the former SDLP leader, who claimed he sought to divert money away from North-South infrastructure schemes towards community projects involving former loyalist paramilitaries. Earlier this week, Ms Ritchie told MPs that loyalist groups were “getting restless” and alleged Mr Robinson had raised the issue with the Irish government. “As far as the working class Protestant areas go, I do want to see them getting more funding because I do think they are getting a thoroughly bad deal at the present time and I will continue to argue for that, Margaret Ritchie or not,” Mr Robinson added. With planning approvals in place and EU support confirmed last month, the cross-border bridge has moved a step closer, promising a new link intended to boost regional connectivity and economic development.

Discussions between Northern Ireland’s main political parties continued on Thursday, but the prospect of a swift breakthrough remained uncertain as Sinn Féin warned of inadequate engagement while the DUP expressed optimism. Sinn Féin’s Conor Murphy said there was not the level of engagement needed to break the political stalemate at Stormont. “We are seriously concerned given the timeframe we are operating in, given the lack of visibility in terms of the deal that’s being negotiated between the DUP and the British government that time is fast running out on this process,” he said. “The ability to reach a conclusion to this is being greatly hampered by the approach of the British government.” The parties have until 29 June to reach agreement, a deadline set by Secretary of State James Brokenshire, who has warned that failure could lead to the reintroduction of direct rule from London. Offering an upbeat assessment, the DUP’s Simon Hamilton said his party remained focused on restoring devolution. “The DUP is able to multi-task and to represent the people of Northern Ireland, both in London and here in Belfast,” he said. “The DUP is focused on getting a good deal for the people of Northern Ireland, bringing stability to the United Kingdom as a whole and of course getting devolution up and running here in Northern Ireland.” Northern Ireland’s power-sharing institutions collapsed amid a bitter row between the DUP and Sinn Féin over a botched green energy scheme. The late deputy first minister, Martin McGuinness, resigned in protest, triggering a snap election and ushering in months of stop-start negotiations.

Bosnian Serbs Back Controversial 9 January Holiday in Defiance of Court Ban Bosnian Serb authorities say voters overwhelmingly backed keeping 9 January as a regional holiday in a referendum held Sunday, defying a ban by Bosnia and Herzegovina’s top court and prompting warnings of escalating political tension. With more than 70% of ballots counted, officials reported that 99.8% supported the holiday. About 1.2 million people were eligible to vote, and turnout was put at more than 56%. The Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, based in Sarajevo, had ruled that celebrating 9 January as a public holiday in Republika Srpska discriminates against Muslim Bosniaks and Catholic Croats and ordered the date to be changed. The court also suspended the referendum, declaring it illegal and unconstitutional. Despite the suspension, the vote proceeded across the mainly Serb entity, one of two that make up postwar Bosnia alongside the Bosniak-Croat Federation. Bosnian Serb President Milorad Dodik hailed the ballot as a historic moment, calling it the “day of Serb determination.” “I am proud of the people of Republika Srpska, of all those who came out and voted,” he said in the town of Pale. Dodik’s decision to press ahead has challenged the authority of the state judiciary and ignored pressure from the European Union, the international high representative, and Serbia. The 9 January date is deeply contentious. It marks the day in 1992 when Bosnian Serb leaders declared the creation of their own state within Bosnia, a step that helped ignite a war in which around 100,000 people were killed. It also coincides with an Orthodox Christian religious holiday, underscoring the court’s finding that it marginalizes non-Serbs. International High Representative Valentin Inzko condemned the referendum, telling the BBC it was “illegal and unconstitutional,” and stressing that Constitutional Court decisions are “final and binding.” The Office of the High Representative retains powers under the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement to remove officials who threaten the accord, though such measures have been used rarely in recent years. Bosniak leader Bakir Izetbegovic accused Dodik of “playing with fire,” while analysts warned that the vote has already strained Bosnia’s fragile interethnic relations and could undermine the credibility of international oversight. Some fear Dodik’s defiance could foreshadow a push for a broader secession referendum, a move that would directly test the postwar settlement. Bosnia remains divided along ethnic lines between Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation, with federal institutions meant to bridge the divide. By flouting the state court’s ruling, observers say, Republika Srpska’s leadership has put the country’s delicate peace framework under renewed pressure.

The winners are to lead the carnival parade on its way around the city from Potternewton Park on Monday. Charis Betts of Leicester was crowned Carnival Queen with Dreamcatcher, a striking costume she co-designed. Elroy Condor was named Carnival King for Flight of Fantasy, a half-bird, half-man ensemble created by his uncle, veteran designer Hughbon Condor. Hughbon, from Leeds, secured a fourth Carnival King title in six years and has designed more than 20 winning Queen costumes since 1979. Betts said Dreamcatcher draws on Native American influences and features LED lighting and a smoke machine for dramatic effect. Friday night’s competition featured five Kings and 11 Queens, showcasing craftsmanship and creativity at the heart of the event. The Leeds Caribbean-themed extravaganza was launched in 1967 by Arthur France after he became homesick for his native St Kitts and Nevis. Widely regarded as the oldest event of its kind in Europe, it is now in its 48th year. The three-day bank holiday celebration culminates with Monday’s parade through Chapeltown and Harehills, attracting crowds often estimated at around 150,000, led by the newly crowned King and Queen departing from Potternewton Park.

title: Media playback is not supported on this device The BBC and ITV have won the rights to broadcast rugby's Six Nations competition for the next six years. The Six Nations will remain on free-to-air television after the BBC and ITV secured a joint deal to broadcast the championship for the next six years, starting in 2016. The agreement guarantees widespread access to one of rugby’s marquee tournaments, a move warmly welcomed by leading commentators and fans alike. Under the arrangement, all of Wales’ home matches will be shown live on the BBC, alongside France and Scotland home fixtures. ITV will screen England, Ireland and Italy home games, creating a shared schedule designed to maximise audience reach across the UK and beyond. Welsh-language channel S4C confirmed that Six Nations games broadcast by the BBC will also be available in Welsh on S4C, with any additional rights subject to further negotiations. Former international and ITV Rugby World Cup commentator Miles Harrison Taylor hailed the decision as a major victory for the sport’s visibility and growth. “In terms of the importance to the game, it’s brilliant,” he said. “I think it’s often underestimated how important it is to be free-to-air so the whole nation can see it. In somewhere like Wales, where we need that stimulus, it really counts, because there is no question audiences suffer when you go over to Sky or BT.” The appetite for accessible coverage was underlined in 2015, when almost 10 million viewers tuned in to the dramatic finale of the Six Nations on the BBC. Taylor, who commentated on the 2003 Rugby World Cup final for ITV, expressed surprise at the level of cooperation between two traditional rivals. “I’m quite amazed,” he said. “In my day it was ‘never the twain shall meet’ and we were head-to-head for everything. The idea of cooperation was something that never came into it. In the last year you’ve already seen the precursor, with presenters crossing over to work on both ITV and the BBC—it seems a complete change of culture now.”

Paramilitary forces fired bullets and shotgun pellets as people protesting against Indian rule stormed polling stations near Srinagar on Sunday. Separatist leaders had called for a boycott of the vote in the Muslim-majority region, which has been at the centre of a decades-old territorial dispute between India and Pakistan. Reports said turnout was about 7%, the lowest in three decades, as violence and intimidation marred the by-election in Budgam district. Authorities said thousands of protesters charged into multiple polling centres, damaging and snatching voting machines. The state’s chief electoral officer, Shantmanu, told AFP that more than 200 incidents of violence were recorded, including petrol bomb attacks and a polling station set on fire. Clashes erupted when police and paramilitary troops moved in, first using tear gas and later opening fire, while protesters fought back by pelting stones. Polling had to be suspended in some places as voters largely stayed away. The disturbances followed days of heightened security. The Indian government deployed around 20,000 additional troops ahead of the vote and shut down internet services in an attempt to ensure a peaceful poll. On Monday, authorities tightened restrictions further, blocking roads with barricades and suspending some train services across the region. The Times of India reported two schools were set alight by unknown protesters. Kashmir remains a flashpoint between India and Pakistan, with both nations claiming it in full while administering different parts. India accuses Pakistan of backing separatist sentiment, a charge Islamabad denies. Tensions have escalated since July last year, when influential militant Burhan Wani was killed by Indian forces, triggering months of unrest. Rebel groups in Indian-administered Kashmir have long called for independence or union with Pakistan, rejecting local elections as illegitimate. Sunday’s poll was conducted to fill a parliamentary seat after a politician resigned, citing what he described as the “anti-people” agenda of the Indian government. Separatist leaders urged voters to boycott the by-election, and their call appeared to resonate amid widespread anger. Farooq Abdullah, a former chief minister and a candidate in the by-election, condemned the violence. “Elections should have been peaceful. This government has failed in giving a peaceful atmosphere for people to come and vote,” he told reporters. A separate by-election for another parliamentary seat is scheduled in Anantnag district on 12 April. Results for both contests are expected on 15 April, with authorities bracing for further unrest as political tensions persist.

Members of the GMB union voted strongly in favour of a new pensions deal at Diageo, but the agreement was rejected by Unite, leaving the outcome of a high-profile dispute uncertain across whisky sites in Scotland and other UK locations. The row centres on company plans to move staff away from a final salary pension scheme, a change that prompted both unions to back industrial action last month at facilities in Scotland, Northern Ireland and Cheshire. Following further talks with the drinks giant, a deal appeared to have been reached. GMB, which represents about 1,200 Diageo employees in Scotland, endorsed the proposal by almost three to one. Unite members, however, voted it down by 62% to 38%. Diageo, the world’s largest producer of Scotch whisky, said it was awaiting formal confirmation from Unite of its position, while the union has yet to comment publicly on its ballot outcome. It is understood Unite officials will meet workplace representatives at Diageo in the coming days to consider next steps. At the heart of the dispute are concerns over the sustainability and cost of Diageo’s final salary pension scheme. In a statement, the company said it is committed to providing competitive and sustainable pensions and noted that, over the past decade, it has invested an additional £1.1bn into the final salary scheme beyond normal employer contributions. With costs escalating, Diageo argues the scheme is no longer sustainable and has held extensive talks with UK employees since February on proposed changes. The GMB union’s Scotland organiser, Louise Gilmour, welcomed the vote in favour, saying members would retain a pension scheme that ranks among the very best in the UK private sector. She added that GMB would now sit down with Diageo to discuss the future and ensure members’ interests remain central to a hugely profitable global company vital to the Scottish economy. Diageo said the GMB, its majority union, had accepted the company proposal, while its minority union, Unite, had rejected it. The firm plans to engage with GMB and other employee forums to move forward. In Scotland, Diageo operates 29 distilleries and bottling plants at Leven in Fife and Shieldhall in Glasgow, producing brands including Johnnie Walker, Bells, Talisker and Dalwhinnie. Whether Unite’s decision leads to renewed strike action remains to be seen. Industrial action mandates secured last month remain in place, pending Unite’s deliberations, raising uncertainty for operations beyond Scotland too.

Victoria Azarenka says her participation at this year’s US Open is in doubt as she navigates an ongoing family situation following the birth of her son, Leo, in December. The Belarusian former world number one, 28, returned to the tour in June but separated from Leo’s father in July. In a statement, Azarenka said the pair are working “to resolve some of the legal processes,” and revealed that “the way things stand now is that the only way I can play in the US Open this year is if I leave Leo behind.” The US Open runs from 28 August to 10 September at Flushing Meadows. Azarenka, a two-time Australian Open champion in 2012 and 2013, reached the US Open final in those same years. She was knocked out in the fourth round at Wimbledon this season and withdrew from last week’s Cincinnati Open citing “a family matter.” “Like most working mothers I am faced with a difficult situation which may not allow me to return to work right away,” her statement continued. “Balancing childcare and a career is not easy for any parent, but it is a challenge I am willing to face and embrace. I want to support men and women everywhere who know it is OK to be a working mother – or father. No-one should ever have to decide between a child and their career, we are strong enough to do both.” Azarenka added she remains hopeful an agreement can be reached that would allow her to compete while ensuring Leo has “a consistent presence from both of his parents.” “I remain optimistic that in the coming days Leo’s father and I can put aside any differences and take steps in the right direction to more effectively work as a team and agree on an arrangement for all three of us to travel and for me to compete,” she said. Tournament organizers have not commented on her status.

Former Army officer Henry Worsley is set to embark on an 80-day, 1,100-mile trek across Antarctica in a bid to raise £100,000 for the Endeavour Fund, which supports injured and sick servicemen and women. The 55-year-old will travel solo and unsupported, pulling a sledge laden with food, a tent, and equipment, with no supply drops or assistance from dog teams. He plans to set off in November and expects to lose around two stone (12.7kg) during the challenge. “There is no black art to driving one ski in front of the other,” Worsley told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “What is driving me on is the money for these wounded soldiers.” Worsley will fly to Chile on Tuesday and from the country’s southernmost tip will travel to Union Glacier in early November, which will serve as his Antarctic logistics base. From there, he will continue to his start point at Gould Bay, the closest accessible location to Sir Ernest Shackleton’s intended start at Vahsel Bay on the edge of the Weddell Sea. Shackleton’s famed attempt to complete the first crossing of the Antarctic continent was thwarted in 1915 when his ship, Endurance, was trapped and crushed by pack ice, leaving the expedition stranded. Worsley’s journey pays tribute to that historic endeavor while aiming to achieve a modern feat of endurance and resilience. The Duke of Cambridge, patron of the challenge, presented Worsley with a replica of the flag given to Shackleton before his expedition. Worsley will carry it during the trek. “It’s a huge challenge, but there’s no better person than you,” the Duke said. “We’ll be thinking of you at Christmas.”

Chris and Colin Weir donate £1m to help create National Theatre of Scotland’s new Rockvilla HQ in Glasgow Chris and Colin Weir, the Ayrshire couple who won a £161m EuroMillions jackpot in 2011, have donated £1m to the National Theatre of Scotland (NTS) to support the transformation of a former warehouse at Speirs Wharf into a new headquarters and production hub. The contribution, described by NTS as a “major gift,” helped close the funding gap for the Rockvilla complex on the banks of the Forth and Clyde Canal and reduce the need for borrowing. Launched in October 2015, the public campaign for Rockvilla has attracted more than £3m in support from the Scottish government, Glasgow City Council and the Vacant and Derelict Land Fund, against total project costs of £6.5m. To date, the theatre has raised £5.1m, with fundraising continuing as staff move into the completed facility ahead of an official opening early next year. “It’s a great pleasure for us to support this next exciting chapter of the National Theatre of Scotland,” Mr and Mrs Weir said. “As well as becoming a beacon that will attract some of the world’s finest artists to come and make work here in Scotland, we are excited about the possibilities that Rockvilla will create for our young people and communities to engage in life-changing arts activity and to nurture theatre-making talent for generations to come.” An NTS spokeswoman said the organisation is “delighted to be part of an emerging cultural hub in this area of Glasgow.” Neighbouring institutions include Scottish Opera, the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland, Glasgow Sculpture Studios, The Glue Factory and Whisky Bond, consolidating Speirs Wharf as a creative quarter.

However, Kim Davis questioned on Monday whether licences without her signature would be valid. Rowan County clerk Kim Davis on Monday questioned whether marriage licences issued by her office without her signature would be valid, escalating a standoff in eastern Kentucky that began after the US Supreme Court legalised same-sex marriage in June. Davis, an elected Democrat, argues her Christian faith should exempt her from authorising licences to gay couples. "I don't want to have this conflict. I don't want to be in the spotlight. And I certainly don't want to be a whipping post," Ms Davis said. "I am no hero. I'm just a person that's been transformed by the grace of God, who wants to work, be with my family. I just want to serve my neighbours quietly without violating my conscience." Shortly after Davis addressed reporters, a deputy clerk issued a marriage licence to a lesbian couple without incident. Despite Davis’s claims, several Kentucky officials, including Governor Steve Beshear, said licences issued by her deputies are valid. Two federal courts and the US Supreme Court have ruled against Davis after she repeatedly refused to issue marriage licences following the June decision. Couples seeking licences have continued to receive them from deputy clerks. On 3 September, US District Judge David Bunning found Davis in contempt of court and ordered her jailed after she continued to defy court orders. The next day, several of her deputies began issuing licences. Bunning released Davis on 8 September after five days in jail on the condition that she not interfere with her deputies’ work. Upon her release, Davis was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters outside the Carter County Detention Center. Davis has become a heroine to many conservative Christians who believe marriage is only between a man and a woman, and her case has reverberated through the Republican presidential race. Former Arkansas governor Mike Huckabee and Texas senator Ted Cruz have championed her cause, casting the dispute as a fight over religious liberty. Because Davis is elected, she cannot be fired; she could be impeached by the Kentucky legislature, but it is not currently in session.

US firm Corning said its Antimicrobial Gorilla Glass contains ionic silver, a substance that has been used to fight germs for more than 100 years. The specialty glass-maker said the built-in protection against microbes would last for the lifetime of devices that use it, creating a new hygiene-focused option for phone, tablet, and other smart device makers. The company said the ionic silver embedded in the glass surface continuously inhibits the growth of algae, mold, mildew, fungi, and bacteria. Marketing materials note that “thousands of bacteria live on the average mobile device,” an assertion likely to resonate with consumers who are increasingly sensitive to cleanliness and sanitation. Corning’s move comes as hygiene has become a higher priority across consumer and professional environments. Bob O’Donnell, chief analyst at Technalysis Research, said the feature could carve out a narrow but meaningful niche. “This gives Corning an edge, even if it’s a bit of an odd edge,” he said. “There are clearly folks in the world who are very concerned about germs and carry antibacterial hand gel in their pockets. If vendors opt to pay extra for this glass I’m sure they will talk about its abilities. But it’s likely to be only a small niche of people for whom this would be the deciding factor when choosing between products.” Other companies, including CaseCrown and S-View, already sell anti-bacterial films that can be fitted to tablets and smartphones as an alternative. Unlike add-on films, Corning’s antimicrobial capability is built directly into the glass, which the company says avoids compromising clarity, touch sensitivity, or durability. Gorilla Glass is widely used by leading manufacturers including Apple, Amazon, LG, HTC, and Samsung, and has become one of the few publicly recognized brands in the glass industry. The line has generated more than $1bn (£610m) in annual sales, underscoring its importance to Corning’s business. Some investors have worried that rival GT Advanced Technologies could lure customers with sapphire glass, which promises greater scratch resistance. Corning believes the antimicrobial feature gives device makers an extra reason to stay loyal. “This innovation combines best-in-class antimicrobial function without compromising Gorilla Glass properties,” said James Steiner, Corning’s senior vice president. Health experts urge perspective. Prof Charles Gerba, a microbiologist at the University of Arizona, previously told the BBC that while touchscreens can harbor a wide range of microbes, they are not a major risk if devices are not shared. “If you are the only one using it, it’s only your germs,” he said. Corning said the new glass is ready for high-volume production and is being tested by several unnamed tech manufacturers. Beyond consumer electronics, the company plans to market the material to healthcare, hospitality, and transportation industries where shared surfaces and sanitation standards are top priorities.

A vehicle struck the 4.5m (14ft) bridge on Wootton Bassett Road shortly before 08:50 GMT, prompting closure of the A3102 while engineers worked to free it. British Transport Police said the driver was unhurt. Wiltshire Police advised the road would remain closed for a couple of hours. As a precaution, Network Rail imposed a 5mph speed limit on trains crossing the bridge. A spokeswoman later confirmed engineers had inspected the structure and found no damage, allowing services to return to normal. Motorists were advised to avoid the area until the road fully reopens later today.

South Wales Police have stepped up patrols at key locations across the region following deadly explosions in Brussels that are feared to have killed at least 31 people. Assistant Chief Constable Jon Stratford said the move is a precaution to protect the public and provide reassurance, stressing there is no specific intelligence pointing to a threat in Wales. “Our thoughts are with the people of Brussels following this morning’s horrific attacks,” ACC Stratford said. “As a precaution forces across Wales have increased policing presence at key locations, including transport hubs, to protect the public and provide reassurance. This is not in relation to any specific information or intelligence.” He added that the number of officers deployed will be regularly assessed and that the additional presence is part of wider reassurance measures. The UK’s national threat level from international terrorism remains at severe—meaning an attack is considered highly likely—where it has been since August 2014. Earlier, Prime Minister David Cameron said Britain faces “a very real terror threat” and announced increased patrols at ports, airports, Tube stations and major railway stations across the country to bolster security and public confidence.

Kareena Kapoor and Saif Ali Khan announced the birth of their son, Taimur Ali Khan Pataudi, on Tuesday, sharing the news in a signed statement. “We are very pleased to share with you all the wonderful news about the birth of our son: Taimur Ali Khan Pataudi, on the 20th of December 2016,” the couple said, confirming mother and baby are doing well. The Bollywood power couple, dubbed “Saifeena” by the paparazzi, married in Mumbai in 2012 after a five-year courtship. On Monday, ahead of the announcement, Khan reflected on the milestone in a press release: “To have a child now completes us. There is something about a baby that is kind of half mine and half of hers, so, it’s a nice feeling.” Congratulations poured in across social media from colleagues and fans, with filmmaker Karan Johar among the first to post his wishes. The arrival of Taimur has been greeted with particular excitement given the couple’s prominent film lineage. Khan, 46, is the son of the late Indian cricket captain Mansur Ali Khan Pataudi and veteran actress Sharmila Tagore. Kapoor, 36, hails from the storied Kapoor family, with her parents and grandparents among Bollywood’s most celebrated actors. This is Kapoor’s first child. Khan was previously married to actress Amrita Singh; they have two children who are now teenagers. Both actors are among Hindi cinema’s most recognizable stars. Khan has appeared in more than 40 films and won acclaim for his performance in Omkara, Vishal Bhardwaj’s adaptation of Shakespeare’s Othello. Kapoor has starred in nearly 50 films and won the Filmfare Award for Best Actress for her 2007 hit Jab We Met. The family’s announcement capped days of anticipation, with fans and industry peers welcoming Bollywood’s newest star kid.

Broadcaster Rani has been confirmed for the 13th series of BBC One’s Strictly Come Dancing, announcing the news on The One Show, where she previously worked as a roving reporter. Rani, 37, said joining the ballroom contest fulfils a family dream inspired by the original series, Come Dancing. “When my mum first came from India to the UK, she'd watch the original series of Strictly [which was called Come Dancing] and would dream of dancing and wearing those gorgeous dresses and now I'm able to realise her dream,” she said. “That makes me feel amazing. My mum devoted her life to me and my brother and it's great to be able to do things to make her proud.” Born and raised in Bradford, Rani studied at the University of Leeds and began her career with the BBC as a researcher before moving into presenting. Her credits include co-presenting Watchdog alongside Anne Robinson in 2009, hosting on BBC Asian Network, and fronting programmes across BBC, Sky, Channel 4 and Channel 5. Strictly’s new series will begin in September, with the full celebrity line-up continuing to be unveiled. Former The Wanted singer Jay McGuiness became the 10th contestant to be announced, revealing his participation live on BBC Radio 1 with Matt Edmondson. Rani and McGuiness join a roster that already includes Jeremy Vine, Ainsley Harriott, Kellie Bright, Georgia May Foote, Katie Derham, Carol Kirkwood, Peter Andre, Daniel O'Donnell and Anthony Ogogo.

Essex cruised to a 10-wicket victory over Gloucestershire as England captain Alastair Cook and opener Nick Browne polished off a modest target with authority at Chelmsford. Cook, who struck a composed 105 in the first innings, added an unbeaten 35 to guide the hosts to 94-0, while Browne led the way with a confident 55 not out, laced with nine fours. Browne, Essex’s leading Championship run-scorer last season, ended the match in fitting style by threading the winning boundary, having earlier been given a life when Ian Cockbain spilled a chance at point. The result capped a dominant performance across the match for Essex, who controlled proceedings from the outset and never loosened their grip. Cook hailed the perfect opening to the campaign and the depth within the squad as they embark on what he called a “new era” at the club. “It’s great to start the season well. We’d have gone into this game as favourites. That doesn’t always count for much, but to dominate all the days is a pleasing start,” Cook said. “It’s the start of a new era here and it’s a great way to start, to win by 10 wickets – but 15 more games to go. The slight difference for Essex now is that if we had to put out a second team, we’d manage to have a good bowling attack. Four or five bowlers who missed out in this game could easily come and fit in. Next week away from home at the favourites (Sussex) will be a good marker.” BBC Essex’s Nick Gledhill praised Browne’s assurance and highlighted Jack Taylor’s enterprising off-spin, which nearly saw Cook stumped. He noted Gloucestershire leaned heavily on Taylor and captain Gareth Roderick, while Essex’s balance suits early-season conditions. Essex head to Hove next, eyeing momentum against pre-season favourites Sussex.

Jay Emmanuel-Thomas has left Gillingham after a season-long loan from QPR was cut short. The 26-year-old striker scored 10 goals in 35 appearances for the Gills, but failed to find the net in six outings under new boss Ady Pennock, appointed on 4 January. The former Arsenal trainee is not eligible to play for QPR this season. His final appearance for Gillingham came in Saturday’s 2-1 defeat at Coventry, where the ex-Ipswich and Bristol City forward was substituted at half-time.

Floodwaters receded on Sunday but many villages were still inundated Floodwaters in Sri Lanka began to recede on Sunday after days of torrential rain, but vast swaths of the country remain submerged and cut off, with officials reporting at least 151 deaths and nearly 500,000 people displaced. Another 111 people are missing, authorities said, as military boats and helicopters ferried rescuers and supplies to stranded communities during a brief break in the weather. Correspondents say emergency crews are racing to deliver food, water, and medical aid to the worst-hit districts before another round of rain forecast for Monday. The Disaster Management Centre (DMC) warned that the situation could rapidly deteriorate again if river levels rise further. In Weyangala village in the southern Kalutara district, floodwaters still stand well above homes, shops, places of worship, and schools. The district is among the worst affected, with more than 50 fatalities reported. Roads are completely under water, forcing residents to rely on boat services to reach their homes or find supplies. Families with children were seen waiting for aid, as thousands remain displaced and cut off from basic services. The village also suffered a deadly mudslide that killed seven people, including six children. Water levels are slowly falling in parts of the country, but anxiety is high with more rain expected. At least five mudslides were reported across Kalutara district, and residents in the town of Baduraliya said it had been badly affected. “Water came to our house. It’s very bad for us because we can’t go to school, tuition classes, and we can’t go to the town. And many people face this situation. Many houses are flooded,” Devindi Dissanayake told Reuters. Sri Lanka’s Daily Mirror reported that a second Indian naval ship, INS Shardul, arrived in Colombo on Sunday carrying relief supplies and inflatable boats, following the arrival of INS Kirch on Saturday. The additional support bolsters ongoing military-led rescue and relief operations. The DMC issued evacuation notices to residents along the Kelani River, which flows through the capital, Colombo, where water levels were rising rapidly. The flooding is believed to be the worst since May 2003, when a similarly powerful southwest monsoon destroyed 10,000 homes and killed 250 people. Authorities urged vigilance as the country braces for potential new downpours.

The Football Association has charged both Queens Park Rangers and Fulham after clashes between staff and players marred their 1-1 draw at Loftus Road. At an independent hearing, both clubs admitted two breaches of FA rules for failing to ensure their players and officials conducted themselves in an orderly fashion. QPR coach Marc Bircham and Fulham medical manager Marco Cesarini were each fined £2,000 for misconduct. The incident escalated in the 91st minute when members of both benches and several players became involved in a confrontation. Referee Keith Stroud later booked Fulham’s Tom Cairney and Chris Martin, along with QPR defender Joel Lynch, following an off-the-ball incident in the 94th minute. The FA’s disciplinary process and fines conclude the matter for the individuals.

Sheridan Smith to Take Short Leave from West End’s Funny Girl; Understudy Natasha J Barnes Steps In Sheridan Smith will take between two and four weeks away from the West End production of Funny Girl at the Savoy Theatre, producers announced, citing the need for the 34-year-old star to receive “the rest and support she needs.” During her absence, the role of Fanny Brice will be played by understudy Natasha J Barnes, who has previously covered the part to strong audience reaction. “The entire team at Funny Girl is thinking of Sheridan, and know she is getting the rest and support she needs during this very difficult and stressful time,” the production said in a statement. “We will all miss her enormously and send her our love and best wishes — and we are looking forward to her return to the show in due course. Meanwhile, we are thrilled to support the wonderful Natasha J Barnes who will be taking on the role of Fanny Brice until Sheridan’s return.” Producers added that Barnes has received “high praise from audiences on the occasions that she has appeared.” On Wednesday, Barnes thanked audiences on Twitter for their support. Smith, who has earned rave reviews for her turn as Brice, has missed a small number of performances in recent weeks. She previously wrote on Twitter that she was “not strong enough” and apologized to audiences for the shows she had to miss; her account has since been made private. A two-time Olivier Award winner for Legally Blonde and Flare Path and appointed OBE last year, Smith has described playing Fanny Brice as her “dream role.” Funny Girl transferred to the Savoy Theatre in April following a sell-out run at the Menier Chocolate Factory, during which Smith withdrew from two performances after her father became unwell. Funny Girl is booking at the Savoy Theatre until 8 October. Producers said they look forward to welcoming Smith back to the production in due course.

Accused arson suspect Robert Seman Jr. died in an apparent suicide at the Mahoning County Courthouse on Monday, Sheriff Jerry Greene said. Seman, who was being escorted by two deputies following a status hearing ahead of his trial, was not in handcuffs at the time, according to Greene. Surveillance video reviewed by investigators showed no struggle before the incident, the sheriff said. Seman was charged in connection with a fatal March 2015 house fire in Youngstown that killed Corinne Gump and her grandparents, Bill and Judy Schmidt. Prosecutors alleged he set the blaze because the girl was expected to testify against him in a separate rape case, in which he was accused of molesting her. He had pleaded not guilty and was awaiting trial. “We watched the video, and it’s an apparent suicide,” Greene said, adding that investigators found nothing to suggest a confrontation before Seman’s death. Assistant Prosecutor Dawn Cantalamessa said Seman’s actions reflected the strength of the case. “I think it’s very telling,” she said. “He knew the evidence against him. Every witness we talked to in preparation for the case didn’t know why he wasn’t pleading guilty or asking for some sort of plea.” If you or someone you know is struggling, help is available. In the U.S., call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or seek local emergency support.

The actress was part of a series of adverts which showed images of breasts with visible evidence of cancer. A bold Scottish breast cancer awareness campaign has prompted a surge in women seeking medical advice, with 21,000 women visiting their GP in the three months after the initiative launched in September 2012. That compares with 14,000 consultations during the same period the previous year, indicating a significant uptick in women acting on concerns and seeking professional guidance. Fronted by an actress and using striking images that highlighted visible signs of breast cancer, the campaign carried the message that “lumps aren’t the only sign of breast cancer.” Its aim was to broaden public understanding of the disease beyond the most commonly known symptom and to encourage women to report any unusual changes. The adverts formed part of the Scottish government’s £30 million Detect Cancer Early drive, which targets a 25% increase in early cancer diagnosis across the country. “It is welcome news that women have responded to this campaign by going to their GPs to get any possible breast cancer symptoms checked out,” said James Jopling, Scotland director at Breakthrough Breast Cancer. “We know that early detection can save lives as the earlier a diagnosis is made, the better the chance of successful treatment. Breast cancer remains the most common cancer among women in Scotland with nearly 4,500 women diagnosed every year.” Health Secretary Alex Neil said the response shows the value of clear, accessible information. “The earlier a cancer is diagnosed the greater the chance it can be treated successfully and that is why it is so important that women know how to spot the signs of breast cancer early on,” he said. “These figures show that our bold breast cancer campaign has been effective in getting people talking about breast cancer, and in encouraging women to contact their GP if they are worried about changes in their breasts.” The figures were released as Mr Neil visited the Breast Clinic at the Western General Hospital in Edinburgh, where he met breast cancer survivor Angela Moran. Now 53, Moran was diagnosed at 46 and has been free of the disease for six years following chemotherapy and a mastectomy. “I remember sitting in the waiting room and worrying that I was wasting the doctor’s time,” she said. “However the doctor was very supportive and confirmed that there was indeed a lump and acted right away to get me referred.” Moran urged women to be vigilant. “I’m always amazed by the amount of women who don’t regularly check their breasts or go for mammograms. These simple steps could save your life. If you do find something that you’re worried about it is always best to face up to it—no matter how frightened you are.” NHS Scotland data show that between October and December 2012, 95.8% of patients began treatment within 62 days of an urgent referral with suspicion of cancer, underscoring progress in timely care alongside rising awareness and earlier presentation.

Departing US Ambassador to the United Nations Susan Rice used her final press appearance to sharply criticize Russia and China for vetoing three Security Council resolutions that would have increased pressure on Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. While calling the Council’s inaction on Syria “a moral and strategic disgrace that history will judge harshly,” Rice also described her UN post as “the best job I’ve ever had.” Rice is leaving the ambassadorship to become President Barack Obama’s national security adviser. To succeed her, Mr Obama has nominated Samantha Power, a Pulitzer Prize-winning author and former White House adviser, whose appointment must be confirmed by the US Senate. Rice said her tenure had been “a remarkable period,” but she regretted that more was not done to stem Syria’s bloodshed. Citing UN figures, Rice noted that more than 90,000 Syrians have been killed and millions displaced since the conflict began. On Wednesday, the UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights put the death toll even higher, at 100,191. The group said more than 36,000 of those killed were civilians, including more than 3,000 women and over 5,000 children under 16, and cautioned the true number of combatants could be twice what it had documented due to both sides’ secrecy in reporting casualties. Rice rejected suggestions that the failure to act was a US shortcoming. “I don’t know how in any circumstance one could ascribe that to a failure of US policy or US leadership,” she said, “when the vast majority of the council was ready and willing to move ahead.” Russia and China used their veto powers once in 2011 and twice in 2012 to prevent resolutions that condemned the violence, demanded an end to human rights violations by Syrian government forces, and threatened non-military sanctions. The Russians criticized the proposed measures as tantamount to taking sides in a civil war, and China backed the view that the texts risked deepening the conflict. Despite her sharp words on Syria, Rice said it was not inevitable that “complex and multifaceted” US relations with Russia should sour, noting that “on issues as important as Iran and North Korea, and many others, we have been able to find common ground.” Power’s nomination signals continuity on multilateral engagement as Washington weighs its next steps amid Syria’s grinding war and persistent Security Council divisions. Global stakes remain high.

Cheshire school leaders have warned parents against allowing children to play over-18 video games, citing concerns about exposure to extreme violence and adult themes. In a letter sent by the Nantwich Education Partnership to families at 16 schools across the county, headteachers named titles such as Grand Theft Auto and Call of Duty as inappropriate for younger players and cautioned that, in some cases, parents could be reported for neglect. The heads say that playing age-restricted games or accessing certain social media platforms can contribute to early sexualised behaviour and may leave children vulnerable to grooming for sexual exploitation. They urged families to adhere to age ratings and to take a more active role in monitoring online activity and gaming content. Mary Hennessy Jones, the headteacher who drafted the letter, said: “We are trying to help parents to keep their children as safe as possible in this digital era. It is so easy for children to end up in the wrong place and parents find it helpful to have some very clear guidelines.” The intervention comes amid wider national scrutiny of safeguarding responsibilities. Prime Minister David Cameron announced this month that adults in positions of responsibility could face prison sentences of up to five years if they fail to report allegations of neglect or abuse of children, reinforcing expectations around mandatory reporting. Housing Minister Gavin Barwell has signalled a shift in the government’s housing strategy, promising minimum tenancy standards and a larger push to build homes for rent as part of what he called a “change of tone” from previous Conservative policy. Speaking on the BBC’s Sunday Politics, Barwell said ministers would unveil a package of measures in a White Paper due on Tuesday, aimed at tackling spiralling costs for both renters and would-be buyers. Barwell said the government remained committed to expanding home ownership, insisting it had not given up on the aspiration that “everyone who works hard should be able to own a home of their own.” But he acknowledged that policies must also address the needs of the growing number of private renters—now estimated at about 4.3 million—who are struggling with affordability. The forthcoming proposals will focus on boosting investment in build-to-rent schemes and expanding the supply of affordable rental homes. Barwell defined “affordable rent” as at least 20% below prevailing market rates and said councils would be encouraged to take a more active role in delivering this type of housing. Ministers have already announced a ban on letting agents in England charging fees to tenants, and Barwell indicated the White Paper would set out plans for minimum tenancy terms to improve stability for renters. “Whether you’re trying to buy or you’re trying to rent, housing in this country has become less and less affordable because for 30 or 40 years governments have not built enough homes, and this White Paper is fundamentally trying to do something about that,” he said. Barwell admitted that the latest official figures showing the number of new affordable homes at a 24-year low were “embarrassing,” attributing the drop to the early stages of a new five-year programme. He also reaffirmed the government’s pledge to build one million new homes in England by 2020, while conceding that delivery was currently behind schedule. Addressing concerns over development on protected land, Barwell said the government would not alter existing green belt rules, which restrict building to “exceptional circumstances.” “This idea that we can only fix our broken housing market by taking huge swathes out of the green belt is not true,” he added. Labour criticised the plans as inadequate. Shadow housing secretary John Healey said: “Ministers continue to do next to nothing to help people who rent from a private landlord and have consistently blocked Labour’s attempts to change the law to control costs and give renters security.” The government’s White Paper is expected to detail timelines, funding mechanisms, and planning reforms designed to accelerate building and increase the mix of tenure across England.

British sprinter Jonnie Peacock stormed to Paralympic T44 100m gold in Rio, clocking 10.81 seconds. Speaking to Newsround, he said the victory felt “absolutely crazy” and “amazing,” adding: “Everything is possible. If you get yourself with the right team and keep your head in the game, you can achieve what you want to do.” Posted 11 September 2016. Watch the interview for more.

A major search operation is under way after a man fell into the River Tay shortly after 04:00 on Saturday. Multi-agency teams from Police Scotland, the coastguard, ambulance and fire services responded, with RNLI Broughty Ferry’s inshore lifeboat and a search-and-rescue helicopter assisting. The force’s dive and marine unit conducted targeted searches near Moncrieffe Island on Monday, as efforts to locate the missing man continued along stretches of the river. The Police Investigations and Review Commissioner (PIRC) has been instructed to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident and will submit its findings to the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS). A Police Scotland spokeswoman said it would be inappropriate to comment further while the watchdog’s inquiry is ongoing.

The islanders have gone to the Supreme Court to challenge a decision made by the House of Lords in 2008, which dashed hopes of a return home. Their legal team argues information about a feasibility study was not disclosed before the decision was made. The court reserved its judgement. Chagossian families were forced to leave the Indian Ocean archipelago in the 1960s and 1970s to make way for a United States Air Force base on Diego Garcia, the largest island in the group. An Immigration Order issued in 1971 barred anyone from returning, setting the stage for a decades-long legal struggle over the right to resettle the islands. Monday’s hearing marked the latest chapter in that fight. In 2000, the High Court ruled that Chagossians could return to 65 of the islands, though not to Diego Garcia. Four years later, the government used the royal prerogative—powers exercised by ministers in the Queen’s name—to effectively nullify that ruling. In 2007, the Court of Appeal overturned the government’s order and rejected arguments that the prerogative was immune from judicial scrutiny. However, in 2008 the government prevailed when the House of Lords ruled that the exiles could not return. At the Supreme Court, Edward Fitzgerald QC, leading the islanders’ legal team, told a panel of five justices that the Law Lords’ 2008 decision relied heavily on a 2002 feasibility study into resettlement. That study concluded that sustaining long-term habitation on the outer islands would be prohibitively expensive and that life there would be precarious. Fitzgerald argued it has since become clear that relevant materials were not disclosed, preventing a Chagossian leader from properly challenging the study’s findings. He said the non-disclosure amounted to a significant injustice in the earlier proceedings and provided grounds to reopen the case. “There has been a significant injustice in the earlier proceedings, whether or not there was bad faith,” he told the court. “And there is clearly no alternative remedy.” The Supreme Court reserved judgment to a later date. If the case is reopened, it could have far-reaching implications for the islanders and for how government decisions made under the royal prerogative are scrutinized, reviving hopes of a return to their homeland after more than half a century in exile.

Former UK prime minister Tony Blair has urged governments to open education systems to a wider range of providers and ideas, including the possibility of for-profit operators, arguing that innovation and effectiveness should take precedence over ideology. Speaking at the Global Education and Skills Forum, Blair said many countries—particularly developing nations—could benefit from allowing diverse organizations to run schools, provided they can demonstrate results. “The public sector is not good at innovating,” he said, calling for more partnerships that encourage experimentation with different models of teaching and school management. “Nothing should stand in the way” of improving schools, he added, emphasizing that technology and new delivery methods must play a larger role in raising standards and widening access. Blair reflected on the political challenges of reform, recalling the pushback he encountered while in office. “When you first propose it, people tell you it’s a terrible thing. When you’re doing it, it’s hell, and after you’ve done it, you wish you’d done more of it,” he said. He described a persistent gap between general support for reform and resistance when changes affect individual communities. “You have major interests that often stand in the way of it,” he noted, urging current education ministers to “scour the world” for ideas that work and avoid the trap of assuming their challenges are unique. He did not rule out private sector involvement, including for-profit schools, if they can operate effectively and improve outcomes. The priority, he argued, should be delivering high-quality education at scale, not protecting institutional turf. “Governments always make the mistake of thinking their problems are unique,” he said, arguing that proven strategies from elsewhere can be adapted and adopted. Blair steered clear of commenting on US presidential candidate Donald Trump or UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, saying, “When I look at politics today, I am not terribly sure that I quite understand it.” He warned, however, about the rise of political populism feeding on widespread resentment and economic frustration. Debates over migration, he said, reflect concerns that “incomes are stagnating and they aren’t really getting anywhere in life.” The answer, he argued, is not to “blame migrants,” but to invest in “education and skills” that lead to better jobs, higher productivity, and greater opportunity.

UK inflation holds at 2.6% as rail-fare measure rises to 3.6%, easing sterling effects but pressures persist UK consumer price inflation remained unchanged at 2.6% in July, according to latest figures, while the Retail Prices Index, used to set regulated rail fares, edged up to 3.6% from 3.5%. The divergence means commuters face higher fare increases even as headline inflation stabilises. The principal driver of higher prices over the past year has been the sharp fall in sterling following the Brexit referendum. The pound is down about 14% over the past year on a trade-weighted basis, making imports more expensive for firms and households. However, more than a year after the currency’s initial drop, imported goods are now not much pricier than they were a year ago, suggesting the peak impact of the depreciation is fading. Data from the Office for National Statistics show pipeline cost pressures continued to ease in July. Input prices paid by manufacturers rose 6% year-on-year, down from 10% in June. Prices charged at factory gates also moderated slightly to 3.2% from 3.3%. These trends point to a gradual cooling of external cost pressures filtering through the supply chain. CPI had fallen unexpectedly to 2.6% in June from 2.9% in May, and its stability in July may indicate that the worst of the imported inflation shock has passed. Even so, price rises have not disappeared. Food, clothing and household goods continue to climb, keeping pressure on family budgets. Household costs look set to increase further. Price comparison site uSwitch estimates energy suppliers will lift gas and electricity tariffs by 7% to 10% this year. The RPI-linked increase in regulated rail fares due next year will compound the squeeze on commuters. The Bank of England has warned that domestic forces could take over as the import shock wanes. “As the effect of rising import prices gradually diminishes, domestic inflationary pressures will gradually pick up,” Governor Mark Carney said in this month’s inflation report.
