Yael Selfin, chief economist at KPMG UK, said the weaker pound has squeezed company margins. “We have seen some of these costs passed on to consumers but there’s likely to be more in the pipeline,” she said. She added that higher oil prices, further sterling weakness against the euro and a still-resilient, if slower-growing, economy are likely to “encourage further rises to consumer prices.” KPMG expects inflation to average about 2.6% over the next two years. With wages unlikely to keep pace, households are set to become poorer in real terms.

The carmaker said it would withhold a portion of bonus payments for now, but could award them at a later date. Last year VW admitted to cheating on diesel emissions tests, with net losses for 2015 reaching €5.5bn. Chief executive Matthias Mueller apologised for the firm's actions. At a press conference, he acknowledged that the carmaker "disappointed many people who trusted Volkswagen". Mr Mueller has been promised a 2015 pay package of €4.76m, of which €880,000 has been postponed. Meanwhile former chief executive Martin Winterkorn, who resigned in the wake of the scandal, agreed to delay 30% of his variable pay but will still collect a total of €7.3m. Hans Dieter Posch will receive €5.2m for his previous work as chief finance officer, as well as fixed pay of €13.4m for his new role chairing Volkswagen's supervisory board. The German company has set aside €16.2bn to pay costs associated with the scandal, almost half of which is devoted to buying back or repairing diesel cars that possess the emissions cheating software. Mr Mueller said that the recall process would be the company's "most important task until the very last vehicle has been put in order". Earlier this week, Volkswagen said it was postponing a recall plan for tens of thousands of Passat models in Germany, while it waited for the repair process to be approved by regulators. The company has previously failed to win approval for a recall of its Golf models, as it struggles to fix 8.5 million vehicles in Europe alone.

Swiss pilot Yves “Jetman” Rossy has completed a series of spectacular flights over Japan’s Mount Fuji, piloting his self-designed jetpack with carbon-fibre wings and four jet engines. Rossy made nine passes above the iconic volcano, calling it “a perfect form..... a presence that you can feel on the ground and also in the air.” The pioneering aviator is renowned for high-profile adventures, including crossing the English Channel, flying over the Grand Canyon, and soaring above Rio de Janeiro. He has also flown in formation with jet aircraft and a vintage Spitfire. Rossy’s latest achievement highlights the continued evolution of personal aviation and his quest to expand the limits of human flight, combining precise engineering with daring skill over one of the world’s most recognizable natural landmarks.

Digital connectivity is set for a significant test in the Scottish Borders this weekend as organisers of the Tweedlove Bike Festival trial “TV white space” technology in Glentress Forest to power live streaming and on-site internet access for spectators and competitors. The ground-breaking pilot aims to deliver reliable wireless coverage across the thickly wooded, mountainous terrain during the festival’s flagship 80km Enduro event. About 600 mountain bikers and thousands of spectators are expected to descend on Glentress for the multi-day festival near Peebles. If the technology proves successful, organisers hope it will enable real-time broadcasts from deep within the forest and allow fans to follow racing action on their smartphones and tablets. Beyond the event, backers believe the trial could pave the way for improved communications services in rural areas across Scotland where mobile and broadband signals are currently limited. TV white space refers to unused frequencies in the spectrum allocated to broadcasting services. These gaps vary by region but can be harnessed by specially configured devices to carry data over longer distances and through obstacles that typically disrupt conventional signals. The Glentress trial is designed to stress-test the approach in a challenging environment of dense trees and steep hills, where network coverage is notoriously difficult to provide at scale. The initiative is led by Scottish Enterprise, the Mountain Bike Centre of Scotland—based at Glentress—and Microsoft, which has been piloting white space solutions in a variety of settings. Moira Forsyth of the Innovation Directorate at Scottish Enterprise described the technology as a major opportunity for local businesses and the wider tourism sector. “TV white space technology has the potential to provide a major boost for Scottish tourism,” she said. “Like many rural tourism businesses the majority of mountain biking locations have no or very poor connectivity—whether mobile or internet access. This lack of connectivity to stream live events also significantly limits the international viewing opportunities when Scotland hosts global events such as the Enduro World Series.” Danny Cowe, business development manager at the Mountain Bike Centre of Scotland, said poor connectivity can undermine the visitor experience by hindering social sharing and discovery of local services. “Beyond this they cannot use smart phones or other mobile devices in order to view or look and book with local businesses—for example local restaurants,” he noted. “We can see how this clever new technology could hugely improve both the spectator experience and improve their time at centres such as Glentress.” Microsoft’s Jim Beveridge, senior director of international technology policy, highlighted the versatility already demonstrated by white space pilots. “We’ve successfully trialled it in everything from lifeboats to businesses and now in sport,” he said. “It brings people together in a way that just wasn’t possible five years ago and it just might bring some of the superstars here this weekend direct to your mobile.” Local enterprise Dirt School sees immediate potential. Head coach Andy Barlow said the team is launching a coaching app and virtual training programmes. “It is vital that we are then able to connect with our students to provide feedback instantly,” he said. “TV White Space technology could enable us to do that at Glentress.” With spectators keen to share and stream their experiences, the trial’s success could mark a turning point for rural connectivity, offering new opportunities for tourism promotion, community engagement, and business growth far beyond the forest.

Two rival groups are planning to stage an amateur cycling event in Lincoln on the same day and over the same route next May, leaving riders uncertain over which to enter and prompting legal consultations. ITP Events, which has organised the Lincoln Grand Prix Sportive for the past five years, says it intends to continue with its established ride. A separate team behind the Lincoln Festival of Cycling is promoting a new Lincoln Sportive as part of a three-day weekend of activities. Both events are proposed for Saturday 14 May and would follow a course starting at Yarborough Leisure Centre and finishing in Castle Square. The clash has led to confusion among cyclists and concern within the local cycling community. Lawyers have been contacted in an effort to resolve questions around the staging and marketing of the overlapping events. Ian Pemrose of ITP Events said his company had built up the sportive over several years and would proceed under its existing trademark. “We’ve run five editions of the Lincoln Sportive. We created that event and we’re just carrying on with what we do under our trademark,” he said. “If you’d spent five years building up a business and then somebody said ‘actually I want to do that’, would you do that?” Dan Ellmore, organiser of the Lincoln Festival of Cycling, praised the city’s cycling scene but criticised the dispute. “It’s one of the best events I’ve ever seen,” he said. “Dragging the name through the mud like this doesn’t do anyone any good and is really a destructive and negative approach. If the ITP event goes ahead as planned on the 14th, we’ll move, however it seems a little crazy to me to move a three-day weekend.” Lincoln hosted the British Cycling National Road Championships in 2015, drawing thousands of spectators and cementing its reputation as a premier cycling destination. Organisers on both sides say they want a solution that preserves that momentum.

Cardiff Blues have appointed Jones to spearhead a revamped academy structure as part of a reshuffle following the departure of rugby general manager Billy Millard. A former director of rugby at Pontypridd, Jones has extensive experience working with college and youth sides in the Rhondda and will oversee pathway development as the region intensifies its focus on homegrown talent. Chief executive Richard Holland said the academy system must “maximise the potential from within” amid ongoing financial pressures. “Due to the ongoing financial challenges the business faces, we must put all our efforts into developing from within if we want to be competitive in the future,” he told the Blues’ website. “This fits into the Welsh Rugby Union’s strategy and there will be further investment into our realigned academy system to ensure we maximise the potential from within.” Jones has led the Coleg y Cymoedd rugby academy, which has produced 34 age-grade internationals over six years. He rose to prominence with brother Chris in the 1990s, steering Treorchy Zebras to third in Welsh club rugby’s top flight and qualification for European competition.

Kent piled up 575 against Sussex after resuming 310-3 at Canterbury. Darren Stevens fell for 63, but captain Sam Northeast and Alex Blake (61) added 127 for the fifth wicket to keep the hosts in control. Northeast top-scored with 190 before falling to Steve Magoffin, and wicketkeeper Callum Jackson chipped in 38 to push the total past 550. Sussex lost Harry Finch early in reply, but Chris Nash’s unbeaten 48 guided them to 69-1 at stumps. Northeast is six short of 1,000 Championship runs this season.

Nigerian refugee dies after street attack in Italy; suspect arrested on manslaughter charge A 36-year-old Nigerian refugee has died after a confrontation in the Adriatic town of Fermo, Italy, that began when his partner was subjected to racist abuse, authorities said. Police reported that an argument erupted on Tuesday evening after slurs were directed at the partner of Emmanuel Chidi Namdi. The dispute escalated and a traffic pole was pulled from the ground during the struggle. Namdi was taken to hospital in a coma and later died. A local man, identified as 35-year-old Amedeo Mancini, has been arrested on suspicion of racially aggravated manslaughter. Mancini, described by locals as a well-known “ultra” football fan, is being held in connection with the incident. His lawyer said his client “did not mean to kill” and claimed he had punched Namdi in self-defence. The exact sequence of events remains under investigation. Police believe the confrontation began when the attacker subjected Namdi’s partner, 24-year-old Chinyery, to racist chanting and allegedly grabbed her. What followed is unclear, but the clash turned violent and left Namdi fatally injured. Namdi and Chinyery had fled Nigeria after their families were killed in a 2015 attack on a church attributed to the jihadist group Boko Haram, Italian media reported. During their journey across the Mediterranean, the couple’s baby died. They arrived in Fermo in November and were taken in by a local Christian charity. In January, they held an unofficial wedding ceremony conducted by Father Vinicio Albanesi because they had lost their documents, according to Rai TV. Father Albanesi said local churches that assist migrants have recently been targeted by small bombs, adding to tensions in the area. News of Namdi’s death sparked widespread outrage. Prime Minister Matteo Renzi expressed his disgust on social media, using the hashtag Emmanuel. “The government today is in Fermo with Don Vinicio and the local institutions in memory of Emmanuel. Against hate, racism and violence,” he wrote. Interior Minister Angelino Alfano visited Fermo on Thursday, declaring that “the seed of racism had to be stopped before it could bear fruit” and saying, “The heart of Italy isn’t represented by those who carried out this murder.” He also announced that Chinyery has been granted refugee status. Authorities said the investigation was continuing.

Historic south coast pier retained by Noble Group after review Noble Group, owner since 1984 of the Grade II* listed pier, has withdrawn the landmark from sale, choosing to keep it within its long-term plans. The company put the 1,760ft (533.3m) attraction on the market in June 2011 and says last year’s marketing generated strong interest and several substantial offers, but a strategic rethink prompted the decision to retain the asset. The pier, home to funfair rides, two amusement arcades and several bars, has seen about £35m invested by its present owners. Noble Group did not clarify what is now being considered, but said the pier will form part of broader group plans. Construction of the pier began in 1891 at a cost of £27,000 and it opened in May 1899. Its long history includes wartime alterations—on War Office instruction in May 1940, part of the structure was dismantled to prevent potential use by invading forces—and several incidents of storm and fire damage. In 1973 a barge that broke free in severe weather struck the pier, and in February 2003 it suffered limited fire damage. One of the south coast’s best-known landmarks, the pier employs about 300 people at the height of the tourist season. Local businesses and visitors welcome the stability, while awaiting further details.

Neonatal intensive care for babies in north Wales will be centralised at Ysbyty Glan Clwyd, with the most complex cases transferred to Arrowe Park Hospital on the Wirral, following an independent review by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH). The decision, welcomed by Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, sets out a new model of care after years of debate over the best way to deliver specialist services. The RCPCH review examined options including making Wrexham Maelor Hospital the sole site for neonatal intensive care. However, it concluded that, in the short to medium term, the necessary investment and medical expertise to provide the highest level of care entirely within north Wales would not be available. As a result, babies requiring the most intensive support—estimated at around 36 each year—will be treated at Arrowe Park, while intensive care for north Wales will be concentrated at Glan Clwyd in Denbighshire. Currently, both Ysbyty Glan Clwyd and Wrexham Maelor provide specialist neonatal care at level 3. The announcement confirms a shift to a single centre within north Wales, alongside a pathway to Arrowe Park for the most complex cases. Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, the largest health organisation in Wales, said it will now develop the business case for a “sub regional neonatal intensive care centre,” detailing investment, staffing, and service configuration. The board had faced a sustained campaign from local people and opposition from Assembly Members across all four parties after its 2012 consultation, Healthcare in North Wales is Changing, proposed moving specialist intensive care across the border. In a statement welcoming the decision by First Minister Carwyn Jones, board chair Dr Peter Higson said: “It ends a period of uncertainty for our dedicated and committed staff, as well as local people.” The health board will set out next steps and timelines as the business case is prepared.

Tight races emerge across Merseyside as Conservatives eye Wirral gains Wirral West has emerged as one of the Conservatives’ most tantalising targets on Merseyside, a seat some in the party still view as rightfully theirs. Former Department for Work and Pensions minister Esther McVey was ousted there in 2015 after a bitter campaign, with Labour’s Margaret Greenwood taking the constituency on a wafer-thin majority of 417. That margin leaves the seat firmly within Conservative reach. The Tories have selected cushion magnate Tony Caldeira, who is buoyed by his recent performance in the city region metro mayor election, where he finished second with 20% of the vote. Neighbouring Wirral South is also in Conservative sights. Labour’s Alison McGovern won in 2015 with a majority just under 5,000, or 11%, and the Conservatives hope to close the gap with Wirral councillor Adam Sykes as their candidate. McGovern’s campaign benefits from a large local team, but the outcome may hinge on whether the Conservatives can mobilise enough door-knocking to shift votes. Elsewhere on Merseyside, Southport is shaping up as a genuine three-way contest. The seat, held by Liberal Democrat John Pugh since 2001, stayed Lib Dem in 2015 thanks largely to Pugh’s personal popularity while many of his colleagues elsewhere lost. With Pugh standing down, the Liberal Democrats have turned to Sefton councillor Sue McGuire. She faces a formidable challenge from Conservative Damien Moore, who finished second in 2015, while Labour also senses an opportunity. Across Liverpool, Knowsley and St Helens, Labour’s dominance remains pronounced, with some staggering majorities that are unlikely to be significantly dented. Liverpool Walton is guaranteed a new MP after Steve Rotheram stood down following his election as metro mayor. Labour’s replacement candidate, Dan Carden, has encountered opposition from some local Labour members concerned about his relative inexperience. Local businessman Terry May, a former Labour member, is standing against him. UKIP is contesting fewer seats across Merseyside this time and will not field a candidate in places such as Bootle, where party leader Paul Nuttall finished second in 2015. The Green Party is targeting Knowsley and St Helens, arguing that controversy over green space development is eroding Labour support and could open the door to stronger Green showings.

The Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy has urged the government to begin the next round of national security review planning “immediately,” warning that the economic and strategic consequences of Brexit could undermine the UK’s defence ambitions. In a report published on Tuesday, the cross-party committee criticised ministers for failing to set out contingency plans for a Leave vote in last year’s Strategic Defence and Security Review (SDSR), accusing them of “putting political interests ahead of national security.” The SDSR 2015 included a commitment to meet NATO’s 2% of GDP defence spending target for the rest of the decade. That pledge implied an annual real-terms rise of 0.5% above inflation in the Ministry of Defence budget, lifting spending from £34.3bn in 2015-16 to £38.1bn in 2019-20. The committee warns those projections are now in doubt amid a weaker economic outlook following the EU referendum. Citing analysis highlighted by the Institute for Fiscal Studies, the report notes that UK GDP could be reduced by between 2.1% and 3.5% in 2019 as a result of Brexit. After accounting for a lower net contribution to the EU, such a slowdown would still imply a hit to the public finances of between £20bn and £40bn in 2019-20, it says. “In that context, even if the new government were again to commit to spending at least 2% of GDP on defence, a stagnant or contracting UK economy might mean that the defence budget would be significantly reduced in real terms,” the committee concludes. The report warns that Brexit “could impact on the aspirations and capabilities set out in the National Security Strategy,” arguing that any economic contraction would “limit the ability of the armed forces to fulfil their role effectively.” It adds that the National Security Strategy (NSS) and SDSR 2015 should have addressed the immediate steps required in the event of a Brexit vote. “The failure to outline a plan to address that contingency indicates the prioritisation of political interests above national security,” it says. “If the National Security Strategy is to be credible, it must prioritise the maintenance of national security above political expediency.” Beyond the domestic fiscal implications, the committee highlights a shifting regional security landscape. It says the European Union is facing “significant security challenges,” including large-scale migration and an emerging domestic terrorist threat. “These challenges also have implications for the UK, regardless of whether it is a member of the EU,” the report says. “A new security review must address how the UK will engage with these issues from outside the EU.” On force levels, the government has pledged to maintain the regular Army at 82,000 personnel and to increase the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force by a total of 700 regulars. However, the committee argues that “the manpower fielded by the UK armed forces is inadequate bearing in mind the range, complexity and potential concurrency of tasks expected of them.” It also cautions that planned reductions in Ministry of Defence civilian staff could undermine the effective use of new, state-of-the-art equipment promised in the NSS and SDSR 2015. Calling for review planning to start at once, the committee says the government must reassess the assumptions underpinning the current strategy and set out a clear plan for sustaining capabilities under tighter fiscal conditions, while redefining how the UK will tackle shared security challenges from outside the EU.

Four men and two women were arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of destroying or damaging Stonehenge after a group set grass alight inside the stone circle. English Heritage said 14 people entered the monument and doused the turf with paraffin, in what is believed to be a protest against an alcohol ban and new parking charges for the Summer Solstice. “How can people who claim to honour the stones deliberately disrespect and damage them like this?” said Kate Davies, Stonehenge’s general manager.

Saudi Prince Alwaleed Pledges Personal Fortune to Global Philanthropy, Cites Gates Foundation as Inspiration Saudi billionaire Prince Alwaleed bin Talal, a 60-year-old nephew of King Salman and one of the world’s richest people, has pledged to donate his personal wealth to philanthropy, unveiling a long-term plan to support global causes from disaster relief to women’s empowerment. The funds will be channeled through Alwaleed Philanthropies, the prince’s charitable organization, to which he has already contributed $3.5bn. Announcing the decision during Ramadan, when Muslims are encouraged to give to those in need, Prince Alwaleed said the initiative was inspired by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, founded in 1997. “This is very much separate from my ownership in Kingdom Holding,” he said, emphasizing that the commitment involves his personal wealth and will be executed over several years. “Philanthropy is a personal responsibility, which I embarked upon more than three decades ago and is an intrinsic part of my Islamic faith.” He said the gift aims to “help build bridges to foster cultural understanding, develop communities, empower women, enable youth, provide vital disaster relief and create a more tolerant and accepting world.” A board of trustees led by the prince will oversee the disbursement. Bill Gates welcomed the announcement, calling it “an inspiration to all of us working in philanthropy around the world.” Prince Alwaleed ranks 34th on Forbes’ list of the world’s richest people. Though he holds no official government position, he chairs Kingdom Holding Company, an investment firm with stakes in hotel brands Four Seasons, Fairmont and Raffles, and in major corporations including News Corp, Citigroup, Twitter and Apple. He said he hopes the donation will catalyze partnerships and measurable impact across regions and sectors in the years ahead.

Four young people have died following a collision involving a quad bike and a car on the A6201 between Upton and Hemsworth in West Yorkshire early on Sunday, police have confirmed. The victims, named in reports as Terrie Kirby, and friends Alexandra Binns, 18, Ryan Beal, 20, and Brandon Brown, 20, were riding the quad bike when it was involved in the crash. Three were pronounced dead at the scene; one of the men later died in hospital from his injuries. West Yorkshire Police said the quad bike was unregistered and believe a Nissan car travelling towards Hemsworth collided with it on the A6201. At a press conference, Det Ch Insp Richard Homes stated the car was seen parked on the bypass prior to the incident. Two men who were in the car were questioned about the crash and have been bailed as inquiries continue. The force has appealed for witnesses and dashcam footage to help establish the full circumstances of the collision. The tragedy has prompted an outpouring of grief from friends and family on social media, with one contributor saying Terrie died on her birthday. Ashleigh Lynch wrote on Facebook: “I don’t actually know what to do with myself. Absolutely wounded, my heart’s actually melting. Why does it have to [be] the best ones? My best friend out of it all. And on her 16th birthday. You’re my angel. My beautiful Alexandra, Beal..... and Drea will show you how to have a good time.” Jeorgia Lynch added: “Can’t believe it, doesn’t seem true. Going to miss you Ryan Beal, Terrie Lynch. Fly high, don’t party too hard up there, beautiful angels. Love you Alexandra Binns..... too young, taken too soon.” Ray Henshaw, principal of Minsthorpe Community College, said the deaths were “devastating.” He confirmed Terrie Kirkby was a current pupil, and that both Alexander Binns and Ryan Beal had previously attended the college. “We are trying to help our young people come to terms with it, the understandable grief and loss,” he said. “The sense of devastation is [because of] the age of these young people, the tragic loss and the fact they had so much of their lives left ahead of them.” A statement from glazing firm Safestyle, where Ryan Beal worked as a fitter, said staff were in mourning. “We are deeply saddened and shocked by the news. Our heartfelt condolences go out to the family and friends of Ryan,” the company said. The A6201 remains closed as collision investigators work at the scene, with rush-hour traffic diverted and delays expected in the area.

Keshi demands payment and defamation damages from NFF after July dismissal Former Nigeria coach Stephen Keshi has formally demanded payment of outstanding entitlements and damages for defamation from the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) following his early-July dismissal, which saw him replaced by Sunday Oliseh. In a letter sent through his lawyers, Keshi alleges the federation’s disciplinary process tarnished his name and seeks compensation. Senior NFF officials say the claim lacks substance and are confident the body will not be compelled to pay. BBC Sport understands Keshi is anxious to safeguard his reputation and standing within football circles after the NFF disciplinary committee made a series of allegations against him. He has yet to file a suit in court, signalling a preference to resolve the matter amicably if possible. The dispute makes Keshi the second former Nigeria coach in five years to challenge his dismissal. His predecessor Samson Siasia launched legal action in October 2011 but later withdrew the case, saying he wanted to move on. Keshi, a former Super Eagles captain, enjoyed a decorated tenure as national team manager. He led Nigeria to the 2013 Africa Cup of Nations title in South Africa and guided the team to the Round of 16 at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil. Despite those achievements, his contract was not renewed after the World Cup. He returned on a match-by-match basis, a short-term arrangement that ended in November after Nigeria failed to qualify for the 2015 Nations Cup. As caretaker coach, Keshi endured a turbulent 2014, at one point being sacked by the NFF before being reinstated following intervention from then President Goodluck Jonathan. He came back for a third spell in April, overseeing a 2-0 home win over Chad in a 2017 Africa Cup of Nations qualifier in June, but was dismissed less than three months into a two-year deal.

Highgate United has renamed a stand in honour of defender Tony Allden, who died after being struck by lightning during an FA Amateur Cup quarter-final in 1967. The Tony Allden Stand was unveiled at 14:00 GMT at the club’s ground, marking a poignant tribute to the 23-year-old, who had recently married before the tragedy. Allden collapsed when a bolt of lightning hit the pitch on 25 February 1967. The match against Enfield was halted in the 28th minute with the visitors leading 1-0. Team-mate Roy Taylor recalled: “The chances of it happening must be millions to one..... [there was] just a flash and a lot of the players went down like a pack of cards.” Taylor and his brother Eric, also a former Highgate player, were taken to hospital and treated for shock. More than 3,000 people attended the original tie involving the Solihull club. The rearranged match was staged at Villa Park before a crowd of 30,000, with all proceeds donated to Allden’s family. Enfield won the replay 6-0. Ken Barnett, who played football and cricket with Allden and was at the Highgate game, said: “Obviously I was heartbroken really because he was a good mate of mine and he didn’t deserve to have his life cut that short..... from a freak incident.”

Providing prisoners with access to education significantly reduces the risk of reoffending, according to new research commissioned by the Ministry of Justice. In a sample of 3,000 inmates who were able to study while in custody, 19% reoffended within a year of release, compared with 26% among a matched group of 3,000 who did not have study opportunities. Participation in distance learning emerged as the most effective single intervention, outperforming other voluntary and community sector initiatives examined in the broader review. The study covered a range of courses, from Open University degrees to vocational qualifications, many funded by the Prisoners’ Education Trust (PET). PET chief executive Rod Clark said the findings underline the value and cost-effectiveness of education behind bars. “Courses we fund typically cost £250 a piece,” he said, “which is a minor cost when set against the £37,648 annual cost of a prison place.” He added that expanding educational access is vital “if we want to stop people falling back into a life of crime when they leave,” and urged policymakers to scale up proven programmes.

The box tree caterpillar - the larva of a moth - is native to Asia and feeds on box plants, commonly used in formal gardens for hedges and shrubbery An invasive garden pest is rapidly spreading across south-east England, displacing slugs and snails for the first time in nearly a decade at the top of the Royal Horticultural Society’s most-unwanted list. The box tree caterpillar, the larval stage of the moth Diaphania perspectalis, was first detected in UK private gardens in 2011 after adult moths were reported in 2008. Since then, it has moved beyond its initial London stronghold, alarming gardeners and heritage institutions that rely on box (Buxus) to shape formal garden designs. The RHS says enquiries to its entomology team in 2015 reflect the surge in concern: the box tree caterpillar accounted for 433 queries, or 17% of all pest-related enquiries, placing it at number one. Slugs and snails, the perennial scourge of beds and borders, fell to second with 122 enquiries. Experts warn the “invasive bug” could continue to spread more widely in the UK if not actively managed. Native to Asia and believed to have originated in China, the moth is thought to have reached Britain either by flying across the English Channel or by hitching a ride among imported plants. Once established, it can devastate box plants. Females lay overlapping sheets of pale yellow eggs on the undersides of leaves. After hatching, the green-and-black striped larvae feed within protective webbing, spinning silken structures around leaves and twigs to conceal themselves. As they grow to around 4cm long, caterpillars can completely defoliate box shrubs, leaving brown, skeletonised foliage and weakened plants. The RHS advises several control measures, including physically removing caterpillars by hand where feasible, or deploying biological controls and approved insecticides to reduce populations. Early detection and regular inspection of box hedges and topiary are critical to limiting damage. Experts stress that the caterpillar is unrelated to box blight, a fungal disease that causes bare patches and dieback, where leaves die back from their tips. Nonetheless, 2025 has been challenging for box plants overall, with box blight among the most frequently reported garden diseases. High spring temperatures combined with rainfall created ideal conditions for fungal spread, leading to a spike in enquiries. The warmest, wettest December on record further fuelled unexpected disease activity that is normally suppressed by colder weather. Because box plants underpin the structure of many historic formal gardens, both the caterpillar and box blight pose a serious risk to the UK’s horticultural heritage. The RHS is urging vigilance, prompt treatment, and careful plant sourcing to slow the pest’s advance and protect cherished landscapes.

A 22-year-old man has been refused bail over alleged involvement in serious disorder surrounding a contentious Orange Order parade in north Belfast last month. Christopher Stitt, of Carrick Hill in the city, faces charges of riotous assembly, hijacking, and attempted grievous bodily harm with intent in connection with violence in the Ardoyne area. The court heard that twenty police officers were injured as petrol bombs, fireworks and other missiles were thrown by hundreds of people from both sides of the sectarian divide. Ten shots were also fired at police from a semi-automatic rifle during the clashes. Opposing the bail application, a prosecution barrister said Stitt was identified on CCTV footage of the disturbances and by a distinctive tattoo on his neck. He was allegedly seen throwing missiles at police lines and supplying others with crates of bottles used in attacks. According to the prosecution, Stitt filled some bottles with brown paint at the scene; paint marks were later said to have been found on his footwear following his arrest. The court was told that Stitt is alleged to have driven a hijacked Citroen Picasso up Brompton Park during the unrest. He then got out before another man allegedly attempted to use the vehicle to ram another car at police lines. It was further claimed that Stitt was linked to an attempt to shunt a burning vehicle into officers amid the violence. Stitt provided a prepared statement to police in which he accepted being the person identified by officers, but he denies involvement in the alleged offences, including the hijacking incident. His barrister argued that he should be released pending trial. However, Lord Justice Coghlin refused bail, citing the risk of further offending given the nature of the allegations and the ongoing tensions surrounding the marching season. The judge said a further bail application could be made once the marching season is over. Stitt remains in custody as the investigation continues. Police have appealed for information as they review extensive footage from the disorder.

The domestic cricket summer will begin earlier than usual, with the County Championship starting on 10 April as promoted Surrey travel to Trent Bridge to face Nottinghamshire. Yorkshire, the reigning champions, will actually kick off their year a fortnight sooner with a showcase fixture against the MCC in Abu Dhabi on 20 March. The broader structure of the season remains familiar: most Championship matches will start on Sundays, while the NatWest T20 Blast continues to anchor Friday evenings. However, one significant change arrives with the scrapping of the mandatory coin toss in both Championship divisions, handing the visiting captain the option to bowl first; if he declines, a traditional toss will be held. The opening round of Division One Championship fixtures also pits Durham, champions in 2008, 2009 and 2013, against Somerset, while Hampshire—who stayed up on the final day of 2015—meet Warwickshire. In Division Two, relegated Worcestershire host Kent at New Road and Sussex visit Northants, with Essex welcoming Gloucestershire to Chelmsford under a new head coach following Paul Grayson’s departure last September. The second round of Division One sees Yorkshire host Hampshire at Headingley and Lancashire begin their campaign against Nottinghamshire, who will have Australian fast bowler Peter Siddle available. The first Roses match of the summer between Yorkshire and Lancashire is set for Headingley on 29 May, with the reverse fixture starting at Old Trafford on 13 August. Lancashire, the reigning T20 Blast champions, open their title defence against Derbyshire on Saturday, 21 May, as the nine-team North and South group format is retained from 2015. Beaten finalists Northants will start away at three-time Twenty20 winners Leicestershire and will be without England all-rounder David Willey after his move to Yorkshire. The group stage’s final round of 14 matches lands on Friday, 29 July, with the quarter-finals scheduled for 8-11 August. Edgbaston hosts finals day for the eighth time on Saturday, 20 August, bringing the showpiece nine days earlier than last summer. The 50-over Royal London One-Day Cup will be staged across two compact windows to fit around the Championship, with group fixtures played from 5-15 June and again from 24 July to 2 August. The groups mirror the T20 Blast: Group A comprises Warwickshire, Durham, Yorkshire, Lancashire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Worcestershire and Northants; Group B features Kent, Essex, Sussex, Hampshire, Middlesex, Surrey, Gloucestershire, Somerset and Glamorgan. The Lord’s final, where Gloucestershire edged Surrey by six runs in 2015, will take place on Saturday, 17 September. The season’s climactic Championship round begins on 20 September, highlighted by Yorkshire’s visit to Middlesex—significant given Middlesex were the only side to beat Jason Gillespie’s team in first-class cricket last year. With an earlier start, a streamlined white-ball calendar, and the innovative toss reform aimed at encouraging fairer pitches and more positive cricket, the 2016 county season promises compelling storylines across red and white ball formats from spring through to the autumn finale at Lord’s and the Championship denouement.

On International Holocaust Day, marking 70 years since Auschwitz’s liberation, luthier Amnon Weinstein showcases “Violins of Hope,” a collection of restored violins and cellos played by Jewish musicians, including instruments from a prisoners’ orchestra at the death camp. Weinstein describes the painstaking work of bringing the instruments—and the memories they carry—back to life, honoring those silenced by the Shoah through music. The interview was recorded by Gidi Kleiman, with performances by Professor Tzvi Plesser of the Jerusalem Music Academy. Photographs by Noam Sharon, with additional images from AFP, AP, EPA, Getty, Yad Vashem, and Phil Coomes. A photofilm produced by Phil Coomes. The piece is best viewed full screen.

French authorities deployed about 2,000 riot police in Paris on Thursday to prevent a repeat of the violent clashes that marred a previous demonstration on 14 June. Before the march set off from the Place de la Bastille, police said they arrested roughly 100 people, most for wearing scarves or other items that could be used to conceal their identities. Interior Minister Bernard Cazeneuve said the march took place under “optimal conditions,” with no clashes or damage reported. “No teargas was fired..... no-one was injured,” he said. The demonstration had initially been banned, but ministers reversed the decision after a public outcry, allowing the protest to proceed. The rallies target government labour reforms designed to make it easier for employers to hire and fire workers and to relax limits on working hours. Despite months of unrest, President François Hollande has insisted the government will not retreat. “We will take this bill to the finish line,” he told reporters. Protests were also held in other cities. In Rennes, in western France, demonstrators torched a car, attacked police headquarters and smashed storefronts, according to the AFP news agency.

Gary Clampett, 39, died after a disturbance at Fernie Place in early hours of Sunday, 18 June. At Peterhead Sheriff Court, Barry Martin, 31, Gary Martin, 36, Joseph Martin, 39, Thomas Martin, 44, David Graham, 45, and John Henderson, 46, made no plea. All were charged with murder and two counts of attempted murder. Six were remanded in custody.

Former Indian Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and several co-accused have denied criminal conspiracy amid a probe into the allocation of coal blocks. They appealed to the Supreme Court against an order requiring them to appear on 8 April. The case stems from a 2012 federal audit that claimed India lost $33bn because coalfield rights were sold off cheaply. Mr Singh maintains his innocence and says he is open to legal scrutiny. Those accused alongside him include a former bureaucrat and a leading businessman. Though not formally charged, Mr Singh is being investigated for criminal conspiracy, criminal breach of trust, and corruption-related offences; a conviction could carry a life sentence, which observers deem unlikely. “There was no criminal intent—it was an administrative decision and not an illegality,” Mr Singh’s lawyer and former minister Kapil Sibal said on Wednesday. Last September, India’s Supreme Court cancelled nearly all of more than 200 licences awarded since 1993, calling them illegal and arbitrary. The Congress party was in power when most allocations were made, while the ruling BJP government has begun re-auctioning the coal licences, saying it aims to recover the true value of the reserves and improve transparency. The proceedings have reignited debate over accountability in resource allocation and the balance between policy discretion and criminal liability. The case continues to draw scrutiny from investors, industry and the public, with the outcome expected to influence future oversight of natural resources.

Wales wing Alex Cuthbert faces up to six weeks on the sidelines after suffering a shoulder ligament injury in the 24-6 win over Tonga at Eden Park. The 27-year-old scored the opening try before being forced off, and will now withdraw from the tour. “Alex has been in excellent form leading into this tour, so it’s a shame he’s had to leave us at this juncture,” said head coach Robin McBryde. “He’s also been a great influence off the field with the younger players in the squad. I know he’ll work hard now to be back in action for Cardiff Blues’ pre-season.” Cuthbert’s absence compounds Wales’ personnel challenges after Kristian Dacey, Tomas Francis, Cory Hill and Gareth Davies departed to join the British and Irish Lions. Despite the reduced numbers, Wales do not plan to make additional call-ups as they turn their focus to facing Samoa in Apia. Captain Jamie Roberts backed the remaining squad to step up. “We have a big squad. Some players missed out against Tonga and now others will get an opportunity,” said the centre. “We have to develop our strength in depth across the senior playing group in Wales. We’re doing that well at the moment with the young players in this squad and we have the artillery to come in.”

Police are appealing for information after an incident on a bus travelling along Bath Street in Glasgow at around 22:15 on 30 August, which left a 17-year-old woman greatly distressed. Officers want to trace a man described as of Asian appearance, aged 50 to 60, about 5ft 8in, medium build, with dark hair and a moustache, and carrying a silver walking stick. He was wearing a grey striped T-shirt, dark trousers and a black jacket. Anyone who witnessed the incident or recognizes the man is urged to contact PC Paul Lorenzetti via 101. Information can be provided anonymously.

Leyton Orient have highlighted Dave Mooney’s contributions, noting he scored nine goals in 46 outings for Southend United after moving from Orient in July 2015. Mooney previously netted 38 in 140 games for Orient after joining in 2011. In other club news, 20-year-old goalkeeper Charlie Grainger has agreed a new contract lasting until 2019. Find the latest football transfers on our dedicated page.

Derbyshire Constabulary will reduce front counter provision this summer, cutting the number of desks from 16 to four in total following a property review announced in January. Seven offices are to shut on 12 June: Glossop, Matlock, Clay Cross, Bolsover, Long Eaton, Cotton Lane in Derby and Swadlincote. Bakewell and Derby’s Assembly Rooms will close the next day. A further three sites—Ashbourne, Ripley and Ilkeston—will go by 18 September, with dates to be confirmed closer to the time. The decision forms part of plans to save up to £26m over the next five years. Senior officers say footfall at counters has declined sharply, with residents increasingly contacting the force online, by phone, and through scheduled appointments. The remaining counters will be at Buxton, Chesterfield, and two Derby locations: St Mary’s Wharf and Pear Tree. Assistant Chief Constable Gary Knighton said the changes would allow investment in frontline services: “This will save us a significant amount of money which will go towards keeping people safe. The way people contact us has changed.” Knighton stressed that only the front counters are closing, not police stations, and officers will continue to operate from the affected buildings.

Welsh rugby faces a nail-biting finale this weekend as Scarlets and Ospreys enter a decisive round with their fortunes intertwined and the stakes stretching from domestic play-offs to European qualification. Fifth-placed Scarlets are chasing Ulster for the fourth and final play-off berth, while Ospreys host Ulster needing to overhaul Munster to secure sixth place and a coveted spot in next season’s European Champions Cup. Scarlets travel to Thomond Park to face Munster, knowing a win could simultaneously keep their own season alive and assist their Welsh rivals’ European hopes. For Ospreys, the path to Europe begins in Limerick. The simplest scenario sees Scarlets beating Munster and denying the Irish side a two-bonus-point return, which would allow an Ospreys victory over Ulster to clinch sixth place. Should Munster escape with a losing bonus point, Ospreys would need to claim a bonus-point win themselves against Ulster. And if Munster manage both a losing bonus point and four tries — the double-bonus haul — Ospreys’ Champions Cup ambitions will end, consigning them to a season on the sidelines of Europe’s elite competition. Scarlets’ equation is equally stark. To leapfrog Ulster into the play-offs, they must secure at least one more league point this weekend than their Irish rivals. An Ospreys win over Ulster would be a significant help, potentially leaving Scarlets needing only to edge Munster on points. But if Ulster win in Swansea, Scarlets would require a bonus-point victory at Thomond Park — a formidable task in one of the toughest venues in the league. Should Ulster collect a bonus-point win, Scarlets’ season will be over, while Ospreys would confront the prospect of a campaign that fell short of their established standards. Ospreys forward James King captured the mood of mutual dependency. “Obviously we’ll be supporting the Scarlets. We need to go for five points and hope that Scarlets don’t let Munster have anything really, but that’s a big ask at Thomond Park,” he said. “I might send a text or two later to ask them to see if they can do us a favour.” Scarlets back Gareth Owen acknowledged the irony of rivals hoping to help each other. “It would be nice for them to do us a favour wouldn’t it?” he said. “I don’t know if they think they owe us a favour or not, but the Ospreys have something to play for. I haven’t spoken to any of the players yet — they’d probably tell me where to go, I guess.” Ospreys backs coach Gruff Rees added: “Yes, they would be doing us a favour if they beat Munster and vice versa, ironically enough. We have to have one eye on Thomond Park — if Scarlets can pick up that extra point on them regardless of winning, then Ulster may have to chase some tries as well so the dynamic may have to change during the game.” Scarlets head coach Wayne Pivac underlined the live nature of the permutations. “I’ll have a laptop set-up next to me with all scores on it — they’ll be streamed as it’s happening so we’ll know exactly what the equation is so if we need to change our tactics we’ll have the ability during the game.” With so much riding on two fiercely contested fixtures, Welsh eyes will be trained on both Swansea and Limerick, where every point, try, and bonus could reshape the season’s endgame.

An improvement team will help Betsi Cadwaladr managers set key milestones to be reviewed every six months. Deputy Health Minister Vaughan Gething said the aim was to provide "the right support at the right time". Acting chief executive Simon Dean will return to his role as deputy NHS Wales chief "in due course", he added. The Welsh Government has announced the additional support as part of efforts to restore confidence and stability at Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board, which has been under the highest level of intervention since June. Health Minister Mark Drakeford described “serious and outstanding concerns” about the board’s leadership when special measures were first imposed, a status that was extended for a further two years in October. The decision followed a series of grave issues, including a May report that found “institutional abuse” at the Tawel Fan mental health ward in Glan Clwyd Hospital. In June, it also emerged that aspects of the board’s spending plans were the subject of a fraud investigation, further intensifying scrutiny of governance and oversight. Announcing the extra support on Wednesday, Mr Gething said he expects to see a health board with “strong leadership and robust governance” emerge over the next two years. He said the move had been informed by a review of how NHS trusts in England are supported through special measures. “The English experience has highlighted the importance of providing the right support at the right time,” he said. “It is also clear that organisations need time to achieve a successful and sustainable turnaround.” Mr Gething said the establishment of a health board improvement team, alongside the appointment of a new permanent chief executive, would add capacity and focus to the turnaround programme. Specific areas identified for improvement include governance, mental health services, out-of-hours primary care, and public engagement. Betsi Cadwaladr chairman Dr Peter Higson welcomed the intervention. “I believe it will enable us to build on our programme of improvement, which has delivered progress in a number of areas over the past four months,” he said. Welsh Conservative Shadow Health Minister Darren Millar AM said: “Change cannot come soon enough for north Wales and Labour ministers should set an urgent timetable for immediate improvements.”

Alexander Elliott, a young patient with a brain tumour at University Hospital Southampton, has died after a court authorised doctors to withhold further chemotherapy deemed “futile.” He passed away on Thursday, bringing to a close a contentious legal and medical dispute between his parents and the hospital trust over whether life-preserving treatment should continue. Specialists concluded in February that additional chemotherapy would not benefit Alexander. At the Court of Protection, Mrs Justice Hogg granted University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust permission to withhold treatment, ruling that stopping further intervention was in his best interests amid a deteriorating condition. Alexander’s parents, Brian and Olya Elliott, argued that his therapy should continue. Paying tribute to his son, Mr Elliott said: “My son was a courageous fighter, and the very definition of brave. He went in his own time, with his dignity and autonomy intact, and not at the behest of the hospital trust who, since February, have repeatedly told the court that it was in his best interests for further life-preserving treatment to be stopped, and for him to be left to die.” In recent weeks, judges heard that Alexander had “surpassed all expectations,” a development that briefly fuelled hopes among his family. A spokesperson for University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust said: “We are deeply saddened by Alex’s death at a tragically young age. This is an extremely difficult and distressing time for his parents and we are doing all we can to support them. Although very upsetting for his family, Alex had reached a point where all medical and surgical treatment options had been exhausted and, due to his deteriorating condition, any further intervention would have been futile and risked causing him great distress.” The trust was previously involved in the 2014 case of Ashya King, whose parents removed him from the UK so he could receive treatment in Europe.

Premier Foods reported a modest rise in annual profits and sales and deepened its alliance with Nissin Foods, announcing the appointment of the Japanese noodle maker’s managing director, Tsunao Kijima, to its board as a non-executive director. In the year to 2016, pre-tax profits increased 3.5% to £86.1m, while sales edged up 0.6% to £771.7m. The move strengthens ties with Nissin, which holds a 19.9% stake in Premier, and follows the UK company’s decision in April to partner with Nissin after rejecting a takeover approach from US spice maker McCormick. Premier said the collaboration with Nissin is focused on exploring areas for co-operation, including sharing intellectual property and technical expertise to accelerate new product development. The partnership could also pave the way for Premier to distribute Nissin products in the UK and leverage Nissin’s international reach to bring Premier brands to key overseas markets. “The potential opportunities presented by our partnership with Nissin are very exciting,” said Gavin Darby, Premier’s chief executive. Performance across Premier’s portfolio was mixed. Six of its eight largest brands, including Bisto, Oxo and Mr Kipling, grew sales by an average 3.4%, driven by increased investment in marketing and innovation. However, Ambrosia and Batchelor registered a 2.9% decline. Looking ahead, Premier plans to boost sales by expanding its cake brands in the US and other international markets and broadening its range of products aimed at health-conscious consumers. International growth gathered momentum over the year. Sales in Australia surged 47% and US revenues rose 23%, supported in part by strong demand for Sharwoods Indian cooking sauces. Reflecting its ambitions abroad, Premier’s international business unit has expanded to 28 employees from nine a year earlier. The company is also sharpening its focus on nutrition. It has already launched a reduced-salt version of Bisto and increased the vegetable content in several cooking sauces. Over the next three years, Premier intends to roll out more products offering nutritional benefits, such as reduced calories and lower levels of sugar and salt. McCormick withdrew its bid for Premier on 13 April after the UK firm rejected an initial 52p-a-share offer in February and a subsequent 65p-a-share proposal on 30 March. Nissin agreed to acquire a 17.27% stake in Premier on 24 March and later increased it. Following McCormick’s exit, Premier said it sees “a strong future for an independent Premier Foods,” with longer-term prospects enhanced by its collaboration with Nissin.

An overnight blaze aboard the cargo vessel MV Parida forced the precautionary evacuation of 52 workers from an oil platform in the Moray Firth after the ship lost power and began drifting toward the installation, authorities said. The fire, which broke out Tuesday night in one of the ship’s two funnels, was brought under control, and tugboats towed the Parida to the Port of Cromarty Firth at Invergordon, where it has been secured for repairs. Police Scotland said there is no risk to the public. The Parida, built to handle heavy and potentially dangerous cargoes, is carrying two containers, each holding three 500-litre drums of intermediate-level waste. The material is a by-product of radioactive material from Belgium that was reprocessed at the Dounreay nuclear site near Thurso in Caithness in the 1990s and is now being returned. The Nuclear Decommissioning Authority said the vessel and its cargo had been categorised at the lowest level of safety concern. Police Scotland said the Parida is tied up at a secure pier within the Port of Cromarty Firth to allow repairs, stressing there are no public safety concerns and that the integrity of the vessel and cargo was not affected. The ship will remain alongside with security measures until a final inspection clears it to resume its journey. Dounreay Site Restoration Limited confirmed that other radioactive material could be shipped to Sellafield in Cumbria for reprocessing or storage, and said a trial run of the proposed shipments was completed last week. Tuesday’s incident has renewed calls from Comhairle nan Eilean Siar and Highland Council for a dedicated emergency tug to cover the west coast and the Western Isles. Government-funded emergency tug cover for the area was removed in 2012. For a decade, two tugs were hired by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency to assist stricken vessels around Scotland, but the UK government moved to end the contracts in late 2011, agreeing only short extensions until March 2012. In June 2012 it announced funding for one tug to work “around Scotland’s coast as required” until 2015, and in February last year a deal with BP provided an oil company vessel for emergency cover in the Northern Isles. Officials said investigations into the cause of the funnel fire are under way. Further updates on repairs and the ship’s departure will be provided following inspection.

TP Mazembe will host JS Kabylie on Sunday in Lubumbashi in the first leg of the Confederation Cup play-offs, aiming to repeat last season’s recovery after a Champions League exit. The Democratic Republic of Congo giants dropped into Africa’s second-tier competition following a round-of-32 loss, just as they did last year before storming to the title with a 4-1 aggregate victory over Mouloudia Bejaia. The path looks tougher this time, with 10 other clubs boasting Confederation of African Football honours in the draw. Kabylie, one of the continent’s storied teams, can point to six African triumphs and arrive with momentum. Mazembe’s recent form has been uneven. They fell to CAPS United of Zimbabwe on away goals last month, a setback that cost French coach Thierry Froger his job barely a month after his appointment. Assistants David Mwakasu and Pamphile Mihayo have stepped up to guide the team through the play-offs. The hosts also lack a consistent scorer following the departure of Jonathan Bolingi, one of three Mazembe stars signed by Belgian side Standard Liege. In contrast, Kabylie edged Etoile of Congo Brazzaville in the previous round thanks to a last-minute strike from Mohamed Boulaouidet, his third goal of the competition this season, underlining the Algerians’ knack for decisive moments. They are not the only teams to have dropped into the Confederation Cup. Fifteen other Champions League losers have been demoted into this phase, including Rail Kadiogo of Burkina Faso, who face CS Sfaxien of Tunisia. That match will be staged behind closed doors in Ouagadougou as a disciplinary measure following bottle throwing and pitch invasions during a Champions League tie last month. Sfaxien, record three-time winners of the Confederation Cup, are coached by Nestor Clausen, a member of Argentina’s 1986 World Cup-winning squad, and feature in-form Senegalese poacher Waliou Ndoye. Zambia’s Zesco United, semi-finalists in last year’s Champions League, continue to benefit from a multinational set-up. Goals from Kenyans Jesse Were and David Owino helped secure their play-off berth, and they now travel to face Nigeria’s Enugu Rangers, whose lone Caf title came 40 years ago in the defunct African Cup Winners Cup. Elsewhere, Club Africain’s plans were disrupted when players delayed departure by a day in protest over unpaid wages ahead of their tie against Association Sportive Port Louis in Mauritius. Morocco provides the only domestic clash, with former Confederation Cup winners FUS Rabat and MAS Fes meeting for a place in the group stage. Play-off winners will advance to the groups, which begin next month, setting the stage for a fiercely contested chase for continental silverware.

Bus Carrying Tourists Plunges Off Nepal’s Prithvi Highway Near Kathmandu, Injured Taken to Hospitals A tourist bus traveling from Kathmandu to Gorakhpur plunged nearly 1,000ft (300m) into a river after veering off the Prithvi highway about 16km (10 miles) west of the capital, a police officer said. Tejendra, speaking to the Associated Press, reported that the injured were transported to multiple hospitals in Kathmandu. The cause of the crash was not immediately known, but accidents are common in Nepal’s mountainous regions, often linked to poor road conditions, badly maintained vehicles, reckless driving and overloading. The incident underscores a spate of deadly bus crashes in the country: in November, 47 people died when a bus fell into a river in western Nepal, and in October an overloaded bus plunged into a gorge, killing at least 29. Many passengers in those cases were traveling to meet family for Hindu festival celebrations.

The temporary break follows the discovery of the body of a third man on Wednesday. Ken Cresswell, 57, and John Shaw, 61, from Rotherham, and Chris Huxtable, 34, from Swansea, have been missing since the collapse in February. Police said the search would resume when recovery work in the area where the body was found was completed. The body was taken from the site yesterday but formal identification has not yet taken place. Emergency services and workers who carried out the search formed a guard of honour as the body was driven from the site in the early hours of the morning. Steve Hall, Mr Cresswell's son-in-law, said the family had been hoping for a breakthrough for six months. He added: "There's nothing you can do. Obviously we are hoping this is him, and not in a selfish way to the other two families, because I'm sure they're hoping it's them as well." The body of a fourth man, Michael Collings, 53, from Brotton, Teesside, was previously recovered from the site. The building was due for demolition when it partially collapsed in February. The remaining section was brought down using explosives in July. Police confirmed a temporary pause in search operations to allow specialist recovery and safety work in the immediate vicinity. They said teams would return to the wider site once that work was complete. Families of the missing men have been kept informed of developments and continue to receive support from liaison officers. Authorities reiterated their commitment to recovering all those unaccounted for and to conducting a full investigation into the circumstances of the collapse.

Snowdonia Enterprise Zone chairman John Idris Jones is to make the case for small modular reactors (SMRs) at a government-sponsored conference on Monday, as the former Trawsfynydd nuclear site in Gwynedd emerges as a potential host. Advocates argue SMRs—derived from designs used on nuclear submarines—could be cheaper and faster to deploy while delivering power comparable to older reactors, but opponents warn the technology remains untested and question the rationale for choosing remote locations. “I would hope that Trawsfynydd will be one of the main sites for this type of reactor,” Mr Jones told the Newyddion 9 programme. “We have all the necessary resources, the lake for cooling water, we have connections to the national grid and we have an educated local workforce. If the 300 megawatt reactor was built there that would lead to 300 jobs as well as 300 associated jobs in the local area.” Trawsfynydd, the UK’s only inland nuclear power station, was mothballed in 1991 after 26 years in operation. Its existing infrastructure and proximity to a cooling water source are viewed by supporters as key assets for a new generation of nuclear technology that aims to reduce capital costs and construction times through factory-built modules. However, local campaigners and environmental groups remain sceptical. Deilwen Evans of the anti-nuclear group CADNO said the community faces a stark choice. “It is always the case that we accept jobs that imperil the community or do we go for jobs at any cost?” she said. “Maybe ‘small nuclear reactor’ gives the impression that these are safer but they are totally experimental and totally new so we have nothing to go on apart from their say so. My concern is they have not been tried or tested. I don’t believe in nuclear power because of the waste it makes and I believe there should be a public inquiry into the health effects of the last power station in this area.” The debate comes as the UK wrestles with the cost and complexity of large-scale nuclear projects such as the £18bn Hinkley C in Somerset. Some industry voices argue the future lies with smaller reactors, a topic set to feature prominently at Monday’s London conference. US-based NuScale Power hopes to have a small-scale reactor operating in the United States by the mid-2020s, while the first UK unit may not arrive until around 2030. The UK government has invited companies, including Rolls-Royce, to submit SMR designs and is expected to outline further policy measures in the coming year. For Trawsfynydd, any decision would pit hopes for high-skilled jobs and regional regeneration against concerns over safety, waste, and the legacy of nuclear power.

Bulgarian national Denis Petkov died following an incident on East Hanningfield Road in Rettendon. Mihal Dobrev, of East Hanningfield Road, was due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday. A 21-year-old man from Chelmsford arrested over the incident has been released on police bail until 27 July. Three men, aged 24, 42 and 30, were arrested but have since been released without charge.

Emirates has been forced to clarify its uniform policy after a leaked internal email instructed cabin crew to “follow the One China policy,” telling Taiwanese staff to remove their Taiwan flag pins and replace them with China’s. The directive, which the airline now says was issued in error and subsequently withdrawn, sparked online backlash and raised questions over whether Chinese authorities had complained about the display of the Taiwan flag. According to excerpts reported by the South China Morning Post and other Asian media, the initial message said the airline had been “instructed by the Chinese government” to align with Beijing’s stance. “This means you must remove the Taiwanese flag from your service waistcoat and replace it with the Chinese flag,” wrote Nicola Parker, Emirates’ uniform standards and development manager, adding that new stocks of China flag badges were being ordered. Hours later, a follow-up email from Parker reversed course, calling the earlier instruction “incorrect and inappropriate” and apologizing “for any upset I may have caused.” That message told staff: “Please refrain from wearing your Taiwanese flags on flights until further notice. Therefore no flag is required on your uniform.” Emirates told the BBC the incident stemmed from a “communication error,” explaining that an internal email had improperly told crew to replace one flag pin with another. “This email was sent in error and has since been retracted,” a spokesperson said, adding that the airline’s intent was to recall flag pins for all cabin crew as part of an ongoing uniform update based on staff feedback. “All cabin crew are no longer required to wear a flag pin as part of their uniform.” Flag pins have been used by Emirates to indicate a crew member’s nationality and languages. The airline did not clarify why, if the change was system-wide, the initial instruction appeared to single out Taiwanese crew for replacement with the Chinese flag. The BBC said it asked whether Chinese authorities had lodged a complaint about Taiwan flag pins, but Emirates had not responded to that question. China views Taiwan as a breakaway province and insists the self-governed island is an inalienable part of a single China to be reunified in the future, making corporate references to “One China” a sensitive diplomatic tightrope. The episode drew swift reaction on social media, where users posted images of the Taiwan flag on Emirates’ Facebook page and some called for a boycott. China remains a critical growth market for global carriers. Industry group Iata has forecast that China will overtake the United States as the world’s largest aviation market by 2029. Emirates operates dozens of weekly flights between Dubai and Chinese cities including Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Yinchuan and Zhengzhou, and says it carried more than 1.3 million passengers and 106,000 tons of cargo on China routes in 2015.

A Dutch court rejected attempts by a group of shareholders to force a special shareholder meeting aimed at ousting the company's chairman. Antony Burgmans is seen as the main obstacle to the PPG takeover bid. A Dutch commercial court has dismissed a bid by activist investors to compel Akzo Nobel to hold an extraordinary general meeting aimed at removing chairman Antony Burgmans, dealing a setback to efforts to push the Dutch paints and coatings company to engage with U.S. rival PPG Industries. The Enterprise Chamber ruled Akzo was not obligated to convene the special meeting or to include investors in shaping its response to PPG’s takeover approach. Hedge fund Elliott Advisors, which led the legal challenge, said it was disappointed with the decision and is evaluating its options. “Elliott is considering the implications of this judgment for shareholder rights in the Netherlands and for its next steps in relation to Akzo Nobel,” a spokesperson said. Elliott has argued that Burgmans is a key obstacle to talks with PPG. Akzo has rebuffed three takeover proposals from PPG since March, asserting that the latest €26.9bn (£22.8bn) offer undervalues the company and reflects a “lack of cultural understanding of the brand.” The company maintains that its standalone strategy offers superior value to investors. The Dutch government and Akzo’s workforce have also urged the company to resist a merger. The court ruling forces PPG to consider whether to walk away or take its offer directly to Akzo’s shareholders in a hostile bid. PPG signaled earlier this month that its third proposal was its last friendly attempt, though it has not ruled out appealing directly to investors. Under Dutch takeover rules, PPG has until 1 June to decide on its next move. Following the decision, PPG reiterated that it “remains willing to meet with Akzo Nobel regarding a potential combination of the two companies,” but cautioned that “without productive engagement, PPG will assess and decide whether or not to pursue an offer for Akzo Nobel.” Akzo has outlined alternative plans, including spinning off its chemicals division into a separate business, increasing its 2017 dividend by 50%, and paying a €1bn special cash dividend in November, measures it says will better serve shareholders.

Margaret Stewart, 47, has admitted embezzling money from Canadian property company Ivanhoe Cambridge, the former owners of Glasgow’s St Enoch Centre, by diverting cheques through a youth football club where she served as treasurer. Her sentence was deferred and bail continued following a hearing at Glasgow Sheriff Court. The court was told Stewart, from Hamilton, South Lanarkshire, worked in the accounts department at Ivanhoe Cambridge UK, which sold the St Enoch Centre in 2013. Between May 2008 and January 2011, she arranged for managers to sign cheques intended for legitimate company payments. She then altered the payee details, inserting the name of the Rangers Supporters’ Association Boys Club, and paid the cheques into the club’s account before taking the cash herself. The scheme came to light when a bank identified an irregularity with one of the cheques and contacted her office. Stewart immediately confessed to her superiors, and a repayment plan was established. Although more than £5,000 was returned, the plan ultimately failed. Stewart put her home on the market to raise funds, but it was deemed worthless due to the presence of Japanese Knotweed. She was subsequently reported to police. Stewart pleaded guilty to embezzlement. The court heard that the Rangers Supporters’ Association Boys Club, founded in 1960, serves boys aged five to 17 and has produced several notable players, including Barry Ferguson, Lee McCulloch, Graham Dorrans and Charlie Miller. No further details of the deferred sentence were given. Ivanhoe Cambridge was not reported to have suffered operational impacts, and the St Enoch Centre’s ownership change in 2013 was unrelated to the embezzlement period. The case will return to court at a later date.

Hugh Henry has stood down as justice spokesman and has been replaced by Graeme Pearson. The change comes as new Scottish Labour leader Kezia Dugdale unveiled her frontbench line-up in Edinburgh, just days after securing the party leadership. Dugdale’s reshuffle is designed to sharpen Labour’s message ahead of next year’s Holyrood elections while maintaining a gender-balanced team. Her rival for the top post, Ken Macintosh, has been appointed community spokesman, with a brief spanning housing, local government, cities, planning and island communities. Dugdale said she was determined to put unity and renewal at the heart of her leadership and has ensured five women join her frontbench alongside six men. “I am excited about the future. We all know the big task that faces Scottish Labour in the months and years ahead, but we’re up for it,” she said. “The most important goal of any party must be to ensure that the life chances of our young people are determined by their potential, work rate and ambition, not by their background. These values will drive my team in every portfolio.” Dugdale succeeded former MP Jim Murphy, who resigned in June after Labour lost 40 of its 41 Scottish seats at Westminster in May. Much of her new team mirrors the line-up assembled by Murphy, signalling continuity amid change; however, there are notable adjustments to remit and emphasis, and Henry’s departure from justice marks one of the few personnel shifts. Former senior police officer Graeme Pearson takes over the justice and policing brief. Pearson backed Macintosh in the leadership contest, but Dugdale stressed she does not bear grudges and wants talent from across the party on the frontbench. The message is one of consolidation and shared purpose after a bruising period for Labour in Scotland. Dugdale has retained Jenny Marra, Iain Gray and Jackie Baillie in key positions, with their roles expanded and rebranded to reflect Labour’s core values. Marra becomes Equality spokeswoman, covering health, equalities, welfare, care and social inclusion. Gray is Opportunity spokesman, responsible for schools, childcare, skills, lifelong learning, sport, science and workplace issues. Baillie takes on Public Services and Wealth Creation, covering finance, infrastructure, business, public service delivery and tourism. The new titles are intended to frame Labour’s priorities in terms of fairness, aspiration and effective services. Dugdale wants her team to champion what the party stands for, while rigorously holding SNP ministers to account on policy and performance. Deputy leader Alex Rowley will cover policy and strategy. Sarah Boyack is Environmental Justice spokeswoman, handling transport, environment and rural affairs, land reform, climate change and energy, including oil and gas. Claire Baker takes the Democracy brief, covering the constitution, Europe, culture and the distribution of power in society. Mary Fee will lead on Reform, focused on party and parliamentary change. James Kelly becomes Business Manager, with Neil Bibby serving as Chief Whip, underscoring an emphasis on discipline and delivery as Labour seeks to rebuild. Dugdale’s team now turns to the challenge of reconnecting with voters and setting out a compelling alternative at Holyrood.

Women born after 6 April 1951 should all have been warned that they would not receive a state pension at 60 as the retirement age was gradually raised, but thousands say they were not given proper notice of the change. The government insists all affected women were contacted directly, setting up a dispute that has galvanized campaigners and prompted calls for compensation. “They deserve compensation. They were wronged,” said Baroness Bakewell, a former government “tsar” for older people. “They expected that their pension would start at a certain age — 60 — and then the law was changed quite suddenly.” Under the 1995 Pensions Act, ministers set out plans to equalise the state pension ages of men and women by 2020. Previously, women retired at 60 while men retired at 65. In 2011, the timetable was accelerated, bringing faster increases that mean some of those born between April 1951 and 1960 will not qualify until the age of 66. Campaigners from Women Against State Pension Inequality (WASPI) argue that many women had very little notice that they would not receive their state pension at 60. Norah Hickey, a 61-year-old former teacher from Solihull in the West Midlands, said she had only two years’ warning. “When I was informed at the age of 58 that I wouldn’t be getting it, it really was a big shock,” she told the BBC. Instead of getting her pension at 60, she will now get it at 65, and estimates she will have lost at least £30,000 in state pension payments. Hickey said she had lived at the same address for 26 years, so there was no excuse for not writing to tell her. The government maintains that all those affected were written to, using address details recorded by HM Revenue and Customs, and says it will not be revisiting the arrangements. “I can’t see any way in which the government would undo a law that was properly made in 2011, and which is potentially going to cost billions of pounds,” pensions minister Baroness Altmann told the BBC. “I really do feel for them. But at the end of the day most of these women will still get their state pension before a man born at the same time,” she said. More than 35,000 people have signed a petition urging ministers to make transitional arrangements to ease financial difficulties faced by those whose retirement plans have been upended. While the government’s state pension calculator can help individuals check their entitlement, campaigners say clearer, earlier communication would have prevented hardship.
