Those whose pension ages are raised after 2017 are likely to be given at least ten years’ notice of changes, but for many women already affected, the debate over fairness and compensation is far from over.

The victim was plied with drink and drugs between the ages of 13 and 15 and passed around "like a piece of meat". The offences included rape and indecent assault. On one occasion the girl was taken to woodland and told she would have her neck snapped. She was in the care system when the abuse started and it continued between 1999 and 2007. The defendants, charges, and sentences: Prosecutors said the crimes took place in wooded areas around Oxford and private addresses. A six-week trial at Oxford Crown Court heard how the girl, then a child in care, was targeted, groomed and repeatedly sexually abused over several years. Jurors deliberated for more than 45 hours before reaching their verdicts. Owais Khan, 32, was found not guilty of five counts of rape and Alladitta Yousaf, 46, was cleared of four counts of indecent assault. In sentencing remarks, Judge Ian Pringle condemned the exploitation, saying the survivor had been “perfect prey for those who wanted to sexually exploit her. There was clearly never any consent given.” He described the threats to kill as “shocking” and identified Akhtar Dogar as the “principal player” in those threats, telling the court Dogar “used friendly companionship and turned it into an opportunity to serve his sexual desires.” On one occasion, the court heard, the child was taken to a wooded area and told her neck would be snapped, reinforcing the climate of fear that kept her under control. The abuse was carried out in isolated locations and at private addresses around Oxford, with alcohol and drugs used to facilitate the offences and dull the victim’s resistance. Following the verdict, the woman, who cannot be named to protect her identity, issued a statement describing the process as “challenging and painful.” She added: “Looking back now I am relieved that I found the strength to speak out. It was easier to make myself heard than it was to hold it all inside. This process has been therapeutic for me, as I now feel stronger and I am no longer consumed by my past.” Det Ch Insp Mark Glover praised her “immense bravery” in coming forward and “reliv[ing] the abuse..... in court,” noting the emotional toll such testimony takes on survivors. Adrian Foster, chief crown prosecutor for Thames and Chiltern Crown Prosecution Service, said the victim was a “vulnerable girl with a difficult background” who was “robbed of her childhood.” He detailed the tactics used to condition her compliance, including “insincere flattery, the giving of gifts, plying with alcohol and drugs, and the use of threats,” adding: “Ultimately, fear of non-compliance eroded her free will to consent. Emotional abuse, coercion and bribery provide no basis for free consent in law.” Several of the men involved had already received prison terms for their roles in a separate grooming ring that abused children between 2004 and 2012. In 2013, as part of Operation Bullfinch at the Old Bailey, brothers Akhtar and Anjum Dogar were jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years, while Assad Hussain was sentenced to seven years for sexual activity with a child. The latest case addressed earlier offending against the same victim, spanning 1999 to 2007.

Somerset County Council leader Ken Maddock is holding talks with South West MPs to open more dual-carriageway sections on the A303, a move he says will cut journey times and improve reliability, boosting tourism and the local economy. Calling the upgrades “crucial for encouraging inward investment, moving goods and creating new jobs,” Maddock is working through a multi-agency task group developing proposals that also cover improvements to the A358 and A30. The A303 runs 92 miles (148km) through five counties: Wiltshire, Somerset, Cornwall, Devon and Dorset. Representatives from the Highways Agency and county councils in those areas are collaborating to shape options. “Improving these roads is vital for Somerset and therefore it is important that we work closely with MPs in order to form one strong voice,” Maddock said.

The singer and celebrity chef are among 63 alleged victims to have issued a bid for compensation at the High Court. A fresh wave of phone-hacking and unlawful information-gathering claims has been lodged against News Group Newspapers (NGN), with 63 alleged victims seeking damages in proceedings that now encompass stories published by the Sun. The new filings add to 28 existing claims, bringing the total being led by Hamlins Solicitors to 91. NGN, publisher of the Sun and the now-defunct News of the World (NoW), denies that phone hacking took place at the Sun. More than 1,000 people have previously reached settlements with NGN over historic wrongdoing at the NoW. The latest claims follow an April 2016 High Court ruling that there was sufficient evidence for allegations concerning the Sun to be heard, prompting an expansion of the litigation. The phone-hacking scandal led to the closure of the NoW in 2011 after it emerged journalists had intercepted the voicemail of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler. Since then, celebrities including Hugh Grant and Charlotte Church have settled claims against the NoW, while other cases, including one involving actor David Tennant, remain before the courts. Christopher Hutchings of Hamlins Solicitors, the lead firm for the 91 claimants, said the inclusion of the Sun had encouraged more alleged victims to come forward. “This surge in the number of claimants is a reflection of the expansion of the case to cover the Sun,” he said, adding that some are also seeking damages for alleged concealment and destruction of evidence by NGN. Singer Sophie Ellis-Bextor and theatrical agent Caroline Chignell are among those taking action, alongside a range of sporting figures, actors and entertainers. NGN continues to contest the claims.

Paralympic bronze medallist Tyrone Pillay says he was prevented from boarding a South African Airways flight from Johannesburg to Durban, alleging “disrespectful” treatment over his prosthesis. He tweeted that he was denied access to the cabin with his prosthetic leg. SAA acknowledged he should have been permitted and has launched an investigation. “Our policy makes provision for passenger assistive devices to be carried into the cabin,” spokesperson Tlali Tlali said. “Mr Pillay’s prosthetic legs fall under this classification and should have been allowed.” Tlali said it was unclear what had happened to the prosthesis after he was told he could not keep it in the cabin. He noted Pillay had carried the device on SAA’s Sao Paulo–Johannesburg service, calling the handling “inconsistent.” The airline said it would establish the facts with staff and review procedures to ensure compliance and consistency.

Grand Jury Indicts Officer Michael Slager in Fatal Shooting of Walter Scott A South Carolina grand jury on Monday returned a murder indictment against North Charleston police officer Michael Slager in the April 4 shooting death of Walter Scott, 50, clearing the way for a formal trial. Slager, 33, now faces up to 30 years in prison if convicted. He has been held in jail since charges were announced in April. The case drew national attention after a bystander’s mobile phone video appeared to show Slager firing multiple times at Scott as he ran from a traffic stop. Slager has said he feared for his safety because Scott tried to grab his stun gun during the encounter. At a press conference, Scott’s brother, Rodney, said the family is “very happy and pleased” with the indictment but emphasized it is only the first step. He added that the family plans to file a civil lawsuit in the coming months. Scarlett Wilson, solicitor for the North Charleston court, cautioned that despite the video evidence, prosecutors must still prove the murder charge in court. “Just because you have video in this case, it doesn’t mean it’s the be-all and end-all,” Wilson said. “The issue is the people who were there who were involved, who saw or heard anything, who can demonstrate what they saw and heard.” Authorities have not set a trial date. Officials encouraged potential witnesses to come forward as the case proceeds, underscoring the importance of testimony alongside the widely viewed video.

The Central African Republic’s presidential race appears headed for a run-off on 31 January after a crowded first round produced no clear majority winner, according to partial results released by electoral officials and cited by AFP. Thirty candidates contested the 30 December vote, which was conducted under the protection of UN peacekeepers amid hopes that a return to elected government will help stabilize a nation scarred by years of sectarian conflict. With a little over 23% of ballots counted so far, former prime minister Faustin-Archange Touadéra holds an early lead. His closest rival is another ex-prime minister, Anicet Georges Dologuélé, on about 13%. Désiré Kolingba, the son of a former president, is currently in third place. Officials cautioned that votes from outside the capital, Bangui, as well as ballots cast by refugees and citizens abroad, have yet to be tallied, leaving the race open as counting continues. If no candidate secures more than 50%, the top two will face off at the end of the month. The winner will succeed interim President Catherine Samba-Panza, who was installed to guide the transition after the Seleka rebel coalition seized power in March 2013, toppling ex-President François Bozizé. Seleka’s takeover plunged the majority-Christian country into violence along religious lines, prompting the emergence of largely Christian anti-Balaka militias. The turmoil forced more than a quarter of the population from their homes; over one million people fled during the height of the fighting. Touadéra, 58, a former university mathematics lecturer who entered politics and served as prime minister under Bozizé, ran as an independent, presenting himself as a technocrat capable of rebuilding state institutions. Dologuélé, a former central bank official and prime minister, campaigned on restoring investor confidence in a country that is among the world’s poorest despite abundant natural resources. Parliamentary elections for the 149-seat National Assembly were held alongside the presidential vote, part of a roadmap backed by the interim authorities and international donors to restore constitutional order. After Seleka’s rise, Michel Djotodia briefly became the country’s first Muslim head of state before stepping down under pressure from regional leaders and France, paving the way for Samba-Panza’s interim administration. Roughly 1.8 million citizens registered to vote out of a population of about five million.

George Shields has been appointed Montrose manager on a permanent basis and has named former Scotland defender Lee Wilkie as his assistant, following the departure of Stuart Garden by mutual consent. Shields steps up from his role as Garden’s assistant after a three-week caretaker spell that culminated in a 2-1 win over second-top Annan Athletic. “My last game as caretaker manager was a 2-1 win over Annan,” said Shields. “And hopefully we can build on that in my first game in charge officially.” Garden left after Montrose’s hopes of reaching the League Two play-offs were ended, drawing a line under their push for promotion. Despite that, a win away to East Stirlingshire on Saturday would lift the Gable Endies above their hosts into sixth place. Under Shields, Montrose drew away to bottom side Queen’s Park and lost to Clyde before the morale-boosting victory over Annan. “The players were terrific against Annan and, despite not having anything to play for, they fought for everything,” he told the Scottish Professional Football League website. “I am sure the way they went about things impressed the board. It certainly impressed me and I have to thank the players for it.” Shields, a former Dundee, Arbroath and Forfar Athletic player who previously managed junior side Dundee Violet and served as head of youth development at Links Park, added that commitment within the squad has been notable. “During my three weeks in charge, I have also had a full turn-out at every training session. The players have backed me and I am really pleased with that.” In a club statement, Montrose confirmed they had interviewed several candidates before settling on Shields: “George was very impressive in the interview stage against equally strong candidates and the club is positive George, with his management team, will build a strong team for the coming season and competing for promotion to SPFL League 1.” Wilkie, capped 10 times by Scotland, will remain with Lochee United as assistant manager until the end of the season before joining Montrose. The 34-year-old made his name with Dundee and Dundee United before a knee injury forced his retirement in 2010, and he also had loan spells with Plymouth Argyle, Notts County, Falkirk and Ross County. Goalkeeping coach John McCafferty completes the management team at Links Park.

A 31-year-old man has been arrested in connection with an alleged assault that left two males, aged 16 and 20, with serious neck injuries in Saughton Mains Park, Edinburgh. The incident occurred about 20:40 on Friday 16 December after the pair left a house party. Police said the victims became involved in an argument with a passerby who allegedly attacked them before fleeing. They were taken to the Royal Infirmary; officers described the incident as an unprovoked attack and said one injury could have been life-threatening. The man is due to appear at Edinburgh Sheriff Court on Thursday.

He told Fox News that the Democratic Party was using the row over his remarks to deflect from bigger issues. Donald Trump on Thursday defended his controversial call for Russia to locate Hillary Clinton’s missing emails, telling Fox News he was being sarcastic and accusing Democrats of using the uproar to distract from damaging revelations about the Democratic National Committee. “Of course I’m being sarcastic,” Trump said, adding, “The real problem is what was said on those emails from the Democratic National Committee. What they said on those emails is a disgrace and they’re just trying to deflect from that.” At a news conference on Wednesday, Trump had declared, “Russia, if you’re listening, I hope you’re able to find the 30,000 emails that are missing. I think you’ll be rewarded mightily by our press.” He later tweeted that if anyone possessed the emails, they should turn them over to the FBI. The remarks referenced roughly 30,000 emails that Clinton did not hand over during an FBI inquiry into her use of a private email server while serving as secretary of state, saying the messages contained personal information. The Trump campaign has kept steady pressure on Clinton over the FBI investigation, while Democrats seized on his comments as irresponsible. Jake Sullivan, Clinton’s senior policy adviser, said Trump’s remarks elevated the issue beyond politics. “This has gone from being a matter of curiosity, and a matter of politics, to being a national security issue,” he said Wednesday. The dispute erupted as U.S. officials and cybersecurity experts alleged Russia was behind the hacking of DNC emails, which were published by WikiLeaks last Friday. Both Moscow and Trump have denied any coordination or Russian role in aiding his campaign. The leaked emails appeared to show DNC officials, who are expected to remain neutral during the primary process, favoring Clinton and disparaging her Democratic rival, Bernie Sanders, leading to charges of bias and the resignation of DNC Chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz. President Barack Obama declined to rule out Russian involvement in the DNC breach, noting the country’s history of cyber intrusions. “What we do know is that the Russians hack our systems. Not just government systems, but private systems,” Obama said. The Kremlin strongly rejected the accusations. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the claims “a vivid example of the use of anti-Russian sentiment for electoral purposes in the United States,” saying, “It is so absurd it borders on total stupidity.” He added, “As regards these (DNC email) batches, that is not our headache. We never poke our noses into others’ affairs and we really don’t like it when people try to poke their nose into ours.” Peskov urged Americans to resolve the controversy themselves: “The Americans needs to get to the bottom of what these emails are themselves and find out what it’s all about.” Russia has also accused U.S. candidates of stoking anti-Russian sentiment, a charge echoed as the 2016 campaign increasingly intertwines cybersecurity, foreign interference, and domestic politics.

A Saudi-led coalition naval force has intercepted a fishing vessel allegedly carrying a cache of weapons bound for Yemen’s Houthi rebels, the coalition said in a statement. The boat was stopped on Saturday about 241km (150 miles) south-east of the Omani port of Salalah, and its 14 Iranian crew members were detained, according to the statement. Iranian authorities had not commented on the report as of Tuesday. The coalition listed the seized materiel as including 18 anti-armour Concourse shells, 54 anti-tank BGM17 shells, 15 shell battery kits, four firing guidance systems, five binocular batteries, three launchers, one launcher holder and three batteries. Saudi Arabia and its allies have repeatedly accused Iran of supplying the Houthis with weapons and training, charges Tehran denies. The seizure comes amid renewed diplomatic sparring over Iran’s role in Yemen’s conflict. Addressing the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Yemen’s internationally recognized president, Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi, accused Iran of seeking the country’s “destruction” and praised Saudi King Salman for his “utter determination” in leading a military campaign to restore his government. A senior Iranian foreign ministry official, speaking to Reuters, rejected the accusations, saying: “Iran has never interfered in any country’s state matters and will never do it. We support peace and stability in the region.” The Saudi-led coalition launched air strikes in Yemen six months ago after Hadi fled abroad as Houthi forces advanced on Aden, the country’s second city. Hadi returned to Aden last week, where his government has established a temporary base as southern militias and coalition-backed forces push northward toward the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa. The United Nations estimates that about 5,000 people have been killed since March 26, including 2,355 civilians, amid air strikes and ground fighting. The coalition’s blockade of Yemen’s air and sea ports has further worsened what the UN describes as an “extremely dire” humanitarian situation. Approximately 21 million people—roughly 80% of the population—now require some form of aid, and nearly 1.5 million have been displaced internally. Humanitarian agencies continue to warn of acute shortages of food, fuel, and medical supplies across the country.

Chelsea produced a slick performance and moments of brilliance to progress to the last 16 in their maiden season in European competition, sweeping past Glasgow City 3-0 in the second leg to seal a comprehensive aggregate victory. Goals from Eniola Aluko, Fran Kirby and Gilly Flaherty settled the tie in Glasgow, and with Liverpool’s defeat to Brescia, Chelsea stand as the sole British representatives in the next round. Arriving in Scotland with a narrow first-leg advantage courtesy of England striker Kirby, the visitors signaled their intent from the outset. Kirby was central to the early thrust, threading a lovely reverse pass into the path of captain Katie Chapman. City goalkeeper Lee Alexander read it well, smothering the shot at source, but the move foreshadowed the danger posed by Chelsea’s incisive front line. With Glasgow enjoying spells of possession and pushing for the crucial equalizer, a lapse in space afforded to Aluko proved costly. Collecting the ball on the left, the forward cut across the face of goal and unleashed a fierce, curling strike into the top-right corner, doubling Chelsea’s aggregate cushion and deflating the home crowd. City head coach Scott Booth responded by introducing Claire Shine for Erin Cuthbert and switching to two up front in an effort to unlock a disciplined Chelsea backline. Shine soon fashioned Glasgow’s best moment, stretching to meet a teasing cross from the left, but her touch lacked the direction to beat Hedvig Lindahl in the Chelsea goal. The visitors punished City immediately. Breaking from that passage, Kirby tried her luck from distance; her skidding effort caught Alexander off guard and crept in over the keeper’s outstretched boot to effectively put the contest beyond reach. Moments later, defender Flaherty compounded City’s woes by rising to head home Chelsea’s third, capping a ruthless spell that showcased the visitors’ potency on the break and at set pieces. Aluko and Gemma Davison continued to torment Glasgow with nimble footwork and pace, and Chelsea might have added more, with Aluko particularly wasteful as further chances came and went. For Glasgow City, attention turns back to domestic duties as they remain on course for a fourth consecutive treble. Chelsea, meanwhile, can savor a landmark achievement in their debut European campaign and look ahead to Monday’s last-16 draw, armed with momentum and the distinction of being Britain’s last team standing.

A long-standing wedding and conference venue in Desborough is preparing to drop the “Ritz” name after receiving a legal challenge from the owners of London’s famed Ritz Hotel. The venue, known locally as The Ritz since the 1930s, was asked last month to sign a name-change agreement by solicitors representing Ellerman Investments Limited, which owns The Ritz in Piccadilly. Owner Kris Malde said he was “very sad” to comply but could not justify the costs of any court action. “I have talked to my legal advisor, who said the costs involved could not be justified,” he said. “I am very sad. The locals are deeply upset and I have had letters sent to me from many people. The public sympathy has been unbelievable.” Malde estimates rebranding and updating marketing materials will cost between £20,000 and £30,000. He said he plans to approach the London hotel to request a contribution toward those expenses out of “goodwill,” noting that the venue has used the name for generations without issue. The London Ritz was unavailable for comment. The Desborough venue will run a competition in the local press to find a new name, with the winning suggestion likely to be announced next week. Malde said he hopes the community will help choose a title that reflects the site’s heritage while avoiding further legal complications. In a letter sent to Malde, solicitors for Ellerman Investments wrote: “Our clients are concerned to discover that you are using the domain name in connection with a business which appears to be trading as ‘The Ritz’ and offering banqueting and conference services. Our clients cannot allow their trademarks to be used without consent. The Ritz Hotel was opened by Cesar Ritz in 1906 and since then its owners have built up a very substantial reputation and goodwill throughout the world.” The Desborough venue recently completed a £1 million refurbishment and features rooms including the Berkeley Suite, Kensington Lounge and the Eton Room, with capacity for up to 600 guests. The Berkeley Suite measures 12m x 7m, accommodates 100, and offers a private bar and lounge, mood lighting, and facilities for civil ceremonies. By contrast, the Berkeley Suite at the Piccadilly Ritz offers 1,200 sq ft of luxury accommodations, including a marbled lobby, two bedrooms, two bathrooms, a dining area, study and pantry, and commands a nightly rate in the many thousands of pounds.

David Marshall, 68, of Birks Street, Stoke-on-Trent, has admitted murdering Eni Mevish, 20, and wounding a 22-year-old man at Wolverhampton Crown Court. Mevish was found with stab injuries on Cauldon Road, Shelton, in November. Police said both victims were stabbed; Mevish, a university crime science student, later died. Marshall will be sentenced at Stafford Crown Court on 10 April. Officers continue their investigation and support for the victims’ families has been offered.

Holiday park operator Parkdean, which runs Trecco Bay in Porthcawl and Pendine Sands in Carmarthenshire, is to merge with Park Resorts Group, creating a combined company with 73 sites. Electra Private Equity, a part-owner of Park Resorts, announced the deal, saying it would form a "business of real scale." The enlarged group is expected to generate £100m in earnings before interest and tax.

Dundee United have parted company with manager Jackie McNamara after a prolonged run of poor results left the club second bottom of the Scottish Premiership. The decision, confirmed on Monday, followed Saturday’s 2-1 defeat by 10-man St Johnstone, a loss that kept United on five points after nine league games. Chairman Stephen Thompson said the board had been reviewing the team’s performance “for a while” before removing McNamara. “The board had been discussing it ongoing for a while – where we were as a club, where we think we should be and the support we had given to the manager,” he explained. “It was very, very hard on a personal level because, as a chairman, you build a relationship with your manager. You speak two, three, four times a day. As a board, we decided it was the right thing for the club.” Thompson stressed there is no time limit on appointing a successor and that the search is wide-ranging. “We’re going to have to think rationally and calmly and get the right person in here to run what we believe is a great opportunity for somebody,” he said. “Me, as chairman, I would not be bringing in someone that’s never managed before. The world’s a small place, they could be from anywhere in the world.” He added that those initially approached are currently out of work, indicating United aim to avoid compensation issues and move swiftly once the right candidate is identified. McNamara, 41, had been at Tannadice since January 2013, overseeing 119 games with 51 wins and 23 draws. His tenure included notable highs, guiding United to the Scottish Cup final in 2014 and the League Cup final in 2015. However, results in 2015 have been poor. United opened this season with defeat to Aberdeen, followed by a win over Motherwell, but since 8 August have managed only two league draws. Despite league struggles, United have advanced to the quarter-finals of the Scottish League Cup and will visit Hibernian in the last eight. Thompson insisted the board had backed McNamara, including signing players late in the transfer window, but concluded change was necessary. “It’s always a difficult decision to make in football,” he said, pledging a careful process to appoint a new manager capable of stabilising United’s season.

Teenage defender Ethan Ampadu has received a first senior Wales call-up as Chris Coleman names his squad for a pre-Serbia training camp at Vale do Lobo in Portugal and June’s World Cup qualifier in Belgrade. The 16-year-old, who has represented Wales up to Under-19 level and is also eligible for England, made his professional debut in August 2016 and was named Wales’ young player of the year in November. He was on standby for the World Cup qualifier against the Republic of Ireland in March. Everton’s Gethin Jones and Bristol Rovers centre-back Tom Lockyer are included, while Barnsley forward Marley Watkins earns a maiden call-up after scoring 10 goals in the Championship this season. Watkins, 26, began at Swansea City’s academy, played for Inverness Caledonian Thistle, and is the grandson of Welsh poet Vernon Watkins. He has rejected a new deal at Barnsley. Coleman’s group also features several other uncapped players: MK Dons defender Joe Walsh, Wolverhampton Wanderers midfielder Lee Evans, and Liverpool forward Ben Woodburn. Woodburn is joined by Liverpool team-mate Harry Wilson, Wales’ youngest ever senior international. Wales will be without Real Madrid forward Gareth Bale and Aston Villa full-back Neil Taylor, both suspended for the match in Belgrade on 11 June. Coleman’s side sit third in Group D after four consecutive draws, four points behind leaders Serbia with five games remaining, making the clash pivotal to their qualification hopes. Jones, who spent the second half of the season on loan at Barnsley and made 17 appearances, was born in Perth, Australia, and has attracted interest from the Socceroos. Coleman, however, says the Everton defender is fully committed to Wales. Midfield experience comes from Joe Allen (Stoke City), Joe Ledley (Crystal Palace), and Aaron Ramsey (Arsenal), while Sam Vokes (Burnley), Hal Robson-Kanu (West Bromwich Albion), and Tom Bradshaw (Barnsley) bolster the attacking options. Wales squad (selected): Goalkeepers: Wayne Hennessey (Crystal Palace), Danny Ward (Liverpool, on loan at Huddersfield Town), Owain Fôn Williams (Inverness Caledonian Thistle). Defenders: Ben Davies (Tottenham Hotspur), James Chester (Aston Villa), Declan John (Cardiff City), Joe Walsh (MK Dons), Chris Gunter (Reading), Jazz Richards (Cardiff City), Ashley Williams (Everton), Tom Lockyer (Bristol Rovers), Gethin Jones (Everton), Ethan Ampadu (Exeter City). Midfielders: Joe Allen (Stoke City), Dave Edwards (Wolverhampton Wanderers), Tom Lawrence (Leicester City), Emyr Huws (Cardiff City), Lee Evans (Wolverhampton Wanderers), Joe Ledley (Crystal Palace), Aaron Ramsey (Arsenal). Forwards: Marley Watkins (Barnsley), Hal Robson-Kanu (West Bromwich Albion), Tom Bradshaw (Barnsley), Sam Vokes (Burnley), Harry Wilson (Liverpool), Ben Woodburn (Liverpool).

Ulster sign Ireland tighthead Rodney Ah You Ulster have secured the signature of 27-year-old tighthead prop Rodney Ah You, a former New Zealand age-grade international who qualified to play for Ireland in 2013 and made his senior debut the following year against Argentina. Ah You, who progressed through the Canterbury system and was capped at U19 and U20 levels by New Zealand, was part of the Junior World Championship-winning side in 2008. He moved to Connacht in 2010, establishing himself in the PRO12 and earning Ireland selection after completing his residency qualification. “I’m really excited about the challenges that lie ahead with Ulster – they are a side with big ambitions,” Ah You said. “I feel that the environment at Ulster will allow me to reach my potential and help me to realise my ambitions in the game. With so many players pushing one another for starting places, it will hopefully spur me on to a new level. I feel, at 27, that my best years are ahead of me and I want to push hard for more international recognition too.” Ulster director of rugby Les Kiss hailed the addition, highlighting Ah You’s power and potential impact in the scrum. “We are delighted that Rodney has decided to commit to Ulster as he will add real strength to our front row department,” Kiss said. “As a 27-year-old prop, there is still room for him to develop and as a coaching group we will endeavour to get the very best out of Rodney.” Ah You’s arrival bolsters Ulster’s options as the province looks to build on recent campaigns.

Guided-missile destroyer USS Lassen breached the 12-nautical mile zone China claims around Subi and Mischief reefs in the Spratly archipelago, in a high-profile freedom of navigation operation that directly challenges Beijing’s expansive territorial assertions in the South China Sea. The sail-by, carried out early Tuesday local time, marks one of Washington’s most assertive moves in the contested waters and comes amid rising tensions over land reclamation and suspected militarization of artificial islands. China’s foreign ministry condemned the operation as illegal. In a statement, ministry spokesman Lu Kang called the transit a “threat to China’s sovereignty,” and warned that Beijing would “resolutely respond to any country’s deliberately provocative actions.” China claims most of the South and East China seas, where several Southeast Asian nations also assert sovereignty over features in the Spratly Islands, Paracel Islands, and Scarborough Shoal—areas believed to have resource-rich waters and critical maritime routes. The United States framed the mission as routine and lawful. “The United States is conducting routine operations in the South China Sea in accordance with international law,” said US Defense Department spokesman Commander Bill Urban. US Defense Secretary Ash Carter had previously signaled such a move, stating the US would “fly, sail and operate wherever international law allows.” A senior US defense official told Reuters the USS Lassen began its mission near Subi and Mischief reefs and would spend several hours there. The destroyer was expected to be accompanied by a US Navy P-8A surveillance aircraft and a P-3 surveillance plane, according to US media reports. Additional patrols could follow in the coming weeks, the official added. The US Freedom of Navigation program is designed to challenge what Washington views as “excessive claims” over oceans and airspace, promoting adherence to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), even though the US has not formally ratified the treaty. International maritime law permits countries to claim a 12-nautical mile territorial sea around natural islands, but does not grant such rights to submerged features that have been elevated through human intervention. Subi and Mischief were previously submerged reefs that China transformed into artificial islands through extensive dredging and construction beginning in late 2013. Beijing maintains the work is legal. In a meeting with US President Barack Obama last month in Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping said China had “no intention to militarise” the islands. Washington, however, believes China is building military facilities to reinforce its disputed claims across a key global shipping corridor. US records show that in 2013 and 2014, Washington conducted various Freedom of Navigation operations challenging maritime claims by China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Vietnam—each of which maintains positions in the South China Sea. USS Lassen Source: US Navy

There are hopes microalgae, which cannot be seen by the naked eye, could replace synthetic sunscreens. The natural products, found in the sea, have a high absorbance of damaging sun rays. Dr Carole Llewellyn, who has led the research, said algae sunscreen would be better for the environment. “What we found is that algae have their own process of protecting themselves against the damaging ultra-violet rays,” said Dr Llewellyn, an associate professor in applied aquatic bioscience. “We’re really interested in finding out how they do this and applying it to products we want to use.” The team is exploring how the microscopic organisms’ natural UV-shielding compounds can be harnessed for human use, potentially offering a sustainable alternative to widely used sun-care formulations. Environmental concerns are a driving force behind the research. “There’s increasing evidence that some of the synthetic sunscreens are quite harmful to the environment when they wash off in the sea,” Dr Llewellyn said. “Many sunscreens are produced from petroleum sources and the industry is looking for something more sustainable.” With rising consumer interest in natural products, algae-derived sunscreens could meet demand for eco-friendlier options while reducing the impact on marine ecosystems. Microalgae can be cultivated in a laboratory, and the university has a facility where they are grown in photobioreactors or small flasks. Once the quantities are large enough, the algae are removed from the water they are growing in and concentrated. The cells are then broken down — a process known as down streaming — to extract the colourless sunscreen compounds. These bioactive molecules are of particular interest because they can provide broad-spectrum UV protection without adding dyes or pigments to formulations. For anyone who might initially feel squeamish about using an algae-based product, Dr Llewellyn offered reassurance: “Think about the sunscreen you are currently using and where the ingredients have come from. To use a natural alternative seems like a much better way forward.” While companies have expressed interest, she acknowledged challenges remain. The main hurdle is making algae sunscreen a commercial reality, as synthetic sunscreens are cheap to produce at scale. “That doesn’t mean to say in the future the cost of the process [with algae] won’t come down and then it will look like an economically viable product,” she added.

Title: Demonstrators had gathered outside a police station on Monday to pay homage to the dead man. His family denies he attacked an officer with scissors as they responded to reports of a domestic dispute. A French inquiry is under way. China has made a complaint and is calling for its nationals to be protected. A day after the fatal police shooting of a Chinese man in Paris, tensions rose as mourners and demonstrators gathered outside a police station on Monday to pay homage and demand answers. The victim, 56-year-old father-of-five Liu Shaoyo, was shot dead on Sunday night in the city’s 19th arrondissement during a police response to reports of a domestic dispute. Police say Liu attacked an officer with a sharp object as he opened the door, and that the officer was only saved by a bullet-proof vest. A second officer then fired the fatal shot. The family’s lawyer “totally disputes” the police account, and relatives insist Liu did not assault officers. One of Liu’s daughters told French media that her father, who spoke little French, had gone to the door holding a pair of scissors he had been using to prepare fish. “They smashed the door in, the shot went off and my father ended up on the floor,” she told Le Parisien. French authorities have opened an inquiry, and the national police watchdog is due to interview the family later on Tuesday. At least 150 people took part in Monday’s protest, where some demonstrators shouted “murderers!” at baton-wielding police. China’s foreign ministry lodged an official complaint, urging a full investigation and calling for the “security and rights” of Chinese nationals in France to be protected. France’s foreign ministry responded that the safety of Chinese people in the country is a high national priority. The Chinese intervention is unusual, according to BBC correspondent Hugh Schofield, who noted that while Beijing has previously raised concerns about criminal gangs targeting Chinese tourists in Paris, this is the first time it has implicitly criticized police actions. France’s Chinese community, estimated at more than 600,000 people, is considered Europe’s largest. The shooting has rekindled broader concerns about police conduct, following accusations last month after a young black man alleged he was sodomised with a truncheon during a police encounter. The officer involved said any injury was accidental, and an investigation is ongoing. Calls for clarity and accountability continue as both the French and Chinese governments watch the case closely.

Ireland’s women edged Malaysia 2-1 to maintain a perfect start so far at their World Cup qualifying tournament. Skipper Chloe Watkins opened the scoring with a fifth-minute field goal before Anna O’Flanagan doubled the advantage in the 52nd minute. Hanis Onn replied late for Malaysia, but they could not find an equaliser as Ireland claimed their second win in as many games. The result follows a thumping 12-0 opening victory over Kazakhstan. The squad complete their group programme against Hong Kong on Tuesday (10:15 GMT) as they target a top-two finish to progress to World League 3, which will be staged in Belgium (21 June-2 July) or South Africa (8-23 July), depending on rankings. Ireland are the second-highest ranked nation at the event at 16th in the world, with only Italy (15th) above them. Pool A features Italy alongside Thailand, Wales and Singapore, ranked 15, 31, 32 and 43 respectively.

WhiteHat Security to create 80 jobs in Belfast with government support WhiteHat Security, which provides web security services to businesses in e-commerce, financial services and healthcare, will create 80 jobs in Northern Ireland following the establishment of a threat research centre, customer support and software engineering operation. Invest NI has offered the company an employment grant of £400,000. The firm will also receive £80,000 under Invest NI’s Skills Growth Programme to develop its Belfast team, while the Department for Employment and Learning has offered up to £240,000 towards pre-employment training costs. Over the next three years, WhiteHat Security will recruit 50 security engineers, 20 software engineers and 10 customer support staff. Enterprise Minister Arlene Foster welcomed the investment, saying: “It is very welcome news that another leading ICT company has decided to locate in Northern Ireland. WhiteHat Security is a rapidly expanding company that is leading the field in the area of web security. The ICT sector is an important and growing cluster for Northern Ireland; and WhiteHat is a welcome addition to our important IT security sub sector.”

Romanian forward Sergiu Buș, 24, has left Sheffield Wednesday after his contract was terminated by mutual consent. Buș joined the Owls from CSKA Sofia on a three-and-a-half-year deal in February 2015 but struggled to break into the first team, making just nine Championship appearances. He has returned to his homeland on an 18-month deal. For transfer updates, visit our dedicated page or follow the Premier League tracker.

Sub Lt Samuel Mitchell, 27, is on trial at a court martial in Portsmouth accused of raping a woman at the Britannia Royal Naval College in Devon. He denies two counts of rape relating to an alleged incident on 8 May 2015, following a Victory in Europe Day ball. Prosecutor David Richards told the court the complainant was so intoxicated that friends had to carry her back to her room, where she later fell asleep. Mr Richards said Mitchell entered the room while the woman slept, removed both their clothing, and climbed on top of her. The court heard that the complainant crossed her arms over her chest and told Mitchell “no sex.” She allegedly awoke the next morning “in a cold sweat and shaking.” According to the prosecution, Mitchell went to the complainant’s room after his advances were rejected by another woman earlier in the evening. In an effort to make him stop, the complainant asked Mitchell to put on a condom, Mr Richards said, prompting him to leave, retrieve one from his room, and return before continuing. The prosecution argues that the woman did not consent at any point and that Mitchell was aware of her level of intoxication. “He knew she was drunk and that her passivity didn’t reflect a choice she had made, but the fact that she didn’t have the wherewithal to resist him,” Mr Richards told the court. Mitchell denies the charges. The court martial, held at Portsmouth Naval Base, continues, with further evidence and legal argument expected in the coming days.

Wales defender Chris Gunter insists the national team can keep their World Cup ambitions alive in Belgrade despite the suspension of talisman Gareth Bale and a mounting absentee list. Chris Coleman’s side sit third in Group D, four points adrift of leaders Serbia and second-placed Republic of Ireland, with five qualifiers remaining. After an opening win over Moldova, Wales have been held to four straight draws by Austria, Georgia, Serbia, and the Republic of Ireland, leaving little margin for error as the campaign enters its decisive phase. “We have shown in the past in big games we can go and win matches people think we probably can’t,” Gunter said. “We are in a situation where we have to go to Serbia and perform and pick something up. If we go and play as we have done over the course of the last two to three years, we give ourselves a really good chance.” Bale, 27, will miss Sunday’s trip to Belgrade after collecting a suspension, sidelining him for his first competitive Wales match since October 2013. Aston Villa full-back Neil Taylor is also suspended, while defender James Collins and midfielder Andy King are out injured. The absence of Real Madrid forward Bale is a significant blow, but Gunter believes Wales have the depth and resilience to cope. “You always want your best eleven out but we have shown in the past we have been able to manage,” he said. “We have some really good players ready to come whatever way the manager wants to go.” The Newport-born full-back, in line to win his 79th cap after making his senior debut against New Zealand in May 2007, described the campaign as “a strange group” in which Wales “haven’t done a lot wrong” yet feel they “could have a couple more points.” “At the start of a group you know to qualify you need to put a run of wins together and we haven’t done that in the first-half, but it doesn’t mean you can’t in the second half of the group,” Gunter told BBC Wales Sport. “We come away from Serbia with something and we are right in the group with the games we have left to play.”

Cervical screening uptake in Scotland has fallen to 76.6% among nearly 1.5 million eligible women, prompting warnings from Jo’s Cervical Cancer Trust that urgent action is needed to reverse a long-term decline. The charity said attendance had dropped across all age groups and estimated that incidences of cervical cancer could be reduced by 21% within a year if uptake reached 85%. According to Jo’s Cervical Cancer Trust, five-year cervical screening coverage has been decreasing since 2001-2002, when it stood at 86.5%. The only interruption to that downward trend came in 2009, when the death of reality TV personality Jade Goody from cervical cancer led to a temporary surge in attendance as awareness spiked. The charity says the renewed drop-off underscores the need for sustained, targeted efforts to ensure women attend routine smear tests when invited. The charity’s chief executive, Robert Music, described cervical cancer as a preventable disease and said continued declines in screening uptake cannot be allowed to persist. He urged policy makers and health professionals to invest in targeted approaches that address barriers to screening for women of every age, ethnicity, location and circumstance. Music highlighted that tailored outreach and better access could help close gaps in participation that have widened over time. Jo’s Cervical Cancer Trust will relaunch its #SmearForSmear awareness campaign at the start of Cervical Cancer Prevention Week, following evidence it boosted attendance among women aged 25 to 29 when it ran last year. The new push will also highlight a clear trend of declining participation as age increases. In Scotland, coverage for women aged 50 to 54 fell to 82.1% last year, down from 89.3% nine years ago. Among women aged 55 to 59, coverage dropped from 86.8% to 78.7% over the same period. Public Health Minister Maureen Watt said early detection is critical, noting that screening remains the most effective way to identify cervical cancer at its earliest, most treatable stage. She pointed to the Scottish Government’s £39 million Detect Cancer Early programme, which aims to increase the proportion of cancers found at an early stage, raise awareness of screening among the public and professionals, and save more lives each year. The minister added that while 70% of eligible women took up their screening invitation within the last three years, it is essential that every eligible woman in Scotland attends when invited to help prevent more cases and reduce mortality.

A man has been jailed for a minimum of 18 years for killing 44-year-old Khalilur Rahman at a hotel in Woking, Surrey. Jermaine Lee, 32, of Gorse Road, Croydon, was sentenced at Guildford Crown Court after Mr Rahman’s body was found at the Woking Hotel on 26 August 2015. During the hearing, the court was told that hotel staff discovered Mr Rahman dead in one of the rooms on the morning of Wednesday, 26 August 2015. A post-mortem examination found he had suffered 15 blows to his face, body and arms and died as a result of a head injury. Surrey Police said Lee’s attack was “unprovoked” and followed a brief verbal altercation in the hotel room. Lee punched Mr Rahman several times before striking him with a piece of wood, officers said. Lee admitted manslaughter at the start of the trial but denied murder. The jury convicted him, and the judge imposed a minimum term of 18 years. Lisa Warner, 35, of no fixed address, admitted assisting an offender and is due to be sentenced on 7 July. Det Supt Karen Mizzi of Surrey Police said: “This was a tragic incident where a man has lost his life. He died as a result of a viciously brutal and sustained assault by Jermaine Lee and the sentence given demonstrates the severity and impact of this horrendous crime.” She added that Mr Rahman’s family had shown “tremendous dignity” throughout the proceedings and hoped the outcome would help them feel justice had been done. In a statement, Mr Rahman’s family said: “Khalilur was caring, kind, loving and full of life but ultimately a dedicated family man, husband and father-of-two. His wife and boys were his life. His murder has left the family devastated, a void that will never be filled.”

The brother of a man murdered in Great Yarmouth more than three decades ago has accused Norfolk Police of “stealing” his family’s chance of justice after vital exhibits from the case were destroyed years after the killing. Peter Miller, 24, was found stabbed to death on the kitchen floor of the family home in Camden Place on 9 December 1984. He was last seen by a neighbour that afternoon. His brother Tony Miller, now a 54-year-old plumber from Gorleston, was initially arrested following the discovery of the body but was released soon afterwards. Subsequent investigations led to several other arrests, yet no-one was ever charged. Last year Norfolk Police confirmed that evidence had been destroyed or returned to original owners in 1991, just seven years after the murder, although the force said the total number of items was not known. Correspondence seen by the BBC indicates that 170 exhibits were cleared out, severely limiting the potential for any modern forensic reassessments of the case. In the letters, police said officers had been “unable to ascertain who it was who took the decision to destroy the exhibits,” and acknowledged that it was “disappointing” the force no longer had access to them. The documents also highlight that a can of CS spray recovered from the crime scene and classified as “clearly significant” is “unaccounted for.” Norfolk Police said the can was handed to the original senior investigating officer two months after the killing, but when recently asked about its fate the force reported that he “simply cannot remember.” Tony Miller said the loss of evidence and gaps in the original investigation have compounded years of trauma. He described being “fobbed-off” by police on multiple occasions and believes there were numerous “missed opportunities” in the 1980s inquiry, including the failure to collect formal statements from neighbours despite assurances they would be taken. “I’m going to continue fighting for Peter’s justice because they [Norfolk Police] have stolen it,” he said. “I want to show them that I will always be there, so deal with it now. I want them to stand up and say ‘we’re sorry, these are the mistakes we’ve made’. It’s got to a point now where maybe an apology isn’t enough – it’s taken my life away. They’re still trying to make excuses for the past.” Norfolk Police said it remains committed to the investigation and is pursuing a new line of inquiry that emerged in April 2013. The force added that officers continue to support the Miller family and appealed for fresh information. “As 31 years have passed since Peter Miller’s death, we hope that people who may have not been prepared to come forward at the time may now feel able to provide information,” a spokesman said.

PCC Sir Clive Loader Calls for Return to Pub Closing Times Amid Strain on Services Conservative Police and Crime Commissioner Sir Clive Loader, a retired RAF Air Chief Marshal elected as the county’s first PCC in 2012, has called for a national debate on late-night drinking and urged a return to traditional pub closing times. He believes extended opening hours are putting an unsustainable strain on police and hospital services, and says he is “appalled” by the behaviour of some people at weekends. “When asked if he believed the law should be changed, he said: ‘Yes, I do. I would like us to go back to something that looks like a closing time.’” Prior to changes introduced in 2005, most pubs were required to close at 11pm unless they had a special licence extension. Sir Clive argues that the relaxation of these rules has contributed to rising disorder and placed additional demands on frontline staff. “The police have to put on a lot of extra people on a Friday night, assaults go up fourfold—I think we should be doing more to look after our youngsters,” he said. “I’m not a killjoy..... but I don’t think we need places open, as we do in the city, until six or seven in the morning—I don’t think that’s looking after the people who do the drinking. I’m appalled that the very people who are helping those who have had too much to drink, they assault them—they assault nurses and doctors.” Sir Clive, who sets priorities for the force and oversees its budget, says his focus has included establishing the county’s first youth commission, created to give younger people a clear voice in how they are policed. He believes engaging youth is a key part of reducing harm and improving community safety. He also highlighted growing collaboration among police forces in the East Midlands, noting that forces are sharing more resources through a “strategic alliance.” While he does not expect a full merger imminently, he suggested it could be likely in the next 10 to 15 years as crime becomes increasingly complex and international. “[Crime] can be so complex and international, crossing not just force borders but national borders, so I think the move is generally in that direction,” he said. “The trick will be to get the balance right and not losing sight of the fact that you need eyes and ears on the ground at estates in Leicester city and farms in Rutland.” Sir Clive’s comments are expected to fuel debate over licensing laws, balancing nightlife economies with public safety and the wellbeing of communities and emergency workers.

The Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for comic writing has unveiled its shortlist, featuring comedienne Helen Lederer, columnist Caitlin Moran, Irish novelist Joseph O’Neill, and former nanny-turned-author Nina Stibbe. The prize, presented at the Hay Festival, honours the book that best captures PG Wodehouse’s comic spirit, with the winner receiving a Gloucestershire Old Spot pig named after the victorious novel. Festival founder Peter Florence hailed the contenders, saying, “These astonishingly gifted writers can turn phrases, create characters to love and rattle good yarns.” The winning book will be announced shortly before this year’s Hay Festival opens on 21 May. Past recipients of the award include the late Sir Terry Pratchett, Will Self and Howard Jacobson, who won the inaugural prize in 2000 and again in 2013. The shortlist underscores the continued vitality of comic fiction across a diverse range of voices.

UK trading standards warn of dangerous hoverboards ahead of Christmas rush Trading Standards officers have issued a stark warning over the safety of self-balancing scooters, commonly known as hoverboards, as the devices surge in popularity ahead of Christmas. Officials say many boards are in danger of overheating, exploding or catching fire, with the London Fire Brigade reporting at least three house fires linked to such devices over a 10-day period in October. Celebrities including Lilly Allen have helped fuel the craze, but authorities caution that the trend should not cloud consumer judgment. National Trading Standards said that 88% of hoverboards seized around the UK were found to be defective. The majority were intercepted at the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk, with additional consignments discovered at East Midlands Airport and in Glasgow. Many of the suspect boards are believed to have originated in East Asia and China and fail to meet European safety standards. Officials noted that most were unbranded products ordered by websites or small traders seeking to sell to bargain-hunting shoppers. “We suspect that most of these products are being imported for onward sale domestically as Christmas approaches. We urge consumers to be on their guard when purchasing these products,” said Lord Harris, chair of National Trading Standards. Consumers are advised, at a minimum, to check that the three-pin plug meets the BS 1363 standard. Safety laboratories have been flooded with suspect products, prompting some to hire extra staff to cope with demand for testing. Trading Standards officers cite common faults with plugs lacking fuses, substandard cables and chargers capable of bursting into flames. “Consumers should not let a new fashion or craze cloud their judgement and remain vigilant at all times,” said Leon Livermore, chief executive of the Chartered Trading Standards Institute. In Salford, Greater Manchester, officers seized 90 hoverboards last month over similar safety concerns. Fires linked to hoverboards have also been reported in the US, Australia and Hong Kong. Despite their name—borrowed from a device featured in the 1989 film Back to the Future 2—it is illegal to ride hoverboards on UK pavements or roads. They may only be used on private land with permission. Anyone who encounters suspect devices for sale is urged to contact the Citizens Advice helpline on 03454 04 05 06.

Straw-stuffed spacemen, space dogs and a scarecrow Chewbacca headline this year’s Wray Scarecrow Festival, held since 1993 and themed around "explorers." The Lancashire village’s whimsical displays also include a tribute to the late pop icon David Bowie. Crowds are flocking to admire the creations, while BBC North West Tonight reports from the event, capturing community spirit and craftsmanship.

A leading cybersecurity researcher has asserted that the Stuxnet computer worm was purpose-built to cripple industrial systems tied to Iran’s nuclear ambitions, and suggested the United States was the principal force behind the operation, with Israeli involvement. Speaking at the TED conference in Long Beach, California, Ralph Langner — one of the first analysts to demonstrate how Stuxnet could seize control of industrial machinery — said the malware was designed to sabotage equipment that could help build an Iranian bomb. “My opinion is that Mossad is involved,” he said, referring to Israel’s intelligence agency. “There is only one leading source, and that is the United States.” In a recent technical assessment, security firm Symantec concluded the sophisticated worm likely required a team of five to ten developers working for about six months. Langner argued that its creators had extraordinary access to operational details inside targeted facilities, remarking that “they probably knew the shoe size of the operator.” The malware first drew global attention in July 2010, with telemetry showing that nearly 60% of reported infections were inside Iran. Stuxnet targets programmable logic controllers (PLCs) manufactured by Siemens, the ubiquitous industrial devices that govern automated processes across factories, power plants, and other critical infrastructure. While PLCs are used in many settings, experts believe the intended focus was the control systems inside Iran’s nuclear sites. Analysts who have dissected the code say Stuxnet could manipulate and damage centrifuges, the machines essential to enriching uranium for civilian power generation or, at higher purities, for nuclear weapons. The United States and Israel have led international efforts to constrain Iran’s nuclear program, but neither country has been conclusively linked to the malware’s development, and both have declined direct comment. Earlier this week, Iran’s Interior Ministry denied that Stuxnet caused a shutdown at the Bushehr nuclear reactor. An International Atomic Energy Agency report noted that Russian engineers at the plant had removed 163 fuel rods; Iranian officials said the move addressed problems with the rods, not sabotage. The episode underscores the rise of state-sponsored cyber operations against critical infrastructure worldwide.

"Let us end the process of having people with bigoted religious views treating women as second class citizens," he told Labour MPs. "I think you should all take the pledge - no more segregated meetings," he added. It follows reports of Labour meetings where Asian men and women have been separated along gender lines. Prime Minister David Cameron’s comments have reignited a debate over gender segregation at political events, urging Labour MPs to commit to ending any practice that separates attendees by sex. His intervention comes amid scrutiny of past Labour gatherings where seating arrangements placed men and women on different sides of the room. A Labour Party spokesperson rejected Cameron’s claims, saying: “David Cameron is trying to imply that the Labour Party condones segregation. This is absolutely untrue. We make sure that everyone is treated equally and respectfully and our record on gender equality speaks for itself.” In May last year, Labour’s then deputy leader Harriet Harman told LBC radio she did not “agree” with a Labour rally she attended in Birmingham where Asian men and women were seated separately. Harman said it would have been better if the meeting had decided to “sit round in a big circle,” but she did not “like to be rude” by walking out. She added that the event was organised by a male Labour councillor and a female Labour councillor, who were trying to ensure there were no men-only meetings. “It was actually bringing the women from the community into the meeting,” Harman told LBC. At the time, the Labour Party said: “There was no forced segregation. Speakers at the event included both women and men.” Labour’s current deputy leader Tom Watson, Harman’s husband and Labour MP Jack Dromey, and Birmingham MPs Liam Byrne and Khalid Mahmood were also reported to be present. Cameron’s call for a pledge underscores ongoing tensions over how political parties engage with diverse communities while upholding principles of equality.

US seeks to try former FIFA vice-president Jack Warner on corruption charges, as extradition fight continues The United States is seeking to prosecute Jack Warner, 72, a Trinidadian national and former FIFA vice-president, on corruption charges alleging he accepted millions of dollars in bribes over many years. Warner, who denies the allegations, is contesting a US extradition request from Trinidad and Tobago. His case has been adjourned until Friday due to a legal dispute over a technicality. Warner was among 14 current and former FIFA officials indicted by US authorities in May as part of a sweeping investigation into corruption in international football. Prosecutors allege Warner engaged in corrupt practices for more than two decades. He has maintained his innocence. The case forms part of a broader crackdown that has seen multiple arrests and extradition proceedings across jurisdictions. Last week, Switzerland approved the extradition of former FIFA vice-president Eugenio Figueredo of Uruguay to the United States. Figueredo was detained in May in Zurich while attending a FIFA congress. So far, only one of the officials arrested in Switzerland has agreed to be extradited to the US. Jeffrey Webb, a former FIFA vice-president from the Cayman Islands, was transferred to New York, where he pleaded not guilty to charges of accepting bribes worth millions of dollars related to the sale of marketing rights. He was placed under house arrest on $10 million (£6.4 million) bail. As former head of North, Central American and Caribbean football (Concacaf), Warner was one of world football’s most influential figures, with his support often deemed crucial to World Cup host bids. He has long faced allegations of corruption, and a BBC investigation in June 2015 reported evidence of bribes paid to Warner. The US-led probe into FIFA continues to unfold, with further legal proceedings expected in the coming weeks.

UK FTSE chief executives’ median pay has fallen to £3.5m this year from £4.3m in 2016, according to a new remuneration report by Deloitte, which said policies introduced in recent years to curb top pay are beginning to have an impact. The accountancy firm described this year’s annual general meetings as “calmer than expected,” suggesting that remuneration committees are responding to investor pressure and tougher rules on transparency and voting. “The fall in executive pay demonstrates that remuneration committees are making a real effort to address shareholder concerns,” said Stephen Cahill, vice chairman at Deloitte. “This is the first cycle where the legislation introduced in 2013 and primarily voted on during the 2014 AGMs will have taken effect. It seems the current legislation is working.” Deloitte’s report also highlights a reduction in annual bonuses and pension allowances for newly appointed bosses, changes that align with investor calls for more restrained and performance-linked pay. The findings tally with research published by the High Pay Centre, which indicated the average pay of FTSE bosses has dropped by 17% this year. However, the High Pay Centre urged caution in interpreting the decline. Its director, Stefan Stern, suggested the fall might prove to be a “one off,” noting that headline figures could be skewed by significant pay cuts for one or two high-profile individuals rather than a broad-based reset. The think tank also reported that the average pay ratio between FTSE 100 chiefs and their employees fell to 129:1 from 148:1 in 2015. In practice, that means for every £1 earned by the average employee, a FTSE 100 chief executive receives £129. The shifts come against a backdrop of sustained political and public concern over executive remuneration. Reforms introduced in 2013 require companies to disclose top pay more clearly in relation to the wider workforce and to submit pay policies to a binding shareholder vote at least every three years. Despite these measures, discontent has persisted, prompting Prime Minister Theresa May to promise further changes to tackle what she called an “irrational, unhealthy and growing gap” between bosses’ and workers’ pay. Investor criticism at AGMs this spring was more subdued than anticipated, Deloitte said. Mr Cahill argued that further intervention is unnecessary for now. “With many companies renewing their policies this year we are seeing further moves to incorporate the best practice provisions shareholders now expect. The current framework is working well and we do not believe further regulation is needed to move things forward,” he said.

A graduate from Nottingham University has sparked a national debate over student loan interest after a letter to his local MP went viral, drawing tens of thousands of responses on social media. Simon Crowther, who began a civil engineering degree in 2012 as part of the first cohort subject to £9,000 annual tuition fees, says he did not fully understand the terms of his student loan when he signed up at 18 and now believes he has been mis-sold. In a letter sent to Vernon Coaker MP and copied to the prime minister, Crowther writes that he thought his borrowing would carry a very low interest rate, around 0.5%, when he agreed to the loan while still in sixth form. “I had no experience of loans, credit cards or mortgages,” he wrote. “Like all the other thousands of students in the UK, we trusted the government that the interest rate would remain low.” Crowther says he graduated last year with what he describes as a “huge debt” and was shocked to see the interest charged since then. He claims his loan has been accruing interest at the rate of inflation, currently 0.9%, plus 3%. In some months the interest exceeded £180, he says, amounting to £1,828 in the year to March. His total balance has risen to £41,976. “I feel we have been mis-sold the loan,” he wrote, adding that he believed interest rates were increased after loans were sold to a private company. That claim was later shown to be incorrect, but his post has clearly struck a chord: his letter has been shared about 38,000 times on Facebook and attracted close to 50,000 likes since being posted on Tuesday. Other graduates responded with alarm, with one saying she had “nearly passed out” upon seeing her statement. Another commenter suggested that the issue could prompt a class action. The government and Student Loans Company (SLC) insist the interest arrangements were clear from the outset and have not changed since Crowther took out his loan. “It is not the case that this individual’s interest rate has increased or that their loan has been sold,” a spokesman for the SLC said. “The variable interest rates that would apply to his student loan are unchanged from those in force at the time of his application in 2012. All students that take out a loan must sign a declaration confirming that they have read the terms and conditions of the loan before it will be paid. These terms and conditions clearly set out the interest rates that the student will be charged, when they will start repaying and when interest starts accruing.” The Department for Business, Innovation and Skills defended the system, calling it fair and sustainable and noting recognition from the OECD. “It removes financial barriers for anyone hoping to study and is backed by the taxpayer, with outstanding debt written off after 30 years,” a spokesman said. “Graduates only pay back at 9% on earnings above £21,000 and enjoy a considerable wage premium of £9,500 per year over non-graduates.” Crowther’s case highlights ongoing confusion and frustration among some graduates over the complex rules governing post-2012 loans, which carry variable interest linked to inflation, rising by up to three percentage points depending on circumstances. His letter has reignited debate on how these terms are communicated to young people as they make life-defining financial decisions.

Fleetwood Town have bolstered their squad with the signings of striker Aaron Amadi-Holloway, 23, and goalkeepers Chris Neal, 30, and Alex Cairns, 23. Amadi-Holloway scored eight goals in 64 appearances for Wycombe after joining in 2014 following his release by Newport County. Neal departs Port Vale having made eight appearances last season, and spent March on loan at Bury, while Cairns was released by Championship side Rotherham without making a senior appearance. Holloway told BBC Radio Lancashire that promotion is the target, praising the club’s facilities and the support network highlighted by his agent: “It’s a no-brainer when you see those.” The trio join on free transfers as Fleetwood prepare for the new campaign, adding experience and depth across the pitch before the new season.

The Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument will become the largest network of oceanic protected areas in the world President Barack Obama has signed a memorandum expanding protections across the Pacific Remote Islands Marine National Monument, creating the largest network of oceanic protected areas in the world and banning commercial fishing, deep-sea mining, and other extraction of underwater resources within its boundaries. The move, hailed by environmental campaigners as a landmark for ocean conservation, extends no-take protections to 200 nautical miles from shore around select islands and atolls, up from the previous 50 nautical miles. “The Pacific Remote Islands Area consists of seven scattered islands, atolls and reefs that lie between Hawaii and American Samoa,” the White House noted. The surrounding waters shelter corals, seabirds, sharks, and unique vegetation found nowhere else on Earth. Established by President George W. Bush in 2009, the monument’s expansion now covers about 490,000 square miles (1.2 million sq km) — roughly three times the size of California. “This really is a matter of stewardship. It’s also a matter of generational responsibility,” said US Secretary of State John Kerry. “We have a responsibility to make sure..... the future has the same ocean to serve it. Not to be abused, but to preserve and utilise.” Mr Obama first signalled his plans in June and invited comments from fishermen, lawmakers, and scientists on the final boundaries. Environmental groups quickly applauded the decision and expressed hope it would spur similar steps by other nations. “The president acted expeditiously, while the area is still largely pristine and undisturbed,” said Frances Beinecke, president of the Natural Resources Defense Council. However, some critics argue the expansion falls short of the strongest protections available under presidential authority. The islands are divided into five regions, and the expansion only involves three of them. Had all five regions been included, environmentalists say, more than 780,000 square miles could have been shielded from industrial activity. Supporters counter that expanding protections now will preserve vital habitat and biodiversity while aligning US policy with global efforts to safeguard the high seas. They say the new boundaries will help ensure these remote ecosystems remain intact for future generations.

Exeter City veteran Matt Oakley has been lauded by manager Paul Tisdale as the 39-year-old nears a potential final flourish in the League Two play-offs. Oakley, who has amassed 694 career appearances, first rose to prominence with Southampton, making 311 appearances over 12 years and featuring in the 2003 FA Cup final. He later won promotions with Derby County and Leicester City before joining Exeter following an initial loan in 2011. Since arriving in Devon, Oakley has played 172 times without scoring, a testament to his deep-lying, disciplined role. “He’s been a great servant to Exeter in the five-and-a-half years he’s been at the club,” said Tisdale. “There are few players in modern football with his CV and achievements at the top level, who actively give something back to the game at the lower level once their elite playing days are over.” Oakley could still play a part as Exeter bid for promotion via the play-offs — a success that would see the midfielder complete promotions from all three EFL divisions.

Tributes have been paid to Caerphilly council leader Keith Reynolds, who has died following nearly 40 years as a councillor. Reynolds, who represented the Aberbargoed ward since 1979, began his career as a colliery blacksmith before becoming a community health council chief officer. He had announced he would stand down in May. First Minister Carwyn Jones hailed Reynolds as “a dedicated public servant who worked tirelessly for the people of Aberbargoed,” adding that his passing will be felt deeply by his family, friends and communities across Caerphilly, where he made his impact as a councillor, local campaigner and civic leader. Caerphilly council’s deputy leader David Poole called him “an outstanding public servant” with unwavering drive to serve his community. He was widely respected locally.

Edward Hughes, known locally as Iori, died after being struck by a black Vauxhall Insignia at the junction of Wian Street and London Road in Holyhead on 3 June. He was taken to hospital in Stoke but later succumbed to his injuries. Tributes described him as a popular character who will be sorely missed. North Wales Police are appealing for witnesses and footage to assist investigation.

A federal agency is probing allegations that Rolls-Royce paid bribes for supply of aircraft engines. Rolls-Royce said it would "cooperate fully" with Indian authorities. The company is the world's second biggest manufacturer of aircraft engines. India’s defence ministry has put on hold all existing and future contracts with Rolls-Royce while a federal investigation examines allegations of bribery tied to the supply of aircraft engines to state-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), local media reported on Monday. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has opened an inquiry into the purchase of fighter jet engines in a deal valued at $1.6bn (£960m) between 2007 and 2011, after an internal vigilance report at HAL flagged possible discrepancies, officials said. A defence official, quoted by AFP, said the CBI would scrutinize findings from HAL’s report to determine whether improper payments were made to secure the contracts. Press Trust of India said the suspension covers all current and prospective agreements until the probe concludes. Rolls-Royce said it would cooperate fully with Indian authorities and reiterated its zero-tolerance stance on misconduct. "We await clarification from the authorities in India. We have made clear that we will cooperate with regulators and will not tolerate misconduct of any sort," a company spokesperson told the BBC. The UK’s Serious Fraud Office last year opened a formal investigation into possible bribery involving the company’s activities in China and Indonesia, and two people were arrested in London last month as part of that inquiry. The latest allegations add to mounting controversy around India’s defence procurement. In January, New Delhi cancelled a helicopter deal with Italian defence group Finmeccanica following corruption claims. The governing Congress party has faced a string of scandals in recent years, and opposition leaders have used the defence furore to renew calls for Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to step down.

Jama Ahmed, 26, and Asif Yousaf, 33, are on trial at Sheffield Crown Court charged with the murder of Jordan Thomas, 22, who was fatally shot on Derek Dooley Way in December 2014. Both men, from Sheffield, deny murder. They also deny the attempted murder of the car’s driver, Neshaun Ferguson. Yousaf’s father, Mohammed Yousaf, 61, also of Sheffield, denies attempting to pervert the course of justice. Prosecutors allege Mr Thomas was targeted by a lone gunman who got out of a burgundy Mitsubishi Shogun and opened fire at about 22:15 GMT on 21 December 2014. Mr Thomas was struck twice in the chest as he sat in the passenger seat, while a third shot was fired at Mr Ferguson. The prosecution has suggested the shooting was linked to tensions following the fatal stabbing of Mubarak Ali in 2011, a killing carried out by Mr Thomas’s cousin, James Knowles. The Crown says the attack formed part of a retaliatory feud. Taking the stand, Ahmed told the court he was not involved in the killing and had been watching DVDs at an address in Broomhall before returning home. Asked if he knew who shot Mr Thomas, he replied: “I would love to know. I’m completely innocent.” Jurors heard that Ahmed and Thomas were allegedly caught up in an altercation between two groups outside a Sheffield nightclub two days before the attack. Ahmed said he had gone to the club to sell drugs but insisted he was not part of the incident.
