He told the court he and Mr Thomas had previously played on the same football team and that there had “never been a problem” between them, though he was aware some people he knew “did not like anyone related to James Knowles.” Co-defendant Yousaf testified that he had acquired the Mitsubishi Shogun in exchange for crack cocaine but maintained he was not in the vehicle when the shots were fired. He told jurors he later handed the car to Ahmed in Philadelphia Gardens, Upperthorpe. Ahmed disputed that account, saying he had not been to that address and accusing Yousaf of lying. Ahmed is of Broomhall Place, while Yousaf is of Violet Bank Road. All three defendants deny the charges against them. The jury continues to hear evidence, and the trial remains ongoing.

Shiseido has cut its full-year profit forecast as the strong yen and the cost of recent acquisitions weigh on results, sending its shares down sharply. The Japanese beauty group now expects net profit of 30 billion yen ($296m; £227m) for the year, compared with a previous projection of 34.5 billion yen. The stock fell 7.5% after the guidance revision. “There is a growing sense of uncertainty regarding the future,” Shiseido said in a statement, citing further appreciation of the yen, declines in stock prices, mounting anxiety over overseas economies, and signs that corporate earnings and consumer spending have stalled. A stronger yen reduces the value of overseas earnings when translated back into Japanese currency and can dampen inbound tourism spending—both important to Shiseido’s performance. The 140-year-old company has been pushing to expand its global footprint through acquisitions and licensing deals to lift sales. In June, Shiseido agreed to buy Gurwitch Products, the owner of make-up brand Laura Mercier and skincare line ReVive, for an undisclosed amount. Integration and restructuring costs tied to the deal are hitting profits earlier in the year than many analysts had anticipated. “If you remove currency fluctuations from the picture you see that sales are flagging in international markets such as the U.S.,” said Andrew Hall, retail consultant at Verdict Retail. “Recent acquisitions will also be taking its toll on profit as Shiseido must invest in restructuring these acquisitions to align with the rest of the business. However the brand still has a number of strengths including licence agreements with coveted brands such as Dolce & Gabbana.” Hall added that geopolitical turbulence remains a persistent headwind, creating volatile currency markets and shifting tourist dynamics. “For such a large company as Shiseido and one for which tourism has been an important source of sales, these issues are particularly pertinent,” he said. Shiseido is also the licensee for fragrances by Dolce & Gabbana, Issey Miyake and Elie Saab, and has said it is “making every effort to become a global beauty company..... with its roots firmly entrenched in Japan.” The company aims to lift annual sales to more than $9bn by 2020, and is currently ranked fourth in the U.S. beauty market behind Estée Lauder, L’Oréal and LVMH.

Alderney’s Gambling Control Commission has suspended the eGambling license of Full Tilt Poker, effectively shutting down the American-run online poker site registered on the Channel Island. Executive director Andre Wilsenach said the decision was “in the public interest” and that “because of the seriousness and urgency of the matter, it required that immediate action was taken ahead of the regulatory hearing.” The move comes as U.S. authorities pursue an investigation launched in April into money laundering, illegal gambling and bank fraud linked to several online poker operators. Eleven people, including the founders of Full Tilt Poker, have been charged in connection with the alleged offenses, marking the most aggressive action since Washington’s 2006 Unlawful Internet Gambling Enforcement Act. That law was designed to halt money transfers to online gaming sites and triggered a retreat by major firms from the U.S. market, with PokerStars basing operations on the Isle of Man, Absolute Poker in Canada, and Full Tilt in Alderney. Alderney’s commission said an internal investigation indicated that Full Tilt employees and associates had operated contrary to its gambling regulations. A regulatory hearing is scheduled in London on 26 July to consider the case. Full Tilt Poker has not commented on the suspension. Players were unable to access the site following the suspension.

Falco, a black German shepherd police dog, has been taken off active duty after a Yorkshire terrier named Barbie was fatally bitten, Lincolnshire Police confirmed. The force has referred two incidents involving the same dog to the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC), and suspended Falco’s operational licence pending the outcome of investigations. A spokesperson for the commission said: “The IPCC is investigating two complaints relating to the same Lincolnshire Police dog. The IPCC received two complaint referrals from the force, one relating to the dog biting a member of the public in the Moulton Marsh area on 27 February, and another incident where it is alleged to have bitten another dog near Fishtoft on 29 February.” The incident involving Barbie occurred on a private lane while Falco was with handler Mick Judge. The three-year-old terrier was put down because of the extent of her injuries. Police are yet to comment on the circumstances of the incident involving the member of the public. Lincolnshire Police said the licence suspension was normal practice during such inquiries and “not a pre-judgement of the circumstances.” Barbie’s owner, Charles Giermak, said the attack could have been avoided if Falco had been muzzled. More on this and other stories from across Lincolnshire is available on our live page.

High winds brought a tree down onto a car in Shropshire on Thursday morning, leaving a front-seat passenger in his 80s critically injured on the A49 just north of Church Stretton. He died in hospital on Sunday. Two other people were in the vehicle: the man’s wife, who was sitting in the back, was uninjured, while the 75-year-old driver was taken to hospital for precautionary checks. In a separate incident in Wolverhampton, Tahnie Martin, 29, from Stafford, was killed after being struck by a large piece of wooden roofing. She was walking past a Starbucks coffee shop on Dudley Street with colleagues from the University of Wolverhampton when the debris fell. West Midlands Police said it is working with Wolverhampton City Council and the Health and Safety Executive to determine which building the roofing came from. Officers have appealed for anyone who witnessed the incident to come forward. The severe conditions, with gusts recorded up to 94mph across the UK on Thursday, led to widespread disruption and a number of injuries. Authorities and emergency services continue to assess damage and investigate the circumstances around the incidents, urging the public to remain cautious in the aftermath of the extreme weather.

A 20-year-old woman from Leeds says draft guidance advising against NHS use of the cystic fibrosis drug Orkambi leaves her fearing "the same fate" as her sister, who died from the disease last November. Hannah Lindley said the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) decision that Orkambi is not a "cost effective use of NHS resources" amounts to denying her a chance at a longer, healthier life. Her sister Iona, 19, died in November. "With CF you can be OK one minute and you can have a chest infection and be dead a month later, so I don't know how long that will take," Ms Lindley said. "I'm going to have a life of worry and sickness, basically. Not having this drug will mean I will have the same fate as my sister, which is deterioration until ultimate death and why should I be given a death sentence for something I did nothing to cause?" Orkambi, which costs about £104,000 per patient per year, reduced instances of sudden worsening of symptoms that required hospital treatment in clinical trials. However, NICE said the overall benefits compared with current care were modest in relation to the price. James Barrow of the Cystic Fibrosis Trust called the situation "wholly wrong," saying people with a life-shortening condition are "caught up in a cross fire between a pharmaceutical company and the NHS over long-term effectiveness and data." He urged a compromise: "give the treatment to people with the condition and then measure the impact it's having while they are receiving it." Prof Carole Longson, director of NICE's Centre for Health Technology Evaluation, said it was "disappointing" the agency could not recommend Orkambi. The draft guidance will now go out to public consultation.

A new week-long round-robin T20 competition will bolster the match experience of eight associate nations, with Ireland naming a strengthened squad for the UAE-hosted event. After opening their campaign earlier in the week, Ireland face Namibia in Abu Dhabi on 17 January before meeting hosts United Arab Emirates in Dubai on 18 January. The semi-finals and final are set for Dubai on 20 January this month. Experienced trio Boyd Rankin, Stuart Thompson and Andrew Balbirnie return to the fold after missing most of 2016. Rankin is back from a broken leg, Balbirnie from a hip injury, and Thompson after addressing performance anxiety. Niall O’Brien has been omitted, with selectors opting for Gary Wilson as the sole wicketkeeper, while Middlesex seamer Tim Murtagh also misses out. Emerging talents Jacob Mulder and Josh Little keep their places following T20 debuts against Hong Kong, and Greg Thompson’s impressive comeback in that match—ending an eight-year absence—earns him a spot on tour. Ireland squad: William Porterfield (capt), Andrew Balbirnie, George Dockrell, Josh Little, Jacob Mulder, Andy McBrine, Barry McCarthy, Kevin O’Brien, Boyd Rankin, Paul Stirling, Greg Thompson, Stuart Thompson, Gary Wilson, Craig Young.

Big Pit National Coal Museum in Torfaen has appointed two mining craft apprentices as it prepares for the retirement of many former miners who have long maintained the underground workings and guided visitors through the historic pit. More than thirty years after the last coal was dug, the museum has relied on ex-colliers to keep its tunnels safe and its tours authentic. With many retirements looming, managers drew 52 applicants for two new posts. David Powell, from Treharris, and Ben Monro, from Caerphilly, were selected. “I am extremely excited at the prospect of becoming a part of Welsh industrial heritage and to contribute to Big Pit’s aims and objectives as a world class museum,” said Mr Powell. Mr Monro added: “I feel passionate about encouraging individuals and families from all backgrounds to visit our national museums and look forward to increasing understanding and appreciation of our history and culture.” The pair will receive vocational training and hands-on experience alongside the maintenance team, while also serving part-time with the local Mines Rescue Team. If successful, after six months they are expected to qualify as underground guides. “The apprenticeships are an important part of the succession plan at Big Pit and will help to ensure that the public can continue to enjoy the underground experience at the museum and learn about the history of the mining industry in Wales,” said mine manager Huw Jones. “We are hopeful that the apprenticeship initiative will continue year on year.”

Northern Ireland's Historical Abuse Inquiry has begun an examination on the activities of Fr Brendan Smyth. Smyth was at the centre of one of the first paedophile priest scandals to rock the Catholic church in Ireland. The inquiry heard he told a doctor in 1994: "Over the years of religious life, it could be that I've sexually abused between 50 and 100 children. That number could have been doubled, or perhaps even more." Smyth was convicted of more than 100 indecent assaults against children across Ireland, offences which took place over a 40-year period. He died in prison in 1997 after a heart attack. The wide-ranging inquiry is conducting a week-long focus on how Smyth evaded detection and accountability for so long. Proceedings on Monday were told Smyth abused children in Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland and also faced allegations of similar abuse in Scotland, Wales and the United States. The inquiry is examining whether systemic failures, institutional culture, and individual decisions allowed the priest to continue offending for decades despite concerns being raised. Evidence presented indicated that suspicions about Smyth’s behavior first arose while he was in Rome studying for the priesthood. One church figure subsequently opposed his ordination but was overruled. In a statement provided to the inquiry, Fr William Fitzgerald of the Norbertine Order—of which Smyth was a member—said “warning signs had surfaced” prior to Smyth’s ordination. “I am unable to say how clear those warning signs were, but in light of what we now know the pattern of behaviour by which Brendan Smyth maintained his freedom to do as he chose was already apparent while he was in formation,” his statement read. “He ought never to have been ordained to the priesthood.” Fr Fitzgerald added that Smyth had been able to “silence and ridicule those who would oppose him.” He continued: “It is clear he used his intelligence and naked cunning not only to engineer circumstances where he could conduct abuse of children, but also to intimidate and effectively oppose the efforts of those who sought to confront him or restrict his activities. Brendan Smyth should not have been permitted to exercise ministry after it had become known that he was perpetrating acts of child sexual abuse.” A witness statement provided to the inquiry on behalf of the Archdiocese of Armagh said “the church today can only look back on all this with shame and in disgrace.” The retired Cardinal Seán Brady is expected to give evidence later this week on his involvement in a church examination of Smyth in 1975, an internal process now under renewed scrutiny. Junior counsel Joseph Aiken said the inquiry will consider whether there were “missed opportunities” to halt Smyth’s abuse by individuals in prominent and important positions. The inquiry is led by retired judge Sir Anthony Hart and was established by the Northern Ireland Executive to investigate child abuse in residential institutions over a 73-year period up to 1995. Its current focus seeks to understand how clerical and institutional structures failed children and what lessons must be applied to ensure accountability and protection in the future.

Dunkirk Veterans Return to Allied Beach Memorial for 75th Anniversary of Operation Dynamo Seven veterans of Operation Dynamo gathered at the Allied Beach Memorial in Dunkirk to pay their respects during a poignant service marking the 75th anniversary of the mass evacuation. Arthur Taylor, 94, described feeling “enormous tears” as he laid a wreath, flanked by his military grandsons, in a ceremony that brought together veterans, families, and dignitaries to honor one of World War Two’s defining moments. Operation Dynamo, staged between 26 May and 4 June 1940, saw hundreds of vessels—naval ships, merchant craft, and civilian “little ships”—rescue 338,000 Allied troops from the beaches of northern France after they retreated before advancing Nazi forces. Though hailed as a triumph of courage and coordination, the operation also carried a heavy toll, with about 90,000 left dead, wounded, or taken prisoner. Historians regard the feat as a pivotal turning point that helped sustain Britain’s war effort. Under grey skies, a crowd of onlookers gathered in the memorial square to witness the service. Wrapped against the cold, the veterans listened as the French army performed music, followed by schoolchildren reading aloud a newspaper account written in the days immediately after the evacuation. The intergenerational tribute set a reflective tone for the ceremony. Wreaths were laid at the foot of the memorial wall by French and British dignitaries, including Prince Michael of Kent, honorary admiral of the Association of Dunkirk Little Ships. Applause broke out spontaneously as Mr. Taylor stepped forward to place his wreath on behalf of the Bournemouth branch of the Dunkirk Veterans’ Association, supported by his grandsons—Royal Marines Major Stuart Taylor, 41, and Warrant Officer Second Class Ian Taylor, 39, of the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers. “I appreciated them all clapping. I didn’t expect it,” Mr. Taylor said afterward, admitting to “enormous tears” during the tribute. Major Taylor called it a “real honor” to be present for the service and described the moment as “very proud” for the family. As God Save the Queen rang out, those veterans able to stand saluted before making the short journey down to the beach. The commemorations began on Thursday as around 50 “little ships” that participated in the 1940 rescue crossed from Kent to Dunkirk. On Friday, a handful of veterans gathered at the British Memorial in the Dunkirk Military Cemetery for another remembrance service. Leading that ceremony, Royal Navy chaplain Gordon Warren offered a solemn reflection: “Whilst we thank God this weekend for those wartime miracles during the evacuation, let us never forget the precious souls who are commemorated here and who never came back. We will remember them.” Observances continue on Sunday with the unveiling of a memorial plaque at the site of the MV Crested Eagle, a paddle steamer sunk with 300 soldiers aboard, and a commemorative service for the Association of Dunkirk Little Ships on the quayside. Together, the events underscore the enduring legacy of Operation Dynamo and the bond between generations united by memory and sacrifice.

St Helens responded to their Challenge Cup disappointment with a composed six-try victory over Salford Red Devils, climbing to fourth in the Super League table and restoring momentum after a bruising week. Five days on from a 47-18 defeat by Hull FC, Keiron Cunningham’s side showed steel and invention at home, overcoming a Niall Evalds hat-trick and a spirited Salford fightback to secure the points. Salford struck first when Evalds finished crisply on the edge, but Saints settled quickly and hit back through Louie McCarthy-Scarsbrook and Mark Percival to turn the scoreboard in their favour before the interval. Dominique Peyroux crossed as the hosts tightened their grip, and Jonny Lomax added another either side of the break to keep Salford under sustained pressure. Evalds, however, kept the visitors alive with two further tries to complete his treble and drag the contest back to 22-20 in the second half, raising hopes of an upset among the travelling support. Those hopes were short-lived. Former Salford scrum-half Theo Fages darted over to restore daylight for St Helens, before a powerful surge from Kyle Amor, arriving on the end of a move initiated by Fages, pushed the hosts out of reach. With their pack asserting control and the spine dictating tempo, Saints closed out the game with minimal fuss to notch a timely win and consolidate their league form. “It was a really good performance and the final scoreline did not justify the game,” said St Helens boss Keiron Cunningham. “We bombed a few chances but all credit to Salford, who showed a lot of resilience. This club has a prestigious affiliation with the Challenge Cup and we have been hurting deeply all week but this was the perfect response. The players worked their socks off and big Alex Walmsley was back to his best. Young Morgan Knowles gets better and better and skipper Jon Wilkin ran his blood to water, it was between him and Louie McCarthy-Scarsbrook for man of the match. Our league form is pretty good and I am happy where we are heading. This game could quite easily have gone against us but we were the dominant team all night and deserved the win.” Salford head coach Ian Watson praised his side’s resilience but expressed frustration with the officiating by referee Chris Kendall. “We were on the rough end of some iffy decisions,” he said. “I told him after the game I didn’t think his performance was the best and he did not disagree. The Rugby League should not have put a young lad into a match like this. He was under pressure from the home crowd from the start.” Watson hailed Evalds’ display too: “He’s lost his spot to Gareth O’Brien but he’s a real team player and has applied himself brilliantly.” Saints’ win, coupled with Hull FC’s victory over Wigan, lifts them to fourth, while Salford remain 10th.

Blaze at Coventry Castings prompts road closures and smoke warning in Potters Green About 30 firefighters tackled a blaze at Coventry Castings on Barlow Road in Potters Green after it erupted at around 05:30 GMT. Barlow Road was closed in both directions at the junction with Dutton Road while crews worked to bring the incident under control. Firefighters said the fire is believed to have started accidentally when molten metal from a casting ignited materials on site. Smoke lingered over the area due to calm conditions, prompting a precautionary advisory for residents to keep doors and windows closed. “There was a fair bit of smoke, and with the current weather conditions the smoke is not dispersing,” Group Commander Steve Harris told the BBC at the scene. The smoke warning was lifted by 08:00 as conditions improved and crews ventilated the premises. No injuries were immediately reported. An investigation into the circumstances is under way.

Australia’s central bank delivered a widely expected interest rate cut, citing a recent run of weak inflation readings and a desire to bolster hiring and growth as the economy transitions away from its mining-led past. “The Board judged that prospects for sustainable growth in the economy, with inflation returning to target over time, would be improved by easing monetary policy at this meeting,” Reserve Bank of Australia governor Glenn Stevens said. Policymakers are seeking to support business investment and household demand as Australia moves toward a more diversified growth profile following the end of an unprecedented mining boom. Markets were cautious. Australia’s benchmark ASX/200 fell 0.8% to 5,540.54, with rate-sensitive sectors mixed as investors weighed cheaper borrowing costs against lingering concerns about sluggish price pressures. Across the region, sentiment remained fragile. In Tokyo, shares declined ahead of details on the government’s latest stimulus effort, with the Nikkei 225 down 1.5% to 16,391.45. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe is set to outline a 28 trillion yen ($265 billion; £200 billion) package announced last week. While the headline size exceeded expectations, many economists questioned whether the measures would deliver a meaningful boost after three years of Abenomics have failed to lift Japan decisively out of a two-decade stretch of low growth and weak consumer spending. South Korea’s Kospi mirrored the cautious tone, slipping 0.5% to 2,019.03. Mainland Chinese equities edged higher, with the Shanghai Composite up 0.5% at 2,968.67, as investors assessed policy signals and corporate earnings. In Hong Kong, trading was halted, with the Hang Seng index closed as Typhoon Nida swept through the city, curtailing activity across financial markets and businesses.

Cardiff Devils have bolstered their forward ranks ahead of the new Elite League campaign, confirming the return of Patrick Asselin and Luke Piggott and the addition of veteran centreman Paul Crowder. The trio adds experience, size, and two-way reliability as the reigning champions aim to defend their title. Asselin, 30, re-signed after an impressive debut season in Cardiff, where he returned from a year’s break to post 21 goals and 38 assists. Skating alongside linemates Joey Haddad and Layne Ulmer, Asselin formed part of an imposing top-six that gave the Devils two potent scoring lines. “Patrick is a great two-way forward and as good as he is offensively, he is responsible on the back check and in his own end,” said player-coach Andrew Lord. “He is a big-game player and can make those game-changing plays that have you just in awe. It wasn’t just important for us to get him back, it was vital.” Crowder, 32, arrives with familiarity and pedigree. A former teammate of Lord’s, he played with the Devils coach and current forward Joey Haddad during the 2010/11 season for the Wheeling Nailers in the ECHL. Crowder last featured in 2015/16, splitting his time between Amiens in France’s top division and Fort Wayne in the ECHL, tallying 15 goals and 39 assists across 53 games. “I know Paul very well and I know what type of guy he is, the way he plays and what he brings to a team,” Lord said. “He has always produced offensively and is another big body up front and a solid two-way centreman.” Piggott, 31, returns for a seventh successive season, underscoring the club’s continuity and culture. “Luke Piggott epitomises what the Cardiff Devils are all about,” Lord added. “He is a great team-mate, he is unselfish, works hard every day and will do anything for the team. The bottom line is, we wanted him around and we want him part of this team, which is exactly what he wants as well.” With Asselin’s scoring touch, Crowder’s playmaking and size, and Piggott’s relentless work ethic, the Devils look primed for another strong campaign.

Debt charity StepChange has urged policymakers and employers to help build emergency savings buffers, warning that a £1,000 cushion could prevent around 500,000 households from tipping into problem debt. Its analysis finds low-to-middle income workers, tenants, and parents with young children are least likely to have accessible savings and most exposed to income shocks and unexpected bills. StepChange proposes adapting auto-enrolment mechanisms so workers can divert part of money routed to pensions into an available emergency pot. Chief executive Mike O’Connor said: “Our research highlights a national savings crisis with far too many families living without a financial safety net and at real risk of problem debt. Adapting the existing approach to pension saving would ensure each adult is better able to cope with an unexpected bill and a loss of income without sinking into debt.” The charity urged trialling prize-linked savings accounts, which offer chances to win cash awards and have proved effective at engaging lower-income savers. In addition, it called for the renewal of matched savings schemes, under which government tops up deposits made into designated accounts, to jumpstart precautionary savings.

Worcestershire seized control of their County Championship clash with Northamptonshire at Wantage Road, posting 434 all out to claim a first-innings lead of 196. Former captain Daryl Mitchell, who resumed on 52 overnight, anchored the innings with 161 before falling lbw to Nathan Buck, who led the hosts’ attack with 5-90. Mitchell shared key stands with Tom Kohler-Cadmore, who struck 76, and captain Joe Leach, who added 50, as the visitors advanced from 108-2 into a position of dominance. Northamptonshire closed on 53-2 in reply, with Ben Duckett unbeaten on 25, leaving the hosts facing a substantial deficit on a surface Mitchell described as deteriorating. “The pitch didn’t do as much. We bowled well in patches and produced periods of pressure,” Buck told BBC Radio Northampton. “But we leaked a few too many and didn’t put the ball in good areas consistently.” Mitchell told BBC Hereford & Worcester: “Northants have been a bogey team for me, so it’s nice to get a few. Four hundred is our target and we got there with partnerships. We’ve had two good days and hopefully can press home the advantage.”

Schaffhausen Manhunt: Town Center Sealed Off After Office Attack; Suspect at Large Central parts of Schaffhausen, a historic Swiss town on the German border, were sealed off on Monday as police launched a major manhunt for an attacker who stormed office buildings and assaulted several people. Police and ambulances flooded the area and rescue helicopters circled overhead, spokeswoman Cindy Beer said. Authorities stressed the incident is not related to terrorism. Officers released a photograph of the alleged suspect, who remains on the run, but did not disclose his name. He is described as about 190cm (6.2ft) tall, with an unkempt appearance, and is considered dangerous. Local shops have been shut and residents have been urged to avoid the vicinity. The alarm was raised at 10:39 local time (08:39 GMT) after reports that an armed man entered offices, including the local branch of a health insurance company, according to Swissinfo. At a news conference, police reassured the public that a large number of officers had been deployed and urged witnesses to come forward. According to news agency ATS, the vehicle the suspect was believed to be driving—a white Volkswagen—has been found, but the attacker remains at large. Schaffhausen, capital of the canton of the same name, has a population of about 36,000. Police continue to search the area and have asked people to follow official guidance and avoid speculation.

Prosecutors said Danielle Watson, 24, of Rowhedge near Colchester, conned fundraisers in 2012 by claiming she needed to raise money for therapy. The court heard she had already been given the all-clear by doctors. A 24-year-old woman who falsely claimed to have stage four cervical cancer to obtain donations and free services has pleaded guilty to fraud at Basildon Crown Court, sitting in Southend. Danielle Watson, from Rowhedge near Colchester, admitted her deception on the first day of her trial after initially denying six counts of fraud. In January 2012, Watson announced she had advanced cervical cancer and said she had brought forward her wedding to April, explaining it would take place before radiotherapy and chemotherapy caused her hair to fall out. Her story garnered widespread attention in local media, prompting offers of free or discounted services, including haircuts, a wedding dress, and a wedding reception at the Ivory Rooms in Billericay. At fundraising events, she raised nearly £10,000, which she claimed would pay for “vitamin C treatment.” Marcus Croskell, prosecuting, told the court that Watson had undergone keyhole surgery that month for a common and treatable gynaecological condition, and had already been given the all-clear regarding cancer. “At no stage was she told by a medical professional that she had any form of cancer, let alone stage four cervical cancer, and she has never had treatment for it,” he said. “Any such assertions are dishonest and false.” Fundraisers began to doubt her claims when she failed to provide direct evidence of her illness or treatment. Concerns escalated after Watson used Facebook to announce she was pregnant in June 2012, and police were contacted. Det Con Rob Lewis of Essex Police described Watson’s conduct as “cold and calculated.” He said: “She befriended and abused the trust of kind and generous people who wanted to help a person they thought was dying. Everyone involved will be that bit more cautious and cynical the next time they are asked to make a donation.” Essex Police said some supporters withheld money and were able to donate £6,563 to the Mercedes Curnow Foundation, a cervical cancer charity, earlier this year. Watson is due to be sentenced on 9 January.

Former Egyptian president Hosni Mubarak has left a military hospital in southern Cairo and returned to his home in the northern suburb of Heliopolis, his lawyer said, marking the most significant step in his reemergence since the 2011 uprising that ended his three-decade rule. The move follows a decision earlier this month by Egypt’s top appeals court clearing Mubarak, 88, of charges related to the deaths of protesters during the revolt. Mubarak, who became president in 1981 after the assassination of Anwar Sadat, had been held at Maadi Military Hospital since 2013, when he was transferred there on bail from Cairo’s Torah prison. He was initially sentenced to life in prison in 2012 after being convicted of complicity in the killing of protesters in February 2011. A retrial and subsequent rulings culminated in a judge decreeing in May 2015 that he could be released, though the government under President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi was reportedly reluctant to free him amid concerns about potential public backlash. Sisi, a former military intelligence chief under Mubarak, led the military’s overthrow of democratically elected president Mohammed Morsi in 2013. The 2011 uprising, which lasted 18 days and forced Mubarak to resign, saw security forces clash with protesters across Cairo, Alexandria, Suez and other cities. More than 800 people are believed to have been killed during the unrest. Mubarak’s return home underscores the shifting political landscape in Egypt six years after the revolt.

European newspapers offered a starkly mixed verdict on Chancellor Angela Merkel’s declaration that Germany is willing to receive large numbers of refugees, a pledge that has placed Berlin at the moral center of the continent’s migration debate and reignited arguments over burden-sharing across the EU. Germany’s major dailies reflected both urgency and resolve. Munich’s Sueddeutsche Zeitung proclaimed “Germany is a land of hope,” casting Merkel’s stance as a humanitarian beacon amid Europe’s turmoil. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung highlighted the message of shared duty with the headline “Merkel: Share responsibility for refugees,” while Berlin’s Der Tagesspiegel emphasized the chancellor’s determination with “We’ll get it done,” echoing her call for confidence and coordination as arrivals surge. Praise was particularly strong in Austria, where commentators framed Berlin’s move as both generous and catalytic. “It’s a great humanitarian gesture,” wrote Oliver Pink in Die Presse, applauding Germany’s decision to accept up to 800,000 migrants. Paul Lendvai in Der Standard noted that Germany is set to receive almost 45% of all asylum applications, underscoring the disproportionate load carried by Europe’s largest economy. Both, however, insisted that other EU states—especially newer members in post-communist eastern Europe—must do more. “European solidarity now means not leaving the Germans alone,” Pink argued. Germany’s tabloid Bild pushed the point with characteristic bluntness. Under the headline “Europe’s shirkers,” columnist Dirk Hoeren accused several EU leaders of “taking far fewer refugees than they could,” placing the UK’s David Cameron at the center of a graphic alongside France’s Francois Hollande, Italy’s Matteo Renzi, Lithuania’s Dalia Grybauskaite and Slovakia’s Robert Fico. A more restrained critique came from Christoph B Schiltz in Die Welt, who titled his piece “The EU has become a club of egoists.” He urged Merkel to remind eastern European governments of their obligations and to “loudly condemn people such as David Cameron” for language like “swarm” to describe refugees. In the Balkans, where many refugees transit, Serbian papers captured both strain and uncertainty. Belgrade’s Politika described “a helpless Europe struggling with a stream of migrants,” while Vecernje Novosti warned that the “migrants crisis assumes new dimension” and reported “Europe reintroducing borders over migrants,” accompanied by an image of lorries queuing toward Austria as controls tightened. The debate has intensified beyond Europe. In Bahrain’s opposition daily al-Wasat, Mansur al-Jamri lamented Arab governments’ failure to prevent the exodus. “How long will we watch people fleeing their countries to Europe for?” he asked. In Lebanon’s al-Nahar, Ruzana Bumunsif blamed the crisis and its “dangerous repercussions” on the West’s failure to end the Syrian war. Russian pro-Kremlin outlets placed responsibility squarely on Washington and its allies. Yevgeny Shestakov in Rossiyskaya Gazeta said the United States worked to create “controllable chaos” on Europe’s doorstep, while Yegor Kholmogorov in Izvestiya argued that the “deconstruction of authoritarian regimes” in the Middle East delivered only collapse—erasing the basic stability that once kept people from fleeing. The cross-border commentary underscores Merkel’s gamble: a bid for European solidarity that, so far, reveals a continent divided over duty, capacity and compassion.

IS militants are being smuggled into Europe on boats carrying migrants across the Mediterranean, a Libyan government adviser has alleged, claiming extremist operatives are concealed among passengers departing from parts of North Africa. Abdul Basit Haroun said his assertions are based on conversations with boat owners operating in areas under the influence of the so-called Islamic State (IS), and that the group permits smugglers to continue their trade in exchange for half of their earnings. According to the UN refugee agency, an estimated 60,000 people have attempted the dangerous sea crossing so far this year. More than 1,800 are feared to have died in 2015 alone, a steep rise compared with the same period in 2014, as migrants and refugees continue to risk the journey in overcrowded and unseaworthy vessels. Speaking to BBC Radio 5 live Investigates, Haroun said IS uses “the boats for their people who they want to send to Europe as the European police don't know who is from IS and who is a normal refugee or not.” He added that suspected militants often sat apart from other migrants and appeared unfazed by the crossing, insisting they were “for IS – 100%.” Haroun also alleged that boat operators are allowed to work provided they hand over 50% of their takings from each trip. He suggested the group is positioning operatives for potential future attacks in Europe. Earlier this year, the EU’s border agency, Frontex, warned it was “possible” that foreign fighters could exploit irregular migration routes to enter the bloc. IS, which holds territory in Iraq and Syria, has expanded its presence in Libya by exploiting the country’s political turmoil following the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi. In March, the group claimed responsibility for the attack in Tunisia’s capital, Tunis, in which 22 people were killed. While Haroun’s claims have not been independently verified, they underscore growing fears about the intersection of migration flows and security threats in the Mediterranean.

Spain’s Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy appeared bruised and without his glasses after being struck during a walkabout on Wednesday, but he said the incident would not deter him from campaigning on the streets ahead of Sunday’s general election. “I am drawing no political conclusions from the incident yesterday and ask that nobody does,” Mr Rajoy tweeted, adding that he was fine. Spaniards head to the polls this weekend in a closely watched vote, and Rajoy’s decision to continue engaging with voters underscores both the importance of personal contact in modern campaigns and the persistent risks public figures face. Spanish media reported that the attacker was a 17-year-old youth. While Rajoy’s injuries do not appear to be severe, episodes like this highlight the balance politicians must strike between accessibility and security, especially as an election nears and the demands on a sitting prime minister’s protection detail intensify. Security teams typically adjust protocols to rising crowds, unpredictable settings, and heightened emotions—factors that can make even routine campaign stops more complex and potentially hazardous. Similar incidents have punctuated political life elsewhere. In December 2009, then Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was attacked at a rally in Milan by a man wielding a souvenir model of the city’s cathedral, suffering a broken nose and requiring hospital treatment. In New Zealand, Prime Minister John Key—already recovering from a broken arm—was “quite shocked” after two protesters grabbed him at a Maori memorial at Waitangi in February 2009; the men were later charged with assault. And in the United Kingdom, then Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott famously retaliated after a protester threw an egg at him in 2001, an episode that later became a local curiosity marked with a plaque in the north Wales town of Rhyl. While such scenes can be unpleasant—and occasionally inspire moments of humor—they exist alongside far graver dangers. History is marked by deadly attacks on leaders, including the assassinations of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995, Sweden’s Olof Palme in 1986, and India’s Indira Gandhi in 1984, tragedies that reshaped national politics and security practices. Assessing the actual risk of a fatal attack, economists Benjamin F. Jones and Benjamin A. Olken examined 298 assassination attempts on world leaders from 1875 to 2004 in a study published in 2007. They found that the probability of a given leader being assassinated in a given year is currently below 0.3%, down from nearly 1% in the 1910s. For Rajoy and his team, the focus now turns to balancing visibility with vigilance as Spain prepares to vote.

Photojournalist and four women found shot dead in Mexico City; authorities vow thorough probe A 31-year-old photojournalist for the investigative magazine Proceso and four women were found dead in a Mexico City apartment on Friday, all with bullet wounds to the head, authorities said. Investigators disclosed that three of the women were raped. The killings have stirred outrage among press freedom advocates and renewed scrutiny of the risks journalists face in Mexico. The victim, identified by colleagues as Mr Espinosa, had recently moved to the capital from the eastern state of Veracruz, saying he had been threatened, harassed, followed, and intimidated in Xalapa, where he covered social movements. Friends said he began receiving threats after Proceso ran an unflattering cover photo he shot of Veracruz governor Javier Duarte. The governor condemned the killings and said he would cooperate with the police investigation. Veracruz is regarded as one of Mexico’s most dangerous states for journalists. According to rights group Article 19, 17 journalists have been killed there since 2000. Mr Espinosa’s death has heightened concerns that intimidation and violence against reporters are spreading beyond state boundaries. Mexico City Mayor Miguel Ángel Mancera pledged that there would be “no impunity in this matter,” telling reporters Monday that “no line of investigation will be discarded.” Prosecutors said Sunday that robbery may have been a motive, noting that belongings were missing from the apartment. But Proceso editor Rafael Rodríguez Castañeda argued the brutality of the crime suggested it was not a simple robbery. Authorities have not publicly released the names of the four women, only their ages: 40, 32, 29, and 18. Proceso identified the 32-year-old as Nadia Vera Pérez, a social activist from the southern state of Chiapas who had worked with Mr Espinosa in Veracruz and belonged to a student movement calling for greater transparency in Mexican politics. Vera Pérez told reporters a year ago that she had received death threats. Local media reported the 29-year-old may have been Colombian. The 18-year-old is believed to have shared the flat with Vera Pérez and the 29-year-old. The oldest victim is thought to have worked as a cleaner in the apartment. The case has sparked calls for a swift, transparent investigation that examines both criminal and potential targeted motives, amid fears that violence against journalists and activists continues to escalate.

People with mental illness and psychiatric disorders are excluded too. Last year, the Canadian Supreme Court struck down a law banning doctors from helping someone die. This bill, which is backed by Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, must now be studied by committee and then voted on by both House and Senate. It seeks to protect "the conscience rights of medical practitioners", said Canadian Justice Minister Jody Wilson-Raybould. Asked why foreigners would be excluded from the new legislation, she refused to answer. "We have considered this question in the context of Canada and Canadians," she said at a press conference. Cases brought on by the families of two deceased British Columbia women spurred last year's decision by the court to strike down the law. The court said outlawing assisted suicide deprives people of dignity and autonomy. Prior to that, counselling, aiding or abetting suicide was illegal in Canada. The Liberal government had four months to come up with a new law, a time period that was extended. Last year Quebec's top court ruled that the province can allow terminally ill patients the right to die with medical help. Currently, assisted suicide is legal in Switzerland, Germany, Albania, Colombia, Japan and in US states Washington, California, Oregon, Vermont, New Mexico and Montana. What different countries say about assisted dying More US states introduced aid-dying legislation last year, but only California's became law. The proposed federal framework would exclude requests from people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness, and would limit access to adults who meet strict eligibility criteria. Supporters say the bill balances personal autonomy with necessary safeguards and respects providers who object on moral grounds. Critics argue the exclusions leave many suffering Canadians without options and call for broader access and clearer federal-provincial coordination as the legislation moves through Parliament.

South Wales Police were called to the area around 08:00 GMT on Tuesday, police said, where a man was found and later identified as Lee Turner, 45, from Plasmarl, Swansea. Turner had been missing since 7 November. Officers confirmed his family have been informed and said the death is not being treated as suspicious. The circumstances will be investigated on behalf of the coroner.

Dembele double powers Fulham to 4-1 win at Bristol City as McCormack and Tunnicliffe seal rout Fulham surged to a convincing 4-1 victory at Bristol City, sparked by a blistering start that saw Moussa Dembele net twice inside the opening 36 minutes before Ross McCormack and Ryan Tunnicliffe completed the scoring. Jonathan Kodjia’s stoppage-time finish provided scant consolation for the hosts, who slipped perilously close to the Championship drop zone. The visitors were in front almost immediately. James Husband broke in behind City’s back line and squared for Dembele to tap in from close range with fewer than two minutes on the clock. Fulham’s press and pace continued to unsettle the home side, and a costly error from Aden Flint set the tone for a punishing half. The defender’s loose crossfield pass was picked off by McCormack, who fed Tom Cairney on the right; Cairney’s pinpoint delivery found Dembele at the far post for a composed side-footed second. Just after the half-hour, McCormack added a third in style, bending a sweetly struck free-kick from around 30 yards beyond Frank Fielding. Fulham were rampant, and Tunnicliffe made it 4-0 before the break, racing onto a bouncing ball that split the City defence and lifting a clever lob over the advancing keeper to put the result beyond doubt. Bristol City rallied after the interval and, despite the deficit, kept pressing for a response. They finally found a breakthrough in injury time when substitute Simon Cox delivered from the right and Kodjia swept a first-time shot past Andy Lonergan from eight yards. The defeat leaves City just a point above the relegation zone, with only Charlton, Rotherham and Bolton beneath them. Fulham, meanwhile, climb to 10th, four points outside the play-off places. “We made a couple of mistakes to give Fulham a leg-up in the game and we are very disappointed with the goals conceded,” said Bristol City manager Steve Cotterill. “We came up against opponents with that bit more quality than us and they took their chances. We are in for training tomorrow and will dust ourselves down in time to face Wolves on Tuesday.” Fulham boss Kit Symons praised his side’s cutting edge. “First half I thought we were excellent and took our goals really well,” he said. On 19-year-old Dembele’s future, Symons added: “Talks over a new contract are in progress and we want him to sign.”

Police were called at 03:10 BST after a lorry left the carriageway a mile north of Rivington services and struck wooden fencing. Workmen found the driver, pronounced dead at the scene. The motorway was closed between Horwich and Chorley for several hours, reopening at 09:00. One lane remains shut for recovery. Officers are appealing for witnesses and urging anyone who saw the crash to contact Lancashire Police.

The champions are five points ahead of the Blues while the final five rounds of matches will also determine the European play-off places. At the other end of the table there's the fight to avoid relegation. Warrenpoint sit bottom and occupy the automatic relegation place with Carrick Rangers in the play-off position. The Danske Bank Premiership enters its post-split run-in with five decisive rounds that will shape the title, European play-offs, and survival scrap. In Section A, the champions lead Linfield by five points, setting up a pivotal opener on Saturday, 9 April, when Crusaders host the Blues, alongside Cliftonville v Glenavon and Coleraine v Glentoran. Section B begins with Dungannon Swifts v Ballymena United, Portadown v Ballinamallard United, and a vital basement clash as Warrenpoint Town face Carrick Rangers. On Saturday, 16 April, Glenavon meet Crusaders, Linfield host Coleraine, and Cliftonville play Glentoran, while Section B features Portadown v Dungannon, Carrick v Ballymena, and Ballinamallard v Warrenpoint. A midweek slate on Tuesday, 19 April (19:45 BST) sees Cliftonville v Crusaders, Glentoran v Linfield, and Glenavon v Coleraine, with Dungannon v Ballinamallard, Warrenpoint v Ballymena, and Carrick v Portadown in Section B. The penultimate weekend, Saturday, 23 April, brings Crusaders v Coleraine, Linfield v Cliftonville, and Glentoran v Glenavon, plus Dungannon v Carrick, Ballymena v Ballinamallard, and Warrenpoint v Portadown. The season closes on Saturday, 30 April: Glentoran v Crusaders, Glenavon v Linfield, Coleraine v Cliftonville, with Warrenpoint v Dungannon, Ballymena v Portadown, and Carrick v Ballinamallard likely to decide European spots and who stays up.

Emergency services were called to The Shambles near the Argos store before 09:20 BST following an incident. West Mercia Police closed the road between Trinity Street and St Nicholas Street. A woman was pronounced dead at the scene. Police urged people to avoid the area for hours. No other vehicles were involved.

Police closed the road between Junction 30 and the A13 in Thurrock, Essex, for hours after two horses wandered onto the motorway. Officers initially herded the animals to safety, but one broke loose while efforts to trace its owner continued. Firearms officers then shot the horse, citing the safety of motorists and the need to prevent further suffering. The road later reopened. Essex Police are investigating, appealing for witnesses and dashcam footage.

Kerry urges Haiti to press ahead with Oct. 25 vote, calls for calm and credibility U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry urged Haiti to move forward with its Oct. 25 presidential election “without violence and without intimidation,” despite lingering security concerns after a turbulent first round of legislative voting in August. During a brief stop in Port-au-Prince on his return from a conference in Chile, Kerry said Haiti’s stability depends on credible balloting and the swift restoration of confidence in democratic institutions. “Haiti needs governing institutions that are legitimate and representative, and those cannot come into being without free and fair elections that take part without intimidation, without violence,” he said. “Over the next three weeks there is all the opportunity to take advantage of the election process.” August’s parliamentary vote was marred by sporadic violence, low turnout and allegations of fraud. Only a handful of candidates have been officially elected, and new polls will be required in a number of constituencies. Earlier scheduled elections were canceled in 2011 and 2014, triggering months of violent street protests against President Michel Martelly. Kerry described his meeting with Martelly as “productive.” Martelly, who is constitutionally barred from seeking re-election, conceded that the Aug. 9 vote had been “far from perfect,” but said the presidential election would be better organized. More than 50 candidates are on the ballot, many with limited national profiles, and analysts say none is likely to surpass the 50% threshold needed to avoid a second round. A runoff is expected on Dec. 27. Haiti remains the Western Hemisphere’s poorest nation. Since the devastating 2010 earthquake, the country has relied heavily on international donations and foreign aid from the United States and other partners, heightening pressure for a credible vote to anchor longer-term recovery and governance.

In the first attack, two Israelis were stabbed to death by a Palestinian man at the entrance of a shop that serves as a synagogue in the city of Tel Aviv. Later, a third Israeli, a Jewish American and a Palestinian were killed in an attack near a Jewish settlement. A wave of violence over the past two months has claimed the lives of 15 Israelis and dozens of Palestinians. Many of the Palestinian fatalities were knife-wielding attackers of Israelis, shot by their victims or security forces. Others have been killed in clashes with troops in the West Bank or in cross-border violence in Gaza. The stabbing in Tel Aviv unfolded Thursday afternoon inside a busy commercial building on Ben Tzvi Road in southern Tel Aviv, where worshippers had gathered for prayers. Witness Shimon Vaknin told the Jerusalem Post that the afternoon service had just begun when a man attacked several worshippers near the entrance. Vaknin said congregants managed to push the assailant outside and barricaded the door to prevent him from re-entering. Emergency responders from the Magen David Adom ambulance service declared one victim, a man in his 20s, dead at the scene. A second victim was rushed to Tel Aviv’s Ichilov Hospital but was pronounced dead upon arrival. Security officials identified the suspect as a 36-year-old resident of Dura, a village in the West Bank. He was reportedly lightly wounded and taken into custody. Shortly after the incident, the militant Palestinian Islamist movement Hamas posted a message on social media praising what it called “the heroic attack in Tel Aviv” and urged further assaults. Hours later, an attacker in a car opened fire at a busy junction near a Jewish settlement before crashing into a group of pedestrians, according to the Israeli military. Three people were killed and several others wounded. Authorities identified two of the victims as Jewish—a 50-year-old Israeli and an 18-year-old American tourist—and the third as a Palestinian. The assailant was apprehended and was being questioned, while security forces launched searches in the area for possible accomplices. The Tel Aviv stabbings marked the first Palestinian attack on Israelis since Friday, when a rabbi and his son were shot dead south of the West Bank city of Hebron, the newspaper Haaretz reported. The last attack in central Israel prior to Thursday occurred two and a half weeks ago, when four people were stabbed and wounded in separate incidents in Rishon Lezion and Netanya. This latest surge in violence began in September amid heightened tensions at a contested holy site in Jerusalem revered by both Jews and Muslims. Rumors that Israel intended to relax long-standing rules to bolster Jewish rights at the compound fueled unrest; Israeli authorities have repeatedly denied any such plans.

James McDonald had initially denied murdering Sophie, 36, at their flat in Devon, in January, but changed his plea at Exeter Crown Court. James McDonald, 37, has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 17-and-a-half years after admitting the murder of his wife, Sophie, at their home in Dawlish, Devon. McDonald initially denied the charge but changed his plea at Exeter Crown Court. The court heard that after choking his wife, he wrapped her body in plastic and hid it beside bins in a rubbish store at Iddesleigh Terrace, where it was later discovered following a missing person report. Jurors were previously told that McDonald was concealing his wife’s body as police knocked on his door. McDonald, of Iddesleigh Terrace, Dawlish, later told the court he killed Sophie in what he described as a “cowardly attack,” saying he lost control during an argument and strangled her with the flex from a tumble drier. He then wrapped her in layers of plastic and hid her body in the building’s refuse area. Det Insp Steve Davies of Devon and Cornwall Police praised the dignity shown by Sophie’s family throughout the investigation and court proceedings. “Two parents have lost their daughter, a brother has lost his sister and three children have lost their mother,” he said. “I now hope that this result in some way will assist them to move forward in their lives.” Following sentencing, Sophie’s family said it “isn’t possible for justice to have been done for such a terrible thing” and that forgiveness was not “something that will come easily.” Her parents added: “Sophie has been murdered there clearly are no winners. We can only now begin to come to terms with the reality of this situation. He will eventually be released to rebuild a new life. However, we are all serving a life-long sentence.”

Berlin police have raided 15 apartments and two commercial premises across the city in a large-scale operation targeting a banned Islamist organization linked to last year’s Christmas market attack. About 460 officers took part in the searches, which also included six prison cells, authorities said. The Berlin association, Fussilet 33, which ran a mosque frequented by the attacker, was officially banned in mid-February and closed a week ago. Prosecutors say Anis Amri, a Tunisian asylum seeker who killed 12 people and injured more than 50 others in the 19 December attack, visited the mosque frequently, including on the day of the rampage. Police suspect the venue served as a hub for radicalizing recruits for so-called Islamic State in Syria and for collecting funds to support IS operations. The mosque had been under observation, with officers monitoring a camera positioned opposite its entrance, officials added. Berlin State Interior Minister Andreas Geisel said additional searches were carried out at apartments in the neighboring state of Brandenburg and in the city of Hamburg. He noted that leading figures associated with Fussilet 33 were already in custody and under investigation on allegations of supporting terrorism abroad or preparing terrorist acts. Those detained include former imams and members of the organization’s board. “With this strike against Islamist terrorism, Berlin is sending a clear signal that people who act against our free democratic basic order, people who are committing violent acts or preaching violence, don’t have a place in this city,” Geisel told reporters. Amri launched his attack by hijacking a lorry, killing its Polish driver, and then driving the vehicle into crowds at a packed Christmas market in central Berlin, where 11 more people were killed and dozens injured. He fled Germany and was tracked to Italy, where he was shot dead by police days later. Authorities say the raids focused on properties used by those who ran the banned association.

Wolverhampton Wanderers head coach Kenny Jackett has confirmed an agreement to bring Polish international Zyro to Molineux, with the deal to take effect at the start of January. The 23-year-old left-footed forward, capped four times by Poland, is comfortable across the attacking line, a versatility Jackett says will add balance. “We have a deal agreed and it’ll be kicking in at the start of January,” he told BBC WM. “He can play in any of the attacking positions and, being left-footed, he brings a balance.” Jackett wants reinforcements after Wolves’ Championship play-off push has faltered, with just one win in eight matches, and remains confident the board will back his plans. “There’s no doubt we are on the same page and want the same thing — success. To try and bring in some players in January is something we’re all focused on,” he said. Wolves, nine points off the top six, host Reading on Boxing Day.

The development near Charing has been approved by Ashford Borough Council. Ashford Borough Council has approved a housing development near Charing that will deliver 61 new homes, including a significant tranche of affordable housing. For the first time, the council will directly build and manage eight shared ownership properties. Of the total, 21 homes will be available for affordable rent to the local community, a council spokesman said. To support the scheme, the borough council will borrow £1.4 million via the Housing Revenue Account borrowing programme, which allows local authorities to retain rental income. After servicing loan interest, councils can decide how best to manage their housing stock, enabling long-term investment and responsiveness to local needs. Construction is expected to begin next spring, with completion scheduled for March 2016. The project adds to momentum in the area, where 390 homes have been built through the government’s Affordable Homes Programme. Councillor Aline Hicks said rural homes help residents remain rooted and “give rural communities a chance to thrive.”

England captain Steph Houghton lined up alongside ex-stars Hope Powell and Marieanne Spacey in an All Star XI, managed by Kelly Smith, for a celebratory friendly at Boreham Wood FC. Former World Cup final referee Howard Webb officiated as Arsenal’s current Gunners side prevailed 4-2 in front of 2,351 supporters. Smith, England’s record goalscorer with 46 in 117 appearances, did not feature from the start after recently announcing her pregnancy, but she later came on to convert a late penalty, adding another to her glittering tally. Powell, Smith’s England manager at six major tournaments, told BBC Sport she “enjoyed the warm-up more than the game,” admitting her body is no longer used to the demands but calling it “a good run-out.” She praised the turnout for Smith and noted the emotional significance of the day. “It was a lot of fun, with banter in the changing rooms and, for her, a really special day,” Powell said.

The couple went by boat to the city hall building where the brief procedure was conducted. At the weekend, a host of famous guests including Matt Damon and Bill Murray attended a lavish wedding reception for the couple. Clooney's publicist broke the news of their nuptials in a brief statement to the press on Saturday. The couple emerged from the town hall some 10 minutes after their arrival and were whisked away in a water taxi, surrounded by other boats and watched by well-wishers. Clooney was dressed in a charcoal grey suit, while Alamuddin wore a smart-casual white outfit and a wide-brimmed sunhat. At city hall, the pair were officially married under Italian law by former mayor of Rome Walter Veltroni, a long-time friend of the film star. Earlier in the day, he was seen getting ready for the ceremony at the Hotel Cipriani, where the wedding party have been staying. The couple were engaged in April. Clooney was previously married to Talia Balsam, who he divorced in 1993. One of the world's most recognisable actors, the American has two Oscars to his name: for best supporting actor in Syriana (2006) and for best picture as producer of Argo (2013). Other than his film work, he has embraced human rights causes such as the Darfur crisis in Sudan. Lebanese-born British lawyer Amal Alamuddin has defended Julian Assange of Wikileaks and former Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko among others. She met Clooney through her work. George Clooney and Amal Alamuddin sealed their marriage in Venice on Saturday with a civil ceremony at the city’s town hall, capping days of festivities along the Grand Canal. The couple arrived by boat for the brief legal formalities, conducted by Walter Veltroni, a former Rome mayor and close friend of the actor. They departed minutes later by water taxi, cheered on by crowds lining the canals. A star-studded reception over the weekend featured guests including Matt Damon and Bill Murray, adding Hollywood sparkle to the Venetian celebrations. Clooney, a two-time Oscar winner known for roles in Syriana and his producing turn on Argo, has long coupled his screen success with activism, notably on Darfur. Alamuddin, a Lebanese-born British barrister renowned for high-profile human rights cases, has represented figures including Julian Assange and former Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko. The pair, engaged in April, were based at the Hotel Cipriani during the festivities, where Clooney was seen preparing for the ceremony. Saturday’s proceedings were confirmed in a brief statement from Clooney’s publicist. Clooney, previously married to actress Talia Balsam until their 1993 divorce, and Alamuddin met through their professional circles. Their Venetian wedding blended understated legal formalities with exuberant celebrations, drawing locals and tourists alike to witness the couple’s canal-side exit. As the newlyweds departed surrounded by a flotilla of boats, well-wishers waved and snapped photos, marking the end of a closely watched romantic milestone.

British skeleton slider Swift sealed a first senior victory in Switzerland, ending a wait of more than 80 races for the 31-year-old from Devon. The breakthrough follows previous bronze and silver medals on the Intercontinental Cup and Europa Cup circuits, and marks his maiden gold. “It’s taken a long time, but it’s such a nice feeling hearing the national anthem blaring out,” said Swift. “I had high expectations, but there’s a big difference between performing well in training and racing. That’s something I’ve struggled with historically.” Swift split his season between the World Cup and Intercontinental Cup and hopes to earn selection for Great Britain’s World Championship team, due in early February.

Kent have signed 23-year-old, Zimbabwe-born wicketkeeper-batsman Adam Rouse on a permanent deal after a trial spell at the start of last season and appearances for their Second XI in 2014. The former England Under-19 international said: “I’m delighted to be rejoining Kent on a more permanent basis. I really enjoyed my time at the beginning of last year. Hopefully I can use this opportunity to push on and secure a regular first-team spot.” Rouse has played five first-class matches since his Hampshire debut in 2013, plus 10 limited-overs games.

Government drops abortion counselling consultation, says no changes to law or guidance Public health minister Anna Soubry has told MPs the government does not intend to change either the law or the guidelines governing abortion counselling, reversing plans for a separate consultation while pledging to consider recommendations from a cross-party inquiry into unwanted pregnancy. Addressing the Commons during a debate called by Conservative MP Nadine Dorries, Ms Soubry said ministers would examine evidence gathered by a cross-party group of MPs but ruled out pursuing new regulations at this stage. “I am aware that there is a cross-party inquiry into unwanted pregnancy and I think there is some important work that they will do and evidence which they will hear,” she said. “But the simple reality is as follows — we no longer plan to undertake a separate consultation and I am sorry if that disappoints those members of the committee. I am grateful for the work that they did and I want to thank them for all their efforts. I am sorry if, as I say, there is some disappointment, but the reality is that we now don’t intend to change the law so it is now an otiose exercise.” The cross-party group was established after MPs voted last September against proposals that would have stopped abortion providers from offering counselling to pregnant women. Those proposals, backed by three cabinet ministers and brought forward by Ms Dorries, argued that counselling should be provided by professionals independent of abortion services. Anti-abortion campaigners contend there is an inherent conflict of interest when clinics that perform abortions also counsel pregnant women, noting that many women who receive counselling at such clinics subsequently go on to have terminations. They have urged that counselling be delivered by a separate provider, such as a GP, to ensure impartiality. Following last year’s vote, the government had said it would look at ways of incorporating the “spirit” of Ms Dorries’ proposals into new regulations and indicated a consultation would be launched. Ms Soubry’s statement signals a change of course, focusing instead on the findings of the parliamentary inquiry. Ms Dorries accused the minister of cancelling the consultation because of her personal beliefs. “This is quite bizarre. What Anna Soubry has said today doesn’t improve services for women. The government has decided that it is not the right decision, and what makes it even more bizarre is that the British Medical Association voted to support the consultation,” she said. “Anna Soubry has a personal belief. What she has done is try to impose her personal belief on her role and that is out of order.” After the debate, the British Medical Association responded to Ms Dorries’ reference, clarifying its position. “Our policy states that we support timely and impartial counselling and advice for women requesting abortion should they wish to receive it. However, we have not called for consultation,” the BMA said. Shadow public health minister Diane Abbott, who left the cross-party group earlier this year, welcomed the cancellation as a “victory for women.” She added: “The message that people have forced this government to listen to is that British women’s right to choose is here to stay. I think it’s been a particularly tough period for those people who provide care and support for women seeking an abortion, who have repeatedly faced the most appalling attacks, smears and misinformation about their work in the media, and in Parliament.” The government says it will review the inquiry’s recommendations when they are published but, for now, confirmed that existing laws and guidance remain unchanged.

Court hears allegations Patrick Curran strangled Joan Roddam in 2003 Truro Crown Court has been told that Patrick Curran allegedly strangled 71-year-old Joan Roddam at her bungalow in Delabole, Cornwall, in November 2003. The prosecution says Curran, then 27, set fires later that evening to destroy “very significant items,” including clothing and the hard drive from his computer, and left the town two days afterward. Curran, now 38, denies murder. He was arrested in March 2014 after police re-opened the investigation. Addressing the jury, prosecutor Simon Laws invited them to consider Curran’s movements on the morning of the attack. He said the scene left behind was a dead woman “of an age group he found sexually attractive,” covered with a blanket carrying DNA attributed to Curran. He added that Roddam was wearing clothing with fibres matching “not one but two items” owned by the defendant, and argued the crime scene was “strongly suggestive” of involvement by a local man. Laws told the jury that, in front of Curran, lay “an evening of setting fires,” and that two days later he left Delabole. “He was in the right place at the right time to have killed that woman,” Laws said, asserting that Curran’s explanation—that the apparent links are coincidental—was implausible. “The prosecution say to you nobody could be so unfortunate.” The court previously heard that Curran had a sexual interest in much older women and that Roddam was allegedly strangled after rebuffing his advances. Curran, who is in custody, is being tried in his absence and does not have legal representation. The case, revived more than a decade after the killing, continues as jurors weigh the prosecution’s account against Curran’s denial and the defense’s contention that the apparent connections are a matter of chance.

Usha Ram says her manager gave her permission to take home the food. A British Columbia judge has ordered damages for a longtime Burger King employee who was fired after taking a fish sandwich, fries, and an orange soda without paying, ruling the dismissal was “unreasonable, unfair and unduly insensitive.” Usha Ram, a 55-year-old immigrant from Fiji, had worked at various Burger King locations around Vancouver for 24 years and was the sole earner for her household. Justice Lisa Warren found that Ram’s employers failed to properly consider her age, limited education, and English skills when they terminated her in January 2014. At the time, Ram earned about $21,000 a year working full-time. Her husband is physically disabled, and she supports an adult daughter with a mental disability. The incident occurred on Boxing Day in 2013, when Ram asked store manager Tayyaba Salman in Hindi if she could take home some food because she had forgotten her wallet. “Can I have a fish?” Ram asked, using her native language. The restaurant’s policy permits employees to have free beverages during their shift and receive a 50% discount on food; managers are allowed to make exceptions. According to court documents, the dispute hinged on what Ram meant by “a fish”: she testified she intended a combo meal, while Salman interpreted the request as a single sandwich. Salman told the court there is no word for “sandwich” in Hindi. Ram left the restaurant with a fish sandwich, medium fries, and an orange soda without paying. Salman reported the incident to franchise co-owner Janif Mohammed. After applying the employee discount, the value of the fries and drink was approximately 50 cents. On December 30, Ram was called into the office with Salman and Mohammed, where she was accused of theft. Ram began to cry and offered to pay for the food, but Mohammed told her to go home. He later told the judge that her offer to pay was an admission of theft. Ram was fired shortly afterward without severance. Mohammed, who defended himself in court, described Ram as an exemplary employee, a “wonderful lady” and a “good worker.” The two had worked together since 1989. Nevertheless, he said he terminated her to send a warning to other staff against theft. Justice Warren rejected that approach, emphasizing that the circumstances called for greater care. “Had he simply turned his mind to the specific words that Ms Salman said Ms Ram used when she asked to take the food, or the fact that Ms Ram made no attempt to conceal what she was doing, he would likely have appreciated the significant possibility of a misunderstanding between Ms Ram and Ms Salman,” she wrote. The judge ordered Mohammed and his co-owner, Michael Lacombe, to pay Ram $21,000 in general damages, equivalent to one year’s severance, and $25,000 in aggravated damages for emotional distress. The ruling underscores the importance of considering language barriers and employee vulnerabilities when imposing discipline in the workplace.

England seized a dramatic victory in the first Test against South Africa in Durban, claiming six wickets for just 38 runs on the final morning to wrap up the match and take a 1-0 lead in the series. The visitors, who regained the Ashes this summer but lost a series to Pakistan last month, closed out their year with a composed performance built on disciplined batting and relentless bowling, making it six wins from 14 Tests in 2015. Captain Alastair Cook praised his side’s resilience and potential, while warning that sustained hard work will be required to turn promise into a consistent run of results. “Potentially this team can do some really good things,” Cook said. “There’s so much talent in this side but it will take relentless hard work.” Cook also cautioned against complacency ahead of the second Test in Cape Town, which starts on Saturday. England have not won at Newlands since 1957, when Denis Compton played a pivotal role in a 312-run victory—a poignant link given that his grandson, Nick Compton, anchored England’s first innings in Durban with a patient 85 from 236 balls. “The way Nick played really set up the first innings,” Cook said. “He was a rock for us in that first innings. From that moment on, the guys bowled particularly well to take 20 wickets and we scored enough runs in the second innings.” Compton’s return to the Test side after being out since May 2013 was one of several key contributions from England’s lineup, complemented by controlled spells from the seamers and timely breakthroughs from the spinners that steadily applied pressure to South Africa’s batting. The hosts’ collapse on day five underscored England’s ability to close out sessions and capitalize on small openings. There was encouraging news on James Anderson, England’s leading Test wicket-taker, who missed the Durban Test with a calf injury but was seen bowling at the ground before the final day began. “He has had a tough week, bowling a lot and doing rehab. Hopefully he’ll be fit,” Cook said. “He is hopeful of playing and it’s looking good but we’ll know in the next 48 hours.” Wicketkeeper-batsman Jonny Bairstow expressed relief after claiming England’s first stumping in 38 Tests, dismissing Temba Bavuma a day after he missed a similar chance to remove AB de Villiers. “It doesn’t necessarily make up for it because I was desperately disappointed to miss it. You work so hard on your game that when the opportunity arises you like to take it,” Bairstow told BBC Test Match Special. “To get another one and get into the game was really pleasing and something I can take forward.” Despite South Africa’s batting frailties in Durban, Bairstow echoed Cook’s respect for the world’s top-ranked Test side. “They are not the number one side in the world for nothing,” he said. “We’ve got to be mentally and physically prepared for what is going to be a very tough battle in the New Year Test match.” With momentum on their side, England now turn their focus to Cape Town, aiming to press home their advantage while staying grounded against a proud, formidable opponent on home soil.

Supreme Court president Lord Neuberger has warned that reduced access to legal aid risks producing inefficient claims that ultimately cost the court system more, while denying justice to those most in need. In a speech delivered at the annual Tom Sargant Memorial Lecture, organized by legal campaign group Justice, he cautioned that recent changes to legal aid and proposals to curb judicial review could undermine the rule of law. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) argues the legal aid budget is unsustainable, describing the annual £2bn bill as “costing too much” and defending plans to cut £350m from the system. An MoJ spokesperson said the reforms will “create a sustainable legal aid system that will still be one of the most generous in the world,” adding that the sector cannot be immune from the government’s broader drive to secure better value for taxpayers.
