Lord Neuberger countered that cutting legal aid disproportionately affects those who most rely on the courts. “Cutting the cost of legal aid deprives the very people who most need the protection of the courts of the ability to get legal advice and representation,” he said, noting that recent changes have reduced the types of claim eligible for support and increased the stringency of the criteria. He warned of two likely consequences when people with potential claims cannot access legal aid. “The first is that the claim is dropped—that is a rank denial of justice and a blot on the rule of law,” he said. “The second is that the claim is pursued, in which case it will be pursued inefficiently, and will take up much more of the court staff’s time and of the judge’s time in and out of court.” Such cases, he argued, lead to greater costs and delays across the system. Lord Neuberger also urged ministers to be “very careful” about restricting the right to judicial review, the legal mechanism by which individuals can challenge decisions of local councils and public authorities. While acknowledging that moves to discourage weak applications are “understandable, even laudable,” he stressed the fundamental importance of judicial review. “One must be very careful about any proposals whose aim is to cut down the right to judicial review. The courts have no more important function than that of protecting citizens from the abuses and excesses of the executive—central government, local government, or other public bodies.” The debate underscores the tension between making public services more efficient and safeguarding access to justice, with senior judicial figures urging caution as the government pursues savings in the justice system.

Video shows Mr Trudeau walking into a crowd and taking Opposition Whip Gord Brown by his arm in an apparent attempt to steer him to his seat. New Democratic Party MP Ruth-Ellen Brosseau said she was "elbowed in the chest" in the ensuing scuffle. Mr Trudeau later apologised to Ms Brosseau of Quebec "unreservedly". Liberal Party leader Mr Trudeau also had a heated verbal exchange with New Democratic Party leader Tom Mulcair. "What kind of man elbows a woman? It's pathetic! You're pathetic!" Mr Mulcair shouted at Mr Trudeau in the incident caught on video. The CBC reported that Mr Trudeau lost his temper and shouted an expletive. The incident is considered a rare misstep for the young prime minister who is popular at home and abroad. "I have never seen a display of bully behaviour by a Canadian politician let alone a prime minister as I witnessed just now in the chamber," said David Sweet, a Conservative MP from Ontario. The row appears to have begun when Mr Trudeau sought to put an end to Mr Brown's speech in the House after accusing him of deliberately speaking slowly. Elizabeth May, a Green Party MP from British Columbia, said opposition MPs were engaging in "mischief" to delay the vote. Several lawmakers were concerned about the breakdown in civility in the House of Commons. "We don't want to become a House of Commons from some country you watch on CNN," Ms May said. The confrontation intensified scrutiny of parliamentary decorum, underscoring tensions over procedural tactics and the prime minister’s handling of an unusually chaotic moment on the floor. Trudeau’s swift apology sought to contain the fallout, but the video sparked wider debate on standards of conduct in Canada’s legislature.

Unlike the SNP and the Greens, Plaid have not seen any rise in support reflected in recent polls Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood has said she expects an improvement in her party’s polling following last week’s televised leaders’ debate, arguing that Plaid presented a strong and distinctive platform for Wales. Speaking on BBC Wales’ Wales Today on Friday, Wood urged observers to “let us see the result of the polls that would have been taken after the TV debate that has been quite a success for Plaid Cymru.” The debate was broadcast on 2 April. Wood said feedback from viewers suggested Plaid had effectively communicated its priorities, including securing a “decent funding settlement” for Wales and addressing what she described as the country’s “powers problems.” “We have managed to get across a strong platform for Wales,” she said, adding that she believes “the next polls should see an improvement in our fortunes.” She also clarified Plaid Cymru’s stance on potential post-election cooperation, reiterating that the party would consider a deal with Labour only in the event of a hung parliament. “I do not think people in Wales would find it very acceptable for Plaid Cymru to allow another Conservative government,” Wood said. “People in Wales have never given the Conservatives a mandate. In many communities in Wales people feel very, very strongly against the Conservatives because of Mrs Thatcher’s deliberate de-industrialisation.” Defending her call for the Welsh Assembly to receive an additional £1.2bn from Westminster, Wood argued that Wales is “trying to close the gap with our hands tied behind our backs.” She highlighted limited Welsh powers over natural resources as a barrier to economic growth, and said achieving parity with Scotland in both resources and devolved powers is a central issue for Plaid in this election. The interview with Wood was the fourth in a Wales Today series featuring Welsh political leaders, as parties seek to define their positions ahead of the upcoming vote.

Heat expert says Pte Gavin Williams’s heat illness was not recognised before fatal ‘beasting’ on one of 2006’s hottest days Pte Gavin Williams, 22, of Hengoed, Caerphilly county, collapsed at Lucknow Barracks in Wiltshire on one of the hottest days of 2006 and later died after being made to complete intensive exercise as an informal punishment for drunken behaviour and being absent without leave, an inquest heard. Heat expert Dr Daniel Roiz De Sa told the coroner, Judge Alan Large, that the hot weather risk level on the day Williams died was high and established guidance suggested he should not have been exercising for more than one hour within any 90-minute period. He said Williams’s heat illness symptoms were not recognised and there was “no clear assessment of the risk that the environment would have on the exercise of an individual” that day. The inquest has previously been told that ecstasy was found in Williams’s bloodstream when he died and that he was likely to have been dehydrated before the “beasting”. Witnesses have disputed how long he was made to exercise, with some suggesting it lasted for more than an hour, potentially breaching the recommended limits given the extreme heat. The hearing also learned that a doctor who treated Williams had already seen another soldier for heat-related illness earlier in the day. However, no information was disseminated to other staff to warn them about the heightened risk posed by the conditions, the inquest was told. The proceedings aim to establish the circumstances surrounding Williams’s death and whether adequate safeguards, communication, and risk assessments were in place to protect personnel during extreme heat. The inquest continues.

The firm has produced UK future energy scenarios covering four different approaches in policy. Even in the most environmentally minded scenario, the UK is projected to fail in its target of producing 15% of total energy from renewables. The government no longer claims the 2020 target will be hit but a spokesman said the UK was making good progress. The National Grid also says the UK will not achieve its own independently set long-term CO2 reduction plans unless tougher policies are imposed very soon. The Climate Change Act mandates emissions cuts of 80% by 2050. The government spokesman said the UK was still committed to the act, and last week ministers announced a world-leading interim step towards that goal. But the government’s independent advisers, the Committee on Climate Change (CCC), have warned of a sizeable gap between ministerial ambition and the policies currently in place to deliver it. Their assessment echoes concerns in the National Grid’s scenarios, which explore four pathways and consistently highlight the need for accelerated action across transport and heating, not just electricity. The report notes that Britain’s progress in wind and solar-powered electricity has been faster than many anticipated, helping to decarbonise the power sector. However, meeting the wider EU 2020 renewables obligation—which spans electricity, heat, and transport—will require a dramatic uptick elsewhere. The rate of progress towards electric and hydrogen vehicles must nearly triple, rising from 15 terawatt hours (TWh) to 40 TWh. Uptake of clean heating systems such as heat pumps faces an even steeper climb, increasing from 35 TWh to 95 TWh. On National Grid’s low-ambition scenario, the UK misses the targets by nine years; even the greenest scenario reaches compliance only by 2022. The renewables targets are legally binding, and the EU may consider penalties for nations that fall short. The UK’s energy system is tightly interconnected with Europe, benefiting from electricity imports via undersea interconnectors. It remains unclear how these links might evolve following the UK’s 23 June referendum decision to leave the EU, but whatever the future relationship, the domestic Climate Change Act will continue to set the trajectory for emissions reductions. To ensure a cost-effective pathway to 2050, the National Grid outlines a balanced technology mix: 22 gigawatts (GW) of nuclear capacity, 100 GW of renewables, and 20 GW of fossil fuel generation fitted with carbon capture and storage (CCS). “The 2050 targets are still achievable, but we need much more momentum,” a spokesman told BBC News. “The government has to change the trajectory or we are going to fail. We need to learn our lessons from where things have gone wrong so far.” Yet the government faces hurdles. It has struggled to bring new nuclear plants to fruition and scrapped a dedicated CCS funding program, despite then-Prime Minister David Cameron previously calling the technology “crucial.” He later said CCS was “not working,” citing costs that had not fallen as expected. The findings add urgency to calls for clear, durable policy and investment signals to bridge the gap between ambition and delivery.

title: After high-level talks between both sides, one Russian official involved said the row had "almost" been resolved. A long-running diplomatic dispute between Washington and Moscow over two Russian government compounds shut down in the United States appears close to resolution after high-level talks in the US capital. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov, speaking to reporters following a three-hour meeting with US Undersecretary of State Thomas Shannon on Monday, said the spat was “almost” settled, signaling a potential breakthrough after months of recriminations and stalled dialogue. US officials offered no immediate comment and there was no formal readout of the meeting, leaving details of any emerging compromise unclear. The talks had been postponed since June, when the US expanded sanctions over Russia’s activities in Ukraine by adding 38 individuals and entities to its blacklist. That move prompted Moscow to cancel a previously scheduled session in St Petersburg and harden its stance on the compounds. The dispute dates back to December, when the Obama administration expelled 35 Russian diplomats and closed two recreational properties used by Russian personnel in Maryland and New York, citing suspicions of Kremlin-directed meddling in the US presidential election. Then-President Barack Obama’s punitive measures followed US intelligence assessments that Russian state actors hacked Democratic Party computers to undermine Hillary Clinton’s campaign, allegations the Kremlin has consistently denied. Moscow has demanded unconditional restoration of access to the facilities, portraying the US actions as violations of diplomatic norms. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said before the latest talks that Russia considered it “absolutely unacceptable to place conditions on the return of diplomatic property,” insisting the sites “must be returned without any conditions and talking.” Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov went further, calling the US move “daylight robbery” and arguing it was not how “decent and well-brought-up people” behaved. “How can you seize property which is protected by a bilateral, inter-governmental, ratified document and, to return it, act according to the principle ‘what is mine is mine, and what is yours we’ll share’?” he said during a visit to Belarus. Russia has warned it would retaliate if the compounds are not returned, with officials floating “specific measures” including the expulsion of up to 30 American diplomats and the seizure of US state property inside Russia. The newspaper Izvestia reported that a failure to reach compromise in the Shannon–Ryabkov talks would trigger those steps, underscoring the stakes for both sides. The broader political climate in Washington complicates any settlement. President Donald Trump’s team remains under investigation over alleged Russian collusion during the 2016 campaign, and congressional and special counsel inquiries into election interference have intensified scrutiny of US–Russia contacts. That makes concessions to Moscow politically fraught, even as the White House has sought improved ties. Russia, for its part, said President Trump presented “no plan to resolve the crisis” when the issue was raised at the G20 summit in Hamburg on 7 July, though officials praised the tone of the leaders’ meeting. A resolution on the compounds could remove a prominent irritant in relations already strained by sanctions, competing narratives about the 2016 election, and deep mutual suspicion. But with no US briefing and Moscow insisting on unconditional terms, it remains uncertain what framework is being considered. If talks falter, a new round of expulsions and property seizures could follow, further complicating already delicate diplomacy. For now, both sides appear to be testing whether the impasse can be defused without igniting a broader confrontation.

Lincolnshire Trust For Cats has almost 80 cats living out the end of their nine lives, with luxuries including heated beds, sofas and an open fire. Some of the cats live there because their owners have died, while other owners have moved abroad. Finding new homes for elderly cats like these is more difficult because people prefer to adopt young cats. Older cats can also be more expensive to look after, due to veterinary bills, so many are put down when their owners die. Trust founder Jain Hills believes the home is unique. "I know of some charities that have a few elderly cats, but they are not doing it on the scale we are," she said. "For cats to come to us people have either got to make a provision in their will, or people come to look round. I don't think anywhere else does it because people come all the way from London with the cats to come here." Set on seven acres on the outskirts of Osgodby, the sanctuary offers a retirement home tailored to feline comfort. “There's three sitting rooms and they are connected by enclosed outdoor areas,” Hills said. “It's all south-facing which means the cats have a lot of sunbathing options.” Heated beds, sofas, and an open fire create a homely environment where elderly cats can relax without the stress of competing for attention in traditional shelters. While the retirement home cares for nearly 80 senior residents, the trust looks after about 400 cats in total, running a separate rescue facility for abandoned cats in need of new owners. Hills says demand for places often comes from families settling estates or people heading overseas, and she encourages owners to plan ahead. “For cats to come to us people have either got to make a provision in their will,” she noted. Despite presiding over hundreds of cats, Hills says she is “a bit of a dog person.” “I've got five dogs at home,” she said. “When you work with 400 cats all day you need to go home to a dog. I couldn't run a dog charity but I can run a cat charity because I can stand back from it. I don't get emotionally involved.”

Liverpool City Council has confirmed it is in talks with two city-based organisations to take on the management of St Luke’s Church, the Grade II* listed landmark left roofless after a 1941 air raid. The move follows speculation that a Manchester company was involved; the council said the proposals now under consideration come from within Liverpool and that it will retain the site’s freehold. “We want to achieve the best possible outcome,” a spokesman said. “Once these discussions have concluded and an agreement has been reached, a recommendation will go to the Cabinet for a decision to be made.” Located at the corner of Leece Street and Berry Street, St Luke’s has remained without a roof since wartime damage. A survey after severe winter storms in 2015 found the structure needed to be made safe. Full restoration, valued at £500,000, would include works to the tower, masonry and low-level stonework, the installation of a roof on the church tower, and repairs to decorative stonework.

A police officer assigned to investigate an assault on a woman at her home in north Belfast has been found guilty of misconduct and disciplined, following a Police Ombudsman investigation that uncovered significant failings in how the case was handled. The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) accepted the Ombudsman’s recommendation that the officer attend a formal disciplinary hearing after the victim’s criminal case collapsed in court 11 months after the incident. The attack took place when a group of women confronted the victim at her property, apparently in retaliation for an alleged assault on one of their daughters the previous evening. According to the victim, she was dragged into her garden, kicked and punched to the body and head, and struck with a golf umbrella. The assault ended only when a man intervened. After the case was dismissed, the victim lodged a complaint with the Police Ombudsman’s office, alleging that failings in the police investigation had contributed to its collapse. She also said a prosecuting officer from the Public Prosecution Service (PPS) had told her there were gaps in the police case file. Ombudsman investigators obtained police documentation relating to both the attack and the incident the night before, which had apparently triggered the confrontation. They interviewed the investigating officer, his sergeant, and two inspectors. The PPS prosecuting officer provided a written account detailing concerns about the completeness and quality of the case file submitted by the investigating officer. The Ombudsman’s enquiries revealed what was described as “an alarming number of missed investigative opportunities.” No witnesses were interviewed, there was no house-to-house canvass or CCTV enquiries, and no searches were conducted at the scene or at the suspects’ homes. Investigators found that no consideration had been given to forensic opportunities, no photographs of the victim’s injuries were taken, and there was no formal process to identify those responsible. There were also delays in interviewing suspects, and when interviews did occur they were of poor quality with no follow-up questioning. The investigating officer failed to communicate with a colleague looking into the earlier incident and did not reference that incident in the file sent to the PPS. He ignored printouts of relevant Facebook messages provided by the victim and did not adequately update her on the progress of the case. Additionally, he disregarded directions from supervising officers and misled them about the steps taken to advance the investigation. When interviewed by Police Ombudsman investigators, the officer’s account was found to be misleading and lacking credibility. The Ombudsman recommended that he be required to attend a formal disciplinary hearing. The PSNI accepted the recommendation, and the officer was found guilty of misconduct and disciplined. The investigation concluded that the inspectors involved had not committed misconduct, as they had been misled about the progress of the case. The sergeant overseeing the investigation was also misled, but the Ombudsman determined he should have given the case closer scrutiny. The PSNI has implemented the recommendation that the sergeant be disciplined.

Waverley Borough Council said preparatory work on Farnham’s Brightwells redevelopment will begin in September, after the government confirmed a compulsory purchase order for the Marlborough Head pub and approved the removal of two public footpaths. The long-delayed scheme, first approved in 2008, includes a new town square, cinema, shops and 239 homes. It was held up by protests over the loss of the theatre, increased traffic, tree removal and impacts on historic features.

The Supreme Court ruled that oil and gas exploration near the community of Clyde River cannot go ahead. The unanimous decision stated Canada failed in its duty to consult the tiny Inuit hamlet about the impact of seismic testing near their community. The court heard the case in November. Wednesday's decision helps clarify the federal government's duty to consult with indigenous groups on development projects. In a unanimous ruling, Canada’s highest court quashed National Energy Board (NEB) authorization for offshore seismic testing near Clyde River, Nunavut, finding that federal officials failed to adequately consult the Inuit community about potential impacts on their treaty rights and way of life. While the Court affirmed that Ottawa may rely on the NEB’s regulatory process to fulfill its duty to consult on energy projects, it held that, in this instance, the process fell short of constitutional standards. The decision stems from a 2014 NEB approval allowing three energy companies to conduct a five-year seismic survey under the ocean around Baffin Island. Clyde River, a northern hamlet of fewer than 1,000 residents, relies heavily on hunting and fishing for food and trade, and holds established rights to harvest marine mammals. The community argued that the loud underwater blasts used in seismic testing could harm marine wildlife and disrupt migration routes—concerns the NEB’s own environmental assessment acknowledged as risks. The Court noted that although consultations took place, they were inadequate in substance and accessibility. Community members asked basic questions about effects on marine mammals, but proponents were unable to answer many of them. Key documents were difficult to download due to their size, and only a fraction was translated into Inuktitut, the local language, limiting meaningful participation. Jerry Natanine, former mayor of Clyde River, welcomed the outcome of what he called a “seemingly impossible case.” He said, “Justice is on our side. We’re fighting for our life, our way of life.” Natanine emphasized that residents are not opposed to development but want transparent discussions and negotiations about risks and compensation before projects proceed. The campaign against the survey drew national and international attention, with support from celebrities including Leonardo DiCaprio, Emma Thompson, Jane Fonda, and Oprah Winfrey. Greenpeace Canada also backed the effort, contributing to legal costs. The ruling provides important guidance on how the federal duty to consult Indigenous communities must be met, particularly in resource development. It clarifies that while the NEB can serve as the vehicle for consultation, the Crown remains ultimately responsible for ensuring the process is robust and responsive to community concerns. The Clyde River decision was issued alongside a separate case involving the Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, which challenged Enbridge’s plan to reverse and expand its Line 9 pipeline in southwestern Ontario. In that matter, the Supreme Court found that the community had been adequately consulted, underscoring that the sufficiency of consultation depends on the specific circumstances and the quality of engagement in each case.

Murder investigation after man found collapsed at Benson Road tram stop in Winson Green British Transport Police launched a murder investigation after a man in his 50s was found collapsed at Benson Road tram stop in Winson Green and pronounced dead at the scene. Officers were alerted around 16:50 BST; they are working to determine whether the victim was stabbed on the platform approach or injured elsewhere. Det Chief Insp Tony Fitzpatrick, leading the inquiry with West Midlands Police, said detectives are still establishing how the man sustained his injuries and urged anyone in the area during rush hour to come forward. Witnesses or anyone with CCTV, mobile footage, or information are asked to contact BTP. Investigators appealed to commuters to check phones and dashcams for images that might assist.

Johnston Press has announced a restructuring of its editorial operations in Scotland as it grapples with the accelerating shift in media consumption and mounting pressure on traditional print businesses. The Edinburgh-based publisher said it is overhauling its newsroom structure to address audiences migrating to digital platforms and the influence of industry giants such as Google and Facebook, which it says have reshaped how people discover and read news. While the company did not disclose how many jobs could be lost, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) said 25 posts are under threat across 24 of Johnston Press’s 28 Scottish weekly titles. In a statement, the publisher acknowledged the pace of change in the media industry “is showing no signs of abating” and noted that over the past year, numerous newspapers have closed or been put up for sale as publishers struggle to adapt. “This restructure is designed to ensure our news brands are able to continue to serve their communities—as their only source of trusted local news,” the company said. “However, it does mean that there will be a significant reduction in the number of editorial roles. We are working closely with the NUJ in Scotland, and will continue to do so, in order to ensure we can achieve the best outcome for affected staff within the new structure.” NUJ Scottish organiser Paul Holleran said members were “shocked at the scale of proposed job losses” and now recognized the long-term precarious position of 24 Johnston Press Scottish titles. Holleran added that management has so far worked closely with the union, providing information, maximizing consultation, and responding positively during initial talks. “We have been told that their plans will put these titles into profitability,” he said. “From our point of view we want to save all the titles, protect the journalists who will continue to work on these papers and get the best possible deal for those members who choose to leave the business. They have agreed a sensible timeframe for consultation and negotiation and I am hopeful agreement can be reached as soon as is practicable.” According to the NUJ, four titles are not facing job cuts: the Falkirk Herald, Fife Free Press, Southern Reporter, and Stornoway Gazette. The union said these have been identified as “prime” titles that will receive additional support to target potential growth. The restructuring underscores the challenges facing local news providers as they navigate rapid digital transition, changing reader habits, and the dominance of global platforms, while seeking to remain viable and maintain trusted coverage in the communities they serve.

Bangladesh is grappling with targeted violence after five secularists were killed in recent months, amid claims by an Islamist group that it carried out the latest attack on a publisher. Professor Anisuzzaman, a scholar of Bengali literature at Dhaka University, said he received a death threat by text message and filed a police complaint. He joined several public figures in urging the government to act. The United States has issued a travel alert for Bangladesh, urging Americans to be cautious following the recent killings of two foreigners. A Japanese man was shot dead last month and an Italian aid worker was killed in Dhaka in September in attacks claimed by the Islamic State militant group. “There is reliable information to suggest that terrorist attacks could occur against foreigners in Bangladesh, including against large gatherings of foreigners,” the State Department said. Anisuzzaman told bdnews24.com the message “asked in proper English why I support bloggers and if I wanted to die on being struck by machete,” highlighting risks for secular voices. The attacks have stoked fear among academics and publishers, prompting calls for protection.

Great Britain opened their Sultan Azlan Shah Cup campaign with a 1-1 draw against India in Ipoh, Malaysia, after a two-hour delay caused by an electrical storm. India struck first in the second quarter when Akashdeep Singh reacted quickest to a penalty corner rebound. Tom Carson levelled before half-time with a fine finish, but Mandeep Singh restored India’s advantage from close range early in the third period. A trademark poacher’s goal from Alan Forsyth in the final quarter ensured GB took a point. The match marked the first use of video referrals at the tournament, and Britain benefited when a third-quarter penalty corner awarded to India was overturned. GB had a late penalty corner of their own but could not convert, leaving the sides even at the whistle. Defending champions Australia began their bid for a record-extending 10th title with a 1-1 draw against New Zealand. The six-team event features round-robin, four-quarter matches. GB, who last won the trophy in 1994 when competing as England, face outsiders Japan on Sunday.

Title: Sgt Elor Azaria, 19, shot Abdul Fatah al-Sharif in the head while the 21-year-old was apparently incapacitated in Hebron, in the West Bank, in March. The soldier denies violating the Israeli military's rules of engagement without operational justification. The incident, which was caught on video, has divided opinion in Israel. Human rights groups say Sgt Azaria carried out an extra-judicial killing, while thousands of people who believe he did nothing wrong attended rallies in support of him last month. The trial of Israeli army medic Sgt Elor Azaria began Monday, drawing intense public attention and exposing deep divisions in Israeli society over the rules governing force and accountability in conflict zones. Azaria is accused of shooting dead Abdul Fatah al-Sharif, a 21-year-old Palestinian, in Hebron in March after Sharif had allegedly taken part in a stabbing attack and was lying wounded on the ground. As the proceedings opened, Azaria sat on a bench inside the courtroom while the head of the three-judge military panel read out the indictment. Prosecutors allege that Azaria “violated the rules of engagement without operational justification as the terrorist was lying on the ground wounded and represented no immediate threat for the accused or others who were present.” The soldier has denied wrongdoing, insisting he acted out of concern for the safety of those at the scene. Defense attorney Binyamin Malka told reporters, “The truth will come out. The path will be long. We will endure,” signaling that the defense will challenge both the prosecution’s interpretation of the rules of engagement and the circumstances captured on video. Sharif and another Palestinian, Ramzi Aziz al-Qasrawi, had stabbed and wounded an Israeli soldier in Hebron on March 24 before troops shot Qasrawi dead and wounded Sharif. Video recorded by a Palestinian witness and released by an Israeli human rights group shows Sharif alive several minutes later, when a soldier identified as Azaria cocks his rifle and shoots Sharif in the head from several meters away. Azaria told military police that he perceived a continuing threat, observing Sharif move his head and hand toward a knife and fearing the possibility of an explosive device. However, army investigators reported that before firing, Azaria told a comrade the wounded man “deserved to die” for stabbing his friend. On Sunday night, Israel’s Channel 2 aired new footage that appeared to show the knife at least one meter away from Sharif. The case has sparked large-scale demonstrations and a polarized debate over soldier conduct and oversight. Human rights organizations have condemned the shooting as an extra-judicial killing, while thousands rallied last month in support of Azaria, arguing he acted reasonably in a tense, dangerous environment. The incident unfolds amid a broader wave of violence since October, in which 29 Israelis have been killed in stabbings, shootings, or car-rammings carried out by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. About 200 Palestinians have been killed in the same period, most while attacking or during clashes, according to Israeli authorities. The trial is expected to continue for weeks, with testimony from witnesses, forensic experts, and commanders central to determining whether Azaria’s actions violated military law.

Police are appealing for witnesses after a three-car crash on the B921 between Kinglassie and Cardenden around 14:30 this afternoon. The incident involved a Jaguar, BMW and Citroen. The BMW’s 42-year-old driver is being treated for serious injuries at Edinburgh Royal Infirmary. The 62-year-old woman driving the Citroen and her young female passenger were also seriously hurt and taken to Victoria Hospital in Kirkcaldy. Four others sustained minor injuries: the 75-year-old Jaguar driver, two passengers in the BMW, and a second passenger in the Citroen. Insp Brenda Sinclair urged anyone who was on the road at the time and witnessed the collision to contact police immediately as inquiries continue.

The Premier League is facing mounting scrutiny over its pledge to improve stadium facilities for disabled fans, amid warnings that a significant number of clubs will miss an August 2017 deadline to comply with official guidance. The commitment, made last year, followed a 2014 BBC investigation that found 17 of the 20 top-flight clubs failed to provide enough wheelchair spaces. Advocacy groups say progress has been too slow despite the league’s wealth and global profile. Joyce Cook, chair of the fan-led charity Level Playing Field, described the delays as “unacceptable” and warned that the problem is more widespread than the league admits. “We think up to a third of clubs are not going to meet this pledge,” she said. “This is a promise that they made themselves, they set their own deadline.” It is understood that Liverpool are among the clubs set to miss the deadline, even after spending £100m to redevelop Anfield’s Main Stand. While the club has upgraded facilities for disabled supporters, the improvements reportedly do not yet go far enough to meet the requirements set out in the Accessible Stadia Guidelines. Liverpool did not comment when contacted. Chelsea are also expected to fall short. A spokesperson acknowledged the issue’s importance but pointed to structural limitations at Stamford Bridge. “This is an issue we take very seriously, however we are constrained by an old stadium,” the spokesperson said. The club has submitted a planning application for a comprehensive redevelopment of the ground. “If approved, [it] will see the construction of a new stadium that will exceed the Accessible Stadia Guidelines,” the spokesperson added. Pressure on the league has intensified, with Lord Holmes of the Equality and Human Rights Commission warning that clubs could face legal action if they fail to comply. “There are clear sanctions in the Equality Act which Premier League clubs may find themselves on the end of,” he said. Criticising what he sees as misplaced priorities, he added: “HD cameras, extensions to hospitality areas, that’s done in a heartbeat. I think anyone out there would understand that it’s perfectly reasonable for a Premier League club to be accessible. We have the richest, the most profitable league on the planet. That has to be the most inclusive league as well otherwise it is morally bankrupt.” Level Playing Field, which campaigns to ensure all fans can enjoy an equal experience at live sports events, has called for strong penalties for clubs that do not meet the standards. “We certainly look at sanctions when it comes to things like financial fair play, and this should have the same impact,” Cook said. The Premier League, when approached by BBC Sport, insisted it is working hard to improve disabled access across all grounds. “The commitments made in this area are wide-ranging and will set new standards for sport and other sectors,” a statement read. “All clubs are working towards making their grounds meet the appropriate standards in the agreed timescale.” Some clubs say they are on track. Watford stated they are “very confident” of being fully compliant by August 2017. Crystal Palace said they have “met with architects” and are “working diligently on all aspects of the Accessible Stadia Guidelines and will continue to do so over the coming months.” As the deadline approaches, campaigners and regulators alike will be watching closely to see whether the league’s richest teams can deliver meaningful change for disabled supporters.

Amazon has urged customers in the UK to dispose of certain self-balancing scooters, commonly known as hoverboards, after safety concerns prompted a widespread crackdown by authorities and retailers. In an email to buyers, the company told customers who purchased devices with “non-compliant UK plugs” to take the products to a recycling centre registered to handle electrical items “as soon as possible,” and said refunds would be processed automatically within three days. The company said: We regret the inconvenience this may cause you but trust you will understand that your safety and satisfaction is our highest priority. The move follows action by Trading Standards, which recently seized 15,000 unsafe boards attempting to enter the UK. Officials said that 88% of the scooters examined since 15 October were detained, largely due to non-compliant electrical components that could overheat, catch fire, or explode. Many boards were found with plugs lacking fuses, cut-off switches that failed during testing, and chargers, cabling and batteries that did not meet safety standards. The London Fire Brigade has warned about the risks, reporting that at least three house fires in a 10-day period in October were linked to hoverboards. Authorities have urged consumers to be vigilant and to avoid using products that show signs of electrical faults, as well as to ensure charging is done safely and in accordance with manufacturer guidance. Retailers have moved swiftly in response. Amazon is understood to have stopped selling the devices, while Argos and John Lewis have reportedly pulled them from sale. A Tesco spokesman said: We’ve suspended the sale of all hoverboards both in store and online as a precautionary measure. In addition to issuing refunds for units with non-compliant plugs, Amazon said it had sent a separate email to customers who purchased boards with compliant UK plugs, offering guidance on safe battery and plug use as a precaution. Those customers who prefer not to keep their product have been advised to contact Amazon customer services. Consumer groups and watchdogs have backed the crackdown. The Retail Ombudsman urged UK retailers to remove unsafe devices from sale or face the risk of the full force of the Consumer Protection Act. Chief ombudsman Dean Dunham said retailers could be held liable for injuries caused by unsafe goods, and told BBC Radio 5 live that people who have bought any type of hoverboard should return them to the place of purchase for a refund. I think you’ve got to err on the side of caution and take it back, he said. We don’t know enough information about these to be able to go out to the public and say, ‘If you spend a lot of money on one of these, it will be fine.’ Trading Standards is advising consumers to report suspect products and sellers. Anyone who finds such items for sale is urged to contact the Citizens Advice helpline on 03454 04 05 06. Reflecting mounting safety concerns, several major airlines, including American, Delta and United, have banned hoverboards from flights, citing the fire risk posed by their batteries.

Aviva chief decries ‘dysfunctional’ UK car insurance as premiums jump 11% Aviva’s chief executive has called the UK car insurance market “dysfunctional”, accusing firms of enticing new customers with “too low” prices and then pushing up premiums for existing policyholders. “I think that the UK car insurance market is dysfunctional, I don’t think it works properly,” Mr Wilson told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “The entry level is too low and then it gets put up for all existing customers.” His comments came as the Association of British Insurers said average car insurance premiums have risen 11% over the past year, taking the typical annual bill to £484. Mr Wilson said Aviva has developed a suite of products, due before the end of the year, aimed at rewarding loyal customers rather than prioritising introductory deals. “Let’s see how it goes,” he added, noting that motor insurance represents just 2% of Aviva’s overall business. Aviva shares rose about 0.5% after the insurer reported an 8% rise in first-half 2017 operating profits. Sales of annuities, bulk annuities and equity release products increased, with growth particularly strong in the UK. The board lifted the dividend by 13%. Asked about his own remuneration, Mr Wilson declined to say whether he is paid too much. “I think I’ll let the shareholders answer that one,” he said. He added that Aviva would be happy to publish the ratio of its highest paid employee to its lowest once the government decides how it should be calculated. Aviva already pays staff the National Living Wage and requires all contractors to do the same.

Police are treating as arson a blaze that damaged the clubhouse at Wellingborough Town’s Dog & Duck ground, shared with AFC Rushden & Diamonds. The fire broke out in the early hours of Monday at the stadium behind the Dog & Duck pub, destroying club memorabilia and damaging bar stock, furniture and toilets. While the clubhouse remains out of action, electricians are checking the site and a local firm has installed a pop-up bar so the Diamonds can continue to operate on matchday. AFC Rushden & Diamonds said the changing rooms are being professionally cleaned and confirmed Saturday’s home fixture against Beaconsfield SYCOB will go ahead as normal. “The club would like to place on record its gratitude to the numerous offers of help,” a statement added. The non-league ground is home to both the Diamonds and Wellingborough Town; the Doughboys are due to play away at Wisbech on Saturday. Police inquiries continue.

Illnesses associated with working in the construction industry are thought to kill more than 4,000 people across the UK every year, with experts warning that 2015 will see a peak in cases. Campaigners and clinicians are urging earlier detection to improve outcomes, as families affected by asbestos-related disease call for routine screening. Clydeside Action on Asbestos, Scotland’s largest asbestos charity, said enhanced screening could extend lives by catching conditions such as mesothelioma sooner. At its annual general meeting on Saturday, the charity called for investment in routine X-rays or a simple blood test capable of detecting asbestos-related illnesses at an earlier stage. Chairwoman Phyllis Craig said early diagnosis enables people “to start making plans for their life and their families and so forth, but also to receive any form of treatment that may be available.” Mesothelioma is a form of cancer most commonly caused by exposure to asbestos, which was widely used in construction and other industries for decades. The disease is frequently diagnosed late, when symptoms such as breathlessness and chest pain become apparent, limiting treatment options and survival. Lynsey Innes, 40, from Scotland, told BBC Scotland how her father, Gordon Roberts, died of mesothelioma this year. A joiner by trade who retired at 62 and kept fit by swimming, Mr Roberts developed breathing difficulties last summer. An X-ray revealed mesothelioma and he was given a prognosis of nine to 12 months. He died at Easter, aged 70. Ms Innes said her uncle, who had been a plumber, also died of mesothelioma after first experiencing pains in his shoulder. “It was just a simple X-ray that picked up my dad’s cancer,” Ms Innes said. “It doesn’t cost a lot of money to give an X-ray to somebody. [Carrying out screening] within a certain generation, over a certain period of time, would be ample to try and catch it at an early stage. If you catch it at an earlier stage the chemotherapy may shrink the tumour, you may then not get nine to 12 months — you can get up to five years.” A Scottish government spokesman said national screening programmes are introduced only after a detailed assessment of clinical and cost effectiveness and public health benefit, based on advice from the National Screening Committee. “The National Screening Committee has not considered screening for asbestos exposure,” he said. He encouraged anyone with symptoms such as difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, coughing and chest pains, and with a history of working in occupations associated with asbestos exposure, to contact their GP.

LVMH, the world’s largest luxury goods group, reported a 16% rise in 2015 revenue to €35.67bn (£27bn), with like-for-like sales up 6%, as strength in Europe, the US and Japan offset softer demand in Asia. The company owns famous brands including Louis Vuitton and Christian Dior. Chief executive Bernard Arnault said trading in France—where LVMH generates about 10% of sales—was “almost back to normal” after the November Paris terror attacks, which triggered declines of up to 50% at some stores and left sales still 4% to 5% lower. “Over time, sales are coming back to normal,” he said. Despite the top-line growth, net profit fell to €3.57bn, below analysts’ €3.71bn consensus and down 37% from 2014, when results were boosted by €2.8bn in capital gains from the sale of its stake in rival Hermès. LVMH shares rose €9.65 to €154.80 in Paris on Wednesday morning after the update, as investors focused on solid operational momentum. The fashion and leather goods division, home to Louis Vuitton and Fendi, posted 3% fourth-quarter growth, beating expectations for 1%. For the year, like-for-like sales in the division rose 4%, while perfumes and cosmetics advanced 7% and watches and jewellery climbed 8%. Arnault said Louis Vuitton delivered “double-digit” growth, with Fendi up more than 20%, though he noted the figures benefited from a weak euro. Analysts welcomed the performance. Exane BNP Paribas’s Luca Solca called it “a solid set of numbers with a good beat on fashion and leather,” noting the strength of key houses despite uneven Asian markets. Reflecting confidence in cash generation, LVMH will raise its dividend by 11% to €3.55 a share. Investment banks responded positively. Goldman Sachs increased its price target on LVMH from €164.90 to €171.90 and reiterated a “buy” rating, citing resilient demand in core markets and continued brand strength to offset regional volatility.

Stephen Cummings, 32, has been jailed after police discovered almost eight kilos of cannabis in his van on the A737 Johnstone bypass in Renfrewshire on 7 July this year. Paisley Sheriff Court heard that passing officers stopped to offer assistance when they saw the vehicle’s hazard lights on. When Cummings lowered his window, officers smelled cannabis and searched the van, finding eight taped blocks, each weighing close to a kilo, sealed inside a carrier bag. Cummings admitted being concerned in the supply of the drug. He was handed a 30-month sentence, which will begin after he completes an 18-month jail term he is currently serving for another offence.

A selection of candid remarks from the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia is resurfacing as debates over judicial philosophy and the role of the courts continue to animate American public life. Across interviews and speeches from 2002 to 2015, Scalia’s own words sketch a portrait of a jurist who relished argument, insisted on constitutional fidelity, and embraced the consequences of principled decision-making even when the outcomes were unpopular. “I love to argue,” Scalia told CBS News in 2008. “It may well be that I’m something of a shin kicker. It may well be that I’m something of a contrarian.” That contrarian streak was matched by a robust insistence on intellectual clarity and discipline: “The main business of a lawyer is to take the romance, the mystery, the irony, the ambiguity out of everything he touches,” he said in a 2005 speech at Juilliard. Scalia’s quips often captured complex ideas in strikingly accessible terms. In a 2005 address to the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, he asked, “What is a moderate interpretation of the text? Halfway between what it really means and what you’d like it to mean?” The line encapsulated his originalist method: interpret the Constitution according to its public meaning at the time of enactment, not as a flexible vessel for modern policy preferences. He joked about the label’s reputation during a 2008 talk at Oxford: “Sometimes people come up to me and inquire, ‘Justice Scalia, when did you first become an originalist?’ As though it’s some weird affliction.” His fidelity to constitutional protections included speech he personally disliked. “I do not like scruffy people who burn the American flag, [but] regrettably, the First Amendment gives them the right to do that,” he said in 2002 at Lewis & Clark Law College. And he recognized that judging would not always align with personal viewpoints: “If you’re going to be a good and faithful judge, you have to resign yourself to the fact that you’re not always going to like the conclusions you reach,” he told Chapman Law School in 2005. Scalia’s bracing frankness extended beyond legal theory. “A man who has made no enemies is probably not a very good man,” he said in 2012. His advice was similarly uncompromising: “Never compromise your principles,” he remarked in 2015—“unless of course your principles are Adolf Hitler’s.” For Scalia, clear thinking, sharp debate, and a steadfast approach to the law were hallmarks of both his jurisprudence and his public persona.

James Lovelock told Radio 4's Today programme he was "shocked" at the lack of coverage so far. James Lovelock, the eminent environmentalist and creator of the Gaia theory, has criticised what he described as a troubling silence from political leaders on climate change, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme he was “shocked” by the lack of attention and urgency. His concerns were echoed by Professor Sir Brian Hoskins, director of the Grantham Institute for Climate Change at Imperial College London, who said there had been a “total lack” of vision from the main parties. “This is a key thing that they should be talking about,” Lovelock said, warning that “in a way we are fiddling while Rome burns and we certainly could be looking at a lot of suffering and a lot of unpleasantness.” He praised former Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, herself a trained scientist, as the rare politician who “fully understood the issue,” adding: “She understood very well and got us thinking the right way. But there has been no politician since that has been able to do that.” Hoskins argued that short-term political calculus is overpowering the long-term planning needed to confront the climate crisis. “It seems that when we get to the discussions it all goes down to the lowest level of what’s going to make someone happy for the next five minutes and the politicians seem to think that’s going to buy their votes,” he told Today. He added that the main parties have failed to set out distinct visions, saying: “I can’t say that I can see any big difference in the statements they have been making just recently.” Calling this “an incredibly important year for the world,” Hoskins said decisions now will set the framework for the next 30 years. Both figures urged politicians to elevate climate policy in debates, and for media and voters to demand clear, credible plans to drive decarbonisation, resilience, and long-term prosperity.

Five Daughters wins Drama Serial award, honors victims of Ipswich murders The three-part drama Five Daughters has won the Drama Serial award, with its creators dedicating the honor to the women whose lives it portrayed. Director Philippa Lowthorpe said, “We would like to dedicate this award to the women who lost their lives,” underscoring the production’s focus on the victims rather than the perpetrator. Five Daughters explored the family relationships and everyday lives of the five women murdered in Ipswich by Steve Wright, who was convicted in 2008. Judges praised the BBC drama as “a sensitive, skilfully acted dramatisation of an appalling true story,” calling it “ground-breaking television.” By centering the women—Gemma Adams, Tania Nicol, Anneli Alderton, Annette Nicholls and Paula Clennell—the series “succeeded in giving the five women back some dignity and humanity,” the panel said, hailing it as “powerful and important” and “TV drama at its very best.” Writer Stephen Butchard was shortlisted in the Writer-Drama category, which ultimately went to Jack Thorne and Shane Meadows for This Is England ’86. Five Daughters was the result of a year-long research process by its writers, actors, and producers, who worked closely with some of the victims’ relatives, Suffolk Police, and the Ipswich drugs rehabilitation charity the Iceni Project. Liz Harsant, leader of Ipswich Borough Council and a trustee of the Somebody’s Daughter Memorial Fund, welcomed the award. “We met the actors and producers and all of them were touched by the stories the parents had told them,” she said. “I can’t say how pleased I am that they’ve won the award. It’s not something you want to relive every day of your life, but I think people had to know about it.” Lowthorpe said the team hopes the drama continues to spark debate about drug addiction and the vulnerability of girls on the street, and that charities like Iceni receive sustained support for their “tremendous work.”

Wenger admits top-four uncertainty as Arsenal slip to sixth after Palace defeat Arsenal’s hopes of securing Champions League football were dealt a major blow with Monday’s 3-0 defeat at Crystal Palace, leaving the Gunners sixth in the Premier League, seven points behind fourth-placed Manchester City with eight games remaining. Asked about the club’s top-four prospects, manager Arsene Wenger was candid: “We might get there, we might not get there.” Wenger’s contract expires this summer, and while he has been offered a new two-year deal, he has yet to announce whether he will continue. The Frenchman has delivered top-four finishes in each of his 20 seasons in charge, a record now under serious threat. Five defeats in their past 10 league matches have intensified dissatisfaction among some supporters, with calls for Wenger to step down growing louder. Addressing his future on Friday, Wenger said: “What is happening at board level is not down to me. I focus on what is down to me, the performance of the team and what the fans are interested in is the performance of the team.” Arsenal travel to struggling Middlesbrough on Monday (20:00 BST) seeking to arrest their recent slump and revive their top-four challenge. Wenger refused to comment on reports that forward Alexis Sanchez has been offered a £300,000-a-week contract to extend his stay. The 28-year-old Chile international, under contract until the summer of 2018, was this week nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award after an outstanding campaign featuring 18 league goals and nine assists. “I’m very happy because it rewards a very strong season if you look at his numbers,” Wenger said of Sanchez. “He basically prefers to play wide rather than up front because he can get the ball more. He has to keep that balance between providing and goalscoring because he has both in the locker.” With the season entering its decisive phase, Arsenal face a pivotal run-in amid mounting pressure and unresolved questions about the manager’s future.

The European Central Bank held the euro area’s key interest rate steady in October and confirmed it will maintain its quantitative easing (QE) programme, which is scheduled to run until March 2017. ECB President Mario Draghi said there had been no discussions yet on ending QE, but signalled the topic would be addressed at the Governing Council’s December meeting and is likely to be gradually wound down, or “tapered,” rather than halted suddenly. “Our decisions in December will tell you what we are going to do. That will define the monetary policy environment for the coming weeks and coming months,” Draghi said at a press conference. He added it was “unlikely” there would be an abrupt end to the bond-buying scheme, emphasizing that policymakers are waiting until December to consider all relevant information. “We want to see all the inputs that are useful to have this discussions,” he said, to “ensure the smooth implementation of our purchase programme until March 2017 or beyond if necessary.” Investors have been searching for clues on whether the ECB will extend QE beyond March next year, as the eurozone faces a complicated mix of slowly rising inflation and weakening growth. Headline inflation rose to 0.4% in September, while quarterly economic growth decelerated from 0.5% in the second quarter to 0.3% in the three months to September. Draghi cautioned that the European economy remains vulnerable to downside risks, pointing to “subdued foreign demand” and lingering structural issues. “We will continue to act, if warranted, by using all the instruments available within our mandate,” he said. Reaction in bond markets was mixed, with some participants expressing frustration at the lack of explicit guidance on tapering. James Athey, a fixed income investment manager at Aberdeen Asset Management, said: “This was not Draghi’s finest hour. He really wanted to shut down any suggestion that the ECB is going to taper any time soon. But what he actually did was to tell people to come back in December and see what the ECB thinks then.” He added that the uncertainty would “leave enough unanswered questions to keep bond markets volatile,” noting that “an already nervous market will not take much comfort from his obfuscation today.” Draghi underscored the broader challenges facing the euro area, saying the recovery is expected to be dampened by “still subdued foreign demand, the necessary balance sheet adjustments in a number of sectors and sluggish pace of implementation of structural reforms.” He reiterated that “the risks to the euro area growth outlook remain tilted to the downside and relate mainly to the external environment.” The ECB meeting coincided with UK Prime Minister Theresa May’s arrival in Brussels for her first European Union summit since taking office after Britain’s vote to leave the EU. May said: “This is my first European Council and I’m here with a very clear message: The UK is leaving the EU but we will continue to play a full role until we leave and we’ll be a strong and dependable partner after we have left. It’s in the interests of both the UK and the EU that we continue to work closely together, including at this summit.”

The Competition and Markets Authority will determine whether the merger could result in "a substantial lessening of competition" for consumers. The CMA decision has surprised some analysts. Richard Perks, retail director at Mintel, said the watchdog had every right to examine the deal, but he described the move as "rather odd". Although the supermarket planned to close dozens of Argos stores and relocate them in Sainsbury's outlets, he said that almost half of Argos sales were now online. That made it difficult to see how the deal would reduce competition for consumers, Mr Perks said. The CMA has launched a phase one inquiry into J Sainsbury’s proposed takeover of Home Retail Group, owner of Argos, to assess potential impacts on consumer choice and pricing. A Sainsbury’s spokesperson said: “The combination of both businesses will create a multi-product, multi-channel proposition with fast delivery networks, benefiting customers by accelerating our strategy to give them what they want, where and when they want it. We look forward to the successful completion of the deal.” The CMA will accept responses until 13 June and should make a decision by 25 July. Separately, the watchdog is investigating German drugs distributor Celesio’s £125m acquisition of Sainsbury’s pharmacy business, with a decision expected on 8 August. Sainsbury’s made a £1.4bn bid for Home Retail Group in March that aimed to “future-proof” its business amid rapid shifts in retail. Shares in Sainsbury’s closed up 0.6% at 269.3p on Friday.

Joshua Martin, 19, has been convicted of manslaughter over the death of his three-month-old daughter, Ezmai, who was found not breathing at a flat in Bordon, Hampshire, in June 2015. A jury at Winchester Crown Court cleared Martin of murder but found him guilty of causing the fatal injuries, which experts said were consistent with the baby being “deliberately shaken” and included rib damage. Ezmai’s mother, Jemma Pethybridge, 19, told the court she left the infant for about 20 minutes while she went to the bathroom and returned to find her lifeless, with “milky vomit” coming from her nose and mouth. Ezmai was transferred to St George’s Hospital in London, where she died the following day. A post-mortem examination found a head injury had led to a subdural haemorrhage and severe brain damage. Prosecutors said that although no attack was witnessed, Martin caused the injuries. The court also heard that while his partner and daughter were at the Royal Surrey County Hospital in Guildford on an earlier occasion, Martin “trashed” their flat, overturning furniture and pulling down curtains. Martin, of Salisbury Road, Alton, was sentenced to seven years in a young offenders’ institution, with an extended five-year licence period.

Cambridge University Botanic Garden braces for rare titan arum bloom within days A titan arum at the Cambridge University Botanic Garden is poised to flower for the first time, with staff expecting the dramatic event in the next day or two. Another specimen at the garden last bloomed in 2004. The fleeting spectacle, which typically lasts only a few days, is known for its intense night-time odor designed to lure pollinators. To give the public a chance to experience the phenomenon, the garden plans to extend opening hours until 22:00 BST on the two nights the flower is open. “The tricky thing is, we don’t know when it’s going to open,” said Prof Beverley Glover, director of the garden. “When it flowers, we want visitors to smell it at its night-time stinkiest.” Scientifically named Amorphophallus titanum, the titan arum is native to Sumatra and spends much of its life as an underground tuber. “Every year it puts out one gigantic leaf several metres tall that lasts for the growing season,” Prof Glover explained. “This year it’s decided not to put up a new leaf, but to put up a flower instead.” The current specimen has been in Cambridge for about 10 years and has never flowered before. When it does, Prof Glover said, it produces “the biggest single flower known in the world,” which can reach about two metres (80 inches) across. To attract carrion beetles—the plant’s natural pollinators—the bloom heats itself to around 40C (104F) and emits what Prof Glover described as “the most appalling scent of rotting flesh and decay,” driven by a mix of sulphur compounds. The garden has two titan arum plants and will provide updates on the bloom’s timing as it approaches.

A major new facility dedicated to advancing cancer and genetic research has opened at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, providing a significant boost to the Institute of Medical Genetics. The Cancer Genetics Building offers two laboratory floors focused on diagnosis and treatment, expanding capacity for work that has already identified genes linked to bowel cancer and Huntingdon's Disease. The centre is designed to accelerate research into conditions such as Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC), a genetic disorder that causes tumours in the brain, heart and kidneys and is associated with epilepsy, autism and severe learning disabilities. A team from the Institute of Medical Genetics was part of the group that first identified TSC genes, enabling clinical trials of potential treatments that were previously out of reach. Among those hoping to benefit from the breakthrough research is 24-year-old Trystan James from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, who was diagnosed with TSC at eight months old. Invited to the opening ceremony on Thursday, his family described the emotional toll of the condition and their hopes for the future. “To learn that one's child has a serious genetic disorder, with all its implications, is a shock,” said his mother, Marie. “To learn that the condition can be fatal, will probably result in learning disabilities, with the almost certain prospect of epilepsy, plus the prospect of severe facial skin problems, marring appearance for life is, to say the least, frightening. “The course of the condition cannot be predicted. There is as yet no cure,” she added. “We can but cope from day to day to watch, care, hope and wait. The advancement in research that the Cardiff team have developed is something we didn't dare hope would come in Trystan's lifetime.” Professor Julian Sampson, Head of the Institute of Medical Genetics, said the new building will play a pivotal role in pushing scientific boundaries. “The new cancer genetics building offers a real boost for our research and helps enhance our work unravelling the genetic changes and mechanisms that lead to cancer,” he said. One of the centre’s core aims is to bridge the gap between identifying DNA changes associated with cancer and understanding their impact on the proteins within cancer cells. Professor Ray Waters, of Cardiff University’s School of Medicine, emphasised the urgency of this work. “Every day the body experiences millions of DNA damaging events within the cells that make up the body. We can repair much of this damage, but the precise details of how this happens is still unknown. If DNA damage is not repaired it can cause mutation and cancer.” The research centre is to be officially opened by First Minister Carwyn Jones.

The job advert on Facebook for a constable post on the Isles of Scilly has gone viral, drawing interest from as far afield as Thailand and Australia after Sgt Colin Taylor described it as “possibly the most enviable policing post in the UK or even the world.” Taylor, who posted the listing, said the phones at the island police station were “red-hot” all weekend as inquiries poured in. The Isles of Scilly, with a population of around 2,200 and just five miles of roads, typically see modest crime levels. Between March 2014 and February 2015, officers recorded 24 cases covering violence, sexual offences, criminal damage and arson. Last year brought three stolen bicycles—though, with limited road space, there’s not far for thieves to go. Quirky incidents add to the island’s reputation, including a recent break-in at a shed containing footballs where a fried egg was inexplicably left at the scene. Taylor acknowledged he may have “overcooked” the advert’s allure and clarified the role is only open to serving officers in Devon and Cornwall Police, with applications closing on 3 April. Among the qualities listed was the “resolve to issue a parking ticket to your spouse so tactfully so as not find dinner in the dog thereafter,” a line that helped the post capture public imagination. Despite the restrictions, interest came from around the globe. “Commiserations go to hopefuls who contacted us from Ukraine, Texas, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Philippines, Thailand, Spain, Greece, loads from Italy, Australia, Germany, Portugal, South Africa and a smattering from England, Scotland and Ireland,” Taylor said, thanking applicants for their enthusiasm.

Coach driver jailed over Looe crash as victim’s family urges tougher mobile phone penalties Coach driver Martin Chun has been jailed for five years after being found guilty of causing death by dangerous driving and causing serious injury by dangerous driving. The conviction follows a May 2014 crash near Looe in Cornwall in which two women died, including 59-year-old Margaret Luxton. The court heard Chun was using a hands-free mobile phone at the time of the crash. While hands-free use is legal, drivers can still be penalised if they are distracted and not in proper control of their vehicle. The Confederation of Passenger Transport UK said the penalty mirrors that for using a handheld mobile: a £100 fine and three penalty points. Mrs Luxton’s son, Terry, said the case showed the need for tougher penalties. “We know now the driver was using his mobile phone and we need tougher legislation for drivers using mobile phones while driving — it should be as tough as drink driving,” he said. “People use their mobile phones willy-nilly thinking ‘yeah it’s fine’. It’s a distraction; if your eyes aren’t 100% focused on the road it is a distraction and you can kill people.” By contrast, anyone caught drink-driving or attempting to drink-drive can face up to six months in prison, an unlimited fine and a driving ban of at least one year. Campaigners argue that parity in penalties would better reflect the risks posed by distraction behind the wheel and serve as a stronger deterrent. Terry Luxton said his mother’s death continues to have a profound impact on the family. “It’s been more than two years, and my father is suffering from depression and anxiety — he’s really not in a good place,” he said. He hopes the case will prompt action to make roads safer and prevent similar tragedies.

Gale-force winds and heavy seas have battered Devon and Cornwall, toppling trees and triggering rescues as forecasters warn of further disruption across the South West and beyond. Gusts approaching 60mph (97km/h) and storm-driven waves up to 5m (16ft) swept the coastline on Thursday, with the Environment Agency issuing multiple flood alerts for rivers and coastal areas, and the Met Office placing an amber warning urging the public to take extra care. Near Tavistock in Devon, a 30ft (9m) beech tree crashed onto a car at Gulworthy, trapping a woman inside while her two children managed to escape. Tavistock fire station crews used cutting gear to release the woman, who was taken to hospital with cuts and bruises. Firefighters said passers-by are thought to have freed the children before emergency services arrived. The operation to extricate the driver took around 30 minutes. Keith Pascoe, from the fire service, described the near-miss as “incredibly lucky,” saying: “It appears the tree was falling as the car went under it. They could have been accelerating to get away from it, but part of the tree went through the car. They were incredibly lucky. Another couple of seconds and they would have been engulfed by the tree. It could have been a fatality. It’s a huge tree – large enough to completely block the road.” At sea, conditions were equally perilous. A Jersey yachtsman was airlifted to safety off the Cornish coast, while 54-year-old sailor Peter Evans was rescued about 40 miles off the Lizard after his 22ft yacht Federwolke was swamped by waves in a Force 9 gale and capsized twice. Evans, who had set off solo from Plymouth on the Jester Challenge race to the Azores, was forced to turn back amid the relentless battering. “I didn’t get any sleep at all last night, the sea was so rough. I’ve never seen anything like it,” he said. He was winched by a crew from RNAS Culdrose in Cornwall and looked after by rescuers, who also provided him with new clothing. Terry Collins, watch manager at Falmouth Coastguard, which coordinated the rescue, urged mariners to plan cautiously: “We do advise anyone setting out on the water to take heed of weather forecasts and do not make journeys in conditions unsuitable for their vessel.” Forecasters expect the centre of the storm to move slowly north-east through Thursday and into Friday morning, brushing north Wales and exiting Britain as far north as Northumberland. For Friday, Met Office wind and rain warnings extend to south Wales and many parts of southern England as well as the South West. Mark Seltzer from the Met Office advised road users: “People towing caravans should be aware of the strong winds because it could cause some snaking.” Authorities continue to monitor river levels and coastal conditions, urging residents and travellers to stay alert to updated guidance.

Dozens of schoolchildren and several adults were treated in hospital after a school bus and a car overturned on the Omagh Road in Drumquin, County Tyrone, on Monday morning. Emergency services were called to the scene at approximately 8:20am after the Ulsterbus, carrying pupils from Castlederg to secondary schools in Omagh, collided with a car. Both vehicles came to rest on their sides in a nearby field. While initial fears were high, authorities said it is not thought that any of those involved sustained serious injuries. A total of 27 people were taken to Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry and 25 to the South West Acute Hospital (SWAH) in Enniskillen. Rosemary Watterson, of the Western Education and Library Board, said all patients treated at SWAH had been discharged, along with a significant proportion of those assessed at Altnagelvin. Ambulance Service spokesman John McPoland said the “vast majority” of passengers needed to be checked because of their age. He added that six people had injuries “slightly more than minor,” including children who banged their heads against bus windows during the impact. “No one went through any windows,” he said. Three patients were transported by Ambulance Service A&E crews for further assessment due to the nature of their injuries, which, although not serious, warranted additional attention. To manage the large number of casualties, the children and occupants of the car were moved from the scene on two Translink buses, accompanied by paramedics, to both hospitals for precautionary checks. Katie Devlin, 18, who was on the bus, described the crash as “really scary.” “We are all very lucky that it wasn’t any worse,” she said. “I wasn’t even worried about myself, it was everybody else, I was worried for them. I was checking everybody was OK and then I realised I was sore myself. It was just like your life flashing before your eyes. Everybody is still very shaken up. Emergency services were excellent.” Local councillor Frankie Donnelly, who visited the scene, said it was fortunate that “everybody has come out of it relatively unscathed.” He noted that on that stretch of road, “early in the morning, a bright sunny morning, there would be a very low sun there and that may have been a factor in this accident.” Translink, which operated the Ulsterbus, said in a statement: “We can confirm that an incident has occurred involving an Ulsterbus carrying school pupils and a car on the Drumquin Road, County Tyrone, at approximately 8.20am. Emergency services were called to the scene and an investigation is under way.” Education Minister John O’Dowd said his department would engage with all schools involved “to ascertain if we can be of further assistance and ensure that any help that can be provided will be provided.” The Western Education and Library Board said its critical incident response team had contacted schools to offer support.

Middlesbrough forward Kike has joined La Liga side Eibar on a two-and-a-half-year deal. The 26-year-old scored 16 goals in 75 appearances for Boro after arriving from Real Murcia in July 2014. This season he featured 24 times under Aitor Karanka but has found the net only once since August. Boro strengthened their attack in January with the signings of Jordan Rhodes and Enrique Sola and sit second in the Championship, one point behind leaders Hull. BBC Tees reports Kike cannot play for Eibar until next season due to paperwork delays.

Darren Clarke has emerged as the leading candidate to captain Europe at the 2016 Ryder Cup, with an official announcement expected next Wednesday, 18 February. The 46-year-old Northern Irishman, a Ryder Cup winner four times as a player, is tipped to get the nod ahead of Spain’s Miguel Ángel Jiménez. “If it’s Miguel, I would be delighted for him, but I would love to do the job,” Clarke told BBC Northern Ireland. “To be the captain is huge, but he is only there to steer the players. It’s not about the captain, it’s about the team.” A five-man European Tour selection panel, which includes 2014-winning captain Paul McGinley, will choose McGinley’s successor. Europe retained the trophy in September at the 40th Ryder Cup, defeating the United States 161⁄2–111⁄2 at Gleneagles in Scotland — their eighth win in the last 10 meetings. Clarke added: “I’ve got very special memories of the event and I’m fortunate to have played in many winning teams. Those memories I will cherish for ever.” The United States will host 2016 match at Hazeltine from 30 September to 2 October.

Heavy security at Brussels Airport leads to long queues as operations resume Brussels Airport reopened portions of its departure hall under tight security following the 22 March attacks claimed by IS that severely damaged the terminal. Authorities have advised passengers to arrive at least three hours before departure, but the enhanced checks have triggered long queues and mounting frustration. Local media reported lines stretching for two hours outside the hall, with some travelers missing flights despite the extended lead time. Among those affected was former Belgian Prime Minister Yves Leterme, while others voiced uncertainty as they waited, unsure they would reach their gates in time. On Sunday, a limited number of passengers boarded select flights, and from Monday check-in reopened at more than 100 desks in the departure hall. Airport officials caution that operations will ramp up gradually and are not expected to reach full capacity until mid-June. Complaints flooded the airport’s Facebook page, where users labeled the situation “ridiculous,” “chaotic,” and a “nightmare,” and warned business travelers could be deterred by the three-hour check-in window. Some passengers, however, expressed understanding, noting the extraordinary circumstances after the attacks, which also included a suicide blast on a metro train that killed 16 people. “At the moment it’s fine, we know what happened and all. But for the future, it has to be faster,” one woman said, as a spokeswoman promised improvements in coming days.

Stockholm truck attack leaves at least a dozen injured on Drottninggatan; PM calls it terrorism, one arrested At least a dozen people were injured on Friday afternoon after a lorry drove into crowds on Drottninggatan (Queen Street), one of Stockholm’s busiest pedestrian thoroughfares, before crashing into the front window of the Ahlens department store.
