Swedish Prime Minister Stefan Lofven described the incident as a terror attack and vowed that Sweden’s values of democracy and freedom would not be undermined by hatred. He announced that Sweden had strengthened border controls as authorities responded to the unfolding situation. The crash occurred just before 15:00 local time (13:00 GMT), prompting a large-scale emergency response and the swift evacuation of Stockholm’s central station, which sits close to the store. The metro, central roads, and various bus lines were shut down following the attack, and city authorities made several spaces, including school buildings, available for people stranded by transport disruptions. Officials also urged the public not to share photographs of victims online. Police said one man had been arrested after they released a CCTV image of a person who may be connected to the case. Shots were reportedly fired in another part of the city earlier in the day, but police told local media there was no link between that incident and the truck crash. Investigators continued to comb the area late into the evening, while officers maintained a heightened presence across the capital. Eyewitnesses described scenes of panic and confusion as the lorry barreled down the pedestrian street. “There was blood everywhere,” said Annevi Petersson, who told the BBC she was in the store’s fitting room when she heard screams and rushed to find the aftermath. Others reported the vehicle appeared to be trying to hit people, sending shoppers and passersby scrambling for safety. Swedish brewery Spendrups said the lorry involved had been stolen earlier in the day while on its way to deliver to a restaurant. “Someone jumped into the driver’s cabin and drove off with the vehicle while the driver was unloading,” a spokesperson told the TT news agency, adding that the company was cooperating with authorities. Security observers noted that Sweden has faced relatively few large-scale attacks in recent years; the last notable case was in 2010, when a failed suicide bomber blew himself up in central Stockholm. While Sweden’s intelligence service, Sapo, is regarded as capable, some insiders have expressed concerns that legislation has lagged behind emerging threats. Officials cautioned that it remains important to keep an open mind about the perpetrator’s motive, acknowledging the possibility of personal or psychological factors alongside potential political intent.

Barcelona defender Gerard Piqué said he will retire from Spain duty after the 2018 World Cup, citing relentless criticism that resurfaced during Sunday’s 2-0 win in Albania. The 29-year-old, unpopular with some fans for supporting Catalan independence, faced backlash when his shirt appeared without the Spanish flag trim seen on teammates’ sleeves. After a social-media outcry, the Spanish football federation defended Piqué and clarified the kit. It said the long-sleeved jersey worn by Piqué—also by Real Madrid captain Sergio Ramos—does not include the flag. The federation added that Piqué had cut the sleeves for comfort, as other players have done. “I have tried everything, but I can’t bear this anymore,” said Piqué, a 2010 World Cup and Euro 2012 winner. “Today’s issue of the sleeves is the straw that breaks the camel. They’ve managed to make me lose the excitement of coming here and although after Russia I’ll only be 31, I’ll leave.”

St Mary’s Catholic School in Bishop’s Stortford, the former school of Grammy- and Oscar-winning singer Sam Smith, will not offer GCSE music to next year’s Year 10 cohort after only three students opted to take the subject. The Herts and Essex Observer first reported the change, which school leaders described as a difficult but practical decision based on uptake. Headmaster Andrew Celano said the school remains committed to nurturing students’ musical interests despite suspending the GCSE class. He said the three pupils who selected the course will receive curriculum-time music tuition so they can continue their studies, adding that the school “remains very focused on all the performing arts.” St Mary’s said it has a strong tradition of music education and plans to reintroduce the GCSE course in the future if interest rises. The move has prompted reflection on access to music education, particularly for students who may not receive private support. Joanna Eden, a singer-songwriter and vocal coach who taught Smith from the age of 10 through 18, called the low sign-up “disappointing but not surprising.” She noted that Smith benefited from parents who recognized his talent and could fund lessons, suggesting that fewer opportunities in schools can limit students’ belief that music is a viable path. “If that sense of empowerment isn’t there, they’re less likely to choose it,” she said. Smith, who rose to global fame with multiple chart-topping singles and won an Academy Award for the James Bond theme “Writing’s On The Wall,” did not comment on the school’s decision. A spokesperson for the artist declined to respond when asked. The school emphasized that extracurricular opportunities and performance activities will continue alongside its broader arts provision.

A man was killed in a road accident at McClays Corner on the Letterkenny side of Stranolar at about 02:50 BST. The road was closed and diversions are in place. Gardaí appealed for witnesses to contact them. The victim’s name has not yet been released as investigations continue following the collision.

Ipswich Central urges firms to back BID plan promising major retail growth Ipswich Central is asking town-centre businesses to back a new five-year Business Improvement District (BID) strategy that it says could unlock 500,000 sq ft (46,000 sq m) of new retail space and accelerate the town’s transformation. The umbrella business organisation, which represents around 700 firms, argues that renewed investment would help tie together Ipswich’s waterfront with the historic town centre and attract national retailers that have expressed interest in locating there. A BID is a defined area where businesses pay into a central fund used to drive economic development, town centre management, and marketing. Ipswich Central says that since its first five-year term began in 2007, it has overseen £3.3m of spending on initiatives including improved streetscapes, street rangers, enhanced security systems, and efforts to recruit new retailers. “The town centre has improved immeasurably over this period,” said Steve Hardy, managing director at AXA, one of the businesses involved with Ipswich Central. “It is a brighter and safer place, largely thanks to the work of Ipswich Central.” The organisation is now seeking approval from its 700 member businesses for the next five-year strategy, which it estimates would raise £3.75m. Paul Clement, executive director of Ipswich Central, said the focus reflects business priorities. “The area that businesses want us to lead on is in marketing the town centre—not just to visitors and consumers but to new investment. We’ve got a whole host of name retailers who would take space here tomorrow morning but the space doesn’t exist,” he said. Ipswich Central has identified several sites with redevelopment potential, including the Tower Ramparts bus station and the Lower Brook Street site currently occupied by the Archant local newspaper group. Clement added that the town’s unique selling point is its waterfront, but stressed the need to better integrate it with the “old” town centre. The vote comes as competition intensifies, with the Westfield shopping centre opening at the Olympic site in London, less than an hour by train from Ipswich. “For years, we’ve been talking about Norwich as a better retail location than Ipswich and we’ve never really done anything about it,” Clement said. “It’s about regaining that sense of pride in Ipswich and not concerning ourselves too much with the opposition, but doing what we know is right for this place.”

Council leader Jenny Laing said the UK and Scottish governments, trade unions and industry bodies needed "to get round the table as soon as possible" Aberdeen City Council leader Jenny Laing has called for an urgent summit bringing together the UK and Scottish governments, trade unions, industry bodies and local representatives to agree a strategic plan to protect jobs amid a sharp fall in oil prices. The Labour councillor urged First Minister Nicola Sturgeon and Prime Minister David Cameron to attend, warning that swift, coordinated action was needed to shore up confidence in the North Sea sector and prevent job losses in Europe’s oil capital. Her intervention follows stark warnings from parts of the industry. On Thursday, Robin Allan, chairman of the independent explorers’ association Brindex, told the BBC the UK’s oil industry was “close to collapse,” claiming almost no new North Sea projects were profitable with oil below $60 a barrel. However, Sir Ian Wood, another leading industry figure, said Mr Allan’s warning was “well over-the-top and far too dramatic,” and predicted conditions would begin to recover next year. Ms Laing said it was her responsibility, as leader of Aberdeen City Council, to work with governments in Edinburgh and Westminster and the oil industry to ensure jobs were protected and companies remained based in the city. “I have today instructed Angela Scott, our chief executive, to arrange a summit between senior politicians, government officials, industry representatives, trade unions, and local politicians,” she said. “The aim will be to ensure an agreement to develop a strategic plan to ensure job losses are either avoided or kept to a minimum. It must concern us all that the price of oil has dropped so heavily in such a short space of time and we need to agree a strategy to deal with fluctuations that undermine confidence in the North Sea.” She said the council chief executive would write to politicians within both the UK and Scottish governments, as well as UK Oil and Gas, other industry leaders and trade unions to encourage participation. Scottish Labour has pledged to send its new leader, Jim Murphy. A Scottish government spokesman said ministers were continuing to do all they could to support Scotland’s oil and gas sector. “As we have long said, what the industry requires is a stable predictable fiscal regime, and that substantial tax incentives are needed to achieve the objective of maximising recovery,” he added. “Unless the UK government acts to bring in further measures, the likelihood is some fields will cease production early.” The UK government’s Department of Energy and Climate Change said it was important to highlight that there was “very little evidence of new projects being cancelled or deferred in reaction to lower oil prices.” A spokesman added: “The government recognises the challenges currently faced by the oil industry and that’s why earlier this month the Treasury announced a package of fiscal changes and initiatives to stay on the front foot in dealing with them. We understand the particular concerns recent sharp reductions in oil prices have raised for companies active in the North Sea and will continue to engage with the Scottish government on this issue, including at this summit.” With opinions divided over the severity of the downturn, Ms Laing’s proposed summit seeks to establish a united approach to navigating volatile market conditions and safeguarding employment across the region’s vital energy supply chain.

Hunt for missing £33m Lotto winner triggers flood of claims in Worcester The search for a missing £33 million Lotto ticket-holder has prompted hundreds of people to come forward with stories of lost, damaged or stolen tickets, according to operator Camelot. The unclaimed prize represents half of a record £66 million jackpot from the 9 January draw, the other half having been claimed within days by a couple from Hawick. Camelot has confirmed the winning ticket was purchased in Worcester but says it will not comment on unverified claims while its investigation continues. “Given the interest in the missing £33m ticket-holder, we have received hundreds of claims of this nature,” a Camelot spokesman said. “All of these are currently being considered on a case-by-case basis, and we will follow up with all claimants directly to advise them whether their claim will be investigated further.” One claimant told a local shopkeeper she had washed her ticket in a pair of jeans, while others have reported theft or damage. Natu Patel, who runs Ambleside News in Warndon, Worcester, said a woman visited his newsagent with a ticket showing the winning numbers but with an illegible date and barcode. The winning numbers were 26, 27, 46, 47, 52 and 58. Camelot has not released details of the shop that sold the winning ticket and says no retailer has been told they sold it. The operator also outlined its rules for paying prizes in cases where tickets are stolen, lost or destroyed. Players must submit a written claim within 30 days of the relevant draw. If sufficient evidence is provided, Camelot will investigate and, at its discretion, may validate the claim and pay the prize 180 days after the draw. Despite the jackpot being shared, the £33 million sum remains the largest individual win since the National Lottery began in November 1994. Camelot urged anyone who believes they have a valid claim to come forward promptly as checks continue to identify the rightful winner.

Afua Hirsch’s call to reassess Britain’s colonial past has ignited debate in Norfolk over the legacy of Admiral Horatio Nelson, long celebrated as a national maritime hero. Writing in the Guardian, the author and broadcaster argued that the country should confront the full histories of its most venerated figures, drawing parallels with events in the United States where statues of Confederate leaders linked to slavery have been torn down. Hirsch contended that Nelson, revered in the county where he was born and educated, used his influence to defend slavery at a time when abolitionist momentum was growing. “One of the obstacles abolitionists had to overcome was the influence of Nelson, who was what you would now call, without hesitation, a white supremacist,” she wrote. “While many around him were denouncing slavery, Nelson was vigorously defending it.” She added that he “used his position to perpetuate the tyranny, serial rape and exploitation organised by West Indian planters, some of whom he counted among his closest friends.” Defending her stance on BBC Radio Norfolk, Hirsch said many people had “no idea that Nelson was an advocate of slavery” and urged local residents to consider “why they’ve been content to put that part of history on a pedestal but not the full picture.” The comments prompted a robust response from Nelson’s admirers in Norfolk. Bruno Peek, the Great Yarmouth-based pageantmaster who led national bicentennial celebrations in 2005, said the admiral’s global renown should be recognised. “We cannot change the past,” he said. “Nelson is loved in Norfolk because he’s from here. It’s no different to any other famous person being celebrated in the place of their birth. His memory should be protected. He is one of our greatest maritime heroes.” Great Yarmouth mayor Kerry Robinson-Payne, who also curates the town’s Nelson Museum, said the admiral remains an “adopted son” cherished locally. “Nelson was revered by his sailors, of all nationalities,” she said. “He looked after all his men no matter where they came from.”

Cameroon head coach Hugo Broos has threatened to walk away from his post, citing what he called “unprofessional” working conditions and a lack of support from football authorities, despite leading the Indomitable Lions to the Africa Cup of Nations title in February. Speaking after a 2-1 friendly defeat to Guinea in Belgium on Tuesday, the Belgian coach said he is “seriously considering whether I should continue or not.” Broos, appointed in February 2016, said the issues have persisted throughout his tenure and have now reached a breaking point. “One year ago when I started working with Cameroon I met many problems. Despite all this we worked hard and reached a new level. But the working conditions are not professional,” he said. “Today I am saying that this is the last straw.” He detailed a series of logistical and administrative failings. Broos claimed a trip to South Africa was delayed by more than two hours on the tarmac because officials attempted to add unnecessary passengers to the plane. He said the team’s doctor had to purchase medicines and bandages with his own money during a recent trip to Nantes and has yet to be reimbursed. The squad, he added, traveled without training kits and equipment because it was deemed too expensive to transport them. Most alarmingly, he said the players did not receive lunch on the day of the Guinea match because the hotel bill had not been settled. “No food? Hotel not been paid? This is the national team. We want better conditions,” Broos said. He also accused certain officials within the Cameroon Football Federation (Fecafoot) of “sitting in their chairs doing nothing.” Broos linked the subpar preparations directly to the defeat against Guinea. In a brief response, Fecafoot said via its official Twitter account that it would launch an inquiry into the circumstances behind Broos’s remarks. The federation did not immediately address the specific allegations. Broos led Cameroon to a surprise Africa Cup of Nations triumph in Gabon earlier this year, a success achieved amid ongoing disputes over bonuses and logistics that have long dogged the national setup.

Nottinghamshire have signed 29-year-old Australian Test pace bowler Jackson Bird as a replacement for Peter Siddle, confirming the deal on Monday, four days after Siddle was ruled out with a back injury. Director of cricket Mick Newell said it was "one of the easier contracts to pull together," adding that Trent Bridge is "an easy place to sell" and "we don't have to embellish." Newell revealed there were early signs Siddle's back problem was serious, giving the club time to assess options with the County Championship season six weeks away. He credited batsman Michael Lumb, who faced Bird in Australia's Big Bash, and former Notts limited-overs international David Hussey with helping persuade Bird to commit to the opening 10 Championship matches. "They both put in a good word for Trent Bridge and Notts and how we do things," Newell told BBC Radio Nottingham, ahead of the new season.

Great Yarmouth College and Lowestoft College are exploring deeper collaboration to strengthen course quality and better serve local industries, with options ranging from shared delivery to a joint management team or a full merger. The colleges, which each operate on annual budgets of about £14 million, say they offer many similar programmes aligned to the region’s needs and see partnership as a way to expand provision efficiently amid tightening further education funding. Final decisions will be taken by the governing boards, with governors at both institutions set to meet next month. A further period of staff consultation will follow before any announcement. Leaders caution that impacts on staffing cannot be predicted until the scope of collaboration is defined. “The main driver for these discussions is to improve the quality of learning, but we do need to bear in mind the changes and reductions in further education funding and how we can work together within that,” said Simon Summers, principal at Lowestoft College. “Both colleges are developing their energy and engineering offering and the courses are expensive to set up, so collaboration gives us the chance to offer a greater range of courses that will support local industry.” Great Yarmouth College principal Penny Wycherley highlighted existing joint activity: “We’ve already started a programme in marine engineering and energy and students go to both campuses and we bus them between the two. What we’re looking at is trying to widen the courses and training that we offer both within the colleges and at employers’ premises. Staff are worried, but what I hope they will see is that this assures the long-term future of both colleges.” In the event of a full merger, the colleges would operate under a joint corporation while retaining their individual names, reflecting their distinct identities within a single governance framework.

Media playback is not supported on this device The 40-year-old was linked with the position of attack and skills coach. Northampton Saints assistant coach Alex King has dismissed speculation linking him with a role in Eddie Jones’s England backroom team, insisting he was never in contention and remains committed to the Premiership club. King, 40, had been reported as a candidate to join the national set-up as attack and skills coach following Jones’s appointment as head coach. Speaking to BBC Radio Northampton, the former Wasps fly-half said Jones has held conversations across the English game as part of his fact-finding, but that did not equate to an approach. “Just because you have a conversation with Eddie Jones doesn’t mean there’s more to it,” King said. “I was always staying at Saints.” Saints director of rugby Jim Mallinder had earlier complained the club had been “kept in the dark” about any interest in King. On Friday, King reiterated there was no prospect of him joining England, adding that Jones intends to lead the attack himself. “I think Eddie wants clarity on what he wants to bring and that’s probably one of the reasons he doesn’t want another coach. Four coaches is enough at this stage,” he said. Jones is expected to oversee England’s attack for the Six Nations, with Ian Peel taking charge of the scrum and Paul Gustard and Steve Borthwick completing the coaching line-up on defence and the forwards respectively. King admitted the rumours had been frustrating but welcomed confirmation of England’s structure. “I’m looking forward to seeing how England play and the squad he picks,” he said.

David Bowie’s family has announced plans for a private ceremony to honor the late singer, while emphasizing that upcoming public tributes are not officially sanctioned by them. In a statement titled “Thank you,” shared on Bowie’s official Facebook page on Thursday, the family expressed gratitude for the outpouring of love and support following his death and asked for continued respect for their privacy during a “most sensitive” time. “The family of David Bowie is currently making arrangements for a private ceremony celebrating the memory of their beloved husband, father and friend,” the statement read. “They ask once again that their privacy be respected at this most sensitive of times. We are overwhelmed by and grateful for the love and support shown throughout the world. However, it is important to note that while the concerts and tributes planned for the coming weeks are all welcome, none are official memorials organized or endorsed by the family. Just as each and every one of us found something unique in David’s music, we welcome everyone’s celebration of his life as they see fit.” Bowie died of cancer on Sunday at the age of 69. According to multiple reports, including from the Daily Mirror, his body was privately cremated in New York, with no family or friends present, in line with the artist’s wishes. A publicist for Bowie told the BBC they were “neither confirming nor denying” the cremation reports. The singer released his final album, Blackstar, just two days before his death. The record’s stark imagery and lyrics—such as “Look up here, I’m in heaven”—have been widely interpreted as a farewell. Yet longtime collaborator and producer Tony Visconti told Rolling Stone that Bowie had remained creatively active until shortly before his death, writing and demoing five new songs and even planning a follow-up to Blackstar. “I was thrilled,” Visconti said, noting that Bowie had called him about a week before he died. “I thought, and he thought, that he’d have a few months, at least. So the end must’ve been very rapid. I’m not privy to it. I don’t know exactly, but he must’ve taken ill very quickly after that phone call.” Visconti, who worked with Bowie on seminal albums including The Man Who Sold the World, Low, and 2013’s The Next Day, will be among the performers at a memorial concert at New York’s Carnegie Hall in March. Initially conceived as a tribute show, The Music of David Bowie—featuring artists such as Cyndi Lauper and The Roots—will now serve as an opportunity for fans to mourn and celebrate Bowie’s legacy. Further tributes are planned in the UK. Next month’s Brit Awards will include a special performance honoring “the extraordinary life and work of one of our greatest icons,” organizers said. In the wake of his death, Bowie’s music has seen a dramatic surge. Blackstar is poised to become his first number one album in the United States, while it is also tracking toward the top spot in the UK. Meanwhile, 13 of Bowie’s earlier albums are expected to re-enter the UK top 100. Fans can revisit Bowie’s career through a special tribute program, David Bowie: Sound and Vision, available on BBC iPlayer.

The fare system allows bus passengers to make an extra journey within an hour of touching in when using an Oyster card or contactless payment. Previously, customers were obliged to pay £1.50 each time they boarded a bus. The hopper-fare will “help ensure everyone will be able to afford to travel around the city,” Mayor Sadiq Khan said, confirming the policy is scheduled to be introduced in September. Unveiling his first major transport measure since taking office, Mr Khan framed the change as both personal and practical. “My dad drove the number 44 bus and transport in London has always been a big part of my life,” he said. “The cost of a fare in London has risen for eight years in a row and now that I’m mayor I am determined to prevent the cost of travel from becoming a barrier to work.” Under his predecessor Boris Johnson, bus fares rose in successive years, a trend Khan says he is keen to reverse or mitigate. Under the new hopper-fare, a single bus journey will still cost £1.50, but passengers will be able to board a second bus within 60 minutes of their first tap without paying again. The change applies to Oyster and contactless payments; London buses stopped accepting cash in 2014, and riders today either purchase single tickets or use travelcards that cover multiple journeys in a day. Unlike the Tube, where prices are calculated by zones with automatic transfers via the same fare, bus passengers currently pay for every boarding, a disparity many have argued is unfair. Transport for London (TfL) said it does not yet have the technology to allow unlimited bus transfers within a one-hour window but aims to upgrade its ticketing systems in 2017, with the possibility of introducing unlimited timed bus fares by the end of 2018. TfL has previously estimated a one-hour bus ticket would cost around £50 million a year. Officials described the move as a clear signal of intent to deliver on the mayor’s priorities as it modernizes its payment infrastructure. The policy arrives in a network that carries about 2.5 billion bus journeys annually. Of those, roughly 600 million are pay-as-you-go fares, and an estimated 86 million riders make more than one bus trip in an hour—people who stand to benefit directly from the hopper-fare. “It’s Mayor Sadiq Khan’s first big transport policy announcement and perhaps there is little surprise — that from the son of a bus driver — it involves buses,” said BBC London transport correspondent Tom Edwards. Supporters say the change will ease costs for commuters and shift workers who rely on multiple bus connections, improving access to jobs and services across the capital. While unlimited transfers are not immediate, Khan and TfL say the September rollout is a significant step toward a fairer, more integrated bus fare system.

The mock hangings involved two blow up dolls, one with a Rangers scarf, the other with an Orange sash Police in Scotland have launched a public appeal for footage following disorder and vandalism at a recent match, including the mock hangings of two blow-up dolls and damage to toilets in the away section. A dedicated email address has been set up to collect videos and images as officers work to identify those responsible. Detective Inspector David Stewart, who is leading the investigation, urged supporters and witnesses to come forward with mobile phone footage of vandalism within the away support toilets. “Today specifically, we are requesting people with mobile phone footage of vandalism within the toilets of the away support section to contact us,” he said. “I would ask anyone who witnessed or who captured this vandalism to contact police, as it may assist with our enquiry.” He added that police are reviewing CCTV and obtaining footage from broadcasters to track individuals involved in disorder, vandalism and offensive or antisocial behaviour. “I understand there were a number of images and video shared online of this and I would be keen for people to contact us directly with any information they may have,” DI Stewart said. Both clubs issued statements condemning fan behaviour. Anyone with information or footage is asked to email CelticRangersDisorder@scotland.pnn.police.uk.

Abubakar Audu, 68, the All Progressives Congress candidate in Kogi state, died on Sunday under unclear circumstances as vote counting continued, the BBC’s Chris Ewokor reports. Audu was believed to be leading when results were halted amid reports of irregularities. He was buried Monday according to Islamic rites in his hometown, Ogbonicha. The uncertainty has raised questions over the next steps in the gubernatorial race. Audu, a former Kogi governor, had previously faced allegations of misappropriating public funds, which he denied. Authorities have yet to clarify the cause of death or the election outcome.

Humberside Police overhaul drew “substantial difficulties” as force rated inadequate, federation says Humberside Police’s rapid shift to a new “One Force” operating model triggered “substantial difficulties” and a “very difficult period” for frontline officers and the public, the Humberside Police Federation has said, speaking out in the same week national inspectors branded the force inadequate at keeping people safe and reducing crime. The federation’s chairman, Paul Yeomans, said the organization had warned senior leaders before the change that the plans posed significant risks but that the force pressed ahead regardless. “We advised the force quite robustly that we had significant concerns, however, the force went live with the model and the new shift pattern and, as has been borne out in the report, there were some substantial difficulties...in delivering the quality of service to the public,” he said. He added that a sudden, rather than phased, introduction left staff grappling with teething problems that “quite quickly...became very significant,” and credited the “goodwill of our members” with helping the force through. Humberside scrapped its geographical divisions in April in favor of four force-wide departments and introduced new shift patterns intended to improve efficiency. But a June inspection by Her Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary concluded that “due to serious difficulties in implementing the new operating model [the force] cannot be judged any higher than inadequate.” Inspectors cited a shortage of skilled staff in the command hub that risk-assesses public calls, weak workforce planning, and increased workloads. Yeomans linked some of the strain to national austerity measures, saying he could not “completely blame the force” given “the corporate spending review and the draconian cuts placed on policing.” He also noted there had been “significant improvements” since the inspection. Chief Constable Justine Curran acknowledged the concerns, saying “there are always lessons to be learned,” but defended the strategy. “I am confident the One Force model is right for us and will deliver the efficiencies and service levels we expect,” she said, adding that “any major change brings with it challenges and difficulties and we were prepared for this.” Both the federation and the force say work is ongoing to stabilize the model and sustain improvements following the inspectors’ findings.

DC legalizes private marijuana use, setting up clash with Congress Washington, DC, has legalized the private use of marijuana, intensifying a dispute between the city’s leaders and Congress over the limits of local autonomy in the federal district. As of midnight on Thursday (05:00 GMT), adults 21 and over may possess up to 2 ounces (56 grams) of cannabis and grow a small number of plants at home. Buying and selling the drug remains illegal, as does smoking it in public. The change places the nation’s capital alongside Alaska, Colorado, and Washington state as the only US jurisdictions permitting recreational marijuana use. It follows a referendum last November in which voters overwhelmingly approved the measure. Unlike US states, Washington, DC, is a federal district, and many of its laws are subject to congressional oversight. That unique status has reignited tensions. In a letter sent Tuesday, two members of Congress warned Mayor Muriel Bowser that moving forward with legalization would violate federal law, citing a national budget bill passed in December that includes a provision aimed at preventing the District from legalizing marijuana. Bowser and other city officials argue the voter-approved initiative remains valid because it was sanctioned before the budget restriction took effect. In their letter, the congressmen cautioned that by enacting the new rules the mayor would “be doing so in knowing and wilful violation of the law.” Representative Jason Chaffetz, one of the letter’s signatories, told the Washington Post that Bowser could face “very severe consequences,” adding, “You can go to prison for this.” “We do disagree on a matter of law,” Bowser said, emphasizing that there are “reasonable ways to resolve” the dispute without threats. While any criminal prosecution would fall under the US Department of Justice, Congress could seek to pressure the District by withholding funds for other initiatives. With private possession and home cultivation now permitted but sales and public consumption banned, the District enters a legally fraught phase that may ultimately be resolved in the courts—or through further action by Congress.

Heart of Midlothian are set to complete the signing of United States international Perry Kitchen after the 24-year-old returned to the USA to finalise paperwork following the approval of his UK work permit. Head coach Robbie Neilson said the move should be completed next week and admitted he was surprised to land the midfielder given rival interest. “I was pleased to get him and quite surprised,” Neilson said. “He had a big offer in the MLS, but he wanted to come to Europe to get into the USA team more consistently.” Kitchen, capped three times by the USMNT and with D.C. United since 2011, had also been close to a switch to Germany before that deal collapsed late in the process. “He had an offer from a German team, which fell through at the last moment, and, because it was February, he couldn’t make a move there because their window shuts,” Neilson explained. “But we can still bring in free agents and it was a chance to get him in.” Describing his prospective signing, Neilson added: “He is a defensive midfield player who sits in front of the back four, he’s very mobile, athletic and a good player. He has played in the US national team, which is a really good level.” In a separate update, Hearts have been dealt a blow with right-back Callum Paterson ruled out for around a month after sustaining a shoulder ligament injury against Kilmarnock last week. “He went over on it, but it felt a lot better and we were hopeful he had jarred it,” Neilson said. “But the scan showed a little tear, so it is important to let it settle down. He has been one of the key players, but we have a squad and strength in depth.”

Nottinghamshire’s Vitality Blast clash with Leicestershire was abandoned after rain. Riki Wessels hit 63 off 37 and Alex Hales made 51, his third straight fifty, as Notts posted 210-8 from 20 overs. After a delay, Leicestershire were set 68 from five overs under DLS, but further showers ended the game before a result was possible. The washout gives Notts a point, lifting them to fifth in the North Group, level on 10 points with Northamptonshire, who occupy the final qualifying spot.

PCC seeks fairer funding for policing Conservative conferences in Birmingham West Midlands Police could face costs of about £500,000 each time the Conservative Party holds its annual conference in Birmingham, PCC David Jamieson has warned. He said the party will meet in the city this October and is due to return in 2018 and 2020. Jamieson has asked Home Secretary Amber Rudd for talks on a “fairer arrangement” to cover planning and policing. The Home Office said conference funding has been reviewed and is now “fairer” than previous schemes after consultation with policing partners. A spokesman said a government grant will pay for policing, noting earlier rules reimbursed 85% of operational costs plus planning. He added that forces should plan for party conferences as they do other large events without extra funding. Jamieson argued that making the conferences safe requires meticulous, extensive preparation by West Midlands Police. He said the dedicated planning team, which began work last autumn, is costing approximately £460,000 this year and will not be recouped. In 2014, when Birmingham last hosted the Conservative conference, planning costs reached £520,000, he noted. The PCC warned that over the next four years the burden could reach £1.5m if the gap remains. At its peak, the planning team will include three chief inspectors, five inspectors, eight sergeants, four constables and four police staff. In total, 24 police employees will work on planning, split between 12 full-time and 12 part-time posts. Birmingham’s International Convention Centre last hosted the conference in September 2014, and the city remains a regular venue for national political gatherings. Jamieson said West Midlands Police will continue to prioritise public safety but urged the government to reconsider how conference-related planning costs are covered to prevent further strain on local policing budgets.

It said CIA officers acted reasonably in searching computers after concerns they contained classified material. The finding contradicts allegations from lawmakers and an admission from the agency’s own inspector general. An internal CIA review board launched an inquiry after the agency appealed findings by David Buckley, the inspector general, who determined that employees had “improperly” gained access to computers used by Senate staff. The board concluded that while there had been some “inappropriate access” to a secured network used by Senate workers, the actions did not constitute wrongdoing and no laws were violated. Officials said officers acted to protect sensitive information they believed might be improperly stored on the system. The allegations arose during the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into claims of torture by the CIA following the 9/11 attacks. Senate staff had been using computers at a CIA facility to examine agency documents related to interrogation practices. Those records formed the basis of a damning report released in December 2014, which found the CIA had carried out “brutal” interrogations of al-Qaeda suspects. Dianne Feinstein, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, rejected the board’s conclusions and criticized the absence of consequences. “I’m disappointed that no-one at the CIA will be held accountable,” she said in a statement. “The decision was made to search committee computers, and someone should be found responsible for those actions.” The board’s conclusion comes a week after Buckley announced he was stepping down, though officials said his resignation was unrelated to matters he investigated. The dispute highlights enduring tensions between the CIA and its congressional overseers over access, accountability, and the handling of classified information.

Jose Mourinho has downplayed mounting speculation linking him with Manchester United, describing his future as "the one million dollar question" and insisting he does not yet know his next move. Speaking at a school event in Singapore, the 53-year-old former Chelsea manager said he has read "so many different things" about his plans but suggested that starting next season with a fresh club and project is "probably the best" option. BBC Sport reported earlier this month that United had held talks with representatives of the Portuguese coach. Mourinho, who was dismissed by Chelsea in December just seven months after guiding them to the Premier League title, has also been linked with returns to Inter Milan and Real Madrid. Uncertainty continues to surround Louis van Gaal’s position at Old Trafford. The 64-year-old Dutchman, whose contract runs until the end of next season, has faced persistent questions about his future. United sit fifth in the Premier League, six points behind fourth-placed Manchester City in the race for Champions League qualification. The club exited this season’s Champions League at the group stage but remain in contention domestically, having reached the FA Cup quarter-finals. In Europe, they face FC Midtjylland on Thursday in the Europa League round of 32, trailing 2-1 from the first leg. For now, any decision appears likely only in the summer months ahead.

Naomi Folkard and Patrick Huston have been selected to represent Team GB in the individual recurve archery event at the Rio Olympics. Folkard, 32, will make her fourth Olympic appearance, having competed at London 2012. Belfast-born Huston, 20, ranked 39th in the world, earns his Olympic debut after taking bronze at the European Championships in May. He was also part of the Team GB squad that narrowly missed a bronze at the Archery World Cup. Great Britain will look to add to their nine Olympic archery medals in Rio.

Police are investigating an early-morning assault on Ballyvannon Road in Glenavy, reported shortly after 04:00 BST. The victim was taken to hospital with injuries not believed to be life-threatening. A car found burnt out on Lurgan Road in Glenavy a short time later is being linked to the incident. The vehicle, a black Renault Clio, had been stolen earlier from a house in the Dunmurry area. Police have appealed for information.

Sterling slipped to its lowest level in months on Tuesday, dropping as far as $1.4618 before recovering slightly in late trading, as softer UK industrial data and rising political uncertainty pressured the currency. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) reported that industrial output rose just 0.1% in February from January, undershooting analysts’ expectations for a 0.3% gain. Within the headline figure, manufacturing delivered the strongest performance, climbing 0.4% in February and bouncing back from a 0.6% decline in January. However, oil and gas production fell sharply, and the construction sector contracted by 0.9% in February, compared with forecasts for a 2% rise. The mixed picture adds to signs the economy has slowed early this year following robust 2.8% growth in 2014. “Clearly this all bodes ill for economic growth in the opening quarter of the year,” said Chris Williamson, chief economist at Markit. “It’s now looking like the economy slowed, and possibly quite markedly, compared to the 0.6% expansion seen in the closing quarter of 2014. The trend should improve in March, however, according to survey data.” Sterling’s slide was compounded by a series of opinion polls showing Labour ahead of the Conservatives, unsettling traders ahead of the general election. Some market participants warned the pound could fall further if the vote produces no dominant party and a prolonged struggle to form a government ensues. “A $1.40 level for sterling/dollar is certainly not out of reach if the election aftermath turns ugly,” said Steve Barrow, currency strategist at Standard Bank. The ONS said its industrial output measure covers 14.6% of the UK economy. The first official estimate of gross domestic product for the first quarter will be released about a week before the general election, offering a clearer snapshot of momentum as political risks intensify.

Pink-clad mourners honour social worker John Stollery at Walesby funeral About 200 people gathered at St Edmund’s Church in Walesby to pay their respects to John Stollery, the 58-year-old social worker from Nottinghamshire who was among 30 UK victims killed in the attack near Sousse, Tunisia. A guard of honour from members of 2 Para, the regiment Stollery served with before entering social work, lined the church path as the cortege arrived, reflecting his service and the esteem in which he was held. Mourners wore pink, Stollery’s favourite colour, as a heartfelt tribute. His wife, Cheryl, described him as a “much loved husband, father and exceptional social worker,” and spoke movingly about their life together. “John was a devoted husband, my best friend and a fantastic dad to our son Matthew, and we miss him every moment of every day,” she said. “I feel privileged to have been his wife and I’m so proud of the outstanding tributes that have been paid in his memory. John, you always gave of yourself to others and to us so we could have a brighter future. Shine brightly with the stars above. Love and miss you forever.” Reflecting on the circumstances of his death, she added: “Matt and I are finding it extremely difficult to come to terms with the way John was taken from us in such a horrific and tragic way when we were just on a family holiday together.” She also extended her thoughts to other families affected, and offered thanks for the kindness and support they have received in recent weeks. Stollery worked at Nottinghamshire County Council for 33 years, dedicating the last 16 to supporting children in care. Colleague Steve Edwards said: “We have lost a truly magnificent social worker and there will be a huge gap in the lives of the children he cared for.” Books of condolence have been opened at county council offices across Nottinghamshire, giving residents the opportunity to pay tribute. As the community gathered to remember Stollery’s life and service, the outpouring of respect and gratitude underscored his lasting impact on the families and children he supported.

Birmingham City Women have re-signed Leicester-born forward Rachel Williams on a free transfer after Notts County Ladies folded in April. Williams, 29, returns to the Blues, where she spent two seasons between 2011 and 2013 and established herself as one of the WSL’s leading strikers. She is the third former Notts County player to secure a new club on the same day, following England defender Amy Turner’s move to Liverpool and Wales international Angharad James’s switch to Yeovil. Williams was voted Players’ Player of the Year at the FA Women’s Football Awards in 2011 and etched her name into Birmingham folklore with an injury-time equaliser that led to a penalty shootout victory over Chelsea in the 2012 Women’s FA Cup final. She was also part of the Blues side that narrowly missed out on the WSL title on the final day in 2014, scoring 14 goals in as many games. Having started at hometown club Leicester City before joining Doncaster Belles, Williams signed for Chelsea in 2014 and moved to Notts County in 2015.

Justine Roberts has revealed she was the target of a “swatting” incident in the UK last week, after police were falsely alerted to an armed intruder at her home while she was away on holiday. Speaking to the BBC, Roberts said the first she knew of the hoax was a message from her au pair the following morning, describing a late-night raid. At around 03:30, five armed officers, three unarmed officers and a police dog arrived at the property in response to a report of a man prowling with a gun. Roberts noted that while such harassment has become more common in the United States, it remains relatively rare in Britain. She said officers initially seemed unsure whether the incident would be treated as a criminal matter because there were “no actual real victims.” However, Roberts warned that swatting is taken seriously in the US due to the potential for copycat attacks, disruption and the significant cost to emergency services. The incident raises questions about how UK authorities record and pursue false emergency reports to intimidate targets. No injuries were reported. Police have not confirmed whether an investigation is under way, but Roberts’ account highlights concerns about online-enabled harassment spilling into real-world risks.

The body of Andrei Karlov, shot by off-duty Turkish policeman Mevlut Mert Altintas, was flown home on Tuesday. President Vladimir Putin took part in a solemn ceremony at Russia’s foreign ministry ahead of a planned state funeral, underscoring the importance Moscow has placed on the veteran diplomat’s service and death. Karlov, 62, was assassinated at a photo exhibition in Ankara on Monday evening. Witnesses reported that Altintas, a 22-year-old member of Ankara’s riot police, shouted that the attack was revenge for Russia’s involvement in Aleppo, where Moscow-backed Syrian government forces had recently taken control. Altintas was later killed in a gunfight with Turkish officers. Authorities have not yet clarified whether he had links to any militant group. Despite initial fears that the shooting might derail a fragile rapprochement between Russia and Turkey, both governments have emphasized their alliance and pledged cooperation. BBC Moscow correspondent Sarah Rainsford reports that joint investigative teams from Russia and Turkey are working together on the murder inquiry, a sign of the political determination to keep relations on track. The sombre ceremony in Moscow began with mourners including Mr Putin, Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev and Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov laying flowers beside Karlov’s open casket in the foreign ministry’s grand hall. Karlov’s coffin had been returned to Russia following a formal ceremony at Esenboga airport in Ankara, attended by senior Turkish officials and an honour guard of six soldiers. In scenes unusual for a predominantly Muslim country, a Russian Orthodox priest said prayers and swung incense over the coffin at the Ankara ceremony, as a Turkish soldier stood holding a photograph of the slain diplomat. Karlov’s widow, Marina, wept as she paid her respects; she was present when Altintas opened fire. Karlov was a seasoned diplomat, serving as the Soviet ambassador to North Korea for much of the 1980s. His posting in Ankara began in 2013 and coincided with several crises, including the 2015 downing of a Russian jet by a Turkish plane near the Syrian border. Moscow demanded an apology and imposed sanctions—most notably a freeze on charter flights by Russian tourists—before the two sides recently repaired ties.

Concerns raised over Welsh‐medium school access as councils’ plans scrutinised Since last year, Welsh councils have been required to submit proposals to ministers outlining how they intend to meet local demand for Welsh‐medium education. Ministers can accept, amend or refuse these plans. However, Welsh Language Commissioner Meri Huws told the Senedd’s education committee she is worried the system lacks teeth, noting the government “cannot force councils to implement their schemes.” Liberal Democrat AM Aled Roberts said the arrangements are already failing some families, citing a north Wales constituent who speaks Welsh with her children but was unable to secure a place at a Welsh‐medium primary school. “This shows the system is not delivering for parents who want Welsh‐medium education,” he argued. Responding, Wrexham Council said it believes provision is sufficient across the county borough. “Some parents have, however, been unable to get their children into their preferred school and have been offered a place in an alternative Welsh‐medium school,” a spokesperson said, adding that “the criteria used for over‐subscription is exactly the same as for English‐medium schools.” Education Minister Huw Lewis acknowledged shortcomings in the first round of plans, revealing he has “sent 17 of the 22 proposals back to the councils” for revision. He cautioned, though, that it remains “too early to see how effective the new system has been,” and said monitoring will continue as councils adjust their strategies to meet demand.

Introducing bonus points is aimed to be an incentive for teams to attack. Wales will balance ambition with pragmatism in Rome as the Six Nations’ bonus-point system encourages teams to attack, according to kicking coach Neil Jenkins. The introduction is intended to incentivise attacking play across the Championship, but Jenkins insisted pragmatism remains paramount. Jenkins, the only Welshman with more than 1,000 Test points, said Warren Gatland’s side are prepared to “bring our A-game” and play from anywhere on the field, but will not hesitate to resort to a territorial battle if conditions or the contest demand it. “We’ve got to be ready to play from anywhere and be ready to play territory as well,” he told BBC Wales Sport. “It’s going to be a tough game. Italy are looking forward to playing us.” Wales have not lost to Italy since 2007, though the Azzurri have beaten them twice in Rome, in 2003 and 2007. In contrast, the last two Championship meetings have ended in heavy Welsh wins, with Italy conceding more than 60 points on each occasion. Jenkins cautioned against reading too much into those scorelines, aligning with Italy captain Sergio Parisse’s view that Wales only pulled clear late. “You look at the scores the last two years — they’ve been blown out a bit — but the games have been tough from the word go,” he said. “As Sergio says, we got away in the last 20 minutes and scored quite a few tries in both games.” With rain forecast for Sunday afternoon, Jenkins stressed that Wales will take points as they come. “You’ve got to earn your right to put points on the scoreboard, and sometimes that’s three, six, nine, 12, and not seven, 14, 21,” he said. “Test matches are all about winning, it’s as simple as that. If the bonus point comes into play, so be it.” He added that Wales have a clean bill of health, with no injury concerns on the eve of the match.

The diamond measures 2.69cm by 2.06cm (1.06 inches by 0.81 inches) and is set on a ring. A spectacular pink diamond has shattered the world auction record in Geneva, selling for $83 million including commission and instantly becoming one of the most valuable gemstones ever sold under the hammer. The 59.60-carat stone, previously known as the Pink Star and now renamed the Pink Dream by its buyer, New York diamond cutter Isaac Wolf, drew swift and intense bidding before the hammer fell. The winning offer was 68 million Swiss francs ($74 million) before fees, eclipsing the previous diamond auction record of $46.2 million set three years ago by the Graff Pink, a stone roughly half the size. After a tense exchange that saw a telephone bid of 67 million francs countered by the final offer in the room, Sotheby’s auctioneer David Bennett declared, “Ladies and gentlemen, 68 million is the world record bid for a diamond ever bid and it’s right here,” before confirming the sale. To mark the moment, the auction house played the theme from the Pink Panther. Geneva’s jewelry sales are renowned for glamour and headline-making prices, with past highlights including pieces once owned by Gina Lollobrigida and Wallis Simpson. Despite broader economic uncertainties, the appetite for exceptional gems shows little sign of waning, and tonight’s sale underscored the market’s focus on rarity and provenance. According to Sotheby’s, the Pink Star was mined by De Beers in Africa in 1999, though the specific country was not disclosed. In its rough state, the diamond weighed 132.5 carats and required two years of cutting and polishing to achieve its current size and vivid hue. Pink diamonds of any size are rare, and most weigh under five carats; at 59.60 carats, the Pink Dream is more than double the size of the next largest diamond in its class to appear at auction. “It’s really extraordinarily rare,” Bennett said. “Very, very few of these stones have ever appeared at auction.” The $83 million price includes Sotheby’s commission and contributed to a record-setting evening for the auction house, which said it has sold nearly $200 million worth of jewelry in its current Geneva auction—its highest total for a single jewelry sale. The Pink Dream, mounted on a ring, now ranks as a benchmark for the top end of the colored diamond market and a testament to collectors’ willingness to pay unprecedented sums for truly exceptional stones.

Mr Bean retires at the end of the month after almost 14 years at the bank, capped by a knighthood recognizing his services to monetary policy and central banking. The honour headlines a list that highlights leading figures across finance, consumer advocacy, industry and infrastructure. Martin Lewis, founder of the Money Saving Expert website, is appointed OBE for services to consumer rights and charity, acknowledging his high-profile campaigning and the impact of the MSE charity fund. Pensions specialist Ros Altmann receives a CBE, credited for her role in campaigning for the end of compulsory annuities, while economist Kate Barker, a former member of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, is made a dame. Nominees from industry and the economy make up 11% of this year’s list. Gerry Grimstone, chairman of asset manager Standard Life, is awarded a knighthood for public service to defence and business. In transport safety, Chris Hanson-Abbott, chairman of Brigade Electronics, earns an OBE for services to road safety, reflecting the company’s role in introducing reversing alarms for trucks in the UK. Louise Makin, chief executive of British Technology Group, becomes a dame for services to the life sciences industry. Philip Dilley, former chairman of engineering and consultancy firm Arup, receives a knighthood. Jim O’Neil, the former chief executive of UK Financial Investments, the body that oversaw the sale of government stakes in bailed-out banks, is appointed OBE for services to the banking industry.

Twitter disclosed Thursday it had received a U.S. government demand to unmask the person or people behind @ALT_USCIS, a pseudonymous account claiming to be employees of a border protection agency and sharply critical of the new President. The company refused, framing the request as a free speech issue, and challenged it in court. By Friday, according to court filings, the Justice Department informed Twitter the demand “no longer has any force or effect,” withdrawing the order and ending the legal confrontation.

Neymar-led Brazil held again as Iraq resist; Gnabry rescues Germany; Mexico, Portugal win; Nigeria into quarters Brazil’s quest for a first Olympic football gold stuttered once more as the hosts were held to a second successive goalless draw, this time by a stubborn Iraq side in Brasilia. Despite the presence of Barcelona forward Neymar and a buoyant home crowd of more than 60,000, Brazil could not find a breakthrough and were met with jeers at full-time after another frustrating 0-0 stalemate following their opening draw with South Africa on Thursday. Rogerio Micale’s team dominated with 20 attempts, but only six were on target as composure deserted the Selecao in the final third. “We need to apologise to the fans, to the people,” said the Brazil coach. “As the time passes and we can’t score, the anxiety increases, and in this situation it’s easier to make mistakes.” Iraq, who defended diligently and countered selectively, celebrated a landmark result. “It’s a historic day for Iraq to be able to draw against Brazil at its home,” said coach Abdulghani Alghazali. “It’s a great achievement for Iraqi football.” In Group A’s other fixture, Denmark moved top with four points thanks to Robert Skov’s 69th-minute strike in a 1-0 win over South Africa. The result leaves Brazil and Iraq on two points apiece and South Africa with one, tightening the race for the quarter-finals heading into the final round of matches. Group C provided high drama and a flurry of goals. Defending Olympic champions Mexico roared back from a shock halftime deficit to dismantle Fiji 5-1 in Salvador, with Erick Gutierrez scoring four times after the interval. Fiji, who conceded eight against South Korea in their opener, stunned the Mexicans through a Roy Krishna header before wilting under sustained second-half pressure. Mexico now sit level on four points with South Korea, who were denied victory by Germany in a pulsating 3-3 draw. Arsenal winger Serge Gnabry delivered an injury-time equaliser with a deflected free-kick to complete his brace and salvage a point for the Germans. Germany, who drew 2-2 with Mexico in their first match, have two points from two games. Portugal maintained their perfect start in Group D with a 2-1 victory over Honduras in Rio. Alberth Elis fired Honduras ahead inside the first minute, but Tobias Figueiredo and Goncalo Paciencia turned the match around to keep Portugal atop the group after their opening 2-0 win over Argentina. The Argentines revived their campaign by eliminating Algeria with a 2-1 win, as Atletico Madrid’s Angel Correa scored and set up Jonathan Calleri’s decisive strike. A fiery contest saw both sides finish with 10 men following red cards to Argentina captain Victor Cuesta and Ayoub Abdellaoui. Nigeria became the first team to clinch a quarter-final berth, edging Sweden 1-0 in Group B. Sadiq Umar’s first-half goal gave the African champions a second straight win, moving them to six points from two matches and underlining their credentials as contenders.

Scotland’s First Minister and SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon has set out key conditions for any post-election deal at Westminster, ruling out an electoral pact with the Conservatives while signalling she could reach an understanding with Labour. Speaking after a meeting of the Joint Ministerial Council, which brings together UK ministers and leaders of the devolved administrations, Sturgeon also renewed calls for the SNP to be included in TV debates. She argued that excluding the party, along with Plaid Cymru and the Green Party, would be “indefensible” given the SNP is the third-largest party in the UK by membership. Sturgeon later held talks with Prime Minister David Cameron, during which he agreed to devolve powers allowing the Scottish Parliament to lower the voting age in time for the 2016 election, following the participation of 16- and 17-year-olds in the independence referendum. Outlining her terms for cooperation with other parties in the next Parliament, Sturgeon said the SNP could not support any government committed to replacing the Trident nuclear missile system. While she avoided using the phrase “red line,” BBC Scotland’s Westminster correspondent David Porter reported that Sturgeon made clear opposition to Trident renewal would be required before the SNP could back a deal. In a show of alignment on shared priorities, Sturgeon joined Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood and Green Party leader Natalie Bennett in pledging to work together “whenever possible” to challenge what they described as Westminster parties’ fixation on austerity. The trio said May’s general election presents an opportunity to reshape UK politics, redirecting economic policy toward investment and fairness. Sturgeon’s intervention underscores the SNP’s growing influence at Westminster and sets the parameters for any negotiations that could follow a hung Parliament, while intensifying pressure on broadcasters to broaden the lineup for televised debates.

Welsh-born actor Roger Rees, a Tony and Olivier Award winner celebrated for both stage and screen, has died after a short illness. He had lived in the United States for the past 25 years and made New York City his home with his husband, playwright Rick Elice, his partner since 1982. Rees was born in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, and spent most of his childhood in south London, where he acted in church and Boy Scout productions before studying art and painting. He began his career in show business as a scenery painter, turning to acting full-time in the mid-1960s. His breakthrough came with the Royal Shakespeare Company’s epic adaptation of Charles Dickens’s The Life and Adventures of Nicholas Nickleby, for which he won both the Tony and Olivier awards in 1982, a performance that established him as a leading figure of the stage. On television, Rees became widely known to American audiences as millionaire Robin Colcord in the 1980s sitcom Cheers, where he played a love interest to Rebecca Howe, portrayed by Kirstie Alley. Paying tribute, Alley wrote on Twitter: “He is the sweetest man in the world! Lucky to have had him as a friend and to have worked beside such greatness.” Rees later appeared in the acclaimed political drama The West Wing from 2000 to 2005, bringing scene-stealing flourish to the role of Lord John Marbury, Britain’s eccentric ambassador. His film credits included a turn as the pompous Sheriff of Rottingham in Mel Brooks’s slapstick comedy Robin Hood: Men in Tights and the titular detective in a 1988 adaptation of The Hound of the Baskervilles. On stage, Rees continued to shine, playing Gomez Addams in the 2011 musical The Addams Family and starring opposite Sir Ian McKellen as Vladimir in Waiting for Godot. Tributes from across the arts poured in. Actor and director Samuel West tweeted that he woke to “the sad news of Roger Rees’s death,” while choreographer Matthew Bourne remembered him as “a lovely, generous & kind man & an heroic & passionate actor.” Musician Rick Wakeman called him “a truly lovely man and very talented too.” Rees leaves a legacy of wit, elegance, and versatility that resonated on both sides of the Atlantic.

Sebastian Vettel has been named the BBC Overseas Sports Personality of the Year after a season of remarkable dominance in Formula 1. The 26-year-old Red Bull driver clinched a fourth consecutive world title with four races to spare and closed the campaign by winning the finale in Brazil, equalling Alberto Ascari’s 1952-53 benchmark of nine successive grand prix victories. Vettel’s run after the summer break delivered nine straight wins and lifted his 2013 total to 13, matching Michael Schumacher’s single-season record. The surge took the German’s career tally to 39 wins, moving him to fourth on the all-time list, behind Schumacher, Alain Prost and Ayrton Senna. “It’s something very special if I look at the list of previous winners,” said Vettel, who did not attend the ceremony in Leeds. “Thank you very much for the award. It’s been a fantastic year.” The BBC Overseas Sports Personality award has previously gone to Usain Bolt, Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, Roger Federer and Shane Warne among others. The first half of the campaign was more open, with five different winners in the 10 races before the break — Kimi Raikkonen, Fernando Alonso, Nico Rosberg, Lewis Hamilton and Vettel each stood on the top step. But after the restart, Vettel and Red Bull were untouchable, sealing the title at the Indian Grand Prix and confirming his status among the sport’s greats. “I’m speechless,” he said in Delhi after securing the championship. “It has been an amazing season; the spirit in the team is great.” Vettel, who made his F1 debut in 2007, celebrated the title with a series of exuberant doughnut spins on the start-finish straight, a fitting flourish to a campaign that underlined his place alongside Juan Manuel Fangio, Alain Prost and Schumacher as a four-time world champion.

There were no reports of violence when the 35 Roma people were forced out of the city's Creneaux estate. A group of residents in Marseille’s 15th arrondissement forced around 35 Roma individuals to leave a makeshift camp on Thursday evening, amid rising tensions in one of the city’s poorest districts. The camp, erected earlier in the week on wasteland and consisting largely of tents, became the focus of local anger over alleged burglaries and public nuisance. Although police reported no violence at the time of the expulsion, images from the scene showed furniture and other items being set on fire. According to reports in Le Monde, the confrontation unfolded at approximately 19:30 local time (17:30 GMT) when around 30 vigilantes arrived at the Creneaux estate and ordered the Roma to depart. By the time police reached the area, the group was already leaving, and officers found no evidence of physical assaults. La Provence reported that police recorded the incident without noting any crimes, despite visible fires at the camp site. Earlier that day, residents from Marseille’s 15th and 16th arrondissements had approached Mayor Samia Ghali to complain, accusing the Roma of burglaries and other disturbances. “Some of the residents accused the Roma of fouling everything and entering buildings,” Ghali told AFP, summarizing the grievances presented to her. The 15th arrondissement, a northern neighborhood with a large immigrant population, has experienced repeated friction around temporary Roma encampments on patches of bare ground. One resident, identified only as Sabrina, told La Provence that locals felt abandoned by authorities. “We were given to understand that we had to sort out the matter ourselves,” she said. “So fine, that’s what we did. In the afternoon we phoned each other and turned up at the camp. We all know each other here. It happened very fast.” Roma rights advocates condemned the expulsion. Caroline Godard of Rencontres Tsiganes said she was “horrified” by the events, warning that actions by vigilantes risk escalating tensions and endangering vulnerable families. Godard’s remarks reflect broader concerns among human rights groups about increasingly confrontational responses to Roma settlements in parts of France. The incident in Marseille comes amid a broader national debate over Roma communities and policy enforcement. France’s new Socialist government has continued dismantling illegal camps and deporting inhabitants to Eastern Europe, a controversial approach that mirrors measures taken by the previous conservative administration. Authorities estimate that around 15,000 foreign Roma were living in illegal camps across the country this summer. Most of these Roma originate from Bulgaria and Romania. While citizens of those countries can enter France without a visa, they must secure work or residency permits to stay beyond three months under transitional EU rules. From January 2014, Romanians and Bulgarians are set to enjoy full freedom of movement within the European Union, potentially reshaping policy and enforcement landscapes in cities like Marseille.

The 21-year-old completed a four-under-par 68 on Friday, resuming after high winds stopped play on Thursday. France's Karine Icher, American Cristie Kerr and Germany's Caroline Masson are tied for the lead. Teenage amateur Seong Eun-jeong hit a hole-in-one to help move her into early contention on day one. The 17-year-old South Korean carded an impressive four-under 68, and is joined by Hull in a six-way tie for fourth place. Seong, who last year became the first player to win the US Women's Amateur and US Junior titles in the same season, birdied the first two holes before her hole-in-one at the 182-yard par-three fifth. Almost half the field were forced to complete their first rounds on Friday, with winds of 25mph and gusts of 35mph blowing when the players were taken off on day one at Mission Hills Country Club in California. World number 16 Hull hit six birdies and two bogeys in her round. Compatriots Mel Reid and Jodi Ewart Shadoff finished level par and one over respectively. Scotland's Catriona Matthew shot a three-over 75 and is in danger of missing the cut. Full leaderboard Charley Hull, 21, carded a four-under 68 on Friday as play resumed at Mission Hills Country Club after high winds halted the opening round on Thursday. France’s Karine Icher, American Cristie Kerr and Germany’s Caroline Masson share the lead following a blustery start that forced nearly half the field to complete their first rounds a day late, with 25mph winds and gusts up to 35mph disrupting day one. Teenage amateur Seong Eun-jeong produced the shot of the day, making a hole-in-one at the 182-yard par-three fifth. The 17-year-old South Korean, who last year became the first player to win the US Women’s Amateur and US Junior titles in the same season, added two early birdies and finished with an impressive four-under 68. She joins Hull in a six-way tie for fourth, keeping both in contention heading into the weekend. World No. 16 Hull balanced six birdies against two bogeys to sit off the pace. Fellow English players Mel Reid and Jodi Ewart Shadoff posted level par and one-over respectively, while Scotland’s Catriona Matthew signed for a three-over 75 and faces a fight to make the cut.

Rev Dan Woodhouse, a Methodist minister from Leeds, and Quaker activist Sam Walton were arrested after allegedly entering BAE Systems’ Warton site in Lancashire to “disarm” warplanes destined for Saudi Arabia. Lancashire Police said they are being held on suspicion of criminal damage. In a statement, Rev Woodhouse said stopping or delaying aircraft would save lives in Yemen and prevent war crimes. BAE Systems confirmed the incident is under investigation and said it is assisting police with inquiries. The company declined further comment while the probe continues, after an intrusion at the facility.

H5N8 avian flu confirmed in Settle backyard flock; public health risk ‘very low’ A small backyard flock in Settle has tested positive for the H5N8 strain of avian influenza, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) has confirmed. The flock consisted of about 17 birds. Defra said the risk to public health is “very low.” The UK’s chief veterinary officer, Nigel Gibbens, said some of the birds had died from the disease and the remainder were humanely culled to prevent further spread. To contain the outbreak, authorities have established a 1.6-mile (3km) protection zone and a six-mile (10km) surveillance area around the affected premises. The strain detected is the same as that found in Wales on 3 January and at a farm in Lincolnshire in December. Mr Gibbens urged all poultry keepers, including those with small or pet flocks, to strengthen biosecurity and keep birds separate from wild birds. “This finding in a back-yard flock shows how essential it is for all poultry owners, even those who just keep a few birds as pets, to do everything they can to keep them separate from wild birds and minimise the risk of them catching avian flu via the environment,” he said. Defra introduced an Avian Influenza Prevention Zone on 6 December, in place until 28 February, requiring keepers of poultry and other captive birds to keep them indoors or implement measures to prevent contact with wild birds. The zone covers England, with similar restrictions introduced in Scotland and Wales. The measures followed the discovery of H5N8 in poultry and wild birds across 14 countries, including Germany and France. Authorities continue to monitor and enforce the containment zones to reduce the risk of further spread.

Incidents of “concerted indiscipline” in prisons across England and Wales have surged by more than 200% since 2012, according to Ministry of Justice figures. Parc Prison in Bridgend recorded the highest number, rising from 13 incidents in 2014 to 25 last year. The MoJ introduced new standards for reporting last summer, and defines “concerted indiscipline” as situations where two or more prisoners act together to defy instructions or the establishment regime, including major disturbances such as riots. Cardiff and Swansea prisons reported two incidents over the past four years, while Prescoed and Usk recorded none. The Howard League for Penal Reform said expanding the prison estate is not the solution. “Evidence shows that building additional prisons only compounds overcrowding and its consequent problems as the courts send more people to prison every day,” said chief executive Frances Crook, urging policymakers to tackle causes of disorder.

So it is playing out again, as Greece has struggled to secure adequate loans from its eurozone and International Monetary Fund (IMF) creditors to avoid the disaster of failing to keep up its payments to the IMF. With time rapidly running out and the prospect of a de facto default looming, Greece’s banking system has been pushed to the brink. Weeks of uncertainty and faltering negotiations eroded public confidence, triggering a flight of deposits that left banks perilously short of the collateral needed to access emergency funding. Against this backdrop, Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras has presented a revised plan that eurozone leaders now view as a credible foundation for an agreement. The proposal, currently the subject of intensive technical talks, centers on raising taxes on businesses and the wealthy, increasing pension contributions, and selectively hiking value-added tax. If these measures are finalized, officials say a deal to unlock urgently needed financing could be reached by the end of the week, offering Greece temporary relief and buying time to stabilize its finances. Yet, in keeping with the familiar eurozone crisis script, the drama is unlikely to end quickly. Crucial discussions on easing Greece’s heavy debt burden—considered by many economists essential for a durable recovery—have been deferred to the coming months. Meanwhile, the banks’ liquidity position remains acute. The scale of deposit outflows has been so severe that institutions have nearly exhausted the assets they can pledge for support from the Bank of Greece and the European Central Bank. Restoring confidence will be vital. Without savers bringing cash back from “under the mattress” and redepositing it, Greek banks will stay dangerously close to collapse and remain constrained in their ability to extend credit. That, in turn, threatens to prolong the financial squeeze on households and businesses, undermining the broader economy just as policymakers seek a path out of crisis.

Essex have handed 22-year-old seamer Paul Walter a one-year extension after a busy 2016. Walter, who signed his first professional deal in June, featured in two first-class and seven T20 matches, taking the new ball in the closing stages of the T20 Blast. He claimed eight wickets across all formats. “It’s always been a dream to play for Essex, and I jumped at the chance to stay another year,” Walter told the club website. The extension keeps him at Chelmsford through next season.

Doubts are growing that a solution to Greece's debt problem will be found, and German finance minister Wolfgang Schaeuble says he is not optimistic UK stocks slipped on Tuesday as renewed concerns over Greece’s debt negotiations weighed on investor sentiment, with German finance minister Wolfgang Schaeuble warning he was not optimistic a resolution would be found. The benchmark FTSE 100 index fell 16.5 points to 6,857.05, as risk appetite faded across European markets.
