Centrica led decliners among blue chips, dropping 2.8% to 278.80p after Citi cut its price target on the British Gas owner to 285p. The move came amid reports that the energy group will post a near-30% fall in annual operating profits when it reports results on Thursday, adding to pressure on the stock. Mining group Fresnillo was also under fire, slipping 4.3% after Morgan Stanley advised investors it was “time to take profits” on the precious metals producer, citing valuation concerns. Outside the FTSE 100, 888 Holdings tumbled 11% after the online gambling firm said takeover talks with bookmaker William Hill had been scrapped due to a “significant difference of opinion on value with a key stakeholder.” William Hill shares gained 0.76% on relief that it will not proceed with a potentially costly transaction. In brighter fashion, luxury shoemaker Jimmy Choo climbed nearly 4% after HSBC raised its rating to “overweight” from “neutral,” pointing to improving momentum. On currency markets, sterling weakened 0.3% against the dollar to $1.5355, while it was little changed against the euro at €1.3503, as traders assessed political risks and upcoming earnings.

Uganda FA chief Moses Magogo says most members of the national team have received presidential rewards promised for qualifying for the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations, but a handful of players and officials are still awaiting payment. President Yoweri Museveni had pledged cash rewards after hosting the Cranes at State House earlier this month to mark their first Nations Cup qualification in 39 years. “Yes, 30 players and six officials have received their payment,” Magogo told BBC Sport, thanking the President for what he called a generous gesture. He added that the federation and the team will “continue to work hard to develop and promote football.” However, Magogo said six other players and four officials have not yet been paid despite submitting their bank details. He attributed the delays to authorities in the President’s office “reducing the numbers” during the processing of payments. Among those yet to receive funds are defenders Hassan Wasswa Mawanda and Nicholas Wadada. “I have not received my money yet, but I have been told they are working on the matter so that I receive the money,” Mawanda told BBC Sport. While President Museveni initially promised US$15,000 per recipient, the Ministry of Education and Sport clarified that US$10,000 has been disbursed, with a view to raise the total to US$15,000 in future to align with rewards offered by other nations. Uganda is the only Cecafa region country to have reached the 2017 finals and remains in the group stage of the 2018 FIFA World Cup qualifiers, underscoring the Cranes’ resurgence on the continental stage.

Investigators probing the 1989 Hillsborough disaster have released images of 100 people who attended the Liverpool v Nottingham Forest FA Cup semi-final in Sheffield, where 96 fans died in a crush. The photos, issued across 10 appeals by Operation Resolve, aim to trace potential witnesses. So far, 47 individuals have been identified or have come forward. Images of those yet to be traced are available on the Operation Resolve website. New inquests into the tragedy are under way in Warrington, Cheshire.

IKO Creative Prosthetic System Wins Netexplo Grand Prix With Lego-Compatible Bionic Arm A playful, modular prosthetic arm designed to work with Lego has won the Grand Prix at the Netexplo digital technology summit. The IKO Creative Prosthetic System combines a battery-powered arm with a 3D-printed socket and interchangeable Lego attachments — including a remote-control digger — to turn assistive technology into a customizable, collaborative tool. Creator Carlos Arturo Torres, a former intern at Lego’s Future Lab research department, said he hopes to secure investment to move the project toward wider production this year. “I’m super happy with it. I wasn’t expecting the Grand Prix,” he told the BBC. Reflecting on his Colombian upbringing, he added that growing up amid armed conflict heightened his awareness of people living with limb loss and motivated a more empowering approach to prosthetics. Torres envisions IKO as a social project that encourages children to co-design and build their own attachments with friends and classmates. “When I was at Lego, I realised how social toys can be,” he said, noting that the system aims to foster creativity and inclusion alongside functionality. The prosthetic is expected to retail for about $5,000 (£3,500), with additional 3D-printed sockets priced around $1,000 as young users grow and their needs change. Jo Dixon, national co-ordinator at children’s charity Reach, said using cheaper materials makes prosthetics “far more affordable” and easier to maintain. The rise of simple 3D-printed designs, including build-your-own Lego-style kits, with their robotic look and bespoke colors, can “increase self-confidence” and support the “acceptance of difference rather than being a functional replacement hand,” she said.

Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd is defending the arrests of two Florida girls, aged 12 and 14, accused of cyberbullying Rebecca Sedwick in the year leading up to the 12-year-old’s death, saying he has no regrets and that the action ensured the girls “receive the services they need.” “Our goal is that these kids never bully anyone again, never torment anyone again,” Judd said, a month after Sedwick died on September 9 by jumping from a tower at an abandoned concrete plant in Lakeland. Authorities said the harassment began last year after the 14-year-old objected to Sedwick dating a boy she had previously seen. Investigators alleged the two girls targeted Sedwick through online message boards and text messages. On Wednesday, Jose Baez, the attorney for the 12-year-old, challenged the basis for the arrest, saying he had found “zero evidence having to do with my client that would rise to the level of a criminal act.” He described his client as a “troubled young girl” who had been bullied herself and demanded an apology from Sheriff Judd. Baez said he has not ruled out filing a lawsuit against the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, calling the arrests and the public release of his client’s name and booking photo “reckless.” A lawyer for the 14-year-old confirmed to the Associated Press that charges against her had been dropped as well. The Sheriff’s Office did not immediately comment on the status of the 12-year-old’s case. The high-profile case has intensified debate over how law enforcement should respond to cyberbullying involving minors and where to draw the line between intervention and criminalization. Complicating the backdrop, the 14-year-old’s stepmother, Vivian Vosburg, was arrested last month on separate child abuse charges after a Facebook video allegedly showed her punching two boys.

The Superhero Series allows disabled and non-disabled people to take part in triathlons - either solo, or in a team A pioneering triathlon initiative is opening up the sport to disabled and non-disabled participants alike, inviting people to race solo or team up with friends and family. The Superhero Series, led by former T35 sprinter Warner, aims to remove barriers that have long made recreational sport feel out of reach for many. “As a person with a disability looking to do sport for fun I’ve found it a real struggle,” Warner said. “I know what a positive impact sport can have on a person’s life – I believe everyone should have the chance.” Warner, who has cerebral palsy, became the first disabled person to enter the London Triathlon in 1998. Even as an elite athlete, she recalled finding it difficult to keep pace with the event’s logistical demands. “I had to ask other participants for help with my wetsuit and to get my bike down from the bike rack,” she said. “I’ve also taken part in fun runs where the roads have reopened and organisers have started clearing up before I’ve had a chance to finish.” Described as being “dedicated to the everyday superhero – the UK’s 12 million people with disabilities – and their friends and families,” the Superhero Series puts disabled participants firmly in control. “The idea is simple: to create fun, gutsy events where people with disabilities call the shots and don’t have to worry about cut-off times or equipment restrictions,” Warner added. “If you need flippers or floats in the water, or want to use your powered wheelchair, we make it possible. In fact, as far as I’m concerned, anything goes.” Entrants can complete the full triathlon or choose one or two stages as part of a relay, mixing disabled and non-disabled team members. With three distances available, the series is designed to be as accessible and flexible as possible. All disabled participants are also invited to bring along a free “sidekick” to assist them in completing the course. “We’ve gone all out to try to think of everything we can to ensure everyone can be a superhero for the day,” Warner said. Competitors also have the chance to join celebrity teams, racing alongside figures such as Rio cycling and athletics Paralympic medallist Kadeena Cox and Channel 4 presenter Sophie Morgan. Twenty “celebrity captains” will each select two athletes to form their team, with entrants asked to submit reasons they should be chosen.

New Zealander Lydia Ko, 18, secured the season-long title, clinching the Race to the CME Globe and its $1 million bonus, after finishing tied seventh at the CME Group Tour Championship in Naples, Florida. Cristie Kerr captured the $500,000 tournament at 17 under par, while South Korea’s Ha Na Jang and American Gerina Piller shared second, one stroke behind. Ko posted a level-par 72 on Sunday, missing a birdie putt at the last, and learned she had sealed the top spot after leaving the green. “It was kind of a tough day. The hole is smaller than the ball today,” said Ko, who in September became the youngest major winner by lifting the Evian Championship. “Every emotion went through me. I’m happy that the season is over and I can relax now.” American Lexi Thompson shot 68 to finish fourth at 14 under, and world No.2 Park In-bee placed sixth, two shots further back, after both missed birdie chances at the 17th that could have overtaken Ko in the standings.

Chelmsford custody suite temporarily closed after buzzer failure as Colchester cells remain shut Police custody provision in Essex faced further disruption this week after cells at Chelmsford were temporarily closed due to a fault with their buzzers, BBC News has learned. The closure came amid ongoing works at Colchester police station, whose custody suite was shut last month following a routine inspection that identified defects with potential health, safety and welfare implications for detainees. With Colchester’s cells unavailable for a number of weeks while improvements are carried out, those arrested have been diverted to Chelmsford or Clacton. However, on Tuesday, the Chelmsford custody suite also shut to allow essential maintenance, forcing officers and solicitors to make alternative arrangements and travel farther afield. Caroline Woodley, a defence solicitor working in the north of the county, told the BBC that the Chelmsford closure was due to non-functioning cell buzzers. “This means officers having to travel to other stations and some officers have been just deployed as a taxi service ferrying people between the two,” she said. “Voluntary attendees at Colchester police station are finding it impossible to get into custody. We are obviously having to travel further afield which will in turn cost the taxpayer in legal aid.” Woodley added that last week a colleague and a police officer abandoned attempts to access custody for an interview and instead conducted a contemporaneous note interview at the client’s house. She said a complaint had been lodged with Chelmsford police after her firm was not contacted about two clients. Essex Police confirmed the temporary closure at Chelmsford on Tuesday to carry out essential maintenance and said the problems have since been fixed, with the cells reopened. A spokesman said the Colchester custody suite remains shut while a programme of works is completed, following a routine inspection which highlighted defects “that could have health and safety or welfare implications for detainees.” The force said custody suites in Chelmsford and Clacton will be used to detain prisoners until Colchester reopens. The former custody suite at Braintree police station is permanently closed.

The Simon Andrews Legacy Lap, established in 2014 following the Worcestershire TT star’s death at the North West 200, will return with added poignancy this year after recent fatalities. “It is very important that fallen racers are not forgotten. Last year the procession stretched back for 15 miles, which shows the respect that exists,” said Simon’s sister, Claire Jupp. The mood has been darkened by further tragedy. On Saturday, two competitors were killed on the Isle of Man TT’s opening day: sidecar driver Dwight Beare, 27, crashed near the Rhencullen section of the Mountain Course, while Paul Shoesmith, 50, from Cheshire, died following a crash on Sulby Straight during solo practice. Earlier this season, Manx soldier Billy Redmayne, 25, died in April from serious head injuries sustained at the Oliver’s Mount Spring Cup in Scarborough. Malachi Mitchell-Thomas, 20, from Chorley, Lancashire, died this month after a crash during the Supertwins race at the NW200 in Northern Ireland. Both had hoped to make their TT debuts. More than 5,000 riders took part in last year’s tribute lap, with the procession stretching back for 15 miles. This year’s Legacy Lap will have a full police escort and is scheduled to set off from the TT Grandstand at 10:00 BST, uniting the racing community in remembrance and underscoring the enduring respect for competitors who have lost their lives pursuing the sport they love.

Mick Creedon, now Derbyshire chief constable, said there was enough evidence to prosecute the MP in 1991. He spoke following publication of an independent inquiry into allegations against Lord Janner. The late peer's family deny the allegations. Derbyshire’s chief constable Mick Creedon has said that the Crown Prosecution Service, not the police, made the decision that prevented a 1991 prosecution of the late Lord Janner, insisting there was sufficient evidence at the time to bring charges. “It remains a simple and regrettable fact that Lord Janner should have been prosecuted 25 years ago,” he said. “This report confirms that the reason he was not [prosecuted] was a direct decision made by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and not by Leicestershire Constabulary.” Creedon, then a detective sergeant with Leicestershire Police, became aware of allegations against Greville Janner—MP for Leicester West at the time—during an investigation into Frank Beck, a convicted sex offender who abused children in Leicestershire care homes. Creedon and his colleague, Detective Inspector Kelvyn Ashby, interviewed a complainant referred to in the inquiry as Complainant 1, who alleged he was groomed by Janner and engaged in sexual activity with him in 1974–75, when he was under 16 and living in a children’s home. On 13 March 1991, Creedon and Ashby interviewed Janner under caution. Janner replied to every question: “As advised by my solicitor, I do not wish to answer.” Despite this, Creedon says officers gathered supporting material, including personal letters from Janner that corroborated aspects of Complainant 1’s account. Creedon maintains he wanted to arrest Janner, which would have allowed a search of the MP’s home, but was instructed to interview him by appointment instead. “I believed the victim’s account of abuse,” he said. His intervention comes after a report by Sir Richard Henriques, a retired High Court judge, into past decisions not to prosecute Janner. Henriques concluded that the primary cause of the failure to prosecute in 1991 was “an inefficient investigation by police.” However, he also found that by December 1991 there remained enough evidence to offer “a realistic prospect of conviction,” and that the decision not to charge was wrong. Creedon rejected the report’s criticism of the police as unfair, saying: “I do not recall us receiving any requests for further investigative work from either counsel or the CPS.” He has already given preliminary evidence to the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse, chaired at the time by Justice Lowell Goddard, which is examining institutional failings. The Janner family has consistently denied the allegations. The renewed focus on the 1991 decision underscores the high stakes for the reputations of those involved and the wider search for accountability in historic child abuse cases.

Over a long time it is thought that when bigger animals become extinct rats will grow to fill the environment that they lived in. Rats are known to be really good at changing to survive wherever they live. The way animals change over a long time is called evolution. So scientists think that rats will evolve to grow bigger and bigger, potentially reaching the size of other large animals. Dr Jan Zalasiewicz of the University of Leicester said, “Given enough time, rats could probably grow to be at least as large as the capybara, the world’s largest rodent alive today, which can reach 80 kilos.” He added that size is only one part of the story, predicting a wide range of future rat adaptations. “There will be future thin rats, future fat rats, slow and heavy rats, fast and ferocious rats, probably future aquatic rats—the list goes on.” According to Zalasiewicz, other adaptable species such as domestic cats, rabbits, goats and more could follow similar evolutionary paths, diversifying to fill vacant ecological niches. History offers striking precedents. The largest extinct rodent known, Josephoartigasia monesi, lived around three million years ago in South America. It was larger than a bull and may have weighed over a ton, dwarfing its modern relative, the sheep-sized capybara. Such examples show how rodent lineages can expand dramatically under the right conditions. Even so, experts caution that these changes unfold over vast timescales. Evolution operates across thousands to millions of years, meaning no one should expect giant rats anytime soon. As a reminder of how dramatically species can transform, scientists note that about 50 million years ago a relative of today’s blue whale was roughly the size of a wolf—proof that life can scale up in extraordinary ways when environments and opportunities shift.

Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge, has revealed a personal glimpse into her relationship with Queen Elizabeth II, recalling the anxiety of choosing a Christmas gift for the monarch and how a simple homemade present became a cherished moment. Speaking to ITV for the documentary Our Queen at Ninety, the Duchess recounted deciding to make chutney using her grandmother’s recipe after wondering what to give “the woman who has virtually everything.” “I was worried what to give the Queen as her Christmas present. I was thinking, ‘Gosh, what should I give her?’” she said. “And I thought back to what would I give my own grandparents. And I thought, ‘I’ll make her something.’ Which could have gone horribly wrong. But I decided to make my granny’s recipe of chutney.” Her concern quickly turned to relief when she saw the jar placed on the table at Sandringham the following day. “I’ve noticed since she’s done that on lots of occasions and I think it just shows her thoughtfulness, really, and her care in looking after everybody,” Catherine added. While the Duchess did not specify the exact recipe, “Granny’s Marrow Chutney” is a likely candidate. The dish, featured in Pippa Middleton’s book Celebrate, is described as a traditional family recipe and a practical way to use large marrows or courgettes. In what is Catherine’s first solo television interview, she also spoke about the Queen’s close bond with her great-grandchildren. “George is only two-and-a-half and he calls her Gan-Gan,” she said. “She always leaves a little gift or something in their room when we go and stay and that just shows her love for her family.” Catherine praised the Queen’s “gentle guidance” in helping her adapt to her royal role. The two-hour ITV documentary, airing to mark the Queen’s milestone birthday in April, features interviews with 11 members of the Royal Family, including the Prince of Wales and the Duchess of Cornwall, the Duke of Cambridge, Prince Harry, the Duke of York, and Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie. It offers a rare, intimate portrait of the monarch through the eyes of her children and grandchildren. The Duke of Cambridge noted the powerful impact his grandmother has on the public. “I’ve seen people literally faint in front of her,” he said. “There’s a lot of trembling knees and people can’t talk sometimes.”

Herero and Nama Descendants Sue Germany in U.S. Court, Seek Reparations and Role in Namibia Talks Descendants of the Herero and Nama peoples have filed a lawsuit in U.S. federal court seeking reparations from Germany and a formal role in ongoing negotiations between Berlin and Namibia over atrocities committed during colonial rule. The complaint, lodged in the U.S. District Court in Manhattan under the Alien Tort Statute, a 1789 law often used in human rights cases, alleges genocide, expropriation, and forced labor stemming from the 1904–1908 campaign by German colonial forces in what was then South West Africa. Historians estimate that about 100,000 people were killed as German troops crushed an uprising beginning in 1904. Studies cited in the suit say colonial authorities confined captives in concentration camps and shipped thousands of human remains, including skulls, to Berlin for now-discredited racial “science.” Germany has recently acknowledged the killings as genocide and is in talks with Namibia on a joint declaration addressing the massacres. However, representatives of Herero and Nama descendants say they have been excluded from those discussions and insist that any settlement must include direct participation and compensation. “There is no assurance that any of the proposed foreign aid by Germany will actually reach or assist the minority indigenous communities that were directly harmed,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Ken McCallion, said in an email to Reuters. “There can be no negotiations or settlement about them that is made without them.” Germany has rejected paying reparations akin to those awarded to victims of Nazi-era crimes, arguing that it supports Namibia through significant development aid. The plaintiffs contend that aid to the state is not a substitute for restorative justice owed to the communities directly affected by the colonial-era abuses. A hearing date has not yet been set.

High Court backs government plan to close Independent Living Fund in June 2015 The High Court has upheld the government’s decision to close the Independent Living Fund (ILF), a £320m scheme that provides support to around 18,000 severely disabled people across the UK, ruling that ministers acted lawfully in planning to end the fund on 30 June 2015. Delivering her judgment, Mrs Justice Andrews expressed sympathy for those affected, acknowledging the closure would be a “great disappointment” for many, but concluded that the legal challenge did not establish that the decision breached equality duties. The ILF, established to help disabled people live independently rather than in residential care, offers payments that many recipients use to employ personal assistants and access support tailored to individual needs. During an October hearing, David Wolfe QC, representing two severely disabled claimants in lead cases, argued that the Work and Pensions Secretary had unlawfully failed to discharge his public sector equality duty under the Equality Act 2010. He told the court the claimants receive between £450 and £500 per week from the ILF, funding he said was critical to enabling them to live in their own homes, work, and study. The application for judicial review dismissed on Monday marked the second legal battle over the closure. In November 2013, the Court of Appeal overturned an earlier ruling from April 2013 that had found the government’s original decision to be lawful. Following that setback, ministers announced a fresh decision to close the fund, underpinned by new equalities analysis prepared by the Department for Work and Pensions, which was subsequently challenged again in court. The government argues that reforms to social care have called into question the need for a separate funding stream, asserting that the vast majority of disabled people with care needs are already supported through the adult social care system administered by local authorities. Under the plan to close the ILF, funding is to be transferred to councils. However, disability rights advocates have warned of serious consequences. The charity Scope said disabled people could be left without enough support, with chief executive Richard Hawkes describing the care system as “on its knees.” He cautioned that closure is “likely to lead to fewer disabled people being able to live independently,” adding: “Funding will be transferred to councils, but there will be no guarantee that the money will be used to support disabled people to live independently, or that former ILF users will receive the same levels of support, given the pressures on local authority finances.” Wheelchair user John Kelly, 45, from Wimbledon, who attended the ruling, called the decision “bonkers.” “I am absolutely gutted — not just for myself but for the thousands of people this decision will impact on,” he said. The Equality and Human Rights Commission has previously warned that closing the ILF would “result in loss of dignity and independence for many ILF recipients,” and could put the UK at risk of breaching international commitments to support disabled people.

Dean Stansby, 41, died after suffering stab wounds to the abdomen near Ancaster Road in Ipswich on Wednesday. He was found injured and taken to Ipswich Hospital, where he died a short time later. A 39-year-old man from Ipswich and a 16-year-old boy were arrested on suspicion of murder and have been bailed. On Monday, a 31-year-old man of no fixed abode was arrested and has been bailed until 21 May. Detectives continue to investigate and have appealed for witnesses or information to come forward.

Tomlinson’s Dairies in Minera plans a £14m expansion after outgrowing its facilities, with Wrexham council planners recommending approval ahead of a planning committee meeting on Monday. The three-phase project would double output to 195 million litres of milk annually. The dairy, which employs about 170 staff, says the growth will secure jobs and increase capacity to meet demand. Founded in 1983 by brothers Philip and John Tomlinson, the business grew from a doorstep round using milk from the family farm in Minera.

Venezuela opposition’s supermajority at risk as Supreme Court reviews election challenges Venezuela’s opposition coalition faces a pivotal test as the Supreme Court reviews challenges to key legislative races that delivered the bloc a two-thirds supermajority in the incoming National Assembly. The court said Tuesday that several losing candidates had filed appeals, though it did not specify the grounds. It remains unclear how long the tribunal will take to rule. Members of the new legislature are set to be sworn in Tuesday, marking the first time in 16 years that the opposition Democratic Unity Roundtable (MUD) will control the chamber. The opposition secured 112 seats, the threshold required for a two-thirds majority in the 167-seat Assembly. However, if the Supreme Court upholds even one challenge, the MUD would fall below that mark, significantly curbing its leverage. A supermajority would grant the opposition sweeping powers, including the ability to remove Supreme Court justices, appoint key officials such as an independent attorney general, and advance constitutional amendments, which would then require ratification by referendum. MUD secretary-general Jesús Torrealba condemned the legal challenges, accusing the government of using judicial maneuvers to undermine the vote. “You can’t use legal tricks to steal something the voters didn’t want to give you,” he said, adding, “We’re not living in a functional democracy.” President Nicolás Maduro countered that it was the opposition that was “playing dirty,” alleging that “criminals were buying votes.” His government has not provided details supporting the claims. The opposition has also denounced last-minute actions by the outgoing, socialist-led National Assembly, which convened extraordinary sessions to appoint 13 new Supreme Court judges and 21 substitutes. Outgoing Assembly president Diosdado Cabello oversaw the appointments, prompting accusations that ruling-party allies are seeking to retain influence beyond the legislative term. Amid the mounting institutional clash, Maduro has called a January gathering of socialist supporters to chart the next phase of the “Bolivarian revolution,” signaling a protracted struggle over the direction of the country’s political and judicial institutions.

Hebe de Bonafini has refused twice to appear in court to give evidence over the alleged embezzlement of millions of dollars from a low-income housing project. Mrs Bonafini, who is 87, is not personally accused in the case. Her organisation has been leading the fight for justice for victims of the 1976-83 military regime in Argentina. Later, it became a close ally of the former president, Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner. Police were dispatched to escort Mrs Bonafini after she declined two summonses to testify, but she apparently evaded officers and boarded a minivan bound for the Plaza de Mayo, where the Mothers and their sister group, the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, have marched in protest every Thursday since 1977. Bonafini’s two sons were among those “disappeared” during the dictatorship, a personal loss that helped galvanize the movement’s enduring presence and influence in Argentine public life. The case centers on a social initiative the Mothers launched to carry forward the work many of their children—mostly left-wing activists—might have undertaken had they survived. The program, valued at $53 million, aimed to build housing, schools, and health centers in low-income neighborhoods before being abruptly halted in 2011. Prosecutors are investigating the alleged diversion of millions of dollars from the initiative. The renewed focus on past abuses and accountability comes as the United States prepares to release additional documents related to Argentina’s “dirty war,” a trove that may further illuminate the period’s human rights violations and state repression. Bonafini’s defiance underscores the tensions between her movement’s moral authority and the judiciary’s pursuit of answers in a high-profile probe.

The analysis shows that the average body size of four whale species declined rapidly during the second half of the 20th Century in response to hunting. But warning signals were visible up to 40 years before whale stocks collapsed. The work appears in Nature Ecology and Evolution journal. A new study led by Christopher Clements of the University of Zurich has found striking reductions in the average body size of blue, fin, sei, and sperm whales during the industrial whaling era, with early indicators of stress detectable decades before populations crashed. The team examined historical catch records spanning 1900 to 1985, the period preceding the global moratorium on commercial whaling, to track changes in abundance and body measurements. “We looked at data on blue, fin, sei and sperm whales and found significant declines in body size, with sperm whales taken in the 1980s four metres shorter on average than those in 1905,” said Dr Clements. He attributed the shrinkage largely to selective harvesting, in which the largest individuals were preferentially targeted. “This means that warning signals were detectable up to 40 years before a population collapse,” he added. The researchers note that similar trends have been documented in fish populations under heavy fishing pressure, where reductions in mean size serve as a precursor to declines in stock resilience. By monitoring changes in average body size, managers could identify populations at risk sooner and deploy conservation measures before numbers fall precipitously. “Our technique could be used to help provide other species of conservation concern. Moreover, it could allow interventions to be put in place to stop this happening,” said Clements, emphasizing the value of historical catch data and continuous biological monitoring in safeguarding marine wildlife.

Simon Collis made the holy trip - which it is a duty for all able-bodied Muslims to make at least once in their life - with his wife Huda Mujarkech. The 60-year-old is the first UK ambassador to perform Hajj. Mr Collins has been pictured wearing the white robes traditionally worn for the pilgrimage which re-enacts the actions of the Prophet Muhammad. The photograph was posted on the twitter account of Saudi Arabian writer and female activist Fawziah Albakr, who wrote in Arabic: "First British ambassador to the Kingdom undertakes the Hajj following his conversion to Islam. Simon Collis with his wife Huda in Mecca. Praise be to God." Saudi social media users quickly amplified the news, with among the well-wishers Saudi Arabia’s Princess Basmah bint Saud, who tweeted: “Special congratulations to the ambassador and his wife.” Collis responded on Twitter to thank supporters and clarified the personal journey behind his decision, writing: “In short, I converted to Islam after spending 30 years in Muslim societies and before getting married to Huda.” Collis has served as the British ambassador to Saudi Arabia since 2015, a capstone to a distinguished career with the UK’s Foreign Office. He previously held ambassadorships in Iraq, Syria and Qatar. In 2012, he was withdrawn from Damascus amid escalating violence and security concerns, and has openly criticised the Assad regime’s conduct in the Syrian civil war. His earlier roles include British consul-general postings in Dubai and Basra, with additional diplomatic assignments in Tunis, New Delhi and Amman. Hajj, one of the five pillars of Islam, brings millions of pilgrims to Mecca each year. Collis’s public participation, following his conversion, marks a notable moment for a senior British diplomat in the region and drew widespread praise from Saudis and international observers alike.

Victory would pull her closer to Muriel Ferguson's record of seven titles in a row in the 1960s, while Susan Egelstaff won the event six times between 2001 and 2011 and Anne Gibson was victorious nine times in the 1990s. Gilmour is returning from knee surgery. Commonwealth and European silver medallist Kirsty Gilmour will make her competitive return at the Scottish National Badminton Championships at Bell’s Sports Centre, aiming to add another women’s singles crown after an injury-hit 2016. The 23-year-old from Hamilton, who is top seed, has been out since undergoing surgery in October to repair a meniscus tear that troubled her before and during the Olympic season. A win this weekend would nudge Gilmour closer to some of Scotland’s storied landmarks in the women’s game. Muriel Ferguson captured seven consecutive national titles in the 1960s, while Susan Egelstaff amassed six between 2001 and 2011. Anne Gibson dominated the 1990s with nine victories, setting a benchmark Gilmour openly admires as she rebuilds toward peak form. Gilmour chose to compete through discomfort last year, playing the Australian Open and continuing until after Rio, where she beat Switzerland’s Sabrina Jacquet before losing to Bulgaria’s Linda Zetchiri in the group phase. “I can’t wait to get back on court,” she told BBC Scotland, admitting the transition from rehab to competition will feel unfamiliar but energising. She added that training has gone well and she is keen to experience “a consequence to points and rallies” again. Under national assistant coach Andy Bowman, Gilmour has progressed carefully, moving from controlled, predictable drills on a small court to full-court, reactive sessions. This week marks her first complete training load in four months, a milestone she says has sharpened her tactics as much as her fitness. A positive mindset, she noted, has been central to recovery, and conversations with athletes who underwent similar procedures gave her confidence about the timeline and outcomes. While she now has less cushioning in her knee, Gilmour has adapted with practical measures, including silicone beneath her insoles to absorb impact. She acknowledges she will have to manage workload and recovery intelligently, but believes the foundations are in place for a successful return across multiple events. In singles, Edinburgh’s Julie MacPherson and Mauchline’s Holly Newall are considered her principal challengers. Gilmour will also chase a first mixed doubles title, partnering Kinross’s Patrick MacHugh on Friday evening. The draw features strong pairings throughout, promising a competitive backdrop to her comeback. Top seeds include Kieran Merrilees in men’s singles ahead of defending champion Matthew Carder, and Alex Dunn with Adam Hall in men’s doubles. Rebekka Findlay teams with Caitlin Pringle atop the women’s doubles list, while Adam Hall and Eleanor O’Donnell lead the mixed. The nationals form part of Scotland’s build-up to hosting the BWF World Championships from 21–27 August, a focal point of the country’s badminton calendar.

With the Football League loan window closing on 27 March, clubs will rely on free agents and emergency loans to reinforce squads. League rules also allow long-term loans to become permanent outside a transfer window. Confirmed moves include Neil Danns leaving Leicester for Bolton on a free and team-mate Martyn Waghorn joining Wigan, also free. Sunderland’s David Vaughan heads to Nottingham Forest on a free, and Crystal Palace goalkeeper Lewis Price has joined Mansfield on loan. Abroad, Hertha Berlin striker Adrian Ramos is set for Borussia Dortmund for an undisclosed fee. Eintracht Frankfurt’s Sebastian Rode will join Bayern Munich on a free, and VfB Stuttgart winger Ibrahima Traoré will switch to Borussia Mönchengladbach, also free. Chesterfield have signed defender Charlie Raglan from FC United of Manchester for an undisclosed sum. Deals marked with an asterisk will go through at season’s end. For managerial changes, see our ins and outs page, and visit the gossip column for daily transfer rumours.

Ystradgynlais and Newtown have been identified to receive Syrian refugees as part of the second wave to Wales under the UK’s Vulnerable Persons Relocation Scheme. The move follows plans for Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, to welcome families before Christmas, and aligns with Prime Minister David Cameron’s pledge for Britain to resettle 20,000 refugees by 2020. Councillor Darren Mayor, cabinet member for housing and property, said both towns are well placed due to available family housing and adequate capacity in local schools. The first families are expected to arrive before the end of March 2016, with services preparing to support integration and community cohesion.

The last weekend before the Christmas holiday could see alcohol-related emergencies surge by up to 50%, officials warn, as festive celebrations peak and drinking intensifies across the UK. Health campaigners estimate alcohol sales in December could reach £2.3bn, with Public Health England (PHE) urging people to consider a “Dry January” to give up alcohol in the new year. Figures from PHE and Alcohol Concern show that alcohol sales in pubs, clubs, restaurants and hotels across the UK jumped by 142% on the final Friday before Christmas last year, underscoring the strain on emergency services at this time of year. The London Ambulance Service said its paramedics could attend more than 700 emergencies over the coming weekend, attributing the rise to increased festive drinking. “We can be called to people who have fallen in the road or on railway tracks or been involved in fights — often because they’ve had too much to drink,” said Paul Woodrow, director of operations at the London Ambulance Service. West Yorkshire Police expect calls to the force to rise by about 50% over the weekend, noting that a significant proportion will be alcohol-related. In the West Midlands, a temporary minor injuries unit will be set up in Birmingham city centre to help treat “worse for wear revellers” and reduce attendances at accident and emergency departments. Dr Yvonne Doyle of Public Health England said people drinking “much more than usual” over the Christmas period can lead to “the NHS and police dealing with more drinking-related accidents and emergencies.” “It’s not surprising that many of us feel ready to take a break from alcohol,” she added. “A period of abstinence could help encourage less harmful, better drinking habits in the long-term — even six months later, evidence from Dry January shows that more than two-thirds of participants are still drinking less.” “As the festive season continues, we’re urging people to take a break and get their 2016 off to a positive start by signing up for Dry January,” Dr Doyle said, highlighting the campaign’s role in promoting healthier choices and easing pressure on public services during the busiest time of the year.

Denbighshire council is standing by an enforcement officer who issued a fixed penalty notice in Ruthin after a woman was accused of littering. The woman, who asked not to be named, said she did not realise anything had fallen to the ground. The case sparked debate online, and residents launched a collection after the incident was highlighted on Facebook, with some saying she had been treated unfairly. The council acknowledged that littering “can prove an emotive issue” but said it had decided to act on the evidence. “She has the right to challenge the fixed penalty notice, and process is outlined in the notice,” a spokesman said.

An award-winning museum that honours a famous regiment amalgamated in 1994 to become part of the Highlanders, with Prince Charles its last colonel-in-chief, has warned of severe financial pressures as the oil price slump hits its core income. The attraction, which marks its 20th anniversary this year, relies heavily on bookings from oil and gas firms for conferences, training days and dinners. Despite rising visitor numbers and school tours involving children from more than 50 schools last year, the museum reports an 80% drop in profits. To safeguard its future, it must raise £100,000 annually for the next three years, with an official fundraising campaign launching next week. The museum last re-opened in 2006 following a £1.2m refurbishment, and says community support will be vital to keep its doors open.

Bonmarché has warned that colder weather dampened demand for spring stock and that UK consumer confidence remains subdued, prompting a cautious outlook for the year ahead. Chief executive Beth Butterwick said trading conditions are likely to remain challenging and that profit will be lower than expected. Shares in the fashion chain fell 10% to 170p, valuing the business at about £85m. The retailer, which operates 312 UK stores, reported like-for-like sales were broadly flat over the past 12 months. The update comes as Marks & Spencer reported a fall in clothing sales, and Next warned 2016 could be the toughest year since 2008. “Our expectation is that trading conditions will remain challenging, and our outlook for fiscal year 2017 is cautious,” Butterwick said.

Rain denied Derbyshire a famous County Championship victory over Nottinghamshire as bad light and heavy showers ended a compelling chase with the visitors just 26 runs short of their target. Play on the final day did not begin until 13:45 BST after morning rain, with Nottinghamshire resuming on 313-6. They added only 36 runs before being dismissed for 349, thanks to a burst from Tom Taylor, who claimed three quick wickets to finish with figures of 4-67. That left Derbyshire needing 216 for victory, a target that looked well within reach after a vibrant counterattack led by Wayne Madsen. Derbyshire slipped to 36-2 but Madsen, timing the ball beautifully, anchored the chase with 61. In partnership with Shiv Thakor, who made 25, he put on 67 at better than a run a ball to swing the momentum firmly in Derbyshire’s favour. Their positive intent kept the required rate manageable and, as the target came into view, the visitors appeared poised to secure their first Championship win over Notts since 2002. However, the closing stages were fragmented by interruptions. With Derbyshire edging to 180-4 and needing 36 more, the players were taken off for bad light, a stoppage that left nine overs available to reach the finish line. The restart lasted just seven balls, enough time for Alex Hughes, on 24, to be trapped lbw by Luke Fletcher, who took 2-46 and briefly checked Derbyshire’s momentum. Moments later, heavy rain swept in and forced the players off for the final time, with Derbyshire stranded at 190-5 and still requiring 26 with 7.5 overs left. The draw extends Nottinghamshire’s advantage at the top of the table. They are now 13 points clear of second-placed Kent, who did not play this week, while Derbyshire sit eighth with 36 points from five matches. Notts head coach Peter Moores praised the opposition’s efforts and acknowledged the role the conditions played. “I think we have to give credit to them. Derbyshire were in a great position to win the game. It was unfortunate for them that the weather came at the wrong time, but credit to how they played,” he said. “We prepared as if we were going to play but we wanted to get a lead of 250-270. They bowled well at us and it was a good run chase from them. They put us under pressure.” Derbyshire captain Billy Godleman reflected on a performance he believes merited victory. “Obviously we are disappointed that we weren’t able to play the game through and seal the victory,” he said. “It has been a real team effort and everyone has contributed. We are just disappointed that the weather and light intervened and stopped us from a certain victory.”

The home side declared on 318-9 at lunch on the final day, setting India 384 to win in 70 overs. Australia secured the Border-Gavaskar Trophy after drawing the third Test, with India surviving a tense final session to close on 174-6 in pursuit of an imposing fourth-innings target. Resuming their second innings at 261-7, the hosts were expected to attack quickly before declaring, but Shaun Marsh and Ryan Harris opted for caution, adding 69 in a measured stand that tightened Australia’s grip on the series. Marsh fell agonizingly short of a maiden Test hundred on home soil, run out for 99 as he chased a risky single moments before the interval. Set 384 in 70 overs, India’s chase faltered immediately. Harris struck with the second ball of his second over to remove Shikhar Dhawan for a duck, before debutant Lokesh Rahul’s tough initiation continued when he gloved a Mitchell Johnson short ball to fall for one, having scored three in the first innings. Josh Hazlewood then trapped Murali Vijay lbw for 11, his first wicket of the match, leaving India reeling at 19-3 after 8.2 overs. Virat Kohli and Ajinkya Rahane steadied nerves with a composed 74-run stand, pushing the game deep into the final session and leaving Australia needing seven wickets. But the pressure returned immediately after tea: Kohli was caught at backward square leg off the first ball, Cheteshwar Pujara was bowled by Johnson for 21, and Rahane was taken at mid-wicket off Hazlewood, reducing India to 142-6 with 15 overs remaining. Captain MS Dhoni and Ravichandran Ashwin then dug in, navigating 11 overs through fading light and mounting tension. With four overs left, the teams agreed to a draw. Soon after, Dhoni announced his immediate retirement from Test cricket, bowing out after guiding India to safety. The result ensured Australia retained the Border-Gavaskar Trophy and solidified their series advantage, with the hosts’ disciplined final-day tactics proving decisive.

Cardiff Council has begun rolling out new 20mph zones in Riverside and Canton as part of a wider plan to improve public safety and promote walking and cycling. The move follows a map unveiled in March outlining areas the authority hopes to enforce by 2021, and comes after a trial in Cathays that officials say reduced average speeds. The latest phase covers streets between Llandaff Road and Cowbridge Road East, stretching up to the edge of Pontcanna Fields. However, some key routes will remain at 30mph, including Wellington Street and sections of Cowbridge Road East up to Cardiff Bridge. The council said retaining higher limits on these roads is designed to prevent drivers cutting through smaller residential streets, “which goes against the principle of the scheme.” A public consultation has opened on the next stage, which would extend 20mph limits to parts of Canton, south Riverside, and areas west of Llandaff Road to Victoria Park Road West, down to Cowbridge Road East. Councillor Caro Wild, cabinet member for strategic planning and transport, said the rollout follows the “success” of the Cathays pilot, which “did decrease average speed limits.” Residents have offered mixed reactions. Richard Cook tweeted that “Cardiff should have blanket 20mph. Changing limits are confusing,” while Wilhelm Von Jones wrote, “I’m all for it but the reality is people unfortunately ignore. Our St has been 20mph for years, nobody obeys it.” Others were more critical, with Roger Swan calling the initiative a “complete waste of time and money.” The council said it will monitor compliance and feedback as the programme expands.

Victor Lownes, the Playboy executive who helped export the brand’s glamour to Britain, first met founder Hugh Hefner in 1954 and quickly rose to promotion director. He proposed launching Playboy Clubs and conceived the Bunny-hostess role, ideas that became central to the company’s cachet. After relocating to London, Lownes embodied the Playboy lifestyle, opening a string of successful clubs and casinos and hosting lavish, star-studded parties at his Hertfordshire mansion. He married Marilyn Cole, a former Playmate of the Year, and for a period was reputedly Britain’s highest-paid executive. His career faltered in 1981 when Playboy dismissed him as the gambling arm ran into regulatory trouble. Lownes’ imprint endures in the brand’s UK legacy. He remained a charismatic figure in British nightlife, courting celebrities and controversy in equal measure.

The 26-year-old retired from boxing earlier this year after he had to be put into an induced coma following a defeat by Chris Eubank Jr. Nick Blackwell has been taken to hospital after reportedly taking part in a sparring session despite no longer holding a boxer's licence, prompting shock across the boxing community and an immediate investigation by the British Boxing Board of Control. Blackwell, who retired earlier this year following a life-threatening brain injury sustained in his bout with Chris Eubank Jr, is said to be in a stable condition after falling ill on Tuesday, 22 November. His former trainer, Gary Lockett, expressed disbelief that the former middleweight contender would risk getting back into the ring after his previous injury. "I couldn't believe Nick would be so stupid as to put his health at risk," Lockett said. "I can't believe the boxer he sparred with, and coach or coaches involved, would ever allow Nick to spar when he's had a brain injury. In due course, I hope they are dealt with by the British Boxing Board of Control in the correct manner." Lockett said he was "shocked" when Blackwell’s brother, Dan, also a former boxer, told him the news. "I couldn't believe it. At this time, all our thoughts are with Nick and his family," he added. Lockett explained that he had encouraged Blackwell to pursue coaching and secure a trainer’s licence, which he did, and that Blackwell had been scheduled to be in Liam Williams’ corner for Saturday’s fight in Cardiff. "We thought that was all going very well and while we knew Nick missed boxing, we obviously didn't realise the extent to which he missed it," Lockett told BBC Wales Sport. "I am deeply saddened by what has happened. Nick is not just an ex-boxer of mine, but also someone I consider to be a friend." Robert Smith, secretary of the British Boxing Board of Control, confirmed an investigation would begin on Monday. "What we understand is that Nick Blackwell sparred, he was taken ill and taken to hospital where he is in a stable condition," he told the Telegraph. "He no longer has a boxer's licence, but he does have a trainer's licence, which is a completely different thing. He should not have been boxing. I'm sickened by it. It's a very tough sport and the doctors here did a wonderful job to save his life. He made remarkable recovery and for somebody to go and do what he's done, for what I thought was a very sensible young man, is just beyond belief." He also told the Daily Mail: "We need to find out how this was allowed to happen. I really can't believe Nick has got in the ring again after what had happened, I honestly can't. I don't know what he was doing - it makes no sense." Chris Eubank Jr expressed support on social media, tweeting: "Nick Blackwell is back in hospital, after he tried to start sparring again. He's a tough, tough kid, I know he'll get himself through it again. I honestly hope everything is OK and the procedure he's had is not a serious one."

Holland paceman Timm van der Gugten and on-loan Middlesex youngster Harry Podmore are in line for competitive debuts as Glamorgan open their County Championship Division Two campaign against Leicestershire, with both seamers named in the hosts’ squad for Cardiff. The visitors are set to field a reshaped and more experienced batting unit, having recruited Paul Horton from Lancashire, Neil Dexter from Middlesex and Mark Pettini from Essex over the winter in a bid to build on last season’s late momentum. Glamorgan finished fourth in Division Two in 2015, while Leicestershire ended ninth. The Welsh county took the honours in last year’s meeting in Cardiff and drew the season opener at Grace Road, but the Foxes, after two barren years in the four-day game, went on to claim two Championship wins later in the campaign under captain Mark Cosgrove. Head coach Robert Croft believes Leicestershire will present a significantly stiffer challenge this time. “They’ve recruited really well over the winter, they’ve bought in a lot of experience into their side so I don’t expect the same sort of team as we saw a couple of years ago,” Croft told BBC Wales Sport. “They’ll be quite a tough nut to crack but you’ve got to concentrate on what you do. It’s about our strengths and playing to those strengths.” Cosgrove, a former Glamorgan favourite after four seasons in Cardiff, returns determined to set the tone early. “It’s always nice to go back to Cardiff and say hello to old friends, but make no mistake, I’m back there for business, the plan is to start as we mean to go on,” he told BBC Radio Leicester. The Australian ended 2015 in prolific form, striking three centuries in his final eight innings, and says he grew into the captaincy despite challenges. “I finished the season really well, and if I can start the way I finished, I’ll be happy with that. I definitely learned as a captain—it was tough at times, but it was exciting at times as well, and I learned a lot about captaincy and managing people. We probably lacked a couple of senior players and experience sometimes—we’ve brought that in and hopefully we’ll be able to get on the front foot and play a lot of attacking cricket.” Home captain Jacques Rudolph expects the match to begin with a toss rather than Cosgrove exercising the visiting captain’s option to bowl first under the new regulations, noting only six wickets fell in two days of Glamorgan’s draw with Cardiff MCCU. Leicestershire, meanwhile, completed a competitive warm-up against Loughborough MCCU. Glamorgan must decide which batsman to omit with South African international Colin Ingram set to return. Squads: Glamorgan (from) Rudolph (capt), Kettleborough, Bragg, Ingram, Cooke, Donald, Lloyd, Wagg, Meschede, Wallace (wk), Salter, Hogan, van der Gugten, Podmore. Leicestershire (from) Cosgrove (capt), Horton (vice captain), O’Brien (wk), Robson, Dexter, Pettini, Ali, Naik, White, Raine, McKay, Chappell, Shreck.

MPs are poised to back a rare parliamentary reprimand of two former newspaper executives found in contempt of Parliament over evidence they gave in the phone-hacking scandal. Colin Myler, former editor of the News of the World, and the paper’s ex-legal manager Tom Crone were ruled in September to have misled the Commons culture, media and sport committee. On Thursday, MPs are expected to support a report admonishing the pair, and an amendment that would summon them to the Bar of the House to be formally rebuked by the Speaker. The move, led by phone-hacking victim and former Labour minister Chris Bryant, would mark the first time in nearly 60 years that non-MPs have been punished in Parliament under its contempt powers. Bryant said the sanction was necessary because the two men “have effectively been putting two fingers up to the Commons culture, media and sport committee and to parliament.” He added: “They dispute the findings, they dispute the committee’s right to do what it has done, they dispute the whole process. Parliament should take this seriously.” Myler and Crone appeared before the culture committee in 2009 and 2011 to answer questions on the extent of phone hacking at the News of the World. Initially, the newspaper claimed the illegal practice was confined to a single reporter and a private investigator. However, subsequent evidence indicated widespread wrongdoing, culminating in the paper’s closure in 2011 amid public outrage and legal fallout. The Commons privileges committee concluded that Myler misled MPs by denying awareness of phone hacking or other misconduct by staff beyond royal correspondent Clive Goodman, who was jailed in 2007 for hacking-related offences. It also found Crone misled the committee on the same point, as well as on the “significance of confidentiality” in a settlement with Professional Footballers’ Association chief Gordon Taylor, whose claim became a key marker in uncovering the breadth of the scandal. Responding at the time, Myler described the findings as “profoundly disappointing.” Crone said he did not accept the conclusions and stood by his evidence on the matters for which he was criticised. Bryant, who was awarded £30,000 in damages after his phone was found to have been hacked, insisted the call to admonish the former executives was not personal. “In the end it is our job as representatives of our constituents to hold the mighty to account, whether they are government ministers or senior executives in business, and if we can’t rely on witnesses giving truthful, honest answers, then democracy flounders,” he said. If approved, the summons would be the first of its kind since 1957, when Sunday Express editor John Junor was admonished for publishing an article that questioned MPs’ integrity over petrol allowances. The Bar of the House procedure is a formal mechanism by which non-members can be brought before the Commons to receive a public reprimand, underscoring Parliament’s authority to enforce standards and the seriousness with which it views misleading testimony.

Goldman Sachs reported a sharp drop in third-quarter earnings, as a market sell-off and muted client activity hit trading revenues. Net profit for the three months to 30 September fell more than a third to $1.43bn (£927m), while revenue slid nearly 20% to $6.9bn. The bank said advisory and underwriting lifted investment banking, but weakness in market making and bond trading offset those gains. “We experienced lower levels of activity and declining asset prices during the quarter, reflecting renewed concerns about global economic growth,” chief executive Lloyd Blankfein said. Other big US banks also reported slower trading, after equities tumbled in August amid fears of a Chinese slowdown. Results contrasted with Citigroup, which posted a 50% jump in quarterly profit to $4.29bn. Citi’s revenue fell 5% to $18.69bn, but aggressive expense cuts and tighter risk management boosted earnings. “Despite revenue headwinds, we once again proved our ability to manage our risk, our expenses and our capital,” chief executive Michael Corbat said. The diverging performances highlight how cost discipline and business mix are shaping bank results in a volatile environment.

Manager Gary Johnson says the 17-year-old Bower has enjoyed a really good pre-season, underscoring his progress through the academy. The youngster made his first senior start against Oxford City in an FA Trophy replay on 26 January last season. Speaking after that match, Bower told BBC Radio Gloucestershire it was surreal for his dad and brother to watch him play for the team they all support. A product of the club since Under-13 level, Bower acknowledged he must add physicality, saying he needs to bulk out massively to compete at senior level, where opponents can be too physical. Johnson hinted at further opportunities.

Derbyshire’s new-look line-up made a steady start against Northamptonshire on day one at Derby, anchored by Ireland international Gary Wilson’s 72 before he fell lbw to Nathan Buck seven balls before the close. Buck led the visitors with 3-54, while Ben Sanderson claimed two and Rory Kleinveldt one as all of Derbyshire’s dismissed batsmen reached double figures without pushing on. Wilson, who joined from Surrey in September, struck 10 fours in a 104-ball knock and shared the day’s highest stand of 92 with fellow debutant Daryn Smit, who made 19. With 71 overs completed, Alex Hughes and Jeevan Mendis were unbeaten at stumps, as four Derbyshire debutants featured, including Mendis and Luis Reece.

Stephane Dujarric said the secretary-general was alarmed by reports of air strikes involving incendiary weapons and bunker-busting bombs. The Syrian government has stepped up strikes on rebel-held areas of the city since a ceasefire collapsed last week. The UN Security Council is due to meet on Sunday morning in New York. The meeting was requested by the US, the UK and France. The United Nations sounded the alarm over intensifying aerial bombardments in Aleppo, with the spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon warning of repeated reports of incendiary weapons and advanced munitions being used in densely populated areas. “Since the announcement two days ago by the Syrian army of an offensive to capture eastern Aleppo, there have been repeated reports of air strikes involving the use of incendiary weapons and advanced munitions such as bunker-buster bombs,” Stephane Dujarric said in a statement. “The secretary-general considers this a dark day for the global commitment to protect civilians.” The northern city of Aleppo has become a central battleground in Syria’s five-year civil war, and the collapse of the US-Russia brokered ceasefire last week has been followed by a dramatic escalation in fighting. Last Tuesday, Ban launched a stinging attack on the Syrian government from the UN podium, saying it had killed the most civilians in the conflict. Amid mounting outrage, the UN Security Council will convene in emergency session on Sunday, following requests from the United States, the United Kingdom and France. Western governments are pressing for accountability after the deadly attack on an aid convoy near Aleppo last week, which killed humanitarian workers and destroyed vital supplies. UK Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson suggested the strike could have been deliberately carried out by Russian aircraft, saying that if confirmed it could amount to a war crime. In an interview with the BBC’s Andrew Marr, Johnson said Russian President Vladimir Putin was “not only..... handing [Syrian President Bashar] Assad the revolver. He is in some instances actually firing the revolver himself.” Russia has denied any role in the convoy attack, blaming rebel artillery. On the diplomatic front, Syrian Foreign Minister Walid al-Moalem told the UN General Assembly in New York on Saturday that government forces were making “great strides” against “terrorism,” a term Damascus uses to describe all armed groups opposing President Bashar al-Assad. He said his belief in ultimate victory was stronger than ever. Earlier, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov insisted any revival of the cessation of hostilities could not hinge on unilateral concessions by Moscow alone, calling instead for a collective effort involving all parties. The humanitarian situation in Aleppo has deteriorated sharply. The UN says nearly two million people have been left without running water. Unicef reported that fierce air strikes on Friday halted repairs to a damaged water pumping station serving rebel-held eastern districts, and that, in retaliation, a nearby station supplying government-held western areas was switched off. Unicef spokesman Kieran Dwyer said water was being used as a weapon of war by all sides, forcing residents to rely on contaminated sources and heightening the risk of waterborne diseases. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said 25 people were killed in fresh bombardments on Saturday. Activists say both Syrian and Russian warplanes are participating in the offensive, though Russia has not confirmed its involvement. Russia backs the Syrian government, while the United States supports elements of the opposition, and the two powers continue to accuse each other of failing to rein in their respective allies on the ground.

Nike will supply Chelsea’s kits from the 2017-18 season in a long-term partnership, after the Premier League club ended its Adidas agreement six years early. The deal is reported to be worth £60m per season over the next 15 years, though Chelsea did not disclose financial details. Under the arrangement, Nike will produce strips for the men’s first team, academy and women’s sides, as well as replica kits and lifestyle apparel for supporters worldwide. The tie-up underscores Chelsea’s push to grow its fan and commercial footprint in East and South East Asia and North America. Chelsea director Marina Granovskaia said: “We believe Nike will be able to support our growth into new markets as well as helping us maintain our place among the world’s elite football clubs.” The Nike contract is believed to be roughly double the value of Chelsea’s previous Adidas deal, which was worth around £30m annually. Chelsea’s announcement follows a trend of soaring kit partnerships among elite clubs. Rivals Manchester United hold the most lucrative Premier League agreement, a 10-year Adidas contract signed in 2014 valued at £750m. The Stamford Bridge club described the Nike partnership as “an incredibly exciting and important deal” for its future.

The US 5th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a Texas judge’s injunction blocking the Obama administration’s plan to expand deportation relief for undocumented immigrants. The program, challenged by 26 states as executive overreach, would have allowed the government to defer deportations for groups, including some brought to the United States as children, while granting work authorization. The appeals court rejected the administration’s argument that the states lacked standing to sue and found the plan likely violated administrative law. President Obama argues that setting enforcement priorities and deferring removals fall within executive authority. “We strongly disagree with the 5th Circuit’s decision,” a White House official told the Associated Press, noting that Congress and the Supreme Court have affirmed the federal government’s ability to prioritize immigration enforcement. Texas Governor Greg Abbott praised the ruling, calling the proposal “lawless.” In a dissent, one judge argued the actions were lawful and “quintessential exercises of prosecutorial discretion.” Appeals take months, and the case may not be resolved before Mr Obama leaves office. The National Immigration Law Center urged an immediate Supreme Court appeal.

British and Irish Lions head coach Warren Gatland says Conor Murray must play before the squad departs for New Zealand. The 27-year-old scrum-half has been sidelined since being hurt against Wales last month. Gatland named Murray in his Lions squad on Wednesday but stressed the Munster star “is going to need to play before he gets on the plane — that’s important for us.” Murray has met a neurologist over a nerve issue and has been ruled out of Munster’s European Champions Cup semi-final against Saracens on Saturday. With a maximum of four Pro12 games remaining, opportunities to prove fitness are limited. The New Zealand tour is fast approaching, heightening the urgency around Murray’s return to action. “He’s got a nerve issue and it is a concern. He was hoping to be fit this week but he had a setback a couple of weeks ago,” Gatland said. “I would be reluctant to take someone to New Zealand with a neck injury who hasn’t played.” “He’s incredibly fit, and hopefully he’s going to be right in a couple of weeks — the neurologist is confident he is going to be okay.”

Manchester United forward Robin van Persie has welcomed the arrival of Radamel Falcao, insisting the Colombia international will strengthen the team and bring healthy competition for places. Falcao, 28, joined United on transfer deadline day in a £6m season-long loan from Monaco. “I welcome his arrival, he makes us better,” Van Persie told Fox Sports NL. “At a top club you should always go for the best, which also fits my philosophy. Falcao must fight for his place, as I also have to.” Falcao scored 11 goals in 20 appearances for Monaco last season before suffering a knee injury in January that ruled him out of the World Cup in Brazil. His move to Old Trafford sparked speculation he was signed to replace Van Persie, 31, amid reports the Dutchman required knee surgery. Van Persie dismissed the rumours, saying, “I am impressed that people have the imagination to invent something like that. I do not know where it comes from and can say with my hand on my heart that I won't be in a hospital to have the operation.” Van Persie joined United from Arsenal for £24m in August 2012 and netted 26 league goals in his first campaign, helping the club to the Premier League title.

Fire crews in South Wales battled a major hillside blaze near Cwmparc, Treorchy, after being called at 21:55 GMT Saturday. SWFRS worked overnight to contain a fire spanning 166 hectares (410 acres), equivalent to at least 200 football pitches. Crews later withdrew and allowed the fire to burn out naturally under monitoring, officials said. A separate wildfire on Penrhys mountain, covering 20 hectares (50 acres), has also been extinguished. Over the weekend, SWFRS responded to 36 grass fires in 24 hours and believes most were started deliberately. Mid and West Wales Fire Service reported 27 grass fires in the same period, while North Wales Fire and Rescue said it had tackled “a few.” Fire services urged the public to avoid risky behaviour and report suspected arson promptly.

Play resumed on Saturday at the event after high winds forced Friday's suspension of the second round. The disrupted schedule forced many to play well into the evening as they chased position before Sunday's finish. Sergio Garcia moved three clear at 16 under par, completing his delayed second round at 12 under before adding a four-under 68 in round three. The 37-year-old capped a marathon day with a birdie at his 31st hole and admitted he couldn't really see much on the last three shots as light faded. Garcia's last European Tour win was the 2014 Qatar Masters. Open champion Henrik Stenson carded a five-under 67 to reach 13 under. Ian Poulter matched that 67 and is two shots further back, tied with Thailand's Prom Meesawat. England's Tyrrell Hatton produced the round of the day, a seven-under 65, to share seventh at nine under. Three players, Jason Scrivener, Gregory Bourdy and Bradley Dredge, still have two holes to complete in the third round and will resume at 04:30 GMT on Sunday. The final round is scheduled to start 90 minutes later with a two-tee start.

The European Boxing Union has stripped Igor Mikhalkin of the EBU light-heavyweight title after he failed a drugs test on 12 March, following his unanimous points victory over Frenchman Patrick Bois in Paris. The Russian champion, who had successfully defended the belt three times, tested positive for meldonium, a substance added to the World Anti-Doping Agency’s banned list in January. “Igor Mikhalkin tested positive for an illegal substance last month and, in accordance with the rules of the EBU, he was stripped of his belt,” EBU general secretary Enza Merchionne Jacoponi said. “The illegal substance in question was meldonium, which is now on WADA’s banned list but was not on the list until January of this year. We asked him if he had taken the drug, and he confirmed it. That is why no counter-analysis of a B sample has taken place.” More than 100 athletes have tested positive for meldonium since it was prohibited, including former Wimbledon champion Maria Sharapova. On 25 March, Russian sports minister Vitaly Mutko confirmed 27 Russian sportspeople had returned positive tests for the drug this year.

Wael Shalaby, a former secretary general of Egypt’s State Council, resigned on Saturday and was arrested the following day as part of a widening corruption inquiry, according to the public prosecutor. Shortly after his death in custody was confirmed, Prosecutor-General Nabil Sadek imposed a gag order on all media coverage of the case until investigations are concluded. The probe centers on allegations that officials received bribes. Authorities said Shalaby’s arrest is linked to the detention of Gamal al-Din al-Labban, a procurement manager at the State Council, who was charged last week with accepting bribes worth millions of Egyptian pounds. The public prosecutor described the two arrests as part of the same case. Alongside his role at the State Council, the umbrella organization for Egypt’s administrative courts, Shalaby also served as a deputy chief justice in the administrative courts, according to Reuters. Shalaby’s lawyer, Sayed Beheiry, told Reuters his client died by hanging himself with a scarf during questioning, describing Shalaby as being in a severe psychological state. “It is very hard to be a big important judge and suddenly you lose everything and sit in front of an investigator being accused of taking a bribe,” Beheiry said. He also told Daily News Egypt that his client had been interrogated for nearly 40 hours without sleep and argued the arrest was unlawful because prosecutors had not issued a warrant. Egypt’s Interior Ministry, which oversees the prison system, has not commented. The public prosecutor has ordered an autopsy, state news agency MENA reported. The gag order underscores the sensitivity of corruption investigations in Egypt, where local and international non-governmental organizations say graft is widespread. Transparency International ranked Egypt 88th out of 168 countries in its 2015 Corruption Perceptions Index. The State Council case has prompted intense public interest, but with the media blackout now in force, official findings are unlikely to be known until investigators conclude their work.

Welsh striker Craig Davies, 31, has rejoined Oldham Athletic, returning to the club where he scored 13 goals in 55 appearances between 2007 and 2009. The Wales international arrives after stints with Brighton, Chesterfield, Barnsley, Bolton and Wigan, and a spell at Scunthorpe, where he failed to score in 21 outings. Davies becomes Oldham’s second summer signing following midfielder Dan Gardner’s move from Chesterfield, as the Latics bolster their squad ahead of the new campaign and seek firepower.

title: Wales face Fiji on Thursday having had only four days to recover from their bruising win against England. Warren Gatland says Wales will not lean on a demanding schedule as an excuse ahead of their Rugby World Cup clash with Fiji on Thursday, but believes the sport must confront the growing strain short turnarounds place on player welfare. Wales have had just four days to regroup following their physically intense victory over England, a quick reset Gatland accepts as part of tournament planning while urging World Rugby to consider longer gaps between matches in future editions. “It’s something we all need to be aware of because it’s a pretty brutal game at the moment,” the Wales head coach said. “It’s important we consider and look after the welfare of our players as well. I’m not complaining about the short turnaround because we’ve known about that for a long time. We’ve had to prepare for that.” Wales sit second in Pool A after opening wins over Uruguay and England, with Fiji next at the Millennium Stadium before a decisive final group fixture against leaders Australia at Twickenham on 10 October. Australia face England on Saturday in a match that could further reshape the pool’s dynamics. Short rest periods have impacted other teams at this World Cup. Japan, who shocked South Africa, had only three days to recover before losing to Scotland, a stark example cited by Gatland as evidence that the sport’s physical intensity is rising faster than scheduling practices have adapted. “We’ve still got guys who are battered and bruised this morning and we’ve got a game in two days,” Gatland added. “I don’t know whether four or five-day turnarounds in World Cups are too short.” Reflecting on his British and Irish Lions tours, he said the difference in collisions and tempo has grown markedly. “From South Africa in 2009 to Australia in 2013, the step-up in physicality and intensity increased massively.” Wales will seek to manage their squad carefully against a dangerous Fiji side, balancing momentum with recovery as the pool stage approaches its decisive phase.

World Bank Urges Criminal Justice Crackdown on Illegal Logging Most illegal logging operations are controlled by organized crime and channel profits to corrupt officials, the World Bank warns in a new report calling for a tougher criminal justice response to protect forests and communities. The study, titled Justice for Forests, identifies Indonesia, Madagascar and several West African nations among those heavily affected, and says targeted prosecutions and stronger law enforcement capacity can deliver swift, measurable impact. “We need to fight organised crime in illegal logging the way we go after gangsters selling drugs or racketeering,” said Jean Pesme, manager of the World Bank Financial Market Integrity team. The report argues that the illegal timber trade mirrors other prohibited commodities, with sophisticated networks laundering wood, bribing officials, falsifying documentation and exploiting weak governance. Analysts estimate that an area of forest the size of a soccer pitch is illegally logged every second. Despite the scale, most forest crimes go undetected, unreported or ignored, the report says.
