Investigations, when they occur, are often “amateurish and inconclusive,” and prosecutions too frequently target minor players driven by poverty while leaving higher-level profiteers untouched. Illegal logging ranges from mechanized crews stripping vast tracts to individual villagers gathering fuelwood, underscoring the need for responses that distinguish between subsistence and organized criminal activity. Some countries are beginning to turn the tide. Indonesia and Papua New Guinea are moving to strengthen enforcement and bring cases against figures higher up the criminal food chain. The World Bank urges aid donors to support programs that build the capacity of law enforcement agencies, prosecutors and courts to pursue complex timber crime, including financial investigations that trace profits and expose corruption. Western governments, consumers and businesses have a key role in cutting off demand for illicit wood. The United States strengthened the Lacey Act three years ago, making companies liable for ensuring that wood sold in the US comes from legal sources. Several firms have faced scrutiny under the amendment, including the iconic Gibson guitar company. The European Union has introduced similar due diligence requirements, and a growing number of buyers now insist on timber that is demonstrably legal and sustainably harvested. A 2010 study by the London-based Chatham House think-tank found that such measures had reduced illegal logging by about a quarter over the previous eight years. It urged Japan, a major timber consumer, to enact its own legislation. With Chinese consumption rising rapidly, campaigners are increasingly focusing on Beijing. Two years ago, the Environmental Investigation Agency reported beds made from illegally sourced Madagascan rosewood selling in the Chinese capital for up to $1 million, illustrating both the profits at stake and the urgency of closing global loopholes.

Ten companies have been hit by a series of ransomware attacks that lock businesses out of their computer systems until a payment is made, prompting warnings from Guernsey Police and local IT specialists. Investigators say no engineer has yet succeeded in recovering encrypted files for affected customers. In one case, a victim attempted to pay the ransom, only to see the price escalate from £400 to £1,000 within 24 hours. “We would always urge any business that has been the subject of a cyber-attack to inform us,” detectives said. “We have specialist officers who would investigate to attempt to try and locate those responsible.” Computer engineer Paul Domaille described how one company was compromised after opening an email titled “remittance advice enclosed.” He said: “I clicked on this email, the screen went black, clicked a few times and when I tried to look at QuickBooks it was all gone. Everything stored on the computer was quickly encrypted. Messages then started to appear on screen asking for a ransom, in order to get the data back. The advice is not to pay it, go back to backup and that’s the only way to recover your files.” Victims include hotels, restaurants, small businesses, and individuals, with every case involving a demand for money to unlock the computer. Authorities are advising vigilance and robust cybersecurity measures, particularly around email. Guernsey Police said: “We would always encourage businesses to have appropriate levels of cyber security and advise against clicking on emails from unknown sources. Additionally, we would advise businesses that regular reliable backing up of data, which is kept apart from their main system, would aid their rapid recovery from such an attack.” Businesses are encouraged to report incidents promptly and to maintain offline backups to minimize downtime and reduce the impact of ransomware. Police investigations into the source and scope of the attacks are ongoing.

Whistleblower Yuliya Stepanova condemns IOC ban, warns of chilling effect ahead of Rio 2016 Russian 800m runner Yuliya Stepanova has condemned the International Olympic Committee’s decision to bar her from competing at the Rio Olympics, despite her prominent role in exposing systemic doping in Russian sport. Stepanova, who had been cleared by athletics’ governing body, the IAAF, to compete under a neutral flag next month, said the IOC ruling was “based on wrong and untrue statements” and would discourage future whistleblowers from coming forward. On Sunday, the IOC stopped short of imposing a blanket ban on Russian athletes following last week’s McLaren report, which documented widespread, state-sponsored doping and manipulation of testing. Instead, the IOC said eligibility would be determined by individual sports federations, with the stipulation that any athlete previously sanctioned for doping would be ineligible for Rio. Applying that standard, the IOC specifically ruled that Stepanova could not take part, despite her earlier clearance, because she was sanctioned in 2013. In a statement, the 30-year-old argued the decision contradicted prior rulings by the Court of Arbitration for Sport and asked the IOC to review its position “on the basis of the information provided.” A covering letter addressed to IOC director general Christophe de Kepper urged the organisation to reconsider, noting that Stepanova sought “not to receive an extraordinary benefit, but to simply restore her to the position she would have been in had she never exposed Russia’s systemic doping program.” Stepanova and her husband, Vitaly, a former official at the Russian Anti-Doping Agency, were central to the chain of revelations that led to the current crisis. Their testimony to a German documentary in 2014 prompted the World Anti-Doping Agency to commission an independent investigation that uncovered the scale of doping among Russian athletes. WADA then commissioned the McLaren report, which further detailed the breadth of the state-backed scheme. Although Stepanova admits her own doping violation, she has long maintained she was trapped within a system that normalized and enforced cheating, and says her cooperation with investigators was critical to dismantling that system. She competed at the European Championships earlier this month under neutral status and was praised by peers as a “symbol” for clean sport. The IOC says it considered her circumstances but will uphold the ineligibility of any athlete previously sanctioned for doping. The decision has intensified debate over how sport balances punishing past offenders with protecting whistleblowers, as federations now race to assess Russian entries with the Rio Games fast approaching.

Crew Manager Paul Wilkens, a 47-year-old father of four, was found dead while on duty at Castle Donington Fire Station on Tuesday morning, Leicestershire Fire and Rescue Service has confirmed. Wilkens, who had served with the service for 14 years, was discovered at the station. The cause of death has not yet been disclosed. Chief Fire and Rescue Officer Steve Lunn said the organisation was “devastated and shocked” by the loss. “At this hugely sad time our primary concerns are very much focused on Paul’s partner, his children and his immediate and close family. As a service, we are doing everything we possibly can to support them,” Lunn added. Before joining the fire service, Wilkens served in the armed forces with the Corps of Royal Engineers. A JustGiving page set up to support his partner, daughter, son and two stepchildren has already raised thousands of pounds. A tribute on the page said Wilkens was affectionately known as “TL” — short for “too loud” — and remembered for his positivity and kindness: “You certainly knew when TL entered a room, a party and even an incident.” Tributes poured in from colleagues. The fire service said further information would be shared in due course and asked the public to respect the privacy of Wilkens’ family during this time.

Firefighters rescued a man from a burning flat on Lydgate Road as a woman fled the property early Wednesday. Hampshire Fire and Rescue Service crews from Hightown and St Mary’s were called at 02:30 GMT. Three more people were brought to safety from a neighbouring flat’s balcony using a ladder, and eight others were led outside by crews. South Central Ambulance Service said a 20-year-old man was taken to Southampton General Hospital for treatment for smoke inhalation. The cause of the fire is under investigation by authorities.

St Mary’s Church in Llanfair Talhaiarn has secured Heritage Lottery funding to carry out repairs and restoration after the historic building was temporarily closed last year when plaster fell from the ceiling. The churchyard also contains the gravestone of 19th-century bard John Jones, known as Talhaiarn, underscoring the site’s cultural significance. Maryann Williams, involved in the grant application, said the award will allow the community to preserve the existing fabric while developing the church and its surroundings for future use, enhancing accessibility, safety, and heritage engagement.

Mourners Stream to Bangkok’s Grand Palace as King Bhumibol Lies in State Crowds have gathered outside the Grand Palace in Bangkok since King Bhumibol Adulyadej died two weeks ago, but Friday marked the first time members of the public were allowed to view his coffin, concealed behind an ornate gilded funeral urn inside the throne hall. Authorities said up to 10,000 mourners will be permitted inside each day, as Thailand begins a long, formal farewell to the monarch who reigned for seven decades and was revered across the nation. By dawn, a thick line of black-clad mourners stretched across and around the royal park adjacent to the palace. Some had waited overnight to secure a place. “I have been waiting here since 01:00,” said 84-year-old Saman Daoruang, seated in a long queue and clutching portraits of the late king. “I haven’t been able to sleep because I was so thrilled and proud to come here.” Many wiped away tears as they emerged from the hall. In older times, the king’s remains would have been interred in the urn. King Bhumibol requested that his body be placed in a coffin instead, which is concealed behind the ceremonial vessel. Official mourning is set to last a year, and the government has asked citizens and institutions to observe somber dress and tone, with the first stage of public mourning due to end in two weeks. Images of the king are ubiquitous in Bangkok. Screens at train stations and shopping malls loop archival footage of Bhumibol at work, underscoring the deep affection many Thais felt for a monarch often regarded as semi-divine. The surge of visitors is straining resources around the palace, where new toilets are being hastily installed and rubbish disposal has become a challenge. There has been no announcement on when Crown Prince Maha Vajiralongkorn will formally ascend the throne. Officials say he has asked for time to mourn his father. The late king’s cremation is not expected for at least a year, prolonging a period of collective remembrance in a country still absorbed by memories of its longest-serving sovereign.

An anniversary auction celebrating 150 years since the birth of Beatrix Potter has raised £101,952, with more than 50 lots spanning sketches, letters and rare editions drawing global interest. Most of the memorabilia was consigned from the collection of John Cawood, a Lake District enthusiast who began acquiring Potter material in 1972 with the ambitious goal of assembling a complete set of first editions. His trove reflected the breadth of Potter’s creativity—from her finely observed illustrations to the business savvy that helped make her characters household names. Among the highlights was an original illustration for The Story of Miss Moppet, accompanied by the author’s instructions detailing how the artwork was to be shrunk to fit the title page, offering a rare window into Potter’s production process. A handwritten letter dated February 1924, signed under her married name, Beatrix Heelis, was estimated at up to £1,200 but surpassed expectations to sell for £2,700. Several first editions also featured in the sale, underscoring ongoing demand for early printings of her “little books.” Clive Moss, an auctioneer at Dreweatts & Bloomsbury Auctions in London, said bids were “received briskly from within the auction room, online and on the telephone from a world-wide audience,” reflecting Potter’s enduring international appeal. That appeal stretches far beyond publishing. In 1903, Peter Rabbit became the first literary character to be licensed and turned into a doll—an innovation instigated by Potter herself. She followed with a Peter Rabbit board game in 1904 and painting books featuring her animal protagonists, establishing a template for literary merchandising that remains influential. Potter’s legacy continues to be a significant draw for the Lake District. Her “little books” have sold 100 million copies in 35 languages, while the properties and landscapes she bequeathed—4,000 acres and 15 farms transferred to the National Trust—anchor a thriving heritage economy. Hill Top, her former home in Cumbria, attracts around 100,000 visitors annually, and The World of Beatrix Potter experience welcomes about 15,000 visitors from Japan each year, where her characters have even served as mascots for banks. Royal Mail stamps featuring Peter Rabbit and Mrs Tiggy-Winkle have been released to mark the milestone anniversary, further cementing the timeless resonance of Potter’s creations.

Two people suffered serious injuries after a black Renault Laguna crashed into parked vehicles on the A4054 Cardiff Road at about 02:40 BST on Saturday. The driver and front-seat passenger were taken to Prince Charles Hospital in Merthyr Tydfil. The road, near the junction with Gray's Place in Merthyr Vale, was closed for investigations but has since reopened. South Wales Police said the car had been travelling towards Merthyr from Edwardsville before the collision. Officers are appealing for witnesses and anyone with dashcam footage who saw the vehicle prior to the crash to contact them via the non-emergency 101 number. Police inquiries continue.

Swansea City have completed the signing of Ghana forward André Ayew after his contract with Marseille expired this month, bringing one of Ligue 1’s longest family associations to a close. Ayew, 25, has been at Marseille since 2006, scoring 52 goals in 181 appearances and earning 62 caps for his country. The former BBC African Footballer of the Year said the move fulfills his ambition to test himself in England’s top flight. “I felt this was the right place for me,” Ayew said. “I felt that my desire to play in the Premier League and wanting to grow as a player meant that Swansea was the best solution for me in every way. Seeing the honesty and desire of the club made me feel that they really wanted me to come. They have proved that in all ways.” Swansea have been reshaping their forward line since selling Ivory Coast striker Wilfried Bony to Manchester City in January. Nelson Oliveira, who arrived as a short-term replacement, has returned to Benfica following his loan at the Liberty Stadium, leaving room for Ayew to take a central role in the attack. Ayew’s departure ends a 28-year link between the Ayew family and Marseille. His father, Abedi Pele, joined the club in 1987 and was part of their 1993 Champions League-winning side, while younger brother Jordan began his career at the Stade Vélodrome before moving to Lorient. Ayew held talks with QPR in January and said in May he was weighing options in England, Italy and Germany, admitting the Premier League’s appeal was strong. Swansea’s pitch proved decisive, with the club’s ambition and approach convincing the Ghanaian to make South Wales his next challenge.

The Foxes are currently two points clear at the top with 12 games remaining despite being bottom of the table at the same stage last season. Leicester City midfielder Andy King insists the Premier League leaders feel “no pressure” as they enter the decisive phase of the season, despite a last-gasp defeat at Arsenal on 14 February. Reflecting on the contrasting emotions of fighting relegation a year ago and leading the title race now, the 27-year-old says perspective is keeping spirits high. “I have heard people saying that we are under pressure, but we are under no pressure. That was last season, trying to stay in the top division,” King said. “It was disappointing, the way we lost to Arsenal, but we will bounce back.” King believes the Foxes can be satisfied with their recent run against top opposition. “We were of course disappointed to lose last week, especially the manner of the defeat, but if you had offered us six points from Liverpool, Man City and Arsenal, we would certainly have taken it,” he told BBC Radio Wales. He added that the mood around the club reflects their remarkable position after starting last season in the drop zone. “Things are going well and you can imagine the training ground is buzzing at the moment. It is brilliant to be playing for the team top of the Premier League. I am enjoying every minute of it.” Having made 25 appearances this season, King also believes Leicester’s title challenge can sharpen him for Wales’ European Championship campaign this summer. “I think it will help me with Wales, playing in these big matches,” he explained. “We are all new and inexperienced at big tournaments, so the more big games you can play the better. We have Gareth Bale and Aaron Ramsey used to playing at this level, but for other players, playing in these big games can only stand us in good stead for the summer.”

Venezuela releases first health data in two years, showing maternal mortality up 65%, child deaths up 30% Venezuela’s Health Ministry has published its first health statistics since 2015, revealing sharp deteriorations across key public health indicators amid the country’s deepening economic crisis. The newly released bulletin reports a 65% rise in maternal deaths and a 30% increase in child mortality, alongside surges in illnesses such as malaria and diphtheria. The figures have intensified the debate over responsibility for the nation’s health emergency. Opposition leaders say years of government mismanagement and underinvestment have crippled hospitals and disrupted supply chains, while President Nicolás Maduro argues that medicines are being hoarded by political opponents to foment a coup. Venezuela has the largest proven oil reserves in the world, but the collapse of oil prices several years ago triggered a prolonged recession and slashed access to foreign currency, undermining imports of medical equipment, food, and pharmaceuticals. Shortages now span basic staples and critical treatments, with a leading pharmaceutical association estimating that roughly 85% of medicines are scarce. Hospitals report failing infrastructure, intermittent electricity, and limited supplies, forcing many patients to seek care abroad. Thousands of Venezuelans have crossed into Brazil and Colombia to buy medicines and obtain treatment in public facilities; Brazil’s border state of Roraima has declared a state of emergency to manage the influx. A recent national survey found that three-quarters of Venezuelans say their health has deteriorated, many eating fewer than two meals a day and reporting an average weight loss of about 9 kilograms (19 pounds). The health sector is facing a significant brain drain, as large numbers of doctors have emigrated amid worsening conditions and pay. “The striking part is the turmoil in almost all categories that this bulletin addresses, with particularly significant increases in the infant and maternal health categories,” Dr. Julio Castro, an infectious disease specialist and critic of the government’s health policies, told Reuters. It remains unclear why the Health Ministry decided to resume publishing data after halting releases in July 2015. The publication comes as Venezuela endures more than a month of near-daily, increasingly violent protests demanding elections, with the country’s political crisis compounding its humanitarian emergency. Aid groups and UN agencies have been urged to expand support to bridge the growing gaps in care and supplies.

An empty CrossCountry passenger train derailed at low speed at Eastleigh, blocking lines through the station and disrupting signalling arrangements. The incident, which occurred before the train had entered service, forced South West Trains to reduce the number of services while recovery work took place. The operator had warned cancellations and delays could persist until 18:00 BST, but the train was re-railed and moved to a nearby depot sooner than expected. Services are now resuming, with small residual delays reported as the network clears. CrossCountry described the event as a “minor low-speed derailment.” An investigation has begun into the cause and the impact on signalling infrastructure. No injuries were reported.

The statement on the future of the 59-year-old, in charge since June 2011, ends speculation about Allardyce's role at Upton Park. West Ham United have confirmed that manager Sam Allardyce will remain in charge for next season, setting clear expectations for on-field progression and a more entertaining style of play. The announcement follows an end-of-season meeting between Allardyce and the club’s board, during which plans for the 2014-15 campaign were reviewed before a decision was made. Allardyce, who led the Hammers to a 13th-place finish in the Premier League, has faced criticism from sections of the support, particularly in the latter stages of the campaign. In a club statement, West Ham said: “The club have made clear that they want to see progression on the pitch,” adding that the manager has agreed to recruit a new attacking coach “to ensure the team provides more entertainment next season.” The club also set a target of at least a top-10 finish in the table. The board’s directive includes significant changes behind the scenes. “After listening to feedback from supporters, the board have insisted on improvements to the set-up of the playing and backroom staff to ensure the team provides more entertainment next season,” the statement continued. “The manager has agreed to recruit a new attacking coach to complement the existing coaching set-up as well as an overhaul of the club’s scouting and recruitment operation.” West Ham said that the board will have a greater say in player acquisitions, reflecting plans to invest substantially over the summer. “That will see the board have a greater involvement in the players who are signed, as the board will once again be investing considerable funds into the club this summer,” the statement added. “The club have made clear that they want to see progression on the pitch and at least a top 10 finish as a result.” Allardyce took the helm in 2011 after West Ham were relegated under Avram Grant, guiding the team back to the Premier League via the Championship play-offs at the first attempt. He followed that with a 10th-place finish in 2012-13. This season, however, a strong run of four consecutive wins in February was followed by a difficult end to the campaign, with eight defeats in the final 11 matches. Some fans voiced their displeasure during the 1-0 defeat by West Brom on 26 April. “We are absolutely committed to taking West Ham United to new heights and we want to see the club continue on an upward trajectory next season,” said joint-chairmen David Sullivan and David Gold. “The 2014-15 campaign is crucial to our future and we are confident that Sam has the passion, experience and determination to make sure it is a success.”

Maracanã stadium ransacked amid management dispute, Rio federation warns Rio de Janeiro’s football federation says the iconic Maracanã stadium has been ransacked and vandalized in recent weeks, with windows smashed and items stolen, as a long-running dispute over its management leaves the venue effectively abandoned. The stadium, owned by the state government of Rio de Janeiro, has sat largely empty since its last official event in September, despite undergoing costly modernizations for the 2014 World Cup and the 2016 Olympic Games. The federation warned that “the worries over the present and the future of the stadium are only increasing,” and has called a meeting with the city’s clubs to discuss interim management. O Globo reported that thieves have stripped copper wiring from walls and ceilings and taken fire extinguishers, hoses, televisions, and even a bust of journalist Mario Filho, for whom the stadium is officially named. To cut costs, lights have been switched off at night, and the pitch has deteriorated, with dry turf dotted by holes. The Maracanã—one of the most famous football venues in the world—hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the Rio Olympics and the 1950 World Cup final. Traditionally, it has served all four of Rio’s major clubs: Botafogo, Flamengo, Fluminense, and Vasco da Gama. But Brazil’s deep economic crisis has hit the state government hard, complicating maintenance obligations and fueling disagreements between clubs, authorities, and private operators over who should manage the facility. Local football leaders hope an urgent agreement can prevent further damage and return the stadium to regular use before the situation deteriorates further.

Two men have denied charges following incidents at Celtic’s 2-1 win on 31 December. Michael Thomson, 51, from Dalry, North Ayrshire, is alleged to have been drunk, used abusive language and struggled with police during the match, which kicked off at 12:15. Gerard Donnelly, 24, from Coatbridge, North Lanarkshire, is accused of throwing a smoke bomb onto the pitch. Both men appeared from custody at Glasgow Sheriff Court, pleaded not guilty and were granted bail. They are due to go on trial in May.

Two people aboard an 11ft (3.4m) yacht were rescued after getting into difficulty a mile off Douglas at about 20:35 BST on Monday. The powerless vessel drifted three miles from the Isle of Man before the Douglas volunteer RNLI crew located it and towed it to Battery Pier, where coastguards assisted. No injuries were reported by officials.

Waghorn boosts Rangers ahead of cup final with sharp return from knee injury Rangers striker Martyn Waghorn has handed Mark Warburton a timely selection boost after playing an hour on his comeback from a knee injury in Sunday’s 2-2 draw with St Mirren. The 28-goal forward had been sidelined for 11 weeks since damaging his knee in the 2-1 Scottish Cup quarter-final win over Kilmarnock on 16 February, but looked lively on his first start back in the Championship title winners’ final league match. Warburton said Waghorn is firmly in contention to start the Scottish Cup final against Hibernian at Hampden on 21 May. “He has a chance of starting. He’s worked hard and looked really fit,” the Rangers manager noted, praising the player’s sharpness and application on a difficult surface in Paisley. Warburton added that Waghorn “looked as if he hadn’t been away,” lauding the efforts of the club’s medical team and the striker’s determination to return in top condition. Rangers have arranged a behind-closed-doors friendly with Tottenham Hotspur on 11 May to maintain match fitness during a long gap before the final, and Warburton plans to give Waghorn further minutes to build rhythm and confidence. Opponents Hibernian, who finished third behind Rangers and Falkirk, could arrive at Hampden on the back of three taxing promotion play-off ties, a factor Warburton hopes will tip the balance. Despite the draw at St Mirren extending Rangers’ run to four matches without a win since defeating Celtic in the Scottish Cup semi-final, Warburton insisted he is unconcerned by the dip. He said he was encouraged by the second-half display, highlighting his side’s bravery in possession, energetic running and chances created, including strikes against the woodwork. The late 92nd-minute equaliser “dampened things a bit,” he admitted, but believed the response was exactly what he wanted after the loss to Livingston. Warburton also played down speculation linking him with Everton should the Premier League club part ways with Roberto Martinez, dismissing the rumours with a smile. “Who is it this time?” he joked, adding that perhaps Barcelona and Real Madrid would be next to be mentioned. His focus, he stressed, remains firmly on guiding Rangers to a first Scottish Cup triumph since 2009.

MPs will debate later this month whether the US presidential hopeful should be refused entry. It follows the billionaire property tycoon calling for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the US. More than half a million people backed a petition calling on the tycoon to be barred for his comments, triggering a debate in the Commons. However, there will be no vote at the end of the debate and it will be up to Home Secretary Theresa May to decide whether or not Mr Trump should be excluded from the UK. The debate stems from widespread criticism of Donald Trump’s proposal to halt Muslim entry to the United States, remarks that prompted a surge of signatures on Parliament’s petitions website. While MPs will air views from across the political spectrum, the session will be non-binding, leaving the Home Secretary with the final say on any exclusion decision. Mr Trump has substantial business interests in Scotland, owning the Turnberry golf resort in South Ayrshire and Trump International Golf Links near Aberdeen. In a statement, the Trump Organisation said it had planned to invest more than £200m at Turnberry and a further £500m at the Aberdeenshire course. It warned that any action to restrict Mr Trump’s travel would force it to “immediately end these and all future investments we are currently contemplating in the United Kingdom.” The company added that barring the candidate would set a “dangerous precedent” and send a message that the UK “opposes free speech” and is uninterested in attracting inward investment. It said such a move would also “alienate the many millions of United States citizens who wholeheartedly support Mr Trump” and argued that addressing sensitive issues requires open discussion. Political leaders in the UK remain divided. Scottish First Minister Nicola Sturgeon has joined calls for Mr Trump to be considered for exclusion. Prime Minister David Cameron previously labelled Mr Trump’s comments “stupid” but said he did not support a ban, telling MPs the tycoon would “unite us all against him” if he visited the UK. The Home Office has not indicated when a decision might be made.

Economy Secretary Keith Brown has faced questions over transparency in the Scottish Government’s Enterprise and Skills Review after MSP Tavish Scott claimed Professor Lorne Crerar told MSPs he is not permitted to speak publicly about the process, which covers the work of Highlands and Islands Enterprise (HIE). Scott raised the issue during a meeting of Holyrood’s Education and Skills Committee on Wednesday, asking Brown to confirm whether Crerar, who chairs the review’s advisory board, is barred from commenting and to provide a list of organisations and individuals supporting the creation of a single statutory board. Brown said he could not comment on private conversations, noted that all submissions have been published, and pledged to examine the minutes of the ministerial review group. In October, ministers outlined Phase 1 proposals to reform Scotland’s enterprise and skills agencies, including plans for a new Scotland-wide statutory board to coordinate Scottish Enterprise and HIE. The government has insisted services in the Highlands and Islands will be protected under any changes. Crerar, in an online statement last month, said HIE would continue to exist in its present form despite alterations to how it is overseen. HIE provides support to businesses and community initiatives across the Highlands and Islands, Northern Isles, Moray and Argyll. The debate underscores tensions around the balance between national coordination and regional autonomy, and the level of public scrutiny applied to reforms affecting economic development. The session was Wednesday.

Three new laboratories in Blantyre, Malawi, will compare heart disease data with the South Lanarkshire town Three new laboratories in Blantyre, Malawi, are being established to compare heart disease data with Blantyre in South Lanarkshire, as part of a £2m health research partnership between the University of Glasgow and Malawi’s College of Medicine. The Scottish Government will fund half of the five-year project, which aims to strengthen healthcare in Malawi while shedding light on the causes of poor health in parts of western Scotland. The initiative follows a rise in conditions such as cardiovascular disease, hypertension and arthritis among Malawians, and will support joint research, diagnostics, and training. International development minister Alasdair Allan told MSPs at Holyrood the collaboration would deliver benefits on both sides. “Although what we do in Malawi is for Malawi’s sake, in many cases our partnership working has created real benefits for Scottish people too,” he said. Prof Iain McInnes of the University of Glasgow called the project the “true spirit of partnership.” “This represents a remarkable fusion of expertise in Glasgow and Blantyre, Malawi, that will allow a transformation in the way that diseases are recognised, treated and studied in Malawi,” he added.

This was an unusual departure for TfL; it doesn't normally operate like this. This was a methodical mugging. It told the Transport Committee of the London Assembly the Aviation Commission's assessment was "substantially underestimating the impact of the third runway". The criticism went further. TfL says the Aviation Commission did not use the maximum capacity of the runway in its modelling. So instead of 385,000 extra trips per day on the transport network, there could be 450,000. It said the modelling didn't take into account freight and those trucks would have a huge impact on surrounding roads. Crucially, the officials also estimated it would cost £15bn to £20bn in investment to build the new rail links required. And the third runway could create "congestion on road and the rail network and overcrowding on a level we haven't seen". The sentiments may not be new from TfL; some have implied the officials there are just doing the mayor's bidding - but if they're to be believed. the figures certainly show you the impact a third runway could have on surrounding transport infrastructure. Update: Heathrow airport has been in touch: "Heathrow's expansion will come with a step-change in rail access to the airport. With new rail lines to the north, south, east and west, Heathrow can increase the number of passengers taking public transport, and ensure that even with expansion, there is no more airport-related traffic compared to today. "We are confident in our plans because we already have an outstanding record in increasing the use of public transport to get to the airport and encouraging people to shift out of their cars. Over the last 20 years, our passenger numbers have risen by almost 80% but airport related traffic has remained static."

Regional media react to UK airstrikes in Syria and Cameron’s remarks The British House of Commons vote to extend airstrikes against Islamic State (IS) into Syria, and Prime Minister David Cameron’s remarks surrounding it, have drawn sharply divergent reactions across Middle Eastern and Iranian media, ranging from outright condemnation to measured, factual reporting. Syria’s pro-government press was scathing. Al-Thawra accused the House of Commons of “vaulting over international legitimacy as usual” in response to what it described as “Prime Minister David Cameron’s lies,” questioning why the US-led coalition “does not target Islamic State leaders’ bases, or the smugglers’ oil pipelines to Turkey.” Al-Baath, another state-aligned outlet, portrayed Cameron’s push as a “PR campaign” designed to bolster a “US-led show in violation of the UN Charter.” By contrast, Syria’s privately owned Al-Watan highlighted potential diplomatic convergence, focusing on Cameron’s remark about a “narrowing gap” between the West and Russia over the fate of President Bashar al-Assad. The opposition weekly Inab Biladi, published from Turkey, trained its attention on the UK domestic scene, reporting on large anti-bombing protests in London with the chant: “Shame on you Cameron, no to bombing Syria!” Syrian state TV echoed the government press in tone but also seized on one of Cameron’s claims: that defeating IS could help 70% of Syrian refugees return. Broadcasters underscored that this was, in their view, the first time Britain had acknowledged terrorism as the driver of Syria’s mass displacement. Iranian media devoted extensive and sceptical coverage to the decision. State television said Britain had intervened “under the pretext of fighting terrorism.” English-language Press TV amplified voices from anti-war demonstrations in London, airing footage of placards reading “No bombing in Syria” and “Bombing does not kill an ideology. It feeds it,” and quoting one protester’s warning that “the bombs will further deepen the Syrian people’s pain.” Across the wider Arabic press, reporting was more restrained. Several outlets relayed developments with minimal comment. Rafiq Khouri of Lebanon’s private Al-Anwar argued that air campaigns alone cannot defeat IS: “The critical factor in an aerial war, which those who launch it admit, is that it cannot eliminate IS without ground troops.” He added that Russian strikes had achieved “in one month more than what Washington did in over a year.” In a separate analysis, Ghazi Dahmani in Saudi-based Al-Hayat framed the UK move as a reaction to IS’s “new operational pattern of taking war abroad.” Saudi daily Asharq Al-Awsat featured a front-page image of the marathon UK debate under the headline: “Ten hot hours in the British House of Commons.” Qatar’s Al-Watan led with Cameron’s vow that “IS is planning to kill and we will not be silent,” while pan-Arab broadcasters Al-Jazeera and Al-Arabiya topped morning bulletins with factual packages on the vote and ensuing strikes. As of publication, IS has not reacted publicly to the Commons decision, and its online supporters have offered little guidance on any potential response. BBC Monitoring tracks and analyzes media worldwide and contributed to this overview.

title: Governing body the UCI announced on Monday that the event will take place in Los Angeles from 2-5 March. The UCI announced on Monday that the UCI Para-cycling Track World Championships will be held in Los Angeles from 2-5 March, filling a 2017 calendar that previously had no major track events. The short notice has drawn mixed reactions, coming less than six months after the Rio Paralympics as many riders and staff are only just resuming full training. Teams are now scrambling to secure travel, funding and selections. Britain’s Jody Cundy, 38, a double gold medallist at Rio 2016, told BBC Radio 5 live: “I can not imagine any other sport doing the same. I know of athletes not going because it is too close for them to even get back on the track, while other nations are not going because they do not have the funding. I’m not sure the message it sends to go to Los Angeles with half of the normal competitors. It takes away from the level of competition and makes it look Mickey Mouse.” He said he only returned to training last month, for the first time since September’s Paralympics, adding: “It would be nice to go in prime condition, rather than last-minute panic-training.” Barney Storey, coach and husband of multiple Paralympic champion Sarah Storey, echoed the concern on social media, tweeting: “Para-track worlds in seven weeks, the UCI are NOT helping progress the sport. ‘Helping’ the sport to be mediocre is not progress.” UCI president Brian Cookson said the organisation is conscious some athletes have yet to reach full intensity but argued the timing represents progress: “Holding these championships for the first time in a post-Paralympic season will enrich the calendar as the discipline continues to develop.”

She came to power determined to change a Britain she believed was in terminal decline Margaret Thatcher’s premiership left an indelible mark on Scotland, reshaping its economy, politics and public life in ways still debated today. Supporters argue she confronted a failing system with uncompromising clarity; critics say her policies brought lasting social damage and fueled a new Scottish political consciousness. Former Scottish Secretary Lord Lang recalls a country already in deep trouble when she arrived in Downing Street. “All she was doing was clearing away the debris of what was already a desert on a life support machine,” he says. “The life support machine was one fed by taxation pumped in by the Westminster government.” State-supported heavy industry, long central to many Scottish communities, was left to decline. British Steel’s mill at Gartcosh, the Invergordon aluminium smelter and the Corpach pulp mill were among the casualties of a new economic approach that favored market discipline over public subsidy. The most dramatic confrontation came with the miners’ strike, a year-long dispute that became a defining battle of the 1980s. Thatcher famously labeled striking miners “the enemy within,” a phrase that crystallized both her resolve and her polarizing effect. “Miners were proud people. Proud to work in the industry and she took that from us, her and her government, during that period,” says Nicky Wilson of the National Union of Mineworkers. “I personally don’t think anybody involved in that time will ever forgive her.” Yet one policy proved widely popular across Scotland: the sale of council houses. Even where her party struggled at the ballot box, tenants embraced the opportunity to buy their homes, transforming the housing landscape and wealth ownership for many families. Thatcher articulated the moral case for her economics in her “Sermon on the Mound,” addressing the Church of Scotland’s General Assembly in May 1988. “It is not the creation of wealth that is wrong but the love of money for its own sake,” she told the Kirk, seeking to align enterprise with ethical purpose. Another flashpoint was the Community Charge—better known as the Poll Tax—introduced in Scotland first. The flat-rate levy, applied equally to rich and poor, ignited anger, street protests and widespread non-payment. Former Labour MP and MSP Dennis Canavan argues the policy galvanized demands for devolution. “This was such a blatant injustice—this Poll Tax—that people then began to see that this could never happen if we had a Scottish Parliament.” The tax proved untenable in England too, hastening Thatcher’s downfall and rebellion within her own party. Former Scottish Secretary Malcolm Rifkind says her style grated: “She was a bossy English woman. They could probably have put up with one or even two of these but all three simultaneously was a bit too much.” Her legacy, says SNP leader and First Minister Alex Salmond, is etched into the concrete of Holyrood. “What Margaret Thatcher did was turn the Scottish Parliament from being a nice idea—democratic advance—to being something absolutely essential.” To many, her strengths were her weaknesses: tough, decisive, and, critics insist, inflexible—qualities that defined the Iron Lady and a transformative, contested era.

"You must do something for the children of Syria because they are like your children and deserve peace like you," she wrote. Seven-year-old Syrian girl Bana Alabed has appealed directly to U.S. President Donald Trump to help end the suffering of children in Syria, in a letter shared shortly before his inauguration. Bana, who escaped besieged eastern Aleppo with her family during mass evacuations in December and now lives in Turkey, became known worldwide for posts from her Twitter account chronicling life under bombardment in Aleppo. Her mother, Fatemah, who helps manage the account, sent the text of Bana’s letter to the BBC, explaining that her daughter wrote it because “she has seen Trump many times on the TV.” “My name is Bana Alabed and I am a seven years old Syrian girl from Aleppo,” the letter begins. “I lived in Syria my whole life before I left from besieged East Aleppo on December last year. I am part of the Syrian children who suffered from the Syrian war. But right now, I am having a peace in my new home of Turkey.” Bana describes how her school in Aleppo was destroyed by bombing and how friends were killed in the fighting. “I am very sad about them and wish they were with me because we would play together by right now,” she wrote. “I couldn’t play in Aleppo, it was the city of death.” Now in Turkey, she says she can go outside and hopes to attend school soon. “That is why peace is important for everyone including you.” Her appeal urges Trump to act: “However, millions of Syrian children are not like me right now and suffering in different parts of Syria. They are suffering because of adult people. I know you will be the president of America, so can you please save the children and people of Syria? You must do something for the children of Syria because they are like your children and deserve peace like you.” She concludes by offering friendship if he pledges to help: “If you promise me you will do something for the children of Syria, I am already your new friend. I am looking forward to what you will do for the children of Syria.” Turkey, where Bana and her family now live, backs Syrian opposition forces. President Trump’s approach to the conflict remains unclear. He has emphasized a desire for a stronger relationship with Russia and praised President Vladimir Putin, whose government is a key ally of Syria’s President Bashar al-Assad. During the campaign, Trump spoke of ending U.S. aid to Syrian rebels, but he has more recently floated the idea of establishing “safe zones” in Syria, which could bolster opposition-held areas. Bana’s plea comes as Iran, Russia, and Turkey have pledged to enforce a three-week ceasefire amid ongoing peace talks. Without firm agreement from the Assad government or rebel factions, however, the durability of any truce remains uncertain.

Thai Airways has swung to a quarterly profit as its year-long turnaround effort begins to show results, even as the carrier remains loss-making for the full year amid persistent industry headwinds. Officials confirmed to the BBC that the airline posted a net profit of 5.1 billion Thai baht ($141.7 million) in the latest quarter, a sharp reversal from a 6.4 billion baht loss in the same period a year earlier. For the full year, net loss narrowed to 13.05 billion baht from 15.57 billion baht the previous year. The national flag carrier, 51% owned by the Thai government, said operating losses were “substantially reduced,” attributing the improvement in part to a roughly 20% decline in fuel expenses. The gains come after Thai Airways launched a transformation plan in January last year aimed at “stop[ping] the bleeding,” as management described it, and restoring financial stability following a period of tough competition and weakening demand across the region. Over the past 12 months, Thai Airways has cut unprofitable routes, reduced flight frequencies, and implemented cost-saving measures throughout the business. The airline said it plans to focus on voluntary retirements this year to further streamline operations. In fleet management, the carrier decommissioned several aircraft in 2015 while taking delivery of eight new planes, reducing its total fleet to 95 aircraft from 102 a year earlier. Despite the financial improvement, Thai Airways cautioned that global aviation remained under pressure in 2015 due to economic and political uncertainty and a broader global slowdown. The company highlighted China’s deceleration, a “heavy expansion” of low-cost carriers, and volatile exchange rates as key challenges affecting demand and yields across the industry. The airline also addressed concerns about its international flight safety reputation following regulatory scrutiny of Thailand’s aviation oversight. In December, the US Federal Aviation Administration downgraded Thailand’s safety rating after earlier findings by the International Civil Aviation Organization indicated non-compliance with certain standards. While experts warned the move could jeopardize code-share arrangements in the United States, Thai Airways said it had not been affected. The carrier added that the European Commission had not recently placed any Thai airlines on its air safety blacklist and noted it had recently passed the European Aviation Safety Agency’s safety standards audit. Thai Airways said it remains committed to its turnaround program and will continue to adjust capacity, optimize its network, and strengthen its balance sheet to navigate ongoing industry challenges.

Mark Cavendish surrendered the overall lead at the Tour of Qatar despite a strong performance in Wednesday’s individual time trial, as Norway’s Edvald Boasson Hagen powered to stage victory and seized control of the race. The 30-year-old Briton, who won the event in 2013, placed seventh in the 11km Lusail time trial, finishing 44 seconds down on Boasson Hagen’s benchmark. Dimension Data teammate Boasson Hagen stopped the clock in 13 minutes 26.98 seconds, winning by 25 seconds over Jos van Emden of Team LottoNL-Jumbo, with BMC Racing’s Manuel Quinziato a further four seconds back in third. Boasson Hagen’s emphatic ride catapulted him into the race lead with an overall time of 6 hours 53 minutes 35 seconds. Cavendish now sits second, 26 seconds adrift, while Quinziato is third at 32 seconds and Greg van Avermaet fourth at 34 seconds, both for BMC. Alexander Kristoff of Katusha rounds out the top five at 45 seconds. The five-stage race concludes on Friday at Doha Corniche, where crosswinds and sprint dynamics often dictate the final outcome. Cavendish has started his season brightly, going close in two stages at the Dubai Tour and claiming Tuesday’s opening stage in Qatar, yet he faces a packed slate in 2016 that includes a potential tilt at the track World Championships in London next month and the Olympic Games in Rio in August. He has said he will decide during the race whether to pursue the track Worlds, acknowledging uncertainty over how a winter split between road and track could affect him. “I could be flying, I could be catastrophic, I could be indifferent,” he told BBC Sport in January. Behind Boasson Hagen and van Emden on the day, van Avermaet finished fourth at 32 seconds, Dmitriy Gruzdev fifth at 40 seconds, and Lieuwe Westra sixth at 43 seconds. Cavendish, seventh, led a cluster that included Jordan Kerby on the same time, Soren Kragh Andersen at 45 seconds, and Daniel Oss at 47 seconds. With two stages remaining, the race remains finely poised. Cavendish will look to capitalize on sprint opportunities and team support, while Boasson Hagen aims to defend the leader’s jersey to the finish on the Corniche.

Sweden mounted a stirring comeback to eliminate Japan and reach the challenger final, overturning a 3-1 deficit with three straight wins on Thursday before clinching the series by taking Friday’s opening race. “We’re absolutely stoked,” said Swedish skipper Nathan Outteridge. Friday’s showdown was tight and turned on a tactical mistake by Japanese skipper Dean Barker, who was forced to a standstill when Outteridge shut the door as Barker attempted to pass in the middle of their head-to-head duel. “That was obviously the key moment,” Outteridge added. The Swedes will face New Zealand, who knocked out Great Britain, in a first-to-five-wins challenger final beginning Saturday. The winner will advance to meet holders Oracle Team USA for the America’s Cup, the sport’s most coveted prize, also known as the Auld Mug. The America’s Cup Match is first to seven points, with up to 13 races scheduled across June 17-18 and 24-27. First contested in 1851 around the Isle of Wight, the America’s Cup is the oldest competition in international sport and has been won by only four nations.

Calhoun College will be renamed to honour Grace Murray Hopper, who helped transform the way people use technology. Hopper earned Yale degrees in the 1930s and became a US Navy rear admiral. Saturday’s announcement, which follows years of debate, reverses a decision made last year and aims to end a long-running controversy over the former politician and defender of slavery John C. Calhoun, whose legacy sparked campus protests beginning in 2015. Yale University President Peter Salovey said the residential college, named in the early 1930s, presents an exceptional case because Calhoun’s legacy is at odds with the university’s values. “We have a strong presumption against renaming buildings on this campus,” Salovey said, adding, “I have been concerned all along and remain concerned that we do not do things that erase history.” The decision comes after Salovey, who announced in April that Yale would retain the Calhoun name, later appointed an advisory panel to reassess whether that choice was correct. Tensions around the issue remained high as recently as Friday, when four people were arrested during a peaceful protest after blocking a road near the residential college. Advocates for change argued that honouring Calhoun—an influential senator from South Carolina, Yale class of 1804, and a leading voice against abolishing slavery—was incompatible with a modern, inclusive academic environment. Calhoun served as vice president from 1825 to 1832. Yale said it will not remove existing symbols of Calhoun from campus and will allow alumni to continue associating with the Calhoun name if they choose, rather than the new designation, Grace Hopper College. Salovey expressed hope that the university community would “embrace Grace Hopper and get to know her better.” Hopper graduated from Yale in 1930 and earned a doctorate in mathematics and mathematical physics in 1934. She later enlisted in the US Navy and, according to the university, “used her mathematical knowledge to fight fascism during World War Two.” A pioneering computer scientist, Hopper developed the first computer compiler, a breakthrough that helped computers process human-readable commands and laid groundwork for modern programming languages. She retired from the Navy as a rear admiral at age 79 and died in 1992 at 85. The renaming underscores Yale’s effort to reconcile institutional history with present-day values, while preserving historical context and allowing alumni traditions to continue.

Police are investigating a stabbing after an altercation among several men in Ardcarn Park around 05:00 GMT on Saturday. A man in his 40s suffered a stab wound to the head, while two men in their 20s sustained stab wounds to their bodies. Injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. Officers appealed for witnesses, anyone in Ardcarn Park, Nursery Drive or Springfarm Heights at the time, to contact them.

Glasgow Warriors flanker Tyrone Holmes has undergone surgery following an injury sustained in a Warriors A match against Edinburgh last month, the club has confirmed earlier this week. Head coach Gregor Townsend said Holmes has suffered bad luck with injuries over the past two seasons, noting he had started the campaign well. Holmes is expected to be sidelined for the next few months, ruling him out of a pivotal stretch in Glasgow’s season. The Warriors host Pro12 rivals Leinster this weekend before a Champions Cup double-header against Scarlets. That is followed by back-to-back league meetings with Edinburgh, with their European pool concluding against Racing 92 on either side of a trip to Northampton Saints. “We wish him all the best with his rehab,” Townsend added. No timeline for his return was given.

Kelvin Muriuki, once top of his class in 2016, was forced by poverty to abandon school and work in a quarry, his family says. His prospects changed when the Kenya Air Force Veteran Officers Association stepped in, pledging to cover his annual school fees of $530 (£430) through to 2020 and arranging a helicopter ride to his new school. Muriuki, who dreams of becoming a pilot, arrived in the central Kenyan town of Karicheni after a 20-minute flight from his previous school, according to the BBC’s Abdinoor Aden in Nairobi. The gesture has spotlighted the struggles of many Kenyan children who drop out because families cannot afford tuition and costs. Supporters hope the intervention will keep Muriuki on track through secondary education and inspire similar efforts to keep promising students in class.

Because today's Budget is massively less austere than the one forged with them in March, just before the election The chancellor’s latest Budget represents a notable softening of austerity compared with plans outlined before the general election. By the end of the parliament, George Osborne now intends to reduce spending on public services by just under £18bn a year—still significant, but less than half the £42bn in annual cuts previously proposed for 2018-19. As a result, the scale of retrenchment is no longer widely viewed by economists and politicians as ideologically driven or implausible. The lesser squeeze is financed in large part by tax rises that collectively outweigh headline-grabbing giveaways. According to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the measures will raise £47bn over five years. Key components include reform of dividend taxation, expected to yield around £2bn annually, and a rise in insurance premium tax projected to bring in £1.5bn per year. Against these increases stand around £25bn in tax cuts, most visibly through higher personal allowances and an increase in the threshold for the 40% income-tax band, alongside a two percentage point reduction in the main rate of corporation tax. With a pledged corporation tax rate of 18%, Britain could start to look to some multinationals like a near-tax haven, intensifying competitive pressures on other jurisdictions. Welfare and social security are still slated for deep reductions, albeit more slowly than first advertised. The £12bn of cuts will be phased over four years rather than two, spreading the impact though not diminishing its severity. Millions are expected to feel the strain, particularly middle-income families, who will absorb much of the effect of tax-credit reforms forecast to raise around £4.5bn each year. In a striking departure for a Conservative administration that espouses market solutions, the Budget also creates a new official living wage—effectively an intervention to set the price of labour above the current minimum wage. Critics liken the move to 1970s-style Labour price-setting, noting the tension it introduces for businesses facing higher staffing costs. Osborne’s timetable for restoring the public finances has slipped. The surplus he said would arrive in 2018-19 is now forecast for 2019-20. The OBR estimates the national debt will be £18bn higher by 2020 than promised in March, with £3.5bn of that directly attributable to decisions announced today. In short, the chancellor’s effort to “mend the roof while the sun is shining,” to use his preferred phrase, is proceeding more slowly than previously pledged—even as the Budget’s mix of tax rises, targeted reliefs, and phased welfare cuts reshapes the UK’s fiscal landscape.

Simon Hart has been cleared by the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards over allegations he used pre-paid House of Commons envelopes to campaign for a Conservative council candidate ahead of the 4 May poll. The complaint was lodged by Plaid Cymru rival, councillor Jonathan Preston, who alleged the Carmarthen West and South Pembrokeshire MP breached rules by deploying parliamentary stationery for party political purposes. An investigation was opened by Commissioner Kathryn Hudson, as using Commons-funded materials for campaigning would constitute a breach of parliamentary rules. In his response, Mr Hart said the claim arose from a confusion between two separate mailings sent in March. He explained that on 11 March he posted a letter to constituents inviting them to a public meeting, which was correctly sent in parliamentary envelopes. A second mailing, dated 30 March, endorsed a Conservative candidate in the upcoming council elections and, he said, was sent by the local Conservative Association using plain stationery and paid for through its own Royal Mail account. Mr Hart also noted the two letters were different sizes, making it difficult to fold the campaign letter into a Commons envelope. The commissioner accepted his explanation and rejected the complaint, with no further action taken.

UEFA has opened disciplinary proceedings against FK Shkendija over the alleged use of a laser pointer during their Europa League qualifier against Aberdeen in Skopje. The case, citing Article 16(2) of the UEFA Disciplinary Regulations, will be reviewed by the UEFA Control, Ethics and Disciplinary Body at its meeting on 23 July. Aberdeen reported the incident to a UEFA delegate after the match at the National Stadium. The first leg finished 1-1, with Hristijan Kirovski cancelling out Niall McGinn’s opener. Aberdeen handed goalkeeper Danny Ward, on loan from Liverpool, an immediate European debut for Aberdeen.

Gavin Grimm filed the lawsuit after the school board adopted a policy that required students to use a private toilet or one that corresponds to the sex listed on their birth certificate. Grimm, who identifies as male, said the policy was stigmatizing. How transgender people use public toilets is a divisive issue in the US. A number of places in the US - most recently North Carolina - have passed laws requiring transgender people to use a public toilet that corresponds to the sex listed on their birth certificate. The North Carolina law in particular has been sharply criticised as discriminatory and several companies have stopped doing business in the state as a result. In the Grimm case, the three-judge panel found the Gloucester County District policy violated Title IX, a federal law which prohibits gender discrimination at schools that receive federal funding. The Gloucester County District said the policy was meant to respect the privacy of all students. A federal judge had earlier rejected Grimm's sex discrimination claim, saying Title IX only protects students from discrimination based on biological sex, not gender identity. Other federal rulings in similar cases have also ruled that Title IX does not apply to transgender students. This federal ruling could have wider implications because it creates a legal precedent in five states including North Carolina. The America Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and others have already filed a challenge to North Carolina's transgender law. Some supporters of these policies said allowing transgender people to choose their restroom could lead to women and children being attacked. They said they feared that predatory men could pose as transgender people and use legal protections as a cover. Gavin Grimm filed the lawsuit after the Gloucester County School Board in Virginia adopted a restroom policy requiring students to use either a single-stall facility or the restroom corresponding to the sex on their birth certificate. Grimm, a transgender boy, argued the rule was stigmatizing and violated his rights under Title IX, the federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in schools receiving federal funds. A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals ruled the district’s policy unlawfully discriminated against Grimm, reversing an earlier federal district court decision that held Title IX protects only against discrimination based on biological sex, not gender identity. The Gloucester County School Board defended the policy as a measure to respect the privacy of all students. But the appellate decision establishes a legal precedent across the Fourth Circuit, which covers five states including North Carolina, potentially influencing disputes over transgender students’ access to school facilities. The case arrives amid a broader national debate over how transgender people use public restrooms. Several jurisdictions, most recently North Carolina, have enacted laws mandating that individuals use facilities matching the sex listed on their birth certificates. North Carolina’s law has drawn sharp criticism from civil rights groups and businesses, with companies curtailing operations in the state. The American Civil Liberties Union and allied organizations have filed legal challenges to North Carolina’s statute, arguing it discriminates against transgender residents and violates federal protections. Supporters of birth-certificate-based policies contend that allowing people to choose restrooms according to gender identity could endanger women and children, warning that predatory men might exploit protections by posing as transgender. Opponents say such claims lack evidence and restricting access harms transgender individuals by singling them out.

Four paintings stolen from the Westfries Museum in Hoorn in 2005 have been recovered in Ukraine, officials said. The 16th and 17th Century works, valued at €50,000 (£40,000; $56,000) when taken, had been “in the possession of criminal groups,” Ukraine’s foreign minister said. Local reports said the artworks were retrieved from Ukrainian ultra-nationalists, though authorities offered no additional details about the operation. In December, the museum reported that two men, reportedly linked to a Ukrainian nationalist militia, presented a photo of one of the missing paintings to the Dutch embassy in Kyiv. Dutch media said the men claimed to have located the entire stolen collection and demanded millions of euros for its return. Vasyl Grytsak, head of Ukraine’s state security service (SBU), told a press conference that the first painting was recovered in early March, a second in early April, and two more on Thursday. “A preliminary examination has determined they are authentic,” he said. Dutch authorities are working to secure their return. Ultra-nationalist militia groups are among forces engaged in fighting a pro-Russian insurgency in parts of eastern Ukraine. The conflict has killed more than 9,200 people since April 2014.

Government proposes new limits and oversight for pre-charge police bail Theresa May has unveiled plans to overhaul pre-charge police bail in England and Wales, introducing time limits and new oversight requirements amid mounting concern over suspects being kept on bail for extended periods without charge. Under the proposals, a senior police officer would have to authorise any bail period beyond 28 days, and a magistrate would be required to approve extensions beyond three months. At present, there is no statutory time limit on pre-charge bail and no requirement for police to seek external approval to extend it. Mrs May said the reforms would be taken forward in the next Parliament, describing it as “simply not acceptable” that pre-charge bail could last “months or years.” She also announced a “new presumption” in favour of releasing suspects without bail, with conditions to be imposed “only where it is necessary or proportionate,” in a bid to drive down what she called the “inappropriate use” of bail. The Home Office said the revised approach reflects feedback on earlier proposals that would have required court approval after 28 days. Under the new plan, a superintendent could authorise an extension at 28 days, but only in exceptional circumstances and up to a total of three months. Any further extension beyond three months would need to be sanctioned by a magistrate. Mrs May added that some elements, including issuing national guidance and collecting data on the use of police bail, would not require legislation and could begin immediately. The Association of Chief Police Officers (Acpo) said pre-charge bail remained “an essential tool in securing justice,” but agreed the system should be “efficient and proportionate” for both victims and suspects. “Each and every investigation follows a different path. Less than 2% of arrests result in a person being on bail for more than six months. However, in an increasingly globalised and digitised world some cases are complex..... and cannot be rushed,” an Acpo spokesman said. Calls for reform have intensified following high-profile cases. Earlier this month, broadcaster Paul Gambaccini urged MPs to impose limits on pre-charge bail, recounting how officers and prosecutors “sat” on his case for 12 months before informing him he would not be charged over an allegation of historical sexual abuse. The government’s proposals will be subject to parliamentary scrutiny in the next legislative session.

The bid, made late on Sunday, was £25m plus add-ons but United maintain the 27-year-old is not for sale. Chelsea have had a second offer for Wayne Rooney rejected by Manchester United, with the Premier League champions reiterating the striker is not available despite his desire to leave. The latest bid, worth £25m plus add-ons, follows an initial proposal of around £20m in July that was also turned down. Rooney has been left out of United’s squad for Tuesday’s pre-season friendly in Stockholm due to a shoulder injury, understood to have been sustained during a behind-closed-doors match against Real Betis on Saturday. The absence comes amid growing uncertainty about his future, with the forward intent on moving and Chelsea manager Jose Mourinho determined to bring him to Stamford Bridge. United boss David Moyes has consistently stated Rooney will remain at Old Trafford, but the player is believed to be angered and confused by recent signals from the club, notably the suggestion that Robin van Persie is the preferred option up front. The situation could escalate later this week, with Rooney considering submitting a formal transfer request to force a move. Rooney previously attempted to leave United in October 2010, citing concerns over the strength of the squad, before signing a new five-year contract days later. He flew home early from the club’s pre-season tour in Thailand in July with a hamstring problem and has not played for United since a substitute appearance in the 1-0 defeat to Chelsea on 5 May. Since joining from Everton, Rooney has made 402 appearances and scored 197 goals for United. He has 83 England caps with 36 goals and a decorated trophy haul that includes five Premier League titles, two League Cups, the Champions League, the FIFA Club World Cup, and the PFA Player of the Year award in 2010. With the season approaching, United’s stance and Chelsea’s pursuit set up a tense standoff.

Australia will tighten the assets test for the age pension, boosting payments for retirees with modest holdings while reducing or removing benefits for wealthier homeowners, as the government seeks savings ahead of the 12 May budget. The move comes amid a sharp fall in revenue, with the deficit expected to blow out due largely to lower royalties from commodities such as iron ore. Social Services Minister Scott Morrison said the overhaul would save about A$2.4bn (US$2bn; £1.3bn) a year and better target support. “We want the welfare system to be focused on those in greatest need and in the pension system, that’s those with low or modest assets,” he told the ABC. Under the changes, the government estimates roughly 172,000 pensioners will be A$30 a fortnight better off. About 91,000 retirees who own their homes and have other assets worth more than A$823,000 would lose access to the part-pension. The package replaces the government’s earlier, highly contested plan to alter pension indexation by tying increases to inflation rather than wages. Seniors’ groups argued that linking to inflation would have left pensioners worse off over time because prices were rising more slowly than average earnings. The government has now scrapped that proposal, keeping the existing wage-based indexation. Advocacy groups broadly welcomed the pivot to the assets test. Combined Pensioners and Superannuants’ Association spokesperson Amelia Christie said tightening the test was “definitely fairer” than cutting indexation. “Tightening the pension asset test makes more sense both from a financial and fairness perspective if you compare it with the 2014 budget proposal to cut pension indexation and reduce the value of the pension over time,” she said. However, Christie noted the changes still conflict with the government’s pre-election pledge not to touch pensions. She urged ministers to focus instead on superannuation tax concessions, which she said overwhelmingly benefit high-income earners. “This lost revenue should be tackled before pensioners face a hit to their incomes,” she said. The government says the reforms will refocus support on those most in need while contributing to broader efforts to rein in spending as revenue pressures mount.

Syrian government forces and allied militias, backed by Russian air strikes, have advanced into western Palmyra, seizing parts of a neighborhood and reaching the hilltop citadel that overlooks the city’s famed Roman-era ruins, according to multiple reports on Thursday. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said heavy clashes and shelling erupted across the historic city as the offensive unfolded. A media unit linked to Lebanon’s Hezbollah said pro-government units had reached the citadel, while Syria’s state news agency SANA reported the army had also taken control of the so-called Palmyra triangle, a strategic area on the approaches to the city. Islamic State militants recaptured Palmyra, known locally as Tadmur, in December after being ousted by a Russian-backed government campaign in March 2016. The group first seized the site in May 2015, holding it for 10 months and destroying internationally treasured antiquities, including the Arch of Triumph, funerary towers, and the Temple of Bel — once among the most important religious structures in the 1st Century AD in the East. In January, satellite imagery indicated further damage, showing the destruction of the tetrapylon—largely reconstructed elements—and parts of the Roman Theatre. The latest push highlights the city’s military and symbolic significance. Control of Palmyra opens routes across Syria’s central desert and sits near key gas fields. Independent verification of battlefield claims remains difficult, but the reports suggest a coordinated effort by Damascus and its allies to roll back Islamic State gains while securing heritage sites that have suffered severe damage. In a separate development, the United States said Russian and Syrian aircraft struck positions held by US-backed Syrian Arab Coalition fighters near the Islamic State-held town of al-Bab in northern Syria. “I believe they thought they were held by ISIS, yet they were actually—on the ground—some of our Syrian Arab Coalition forces,” Lt Gen Stephen Townsend told reporters, using an acronym for Islamic State. He said US forces quickly communicated with Russian counterparts to halt the strikes.

Somerset have signed 23-year-old Netherlands seamer Paul van Meekeren on a two-year deal after he impressed in 2016. Mostly with the Second XI, he made two first-team T20 Blast outings and has 15 T20Is and two ODIs for the Dutch. “He’s shown he offers something a bit different,” said director of cricket Matt Maynard. “We look forward to having him for the next two seasons.”

Richard Clay, 50, and his business partner Kathryn Clark, 52, have been sentenced over a multimillion-pound investment fraud run through their Nottingham-based firm, Arck LLP. The pair persuaded “several hundred” investors to part with significant sums, including pension funds and life savings, by promising returns linked to property development projects, including in Cape Verde. The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said the “elaborate scam” was uncovered in 2012 following civil proceedings, which led to their arrests in March that year. Arck LLP received around £47.5 million from investors before the scheme collapsed. According to police and the SFO, Clay and Clark used forged documents to reassure anxious clients about the firm’s financial position. Clark, of Edwalton, Nottinghamshire, who held authorisation under the Financial Services Act, helped fabricate bank statements that lent a veneer of credibility to the operation. In one instance, a statement was altered to suggest there was more than £12 million in Arck’s account when the balance was just £25, an Insolvency Service hearing was told. SFO director David Green described the pair’s activities as a “pernicious fraud.” Clay, of Belper, Derbyshire, was identified as the “directing force” behind Arck’s schemes. At Southwark Crown Court, he was sentenced to 10 years and 10 months in prison and given a serious crime prevention order lasting five years. Clark received a two-year suspended sentence and was ordered to complete 300 hours of unpaid work. Both had previously admitted multiple offences: Clay pleaded guilty to three counts of fraud, while Clark admitted three counts of fraud and two of forgery. Earlier this year, the Insolvency Service disqualified Clay and Clark from serving as company directors for 15 and 14 years respectively. A hearing to consider confiscation proceedings is scheduled for March, as authorities continue efforts to recover funds for victims.

Interior Minister Rehman Malik said the bodyguard who shot Mr Taseer said he had done so because of the governor's opposition to Pakistan's blasphemy law. Pakistan was reeling after Punjab Governor Salman Taseer was shot dead by a member of his own security detail, an attack that officials say was motivated by his outspoken criticism of the country’s blasphemy statutes. Interior Minister Rehman Malik said the bodyguard confessed to killing Taseer over the governor’s public stance on the law, which has long divided opinion across the nation. As shock turned to uncertainty, Islamabad moved swiftly into lockdown. Residents reported empty streets, shuttered shops and markets, and a heavy police presence as authorities sought to prevent unrest. “Islamabad is in lockdown as people prepare for the backlash to the assassination of the governor. Already the streets are empty, shops and markets have closed and there are lots of police vehicles racing around the city,” said Saj Malik from the capital. Voices from across Pakistan reflected the breadth of emotion and debate triggered by the killing. In Karachi, Rehman called religion “a very sensitive issue in our part of the world,” noting that even moderates felt Taseer’s comments were ill-judged, and recalling how the Muslim world was angered by the publication of blasphemous caricatures in a Danish newspaper. Others emphasized personal safety concerns. “The concern for most of the residents here is their own security—people worry about any possible backlash after his assassination,” said Junaid from Lahore, who added that Taseer was widely disliked by some segments of society. Despite political and religious differences, several contributors condemned the violence. Muhammad Ramzan from Sargodha, who identified himself as an orthodox Sunni and a supporter of the opposition PML-N, said he did not like the governor but called the killing “religiously and morally a sin.” He argued that the blasphemy law is man-made and therefore open to critique and reform.
