Another reader, Akhtar Rind from Hyderabad, described Taseer as “a brave man who stood openly against terrorism and the blasphemy law,” saying the murder underscored fears that extremists have penetrated security agencies. While many saw the assassination as a direct result of Taseer’s stance, some urged a wider view. “It would be very short-sighted to assume that a lone gunman decided to execute him for this reason alone,” wrote Nameer Rehman from Karachi, who suggested broader political calculations may be at play. From Peshawar, Nadi Yousafzai called the killing “alarming” with “serious implications in political circles,” arguing it could offer temporary relief to the ruling party amid instability, and warning that those who challenge prevailing public sentiment risk severe consequences. He urged that the blasphemy issue be resolved through legal means. The tragedy also prompted calls for deeper social change. Shahmeer Naveed Arshad from Lahore said Taseer had not only proposed amendments but labeled the statute a “black law,” adding that the incident exposed inefficiencies in security forces and highlighted social prejudice. He urged the international community to support human development initiatives such as education to address root causes of intolerance. As authorities continue their investigation and tighten security nationwide, Taseer’s assassination has reignited a polarizing debate over blasphemy legislation, freedom of expression, and the state’s capacity to protect public officials. The coming days are likely to test both political unity and the resilience of Pakistan’s institutions.

Kevin Nunes, 20, a suspected drug dealer from Wolverhampton, was found dead in Pattingham, Staffordshire. Five men jailed for his murder were cleared on appeal in March 2012. A redacted internal Staffordshire Police report, released following Freedom of Information requests by the Express & Star, has revealed deep-rooted failings within the force’s former “sensitive policing unit” during the period it was involved in the Nunes investigation. The November 2006 management review concluded the unit required “radical restructuring,” and it was subsequently disbanded in 2007. The 2006–07 Management Review said a complaint by an officer “exposed failings in the structure, procedures, working practices, culture and management” of the unit. Among the issues documented were a breakdown in trust between officers, concerns about drinking, poor morale, and friction among staff. The review found that a decision to change personnel assigned to protected witnesses in the Nunes murder case created “open resentment” and “unrest” within the team and led to complaints by the witnesses against one officer. The review was commissioned following an informal meeting between the unit’s head and the head of professional standards at Staffordshire Police, Supt Jane Sawyers, who is now the force’s Chief Constable. The review team focused particularly on the unit’s involvement with the Nunes investigation, “which was the main reason why DI [name redacted] decided to approach Supt Sawyers,” according to the report. In March 2012, five men convicted of Mr Nunes’s murder were cleared by the Court of Appeal. The court heard that concerns about the credibility of a key prosecution witness had not been disclosed to the defence. Two of the men later launched legal action against Staffordshire Police. The force said the “sensitive policing unit” was disbanded in 2007 and that since 2012, the management of protected witnesses has been handled on a national basis. Last March, the Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) announced that four senior officers, including Chief Constable Sawyers, would not face misconduct hearings over allegations they failed to declare evidence related to the shooting of Mr Nunes. The watchdog said it found “no evidence of a cover-up or of wilful omission.” Nick Baker, Staffordshire’s Deputy Chief Constable, said: “The content of the report shows that the actions of some of those in the unit 10 years ago is not one that now, or at the time, met the high standards we expect of officers and staff working for Staffordshire Police. Any mistakes or misconduct were of a professional, not criminal nature, and tackled according to the force’s disciplinary process, as set out in the review.” For more on this story and other Staffordshire news, visit the Express & Star.

Private funding for Brighton’s i360 tower has been withdrawn, but the project’s architect insists the £38m seafront landmark will still be built, with public support and new investment being sought. David Marks, of Marks Barfield Architects and co-designer of the London Eye, disclosed during a briefing with councillors that the scheme’s private backers pulled out in the summer of 2012, a development only now made public. Despite the setback, Brighton and Hove City Council confirmed its £15m loan offer remains on the table, alongside a separate £3m enterprise loan. Marks said the investors had been “very reluctant to pull out,” stressing their decision was driven by broader market conditions and sentiment within their funds rather than concerns over the project itself. “The reasons they said had much more to do with the market and investor sentiment in their funds than the project, which is resilient and financially viable,” he said. He added that discussions are underway with alternative investors and revealed that he and his wife, Julia Barfield, have put their own money into the i360 to help bridge the financing gap. “We care deeply about this project,” Marks said. “We believe it’s iconic in scale and design and it’ll raise the profile of the city. We think it’ll do a lot of good things for the city, it’ll create jobs, it’ll bring in visitors, it’ll help more people stay overnight and it’ll be a fantastic thing for the city. We will do this, this will happen.” Councillor Geoffrey Bowden, chair of the council’s economic development and culture committee, said he had confidence in Marks and the scheme’s prospects. However, local developer Mike Holland, who has previously expressed interest in buying the nearby ruined West Pier, dismissed the i360’s chances of revival. “Let’s be honest about it, Nelson has more chance of getting his eye back than David Marks does of finding backing for this scheme,” he said. Holland urged the city to “stop being silly” and focus on tidying the seafront, either rebuilding the pier in a classic or modern style, or removing the remains to improve the area for traders. The i360 team believes the observation tower could attract up to 670,000 visitors annually. Talks with potential investors are continuing while the council’s loan offer stands.

Ireland wicketkeeper Niall O’Brien faces up to six weeks out after suffering a grade-two tear during Leicestershire Foxes’ nine-wicket Cup defeat to Warwickshire on Tuesday. The 34-year-old’s brother and team-mate Kevin O’Brien told BBC Radio Leicester a 4-6 week recovery is likely, adding: “It could have meant more time on the sidelines, but it’s a grade two tear. Hopefully he can get back quickly.” Niall will miss Ireland’s two ODIs against Sri Lanka in Malahide on 16 and 18 June, and is likely to sit out July’s five-match series against Afghanistan. He will target a return for Pakistan’s two ODIs on 18 and 20 August.

Air India, which carries nearly 20% of India’s domestic air passengers, has launched a restructuring plan it says will save more than $200m (£132m) after receiving a government bailout. The overhaul aims to cut costs, streamline operations and improve reliability as competition intensifies. Officials say the savings are crucial to restoring financial health and bolstering market share. The report originated from Mumbai.

Amber Heard has been ordered to appear in an Australian court after authorities alleged she illegally brought her two Yorkshire terriers, Pistol and Boo, into the country without declaring them. Australia’s Department of Agriculture confirmed that the actress was served with a summons on July 14 by the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions (CDPP), following an April visit by a biosecurity officer to a Gold Coast property where two dogs were found and alleged to have been illegally imported. The incident sparked a high-profile dispute earlier this year, highlighting Australia’s stringent biosecurity laws designed to prevent the introduction of pests and diseases. At the time, Agriculture Minister Barnaby Joyce warned that the dogs would be euthanized if they remained in the country, bluntly stating, “It’s time Pistol and Boo buggered off back to the United States.” The animals departed Australia unharmed a few days later. A subsequent Senate hearing underscored the seriousness of the alleged breach, revealing that Heard and her husband, actor Johnny Depp, could face penalties including up to 10 years in jail or a fine of up to $265,000 (£172,000) if found guilty of illegally importing the pets. Depp is currently in Australia filming the latest installment of the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise on the Gold Coast, but authorities said it is Heard, known for roles in Friday Night Lights and Magic Mike XXL, who has been ordered to appear in court. “All animals entering Australia must have an import permit, and have undergone relevant testing and health checks signed off by a government veterinarian from the exporting country to ensure pests and diseases from overseas are not brought here,” the Department of Agriculture said in a statement. Heard has previously criticized the handling of the case and suggested she would avoid returning to Australia. “I have a feeling we’re going to avoid the land Down Under from now on, just as much as we can thanks to certain politicians there,” she told Australia’s NBC. “I guess everyone tries to go for their 15 minutes, including some government officials.”

Southampton’s director of scouting and recruitment Ross Wilson has rejected an approach from Rangers to lead the Ibrox club’s revamped football structure, choosing to remain with the Premier League side. The 34-year-old had been identified as a key appointment following the departure of manager Mark Warburton, with Rangers undertaking a wider overhaul after head of recruitment Frank McParland and assistant manager David Weir also left last month. McParland has since become director of football at Nottingham Forest, while Portuguese coach Pedro Caixinha is among those linked with the managerial vacancy at Ibrox.

Black riders faced longer wait times and more frequent cancellations than white riders, the research indicates. Women were more likely to be overcharged or taken on elongated routes, it says. Researchers took nearly 1,500 rides in Seattle and Boston, gathering data from three taxi-hailing companies. The two-year study was conducted by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Stanford and the University of Washington. Undergraduates were given identical phones with three ride-sharing apps—Uber, Lyft and Flywheel—and instructed to take a handful of prescribed routes. They recorded a range of service metrics, including how long it took for trip requests to be accepted, whether drivers cancelled rides and how routes and fares compared across passengers. In the Seattle experiment, the researchers came from a range of different racial backgrounds and used their real identities to request trips. In the Boston test, each researcher requested rides under two different names—one “white sounding” and the other a “distinctively black name”—to isolate the potential effect of perceived race on driver behavior. The results were stark. In Seattle, trip requests from Black riders took up to 28% longer to be accepted by both UberX and Lyft than those from their white counterparts. In Boston, the cancellation rate for Black-sounding names was more than twice as frequent as for those using white-sounding names. The disparities were even more pronounced in lower-density areas, where male passengers with Black-sounding names were more than three times as likely to have their trip cancelled. The study also identified gender-based differences in treatment. Female travellers were more often driven further than necessary. Female researchers reported “chatty” drivers who drove extremely long routes, on some occasions even driving through the same intersection multiple times. “The additional travel that female riders are exposed to appears to be a combination of profiteering and flirting to a captive audience,” the researchers noted. The report’s authors contextualized their findings within broader transportation history. “Passengers have faced a history of discrimination in transportation systems,” they concluded. “Peer transportation companies such as Uber and Lyft present the opportunity to rectify long-standing discrimination or worsen it.” The team warned that design choices intended to reduce bias could have unintended consequences. “Removing names from trip bookings may alleviate the immediate problem but could introduce other pathways for unequal treatment of passengers,” the report stated. Ride-hailing companies responded by emphasizing their efforts to expand access and enforce anti-discrimination policies. In a statement provided to the BBC, Rachel Holt, head of North American operations at Uber, said: “Ridesharing apps are changing a transportation status quo that has been unequal for generations, making it easier and more affordable for people to get around—no matter who they are or where they live. Discrimination has no place in society, and no place on Uber. We believe Uber is helping reduce transportation inequities across the board, but studies like this one are helpful in thinking about how we can do even more.” Lyft spokesman Adrian Durbin said in a statement: “We are extremely proud of the positive impact Lyft has on communities of colour. Because of Lyft, people living in underserved areas—which taxis have historically neglected—are now able to access convenient, affordable rides. We provide this service while maintaining an inclusive and welcoming community and do not tolerate any form of discrimination.”

Hibernian have completed the signing of Scotland Under-21 international John McGinn, with the 20-year-old choosing an Easter Road move after rejecting a new contract from St Mirren following the Paisley club’s relegation. McGinn, who considered several offers over the summer, said he was convinced Hibs represented the best next step in his career as the Edinburgh side target a return to the Premiership. “Once I weighed it all up, I quickly realised that Hibs was the right move for me at this stage,” McGinn said after sealing the switch. “The manager is really ambitious and I wanted to be part of his plans to move Hibs forward and get the club back into the Premiership. I’m still a young player and I believe Alan Stubbs will help me to develop into becoming a better player.” Head coach Alan Stubbs hailed the deal as a statement of intent from Hibernian without casting McGinn as a replacement for sought-after playmaker Scott Allan. “His arrival symbolises our ambitions for the future,” Stubbs told the club’s website. “He is an extremely talented young player with huge potential and I’m looking forward to seeing John continue his development here at Hibernian. John had other options, so we’re really pleased that he has chosen Hibernian and the aim is for him to achieve his career goals at our club.” McGinn had held talks with Major League Soccer side Houston Dynamo earlier in the summer, but ultimately opted to remain in Scotland with St Mirren’s Championship rivals. Stubbs, addressing whether the move should be seen as a response to the uncertainty surrounding Allan, was unequivocal. “People will ask, is it a statement, but it’s just the club looking to sign good players,” he said. Allan, 23, last season’s Scottish Championship Player of the Year, has submitted a transfer request amid firm interest from Rangers, but Hibs have rejected two bids and insist he will not be sold to a direct rival. Stubbs reiterated that the club’s stance remains unchanged. “I know people have tried to link it to that, but the position with Scott has not changed and it won’t,” he said. “I understand Scott’s position completely, I don’t dismiss it one bit. I understand where he’s coming from, but people have to respect the position of the football club.” Chief executive Leeann Dempster backed that position while stressing Allan’s ongoing importance to the squad. “Scott has every right to put in a transfer request and the club has every right to reject it. He’s still a Hibernian player, we will continue to look after him and he’s still a very big part of our squad here,” she said. Stubbs and his coaching staff signed extended contracts on Wednesday, with the head coach stressing the timing was unrelated to the Allan situation. “People have tried to link it, that I’ve held the club to ransom, but that’s very wrong and very unfair. We’ve been in negotiations for a number of weeks, a couple of months actually. I wanted to make sure that we signed all the players we wanted to sign and mine would take care of itself,” he added. With McGinn on board and Allan still in situ, Hibs are sharpening their focus on a promotion push, confident their blend of youth and experience can lift the club back to Scotland’s top flight.

A lightning strike at an outdoor activities centre in Lathus-Saint-Rémy, central-west France, injured eight youths on Monday, leaving a 15-year-old with cardiac arrest and burns. He is being treated in Tours, about 120km north of the site. Two others remain hospitalised, and five more sustained injuries, with several reporting tinnitus, officials said. The group of 16 had arrived that morning for a week-long stay and were outside with an instructor when the storm hit. While 13 French departments were under “orange alert” for violent storms at the time, the Vienne department, where the centre is located, was not included. Emergency services responded swiftly, and psychological support is being provided to those affected. Authorities are assessing the incident and weather conditions as the centre works with families and local officials.

Former Dragons forward Hugh Gustafson has joined Ospreys and will continue his switch from prop to the middle of the front row. The 28-year-old captained Wales Under-20s in 2007 and made 149 appearances for the Dragons at Rodney Parade. Calling the move “nerve-wracking, but a great opportunity,” Gustafson said he was embracing a “challenging environment” where players “have to want to be at your best in everything you do, every day.” Ospreys rugby general manager Andrew Millward welcomed the signing, describing Gustafson as “someone who wants to compete for the shirt and is eager to push on with us.” Millward added that Gustafson’s growing coaching experience and aspirations could make him “a huge asset” off the field as well.

Twenty-year-old goalkeeper Ryan Fulton, yet to make a first-team appearance for the Reds, made 13 outings on loan at Portsmouth in 2015-16. He could start the season as Chesterfield’s number one, with Tommy Lee set for shoulder surgery. The Scotland youth international has travelled to Hungary to join the Spireites’ pre-season camp ahead of the new campaign. Follow all the latest football transfer news and moves on our dedicated page.

Stephen Robinson has been appointed Motherwell’s permanent manager on a deal running until May 2018, two weeks after Mark McGhee was sacked and amid a push to stabilize the club’s Scottish Premiership campaign. Robinson, 42, stepped in as interim boss following McGhee’s departure and believes that short spell gives him crucial momentum. “It gives me a head start,” he said. “I know the vast majority of the players really well and I know what’s needed. Both previous managers let me take a lot of the training — I’m used to that. I don’t think loads will change from what I’ve done in the last two weeks. We tried to put a structure in place where we’re hard to beat and stop conceding goals, and we’ll continue to do that to stay in this division.” The Northern Irishman rejoined McGhee’s coaching staff in February after being sacked by Oldham Athletic in January. He had previously served as assistant to McGhee and his predecessor Ian Baraclough at Fir Park. Robinson said McGhee offered his full support during the transition. “I spoke to Mark in depth on Tuesday morning when he offered me his advice and best wishes, hoping I got the job,” Robinson explained. “So it’s with Mark’s blessing we do this, and I’ll give it my best shot to turn the football club around again.” Robinson underlined his pride at leading a club he knows intimately. “I’m delighted and honoured to be working for this club,” he said. “It’s got a great history and tradition and, as I’ve said numerous times, there are a lot of good people around the football club that we owe performances to.” With the transfer window closed, Robinson stressed that immediate priorities are rooted in tightening the squad’s shape and managing fitness. “The be all and end all is to keep the club in the Premiership,” he added. “We’ll worry about things after that and we’ll make plans for going forward after that, because at this time we can’t sign any other players — we have to deal with what we’ve got. We’ve got to deal with the injury situation which we have and rectify that and make sure we get through to the end of the season.” Robinson confirmed James McFadden will remain as assistant manager until the end of the season. “I’m conscious there’s an identity at the football club,” he said. “There are a lot of boys that have been here a long time, so we need to retain that as well.”

Nine people, Protestant and Catholic, were killed when three bombs exploded in the County Londonderry village in July 1972. Families of the Claudy bombing victims say their case remains in limbo, with pleas for greater transparency and the release of official files. Mark Eakin, whose sister Kathryn was eight years old when she died, said relatives remain “broken hearted” more than four decades on. “We are broken hearted. All I am asking of him (James Brokenshire) is to do his utmost to get whatever files and information on Claudy released to the public so that the people there can eventually have the truth,” he said, adding that he understood there were “secret files” that had not been released. Northern Ireland Secretary of State James Brokenshire said the government would not rush legacy issues to meet an artificial deadline or timescale. He noted that work was ongoing behind the scenes but could not be fast-tracked without agreement among parties. It is nearly a year since the Fresh Start Agreement was signed, setting out new proposals to address the past, and Brokenshire said achieving consensus remains essential. The Claudy bombing struck a mixed community in July 1972, when three devices detonated in the village, killing nine people and injuring many others. The victims were: Kathryn Eakin, 8; Joseph McCloskey, 39; David Miller, 60; James McClelland, 65; William Temple, 16; Elizabeth McElhinney, 59; Rose McLaughlin, 51; Patrick Connolly, 15; and Arthur Hone, 38. Kathryn, the youngest victim, was cleaning the windows of her family’s grocery store when the first bomb exploded. In 2010, a report by the Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland said detectives had concluded that the late Father James Chesney was a suspect and that the police, the state, and the Catholic Church had covered up his suspected role. Fr Chesney, who was later moved to the Republic of Ireland, died in 1980 and no action was ever taken against him. For families like the Eakins, the priority remains clear: access to information and acknowledgement, so that the truth of what happened in Claudy can finally be established.

Woolacombe Beach has been hailed in TripAdvisor’s Travellers’ Choice Beaches Awards, with reviewers calling it a “magnificent stretch of sand” offering “great surf.” Cornwall dominated the top 10 more than any other county, with four entries including Perranporth Beach and Fistral Beach. Beaches in Weymouth, Jersey, Swansea, and Bournemouth also featured among the UK’s favourites. Phil Hill, RNLI lifeguard manager at Woolacombe, said that “having such a beautiful beach in a beautiful setting with all those facilities” makes it “a great destination to take your family.” Set on north Devon’s coastline, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, Woolacombe combines scenery with convenience: nearby parking, surf hire, showers and toilets, plus plenty of cafes, pubs and shops. The Travellers’ Choice honours are based on the quality and quantity of traveller reviews and ratings for beaches collected over the past 12 months, reflecting consistent visitor satisfaction across the season.

Barcelona have agreed a £75m deal to sign Liverpool striker Luis Suarez, but the Uruguayan will not be presented to supporters or allowed to train with his new teammates until late October due to a four-month ban from football-related activities. The suspension was imposed by FIFA after Suarez bit Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini during the World Cup, an incident that led to the longest ban ever issued at the tournament. Barcelona confirmed they have lodged an appeal with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in an attempt to ease the restrictions, though club officials say they planned for the delay. Andoni Zubizarreta, Barcelona’s director of sport, said Suarez is already fully part of the club despite the complications. He described the forward as a positive addition who will be embraced “imperfections and all,” emphasizing Barcelona’s belief that the striker will contribute significantly once eligible. New head coach Luis Enrique echoed that view, saying the team anticipated the situation and will adapt in the short term. “It’s not ideal that he won’t be with us from the start, but it’s not a tragedy,” Enrique noted, adding that other players will step in until Suarez can play. He also highlighted the prospect of fielding a forward line featuring Suarez alongside Lionel Messi and Neymar, a trio he suggested any coach would relish. Suarez, 27, was last season’s Premier League top scorer and joined Liverpool from Ajax in January 2011 for £22.7m. He had four years remaining on his Liverpool contract. When he is finally cleared to play, he is expected to take the number nine shirt at Barcelona, bolstering an attack that the club hopes will spearhead a renewed push for major honours. Enrique was appointed in May to lead a rebuild after Barcelona finished last season without a significant trophy for the first time in six years. If confirmed at £75m, Suarez’s transfer fee would be the third largest in football history, behind Gareth Bale’s £86m move to Real Madrid and Cristiano Ronaldo’s £80m transfer to the same club. FIFA has informed Barcelona that, under the terms of the ban, they cannot hold a public unveiling for Suarez of the type the club has staged for previous marquee signings. Barcelona famously drew an estimated 90,000 fans to the Camp Nou for Neymar’s presentation in June 2013. In a separate move, Barcelona have allowed 22-year-old forward Cristian Tello to join Porto on a two-year loan. The Portuguese club holds an option to buy the Spain international at the end of the loan, while Barcelona have included a clause enabling them to recall Tello after one season. The deal gives Tello the chance to gain regular minutes and provides Barcelona with flexibility as Enrique reshapes the squad ahead of the new campaign.

One Dead, Several Injured After Ride Malfunctions at Columbus Fair; Governor Shuts Down All Rides A mechanical failure on the Fire Ball ride at a fair in Columbus on Wednesday evening resulted in passengers being thrown from their seats, leaving at least one person dead and several injured, including at least one in critical condition, authorities said. The incident occurred on the fair’s opening day. Columbus Fire Chief Steve Martin told local media that victims were ejected from the attraction, which swings side to side while spinning riders at high speed. The Fire Ball is marketed in Europe as the “Afterburner.” Ohio Governor John Kasich confirmed at least one fatality and ordered all fair rides shut down pending safety inspections. He said a full investigation would be carried out to determine the cause and ensure public safety before rides reopen. A doctor treating some of the injured described the forces involved as comparable to a vehicle crash. “Passengers were ejected at high speed with high energy, many feet—at least 20 or 30, if not more—into the air, and then crashed at a significant distance from the ride,” the doctor said. A video circulating online appears to show a passenger carriage breaking loose near the bottom of the pendulum swing, tossing riders into the air as the arm rises again. The footage has not been independently verified. The state fair confirmed on Twitter that there was “a report of a ride incident” but provided no additional details. Local NBC affiliate WCMH reported that one of the injured is a 13-year-old child. Multiple local outlets said the deceased is an 18-year-old. The Columbus Dispatch reported that safety inspections of the rides had taken place earlier in the week. Emergency crews responded quickly, securing the area and transporting victims to nearby hospitals. Fair organizers said they are cooperating with authorities. No timeline has been given for the rides’ reopening.

Exeter Chiefs head coach Rob Baxter confirmed centre Michele Campagnaro, 23, will start for Italy against England in the Six Nations on Sunday and has agreed a one-year extension with the club. Veteran full-back Phil Dollman, 31, Baxter’s first signing in 2009 when Exeter were in the Championship, remains a key presence. Winger Ollie Woodburn, 25, has scored seven tries in 20 appearances this season. Baxter praised their adaptability, saying the squad is being challenged in different ways and the trio have embraced change and thrived on those challenges.

Campaigners say the former Volkswagen garage in central Oxford, owned by Wadham College, has become “Oxford’s unofficial homeless shelter,” intensifying a debate over its future as the site faces a handover deadline this spring. The leaseholder, The Midcounties Co-operative, said it is “very confident” an agreement can be reached that would allow the squatters to remain until April, when its lease expires. “In April we have a legal obligation to hand the site back, with vacant possession, to our landlord Wadham College,” said Kevin Brown, group general manager at The Midcounties Co-operative. “To ensure we’re able to meet that requirement, we will request a repossession order but our preference is not to use it.” Campaigners have urged the site be formally designated as homeless housing, arguing it offers a vital refuge during winter. Wadham College, however, hopes to redevelop the building into student accommodation, and has not yet confirmed its next steps. Last week, the college said it was “exploring everything” and had not decided whether to pursue legal action, stressing that its chief concern was the “safety implications” for those who had moved in. The college highlighted its longstanding relationship with the Gatehouse homeless project and pledged to consult widely. “The college will be making every effort to speak to representatives of this homeless group as well as local residents, safety experts and the site developers,” a statement said. For those living there, the building offers stability and a path forward. “It’s a bit of a godsend really,” said Lewis Cairns, who is homeless and has been staying in the squat. “I feel like I can get somewhere now. I can start applying for university and get things done.”

Izzet Eren was being transferred to Wood Green Crown Court from jail on 11 December when a plot to spring him sparked a police operation in north London. Jermaine Baker, 28, was shot dead as officers moved to foil the escape attempt. At Woolwich Crown Court, Eren, 32, alongside Nathan Mason, of Vicarage Road, Tottenham, and Gokay Sogucakli, 18, of the Roundway, Tottenham, admitted their involvement in the plan and pleaded guilty to possessing an imitation firearm with intent. The trio were remanded in custody and will be sentenced at a later date. Two other defendants, Ozcan Eren, 31, of Douglas Road, Wood Green, and Eren Hayser, 25, of Kettering Road, Enfield, appeared earlier and pleaded not guilty to the same charges. They were also remanded, with a further pre-trial hearing scheduled for 18 March. The Independent Police Complaints Commission continues to investigate the circumstances surrounding Mr Baker’s shooting.

Tim Bresnan staged a vital late rescue as Yorkshire closed just 13 runs behind Worcestershire on an eventful opening day that swung repeatedly between the sides. Batting at number seven, Bresnan compiled a composed, unbeaten 78 to lift the visitors from the perilous position of 193-7 to 298-9 at stumps, keeping Yorkshire firmly in contention after captain Alex Lees had laid a stylish foundation earlier with 87 off 135 balls. Worcestershire had begun the day by extending their first innings from 264-8 to 311 all out, with all-rounder Gareth Andrew moving briskly from his overnight 42 to a 59-ball half-century, the 17th of his first-class career. His momentum was checked when he was caught at second slip by Lees off Jack Brooks, attempting to flick into the leg side. Sri Lankan off-spinner Sachithra Senanayake and seamer Charlie Morris nudged the total past 300 to secure a third batting bonus point, before Senanayake was taken at deep mid-wicket, giving Brooks his fifth wicket to complete figures of 5-56. Yorkshire’s reply faltered immediately as Andrew and Morris made early inroads. Will Rhodes edged Andrew to Daryl Mitchell at second slip for nought, and Indian Test batsman Cheteshwar Pujara, on debut, was snapped up at third slip by Morris, also without scoring, leaving the visitors reeling at 3-2. Lees, captaining at just 21 in the absence of the suspended Andrew Gale, responded with authority alongside Richard Pyrah. The pair counter-attacked at close to five an over, adding 108 in an enterprising stand that wrested back momentum. Jack Shantry then shifted the balance again, removing Pyrah for 43 and shortly after dismissing Jack Leaning. Lees continued to bat fluently but fell lbw to Andrew, 13 short of a deserved century, as Yorkshire went to tea on 179-5. Wickets continued to tumble early in the evening session: Andy Hodd, who made 30, nicked Andrew to Mitchell for the slip fielder’s third catch of the day, and Shantry bowled Steven Patterson for nought. Bresnan, however, found crucial support. He and Ryan Sidebottom took Yorkshire past 200 before Sidebottom, on 10, was forced to retire hurt with a calf strain after attempting a quick single. Bresnan then added a valuable partnership with Brooks, who contributed 26 before edging Andrew behind. Shantry returned to remove Karl Carver, but Sidebottom limped back to the crease as Yorkshire closed at 298-9, nearly erasing the first-innings deficit. Andrew finished with four wickets, matched by Shantry’s incisive spell, while the evergreen Brooks shone earlier with his five-for. After play, Yorkshire coach Jason Gillespie suggested Sidebottom is unlikely to bowl in the second innings. “Everyone could see that Sid was in a bit of discomfort. He’s hurt his calf and we’ll assess that over the next 24 hours. You’d say it’s pretty unlikely he’ll bowl in the rest of this match, and he’s gutted about that – but we’ve got a couple of other options,” Gillespie said. He praised Yorkshire’s fightback: “I’m delighted with the positive way we played to get back into the game. I think we’ve made a psychological blow already getting so close to their score, even if we don’t get a lead in the morning.”

Natalia Doherty was last seen on 15 April 2003 in Eastbourne, where she was living at the time. On Wednesday a Luton man, aged 66, was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and preventing a lawful burial Last week a 71-year-old man from Port Glasgow, Inverclyde, was arrested on suspicion of the same offences. A house in Icknield Way in Luton has been searched as part of the investigation. When Ms Doherty disappeared she was thought to have travelled to Luton to stay with her ex-husband, Gerald Doherty, who has since died. Officers from the Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire major crime unit launched an investigation in January 2014 into the case, which has led them to believe Ms Doherty was murdered in 2003. A police spokesman said: "Proof-of-life enquiries have since failed to show any sign she is alive. "Investigators are keen to trace Natalia's final movements and anyone who recognises her or Gerald from their time at the now-demolished pub, the Regents Arms in Hastings Street, Luton, or has any information relating to her disappearance, is asked to contact the police." Police investigating the 2003 disappearance of Natalia Doherty have arrested two men on suspicion of assisting an offender and preventing a lawful burial. On Wednesday, a 66-year-old man from Luton was detained; last week, a 71-year-old man from Port Glasgow, Inverclyde, was arrested on suspicion of the same offences. Officers searched a property on Icknield Way in Luton. Doherty, who was living in Eastbourne, was last seen on 15 April 2003 and was believed to have travelled to Luton to stay with her ex-husband, Gerald Doherty, who has since died. The Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire major crime unit opened a new investigation in January 2014, leading detectives to believe she was murdered in 2003. A police spokesperson said proof-of-life enquiries have found no evidence that Natalia is alive. Investigators are appealing for information to trace her final movements, particularly from anyone who knew Natalia or Gerald during their time at the now-demolished Regents Arms pub on Hastings Street, Luton. Anyone with information Natalia Doherty’s disappearance is urged to contact police or report via Crimestoppers.

The Scottish government advisors also said efforts to raise attainment should not result in the broader development of a child being overlooked. Education Secretary John Swinney has made it clear he expects the group to challenge him on policy and delivery. The panel was set up after last year's Holyrood elections. It includes members from Australia, the US, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Malaysia and the UK. Recommendations from the group are contained in a short report produced by the Scottish Government’s International Council of Education Advisers following its most recent meeting in Edinburgh in February. The council’s role is to generate ideas for improvement and provide robust challenge to ministers as reforms are taken forward. The report warns that one of the core aims of Curriculum for Excellence (CfE) risks being diluted by the way plans to drive up performance are implemented. CfE was designed to focus on the “whole child”, ensuring education supports young people to become successful learners, confident individuals, effective contributors and responsible citizens, rather than concentrating solely on academic outcomes. In parallel, the National Improvement Framework (NIF) has been established to raise attainment, with key goals including improving literacy and numeracy and closing the gap between the most and least disadvantaged pupils. While the council said CfE and NIF share a clear and positive narrative, it expressed concern that system pressures could push schools away from the whole-child approach toward a narrower focus on what is easier to measure. It highlighted three priority areas, and noted evidence of collaborative intent across the system, but concluded that collaboration remains uneven and insufficiently embedded in practice. The advisors also cautioned against an overemphasis on structural changes. They argued that culture and capacity are, arguably, more important drivers of improvement than reorganising governance or management arrangements. The Scottish Government recently announced plans to give head teachers more formal powers in an effort to accelerate school-level decision making. Some members of the panel had previously told BBC Scotland that changing structures alone would not deliver better outcomes. A Scottish government spokeswoman said: “We value the council’s expertise, robust challenge and input into our policy thinking, and our decision to further empower schools and teachers took their advice into account alongside other evidence.” Mr Swinney has encouraged the council to test and challenge the government’s approach as reforms are developed and implemented. A formal report on the actions required by the Scottish Government to deliver its vision for education is expected to be produced by the advisors next year, building on the initial findings from the February meeting and setting out detailed recommendations for policy and delivery.

China’s Ren Qian claimed women’s 10m platform gold after seizing the lead on her third of five dives and sealing victory with a superb inward three-and-a-half somersault on her fourth. Compatriot Si Yajie took silver, while Canada’s Meaghan Benfeito earned bronze. Britain’s Tonia Couch, competing in her third Olympics, finished 12th, with a reverse two-and-a-half somersault. “The last few days I haven’t dived my best, I’ve been a bit flat,” the 27-year-old from Plymouth told BBC, adding that making the final was her goal.

Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega says he is seriously considering entering the race to become Fifa’s next president as the organisation grapples with unprecedented turmoil at the top. The Swiss former international, 44, told BBC Sport he could stand in February’s election if he can help drive reform, amid the suspensions of outgoing president Sepp Blatter and Uefa chief Michel Platini over corruption allegations. “If I am the catalyst to reforming Fifa then I’m definitely considering going forward,” Vega said. He added that the current crisis presents an opportunity for a former player to lead world football. “Without a doubt,” he replied when asked if the time was right. “We are the product, we smell the grass, we smell the dressing room, we know the rules, the ins and outs, and the politics.” Vega, who also played for Celtic and Watford during a British spell from 1997 to 2002, retired in 2004 and has since built a career in finance. He says his background offers “the experience of two worlds of football and finance,” and revealed he has been approached by “various federations in Europe” to run, with a decision expected in the coming days. Fifa’s executive committee meets on Tuesday to decide whether to postpone February’s presidential vote, complicating a field already marked by uncertainty. Platini, 60, insists he will still stand and says he has been treated “shamefully” despite his suspension. Jordan’s Prince Ali bin al-Hussein and former Trinidad and Tobago midfielder David Nakhid have confirmed their candidacies. Bahrain’s Shaikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa has not yet submitted his bid but says “senior” figures in world football have encouraged him to enter before the 26 October deadline. The Football Association has suspended its backing of Platini pending a Fifa ethics committee investigation into an alleged “disloyal payment” from Blatter. Vega said he would welcome FA support, calling it “a strong voice in the football world.” Blatter, who is due to step down in February, is under criminal investigation over claims he authorised a £1.35m payment to Platini in 2011 and signed a contract “unfavourable” to Fifa. Both men deny any wrongdoing. The coming days are set to be pivotal, with Fifa’s leadership vacuum and reform agenda shaping the slate—and the stakes—for football’s most powerful job.

UCU to ballot for industrial action as university redundancy dispute escalates The University and College Union (UCU) has announced a ballot for industrial action after what it says were serious breaches of agreed procedures in a growing dispute over job cuts. The union claims more than 250 staff now fear for their jobs, while the university insists no one faces compulsory redundancy and has offered further talks. “We now feel we have no alternative but to ballot for industrial action,” said UCU regional official Martyn Moss. “Out of the blue, 37 people who thought they were safely on the books of the university suddenly faced a redundancy process..... to make it worse, another 219 staff are also at risk of losing their jobs.” The dispute began in April when 37 staff who had been on the university’s redeployment register for three months or more were told they could face redundancy. The union says the move marked a dramatic departure from the university’s long-standing policy of allowing staff to remain on the register until redeployed without fear of redundancy. It alleges managers rode roughshod over procedures while the redeployment policy was being revised and “simply went ahead and issued 37 ‘at risk of redundancy’ notices.” Tensions escalated in July when 219 employees in the computer support and maintenance team were informed the university planned to cut 68 posts. The university disputes the union’s characterization, saying no compulsory redundancies are planned and that letters sent to staff were requests for volunteers. A university spokesman said management had offered “further discussions to try to resolve any issues.” Formal talks broke down last month. UCU members have until 20 November to vote on industrial action. Both sides say they remain committed to further discussions, potentially with the assistance of the arbitration service Acas.

The planters separate the road and pedestrian route for cruise liner passengers arriving at the Albert Pier, in St Peter Port. Residents have branded them "tacky" and have criticised the colour. But, Deputy Scott Ogier said if people found them "so horrendous" they would be adjusted next season. The States expects more than 130,000 people to arrive at the pier during the season. Commerce and Employment Minister Deputy Kevin Stewart, who plans to make an official complaint, said: "They are really ugly planters. I also think they're the wrong colour." Pat Johnson, from Floral Guernsey, which promotes island events, said: "I'm stunned. There were 18 colour choices, this is almost certainly the worst one. He said that the planters "were something you wouldn't want to show the judges" of floral competitions. Some people on the BBC Radio Guernsey Facebook page branded them "tacky", "a waste of money" and said they resembled "upside-down Lego bricks". But, Deputy Ogier, Public Services Minister, said: "The colour was chosen to merge in with the backdrop of the harbour. "The purpose is when people come ashore [from cruise liners] they'll see some beautiful plants and flowers. "We're effectively talking about the colour of flower pots..... it's a minor issue, but important."

Local officials say a truck driver fell ill and died after a scuffle with police in Longmatan district on Wednesday evening, sparking overnight protests amid claims he had been beaten to death. Photos circulating on Chinese social media showed large crowds converging on the streets, with cars overturned and set ablaze, and police vehicles damaged. By dawn on Thursday, state media reported that calm had been restored. In a statement, the local government identified the driver as Gan Junyuan. Officials said auxiliary traffic police asked Gan to move his truck, prompting an argument and scuffle during which he “suddenly felt uncomfortable.” Gan reportedly took medication from his vehicle, but his condition worsened. Paramedics were unable to resuscitate him at the scene, and he was pronounced dead. An eyewitness quoted by Hong Kong’s South China Morning Post said she rushed to the scene and saw the man “suffering from some kind of heart attack,” adding she did not notice visible injuries on his body. The account contrasted with online claims that Gan had been fatally beaten, which fueled the unrest. The official Global Times, in a report posted on its accredited microblog before it was later removed, said as many as 10,000 people participated in the protests. A local resident told Reuters that several thousand people had taken to the streets. Images shared by users on Weibo-like platforms showed flames engulfing vehicles and police cars overturned, while another purported local resident posted a photo of paramilitary police in riot gear deployed at the scene. Authorities have pledged an investigation into Gan’s death and the events that followed. The incident comes just weeks before the Communist Party’s national congress, scheduled to open on November 8, during which China’s leadership undergoes a once-in-a-decade transition. In a separate development this week, Zhou Yongkang, the party’s security chief, urged local officials to maintain social harmony and stability during a visit to Sichuan, state media reported. As of Thursday morning, officials said order had been restored. However, the removal of the Global Times post and the scale of the unrest highlighted ongoing public sensitivity to allegations of police misconduct and the rapid mobilization power of social media in China.

Hunt said she was "proud of what has been achieved on BBC One" but "could not resist the chance to join Channel 4 at such an exciting time." Jana Bennett, the BBC's director of vision, said Hunt had "led BBC One with great commitment and creative flair." Her appointment follows that of David Abraham, who was made Channel 4's new chief executive in January. "Channel 4 requires a fearless creative leader to help steer us through our next phase," he said. "Jay has demonstrated..... her appetite to challenge the status quo, create and lead change, and promote new talent." Julian Bellamy is currently Channel 4's acting chief creative officer and will leave the station after "a short period of transition". The newly created chief creative officer role combines the channel's former two most senior creative posts, Head of Channel 4 and Director of Television and Content. Hunt's successes at BBC One include the modern update of Sherlock Holmes, crime thriller Luther and hard-hitting drama Five Daughters. She was previously controller of BBC Daytime and worked as editor of the One O'Clock and Six O'Clock News. Hunt was director of programmes at Five when she was appointed BBC One's controller in 2007. Jay Hunt has been appointed Channel 4’s chief creative officer, departing her role as BBC One controller. Her appointment follows David Abraham’s arrival as Channel 4 chief executive in January. The newly created role combines the former posts of head of Channel 4 and director of television and content. Julian Bellamy, currently acting chief creative officer, will leave after a short transition. At BBC One, Hunt oversaw the modern update of Sherlock, crime thriller Luther and hard-hitting drama Five Daughters. Jana Bennett, the BBC’s director of vision, said Hunt had “led BBC One with great commitment and creative flair.” Before becoming BBC One controller in 2007, Hunt was director of programmes at Five, and previously controller of BBC Daytime and editor of the One O’Clock and Six O’Clock News. Her move underscores Channel 4’s drive to refresh its creative leadership.

Irish police have intensified searches at a farm near Castleblayney, on the Armagh-Monaghan border, as part of the investigation into the 2007 killing of a 21-year-old found beaten to death in a barn in Oram, County Monaghan. The operation began around 09:00 local time on Thursday. A man in his 50s arrested that morning remains in custody. The BBC understands specialist ground-penetrating radar was deployed, revealing a large amount of buried material initially thought to include a van linked to the gang suspected of killing Mr Quinn. A digger was brought in to excavate the site, but the items uncovered were illegal waste, including large household objects. Gardai will now sift through the waste for potential evidence that could assist the inquiry. Searches are continuing in the area, with officers maintaining a presence.

Regional Leaders Sign Peace Accord in Addis Ababa, Paving Path Toward Stability in Eastern DR Congo A landmark peace agreement aimed at ending years of instability in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) was signed in Addis Ababa in the presence of UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon, who expressed hope the deal would usher in “an era of peace and stability” for the Great Lakes region. Leaders and representatives from 11 countries signed the accord, which could pave the way for a special UN intervention brigade to be deployed to eastern DR Congo alongside renewed political efforts to consolidate peace. “As many as 800,000 people have been displaced since the March 23 (M23) rebel group took up arms against the Kinshasa government last May,” Mr Ban noted, cautioning that the agreement was “only the beginning of a comprehensive approach that will require sustained engagement.” An earlier attempt to secure signatures last month was called off at the last minute, underscoring the fragility of recent diplomatic efforts. Heads of state and officials from Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Congo Republic, and South Sudan attended the ceremony, reflecting the regional scope of the crisis and the shared interest in finding a lasting solution. The M23 movement says its campaign is driven by the need to improve living conditions in eastern DR Congo, but the United Nations has long alleged that the group is backed by Rwanda, whose security landscape has been intertwined with DR Congo’s since perpetrators of the 1994 genocide fled across the border. Bosco Ntaganda, widely accused of being among the M23’s leaders, previously served as an officer in the Rwandan army before joining a DR Congo rebel movement. He is wanted by the International Criminal Court for allegedly using child soldiers, while the UN says he controls several mines in the country’s east. The group briefly seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, last November after carving out territory in the area. Talks between DR Congo’s government and M23 representatives have been taking place in Uganda to address a range of issues. The rebels declared a unilateral ceasefire in January, though a previous effort collapsed in December after they accused President Joseph Kabila of failing to honour a deal to integrate fighters into the national army. For over 15 years, the region’s mineral wealth has been heavily exploited by multiple actors, with little investment in DR Congo’s infrastructure—an imbalance the new agreement seeks to help redress.

Hull man Lewis Skelton, 31, named as victim Tasered and shot by police; IPCC launches investigation Lewis Skelton, 31, has been identified by his family as the man who was Tasered and shot by police on Francis Street in Hull on Tuesday. He later died in hospital. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) confirmed that officers fired more than one shot during the incident and has opened an investigation into the circumstances. In a statement, Mr Skelton’s sister, Laura Skelton, said: “My heart is breaking right now for my brother. He was a kind and caring person. What happened was out of character. We are all heartbroken.” Floral tributes have been left at the scene, with one message reading: “Fly high with the angels..... we love you,” and another stating: “Such a loss. What a lovely person he was. Words can’t express the sadness we all feel, you didn’t deserve this.” Neighbours described Mr Skelton as “mild mannered and polite.” Paul Mitten, who lived in the flat above him on Durham Street, said: “When I found out I just started crying because it just hit me for six knowing that what’s happened over there was the lad who lived under me. He was quiet, placid, looked after his animals. I can’t believe it. I can’t get over it. I’ve not been able to sleep. He’s always been polite to people, he’s always said ‘hi’ when he’s walked past..... can’t say a bad word about him.” Humberside Police said armed officers were deployed to the Holderness Road area at about 09:20 GMT following reports of a man carrying an axe, responding to calls from members of the public. The IPCC said it is searching a flat on Durham Street as part of its inquiry and will examine police actions leading up to the shooting. The watchdog has appealed for witnesses and urged anyone with information to come forward.

Police believe Roger and Christine Solik, from Abercynon, Rhondda Cynon Taff, were killed in an armed robbery at their farmland estate in the Kwazulu-Natal province in February. The suspects are due before magistrates on Monday. A 43-year-old man has already appeared in court charged with the couple's murder as well as kidnap and robbery. The body of Mrs Solik, 57, originally from Mountain Ash, was found bound in the Inzinga river in Impendle, 50 miles (80km) from her home on 17 February. Mr Solik, 66, who suffered from Parkinson's disease, was found dead almost two miles (3km) downstream from her three days later. South African police said the latest arrests were the result of a "breakthrough" on Friday night. They said the main suspect was arrested in Umlazi and further investigation led them to Impendle where two other suspects were arrested. Police said they were found in possession of suspected stolen property and two unlicensed firearms, which will be sent for ballistic testing. The Soliks moved to South Africa in 1981 after getting married in Wales the previous year.

A 78-year-old Florida man died after suffering “massive” injuries in a June 9 collision in Palm Beach Gardens that police say was caused by tennis star Venus Williams, according to attorneys for the victim’s family and a police incident report. Jerome Barson, who was riding in the passenger seat of his wife’s car, was hospitalized for 14 days following the crash and underwent multiple surgeries before succumbing to his injuries on June 22, his widow’s attorney said. Williams, 37, is in London preparing for her 20th Wimbledon appearance, scheduled to begin Monday. According to a police report obtained by U.S. media, Linda Barson told officers she was driving their 2016 Hyundai Accent through an intersection on a green light when Williams’ 2010 Toyota Sequoia crossed in front of their vehicle. Williams told police she became stuck in the middle of the intersection due to other traffic, the report states. Witnesses told police Williams’ SUV “suddenly darted” into the Barsons’ path and could not clear the junction in time because of traffic congestion. The incident report estimated the speed of Williams’ vehicle at approximately 5 mph (8 km/h) at the time of impact. The police report concluded Williams “is at fault for violating the right of way” of the Barsons’ car. Authorities did not issue citations at the scene, and Williams has not been criminally charged in connection with the crash. In a statement to U.S. media, Williams’ attorney Malcolm Cunningham said the player entered the intersection on a green light and offered condolences to the Barson family. “This is an unfortunate accident and Venus expresses her deepest condolences to the family who lost a loved one,” Cunningham said. Michael Steinger, an attorney for Linda Barson, told ABC’s Good Morning America that his client is devastated. “Mrs Barson is suffering intense grief and doesn’t know how she will go on,” he said. “Her husband of 35 years was struck by Venus Williams, who was at fault in a car accident, which ultimately resulted in Mr Barson being hospitalised 14 days with multiple surgeries which resulted in his death.” A wrongful death lawsuit filed by the couple’s daughter, Audrey Gassner-Dunayer, asserts that Jerome Barson’s injuries included “severed main arteries, massive internal bleeding, a fractured spine, and massive internal organ damage.” The filing also describes extensive damage to the Barsons’ vehicle: the front windshield shattered, airbags deployed, crush damage to the rear on the driver’s side, and the back window shattered. Steinger said the family is working to preserve and access evidence related to the collision. Jerome Barson died on June 22, which was Linda Barson’s 68th birthday. She was also hospitalized after the crash. Williams was not hurt. The accident occurred just days after the seven-time Grand Slam champion was eliminated from the French Open. Williams is currently training in London for Wimbledon, which she has won five times, most recently in 2008. The All England Club tournament begins Monday.

It is understood the complaint is that Fermanagh politician Tom Elliott announced his candidacy too early. Fermanagh MLA Tom Elliott faces an internal complaint after declaring in June his intention to run for the party leadership, weeks before party leader Sir Reg Empey officially confirmed his resignation last week. Elliott described the complaint as “incredibly petty,” arguing there is no rule preventing early announcements of leadership bids. Sir Reg had indicated earlier this year that he would step down following disappointing general election results. A selection meeting to choose the new leader is scheduled for September at the Waterfront Hall in Belfast. The party expects the new leader to be in place ahead of its conference in late October or early November. The dispute underscores sensitivities around succession timing as preparations for the leadership contest gather pace.

Residents have been evacuated from within a two-mile (3km) zone around the site of Wednesday’s huge explosions at an industrial estate warehouse housing hazardous chemicals, as the death toll rose to more than 100 with at least 700 injured. Authorities have advised people in affected neighborhoods to wear protective masks and take extra precautions if rain is forecast, amid concerns about potential contaminants. “The area where we live now is pretty much like a ghost town and anybody who is there is wearing protective safety masks,” said Roy Keld, a mechanical engineer from Sedgefield who has lived in China for six years. “We’ve been warned if it rains to wear long-sleeved clothes, long trousers, that kind of thing, and use an umbrella. So they’re pretty worried about what could come out of the sky if it does rain. It’s going to be crazy for a long time, I think.” Keld, who lives near the blast site with his Chinese wife and son, said the family has relocated to a hotel about 20 miles (30km) away. He described widespread anger and frustration among residents about the scarcity of official information. “That’s pretty much China all over – they don’t tell you unless they really have to,” he said. “There’s a lot of frustration with the general public who were actually involved in what’s going on.” With the area densely populated, Keld said many displaced residents have taken shelter in schools and tents as authorities continue to clear the area and assess damage. “There’s a lot of people just living in schools at the moment, and tents. It’s a very densely populated area. So where do you put people?” he said. The China Earthquake Networks Centre said the magnitude of the first blast was equivalent to detonating three tonnes of TNT, while the second was equivalent to 21 tonnes. Keld’s employer, UK-based Heat Tech Tooling, located about 25 miles (40km) from the blast site, has not been affected.

The deal marks F1's first commercial tie-up with a major digital service that appears on mobile devices first. The partnership will kick off this weekend, with coverage of the British Grand Prix on Sunday via Snapchat’s Our Stories format. Formula 1 is moving to broaden its presence across digital platforms, and the new arrangement will see footage from the racing season hosted on Snap’s editorially curated Our Stories. The feature compiles videos and photos submitted by users at F1 events and locations around the world, aiming to deliver a fresh perspective distinct from traditional broadcast coverage. Material from the British Grand Prix that appears on the Our Story stream will be available to users in the UK and the US, with plans to extend coverage to races in Singapore, Japan, the US, Mexico, Brazil, and Abu Dhabi. “Our Stories allow Snapchatters at the same event to contribute their unique perspectives through video and photo Snaps to one collective Story, capturing the atmosphere and excitement,” Snapchat said in a statement. Frank Arthofer, head of digital at F1, called the collaboration a key step in the sport’s evolving social media strategy. “This is the first step towards expanding our social media strategy. We need to continue to bring new fans to the sport—by reaching out to them on social media platforms with behind-the-scenes, fun and engaging content. Snap’s platform is one of the most popular among millennials, a sector we are particularly keen on attracting, as it represents the future of our sport.” The partnership underscores F1’s push to engage younger audiences and deliver mobile-first experiences, reflecting changing media consumption habits across global sports.

The FTSE 100 extended losses on Tuesday, slipping 15.98 points, or 0.28%, to 5,673.38 by late morning, after a 2.7% tumble on Monday. Analysts said sentiment toward financial shares has soured amid concerns over faltering global growth, while miners bore the heaviest selling. Antofagasta led fallers, plunging 9.4%, and Anglo American dropped 9.3%. In commodities, oil prices inched higher: Brent crude rose 1% to $33.22 a barrel and US West Texas Intermediate added 1.6% to $30.16. Sterling weakened slightly, down 0.03% against the dollar at $1.4428 and 0.29% against the euro at €1.2854, reflecting lingering risk aversion despite the uptick in crude. Broader market volatility kept investors cautious throughout.

Japan’s exports fell sharply in July, highlighting persistent headwinds for the world’s third-largest economy and sending local shares lower as the yen strengthened. Overseas shipments dropped 14% from a year earlier, while imports slid 24.7%, leaving a trade surplus of 513.5bn yen ($5.2bn; £4bn). Both declines were the steepest since 2009, underscoring weak global demand and the drag from a stronger currency. The benchmark Nikkei 225 closed down 1.6% at 16,486.01, and the broader Topix index matched the fall, ending at 1,290.79. The yen advanced again on Thursday, briefly moving past the psychologically important 100-per-dollar mark for the third time this year, pressuring exporters’ earnings prospects. “Looking ahead, we expect the yen to weaken against the dollar towards the end of the year, so the annual growth rates of export and import values should start to recover in coming months,” said Marcel Thieliant, senior Japan economist at Capital Economics. “But with external demand sluggish, trade volumes are unlikely to stage a strong rebound.” Asian markets were mixed following minutes from the US Federal Reserve that tempered expectations of a rate hike next month. South Korea’s Kospi rose 0.6% to 2,054.89, while China’s Shanghai Composite dipped 0.2% to 3,104.11. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 1% to 23,028.08, buoyed by Tencent shares after the internet giant reported stronger-than-expected quarterly profit. In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.5% to 5,507.80 despite jobs data beating forecasts. The unemployment rate eased to 5.7% in July, driven by an increase in part-time positions around last month’s national election. Shane Oliver, head of investment strategy and chief economist at AMP Capital, called the figures “reasonably solid,” but cautioned the labor market is “not quite as strong as it looks” given the decline in full-time employment. Investors remain focused on currency moves and global demand signals as regional markets navigate uneven growth and policy uncertainty.

Sony said a planned sale will help finance increased production in its image sensor business, aiming to raise about 440bn yen ($3.6bn; £2.28bn). The move aligns with a February announcement to spin off its video-and-audio division as the electronics giant seeks a return to long-term profitability. Sony has set a target of 500bn yen in operating profit by March 2018, underpinned by a greater focus on image sensors used in smartphones and cameras. The company previously spun off its TV unit and exited the personal computer market. Despite the strategy shift, Sony’s shares closed down 8.26% in Japan at 3,461 yen, reflecting investor caution over the restructuring and funding plans.

The department has ordered all schools and colleges in England to carry out fire safety checks, with immediate steps taken to assess and mitigate risks in the wake of the Grenfell Tower tragedy. In a statement, the Department for Education (DfE) said cladding on two London schools—a secondary academy and a primary special school—was found to be “not of limited combustibility.” The schools, London Enterprise Academy in Tower Hamlets and The Bridge primary school in Islington, underwent additional inspections and have been declared safe for continued use. “As a precautionary step, both schools have already been inspected by the fire and rescue service, who confirmed appropriate measures are in place to mitigate the risks from potential fire, and the buildings have now been declared safe for continued use,” the DfE statement said. The nationwide move follows the devastating blaze at west London’s Grenfell Tower, in which at least 80 people are believed to have died. The DfE ordered all of England’s 22,000 schools to complete a fire safety survey, and a spokesman said thousands of responses have already been received. Schools with buildings over 18 metres—around four storeys—were asked to send samples of any cladding that is similar in type and structure to the aluminium composite material used at Grenfell for testing at the Buildings Research Establishment in Hertfordshire. While the cladding at London Enterprise Academy and The Bridge failed these safety tests, fire experts have visited both sites to confirm evacuation systems and other safety measures are robust. Officials advised that the buildings’ design means the risk profile is different from that of residential housing, and not of the same order. Elsewhere in the UK, the Scottish government says checks have found no Scottish local authority-owned school buildings above 18 metres contain aluminium composite cladding of the type used at Grenfell. Universities and colleges in Scotland have been asked to carry out fire assessments, and some cladding is being removed from a hall of residence at Edinburgh Napier University. In Wales, the government has written to schools requesting cladding checks, with particular attention to buildings more than six storeys high. Authorities across the UK continue to coordinate on guidance and testing to ensure pupil and staff safety.

In his conference speech, Mr Khan said Labour needed to be "not just talking the talk, but walking the walk too". London Mayor Sadiq Khan issued a forthright call for Labour to refocus on winning and wielding power, telling delegates that being in opposition would “never ever be good enough.” Speaking at the party’s annual conference in Liverpool, Khan used the word “power” 38 times, underscoring his central message that Labour must turn its ambitions into action. Khan, who backed Owen Smith in the unsuccessful leadership challenge, nonetheless said Jeremy Corbyn could lead Labour to victory. Asked by the BBC whether Corbyn could win a general election, he replied: “Sure he can.” But he warned against Labour becoming a “protest party,” adding: “We are not a party set up to make ourselves feel better,” and urging members to resist the “comfort zone” of opposition. The London mayor received a standing ovation after detailing how Labour in power translates into concrete improvements: more affordable housing and transport, cleaner air, and better pay and conditions for workers. He described the scale of rough sleeping as a “stain on our nation” and vowed to tackle London’s “filthy” air, framing these issues as emblematic of the stakes when Labour is and isn’t governing. “The people who need us the most are those who suffer the most when Labour is not in power,” he said. Khan hailed Labour’s success in the Bristol mayoral race and its continued government in Wales, but stressed the party is absent from the place where it can “have the biggest impact on our country — in Parliament.” “It’s in government that Labour can make the biggest changes to people’s lives,” he said. “Every day now we see what happens when Labour’s not in power.” He also took aim at the Conservative government, arguing plans to expand grammar schools would “deepen inequality” and accusing ministers of having “no plan” for leaving the European Union, sharpening Labour’s critique on education and Brexit. Reactions in the hall captured the speech’s resonance and its tensions. Gavin Stamp, BBC political reporter in Liverpool, spoke to attendees streaming out afterward. Martin Hodges called it a “good rallying call which went down very well” and hoped the emphasis on power “will be carried through.” Aaron Rice described the address as “inspirational,” adding it was “good to hear from someone who is actually in power for Labour.” Another delegate praised the delivery but felt it carried a “pretty unhelpful subtext,” suggesting some in Labour would rather sit on the sidelines than make decisions. Khan’s message was clear: ambition is not enough—Labour must turn words into governing power.

Plans for a ski centre, 5,000-seat concert venue and cinema at Swindon’s Oasis leisure centre have been revived after work stalled. Swindon Borough Council said developer Moirai Capital Investment Ltd failed to meet key targets and intended to terminate the development agreement. The council has now withdrawn that notice after Seven Capital Investments Ltd agreed to take over the project. Seven Capital has indicated it will work alongside Moirai on the North Star site and views the scheme as “an ideal opportunity” to invest in the leisure market, the council said. Both parties will undertake a period of due diligence, and, if successful, the proposal will go to the council’s cabinet for approval. Garry Perkins, cabinet member for economy, skills and regeneration, said Seven Capital could help deliver “a landmark regeneration project for the town.” The North Star plans are seen as key to boosting Swindon’s leisure offer.

Audi to let DHL deliver Amazon Prime packages to car boots in Munich pilot Audi will pilot in-car delivery in Munich in May, letting Amazon Prime customers receive purchases in their parked vehicles to avoid missed drop‐offs. Partnering with DHL, the automaker’s Connect system allows couriers to locate a customer’s car during an agreed time window. Drivers get a one-time digital code to open the boot, place the parcel inside and relock the vehicle; the credential expires once the boot is shut. The trial is limited to Prime members and compatible Audi models. The move reflects a broader last-mile delivery push. In March, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration cleared Amazon to test Prime Air drones, highlighting industry efforts to speed fulfillment. Audi and DHL say time-bound tracking and expiring digital keys address security and privacy concerns. The initiative aims to end the frustration of missed deliveries.

A Norwich woman is trying to reunite a hidden trove of family photographs with their rightful owners after discovering a wartime-era album lodged behind a drawer in a second-hand chest. Clare Sherwood said she bought the furniture from a charity shop in Norwich about a year ago but only recently pulled out one of the drawers, revealing a dark red photography album wedged behind it. The book appears to date from 1937 and seems to have belonged to a couple, with images continuing through to the mid-1940s. The album contains holiday snapshots and family moments captured during World War Two, offering a vivid glimpse into local life across Norfolk. Among the locations featured are Sandringham, Caister and Hembsy, with scenes of children at the seaside and family outings. One striking photograph shows people fundraising for the war effort outside Tudor Hall in Norwich, a building that is now a tattoo parlour. Despite the detailed images, the album offers few clues to identify those pictured beyond first names. A caption under a photo of a mother and baby references the name Jean-Muriel and is dated 1938, but no surnames are included. “For us it’s fascinating, and it’s great local history, but I think it would be really wonderful to get this to someone who knows the people in it,” Ms Sherwood said. Her partner, Mr Kinghorn, added: “It’s been great fun looking through the pictures and putting lives together for different people, but it’d be nice to have that moment to give it to someone who, hopefully, it means something to.” Because the chest of drawers was donated anonymously, the couple were initially unsure how to proceed. After some of the photographs were shown on the BBC, Ms Sherwood said a woman had come forward claiming to recognise some of those in the images. She hopes this lead will help verify the family and allow the album’s precious memories to be reunited with relatives. Anyone who believes they may know the people pictured is encouraged to come forward.

The health minister was speaking ahead of a political summit to be held in February on health and social care. Northern Ireland’s Health Minister, Mr Hamilton, has urged political parties to forge consensus on long-term reforms to the region’s health and social care system, saying progress depends on taking politics “out of it as best as we possibly can.” Speaking to Radio Ulster’s Sunday News, he stressed that agreement across party lines is essential to deliver the world-class service envisioned by former Chief Medical Officer Sir Liam Donaldson. “I think it is incredibly important that the political parties sit down and agree in so far as they can,” Mr Hamilton said. “If we are to get this right and if we are to deliver the world class health social care system Liam Donaldson says we can have, then we need to get political agreement.” His comments come after more than 50 health and social care organisations called on Stormont politicians last week to take urgent action to transform services, citing mounting pressures and the need for a sustainable model. In response, Mr Hamilton has established a panel of health experts to redesign local services in line with recommendations from the Donaldson report published last year. The panel is chaired by Prof Rafael Bengoa, director of the health department at the Deusto Business School in Spain, and is tasked with proposing structural reforms to improve outcomes, efficiency, and resilience. The minister said the greatest obstacle to change has not been clinical resistance but political division. “What I think has been the biggest barrier to the level and degree of change that we have needed in social health care system..... has not been a lack of willingness on the part of clinicians and those within the system,” he said. “People understand that change in Northern Ireland needs to happen.
