We need to get political consensus around these very difficult issues or else they are not going to go anywhere.” The panel is expected to deliver its report by the summer. Hear more on Radio Ulster’s Sunday News at 13:00 GMT.

A Blue Air Boeing 737 bound for Bucharest returned to a UK airport after a suspected bird strike, burning off fuel over the Irish Sea and north Wales before landing safely shortly after 12:30 BST local time, airport officials said. Flight OB134 had departed at 10:10 BST when, about 20 minutes into the journey, the pilot reported the suspected strike but did not declare an emergency. The aircraft is undamaged and passengers remain on board as the jet is refuelled for a planned departure, a spokesman added. Bird strikes typically occur during take-off and landing when airborne animals are ingested into engines. Earlier this year, researchers from Swansea University and Argentina’s National University of Comahue warned such incidents involving aircraft and other man-made structures are increasing.

Gambian goalkeeper Fatim Jawara has died while attempting to cross the Mediterranean from Libya to Europe, the Gambia Football Federation (GFF) has confirmed. Jawara was on board a boat that ran into trouble last month, and her family has confirmed news of her death, association president Lamin Kaba Bajo said. Many of the undocumented migrants who arrive in Italy are Gambians, and her death has reignited debate at home about the risks people take on the so‐called “Back Way” route to Europe. The Gambia’s President Yahya Jammeh has been accused of intimidating the opposition, charges he denies, and the mounting pressures at home are often cited as factors pushing young people to leave. Jawara made her debut with the national women’s side a year ago after progressing through the junior ranks. “She will be remembered for saving a penalty kick in a friendly encounter involving the national soccer team and the Glasgow Girls from Scotland,” Mr Bajo told AFP. In a Facebook post, the federation said the manner in which she died was “shocking” and offered condolences to her family, teammates, and supporters. At club level, Jawara played for Red Scorpions FC in Serekunda, just outside Banjul, where she earned her place as first‐choice goalkeeper, leading to her selection for the national team. Red Scorpions coach Chorro Mbega described Fatim as “a very lovely person who always smiled.” Mbega told the BBC’s Focus on Africa that Jawara had been a member of the squad that represented the Gambia at the 2012 under‐17 Women’s World Cup in Azerbaijan, having joined the team in 2009. “Fati was a player who can play anywhere on the field. I’m really sad about this because she fought so much to be number one,” Mbega said, adding that Red Scorpions players were not paid salaries, though she was not aware of Jawara being frustrated. Her absence was widely noticed when the Gambia national women’s team was scheduled to play Senegalese club Casa Sports during celebrations marking a girls’ football festival recently. As rumours grew that she had taken the “Back Way,” Red Scorpions captain Fatu Fatty said confirmation came from Jawara’s family after an agent contacted them to say Fatim was among those on a boat that capsized. “She was everyone’s friend in the team. Jovial and funny to an extreme,” Fatty said in tears. Figures from the International Organization for Migration show more than 4,200 migrants fleeing conflict and poverty have died or gone missing in the Mediterranean this year. Recent shipwrecks off Libya have killed hundreds, and migrant deaths are at a record high. A GFF official noted Jawara was not the first footballer to suffer such a fate, but she is one of the most high‐profile athletes to have died this way. Her death has shocked Gambians and brought the issue of illegal migration into sharper focus, underscoring the tragic human toll of dangerous journeys undertaken in search of opportunity.

Aston Villa have scrapped their end-of-season awards ceremony as the club edges toward relegation from the Premier League after a dismal campaign marked by fan unrest and managerial upheaval. Villa are nine points adrift at the bottom, having won just three games all season, and could be relegated on Saturday. “In the current circumstances, we are sure our supporters will understand,” a club spokesman said, confirming the decision to cancel the event. The move follows a series of protests against owner Randy Lerner, including during the recent home defeat to Chelsea, when supporters displayed banners reading: “Proud history, what future?” Discontent has intensified in recent weeks, with fans organising walkouts and demonstrations at Villa Park. “There is a toxic atmosphere at the club at the moment. The players are not generally well liked,” said Villa supporter Mike McKenna, who helped organise fan walkouts during home games against Everton, Tottenham and Chelsea. “Unfortunately, the complaints about the likes of [Micah] Richards, [Gabriel] Agbonlahor, etc have rubbed off on other players. Maybe Jordan Ayew deserved an award but, with the toxic atmosphere, the club have thought it would only garner bad publicity to garnish the players with awards. Generally, I would think the supporters support the decision not to have awards as there is nothing to celebrate.” Villa have dismissed two managers this season—Tim Sherwood in October and his successor, Remi Garde, last month. Interim boss Eric Black has overseen two successive defeats, the latest a home loss to Bournemouth on Saturday. Relegation could be confirmed in Saturday’s early kick-off if Norwich avoid a home defeat by Sunderland at 12:45 BST. Even if Norwich lose, Villa would need to win later in the day at Manchester United’s Old Trafford to keep their faint hopes of survival alive.

An Irish former soldier detained in Iraq after allegedly crossing the border illegally has been released, along with two British citizens, the Irish government and family members confirmed. Joshua Molloy, 24, from Ballylinan, was held for over a week in the Kurdish city of Erbil. He is a former member of the Royal Irish Regiment and was reported to have been fighting alongside Kurdish forces opposed to the Islamic State group. Minister for Foreign Affairs Charlie Flanagan said arrangements were under way to reunite Mr Molloy with his family in the coming days. He thanked those who helped facilitate the release and said his department would continue to provide consular assistance. Mr Molloy had been detained with two Britons, Jac Holmes from Bournemouth and Joe Ackerman from Halifax. The trio were picked up after entering Iraq from Syria. Declan Molloy, Joshua’s father, told RTÉ he received a phone call late on Saturday from Mr Flanagan confirming the release. “We are all delighted here. We are jumping with joy to know that he is out,” he said. “You know that Christmas morning feeling, it’s a bit like that, when you find your most sought-after present under the tree, the dream present. That’s how we feel.” He said he had spoken to his son via Facebook on Sunday and that he was “fine” but would need some time alone after the ordeal. He reiterated that his son was not a mercenary or a freedom fighter, and had travelled to Syria last year for humanitarian reasons. No further details of their detention have been released.

Flood support workers in Carlisle estimate 80 people across the county have been left in limbo after their home insurance policies were declared void following recent floods. The insurer Integra says a number of customers provided inaccurate information when taking out cover, but those affected argue they made innocent mistakes and are now pinning their hopes on an appeal to the insurance industry ombudsman to reinstate claims. Steven Boyd, from Carlisle, told the BBC he was informed by Integra that his policy was void because he lives in an area that had previously flooded and had not paid an additional flood premium. Three months after his property was stripped during the clean-up, Boyd and his wife are living in upstairs rooms. He says he is considering using money from his pension fund to pay for repairs. Insurance expert Joel Zimelstern said he understands Boyd should not have been required to declare his property as at risk, citing flood prevention measures installed by the Environment Agency in recent years. Paul Hendy, who leads the Carlisle Flood Recovery Centre, said he is taking multiple cases to the ombudsman on behalf of residents whose claims have been voided. “It’s bad enough going through a flood, it’s bad enough having your home stripped out, it’s bad enough losing all your personal possessions in a skip,” he said. “We have people in the centre sobbing their eyes out because this is unreal.” Carlisle’s Conservative MP John Stevenson said most cases he had seen involved “innocent error,” adding insurers should have known whether an address was in a flood area and clarified any issues at the point of sale. He appealed for anyone affected to contact his office. Integra said it does not discuss individual customers’ details with the media.

UK Coaching honoured the nation’s leading coaches and organisations over the past year at the UK Coaching Awards. The ceremony showcased outstanding success achieved over the previous 12 months. Rugby league coach McDermott was recognised after leading his side to an historic treble, topping the Super League table before defeating Wigan Warriors in the Grand Final and lifting the Challenge Cup. “Whenever one person gets recognised for coaching there are so many more people that are part of it. The whole club has a part to play, so personally I am unbelievably proud, but I am proud for the whole club,” McDermott said, adding that the emotion at the end of the season was “relief.” Danny Kerry, head coach of England and Great Britain’s women’s hockey teams, was named High Performance Coach after guiding England to the European Championship title for the first time in 24 years. He also steered the team to Commonwealth silver and Olympic qualification with a 100% win record. British Cycling enjoyed a strong night, collecting three awards. Coaches Richard Shepherd and Andrew Pink received the Coach Developer of the Year and Heather Crouch Young Coach of the Year honours, while British Cycling was named Governing Body of the Year. The accolades capped a year of exceptional achievement across UK sport, highlighting the impact of world-class coaching on team success and athlete development.

English Heritage has approved the replacement of Charminster’s 16th-century bridge after concluding its small arches restricted the flow of the River Cerne, exacerbating flood risk. The historic crossing, previously protected from alteration, was blamed for nearly wrecking the nearby grade I-listed church during the January 2014 floods. Dorset County Council, working with the Environment Agency, said the new structure will echo the character of the original while improving river capacity. As many of the original bricks as possible will be reused, and the existing historic parapets will be incorporated into the design. Construction is scheduled to begin in May, with the road surface raised by 30cm to accommodate larger arches. The road will be closed to vehicles and pedestrians until October. Officials say the project balances heritage conservation with public safety, aiming to reduce flood impacts while preserving the village’s identity.

Scott Brown’s red card downgraded; available for Old Firm, banned for next two league games The 31-year-old midfielder’s sending-off has been downgraded to a caution for “recklessly dangerous play” after Celtic won an appeal to the Scottish FA. Scott Brown was dismissed for a stoppage-time challenge on Liam Boyce in a 2-2 draw, but disciplinary hearings were delayed over Easter, allowing him to feature in Sunday’s Scottish Cup semi-final win over Rangers at Hampden. The downgrade makes Brown eligible for Sunday’s Old Firm derby at Ibrox; however, the yellow card pushes him beyond the disciplinary threshold, triggering a two-match ban. He will miss subsequent Premiership fixtures against St Johnstone and Aberdeen. The decision follows Celtic’s appeal of the dismissal and brings immediate clarity to their run-in.

Openreach will lay ultrafast fibre to homes in Altnaharra and Skerray, near Bettyhill in Sutherland, boosting connectivity for 45 households linked to the Altnaharra telephone exchange and 100 premises in Skerray. The project is being delivered with local support: workers from Altnaharra Estate will install cable across the estate, while skilled residents in Skerray will undertake digging to Openreach-agreed specifications. The community-assisted rollout aims to accelerate gigabit-capable broadband access in remote areas, enhancing reliability and future-proofing connectivity.

Shenol Erol Ali, 32, a Bulgarian national, was found dead with multiple stab wounds at the Bill Nicholson pub in Northumberland Park, Tottenham, on 3 February. Gyuldzhan Hadzhieva, 37, of Northumberland Park, has been charged with murder and is due to appear at Hendon Magistrates’ Court later.

Amateur comedians submitted contemporary Christmas cracker jokes to TV channel Gold for 2014. Around 2,000 people voted for a top 10 from a shortlist drawn up by judges. The winning quips riff on Luis Suarez’s World Cup bite, UKIP, The Great British Bake Off and Game of Thrones. Highlights include: “What do the royal family play at Christmas instead of musical chairs? Game of Thrones,” and “Why is Bake Off festive? Because the star is in the yeast.” “Santa only comes if you sleep, not if Ukip.” An orange “bite-sized” Suarez gag and a cheeky “Twerky” pun also drew laughs, though the latter missed the top ten. The competition aims to refresh the classic cracker tradition with timely, family-friendly humor that nods to the year’s biggest cultural moments.

CBI president Paul Drechsler will use a speech in London to back the government’s pursuit of an ambitious post-Brexit trade agreement with the European Union while warning that it is “wrong and irresponsible” to treat leaving without a deal as the UK’s first or only option. He will say he agrees with the prime minister that a deal can be done, and argue that both British and European firms fear a “worst-case scenario” of no agreement. Drechsler will stress that business supports the government’s plan for a comprehensive trade deal and that the CBI is working with business groups across EU member states to secure an outcome in everyone’s interests. He will say companies on both sides of the Channel want a smooth Brexit and continued cooperation, and that industry is focused on practical solutions to protect jobs, investment, and supply chains. “But to those whose first and only choice is for Britain to walk away without a deal, I say you’re not only wrong but irresponsible,” he will say, warning that reverting to World Trade Organisation terms would bring immediate costs. He will argue that, without an agreement, British firms would face tariffs on around 90% of their exports to the EU, alongside new regulatory hurdles that would disrupt trade and raise prices, hurting businesses and consumers across the bloc. Drechsler will note that while some companies are preparing for such a “worst-case scenario,” many are unable to do so because the costs are too high or the operational requirements too complex. He will call for clarity, pragmatism, and early progress on transitional arrangements to avoid cliff-edge changes when the UK formally leaves the EU. His remarks come as Prime Minister Theresa May prepares to trigger Article 50 by the end of the month. While the government says it is determined to secure an agreement, May has also insisted that “no deal is better than a bad deal.” Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson has said the UK can be “ever-more European and ever-more internationalist” simultaneously, and that there is every reason to believe a “win-win” EU deal can be struck within the two-year timeframe for negotiations. Drechsler’s intervention follows similar warnings from the British Chambers of Commerce and former chancellor George Osborne earlier this week, underscoring persistent concern in business circles about the potential disruption of a disorderly departure. He will say a “smooth Brexit” is in everyone’s interest and urge negotiators to focus on outcomes that maintain the UK’s global competitiveness. Pro-Brexit group Change Britain accused the CBI of being “proven wrong time and again on Europe” and urged the business body to be “more optimistic” about the UK’s prospects. Spokeswoman Chloe Westley said it is “overwhelmingly in the EU’s interests to strike a free trade agreement with the UK,” and that the CBI should support the government in getting the best deal for Britain. Patrick Minford, chairman of Economists for Brexit, said it was wrong to assume a no-deal Brexit would harm the UK. He argued that unilaterally removing all import tariffs, even without EU reciprocity, could add 4% to GDP and 7.3% to Treasury receipts compared with the status quo. “Our economy can and will flourish outside the single market and we do not need a trade deal with the EU to deliver that,” he said.

His music has been a regular fixture on screens big and small for more than five decades, but across the island of Ireland, German bandleader James Last is best remembered by many for one piece of instantly recognisable music: the theme song from RTÉ’s The Sunday Game. Known as Jagerlatein (Hunters’ Yarns), the tune’s distinctive blasts of brass and quickstep marching beat have introduced the broadcaster’s flagship Gaelic games programme since it first aired in 1979. For GAA fans, Jagerlatein is the sound of the summer, synonymous with early starts and car journeys to far‐flung stadiums, ham sandwiches on the terraces, and championships won and lost on the turf of Croke Park. It is also an insidious earworm—one brief bar is enough to lodge it in the brain, likely to have supporters humming along all week after hearing even a snatch on any given Sunday. Its popularity is such that when RTÉ replaced the theme in 2004 as part of a “remodernisation of The Sunday Game,” it sparked uproar among viewers. The network reversed course four years later, reinstating Last’s composition after a groundswell of public pressure. Speaking at the time, Paul Byrnes, the programme’s editor, said RTÉ had been “inundated with requests from the public” to bring back the theme. “Travelling the length and breadth of the country with The Sunday Game over the last few years, the replacement of the theme tune was always much talked about and lamented,” he said. Michael Lyster, the longtime presenter of The Sunday Game, told RTÉ’s The Late Late Show in April that “people just demanded that it be brought back again and rightly so as well.” He also admitted there are drawbacks to spending so much time within earshot of such a catchy slice of Irish television history. “At the end of the season of The Sunday Game, you park the whole thing for a couple of months and you get a break from it all,” he said. “But you hear The Sunday Game music so often and it’s not just on the Sundays, but obviously in the office there’s somebody rehearsing a piece of footage—and over and over and over again and you get to the point where you think to yourself, if I hear this one more time, I’m actually going to go scatty.” As tributes are paid, Lyster will surely forgive fans if they break into a chanted, hummed, or whistled version of Jagerlatein in memory of the man who inadvertently gave Gaelic games their most iconic theme. For generations, James Last’s brass‐driven anthem has been the soundtrack to Irish summers—and it will remain so for years to come.

A new cross-Wales research network aimed at tackling stroke has been announced as fresh figures show significant progress in reducing deaths from the condition. British Heart Foundation (BHF) Cymru said 66,000 people in Wales are living with the long-term effects of stroke, while highlighting a 22% fall in stroke mortality between 2010 and 2015. Despite the improvement, the charity estimated that 13 people per day still suffer a stroke in Wales. Prof Nilesh Samani, medical director at BHF, said more investment in research is urgently needed to build on recent gains and expand treatment options. “There are 66,000 people living in Wales with the cruel and debilitating after-effects of this devastating disease,” he said. “Although some exciting new developments have been made in stroke treatment, the options at our disposal for treating stroke patients are still far too limited. We urgently need to fund more research to better understand the causes of strokes so that we can prevent them occurring and develop new treatments for all types of stroke in order to save more lives.” BHF Cymru described research as “fundamental” to delivering new treatments for both ischaemic stroke, caused by a blood clot, and haemorrhagic stroke, caused by bleeding in or around the brain. The charity welcomed the creation of the Cross-Wales Stroke Research and Innovation Network, which will be hosted by Cardiff Metropolitan University and launched in the autumn. The network will bring together members of Wales’ Stroke Implementation Group (SIG), established to deliver the Welsh Government’s five-year strategy on stroke. Prof Philip James, associate dean for research at Cardiff Met’s School of Health Sciences, who helped to create the network, said: “Our aim is to create and sustain a collaborative, robust research infrastructure in Wales and help facilitate world-leading research and innovation in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of stroke, thus saving lives and ultimately reducing the debilitating impact on stroke patients.” Ana Palazon, director for the Stroke Association in Wales, said investing in “world-class research” is key to reducing the condition’s “devastating impact,” noting the need for collaboration across health services, academia and charities to accelerate discovery and improve care. A Welsh Government spokeswoman said “good progress” was being made across stroke care. “More people are surviving strokes, with 22% fewer deaths from strokes since 2010, and staff skills and expertise is continually improving,” she said. “To support these ongoing improvements a Stroke Implementation Group was formed in 2013 to provide national leadership and support for the delivery of effective person-centred stroke care in Wales.”

Ryan Simpson, 29, of Elgin, has been jailed for 16 months after admitting sexually assaulting a child and possessing indecent images. The hotel worker sent a video of himself kissing an infant to his boyfriend. The case, initially heard at Elgin Sheriff Court, was referred to the High Court in Aberdeen in Scotland for sentencing, where Simpson was also placed on the sex offenders register for 10 years. At an earlier hearing, fiscal depute Alison Wylie told the court the baby was “distressed and crying” in the footage. Defence lawyer Jonathan Crowe said Simpson endured a difficult upbringing and claimed he had been pressurised by his then partner to commit the assault, adding that his client was horrified by his actions. Sentencing, Lord Woolman urged Simpson to engage fully with rehabilitation, saying: “It is in your best interests that you engage in every social work programme which is recommended to you.” The case underscores the gravity with which Scottish courts treat offences against children and the importance of offender rehabilitation.

Wycombe Wanderers striker Adebayo Akinfenwa, famed as “the Beast” and often dubbed the strongest man in football, delivered a wrestling-style celebration in Saturday’s 3-2 win over Port Vale. After scoring his second goal, Akinfenwa dropped the “People’s Elbow” on team-mate Luke O’Nien, mimicking WWE icon Dwayne “The Rock” Johnson’s signature move. Johnson noticed and applauded the homage, tweeting: “Heart stoppin’ elbow droppin’..... well done brotha.” O’Nien saw the funny side, joking on Twitter: “Just got out of A&E. Planning my pay back celebration.” The eye-catching moment capped a lively League Two clash and sent social media buzzing, with fans quoting The Rock’s catchphrase: “Do you smell what The Rock is cooking?”

German court rules Facebook not obliged to proactively remove defamatory posts about Anas Modamani A court in Wuerzburg has ruled that Facebook is not required to proactively seek out and delete posts that falsely linked Syrian refugee Anas Modamani to terrorism and violent crime, rejecting a bid to force broader policing of the platform. The 19-year-old became a social media figure after a widely shared photo in 2015, but his image was later misused in posts that tied him to attacks in Brussels and at a Berlin Christmas market, as well as crimes including an arson attack on a homeless man in Berlin. Facebook removed some of the malicious posts, but Modamani sought an injunction compelling the company to identify and eliminate such content without waiting for users to flag it. The Wuerzburg court acknowledged that the posts amounted to “undisputable defamation,” yet concluded that because Facebook had not created the slanderous content, it was not obliged to actively seek and delete it. Modamani, who is taking German classes and working in a restaurant, said the false claims had harmed him, according to AFP. Lawyers for Facebook argued that the platform hosts billions of postings each day and that detecting every misuse would require “a sort of wonder machine.” They contended that responsibility should lie with the individuals who originally posted the defamatory images. Modamani’s lawyer countered that Facebook has the technical capacity to detect and block other types of content, such as pornography, and should be able to prevent repeated misuse of his photo. The ruling comes amid heightened scrutiny of social media companies over the spread of fake news. Facebook has introduced filtering systems in the United States, Germany, and France after suggestions that fabricated reports influenced the outcome of the U.S. presidential election. In France, the company has teamed up with Google and eight news organizations to deploy fact-checking tools ahead of the April presidential vote. Germany, which holds elections in September, is considering fines for each fake news article that platforms fail to remove, reflecting intensifying pressure for more aggressive moderation.

Adam Rooney’s ninth European goal for Aberdeen sealed a 4-0 aggregate victory over FK Ventspils, sending the Dons into the Europa League third qualifying round for the third successive season. Derek McInnes’ side will face Slovenian outfit Maribor next, with the Aberdeen manager welcoming the challenge while warning it will be a step up in quality. “We already know that it will be a step up in quality when it comes to this tie,” McInnes told BBC Scotland. “There’s no doubt we will look forward to a crowd of 17 or 18,000 at Pittodrie next Thursday night for another great occasion. Hopefully now we can look forward to going at least that one step further in the competition this time. It would be good to put ourselves in the position to qualify for the group stages but it won’t be easy as it gets tougher as you progress in any tournament. I think we are improving as we move on and we will be looking forward to it.” Rooney had a first-half effort ruled out for offside before eventually striking to put the tie beyond doubt, his seventh goal against Latvian opposition in Europe. McInnes praised his striker’s reliability on the continental stage, saying: “We thought one would kill the tie and Rooney gets his traditional goal. It was a fantastic goal and he led the line well.” The manager reserved special praise for goalkeeper Joe Lewis, who produced a superb double save to keep out a controversial first-half penalty and its rebound, with McInnes sharply critical of the officials. “It was never a penalty,” he said, referencing Serbian referee Danilo Grujic and his assistants. “That was frustrating and I thought the standard of the refereeing was poor at times, but thankfully big Joe has made a brilliant save and played his part keeping out the rebound as well. I was confident he would save it if the player went to his right-hand side as it is his favoured side to put it in.” McInnes added that Aberdeen’s control, particularly after the break, underlined the professionalism of the performance away to a team that “normally win at home.” He concluded, “I thought we defended brilliantly in the second half and we certainly feel we should have scored more, but it was a professional performance.”

Essex secured a draw after resuming 163-4, 73 ahead, focusing on saving the game. Captain Ryan ten Doeschate anchored with 109, setting platform before Graham Napier unleashed 124, his seventh first-class century, featuring three late sixes in one over. Essex declared at 470-8, handshakes followed. David Masters finished unbeaten on 47; Tom Westley added 44. The 11-point haul lifts Essex back to the top of County Championship Division Two, one point clear of Kent. Sussex, still unbeaten in 10 fixtures, remain sixth and now sit 41 points off the summit. The result underscores Essex’s title push and Sussex’s consistency without victories, as the Chelmsford deck offered few alarms for bowlers on the final day.

Royal Mint offers silver pennies to babies sharing birthday with new princess The Duchess of Cambridge has given birth to a daughter, prompting a nationwide celebration and a special gesture from the Royal Mint. The palace confirmed the Duke of Cambridge was present for the birth on Saturday. The new princess weighed 8lb 3oz, and both Catherine and her daughter are doing well. To mark the occasion, the Llantrisant-based Royal Mint is gifting silver pennies to babies born on the same day as the royal newborn. Each coin will be struck with the child’s year of birth, continuing what the Mint describes as an age-old tradition of giving silver to celebrate a new arrival and bring good luck. Parents of eligible newborns will need to register their child’s birth via the Royal Mint’s Facebook page within 60 days to receive the commemorative penny. The initiative mirrors a similar giveaway in 2013, when the Mint distributed 2,013 silver pennies to infants born on the same day as Prince George. The first family to receive one of the coins is Chantal and Miguel Abel, whose daughter Sofia was born at 11:30 BST on Saturday at Chelsea & Westminster Hospital in London. “It’s a special day for us and we’re excited to be one of the first families to receive a lucky silver penny and be part of the celebrations,” the couple said in a statement. Shane Bissett, the Royal Mint’s director of commemorative coin, said the gift reflects a shared moment of national joy. “The birth of the new royal baby is a joyous occasion not just for their Royal Highnesses the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge but also for the whole nation, as we celebrate another remarkable milestone in their life journey together,” he said. “However, it is also a special day for many mothers and fathers across the country as they too welcome the arrival of their new babies, hence why we wanted to extend this historical moment to them with a unique and timeless gift that can be treasured for years to come.” In addition to the silver pennies, the Royal Mint will release a £5 coin to commemorate the princess’s birth, following the tradition established for the arrival of Prince George.

The secretary of state said Downing Street and the Treasury were now considering the proposal. Downing Street and the Treasury are examining a package submitted by Northern Ireland’s five parties aimed at breaking the deadlock over welfare reform. The move follows 10 weeks of talks at Stormont Castle addressing disputes over flags, parades, the legacy of the Troubles and welfare. Northern Ireland Secretary Theresa Villiers said the talks had reached a “crunch point” and confirmed the government was looking “very seriously” at the paper tabled by parties. Central to the proposals are plans to improve Stormont’s borrowing powers and to have welfare penalties imposed by the Treasury written off. Northern Ireland is paying fines for failing to implement welfare reforms passed at Westminster in February 2013. The BBC understands the document also seeks funding for new bodies to examine the past and the creation of a peace investment fund to support communities still affected by conflict. Villiers, who declined to detail the proposals, said “there does seem to have been a degree of progress between the parties,” but cautioned that “our response is going to have to take into account the deficit that we inherited and the limited resources we have.” She added there were no plans for Prime Minister David Cameron to return to Northern Ireland before Christmas. Earlier, Sinn Féin’s Martin McGuinness said there had been a “step change” in the negotiations, tweeting: “Our team focussed but more to do.” Sinn Féin has resisted the implementation of welfare reforms in Northern Ireland, and a paper it circulated earlier in the week was dismissed by other parties as unrealistic and unaffordable. Negotiators from the five executive parties are continuing their discussions, with UK ministers weighing whether the financial concessions sought can be accommodated. Further meetings are expected in the coming days.

A consumer watchdog report last year found residents suffered unscrupulous, intimidating or criminal behaviour from some site owners and operators. A landmark private member’s bill from Liberal Democrat AM Peter Black has been passed by the Welsh assembly, introducing clear rights and protections for residents of park home sites and setting out responsibilities for site owners. The legislation follows concerns highlighted by Consumer Focus Wales (CFW), which reported widespread problems including high rents, poor maintenance and operators blocking legitimate home sales, leaving some residents thousands of pounds out of pocket. Mr Black said many of Wales’s 96 park home sites are well run, but that under current law there is little protection for residents when disputes arise. “Under the current law there is little protection for residents from unscrupulous park homes site owners, a minority of whom may exploit their position for personal gain,” he said. “Problems can include poor site management and vetoing or deterring legitimate sales. My bill will stop this unfairness. Wales will have a new system that will protect people by bringing in fair, easy-to-use processes and clear rights for both residents and site owners.” The new law applies only to sites where people have permanent homes and excludes holiday parks. Key measures include a “fit and proper” persons test for site owners and a licensing system designed to give homeowners confidence that their site is effectively managed. Site owners who breach their licence conditions could face fines of up to £10,000. Mr Black said the reforms would create accessible avenues to resolve disputes and raise management standards across the sector. The bill is the first private member’s measure to be passed in Cardiff Bay under powers devolved from Westminster in 2011. The British Holiday and Home Parks Association, representing park operators, has argued most site owners are law-abiding and that authorities should focus on enforcing existing laws.

A man who attacked an ambulance while paramedics were inside a nearby house treating a patient has been handed an 18-month community order. Josh Thacker, 24, who lives at the YMCA in Leicester, admitted criminal damage at Leicester Magistrates’ Court following the incident in the Highfields area on 18 January. The court heard Thacker kicked and punched the ambulance and threw projectiles at it as the crew worked. Paramedics, alerted by shouting outside, filmed the incident on a mobile phone from the patient’s window. East Midlands Ambulance Service (EMAS) said the vehicle was taken off the road for six days while repairs were completed, warning that the money spent could have funded lifesaving equipment. “I, once again, find myself saddened and appalled by the mindless actions of an individual,” said Mark Gregory from EMAS. “Our staff work hard every day to deliver the best possible care to the public we serve. Actions like this make their job even harder, not to mention the anxiety they and the patient must have experienced during this attack.” Thacker was ordered to pay compensation as part of his sentence. He also admitted damaging a job centre on 24 November and damaging clothing belonging to a shop on 12 December. In addition, he pleaded guilty to using threatening words or behaviour in a racially aggravated offence on 12 December. EMAS reiterated that assaults on ambulances disrupt critical services and can delay emergency responses.

The explosion had been caused by “irresponsible human error,” the National Petroleum Authority (NPA) said, after a devastating fire erupted at a gas facility near Accra’s Labadi Trade Fair site on Thursday evening. The regulator, which inspected the scene, said a fully loaded gas tanker was discharging Liquid Petroleum Gas (LPG) when two bolts that should have tightened the tanker’s lid were found to be missing, allowing pressure to build dangerously. Witnesses reported hearing a loud bang before seeing flames billowing into the night sky. Injured persons suffered severe burns and were rushed to nearby hospitals for treatment. Several images showing charred bodies were shared across social media, underscoring the ferocity of the blast and intensifying public grief and anger. NPA head Moses Asaga told local radio station Joy FM that “The pressure built up and because the lid was not tight, the pressure was able to force the lid open.” He described the force as “missile-like,” adding that the lid “spewed out 200 meters into the Labadi Trade Fair site and caused the fire.” Local media reported the explosion occurred at about 18:00 local time, and fire officers battled for several hours to bring the blaze under control. A blackout was reported in the area, which houses a national exhibition center and a university, after some electricity cables caught fire. The tragedy has revived concerns about the siting of fuel and gas stations, many of which are located close to residential neighborhoods. In a Facebook post, Ghana’s incoming President Nana Akufo-Addo called for a “second look” at the location of gas stations nationwide and “strict enforcement” of safety regulations to prevent “such avoidable incidents.” President John Dramani Mahama also expressed his condolences to victims via Twitter. Ghana last faced a similar calamity in 2015, when a deadly explosion at a fuel station in Accra claimed more than 150 lives. Thursday’s blast has renewed calls for tougher oversight, improved maintenance protocols, and urgent reforms to protect communities from industrial hazards.

Steve Claridge linked with Salisbury City job as club fights for league place BBC pundit Steve Claridge has been linked with the vacant Salisbury City managerial role as the troubled club seeks both a new boss and confirmation of which division it will play in next season. The 48-year-old, who clocked up more than 1,000 professional appearances during a 24-year playing career, has extensive experience in the dugout and the lower leagues. Salisbury finished 12th in the Conference Premier last term under Mikey Harris but were thrown out of the Football Conference this summer after failing to meet deadlines to pay football creditors. Harris resigned last month to join Portsmouth as youth-team coach, leaving the Whites without a manager as off-field turmoil deepened. A consortium completed a takeover on Friday, ousting former chairman Outail Touzar, and has pledged to stabilise the club’s finances. The new owners plan to appeal for reinstatement into Conference South for the coming campaign while beginning the search for a permanent manager. Claridge began his professional career at Bournemouth in 1984 and later had spells with Aldershot, Cambridge United, Birmingham City, Leicester City, Wolves and Millwall. At Leicester he scored the decisive goal in the 1996 First Division play-off final to secure promotion to the Premier League and netted the winner in the 1997 League Cup final against Middlesbrough. He went on to score 34 goals in three years at Portsmouth and spent four months as Pompey manager between October 2000 and February 2001. Claridge later managed Millwall and Weymouth, returned to semi-professional football in 2007, and most recently played for Gosport Borough, helping them win promotion to the Southern League in 2012.

Paul Hemming has admitted manslaughter but denies murdering his partner, Natalie Hemming, whose body was found in woodland near Chandlers Cross, Hertfordshire, on 22 May. Opening his trial at Luton Crown Court, Hemming told jurors that a heavy ornamental egg made of jade struck the 31-year-old’s head, causing her to fall into a coffee table. He said he then realised she was not breathing. “I couldn’t believe I had done it. I just thought..... I’m in trouble. How am I going to explain it to the kids upstairs? So then I thought I am going to cover this up,” he told the court. Asked why, he replied: “Because I knew I had killed her.” He insisted he had not intended to kill her. Natalie Hemming was last seen alive in Hemel Hempstead on 1 May. The court heard that after her death, Hemming drove her body about 30 miles from the couple’s home in Alderney Avenue, Newton Leys, Milton Keynes, and left it in undergrowth in a wooded area. Jurors have been told the couple’s relationship was strained and that Ms Hemming had told her partner she wanted to leave him for another man. In evidence, Hemming said he was “heartbroken” at the prospect of a split, but he denied being violent towards her shortly before her death. When asked what he was thinking when he threw the £1,000 jade egg, Hemming said: “I have no idea what was in my mind.” He reiterated he had not intended to kill her and entered a plea to manslaughter at the outset of proceedings. The trial continues at Luton Crown Court.

UK Treasury Minister Greg Hands has been criticised for taking a holiday in France as negotiations over the fiscal framework underpinning the new Scotland Bill reach a crucial stage. Mr Hands, the UK government’s chief negotiator, spoke by phone with Scotland’s Deputy First Minister John Swinney about the financial arrangements that will support the legislation, but MPs and MSPs say in-person talks are needed now to secure a deal. Holyrood members have called for an agreement before 23 February to allow time to scrutinise the plans. Despite months of discussions, the deadline for reaching a settlement was pushed back earlier this month amid continuing differences between the UK and Scottish governments. A Treasury spokeswoman said Mr Hands would return “at any time” if the Scottish government was “willing to make a substantial move.” However, First Minister Nicola Sturgeon’s spokesman condemned the timing of the trip. “This beggars belief,” he said. “Having secured an extra week for negotiations, the deputy first minister offered to clear his diary to go to London on Monday and do whatever was required during this week to thrash out a deal. We now find out that the reason a Monday meeting was not agreed to is that the UK government’s chief negotiator has gone on holiday to France – before even having the courtesy to respond to the revised proposal submitted by the Scottish government last week.” He added: “It is time for the UK government to decide if they are really serious about reaching a deal. Otherwise, they will stand accused of breaking their vow.” SNP MP Pete Wishart, who chairs the Scottish Affairs Committee at Westminster, told BBC Scotland it was “ridiculous” for Mr Hands to be away at a “crucial” point in the talks. The Perth and North Perthshire MP said the decision showed a “lack of respect for the process” and urged him to return to the UK. Labour’s shadow secretary of state for Scotland Ian Murray also criticised the move. “It beggars belief that Greg Hands thought he could take a holiday at this crucial stage in the negotiations,” he said. “If the Treasury won’t take this seriously, David Cameron must get involved. Both governments must do whatever it takes for as long as it takes to reach an agreement.” The fiscal framework is central to the implementation of the Scotland Bill, setting out how Scotland’s budget will be adjusted as new tax and welfare powers are devolved. The two governments remain divided over the Smith Commission’s “no detriment” principle, which states that neither the UK nor Scottish budgets should be worse off as a result of the changes. With time running short, pressure is mounting for a breakthrough that satisfies both sides and allows MSPs proper scrutiny before the February deadline.

About 300 people braved sub-zero temperatures in Edinburgh’s Charlotte Square on 15 December for Social Bite’s CEO Sleepout, a mass fundraising event that has surpassed its goal to build a pioneering “homeless village” in the city. A statement posted on Tuesday confirmed the total raised at £564,545, exceeding the original £500,000 target needed to construct 10 purpose‐built homes in Granton. Designed to house up to 20 people, the village will offer stable accommodation alongside intensive wraparound support tailored to help residents rebuild their lives. “The money will not only be put towards the physical build but also towards an intensive support structure for the residents to help them get back on their feet,” Social Bite said, thanking supporters for “making the first steps on that journey.” Participants in the overnight vigil included Olympic cycling legend Sir Chris Hoy, while First Minister Nicola Sturgeon served breakfast to sleepers the following morning. Work on the village is expected to begin early next year, with the first residents moving in by the summer. The project will be operated by Social Bite in partnership with the EDI Group and the City of Edinburgh Council. Founded as a social enterprise tackling homelessness through employment and community initiatives, Social Bite has attracted international attention. Co‐founder Josh Littlejohn received an MBE earlier this month for services to social enterprise and entrepreneurship in Scotland. The organisation’s work has also been championed by high‐profile visitors: Leonardo DiCaprio lunched at Home, Social Bite’s west‐end venture, in November, following George Clooney’s visit to its Rose Street branch a year earlier.

UK services activity accelerated in October, with the Markit/CIPS services PMI rising to 54.5 from 52.6 in September, the highest reading since January and signaling solid expansion at the start of the final quarter of 2016. The survey showed employment rising for the third month in a row, while new business increased at the fastest pace in nine months, with the weaker pound helping to generate new contracts and opportunities. However, firms faced stronger cost pressures, as input prices climbed at the fastest rate since March 2011, reflecting currency-driven import costs and higher supplier charges. “The dominant UK service sector moved up a gear at the start of the final quarter of 2016,” the report said. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at IHS Markit, warned that inflation could temper the outlook: “An encouraging picture of the economy gaining further growth momentum in October is marred by news that inflationary pressures are rising rapidly. The increase in prices threatens to curb both corporate hiring and consumer spending, as firms seek to reduce staff costs and households see their pay eroded.”

Paul Michael Sadler, 35, from Broughton, died in hospital after a collision on the A5104 in Broughton at about 21:30 GMT on Saturday. He passed away in the early hours of Monday, North Wales Police said. A 26-year-old local van driver was arrested after failing a roadside drug swipe test, police said, and has been released on police bail pending the result of further tests. Mr Sadler’s family said they were “completely heartbroken,” in a statement issued by police.

Its service centre in Llanelli will shut as will three job centres at Pyle in Bridgend, Mountain Ash in Rhondda Cynon Taff and Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) is closing its Llanelli service centre alongside job centres in Pyle, Mountain Ash and Tredegar as part of a wider reorganisation in Wales, prompting warnings about the impact on local jobs and services. Plaid Cymru Assembly Member Simon Thomas said the Llanelli decision alone would mean the loss of 146 jobs in the Carmarthenshire town, describing the move as a major blow to the community. Mr Thomas, who represents mid and west Wales, said the closures would have a “huge impact” on Llanelli. “The spin-off in terms of the local economy has been overlooked by the Conservative government in Westminster,” he said. “Once again they look just at the spreadsheet economy, rather than how we can start to re-build our communities after austerity.” The DWP insisted the changes were not about cutting jobs but “delivering a more efficient and modern employment service.” It said all staff affected are being offered the opportunity to relocate to other sites, and those who choose not to move will be offered a redundancy package. The department added that more people now access benefits online, leaving many buildings underused. UK Employment Minister Damian Hinds said: “We will always make sure that people have the support they need to get into and progress within work. These changes reflect the fact that more people access their benefits online resulting in many of our buildings being underused. We’re merging some offices and locating other jobcentres with local authorities to make sure that the welfare state and our employment support works for those who need it and those who pay for it.” However, the PCS union condemned the plan, saying it would “decimate services to the public.” Wales chairwoman Katrine Williams said: “The DWP should not be removing jobs and services from areas of high unemployment and threatening our members with the risk of redundancy. There is a massive amount of work and support that we need to deliver to the public and the best way to do this is with sites and our members based in the local communities.” The DWP said it will continue engaging with staff and unions as the reorganisation proceeds.

Media playback is not supported on this device De Villiers took Rashid Khan for four sixes and a four in his 29-ball 64 to propel the Proteas to 209-5. AB de Villiers unleashed a blistering display of power hitting to ignite South Africa’s ICC World Twenty20 campaign, smashing a 29-ball 64 as the Proteas defeated Afghanistan by 37 runs at the Wankhede Stadium. His assault, highlighted by an over off 17-year-old leg-spinner Rashid Khan that yielded four sixes and a four, transformed South Africa’s innings and set up a formidable 209-5. Afghanistan, buoyed early by the explosive Mohammad Shahzad, were eventually bowled out for 172, with Chris Morris spearheading the defense through figures of 4-27. South Africa, stung by their run-fest defeat to England in their opening match, looked in danger of posting a par score until de Villiers arrived and shifted the momentum decisively. The Proteas plundered 71 runs from the final four overs, propelling them to the sixth-highest total in World T20 history. De Villiers’ takedown of Rashid was among the most destructive in tournament annals, equaling the fourth-most expensive over at a World T20. He followed with another six off the first ball of the next over, sweeping Mohammad Nabi, before holing out at mid-wicket, his job effectively done. Earlier, South Africa’s reshaped attack, with Dale Steyn omitted in favor of David Wiese, had to contend with the unorthodox and fearless Shahzad. The opener swung and swiped his way to 44 off 19 balls, including five sixes—four dispatched over the leg side—as Afghanistan raced to 47-0 after just three overs. The burst brought back memories of England’s brutal chase on the same surface, but Morris checked the surge by bowling Shahzad at the end of the fourth over, a pivotal moment that halted Afghanistan’s charge. From there, South Africa tightened their grip with regular wickets. Kagiso Rabada, Kyle Abbott and Imran Tahir each claimed two, complementing Morris’s aggression and accuracy. Afghanistan’s middle order lost traction under pressure and rising required rates, and despite glimpses of resistance, they were dismissed off the final ball of the innings for 172. Proteas captain Faf du Plessis admitted the early onslaught evoked a sense of déjà vu. “I did feel a little bit of déjà vu when Shehzad was batting. There were some really good shots being played and immediately you’re under pressure in the field. Chris Morris stood up for us and gave us a bit of aggression. Once again our batting was really solid, but our extras let us down and that’s why we let teams get closer than they should. I think we’re going to a different continent for the next game, so obviously that means a change of strategy.” Afghanistan captain Asghar Stanikzai praised the pitch but conceded his side lacked the experience to defend such a target. “The wicket was good for batting. We lack experienced bowlers and their total was a bit high for us. Shehzad started very well, but we lost his wicket very early.” With Group 1 potentially set to hinge on net run-rate, South Africa still have challenging fixtures against West Indies and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan, the only non-Test nation remaining in the tournament, will be eliminated if they lose to England on Wednesday, though they once again showed they can compete at this level.

Mr Brokenshire said he will brief politicians and business leaders in the United States on the political situation in Northern Ireland. He is expected to hold bilateral meetings with senior political figures. These will include Conrad Tribble of the US State Department and the US vice-president's national security advisor Andrea Thompson. Former US Senator George Mitchell and various members of Congress will also be updated on the government's priorities in Northern Ireland. Mr Brokenshire will travel to Washington amid an ongoing political stalemate in Northern Ireland, where devolved government has not been functioning since January. The power-sharing executive, led by the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and Sinn Féin, collapsed following a controversy over a green energy scheme, triggering months of deadlock. Speaking ahead of the trip, Mr Brokenshire described the visit as taking place “against a backdrop of political stalemate in Northern Ireland,” but called it a “timely opportunity to brief members of the US administration, who throughout history have done so much to support our efforts in moving forward the political process, on the current situation.” He added: “I also want to reassure them that the UK government is determined to see devolved, power-sharing government restored.” In addition to political discussions, Mr Brokenshire said he will underline the “continued need for strong foreign direct investment” into Northern Ireland and “offer reassurance on current issues including the UK’s exit from the European Union.” During a reception at the Northern Ireland Bureau in Washington on Monday evening, he is expected to “praise the expertise and capabilities of Northern Ireland firms.” The meetings with US officials and lawmakers are intended to sustain American engagement with Northern Ireland’s peace and economic priorities while efforts continue to break the impasse at Stormont.

The National Executive Committee (NEC) has voted to include representatives of Labour leaders in the two nations. Labour’s National Executive Committee has backed a plan to give the Scottish and Welsh parties formal seats on the NEC as part of a wider devolution package, setting up a key vote at the party’s annual conference in Liverpool on Tuesday. The reforms would hand Scottish and Welsh Labour greater autonomy over issues including Westminster candidate selection, disciplinary matters, and the election of their respective leaders, while ensuring direct representation at the top of the UK party. Allies of Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn have opposed the move in its current form, arguing that any Welsh and Scottish NEC representatives should be elected by members rather than appointed by party leaders. However, sources said Welsh First Minister Carwyn Jones delivered a “powerful address” to the NEC on Monday, urging members not to “let Wales down” and to resist attempts to “water down” the package. He told the committee that Welsh Labour is the party’s most successful arm, having governed Wales continuously since devolution in 1999, and said the reforms would counter nationalist claims that Welsh Labour functions merely as a “branch” of the UK party. In an interview with BBC Wales, Mr Corbyn said he was open to the idea of a Welsh member sitting on the NEC. “I’m not resistant to the idea of there being a Welsh member of the NEC at all,” he said. “What I want to do is have agreement within the party about how the nomination should take place to the NEC so it enjoys the confidence of the executive and so on in Wales.” Scottish Labour leader Kezia Dugdale said the proposals would be presented to conference as agreed. “Exactly what we agreed yesterday is exactly what is happening tomorrow in a vote on the conference floor,” she told the BBC. She added that the reforms are clear: the leaders of the Scottish and Welsh parties would either take the NEC seat themselves or nominate someone to fill it, mirroring how Mr Corbyn nominates members of the shadow cabinet who sit on the NEC. Not all NEC members were persuaded. Darren Williams, a Cardiff councillor who sits on the committee, told BBC Wales he had voted against the plan, preferring that the Welsh representative be elected by rank-and-file members. The conference vote will determine whether the devolution package is adopted in full.

A man was executed by firing squad in Jamame, Lower Juba, after pleading guilty in a Sharia court run by al-Shabab, witnesses said. The BBC Somali Service reported that the group has previously killed alleged spies and apostates. The execution underscores the militants’ grip on parts of rural Somalia, even as African Union and Kenyan forces press their offensive to reclaim territory. Last month al‐Shabab carried out a massacre at Garissa University College in neighboring Kenya, killing 148 people. The Islamists have waged an insurgency against Somalia’s internationally backed government for nearly a decade, using courts and public punishments to enforce their interpretation of Islamic law. In response to cross-border raids, Kenya has begun constructing a barrier along the Somali frontier to deter incursions. Despite military setbacks, al‐Shabab retains the capacity to mount deadly attacks.

A Commons committee has urged sweeping changes to boost voter turnout, drawing lessons from Scotland’s 2014 independence referendum, which achieved an 85% participation rate. The political and constitutional reform committee says the sense that every ballot mattered in Scotland drove engagement, and is calling for measures to replicate that motivation across UK elections. Its report backs extending the franchise to 16- and 17-year-olds in all polls, piloting online voting in the next Parliament, and allowing same-day voter registration, so citizens can sign up on polling day. To further remove barriers, the committee recommends making election day a public holiday. MPs warn that turnout has drifted downward in recent elections and argue that modernization and accessibility reforms are overdue. They say action is needed to ensure every vote counts, and urge support to implement changes ahead of future contests.

US stocks rebounded Friday, broad-based gains after midweek selloff; S&P +0.68% to 2,381.73; Dow +0.69% to 20,804.84; Nasdaq +0.47% to 6,083.70. Rally buoyed by industrials and blue chips: Deere +7% after fiscal Q2 results; net sales $5.8bn up 1%; full-year sales seen rising 9%, aided by 20% jump in South America farm equipment; optimism spread to Caterpillar +2.2%. Dow components Chevron and Walmart added support. Campbell Soup -2% on disappointing quarter; warned full-year sales could fall. The advance followed a volatile week as investors reassessed the policy outlook amid growing political scrutiny of President Trump. On Wednesday, S&P and Dow suffered their biggest single-day drops since September after the dismissal of FBI Director James Comey and reports the president sought to influence the Russia probe, sparking impeachment talk. Despite lingering uncertainty, equities remain higher in recent months on expectations for business-friendly tax and regulatory reform. Traders said Friday’s bounce reflected bargain-hunting and relief that earnings and outlooks from companies continue to underpin the expansion. Market participants will watch Washington developments and economic data for clues to the trajectory of growth and corporate profits in the weeks ahead. Analysts said the week’s sharp swings underscored how sensitive markets remain to policy progress in Washington. While corporate earnings have largely beaten expectations, investors are weighing whether reforms on taxes, infrastructure and deregulation will arrive fast enough to sustain the rally.

Talks raise hopes for revival of historic Vale of Glamorgan funfair Worcestershire-based fairground operator Henry Danter has held talks this week with the site’s owners and the Vale of Glamorgan council, raising hopes that the historic seaside attraction could be restored and enhanced after years of uncertainty. The council said it wanted the site to continue to be used “and enhanced” for leisure purposes, underscoring ambitions to secure a future that preserves its character while improving facilities. The fair has been a draw since 1920, recording a remarkable 400,000 visitors over a bank holiday at its peak in 1934. In recent years it found renewed fame through the TV comedy Gavin and Stacey, after featuring in the BBC show. However, the attraction has struggled since the closure of the nearby Butlins holiday camp 18 years ago, a blow that reduced footfall and led to prolonged decline. Two years ago, an application was submitted proposing restaurants, a cinema, a bowling alley and 124 flats on the site. Senior councillors have since stressed their determination to retain a “vibrant fairground” at the heart of any redevelopment, and have been helping to bring together the owners, Hilco, and businessman Ian Rogers with an investor to advance plans. Progress has been “at times frustrating” and “slow,” councillors admitted last month, as the site deteriorated and became an eyesore. Debris blown from the funfair temporarily closed surrounding roads, prompting renewed scrutiny. Officials described it as “puzzling” that the first phase of the most recent plans mostly involved housing. “We have made it clear to the applicant on several occasions that any redevelopment has to have regard to the future use of the funfair site,” said Rob Thomas, director of development services. “To this end, how and when the funfair site is brought forward is of utmost importance, and these are discussions that we continue to progress.” Danter, who runs the Treasure Island fairground in Stourport-on-Severn, visited the fair as a child and brings 50 years of fairground experience to the talks. His involvement is seen as a positive step toward safeguarding the site’s leisure legacy.

Leeds United midfielder Liam Bridcutt made 27 appearances last season after joining on loan from Sunderland in November. The 27-year-old moved to Sunderland from Brighton for £3m in January 2014 but featured only 30 times in the Premier League for the Black Cats. A Scotland international, Bridcutt debuted against Serbia in 2013 and won his second cap in a 1-0 win over Denmark in March. Follow all the latest football transfers and deals on our dedicated page.

**Ceasefire Extended as Pakistan and TTP Hold First Direct Talks, Despite Skepticism** Local media reported that a temporary ceasefire between the Pakistani government and the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) has been extended, though neither side has officially confirmed the agreement. The talks, the first direct contact between the two parties since peace efforts began last month, took place in an area near the Afghan border, where a delegation of four Pakistani officials traveled by helicopter to meet with militant representatives. The TTP, which has waged a deadly insurgency across Pakistan since 2007, remains a major challenge for Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif’s administration, which has faced growing pressure to end the conflict. The BBC’s Shumaila Jaffery in Lahore noted that Sharif, under domestic political strain, is seeking to avoid further military escalation that could fuel violence. However, many in Pakistan remain skeptical, fearing the talks may only buy time for militants to regroup. Previous attempts at dialogue with the TTP have collapsed, and analysts argue the group’s rejection of Pakistan’s constitution and its demand for a strict Islamic system make a lasting deal improbable. The TTP’s fractious internal factions further complicate negotiations. Sharif has publicly endorsed peaceful resolution but warned that stronger military action could follow if talks fail. Critics accuse his government of lacking a coherent strategy to counter the militants, whose attacks have claimed thousands of lives. Observers also question whether the ceasefire, if real, reflects genuine intent or tactical maneuvering. With past agreements unraveling swiftly, public trust in the peace process remains fragile. For now, the lack of official confirmation from either side underscores the precariousness of the situation, as Pakistan grapples with balancing hope for peace and the specter of renewed violence.

**Senator Thom Tillis Defends Deregulation Stance Amid Controversy** U.S. Senator Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) sparked debate on Monday during a speech criticizing federal regulations, arguing businesses should be free to decide how to comply—or not—with certain rules. The newly elected lawmaker contended that marketplace forces, rather than government mandates, should govern practices like food safety. “If a restaurant didn’t require handwashing and it led to illness, they’d go out of business. That’s how it works,” Tillis said, using the example to advocate for reducing regulatory burdens. However, he acknowledged the need for transparency, suggesting such establishments could be required to post prominent signs notifying customers of lax practices—a move critics argue still constitutes regulation. When questioned later at the U.S. Capitol, Tillis defended his stance, telling the Associated Press, “Sometimes we set a direction but let those regulated decide if it makes sense. They might pay a huge price, but they get to make that decision versus the government.” His remarks come amid growing GOP skepticism toward mandates, including vaccine requirements. At least two Republican presidential hopefuls have argued parents should be allowed to bypass school vaccine rules, even during a measles outbreak. Tillis’s comments have reignited discussions about balancing public health and regulatory freedom, with critics warning that such policies could endanger communities. Tillis’s position reflects a broader conservative push to roll back federal oversight, though public health experts emphasize the risks of minimizing safety standards. The debate underscores deepening partisan divides over the role of government in protecting public welfare.

**Man Found Guilty in Stabbing Death of 26-Year-Old After Attempt to Halt Fight** A 26-year-old man has died after being stabbed in the chest following a violent altercation in Eccles, Greater Manchester, on 29 August. Wesley Lennon, of Winton, was attempting to intervene in a dispute between two groups when he was targeted and attacked in Cambrai Crescent. Adam Akhtar, 19, of Somerset Road, was found guilty of murder at Manchester Crown Court. He was sentenced to a minimum of 18 years in prison and received an additional 12-month concurrent sentence for possession of an offensive weapon. Akhtar denied the charge but was convicted after police revealed he had rushed to aid his friends, stabbing Lennon before fleeing the scene shortly before midnight. Greater Manchester Police stated the fight began around midnight, with Lennon’s fatal injury occurring as he tried to de-escalate tensions. Detective Chief Inspector Richard Eales condemned the attack, stating, “This is a terrible incident where a young man has lost his life after he tried to do the right thing and stop an escalating and violent fight.” The court heard that Lennon’s actions were in an effort to prevent further harm, underscoring the tragedy of a life lost while attempting to protect others.

**Miami Medical Centre Hit by Unusual Ransomware Attack** A Miami-based medical clinic is grappling with a rare cyberattack that has left its systems locked and its data encrypted, with hackers demanding 4,000 Australian dollars (approximately $4,200 or £2,610) for the decryption key. The Miami Family Medical Centre has ruled out a virus as the cause, instead suggesting that attackers directly hacked into their server—a tactic experts describe as unprecedented in ransomware cases. David Wood, co-owner of the clinic, told ABC News in Australia that while standard antivirus protections were in place, “there’s no sign of a virus. They literally got in, hijacked the server, and then ran their encryption software.” The breach has exposed sensitive patient data, including confidential medical records, leaving the clinic in a precarious position as it works to resolve the crisis. Most ransomware attacks typically involve malware—such as a phishing email attachment or malicious link—that infiltrates a system and encrypts files. Rik Ferguson, a security expert at Trend Micro, explained to the BBC that such attacks often display fake messages from authorities, accusing victims of possessing illegal content and demanding small fines for “unblocking” their devices. “People pay because they’re embarrassed or it’s more convenient,” he said. However, the Miami case defies this pattern. “Ransomware itself has become a common tool for cybercriminals, but it does have a malware front end. You click a link and an infection encrypts your data,” Ferguson noted. He described the clinic’s claim of a direct hack as “unusual” and “the first time I’ve heard of that happening.” Cybercriminals based in Russia and former Soviet states are frequently linked to such attacks, he added, though the perpetrators in this case remain unidentified. Security professionals are divided on how to respond. Nigel Phair, an Australian cybersecurity expert, told ABC that paying the ransom might be the clinic’s only option at this stage. “Though it’s not the best option, because as we know from extortion, once you pay, they’ll follow up,” he warned. Ferguson emphasized the need for robust data security, urging organizations to store sensitive information offline and use encrypted backups. “A lot of stuff does need to be connected online, but you would only need to have your front-end server directly connected,” he said. As IT teams race to recover the clinic’s data without compromising further, the incident highlights the evolving tactics of cybercriminals—and the urgent need for vigilance in an era where digital threats are increasingly sophisticated. For the Miami Family Medical Centre, the stakes are both financial and reputational, with patient trust hanging in the balance.

**U.S.-China Tensions Escalate Over Taiwan and South China Sea Amid Trump’s Policies** BEIJING — A Chinese official has warned that continued U.S. interference in cross-strait relations could derail U.S.-China ties and destabilize the Taiwan Strait. The comments came as growing concerns mount over President-elect Donald Trump’s stance on the “One China” policy, a cornerstone of diplomatic relations between the two nations. An Fengshan, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, stated on Wednesday that upholding the “One China” principle is the “political basis” for peaceful U.S.-China relations and regional stability. “If this foundation is interfered with or damaged, the healthy, stable development of China-U.S. relations is out of the question,” he said, adding that the Taiwan Strait’s peace could be “seriously impacted.” The remarks follow recent tensions sparked by Trump’s public actions regarding Taiwan. The incoming U.S. leader, who has expressed skepticism about the policy, took a controversial phone call from Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and later tweeted about the conversation—a move China condemned as a breach of diplomatic norms. In a statement on Monday, China said it was “seriously concerned” by Trump’s actions and urged “sensitivity” on the issue. The “One China” policy, upheld by the U.S. government, acknowledges Taiwan as part of China but maintains unofficial ties with the island. However, Trump’s rhetoric and interactions with Taiwan’s leadership have alarmed Beijing, which views any U.S. support for Taiwanese independence as a direct threat. **England Fans Face FA Sanctions After WWII Chants at Dortmund Match** Some England fans booed Germany’s national anthem and sang WWII-era chants during the 1-0 defeat in Dortmund, prompting condemnation from FA chairman Greg Clarke, who called the behavior “disrespectful and disappointing.” The FA confirmed investigations into the disturbances, with 34 members under scrutiny. Twelve individuals have already been suspended from the England Supporters’ Travel Club, and the UK Football Policing Unit is pursuing potential football banning orders. The FA stated it is collaborating with authorities to hold offenders accountable, emphasizing its commitment to “upholding the values of the game.” The incident has reignited debates over fan conduct in international football.

**Paris Fashion Week Shines with Tributes, Controversies, and Celebrity Appearances** Paris Fashion Week unfolded as a whirlwind of creativity, controversy, and celebrity flair, blending artistic expression with activism and high-profile drama. Among the standout moments was Stella McCartney’s poignant tribute to the late George Michael during her autumn/winter collection debut. Models strutted down the runway to a reimagined version of his hit “Faith,” ending with a choreographed dance that had audience members—including McCartney’s sister, Mary—rising to join the rhythm. Meanwhile, animal rights advocates disrupted the fashion frenzy. Three women in animal masks staged a protest near the Eiffel Tower, holding signs reading “I am not leather,” “I am not wool,” and “I am not fur” as part of Peta’s campaign against fur use. The demonstration underscored growing ethical scrutiny of the industry. Balenciaga faced backlash after firing its casting agency amid allegations of mistreatment. The agency was accused of leaving 150 models stranded for three hours without food or bathroom access. Prominent casting director James Scully highlighted the “sadistic and cruel” conditions on social media, shifting focus from the brand’s rubber-car-mat-inspired skirts. British designer Clare Waight Keller closed her five-year tenure at Chloe with a nostalgic final collection, sparking speculation about her rumored move to Givenchy. Meanwhile, pop culture dominated headlines when rapper Nicki Minaj stole the show at Haider Ackermann’s presentation. Her daring ensemble—leaving her left breast exposed save for a small silver detail—outshone the catwalk designs. Rihanna continued her Fenty x Puma collaboration with a vibrant, school-inspired collection unveiled at France’s National Library. The third installment in the line celebrated youth culture with bold colors and eclectic styles. Chanel’s space-themed showcase, however, captivated audiences with a towering rocket at the Grand Palais. Under Karl Lagerfeld’s visionary direction, models in sci-fi-inspired designs walked under the iconic rocket, while Lagerfeld himself brought his godson, Hudson Kroenig, to the front row. Paris Fashion Week proved a dynamic mix of art, activism, and A-list presence, leaving a lasting impression long after the final show.
