**Lost Mother’s Letter Reunited with Daughter 21 Years Later** Bethany Gash, now 21, never imagined she would see the heartfelt letter from her late mother again—until a second-hand bookshop owner tracked her down. The touching message, written in 2001 and tucked inside a book that vanished during a house move, was discovered this week by Gordon Draper of Bondgate Books in Bishop Auckland. The letter, addressed to Bethany, contains a poignant message from her mother, Lisa, who passed away when Bethany was just a toddler. In it, Lisa writes, “If your dad is reading this to you, it is because I have died and gone to heaven..... Don’t forget me because I’ll always be your mam.” The envelope also holds a cherished photograph of Bethany sitting on her mother’s knee. “When I found it, I just had to do something,” Mr. Draper said. After learning Bethany lived nearby, he contacted BBC Tees, which facilitated their reunion. “I can’t emphasise how pleased I am,” he added, expressing his awe at the serendipity. For Bethany, the letter is irreplaceable. “It’s absolutely overwhelming considering something so small can mean so much to someone,” she said, acknowledging the letter’s emotional weight. Though she suspected the book was lost during a move, she admits she “never actually acted upon that” feeling. Ms. Gash recalls her father reading the letter to her after Lisa’s death, a moment etched in her memory. “A lot of people would just disregard it as something stupid, just a little old letter,” Bethany noted. “But it meant absolutely the world.” The bond between mother and daughter, preserved in the letter’s words and photo, has been restored—a testament to love that transcends time. As Bethany reflects, the reunion is a reminder of how even small acts of kindness can bridge the past and present.

**Allen Concedes Unfair Result as Higgins Stages Stunning Comeback** Northern Irish snooker star Mark Allen, 31, faced a brutal lesson in consistency as four-time world champion John Higgins stormed back from a deficit to clinch a 13-9 victory in a dramatic World Open semi-final showdown. Allen, who led 5-3 after a dazzling first session highlighted by three century breaks, found himself outmaneuvered in Saturday’s morning session, where Higgins reeled off six frames in eight to seize control. The world number 11, known for his flair and precision, later admitted the result “wasn’t a fair reflection” of the match but bore little hope of redemption once Higgins shifted into his dominant form. Allen’s initial brilliance on Friday set the tone, with the Northern Irishman showcasing his trademark aggression and tactical prowess to build a two-frame advantage. However, Higgins, 46, capitalized on Allen’s uncharacteristic lapses in concentration during the second session, leveraging his experience and composure to extend his lead to 9-7. “John played really well himself,” Allen conceded, quick to acknowledge his rival’s brilliance. “He closed out the match the way you’d expect John Higgins to do.” The momentum briefly shifted in Allen’s favor during the final session, as he won the first frame to narrow the gap to 9-8. But a pivotal moment arrived in the next frame, where a disruptive ball “kick” while Allen was on a 58-break sequence handed Higgins a crucial second frame, silencing the hosts’ hopes. Allen later lamented the moment, stating, “I felt like I really played well in spells but a couple of things went against me.” Beyond the table, Allen pinpointed his own preparation as the root of the setback. Admitting he began training at 12 p.m. for a 10 a.m. match—a stark contrast to his usual leisurely morning routine—he acknowledged the mismatch between his habits and the tournament demands. “I don’t prepare properly for these tournaments,” he said. “I just wasn’t prepared for a 10 o’clock match.” When asked if he would adjust his schedule in the future, Allen shrugged: “Probably not.” The defeat comes as Allen continues his broader efforts to refine his game, including a fitness-focused regimen to shed weight. Since the Masters, he has lost 1.5 stone, with a target of seven remaining. “I’ve got to keep working hard,” he said, though the absence of former coach Terry Griffiths, who declined to resume their collaboration, adds another layer of challenge. “That’s a hard one for me,” Allen added, reflecting on the fractured partnership. Despite the setback, Allen remains undeterred, buoyed by his three ranking titles in a 12-year career and the knowledge that Higgins’ triumph, while authoritative, did not define the entirety of the contest. “I think 13-9 wasn’t really a fair reflection,” he insisted. As he turns his focus to future challenges, the lessons of this gritty battle—both on and off the table—will linger.

**Astoria Deploys Fake Orca to Scare Sea Lions Amid Job Crisis** Astoria, Oregon—City officials have turned to a 32-foot fiberglass orca in a last-ditch effort to drive sea lions away from the port, as the marine animals threaten the city’s fishing-dependent economy. The decoy, borrowed from a whale-watching business in Washington state, arrived in the coastal city after other methods—electric mats, colorful beach balls, and loud noises—failed to deter the growing sea lion population. The fake orca, intended to mimic a natural predator and scare the sea lions off, faced immediate setbacks when its motor flooded on Thursday, halting the first deployment. Authorities plan to retry the tactic Friday, calling the measure a “desperate but necessary” response to a crisis that jeopardizes thousands of local jobs. “This is a sign of how far we’re willing to go,” said Jim Knight, Port of Astoria Executive Director, in a press statement. “We simply lack the funds to build physical barriers. Every option must be on the table.” The sea lions, which congregate near fishing docks, disrupt commercial and recreational operations vital to Astoria’s 10,000 residents. Knight emphasized that their presence risks “crippling” the city’s economy, with hundreds of workers depending on seasonal fishing activities. The fiberglass orca, transported overland from Washington, marks a creative, low-cost solution amid budget constraints. Previous tactics, including bright lights and sonic devices, proved ineffective as the sea lions ignored them. If the revised strategy succeeds, officials hope to restore order to the docks by September, when fishing seasons peak. “Time is not on our side,” Knight added. The city remains hopeful the orca will act as a temporary fix while long-term solutions are explored. For now, residents await the outcome of Friday’s second attempt, bracing for yet another twist in the battle for Astoria’s future.

**Two Charged with Murder After 81-Year-Old Man Killed in Rotherham** Rotherham community members mourn the death of Mushin Ahmed, 81, who was fatally attacked near Fitzwilliam Road on 10 August. Damien Hunt, 29, of Doncaster Road, and Dale Jones, 29, of East Bawtry Road, have been charged with murder and remanded in custody. They are scheduled to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on 20 November. In a heartfelt statement following Mr. Ahmed’s funeral, his family described him as a “gentle, loving, and friendly” man who cherished community bonds. They expressed gratitude for the “overwhelming support” from locals and beyond during their grief. The family emphasized their desire to transform their loss into positivity, urging efforts to prevent other families from enduring similar pain. “Mushin would have wanted something positive to come out of our grief,” they said, highlighting the community’s unity in mourning their “husband, father, and friend.” The attack has sparked outrage, with residents calling for justice. Police confirmed ongoing investigations into the incident, which remains under scrutiny. The court case will proceed in November, as the community grapples with the tragedy and honors Mr. Ahmed’s legacy of kindness.

**European Banks Propose New Security Measures for Online Transactions Over €10, Sparking Industry Concerns** The European Banking Authority (EBA) has proposed new rules requiring consumers to enter passwords or one-time codes for online transactions exceeding €10 (£8.50), aiming to curb fraud while balancing convenience. However, the plan has drawn sharp criticism from payment giants, banks, and retailers, who warn it could disrupt e-commerce and harm digital shopping habits. Under the proposed regulations, shoppers would need to verify payments above €10 through multi-factor authentication, such as entering a password, a one-time code sent to a mobile device, or another form of identity check. The EBA described the move as a “difficult trade-off” to enhance security in retail payments, but critics argue it risks frustrating consumers and stifling online commerce. Visa has labeled the rules “catastrophic,” highlighting the potential disruption to seamless shopping experiences, particularly during peak periods like Black Friday, which begins this week. The company noted that “express checkouts”—such as one-click payments and automatic app transactions—now account for half of Europe’s e-commerce sales. Blocking these for transactions over €10 could significantly dampen online activity, with the UK hit hardest due to its high levels of digital shopping and reliance on e-commerce for economic growth. Kevin Jenkins, managing director of Visa UK and Ireland, stressed the gravity of the issue: “We do not normally take such a strong position on regulation. It’s just that in this particular instance, we feel so strongly that the risk of rushing into legislation..... is catastrophic.” Visa’s chief risk officer for Europe, Peter Bayley, added there was no evidence the added friction would reduce fraud, suggesting the rules could force the sector “back 10 or 15 years.” MasterCard and PayPal have also raised concerns. MasterCard criticized the “overly prescriptive approach” of mandating specific security measures, arguing it might undermine the regulator’s goal of reducing fraud. PayPal warned that “unfriendly” security checks would negatively affect most digital payments, regardless of actual risk. The proposal forms part of the European Commission’s updated Payment Services Directive (PSD2), aimed at modernizing financial services and enhancing consumer protection. However, industry experts like Tim Richards of Consult Hyperion note the focus on the €10 threshold has dominated consultations, with UK banks and payment firms actively pushing back. “They do not think this is something they can ignore,” Richards said. The EBA is now reviewing feedback, with final technical standards expected by early 2018. If approved, the rules would take effect months before the UK’s planned exit from the EU, adding urgency to the debate. While the EBA insists it is striving for the “right balance” between security and convenience, stakeholders warn that overly rigid measures could undermine the very goals of fostering trust

Shane Geraghty’s early penalty put the visitors ahead, but a 10-point halftime burst from Armand Batlle and Nigel Hunt’s tries shifted momentum, with Grenoble leading 21-6 at the break. Charl McLeod’s second-half try and 13 points from Jonathan Wisniewski’s boot sealed the win, despite late consolation tries from Dom Waldouck and Alex Lewington for the Irish. London Irish, who rested 11 players following their Premiership win over Newcastle, now trail second-placed Edinburgh by five points in the pool, with their fate resting on a final showdown against Agen. **Macy’s Announces Major Restructuring: Job Cuts, Store Closures Amid Sales Decline** Macy’s Inc., the U.S.’s largest department store chain, is undergoing a significant restructuring plan, impacting 3,000 jobs and closing 36 stores by early spring. The company revealed that approximately half of the affected employees will be repositioned within the company, while 600 roles will vanish from back-office operations and 750 jobs will be lost due to the closure of a call center. Same-store sales, a key metric for retailers, are now projected to decline 2.7% for the year ending January 2025—worsening from the initially predicted 2.2% drop. “In light of our disappointing 2015 sales and earnings performance, we are making adjustments to become more efficient and productive,” said CEO Terry J. Lundgren in a statement. “In some cases, there will be short-term pain as we tighten our belt and realign our resources.” The struggling retail giant cited a combination of factors for its poor performance during the winter holiday season, including a strong U.S. dollar, reduced tourist spending, unseasonably warm weather, and an inventory surplus. Consumer behavior shifts also played a role, with shoppers prioritizing travel and electronics over discretionary purchases like apparel and cosmetics. Additionally, competition from e-commerce behemoths like Amazon and discount retailers such as TJ Maxx has intensified pressure on the company. Macy’s, which operates the upscale Bloomingdale’s chain, aims to save $400 million through these cuts and closures. Last year, the company announced plans to shutter 40 stores in early 2015. Shares rose over 3% in after-hours trading as investors reacted positively to the cost-saving measures. The restructuring underscores the broader challenges facing traditional retailers in an era of shifting consumer preferences and digital disruption. While the short-term pain is evident, Macy’s is betting on long-term operational efficiency to stabilize its market position.

The accused, a 22-year-old man from Cairns, was arrested after a road trip through Queensland’s outback, which police said spanned from February 3 to March 5, contrary to earlier reports of a two-month period. The woman, originally from Liverpool in the UK, met the accused at a Cairns party on January 27, according to police. Their relationship allegedly soured, leading to a month-long period of abuse. Police intercepted the vehicle shortly after, finding the accused hiding in the back when arrested. Charges against the man include four counts of rape, eight of assault, four of strangulation, and two counts of depriving the woman of liberty, alongside lesser offenses such as drug possession and obstructing police. As the legal process unfolds, the incident serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of domestic abuse and the challenges of tracking crimes in remote areas. **Migrant Discovery at Rugby Service Station Sparks Police and Border Force Response** Rugby, Warwickshire — A dramatic scene unfolded at Mangrove Service Station on the A45 London Road after a group of individuals were discovered inside a refrigerated lorry, prompting a multi-agency response. Police confirmed that three of the individuals required medical treatment for suspected heat exhaustion and were transported to University Hospital Coventry and Warwickshire. The remaining migrants, whose nationality is suspected to be Middle Eastern, were taken into custody, while the incident has been referred to Border Force for further investigation. Warwickshire Police described the vehicle as an “overseas lorry,” with officers and forensic teams meticulously inspecting approximately 100 square boxes removed from the trailer. The lorry, believed to be of Romanian origin, was parked near the service station amid a chaotic scene. Authorities closed the A45 Westbound between the M45 and the A4071 for several hours, later reopening the road after the operation was completed. Lorry driver Will Fry, who witnessed the operation, told the BBC that he noticed “a large number of police cars, ambulances, and officers” as he approached the service station. He described seeing the men “wrapped in blankets and silver foil,” with some appearing visibly unwell. “The fridge lorry’s freight was strewn across the floor,” Fry said, noting the presence of bearded individuals who appeared to be in distress. Tunde Kosa, a hotel worker at the nearby Travelodge Rugby Dunchurch Hotel, confirmed encountering police outside the premises upon arrival for her shift. “It was an unusual sight, but the hotel wasn’t affected by the closure,” she said. West Midlands Ambulance Service confirmed paramedics treated the three men for heat-related symptoms at the scene before their hospitalization. A Border Force spokesperson declined further comment, citing ongoing investigations. The incident has raised concerns about smuggling operations using refrigerated vehicles, a method previously reported across Europe. Warwickshire Police have urged the public to remain vigilant and report suspicious activity. As authorities continue to examine evidence, the lorry’s origin and the migrants’ route remain under scrutiny. This event underscores the challenges faced by UK law enforcement in combating irregular migration, particularly along key transport routes like the A45. No further details about the migrants’ condition or immigration status have been released.

**British Transport Police Partner with Unions to Curb Anti-Social Behavior on Trains** The British Transport Police (BTP) has collaborated with the RMT union and train operators to address rising concerns over alcohol-fuelled anti-social behavior on rail services. Officers patrolled 350 trains across key routes from Aberdeen, Inverness, Dundee, Glasgow, Edinburgh, and Newcastle, monitoring over 2,000 workers, including offshore personnel. BTP reported a "noticeable improvement" in conduct following the initiative. Sgt Ashley Forbes highlighted that warnings issued by BTP and operators appeared to have been "heeded," but emphasized the force would maintain vigilance. "High-visibility patrols at stations and on trains will continue," she said, adding that collaboration with industry partners remains critical. The effort aims to ensure safe travel for passengers and staff, including RMT members, who often face disruptive behavior from offshore workers traveling to and from employment. BTP reiterated that anti-social conduct, particularly involving alcohol, will not be tolerated, underscoring ongoing partnerships to uphold safety across the rail network.

**Malaysian Police Detain Kosovo Hacker Linked to IS Data Breach** Malaysian authorities have arrested a 20s-year-old man suspected of hacking a U.S. company and sharing sensitive data with Islamic State (IS) operatives. Identified by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) as Ardit Ferizi, known online as “Th3Dir3ctorY,” he is believed to lead the hacker group Kosova Hacker’s Security (KHS). Ferizi, a Kosovo national, will face extradition to the U.S. to stand trial for computer hacking and identity theft, charges that could result in a 35-year prison sentence. According to a U.S. DOJ statement, Ferizi infiltrated a U.S. company’s systems

**Worcester Warriors Strengthen Squad with Phil Dowson and Carl Kirwan Signings** Worcester Warriors have bolstered their squad ahead of the 2024 season, securing the signing of Northampton Saints’ experienced flanker Phil Dowson and agreeing a deal for London Welsh’s Carl Kirwan to join in the summer. The moves mark a pivotal step in Dean Ryan’s ambitious plans to build a competitive side for sustained success. Dowson, 33, brings over six years of experience at Franklin’s Gardens, where he made 179 appearances and earned seven England caps. Despite recently expressing hopes of extending his stay with Saints, the former Newcastle and England forward will now play a central role in Warriors’ evolution. Ryan praised Dowson’s leadership, highlighting his ability to “influence successful environments” and drive the development of Worcester’s youthful squad. “To attract a player of Phil’s calibre is a huge coup,” Ryan said, emphasizing the club’s commitment to progressing “season after season.” Alongside Dowson, Warriors have secured the services of Carl Kirwan, who joined London Welsh from Rotherham in 2013 and played a key role in their Championship promotion last season, scoring eight tries. Kirwan, who previously balanced rugby with a scaffolding job in the North Sea, had evaded Worcester’s advances the previous year. Ryan admitted the club’s renewed pursuit was successful this time, with Kirwan adding “balance” to their growing ambitions. Worcester, currently top of the Championship, have won 13 of their 14 league matches this season, one point ahead of Bristol. Ryan hinted at further arrivals, stating: “We have others to come and we’re really excited about where we’re heading.” The dual signings underline Warriors’ determination to bridge the gap between the Championship and Premiership, with Dowson and Kirwan set to anchor a side poised for a bold push in 2024.

**Man Granted Bail Over Alleged IRA-Related Speech Faces Strict Court Conditions** Damien “Dee” Fennell, a 33-year-old activist from north Belfast’s Ardoyne area, has been granted bail following his arrest over allegations of inviting support for a proscribed organization, but is subject to stringent conditions including a ban on public speaking and internet activity. The decision was made at the High Court in Belfast on Wednesday, after Fennell agreed to adhere to all court-imposed restrictions. The charges stem from a speech Fennell delivered at a 1916 commemoration event in St Colman’s graveyard, Lurgan, County Armagh, on Easter Sunday. The address, which was recorded and later removed from the internet after media reports of an investigation, reportedly referenced the IRA’s armed struggle and included a remark about a “British micro-minister” attending the same location—a comment prosecutors claim alludes to a Sinn Féin minister at Stormont. During police interviews, Fennell’s lawyer read a prepared statement denying any encouragement of terrorism, emphasizing that comments about the IRA were expressed as personal opinions. However, prosecutors argued that the speech “invited support” for a banned group, noting that a handwritten copy of the speech was recovered behind a kitchen microwave during a search of Fennell’s home on April 20. Fennell, a prominent figure in the Greater Ardoyne Residents Collective, which campaigns against Orange Order marches, appeared via video-link from prison to answer questions about bail. The judge asked whether he would comply with release conditions and attend future court dates. Fennell replied, “I will,” prompting the judge to grant bail on the basis of his assurance. The bail conditions include a 24-hour ban on publishing material online or on social media, a prohibition on public speaking, and a requirement to reside at a non-publicized home address. Fennell must also report to police three times weekly. The judge warned, “You are to refrain from any public speaking and from posting or causing to be posted any material on the internet pending the outcome of this case.” The prosecution opposed bail, asserting F

**Body of Missing Kayaker Found in Rum, Family Informed** The body of Jason Chung Wai-Ho, 33, a kayaker reported missing from the Arisaig area on January 13, has been recovered by police and coastguard teams from the Isle of Rum. Though no formal identification has been confirmed, his family has been notified. The discovery was made by a member of the public, with assistance from search teams including Mallaig and Eyemouth lifeboats, coastguard rescuers, a helicopter, and police dogs. Mr. Chung Wai-Ho was last seen departing in a red inflatable kayak after being cautioned by an off-duty officer about unstable weather conditions.

**Vue Cinemas to Challenge York Council’s Decision on Expanded Stadium Cinema** Vue Cinemas has announced plans to contest the City of York Council’s approval of a larger cinema at the York Community Stadium site, according to the *York Press*. The council initially agreed to a 12-screen design in 2009 but later sanctioned an additional screen and 400 extra seats at the Monks Cross development, a decision made in June 2016. Vue, which operates a 12-screen cinema at York’s Clifton Moor Centre, argues this expansion threatens its business and the city’s cinema landscape. The council confirmed it had accepted Vue’s application for a judicial review, with a hearing expected in early 2017. A spokesperson stated the authority remained “fully committed” to the stalled stadium project, despite legal challenges. The proposed 13-screen cinema, part of a £44m stadium and leisure facility, is intended to become the home ground for York City Football Club and York City Knights Rugby League Club. The development has faced repeated delays and cost overruns, with its opening pushed back from Spring 2017 to 2018. Originally budgeted at £37m, the project’s expenses have risen by £7m. A council report highlighted concerns that the expanded cinema’s “directly comparable format” would disproportionately affect Vue’s existing Clifton Moor Centre site, one of only three cinemas in York. Vue has yet to issue an official statement, though the BBC has sought clarification. If the judicial review succeeds, the council may be required to revoke the revised planning permission. The outcome could influence the stadium’s timeline and the city’s cultural and commercial landscape. For now, the council maintains its focus on delivering the long-anticipated leisure and sports facility.

**Cornwall Beach Pollution Dispute Sparks Concern Over Testing Methods** Godrevy, a popular Cornwall beach, faced nine "sewer overflow events" this bathing season, with heavy rainfall turning the sea a discolored brown, alarming locals and visitors. Despite these incidents, the Environment Agency (EA) reported the beach as one of 65 in Cornwall rated "excellent" for water quality, sparking a debate over the validity of the results. Surfers Against Sewage (SAS), an environmental group, has criticized the EA’s methodology. Andy Cummins, SAS campaigns director, accused the agency of sampling in areas untouched by pollution. "Only two of the nine overflows occurred on days EA collected samples, meaning seven went unmonitored," he said. He added that the agency avoids testing near the Red River, a key point of pollution where untreated sewage and surface water flow into the sea. The EA defended its approach, stating samples are taken where bathers are most concentrated. Bruce Newport, EA’s environment manager for Devon and Cornwall, noted the Red River’s discoloration after rainfall is often due to runoff from an abandoned mine at Dolcath, not necessarily sewage. "Combined sewer overflows can release diluted waste after heavy rain, but we prioritize areas with the highest public use," he said. In 2014, a surfing competition at Godrevy was canceled after similar discoloration, raising fears of contamination. Cummins emphasized the risk to public health, arguing that the EA’s sampling strategy "ignores regular pollution hotspots." The EA acknowledged the presence of combined sewer overflows but maintained that its standards align with EU bathing water directives. The dispute highlights tensions between regulatory testing and community concerns, as beachgoers continue to question whether the "excellent" rating accurately reflects the true state of coastal water quality.

**Wales’ Busiest Speed Cameras Highlight Persistent Speeding Challenges** Cardiff’s southbound North Road speed camera emerged as the most prolific in Wales and South Wales Police’s jurisdiction in 2016, capturing thousands of speeding offences. The camera’s data, part of a broader snapshot of Wales’ enforcement efforts, reveals a slight annual increase in recorded violations, with 171,000 offences logged in 2016 compared to 169,000 in 2015—a 1.1% rise. The figures, obtained via a Freedom of Information request by BBC Radio Wales’ *Dot Davies* programme, underscore the disparity between high-traffic areas and the proportion of drivers exceeding speed limits. Teresa Healy, operations manager for the Go Safe road safety partnership, emphasized that while cameras in busy corridors like North Road and the M4 near Newport captured the most offences, the violations represented a small fraction of total traffic. “These locations reflect traffic volume, not the norm,” she said, noting that most drivers adhere to speed limits. However, RAC Foundation director Steve Gooding raised concerns about the effectiveness of speed cameras. He criticized the high number of fines at certain sites, arguing that “the best camera would detect no one speeding.” The fact that hundreds to thousands of drivers are caught daily, he said, signals a flaw in the approach. Potential solutions, he suggested, could include clearer speed limit signage, road design reviews, or additional safety measures. Gooding also reiterated a long-standing call for authorities to release accident data for camera sites to assess their true impact on road safety. Key offenders in 2016 included the A483 at Rossett in Wrexham (4,500 offences) and the westbound M4 near Newport (4,400), the busiest in Gwent. The A44 in Ceredigion recorded 650 violations, the highest in Dyfed-Powys. Penalties for speeding in the UK now start at £100 and include three penalty points. If all 2016 offences in Wales were upheld, they could generate at least £17.1 million in fines. Recent data also highlighted a surge near Newport, where 13,000 drivers were caught over six months—an average of 84 daily—since enforcement intensified. While proponents argue cameras deter dangerous driving, critics like Gooding warn against viewing them as revenue tools. “Safety, not profit, must be the goal,” he said. The debate continues as authorities balance enforcement with public trust.

Former Poland international coach Lucien Goet was recently dismissed from his role with the Tunisian national team, the Carthage Eagles, after leading the squad since July 2015. Under his guidance, Tunisia was eliminated from the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations by Burkina Faso and suffered recent 1-0 defeats to Cameroon and Morocco. The Tunisia Football Federation announced that a new manager will be appointed by the end of the month. The team's campaign for the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations begins with a home match against Egypt, followed by World Cup qualifiers against DR Congo in September. Both Tunisia and DR Congo have secured victories in their preliminary fixtures.

**Conservatives Maintain Double-Digit Lead in UK Polls Amid Political Realignment** The Conservative Party has secured a commanding double-digit lead in British politics, with an average of five April polls placing them on 42.9% support compared to Labour’s 25.3%, a 17-point gap. In some individual surveys, the Tories’ advantage has surged beyond 20 points, marking the largest lead since the 2015 general election, when they won a majority of 12. That year’s election also saw the Conservatives begin their sustained dominance in polling averages, which have never placed them behind Labour since. **A Historic Lead for the Conservatives** Theresa May’s party now enjoys a position of strength reminiscent of Margaret Thatcher’s 1983 landslide victory, when she led Labour by a similar margin. **Moroccan UN Soldier Killed in Central African Conflict** A Moroccan peacekeeper was killed and three others injured in an attack by Christian militia in Bangassou, a southern diamond-mining town, authorities reported. The assault targeted a cathedral sheltering hundreds of displaced Muslims, who have sought refuge there since ethnic violence erupted in May. The Red Cross previously recovered 115 bodies from Bangassou following clashes between Christian and Muslim groups, with victims dying from knives, clubs, and bullets. The conflict, which has claimed thousands of lives, traces back to 2013 when predominantly Muslim Seleka rebels ousted President Francois Bozize, sparking a Christian militia backlash. Tensions remain high as religious and ethnic divisions fuel cycles of violence. The United Nations condemned the attack, calling for accountability. “The security situation is extremely volatile,” a UN spokesperson stated, urging all parties to protect civilians.

**Graham Short’s Rare Engraved £5 Notes Spark Nationwide Hunt** Micro-artist Graham Short has ignited a search for five intricately engraved £5 notes, each now valued at £50,000. In 2016, Mr. Short discreetly spent the first in a Welsh café, where it was swiftly discovered. Four notes were released into circulation, with three recovered since. A Scottish note was found tucked inside a Christmas card, while another was donated to charity by a pensioner. The fourth, spent in Leicestershire, remains missing. The fifth note was gifted to the Jane Austen Centre in Bath during a commemorative event marking the bicentenary of Austen’s death, following a minute’s silence. Displayed there, it bears one of five unique serial numbers (AM32 885551–885554) and a poetic quotation. The hunt continues for the final elusive note, with collectors eagerly scanning for the tiny engravings. Each discovery underscores the blend of artistry and serendipity fueling this unique national treasure hunt.

**Fin Whale Carcass Found on RSPB Land Near Harwich, Suspected Ship Strike** A significant portion of a fin whale’s carcass, measuring 10 meters (33 feet), was discovered on RSPB land near Harwich, Essex, last week. The remains, which accounted for two-thirds of the body, were dragged ashore on the front of a cargo vessel. Experts suspect the whale may have been struck by another ship, though the exact cause of death remains under investigation. Rick Vonk, site manager of the RSPB Stour Estuary, expressed bewilderment at the incident. “Fin whales are a very northerly species. We don’t know what it was doing to get hit, presumably by a container vessel,” he told the BBC. The whale’s presence in the region is rare, as the species typically inhabits colder waters. “It’s unfortunate this has happened—we like to see live whales rather than dead ones,” he added. The carcass, found on private land with no public access, will remain in place to avoid damaging the local habitat, as removing it would pose ecological risks. Rob Deaville, project manager of the Cetacean Strandings Investigation Programme (CSIP), confirmed this decision. “Leaving it in place was the most pragmatic option,” he said. Deaville noted that fin whales are vulnerable to ship strikes, though such incidents are exceptionally rare in UK waters. His team has encountered only two similar cases in the past 25 years. Approximately 600 cetacean strandings occur annually in the UK, with just two to three involving fin whales. Deaville emphasized the need for vigilance in reducing human impacts on marine life, such as shipping activity and habitat disruption. The discovery underscores the fragility of marine ecosystems and the growing challenges faced by migratory species. As investigations continue, conservationists hope the event will highlight the importance of protecting these endangered giants.

**British 800m Runner Shelly-Ann Leonard Left Off Team GB Despite Qualifying Standards** A British 800m runner has been omitted from the Team GB squad for the Rio Olympics despite meeting the qualifying time six times and finishing third at the trials. Shelly-Ann Leonard, 26, expressed her dismay in a post on eightlane.org, stating, “I accept I will never win an Olympic medal.” UK Athletics declined to comment on individual selection decisions when contacted. Only two 800m runners, Shelayna Oskan-Clarke and Lynsey Sharp, were named for Rio, leaving a third spot unfilled. Leonard, who clocked 2 minutes 2.45 seconds—just behind Oskan-Clarke and Sharp—at the British Championships in July, criticized the decision. “To leave a space empty when several athletes have the qualifying standard is an insult to the effort athletes put in,” she said. Leonard argued that the selection process devalued the sacrifices athletes make. “The early mornings, icy runs, hill reps, missed parties—none of it matters if you’re not making the final,” she added. **Enda Kenny Resigns: A Legacy of Economic Recovery and Transition Amid Political Challenges** Enda Kenny delivered his final address to the Dáil (Irish parliament) on Tuesday, marking the conclusion of his six-year tenure as taoiseach (prime minister) and his departure from the political stage after a 40-year career. As the longest-serving Fine Gael leader and the first in his party to hold the taoiseachship for two consecutive terms, Kenny leaves office amid a mixed legacy of economic revival, divisive austerity, and the looming specter of Brexit. Kenny assumed power in 2011, just months after Ireland entered an international financial bailout—a period of profound uncertainty for the nation and the Eurozone. His government oversaw a dramatic economic turnaround, exiting the EU bailout program in 2013 and steering the Republic toward recovery. The landmark 2015 same-sex marriage referendum, a resounding public victory, further cemented his legacy as a transformative leader. Yet his time in office was not without controversy. Opposition parties criticized his administration’s budgetary adjustments, which included €10 billion in austerity measures during the recession, arguing that the burden fell disproportionately on the Irish public. In his final speech, Kenny acknowledged shortcomings but emphasized his unwavering commitment to the people’s interests. “I will be the first to admit I didn’t get everything right,” he stated. “But my motivation has always been to serve the Irish people.” He also addressed the growing disillusionment with politics, urging colleagues to “treat each other with respect” as a means to rebuild public trust. Kenny’s successor, Leo Varadkar, was elected Fine Gael leader earlier this week and will formally assume the taoiseachship following a Dáil vote on Wednesday. Varadkar, who defeated rival Simon Coveney in a heated leadership contest, has named Coveney as his deputy, signaling a strategic alliance to re-energize the party. Varadkar pledged unity, stating the duo would “guide Fine Gael’s role in government” as the nation confronts new challenges. Among these challenges, Brexit looms largest. **Sunderland Midfielder Faces Trial Over 2015 Allegations** Adilson Tavares Varela, known as Cabral, will stand trial at Newcastle Crown Court on 25 April following his arrest in January 2015 on alleged sexual offence charges linked to an incident in Gateshead. The 27-year-old, who played one Premier League match for Sunderland during the 2013-14 season, previously pleaded not guilty. The club confirmed his departure in February 2015 via mutual consent. A former Swiss Under-21 international, Cabral previously represented Lausanne, Sevilla, and FC Basel before joining FC Zurich. Sunderland AFC declined to comment on the ongoing legal proceedings. The case follows high-profile sentencing of former teammate Adam Johnson, 28, who will be sentenced on 24 March for sexual activity with a 15-year-old. Johnson, an England caps holder, was convicted in a separate case. Both incidents have cast a shadow over the club’s recent history.

**Venezuelan Businessman’s High-Profile Drug Trial Sparks Political Controversy** Caracas, Venezuela — The trial of Carlos von Mühlen, a once-prominent Venezuelan businessman and U.S.-wanted figure, has ignited political tensions after his extradition from Colombia in 2011. Makled, whose family controlled a transport empire, airline, and warehouses, has been accused of leading one of the world’s largest drug trafficking networks, along with two counts of murder. U.S. authorities have labeled him a global kingpin, while Venezuela’s government claims his allegations of bribery involving senior officials are a ruse to evade prosecution. Makled’s case took a contentious turn after his arrest in 2010, following his brothers’ 2008 arrest when cocaine was discovered at their ranch. His 2011 extradition to Venezuela, hailed as a diplomatic win for regional cooperation, has since been overshadowed by his prison interview claims that he paid millions to top officials—a charge dismissed by the government as fabricated. Makled denies all accusations, asserting state authorities framed him to seize his businesses. The trial, now underway in a Caracas court, has drawn scrutiny for its secrecy. Journalists were barred from attending, with officials citing limited space—a decision criticized by opposition leader Miguel Ángel Rodríguez as a setback for transparency. “The trial has begun, but the prosecution’s 900-page case is dragging proceedings,” defense lawyer Rafael Ojeda told reporters. Rodríguez called the closed-door process “unacceptable” for such a politically charged case. As the trial unfolds, the case remains a flashpoint for Venezuela’s tangled web of legal and political disputes, with observers watching for signs of judicial independence or partisan interference. Makled’s fate could further strain Venezuela’s fragile diplomatic and domestic standing.

Ten candidates compete for the Lincolnshire constituency seat as polls open at 07:00 GMT. Voters cast ballots in cloudy but dry conditions, with temperatures peaking at 13°C. Results are projected by 04:00 GMT Friday, after the 22:00 GMT deadline. The race remains tight, with no clear front-runner emerging ahead of the final count.

**St Helens Continue Rise as Castleford Stumble in Narrow Defeat** St Helens edged out Castleford Tigers 26-20 in a thrilling Super League clash at the Halliwell Jones Stadium, with the hosts claiming their first back-to-back victories of the season to close the gap on the top three. Early exchanges were fiery, with Tigers’ Grant Millington bursting through for the opening try within the first 10 minutes. Saints responded swiftly as Adam Swift touched down to level, followed by Mike McMeeken’s try for the visitors after a neat offload from Ben Crooks. However, Saints seized control with two quick tries from Atelea Vea and Tommy Makinson’s replacement, Sam Conway (Dawson), to lead 16-14 at halftime. After the break, the hosts extended their dominance. Louie McCarthy-Scarsbrook’s clinical run and a second from Dawson stretched the lead to 26-14. Tigers’ hopes of a comeback dimmed when prop Millington exited with a hand injury, compounding an earlier blow as stand-off Ben Roberts went off injured. Adam Milner’s consolation try offered a late spark, but it proved insufficient for the Tigers, who remain in the drop zone. For Saints, the win moves them within two points of the top three, with captain Willem Alberts and key duo Vea and Dawson central to their resurgence. Castleford’s inconsistency deepens as injuries and a fragile defense hamper their title ambitions. Referee James Child enforced a tight contest, with six goal-line drop-outs reflecting the physicality. The result leaves Saints buoyant, while Tigers face a tense wait for the Play-Offs. **St Helens:** 26 (Vea, Dawson x2, McCarthy-Scarsbrook, Milner tries) **Castleford Tigers:** 20 (Millington, McMeeken, Milner tries) **Attendance:** 7,500.

**RHS Announces Ambitious Restoration of Worsley New Hall for Its Fifth Garden** The Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) has unveiled plans to transform the historic grounds of Worsley New Hall into RHS Garden Bridgewater, a £100m project set to open in 2019. Nestled beside the iconic Bridgewater Canal in Salford, the initiative aims to revitalize the 19th-century estate and establish one of the UK’s most remarkable gardens. As the RHS’s fifth garden—joining collections in Surrey, Devon, Essex, and North Yorkshire—the site will feature a 10-acre walled kitchen garden, once demolished in 1949, now to be meticulously restored. Historical elements, including tree-lined pathways and terraces between the estate’s lake and the former hall, will be revived to honor the site’s heritage. A key component of the project is a state-of-the-art learning center, designed to educate schoolchildren about horticulture and sustainability. The RHS’s 10-year, £100m investment program, which seeks to “make the UK a greener and more beautiful place,” underscores the garden’s role in environmental and educational outreach. Sue Biggs, RHS Director General, emphasized the project’s potential: “With its stunning landscapes and excellent transport links, Worsley New Hall was an opportunity we couldn’t miss. This garden will showcase the best of British horticulture and attract a million visitors annually.” Salford City Mayor Ian Stewart praised the development as a milestone in the city’s evolution: “Creating a garden of national and historical significance here reflects Salford’s ongoing transformation.” The project, a collaboration between the RHS, Salford City Council, and estate owners Peel Land and Property, will blend heritage preservation with modern innovation. By blending the estate’s historic charm with contemporary design, RHS Garden Bridgewater promises to become a cornerstone of the UK’s horticultural landscape, celebrating nature and inspiring future generations.

**Nick Goode Announces Retirement from Professional Rugby** London Irish fly-half Nick Goode has retired from professional rugby at 35, ending a storied 17-year career that included 17 Test caps for England and a place among the Premiership’s all-time greats. The 35-year-old, who joined London Irish this summer after leaving Wasps, will hang up his boots following medical advice. Goode, the second-highest points-scorer in Premiership history, expressed pride in his journey across clubs, including Leicester, Saracens, Worcester, and a return to the Exiles. “I’ve loved playing for every team and feel immensely proud of my achievements,” he said. Joining Irish with hopes of one final season, the decision to retire came after discussions with club and personal medical staff. A key figure in Leicester’s dominant era, Goode helped secure four consecutive Premiership titles and two European Cups. His career also spanned South Africa’s Sharks in Super Rugby and Brive in France’s Top 14. Reflecting on his time with London Irish, he said: “I’m disappointed I can’t continue, but I’ve enjoyed my short period with them.” Goode’s legacy combines consistency, creativity, and a passion for the game, leaving a lasting mark on English rugby.

**Mastercard Trials Selfie-Style Facial Recognition for Secure Transactions** Mastercard is testing a facial recognition system that allows users to authenticate payments by holding their phones up like a selfie, aiming to modernize digital security for a tech-savvy generation. The trial, involving 500 users in the United States, requires participants to blink to confirm their identity. Ajay Bhalla, Mastercard’s head of security, told CNN the approach aligns with younger users’ habits. “The new generation, which is into selfies..... I think they’ll find it cool,” he said. However, security experts warn that facial recognition alone remains vulnerable to spoofing. Ken Munro, a researcher at Pen Test Partners, highlighted past flaws in biometric systems. Google, for instance, initially struggled with Android’s facial unlock feature, which users could trick using static photos. Similarly, Mastercard’s app previously required a blink to prevent photos from being used, but Munro noted that attackers had previously circumvented this by animating photos with added eyelids. Mastercard’s facial recognition technology aims to replace its SecureCode system, which requires a password for online purchases. Last year, SecureCode protected three billion transactions, underscoring the scale of the shift. The company also mentioned exploring fingerprint and voice recognition as alternatives. Despite advances, experts stress the need for layered security. “Ideally, I’d like to see facial recognition used in conjunction with a PIN,” Munro said. Both systems have weaknesses, but combined, they offer stronger protection. He warned that biometric data poses unique risks: “If your facial recognition data gets stolen, you can’t change your face.” Meanwhile, competitors like Alibaba have demonstrated facial recognition tech, though it remains unlaunched. Mastercard’s trial reflects broader industry efforts to balance convenience with security. While the company emphasizes its commitment to safety, Munro noted, “People want something less cumbersome, but true security often requires compromise.” Mastercard’s approach mirrors a growing trend toward biometrics, yet the debate over how to safeguard personal data continues. As the trial unfolds, the challenge will be proving that convenience doesn’t come at the cost of consumer trust.

**Disabled Protesters Demand Financial Support and UN Report Release** Hundreds of disabled activists, including around 150 in wheelchairs, gathered outside Parliament to protest against government welfare cuts, according to Disabled People Against Cuts (DPAC). The demonstration, part of a week of action, demanded improved financial support for disabled people and the immediate publication of a UN inquiry into the UK’s treatment of disabled citizens, currently delayed until 2017. Ellen Clifford of DPAC condemned the government’s policies, highlighting changes to Personal Independence Payments (PIPs)—a welfare scheme for those aged 16-64—and cuts of up to £30 per week for some Employment Support Allowance (ESA) claimants. “The Paralympics celebrate disabled achievement, yet these cuts push others into crisis,” she said, emphasizing impacts on “dignity, care, and lives.” The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) acknowledged ongoing challenges, stating, “More needs to be done to support people with disabilities or health conditions.” However, the government defended its £50bn annual spending on disability-related support. Protesters faced heavy police presence, with Clifford accusing officers of using excessive force, including deploying bolt cutters and detaining a personal assistant. “We’re surrounded by police, not protesters,” she said. Scotland Yard confirmed two arrests for obstructing a public highway. The dispute centers on welfare reforms critics argue undermine disability rights. The UN inquiry, delayed until 2017, has drawn sharp rebukes from DPAC, which urges transparency. As tensions escalated, the contrast between the government’s spending claims and protesters’ lived experiences underscored the growing divide over disability policy in the UK. With the Paralympics symbolizing inclusion, the rally highlighted fears that austerity measures risk eroding progress for disabled communities. The outcome of the UN report and future welfare debates will remain pivotal for activists fighting for equitable support.

**NHS Scotland Reports Slight Rise in Operation Cancellations Amid Capacity Challenges** New data reveals a modest increase in operation cancellations across NHS Scotland in April, with 578 procedures (1.9% of 31,213 scheduled) postponed due to non-clinical capacity issues, up from 467 (1.6%) the previous month. Health Minister Aileen Campbell emphasized that cancellations are avoided whenever possible, citing factors such as bed shortages, staff absenteeism, equipment delays, and theatre overruns as primary causes. Ms. Campbell, Scotland’s public health minister, stated: “Decisions to cancel planned operations are never made lightly. We work closely with health boards to manage capacity and ensure cancellations remain minimal.” She noted that the rise aligns with seasonal fluctuations, particularly during winter months when demand on the health service surges. While the percentage of cancellations remains low, the government has reiterated its focus on rescheduling postponed procedures promptly and prioritizing patients with urgent clinical needs, such as cancer treatments. However, Scottish Labour’s health spokesman, Anas Sarwar, criticized the Scottish National Party (SNP) government for what he described as neglect of the NHS in favor of preoccupying itself with EU referendum fallout. He warned: “This increase is a wake-up call that SNP ministers are failing to address long-standing pressures on our health service.” Mr. Sarwar highlighted staff shortages, with a recent survey showing only a third of NHS workers believe there are adequate numbers to fulfill duties. He accused the SNP of adopting a “crisis management” approach to healthcare for nearly a decade, urging increased investment and a long-term strategy to address systemic issues. The data comes amid ongoing concerns over NHS capacity, with health boards citing winter pressures and staff retention challenges as key hurdles. While the government maintains cancellations are kept to a “very small percentage” of total operations, opposition leaders argue the figures underscore the need for urgent action to prevent further disruptions. The Scottish government has pledged to review capacity planning and improve coordination between health boards, but with winter likely to bring renewed strain, the debate over funding and workforce planning is expected to intensify. Patients and healthcare professionals alike are calling for measures to ensure timely care and prevent the erosion of public trust in the NHS. For now, the focus remains on minimizing cancellations and addressing the root causes of capacity constraints—a challenge that both supporters and critics agree requires sustained attention.

**Leeds Outclass Sheffield Wednesday as Monk Defends Tactics Amid Owner Pressure** Leeds United secured a crucial 2-0 victory over Sheffield Wednesday at Hillsborough, ending a turbulent week for manager Garry Monk. The win came amid speculation that Monk faced potential sacking by owner Massimo Cellino, who had reportedly grown frustrated with his team’s 1-2-0 start to the season. Monk, whose one-year contract remains intact, dismissed pressure claims, telling BBC Radio Leeds: “I’m not under any pressure..... my plan isn’t an overnight fix. We’re at the start of something new.” He highlighted the rebuilt squad, emphasizing long-term growth: “We’re not miracle workers. You can see the players’ belief in this project.” The manager acknowledged challenges ahead, noting, “We’ll have ups and downs,” but expressed confidence in the team’s potential. **Rural Youth Face Education Challenges Due to Transport and Broadband Gaps, Report Finds** A new report from Rural England warns that inadequate public transport and uneven broadband access are stifling educational and employment opportunities for young people in rural areas, exacerbating inequality between rural and urban communities. The *State of Rural Services* report highlights how patchy and costly transportation, coupled with digital divides, are limiting students’ access to secondary schools, further education, and apprenticeships, raising concerns about a widening skills gap. The report emphasizes that young people in rural England are disproportionately affected by unreliable or non-existent public transport. Half of those in smaller villages have no access to buses, trains, or other services, forcing reliance on parental or private transport. For many, this restricts their ability to attend schools or colleges outside their immediate area, effectively narrowing educational choices based on proximity rather than quality or suitability. Margaret Clark, a spokesperson for Rural England, stressed that “poor transport services” are leaving rural youth at a disadvantage, with their futures constrained by geography. Financial burdens are also mounting. The study reveals that rural students spend 20% more on transport than their urban peers, a cost that can act as a barrier to pursuing further education or training. Local authority funding for rural bus services has plummeted by 25% over four years, leaving many areas without affordable, regular transit options. Without reliable transport, the report warns, young people are more likely to remain in local schools with limited resources or forgo post-16 education

**African Legacy and Fan Connection Shines in Premier League** Since its inception in 1992, the Premier League has welcomed 246 African players, who have scored 1,776 goals across 14,210 appearances. Chelsea legend Didier Drogba tops the charts as the highest scorer (104 goals), while Ivory Coast’s Kolo Toure made the most appearances (349). Nigeria leads African nations in contributions, with 35 players representing the league. As the Premier League live fan park arrives in Cape Town this weekend, the rich history of African involvement in England’s top flight takes center stage. While Nigeria leads in player numbers, Egypt dominates in digital fan engagement. Over 3.1 million Egyptians follow Chelsea on Facebook, with nearly 2.2 million backing Arsenal. This reflects the deep cultural ties between the Premier League and African audiences. Notably, Leicester City’s surge to the league summit has sparked a unique fandom in Algeria: 347,998 Algerians follow the club on Facebook—16.6% of their global fanbase—surpassing UK followers (139,982). The phenomenon is likely tied to Riyad Mahrez, the Algerian winger whose heroics have propelled Leicester’s “Cinderella” story. With the fan park celebrating the Premier League’s global reach, these stats underscore Africa’s pivotal role in shaping—and being shaped by—the league’s legacy.

**Vandals Attack Beloved ‘Gnome Village’ at Warwickshire Attraction, Prompting Outpouring of Public Support** A cherished “gnome village” at Echills Wood Railway, part of Kingsbury Water Park in Warwickshire, has been targeted in a reported act of vandalism, leaving over 40 handcrafted figurines smashed and scattered across the track. The incident, which occurred between 21:00 BST on 8 September and 09:00 the following day, also damaged signs, a crocodile head, and other features at the family-friendly attraction. The gnome village, a popular centerpiece for visitors, was reduced to rubble by an unknown offender or offenders. Park staff expressed shock at the destruction, sharing photos of the damage on Facebook. The post quickly gained traction, viewed by thousands and shared hundreds of times, sparking an overwhelming public response. Dozens of people offered to donate replacement gnomes, with many condemning the act as senseless. Countryside ranger Rachel Hextall described the reaction as “profound,” noting the emotional connection people feel to the whimsical display. “Who knew gnomes could be so emotive?” she said. Social media was flooded with outrage, including from Helen Perkins, a parent who wrote, “My children love the village. What the hell is wrong with some people? Next time we come, we’ll donate a gnome,” and Faye Nethercot, who called the act “vile, vicious” and expressed hope for a swift rebuild. Warwickshire Police confirmed a report of criminal damage to the site, including “a significant number of ornamental gnomes,” but no arrests have been made. Staff are now working to restore the village, buoyed by public generosity. “We’re determined to rebuild, thanks to the incredible support from our community,” said a park representative.

**BBC Breakfast Presenter’s Surprise Role as Baby Midwife as Colleague Gives Birth Unexpectedly** BBC Breakfast presenter Victoria Fritz gave birth to a baby boy at Manchester’s St Mary’s Hospital, with co-host Sally Nugent stepping in to support her when Fritz’s husband was stranded on the M6 motorway. The unexpected event unfolded after Fritz, who was due to deliver in early December, went into labor prematurely following her business news segment on Wednesday. Fritz’s waters broke shortly after she left the studio, prompting an urgent trip to the hospital. Her husband, however, was stuck in traffic, and Nugent, who had initially gone to the hospital to keep Fritz company, remained by her side throughout the birth. A BBC spokesperson confirmed that Nugent “intended only to keep her company” but ended up witnessing the arrival of Fritz’s first child when the father-to-be failed to reach the hospital in time. Nugent later tweeted, *“You won’t believe what happened after work yesterday. Huge congrats to our very clever @VFritzNews. It’s going to be a brilliant story for his 21st birthday!”* The presenter also shared a photo of Fritz with her newborn, captioning it: *“Breaking Breakfast Baby News! He was in a bit of a rush to greet the world...”* The baby, born three weeks early, is thriving alongside his mother, though he remains unnamed. Social media users expressed surprise at the news, noting Fritz’s subtle appearance during her on-air segments. BBC Breakfast shared the joyous update with fans, highlighting the “team effort” behind Fritz’s delivery. Viewers are invited to share story ideas via email at *entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk* or follow @BBCNewsEnts on Twitter for more updates.

**Indonesia Sentences IS Supporters for Recruitment to Syria; Calls for Stronger Laws Emerge** An Indonesian court has handed down the first jail sentences for recruiting and aiding individuals to travel to Syria and join the Islamic State (IS). The verdict, delivered Tuesday, follows a deadly IS-linked attack in Jakarta last month and underscores growing concerns over homegrown extremism. The judge ruled that supporting IS constitutes terrorism, a key legal shift in combating the group’s influence. Four defendants had traveled to Syria for IS military training, while three assisted in buying travel documents and recruiting fighters. However, security expert Sidney Jones told the BBC the sentences were lenient, citing weaknesses in Indonesia’s anti-terrorism laws. She called for stronger legislation to address evolving militant tactics. The attack in Jakarta—comprising explosions and gun violence—sparked public demands for harsher penalties. Yet, members of parliament have resisted expanding security forces’ powers, fearing abuses by agencies with a poor human rights record, per BBC correspondent Rebecca Henschke. Experts warn that Indonesia’s “new breed” of militants, inspired by IS, poses a persistent threat. While the verdict marks progress, balancing security and human rights remains a contentious challenge.

Of 25 bonfire-related cases, NIFRS crews intervened seven times, while other incidents saw minimal action. No major injuries reported.

The company stated that a faulty code may activate upon a significant impact, increasing injury risks. The recall, set to begin in late June, affects models sold across the U.S., Canada, Mexico, and international markets. FCA reported one fatality, two injuries, and two accidents potentially linked to the issue. A statement read, “The company is aware of these incidents and is addressing the problem.” Owners will be notified to reprogram their vehicles. As a temporary fix, FCA advises turning the vehicle off and then on again if a warning light appears, per the summary. Affected models include [insert list], though specifics were not detailed in the summary. The recall underscores ongoing safety concerns linked to vehicle software systems.

**Ancient Egyptian Figurine Sekhemka Sold to US Amid Export Controversy** The 4,000-year-old Sekhemka figurine, believed to depict an ancient Egyptian high court official, was sold by Northampton Borough Council in 2014 for nearly £16 million. Initially, the UK government imposed an export ban, citing the statue’s “outstanding aesthetic importance” and cultural value. However, after no UK buyer emerged, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport granted an export license to the US in April. Auctioneers Christie’s had withheld buyer details at the time, sparking rumors the artifact might have entered a private collection in Qatar. Egypt’s Antiquities Ministry opposed the sale, arguing it undermined heritage preservation. Last week, BBC News revealed the council faced legal warnings against selling for “financial motives.” The council defended the decision, stating proceeds funded a £14 million museum and art gallery extension. The sale, controversial from its outset, highlights tensions between preserving cultural heritage and municipal financial needs. While the license now cleared its export to the US, the artifact’s legacy remains entangled in ethical debates over ownership and accessibility.

**Morriston Hospital Review Highlights Deep-Seated Issues in Cardiac Surgery Service** An independent review of Swansea’s Morriston Hospital has revealed "deeply unsatisfactory" patient outcomes, including preventable deaths linked to delays in cardiac surgery, prompting urgent reforms. The external panel, commissioned by Abertawe Bro Morgannwg University Health Board (ABMU), identified systemic problems such as low staff morale, bullying by surgeons, and poor teamwork as key factors undermining care. The findings were presented to the health board on Thursday, alongside a 34-point action plan to address the crisis. The review, conducted by an expert team, highlighted a toxic work environment, with staff describing "intolerable working conditions," excessive hours, and inequitable pay. Many reported being "bullied and abused" by senior surgeons, while leadership was criticized for a lack of support. The report warned that such issues have led to high staff turnover, rising sickness rates, and a culture of demoralization, all of which contributed to prolonged waits for critical surgery. Paul Roberts, ABMU’s chief executive, acknowledged the gravity of the findings, stating, "Our patients deserve the best possible cardiac surgery service, and I sincerely apologise that these long-term issues have not been resolved much earlier." While Roberts emphasized the hospital’s historic excellence in cardiac care since 1997, he confirmed that the service had "deep-rooted problems" requiring immediate intervention. Among the recommendations are urgent measures to halt harmful practices, improve staff support, and enhance collaboration. The health board has pledged to implement changes, including restructuring leadership and addressing workplace bullying. A detailed action plan will be unveiled in the coming weeks, with a focus on restoring trust and prioritizing patient safety. The report underscores a stark warning: without systemic reforms, the legacy of poor practices could persist, risking further harm. As ABMU moves forward, the pressure is on to translate promises into tangible improvements, ensuring the cardiac surgery service can once again deliver the care its patients deserve.

**Swansea Unveils Ambitious Coastal Transformation Plans** Swansea Council has outlined bold plans to revitalize the coastline from the Marriott Hotel to the civic centre, aiming to create a vibrant hub of tourism, hospitality, and public space. The project, which includes a five-star hotel, restaurants, bars, and a proposed aquarium developed in partnership with Swansea University, seeks to connect the city centre with the beachfront. A developer will be selected in November, though details of the five bidders’ proposals remain confidential. The vision extends beyond leisure: the council envisions public spaces, tourist attractions, and housing on the current civic centre site, which is up for sale. A key feature will be a walkway over the main road linking to the former St David’s shopping centre site, set to house a retail and leisure complex. Councillor Rob Stewart hinted at the project’s potential during a recent business event, stating, “It would provide a new city space,” while comparing the development to Cardiff Bay’s Mermaid Quay. “Swansea’s city beach could surpass it,” he suggested, signaling ambitions to attract visitors and boost the local economy. The plans underscore Swansea’s push to leverage its coastal assets, blending academic research, tourism, and urban renewal. With a focus on connectivity and innovation, the project aims to redefine the city’s waterfront identity.

Campbell was fatally shot on High Street, West Bromwich, on 27 December. **Vietnamese National Sentenced for Supporting AQAP in 2011 Plot** Minh Quang Pham, 33, a former Vietnamese national residing in London, was sentenced in New York for supporting al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) in a 2011 terror plot. Pham admitted to three counts of terrorist-related activity in January, including providing material support to AQAP, conspiring to receive military training from the group, and possessing a machine gun for violent crimes. He denied intent to carry out attacks, though no assault materialized. Pham, also known as Amin, was arrested in the UK in June 2012 and extradited to the U.S. in February 2015. Scotland Yard’s counter-terrorism command played a pivotal role, providing critical evidence that shaped the case. Prosecutors revealed Pham was directed by AQAP leader Anwar Al-Awlaki—killed in 2011—to detonate explosives at Heathrow Airport’s arrivals area after months of training in Yemen. Judge Alison Nathan called for an “exceptionally severe sentence,” noting Pham’s status as a “trusted asset” for the group. During his time with AQAP, he worked as a graphic artist on *Inspire*, the terror group’s magazine, which was referenced by the Boston Marathon bombers in 2013. At the sentencing, Pham expressed regret, calling his actions a “terrible mistake” and renouncing terrorism in a letter to the court. Despite his remorse, the judge emphasized the gravity of his crimes, underscoring the threat he posed to global security. The case highlights the transnational reach of AQAP and the challenges of combating radicalization networks.

**Skyscanner Acquires Chinese Travel Comparison Site Youbibi to Boost Domestic and International Travel Services** Edinburgh-based travel tech firm Skyscanner has acquired Youbibi, a Shenzhen-based Chinese startup specializing in comparing flights, hotels, and package holidays, marking a strategic expansion in the Asia-Pacific market. The move follows a partnership with Baidu, one of China’s leading search engines, established two years ago. Founded in 2010, Youbibi will continue as a Skyscanner subsidiary, with its engineering team remaining in Shenzhen, while Skyscanner’s commercial and marketing operations for China will stay in Beijing. Skyscanner, which operates under the Tianxun brand in China, currently attracts 1 million monthly visits in the country—10 times Youbibi’s current rate. CEO Gareth Williams highlighted the acquisition’s potential: “Since launching our China team in 2012, traffic to our platforms has grown tenfold, yet we’re only at the start of this market’s potential. Merging Skyscanner’s global reach with Youbibi’s expertise in domestic Chinese travel and traveler insights creates a unique advantage.” The acquisition positions Skyscanner as a comprehensive global travel provider for Chinese consumers, offering both international and domestic travel solutions. Williams emphasized the opportunity to “combine the best of both worlds,” leveraging Youbibi’s local knowledge to enhance Skyscanner’s services in one of the world’s fastest-growing travel markets.

**Historic Tribute Held for 1942 Plane Crash Victims** A poignant memorial event took place near Ilkeston on 12 July to honor the five men who died in a secret experimental flight crash 75 years ago. The occasion, held in Stanley, Derbyshire, featured a flypast by a Dakota aircraft from the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight, a tribute to the crew of the W5795 bomber that tragically crashed in 1942. The doomed flight, part of a high-altitude test to assess whether bombers could evade German fighters by flying at 35,000 feet, ended in disaster when a propeller sheared off, tearing through the pressurized cabin. The crash site, a field in Stanley, became the focal point of the day’s commemorations, which included a solemn service at St Andrew’s Church followed by a 1942-themed parade. Among the attendees was Hillary Eddleston, whose father, Mr. Radford, served as the rear gunner on the ill-fated flight. “This has brought closure to our family,” she said. “The bomber crashed when my mother was only six weeks pregnant with me—I never got to know my father.” Eddleston was joined by her children and grandchildren, marking the anniversary with emotional resonance. Rosin Eddleston-McGrath, Mr. Radford’s great-granddaughter, echoed the sentiment: “All the men died so we could have peace and a future. It’s special to honor their sacrifice today.” The event was organized by ex-serviceman Terry Hall and church warden Bernard Walters, who, as a child, witnessed the crash in 1942. The pair spearheaded efforts to commission a permanent memorial for the crew, ensuring their legacy endures. The tribute highlighted the enduring impact of World War II’s unsung heroes, blending history with heartfelt remembrance.

**Newcastle Falcons Secure Prop Signing as Sixth Addition for Next Season** Newcastle Falcons have bolstered their pack with the signing of 24-year-old prop Ben Sowrey from Worcester Warriors, marking their sixth addition for next season. Sowrey, who made eight appearances for Worcester this term, including three in the Premiership, expressed excitement about joining a club "set to go places." Director of Rugby Dean Richards praised the tighthead as a "quality player," highlighting his "strong scrummage," line-out expertise, and all-around skillset. Sowrey joins fellow recruits Sam Egerton, Vereniki Goneva, Sam Lockwood, Joel Hodgson, and Harrison Orr. Despite currently sitting second-bottom in the Premiership, seven points ahead of London Irish with two games left, Newcastle remain optimistic ahead of the new season. Sowrey’s arrival underscores their ambitions to climb the table.

**Celtics Top Warriors in Heart-Stopping Finish at Oracle Arena** Boston Celtics’ Isaiah Thomas sank a decisive driving lay-up with 8.3 seconds remaining, securing a 110-108 victory over the Golden State Warriors on Friday. Thomas finished with 22 points, including clutch free throws in the closing seconds, while Stephen Curry missed a desperation three-pointer to force overtime with 5.3 seconds left. The loss marked the Warriors’ first defeat at Oracle Arena since January 2015, snapping a 36-game home winning streak this season. Despite the setback, the Warriors—NBA champions with a 68-8 record—maintain a 4.5-game lead over the San Antonio Spurs in the Western Conference. They’ll face the Portland Trail Blazers at Oracle Arena on Sunday. Curry, 28, expressed frustration, calling the loss “a weird feeling” but acknowledged the lesson for the playoffs: “We don’t want this feeling.” The Warriors need five wins in their final six games to surpass the Chicago Bulls’ 1995-96 record of 72 regular-season victories. The Celtics’ gritty win highlighted Boston’s resilience and underscored the Warriors’ upcoming challenges as the play-in race intensifies.

**Government Reverses Tax Plans on Pasty Sales and Caravans After Outcry** *VAT on static caravans cut to 5%, with new rules on hot pasties following backlash* **By Nick Robinson, Political Editor** In a significant policy U-turn, the UK government has abandoned plans to impose a 20% VAT increase on static caravans and revised rules for taxing hot pasties and savouries, following fierce protests from businesses and the public.
