The Treasury confirmed that the original 20% VAT rate on static caravans—currently zero-rated—will now be reduced to 5%, with implementation delayed from October to April 2016. Separately, the government will no longer tax food such as pasties, pies, or sausage rolls sold on supermarket shelves or in bakeries, provided they are not kept hot in temperature-controlled cabinets. The change aims to address concerns that enforcing a tax based on the precise temperature of food items would be impractical. The policy shift followed intense parliamentary scrutiny. During a heated debate, MPs from all three main parties condemned Osborne’s initial proposals as unenforceable and economically damaging. Conservative MP Sheryll Murray, representing South East Cornwall, praised the government for heeding concerns about “thermometer-wielding tax inspectors” and the ambiguity of “ambient temperatures.” Liberal Democrat MP Stephen Gilbert hailed the decision as a victory for Cornish communities, predicting “dancing in the streets from Land’s End to the Tamar.” Currently, VAT is zero-rated on most food and hot baked goods but applies to takeaway items sold for immediate consumption. The Treasury had proposed extending VAT to hot savouries sold at room temperature, citing inconsistencies. However, critics argued the policy would burden small businesses and disrupt traditional food retail. The revised rules now exempt pasties and similar items if sold on open shelves, effectively reinstating the status quo. A Treasury spokesperson said the policy had been “improved” after extensive engagement, aiming to simplify enforcement while removing “inconsistencies” in VAT treatment. The government stressed that businesses would no longer face obligations to monitor product temperatures, though the revised 5% caravan tax will still apply to new static homes. Labour’s shadow Treasury minister, Chris Leslie, criticized the government for “incompetent” policy-making, arguing the reversal exposed a lack of foresight. He accused ministers of failing to consult adequately before making announcements, leading to last-minute revers

**Memorial Marks 1965 Cambrian Colliery Disaster in Emotional Service** On the anniversary of the 1965 Cambrian Colliery explosion that claimed 31 lives, a solemn remembrance service unfolded at Cambrian Memorial Park, Rhondda Cynon Taff. Organized by the Cwm Clydach Community Development Trust with support from Rhondda Cynon Taff Council, the event honored victims of the disaster caused by a buildup of flammable firedamp due to inadequate ventilation. First Minister Carwyn Jones and Rhondda Cynon Taff mayor John Watts joined survivors and families, including 83-year-old John Benbow, a former underground mechanical fitter; 87-year-old Alwyn Davies, an ex-worker; and 87-year-old Betty Thomas, a canteen assistant. The open-air ceremony began with a prayer by Father Haydn England-Simon, followed by the mayor’s address. A 33-bell toll symbolized not only the 1965 tragedy but also earlier mining disasters at the same colliery in 1905 and 1900, and incidents at Ffynnon Dwyn and Blaenclydach collieries. At 13:00 BST—the hour of the 1965 explosion—a minute’s silence was observed, followed by wreath-laying, a roll call of the deceased, and music performed by soprano Lucy Rees and the Cambrian Male Choir. Concurrently, at Senghenydd’s National Mining Memorial, a floral tribute was placed at the Cambrian tablet, with a separate minute’s silence held by the Senghenydd Colliery Memorial Society and local residents. First Minister Jones emphasized the importance of remembering those lost to mining’s dangers, while the mayor highlighted the enduring legacy of resilience in the community. The service served as a poignant reminder of the human cost of industrial progress, uniting past and present in shared remembrance.

**£1.5m Cancer Support Centre Approved for Redhill** The £1.5m Macmillan Cancer Information Support Centre in Redhill has secured planning consent, with NHS managers now finalizing construction timelines. Michael Wilson, CEO of Surrey and Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust, hailed the project as a transformative step for cancer care in the region, promising a "revolution" in patient support. The center, a collaboration with Macmillan Cancer Support, will offer a comprehensive suite of services, including welfare advice, counseling, alternative therapies, and psychological support. It will also feature exercise classes and a dedicated space for families, marking a first for the area. Mr. Wilson emphasized its holistic approach, complementing the radiotherapy unit that opened in July 2024. “To have all of those things in east Surrey and north east West Sussex for our whole population is absolutely fantastic,” he said, noting that chemotherapy and radiotherapy often take a physical and emotional toll. Set in a single-story building with a large reception, therapy rooms, activity spaces, and a garden, the facility will provide a calming environment. Reigate Council approved the plans this week, recognizing its role as a vital community hub. Papers submitted by the trust highlighted the center’s potential to support patients and families during treatment journeys. With nearly 5,000 new cancer diagnoses annually in Surrey, Macmillan is launching a fundraising campaign to secure the full £1.5m needed for construction. Mr. Wilson stressed the importance of local care, reducing the burden of travel for patients and ensuring support is “closer to home.” The new center aims to address the emotional, practical, and physical challenges of cancer, offering a one-stop resource for patients navigating their treatment and recovery. Construction is expected to begin once funding is secured, with the trust hopeful for a swift start to bring this critical service to the community.

**Local Cyclist Dies During RideLondon Event After Personal Fight Against Cancer** Robin Chard, 48, of Bicester, tragically passed away on Sunday after suffering a cardiac arrest during the annual RideLondon cycling event. The incident occurred as he approached the 25-mile mark, with medical teams and fellow riders immediately responding at Kingston Bridge. Despite emergency care, Mr. Chard succumbed to his injuries later at Kingston Hospital. A passionate advocate for cancer research, Mr. Chard participated in the 100-mile ride as a "personal crusade," driven by the loss of his father, stepfather, and several other family members to the disease. His wife, Vickie, shared, "Robin was doing something he loved to raise money for Cancer Research UK, a cause that was very important to him." As of Monday, his fundraising page had surpassed £15,000, with donors praising his dedication. RideLondon organizers expressed deep sorrow over the incident, stating, "Everyone involved..... would like to express sincere condolences to Robin’s family and friends." The event, which drew hundreds of cyclists, stewards, and volunteers, highlighted both the risks of endurance sports and the resilience of those battling personal and communal health challenges. Tributes poured in online, with heartfelt messages from loved ones and strangers. One note read, "Hi daddy, I’m so proud of you," from what appears to be a child, praising his fundraising efforts. Another, signed by Ashley, called the page "a legacy of your hard work," while Judie Pierce wrote, "A sad ending to someone doing an act of generosity..... May you rest in peace." On his JustGiving page, Mr. Chard humorously described his mission: "Just a bike 100 miles in and around London," adding that his goal was to help "find more effective and permanent cures." **What is RideLondon?** RideLondon is a flagship cycling event organized by Sport London, in partnership with the Prudential, aiming to promote physical health and raise funds for charities. Annual routes weave through London and surrounding areas, attracting amateur and professional riders alike.

**Writers Guild Awards: Top TV Shows Vie for Writing Honors in 2023** The Writers Guild of America (WGA) has unveiled its nominees for the 2023 Awards, spotlighting groundbreaking TV series in drama, comedy, and new shows. AMC’s *Better Call Saul*, a prequel to *Breaking Bad*, leads the drama series and new series categories, with its debut episode also earning a nod in the episodic drama category. The show’s star, Bob Odenkirk, reprises his role as the morally ambiguous attorney in a story that expands the *Breaking Bad* universe. Competition in the drama series category is fierce, with *Game of Thrones*, *Mad Men* (in its final season), *Mr. Robot*, and *The Americans* all vying for top honors. *Mr. Robot*, which premiered on USA Network and later online, centers on a programmer joining a group of hacktivists, while *The Americans* continues to captivate with its Cold War-era intrigue. In the comedy series category, HBO’s *Veep* faces off against Amazon’s *Transparent*, a poignant series about a retired professor transitioning later in life. *Veep* also earned an episodic comedy nomination for its season-five episode *Joint Session*, which humorously dramatized political gridlock. Meanwhile, *Breaking Bad*, which won six WGA Awards over its run, looms large as a past champion. The WGA, which honors writing in TV, radio, and animation, will announce winners on 13 February. With bold storytelling and sharp dialogue, the nominated series reflect the evolving landscape of scripted television. As creators and fans await the results, the awards highlight the power of writing to shape the most iconic shows of the decade.

A baby wallaby, found alone near the Curraghs on the Isle of Man last week, is now under the care of the Manx Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (MSPCA) in Ard Jerkyll. The joey, believed to be around three weeks old, is being nurtured by Jenny Corran, who usually tends to rescued seals. Ms. Corran explained the joey may have fallen from her mother’s pouch or been rejected at birth. “She’s very fragile but coping well,” she said. The Curraghs, home to 120 wallabies descended from a pair that escaped a wildlife park in the 1970s, provides a thriving habitat for these Australian natives. Ms. Corran, using a backpack as a surrogate pouch filled with a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel, feeds the joey milk every three hours. She has also started nibbling grapes, a promising sign of progress. The MSPCA is collaborating with Blackpool Zoo and the Curraghs Wildlife Park to determine the joey’s future. For now, the focus remains on her survival. “We’re doing everything we can to give her a chance,” Ms. Corran added. The joey, yet to be named, continues to show resilience, offering hope for her recovery and eventual reintegration into the wild.

**Former Irish Taoiseach Albert Reynolds, Architect of Northern Ireland Peace, Dies at 81** Former Irish Taoiseach Albert Reynolds, a pivotal figure in advancing peace during the Northern Ireland conflict, has died at the age of 81. His passing on Thursday marks the end of a legacy defined by relentless advocacy for reconciliation, as mourners and world leaders hailed his efforts to bridge divides during one of Ireland’s most turbulent periods. Reynolds, a Fianna Fáil politician born in Rooskey, County Roscommon, served as Ireland’s prime minister from 1992 to 1994. During his tenure, he worked closely with then-British Prime Minister Sir John Major to craft the 1993 Downing Street Declaration. This landmark agreement laid the groundwork for the 1994 IRA ceasefire and the subsequent Good Friday Agreement, reshaping the political landscape of Northern Ireland. “He knew that peace was not achieved only by talking to your friends, you must talk to your enemies and make peace with them,” said Fr Brian D’Arcy, a priest who spoke at Reynolds’ funeral Mass at Sacred Heart Church, Donnybrook, Dublin. The gathering drew an unprecedented cross-section of political leaders from across Ireland, Britain, and the Catholic Church. Sir John Major’s attendance, met with a standing ovation, underscored the significance of their collaboration. “His words were typical: ‘Where else would I be on this day?’” Fr D’Arcy noted, highlighting Major’s deep respect for Reynolds’ vision. The funeral, attended by Taoiseach Enda Kenny, Irish President Michael D. Higgins, and former leaders such as Bertie Ahern, John Bruton, and Liam Cosgrave, reflected the unifying ethos Reynolds championed. Among the mourners were Sinn Féin’s Gerry Adams and Martin McGuinness, SDLP leaders John Hume and Alasdair McDonnell, and Northern Ireland Secretary Theresa Villiers. The presence of figures from deeply divided political factions illustrated Reynolds’ unique ability to foster dialogue. Atkinson’s move underscores growing transnational cooperation among far-right and Eurosceptic forces, amplifying their influence in shaping EU policy debates. **Plymouth Tops National Stroke Care Rankings in CQC Review** *Plymouth’s stroke care services have been recognized as the best performing in the UK by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), a major accolade highlighting the region’s commitment to patient recovery and support.* In a comprehensive review of health and social care services, the CQC evaluated trusts and providers across critical areas including acute care, hospital discharge, access to rehabilitation, and long-term support. Plymouth emerged as the top-performing area, boasting one of the nation’s lowest mortality rates for stroke patients. Neighboring regions Torbay and Devon were also commended as “better performing,” underscoring a regional focus on stroke care. A stroke—caused by a blood clot or burst blood vessel—remains the leading cause of severe disability in the UK, often resulting in paralysis, impaired coordination, vision loss, and language difficulties. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are vital, particularly for ischemic strokes (caused by clots), which can be addressed with thrombolysis (clot-busting drugs). Plymouth’s care model emphasizes speed and specialization, with Derriford Hospital’s dedicated stroke unit providing immediate access to a multidisciplinary team of doctors, nurses, physiotherapists, and speech and language therapists. Patients experiencing transient ischemic attacks (TIAs, or “mini strokes”) can also be referred to a TIA clinic within 24 hours, ensuring timely intervention. Beyond acute care, Plymouth’s success lies in its holistic support network. Adult social care services, led by Plymouth City Council, include a specialist counseling program for stroke survivors, carers, and families, alongside weekly communication support groups and exercise classes to rebuild strength and mobility. These initiatives were praised in the CQC review for fostering community reintegration, though the regulator noted a shortfall in facilitating patients’ timely return home. Plymouth City Councillor Grant Monahan welcomed the recognition, stating, “Our development of the stroke services directory and specialized counseling service go a long way to helping those who’ve suffered a stroke get the help they need once they leave hospital.” He emphasized the “lifeline” provided by partnerships between health and social care providers. A statement from Plymouth Hospitals Trust echoed this, highlighting two years of collaborative efforts to enhance stroke care as reflected in the CQC’s rating. While the CQC’s criticism of post-discharge support offers room for improvement, Plymouth’s achievements underscore a robust system that prioritizes both clinical excellence and patient-centered recovery. For stroke survivors and their families, the region’s services represent a beacon of hope in a condition that can otherwise devastate lives. As national leaders in stroke care, Plymouth’s model may serve as a benchmark for others striving to improve outcomes for one of the UK’s most challenging health issues.

**Legal Complaint Urges Probe into 2006 Parliamentary Remarks by Northern Ireland’s First Minister** A Belfast businessman has lodged a formal complaint with police, calling for an investigation into remarks made by former First Minister Peter Robinson in 2006. The legal action, brought by Peter Curistan, the developer of Belfast’s Odyssey complex, alleges that Robinson’s parliamentary claim linking him to “IRA dirty money” constitutes *misfeasance in public office*. Robinson, who was First Minister from 2008 to 2015, responded dismissively to the BBC, stating, “The police may have to waste their time with this but I do not.” Curistan’s case hinges on whether political statements with no supporting evidence—and alleged long-term harm—warrant legal action. The PSNI has yet to comment on the matter. The dispute resurfaces amid ongoing tensions over historical claims and accountability in Northern Ireland’s political landscape.

**Two Teenagers Arrested Over Arson Suspected at Baitul Futuh Mosque in Morden** Two teenagers, aged 16 and 14, were arrested on Sunday on suspicion of arson following a major fire at the Baitul Futuh Mosque in Morden, south London. We are thankful for the bravery of emergency services and the solidarity of our community.” The mosque’s community center and front hall sustained partial damage, but no injuries or fatalities were reported. The two arrested youths remain in police custody at a south London station as investigations continue into the incident’s cause. **Innovative “Robojelly” Robot Inspired by Jellyfish Could Revolutionize Underwater Rescue** Scientists are developing a soft-bodied robot inspired by jellyfish, nicknamed *Robojelly*, which could one day aid in underwater rescue missions. Researchers at the University of Texas at Dallas, led by Yonas Tadesse, have published a study in *Smart Materials and Structures* detailing the robot’s novel design and propulsion system, which uses external hydrogen as fuel—a first in underwater robotics. The project draws from the jellyfish’s simple yet efficient movement. Natural jellyfish propel themselves by contracting their bell-shaped bodies, expelling water. To mimic this, *Robojelly* uses shape memory alloys (SMAs)—materials that return to their original shape when heated. These SMAs are wrapped in carbon nanotubes and coated with platinum black powder, a catalyst for chemical reactions. When hydrogen and oxygen in water interact with the platinum, heat is generated, triggering the SMAs to flex and replicate the jellyfish’s undulating motion. “What sets this robot apart is its fuel source,” said Dr. Tadesse. “To our knowledge, this is the first successful powering of an underwater robot using external hydrogen as a fuel source.” The system eliminates the need for batteries, offering a sustainable energy solution for deep-sea operations. Currently, *Robojelly* flexes all eight segments of its bell simultaneously. However, the team aims to develop independent control for each segment, enabling more precise movement and maneuverability. This advancement could allow the robot to navigate complex environments or deliver aid in rescue scenarios. Funded by the U.S. Office of Naval Research, the project underscores efforts to create adaptive technologies for the Navy and Marine Corps. While still in early development, *Robojelly* represents a promising step toward bio-inspired robotics capable of tackling underwater challenges previously deemed insurmountable by traditional machines. As researchers refine its design, the future of underwater exploration and emergency response may hinge on this unique blend of biology and engineering.

A new internet-based system will restrict recruitment to licensed Saudi agencies, aiming to prevent unscrupulous intermediaries from exploiting vulnerable laborers. Residents often opt to shop in nearby towns like Chester or Runcorn to avoid the delays, with Hooper noting that the 40-minute bridge wait could instead allow a round-trip to Chester’s city center. Osborne called the queues “unacceptable” and urged the construction of a second bridge between Barnton and Winnington. He has lobbied Cheshire West and Chester Council, neighboring MP Graham Evans, and the transport secretary for a solution. The council confirmed a feasibility study will soon begin, but campaigners warn the situation is worsening. With plans for 4,300 new homes in Northwich, traffic is expected to soar. “This is a critical infrastructure gap,” Hooper said. “Without action, our community risks being strangled by congestion.” While the bridge’s historical significance complicates expansion plans, Osborne insisted progress is vital. “Modernizing this link is not just about easing traffic—it’s about future-proofing our economy,” he said. The council declined to comment further, citing the ongoing study. For now, residents remain stranded, caught between heritage and the demands of a growing town.

Under his regime, opposition has been ruthlessly suppressed, with the specter of Islamic militancy used to justify restrictions on civil rights. Speculation about Karimov’s successor gained traction internationally when his eldest daughter, Gulnara Karimova, emerged as a prominent political and business figure. In 2014, Gulnara was charged with leading a crime ring allegedly responsible for stealing £40 million ($65 million) in assets, marking her abrupt fall from grace. Analysts suggest her downfall stemmed from family infighting and a rivalry with Rustem Inoyatov, the influential head of Uzbek security services. Uzbekistan’s political structure remains a one-party system, with the December 2014 parliamentary elections—only the second since 1995—highlighting the regime’s consolidation of power. The parliament, meeting sporadically, functions as a rubber stamp, endorsing government policies without meaningful debate. Genuine opposition operates in exile, as the state criminalizes dissent. Karimov’s rule, now in its third decade, has entrenched a system where power is concentrated at the top, leaving a vacuum in governance and accountability. With no credible mechanism for democratic transition, the future of Uzbekistan remains uncertain, its trajectory shaped by the enduring shadow of its autocratic leader.

**Beamish Museum to Replicate Home of Legendary North East Artist Norman Cornish** The historic home of Norman Cornish, the celebrated painter renowned for capturing the essence of the industrial North East, is set to be recreated at Beamish Museum’s new £17 million 1950s Town and Farm. The 1950s house at 33 Bishop’s Close Street in Spennymoor, where Cornish lived as a child and later with his wife and children, will be joined by a replica of the artist’s studio, offering visitors a glimpse into his life and legacy. Cornish, a miner turned artist, began sketching and painting as a teenager while working in the mines at just 14. His passion for art flourished through the Spennymoor Settlement, a community initiative established in 1930 to provide working-class families with access to the arts. Known as the Pitman’s Academy, the settlement nurtured talents like writer Sid Chaplin and artist Tom McGuinness. Cornish, a standout student, left the mines in 1966 due to a back injury and dedicated himself to art full-time. The Cornish family resided in Bishop’s Close Street until 1967, when they moved to Whitworth Terrace in Spennymoor. Before his death at 94 in 2014, Cornish arranged for the museum to receive over 100 unfinished paintings, dozens of sketches, and personal items—including his paint-stained chair and carpet—offering a poignant insight into his creative world. The replica at Beamish will not only showcase the artist’s family life but also highlight the social and cultural impact of the Spennymoor Settlement. “We’re delighted to be sharing the story of Norman Cornish and the Spennymoor Settlement in our planned 1950s Town,” said Lisa Peacock, a project officer at Beamish. “We’re honoured to have received these amazing pieces of history from the studio and home of someone who so skilfully captured everyday life in the North East.” By recreating this slice of history, the museum aims to preserve Cornish’s legacy and celebrate the transformative power of art in a community rooted in industry. **South Korea Postpones Presidential Trip Amid Escalating MERS Outbreak** South Korean President Park Geun-hye has delayed a scheduled trip to the United States to address a rapidly spreading outbreak of the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), which has now claimed nine lives and infected 108 people. The announcement came as health authorities confirmed two additional deaths and 13 new infections, marking the worst outbreak outside the Middle East, where the virus was first detected in 2012. The crisis began last month when a South Korean citizen returned from a business trip to Saudi Arabia carrying the virus, triggering a chain of transmissions. Critics have accused authorities of inadequate response, with some alleging delayed containment measures fueled public panic. Over 3,439 individuals now in isolation—a surge from 2,500 on Monday—and nearly 2,500 schools and universities, primarily in Seoul and Gyeonggi province, have closed to curb spread. Park’s office stated the postponement of her Washington visit was to “prioritize public safety and expedite containment of MERS.” The trip, originally set for June 16, was to include a meeting with U.S. President Barack Obama to discuss security and economic ties, including tensions with North Korea. A spokesperson emphasized rescheduling for the “earliest mutually convenient time.” The outbreak has also reached China, with one confirmed case reported in a man now in stable condition. Chinese authorities noted 75 quarantined individuals tested negative for MERS. MERS, a coronavirus with no known cure, carries a high fatality rate and has raised global concerns. South Korea’s Health Ministry faces mounting pressure to strengthen containment efforts amid public frustration. As the situation evolves, the government has urged citizens to adhere to health guidelines and avoid unnecessary travel. The crisis underscores the challenges of managing infectious diseases in an interconnected world, with South Korea’s experience likely to influence global health strategies. For now, the focus remains on halting the spread before it escalates further.

**Short SC1 Aircraft Honored with Prestigious Engineering Heritage Award** The Short SC1, the first British fixed-wing vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) aircraft, has been awarded the 76th Engineering Heritage Award by the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (IME), recognizing its groundbreaking role in advancing aviation technology. The accolade, presented on Thursday in Belfast, underscores the aircraft’s historic significance as a pioneer in VTOL innovation and its lasting legacy on military aviation. Developed by Shorts in the 1950s at its experimental workshops in Belfast, the SC1 first took to the skies in 1957. It made history in 1960 as the first British fixed-wing aircraft to transition seamlessly between vertical and horizontal flight, a feat achieved through its revolutionary autostabilizer control system. This technology laid the foundation for the iconic Harrier Jump Jet family, which became a cornerstone of global VTOL aviation. The SC1’s design and testing provided critical insights that propelled the UK to a world-leading position in vertical flight technology. The aircraft, now preserved at the Ulster Folk and Transport Museum in County Down, will be honored in a permanent display, allowing visitors to explore its engineering marvel. Dr. Jim McGreevy, Director at National Museums Northern Ireland, accepted the award on behalf of the museum. “The SC1 holds a special place in our collection,” he said. “It exemplifies the ingenuity of Northern Ireland’s engineering heritage and offers a unique opportunity for people worldwide to learn about this remarkable achievement.” The award was presented by Professor Isobel Pollock, President of the IME, who hails from Ballymoney, County Antrim. A proud moment for Northern Ireland, Pollock described the honor as “particularly delightful” as it marked the first IME Engineering Heritage Award for the region. The accolade joins an elite list of previous winners, including the Thames Barrier, the Channel Tunnel, Tower Bridge, and the Falkirk Wheel. “The SC1 is a worthy recipient and a testament to engineering excellence,” Pollock said, noting its role in enabling military operations from unconventional locations such as car parks or fields, eliminating the need for vulnerable runways or airbases. Vertical takeoff and landing capabilities, pioneered by the SC1, proved invaluable for naval operations, allowing aircraft to operate from smaller carriers. The research and development behind the SC1 not only advanced the UK’s aerospace sector but also inspired future innovations in military and commercial aviation. The IME, founded in 1847 by railway pioneer George Stephenson, continues to celebrate engineering milestones that shape society. The SC1’s recognition reaffirms Northern Ireland’s contributions to global technological progress and highlights the enduring impact of its engineering legacy. As the aircraft remains a centerpiece at the Ulster Folk and Transport Museum, visitors can now appreciate a pivotal chapter in aviation history that took flight from Belfast.

Elphicke emphasized the urgency of resolving the crisis, stating, “What’s more important than compensation is for people to know what the situation will be when they return after the holidays.”

**QPR Boss Redknapp Backs Financial Fair Play Reforms as Club Faces Potential £54m Fine** QPR chairman Tony Fernandes has signaled his intention to appeal a potential £54 million fine from the Football League (FL) over alleged breaches of Financial Fair Play (FFP) regulations. The penalty, linked to the club’s 2013-14 financial losses, could block Rangers from FL competitions if unpaid. The figure is based on comparisons with their £65.4 million losses in 2012-13, which triggered previous FFP scrutiny. Manager Harry Redknapp, a long-time advocate for financial equality, criticized the current system, arguing: “Fair play would be everyone having £30 million a year to spend.” He expanded, referencing QPR’s upcoming clash with Manchester United: “To make it fair play, we should be able to spend as much as Manchester United have spent before we play them. If fined, the FL risks struggling to enforce penalties against a club no longer in its jurisdiction, complicating enforcement. Financial figures for 2013-14, expected before November’s end, will likely dictate next steps. FFP penalties often target relegated clubs, whose Premier League wage costs—despite brief top-flight spells—can inflate losses. Redknapp, in charge since November 2012, may secure a new deal by Friday, reiterating his commitment to Loftus Road. The case underscores tensions between financial regulations and club mobility, as the FL and Premier League navigate FFP enforcement in an era of soaring expenditures. For QPR, the appeal process and potential sanctions could shape their Championship journey.

**Global Spread of C. difficile Traced Through Genetic Analysis** Researchers have used genetic code analysis to trace the global spread of antibiotic-resistant strains of *Clostridium difficile* (C. difficile), revealing how two particularly virulent strains emerged in North America and radiated across continents, fueling outbreaks in hospitals worldwide. The findings, published in *Nature Genetics*, highlight the role of antibiotic resistance in driving the evolution and persistence of this deadly pathogen. C. difficile is a leading cause of hospital-acquired infections, linked to 14,000 deaths annually in the U.S. alone. While present in healthcare settings for decades, concerns intensified in the past ten years due to large-scale outbreaks in Europe, the U.S., and Canada. These were driven by a rare variant of C. difficile, now the most common cause of the infection in North America. By analyzing the rapidly mutating genetic code of 151 C. difficile samples collected from 19 countries, researchers mapped the global transmission routes of two antibiotic-resistant strains: FQR1 and FQR2. Strain FQR1 originated in the U.S. and spread domestically to Switzerland and South Korea, while FQR2 emerged in Canada before expanding across North America, Europe, and Australia, with four documented introductions into the UK. The study underscores how interconnected global healthcare systems are, as resistant strains can spread internationally within months. Dr. Trevor Lawley of the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute emphasized the implications: “Understanding how these strains emerged offers lessons for future outbreaks. The fact that two distinct strains became dominant shows such events are more frequent than previously realized—and antibiotic resistance is a key driver.” The rise of fluoroquinolone resistance appears to have transformed C. difficile into a more severe and transmissible threat. Prof. Brendan Wren of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, who has studied the bacteria for 25 years, explained: “Once it became resistant to fluoroquinolones, it not only evaded treatment but also gained a competitive edge in hospitals. This resistance has been critical to its evolution and persistence.” Advances in genomic sequencing have made tracking such outbreaks faster and more affordable. The cost to sequence a bacterium’s genome has dropped to £40–60, and the process now takes less than a day. **Valeant Pursues Allergan Takeover Amid Board Rejection** Valeant Pharmaceuticals has vowed to escalate its bid for Allergan, despite the Irish drugmaker’s rejection of its offer earlier this week. Combined with lingering effects from a previous coronal hole, the BGS warns of “stormy conditions again, with a chance for some isolated G3 periods.” Visibility will peak on Thursday, with the best opportunities for observers in Scotland, northern England, and Northern Ireland. Recent confirmed sightings include the Isle of Lewis, Aberdeenshire, and Northumberland, where the aurora has already dazzled onlookers this week. “We’re in a prime window for aurora viewing,” said a BGS spokesperson. “Clear, dark skies overnight Wednesday and Thursday will maximize chances, especially in the north.” Weather permitting, stargazers are advised to head to rural locations away from light pollution. Zahran, who has been praised for his community engagement and culinary reputation, faces an uncertain future despite local efforts to preserve his tenure. The upcoming meeting between Zahran and Enterprise Inns remains the focal point of a tense standoff, with residents hoping for a resolution that honors the pub’s legacy. As the community rallies behind Zahran, the outcome of these discussions could set a precedent for landlord-tenant relations in the hospitality sector, where local businesses often grapple with corporate decisions perceived as prioritizing profit over people. *For updates on this and other local stories, stay tuned to Coventry and Warwickshire news outlets.*

**European Space Agency Awaits Clarity After Schiaparelli’s Mars Landing Failure** The European Space Agency (Esa) faces uncertainty after its Schiaparelli lander lost contact just minutes before its scheduled descent onto Mars. Initially expected to touch down on the Red Planet at 14:58 GMT (15:58 BST), the mission lost radio signals from the craft just 60 seconds prior. A satellite tasked with monitoring the landing, Mars Express, also failed to provide additional details about the final moments of the journey, leaving the mission’s fate unclear. Esa has emphasized it will not draw conclusions until further data from other orbiters at Mars becomes available. These satellites may have captured insights missed by Mars Express, offering a chance to identify what went wrong. In a silver lining, Esa confirmed the Trace Gas Orbiter, Schiaparelli’s mothership, has successfully entered its intended orbit around Mars. Over the coming years, the orbiter will study the planet’s atmosphere, searching for gases like methane that could hint at geological or biological activity. Landing on Mars remains a notoriously high-stakes endeavor. Schiaparelli, a 130kg test probe, relied on a heat shield, parachute, and retro rockets to slow its descent through the planet’s thin atmosphere—a process dubbed “seven minutes of terror.” Even minor errors in timing or trajectory can lead to catastrophic failure. If Schiaparelli is confirmed lost, it would echo Esa’s earlier disappointment with the Beagle-2 lander in 2003, which failed shortly after touching down despite a safe descent. Schiaparelli was designed as a technology demonstrator, paving the way for a more ambitious mission: a six-wheeled rover planned for 2021. That project, ExoMars, will depend on the landing systems tested by Schiaparelli, including its Doppler radar for altitude sensing and advanced navigation algorithms. “Mars has a reputation for being a harsh judge,” said BBC science correspondent Jonathan Amos, noting the 40% success rate of missions to the planet. Esa’s next steps hinge on data from its orbiters, which could shed light on whether Schiaparelli’s systems failed during entry, descent, or after landing. For now, the agency balances cautious hope with the sobering reality that Mars remains a formidable challenge. *Contact Jonathan Amos at [email protected] or follow him on Twitter: @BBCAmos.*

**Phillip Simmons Faces Double Murder Charges in Hull** Phillip Simmons, 38, of May Street, has been charged with two counts of murder and one of burglary following the discovery of two men’s bodies at a house on the street last Friday. Daniel Hatfield, 52, and Matthew Higgins, 49, were found with “significant multiple injuries.” Simmons, remanded in custody after appearing at Hull Magistrates’ Court, is due to face Hull Crown Court on Wednesday. Two women arrested in connection with the deaths have been released: a 36-year-old on police bail until next month and a 27-year-old unconditionally. Authorities have not disclosed further details about the investigation. The case remains under active review, with ongoing inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the fatal incidents. Updates will be provided as more information emerges.

**Tragedy and Remembrance: Memorial Held for Eight Children in Queensland** A solemn memorial service, *Keriba Omasker*—meaning “our children” in the region’s ancestral language—was held in Cairns, Queensland, for eight children killed in a devastating incident. Prime Minister Tony Abbott attended, tweeting, “Today in Cairns. Sad beyond words. Keriba Omasker.” The victims, four boys and four girls aged 18 months to 14 years, were murdered by their mother, Mersane Warria, 37, who has been charged with their deaths. Another victim was her niece. Over 5,000 people gathered for prayers and tributes, as leaders, including Mr. Abbott, laid wreaths. The children’s bodies were transported to Martyn Place Cemetery for burial. Warria, hospitalized but not at the funeral, faces legal proceedings. Authorities plan to demolish the family home, replacing it with a public memorial to honor the children. The tragedy has left the community reeling, with calls for support for First Nations communities grappling with systemic challenges. The service underscored a collective grief, blending cultural traditions and national solidarity in mourning the loss of young lives.

**Vandals Damage Northern Ireland’s Iconic Rope Bridge; Authorities Aiming for Quick Reopening** *National Trust Works to Repair Structure After Ropes Were Cut, Threatening Popular Tourist Attraction* A historic rope bridge in Ballintoy, County Antrim, was closed Wednesday after vandals cut through critical ropes, sparking a safety inspection and leaving hundreds of visitors unable to cross the popular tourist spot. The National Trust, which manages the site, announced the damage had been repaired and expressed hope to reopen the bridge by Thursday, pending no further issues. The 100-foot (30-meter) suspension bridge, linking two cliffs above the North Atlantic, was damaged overnight when an unknown individual partially severed the hand rope and supporting cables. Frank Devlin of the National Trust told BBC Radio Ulster’s *Evening Extra* that staff discovered the vandalism before the bridge opened to visitors, preventing potential accidents. “We’re thankful to get the engineers on site promptly this afternoon to begin repairs,” he said, adding that the vandalism could have led to prolonged closures had repairs not been swift. The attack, described as “mindless” by the National Trust, prompted police to investigate as an act of criminal damage. PSNI Inspector Colin Reeves stated that a padlock on the bridge’s gate was removed sometime between 6:30 p.m. Tuesday and 9:30 a.m. Wednesday, enabling the damage. “The hand rope on the right side and supporting ropes were partially cut, posing serious risks,” he said, urging witnesses to come forward. The bridge, first erected in 1755 by local fishermen, has become a magnet for thrill-seekers and photographers, drawing record numbers last year. To manage crowds, the National Trust introduced timed tickets, a measure now under threat due to the vandalism. Devlin emphasized the bridge’s economic importance, noting that prolonged closure could have severely impacted tourism in the region. The National Trust initially tweeted the bridge would be closed “indefinitely,” but revised its stance after engineers assessed the damage. “Our staff’s vigilance was crucial in identifying the harm before anyone could access the bridge,” Devlin added. Visitors turned away Wednesday expressed frustration, though

**Teacher Exploited Role as Educator and Guide Leader to Coerce Girls, Court Hears** Nicholas Taylor, 27, a former primary school teacher and Girl Guide leader from Barnet, north London, has been handed a lifetime sexual harm prevention order after using his position of trust to exploit girls aged 10–15 on Instagram, a court was told. St Albans Crown Court heard how Taylor, who worked at a south Hertfordshire school, posed as a 13-year-old boy to befriend victims. He coercively encouraged them to send nude images, threatening to post the material online or take his own life unless they complied. Prosecutor Peter Shaw emphasized the psychological manipulation, stating Taylor exploited “the threat to humiliate and cause distress” to ensure obedience. The court was shown how Taylor shared the explicit photos with other children, escalating the abuse. Judge Jonathan Carroll condemned Taylor as “every parent’s worst nightmare,” highlighting the profound betrayal of trust by a figure entrusted to nurture children. “The levels of abuse you have sunk to simply beggars belief,” he said, underscoring the sacred responsibility teachers hold in shaping young lives. Impact statements revealed the lasting trauma on victims, who now struggle with distrust of online strangers. At an earlier hearing, Taylor pleaded guilty to six counts of inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, two counts of making indecent photographs of a child, and one count of distributing such material. The case has sparked renewed concern over the risks of online grooming, particularly by those in positions of authority. A spokesperson for the NSPCC noted the incident underscores the need for vigilance in safeguarding children’s digital interactions. Taylor’s sentencing, including the indefinite prevention order, marks a severe punishment for crimes that have left victims grappling with the violation of their childhood trust. The court emphasized the gravity of preying on the vulnerable, sending a clear message that such exploitation will not be tolerated.

**Cambridgeshire Artist Wins Prestigious BP Portrait Award for Enigmatic “Girl in a Liberty Dress”** The Cambridgeshire-based artist James Drummond has been announced as the winner of the 2016 BP Portrait Award for his evocative work *Girl in a Liberty Dress*. The £30,000 prize, along with a £5,000 commission, recognizes the painting’s “subtle, enigmatic nature” and the “indelible impression” of the artist’s technical mastery. The piece, featuring artist Victoria Buchanan, is the latest in a series of notable works by Drummond, whose portraits have been celebrated in the BP Portrait Award exhibitions for over a decade. Drummond’s portrait of Buchanan, created during a collaborative exhibition with the William Morris Society, is imbued with symbolism. Buchanan wore a vintage Liberty dress for the piece, a nod to the shared connection between both artists and the William Morris aesthetic. “The dress became a narrative thread,” Drummond explained, linking his work to the Arts and Crafts movement that Morris championed. This is not the first time Drummond has captured Buchanan; she also posed in the 2013 and 2014 BP Portrait exhibitions, with her likenesses earning acclaim for their depth and emotional resonance. The competition, now in its 26th year, draws entries from artists worldwide, with a jury of art experts selecting works that balance technical excellence with emotional impact.

**Young Dolphin’s Resilient Journey from Stranding to Recovery Captivates Scientists** In a remarkable story of survival and scientific breakthrough, a juvenile bottlenose dolphin named Spirtle has made a triumphant return to the Moray Firth after being rescued from a life-threatening stranding in May. The young animal’s journey, now being closely monitored by researchers, marks the first time in the UK that scientists have tracked a dolphin’s behavior following such an event. Spirtle’s ordeal began on 29 May when a couple, who had become disoriented while driving to a dolphin-watching hotspot at Chanonry Point, stumbled upon the stranded dolphin at the Cromarty Firth. The pair, navigating the tidal mudflats by mistake, spotted the animal floundering in the exposed silt and immediately alerted local authorities. A collaborative rescue effort involving Scottish Marine Animal Stranding Scheme (SMASS) officers, British Divers Marine Life Rescue volunteers, the Scottish SPCA, and North 58 Sea Adventures swiftly refloated the animal and returned it to deeper waters. Now, nearly a month later, Spirtle has reappeared in the Moray Firth, where University of Aberdeen researchers have documented her recovery. The dolphin, identified by a severe blister on her right flank—a wound SMASS described as “horrific” but now showing signs of healing—has returned to normal behaviors, including foraging. Barbara Cheney, a research fellow at the university’s Lighthouse Field Station in Cromarty, called the case “unique” and emphasized its significance. “We’ve not seen anything like this before,” she said. “Being able to track her recovery provides invaluable insights into post-stranding rehabilitation in wild populations.” The injury, caused by unknown factors, has surprised scientists due to its severity. “Dolphins’ skin composition likely helped her survive a wound that other animals might not have,” explained Dr. Andrew Brownlow of SMASS, who called the initial rescue “a miracle.” The mudflat where Spirtle was found dries out almost entirely at low tide, leaving stranding a near-certainty for the animal. **Lynx House Scraps Controversial Wristband Policy Amid Scrutiny Over Conditions** Lynx House, a shelter for asylum seekers in Wales, has abandoned a contentious wristband policy criticized as dehumanizing and a potential target for abuse. The decision follows allegations of overcrowding and substandard living conditions. Welsh Affairs Committee chair David Davies announced a parliamentary visit to the site, emphasizing the need to “see the place for ourselves” and “scrutinize behind the headlines.” He noted Wales hosts over 1,000 asylum seekers, urging urgent oversight amid an ongoing refugee crisis. The Clearsprings Group, which operates the service, previously defended the wristbands as a “reliable and effective way” to manage support but confirmed their discontinuation. Davies stressed the committee’s commitment to ensuring accountability as challenges in the asylum system persist. Critics argue the policy shift is long overdue, with concerns over dignity and safety remaining unresolved. The visit aims to assess current conditions and policy reforms.

**Moon Jae-in’s Victory Marks Shift in South Korea’s North Korea Policy Amid Domestic Renewal** South Koreans have elected Moon Jae-in as their new president, signaling a potential reset in the nation’s approach to North Korea and a desire to move beyond the political turmoil that led to the country’s first ever presidential impeachment. With 80% of votes tallied, the center-left Democratic Party candidate led with 40% of the vote, according to the National Election Commission, comfortably ahead of conservative challenger Hong Joon-pyo (25.5%) and centrist Ahn Cheol-soo (21.4%). The election, called after a corruption scandal forced the removal of former President Park Geun-hye, who faces charges of allowing her close confidante, Choi Soon-sil, to extort money from companies, underscores voters’ yearning for change. Park, the daughter of late military ruler Park Chung-hee, denies wrongdoing. Moon, a 64-year-old human rights lawyer and former senior aide to the late liberal President Roh Moo-hyun, pledged to be “a president for all South Koreans” in a speech to supporters in Seoul’s Gwanghwamun Square. His victory is expected to bring a dramatic shift in inter-Korean relations. Unlike Park’s administration, which severed most ties with Pyongyang and aligned closely with U.S. sanctions, Moon advocates a return to dialogue with North Korea.

**Tragedy at Bolton Apartment Block: Property Firm Admits Negligence in Fatal Lift Incident** In a tragic case of avoidable negligence, a property management company has been held accountable for the death of 27-year-old Craig Jones, who fell five floors down a lift shaft in Bolton town centre in August 2014. Warwick Estates Property Management admitted breaching health and safety regulations at Bolton Crown Court, following a harrowing incident that highlighted systemic failures in maintaining the lift at Marsden House. The court heard that Mr. Jones and a friend became trapped between the fourth and fifth floors of the lift on August 30, 2014. After pressing the emergency alarm, they found the call system unresponsive—a recurring issue that had plagued the lift for months. Desperate to escape, Mr. Jones lost his footing while climbing and plummeted to his death when an item of clothing caught on an unknown object. Judge Clayton condemned the company’s inaction, stating the faults had gone “unaddressed for a substantial period of time,” turning the lift into “a serious accident waiting to happen.” Investigations revealed the lift had broken down repeatedly, with the emergency system failing intermittently and no mobile signal to aid trapped residents. The court also learned that other occupants had attempted “self-rescue” after being stranded, underscoring a pattern of neglect. Warwick Estates admitted it had failed to maintain the lift systems and neglected to scrutinize maintenance reports on five occasions. The judge emphasized that if these reports had been reviewed, “serious faults” might have been identified and rectified. Speaking after the sentencing, Mr. Jones’ mother, Samantha, described the ruling as “comforting,” reiterating that her son’s death was “completely unnecessary and avoidable.” She added: “He had no choice and that has been shown clearly now. [My son] had his whole life in front of him, and it was taken away by incompetence.” The firm was ordered to pay £45,000 in costs. The case serves as a stark reminder of the consequences of corporate negligence in safety-critical infrastructure, leaving families and communities demanding stricter accountability. Mr. Jones’ death has sparked renewed calls for rigorous maintenance checks and transparency in property management, ensuring such tragedies are never repeated.

**Lions Part with Several Players After Wembley Defeat** Carlisle United have confirmed the release of four senior players, including Carlos Edwards, Ed Upson, Lee Martin, and John Marquis, as well as three under-21s—Jack Powell, Chris Parr, and Keaton Wood. Goalkeeper Mark Beevers is in contract negotiations, while defenders Byron Webster and Joe Martin have triggered one-year extension clauses. The club’s relegation to the EFL after a 3-1 Wembley play-off final loss to Barnsley has prompted restructuring as they aim to rebuild for next season.

**Global Report Highlights Persistent Gender Gap in Work Hours and Economic Inequality** A new report by the World Economic Forum (WEF) reveals that women, on average, work 50 minutes more per day than men—a disparity rooted in unpaid labor and systemic economic inequalities. According to the WEF’s Global Gender Gap Report, closing the gender economic gap could take 170 years at the current pace, marking the largest gap in economic opportunity since 2008. Despite nearly 240 million women joining the global workforce in the past decade, progress remains uneven, with unpaid domestic and caregiving responsibilities disproportionately burdening women. The report underscores that while men perform 34% more paid work than women, women still spend significantly more time on unpaid tasks such as housework, childcare, and elder care. When combined with paid work, this translates to women working over a month more annually than men. The disparity is most pronounced in countries like India, Portugal, and Estonia, where women work more than 50 additional days per year. In the UK, women contribute nearly 12 more workdays than men. Only six nations globally see men outworking women, including Nordic countries such as Iceland, Sweden, and Norway. In these regions, shared parental leave policies encourage more equitable distribution of caregiving, fostering higher female labor participation. Shared parental leave, experts note, is critical for balancing career and family life. Vesselina Ratcheva, a WEF data analyst, told the BBC that such policies “allow families to plan their lives, fit having children with their careers, and share responsibilities.” However, parental leave remains heavily skewed toward mothers, with governments more likely to fund maternity than paternity leave. In some Eastern European countries, extended paid leave exceeding two years has paradoxically reduced women’s workforce participation, suggesting limits to the policy’s effectiveness. Economists argue that addressing the unpaid care economy could spur global economic growth. The International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC) estimates that investing just 2% of a country’s GDP into care sectors could create millions of new jobs. For instance, such an investment could generate nearly 13 million jobs in the U.S., 3.5 million in Japan, and 1.5 million in the U.K. The report calls for systemic reforms, including better childcare infrastructure,

**Sky to Transition 950 Customer Service Staff to New Supplier by April 15** Sky has confirmed the termination of its contract with Response on April 15, marking a significant shift in its customer service operations. The satellite broadcaster is streamlining its outsourced supplier base, reducing the number from nine to two, with Falkirk-based firm HEROtsc set to assume the Sky account. Around 950 Response employees, who previously supported Sky’s customer service, will transition to the new provider. The affected staff, currently based in Falkirk, will relocate to HEROtsc’s newly established call center at Glasgow’s Atlantic Quay. Brian Bannatyne, managing director of Response, expressed gratitude for the team’s dedication, stating, “Our people employed on the Sky account have delivered a great service to Sky’s customers. We are confident they will continue to do so.” He emphasized Response’s commitment to business transformation and future growth, calling the move an exciting opportunity. Chris Stylianou, managing director of Sky’s customer service group, praised the expertise of the workforce, noting, “We have particularly valued the contribution of many of the committed and talented customer service advisors who Response has helped train and nurture.” He added that Sky is “delighted” these employees will continue supporting its customers under HEROtsc. HEROtsc has pledged to collaborate closely with Response during the transition, ensuring a “smooth and straightforward” process for affected staff. A spokesperson stated, “We fully understand this can be a confusing time..... and Response and HEROtsc are working together to make the transfer process as simple as possible.” The transition reflects Sky’s ongoing efforts to optimize its operations, with HEROtsc expected to inherit a team renowned for its customer service expertise. Response and HEROtsc will initiate a formal consultation process to facilitate the staff handover, underscoring a shared focus on stability and continuity for Sky’s customers.

A man died a week after being struck by a Ford Focus on Grove Lane, Handsworth, at 17:55 BST on 24 June, West Midlands Police confirmed. The 23-year-old driver was questioned at the scene, while officers urge witnesses to come forward. The collision occurred near the site where two sisters were killed in 2022; the driver there received a four-year sentence for causing death by dangerous driving. Authorities reiterated safety concerns in the area, emphasizing the need for public assistance to prevent further tragedies.

**Rio Police Families Demand Resources Amid Rising Violence and Deaths** Hundreds of mourners and supporters gathered along Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana beach this week to demand urgent action as the city’s police face a deadly surge in violence. With 91 officers killed in Rio state so far this year—already exceeding the 2016 total—families of fallen officers are sounding the alarm over inadequate resources, dangerous working conditions, and a deepening crisis in public security. “We see families being destroyed every day,” said Rogeria Quaresma, wife of a police officer, at the protest. “I don’t accept becoming the next widow.” Her words echoed the desperation of hundreds who marched to honor colleagues and call for government support. The march followed the fatal shooting of Sgt. Hudson Araujo in the Vidigal favela over the weekend, the latest in a string of violent encounters linked to Rio’s entrenched criminal networks. The Brazilian government announced last week it would deploy an additional 1,000 federal agents to assist local police, but families argue such measures are insufficient. Since the end of the 2016 Olympics, violence in Rio has spiked, exacerbated by Brazil’s worst economic recession and a collapsing state budget. Political instability has further muddied the outlook, with no clear solutions in sight. Police officers are also pushing for changes to the penal code to classify attacks on law enforcement as “heinous crimes,” currently treated less severely than other murders. They criticize the media for highlighting alleged abuses during security operations while overshadowing the sacrifices of honest officers. “The hard work of those who protect this city is invisible,” said one protest organizer. Amnesty International has raised concerns about escalating police-related deaths, noting over 800 civilians killed in Rio state alone in 2016. Yet families argue that the true human cost lies with officers, whose lives are increasingly expendable in the war against organized crime. As protests continue, advocates stress that without adequate funding, equipment, and legal reforms, Rio’s security forces remain vulnerable—and the cycle of violence will only intensify.

**Road Closure Following Emergency Incident in Merthyr Tydfil** The Welsh Ambulance Service responded to a 999 call at 15:10 BST, transporting a casualty to Prince Charles Hospital. The road between Cefn Coed roundabout and B4276 Merthyr Road remains shut in both directions. Authorities have yet to confirm the individual’s condition. Travelers are advised to check for route disruptions.

A man was shot in the leg at his home on Butler Walk at 22:00 BST Tuesday. He answered the door but heard a loud bang before realizing he’d been wounded. He was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. His partner and four children were present. Detective Chief Inspector Peter Mullan condemned the "appalling incident" and urged witnesses to come forward. Authorities are investigating.

**Nine Injured in Tsunami Ride Derailment as HSE Bans Inspector** Nine people were injured, including several children, when five gondolas from the Tsunami inverted rollercoaster derailed at M&D’s amusement park in Scotland on June 26. The incident has prompted the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) to issue a prohibition notice barring the inspector responsible for certifying the ride’s safety. The HSE also ordered additional checks on all rides the inspector had deemed compliant, raising concerns about oversight in the amusement industry. According to an HSE interim investigation update, the inspector had issued a Declaration of Operational Compliance (DoC) for the Tsunami ride on June 10—a document confirming the attraction met safety standards just weeks before the accident. Enforcement action was taken against the inspector after the HSE concluded he failed to demonstrate “due diligence” in his work. The prohibition notice halts him from inspecting fairground attractions until its conditions are met, with 21 days to appeal the decision. During the incident, 10 individuals, including a 25-year-old woman later confirmed unharmed, were rushed to hospitals in Glasgow and Wishaw. Park officials reported the rollercoaster was operating when five gondolas detached from their rails at a bend, causing a dramatic fall to the ground. M&D’s amusement park remains closed indefinitely, though indoor attractions have reopened. A spokesperson for the park stated, “We’re unable to comment on any decisions taken by HSE.” The HSE emphasized it is collaborating with industry bodies to notify affected ride owners and ensure compliance with safety protocols. This marks a significant escalation in regulatory scrutiny, as the incident highlights potential gaps in fairground safety certification processes. The probe into the Tsunami derailment continues, with the park under pressure to address concerns over ride safety before reopening.

**Ford and Argo AI Partner to Launch Autonomous Vehicles by 2021** Ford has announced a collaboration with Argo AI, a self-driving technology firm, to develop a virtual driver system for autonomous vehicles. The automaker aims to deploy a fully driverless car by 2021, with Argo as its primary partner. Ford now holds a majority stake in Argo, which was co-founded by CEO Brian Salesky and COO Peter Rander, both former leaders of self-driving teams at Google and Uber. “Autonomous vehicles will redefine society as profoundly as Ford’s assembly line did a century ago,” said Ford CEO Mark Fields, emphasizing the transformative potential of the technology. Despite ambitious goals, Ford’s progress in California testing has lagged. In 2016, its autonomous vehicles logged just 590 miles, with three disengagements, including two aborted lane changes. This pales compared to BMW’s 638 miles and one disengagement, and Google’s 636,000 miles with 124 interventions. California’s reporting requirements highlight industry transparency gaps, as many states do not mandate mileage or disengagement data. Ford and Argo claim their partnership accelerates innovation, but the company faces mounting pressure to catch up to tech rivals.

**Campaigners Press Football Club to Reject Ex-Player Convicted of Rape** A growing online campaign led by blogger Jean Hatchet has intensified pressure on Oldham Athletic Football Club to reject a potential deal for former Wales international Lee Evans, a player convicted of rape in 2011 but who denies wrongdoing. Hatchet’s petition, which argues that Evans’ refusal to acknowledge his crime poses a dangerous precedent, has garnered over 45,000 signatures since launching last weekend. Oldham, currently considering a move for the 26-year-old striker, has yet to confirm its stance. Evans, who served half of a five-year prison sentence for the 2011 rape of a 19-year-old at a hotel in Rhyl, Denbighshire, was released in October and remains on probation. Hatchet, whose earlier campaign against Evans’ reinstatement at Sheffield United amassed 169,000 supporters, emphasized that his “atrocious crime” has not been fully addressed. “He hasn’t served his time—he’s still on licence,” she told BBC News. “Crucially, he hasn’t reformed or rehabilitated. He doesn’t acknowledge what rape is.” The petition calls on football authorities to “take a stand” against players returning to high-profile roles after violent offenses. Evans’ previous bid to return to Sheffield United—a club that briefly allowed him access to training facilities—was abandoned after public outcry, including criticism from Olympic heptathlon champion Jessica Ennis-Hill. Evans continues to maintain his innocence, with the Criminal Cases Review Commission currently investigating his conviction. The Football Association and Professional Footballers’ Association have faced calls to address their policies on players with criminal records. Oldham’s decision could set a significant benchmark for how sports organizations handle similar cases. As the debate unfolds, Hatchet reiterated her belief that football must prioritize moral responsibility over financial interests. “This is about sending a message that such behavior is unacceptable,” she said. The club’s final decision remains pending.

**Macedonia Tightens Border Controls Amid Rising Tensions and Fears of Closure** Under a drizzle of rain, hundreds of migrants and refugees huddle near the Macedonian-Greek border, waiting in line for their chance to cross into what they hope is safer ground. A single metal gate, operated by a Macedonian police officer, stands as a stark barrier between them and their destination. But as the officer methodically checks documents—demanding proof of Syrian, Iraqi, or Afghan nationality and a Greek stamp marking their initial entry—the gate is repeatedly opened and shut, leaving those waiting in limbo. The tension between Macedonian and Greek authorities has escalated, with Greek officials expressing frustration over what they perceive as insufficient cooperation. “They had been queuing in the rain when they could have been warm and dry in their tents,” said a Greek border officer, her voice laced with anger. The situation highlights the growing divide between EU member states over how to manage the migrant crisis, as Macedonia and its allies tighten controls to stem the flow of people toward Western Europe. Aid workers and humanitarian organizations warn that the increasing restrictions risk triggering a complete border closure, exacerbating the plight of vulnerable individuals. “The authorities and all humanitarian actors must have contingency plans,” said Alexandros Voulgaris of the UNHCR, which has been erecting additional family tents to prepare for potential surges in arrivals. “We are working on that now.” Macedonia is not acting alone. Teams of foreign police officers from Slovenia, Hungary, Croatia, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Serbia have joined Macedonian forces in patrolling the border. More EU nations are expected to participate, providing surveillance technology, registration support, and manpower. Foreign Minister Nikola Poposki hailed the collaboration, stating, “Our effort to decrease illegal migration is being made in an efficient manner with assistance from these countries.” He revealed that up to 350 to 400 foreign officers could be deployed, adding that

**Welsh Champions Set for Gibraltar Clash in Europa Qualifiers** Welsh Premier League champions Connah’s Quay Nomads will face Gibraltar’s Europa FC in the UEFA Europa Conference League first qualifying round, with the two-leg tie set for 27 June (home) and 4 July (away). Manager Gary Roberts has urged his squad to focus on the immediate challenge rather than potential next-round opponents. If the Reds secure progression, they will meet Croatian champions HNK Rijeka in the second round. However, Roberts insists attention remains firmly on the Gibraltar side. “We’re not thinking of the Croatian champions yet,” Roberts said. “These two games are our priority. We’ll respect Europa but remind players we’re the seeded team. We’ll be the favorites, but I won’t emphasize that—let’s focus on doing the job in the first leg.” Roberts emphasized a disciplined approach, stating, “Play your normal way, respect the opposition, but remember our status. Our message is simple: get the work done in June, then assess the second leg in July.” The first leg will be held at Park Hall, followed by the return fixture in Portugal.

**El Al Ordered to Halt Gender-Based Seat Swap Requests After Landmark Ruling** A Jerusalem court has ruled that Israel’s national airline, El Al, violated anti-discrimination laws by accommodating requests from strictly Orthodox Jewish passengers to swap seats with women, following a lawsuit brought by 83-year-old Holocaust survivor Renee Rabinowitz. The decision, announced by the Jerusalem Magistrate’s Court, marks a significant legal victory in a years-long debate over gender segregation in public spaces. Ms. Rabinowitz, who sued the airline after being asked to change seats during a 2015 flight from Newark to Tel Aviv, described the incident as “humiliating.” The court found that El Al staff had improperly acquiesced to requests from Orthodox men, who avoid physical contact with women outside their families under Jewish law (a practice known as *negiah*). The airline, however, denied pressuring passengers to comply with such demands, stating in court that it opposes discrimination. The Israel Religious Action Center (IRAC), a civil rights group representing Ms. Rabinowitz, hailed the ruling as a “huge victory” in the fight against gender segregation. The court ordered El Al to inform employees that facilitating seat swaps based on religious gender norms is illegal and awarded Ms. Rabinowitz 6,500 shekels (approximately $1,800) in damages. Similar requests have sparked frequent disputes and flight delays, according to *The Jerusalem Post*, with Orthodox men refusing to board until reseated away from women. The ruling ends a contentious policy that rights groups argued perpetuated discrimination. Ms. Rabinowitz told *The New York Times* the case was never about money but about “changing El Al’s policy,” a goal now achieved. While the airline has not announced specific plans for staff training, the court’s order could set a precedent for other airlines and public institutions grappling with balancing religious practices and equality laws. For Ms. Rabinowitz, the verdict is a personal and symbolic win: “The judge understood the issue,” she said. “It’s about fairness.”

**Scottish Government Advances Ferry Contract Process with Data Access for Bidders** The Scottish government has taken a significant step in the tendering process for the next Clyde and Hebrides Ferry Services contract by granting CalMac Ferries Ltd and Serco Caledonian Ferries Ltd access to critical data to inform their bids. **Yorkshire Building Society Rebrands N&P, Closes Current Accounts Without Deadline** The Yorkshire Building Society, the UK’s second-largest mutual, has announced that its plan to phase out the National & Provincial (N&P) brand, close branches, and discontinue current accounts will proceed without a fixed deadline for customers. While the original August 2023 target for account closures was set in January, the society now emphasizes flexibility, urging affected customers to complete the process within six months of receiving official communications. Approximately 35% of the 100,000 customers impacted by the transition—either closing accounts, switching banks, or in the process of doing so—have already acted, according to the Yorkshire. The society is staggering the delivery of letters to avoid overwhelming customers, with 70% of affected individuals already notified. The remaining correspondence will be sent by the end of July. Under the rebranding strategy, 28 N&P branches will close this year, while the remaining locations will transition to the Yorkshire Building Society name. A spokeswoman for the society clarified: “We are continuing to work closely with other financial providers to assist customers in switching or closing accounts. Customers who receive their letter should complete the process within six months. If not, we will support them on a case-by-case basis to facilitate a switch or closure.” Notably, N&P is not part of the UK’s Current Account Switching Service (CASS), which typically allows moves to occur within a few days. As a result, customers transferring to new providers may face a 12-day delay. However, many rival banks have extended cash incentives and perks to N&P customers, softening concerns over the slower process. Mike Regnier, chief executive of the Yorkshire Building Society, told BBC Radio 4’s *Money Box* earlier this year that the decision to end current accounts was “a real shame.” He explained that maintaining compliance with financial regulations for current accounts would require significant investment, which the mutual instead plans to redirect toward savings and mortgage products. The society assured that customers can continue to deposit funds or conduct standard banking activities via N&P current accounts until they decide to close or switch. The phased approach aims to minimize disruption, though the absence of a final deadline marks a shift from earlier timelines. The move reflects a broader strategy to focus on the Yorkshire’s core strengths in savings and home loans, aligning with its mutual ethos. As the transition unfolds, the society will provide ongoing support to ensure a “smooth and manageable” shift for all affected customers.
