The Unite leadership contest, coupled with the political standoff over North Sea policy, underscores the sector’s political significance. As McCluskey seeks re-election, the debate over government support highlights tensions between local and national priorities, with the industry’s future hanging in the balance. Both governments face mounting pressure to reconcile their rhetoric with concrete action as oil prices remain volatile and climate pressures mount.

**Coroner Concludes Azaria Chamberlain’s Death Was Caused by a Dingo, Ending a 40-Year Mystery** After decades of public scrutiny and legal battles, a coroner has officially concluded that eight-week-old Azaria Chamberlain was killed by a dingo in 1980, exonerating her parents once and for all. The ruling, delivered in Darwin by Northern Territory Coroner Elizabeth Morris, marked the end of a case that captivated Australia and split the nation for nearly 40 years. Lindy Chamberlain-Creighton and her husband, Michael Chamberlain, have long maintained that their daughter was taken by a dingo while the family was camping near Uluru (Ayers Rock) in the Northern Territory. In 1982, Lindy was convicted of Azaria’s murder and sentenced to life in prison, while Michael was found guilty of being an accessory. Both were released in 1986 after new evidence, including a fragment of Azaria’s dress found in a dingo-infested area, supported their account. However, the case remained shrouded in controversy, with courts previously issuing an open verdict that left lingering doubts about the couple’s innocence. Speaking outside Darwin’s courthouse, Lindy Chamberlain-Creighton expressed relief and gratitude. “Obviously we are relieved and delighted to come to the end of this saga,” she said, adding, “No longer will Australia be able to say that dingoes are not dangerous. We live in a beautiful country, but it is dangerous.” Michael Chamberlain echoed her sentiment, stating, “The truth is out. Now, some healing and a chance to put our daughter’s spirit to rest.” Coroner Morris delivered her verdict with deep emotion, offering her “sincere sympathy” to the Chamberlains for their loss. “Time does not remove the pain and sadness of the death of a child,” she said, releasing a formal death certificate and posting final findings on her office’s website. The couple’s campaign to officially blame dingoes for Azaria’s death gained momentum after presenting evidence of multiple dingo attacks on humans. Their efforts were bolstered by recent inquests, including a 2023 coroner’s review that confirmed a dingo likely took Azaria. The case has remained a cultural touchstone since 1980, even inspiring the 1988 film *A Cry in the Dark*, starring Meryl Streep. Three previous coroner’s inquests had failed to reach definitive conclusions, but the latest ruling finally brings closure to a family and a nation grappling with questions of justice, truth, and the untamed dangers of the Australian outback. As the Chamberlains’ ordeal ends, their daughter’s story continues to serve as a poignant reminder of the intersection between human vulnerability and the natural world’s unpredict

**Exhumation Ordered in Reinvestigation of Argentine Heir’s Death** A judge has ordered the exhumation of Carlos Saúl Facundo Menem’s remains as part of a renewed probe into his death, 29 years after the 26-year-old heir to Argentina’s former president died in a helicopter crash. Menem, known as *Carlitos*, perished on March 15, 1995, when the aircraft he was piloting struck high-voltage cables. However, his mother, Zulema Yoma, has long alleged it was a *terrorist attack*, claiming he was shot in the head and that his body may have been swapped to conceal bullet wounds. The remains will be exhumed on Wednesday from the San Justo Islamic Cemetery in Buenos Aires province for new DNA testing. Menem’s father, former president Carlos Menem, initially backed the official finding of an accidental death. However, he later accused Lebanon’s Hezbollah of orchestrating his son’s killing, linking it to the 1994 bombing of the Argentine-Israeli Mutual Association (Amia) cultural center in Buenos Aires—a deadly attack that killed 85 people and for which Argentine courts blamed Iran and Hezbollah. Iran has denied any involvement. Menem claimed he withheld Hezbollah’s alleged role for years due to “state secrets,” asserting his son’s death was meant to intimidate him into halting the Amia investigation. Yet he now faces charges of obstructing the same inquiry, with a trial opened in 2022. The Hezbollah connection resurfaced amid its ongoing investigations, as prosecutors accuse the group of carrying out the 1994 bombing. Forensic experts aim to resolve the decades-old mystery through DNA analysis, as both familial claims and political tensions complicate the case. The exhumation underscores lingering questions about accountability for Argentina’s deadliest terror attack—and whether Menem Jr.’s death was a tragic accident or a deliberate act of intimidation.

**Dash Cam Video Captures Close Call on A9 Tomich Junction** A tense moment unfolded on the A9 near Invergordon on Monday, as a dashboard camera video titled “A9 Tomich close shave” shows a car swerving to avoid a lorry suddenly pulling out at Tomich junction. The footage captures the vehicle mounting the verge, with slush sliding from its roof onto the windscreen. Police confirmed awareness of the incident, stating, “Police have been made aware of video footage of a lorry on the A9 at the Tomich junction, near Invergordon.” The clip has sparked concerns over road safety on the busy route.

**Harris Tweed Granted Historic Coat of Arms to Safeguard Heritage** The iconic Harris Tweed industry has been awarded a coat of arms by the Lord Lyon, King of Arms, marking a historic milestone in its decades-long mission to protect its unique heritage and quality. The design features an orb incorporated into a shield, symbolizing the global reach and craftsmanship of the handwoven cloth, traditionally made from wool of island sheep in Scotland’s Western Isles. The Harris Tweed Authority, which oversees the brand, emphasized that the grant adds an official layer of legal protection against imitations. Norman Macdonald, chairman of the Authority, hailed the move as the “ultimate protection” for a fabric renowned worldwide for its authenticity and craftsmanship. “Being awarded a Grant of Arms is a historic milestone for Harris Tweed, which has fought for decades to protect the sanctuary of our cloth,” he said. “It ensures the security of our heritage for generations to come.” The grant underscores the significance of Harris Tweed as a symbol of Scottish tradition, with the new coat of arms reinforcing its legacy of quality and artisanship.

**Sir Bradley Wiggins Aims to Shatter Hour Record in Lead-Up to Rio 2016** Four-time Olympic champion Sir Bradley Wiggins is set to tackle the individual world hour record as part of his preparation for the Rio 2016 Olympics, leading a new initiative called Team Wiggins. The 34-year-old British cyclist, who became the first British rider to win the Tour de France in 2012, expressed his gratitude for the sport that has shaped his career. “Cycling has given me everything,” Wiggins said. “I want to build something to inspire kids and to reach all those people who might be on the fringes of the sport.” His message is clear: “If I can do it, then so can you.” Team Wiggins will feature a roster of young British talent, including England’s Andy Tennant, Jon Dibben, Steven Burke, Daniel Patten, and Mike Thompson, alongside Welsh cyclist Owain Doull, Isle of Man’s Mark Christian, and Scotland’s Iain Paton. The team’s calendar of UK-based track and road events will be announced in spring 2015, offering riders opportunities to gain experience and train collectively. While operating independently of British Cycling, the organization has endorsed the venture, recognizing its potential to support Olympic ambitions. British Cycling CEO Ian Drake praised Wiggins’ leadership, noting, “Sir Bradley won his first Olympic medal in Sydney in 2000 and it’s impressive to see him still breaking new ground now, 15 years later with his Wiggins team.” Wiggins, who will continue with Team Sky until April 2015, aims to transition fully to track cycling as he targets the Rio Games. His hour-record attempt, a historic challenge in cycling, underscores his relentless pursuit of excellence and commitment to fostering the next generation of riders. With a blend of elite ambition and grassroots inspiration, Team Wiggins seeks to leave a lasting legacy beyond the velodrome.

**Nationwide Labor Disruptions Erupt as Workers Protest Trump’s Immigration Policies** Dozens of workers across the United States, including construction laborers and restaurant employees, were reportedly fired after participating in a nationwide strike on Thursday to protest President Donald Trump’s hard-line immigration policies. The walkout, which disrupted businesses and schools, aimed to highlight the contributions of immigrants to the U.S. economy and society. JVS Masonry owner Jim Serowski of Commerce City, Colorado, became one of the most high-profile figures in the controversy after terminating approximately 30 bricklayers who stayed home. “They were warned: if you do this, you’re hurting the company, and if you go against the team, you’re not a member of the team,” Serowski told CNN, expressing no remorse. Similarly, a commercial painting company in Nolensville, Tennessee, fired 18 employees, while 12 restaurant workers in Tulsa, Oklahoma, lost their jobs, according to Fox News and NBC. The exact total of firings remains unclear. The protests coincided with Trump’s announcement of a new executive order targeting immigrants from seven predominantly Muslim countries—Iran, Iraq, Syria, Yemen, Somalia, Sudan, and Libya. The plan follows the judicial rejection of his previous travel ban, which sparked nationwide backlash. At a press conference, Trump vowed to move forward, framing the policy as a security measure. Meanwhile, demonstrations erupted nationwide. In New York’s Times Square, crowds rallied to support Muslim Americans and oppose Trump’s immigration stance. Boston saw hundreds of scientists march against the administration’s approach to climate change and scientific research. Protesters also marked the upcoming Presidents’ Day weekend, with thousands expected to gather in cities across the country. Trump is scheduled to return to Washington from his Florida retreat as tensions over his policies intensify. Labor advocates condemned the firings as retaliation, calling on companies to reinstate employees. “Standing for your beliefs shouldn’t cost your livelihood,” said one organizer. The strike underscores growing divides over immigration, with workers and activists vowing to challenge policies they view as discriminatory. As the debate continues, the U.S. grapples with balancing economic demands and civil liberties in an era of shifting political priorities.

**Nigeria’s Army Claims Injuring Boko Haram Leader, but Past Claims Cast Doubt** The Nigerian military announced on Friday that an airstrike in Borno State’s Sambisa Forest severely injured Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau. However, the claim lacks independent verification, and a history of false assertions about Shekau’s death underscores the need for caution, BBC Africa Security Correspondent Tomi Oladipo noted. The army stated warplanes targeted a militant gathering during Friday prayers at a remote village in the forest, a key Boko Haram stronghold. The attack occurred as U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry visited Nigeria, where he emphasized addressing the root causes of the insurgency. “Building public trust in government also requires cooperation from the military and law enforcement. Extremism can’t be defeated through repression or fear,” Kerry said in Sokoto, urging Nigeria to pursue inclusive solutions. Boko Haram, which seeks to establish an Islamic state in northern Nigeria, has been weakened in recent years by a joint military offensive led by Nigeria and neighboring countries. The group now controls little territory but remains a threat, holding hundreds of captives, including over 200 Chibok schoolgirls abducted in 2014. The Sambisa Forest, a vast jungle region, is believed to be one of the girls’ detention sites. The latest claim about Shekau’s injury comes amid internal Boko Haram upheaval. In May, the Islamic State (IS), to which Shekau pledged allegiance in 2015, declared him replaced by Abu Musab al-Barnawi, son of the group’s founder, Mohammed Yusuf. This leadership shift has fueled speculation about factional tensions within the group. While Nigeria’s military has made territorial gains against Boko Haram since 2021, challenges persist. Analysts warn that without addressing poverty, governance failures, and local grievances, the conflict could reignite. Meanwhile, the international community continues to press Nigeria for transparency and accountability in its counterinsurgency efforts. For now, the truth behind Shekau’s reported injury remains unconfirmed, adding to a pattern of unverified claims that have long complicated efforts to assess Boko Haram’s capacity.

**Fulham’s Grimmer Eyes Fresh Challenge as Ebanks-Blake Shines at Derby** Scottish defender Andrew Grimmer, 22, is poised to leave Fulham after a 12-month loan with League One side **Town**, which included a pivotal FA Cup goal. The full-back, who had two prior spells at the club, played seven times during his 2014 loan and was instrumental in their survival last season. His stoppage-time strike against Sheffield Wednesday in January 2016, securing a fifth-round tie against Manchester United, remains a standout moment. With his Fulham contract expiring in June, speculation grows over his next move. Meanwhile, Derby County’s Darius Charles Ebanks-Blake, 30, continues to impress, netting 10 times in 33 League One games since joining in 2015. A former Manchester United trainee, the striker has scored 64 goals across 193 appearances for clubs including Plymouth and Wolves. Both players’ performances highlight their clubs’ ambitions as the January transfer window approaches. *Follow our dedicated transfer page for real-time updates.*

**Bristol Arena Project Secures £53m Funding from LEP, Awaits Final Approval** The West of England Local Enterprise Partnership (LEP) has pledged £53 million from the City Deal to fund a new 12,000-capacity indoor arena in Bristol, with the city council set to cover the remaining £38 million. The venue, located in the Temple Quarter Enterprise Zone near Bristol Temple Meads station, is expected to drive economic growth and job creation in the region. A final decision on the project will be debated at Bristol City Council’s budget meeting on 18 February. Mayor of Bristol George Ferguson welcomed the LEP’s support, stating, “It’s very encouraging that the LEP recognises the importance of using the City Deal funding for the development of an arena, which will give a massive boost to the local economy.” The arena is part of a broader regeneration plan targeting 70 hectares of land around the station, aiming to attract businesses and tourism. Colin Skellett of the LEP emphasized the project’s potential to unlock regional growth, noting, “The economic benefits to the region from having an arena are well recognised..... the fund is there to unlock jobs and growth.” The council plans to recruit an independent operator for the venue, with construction potentially starting next month. If approved, the arena could open by June 2017, funded in part by operator rents and other revenues. The City Deal scheme, which devolves decision-making power from central government to local authorities, enables cities like Bristol to direct public funds and shape economic strategies. The arena joins other projects under the initiative, reflecting Bristol’s ambition to transform its economy through large-scale infrastructure. With backing from key stakeholders, the project now hinges on the council’s approval. If successful, it will mark a significant step in revitalizing Bristol’s enterprise zone and boosting its status as a cultural and economic hub.

**National League Boss Calls for Promotion Reform** National League side Gloucester City manager Paul Vince has called for an expansion of promotion opportunities from the fifth tier to address what he describes as a “glass ceiling” between the National League and EFL League Two. Speaking to BBC Sport, Vince argued that the current system—where only one team is promoted automatically each season, with a play-off for a second spot—fails to reflect the competitiveness of the league. “There is a good reason for four teams being promoted and relegated between Leagues Two and One. That model should extend to the National League,” Vince said. His club, currently third in the table with 15 games remaining, trails National League leaders Lincoln City by four points. Gloucester narrowly missed out on promotion last season, losing the play-off final to Grimsby Town at Wembley after finishing second. Vince highlighted the disparity in FA Cup progress as evidence of the National League’s strength. Lincoln, who beat Championship sides Brighton and Ipswich to reach the fifth round, and Sutton United, 17th in the league, have both advanced further than any League Two clubs. “There are some very strong, capable teams in the National League,” Vince added. “They are kept in this league, restricted by the promotion opportunities.” The FA’s classification of teams below League Two as “non-league” further exacerbates the issue, he argued. Vince called for a “proper exchange” of clubs between the tiers to create a more balanced structure. The National League introduced play-offs in 2002, increasing promotion chances from one to two per season, but critics argue the system remains outdated. In 2013, Cambridge United manager Richard Money similarly dismissed the format as “nonsense.” With Lincoln preparing to face Premier League leaders Burnley in the FA Cup and Sutton hosting Arsenal, the debate over tier promotion highlights the growing divide between the National League and the EFL. Vince’s call for reform underscores a broader push to level the playing field for clubs striving to break into the professional tiers above.

**Protesters Demand Return of Vital Hospital Services to Pembrokeshire** *Demonstrators in Cardiff Bay highlight concerns over safety and access after key services were moved in 2014.* A growing campaign to reverse the relocation of critical healthcare services from Withybush Hospital in Haverfordwest to Glangwili Hospital in Carmarthen has intensified, with protesters gathering in Cardiff Bay to voice their frustration. The children’s overnight care unit and consultant-led maternity services were moved in 2014 by Hywel Dda University Health Board, which claimed the decision would improve patient care through centralized resources. However, local residents and medical professionals argue the move has left Pembrokeshire’s communities at risk. Glan Phillips, a retired orthopaedic consultant and longtime Withybush advocate, described the protests as a response to “years of feeling ignored” by decision-makers. “We are in a dangerous situation with paediatrics and obstetrics,” he said. “The poor road infrastructure, combined with potential delays from bad weather or traffic, puts lives at risk. People are likely to die because they can’t reach Glangwili in time for emergencies.” Save Withybush Action Team, which has spearheaded the campaign, warns that the lack of on-site specialist services in Haverfordwest has increased reliance on a single facility 50 miles away. Local politicians have joined the chorus of criticism, with Welsh Conservatives accusing the Welsh Labour government of “isolating communities” through “reckless reconfiguration” of services. A party spokesman pledged to reverse such closures, stating they “place unsustainable strain on hospitals and endanger patients.” Plaid Cymru echoed these concerns, rejecting the Welsh government’s “downgrading of local hospitals.” The party reaffirmed its commitment to ensuring consultant-led maternity and emergency services are accessible within one hour of rural areas, emphasizing the need for “life-saving care close to home.” The Welsh Liberal Democrats also condemned the removal of key services, calling it a “huge blow” to Pembrokeshire communities and vowing to “maintain paediatrics, A&E, and maternity care” if elected. Welsh Labour, however, defended the 2014 decision, citing an independent expert report that deemed the changes “safe and sustainable.” A spokesman acknowledged the “huge strength of feeling” about the move but stressed the importance of adhering to clinical advice. The party argued that the consolidation of services has led to “better outcomes” for patients. UKIP Wales accused all parties of “navel-gazing” and “sniping” instead of addressing the crisis in healthcare. A spokesman criticized the “failure of the NHS” due to political infighting, stating that blame-shifting “does nothing to protect patients.” As the debate continues, campaigners remain undeterred. “This isn’t just about hospitals,” Phillips said. “It’s about trust, safety, and the right to access care in a timely manner—no matter where you live.” The protest underscores a deepening rift between rural communities and policymakers, with the future of Withybush Hospital’s services hanging in the balance.

**Ferry Disruptions Leave Passengers Stranded, Demand Compensation** Sailings between the Channel Islands and the UK faced severe disruptions over the weekend after the high-powered trimaran *Liberation* was forced to cancel services due to steering issues on Friday. Passengers scheduled to travel on the *Liberation* were rerouted to the *Clipper* ferry for onward travel to Portsmouth, but the *Clipper* itself broke down on Saturday morning, stranding 110 people and 44 cars for over 12 hours. Among those affected was Kit Ashton, a passenger from Jersey, who had been booked on the *Liberation* service to Poole but was transferred to the *Clipper*. After the ferry’s ramp failed, Ashton and others remained onboard for more than a day, with some only disembarking at 1 a.m. after a 24-hour delay. “More than 12 hours after arriving in Portsmouth, I was finally able to disembark and begin my drive to Exeter,” he said. “I eventually arrived at my final destination at 1 a.m.—about 24 hours after I would originally have arrived.” Ashton and other passengers are now seeking compensation beyond the full refunds offered by operator Condor. He has requested an additional 50% of his ticket price as recompense for “two failed journeys” and the “huge disruption, inconvenience and lost time.” A Condor spokesman apologized, stating the company complies with EU passenger rights regulations, which mandate refunds and support during disruptions. “We not only refund passengers a proportion of their fare as set out in the regulation but also look after them at our expense during the disruption,” they said. Services have since resumed, but Ashton reported no response from Condor to his compensation request, highlighting ongoing frustration among affected travelers.

**Charity Accuses One Direction of Animal Abuse in Music Video** A charity has sparked controversy by releasing a full-page advert in *The Hollywood Reporter*, questioning One Direction’s music video for using animals amid allegations of industry-wide mistreatment. The ad, headlined “‘No animals were harmed,’ really One Direction?”, criticizes the band’s video for featuring a lion, flamingos, sheep, and a chimpanzee, while accusing the film industry of employing “abusive training methods” to control wild animals. The campaign, led by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA), specifically targets Steve Martin, the animal trainer used in the video, alleging he has a poor record on animal welfare. PETA urged the band last week to remove the animal scenes, pledge never to work with animals again, and donate a portion of the song’s proceeds to a chimpanzee-rescue organization. “We vetted Steve Martin closely and chose him based on his exemplary treatment of animals,” production company Fulwell 73, which produced the video, countered in a statement. The company highlighted Martin’s use of reward-based training and his history of collaborating on films such as *The Bourne Legacy*, *True Blood*, *The Zookeeper*, and *Dances With Wolves*, emphasizing his contributions to animal conservation programs. PETA dismissed these claims, reiterating that Martin’s past work has been criticized for cruelty. The charity accused Fulwell 73 of downplaying concerns, despite its public commitment to “exemplary treatment.” The production company reaffirmed its respect for animal welfare groups, calling PETA’s actions “passionate and dedicated,” while standing by its choice

**Labour Faces Internal Division Over Immigration Strategy Post-Brexit** The Labour Party is grappling with a growing divide over its approach to immigration, with prominent voices within the party clashing over how to address public concerns in the wake of the EU referendum. While leader Jeremy Corbyn insists the focus should be on managing the "real issues" of immigration—such as its impact on public services—others, including Welsh First Minister Carwyn Jones, argue the party’s stance is too "London-centric" and risks alienating voters in other parts of the UK. Corbyn has repeatedly defended free movement of people as a cornerstone of EU membership, emphasizing that Labour should prioritize addressing pressures on housing, healthcare, and education caused by immigration rather than enforcing numerical caps. This position was echoed by Shadow Home Secretary Diane Abbott in November, who acknowledged public "disaffection" over immigration in traditional Labour strongholds but urged the party to maintain its pro-immigration stance. However, Jones, a senior Labour figure and staunch advocate for remaining in the EU, warned that the party’s current approach overlooks regional differences. In an interview with *The Guardian*, he argued that areas outside London, such as northern England, view immigration through a different lens. "London is a cosmopolitan city with a history of immigration," he said. "But many other parts of the UK are not." Jones expressed concern that failing to address these regional concerns could drive disaffected voters to UKIP, a party he warned against as a growing threat. The tension highlights the party’s struggle to reconcile its metropolitan base with working-class voters who helped propel Brexit. During the EU referendum, Jones campaigned for Remain, but 52.5% of Welsh voters chose Leave. He recalled hearing from supporters who said, "We’re voting out, but we’re still Labour," and stressed the need to retain their loyalty. Abbott and others have defended Labour’s position as principled, but Jones’s critique underscores a broader challenge: balancing a unified message on immigration with the diverse realities across the UK. As the debate continues, the party faces pressure to craft a strategy that addresses both global mobility and the anxieties of communities feeling left behind. Labour has not yet commented publicly on the dispute.

**Man Assaults Woman in Coatbridge, Police Appeal for Witnesses** A 26-year-old woman was assaulted in Coatbridge on Sunday morning, prompting a police appeal for public assistance in tracing the suspect. The incident occurred at approximately 00:40 on Calder Street when a man pulled the victim to the ground outside a property. The woman sustained minor injuries and screamed during the attack, which alerted nearby individuals and caused the suspect to flee. Det Con Steven Scullion of Police Scotland confirmed the suspect, described as a man in his 30s, possibly of Eastern European origin, with dark hair, a medium build, and dressed in a grey hooded top and dark trousers. Police believe the suspect approached from the direction of shops near Elm Street, heading toward Calder Street at Southfield Crescent. After the assault, he ran across the road, ducked through bushes, and disappeared into the business estate on North Caldeen Road. "Extensive inquiries are ongoing to trace the individual responsible," Det Con Scullion stated. "We are committed to ensuring residents do not feel unsafe in their community." Authorities have not received additional reports of similar incidents and are treating the case as isolated. Investigators are focusing on retrieving CCTV footage and urging anyone who observed a man acting suspiciously in the early hours of Sunday or heard the disturbance to come forward. "Even seemingly insignificant details could aid our investigation," the officer added. Local residents are advised to report any relevant information to Police Scotland. The force is treating the case with urgency, emphasizing transparency to reassure the community. Anyone with information is encouraged to contact officers or Crimestoppers anonymously

**MP’s Use of Longest Word in Youth Committee Sparks Mental Health Debate** Michael Bryan, a teenager from Bournemouth, sparked a lively discussion during a Youth Select Committee meeting on 14 July when he cited the 45-letter term *pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis*—a lung disease—to highlight disparities in mental and physical healthcare funding. However, as the meeting was not a formal parliamentary proceeding, the use of the word will not be recorded in Hansard, the official parliamentary transcript. Instead, the exchange will appear on the British Youth Council’s website. Bryan, who begins sixth form in Dorset in September, addressed body image therapist Liz Ritchie, referencing the 2015 Youth Select Committee report that dubbed mental health services as the “Cinderella of Cinderella services.” He asked: “Do you agree that there should be parity of esteem between mental conditions such as body dysmorphia and physical conditions such as pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis?” The term, which Oxford Dictionaries describes as an “invented long word” meaning a lung disease caused by inhaling fine ash and sand, dates back to the 1930s and is often attributed to Everett M. Smith, then president of the National Puzzlers’ League. While Bryan’s use of the word does not break Jacob Rees-Mogg’s 2012 Hansard record—*floccinaucinihilipilification* (29 letters)—it underscores a broader debate on mental health awareness. Bryan clarified he did not aim to set a record but sought to illustrate the imbalance in treatment priorities. “I wanted to show the disparity between mental and physical conditions,” he said. “Even if just one person is inspired, I’ve done my job.” A House of Commons spokeswoman confirmed the Youth Council’s online record of the meeting, acknowledging Bryan’s contribution to the ongoing conversation about mental health funding and recognition. The exchange has reignited discussions about the need for equal resources and societal attention for mental health, a cause championed by young advocates like Bryan

**UN and Global Powers Reaffirm Syria Stance Amid Escalating Violence and Humanitarian Crisis** The United Nations Security Council has reaffirmed a unified stance on Syria for the second time in a week, underscoring urgent concerns over the conflict’s escalating violence and the dire humanitarian situation. This follows a previous resolution aimed at eliminating Syria’s chemical weapons, a move seen as a rare consensus in an otherwise fractured international response. Disarmament experts began their work in the country on Tuesday, but their mission faces immediate challenges due to persistent fighting across Syria. Clashes between anti-regime factions have intensified, complicating efforts to address the broader conflict. In Barzeh district, north of Damascus, at least 19 government troops and pro-regime militiamen were killed in rebel attacks since Monday, according to the UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. Meanwhile, in the northern border town of Azaz, heavy fighting erupted between al-Qaeda-linked Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant (ISIS) and Western-backed Free Syrian Army (FSA). The conflict, driven by territorial disputes, resource control, and ideological rifts, has deepened the complexity of a war that has claimed over 100,000 lives in two years. The Security Council’s latest statement, adopted on Wednesday, condemned the “unacceptable and escalating level of violence” and highlighted the plight of nearly six million internally displaced Syrians, nearly half of whom are children. It emphasized the urgent need for humanitarian aid, warning that without immediate assistance, “lives will be at risk.” The Council also condemned widespread human rights violations by both the Syrian government and armed groups, reiterating that the regime bears a primary responsibility to protect its population and ensure unhindered aid access. However, aid agencies report that the Syrian government has obstructed foreign aid operations by restricting visas and limiting the number of international groups allowed to work in the country. UN humanitarian chief Valerie Amos stressed the Council’s need to “turn these strong words into meaningful action,” while Syria’s UN ambassador, Bashar Jaafari, said his government would study the statement before responding. Meanwhile, the opposition Syrian National Coalition has issued a dire warning: thousands of families in Damascus suburbs, including Moadamiye, face starvation due to sieges by pro-government forces. Seven people have already died of hunger

**Crucible’s 40th Anniversary: Fans Crown 1985 Final as Greatest Moment** As the Sheffield Crucible celebrates four decades of hosting the World Snooker Championship, fans have voted their favorite moment in history. The 1985 black-ball thriller between Dennis Taylor and Steve Davis, won by Taylor in one of sport’s most iconic finishes, claimed 55% of votes. Ronnie O’Sullivan’s record-breaking 5-minute 147 in 2012 followed with 22.25%, while Alex Higgins’ emotional 1982 triumph ranked third at 7.64%. The poll, conducted by the BBC ahead of the anniversary, highlighted the tournament’s legacy of drama and skill. Full results are now available for those with compatible devices, and readers can sign up to My Sport for live updates and coverage via the BBC app. *Media playback restrictions apply on some devices. Join the conversation and stay updated with expert analysis throughout the championship.*

**Daallo Airlines Flight Incident Sparks Bomb Fears Amid Somalia Security Concerns** A Daallo Airlines flight from Mogadishu to Djibouti came under scrutiny after a mysterious hole appeared in the aircraft shortly after takeoff on Tuesday, raising fears of a bomb attack. The incident, which injured two passengers and saw a body reportedly fall from the plane, has left authorities and aviation experts scrambling to determine the cause. According to reports, the plane, carrying 60 passengers and crew, developed a large hole in its fuselage as it climbed to an altitude of approximately 11,000 feet. Serbian captain Vlatko Vodopivec, one of the few survivors from the cockpit, described the moment of the explosion as “my first bomb; I hope it will be the last.” He and the crew were initially told the blast was caused by a bomb, though Somalia’s civil aviation authority later stated no evidence of a criminal act had been found. Eyewitnesses and technical assessments have painted a conflicting picture. Mohamed Hassan, a police officer in the northern town of Balad, reported that residents discovered the body of a man believed to have fallen from the plane. However, Abdiwahid Omar, director of Somalia’s civil aviation authority, said it was unclear if the deceased was a passenger. Meanwhile, Darren Howe, whose colleague was aboard the flight, suggested the incident was a fuselage failure rather than an explosion. Photographs of the damaged aircraft show intact seats near the hole, leading some experts to speculate that any explosive device may have been stowed in an overhead compartment. The plane’s low altitude and unpressurized cabin at the time of the incident likely saved lives. If the blast had occurred at higher altitudes, the cabin could have ruptured catastrophically, risking fatalities from rapid decompression. Captain Vodopivec credited emergency procedures for allowing a safe return to Mogadishu’s Aden Adde Airport. “It would have been much worse if we were higher,” he said, describing the harrowing landing. The incident has reignited concerns about aviation security in Somalia, where al-Shabab militants continue to target infrastructure.

**Christopher Steele’s FIFA Bid Investigations Tied to Trump Dossier Scrutiny** Christopher Steele, the former British intelligence officer, has been linked to a probe into FIFA’s World Cup bidding process, including Russia’s successful 2018 bid. Acting through his London-based firm Orbis, Steele gathered intelligence on the tournament’s allocation, which has resurfaced amid renewed attention on the so-called “Trump dossier.” This document, authored by Steele, contained allegations of Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election. President Donald Trump has repeatedly dismissed these claims as “fake news” and “phoney stuff.” While it remains unclear if Steele’s findings directly triggered investigations into FIFA corruption, he reported his information to the FBI’s Eurasian crime division. Russia secured the 2018 World Cup, and Qatar won the 2022 edition, both under Swiss-led corruption inquiries. U.S. officials, according to Reuters, cited Steele’s work on the bidding process as lending “credence” to the Trump dossier. Steele’s dual role in FIFA and U.S. election controversies underscores his prominence in transatlantic investigations. The FBI and Swiss authorities continue to examine ties between sports governance and political influence, as the legacy of both World Cup hosts faces scrutiny. For now, the intersection of sports diplomacy and political intrigue remains under a cloud.

**North Weald Airfield Celebrates Centenary of RAF Legacy** This Sunday, North Weald in Essex marks a century since its establishment as a Royal Air Force base with its Centenary Air Fete, a celebration of its storied history and enduring legacy. Located just off the M11 near Epping, the airfield opened in 1916 as a critical defense post during World War I, safeguarding London from German airship raids. However, it was during the Battle of Britain in 1940 that the site rose to national prominence as a pivotal RAF Fighter Sector Station. Equipped primarily with Hawker Hurricanes, the base defended the eastern approaches to London, with pilots from Allied nations—including Norway, the USA, New Zealand, Czechoslovakia, and Poland—playing vital roles in the war effort. Arthur Moreton, chairman of the North Weald Royal Air Force Association, emphasized its significance: “It was involved in the defense of London in WWI, but it really came to public prominence during the Battle of Britain..... Spitfires arrived later, and its role continued during the Cold War.” However, the expansion of civilian aviation around London’s major airports in the 1960s rendered the site impractical for the RAF, which withdrew in 1964. Today, the airfield—owned by Epping Forest District Council—thrives as a hub for private aviation, historic aircraft restoration, and the North Weald RAF Museum. Ash Bailey of EM Aviation Services, organizer of the centenary event, highlighted its special focus: “We’re most excited about the return of three Norwegian veterans who flew from here for the RAF during WWII.” The event promises a fitting tribute, with the weather forecast adding optimism to the proceedings. North Weald’s journey from wartime stronghold to a vibrant civil aviation center underscores its adaptability and enduring connection to aviation history. As the centenary air fete takes flight, it honors a century of service, resilience, and international camaraderie.

**Gloucestershire Close Day on 69-0 as Rain Halts Play, Norwell Shines for Leicestershire** Gloucestershire closed day’s play at 69-0 after 45.3 overs on a rain-interrupted day at the County Ground, with Leicestershire’s chase falling short at 334 for 10. The home side collapsed in the face of Liam Norwell’s (4-72) aggressive spell, ending their innings shortly after lunch, while Gloucestershire’s reply started strongly before a premature halt. The pivotal moment came when all-rounder Chris Dent, on 107 not out overnight, added 29 runs before a sharp slip catch by Dent himself ended a 86-run partnership with Clint McKay. The Australian McKay, in particular, accelerated to a 47-ball half-century, only to depart for 55 when he mis-timed a delivery from Norwell. Leicestershire’s hopes of enforcing a follow-on were dashed as Gloucestershire’s openers Chris Dent (34*) and Gareth Roderick (23*) calmly navigated the remaining overs. Rain, however, intervened mid-afternoon, with umpires Steve Garratt and Nigel Cowley calling play at 17:00 BST. In club news, Leicestershire confirmed the departure of elite development coach Keith Piper by mutual consent for family reasons. Meanwhile, on-loan seamer Richard Jones praised the County Ground pitch: “It’s one of those where you need to be patient, bowl consistently short of a good length, and let the wickets come. I felt solid today, though I’d have liked one or two.” Jones’ insights underscored the patience required to navigate the challenging conditions, as both teams prepare for the second day’s potential resumption.

**Chancellor Philip Hammond Balances Pragmatism and Prudence in Budget Response to Brexit Uncertainty** In a pragmatic and carefully calculated Budget, Chancellor Philip Hammond avoided bold gestures, opting instead for measured interventions to support vulnerable households while reaffirming his commitment to economic stability in the shadow of Brexit. The announcement, delivered under pressure of looming uncertainty, prioritized modest but targeted measures aimed at upholding Prime Minister Theresa May’s vision of a “Government for all,” while leaving room to navigate the unpredictable economic tides of Britain’s departure from the EU. Key among the limited giveaways was a reduction in the rate at which benefits are withdrawn for low-income workers, easing financial strain on those “just about managing.” A ban on letting fees for private renters and a 6.1% increase in the National Living Wage to £8.21—an advance publicized to curb media attention—also featured. These measures were designed to address immediate concerns without overextending fiscal flexibility. Hammond shifted away from his predecessor’s rigid deficit reduction targets, instead pledging to achieve a budget surplus “as soon as possible.” The new approach focused on long-term productivity gains, with announcements of increased investment in housing, roads, and research and development. While welcoming as a nod to infrastructure modernization, critics noted the lack of grand spending pledges, with Hammond emphasizing restraint to maintain market confidence. The Chancellor’s strategy hinged on balancing immediate needs with contingency planning. With forecasts of rising borrowing and slowing growth, Hammond sought to preserve fiscal firepower to cushion against potential Brexit-related shocks. He struck a conciliatory tone, acknowledging challenges while highlighting opportunities, declaring the UK a “great nation” poised for resilience. Yet the cautious approach drew swift criticism from Labour. Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell lambasted the government’s long-term economic plan as an “abject failure,” accusing the Treasury of abandoning ambitious growth targets in favor of short-term survival. **Hope Renewd as #Bringbackourgirls Campaign Member Found Alive** The #Bringbackourgirls global social media movement, championed by figures like First Lady Michelle Obama, Malala Yousafzai, and Ellen DeGeneres, has sparked renewed hope after Amina Ali Nkeki, one of 276 girls abducted by Boko Haram in 2014, was found. Thousands on Twitter celebrated the news, urging continued efforts to locate the remaining missing girls. "Amina’s rescue offers light in darkness," tweeted one supporter. Activists and families remain determined to bring all the girls home.

**Rise of ‘Creepy Clown’ Fad Sparks Childline and Police Intervention in Scotland** A surge in reports of “creepy clown” sightings across Scotland has prompted Childline and police to act, as concerns grow over the impact on children’s safety and mental health. According to the NSPCC, Scotland’s two Childline bases have conducted 22 counselling sessions since the trend began last week, with frightened children reaching out over fears of being targeted. The US-born craze, which has seen individuals dress as distorted clowns to scare others, has left schools and communities on edge. In Dunbar, East Lothian, a clown was spotted chasing terrified schoolchildren, causing traffic chaos by jumping into the road. Police have warned pranksters will face arrest, with incidents including clowns brandishing weapons such as knives and baseball bats. Childline reported that 25% of calls about the phenomenon came from children under 11, while over a third were from 12- to 15-year-olds. In Glasgow, staff handled 12 sessions, and in Aberdeen, 10. The charity also highlighted a disturbing online case: a 13-year-old girl received threatening messages on Instagram from someone posing as a clown, who allegedly claimed they would “cut her throat and rape her.” NSPCC Scotland spokespersons condemned the trend, calling it a “twisted” abuse of a traditionally joyful symbol. “Clowns are meant to make children laugh, but these individuals are exploiting the idea to intimidate and scare,” they said. They urged parents and authorities to address the issue urgently, noting fears that some clowns are using the trend to commit crimes or bully. Authorities have advised children to report sightings of suspicious figures to adults or the police. As the craze spreads, the NSPCC emphasized the need to protect vulnerable young people from a trend that “needs to be stamped out.”

**St Fagans Museum to Unveil £17.5m Expansion Project, Telling 200,000 Years of Welsh History** The Heritage Lottery Fund (HLF) has announced a landmark £11.5 million investment for St Fagans National History Museum near Cardiff, with the Welsh government contributing an additional £6 million. Together, these funds will fuel a transformative expansion aimed at reimagining the museum as Wales’ first dedicated National Museum of History. The project, set to cover 200,000 years of Welsh heritage, marks a significant leap beyond the site’s current focus on 500 years of life in Wales. The museum, which welcomes over 600,000 visitors annually, faces a £7.5 million shortfall to complete its £29 million overhaul. To bridge this gap, a public appeal has been launched, inviting visitors to donate £1 per visit. This initiative mirrors a historic fundraising campaign by scholar and poet Iorwerth Peate in 1946, who galvanized support to establish St Fagans as a cultural landmark. Plans for the revamp, first revealed in January, were bolstered by planning permission secured in May after the museum applied to Cardiff council. The overhaul will introduce new buildings, galleries, and immersive projects, including reconstructions of iconic sites such as the Iron Age settlement Bryn Eryr on Anglesey and the medieval court of Llys Rhosyr, once the seat of the Princes of Gwynedd. These additions will deepen visitors’ understanding of Wales’ rich history and its evolving relationship with the environment. **Aberdeen Secure Signing of Experienced Chris Burke** Aberdeen FC have confirmed the signing of 32-year-old Scotland international Chris Burke, who recently trained with Kilmarnock after departing Nottingham Forest. Manager Jim McIntyre expressed enthusiasm about the acquisition, stating: "We are delighted to announce the signing of Chris. He will provide much-needed competition on the flanks and bring a wealth of experience from top-level football." Burke rose to prominence with Rangers, netting on his debut in a 5-0 victory over Kilmarnock in 2002. However, limited opportunities at Ibrox led to a 2009 free transfer to Cardiff City, where he earned over 100 league appearances. A move to Birmingham City followed, where he scored 28 goals in 155 games across three seasons. After spells at Nottingham Forest (50 league games) and a loan at Rotherham, Burke became a free agent this summer. The addition of the versatile full-back underscores Aberdeen’s focus on depth and experience ahead of the new season.

**Leaked Iranian Document Reveals Pressure on Media to Curb Hardliner Dissent Over Nuclear Deal** A top-secret directive from Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), recently surfaced online, has exposed the government’s efforts to suppress criticism of the landmark nuclear deal reached in Vienna on July 14. The document, which marks a departure from past practices, targets hardline newspapers that have openly criticized the agreement, signaling rising internal tensions over its implementation. For hardliners, who hold influential positions in the Revolutionary Guards and other power centers, the agreement represents a strategic compromise. Under the deal, Iran is barred from enriching uranium beyond 3.67% purity and will reduce its centrifuge stockpile by two-thirds. The SNSC’s directive suggests the government is anxious about dissent from these factions, whose vocal opposition could jeopardize the deal’s ratification by parliament. **Mariah Carey’s Troubled Times Square Performance Sparks Controversy Over Sound Issues and Producer Accusations** Mariah Carey’s highly anticipated live appearance at New York’s Times Square during *New Year’s Rockin’ Eve* on ABC turned chaotic just before midnight, as the pop star faced severe sound difficulties that derailed her performance and ignited a bitter public feud between her team and the show’s producers. Beginning with a rendition of “Auld Lang Syne” to ring in the new year, Carey transitioned into her 1991 hit “Emotions” but quickly hit technical snags. The singer, visibly frustrated, repeatedly gestured to her earpiece, claiming she could not hear the music. Can I not have one? Instead of fixing the issue, they went live.” Perna emphasized that Carey, “flying blind” on stage, relied on a backing track out of necessity, not premeditation. **Bank of America Faces Fraud Liability Over Countrywide’s “Hustle” Scheme** *Former Executive Ordered to Pay $1M; Bank Questions Penalty’s Scale* A California federal court has ruled that Bank of America’s former mortgage subsidiary, Countrywide Financial, was guilty of defrauding U.S. mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac through a high-pressure loan program dubbed the “hustle” in 2007. The program, known internally as the “high-speed swim lane” (HSSL), incentivized employees to rapidly approve mortgage applications without proper underwriting, leading to the sale of thousands of defective loans. In October, a judge found Countrywide liable for fraud but has yet to determine a financial penalty. Former Countrywide executive Rebecca Mairone, who oversaw the program, was ordered to pay $1 million in penalties. Bank of America, which acquired Countrywide in 2008 during the financial crisis, has disputed the scale of the alleged misconduct, calling the proposed liability disproportionate to the short-lived initiative. “This figure bears no relation to a limited Countrywide program that lasted several months and ended before our acquisition of the company,” said spokesperson Lawrence Grayson, adding the bank is reviewing appellate options. The case stems from a whistleblower complaint by Edward O’Donnell, a former Countrywide executive, who exposed the HSSL’s lax screening processes. Government investigations revealed 43% of loans sold to Fannie and Freddie through the program were defective. The ruling underscores ongoing scrutiny of banks’ roles in the 2008 housing collapse, with Bank of America already spending nearly $40 billion on related legal matters. The bank is also expected to announce a multi-billion-dollar settlement with U.S. regulators in the coming weeks. Despite the ruling, investors showed muted reactions, with Bank of America shares rising slightly midday. The outcome reflects the complexity of financial sector litigation, where settlements have become routine, even as penalties remain a flashpoint for debate over accountability.

**Nevada Pioneers Online Poker Legalization as U.S. States Eye Expansion** Nevada became the first U.S. state to legalize online poker in February, marking a potential turning point for the gambling industry. The Nevada Gaming Control Board has granted a 30-day license to allow websites to compete for customers, with UltimatePoker.com—the first to launch—serving as a testbed for the new market. Experts predict that states like New Jersey and Delaware may soon follow, capitalizing on an industry projected to generate billions in annual revenue for U.S. authorities. Online poker is already popular among an estimated 10 million Americans, though most platforms operate offshore, depriving state and federal governments of tax revenue. This dynamic could shift as states push to relax rules imposed by Congress in 2006, which banned internet gambling. Under Nevada’s new framework, players must be residents of the state and at least 21 years old, with online poker as the initial offering. UltimatePoker, a subsidiary of Station Casinos—operator of 16 Las Vegas properties—will test the waters under these regulations. Critics, however, warn of societal costs. The Stop Predatory Gambling group has condemned the partnership between government and the gambling industry, arguing it “actively encourages people to lose money.” Similar debates surround the UK, a global leader in online gambling regulation. While British sites are required to verify user identities and provide addiction support, the country has seen a surge in problem gambling. In 2010, the UK Gambling Commission estimated 450,000 problem gamblers, a 200,000 rise since 2007, with an average debt of £17,500. The online gambling boom traces back to 1994, when Microgaming Software Systems on the Isle of Man launched the world’s first virtual casino. As the U.S. considers its next steps, the balance between economic gain and public safety remains a pressing question.

**Rosberg Dominates Belgian GP Practice as Hamilton and Verstappen Face Challenges** Mercedes driver Nico Rosberg set the pace in both Friday practice sessions for the Belgian Grand Prix, leaving his title rival Lewis Hamilton struggling for form at Spa-Francorchamps. The German, currently 21 points adrift in the championship, claimed he is “one step ahead of Lewis at the moment” as he seeks to close the gap before the season’s final six races. Hamilton, who finished 0.6 seconds behind Rosberg in the second session, hinted at dissatisfaction with his car’s performance. Rosberg, however, remained confident, stating: “It is going well for now. I’m feeling comfortable. I think Alain Juppe offers an alternative.”* Juppe, 71, who lost the primary to Fillon with just 33% of the vote, has remained low-profile since his defeat but has not ruled out a return. Sources close to Juppe said he would only re-enter the race with “unanimous support from the party” and if Fillon voluntarily stepped down. Juppe’s camp has described the situation as a “collective suicide” for the Republicans, emphasizing the need for unity. **Dundee and Celtic Eye Historic Premiership Match in North America** Dundee FC and Celtic have confirmed ongoing discussions to stage a Scottish Premiership fixture in North America, marking a potential landmark move for Scottish football. The proposal, expected to be formally submitted to the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL) in the coming weeks, could see the December 30 clash between the two clubs played in either Boston or Philadelphia. The idea has sparked enthusiasm and debate, with supporters and officials weighing the opportunities and challenges of internationalizing domestic league matches. Celtic’s Australian midfielder, Adam Rogic, expressed support for the initiative, calling it a “positive idea” to elevate Scottish football’s global profile. “It’s a good opportunity to expand the game and broadcast Scottish football on a world stage,” he said. “Celtic has a massive fan base, and it would be fantastic to give some fans over there the chance to see us play.” Rogic, who grew up in Australia with a deep admiration for Celtic’s heritage, acknowledged the logistical hurdles but emphasized the benefits of tapping into the clubs’ international followings. “We have a few international boys used to travel, so it’s not a huge issue,” he added. The proposed match aligns with Celtic’s long-standing presence in the United States, where the club has played high-profile friendlies, including against the New York Cosmos and former AC Milan star Zlatan Ibrahimović. In October, Celtic revealed plans to explore the feasibility of establishing a franchise in the U.S., a move that could further strengthen their North American ties. Dundee, meanwhile, has a unique connection to the region: Texas-based chairman Tim Keyes and managing director John Nelms, who have led the club since 2013, may view the venture as a strategic opportunity to engage U.S. audiences. However, the proposal faces regulatory scrutiny. The SPFL must approve any overseas league match, and international governing bodies have issued cautious responses. A UEFA spokesperson stated that while the SPFL and national associations hold primary responsibility, “the framework of the game worldwide is based on association football and the rules which apply.” FIFA reiterated that any such match would require approval from member associations and could only proceed if “procedures are respected.” The organizations’ ambiguity highlights the complex bureaucratic hurdles facing the clubs. Alan McEwan, director of the Dundee FC Supporters Society, voiced optimism. “We look forward to hearing more details on what certainly sounds like a forward-thinking and incredible opportunity for both clubs,” he said. For fans, the prospect of witnessing a top-tier Scottish derby in North America is enticing, but concerns linger about disrupting the domestic schedule and the feasibility of competing with other global sporting events. The proposed match would not only test the boundaries of football’s traditional structures but also signal a bold new era for Scottish clubs seeking to expand their influence. As discussions progress, all eyes will be on the SPFL and international football authorities to determine whether this ambitious vision can become a reality. **Renewed Search for Seamus Ruddy’s Remains Offers New Hope for Family** A renewed search for the remains of Seamus Ruddy, a man abducted and murdered by republican paramilitaries in 1985, has begun in a forest near Rouen, northern France. The Independent Commission for the Location of Victims’ Remains (ICLVR) launched the operation after receiving new intelligence from the Irish Republican Socialist Party (IRSP), which maintains ties to the INLA, the group responsible for his abduction. Seamus Ruddy, 32, was a Newry native working as a teacher in Paris when he was seized by the INLA on May 9, 1985. His body was never found. The search, focused on the Pont-de-l’Arche forest, is the latest in a series of efforts over decades, including a 2008 attempt that yielded no results. Geoff Knupfer, ICLVR lead investigator, stated the recent information was “as accurate as it can be, given the passage of time,” and that those providing the details “genuinely desire to resolve this by finding where Seamus is buried.” Ruddy is among four of 16 individuals known as the “Disappeared”—victims abducted, murdered, and secretly buried during Northern Ireland’s Troubles. The others missing are Columba McVeigh, Joe Lynskey, and Captain Robert Nairac. For Ruddy’s family, the search marks their “best hope yet,” as his sister, Anne Morgan, was the last to see him alive. The ICLVR has relied on community cooperation to locate victims’ remains since its 2003 formation, with this case highlighting the enduring legacy of conflict and the pursuit of closure for families. If successful, the search could finally lay to rest the decades-long quest for justice and reconciliation.

**Condor Liberation Crossing Canceled After Storm Damage in Poole Harbour** The Condor Liberation ferry service between the Channel Islands and the UK was canceled after severe damage to the vessel during Storm Frank on Wednesday. The £50m ship, which operates the region’s only fast ferry route since March, was blown against its berth in Poole Harbour, damaging its protective belting above the waterline. Condor Ferries confirmed the cancellations stem from the storm’s impact and assured a contingency plan is in place for affected travelers. Passengers can choose a full refund or rerouting. Wind speeds in the harbor reached 55 knots (63mph) during the storm, prompting crew and harbor staff to hastily install extra protective barriers between the ship and the berth to minimize further harm. Captain Fran Collins highlighted the crew’s 24/7 vigilance, stating: “Like all our ships, Condor Liberation has a crew 24 hours a day, whether she is undertaking passenger services or not. The crew acted quickly with assistance from Poole Harbours to put additional protection in place.” The disruption underscores the vulnerability of the vital route, which connects Guernsey, Jersey, and the UK. Condor Ferries reiterated its commitment to resolving the issue while prioritizing safety. Affected passengers are urged to contact the company for travel adjustments.

**Southampton Striker Faces 2-3 Month Ankle Injury as Transfer Search Falters** Southampton manager Claude Puel confirmed that Dutch defender Virgil van Dijk will miss two to three months with an ankle injury sustained in a challenge by Leicester City’s Jamie Vardy during the 3-0 win on 22 January. The 25-year-old’s absence looms as a blow ahead of the FA Cup final against Manchester Arsenal on 26 February, following Southampton’s recent victory over Liverpool. Puel admitted the club pursued a replacement before the transfer window closed on Tuesday but faced setbacks. “We studied many options, but no suitable defender emerged,” he said. The Saints boss remains optimistic about fielding a strong squad despite the injury hurdle, though the focus now shifts to maintaining momentum in the Premier League and FA Cup campaigns.

**Olympics Enthusiast Chen Guan Ming Pedals to Rio on Rickshaw, Befuddles UK Police** In a remarkable display of dedication to the Olympic spirit, 58-year-old Chen Guan Ming from Xuzhou, China, is cycling his rickshaw across Europe to attend the 2016 Rio Olympics. The passionate fan, who previously made headlines during the 2012 London Games, began his latest journey in Cambridge, England, and recently encountered local authorities while navigating a high-speed dual carriageway. Chen’s rickshaw, adorned with a banner proclaiming “Promote the Olympic Spirit,” became the center of attention on Wednesday when he was spotted on the A14, a 70mph (110km/h) dual carriageway in Cambridgeshire. Police intervened after reports of traffic disruption, advising him to take a safer route. “He was not committing an offence, but we offered him a map and words of caution,” said a Cambridgeshire Police spokesman. Chen, who understands only four words of English, declined the map but continued his journey. This is not Chen’s first global adventure. In 2012, he cycled his rickshaw from China to London for the Olympics, later returning home. For Rio 2016, he secured a courtesy flight from a British airline to restart his quest in the UK. Funding the remainder of the trip himself, Chen relies on odd jobs and offers rides in his rickshaw, which serves as his nighttime shelter. The police spokesman noted uncertainty about Chen’s next destination but speculated he might head to Liverpool. Despite the challenges—ranging from language barriers to road safety advisories—Chen remains undeterred, driven by his lifelong passion for the Olympics. His rickshaw, a symbol of his perseverance, carries not just supplies but a message of global unity. As Chen peddles onward, his journey underscores the lengths to which one man will go to celebrate the world’s greatest sporting event—a feat as unconventional as it is inspiring.

**Boy, 5, Dies After Dog Attack in Sunderland** Reggie Young tragically died after being attacked by a small terrier-type dog at a home in Falkland Road, Sunderland, on Saturday morning. Police have taken the dog into custody and placed it in secure kennels, with authorities indicating the animal may be destroyed. A growing display of flowers, cuddly toys, and heartfelt messages has appeared outside the semi-detached house, including a poignant tribute: *“Our thoughts and prayers are with you at this tragic time. Shine like a bright diamond, little one. Beautiful boy gone too soon.”*

**Ralph Waite, Beloved “The Waltons” Star, Dies at 86** Ralph Waite, the acclaimed actor best known for his iconic role as John Walton, Sr. on the classic TV series *The Waltons*, passed away at the age of 86. Tributes have poured in from colleagues, fans, and loved ones, celebrating a career spanning decades and a legacy rooted in warmth, integrity, and mentorship. Born Richard Ralph Waite in 1931, he served as a Marine before studying theology and becoming an ordained Presbyterian minister. In the 1960s, he transitioned to acting, making his Broadway debut opposite Faye Dunaway in *Hogan’s Goat*. His stage success led to small-screen roles alongside Hollywood legends like Paul Newman and Jack Nicholson in films such as *Cool Hand Luke* and *Five Easy Pieces*. However, it was his portrayal of the Depression-era patriarch in *The Waltons*—which premiered in 1972—that cemented his status as a global icon. “Ralph was a good honest actor and a good honest man,” said Michael Learned, who played his on-screen wife, Olivia Walton. “He was my spiritual husband. We loved each other for over 40 years. He died a working actor at the top of his game..... a mentor to many and a role model to an entire generation.” Waite’s character, John Walton, Sr., embodied resilience and moral strength, guiding his seven children through hardship with humor and compassion. The show’s unexpected nine-season run resonated worldwide, inspiring stories of its profound impact. In a 2021 interview with *The Lancaster News*, Waite recalled a fan who credited the series with motivating her to attend college and become a lawyer: “She said, ‘Now, I’m a lawyer and I don’t think I would be if I hadn’t seen that show.’ I’m still amazed by that,” he shared.
