She will no longer work for us.” Bunte, who did not directly interact with children in her role, criticized the decision as “out of proportion and judgemental.” In an interview, she defended the novel’s explicit content, stating, “Some novelists stop at the bedroom door; I went in with them and tried to describe a relationship that was central, that was passionate..... in fairly graphic detail.” She emphasized the fictional nature of the work but added that she had sought permission from her superiors to speak to the media about it. KCC, however, acted swiftly after her public comments, despite her four-year tenure at the Joy Lane centre. The case has sparked debate over the boundaries between personal expression and professional conduct. Bunte’s legal team is reviewing the dismissal, while KCC reiterated its commitment to “maintaining appropriate standards” in its services. The council did not specify whether it notified her agency prior to ending her contract. Bunte’s novel remains available for purchase online, though its distribution has drawn mixed public reactions. The incident underscores the challenges faced by public sector employees navigating the intersection of personal creativity and workplace expectations.

**Sheffield City Council Considers Early Termination of Veolia Waste Contract, Threatening 180 Jobs** Sheffield City Council has warned that up to 180 jobs could be at risk if it proceeds with terminating its contract with waste management firm Veolia, which has handled the city’s waste collection and disposal since 2001. The current deal, valued at £620 million, is scheduled to expire in 2036, but the council claims it no longer aligns with financial demands imposed by central government. A decision is set for a cabinet meeting on 18 January. Councillor Bryan Lodge, the city’s environment portfolio holder, stated the existing contract fails to meet “crucial savings targets” outlined in the council’s 2016 budget. “We’re operating in a tough financial landscape, and the contract is no longer meeting our needs,” he said. Veolia, which manages Sheffield’s Bernard Road incinerator, recycling centres, district heating network, and bulky item collections, has faced ongoing disputes with staff. Employees have staged multiple strikes in recent years over pay disputes and allegations of “aggressive” management practices, including 96 gross misconduct cases recorded in a single year. The GMB union, representing Veolia workers, dismissed the council’s announcement as a “negotiating tactic.” Pete Davies, the union’s spokesperson, expressed skepticism, adding that members had been alerted to safeguard their jobs and conditions. “We suspect this is all part of a negotiation strategy, but we’ll challenge any attempt to undermine our members’ rights,” he said. Veolia has not yet responded to the potential contract termination. The council emphasized it would aim to maintain waste services seamlessly if the deal is cut short. However, unions and workers remain wary, given the firm’s history of labor tensions. With a decision looming in January, the city’s waste management future—and the livelihoods of 180 employees—hang in the balance.

A set of 38 historic photographs from Robert Falcon Scott’s ill-fated Antarctic expedition has been re-auctioned after failing to sell at Wiltshire’s Henry Aldridge. The images, captured by expedition photographer Herbert Ponting, include Scott’s final birthday, killer whales, and frostbitten hands. Scott and his five-man team perished in 1912, outpaced to the South Pole by a Norwegian team. Ponting, who did not join the pole attempt, survived a near-fatal killer whale attack and returned to civilization. The lot, initially estimated at £400–£600, will be re-auctioned. Ponting died in 1935.

Megan Lee, 46, from Oswaldtwistle, Lancashire, died on January 1 after being hospitalized for two days. Two men, both staff at the Royal Spice Indian takeaway on Union Road, were arrested and held on suspicion of involuntary manslaughter by gross negligence. Aged 37 and 38, they are from Rossendale and Blackburn. Lancashire Police and trading standards continue their investigation. A post-mortem was conducted, but police confirmed results will take time. The suspects remain in custody for questioning as authorities probe potential links between the takeaway and Ms. Lee’s death.

James Cox (real name James Russan), a 2006 Commonwealth Games gold medallist, faces charges including common assault, harassment, violence to secure entry, and criminal damage after a 16 July incident on Lambeth Road, Kennington. The 28-year-old’s case at Camberwell Green Magistrates’ Court was adjourned, with a next hearing set for Croydon Magistrates’ Court on 12 January 2016.

**Powys Council Recovers Nearly Full £4m Investment Following Complex Process** Powys Council has recovered £4,077,799—including interest and legal costs—after a "long and complicated issue" involving £4m invested in Icelandic banks Glitnir and Landsbanki. The council was among eight local authorities, three universities, and three former police bodies that collectively invested nearly £75m in the banks. Council officials emphasized the lengthy resolution, which ultimately secured almost the entire original sum.

**Teenager Assaulted in Whitehall Road Playground, Kent Police Appeal for Witnesses** Kent Police confirmed a teenage girl was attacked at Toddler’s Cove playground off Whitehall Road just before midnight Friday. The victim reported the incident early Sunday, prompting a cordon to be erected for investigations. Authorities urge witnesses to come forward.

**Accrington and Cambridge Share Points in Thrilling Encounter** In a tight match at Accrington, the visitors struck first with a fortuitous goal. Tom Davies’ clearance deflected off Jimmy Spencer, 12 yards out, nestling into the bottom corner. The home side responded swiftly: on-loan winger Tariqe Fosu latched onto a breakaway, slotting past the keeper from 10 yards. A 1-1 draw leaves Accrington slipping to fifth in the table, while Cambridge remain 12th, still five points from the play-offs.

**England Set to Face Argentina in BBC Rugby Fixtures** England, led by Stuart Lancaster, will take on Argentina’s Pumas in two Tests this June. The matches are scheduled for **Saturday, 8 June** in Salta and **Saturday, 15 June** in Buenos Aires, both kicking off at **20:10 BST** on **BBC Two**. The broadcast team features renowned pundits Sir Clive Woodward, Jonathan Davies, Brian Moore, and Keith Wood, alongside presenters John Inverdale and Jason Mohammed. Eddie Butler will provide commentary. Philip Bernie, BBC Head of TV Sport, stated: “We’re delighted to cover England’s Tests in Argentina, a nation offering a formidable challenge. These games add to our extensive international rugby lineup.” The fixtures promise intense rivalry, with both teams eager to showcase their strength on the global stage.

**Monaco Move Top as Nice Miss Late Winner in Marseille Thriller** Monaco claimed the Ligue 1 summit with a dominant 4-0 victory over Marseille on Saturday. Meanwhile, Nice moved to within one point of the leaders as Alassane Plea’s header was followed by Enzo Crivelli’s equalizer before Plea struck the crossbar in stoppage time. Paris St-Germain, champions, maintained third place with a 2-1 win over Lyon on Sunday, with Edinson Cavani scoring twice.

Newport County have signed 30-year-old midfielder Max Blanchard on a free transfer after his departure from League of Ireland side Shamrock Rovers. Blanchard, their 14th signing of 2017, started in Friday’s 0-0 draw with League Two leaders Doncaster Rovers, playing the full 90 minutes. Exiles manager Graham Westley stated: “Max was on a game-to-game basis. He’s moved on, and we wish him well.”

**Project Propeller Celebrates 19th Year with Flight for WWII Veterans** Project Propeller, now in its 19th year, brought together war veterans for a poignant fly-in at Staverton, organized by 120 volunteer pilots using private light aircraft. Air Operations Manager Graham Cowie called it “a privilege and honour to be part of it all.” Among the veterans is 101-year-old Mary Ellis of Sandown, Isle of Wight, one of the last surviving Air Transport Auxiliary (ATA) pilots. During WWII, she delivered Spitfires and bombers, a role critical to Allied efforts. Gloucestershire Airport, where the event took place, served as an RAF base before becoming a commercial airfield. Also participating are three ex-POWs who endured the Long March—a 600-mile Nazi-led forced march in 1945 to evade advancing Soviet forces. The event honors their resilience and legacy, with volunteers ensuring these history-makers receive a final tribute. Over 1,000 veterans have flown with Project Propeller since its inception, celebrating their sacrifices and preserving their stories for future generations.

**Rio Tinto’s Ben Nevis Aluminum Smelter Faces Uncertain Future** Rio Tinto’s Lochaber aluminum smelter, a cornerstone of the local economy for nearly 90 years, is at a crossroads after the mining giant announced a potential sale of its UK operations. Located near Ben Nevis, the smelter is the only active aluminum plant in the UK and employs around 170 people, making it a major employer in the Fort William area. In January, Rio Tinto initiated a review of the site’s future, informing staff this week that a sale is not guaranteed. If no deal materializes, the company may explore alternatives, including maintaining current operations. A spokesperson emphasized that a sale, following a thorough review, is deemed the best route to secure long-term sustainability for the site, workers, and the broader Fort William economy. However, the lack of automaticity in the process has left employees and the community in suspense. The smelter’s future will hinge on negotiations and the outcomes of ongoing assessments.

**Severn Trent Secures £84m Takeover Approval as Dee Valley Shares Bid for Clarity** The High Court has approved the £84 million acquisition of Wrexham-based Dee Valley by utilities giant Severn Trent, ending a protracted legal battle. Shareholders, who had dubbed their challenge a “David versus Goliath” dispute, withdrew their objection to resolve uncertainty. Dee Valley confirmed it will proceed with the takeover immediately, stating shareholders had agreed not to pursue an appeal. A spokesperson noted the scheme is expected to finalize this week, with further details to follow. “We always said we would abide by the court’s decision and we have done so,” the company added, signaling a resolution to the months-long saga.

**Heartfelt Donation Aims to Save Premature Babies’ Lives in Memory of Lost Triplets** Garreth and Nicola Wood, a couple from Wishaw, have made a profound commitment to improving neonatal care in Scotland after losing their triplets in 2013. Their £400,000 donation to install the Heart Rate Observation (HeRO) system at Wishaw General Hospital’s neonatal unit seeks to give vulnerable premature babies a fighting chance against life-threatening infections—a cause close to their hearts. The Woods’ journey with neonatal care began in 2010 when their first daughter, Ezra, was born prematurely at 32 weeks. After receiving care at Wishaw Hospital, the couple became vocal advocates for better facilities, previously donating £35,000 for staff training and £5,000 for breathing equipment. Tragedy struck again in 2013 when their triplets—Asha, Oren, and Willow—were born at 24 weeks and survived only two weeks. “A couple of our girls had infections,” Nicola Wood shared. “Though these machines might not have saved them, they could give other babies a chance we never had.” The HeRO system, which the Woods funded, uses advanced algorithms to analyze a baby’s heartbeat and detect early signs of infection, a leading cause of death in preterm infants. By identifying subtle changes in heart rate patterns, the device enables medical teams to intervene before symptoms become severe. Dr. Samuel Ibhanesebhor, consultant neonatologist and clinical director at Wishaw Hospital, emphasized its critical role: “Infection is a major killer of preterm babies globally. Early detection is key to saving lives.” The system, now operational in all 28 cots of the hospital’s neonatal unit, is backed by independent research suggesting it could reduce mortality rates in preterm infants by 20%. The remaining cost of installation and operation was covered by NHS Lanarkshire. Garreth, managing director of a pub and restaurant chain, underscored the donation’s emotional significance. “We wanted to do something in their memory,” he said. The couple’s generosity follows a £10 million car park donation

**Youth Arraigned in Death of Man in His 40s After Warrington Street Attack** Bradley Moore, a man in his 40s, died in hospital following an attack on Warrington Street, Ashton-under-Lyne, on Wednesday night. Four teenagers, aged 12 to 17, appeared at Manchester Crown Court on Thursday for a preliminary hearing. The 12-year-old defendant was remanded into local authority care, while his three co-accused—aged 13, 15, and 17—were placed in youth detention. Family members attended the brief hearing. As the youngest defendant left the dock, he blew a kiss to his mother, a moment noted by court observers. Judge Patrick Field QC scheduled a provisional trial for January 2024, with a plea hearing set for August. A bail application for the 12-year-old will be heard at the same court on Wednesday. All four had previously faced magistrates in Oldham. The case, which has drawn attention due to the defendants’ ages, will be closely monitored as it progresses. Further details are expected during upcoming court proceedings.

The revelations follow a demand from a local regulator for companies to release “vehicle disengagement reports,” detailing incidents where autonomous systems ceded control to a human driver. Google and six other car tech firms complied, but critics argue the data underscores the risks of removing traditional safety features. The 32-page report submitted by Google reveals that during 15 months of testing on California roads, its self-driving vehicles experienced 18 disengagement incidents, where human intervention became necessary due to technical malfunctions or external factors. While Google emphasizes that such events are rare—highlighting 230,000 autonomous miles driven without an incident between April and November 2015—Consumer Watchdog’s privacy project director, John Simpson, contends the data contradicts the company’s vision. “How can Google propose a car with no steering wheel, brakes, or driver?” Simpson questioned. He urged the release of video footage and technical data from incidents to “fully understand what went wrong” and ensure public accountability. Google maintains that its engineers rigorously analyze disengagement events to refine safety protocols. “We are generally driving more autonomous miles between these events,” the report states, reflecting progress. However, Simpson argues that transparency remains insufficient, noting that most other companies submitting reports to the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) provided even less detail. The DMV has proposed regulations requiring licensed drivers to remain present in autonomous vehicles, a stance Google challenges. **Hotelier Denies Aviation Charge in Upcoming Trial** A 76-year-old hotelier from Newton Abbot, Devon, has denied a charge brought by the Civil Aviation Authority after alleged flying incidents at his Falmouth Hotel in August 2014. Keith Richardson, self-representing at Truro Magistrates, faces trial for the offence, scheduled for August. Mr. Richardson, owner of Richardson Hotels—covering the Fowey, Falmouth, Metropole, Padstow, Grand, and Grosvenor hotels—maintained his innocence, with the case set to determine the validity of the CAA’s claim.

**Manchester United End Winless Streak Amid Injury Woes as Mourinho Praises'Brave' Mentality** Manchester United ended a four-game winless run in the Premier League with a crucial 3-0 victory over Swansea City, thanks to goals from Zlatan Ibrahimovic, Paul Pogba, and a dominant display at Old Trafford. The result, however, came amid a severe injury crisis that forced manager José Mourinho to field a makeshift defensive line-up, with key players sidelined. Defender Chris Smalling, out since 23 October with a foot injury, and left-back Luke Shaw, who played in the Europa League defeat by Fenerbahçe on Thursday, were ruled out due to lingering pain. Before the game, Mourinho confirmed: “Smalling doesn’t feel that he can play 100% with his pain. Shaw told me this morning that he was not able to play.” The Portuguese manager, serving a touchline ban and watching from the stands, later reflected on the challenges of fielding a weakened squad. “Football is about making tough decisions. For the team, you have to do anything,” Mourinho said. He emphasized the importance of “brave” players willing to play through minor injuries, contrasting them with those who let discomfort dictate their participation. “How many times do you play and you’re not 100%? In every sport, it’s part of the game.” The manager’s comments came as United dealt with the absence of four defenders: Smalling, Shaw, Eric Bailly (knee injury), and Antonio Valencia (arm surgery). **French Protests Escalate as Unrest Over Labor Reforms Intensifies** Trade unions and demonstrators blocked streets nationwide as thousands marched against a proposed labor law, with police using tear gas after youths hurled missiles, reports AFP. The protests, entering their second month, saw several officers injured during clashes Thursday. The draft law, set for parliamentary debate on Tuesday, aims to weaken worker protections against layoffs to boost hiring and combat 9.4% unemployment. President Macron’s government argues the reforms are vital to revive France’s stagnant economy, but critics warn they could erode rights to fair pay, rest periods, and overtime. Unions accuse the administration of sidelining worker voices, fueling tensions as strikes and violence persist. The crisis raises broader questions about France’s struggle to balance economic modernization with social cohesion.

**EU Parliament Votes to Halt Talks with Turkey Amid Tensions with Erdogan** The European Parliament has passed a non-binding resolution urging the European Commission and EU member states to impose a "temporary freeze" on accession talks with Turkey, amid deepening political rifts with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. The vote, backed by 479 members (479 in favor, 37 against, 107 abstentions), was dismissed by Erdogan as "worthless," reflecting the soured state of EU-Turkey relations. Turkey’s EU accession negotiations, which began in 2005, have progressed agonizingly slowly, with only one of 35 required policy chapters closed. The EU has long held that a country must meet all 35 chapters’ criteria to qualify for membership, a threshold Turkey remains far from achieving. The resolution underscores growing concern among MEPs over Erdogan’s government, which has intensified repression following the 2016 coup attempt. Over 120,000 public sector workers, 40,000 suspects, and dozens of journalists have been dismissed, arrested, or detained since the failed coup, according to the parliament. Erdogan accused the EU of supporting “terrorism” rather than standing by Turkey during the crisis, while MEPs argue his crackdown on dissenting voices and pro-Kurdish opposition has eroded Turkey’s democratic foundations. The resolution warns that such measures are “diverting Turkey from its European path” and demands a review of the EU’s stance once repression is halted. Despite the symbolic rebuke, EU leaders are unlikely to act on the resolution, according to BBC correspondent Mark Lowen. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Federica Mogherini, urged continued engagement with Turkey, stressing its strategic importance in curbing migrant flows and countering Islamic State threats. The EU-Turkey deal, struck in March 2016 to reduce irregular migration to Europe, remains a critical component of European security, though fears linger that Erdogan’s growing anti-Western

**UK to Ban Legal Highs as Rochdale Cases Highlight Risks** A new law banning the manufacture and sale of so-called “legal highs” is set to take effect in the UK on the eve of alarming reports from Rochdale, where four individuals have required medical treatment after taking potentially lethal substances. Two men remain in custody following arrests linked to a shop closed for suspected drug offenses, as authorities warn of the dangers posed by these unregulated products. The incidents began last week when a man suffered a cardiac arrest after consuming “Clockwork Orange,” one of several legal highs sold at Clear Vapour, a now-closed shop in Rochdale. He was placed in intensive care, while another man, who had fallen seriously ill and been put into an induced coma, has since recovered and been discharged. Police confirmed the arrests of a 61-year-old and a 34-year-old on suspicion of supplying class B drugs, as part of an investigation into whether the substances contained illegal ingredients. Greater Manchester Police’s Supt Alistair Mallen described the surge in legal high use as “alarming,” noting that drugs such as Kronik, Pandora’s Box, and Annihilation—often marketed as legal alternatives to illicit drugs—are sold with “unclear chemical content.” “These substances are not just harmful; they’re potentially lethal,” he said, reiterating warnings about the growing trend. Legal highs, or psychoactive substances, mimic the effects of drugs like cocaine, cannabis, and ecstasy but often contain synthetic chemicals with unpredictable and severe health risks. Greater Manchester Mayor Tony Lloyd emphasized that the misconception of safety is “costing lives,” citing Spice—a legal high he called “more dangerous than marijuana”—as a product with “fatal consequences.” The impending ban, part of the Psychoactive Substances Act, will make it illegal to produce or sell any substance intended for psychoactive use, with exceptions for alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine. Offenders face up to seven years in prison. Home Office Minister Karen Bradley cited an expert panel’s findings, stating that over 400 lives have been lost to legal highs since 2014. “This threat must be taken seriously,” she said, defending the government’s approach. However, Rochdale Labour MP Simon Danczuk criticized the legislation as “wholly inadequate,” arguing that loopholes will persist. “The wording of the bill fails to disrupt the trade effectively,” he said, urging the government to strengthen the law to prevent continued harm. The app’s free-to-play demo offers a brief taste of the game, but unlocking all three modes—Classic, Toad Rally, and Kingdom—requires payment. As players download the title, social media reactions highlight a divide between those who deem the price too steep and defenders who argue it reflects the value of quality entertainment. **Critics Call the Cost “Absurd”** Some players have taken to Twitter to voice their frustrations, comparing the price to Nintendo’s free-to-play hit *Pokémon Go* or older Mario games. I was expecting more.”* Such sentiments reflect a broader skepticism toward paid mobile games in an era dominated by free-to-play models with optional in-app purchases. **Defenders Highlight Value and Fair Pay for Developers** Nintendo supporters, however, argue the price is fair. “Wow..... people are actually complaining..... Have we become so addicted to free-to-play?” tweeted user titowrestling. **Australian Heavyweight Champion Lucas Browne Fails Drug Test Amid Drug Scandal Concerns** Australian boxer Lucas Browne, 36, faces a potential ban after testing positive for a fat-burning drug following his victory over Ruslan Chagaev to claim the WBA heavyweight title. Browne, who has denied wrongdoing, vows to prove his innocence, but the incident has reignited calls for stricter anti-doping measures in boxing. WBC cruiserweight champion Tony Bellew criticized the sport’s lax approach to drug testing, stating, “Professional boxing has a major problem with drugs. There are not lives at risk in a 100m race. There are in a boxing ring, and that is why it is so alarming.” Bellew highlighted the physical advantages gained from steroids, which he claims allow fighters to “train much harder and recover quicker,” giving users an “unfair advantage” in high-stakes matches. The issue has long plagued the sport. In 2015, negotiations between Floyd Mayweather and Manny Pacquiao were deadlocked over unannounced testing demands. Meanwhile, Sheffield’s Kid Galahad was banned for six months in 2014 after testing positive for Stanozolol, a performance-enhancing steroid. Bellew argues such cases underscore the need for harsher penalties, advocating for “nothing less than a lifetime ban.” “It shouldn’t take someone dying in the ring at the hands of a steroid-user for this to happen,” he added. Bellew, set to face Congo’s Ilunga Makabu for the WBC cruiserweight title this summer, confirmed Goodison Park as a potential venue. His comments echo growing frustration over doping in boxing, with fans and fighters alike demanding transparency. As Browne fights to clear his name, the sport faces mounting pressure to address its credibility crisis. *Read more: “It was like fighting two people” – athletes’ firsthand accounts of doping scandals.*

**Santander Seeks €7.5bn from Shareholders Amid Leadership and Strategic Shifts** Santander, Spain’s largest bank, has announced a €7.5bn (£6bn) capital increase, equivalent to 10% of its capital value, as it seeks to bolster its financial resilience amid economic uncertainty in the eurozone. The move prompted a temporary suspension of its shares on the Madrid stock market ahead of the official announcement. Despite recently passing a European Central Bank stress test with “comfortably” sufficient capital, speculation had swirled about the bank’s need for additional funds, with some analysts questioning whether it might spin off its UK operations or pursue a major acquisition. Shares in Italy’s Monte Paschi surged 8% following the news, as the historic bank—facing its own post-stress-test challenges—hopes to attract bidders. The capital raise comes as Santander’s new leadership under Ana Botín, who assumed control in September after the death of her father, Emilio Botín, embarks on a restructuring effort. Ms. Botín, previously head of the UK division, has already reshaped the top team, replacing CEO Javier Marín with finance director José Antonio Álvarez and making other senior board changes to solidify her vision. In a further signal of fiscal discipline, Santander also announced a dividend cut—a reversal of its past strategy of maintaining payouts even during Spain’s property crash and financial crisis. Analysts broadly endorsed the capital call as prudent amid weakening eurozone conditions, though some expressed surprise. “We met with Santander one month ago, and they didn’t mention needing a capital increase,” Yohan Salleron of France’s Mandarine Gestion told Reuters, underscoring the abruptness of the decision. Ms. Botín has acknowledged heightened competition and regulatory pressures as key challenges, with the bank likely positioning itself for strategic opportunities, including potential acquisitions or divestments. While the cash infusion is expected to strengthen Santander’s balance sheet, questions linger about its immediate strategic priorities. As Monte Paschi’s share price reaction suggests, the move could signal broader shifts in the banking sector, where stability and consolidation remain central themes.

**St Mary’s Christmas Tree Festival Kicks Off with Festive Spirit** St Mary’s Church in Melton Mowbray has launched its annual Christmas tree festival, aiming to top last year’s impressive total of 916 decorated trees. The event, running until Tuesday, showcases creations by schools, charities, businesses, and community groups from across the UK. Adding to the festive cheer, The Rev Kevin Ashby embraced the spirit by dressing as a Christmas tree, delighting visitors during the festival’s opening. Similar tree festivals are common in churches nationwide, combining seasonal charm with fundraising for charitable causes. The event coincides with Melton’s Victorian Christmas weekend in the town center, enhancing the traditional holiday atmosphere. As part of the program, the church will host carol singing services on Saturday and Sunday evenings, inviting the community to join in the celebration of light and generosity.

**Ilex to Close a Year Early Amid Leadership Turmoil and Transfer of Responsibilities** The Office of the First Minister and Deputy First Minister (OFMDFM) announced on Thursday that Ilex, the regeneration company established in 2003 to revitalize former army bases at Fort George and Ebrington in Derry, will close earlier than expected. The decision accelerates its original closure date by one year, ending operations by 31 March 2016. The announcement follows a critical independent review published in July, which highlighted Ilex’s failure to attract private investment and its reliance on public funding. Despite this, the company is credited with significant achievements, including the Peace Bridge, the Science Park at Fort George, and the successful City of Culture initiative in 2013. The remaining capital work projects, including developments at Ebrington, will now be managed by OFMDFM and Derry City and Strabane District Council. This shift aligns with the review’s recommendation that such responsibilities should transition to local authorities. First Minister Peter Robinson acknowledged Ilex’s contributions, stating, “We are grateful for all the work undertaken..... which has opened the site up for all the people of Londonderry and beyond.” Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness reiterated that the council’s long-term management of the Ebrington site remains the goal, ideally achieved by 2017. However, recent leadership instability has hastened the change. Last month saw the resignation of Mel Higgins, Ilex’s fifth chief executive in 12 years, prompting the decision to transfer control. All affected staff will be eligible for redundancy entitlements. While Ilex’s early closure marks the end of an era, it underscores the transition of regeneration efforts to public bodies, ensuring continuity for ongoing projects in the region. This move reflects a strategic pivot to stabilize the Ebrington redevelopment amid management challenges, with local authorities set to lead future initiatives.

Led by a consortium of UK universities and businesses, including Queen’s University Belfast, this $344 million (£226m) telescope will be the largest of its kind, offering unprecedented detail of the Sun’s surface. Its mission? To study the buildup of magnetic energy that drives explosive solar events, which can disrupt power grids, communications, and aviation. The threat posed by solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) is no small concern. A massive solar storm in 1989 caused a 12-hour blackout in Quebec, Canada, crippling the region’s power grid. “We are trying to predict when these explosions will happen so that we can issue a warning,” explained Prof Mihalis Mathioudakis from Queen’s University Belfast. He emphasized that advance alerts could allow power companies to prepare for outages and airlines to reroute polar flights, which face heightened radiation risks during solar storms. **Storm-Generated S Waves Unveiled, Offering New Window into Earth’s Depths** In a groundbreaking discovery, scientists have for the first time traced storm-generated S waves to their source deep within the Earth, opening a new avenue for probing the planet’s hidden layers. The achievement hinges on a “weather bomb”—a powerful low-pressure storm off Greenland that made headlines in the UK in late 2014. This storm, along with others, creates faint seismic signals known as microseisms, which ripple through the Earth’s crust and mantle. While scientists had long detected the faster-moving P waves from these storms, the elusive S waves—responsible for the most violent shaking during earthquakes—had never been traced to their origin. A new study published in *Science* reveals how this barrier has finally been overcome. Microseisms are continuous tremors generated when storm-driven ocean waves collide, sending energy cascading into the seafloor. This energy splits into two faint seismic wave types: P waves, which travel through solids and liquids, and S waves, which only propagate through solids. During earthquakes, these waves appear in violent form, with P waves arriving first and S waves following seconds later. While P waves from storms have been routinely observed—such as signals from Pacific typhoons picked up in California—the S counterparts have remained a mystery until now. The breakthrough came from a high-density network of 202 seismic stations in southern Japan’s Chugoku region, operated by researchers Kiwamu Nishida of the University of Tokyo and Ryota Takagi of Tohoku University. By aggregating data from this array, the team isolated the faint S waves generated by the 2014 Greenland storm and traced them back to their source in the north Atlantic. This feat was only possible through the array’s scale and precision, which allowed the researchers to distinguish the subtle S signals from background noise. The study’s implications are profound. “Most of our knowledge about Earth’s interior comes from studying earthquake waves,” explained Peter Bromirski, a seismologist at the University of California San Diego and co-author of a *Science* commentary on the research. “But earthquakes are sparse in some regions, like the mid-Pacific. Storm-generated microseisms could fill these gaps, offering a new seismic ‘light’ to illuminate Earth’s structure where data are scarce.” S waves, in particular, are critical for mapping the Earth’s solid layers, as they cannot travel through liquid. By detecting these storm-driven signals, scientists may now gain unprecedented access to areas of the planet that have been seismically “dark,” such as vast portions of the Pacific. This could refine models of the mantle and core, and even improve hazard assessments by revealing how tectonic stresses build in less monitored regions. The research also underscores the interconnectedness of Earth’s systems. Storms, long seen as distant drivers of weather and climate, now emerge as inadvertent geophysical tools. As Bromirski noted, “The Earth is constantly talking to us—through both storms and earthquakes. We’re just learning how to listen more closely.” With this new technique, seismologists may soon unlock secrets buried thousands of miles beneath the surface, guided not by earthquakes, but by the quiet rumble of the oceans. *BBC iWonder: How often do forecasters actually get the UK weather right?*

**Cambridge Folk Festival Concludes with Record Attendance and Sunny Finale** Over 14,000 music lovers celebrated at the UK’s premier folk festival as the four-day event ended under sunny skies at Cherry Hinton Hall. Despite intermittent rain earlier in the week, the finale proved a triumph, with highlights including a high-energy set from Saturday’s headliner, Frank Turner and The Sleeping Souls. Neil Jones of Cambridge Live praised the event’s success, stating, “It’s a bumper year..... the energy of the crowd has been incredible, with some amazing performances.” Renowned artists like Lisa Hannigan, former collaborator of Damien Rice, and Orkney group Fara captivated audiences, while emerging talents shone. Norfolk band Morganway, Cambridge’s Kerry Devine, and Bedford’s Danni Nichol all delivered standout acts. Devine, who performed at The Den on Saturday, expressed pride in playing her hometown festival: “I was born in Ely and raised in Cambridge, so this is really special.” Running from Thursday to Sunday, the festival showcased the breadth of folk music, blending tradition with innovation, and leaving attendees eager for next year.

**Spittleborough Roundabout Upgrade Begins to Ease Traffic from Wichelstowe** Plans to upgrade Spittleborough roundabout, near Swindon, have commenced to manage growing traffic from the Wichelstowe housing development. The project, funded by the Local Enterprise Partnership, local councils, and Highways England, includes widening motorway slip roads to four lanes, adding a dedicated right-turn slip road for Swindon-bound traffic onto Hay Lane, and expanding the Great Western Way carriageway. Clearance work is underway, with major construction set to follow. Completion is targeted for spring 2018, or when the 1,100th Wichelstowe home becomes occupiable, per planning conditions. The improvements aim to ease congestion and support the new neighborhood’s growth. Local authorities stress the upgrades are vital for sustainable transport and regional connectivity.

**Radwanska Staves Off Broady to Move Closer to World Number One** *New York, NY* — Agnieszka Radwanska edged a grueling first-set tie-break and held off a valiant effort from Britain’s Heather Broady to claim a 7-6 (11-9), 6-3 victory at the US Open on Wednesday. The win, coupled with other results, could propel the Polish star to the world number one ranking if she continues strong in the coming days. Broady, ranked 82nd in the world, reached the second round of a Grand Slam and faced a top-five opponent for just the second time in her career. The 26-year-old from Stockport made it a challenge, using her 6’2” frame to blast 120mph serves and tally 35 winners from the net. Radwanska, however, held her nerve in a dramatic tie-break after falling 5-2 down, saving four set points as Broady faltered on returns and a final forehand floated long. “She was serving unbelievable,” Radwanska said. “120mph serves are not easy to return.” The 27-year-old Pole recovered from 2-0 down in the second set, capitalizing on Broady’s growing errors. A sharp backhand winner from the wide angle clinched the decisive break at 4-4 before Radwanska closed it out in 1 hour and 43 minutes. “I’m so pleased I could come back in that first set,” Radwanska said. “It was the key set. There was a lot of running and a lot of struggling, but it was another two sets for me.” Meanwhile, top seed Serena Williams advanced to the third round with a 6-3, 6-3 victory over fellow American Vania King. **Farage Hails UKIP’s Welsh Gains Amid EU Critique** Nigel Farage, UKIP leader, asserted that the party is gaining momentum in Wales, trailing Labour by just 5,000 votes in the 2019 European elections. Speaking to BBC Radio Wales, he highlighted shifting political tides, noting ex-Labour voters are turning to UKIP as the party aims to challenge in May’s general election. Farage criticized EU membership for stifling Welsh manufacturing, fishing, and small businesses, claiming European funds have failed to revitalize the economy. He cited a stark imbalance: “For every job created in the green economy, four traditional manufacturing roles are lost,” he stated on the *Good Morning Wales* program, underscoring his party’s anti-EU stance.

**U.S. Social Security Payments to Nazi War Criminals Spark Outcry** An Associated Press investigation has revealed a troubling legal loophole allowing former Nazi war criminals, including guards at World War II labor camps where millions perished, to continue receiving U.S. Social Security benefits after renouncing citizenship and leaving the country voluntarily. At least four WWII-era suspects remain alive and collecting payments, including Auschwitz patroller Jakob Denzinger and former SS guard Martin Hartmann, who moved to Germany and Croatia after decades in the U.S. Congresswoman Carolyn Maloney (D-NY) called the situation “absolutely outrageous,” condemning the use of taxpayer funds to support individuals deemed war criminals. She announced plans to propose legislation to close the loophole, which critics argue permits “Nazi war criminals” to evade accountability while enjoying U.S. retirement benefits. The U.S. Justice Department’s Office of Special Investigations (OSI) has long relied on voluntary renunciation as a faster alternative to deportation hearings. While federal law terminates benefits for those ordered to leave by courts, voluntary departures after citizenship revocation allow payments to continue. Between 1985 and 2020, 38 of 66 Nazi suspects who left the U.S. under this arrangement retained Social Security and Medicare benefits, according to the AP. Justice Department spokesman Peter Carr stated in a release that Congress mandated the “expeditious” removal of Nazi criminals in 1979. “If someone is ordered removed, benefits stop. But voluntary departures may permit continued payments,” he noted, citing current legal boundaries. The practice has sparked ethical debates, as survivors’ groups and lawmakers argue it undermines U.S. war crimes commitments. Hartmann, who fled Arizona to Germany in 2007, and Denzinger, who left Ohio for Croatia in 1989, exemplify the lingering impact of this policy. With no known legal framework to claw back benefits retroactively, the AP report highlights a systemic gap that critics say demands urgent congressional action.

**Inquest into 2013 Brecon Beacons Tragedy Begins as Families Question Military Response** The inquest into the deaths of three soldiers during a grueling 2013 training march in the Brecon Beacons has begun, with families alleging the military failed to act on warnings about extreme heat conditions that led to the tragedies. The soldiers, who were carrying 49lb (22kg) rucksacks, collapsed in staggered incidents throughout the march, with L/Cpl Roberts activating his “man-down” beacon at 15:36 BST. **Dubai Surpasses Heathrow as World’s Busiest Airport** Dubai International Airport handled nearly 70.5 million passengers in 2014, edging past Heathrow’s 68.1 million to claim the title of the world’s busiest airport, Dubai Airports announced. The milestone marks a historic shift in global aviation leadership. Heathrow, operating at 98% capacity, has long sought expansion to maintain its edge. “After 350 years as the hub of air travel, the UK has inevitably ceded the crown to Dubai due to capacity constraints,” said a Heathrow spokesperson. Dubai’s passenger numbers grew 6.1% year-on-year, driven by strategic investments. Sheikh Ahmed Bin Saeed Al Maktoum, Dubai Airports chairman, emphasized the emirate’s ambition: “Our goal is to establish Dubai as a global aviation center.” The shift underscores Dubai’s rapid rise as a key player in international travel, challenging long-standing Western dominance in the sector.

**Rare British Guiana Stamp Fetches Record Price at Sotheby’s** In a swift yet historic transaction, the British Guiana one-cent magenta stamp was sold to an anonymous bidder in just two minutes at Sotheby’s, setting a new world record for the highest price ever paid for a single stamp. The 1-inch-by-1-inch (2.5cm) relic, often hailed as the “most famous and valuable stamp in the world,” was auctioned after remaining hidden from public view since 1986. Sotheby’s confirmed the sale not only broke the previous stamp auction record but also marked the most expensive item ever sold by weight and size. The previous benchmark, a $2.3 million price tag set by an 1855 Swedish stamp in 1996, has been surpassed, cementing the British Guiana’s status as philately’s Holy Grail. The stamp’s unique history adds to its allure: it was hastily printed in 1856 when a shipment of British stamps was delayed, prompting local printers to create three emergency denominations—1-cent magenta, 4-cent magenta, and 4-cent blue. Only the 1-cent magenta survives today, featuring a three-masted ship and the colony’s motto: “We give and expect in return.” The stamp’s last owner, John du Pont, heir to the DuPont chemical empire, acquired it in 1980 for $935,000. Du Pont, who died in prison in 2010 after serving time for murder, left the stamp to his estate. Proceeds from the sale will partially fund the Eurasian Pacific Wildlife Conservation Foundation. Sotheby’s emphasized the stamp’s scarcity and cultural significance, noting it “represents a confluence of history, art, and rarity.” The 1856 artifact, with its crimson hues and storied past, now stands as a testament to the enduring fascination with philately’s crown jewel—a symbol of both colonial history and the relentless pursuit of collectors worldwide.

**Hibernian Miss Chance to Close Gap on Falkirk as Stubbs Praises Resilience Amid Slippery Surface** Hibernian squandered a golden opportunity to narrow the gap on Championship second-placed Falkirk as Jason Cummings’ goal was ruled offside in a 0-0 draw at Easter Road. Manager Alan Stubbs, however, remained optimistic, emphasizing the team’s resilience and the exciting run-in ahead. The visitors, who remain three points behind Falkirk with a game in hand, were frustrated by a pitch Stubbs described as “not a great surface to try and play football on.” The Scottish boss noted his players were “worrying too much about the bobbles rather than trusting their technique,” a factor that disrupted their rhythm in a tight encounter. Despite the challenges, Hibs earned a clean sheet and a valuable point, with goalkeeper Mark Oxley making a crucial save that struck the post. Cummings’ disallowed goal, which appeared onside to many, summed up the day’s officiating frustrations. “The officials didn’t get a lot of things right today to be honest,” Stubbs admitted. While the result left Hibs’ promotion ambitions in their own hands, the manager remained upbeat, highlighting their Scottish Cup Final appearance and the “exciting end to the season” as motivation. The result extended Hibs’ league unbeaten run to four games as they prepare for their final two matches against Dumbarton and Queen of the South. Falkirk, meanwhile, host Morton next, with both teams vying for automatic promotion. Stubbs, unfazed by the narrow escape, insisted his squad was “full of optimism.” “We have been to a final, we are in the Scottish Cup Final and we still have a chance of promotion,” he said. “I’m surprised how people think sometimes it’s doom and gloom. We have an unbelievable end of the season to play for.” For Morton, the point was a missed opportunity to leapfrog Hibs, though manager Jim Duffy accepted the result. A Bobby Barr strike hit the post earlier in the match, and Duffy acknowledged the near-miss. “If that goes in, there is every likelihood we could have picked up the three points,” he said. “But a point against a side of Hibs’ quality is not a bad result for us.” Duffy praised the top four teams for their consistency but noted Morton had “at least deserved” a mid-table finish this season. As the Championship approaches its climax, both Hibs and Falkirk aim to maximize their remaining fixtures. For Stubbs, the focus remains on the “unbelievable end of the season” and seizing the moment. “Let’s see what happens for the next three or four weeks,” he said.

**Jono Dunnett Completes Historic Windsurfing Journey Around Britain Without Support Team** Jono Dunnett, 41, has become the first person to windsurf around Britain without a water-based support team, completing a 2,200-mile (3,540 km) journey that began and ended at Clacton Pier in Essex on 7 June. The intrepid adventurer, who fished for food and sailed alongside dolphins, relied on the kindness of strangers and a makeshift tent crafted from his sail to survive the challenging expedition. Inspired by Tim Batstone, the first windsurfer to circumnavigate Britain in 1984 with a support boat, Dunnett meticulously planned his trip after seeking advice from windsurfers and a round-Britain yachtsman. “I got to see this island I call home in a unique way,” he said, noting the “painstaking risk-assessment” behind the endeavor. While he had no water-based team, Dunnett received “some van-based support” and used a GPS tracker. His longest single-day push covered 100 miles along the south coast. The journey tested his endurance, particularly in cold, wet conditions. Strangers occasionally offered shelter after reading his blog, leaving him “in awe of the fundamental niceness of people.” Yet, some stretches, like the perilous Land’s End, were “a part I would never do again.” Dunnett’s trip also aimed to raise funds for the Pancreatic Cancer Research Fund and Supporting Tanzanian Orphans and Widows, combining personal challenge with philanthropy. Returning to Clacton later this year, he has etched his name in history as a pioneer, proving the sport’s potential for solo, unaided feats. His journey underscores not just human resilience but also the enduring spirit of camaraderie that can emerge from such extremes.

**Colossal Steel Centurion Sculpture Unveiled at Hadrian’s Wall** Wallsend, UK – A striking 8ft 8in Corten steel sculpture, *Sentius Tectonicus*, has been installed at Segedunum, marking the eastern terminus of Hadrian’s Wall. Created by artist John O’Rourke for North Tyneside Council, the three-tonne figure mirrors the durability of the Angel of the North, also constructed from Corten steel. The name, derived from a nearby inscription, honors a Roman centurion, Sentius, who oversaw wall construction. The sculpture features a central opening with ladders ascending four levels, blending accessibility with historical homage. O’Rourke emphasized Wallsend’s industrial legacy, stating the use of steel and fabrication methods ties the artwork to the area’s historic shipbuilding industry. “This piece bridges the ancient and modern, anchoring the site’s Roman past with its working-class roots,” he said. The structure stands as a dynamic tribute to the region’s layered heritage, inviting public interaction while preserving historical continuity.

**Astronomers Unveil 16 New Super-Earths, Boosting Hopes for Alien Life** A groundbreaking study led by an international team of scientists has revealed the discovery of 16 "super-Earths"—planets more massive than Earth but far less dense than gas giants like Jupiter—alongside Neptune-like worlds. The findings, presented at the Extreme Solar Systems conference in Wyoming and set to be published in *Astronomy and Astrophysics*, mark a surge in the hunt for Earth-like exoplanets and their potential to host life. The planets were identified using the High Accuracy Radial Velocity Planet Searcher (Harps), a state-of-the-art spectrograph at Chile’s La Silla Observatory. This instrument detects planets by measuring the subtle "wobbling" of stars caused by gravitational tugs from orbiting bodies—a technique known as the radial velocity method. Dr. Michel Mayor, lead author from the University of Geneva, hailed the discovery as "an exceptionally rich population of super-Earths and Neptune-type planets hosted by stars similar to our Sun," emphasizing the accelerating pace of exoplanetary research. Among the 16 super-Earths, one is located in the "habitable zone"—the region around a star where conditions could allow liquid water, a key ingredient for life, to exist. Another notable find is HD 85512 b, a super-Earth with 3.6 times Earth’s mass, situated at the edge of its star’s habitable zone. While not yet confirmed to support life, its position raises intriguing possibilities for future exploration. The study also highlights five planets with masses less than five times that of Earth, deemed prime candidates for next-generation space telescopes. Dr. Francesco Pepe of the Geneva Observatory noted these worlds could be scrutinized for biosignatures, such as atmospheric oxygen, using advanced instruments. Additionally, the research sheds light on the frequency of low-mass planets around sun-like stars. Observations suggest 40% of such stars host at least one planet less massive than Saturn, reshaping our understanding of planetary system diversity. Harps, with its unprecedented precision, has been pivotal in uncovering these trends. "These discoveries not only expand our cosmic neighborhood but also bring us closer to answering whether life exists beyond Earth," said Mayor. With future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope, scientists aim to analyze the atmospheres of these newly discovered worlds, potentially uncovering traces of life. As the search for habitable planets intensifies, the Harps instrument continues to revolutionize astronomy, revealing that Earth-like worlds might be far more common than once imagined

**Wycombe Edge Past Rovers in Thrilling League Two Encounter** Wycombe Wanderers secured a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Bristol Rovers at the Memorial Stadium, with a pivotal set-piece goal from Tom O’Nien earning the Chairboys a crucial three points. The match remained goalless until the 30th minute when Rovers’ Steve Mildenhall produced a stunning save, pushing Joe Jacobson’s free-kick wide. However, the visitors struck first in the 63rd minute as O’Nien powered home Jacobson’s set-piece delivery, leaving Mildenhall with no chance. Rovers pressed for an equalizer, with Mildenhall again denied a second clean sheet by Ryan Allsop, who made vital stops to thwart Lee Mansell and Ollie Clarke. Despite the efforts, Wycombe held firm, capitalizing on their defensive resilience and tactical discipline. The win lifts Wycombe to sixth in League Two, surpassing Bristol Rovers, who now occupy 10th place. Manager Gareth Ainsworth praised his team’s performance, stating, “It’s a huge three points. We reduced Bristol into a long-ball team and worked hard to exploit set-pieces. I owe a debt of gratitude to my coaching staff—they’ve been instrumental this week.” With the result, Wycombe’s playoff hopes gain momentum, while Rovers face mounting pressure to climb the table in the weeks ahead.

**Legendary Lokomotiv Moscow Forward Sergey Loskov Retires with Emotional Farewell Match** Sergey Loskov, one of Russia’s most decorated footballers, retired with a poignant farewell after making a 420th and final appearance for Lokomotiv Moscow in a 4-0 home win over Orenburg. The 42-year-old, who left the club in 2013 after 18 years, returned to the pitch in February 2023 after serving as assistant manager, seeking a proper send-off before a home crowd. The capital club, currently mid-table in the Russian Premier League, marketed the match as a tribute to the veteran. Loskov, the second-oldest player in the league and the first to appear in 20 different RPL seasons, captained the side wearing his iconic No. 10 shirt. Fans roared his name for the first 11 minutes of the game before he was substituted to a standing ovation, making way for Russia international Aleksei Miranchuk. Loskov, visibly emotional, handed his shirt to his son on the touchline after his departure. The match followed Lokomotiv’s recent Russian Cup victory, and the win marked their first home game since the trophy celebration. “This is my dream come true,” Loskov said post-match, expressing nerves after a lengthy layoff. “I want to thank the president, the fans, and the club for this unforgettable chance to finish my career on the pitch. Now, I can hang up my boots and let the young players take over.” A symbol of Lokomotiv’s golden era, Loskov’s farewell encapsulated a career spanning over two decades, leaving a legacy etched in Russian football history.

**Morrison Shines as QPR Secure Crucial Victory Over Birmingham** Ravel Morrison, on loan at Queens Park Rangers from West Ham United, was the star of the show as his brace secured a 2-0 victory for the Hoops against Birmingham City. The 21-year-old, who has spent much of his career bouncing between clubs on loan, showcased his potential with a composed performance that left his manager, Steve Clark, effusive in praise. Morrison, who previously spent the 2022/23 season on loan at Birmingham under Clark, was a revelation in the middle of the park. His first goal came in the 28th minute, a clinical finish after a quick counterattack, while he doubled QPR’s lead in the 67th minute with a well-timed run and strike. The win lifts QPR closer to their Championship safety hopes, though Morrison’s future remains uncertain amid speculation over his place in England’s World Cup squad. Gascoigne, the legendary England midfielder known for his flair and technical brilliance, is widely regarded as one of the nation’s greatest talents. Clark, who played alongside Gascoigne, argued that the latter’s career might have reached even greater heights had he avoided a career-altering knee injury. Despite his praise, Clark identified Morrison’s attitude as a barrier to international recognition. “Ravel can score goals and change games,” he said. “The only thing is he doesn’t know who Paul Gascoigne is!” The manager believes working under QPR manager Harry Redknapp—a proponent of creative players—could be the key to unlocking Morrison’s full potential. Morrison, who joined QPR on a season-long loan in February, has 11 games remaining to prove his worth. Clark added: “I’d love to see him on that plane to Brazil. He’s capable of doing something for England even in a short appearance.” For now, his focus is on steering QPR away from relegation trouble, with his performance against Birmingham offering a tantalizing glimpse of what the future might hold.

**San Francisco 49ers Fullback Bruce Miller Released After Alleged Attack** The San Francisco 49ers announced Monday they have released fullback Bruce Miller (29) following his arrest in connection with an alleged assault on a 70-year-old man and his son at a Fisherman’s Wharf hotel on Sunday night. Both victims required hospital treatment, with authorities reporting the incident stemmed from a dispute over a hotel room. Local broadcaster KTVU confirmed the altercation occurred during the late evening hours at an unspecified venue in the popular tourist district. Miller, a 6ft 2in, 248lb (112kg) player with the 49ers since 2011, faces unspecified charges, though no formal statement from police has been released. The team’s brief announcement emphasized their decision to part ways with Miller, who now joins a roster already under scrutiny following quarterback Colin Kaepernick’s controversial anthem protests. Kaepernick, who recently sparked national debate by refusing to stand for the national anthem to highlight racial injustice, received support from former President Barack Obama, who defended the player’s right to express his views. As the 49ers navigate off-field controversies, Miller’s arrest adds further pressure on the team amid a turbulent period for NFL players facing public and institutional scrutiny.

**By-Election Sparks in Sleaford as Brexit Rift Deepens** A by-election in Sleaford and North Hykeham has been triggered after Conservative MP Stephen Phillips resigned last week, citing “irreconcilable policy differences” with the government over Brexit. The contest, expected to take place before year-end, has intensified as UKIP’s Joanne Evans aims to unseat Conservative hold, vowing to challenge the government’s approach to EU withdrawal. Evans, a former Conservative and current UKIP candidate, emphasized her campaign’s focus on honoring the 2016 referendum result. “The people of Lincolnshire voted to leave the European Union, and it looks as though the establishment is trying to renege on that,” she stated. Her remarks follow a High Court ruling on Thursday that the government cannot unilaterally notify the EU of its exit intention without parliamentary approval—a decision she called an “unacceptable” attempt to undermine the Brexit mandate. The Lincolnshire constituency, which recorded over 75% support for Leave in 2016, has become a battleground. Recent years have seen an influx of EU workers into its agricultural sector, complicating local attitudes toward the EU. Phillips, who secured a 24,115 majority in 2017, argued the government’s Brexit strategy was misaligned with local priorities. Evans faces competition from Conservative councillor Richard Davies, Independent Joseph Hyatt, and UKIP’s Victoria Ayling and Robin Hunter-Clarke. Meanwhile, UKIP’s leadership contest, due November 28, features Evans against Paul Nuttall and John Rees-Evans, adding uncertainty to the party’s trajectory. The by-election highlights the deepening political rift over Brexit’s execution. With the High Court decision emboldening pro-Leave factions, Evans pledged to pressure Prime Minister Theresa May to “get us out” of the EU, warning against what she called the “establishment’s kowtowing” to Brussels. **BBC to Deliver 180 Hours of Free Coverage for 2018 Commonwealth Games on Gold Coast** The BBC has confirmed it will provide 180 hours of live coverage across its platforms for the 2018 Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast, Australia, marking its 17th consecutive partnership with the event. The broadcast will span BBC One, BBC Two, the BBC Sport website, iPlayer, and radio, ensuring free access to audiences across the UK. The BBC’s inclusive, innovative coverage from Glasgow ensured UK fans felt part of the action, and I’m confident they’ll deliver another unforgettable experience.” The Games will also feature a landmark expansion of para-sport, with 300 athletes competing in 38 medal events across seven sports—the largest para-sport program in Commonwealth history. With two years until the Games, anticipation is building for a celebration of unity, athleticism, and record-breaking performances, all brought to UK audiences free of charge by the BBC.

As Venezuela’s economic and political crisis deepens, the standoff underscores growing fears of authoritarian governance and eroding democratic norms in the region.

**Libya’s Eastern Government Imposes Travel Ban on Women for “National Security”** Tripoli and al-Beyda — Libya’s eastern authorities have enforced a new travel ban restricting women from transiting through the region, citing “national security reasons.” The measure, first implemented at al-Beyda’s Labraq International Airport, affects all passengers passing through the eastern part of the country, according to BBC North Africa correspondent Rana Jawad. Controlled by General Khalifa Hafter’s forces, eastern Libya—which stretches from Ajdabiya to Tobruk—has seen the ban applied to land, air, and sea travel. A spokesman for the eastern government’s Chief of Staff, Abdulrazzak al-Naduri, told the BBC in a TV interview that the restriction targets women affiliated with civil society groups, accusing them of being “used by foreign intelligence.” Despite lacking parliamentary approval, the directive is already in effect, with military officers enforcing it without legal oversight. The decision underscores Libya’s deepening fragmentation, where rival administrations in Tripoli and the east impose competing rules. While the internationally recognized government in Tripoli faces challenges from Islamist militias, Hafter’s eastern bloc continues to consolidate power, often bypassing democratic processes. Analysts link the travel ban to broader efforts by Hafter to centralize control in the east, where he has long advocated for a more “traditional” social order. Libya’s political instability dates to the 2011 NATO-backed overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi, which left the country fractured and vulnerable to factional conflicts. The current restrictions reflect how security concerns and ideological agendas intersect in the east, further complicating hopes for national unity. As the ban sparks international scrutiny, it highlights the precarious balance of power in a region where authority is as much about control as it is about law.

The incident involved a black Renault Clio that veered off the road on a bend between a resort and Penrhyn Bay, crashing into a field. The collision occurred between 5:30 PM and 9:30 PM on Friday. The vehicle’s driver, a woman with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, was hospitalized in Stoke. North Wales Police are appealing for information from the driver or passengers of a small van or SUV reportedly parked on the grass verge of Gloddaeth Lane near the crash site at approximately 6:15 PM. Sgt Nikki Grimes-Williams stated, “We believe this vehicle may hold crucial details about what happened.” The crash remains under investigation, with authorities urging witnesses or those with dashcam footage to come forward. **Drought and Water Crisis Threaten Italian Agriculture, Spur Urgent Action** Italy’s agricultural sector is grappling with a severe drought, with dairy farmers, olive groves, tomato growers, and wine grape producers among the hardest hit, warns Coldiretti, the country’s farmers’ association. A crippling lack of rainfall, compounded by a persistent heatwave, has left 60% of farmland under threat, sparking fears of reduced harvests and soaring prices for key crops. Milk production has also dipped as livestock struggle in the extreme heat. The crisis has escalated in northern regions, where a state of emergency was declared in two provinces. Meanwhile, southern Italy faced wildfire emergencies earlier this month, forcing hundreds to evacuate as flames raged through rural areas. Farmers in at least 10 regions are now seeking a “natural calamity” declaration from the agriculture ministry, citing the devastating impact on livelihoods, reports Ansa. Rome, already reliant on dwindling water reserves, is bracing for drastic rationing. Local authorities in the Lazio region halted water pumping from Lake Bracciano, 30km north of the capital, after levels dropped to dangerous lows. The lake, which supplied 8% of Rome’s water, is now at risk of an environmental collapse, according to Lazio Governor Nicola Zingaretti. “We must act quickly,” he urged, as utility company Acea has already begun shutting off iconic drinking fountains. Residents may face up to eight hours daily without running water, further compounding the crisis. The convergence of drought, heat, and wildfires has placed Italy’s food security and economy in jeopardy. With agriculture a cornerstone of the nation’s exports, the government faces mounting pressure to implement urgent solutions to avert long-term damage to rural communities and global markets.

The aircraft landed safely at 08:48 GMT, using only one engine. Divisional officer Neil Fenwick, who responded to the incident, praised the “textbook operation.” He confirmed no injuries were reported and emphasized the successful coordination between emergency services and the crew. “This had the potential to be extremely serious, but everything which should happen did,” he said. The airline confirmed the flight adhered to safety procedures and noted engineers were inspecting the aircraft at Southend. “Initial indications are that no fire took place,” the company said. Passengers on the diverted flight are reported to be unharmed, and the incident has not disrupted regular operations at either airport. The cause of the false alarm remains under investigation.

**County Cricket 2017: ECB Announces Format Overhaul** The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has unveiled sweeping changes to domestic cricket for the 2017 season, reshaping the structure of county competitions to enhance fan engagement and player development. ECB chairman Colin Graves described the changes as beneficial for fans, players, and international teams, stating they create a “clearer season structure” that allows players to focus on specific skills and balances all three formats. The T20 Blast will remain a single-tier competition until 2019, with plans for a city-based franchise model postponed for now. Meanwhile, four-day cricket will face a two-month break during July and August, accommodating the revised One-Day Cup schedule and T20 fixtures. Graves emphasized the changes simplify the cricket calendar and improve accessibility for audiences. The ECB’s move follows calls for innovation, including former England captain Michael Vaughan’s recent suggestion that county cricket needs a new tournament. Fans are encouraged to track updates via the BBC Sport app, which offers customizable alerts for cricket scores and other sports events.

**Brain Study Links Amygdala Size to Social Network Complexity** A groundbreaking study published in *Nature Neuroscience* reveals a potential evolutionary role for the amygdala, a brain region long associated with emotions, in managing complex social networks. Researchers led by Dr. Lisa Feldman Barrett of Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School found that individuals with larger, more intricate social circles tend to have a larger amygdala, even when accounting for factors like age and overall brain size. The study, which involved 58 healthy volunteers, used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to analyze brain structure while participants detailed their social connections. The results showed a clear correlation between the amygdala’s volume and both the size and complexity of a person’s social network. “We found that amygdala volume correlates with the size and complexity of social networks in adult humans,” the team wrote, underscoring the region’s critical role in social behavior. The amygdala, traditionally linked to processing emotions and threats, may have evolved to support the demands of human social life, which grows increasingly complex over time. Dr. Barrett explained to the BBC that a larger amygdala could enhance an individual’s ability to interpret social and emotional cues, enabling more effective navigation of relationships. “This allows us to develop strategies to get along and get ahead in life,” she added. The findings align with earlier research on the amygdala’s role in social cognition and provide new insights into how brain structure adapts to societal demands. The team is now exploring how abnormalities in the amygdala and related brain regions might contribute to social challenges in conditions like autism or schizophrenia. This study highlights the interplay between neuroscience and social behavior, offering a window into the evolutionary pressures that have shaped the human brain. As the researchers continue their work, understanding these connections could pave the way for innovative approaches to treating social and psychiatric disorders.

**Ex-Head Teacher Jill Evans Faces Two-Year Teaching Ban After Council Upholds Conduct Charges** Jill Evans, 54, a former head teacher at Heolgerrig Community Primary School in Merthyr Tydfil, has been banned from teaching for two years after a General Teaching Council for Wales panel upheld three charges of unacceptable professional conduct. During a hearing in Cardiff, Evans denied all nine allegations brought against her, but the council found three actions proved and two partially proven. The upheld charges included intimidating staff to sign a letter opposing a proposed new playground at the school, a move the panel described as "beyond firm management." Additionally, she was accused of appointing her son’s partner as a teaching assistant, violating council guidelines on recruitment processes. Chair of the panel, Jacquie Turnbull, emphasized that Evans’ behavior demonstrated a failure to uphold professional standards. However, the council did not find sufficient evidence to support allegations of misuse of grant funding, breach of confidentiality, or failure to address health and safety concerns. Claims that Evans falsified staff meeting minutes were also dismissed. Gwilym Roberts-Harry, representing Evans, noted her "excellent career" prior to the allegations, citing positive inspection reports from Heolgerrig and other schools she had led. While the panel acknowledged her past contributions, Turnbull stated the findings justified a two-year ban. Roberts-Harry said it was "unlikely" Evans would return to teaching, with her instead planning retirement. Evans has 21 days to appeal the decision, which could impact her future in education. The case highlights ongoing scrutiny of leadership conduct in schools and the council’s role in upholding ethical standards.
