The U.S.-backed campaign faces persistent threats from IS, which continues to employ asymmetric tactics to destabilize regional efforts.

**Morocco Unilaterally Withdraws Troops from Western Sahara Buffer Zone Amid Stalemate** A tense standoff in Western Sahara has taken a new turn as Morocco announced a unilateral withdrawal of its troops from the Guerguerat border zone, a move described as a gesture of goodwill toward the United Nations amid a decades-old conflict. The decision, reportedly taken personally by King Mohammed VI following a call with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, marks a symbolic but limited shift in Morocco’s long-standing stance on the disputed territory. The Guerguerat buffer zone, established under a 1991 UN-brokered ceasefire, has been a flashpoint since Morocco deployed forces into the area in 2015, breaching the agreement. The Polisario Front, which seeks independence for Western Sahara, dismissed the recent withdrawal as a “window dressing,” arguing that the move involves a mere “few hundred metres” of retreat and does not address the core issue: the unresolved status of the territory. Western Sahara, a sparsely populated desert region on Africa’s northwest coast, was annexed by Morocco in 1975, sparking an armed struggle by the Polisario. A 16-year conflict ended with a truce, but a promised UN referendum on independence has never materialized. Morocco controls two-thirds of the territory, while the Polisario administers the rest, with over 100,000 Sahrawi refugees living in camps in Algeria. Morocco’s re-entry into the African Union (AU) in January 2017—after a 33-year absence—highlighted its renewed diplomatic efforts to secure international recognition of its sovereignty over Western Sahara. The AU had previously recognized the Polisario as the territory’s legitimate government. King Mohammed VI’s recent visits to African nations and the AU rejoining underscore Morocco’s strategy to isolate the Polisario diplomatically. The UN’s role remains pivotal. Guterres’ call for Morocco’s withdrawal followed criticism of his predecessor, Ban Ki-moon, who in 2016 called the Moroccan occupation an “occupation,” prompting an apology from the UN. Guterres’ engagement with Rabat appears aimed at reviving dialogue, though skepticism persists. For the Polisario, the partial retreat does little to alleviate concerns over Morocco’s commitment to a referendum. “The Moroccan decision is window dressing,” a Polisario statement declared, emphasizing that the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination remains unfulfilled. Analysts suggest the move reflects Morocco’s dual strategy: aligning with the UN to avoid further international friction while maintaining its territorial claim. However, without progress on a referendum, the conflict’s resolution remains distant. The Guerguerat withdrawal may ease immediate tensions but fails to address the

**Historic Allegations Against Late Cardiff MP Under Police Review** Historical abuse allegations involving the late Welsh MP George Thomas, who died in 1997, have resurfaced, prompting an investigation by British Transport Police (BTP). A second report of sexual assault was submitted to Gwent Police, detailing an incident allegedly occurring between 1964 and 1966 during a train journey from Newport to London Paddington. The alleged victim, a man who was 16 or 17 at the time, stated he was assaulted but did not provide a formal statement to police. BTP confirmed awareness of two allegations against Thomas, who represented Cardiff as a Labour MP and was born in Port Talbot. The first claim involves “inappropriate touching” on a 1959 train from London to Aberystwyth. Both reports have been forwarded to Operation Hydrant, a team handling historical child sexual abuse inquiries, including Operation Pallial (linked to north Wales abuse) and Operation Yewtree (prompted by Jimmy Savile’s abuse cases). A BTP spokesperson emphasized the ongoing review of evidence, noting the complexity of historical investigations. While Thomas is deceased, authorities are committed to addressing these claims to support survivors and uncover truth. The case underscores renewed scrutiny of historical figures amid broader efforts to confront past abuses.

**BBC Unveils Unprecedented Coverage of Hay Festival as New Three-Year Partnership Begins** From May 22 to June 1, the Hay Festival will be transformed into a global stage, with the BBC delivering its most extensive live coverage yet. Radio and television shows will broadcast from the iconic Welsh literary gathering, reaching audiences worldwide through BBC World News and online platforms. The festival’s 27th edition marks the start of a landmark three-year partnership with the BBC, replacing Sky Arts’ previous coverage and signaling a major shift in the event’s media strategy. The BBC’s multi-platform approach will see a full program of events aired across BBC Radios 2, 3, 4, 6 Music, as well as BBC Radio Wales and Radio Cymru. Highlights will include live streams of headline events on the BBC website, appearances by prominent presenters at a dedicated BBC Tent, and a special performance from singer Cerys Matthews. *The One Show* will broadcast live from Hay for the first time, while the *Talking Books* program will feature five special episodes centered on the festival. BBC Wales will contribute live coverage and a documentary exploring the festival’s impact on the town of Hay-on-Wye, with BBC Four also set to air a feature on the event. Daily updates, videos, and live feeds of popular sessions will ensure global accessibility, aligning with the BBC’s ambition to “join up arts like never before.” Tony Hall, BBC Director General, emphasized the broadcaster’s commitment to bridging arts and culture: “Our coverage will give the public access to the greatest writers, performers, and thinkers in a way no one else can.” Peter Florence, Hay Festival’s director, hailed the partnership as a way to “give everyone, everywhere, the best seat at the table.” Rhodri Talfan Davies, BBC Wales director, praised Hay as a “festival of ideas” that brings together global leaders in thought and literature. Once described by former U.S. President Bill Clinton as “the Woodstock of the mind,” the Hay Festival has long been celebrated as a hub for intellectual exchange. With this new collaboration, the BBC aims to amplify its reach and reaffirm its role as a cultural cornerstone. As the festival unfolds, audiences worldwide will witness its magic through a unified lens of television, radio, and digital innovation.

**Winchester to Replace Aging Leisure Centre with New Out-of-Town Facility** Winchester City Council has approved plans to replace the 42-year-old River Park Leisure Centre, which requires £3 million in repairs, with a modern out-of-town complex at Bar End. The new £25m facility, expected to take three years to build, will feature a 50m swimming pool, state-of-the-art fitness areas, and community spaces. The council aims to fund the project through loans and potential partnership funding from the University of Winchester. The existing centre at North Walls will be demolished, with the site repurposed for other uses. This follows controversy in 2013 when proposed expansions into nearby parkland sparked protests from campaigners, who argued the plans threatened “Winchester’s only park.” Councillors emphasized the new Bar End site will alleviate pressure on green spaces while providing improved facilities. Final designs and a business case will now be developed, with the project subject to further council approval.

**China Cracks Down on'Bizarre' Architecture, Banning Over-the-Top Designs** The Chinese government has launched a crackdown on what it deems "bizarre" architecture, targeting "oversized, xenocentric, weird" structures. Landmarks like a teapot-shaped building and a skyscraper resembling trousers now face scrutiny. The new directive mandates buildings must be "economical, functional, aesthetically pleasing," and "environmentally friendly," signaling a shift toward practical urban design. Amid the cleanup, entrepreneur Chairman Zhang has sparked a construction revolution. His 57-storey flatpack skyscraper, assembled in 19 days, exemplifies rapid, cost-effective innovation. While his futuristic vision may align with the government’s goals, the directive’s impact on such bold projects remains uncertain. China’s architectural landscape is poised for a dramatic transformation, blending tradition with modernity in a race to redefine its skylines.

**Flight Diverted to Heathrow Over Possible Birth Onboard, Airport Confirms** Heathrow Airport confirmed flight SV21 was diverted on Friday for a medical emergency. Air Live reported at 10:47 BST that "a woman is giving birth" onboard. London Ambulance Service responded at 10:32 BST, meeting the plane as it landed and transporting the woman to a hospital urgently. Officials have not confirmed whether the birth occurred during the flight or after the diversion.

**Crusaders Target Historic Title Retention in Clutch Clash with Linfield** Crusaders sit five points clear at the top of the Irish Premiership with five games remaining, but their quest to retain the league title for the first time in their history will be put to the test this weekend when they face in-form Linfield. Manager Stephen Baxter’s side, buoyed by a strong record against the Blues, aim to shut down David Healy’s outfit during a critical post-split fixture. While Crusaders defender Ryan Coates admits the challenge is formidable, he remains confident in his team’s ability to overcome Linfield. “It’s going to be a tough ask against a good Linfield team, but we have the tools here to win,” Coates said. The Blues, however, will enter the match without key midfielder Aaron Burns, who is serving a two-match suspension after scoring a hat-trick in the Irish Cup earlier this week. Linfield, who have lost just once in their past 15 league games, are mounting a determined push for the Gibson Cup, with Healy’s side showing increased hunger this season. However, Crusaders hold a psychological edge, having lost only three of their last 16 Premiership encounters against the Blues. “We’ve been at the top since October, and the pressure has been on us since then,” Coates added. “But we’re enjoying it because that’s where you want to be in football.” The Northern Irish champions acknowledged their inconsistent fluency this term but emphasized their knack for raising their game in crucial moments. “Sometimes we perform better in the big matches, and that’s what we’re banking on,” Coates said. He also highlighted Linfield’s recent intensity: “They look hungrier than in previous seasons, but we’re looking to end that run.” Meanwhile, the first round of post-split fixtures also features key encounters at the bottom of the table. Warrenpoint Town could move off the relegation zone with a win at Carrick Rangers, while Portadown seek to halt their slide in a home clash against 11th-placed Ballinamallard United. With the title race entering its final stretch, Crusaders’ pursuit of a historic first-ever title defense promises a thrilling conclusion to a season defined by resilience and rivalry.

**Rare Albino Bat Spotted in Scottish Garden—A “Once-in-a-Lifetime” Discovery** A rare albino bat has been captured on camera in a quiet garden in Monikie, Angus, sparking excitement among experts who describe the sighting as a “once-in-a-lifetime” event. The bat, likely a pipistrelle, was filmed by local resident Brian Whyte in September as it swooped and clung to a garden wall. Its significance came to light only recently when Whyte shared the footage with the Tayside Bat Group, revealing a genetic marvel: a mammal with no natural pigmentation, a phenomenon with only six or seven known sightings in the UK. Dr. Amanda Wilson, chairwoman of the Tayside Bat Group, called the discovery “very exciting.” “We’ve been active for 30 years and never encountered one before,” she said. “Albinism is incredibly rare in bats, so this is a remarkable find.” The bat’s white fur and pink eyes—hallmarks of albinism, a genetic condition that leaves mammals without pigment—are visible in the footage. Experts suggest the lack of color could make the creature more vulnerable to predators like owls or cats, reducing its chances of survival. Whyte, 58, described the moment he noticed the bat: “It was almost tame. I saw it flying around in daylight, fluttering about and landing frequently. I thought it looked tired.” Bats typically avoid daylight, but Dr. Wilson explained the mammal might have been “confused” due to seasonal changes. Most UK bats are now entering hibernation, making a reappearance this year unlikely. The discovery has also raised questions about the potential for other albino bats in the area, as albinism can occur sporadically in populations. However, Dr. Wilson noted that such individuals rarely survive long. “Pipistrelles can live up to 16 years, but this one may not reach that mark,” she said. Next summer, Dr. Wilson plans to return to Monikie in hopes of locating the bat again. “Its survival will depend on avoiding predators and adapting to its environment,” she added. For now, the footage serves as a rare glimpse into the hidden wonders of nature. “It’s a reminder of how much we still don’t know,” Dr. Wilson said, as the bat group celebrates what may be a fleeting, magical moment in bat conservation.

**Naomi Watts to Join Glantraeth FC Board as Club President** Naomi Watts, renowned for her roles in *Mulholland Drive* and *King Kong*, has expressed excitement about joining Glantraeth FC’s board as its new president. The English-born actress, who spent three years of her childhood on her grandparents’ farm near the Welsh village of Malltraeth (population 400), will take the helm of the small-town football club, which plays in the Welsh Alliance League’s third tier. Glantraeth FC typically draws crowds of just 40 fans per match. The appointment follows the resignation of former president Sir George Meyrick in August. Club secretary Stan Strickland, inspired by Watts’ local ties, wrote to her Los Angeles-based agent via Sunset Boulevard, securing a positive response this week. “She attended school in Llangefni before becoming a global star,” Strickland noted, adding, “If you don’t ask, you don’t get.” He hinted the collaboration could attract international attention, with Watts’ publicist now involved—potentially drawing media like the *New York Times*. Watts’ name will feature on the club’s website, matchday programs, and letterheads. Strickland expects ongoing discussions to outline her role, including annual performance updates. For Glantraeth FC, the partnership marks a bold step for a club with a modest footprint, bridging local heritage and Hollywood glamour.

The single currency fell 0.5% to $1.0894 on Thursday, pressured by expectations that the European Central Bank (ECB) will keep its accommodative monetary stance for an extended period. Meanwhile, markets are increasingly pricing in tightening cycles in the UK and US. Central bank rhetoric intensified the euro’s decline. Bank of England Governor Mark Carney signaled that UK rate hikes were “moving closer” following Tuesday’s comments, while Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen reiterated on Wednesday that US interest rates could rise before year-end. The contrast in policy trajectories underscored the euro’s vulnerability, as higher yields in London and Washington typically draw capital flows away from the eurozone. Equity markets showed resilience, with the UK’s FTSE 100 climbing 0.63% to 6,796.45, buoyed by Greece’s approval of a new bailout agreement. European bourses outperformed, with Germany’s Dax rising 1.53% and France’s Cac 40 gaining 1.47%. Retail stocks drew attention: Dixons Carphone, the merged electronics and mobile retail giant, saw shares rise 1.45% after reporting a 21% surge in underlying annual profits to £381 million. The firm hailed the result as a “terrific year” following its integration. Sports Direct shares inched up 0.27% despite cutting its 2016 core earnings target to £420 million from £480 million, citing missed acquisition plans in 2015. The mixed signals from central banks and corporate earnings highlight the fragility of investor confidence, as markets balance optimism over fiscal measures with uncertainty over global growth.

**Dumfries Ukulele Festival Set for Record-Breaking Run** The Dumfries Ukulele Festival, now in its second year, is set to captivate audiences on the Crichton Campus until Sunday, featuring over 70 acts from local and global artists. Headliners include Scottish talents Zoe Bestel and Claire Hastings, alongside an international lineup that promises a diverse musical experience. Organizers announced that early ticket sales have already surpassed those of last year’s inaugural event, hinting at a larger audience. Festival director Linda Butterworth highlighted the success as a testament to the “brilliant venue, great programme, and meticulous organisation,” along with the dedication of volunteers and carefully curated performances. “We’re proud to showcase Dumfries as a hub for international quality events,” she said. Butterworth emphasized the festival’s inclusive spirit, noting that “you don’t have to play the ukulele to enjoy it.” She urged attendees to embrace the vibrant atmosphere, joking that they might leave with a new instrument—and a list of new friends. With a mix of local pride and global flair, the festival aims to deliver “something special” for all.

**Tom Elliott Steps Down as UUP Leader Amid Internal Strife and Political Challenges** Tom Elliott’s tenure as leader of the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has come to an end amid allegations of internal division, controversial statements, and a struggle to chart a clear path forward. The Fermanagh MLA resigned on Thursday, blaming factional hostility and a lack of support for advancing key initiatives. While the exact reasons for his departure remain opaque, speculation centers on conflicts with colleagues such as David McNarry over media revelations about talks with the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), and tensions with Danny Kennedy over the A5 road upgrade—a project the DUP has long opposed. Elliott acknowledged that “obstruction and hostility” emerged soon after his election as leader and persisted relentlessly. However, he added that such dynamics are “part and parcel of politics,” where leaders must “make their own luck.” Known for his courteous, low-key demeanor, Elliott’s leadership has been marked by missteps, including inflammatory remarks about Gaelic matches and a controversial label for Sinn Féin as “scum,” which drew widespread criticism and are revisited in a recent analysis on the UUP website. The party now faces a critical juncture. With a contested leadership race set to conclude in a week, Elliott’s Fermanagh supporters—comprising a significant portion of the UUP’s internal electorate—could wield considerable influence over his successor. Questions loom over whether the new leader can avoid political pitfalls and steer the party away from decline. The UUP, already a diminished force in Stormont’s 90-member assembly, risks further marginalization if it continues its current trajectory. A shift to opposition could reshape Stormont’s political landscape, but it also risks alienating voters unaccustomed to such a stance. Elliott’s exit underscores the UUP’s broader challenges: balancing tradition with modernity, and unity with internal dissent. As the party searches for renewal, the pressure to chart a viable future intensifies. Whether the next leader can navigate these treacherous waters will determine if the UUP can avoid becoming a relic of Northern Ireland’s political past.

The search, however, has yet to locate Zaani. **Man Sentenced for Hospital Staff Fraud Scheme** A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to four years in prison for defrauding hospital staff in Hampshire and Dorset. David Coombs, of Hunston Road, Chichester, admitted nine fraud offences in 2015 during a hearing at Southampton Crown Court. Targets, aged between 49 and 83, were befriended by Coombs, who claimed to be a wealthy businessman with multiple properties and offshore accounts. He allegedly spun tales of needing money after saying his wallet was stolen or his bank card blocked. The scheme, spanning 22 months, came to light when a former romantic partner reported Coombs for harassment, prompting police investigation. Detective Sergeant Will Whale condemned the “web of lies,” stating the fraud had “immeasurable” financial and psychological effects on victims. Coombs, employed as a designer, exploited trust by cultivating relationships before making money requests. His deception ended when the relationship soured, revealing the extensive fraud. The court heard victims were left distressed, with one woman contacting authorities after his harassment intensified. Police emphasized the need for vigilance in similar cases, urging reporting of suspicious activity to prevent future harm.

**Hearts Midfielder Josh Nicholson Joins Minnesota United on Free Transfer** Heart of Midlothian (Hearts) midfielder Josh Nicholson, 22, has joined Major League Soccer side Minnesota United on a free transfer, with the Scottish club including a sell-on clause in the deal. Nicholson, who spent nearly a decade with Hearts’ youth academy before making his senior debut in 2013, appeared 127 times for the club, scoring 16 goals. The transfer marks his exit without direct compensation for Hearts, though the sell-on clause may provide future financial benefits. Speaking to Minnesota’s official website, Nicholson said, “It was an easy decision after speaking with the coaching staff; everyone made me feel at home straight away.” The versatile midfielder, who also featured eight times for Scotland’s Under-21s, praised the club’s approach. Minnesota head coach Adrian Heath highlighted Nicholson’s adaptability: “He can cut inside from either side, has two good feet, and can beat his man. It’s rare to bring in a European player who sees MLS as a step up. We’re delighted to have him.” Nicholson’s move underscores his ambition to develop in North America while offering Minnesota a dynamic attacker. Hearts confirmed they receive no immediate compensation but retain potential future rewards via the sell-on clause.

**Women Take Up Arms to Clean a Polluted Village in Nalanda** In a village of 275 homes in Nalanda district, a group of 16 women is waging a quiet battle against open defecation, urging residents to avoid soiling roads and fields near homes. With most households lacking toilets, villagers have long resorted to relieving themselves along a 10ft-wide main road, turning it into a health hazard. “The road is 10ft wide, but because of excreta along the sides, we find it impossible to walk on it,” said Sudama Prasad, a resident who described the stench and filth as unbearable. The issue is not isolated to this village. Over 500 million Indians still lack access to latrines, according to the World Health Organisation, leading to widespread contamination of water bodies and the spread of diseases. Concerned about the filth and frequent outbreaks, 52-year-old Girija Devi began patrolling the roads last October. Her solo effort soon inspired others, and the group swelled to 16 women. “We split into groups of four and patrol the roads at dawn or dusk, when most people go outdoors,” Devi explained. Armed with bamboo sticks and torches, the women confront offenders, pleading with them to use distant fields instead. But resistance has been fierce. “Many people in the village are upset with us; some have even stopped talking to us,” admitted Raj Munni Devi, another patroller. Despite the backlash, the group remains resolute, working in darkness to uphold hygiene. Their mission, however, extends beyond cleanliness—it is a push for dignity. “A clean village means healthy lives for our children,” said Devi. As they continue their patrols, the women hope their efforts will spark lasting change in a community long trapped in a cycle of neglect.

**Tragic Collision on Rivington Road Claims Life of 43-Year-Old Man** A man from St Helens has died after a collision with a Yamaha motorcycle on Rivington Road near Belmont on Sunday afternoon. The 43-year-old was hospitalized at Royal Preston but succumbed to injuries. The motorcyclist sustained facial trauma and was treated at Salford Royal. The road remained closed for three hours post-crash. Lancashire Constabulary’s Sgt Claire Pearson stated officers are investigating the incident and urging witnesses to contact them for details.

**Two Admit Culpable Homicide in 2014 River Clyde Killing** Kevin Caughey, 33, and Margaret McKellar, 31, have been jailed for their roles in the fatal attack of 41-year-old Scott McGuire at a suspension bridge in Carlton Place, Glasgow, on July 8, 2014. Both pleaded guilty to the reduced charge of culpable homicide, initially charged with murder. Caughey was sentenced to eight years and one month in prison, while McKellar received six years and four months. The incident began after McGuire struck McKellar with a bottle during a confrontation, the High Court in Glasgow heard. In response, the pair launched a violent attack, stabbing McGuire in the head and body before pushing him into the River Clyde. The victim hit his head on a rock during the assault and drowned. His body was recovered later that day. Judge John Beckett QC condemned the "senseless killing," emphasizing the devastating impact on McGuire’s family. He noted: "While Mr McGuire may have triggered the attack with initial violence, you reacted with wanton violence. You left the scene without aiding him or seeking help." The court was told that superficial stab wounds were inflicted during the assault, and the attack stemmed from a row between the individuals. Caughey, who has 74 previous convictions—including seven for weapon possession—and McKellar, with 60 prior convictions including assault, both have extensive criminal histories. Their guilty pleas were accepted by the Crown, which acknowledged their remorse but stressed the severity of the offense. McGuire, survived by his father and four adult children, was described by the judge as a man whose life was "cut tragically short." The case underscores the consequences of escalating conflicts into lethal violence, with the court emphasizing the need for accountability. The sentencing concludes a decade-long legal process, offering a measure of closure to a grieving family.

**Mudslides Devastate Tetovo, Spark Rescue Efforts and Nationwide Mourning** Mudslides triggered by a 30-year-rainstorm have overwhelmed mountain villages near Tetovo, North Macedonia, leaving roads impassable and displacing residents. Mayor Teuta Arifi described the deluge as unprecedented, with rescue teams searching for missing individuals, including a six-year-old girl. Deputy PM Vladimir Peshevski reported over 200 damaged homes and critical infrastructure in the region. “Sipkovica looked as though a huge tsunami had gone through it,” he told reporters, as per the Associated Press. The government has declared Wednesday and Thursday national mourning days, underscoring the disaster’s severity. Emergency crews continue recovery operations as the country grapples with the aftermath.

**Scotland’s Gary Strachan Praises Brave Performance but Laments Defeat to Slovakia** *October 15, 2023* Scotland’s Euro 2020 qualifying campaign faced a setback as they fell to a 3-0 defeat against Slovakia in Trnava, leaving them fourth in Group F with four points from three games. Manager Gordon Strachan expressed pride in his team’s efforts but admitted to sympathy for both the players and their supporters after a challenging match. Two goals from Robert Mak and a third by Adam Nemec secured Slovakia’s victory, though the result was clouded by controversy. Scotland’s players believed a foul by Jan Durica on Steven Fletcher preceded Mak’s opening goal, a decision Strachan described as “just when they need a break, the decision being on their side, it goes against them.” The home side capitalized on defensive lapses, with Mak and Nemec exploiting space in Scotland’s penalty box to extend their lead in the second half. Despite the loss, Strachan praised his squad for their “bravery on the ball” and “effort to create chances,” acknowledging that the second goal shifted the game’s momentum. “It was uphill after that,” he said, reflecting on the 11th-minute strike that dented Scotland’s confidence. The defeat follows a mixed October double-header, with Scotland drawing 1-1 against Lithuania at Hampden to claim just one point from their two fixtures. Now one point adrift of a potential play-off position, Strachan remains optimistic about the group’s second-place race. “Form can change in a couple of weeks,” he noted, emphasizing the long-term nature of the 12-month campaign. A key test looms on November 11, when Scotland face Group F leaders England at Wembley. Strachan, in charge since January 2013, stressed his belief in the squad’s resilience. “Every time I get together with these guys, they rejuvenate me,” he said. “We’ve given it our best shot..... **Shift from Reactive to Proactive Cybersecurity Urged by Experts** Cybersecurity experts are warning that many firms remain trapped in outdated, reactive approaches to detecting and removing cyber threats, leaving them vulnerable to prolonged intrusions. At Infosecurity Europe, a leading cybersecurity conference in London, Mandiant—a global incident response firm—highlighted a critical flaw in how companies respond to breaches. Instead of actively hunting intruders, organizations often rely on software alerts, enabling attackers to linger undetected for months and expand their foothold in networks. Mandiant’s research reveals that the average breach involves hackers gaining control of around 40 machines. Yet, in most cases, only a handful of compromised servers are cleaned up, leaving attackers free to move laterally within networks. Bill Hau, a senior executive at Mandiant, emphasized that traditional investigative methods are inadequate. “Most companies have a very old-fashioned way of investigating a breach,” he said. “They use tools that make them think they’ve remediated an issue, but attackers are still hiding.” This reactive model, he added, allows intruders to dwell in networks for extended periods, seeking administrative access to erase evidence and disrupt investigations. The financial stakes are rising. Global cybersecurity spending reached $77 billion in 2018 and is projected to soar to $170 billion by 2020, reflecting growing awareness of cyber threats. However, even as budgets expand, many firms remain ill-equipped to tackle sophisticated attacks. Mandiant and similar incident response firms are increasingly called in when traditional tools fail to identify and eliminate vulnerabilities. Hau stressed the need for a cultural shift: “Companies must stop waiting for alerts and start actively hunting threats in their own networks. If they look hard enough, they’ll find trouble.” Patrick Grillo, a senior director at Fortinet, echoed these concerns, pointing out that while organizations often prioritize securing network perimeters, internal defenses remain “soft and chewy.” Once malware bypasses initial barriers, attackers can freely navigate systems to access sensitive data, such as credit card details or customer information. “The perimeter is just the first line of defense,” Grillo said. “The real danger lies in the unchecked movement inside networks.” He urged firms to conduct internal “drills” to train security teams and simulate real-world attack scenarios, ensuring they can identify and neutralize threats proactively. As cyber threats evolve, experts agree that reactive strategies are no longer sufficient. By shifting to a proactive, “hunting” mindset and strengthening internal network monitoring, companies can reduce dwell times and limit the damage caused by intrusions. The message is clear: in a world where hackers exploit inaction, survival depends on taking the fight to the enemy.

**Lib Dem Leader Warns Brexit Threatens UK Security Over Schengen Database Dispute** Liberal Democrat Brexit spokesman Nick Clegg has accused the government of pursuing a “reckless” Brexit strategy, warning that losing access to the EU’s Schengen Information System (SIS) would jeopardize national security. The SIS operates across the Schengen zone, which allows passport-free travel between member states. Non-Schengen countries like the UK and Ireland use the system with “special arrangements” to access its data. **UK Sees Sharp Drop in Personal and Corporate Insolvencies Amid Economic Recovery** The number of individuals declaring insolvency in England and Wales has plummeted to its lowest level in nearly two decades, according to the latest figures from the Insolvency Service. Analysts attribute the decline to a strengthening economy and a return to real-terms wage growth, which has helped individuals and businesses manage debts more effectively. “With wages now outpacing inflation, people are finding it easier to meet their financial obligations without turning to insolvency,” said Phillip Sykes, president of R3, the UK’s insolvency trade body. This represents a 2.7% increase from May and brings the total close to the recent peak seen in April. The rise in homeownership underscores growing consumer confidence, though experts caution that this trend may mask underlying vulnerabilities. However, the outlook for businesses is more concerning. Howard Archer, chief UK and European economist at IHS Global Insight, warned that the sharp decline in bank lending “raises serious questions about business activity and investment.” The contrast between household and corporate finances has left some economists puzzled, with many pointing to tighter credit conditions and ongoing uncertainty about economic growth. While the fall in personal insolvencies has been welcomed by the Money Advice Trust (MAT), which runs the National Debtline service, the organization has raised concerns about rising household debt levels. Jane Tully, head of insight and engagement at MAT, noted that many families are relying on credit to cover budget shortfalls. “The economic recovery is helping some households, but we fear others will fall into debt traps,” she said. The Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts that household debt will reach 169% of income by 2020, driven in part by rising mortgages and borrowing. Changes to tax credits in the coming years could further strain vulnerable households, the MAT warned. The latest data reflects a complex economic landscape: while personal and corporate insolvency rates are declining, underlying risks—such as business lending cuts and growing household debt—suggest the UK’s recovery may still be fragile.

**Royal Mint Launches Gold Bullion Investment in Pensions Scheme** The Royal Mint has expanded its investment options by allowing customers to store gold bullion within Self-Invested Personal Pensions (SIPPs), offering a new avenue for investors seeking to diversify their retirement savings. The initiative, unveiled in South Wales, enables investors to purchase 100g or 1kg gold bars, or even fractional portions of a larger 400oz bar, with storage secured in a Ministry of Defence-guarded vault at Llantrisant. James Craigen then doubled the lead with a first-half penalty following Chris Higgins’ handball. Rovers dominated the second half but failed to add to their tally. The win moves them seven points clear of Doonhamers in the race for the promotion play-off spot, tightening the race for the top.

**National League Club Set for Sale to Gaming International in Landmark Deal** The National League club is on the brink of a major ownership shift, with Gaming International poised to finalize a deal to take control from the current board. But new owners may bring fresh ideas, and if that’s the case, I’ll continue supporting the club as a Torquay fan.” Nicholson paid heartfelt tribute to outgoing chairman David Phillips and his team, who took over in June 2015 after former owner Thea Bristow stepped back from the club. “They’ve given this club life-support and laid a solid foundation,” he said. “We’re in a position now where the new owners can shape the club’s future.” Under Phillips’ leadership, the club weathered financial challenges and secured its place in the National League. Nicholson emphasized that the sale arrives at a “strong” point for the club, with infrastructure and stability in place. The deal, expected to close soon, marks a new chapter for the historic side, as Gaming International prepares to inject fresh resources and vision into the team’s ambitions.

**Tournament Highlights: Kerber and Kvitova Advance, Muguruza Stumbles** Germany’s second seed Angelique Kerber edged Shuai Peng 7-6 (7-3), 6-3, while Czech Petra Kvitova defeated compatriot Lucie Safarova 6-3, 6-2. **Police Respond to Youths Near Main Street Bridge After Girl Injured** Police were called to an area near Main Street bridge Saturday evening following reports of unruly behavior by youths aged 12–17. Authorities said the incident involved an intoxicated young female who had injured herself while receiving assistance from the group. Officers accompanied her to hospital for treatment. A PSNI spokesperson expressed concern over the youths’ intoxication and actions, stating, “Such behavior could result in criminal records.” The investigation is ongoing.

**Scotland’s Europa League Teams to Benefit from Schedule Shift as Aberdeen Eyes Seeded Advantage** Scotland’s three Europa League representatives—Aberdeen, Rangers, and St Johnstone—have been handed a crucial scheduling reprieve after the unexpected exit of UEFA Champions League finalists Manchester United and Ajax. With both clubs failing to qualify for the Champions League group stage via their domestic leagues, Scotland’s position in the Uefa rankings has risen from 25th to 24th, altering the timeline for the Europa League. This shift grants one Scottish team an extra two weeks of preparation before entering the competition on 13 July, instead of the original start date of 29 June. Aberdeen are the strongest contenders to secure the advantageous slot, having established a commanding lead in the Scottish Premiership. With six points and a far superior goal difference over third-placed Rangers, the Dons appear poised to clinch third place in the league, ensuring a delayed start. Their consistent Europa League performances—reaching the third qualifying round in three consecutive seasons—also position them as a likely seed in the upcoming qualifiers. The first and second qualifying rounds draw will take place on 19 June, with Rangers and St Johnstone also learning their opponents on that day. The scheduling change stems from Ajax finishing second in the Eredivisie and Manchester United’s 2-1 Premier League defeat to Tottenham, which ruled them out of the top four. This opens a Europa League qualifiers spot regardless of the 2023 final’s outcome on 24 May in Sweden, as the winner will still gain direct Champions League entry. Celtic, meanwhile, will discover their Champions League second qualifying round opponents separately. With the draw set to emphasize strength and seeding, Scotland’s teams are capitalizing on the recalibrated landscape to maximize their continental campaigns.

**Historian Unveils Hitler’s Hidden Autobiography, Revealing Early Political Mastery** A groundbreaking discovery by historian Thomas Weber has upended long-held assumptions about Adolf Hitler’s early career, revealing that the Nazi leader authored a provocative 1923 book under a pseudonym to advance his political ambitions. The book, *Adolf Hitler: His Life and his Speeches*, was originally attributed to German aristocrat Victor von Koerber but is now proven to have been written by Hitler himself, according to compelling evidence uncovered by Weber in a South African archive. Published just two years before *Mein Kampf*, the 1923 work depicted Hitler’s political rise as a divine mission, drawing parallels to “Jesus’ resurrection” and calling the book the “new bible of today.” Historians previously assumed von Koerber, a high-profile supporter of Hitler’s early party, was the author. However, Weber’s research—detailed in an upcoming book—shows von Koerber was merely a “front” for Hitler’s self-promotion. Weber, a professor at the University of Aberdeen, discovered signed testimony in von Koerber’s private papers, now housed at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. These documents, never before examined in this context, confirm Hitler’s authorship and challenge the notion that he lacked the strategic foresight to envision himself as Germany’s revolutionary leader in 1923. “The book demonstrates Hitler’s mastery of political narrative and manipulation,” Weber stated. “He was already framing his story as a sacred mission, using rhetoric like ‘holy’ and ‘deliverance’ to position himself as Germany’s savior. This was not the work of an amateur but a calculated public relations campaign.” The findings suggest Hitler began crafting his mythos years earlier than previously thought, using the book to amplify his profile ahead of the failed 1923 Beer Hall Putsch. Weber argues this early autobiography, rather than *Mein Kampf*, marks the true beginning of Hitler’s bid for power. “This discovery reshapes our understanding of Hitler’s political evolution,” Weber added. “It shows he was a manipulative operator with a clear vision from the start.” Weber’s as-yet-untitled book will be published in the UK next year, offering further insights into Hitler’s transformation into a Nazi leader. The revelations underscore the importance of re-examining historical narratives and highlight how propaganda, even in its earliest form, played a central role in Hitler’s ascent to power.

**Finnish PM Faces Dual Scrutiny Over Contract Claims and Alleged Censorship of Media** Prime Minister Juha Sipilä has found himself at the center of a growing political and media controversy in Finland, a nation ranked highest in global press freedom for five consecutive years. Sipilä has denied claims of a conflict of interest involving a contract awarded to a steel company owned by his relatives by a state-run mine. However, the dispute has escalated into a heated debate over press freedom after revelations that the PM sent critical emails to Finland’s public broadcaster, YLE, over its coverage of the issue. Sipilä, addressing reporters on Wednesday, rejected allegations of censorship, stating he had not sought to limit press freedom or influence YLE. “I was not given a fair opportunity to respond to the claims against me,” he said, emphasizing that YLE’s reporting had unfairly suggested fraud by him or his relatives. The controversy intensified when Suomen Kuvalehti reported that Sipilä had sent a series of pointed messages to a YLE reporter on November 25, urging changes to the coverage. YLE, which leads Finland’s media landscape, confirmed that a story assessing the conflict of interest allegations was dropped on Friday. A further piece written on Monday about Sipilä’s emails was also shelved, according to three sources within the broadcaster. Talk show host Ruben Stiller alleged on Twitter that he was barred from discussing the issue on his program, a claim he later confirmed was lifted after pressure. YLE’s news editor, Atte Jaaskelainen, denied claims of censorship in a public statement, asserting that the broadcaster had allowed “unprecedented visibility” to the story across all platforms for four days. However, he explained that YLE had withheld stories questioning Sipilä’s involvement in contract decisions until ongoing investigations into potential conflicts of interest could conclude. “We must ensure accuracy and fairness,” Jaaskelainen wrote, stressing that the PM’s emails had not influenced the reporting process. The row has reignited debates about the balance between political accountability

**Villa Midfielder Bacuna Faces Extended Ban After Barging Official** AFC Bournemouth midfielder Lucien Bacuna has been hit with a four-match ban and a £20,000 fine after admitting violent conduct for barging a match official during last Saturday’s game. A Dutch-born Curaçao international, Bacuna now faces a prolonged absence as Villa navigate a tight relegation battle. The Football Association confirmed the punishment on Monday.

**Chaotic Stag Party Ends in Mid-Flight Arrests After Drunken Outburst on Ryanair Jet** A rowdy stag party descended into chaos during a Ryanair flight from Luton to Bratislava on Friday, prompting an unscheduled landing in Berlin and the arrest of six men from Hampshire. However, eyewitnesses described a scene of “unacceptable” disorder from the outset. Tensions reached a breaking point when a fight erupted between members of the group. A video shared by *The Sun* captured a man swearing and threatening another passenger before launching a punch. “One of the very drunken members tried to stop the fight but failed,” said Mr. Heravi. “That’s when the crew decided to divert to Berlin.” The pilot made an emergency landing at Schönefeld Airport after assessing the threat to safety, he added. Six men were removed from the aircraft, with German police charging them with violating aviation security laws—a misdemeanour punishable by fines up to €25,000. Darius Davies, another passenger, described the group as “boisterous” and recalled further antics, including one man being left without trousers after they were hidden by friends and others inflating their life-vests for no reason. “We were stuck for hours trying to get back. Joshua Mariner, the groom from Southampton, denied being among those arrested in a statement to the *Southern Daily Echo*. “The lads’ behavior was unacceptable, and they will now face the consequences,” he said. However, he emphasized: “It was reported I was arrested, which isn’t true. I will seek legal advice as it has caused distress for my family and me.” Police in Berlin have confirmed the arrests, but no official list of the detained individuals was released. Ryanair condemned the incident in a statement, reiterating its zero-tolerance policy on “unruly behavior.” A spokesperson said: “The safety and comfort of our passengers and crew are our top priority. This matter is now in the hands of local authorities.” The airline has also reserved the right to pursue civil damages from the men involved. Eyewitnesses highlighted the severity of the drunkenness

**Hospital Staff Expose Crisis in Care for Vulnerable Patients** Behind the sterile walls of Belfast’s hospitals, a quiet but alarming crisis is unfolding. Frontline healthcare workers, in a rare and blunt letter to hospital management, have laid bare the challenges facing vulnerable patients and overstretched staff. Their revelations paint a harrowing picture of a system buckling under unsustainable pressures, with consequences for patient care and staff morale. The letter, shared anonymously with the BBC, claims that patients—many of whom are elderly or frail—are being treated “inequitably,” often without their consent or knowledge. Staff describe being forced to transfer patients between hospital sites late at night via ambulance, a practice that has sparked outrage among consultants who argue it violates clinical standards. Meanwhile, the shortage of hospital beds has triggered a cascade of cancellations, particularly in orthopedic surgery. In January, Musgrave Park Hospital saw over 100 scheduled operations canceled due to bed shortages. By March, the total number of orthopedic procedures performed in the first quarter of 2024 had fallen by 250 compared to the same period last year. Compounding the issue is a severe staff shortage. With no additional nursing posts, the number of beds available for critical work has been slashed from 80 to 40. Nurses report working at capacity, often without adequate support, while orthopedic surgeons and other specialists are in short supply. Sick leave gaps frequently remain unfilled, straining remaining staff and eroding patient safety. These challenges were underscored in last week’s RQIA (Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority) report, which highlighted systemic failures in elderly care, including inadequate staffing and poor communication. For the whistleblowers, the decision to speak out was a last resort. “We can’t stand by and allow vulnerable patients to be treated this way,” one staff member wrote. The courage required to break silence is immense, especially in a system where speaking up often invites retaliation or indifference. Yet these staff members insist their actions are necessary to advocate for those unable to do so themselves. The fallout extends beyond hospital walls. Patients face prolonged suffering, delayed surgeries, and abrupt relocations. Nurses grapple with emotional and physical exhaustion. Consultants, once respected as partners in care, now feel sidelined. As the health service teeters on the edge, the question remains: how long can this broken system sustain itself? With no immediate resolution in sight, the voices of those on the frontlines offer a stark warning: without urgent investment in beds, staffing, and patient dignity, the crisis will only deepen. For now, the hope lingers that these whistleblowers’ cries for change will be heard.

**Farmer Secures British Superbike Victory Amid Drama at Lincolnshire Circuit** The Clogher rider overcame a fierce challenge from Andrew Irwin in the British Superbikes race at the Lincolnshire circuit, clinching the win as Irwin crashed while leading. **New Horizons Probe Nears Historic Pluto Flyby, Captures Sharpest Images Yet** The NASA New Horizons probe has transmitted its sharpest images of Pluto to date, offering tantalizing glimpses of the enigmatic dwarf planet ahead of its historic flyby on 14 July. The latest images, captured on Tuesday when the spacecraft was approximately 8 million kilometers from Pluto, reveal a surface marked by extreme contrasts: a sprawling, heart-shaped bright region spanning 2,000 kilometers and a dark, equatorial expanse dubbed “the whale.” By Thursday, New Horizons had closed the distance to six million kilometers, hurtling toward its closest approach at 12,500 kilometers on 14 July. This milestone follows a brief communications hiccup over the weekend, during which the probe temporarily lost contact with Earth. The newly released images are the first to be received since the anomaly was resolved. “They’re still a little blurry, but they’re by far the best pictures we’ve ever seen of Pluto,” said Dr. John Spencer, a co-investigator from the Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) in Colorado. “And they’re only going to get better.” The images combine data from New Horizons’ high-resolution Long Range Reconnaissance Imager (LORRI) and the Multispectral Visible Imaging Camera (MVIC) on Ralph, the probe’s color imaging system. LORRI’s black-and-white images provide clarity down to 100 meters per pixel, while Ralph adds color to highlight Pluto’s dramatic surface variations. “Pluto is really weird,” Dr. Spencer noted. “It has some extremely dark areas, some extremely bright ones, and we don’t know what any of them are yet.” Scientists speculate that the heart-shaped region might be coated in frozen carbon monoxide, while the dark “whale” could be a deposit of hydrocarbons formed by UV light and cosmic rays interacting with Pluto’s atmosphere. However, these remain educated guesses until the probe’s closest approach, which will deliver images 500 times sharper by 12 July. New Horizons will traverse Pluto’s system at a blistering speed of 14 kilometers per second, too fast to enter orbit. Instead, it will execute an automated reconnaissance, capturing data on Pluto and its five moons—

Investigators are using CCTV footage to track the perpetrators, with authorities alerted at airports, ports, and border crossings to locate them. The Foreign Office confirmed it is supporting George’s family and coordinating with Cypriot authorities. Relatives plan to travel to Ayia Napa to bring George

**Dyson Reports Strong Growth Amid Global Expansion and R&D Focus** Dyson, renowned for its innovative bag-less vacuum cleaners, announced a 13% rise in profits to £367 million, driven by robust international sales and strategic investments in cutting-edge technology. **U.S. Senate Probes Link Between Megrahi’s Release and BP Oil Deal; Scottish Officials Refuse to Attend Hearings** The U.S. Senate’s foreign relations committee has intensified scrutiny into allegations that the compassionate release of Libyan terror convict Abdelbaset Ali al-Megrahi in 2009 was influenced by BP’s lobbying to secure an oil deal in Libya. The Scottish government has firmly rejected the claims, with a spokesperson stating that the “decision was solely based on medical grounds and was made under Scottish law.” They emphasized that the release process adhered to Scotland’s legal framework and that further inquiries should focus on U.S. domestic matters, as the Senate’s jurisdiction does not extend to Scottish judicial decisions. The spokesperson added that the Scottish Parliament’s justice committee had already conducted a thorough review of the case, deeming it “right and proper” to conclude the matter within their system. Jack Straw, the former UK Justice Secretary, has not yet decided whether to attend the hearing. He stated he would consult former Prime Minister Tony Blair, who was initially invited but had his invitation retracted after a draft letter was mistakenly published. A BP spokesman confirmed the company was “considering” the invitation but has not committed to a response. The Scottish government’s decision not to send MacAskill or Fraser to the hearing

**Amazon Expands Original Lineup with Four New Series Greenlights** Amazon has announced the selection of four new original series—*The After*, *Mozart in the Jungle*, *Bosch*, and *Transparent*—following a second round of pilot feedback from viewers. The picks mark a strategic push into drama, with *The After* and *Bosch* becoming the streaming giant’s first drama commissions, positioning Amazon to compete with Netflix’s acclaimed originals like *House of Cards* and *Orange is the New Black*. The newly commissioned shows include a diverse array of genres. *The After*, written and directed by *The 100* creator Jason Rothenberg, follows eight strangers thrust together by mysterious forces, who must navigate a violent world while relying on one another for survival. **Sarkozy Announces UMP Leadership Bid, Eyeing 2017 Presidential Run** French ex-president Nicolas Sarkozy has declared his intention to contest leadership of the opposition Union for a Popular Movement (UMP) party, signaling a potential return to politics as he aims for a 2017 presidential bid. He faces multiple investigations, including a formal probe into alleged attempts to influence judges examining his finances, as well as inquiries into ties with former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi and accusations of illegal 2012 campaign funding. Sarkozy has consistently denied wrongdoing. While his supporters argue his leadership is essential to address France’s stagnation, critics warn that his legal entanglements and divisive style could hinder the UMP’s unity and viability. **Canadian Researchers Uncover Why Specific Brain Cells Deteriorate in Parkinson’s Disease** A groundbreaking study by Canadian researchers may finally explain why Parkinson’s disease selectively destroys only certain brain cells, offering fresh hope for new treatments. Published in *Current Biology*, the research reveals that the neurons most vulnerable to the condition are structurally and metabolically distinct, making them prone to damage and death. Parkinson’s, which affects an estimated 127,000 people in the UK, is characterized by the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in specific brain regions. However, why these cells are disproportionately affected has long puzzled scientists. To investigate, a team from the University of Montreal analyzed neurons in mice models of the disease. They discovered that the at-risk neurons—particularly those in the substantia nigra region—were far more complex than neighboring cells, with intricate branching and significantly higher energy demands. Prof. Louis-Eric Trudeau, the study’s lead author, explained: “Like a motor constantly running at high speed, these neurons need to produce an incredible amount of energy to function. They appear to exhaust themselves and die prematurely.” The team found that the intense energy production generates toxic byproducts, a process known as oxidative stress. Over time, this accumulation of waste overwhelms the cells, triggering their demise. The findings align with a long-standing hypothesis that oxidative stress plays a central role in Parkinson’s pathology. Dr. Arthur Roach of Parkinson’s UK emphasized the study’s importance: “Out of the billions of cells in the brain, it is always the same small group that degenerate and die in Parkinson’s. We don’t know why only these cells are affected. This study provides strong support to the idea that their unique structure and function make them especially susceptible to oxidative stress.” The research could pave the way for innovative therapies. By targeting the energy inefficiencies of these vulnerable neurons, scientists hope to develop drugs that reduce energy demands or enhance cellular resilience. “This could lead to new treatments based on the most up-to-date ideas about oxidative stress,” Dr. Roach added. While the study focused on mice, its implications for human patients are promising. Researchers hope the findings will inspire further exploration into experimental models and potential interventions to slow or halt Parkinson’s progression, bringing relief to millions worldwide.

**Teenagers Admit Reckless Arson in Barnstaple Market Incident** Exeter Crown Court has heard harrowing CCTV footage of a lit piece of cardboard placed on a sleeping bag in Barnstaple’s Pannier Market on 2 December. Two 16-year-old boys admitted to arson while reckless as to whether life was endangered but denied charges of arson with intent to endanger life. The Crown Prosecution Service has been granted time to decide whether to accept their pleas. Footage revealed a group approaching a figure huddled in a sleeping bag in a market corner. A lit cardboard was placed on the bag, burning briefly before a girl extinguished it. The same group later reappeared, positioning the cardboard onto a nearby wheelchair. The victim, identified as 71-year-old Robert Newton, was unharmed. Judge Cottle adjourned the case, remanding the teenagers to a secure unit in Bristol pending further review. A third defendant, 23-year-old Adam Scott, faces charges of arson with intent to endanger life and is due to appear on 5 February. The court heard the incident occurred in a densely populated public space, raising concerns over potential fatalities. Prosecutors emphasized the “extreme recklessness” of the accused, despite their denials of intent. As the case develops, local authorities have urged vigilance, with Newton’s family expressing relief at his survival. The outcome could hinge on the CPS’s decision on the teenagers’ plea agreements, while Scott’s trial remains a separate but critical component of the proceedings.

**World War One Soldier’s Century-Old Scotch Heads to Auction** A rare bottle of *Croft Blend Fine Old Scotch*, untouched for over a century, is set to go under the hammer later this week. The whisky, carried to France by Cpl William Mill in 1914 and never opened during World War One, has remained sealed in a suitcase beneath a family bed in Scotland for decades. Now, it will be auctioned online by Scottish Whisky Auctions, with bids starting at £2,000. Cpl Mill, a member of the 3rd Volunteer Battalion of the King’s Own Scottish Borderers, took the bottle with him when he returned home after the war. Passed down through generations, it has become a cherished family relic. Alongside the whisky, a personal note written by Cpl Mill on the back of a 1908 photograph of him will also be included in the lot, adding historical significance to the sale. The bottle, the oldest ever offered on the Glasgow-based auction site, was produced by glassmaker Cannington, Shaw & Co between 1889 and 1908. The company’s distinctive stand format, visible on the bottle’s base, narrows its production window. Despite extensive research by auctioneer Peter Burns, the whisky’s exact blend and origin remain unknown. “It’s a true mystery,” Burns said. “We’ve consulted archivists, whisky experts, and historical institutions, but no one can identify it. It’s likely one of a kind.” With its wartime history and enigmatic contents, the bottle is expected to attract intense interest. Bidding opens on Friday and runs for 10 days, with Burns predicting “fierce competition” given its rarity. The sale highlights the enduring fascination with whisky and the stories that shape its legacy. Whether it fetches a record price or not, the bottle’s journey from the front lines to the auction block promises to captivate collectors and history buffs alike.

**Patient Sues Spire Manchester Hospital Over Alleged Surgical Error** Helen Reynolds, a 50-year-old from Rugeley, Staffordshire, has filed a claim against Spire Manchester Hospital after allegedly suffering severe complications following a gastric bypass surgery in January 2023. The procedure, undertaken to ease chronic knee and back arthritis, was followed by months of excruciating abdominal pain, with a scan this May revealing a foreign object inside her body—surgical tubing that was never removed. Irwin Mitchell, the law firm representing Reynolds, described the incident as a “never event,” a term reserved for wholly preventable medical errors under national safety guidelines. Reynolds, who paid for the private procedure, claims she endured a year of agony before requiring further surgery to remove the tubing. “I can only describe the pain as like labour pains,” she told the BBC. “I couldn’t leave the house for months and relied on painkillers constantly.” Her general practitioner initially attributed her symptoms to ovarian cysts, but a scan confirmed the presence of the foreign object. Reynolds, who had sought weight loss surgery to improve her quality of life, expressed shock at the ordeal. “I’m flabbergasted at how this has happened,” she said through her legal team. Spire Healthcare, the hospital’s parent company, stated in a response that patient safety is its “top priority” and that it adheres to “extremely high standards.” However, the firm declined to comment on individual cases, citing confidentiality. Irwin Mitchell emphasized that its investigation is ongoing, with medical evidence being compiled to determine accountability. Reynolds’ case highlights concerns about surgical safety in private healthcare settings. The National Patient Safety Agency defines “never events” as incidents that should never occur if proper protocols are followed, including foreign object retention. The hospital has not yet disclosed internal findings, but Reynolds’ legal team is seeking compensation for her prolonged suffering. As the investigation continues, the case underscores the importance of rigorous post-operative checks and transparency in medical procedures. For Reynolds, the ordeal has been a devastating setback to her health goals, leaving her to confront the physical and emotional toll of a mistake she calls “unacceptable.”

**Teen Involved in Forklift Chaos to Be Sentenced After Police Helicopter Scramble** A 16-year-old from Henley-on-Thames faces sentencing after a reckless incident involving a stolen forklift truck in September last year. Oxford Magistrates’ Court heard how the teenager stole the vehicle from Oliver Agriculture in Cane End, Reading, and drove it two-and-a-half miles to Sonning Common, where it caused chaos in Hazel Gardens. Police were alerted as the truck “drove erratically,” prompting a helicopter response. During the incident, the boy tipped a Fiat Punto onto its side, a prosecutor stated. Admitting aggravated vehicle taking, careless driving, and possession of an unloaded firearm, the teenager told the court: “It probably wasn’t the best thing to have done.” Chairman Colin McGuire branded the forklift “a lethal machine” and ordered a Youth Justice Service report. The unnamed youth, whose identity is protected, will be sentenced on 16 August. The case highlights risks posed by young offenders accessing heavy machinery, with magistrates emphasizing the severity of the actions.

**Chelsea Inflict First Defeat on Liverpool in Nail-Biting WSL Encounter** In a thrilling Women’s Super League clash at Kingsmeadow, Chelsea Ladies secured a 2-1 victory over Liverpool, handing the Reds their first league defeat of 2016. South Korean forward Ji So-Yun opened the scoring in the first half with a clinical low strike, before Gilly Flaherty, who signed a new two-year contract earlier in the day, doubled the advantage with a composed header from a second-half corner. Liverpool fought back valiantly, with Katie Zelem coming close to an equalizer before Caroline Weir’s 80th-minute strike—a deserved consolation goal—brought the Reds within one. The visitors pushed for an equalizer, but Chelsea’s resilience was tested when goalkeeper Hedvig Lindahl, who had made crucial first-half saves to deny Weir, had to be substituted after a knock. Her replacement, Rebecca Spencer, produced a stunning late reaction save to thwart Niamh Charles and preserve the lead. Liverpool boss Scott Rogers praised his team’s performance, stating, “We deserved a point. They’re champions for a reason, and we caused them problems.” Chelsea manager Emma Hayes, meanwhile, acknowledged Liverpool’s effort but highlighted her side’s shortcomings: “Credit to them, but we lacked experience in midfield and have work to do.” The result extends Chelsea’s unbeaten run and maintains their dominance, while Liverpool remain in second place. Elsewhere in the league, Arsenal Ladies moved into third with a win at Reading, and Birmingham earned their first points of the season. With the title race heating up, both managers will reflect on a hard-fought contest that underscored the growing competitiveness of the WSL.

Haskell, who earned 70 caps and was named man of the series for his performances, had also played a pivotal role in England’s recent Six Nations Grand Slam triumph. Wasps director of rugby Dai Young expressed disappointment, stating, “James’ performances with England have been hugely impressive. Everyone at Wasps knows how hard he works and wishes him a speedy recovery.” Despite the setback, Haskell is expected to remain in top condition, with his determination to return highlighted by Young. The injury adds a challenge for England ahead of their upcoming fixtures, as Haskell’s leadership and experience are vital to their squad.

**Former Indian General Stabbed in London, Nine Arrested in Connection** Lt-Gen Kuldeep Singh Brar, a retired Indian army officer, was stabbed in an attack by four men on Sunday near Oxford Street’s Old Quebec Street. The 79-year-old was hospitalized with a neck wound but has since been discharged. A woman and seven men were arrested at the scene and are being questioned by London police. Separately, two men and one woman from the West Midlands, arrested earlier this week, remain in custody. Three others were detained on unrelated immigration offenses. Brar, who led India’s 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar—resulting in hundreds of deaths—has long faced threats from extremist Sikhs. Police have not confirmed the attackers’ identities, though suspicion of retaliation persists. The operation, condemned internationally, remains a flashpoint for tensions within the Sikh community. Authorities continue investigating the assault, which has reignited debates over security and extremism in the UK.

**Smoking Linked to Higher Risk of Type 2 Diabetes in Major Global Study** A new international study, analyzing data from nearly six million people, has reinforced evidence of a significant link between smoking and an increased risk of type 2 diabetes. Published in *The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology*, the research highlights the potential role of smoking cessation in reducing the global diabetes burden. The study, conducted by an international team, pooled data from 88 global studies to assess the relationship between smoking and diabetes risk. Results revealed that current smokers face approximately 1.4 times higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared to non-smokers. While the risk remains elevated for several years after quitting—peaking at 1.5 times the risk—it gradually declines, returning to 1.2 times after five years of not smoking. Prof Naveed Sattar of the University of Glasgow, commenting on the findings, urged healthcare professionals to include smoking in diabetes risk assessments. “Smoking should be recognized as a diabetes risk factor, alongside its well-known links to heart disease and cancer,” he said. However, he noted that the effect size is smaller than, for example, smoking’s impact on lung cancer risk. Although the research does not definitively prove causation, experts estimate that 12% of diabetes cases in men and 2% in women worldwide could be attributed to smoking if a causal link is confirmed. Dr. Richard Elliott of Diabetes Research UK emphasized the added danger for people with diabetes, who face heightened risks of cardiovascular complications. “Smoking exacerbates these risks, making quitting critical for both smokers with and without diabetes,” he said. The findings underscore the potential public health benefits of smoking reduction strategies. Researchers suggest that global anti-smoking campaigns could significantly curb diabetes prevalence, particularly in regions with high smoking rates. For now, the study serves as a call to action: public health messaging should highlight smoking as a modifiable risk factor for diabetes, alongside obesity and sedentary lifestyles. As Prof Sattar noted, “Encouraging smokers to quit is not just about reducing cancer or heart disease—it’s also a step toward diabetes prevention.” The research adds to a growing body of evidence urging a holistic approach to diabetes prevention, with smoking cessation emerging as a vital, yet often overlooked, component.

Edwards, the pioneer of in vitro fertilization (IVF), has sparked sharp criticism from a senior Vatican official. Carrasco, the Vatican’s bioethics spokesperson, emphasized that IVF had led to the destruction of millions of embryos, stating, “There would not be a large number of freezers filled with embryos in the world” without Edwards’ work. The Nobel committee in Sweden defended the decision, highlighting Edwards’ breakthroughs as a “medical triumph” that brought “joy to infertile people worldwide.” Over four million babies have been born via IVF since the 1978 birth of Louise Brown, the world’s first “test tube baby.” Edwards’ work addressed infertility, a condition affecting more than 10% of couples globally, the committee noted. Louise Brown, now 45, welcomed the award as “fantastic news,” expressing pride in Edwards’ recognition. “Me and Mum are so glad that one of the pioneers of IVF has been given the recognition he deserves,” she said, referring to her late father, Robert Edwards. **New Clinical Trial to Test Amlodipine as Potential Treatment for Vascular Dementia in Northern Ireland** A groundbreaking clinical trial at Queen’s University Belfast is investigating whether a common blood pressure drug could become the first treatment for vascular dementia, a condition affecting over 18,000 people in Northern Ireland. Funded by the British Heart Foundation (BHF) Northern Ireland and the Alzheimer’s Society with £2.25 million, the trial focuses on amlodipine, a medication widely used to manage hypertension. Vascular dementia, caused by reduced blood supply to the brain, currently has no licensed therapies to halt its progression. Researchers hope the drug’s ability to improve blood flow might delay symptom deterioration and enhance quality of life. Professor Peter Passmore, leading the study, emphasized the trial’s potential: “If amlodipine proves safe and effective, it could rapidly become the first treatment for subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia, given its existing approval for other conditions.” The trial urgently seeks volunteers from Northern Ireland living with the disease. Participation is critical to advancing understanding and developing targeted care. With vascular dementia ranking as the second most common form of the illness globally, this research represents a vital step toward addressing unmet medical needs. Researchers remain optimistic about repurposing an established drug to transform patient outcomes.

**Amanda Knox Considers Return to Italy for Retrial Amid Autobiography Release** Amanda Knox, the American ex-convicted in the 2007 murder of British student Meredith Kercher, has said she is “still considering” whether to return to Italy for a retrial that could reinstate her conviction, following the overturning of her 2011 acquittal. In an interview with *USA Today* published on Tuesday, Knox, 25, expressed uncertainty over the legal and emotional weight of facing the Italian justice system again but acknowledged the importance of her presence to assert her innocence. The case, which has gripped international media and sparked scrutiny of Italy’s legal procedures, resurfaced last month when an Italian appeals court vacated the 2011 decision that had cleared Knox and her former boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, of murder. Prosecutors now seek to retry the pair for their alleged roles in the death of Kercher, 21, who was found stabbed to death in the Perugia apartment she shared with Knox. While an Ivorian man, Rudy Guede, was convicted in 2008 and sentenced to 16 years for the killing, his conviction has not prevented prosecutors from pursuing charges against Knox and Sollecito, whom they allege were involved in a “brutal sex game gone wrong.” Knox, who has since returned to the U.S., described the prospect of returning to Italy for the retrial as “scary,” though she emphasized her commitment to defending her name. “This is not just happening far away and doesn’t matter to me,” she told *USA Today*. “If my presence is what is necessary to convey that, then I’ll go.” Italian authorities cannot compel her to return, but they may request her extradition, a decision that would rest with U.S. officials. In a separate interview with ABC TV, Knox rebuked media portrayals of her as a “she-devil” and “heartless manipulator,” calling the accusations “surreal” and asserting that the trial’s toll left her “living as a murderer, whether I was or not.” She also sought to reconcile her own pursuit of justice with the grief of Kercher’s family, expressing hope “that eventually I can have their permission to pay respects at her grave.” The interviews coincided with the release of Knox’s autobiography, *Waiting to Be Heard*, which she co-wrote and for which she reportedly received over $4 million. The book details her life in Perugia, where she studied abroad, and maintains her claim that she was with Sollecito at his home, watching a movie and smoking marijuana, on the night of Kercher’s death in November 2007.
