**NHS Trusts Unite in Health Alliance Amid Local Criticism** South Tyneside NHS Foundation Trust and City Hospitals Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust have announced a new alliance to restructure healthcare delivery for their 430,000 patients. The partnership aims to improve service efficiency and sustainability, with both trusts emphasizing that closer collaboration will ensure “high-quality” care for the communities of South Tyneside and Sunderland. However, the decision has sparked strong criticism from local politicians and members of the public. South Shields MP Emma Lewell-Buck called the move “quite shocking,” accusing the trusts of bypassing essential consultation. “There’s been no discussion with myself as a local member of parliament, but worse, it’s absolutely disgusting that there’s been no consultation with the people of South Tyneside who use these services,” she stated. The lack of public engagement has raised concerns about transparency and patient involvement in the reconfiguration plans. The trusts, which already collaborate on services such as stroke and pediatric care, argue that deeper integration is necessary to address financial pressures and safeguard healthcare’s future. Steve Williamson, chief executive of South Tyneside NHS Hospital Trust, stated, “By forming an alliance, we can make the most effective use of our resources. This is key to delivering sustainable, high-quality services in both areas.” Under the new partnership, known as the South of Tyne Healthcare Group, roles will be divided: Sunderland will prioritize emergency surgical and planned care, while South Tyneside will focus on rehabilitation and screening. Peta Clark of the Royal College of Nursing noted that the partnership builds on existing collaboration and could free up funds for frontline care. “The NHS faces huge financial challenges. Working together allows trusts to become more efficient,” she said. Despite the reorganization, both trusts will retain their status as statutory NHS Foundation Trusts. The outcome of the partnership will likely depend on balancing operational efficiency with addressing community concerns over consultation and local input.

**Liverpool Manager Denies Interest in Derby’s Young Star Amid Transfer Speculation** Brendan Rodgers has firmly denied reports linking Liverpool to 18-year-old Derby County midfielder Harvey Hughes, emphasizing the player’s development is best served at Pride Park. The Reds have been heavily connected with the youngster, but the manager dismissed rumors of a bid as “baseless.” “I read we had put in a bid or something had been agreed, but there has been nothing,” Rodgers said ahead of Liverpool’s latest fixture. “I think he is a wonderful young talent who just needs to play football—and for me, he is probably at the best place he could be.” Hughes, who recently scored for England U21 in their 9-0 victory over San Marino, has emerged as a standout performer for Derby since his first-team debut in 2011. The midfielder, who joined the Rams from Nottingham Forest at 12, has made 18 appearances this season, scoring four goals. Rodgers stressed the importance of Hughes staying at Derby, where he plays under manager Steve McClaren. “This is a young kid learning the game—he is at an outstanding club, with a great manager there,” Rodgers added. “We sent one of our young players [Andre Wisdom] to Derby to develop, so it’s a place we respect.” The Liverpool boss also criticized the media for “constantly linking” Hughes to Anfield, arguing the speculation distracts from the player’s growth. “I don’t normally comment on speculation, but I will because I have the interest of the player at heart.” With Hughes thriving in the Championship, all eyes remain on whether Derby can keep the rising star from becoming a transfer target next season.

**Jamaican Sprinter Yohan Blake Banned for Doping Violation, Appeals Decision** Jamaican sprinter Yohan Blake, 31, has been suspended for three years by Jamaica’s Anti-Doping Disciplinary Panel after testing positive for the banned stimulant oxilofrine at the 2013 National Championships. The ban, backdated to the date of the offense, will expire on December 20, 2014, allowing Blake to compete in 2015. Blake, a two-time Olympian and former world record holder in the 100m, called the ruling “unfair and unjust,” claiming the substance entered his system via a contaminated legal supplement, *Epiphany D1*, provided by his Canadian physical trainer, Chris Xuereb. Xuereb has denied supplying performance-enhancing drugs. Blake plans to appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS). The suspension, along with a three-year ban for training partner Sherone Simpson (a two-time Olympic relay medalist) and a two-year ban for discus thrower Allison Randall, casts a shadow over Jamaica’s athletics community ahead of the 2014 Commonwealth Games. Blake and Simpson, who provided samples on June 21, 2013, will miss the Glasgow event. The panel ruled Blake “negligent” for using *Epiphany D1* without verifying its contents, despite his claims it was mislabeled or contaminated. Blake, once Jamaica’s top sprinter before Usain Bolt’s rise, has a storied career. His personal bests include a 9.72-second 100m (2009) and a 200m record of 19.90 seconds (2008). He won Olympic gold in the 4x100m relay (2008) and three World Championship medals. The suspension forced his withdrawal from the 2013 World Championships, further sidelining his career. Blake’s coach, Stephen Francis, criticized Jamaica’s anti-doping agency in the wake of the ruling, urging Prime Minister Portia Simpson-Miller to outsource testing to overseas agencies like those in Germany or the UK. Francis referenced the recent case of Veronica Campbell-Brown, cleared of doping charges by CAS, as evidence of systemic flaws. “Embarrassment after embarrassment after embarrassment,” he said, citing a pattern of failed oversight. At the start of the show, Harry Styles addressed the crowd, declaring, “You have no idea how much we love you right now,” as fans cheered from a sea of glowing phones and handheld lights. However, the absence of the former member—whose face was conspicuously removed from a pre-show video montage—loomed over the event. Malik, 22, left the band in March, citing a desire to “relax and have some private time out of the spotlight” after five years of global tours and relentless fame. Earlier this month, he had abruptly walked away from the band’s world tour after being hospitalized for stress. While the remaining members—Styles, Niall Horan, Liam Payne, and Louis Tomlinson—have insisted they are “staying together” to record a fifth album, fans expressed mixed emotions. At the Johannesburg gig, Niall and Louis reportedly stepped in to cover Zayn’s solos, but many in the crowd were visibly heartbroken. Teen fan Bianca, 15, told BBC Newsbeat: “Come back Zayn. We respect your decision but we needed to see your beautiful face. South Africa loves you.” Another fan lamented: “It’s disappointing but things change, things happen. I think sooner or later they will break up, but I don’t want it to happen. He must rejoin them.” Zayn has since shifted focus to a solo career, rumored to be collaborating with producer Naughty Boy, who has worked with Emeli Sandé and Sam Smith. In a statement, he said, “My life with One Direction has been more than I could ever have imagined. But, after five years, it’s the right time for me to leave. I’d like to apologise to the fans if I’ve let anyone down.” While the band continues, fans worldwide are left speculating about the future—both for the group and the ex-member. As the Johannesburg crowd chanted the band’s hits, one message rang clear: Zayn’s absence is deeply felt, and the door to reconciliation remains open. *Follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube for more updates.*

Three of the four runners-up—whose concepts included smart curtains, a smart fridge, and a sleep monitor—were submitted by girls. EDF clarified on Twitter that while the Pretty Curious program originally targeted girls, the challenge was “gender-neutral,” with a judging panel that included the all-female team from its Glasgow workshop. **Adrian Purtell Poised for Comeback as Specialist Clears Return Ahead of Hull KR Clash** Bradford Bulls forward Adrian Purtell has been given the green light to return to action following medical clearance after a recent health scare. The 28-year-old, who was cleared to resume training in December, suffered a setback after a defeat to Leeds Rhinos at Magic Weekend. However, a specialist’s recent verdict has revived hopes of his return, with Purtell potentially set to feature in Sunday’s crunch Super League clash against Hull KR. “I’m delighted with the verdict of the specialist and can’t wait to pull the shirt on,” Purtell said in a statement on the club’s website. The Australian had previously admitted in September 2023 that he was uncertain whether he could continue his career. He expressed gratitude to medical teams and the club for their unwavering support over the past 10 months, stating, “I just want to put this behind me now and concentrate on my career.” Bradford head coach Francis Cummins hailed Purtell’s progress as a “fantastic boost,” noting the team’s strong start to the season—three wins and one draw from six games. “It’s like having a new player on board,” Cummins said, emphasizing the significance of Purtell’s return. “I’m really looking forward to seeing Adrian play the game he loves again.” Purtell’s potential return offers both a morale boost and tactical depth as the Bulls aim to maintain momentum in their Super League campaign.

**Glasgow Warriors Bolster Backline with Acquisition of New Zealand-born Sean Maitland** Glasgow Warriors have secured the signing of versatile New Zealand-born winger Sean Maitland, who will join the club under a three-year deal pending medical and visa formalities. The 33-year-old, eligible to play for Scotland through both grandfathers, can also operate at full-back and is set to enhance the Warriors’ backline depth. “We’re delighted to welcome a player of Sean Maitland’s calibre,” said head coach Gregor Townsend. “The back three is already strong, but Sean’s experience and skill will add another layer of quality as we enter a busy season.” Maitland, a former New Zealand Under-19 and Under-20 World Cup winner, has a storied career that includes stints with Canterbury provincial and New Zealand Maori sides. The Warriors now turn their focus to finalizing Maitland’s transition ahead of a pivotal campaign.

**New Music Initiative Bridges Generations to Tackle Loneliness in Gwynedd** Gwynedd Council has backed an innovative project, *Memories Through Music*, aimed at combating loneliness among older residents through intergenerational collaboration. Run by the William Mathias Centre in Caernarfon, the initiative brings together the elderly and children in shared musical experiences, fostering connection and community spirit. The program currently runs weekly singing and music sessions at Awel y Coleg residential home in Bala, with a similar scheme planned for Gellilydan. Starting next year, children from Ysgol Bro Tryweryn in Frongoch will join the project, working alongside residents to “enrich the lives of both generations,” according to project manager Meinir Llwyd Roberts. She highlighted the project’s dual focus: addressing isolation in both bustling urban areas and remote communities. “Individuals can feel lonely in a busy town if they’ve relocated later in life, just as those in quiet areas might feel disconnected,” she said. By uniting the oldest and youngest members of society through music, the initiative aims to give the elderly a stronger voice in their communities. Residents at Awel y Coleg have embraced the sessions. Sylwen Davies, a regular participant, praised the project for “enriching our lives” and calling it “wonderful,” while Lily Williamson noted it made residents feel “more active and more normal.” Meanwhile, Ysgol Bro Tryweryn headteacher Heledd Owen emphasized the educational value for children, stating the project offers “a great opportunity to engage with the community and meet new people.” By blending tradition with innovation, *Memories Through Music* seeks to create lasting bonds, proving that shared experiences—rooted in song—can bridge divides and restore a sense of belonging across generations.

**Mercy Rimell: A Trailblazer in Jump Racing** Mercy Rimell, a legendary figure in British horse racing, has passed away, leaving behind a legacy as one of the sport’s most successful trainers. Alongside her late husband, Fred, she saddled four Aintree Grand National winners—*ESB*, *Nicolaus Silver*, *Gay Trip*, and *Rag Trade*—equalling a historic record. After Fred’s death, she bravely took over the training licence, continuing their family’s racing dynasty. In 1983, Rimell made history as the first woman to win the Champion Hurdle at Cheltenham with *Gaye Brief*. Her triumphs extended to the 1984 Stayers’ Hurdle (*Gaye Chance*) and the 1987 Arkle Trophy (*Gala’s Image*), cementing her status as a master of jump racing. She retired from training in 1989 but remained a vital force as an owner and breeder. Her grandson, Mark Rimell, honored her impact: “She had a great life and passed away in peace..... She was a great woman and left her mark in a great sport.” BBC correspondent Cornelius Lysaght praised the Rimells’ partnership, describing them as “among the most formidable training combinations jump-racing has known.” Even in her 80s, Mercy’s passion endured. In 2007, she famously lobbied for a low weight for her Grand National contender *Simon*, stating: “I’m old, and won’t be around to see him for much longer.” The horse competed in 2007 and 2008, a poignant testament to her enduring love for the sport. Mercy Rimell’s legacy transcends her victories. She redefined barriers, blending strength, strategy, and heart. Her family’s stables near Worcester produced champions like *Comedy of Errors* and *Royal Frolic*, while her wit and determination inspired generations. Though she has left the racetrack, her mark on jump racing remains indelible.

**Venezuela’s Deepening Crisis: 40-Day Power Cuts Amid Drought and Economic Collapse** Venezuela’s energy minister announced on Thursday that the country will face 40 days of electricity cuts, exacerbating its worsening crisis as a severe drought limits hydroelectric output. The restrictions, which will be detailed daily in newspapers and online, will avoid the 20:00–midday window but will otherwise disrupt daily life. The move follows months of declining energy infrastructure and a spiraling economic downturn. The crisis has hit key industries hard. Venezuela’s largest brewer, Polar—which produces 80% of the nation’s beer—has suspended operations, citing a lack of foreign currency to import grain. The shutdown will affect 10,000 workers, deepening unemployment and hardship in a country already grappling with hyperinflation and severe shortages of basic goods. President Nicolás Maduro has blamed the energy crisis on the “selfishness” of Venezuela’s business elite and U.S. interference, accusing Polar’s owner, Lorenzo Mendoza, of collaborating with the opposition-led National Assembly. However, opposition leaders and economists point to decades of government mismanagement, including strict currency controls introduced under late president Hugo Chávez in 2003, as the root cause of collapsing industries and dwindling oil revenues. Oil, which accounts for nearly all of Venezuela’s export earnings, has seen its value plummet, compounding the crisis. In February, the government ordered shopping malls to reduce operating hours and install backup generators, a measure now dwarfed by the latest blackout plan. With inflation soaring and food shortages persistent, citizens are bracing for prolonged instability. Analysts warn that without urgent reforms, Venezuela’s reliance on oil and its inability to adapt to global market shifts will continue to erode the economy. As power cuts loom, the country’s political divisions and public discontent threaten to escalate further, leaving millions in the dark—literally and economically.

**46 Patients and 12 Staff Affected by Sickness Outbreak at Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary** Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary is grappling with a surge in a highly contagious sickness and diarrhoea bug, infecting 46 patients and 12 staff. Ward 14 remains closed, though three other wards have reopened. Infection control manager Elaine Ross highlighted the virus spreads easily, particularly through vomiting, which “makes it much more easy to transmit.” Restrictions on visiting, imposed during a holiday period, aim to curb transmission. Ross expressed regret but thanked staff and the public for their “continued support and patience.” The outbreak has strained hospital operations, with vomiting as a prevalent symptom exacerbating challenges. Authorities urge visitors to follow hygiene guidelines to minimize risks. Ross emphasized efforts to contain the outbreak while balancing patient care, stating, “We endeavour to minimise the impact of this horrible bug.”

**Uganda’s Museveni Sidesteps Debate, Eyes Fifth Term Amid Looming Election** Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni, 71, skipped the nation’s first pre-election debate last month, dismissing such events as “for schoolchildren,” as he seeks a fifth term in power. The upcoming elections, scheduled for Thursday, will decide the 71-year-old leader’s attempt to extend his three-decade rule. The second and final debate, held recently, focused on foreign policy and national security—areas where Museveni is widely seen as strongest. The first debate had centered on domestic issues like health and education, with observers noting Museveni’s calm demeanor and concise remarks, according to BBC correspondent Catherine Byaruhanga. However, the second debate drew less scrutiny from moderators, raising questions among analysts. “Did the president set conditions for attending, such as softer questioning?” Byaruhanga posited. Museveni dismissed rival accusations of corruption as “fiction” and defended his economic policies and healthcare system, despite ongoing criticism. Eight presidential candidates will vie for power, with Museveni’s National Resistance Movement (NRM) facing unprecedented challenges from Kizza Besigye of the Forum for Democratic Change and Amama Mbabazi, a former prime minister running independently with the GoForward group. Both Besigye and Mbabazi are seen as formidable opponents, capitalizing on voter frustrations over high unemployment, corruption, and poor public services. The elections, the first since Museveni’s controversial 2017 constitutional amendment allowing indefinite rule, will also decide parliamentary and local representatives. With tensions high, the outcome could mark a pivotal shift in Uganda’s political landscape after decades of NRM dominance.

**Bomb Alerts Disrupt Derry as Railway Closures and Evacuations Spark Political Outcry** Derry’s main train station was evacuated, and Quarry Steps on Spencer Road were cordoned off on Tuesday after separate bomb alerts prompted a major police operation. The railway line between Coleraine and Derry was temporarily closed as authorities conducted searches, causing widespread disruption ahead of the Apprentice Boys of Derry annual parade. All roads and the station have since reopened following a thorough investigation that found no evidence of explosives. The initial alert at the train station led to the evacuation of staff and passengers, while Quarry Steps, a key city center location, was sealed off as a precaution. Police bomb disposal units were deployed, and the area remained under investigation for several hours. A detailed search of the station and surrounding roads was conducted, with authorities confirming the all-clear late Tuesday. Ch Insp Tony Callaghan of the PSNI praised the public’s cooperation during the operation. “Our priority was to keep people safe,” he said, urging residents to remain vigilant and report suspicious objects. “If you see anything unusual, please contact police immediately by dialling 999.” The alerts, which coincided with the Apprentice Boys parade—a contentious but officially respectful event—sparked sharp political reactions. SDLP leader Colum Eastwood condemned the incidents as an attempt to “raise tension” and “diminish our peace.” He accused perpetrators of seeking to “blow our peace apart” and emphasized that divisions in Derry now lie “between those who want to destroy peace and those who stand to protect it.” Sinn Féin MLA Raymond McCartney criticized the alerts for harming Derry’s reputation as a “forward-looking city” and disrupting traders already affected by a quieter Christmas period. He praised ongoing efforts by the community, the Apprentice Boys, and the PSNI to foster respect and minimize disruption. DUP MLA Gary Middleton echoed these sentiments, stating the alerts “achieved nothing” and “inconvenienced many locals and visitors

**Cubestormer 3 Shatters Rubik’s Cube World Record in Stunning 3.253 Seconds** At Birmingham’s NEC, engineers David Gilday and Mike Dobson made history with Cubestormer 3, a robot that solved a Rubik’s Cube in an astonishing 3.253 seconds—a full two seconds faster than the previous record of 5.27 seconds, also set by the duo three years ago. The achievement, verified by Guinness World Records editor Craig Glenday, underscores the power of accessible technology and innovative engineering. Cubestormer 3 leverages a smartphone camera to analyze the cube’s scrambled state before calculating the optimal solution in under a second. Four precision robotic hands then execute the moves, powered by an ARM processor—a fitting component given Gilday’s role as a principal engineer at the company. The pair spent 18 months designing and building the robot in their spare time, balancing their professional work with this ambitious project. “We knew Cubestormer 3 had the potential to beat the existing record,” Gilday said, “but with the robot performing operations faster than the human eye can track, there’s always an element of risk.” The challenge, he emphasized, was not just technical but also motivational: “Our real focus is to inspire young minds into STEM.” By demonstrating what can be achieved with off-the-shelf components, the team aims to spark curiosity in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. During the same event at the Big Bang Science and Engineering Fair, Gilday also broke records for the fastest 4x4x4 and 9x9x9 cube solves—far more complex puzzles. As he reflects on the success of Cubestormer 3, Gilday’s next challenge is clear: “Can we make it even faster?” The feat not only highlights the rapid advancement of robotics but also serves as a testament to what passion and ingenuity can accomplish outside the lab.

**Olympic Flame to Traverse North East with Unusual Travel and Historic Landmarks** The Olympic torch will embark on a unique and scenic 70-day relay through the North East of England, passing by iconic landmarks and offering communities a chance to celebrate the 2012 London Olympics. The journey, beginning in Berwick-upon-Tweed on 14 June, will feature one of its most unusual travel methods during the region’s leg, with the flame set to be carried through Ashington, Northumberland, twice in a single day. The torch will traverse Northumberland’s coastline and the Tyne and Wear areas before reaching Teesside, highlighting the region’s rich heritage. Among the landmarks to host the flame are Hadrian’s Wall, the Angel of the North, St Mary’s Lighthouse, and the Penshaw Monument. Three overnight stops will punctuate the North East leg, with evening celebrations in Alnwick (14 June), Newcastle (15 June), and Durham (16 June), each offering local communities a chance to participate in the global event. Councillor Neil Bradbury of Northumberland County Council emphasized the region’s enthusiasm: “Towns and villages along the route are already preparing welcome celebrations to showcase their pride and hospitality.” The relay will pass through 34 locations in Tyne and Wear over two days, including Bamburgh, Amble, Newcastle, and South Shields. On 16 June, the flame will reach Sunderland, where Councillor Paul Watson, leader of Sunderland Council, hailed the visit

**Nigerian Lawmaker Farouk Lawan Faces Bribery Charges Over Fuel Scandal Probe** Abuja, Nigeria – Farouk Lawan, a prominent Nigerian lawmaker and chair of a parliamentary committee probing a fuel subsidy scandal, has been arrested and charged with corruption after allegedly accepting $500,000 of a $3 million bribe from oil tycoon Femi Otedola. The 57-year-old legislator, who pleaded not guilty in court on Tuesday, was remanded in custody until a bail hearing on February 8. His arrest has sparked a political firestorm, with supporters alleging he is being framed by those implicated in the probe he led. The case stems from an investigation into a massive fuel subsidy fraud that revealed billions of dollars in losses due to overcharging by fuel importers. Lawan’s committee, established after nationwide protests against a 2012 fuel subsidy removal, accused powerful individuals and companies of systemic corruption, including Zenon, Otedola’s firm. The report called for a complete overhaul of the oil ministry and prosecution of those involved. Otedola, a close ally of President Goodluck Jonathan and a major financier of the ruling People’s Democratic Party (PDP), has claimed Lawan demanded the $3 million bribe to remove Zenon from the scandal report. “In the course of your official duty, you corruptly asked for $3 million for yourself,” prosecutors quoted Reuters as stating during a court hearing. Otedola, who handed over part of the money and provided a video of the transaction to police, is not facing charges, though critics question why the billionaire is not being investigated. Lawan has defended the cash exchange, stating he accepted the funds to “expose blackmail” and alerted both the anti-corruption Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) and his committee. However, the committee’s deputy leader denied receiving any notification or money, and the EFCC has remained silent on the matter. Another committee member, Emenalo Boniface, was also charged with corruption for allegedly accepting $120,000 from Otedola. The case has deepened political tensions. Lawan’s supporters argue he is a victim of a vendetta by those targeted in his investigation. Meanwhile

**Wells Fargo Profits Dip Amid Scandal Fallout, Executives Step Down** Wells Fargo’s third-quarter net income fell 2% to $5.64 billion as the bank grappled with the fallout from a widespread scandal involving unauthorized account openings. Investigations revealed employees created as many as two million accounts without customer consent to meet aggressive sales targets. The crisis escalated in September when the bank was fined $185 million and CEO John Stumpf resigned. Over 5,300 staff were fired in connection with the misconduct, while federal and state probes continue. Rising litigation costs contributed to a spike in fixed expenses to $13.3 billion in Q3, up from $12.9 billion the previous quarter. JP Morgan Chase also reported a 8% decline in third-quarter net income to $6.286 billion, though results exceeded expectations. Despite setting aside more funds for potential loan losses, the bank’s investment banking division surged, nearly doubling profits to $2.9 billion. “We delivered strong results with all businesses performing well,” CEO Jamie Dimon said. Citigroup saw net income drop 10.5% to $3.8 billion, yet the figure surpassed analyst projections. While Wells Fargo and peers face challenges, market reactions highlight resilience amid regulatory pressures and shifting economic conditions. The banks’ ability to recover will hinge on navigating legal scrutiny and restoring consumer trust.

**Williams Joins Birmingham Ahead of WSL Spring Series** Birmingham City have secured the services of 21-year-old left-back Williams, who returns to the UK after two seasons in Italy. The former ACF Brescia and AGSM Verona player claimed Serie A and Coppa Italia titles with Brescia before leaving England for professional opportunities abroad. A England Under-23 cap holder and FA Cup finalist in 2014 with Everton, Williams becomes manager Marc Skinner’s third signing for the WSL Spring Series, following Ellen White and Sarah Mayling. Authorities confirmed the arrests were part of a broader counter-terrorism operation. **Man Sentenced for Stalking, Assault After Non-Custodial Deal** Kieran Dorian, 20, from Broughty Ferry, Dundee, has been handed a three-year supervision order after admitting to a string of serious offenses, including stalking, assault, and making lewd sexual remarks to minors. The sentences follow a four-year campaign of harassment against women he knew from school, alongside a separate incident involving a police officer. Dorian pleaded guilty to four stalking charges committed between October 2011 and May 2015. During this period, he also assaulted a female officer, spat blood at her feet, and made sexually offensive remarks. Additionally, he admitted to targeting two 13-year-olds with inappropriate comments while they queued at a Dundee McDonald’s on July 30, before sexually assaulting one of the girls that same day. At Dundee Sheriff Court, Sheriff Alastair Carmichael emphasized that Dorian’s conduct “is firmly within the custodial range of sentences.” However, acknowledging that Dorian had already served time in custody, the sheriff opted for a non-custodial approach. Dorian was ordered to complete 120 hours of unpaid work, register as a sex offender for three years, and comply with a five-year sexual offenses prevention order (SOPO) and non-harassment order. The SOPO includes strict conditions governing his behavior, while the non-harassment order prohibits contact with his victims. Defense solicitor Douglas McConnell stated Dorian aims to avoid custody by adhering to the court’s conditions. Sheriff Carmichael warned that any breach of the orders would “very likely” result in imprisonment. The case underscores the legal system’s focus on rehabilitation and monitoring for non-violent offenders, while safeguarding victims from further harm.

**Wales School Launches Video to Warn Students About Snapchat Location Feature** Ysgol y Preseli, a school in Crymych, Wales, has taken a proactive step to address growing concerns about Snapchat’s location-sharing feature, Snap Map. The initiative follows widespread unease among staff and parents about the potential for students to unknowingly expose their whereabouts to others. Snap Map allows users to share their exact location with selected “friends” in real time. While Snap, the app’s parent company, states the feature is an “opt-in” setting that can be turned off at any time, educators at Ysgol y Preseli argue the tool poses significant privacy risks. Teacher Serena Davies explained that the video was created due to “huge concerns” about individuals tracking pupils’ movements, including home addresses, travel routes, and school locations. “Our pupils have responded positively to the video and even offered suggestions about other apps they think require attention,” she added. The school’s outreach has sparked a broader conversation, with multiple institutions across Wales sharing the video online and planning to integrate it into classroom discussions and assemblies. This follows similar concerns raised in England, where schools warned that Snap Map could be exploited to compile sensitive data, such as personal addresses or workplace locations. Although location sharing is restricted to users’ “friends” lists, there are fears this could include individuals met through other apps or websites, introducing potential strangers into private circles. Snap has defended the feature, emphasizing it is disabled by

**Security Forces Clash with Poachers at Popular Tourist Site** Security forces in South Africa faced off with a gang of five suspected rhino poachers at a renowned tourist attraction, leaving one individual wounded. Authorities recovered a firearm, ammunition, and poaching equipment from the scene, marking another effort to curb the escalating crisis. Rhino horn demand, driven by Asian beliefs in its medicinal value, has surged, fetching £35,000 ($55,000) per kilogram on the black market. Last year alone, South Africa recorded over 300 poaching incidents. Despite heightened prosecutions, the lucrative trade persists, underscoring the urgent need for global cooperation to protect endangered rhinos from extinction.

**PLA Troops Incursion into India Downplayed by New Delhi Amid Lingering Border Tensions** According to reports from the Press Trust of India, Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) soldiers briefly entered Indian territory in the Chaglagam sector on the India-China border between August 11 and 15. Defense sources cited by the agency confirmed the incursion, which followed recurring disputes in Himalayan border regions. However, India’s Ministry of External Affairs dismissed the incident as a “non-event,” with spokesperson Syed Akbaruddin stating, “We don’t take up non-events in diplomatic practice.” He referred queries to border security forces, which have not publicly addressed the matter. Beijing has yet to comment on the reports. The latest development adds to a long-standing territorial rivalry rooted in the 1962 Sino-Indian War, with both nations contesting control over Arunachal Pradesh and the Aksai Chin area of Ladakh. Earlier this year, India accused China of illegally stationing troops near the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in Ladakh, prompting diplomatic calls for withdrawal. Despite multiple rounds of border talks since 2020, no resolution has been reached, and tensions persist. Sources indicated the Chinese troops withdrew after a meeting with Indian border personnel, though the circumstances remain unclear. New Delhi’s refusal to escalate the narrative contrasts with past episodes of heightened friction, including a 2020 clash in Galwan Valley that left 20 Indian soldiers dead. Analysts suggest the brief incursion reflects the fragile status quo, where military posturing often precedes diplomatic engagement. With both sides maintaining conflicting claims, the LAC remains a flashpoint, underscoring the challenges of resolving one of the world’s most complex territorial disputes.

**Man Missing from Offshore Rig in Mariner Field as Search Continues** A 49-year-old man is missing following an extensive search operation at the Noble Lloyd Noble rig, located in the Mariner Field, approximately 90 miles (150km) east of Shetland. The alarm was raised at around 21:20 on Tuesday after a routine check of the offshore installation failed to locate the individual, believed to be from the Aberdeen area. Coastguard search and rescue teams were initially deployed, but their helicopter returned to base after no trace of the man was found. Two standby vessels and a platform supply vessel have since continued the search, scanning the surrounding waters. Police Scotland confirmed that a team of officers had flown offshore to the rig to assist in the investigation and support personnel on-site. Det Insp Norman Stevenson, leading the inquiry, stated: “An extensive search has been conducted, involving a helicopter, standby vessels, and a platform supply vessel. While we are still in the early stages, there are no apparent suspicious circumstances at this time. The man’s next of kin have been informed, and further updates will be provided as more information becomes available.” The Noble Lloyd Noble, one of the world’s largest jack-up rigs, is equipped with long support legs that stabilize it on the seabed. Noble Drilling, the operator of the rig, confirmed that emergency response teams had been mobilized in Aberdeen and Stavanger to aid the search. The company added: “Statoil vessels have assisted in a comprehensive search of the waters surrounding the rig. We remain focused on the safety of all personnel, the ongoing search for the missing individual, and supporting their loved ones and colleagues. All operations on the rig have been suspended until the investigation concludes.” Statoil, which is developing the Mariner Field with its first oil expected in 2018, is collaborating with Noble Drilling to coordinate the effort. Authorities emphasized that the search remains active

**Slovakia’s EU Presidency Confronts Brexit Uncertainty and Migration Tensions** Slovakia is set to assume the European Union’s rotating presidency for the first time this week, with Prime Minister Robert Fico acknowledging that the UK’s decision to leave the bloc will cast a long shadow over his country’s six-month leadership. The presidency, which begins on Friday, arrives amid heightened uncertainty following the June 23 Brexit referendum, which has left EU institutions scrambling to prepare for a future without the UK’s membership. Fico, speaking at a press conference alongside European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, emphasized that Slovakia’s agenda for the presidency was finalized only yesterday to reflect the “fallout from Brexit.” He stated that while Slovakia has a distinct plan focused on economic growth, digital transformation, and infrastructure, the UK’s departure would exert “considerable influence” on EU priorities. “These are turbulent times,” Fico said. “We have to ensure the next six months are a success for Slovakia and the EU.” The summit comes as the EU awaits formal notification from the UK to trigger Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty, the legal mechanism required to begin the Brexit process. Juncker reiterated that no negotiations would commence until such notice is received, a stance echoed by Fico. The UK has yet to issue the Article 50 letter, with Prime Minister Theresa May delaying the move amid domestic political pressures. Fico also addressed the divisive issue of migration, a challenge that has tested EU unity since the 2015 refugee crisis. Slovakia, which resisted participating in the EU’s quota system for distributing asylum seekers, aims to foster “space for discussion” on managing migration flows. Fico stressed the need for better communication to “sell the European project to our citizens,” acknowledging public skepticism but ruling out “radical steps” that could destabilize the bloc. Juncker, meanwhile, reflected on the Brexit vote, stating that “freedom of movement” was a central concern for UK voters. However, he dismissed calls to alter the EU’s founding principles, insisting that access to the single market remains tied to accepting free movement. “There will be no negotiation over these rules until the UK formally leaves,” he added. As Slovakia prepares to guide EU policy, Fico framed the presidency as an “exceptional event” requiring both stability and adaptability. With Brexit and migration dominating the agenda, the Slovak leadership faces a delicate balancing act: advancing its own priorities while addressing crises that threaten the EU’s cohesion. The coming months will test Slovakia’s ability to navigate these challenges and reinforce the bloc’s unity in an era of uncertainty.

**Singapore Grand Prix: A Nighttime Spectacle That Captures the Soul of F1** When it comes to Formula 1, few circuits rival the allure of Singapore’s Marina Bay. Nestled in the heart of a bustling metropolis and bathed in a kaleidoscope of neon lights, the Singapore Grand Prix has carved out a reputation as one of the most distinctive and desirable events on the Formula 1 calendar—second only to Monaco in its ability to blend racing with high-stakes business and luxury. The race’s magnetism begins with its location. As a global hub at the crossroads of Southeast Asia, Singapore offers a unique blend of colonial history, futuristic architecture, and cultural richness. But it’s the nighttime setting that truly sets this race apart. As the sun dips below the horizon, the Marina Bay Circuit transforms into a glittering spectacle. The track winds through the city center under a canopy of lights, with Chinese lanterns casting vibrant hues and the skyline of towering glass-and-steel buildings serving as a breathtaking backdrop. The humid tropical air cools slightly, and the atmosphere shifts into something surreal—a heady mix of elegance and energy that captivates both spectators and those behind the scenes. For the teams and staff who work tirelessly through the race weekend, the experience is anything but ordinary. The inverted schedule—starting track sessions at dusk and racing under the stars—means waking at 2pm, working through the night, and retiring at 6am. While hotels cater to this rhythm with 24-hour dining, many opt for the vibrant all-night hawker markets, where affordable, flavorful local cuisine offers a taste of Singapore’s culinary soul. Yet, beyond the ambiance, Singapore’s challenge as a race track is formidable. The Marina Bay Circuit boasts 23 corners, a grueling two-hour race duration, and a lengthy lap that ranks among the longest in Formula 1. The intense humidity tests drivers’ endurance as much as their skill, making it arguably the toughest race of the season—only Malaysia comes close. While it lacks the natural flow of circuits like Spa-Francorchamps or Suzuka, its character lies in its relentless physicality and the precision required to navigate its undulating layout. The event’s success also lies in its ability to attract business and glamour. Executives and investors flock to the race, drawn by its prestige and the city’s reputation as a nexus of commerce. For fans, it’s a chance to witness F1 in a setting that defies convention. As Andrew Benson, the BBC’s chief F1 writer, notes, Singapore is a race not to be missed. It’s a fusion of sport, culture, and spectacle that leaves an indelible mark on all who experience it. Subscribe to the BBC Sport newsletter for more F1 insights and highlights.

**O'Sullivan Dominates Murphy to Set Up Crucible Quarter-Final Clash** Ronnie O’Sullivan, the four-time world champion, delivered a masterclass performance at the Crucible Theatre, racing into a commanding 3-1 lead over world number five Shaun Murphy in their last-16 snooker clash. The Rocket, known for his unrelenting pace and tactical brilliance, showcased his prowess with breaks of 91, 75, and a staggering 128 to assert his dominance in the opening session. Despite Murphy’s efforts to level at 1-1 with a composed 84 and fleeting opportunities in frames five and six, O’Sullivan’s clinical precision proved insurmountable. The 41-year-old icon, chasing a sixth world title and 29th ranking title, rounded off the session with a stylish 74 to leave Murphy trailing in his wake. A second consecutive early exit for Murphy at the Crucible looms large, echoing their 2014 quarter-final where O’Sullivan triumphed 13-3. This result would mark Murphy’s third career defeat by the Rocket in a major tournament, intensifying their storied but fraught rivalry. Beyond the table, tensions simmered as Murphy dismissed O’Sullivan’s recent allegations of bullying by snooker officials, a comment that further strained their already uneasy relationship. O’Sullivan, visibly incensed ahead of the match, prowled the Crucible corridors with a palpable sense of fury, as BBC commentator George Riley observed: *“You could tell he wanted to hammer Murphy.”* The animosity between the two legends stems from contrasting personas—Murphy, the eloquent, measured professional, and O’Sullivan, the enigmatic maverick who thrives on unpredictability. In other Crucible action, 2013 runner-up Barry Hawkins eased past Leicester’s Tom Ford, winning 7-2 overnight and extending his lead to 10-3. The victory sets up a last-16 showdown with Scottish veteran Graeme Dott. As O’Sullivan advances to face either Ding Junhui or Liang Wenbo, the snooker world braces for a blockbuster quarter-final. With his peerless skill and fiery resolve, the Rocket remains a formidable force, turning past accusations into present triumphs. The Crucible, as ever, continues to witness drama both on and off the table. *382 words

**Roger Croft, West Berkshire Council Leader, Dies Following Collision in France** Roger Croft, leader of West Berkshire District Council, has died following a collision in France while traveling with his wife, Grizelda. The incident occurred at an undisclosed location, leaving him seriously injured before his passing. News of his death was announced by Conservative MP for Newbury, Richard Benyon, on Twitter, who described Croft as “a decent and kind man” and expressed deep sadness at the loss of a close friend. Councillor Emma Webster paid tribute to Croft, calling him an “inspiring leader, amazing man & great friend,” noting his reunification with his late wife, Zelda, whom he was close to. West Berkshire Council confirmed deputy leader Graham Jones has temporarily assumed the leadership role pending further arrangements. Croft’s passing has prompted widespread mourning, highlighting his respected role in local governance and community. The cause of the collision remains under investigation.

The 30-year-old will compete with Ross Etheridge for a starting berth in John Coleman’s squad. **European Tour Shifts 2017 Irish Open to Links Course Amid Lough Erne Disappointment** The 2017 Irish Open will no longer be held at the Lough Erne Resort in Fermanagh, marking a significant setback for the Northern Ireland venue. The European Tour confirmed on Monday that the tournament will instead be staged at a traditional links course, with Portstewart Golf Club emerging as a likely candidate. The decision ends a four-year hosting agreement, as the resort had been previously selected to host the event in 2014 with support from the Northern Ireland government. The Lough Erne Resort expressed deep disappointment over the announcement, stating that the European Tour opted for a "links course strategy" for future Irish Opens. Despite efforts by the resort’s management to maintain the partnership, the decision was finalized after months of discussions with tour officials. A spokesperson for the resort noted that the venue had remained committed to its original agreement but could not persuade the Tour to honor its commitment to the region. In a statement, European Tour Chief Executive Keith Pelley acknowledged the significance of the Lough Erne Resort, praising its "outstanding championship golf course" designed by Sir Nick Faldo. Pelley emphasized that the Tour values its relationship with the resort’s new ownership and expressed confidence in future collaboration. However, he stated that the shift to a links course aligns with the Tour’s broader vision for the Irish Open. The resort, which had invested heavily in infrastructure upgrades ahead of the 2017 event, lamented the missed opportunity to showcase the region. “We have spent the last few months working at the highest level to convince the Tour to maintain its commitment,” the resort said. “Despite our efforts, the decision to change the venue has been made.” Portstewart Golf Club, a storied links course on Northern Ireland’s Causeway Coast, has already been evaluated by European Tour officials. The shift marks a return to traditional links venues for the Irish Open, which last moved to Lough Erne in 2014. In a positive note, golf fans will see Masters champion Danny Willett compete at the K Club in July, marking his first European Tour event since his historic victory at Augusta National. The decision underscores the European Tour’s evolving strategy, balancing historical traditions with modern tournament demands while leaving Lough Erne with lingering questions about its future role in the golfing calendar.

**Two Arrested After Deadly Crash on Balls Pond Road** A fatal collision occurred at 11:00 GMT Sunday on Balls Pond Road after two cars raced, according to eyewitness Khurran Shazad. He described how one driver lost control, veering onto the footpath. "It was a very terrible scene..... injured people and blood," he told the BBC. Three pedestrians were treated at the scene; two remain hospitalized in serious but stable condition, per the Met. Police arrested two men on suspicion of dangerous driving. Investigations continue.

**Celtic Target Cup Glory in All-Premiership Clash as Hibs Take On St Johnstone in Semi-Final Showdown** The Scottish Cup semi-finals take center stage on consecutive weekends as Celtic face an all-Premiership tie at Hampden Park on **Sunday, 31 January**, while Championship side Hibernian clash with St Johnstone at Tynecastle Stadium on **Saturday, 30 January**. Both matches kick off at **15:00 GMT** and will be broadcast live on **BBC Radio Scotland**, with coverage also streamed on the **BBC Sport website** featuring highlights. Defending champions Celtic reached the last four by defeating Hearts, continuing their impressive form after last season’s final win over Dundee United. St Johnstone earned their spot by staging a dramatic comeback against Greenock Morton, while Hibs made history by overcoming Premiership sides Aberdeen and Dundee United, cementing their underdog status. The semi-finals promise thrilling encounters as clubs vie for a place in the final.

**Indonesian Authorities Advise Australians of Imminent Executions** Indonesian officials notified two Australian citizens, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, and a Filipino woman, Mary Jane Veloso, on Saturday of their upcoming executions, though no formal date has been set. Under Indonesian law, convicts must receive 72 hours’ notice before an execution. The trio, along with others, is detained on the high-security prison island of Nusakambangan in Central Java. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop confirmed the notification, stating the government would continue to seek clemency for Chan and Sukumaran, the ringleaders of the 2005 “Bali Nine” drug smuggling ring. They were sentenced to death in 2006 for organizing a plot to smuggle 8.3 kilograms of heroin from Indonesia to Australia. “We remain determined to pursue every possible avenue for mercy,” Bishop said in a statement. Veloso, convicted of drug trafficking, was visited by her family, including her sons and sister, on Saturday. The French national’s case remains under appeal. President Joko Widodo, who has adopted a hardline stance on drug crimes since taking office in 2014, has approved multiple executions this year, including six in January for foreign nationals convicted of drug offenses. Among the 10 prisoners awaiting execution are also nationals from Brazil, Nigeria, and the Philippines. The Bali Nine case has drawn global attention, with advocates urging clemency, while Indonesia maintains its strict anti-drug policies. As appeals for Chan and Sukumaran face rejection, the prospect of imminent executions looms, underscoring the tension between Indonesia’s legal stance and international calls for mercy. *Who were the Bali Nine?* The group of nine Australians was arrested in 2005 for attempting to smuggle heroin from Indonesia to Australia, sparking widespread debate over drug laws and foreign nationals in the justice system.

**Two Men Arrested Over Attempted Murder in Banbury** Thames Valley Police have arrested two men on suspicion of attempted murder following a serious incident in Banbury, Oxfordshire. The altercation, involving weapons and multiple individuals, occurred at approximately 19:45 on Friday. Both suspects, aged 38 and 26, are local residents. Authorities confirmed no further public danger is anticipated. Roads in Coopers Gate and Cope Road remain closed as investigators secure the scene. Detective Inspector Jon Capps urged witnesses to come forward, particularly regarding a silver Volkswagen Passat in the area at the time. "This was a serious incident, and we continue to investigate," he stated. "We have scene watches in place and are keeping an open mind, but there is no wider threat to the public." The police are appealing for anyone with information to contact them. No further details about the victims or motivations were disclosed.

**Welsh Ambulance Service Warns of Misused 999 Calls Putting Lives at Risk** The Welsh Ambulance Service NHS Trust has revealed that 19,151 "non-urgent" calls were made to emergency services between August 2014 and April 2015, with only 318 resulting in an ambulance deployment. Such incidents are straining resources and delaying critical care for severe emergencies, officials say. Examples highlighted include a woman in Rhyl, Denbighshire, who reported pulling her side while reaching for a phone charger. In Pontypool, Torfaen, a caller claimed a burning face after eating a Scotch bonnet chilli pepper, while a Wrexham resident reported injuries from punching a punch machine. Richard Lee, head of clinical services, stated, “Calls of this type put people’s lives at risk..... An ambulance attending a non-urgent call cannot respond to a serious road accident, heart attack, or stroke.” The trust urges the public to “choose well,” reserving 999 for genuine emergencies. These incidents underscore the need for better public awareness to ensure emergency services remain accessible for life-threatening situations.

**Facebook Introduces New Measures to Combat Fake News Amid Persistent Criticism** Facebook has rolled out updated measures to combat the spread of misinformation, including a new “Related Articles” feature in the U.S., France, Germany, and the Netherlands. However, experts argue the initiatives fall short of addressing the platform’s role in amplifying false narratives that have swayed public opinion during critical elections, including the 2016 U.S. presidential race and the 2015 French presidential contest. The social media giant has long faced scrutiny for its handling of fake news, particularly after allegations that hoax stories influenced voter behavior in high-stakes political events. In response, Facebook previously relied on a hybrid system of artificial intelligence (AI) and user reporting to flag potentially false content for independent fact-checkers. If verified as false, posts receive a warning label, reducing their reach. Yet the company has resisted directly removing such content, asserting it does not wish to act as an “arbiter of truth.” The latest updates include enhanced machine learning algorithms to detect dubious content more efficiently. A blog post by product manager Sara Su announced that fact-checked articles would now be displayed beneath flagged posts, offering users “additional perspectives and information.” However, the company clarified that these links would not directly counter false stories but instead provide alternative, credible reporting. The rollout of the “Related Articles” feature marks the first time Facebook has systematically introduced competing narratives, testing the strategy in April before its full launch this week. While some media watchdogs welcomed the move, others criticized it for addressing symptoms rather than the root cause of misinformation. Tom Felle, a senior lecturer in digital journalism at City University, noted that while contextualizing content is helpful, the measures fail to curb traffic to fake news creators who profit from viral falsehoods. Similarly, Brooke Binkowski of fact-checking magazine *Snopes* praised Facebook’s “flooding out” approach but warned that AI, despite being a “good tool,” remains too broad to effectively identify nuanced misinformation. Felle emphasized that Facebook’s true responsibility lies in supporting quality journalism. “If Facebook wants to help journalism, it needs to put its hand in its pocket and support quality, trusted news organizations to better reach audiences and advertisers,” he said. Binkowski echoed the sentiment, urging the platform to invest in partnerships with credible news outlets to restore public trust. As the debate over tech companies’ role in democracy continues, Facebook’s latest steps reflect a shift toward indirect intervention. Yet, with misinformation evolving rapidly and financial pressures mounting on traditional media, many argue the firm must do more than tweak algorithms. Without sustained investment in journalism and robust, real-time solutions, critics warn, fake news will remain a persistent threat to informed public discourse.

The incident occurred at approximately 21:30 BST, with Lancashire Police confirming paramedics treated the individual at the scene before transporting him to Royal Preston Hospital. Authorities stated his injuries are not life-threatening. Eyewitness Robert Simmill described the harrowing moment, recounting, “I just saw the body fall..... then there was a loud thud. Everyone around me got up, screaming and shouting.” The man, who landed on the shoulder of a woman seated in the front row, had not injured her, police added. However, Simmill said the atmosphere was chaotic, with audience members urging the cast to halt the performance

**Dispute Over Welsh Language Recognition in Cardiff’s New Development Plan** A heated debate has erupted in Cardiff over the role of the Welsh language in the city’s Local Development Plan (LDP), following a controversial letter from Council Leader Phil Bale to the Welsh Language Society (Cymdeithas yr Iaith Gymraeg). Bale’s remarks, described as “completely ignorant” by the society, have sparked accusations of institutional neglect toward Wales’ official language. In his letter, Bale asserted that evidence presented to the council suggested the Welsh language was “not part of the social fabric” of Cardiff, according to national planning guidelines. He argued that development proposals outlined in the LDP would not “materially affect the linguistic balance of communities,” and concluded no specific policies were needed to protect the language in the plan. This stance has drawn sharp criticism from pro-Welsh groups, who argue the language is foundational to the city’s identity. Local Cymdeithas yr Iaith chair Carl Morris condemned Bale’s claim as “daft and completely ignorant,” writing to the Welsh government’s Planning Inspectorate to demand accountability. Morris suggested the remark reflected “the ignorance of officers in the planning department,” rather than the council leader’s personal stance. He urged planners to ensure the LDP includes measures to support Welsh, including provisions for language-friendly schools and community services. Cardiff Council has defended its position, stating the disputed wording in Bale’s letter was taken from a national planning guidance document and “technically” presented. A council spokesperson insisted the language was “used selectively” without its full context, which includes broader considerations for linguistic needs. The council also expressed disappointment that concerns were raised only now, after “ample opportunity” for public consultation during the LDP drafting process. Bale’s leadership has been under scrutiny since a May challenge within Cardiff’s Labour group, where his position was narrowly upheld. His recent comments have reignited tensions over the council’s commitment to Welsh language rights. The LDP, currently under review by the Welsh government’s planning inspector, will determine how future development projects address linguistic and cultural priorities. The Welsh Language Society and advocates argue that excluding language-specific policies undermines the 2011 Welsh Language (Wales) Measure, which mandates public bodies to promote equal status for Welsh and English. They emphasize that Cardiff, with over 21,000 Welsh speakers and numerous bilingual communities, cannot afford to overlook the language in urban planning. As the inspector’s evaluation progresses, the dispute highlights deepening divides over how local authorities balance growth, heritage, and linguistic rights. For now, the debate over Welsh in Cardiff’s future remains unresolved—a clash of priorities with broader implications for Wales’ cultural identity.

**Calls for Mobile Phone Unlocks to Promote Fair Competition** The consumer advocacy group Which? has urged mobile phone companies to stop locking devices to specific networks, arguing that the practice stifles competition and disadvantages customers seeking better deals. The organization claims that pay-as-you-go phones should never be locked, while contract phones should be unlocked automatically at the end of agreements. Current industry practices, it says, often obscure the best options for consumers and tie them to unsuitable contracts. When purchased from a mobile operator, phones are typically locked to the provider’s network until a contract expires or the customer requests an unlock. This prevents users from inserting SIM cards from rival networks. Which? executive director Richard Lloyd emphasized that mobile phones are now essential tools for many people, and consumers should not be “locked into contracts that do not suit their usage.” The group is pushing for operators to alert customers when their contracts are nearing their end and to unlock devices for free, enabling users to compare deals and switch providers. A survey conducted by Which? of 2,100 customers revealed that 70% would be more likely to seek better value for money if phones were unlocked automatically. However, most operators currently charge fees for unlocking. O2, for example, waives the cost for contract users but charges £15 for pay-as-you-go customers, citing the need to recoup subsidies and deter fraud. EE and Vodafone levy higher fees of £20.42 and £19.99, respectively, with EE only unlocking devices after six months. Three has taken a different approach, offering free unlocks for all pre-January devices and selling unlocked phones since that date. Operators defend the practice, with O2 stating that locked pay-as-you-go phones risk “box breaking”—a scheme where devices are bought, unlocked, and resold overseas for profit. The company claims the £15 fee covers subsidies, administrative costs, and fraud prevention. Similarly, EE and Vodafone argue that locking phones ensures compliance with subsidy agreements and safeguards against misuse. Critics, however, argue that these policies limit consumer choice. Richard Lloyd said the industry should prioritize transparency, including notifying customers of the best available deals after contracts end. Financial advice website Moneysavingexpert.com supports this stance, noting that even with upfront unlocking fees, long-term savings from cheaper plans or international SIM cards often outweigh the cost. As the debate over phone locks continues, Which? is calling for stricter regulations to ensure fairness. With mobile networks increasingly competing on price and flexibility, the pressure to align with customer needs is growing. For now, the burden of unlocking remains on consumers, though advocates insist that open competition—and unlocked devices—would ultimately benefit everyone.

**Home-Schooled Prodigy Edith Fuller Claims Regional Spelling Bee Crown, Eyes National Stage** TULSA, Okla.—Edith Fuller, a home-schooled 13-year-old, emerged victorious at the Scripps Green Country Regional Spelling Bee on Saturday, outpacing over 50 competitors to secure her spot in the National Spelling Bee in Washington, D.C., this May. Her champion word, “jnana,” a Sanskrit term for “knowledge” in Indian philosophy, sealed her triumph in a competition that tested even the most advanced young linguists. Fuller’s road to victory was paved with formidable words, including *Panglossian* (excessively optimistic), *Baedeker* (a reference to German travel guidebooks), *nisei* (an American or Canadian of Japanese immigrant descent), and *Croesus* (a symbol of extreme wealth, named after a 6th-century BC Lydian king). She also correctly spelled “sarsaparilla,” a term for both a tropical plant and a root-based beverage. The win marks a milestone for the Tulsa-native, who faced off against students from northeast Oklahoma’s primary and middle schools. Her mother, Annie Fuller, expressed pride in her daughter’s resilience. “I knew she’d be a novelty, so I’m proud she held her own,” she told the *Tulsa World*. The family first recognized Edith’s potential last summer when she spelled “restaurant” correctly on her own, a word she hadn’t been formally taught. Edith, who describes herself as “thankful” for her victory, will join other top spellers at the national stage in May. The competition is open to students who haven’t completed the eighth grade, with no minimum age requirement. Last year’s youngest contestant, 6-year-old Akash Vukoti, was eliminated after misspelling “bacteriolytic” in an early round, underscoring the contest’s rigor. The National Spelling Bee continues to draw a mix of prodigies and underdogs, and Edith’s blend of home-schooling and natural aptitude positions her as a formidable contender. As her mother noted, “It’s fun to share her with everyone.” For now, the Fuller family is savoring their daughter’s regional triumph—a step closer to spelling history.

**UK's Economic Growth: Major Achievement or Missed Opportunity?** The UK’s 2014 economic growth of 2.6%, as forecast by the IMF in January 2015, outpaced all other G7 nations, including the US (2.4%) and Germany (1.5%). However, this progress pales in comparison to emerging giants like China (7.4%) and India (5.8%), which many economists classify as “major economies.” While the UK’s performance edged ahead of its G7 peers, the IMF’s data highlights a critical nuance: growth alone does not define economic success. China and India, with vastly larger populations and GDPs, expanded far more rapidly, challenging the narrative of the UK as a standout performer. Adding complexity, the UK’s Office for National Statistics reported 2014 growth at 2.8%, slightly higher than the IMF’s estimate, though both remain provisional. The IMF also predicts the US will surpass the UK in growth for 2015, potentially shortening the UK’s lead. Political claims about economic strength often rely on selective metrics, underscoring the need for context. As the BBC Reality Check notes, growth rates must be weighed against population size, global economic trends, and future projections. While the UK may have led the G7 last year, its position as a global economic leader remains contested, particularly against faster-growing economies. Ultimately, the truth behind the numbers depends on which economies are measured—and which stories are told.

**Tranmere Rovers Midfielder Joe Thompson to Undergo Chemotherapy After Cancer Diagnosis** Tranmere Rovers’ 24-year-old midfielder Joe Thompson has begun a six-month course of chemotherapy after being diagnosed with nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma. The Rochdale-born player, who recently reported feeling unwell, received the diagnosis following medical tests. His treatment marks the start of a challenging but hopeful journey for the young athlete and his family. Nodular sclerosing Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common type of the disease in the UK, accounting for nearly 60% of cases. According to Cancer Research UK, it often presents at an early stage, with enlarged lymph glands in the neck being a typical sign. The organization emphasizes that early detection significantly improves outcomes, offering a sense of optimism for Thompson’s recovery. Tranmere’s chief executive, Mick Horton, expressed the club’s deep concern and solidarity with Thompson. “Joe will get all the love and support we can give him as he undergoes treatment,” Horton said. “We are stunned by this news, and all our thoughts are with Joe and his family. We ask that their privacy be respected and will share updates as they become available.” Manager Ronnie Moore praised Thompson’s character, stating, “Joe is a fantastic young man, and we will do everything we can to help him make a full recovery.” Thompson, who made over 100 appearances for Rochdale before joining Tranmere in 2012, is widely respected within the club. His absence will be felt both on and off the pitch. Fans and the football community have rallied behind Thompson, with the club urging supporters to send well-wishes during his treatment. As the midfielder embarks on his fight against cancer, Tranmere Rovers remain committed to supporting him every step of the way.

**FARC Unveils New Ceasefire Amid Escalating Violence, Government Calls for Greater Commitment** The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) announced a unilateral ceasefire beginning July 20, aiming to create conditions for a bilateral truce with the Colombian government. FARC’s chief negotiator, Ivan Marquez, stated the move could “advance toward a definitive ceasefire,” signaling hope after years of stalled peace talks. However, the government, while acknowledging the gesture, emphasized the need for concrete action to accelerate negotiations. President Juan Manuel Santos tweeted, “We appreciate the FARC’s unilateral ceasefire, but more is needed—especially commitments to speed up talks.” The renewed ceasefire follows a recent surge in violence, including the June detonation of an oil pipeline in Catatumbo, which contaminated water supplies and displaced 16,000 residents. Since the previous FARC ceasefire collapsed in May, clashes have killed dozens of rebels and soldiers. A December 2023 truce had similarly failed, with clashes resuming after 11 soldiers were killed in April. Four nations facilitating the talks—Cuba, Norway, Chile, and Venezuela—urged de-escalation, highlighting the fragile progress in Havana negotiations that began in 2012. These talks aim to end Colombia’s 58-year civil war, which has claimed over 200,000 lives. While agreements have been reached on several issues, the conflict remains unresolved, with sporadic violence undermining trust. FARC’s latest proposal reflects growing pressure to finalize peace, but the government’s cautious response underscores deep-seated skepticism. Analysts warn that without mutual steps to address lingering disputes—such as land reform and transitional justice—lasting peace may remain elusive. For now, the ceasefire’s success hinges on whether both sides can bridge the gap between rhetoric and action in a conflict as entrenched as it is complex.

**FIFA Faces Corruption Fallout as Blatter Re-elected Amid Crisis** FIFA, the global football governing body, has been rocked by a corruption scandal this week, with seven senior officials arrested in Switzerland on Wednesday (27 May) over allegations of multimillion-dollar bribe-taking. The arrests, made at a Zurich hotel, mark the latest blow to FIFA’s reputation, which has long faced scrutiny over financial impropriety. Sepp Blatter, FIFA’s president, faced intense pressure to resign but was re-elected on Friday, despite widespread criticism. His decision to stay in office has sparked calls for a boycott of the 2018 World Cup in Russia, with some nations threatening to withdraw in protest. “I am very much linked to FIFA and its interests. Those interests are dear to me,” Blatter stated, defending his leadership. Critics argue the scandal has undermined the sport’s integrity. FIFA announced plans for a new election “as soon as possible” to appoint a leader capable of restoring public trust. The organization, which oversees international competitions, now faces urgent challenges in addressing systemic corruption and regaining global confidence. The arrests and ongoing turmoil highlight deep-seated issues within FIFA’s governance, as stakeholders demand accountability and reform.

Former health secretary Alex Neil MSP accused the board of adopting a “high-level finger in the air estimate” instead of a rigorous business plan. “You need a detailed roadmap to pay off debt without slashing services,” Neil demanded, warning that the current approach risked a Scottish government bailout. **EIS Union Payouts Highlight Safety Concerns in Scottish Education Sector** The Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS) union has revealed that £608,925 was paid to members in compensation claims for injuries sustained at work during the year, including a £55,000 payout for a teacher assaulted by a pupil. The incident occurred when the educator attempted to de-escalate a situation with the student. Other notable claims involved injuries from accidents, with £12,000 awarded to a teacher who fractured a knee after tripping over a metal door wedge and a similar sum for a colleague who broke an arm after slipping on black ice in a school car park. Additionally, £12,500 was paid to a staff member who developed back pain from lifting a heavy box without handles. EIS General Secretary Larry Flanagan emphasized that the total payout underscores the urgent need for improved workplace safety in schools, colleges, and universities. “The most common causes of injuries remain preventable incidents like slips, trips, and falls,” he stated. “While no environment can be entirely risk-free, adherence to health and safety protocols is critical to protect staff and students alike.” Flanagan rejected claims that the figures reflect a “compensation culture,” arguing that quicker liability admissions by insurance firms could reduce settlement costs. “If insurers act promptly, the financial burden on institutions—and, ultimately, on staff—could decrease significantly,” he added. The EIS has called for systemic changes to address avoidable hazards, including better training and risk assessments. With nearly £610,000 spent on compensation, the union reiterated its commitment to advocating for safer working conditions across Scotland’s education sector. The revelations come amid ongoing debates over workplace safety standards and the balance between accountability and employee welfare in public services.

**North Yorkshire Pushes for 95% Broadband Coverage by 2019 Amid Rural Challenges** North Yorkshire County Council has set a target to deliver high-speed broadband to 95% of households by 2019, acknowledging the difficulties of providing services across its sprawling 3,000-square-mile area. Council leader Carl Les admitted the goal, though ambitious, reflects revised expectations after initial optimism for universal coverage. “We thought 100% was realistic,” he said, “but experience has shown it’s more complex than we anticipated.” Currently, 91% of the region’s premises will achieve a minimum speed of 25Mbps by June 2019, with £35 million allocated to date. A further £21 million has been approved for the final phase, aiming to close the gap to 95%. However, Les acknowledged lingering frustrations for the remaining 5% of households. “Those left out will be very disappointed,” he said, citing the challenges of remote, rural properties. To bridge the gap, some communities are taking matters into their own hands. In Clapham cum Newby, a grassroots initiative led by Simon Peach raised £250,000 to install 20 miles of fiber-optic cable, connecting 100 homes with speeds up to 1,000 Mbps. “We did the right thing,” Peach said, but added that securing land access and relying on volunteer labor highlighted systemic barriers. “Rural properties are last in the queue—a frustrating reality.” While progress is notable, with over 90% of areas now covered “in a short time,” the council and communities face a shared mission: ensuring no one is left behind in an increasingly connected world. The combined effort of public funding and local innovation underscores the complexity—and resolve—of addressing digital inequality in one of the UK’s largest counties.

**Amazon Enters Singapore E-Commerce Race with Two-Hour Delivery Service, Directing First Asian Clash with Alibaba** Amazon has launched its Prime Now delivery service in Singapore, marking a bold step into Southeast Asia and igniting its first direct competition with Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba in the region. The service promises two-hour delivery on thousands of items, including groceries, electronics, and food, positioning Amazon to challenge local players like Redmart, owned by Alibaba-backed Lazada. The move underscores Amazon’s aggressive expansion into a market of 600 million people, with Singapore serving as a strategic testing ground. The city-state’s developed infrastructure and affluent population make it an ideal entry point, though analysts caution that the broader Southeast Asian market remains highly fragmented, with diverse cultures, languages, and regulatory challenges. Initially, Singapore customers can use Prime Now without a paid subscription, gaining access to electronics, toys, sports gear, and groceries. However, key Amazon Prime features like video streaming, Prime Video, and Amazon Echo devices are excluded. Books also appear unavailable for purchase, indicating a phased rollout of the service. Amazon’s presence in Asia has grown steadily, with significant footholds in India and Japan. Yet Southeast Asia represents a critical battleground. The region’s potential $70 billion e-commerce market has drawn global giants, but local knowledge and logistics networks are vital. Alibaba’s Redmart already dominates the instant delivery space in Singapore, while Lazada’s regional footprint in countries like Indonesia and Thailand gives it a first-mover advantage. Logistics hurdles loom large. While Singapore’s compact size and efficiency enable two-hour deliveries, scaling this model to larger, less-developed markets like Indonesia and Vietnam poses challenges. Alibaba’s deep understanding of local markets and established networks could prove decisive. Despite these obstacles, the rivalry is likely to benefit consumers. However, cybersecurity experts have criticized the company for failing to implement basic security measures that could have mitigated the damage. **Lack of Salted Hashing Leaves Passwords Vulnerable** Rik Ferguson, a senior security researcher at Trend Micro, highlighted that Vtech stored customer passwords using a hashing algorithm but did not employ “salting”—a critical security practice that randomizes the hashing process. Without salting, identical passwords across accounts produce the same hash, making them susceptible to “rainbow table” attacks. These attacks use precomputed tables of hashes for common passwords to reverse-engineer sensitive information. Secure websites avoid storing passwords in plain text, instead using hashing algorithms to convert passwords into unique, scrambled strings of code. When a user logs in, the entered password is rehashed and compared to the stored hash. While hashing is designed to be a one-way process, the absence of salting in Vtech’s system creates a critical vulnerability. “If attackers know the hashing algorithm, they can match hashes to common passwords using a rainbow table,” Ferguson explained. **ESA’s Sentinel-3a Unveils Ocean Dynamics: A New Era in Climate Monitoring** The European Space Agency (ESA) has released its first data from the Sentinel-3a satellite’s altimeter instrument, revealing striking images of the Gulf Stream—a powerful current of warm water that shapes global climate patterns.
