**Zero-Hours Workers’ Rights and Legal Complexities Unveiled** Workers in the UK enjoy fundamental rights, including annual leave and the National Minimum Wage, but the extent of their protections depends on their employment status. While all “workers” have these entitlements, “employees” receive additional safeguards, such as protection against unfair dismissal, maternity rights, and redundancy pay. The line between the two categories hinges on contractual terms and practical working arrangements. Zero-hours contracts—common in sectors like hospitality and retail—typically classify workers as non-employees, as employers aren’t obligated to offer work, and workers aren’t required to accept it. However, Employment Tribunals have occasionally ruled that zero-hours workers should be reclassified as employees if their work patterns show consistency, such as regularly accepting shifts. The House of Commons Library highlights that the distinction is “complex” and subject to ongoing debate, with real-world practices often outweighing contractual language. Legal experts stress that employers and workers must scrutinize the “reality” of the relationship, not just the contract. Misclassification can strip workers of critical rights, while employers risk penalties for non-compliance. As political leaders debate labor reforms, understanding these nuances becomes vital. **Chris Brunt Reflects on Setback and New Chapter Amid Recovery from Major Knee Injury** West Bromwich Albion’s veteran utility man Chris Brunt has spoken of his mixed emotions following the rupture of his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in early March, an injury that will sideline him for at least six months. I haven’t made up my mind yet, but it’s a great opportunity to be around the lads and the coaching staff.” Brunt, who has scored 43 goals for West Brom, has found a silver lining in the forced absence. “Being out has given me more time with my kids, which I’ve been missing when I was training and playing,” he said. “I knew straight away this was a bad one. My knee was three times its normal size by the next day.” The injury overshadowed a period of controversy in March when a fan hurled a coin at Brunt post-match, cutting his cheek and sparking outrage. Though Brunt remains reluctant to dwell on the incident, he praised the Albion fans’ response. “One person did something awful, but the support I received was incredible,” he said. “The bucket collections for charity at the Palace game were a great show of solidarity, and I’ve been overwhelmed by the messages. I’ve always had a good relationship with the fans, and I don’t see that changing over this.” As Brunt prepares for a long rehabilitation, his focus remains on returning stronger for West Brom and contributing to Northern Ireland’s European campaign. “If I can help the team from the sidelines, even as a non-playing member, that would mean a lot,” he added. “The Euros are just weeks away, and I’m eager to see the lads do well.” With 43 goals in 314 games, Brunt’s career resilience mirrors his approach to this latest challenge—a blend of pragmatism, gratitude, and a commitment to supporting both club and country.

**Court Upholds EU Ruling on Mastercard’s Interchange Fees, Ending Seven-Year Legal Battle** The European Court has rejected Mastercard’s appeal against a decision to cap interchange fees, affirming regulators’ stance that the charges were excessive and anti-competitive. The ruling maintains the cap at a weighted average of 0.2% for debit and 0.3% for credit card transactions, a move welcomed by retailers and competition authorities. Mastercard, the second-largest card network after Visa, faced a year-long investigation over its fee structure in Europe. Javier Perez, president of Mastercard Europe, called the outcome “disappointing” but insisted it would have “little or no impact on operations.” He confirmed the company would continue complying with the cap, which has been in place for years, and retain its cross-border fees. UK retailers praised the decision as a victory for fair competition. Helen Dickinson of the British Retail Consortium hailed it as “historic,” stating that capping fees would help the industry invest, innovate, and pass savings to consumers. “This ruling supports our ability to deliver lower prices and value,” she added. The court’s decision marks the end of Mastercard’s seven-year challenge to the EU’s competition watchdog. Regulators argued that high interchange fees unfairly burdened retailers, stifling competition and raising costs for consumers. With the appeal dismissed, the policy is now likely to remain in effect, reinforcing the EU’s commitment to curbing anti-competitive practices in the financial sector.

**106-Year-Old British Fruitcake Defies Antarctic Time, Outlives Tragic Expedition** A 106-year-old fruitcake, preserved in the harsh Antarctic environment, has emerged as an unexpected survivor in a tale of historical exploration. Discovered by the New Zealand-based Antarctic Heritage Trust on Cape Adare, the cake is believed to have belonged to British polar explorer Robert Falcon Scott, renowned for his ill-fated Terra Nova expedition of 1910–1912. The confection, stored in a rusted tin but described as being in “excellent condition” with an edible aroma, was found in Antarctica’s oldest building—a hut constructed in 1899 by Norwegian explorer Carsten Borchgrevink’s team and later used by Scott’s crew. The fruitcake, produced by the British biscuit company Huntley & Palmers, was a staple for early Antarctic explorers. According to Lizzie Meek, the Trust’s conservation manager for artefacts, such cakes were favored for their high-fat, high-sugar content—a critical energy source in frigid conditions. “They go very well with a cup of tea, too,” Meek noted, emphasizing their historical and practical appeal. The Trust, excavating the hut since May 2016, has recovered 1,500 items, including tools, clothing, and jars of “rather nice-looking” jams, though other foodstuffs like meat and fish have deteriorated. The cake’s preservation is starkly contrasted by the fate of Scott and his team. After reaching the South Pole in January 1912, they found Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen had beaten them by 33 days. Scott and his companions perished on their return journey. The hut, now a museum, houses restored artefacts returned to their original locations—a testament to the explorers’ resilience and the enduring legacy of their hardships. While the fruitcake endures as a curious relic of ingenuity, it also serves as a poignant reminder of the human cost of exploration in Earth’s most unforgiving landscapes.

**Ben Forster and Kimberley Walsh Lead ‘Elf’ in Costly, Divisive West End Musical** The West End’s latest holiday spectacle, *Elf*, starring *Jesus Christ Superstar* alumnus Ben Forster as Buddy the Elf and former *Girls Aloud* singer Kimberley Walsh as Jovie, has sparked a frenzy of praise and controversy since its opening. Based on the 2003 film, *Elf* retells the story of a 30-year-old man raised by elves who journeys to New York to meet his human father. **CAA Announces Enhanced Safety Measures for Air Displays Following Shoreham Crash** The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) has unveiled a comprehensive overhaul of air display safety protocols in the wake of the tragic Shoreham Airshow crash, which claimed 11 lives on August 22. A vintage Hawker Hunter jet, performing aerobatics at the event, crashed onto the A27 motorway, prompting immediate scrutiny of airshow regulations. This year’s Shoreham Airshow has been cancelled, and the CAA has introduced stricter requirements to ensure public safety at future events. Tony Rapson, the CAA’s head of general aviation, confirmed that while the exact cause of the Shoreham disaster remains under investigation by the Air Accidents Investigations Branch (AAIB), the authority is implementing new safeguards. These include tightened permission processes for air shows, enhanced training for display directors, and stricter assessments of pilots’ experience, skills, and health. From 2017, display directors will be required to complete a formal two-day course, while immediate measures this year mandate participation in a pre-season symposium or individual briefing. In the aftermath of the crash, the CAA also imposed lasting restrictions, such as grounding all Hawker Hunter jets, limiting ex-military aircraft to fly-pasts over land, and requiring enhanced risk assessments for air displays. Rapson emphasized that these precautions would remain in place until the AAIB concludes its investigation and provides recommendations. “We still don’t know the cause of the Shoreham accident,” he stated, “but when the AAIB makes its recommendations, the CAA will respond.” The changes reflect the CAA’s commitment to balancing public accessibility with safety, as air displays attract millions—5.7 million in the UK alone in 2014. Rapson reiterated the authority’s goal to ensure displays remain “even safer and even better.” Colin Baker, a director of the Shoreham Airshow, expressed full support for the CAA’s initiatives, noting the show had always adhered to regulations. “We will closely examine both the updates announced today and the CAA’s next report, due after the AAIB investigation is completed, when we consider the future of the airshow from 2017 onwards,” he said. The CAA and AAIB have yet to publish final reports, but the tragedy has undeniably reshaped the landscape of air display safety in the UK. As the aviation community awaits the AAIB’s findings, the Shoreham crash serves as a sobering reminder of the risks and responsibilities inherent in such events.

**Welsh Leaders and Notable Figures Caught in Memorable Mishaps** As Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies opened his party’s conference in Manchester on October 4 with a confident declaration that “We’ve had a successful breakfast,” it became clear he was conflating the event with Brexit—a mix-up not uncommon in the political landscape. Yet, this was far from the first time Welsh public figures have made headlines for unexpected gaffes. From social media storms to missteps on live television, here are some iconic moments that left Wales—and beyond—amused, baffled, or both. One of the most infamous blunders came in February 2011 when First Minister Carwyn Jones hinted during a BBC interview that his children might no longer believe in Santa Claus. “It’s the first year they won’t believe in St Nick,” he remarked, prompting a Twitter and Facebook frenzy. The Prime Minister at the time, David Cameron, playfully replied: “I’m sure Father Christmas will be quite happy to intervene.” The incident highlighted the delicate balance between political candor and tradition. Earlier, in 2008, a high-profile confusion at the National Book Awards at the Hilton Hotel saw a mix-up that stunned attendees. Culture Minister Rhodri Glyn Thomas mistakenly announced Tom Bullough as the winner of the English-language book category. As the former Wales poet laureate made his way to the stage, Thomas hastily corrected himself, revealing the true winner: Dannie Abse for *The Presence*, a poignant work about losing his wife. The flub underscored the unpredictability of live events, even in the literary world. Dylan Iorwerth, a seasoned journalist known for uncovering major stories, found himself in an unexpected role during the 2023 National Eisteddfod in Powys. While live on TV debating with Dewi Llwyd and Karen Owen, Iorwerth’s phone rang, forcing him to apologize and mute himself. The awkward interruption, though minor, reminded audiences that even seasoned professionals aren’t immune to technical mishaps. Perhaps the most colorful mix-up involved former Wales striker Dean Saunders. During the 2016 Euros, Saunders was tasked with BBC commentary for Wales’ matches but misjudged his parking spot at Birmingham Airport, leaving his car over a mile from the stadium. As Gareth Bale and Hal Robson-Kanu graced the field, Saunders faced a parking fine totaling £1,000. The tale of his misplaced confidence became a running joke among colleagues, with some dubbing it “the greatest parking maneuver of the tournament.” These incidents, while humorous, offer a glimpse into the human side of public figures. Whether it’s a misplaced Santa reference, a literary award snafu, or a costly parking error, such moments remind us that even those in the spotlight aren’t above the occasional blunder. As Wales moves forward, these stories will likely endure as quirky footnotes in its political and cultural history. For now, as the political class continues its quest for perfection, one thing remains certain: the past is replete with tales where “successful breakfasts” sometimes taste like unintended chaos.

**Cliftonville Edge Toward Europa League Second Leg with Crucial Away Goal** Cliftonville manager Gerard Lyttle’s side head into next week’s Europa League first qualifying round second leg at Solitude with a vital away goal, thanks to Lee Lavery’s decisive header in the first leg. The match, played against an unfamiliar opponent, showcased resilience from the Reds as they secured a 1-0 advantage. New goalkeeper Jason Mooney made an early impact, saving a strong effort from Yeye Jordann, while Omar Er Rafik broke the deadlock in the 38th minute with a composed finish. Home keeper Julien Weber then denied Martin Donnelly late in the game, underscoring the tactical battle. Cliftonville, who secured their place in the competition with a thrilling 3-2 Irish League victory over Glentoran in May, faced challenges this time without suspended defender Jaimie McGovern. Jason McGuinness, making his competitive debut after joining from St Patrick’s Athletic, stepped in and impressed. Lyttle praised his team’s adaptability, stating: “We aimed to get a goal here, and we worked hard against a team we knew little about. We sussed them out in the first half and were a different team after the break. Ross [likely Lavery] has a bright future—his talent, energy, and strength made tonight a dream come true.” With the second leg at Solitude looming, Cliftonville will look to build on their advantage as they chase a spot in the next round.

**Retired Pastor’s Death Under Investigation After Shed Fire** The body of David Wynn, 79, was discovered outside his Cilcain, Flintshire, home on October 20 following a shed fire. An inquest in Ruthin revealed Mr. Wynn, a retired minister of Ebenezer Baptist Church in Mold, had been welding as a hobby when the blaze occurred. Police confirmed his death is not being treated as suspicious. The alarm was raised by members of the public who spotted the fire. A full post-mortem and further tests are underway, with the inquest adjourned until April for a comprehensive hearing. Mr. Wynn, who retired from the church 13 years ago, remained active in his community. Investigators are examining the fire’s cause but have ruled out foul play.

**Blues Midfield Shake-Up as Allen Faces Uncertain Future** Cardiff Blues’ Welsh centre Rhys Allen, 24, has been sidelined this season as New Zealand imports Rey Lee-Lo and Willis Halaholo dominate the midfield. With the club securing Leicester’s Jack Roberts for next season, competition for starting spots is intensifying. Allen, who earned four Wales caps and notched a hat-trick in Wales’ 2015 World Cup win over Uruguay, faces an uncertain future after suffering a hamstring injury in that match. Blues head coach Danny Wilson confirmed Roberts will battle Lee-Lo, Halaholo, Garyn Smith, and Harri Millard for a centre role next term. Allen, whose contract expires this summer, has been linked with Pro12 rivals Ospreys amid speculation about his status. Wilson reiterated that current first-team options are prioritized: “The names mentioned will compete for that position next season.” Allen’s absence this year highlights the Blues’ reliance on international signings, though his potential exit could open doors for younger talent or new recruits as the team reshapes its midfield ambitions.

**Prison Officers Across Five Jails Walk Out Over Safety Fears** *By Danny Shaw, BBC Home Affairs Correspondent* Largely unnoticed and seldom praised, prison officers perform a vital role in managing some of society’s most challenging and volatile individuals. Yet when staff at five separate prisons down tools, it signals a crisis. Recent walkouts, driven by escalating safety concerns, underscore a systemic issue within the UK’s prison system—one that threatens both staff well-being and the government’s reform agenda. Last year, nearly 5,000 assaults were recorded against prison staff, the highest figure in a decade. The Prison Officers Association (POA), whose members are legally barred from striking, has cited these alarming statistics as a key reason for the recent wave of unofficial walkouts. Officers at Wetherby Young Offenders Institution in West Yorkshire and Wormwood Scrubs in London stopped work in May, but similar actions at three other prisons—Mount Prison in Hertfordshire, Holme House in County Durham, and Swinfen Hall in Staffordshire—only came to light recently. At Mount Prison, four staff members refused to carry out duties, while 40 officers at Holme House withdrew in protest against regime changes. Most recently, officers at Swinfen Hall left prisoners locked in their cells, citing fears of a “significant and imminent threat” to their health and safety. Mike Rolfe, chairman of the POA, highlighted the growing divide between staff and inmates, exacerbated by chronic understaffing. With limited time for informal interactions—essential for de-escalating tensions—officers are overwhelmed by administrative tasks like cell checks and searches. “The safety of our staff is non-negotiable,” Rolfe said. “We’re in a crisis where basic welfare needs are being neglected.” The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has responded by announcing £13 million in funding to improve safety across 69 prisons, including those affected by recent walkouts. This comes alongside a £1.3 billion investment to modernise prison infrastructure and a net increase of 530 officers since January last year. A MoJ spokesperson dismissed claims of “significant disputes” at the affected prisons as “wholly inaccurate,” insisting safety and staffing levels remain a priority. However, critics argue that funding alone cannot address the root causes of the crisis. Rising rates of mental illness, drug use, and violent extremism in prisons have created an environment where even experienced officers struggle to manage risks. **Horse-Mounted Volunteers Aid Northamptonshire Police in Traffic Crackdown** Northamptonshire Police has launched a pioneering initiative to tackle speeding and road safety, recruiting over 50 volunteers trained by the British Horse Society to patrol on horseback. Equipped with high-visibility jackets bearing a police volunteer logo, the riders will serve as an “extra set of eyes and ears” but will not confront lawbreakers directly. The force hopes the presence of uniformed riders will encourage motorists to reduce speeds, particularly in rural areas. Volunteers, who provide their own horses, will receive out-of-pocket expenses but will not follow fixed patrol routes. Instead, they will be asked to report issues as they ride through lanes and bridleways. The scheme also marks the appointment of Tash Fountain as the force’s first Mounted Police Community Support Officer (PCSO), riding her horse, Cody. Similar programs exist in other English forces. Norfolk Police reintroduced mounted patrols in 2012, with Special Constable Richard Tallent noting the unit’s success in addressing issues like fly-tipping, drink driving, and anti-social behavior. “Every year, we complete 100 hours of patrols,” he said. “We’ve already seen measurable results.” Northamptonshire Police emphasizes that while the initiative is voluntary, it aligns with broader efforts to build community engagement and enhance safety. The focus remains on deterrence and reporting rather than enforcement, reflecting a collaborative approach to policing.

**Eighth Annual “Snow Census” to Track Lingering Winter** The eighth annual “snow census” in Scotland kicks off this August, surveying persistent snow patches from the Cairngorms to Glencoe and the Nevis Range. Researchers anticipate a record haul of data due to unusually high snow retention this summer. The weekend-long survey, reliant on volunteer efforts, aims to map patches across rugged terrain. Last year’s tally—nearly 300 patches, including a 10m-deep remnant on Ben Nevis—highlighted climate shifts. This year’s results could further reveal trends in Scotland’s changing landscape. Volunteers will document locations, depths, and conditions, offering insights into how winter’s grip lingers into autumn.

**Urgent Repairs Needed for Canterbury Cathedral** **Christchurch Gate Requires Immediate Attention as Cathedral Seeks Funding for Restoration Project** Canterbury Cathedral faces a critical repair crisis, with two-thirds of its structure—most notably Christchurch Gate, the primary tourist entrance—urgently requiring restoration. Andrew Edwards of the Canterbury Cathedral Trust warned that a single stone falling from the unstable gate could force the cathedral to close indefinitely. The trust plans to resubmit its funding bid in 2014 for a five-year conservation project, with 68% of the cost dedicated to urgent repairs identified by architects. “The funding is absolutely critical,” Edwards emphasized. “If a piece of stone falls, we’re closed for business.” With limited domestic resources, the cathedral is now appealing to international donors to safeguard its historic site. The project aims to preserve the iconic structure and ensure it remains open for future generations.

**Anglican Communion Seeks Unity Amid Deepening Divides Over Social Issues** The Anglican Communion, the third-largest Christian denomination globally, faces a pivotal moment as its leaders gather to address escalating tensions over contentious social issues, including the role of female priests and same-sex relationships. The meeting’s agenda includes contentious topics such as human sexuality, religiously motivated violence, child protection, and environmental stewardship, reflecting the communion’s broader challenges. The roots of the conflict trace back to 2003, when the U.S. Episcopal Church consecrated Gene Robinson, a divorced man in a same-sex relationship, as bishop of New Hampshire. This sparked mass protests and a boycott of the 2008 Lambeth Conference by a quarter of attending bishops. Now, with societal values evolving rapidly in the Global North, Welby faces immense pressure to reconcile divergent views without fracturing the communion entirely. **Tragic Loss Shocks Spalding Community as Family Mourns Sudden Deaths** A devastating tragedy has shaken the Lincolnshire town of Spalding, where 57-year-old Lance Hart was identified as the man who shot and killed his wife, Claire Hart, 50, and their daughter Charlotte, 19, on July 19 near the Castle Sports Complex. The family’s funeral took place this week at All Saints Church in Moulton, drawing an overflow crowd as loved ones paid tribute to the women described as “a force of love and light.” The heartfelt ceremony saw Reverend Barbara Hutchinson deliver a poignant reading of a tribute penned by Claire and Charlotte’s sons, Ryan and Luke. “We were always awestruck that the universe could create something as beautiful as you both,” the siblings wrote, their words echoing through the church. The message highlighted their mother and sister’s “unconditional love” and resilience, urging mourners to “not be defeated” in the face of their loss. The service, relayed via loudspeakers for those unable to enter the packed church, included a moving tribute to Michael Bublé’s “Home,” a song the women cherished. Reverend Hutchinson, visibly emotional, described the tribute as “heart-wrenching to read” and praised Ryan and Luke for their remarkable composure during the ordeal. An inquest last month revealed the victims were shot by Lance Hart using a single-barrel shotgun. While the exact motive remains under investigation, a full inquest is scheduled for October. The community, still reeling from the violence, has rallied around the Hart family, with many describing Claire and Charlotte as pillars of strength and kindness. As the family grapples with their unimaginable grief, friends and neighbors continue to honor their memory through shared stories and a legacy of love. “We hope to make you as proud as you have made us,” the sons concluded in their tribute, a sentiment that resonates deeply across Spalding.

**Sam Burgess departs Bath for rugby league return as England’s World Cup disappointment sparks criticism from former coach** Sam Burgess has confirmed his return to rugby league, ending his 12-month stint at Bath after the English rugby union team’s early exit from the 2019 World Cup. The former England international will rejoin South Sydney Rabbitohs in Australia, citing personal and family reasons for the move. His departure has reignited debates over English rugby’s struggles, with former England coach Sir Clive Woodward slamming the sport as being at an “all-time low.” Burgess, 29, made 21 appearances for Bath since his summer 2018 switch from league, scoring four tries while adapting to the union code. His selection for the World Cup squad, however, proved contentious. Despite making his England debut in August 2018, he was chosen ahead of experienced Northampton centre Luther Burrell, who had been a mainstay in the Six Nations. Burgess, who played blind-side flanker for Bath, was deployed at centre for the hosts’ opening World Cup clash against Wales, a decision criticized for prioritizing star power over positional expertise. England’s group-stage elimination—only the third time a host nation failed to reach the semifinals—fueled speculation over the team’s tactics and leadership. Woodward, who led England to World Cup glory in 2003, blamed the Rugby Football Union (RFU) for the sport’s current turmoil, absolving Burgess of responsibility. “We are the laughing stock of world rugby,” Woodward wrote in the *Daily Mail*, accusing the RFU of arrogance and complacency. He condemned the governing body’s self-congratulatory approach over the past four years, arguing that off-field mismanagement has directly harmed on-field success. “The saddest part is the players and fans have been let down,” he added. Bath head coach Mike Ford expressed regret over Burgess’s exit, acknowledging the player’s potential in union. “We hoped he would stay,” Ford said. “Given time, he could’ve been a great rugby union player. Unfortunately, for personal reasons, he is returning to Australia.” Burgess’s return to league marks a career shift back to the sport where he earned fame, including an NRL Premiership with Rabbitohs in 2014. As English rugby faces calls for reform, his departure underscores the challenges of integrating code-hopping stars into a struggling national team. With the RFU under scrutiny, the question remains whether structural changes can reverse the tide ahead of the next World Cup.

**Barr Reports Strong Profit Growth Amid Challenging Soft Drinks Market** Cumbernauld-based Barr has announced a 10% rise in pre-tax profit to £41.9 million for the year ending 25 January, alongside a 2.7% increase in total turnover to £260.9 million. The company attributed the success to robust performance across its core brands, including Irn Bru, Barr, Rubicon, and Strathmore, all of which outperformed the broader market. Despite the positive financial results, Barr cautioned that the UK soft drinks industry is grappling with price deflation, which could hinder growth for many firms. Roger White, chief executive, acknowledged the “difficult market conditions” but emphasized the company’s focus on sustainable, profitable expansion. “We have delivered an excellent financial performance..... whilst continuing to build the platform required for sustained long-term growth,” he stated. Strathmore, Barr’s water brand, saw a standout year, with sales in the stills segment surging over 20%. The growth was driven by the brand’s sponsorship of the Glasgow 2014 Commonwealth Games and the rising consumer demand for bottled water. Meanwhile, Irn Bru, Scotland’s iconic soft drink, achieved a 1.6% rise in invoiced sales. Its ice cream variant generated nearly £1 million in revenue, and the sugar-free version saw sales climb by more than 20%. **Mexican Tourists Killed in Egyptian Western Desert Ambush Amid Security Operations** CAIRO — At least two Mexican tourists and two Egyptians were killed, and ten others injured when four unauthorized vehicles carrying foreign visitors entered a restricted zone in Egypt’s Western Desert during a joint military-police operation, authorities said Monday. The incident, described by Egypt’s Interior Ministry as a “mistakenly dealt with” engagement, has triggered diplomatic concern and raised questions about security in a region plagued by militant activity. The vehicles entered the restricted area in Wahat, part of the Western Desert, on Sunday, a statement from the Egyptian ministry said. The area, which borders Libya and serves as a transit route for militants, was off-limits to foreign tourists, though the exact location of the clash was not disclosed. Egypt’s Tourism Ministry confirmed the tour company involved did not possess valid permits or notify authorities before the trip. A ministry spokesman, Rasha Azaz, told AP News that the lack of proper authorization left authorities unprepared for the group’s presence. Among the injured, five Mexican nationals were reported in stable condition after being treated at a local hospital. Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto condemned the incident, vowing to demand a “thorough investigation by the Egyptian government.” The Mexican Foreign Ministry confirmed at least two of its citizens died but is still verifying the identities of the remaining victims. Ambassador Jorge Alvarez Fuentes visited the hospital and provided support to the survivors, according to a ministry statement. **Blaenau Gwent Film Academy Launches to Cultivate Young Talent and Revitalize Local Culture** Tredegar, Wales — A new film academy aims to transform Blaenau Gwent into a thriving creative hub by equipping hundreds of young people with skills in scriptwriting, filming, and editing. Based at The Circle in Tredegar, the Blaenau Gwent Film Academy has been established through a partnership between Cymru Creations, Made in Tredegar, and the Workers’ Educational Association. The initiative, supported by local funding bodies, will offer training and hands-on experience to aspiring filmmakers, with its first production set to debut this summer. The academy’s founders, who have collaborated with local schools for four years, aim to bridge the gap between the area’s untapped talent and industry opportunities. Kevin Phillips, a key figure in the project, emphasized the region’s potential. “There are so many talented youngsters who want to work and pick up skills quickly,” he said. “In London or Cardiff, they’d get opportunities fast, but here, they’re struggling.” The academy’s curriculum is designed to empower participants with qualifications and practical experience, enabling them to pursue careers in media. The first production, a supernatural horror film titled *The Werewolf* or *Shadow Beyond the Gates*, will be filmed at a local Victorian manor house in August. Written by 29-year-old Leigh Jones—whose transition from office work to screenwriting was inspired by Stephen King—the film follows a group of teenagers lured into a deadly game by a werewolf. “The house and park are perfect for this eerie setting,” Jones explained. The project will employ local youth in roles ranging from acting to production, fostering community engagement. Beyond film, the academy will also mentor participants in musical theatre and performance, as seen with Iwan Smith, who aspires to a stage career. The initiative will expand into documentary projects, including “500 Photos for 500 People,” a Heritage Lottery Fund-funded program. Participants will research and film stories based on historical photos of the area, blending education with creative storytelling. Alan Terrell of Made in Tredegar, whose team previously produced the award-winning Welsh-Polish film *The Bench*, hailed the academy as a “life-changing opportunity” for the valleys. With ambitions to train up to 200 young people annually, the project underscores a commitment to nurturing local talent while celebrating Blaenau Gwent’s unique heritage. As Phillips noted, the academy’s success hinges on the “passion and ambition” of its participants—a testament to the region’s creative potential.

**Local Artists Secure £100,000 Grant to Revolutionize Floating Image Technology** Newton Stewart-based artists Chris Helson and Sarah Jackets are set to develop a commercial prototype for their groundbreaking invention, Help Me Obi, thanks to a £100,000 Smart:Scotland grant. The technology, originally conceived as an art project in 2008, has evolved into a versatile tool with potential applications across industries, from medical education to virtual conferencing. The duo’s project draws inspiration from the work of 19th-century physicist James Clerk Maxwell, who experimented with a zoetrope (a precursory animation device) by inserting lenses to create the illusion of floating images. Helson and Jackets have taken this concept further, engineering a system that stabilizes and controls light to produce vivid, three-dimensional visuals. Their breakthrough in 2014 marked a turning point, enabling the technology to move beyond abstract, flickering images to a refined, interactive format. The grant, secured with support from Business Gateway Dumfries and Galloway, has opened new avenues for the artists. “If we hadn’t gone to Business Gateway 18 months ago, I don’t think we’d have fully realized the scale of the opportunity,” said Helson. The organization’s adviser, Angus Robertson, helped the pair refine their business model, identify funding streams, and navigate intellectual property strategies. This guidance led to partnerships with Interface, Heriot-Watt University, and Scottish Enterprise, positioning Helson and Jackets Technology Ltd as a high-growth tech start-up. Helson envisions Help Me Obi transforming multiple sectors

**Judy Murray Urges Immediate Action to Grow Tennis in Scotland After Andy’s 500th Win** As Andy Murray reached a historic 500th career victory, his mother, Judy Murray, has called for urgent efforts to expand tennis in Scotland. Speaking at a “Tennis on the Road” initiative in Dumfries, she emphasized the need to capitalize on the sport’s growing popularity, citing the recent success of the Davis Cup match in Glasgow. “Tennis is at a massive, massive opportunity to grow in Scotland,” Murray said. “For five or six years now, we’ve had players like Andy and Jamie [Murray] dominating the global stage. Andy has been in the top five for seven years and holds Grand Slam titles, while Jamie has his own Grand Slam success. Their performances, especially in high-profile events like the GB-USA Davis Cup clash, have shown how passionate the public can be.” Murray stressed the importance of acting immediately to secure tennis’s future. “There’s no point in waiting for a legacy after the players are gone,” she said. “Andy is 27, still at his peak, but you never know when he might retire. When he’s gone, I want the game to be in a strong place for the long term.” Jamie Murray, a doubles specialist and 2007 Wimbledon mixed champion, has previously voiced concerns about the lack of a clear legacy plan in Scotland. He warned that failing to inspire the next generation could be a “tragedy,” as many young players are eager to follow in the brothers’ footsteps. During the two-day road show in Dumfries and Galloway, Murray worked with schools to train parents, teachers, and students in delivering tennis lessons. “We’re building a workforce of volunteers to create opportunities for everyone,” she said. “Whether you’re a child or an adult, there should be a way to start playing.” The initiative aims to embed tennis in local communities, ensuring accessibility and sustainability. Murray’s message is clear: while the Murray name commands attention, the future of Scottish tennis depends on collective action—starting *now*.

**Controversial Facebook Post Sparks Calls for Missouri Senator’s Resignation** Democratic Missouri state Senator Maria Chappelle-Nadal has faced widespread backlash after posting a Facebook comment expressing a wish for President Donald Trump’s assassination. The senator, representing St. Louis, initially responded to a comment on her page with the statement: “No. I will. I hope Trump is assassinated!” before deleting the post. The Secret Service confirmed it is investigating the remarks, as part of its mandate to examine all threats against the president. Chappelle-Nadal later told the *St. Louis Post-Dispatch* she did not intend the comment to reflect her views. “I didn’t mean what I put up. Absolutely not,” she said, adding that the post should have been deleted immediately. However, she ruled out resigning, insisting she would continue addressing the “frustration and anger” she claims many Americans feel. Her remarks drew swift condemnation from across the political spectrum. Democratic colleagues, including Senate Democratic Caucus leader Gina Walsh, called the post “toxic” and urged Chappelle-Nadal to step down. “She should be ashamed of herself for adding her voice to this toxic environment,” Walsh said. U.S. Senator Claire McCaskill, also a Democrat, called the comment “outrageous” and echoed calls for resignation. Republican Missouri Governor Eric Greitens similarly condemned the post, stating: “No one should encourage political violence. The senator should resign.” Chappelle-Nadal, however, defended her right to free speech. “I refuse to resign for exercising my First Amendment rights, even though what I said was wrong,” she said. The incident highlights tensions over how to balance political dissent with calls for accountability, particularly in polarized climates. The Secret Service’s ongoing investigation underscores the seriousness of threats against public figures, while Chappelle-Nadal’s defiance reflects broader debates over free speech and political expression. As the fallout continues, the senator remains a focal point of controversy in Missouri politics.

The former hairdresser, who has no fixed address, was also banned from driving for three years following the incident. On October 30, 2016, Walsh, then a mother of one, took the keys to her uncle’s Ford Mondeo during the night and drove off on the A6 near Luton while under the influence of wine, lager, and whisky. Prosecuting lawyer Rachel Law described how Walsh, who had been offered accommodation by her aunt and uncle days prior, sped northward toward Barton in a dangerous and reckless manner. Police attempted to stop her, but she overtook vehicles dangerously and accelerated further. By the time she reached Elstow, the car had two flat tyres and was emitting black smoke, leading to a crash after she misjudged a roundabout. Walsh was found unconscious, with deployed airbags, and later tested twice over the legal alcohol limit. In her defense, Jane Anderson noted that Walsh had led a “productive life” as a hairdresser and mother before being influenced by a partner who introduced her to drugs. “She is working hard to change her lifestyle,” Ms. Anderson told the court. Judge Philip Bartle QC condemned Walsh’s actions as “incomprehensible,” stressing the extreme danger she posed to herself and others. “It is nothing short of a miracle that no one was killed,” he said. The case highlights the consequences of drunk driving and the risks of unauthorized vehicle use. Walsh’s sentence reflects the court’s determination to hold her

**Royal County Down Climbs to Top of Golf Digest Global Ranking** Northern Ireland’s Royal County Down has dethroned New Jersey’s Pine Valley to claim the top spot in Golf Digest’s latest global rankings. Pine Valley fell to third, while Augusta National secured second place. Completing the top six are California’s Cypress Point, Scotland’s Royal Dornoch, and Australia’s Royal Melbourne. St Andrews and Muirfield in Scotland ranked seventh and eighth, respectively. Among Irish courses, Portmarnock and Royal Portrush occupied 25th and 27th positions, with Lahinch (65th) the only other Irish entry in the top 100. Royal County Down’s rise is attributed to its 2023 Irish Open hosting, which bolstered its global profile. The rankings, compiled from over 1,800 course evaluations, highlight the venue’s ascent from fourth last year to the top.

**Carnegie Mellon University Wins Landmark Patent Case Against Marvell, Jury Awards $1.17 Billion in Damages** *Verdict Could Be Tripled to $3.96 Billion, Rivaling U.S. Patent Award Records* A Pittsburgh jury has delivered a landmark ruling against semiconductor giant Marvell, ordering the company to pay Carnegie Mellon University $1.17 billion in damages for infringing two patented hard disk innovations. The verdict, which could escalate to as much as $3.96 billion if the judge applies a “wilful infringement” multiplier, threatens to reshape the semiconductor industry’s legal landscape and could rank among the largest patent awards in U.S. history. The dispute centered on technologies developed by a Carnegie Mellon professor and student to enhance hard disk drive precision at high speeds. The university alleged Marvell used these inventions in its chips from 2003 to 2012, selling 2.3 billion units incorporating the disputed technology. The jury rejected Marvell’s defense, which argued it never utilized the university’s patented methods and claimed the patents were invalid. The financial stakes are staggering. The $1.17 billion award alone is roughly 35% of Marvell’s current market capitalization of $3.33 billion, but if the judge deems the infringement “wilful,” the total could triple to $3.96 billion—a sum that would effectively erase the company’s stock value. **Poland-EU Dispute Escalates Over Judicial Reforms** The European Commission has warned Poland that it risks losing its voting rights in EU institutions if it proceeds with controversial judicial reforms, triggering a sharp rebuke from Warsaw, which accused the bloc of “blackmail.” The dispute centers on a proposed law mandating the retirement of all Supreme Court judges by 2020, a move the EU claims would severely undermine judicial independence. Despite Polish President Andrzej Duda vetoing two of the most contentious bills earlier this week, the ruling Law and Justice (PiS) party has vowed to push the reforms through, defying mass street protests and international pressure. Commission Vice-President Frans Timmermans reiterated that the laws would have a “very significant negative impact on the independence of the Polish judiciary” and announced immediate legal action, including a potential invocation of Article 7—a mechanism to suspend voting rights that requires unanimous EU approval. Hungary has pledged to support Poland, making the measure unlikely for now. Instead, the Commission has opted to sue Poland over alleged breaches of EU law, with a focus on judicial independence and gender discrimination, as the bills impose a gendered retirement age for judges. President Duda, a PiS ally, called for revisions to the vetoed laws but approved a third bill, declaring his support for a “wise reform” to overhaul the judiciary. Prime Minister Beata Szydło reiterated the government’s resolve, stating Poland would not “yield to pressure from the street and from abroad.” The parliament may now attempt to override the presidential veto or revise the bills to secure Duda’s approval. Poland has one month to respond to the Commission’s legal challenge, which could result in hefty fines from the European Court of Justice (ECJ). The ECJ has already ruled against Poland’s judicial reforms in previous cases, citing rule-of-law violations. A government spokesman dismissed EU criticisms as unfounded, asserting Poland’s sovereignty over its legal system. The crisis has deepened tensions between Warsaw and Brussels, with the EU accusing PiS of a coordinated effort to consolidate political control, while Poland frames the reforms as necessary to address systemic corruption. Public opposition remains strong, with protests continuing nationwide. As the standoff intensifies, the outcome will test the EU’s ability to enforce its rule-of-law principles and Poland’s defiance of external pressure. With no clear resolution in sight, the dispute underscores the fragility of EU unity and the challenges of balancing national sovereignty with collective governance.

**The Return of the Eurasian Lynx: From Extinction to Revival** The Eurasian lynx, once eradicated in Scotland over 1,000 years ago, has seen a remarkable comeback in parts of Europe. While the species vanished from the British Isles by around 500 A.D.—as noted by the Lynx UK Trust—populations endured in Scandinavia, the eastern Baltic, the Carpathian Mountains, and the Balkans. By the mid-20th century, lynx numbers in these regions had plummeted due to hunting and habitat loss, but recent conservation efforts have spurred their resurgence. As the third-largest predator in Europe after the brown bear and wolf, the lynx is distinguished by its iconic black ear tufts and elusive nature. These solitary hunters rely on stealth and explosive pounce tactics to ambush prey four times their size, delivering precise neck or snout bites to fell deer. Their efficiency as predators has earned them a fearsome reputation, though a centuries-old myth persists: the belief that lynx “suck blood.” This misconception, recorded in a 2011 study of Balkan lynx published in the *International Journal of Conservation*, stems from their preference for throat strikes during hunts. Though absent from Scotland for millennia, the lynx’s survival in continental Europe highlights its adaptability and resilience. Conservationists now monitor its recovery, raising questions about potential reintroduction efforts. Once a shadow in Britain’s forests, the lynx may yet reclaim its place in the wild.

**Cecafa in Crisis: Musonye Slams "Politics and Mediocrity" in Regional Football** In a scathing critique of regional football governance, Cecafa Secretary General Charles Musonye has accused Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and Rwanda of undermining the organization and stifling progress in East and Central African football. Since Gafe’s leadership, Cecafa has collapsed in organizing its flagship tournaments—the Club Championship and Senior Challenge Cup—leaving fans and stakeholders in limbo. “Dark clouds descended on Cecafa after 2015,” Musonye told the BBC. “There is a lot of politics creating confusion, and four countries are actively undermining progress. They cannot accept Gafe’s legitimate election and are sabotaging the organization.” Musonye accused the four nations of fostering a sense of superiority, insisting they treat themselves as “more equal than others.” He criticized their refusal to support Gafe’s leadership, despite the Sudanese president’s election in a process he described as “open and free.” “Cecafa is not my company,” he emphasized. “If they want to destroy it, let them proceed. It’s their organization, their baby.” The fallout has had dire consequences for the region’s football. Musonye pointed to poor administrative leadership as a root cause of the decline in team performances, including repeated failures to qualify for the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON). “Mediocrity in organization has crippled us,” he said. “While other nations flourish in AFCON, we stagnate because our leaders prioritize politics over progress.” Compounding the crisis, Musonye revealed that member associations—many of which rely on unpaid participation fees—routinely neglect financial obligations. “They expect to play for free, but this undermines the integrity of Cecafa,” he added. The secretary general’s remarks highlight a deepening rift between regional powers and smaller member states. If left unresolved, the crisis risks further eroding Cecafa’s influence and dimming the prospects of its national teams on the continental stage. As Musonye’s frustration mounts, the question remains: who will step up to save the organization—or let it crumble under the weight of its own divisions?

**German Politician Faces Charges Over Nazi-Era Slogan Tattoo** A German politician affiliated with the far-right National Democratic Party (NPD) has been charged under strict anti-Nazi laws after a photograph surfaced of him displaying a tattoo linked to a slogan from the Buchenwald concentration camp. While Zech has not publicly commented, the case reignites debates about far-right extremism in a country still grappling with its Nazi past. Zech’s case echoes that of artist Jonathan Meese, who was acquitted in 2013 after arguing his Nazi salutes were part of a performance art piece. Unlike Meese, Zech’s political affiliations amplify concerns about the resurgence of far-right violence. This follows recent clashes at migrant reception centers, with a senior German intelligence official recently telling the BBC that Germany’s asylum policies are fueling extremist sentiment. As the trial approaches, the case underscores the fragility of Germany’s postwar democratic values amid rising tensions over immigration and far-right activism.

**Miroslav Klose Retires from German National Team After Historic World Cup Legacy** Miroslav Klose, the Polish-born German striker, has announced his retirement from the German national team following a historic 13-year career capped by victory in the 2014 FIFA World Cup. At 36, the Lazio forward concluded his international journey with 71 goals in 137 appearances, cementing his place as Germany’s all-time leading scorer and surpassing Gerd Müller’s 40-year-old record in June 2014. Klose’s triumph in Brazil marked the pinnacle of his career. Scoring twice during the tournament, he notched 16 World Cup goals—a record that eclipsed Ronaldo’s previous mark of 15—to become the first player ever to score at four World Cup finals. “Winning the title in Brazil was a childhood dream come true,” Klose said in a statement, expressing pride in contributing to German football’s greatest success. The striker, who made his national team debut in 2001, also became only the third player to participate in four World Cups, alongside legends like Brazil’s Pelé and Germany’s Lothar Matthäus. Germany manager Joachim Löw praised Klose’s legacy, calling his decision to retire “irreversible” and lauding his reliability. “You can always count on Miro to keep his word,” Löw said, referencing Klose’s pivotal role in Germany’s World Cup campaign. The forward joins captain Philipp Lahm in exiting the squad post-tournament, signaling a new era for the national team. Born in Poland, Klose’s journey to football immortality includes 14 major trophies with clubs like Bayern Munich and Lazio. As he steps away from international play, his records and four World Cup appearances stand as a testament to a career that redefined excellence on football’s grandest stage.

Hasenhuttl emphasized the midfielder’s importance to the team, particularly as they prepare for European competition. “Everyone can see how important Naby is for our game,” he said. “We have very young players, and this season is a chance to grow in the Champions League together.” The coach also highlighted Keita’s renewed focus, noting the player’s energy and commitment in pre-season. “He is more focused and happier now than last year,” Hasenhuttl added. With Keita poised to lead Leipzig’s charge in their first Champions League campaign, the club has made it clear their prized asset is staying put.

**Bombardier Announces 130 Contract Job Cuts in Northern Ireland Amid Ongoing Challenges** Aerospace giant Bombardier has announced the layoff of up to 130 contract workers in Northern Ireland, marking the latest in a series of job reductions that have seen over 500 roles eliminated in just six months. The company described the cuts as “regrettable” but necessary to maintain competitiveness amid ongoing financial struggles. The affected positions belong to Bombardier’s “complementary labour force,” consisting of temporary and contract staff. The Belfast base, Northern Ireland’s largest Bombardier site, employs approximately 5,000 permanent workers and 1,000 temporary staff. The current cuts follow significant job reductions last year, including 300 temporary and 90 permanent roles. Unite, the trade union representing workers, condemned the move, calling it “another savage blow” to an already vulnerable workforce. Bombardier cited fluctuating demand and the need for “adjustments to staffing levels” as the primary drivers of the decision. A company statement noted that the complementary workforce had expanded by over 1,000 positions by mid-2014 but has since required reductions due to shifting customer needs. The firm’s challenges have been exacerbated by years of delays in developing its C Series aircraft—a project costing over $5 billion—and the suspension of a business jet initiative. The appointment of a new chief executive, Alain Bellemare, last week signals a fresh attempt to stabilize the company. Bellemare faces the urgent task of securing orders for the C Series to offset mounting costs and stabilize operations. Unite regional officer Davy Thompson criticized the lack of protections for agency workers, who comprise an increasing share of Northern Ireland’s labor force. “This announcement highlights the inadequacy of existing employment protections,” he said, urging Stormont politicians to act on job security measures, particularly in manufacturing. Thompson warned of a “real risk of de-skilling” in the sector without intervention. Bombardier’s cuts underscore broader industry pressures, with the company’s financial woes reflected in its shrinking Northern Ireland workforce. As the firm navigates leadership changes and operational restraints, workers and unions remain anxious about the long-term stability of one of the region’s key employers.

Wigan Warriors delivered a commanding performance at the DW Stadium, securing a 34-0 victory over Catalans Dragons with eight tries, a result that highlighted their home form despite ongoing struggles on the road. The reigning Grand Finalists, who lost last year’s title decider, showcased their intensity and precision to record their fifth consecutive home league win. Head coach Shaun Wane praised his side’s professionalism but acknowledged there is still room for improvement. “I’m not saying that in an arrogant way, I genuinely believe that we can play a lot better than we are doing,” Wane told BBC Radio Manchester after the match. While he admitted, “We’re not playing well,” he highlighted the team’s “very professional” display, offering rare commendations to his players. “I don’t give praise out that much to the players, but I’ve just given them lots as it was a really good, professional win.” Wigan’s inconsistent away record—just one point from their first five league games on the road—remains a concern. Their sole success away from home was a 24-24 draw at Widnes in the season opener. However, the club’s dominance at the DW Stadium has been a bright spot, with the team winning all five home fixtures so far. The victory also marks a key development for Wigan as Wales forward Ben Flower returns from a six-month ban. Flower, who was sent off in the Grand Final for striking Lance Hohaia, is set to join the squad for Thursday’s clash against Warrington. Wane confirmed: “I want Ben to play and he will be playing on Thursday. If there’s a middle that’s not up to standard then he’s going to miss out.” With Flower’s return and a strong home record, Wigan aim to build momentum ahead of a challenging season.

**Polaroid and GoPro Face Off Over Cube-Shaped Camera Design Patent** C&A Marketing, the company behind Polaroid cameras, has accused GoPro of infringing on a U.S. design patent for the Polaroid Cube, a compact, cube-shaped video camera released in 2014. The dispute centers on GoPro’s Hero 4 Session, launched months after the Polaroid Cube, which shares a similar form factor, including a lens on one face and a record button on another. C&A Marketing is seeking damages that could include all of GoPro’s profits from the Session model, alleging that its patented design elements—such as rounded edges, a recessed lens, and a single top-mounted button—were unlawfully replicated. Design patents, which protect aesthetic features rather than functional aspects, are often contentious in tech disputes. Chartered patent attorney Rob Jackson explained to the BBC that GoPro’s legal team is likely searching for “prior art”—publicly available designs predating Polaroid’s patent—to prove the Cube’s look wasn’t novel. “Just because a design is simple doesn’t mean it can’t be protected,” Jackson noted, but prior examples could weaken C&A’s case. C&A Marketing emphasized its investment in creating a “unique” product, arguing that GoPro’s Hero 4 Session mirrors key design elements. In a statement, the company said, “All important design elements” of the Cube were replicated in the Hero 4 Session. GoPro, however, denied infringement, asserting that the Hero 4 was developed independently and that its design lacks the specific features outlined in the Polaroid patent. The company added that the competitor’s patent does not cover the Session’s “overall design.” Both companies have launched cube-shaped cameras to cater to users seeking portable alternatives to bulkier action cameras. The outcome of this legal battle could set a precedent for design patent protections in the tech industry, particularly for minimalist aesthetics. As the case unfolds, it highlights the fine line between inspiration and infringement in innovation.

Guiseley sit 16th in the National League, seven points above the relegation zone with seven games remaining. Follow the latest football transfers on our dedicated page.

**Six Men Face Corruption Charges Over £245m HBOS Scandal** Southwark Crown Court heard this week that six individuals have pleaded not guilty to a sprawling corruption scheme linked to HBOS, now part of Lloyds Banking Group. The case centers on allegations that a web of former bankers, consultants, and accountants exploited vulnerable small businesses between 2003 and 2007, draining the bank of £245 million in bad loans and siphoning millions into personal accounts. At the heart of the scandal was Lynden Scourfield, a former HBOS manager in Reading responsible for overseeing the recovery of troubled small business customers across southern England. Prosecutors claim Scourfield, who is not on trial, used his position to force struggling businesses to take out additional loans “well past the point when any honest banker would have known the debt could never be repaid.” Instead of helping these firms recover, he allegedly steered them toward Quayside Corporate Services, a consultancy run by David Mills, a former banker and one of the accused. Mills, alongside his wife Alison, is accused of using Quayside to extract “huge consultancy fees” from the businesses. Over £28 million passed through the Millses’ personal accounts, prosecutors allege, while the defendants allegedly seized control of some firms to enrich themselves. The scheme, described by prosecutor Brian O’Neill QC as “callous,” left business owners facing “great financial loss and considerable personal trauma” as they lost livelihoods and life savings. Scourfield himself, it is claimed, reaped “huge rewards” for his role, including luxury holidays, cash, gifts, and relationships with “high-class escorts.” In turn, he facilitated the exploitation of HBOS’s lending practices, enabling Mills and others to profit. The court heard that Scourfield’s mismanagement directly led to the bank’s £245 million in losses. The six defendants—David and Alison Mills, Michael Bancroft (who co-ran Quayside), Jonathan Cohen and Tony Cartwright (accountants), and Mark Dobson (a former HBOS manager)—face six counts of conspiracy to corrupt, fraudulent trading, and concealing criminal property.
