**Cardiff Blues Fly-Half Rhys Patchell Faces Uncertain Future Amid Transfer Interest** Rhys Patchell, the 22-year-old Cardiff Blues fly-half, is set to make a pivotal decision on his future as his contract nears expiration at the end of the season. Linked with a move to Welsh rivals Scarlets, the twice-capped international has been a key figure in ongoing transfer speculation, with Blues director of rugby Danny Wilson confirming interest in the player from both Wales and abroad. Patchell, who earned his Wales debut in 2013, has been sidelined as a fly-half since the arrival of Gareth Anscombe at the Blues in 2014. Anscombe, whose national dual contract is 60% funded by the Welsh Rugby Union, secured a World Cup call-up as injury cover, starting at full-back during the 2015 tournament, while Patchell was omitted from Warren Gatland’s final squad. However, Anscombe’s recent ankle injury has shifted the dynamic, thrusting Patchell into the spotlight as the Blues’ first-choice fly-half for the 2016 Six Nations. Wilson acknowledged the Blues’ efforts to retain Patchell but emphasized the club’s need for players “who want to be here and play for Cardiff Blues.” He noted: “We’re in discussions with Rhys and others. He’ll make the appropriate decisions at the right time.” Scarlets coach Wayne Pivac offered no confirmation of a potential move but hinted at the Blues’ dilemma: “I understand he’s not going back to the Blues, and that’s disappointing for them.” Pivac’s remarks underscore the growing momentum around Patchell’s potential departure, though no formal offer has been made. For Wales, Patchell’s decision carries broader implications. His talent and versatility—playing both fly-half and full-back—make him a valuable asset, yet his development has been overshadowed by Anscombe’s emergence. As the 2016 Six Nations approaches, all eyes will be on how this high-stakes chapter unfolds for the promising young star.

**Northern Ireland Construction Firms Shift Focus to Great Britain Amid Local Sector Challenges** A new survey by the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) and Tughans reveals that Northern Ireland (NI) construction firms are increasingly seeking projects in Great Britain (GB) due to stagnant growth in the local market. The latest *RICS & Tughans Construction Market Survey* highlights that while NI’s construction sector saw modest workload increases in the final quarter of 2023, activity remains far below levels in other UK regions, driven by weak infrastructure development and limited recovery in non-housing sectors. Private housing was the sole bright spot, with a notable rise in activity. However, infrastructure workloads fell sharply in Q4, marking the ninth consecutive quarter of declining or flat demand. Jim Sammon, RICS Northern Ireland spokesperson, noted that while NI firms demonstrated competitiveness by securing work in Scotland and England—regions experiencing stronger construction growth—the reliance on external projects “hides the broader challenges at home.” Sammon emphasized that overall workloads in NI increased in all four quarters of 2023, but growth remained weak compared to UK peers. “The sector is recovering from a low base, yet the lack of momentum, particularly in infrastructure, is concerning,” he said. “Firms deserve more opportunities locally, especially in vital sectors like transport and utilities.” The survey underscores a persistent imbalance, with local firms leveraging their expertise abroad to offset domestic stagnation. While this reflects resilience, the call for greater investment in NI’s infrastructure projects grows louder, as businesses and policymakers seek to stimulate sustained growth within the region.

**Nick Jones Focuses Fully on Welsh Transport Role** Since 2007, Nick Jones has overseen licensing and regulation of buses, coaches, and goods vehicles. Previously juggling a part-time role covering the West Midlands, from October he will work exclusively in Wales, supported by three bilingual staff. Economy Secretary Ken Skates emphasized the move would enable “increased and more effective engagement” with the transport sector. He highlighted Welsh infrastructure projects, including the M4 upgrade around Newport and Metro proposals, as pivotal in addressing long-standing traffic challenges. The Welsh Government’s new funding, alongside Mr. Jones’s existing UK Department for Transport budget, aims to bolster progress in improving Wales’s transport network.

**Edublogs Outage Sparks Debate Over Hosting Rights and Copyright Enforcement** A one-hour blackout of the popular educational blogging platform Edublogs last week ignited a contentious debate over the responsibilities of hosting companies in copyright disputes. The outage followed a decision by ServerBeach, Edublogs’ hosting provider, to shut down the entire site after a copyright claim from Pearson, a major academic publisher. Pearson alleged that a 2007 blog post on Edublogs had been illegally sharing a copy of the Beck Hopelessness Scale, a psychological questionnaire it owns. ServerBeach, which hosts Edublogs, initially requested the removal of the content twice, claiming Edublogs ignored the demands. After automated systems detected the disputed blog entry still lingering in Edublogs’ internal cache—used to speed up page loading—ServerBeach took the drastic step of disabling the site entirely. Edublogs had already taken down the post publicly in late September following Pearson’s first notice, but the cached copy, invisible to users, triggered further action. In a statement to *Ars Technica*, ServerBeach defended its decision, stating it lacked the tools to remove individual blog content as a hosting provider. “We had no way to control or isolate the infringing material without affecting the entire platform,” the company said. Edublogs founder James Farmer, however, criticized the move as overly aggressive. In a post-dispute blog entry, he expressed surprise at ServerBeach’s “extreme reaction” and accused the firm of avoiding a simpler resolution, such as contacting Edublogs via the three phone numbers it possessed. The incident underscores the complexities of balancing copyright enforcement with the operational realities of hosting services. While ServerBeach acted under takedown policies designed to protect intellectual property, critics argue the outage disproportionately affected Edublogs’ community. The Beck Hopelessness Scale, a widely used academic tool, remains a point of contention, highlighting how even outdated content can reignite legal battles. As the dust settles, the episode raises questions about the need for clearer communication protocols between hosts, platform operators, and copyright claimants—especially when automated systems inadvertently resurrect archived content. For now, Edublogs has reinstated its service, but the fallout may prompt a reevaluation of how hosting firms handle such disputes.

**Teenager Shot in Liverpool – Police Den Gang Fight Claims** A 16-year-old boy has died after being shot in Vauxhall, Liverpool, with police dismissing claims that a gang-related confrontation involving quad bikes occurred at the scene. Lewis Dunne was found on a towpath near Burrows Court on Sunday evening and later succumbed to his injuries in hospital. A post-mortem examination confirmed he died from a single shotgun wound to the back. A 20-year-old man from Everton is currently in custody at a Merseyside police station for questioning. Detectives have ruled out rumors circulating in the community that an “arranged fight involving groups on quad bikes” took place. Detective Chief Inspector Tom Keaton stated: “There has been speculation about an organized confrontation, but we have no evidence to support this. We are still working to determine why Lewis was shot.” The inquiry has focused on establishing Lewis’s movements between 10:15 PM and 11:10 PM, the timeframe he was last seen leaving home to visit a local shop. Officers have recovered mobile phones, jackets, and other items from the canal near the towpath, which are being forensically analyzed. CCTV footage from the area is also under review. Lewis’s family and community have been left “devastated” by the tragedy. Described as a “vivacious young man who was very popular,” he is remembered for his warmth and engagement in local life. Det Ch Insp Keaton emphasized the bafflement of those close to him: “Friends and family are struggling to understand how this could happen.” Authorities have urged the public to share any information that could assist the investigation. A neighbor noted, “This area isn’t known for violence like this,” underscoring the shock of the incident. Police remain tight-lipped about the motive but reiterated their commitment to uncovering the truth. Updates will be shared as the probe progresses. Lewis’s death has sparked calls for increased safety measures in Vauxhall, as residents grapple with the loss of a young life cut short.

**Argentina Grapples with Record Heatwave and Power Crisis** Argentina is battling its worst heatwave in over a century, with temperatures in northern provinces like Santiago del Estero surpassing 45°C (113°F). Compounding the crisis, widespread power outages have crippled air-conditioning use, leaving residents to endure stifling heat with limited relief. Meteorologists have labeled the event the most severe since record-keeping began in 1906, triggering a public health emergency. In Santiago del Estero, 1,100 km (680 miles) north of Buenos Aires, hundreds have sought medical attention for heat-related illnesses. Doctors are urging people to stay indoors during peak temperatures, but the aging national power grid has failed to meet surging demand, plunging entire regions into darkness. Ice cream parlors and businesses have lost perishable stock due to the blackouts, while authorities blame the energy shortages on the unprecedented heat. However, the opposition accuses the government of mismanagement, citing a lack of infrastructure investment. Protests have erupted nationwide as frustration mounts. In Buenos Aires, some areas have faced power cuts for over two weeks, prompting residents to burn rubbish and tires on roads, worsening traffic and disrupting New Year’s travel. Mayor Mauricio Macri, a former ally of President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, criticized the federal government for failing to prioritize energy infrastructure. “The main responsibility lies with the federal government,” he said, stressing the need for a long-term investment plan. As temperatures persist and tensions rise, Argentina’s dual crisis of climate extremes and crumbling infrastructure underscores a political and humanitarian reckoning. With the heat showing no sign of abating, the nation braces for further challenges in the coming weeks.

**Wales Name Adjusted Side for Crucial Six Nations Clash Against Italy** Wales head coach Warren Gatland has made three changes to his starting XV for Saturday’s pivotal Six Nations clash against Italy in Rome, with injuries forcing alterations in the front row and at scrum-half. Rob Evans returns to the loose-head prop position for his first start in over a year, while Aaron Jarvis comes in at tight-head. The duo replaces the injured Samson Lee (Achilles) and Gethin Jenkins (hamstring), who suffered setbacks during Wales’ 23-16 victory over Ireland last weekend. With Richard Hibbard ruled out with a back injury, Gatland has bolstered his bench with Rhys Gill, Ken Owens, and Scott Andrews to cover front-row contingencies. Meanwhile, Scarlets’ scrum-half Gareth Davies earns his first start for Wales in nearly a decade, replacing the experienced Mike Phillips. Gatland emphasized the importance of the Italy match, stating, “Obviously it’s disappointing for Gethin and Samson, but Rob and Aaron stepped up well last weekend and we expect the same on Saturday.” He added that the team must deliver a commanding performance to set the tone for the remaining championship fixtures. Wales currently sit third in the table, with three wins but a points difference trailing Ireland and England. A win against Italy could position them to claim the title, but Gatland warned of the challenge ahead: “The first job will be to simply get the result.” Italy, who host Wales at 12:30 GMT, pose a threat through their scrum and line-out, areas Gatland

**Hamilton Prioritizes Preparation Over Fan Events Ahead of British Grand Prix** Lewis Hamilton has confirmed he skipped the Formula 1 event in central London this week to focus on preparation for the upcoming British Grand Prix, calling the race his “must-win” of the season. The Mercedes driver emphasized the importance of balancing championship ambitions with the pride of competing on home soil, stating, “The championship is the most important thing, but a very close second is your home grand prix.” The London event, held in Trafalgar Square and Whitehall, featured appearances by all 19 other drivers but was missed by Hamilton, who has been 20 points behind title rival Sebastian Vettel of Ferrari since finishing fourth in last Sunday’s Austrian Grand Prix. A gearbox penalty in Austria had initially placed Hamilton eighth on the grid, complicating his chances. The decision to forgo the event was made in advance, reflecting Hamilton’s focus on the high-stakes battle for the championship. “The intensity of the season is weighing heavily on everyone,” he said. “This is the closest battle I’ve ever had in a championship. It’s going to be the hardest to win, so you make sacrifices.” Hamilton, who has won the last three British Grands Prix, aims to tie the record of five wins held by legends Alain Prost and Jim Clark. “I want to win the British Grand Prix,” he said. “I have not won the last two races. The pleasure it would give me, you can’t measure that.” The race, held at Silverstone—the “home of motorsport”—attracts an electric atmosphere, with Hamilton crediting the passionate British fans for the event’s unique energy. “There’s no other race with this atmosphere,” he said. “You want to be the one who delivers for them. Look out and see the British flags—it’s no better feeling.” Hamilton also previewed the challenges of the 2017 season, citing the “spectacular” speed of the new cars and the physical demands they impose. “The g-force levels are going to be one up at each corner,” he said, predicting a tight contest between Mercedes, Ferrari, and Red Bull. Despite the pressure of the title race, Hamilton remains resolute. “I am happy with how I’ve performed,” he said. “The real fans know that when they come here, you have to do what’s right to make yourself the best prepared you can be.” With Silverstone’s blend of history and intensity, Hamilton is determined to turn his home race into a pivotal moment in his championship campaign.

**J.K. Rowling Unveils New ‘Magic in North America’ Series to Precede ‘Fantastic Beasts’ Film** British author J.K. Rowling has launched a new online series, *The History of Magic in North America*, via Pottermore, setting the stage for the release of her *Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them* film this November. The four-part series, beginning with the 14th to 17th centuries, explores lesser-known aspects of the magical world, including Indigenous legends, the Salem witch trials, and the development of American wizardry. Rowling reveals that North American wizards were aware of the continent long before non-magical “Muggles,” noting that the term for Muggles there differs from the British usage. The first instalment delves into the rich traditions of Native American magical communities, offering a nuanced perspective on their coexistence with enchanted creatures and early settlers. Subsequent chapters will introduce *Ilvermorny*, Rowling’s version of a North American Hogwarts, and the *Magical Congress of the United States of America* (MACUSA), the U.S. counterpart to the British Ministry of Magic. The *Fantastic Beasts* film, starring Eddie Redmayne as magizoologist Newt Scamander, adapts Rowling’s 2001 Hogwarts textbook. Newt’s adventures with magical creatures will be contextualized by the newly released series, which provides historical and cultural depth to the cinematic universe. Rowling, who wrote the screenplay, aims to expand the wizarding world beyond Europe, blending folklore and her own lore. With the film hitting theaters in November, fans are eager to immerse themselves in the newly unveiled North American magic system, setting the scene for an eight-film franchise. Rowling’s series not only enriches the *Fantastic Beasts* narrative but also underscores her dedication to crafting a globally diverse magical world.

**Sarkozy Faces Fallout Over Fukushima Visit Claim in Heated Election Rivalry** Former French President Nicolas Sarkozy has come under fire after admitting he never visited the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant in Japan, despite earlier claiming he did during an election rally. The controversy has intensified as the future of France’s nuclear power industry remains a central issue in the presidential race. The dispute began when Socialist candidate François Hollande challenged Sarkozy’s assertion that he had visited Fukushima in 2011. On I-tele, Sarkozy backtracked, stating, “I’m not an engineer, I don’t need to stick my nose in the situation at Fukushima.” He clarified he had traveled to Japan with his then-ecology minister, Nathalie Kosciusko-Morizet, to meet Japanese authorities and discuss the crisis but did not personally visit the plant. Hollande seized on the admission, accusing Sarkozy of fabricating the visit. “It’s the first time in the history of the Republic that an outgoing candidate has described a trip he never made,” he said, mocking Sarkozy’s tendency to “pioneer” falsehoods. The claim was corroborated by the World Nuclear Association, which confirmed no record of Sarkozy’s visit exists. The incident has reignited debate over France’s nuclear energy policy, a key election issue. The Socialists, led by Hollande, have pledged to reduce nuclear power’s share of electricity generation from 75% to 50% by 2025. In contrast, Sarkozy’s center-right UMP government defends nuclear energy as economically vital, citing job creation, exports, and its role as a reliable, low-carbon energy source. Sarkozy defended his original statement, arguing that linking Fukushima to France’s nuclear plants was “absurd.” He noted that the Fukushima disaster stemmed from a 42-meter tsunami that disabled cooling systems, not a nuclear failure. “To say as a result of Fukushima that you should shut Fessenheim [a French plant] in Alsace, that seemed to me a particularly remarkable absurdity,” he said. This is not the first time Sarkozy has faced scrutiny over past claims. In 2009, he posted a photo on Facebook purporting to show him chipping away at the Berlin Wall on November 9, 1989, the day it fell. The photographer later confirmed the image was taken the following day. As the election looms, the fallout underscores the challenges both candidates face in balancing energy policy with public trust. With voters closely watching their leaders’ credibility, Sarkozy’s admission risks further eroding his credibility, while Hollande’s relentless pursuit of the issue aims to frame his rival as dishonest. The debate over France’s nuclear future—and the political fallout from one disputed trip—will likely remain a focal point in the weeks ahead.

**Post Office Strike Escalates as Unions Warn of Further Industrial Action** Members of the Communication Workers Union (CWU) and Unite began a 24-hour strike at 03:00 GMT on Monday, marking the second major walkout in two months and signaling potential further disruption before Christmas. The action, affecting Crown Post Offices—typically larger high-street branches—has closed over 80 locations, though the Post Office emphasized that the majority of its 11,500-branch network remains open. Unions, however, warned that more strikes could follow if unresolved disputes over job security, pensions, and franchising plans persist. The walkout involved an estimated 3,000 workers across 300 branches, according to the unions, though exact turnout remains unconfirmed. A rally at Post Office headquarters in central London drew solidarity from striking staff, with Brian Scott, Unite’s union officer for the Post Office, vowing to escalate action if necessary. “We are hoping the Post Office sees sense and gets around the table, but they can’t reject everything we put forward,” Scott told the BBC. “It may well be that there has to be other action in the run-up to Christmas, but we are willing to talk.” The dispute centers on the Post Office’s strategy to restructure its operations, including the closure of the final salary pension scheme for Crown Post Office staff, job losses linked to branch relocations, and a plan to franchise Crown branches to private businesses. In 2016, the Post Office announced the transfer of up to 61 Crown branches to WH Smith stores, a move officials described as part of a 10-year cost-saving initiative to “safeguard the future of the network.” However, unions condemned the plan as a threat to jobs and community services. The CWU reported that the pension scheme’s closure could impact thousands of workers, with members voting overwhelmingly—83% in favor—during a strike ballot in August. Over 3,500 members participated, leading to the first 24-hour strike on 15 September and a second on 31 October. Dave Ward, CWU general secretary, called the current strike a reflection of public support for workers. “We are now calling upon the government and the company to bring all stakeholders together to thrash out a new future for the Post Office that is more than a glorified closure programme,” Ward said. The Post Office defended its plans, arguing that integrating post office services into retail outlets like WH Smith would extend opening hours and better meet customer needs. Kevin Gilliland

**Scrabble Gets a Modern Makeover: 6,500 New Words, Including Slang and Tech Terms, Added to Word List** The latest edition of the Collins Scrabble Word List has undergone its first major update since 2011, welcoming approximately 6,500 new words. Among the additions are slang terms popularized on social media and in text messages, such as *twerking*, *emoji*, *bezzy* (a shortcut for "buzzing"), and *ridic* (short for "ridiculous"). The update reflects the evolving landscape of modern English, incorporating language from Australia, Canada, South Africa, the UK, and the US into a unified list. High-scoring newcomers include *quinzhee*, an Inuit-style snow shelter, which earns 29 points—among the most valuable additions. Other notable entries span fashion (*shootie*, a trendy ankle-covering shoe), politics (*devo*, for devolution), and technology (*facetime*, *hashtag*, and *sexting*). Informal exclamations like *augh*, *blech*, *grr*, and *yeesh* also make the cut, capturing digital-age expressions. Helen Newstead, head of language content at Collins, highlighted the role of digital communication in shaping modern vocabulary. “Dictionaries have always included formal and informal English, but it used to be hard to find printed evidence of slang,” she explained. “Now, social media, tweets, blogs, and text messages provide a treasure trove of informal language that simply didn’t exist before.” The update not only enriches the game but also underscores how digital culture continues to redefine linguistic norms, ensuring Scrabble remains a dynamic reflection of contemporary speech.

A helicopter carrying two individuals for a U.S. reality TV shoot crashed into Argentina’s Potrerillos de Mendoza dam in western Mendoza province, authorities confirmed. The MTV show *The Challenge* was the intended destination, but neither of the deceased—identified as non-cast or crew members—were associated with the production, the network stated. The aircraft was found submerged at 60 meters (200 feet), complicating recovery efforts. Mendoza’s security minister, Gianni Vernier, told *Telam* that divers faced significant challenges retrieving the bodies. This marks the second fatal helicopter accident involving a reality TV production in Argentina this year. In March, a collision during filming of the French show *Dropped* in northwest Rioja province killed 10, including athletes Florence Arthaud, Camille Muffat, and Alexis Vastine. The crash there claimed five French nationals and two Argentine pilots. Both incidents highlight risks in high-stakes filming, with Mendoza’s rugged terrain and deep waters adding to the dangers. Investigations into the latest crash are underway, with no further details on the victims released to date.

**Sewer Collapse Closes Newport Road; Repairs Underway** A significant sewer collapse at Gibbs Road in Newport’s Beechwood area prompted emergency response by council officers at 04:30 BST on Wednesday. The road remains closed as Welsh Water investigates the incident. The utility firm confirmed the affected sewer is part of its network managing wastewater from homes and businesses. “We are working diligently to ensure the road can reopen as quickly as possible,” a Welsh Water spokesman stated. While repairs are ongoing, the company assured no disruption to wastewater services, though apologizing for the inconvenience caused. “This essential work requires temporary closures, and we regret any disruption to the community.” Residents are advised to seek alternative routes until further notice.

**Stolen 19th-Century Painting Recovered from Sotheby’s Auction** A long-lost painting, *Blanchisseuses souffrant des dents* (1869) by an unknown artist, was removed from a Sotheby’s auction in New York after French authorities confirmed its 1973 theft from the Havre Museum in Normandy. The work, stored by the Louvre since 1960, had been expected to sell for $350,000–$450,000 as part of an impressionist art sale. A museum staff member identified the piece in the auction catalogue, prompting French officials to alert Sotheby’s, which promptly withdrew it. “We contacted Sotheby’s, which agreed to withdraw it,” a French official told AFP. While the owner remains anonymous, authorities plan “friendly negotiations” to recover the artwork. U.S. and French police are investigating how the painting resurfaced, despite not being listed on Interpol’s stolen art database. The incident highlights challenges in tracking stolen cultural artifacts.

**Irish Government Survives Vote Amid Whistleblower Controversy** The Irish government faces mounting scrutiny over its handling of sex crime allegations against former Garda (police) whistleblower Maurice McCabe, as Sinn Féin accuses ministers of a cover-up. The controversy, which has dominated political discourse for over three years, began when McCabe and retired officer John Wilson exposed alleged corruption in the country’s driving license penalty points system. Sinn Féin has demanded transparency, asserting the government is concealing details of “who knew what and when.” However, Fianna Fáil, the main opposition party, will abstain from a crucial confidence vote, effectively allowing the government to avoid a no-confidence defeat. At the center of the storm is Garda commissioner Nóirín O’Sullivan, who has denied instructing journalists to report allegations of sexual misconduct against McCabe. Irish Labour Party leader Brendan Howlin leveled the accusation in the Dáil (parliament), which O’Sullivan swiftly refuted. **Copyright Alert System Ends After Mixed Success, Critics Question Effectiveness** The Copyright Alert System (CAS), a controversial "six strikes" initiative aimed at curbing online piracy, has officially concluded after four years of operation. Designed to notify internet subscribers whose accounts were suspected of being used to download copyrighted content illegally, the program was championed by copyright holders as a step toward reducing piracy. However, critics and experts have long questioned its real-world impact, arguing that there is little evidence to suggest it significantly lowered infringement rates. Launched in 2013, the CAS was a collaboration between major U.S. internet service providers (ISPs), including Comcast, Verizon, and AT&T, and content industry giants like the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and the Motion Picture Association of America (MPAA). The system operated on a tiered structure: the first two alerts were purely informational, aiming to educate users about copyright laws. Subsequent strikes escalated in severity, requiring responses from users by the third and fourth levels. The fifth and sixth strikes could result in punitive measures, such as throttling internet speeds or even terminating accounts—decisions left to the discretion of individual ISPs. According to the Center for Copyright Information (CCI), which administered the program, the CAS concluded after "extensive consumer education and engagement," with the organization claiming it demonstrated the potential for collaboration between content creators, ISPs, and consumer advocates. However, data on the program’s effectiveness remains sparse. Over the first 10 months of its operation, 1.3 million alerts were issued, but fewer than 3% of recipients received the sixth and final warning. Notably, there is no public record of any user being terminated for reaching six strikes, and the CCI did not specify how many accounts faced throttling. Supporters, including RIAA and MPAA, argued the system achieved its educational goals. Steven Fabrizio, a lawyer for the MPAA, stated that "a significant number of users who received alerts stopped engaging in piracy," though he acknowledged that "hard-core, repeat infringers" remained unaffected. However, piracy watchdogs and industry analysts painted a different picture. Ernesto van der Sar, editor of TorrentFreak, highlighted that the CAS failed to adapt to shifting trends in piracy. "A lot of copyright infringement has moved away from BitTorrent networks to streaming and direct downloading, which the system doesn’t address," he told the BBC. The MPAA itself cast doubt on the CAS’s efficacy in 2015 when the Internet Security Task Force, representing major film studios, criticized the program as insufficient. Citing the film *Expendables 3*, the task force noted it had been "illegally viewed more than 60 million times," despite CAS efforts.

He noted that retailers planned to maintain momentum with “attractive promotions” and “strong consumer value,” including mobile and online enhancements, through December. Online sales surged, with Comscore reporting $1.25 billion in digital transactions on Black Friday—a first-time $1 billion threshold—while Thanksgiving Day sales jumped 33% year-on-year. Cyber Monday is projected to add another $1.5 billion online, a 20% increase from 2022. Despite the blockbuster weekend, the NRF tempered expectations for the full holiday season, forecasting a 4.1% rise in retail sales for November and December, down from last year’s 5.6% growth. Analysts cited concerns about economic uncertainty, inflation, and potential spending shifts toward essentials rather than discretionary purchases. “This holiday season has already shattered weekend records, but challenges like rising prices and tighter budgets may dampen overall consumer optimism,” said one industry expert. As retailers navigate a mix of record-breaking days and lingering macroeconomic pressures, the final tally for the festive period remains a critical barometer for 2023’s economic health.

**Bournemouth Midfielder Extends Stay as Club Pushes Ahead with New Stadium Ambitions** Bournemouth midfielder Harry Arter has signed a new contract with the club, reinforcing his commitment to Eddie Howe’s side as they continue their Premier League journey. The project aims for completion by summer 2020, despite earlier concerns about a “significantly bigger stadium” in the area. The club’s vision underscores its ambitions to grow alongside its on-field success, with Arter’s commitment adding stability as the club navigates this transformative phase.

**Salford Players Clashes with Fans Over Safety Concerns After Super League Match** *By [Your Name], BBC Sport* A tense clash between Salford Red Devils players and fans erupted following Monday’s Super League match against Huddersfield Giants at the John Smith’s Stadium, with players intervening to protect children after a flare was thrown onto the pitch. The incident, described as the “worst I’ve seen” by England international Tom Briscoe, left families and officials deeply unsettled. The game, which Salford won 26-24, ended in chaos when a flare was launched from the Salford end, triggering panic among supporters. As players departed the field, two fans were ejected for pitch encroachment, with stewards scrambling to regain control. Salford winger Justin Carney and centre Junior S’au were photographed in heated exchanges with spectators after rushing into the stands to ensure the safety of their young children and other families. “Lives were in danger,” said Briscoe, whose wife and children were in the crowd. “The players were just protecting their families. It’s the natural thing to do. I would have done the same.” He described scenes of distress, with “women crying and kids walking out in shock,” adding that “newborn babies were being trampled.” Salford head coach Ian Watson confirmed that Carney’s children, along with those of team conditioner Greg Brown, were “a little bit shaken” by the ordeal. He praised the players’ actions, stating, “They prioritized safety over anything else.” Huddersfield Giants issued a statement clarifying that the flare-thrower and igniter were not identified. West Yorkshire Police, who were not in attendance but were called after full time, assisted stewards in managing the crowd. No criminal charges have been reported, and no arrests were made. Rugby Football League (RFL) chief executive Nigel Wood has announced a full investigation into the incident. “This doesn’t happen all the time,” Briscoe emphasized, urging lifelong bans for those responsible. “There’s no place in rugby league for this. Salford’s players, however, remain focused on the emotional impact. “The players’ wives were there with small children,” Briscoe said. “This is about protecting the heart of what rugby league is: family.” With tensions simmering post-match, the RFL faces mounting pressure to address safety protocols and fan behavior ahead of the season’s climax. As investigations proceed, the league reaffirmed its commitment to safeguarding matchday experiences for all attendees.

**Labor Pushes for Republic as Monarchy Debate Resurfaces Ahead of Election** The Australian Labor Party is set to reignite the long-dormant debate over Australia’s constitutional ties to the British monarchy, with a motion advocating for a republic likely to be debated at its national conference this week. The proposed resolution, backed by prominent members including Senator Lisa Singh and Shadow Parliamentary Secretary Matt Thistlethwaite, aims to revive the push for a democratic head of state, positioning the issue as a key policy differentiator from the ruling Coalition. The motion, slated for a vote on Friday, would formalize Labor’s commitment to a “roadmap” for transitioning Australia into a republic. While party policy documents have long referenced the need for such a shift, this marks the first time the issue has been elevated to a central campaign plank ahead of a looming election. If adopted, the party plans to appoint a ministerial portfolio dedicated to advancing the republic cause, underscoring its seriousness as a national priority. The timing is politically charged. Prime Minister Tony Abbott recently faced backlash for his decision to knight Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh, in January. Critics argued the move, which occurred during the late Duke’s final months, was anachronistic and at odds with Australia’s modern identity. Senator Singh, a key architect of the Labor motion, cited this controversy as evidence of the monarchy’s growing irrelevance. “Australia’s collective shock at the Prince Philip knighthood shows how alien the concept of knights and dames is to our contemporary identity,” she told the BBC. The debate resurfaces amid shifting public sentiment. A 2023 Fairfax poll revealed only 42% of Australians support becoming a republic, the lowest level in over three decades, with 51% deeming the move unnecessary. This follows a post-2019 dip in enthusiasm, partly linked to the high-profile visit of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. The 1999 referendum on a republic also faltered, partly due to division over the proposal for a parliamentary-appointed president. Yet Labor leaders argue the time is ripe for renewed efforts. Thistlethwaite emphasized that the motion reflects a desire to “recognize Australia’s independence, maturity, and unique identity.” He claimed the policy would set Labor apart from the government, asserting, “I think it’s pretty clear that you’re only going to see a republic come about through a Labor government.” The party’s roadmap could also align with speculation that Abbott may call an early election this year, though the Coalition has yet to respond. Support for a republic has waxed and waned since 1999. Former Governor-General Quentin Bryce briefly reignited the discussion in 2013 by publicly endorsing a republic, but recent years have seen little progress. Labor’s push, however, signals a deliberate strategy to frame the issue as both pragmatic and symbolic—a move toward self-determination

**Aberdeen Airport to Undergo Major Expansion in £20m Investment Boost** Aberdeen Airport is set for its most significant transformation since the current terminal opened in 1977, with a £20 million investment aimed at modernizing facilities to meet rising passenger demand. The £20m investment is part of a broader strategy to position Aberdeen as a key transport hub, supporting tourism, trade, and local employment. As the northeast navigates a shifting industrial landscape, the dual focus on infrastructure and workforce retraining signals a coordinated effort to secure long-term prosperity. For now, the airport’s transformation marks a landmark step forward.

**Brazil’s Meat Export Crisis Sparks Global Restrictions Amid Corruption Scandal** A major scandal has rocked Brazil’s meat industry, prompting some of its largest trade partners to suspend imports as evidence emerged of widespread safety violations. China, the European Union, Hong Kong, South Korea, and Chile have all imposed restrictions on Brazilian meat products following a massive federal police investigation, codenamed *Operation Weak Flesh*. The operation, launched after a two-year probe, uncovered evidence that meat-packing companies had been selling rotten and substandard products for years, undermining Brazil’s reputation as the world’s top red meat and poultry exporter. The crisis began with a sweeping federal police raid on Friday, targeting meat-processing plants across six Brazilian states. Over 1,000 officers searched 194 locations, leading to the arrest of more than 30 individuals, including company executives and government officials. The government suspended 30 senior civil servants suspected of turning a blind eye to unhygienic practices and corruption. Three plants were immediately closed, and 21 others are under investigation. President Michel Temer downplayed the scale of the issue, noting that only 21 of Brazil’s 4,837 inspected meat-processing units face allegations, with just six having exported products in the past 60 days. Despite Temer’s efforts to reassure international markets—including a diplomatic dinner at a steak house over the weekend—the damage has been significant. China, Brazil’s largest meat buyer, halted imports from implicated companies, while the EU announced it would also cease purchases from those under scrutiny. Hong Kong’s Centre for Food Safety suspended frozen and chilled meat and poultry imports “in view of the questionable quality of Brazilian products.” Together, these markets accounted for nearly a third of Brazil’s meat exports in 2016, according to *O Globo* newspaper, highlighting the economic stakes. Brazil’s meat industry, a cornerstone of its economy, now faces a credibility crisis. Temer reiterated the government’s confidence in the sector, stating, “The Brazilian government reiterates its confidence in the quality of a national product that has won over consumers and obtained the approval of the most rigorous markets.” However, the scandal has exposed systemic flaws, including regulatory failures and corruption, which investigators allege enabled unsafe practices for years. The fallout underscores the challenges Brazil faces in balancing economic growth with food safety and transparency. As investigations continue and global demand for its exports wavers, the government’s ability to restore trust will be critical in mitigating long-term damage to its vital agribusiness sector.

**Rangers Confirm Acceptance of Warburton’s Resignation Amid Legal Dispute** Rangers Football Club announced on Friday that it had accepted the resignations of manager Mark Warburton, assistant David Weir, and head of recruitment Frank McParland. Rangers’ statement did not clarify how Warburton’s contract, which runs until 2019, will be affected by the resignation. **FDA Announces Policy to Curb Nicotine Levels in Tobacco Products to Reduce Addiction and Deaths** The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) unveiled a groundbreaking policy on Friday aimed at reducing nicotine levels in tobacco products to curb addiction and save lives. The initiative, which seeks to make cigarettes “minimally addictive,” targets one of the leading causes of preventable death in the U.S., where tobacco use is responsible for 480,000 annual deaths and $300 billion in medical costs. The policy, which applies to traditional cigarettes and e-cigarettes, drew an immediate reaction from Wall Street. Shares in major tobacco firms plummeted, with Altria (owner of Philip Morris) losing up to 17%, British American Tobacco (BAT) dropping 11%, and Philip Morris shares falling 7% before partial recoveries. FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb emphasized that nicotine addiction is central to tobacco’s deadly toll, stating, “The only legal consumer product that kills half of long-term users when used as intended is cigarettes.” Tobacco companies, including BAT, have framed the move as an opportunity for industry innovation. BAT’s U.S. subsidiary, Reynolds American Inc., pledged to drive a “transformation” in tobacco, promoting harm-reduction products like heated tobacco or nicotine pouches. A BAT spokesperson noted, “We believe future success will require transformative products and shifting the conversation about tobacco harm reduction.” The FDA also announced plans to address flavored tobacco products, including menthol, through a public consultation period. This dialogue will shape a final policy recommendation, which could expand restrictions to all nicotine delivery systems. The agency stressed that reducing addiction will require ongoing research and collaboration, with e-cigarettes—often marketed with appealing flavors—falling under the same regulatory umbrella. Public health advocates hailed the move as a critical step toward reducing smoking-related illnesses, though opponents warn of potential black-market risks. The policy, if finalized, could mark a historic shift in tobacco control, prioritizing long-term health over industry profits. As the FDA initiates its public dialogue, the tobacco sector faces an uncertain future, balancing compliance with innovation in a rapidly evolving regulatory landscape.

**Tributes Paid to South Yorkshire Officer Killed in Car Crash** South Yorkshire Police Constable Hassan Ali, 44, has died in hospital nine days after being struck by a car while walking in Sheffield on January 28. The incident occurred on Staniforth Road, Darnall, when a blue Vauxhall Corsa hit him. Last month, the watchdog announced it was investigating 10 officers from the force over failures in handling child sexual exploitation cases. PC Ali, a neighborhood officer based in Rotherham, was described by Chief Constable David Crompton as a “well-liked officer” whose death has left colleagues “devastated.” Crompton added: “All of our thoughts are with Hassan’s family at this incredibly difficult time.” The collision has raised questions about road safety, with police emphasizing the need for public assistance to piece together the circumstances of the crash. While no criminal charges have been filed, inquiries into the IPCC’s ongoing investigations and the broader Rotherham scandal continue to dominate discussions about accountability within the force. PC Ali’s death underscores the complex challenges faced by South Yorkshire Police, balancing public duty with the weight of historic failures. Colleagues and community members are mourning the loss of a dedicated officer as the force grapples with its troubled legacy.

**Horsey McHorseface Joins the Ranks of Quirky Boaty McBoatface Tributes** A thoroughbred named *Horsey McHorseface* has become the latest nod to the internet-fueled campaign to name a British polar research ship *Boaty McBoatface*. **Deaf Swimmer Completes Historic English Channel Crossing** On Sunday, 17 July, Welshman 48-year-old Neil Rees, a former member of Great Britain’s deaf swimming team in the 1990s, achieved a remarkable milestone by becoming the first profoundly deaf athlete to swim the English Channel. The 15-hour marathon, which began at Semphire Hoe beach near Dover, concluded at Sangatte beach in France at 11:30 BST. Rees, who is profoundly deaf, faced formidable challenges during the crossing. After a smooth start, he encountered treacherous conditions in French waters: 23-knot winds (approximately 26 mph) and waves towering 2.5–5 meters disrupted his strokes, testing his endurance and focus. Despite these obstacles, Rees persisted, driven by a message he hopes will inspire others: “Don’t let your deafness stop you from doing what you really want to do. There are no barriers if you really want it.” The moment of triumph came when Rees felt sand slip through his fingers—proof he had reached France. “It was a tough swim, but when I felt the sand, I knew I’d made it,” he said. “Relief washed over me, alongside thoughts of my family, friends, and those no longer with us. I wondered what they’d say about this.” Supported by the boat *Louise Jane*, Rees raised over £6,000 for the current Great Britain Deaf Swimming team. The funds aim to assist athletes, many of whom lack financial support, in competing at the 2017 Deaflympics. Rees emphasized the importance of adaptation, noting that technology and shifting attitudes can empower individuals with disabilities. “There are ways to improvise or adapt,” he said, underscoring the potential for innovation to overcome limitations. His journey serves as a testament to resilience, proving that physical challenges need not define one’s limits. As he urged others to pursue their passions, Rees’ achievement stands as both a personal victory and a rallying cry for inclusivity in sport. *Inspired to take up swimming? **Presiding Officer to Welcome Scotland’s Iconic Tapestry at Parliament** Presiding Officer Tricia Marwick will formally receive *The Great Tapestry of Scotland*, a monumental 143-meter-long artwork chronicling the nation’s history, during a ceremony at the Scottish Parliament. Marwick will also invite people nationwide to contribute to a new “People’s Panel,” a vibrant tribute to the parliament building and its connection to the tapestry. The event will feature renowned tapestry artist Andrew Crummy, author Alexander McCall-Smith, and historian Alistair Moffat. The tapestry, stitched over 50,000 hours by 1,000 volunteers, spans 160 panels—from the Battle of Bannockburn to the 1999 reconvening of Scotland’s parliament. Outstripping the Bayeux Tapestry by 70 meters, it stands as the world’s longest embroidered artwork. The charitable trust overseeing the tapestry will display it at the parliament until September 13, inviting the public to engage with its legacy. Marwick emphasized the People’s Panel as a chance for communities to “weave their stories into Scotland’s national narrative,” ensuring the tapestry remains a living testament to the nation’s shared history.

**RMT Union Strikes Set to Disrupt UK Rail Network Amid Government Crackdown on Industrial Action** Rail services across the UK face widespread disruption in July as the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union escalates its campaign against Southern Rail, Northern Rail, First Great Western, and London Underground. The dispute centers on fears of job cuts linked to the introduction of Hitachi Inter-City trains from 2017, as well as disputes over staff roles and responsibilities. Northern Rail staff, meanwhile, have also voted 4-1 to strike, citing concerns over the elimination of permanent posts, the replacement of full-time roles with zero-hour contracts via a private security firm, and cuts to station booking offices. The RMT accused Northern Rail of failing to commit to preventing compulsory redundancies beyond its current franchise, which expires in February 2016

**South Korea Halts Operations at Kaesong Industrial Complex Amid Escalating Tensions** South Korea announced the immediate suspension of all operations at the Kaesong Industrial Complex, a cross-border economic zone in North Korea, citing concerns that Pyongyang is diverting revenue to fund its nuclear and missile programs. The decision, unveiled on Tuesday, marks a significant escalation in tensions between the two Koreas, with Seoul accusing the North of exploiting joint projects for military development. The Kaesong complex, one of the last major symbols of inter-Korean cooperation, has long been a critical source of income for North Korea. South Korea’s Unification Minister Hong Yong-pyo stated, “All our support and efforts..... were taken advantage of by the North to develop its nuclear weapons and missile programmes.” The move follows North Korea’s January 6 nuclear test and a February rocket launch, which South Korea, the U.S., and Japan condemned as a covert missile test. Japan responded by imposing sanctions, including a ban on North Korean vessels entering its ports and restrictions on ships from other countries that have visited Pyongyang. The U.S. also warned that North Korea may soon possess sufficient plutonium for multiple nuclear warheads. Amid these developments, unconfirmed reports surfaced that North Korea executed its military chief, Ri Yong-gil, on corruption charges. South Korean state media cited unnamed sources, while Reuters reported the claim without disclosing its source. Pyongyang has not verified the report, leaving details unclear. The Kaesong shutdown reflects a hardening stance by Seoul amid deepening regional security threats. With inter-Korean relations at their lowest in years, the move underscores the global community’s efforts to isolate North Korea over its nuclear ambitions.

**New Scottish Bill Aims to Ban Smoking in Cars with Children, Proposed £100 Fines** By [Your Name], March 2024 A groundbreaking bill to protect children from second-hand smoke in vehicles has taken a major step toward becoming law, with Scottish politicians and health advocates rallying behind the proposal. Introduced by Liberal Democrat MSP Jim Hume, the *Smoking Prohibition (Children in Motor Vehicles) (Scotland) Bill* would impose a £100 fine on drivers who allow smoking in cars with minors under 18 present. **Reserve Bank of India Cuts Repo Rate to 6.25% in First Move Under New Governor Urjit Patel** The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reduced its benchmark repo rate to 6.25% from 6.50% on Tuesday, marking the first interest rate decision under Governor Urjit Patel since he assumed office in September. Patel’s appearance before the media, however, was notably shorter than his predecessor’s. He fielded only five questions, a stark contrast to Rajan’s detailed and engaging interactions. Observers interpreted the brevity as a deliberate effort to maintain a low profile, a departure from the transparency and public outreach Rajan championed. “This signals a more cautious approach to communication,” said Abheek Barua, chief economist at HDFC Bank. “But the policy direction seems aligned with market expectations.” The MPC’s dual mandate—“maintaining price stability while supporting growth”—is now central to India’s economic strategy. **Celtic’s Unbeaten Domestic Streak Sets Stage for Fierce Old Firm Clash** Celtic enter Sunday’s Scottish Cup semi-final against Rangers with an unblemished domestic record this season, but ex-Rangers striker Nicklas Lovenkrands insists the Ibrox side have more than just pride at stake. In 2015, four secular bloggers—all named in a 2013 Islamist list of 84 “atheist bloggers”—were also murdered with machetes. Victims now include academics, Shia and Sufi Muslims, Ahmadi Muslims, Christians, and Hindus, with assailants often wielding knives. The pattern of violence has sparked debate over the perpetrators. While groups like IS and Ansar al-Islam claim responsibility, Bangladeshi officials frequently dismiss these assertions, blaming local extremists or political opposition instead. However, few attacks have led to convictions, and the government faces criticism for failing to protect vulnerable communities. A university professor, whose family described him as a devout believer in God, was among recent victims, underscoring the widening scope of threats. Human rights advocates warn that the growing diversity of targets—spanning religious, ideological, and sexual orientations—reflects a broader campaign of intimidation. As Bangladesh’s government grapples with maintaining stability, its refusal to acknowledge foreign extremist ties and lack of progress in prosecuting attackers risk fueling further unrest. For minorities and dissenters, the message remains chilling: speak out, and you may pay the ultimate price.

**Census Aims to Shed Light on Rohingya Plight in Bangladesh** Bangladesh has launched a comprehensive census to better understand the socio-economic conditions of the Rohingya, an ethnic Muslim minority fleeing persecution in Myanmar. Over half a million Rohingyas live in the country without authorization, many stateless and vulnerable to trafficking. The census, conducted with the International Organization for Migration (IOM), involves house-to-house surveys and is expected to last weeks. Organizers hope to gather critical data to address the community’s dire needs, as most live in poverty or in two overcrowded refugee camps. The Rohingyas, who claim ancestral ties to Arab traders in the region for generations, are denied citizenship in Myanmar, where successive governments since the 1970s have imposed harsh policies. Myanmar officials dismiss them as “Bengali migrants,” a stance that has justified systemic repression. Basic rights are restricted, and in 2012, violent attacks erupted following the gang rape of a Buddhist woman, targeting Rohingya communities. Many fled to Bangladesh, only to face further hardship. In 2015, tens of thousands of Rohingyas were stranded at sea as neighboring countries refused entry, underscoring their limbo status. The latest census marks the first large-scale effort to document their situation, as previous assessments relied on limited research. Experts warn that without accurate data, addressing issues like poverty and human trafficking remains challenging. The Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK highlights decades of persecution, including denied services and movement. As Bangladesh seeks clarity through this initiative, advocates stress the urgency of international support to protect a community long labeled “unwanted.” The census, they argue, is a vital step toward acknowledging the Rohingyas’ plight and securing their rights.

**A Lifetime of Reporting: The Extraordinary Journey of Mrs. Hollingworth** In August 1939, as Europe teetered on the brink of war, journalist Mrs. Hollingworth unknowingly captured one of history’s most consequential scoops. Crossing the border from Poland to Germany, she observed a surge of military vehicles and intense activity along the roads, a clear precursor to the German invasion of Poland. Her report for the *Daily Telegraph* on August 29, 1939, detailed the eerie scene: “Everywhere I saw signs of the most intense military activity. In the two miles between Hindenburg and Gleiwitz I was passed by 65 military despatch riders on motorcycles. The only cars to be seen were those belonging to the military.” This moment marked the start of a legendary career. Born on October 10, 1911—the same day Sun Yat-Sen helped overthrow China’s Qing dynasty—Hollingworth’s life seemed intertwined with global upheaval. Over decades, she reported on pivotal events, from the Vietnam War and Algeria’s struggle for independence to the decline of British colonial rule in Aden. She interviewed Iran’s Shah and witnessed Chairman Mao Zedong’s final days in Beijing. Notably, she maintained ties with British spies Donald McLean and Kim Philby after their defection to the USSR, offering a rare journalist’s perspective into Cold War intrigue. When asked why she became a reporter, Hollingworth simply replied, “Because I just enjoyed it, nothing else.” Her passion for storytelling and commitment to truth defined her work. Even in her later years, she remained engaged with the world, tuning into the BBC World Service hourly. At 112, Mrs. Hollingworth’s legacy endures—a testament to a career that bridged continents, conflicts, and centuries. Her life reminds us that curiosity and courage can illuminate history’s darkest moments.

The findings underscore a growing concern over the enforcement of hygiene practices within the healthcare sector.

**Rea Clinches Double Win at Italian Circuit, Extends Dominance in WorldSBK** Northern Irish rider Jonathan Rea claimed his 10th career double victory in the World Superbike Championship after securing a commanding triumph at the Misano World Circuit on Sunday. The Kawasaki Racing Team rider outpaced teammate Tom Sykes by 2.96 seconds in the second race, following a nail-biting 0.09-second margin win in Saturday’s opener. His Kawasaki teammate Sykes, who finished second for the second consecutive day, remains a key contender, having secured four wins this season and both races at last month’s Donington Park round. Italian rider Davide Giugliano (Aruba Italia Racing) claimed third place in the Sunday race, while Huddersfield’s Chaz Davies crashed out on lap two, a stark contrast to his earlier threat in race one, where he forced a last-corner showdown with Rea before contact with Michael van der Mark. Rea’s 16 podium finishes from 16 starts this season have stretched his championship lead, a testament to his consistency since his 2009 Misano debut. With five wins in the opening eight races this year, he is now just 14 victories shy of the all-time WorldSBK record. The championship heads to Laguna Seca, USA, for the next round on July 9–10, followed by an eight-week break before resuming in Germany, France, and Spain, concluding in Qatar on October 29–30. With the title race heating up, Rea’s double win at Misano reaffirms his status as the series’ dominant force.

George passed away peacefully surrounded by loved ones; one month before his eighth birthday.”* Born the runt of a litter of 13 puppies, George defied his small start, growing to an astonishing 43 inches tall from paw to shoulder and weighing over 111kg (17.5 stone). In 2010, he was named the *tallest living dog* and *tallest dog ever* by Guinness World Records, surpassing his rival Titan, a Great Dane from California, by three-quarters of an inch. The achievement earned him a place on shows like the *Oprah Winfrey Show* and *Good Morning America*, as well as his own website and social media accounts. George’s colossal size necessitated extraordinary accommodations. On a 2010 media trip to Chicago, he was allotted three airline seats. He consumed 50kg of food monthly and slept in a custom queen-sized bed. His online presence—boasting over 53,000 Facebook followers—highlighted his celebrity status as a beloved pet and symbol of gentle giant breeds. Nasser described George as a “gentle giant” who brought joy to countless people. The dog’s legacy includes raising awareness for large-breed health challenges and inspiring admiration for his remarkable life. Tributes from fans have poured in, celebrating his unique journey from a small puppy to an international icon. George’s passing marks the end of an era for dog lovers worldwide, but his story of resilience and record-breaking stature will endure.

The revisions aim to expand law enforcement and intelligence agency capabilities while addressing concerns over privacy safeguards. The changes, which build on the controversial draft Investigatory Powers Act, include new provisions on internet monitoring, hacking, and data handling, sparking renewed debates over the balance between national security and civil liberties. **Expanded Internet Monitoring Powers** One of the most contentious updates allows public authorities to apply for access to individuals’ “internet connection records”—detailed logs of websites, apps, and social media platforms accessed. A newly added clause broadens the scope of these requests to include investigations into serious crimes such as human trafficking. For instance, police could examine web browsing history to determine if a suspect booked airline tickets, transferred funds, or searched for specific locations. This marks a shift from the original bill, which lacked explicit mention of such investigative applications. **Urgent Hacking Warrants for Emergencies** The revised code introduces “urgent equipment interference warrants,” permitting police and intelligence agencies to hack smartphones or computers in real-time. Previously, hacking required pre-approved warrants. Now, authorities may bypass this process if an “imminent threat to life or serious harm” is identified—such as a kidnapping or the disappearance of a vulnerable person. The victories have set the tone for their campaign, with manager Alan Forsyth praising both offensive firepower and defensive resilience. “We’ve scored a lot of goals, but defensively it’s great credit to the boys at the back that we’re holding out,” Forsyth told BBC Scotland. With six points from six in the group stage, Scotland is virtually guaranteed a top-two finish to advance to round two. Meanwhile, his brother David, who plays for Qui Vive in the Netherlands, has set his sights higher. The Forsyth siblings both emphasized the historic opportunity to qualify for the 2018 World Cup in India, dependent on a strong World League round two in March 2017. “For Scotland alone the World Cup is the biggest competition and it would be a massive achievement to get there,” David told BBC Scotland. **Flash Floods Wreak Havoc Across Texas and Mexico** Hurricane Patricia, once the most powerful storm ever recorded in the Americas, unleashed chaos after triggering flash floods in Mexico and Texas, though its intensity rapidly diminished over rugged terrain. While damage in Mexico was less severe than feared—with no reported fatalities—floods damaged homes and disrupted utilities in sparsely populated Costa Alegre. Authorities expressed relief but noted ongoing recovery efforts. In the U.S., Patricia’s remnants merged with a separate storm system, deluging Texas with over a month’s worth of rain in some areas. Houston Mayor Annise Parker urged residents to avoid roads at night, as several motorists were stranded in rising waters. The town of Powell, 60 miles south of Dallas, bore the brunt of the deluge, with 20 inches of rain reported. A freight train derailed near Corsicana on Saturday when tracks were washed away, but both crew members swam to safety. Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport canceled flights due to flooding. The storm also impacted the U.S. Grand Prix, forcing disruptions at the Circuit of the Americas near Austin. In San Antonio, a man was swept into a drainage ditch and declared missing, prompting search efforts. Flood warnings spanned eight southeast Texas counties, with meteorologists predicting rain would shift toward Louisiana, Mississippi, and Georgia by Sunday. Though Patricia weakened swiftly after hitting Mexico, its merged system underscored the unpredictability of tropical systems. Officials remain vigilant as recovery operations continue, balancing relief at minimal loss of life with the challenges of extensive flooding and infrastructure damage.

**Lewis and Stars to Bear Muhammad Ali’s Final Journey** The funeral of boxing legend Muhammad Ali, who died aged 74 in Phoenix, Arizona, last Friday, will be held in his hometown of Louisville, Kentucky. Among the pallbearers is Lennox Lewis, the London-born former world heavyweight champion, 50, who became undisputed champion in 1999. Lewis expressed profound honor at carrying Ali, his hero, to his final resting place. “Ali transformed the world of sport and used it to transform the world,” he said, reflecting on the influence Ali had on his career and life. Other pallbearers include Jerry Ellis, brother of Ali’s former sparring partner Jimmy Ellis; Ali’s cousins John Grady and Jan Wadell; nephew Ibn Ali; former brother-in-law Komawi Ali; and family friend John Ramsey. The service, starting at 19:00 BST, will be open to the public and live-streamed online. Global leaders, celebrities, and dignitaries are expected to attend, paying tribute to the three-time world champion and civil rights icon. Ali, who retired in 1981 after battling Parkinson’s disease, left an indelible mark on sports and society. His funeral, a blend of private reverence and public celebration, honors a life of triumph, activism, and unyielding charisma. As tributes pour in from around the world, the event underscores the enduring legacy of a man who transcended boxing to become a global symbol of resilience and grace. **Obituary: Muhammad Ali | Muhammad Ali – in his own words | World Pays Tribute to Boxing Legend**

**Emma Stone and Sandra Bullock Lead Forbes’ Highest-Paid Actresses List** Forbes has unveiled its 2016 rankings of the world’s highest-paid actresses, with **Emma Stone** claiming the top spot for the second consecutive year. The Oscar-winning star earned an estimated **$46m (£34.9m)** before tax in the 12 months to June 2016, driven by her roles in *Joy* and the final *Hunger Games* film, *Mockingjay: Part 2*. **Melissa McCarthy** rose to second place with **$33m (£25m)**, buoyed by her starring roles in the all-female *Ghostbusters* reboot and the box office hit *The Boss*, which topped the US charts. McCarthy now ranks as the world’s second-highest-paid actress. Scarlett Johansson, who held the top spot last year, slipped to third with earnings of **$25m (£19m)**. Her filmography included *Captain America: Civil War*, *The Jungle Book*, and *Hail, Caesar!*. Rounding out the top five were Jennifer Aniston (*Friends* star, fourth with $21m) and China’s Fan Bingbing (fifth with $17m). The list also welcomed Bollywood actress **Deepika Padukone**, who earned **$10m (£7.6m)** to secure 10th place. While her film roles in India generate lower pay than Hollywood counterparts, Padukone’s lucrative endorsements bolster her income. Other top-10 stars included **Charlize Theron**, **Amy Adams**, **Julia Roberts**, and **Mila Kunis**. Forbes noted that the actresses’ earnings reflect both global box office success and commercial endorsements. A separate list of the highest-paid male actors will be released this week. *Follow the latest updates on @BBCNewsEnts, on Instagram, or email entertainment.news@bbc.co.uk for story suggestions.*

**Delek Completes $518M Takeover of Ithaca Energy, Expanding UK North Sea Presence** Herzeliya, Israel — Delek Group, Israel’s leading integrated energy company, has finalized a £518 million ($658M) equity acquisition of Ithaca Energy, a Toronto-listed firm headquartered in Scotland and active in the UK’s offshore oil and gas sector. The all-cash deal, valued at £1 billion ($1.26B) including debt, marks a significant strategic move for Delek to bolster its North Sea operations. The transaction, announced earlier this month, offers Canadian $1.95 per share for Ithaca, a 12% premium over its closing price on February 3 and a stark increase from the 40% surge in Ithaca’s share price over the past two months. Ithaca’s shares rose another 10% following the deal’s confirmation. The acquisition coincides with the imminent start of production at Ithaca’s 55%-owned Stella field in the central North Sea. Remedial work on the field’s electrical systems has cleared the way for output to begin, underscoring the timing of the takeover as a pivotal moment in Ithaca’s operational trajectory. Brad Hurtubise, Ithaca’s non-executive chairman, stated the offer “secures a premium cash value following a sustained period of share price growth at a favourable point in the company’s evolution.” Delek, which has operated in the Eastern Mediterranean since its landmark Tamar and Leviathan gas discoveries, already held a 20% stake in Ithaca since 2015. The acquisition adds to its expanding portfolio of upstream assets, complementing its 13% stake in Faroe Petroleum, an Aberdeen-based firm focused on the UK and Norwegian North Sea. “We are positioning Delek as a major player in the UK’s offshore energy landscape while leveraging our expertise in exploration and production,” said a Delek spokesperson, referencing the company’s transformation of the Levant Basin into a key energy hub. The deal underscores Delek’s ambition to integrate its Mediterranean successes with North Sea growth, as global energy markets navigate shifting demand and production trends. With the Stella field now operational, the transaction could catalyze further investment in the region’s aging but revitalized infrastructure.

**Sky’s Broadband Ad Banned for Misleading Reliability Claims, ASA Rules** The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) has ruled that Sky’s recent broadband ad featuring *The Secret Life of Pets* cast misleadingly claimed its service was “super reliable.” The ad, which showed a dog becoming frustrated with broadband connectivity, prompted Virgin Media to challenge the portrayal. The ASA cited Ofcom data to support Virgin’s complaint, stating the ad implied all Sky broadband packages were highly reliable, which is not true for Sky’s ADSL2+ offering. A similar Sky ad starring Lego Batman was also banned in January 2023 for falsely claiming to provide the UK’s lowest-priced fibre service. This dispute underscores the fierce competition in the telecoms industry, where rival companies frequently challenge each other’s ads. In 2016, Virgin Media faced backlash after an ad featuring Usain Bolt was banned for exaggerated speed claims following complaints from BT and Sky. More recently, BT’s Ryan Reynolds-fronted campaign was prohibited in 2022 for implying its 52Mbps package was the fastest and cheapest in the UK. An ASA spokesperson emphasized that while the sector is highly competitive, the body encourages companies to resolve disputes directly before lodging formal complaints. “We only intervene when ads breach the rules,” they said, noting the ASA seeks to avoid a “tit-for-tat” cycle by requiring evidence of prior attempts at resolution. The latest ruling highlights the importance of transparency in advertising, particularly in a market where consumers increasingly rely on marketing to navigate complex service offerings. With telecoms providers vying for market share, regulatory scrutiny remains a key tool in maintaining fair competition and consumer trust.

**Cumbria Police Urge Public to Avoid Nuisance Calls to Emergency Lines** Cumbria Police are urging residents to refrain from contacting 999 or the non-emergency 101 number for non-urgent inquiries, warning that such calls could delay critical responses. Chief Superintendent Steve Johnson highlighted that the force has fielded requests for taxi numbers, directions, and even cooking advice—such as oven temperatures for roasting chicken. “While these may seem trivial, they divert resources from life-threatening situations,” he said. The force revealed a campaign to educate the public on appropriate contact methods, stressing that 999 should be reserved for emergencies and 101 for non-urgent issues. Johnson added: “We’re asking people to pause before calling. Every call we can’t answer due to misuse has real consequences.” The initiative aims to reduce unnecessary demand and ensure police can respond swiftly to genuine crises.

**Sunderland Lighthouse Secured in Major Seafront Revamp** Sunderland City Council has pledged to restore the iconic Seaburn Grade II* lighthouse as part of a broader seafront regeneration project. The 1856-built structure, relocated to Cliffe Park from the South Pier in 1983, was officially labeled “at risk” in 2014 due to structural concerns. Council cabinet secretary Mel Speding emphasized its sentimental and historical value, stating, “It’s one of the most recognisable landmarks in the city” and “has a very special place in people’s hearts.” Funding has now secured its future, with the council aiming to remove it from the at-risk register. Restoration work will commence after the Sunderland International Airshow in July and conclude in autumn. The project aligns with £10m invested in Roker and Seaburn’s seafront since 2010, underscoring the council’s commitment to preserving the area’s heritage. Speding added, “I’m delighted we’ve found the money to secure its future,” ensuring the lighthouse remains a cherished symbol of the city for generations.

A man was pronounced dead overnight, though his identity remains unconfirmed. A second victim, hospitalized with multiple stab wounds, was later discharged. Police responded to the scene on Queens Road at 21:25 GMT. Investigations are ongoing.
