Barnes & Noble's founder and largest shareholder, Leonard Riggio, has sold 3.7 million shares of the company, sparking a significant decline in stock price. The shares were sold at $17.30 each on Thursday, prompting investors to follow suit and causing the company's shares to plummet 12.5% to close at $16.26 per share on the US markets. Despite the sale, Riggio remains the largest shareholder of Barnes & Noble. He stated that the sale is part of his long-term financial and estate planning and does not plan to sell more shares this year. This is not the first time Riggio has sold a significant number of shares, having sold 2 million shares in December 2013. The sale comes as Barnes & Noble continues to face challenges from online rivals, including Amazon. The company operates around 700 stores across the US and has been struggling to compete with the rise of e-book sales and online bookstores.

Noshir Gowadia, a 67-year-old Indian-born engineer, has been found guilty on multiple counts of conspiracy and money laundering. Gowadia, who played a key role in designing the propulsion system for the B-2 bomber, faces a possible life sentence in prison. The verdict is part of a series of high-profile prosecutions targeting alleged Chinese espionage in the US. According to prosecutors, Gowadia helped China design a stealth cruise missile, including an exhaust nozzle that could evade infrared radar detection and US heat-seeking missiles. Between 2003 and 2005, Gowadia traveled to China, where he was paid $110,000, which he used to pay off a mortgage on his luxury home in Maui. Gowadia's defense team argued that the exhaust nozzle design was based on publicly available, unclassified information and was "basic stuff." However, the jury rejected this argument, finding him guilty on several counts. Gowadia was acquitted on three counts of communicating national defense information to a foreign nation. He has been in custody for nearly four years and is scheduled to be sentenced in November. The case highlights the ongoing concerns about Chinese espionage in the US and the severe consequences for those found guilty of compromising national security.

Community Buyout Plans for Wanlockhead Gain Momentum A community-led initiative to purchase the village of Wanlockhead from the Duke of Buccleuch is gaining traction. The proposal, which began taking shape after neighboring village Leadhills started a similar process in 2014, aims to provide economic development opportunities for the village. A recent meeting attended by representatives from Community Land Scotland and the Scottish government discussed the potential buyout, with plans to turn Wanlockhead into a "tourism centre" based on its rich mining heritage and recreational opportunities on the Lowther Hills. The proposed buyout comes amidst plans for up to 140 turbines in the area, which has sparked concerns among local residents. To move forward, the community group will establish a community company to register an interest in buying the land under current legislation. South of Scotland MSP Claudia Beamish, who attended the meeting, expressed her support for the initiative, stating that local people have "highlighted an inspiring range of opportunities for the future." If the buyout is successful, decision-making will be in the hands of the community, with support and funding advice from Scottish government bodies. As a member of the Rural Affairs, Climate Change and Environment Committee, Beamish is working to strengthen the Land Reform Bill, which will provide a safety net if landowners refuse to negotiate with the community. The bill will enable communities to take control of their land and make decisions that benefit the local population. With the community's enthusiasm and determination, the future of Wanlockhead looks promising, and the group is poised to take the next step towards realizing their vision.

Novak Djokovic advanced to the final with a 6-4, 6-4 win over a French opponent. However, the match was interrupted when Djokovic complained of smelling weed, saying it made him dizzy. He expressed his frustration, joking that the culprit was "really enjoying his life" around the court. Djokovic noted that this was the second incident, also occurring during a doubles match on Friday. Despite the distraction, he secured the semi-final victory and will face Britain's Andy Murray in the final on Sunday. Djokovic hopes the issue will be resolved before the final match.

Roberts, 39, has been released from his post as manager after six years. Assistant Andy Millen takes caretaker charge. The Scottish League One club aims to appoint a new boss by January 6, following a board meeting on Monday.

A man in his 50s from Lancashire died after a solo crash on the A487 in Pantperthog, Wales, on Saturday. He was airlifted to hospital and passed away Friday morning. Police are seeking witnesses to the incident.

A Historic Reunion: The Cullinan Diamond Exhibition at Buckingham Palace In a rare and exciting event, seven of the nine principal stones cut from the iconic Cullinan Diamond will be reunited for the first time in a special exhibition at Buckingham Palace. The exhibition, which starts on June 30, will be part of the summer opening of the palace and will showcase the stunning stones in various settings, including brooches, a ring, and a necklace, many of which have been worn by Queen Elizabeth II during her 60-year reign. The Cullinan Diamond, discovered in 1905 at the Premier Mine near Pretoria, South Africa, weighed an impressive 3,106 carats in its rough state. Named after the mining company's chairman, Thomas Cullinan, the diamond was initially thought to be a worthless crystal and was even thrown out of the mine manager's office window. However, its extraordinary blue-white color and exceptional purity soon made it clear that this was a gem of unprecedented size and significance. After being sent to London, the diamond was inspected by King Edward VII at Buckingham Palace, and for two years, it was shown to prospective clients, but no buyer could be found due to the daunting task of cutting it. Eventually, the Prime Minister of the Transvaal suggested that the government acquire the diamond and present it to Edward VII as a token of loyalty. The uncut stone was then conveyed to Sandringham House in Norfolk, where the King was celebrating his 66th birthday. The celebrated firm of IJ Asscher of Amsterdam was entrusted with the task of cutting the stone, and in 1907, they produced nine principal stones, 96 smaller stones, and nine carats of unpolished fragments. The two largest gems are now part of the Crown Jewels, with one set at the head of the Sovereign's Sceptre and the other into the Imperial State Crown. The remaining seven stones were mounted in various settings for Queen Mary, wife of George V, and will be on display at the exhibition. According to exhibition curator Caroline de Guitaut, "Until 26 January 1905, no one had ever seen a diamond of this size. Now, for the first time, our visitors will be able to see seven of the nine principal stones cut from this magnificent and highly important diamond." The exhibition will not only showcase the Cullinan Diamond's stunning stones but also highlight the many ways in which diamonds have been used and worn by British monarchs over the last two centuries. The exhibition will run from June 30 to July 8 and then from July 31 to October 7, offering a unique opportunity for visitors to see these historic gems up close. As part of the summer opening of Buckingham Palace, the exhibition promises to be a must-see event for anyone interested in history, jewelry, and the British monarchy. With its rare and stunning displays, the Cullinan Diamond Exhibition is set to be a highlight of the summer season in London.

A US soldier has been killed in combat while fighting the Islamic State (IS) in eastern Afghanistan's Nangarhar province. The region, which borders Pakistan, is notorious for being a hub of IS militancy. US forces have launched multiple air strikes on jihadist bases in the area, aiming to dismantle the group's strongholds. IS announced the establishment of its Khorasan branch in January 2015, marking its first official expansion outside the Arab world. The group quickly appeared in at least five Afghan provinces, including Helmand, Zabul, Farah, Logar, and Nangarhar, in an attempt to establish pockets of territory from which to expand. Despite initial gains, IS has struggled to build a wide political base and garner indigenous support in Afghanistan. The group has made enemies of almost everyone, including the Afghan Taliban, which has challenged IS's dominance over the local insurgency. In recent years, IS has been largely eliminated from southern and western Afghanistan by the Afghan Taliban and military operations conducted by Afghan and US/Nato forces. Estimates suggest that IS's numerical strength inside Afghanistan ranges from 1,000 to 5,000 fighters. The group is also attempting to establish a foothold in northern Afghanistan, where it aims to link up with Central Asian, Chechen, and Chinese Uighur militants. The US military continues to support Afghan forces in their efforts to combat IS and other terrorist groups in the region. The latest casualty highlights the ongoing challenges faced by international forces in Afghanistan as they work to stabilize the country and eradicate militant groups.

Coventry City has signed 21-year-old Gareth Rodger on a temporary deal until January, pending international clearance. The move was facilitated by former Sky Blues manager Tommy Wright, now at St Johnstone. Manager Ferguson expressed gratitude to Wright and anticipation for Rodger's debut. Rodger joins from St Johnstone, where he has been since 2010, with loan spells at Montrose and Brechin City. The signing aims to boost United, who are struggling in the Premiership with three losses and 13 conceded goals, including a 2-0 defeat to Coleraine on Saturday.

A 19-year-old man from East Jerusalem has been brutally executed by the Islamic State (IS) on claims that he was working for Israel's Mossad foreign intelligence service. The young man, identified as Mohammed Said Ismail Musallam, had left his home in East Jerusalem for Turkey last year, apparently intending to fight in Syria. However, his family and Israeli officials have vehemently denied the allegations that he was an Israeli spy. According to his family, Musallam had been recruited by IS through the internet, with promises of a house, money, and marriage. He had grown a beard and was carrying a Kalashnikov rifle by the time he contacted his family from Raqqa late last year. However, his father, Said Musallam, claims that his son had become disillusioned with the group and wanted to return home. Tragically, Musallam's attempt to escape was thwarted, and he was caught and accused of being an Israeli spy. His family says that there was no way IS was going to let him go, given that he had seen their weapons and had been with the group for three months. The IS magazine Dabiq carried a long interview with Musallam in February, which contained what purported to be a confession that he had been sent by Israel to infiltrate the jihadist group. The article gave sketchy details about his alleged training and mission, but its publication was a clear signal that he had fallen foul of the group and was in grave danger. On Tuesday evening, IS's Furqan media outlet published a 13-minute video showing Musallam sitting in a room wearing an orange jumpsuit, talking about how he was recruited and trained by Israeli intelligence. The video then shows Musallam kneeling in an empty field, facing the camera, with two figures in camouflage fatigues standing behind him. One of the figures, who appears to be a boy, shoots Musallam in the head with a handgun and then fires further shots into his body. The video carries a warning from an older, French-speaking militant aimed at the Jewish people, who has been identified as Sabri Essid, reportedly a half-brother of Mohamed Merah, who carried out a series of deadly attacks in France in 2012. The authenticity of the video has not been independently verified, and Israeli officials have said that they cannot confirm its authenticity. However, the footage has sent shockwaves through Musallam's family and community. His mother, Umm Ahmed, is devastated by the loss of her son, recalling the shock she felt when she discovered that he had run away to join IS fighters in northern Syria. The incident highlights the dangers faced by young people who are recruited by extremist groups through the internet. Musallam's family says that he was lured by promises of a better life, but ultimately paid the ultimate price for his naivety. The case also raises concerns about the treatment of individuals who are accused of being spies or traitors by extremist groups, and the brutal methods used to punish them. As the conflict in Syria and Iraq continues to rage on, the incident serves as a reminder of the human cost of the war and the devastating impact it has on families and communities. Musallam's family is now left to mourn the loss of their loved one, who was brutally executed by a group that he had once been drawn to. The incident is a tragic reminder of the dangers of extremism and the importance of protecting young people from its influence.

US Ambassador to the United Nations, Nikki Haley, has warned that holding a meeting to discuss North Korea's latest missile test without taking significant action would be counterproductive. In a statement, she emphasized that an additional Security Council resolution that does not substantially increase international pressure on North Korea would be "of no value" and would only serve to embolden the North Korean dictator. Haley's comments come after North Korea test-fired its second intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) in three weeks, with the state claiming that the entire US is now within its range. The US has responded by testing its anti-missile system and conducting bomber exercises over the Korean peninsula. The Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad) system, which is being installed in South Korea despite China's objections, successfully intercepted a projectile fired by the US Air Force over the Pacific. The US has been urging China, North Korea's closest economic ally, to rein in the isolated state's weapons program. Haley stated that "China must decide whether it is finally willing to take this vital step. The time for talk is over." US President Donald Trump has also criticized China for not doing enough to stop Pyongyang's nuclear ambitions, tweeting that he was "very disappointed" with China's inaction. However, Chinese officials have pushed back against Trump's comments, with former diplomat and government adviser Victor Gao describing the US as acting like a "spoiled child." China has condemned North Korea's latest test launch and urged restraint on all sides, while also calling for a peaceful resolution to the crisis. The Thaad system, which is designed to shoot down North Korean missiles fired at South Korea, consists of a radar system, command and control center, and interceptor missiles. The system works by detecting the launch of an enemy missile, relaying the information to the command center, and then firing an interceptor missile to destroy the enemy projectile. The US has been working with its allies, including South Korea and Japan, to increase pressure on North Korea to abandon its nuclear program. US B-1 bombers conducted exercises over the Korean peninsula with South Korean and Japanese planes on Saturday, in a show of military strength and solidarity. Despite the tensions, China and the US have been in talks over how to address the North Korean threat. After a meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this year, US officials said that the two countries were working on "a range of options" to deal with North Korea. However, Friday's ICBM launch demonstrates a defiance from the North, which is showcasing "a significant advancement in technology," according to South Korea. As the international community grapples with how to respond to North Korea's latest provocation, Haley's warning that a weak Security Council resolution would be counterproductive highlights the need for a unified and robust response to the crisis. With the US and its allies pushing for increased pressure on North Korea, and China urging restraint, the situation on the Korean peninsula remains highly volatile and uncertain.

Dog owners and their pets gathered in Weymouth on Sunday to protest against a new ban that prohibits dogs from being on the beach from Easter to October. The ban, implemented by Weymouth Borough Council, has sparked outrage among dog owners who claim that the decision was made despite the majority of respondents to a public consultation wanting the original dates to remain in place. The original ban, which lasted from May to September, was extended after the council received nearly 1,700 responses to the consultation. However, protesters argue that 63% of respondents wanted the dates to stay the same, and that the council's decision to extend the ban was not representative of the community's views. A petition started by Judi Moore, which has gained over 1,000 signatures, calls for the changes to be revoked. Moore argued that the ban is a "retrograde step" and that dogs were previously a welcome addition to the town's attractions. She also pointed out that the weather in April and October is often unsuitable for beachgoers, making the ban unnecessary. Despite the protests, the council has defended its decision, stating that the correct information from the consultation results was taken into account. Councillor Richard Kosior said that the Policy Development Committee made the decision to extend the ban after considering the consultation results, while Community Protection Councillor Francis Drake acknowledged that the majority of respondents wanted the dates to stay the same, but ultimately supported the committee's decision. The protest highlights the ongoing debate between dog owners and the council over the ban, with no clear resolution in sight.

Diageo, the British spirits company, is optimistic about its growth prospects in Asia despite a crackdown on extravagant spending in China that dented its sales last year. Chief Executive Ivan Menezes told the BBC that the region's strong fundamentals, including 60 million people turning the legal drinking age every year, will drive growth. The company reported lower-than-expected sales for the second half of 2014, with profits falling by 18% to £1.7bn. In China, sales of Scotch whisky were down 22% due to the government's austerity drive. However, Mr. Menezes sees Asia accounting for 25% of Diageo's business in the future, up from the current 20%. He believes that China, India, and South East Asia have good growth prospects, particularly as the emerging middle class grows. Diageo, which makes Johnnie Walker whisky, Smirnoff vodka, and Guinness, is turning to emerging markets to drive growth in the next decade. With low growth in developed markets such as the US and Europe, Diageo is focusing on Africa and India, which Mr. Menezes describes as "hugely attractive" markets. The penetration of spirits among the growing middle class in these regions is still low, making them ripe for expansion. As consumers' purchasing power increases, they are more likely to spend on spirits, making them an attractive market for Diageo. Over the next 10 years, about a billion consumers are expected to cross the threshold of $5,000 a year in purchasing power, which Mr. Menezes believes will be a "big difference-maker" for Diageo.

London's New Routemaster Buses Plagued by Technical Issues, Including Power Steering Problems London's New Routemaster buses, touted as a revolutionary transportation solution, have been beset by a series of technical issues, with the latest revelation concerning problems with the power steering system. According to reports, wiring in the power-assisted steering had to be replaced in 468 of the buses, prompting a recall notice from the government's Vehicle and Operator Services Agency (VOSA). The recall was issued due to concerns that the power-assisted steering may become non-functional, which could potentially pose a risk to passenger safety. Fortunately, the replacements were carried out by the manufacturer, Wrightbus, at London garages between October 2015 and February 2016, and TfL claims that there was no impact on passenger safety or service. This is not the first time the New Routemaster buses have been plagued by technical issues. Previous problems have included battery failures, which forced some of the hybrid buses to run on diesel, and complaints from drivers about poor acceleration. The buses have also been criticized for their lack of windows, which led to sweltering temperatures on the top deck, particularly during the summer months. It was only recently that Transport for London (TfL) bosses agreed to install windows to address this issue. The latest glitch will likely fuel criticism that the New Bus for London scheme is a vanity project that has been rushed into operation without adequate testing. Critics argue that it would have been more sensible to purchase cheaper existing hybrid buses, rather than investing in a bespoke design that has been plagued by technical issues. Mike Weston, TfL's director of buses, has sought to downplay the issue, stating that the precautionary work was completed at no cost to TfL or the taxpayer. However, the ongoing problems with the New Routemaster buses are likely to continue to raise concerns about the viability of the project.

French President Francois Hollande has awarded citizenship to a group of African veterans who fought for France during World War II and other conflicts. The ceremony, held at the Elysee Palace in Paris, marked a significant step towards recognizing the contributions and sacrifices of these individuals. Many of the veterans, who hailed from countries such as Senegal, had been long-term French residents but lacked official citizenship. President Hollande acknowledged the debt of gratitude France owed to these veterans, stating that "France is proud to welcome you, just as you were proud to carry its flag, the flag of freedom." The move is seen as a gesture of reconciliation and a step towards healing old wounds. Mohamed Toure, one of the veterans granted citizenship, praised President Hollande's decision, saying it "repairs a lot of things." The ceremony is the result of years of campaigning by activists, including Aissatou Seck, the granddaughter of a Senegalese soldier. Seck's petition last year gained tens of thousands of signatures, highlighting the plight of African veterans who had been denied equal rights and benefits. Until 2010, these veterans received lower pensions than their French counterparts, and they often faced difficulties when traveling. While the citizenship ceremony is a positive step, many veterans are still seeking a full apology for past injustices, including the 1944 shooting of dozens of West African soldiers by French troops. Further naturalization ceremonies are expected to follow for other veterans in France.

Rory McIlroy Secures Victory at Deutsche Bank Championship In a thrilling turn of events, Northern Irish golfer Rory McIlroy clinched the Deutsche Bank Championship title, finishing two shots clear at 15 under par. McIlroy, 27, started six shots behind overnight leader Paul Casey, but a stunning six-under-par 65, including seven birdies, propelled him to the top spot. England's Casey, 39, came close to forcing a play-off, but missed an eagle putt on the final hole at TPC Boston. This victory marks McIlroy's first tournament win since the Irish Open in May and his first PGA title since May 2015. Notably, it comes just a week after he made significant changes to his putter and putting coach. McIlroy expressed his excitement, stating, "I knew my game was in good shape, I just needed to do something with the putting..... I found something." He acknowledged that there is still room for improvement, but is optimistic about his game's direction. The win will see McIlroy rise 34 places to fourth in the FedEx Cup standings, bringing him closer to the $10m prize for the winner. With this momentum, McIlroy is poised to make a strong showing in the upcoming Ryder Cup.

A hidden pencil caricature has been discovered by volunteers during the restoration of an 1890 carriage at the Midland Railway Trust in Butterley, Derbyshire. The drawing, found on the back of a wooden panel, depicts a man with a high collar, pointed moustache, and satisfied smirk. It is believed to have been created by a builder as a tease aimed at the management. The carriage, a third-class coach, was found in 1999 being used as a changing room for a tennis court. Despite its humble origins, the restoration process involved repairing or replacing relatively luxurious fittings, including velvet seats, gas lights, and mahogany panelling. It was during this work that the doodle was uncovered. According to Alan Calladine, the trust's development officer, the caricature is a unique find, offering a glimpse into the lives of the people who built the carriage. The drawing is thought to represent one of the carriage works' managers, given the subject's posh attire and striking moustache. Calladine speculates that the caricature may have been created by a worker as a quick joke, perhaps as the boss walked by. The drawing has been carefully preserved and will remain hidden from view once again. The restored carriage will be unveiled to the public during the May Day Bank Holiday, giving visitors a chance to experience a piece of history. The discovery of the caricature has added a new layer of interest to the project, highlighting the human side of the carriage's construction and the people involved in its creation.

Glamorgan Cricket Club has secured a crucial draw against Leicestershire, earning 13 valuable points in the process. The team, led by 20-year-old captain Tom Donald, was set a target of 355 to win, but instead opted for a cautious approach, with Donald himself scoring an unbeaten 66. This result comes as a welcome respite for Glamorgan, who had suffered defeats in their opening two games of the season. Donald expressed his satisfaction with the team's performance, stating that it was "nice to get a few points on the board." He highlighted key moments in the game where the team demonstrated their strength and resilience, which had been lacking in their previous matches. The young captain believes that this draw has put the team on the right track, particularly with the Royal London One-Day Cup looming. Glamorgan is set to face Gloucestershire in the first game of the competition on April 27. Donald is confident that the team's white-ball squad, bolstered by the addition of Marchant de Lange, will pose a significant challenge to their opponents. The potential return of injured players Will Bragg and Timm van der Gugten will further strengthen the team's chances. With a quarter-final spot in their sights, Glamorgan is ready to take on Gloucestershire, the 2015 competition winners, and make a strong impression in the tournament.

The recent downing of a Malaysia Airlines plane over Ukraine has sparked widespread concern over the safety of commercial air travel, particularly in areas of conflict. Jim McAuslan, the general secretary of the British Airline Pilots Association (Balpa), has emphasized the need for a uniform level of safety in the aviation industry, rather than leaving it to individual airlines to decide. McAuslan's comments come as airlines continue to fly over areas of hostility, including northern Iraq and Syria, despite the risks. While airlines have stopped flying over Ukraine, where separatists are in control of parts of the east, passenger planes have still been flying over other conflict zones. Some US and European airlines, including Easyjet, have suspended flights to Israel after a rocket landed near Tel Aviv airport. The Balpa general secretary stressed that pilots need to have absolute confidence in the safety of their flight plans, and that the current risk assessment approach can be influenced by commercial pressure and other factors. "Individual pilots looking at their flight plans need to have absolute confidence that the right calls are being made," he said. "The process behind the choice of airspace routing is based on a risk assessment, both by a country's national aviation security services in the advice that they give to their airlines, and by the airline in how they assess this advice." McAuslan also called for greater leadership from the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), the United Nations body responsible for coordinating the safety and order of global aviation. He argued that ICAO should have a greater role in declaring airspace unsafe and should be better resourced to do so. "ICAO's purpose should be to lead where national authorities cannot and it should have the tools to do that," he said. The crash of flight MH17, which killed all 298 people on board, has highlighted the need for improved safety measures and greater international cooperation. While the ultimate responsibility for the tragedy lies with those who launched the missile, McAuslan emphasized that the failures that led to the outcome must be addressed to prevent similar incidents in the future. Balpa is also calling for ICAO to reflect on its rules of membership and to consider revoking privileges from states that do not meet their responsibilities, such as sharing information and allowing access to accident investigations. "Participating states enjoy privileges such as free movement, but with that comes responsibility," McAuslan said. "If a state does not live up to that responsibility, then membership and privileges should be reconsidered." As the investigation into the MH17 crash continues, the aviation industry is under increasing pressure to improve safety measures and to provide greater protection for passengers and crew. The Balpa's calls for greater leadership from ICAO and a uniform level of safety are likely to be echoed by other industry groups and regulators in the coming weeks and months. Ultimately, the goal is to ensure that commercial air travel is safe and secure, even in areas of conflict, and that the tragic events of MH17 are never repeated.

Colombia's Government and ELN Rebels to Hold Peace Talks in Quito The Colombian government and the country's second-largest rebel group, the National Liberation Army (ELN), are set to begin peace talks in Quito, Ecuador. The negotiations follow the successful peace accord signed with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) in December. President Juan Manuel Santos has expressed his desire to achieve "complete peace" in Colombia, and the talks with the ELN are a crucial step towards this goal. The ELN, founded in 1964, has been fighting against Colombia's unequal distribution of land and riches. The group had been holding a former congressman, Odin Sanchez, hostage for 10 months, but released him last Thursday after the government agreed to pardon two ELN members serving time in Colombian jails. The two released rebels are expected to serve as negotiators at the peace talks. The talks were initially scheduled to begin at the end of October but were delayed due to the government's refusal to negotiate while the ELN still held hostages. However, with the release of Sanchez and a soldier, Freddy Moreno, who was held for two weeks, the path has been cleared for the negotiations to proceed. The peace agreement with the Farc, reached after four years of negotiations in Havana, has set a precedent for the talks with the ELN. Members of the Farc are currently demobilizing and laying down their weapons in designated "transition zones" under the supervision of United Nations monitors. The Colombian government hopes to replicate this success with the ELN, bringing an end to decades of conflict and violence in the country. The talks in Quito are expected to be challenging, but both sides have expressed their commitment to finding a peaceful resolution.

Saracens have secured the long-term futures of two of their key players, Maro Itoje and George Kruis, with the second-rowers signing contract extensions until the summer of 2019. The pair played crucial roles in England's Six Nations Grand Slam victory earlier this year, with Itoje, 21, and Kruis, 26, being hailed as two of the brightest talents in the sport. Sarries boss Mark McCall praised the duo, saying they have been in "superb form" for both club and country. Itoje, who made his international debut against Italy in February, has made rapid progress, earning praise from England coach Eddie Jones, who likened his development to upgrading from a "Vauxhall Viva to a BMW". McCall described Itoje's progress as "phenomenal", noting that he has already experienced many big games for the club and country. Kruis, a product of Saracens' academy, has won 15 England caps since his debut against New Zealand in 2014. McCall praised Kruis as "one of the finest lock forwards around", highlighting his consistent improvement and vast potential. The contract extensions are a significant boost for Saracens, who will be looking to build on their recent success with two of their most talented players committed to the club for the next three years.

Poland's Temple of Divine Providence, a project over two centuries in the making, has finally been inaugurated in Warsaw. The cornerstone of the temple was laid in 1792, but its construction was stalled by a Russian invasion and two world wars. The most recent work on the temple began in 2003, with private donations totaling €50m. The temple has become an emblem of perseverance and nationalism for Poland's conservative government, which sees it as a symbol of the country's strong Roman Catholic heritage. The inaugural Mass was attended by Poland's Prime Minister Beata Szydlo and President Andrzej Duda, as well as Archbishop Stanislaw Gadecki. In his address, Archbishop Gadecki cited John Paul II, the Polish former Pope, and called for a "responsible" use of freedom and warned against the "arrogance of power". Despite the temple's completion, some work remains to be done, including finishing the painting and installing stained-glass windows. An additional €7m in donations is needed to complete the project. The temple's design has not been without controversy, with some critics nicknaming it "the giant lemon juicer" due to its stylized rotunda. However, the complex also includes a pantheon of great Poles and a museum commemorating Pope John Paul II and Stefan Wyszynski, the leader of the Catholic Church in Poland under Communist rule. To mark the nation's 98th Independence Day, the temple was lit up in Poland's national colors of red and white. Visitors to the temple will be treated to superb acoustics and lighting that can be changed to reflect different periods of the Church calendar.

Inverness and Partick Thistle played out a tense and tightly contested 0-0 draw, with neither side able to capitalize on their scoring opportunities. The hosts, Inverness, started strongly, with Miles Storey going through on goal in the early stages, only to be denied by a brave block from Tomas Cerny. Andrea Mbuy-Mutombo also had a chance to open the scoring, but his strike was dragged wide, while Iain Vigurs saw an effort from outside the box creep narrowly over the bar. Despite their dominance, Inverness were unable to find the breakthrough, with Cerny making several crucial saves to keep the score level. Partick Thistle, on the other hand, struggled to create chances, with Kris Doolan's scooped effort from the edge of the box being their best opportunity. However, they defended stoutly, particularly after the opening period, and limited Inverness to few clear-cut chances. The second half was a scrappy affair, with both sides struggling to create meaningful opportunities. However, Storey did come close to scoring a sensational opener with a fierce long-range drive, which Cerny had to tip over. Later, Storey created another chance when he got to the bye-line and cut back for Liam Polworth, but the midfielder somehow steered the ball wide of the post. The draw may be seen as a better result for Partick Thistle, who defended well and eased themselves away from the bottom of the table with games in hand. For Inverness, the point will be seen as a missed opportunity to take a significant step forward, but they will be encouraged by their dominant display in the early stages. Ultimately, the match will be remembered for its lack of clear-cut chances and the impressive goalkeeping display from Cerny.

A man has died after a fight involving multiple individuals on Holborn Way, Mitcham. The incident occurred on Monday at 19:20 GMT, leaving the victim with serious head injuries. He passed away two days later. Several others were injured, and a 21-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. Five more were held and bailed for violent disorder.

A rare Great Mormon butterfly with a unique sex division has been discovered at Butterfly World in St Albans. The butterfly exhibits a distinct pattern, with the female half on the right side of its body and the male half on the left, visible in its wing patterns. This natural phenomenon, occurring in only 0.01% of butterflies, is a result of improper sex chromosome division during development. According to lepidopterist Louise Hawkins, this makes the creature infertile and reduces its life span due to mixed-up internal organs. Staff at the centre are fascinated by the butterfly, with many visiting to see it. The centre plans to have the butterfly on display for the next few days, offering a rare opportunity for visitors to witness this unusual phenomenon. The discovery has sparked excitement among staff and is expected to attract visitors from around the area.

Australian Social Media Celebrity Speaks Out Against the "Unhealthy" Ideals of Social Media In a shocking move, 18-year-old Australian social media celebrity Essena O'Neill has spoken out against the "unhealthy" ideals of social media, revealing that her picture perfect online persona left her feeling empty and addicted to social media likes. With over 500,000 followers on Instagram, O'Neill had built a career posting images of her seemingly flawless lifestyle, but now she's taking a stand against the cult of social media. In a 17-minute video uploaded to her YouTube account, O'Neill vows to act against the unrealistic expectations and manipulations of social media. She has also set up a website to fight against the negative effects of social media, which she believes can lead to narcissism, low self-esteem, and addiction. As part of her crusade, O'Neill has deleted over 2,000 photos from her Instagram account, which she claims "served no real purpose other than self-promotion." O'Neill has also re-edited the captions on her remaining Instagram photos to reveal the manipulation and insecurity behind them. For example, a previous post showing her in a bikini has been re-captioned to highlight the strategic pose, sucked-in stomach, and pushed-up boobs, which she says was all done to get attention. Another post showing her work-out selfies has been re-captioned to reveal the excessive exercise and calorie restriction that went into her daily routine. O'Neill's followers have largely reacted with praise for her honesty and vulnerability, with many commenting on her Instagram posts to thank her for speaking out against the evils of social media. "Your honesty and vulnerability are so powerful. I'm very proud of the direction you are taking," commented one user. Another user added, "We are all aware of the evils that social media brings; particularly relating to one's public image on them that only serves to reinforce narcissism and low self-esteem. Good on Essena for waking up and trying to change this one step at a time." O'Neill's decision to speak out against social media has sparked a wider conversation about the impact of social media on our lives. She has emphasized that social media is not real and that it's a system based on social approval, likes, and validation. "I've also spent hours watching perfect girls online, wishing I was them. When I became'one of them', I still wasn't happy, content or at peace with myself," she said. By speaking out against the cult of social media, O'Neill hopes to inspire others to think critically about the media they consume and to promote a more realistic and healthy approach to social media.

Parking fees at Stepping Hill Hospital in Stockport are set to rise from September 1, with a four-hour stay increasing from £6 to £8 and short stays rising from £2.50 to £3.50. The move is part of the Stockport NHS Foundation Trust's efforts to make "savings in areas which do not affect patient services". However, residents are concerned that the hike will lead to more parking problems on nearby streets, as visitors may seek alternative, free parking options. Homeowners in the area are calling for measures such as resident-only parking to be introduced to mitigate the issue. The trust has already announced significant cost-cutting measures, including job losses and ward closures. While concessions have been made for certain patients, including free parking for cancer patients and reduced rates for those with long-term conditions, the increase is likely to be unpopular with visitors and staff.

UK Retirement Communities Face Scrutiny Over "Hidden" Fees A two-year investigation by the Law Commission has revealed that some retirement community operators in the UK are charging residents hefty fees when they move out or need a carer to move in, with some fees reaching up to 30% of the property's value. The Commission has warned of a "real potential for abuse" in the charging of these event or transfer fees, which are often buried in the small print of complicated leases. The fees are supposed to cover running costs and service charges in retirement communities, which are becoming increasingly popular in the UK. However, the Commission found that some rogue operators are taking advantage of residents by keeping these charges hidden. The Law Commission has stopped short of banning the fees, instead recommending that they should be more transparent. The issue has sparked outrage among some families who have been affected by these fees. Ken Ward, from Rayleigh in Essex, told the BBC that his family was unaware of the fees when his father-in-law, Bert Elley, moved out of a retirement home shortly before he died last year. The family was charged an extra £1,725 for administration, on top of service charges and losses on the value of the property itself. "They fleeced him," Ward said. "The whole thing has not been a good experience." The Law Commissioner, Stephen Lewis, acknowledged that exit fees can work well for many people by deferring bills until after they sell their home. However, he warned that "in the worst cases, a few unscrupulous landlords are getting away with very high hidden fees buried deep in the small print of a long and complicated lease." Lewis has urged the government to regulate the sector and ensure that consumers are fully informed about the fees they will be charged before signing a lease. The Leasehold Knowledge Partnership (LKP), which represents the interests of leaseholders, has criticized the report for not going far enough in addressing the issue. The LKP argues that the Law Commission has given the green light to exit fees, which it believes are unfair and exploitative. On the other hand, the industry has welcomed the report, saying that it wants more regulation of the sector, not less. The Association of Retirement Community Operators (ARCO) argues that event fees are used to cross-subsidize running costs and enable older people to use their housing equity to "enjoy now and pay later." There are currently around 160,000 retirement properties of this type in the UK, and the industry is expected to continue growing in the coming years. As the debate over exit fees continues, the government is under pressure to take action to protect vulnerable residents from exploitation. The Law Commission's report is a step in the right direction, but more needs to be done to ensure that retirement community operators are transparent and fair in their charging practices. With the industry expected to continue growing, it is essential that regulators take a closer look at the sector to prevent abuse and ensure that residents are treated fairly.

Cardiff City's woes continue as they sit at the bottom of the Championship table, reeling from four consecutive defeats. Their latest loss, a 2-0 drubbing at the hands of Leeds, has raised concerns about the team's future and the leadership of manager Paul Trollope. Former Bluebirds player Jason Perry has expressed his doubts about the club's ability to make the right decisions, citing a lack of footballing expertise on the board. Perry's comments come after Trollope claimed to have the backing of club owner Vincent Tan, despite the team's poor performance. However, Perry remains skeptical, suggesting that the problems plaguing the team are deeper-seated and have been ongoing since last season. He points to a lack of pace in the squad, a shortage of forward players who can stretch defenders, and a midfield that is struggling to keep up. Fellow former Bluebird Danny Gabbidon has called for Trollope to be given the same amount of time as his predecessor Russell Slade, who was in charge from 2014 to 2016. However, Gabbidon acknowledges that the pressure is mounting, and the team's recent performances have been worrying. The Bluebirds have scored just six goals and conceded 14, winning only once in eight games. Former Cardiff striker Nathan Blake is even more pessimistic, suggesting that the team's problems run deeper than just the players on the pitch. "There's something missing throughout the club," he said. "There's a spark missing. What you see there on the pitch on a Saturday is just the evidence of the overall feeling at the club." With their next game against Rotherham, a team just three places above them in the table, the Bluebirds face a tough test. As Blake warns, "It's only going to get tougher." The team will need to turn their fortunes around quickly if they hope to avoid a long and difficult season.

A devastating house fire in East End Park claimed the lives of three people: Joanne Semple, 36, Kelly Taylor-Hackett, 28, and Stephen Fitzgerald, 18. Their bodies were found along with three dead Rottweilers. Post-mortem results confirmed fire as the cause of death. West Yorkshire Police are investigating the unexplained tragedy.

Rescue Efforts Continue in Manhattan Building Collapse A massive rescue operation is underway in Manhattan, where a building collapse on Wednesday has left one person still unaccounted for. Authorities are scouring the rubble for survivors, using telescopic cameras and sound devices to search small spaces in the wreckage. Despite the challenging conditions, rescue teams remain hopeful, with Fire Department of New York Chief Edward Kilduff stating, "We have to think of survivors and work in that way, with hope." The incident, which injured over 60 people, has raised concerns about the city's aging infrastructure. The suspected cause of the explosion is a gas leak, and city officials and utility company Con Edison are investigating whether the city's old gas and water mains, some of which date back to the 1800s, played a role. New York City still uses an estimated 3,000 miles of old cast-iron pipe to deliver gas, posing a "fundamental challenge" according to Mayor Bill de Blasio. Bulldozers are working to remove debris from the site, located in the Park Avenue and 116th Street area, with the goal of reaching the first floor by Saturday and then searching the basement for victims. Local residents had reportedly complained about strong gas smells in the area recently, but Con Edison claims that only one gas odor complaint was on record from the address, which was from last May and involved a small leak. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are working tirelessly to locate the missing person and determine the cause of the tragic incident.

Beloved Comedian Don Rickles Passes Away at 90 The entertainment world is mourning the loss of legendary comedian Don Rickles, who passed away on Thursday at his Los Angeles home due to kidney failure. Rickles, best known for his sharp wit and distinctive voice, was 90 years old. The news of his passing has sent shockwaves throughout the industry, with many of his colleagues and friends taking to social media to pay tribute to the comedy legend. Rickles was a household name, with a career spanning over 60 years. He was perhaps most famous for his role as the voice of Mr. Potato Head in the Toy Story franchise. Tom Hanks, who played Woody in the movies, tweeted a heartfelt message, saying "A God died today. Don Rickles, we did not want to ever lose you. Never. Hanx." Hanks' tweet reflects the sentiment of many in the industry, who are struggling to come to terms with the loss of a true comedy legend. Jimmy Kimmel, host of the popular US talk show, paid an emotional tribute to Rickles on Thursday night's show. Kimmel, who had become close to Rickles over the years, was visibly moved as he began a 12-minute tribute to the comedian. "I'm going to cry, I'm already crying," he said, his voice cracking with emotion. "I know it sounds crazy to say he was too young [to die] but he was, because he was youthful and funny and sharp and generous." Rickles was set to reprise his role as Mr. Potato Head in the upcoming Toy Story 4, which is due for release in 2019. While it is unclear whether he had already recorded his dialogue for the film, it is likely that his passing will have an impact on the production. The film is currently in the pre-production stage, and it is possible that the script and voice recordings had not yet been completed. Tributes have been pouring in from all corners of the entertainment industry. Martin Scorsese, who worked with Rickles on the film Casino, described him as "a giant and a legend". Mel Brooks tweeted, "Don Rickles. One of the bravest, funniest, and sweetest guys that ever performed. A dear pal that we will all sorely miss." Other stars who paid tribute on social media included Barbara Streisand, Jim Carrey, Chris Rock, Mark Wahlberg, and Danny DeVito. Don Rickles' passing is a significant loss to the entertainment industry, and he will be deeply missed by his fans and colleagues alike. His legacy, however, will live on through his body of work, including his iconic role as Mr. Potato Head. As the industry continues to mourn his passing, it is clear that Rickles' impact on comedy and entertainment will be felt for generations to come.

William "Wink" Bertram, a well-liked man from Eddleston, died after his car crashed near Howgate while driving to work, leaving his family and community in mourning for the hard working and fun loving individual.

A funeral was held for 17-year-old Corey Price at St Mary's Church in Barry, Vale of Glamorgan. His white coffin featured a blue Cardiff City football shirt, honoring his time in the team's academy. The service followed funerals for Alesha O'Connor, Rhodri Miller, and Margaret Challis, who also died in the A470 crash. Seven teenage drivers arrested after the incident have been bailed. The community continues to mourn the loss of these lives.

A Police Dog's Brave Sacrifice: The Fight for "Finn's Law" On October 5th, a disturbing incident occurred in Stevenage, Hertfordshire, when PC Dave Wardell and his German shepherd, Finn, were brutally stabbed while attempting to apprehend a suspect. The suspect, who had allegedly robbed a taxi driver at gunpoint, attacked Finn with a knife, stabbing him in the head and chest. PC Wardell also suffered a stab wound to the hand. According to PC Wardell, "Finn was stabbed trying to protect me..... He got it first." Thanks to the quick thinking of PC Wardell, who rushed Finn to a nearby vet, the dog's life was saved. The vet performed emergency surgery, and Finn has since been recovering at home with his family, including sniffer dog Pearl, a spaniel. Despite the traumatic experience, Finn is making a remarkable recovery, with PC Wardell describing him as "being very cheeky" and already getting into mischief. The incident has sparked a nationwide outcry, with many calling for greater protection for police animals. A petition, known as "Finn's Law," has been set up on the UK government's petition site, proposing that police animals be given greater protection and recognition for their service. The petition has garnered over 57,000 signatures since its launch on October 9th. A 16-year-old boy from Lewisham, south-east London, has been charged with assaulting an officer and criminal damage in connection with the incident. As Finn continues his recovery, his future as a working police dog remains uncertain. His stitches are set to be removed next week, but it may be several weeks before vets can determine whether he will be fit enough to return to duty. Regardless of the outcome, Finn's bravery and loyalty have earned him a special place in the hearts of the nation, and his story will continue to inspire calls for greater protection and recognition for police animals.

Nigerian entrepreneur, Ms Williams, is making waves in the agribusiness sector with ReelFruit, her company founded in 2012. Producing brightly colored packets of dried fruit in Lagos, she aims to showcase Nigerian products as world-class. With huge potential for wealth and job creation, Ms Williams is paving the way for women in business. Featured in the BBC's Women of Africa season, she is one of eight inspiring female entrepreneurs finding success in their country and beyond, proving Nigerian products can compete globally. Her innovative approach is a testament to African women's growing presence in the business world.

Disaster Strikes for Ernie Els at the Masters In a shocking turn of events, four-time major winner Ernie Els suffered a meltdown on the first hole of the Masters, taking a staggering nine putts to complete the par four. The 46-year-old South African, who has struggled with putting in recent times, was left reeling after the disastrous hole, which saw him slip back to six over par. Els, who won his last major title at the 2012 Open Championship using a belly putter, has been forced to adapt to a short-handled club since anchored strokes were banned on January 1. However, the transition has not been smooth, and he has been plagued by putting problems, including missing an 18-inch putt at the SA Open in January. Former PGA tour professional Jay Townsend expressed his sympathy for Els, saying, "It is really disappointing. It ruins your week. There is no way back, even if you play well." Townsend also noted that Els has been struggling with the "yips" for a while, which has clearly affected his game. Els's score of nine on the first hole is one of the worst in Masters history, surpassing the previous worst score on the first hole of eight strokes, recorded by four players. The worst one-hole scores in Masters history remain the 13s taken by Tsuneyuki Nakajima and Tom Weiskopf in 1978 and 1980, respectively. The most recent double-figure score was recorded by American David Duval with his 10 at the par-five second in 2006. As Els looks to recover from this setback, it remains to be seen how he will bounce back from this disappointing start to the tournament.

Helen Jenkins Ready for Rio Despite Playing Down Medal Hopes With just a few months to go before the Rio Olympics, British triathlete Helen Jenkins is gearing up for the biggest event of her career. The 32-year-old, who finished fifth at the London 2012 Olympics, has qualified for Rio and is set to compete in the penultimate World Series event in Stockholm alongside compatriots Non Stanford and Vicky Holland. Despite her impressive track record, Jenkins is playing down her medal hopes, insisting that she doesn't want to put pressure on herself. "Running in Rio is a bonus; I didn't really expect to be going," she said in an interview with BBC Wales Sport. "So I don't want to put that pressure on myself at the moment. Winning a medal is something I won't allow myself to think about." Jenkins' cautious approach is likely due to her experiences four years ago, when she suffered a serious injury just 10 weeks before the London Olympics. Despite the setback, she managed to finish fifth, a feat she is now proud of. "In London, it was all about gold or getting a medal, and this time around, really all I am focusing on is lining up fit and healthy," she explained. The Welsh triathlete believes that she has learned valuable lessons from her past experiences and is now more focused on producing her best performance rather than winning a medal. "If I can do that and produce the best performance that I can, I will come back happy. That's what I want to do really," she said. Jenkins is not the only British woman with medal hopes, as Non Stanford and Vicky Holland are also major contenders. The trio will compete in Stockholm, which will provide valuable race practice and experience before the Rio Olympics. "It is going to be a lot tougher in Rio than it was in London, the course is harder, we have a sea swim, which tends to break things up a bit more, and we have a bike course with a very steep hill in it, so it is a very technical ascent," Jenkins said. Despite the challenges, Jenkins believes that the Rio course suits her and Stanford, who are both strong cyclists. "It is a great course for us," she said. Jenkins had considered skipping the Stockholm event, but ultimately decided to compete in order to get some much-needed race practice. "Choosing to go to Stockholm, it is an important decision, I haven't raced too much this year, and just for race practice and race feel, it should help," she said. The ultimate aim for Jenkins is to make it to the start line in Rio fit and healthy, and she is taking a flexible approach to her training and competition schedule. "We will play things by ear. We need to have a plan, but a very flexible one," she said. With her experience and determination, Jenkins is sure to be a strong contender in Rio, and her fans will be eagerly watching her progress in the coming months. As the triathlon season heats up, fans can follow all the latest news and reports on the BBC app, and find out how to get into the sport with the BBC's special guide. With the Rio Olympics just around the corner, the excitement is building, and Helen Jenkins is ready to take on the challenge and make her country proud.

Samsung has announced that its new flagship devices, the Galaxy S8 and S8+, will ship without English voice control for its Bixby voice-powered assistant. The feature was highly anticipated, allowing users to search and categorize photos and access information using voice commands. However, the Korean version of Bixby's voice control will be available, and Google's voice assistant will also be included. Samsung has promised to release the full Bixby as an update later this spring. Early tests suggested that the software was not yet ready for launch. Despite the delay, key features of Bixby, including Vision, Home, and Reminder, will be available with the global launch of the Galaxy S8 on April 21. The company has not given a reason for the delay, but users can expect the full Bixby experience to arrive soon. The Galaxy S8 and S8+ will still be available on schedule.

A former cult member has testified against Aravindan Balakrishnan, the 75-year-old leader of the Workers Institute commune in south London. The 64-year-old woman told Southwark Crown Court that Balakrishnan made her write explicit "sex diaries" as a form of psychological abuse. She claimed that he would share extracts from these diaries with the group to humiliate her. Under cross-examination, the woman acknowledged that the diaries were written as "love letters" to Balakrishnan, but stated that this was a result of his manipulation. The woman alleged that Balakrishnan's abuse started with kissing and escalated to sexual assault and rape. She felt powerless to refuse due to the verbal abuse and dehumanization she suffered at his hands. A former follower described Balakrishnan's belief that women were the "weakest link of bourgeois culture". Balakrishnan denies four counts of rape and seven counts of indecent assault. The trial is ongoing, with the woman's testimony providing insight into the alleged abusive dynamics within the commune. The court will continue to hear evidence as the case unfolds.

In a bizarre case of mistaken identity, a US band called "The Priests" has been confused with a group of Northern Irish clerics of the same name. The US band, which includes two women members, has been promoting their upcoming tour on music websites, with photos of the three Northern Irish priests inadvertently being used to advertise their gigs. The US band has responded to the mix-up with humor, extending "warm wishes to our brethren'The Priests'" and appreciating that the clerics recognize them as Priests despite some members being women. The band's new album, "Nothing Feels Natural", is set to be released in January and promises to expand on their lo-fi post-punk sound with influences from pop, R&B, and industrial noise. The Northern Irish priests, who debuted in 2008 with a classical album featuring traditional hymns, have also seen the funny side of the situation. Fr Eugene O'Hagan noted that fans had contacted them about tickets for the non-existent US gigs, and joked that if they were to walk out on stage, it would be a shock for both their own fan base and the US band's audience. The websites involved in the mix-up, including Songkick, have since removed the incorrect gig listings. Despite the confusion, it's clear that these two groups of "Priests" are worlds apart in terms of their music and style.

A fuel station on Stockmans Lane was robbed Saturday at 19:00 BST. Two men, one with a machete, stole cash and attempted to flee. Police arrested the 20 and 21-year-old suspects nearby. Staff were shaken but uninjured. The men were detained for robbery and possession of an offensive weapon.

A pair of golfers took the lead at the PGA Tour's final event of the year, hosted by Greg Norman at the Tiburon Golf Club. Playing alternate shots, they posted a six-under-par 66, securing a one-stroke advantage over first-round leaders Jerry Kelly and Steve Stricker. Charles Howell III and Rory Sabbatini, and Kevin Chappell and Kevin Kisner trail by four shots. Meanwhile, Lexi Thompson and Bryson DeChambeau are in 10th place at 11 under, with Thompson making history as the second woman to compete in the event. The 12-team tournament features varying strokeplay formats over three days, concluding with a better-ball format on Saturday.

A Mother's Worst Nightmare: The Dangers of Underage Drinking In a shocking and disturbing incident, a teenager from Northern Ireland was hospitalized after consuming vodka with her friends in Portadown town centre. The girl, Catherine, was found by police at around 17:00 GMT, drunk and with a head injury, just a few hours after she had left her home to go shopping with her friends. Catherine's mother, Paula, who wishes to remain anonymous to protect her daughter's identity, has spoken exclusively to the BBC about the terrifying ordeal. Paula received a call from the police on a "normal" Saturday afternoon, informing her that they had found Catherine and taken her to Craigavon Area Hospital. When Paula arrived at the hospital, she was met with a devastating sight: her daughter lying in a hospital bed, grey and soaked in wet clothes. According to Paula, Catherine had told her that she was going into town to do some shopping with her friends at around 14:30 GMT. However, it appears that the group of friends had arranged for someone to buy them a bottle of vodka, which they all contributed £2 to pay for. Catherine claimed that she did not know the person who bought the alcohol and had never had a drink before. The vodka, which cost a mere £2, had a devastating impact on Catherine. She was hospitalized overnight and required a CT scan for a head injury, as well as treatment for hypothermia. Paula has since learned that her daughter does not remember anything after consuming the alcohol, a fact that has left her shaken and scared. Paula praised the police officers who took Catherine to hospital and have since visited her at home. She expressed her gratitude for their prompt action, which potentially saved her daughter's life. "It scares me to think what could have happened if the police hadn't come across Catherine," Paula said. "She doesn't remember anything, and we've now had a full and frank discussion about how much danger she was in." The incident has highlighted the dangers of underage drinking and the ease with which young people can access alcohol. Paula emphasized that she had always trusted her daughter to make responsible decisions, but the incident has left her feeling fearful and anxious about Catherine's safety. "You cannot keep children in the house forever," Paula said. "Catherine won't be allowed out again until the trust that we had is built back up, but it won't stop me from being afraid of what could happen to her now." As Catherine begins her recovery, Paula hopes that her story will serve as a warning to other parents and young people about the risks of underage drinking. The incident has left a lasting impact on the family, and Paula is determined to rebuild the trust that was broken. However, she knows that she will never forget the sight of her daughter lying in hospital, a stark reminder of the dangers that lurk in everyday life.

Glasgow City's Champions League Hopes Dashed by Chelsea Glasgow City's European adventure came to an end on Wednesday as they suffered a defeat at the hands of English opponents Chelsea. Trailing 1-0 from the first leg, the Scottish champions found themselves further behind after Eniola Aluko's strike, with Fran Kirby and Gilly Flaherty adding to the tally. Despite the loss, City's manager, Scott Booth, was full of praise for his team's performance. "I'm proud of my team, I think they've done great," said Booth. "Each year, in the Champions League, we come across teams like that. Last season it was PSG that put Glasgow City out, this season it's Chelsea." Booth acknowledged the significant gulf in finance and resources between the two teams, but was impressed by his players' commitment and dedication. "We were totally committed again, over the two legs. I'm not disappointed in my team one bit. We did very, very well and I'm still proud of them." Booth identified pace as a key factor in Chelsea's victory, stating that "at times, just that little bit of pace" made all the difference. "Even defensively, they've got quick players. I think that, at times, has been the difference." Despite this, Booth was pleased with his team's approach to the game, saying "we commit everything to this club and that gives me loads of energy to keep going for them." This was Booth's first Champions League campaign as City boss, having taken over from Eddie Wolecki Black in July. He expressed his enjoyment of the experience, saying "I'm loving it, I really am. They're brilliant to work for. I feel like I work for them." Booth also highlighted the growth of the women's game, stating "every year, you feel that the women's game is getting stronger and stronger. It certainly is in our country and there's lots of good players coming through." As Glasgow City's season comes to a close, Booth will be looking to build on the team's performance and continue to grow the women's game in Scotland. With a dedicated squad and a passionate manager, the future looks bright for the Scottish champions. Despite the disappointment of their Champions League exit, Booth's pride in his team is evident, and he will be eager to see them bounce back stronger than ever in the coming season.

Murray Brothers Set to Make History at Wimbledon The Murray brothers, Andy and Jamie, are likely to make history at this year's Wimbledon Championships by competing together in the doubles tournament. According to their mother, Judy Murray, the pair will "have a crack" at playing doubles together at the Grand Slam event. This would be the first time the brothers have played together in a Grand Slam tournament, despite previously partnering in other competitions such as the Davis Cup and Olympics. Jamie, 31, is currently one of the top-ranked doubles players, having reached the top spot in March and winning two Grand Slams in 2016. Andy, 30, is the current world number one in singles, having won three Grand Slams and two Olympic gold medals. Judy Murray believes that the brothers will play together at Wimbledon before they end their careers, driven by their desire to win big titles. The Murray brothers' potential partnership has generated excitement among tennis fans, who are eager to see the siblings compete together on the biggest stage. With Andy set to defend his singles title at Wimbledon, which begins on July 3, the possibility of the brothers playing doubles together adds an extra layer of anticipation to the tournament.

A federal appeals court in California has revived a lawsuit against Internet Brands, the operator of modeling website Model Mayhem, in a decision that could have significant implications for online companies. The lawsuit, filed by a woman known as Jane Doe, claims that she was drugged and raped by two men who contacted her through the website in 2011. According to court documents, Jane Doe had created a profile on Model Mayhem as an aspiring model and was invited to a casting session, which turned out to be a sham. The lawsuit alleges that Internet Brands was aware that people were using the website to target and lure women into similar situations, but failed to warn its members. Two men were jailed in 2012 for running a similar scam, and Jane Doe claims that Internet Brands had knowledge of these activities but did not take adequate steps to protect its users. The lawsuit argues that Internet Brands was negligent under California law by failing to warn its members about the potential dangers. Internet Brands had initially succeeded in having the lawsuit dismissed in 2014, citing the US Communications Decency Act (CDA), which protects websites from being held responsible for content posted by their users. The company argued that it was not liable for the actions of the men who contacted Jane Doe through the website. Online giants such as eBay and Facebook had also weighed in on the case, warning that the lawsuit could have a "chilling effect" on the internet. However, the federal appeals court has now overturned the dismissal, ruling that the lawsuit does not concern the content posted on Model Mayhem, but rather Internet Brands' failure to warn its users about the potential dangers. The court noted that Internet Brands could have taken steps to warn its users, such as posting a notice on the website or sending an email alert. The case will now proceed to a trial court, which will decide whether the "failure to warn" lawsuit can go ahead. The decision has significant implications for online companies, which may be held liable for failing to protect their users from harm, even if they are not directly responsible for the content posted on their websites. The case highlights the importance of online companies taking steps to protect their users and warn them about potential dangers. As the lawsuit proceeds, it will be closely watched by the tech industry and could have far-reaching consequences for online companies and their users.

US New Home Sales Reach Six-Year High, Defying Expectations According to the Commerce Department, sales of new homes in the US have surged to their highest level since May 2008. The seasonally adjusted annual sales rate rose by 18.6% to 504,000, exceeding economist predictions. This uptick suggests that the housing market may be regaining momentum after a slowdown in the second half of 2013. However, the S&P/Case-Shiller index revealed that house price increases slowed in April, with a 0.2% rise on a seasonally-adjusted basis and a 10.8% annual increase. David M. Blitzer, chairman of the Index Committee at S&P Dow Jones Indices, noted that while prices are still rising, the annual gains have weakened. Despite this, recent data indicates that the housing market is starting to improve. Cooper Hawes from Barclays Research described the new homes figure as "the strongest level since the end of the recession" and an "encouraging sign" of improved housing activity in the second quarter. Additionally, sales of previously owned homes saw their largest increase in over three-and-a-half years in May, further supporting the notion of a rebounding housing market.

Veteran cricketer Marcus Trescothick has expressed his desire to continue playing for Somerset. With over 800 appearances for the county, the 40-year-old is eager to extend his career. Trescothick has had a storied career, playing 76 Tests and 123 one-day internationals for England. He stated, "I'm really enjoying my cricket and I still have the hunger to succeed." As Somerset enters an exciting period with emerging talent, Trescothick is looking forward to the next 12 months. The 2017 season will mark his 25th year with the first team, a testament to his dedication and passion for the sport.

Former Oldham Athletic player Jack Tuohy has been found not guilty of five sexual offences against a child. The 20-year-old midfielder was accused of engaging in sexual activity with a child, causing or inciting a child to engage in sexual activity, and meeting with a child following sexual grooming. Tuohy claimed he believed the girl was 16 and denied her claim that she told him her real age. A jury at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court took just an hour to deliver the verdict. The allegations dated back to 2015 when Tuohy met the girl at a schools tournament hosted by Oldham Athletic. Tuohy's family released a statement saying his life had been "on hold" for 18 months, causing him "severe stress." They have asked for privacy so Tuohy can resume his promising career. The verdict brings an end to a lengthy and stressful ordeal for Tuohy.

BBC One has announced that six additional episodes of the popular sitcom Still Game have been commissioned, with the eighth series set to air in 2017. The show, which follows the antics of Glaswegian pensioners Jack Jarvis and Victor McDade, will be filmed in Dumbarton and on location around Glasgow. The news comes after the show's highly successful return to the BBC in October, which attracted its highest ever overnight audience for a single episode. The live shows at the SSE Hydro in Glasgow also saw huge demand, with five extra dates added to the February run of performances. Written and created by its stars Greg Hemphill and Ford Kiernan, the comedy originally ran for six series between 2002 and 2007. The new series will see the return of the core cast, including Paul Riley, Jane McCarry, Mark Cox, Sanjeev Kohli, and Gavin Mitchell. Kiernan expressed his excitement about the show's return, stating that he and Hemphill have been working on "absolute corkers" and can't wait to share them with the audience. Hemphill added that they have "lots of surprises in store" for viewers. Filming at BBC Scotland's Dumbarton Studios is set to begin in the summer. Shane Allen, the controller of comedy commissioning at BBC Scotland, praised the show's enduring popularity, saying that it's "rare for a show to attain the status of comedy classic whilst it's still on air." With the show's previous audience figures in mind, Allen jokingly warned that the national grid may struggle to handle the demand. Fans of the show can look forward to more hilarious adventures with Jack and Victor in 2017.

A 70-year-old former teacher, Patrick Marshall, has been found guilty of multiple counts of indecent assault against young boys and teenagers. The incidents occurred between 1969 and 1981, while Marshall taught at Windsor Grammar School and later at St Paul's in Barnes. The Southwark Crown Court heard that the assaults took place in various locations, including Marshall's car, the victims' homes, and abroad. One witness testified that he was assaulted by Marshall at a secluded school building, describing feeling "intense discomfort" and being unsure of how to stop the abuse. After a six-week trial, a jury of seven men and five women delivered a unanimous verdict, convicting Marshall of 24 counts of indecent assault and one count of indecency with a child. Marshall, a father of three, showed visible distress as the verdicts were read out.

A 45-year-old man from York, John O'Neill, has been given a strict set of conditions to follow after a judge deemed him a risk to women. Despite being cleared of rape at Teesside Crown Court in November last year, District Judge Adrian Lower imposed 12 conditions on Mr O'Neill, including requiring him to inform police "as soon as is reasonably practicable" if he intends to form a sexual relationship with a partner. Mr O'Neill's internet usage will also be monitored by North Yorkshire Police, and he is not allowed to discuss his fantasies and sadomasochistic tendencies with medical staff without a third party present. The judge described Mr O'Neill as a "manipulative man" and stated that he is "quite satisfied" that Mr O'Neill poses a risk to women. The conditions were imposed as part of a sexual risk order, which was applied for by North Yorkshire Police after Mr O'Neill made comments to health professionals that raised concerns. During an earlier hearing, the court heard details of confessions made by Mr O'Neill to medical staff, including choking a woman unconscious and thinking about killing her. Mr O'Neill has expressed his intention to possibly appeal against the order, stating that he has complied with it due to the "threat of prison". He also claimed that every medical assessment has determined him to be no risk, and that the new law allows predictive allegations of sex crimes to be dealt with in a civil court rather than a criminal one. North Yorkshire Police have defended their actions, stating that the sexual risk order and prohibitions applied show that the force has taken the "correct course of action" to protect the public from the risk posed by Mr O'Neill. The case highlights the use of civil orders to manage individuals who are deemed to pose a risk to others, even if they have not been convicted of a crime. Mr O'Neill's situation has sparked debate about the balance between public protection and individual rights.
Two men, Tosief Ahmed, 21, and Asad Majeed, 22, died in a crash near junction 21 on Sunday, prompting a police appeal for witnesses.

England's women's hockey team secured a crucial victory over Germany in their Pool A encounter, thanks to Jo Hunter's decisive goal in the third quarter. This win marks their second triumph in the tournament, following a 3-0 victory over Poland in the opening match.
