Despite a subsequent 1-0 loss to Japan, England remains in contention, sitting second in the table. Head coach Danny Kerry praised his team's performance, saying, "This evening we were exceptional at being intelligent, fast and constantly threatening." Captain Alex Danson, who bravely continued playing after taking a blow to the head, added, "We are delighted. It was a fantastic performance against a great Germany side." England will face Ireland in their final group match on Sunday. The top four teams from each pool will advance to the quarter-finals on Tuesday, with four teams ultimately qualifying for the World League Finals in New Zealand in November.

UK Service Sector Sees Slight Uptick, but Growth Remains Sluggish The UK's service sector has shown a slight improvement in growth, with the latest Markit/CIPS services Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) rising to 53.7 in March. This is up from February's near three-year low of 52.7, and indicates a moderate expansion in the sector. However, despite this uptick, growth remains sluggish, with global economic uncertainty and the upcoming EU referendum weighing on the sector. The service sector is a crucial component of the UK economy, accounting for more than three-quarters of the country's economic output. However, the latest survey suggests that the sector's growth is being hindered by concerns about the global economy and domestic uncertainty. The Markit/CIPS survey found that growth in new business in the service sector hit its slowest pace since January 2013. According to Chris Williamson, chief economist at Markit, the surveys indicate a slowdown in economic growth in the first quarter, with GDP expected to increase by just 0.4%. This is down from 0.6% in the previous quarter. Williamson noted that business confidence remains low, with concerns about the global economy and uncertainty at home, including the prospect of Brexit and further government spending cuts. As a result, it is unlikely that the slight uptick in growth seen in March will mark the start of a longer-term upswing. Instead, the survey data suggests that growth is likely to weaken further in the second quarter.

Paralympic Champion Kadeena Cox Among New Year Honours Recipients The New Year Honours list has been announced, and several notable athletes have been recognized for their outstanding contributions to their respective sports. Olympic boxers Nicola Adams and Ed Clancy, who are already Members of the British Empire (MBE), have been appointed Officers of the British Empire (OBE) for their services to boxing and cycling. Cyclist Brian Robinson, a pioneering figure in British cycling, has been awarded a British Empire Medal (BEM) for his services to the sport and charity work. Robinson made history by becoming the first Briton to win a Tour de France stage. Paralympic medallist Kadeena Cox, 25, from Leeds, has been awarded an MBE for her services to athletics. Cox, who won four medals in Rio, including a gold in the T38 400m sprint, expressed her delight at the honour, saying it was "the cherry on top" of an already incredible year. She hopes her recognition will inspire young people in her community to pursue their dreams and "break the mould". Other athletes honoured include Paralympians Stephen Bate and Adam Duggleby, who receive MBEs for services to cycling, and Paul Bennett, who is recognized for his services to rowing. Olympic diver Christopher Mears is also set to receive an MBE for his contributions to diving. The New Year Honours list recognizes the achievements of individuals from various fields, and these athletes are a testament to the excellence and dedication that exists in British sports.

A medical charity hospital in the rebel-held town of Maarat al-Numan, Syria, was attacked on Monday, resulting in the disappearance of eight staff members and the deaths of at least nine people, including a child. The hospital, which was supported by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), was hit by four rockets within minutes of each other, causing significant damage and destruction. According to MSF, the hospital had 54 staff members, including doctors and nurses, and provided medical services to the local population of around 40,000 people. The facility had two operating theaters, an outpatients department, and an emergency room, making it a vital healthcare provider in the area. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, a UK-based monitoring group, reported that Russian aircraft had targeted the town, resulting in the deaths and injuries. However, MSF did not identify who was responsible for the attack. The strike comes just days after Russia and other world powers agreed to a limited cessation of hostilities in Syria, aimed at reducing violence and allowing humanitarian aid to reach affected areas. The conflict in Syria has resulted in the deaths of over 250,000 people and the displacement of 11 million others, with forces loyal to President Bashar al-Assad and those opposed to his rule battling each other, as well as jihadist militants from the so-called Islamic State (IS). MSF condemned the attack in the strongest possible terms, stating that it appeared to be a deliberate attack on a health structure. The organization's head of mission in Syria, Massimiliano Rebaudengo, said that the destruction of the hospital would leave the local population without access to medical services in an active zone of conflict. This is not the first time an MSF-supported hospital has been attacked in Syria. On February 5, a hospital in the southern province of Deraa was hit in an air strike, resulting in the deaths of three people and injuring six others. MSF has reported that 14 health facilities in Syria have been hit since the start of the year, further depleting the country's already exhausted healthcare system and preventing people from accessing desperately needed medical care. The repeated attacks on medical facilities in the ongoing conflict constitute a flagrant violation of international laws, according to MSF. The organization has called for an immediate end to the targeting of healthcare facilities and for all parties to the conflict to respect the neutrality of medical staff and facilities. As the conflict in Syria continues, the need for humanitarian aid and protection of medical facilities has never been more urgent.

Rolling Stone Managing Editor Will Dana has issued a formal apology to readers and those affected by the magazine's discredited article about a gang rape at the University of Virginia. The November 2014 piece, "A Rape on Campus," sparked widespread outrage and protests, but was later found to be based on unverified claims. A four-month police investigation found no evidence to support the allegations of a gang rape at the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity house in 2012. While police chief Timothy Longo acknowledged that the lack of evidence did not necessarily mean that nothing happened to the student known as Jackie, the article's credibility was severely damaged. An independent report by the Columbia School of Journalism, commissioned by Rolling Stone, described the article as "a story of journalistic failure." The report criticized the magazine's failure to verify the details of the story, which relied heavily on Jackie's account. The journalist who wrote the piece, Sabrina Erdely, did not contact the alleged attackers, and subsequent investigations by other reporters and Erdely herself identified errors in the reporting. The Columbia report said that Rolling Stone's failures were "systematic" and encompassed reporting, editing, editorial supervision, and fact-checking. The article's publication was widely criticized for spreading the idea that many women invent rape allegations, which undermined efforts to stop sexual violence. Dana described the report as "painful reading" and apologized to all those affected by the story, including members of the Phi Kappa Psi fraternity and University of Virginia administrators and students. Erdely also issued a statement apologizing for her role in the article's publication. The magazine has committed to implementing the report's recommendations to improve its journalistic practices. The incident highlights the importance of rigorous fact-checking and verification in journalism, particularly when reporting on sensitive topics like sexual violence. As Dana noted, sexual assault is a serious problem on college campuses, and it is crucial that victims feel comfortable coming forward without fear of being disbelieved or ridiculed. Rolling Stone's failure to uphold basic journalistic standards has damaged the trust of its readers and may have unintended consequences for victims of sexual violence.

Afghanistan Mourns After Deadly Islamic State Attack on Hazara Minority A day of national mourning has been declared in Afghanistan after a devastating attack on a gathering of Shia Muslim Hazara minority in Kabul. The so-called Islamic State (IS) has claimed responsibility for the attack, which left many dead and injured. The attack occurred on Saturday in Deh Mazang square, where thousands of Hazaras were protesting against a new power line that bypasses provinces where many of them live. In a televised address, President Ashraf Ghani vowed to take revenge against those responsible for the attack, describing it as a brutal act of terrorism. The United Nations mission in Afghanistan has also condemned the attack, calling it a "war crime" that targeted a large number of civilians. Tadamichi Yamamoto, head of the UN assistance mission, expressed his outrage and sadness at the senseless killing of innocent people. The IS-linked Amaq news agency claimed that two fighters had detonated explosive belts at the gathering, intentionally targeting the Shia minority. This is the first time that IS has admitted to carrying out an attack in the capital, and it is seen as an attempt to foment sectarian strife in the country. The Taliban, Afghanistan's most prominent Islamist militant group, has condemned the attack, distancing themselves from the violence. The Hazara minority has long faced discrimination and persecution in Afghanistan, and this attack has sparked widespread outrage and condemnation. The government has promised to take action against those responsible and to protect the rights of all citizens, including the Hazara minority. As the country mourns the loss of life, there are fears that this attack could escalate tensions and violence in the region. The international community has urged calm and restraint, and has called for those responsible to be brought to justice.

Merthyr coach Lee Jarvis has revealed that former Wales coach Nigel Davies is in talks to join the team. Although the specifics of Davies' potential role are unclear, Jarvis confirmed that discussions have taken place. Davies has met with Merthyr chairman Sir Stanley Thomas, sparking speculation about his involvement. Meanwhile, Jarvis and assistant Dale McIntosh are focused on the upcoming Welsh Premiership final against Aberavon on May 21. Merthyr finished third in the regular season, and the coaching duo is concentrated on securing a win, leaving discussions about Davies' potential appointment for another time.

Team Jets Set to Begin New Campaign Without Key Players The island's top netball team, Team Jets, are preparing to kick off their second season in the second tier of English club netball without three of their key players. Abbie Hazley, Sophie Holmes, and Georgia Hickey will not be part of the squad due to personal commitments. Hazley recently got married, Holmes has taken up a new job, and Hickey will be spending more time off the island, making it impossible for them to commit to the team's training and match schedule. Coach Andrews expressed that the team was "gelling really well" last season, but the loss of these players will require adjustments. "We'll probably look to try and consolidate and give more girls court time," she told BBC Radio Jersey. Despite the setback, Andrews remains optimistic about the team's chances, although she acknowledges that promotion may be a more challenging goal without the full squad. The door is still open for new players to join the team, with Andrews actively scouting for talent in the local league. "I've been looking to see if there's somebody out there who hasn't put their name forward yet and is of the right calibre," she said. Team Jets will open their campaign at home to Telstars on Sunday, 2 October, and Andrews invites any interested players to attend their open training sessions. With a mix of experienced players and new talent, the team is ready to face the challenges of the new season.

US Economy Sees Significant Job Growth, Boosting Dollar and Japan's Nikkei Index The US economy has exceeded expectations with a significant addition of 271,000 jobs in October, surpassing the forecast of 185,000 jobs by economists. This substantial growth has given the US dollar a considerable boost, particularly against the yen, which is expected to benefit Japan's major exporters. The weaker yen makes Japanese goods cheaper for overseas buyers, providing a competitive edge in the global market. The strong job numbers in the US have also reinforced expectations of a rate hike by the Federal Reserve in December. According to Evan Lucas from IG Markets, the recent testimony by Fed Chair Janet Yellen and the impressive non-farm payrolls have realigned the year's expectations, which initially anticipated at least one rate hike. This development has contributed to the strengthening of the US dollar, which is likely to have a ripple effect on global markets. In Asia, the impact of the US job growth was evident, with Japan's Nikkei index closing up 1.96% at 19,642.74. However, other markets in the region were not as fortunate. The S&P/ASX 200 index in Australia closed down 1.83% at 5,119.50 points, primarily due to falling commodity prices. South Korea's Kospi index also closed down 0.75% at 2,025.70 points. Meanwhile, in Australia, mining giant BHP Billiton's shares took a significant hit, closing down 5.64% on Monday. The decline followed a fatal accident at an iron ore operation in Brazil, which is jointly owned by BHP and Vale. The incident resulted in the collapse of two dams holding waste water, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. BHP has confirmed at least one fatality and 13 missing workers, with details still emerging. In China, investors were closely watching the markets following disappointing trade numbers and the lifting of a five-month ban on mainland initial public offerings (IPOs). The Shanghai Composite closed up 1.58% at 3,646.88, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng index ended down 0.6% to 22,726.77 points. China's imports have declined for the 12th consecutive month, with a drop of 18.8% in October, raising concerns about the country's economic growth. Exports also fell by 6.9%, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline. Despite the disappointing trade numbers, shares of China International Capital Corp (CICC) made a positive debut in Hong Kong, finishing up 1.1% after being higher by as much as 6% in early trade. The state-backed lender raised $811m in its IPO last month, providing a glimmer of hope in an otherwise uncertain market. As global markets continue to navigate the complexities of economic growth, trade, and monetary policy, investors will be closely watching the developments in the US, Asia, and beyond.

A 31-year-old woman, Katy McAllister, has been found not guilty of causing the death of Louise McGowan at a tattoo parlour in Dundee. The verdict was delivered at the High Court in Edinburgh, where McAllister had been accused of culpable homicide. Prosecutors had alleged that McAllister had administered drugs to Mrs McGowan, who died a day later after suffering a cardiac arrest. However, Judge Graham Buchanan QC ruled that the prosecution had failed to provide sufficient evidence to support the charge. McAllister was convicted of other drug-related offences, including supplying or offering to supply Diazepam and Temazepam to other individuals. She also pleaded guilty to possessing magic mushrooms and the controlled drug Midazolam at her home. The court heard that Mrs McGowan had been anxious about getting a tattoo at Voodoo Tattoo in Dundee's Perth Road, where she had taken the drugs. The defence argued that the prosecution had not presented enough evidence to link McAllister to Mrs McGowan's death, and Judge Buchanan agreed. The acquittal prompted the crown lawyers to consider an appeal, but they ultimately decided not to pursue it. McAllister will be sentenced for the drug offences at the High Court in Glasgow next month. Judge Buchanan described the evidence against her as "somewhat concerning" and noted that there were "troubling aspects" to her recent activities. The case has raised concerns about the dangers of drug use and the importance of ensuring that those who supply drugs are held accountable.

Tragedy struck on the A57 Snake Pass on Sunday evening when a three-vehicle accident claimed the lives of two young men. Ehtisham Hanif, 29, from Sheffield, and Joshua Rosenberg, 18, from Winsford, were killed in the crash. The accident occurred when the BMW Mr. Hanif was in, which was reportedly driving erratically, collided with other vehicles. Five people were taken to hospital, with several suffering serious injuries. The road was closed until 07:00 on Monday to allow emergency services to clear the debris. Police are investigating the incident, which also involved a second, non-injury collision between a Vauxhall Corsa and a Volkswagen Polo. The community is in shock following the loss of two young lives in this devastating accident.

UK Farmers Face Uncertainty Over EU Subsidies. The UK's potential exit from the European Union has sparked concerns among farmers. The EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) provides subsidies to farmers, ensuring a stable food supply. The EU spends £42 billion on agriculture annually, with £3.2 billion coming from the UK. Those in favor of leaving the EU argue that this is too much and the saved funds could be allocated elsewhere. However, proponents of remaining in the EU worry that farmers may lose out on crucial cash if the UK leaves. The decision could significantly impact farming and everyday life. Farmers like Baa-rry the sheep and Moo-reen the cow are waiting anxiously to see how the outcome will affect their livelihoods.

Swansea City's struggles in the Premier League continued on Saturday as they suffered a humiliating 4-0 defeat at the hands of Arsenal. The loss has left the team at the foot of the table, and manager Paul Clement is looking to bolster his squad with new signings. Defender Martin Olsson from Norwich and midfielder Tom Carroll from Tottenham Hotspur are set to join the Swans, with midfielder Jack Cork welcoming the new additions. "It's always nice in January to get new bodies in, new faces and fresh legs," said Cork. "It will be good to see how they fit in. It's good to have different people around the club and hopefully that can give us a bit of a lift." Cork is particularly familiar with Carroll, having played alongside him during his loan spell at Swansea in the 2014-15 season. "He's a good player, has good quality. He's good on the ball, with good technique. Hopefully he will fit in well with the team," Cork added. However, despite the incoming signings, Swansea face a tough relegation fight and Cork is aware that the club must hold onto their key players. Gylfi Sigurdsson and Fernando Llorente are once again being linked with moves away from the club, with Everton and Chelsea respectively showing interest. "It's definitely important (we keep them)," said Cork. "Gylfi has scored or assisted nearly all of our goals. He's a huge part of this team. Fernando has scored a few as well. We need to keep hold of them if we can." The Swans' defensive record is a major concern, having conceded 49 goals in 21 games, the worst record in the top-flight. Cork believes that it is the responsibility of the entire team to stop leaking goals. "It's all of us really," he said. "We are trying to work hard to stop it. It just seems once one goes in, heads go down and it is hard to get going. We really need to, when we concede a goal, stick together, keep our shape, and make it harder to concede the second one." With the January transfer window in full swing, Swansea City will be hoping to bring in some much-needed reinforcements to aid their survival bid.

Scottish Golfer David Drysdale Hopes to Continue Fine Form at Scottish Open As the Scottish Open gets underway at Dundonald Links on Thursday, David Drysdale is looking to build on his impressive recent form. The 42-year-old Scot, who finished joint fourth at the Irish Open on Sunday, is feeling confident and optimistic about his chances. Drysdale's success can be attributed, in part, to the influence of his caddie, Vicky, who has been providing a unique perspective on his game. According to Drysdale, Vicky's positive and determined approach has been a significant factor in his improved performance. "She is so positive and determined," he said. "It's been working well, so I hope it continues." Vicky's influence extends beyond just providing technical advice, as she is not afraid to offer a "kick up the backside" when needed. This honest approach has been a refreshing change for Drysdale, who acknowledges that some of his previous caddies may have been hesitant to speak their minds. Drysdale's recent results have been impressive, with a top-20 finish at the French Open and a joint fourth place finish at the Irish Open. His performance at the Irish Open was particularly notable, as he carded seven birdies in his final seven holes to secure his place at The Open at Royal Birkdale, starting on July 20. This consistent form has Drysdale feeling hopeful about his chances at the Scottish Open, an event he considers to be one of the highlights of his calendar. As a regular on the European Tour for the past nine years, Drysdale has had his share of successes and setbacks. However, he believes that he is now finding a nice rhythm at the right time, with several major events on the horizon. His best result to date was a second-place finish at the 2009 Open de Andalucía, but he is eager to improve on this and make a strong showing at the Scottish Open. Consistency has been the key to Drysdale's success, and he is aware that he needs to put together four solid rounds to achieve his goals. While he has had some impressive individual rounds, he has struggled to maintain this level of performance over the course of a entire tournament. Despite this, Drysdale remains optimistic and is looking forward to the challenge of the Scottish Open. For Drysdale, the Scottish Open is more than just another tournament - it's an opportunity to compete in front of his home crowd and make a strong impression. "Certainly, the Scottish Open for me is the biggest event I look forward to every year," he said. "I really enjoy it and have great support from all the Scottish fans." With Vicky by his side and his recent form to build on, Drysdale is ready to take on the best golfers in the world and make a strong showing at Dundonald Links.

Russian President Dmitry Medvedev has appointed Sergei Sobyanin, a 52-year-old former governor and chief of staff, as the new mayor of Moscow. Sobyanin's appointment comes after the sudden dismissal of Yuri Luzhkov, who had held the position since 1992. Luzhkov's removal was reportedly due to Medvedev's loss of trust in the longtime mayor, who had been facing intense criticism from state-run TV channels over issues such as traffic congestion and the demolition of historic buildings. Luzhkov, 74, and his billionaire wife, Yelena Baturina, have also been accused of corruption, which they have vehemently denied. The former mayor has threatened to sue the TV channels that aired the allegations, calling them "total rubbish" designed to discredit him. Medvedev announced Sobyanin's appointment at a meeting at the presidential country residence in Gorki, outside Moscow, on Friday. The president urged Sobyanin to prioritize addressing Moscow's most pressing problems, including corruption and traffic jams. Sobyanin's experience in running a major Russian region, as well as his background as chief of staff to former President Vladimir Putin, make him a strong candidate for the position. While Sobyanin still needs to be confirmed by Moscow's city legislators, the vote is expected to be a formality due to the dominance of the pro-Kremlin United Russia party in the parliament. Sobyanin's appointment may also signal a further consolidation of power for Putin, who has hinted at a possible return to the presidency in the 2012 elections. With Sobyanin at the helm of Moscow, Putin's influence is likely to remain strong in the run-up to the elections.

The Round the Island Race saw a dramatic day of rescues on Saturday. The 16 lifeboats on duty responded to several emergencies, including a man overboard, head injuries, sea sickness, and a broken arm. The Portland coastguard helicopter airlifted two individuals, including a competitor and a lifeboat crew member. A competing yacht ran aground off Ventnor, but was towed to safety by lifeboats from Sandown and Bembridge. Over 1,500 vessels participated in the annual event, with more than 100 retiring before completing the circuit. Fortunately, the rescue efforts ensured a safe outcome for all involved.

A shocking leaked document has revealed that call handlers at the South East Coast Ambulance trust (Secamb) were instructed to inform patients that ambulances had been dispatched, even when they had not. The document, which is set to be published by NHS England on Thursday, raises serious concerns about the trust's handling of emergency calls and the potential harm caused to patients. The trust had been operating a secret pilot project, known as R3/G5, which involved transferring certain 111 calls to the 999 system in order to gain up to 10 additional minutes to assess patients' conditions. However, this project was launched without the knowledge of 111 staff, board non-executives, the medical director, or local commissioners of services. The document examines seven "serious incidents" related to the project, including the death of a 60-year-old man from Horsham who had suffered a cardiac arrest. The report found that there was a "missed opportunity" to improve the man's outcome and that the trust's efforts to check whether harm was done to patients were neither "appropriate" nor safe. The document also states that it is impossible to conclude that patients were not harmed by the project, as all the facts are not known for the calls that went unanswered or for the callers who experienced significant delays. The Patients Association has condemned the trust's actions, with Chief Executive Katherine Murphy describing the reports as "truly shocking". She stated that there had been a "complete disregard for patient safety" through a policy that had put thousands of patients at risk. Health regulator Monitor has also added a condition to Secamb's licence, which could result in the leadership team being changed if insufficient progress is made to address the concerns. Despite the serious findings, Secamb has defended the project, with Chief Executive Paul Sutton stating that the purpose of the process was to protect patient safety by ensuring that the most seriously ill patients received the care they needed as quickly as possible. However, the trust has acknowledged that the project was not properly communicated to staff or stakeholders, and that the handling of emergency calls was not always adequate. The council of governors at Secamb met with the trust's chairman, chief executive, and non-executive directors on Tuesday to discuss the issue and was given further information on the grounds for concerns and the process that will follow. Brian Rockell, Secamb's lead governor, expressed confidence that the process outlined will allow the council to fulfill its statutory duties and be assured that a quality service is provided to patients. The incident has raised serious questions about the trust's handling of emergency calls and the potential harm caused to patients. The publication of the leaked document on Thursday is expected to shed further light on the issue, and it remains to be seen what actions will be taken to address the concerns raised. One thing is certain, however: the trust must take immediate action to ensure that patient safety is prioritized and that emergency calls are handled in a timely and effective manner.

Border staff at UK airports have been instructed to confiscate tobacco and alcohol from passengers who exceed their duty-free limit, regardless of how small the excess may be. However, staff have expressed concerns over the paperwork involved in such seizures, arguing that it is not cost-effective and may lead to confrontations with passengers. A report by the Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration, David Bolt, found that staff at Terminal 5 were using their discretion in some cases, allowing passengers to keep their goods if they were only slightly over the limit. In one instance, two women, one of whom was elderly, were found to be carrying excess cigarettes and tobacco but were allowed to pay the duty and keep their goods. Senior managers have expressed disappointment that staff are not adhering to the "zero tolerance" rules, but staff argue that a more flexible approach is needed to avoid alienating passengers. The report highlights the challenges faced by border staff, who are often called away from customs channels to assist with immigration controls, making it difficult for them to function efficiently without exercising discretion. Despite this, senior managers insist that a hard-line approach is necessary, citing the increasing use of intelligence-led customs work.

Hate Crimes Surge in Manchester Following Arena Bombing A disturbing trend has emerged in Manchester, as the city struggles to come to terms with the devastating bombing at the Manchester Arena on Monday. According to Greater Manchester Police (GMP), a total of 56 hate crimes were reported on Wednesday, a significant increase from the 28 incidents recorded on Monday. Chief Constable Ian Hopkins has acknowledged the rise, stating that while there is no direct link to the bombing, the force is closely monitoring the situation. The bombing, which claimed the lives of 22 people, including seven children, has sparked widespread condemnation and an outpouring of support for the affected families. However, it has also led to a surge in hate incidents, with many targeting the Muslim community. A GMP log obtained by the BBC reveals a string of disturbing incidents, including racist and Islamophobic attacks. Despite the rise in hate crimes, Chief Constable Hopkins has praised the city's resilience and compassion, saying that the community has largely come together in the aftermath of the attack. He has also reached out to faith leaders and places of worship, thanking them for their support and emphasizing that hate crime will not be tolerated. "It is essential that people report any incidents so that they can be investigated, and we can support victims and their families," he said. Mohammed Ullah, a Muslim chaplain at Manchester Metropolitan University, has expressed concern over the reported figures, suggesting that many more incidents may be going unreported due to fear. "These are just the reported figures, other people are very scared to talk," he said. As the city continues to heal and rebuild, it is clear that addressing hate crime and promoting unity and understanding will be a crucial part of the recovery process.

Tri o weithwyr ym meithrinfa Bright Sparks ym Mhort Talbot wedi eu dod o dan ymchwiliad am honiadau o greulondeb at blant, ond maent wedi cael eu rhyddhau o'r cyhuddiadau. Katie Davies, perchennog y feithrinfa, a'i chydweithwyr, Shelbie Forgan a Christina Pinchess, oedd y tri a gafodd eu cyhuddo o fod yn greulon tuag at blant dan 16 oed. Cafodd ymchwiliad ei gynnal yn dilyn honiadau gan bedwar myfyriwr bod plant yn cael eu cam-drin yn y feithrinfa. Yn ystod yr achos yn Llys y Goron Abertawe, clywodd y llys bod myfyrwyr wedi "gorliwio" yr hyn a welsant yn y feithrinfa. Cyhoeddwyd hefyd bod Ms Davies wedi gwneud cwyn yn erbyn dau o'r myfyrwyr I'w tiwtor. Y Barnwr Geraint Walters a diolchodd I'r rheithgor am eu gwaith yn yr achos, gan ddweud "Ar ôl clywed y dystiolaeth, gallaf ddweud bod hwn yn amlwg yn achos oedd angen ei ymchwilio - nid oes amheuaeth o hynny." Ychwanegodd nad oes "dim cwestiynau" I'w ofyn am y ffordd y mae'r heddlu wedi cynnal eu hymholiadau. Ar ddiwedd yr achos, fe safodd y tri diffynnydd ar risiau tu allan I'r llys, tra darllenodd y cyfreithiwr, Giles Hayes, ddatganiad ar eu rhan. "Mae'r tair sy'n sefyll nesaf I mi yma yn gymeriadau hollol di-fai, ac mae eu bywydau wedi cael eu troi ben I waered," meddai. Y feithrinfa ym Mhort Talbot gaeodd y llynedd yn dilyn y pryderon, ond mae'r tri merch bellach yn gobeithio gallu rhoi'r achos y tu ôl iddynt er mwyn symud ymlaen gyda'u gyrfaoedd. Mae eu cyfreithiwr wedi galw am ymchwiliad llawer mwy trylwyr cyn iddo ddilyn y broses I'r llysoedd troseddol.

Oxford University Vice-Chancellor Louise Richardson has expressed reservations about the government's proposal to involve universities in setting up and running schools. The proposal, part of the government's plans to expand grammar schools, suggests that universities should either sponsor a school or help establish a new one in order to charge higher tuition fees. However, Prof Richardson believes that this would be a "distraction from our core mission" and that Oxford University should focus on what it does best: delivering higher education. According to Prof Richardson, Oxford University has "no experience" of running schools, and it would be inappropriate for the university to take on this responsibility. She emphasized that the university is "very good" at running a university, but that its expertise lies in higher education, not in primary or secondary education. Prof Richardson also noted that it would be "insulting" to head teachers and school leaders to suggest that universities could do a better job of running schools. The government's proposal is part of its efforts to improve social mobility through education. The idea is that universities can harness their expertise to improve schools and drive social mobility. About 60 universities, including Birmingham and King's College London, already sponsor or support schools. However, Prof Richardson argued that Oxford University's extensive relationships with schools, including its outreach projects, are separate from running a school and that the university should not take on activities that would "distract our time, energy and resources". Oxford University has a strong track record of promoting social mobility through education. The university recently announced that it would be admitting the highest proportion of state school students for at least 40 years, following significant investment in outreach projects with schools. However, Prof Richardson believes that this work is distinct from running a school and that the university should prioritize its core mission. In addition to her comments on the government's proposal, Prof Richardson also emphasized the importance of free speech and allowing university students to hear views they might find "objectionable". She expressed opposition to the government's Prevent anti-extremism strategy and the idea of "safe spaces" on campus, where views that students find offensive would not be allowed. The Department for Education has defended its proposal, arguing that universities have expertise that can help improve the education system. A spokeswoman noted that there are already excellent examples of universities sponsoring schools and that it is in their own interests to improve attainment in schools. With 1.25 million children in underperforming schools, the government believes that the higher education sector can play a crucial role in making more good school places available. However, Prof Richardson's comments highlight the concerns of some universities about the government's proposal and the potential distractions from their core mission.

Scottish Racer Graham Carroll Set to Compete in World's Richest Sim Race This Sunday, 26-year-old Graham Carroll from Scotland will take part in the highly anticipated Visa Vegas eRace, a 28-lap virtual racing competition with a staggering $1 million (£812,000) in prize money. The event, which starts at 00:00 British time, will see Carroll competing against 20 professional drivers from the FIA Formula E Championship. Carroll's journey to the Visa Vegas eRace is a remarkable one. Having won two Formula Ford titles in 2008, he was forced to abandon real-life racing due to a lack of funds. However, he has since found success in the world of sim racing, and his skills have earned him a spot in the prestigious competition. Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland's Kaye Adams Programme, Carroll admitted that the high stakes are nerve-racking, but he is confident in his abilities. "These days, the simulator is pretty much as real as you're going to get," he said. "The simulators I've been using over the last few years can get you ready for driving a real car because they are so like real life." Carroll's dedication to the competition has been impressive, with the Scotsman revealing that he spent six hours a day, six days a week, preparing for the qualifying rounds. His hard work paid off, as he won the first round of the series and secured his spot in the Visa Vegas eRace. The event, which coincides with the final day of the CES tech expo in Las Vegas, promises to be an exciting and closely contested competition. With a minimum prize of $20,000 (£16,000) and the potential to earn up to $25,000 for pole position, the pressure is on. However, Carroll is ready for the challenge, and his experience and skill make him a strong contender in the world's richest sim race.

Lithuania Distributes Survival Guide Amid Fears of Russian Aggression The Lithuanian government has distributed a 75-page survival guide to tens of thousands of its citizens, warning them of the potential dangers of Russian espionage and military invasion. The guide, published by the Ministry of Defence, includes sections on spotting Russian tanks, bullets, and mines, as well as techniques for surviving in the wild. It also urges citizens to be vigilant and report any suspected spy activity to the authorities via a new telephone hotline. According to Darius Jauniskis, the head of the state security department, "every Lithuanian citizen can become a target" of spying. The guide takes a serious tone, emphasizing the importance of civilian awareness and resistance in the face of aggression. Lithuania's relations with Russia have deteriorated significantly since the annexation of Crimea in 2014, and the country has expressed fears of a potential Russian invasion. As a member of NATO since 2004, Lithuania is seeking to bolster its defences, with plans to reintroduce conscription for men aged 19-26. The country shares a border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, and NATO allies are set to send more troops and equipment to the region. The distribution of the survival guide is a clear indication of the government's concerns about the ongoing tensions with Russia, and its determination to prepare its citizens for any eventuality.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has given its stamp of approval to a new set of sports to be included in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. Skateboarding, surfing, karate, sports climbing, and baseball/softball have been dubbed "a dynamic and exciting package" by the IOC, with all five sports likely to be confirmed. A final decision is expected to be announced on August 3 in Rio de Janeiro, just two days before the 2016 Games begin. Each sport was carefully analyzed in a detailed report, which concluded that their addition would bring a mix of traditional and emerging events, popular both in Japan and internationally. The IOC hopes to attract new, younger audiences by incorporating these youth-oriented sports. The additions are also expected to have a positive impact on gender equality and leave a lasting legacy. If approved, the five new sports would add 18 events and 474 athletes to the Olympic schedule, without replacing any of the existing 28 sports. For Britain, the inclusion of sports climbing could bring medal hopes, following Shauna Coxsey's recent win in the Bouldering World Cup. Baseball and softball, which were previously included in the Olympics from 1992 to 2008, have made a joint bid to return to the Games. The IOC's decision is a significant step towards revitalizing the Olympic program and appealing to a new generation of fans.

A man in his 30s has come forward to accuse a former BBC radio presenter and her husband of sexually assaulting him when he was a teenager. The alleged victim claims to have had sex with Julie Wadsworth up to 15 times, including one incident where her husband Tony joined in. The couple, who worked for BBC Radio Leicester and BBC WM, deny the allegations. The man first met Mrs. Wadsworth when he was 14 years old in 1995, while she was sunbathing in a park. He claims that their sexual relationship continued for four years, until he was 18, with meetings arranged in secret. The alleged victim only discovered the couple's identities later, while listening to the radio and recognizing their voices as they co-presented an evening program. The man's decision to come forward was prompted by child protection training he received, which brought up memories of the incidents. He told police that he had never spoken about the alleged abuse before, but felt compelled to report it after realizing the significance of what had happened. The Wadsworths, from Broughton Astley, Leicestershire, deny five counts of outraging public decency and multiple counts of indecent assault, which allegedly took place between 1992 and 1996. Mrs. Wadsworth, 60, has pleaded not guilty to 12 charges of indecent assault, while her 69-year-old husband denies 10 counts of the same offense. The couple's trial is ongoing, with the jury watching video interviews of the alleged victim's testimony. The man's account provides a detailed and disturbing picture of the alleged abuse, which he claims occurred at the Wadsworths' home in Long Street, Atherstone. The case has sparked widespread concern and highlights the importance of reporting suspected child abuse.

A major expansion project is underway at Parc Prison in Bridgend, with the construction of a new cell block and additional facilities. The project, led by G4S, the company that runs the prison, will create 78 new jobs and increase the prison's capacity to 1,723. The new cell block will have over 200 cells and is expected to be operational by December next year. As part of the expansion, a new visitors' centre, prison workshop, and educational facilities will be built. A new car park with 350 spaces, extended perimeter walls, and security fencing will also be constructed. Preparatory work has already begun on the site, which has been in operation since 1997. According to David Morgan, managing director of G4S Care and Justice Services, the expansion will not only create new jobs but also allow more prisoners to be located closer to their homes and families, which is a key factor in rehabilitation. The Ministry of Justice gave the initial go-ahead for the project in January, and the announcement comes as part of a series of updates on UK prisons, including the planned construction of a new super-prison in Wrexham. The project is expected to have a positive impact on the local community and support the rehabilitation of prisoners.

Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has decided to retain the ban on dogs on Metrolink trams. The decision follows a consultation with over 2,400 respondents. Councillor Andrew Fender cited safety concerns, stating that not all dog owners can guarantee their pets' behavior. Assistance dogs are exempt from the ban. Despite a social media campaign by dog lovers to lift the ban, TfGM has chosen to maintain the policy, which has been in place since Metrolink's launch in 1992. The authority prioritizes passenger safety, avoiding potential nuisances or risks posed by unrestrained dogs. The ban remains in effect.

Lizzie Armitstead and Peter Sagan took the top spots in the Tour of Flanders, with impressive solo victories in the women's and men's races respectively. Armitstead, riding for Boels-Dolmans, edged out Sweden's Emma Johansson in a nail-biting finish, with the pair breaking clear on the final climb. The 27-year-old Briton's win marked her fourth victory of the season, following successes at Omloop het Nieuwsblad, Strade Bianche, and Trofeo Binda. In the men's race, Sagan dominated the field, crossing the finish line 25 seconds ahead of three-time winner Fabian Cancellara. The Slovakian cyclist dropped Sep Vanmarcke on the notorious Paterberg climb and held off Cancellara's challenge in the final 5km of the 255km race. Britain's Luke Rowe finished fifth, 48 seconds behind Sagan, while teammate Geraint Thomas came in 12th. The Tour of Flanders is one of the most prestigious one-day races in the cycling calendar, and this year's event did not disappoint. The women's race, now part of the Women's WorldTour, saw a group of nine riders unable to catch Armitstead and Johansson, who sprinted to the line in a thrilling finale. Armitstead's victory cemented her position as one of the leading female cyclists in the world, and she will look to build on this momentum in upcoming events. With Sagan's win, he proved once again why he is a force to be reckoned with in the men's peloton.

Spanish Politics Take a Personal Turn as MP Breastfeeds in Parliament In a move that has sparked both praise and criticism, Carolina Bescansa, a member of the anti-austerity Podemos party, breastfed her baby in the Spanish parliament on Wednesday. The incident occurred during the first session of parliament following the December 20 election, which saw the conservative People's Party (PP) win the most seats but fall short of a majority. Bescansa, who was standing as a candidate for speaker, had previously promised to breastfeed in parliament during her campaign. She defended her actions, stating that every parent has the right to raise their child in whatever way they choose. The MP, who has been fortunate enough to not have been separated from her baby, Diego, since his birth, asked photographers not to broadcast her child's face. However, not everyone was supportive of Bescansa's decision. Acting Interior Minister Jorge Fernandez Diaz, of the PP, criticized the move as "lamentable," while Socialist MP Carme Chacon described it as "frankly unnecessary." Some critics accused Bescansa of attention-seeking, pointing out that a nursery is available in the parliament building to help MPs manage childcare. Despite the controversy, Bescansa is not the first politician to bring her baby into parliament. In 2012, Iolanda Pineda, of the Socialists' Party of Catalonia (PSC), took her baby into Spain's upper house of parliament. Similarly, Italian politician Licia Ronziulli was pictured with her baby in the European parliament in 2010, and has since documented her daughter's growth through photos. The incident has highlighted the challenges faced by working mothers in politics. In the UK, a group of MPs recently called for a ban on breastfeeding in the House of Commons chamber to be overturned. Bescansa's actions have sparked a debate about the need for greater support and flexibility for parents in politics. Meanwhile, the formation of a government remains deadlocked. Mariano Rajoy's Popular Party is pushing for a coalition with the Socialists (PSOE) and the centre-right Ciudadanos (Citizens) party, but the Socialists are seeking a deal with Citizens and Podemos. Podemos has refused to drop its demand for a referendum on independence in Catalonia, which the two other parties reject. As the political stalemate continues, King Felipe VI may be forced to ask a party leader to form a government, which would then be put to a vote in parliament. If the main parties fail to reach an agreement, new elections may be held. For now, the country waits with bated breath as its political leaders navigate the complex web of alliances and negotiations. In the midst of this uncertainty, Bescansa's bid to become parliamentary speaker was unsuccessful. Socialist MP Patxi Lopez won the vote, becoming the first ever speaker from a party that did not win the most seats in an election. As the Spanish parliament continues to grapple with the challenges of forming a government, one thing is clear: the country's politicians will have to find a way to work together to move forward.

Army Bomb Disposal Unit Called to St Albans Home After Discovery of Explosives and Firearms A shocking discovery was made at a home in Windmill Avenue, St Albans, on Wednesday, prompting the arrival of an Army bomb disposal unit. Police officers found a cache of weapons, including hand grenades, rifles, mortar shells, and guns, at the property, leading to the evacuation of nearby residents. The Army safely removed the items and conducted a controlled explosion in a farmer's field on the edge of the city. A 48-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of stealing items from protected sites and possessing explosives, firearms, and ammunition. He has since been released on bail. The discovery was made in a garage that police described as a "museum for World War One and World War Two relics." It is alleged that the man obtained the items through illegal metal detecting, a heritage crime. Experts believe that the man targeted protected sites to retrieve "heritage artefacts" and wartime munitions. The incident has highlighted the issue of heritage crime, with Mark Harrison, policing advisor for English Heritage, stating that this is the first time a partnership between the military, police, and other experts has been used to tackle this type of criminal activity. Further explosions may be carried out on Thursday as the investigation continues.

Construction on a major pipeline project at Oxford's John Radcliffe and Churchill hospitals has been halted due to a lack of planning permission. Vital Energi, the company behind the £14.8m scheme, had begun digging on All Saints Road but was forced to suspend work on Wednesday after Oxford City Council intervened. The 18-month project aims to upgrade the hospitals' heating systems with a new 1.6-mile pipeline. However, residents had already expressed concerns about the lack of information regarding the project, which is set to affect several roads in the area, including Woodlands Road, Sandfield Road, and London Road. Oxfordshire County Council has requested that Vital Energi either resume work or fill in the excavated trench and reinstate the road with a temporary surface. The NHS has announced that the existing hole will be temporarily filled in. Mark Neal, head of estates for Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, said the contractor would "clarify its planning requirements" and that the public road would be reinstated with a temporary surface. Vital Energi has been contacted for comment on the situation.

A potential'storm surge' had authorities on high alert, warning of severe flooding in various regions. The rare phenomenon occurs when strong winds and high tides combine, bringing excess water onto land. The Environment Agency predicted the surge would hit on January 13 during the night, prompting evacuations in Norfolk, Essex, Suffolk, and Yorkshire. However, a change in wind direction mitigated the impact, and the waves were not as severe as expected. While some areas, like Hornsea in Yorkshire, still experienced flooding, the damage was less extensive than anticipated. Authorities praised preparation efforts and thanked volunteers for their assistance, noting that readiness was key in minimizing the storm's impact. Despite the flooding, the outcome was less severe than initially feared.

Liverpool Secure Thrilling Comeback Victory Over Bolton In a thrilling FA Cup fourth-round match, Liverpool came from behind to defeat Bolton Wanderers 2-1, thanks to a stoppage-time winner from Philippe Coutinho. The match was marked by controversy, with Bolton manager Neil Lennon criticizing the refereeing decisions made by Darren East. The drama began in the 59th minute when East awarded Bolton a penalty, which Eidur Gudjohnsen converted to give the Championship side a 1-0 lead. However, the Trotters' joy was short-lived, as midfielder Neil Danns was shown two yellow cards in the space of seven minutes, reducing his team to 10 men. Lennon expressed his disappointment with the decisions, stating that the first yellow card was unwarranted and that the referee "spoiled what was a very good game." Despite being a man down, Bolton put up a valiant effort, but Liverpool's pressure eventually paid off. Raheem Sterling equalized for the Reds, setting the stage for a thrilling finale. In the dying minutes of the match, Coutinho scored a stunning winner, securing a 2-1 victory for Liverpool and a fifth-round trip to Crystal Palace on February 14. Lennon was philosophical about the defeat, acknowledging that the sending-off of Danns had changed the complexion of the game. "The sending-off changed the game because I thought at 1-0, and with 11 men, we were OK," he said. "We were comfortable. I didn't feel we were being pegged in. I didn't feel we were under immense pressure, but then the pressure came with being a man down against a quality side." In contrast, Liverpool manager Brendan Rodgers was ecstatic about the win, praising the performance of Coutinho, who had signed a new contract with the club just two days earlier. "You'd pay money to watch that kid and watch how he plays football," Rodgers said. "He is a great role model for many technical players who are technically good and maybe not as big in stature. He's a wonderful player and he's really committed to this club." Rodgers also expressed his confidence in his team's ability, stating that the result was "justice" and that he had expected his side to win. "We created some chances and didn't quite take them and went a goal down to what was never a penalty," he said. "After that, we kept our composure and quality. We scored two, but could have had many, many more. We have got great belief at the moment, and you can't question their character." The win marks a significant boost for Liverpool, who have been in impressive form of late. With their confidence high, they will be looking to build on this momentum as they head into the fifth round of the FA Cup. For Bolton, the defeat is a disappointment, but Lennon's side can take pride in their performance, which pushed Liverpool to the limit.

Crackdown on Public Urination in City Centre In a bid to tackle the ongoing issue of public urination, police in the city centre will begin handing out fixed penalty notices to offenders from this Friday. The move comes two years after the council introduced portable urinals in the area, following complaints from local businesses. Despite the provision of these facilities, the problem persists, and authorities have deemed it necessary to take a tougher stance. According to Chief Inspector Dean Thomas, "Urinating in public is a major irritation to authorities and businesses who are left to clean up their own doorways and streets after people under the influence of alcohol feel it is acceptable to treat the city centre like a toilet." He emphasized that this behavior is "certainly not acceptable" and welcomed the collaboration between the police and council to enforce fixed penalty notices. The council has been deploying portable urinals in known problem areas every weekend, and while they are well-used, some individuals continue to disregard the facilities. As a result, the authorities are now taking a firmer approach, following a warning issued two years ago that those caught urinating in public would face fines or arrest. Local business owners, such as Bruno Nunes, who runs Peppermint bar and Bambu Beach bar, have welcomed the crackdown. Nunes believes that the impact of the fines will not only affect those who are caught but also serve as a deterrent to others, who will be aware of the tough stance being taken by the authorities. Council cabinet member June Burtonshaw stated, "Public urination is a contentious issue that has been troubling authorities, organisations, and businesses working together to create a cleaner, healthier, and safer city centre." She emphasized that while the "soft approach" has had some effect, it is now time to get tough. With toilets provided in every night-time venue, as well as additional portable urinals on the streets, there is no excuse for individuals to urinate in public. The city centre, particularly Wind Street, has faced criticism in recent months for being an area of drunkenness and debauchery. In response, the council has introduced a policy limiting new pub and club licences in the area. The use of portable urinals is not unique to this city, with similar facilities being used in other UK cities, including Manchester, Bristol, Cambridge, and London. As the authorities continue to work together to address the issue, it remains to be seen whether the introduction of fixed penalty notices will have the desired effect in reducing public urination in the city centre.

Great Britain's hockey team is facing a nail-biting finish to their Champions Trophy campaign after a narrow 1-1 draw against Olympic champions Germany. The team's hopes of reaching the gold medal final are still alive, but they require a specific combination of results to achieve this goal. GB trailed behind Germany for much of the match, with Tobias Hauke's rebound effort in the second quarter giving the Germans the lead. However, a stunning penalty corner strike from Ashley Jackson in the final quarter leveled the score. Despite the draw, GB's keeper George Pinner was the hero of the match, making several crucial saves to keep the score close. The team's performance was a significant improvement from their disappointing loss to India earlier in the tournament. A 4-1 win over South Korea on Monday had reignited their campaign, and they began brightly against Germany, with a last-gasp clearance from Martin Haner denying them an opener in the opening quarter. GB's chances of finishing in the top two and reaching the gold medal final are now dependent on other results. They must beat Belgium in their final pool match on Thursday and hope that leaders Australia do not lose to India. Any other combination of results would see GB finish outside the top two, although a top-four ranking would still give them a chance of claiming a bronze medal. "We had enough chances to win the game, but George [Pinner] pulled off four top saves and Barry [Middleton] stopped two on the line, so it could have been a very different story," said Jackson. Pinner added, "We need Australia to do us a bit of a favour against India tomorrow, but it's also down to us with a big game against Belgium and that's something we're looking forward to." The team's fate will be decided in the coming days, and they must be prepared to give it their all if they are to achieve their goal of reaching the gold medal final.

A Romanian man, known to his victims as "the minister", has pleaded guilty to exploiting migrant workers in Northern Ireland. Ioan Lacatus forced his victims to work up to 70 hours a week, often without a break, and provided them with only limited cold food. The workers were also subjected to poor living conditions, with multiple people sharing one toilet and one shower. Lacatus, who has an address in Portadown, took almost all of his victims' wages and controlled their every move. He warned them not to leave the house or speak to fellow workers, and when they complained about the conditions, he told them they could "eat stones". The victims, mostly from a remote part of Romania, had their passports taken away upon arrival in Northern Ireland and were made to sign forms allowing Lacatus and his wife to control their wages. The exploitation was eventually exposed when four of the workers escaped and reported their situation to the police. When officers arrived to rescue the remaining five workers, a doctor had to be called for one of them, and others had to be fed immediately. Lacatus has pleaded guilty to conspiracy to traffic people for exploitation, trafficking into the UK, and other related charges. He, along with his wife Cristina Covaci and her brother Samuil Cavaci, will be sentenced next week at Craigavon Crown Court. The court heard that Lacatus has a history of convictions in France and Italy, and his guilty plea marks a significant step towards justice for his victims.

Pokémon Go Finally Launches in Japan with McDonald's Partnership After weeks of anticipation, Niantic Labs, the software company behind the global phenomenon Pokémon Go, has announced that the game is now available in Japan. The launch, which was met with great excitement on social media, comes with a unique partnership with McDonald's, one of the country's most popular fast-food chains. As of Friday morning, Japanese fans were able to start playing the game, with many taking to Twitter to share their experiences. The partnership with McDonald's is expected to bring a new level of excitement to the game, with the company's restaurants being designated as "PokéStops" or "gyms" where players can catch and train their Pokémon. However, in a bid to avoid any disruptions to customers, a McDonald's spokesman has urged players to be respectful of other patrons, stating that restaurants would "call on players not to become a bother to customers who are eating." For many Japanese fans, the launch of Pokémon Go has been a long time coming. The game was first released in the US, Australia, and New Zealand on July 6 and has since become available in over 30 countries. The game's popularity has been unprecedented, with millions of people worldwide obsessively capturing and training virtual creatures in public spaces. One of the first players to start playing the game in Japan was Samuel Lucas, an Australian YouTuber based in Tokyo. "The moment I found out the servers were up, I jumped right out of bed, got dressed, and ran outside with my iPhone and two extra battery packs," he told the BBC. Lucas's enthusiasm was matched by 21-year-old Tomoharu Kudo, who found a Charmander in his bed and then ventured out to explore the city for more Pokémon. However, the launch of Pokémon Go in Japan has not been without its challenges. After weeks of stories about players in other countries getting into trouble while playing the game, Japanese authorities have taken precautions to ensure player safety. The National Centre of Incident Readiness and Strategy for Cybersecurity has issued a nine-point safety guide, which includes warnings about heatstroke, registering with "cool names" that are different from real names, and being mindful of one's surroundings while playing the game. Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga urged players to abide by the safety guidelines, stating, "I want people to abide by the warning so that people can play it on smartphones safely." Unfortunately, just a few hours after the launch, there were already reports of an accident, with a student at Osaka's Kindai University reportedly falling down the stairs while playing Pokémon Go and being taken to hospital. Despite the risks, Pokémon Go has proven to be a cultural phenomenon, with millions of people worldwide captivated by its unique blend of virtual and real-world gameplay. The game's use of augmented reality technology allows players to catch and train Pokémon in their everyday surroundings, from parks and streets to landmarks and public buildings. The game's success is a testament to the enduring popularity of the Pokémon franchise, which first gained widespread recognition in the 1990s with the release of the Nintendo Game Boy. The trading cards that accompanied the game were a huge hit in school playgrounds, and the new game has managed to build on that legacy, introducing the beloved characters to a new generation of fans. As Pokémon Go continues to take Japan by storm, it will be interesting to see how the game evolves and what new features and partnerships are introduced in the coming weeks and months. For now, Japanese fans can enjoy the thrill of the hunt, exploring their surroundings and catching as many Pokémon as possible. With its unique blend of virtual and real-world gameplay, Pokémon Go is sure to remain a global phenomenon for months to come.

A 45-year-old man from Ayrshire has been sentenced to a 12-month community payback order for assaulting his former partner over a period of seven years. Edward Barr pleaded guilty to assaulting Ann Begg, 51, at addresses in Cumnock and Auchinleck between May 1993 and May 2000. The abuse began when Ms Begg became pregnant, with Barr becoming increasingly violent and controlling. Ms Begg told the court that the relationship was fine at first, but things changed when she became pregnant and was no longer able to give Barr the attention he demanded. She recalled being "pummelled" by Barr while pregnant after a row, and being dragged by the hair from the living room to the hallway. The violence escalated over the years, with Barr pouring a plate of boiling hot custard over Ms Begg as she cooked a meal. The abuse eventually led to Ms Begg seeking refuge in women's shelters. The pair split up in 2000 when Barr started seeing someone else. Lord Clark ordered Barr to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work as part of his community payback order. Barr has already spent the equivalent of eight months on remand. He was earlier cleared of 10 further charges of domestic violence due to a key witness failing to appear in court. Ms Begg had to give evidence against Barr at a trial in Livingston before his guilty plea. The sentence has brought an end to a long and traumatic period for Ms Begg, who has shown courage in speaking out against her abuser.

Local Photographer Wins Prestigious Award with Stunning Landscape Image A breathtaking photograph of Loch Creran, taken by Hugh Nicol from Appin, has won the coveted Jolomo Colours of Scotland Photography Competition. The image, titled "The Audrey, Loch Creran," was captured during an evening cycle ride and showcases the serene beauty of the Scottish landscape. Nicol, an estates manager in Argyll, is a self-taught photographer with no formal training. Despite his lack of experience, his photograph stood out among the competition, impressing renowned Scottish artist John Lowrie Morrison, who launched the competition last year. Morrison praised Nicol's image, saying it "shows the colours of Scotland extremely well" and "expresses a real feel of Scotland and a lovely feeling of movement." The competition attracted a high volume of exceptional entries, with runners-up including Mairead Maclennan from North Uist, Susanne Wilson from East Kilbride, and Raymond Hosie from Campbeltown. Their photographs, featuring stunning landscapes from the Western Isles, demonstrated the diversity and beauty of Scotland's natural scenery. Nicol's winning image was taken on a still autumn evening, when the loch's calm waters reflected the vibrant colors of the surrounding landscape. He attributed his success to the picturesque location, saying, "When you have somewhere as beautiful as Appin to work with, taking the picture was easy." Nicol's achievement is a testament to the power of amateur photography and the enduring appeal of Scotland's breathtaking landscapes.

Australian Scientists Stunned by Discovery of Ancient Volcanoes Off Sydney Coast A team of researchers from Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, has made a groundbreaking discovery of a cluster of volcanoes approximately 250km off the coast of Sydney. The volcanoes, believed to be around 50 million years old, were uncovered during a search for larval lobster breeding grounds. This finding is significant, as it may hold clues to the separation of Australia from New Zealand, which occurred around 40 to 80 million years ago. According to volcano expert Richard Arculus, "This is the first time these volcanoes have been seen." The discovery highlights the vast unknowns of the sea floor, with Arculus noting that the surface of Mars is better mapped than the ocean floor. The largest of the four volcanoes rises 700m off the sea floor, with a crater spanning 1.5km across. The discovery is expected to provide valuable insights into the Earth's crust and the composition of the underlying mantle layer. As Arculus explained, studying the volcanoes is like analyzing someone's "garbage bin" to determine their diet, offering a glimpse into the region's geological history.

A team of treasure hunters has begun excavating a site near the city of Walbrzych in Poland, in search of a legendary train said to be filled with loot and guns. The team, led by Piotr Koper from Poland and Andreas Richter from Germany, claims that ground-penetrating radar results are "very promising" and suggest that the train may be hidden in a tunnel. The dig is expected to take up to 10 days to complete. According to local folklore, the armoured train was carrying gold from Wroclaw as the Soviet army closed in during World War Two. It was said to have gone missing near Ksiaz castle, just a few kilometers from Walbrzych. The Nazis had constructed a complex network of tunnels in the area, which were part of a secret military project that was never finished. Despite the team's optimism, experts have cast doubt on the existence of the train. In December, Prof Janusz Madej from Krakow's AGH University of Science and Technology stated that a geological survey of the site had found no evidence of a train, saying "there may be a tunnel, but there is no train." However, the treasure-hunting team remains hopeful, with spokesman Andrzej Gaik saying that they need to find a railway track and the entrance to a tunnel to confirm the train's existence. The excavation has sparked widespread interest, with many eager to see if the legend of the lost train will finally be proven.

A 47-year-old man was found dead in a Compton Road bedsit on Monday at 20:30 BST. Despite treatment, he was pronounced dead at the scene. Police have informed his family and are questioning three suspects. Forensics experts are investigating the property, with a post-mortem examination to follow.

Education Secretary Justine Greening has announced that the government will not proceed with plans to remove the requirement for academies to have elected parent governors on their governing bodies. The proposal, which was met with widespread criticism from MPs, schools, and teaching unions, was included in the Education for All White Paper released in March. The plan aimed to give academies the "freedom" to choose whether or not to have parent governors, but it was seen as an attack on parents' involvement in their children's education. Speaking to the Commons Education Committee, Greening emphasized the importance of parental involvement in school improvement. She stated that parent governors often play a "vital role" in turning around underperforming schools. Greening drew on her experience as a constituency MP, citing examples of schools that had improved significantly when parents became more engaged and invested in the school's success. The initial proposal sparked an outcry from Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who described it as an attack on parents. Former Prime Minister David Cameron defended the plans, claiming that they did not mean parents would be removed from governing bodies altogether. However, the backlash against the proposal was intense, with many arguing that it would undermine the role of parents in their children's education. Liberal Democrat education spokesman John Pugh welcomed Greening's decision, saying it was a "climb down" from a policy that was "indefensible." Pugh criticized the government's education policy, describing it as "all over the place" and accusing ministers of being "ideologues" who disregard common sense. While Greening has abandoned the plan to remove parent governors, she remains committed to her predecessor's vision of a fully academised school system. However, she has acknowledged the need to improve the financial accountability of these privately run but state-funded schools. The education secretary is currently exploring ways to increase transparency and accountability in academy finances, a move that is likely to be welcomed by critics of the academy system. Greening's decision to retain parent governors on academy governing bodies is a significant concession to critics of the government's education policy. It recognizes the important role that parents play in their children's education and acknowledges the value of their involvement in school governance. As the government continues to develop its education policy, it is likely that the role of parents and the accountability of academies will remain key issues of debate.

Unrest Erupts in Kenya as Guinea Bissau Takes Lead in Qualifying Group A contentious goal awarded to Guinea Bissau in the 81st minute sparked chaos in Nairobi, as Kenya's players and fans disputed the decision, claiming the ball had not crossed the line. The match was halted for 30 minutes as Kenya fans threw objects at the Guinea Bissau bench and the fourth official, prompting concerns about potential sanctions for the home team. The goal, which proved to be the winner, gives Guinea Bissau a crucial 1-0 victory and propels them to the top of their qualifying group with seven points. Kenya, on the other hand, is now facing an uphill battle to qualify for next year's tournament, sitting at the bottom of the group six points off the lead. In other Group E action, Congo and Zambia played to a 1-1 draw, mirroring their result earlier in the week. Jordan Massengo put Congo ahead just after halftime, but Winston Kalengo equalized in the 72nd minute. The result leaves Guinea Bissau in first place, with Congo and Zambia tied for second, one point behind. Elsewhere, Ghana's perfect record in Group H was tarnished by a 0-0 draw in Mozambique. The Black Stars still maintain a four-point lead over Mauritius, but the latter has an opportunity to close the gap with a win over Rwanda on Tuesday. In Group C, Benin thrashed South Sudan 4-1, with Stephane Sessegnon scoring twice, to take the top spot. Mali can reclaim the lead with a win over Equatorial Guinea on Monday. Meanwhile, Comoros suffered a 2-1 defeat to Botswana, just days after securing their first major qualifying win. The loss drops Comoros back down to earth, while Botswana moves level on points with the top two teams in the group, Uganda and Burkina Faso, who face off on Tuesday. With all group winners guaranteed a spot at the 2017 tournament in Gabon, and the best two runners-up also qualifying, the competition is heating up as teams jockey for position. The outcome of the remaining matches will be crucial in determining which nations will secure a coveted spot in the tournament.

Former England football star Ray Wilkins has been handed a suspended prison sentence and a four-year driving ban after pleading guilty to drink-driving. The 59-year-old was caught driving his Mercedes in a bus lane on the A4 in London on July 1, where he also struck a kerb and was seen drinking alcohol from a bottle while behind the wheel. Wilkins, who has two previous convictions for drinking and driving, was nearly three times over the legal limit when he was stopped by police. A passer-by had taken his keys to prevent an accident, and when officers approached him, they noticed his glazed eyes, unsteadiness on his feet, and the smell of alcohol. The Uxbridge Magistrates' Court heard that Wilkins, who played 84 times for England, including at the 1986 Mexico World Cup, is currently undergoing a residential rehabilitation course at the Priory Hospital in Woking. His lawyer stated that he is "ashamed and embarrassed" by his actions, and Wilkins himself acknowledged that "abstinence is the only way I can control this situation". District Judge Tim Boswell appreciated Wilkins' "genuine desire to change" and sentenced him to a 12-week prison sentence, suspended for 12 months. In addition to the driving ban and suspended sentence, Wilkins was ordered to perform 140 hours of community service. Outside court, Wilkins asked not to be judged on his alcohol problem, stating "I am an addict".

Drake Continues to Dominate Music Charts with "One Dance" and "Views" This week, Drake has solidified his position as a leading force in the music industry, with his hit single "One Dance" spending its sixth week at number one on the singles chart. The song, which features WizKid and Kyla, has been a massive success, with 105,000 sales in the past week alone. Notably, about 75,000 of those sales came from streams, highlighting the growing importance of streaming services in the music industry. Meanwhile, Drake's album "Views" has climbed three places to the top of the album chart, marking its second week at number one. The album outsold its closest competitor, Beyonce's "Lemonade", by just under 800 chart sales. This achievement is a testament to Drake's enduring popularity and the widespread acclaim for "Views", which has been praised for its introspective and emotionally charged lyrics. In other chart news, Justin Timberlake's new single "Can't Stop The Feeling" entered the singles chart at number two, despite being at number one in the midweek charts. The song's success can be attributed to Timberlake's well-received performance at the Eurovision Song Contest, which helped to boost its profile. However, it was ultimately unable to surpass "One Dance", which held on to the top spot by a margin of just 6,000 sales. The Stone Roses also made a notable return to the charts, with their new single "All For One" entering at number 17. This is the band's first new material in over 20 years, and its release was met with widespread excitement from fans and critics alike. Although it had been at number four in the midweek charts, it ultimately dropped to 17 by the end of the week. Elsewhere on the charts, Calvin Harris and Rihanna's "This Is What You Came For" dropped to number three, while Sia's "Cheap Thrills" and Mike Posner's "I Took A Pill In Ibiza" remained at numbers four and five respectively. A second Drake song, "Too Good", featuring Rihanna, also appeared in the top 10, climbing 15 places to number eight. On the album chart, Norwegian DJ Kygo was the highest new entry at number three with "Cloud Nine", while Meghan Trainor's new album "Thank You" debuted at number five. Justin Bieber's "Purpose" dropped to number 12, marking the first time it has fallen out of the top 10 in 26 weeks. Other new entries included Corinne Bailey Rae's "The Heart Speaks in Whispers" at number 14, Pierce the Veil's "Misadventures" at number 17, and Foy Vance's "The Wild Swan" at number 28.
