Nigeria's Super Eagles Coach, Samson Siasia, has confirmed that former players Vincent Enyeama and Emmanuel Emenike will not be returning to the team. The duo had retired from international football last October after a disagreement with former coach Sunday Oliseh. Following Oliseh's resignation, Siasia had reached out to the pair, asking them to reconsider their decision, but they have chosen to stick with their retirement. Enyeama, the former goalkeeper, had been stripped of the team's captaincy by Oliseh, leading to his retirement. In a recent interview with Brila FM, he stated that his decision to retire still stands and he does not wish to discuss the matter further. Emenike, a striker, had followed Enyeama's lead and also quit the team. Siasia has respected the players' decisions, stating that Nigeria has a wealth of talented footballers and the team must focus on the future. The coach, along with his assistants Salisu Yusuf and Emmanuel Amunike, is set to finalize the squad for the upcoming game against Egypt. When asked about the potential return of other players, such as Obafemi Martins, Victor Moses, and John Mikel Obi, Siasia remained tight-lipped, emphasizing that the team's focus is on the crucial matches against Egypt. He called for the support of everyone, saying that the players who are committed to giving their all for the country will be crucial in achieving success.

Millions of Syrians Flee to Safety as US Increases Refugee Resettlement Efforts The ongoing conflict in Syria has led to a massive exodus of refugees, with over 4.2 million individuals fleeing their homeland in search of safety and security. Initially, many sought refuge in UN-run camps in neighboring countries, but in recent months, a growing number have embarked on perilous sea journeys to Europe, sparking a migration crisis on the continent. In response to mounting pressure, the Obama administration announced plans to increase the number of Syrian refugees allowed to resettle in the US over the next year. As of now, 2,370 Syrian refugees have arrived in the US, with the majority being under the age of 20. The demographic breakdown of these refugees reveals that 55.69% are under 20, while 30.73% fall between the ages of 21 and 40. Women make up 47.05% of the arrivals, while men account for 52.95%. The process of resettling in the US is a lengthy and rigorous one. Refugees must first leave their home country and register with the UNHCR, which then determines their eligibility for international resettlement. Those referred to the US undergo a thorough security screening process, which can take up to two years to complete. If cleared, they are then assisted by one of nine NGOs in finding a new home in the US. The US government has come under scrutiny for its handling of the refugee crisis, with many arguing that it is not doing enough to provide a safe haven for those fleeing war-torn countries. The recent announcement to increase resettlement efforts is seen as a step in the right direction, but much work remains to be done to address the scale and complexity of the crisis. As the situation continues to unfold, it is clear that a comprehensive and coordinated approach will be necessary to provide protection and support to those affected by the conflict in Syria.

Mental Health Care Under Scrutiny in North Wales After Patient's Death The family of a 49-year-old woman from Anglesey who struggled with depression and a personality disorder has spoken out about their concerns regarding the mental health care she received at a hospital in north Wales. Petra Jones, who had been treated at the Hergest mental health unit at Ysbyty Gwynedd, was found dead in her garage just hours after being released from the hospital in April 2015. According to her daughter, Ffion Jones, Petra had been admitted to the hospital several times and had attempted to harm herself on multiple occasions. Despite the family's requests to have her sectioned, Petra was released from the hospital, and Ffion claims that her warnings about her mother's intentions to harm herself were not taken seriously by hospital staff. Ffion recounted a disturbing phone call with a staff member at the hospital, in which she expressed her concerns about her mother's well-being. "My mother told me over the phone that once she was home, she'd go to the garage and kill herself," Ffion said. "I phoned Hergest and told this to one of the staff, and she said,'well, I understand your concern, but the psychiatrist will say whether or not she's allowed to go home'." Tragically, Petra was released from the hospital, and just a few hours later, she was found dead. Ffion has since filed a complaint with the community health council, citing concerns about the care her mother received and the lack of attention given to her warnings. Ffion's story is not an isolated incident. Other families have come forward with similar concerns about mental health care in north Wales, and the community is calling for improved services and more support for families affected by mental illness. Clwyd West Conservative AM Darren Miller has identified two major problems with the current system: a lack of strong leadership and management, and a shortage of beds and staff. In response to these concerns, Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has stated that mental health services have undergone significant changes over the past year and that patient feedback is taken "extremely seriously." A spokesman for the health board said, "We are fully focused on improving the way mental health services are delivered across north Wales." However, for Ffion and her family, the changes come too late. "I know this won't bring mum back," Ffion said, "but we know this has happened to a lot of families – the same situation. So, we've made a complaint so it doesn't happen again in the future and to get a bit more help for families." As the community continues to grapple with the issue of mental health care, Ffion's story serves as a poignant reminder of the need for improved services and support for those struggling with mental illness.

Malaysian Authorities Arrest 14 Suspects Planning Terror Attacks Malaysian Home Minister Zahid Hamidi announced the arrest of 14 suspects, aged between 14 and 44, who were planning to attack police stations and army bases to gather weapons. Two of the suspects had recently returned from Syria, according to police. The group was also allegedly planning to kidnap high-profile individuals, although the targets were not named. Notes were found describing how to make bombs, written by an Indonesian executed for his role in the 2002 Bali bomb attacks. Two of those arrested were members of the army, raising concerns about the extent of militant influence within the country. The arrests come as the government prepares to debate new anti-terrorism laws in parliament, which have been met with controversy and opposition from human rights groups. The new laws would permit indefinite detention without trial and the revocation of passports for individuals suspected of terrorist activities. Prime Minister Najib Razak has defended the measures as necessary to combat militant Islamist cells and "lone wolf" attacks. However, critics argue that the laws could be used to stifle political dissent, particularly given the government's history of using the sedition law to silence opponents. The sedition law has been controversial due to its broad definition of sedition, which can include speech or actions deemed critical of the government, and its potential for abuse.

A motion has been tabled to the council by Vicky Davidson, representing Selkirkshire, to halt the routine deployment of armed officers in the Borders. Davidson argued that the region is a safe place and that carrying side arms is not necessary. She called for an immediate stop to the practice, which was adopted by Police Scotland last year, and for consultations to be held in each council area before restarting. The move has sparked concerns from various parties, including independent MSP John Finnie and Highland councillors, who question the need for armed officers in areas with low crime rates. The issue is set to be debated, with many calling for a more tailored approach to policing in different regions.

Pope Francis Brings Message of Hope and Unity to Egypt In a historic visit to Egypt, Pope Francis brought a message of hope and unity to the Christian community, who have felt under siege in recent weeks. The Pope's visit comes just three weeks after the devastating attack on two Egyptian churches by the so-called Islamic State, which killed at least 45 people. Despite the somber mood, the Pope's arrival at Cairo's Air Defence Stadium was met with jubilation, as thousands of worshippers waved flags and released balloons. As the Pope made his way through the stadium in an unprotected "popemobile", he was greeted with rapturous applause. In his address, he began by referencing the disciples' despair and disappointment following Christ's crucifixion, but went on to emphasize the transformative power of the resurrection. The Pope then turned to a theme that has been a hallmark of his visit: the importance of compassion and charity in religious faith. "God is pleased only by a faith that is proclaimed by our lives," he said. "The only fanaticism believers can have is that of charity. Any other fanaticism does not come from God and is not pleasing to Him." These words echoed his earlier speech at al-Alzhar University, where he spoke to a largely Muslim audience and argued that hatred and violence have no place in religion. The Pope's message was a challenge to both Christians and Muslims in Egypt to re-examine their faith and to strive for a more compassionate and engaged approach. As the country navigates a three-month state of emergency, the Pope's visit was a rare opportunity for the Christian community to come together and celebrate in the open air. The event was a powerful reminder of the importance of unity and solidarity in the face of adversity, and the Pope's words will undoubtedly resonate with people of all faiths in Egypt and beyond.

Monument Valley Creators Bask in Glory After BAFTA Wins and Presidential Endorsement The team behind the critically acclaimed puzzle game Monument Valley is still reeling from their recent BAFTA wins and an unexpected endorsement from the President of the United States. Daniel Gray, a representative from UsTwo, the company behind the indie hit, beamed with pride on the red carpet, stating, "We feel like we've won, just for being nominated, especially for best game." Although the game missed out on the top category to Destiny, it took home the awards for best British game and best mobile game. But the team's excitement wasn't just about the BAFTAs. They revealed that the game had been featured in an episode of the Netflix original series House of Cards, with President Frank Underwood, played by Kevin Spacey, playing the game in the White House. Gray explained that the show's producers had contacted them six months prior to ask for permission to use the game, to which they readily agreed. The exposure has had a significant impact on the game's downloads, with Gray stating that they saw an eight-fold increase in downloads last week. "It's insane, we never thought it would have that kind of effect," he said. The game has already been downloaded around 2.5 million times, generating over $5.8 million in revenue. Despite the game's massive success, Gray insists that it was not just luck that contributed to its popularity. "A lot of hard work went into coming up with an idea and a concept that we thought would really resonate with people," he said. The game's unique design and engaging gameplay have earned it numerous awards, including an Apple Design Award and iPad Game of the Year. UsTwo Games has also been working on new projects, including a design for in-car displays. Gray hinted that the company is committed to surprising people with their innovative designs, stating, "The idea that the creators of Monument Valley can produce something beautiful for cars is going to surprise you every single time." With their BAFTA wins and presidential endorsement, the team behind Monument Valley is certainly basking in glory, and their future projects are eagerly anticipated.

Tensions Run High at JNU as Students Protest Sedition Charges Against Union Leader The Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) campus is abuzz with passion and protest as hundreds of students gather near the main administrative block to demand the release of their union leader, Kanhaiya Kumar. The air is filled with slogans such as "Free Kanhaiya Kumar" and "Long live revolution" as students express their outrage over the sedition charges levelled against him. The police arrested Mr. Kumar on Saturday, alleging that he organized an event commemorating the hanging of 2001 Parliament attacks convict Afzal Guru, where "anti-India slogans" were raised. The students are adamant that Mr. Kumar is innocent and that the charges against him are baseless. They claim that he had nothing to do with the anti-India slogans raised at the event and that he is being unfairly targeted. Many students are visibly agitated and are demanding that the charges against Mr. Kumar be dropped. However, they are also fearful of speaking out, with many refusing to speak on camera citing concerns for their safety. Student activist Shreya Ghosh spoke of the fear prevailing inside the university, stating that many students have been sleeping in different rooms every night to avoid arrest. Another student activist, Deepshita, claimed that ideological politics lies at the heart of Mr. Kumar's arrest, suggesting that right-wing students are trying to increase their foothold in the university and are using the sedition charges as a means to silence their opponents. The protests have been marked by fiery speeches, with many speakers attacking Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party. Professor Ajith Kanna, one of the speakers, told the cheering crowd that if Kanhaiya is anti-national, then he is also anti-national. He pleaded with the students to remain peaceful and not pay attention to rumors, which are flying across the tension-filled campus. Not everyone is protesting, however. Some students, such as PhD students Bibas Sewa and Bijay Thapa, condemn the arrest of Mr. Kumar but agree that the protests have disrupted their studies. They just want to get on with their work, unaffected by the politics that has gripped the campus. In a separate interview, Saurabh Kumar, a member of the right-wing student group Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), stated that the law will decide whether Mr. Kumar is guilty or not, but they will not tolerate anti-India activities inside the campus. The ABVP has been at odds with the JNU student union, which is dominated by left-wing groups. As the protests continue, it remains to be seen how the situation will unfold. The JNU administration has called for calm and has urged the students to refrain from violent protests. The police have also increased their presence on campus, leading to fears of further clashes. One thing is certain, however - the students of JNU will not back down without a fight, and the controversy surrounding Kanhaiya Kumar's arrest will continue to simmer for some time to come.

The FTSE 100 index rose 0.01% to 6,361.8. Hikma plummeted 5.2% after cutting its revenue forecast. Ashtead gained 2.2% on a stronger US outlook. The pound edged up 0.02% against the dollar to $1.5431 and fell 0.15% against the euro to â‚¬1.3994.

Reforms to the Judicial Pension Scheme are set to reduce the generosity of the scheme, bringing it more in line with other public sector pensions. The changes, which will come into effect in 2015, will affect new and younger judges, who will receive lower pensions and will no longer be eligible for large lump sums upon retirement. However, judges who were within 10 years of retirement as of April 2012 will be exempt from the changes, and will continue to receive the more generous pension benefits. This means that many older judges will be spared the reductions, while their younger colleagues will face a less generous retirement package. According to the Ministry of Justice, the current scheme is one of the most generous in the country, offering judges a pension of half their final salary after just 20 years of service, plus a lump sum of two and a quarter times their annual pension. For example, a High Court judge who retired after 20 years could currently receive an annual pension of £86,500, plus a lump sum of £173,000 after tax. Under the new scheme, however, this would be reduced to £75,000 per year, with no lump sum. Additionally, judges will have to pay an annual allowance tax charge of £11,000 per year, due to the rate at which their pension pot builds up exceeding the forthcoming limit of £40,000 per year. The changes are part of a broader effort to reform public sector pensions, which have been criticized for being too generous. The government has argued that the reforms are necessary to ensure the long-term sustainability of the pension system, and to bring public sector pensions more in line with those offered in the private sector. Justice Minister Chris Grayling has defended the changes, saying that the new pension arrangements will "continue to provide a good way of saving for retirement" and that the judicial pension scheme will remain "among the most generous in the public sector." However, the reforms are likely to be unpopular with many judges, who will see their pension benefits reduced as a result of the changes. The normal pension age for judges will also rise in line with the state pension age, to 66, 67, and eventually 68 in the coming decades. However, judges will no longer have their pension accrual capped at 20 years, and will be credited with pension for as many years as they work. Despite the reductions, the judicial pension scheme will still be considered one of the most generous in the public sector, and will continue to provide a good level of retirement benefits for judges.

Around 1,700 jobs were lost when SSI went into liquidation. Some staff remain to maintain the site, including coke ovens. Additional fuel supplies have been purchased, and the official receiver is in talks with interested parties about the site's future, keeping hopes of production restart alive.

Wigan Warriors' Hooker Waterworth is set to make his first team debut on Monday if selected. Meanwhile, Hull KR has been hit with injuries, losing Chris Clarkson, James Green, Albert Kelly, and Josh Mantellato. They have been replaced by Will Oakes, Kieran Moran, Joe Wardill, and Joe Cator, who has impressed in training sessions. Cator has been handed a squad number after his performances for the City of Hull Academy. Both teams have announced their 19-man squads, with Wigan's including Bateman, Tomkins, and Sarginson, and Hull KR's featuring Allgood, Blair, and Boudebza. The match is expected to be intense with both teams looking for a win.

Yr Ysgwrn, the former home of renowned Welsh poet Hedd Wyn, has been secured for the nation thanks to grants from the Welsh government and the National Heritage Memorial Fund (NHMF). The Grade II* listed building, located near Trawsfynydd, is a significant cultural and historical landmark, and its preservation is a major achievement. Hedd Wyn, whose real name was Ellis Humphrey Evans, was a celebrated bard who tragically lost his life in World War I. His poem, "Yr Arwr" (The Hero), was posthumously awarded the prestigious Black Chair at the National Eisteddfod in 1917. The chair, which is housed at Yr Ysgwrn, is a poignant reminder of the poet's talent and sacrifice. The house, which has been lovingly maintained by Hedd Wyn's nephew, Gerald Williams, will now be looked after by the Snowdonia National Park Authority. The authority plans to develop a heritage centre and agricultural unit on the site, which will showcase the life and work of Hedd Wyn, as well as the history and culture of rural Wales during the early 20th century. First Minister Carwyn Jones announced the news on St David's Day, saying, "Hedd Wyn, his work and his tragic death give him a special place in both the history and culture of our nation." He added that the preservation of Yr Ysgwrn is particularly significant as the country approaches the 100th anniversary of the start of World War I. Dr. Manon Williams, NHMF trustee for Wales, described the project as "very important," saying, "Like so many, Hedd Wyn paid the ultimate price and came to symbolise the loss of an entire generation." She added that his poetry, along with other writing inspired by his death, stands as a poignant testament to the culture of his age. Gerald Williams, who had promised his grandmother to keep the door open as a way of paying respect to his uncle's bravery and success, welcomed the news. "By transferring Yr Ysgwrn to the careful care of the park authority, I know that my promise to my grandmother will be kept and respected, and that Yr Ysgwrn and the Gadair Ddu will stay together as a unit," he said. The Snowdonia National Park Authority plans to develop the heritage centre, which will focus on the life of Hedd Wyn, World War I, poets and writers from the period, social life in rural Wales, and sustainable land management practices. The centre will also highlight the importance of biodiversity and the unique cultural heritage of the area. Around 3,000 people visit Yr Ysgwrn each year, by appointment only. The park authority plans to continue this arrangement for at least the next four years, while finalizing plans for the future development of the site. The preservation of Yr Ysgwrn is a significant achievement, and it will ensure that the legacy of Hedd Wyn and his remarkable poetry continues to inspire future generations.

Nigeria's Super Eagles Overcome Adversity to Top World Cup Qualifying Group The Nigerian national football team, led by captain Mikel, has once again demonstrated its resilience and determination in the face of adversity. Despite arriving in Zambia just 22 hours before their crucial 2018 World Cup qualifier on October 9, the team managed to secure a hard-fought 2-1 victory, solidifying their position at the top of Group B. This is not the first time the Super Eagles have had to contend with challenging circumstances. At the 2016 Olympics in Brazil, the team arrived in Manaus just hours before their first match due to transport issues, yet still managed to win the bronze medal. Mikel, who was a key member of that Olympic team, reflected on the experience, saying, "I don't think anything can beat the problems that we faced at the Olympics. I think it's a miracle that we performed the way we did." While the team's unorthodox journey to Olympic bronze was a remarkable achievement, Mikel acknowledges that the current situation is different, but the underlying issues remain the same. "I wouldn't say it's the same problem we are facing now, but it is still the same issues that need to be sorted out," he said. As a seasoned veteran with 72 appearances for Nigeria, Mikel is well aware of the importance of hitch-free preparations in ensuring the team's success. "For us to succeed, we need to put things in place as early as possible and let the players focus on football, and not dealing with issues like flight and other things off the pitch," he emphasized. Mikel's experience and leadership have been instrumental in keeping the team focused and motivated, despite the challenges they face. He has taken it upon himself to shield his teammates from the distractions and controversies that often surround Nigerian teams, including pay rows and bonus disputes. "I try to take in all the problems, I deal with it myself and I only speak to the players when there is good news," he revealed. As the most experienced player in the current squad, Mikel is determined to use his influence to avert any potential conflicts and ensure that the team remains united and focused on their goal of qualifying for the 2018 World Cup. With his guidance, the Super Eagles are well-placed to clinch the group's sole ticket to Russia, and Mikel is confident that his team can overcome any obstacle that comes their way. The victory over Zambia has given Nigeria a significant boost in their qualifying campaign, and Mikel is eager to build on this momentum. With his wealth of experience and leadership, he is well-equipped to navigate the challenges that lie ahead and lead his team to success. As he looks to the future, Mikel remains committed to his role as captain and is determined to make a positive impact on the team's fortunes.

Inmates in several high-security prisons across the UK have been found in possession of al-Qaeda's publication Inspire, according to the Ministry of Justice. The extremist magazine was discovered in prisons in Durham, London, Manchester, and Milton Keynes over the past five years. Justice minister Sam Gyimah stated that the government will not tolerate such material in prisons, and each copy was promptly removed. The possession of Inspire can be a criminal offense under the Terrorism Act 2006 or the Offender Management Act 2007. The figures were released in response to a parliamentary question, revealing instances of discovery at Belmarsh Prison, HMP Manchester, HMP Woodhill, and HMP Frankland between 2011 and 2015. The government has reaffirmed its commitment to preventing the spread of extremist ideology in prisons.

A comical mix-up has ensued after Kent Police released a suspect image in connection with a robbery, only to be met with ridicule from the public. The image, posted on the force's Facebook page, appears to show a man with an exaggerated "extra sideburn" and a resemblance to a Stone Age character, prompting humorous comments from viewers. The image was released in relation to a robbery that occurred on September 26 in Cliftonville, Margate, where a 75-year-old man was targeted in an alleyway. Despite the seriousness of the incident, the public's response to the suspect image has been largely lighthearted, with many joking about the suspect's apparent prehistoric appearance. Over 100 people have shared the image, with dozens leaving amusing comments, including comparisons to the Flintstones character Fred Flintstone. Kent Police has declined to comment on the response, but the incident serves as a reminder of the challenges faced by law enforcement in releasing accurate and helpful suspect images. The investigation into the robbery remains ongoing.

British Superbike Championship contender Christian Iddon has expressed his interest in making the switch to road racing, with the Ulster Grand Prix being his preferred starting point. The 32-year-old, who currently rides for the Tyco BMW team, has been considering a move to road racing for some time and believes that the Ulster circuit would be an ideal introduction to the sport. Iddon, a former 10-times British Supermoto champion, is drawn to the thrill and excitement of road racing, citing the "immense" buzz he gets from competing on circuits. He is keen to experience the unique challenge of racing on public roads, but is also mindful of his commitments to the British Superbike Championship. With a strong desire to win a title in the series, Iddon must weigh up the potential benefits of competing in road racing events against the potential distraction from his short circuit goals. Should Iddon decide to make the jump to road racing, he could have the backing of one of the most successful teams in the sport, Tyco TAS. The team, owned by Philip and Hector Neill, has enjoyed numerous successes at the Ulster Grand Prix with riders such as Ian Hutchinson, Guy Martin, and Bruce Anstey. Iddon believes that with Tyco's support, he would be in "seriously good hands" and would have a strong chance of success on the roads. However, it remains to be seen whether Iddon will be given the green light to compete in the Ulster Grand Prix. While Hector Neill is reportedly keen for Iddon to make his road racing debut, Philip Neill is more cautious, preferring Iddon to focus on the short circuits. Ulster Grand Prix Clerk of the Course Noel Johnston is optimistic that Iddon will make the switch, commenting that he would be "very, very quick" on the roads and would be a great addition to the paddock. With his talent and experience on short circuits, Iddon has the potential to be a top contender in road racing. If he can secure the backing of Tyco TAS and balance his commitments to the British Superbike Championship, he could be a major player in the sport. As the racing world waits with bated breath to see if Iddon will make the switch, one thing is certain - he would be an exciting addition to the road racing scene.

Uber Secures Funding from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund In a significant move to expand its operations in the Middle East, Uber has secured a substantial investment from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The funding, which values Uber at $62.5 billion, will be used to further establish the company's presence in the region, particularly in Saudi Arabia where 80% of its users are women. Notably, women are currently banned from driving themselves in the country, making ride-hailing services like Uber a vital mode of transportation. As part of the investment, Yasir al-Rumayyan, a managing director of the Public Investment Fund, will join Uber's board. The company has announced plans to invest $250 million in the Middle East, where it has been aggressively expanding its services. The investment is part of Uber's latest fundraising round and demonstrates the company's commitment to growing its user base in the region. The move comes as the European Commission warns against restrictions on "sharing economy" services like Uber and Airbnb. The Commission emphasizes that any restrictions should be proportionate to the public interest and only used as a last resort. With significant investments from various backers, including carmakers Toyota and Volkswagen, Uber is poised for continued growth and expansion in the global market.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi concluded his three-day visit to the UK with a tour of the Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) facility in the West Midlands. The plant, owned by India's Tata Motors, is producing the new Jaguar XE sports saloon. Modi was impressed by the "focus on technology, quality and innovation" at the facility. Earlier in the day, Modi unveiled a statue of 12th Century Indian philosopher Basaveshwara on the bank of the River Thames. He also addressed the recent terror attacks in Paris, condemning them as "barbaric" and expressing his strongest opposition. The visit was largely focused on trade, with the UK seeking to capitalize on India's rapid economic growth. India is now the fastest growing large economy in the world, and British Prime Minister David Cameron is eager to secure a share of the market. Modi, on the other hand, is promoting his "Make in India" policy, encouraging British firms to invest in his country. The visit has seen the unveiling of £9bn worth of commercial deals between India and the UK. Modi was greeted with cheers from a 60,000-strong crowd at Wembley stadium, where he appeared on stage with Cameron. He also had lunch with the Queen at Buckingham Palace. However, the visit has not been without controversy. Modi has faced protests over his record as chief minister of Gujarat, where he is accused of failing to prevent the 2002 religious riots that resulted in the deaths of over 1,000 people, mostly Muslims. Modi has consistently denied these allegations. Despite the protests, Modi's visit is expected to enhance the partnership between India and the UK. The Indian Prime Minister will hope that the positive coverage of his visit, including his appearances at Buckingham Palace and Wembley stadium, will help improve his image back home, following a recent defeat in the state election in Bihar.

Redruth secured their largest win of the season and first away victory, scoring 10 tries. Coach Churcher praised the team, saying "the boys were awesome." Despite the impressive performance, Churcher expressed slight disappointment, citing high standards. The bonus-point win propelled Redruth to fourth in the division, seven points behind leaders Taunton. Churcher emphasized the importance of the away win, noting the team's successful execution of a fast and physical game plan from the start, achieving their desired style of play. This victory marks a significant milestone for the team.

Sir Fynwy: Sut I Fwrw ymlaen â'r Pwysau ar y Farchnad Dai Mae Cynghorydd Peter Fox yn dweud bod angen I Sir Fynwy "gwrdd â'r her" o fod yn lle poblogaidd I fyw. Gyda thollau Pont Hafren yn disgwyl eu haneru yn 2018, mae prisiau tai yn y sir wedi bod yn cynyddu wrth I bobl o Fryste brynu tai yno. Mae Mr Fox yn gweld hyn fel cyfle enfawr I bobl a busnesau sir Fynwy, ond hefyd fel her I'w hwynebu. Wrth I'r ardal ddod yn boblogaidd ac yn ddymunol, bydd pwysau ar farchnad dai ac ein isadeiledd. Mae Bryste, heblaw am Lundain, yn yr economi sydd yn tyfu fwyaf ym Mhrydain, ac mae prisiau tai yn codi yn gynt yno nag unrhywle arall yn y DU. Mae ardaloedd yn Sir Fynwy felly yn dod yn llefydd poblogaidd I bobl sydd yn fodlon cymudo. Mae gwerthwyr tai yn yr ardal yn dweud bod 80% o'r prynwyr bellach yn dod o ardal Bryste. Mae ffigyrau'n awgrymu bod prisiau tai yn yr ardal wedi cynyddu'n gynt na'r cyfartaledd ar draws Cymru. Mae Mr Fox yn dweud: "Wrth I brisiau tai gynyddu bydd yn rhaid I ni allu darparu mwy o dai fforddiadwy er mwyn gwneud yn siŵr bod ein pobl ifanc lleol yn gallu aros yma. Mae hynny yn bryder." Mae angen isadeiledd ychwanegol fel meddygfeydd, ysgolion a ffyrdd mwy bydd yn cael eu hariannu gan y datblygwyr. Mae yna gynlluniau I adeiladu tai yn hen ardal y dociau yng Nghas-gwent a ger yr ysbyty, tra bod stad o dai newydd am gael ei hadeiladu ger Magwyr. Gobaith Mr Fox yw y bydd y lleihad yn y tollau yn denu busnesau yn ôl I'r sir, a bydd pobl ifanc yn penderfynu aros yno. "Rwy'n gynhyrfus ynglŷn â'r swyddi ychwanegol o bosib y byddwn ni yn gallu creu," meddai. "Rydyn ni eisiau I'n plant gael y cyfleoedd I aros yma, I fagu teulu yma, a chael swyddi gyda chyflogau da yma, yn hytrach na'u bod yn gorfod gadael y sir I wireddu eu dyheadau."

Somerset all-rounder Craig Overton has been handed a suspension after being reported for a Level One offence during a Championship game. Umpires Alex Wharf and Ian Gould made the report, which has resulted in a three-point penalty. This is Overton's third such offence, triggering an automatic ban. He will miss Somerset's final County Championship match against Warwickshire and their first Championship game next summer. Teammate Rory Kleinveldt, who was also reported for a Level One offence, received a reprimand as it was his first breach. Overton's suspension comes at a crucial time, with Somerset still needing seven points to ensure safety. They face Warwickshire at home next week, with the visitors currently one place above them in the standings. Despite the setback, Overton was recently named in England's Performance Programme and Lions squad for the upcoming winter tour.

Drainage Work to Begin on A55 in Autumn Drainage work is set to commence on a stretch of the A55 between junction 12, Tal-y-Bont, and junction 13, Abergwyngregyn, this autumn. The work, which is contingent upon landowner agreements, aims to alleviate flooding issues that have plagued the area, including a notable incident on Boxing Day that forced the closure of the road. First Minister Carwyn Jones announced the plans during a visit to the Traffic Management Centre in Conwy, where he emphasized the importance of improving the road's resilience to flooding. A separate £1.9m flood alleviation scheme in Tal-y-Bont is also slated to begin in the spring, with completion expected before next winter. The Tal-y-Bont scheme was promised by Mr. Jones during a visit to the village in January, where residents had been affected by flooding over Christmas. At the time, residents expressed frustration after Mr. Jones drove through the village without stopping, despite their expectations of a meeting. He later apologized, stating he was unaware of their expectations. Regarding the A55 work, Mr. Jones acknowledged that the project requires careful planning due to its scale. He reassured motorists that the goal is not to create perpetual roadworks, but rather to ensure the tunnels are safe for the future. The A55 was originally built on a limited budget, and Mr. Jones noted that modern road construction standards would prioritize better design and resilience. With these improvements, the road will be better equipped to withstand flooding and other challenges, providing a safer and more reliable route for drivers.

Wales' Sporting Success Marred by Participation Concerns Wales has celebrated a record-breaking haul of 10 medals at the Rio Olympics, surpassing the seven medals won at London 2012. However, despite this success, concerns have been raised about the nation's sporting participation and investment in grassroots sports. Baroness Tanni Grey-Thompson, a renowned Paralympic athlete, has expressed her doubts about Wales being a true "sporting nation," suggesting that it is more a nation that enjoys watching sports rather than actively participating in them. In an interview with BBC Radio Wales' Sunday Supplement, Baroness Grey-Thompson emphasized the need for investment in schools and community facilities to encourage people to engage in sports. She noted that while events like Wimbledon may inspire people to take up tennis, sustaining their interest beyond the summer months is a significant challenge. "People call us a sporting nation, but I think we are a nation that really likes watching sport," she said. "But we can't change that and get people active without investment in places like schools." Newport East AM and cabinet minister John Griffiths agreed that investment is crucial, stating that "money wins medals" and that elite athletics can inspire others to participate. However, he also stressed the importance of balancing investment in elite sports with community-focused initiatives to get more people physically active. Griffiths highlighted the need for schools to open their facilities to the public in the evenings and weekends, allowing more people to access sports facilities. Meanwhile, Baroness Grey-Thompson has expressed her concerns about the upcoming Paralympics in Rio, citing budget cuts and logistical challenges that may impact the event's success. Despite assurances that the event will go ahead as planned, she fears that the cuts will hinder the Paralympics' ability to promote disability sports globally. "I'm not sure it will move the Paralympics movement on around the world," she said. "It won't change the world as I hoped it would." With the Paralympics just around the corner, Wales will be watching with bated breath, hoping that its athletes can build on their Olympic success and inspire a new generation of sports enthusiasts.

Advocate General for Scotland, Richard Keen QC, is facing charges for allegedly breaching the Firearms Act 1968. The incident occurred on December 31 last year at his home in Ann Street, Edinburgh, after a reported break-in. According to court papers, Lord Keen, 62, failed to safely secure a 12-bore shotgun, contravening the conditions of his firearms certificate. The charge states that shotguns must be stored securely to prevent unauthorized access. A spokesman for Lord Keen expressed regret over the "inadvertent breach of licence conditions," describing it as a "one-off error." Lord Keen has held a firearms licence for many years and has always adhered to the conditions, as evidenced by multiple police inspections. The case is scheduled to be heard at Edinburgh Sheriff Court on March 1. Police Scotland initially responded to a report of a housebreaking at Lord Keen's property, leading to the discovery of the alleged offence. A Police Scotland spokeswoman confirmed that a 62-year-old man had been reported to the procurator fiscal for a firearms licensing offence. Lord Keen is a prominent figure in Scottish law, having served as the Dean of the Faculty of Advocates and being appointed Advocate General in May 2015. He recently represented the UK government in the Supreme Court hearing on triggering Article 50, successfully arguing that the Scottish Parliament's consent was not required before Brexit negotiations began. Lord Keen has also represented high-profile clients, including al-Amin Khalifa Fhima, who was acquitted of the Lockerbie bombing. The UK government has stated that it is aware of the matter and is satisfied that it will not impact Lord Keen's ability to perform his ministerial duties. Despite the charge, Lord Keen remains in his position as Advocate General for Scotland. The incident highlights the importance of adhering to firearms licensing conditions, even for experienced licence holders like Lord Keen. The outcome of the case will be determined at the upcoming hearing in Edinburgh Sheriff Court.

Wikileaks Releases Thousands of Saudi Government Documents, Including Letter Regarding Bin Laden's Death In a massive leak, Wikileaks has released over 60,000 Saudi government documents, including a letter from the US embassy in Saudi Arabia regarding the death of Al-Qaeda leader Osama Bin Laden. The letter, written by Consul General Glen Keiser in 2011, informs Abdullah Bin Laden, Osama's son, that a death certificate for his father cannot be provided. The letter, dated September 9, 2011, explains that it is consistent with US practice not to issue death certificates for individuals killed in military operations. Instead, Keiser provides US court records that confirm Bin Laden's death, along with an Arabic translation as a "courtesy." The reason behind Abdullah Bin Laden's request for a death certificate is not specified. The release of these documents is part of a larger leak, dubbed the "Saudi Cables," which Wikileaks claims will eventually include over 500,000 papers from the Saudi foreign ministry. The majority of the documents released so far are in Arabic, and they touch on a range of topics, including Iranian nuclear talks and the Egyptian revolution. The leak is reminiscent of Wikileaks' 2010 release of US State Department cables, which first brought the organization to prominence. The release of the "Saudi Cables" comes three years to the day that Wikileaks founder Julian Assange sought refuge at the Ecuadorian Embassy in London, where he remains to this day, avoiding extradition to Sweden on rape and sexual assault charges. It is not clear how Wikileaks obtained the documents, but the organization references a hack of the Saudi foreign ministry by the Yemeni Cyber Army in May 2015. Over the next month, Wikileaks plans to release hundreds of thousands of additional documents, shedding further light on the inner workings of the Saudi government.

A recent patrol operation targeting "collision hotspots" in the region resulted in 57 warnings and 43 fines for speeding. Two motorists were fined for driving at excessive speeds, 54mph and 52mph, in a 30mph zone. The operation focused on rural roads, including the A84/A85/A82 corridor, and stopped over 120 motorists. Two cars were seized due to lack of insurance, and additional fines were issued for invalid MOTs and unpaid vehicle tax. Sgt Adam Weir emphasized the goal of promoting road safety to reduce collisions and casualties, and warned that authorities will continue to address dangerous behavior by all road users.

A British Columbia court has sentenced Brandon and Gail Blackmore to a combined 19 months in jail for their role in taking a 13-year-old girl across the border to marry the leader of a fundamentalist Mormon sect. The pair, who are former spouses, were convicted in February of transporting a minor for sexual purposes. Brandon Blackmore, 71, received a 12-month jail sentence, while Gail Blackmore was given seven months. Both were also handed 18 months' probation. The girl was married to Warren Jeffs, the 60-year-old leader of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, which is based in Bountiful, British Columbia. Jeffs, who refers to himself as a prophet, has been sentenced to life in prison in the US for sexually assaulting underage girls. The sect, which has approximately 10,000 members, believes polygamy is the key to heaven and has been the subject of controversy and scrutiny in recent years. The Blackmores' case dates back to 2004, when they brought the 13-year-old girl to Utah to marry Jeffs. The sect's practices were exposed in 2008, when police raided their Texas compound and found numerous underage girls who were pregnant or had given birth. Polygamy is illegal in Canada and the Western world, and the Blackmores' sentencing serves as a reminder of the consequences of such actions.

Sweden's Supreme Court has upheld the arrest warrant for WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, issued in 2010 for allegations of sexual assault. Assange, 43, has been residing at the Ecuadorean embassy in London since June 2012, seeking to avoid extradition. The court's decision means Swedish investigators will likely proceed with plans to question Assange in London. Assange denies the allegations, claiming they are part of a plot to extradite him to the US due to WikiLeaks' publication of classified documents. However, he has not been charged with any crime in the US, and no extradition request has been made. Assange's lawyer, Per Samuelson, expressed disappointment with the court's decision, stating that it was made without allowing them to fully argue their case. The ruling comes as no surprise, as the court saw no reason to lift the warrant with plans already in place to question Assange in London. The Australian-born Assange has been living in a small suite of rooms at the embassy since requesting asylum in 2012. The allegations against him stem from a trip to Sweden in August 2010, where two women accused him of sexual assault.

A man from Pembrokeshire is appealing a court decision after he fell 20ft from a hotel balcony in Tenerife while trying to reach his room to let his wife use the toilet. Philip Clay, from Milford Haven, was on a Thomson package holiday with his family at the 4-star Guayarmina Princess hotel in July 2011. After a night of drinks with his parents on their balcony, Mr. Clay and his wife, Valerie, found themselves locked out, and she urgently needed to use the bathroom. In an effort to avoid embarrassment, Mr. Clay, who was wearing only his pyjama bottoms, attempted to climb to his own balcony next door, where he knew the door was unlocked. However, he misjudged a decorative cornice, thinking it was a solid concrete ledge, and fell two floors to the ground below. The cornice, made largely of polystyrene, collapsed under his weight, leaving him knocked unconscious and lying in a pool of blood for 30 minutes. Mr. Clay, a fire safety and security officer, has since recovered from his injuries. He is now appealing a decision by Cardiff County Court, which dismissed his claim for damages against TUI UK Ltd, the company that operated the hotel. The court had ruled that the cornice was not part of the balcony and did not require a warning sign. However, Mr. Clay argues that the hotel breached safety standards and that the cornice should have been weight-bearing or featured a warning sign. The case was heard at the Court of Appeal in London, where Lady Justice King reserved her judgment. Mr. Clay's lawyer argued that the hotel had a responsibility to ensure the safety of its guests, and that the decorative cornice posed a significant risk. The court will deliver its ruling at a later date, which will determine whether Mr. Clay is entitled to damages for his injuries. The case highlights the importance of hotel safety and the need for clear warnings and safeguards to prevent accidents.

Emma Rice, the newly appointed artistic director of the London theatre, has spoken out about the harsh criticism she has faced since taking on the role in January. According to a report by The Stage, Rice expressed her frustration with the negative press she has received, stating that critics do not use the same language when discussing male directors. She made these comments during a panel discussion at the Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, organized by Tonic Theatre, which aimed to celebrate successful female theatremakers. Rice's remarks came in response to a suggestion by Tonic founder Lucy Kerbel that she had received an unusual amount of negative coverage compared to other new artistic directors. Rice acknowledged that she had been protected from the worst of the criticism due to her decision to avoid social media and limit her reading of reviews. However, she emphasized the importance of developing a thick skin and trusting one's instincts in the face of adversity. The criticism Rice has faced has been fierce, with some reviewers accusing her of "wrecking" the Globe's success story. When asked if she believed that loud and opinionated women attracted more criticism, Rice denied being either loud or opinionated, stating that she was simply doing her job to the best of her ability. She questioned whether the same criticism would be leveled against a male director, highlighting the double standard that often exists in the industry. Rice also shared a personal anecdote about being referred to as "naughty" by a figure high up in the arts, which she felt was a patronizing and sexist comment. She wondered if the same word would be used to describe a male director, further emphasizing the need for greater equality and respect in the industry. Despite the challenges she has faced, Rice remains committed to her vision and artistic direction. When asked what advice she would give to directors who may receive similar criticism, she emphasized the importance of perseverance and self-belief. She noted that every great artist has faced criticism at some point in their career and that it is a natural part of the creative process. Rice's comments have sparked a wider conversation about the treatment of women in the arts and the need for greater equality and respect. As a prominent figure in the industry, Rice's experiences and insights serve as a reminder of the challenges that many women face in achieving success and recognition in their field. By speaking out and sharing her story, Rice hopes to inspire and empower other women to pursue their passions and push against the boundaries of what is expected of them.

Doncaster Belles manager Andy Butler's departure was reported by BBC Sport. The team, promoted last season, currently sits bottom of the Women's Super League One after three losses. They face Notts County on June 26 following a month-long break, seeking to turn their season around after defeats by top teams.

Hearts Ready to Take on Aberdeen After Recovering from Gastroenteritis Outbreak Hearts head coach Robbie Neilson has confirmed that his team is ready to face Aberdeen on Friday evening after a bout of gastroenteritis left the Edinburgh club with "few fit players" earlier in the week. The illness forced the postponement of their previous match, but Neilson is confident that his players have fully recovered and are raring to go. The team's Riccarton training base was closed on Tuesday and Wednesday to prevent the bug from spreading further, with players instead doing individual workouts at their own gyms. Despite the disruption to their preparation, Neilson is optimistic about his team's chances against Aberdeen, who are currently 12 points ahead of third-placed Hearts. Hearts have a game in hand over Aberdeen, and Neilson believes that if they can win on Friday, they can overhaul the Dons and challenge for second place. "It's a huge game," he said. "Aberdeen are desperate to win to keep close to Celtic and we're desperate to win to keep close to Aberdeen." The return of full-back Callum Paterson from a shoulder injury is also a boost to the team. With a full house expected at Tynecastle, Neilson is confident that his team will have the energy and momentum to take on Aberdeen and come out on top.

Scotland Edges Out Namibia in Rain-Affected World Cricket League Match The World Cricket League match between Scotland and Namibia was halted twice by rain on Sunday, but the home team managed to secure a win. Scotland finished their innings on 268-5, with Richie Berrington scoring an impressive 110, his highest score in a one-day international. Namibia, who opted to field first after winning the toss, reached 26-0 before play was abandoned due to rain. The match resumed on Monday, with Namibia scoring 217 from 39.4 overs. Zhivago Groenewald top-scored for the visitors with 42 before being caught by Calum MacLeod. Scotland captain Kyle Coetzer praised Berrington's performance, saying it was a "fine knock" and that the team's batting and bowling lineup is showing promise. Coetzer noted that Berrington's achievement was even more impressive given the challenging weather conditions, which forced him to come on and off the field multiple times. The two teams will meet again on Tuesday at Edinburgh's Grange for their second WCL match. Scotland will be looking to build on their win, while Namibia will aim to bounce back from their defeat. With a strong batting and bowling lineup, Scotland is poised to make an impact on the international scene. The team's captain is confident in their abilities, citing a "pack of bowlers" and batters who are coming into their prime.

A Mother's Desperate Plea: Terminally Ill Candidate Highlights Healthcare Crisis in Northern Ireland In a powerful display of determination and conviction, Melanie Kennedy, a mother of two from County Down, ran as an independent candidate in last week's election, polling an impressive 1,246 first preference votes in North Down. Despite her terminal cancer diagnosis, Kennedy felt compelled to take a stand against the state of the health service and the lack of stable government in Northern Ireland. Kennedy's journey into politics began when she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2013. Initially optimistic about her recovery, she was later told that the cancer had spread to her liver, leaving her with a terminal prognosis. However, it was the discovery that patients in Northern Ireland cannot access the same specialist drugs as those in England that drove her to take action. "For someone in my situation who is on quite harsh treatment, I was driven to this - it took a lot for me to act and create a campaign, but I felt I had to try and fight for justice for cancer patients," she explained. Kennedy's campaign highlighted the critical issues affecting the health service, including the lack of access to cancer drugs, lengthy waiting lists, and inadequate mental health support. Her message resonated with many, who share her concerns about the future of healthcare in Northern Ireland. "With no government and no health minister, it makes me feel like there's no one there to fight my corner. It's heartbreaking," she said. The ongoing political impasse in Northern Ireland has prevented vital health and social care decisions from being made, leaving patients like Kennedy feeling abandoned. Health organizations have warned that the continued lack of government is having a devastating impact on the healthcare system, with many patients being denied access to life-saving treatments. Kennedy's experience has given her a unique perspective on the healthcare crisis, and she is adamant that something needs to change. "The health service in Northern Ireland was already behind other parts of the UK, there was a lack of long-term stability and strategy, and now we're back to square one. It is the ordinary people like me who are suffering," she said. As Kennedy faces her own mortality, she is desperate to see action taken to address the healthcare crisis. "Time is a luxury that I and other people who are terminally ill cannot afford. The reason I started all this was that I asked myself,'where do I turn?' I could be told in the next couple of months, there's no more treatment for me, and I should go home and make my plans and say goodbye to my children," she said, her voice filled with emotion. Kennedy's plea is simple: she wants to see a comprehensive cancer strategy implemented, one that prioritizes early treatment and access to specialist drugs. "Early treatment is critical - it can mean the difference between getting well and going on with your life and ending up in my shoes. I don't want anyone else ending up in my shoes," she said. As the people of Northern Ireland await the formation of a new government, Kennedy's story serves as a poignant reminder of the human cost of political indecision. Her bravery and determination have inspired many, and her message will undoubtedly continue to resonate with those who are fighting for a better healthcare system.

Tragedy Strikes Mount Manaslu as Avalanche Claims Lives of Climbers A devastating avalanche on Mount Manaslu has resulted in the recovery of two bodies, with a further seven spotted by rescue pilots. The avalanche struck a base camp near the summit on Saturday, catching climbers off guard as they prepared to ascend to the 8,156m high peak. Among the dead is a Spanish national, according to the Spanish foreign ministry, while four of the deceased and three of the missing are French nationals. At least five climbers have been rescued and flown to hospitals by rescue helicopters, with two of them being French nationals. However, deteriorating weather conditions have hindered further air searches, with police officials forced to suspend operations on Sunday. The climbers were hit at an altitude of 7,000m (22,960ft) as they were preparing to head towards the summit. The avalanche has highlighted the dangers of climbing in the Himalayas, with Manaslu considered one of the most treacherous mountains in the world. Dozens of deaths have occurred on the mountain in recent years, and the autumn climbing season, which began this month, has gotten off to a tragic start. Hundreds of foreign climbers flock to Nepal every year to tackle the country's eight highest mountains, including Mount Everest. As the search for missing climbers continues, the incident serves as a sobering reminder of the risks involved in high-altitude climbing.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has announced a temporary reprieve for citizens who have been subject to a controversial tax decree. The decree, which was adopted in 2015, requires individuals who work fewer than 183 days per year to pay a tax of approximately $250 as compensation for lost tax revenues. However, Lukashenko stated that those who fall into this category will not be liable for the tax in 2017. The decision comes after mass protests erupted last month, with more rallies planned for March. Lukashenko emphasized that the decree will not be scrapped, but rather adjusted during March. He also announced that individuals who paid the tax in 2016 will be fully compensated if they find employment next year. Despite the concession, Lukashenko warned that authorities will take a "tough reaction" to organizers of future street protests against the decree. The move is seen as an attempt to quell dissent and maintain control in a country where little opposition is tolerated. Lukashenko has been in power since 1994 and has been described by some as "Europe's last dictator." However, he has recently sought to improve ties with the West and reduce dependence on Russia. The tax decree has been a major point of contention, with only 50,000 of the 470,000 eligible individuals having paid the tax so far.

Libertarian Gary Johnson sparked controversy when asked about the crisis in Aleppo, responding with "What is Aleppo?" He later admitted to having a lapse in knowledge, but isn't the first White House candidate with knowledge gaps, raising questions about their preparedness for the role.

Violence Erupts in Kashmir as Militants Ambush Military Convoy A standoff between security forces and militants in Kashmir has resulted in the deaths of two army captains, two other soldiers, and a civilian. The violence began on Saturday when up to four attackers ambushed a military convoy, before taking refuge in a government-run training institute. Despite efforts to dislodge them, the militants have continued to exchange gunfire with security forces, with part of the building catching fire. About 100 students and staff were evacuated from the building on Saturday as it was encircled by troops. Security forces are preparing for a final assault on the institute, using reconnaissance drones to gather intelligence. The militants, described as "suspected anti-India rebels," had told civilians in the complex to move to a nearby hostel as they broke into the premises. The region of Kashmir has been a flashpoint for over 60 years, with both India and Pakistan claiming it in its entirety. The two countries have fought two wars over the region, and intermittent exchanges of fire near the building could still be heard late on Sunday afternoon. Eyewitnesses report that as many as five gunmen may be holed up in the institute, with security forces working to bring the situation under control.

**Grenfell Tower Fire: Cladding Concerns Raised as Investigation Continues** A devastating fire that engulfed the 24-storey Grenfell Tower in west London has raised concerns about the safety of the building's exterior cladding, which was installed during a recent renovation. According to BBC Newsnight, the cladding used on the tower had a polyethylene core, a type of plastic, instead of a more fire-resistant mineral core. The renovation, which was completed in 2015 at a cost of nearly £9 million, included the installation of new cladding, replacement windows, and additional homes using vacant space in the building. Rydon, the company that completed the renovations, stated that the work met all fire regulations and building control and safety standards. However, experts have questioned the use of cladding with a polyethylene core, citing its potential to spread fires quickly. Christopher Miers, managing director of specialist architects Probyn Miers, told Newsnight that the core of the cladding was "critical" in determining its fire safety. "I think attention on the cladding is because we've seen in the reports and the photographs, burning exterior of the building," he said. "And we've seen enormous areas where the exterior is destroyed." Matt Wrack, general secretary of the Fire Brigades Union, added that residents have the right to ask whether the cladding compromised the safety of the building and called for an "absolutely thorough investigation." The cladding used on Grenfell Tower was sold under the brand Reynobond, which offers two different versions of the cladding - one with a plastic core and one with a mineral core. Newsnight understands that the version with a plastic core was used on the west London tower. Similar cladding has been linked to fires in high-rise buildings in France, the UAE, and Australia. Residents of Grenfell Tower had previously raised concerns about the fire risk of the building, with the local Grenfell Action Group claiming that the block constituted a fire risk. They also warned that site access for emergency vehicles was "severely restricted". As recently as last weekend, residents were told to remain in their flats in the event of a fire, advice that has been called into question by the Fire Brigades Union. The Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation, which manages the tower on behalf of the council, stated that it is too early to speculate on the cause of the fire and its spread. However, the organisation has pledged to cooperate fully with the investigation. As the inquiry into the tragedy continues, concerns about the safety of similar buildings and the use of potentially flammable cladding are likely to grow. Harley Facades, the company that fitted the panels to the building, has denied any link between the fire and the exterior cladding, stating that they are not aware of any connection. However, experts and residents are demanding answers about the safety of the building and the materials used in its renovation. The Grenfell Tower fire has raised important questions about building safety and the need for rigorous fire safety standards, and it is essential that a thorough investigation is conducted to determine the cause of this tragic event.

The FTSE 100 has kicked off the new year on a high note, rising 0.5% to close at 7,177.89 on the first trading day of 2017. This follows a record close of 7,142.83 on the final trading day of 2016. According to Neil Wilson at ETX Capital, "there are no January blues for equity markets" as traders return to their desks in an optimistic mood, carrying momentum from last week's Santa rally. Banks and financial companies led the charge, with Hargreaves Lansdown surging 5% and Barclays up 3.78%. Changes to broker ratings also drove significant moves, with Intercontinental Hotels Group rising 1.3% after Barclays upgraded its rating to "overweight". Conversely, Halfords and Next were hit by downgrades from Deutsche Bank, falling 5.6% and 4.2% respectively. A stronger-than-expected UK manufacturing sector survey boosted the pound, which rose 0.2% against the euro to €1.1766. However, it slipped 0.17% against the dollar to $1.2256. The Markit/CIPS purchasing managers' index suggested manufacturing activity reached a two-and-a-half-year high in December. With Next set to release a trading update on Wednesday, investors will be watching closely to see how the retailer performs. Overall, the FTSE 100's strong start to the year bodes well for equity markets in 2017.

Humberside Police are investigating after a baby's body was found in Hull. A member of the public made the discovery on Saturday at 19:15 BST, prompting a police response. Two people are in custody and police have closed off a nearby path, but say they are not seeking anyone else in connection with the death.

Astronaut Tim Peake is undergoing final training in Britain before his five-month mission to the International Space Station. He will perform experiments and orbit Earth over 2,700 times. Ahead of his launch, Tim will be interviewed at the training base, and the public is invited to submit questions for him to answer, with submissions reopening in the morning.

The Big Burns Supper festival came to a close on Sunday in Dumfries, wrapping up a 10-day extravaganza of music, comedy, and theatre performances. The event saw significant success, with the Le Haggis cabaret drawing in over half of the total audience. This year's festival also marked a change in venue, with the Easterbrook Hall replacing the Spiegeltent in the town centre. Executive producer Graham Main expressed his gratitude to the audience, stating that their feedback would play a crucial role in shaping the festival's future direction. "This is a festival of the people, and they will help us decide what we do next," he said. A survey is currently underway to gather feedback on the venue change, with plans for next year's event expected to be announced in March. The festival has had a substantial financial impact on the local area, with businesses reporting a significant economic boost. Mr. Main praised the festival's volunteers, describing them as "shining stars" who bring a unique atmosphere to the event. Their enthusiasm and energy are contagious, and their contributions are invaluable to the festival's success. As the Big Burns Supper looks to the future, it's clear that the community's passion and support will continue to drive its growth and success. With its unique blend of entertainment and cultural celebration, the festival is sure to remain a beloved fixture in Dumfries for years to come.

Italian Prime Minister Matteo Renzi is facing a daunting year ahead, with his own political future hanging in the balance. Known for his bold ambitions to reform the Italian state, Renzi has set his sights on overhauling the country's parliament, aiming to streamline the system, cut costs, and bring about more stable government. However, his plans may ultimately lead to his own downfall. At the heart of Renzi's reform efforts is a referendum scheduled to take place later this year, which seeks to reduce the powers of the Italian Senate. The prime minister has pledged to resign if the vote does not go in his favor, a promise that is starting to look increasingly realistic. With the UK's David Cameron having recently fallen victim to a referendum defeat, Renzi is not alone in putting his fate on the line in a public vote. Renzi's rise to power in February 2014 was marked by a relatively easy first two years in office, during which he successfully commanded the center ground of Italian politics. However, the country is now experiencing a shift away from the center, with the populist Five Star movement gaining significant traction. Founded by comedian Beppe Grillo in 2009, Five Star has won support for its anti-establishment views, and recent opinion polls show that it has surpassed Renzi's center-left Democratic Party as the most popular party in Italy. The Five Star movement's success has been bolstered by its victories in the mayoral elections in Rome and Turin, and it has now caught the referendum fever, calling for a vote on leaving the eurozone. While a general election is not expected until 2018, Italy's struggling economy and troubled banking sector may make it difficult for the country to reach that point in good shape. The Italian economy is growing slowly, but its banks are struggling with a staggering €360 billion in bad loans. Monte dei Paschi di Siena, the country's oldest bank, is particularly troubled, and eurozone rules dictate that it cannot be bailed out by the Italian state unless its bondholders take losses first. Renzi has suggested that he will find a way around these rules, but it remains to be seen whether he will be able to navigate this complex situation successfully. As Renzi faces numerous challenges, both self-inflicted and otherwise, his ability to push through his reform agenda and maintain his position as prime minister is increasingly uncertain. With the referendum on the horizon, the Italian people will soon have their say on Renzi's plans, and the outcome may ultimately determine the prime minister's own fate. Will Renzi be able to overcome the obstacles ahead and emerge victorious, or will his bold ambitions ultimately lead to his own downfall? Only time will tell.

Tragedy Strikes Esher Community as Mother and Daughter Found Dead A devastating discovery was made in a gated community in Esher on Monday, as the bodies of 47-year-old Lisa Anthony and her 14-year-old daughter Ava were found at their residence. A post-mortem examination revealed that Mrs. Anthony died from a compression to the neck, while further tests are being conducted to determine the cause of Ava's death. The news has sent shockwaves through the community, with Ava's head teacher, Fiona Boulton, describing her as a "wonderful, charming girl" with a "love of life that enriched everyone around her." Ava was a talented student, particularly excelling in drama and the performing arts. She was remembered as a warm, generous, and popular student who was a delight to be with. Concerns had been raised about the mother and daughter's whereabouts after they had not been seen for nearly two weeks. The last confirmed sighting was on June 17. The case has been referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission due to a call made to Surrey Police on June 24 by someone who knew Mrs. Anthony, expressing concerns for her welfare. The case has since been referred back to Surrey Police for investigation. In a related development, Jonathan Anthony, believed to be the husband and father of the deceased, was found dead in southern France on Sunday. A post-mortem examination will be conducted on his body in France. The community is left to mourn the loss of this mother and daughter, and an investigation is ongoing to uncover the circumstances surrounding their tragic deaths.

Historic Strutt's Mills in Belper are facing a severe crisis due to significant water damage and disrepair. According to historian Roger Shelley, the mills are leaking badly, with missing window panes, blocked downpipes, and a leaking roof. The damage is extensive, and the costs of repair are multiplying by the day. Amber Valley Borough Council has expressed concern over the state of the buildings and is considering a compulsory purchase order to protect the Grade I listed North Mill and the Grade II listed East Mill. The council's report highlights the "significant damage" suffered by the mills, which were built by Jedediah Strutt, a key figure in the industrial revolution, in the 18th Century. Despite the challenges, the owners, First Investment, claim to have a strategy in place to convert the mills into a mix of flats and retail space. The company also stated that a maintenance program is ongoing. However, Mary Smedley, a trustee of the Strutt's North Mill Trust, emphasizes the need for "serious TLC" to make the buildings viable for conversion. She urges all parties to work together to find a solution. With the mills' rich history and UNESCO World Heritage Status, it is essential that a collaborative effort is made to restore them to their former glory.

Northern Ireland's World Cup qualifying campaign has been dealt a blow with the news that Stuart Dallas has returned to his club due to a calf injury. The 25-year-old midfielder had been a key player for Michael O'Neill's side, but his injury, sustained during last month's international break, has ruled him out of the upcoming game against Azerbaijan. Dallas's absence is compounded by the loss of forward Jamie Ward, who fractured his wrist while playing for Burton Albion on Saturday. Ward has started Northern Ireland's last six competitive games and scored in the 4-0 win over San Marino, making his absence a significant blow. Despite these setbacks, O'Neill has opted not to call up any replacements at this stage, instead choosing to rely on his existing squad. The absence of Ward could increase Kyle Lafferty's chances of earning a recall, however. Lafferty scored his first league goal since January 2015 on Saturday, netting within four minutes of coming on as a substitute in Norwich City's 3-2 defeat by Leeds United. On a more positive note, Chris Brunt and Will Grigg have both returned to the Northern Ireland squad. Brunt, 31, missed Euro 2016 due to a serious knee injury, but has recently returned to duty with West Brom. Grigg, meanwhile, had asked to be left out of recent squads for personal reasons, but is now back in contention. Northern Ireland currently sit fourth in Group C, three points behind Azerbaijan, who have seven points from their three games. Germany lead the table with a maximum nine points. O'Neill's side will be looking to bounce back from their defeat to Germany last month, and will be hoping to take all three points from their game against Azerbaijan. The squad will be looking to players like Lafferty, Grigg, and Brunt to step up and fill the gaps left by Dallas and Ward.

Laura Robson, the 19-year-old British tennis sensation, has made a triumphant return to the US Open, defeating Lourdes Dominguez Lino 7-5 6-0 in the first round. Despite being seeded 30th, Robson faced a tough opponent in the 32-year-old Spanish veteran, who had previously beaten her in their two encounters. However, Robson's determination and skill ultimately paid off, as she secured a spot in the second round against Frenchwoman Caroline Garcia. The match, played on Court 17, got off to a rocky start for Robson, who had not played a competitive match since Wimbledon due to a wrist injury. Despite her rustiness, Robson made a strong start, breaking Dominguez Lino's serve in the first game. However, the pair struggled to find their rhythm, with six breaks of serve and 11 double faults between them. Dominguez Lino's heavy topspin proved to be a challenge for Robson in the blustery conditions, but the British teenager refused to give up. In a pivotal 11th game, Robson fought off two break points to level the set at 5-5. She then went on to win the next two games, taking the set 7-5. The second set was a completely different story, as Robson found her rhythm and dominated the match, winning six games in a row to take the set 6-0. The match lasted just one hour and 22 minutes, with Robson emerging victorious. Robson, who reached the fourth round at Flushing Meadows last year, was pleased with her performance, despite acknowledging that she was "a little bit rusty" due to her lack of match practice. "I just had to stay focused out there and confident in my game plan," she told BBC Radio 5 live. Robson also revealed that her wrist, which had been taped during the match, was "OK" and would not be a concern for her next match. Robson's victory was a welcome boost for British tennis, which has been struggling in recent years. Dan Evans, the only other British player in action on day one, also secured a victory, beating 11th seed Kei Nishikori of Japan 6-4 6-4 6-2. Robson will now face Caroline Garcia, who defeated American Shelby Rogers 6-3 6-2, in the second round. With her confidence and form on the rise, Robson will be looking to make a deep run in the tournament and build on her impressive performance in the first round.

Former Bishop of Derry, Dr. Edward Daly, has sparked controversy by calling for the Catholic Church to reconsider its stance on celibacy for priests. In his new book, "A Troubled See", Dr. Daly argues that allowing clergymen to marry would help ease the church's problems, including the declining number of priests. The 77-year-old bishop, who served in Derry during the height of the Troubles, believes that priests should have the freedom to marry if they wish. Dr. Daly's comments come as the Catholic Church faces a severe shortage of priests, with many young men deterred from joining the priesthood due to the celibacy rule. The former bishop expressed his concerns about the decreasing number of priests and the aging population of clergy, stating that it is an issue that needs to be addressed urgently. He also shared his personal experience of seeing priests and prospective priests forced to resign or unable to join the priesthood because of the celibacy rule, which he found "heartbreaking". While Dr. Daly's views may not align with current Vatican thinking, he remains resolute in his opinion, stating that he is "not engaged in a popularity contest". The Catholic Church has declined to comment on Dr. Daly's remarks, with a spokesman saying that the former bishop was speaking in a personal capacity. Dr. Daly's comments are likely to ignite debate within the Catholic Church, and his book, "A Troubled See", is set to shed new light on his experiences and views on the church's future. As a prominent figure in the Catholic Church, Dr. Daly's opinions carry significant weight, and his call for reform is likely to resonate with many.

In a thrilling turn of events, Jordan Spieth birdied the final hole to propel his team into a tie for the lead at the Classic of New Orleans. Spieth and his partner are now alongside Australian Ryan Ruffels and American Kyle Stanley, who carded an impressive 66.
