The tournament, which has adopted a team format this year, features 80 pairs competing in a mix of foursomes and fourballs. Stanley and Ruffels got off to a scorching start, reeling off four consecutive birdies to begin their round. Meanwhile, England's Ian Poulter, who recently lost his PGA tour card, carded a respectable 69 with Australian Geoff Ogilvy, leaving them in an eight-way tie for 11th place. Olympic champion Justin Rose and Open winner Henrik Stenson had a slower start, carding a 72. The $7.1m tournament has attracted six of the world's top 10 players, as the PGA aims to revitalize interest in the sport with innovative formats.

Wolves and Bolton Share Spoils in Thrilling Championship Clash Wolverhampton Wanderers and Bolton Wanderers played out a thrilling 2-2 draw at Molineux Stadium, with the visitors earning a crucial point in their battle to avoid relegation. New signing Joe Mason gave the hosts an early lead, poking home from close range after Bolton keeper Ben Amos failed to hold onto Bjorn Sigurdarson's shot. Despite dominating possession for much of the game, Bolton struggled to create clear-cut chances, with Liam Feeney's shot over the bar the closest they came to equalizing in the first half. However, they continued to press after the break, with Josh Vela drawing a save from Carl Ikeme and Silva testing the Wolves keeper from distance. Just as it seemed like Wolves were taking control, James Henry doubled their lead with a beautifully crafted goal, cutting inside and firing left-footed into the far corner. But Bolton refused to give up, and they were rewarded with two goals in the final stages of the game. Silva headed in unmarked from Vela's cross, before Stephen Dobbie's fortunate free-kick, which deflected off a player in the wall, earned the visitors a point. Wolves head coach Kenny Jackett was left to rue his side's failure to hold onto their lead, admitting that they had dropped two valuable points. "We need a heck of a run to make the play-offs, and we know that," he said. "Bolton were in the ascendancy for too much of the game, and I accept that. We should have been able to see it out when we were 2-0 up." In contrast, Bolton manager Neil Lennon was delighted with his side's performance, describing it as "outstanding". "We dominated the game for long periods, and I couldn't believe that we went 2-0 down," he said. "We thoroughly deserved a point, and it gives us a huge lift going into our next game against Rotherham." The draw leaves Bolton bottom of the Championship table, but they will take heart from their performance and look to build on it in their upcoming fixtures.

A 45-year-old man from Cwmbran has denied killing his daughter, Amelia Jones, who was left paralyzed and critically injured after an alleged attack in November 2012. Mark Jones, the defendant, was taking care of Amelia at the time of the incident in Pontnewydd. According to the prosecution, the attack may have been motivated by Jones's strong dislike for Amelia's father, Ian Skillern. On November 17, 2012, Jones called 999 after claiming Amelia had stopped breathing when he went to make a cup of tea. The little girl was rushed to Royal Gwent Hospital in Newport, where she was found to be in cardiac arrest. A consultant paediatrician who treated Amelia stated that she had suffered seizures, had flickering eyes, and was unresponsive. Despite being put on life support, Amelia's condition deteriorated, and she was later transferred to the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff. Tragically, Amelia's parents were informed that their daughter had sustained significant brain damage and would not recover. Life support was subsequently withdrawn, and Amelia passed away. A post-mortem examination revealed that she had suffered a fractured skull, brain swelling, and multiple rib fractures, with evidence suggesting she had been injured on at least three separate occasions. The trial at Newport Crown Court continues, with the jury hearing that Jones had been largely absent from his daughter's life until she was 16 and had a strong dislike for her father.

The Duchess of Cornwall recently visited the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill to commemorate its 75th anniversary. During her visit, she had the opportunity to view the iconic "Critical Mass" installation by renowned artist Antony Gormley, featuring 60 life-size cast iron human figures. The Duchess, who serves as the president of the pavilion, also toured the "Tomok Takahashi Introspective Retrospective" exhibition. Vice-chair of the Pavilion, Sara Stonor, welcomed the Duchess and highlighted the pavilion's rich history. She noted that the 9th Earl De La Warr's vision was to create a "people's palace" in Bexhill, which has been fulfilled through the pavilion's commitment to showcasing international exhibitions and performances. The Duchess also met with 100-year-old George Korner, a cousin of the pavilion's architect, Serge Chermayeff. Following her visit to the pavilion, the Duchess traveled to Chailey Heritage School, where she met with children, staff, and volunteers. She was given a tour of the school's facilities, including the multi-sensory studio and horse riding area, by Principal Sylvia Lamb and Head Teacher Simon Yates. The visit was a heartwarming conclusion to the Duchess's day in East Sussex.

Northern Ireland's economic growth is expected to slow down due to uncertainty over the EU referendum, according to Angela McGowan, chief economist at a major bank. McGowan stated that the uncertainty has "dampened" private sector investment, but a "bounce-back" could occur after the vote. However, she warned that public sector austerity and weaker global conditions would continue to weigh on growth. Certain sectors, such as IT and tourism, are forecast to grow at a rate of over 3%, while manufacturing, construction, and agriculture are expected to grow more slowly than average. McGowan emphasized that Northern Ireland's economy is still expanding, but at a slowing pace. The reduction in public sector jobs and Brexit are major risks to growth, with the latter having already lowered investment and growth in the first half of the year. This forecast is consistent with other economic predictions, including one from PwC, which estimates that economic growth in Northern Ireland will be around 1.5% in 2016. The impact of Brexit on the Northern Ireland economy remains a topic of debate, with some experts, like Dr. Graham Gudgin, suggesting that it will have a limited effect. Nevertheless, the current uncertainty is likely to continue affecting the economy until the outcome of the referendum is known.

British cyclist Becky James is set to make her return to the international stage this weekend as she competes for Great Britain at the Track World Cup in New Zealand. The 24-year-old from Abergavenny has faced a long and challenging journey to get back to this point, having undergone surgery to remove abnormal cells following a cervical screening and suffering a series of injuries, including a knee injury that kept her out of competition for nearly two years. Despite these setbacks, James is determined to make a strong impression in New Zealand, with Olympic qualifying points up for grabs. The sprint and keirin specialist, who won double world championship titles in 2013, has her sights firmly set on the Rio Olympics, which take place in nine months' time. "I really, really, really want to go to Rio," she told BBC Wales Today. "It's been a hard cycle missing out on London and on Glasgow, so all this hard work has got to be worth it." James made her track comeback in August after 18 months out of competition, and has been working tirelessly to regain her fitness and form. She acknowledges that it won't be easy to get back to the top, but is feeling positive about her progress so far. "It's really good to be racing again," she said. "The nationals were only three weeks ago and obviously I'm looking forward to being back in the World Cup. I've gone through the hard phase of training and getting into shape and feeling like a bike rider again." James's career has been severely disrupted since her double world championship win in 2013. She was forced to miss the London Olympics due to injury, and has since faced a series of health scares and setbacks. However, she is now focused on putting the past behind her and concentrating on her goal of making it to Rio. "I'm feeling like my old self again and looking forward to racing again," she said. "I know the rest of the world has moved on, so that's going to be a hard thing for me. I just don't have to get back to where I was being a double world champion, I need to be better than that." With the Track World Cup in New Zealand providing an important opportunity for James to gain Olympic qualifying points, she is determined to make the most of the competition. Her experience and talent make her a strong contender, and she will be hoping to use this event as a springboard to launch her bid for a place at the Rio Olympics. As she looks to the future, James is aware that there is still a lot of hard work to be done, but she is ready for the challenge. "This is a starting point," she said. "I know there is a lot of hard work to do, but I'm feeling positive and looking forward to racing again."

**Bullying in Welsh Schools: A Persistent Problem** A recent report has highlighted the ongoing issue of bullying in Welsh schools, with many institutions failing to effectively address the problem. According to Sally Holland, the Children's Commissioner for Wales, some schools are reluctant to tackle bullying due to fear of being perceived as having a problem. This reluctance has resulted in a lack of consistency in handling complaints, leaving some children feeling isolated and unsupported. The report, titled "Sam's Story," gathered the experiences of 2,000 children and young people, as well as the views of 300 professionals. The findings revealed that children are often bullied due to differences such as ethnicity, poverty, disability, and gender stereotyping. Furthermore, many parents are unresponsive to their children's experiences of bullying, exacerbating the problem. Dr. Holland expressed frustration that despite previous warnings from the schools inspectorate Estyn three years ago, the issues of confusion over what constitutes bullying and a lack of consistent recording remain unaddressed. "Some things have changed, but yes, there are some fundamentals we still need to get right," she said. "We do need to be recording bullying and make sure the best practice, which we know is out there, is available to schools." The Welsh Government has stated that all forms of bullying should be tackled vigorously and that a school behavior policy should be in place by law. However, Dr. Holland argued that more needs to be done to ensure that schools are effectively addressing the issue. She has called on the government to place a statutory duty on schools to record all incidences and types of reported bullying, as well as to develop a clear definition of bullying. Dr. Holland emphasized the importance of schools having an honest conversation with their students and the wider community about how they are tackling bullying. "Let's not keep it in the corner as an embarrassing aspect of school life," she said. "Let's accept that it happens and positively move forward to tackle it." She also stressed that everyone, including parents, teachers, and the wider community, needs to be involved in addressing the issue of bullying. The Welsh Government has stated that it will consider Dr. Holland's report as part of its review of anti-bullying guidance. A spokesman said, "We do not tolerate any bullying in the Welsh education system. We expect schools and education services to make it clear that all forms of bullying are entirely unacceptable and to tackle all incidents vigorously, ensuring that pupils are properly supported." While the government's commitment to addressing bullying is welcome, Dr. Holland's report highlights the need for more concrete action to be taken. The fact that anti-bullying guidance often sits on shelves in schools, unread and unimplemented, is a stark reminder of the work that still needs to be done to ensure that all children in Wales feel safe and supported in their schools. By working together, schools, parents, and the wider community can help to create a culture where bullying is not tolerated and all children can thrive.

Violence Erupts Between Wolves and Birmingham City Fans After Match A clash between Wolverhampton Wanderers and Birmingham City fans near Wolverhampton railway station on Friday night has sparked a police investigation. The incident occurred after Wolves' 2-1 defeat, with West Midlands Police reporting that officers were forced to intervene to quell disorder. According to the police, Wolves supporters threw bottles, seats, and coins following Birmingham City's second goal, prompting a response from law enforcement. Thirteen arrests were made on the night, with eight men believed to be Birmingham City supporters and five thought to be Wolves fans. However, a Birmingham fan who witnessed the incident has raised concerns about the use of force by police officers. Nick Glynn, a former police officer with 30 years of experience, claimed to have filmed "potentially unlawful violence" by officers. He stated that he saw an officer striking a fan with a baton, which he believes was excessive and unjustified. Glynn, who has trained police in the use of force, said that the threat level required to justify such action is very high and that the officers' response seemed disproportionate. "Somebody could've died from getting struck on the head with a baton, and my question would be, for what? For maybe not walking quite quickly enough to a railway station?" he asked. West Midlands Police match commander, Chief Inspector Nick Rowe, defended the officers' actions, saying that they had issued several warnings to no avail and used "proportionate force" to prevent further clashes and protect fans. He stated that the incident was "isolated" and that officers had to take action to maintain order. The police have launched an investigation into the two incidents and will review any complaints received. The force is also working to identify those responsible for throwing missiles inside the stadium and those involved in trouble near the station. The incident has raised concerns about fan safety and the use of force by police officers. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) will be consulted as part of the investigation, and any complaints will be reviewed by the West Midlands Police professional standards department.

Ipswich's Cornhill Revamp to Feature Water Feature and Sculpture Work on the revamped Cornhill in Ipswich is set to begin in January, following approval from the council's planning committee. The new design, created by Belfast-based architects Hall McKnight, features a water feature and sculpture, replacing initial plans for a tower. The revised design was unveiled in March after a public consultation, which led to a more traditional approach. The project has received significant funding, with the New Anglia Local Enterprise Partnership contributing £1.6m and Suffolk County Council and Ipswich Borough Council committing £1.75m. The redevelopment aims to transform the main town centre square, which was previously criticized by former Marks & Spencer boss Sir Stuart Rose. The new design promises to enhance the area's aesthetic and functionality, and locals are eagerly awaiting the transformation.

Two men, George-Hari Constantinescu and Danut Gheorghe, both 30, have been found guilty of assaulting a woman in her 20s in Ipswich. The attack occurred on February 25 as the victim was walking along Rope Walk. According to evidence presented at Ipswich Crown Court, the pair had spent nearly an hour prowling the streets before targeting their victim. In a disturbing revelation, the court heard that Constantinescu and Gheorghe had set out to engage in sexual activity with a woman, regardless of her consent. After being rebuffed in local clubs and venues, they spent 50 minutes searching for a young woman to attack. They eventually spotted their victim and "hunted her" down, attacking her between 03:10 and 03:30 GMT. The assault was brutal, with the men using unnecessary violence and leaving the victim with significant injuries to her face and neck. She was dragged into a nearby car park, where she was beaten and left half-naked. The victim fell unconscious during the attack, which lasted several minutes. Constantinescu and Gheorghe then abandoned her and attempted to evade capture by avoiding CCTV cameras and changing their appearance. The victim has spoken out about the lasting impact of the attack, stating that she still experiences nightmares and lives in fear. Judge Rupert Overbury condemned the men's actions as "callous" and described them as "predators." He emphasized that every woman should be able to walk safely without fear of attack. The pair were arrested after Suffolk Constabulary released CCTV images, and they now face justice for their heinous crime.

UK Borrowing Falls to Lowest May Total Since 2007, But Economists Remain Cautious The Office for National Statistics (ONS) has announced that public sector borrowing, excluding support for state-owned banks, has fallen to £9.7 billion in May, the lowest total for the month since 2007. This figure is down £0.4 billion from the same month last year, but slightly higher than the forecasted £9.5 billion by economists. Despite this decrease, borrowing for the financial year so far, covering April and May, has reached £17.9 billion, which is £0.2 billion higher than the same period last year. The ONS has also revised down its estimate of the amount borrowed in the 2015-16 financial year to £74.9 billion. The government's total current expenditure rose, but receipts from income, corporation, and VAT taxes in May were all higher than a year earlier. The total public sector net debt, excluding banks, stood at £1.606 trillion by the end of May, equivalent to 83.7% of gross domestic product (GDP). While annual borrowing has been falling in general since the peak reached in the 2009-10 financial year, economists remain cautious about the government's ability to meet its projections. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) has estimated that the public sector will borrow £55.5 billion during the financial year to March 2017, a reduction of about £20 billion from the previous financial year. Chancellor George Osborne has pledged to fix the public finances and return a budget surplus by 2020. However, the Treasury and Bank of England have warned that the economy has been hit by uncertainty ahead of the EU referendum. Scott Bowman, an economist at Capital Economics, said that the chancellor "still has a long way to go" to meet his projections, but noted that GDP growth could rebound in the second half of the year if the UK votes to remain in the EU. Ross Campbell, public sector director at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW), criticized the chancellor for "taking his eye off the economic ball." He emphasized the need for a comprehensive strategy to kick-start a faltering economic recovery, regardless of the outcome of the EU referendum. As the UK awaits the results of the referendum, it remains to be seen how the government will respond to the challenges facing the economy and whether it can meet its ambitious targets for reducing borrowing and achieving a budget surplus.

Tragedy in Shanghai: Officials and Executives to Face Charges Over Deadly High-Rise Fire A devastating fire that engulfed a 28-storey building in Shanghai last November, killing numerous residents and injuring 71 others, has led to a crackdown on corruption and safety violations. State media reports have confirmed that local government officials, construction executives, and workers will face charges in connection with the tragedy. The fire, which occurred on November 15, was initially blamed on unlicensed welders, but further investigation has revealed a web of corruption and negligence. According to the Shanghai Prosecutors' Office, some executives from the Jingan District Construction Group, the general contractor responsible for the building's renovation, will be held accountable. China's work safety officials have cited illegal contracting, unsafe materials, and poorly supervised workers as contributing factors to the disaster. The State Council has ordered a nationwide overhaul of fire prevention measures in response to the blaze. The incident has raised concerns about corrupt relationships between construction companies and government bodies, highlighting the need for greater accountability and transparency. As the city of Shanghai, home to over 20 million residents and 5,000 high-rise blocks, continues to grow and develop, ensuring the safety of its citizens remains a top priority.

Aberdeen Manager Derek McInnes Hopes to Retain Niall McGinn Beyond Summer Aberdeen manager Derek McInnes has expressed his desire to retain the services of Northern Ireland international Niall McGinn beyond the summer. McGinn's contract is set to expire, and the player is currently weighing his options. McInnes revealed that the club has made McGinn a "strong offer" to stay at Pittodrie, and he hopes the player will choose to remain with the Dons. McInnes believes that McGinn's indecision is not primarily driven by financial considerations, but rather by the temptation to try a new experience at a different club. "We've made Niall what we feel is a strong offer," McInnes explained. "It's not so much the contract offer for Niall. I think it's just maybe weighing up more what he wants to do next, whether he wants to stay for a bit longer, which we certainly hope is the case, or whether he wants to try something different." McGinn has consistently expressed his love for the club and has enjoyed his time at Aberdeen. McInnes is hopeful that this affection, combined with the club's contract offer, will be enough to persuade McGinn to stay. "He's quite within his rights and we respect that," McInnes said. "What is clear is Niall has never at any point said that he wants to leave. He's always indicated his love for the club and how much he's enjoying it." McGinn's performances on the pitch continue to impress, and his individual display in Aberdeen's 3-0 win over Dundee was a testament to his skill and dedication. The forward scored two goals and laid on the other, showcasing his quality and importance to the team. McInnes praised McGinn's first goal, describing it as "top drawer" and a "fantastic piece of individual play." The win over Dundee moved Aberdeen up to second in the Premiership, and McInnes was pleased with his team's overall performance. "We had to wait longer than we hoped to get in front, but once we made the breakthrough, we brought some real quality," he said. In contrast, Dundee manager Paul Hartley was left to lament his team's defensive shortcomings. "The start was promising, but after that, we didn't defend properly," Hartley said. "For us tonight, not to defend balls coming in, they seemed to switch off and not do their jobs. We've got to do the basics properly. For me, we've got to try and make it as difficult as possible. We didn't do that." Hartley also acknowledged the challenges his team faces in terms of recruitment, citing financial constraints as a major obstacle. "We want to try and bring some players in, but it's not going to be easy," he said. "Financially, it's going to be difficult. We've enquired about some players, but we can't get them because of the financial side of it. We want to add quality, and we need to add quality." As the transfer window remains open, McInnes and Aberdeen will be eager to resolve McGinn's contract situation and ensure the player remains at the club beyond the summer. With McGinn's talent and dedication, the Dons will be keen to retain his services and build on their current success in the Premiership.

Kiribati, a Small Island Nation with a Big Challenge Located in the South Pacific, Kiribati, pronounced Kiribas, is a small island nation that gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1979. With a population of approximately 103,000 people, Kiribati is home to the largest marine reserve in the South Pacific. However, the country faces a significant challenge due to its low-lying atolls, which are at risk from rising sea levels caused by global warming. To address this issue, the Kiribati government has taken proactive measures, including purchasing land in Fiji with the permission of the Fijian government. This move aims to ensure food security and provide a possible refuge for its citizens in the event of a climate-related disaster. The country's economy is largely dependent on exports of copra and coconuts, as well as fishing licenses, foreign aid, and remittances from workers abroad. Kiribati's history dates back to the 11th century when Samoans, Fijians, and Tongans migrated to the islands. The country was named the Gilbert Islands in 1820, after British naval captain Thomas Gilbert, who visited the islands in 1788. In 1892, Britain declared a protectorate over the Gilbert Islands and the neighboring Ellice Islands, which later became the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916. The country has a relatively stable political system, with President Taneti Mamau elected in March 2016. Freedom of speech and media is generally respected, with a government-run radio station and newspaper offering diverse views. The country has a trust fund set up with revenues from phosphate mines on the island of Banaba, which was depleted in 1980, causing significant economic hardship for Kiribati. Despite the challenges it faces, Kiribati remains a significant player in the Pacific region. With its stunning marine reserve and rich cultural heritage, the country is working to balance its economic development with environmental sustainability. As the world grapples with the impacts of climate change, Kiribati's story serves as a reminder of the urgent need for global action to protect vulnerable island nations and their communities.

Abbot Cuthbert Madden of Ampleforth Abbey has denied any wrongdoing amid allegations of misconduct dating back to the 1990s. The 61-year-old Benedictine monk, who has been at the abbey for over 30 years, was voluntarily interviewed under caution by North Yorkshire Police. The allegations involve four pupils at Ampleforth College, the school attached to the abbey, where Abbot Madden previously taught. In a statement, the abbey said Abbot Madden will cooperate fully with the investigation and denied any wrongdoing. The police investigation, which was triggered by reports made in August, is ongoing and has led to safeguarding measures being put in place. Abbot Madden was elected as abbot in 2005 and re-elected in 2013. The abbey has chosen to be transparent about the situation, informing the Ampleforth community and friends about the current investigation. North Yorkshire Police confirmed that the investigation is continuing, with no further details released at this time.

A court challenge brought by Vue Cinemas against the City of York Council's decision to approve an expanded cinema at the Monks Cross stadium site has been dismissed. The council had initially approved a 12-screen design, but later gave permission for a 13th screen and 400 extra seats. The judge found that the decision-making process was correct, paving the way for the development to proceed. The stadium, which is expected to become home to York City FC and York City Knights Rugby League Club, has suffered numerous delays since it was first proposed in 2009. The project was initially forecast to cost £37m and open in spring 2017, but is now expected to cost an additional £7m and will not be operational until next year. The council has welcomed the court decision, describing it as a "great step forward" for the development. The stadium will also feature leisure, retail, office, and community facilities, in addition to the cinema and sports facilities. Vue Cinemas has not commented on the decision. Despite the setbacks, the council remains committed to seeing the project through to completion.

Tragedy of Young Father's Drowning Highlights Dangers of Swimming in Open Water It's been over a decade since 21-year-old Dale Alexander tragically lost his life while swimming with friends in the River Mourne at Sion Mills. The young father, whose wife was pregnant at the time, was an experienced swimmer and angler, having spent his youth exploring the river. However, despite his knowledge of the water, Dale fell victim to the bitterly cold temperatures, with his body going into shock as he swam back across the river. Brendan Winters, chairman of Strabane Lifford anglers and a childhood friend of Dale's, remembers the incident vividly. "Dale had swum across the river, got out of the water, and spoken to people on the far side. But as he was swimming back, his body went into shock," he said. "It just goes to show you that regardless of how well you think you know the water, it's really dangerous. You should never become complacent." The tragedy has prompted warnings from Northern Ireland Water and the Quarry Products Association, urging people to stay away from areas that are not usually open to the public. Michael Bergin of NI Water emphasized the importance of taking precautions, stating that "while a reservoir may look like the perfect place to cool down, it can be very dangerous. You may swim well in a warm indoor pool, but that does not mean that you will be able to swim in cold water." A 2010 inquest into Dale's death heard that his life could have been saved had life-saving equipment, such as life ropes and rings, been in place. Brendan Winters echoed this sentiment, saying that the absence of these safety measures may have contributed to the tragic outcome. Dale's legacy lives on through his two young sons, who were born after his passing and will never get to know their father. As Brendan poignantly noted, "Dale is never far from my thoughts. I wouldn't wish that on any other family or for anyone else to have to lose a friend like that."

Revolutionary Solar Cell Technology Takes to the Skies, Paving Way for Future Space Exploration and Renewable Energy A groundbreaking solar cell, developed by the UK Space Agency and the Algerian Space Agency, is currently orbiting the Earth, generating electricity and offering a glimpse into a future where space-based solar power could become a reality. The tiny satellite, measuring just 30cm by 10cm by 10cm, is equipped with a solar cell that is a mere 0.1mm thick, making it significantly smaller than conventional solar cells. The device is flying at an altitude of 450 miles (724km) and travelling at a staggering 17,000mph (27,359km), completing one orbit around the globe every 90 minutes. According to Dr Dan Lamb, from Swansea University's College of Engineering's Solar Energy Research Centre, the project has the potential to revolutionize space exploration and provide a renewable source of energy on Earth. The solar cell's thin design and compact size make it an attractive option for space missions, where every kilogram of weight counts. With the cost of launching payloads into orbit running into thousands of pounds per kilogram, this new approach to space solar power could offer significant cost reductions. Over the course of the satellite's estimated year-long life, Dr Lamb and his team will be monitoring the amount of electricity generated by the solar cell, as well as its ability to withstand radiation and extreme temperature fluctuations in space. The advantages of space-based solar cells are numerous. With approximately 30% more sunlight available in orbit, the cell can generate more energy than its ground-based counterparts. Additionally, the cell spends less time in darkness, making it a more efficient source of power. However, the team is still uncertain about how the complex solar materials will hold up to the sun's radiation without the protection of the Earth's atmosphere. If the experiment is successful, the technology could have far-reaching implications for space exploration. Dr Lamb believes that it could be used to power future manned lunar or Mars bases, as well as provide electric propulsion for spacecraft. Moreover, the technology could also be used to create orbiting solar arrays that beam electricity back to Earth, providing a green and renewable source of energy. The test satellite was launched from Southern India on 26 September and has already begun transmitting data back to scientists in Swansea and their collaborators at the University of Surrey and Qioptiq Space Technology Ltd. By this time next year, the team hopes to have a better understanding of the technology's potential and be one step closer to making space-based solar power a reality. As Dr Lamb noted, the project is already offering a tantalizing glimpse into the future, and its success could pave the way for a new era in space exploration and renewable energy.

New Research Sheds Light on the Formation of the Moon For decades, scientists have believed that the Moon was formed from debris left over after a massive collision between the early Earth and a planet-sized object approximately 4.5 billion years ago. However, this theory, known as the giant impact hypothesis, has been challenged by the fact that the Earth and Moon have surprisingly similar chemical compositions. Recently, two new studies published in the journal Science have proposed innovative solutions to this long-standing conundrum. One team, led by Matija Cuk from the Seti Institute, suggests that the early Earth may have been spinning much faster than it does today, with a rotation period of just a few hours. Using advanced simulations, the researchers found that this rapid rotation would have allowed debris from the Earth's mantle to be ejected into orbit, forming a Moon with a chemical composition similar to that of our planet. Over time, the gravitational interaction between the Sun and the Moon would have slowed the Earth's rotation to its current 24-hour period. Another team, led by Robin Canup from the Southwest Research Institute, took a different approach. Their simulations involved larger impactors colliding with a smaller Earth at lower speeds. The results showed that this scenario could also produce a Moon with a chemical composition similar to that of the Earth. These new findings provide a significant breakthrough in our understanding of the Moon's formation and offer a fresh perspective on the giant impact hypothesis. The giant impact hypothesis was first proposed in the 1970s and suggests that the Moon formed from debris kicked into orbit after a massive collision between the early Earth and a smaller proto-planet. While this theory has been widely accepted, it has been difficult to reconcile with the fact that the Earth and Moon have identical oxygen isotope compositions. The new research provides a compelling explanation for this similarity and offers a new avenue for exploring the early history of our solar system.

UK's Top Spy Agency Partners with Private Firms to Boost Online Security In a bid to strengthen the country's online security, the UK's most secretive agency, GCHQ, has partnered with several private companies to launch a new cyber security hub in Cheltenham. The GCHQ Cyber Accelerator, which was launched on Wednesday, will provide a platform for start-ups to work closely with the agency's staff and resources to develop innovative solutions to combat cyber threats. Among the companies selected for the program are StatusToday, which uses artificial intelligence to monitor workplace behavior and detect insider attacks, and CounterCraft, which runs decoy computers to fool hackers. These companies will have access to GCHQ's expertise and network of international partners, as well as a £5,000 grant each and access to government tenders. The partnership is seen as a significant step forward in the UK's efforts to boost its £22bn cybersecurity sector. According to Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity expert at the University of Surrey, the government recognizes that innovative ideas on cybersecurity are no longer limited to big companies. The accelerator program aims to attract new businesses to Cheltenham and provide a platform for start-ups to develop and test their products. However, the partnership also raises concerns about security risks. Prof Anthony Glees, the director of the Buckingham University Centre for Security and Intelligence Studies, warned that working with the private sector could be a "twin-edged sword" for GCHQ. While it brings in new ideas, it also increases the risk of sensitive information being compromised. GCHQ has assured that all companies have undergone rigorous background checks and have been selected through a competitive process. The launch of the GCHQ Cyber Accelerator is part of a broader effort to establish Cheltenham as a hub for cybersecurity innovation. The city is already home to a number of defence contractors working with GCHQ, and the new National Cyber Security Centre is also located there. With the support of the government and telecoms firm Telefonica, the accelerator program is set to play a key role in boosting the UK's cybersecurity sector and protecting the country from increasingly sophisticated cyber threats.

A recent report has revealed that the £465m of EU convergence money invested in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly between 2007 and 2013 has been deemed "poor value" by independent consultants. The investment, which was intended to boost the local economy, failed to deliver the expected results, with private sector investment coming in at £440m lower than anticipated. Despite creating 3,557 jobs, the project has been widely criticized, with Kim Conchie, chief executive of the Cornwall Chamber of Commerce, describing the findings as "pretty damning". The report highlights that the cost per job in the research and development fund was a staggering £160,000 per person, raising serious questions about the effectiveness of the funding. The region received €654m from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and European Social Fund due to its economic performance being below 75% of the European Union average. The funding was used to support various projects, including the construction of a link road at Camborne and the development of the Wave Hub at Hayle. The ERDF convergence team has acknowledged that the targets set for the program were developed prior to the 2008 financial crisis, but argues that they were retained in order to aim high and achieve the best possible return on investment. However, the report's findings suggest that the uncertain economic climate had a significant impact on the project's performance, leading to "significant under-performance" in achieving its target results regarding jobs, Gross Value Added, and private sector investment. The lessons learned from this program will be carried forward into the next European Funding Programme.

Tottenham Hotspur have rejected a world-record £86m bid from Spanish giants Real Madrid for star player Gareth Bale. Despite the substantial offer, Spurs insist that no deal has been agreed, and they are in no rush to sell their prized asset. The north London club is aware that the sale of Bale could trigger a series of transfers that may ultimately benefit their rivals, including Arsenal, who have been linked with Real Madrid players Karim Benzema and Angel Di Maria. The transfer window is set to close on September 2, and Tottenham is happy to wait and see how the situation unfolds. The club has already missed out on signing Brazilian midfielder Willian, who joined Chelsea for £30m after completing a medical at Tottenham. Spurs have been linked with Roma's Erik Lamela and Chelsea's Juan Mata, although Jose Mourinho has stated that the Spanish playmaker is not for sale. Meanwhile, Bale failed to report for training on Tuesday, following a club-authorised break in Marbella. The reason for his absence is unknown, but it is believed that he is eager to secure a move to Real Madrid. The Spanish club has made two separate bids for the Welshman and is waiting to see if Tottenham will accept either offer. A special stage, nicknamed the "Bale Box," has been erected at the Bernabeu ground, reportedly to unveil Bale to the club's fans. Real Madrid has already spent over £50m this summer, signing Spanish midfielders Asier Illarramendi and Isco from Real Sociedad and Malaga, respectively. The club's next home game is on Sunday against Athletic Bilbao, just a day before the transfer window closes. Bale, who joined Spurs in 2007, was named player of the year by both the Professional Footballers' Association and Football Writers last season after scoring 26 goals for the club. As the transfer saga continues, Tottenham remains firm in its stance, and it remains to be seen what the future holds for the talented Welshman.

Manchester City midfielder Yaya Toure has expressed his discontent with the criticism he has been receiving, stating that it has left him unhappy. In an interview with French sports magazine L'Equipe, the Ivorian captain revealed that winning trophies and earning a substantial amount of money has not brought him the happiness he desired. Toure feels that his name has been tarnished by "lots of bitter people" and is hurt by the lack of recognition for his performances. City manager Manuel Pellegrini has come to Toure's defense, citing his impressive performances over the last four years as proof of his importance to the team. Pellegrini acknowledged that Toure may have concerns about the criticism, but emphasized that it is separate from his overall happiness at the club. Toure has scored just one goal in 11 appearances this season, sparking criticism from some quarters.

Federal Charges Filed Against Suspect in New York and New Jersey Bombings Ahmad Khan Rahami, the 28-year-old suspect in the recent bombings in New York and New Jersey, has been charged with federal offenses, including the use of a weapon of mass destruction, bombing, and use of a destructive device. The Afghan-born US citizen remains in hospital, recovering from gunshot wounds sustained during a police shootout on Monday. The FBI complaint, unsealed on Tuesday in a Manhattan federal court, reveals that 31 people were injured in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan on Saturday, including an unnamed Briton. The victims suffered severe injuries, with one woman requiring the removal of multiple ball bearings from her body, as well as metal fragmentation from her ear and wood shards from her neck. According to the complaint, Rahami was found with a notebook containing writings that suggest a radical ideology. The journal includes passages that praise Osama Bin Laden, Anwar al-Awlaki, and Nidal Hasan, and references jihad and the mujahideen. The writings also express anger towards the US government, stating, "You [USA Government] continue your [unintelligible] slaught[er]" against holy warriors in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and Palestine. The investigation has revealed that Rahami had been preparing for the attack for months, purchasing bomb-making equipment on eBay, including citric acid, a circuit board, and electric igniters for fireworks. The FBI also recovered video footage from a mobile phone belonging to one of Rahami's relatives, which shows the suspect igniting incendiary material in a cylindrical container two days before the blasts. Rahami, who worked at a family-owned fried chicken shop in Elizabeth, New Jersey, is also accused of planting two bombs in Chelsea, one of which failed to detonate. Another bomb exploded in a New Jersey seaside town earlier on the same day, but no one was hurt. He is also accused of leaving explosives in a discarded rucksack in a rubbish bin in Elizabeth, New Jersey. The suspect's wife, a Pakistani national, is being questioned in the United Arab Emirates, according to US media reports. The FBI had previously investigated Rahami for terrorism in 2014, following a complaint from his father, but found no link despite alleged acts of violence. The series of bombings has sparked a heated debate about national security between the two presidential candidates, just days before their first televised debate. The attacks have raised questions about the effectiveness of the US government's counter-terrorism strategies and the need for increased vigilance in the face of growing threats from radical ideologies. Rahami is also facing state charges in New Jersey, including attempted murder of police, stemming from his arrest on Monday outside a bar in Linden, New Jersey. As the investigation continues, authorities are working to piece together the events leading up to the bombings and to determine whether Rahami had any accomplices or connections to larger terrorist networks.

Thieves broke into The Owl and Falconry Centre in Shipley, Wolverhampton, stealing seven birds overnight on September 24. The stolen birds include Gyr Saker Falcons, Barn Owls, and Burrowing Owls. The Gyr Saker Falcons are valued at £7,000 each. Despite the damage to aviaries, the centre will remain open. The falconry, run by volunteers, visits nursing homes and schools for educational tours. The incident is under investigation, with CCTV footage yielding no suspects. The centre, home to about 50 birds and mammals, is seeking support to recover from the loss.

The stage is set for the Irn-Bru Cup Final, with Dundee United set to face St Mirren at Fir Park. The match, scheduled for a 12:30 GMT kick-off, will be broadcast live on BBC Alba. Both teams secured their spots in the final with impressive semi-final wins, with Dundee United edging out Queen of the South 3-2 and St Mirren coming from behind to defeat The New Saints 4-1. This year's competition featured teams from Wales and Northern Ireland, and next season will see the addition of League of Ireland sides Sligo Rovers and Bray Wanderers. Dundee United is seeking their first Challenge Cup title, while St Mirren aims to repeat their 2005 victory. SPFL chief executive Neil Doncaster expressed his delight at hosting the final at Fir Park, where tickets will be available for as little as £5. With excitement building, fans can look forward to a thrilling match between two Championship sides.

A 45-year-old man, Craig Whyte, appeared in the High Court in Glasgow to face two charges related to his involvement with Rangers football club. The charges include one count of fraud and a second allegation under the Companies Act. The alleged fraud occurred between May 2010 and May 2011, during which time Whyte obtained a majority stake in the club. It is claimed that he and his representatives misled then-owner Sir David Murray and others about the availability of funds to make payments. The second charge relates to an £18m payment made in connection with the takeover. Whyte entered no plea and his bail was continued. A provisional trial date has been set for April 2017, with a two-day hearing scheduled for December. Donald Findlay QC represented Whyte, while Alex Prentice QC has taken over as the lead prosecutor in the case. Prentice stated that he would step in as requested by the Lord Advocate. The case will continue to unfold in the coming months.

Crystal Palace midfielder Joe Ledley has been released by the club. The 30-year-old joined Palace in 2014 after stints with Cardiff City and Celtic. The news was announced as Ledley prepares for Wales' World Cup qualifier against Serbia. He is currently with the Wales squad in Belgrade. Meanwhile, Southampton's Lloyd Isgrove is also seeking a new club after being released. Swansea City has confirmed the departures of several players, including Jonathan Dyson, Marvin Emnes, and Gerhard Tremmel. These moves come as the soccer world prepares for upcoming matches and transfers. Ledley's future is now uncertain.

Manx2 has announced flight services between two islands for three months until early September. The company credits last year's short season for boosting tourism. Following a recent Welsh Government contract win, Manx2.com chairman Noel Hayes expressed delight in offering passengers a unique opportunity to visit Anglesey by air, building on positive feedback from last year's trial. The extended season aims to further enhance tourism at both destinations, with services running through the summer.

US and Russia Agree to Ceasefire in Syria A ceasefire has been announced in Syria, following a meeting between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the G20 talks in Hamburg, Germany. The truce, which is also backed by Jordan, is currently in force along a line agreed by Syrian government forces and rebels. This move is a significant development in the six-year conflict, which has resulted in the deaths of approximately 300,000 people and displaced 11 million more. The US and Russia have been supporting opposing sides in the conflict, with Russia backing the Syrian government and the US calling for the removal of President Bashar al-Assad. Despite their differences, US Secretary of State Rex Tillerson stated that the two countries' ultimate goals for Syria are "exactly the same." The ceasefire, which covers the regions of Deraa, Quneitra, and Sweida, is the result of months of secret talks between Russian and US officials. This agreement marks a crucial step towards ending the violence in Syria and working towards a peaceful resolution.

Worcestershire Take Control Against Northants in Championship Clash Worcestershire continued their impressive form in the Championship, taking control of their match against Northants on the first day at Northampton. Skipper Joe Leach led from the front, taking 3-36 as the home side were bowled out for a modest total. Jack Shantry, Ed Barnard, and Josh Tongue shared the other wickets, with Shantry finishing with 3-54. In response, Worcestershire's openers made a solid start, with Brett D'Oliveira and Daryl Mitchell putting on 75 before D'Oliveira fell for 35. Mitchell remained unbeaten on 52, guiding the visitors to 108-2 at the close of play. The partnership between D'Oliveira and Mitchell has been a key factor in Worcestershire's success, with the pair having shared a 243-run stand in their previous match against Derbyshire. Northants captain Alex Wakely expressed his disappointment with the day's events, praising Worcestershire's bowling effort. "They bowled really well this morning, in partnerships and dried the scoreboard," he said. "We were probably going to bat anyway because it looked like a bat first pitch." Wakely acknowledged that his team's bowling had been poor at times, but was hopeful that they could recover on the second day. Worcestershire assistant coach Matt Mason was delighted with his team's performance, citing the bravery of their decision to bowl first. "The pitch had a lot of dead grass, but we took the brave decision to bowl first," he said. "The ball seemed to go through periods of doing something. The key was just sticking to our plans and we got our rewards." With Leach now having taken 25 wickets for the season, Mason will be hoping that his team can continue their winning streak, which currently stands at five matches.

The Bank of Scotland has released its Affordable Cities Review, which reveals that city living in Scotland is more affordable than the UK city average. The average price for a city home in Scotland stands at £175,962, which is 5.24 times the gross annual average earnings. Although this represents a 7% increase on last year, it is still significantly below the peak of 6.12 in 2008. The report suggests that affordability has improved since 2008 due to a combination of a 6% decline in average house prices and a 10% increase in average annual earnings. Stirling remains the UK's most affordable city for the second year running, with an average property price of £158,645, which is 3.85 times the gross average annual earnings. Glasgow and Dundee follow closely as Scotland's most affordable cities. In contrast, Edinburgh is Scotland's least affordable city, with an average house price of £216,424, or 6.11 times the gross annual average earnings. Aberdeen has recorded the biggest price rise of any UK city over the past decade, with an 88% gain, largely due to the strong performance of the oil and gas sector. The report also notes that London has recorded the highest house price growth in recent years, with a 40% rise over the past five years. Overall, the review indicates that city living in Scotland is becoming more affordable, although there are still significant variations between cities.

Intensive Manhunt Continues for Accused Cop Killer Eric Frein in Pennsylvania A massive search operation is underway in the dense north-east woodlands of Pennsylvania for 31-year-old Eric Frein, accused of fatally shooting one police officer and critically wounding another. Over 200 officers are scouring the area, focusing on the vicinity of Frein's parents' home in the Pocono mountains. The search has been hindered by the rugged terrain and heavy forest canopy, which has blocked police helicopters' view of the ground in some areas. According to Lt Col George Bivens of the state police, "I do believe we are close to him at this point." The police have found an AK-47 rifle, ammunition, and other items believed to have been left behind by Frein, a self-described survivalist. Frein has been added to the FBI's 10 Most Wanted List, and a $175,000 reward is being offered for information leading to his capture. The shooting occurred on September 12 outside the Blooming Grove state police barracks during an evening shift change, resulting in the death of Capt Bryon Dickson and injuring State Trooper Alex Douglass. Frein allegedly has a history of making statements about killing law enforcement officers and has received survivalist training. He was also part of a re-enactment group that portrayed soldiers from eastern Europe. Thousands of law enforcement officers recently gathered to pay their respects to Capt Dickson, who was remembered as a devoted and impeccable officer. Fellow officer Derek Felsman praised Dickson's commitment to his work and family, saying he "held himself to the highest standards in every aspect of his life." The search for Frein continues, with police determined to bring him to justice for the tragic attack on their colleagues.

Local Heroes Honoured with Prestigious Awards The New Year's Honours list has recognized the outstanding achievements of several local individuals, including Olympic gold medallist Nick Skelton and football referee Sian Massey-Ellis. Skelton, 58, from Bedworth, Warwickshire, has been honoured for his remarkable career, which includes winning individual gold at his seventh Olympic Games. Despite initially retiring 16 years ago after a serious neck injury, Skelton made a remarkable comeback to become Britain's second-oldest Olympic gold medallist at Rio 2016. Sian Massey-Ellis, 31, from Coventry, has been awarded an MBE for her services to football. The referee has overcome sexism and misogyny in the sport, including a high-profile incident in 2011. Massey-Ellis hopes to inspire the next generation of female officials and footballers, saying, "I love football and it's a privilege to officiate in Premier League and EFL matches." Additionally, football coach Annie Zaidi from Nuneaton has received a British Empire Medal. The 32-year-old has faced racism, sexism, and Islamophobia in her career but has persevered to become a successful coach and role model for young women in the sport. These honours recognize the dedication and perseverance of these local heroes, who continue to inspire and make a positive impact in their respective fields.

Northern Ireland's Aileen Reid has made a remarkable comeback in the triathlon event, finishing 21st overall. Despite a challenging start, placing 32nd in the swim and 36th in the bike stage, Reid gained 15 places in the 10k run. Her strong finish came after a tumultuous training period, hindered by illness. Reid's determination paid off, as she crossed the line just under five minutes behind winner Gwen Jorgensen. The American took gold with a time of 1:56.16, followed by Nicola Sprig of Switzerland. Britain's Vicky Holland secured bronze, outsprinting teammate Non Stanford in a thrilling finish. Reid's result is a significant improvement from her 43rd place finish four years ago, where a cycling crash derailed her Olympic dreams.

Millwall striker Alfie Pavey joins Aldershot Town. The 20-year-old had a spell at Barnet and made six substitute appearances for Millwall. Shots manager Barry Smith praised Pavey's pedigree and coaching. He is eligible to debut against Chester on Saturday, following interest from other National League clubs.

The FIFA awards ceremony is set to take place in Zurich, where the best players and coaches in men's and women's football will be honored. Real Madrid forward Cristiano Ronaldo is fresh from his fourth Ballon d'Or win, having beaten rival Lionel Messi to the award last month. Messi, along with Antoine Griezmann, has also been nominated for the men's prize. The best women's player, as well as the top coaches in men's and women's football, will also be announced. Claudio Ranieri, who led Leicester City to a historic Premier League title, is among the nominees for best coach, alongside Portugal's Fernando Santos and Zinedine Zidane. The winners will be determined by a combination of votes from national team captains and coaches, selected journalists, and an online poll of fans, with each category accounting for 25% of the points. Additionally, the Puskas award for best goal will be presented, and a prize for best fans will be awarded to one of the nominated teams, including Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund, ADO Den Haag, or the Iceland fans who impressed with their clapping salute at Euro 2016. The ceremony promises to be an exciting celebration of the best in football.

Patients and Visitors Share Mixed Views on Addenbrooke's Hospital Following the news that Addenbrooke's hospital has been placed in special measures, the BBC reached out to those who have used the hospital's services to gather their opinions. The responses were varied, with some praising the hospital's care and others expressing concerns and disappointment. Many patients and visitors spoke highly of the hospital, citing the dedication and hard work of the staff. Sue Munro, who has been cared for by the hospital her entire life, said, "Addenbrooke's have cared for me in a timely and efficient way. Without them, I wouldn't be alive. They're great!" Eric and Ern Col also shared their positive experience, stating that their mother received "SECOND TO NONE! Brilliant staff!" care after a hip replacement. However, not all experiences were positive. David Harding expressed his frustration, stating that the hospital has had problems for years and has worked to cover them up. Paul Bernal shared his disappointing experience, where an appointment was delayed by three months due to computer problems. Carole, who worked in the NHS for 14 years, was horrified by the care her late husband received, saying it was "appalling." Some patients acknowledged that the hospital may have its flaws, but overall, they felt that the staff did a brilliant job. Sonya Louise-Bubbles Pledger praised the staff, saying they do a "wonderful job considering their low wages and cutbacks." Phil, on the other hand, felt that the hospital had become "too big and too arrogant," with some consultants being "untouchable and unanswerable." Despite the mixed views, one thing is clear: the patients and visitors of Addenbrooke's hospital are passionate about the care they receive. As Sue said, "Perhaps we should look at the bigger picture here, they do a brilliant job, and waiting a while tells me they have time to spend with each person, to me this feels good." The hospital's placement in special measures may be an opportunity for improvement, and it remains to be seen how the hospital will address the concerns and praises of its patients and visitors.

David Burdett, inspired by Strictly and Billy Elliot, began dancing 18 months ago. He found it "hard, but fun" and plans to continue. The Gorleston, Norfolk resident will star at Gorleston Pavilion Theatre, a notable achievement after just a year and a half of lessons, showcasing his dedication and passion for dance.

Giant panda numbers have seen a significant increase, with the latest count revealing 1,864 individuals in the wild, up from 1,596 in 2003. Nearly 75% of these pandas reside in China's Sichuan province. The population in captivity has also grown, with almost 200 more pandas than in 2003. According to Ginette Hemley of the World Wildlife Fund, this rise is a "victory for conservation" and a cause for celebration. However, the main threat to panda numbers remains the construction of roads and power stations, with over 300 hydropower stations and 800 miles of roads built in panda habitats, posing a significant risk to their survival.

Comedian Matt Lucas Returns to University Roots, Receives Honorary Degree In a humorous and lighthearted ceremony, comedian Matt Lucas was awarded an honorary degree from Bristol University, where he briefly studied Theatre, Film, and Television in 1993. Lucas, known for his work on the hit comedy sketch show Little Britain, which he co-created with fellow university alumnus David Walliams, poked fun at his own university experience. After high-fiving university chancellor Sir Paul Nurse, Lucas jokingly referred to himself as a "charlatan" who left university a year early to pursue a career in comedy. He reminisced about his time at Bristol, saying he quickly realized he was on a "serious course" but struggled to find his place, often spending his days walking up and down nearby Whiteladies Road. Lucas also joked about being "generally useless" at university life, with few friends and a tendency to stay in his room. Despite his humorous take on his university days, Lucas's career has been marked by significant success, including his work on Little Britain and various other TV shows and films. His honorary degree is a testament to his achievements in the entertainment industry, and he was clearly thrilled to return to his university roots, even if it was just to tease his alma mater about bringing the "entire university honours system into question" by celebrating his accomplishments.
Over 15,000 youths competed in singing and dancing at the Urdd in Nelson, Wales' largest youth festival, promoting Welsh language and culture since 1922.

Fidel Castro, the 88-year-old Cuban revolutionary icon, made a rare public appearance on Tuesday, meeting with a delegation of Venezuelan officials on a solidarity mission to the island. According to local press, Castro was "full of vitality" during the encounter, which took place at a local school. The meeting marked one of Castro's few public appearances in recent years, with his last being in January 2014 at a Havana cultural centre opening. Official media released images of Castro, seated in a vehicle, shaking hands with the Venezuelan visitors through the window. He was pictured wearing a baseball cap and windbreaker. The visit highlights the strong alliance between Cuba and Venezuela, which has been in place since the fall of the Soviet Union. Castro has maintained a low public profile since stepping down as president in 2008, handing over to his brother Raul. Despite this, he remains a significant figure in Cuban politics.

Exeter Chiefs' newest recruit, 28-year-old Australian international Joe Turner, has expressed his excitement about joining the club, despite facing stiff competition for a starting spot. Turner, who has won 15 caps for Australia and can play at centre, wing, or full-back, made the move to Sandy Park this week. However, he is aware that he will have to fight for a place in the team, given the impressive form of the club's existing backs, including Jack Nowell, Henry Slade, and Sam Hill. Rather than seeing this as a challenge, Turner views it as an opportunity to improve his game. "I wouldn't want to go somewhere I was guaranteed a position, because you become lazy and complacent," he said. "The growth that you get as a rugby player doesn't happen on Saturdays and Sundays, it happens through the week." Turner is looking forward to learning from and being challenged by his new teammates, while also pushing them to raise their game. Having previously helped the Waratahs reach the Super Rugby final and semi-finals, Turner believes that Exeter have the talent and potential to achieve great things. "They're a very talented group of players and by the end of the season, a lot of people are looking at them now wondering where they're going to be," he said. With Exeter currently sitting in second place, Turner is eager to contribute to the team's success and see where they finish the season.

A bomb disposal team from RAF Wittering safely detonated a World War-era Mills grenade on Gunton Cliff beach in Lowestoft, Suffolk. The device, also known as a "pineapple bomb," was discovered by a metal detectorist at 05:30 BST. The beach was sealed off, but reopened after the controlled explosion at 11:00 BST. Experts confirmed no other explosives were found. The RAF team left the scene just before midday. According to authorities, ordnance washing up on the beach is not uncommon. The successful disposal ensured public safety, and the area has been cleared for normal activities to resume.

London Marathon 2016 Sees Millionth Finisher and New Course Record The 2016 London Marathon has come to a close, with the millionth finisher in the event's history crossing the line on The Mall. The annual race, which was first held in 1981, has become a staple of the British sporting calendar, attracting thousands of runners and spectators each year. This year's event was marked by a number of notable achievements, including a new course record set by men's elite winner Eliud Kipchoge. Kipchoge, from Kenya, completed the 26.2-mile course in a time of two hours, three minutes, and four seconds, just seven seconds outside the world record. The women's elite race was won by Jemima Sumgong, also from Kenya, who pulled clear of Ethiopia's Tigist Tufa despite falling at a drink station earlier in the race. The men's and women's wheelchair races were won by Marcel Hug from Switzerland and Tatyana McFadden from the US, respectively. Britain's David Weir came third in the men's wheelchair race. The winners were presented with their prizes by Prince Harry, patron of the London Marathon Charitable Trust. One of the most unique aspects of this year's event was the participation of astronaut Maj Tim Peake, who completed a marathon distance on a treadmill aboard the International Space Station. Peake recorded a message wishing the competitors good luck, which was shown to the runners on a big screen, and completed his own marathon in a time of three hours and 35 minutes. The event was not without its challenges, however. One runner collapsed at mile 23 near Southwark Bridge and was taken to St Thomas' Hospital after suffering a cardiac arrest. Fortunately, the runner is receiving treatment and is expected to recover. The London Marathon is known for its lively and eclectic atmosphere, with many runners dressing up in costume to raise money for charity. This year was no exception, with runners dressed as Shakespeare, hot dogs, dinosaurs, and Disney princesses taking to the streets. The event also saw a number of celebrity participants, including double Olympic champion Dame Kelly Holmes, former rugby union international Shane Williams, and Games of Thrones actress Natalie Dormer. In a romantic moment, one runner proposed to his girlfriend at Tower Bridge, while another couple got engaged at the finish line. The oldest competitor in this year's race was 88-year-old Bedford grandmother Iva Barr, who has been running marathons for over 30 years and took part in the first London Marathon in 1981. Although she was unable to complete the course, Barr made it past halfway before stopping near Canary Wharf. The London Marathon is a major event in the capital, with road closures in place from 7am to 7pm in some areas. Despite the disruptions, the event is a significant fundraiser for charity, with many runners taking part to raise money for good causes. The event was broadcast live on the BBC, with coverage available to watch again on iPlayer.

A heartwarming memorial has been unveiled for five-year-old April Jones, who was tragically abducted and killed in 2012. The memorial features a teddy bear looking over the top and a poignant verse in Welsh about a small, pink star. April's love for teddies, butterflies, and shooting stars is beautifully captured in the design. April's mother, Coral Jones, and father, Paul Jones, recently visited the grave, where they expressed their relief and gratitude for the memorial. "It's April down to a tee," said Coral, fighting back tears. "We've been waiting two years for this day, and it's lovely that the headstone will be in place for Christmas." The family plans to visit April's grave on Christmas Day, bringing some sense of comfort and closure. April's father, Paul, acknowledged the difficulty of seeing their daughter's name on a headstone but praised the tribute as "really lovely." The family has endured an unimaginable ordeal, with April's body never found despite an extensive search. Her killer, Mark Bridger, was jailed for life in 2013. The memorial brings a sense of peace, and the family can now visit their daughter's grave with a more personal and meaningful tribute.

A British man and his American wife, who were jailed in China last year for their role in the GlaxoSmithKline corruption scandal, are finally returning to the UK. Peter Humphrey and Yu Yingzeng boarded a flight from Shanghai to London, marking the end of a long and tumultuous ordeal for the couple. Peter Humphrey, who was released early on health grounds on June 9, still had seven months left on his two-and-a-half-year sentence. His wife, Yu Yingzeng, a Chinese-born US citizen, was freed two days later with just a month left on her two-year term. The couple's son, Harvey, who resides in the UK, received a call from his parents just before they boarded the flight. According to Harvey, his father was eager to see him, while his mother was overcome with emotion. The couple's troubles began when they helped GSK investigate a secretly filmed sex tape of its top manager in China. They were subsequently found guilty of illegally obtaining Chinese citizens' data and selling it to firms, including GSK China. Although they admitted to buying background information, they claimed they were unaware that this was against the law. The couple's return to the UK brings an end to their ordeal, which has been a long and difficult journey for them and their family.

The FTSE 100 index fell 0.45% to 6,600.54 by lunchtime, with Anglo American down 1.3%. Royal Bank of Scotland dropped 1.5% amid reports of a potential $13bn settlement. The pound declined 0.3% against the euro to â‚¬1.4035 and 0.22% against the dollar to $1.5575. Mining stocks rebounded, leaving only Anglo American in the red.

Bristow Helicopters' revenue fell 19% to $356m in the quarter ending June, down from $440m last year. Offshore earnings dropped 27% due to challenging oil and gas industry conditions. The decline was partially offset by the UK search and rescue contract, the company reported.

A Thai-based company's liquidation has resulted in 2,200 job losses at the Redcar site. To mitigate the impact, over 30 employers are offering new opportunities in various sectors. According to Sue Soroczan, the affected workers possess excellent, transferable skills, attracting interest from local and external companies. A job fair is showcasing vacancies in heavy industry, administration, and logistics, providing hope for those affected by the redundancies.

Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir has arrived in South Africa to attend the African Union summit, despite being wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) for war crimes. The ICC has called on South Africa to detain Bashir, who is accused of war crimes in the Darfur region, but instead, he was welcomed by South African officials upon his arrival in Johannesburg. The ICC issued a statement saying that South Africa should "spare no effort" in detaining Bashir and respecting their obligations to cooperate with the court. However, it is unlikely that South Africa will take action, given the country's history of refusing to arrest Bashir during previous visits. Human rights organizations and South Africa's main opposition party have also called for his arrest, but their pleas are likely to fall on deaf ears. Bashir's visit to South Africa is a contentious issue, given the tensions between the ICC and the African Union (AU). The AU has previously urged the ICC to stop proceedings against sitting leaders, accusing the court of unfairly targeting Africans. Bashir has denied the allegations against him and has restricted his overseas travel to friendly states in Africa and the Middle East. The AU summit, which is being held in South Africa, is expected to focus on a range of issues, including the crisis in Burundi, the conflict in South Sudan, and the fight against terrorism. However, analysts say that discussions will be held, but the outcome will be vague. The summit's official theme is the "Year of Women's Empowerment and Development," but it is likely to be overshadowed by the presence of Bashir and the controversy surrounding his visit. South Africa's hosting of the summit has also been marred by the recent xenophobic violence in Johannesburg and Durban, which has left the country embarrassed. Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Nigeria have lashed out at President Jacob Zuma's government for the attacks, which have put a damper on the summit. Despite the challenges, the AU is expected to press on with the summit, but the presence of Bashir is likely to remain a contentious issue throughout the proceedings.

Tom Daley has taken a significant step towards realizing his Olympic dreams by emerging victorious at the British diving championships. The 22-year-old diver accumulated an impressive 507.95 points from his six routines, surpassing his competitors Matty Lee and Noah Williams, who scored 428.00 and 389.05 points respectively. Daley's outstanding performance has bolstered his chances of being selected for the Team GB lineup at the Rio Olympics this summer. Having made his Olympic debut at the tender age of 14 in Beijing and winning a bronze medal at the London 2012 Games, Daley is now more confident than ever of securing his first Olympic gold medal. He attributes his improved consistency over the past 12 months to his newfound confidence in executing big scores. Meanwhile, Scotland's Grace Reid has also boosted her chances of being named in the Team GB lineup after winning the 3m springboard title. The 20-year-old diver has enjoyed a remarkable year, having secured Britain a place in the women's individual 3m event at the Rio Olympic test event and becoming the first Scottish diver to win an individual European medal in 62 years. Reid's impressive performance has left her hopeful of being selected for the Rio Olympics, which would be a dream come true for the young diver. "It's just amazing, and I'm really pleased not only with the result today but also the new consistency that I've found," she exclaimed. The British diving team will learn later this week whether they have been selected to represent Team GB at the Rio Olympics. With their impressive performances, Daley and Reid are certainly strong contenders for a spot on the team.

South Korean Prosecutors Investigate Samsung's Alleged Ties to President's Friend Prosecutors in South Korea are investigating allegations that Samsung, the country's largest conglomerate, provided millions of euros to a company co-owned by Choi Soon-sil, a close friend of President Park Geun-hye, and her daughter. The funds allegedly bankrolled the daughter's equestrian training in Germany. Samsung confirmed that its offices were raided by prosecutors but declined to comment further. The investigation is the latest twist in a scandal that has been rocking South Korea for weeks. President Park has apologized for her ties to Ms. Choi, who is accused of using their friendship to interfere in politics and solicit business donations. However, the apology has done little to quell the growing calls for the president's resignation. Ms. Choi was arrested on November 3 and charged with fraud and abuse of power. She is alleged to have pushed businesses to donate millions of dollars to foundations she controlled and even helped choose the president's clothes. President Park has admitted that she allowed Ms. Choi to edit her speeches, sparking widespread outrage and protests. Tens of thousands of South Koreans have taken to the streets in recent days, demanding the president's resignation. The scandal has left President Park with a record-low approval rating of just 5%. Opposition leaders have called for her impeachment, and there are growing demands for her to accept a new prime minister recommended by parliament. The raids on Samsung's offices and those of the Korea Equestrian Federation and the Korea Horse Affairs Association mark a significant escalation of the investigation. If the allegations are proven, it could have far-reaching implications for Samsung and the president's administration. As the scandal continues to unfold, it remains to be seen whether President Park will be able to weather the storm and maintain her grip on power. With her popularity at an all-time low, it seems increasingly unlikely that she will be able to survive the crisis.

Linfield FC has announced the resignation of Jim Kerr as chairman and board director. The club expressed deep regret over his departure, midway through the season, but did not disclose the reason. Linfield praised Kerr's immense contribution and hard work, stating the board is unanimous in their appreciation. The club plans to formally recognize Kerr's long service at a later date, paying tribute to his dedication to Linfield over many years. Kerr's resignation has come as a surprise, and the club will likely feel his absence in the remaining season.

The Ebola outbreak continues to ravage Guinea, with clinics struggling to cope. According to the WHO, there have been 15,935 reported cases and 5,689 deaths. The epidemic, which began eight months ago, shows no signs of slowing, with the remote area still in dire need of support and resources to combat the crisis.

Gamba Osaka has been fined 2 million yen (£13,500) by the J-League after a flag bearing a Nazi-style symbol was displayed at a match against Cerezo Osaka. The flag, featuring a double'S' logo, was seen on April 16. In response, Gamba has banned the responsible supporter group and prohibited flags and banners at games. The J-League criticized the club's monitoring efforts, stating they are not sufficient to prevent discriminatory actions.
