Despite the incident, Gamba remains third in the league with 19 points from 10 games, and will face Hokkaido Consadole Sapporo on Sunday. The club has taken swift action to address the issue.

Usain Bolt blamed a "bad race" for his modest 10.09 seconds finish in the 100m. Despite carrying a hamstring problem, the triple Olympic champion claimed it wasn't a factor. Training partner Kemar Bailey-Cole also finished in 10.09 seconds. Bolt plans to review the race with his coach to identify what went wrong. Meanwhile, Antigua's Daniel Bailey took third with 10.23 seconds. In the women's 100m, America's Carmelita Jeter secured a world-leading time of 10.95 seconds, outpacing her competitors in the Cayman Islands event. Bolt's subpar performance has raised questions about his upcoming races.

Violent Protests Erupt in Srinagar After Eid Prayers, 12 Injured At least 12 people were injured in clashes between protesters and riot police in the capital city of Srinagar and other parts of the state after Eid prayers turned violent. The unrest was sparked by the arrest of four prominent religious and separatist leaders, as well as a 40-hour ban on internet services. The ban was imposed after local Muslim leaders urged people to upload pictures of cows being slaughtered for Eid, defying a 1932 law that prohibits the slaughter of cows, considered sacred in Hinduism. Eyewitnesses reported that protesters marched with posters of armed militants, leading to clashes with riot police who fired plastic bullets and tear gas. Tensions have been running high in the mostly Muslim region of India-administered Kashmir, where some religious leaders and separatist groups called for the slaughter of cows instead of traditional sheep and goats. The authorities' decision to block internet access to prevent the uploading of images of cow slaughter further fuelled the anger. The arrests of high-profile separatist leaders, including Mirwais Omar Farooq, Syed Ali Gilani, and Yasin Malik, have also contributed to the unrest. The Indian authorities' decision to enforce the long-dormant law has been seen as an attempt to impose Hindu values on the Muslim-majority region, leading to widespread resentment and protests. The situation remains volatile, with many fearing further escalation of violence in the coming days.

A prison officer at Maghaberry Prison in County Antrim has spoken out about the dire conditions and staffing shortages within the facility, following a damning report that described the jail as being in a "state of crisis". The officer, who wished to remain anonymous, expressed concerns over the safety and stability of both prisoners and staff, citing inadequate staffing levels as a major contributor to the problems. The report, which was published after inspectors visited the prison in May, highlighted significant failures in leadership and raised concerns about the welfare of those held within the prison. The officer's comments corroborate these findings, painting a picture of a prison struggling to cope with the demands placed upon it. "Landings are running with two officers for 50 prisoners and posts are being stood down all over the prison," the officer told the BBC's Evening Extra. The officer described the situation in the prison's pods, where a single staff member is often responsible for overseeing the movement of prisoners, issuing passes, and monitoring cameras. This, they claimed, is a situation that is "crazy" and unsustainable. The recommended staffing level for these areas is at least two people, but the officer said that this is often not the case. The staffing shortages are also having a significant impact on the prison's ability to safely restrain prisoners. The officer explained that the recommended control and restraint techniques require three people, but often only two officers are available. This, they said, means that the techniques are not being used effectively, putting both staff and prisoners at risk. The officer recounted a disturbing incident in which they had to rely on another prisoner to press the alarm while they were restraining a prisoner, highlighting the desperation of the situation. In response to the report and the officer's comments, Stormont Justice Minister David Ford has said that steps have been taken to improve standards within the jail. However, the officer's testimony suggests that much work still needs to be done to address the deep-seated problems within Maghaberry Prison. The situation is a cause for concern, and it remains to be seen whether the measures being taken will be enough to bring the prison out of its "state of crisis" and ensure the safety and well-being of both prisoners and staff.

A trial date has been set for three medical staff accused of manslaughter by gross negligence. Aisha Chithira, 32, died after an abortion at a Marie Stopes clinic in 2012. Dr Adedayo Adedeji, Margaret Miller, and Gemma Pullen denied the charge at the Old Bailey. They will stand trial on March 7. The trio, from various UK locations, were granted bail. The case alleges negligence led to Chithira's death, sparking a lengthy investigation and impending trial, set to commence in early March, with the defendants maintaining their innocence.

Sheffield United signs highly-rated 18-year-old winger Chapman. He played 14 games on loan at Barnsley, helping them earn League One promotion. Manager Chris Wilder praises Chapman's ability as a wide player. The youngster previously played for Boro's under-19 team in the Uefa Youth League.

Celtic Winger James Forrest Rejects Contract Offer, Sparks Debate on Future James Forrest, the 24-year-old Celtic winger, has turned down a four-year contract offer from the club, sparking speculation about his future. The Scotland midfielder's current deal is set to expire at the end of 2016, and his decision has left many wondering what's next for the talented player. According to former Celtic goalkeeper Pat Bonner, Forrest should remain at Celtic Park, where he has the opportunity to prove himself as a regular starter. "He should be a regular fixture in the starting line-up every single week," Bonner told BBC Scotland. "I would love him to stay at Celtic because there is no better place if you are playing really well." Forrest, who has made 13 Scotland appearances, has been linked to English clubs Norwich and Queens Park Rangers. However, Bonner believes that the player's inconsistent form is a mental issue, rather than a lack of ability. "James is a wonderful talent, he has great ability on the ball," Bonner said. "The problem with James is inconsistency. He's had his injuries, but for me, it looks like a mental thing." Despite his inconsistency, Forrest has shown glimpses of brilliance, scoring twice in 32 appearances this season. Bonner believes that the player has the potential to be a fan favorite, saying, "When he is effective, there's nobody better at getting the fans up out of their seats." As Forrest weighs his options, Bonner has warned him that leaving Celtic for more money may not be the right decision. "Sometimes, going away for more money might not be the right decision," he said. "Maybe he feels a wee bit stagnated and thinks he needs a change of scenery just to kick on. That can happen, of course." With his international career also to consider, Forrest must carefully think about his next move, and whether staying at Celtic is the best decision for his future.

Miriam Santiago, the "Iron Lady of Filipino politics," passed away on Thursday morning after a long battle with lung cancer. The former judge and senator died peacefully in a hospital in Manila, according to her husband. Santiago's death has sent shockwaves throughout the Philippines, with many taking to social media to pay tribute to her legacy. Santiago was a prominent figure in Filipino politics, known for her fearless and frank style. She ran for president in May's elections, but ultimately lost to Rodrigo Duterte. Despite her ill health, which plagued her campaign, Santiago insisted that she was fit to hold office. This was not her first attempt at the presidency, having also sought the position in 1992 and 1998. Born in Iloilo city, Santiago announced in 2014 that she was suffering from stage four lung cancer. She turned down a judicial position at the International Criminal Court due to her illness, but continued to be a vocal presence in politics. Her weakening health was a concern during the presidential election, where she was often seen sitting down and resting during televised debates. Santiago was a feisty senator who took bold stands on major issues like corruption and defense agreements. She was known for her quick wit and sharp tongue, which earned her both admiration and fear. Many remember her as being accommodating and jovial, often joking with the media. Filipinos have flooded social media with tributes to the late senator, with many describing her as the "best president the Philippines never had." A Facebook post from the GMA News agency drew over 300,000 reactions and close to 50,000 comments, with many expressing their sadness and gratitude for her legacy. "We just lost a great woman, a great Filipino and a great public servant," said one user. "You could have been one of our greatest presidents. This is a very sad day for the Philippines. We lost a gem," said another. As the nation mourns her passing, Santiago's legacy will undoubtedly be remembered for years to come.

A high-profile trial involving a journalist and two others has been delayed amid a review of prosecutions related to the Metropolitan Police's Operation Elveden. Journalist Greig Box Turnbull, prison officer Grant Pizzey, and his partner Desra Reilly were set to stand trial this week on charges of conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office. However, the trial has been put on hold as the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) re-examines its cases in light of a recent Court of Appeal ruling. The ruling, which overturned the conviction of another journalist, raised questions about the direction given by the trial judge and the impact of the offence on the public interest. The journalist, who cannot be named, had been convicted of illegally paying a prison officer for stories. The Court of Appeal found that the trial judge's direction did not fully consider the seriousness of the offence and its potential harm to the public interest. The delay in Mr. Box Turnbull's trial is the second to result from the Court of Appeal's decision, with nine more trials and re-trials related to Operation Elveden scheduled to take place over the summer. A further hearing in the case of Mr. Box Turnbull, Mr. Pizzey, and Ms. Reilly is set for April 27. The development has thrown Operation Elveden, which investigates payments by journalists to public officials, into disarray, according to home affairs correspondent Daniel Sandford.

Mass Grave Uncovered in Syria, Revealing Horrors of IS Brutality A disturbing discovery has been made in eastern Syria, where a mass grave containing the bodies of 230 people has been uncovered. According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the victims are believed to be members of the Sheitat tribe, who were brutally killed by the Islamic State (IS) group in the summer. The mass grave was discovered near the village of Kashkiya, in Deir al-Zour province, after IS leaders allowed the tribe to return to their homes. The Syrian Observatory reported that the "vast majority" of the victims were civilians, and many had been executed in cold blood. The discovery brings the total number of Sheitat tribespeople killed during the summer to over 900, with hundreds more still missing. The killings are thought to have taken place after negotiations between the tribe and IS broke down, with the tribe's elders refusing to pledge allegiance to the extremist group. IS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi had issued a statement in early November, granting the tribe permission to return home on the condition that they surrendered their weapons and informed on any "apostates". The brutal massacre is just one example of the atrocities committed by IS in their struggle for control of oil resources in the region. Video footage published online appears to show IS fighters conducting mass beheadings of Sheitat tribesmen, with some victims reportedly being forced out of hospital before being decapitated. The UN had previously received reports of a massacre in the area, and the latest discovery confirms the worst fears of human rights groups. The international community has condemned the atrocities committed by IS, and the discovery of the mass grave serves as a stark reminder of the horrors faced by civilians in Syria. The Syrian Observatory has called for further investigation into the massacre, and for those responsible to be held accountable for their crimes.

A car drove down beach steps at 15:00 BST, prompting emergency services to respond. Gardaí and firefighters removed the lodged vehicle. Onlookers expressed relief, calling it "very lucky" and an "absolute miracle" that no one was seriously hurt. The cause of the incident is unknown and police are investigating. Witnesses described the scene as fortunate, with no major injuries reported despite the shocking accident.

Maidstone United signs a 25-year-old after two years with the Fleet. The team has also added Ben Greenhalgh, Kevin Lokko, and Tom Murphy, while Callum Driver, Dumebi Dumaka, and Bobby-Joe Taylor renewed contracts, bolstering their roster after promotion to the top non-league flight.

A former senior police officer has expressed her outrage and disappointment over the decision to pay a convicted child rapist £10,300 for his role in helping to convict 17 men and one woman of abusing girls in Newcastle. Sue Sim, who retired in 2015, said she was "appalled" and "horrified" by the move, which she claimed she would never have agreed to. The controversy surrounds the use of a man known as XY, who provided information that led to the convictions as part of Operation Sanctuary. The current chief constable of Northumbria Police, Steve Ashman, has defended the decision, saying it was "morally" right and that it had helped to put "dangerous men behind bars" and protect vulnerable women and girls. However, Ms Sim, who created the operation, has called for a public inquiry into the matter. She said that while she was delighted with the success of the operation, she was shocked and dismayed by the use of XY as an informant. "I would never have agreed to the payment of a convicted child rapist," she said. "I keep hearing it was a very difficult decision - clearly it was so difficult that they didn't tell me. Probably because they knew I would totally and utterly disagree." Ms Sim also questioned the effectiveness of the evidence provided by XY, saying that she had not seen or heard anything that suggested what evidence he had actually produced. "Two wrongs don't make a right - he was a convicted child rapist and you can never put sufficient safeguards in place," she said. Northumbria Police has responded to the criticism, saying that it had been "open and transparent" in its response to Operation Sanctuary and the use of XY. However, the force said it would not comment on individuals' opinions. The chief constable, Steve Ashman, has maintained that the decision to use XY was "inside the law and inside accepted policy and practice". The controversy has sparked a heated debate about the use of informants in policing and the moral implications of paying a convicted child rapist for his help. Ms Sim has apologized to any rape victims who may feel let down by the decision, saying that the success of the operation should not be tarnished by this, but it does need further serious investigation. The incident has raised questions about the tactics used by police and the need for greater transparency and accountability in such cases.

EU's New Migrant Rescue Operation Raises Concerns Over Future Rescues The European Union's new migrant rescue operation, Triton, is set to replace Italy's Mare Nostrum operation, which has been rescuing migrants off the Libyan coast for the past year. However, concerns have been raised over the reduced budget and changed focus of the new operation, which may put the lives of thousands of migrants at risk. Mare Nostrum was launched in response to the tragic deaths of hundreds of migrants who drowned off the island of Lampedusa. Since then, the operation has rescued over 150,000 migrants, mostly fleeing violence in the Horn of Africa and Middle East. However, this year has seen a surge in migrant boats heading for Europe, with at least 3,000 migrants drowning in the Mediterranean. The new Triton operation will have only a third of Mare Nostrum's budget and will focus on border control, such as vetting asylum seekers and coastal patrols, rather than search and rescue in international waters. Italian Admiral Filippo Foffi has expressed concerns over the reduced scope of the new operation, stating that EU-Italian naval cooperation must continue in international waters to prevent further tragedies. While there has been no official order to stop Mare Nostrum, Italian officials have indicated that they intend to scale down the operation as Triton takes over. The EU's Frontex border agency will lead the new operation, with six ships, two planes, and one helicopter pledged by EU countries so far. However, many operational details, including the amount of time spent in international waters, are still to be determined. Admiral Foffi warned that if the operation is limited to territorial waters, "we won't see people in danger and if they die we won't see it." He emphasized that Frontex relies on member states to provide personnel and equipment, and that the success of the operation depends on the resources offered by EU partners. The UK has announced that it will not support future search and rescue operations, citing concerns that they may encourage more people to attempt the dangerous sea crossing. However, critics argue that this approach is misguided and will only lead to more deaths at sea. As the migrant crisis continues to escalate, the EU must ensure that its new operation prioritizes the safety and dignity of those fleeing persecution and violence.

New Research Reveals Complex Role of "Good" Cholesterol in Heart Health For years, it has been widely accepted that high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, also known as "good" cholesterol, plays a crucial role in maintaining a healthy heart. HDL cholesterol helps to keep arteries clear by shipping excess cholesterol to the liver, reducing the risk of heart attacks and strokes. However, a recent study by researchers at the Cleveland Clinic has shed new light on the complex role of HDL cholesterol in heart health. The study, published in the journal Nature Medicine, reveals that HDL cholesterol can become abnormal and contribute to the development of heart disease. According to Dr. Stanley Hazen, one of the lead researchers, HDL cholesterol can become modified in the walls of the artery, leading to the formation of dysfunctional HDL. This abnormal HDL can then seep back into the bloodstream, where it can be detected and used to predict the risk of cardiovascular disease. The researchers analyzed blood samples from 627 patients and found that levels of abnormal HDL in the blood could be used to predict the risk of heart disease. This discovery challenges the traditional view of HDL cholesterol as simply "good" cholesterol and highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of its role in heart health. Despite these findings, experts emphasize that a healthy diet and lifestyle remain essential for maintaining good heart health. "This data does not change the message of eat healthily," said Dr. Hazen. Instead, the research will be used to develop new tests for abnormal HDL cholesterol and to investigate the development of drugs that can help block its formation. The British Heart Foundation has welcomed the research, noting that it highlights the complexity of HDL cholesterol's role in heart health. "Although traditionally we think of HDL as'good' cholesterol, the reality is much more complex," said Dr. Shannon Amoils, a senior research adviser for the organization. "This interesting research pins down the exact chemical change that causes the'good' HDL cholesterol to become bad, and could allow scientists to monitor coronary artery disease more closely or even target the'bad' HDL with drugs."

England's Rokoduguni Sent Back to Club Despite Impressive Return Roko Rokoduguni's return to Test rugby was short-lived, as the Bath winger was sent back to his club on Tuesday, just days after scoring twice against Fiji. Despite his impressive performance, Rokoduguni will not feature in England's upcoming match against Argentina on Saturday. According to England's defense coach, Paul Gustard, Rokoduguni's exclusion is not a reflection on his abilities, but rather a tactical decision to field the best possible team against the Pumas. "Roko acquitted himself pretty well, and this is one game he is not chosen for," Gustard said. "It is not a reflection of anything that will come after that." Gustard emphasized that the team's priority is to secure a win, and they believe the selected squad is the right one to achieve that goal. Rokoduguni's confidence is not expected to be affected by his exclusion, as he has had a positive conversation with coach Eddie Jones and is aware of the areas he needs to improve. In Rokoduguni's place, Jonny May is expected to return to the right wing, while Elliot Daly and Mike Brown are likely to retain their positions on the left wing and full-back, respectively. Meanwhile, George Kruis has made a speedy recovery from ankle surgery and is expected to start in the second row. Kruis, who has been sidelined for the past month, worked hard to meet his goal of returning to the squad within four to five weeks. England will announce their starting XV and replacements on Thursday morning.

Arsenal has claimed the Emirates Cup trophy despite losing 2-1 to Sevilla in their final match. The Gunners' Alexandre Lacazette scored his first competitive goal for the club, tapping home a cross from Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain. However, Sevilla's Joaquin Correa and Steven N'Zonzi secured the win for the La Liga side. Arsenal won the tournament on goals scored, having beaten Benfica 5-2 earlier. Lacazette was substituted shortly after scoring, but manager Arsene Wenger attributed the change to tactical reasons, not the apparent leg injury. The Emirates Cup win is a confidence boost for Arsenal ahead of their Community Shield match against Chelsea on August 6 and their Premier League opener against Leicester City on August 11.

A stunning collection of miniature houses has found a new home at Newby Hall near Ripon. The "historically accurate" houses, created by collectors and miniaturists Caroline Hamilton and Jane Fiddick, are now on display in the former potting sheds at the historic estate. The collection includes a miniature Adam house featuring a replica of Newby Hall's tapestry room, showcasing the miniaturist's exceptional skills. The houses are made with intricate details, including hallmarked silver, hand-blown glass, real china, and hand-carved wood. The collection was donated to Newby Hall after it became too large for the collectors to house themselves. Newby Hall, built by Sir Christopher Wren in the 1690s and later adapted by Robert Adam, is considered one of Britain's finest examples of Adam-style architecture. The potting sheds were converted at a cost of £150,000, with £97,000 contributed by the Heritage Lottery Fund. The dolls' house collection will be open to the public from June 30 to September 27 and will be a permanent exhibit from April to September each year. According to Ms Fiddick, the hall's Adam rooms are a "miniaturist's dream," making it the perfect setting for the collection.

UK Communities Encouraged to Hold Vigils for Somme Centenary The government and the Royal British Legion are calling on villages, towns, and cities across the UK to organize their own remembrance events to mark the centenary of the Battle of the Somme. The devastating battle, which began on July 1, 1916, resulted in over 600,000 British and French casualties, leaving a profound impact on communities throughout the UK and Commonwealth. To commemorate this significant event, evening vigils are being planned for June 30 or July 1, allowing people to come together and reflect on the sacrifices made by those who fought in the battle. The Right Reverend Nigel McCulloch, head of remembrance at the Royal British Legion, emphasized the importance of remembering the tragic scale and futility of modern industrialized warfare, which the Battle of the Somme has come to symbolize. The vigils are designed to recreate the apprehension felt by soldiers as they waited in the trenches for "zero hour" at 7:30 am, when they would go "over the top" into battle. To support local events, the Royal British Legion has created a toolkit with ideas for organizing vigils, while the government has launched an online guide on remembrance events. Suggestions include gathering at meaningful places, lighting candles, reading poems, listening to music, and sharing photographs of relatives who fought in the battle. Culture Secretary John Whittingdale stressed the importance of honoring the memory and bravery of those who fought in the Battle of the Somme, saying, "It is important that we never forget what happened on the battlefields and honour their memory and bravery for generations to come." National events, including a national vigil at Westminster Abbey and commemorative services in Edinburgh, Cardiff, and Manchester, will also take place to mark the centenary. As the UK prepares to remember the sacrifices of the past, communities are encouraged to come together to pay their respects and ensure that the legacy of the Battle of the Somme is never forgotten.

Nicholas Rhea, a renowned author and former policeman, has passed away at his home in Ampleforth, North Yorkshire. Rhea, whose real name was Peter Walker, died on Friday surrounded by his family after his cancer returned two weeks ago. His daughter, Tricia, described him as a "Yorkshireman to the end." Rhea is best known for his Constable series of books, which inspired the popular Yorkshire Television production that aired from 1992 to 2010. The show followed a young police officer's life in the North York Moors. Rhea's funeral will be held at Our Lady's & St Benedict's Church, Ampleforth, on Friday, a fitting tribute to a man who lived in the village for 50 years. He will be deeply missed by his family and fans alike.

Tories' £12bn Welfare Cut Plan Sparks Fury from Opposition The Conservative Party's plan to cut the welfare bill by £12bn if they win the next election has sparked outrage from opposition parties. While the Tories have not explicitly stated where the cuts will come from, concerns have been raised that child benefit and child tax credits may be targeted. Dolores Kelly MLA slammed the proposal, calling it a "further attack on struggling families." The controversy began when Lib Dem Danny Alexander claimed that the Tories had previously proposed limiting child benefit and tax credits to two children during their coalition government. However, George Osborne denied the claims, stating that they were three years old and never official policy. Kelly criticized the Tories' "slash and burn ideology" and accused local parties of not doing enough to oppose the cuts. She argued that the best way to prevent the cuts is to vote for a strong Labour government, which would be held accountable by social democrats in the SDLP, SNP, and Plaid Cymru. Kelly also took aim at Sinn Féin, accusing them of hypocrisy for claiming to oppose Tory cuts while failing to take action. She alleged that Sinn Féin would "stand idly by" and support the cuts when they come before the assembly. The row highlights the deep divisions between parties on welfare reform and the impact of austerity measures on vulnerable families. As the election approaches, the debate is likely to intensify, with opposition parties pushing for greater transparency on the Tories' plans.

A 37-year-old woman, Nicola Cross, was tragically stabbed to death at her home in Dunlin Road, Hemel Hempstead, on Monday night. Marcin Porczynski, 23, of Claymore Avenue, has been charged with her murder, as well as two counts of kidnap and trespass with intent to inflict grievous bodily harm. Porczynski appeared at Hatfield Remand Court, where he was remanded in custody to appear at St Albans Crown Court on Friday. Using a Polish interpreter, he confirmed his name, age, and address, but did not enter a plea. The police investigation into Mrs. Cross's death is ongoing, and the incident has been referred to the Independent Police Complaints Commission. In a heartfelt tribute, Mrs. Cross's family described her as "kind, generous, and brave." They said she was the "heart and soul" of their family and a "perfect wife and amazing mummy." Her family praised her talent and core values, which she instilled in her children. The community is in shock following the tragic event, and an investigation is underway to determine the circumstances surrounding Mrs. Cross's death. Police were initially called to the scene after reports of a suspicious individual, but they released him without incident. However, they were called back to the area an hour later, responding to a report of a burglary at a neighboring home, where they discovered Mrs. Cross's body. A 19-year-old man arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to burgle has been released on police bail until September 24. The investigation is ongoing, and the community is awaiting further updates on the case.

A private funeral service was held for Courtney Boyle and Philip Tron, victims of the Manchester Arena attack. The pair, from Gateshead, were killed on May 22 while picking up Courtney's sister after the Ariana Grande concert. Family and friends wore yellow to the service at Saltwell Crematorium. A minute's silence was observed at the start of the inquests into the 22 deaths. Meanwhile, a joint funeral for Chloe Rutherford, 17, and Liam Curry, 19, will be held on June 15 at St Hilda's Church in South Shields, followed by private cremations. The community comes together to mourn the loss of these young lives.

A vital mental health support line in Norfolk is set to close at the end of the month after the local NHS clinical commissioning groups (CCGs) decided not to continue funding it. The support line, run by staff from charity Mind, has received over 6,000 calls in its first six months of operation, providing a lifeline for patients in need of mental health support. The pilot project was launched in January by former health minister Norman Lamb, with the aim of providing support for patients over 18 under the care of Norfolk and Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust (NSFT) or those who have been seen by the trust's services within the last 12 months. Despite its success, the CCGs have stated that they are unable to commit sufficient new funds to keep the service running. Amanda Hedley, chief executive of Norwich and Central Norfolk Mind, expressed her disappointment at the decision, stating that the service had been a lifeline for many patients. "We have been able to answer 6,111 calls between January and May, and I am very shocked and extremely disappointed that the funding will not be continued," she said. Service users and advocates have also spoken out against the decision, citing the importance of the support line in meeting the needs of mental health patients. Kevin James, service user governor for the NSFT in Norfolk, said that the support line had filled a gap in services and that he was "beyond concerned" for the welfare of patients who would no longer have access to it. The CCGs have stated that they are exploring alternative models for crisis response, including a new mental health pathway in partnership with the NSFT team. However, for now, the future of mental health support in Norfolk remains uncertain, leaving many patients and advocates worried about the consequences of the support line's closure.

Emma announced a new live-action Beauty and the Beast film, directed by Bill Condon. The 1991 animated classic was a "big part" of her childhood. She'll dance to "Be Our Guest" and sing "Something There". Emma expressed excitement, saying her "six-year-old self is on the ceiling" and her "heart is bursting". A release date has not been set for the highly anticipated film.

Police Officers' Fitness Test Results Revealed: Overall Pass Rate of 98% A recent report released by the College of Policing has revealed the results of the compulsory fitness test taken by police officers in England and Wales. The test, which was taken 93,956 times from September 2014 to August 2015, showed an overall pass rate of 98%. However, 1,863 officers failed to meet the required standard. The results varied across the 43 territorial police forces, with South Yorkshire Police having the lowest pass rate at 95%. This meant that 5% of its officers failed the test. On the other hand, the City of London Police achieved a perfect pass rate, with all 120 of its officers passing the test. The test, which was introduced in 2014, is designed to ensure that police officers are physically fit enough to perform their duties effectively. It involves a 15-metre shuttle run, which requires officers to run 525 metres in three minutes 40 seconds or less. The College of Policing recommends that officers who fail the test be given the opportunity to retake it twice. According to the report, female officers had a lower pass rate than their male counterparts. Of the 23,154 times a female officer took the test, 95.4% passed, compared to 98.9% of male officers. However, the College of Policing has emphasized that it is committed to supporting officers who struggle with the test, particularly female officers. National lead for fitness testing, Assistant Chief Constable Jo Shiner, noted that the College's guidance on fitness tests includes advice on positive action measures such as specialized training and mentoring programs. Despite the few failures, the overall results suggest that the vast majority of police officers are fit and able to protect the public. As Assistant Chief Constable Shiner pointed out, "The public want their officers to be fit and able to protect them in the face of danger, and these results show they are able to do just that." The College of Policing will continue to monitor the results and provide support to officers who need it, ensuring that police forces across England and Wales maintain the highest standards of physical fitness.

Conlan Advances to Finals with Unanimous Decision. Belfast bantamweight Michael Conlan secured a spot in the finals with a unanimous decision win, earning scorecards of 30-27, 29-28, and 29-28. The 23-year-old European champion has already qualified for the 2016 Rio Olympics. Conlan's victory sets him up for a strong finish, while teammates Michael O'Reilly and Joe Ward prepare for their semi-final matches.

The Pirate Bay, one of the internet's most-visited websites, is set to make a comeback this Sunday, February 1, according to a countdown on thepiratebay.se. The website, which provided links to pirated content, was taken offline in December following a raid by Swedish police. The raid, which was prompted by a complaint from the Rights Alliance, resulted in the seizure of servers in Stockholm. Despite previous attempts to shut down the site, including a 2006 raid, The Pirate Bay has consistently managed to reappear online. The site's resilience has been a thorn in the side of the film, music, and software industries, which blame it for billions of pounds in losses. In 2012, UK internet service providers were ordered to block access to the site, but it continues to be accessible through various means. The site's co-founders have also faced legal troubles, with Gottfrid Warg sentenced to three-and-a-half years in prison for hacking and copyright violations, and Peter Sunde sentenced to eight months in prison for violating copyright laws. Another co-founder, Hans Fredrik Lennart Neij, was arrested in November while trying to cross into Thailand from Laos. The Pirate Bay's return is likely to be met with both excitement and concern, as the site's impact on the entertainment industry and internet freedom continues to be debated.

A Bosnian court has sentenced Mevlid Jasarevic to 18 years in prison for committing a "terrorist act" by firing over 100 bullets at the US embassy in Sarajevo. The attack, which occurred in 2011, resulted in the injury of one policeman before Jasarevic was shot and arrested by a police sniper. Jasarevic, a member of a fundamentalist Wahhabi group, was found to have acted alone in the attack, with two alleged accomplices, Emrah Fojnica and Munib Ahmetspahic, being acquitted. The three men were residents of Gornja Maoca, a village known for its Islamist community, which has been the subject of several police raids in recent years. The US embassy was locked down during the attack, and fortunately, no one inside was injured. Judge Branko Peric described the sentence as the harshest ever given for terrorism, intending it to serve as a warning. He also expressed concern over the Islamist community in Gornja Maoca, which refuses to recognize the authority of the Bosnian state. Jasarevic's motivations for the attack are believed to have stemmed from opposition to US policy towards Muslims worldwide. The attack was widely condemned, including by Bakir Izetbegovic, the Bosniak member of the Bosnian presidency, who labeled it a terrorist attack. The incident has raised concerns about the potential for extremist activity in the region, which is still recovering from the bitter 1992-95 conflict.

A fire broke out at a property in the Tiger Court area early Friday morning. Luckily, two brave police officers helped rescue residents from the burning building, and no one was injured. Councillor Neil Kelly praised the officers' actions, saying they put their lives at risk to protect the public. He expressed relief that the incident didn't result in a tragedy, especially during Christmas time. Kelly condemned the arson attack, stating that those responsible have no regard for human life and must be caught by the police. The councillor wished the officers a swift recovery, acknowledging their selfless bravery in the face of danger.

Castleford Tigers' star player Greg Eden's season is likely over due to an injury sustained during Friday's 38-14 win against Salford. Eden, 26, scored his 33rd and 34th tries of the season but suffered the injury while diving over for his second. Tigers coach Powell confirmed the injury would "probably" end Eden's season. Teammate Michael Shenton expressed his disappointment, saying, "I'm absolutely gutted, he's had a superb year..... He's been a massive part of what we've been doing." Eden's impressive form has been crucial to the Tigers' success, and his absence will be felt. Despite the setback, the Tigers remain top of Super League, eight points clear heading into the Super 8s competition. Eden's injury is a significant blow, as he was just six tries short of breaking the record for most tries in a single season, held by former Castleford winger Denny Solomona.

Diageo, the UK-based manufacturer of renowned spirits such as Johnnie Walker whisky and Smirnoff vodka, has reported a 9% decline in net sales to £10.3 billion for the year ending June 30. The company experienced a 5% decrease in sales volume across its Asia Pacific, Africa, Eastern Europe, and Turkey divisions, while sales in North America and Latin America were slightly down, and Western Europe remained flat. The weak performance in certain regions was largely attributed to economic challenges and regulatory changes. In China and South East Asia, sales plummeted by 20% and 25%, respectively, due to anti-extravagance measures and tax increases. Venezuela also posed a significant challenge, with a 47% decline in Scotch whisky sales resulting from currency devaluation and inflation. Despite these setbacks, Diageo's North American operations delivered top-line growth, driven by a 5% increase in US spirits and wines sales. The company remains optimistic about its long-term prospects, particularly in emerging markets. According to John Kennedy, President of Diageo Europe, the growing number of high net worth individuals and increasing consumer wealth will drive demand for premium brands. Notably, sales of single malts surged by 18% compared to the previous year, indicating a strong potential for growth in the high-end Scotch whisky category. Despite the mixed results, Diageo is confident in its ability to capitalize on emerging market opportunities and achieve long-term growth.

Wales international Rhodri Jones has announced that he will be leaving the Scarlets to join the Ospreys on a new contract. The 24-year-old tight-head prop has played 13 internationals for Wales and signed a national contract in December 2014. However, his new deal is solely with the Ospreys and not an extension of his national contract, which was jointly funded by the Welsh Rugby Union. Jones made his 100th appearance for the Scarlets in their recent win over Edinburgh, and despite his loyalty to the region, he has decided to make the move to the Ospreys. The Scarlets' general manager, Jon Daniels, expressed disappointment at Jones' departure but respected his decision. Jones stated that he is excited about the new opportunity and is looking forward to contributing to the Ospreys' success. Jones' opportunities at the Scarlets and with the national team have been limited by the emergence of Samson Lee and Exeter's Tomas Francis. However, the Ospreys' rugby manager, Andrew Millward, believes that Jones has huge potential to become a quality player. Millward welcomes the signing, stating that Jones fits the Ospreys' requirements in terms of ability and character. The Ospreys are confident that they can help Jones improve his set piece work and reach his full potential. Jones will remain with the Scarlets until the end of the season, where he will continue to give his all to help the region secure a Pro12 play-off position.

India has seen a significant number of elephant deaths, with many caused by accidental electrocution. According to Bijayshree Routray, over a third of the elephant deaths were due to electric shock from hanging wires. The country is home to around 26,000 wild elephants, a heritage animal. To address the issue, the government has formed a joint committee to monitor elephant deaths. The committee will comprise members from the forest, environment, and energy departments. Other causes of elephant deaths include poaching, poisoning by farmers, and being hit by trains. As elephants' habitats shrink, conflicts with humans have increased, leading to the deaths of these protected animals. The government's efforts aim to reduce elephant fatalities and preserve the species.

Bloomberg Considers Presidential Bid, Citing "Banal" Debate In a recent interview with the Financial Times, Michael Bloomberg revealed that he is "looking at all the options" regarding a potential presidential bid. This marks the first time the former New York City mayor has publicly acknowledged the possibility of running. Bloomberg's aides had previously hinted at a potential bid, citing his concern over the increasingly polarized nature of the race. Bloomberg expressed his disappointment with the current state of the debate, stating that US voters "deserve a lot better" than the "distressingly banal" discussions currently taking place. He criticized the level of discourse, calling it "an outrage and an insult to the voters." As a former Democrat, Republican, and current independent, Bloomberg's pro-business views and liberal stance on issues like gun control and abortion could make him a wild card in the election. If Bloomberg were to run as an independent, his candidacy could potentially damage the Democratic party's chances. According to BBC North America reporter Anthony Zurcher, Bloomberg's liberal views would likely draw support away from the Democrats, rather than the Republicans. With Donald Trump leading the Republican pack and Bernie Sanders challenging Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination, the 2016 presidential election is already shaping up to be a highly contested and unpredictable race. Bloomberg's potential entry could further shake up the landscape, offering voters an alternative to the traditional party candidates.

A dramatic incident occurred at a Spanish airport when a passenger, who had missed his flight to Gran Canaria, attempted to reach the plane by jumping onto the airbridge. The man, reportedly from Bolivia, had cleared security but missed boarding. In a desperate bid to catch his flight, he jumped 10ft into the air, shouldered his two bags, and ran towards the tunnel. He broke through fire escape doors to access the airbridge, sparking concerns over airport security. The incident was captured on video and posted on Facebook, showing the man's daring attempt to reach the plane. The footage has raised questions about the effectiveness of the airport's security measures, which are currently at level 4, the second-highest alert level. The man could face a fine of up to €45,000 for breaching airport security laws. Ryanair, the airline involved, has stated that the incident is a matter for airport security to handle. The identity of the man has not been officially confirmed, but local media reports suggest he panicked when he saw the plane start to move. An investigation into the incident is likely to follow.

The Introduction of Video Technology in Football: A Step Closer to Reality The debate over the introduction of video technology in football has been ongoing for several years, with many arguing that it is long overdue. Recently, the International Football Association Board pushed back trials in competitive matches by a year, but according to Gijs de Jong, operations director at the Dutch FA (KNVB), the technology will be used in the not-too-distant future. De Jong predicts that it will take no more than five years for video technology to be implemented in the sport. The need for video technology has been highlighted by a number of high-profile errors made by referees in recent matches. In the English top-flight, referees have come under intense scrutiny, with mistakes affecting the outcome of games. For example, West Brom's Gareth McAuley was initially sent off against Manchester City, only for the red card to be transferred to teammate Craig Dawson after the referee admitted his mistake. Similarly, Sunderland's Wes Brown was sent off for a foul that was actually committed by his teammate John O'Shea. Managers such as Tony Pulis and Nigel Pearson have called for the introduction of video technology to help referees make accurate decisions. Pulis suggested a 30-second call-back option, twice a game, to review contentious decisions, while Pearson argued that technology would have prevented a mistaken yellow card being shown to Leicester City's Wes Morgan. De Jong believes that every mistake made by referees strengthens the case for video technology and can help bring forward its introduction. He points to recent examples in the Premier League and Champions League as evidence that the sport is ready for the implementation of video technology. With the support of managers, players, and fans, it is likely that video technology will become a reality in football sooner rather than later. As De Jong said, "When we get some good examples..... then hopefully it'll speed up and we do reach the five year period."

Breakthrough Study Reveals Snakes' Deadly Secret: Constriction Causes Circulatory Arrest, Not Suffocation For decades, it was believed that snakes, specifically constrictors, suffocated their victims to death. However, a groundbreaking study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology has debunked this myth, revealing that the snakes' lethal grip actually restricts blood flow, causing a rapid and efficient circulatory arrest. This innovative research, led by Professor Scott Boback from Dickinson College in Pennsylvania, has shed new light on the unique killing method of these fascinating creatures. To conduct the study, researchers took measurements from anaesthetised rats that were gripped by boa constrictors. The team recorded blood pressure, heart activity, and other vital signs, providing a detailed understanding of the physiological effects of constriction on the prey. The results showed that the snake's grip severely restricted blood flow, effectively cutting off the oxygen supply to the vital organs. This circulatory arrest, the scientists explained, is a much more efficient and rapid way of killing prey than previously thought. According to Professor Boback, restricting blood flow to the brain would cause a rodent to "pass out within seconds." The researchers believe that their findings could have implications beyond the realm of herpetology, as recording during a constriction could reveal useful details about how crush injuries cause complex tissue damage in humans. However, the primary focus of the study remains on understanding the fundamental question of how and why these snakes evolved their unique killing method. As Professor Boback noted, "The thing I find fascinating is that all snakes have is their mouth to engage with prey. A constrictor has to hold a potentially dangerous animal right next to it, and that animal's fighting for its life, so it will absolutely take chunks out of the snake if it can." To measure this life-or-death battle, the researchers presented anaesthetised lab rats to boa constrictors and recorded from the rats' arteries and heart as they were squeezed. The team also took blood samples before and after, revealing how the blood chemistry of a constricted victim changed. The study's findings have significant implications for our understanding of constrictor snakes and their behavior. As Professor Brad Moon from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, who has studied snake movements for two decades, explained, "It shows that constriction is stronger, faster, and more effective than expected." The research also highlights the remarkable adaptability of these snakes, which have evolved to use their bodies to lethal effect. In a previous study, the same Dickinson College team discovered that the snakes were able to sense their victim's heartbeat and stopped squeezing only when it stopped. This latest research builds on that finding, providing a more detailed understanding of the physiological mechanisms underlying the snakes' killing method. As the scientific community continues to unravel the secrets of these fascinating creatures, one thing is clear: constrictor snakes are more efficient and deadly predators than previously thought.

Swansea's Ashley Williams is set to join Everton in a £12m deal after undergoing a medical. The 31-year-old centre-half will bolster the Toffees' defence following John Stones' £47.5m move to Manchester City. Everton have already signed Idrissa Gueye and Maarten Stekelenburg this summer, strengthening their squad ahead of the new season.

Wasps have announced new contract deals for three young players. Full-back Miller, who has scored seven tries in 35 appearances, has committed to the team, along with wing Bassett, who has scored 27 points in 21 appearances. Centre Macken, yet to make his debut, has also signed on. The announcements come as the team prepares for the departure of fly-half Alex Lozowski to Saracens. This news follows recent contract deals for captain James Haskell and Nathan Hughes. Haskell is one of four Wasps players named to England's 33-man squad for the Six Nations, alongside Joe Launchbury, Matt Mullan, and Elliot Daly. These signings demonstrate Wasps' investment in their young talent and veteran players alike.

EastEnders Fans Prepare for Emotional Farewell as Peggy Mitchell Says Goodbye In a highly anticipated and emotional storyline, Dame Barbara Windsor's iconic character Peggy Mitchell will be making her final appearance on the BBC soap EastEnders. The actress, who has been battling terminal cancer, will be joined by her on-screen sons Phil and Grant as the Mitchell family reunites to bid their final goodbyes. Peggy's return to Albert Square, set to air on May 9, promises to be a dramatic and flamboyant one, as she is greeted by her extended family, including grandchildren Ben and Louise, Billy Mitchell, and niece Ronnie Mitchell. Notably, Grant Mitchell, played by Ross Kemp, will be making a comeback to the show after a 10-year absence. Kemp has expressed his gratitude to the show, stating that his time on EastEnders was a significant springboard for his career. Dame Barbara, 78, has played the beloved character since 1994 and has made sporadic appearances since her full-time departure in 2010. Her last appearance was earlier this year, when she revealed to her son Phil that her cancer had returned. The show's executive producer, Dominic Treadwell-Collins, has promised that Peggy's exit will be "one of the most heartbreaking, uplifting, and epic exits an EastEnders character has ever had." Fans are bracing themselves for an emotional farewell as they say goodbye to a true EastEnders legend.

The women's grass court event at Devonshire Park has been a staple of the tennis calendar since 1974. This prestigious tournament traditionally draws top female players ahead of Wimbledon. The 2023 final saw Karolina Pliskova defeat Caroline Wozniacki. Past winners include legends Martina Navratilova and Chris Evert. The Lawn Tennis Association has announced that free coverage will continue on TV, radio, and online. According to Oliver Scadgell, the LTA's director of major events, the BBC's support helps to promote tennis and increase participation, building on the success of players like Andy Murray and Johanna Konta. The event's popularity is set to endure.

Liverpool FC and Liverpool City Council have announced a joint plan to redevelop the iconic Anfield stadium, increasing its capacity to 60,000 and transforming the surrounding area. The £150m project is part of the council's £175m regeneration scheme for the L4 area, which aims to create employment and business opportunities for the local community. The redevelopment will see a number of streets demolished, while hundreds of homes in the area will be refurbished. The project is expected to bring significant benefits to the local community, including the creation of new jobs, improved housing, and enhanced amenities. A public consultation will be held to ensure that residents are kept informed and involved in the planning process. Alan Blundell, chair of the Walton Breck Road Residents' Association, has welcomed the proposals, stating that he is "very pleased" with the plans. However, he emphasized the importance of keeping residents informed and consulted throughout the process, particularly those who may be affected by Compulsory Purchase Orders (CPOs). "We have got a new school, medical centre, housing; the main thing is we have got to involve the community at all stages," he said. The plans have also been cautiously welcomed by fans' union Spirit of Shankly, who have long advocated for the club to remain at Anfield. Paul Martin, a representative of the group, stated that while the proposals are promising, there are still many details to be ironed out. "We will only really believe it when the team is running onto the pitch," he said. The group has also suggested the creation of a "football quarter" around the refurbished ground, featuring bars and restaurants. Liverpool Mayor Joe Anderson has expressed his support for the project, stating that he wants to create a "regenerated Anfield" that will bring employment and business opportunities to the area. Ian Ayre, Liverpool FC's managing director, has emphasized the importance of gaining the support of local homeowners, stating that "any final decision depends on home owners being supportive of the proposed stadium extension." The redevelopment of Anfield is expected to begin in 2014, with a planning application to be submitted next summer. The project is likely to see extensions to the Main Stand and the Anfield Road end, as well as the construction of a new hotel. While there have been false starts in the past, the club and council are hopeful that this project will finally come to fruition, bringing benefits to both the football club and the local community. As Ian Ayre noted, "there's a lot of wounds to heal" in terms of the club's relationship with local residents, but the proposed redevelopment is a significant step towards healing those wounds and creating a brighter future for Anfield.

England is set to face Wales at Twickenham without injured centre Jonathan Joseph, who suffered a chest injury during the team's 35-11 win over Fiji on Friday. Rugby league convert Sam Burgess, 26, will start alongside Brad Barritt, earning only his third England cap. Meanwhile, number eight Ben Morgan will miss the match due to a minor knee injury, with Billy Vunipola taking his place. Joseph's injury is not considered serious, but he is a significant doubt for the upcoming match against Australia on October 3. The 24-year-old centre scored four tries in England's Six Nations campaign earlier this year and is a key player in the team's backline. England attack coach Andy Farrell stated that Joseph's injury would likely keep him out for "not more than a week." The team will face Wales, followed by Australia and Uruguay, with the top two teams from the group progressing to the quarter-finals. Head coach Stuart Lancaster will announce the team on Thursday morning. James Haskell will step up to the bench to face Wales, providing additional support to the team. England will look to build on their strong start to the tournament, and fans can follow the latest rugby union news on Twitter @bbcrugbyunion.

A Bittersweet Reunion: Argentine Grandmother's Hopes Dashed in Search for Abducted Granddaughter In a heart-wrenching turn of events, Maria Isabel Mariani, a 92-year-old Argentine grandmother, was left devastated when DNA tests revealed that the woman she had recently met was not her long-lost granddaughter, Clara Anahi Mariani Teruggi. The young girl was abducted by the military in 1976, at just three months old, and Ms. Mariani had been searching for her for nearly four decades. The announcement of their supposed reunion on Thursday had been hailed as a triumph for the campaign group Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, which was formed to reunite families with their missing children. Even President Mauricio Macri had taken to Twitter to celebrate the news. However, two days later, the prosecutor working on the case, Pablo Parenti, revealed that DNA tests had shown no genetic match between Ms. Mariani and the woman she had met. The woman, identified as Maria Elena Wehrli, had arrived at Ms. Mariani's house on Christmas Eve with the results of a private DNA test, but these were deemed inconclusive by the authorities. The National Genetic Database, the only body authorized to determine identity in such cases, had found no match. According to Juan Martin Ramos Padilla, a spokesman for the Anahi Foundation, which Ms. Mariani founded, the news was a "hard blow" for the elderly grandmother, who is nearly blind. Nevertheless, Ms. Mariani remains determined to continue her search for her granddaughter. Clara Anahi's parents, Daniel Mariani and Diana Teruggi, were members of the left-wing group Montoneros, and their daughter was taken from their home during a military operation in which Diana Teruggi was killed. Ms. Mariani's son, Daniel, escaped but went into hiding and was killed a few months later. The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo estimate that some 500 children were abducted from their mothers in captivity during the military rule in Argentina, which lasted from 1976 to 1983. Many of these children were given for adoption to non-communist families, while others were handed over to orphanages. Despite the setback, Ms. Mariani's resolve remains unbroken. "She is 92 and will continue searching for her granddaughter," said Mr. Ramos Padilla. "We just hope to be able to find her." The Anahi Foundation, which includes one of Clara Anahi's names, will continue to work towards reuniting families with their missing children. The Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo have already reunited 119 children with their families, with the most recent reunion taking place just last month. As the search for Clara Anahi continues, the case serves as a poignant reminder of the atrocities committed during Argentina's military rule, during which an estimated 30,000 people were killed. The Grandmothers' campaign is a testament to the power of perseverance and the human spirit, and their work will undoubtedly continue to bring hope to families who have been torn apart by the brutal regime. For Ms. Mariani, the search for her granddaughter will go on, driven by a mother's unwavering love and a grandmother's unrelenting determination.

Liberia's Senate has voted to jail Finance Minister Amara Konneh for proposing a $1.2m budget cut without proper authority. The move has sparked controversy, particularly given Konneh's reputation as a skilled financial manager, having been named African Finance Minister of the Year in 2014 by Banker Magazine. The Supreme Court has since intervened, halting Konneh's imprisonment "until further notice". The Senate's decision was unanimous, with leader Armah Jallah citing Konneh's lack of power to reduce their budget as the reason. The issue has highlighted the sensitive topic of politicians' salaries, with Liberia's 103 lawmakers earning $13,000 per month. As the country faces economic pressure due to declining foreign-exchange earnings from rubber and iron ore, all government sectors are being forced to cut budgets, leading to increased scrutiny of politicians' pay.

Tragedy Strikes Rare Sea Bird Colony in Hartlepool A devastating incident has occurred at the Crimdon coastal site near Hartlepool, where a colony of little terns, one of the UK's rarest sea birds, has been severely impacted. According to wardens, only 29 nests remain, with evidence suggesting that dogs were deliberately let loose on the site over the weekend, destroying approximately 50 nests. Durham Heritage Coast (DHC), which manages the site, has described the incident as "heartbreaking". The little tern is a protected species, and the site, one of only 20 in the UK, is typically safeguarded by fences and monitored by wardens during the day. Despite these measures, it appears that someone intentionally entered the site with dogs, causing widespread destruction to the nests. The DHC has expressed disappointment and dismay at the incident, citing the significant time and effort invested by staff and volunteers in the Little Tern Recovery Project. Unfortunately, this is not the first time the site has been targeted by vandals and egg thieves. In 2013, 50 eggs were stolen from 65 nesting pairs, and it is believed that some eggs were also taken during the recent incident, while others were likely destroyed or eaten by dogs. The remaining 29 nests are now at risk, and the DHC is holding out hope that they will survive. The colony had previously experienced a difficult year in 2015, and conservationists had been optimistic about this year's prospects due to favorable weather conditions. The DHC will be reviewing its security measures, but funding limitations may hinder its ability to implement more robust protections. The incident is currently under investigation by the police.

Newcastle Falcons bounced back from last week's defeat in France with a convincing 59-14 win over Lyon. The hosts dominated the first half, with Juan Pablo Socino scoring two tries and Sonatane Takulua and Charlie Hodgson also crossing the line. Hodgson kicked seven from seven as the Falcons took a 34-10 lead into the break. Zach Kibirige and Callum Chick added further tries after the interval, securing a strong victory. Lyon earned a try bonus-point with Paul Bonnefond's late score, but the Falcons' win lifts them to third in their group, just a point behind the French side. The result marks a significant turnaround for Newcastle after their 42-12 loss in Lyon last week.

Court of Appeal Upholds Compensation Scheme for Jimmy Savile Victims The Court of Appeal has dismissed a challenge to the compensation scheme set up for victims of disgraced BBC presenter Jimmy Savile, paving the way for hundreds of claimants to receive payments. The scheme, which was established by the Savile estate, the BBC, the NHS, and charity Barnardo's, aims to provide compensation to those who were abused by Savile during his lifetime. The Jimmy Savile Charitable Trust, which is a beneficiary of the estate, had argued that the scheme would not effectively weed out fake claims and that too much money would go to lawyers. However, appeal judges rejected this challenge, ruling that the scheme should proceed as planned. The court also rejected the trust's application to remove NatWest as the executor of Savile's estate. The ruling brings relief to the many victims of Savile who have been waiting for justice. According to lawyers, over 200 people have come forward to make compensation claims, with payments capped at £60,000. Liz Dux, a lawyer representing many of the victims, welcomed the ruling, saying it would bring "great relief" to those who have been living with uncertainty. "They just want some recognition of what they have been through so they can then be able to move on with their lives," she said. The compensation scheme was established after a documentary broadcast in 2012 alleged that Savile was a "serial child abuser and sex offender." The former BBC presenter was accused of abusing people in hospitals and other institutions, and a large number of people came forward to make claims after the programme. In a separate development, abuse survivors who met with Home Secretary Theresa May on Monday announced that the government would be creating a £2m fund to support groups helping people who will give evidence to the forthcoming public inquiry into abuse. A further £1.5m fund will be established to support charities that help abuse survivors. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood said it was represented at the meeting, although the Home Office has not yet announced any details. The ruling and the government's announcement are seen as significant steps towards providing justice and support to the victims of Jimmy Savile and other abuse survivors. As the public inquiry into abuse prepares to get underway, it is hoped that these developments will help to bring closure and recognition to those who have suffered at the hands of abusers.

A young musician from Carnoustie has brought together an impressive array of celebrities to feature on his latest song, "The Highland Road". Craig Weir, 23, has enlisted the help of Hollywood actor Alan Cumming, Queen guitarist Brian May, and The Libertines' Peter Doherty, among others, to contribute to the track. The song begins and ends with a poem written by Craig and his friend Chris Brown, which was inspired by a trip they took along the Highland Road in Canada last year. The poem is bookended by 21 guest voices, including former AC/DC bassist Mark Evans, television presenter Lorraine Kelly, and Kyle Falconer from Dundee band The View. Craig, who has previously performed for Arnold Schwarzenegger in Edinburgh, said the idea for the song had been in the back of his mind for a while. He got in touch with his core contributors, including Brian May and Alan Cumming, and was thrilled when they agreed to take part. Peter Doherty was also a key contributor, recording his line in Buenos Aires while on tour. The contributions were largely recorded on the celebrities' phones and emailed or texted to Craig, who then pieced them together in the studio. Despite initial doubts about how the song would sound, Craig is delighted with the final result. "Now I've got this fantastic piece together with a whole range of voices representing entertainment around the world," he said. The celebrities involved have been similarly impressed with the song, with Alan Cumming describing it as "beautiful" and "really moving". Brian May said he was "happy to pour a little of my Scottish blood into this epic", while Lorraine Kelly said she was "delighted" to contribute and that hearing the final product gave her "goose bumps". Craig, who performs with his band The Cabalistic Cavalry, has had a number of high-profile encounters in the past, including six dates with the Bay City Rollers and a performance of "We Will Rock You" with Queen at the SSE Hydro. Despite his musical success, Craig still teaches music and said his pupils take a "great interest" in his other career. "It's like a Jekyll and Hyde character," he joked. "The bell goes on Friday afternoon and that's me away playing around the world." "The Highland Road" is a unique and exciting collaboration that brings together some of the biggest names in entertainment. With its inspiring poem and array of talented contributors, it's a song that is sure to leave a lasting impression on listeners.

Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn to Raise Human Rights Concerns with Chinese President Xi The upcoming state visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to the United Kingdom has sparked a flurry of diplomatic activity, with Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn announcing his intention to raise concerns about human rights issues with the Chinese leader. Mr. Corbyn's spokesman confirmed that the Labour leader would be "using the opportunity" of President Xi's four-day visit to discuss his concerns, citing Mr. Corbyn's long-standing commitment to human rights causes. The visit, which begins next week, will be President Xi's first to the UK as Chinese leader and will include a state banquet at Buckingham Palace, where Mr. Corbyn will be in attendance. The Labour leader's spokesman stated that discussions are underway to arrange private meetings with Chinese officials during the visit, but did not rule out the possibility of Mr. Corbyn raising human rights issues during the royal function if necessary. Mr. Corbyn's decision to raise human rights concerns comes after Chancellor George Osborne's visit to China last month, where he addressed the issue privately with Chinese officials. However, campaigners had urged Mr. Osborne to be more vocal about the treatment of the Muslim Uighur minority in the restive Xinjiang province, which the Chancellor visited during his trip. The UK government has faced criticism for its approach to human rights issues in China, with some accusing ministers of prioritizing trade and economic ties over human rights concerns. Mr. Osborne has stated that the UK and China have different political systems and traditions, but that this does not preclude cooperation in areas such as commerce and culture. Mr. Corbyn, who has a long history of campaigning on human rights cases, has been critical of the government's approach to human rights issues in the past. As a backbench MP, he urged the release of political prisoners and called on the UK to stop selling arms to "repressive" regimes. In his conference speech last month, he highlighted the case of Ali Mohammed Baqir al-Nimr, a Saudi man who faces beheading after being convicted of crimes including breaking allegiance to the country's king. The government's decision to withdraw from talks about a £5.9m contract to provide services to Saudi jails has been seen as a response to criticism of the country's criminal justice system. However, ministers have denied that the decision was related to any individual case. As for Mr. Corbyn's attendance at the state banquet, his spokesman was unable to confirm whether he would wear the traditional white tie attire, or if he even owned such clothing. However, the spokesman did confirm that Mr. Corbyn would "take full part" in the event, including singing the national anthem, after being criticized for not doing so at a Battle of Britain memorial service last month. During the visit, President Xi is expected to address Parliament and hold talks with Prime Minister David Cameron. The visit marks a significant improvement in relations between the two countries, which were strained in 2012 following a diplomatic row over David Cameron's meeting with the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama. As the visit gets underway, all eyes will be on Mr. Corbyn and his efforts to raise human rights concerns with the Chinese leader, and whether his actions will have any impact on the UK's relationship with China.

Tata Steel's Decision to Cut Jobs Sends Shockwaves Through Welsh Economy The Welsh economy has been dealt a devastating blow as Tata Steel announced plans to cut hundreds of jobs, leaving many to wonder about the future of the steel industry in the region. This news comes at a particularly sensitive time, with an assembly election and a possible EU referendum looming on the horizon. The response from the government is expected to be far more tailored to the steel industry this time around, compared to the more general approach taken during the recession seven years ago. The timing of Tata's announcement is also significant, coming less than a fortnight after Chancellor George Osborne warned about the dangers facing the British economy. Many saw Osborne's warning as a cautionary tale about the risks of leaving the EU, but the counter view is that the steel industry's woes will only serve to fuel anger towards Brussels for failing to tackle cheap Chinese steel imports. This could potentially sway voters to reconsider their stance on EU membership. The losses will undoubtedly dominate the economic debate in the lead-up to the assembly elections. First Minister Carwyn Jones has already come out swinging, suggesting that the UK government's lack of urgency in addressing Chinese imports and energy costs contributed to the job losses. Jones stopped short of declaring all-out war with Westminster, but it's clear that he will be seeking to capitalize on criticism of the UK government's handling of the steel crisis. The UK government has defended its response, citing efforts to address concerns over energy and imports, while also acknowledging that the problem is largely caused by over-capacity in the global steel supply. However, this explanation is unlikely to provide much comfort to the hundreds of workers facing redundancy. In the short term, the Welsh government will focus on providing re-training programs for those affected, but in the longer term, a broader debate will need to take place about the level of financial support that should be committed to the steel industry. Plaid Cymru has already suggested that some form of state-ownership should be considered, but any proposals will ultimately come down to the question of whether it's worth risking resources on an industry that is largely beyond the government's control. As one senior Tata manager noted last year, the steel industry is facing a "new reality" that will require significant adjustments in order to survive. The difference between the current situation and the recession of 2009 is stark. While the previous downturn was seen as a cyclical phenomenon, the current crisis is viewed as a more permanent shift in the global steel landscape. As the Welsh government grapples with the implications of Tata's decision, one thing is clear: the steel industry will never be the same again, and the region will need to adapt quickly in order to mitigate the damage. The coming weeks and months will be crucial in determining the future of the steel industry in Wales, and the impact that it will have on the wider economy.

A British Army major is on trial for causing the death of a 24-year-old man by careless driving. Maj Richard Scott, 40, is accused of driving his Audi A6 at speeds of up to 95mph on a B-road in Wiltshire despite bad weather conditions. On October 6, 2014, Gareth Hicks, a passenger in a Ford Transit van, suffered fatal injuries when the vehicle was hit head-on by Maj Scott's car. Prosecutor Charles Gabb told the court that Maj Scott had crossed the carriageway of the 60mph-limit B390 in Shrewton, near Amesbury, before colliding with the van. The weather at the time was described as "awful" with strong winds and heavy rain. Mr Gabb alleged that Maj Scott's car was "twitching" and may have been aquaplaning before striking a BMW driven by Craig Reed, and then crossing the carriageway again to collide with the van. Maj Scott denies the charge, suggesting that it was actually Mr Reed who had crossed the carriageway, causing the collision. The defendant suffered substantial injuries in the crash and claims to have no memory of the incident. The trial continues, with the jury considering the evidence presented. Gareth Hicks, from Bath, Somerset, was on his way to a construction site in Salisbury when the accident occurred. His family and friends are awaiting the outcome of the trial, seeking justice for his tragic death.

Former Labour Prime Minister Gordon Brown has launched a scathing attack on both Scottish and Brexit nationalism, stating that voters are caught between the "extremes" of these two ideologies. In a campaign speech delivered in Fife, Brown emphasized the need for social justice to be the defining issue of the upcoming general election on June 8. Brown's speech, which made no mention of current UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, centered on the forecasted rise in child poverty in Scotland. According to the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), 320,000 children living in Scotland will be in poverty by 2022. Brown argued that nationalism offers no solutions to this pressing issue and that it is imperative to address poverty through a commitment to social justice. The former Prime Minister also warned against giving Theresa May a "free hand" or "blank cheque" in the election, stressing the importance of sending Labour MPs to parliament to "fight a war against poverty." However, his remarks were quickly countered by SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon, who claimed that Labour is "incapable" of defeating the Conservatives. Sturgeon argued that only the SNP can protect Scotland from the "full force" of policies implemented by a future Conservative government. She criticized Brown's speech as being overly familiar, stating that he has been making the same arguments for years. The SNP leader also highlighted the chaos at the heart of the Labour Party, which she believes has contributed to the Tories' significant lead in England. Scottish Conservative leader Ruth Davidson also responded to Brown's speech, accusing him of taking Scotland back to the 1990s. Davidson called on the SNP to remove the threat of a second independence referendum from the table, emphasizing the importance of the union between Scotland and the rest of the United Kingdom. She positioned the Scottish Conservatives as a forward-thinking party, focused on the future and the well-being of young people. Meanwhile, Scottish Liberal Democrat leader Willie Rennie echoed Sturgeon's sentiments, stating that Labour is incapable of providing a competent opposition to the Conservatives.
