I was really panicking," she told the BBC. Neighbours, who had rushed to the scene to offer assistance, urged Mrs. Philip to evacuate the house. However, she was initially hesitant, fearing that they might be the perpetrators of the attack. It was only when she realized they were trying to help that she opened the door and fled with her children. "I got out and I ran," she said. "It was so scary." The attack has been widely condemned by local politicians and community leaders. UUP MLA for South Antrim, Adrian Cochrane-Watson, praised Mrs. Philip's bravery and quick thinking in getting her children to safety. "This is a young mother who has been living in this country for a number of years, set up home. This is a lady, a professional who is saving lives every day of the week and rehabilitating people who are suffering from heart disease or heart attacks," he said. The local Indian community has rallied around the family, offering support and condemnation of the attack. Siba Thomas, a friend of Mrs. Philip, said he was shocked and saddened by the incident. "We have around 60 Indian families here, most of us work in the Antrim Area Hospital as either nurses or doctors. We work along with the community. Most of our children were born here and go to the local school. The community here is very welcoming, the people are so nice. So it's very unfortunate to see things happening like this, that someone would have that mindset," he said. Police have appealed for information and are treating the attack as a deliberate act of arson. Chief Inspector John Allen said, "We believe that the attack was motivated by racial hatred. Any attack on property is unacceptable, however I totally condemn the racial hate crime element of this attack, which makes it particularly repugnant." The Fire and Rescue Service is also investigating the incident. The community is coming together to support the Philip family, and a fundraising campaign has been launched to help them rebuild their lives. The attack has sent shockwaves through the local community, and many are left wondering how such a horrific incident could occur in their neighborhood. As the investigation continues, one thing is clear: the Philip family will not be alone in their time of need, and the community will rally around them to provide support and comfort.

A 29-year-old father, Kevin Toye, has been sentenced to six years in prison for killing his infant son, Baylee Varley. The sentencing took place at Norwich Crown Court, where it was revealed that Baylee suffered severe brain and retinal injuries in 2008, consistent with shaking. The injuries ultimately led to Baylee's death in 2014. Judge Mr Justice Spencer emphasized that Toye's refusal to acknowledge his role in Baylee's death was a significant aggravating factor. Despite acknowledging that Toye loved his son, the judge stated that his culpability remained high due to the victim being a "tiny, defenceless baby." Detective Constable Mike Proctor expressed that the investigation, which spanned several years, aimed to give Baylee a voice and seek justice for his tragic and avoidable death. The sentence reflects the severity of the crime, bringing closure to a heartbreaking case. Toye's actions have been condemned, and the court's decision serves as a reminder of the importance of protecting vulnerable children.

A recent survey by the CAF has revealed the world's most charitable countries. Thailand took the top spot, with 85% of its population making regular charitable contributions. The UK followed closely, with 79% of its citizens regularly giving to charity. The Irish Republic, Australia, and New Zealand also ranked highly. Despite a slight fall in charitable donations due to the global economic crisis, the survey found that more people are likely to perform charitable acts this year compared to 2010. Interestingly, the richest countries are not necessarily the most charitable, with only five of the top 20 economies by GDP appearing in the CAF's top 20 giving index. The survey highlights the generosity of nations and their people.

Actor Dan Haggerty, best known for his role as Grizzly Adams, has passed away after a battle with cancer. His manager, Terry Bomar, confirmed the news to ABC News. Haggerty's career in Hollywood began as a stuntman and animal handler, with guest appearances on popular TV shows like "CHiPs," "Charlie's Angels," and "The Love Boat." He starred in the 1974 film "The Life and Times of Grizzly Adams," which became a huge success, and later in the NBC TV series of the same name from 1977 to 1978. The film and series were inspired by the true story of James Capen Adams, a 19th-century bear trainer. Haggerty's iconic portrayal of the nature-loving mountain man has left a lasting impression on fans. His legacy will be remembered through his notable work in the entertainment industry.

Aberdeen Takes Down "No Ball Games" Signs to Encourage Outdoor Play Aberdeen has begun removing "no ball games" signs from public areas, with the help of former Manchester United star, Denis Law. The football legend, born in Aberdeen, was on hand to take down the first of hundreds of signs, citing the importance of outdoor play for young people. "You need to get young people out playing - the streets were where we learned our trade," he said. The city's plan to remove the signs was announced in August, with a report deeming them unenforceable and a deterrent to outdoor activity. Law expressed his support for the initiative, stating that parents would be happy for their children to engage in outdoor play, rather than being confined to computer games. The campaign is being assisted by local charity Aberdeen Greenspace, with the goal of improving the health and skills of the city's children. To mark the occasion, hundreds of sports balls will be given to underprivileged children. Law reflected on his own childhood, playing football in the streets without the presence of such signs, and welcomed the change, saying "it's nice to have this come round, taking the signs down."
Northern Ireland's election is underway, with 276 candidates vying for 108 seats. Polling stations were open from 07:00 to 22:00 BST, with counting to begin Friday.

UK Government Unveils New Powers for Welsh Assembly In a significant move towards devolution, the UK Government has announced plans to grant the Welsh Assembly more powers over income tax rates, energy, transport, and its own elections. The Wales Bill, which received an unopposed third reading in the Commons on Monday, marks a major milestone in the devolution settlement for Wales. According to Secretary of State for Wales, Alun Cairns, the new powers will transform the assembly into a "fully-fledged Welsh legislature" and make it a permanent part of the UK's constitutional fabric. The proposed laws will give the assembly the power to make decisions on policies such as setting speed limits and whether fracking should be permitted. Additionally, the assembly will have more control over taxes, making it responsible not only for how money is spent in Wales but also for how it is raised. This move is expected to usher in a new era of devolution, one that will bring clarity and accountability to the people of Wales. However, the Bill has faced criticism from other parties, who feel that it does not go far enough. Shadow Welsh secretary Paul Flynn expressed his disappointment, stating that the Bill is "just a stage" and not the end of devolution. He called for a separate Welsh government with powers similar to those of Scotland. Hywel Williams, Plaid Cymru's Westminster leader, and Welsh Liberal Democrat leader Mark Williams also echoed similar sentiments, saying that the new Bill does not grant enough powers to the Welsh Assembly. One notable omission from the Bill is the establishment of a separate justice system for Wales. Despite this, Mr. Cairns insisted that the move marks a significant step forward in the devolution settlement for Wales, one that is "clearer, fairer and stronger." The Bill will now undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords, where it is expected to face more debate and potential amendments. As the Bill progresses, it is clear that the UK Government's decision to grant more powers to the Welsh Assembly is a significant step towards greater autonomy for Wales. While some parties may feel that the Bill does not go far enough, it is undeniable that this move marks a new era in the devolution settlement for Wales, one that will bring greater clarity, accountability, and powers to the Welsh people.

Stirling Castle has won a prestigious award, beating Edinburgh Zoo and Dynamic Earth. The castle attracts 460,000 visitors annually. Executive manager Liz Grant called the win a "wonderful achievement", noting it recognizes Scotland's heritage attractions. The award was voted on by the public, making it a special accolade for the castle and its contribution to Scotland's tourism and leisure offerings.

A 30-year-old motorcyclist is being treated for a serious head injury after crashing into a wall on the B743 near Dungavel. The incident occurred at 19:25 on Wednesday, with the man losing control of his Suzuki motorcycle. He was airlifted to Queen Elizabeth University Hospital in Glasgow. Two friends, who were travelling on the same road, were nearby at the time of the crash. Police are urging witnesses to come forward, asking anyone with information to contact them on 101. Inquiries into the crash are ongoing, led by PC Dougie Bryson. Witnesses are encouraged to share any information.

President Trump's Advisory Commission on Election Integrity held its first meeting on Wednesday, sparking controversy and concerns over voter suppression. The commission, established by the president in May, aims to investigate voter fraud and election integrity. However, Democrats suspect that the commission's true intention is to disenfranchise left-leaning voters. During the meeting, President Trump pledged his strong support for the commission, emphasizing the importance of ensuring the integrity of the electoral process. "Every time voter fraud occurs, it cancels out the vote of a lawful citizen, and undermines democracy," he said. "Can't let that happen." The president has repeatedly claimed that he would have won the popular vote in the 2016 presidential election if not for millions of illegal votes cast, despite lacking evidence to support this assertion. The commission's chairman, Kris Kobach, echoed the president's sentiments, stating that it is impossible to know the true outcome of the election due to the presence of ineligible voters. "I think the President-elect is absolutely correct when he says the number of illegal votes cast exceeds the popular vote margin between him and Hillary Clinton," Kobach said. However, he acknowledged that even if the commission were to identify ineligible votes, it would be impossible to determine which candidate they voted for. Kobach, who is also the secretary of state of Kansas, has been a vocal advocate for stricter voter ID laws and immigration policies. His involvement in the commission has raised concerns among voting rights advocates, who have dubbed him the "king of voter suppression." The American Civil Liberties Union's voting rights project has criticized Kobach's efforts to restrict voting access, particularly among minority and low-income communities. The commission's request for voter data, including names, addresses, and voting history, has been met with resistance from at least 20 states. Kentucky Secretary of State Alison Lundergan Grimes has refused to submit voter records to the commission, calling it a "waste of taxpayer money" and an attempt to "legitimize voter suppression efforts." Other states have expressed similar concerns, citing the potential for the commission's findings to be used to justify restrictive voting laws. The controversy surrounding the commission has highlighted the deepening partisan divide over voting rights and election integrity. While the president and his allies claim that the commission is necessary to prevent voter fraud, opponents argue that it is a thinly veiled attempt to suppress Democratic votes. As the commission continues its work, it remains to be seen whether it will be able to achieve its stated goals or if it will become a tool for partisan manipulation. One thing is certain, however: the debate over voting rights and election integrity will continue to be a contentious issue in American politics.

Renowned Author Margaret Forster Passes Away at 77 Margaret Forster, the award-winning author of novels such as "Georgy Girl" and "Diary of an Ordinary Woman", has passed away at the age of 77. Forster, who had been suffering from cancer in her back, died on Monday morning at the Marie Curie Hospice in north London. The news was confirmed by her daughter, Caitlin Davies, who took to Twitter to pay tribute to her mother, saying "Her books will live on." Forster's writing career spanned over five decades, during which she published more than 25 novels, as well as several biographies of notable figures such as Dame Daphne du Maurier and William Makepeace Thackeray. Her most famous novel, "Georgy Girl", was published in 1965 and was later adapted into a film starring Lynn Redgrave and Charlotte Rampling. The book told the story of a young woman in 1960s London, navigating a complex web of relationships and identity. Fellow novelist Elizabeth Day paid tribute to Forster, describing her as "an under-appreciated wonder of a writer" who was "once very nice to me as a debut novelist". Forster's husband, writer Hunter Davies, also spoke fondly of his wife, describing her as "the cleverest woman I ever met". He praised her emotional intelligence, saying she had a unique ability to understand people and predict their actions and feelings. Forster's life was marked by her bravery and resilience in the face of adversity. She underwent a double mastectomy 40 years ago, and yet continued to write and publish books until recent years. Her most recent book, "My Life In Houses", was published in 2014 and offered a poignant and introspective look at her life through the places she had lived. Despite her literary success, Forster rarely sought to draw attention to herself, and gave few interviews throughout her career. However, she did appear on Radio 4's Desert Island Discs in 1994, offering a rare glimpse into her life and personality. Her legacy will live on through her books, which continue to captivate readers with their insightful and nuanced portrayals of human experience.

Tragedy Strikes Deganwy as Beloved Business Owners Perish in House Fire A devastating house fire in Deganwy, Conwy, has claimed the lives of Ted and Lucy Hocknell, a well-respected and beloved couple in the community. The blaze, which occurred at their home in Gannock Park West at approximately 07:40 BST on Tuesday, is thought to have been caused by an electrical fault. Despite being brought out of the house, the couple sadly passed away afterwards. Ted Hocknell, 93, was a decorated war veteran who received the Ushakov medal from the Russian government in 2014 for his bravery in keeping Arctic supply lines open during World War Two. A former policeman, he was also known for his heroic actions in the community, including saving two children from the tide on Llandudno's West Shore and apprehending a handbag thief. His friend, Ian Turner, remembered him as a "really nice guy" who would never seek to draw attention to himself. Lucy Hocknell, 88, was a former hairdresser and a "real lady" who was always seen walking arm in arm with her sister in town. The couple owned the popular Bryant and Hocknell furniture shop on Gloddaeth Street, and their presence will be deeply missed in the community. Aberconwy AM Janet Finch-Saunders expressed her shock and sadness at the news, stating that the town will "miss them tremendously."

Thousands of Swansea City fans are set to descend upon Wembley Stadium this weekend as the team prepares to face off against Bradford City in the Capital One Cup final. The club's allocation of 33,000 tickets sold out weeks ago, demonstrating the immense excitement and dedication of the Swansea City faithful. As the big day approaches, the BBC will be providing comprehensive coverage of the event. Fans are encouraged to share their experiences and photos from Wembley, Swansea, or anywhere else in the world where they will be cheering on their team. Photos can be emailed to newsonline.wales@bbc.co.uk, and a selection will be published online. The BBC invites fans to share their stories and comments, which may be published along with their name and location. Fans can also include their phone number if they are willing to be contacted by a BBC journalist. As always, safety is paramount, and fans are reminded to avoid taking unnecessary risks or infringing on laws when sharing their content. A full gallery of fan photos is already available online, and more will be added throughout the weekend.

Indian President Pranab Mukherjee has introduced reforms to the protocols surrounding his office. According to his press secretary, Venu Rajamony, the president felt that certain practices needed to be reformed. As a result, Mr. Mukherjee will now be referred to as "Mr. President" instead of "His Excellency" in domestic contexts. The title "Excellency" will only be used when interacting with foreign leaders, following international customs. This change aims to promote equality, as enshrined in the Indian constitution. Additionally, the president has instructed his office to organize functions within the Rashtrapati Bhavan to minimize public inconvenience and reduce the burden on law enforcement. This move is part of a broader review of protocols undertaken by the new president, who was elected in July. The reforms reflect Mr. Mukherjee's commitment to simplicity and equality.

An incident occurred at HM Naval Base Clyde, home to the UK's Trident nuclear submarines, when a routine fire exercise on a surface ship triggered a fire suppression system. The incident happened at around 05:30, prompting emergency services to be called to the base. Six personnel inhaled a gas and were taken to the Royal Alexandria Hospital as a precaution. Their families have been informed and an investigation has been launched. A Royal Navy spokesman confirmed the incident, stating that all other personnel were declared fit after being checked at the base's sick bay. The cause of the incident is currently under investigation.

Belgian Cisse expressed excitement about his new opportunity, stating, "I am looking forward to showing my qualities." The 23-year-old made 27 appearances for Standard last season and is eager to contribute to his new team. He previously played for KVV Mechelen before returning to his hometown club.

Australian Election Results Remain Uncertain as Counting Continues The Australian federal election results remain too close to call, with counting continuing on Wednesday in several key electorates. According to the Australian Broadcasting Corp. (ABC), the government has secured 71 seats in the lower house, with a possibility of reaching an absolute majority of 76. However, the outcome is still uncertain, and the possibility of a "hung parliament" looms. Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has accepted responsibility for the government's mediocre performance, citing disillusionment with mainstream parties as a contributing factor. The coalition has lost over 20 seats, with many analysts surprised by the close result. Turnbull stated, "I want to make it quite clear that as Prime Minister and leader of the Liberal party, I take full responsibility for our campaign." The ABC's election analyst, Antony Green, predicts that the government will win at least 73 seats, surpassing the opposition Labor Party's tally. Postal votes have favored the government, with results in several electorates hanging in the balance. In the Queensland seat of Forde, the Liberal candidate leads by a mere 94 votes, highlighting the intense competition. If the coalition fails to secure 76 seats, it will face a "hung parliament," requiring them to negotiate with independent crossbenchers to form a government. The coalition is likely to seek support from Queensland rural MP Bob Katter and the Nick Xenophon Team's newly elected MP Rebekha Sharkie. Labor, on the other hand, is unlikely to have the numbers to form a minority government. The poor showing during the coalition's re-election campaign has sparked speculation about Turnbull's position as prime minister. Opposition leader Bill Shorten has repeatedly called on Turnbull to step down, while some MPs have criticized the prime minister's campaign strategy. Turnbull, however, remains committed to his role, stating, "It's too early for definitive judgments..... it will take time to absorb the learnings from the campaign." As Australia waits for the final results, the country's history of frequent leadership changes looms large. With five prime ministers in the past six years, the political landscape remains uncertain. The outcome of the election will have significant implications for the country's future, and all eyes are on the ongoing counting process to determine the ultimate winner.

Pop stars Pixie Lott, Geri Halliwell, and Professor Green attended the Starlight charity party. EastEnders' Jake Wood and McBusted also joined. Starlight grants wishes and provides hospital entertainment for ill children, aiming to distract them from pain and isolation, bringing joy to those in need. The event supported the charity's mission to improve young lives.

Two Saudi women, Loujain al-Hathloul and Maysa al-Amoudi, have been released from detention after being arrested for campaigning against the country's ban on female drivers. Al-Hathloul, 25, was taken into custody on December 1 after attempting to drive into Saudi Arabia from the United Arab Emirates, while al-Amoudi, 33, a Saudi journalist, was detained when she arrived at the border to support her friend. The women's arrest sparked widespread concern, particularly after reports emerged that their case was being transferred to a terrorism court. The move was reportedly due to comments they had made on social media, rather than their actions behind the wheel. Saudi Arabia is the only country in the world where women are forbidden from driving, and those who do risk being fined and arrested. The women's release comes just days after Britain's Prince Charles met with Saudi Arabia's new monarch, Prince Salman. During the visit, Prince Charles raised the case of Raif Badawi, a blogger who has been sentenced to 1,000 lashes and 10 years in prison. The case of the women drivers has highlighted the restrictions faced by women in Saudi Arabia and has put pressure on the new monarch to address human rights concerns. The release of al-Hathloul and al-Amoudi has been welcomed by activists, who believe that the British prince's visit may have played a role in securing their freedom. The women's large following on Twitter had helped to draw attention to their case, with many using social media to campaign for their release. The incident has shone a spotlight on Saudi Arabia's human rights record, and many are now calling for greater reforms to address the country's restrictive laws and practices.

Rentokil has announced the sale of its struggling delivery firm City Link to restructuring specialist Better Capital. City Link has incurred significant losses since 2007, including a £26m deficit in 2012, due to weakening demand from small businesses. Better Capital is expected to invest £40m into the business, which will continue to be run by its existing management team. Rentokil's decision to offload City Link is part of its strategy to focus on its core pest control and hygiene operations. Despite chief executive Alan Brown's optimism that City Link has "turned the corner," Rentokil's shares closed 0.6% down following the announcement. Better Capital has recently invested in Jaeger and Everest, and its investment in City Link is hoped to revitalize the struggling business. The sale marks a significant shift for Rentokil, which acquired City Link in 2006.

French conservatives are heading to the polls today to choose their candidate for next spring's presidential election, with former Prime Minister François Fillon emerging as the favorite to win. Fillon, 62, secured 44.1% of the votes in the first round of the primary election last week, leaving his rival, Alain Juppe, 71, trailing behind with 28.5%. The winner of today's run-off is expected to face off against far-right National Front leader Marine Le Pen in the general election. The primary election, modeled on the US system, has been marked by a heated debate between the two candidates over their economic reform plans. Fillon has campaigned on a promise of radical change, pledging to slash 500,000 public jobs and implement sweeping economic reforms. Juppe, on the other hand, has proposed a more moderate approach, focusing on harmony and diversity, and planning to cut just over half the number of public jobs proposed by Fillon. The debate between the two candidates has become increasingly personal, with Juppe attempting to mobilize centrist and left-wing voters by highlighting Fillon's conservative views on abortion and gay marriage. Juppe has also accused Fillon of being close to Russian President Vladimir Putin, amid growing tensions between the West and Moscow over the crises in Syria and Ukraine. Fillon has hit back, arguing that the EU and the US "provoked" Russia by expanding in Eastern Europe, and calling for an alliance with Russia to fight Islamic State militants in Syria. He has also complained of being portrayed as a "medieval conservative", describing Juppe as a "man of the system" with no real plans for change. The endorsement of former President Nicolas Sarkozy, who was knocked out of the race in the first round, has given Fillon a significant boost. Polls suggest that Fillon is now the favorite to win, with 71% of conservative respondents finding him more convincing in a recent TV debate. Polls across France are due to open at 07:00 GMT and close at 18:00 GMT, with the results expected to be announced later today. The winner of the primary election will go on to represent the Republican party in the general election, where they are expected to face off against Marine Le Pen in a battle for the presidency. With the French economy struggling and the country facing a range of challenges, from terrorism to immigration, the outcome of today's election is being closely watched by politicians and voters across the country.

Actor Tom Chambers has sparked controversy after suggesting that men's salaries should be higher than women's because they often have families to support. The Casualty star, who plays Sam Strachan on the show and its sister program Holby City, made the comments at a book launch, where he also expressed his opinion that his co-star Derek Thompson deserved to be the BBC's highest-paid actor due to his 31 years of service. Chambers, a former winner of Strictly Come Dancing, stated that as the sole breadwinner in his family, his salary was not just for himself, but also for his wife and children. However, his remarks were met with a social media backlash, with many criticizing him for perpetuating the gender pay gap. In response to the backlash, Chambers has since apologized, claiming that his comments were "taken out of context" and that he does not advocate for the gender pay gap. He expressed his mortification at the stories that had run about his comments and emphasized his belief that change is needed to address the issue of gender pay disparity. The controversy surrounding Chambers' comments comes amid ongoing debate about the BBC's pay disclosures, which have highlighted a significant disparity between the salaries of the corporation's male and female celebrities. The issue of gender pay disparity remains a contentious topic, with many calling for greater equality and transparency in pay practices. Chambers' comments have added fuel to the fire, sparking a renewed conversation about the need for change.

Andy Murray has made a strong return to the court, defeating Borna Coric 6-1 6-2 in the Paris Masters. The second-seeded Murray, who was playing for the first time since losing to Novak Djokovic in Shanghai 19 days ago, wasted little time in seeing off the 18-year-old Coric. The young Croatian, ranked 46 in the world, was unable to fashion a single break point as Murray broke serve twice in each set to secure the win in under an hour. Murray's victory sets up a meeting with Belgian David Goffin, which will serve as a warm-up for their likely encounter in the Davis Cup final later this month. The Scot is looking to gain valuable information from their match on the Paris hard courts, which he can take to the indoor clay courts in Ghent. "Any time you spend time on court with opponents you can learn about their game," Murray said. "It's good to play against him but I will obviously, before the tie, watch matches of him playing on clay to learn and understand his game better on that surface." Meanwhile, British number two Aljaz Bedene's run in the tournament came to an end with a 6-3 7-6 (7-3) loss to American 13th seed John Isner. Bedene, who could yet feature in the Davis Cup final pending an ITF ruling on his eligibility to represent Great Britain, had come through two rounds of qualifying and beaten Spain's Marcel Granollers in the main draw. His ranking is set to reach a new high of 46 next week. Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer also progressed in the tournament, with Nadal beating Lukas Rosol 6-2 6-2 and Federer cruising past Italian Andreas Seppi 6-1 6-1. Murray will face Goffin at 09:30 GMT on Thursday, as he looks to build momentum ahead of the ATP Finals in London and the Davis Cup final. With a busy schedule over the next few weeks, Murray will be looking to make the most of his time on court and gain valuable experience that he can take into the upcoming tournaments.

London Launches Dedicated Hub to Combat Online Hate Crime A new hub is being set up in London to tackle online hate crime, with a team of five officers dedicated to supporting victims and identifying abuse. The two-year pilot project, which will cost £1.7m, has received £452,000 in funding from the Home Office. The London Mayor's office has stated that there will be a "zero tolerance" approach to online abuse, with a spokesman emphasizing that there is "no place for hate" in the city. The team will work to identify the location of online crimes and allocate them to the relevant police force. They will also be assisted by a team of volunteers. The Mayor's Office for Policing And Crime (Mopac) has highlighted the challenges posed by social media, which can provide perpetrators with anonymity and make it harder to bring them to justice. Victims of online hate crime can become isolated and fearful, with the potential for online abuse to spill into the real world. The new hub will not only support victims but also provide training for police officers and community groups on how to identify, report, and challenge online abuse. This is the first time a dedicated police team has been set up to detect and respond to hate crimes, and it is seen as a significant step forward in tackling this growing issue. Community groups in London have welcomed the initiative, citing online hate crime as a major concern that has previously received an inconsistent police response.

North West Ambulance Service (NWAS) is facing scrutiny after two separate incidents where patients died after experiencing significant delays in receiving medical attention. The family of 71-year-old Jack Skelly from Burnley has lodged a complaint after he passed away following a 55-minute wait for an ambulance crew. In a separate incident, 65-year-old Richard Hansbury from Wigan bled to death after a staggering 150-minute delay. According to NWAS, patient handovers are causing "significant delays" in their response times. The trust is currently facing its most challenging operating environment on record, with a 7% increase in 999 calls this year. Nurse Jo Needham, the niece of Mr. Skelly, expressed her concerns about the delay in response time, stating that her uncle "would've had a better chance" of survival if the ambulance had arrived earlier. Mr. Skelly had complained of feeling unwell and collapsed in his bathroom on December 19. Despite multiple phone calls made by his family for an ambulance, the crew took 55 minutes to arrive. By the time they arrived, Nurse Needham was attempting to resuscitate her uncle. She believes that if he had collapsed in a public place with access to a defibrillator, his chances of survival would have been higher. In the case of Mr. Hansbury, an ambulance crew had to wait nearly three hours for a second available crew to help them lift the 19-stone patient into an ambulance. His inquest is scheduled for Friday. NWAS has stated that it is fully investigating both incidents and has offered its condolences to the families. The trust attributed the delays to high demand for services and resources being tied up at nearby hospitals. The incidents have raised concerns about the trust's ability to meet national targets for response times. In September, NWAS admitted that it was struggling to hit targets for reaching "red one" and "red two" calls within eight minutes. The trust must also reach non-life-threatening "green" calls within 20 minutes. As the investigation into these incidents continues, the families of the victims and the community at large are left to wonder about the adequacy of the emergency services in the region.

A British student, Hannah Bladon, was tragically killed in a stabbing attack on a tram in Jerusalem on Good Friday. The 20-year-old, from Burton-upon-Trent in Staffordshire, was studying at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem at the time of her death. She had been participating in an archaeological dig that morning and was on her way back when the attack occurred. The incident took place on a tram travelling near the Old City, which was crowded with Christians marking Good Friday and Jews celebrating Passover. A 57-year-old Palestinian man, who had recently been released from a psychiatric hospital, pulled a knife from his bag and repeatedly stabbed Ms. Bladon in the chest. She died shortly after arrival at the hospital. The attacker was detained at the scene by an off-duty policeman who was travelling on the tram with his family. The policeman, who wished to remain anonymous, told the AFP news agency that he heard the cries of "attack, attack" and immediately sounded the alarm. With the help of another passenger, he overpowered the attacker and prevented further harm. Two other people, a 30-year-old pregnant woman and a 50-year-old man, were also injured in the attack. According to BBC Middle East correspondent Tom Bateman, they were either hurt when the tram came to a sudden stop or in the panic to get away from the scene. Ms. Bladon was a student at the University of Birmingham, where she was studying bible studies, archaeology, and Hebrew. Her personal tutor, Dr. Andrew Davies, described her as a "rare treasure" and praised her enthusiasm and dedication to her studies. "She was always the first to be there for lectures, bright-eyed, bushy-tailed, even in the early hours of the morning," he said. The Hebrew University of Jerusalem expressed "deep sorrow" over Ms. Bladon's death, and her family released a statement paying tribute to her memory. "Hannah was the most caring, sensitive, and compassionate daughter you could ever wish for," they said. "She was a talented musician, part of a serving team at her local church, and a member of her local archaeological group. She was an enthusiastic rugby player and a keen Derby County supporter. Her death leaves so much promise unfulfilled." Israel's President Reuven Rivlin said he was "filled with sadness" about the attack and offered his thoughts and prayers to Ms. Bladon's family. The incident has sparked widespread condemnation, and Israeli police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the attack. The suspect, who has been named as a resident of Ras al-Amud in east Jerusalem, is being held in custody and is expected to face charges in the coming days.

The TweedLove Bike Festival has kicked off in the Borders, attracting thousands of visitors. The first week's events included a trail run, mountain bike marathon, and family day in Peebles. Hundreds of children participated in riding events. Now in its eighth year, the festival boasts over 40 events across three weeks. A "mega bike demo" is upcoming, featuring bikes worth up to £10,000 for the public to try, during the second "big weekend" from June 9-11. The festival is the UK's largest cycling celebration.

Notts County and Arsenal played to a thrilling 1-1 draw in front of a crowd of 1,583 at Meadow Lane, with both teams creating numerous scoring opportunities. The hosts took the lead in the 27th minute courtesy of a cool finish from Jess Clarke, who sidestepped two defenders before slotting the ball into the far corner of the net. Clarke, playing up front in the absence of Ellen White, had gone close with a couple of early long-range efforts and her goal was well-deserved. However, Arsenal came out strong in the second half, with Japanese midfielder Yukari Kinga having a header well saved by keeper Carly Telford in the 49th minute. Just four minutes later, the Gunners leveled the score when right-back Alex Scott drilled an 18-yard volley into the far corner of the net. Arsenal continued to push for a winner, with striker Kelly Smith being desperately unlucky not to give her team the lead as her 72nd-minute free-kick hit the bar and bounced clear off the goal line. Substitute Freda Ayisi also had a chance to win the game for Arsenal, but her 12-yard shot was headed off the line by central defender Sophie Bradley. Despite their improved second-half display, the Gunners were unable to force a winner, but will be boosted by their performance ahead of their upcoming fixtures. In the night's other game, Birmingham City fought out a 0-0 draw with Everton at their new Solihull ground in front of 657 fans. The match was a tightly contested affair, with both teams creating scoring opportunities but neither able to find the back of the net. Everton striker Nikita Parris had an early header saved by goalkeeper Rebecca Spencer, while Birmingham's Katie Wilkinson had a shot fly over the bar in the 29th minute. The Toffees continued to look the sharper side in front of goal, with Danielle Turner striking the post and Billie Murphy having a close-range shot saved by Spencer. However, Birmingham almost took the lead eight minutes from time, with Kirsty Linnett driving in a 30-yard shot that hit the bar. The draw will be a welcome point for Birmingham, who face a tough Champions League semi-final against Swedish team Tyreso in just three days' time.

European Athletics Launches Review of Records Amid Doping Scandals In the wake of growing concerns over doping in athletics, European Athletics (EA) president Svein Arne Hansen has ordered a review of European records to ensure they are "100% believable and credible". The move comes as Russian athletes face a ban from competing due to a state-sponsored doping program, and Olympic legend Usain Bolt is set to lose a gold medal after a teammate tested positive for banned substances. The review, which will report back its findings by September, aims to scrutinize the legitimacy of European records, particularly those held by Russian athletes. Currently, the EA website lists 15 European indoor and outdoor athletics records held by Russians, as well as additional records set in the 1980s by athletes from Soviet Bloc countries, including East Germany, which operated its own extensive doping program. Hansen emphasized the importance of records being respected and recognized as beyond question by athletes and fans. "Claiming a European record - after being crowned European Champion - is the pinnacle of our sport in Europe. The holders of these records should be aspirational heroes whose performances are respected and recognised as beyond question by their fellow athletes and the fans of our sport," he said. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) is also taking action, re-testing hundreds of samples from the 2008 and 2012 Olympic Games using up-to-date detection methods. So far, almost 100 athletes have been sanctioned for using banned substances, including Jamaican sprinter Nesta Carter, who was part of the Jamaican quartet that won the 4x100m relay in Beijing in 2008, featuring Usain Bolt. As a result, Jamaica will be stripped of its medal. Hansen has spoken with Lord Coe, head of the IAAF, athletics' world governing body, about the review, and the IAAF will monitor the work closely before deciding on any actions at the world level. The review is a significant step towards restoring integrity and trust in athletics, and ensuring that European records are a true reflection of athletic achievement.

Tragedy struck in Quinta do Conde, a town 30km south of Lisbon, as a dispute over a barking dog turned deadly. A 77-year-old man allegedly opened fire after a row with a neighbor, sparking a chaotic sequence of events. A plainclothes officer, who lived in the area, was fatally shot while investigating the disturbance. A patrol officer responding to the scene was also shot in the head and killed. The officer's son, who attempted to aid his father, was seriously injured in the crossfire and later succumbed to his wounds in hospital. The gunman, who reportedly tried to take his own life with a hunting rifle, was arrested and hospitalized. Neighbors expressed shock, stating that while the man had previously threatened to harm someone over the barking dog, they never thought he would act on it.

Nottingham Forest Chairman Fawaz Al Hasawi has expressed his excitement as manager Billy Davies returns to the club on a three-and-a-half year deal. Davies, 49, previously managed Forest from 2009 to 2011, leading the team to consecutive play-off campaigns. After being sacked in 2011, he has now returned to the City Ground, becoming the fourth manager to work under the Al Hasawi ownership in seven months. Last season, Forest narrowly missed the Championship play-offs, but currently sit fourth in the table after 11 games. Davies' return has brought optimism to the club, with Al Hasawi looking forward to working with him to bring success back to Nottingham Forest. With Davies at the helm, the team aims to build on their strong start to the season and push for promotion.

Labour Pledges to Protect EU Funding for Deprived Regions In a significant commitment, the Labour Party has vowed to safeguard the funding of deprived regions in the UK that currently receive financial support from the European Union. Shadow Foreign Secretary Emily Thornberry announced at the party's conference in Liverpool that a future Labour government would guarantee to make up any shortfall in structural funding into the 2020s and beyond. The move is seen as a key plank of Labour's next manifesto, with Ms Thornberry emphasizing that the communities most affected by Brexit must be protected. She criticized the government's current offer, which guarantees EU-funded projects signed before the Autumn statement and agricultural funding until 2020, as "hedged in conditions" and lacking long-term certainty. Without a clear guarantee of funding, Ms Thornberry argued that the most deprived regions and communities cannot plan ahead, attract investment, or make progress. She pledged that Labour would fill any funding gap, with regions such as Wales, south west England, and the North West set to benefit. Wales is currently allocated £2.1bn, south west England £1.3bn, and the North West £979m under the current seven-year programme. Ms Thornberry also used her speech to praise Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who was re-elected on Saturday, and to attack the government's handling of Brexit. She accused the government of having "no plan" for the UK's exit from the EU and promised that Labour would "stand up" for EU migrants, UK businesses, and workers' rights. Labour has committed to opposing any attempts by the government to scrap legal rights and funding programmes derived from Britain's EU membership. The party will publish a document outlining the full range of benefits that are under threat, with regional funding being a key area of concern. By establishing a domestic fund for less prosperous regions, Labour aims to protect the level of funding currently received from the EU, using the estimated net savings from Britain's withdrawal to prioritize this commitment. The pledge has been welcomed by delegates at the Labour conference, who see it as a vital step in protecting the most vulnerable communities from the impact of Brexit. With the government's Brexit plan still unclear, Labour's commitment to safeguarding EU funding is likely to be a major issue in the run-up to the next general election.

A Call to Ban Hot Food on the London Tube Lord Sherbourne has sparked a debate in the House of Lords by suggesting that hot food should be banned on the London Tube network. He argued that the consumption of hot food on trains is "very offensive" to many passengers and creates litter that can pose a health hazard. The peer pointed out that smoking and alcohol are already prohibited on the network and questioned why hot food should be treated differently. Lord Sherbourne cited cities like Washington DC, which have implemented similar bans, as examples that London could follow. He urged Transport Minister Lord Ahmad to raise the matter with Transport for London (TfL) and consider conducting a passenger survey to gauge public opinion on the issue. In response, Lord Ahmad acknowledged the concern but stated that there are currently "no plans" to introduce a ban on hot food on the Tube. However, he promised to discuss the matter with TfL and noted that the transport authority already has a policy in place to promote good travel etiquette among passengers. While a ban may not be on the horizon, the debate highlights the ongoing efforts to improve the commuting experience for Londoners. The issue is likely to continue to be a topic of discussion among transport officials and passengers alike.

Environment Secretary Enjoys Warm Welcome and Local Fare at Gloucester Services In a lighthearted moment during a recent Parliamentary debate, Environment Secretary Liz Truss was invited to visit Gloucester Services, a renowned motorway stop-off, and enjoy a traditional Gloucester Old Spot sausage. The offer, extended by Gloucester MP Richard Graham, was met with laughter in the Commons, but Ms Truss took him up on it, visiting the services on Friday. Upon arrival, she was treated to a cooked breakfast, complete with a locally-sourced sausage, which she proclaimed "very nice". The sausage, made from Gloucestershire Old Spot meat, was a highlight of her meal, with Ms Truss praising its "really lovely" flavor and the passion of the local producers who made it. Gloucester Services has gained a reputation for defying the typical motorway services stereotype, instead offering upmarket, organic fare from local suppliers. The site, which features independent shops and restaurants, sources produce from 130 local suppliers within a 30-mile radius. Ms Truss praised the services as "a brilliant example of promoting local food" and highlighted its role in bringing together local producers to create an exceptional experience for visitors. The visit comes as part of the government's efforts to promote British food, following the launch of the Great British Food Unit in November. The unit aims to help Britain become a "great food nation" by bringing together "food and drink pioneers" to support the industry. With its commitment to local, high-quality produce, Gloucester Services is a shining example of this initiative in action.

Concerns Over Pencil Use in Voting Prompt Calls for Change The use of pencils to mark ballot papers in the recent EU referendum has sparked widespread concern among voters, with many taking to social media to express their fears that votes could be altered. The issue has prompted the Electoral Commission to receive almost 200 calls from worried voters, and has led to calls for the government to provide alternative writing instruments. Lib Dem Lord Rennard has asked the government to consider providing "special ballot pens" instead of pencils, citing concerns that pencil marks could be easily erased and changed. The Electoral Commission has stated that it is looking into "alternatives to providing pencils for voters in polling stations which could improve confidence" in the voting process. The controversy surrounding pencil use in voting began on social media, where the hashtag #usepens gained traction on Twitter. Many voters expressed concerns that ballot papers filled out in pencil could be rubbed out and changed, potentially altering the outcome of the referendum. In response, the Electoral Commission has noted that voters are able to use either a pen or pencil to mark their ballot paper, and that there is no law requiring the use of one over the other. Despite this, the Commission has acknowledged that the use of pencils may not be the most secure or reliable method of voting. Historically, pencils have been used for practical reasons, as pens can dry out or spill, causing problems with the voting process. However, the Commission is now working with returning officers and national governments to explore alternative options that could improve voter confidence. A Cabinet Office spokeswoman, Baroness Chisholm of Owlpen, has stated that the government is aware of the concerns surrounding pencil use, but has noted that there were no reported cases of ballot papers being changed during the referendum. The Electoral Commission's report into the EU referendum has highlighted the need for alternative voting methods, and it is likely that changes will be made to the voting process in the future to address the concerns of voters.

Russell Knox has maintained his position at the top of the leaderboard at the World Golf Championships in Shanghai, matching Hideki Matsuyama's impressive four-under round of 68. The Scottish golfer now stands at 14 under par, tied with Matsuyama for the lead. American Daniel Berger is close behind, just one shot off the pace, while Bill Haas and Francesco Molinari are a further stroke back on 12 under. Rory McIlroy, the world number three, had a mixed day, carding an up-and-down 70 at Sheshan International. He showed glimpses of brilliance, including a remarkable recovery shot on the eighth hole, but was ultimately hindered by bogeys on the 11th, 12th, and 15th. Despite picking up strokes on the 16th and 18th, McIlroy finds himself eight shots off the lead. Knox, who is bidding to become the second player to retain a World Golf Championships title, came agonizingly close to a hole-in-one on the fourth hole. He then applied pressure on Matsuyama with a shot on the 13th, but found water on the 14th. However, the 31-year-old showed remarkable resilience, holing from 25 feet for an unlikely par before birdying the 15th. As the tournament enters its final stages, Matsuyama is poised to make history as the first Japanese player to win a WGC event. Meanwhile, Ross Fisher and Shane Lowry have made notable moves up the leaderboard, with Fisher tied for sixth on 10 under and Lowry joining McIlroy and Henrik Stenson on nine under. In contrast, Danny Willett endured another difficult day, carding a 75 to leave him 11 over par.

Revolutionary Changes Proposed for Rugby League Structure The Rugby Football League (RFL) has unveiled three groundbreaking proposals to transform the sport's competitive structure, with the aim of introducing positive change and innovation across the entire sport. The proposed changes, which cannot be implemented until the start of the 2015 season, have been met with enthusiasm from clubs and fans alike. RFL chief executive Nigel Wood expressed his optimism, stating, "The interest already shown in these ideas has been very encouraging, and I believe these new proposals will produce positive change and innovation across the whole sport." The current licensing system, which has been in place since 2009, has granted 14 clubs three-year licenses, making them immune to relegation. However, this system has been met with criticism from some clubs, particularly those in the Championship, who are advocating for a return to regular promotion and relegation. In response to these concerns, the RFL has consulted with all Super League and Championship clubs, and a proposal to maintain the status quo was rejected. The three proposed options aim to address the concerns of clubs and fans while ensuring the long-term sustainability of the sport. Option 1 suggests a 12-team Super League competition, with a 10 or 12-team Championship, and one club promoted and relegated each year. Option 2 proposes a two-division Super League, with each division comprising 10 teams. The most radical proposal, Option 3, involves two divisions of 12 teams in Super League, with teams playing each other once before splitting into three groups of eight in mid-season and then playing each other home and away. The third option would culminate in a play-off series and a Grand Final or play-off final, with the final standings determining the makeup of the two 12-team divisions for the following season. This option would result in two teams being relegated from Super League at the end of next season. Wood emphasized the need for a balanced approach, stating, "I do believe that we need to create a pathway into Super League, but it is essential that we are mindful of the challenges that a straight reintroduction of promotion and relegation between part-time and full-time leagues would create." The RFL has sought the expertise of sports industry financial experts KPMG in drafting its proposals, ensuring that the changes are well-researched and sustainable. Wood acknowledged the progress made in recent years and the need to avoid destabilizing the sport. "While there is a recognition that the time is right for change, we fully understand the need to avoid destabilizing the excellent progress that has been made in recent years," he said. The proposed changes have sparked excitement and debate among fans and clubs, with many welcoming the potential for innovation and positive change. As the RFL continues to consult with stakeholders, it is clear that the future of rugby league is set to undergo a significant transformation. With the introduction of these new proposals, the sport is poised to enter a new era of competitiveness, excitement, and growth.

England wicketkeeper Jonny Bairstow led a stunning Yorkshire fightback on the opening day of their County Championship match against Durham at Chester-le-Street. Bairstow hit a magnificent 102 and shared an unbroken seventh-wicket stand of 138 with Tim Bresnan as the visitors closed on 329-6. Yorkshire's batsmen all reached double figures, but it was Bairstow and Bresnan (66 not out) who stole the show. Bairstow's 126-ball innings, which included 16 fours, turned the day on its head after Yorkshire had been struggling on 191-6. Bresnan's equally attacking knock, off just 85 balls, was just as crucial and took his Championship batting average past 65 for the season. Earlier, Durham had won the toss and decided to bowl first under overcast skies. Alex Lees and Will Rhodes played watchfully to see out the majority of the morning session with an opening stand of 56. However, when Rhodes was bowled by Jamie Harrison, who was making his return after 13 months out following a knee operation, wickets began to fall at regular intervals. Yorkshire looked in danger of being bowled out for less than 250 when Adil Rashid became the sixth wicket to fall. But Bairstow and Bresnan's attack on a tiring Durham bowling unit put their side firmly on top and in with a chance of gaining maximum batting points. Bairstow was delighted with his own innings, saying: "The way the openers applied themselves was fantastic. It was highly skilful. It set us up and you always know that one session here can change the game." He added: "I'm delighted with my own innings. I enjoy playing here - we had a lot of our own supporters here and the Durham fans gave me a good reception." Durham's Jamie Harrison, who took 2-62 on his return to first-team action, was happy to be back playing after a long injury layoff. "I'm just happy to be playing," he said. "I've had four years of struggling with injuries and it's been really tough." Yorkshire will be looking to build on their strong start and score as many runs as possible to put pressure on Durham. With Bairstow and Bresnan still at the crease, they will be confident of achieving their goal.

A court in Jhelum has rejected the bail application of Chaudhry Muhammad Shakeel, accused of murdering his ex-wife Samia Shahid. The 28-year-old beautician from Bradford died in July while visiting relatives in Pakistan. Her second husband, Syed Mukhtar Kazam, claims she was killed because her family disapproved of their marriage. Initially, it was reported that Ms Shahid had died of a heart attack, but a post-mortem examination revealed she had been strangled. Ms Shahid's father, Chaudhry Muhammad Shahid, was held as a suspected accessory but has been released on bail. Mr Kazam is seeking to have the case moved, citing threats to his life from Ms Shahid's family. The Lahore High Court is set to hear his application. The Jhelum court has indicated that a higher court may yet consider Mr Shakeel's bail request.

Sue Beatt has been elected as the new Chair of Bowls Scotland, following the retirement of Bill Knox. Beatt, a passionate bowler from Glasgow, has been a director of the organization for two and a half years. She has pledged to sustain the sport for future generations while supporting current members and clubs. Beatt brings a wealth of business experience to the role, as the owner and director of People Solutions (Scotland) Ltd and The Whisky Ambassador Limited. Outgoing chair Bill Knox welcomed Beatt's election, stating that she has the relevant skills for the position and will be a great asset to the board. Beatt expressed her pride at being elected and is committed to working tirelessly for the benefit of the sport. Her appointment has been warmly received by the bowling community.

The Outer Hebrides population has declined to 27,070, according to the latest figures released in June last year. This represents a decrease of 180 people since 2014. In an effort to address this issue, the local authority, Comhairle nan Eilean Siar, is set to develop a framework for a policy to tackle population decline at an upcoming seminar. Islands Minister Humza Yousaf has been invited to attend the event, which is scheduled to take place in the autumn. Councillor Angus Campbell emphasized the importance of attracting people to the islands, stating that positive net migration is crucial to counteracting the negative natural change that the Outer Hebrides is experiencing. The islands offer a good quality of life, but Councillor Campbell noted that providing infrastructure, including good and affordable housing, services, and a multi-agency approach, is essential to fulfilling people's aspirations. Depopulation has long been a concern for the Western Isles, with research suggesting that more women than men are leaving the islands. The Hebrides Migration Study found a long-term decline in population between 1901 and 2001, with the steepest decline in Harris, the Uists, and Barra. The comhairle is working to address this issue and develop a policy to reverse the decline and ensure a sustainable future for the Outer Hebrides.

Violence Erupts at Trump Rallies, Critics Accuse Him of Encouraging Hate The presidential campaign of Donald Trump has been marred by violent clashes between his supporters and protesters, with critics accusing him of encouraging hate and division. The latest incident occurred on Friday in Chicago, where a rally was forced to be called off due to violent clashes between supporters and protesters. The clashes, which took place at the University of Illinois at Chicago, resulted in several injuries and arrests. Democratic candidate Bernie Sanders has been vocal in his criticism of Trump, calling him a "pathological liar" and accusing him of conducting a cynical campaign of hate and fear. Sanders also urged Trump to tell his supporters that violence is not acceptable in the political process. Fellow Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton has also weighed in, accusing Trump of encouraging his supporters to beat up protesters and then offering to pay their legal costs. The controversy surrounding Trump's rallies has been building for some time. On Saturday, a man tried to rush the stage as Trump spoke in Ohio, but was stopped by Secret Service agents. Additionally, a Trump supporter was charged with assault after punching a protester at a rally in North Carolina, with Trump later saying that the supporter's actions were "appropriate". Trump's campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, has also been accused of assaulting a female journalist, Michelle Fields of Breitbart, although he denies the accusation. As the Republican primaries approach, with votes taking place in states including Florida and Ohio on Tuesday, Trump's rivals are seizing on the controversy surrounding his rallies. Marco Rubio, currently in third place, has said that a win in his home state of Florida is vital to prevent the Republican nomination from being "hijacked" by Trump. With the campaign season heating up, it remains to be seen how the controversy surrounding Trump's rallies will impact his chances of securing the nomination. Despite the criticism, Trump has denied using hate speech or playing any part in fostering division. However, his rivals and critics argue that his rhetoric and actions have created a toxic atmosphere that encourages violence and intolerance. As the presidential campaign continues, it is clear that the issue of violence at Trump rallies will remain a contentious and divisive issue. With tensions running high, it remains to be seen how the situation will unfold in the coming days and weeks.

Dennis Kimetto made history yesterday by becoming the first man to run a marathon in under two hours and three minutes. The 30-year-old Kenyan achieved this incredible feat at the Berlin Marathon, finishing with a time of 2:02:57. Kimetto shook off fellow Kenyan Emmanuel Mutai with just under three miles remaining, securing his victory and breaking the previous world record. Mutai, who finished second with a time of 2:03:13, also broke the previous record set by Wilson Kipsang last year. Kimetto had promised to attack the record if conditions allowed, and the perfect weather in Berlin enabled him to keep his promise. The lead group stayed together throughout the race, with Kimetto sprinting to victory in the final stretch. Mutai believes that a two-hour marathon is possible, saying "times are coming down and down. So if not today, then tomorrow." Kimetto's win marks a significant milestone in long-distance running, and his achievement is likely to inspire other athletes to push the boundaries of human endurance. In other results, Scott Overall finished 14th in the men's race with a time of 2:13:00, while Britain's Shelly Woods won the women's wheelchair race.

England's women's team has risen to second in the world rankings. They finished third at the World Cup last year. The team recently came third at the SheBelieves Cup, and will host Belgium on April 8 in Euro 2017 qualifiers, having won their first two games. USA remains top of the rankings, with Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland also placing.

Rosneft, Russia's largest oil producer, has reported a significant decline in net income for the third quarter, with profits reaching 26bn roubles ($400.7m; £318m). This figure is substantially lower than expected, reflecting the challenging environment in the commodity markets. The company's chief executive, Igor Sechin, cited the difficulties in the sector, which have been exacerbated by low crude prices. The news comes as the Russian government, which owns approximately three-quarters of Rosneft, prepares to sell a 20% stake in the company as part of a privatisation programme. The sale is expected to raise £9bn for the cash-strapped government, which has been impacted by the decline in commodity prices. UK oil giant BP, which owns 20% of Rosneft, has also been affected by the sector's struggles, recently reporting a near-halving of its third-quarter profits. The decline in oil prices, which peaked at $115 a barrel in 2014, has had a significant impact on the industry, with many major oil companies reporting lower profits. Despite a recent surge in prices following Opec's agreement to limit production, doubts over the cartel's ability to deliver cuts have seen prices slip, with Brent crude currently trading at $45.77 a barrel. The challenging market conditions are likely to continue, with Rosneft and other oil producers facing ongoing uncertainty.

The pressure to succeed in exams is taking a toll on an increasing number of young people, according to a leading children's charity. Data from ChildLine, a helpline run by the NSPCC, reveals that the charity conducted 3,077 counselling sessions about exam-related stress over the past year, a 9% increase on the previous year. The helpline also reported a significant rise in the number of counselling sessions about exam results, with 1,127 sessions taking place, a 20% increase on 2014/15. The charity says that the pressure to do well is being felt by a growing number of young people across the country, with many struggling to cope with the stress and anxiety of exams. One 15-year-old boy who contacted ChildLine said: "All I can think about is exams and I just can't deal with it anymore. I'm revising all night because I'm so worried I'll fail, and I feel so tired all the time." A 17-year-old girl also admitted: "I feel so overwhelmed at the moment, it's impossible to concentrate on revising. I'm worried that I won't get the grade I'm predicted, and I don't know where to start." NSPCC chief executive Peter Wanless said: "The exam period can be a very stressful and anxious time for young people. We hear from lots of young people each year who are anxious, worried, or panicking about their exams and revision." To help young people cope with exam stress, ChildLine has launched a new video offering tips and advice, including taking regular breaks from revising, exercising, getting a good night's sleep, and thinking positively. The charity is also advising parents and carers to avoid placing unnecessary pressure on children to achieve certain grades, and to help them revise by giving them time and space to do so. Young people can call ChildLine free on 0800 11 11 for confidential advice and support. As the exam season approaches, the charity is urging young people to reach out for help if they're feeling overwhelmed, and reminding them that they're not alone in their concerns.

The BBC's Spotlight programme has won a prestigious Royal Television Society Journalism Award. The award recognizes the team's investigative journalism in exposing secret dealings behind Northern Ireland's biggest property deal in 2014, involving Nama. Secret recordings uncovered by reporter Mandy McAuley revealed hidden transactions. The programme team received the RTS Nations and Regions Current Affairs award in London. BBC Northern Ireland's Director, Peter Johnston, praised the team's dedication to producing high-quality journalism, continuing Spotlight's tradition of award-winning programmes. The award acknowledges the team's hard-hitting investigative work.

Bradford City is set to sign Blackpool's club captain, Colin Doyle. The 31-year-old goalkeeper will undergo a medical early next week. Doyle was a standout performer in League One last season despite Blackpool's relegation. He will join Nicky Law and Nathaniel Knight-Percival as summer recruits. With Ben Williams' departure to Bury, Doyle is likely to become the Bantams' number one. His release clause allowed him to explore options after Blackpool's relegation. The move is expected to be completed soon, ahead of Bradford's season opener against Port Vale on August 6.

The pound experienced a significant surge after a recent survey revealed a strong rebound in manufacturing activity for August. It rose 1% to $1.327 and nearly 1% against the euro at €1.187. The Purchasing Managers' Index jumped to a 10-month high, attributed to the pound's post-Brexit weakness boosting exports. However, this also increased costs for companies. On the stock market, housebuilders saw gains, with Berkeley Group, Taylor Wimpey, and Persimmon rising. In contrast, Vodafone, GlaxoSmithKline, and Shell saw declines of 2-3%. The pound's rebound is a positive sign for the UK's economic recovery.

Guinea is set to hold its presidential election, with seven candidates challenging incumbent President Alpha Conde. Conde's main opponent, Cellou Dalein Diallo, has urged supporters to vote despite the court rejecting his plea for a delay. The election follows a tumultuous period marked by an Ebola outbreak and a slump in bauxite prices. Opposition parties had sought a postponement due to alleged electoral roll anomalies, but the election commission refused. Pre-election violence has claimed at least three lives. Conde is favored to win, but a second round of voting is likely. The outcome will determine the country's future after a transition from military to civilian rule in 2010.

Concerns have been raised over the rising use of synthetic drugs within HMP Birmingham, a privately-run prison, which is reportedly leading to violent outbursts and displays of extreme strength among inmates. According to a recent report by the Independent Monitoring Board, covering the period from July 2015 to June this year, the prison continues to show signs of improvement, but the issue of drugs smuggling and staff shortages remains a pressing concern. The report highlighted the impressive response and support provided by prison staff to inmates, but noted that they regularly face challenges posed by the high rate of sickness and the presence of smuggled drugs. Prison officers at the category B jail have expressed concerns over how to deal with being attacked by inmates under the influence of synthetic drugs, also known as "legal highs". The use of these substances has been linked to at least 19 prisoner deaths between 2012 and 2014, according to the Prisons and Probations Ombudsman. Rodger Lawrence, chairman of the monitoring board, emphasized the urgent need for a solution to the problem of new psychoactive substances (NPS), which continue to impact all aspects of prison life. He also highlighted staff shortages as a major issue affecting morale, wellbeing, and efficiency. In response, Pete Small, G4S director for HMP Birmingham, acknowledged the challenge of tackling the use of NPS and recognized the work being done by his team in collaboration with the police to catch those bringing drugs into the prison. The prison has vowed to work "relentlessly" to stop the influx of drugs and address the concerns of its staff.

Ian Hutchinson Dominates 600cc Class with Seventh Win Yorkshire rider Ian Hutchinson led from start to finish to claim his seventh victory in the 600cc class, setting the fastest lap at 128.26mph. Hutchinson, riding for Team Traction Control, built a 10-second lead over his nearest rival, Michael Dunlop, on the opening lap and maintained a steady pace throughout the race. By the end, he had a 14.3-second advantage over Dunlop, who was later disqualified due to a technical infringement. Dunlop's disqualification moved Dean Harrison up to second place, with James Hillier taking the final podium position. Hutchinson's win was impressive, beating the previous race record by 15.2 seconds. He joins Michael Dunlop as the fourth most successful solo rider in the history of the event. Hutchinson attributed his success to his connection with the bike, saying, "I seem to have a real connection with this bike and I knew I had to push really hard in the first two sectors." He also acknowledged the challenges posed by backmarkers, stating, "I lost a few seconds here and there after I ran into some backmarkers, but I knew it would be the same for Michael." The race saw several high-profile retirements, including Peter Hickman and Bruce Anstey. Manxman Conor Cummins and 23-times winner John McGuinness finished fourth and fifth, respectively, with Lee Johnston and William Dunlop taking sixth and seventh positions. The organisers noted that Dunlop's disqualification was due to a technical infringement, but they do not believe it was a deliberate attempt to gain an unfair advantage.

Denbighshire Council Moves Forward with North Wales Hospital Revitalization Plans The Prince's Regeneration Trust has unveiled proposals for the long-abandoned North Wales Hospital in Denbigh, bringing new hope to the town. Earlier this year, Denbighshire council successfully obtained a compulsory purchase order for the site, citing concerns over the Grade II-listed building's deteriorating state. Although Freemont (Denbigh) Ltd, the current owner, is expected to retain ownership until early 2017, the council plans to transfer the site to the North Wales Buildings Preservation Trust once the ownership changes hands. The trust, a not-for-profit organization, aims to preserve the historic buildings through "enabling development" plans, which involve generating funds by selling new properties on the site. This approach will allow the trust to balance the need for preservation with the need for financial sustainability. The former Victorian asylum has been vacant since its closure in 1996, and despite Freemont's purchase of the site in 2003, no redevelopment work has taken place. Denbighshire council has already invested £900,000 in emergency repairs to protect the building from further deterioration. The latest proposals, approved by the council's planning committee, have been met with enthusiasm from local councillor Colin Hughes, who believes the development will bring significant benefits to the town, including an increase in residents and visitors. "The importance of this development to the future of Denbigh is immeasurable," he stated, emphasizing the need to revitalize the site after 21 years of neglect. Despite opposition from Freemont, the council remains committed to moving forward with the plans, marking a new chapter in the hospital's history.

Warrington Wolves dominated St Helens 28-6 at Langtree Park, with Chris Sandow playing a key role in the victory. Sandow's dummy set up Ben Currie for the opening try, before the Australian half-back touched down himself. Ryan Atkins also scored on his 300th career outing, helping Wolves to a 16-0 lead at half-time. The visitors continued their impressive play in the second half, with Stefan Ratchford and Rhys Evans adding to the score. St Helens' only points came from full-back Jonny Lomax. The loss marks six defeats in eight games for Keiron Cunningham's side, leaving them six points off the top four with six games until the Super 8s. The match was marred by a long stoppage in play when Jordan Turner received treatment and was carried off on a stretcher. Warrington will look to build on their momentum when they host leaders Hull on June 10. Meanwhile, St Helens will aim to bounce back from their disappointing performance and close the gap on the top four. Referee James Child oversaw the match, which saw Warrington assert their dominance over their rivals.

Aberdeen City and Aberdeenshire councils have taken a significant step towards securing £2.9 billion in funding by submitting a "statement of intent" to the UK and Scottish governments. The statement outlines the benefits that the funding would bring to the city and surrounding area, with a focus on improving infrastructure, boosting the economy, and supporting innovative technologies. At the top of the councils' list are key projects such as providing more affordable homes, enhancing rail connectivity, and improving links to Aberdeen's harbour and airport. Additionally, research into renewable and hydrogen technologies, as well as international trade, are also highlighted as priorities. According to Jenny Laing, leader of Aberdeen City Council, the statement of intent provides a solid foundation for a City Region Deal that would not only benefit the north east but also the rest of Scotland and the UK. Laing emphasized the need to work towards a deal that maximizes the benefits of coordinated investment in the Aberdeen city region. Co-leader of Aberdeenshire Council, Martin Kitts-Hayes, added that the councils will continue to collaborate with the two governments to deliver a City Region Deal that contributes to the economic vision for the north east of Scotland. Kitts-Hayes noted that the region plays a significant role in contributing to the financial wellbeing of Scotland, the UK, and globally, and that greater collaboration across industry and government can help protect the competitiveness of the oil and gas industry and support future growth. A full bid submission is expected to be drawn up by the end of the year.

Tragedy Strikes Construction Site in High Blantyre A 45-year-old man has lost his life in a fatal incident at a construction site in High Blantyre. Emergency services were called to the Avant Homes site near Shott Farm on Hamilton Road at approximately 09:45. Paramedics treated the seriously injured man, but unfortunately, he died at the scene. The company has launched an investigation into the incident and suspended all work at the site. The man's identity has not been formally released. Police Scotland has confirmed that the death is not being treated as suspicious at this time, and a post-mortem examination will be conducted to determine the cause of death. The Health and Safety Executive has been informed, and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal. Avant Homes has expressed its condolences to the man's family and loved ones, and is cooperating fully with the emergency services to assist in the investigation.

A takeaway in Edinburgh was targeted by a pair of would-be thieves on Friday night. At 23:00, a man and woman entered the Maysum takeaway on Craigentinny Road, with the man demanding money from staff. After being refused, the pair fled the scene, heading east down Craigentinny Road. Police are investigating and reviewing CCTV footage. The suspects are described as a man in his 20s, 5ft 7in tall, wearing a cream jacket, and a woman, 5ft 9in tall, in a black hooded jacket and pink hat. Police are appealing for witnesses to come forward.

Undefeated WBA world super bantamweight champion Guillermo Rigondeaux is set to make his UK debut as he defends his title against Liverpool's Jazza Dickens. The 35-year-old Cuban boxer is widely regarded as one of the world's top pound-for-pound boxers, boasting an impressive record of 16 wins in as many professional bouts.
