Rigondeaux's amateur career was equally impressive, with 475 victories in 487 contests, including gold medals at the 2000 Sydney Olympics and 2004 Athens Olympics. The highly skilled boxer will co-headline a bill featuring WBO world lightweight champion Terry Flanagan's title defense against Mzonke Fana. British and Commonwealth super welterweight champion Liam Williams will also be in action, defending his titles against Gary Corcoran in front of his hometown fans in Wales. Rigondeaux's coach, Pedro Diaz, has high praise for his fighter, calling him "the most complete" boxer in the world. With his unique ability to only fight boxers with winning records, Rigondeaux is poised to put on a show in his UK debut. Fans are eagerly anticipating the event, which promises to be an exciting night of boxing.

CCTV footage of a heist outside Debenhams has been released. A man stole a cashbox from a security van on Monday at 14:15 GMT. Police seek witnesses and are tracing a silver van abandoned in Russell Street. No weapons were used and no one was injured in the incident.

Ikea to Recall 1.7 Million Drawers in China Over Safety Concerns China's regulator has announced that Ikea will recall 1.7 million drawers due to safety concerns. The decision comes after six children in North America were crushed to death when the chests toppled on them. The recall affects drawers made between 1999 and 2016. Last month, Ikea recalled 36 million dressers in the US and Canada, and has since stopped selling the drawers. Initially, the company refused to extend the recall to China, the UK, or the EU, citing that the products met local industry standards. However, following an online backlash in China and a meeting with the country's safety watchdog, Ikea has agreed to the recall. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission found that the Malm drawers can topple over and crush children if not anchored to the wall with screws. Ikea has warned customers to ensure the drawers are properly fixed to walls and has launched an awareness campaign. The company has also offered free home installation and an optional refund to customers in China. Ikea has pledged to "serve as a model" in responding to the challenge of furniture safety. The recall highlights the importance of ensuring household safety and the need for companies to prioritize consumer well-being.

A former paramedic, Andrew Davies, has been found guilty of misconduct by a health profession panel for failing to assist a man who later died of a heart attack. The incident occurred in the car park of Walsall Manor Hospital in June 2012, where 47-year-old Carl Cope was in need of medical attention. Despite the presence of four clinical staff members, including Davies, no aid was provided to Mr. Cope. The Health and Care Professions Council panel heard that Davies had been previously dismissed by his employer, West Midlands Ambulance Service, for gross misconduct. The panel chair, Naseem Malik, stated that Davies' inaction was "conduct falling far below that expected by the public, his profession, and fellow practitioners." Due to a lack of insight into his mistakes, the panel deemed it likely that Davies could repeat such misconduct in the future. As a result, Davies was struck off the HCPC Register, effectively ending his career as a paramedic. This ruling comes after another paramedic, Matthew Geary, received an eight-month suspended jail term for his role in failing to provide adequate treatment to Mr. Cope. The case highlights the importance of medical professionals providing timely and adequate care to those in need, and the severe consequences that can result from failing to do so.

Celebrities React to Dallas Shootings, Call for Peace and an End to Violence The recent shootings in Dallas, which left five police officers dead and several others injured, have sparked an outpouring of reactions from celebrities across the United States. The shootings occurred during a protest against the use of lethal force by police against African Americans, and have reignited a national debate about racism and violence. John Legend, who won an Oscar for his song "Glory" from the film Selma, was among the first to speak out against the violence. "Being against cops killing is not equal to being for killing cops. We need peace in our streets," he tweeted. Legend also condemned the shootings, calling them "horrific" and "morally reprehensible." Other celebrities, including Beyonce and Jay-Z, have also reacted to the shootings. Beyonce held a minute's silence at her concert in Glasgow on Thursday night for the two black men, Alton Sterling and Philando Castile, who were killed by police earlier in the week. She also put their names on a big screen and pleaded for an end to the "war on minorities" in the US. Jay-Z released a new song, "Spiritual," on his streaming service Tidal, and released a statement saying that he was "saddened and disappointed" by the events in the US. "I'm saddened and disappointed in THIS America - we should be further along. WE ARE NOT," he said. He also sent blessings to the families of those who "lost loved ones to police brutality." Michael Moore, who directed the documentary "Bowling for Columbine," tweeted that President Obama's presence was needed to address the crisis. "We need our President to speak to the nation, to address the racism and the violence that is tearing our country apart," he said. Oscar-winning actress Patricia Arquette added her voice to the chorus of condemnation, saying "Just heard about shootings in Dallas Please everyone stop killing each other- no more guns. No more violence. No more murder. Horrible." Other celebrities, including Kevin Hart, Justin Timberlake, and Katy Perry, have also spoken out against the violence. Hart tweeted "Peace is the message..... An eye for an eye leaves everybody blind," while Timberlake said "This IS systemic. We MUST DO BETTER. My heart goes out to the families of #AltonSterling and #PhilandoCastile May they both Rest In Peace." Katy Perry linked to a video of Alton Sterling being shot, saying "You can't just go on with your day, you must watch this & we must face this continual outrageousness #ALTONSTERLING." Canadian rapper Drake also spoke out, saying that it was "impossible to ignore" the strained relationship between black and brown communities and law enforcement. The shootings in Dallas have sparked a national conversation about racism and violence, and it is clear that many celebrities are committed to using their platforms to call for peace and an end to violence. As Cynthia Erivo, who won a Tony for her portrayal of Celie in Broadway's The Color Purple, tweeted, "Dear Lord I ask you to take this world in your arms and brush it with love and peace and understanding. It's gone too far."

Edinburgh Rugby Team Secures Crucial Win Against Zebre, Moves into Fifth Place In a thrilling match at Murrayfield, Edinburgh Rugby Team managed to secure a crucial win against Zebre, moving into fifth place in the league standings. The team's victory was largely due to a strong second-half performance, which saw them score 24 unanswered points against their Italian opponents. The first half of the game was a dismal affair, with Edinburgh managing to score only three points from the boot of Jason Tovey. The team's performance was marred by errors, with fumbles, stray passes, and petty squabbles dominating the opening 40 minutes. Zebre's Kelly Haimona also missed a penalty attempt, and the visitors were denied a try when Oliviero Fabiani's route was cleared by an obstruction. However, the introduction of Sam Hidalgo-Clyne in the second half brought a much-needed spark to the game. The replacement scrum-half threaded a grubber through for Damien Hoyland to run onto, and the winger was able to kick it on and win the race for the line. This try was the catalyst for Edinburgh's dominance in the second half, with Hoyland scoring again soon after. Tovey converted both of Hoyland's tries and also made it three from three when his clever break was supported well by Stuart McInally, with the replacement hooker offloading for Hidalgo-Clyne to waltz through unchallenged. The home team's chances of securing a try bonus point seemed to have slipped away when a late penalty was kicked into touch, only for Zebre to rob the line-out. However, an offside infringement allowed Edinburgh to keep the ball alive, and a patient passing move was finished off by Ben Toolis. Edinburgh's win moves them ahead of Glasgow and Munster into fifth place, with those teams in action on Saturday. If Alan Solomons' side is to hang on to a top-six spot and earn a Champions Cup place, they will need to turn in more performances like their second-half showing at Murrayfield. The team's error-strewn opening 40 minutes was a concern, but their ability to turn the game around in the second half will give them confidence going into their next match. The final score was 24-0 in favor of Edinburgh, with Tovey's conversions and penalties proving crucial in the team's victory. Hidalgo-Clyne's introduction was also a key factor, bringing a much-needed zip to the game and setting up two of Edinburgh's tries. The team will look to build on this performance in their next match, as they aim to secure a top-six spot and a place in the Champions Cup. In terms of team selection, Edinburgh started with a strong lineup, featuring the likes of Jason Tovey, Damien Hoyland, and WP Nel. The team's replacements, including Sam Hidalgo-Clyne and Stuart McInally, also made a significant impact on the game. Zebre, on the other hand, struggled to cope with Edinburgh's pressure in the second half, and their ill-discipline ultimately cost them the game. Referee Leighton Hodges had a busy game, with several penalties and infringements to contend with. However, his decisions ultimately had little impact on the outcome of the match, as Edinburgh's superior performance in the second half secured them the win. Overall, it was a crucial victory for Edinburgh, and one that will give them confidence going into their next match.

The Metropolitan Police's counter-terrorism command is seeking to recruit former jihadists who have abandoned radicalism to help combat terrorist propaganda. According to Commander Richard Walton, these individuals can serve as "powerful voices" in challenging the ideology of militant groups such as Islamic State. The Met is "desperate" to find more former extremists to aid in their efforts, with only a few currently working with them. In the past year, the Met's counter-terrorism command has seen a significant increase in arrests, with 225 people detained on suspicion of terrorism-related offences - a 32% rise from the previous year. Notably, 29 of those arrested were women or girls, and 17 were under the age of 20. The Met has also successfully rescued several families, including young children, who were attempting to travel to Syria from Turkey. Commander Walton emphasized the importance of engaging with terrorists, even those in prison, in an effort to turn them away from extremism. He noted that some individuals convicted of terrorist offences may not have received lengthy sentences and will eventually be released, presenting an opportunity for the Met to work with them. The goal is to develop "counter-narratives" to challenge Islamic State's ideology, with the help of former extremists. With at least 700 people from the UK having travelled to support or fight for jihadist organisations in Syria and Iraq, the Met's efforts to counter terrorist propaganda are more crucial than ever.

A house in Birmingham's Handsworth Wood area was evacuated after a marijuana grow operation sparked an electrical fire. Fire crews responded to the incident on Hamstead Hall Avenue at 06:50 GMT on Sunday. They found a severely overloaded fuse box and a large stash of marijuana. The scene was likened to a Cheech and Chong movie set. Authorities warned that the setup posed a huge threat to public safety, putting neighbors at risk of damage or death due to the hazardous conditions. The West Midlands Police Cannabis Disposal Team is investigating.

A fatal collision occurred on the Shrivenham Bypass near Swindon, killing four people in their 20s from Northampton. The occupants of the other vehicle, including a three-year-old, were injured and hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Thames Valley Police are investigating and urge witnesses to come forward.

Edinburgh Rugby Club is facing an injury crisis ahead of their upcoming Pro12 match against Connacht in Galway on Friday. Stand-off Duncan Weir, 25, underwent surgery on Sunday after a clash of heads with CJ Stander and will be out of action for some time. Fellow stand-off Jason Tovey has made a timely return to training from a wrist injury, but inside centre Phil Burleigh, who can also play at fly-half, is still recovering from a shoulder injury. The club's prop situation is also a concern, with Kevin Bryce awaiting the results of a scan on an elbow injury he suffered in the first scrum against Munster. Simon Berghan is still several weeks away from returning from a foot injury, leaving Nick Beavon as the only back-up to WP Nel. Head coach Alan Solomons is keen to bring in extra tight-head cover to alleviate the pressure. In the meantime, 19-year-old Blair Kinghorn, who replaced Weir in Limerick, could feature at 10 against Connacht. The team has also been dealt a blow with the loss of third-choice hooker George Turner, who sustained an ankle injury playing for Heriot's in the BT Premiership. However, back-row Nasi Manu has returned to training after recovering from a rib injury. The club is also awaiting the outcome of a citing for lock Fraser McKenzie, who was involved in a shoulder charge incident against Munster. A decision is expected on Wednesday. Loose-head prop Alasdair Dickinson is on track to return to training in late October, which will be a welcome boost ahead of Scotland's autumn Tests. With several key players out injured, Edinburgh will be looking to dig deep and find a way to overcome Connacht on Friday.

A 28-year-old man is in critical condition after being assaulted by two men in Union Street. The incident occurred at approximately 05:30, between St Nicholas Street and Broad Street. The victim was taken to the Royal Infirmary with serious injuries. Police are seeking information about the attackers, describing one as 6ft tall with dark hair, wearing a grey T-shirt and dark jeans. The second man is described as 5ft 9in tall with short grey hair, wearing a brown bomber-style jacket and dark blue jeans. Detective Inspector Norman Stevenson is urging witnesses to come forward, appealing for anyone who saw the attack to contact the police and provide information about what they saw.

Energy Giants Consider Reward Programs for Loyal Customers In a bid to address the issue of millions of customers paying too much for energy, two of the UK's major energy suppliers, Npower and EDF Energy, are considering introducing reward programs for their loyal customers. The move comes after pressure from Business Secretary Greg Clark, who suggested that customers who have been on standard variable tariffs for a long time should be rewarded for their loyalty. Npower's managing director of domestic markets, Simon Stacey, revealed that the company is actively exploring the idea of offering rewards to its standard customers, such as a free boiler service. "We want to try and reward customers in a way they wouldn't expect," he told the Business and Energy Committee. EDF Energy's residential sales director, Dan Hopcroft, also confirmed that his company is looking at introducing a loyalty proposition. The move is aimed at the estimated 10 million customers who have been on expensive standard tariffs for at least three years. According to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), 56% of consumers have never switched supplier or are unsure if they have. The CMA has been pushing for reforms in the energy market to encourage more customers to switch to cheaper deals. In a separate development, energy regulator Ofgem has announced plans to conduct trials to test new ways of persuading reluctant customers to switch suppliers. The trials, which are expected to start later this year, will involve tens of thousands of consumers and will explore different approaches, such as renaming standard tariffs to "emergency tariff" or "out-of-contract tariff". Suppliers will also be asked to inform customers about cheaper deals available from rival suppliers. The trials are part of a broader effort to increase transparency and competition in the energy market. Currently, suppliers are only required to show their own cheapest tariff on bills, but not the tariffs of their competitors. By introducing reward programs and testing new approaches to encourage switching, energy suppliers are hoping to address the issue of loyal customers paying too much for their energy.

Fulham Secures Crucial Victory Over Cardiff, Moves 10 Points Clear of Relegation Zone In a thrilling match at Craven Cottage, Fulham secured a vital 2-1 victory over Cardiff City, thanks to a late winner from Emerson Hyndman in stoppage time. The win moves Fulham 10 points clear of the relegation zone, while Cardiff remains five points adrift of the Championship play-off places with only five games remaining. The match got off to a lively start, with both sides creating scoring opportunities in the first half. Aron Gunnarsson's header was saved by Marcus Bettinelli, while Bruno Ecuele Manga headed over from Peter Whittingham's corner. At the other end, David Marshall parried a free-kick from former Cardiff striker Ross McCormack. Cardiff took the lead in the 25th minute when Scott Malone combined with Gunnarsson down the left, and the Icelandic midfielder's cross was met by Lex Immers, who headed home his fifth goal of the season. However, Fulham levelled the score in the opening minute of the second half, catching Cardiff's defence off guard. Moussa Dembele set up former England midfielder Scott Parker, who fired home from a tight angle to score his first goal of the season. The second half saw Fulham gain momentum, with Dembele and McCormack creating scoring opportunities. Gunnarsson and Sean Morrison squandered chances for Cardiff, who struggled to replicate their first-half performance. As the match drew to a close, Fulham's pressure finally paid off when Hyndman struck from close range following a scramble at a corner in stoppage time. Fulham boss Slavisa Jokanovic expressed his delight at the win, saying, "Today is Emerson Hyndman's birthday, and it's a great present for himself and for all of us in the last moment of the game. He's probably one of the more talented players, and I am little bit disappointed with myself that I haven't found more minutes for him this season." Jokanovic also acknowledged that while the win was crucial, there is still work to be done to ensure safety. "We've had one perfect week where we've won three games, but in front of us is five games more. Mathematically, we are 10 points ahead, but we need five points more to be 100 per cent sure." Cardiff City manager Russell Slade was left to ponder what might have been, saying, "We will keep going to the end. It's a setback, and we would have taken a precious point. We've given ourselves a mountain to climb, but there's still time to go." Slade acknowledged that a draw would have been a fair result but was frustrated that his side failed to defend a corner, which led to Hyndman's winner. Despite the setback, Slade remains optimistic, saying, "We've had some real high-level performances recently, and where we want to be is certainly not impossible. We'll keep going, and we've got a home game next week, and all we can control is what's in front of us." The win is a significant boost for Fulham, who have now won three consecutive games. As they look to secure their Championship status, they will be eager to build on this momentum in their remaining five games. For Cardiff, the task ahead is daunting, but Slade's side will be determined to bridge the gap and make a late push for the play-offs.

A disturbing incident occurred on the Britwell estate in Slough, where two young boys, aged six and 10, were abducted from a property on Hemming Way. The offenders, wearing dark clothing and with their faces covered, entered the property between 7:00 and 7:30 GMT and ordered the boys into a white van parked outside. The vehicle travelled to Upper Lees Road, where the boys managed to escape and run back to Hemming Way, fortunately uninjured. Police are currently investigating the motive behind the abduction, with Detective Inspector Nicola Hurdley stating that the incident is "understandably upsetting" for the victims and their relatives. The suspects' van is believed to be a Ford Transit, and officers are appealing for witnesses to come forward with any information. Police are providing support to the affected families as they work to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Russia's central bank has lowered its one-week minimum auction repo rate by 1 percentage point. This decision comes as inflation eased to 15.8% in May, down from 16.9% in March. The bank expressed concern over the economy's "considerable" cooling, predicting a 3.2% contraction in gross domestic product this year. The rate cut was in line with analyst expectations, resulting in little change to the Russian rouble. Western sanctions and falling global oil prices continue to squeeze Russia's economy, which had led to an emergency interest rate hike to 17% last December to stabilize the rouble.

High Court Ruling Paves Way for Resumption of Troubles-Related Inquests A long-awaited ruling at the High Court in Belfast has brought an end to a legal challenge by relatives of victims of the Troubles, clearing the way for the resumption of inquests into their loved ones' deaths. The inquests, which were ordered by Attorney General John Larkin, were halted last November by senior coroner John Leckey, who questioned whether he had exceeded his powers in authorizing the hearings. The move sparked outrage among the families, who claimed that the decision was unlawful and procedurally unfair. Lawyers for the families launched a judicial review challenge, which was due to be heard next week. However, the challenge has now been formally ended, paving the way for the inquests to resume. The inquests will examine the deaths of several individuals, including 11-year-old Francis Rowntree, who was killed by a rubber bullet fired by a soldier in 1972, and Gerard Slane, a 27-year-old father of three who was shot dead by the Ulster Defence Association in 1988. The killings of Gerard Casey, Danny Doherty, William Fleming, and Francis Bradley will also be scrutinized. Outside the court, solicitor Paul Pierce, representing Mr. Slane's widow Teresa, welcomed the decision to lift the suspension on the inquests. "We are pleased that the coroner has lifted the suspension, and we look forward to the inquests proceeding," he said. John Teggart, whose father was killed in the 1970s in Ballymurphy, also spoke out, saying that questions need to be answered about the circumstances surrounding the deaths. The resumption of the inquests is a significant development in the ongoing quest for truth and justice by the families of those who died during the Troubles. The hearings are expected to shed new light on the circumstances surrounding the deaths and may provide long-awaited closure for the families. With the legal challenge now at an end, the families can finally begin to get the answers they have been seeking for so long.

As the UK general election heats up, Labour MPs from the left-wing faction are considering challenging the party's first Queen's Speech, potentially joining forces with the Scottish National Party to oppose cuts. This revelation comes after an interview with John McDonnell, leader of the Socialist Campaign Group, published in the New Statesman. The move could signal a significant rift within the party and potentially jeopardize the passage of key legislation. Meanwhile, Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg is reportedly preparing to demand a "steep price" from the Conservatives in exchange for supporting a referendum on British membership of the EU in the event of a hung parliament. The Financial Times reports that Clegg is seeking to extract significant concessions from the Tories, potentially paving the way for a power-sharing deal. On the campaign trail, Conservative leader David Cameron has come under fire for his claims that families will face a £3,000 tax rise if Labour is elected. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has disputed the claim, undermining Cameron's argument. The Guardian leads with the story, highlighting the ongoing debate over the economy and taxation. In other news, Ed Miliband's credibility on economic issues has taken a hit after business leaders expressed concerns over the use of their quotes in a Labour party advert. The Telegraph reports that the controversy has raised questions about the party's judgment and ability to manage the economy. As the election approaches, minor party candidates are also making their voices heard. Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood has launched her party's manifesto, criticizing the main parties for offering "nothing more than further swingeing cuts" to public services. SNP leader Nicola Sturgeon has also reiterated her opposition to the renewal of Trident, stating that it is a "red line" for her party. With the election just around the corner, the battle for votes is intensifying, and all parties are pulling out the stops to win over undecided voters.

The notorious online drugs marketplace, Silk Road, has been shut down following a lengthy investigation by the National Cyber Crime Unit (NCCU). The interim head of the NCCU, Andy Archibald, revealed that officers were able to identify individuals using the site, but warned that new methods are needed to keep up with the evolving threat of online crime. The success of the operation may not be easily replicated, according to Archibald, as online anonymity services like Tor continually update and resecure themselves. The NCCU will need to adapt and find new ways to infiltrate and disrupt criminal forums. Archibald's comments came as the NCCU announced its first conviction, with 27-year-old Olukunle Babatunde receiving a five year and six month prison sentence for using "phishing" scams to attempt to defraud banks and financial institutions. The conviction marks a significant milestone for the NCCU as it continues to tackle online crime.

Indian Cricketer Ravindra Jadeja Under Investigation for Breaking Safari Rules Indian cricketer Ravindra Jadeja is under investigation for allegedly breaking rules at the Gir National Park and Sanctuary in Gujarat. Photos posted on his Instagram account appear to show him and his wife, Reeva, on foot during a safari, pointing to a pride of lions and taking a photo with one in the background. However, officials at the park stated that it is against the rules for visitors to leave their vehicles, and a penalty may be imposed. The Gir National Park is the only home of the Asiatic lion in the wild, and the animals are listed as endangered. Just days before Jadeja's visit, forestry officials had warned of the dangers of taking selfies with lions. Chief Forest Conservator AP Singh has ordered a probe into the matter, which will consider what penalty to impose on the couple. Jadeja, 27, was part of India's team for the recent World T20 tournament. The incident has sparked concern over the safety and well-being of both the visitors and the animals at the park.

Serge Gnabry has completed a transfer to Werder Bremen, leaving Arsenal after five years. The 21-year-old was joint top scorer at the Olympic Games with six goals. Gnabry made 18 appearances for Arsenal, scoring once, before making the move. Initially, reports suggested a transfer to Bayern Munich with a subsequent loan to Bremen, but the club's sporting director denied any other club's involvement. Gnabry expressed confidence in his new team, citing positive comments from Per Mertesacker and Mesut Ozil. He also praised his talks with management, which led to his decision to join Bremen. Gnabry aims for a successful season, targeting the top half of the table.

Maldives in Crisis: Former President Claims Coup, Successor Denies Allegations The island nation of Maldives is reeling from a deepening political crisis, with former President Mohamed Nasheed claiming he was forced to resign in a coup orchestrated by his successor, President Mohammed Waheed Hassan. In a dramatic turn of events, Nasheed told the AFP news agency that he was coerced into stepping down by armed police and army officers, who threatened to use violence if he refused. According to Nasheed, he was summoned to military headquarters on Tuesday, where he found a group of 18 middle-ranking police and army officers in control. "They told me if I didn't resign, they would resort to using arms," he said, describing the encounter as a thinly veiled threat. Fearing for the safety of his government officials, Nasheed reluctantly agreed to step down. However, President Hassan has categorically denied any involvement in a coup, stating that Nasheed's resignation was a "generous decision" that helped prevent bloodshed. Hassan, who served as Nasheed's vice president before taking over the presidency, criticized his predecessor for wrongfully arresting a top judge, Abdulla Mohamed, last month. The arrest of Judge Mohamed sparked widespread protests, with many calling for Nasheed's resignation. The judge, who was accused of being loyal to the opposition, was released soon after Hassan took power. Hassan has promised to respect the rule of law, uphold the constitution, and protect Nasheed from retribution, while also vowing not to interfere with any police or court action against his predecessor. As the political crisis deepens, concerns are growing for the safety of Nasheed and other senior members of his government. Nasheed's supporters fear that he may face retribution, and there are reports of an investigation into the discovery of bottles of alcohol being removed from outside his residence. Consuming alcohol outside tourist resorts is a crime in the Muslim nation. In an effort to stabilize the country, President Hassan has called for the formation of a national unity government, which he believes can help bring "calm and quiet to the streets." He has also pledged to hold elections in 2013, which would lead to the formation of a new government. The crisis in Maldives has sparked international concern, with many calling for a peaceful resolution to the conflict. As the situation continues to unfold, it remains to be seen whether President Hassan's efforts to build a stable and democratic country will be successful, or if the nation will slide further into chaos. One thing is certain, however: the fate of former President Nasheed and the future of Maldives hang precariously in the balance.

The Unsung Heroes of Formula 1: A Tribute to the Brave and Dedicated Marshals As the Formula 1 season comes to a close, it's time to shine the spotlight on the unsung heroes of the sport: the marshals. These dedicated volunteers give up their free time to ensure the smooth running of every Grand Prix, often putting themselves in harm's way to keep the drivers and spectators safe. From the early morning hours to long after sunset, marshals are on duty, ready to respond to any incident on the track. Their quick thinking and swift action have been instrumental in minimizing delays and keeping the racing action going. This season has seen its fair share of close calls, with marshals narrowly avoiding being hit by speeding cars, including a heart-stopping moment in Russia when a marshal sprinted onto the track just seconds before Sebastian Vettel's Ferrari flew by. Marshals also have to contend with unpredictable weather conditions, as seen during the United States Grand Prix, where they were evacuated due to the risk of lightning strikes. Despite these challenges, they remain steadfast and dedicated, always putting the safety of others first. While their role is often thankless, they occasionally get to let their hair down, such as wearing masks during practice sessions near Halloween or staging mock pitstops with the safety car. It's a testament to their bravery and dedication that the on-track action has rarely been delayed for long this season. As the Formula 1 community looks back on another thrilling season, it's time to give a well-deserved tribute to the marshals, who are truly the stars of the show. Their selflessness, quick thinking, and passion for the sport make them the unsung heroes of Formula 1.

A suspect package report prompted the closure of Swansea's Indoor Market and bus station. South Wales Police reopened the areas at 17:00 BST after investigating. The incident caused significant disruption, but bus services are resuming. Police warned of robust action against hoax activity, urging vigilance while minimizing unnecessary disruption to the community.

Great Wall Motors, China's largest SUV manufacturer, has expressed interest in acquiring some or all of Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA), the world's seventh-largest car maker. According to a Great Wall official, the company has "an intention to acquire" FCA, although Fiat Chrysler has yet to receive a formal approach. The news sent shares in FCA soaring 7.4% in New York on Monday, with the company's valuation now standing at over $19 billion. The potential acquisition has sparked speculation that Great Wall is primarily interested in FCA's most valuable asset: the Jeep brand. Jeep, which celebrated its 75th birthday last year, is a iconic brand with a reputation dating back to World War Two, when its vehicles were extensively used by the US military. Morgan Stanley analysts estimate that the Jeep brand alone could be worth as much as $27 billion, making it a highly prized asset for any potential buyer. The potential takeover has also raised concerns in the White House, with President Trump having previously expressed concerns about China's growing economic influence. His former chief strategist, Steve Bannon, has gone so far as to describe the US as being in an "economic war" with China. While Great Wall's acquisition of FCA may not have an immediate impact on US jobs, as the company could choose to maintain manufacturing operations in the US, it is likely that the Chinese firm is primarily interested in acquiring Jeep's technology and engineering expertise. This has raised eyebrows, given that President Trump has ordered an investigation into allegations of China's theft of US intellectual property. The potential for the takeover to add to the friction between the US and China is high, particularly if the deal is seen as a strategic move by China to acquire valuable US technology and expertise. According to Bill Russo, a former Chrysler executive, Great Wall is likely interested in acquiring the Jeep brand rather than all of FCA, which has debts of around $4.9 billion. "Jeep is the crown jewel of Fiat Chrysler in terms of brand and equity," he said. "A deal would be quite complementary, given Great Wall's focus on SUVs." Yale Zhang, head of Shanghai-based consultancy Automotive Foresight, agrees, stating that "Jeep is the most logical choice, since [Great Wall] wants to be the largest SUV maker in the world." FCA's chief executive, Sergio Marchionne, has been seeking a partner or buyer to help the company manage rising costs, emissions regulations, and the development of electric and self-driving cars. The company also owns Alfa Romeo, Maserati, and RAM trucks, although it is unclear whether Great Wall would be interested in acquiring these brands as part of a potential deal. As the situation continues to unfold, it remains to be seen whether Great Wall's acquisition of FCA will come to fruition. However, one thing is clear: the potential takeover has significant implications for the global automotive industry, and could have far-reaching consequences for the US-China trade relationship. With Great Wall's ambition to become the world's largest SUV maker, and FCA's need for a partner to help navigate the challenges of the modern automotive industry, a deal could be seen as a strategic move by both parties. However, it is likely to face close scrutiny from regulators and politicians on both sides of the Pacific.

The Scarlets have secured the services of their attack coach, Stephen Hayward, on a new contract. Hayward joined the region in August 2014, bringing his experience from coaching the Wales Under-20 side. He praised head coach Wayne Pivac, who also recently signed a two-year deal, for allowing him to take the reins from the start. Hayward expressed his excitement about the team's potential, despite acknowledging defensive improvements are needed. General manager Jon Daniels welcomed the news, citing the coaching staff's commitment to developing the current squad. The Scarlets are currently second in the Pro12 table, just two points behind leaders Connacht after eight matches. This contract extension is a boost to the team as they continue their push for the top spot.

Tiger Woods' Golf Career Hangs in Balance as He Faces Uncertain Recovery In a candid and somber interview, 14-time major winner Tiger Woods has expressed his uncertainty and frustration regarding his return to professional golf. The 39-year-old golf legend has been sidelined since undergoing two operations in September and October to alleviate pain from a pinched nerve. With no clear timetable for his rehabilitation, Woods is facing an uncertain future, leaving fans and the golfing world wondering if he will ever regain his former glory. Woods, who will turn 40 on December 30, revealed that he has not swung a golf club since his operations and has been limited to walking as his only form of physical activity. He has spent most of his time playing video games, a stark contrast to his usual rigorous training regimen. The American golfer admitted that he has not done any rehabilitation work on his back, leaving him without a clear goal or timeline to work towards. This is not the first time Woods has faced a lengthy layoff due to injury. In 2014, he underwent surgery on a pinched nerve in his back and missed three months of the season, playing in only seven tournaments. However, this current setback seems to be the most challenging, with Woods himself describing it as "different from the other surgeries I've had in the past." The lack of a clear recovery timeline has left him feeling uncertain and demotivated, with no "light at the end of the tunnel" to look forward to. Despite his uncertain future, Woods remains hopeful that he can still compete at the highest level. He has been named as one of United States captain Davis Love III's assistants for the 2016 Ryder Cup, but he still harbors ambitions of making the team as a player. Woods has played in seven Ryder Cups, with his most recent appearance in 2012 under Love's captaincy. World number three Rory McIlroy has offered his support to Woods, posting on social media: "Wishing my idol and friend a speedy recovery. Golf without him doesn't bear thinking about. Hope to see you back on the course soon @tigerwoods." However, with no clear indication of when Woods will return to golf, it is difficult to predict if he will be able to regain his former form. Woods' last major victory was at the US Open in 2008, and he has struggled to replicate that success in recent years. He missed the cut at three of the four majors this year and played in only 11 events, leaving him stuck on 79 PGA Tour victories. While he acknowledges that he has achieved a great deal in his 20-year career, Woods is clearly not ready to hang up his clubs just yet. The question on everyone's mind is: will he be able to overcome this latest setback and return to the top of the golfing world? Only time will tell.

A rare solar storm has brought a spectacular display of the Aurora Australis to New Zealand, with the phenomenon visible much further north than usual. The aurora, also known as the southern lights, occurs when cosmic rays or solar wind interact with the earth's upper atmosphere. This week, many New Zealanders braved the cold to capture images of the breathtaking display. Aurora enthusiasts, known as "aurora chasers," were thrilled to witness the spectacle. Photographer Blair Pattinson from Queenstown described it as a "treat" to see such a strong aurora. "It's quite special," he said. "Many people wait years before they see them." The aurora is forecast to be active again on Thursday night, giving enthusiasts another chance to witness its beauty. Despite the cold temperatures, with the South Island dropping to sub-zero temperatures overnight, many were undeterred. Medical practitioner Stephen Voss, who has been chasing aurorae for 15 years, summed up the experience: "There is one word to describe it...freezing." Nevertheless, the opportunity to see the Aurora Australis was too good to miss.

A 64-year-old South Korean monk, Venerable Jung-won, has died after setting himself on fire during a rally against President Park Geun-hye in Seoul. The monk's tragic death has sparked widespread outrage and reignited tensions between South Korea and Japan over the issue of "comfort women" - women who were forced to work in Japanese military brothels during World War Two. Venerable Jung-won staged the protest on Saturday, and his condition deteriorated rapidly before he succumbed to multiple organ failures caused by his burns on Monday night. In a suicide note, the monk called President Park a "traitor", reportedly due to her handling of the comfort women issue. The social justice committee of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism released a statement saying that Venerable Jung-won had "sacrificed his life to convey people's sentiment" and demanded President Park's resignation. The comfort women issue has been a long-standing point of contention between South Korea and Japan. In 2015, President Park reached a deal with Japan, which included a promise to pay into a fund for South Korean women who were forced to work in Japanese military brothels. However, critics argue that the deal does not go far enough in holding Japan responsible for wartime abuses and does not directly compensate the women. Tensions between the two countries escalated last week after Tokyo withdrew its ambassador to South Korea in a row over a statue representing sex slaves. Japan claimed that the statue, which depicts a young, barefoot woman sitting in a chair, was a violation of the 2015 agreement. Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has demanded the removal of the statue, saying that the South Korean side should show its sincerity and implement the agreement as a "matter of credibility". The comfort women issue is just one of several controversies surrounding President Park, who has been embroiled in a scandal involving a close friend charged with corruption. She has been suspended from duties since December, when parliament voted to impeach her. The regular rallies against President Park in Seoul have drawn large crowds, with protesters calling for her resignation and demanding justice for the comfort women. Venerable Jung-won's tragic death has added to the sense of urgency and outrage, with many hoping that his sacrifice will not be in vain.

Tragedy Strikes in Penistone as Father and Son Lose Their Lives in Deliberate House Fire A devastating house fire in Penistone, near Barnsley, has claimed the lives of a father and son, leaving a community in shock. Darren Sykes, 44, and his son Paul were found dead in the property on Tennyson Close on Wednesday evening. A second boy, 12-year-old Jack Sykes, was rescued from the house and remains critically ill in hospital. According to South Yorkshire Police, the fire was started deliberately, and they are not seeking anyone else in connection with the incident. Ch Insp Debbie Mahmood expressed her condolences to the family, stating that a full investigation will be conducted. Emergency services responded to the call at around 18:30 BST, and the three victims were taken to hospital, where Mr. Sykes and his son were pronounced dead. The head teacher of Springvale Primary School, Andy Platt, paid tribute to Paul, describing him as an outgoing and popular boy who will be greatly missed. Jack's mother is currently keeping a bedside vigil, and the house remains cordoned off. The police have declined to comment on whether any substances were used to accelerate the fire. A post-mortem examination is scheduled to take place on Friday. The incident has sent shockwaves through the community, and an investigation is underway to determine the circumstances surrounding the tragic event.

A former lottery winner has been handed a community service order and disqualified from driving for five years after pleading guilty to driving while disqualified and without insurance. Ryan Magee, 34, from Eglinton, appeared before Londonderry Magistrates Court, where he admitted to driving a Ford Focus along the city's Foyle Bridge last December. Magee, who won a staggering £6.4m in the EuroMillions lottery seven years ago, was ordered to complete 200 hours of community service and fined £250. His legally aided barrister described his client's life as a series of unfortunate events, saying "every silver lining has a dark cloud." The barrister added that Magee had been traumatised by recent events and had only recently come to appreciate his responsibilities, particularly when it came to driving. The court heard that police officers on mobile patrol had spotted Magee driving the Ford Focus at 20:40 GMT on December 4 last year. When stopped, Magee admitted to driving while disqualified, replying "yep, that's right" to the officers. This offence occurred just five months into an 18-month disqualification period for failing to provide a specimen. The judge described Magee's criminal record, which includes 17 previous convictions, 12 of them for road traffic offences, as "appalling." He told Magee that he was a "menace" to himself and other road users, and that his actions had caused him "huge concern." The judge warned Magee that if he failed to comply with the community service order, he would face six months in jail. Magee's lottery win had initially brought him a life of luxury, with him spending £170,000 on a Ferrari sports car and purchasing a house equipped with a champagne bar. However, the house is now up for auction, a testament to the tumultuous turn his life has taken. The case serves as a cautionary tale of the importance of responsible behaviour, particularly when it comes to driving, and the consequences of failing to do so.

Alcohol Consumption in the UK: A Growing Concern A recent review by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has found that the average annual consumption of pure alcohol in the UK has risen to 10.6 litres per person, equivalent to 115 bottles of wine. This represents a significant increase from the early 1990s, when consumption was under 10 litres per person. The trend is particularly concerning, as it contrasts with falls in other nations, such as Germany and Italy, which have seen big reductions in drinking rates. The OECD report highlights the UK as one of the heaviest drinking countries among the 34 wealthiest nations, with the average person consuming more than the current OECD average of 9.5 litres. In fact, the UK's drinking rates were below the current OECD average in the early 1990s, but have since surpassed it. The report suggests that the UK should consider implementing measures such as minimum pricing and tougher regulation to reduce consumption. One notable trend highlighted by the report is the high rate of problem drinking among educated women. Nearly one in five women from the highest educated groups drinks to hazardous levels, compared to one in 10 among the least educated group. According to OECD economist Mark Pearson, this trend is "pretty unique" to the UK and appears to be related to the increasing employment opportunities women are getting in traditionally male-dominated sectors, such as the finance industry. The report also notes that the UK has one of the heaviest concentrations of drinking among its population, with the heaviest-drinking one-fifth of the population accounting for nearly two-thirds of all alcohol consumed. Furthermore, there has been a rise in youth drinking, with the proportion of 15-year-olds who have experienced alcohol increasing from 71% to 75% between 2002 and 2010. Although there are signs that this trend may be starting to reverse in recent years, it remains a concern. To address the issue of problem drinking, Mr. Pearson recommends that the UK consider taking tougher steps, including minimum pricing, banning sports sponsorship, and enforcing clear labelling, as well as improving access to treatment. He emphasizes that such measures present "opportunities" to reduce drinking rates, while also acknowledging the need to strike a balance between tackling harmful drinking and penalizing those who drink within recommended levels. Sir Ian Gilmore, chairman of the Alcohol Health Alliance, agrees with Mr. Pearson's assessment, noting that the research shows there is "no silver bullet" and that a range of policies on "pricing, marketing, and availability" are needed to address the issue. He adds that drinking has been seen as a personal choice for too long, rather than a population-wide public health issue. In response to the report, a Department of Health spokeswoman acknowledged that drinking too much too often can have devastating consequences for health and stated that local authorities have been given public health funding to help tackle problems like drinking. The spokeswoman emphasized that more needs to be done to prevent people from getting into dangerous drinking habits. The OECD report serves as a wake-up call for the UK to take a closer look at its drinking culture and to consider implementing policies to reduce consumption and mitigate the negative consequences of excessive drinking. As Mr. Pearson notes, drinking costs a significant amount of money in terms of lost productivity, health spending, and accidents and ill health, making it an issue that any country serious about its economic performance cannot afford to ignore.

Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy has confirmed that he will remain the party's candidate for the East Renfrewshire Westminster seat in the upcoming general election. Despite previously announcing his intention to stand for the Scottish Parliament in 2016 and become the party's candidate for first minister, Murphy's team has clarified that he will retain his current position as MP for East Renfrewshire. Murphy, who was elected leader of the Scottish Labour Party last month, had faced calls to clarify his position on the Westminster seat, which he has held since 1997. A spokesman for Murphy stated that his constituents would be the first to know if there were any changes to his candidacy. It is worth noting that there is no rule preventing Murphy from holding seats in both the Scottish and UK parliaments simultaneously. In fact, former First Minister Alex Salmond previously served as both an MSP and an MP at the same time. However, Murphy has previously expressed his reluctance to pursue this option, stating that it is "not something I'm attracted to". Murphy has given a "cast-iron guarantee" that he will be a candidate in the 2016 Scottish Parliament elections and will stand for the position of first minister. He has also hinted that he may attempt to enter the Scottish Parliament sooner, but has assured his constituents that they will be informed first of any changes to his plans. The confirmation of Murphy's candidacy for the East Renfrewshire seat provides clarity on his immediate political future, but the longer-term question of whether he will attempt to hold seats in both parliaments remains uncertain. For now, Murphy's focus will be on the general election on May 7th, where he will seek to retain his Westminster seat.

Tory Recriminations Begin After Election Setback in Wales The Conservative Party in Wales is left reeling after a disappointing election result, with many questioning the campaign strategy. Despite Theresa May's high-profile visits to Labour-held target seats in Bridgend, Wrexham, and Clwyd South, the party failed to make significant gains. In hindsight, it appears that shoring up support in marginal seats like Cardiff North, Gower, and Vale of Clwyd may have been a more effective approach. The campaign has been criticized for its lack of a Welsh dimension, with sources suggesting that the party's message failed to resonate with local voters. The absence of a clear leader, with three different men representing the party in debates, may have also contributed to the confusion. In contrast, the Scottish Conservatives, led by Ruth Davidson, were able to make significant gains. The election result has sparked a debate about what went wrong for the Tories in Wales. While some argue that the campaign was poorly run, others believe that the country's desire for a softer Brexit may have been a decisive factor. As the party begins to reflect on its performance, it is clear that there are lessons to be learned from the experience. The question now is whether the Welsh Tories can regroup and regain momentum in the face of a resurgent Labour party.

Northern Ireland's First Minister, Peter Robinson, 66, was hospitalized after feeling unwell. A party spokesman confirmed he underwent tests for a heart-related condition. Robinson, in office since 2008, was taken to the hospital by ambulance on Monday morning. His condition remains unclear, with no further details released.

Vin Diesel Reveals Newborn Daughter's Name as Tribute to Late Friend Paul Walker In an emotional announcement on America's Today show, actor Vin Diesel revealed that he has named his newborn daughter Pauline, in honor of his late friend and co-star Paul Walker. Walker, who passed away in a car crash in 2013 at the age of 40, had a profound impact on Diesel's life, and the actor credits him with inspiring him to be more involved in the birth of his children. Diesel recalled the advice Walker gave him seven years ago, before the birth of his first child, Hania. "Paul told me to go into the delivery room and own it, be present, and don't shy away from it," Diesel said. He took Walker's advice to heart and was present for the birth of his daughter, even cutting the umbilical cord. As he did so, he couldn't help but think of his late friend and the impact he had on his life. Pauline is Diesel's third child with his partner, Paloma Jimenez. The couple also has a son, Vincent, aged four. Diesel's tribute to Walker is a testament to the strong bond the two actors shared, both on and off screen. Walker's death was a tragic loss for the film industry, and his brothers stepped in to complete his scenes in the seventh installment of the Fast and Furious franchise. Furious 7, which is dedicated to Walker's memory, is set to be released on April 10.

A Spanish air force pilot, Captain Fernando Lluna Carrascosa, was killed in a Eurofighter jet crash at the Moron air base near Seville. The incident occurred during a routine training flight at around 14:00 local time. Captain Carrascosa, from Madrid, had over 600 hours of experience flying Eurofighter jets. He leaves behind a wife and daughter. The crash is the second fatal Eurofighter incident at the base, following a 2010 accident that claimed the life of a Saudi national. Images on social media showed black smoke rising from the area. The Spanish ministry of defence confirmed the crash and is investigating the circumstances. Captain Carrascosa's death is a tragic loss for the Spanish air force and his family. An investigation into the cause of the crash is underway.

A large fire broke out at a property in Great Haseley on Sunday, engulfing nearly half of the roof. Smoke was spotted at 17:30 BST, prompting a response from up to 50 firefighters. A specialist team used chainsaws to cut fire breaks, protecting the rest of the home. Crews in breathing apparatus tackled the flames from inside. The cause of the fire is unknown. Oxfordshire fire service employed a new technique, using ladders and chainsaws to limit fire spread, allowing for the salvage of personal possessions. This innovative method was praised for its effectiveness in tackling thatch fires.

Scotland's retail sector has shown signs of growth, with the latest retail sales index revealing a 0.8% increase in value and a 1.7% rise in volume in the fourth quarter of 2014. Although these figures are lower than the country-wide averages of 1.5% and 2.3% respectively, they indicate a positive trend for the industry north of the border. On an annual basis, however, Scotland lagged behind Great Britain in both volume and value terms. The volume of sales in Scotland increased by 1.6% year-on-year, compared to a 5% rise for the whole of Britain. This suggests that while the Scottish retail sector is recovering, it still has some ground to make up. The large shops with at least 250 employees, which account for around 70% of retail industry sales, saw a 0.9% increase in sales volumes compared to the previous quarter. Small and medium-sized stores, on the other hand, experienced a more significant growth of 3%. This disparity highlights the ongoing challenges faced by smaller retailers in competing with their larger counterparts. Euan Murray of Barclays Corporate Banking attributed the boost in sales to the "extravaganza of planned promotions" in November and the last-minute Christmas shopping rush. He also noted that non-food products, such as clothing, performed particularly well towards the end of 2014. With the new spring ranges now in stores, fashion retailers will be hoping for milder weather to encourage shoppers to update their wardrobes. Scottish Retail Consortium director David Lonsdale welcomed the resumption of growth in retail sales, citing falling prices at shop checkouts and petrol pumps as contributing factors. However, he cautioned that the recovery in consumer confidence remains fragile and that upcoming public policy decisions, such as the proposed replacement of council tax and the setting of the Scottish rate of income tax, could impact disposable incomes and take-home pay. Deputy First Minister John Swinney highlighted the positive trends in the wider Scottish economy, including record jobs figures, low unemployment, and high employment and economic activity. Scotland Office Minister David Mundell also emphasized the benefits of being part of a strong and diverse UK economy, citing the country's status as the fastest-growing economy in the western world. While there are still challenges to be addressed, the latest retail sales index suggests that Scotland's retail sector is on the path to recovery. As the industry looks to the future, it will be crucial for policymakers to create an environment that supports consumer spending and economic growth. With the right conditions in place, Scottish retailers can continue to thrive and contribute to the country's ongoing prosperity.

UK Retail Sales Disappoint in November Ahead of Christmas Season According to the latest BRC/KPMG survey, sales at UK stores open for more than a year fell 0.4% in November compared to the same month in 2014. The decline is attributed to shoppers holding back on purchases in anticipation of deep discounts on Black Friday, which took place on November 28. However, many retailers failed to deliver the expected discounts, resulting in a relatively flat sales performance. Total sales across all stores increased by a mere 0.7%, significantly lower than the 2.2% rise seen last year. Despite the hype surrounding Black Friday, the event failed to spark a significant surge in sales, with trading up only 25% compared to the beginning of the month. Online sales of non-food items were a bright spot, rising 11.8% year-on-year. The survey also found that sales of furniture and electrical appliances were higher than last year. Nevertheless, the rise of "omni-channel" shopping, where consumers use a mix of online and in-store purchases, has made it challenging for retailers to predict spending patterns during the crucial Christmas shopping period. BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson warned that the conversion of higher disposable income into retail sales should not be taken for granted. As the retail sector heads into the festive season, retailers will be closely watching consumer behavior to gauge the impact of changing shopping habits on sales.

Home Office Delays Police Funding Reform Due to Statistical Error The Home Office has announced a delay in the proposed changes to the police funding formula for 2016/17 due to a statistical error. Minister Mike Penning apologized to the Commons for the mistake, which has caused significant concern among police forces in England and Wales. The error was discovered in a new formula that assesses population size, social and economic factors, and crime rates to calculate funding for each of the 43 police forces. The government had launched a consultation on the proposed changes, but six police and crime commissioners threatened legal action, arguing that the plans were "unjustified and deeply flawed." The Home Office has since revealed that the new formula was based on flawed calculations. As a result, the government will now seek the views of police and crime commissioners and the National Police Chiefs Council before proceeding with the changes. Penning expressed regret over the mistake and apologized to MPs and police forces. The delay is expected to give the government time to re-evaluate the funding formula and ensure that it is fair and accurate. The exact duration of the delay has not been specified, but it is seen as a positive step towards addressing the concerns of police forces and ensuring that they receive the necessary funding to effectively serve their communities.

Tragedy Strikes as Irish Nun Killed in Ecuador Earthquake A devastating 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Ecuador, leaving a trail of destruction and claiming the lives of at least 480 people. Among the victims was Sister Clare Theresa Crockett, a 33-year-old Irish nun from the Long Tower area of Derry. Sister Clare was one of six people killed when a school collapsed in Playa Prieta, including five young women who were entering the religious order. Sister Clare and another Irish nun, Sister Thérèse Ryan from County Limerick, were part of the Home of the Mother order and had been teaching guitar and singing to the postulants when the earthquake struck. It is believed that they were attempting to evacuate the building when they became trapped on a stairway. The Kevin Bell Repatriation Trust has been working tirelessly with the authorities in Ecuador to bring Sister Clare's body back to her family. Colin Bell, founder of the trust, stated that they are making progress, but the process is being hindered by the country's turmoil. "We have been working with a repatriation company and we know that Sister Clare is now with the undertakers. It's only now a matter of getting the paperwork done and getting a flight as soon as possible," he said. Sister Clare's family is anxiously waiting for her body to be brought home, and Mr. Bell is hopeful that this will happen within a week. Before joining the religious order, Sister Clare was a fan of karaoke and had dreams of stardom. Her tragic death has sent shockwaves through the community, and she will be deeply missed. The Kevin Bell Repatriation Trust was set up by Mr. Bell after the death of his son in 2013, and has since helped numerous families bring their loved ones home.

Australian Duo Faces Imminent Execution in Indonesia Amid Bribery Allegations The fate of two Australian men, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, hangs in the balance as they face imminent execution in Indonesia for their roles in a 2005 heroin smuggling operation. The pair, who were sentenced to death in 2006, could be put to death within days, despite a last-ditch effort by their lawyers to have their cases reviewed. In a shocking twist, the men's lawyers have alleged that the judges who presided over their trial in Bali had asked for bribes in exchange for lighter sentences. The claim, which was reported by Australian media outlets on Monday, has sparked outrage and raised questions about the integrity of the Indonesian judiciary. According to the Sydney Morning Herald and Herald Sun newspapers, the lawyers' letter alleges that the six judges who heard the case had offered to reduce the sentences in exchange for money. The letter also claims that the judges were pressured by "certain parts" to hand down the death penalty, which breached ethical standards. The allegations have been met with silence from Indonesian judicial officials, who have not publicly commented on the claim. However, the Australian government has continued to campaign for clemency for the two men, with Prime Minister Tony Abbott and Foreign Minister Julie Bishop urging Indonesia to spare their lives. Speaking to reporters on Monday, Mr. Abbott declined to comment directly on the allegations but said that the Australian government was still making representations to Indonesia about the planned executions. "What we understand is that there are still legal options open to these two Australians and their legal teams," he said. "Until those options are exhausted, Indonesia should not execute these two men." Ms. Bishop also refused to comment on the letter, but said that there were "very serious allegations" and that the lawyers for Mr. Sukumaran and Mr. Chan would continue to raise these matters. She urged the Indonesians to follow all appeals processes, but said that she had to respect its legal systems. The case has sparked widespread outrage in Australia, with a recent poll conducted by the Lowy Institute finding that 62% of Australians opposed the executions of Chan and Sukumaran. The poll of 1,211 randomly selected respondents also found that 69% thought the death penalty should not be applied to drug traffickers. The Indonesian government has been unmoved by the opposition, with President Joko Widodo supporting capital punishment for drug crimes. The country has some of the toughest drug laws in the world and ended a four-year moratorium on executions in 2013. Last month, Indonesia executed convicts from several countries, including Malawi, Nigeria, Vietnam, Brazil, and the Netherlands, as well as one from Indonesia. The move prompted Brazil and the Netherlands to recall their ambassadors in protest, and Australian authorities have threatened to do the same if Chan and Sukumaran are put to death. As the clock ticks down for the two Australian men, their lawyers and supporters are holding out hope that the Indonesian government will grant them a last-minute reprieve. However, with the country's tough stance on drug crimes and the lack of comment from judicial officials, it remains to be seen whether their efforts will be successful.

Work and Pensions Committee Chairman Urges New Rules to Protect Pensions The chairman of the Work and Pensions Committee, Frank Field, has written to Chancellor George Osborne, calling for new rules to be introduced in the Queen's Speech to protect pensions. The committee is currently conducting inquiries into pensions automatic enrolment and pensions regulation, using the collapse of High Street retailer BHS as a case study. BHS's pension scheme has a significant deficit of £571m, highlighting the need for stronger regulations. Mr. Field expressed concern over "gaps in the regulatory framework" that have allowed "potentially unstable master trusts onto the market," putting the retirement savings of thousands of people at risk. Master trusts are defined-contribution workplace schemes overseen by a board of trustees. The committee's inquiry into the Pension Protection Fund and pensions regulation has also raised concerns over the effectiveness of powers available to the regulator and fund trustees. The Pensions Regulator, which oversees work-based pension schemes, and the Pension Protection Fund, which pays compensation when an employer goes out of business, may not have sufficient powers to protect pension funds. The issue has become increasingly pressing following the collapse of BHS, which has put 11,000 jobs at risk. Former BHS owner Sir Philip Green has faced criticism over his role in the company's demise and has been called upon to repay the £571m deficit to the pension fund. Mr. Field has suggested that Sir Philip's knighthood should be removed if he fails to do so. Sir Philip has agreed to appear before the committee to answer questions about the collapse, but has denied any wrongdoing. The committee's inquiry is ongoing, and Mr. Field's letter to the Chancellor highlights the need for urgent action to protect pensions and prevent similar collapses in the future.

Ballymena United midfielder Allan Jenkins has announced his decision to leave the club after eight years of service. The 35-year-old Scotsman, who made 254 appearances for the Braidmen, turned down a new one-year contract due to family and work commitments. Jenkins, who is head of youth development at Stranraer, has been commuting from his home in Scotland to play for the club since 2011. Jenkins stated that he has chosen to prioritize his life outside of football, citing the need to spend more time with his eight-year-old daughter. He described the decision as the "hardest of his life," highlighting his love for the club and the sport. Ballymena boss David Jeffrey paid tribute to Jenkins' service, saying that he was wanted to stay at the club but ultimately understood his decision. Jenkins' departure comes on the heels of a successful season, which saw him score Ballymena's first goal in the League Cup final win over Carrick Rangers. He also helped the team secure a Europa League place by defeating Glenavon in a play-off. The club has already begun to rebuild, releasing six players, including striker Darren Henderson, and signing several new players, including Michael Gault, Stephen McAlorum, and Emmet Friars, as well as defenders Andrew Burns and Steven McCullough. Jenkins will be remembered for his dedication and contributions to the club, and his legacy will be felt for years to come.

A long-lost train rumored to be carrying gold, gems, and guns from World War II has sparked a frenzy of treasure hunting in the south-western Polish city of Walbrzych. The train, which allegedly disappeared in 1945 as Soviet forces approached, is believed to be hidden in the area. Recently, a Polish and German duo claimed to have located the armoured train, and through their lawyers, they are seeking a 10% reward of the value of any findings. However, Polish officials are urging the public to exercise caution and refrain from searching for the train until official procedures are in place to secure the site. According to Piotr Zuchowski, a senior official at the Polish culture ministry, the train may contain hazardous substances and is likely to be booby-trapped. Zuchowski confirmed that he is certain of the train's existence, despite decades of unsuccessful searching. The exact location of the train and the identities of the two men who claim to have found it are being kept secret. Walbrzych's deputy mayor, Zygmunt Nowaczyk, revealed that the train is within the city's administrative boundaries but refused to disclose the exact location. Local folklore suggests that the train went missing near Ksiaz castle, just 3km from Walbrzych. As the search for the train continues, officials are working to ensure that the site is secured and any potential hazards are mitigated.

Peel Ports Medway has been granted approval by Swale Borough Council to build a factory at the Port of Sheerness on the Isle of Sheppey. The move comes after Danish wind turbine firm Vestas cancelled its plans for a manufacturing facility on the island in June, which would have created approximately 1,600 jobs. Despite the setback, Peel Ports Medway remains optimistic about attracting manufacturers to the area. According to Gary Parkinson, managing director of Peel Ports Medway, the company has been in confidential discussions with several manufacturers and believes the Port of Sheerness is an ideal location for wind turbine production and related activities. Parkinson emphasized that the Vestas decision was not a reflection on the site's suitability, but rather a separate issue. With the green light from the council, Peel Ports Medway is poised to invest in the area's infrastructure, reinforcing its commitment to bringing new business and job opportunities to the island. The approval has been welcomed as a positive step towards revitalizing the local economy and exploring renewable energy possibilities.

An appeal has been lodged with the Planning Appeals Commission by sand companies and the Earl of Shaftesbury, who owns the bed of the lough, against an enforcement notice to stop sand extraction. The notice was issued by Environment Minister Mark H Durkan in May, requiring the companies to submit a planning application before resuming operations. Despite a deadline to comply, the appeal allows extraction to continue pending the outcome. Approximately 1.7m tonnes of sand are extracted annually, meeting a quarter of Northern Ireland's construction needs. However, environmentalists argue that the extraction is taking place without permission in a protected bird habitat. The Environment Minister has declined to comment, with his department citing the case as a "live enforcement issue." The appeal will be reviewed, and a decision will be made in due course, determining the fate of sand extraction in the area.

Two Luton men, Ibrahim Anderson, 38, and Shah Jahan Khan, 62, have been accused of supporting a banned organisation. They were arrested by Met Police counter-terror officers and bailed to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on April 21. Anderson also faces a charge of possessing terrorist information. The alleged offences occurred in August and December 2014. Both men are set to appear in court to face the charges.

A heartwarming reunion took place in Sheffield after two young siblings stumbled upon stolen items belonging to 93-year-old Doris Wilcock. Tyler, 10, and Amelia Exelby, 9, discovered the treasures under a blue tarpaulin in woodland, initially thinking they had found lost riches. However, upon taking the items home, their father contacted South Yorkshire Police, who successfully traced the owner. Mrs. Wilcock was overjoyed to be reunited with some of her stolen belongings, describing the children as her "heroes." Although the items held little monetary value, they were sentimental to her. Unfortunately, a pendant given by her late husband was not among the recovered items. The children's selfless act was praised by PCSO Michelle Tatterton, who described the experience as "an emotional and very rewarding end to a busy shift." The reunion highlighted the importance of community kindness and the positive impact it can have on people's lives. Mrs. Wilcock's gratitude was evident as she thanked the young duo for their honesty and kindness.

Scotland's Rugby Team Faces Injury Concerns Ahead of Six Nations Tournament As the Six Nations tournament approaches, Scotland's rugby team is facing injury concerns that may impact their performance in the early rounds. Mark Bennett, a 22-year-old centre, suffered an injury while playing for Glasgow earlier this month, and it was initially feared that he would miss the tournament's early matches. However, head coach Vern Cotter has provided a positive update on Bennett's progress, stating that he is recovering well and that a decision on his availability will be made next week. Cotter described Bennett's chances of playing as "50-50," which highlights the uncertainty surrounding his injury. The team is already dealing with other injury concerns, including a thigh strain sustained by Alex Dunbar during Glasgow's win over Racing 92 on Saturday. Peter Horne is also struggling with a foot problem, while Richie Vernon is a long-term injury absentee. This leaves Matt Scott and Duncan Taylor as the only currently fit centres in Cotter's squad. Cotter has acknowledged that Scotland lacks strength in depth, which could be a significant challenge for the team during the tournament. "We've got some good character and we've got some good individuals, but if we get banged up, we know what that means," he said. Despite these concerns, Cotter believes that his team can be competitive, and he is focusing on building momentum from the start of the tournament. The team is still reeling from their 35-34 defeat by Australia in the quarter-final of the World Cup, which was marked by a controversial penalty decision. However, Cotter wants his players to move on from that loss and focus on improving their performance. "The memory of the World Cup will stay with the players for a long time, but it's part of history now," he said. "I feel for them, but I don't think I need to use it as motivation. The desire in the team is to improve, and that's the energy generated within the team." Cotter has not been set a win ratio target for the tournament, which suggests that the focus is on performance rather than results. The team's goal is to win every game, but Cotter wants to avoid adding stress and weight on the shoulders of his players. Instead, he is emphasizing the importance of starting well and building momentum throughout the tournament. With a "no excuse" mentality, the team is determined to improve and make a strong showing in the Six Nations.

A non-denominational service will be held on November 6 at Aberdeen's Mither Kirk. The event honors infants cremated in the city, whose ashes were secretly mixed with adults' and given to wrong families. Parents were wrongly told no ashes existed. The service addresses the 2013 revelation, which echoed Edinburgh's Mortonhall crematorium scandal.

Trinity College's library has received a remarkable bequest of over 7,000 books from the late Mary, Duchess of Roxburghe. The duchess, who passed away in 2014 at the age of 99, left behind a treasure trove of rare and undiscovered works, including first editions by famous authors such as Wordsworth, Shelley, and Byron. The collection, which had been stored in part in an old blue suitcase, includes previously unknown manuscripts by notable historical figures like Napoleon Bonaparte, George Washington, Florence Nightingale, and Charles Dickens. According to Bamber Gascoigne, the former University Challenge presenter who inherited the duchess's former home, the collection contains "treasures and rarities unknown to anyone" since the death of his aunt's father in 1945. Gascoigne expressed his delight at seeing the books in their new home, stating that it is "thrilling" that they will now be available to everyone. Trinity College's librarian, Dr. Nicolas Bell, described the find as "an extraordinary library - one of the most important private collections in Britain, which offers untold discoveries." The college is eager to make the collection accessible to scholars and the public, uncovering the secrets and stories hidden within its pages.
