A rare painting from Claude Monet's famous Nympheas series is set to be auctioned on May 5, with an estimated value of $30-45m. The piece, unseen in public since 1945, will be sold alongside five other Monet works, including Le Palais Ducal and La Seine a Vetheuil. The six paintings, held in private collections, are expected to raise over $78m. The impressionist masterpieces will be on display in London until April 14, before moving to New York from May 1. This rare opportunity to view Monet's works is highly anticipated, with art enthusiasts eager to catch a glimpse of these stunning pieces.

Tragedy Strikes Taiwan Water Park as Fire Claims First Fatality A 20-year-old woman, Lee Pei-yu, has become the first fatality of the devastating fire that swept through a water park in Taiwan on Saturday. Doctors, with the support of her family, made the difficult decision to turn off her life support ventilator on Monday. Lee suffered second-degree burns over 90% of her body and had been fighting for her life since the incident. The fire, which broke out at around 20:30 local time, injured over 500 people, with at least 200 still in hospital in a critical condition. Among those injured is Lee's 12-year-old brother, who remains in hospital. Eight patients are reported to have life-threatening injuries. The incident occurred when colored powder, sprayed from the stage onto the audience, suddenly ignited, engulfing the crowd in a deadly inferno. The cause of the fire is still under investigation, but officials believe that the flammable powder may have been set alight by cigarette embers, a lighter, or electrical sparks. The powder, which was used to create a party atmosphere, was sprayed into the crowd of over 1,000 people near the stage. Amateur video footage shows the moment the powder burst into flames, sending the crowd into a state of panic as they ran for their lives. The organizers of the event have been questioned by authorities, and the use of colored powder at events has been banned while its safety is assessed. The water park itself remains closed. The seller who provided the powder has stated that the buyer was warned about the risk of fire. Three people, including party organizer Lu Chung-chi, have been arrested and released on bail in connection with the incident. They have been ordered not to leave the island and are likely to face charges of professional neglect and public endangerment. Lu has apologized for the incident and pledged to take responsibility for it. The incident has sent shockwaves through Taiwan, with many calling for greater safety measures to be put in place at public events. The BBC's Cindy Sui, reporting from Taipei, described the scene as "like hell," with many people suffering serious burns. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, and it is likely that more information will come to light in the coming days. For now, the people of Taiwan are left to mourn the loss of Lee Pei-yu and pray for the recovery of those still in hospital.

Reading FC manager Jaap Stam is preparing his team for a crucial play-off meeting with Fulham, while also acknowledging the challenges that lie ahead in the Championship next season. After leading the Royals to a third-place finish in his first season in charge, Stam believes the division will become even more competitive with several big-spending clubs vying for promotion. Stam emphasized the importance of retaining key players, stating, "If you want to make steps yourself as a club, you don't want to sell your best players." He also cautioned that rapid progress can be a double-edged sword, saying, "Sometimes you can have things too quick, but if the opportunity's there to do things well, you need to enjoy it and that's what we're doing." The Royals face Fulham in the first leg of their semi-final at Craven Cottage on Saturday, followed by the return leg at the Madejski Stadium on Tuesday. Stam's initial target of a top-10 finish has been surpassed, and the team is now just three games away from a potential return to the Premier League. The manager admitted that he is worried about losing key players, but is focused on the task at hand. With several clubs investing heavily in their squads, Stam warned that the top six will be increasingly difficult to reach for teams with limited budgets. Despite this, he remains optimistic about Reading's chances and is determined to make the most of their play-off opportunity.

A dramatic incident unfolded in western Sydney's Riverstone suburb on Tuesday morning. Police responded to reports of a man attempting to cut down a power pole. The 51-year-old allegedly threw petrol at officers, and his clothes caught fire when they used a Taser and pepper spray. After extinguishing the flames, the man barricaded himself inside his house. He surrendered an hour later and was treated for minor burns. A police officer, whose eyes were splashed with petrol, was also hospitalized. Charges are expected to be laid against the man. The situation was brought under control without major injuries.

Great Britain's men's hockey team has secured top spot in Pool A despite being held to a draw by Belgium. The British team took the lead three times through Phil Roper, Alastair Brogdon, and Alan Forsyth, but were pegged back on each occasion. Although they didn't play to their full potential, the team achieved their goal of topping the group, thanks to previous wins against Canada and world champions Australia. Captain Dan Fox expressed disappointment with the team's performance but remains optimistic about their chances. On Thursday, they will face hosts India, who finished bottom of Pool B. Fox acknowledged that India has a skilled team and a passionate crowd, but plans to take the game to them. With a much-changed squad, Great Britain aims to reach the semi-finals, and a win against India would bring them closer to achieving this goal.

Morrissey Considered for London Mayoral Candidacy by Animal Welfare Party The Animal Welfare Party has approached renowned singer Morrissey to represent them in the upcoming London mayoral election. A statement on his semi-official website revealed that Morrissey has been asked to stand for the party, citing his long-standing advocacy for animal rights and vegetarianism. Morrissey expressed his desire to "speak out against the hellish and archaic social injustice allotted to animals" and emphasized the need for immediate action to address animal welfare concerns. The party's leader, Vanessa Hudson, stated that they aim to bring attention to animal welfare issues in the mayoral contest, seeking a candidate who will champion London as a leading city for both people and animals. To be eligible, Morrissey would need to meet certain requirements, including being registered to vote in London or having lived, worked, or owned property there for 12 months. He would also require the signatures of 10 registered electors from each London borough and a £10,000 deposit. Nominations for London mayoral candidates close at the end of March, leaving a short window for Morrissey to decide on his candidacy. If he chooses to run, his involvement could bring significant attention to animal welfare issues in the city.

Invest Northern Ireland (Invest NI) has unveiled a new strategy aimed at securing up to £1.2bn in new export orders for local companies. The plan, approved by the Department for the Economy, also promotes the commitment to reduce corporation tax to 12.5%. However, the implementation of this tax cut, initially planned for 2018, remains uncertain due to the need for a functioning executive and assembly. Despite the challenges, Invest NI chief executive Alastair Hamilton reported that Northern Ireland continues to attract significant inward investment, with 22 new companies setting up operations in the region over the past year. The organization promoted 5,600 new jobs in the last financial year, similar to the previous year. Although only 1,300 of these jobs have been publicly announced, Invest NI attributes the delay to "purdah" rules surrounding recent elections and the EU referendum. Hamilton remains optimistic about the region's economic prospects, citing strong investment and job creation.

The British Embassy in Belgrade has partnered with Serbia Post to launch a new set of stamps honoring the bravery and selflessness of six British women who played a crucial role in Serbia during World War I. The stamps feature five Scottish women who worked as doctors, nurses, and drivers, as well as Captain Flora Sandes, the only British female to bear arms during the war. Captain Sandes, who initially went to Serbia as a nurse, enlisted in the Serbian Army and remained in Belgrade after the war, even volunteering to fight against the Nazis in 1941. She was awarded the highest Serbian military medal for her contributions. The stamps are part of a wider campaign by the British Embassy to recognize the efforts of over 600 British women who contributed to the war effort in Serbia, highlighting their roles in promoting universal suffrage, solidarity, and gender equality.

A veteran musician of the Bolshoi Theatre's orchestra has tragically died after an incident at the theatre. Viktor Sedov, 65, who played in the second violins for four decades, passed away in hospital on Wednesday from his injuries. The exact circumstances of the incident, which occurred on Tuesday, remain unclear. Sedov was beloved by his colleagues for his sense of humour and vast knowledge. The Bolshoi Theatre has been plagued by scandals, including an acid attack on ballet director Sergei Filin. The theatre's former head, Anatoly Iksanov, was recently removed from his post. New general director Vladimir Urin has been tasked with leading the theatre out of its crisis. The death of Sedov is the latest blow to the esteemed institution, considered one of the world's greatest theatres. An investigation into Sedov's death is likely to be launched, shedding more light on the incident.

UK Sees Thousands of Children Holding Firearms Certificates, Sparking Debate on Gun Control According to recent Home Office figures, a total of 3,602 children under the age of 18 held firearms certificates in 2016/17, with 327 of them being 13 or younger. These certificates, which allow the holders to possess firearms and/or shotguns, were issued by local police forces after a series of checks, including interviews, visits, and references. The police force with the largest number of children holding firearms certificates was Devon and Cornwall, with 206 certificates issued. This trend is reflected in the overall number of firearms certificates held in the region, with Devon and Cornwall having the highest number of certificates at 11,144, followed by Sussex and North Yorkshire. While the number of children holding firearms certificates may seem alarming, it is worth noting that there are strict controls in place to ensure their safe use. Children under the age of 15 are required to be supervised by an adult aged at least 21 when using shotguns, and those under 18 are prohibited from purchasing or hiring firearms or ammunition. The British Association for Shooting and Conservation has argued that teaching children to use firearms safely and responsibly can have numerous benefits, including promoting self-control and responsibility towards others. Chairman Peter Glenser stated that shooting has many aspects, from pest control to competitive sports, and that an early start in life is essential for those who wish to compete at top levels. However, the fact that children as young as seven have been known to hold firearms certificates has raised concerns about the effectiveness of the current system. The Home Office has emphasized that there are "very strict controls" in place, but some may argue that more needs to be done to ensure that firearms are kept out of the wrong hands. The UK is widely regarded as having some of the toughest gun control laws in the world, and the Policing and Crime Act 2017 has further strengthened firearms legislation by closing legal loopholes exploited by criminals. The number of firearms certificates revoked in 2016/17 fell by 10% compared to the previous year, with 358 firearms certificates and 1,216 shotgun certificates being revoked. Overall, the issue of children holding firearms certificates highlights the need for ongoing debate and discussion about gun control in the UK. While the current system has its strengths, it is essential that lawmakers and regulators continue to monitor and adapt the rules to ensure that firearms are used safely and responsibly by all holders, regardless of age.

Karl Dickson, 32, has made 124 appearances for Quins, scoring 16 tries. Director of rugby Conor O'Shea praised Dickson, calling him "one of the most competitive and best people" he's met. A qualified referee, Dickson also represented England in 2012. O'Shea expects him to continue pushing himself and the team to improve.

Ulster Unionist Party Leader Vindicated by Security Report The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has been vindicated in its decision to withdraw from the Northern Ireland Executive, according to party leader Mike Nesbitt. This comes after a security report revealed that the IRA's ruling army council still exists and has influence over Sinn Féin. The report's findings have sparked widespread criticism of Sinn Féin, with many questioning the party's denials of ongoing IRA activity. The UUP withdrew from government last month amidst allegations that IRA members were involved in the murder of Kevin McGuigan Sr, a former IRA member. The party's decision to pull out of the executive was seen as a bold move, but one that has now been justified by the security report. "I took a principled stand, I took an unambiguous stand that everybody understands," said Mr. Nesbitt. The report's findings have also been welcomed by former UUP leader Sir Reg Empey, who spoke at the party's annual conference on Saturday. Sir Reg criticized First Minister Peter Robinson for returning to "business as usual" despite the report's damning findings. "How awful," he said, "that [Mr. Robinson] goes back to business as usual, sending the clear signal to Sinn Féin that they can get away with it again." Sir Reg also attacked Sinn Féin's denials of ongoing IRA activity, saying that they were "sapping credibility out of politics" and must be reversed if effective devolution is to be achieved at Stormont. He criticized the current administration, saying that it was "the worst so far" and was "failing on nearly all fronts." The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) had also withdrawn its ministers from the executive last month, but returned to government after the security report's release. The report's findings have raised questions about the future of the power-sharing government at Stormont, with many calling for greater transparency and accountability from Sinn Féin. Mr. Nesbitt will address the UUP's annual conference later today, where he is expected to reiterate his party's commitment to principled politics and its determination to hold Sinn Féin to account. The party's decision to withdraw from government has been seen as a significant moment in Northern Irish politics, and one that has sparked a wider debate about the future of the power-sharing executive. As Mr. Nesbitt said, "I set out to do the right thing" by removing the UUP from the executive, and the report has shown that his decision was justified.

Maharashtra Farmers Suspend Protests After Government Agrees to Loan Waiver In a significant development, farmers in the western state of Maharashtra have temporarily called off their protests after the state government agreed to a loan waiver for all sections of farmers. The decision comes after a week-long agitation, which began on June 1, demanding better prices for their produce and relief from debts. Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced on Sunday that a committee would be formed to decide on the specific terms of the loan waiver. The farmers, however, have warned that they will restart their protests if a satisfactory decision is not taken by July 25. "We have decided to temporarily call off our agitation, but if no concrete decision is taken, we will restart our stir," said farmer leader Raju Shetti. The loan waiver is expected to put pressure on the state's fiscal health, according to experts. Meanwhile, a similar standoff continues in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, where five farmers died in police shooting last week. The state government has promised to consider a complete reversal of loans, but farmers are demanding a more comprehensive change in agricultural policy to prevent them from becoming indebted. The issue of loan waivers has also been raised by farmers in other states, with Uttar Pradesh and Telangana already announcing similar measures. The situation remains tense, with farmers across the country seeking better support and relief from their debts.

Emergency services launched a major search operation in Dumfries after a man fell into the River Nith on Sunday evening. The incident occurred near the rowing club in the Greensands area at around 21:00, prompting a large-scale response from multiple agencies. Police Scotland, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service, and the Maritime and Coastguard Agency were among those involved in the search. The man has been identified as 41-year-old Brian Cowie from Queensberry Street in Dumfries. He is described as being around 6ft tall and was last seen wearing a dark jacket, grey hooded top, light-colored jeans, and grey/black shoes. Extensive searches were carried out along the River Nith, downstream to the Solway Estuary, on Sunday night and resumed at first light on Monday morning. A helicopter from the Maritime and Coastguard Agency at Prestwick was also deployed to assist in the operation. Inspector Rory Caldow urged anyone with information to come forward, as searches continue with the help of volunteers from the Moffat Mountain Rescue Team. The public's assistance is crucial in locating Brian Cowie, and police are appealing for anyone who may have witnessed the incident to contact them immediately.

England's rugby hopes have been dealt a blow with the news that promising young flanker Sam Underhill will undergo surgery for a shoulder injury. The 20-year-old Ospreys player suffered a high-grade AC joint injury in training and is expected to be sidelined for around four months. This puts his participation in the autumn internationals in jeopardy, despite England coach Eddie Jones previously tipping him for a role. Underhill had broken into Ospreys' first team last season, making 16 appearances and impressing with his performances. Born in the US, he has pledged his allegiance to England, although he could also qualify for Wales in the future under residency rules. Underhill will have surgery later this week, followed by a rehabilitation program. Ospreys' medical performance manager Chris Towers confirmed the injury and prognosis, saying Underhill's rehabilitation will commence after surgery. This injury is a significant setback for the young player's promising career.

The infamous "Essex Boys" murder case has once again resurfaced, with the family of one of the convicted men, Jack Whomes, continuing to fight for his freedom. On December 6, 1995, three drug dealers, Craig Rolfe, Tony Tucker, and Pat Tate, were shot dead in a Range Rover in Rettendon, Essex. The brutal ambush was reportedly over an unsellable consignment of cannabis. Whomes and his co-defendant, Michael Steele, were jailed for life in 1998 for their murders, following a high-profile trial at the Old Bailey. Despite their convictions, both Whomes and Steele have always maintained their innocence. Whomes' mother, Pam, 77, remains resolute in her belief that her son is innocent and is now pinning her hopes on fresh evidence to overturn his conviction. "He wouldn't put us through this if he had done it," she said. "He would have been out 10 years ago if he admitted it, but he won't confess to something he didn't do." Mrs. Whomes' determination is unwavering, and she hopes to see her son walk out of prison before she passes away. However, not everyone shares Mrs. Whomes' doubts about the conviction. Former Detective Superintendent David Bright, who played a key role in the original investigation, is adamant that justice was served. "I have no doubts whatsoever about the conviction," he said. "It was a long and very thorough trial, and the decision was unanimous by the jury. They were very satisfied with the evidence." Bright also pointed out that the defendants have exhausted almost every avenue for appeal, only to have their claims rejected. The case against Whomes and Steele was built largely on the testimony of a police informant, which was corroborated by mobile phone records. However, these records have since been called into question, casting a shadow of doubt over the conviction. Despite this, two appeals have already been turned down, and Whomes' third bid for freedom was recently rejected before reaching the appeal stage. His legal team is now working to overturn this decision, although the nature of the fresh evidence they claim to have is being kept under wraps. Meanwhile, Michael Steele is also pursuing a separate attempt to overturn his conviction. Whomes, a father of two, is currently detained in HMP Whitemoor in Cambridgeshire, where he has been teaching and has gained an impressive 27 City and Guilds qualifications. His mother remains hopeful that one day he will be exonerated and released from prison. "I think we've got a hell of a struggle the way the legal system is, but I really believe that he will eventually walk out," she said. The "Essex Boys" case continues to be a source of fascination and debate, with the 2000 film starring Sean Bean cementing its place in popular culture. As the fight for justice continues, one thing is certain – the case will remain a topic of discussion for years to come.

Breakthrough in Ultrasound Technology: Dundee University Researchers Create "Sonic Screwdriver" In a groundbreaking achievement, researchers at Dundee University have successfully created a machine that utilizes ultrasound to lift and rotate a rubber disc floating in a cylinder of water. This innovative technology has the potential to revolutionize the field of surgery, enabling more precise and non-invasive treatments. The study, led by Dr. Mike MacDonald of the Institute for Medical Science and Technology (IMSAT), has demonstrated the ability to steer ultrasound waves to specific locations, allowing for more effective treatments. The machine, dubbed the "sonic screwdriver," uses energy from an ultrasound array to form a beam that can both push and rotate objects. By shaping the beam into a helix or vortex, the researchers were able to cause the rubber disc to rotate, a feat that was previously thought to be impossible with ultrasound waves. This breakthrough has significant implications for the medical field, where ultrasound is already used to treat a range of conditions without requiring invasive surgery. The ability to precisely control ultrasound waves could enable surgeons to target specific areas of the body, making treatments more effective and reducing the risk of complications. Additionally, the technology could be used to guide drug capsules through the body, activating them at precise locations, such as inside tumors. The possibilities for this technology are vast, and the researchers are eager to explore its potential applications. The "sonic screwdriver" is part of the EU-funded nanoporation project, which aims to develop new techniques for targeted drug delivery and cellular surgery. The research is also connected to the UK-wide Sonotweezers project, which seeks to bring dexterity and flexibility to ultrasonic manipulation, with applications in regenerative medicine, tissue engineering, and physics. Dr. MacDonald noted that the experiment not only confirms a fundamental physics theory but also demonstrates a new level of control over ultrasound beams. "Like Doctor Who's own device, our sonic screwdriver is capable of much more than just spinning things around," he said. The results of the study will be published in the American Physical Society's journal Physical Review Letters, and the researchers are excited to continue exploring the potential of this innovative technology. With its potential to revolutionize the field of surgery and beyond, the "sonic screwdriver" is an exciting development that could have a significant impact on the medical field and beyond.

Heavyweight Champion Wladimir Klitschko has been cleared to fight after a calf injury forced him to withdraw from his title defense against Tyson Fury. The 39-year-old Ukrainian was set to face Fury on October 24, but the bout was postponed due to the injury. However, it has now been revealed that Klitschko has been declared fit to fight on November 28. The news was announced by Fury himself on Twitter, and the two fighters are now awaiting confirmation from broadcaster Sky Sports to proceed with the new date. Fury, 27, has been vocal about his opponent, previously calling him "boring." The Bolton fighter has been unbeaten in 24 fights and successfully defended his European title in March. Klitschko, who has been unbeaten for 11 years, will be putting his WBA, IBF, and WBO titles on the line in what will be his record-breaking 28th heavyweight title bout. The highly anticipated fight is expected to be a thrilling matchup between two of the sport's top heavyweights.

A double-decker bus destined for Ivory Coast was completely destroyed by a fire on the A11 near Cambridge yesterday. The bus, which was purchased for approximately £6,000, had just been collected from a garage in Croydon and was being driven to Norfolk to be fitted out before its journey to Africa. Fortunately, the three people on board, including the owner Eunice Jokrasset, escaped without injury. The driver managed to steer the bus into a layby on the busy dual carriageway, near Worsted Lodge, after the fire broke out at around 13:30 BST. Ms Jokrasset, who runs the Crown Inn in Smallburgh, north Norfolk, had been fundraising for the bus since February, collecting books and school equipment to fill the vehicle. The community had planned to hold an opening ceremony later this month before the bus was shipped to Ivory Coast in September. The fire service reported that the blaze started in the engine compartment. Ms Jokrasset expressed her devastation, saying "I cannot explain how I'm feeling. It's dreadful." The incident is a significant setback for the community's charitable efforts, and it remains to be seen how they will recover from the loss of the bus.

Wanda Campbell, 43, has lost her appeal against a jail sentence for embezzling £110,000. Campbell, from Auchenmalg, was found guilty at Dumfries Sheriff Court of taking money from James Haugh between 2012 and 2013. She was ordered to pay £110,000 in compensation. The High Court in Edinburgh heard her appeal, which was denied by Lord Brodie and Lord Drummond Young. Campbell had been entrusted with the money for business cash flow, but instead used it for personal expenses, leading to the business's liquidation in 2016. Her conviction and sentence remain in place.

A Heartwarming Reunion: Shamsher Sherin Finds Safety in the UK In a touching turn of events, 13-year-old Shamsher Sherin, a young refugee from Afghanistan, has been reunited with his father in Birmingham, UK. The boy's story gained international attention after he was interviewed by a pop star at a Calais refugee camp, where he had been living for two months. Shamsher's tale of resilience and determination moved the singer to apologize "on behalf of my country for what we've put you through." Shamsher's journey to the UK was not an easy one. He fled his home in Afghanistan and traveled to the Calais refugee camp, where he attempted to cross the border into the UK on several occasions. During one failed attempt, he was kicked and slapped by police. However, he persevered, driven by the hope of reuniting with his father, Hazrat Gul Sherin, who has lived in Birmingham since fleeing Afghanistan in 2005. Thanks to the efforts of the Home Office, Shamsher was among dozens of child migrants brought to the UK on Wednesday to join their families. His father, who had been anxiously waiting for news of his son's safe arrival, was overjoyed to be reunited with Shamsher. According to translator Mohammad Ishaq, Mr. Sherin was "very happy" and "emotional" when he received the news, saying "my dream is completed now." The pop star who interviewed Shamsher took to Twitter to express her relief and happiness at the news of his safe arrival, saying "So happy to see that Sham Sher made it to the UK safely and won't be risking his life jumping on to moving vehicles." Shamsher is now looking forward to starting a new life in England, where he hopes to attend school and build a brighter future. His story serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of compassion and support for refugees and migrants seeking a safer and more stable life.

Bordeaux's Jeremy Menez underwent surgery after a collision with Lorient's Didier Ndong. The 29-year-old was accidentally hit on the head, injuring his ear. Menez had joined Bordeaux just three days prior. He was operated on under local anesthesia and the team wishes him a speedy recovery. Ndong apologized, calling the incident "completely involuntary" with unfortunate consequences. Both teams hope to see Menez back in Ligue 1 action soon.

A fire broke out at the iconic Trellick Tower in Kensal Town, prompting the evacuation of up to 200 people. The blaze, which is believed to have been caused by a discarded cigarette, engulfed a flat in the Grade II listed building just before 9:30pm. Eight fire crews responded to the scene, bringing the fire under control. Fortunately, no injuries were reported. Trellick Tower, designed by Ernő Goldfinger in the brutalist style, has been featured in numerous films and TV shows, and was the inspiration for JG Ballard's novel "High Rise". The incident highlights the importance of fire safety and responsible disposal of smoking materials.

Long-time Labour Party member John Ferrett has announced his resignation from the party after 27 years, citing the party's shift under Jeremy Corbyn's leadership as the reason. Ferrett, who stood in general elections in 2010 and 2015, stated that the party has become a "protest movement that has no interest in winning power". This decision comes after Corbyn's re-election as Labour leader, where he secured 61.8% of the vote, defeating challenger Owen Smith. Ferrett expressed his disappointment with the party's direction, saying it has become "almost impossible to win" in places like Portsmouth, where Labour traditionally had a strong base. He called on members of the Parliamentary Labour Party to create a new political party as a "reasoned social democratic alternative" to the Conservative government. Ferrett will continue to serve as an independent councillor in the Paulsgrove Ward and plans to consult with residents. The Portsmouth Labour Party has expressed disappointment at Ferrett's resignation, with co-chair Sion Reynolds calling on him to resign his council seat to allow residents to "have their say" in a by-election. Meanwhile, Shadow Foreign Secretary Emily Thornberry has urged party unity, stating that opponents of Corbyn need to work for the "greater good" by providing a strong opposition. Ferrett's resignation highlights the ongoing divisions within the Labour Party, with some members calling for a new direction and others urging unity under Corbyn's leadership.

New rules set to take effect in 2016 will revolutionize the way La Liga sells its broadcasting rights. In a bid to modernize and bring the league in line with the Premier League, the rights to show La Liga will be pooled and sold collectively. This change is expected to increase revenue for broadcasters, with the bigger clubs still benefiting, albeit to a lesser extent. The new ruling will regulate the transmission rights for the Spanish first and second divisions, as well as the Copa del Rey and Super Cup competitions. Under the new system, 90% of the total revenue will be distributed among La Liga clubs, with 50% shared equally and the remaining 50% divided based on performance and size. The remaining 10% will go to second division clubs, with 70% of that amount divided equally. According to Sport Ministry spokesman Miguel Cardenal, this change is necessary for Spain to "adapt to modern times." He cited the significant revenue disparity between the Premier League and La Liga, noting that the last-placed Premier League team earned more than current Spanish champions Atletico Madrid. The move aims to bridge this gap, with the Premier League recently selling its television rights for a record £5.136bn.

It's been 20 years since the hit Channel 4 comedy "Father Ted" first aired, and its legacy continues to captivate audiences across the UK and Ireland. The show, which follows the misadventures of three priests and their housekeeper on remote Craggy Island, has become a cult classic with its unique brand of humor. Pauline McLynn, who played the lovable and eccentric housekeeper Mrs. Doyle, recalls the show's humble beginnings. "We didn't think anybody would watch it, or notice it was on," she said in an interview with BBC NI's Good Morning Ulster. "Although we found it funny, that doesn't necessarily mean everybody else would." Despite initial doubts, "Father Ted" went on to become a massive success, attracting a wide range of fans with its simple yet hilarious storylines. McLynn attributes the show's enduring appeal to its innocence and absurdity. "It's about these four people who are stuck with one another, and every week we start at the same place, which is hell," she explained. "It's so simple and so stupid that everybody can enjoy it. By stupid, I mean desperately funny." The show's catchphrases, including Mrs. Doyle's iconic "You will, you will, you will" as she presses tea upon newcomers, have become ingrained in popular culture. McLynn has gone on to appear in other notable roles, including her current stint as Yvonne, Charlie Cotton's mother, in the BBC's "Eastenders." However, she confessed that it took her years to be able to offer someone tea on screen without being reminded of her "Father Ted" days. The show's impact extends beyond its original run, with new generations of fans discovering its humor. McLynn noted that her friend's children, aged five and seven, are "totally devoted" to the show, demonstrating its timeless appeal. The anniversary of "Father Ted" is also a bittersweet reminder of the passing of Dermot Morgan, who played the lovable rogue Fr. Ted. Morgan died suddenly in 1998 at the age of 45, leaving behind a legacy that continues to inspire and entertain. McLynn fondly remembered her co-star, saying, "The best thing would be if he was here. He'd be dining out on Father Ted. But he will never grow old, and he will always be gorgeous." As "Father Ted" celebrates its 20th anniversary, its influence on British comedy and its enduring popularity are a testament to the show's genius and the talents of its cast.

Renowned Artist David Hockney Intervenes to Protect Beloved Country Lane David Hockney, one of the most celebrated artists of our time, has taken it upon himself to ensure that a roadwork project in East Yorkshire does not cause lasting damage to a picturesque country lane that has inspired many of his works. Woldgate, a tranquil and unspoiled lane, has been the subject of Hockney's paintings, drawings, photographs, and films for several years, and the artist is determined to preserve its natural beauty. Hockney has been working closely with roadwork managers, inviting them to his studio to showcase his latest paintings of Woldgate and stressing the importance of minimizing the impact of the construction project on the surrounding environment. The project involves laying a new gas pipe for the town, which requires digging up the road. However, Hockney has provided the workers with a list of specific spots to avoid damaging, including a tree stump and a bluebell wood. According to John O'Grady, communications manager for Northern Gas Networks, Hockney's concerns were taken seriously, and the company has made a concerted effort to avoid disrupting the environment. "His concern was that, because we are putting in this massive new gas pipeline, the environment could have been affected detrimentally," O'Grady said. "We're happy to work with Mr. Hockney and the other local people to ensure that the construction project is carried out with minimal disruption to the natural beauty of the area." Hockney's love affair with Woldgate is evident in the numerous works he has created inspired by the lane. A photographic piece, comprising three 27-foot images of the Bridlington end of the road, taken at different times of the year, has recently gone on display at Salts Mill in Saltaire, West Yorkshire. The exhibition also features pictures created by Hockney on his iPad and iPhone, as well as portraits of his family, friends, and acquaintances drawn on a computer. Next year, the Royal Academy in London will host a major exhibition of Hockney's works, including his Woldgate series. The show will feature a film made by Hockney using 18 cameras, which will be displayed on multiple screens. The artist has described Woldgate as "a lovely little bit of England that is not spoiled," and his efforts to protect it demonstrate his deep appreciation for the natural world and his commitment to preserving its beauty for future generations. As O'Grady noted, Hockney's involvement in the roadwork project has been constructive, and the company is grateful for his input. "He has been down several times and kept a very close eye on what we've been doing," O'Grady said. "We're happy to work with Mr. Hockney and the other local people to ensure that the construction project is carried out with minimal disruption to the natural beauty of the area." Hockney's dedication to protecting Woldgate is a testament to the power of art to inspire and motivate people to take action in preserving the world around us.

Concerns over the availability of Mothers Pride Scottish Plain bread were sparked after a post on Facebook suggested that only one factory was now producing it due to falling sales. The post, which was shared over 13,000 times, prompted an outpouring of support from loyal consumers. However, Hovis, the firm behind the Mothers Pride brand, has reassured fans that it has no plans to stop producing the bread. A spokeswoman for Hovis expressed appreciation for the strong response from Scottish consumers, acknowledging the brand's loyal following. Mothers Pride has been a staple in Scotland for 80 years, with its unique batch baking process setting it apart from other breads. The bread is made in a large baking tray, resulting in a crust only on the top and bottom, unlike pan loaves which are baked in individual trays. The brand's rich history and cultural significance were even immortalized in the classic Scots folk song "Jeely Piece" in the 1960s. Despite a decline in sales, Mothers Pride remains a beloved favorite, and its production will continue at the only batch plant left in the UK, located in Glasgow. Fans of the bread can rest assured that it will remain available, thanks to the dedication of its loyal consumer base.

A talented border collie from Glemsford, Suffolk, has made headlines for retrieving over 20 balls from the open space behind her home. Maggie, the skilled canine, belongs to Meg Brace and has been featured in the East Anglian Daily Times for her impressive ability. The mystery of the missing balls was solved after a public appeal, revealing they had been taken from the Epic Youth Club's kickabouts at the nearby village hall. Youth club manager Stuart Ayling praised Maggie, calling her "one remarkable pet." Maggie's owner, Meg Brace, noted that while her pet can be challenging at times, her talent for retrieving balls is undeniable. Interestingly, Ms Brace's other border collie, Gizmo, has a unique talent of its own - picking up litter from the playing field and bringing it to her to dispose of properly. The incident has highlighted the issue of missing footballs, which Mr Ayling attributed to older teenagers taking them without permission.

Armed police are at Meteor Street in Adamsdown, with a cordon in place. A man in his late teens to early 20s was stabbed, suffering serious but non-life-threatening injuries. He was taken to the University Hospital of Wales, as officers actively search for the offender.

American Couple Sentenced for Murder in Bali A US couple has been sentenced for the brutal murder of the woman's mother, whose body was found stuffed inside a suitcase in Bali last August. Tommy Schaefer, 21, was sentenced to 18 years in prison for the killing of Sheila von Wiese-Mack, 62, a wealthy American academic. His partner, 19-year-old Heather Mack, received a 10-year sentence for her role in the crime. The presiding judge described the killing as "sadistic" and stated that Schaefer's actions had disturbed the public. However, the judge took into account Schaefer's remorse and politeness during the trial, which prevented him from receiving a harsher sentence. Mack's sentence was also influenced by the fact that she had recently given birth to a baby. The couple's troubles began when von Wiese-Mack discovered that her daughter was pregnant, leading to a heated argument at a five-star resort. Schaefer claimed he was defending himself after von Wiese-Mack became angry, and hit her with a fruit bowl. The couple then hid her body in a suitcase and left it in a taxi, which was later discovered by the driver. The police found the couple at another hotel in Bali, leading to their arrest and subsequent conviction.

Lance Bombardier Ben Parkinson Honoured at Buckingham Palace Lance Bombardier Ben Parkinson, a paratrooper who suffered severe injuries in a bomb attack in Afghanistan in 2006, has received a special honour from the Prince of Wales at Buckingham Palace. The ceremony, which took place recently, saw Parkinson recognised for his bravery and determination in the face of adversity. Parkinson, who carried the Olympic flame through his hometown last year on his prosthetic legs, was praised by Prince Charles as an "inspiration". The paratrooper, who broke his pelvis, back, and arm, and lost both legs in the attack, was visibly moved by the Prince's words. "I was surprised at how much Prince Charles knew about me," he said. "He said I was an inspiration. It made me feel so proud." In addition to carrying the Olympic flame, Parkinson has also taken part in a charity trek in Norway, where he and a group of injured veterans travelled 65 miles across the Hardangervidda mountain in challenging conditions. The expedition, organised by the charity Pilgrim Bandits, marked the 70th anniversary of a World War II mission. Parkinson's courage and resilience have made him a role model for many, and his honour at Buckingham Palace is a testament to his inspiring story.

US Deploys Additional Armored Brigade to Europe in Response to Russian Aggression The United States has announced plans to deploy an additional armored brigade to Europe, bringing the total number of brigades to three. This significant reinforcement is seen as a response to increasing tensions with Russia, particularly in the wake of its annexation of Crimea in 2014. The move is the most substantial US reinforcement of NATO since the conflict in Ukraine began. According to General Philip Breedlove, the senior US commander in Europe, the additional presence demonstrates a "strong and balanced approach" to reassuring NATO allies and partners in the face of Russian aggression. Each brigade, comprising approximately 4,200 soldiers, will rotate through the region for nine months, bringing with them modernized equipment and military vehicles. The deployment is part of a broader effort to bolster European defense, with the Pentagon announcing plans to quadruple its budget for European defense in 2017. The increased military presence will enable the US to conduct more frequent and extensive military exercises in the region, enhancing its ability to respond to potential threats. The move has been welcomed by NATO allies, who have expressed concerns about Russian intentions in Eastern Europe. British Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond noted that the situation in Ukraine has "gone backwards" in recent months, with increased ceasefire violations. Russia, however, has accused NATO of using the situation in Ukraine as a pretext to move closer to its borders. The deployment has also sparked speculation about the US military's plans for the post-Obama era, particularly given the views of Republican presidential frontrunner Donald Trump, who has criticized the economic cost of US foreign policy. With 62,000 US service personnel already permanently based in Europe, the additional brigade will further strengthen the US military presence on the continent. The US has 21 bases across Europe, with 25,000 army soldiers currently stationed there. The new deployment will add 4,200 more soldiers to this number, demonstrating the US commitment to European security and defense.

Northern Ireland's unemployment rate has dropped to 5.2%, its lowest level since 2008. Official figures show 300 people came off the jobless register in March, bringing the total to 31,500. Although this decrease is a positive sign, the region still lags behind the UK average of 4.7%. The employment rate also trails the rest of the UK, with 69% of the workforce in employment compared to 75% nationwide. Economist Dr Esmond Birnie notes that the data reveals "a lost decade" with little improvement in employment figures over the past 10 years. The labour market has also seen a shift towards more self-employed and part-time workers. Despite the progress, there is still work to be done to bridge the employment gap with the rest of the UK.

Conservative Party Strategist Lynton Crosby has assured Tory MPs that Labour's lead in the opinion polls is fragile and vulnerable to attack. At a private meeting of the 1922 committee on Tuesday, Crosby presented private polling data indicating that Labour is weak on key issues such as welfare, deficit reduction, and Europe. The meeting, attended by Prime Minister David Cameron and Chancellor George Osborne, aimed to sharpen the party's campaigning strategy ahead of the 2015 general election. Crosby, who successfully ran the 2005 Tory election campaign and Boris Johnson's London mayoral campaign, advised MPs to target Labour leader Ed Miliband and shadow chancellor Ed Balls, who are perceived as weak by some floating voters. He argued that the pair should be held accountable for the country's economic problems. The Conservatives believe Labour has made a significant mistake by suggesting pensioners should lose their winter fuel allowance, and plan to capitalize on this in their upcoming campaigns. With Crosby's guidance, the Tories are gearing up to launch a strong attack on Labour's policies, which they claim will lead to more spending, borrowing, and debt.

President Obama has formally requested that Congress raise the nation's debt ceiling to $16.4 trillion, citing the need for further borrowing to meet existing spending commitments. The proposal, which must be voted on within 15 days, aims to avoid a repeat of last year's near-default crisis. In a letter, Mr. Obama emphasized the necessity of increasing the debt limit to ensure the government can pay its bills. The move is expected to pass, but it will likely provide Republicans with ammunition to criticize the president's handling of deficit reduction. The issue has been a point of contention between the administration and Congress, with an uneasy truce reached last year over long-term deficit reduction plans. To avoid a default, the administration has had to tap into the Exchange Stabilization Fund, and may need to take additional measures, such as suspending pension fund reinvestments, until the debt limit increase is secured.

Wales ended their friendly tournament with a 1-1 draw against Hungary. Henrietta Csiszar scored early for Hungary, but 17-year-old substitute Charlie Estcourt leveled the score on 75 minutes. The result marked Wales' second draw and second defeat in the tournament, with a total of four goals scored. Hungary, ranked 42nd in Fifa's rankings, finished third in Group A after beating the Republic of Ireland 1-0 earlier. Wales finished third in Group B following a 1-0 loss to the Czech Republic. The tournament's final match will feature Group winners Austria and Poland in Larnaca.

A trial is underway at Nottingham Crown Court for Sukhraj Singh Atwal, a 29-year-old man accused of brutally murdering 74-year-old Satnam Singh in Derby. The prosecution alleges that Atwal repeatedly stamped and jumped on Mr. Singh, causing severe injuries that ultimately led to his death. The incident occurred on July 23, 2015, as Mr. Singh was walking to a temple where he volunteered in the early hours of the morning. According to evidence presented in court, Mr. Singh suffered 41 fractures to his ribs, lacerations to his heart, and blunt force injuries to his head and face. The prosecution claims that Atwal's car was seen on local CCTV footage near the scene of the crime, entering the area immediately before the attack and leaving four minutes later. Although the beating itself was not caught on camera, footage from a nearby garage forecourt appears to show Atwal inspecting his light-colored trousers. The prosecution also alleges that Atwal returned to the scene several times, wearing different trousers, to observe the aftermath of the attack. Atwal was initially arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving, but was later arrested on suspicion of murder in April 2016 after forensic tests determined that Mr. Singh had not been hit by a car. Examination of Atwal's phone revealed that he had traveled to a remote location near Carsington Water, where the prosecution believes he disposed of his trousers. The trial is ongoing, with Atwal denying the murder charge. The court will continue to hear evidence in the coming days to determine Atwal's fate.

Team Sky principal Dave Brailsford has expressed his pride and patriotism ahead of the Tour de France, despite facing intense scrutiny over the team's use of banned substances. Brailsford, who has been at the helm of the team since its inception, has been under fire for the team's handling of Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) and the contents of a medical package sent to Sir Bradley Wiggins in 2011. However, Brailsford remains defiant, stating that he has always conducted himself and the team with the utmost integrity. "I've been involved in this sport a long time, and I've tried to do it absolutely in the way that I've always thought it should be done," he said. "I wouldn't want to be doing anything else. I'm proud of cycling in Britain, I'm proud of everything that's been achieved, I'm proud of these guys, proud of Team Sky. I love it, I'm going nowhere." Brailsford's comments come as Team Sky prepares to defend its title at the Tour de France, which begins on Saturday. The team is seeking its fifth win in six years, with Chris Froome aiming for his fourth Tour de France title. Froome, who has been the subject of doping allegations in the past, expressed his full support for Brailsford and the team. "I don't have any trust issues, I can't make it any more plain," he said. Froome, who is close to signing a new contract with Team Sky that would extend his stay until 2021, acknowledged that the team's reputation has been tarnished by the controversy surrounding TUEs and the medical package sent to Wiggins. However, he believes that the team has done nothing wrong and that the criticism is unfair. "Certainly I've learned to grow a thicker skin over the years and I understand where it's coming from given cycling's history," he said. Despite the challenges facing the team, Brailsford remains committed to his "zero tolerance" policy on doping. He has faced intense questioning from the media and lawmakers, including a grilling from the Culture, Media and Sport Committee in December. However, he remains steadfast in his denial of any wrongdoing and is confident that the team will emerge from the controversy with its reputation intact. As the Tour de France gets underway, Team Sky will be looking to put the controversy behind them and focus on winning another title. With Froome leading the charge, they will be a force to be reckoned with, and Brailsford will be hoping that his team can prove their doubters wrong once again.

UK Furniture Market Sees Mixed Results as Consumers Play Catch-Up The UK furniture market has seen a mixed bag of results, with upmarket sofa retailer DFS experiencing a significant boost in sales, while home furnishings retailer Dunelm saw a decline in sales. According to retail analyst Richard Hyman, the market is cyclical, and consumers are playing catch-up after delaying big-ticket purchases during the financial crisis. DFS, which sponsored Team GB at the Rio Olympics, reported a 7.1% increase in annual sales to £756m, driven by a surge in demand for its high-end sofas, including brands like French Connection. Online sales also saw a significant increase, rising 15.6% over the year. The company's chairman, Richard Baker, expressed confidence in the company's ability to weather the uncertainty surrounding Brexit, citing its 47-year history of navigating economic turbulence. In contrast, Dunelm, known for its duvets and curtains, saw a 3.8% decline in same-store sales in the first quarter, attributed to the unusually warm weather that kept consumers outdoors and away from its stores. However, online sales continued to grow, with home delivery sales up 17.9%. The company is looking forward to the second quarter, which includes the Christmas and New Year period, when it plans to invest in extra seasonal space. The mixed results reflect the ongoing recovery of the furniture market, which has not yet returned to its pre-crisis peak in 2007. According to DFS, the market remains 20% smaller in value than its peak, but has recovered from the low point reached in 2011. Retail analyst Patrick O'Brien warned that 2017 may be a tough year for retailers due to the sharp fall in the value of the pound following the UK's vote to leave the EU, which may force companies to pass on higher costs to consumers. Despite the challenges, DFS remains optimistic about its prospects, with Baker stating that the company has "weathered many forms of political and economic turbulence" and is well-positioned to navigate the uncertainty surrounding Brexit. As consumers continue to play catch-up on big-ticket purchases, it remains to be seen how the furniture market will fare in the coming year. One thing is certain, however: the market will be closely watched as retailers navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by the UK's decision to leave the EU.

A man in his 40s, who was acquitted of rape charges last year, is now facing a new challenge as North Yorkshire Police seeks to impose a permanent sexual risk order on him. The order, which was initially imposed in December and extended in January, requires the man to disclose any planned sexual activity to the police at least 24 hours in advance, as well as provide details of his partners, including their name, address, and date of birth. The man, who claims the complainant in his rape trial had consented to sex, has been charged with breaching the terms of the order after refusing to give police the PIN to his phone. He has accused North Yorkshire Police of "sour grapes" in applying for the order, which he believes has devastated his personal life and contravened his human rights. "I had more freedom in prison," the man said, speaking after an adjourned hearing at York Magistrates' Court on Wednesday. "I'm in a state of shock, I cannot believe this is how the justice system works." He claimed that the order has made it impossible for him to form relationships, saying "Can you imagine, 24 hours before sex? Come on." He gave the example of trying to ask a woman out on a date, only to have to inform her that the police would need to be notified beforehand. The man's trial heard that he had an interest in sado-masochistic sex, which he claims was misunderstood by a doctor he had spoken to. He believes that this misunderstanding was seized upon by police and used as evidence against him. He credits the popularity of the book "50 Shades of Grey" with helping to normalize his interests and aid his defense. Sexual risk orders were introduced in England and Wales last year and can be applied to anyone who the police believe poses a risk of sexual harm, regardless of whether they have been convicted of a crime. The orders are civil and can be imposed by magistrates at the request of police. In this case, the police believe that the man poses a risk of sexual harm, despite his acquittal on rape charges. The case is due back in court on July 14, ahead of a hearing on August 19, which will decide whether to grant the police's application to make the interim order permanent. If the order is made permanent, the man could face up to five years in prison if he fails to comply with its terms. The man's lawyers will argue that the order is an infringement of his human rights and that it is not proportionate to the risk he poses. North Yorkshire Police has declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing legal proceedings. However, the man's case has raised questions about the use of sexual risk orders and the balance between public safety and individual freedom. As the case continues to make its way through the courts, it is likely to spark further debate about the role of these orders in preventing sexual harm.

Professor John Beetlestone, founder of the science discovery centre Techniquest in Cardiff, has passed away at the age of 84. The centre announced his death on Friday, following a short illness. Beetlestone dedicated his life to making science and technology accessible and enjoyable for all. Techniquest's chief executive, Lesley Kirkpatrick, praised his contribution to scientific education, saying it will "benefit children across Wales for generations to come." Beetlestone founded Techniquest in 1985 in a gas showroom opposite Cardiff Castle. The centre has since moved to Cardiff Bay and expanded to include a location at Glyndwr University's campus in Wrexham. His legacy will continue to educate and inspire future generations of scientists. Beetlestone's impact on scientific education in Wales will be remembered and celebrated for years to come.

Petra Kvitova's recovery from a stabbing incident is progressing as planned. The 27-year-old tennis champion was attacked by an intruder in the Czech Republic. Initially, doctors estimated a six-month hiatus from competition. However, Kvitova's spokesman, Karel Tejkal, reports her psychological recovery is "very encouraging." She has been fitness training in the Canary Islands and can use her hand for daily activities without issue, despite some weakness. A return date remains uncertain, with Tejkal stating "no-one can give a concrete date" for her comeback to tennis. Kvitova's determination and progress offer hope for her eventual return.

Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust has been granted foundation trust status, giving it the autonomy to set its own financial and operational priorities. This change applies to John Radcliffe, Churchill, Horton, and the Nuffield Orthopaedic Centre hospitals. As a result, local residents can now become members and serve as governors, allowing them to have a greater say in the decision-making process. According to Chief Executive Sir Jonathan Michael, the trust's finances are currently in good shape, but he acknowledges that this is no guarantee of success. "You've still got to run the business effectively and deliver operational performance," he said. The new status, granted by Monitor, the regulator of NHS services in England, is a recognition of the trust's quality services and efficiency. The GMB union, which represents some of the trust's staff, has welcomed the change but highlighted concerns about low pay and job insecurity within the organization. The union's steward, Mark Ladbrooke, urged the trust to address these issues, as well as invest in staff accommodation and resolve long-standing problems with car parking for patients and staff. With its new status, the trust can now manage its services to better meet the needs of the local community.

Government Relaxes Bird Flu Restrictions in England, Allowing Free-Range Birds to Roam The UK government has announced a relaxation of bird flu restrictions in England, allowing poultry farmers to let their birds roam freely outdoors once again. The decision, made by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), brings the rules for poultry in higher-risk areas in line with the rest of England. As of Thursday, normally free-range eggs will no longer require stickers indicating that the birds have been kept indoors for their welfare. The move affects flocks that have been housed or placed under netting to protect them from wild birds, which can carry the highly pathogenic avian flu H5N8 virus. According to Chief Veterinary Officer Nigel Gibbens, the latest evidence suggests that the risk of infection from wild birds has decreased, making it safe for kept birds to be let outside. However, poultry and bird keepers in England are still required to comply with strict biosecurity measures to prevent the spread of bird flu. A ban on poultry fairs and gatherings remains in place, and keepers must take steps to reduce the risk of contamination from the environment, where the virus can survive for several weeks in bird droppings. The restrictions were first put in place in December, as the H5N8 virus was circulating in Europe. Since then, there have been several outbreaks of the virus in poultry and wild birds in the UK. While the Scottish government has chosen to maintain restrictions until the end of April, measures in Wales had previously been relaxed. The relaxation of restrictions in England is a welcome move for poultry farmers, who can now resume normal operations and label their eggs as free-range once again.

A wave of vandalism has swept through Orange Halls in County Tyrone, with three separate incidents reported over the weekend. The attacks began on Friday when windows were smashed at Strawletterdallon Orange Hall outside Newtownstewart. The hall was targeted again on Sunday when an oil drum was placed against a door and set alight, causing damage to the door and wall. Meanwhile, Dergina Orange Hall outside Aughnacloy was also vandalized, with windows smashed and paint thrown over the door. The hall, which was built in 2009, was targeted early on Saturday. Nearby, Mullnahunch Orange Hall was defaced with graffiti. Drew Nelson, secretary of the Grand Orange Lodge of Ireland, expressed relief that the Strawletterdallon hall was not destroyed, thanks to the quick thinking of a passing motorist who raised the alarm. "A tyre was placed at the emergency exit and set on fire, with oil poured over it to accelerate the flames," he said. "We are fortunate the hall was not destroyed." The Orange Order has expressed concern over the apparent upsurge in attacks, with Nelson calling for increased police resources to detect those responsible. Ulster Unionist leader Tom Elliott condemned the attacks, blaming "mindless thugs intent on creating community division." The incidents have raised concerns about community tensions in the region.

Breakthrough in Fight Against Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria: Scientists Discover Key to Disrupting Defensive Barrier In a significant breakthrough, researchers have made a major discovery in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, identifying a key protein complex that plays a crucial role in the construction of a defensive barrier that makes these bacteria so difficult to kill. The study, published in the journal Nature, reveals that the protein complex LptDE is responsible for building the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, which are responsible for a wide range of infections, including salmonella and meningitis. Using the intense X-rays of the Diamond Light Source in Oxfordshire, the researchers were able to map the structure of LptDE, revealing a complex process that involves a "path" and a "gate" that allows the protein to pull up lipopolysaccharide "bricks" from inside the bacterium and insert them into the cell wall. By understanding how this process works, the researchers believe that they can develop new drugs that can interfere with LptDE, effectively disrupting the defensive barrier and killing the bacteria. According to Prof Changjiang Dong, from the University of East Anglia's Norwich Medical School, "We identified how LptDE builds up the outer membrane, and we have shown that if we block the path or the gate, the bacteria will die." The researchers believe that by targeting LptDE, they can develop new antibiotics that do not need to get inside the bacteria to be effective, which is a major advantage over existing treatments. The rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is a major public health concern, with many infections becoming increasingly difficult to treat. Gram-negative bacteria, in particular, are notorious for their ability to resist antibiotic treatments, thanks to the impermeability of their lipid-based outer coating. However, by targeting LptDE, researchers believe that they can develop new antibiotics that can effectively kill these bacteria, without the need for the drugs to penetrate the cell wall. The study has been welcomed by experts in the field, who believe that it offers a promising new avenue for the development of antibiotics. Prof Mark Fielder, from the Society for Applied Microbiology, commented, "The work reported is at a very early stage but does offer some potentially useful information in the fight against bacterial resistance." Prof Brendan Wren, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, added, "New antibiotics against gram-negative bacteria, including many hospital superbugs, are notoriously difficult to develop, and the problem is exacerbated as many of these bacteria are increasingly resistant to currently used antibiotics." While the study is still in its early stages, the researchers believe that their discovery has the potential to lead to the development of new antibiotics that can effectively target gram-negative bacteria. As Prof Dong explained, "If the bacteria do not have the outer membrane, they cannot withstand environmental changes, and it also makes it easier for the human immune system to kill them." With the rise of antibiotic-resistant bacteria posing a major threat to public health, this breakthrough offers a glimmer of hope in the fight against these deadly infections.

Tragedy Strikes Nice: Social Media Unites to Offer Help and Support In the wake of the devastating attack in Nice, France, where a lorry plowed into a crowd of people celebrating Bastille Day, social media has become a powerful tool for people to express their grief, offer help, and show solidarity with the victims. The attack, which has left many dead and injured, has sent shockwaves around the world, and social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook have been flooded with messages of condolence, support, and offers of assistance. One of the most heartwarming aspects of the social media response has been the use of the hashtag #PorteOuverte, or "Open Door," which has been used by Twitter users in Nice to offer their homes to those in need of shelter. Many have also offered to provide free transportation, with taxi drivers giving free rides to those in the area. This outpouring of kindness and generosity is a testament to the resilience and compassion of the people of Nice and beyond. As the search for missing loved ones continues, social media has also become a vital tool for people to connect with each other and share information. The hashtag #RechercheNice, or "search Nice," has been used by thousands to post pictures and descriptions of those who are missing, in the hope of finding them. An account called @NiceFindPeople was quickly set up, which has been circulating a list of names of those reported lost, and has been retweeted almost 500 times. One story that has captured the hearts of many is that of Tiava Banner, a Facebook user who lost her 8-month-old baby in the chaos. She posted a desperate plea for help, asking if anyone had seen her baby, and was later able to update her post to say that the baby had been found, thanks to the help of a woman named Joy Ruez. While the BBC has not been able to independently verify this story, its spread shows the power of social media to bring people together and offer hope in times of tragedy. The #JeSuisNice hashtag, which emerged quickly after the attack, has become a symbol of solidarity with the people of Nice, and has been used by celebrities and political figures around the world to express their condolences and support. However, not everyone has been supportive of the hashtag, with some expressing cynicism and frustration at the use of social media to respond to tragedy. Facebook has also played a crucial role in responding to the attack, activating its safety check feature, which allows users in the affected area to let their friends and family know that they are safe. This feature has been widely used, and has helped to alleviate some of the uncertainty and worry that has followed the attack. As France comes to terms with this latest tragedy, social media will continue to play a vital role in bringing people together, offering support, and providing a platform for people to express their grief and outrage. The state of emergency, which was due to end on July 26, will now be extended, and the people of France will need all the support and solidarity they can get in the days and weeks ahead.

British tennis player Kyle Edmund has advanced to the second round of the Delray Beach Open after his opponent, Adrian Mannarino, was penalized a game for unsportsmanlike conduct. Edmund, 22, was leading 6-3 5-0 with a 15-0 advantage when Mannarino smashed a ball out of the court, resulting in the penalty. The Frenchman had earlier kicked a chair and hit a ball towards a ball boy, displaying his frustration. Edmund will face either American Bjorn Fratangelo or Taiwan's Yen-Hsun Lu in the next round. The world number 49 could potentially meet top seed Milos Raonic in the quarter-finals. Meanwhile, Argentina's Juan Martin del Potro is making his 2017 debut at the tournament after a prolonged off-season following his Davis Cup win in November. Edmund's victory comes after a dramatic previous match, where his opponent was defaulted for hitting an umpire with a ball.

English rugby players are set to receive a significant pay boost, with new terms offering over £20,000 per Test match, excluding bonuses. According to RFU chief executive Ian Ritchie, "these are exciting times for English Rugby" with the deal marking a major uplift from the previous agreement. The RFU posted record profits of over £100m last year, following England's World Cup hosting. Despite a disappointing World Cup, England has since achieved success under coach Eddie Jones, winning the Six Nations Grand Slam and a 3-0 series in Australia. The new deal, negotiated by the Rugby Players Association, covers training fees, image rights, and squad performance bonuses.

Aberdeen Hosts Classes to Educate Seniors on Avoiding Online Frauds In an effort to combat cyber scamming, Police Scotland and the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service (COPFS) have launched a series of classes in Aberdeen aimed at educating seniors on how to avoid online frauds. The sessions, specifically designed for individuals over 60, are being held at the city's Stratosphere and are led by Silver City Surfers, an organization that promotes computer literacy among older adults. The classes focus on raising awareness about various types of cyber scams, including those that use email, websites, chatrooms, and message boards. According to David Bernard, COPFS equality ambassador for age, the goal is to empower seniors with the knowledge and confidence to protect themselves from online threats. "Criminals who prey on the vulnerable are particularly detestable," he said. "Through education, we hope to prevent our older generation from falling victim to these scams and inspire confidence in the criminal justice system." Police Scotland's Det Insp Eamonn Keane emphasized the importance of educating all communities about online safety. "We recognize the internet as a vital part of people's lives, and we welcome this opportunity to improve awareness and prevent crime," he said. By working together, the organizations aim to reduce the risk of cyber exploitation and create a safer online environment for everyone.

JBS plans to sell Moy Park as part of a $6bn fundraising effort. The Brazilian firm acquired Moy Park in 2015 for $1.5bn. Headquartered in Northern Ireland, Moy Park employs over 9,000 people, making it one of the region's largest companies. CEO Janet McCollum stated that the company's priority remains "business as usual," focusing on quality and innovation. Despite the potential sale, McCollum expressed confidence in Moy Park's success, citing its strong financial standing and exceptional workforce. The company will continue to operate normally, delivering high-quality products to customers and consumers. Moy Park's future remains uncertain.

Tragedy Strikes on Lake: Boat Capsizes, Killing Over 100 Refugees A devastating boat accident on Lake Albert has resulted in the loss of over 100 lives, with many more feared dead. The boat, which was carrying refugees from the Democratic Republic of Congo back to their home country, capsized due to overloading. With a capacity of only 80 passengers, the vessel was grossly overcrowded, carrying up to 250 people. According to Uganda's Refugees Minister Hillary Onek, rescue operations are underway, involving the police, military, and civilian fishing boats. So far, 107 bodies have been recovered, including 57 children. The exact number of passengers on board remains unknown. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Antonio Guterres, has expressed his shock and condolences, praising the government's rescue efforts. The boat was one of two that departed from Uganda's Hoima district on Saturday, carrying refugees who had chosen to return to eastern DR Congo from a camp in Uganda. The incident highlights the poor safety standards and frequent accidents on Uganda's lakes, often caused by overloading and lack of life jackets. As the rescue operation continues, the international community is left to mourn the loss of life and support the survivors.

Olympic swimmer Adam Peaty returned to his hometown of Uttoxeter to open a redeveloped sports centre. The facility, named after Peaty, features a 25m pool, gym, and sports hall. It's designed to host competitions, with seating for 140 spectators. Peaty, a Commonwealth Games medalist, unveiled the centre on Saturday, bringing new recreational opportunities to the community.

A 43-year-old man was seriously injured when his car crashed on the B6355 Chirnside to Ayton road on Monday. The silver Seat Alhambra struck a tree and came to rest down an embankment at 16:30. The man was taken to Edinburgh Royal Infirmary, where he is now stable. The road was closed for four hours near Peelwalls Farm. Police are investigating and appeal for witnesses to come forward. PC Davy Johnson urges anyone with information to contact them to help establish the circumstances surrounding the accident. The driver's condition is being closely monitored.

A 21-year-old man from Wolverhampton is facing an uncertain future after his application for British citizenship was rejected, leaving him at risk of being returned to his birth country of Botswana. Brian White, who was adopted by a British family at the age of six, has lived in the UK for most of his life, but a technicality has thrown his future into doubt. Mr. White's family moved to the UK from Botswana when he was 15, and he was granted limited leave to remain, rather than indefinite leave, which is required for naturalization. Despite appealing the decision, his application was rejected in 2014. He is now awaiting the outcome of a new application, but the delay has already had significant consequences. Mr. White was forced to turn down a place to study chemistry at Oxford University in 2016 because he was ineligible for student finance. The situation has sparked widespread concern, with a petition set up by Mr. White's friend, Luke Wilcox, gaining over 4,000 signatures and attracting support from celebrities such as journalist Caitlin Moran and writer Philip Pullman. Mr. Wilcox described the situation as "disgusting" and said it would be "terrifying" for Mr. White to be returned to a country where he has no links, family, or friends. The Home Office has acknowledged the urgency of Mr. White's case and has reassured him that it is working to resolve his application as soon as possible. However, the delay has already taken a significant toll on Mr. White, who is trying to stay focused on his future despite the uncertainty. "I don't think I've ever had time to sit down and think about it," he said. "I'm trying my best to get it out of my mind." With the support of his community and high-profile backers, Mr. White is hoping for a positive outcome and the chance to build a secure future in the country he calls home.

A unique art exhibition has opened at the Old Low Lights Heritage Centre in North Shields, aiming to raise funds for the restoration of Tynemouth Pool. The outdoor pool, which was once a popular visitor attraction, has lain derelict since the 1990s. The exhibition features specially commissioned artworks, including a previously unseen print by renowned photographer Sirkka-Liisa Konttinen. The artworks will be auctioned on November 26 to support the refurbishment efforts. The Friends of Tynemouth Outdoor Pool, formed in 2012, has submitted detailed proposals to North Tyneside Council. The exhibition showcases a variety of mediums and artistic approaches, all sharing the common goal of returning the pool to its former glory. A highlight of the exhibition is an illuminated model of the restoration, created in Lego by architectural photographer Steve Mayes. After the exhibition, the model will be displayed at various locations around North Tyneside, raising awareness and support for the pool's restoration. The event is a significant step towards reviving the iconic pool and restoring it to its former beauty.

Tottenham Hotspur's pursuit of West Brom forward Saido Berahino has hit a roadblock after the Baggies rejected two offers for the 22-year-old. West Brom chairman Jeremy Peace has reiterated that Berahino will not be sold during this transfer window, despite Tottenham's interest.
