According to Peace, the offers made by Tottenham were not only too low but also based on stage-payments and add-ons over a long period, which do not reflect Berahino's ability and potential. Peace emphasized that selling their top goalscorer was never on the agenda this summer, and the club would have needed to find a suitable replacement if Berahino were to leave. Tottenham manager Mauricio Pochettino expressed his admiration for Berahino, likening his desire to sign the player to being in love. "It's like when you are in love with some lady," Pochettino said. "There are a lot of women around the world, but you want only one. Sometimes it is impossible. It's about love. And in football, it is the same." Meanwhile, Tottenham are in talks to sign Bayer Leverkusen and South Korea forward Son Heung-min in a proposed transfer worth 30m euros (£22m). However, their priority remains signing Berahino, who scored 20 goals last season. Berahino was dropped from West Brom's squad last weekend, with manager Tony Pulis citing that the player was not in the right frame of mind to play. With the transfer window still open, it remains to be seen whether Tottenham will make another bid for Berahino or pursue other targets.

Everton Manager Ronald Koeman Pledges Commitment to Club Amid Barcelona Speculation Ronald Koeman, the manager of Everton Football Club, has reaffirmed his commitment to the team despite recent speculation linking him to a return to his former club, Barcelona. In an interview with Catalan newspaper Sport, Koeman expressed his dream of coaching Barcelona, where he spent six years as a player from 1989 to 1995. However, the 54-year-old Dutchman was quick to dismiss any rumors of an imminent departure from Goodison Park. Speaking on Thursday, Koeman stated, "There's no chance that I will leave Everton before the end of my contract." He also downplayed the possibility of becoming the next manager of Barcelona, saying, "I don't see me being the next manager." Koeman's comments come after current Barcelona manager Luis Enrique announced his decision to step down at the end of the season. Koeman, who is in the first season of his contract with Everton, emphasized his ambition to lead the team to Champions League qualification. "We have a very powerful and exciting project and we're going to strengthen as best as possible to try and reach the Champions League next season," he said. The Toffees currently sit seventh in the Premier League with three games remaining and are unlikely to secure a Champions League spot this year. When asked about the possibility of Barcelona approaching him, Koeman replied, "That's a hypothesis we cannot go into too much. In football, like in life, like in business, you can talk and discuss everything." The Everton manager also announced that striker Arouna Kone will be leaving the club at the end of the season. The 33-year-old Ivory Coast striker has been with the Toffees since 2013, joining from Wigan Athletic for £6m. Despite the speculation surrounding his future, Koeman appears focused on the task at hand, guiding Everton to a strong finish in the Premier League and building a team capable of competing at the highest level next season. With his contract commitment and stated ambition to lead the team to Champions League qualification, Koeman's future at Goodison Park seems secure for now.

Violent Protests Erupt in Andhra Pradesh as Kapu Community Demands Job Reservations Protests turned violent in Andhra Pradesh on Sunday as members of the Kapu community took to the streets, demanding that the government fulfill its promise of reserving government jobs for them. The community, which makes up nearly 26% of the state's population, had organized a public meeting that escalated into chaos. Protesters set fire to railway carriages, a police station, and dozens of vehicles, causing widespread destruction. The violence disrupted railway and highway services, with protesters blocking tracks and stopping trains. The Ratnachal Express train was targeted, with four coaches set ablaze after passengers were ordered to disembark. At least 15 policemen were injured in clashes with protesters, who attacked them with stones near the town of Tuni. The local railway station was also ransacked, and 25 cars and other vehicles were torched. The protests were reportedly called off late on Sunday, but not before causing significant damage. Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu condemned the violence, citing the government's commitment to social justice. Despite laws against caste-based discrimination, the influence of the caste system remains strong in India, leading to ongoing demands for job and education quotas. The Kapu community's demands highlight the ongoing struggle for social equality in the region.

Former Maldivian President Mohamed Nasheed's lawyers have accused the government of reneging on a deal to commute his 13-year prison sentence to house arrest. Nasheed was sentenced in March under anti-terror laws, which his lawyers claim is a politically motivated case. The government, however, denies any agreement to commute the sentence, stating that house arrest was only temporarily granted on medical grounds. According to Nasheed's lawyers, they possess a document dated July 19, which proves that his sentence was commuted to house arrest for the remainder of its duration. Nevertheless, presidential spokesperson Ibrahim Muaz Ali has dismissed the document as fake, asserting that the Maldives Correctional Service has not issued any such document altering the Criminal Court's ruling. Amal Clooney, one of Nasheed's lawyers, has condemned the government's actions, stating that they demonstrate "a complete disregard for the rule of law." Nasheed, a former human rights campaigner, was the Maldives' first democratically elected leader, serving from 2008 until his resignation in 2012. His current imprisonment has sparked concerns over the country's democratic trajectory, particularly under the leadership of President Abdulla Yameen, who is the half-brother of former President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom. The situation has raised questions about the independence of the judiciary and the government's commitment to upholding the rule of law in the Maldives.

Flooding Concerns Persist in Clady as Funding Delays Repair Work Residents of Clady are still reeling from the devastating floods that hit their community last December. The storm caused significant damage to homes and businesses, with many still recovering from the aftermath. An initial study has been conducted to replace a damaged floodwall and flood-banks, but progress is now hindered by funding constraints. According to David Porter of the Rivers Agency, the project's viability is being assessed, taking into account affordability and the availability of funds. With many competing priorities for funding, Mr. Porter emphasized the need for residents in at-risk areas to take proactive measures to protect themselves from flooding. This warning comes as a couple in their 60s, Eugene and Mary McShane, continue to live in a caravan after their home on Urney Road was severely damaged by 5ft of water last year. As winter approaches, concerns about repeat flooding are growing, highlighting the urgent need for a long-term solution to Clady's flooding woes.

Linus Torvalds, the creator of the Linux operating system, has been awarded the prestigious Millennium Technology Prize, sharing the honor with Dr. Shinya Yamanaka, a renowned stem cell scientist. The award, presented by Technology Academy Finland, recognizes Mr. Torvalds's significant contributions to the development of shared software, networking, and the openness of the web. Mr. Torvalds, who developed the first version of Linux in 1991 while studying at the University of Helsinki, Finland, has had a profound impact on the technology industry. The Linux kernel, which he created, has undergone numerous revisions and is now used in a wide range of applications, including computer servers, digital video recorders, stock exchange equipment, and Google's Android smartphone platform. The Millennium Technology Prize, awarded every two years, is considered one of the most prestigious awards in the field of technology. This year, the award is being split for the first time, with each winner receiving 600,000 euros ($752,000; £483,000). Dr. Ainomaija Haarla, president of Technology Academy Finland, praised Mr. Torvalds's work, stating that it has "kept the web open for the pursuit of knowledge and the benefit of humanity - not simply for financial interests." Mr. Torvalds, who now works from his home office in Oregon, acknowledged his roots in accepting the award, expressing gratitude to the Technology Academy of Finland and to the thousands of software engineers who have contributed to the Linux project over the years. The Linux kernel has been developed through the contributions of thousands of volunteers, with an estimated 73,000 man-years spent working on the code. The award is a testament to Mr. Torvalds's dedication to the open-source movement and his commitment to keeping the web open and accessible to all. Despite receiving job offers from top companies, including Apple's founder Steve Jobs, Mr. Torvalds has chosen to remain neutral and independent, working with the Linux Foundation, a non-profit organization that promotes and supports the development of the Linux kernel. In a recent interview with the BBC, Mr. Torvalds revealed that he had no intention of leaving the Linux Foundation, citing the importance of his neutral status and the preference of companies involved with Linux for his independence. "I seriously believe that even though the Linux kernel has become a big thing for a number of large companies, people really do appreciate how nice it is that I don't work for any of them," he said. The Millennium Technology Prize is a well-deserved recognition of Mr. Torvalds's contributions to the technology industry, and his commitment to the principles of openness and collaboration. As the Linux operating system continues to play a vital role in shaping the digital landscape, Mr. Torvalds's work will remain an essential part of the internet's infrastructure, promoting innovation and accessibility for generations to come.

Tom Lawrence, the 23-year-old Wales international, is set to leave Leicester after limited appearances. Since joining from Manchester United in 2014, he has featured just four times. Lawrence spent the past two seasons on loan in the Championship with Blackburn, Cardiff, and Ipswich. He impressed with Ipswich, scoring 11 goals in 36 appearances. Derby and Premier League newcomers Brighton are reportedly interested in signing him. Ipswich boss Mick McCarthy had previously stated the club had "no chance" of signing Lawrence permanently due to high demand for the player. A move is expected soon.

A Staffordshire coroner has suggested that there may be a rising trend in suicides linked to concerns over state benefits. Andrew Haigh made the comment after recently presiding over an inquest into the death of Kim Burns, a 51-year-old woman from Codsall, near Wolverhampton. Ms Burns, who suffered from multiple sclerosis, took her own life on January 17, leaving behind a note criticizing the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP). According to her friend, Christine Hammonds, Ms Burns had been struggling with depression and was worried about losing her benefits, including her mobility allowance. She had been receiving personal independence payments, but was concerned that she would lose £1,000 a year in benefits from April. Ms Hammonds described Ms Burns as a proud and independent woman who feared losing her independence and becoming reliant on others. The DWP has disputed the claim that Ms Burns' death was linked to the loss of benefits, stating that she was still receiving the higher rate of mobility allowance and that personal independence payments were not a factor in her death. However, Coroner Haigh believes that the issue is worth exploring, and has noted that he has dealt with similar cases in the past where individuals have taken their own lives due to perceived problems with state benefits. Another case, that of 73-year-old Valerie Grant from Great Bridgeford, is also being investigated. Her son had been told that he would lose his disability allowance on May 3, and her inquest is yet to be heard. While the DWP has declined to comment on Mrs Grant's case, Coroner Haigh has expressed concern that these types of cases may be on the rise. He has called for further exploration of the issue, highlighting the need for greater support and understanding for individuals struggling with the complexities of the benefits system.

Former New Zealand cricket star Chris Cairns is facing prosecution for perjury and perverting the course of justice in a high-profile trial. The charges stem from a libel case in 2012, where Cairns successfully sued Indian Premier League chairman Lalit Modi over a tweet accusing him of match-fixing. During the trial, Cairns testified under oath that he had never cheated at cricket, a claim the prosecution now alleges is untrue. Cairns, who was once considered the "golden boy" of cricket, won damages of $130,000 in the libel case. However, his reputation was tarnished after Modi's tweet in 2010, which accused him of match-fixing while playing for the Chandigarh Lions in the Indian Cricket League. The prosecution claims that Cairns's testimony in the libel case was false and that he had indeed engaged in match-fixing. The trial is expected to hear evidence from current New Zealand cricket captain Brendon McCullum and former teammate Lou Vincent, who were both allegedly targeted by Cairns to help him fix matches. McCullum reportedly refused to participate, while Vincent was "corrupted" by Cairns. The prosecution also alleges that Cairns and his co-defendant, Andrew Fitch Holland, a barrister friend, attempted to induce Vincent to give false evidence in order to help Cairns's case. A recorded Skype conversation between Fitch Holland and Vincent, who has admitted to being involved in match-fixing, was played in court. The prosecution claims that the conversation was an attempt to persuade Vincent to lie to the court and support Cairns's claims of innocence. Cairns and Fitch Holland deny all charges, but the prosecution argues that the evidence will show that Cairns was indeed guilty of match-fixing. The trial is ongoing, with the jury set to hear further evidence in the coming days.

A historic Torah scroll has been returned to a Jewish community in Cornwall after being restored and housed at the Royal Cornwall Museum. The scroll, one of the holiest objects in the Jewish faith, was given back to Kehillat Kernow, a local Jewish group, by the Duke of Gloucester on behalf of the museum. This is believed to be the first Kosher scroll in the country to be returned by a museum. The Torah scroll is considered precious and is typically read using a pointer, or "yad". It will now be used in festivals and ceremonies, including Bar and Bat Mitzvahs and baby blessings. Kehillat Kernow chairman Harvey Kurzfield welcomed the return, saying it provides a "great link with the past" and will be used in a "living, vibrant Jewish community" 350 years after its initial use. The scroll's return is a significant moment for the local Jewish community.

Celtic's Nadir Ciftci has left Scotland on loan for the third consecutive season. The 25-year-old Turkish player joined Celtic in 2015 for £1.5m but made just 11 starts. He last played for Celtic in February and hasn't scored since 2015. Ciftci has had loan spells at Eskisehirspor and Pogon Szczecin, and previously played for Portsmouth in England. Check our football transfers page for the latest updates.

Derry City manager Kenny Shiels has made a shocking allegation against a member of Cork City's backroom staff, claiming he was called a "sectarian name" following Friday night's 2-1 loss at Turner's Cross. The incident occurred after Cork City scored two late goals to secure their first victory over Derry this season, with Kenny Browne netting the winner in stoppage time. Shiels expressed his outrage and disappointment at the alleged abuse, stating that he will "not tolerate" such behavior and is determined to pursue the matter further. However, Cork City chairman Pat Lyons has denied any knowledge of the incident, while manager John Caulfield expressed surprise at Shiels' allegation, attributing it to "excitement" and disappointment. Shiels had taken issue with the home team's reaction after the final whistle, describing their lack of hospitality as "outrageous." He vowed to "fight his own corner" and take action to address the alleged abuse. The incident has sparked controversy, with Shiels insisting that he will not be "walked over" and that Cork City staff will be held accountable for their actions. The matter is likely to be investigated further, with Shiels seeking a resolution to the alleged incident.

A unique weight loss program has proven to be a winning formula for overweight soccer fans in Glasgow. The 12-week program, which involved training sessions at local football clubs, resulted in an average weight loss of 11lb (5kg) per participant, with nearly 40% of men maintaining a weight loss of at least 5% of their original body weight a year later. The program, which was conducted by researchers at Glasgow University, involved 748 overweight men, with half participating in the training sessions and the other half placed on a waiting list. All participants received healthy-eating advice and weight management tips, but only those who attended the training sessions at the football clubs achieved significant and sustained weight loss. Thirteen football clubs took part in the program, including Aberdeen, Celtic, and Rangers, providing a male-friendly environment that encouraged participants to take control of their health. According to Prof Kate Hunt, co-author of the study, the program's success lies in its ability to tap into men's interests and provide a supportive community. "Participants really enjoyed being with other men like them, with a shared interest in football and similar health issues to address," she said. The program's success has significant implications for the development of weight loss programs tailored to men's needs, and its potential for future applications is substantial.

Zambian Referee Janny Sikazwe Invited to Officiate at Under-20 World Cup The FIFA Under-20 World Cup, set to kick off in South Korea on May 20, will feature 22 top referees from around the globe, including Zambia's Janny Sikazwe. The 37-year-old school teacher from Kapiri Mposhi is one of three African referees selected for the tournament, alongside Egypt's Grisha Ghead and Cameroon's Alioum Alioum. Sikazwe's rise to the top has been nothing short of remarkable. Despite hailing from a small town with limited resources, he has consistently demonstrated his skills and dedication to the sport. In Kapiri Mposhi, referees are forced to train on a subpar pitch at a local school, and the town lacks a single stadium. However, Sikazwe remains undaunted, drawing on his experiences to stay focused under pressure. His career has been on an upward trajectory since officiating at the 2015 FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Chile. He went on to referee the 2016 FIFA Club World Cup final between Real Madrid and Kashima Antlers, and most recently, handled the Africa Cup of Nations final between Cameroon and Egypt. Sikazwe's sights are now set on the 2018 World Cup in Russia, where he hopes to represent Africa. With his ambition and determination, he is certainly one to watch in the world of refereeing.

General Motors (GM), the largest US carmaker, has reported a net income of $1.4 billion, a 7.6% decrease from the same period last year. Despite a 9.2% increase in North American car sales, with 794,000 vehicles sold, profits were impacted by a $900 million settlement for faulty ignition recalls and $600 million in civil settlements. However, GM's underlying performance was strong, with North American pre-tax earnings reaching a record $3.3 billion, up 34%. The company also saw improved results in Europe, with losses decreasing to $231 million. GM's shares rose 4% in New York, reflecting the company's overall resilience. Additionally, September saw the strongest US car sales in a decade, with GM selling 814,000 cars in China, albeit at a lower volume than the previous year, but with slightly higher profit margins.

South Korea's Response to MERS Outbreak Criticized as Cases Rise The South Korean government is facing criticism over its handling of the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) outbreak, which has now infected 35 people and resulted in one death. The latest victim, who contracted the virus from another patient in the same hospital room, died in hospital on Thursday. The outbreak, which is the largest outside of the Middle East, has prompted the quarantine of over 1,600 people, with 160 being isolated in state medical facilities and the remainder instructed to stay at home. The criticism stems from the fact that one infected person was allowed to play golf, while another flew to China, potentially putting hundreds of people at risk of infection. The government has been accused of being slow to respond to the outbreak, which was first detected in a 68-year-old man who had recently returned from a trip to Saudi Arabia. As the number of cases continues to rise, public anxiety is growing. Many people in Seoul are now wearing face masks on public transport and in crowded places, and the Korea Tourism Organisation has reported that around 7,000 tourists, mostly from China and Taiwan, have cancelled planned group trips to South Korea. This is a significant blow to the country's tourism industry, with many travellers citing the MERS outbreak as the main reason for their cancellation. Experts say that MERS is not highly contagious and can only spread through close contact in a confined space. However, the virus has a death rate of 27%, according to the World Health Organization, and has resulted in 479 deaths worldwide out of 1,167 reported cases. The South Korean health ministry has confirmed that all of the cases so far are linked to the initial sufferer, and authorities are working to contain the outbreak. However, the government's response has been criticized as inadequate, and there are concerns that the outbreak could spread further if not properly contained. As the situation continues to unfold, the government is under pressure to take more decisive action to prevent the spread of the virus and reassure the public.

St Johnstone Ease Past Stirling Albion in League Cup Clash St Johnstone secured a comfortable 4-0 victory over Stirling Albion in their League Cup match, with the Perth team dominating from start to finish. The Saints took an early lead in the fourth minute, as Steven Anderson headed in a Liam Craig corner at the back post. This set the tone for the rest of the match, with St Johnstone creating numerous scoring opportunities. The home team doubled their lead 12 minutes before half-time, as another Craig corner was flicked on and Steven Maclean netted with an unmarked header. Stirling Albion struggled to create any meaningful chances, with their best effort coming from Bryan Hodge's 25-yard shot that sailed just over the bar. St Johnstone wrapped up their victory with a third goal in the 43rd minute, as Maclean's cross was glanced in by Craig for his first goal of the match. The second half saw a lengthy delay due to an injury to Stirling Albion keeper Chris Smith, who was stretchered off after falling awkwardly while catching a cross. Despite Maclean missing several glaring opportunities to add to the scoreline, he laid on the fourth goal for David Wotherspoon to lash home in stoppage time. The win sees St Johnstone progress comfortably in the League Cup, while Stirling Albion will look to regroup and bounce back from the defeat.

Outrage has erupted in the cycling world after a podium presentation at the Flanders Diamond Tour was marred by controversy. Following Wiggle-Honda's Jolien d'Hoore's win in the Antwerp to Nijlen stage, a picture of the podium was posted on Twitter, showing the winner standing alongside two models in revealing outfits. The image sparked widespread criticism, with Dutch racing cyclist and journalist Marijn de Vries describing the scene as "an utter disgrace". The Lotto Cycling Cup organisers were quick to apologise for the incident, stating that they were not responsible for the podium presentation and found the models "inappropriate". According to the organisers, the local event planners had hired the models from Hostessen Service No Limit, a company that also offers striptease acts. The manager of the company, Gerrid, seemed unfazed by the backlash, stating that he didn't understand what the problem was and that he wouldn't be apologising. However, Johan Molineaux, the local organiser of the event, took a different stance, saying that he would not be using Hostessen Service No Limit again and planned to personally apologise to the competitors. Molineaux explained that the women were supposed to wear cycling shirts but took them off, and he was not present during the presentation. The UCI, world cycling's governing body, has also looked into the incident and contacted the organisers, who apologised. The controversy has sparked a wider debate about the use of podium girls in cycling. British cyclist Helen Wyman, speaking at the launch of the Women's Tour of Britain, said that she thinks podium girls should be a thing of the past. "It's 2015. I'd much prefer to see the race sponsors on the podium, as it's their money that allow us to do what we do, and we'd prefer to see them rewarded," she told BBC Sport. The incident has highlighted the need for greater respect and professionalism in the sport, and it remains to be seen how the cycling world will respond to the controversy in the future.

A 26-year-old man from Edinburgh has been sentenced to 16 months in prison for embezzling over £134,000 from his employer, RS McColl's. Daryl Louden pleaded guilty to the crime, which took place between January and September 2016, and had been deferred for background reports. At Edinburgh Sheriff Court, Sheriff Frank Crowe expressed his disappointment and frustration with Louden's actions, stating that his breach of trust had been "enormous" and devastating for his colleagues. Louden had been a trusted employee and was even in line for promotion to area manager before his addiction took over. The court heard that Louden's gambling habit had spiralled out of control, with him taking out loans and trying to repay them by betting on football and horse racing. When he lost money, he would bet more in an attempt to recoup his losses, eventually leading to the embezzlement of £134,177.46 from the Ferry Road branch. Defence solicitor Jennifer McEvinney argued that Louden's actions were "extremely out of character" and that he had since sought help and turned his life around. She presented a letter from Louden's superior, David Richardson, which expressed concern for Louden's mental health and suggested that he was capable of making amends through community service. However, Sheriff Crowe was unsympathetic, stating that only a prison sentence was suitable for the crime. He emphasized that Louden had wasted public money and disappointed those who trusted him, including his area manager, colleagues, and friends. While reducing the initial sentence of two years to 16 months, Sheriff Crowe also ensured that Louden would receive proper support and help in prison to address his addiction and get his life back on track.

Samsung Sells Shares in Four Companies Amid Galaxy Note 7 Recall Samsung has sold its shares in four companies, including US chipmaker Rambus and hard drive producer Seagate, in a move to efficiently manage its assets. The sales, which raised over 1 trillion won ($888.9m), come as the company faces a major recall of its flagship Galaxy Note 7 phone due to reports of fires caused by faulty batteries. The recall, which affects 2.5 million devices globally, is expected to cost Samsung over $1bn. The shares sold include a 4.2% stake in Seagate, 4.5% of Rambus, and 0.7% of Sharp, as well as half of a 3% stake in Dutch semiconductor firm ASML. Samsung stated that the sale was for "efficient management of assets." The move is seen as an effort to mitigate the financial impact of the Galaxy Note 7 recall, which has already led to a formal recall order from US regulators. With reports of fires in China, despite initial claims that phones in the country were safe, Samsung's woes are far from over. The company has already recalled a small batch of phones in China and is investigating the latest incidents. The recall is a major blow to Samsung's reputation and finances, and the company will be closely watched as it navigates this crisis.

Animal Cruelty Cases on the Rise in England and Wales The RSPCA has released disturbing statistics showing a significant increase in animal cruelty cases in England and Wales. In 2014, a total of 159,831 incidents were investigated, up from 153,770 in 2013. Shocking cases include a rabbit being microwaved to death in Gloucestershire and incidents in Barrow and Peterborough. Despite the rise in cases, the number of people convicted of animal cruelty fell to 1,029, down from 1,371 in 2013. Greater London had the highest number of complaints at 12,202, followed by West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester. The RSPCA reported that 20,258 cases involved deliberate and violent cruelty. Chief veterinary officer James Yeates expressed concern over the inventive and disturbing ways people are being cruel to animals. The charity also highlighted the "Neknomination" online craze, which led to five prosecutions involving the swallowing of live animals. West Yorkshire saw the highest number of convictions at 93, with County Durham and the West Midlands also having high numbers. The RSPCA urges the public to report any cases of animal cruelty and offers welfare advice to prevent neglect and abuse.

Crystal Palace has secured the signing of left-back Patrick van Aanholt from Sunderland. The 26-year-old will be reunited with Eagles boss Sam Allardyce, who he played under last season. Allardyce praised Van Aanholt, stating he brings "great energy" and will increase the speed and energy levels of the squad. Van Aanholt started his career at Chelsea before joining Sunderland in 2014, making 95 appearances for the Black Cats. Allardyce confirmed that Palace has not received bids for any of their players and is hopeful of signing further targets. However, he denied that Norwich's Robbie Brady and Lille's Ibrahim Amadou are among them, citing the high cost of doing business in the current market. The signing is a positive move for Palace, and Allardyce is looking forward to working with Van Aanholt again.

Queen Silvia of Sweden has revealed that she shares her 17th-century Drottningholm Palace with some unexpected "small friends" - ghosts. In a documentary airing on Swedish public broadcaster SVT, the queen expressed her excitement about the paranormal presence, but assured that they are "all very friendly" and don't scare her. The palace, located near Stockholm, has been the permanent residence of the queen and her husband, King Carl XVI Gustaf, for decades. Princess Christina, the king's sister, corroborated the queen's claims, stating that the palace has a lot of energy, which could manifest as ghostly apparitions. The queen's comments have sparked amusement, with Swedish website The Local joking that brave amateur ghost hunters could visit the palace to test the rumors. However, some areas of the palace, including the southern wing, are reserved for the royal family and their alleged ghostly companions. Queen Silvia, who has been Sweden's longest-serving queen for 40 years, has been open about her experiences in the palace. In a 2015 book, she spoke about feeling lonely in her first year as queen, despite the support of her husband and staff. Recently, the queen was hospitalized briefly before Christmas due to dizziness but was released two days later. The documentary, Drottningholm Palace: A Royal Home, offers a glimpse into the queen's life and her unique relationship with the historic palace and its inhabitants, both living and dead.

Emmerdale's rape scene deemed suitable by media watchdog. A controversial scene from the soap opera, in which Rhona Goskirk was raped by her husband Pierce Harris, has been defended by Ofcom. The scene, broadcast at 7pm on April 24, was the culmination of a long-running storyline involving Rhona and her abusive partner. Some viewers felt it was not suitable for broadcast before 9pm, but Ofcom ruled it was "likely to have been in line with what most viewers were expecting." The watchdog noted that a warning had been issued and the scene was limited. Emmerdale producer Iain MacLeod also defended the scene, stating that the show has a responsibility to cover hard-hitting subjects. He added that Emmerdale has always tackled challenging social issues, and this scene was no exception. The ruling has sparked debate about what is suitable for broadcast during early evening time slots.

AFC Telford United, a non-league football club based in Shropshire, has parted ways with manager Rob Smith and his assistant Larry Chambers. This sudden change in management is part of a larger plan to secure new investment and ensure the club's future. According to BBC Radio Shropshire, the club's decision to let go of Smith and Chambers is a result of an offer that was too good to turn down. Director Andy Pryce expressed his gratitude towards the departing management duo, stating that it was tough to part with them. However, he is excited about the future of the club under the guidance of new manager Rob Edwards. Edwards, a 34-year-old Shropshire-born former player, has had a successful career and has made a promising start to his coaching career. He was heavily linked with the manager's job at Shrewsbury Town earlier this year and has now returned to football just four weeks after leaving his role at Wolverhampton Wanderers. Edwards has expressed his commitment to his hometown club, stating that he will work hard to achieve great things and raise the club's profile to a new level. This is a significant development for AFC Telford, who were formed by fans in 2004 following the liquidation of the old Telford United. The club has experienced a mix of promotions and relegations over the years, currently playing in the sixth tier of English football. The new investment is expected to bring about significant changes to the club, including the potential arrival of Football League players on loan. Additionally, the club will receive extra financial support from Wolverhampton Wanderers, who currently use AFC Telford's Bucks Head home to stage their Under-23 games. This support will be on top of their existing agreement and is a major boost to the club's finances. The club's chairman, Ian Dosser, will also be leaving his position, with Andy Pryce taking over as interim chairman. Despite the changes, the club's share structure and name will remain unchanged. The new investment is seen as a game-changer for AFC Telford, and fans are eagerly awaiting the impact it will have on the club's performance and reputation. In a statement, BBC Radio Shropshire's Nick Southall said, "This is a pretty major development for the club. We're talking about pretty major investment, and the prospect of some Football League players joining on loan." The arrival of Rob Edwards as manager and the new investment are expected to bring about a new era of success and stability to AFC Telford United. With the club's future looking brighter than ever, fans are excited to see what the upcoming season holds for their team.

Researchers at King's College London have made a breakthrough in the quest to identify the earliest signs of Alzheimer's disease. By analyzing the levels of 1,129 proteins in the blood of over 200 twins, they discovered a potential link between a protein called MAPKAPK5 and cognitive decline. The study, published in Translational Psychiatry, compared the protein levels with data from cognitive-function tests over a decade and found that individuals with lower levels of MAPKAPK5 were more likely to experience brain decline. The discovery of this protein marker could be a crucial step in the development of early diagnosis and treatment of Alzheimer's disease. Currently, dementia cases are expected to treble globally by 2050, with no cure or treatment available. The disease can take over a decade to progress from the first changes in the brain to the onset of symptoms such as memory loss, confusion, and personality change. According to Dr. Steven Kiddle, a Medical Research Council scientist at King's College London, identifying people at risk of Alzheimer's disease years before symptoms appear could be key to developing effective treatments. "People think it may be hard to reverse 20 years of potential damage to your brain," he said. "But if you could start much earlier in that process, then you might be able to find something that works." While the study's findings are promising, Dr. Kiddle cautions that a blood test for Alzheimer's disease is still a long way off. The twins in the study will need to be followed for many more years to determine whether levels of MAPKAPK5 can predict dementia. Dr. Eric Karran from Alzheimer's Research UK agrees, stating that more research is needed to understand the mechanism linking MAPKAPK5 to cognitive decline. Nevertheless, the study brings hope for the development of new treatments and earlier diagnosis, which is essential for combating this devastating disease.

Scotland's "Living it Up" Initiative Fails to Meet User Targets A Scottish health initiative aimed at helping people over 50 manage their health and wellbeing online has fallen short of its user targets. The "Living it Up" (LiU) programme, launched in 2013, had hoped to attract 55,000 users across Scotland by May 2015, but so far, it has only managed to sign up 15,000 people. Despite the disappointing uptake, NHS 24, which manages the project, remains optimistic about its potential. The organisation pointed out that the website receives an average of 50,000 hits per month, suggesting that there is still significant interest in the service. The LiU website offers a range of tools and resources, including a quiz to help users identify their strengths and interests, a search function to find local community projects, and guides to social media platforms like Twitter and Instagram. The initiative was designed to use technology to match individuals with professional information, local services, and beneficial activities in their community. It was announced by then-Scottish health secretary Alex Neil in November 2013, with the aim of providing accessible health services via familiar technology such as televisions, computers, and smartphones. The project has received £10.375m in funding over three years from the Scottish government, the Technology Strategy Board, Scottish Enterprise, and local health boards and authorities. Despite the significant investment, the cost per patient has worked out at £690, raising questions about the value for money of the initiative. NHS 24 acknowledged that recruitment had been "challenging" but claimed that uptake was now picking up, with a 55% growth in users over the past six months. The organisation described LiU as a "pioneering and ambitious project" that aimed to embed digital tools within health and care service pathways. The project is currently available to patients in several regions, including Forth Valley, Lothian, and the Highlands. While the initiative may not have met its original targets, it remains to be seen whether it can still make a positive impact on the health and wellbeing of Scotland's over-50s.

Northern Ireland's Rail Upgrade Project to Commence in May 2015 The long-awaited rail upgrade project in Northern Ireland is set to begin in May 2015, according to David Strahan, Chief Executive of Translink. Strahan confirmed the start date while giving evidence to a Northern Ireland Assembly inquiry into the rail project. The inquiry was established last year to investigate the significant cost overrun of the upgrade, which has nearly doubled from its initial estimate of £20m to £40m. As part of the inquiry, members of the Regional Development Committee traveled to Derry by train, speaking with passengers about issues on the rail line. The second stage of the upgrade will involve major re-signalling between Derry and Coleraine, as well as the introduction of a passing loop. The work is expected to be completed by 2016. Committee member John Dallat expressed his enthusiasm for the project, stating that Derry needs a proper inter-city service. "I hope that the city of Derry and all the towns in-between will have a new rail service by 2016," he said. "It's not a dream, it's a reality, and I'm absolutely confident because I know that no other city in the world doesn't have a decent inter-city service." Translink has confirmed that an hourly service on the route is a priority, and senior representatives of the company were questioned alongside government officials at the Derry hearing. A Translink spokesperson stated that the work on phase 2 of the project is expected to commence in May 2015, subject to the successful completion of a tender process. With four contractors expressing interest in the project, compared to only one last time, there is optimism that the upgrade will be completed on time and within budget. The new rail service is expected to bring a "new era" to the north west, providing a much-needed boost to the region's transportation infrastructure.

Sweden's Economy Thrives with Unique Public-Private Partnership Model Sweden's economy is experiencing a period of unprecedented strength, with low unemployment rates and a thriving mixed economy. At the heart of this success is the "Swedish model," a public-private partnership developed by the Social Democrats, who governed the country for most of the last 70 years. This model features centralized wage negotiations and a heavily tax-subsidized social security network, providing citizens with a high standard of living and life expectancy. The country's advanced welfare system and strong economy have made it a popular destination for refugees and asylum seekers, with immigrants making up over 10% of the population. Sweden is also known for its commitment to environmental sustainability, having initially phased out nuclear power in the 1990s. However, in 2009, the government reversed this decision, citing concerns over climate change and energy security. Sweden's neutral foreign policy has led to its politicians taking on key international roles, often mediating between conflicting groups. The country joined the European Union in 1995 but declined to join NATO and the single European currency, with voters rejecting euro membership in a 2003 referendum. Today, Sweden continues to thrive, with its unique economic model and commitment to social welfare and sustainability serving as a model for other countries to follow.

A petition is to be delivered to Prime Minister David Cameron and Home Secretary Theresa May, calling for a reversal of a decision to deny visas to the grandparents and aunt of a five-year-old girl who died after being hit by a car in Eastbourne. Andrea Gada's mother, Charity Gada, will be joined by family and friends as she presents the petition, which argues that the family poses no risk to the country and simply wishes to support her and grieve the loss of her child. The case was raised in Parliament by local MP Stephen Lloyd, who urged the Prime Minister to intervene. Although David Cameron agreed to look into the matter, the Home Office has upheld its decision to deny the visas, citing immigration rules. The family's application was reviewed for a second time, with the Home Office considering "compelling and compassionate circumstances," but ultimately deciding against granting the visas. Andrea's mother has expressed her devastation at being separated from her family during this difficult time. She claims that the Home Office denied the visas because her family is "too poor," assuming they would attempt to stay in the UK illegally. The local community has rallied around Mrs. Gada, raising money to help her family attend the funeral. In a heartfelt plea, Mrs. Gada said, "At the heart of it, all I really want is to have my mother at my side whilst I grieve the loss of my child." The petition highlights the human cost of strict immigration policies and the need for compassion in exceptional circumstances.

Charlie Hebdo Releases New Edition with Defiant Cover The French satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo has released a new edition, just one week after a devastating terrorist attack on its offices. The cover features a caricature of the Prophet Muhammad holding a sign that reads "I am Charlie" under the headline "all is forgiven". This move is seen as a defiant statement against extremism, with the magazine's lawyer Richard Malka stating that staff will "cede nothing" to terrorists. The attack on Charlie Hebdo last Wednesday resulted in the deaths of 12 people, including five of the magazine's top cartoonists. The gunmen responsible claimed to have "avenged the Prophet Muhammad" after the magazine had previously published cartoons depicting him. Despite the tragedy, Charlie Hebdo is refusing to back down, with three million copies of the new edition being printed, a significant increase from the usual 60,000. The magazine's staff, who have been working from the offices of another French title, Liberation, have created the new edition without contributions from other cartoonists. The edition is a powerful statement of the magazine's commitment to freedom of speech and its refusal to be intimidated by extremism. As the magazine's financial director, Eric Portheault, stated, the new edition will be created "only by people from Charlie Hebdo", a testament to the magazine's resilience and determination.

Plans for a major shake-up of health services in Herefordshire and Worcestershire have been unveiled, with a focus on merging certain departments and investing more in GP services. The proposed changes aim to keep patients out of hospital and address the significant funding gap facing the local health and social care system. According to the draft NHS plan, despite increased funding, the current projections indicate that it will not be enough to meet future demands. The Herefordshire and Worcestershire Sustainability and Transformation Plan identifies potential savings of £5.4m on planned operations and suggests reducing spending on low-priority treatments. Community hospitals may be transformed into local hubs providing outpatient and support services, allowing patients to receive care closer to home. Sarah Dugan from Worcestershire Health and Care NHS Trust emphasized the need for collective action to address the challenges facing the health and care system. The proposed changes have been welcomed by Dr. Mike Smith, chair of the Patients Association, who stressed the importance of consulting with the community. He noted that treating patients at home is often preferable, provided they can access the necessary social care. The Wye Valley NHS Trust and Worcestershire Acute Hospital are facing significant financial pressures, with required savings of £18m and £24.9m respectively for the 2017-18 period. The plans aim to ensure the long-term sustainability of health services in the region.

Plymouth City Council has taken a significant step towards transforming its waterfront by exchanging contracts to purchase the Quality Inn hotel. The 10-storey building, deemed an "eyesore" by the authority, has been a magnet for anti-social behaviour since its closure two years ago. Council leader Tudor Evans stated that the site would make an "amazing location" for a new hotel, and discussions are already underway with interested parties. The council plans to demolish the building, which was constructed in the late 1960s, to make way for a new development. Although the purchase price remains undisclosed due to "commercially sensitive discussions," a report on the acquisition will be presented to the Cabinet for discussion. This move is expected to revitalize the area and enhance the city's stunning waterfront.

A victim of the 2005 London Tube bombings is still waiting for compensation over a decade after the devastating attack. Stefano Poborko, 52, suffered severe burns and was left using a wheelchair after a suicide bomber detonated a device on a train between King's Cross and Aldgate. The attack, which was one of four explosions targeting three Tube trains and a bus, claimed the lives of 52 people and injured over 770 others. Mr. Poborko, who now lives in Newbridge, Caerphilly county, was running late for a work meeting on the day of the attack. He suffered burns to his back, head, and ear in the blast and witnessed a fellow passenger die in his arms before emergency services arrived. The traumatic experience has had a lasting impact on his life, and he now relies on his fiancée, Louise Britt, as his primary carer. In March 2015, Mr. Poborko applied to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA) for compensation, but he is still awaiting a decision. The CICA is a government body responsible for compensating people who suffer physical or mental injuries arising from violent crime. Despite the authority's claim that it deals with all applications "as quickly and sensitively as possible," Mr. Poborko's case has been plagued by delays, including issues with his medical records being misnamed on the CICA's system. Recent figures show that the CICA took an average of over 11 months to reach a first decision on cases in 2015-2016, which is slightly longer than the previous year. The authority attributes the increase to the "changing nature of our caseload." However, for Mr. Poborko, the wait has been frustrating and debilitating. He hopes to gain compensation as some "recognition" of what he has been through and to improve his quality of life by enabling him to buy his home instead of renting. Mr. Poborko's solicitor, Glyn Maddocks, believes that his client is entitled to compensation despite the claim being outside the two-year limit stipulated. "He was a victim of a crime which was the terrorist outrage on 7 July," Mr. Maddocks said. "He witnessed it, the experiences that he had and what he saw on that day are horrific and life-changing, and he's entitled to receive compensation from the public body because of that." A CICA spokesperson expressed sympathy to all victims of crime and stated that the authority is committed to resolving applications as quickly and sensitively as possible. However, for Mr. Poborko, the wait continues. "I want it sorted – it's ridiculous," he said. "All I was doing was running late for work, and I got blown up. I just want to get on with my life, with Louise, in our home." As he waits for a decision, Mr. Poborko's condition, which includes multiple sclerosis, continues to affect his daily life. He hopes that the compensation will bring some sense of closure and enable him to move forward with his life.

Cardiff City has signed Canadian winger Junior Hoilett after his departure from QPR. The 26-year-old expressed his excitement, stating he's "ready to go" and aims to bring creativity and goals to the team. Meanwhile, striker Marouane Chamakh and centre-back Sol Bamba underwent medicals ahead of their free transfers. Chamakh, a 32-year-old Moroccan, was released by Crystal Palace, while Bamba, 31, left Leeds United due to personal reasons. The additions are expected to bolster Cardiff's squad, with Hoilett eager to get started and make an impact under the team's manager. The new signings are a positive move for the club.

The FTSE 100 experienced a significant surge, rising 45.41 points to 6,873.52, with Tullow Oil leading the charge. The oil company's shares soared 5.1% as the price of Brent crude surpassed $60 a barrel, boosting investor confidence. The upward trend was also evident in mining shares, with BHP Billiton and Glencore increasing by 5% and 3.7%, respectively. Despite reporting a 25% drop in underlying annual operating profit, Anglo American's shares rose 3.3%, demonstrating the sector's resilience. The positive sentiment was further fueled by news of stronger-than-expected growth in Germany, with the economy expanding by 0.7% in the fourth quarter. This growth lifted the German stock index, the Dax, to a record high, and had a ripple effect on the UK market. Rolls-Royce, despite cutting its profit forecast for 2015, saw its shares rise by over 4%. The company's diversified business and cost-cutting measures are expected to help it withstand potential declines in demand. In contrast, BT Group's shares fell 2.4% after Virgin Media announced plans to invest £3bn in its fibre optic broadband network. The move is set to increase competition in the sector, putting pressure on BT to respond. On the currency markets, the pound remained stable against the dollar at $1.5388, while slipping 0.03% against the euro to €1.3486. Overall, the market's positive performance was driven by rising commodity prices and encouraging economic data from Germany, with investors remaining cautious amid ongoing market uncertainties.

Raspberry Pi Foundation Releases Pixel Desktop for PCs and Macs The Raspberry Pi Foundation has announced that its Pixel desktop environment, previously exclusive to Raspberry Pi devices, is now available for PCs and Apple Mac machines. This move aims to provide a consistent user experience across different platforms, making it easier for users to work on projects regardless of the device they are using. According to Eben Upton, co-creator of the Raspberry Pi, the new release is particularly beneficial for schoolchildren who use the Raspberry Pi in class or for personal projects, but often have to continue their work on PCs or Macs. With the Pixel desktop now available on these machines, users can enjoy the same productivity software and programming tools in the same desktop environment, eliminating the need to adapt to different operating systems. The foundation believes that this release will also help to improve the overall quality of the Pixel desktop, as it will highlight areas of the user interface that require attention. Upton noted that the core software underlying Pixel is based on a relatively old computer architecture, making it compatible with "vintage" machines. However, he cautioned that the software is still experimental and may have minor issues or bugs that could affect its performance on some devices. The Pixel desktop was first introduced in September and is based on the open-source Linux software, Debian. The desktop version for PCs and Macs lacks two programs, Minecraft and Mathematica, which are only licensed for use on Raspberry Pi devices. With over 10 million Raspberry Pi devices sold, the foundation is committed to providing the best possible desktop computing experience for its users. The release of Pixel for PCs and Macs is a significant step towards achieving this goal, and the foundation is eager to receive feedback from users to further improve the software.

Met Police Close Lord Sewel Investigation Due to Lack of Evidence The Metropolitan Police have closed their investigation into Lord Sewel, the peer who resigned from the House of Lords in July after being filmed allegedly taking drugs with prostitutes. The decision comes after a thorough inquiry, which included a raid on a property in central London and a forensic examination of the address. According to Scotland Yard, there was "insufficient evidence to proceed" with the case. The incident led to widespread calls for reform of the House of Lords and prompted Lord Sewel, 69, to quit as deputy speaker and chairman of the Lords Privileges and Conduct Committee. He later resigned from Parliament altogether, apologizing for the "pain and embarrassment" caused and stating that his exit would help repair the damage to the reputation of the Lords. The BBC's home affairs correspondent, Danny Shaw, said the decision to close the investigation seemingly draws a line under the episode. The Met Police launched the inquiry on July 27, following a complaint about Lord Sewel's conduct. With the case now closed, attention is likely to turn back to the broader issue of reforming the House of Lords. Lord Sewel's resignation had highlighted concerns about the accountability and conduct of members of the upper house.

Australia's cricket match was abandoned due to rain, leaving their semi-final hopes uncertain. Chasing a target of 183, Australia were 83-1 after 16 overs when the rain arrived, falling short of the minimum required overs for a game. This is Australia's second abandonment, and they now face a must-win situation against England to reach the semi-finals. Captain Steve Smith expressed understanding for the umpires' decision, stating that the groundsmen did their best despite a lack of urgency. Smith was willing to continue playing through the rain but acknowledged the umpires' authority. The abandonment has added pressure to Australia's campaign, and they must now secure a win against England to advance. Australia's previous match against New Zealand was also abandoned, but Smith admitted they "got away with one" on that occasion. The team's fate now hangs in the balance as they prepare for their crucial match against England.

A fire broke out in a downstairs flat on Railway Road, Leigh, at 03:20 GMT Wednesday. Two people were rescued from a bedroom using a nine-metre ladder. They were "shook up but OK". The fire is suspected to have been started deliberately, according to Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service.

Scotland's Parliament Debates Trident Renewal Ahead of Vote The Scottish Parliament has engaged in a heated debate on the issue of Trident renewal, with ministers and MSPs from various parties presenting their arguments for and against the proposed £167bn replacement of the UK's nuclear weapons programme. The debate, which was opened by Minister Keith Brown, highlighted the deep divisions within the Labour party on the issue, as well as the strong opposition from the Scottish National Party (SNP). Minister Brown criticized the massive budget allocated for the Trident replacement, questioning why the funds could not be redirected to offset welfare cuts. He argued that the UK government's prioritization of nuclear weapons over social welfare was misguided, particularly in light of the "massive cuts" being introduced. Brown emphasized that the UK government's enthusiasm for nuclear weapons was misplaced, and that the renewal of Trident would have significant implications for conventional defense forces and public spending. The debate also saw Dumbarton MSP Jackie Baillie, the only Labour member to vote against the call to reject renewal, defend her position. Baillie, whose constituency includes the Faslane naval base, which houses Trident, argued that the base was the largest employer in the area, providing "good-quality, well-paid jobs" to over a quarter of West Dunbartonshire's full-time workforce. She accused the SNP of engaging in "gesture politics" and ignoring the concerns of workers who would be affected by the cancellation of Trident. However, Labour MSP Claire Baker countered that opposition to Trident renewal was her party's "clear position," citing the strong case presented against the programme at the Scottish Labour conference in Perth. Baker acknowledged that cancelling Trident would have significant consequences for the workforce and communities relying on the jobs, but emphasized that the fundamental argument against nuclear weapons was a strong one. Conservative MSP John Lamont criticized Labour's stance on the issue, describing it as "muddled." He pointed out that UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and Scottish leader Kezia Dugdale held different views on Trident, with Corbyn opposing renewal and Dugdale supporting multilateral disarmament. Lamont argued that unilateral disarmament would severely damage the UK's national security and potentially encourage other states to acquire nuclear weapons. The debate reflects the complex and divisive nature of the Trident renewal issue, with different parties and politicians holding strongly opposing views. As the UK government prepares to make a decision on the programme, the arguments presented in the Scottish Parliament highlight the need for careful consideration of the implications of renewal, including the impact on jobs, national security, and public spending. The outcome of the vote will be closely watched, as it may have significant consequences for the future of the UK's nuclear weapons programme.

UK Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson has called for a more balanced distribution of defense spending within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato), stating that it is unjustified for the United States to account for approximately 70% of the alliance's defense spending. In a speech to the Royal Institute of International Affairs at Chatham House, Johnson emphasized the need for all Nato member countries to meet the agreed target of spending 2% of their gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, as well as allocating 20% of their defense budget to new equipment. Johnson's remarks come amidst concerns over the future of Nato, particularly after US President-elect Donald Trump described the Western military alliance as "obsolete" during his election campaign. Trump suggested that the US would think twice about coming to the aid of any Nato ally under attack if it had not paid its "fair share" of defense spending. The UK, which meets the commitment to spend 2% of GDP on defense, has also been urging other countries to increase their contributions. In his speech, Johnson reaffirmed the UK's commitment to collective Nato defense, citing the security guarantee contained in the North Atlantic Treaty Article 5, which states that an attack on any one member shall be considered an attack against them all. He emphasized the importance of this institution, describing Nato as "the most durable and successful defense alliance in history." Johnson also acknowledged that the world is facing significant challenges, including the "cult of the strong man," democracy in retreat, and an "arc of instability" across the Middle East. Despite these challenges, Johnson expressed his confidence in the ability of the UK and its allies to defend and preserve the rules-based international order. He stated that the UK must "redouble our resolve" to prevent a return to "an older and more brutal system where the strong are free to devour the weak." Johnson also committed Britain to working with its allies to address these challenges, including the ongoing tensions with Russia over Crimea and the bombing campaign in Syria. In a notable departure from previous UK policy, Johnson stated that Britain would not oppose attempts by the European Union to form a common defense policy. He emphasized that the UK would not seek to block or impede further steps towards EU integration, provided that EU member states meet their defense spending commitments. This shift in policy reflects the UK's desire to maintain a strong and cooperative relationship with its European allies, even as it navigates its exit from the EU. Johnson also addressed the issue of Russia, stating that strong defense did not preclude negotiations. He believed that pressure could be brought to bear on Russia to halt its bombing campaign in Syria, deliver Assad to peace talks, and abide by the letter of the Minsk agreements in Ukraine. Johnson emphasized that the UK could not "normalize" relations with Russia or return to "business as usual" until these conditions were met. In conclusion, Johnson's speech highlights the UK's commitment to Nato and its desire for a more balanced distribution of defense spending within the alliance. The UK's willingness to support EU efforts to form a common defense policy also reflects its desire to maintain a strong and cooperative relationship with its European allies. As the international community faces significant challenges, the UK's resolve to defend and preserve the rules-based international order remains unwavering.

England cricket star Sarah Taylor has taken a significant step towards returning to the sport after joining the team's training camp in preparation for the World Cup. The 27-year-old wicketkeeper-batter had been on an indefinite break to address anxiety issues. Despite being initially left out of the squad, Taylor has now linked up with the 24-member team. The squad will play two intra-squad games and three matches against Ireland as part of their preparations. Taylor's central contract was renewed in December with the aim of having her fit for the World Cup. Her return to training is being gradually managed, with regular reviews to ensure she reaches full fitness. Coach Mark Robinson confirmed that Taylor is "going really well" and her goal remains to participate in the World Cup. The team has also been bolstered by the addition of former Lancashire all-rounder Tom Smith to the coaching staff. Smith was forced to retire in January due to injury. With Taylor's return and the new coaching appointment, England's prospects for the World Cup are looking increasingly positive.

Tragedy at Chelmsford Care Centre: Inquest Reveals Multiple Failings An inquest into the death of Matthew Leahy, who was found hanged in his room at the Linden Centre in Chelmsford, has exposed a series of shocking failures in his care. The Chelmsford Coroner's Court heard that Mr. Leahy's paperwork was incomplete, and he had not been assigned a key worker. Coroner Caroline Beasley Murray delivered an open narrative verdict, calling for the health trust to consider an inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Mr. Leahy's death. The court was told that Mr. Leahy had been subjected to "multiple failings and missed opportunities" during his time at the centre. Despite his history of drug-induced psychosis and previous threats of self-harm, he did not have a care plan in place. In a disturbing twist, it was revealed that staff had falsified a care plan after his death and back-dated it. One member of staff has been sacked and will face a disciplinary hearing, along with two others. The North Essex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust has insisted that these actions did not affect the quality of care Mr. Leahy received. The inquest highlighted the need for urgent action to prevent similar tragedies from occurring in the future.

Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari has provided an update on his health, stating that he has made significant progress but will remain in the UK for further medical treatment. The 74-year-old leader has spent more time in the UK than in Nigeria since the start of 2017, sparking concerns about his ability to govern the country. In a statement, President Buhari acknowledged that he is eager to return home but is being held back by his doctors. "I feel I could go home, but the doctors are in charge," he said. "I've now learnt to obey orders, rather than be obeyed." The president also expressed gratitude for the support he has received, citing a "tremendous improvement" in his health. The nature of President Buhari's illness remains undisclosed, fueling speculation and demands for transparency from protesters in the capital city of Abuja. Some have called for his resignation, while others have urged the government to be more open about his condition. Deputy President Yemi Osinbajo has been appointed to carry out the president's duties in his absence. President Buhari's health challenges have raised questions about his potential candidacy for the 2019 presidential election. If he is unable to seek re-election, it could lead to tensions between different factions in the country. The health of Nigerian leaders has been a sensitive topic since the death of President Umaru Musa Yar'Adua in 2010, who passed away in office after months of treatment overseas. For now, President Buhari remains in the UK, with his return to Nigeria uncertain.

Arsenal and Everton have discovered their opponents for the upcoming Europa League group stage. The Gunners, who finished fifth in the Premier League last season, will be competing in Europe's second-tier competition for the first time in 20 years. They have been drawn into Group H alongside BATE Borisov, Cologne, and Red Star Belgrade. Everton, who secured their spot in the competition with a play-off victory over Hajduk Split, will face a challenging group. They have been drawn into Group E alongside Lyon, who will host the final on May 16, 2018, as well as Italian Serie A side Atalanta and Apollon Limassol of Cyprus. The Toffees are returning to European competition for the first time since the 2014-15 season. The group stage is set to begin on September 14, with 48 teams competing across 12 groups. Other notable teams in the competition include AC Milan, who will face Austria Vienna, Rijeka, and AEK Athens in Group D, and Athletic Bilbao, who will take on Hertha Berlin, Zorya Luhansk, and Ostersund in Group J. The competition promises to be exciting, with a range of talented teams vying for the top prize.

Young People Share Body Image Struggles in #BodyPositive Campaign An 18-year-old university student, Nikki, has bravely shared her story of struggling with body image issues. Despite pursuing a career as a mental health nurse, Nikki has faced her own demons, including self-harm and suicidal thoughts. With the support of her school and GP, she sought treatment for anxiety and depression. Nikki's story highlights the importance of addressing body image concerns, particularly among young people. According to the charity Young Minds, poor body image can affect many teenagers, exacerbated by media portrayals of the "perfect" body. Those with pre-existing mental health issues may find it even harder to cope. By sharing her story, Nikki hopes to inspire others to open up about their own struggles, promoting a culture of acceptance and support. The #BodyPositive campaign aims to encourage honest and heartwarming accounts from young people.

A 28-year-old man from Edinburgh has been found guilty of attempting to murder an infant in his care. Ross Dunn was left in charge of the baby and her older sister when the child's mother went out on November 17, 2013. However, instead of providing proper care, Dunn shook the little girl and struck her against a surface, leaving her with severe and lifelong disabilities. The child's mother testified in court, describing the devastating impact of the attack on her daughter's life. "She is not mobile," she said. "She is very floppy like a small baby. She will likely never stand, walk, or even sit by herself." The court heard that Dunn had claimed the injuries were the result of an accident, but prosecutors argued that the pattern of multiple injuries was consistent with shaking. The advocate depute, Bruce Erroch, described the consequences of Dunn's actions as "the most appalling combination of disability for a baby to live with for the rest of her life." He also noted that Dunn had admitted to having problems with his temper, which likely contributed to the violent outburst. The sentence has been deferred pending background reports, but it is clear that Dunn's actions will have a lasting impact on the young victim and her family.

A campaign to give on-duty blue light workers priority service at cafes in Ripon has gained momentum after a chance encounter between a paramedic and a local resident. Gail Carpenter was inspired to take action when she saw a paramedic waiting in line at a cafe, only to be called away to an emergency before she could purchase her lunch. Moved by the paramedic's situation, Carpenter wrote a post on Facebook, which was shared hundreds of times and sparked a wave of support for the idea. The post struck a chord with many people, including those who have relied on emergency services in the past. Comments poured in, with individuals expressing their appreciation for the selfless work of paramedics and other blue light workers. Kathy Myers, a commenter, shared her own experience of frequently being called away from food queues, while Jacqui Morrell expressed her respect for emergency services workers, having needed their help herself two years ago. The campaign caught the attention of Liz Guest, owner of Big Bites cafe in Ripon, who has since implemented a priority service policy for on-duty blue light workers. Guest explained that she understood the importance of providing a quick and efficient service to these workers, who often have to sacrifice their breaks to respond to emergencies. By offering priority service, Guest hopes to make a small but meaningful contribution to supporting the local emergency services community. Paramedic Jacqui Pound, who inadvertently sparked the campaign, expressed her gratitude for the outpouring of support. She emphasized the importance of being able to take quick breaks, which can make a significant difference in the ability of paramedics to respond to emergencies effectively. Richard Bentley, a paramedic and Unison member, also welcomed the initiative, acknowledging that while he initially felt hesitant about jumping the queue, he now fully supports the idea. As the campaign continues to gain traction, it is clear that the people of Ripon are eager to show their appreciation for the hardworking men and women who serve their community.

A stunning exhibition of insect photographs, titled Microsculpture, has opened at Oxford's Museum of Natural History. The show features 24 large-format images, some measuring three metres wide, taken by British photographer Levon Biss. Biss's passion for insect photography was sparked by his son's fascination with a ground beetle found in their garden. Using a microscope, Biss was amazed by the beetle's beauty and decided to capture its details through photography. To create the intricate images, Biss photographs each insect in approximately 30 sections, using strobe lights to highlight the micro-sculptural beauty of each section. The individual shots are then merged to form a detailed, large-format picture. The result is a breathtaking display of the tiny creatures' intricate details. The Microsculpture exhibition will be on display at the museum until October, offering visitors a unique glimpse into the tiny world of insects. Biss's work is a testament to the beauty and complexity of these tiny creatures.

Nottinghamshire Police Face Budget Cuts and Potential Referendum Nottinghamshire Police are facing significant budget cuts, resulting in a 25% reduction in community support officer numbers. The force needs to save £2.4m from its budget due to government cuts, which will also lead to the closure of four police stations and five front counters. Unison, the union representing police staff, believes that an above 2% rise in council tax could help mitigate these cuts and is calling for a public referendum on the issue. However, Police and Crime Commissioner Paddy Tipping is skeptical about the success of such a referendum, citing the example of a recent vote in Bedfordshire where a proposed increase in the police precept was rejected by 70% of the population. Tipping stated that he is willing to discuss the issue but does not think that people will vote for an increase. Despite the challenges, a recent report from HMIC found that the force is making good progress towards achieving the required savings while maintaining an effective service to the public. Unison's Dave Ratchford pointed to a consultation conducted by the commissioner last year, which showed that 67% of respondents were willing to pay additional money to protect police services, and 82% were against further cuts. The debate highlights the difficult decisions facing police forces across the country as they struggle to balance budgets and maintain public services.

A 24-year-old man has been jailed for a vicious and unprovoked attack on a stranger in Bellshill. Kieran Kiely, who had absconded from Castle Huntly prison just four days earlier, targeted 37-year-old Christopher Smith on July 17. The High Court in Glasgow heard that Kiely approached Mr Smith as he worked on his Renault Clio 172 sport car and began talking to him about the vehicle. However, the conversation quickly turned violent as Kiely announced his intention to steal the car, punching Mr Smith and smashing a half brick into his face. The attack continued as Kiely kicked and hit Mr Smith with the brick, stealing his car keys, house keys, and mobile phone in the process. Despite being severely injured, Mr Smith managed to immobilize the car by pulling out leads from under the bonnet. As Kiely tried to escape, Mr Smith ran for help, but was chased and continued to be attacked. The ordeal only ended when police arrived, prompting Kiely to flee and discard the stolen keys. Kiely was later arrested and found to be wearing clothes with Mr Smith's blood on them. The victim suffered severe bruising and three head wounds, which will leave permanent scarring. Kiely, who has a history of convictions including car theft and assault, admitted charges of assault, theft, and attempted theft. Judge Lord Boyd condemned the attack as "vicious and unprovoked," stating that it must have been a "terrifying ordeal" for the victim. Kiely was subsequently jailed for his crimes. The court's decision reflects the severity of the attack and the need to protect the public from individuals with a history of violent behavior.

A Devon doctor who came to the aid of an elderly woman on a flight from Gatwick to Thessaloniki, Greece, has been offered a free flight by Easyjet after initially being rewarded with just a free hot drink. Dr Ed Southall, from Totnes, was on the flight in January when he was asked to assist the woman. Despite his good deed, he was only offered a complimentary coffee, and was even told he would have to pay for a Kit Kat. Dr Southall made several requests to Easyjet to inquire about their policy on rewarding passengers who provide medical assistance, but was met with a lackluster response. He was offered free baggage handling, but it wasn't until he wrote to travel reporter Simon Calder that the airline took notice. Easyjet has since apologized and offered Dr Southall a free flight as a gesture of goodwill. The airline stated that they are "grateful for the assistance Dr Southall provided" and acknowledged that they "didn't get this right" on the occasion. Dr Southall expressed that all he wanted was an apology, saying "you would think an airline would encourage people to help." The incident highlights the importance of recognizing and rewarding passengers who provide crucial assistance during flights.

Sir Bob Geldof Brings Together Music Stars for Band Aid 30 In a remarkable display of musical unity, Sir Bob Geldof has gathered some of the biggest names in the industry to record the fourth version of the iconic charity single, "Do They Know It's Christmas?"
