The star-studded lineup includes One Direction, Rita Ora, Olly Murs, Chris Martin, Sam Smith, Bono, and Ellie Goulding, among others. As the musicians came together to lend their voices to the cause, Sir Bob's witty one-liners kept everyone entertained throughout the day. The recording session was filled with memorable moments, including One Direction's soulful rendition of the song's opening lines. Sir Bob was impressed, saying, "It's beautiful. I mean seriously. I never expected that from them. It's very moody the start, and they just come sort of whispering in. It's great." He also noted that many of the younger artists, such as Ellie Goulding, Sam Smith, and the One Direction guys, grew up singing this song at their nativity plays. The new version of the song features changed lyrics that reflect the current Ebola outbreak in West Africa. When asked about the revised lyrics, Sir Bob was tight-lipped, jokingly swearing and saying it was meant to be a surprise. However, he did reveal that there would be a fight over Bono's re-vamped line, which has become a notable aspect of the song. Chris Martin was initially hesitant to sing the line, saying it belonged to Bono, but Sir Bob eventually convinced him to give it a try. After Bono recorded the line, Sir Bob described it as "mega." The song will make its debut on The X Factor results show, but fans won't be able to download it until Monday morning. Sir Bob explained that this is due to technical reasons, and the version played on The X Factor will be a rough edit. He also revealed that Simon Cowell, not many people know, always joins in on these charity efforts and offered him five minutes on The X Factor to promote the single. Other notable artists who were involved in the project include Bastille, who gave up two stadium shows in America to fly back and participate. Sir Bob praised their dedication, saying they didn't receive any compensation for their time or expenses. Unfortunately, not all artists were able to join in, including Adele, who is currently taking a break from music, and Jake Bugg, who had a prior gig commitment in Rio. Sir Bob emphasized that the true spirit of Band Aid 30 is about being part of an event and turning it into a phenomenon. He encouraged fans to support the cause by purchasing the single, rather than streaming it for free. "Don't do any of the free stuff, it's nonsense. Pay for it," he said. With the song's release on Monday, Sir Bob is confident it will reach number one by 8am. As the music world comes together to support this worthy cause, one thing is certain – Band Aid 30 is an event not to be missed.

Co-ordinated Protests Bring UK Cities to a Standstill as Activists Demand Action Against Racial Injustice A wave of protests swept across the UK on Friday, with campaigners blocking major roads and transport links in London, Nottingham, and Birmingham. The co-ordinated action, which saw 19 people arrested, was timed to coincide with the fifth anniversary of the death of Mark Duggan, who was shot by police in 2011. The protests, organized by a national network of anti-racists, brought severe disruption to holidaymakers driving to Heathrow airport, as well as commuters in Nottingham city centre. In London, activists barricaded the junction leading to Heathrow, causing tailbacks and delays for those trying to reach the airport. A spokesman for the airport confirmed that while there were significant delays, no one missed their flight as a result of the action. In Nottingham, protesters lay across tram tracks outside the Theatre Royal, bringing the city's transport network to a standstill during rush hour. The city centre was described as "gridlocked" as traffic struggled to navigate the blocked roads. Meanwhile, in Birmingham, campaigners blocked a road near the city's airport, causing further disruption to traffic. The protests were met with a significant police response, with officers using specialist cutting machinery to remove the activists, who had linked arms and sealed themselves in tubes filled with concrete. In total, 19 people were arrested in connection with the protests, with four people charged with wilful obstruction of a highway by Nottinghamshire Police. The activists behind the protests say they are demanding action against racial injustice and police brutality. Wail Qasim, who helped organize the Heathrow protest, said: "There's a constant disruption of black people's lives in the everyday. We face everyday forms of racism, from stop and search to increased levels of unemployment and over-representation in the prison system." Cara Thompson, part of the Nottingham movement, added: "We need people to listen, to really stop and listen to what is happening to black people - not just in the USA, but here in the UK." The national organization behind the protests says it is seeking to create a movement similar to the Black Lives Matter campaign in the US. In a statement, they said: "We have shutdown roads in London, Birmingham, Manchester, and Nottingham to mourn those who have died in custody and to protest the ongoing racist violence of the police, border enforcement, structural inequalities, and the everyday indignity of street racism." The protests are expected to continue throughout the day, with further demonstrations planned in cities across the UK. As the activists continue to demand action against racial injustice, it remains to be seen what impact their efforts will have on the government and law enforcement agencies. One thing is certain, however: the protests have brought the issue of racial inequality to the forefront of the national conversation, and it will be difficult to ignore the voices of those demanding change.

A former ice hockey player who represented Great Britain has been jailed for sexually exploiting young girls. Tom Squires, 26, pleaded guilty to one count of sexual activity with a child and four counts of inciting sexual activity with a child. The offences took place between 2011 and 2016, against five girls under the age of 16, in the Sheffield area. Squires, who played for the Sheffield Steelers and Hull Stingrays, used social media to approach his victims and request sexual images. He also used his position as an ice hockey coach to groom and exploit the girls, some of whom recognized him as a local hockey star. Squires was sentenced to five years and four months in prison, and will spend an additional three years on extended licence after his release. He has also been barred from working with children. Detective Sergeant Aneela Khalil-Khan praised the bravery of the victims in coming forward, and warned that Squires' actions were a clear abuse of his position of power and trust.

Tragedy Strikes: Cyclist Killed in Accident Involving Beer Delivery Truck A devastating incident occurred on July 3, 2014, in Nottingham city centre, resulting in the loss of a young life. Louise Wright, a 29-year-old cyclist, was fatally dragged under a beer delivery truck driven by Adam Haywood, 31, from Whitwell in Derbyshire. The tragic event has left the community in shock and highlighted the importance of road safety. According to prosecutors, Haywood failed to check his mirrors before turning left at traffic lights, leading to the fatal accident. The trial at Derby Crown Court revealed that Wright had cycled down the left side of the lorry and waited near the front of the vehicle, a practice not recommended by the Highway Code, but not illegal. The prosecution argued that Wright would not have been aware of Haywood's intention to turn left, as he did not have his indicators on. Haywood claimed he had checked his mirrors before turning left but did not see Wright, attributing her presence to his blind spot. However, he could not recall whether he had put on his indicators, which he stated was his usual practice. The Highway Code advises drivers to indicate their intentions, although it is not a legal requirement. The jury delivered a majority verdict, finding Haywood guilty of causing death by careless driving. Judge Jonathan Bennett sentenced Haywood to an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, and banned him from driving for two years. Additionally, Haywood was ordered to perform 150 hours of unpaid work and pay £1,500 in costs. Speaking after the verdict, Wright's mother, Sharon Brown, expressed her emotions, stating, "Nobody is a winner in this. It is just tragic what has happened." She acknowledged the verdict and sentence, saying, "I do feel the right verdict has been reached and the sentence was fair." Brown poignantly reflected on the what-ifs, highlighting the fleeting nature of life and the devastating consequences of a momentary lapse in concentration. Judge Bennett echoed Brown's sentiments, stating, "There are no winners in this particular case." He emphasized the need to "balance justice and mercy" in such tragic circumstances. The incident serves as a stark reminder of the importance of vigilance and responsible behavior on the roads, and the need for drivers and cyclists to be aware of their surroundings and follow safety guidelines. The community mourns the loss of a young life, and the case will undoubtedly have a lasting impact on all those involved.

Mike Phillips, the 33-year-old Welsh scrum-half, is set to join Aviva Premiership club Sale in the summer on a one-year contract from French side Racing 92. When asked if Sale could be his last club before retirement, Phillips remained uncertain, stating that he will assess his body and performance over the next few months. The five-cap British and Irish Lions player has had a storied career, playing for Bayonne, Ospreys, Cardiff Blues, and Scarlets. After five years in France, Phillips is eager to return to the UK and finish his career on a high note. He expressed enthusiasm for Sale, citing positive conversations with former players and coaching staff, and believes the club is "moving in the right direction." Phillips, who retired from international rugby in 2015, is looking forward to this new chapter in his career.

A rare bird species, the White's thrush, has been spotted in Scotland for the first time using a camera trap. The Wildlife Conservation Research Unit (WildCRU) at Oxford University's Zoology Department set up the camera trap in the Woodland Trust Scotland's Ledmore and Migdale Woods, near Bonar Bridge. The primary goal of the camera trap was to monitor for wildcats, but it captured an unexpected surprise. The camera trap, triggered by changes in heat and motion, took a photograph of the White's thrush, which breeds mainly in Siberia and Asia. Project manager Kerry Kilshaw expressed her delight at the discovery, crediting her field assistant Ruiradh Campbell for spotting the bird in one of the camera trap photos. WildCRU director Prof David Macdonald praised the technology, saying it has revolutionized field research, providing "eyes in the backs of our heads" and enabling breakthroughs in monitoring endangered species. The Ledmore and Migdale Woods site manager, Eleanor Garty, highlighted the area's diverse wildlife, including scarce summer visitors such as wood warblers and tree pipits. The discovery of the White's thrush is a significant bonus, demonstrating the woods' importance as a habitat for rare migrants. The camera trap's success underscores the value of innovative technology in conservation efforts, allowing researchers to gather valuable insights into the lives of elusive and endangered species.

BBC England Launches Festive Photo and Video Submission Campaign To celebrate the festive season, BBC England is inviting the public to submit their photographs and videos inspired by the classic "12 Days of Christmas" song. The campaign, titled England's Big Picture, encourages individuals to share their creative and festive captures via email, social media, or Instagram using the hashtag #englandsbigpicture. Those wishing to participate can email their submissions to england@bbc.co.uk or post them on Facebook and Twitter using the handle @BBCEngland. The BBC also has a dedicated Pinterest board, England's Big Picture, where a recent archive of pictures can be viewed. When submitting images, participants are asked to include relevant information and ensure that their photos were taken within the past week. By submitting content, individuals agree to grant the BBC a royalty-free, non-exclusive license to publish and use the material. However, contributors retain the copyright to their work, and their names will be published alongside their accepted images. The BBC reminds participants to prioritize their safety and the safety of others while collecting media and to respect all laws and regulations. While not all submissions are guaranteed to be used, the BBC looks forward to receiving a wide range of creative and festive submissions to showcase on their platforms.

In a surprising move, the British Horseracing Authority (BHA) has ruled that Diore Lia, a 1,000-1 outsider, will not be allowed to compete in the upcoming Derby at Epsom. The decision was made due to concerns over the inexperience of the horse's jockey, Kayleigh Mangan, who has only ridden one winner in her career, back in 2009 at Roscommon. The news has sparked controversy, particularly as the prize money from the race was set to be donated to Great Ormond Street's children's hospital. Owner Richard Aylward expressed his disappointment, stating that he would now refuse to run the horse. Aylward claimed that the BHA had "been got to" and had changed their mind, potentially due to pressure from other stakeholders. The BHA defended their decision, citing the need to prioritize the welfare of both human and equine participants. In a statement, they noted that while Mangan holds a license, her lack of experience, with only 69 rides and one winner, made it a risk to allow her to compete in a high-stakes event like the Derby. The authority emphasized that the unique challenges of the Derby, including its scale and stage, made it an unsuitable platform for an inexperienced jockey. The total purse for the Derby is a record £1.625m, with the winner set to receive £920,913. Despite the charitable intentions of Diore Lia's owners, the BHA's decision has been supported by some in the racing community, who argue that the risk of an incident occurring with an inexperienced jockey is too high. BBC Sport horse racing correspondent Cornelius Lysaght noted that while the story has a "romantic, David against Goliath" quality to it, the authority's decision is likely correct, given the potential consequences of an accident. The incident has sparked debate about the balance between charitable intentions and the need to prioritize safety in high-stakes sporting events.

Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink has parted ways with Queens Park Rangers (QPR) after a disappointing run of results. The 44-year-old Dutchman, who was appointed in December last year, won only 14 of his 47 matches in charge. His departure comes after a 1-1 draw with Nottingham Forest on Saturday, leaving QPR 17th in the table and six points above the relegation zone. Despite their poor form, the team is still within six points of sixth-placed Leeds in a tightly packed league table. Hasselbaink had been under pressure following a run of just two wins since August. The club has stated that an announcement regarding the managerial situation will be made in due course. Former Tottenham and Aston Villa boss Tim Sherwood has been linked to the job. Hasselbaink's tenure was also marred by controversy, including a Daily Telegraph investigation alleging corruption in football.

Gloucester's 22-year-old player, Evans, suffered a serious injury during last Saturday's 18-17 loss to Bath. The injury occurred in the first half after a tackle by Matt Garvey, who received a yellow card. According to Gloucester boss Nigel Davies, the injury appears to be a ligament issue and is "pretty serious." Davies expressed disappointment, stating that Evans had been playing exceptionally well and was close to international honors. Evans, who came through the club's academy, had made significant progress this season, earning his first Premiership and Heineken Cup starts. His injury is a significant blow to the team.

A "data protection issue" has been raised at the annual general meeting of DG Unlimited, a regional arts organization. The meeting, chaired by Cathy Agnew, was attended by members from across Dumfries and Galloway. Agnew confirmed that two members had raised concerns about the handling of private details. The issue is understood to center on the sharing of members' personal information without proper consent. Dumfries and Galloway Council has been made aware of the potential breach and is providing advice and assistance to investigate the matter. Although the council considers it an independent organization's issue, it is offering support to help resolve the problem. DG Unlimited operates four arts hubs across the region, covering Annandale and Eskdale, Nithsdale, the Stewartry, and Wigtownshire. The organization was established after the previous region-wide arts group, dgArts, ceased trading. An investigation is currently underway.

Joe Henson, founder of the Rare Breeds Survival Trust, has been made an MBE for his conservation services. He received the honor at Windsor Castle, accompanied by his wife Gill and children Louise and Adam, a farmer and TV presenter. The Henson family has run the Cotswold Farm Park since 1971. Henson expressed delight at the recognition, citing the park's ongoing work in saving rare breeds. He was particularly pleased to receive the award from Princess Anne, a rare breeds advocate. The honor acknowledges Henson's dedication to conservation and his lasting impact on the field.

A key witness in the trial of Ronnie Coulter, accused of murdering Surjit Singh Chhokar in 1998, has testified that the defendant and his nephew Andrew Coulter made disturbing comments about the victim on the day of the fatal stabbing. Donna Campbell, 33, took the stand at the High Court in Glasgow, recounting a conversation she overheard at Ronnie Coulter's flat in Overtown, North Lanarkshire, on the evening of November 4, 1998. At the time, Ms. Campbell was just 15 years old and had been dating Andrew Coulter for a couple of weeks. She was in the flat with her friend Corrine Chambers, as well as Ronnie and Andrew Coulter. According to her testimony, the men were discussing a plan to meet Mr. Chhokar later that night regarding a £100 Giro cheque. Ms. Campbell initially seemed hesitant to recall the specifics of the conversation, but when pressed by prosecutor Alex Prentice QC, she revealed that Ronnie and Andrew Coulter had been "laughing and joking" about Mr. Chhokar. Ms. Campbell stated that one of the men had mentioned hitting Mr. Chhokar on the knees with a bat, and when asked to elaborate, she referenced a statement she had given to police in 2012. In that statement, she had said that Ronnie and Andrew Coulter were "laughing and joking about going to see Chhokar" and that one of them had said they were going to "batter him." When asked to confirm the accuracy of this statement, Ms. Campbell replied, "Yes." Under cross-examination by defence QC Donald Findlay, Ms. Campbell acknowledged that the conversation had been "not particularly nice" but seemed to downplay its significance. She agreed that the tone had been "joking or light-hearted" and suggested that the men may have been "talking big" to impress her and her friend. However, the jury has already heard that Ronnie and Andrew Coulter, along with David Montgomery, did indeed meet Mr. Chhokar in Garrion Street later that night, and that the encounter ended in tragedy. Mr. Chhokar, 32, was fatally stabbed and left dying in the street. Ronnie Coulter, 48, denies murder and has lodged a special defence blaming his nephew Andrew Coulter and David Montgomery for the crime. The trial, which is now in its third week, continues before Judge Lord Matthews. As the prosecution presents its case, the jury must weigh the evidence and consider the events of that fateful night in 1998. The testimony of Donna Campbell has provided a glimpse into the events leading up to the tragic death of Surjit Singh Chhokar, and the trial will continue to unfold in the coming days.

A young Dublin boy's heartfelt message to boxer Michael Conlan has led to a special gift. Finn McManus, who had written to Conlan after his controversial loss at the Rio Olympics, was presented with custom-made boxing gloves on RTÉ's The Late Late Show. The gloves bear both Finn's and Conlan's names, fulfilling a promise the boxer made after receiving the youngster's message of support. Finn had offered Conlan his school medal and words of comfort after the boxer's quarter-final bantamweight bout against Russia's Vladimir Nikitin. The message, written by Finn's sister Lily, was sent to Conlan via Facebook and later shared on Twitter, where it sparked a "social media storm." Conlan, who won bronze at the London 2012 Olympics, described the message as "very warming" and vowed to send a gift to his young fan. Conlan, who recently confirmed he is turning professional, made headlines at Rio 2016 with his outspoken criticism of the judges who decided against him. Despite the controversy, he remains a beloved figure in Irish boxing, and his gesture to Finn has only added to his popularity. The custom-made gloves are a touching tribute to the young boy's kindness and a reminder of the power of sport to inspire and connect people. Conlan is currently in negotiations with promoters as he prepares to embark on his professional career.

British Cycling Faces Funding Uncertainty Amid Governance Concerns Sport England, the organization responsible for funding grassroots sports, has warned British Cycling that it must meet the highest standards of governance before receiving its allocated £17m in funding. This comes after a draft report into the culture of British Cycling's elite program was leaked, revealing concerns about decision-making within the governing body. The report, which is due to be released imminently, follows accusations of bullying and sexism against elite cyclists. British Cycling's chairman, Jonathan Browning, has already apologized for "failings" within the organization, and the body has begun working on an action plan to address the issues. However, Sport England's chair, Nick Bitel, has stated that more work is required on this plan before funding can be released. Bitel emphasized the importance of ensuring that all sports organizations receiving public funding meet the highest standards of governance. The funding in question is intended for grassroots cycling programs, and Sport England is keen to ensure that it is being used effectively. The organization's board will review the final report of the Cycling Independent Review and a revised version of British Cycling's action plan before making a decision on any additional requirements. This decision is expected to be made within the next month. The warning from Sport England has significant implications for British Cycling, with the potential for the organization's leadership to be called into question. Unless substantial reforms are implemented, there is a possibility that Sport England may demand the replacement of Jonathan Browning as chairman. The fate of the £17m in funding hangs in the balance, and British Cycling must take immediate action to address the concerns surrounding its governance and culture.

A 27-year-old cold case has taken a significant step forward with the arrest of a woman in connection with the death of a newborn baby. The infant's body was discovered at Windmill Pit in Weasenham St Peter, Norfolk, on June 5, 1988. The woman, who has since been released on bail, claimed the baby was stillborn and that she had concealed her pregnancy from family and friends. Norfolk Police exhumed the baby's body last April to conduct tests. While the woman was initially arrested on suspicion of infanticide, the Crown Prosecution Service is considering all options, including charges related to failing to register the birth and preventing a lawful burial. Detective Inspector Andy Guy expressed sympathy for the woman, who has carried the secret for nearly three decades, and confirmed that police do not believe anyone else was involved in the incident.

Trefeglwys Community Council to Dissolve Amid Ongoing Dispute The Trefeglwys Community Council will cease to function after the upcoming polls on May 4, with its responsibilities being absorbed by Powys Council. This decision comes after a three-year dispute that has taken a significant toll on the community council's ability to serve its residents. The row, initially sparked by plans to build pylons in the area, has led to investigations by the Information Commissioner, One Voice Wales, and the police. According to a letter sent to Powys Council, the ongoing dispute has caused "disruption and distress" for the community council, resulting in the resignation of two clerks. The councillors have stated that they are no longer able to effectively serve the community due to the time-consuming and disruptive nature of the issue. The community council has also incurred significant costs, including solicitors' fees and extra hours paid to clerks. Powys Council has announced that temporary councillors may be appointed as an interim measure to ensure a smooth transition. A meeting to discuss the future of the community council will be held on May 18, after the elections. The dissolution of the Trefeglwys Community Council marks the end of a tumultuous period for the community, and residents will be looking to Powys Council to provide stability and effective governance moving forward.

A recent survey by uSwitch has revealed that a significant portion of Britons will be carrying credit card debt into the new year. Approximately 85% of respondents stated that they will still be paying off their credit cards in 2017, with an average debt of £636. Furthermore, over half of those surveyed believe they will still be settling their Christmas expenses by the time next year's festive season arrives. The survey, which questioned 1,261 adults, found that 65% are concerned about their level of debt. This concern is echoed by Bank of England Governor Mark Carney, who has warned about the high debt levels within British households. The survey also revealed that 19% of respondents spent beyond their means over the festive period, with a quarter doing so to capture the "magic of Christmas". The main reasons cited for overspending were the increased expense of Christmas this year and the pressure to keep up with others.

Lena Dunham Takes a Stand Against Unrealistic Beauty Standards with Unretouched Magazine Cover Actress and writer Lena Dunham is making a bold statement against unrealistic beauty standards by appearing on the cover of Glamour magazine's February issue with her cellulite on full display. The issue, which is 100% produced by women, features Dunham alongside her Girls co-stars Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, and Jemima Kirke. Dunham took to Instagram to express her pride and gratitude to the magazine for allowing her to showcase her natural beauty, imperfections and all. In her post, Dunham reflected on her past struggles with body image, revealing that she was often told she was "funny looking" as a teenager. She recalled being self-conscious about her "potbelly, rabbit teeth, knock knees," and feeling haunted by careless comments and hostility. However, Dunham emphasized that she never hated her own appearance, but rather the culture that perpetuated negative body image. Dunham's decision to appear unretouched on the cover of Glamour is a significant statement, particularly given her history of speaking out against the use of Photoshop in the media. Earlier this year, she complained about a Spanish magazine that allegedly used "mad Photoshop" on a photo of her, only to later retract her statement after the magazine claimed it had not altered the image. The actress has long been known for her confidence and willingness to bare her skin on television, but she has also faced criticism and scrutiny over her body. Dunham noted that when her career began, people would often comment on her appearance, framing it as a "bold move" to show her body on TV. However, she argued that this kind of commentary only serves to perpetuate the idea that women's bodies need to be perfected or hidden. By appearing on the cover of Glamour without retouching, Dunham is taking a powerful stand against the unrealistic beauty standards that plague the media. Cellulite, which affects people of all sizes, is a natural and inevitable part of the aging process, and Dunham's decision to showcase it proudly is a refreshing change from the airbrushed and Photoshopped images that typically dominate magazine covers. As Dunham herself said, "I never want to be retouched again," and her commitment to promoting body positivity and self-acceptance is an inspiration to women everywhere.

World Champion Shi Dominates 3m Springboard Event At the recent Olympic games, 24-year-old world champion Shi took home the top prize in the 3m springboard event with a score of 406.05. This impressive score left her nearly 20 points ahead of her nearest rival, compatriot He Zi. Italian athlete Tania Cagnotto secured the bronze medal in her final Olympic appearance. Meanwhile, British diver Grace Reid made history by becoming the first British woman to reach the final of the 3m springboard event since 1972. The 20-year-old finished in eighth place with a final dive score of 67.50. Reid expressed her excitement and satisfaction with her performance, stating that she "loved every second" of the experience. She also joked about her mother, who used to be anxious about her diving, finally being able to watch her compete without worry. Reid's impressive debut has sparked excitement for the future of British diving.

Diego Maradona, the legendary Argentine footballer, has undergone a new gastric bypass surgery in Venezuela. The procedure took place in the city of Maracaibo, 10 years after his initial surgery. Despite the first operation, Maradona had gained weight and developed complications. According to Dr. Carlos Felipe Chaux, Maradona is recovering well and feeling fine with no pain. He will remain in Maracaibo for at least eight days before traveling to Caracas to complete his recovery. Maradona's health issues are well-documented, including struggles with obesity and alcohol addiction. The football icon led Argentina to World Cup victory in 1986 and has been in the spotlight recently, supporting the Argentine rugby team in the Rugby World Cup in England. Fans around the world are wishing Maradona a speedy recovery and hoping he will regain his health and well-being. His legacy as a football great continues to inspire fans globally.

Former lord mayor Nichola Mallon has been selected as the SDLP's candidate for North Belfast, replacing retiring MLA Alban Maginness. Mallon was chosen by party members at a convention in Belfast on Thursday. She expressed her gratitude, calling it a "great honour" to defend the seat and a "privilege" to take over from Maginness. Mallon praised Maginness' dedication to justice and human rights, saying his voice will be "sorely missed" from politics. SDLP leader Colum Eastwood endorsed Mallon, citing her compassion and dedication to the city's people, which made her a successful lord mayor. With her selection, Mallon is poised to bring her unique perspective and experience to the role, building on Maginness' legacy in North Belfast. Her candidacy is expected to be a strong contender in the upcoming election.

A mysterious blast that shook properties and sparked widespread speculation has been linked to activity at a Ministry of Defence (MoD) live firing test site in the Hebrides. The loud bang was heard across the islands, with residents in South Uist, Benbecula, and Barra reporting the incident. Sheila MacCormick, owner of the Borrodale Hotel in South Uist, described the moment the blast occurred, saying the building shook and people were left standing in the road, looking around in confusion. Aviation authorities have ruled out the possibility of an aircraft's sonic boom, while initial speculation about an earthquake has also been dismissed. Instead, it is believed that the blast may have been related to a controlled explosion of out-of-date explosives at the MoD's Hebrides Range. Some residents reported receiving letters alerting them to activity at the rocket range, adding weight to this theory. The incident has caused concern among local residents, who were left wondering what had caused the loud noise. Despite the initial confusion, it appears that the blast was likely a planned event, although the MoD has yet to confirm the details.

Linfield have secured a vital away goal in their first round qualifying tie against Cork, thanks to a strike from Maguire. The goal sets up an exciting second leg at Turner's Cross next week. Northern Ireland goalkeeper Roy Carroll, making his debut for Linfield, played a crucial role in denying Cork a second goal with several fine saves. The match saw both teams create scoring opportunities, with Paul Smyth missing a chance to score from six yards in the first half. Linfield, who finished as runners-up in the Irish Premiership and lost in the Irish Cup final, were without injured defender Sean Ward and Jimmy Callacher, who is on honeymoon. Cork, currently second in the Irish Premier Division, came into the tie with confidence, but were unable to capitalize on their chances. Visiting goalkeeper Mark McNulty made several key saves, including tipping Ross Gaynor's free-kick over the bar and denying Kirk Millar and Karl Sheppard. Maguire's goal broke the deadlock, and he continued to cause problems for the Cork defense, forcing Carroll into a point-blank save and flashing a shot narrowly wide. The second leg is set to be an intense encounter, with Linfield looking to build on their away goal and Cork seeking to overturn the deficit. With both teams creating scoring opportunities, the tie is far from over, and next week's match promises to be an exciting conclusion to the qualifying tie.

England Manager Roy Hodgson's contract is set to expire after Euro 2016, but FA chief Martin Glenn remains confident in his position. Despite a disappointing 2014 World Cup, where England failed to win a game, the team has shown significant improvement under Hodgson, winning all eight qualifying games for the upcoming tournament in France. Glenn stated that Hodgson is "very comfortable" with his situation and would not push for a contract extension if he doesn't perform well. This approach is a departure from the past, as seen with former manager Fabio Capello, who signed a new contract before the 2010 World Cup, only to be eliminated by Germany. Glenn also addressed England's image in the global game, acknowledging that the FA is often perceived as arrogant, but disagrees with this assessment.

A recent video sparked controversy when it appeared to show US President Trump refusing to shake hands with a young boy in a wheelchair at the White House. Renowned author J.K. Rowling was among those who expressed outrage, calling the president's behavior "stunning" and "horrible." However, the boy's mother, Marjorie Kelly Weer, has come forward to set the record straight. According to Weer, the video clip did not accurately represent the interaction between her son, Monty, and President Trump. In fact, Trump had shaken Monty's hand as he entered the room. Weer took to Facebook to clarify the situation, stating that her son wasn't even trying to shake the president's hand and isn't particularly fond of shaking hands in general. Rowling has since apologized for her misunderstanding, tweeting that she had "projected her own sensitivities" onto the situation. While she apologized to the boy and his family, she did not extend the apology to President Trump. The author has deleted her initial tweets on the subject, and the controversy appears to have been resolved. The incident serves as a reminder to be cautious when interpreting video footage and to verify information before jumping to conclusions.

Nottingham Man Admits to Human Trafficking and Forced Labour Charges A 43-year-old man from Nottingham has pleaded guilty to human trafficking and forced labour charges after exploiting a Polish worker. Sajmon Brzezinski, of Overdale Road, Old Basford, admitted to bringing the man to the UK in 2011 and forcing him to work for minimal pay. According to police, Brzezinski paid the worker just £20 to £30 per week, despite earning £480. He also took control of the worker's passport and set up bank accounts in his name, but kept the bank card, preventing the worker from accessing his wages. The worker was told he owed £2,000, which he was forced to pay off through his labour. The exploitation came to light when the worker confided in a colleague at a Christmas party. Brzezinski's arrest followed an investigation by the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority (GLAA) and Nottinghamshire Police. The GLAA's head of operations, Ian Waterfield, said Brzezinski controlled the worker through threats of violence. Brzezinski, who owned multiple cars and properties, including a "palace" with 50 windows in Poland, also admitted to a charge of fraud against another victim. His sentencing is scheduled for June 15. The case has highlighted the issue of modern-day slavery and the need for vigilance in detecting exploitation. Jon Hammond, who employed the worker on a farm near Arnold, Nottingham, described the situation as "shocking" and "abhorrent", saying it was "happening under our nose" without being detected.

Zambian Government Expels South African Opposition Leader Mmusi Maimane In a shocking turn of events, South African opposition leader Mmusi Maimane was expelled from Zambia on Friday, just hours before he was set to attend a court appearance of Zambian opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema. The Zambian government cited concerns that Maimane's presence would put "undue pressure" on the judiciary, but Maimane and his party, the Democratic Alliance (DA), have condemned the move as a clear sign of Zambia's descent into dictatorship. Maimane had planned to show solidarity with Hichilema, who was arrested in April and charged with treason after his convoy allegedly refused to give way to President Edgar Lungu's motorcade. The charges have been widely criticized as "trumped up" and an attempt to silence Hichilema, who narrowly lost to Lungu in last year's disputed presidential elections. According to the DA, Maimane was "aggressively confronted" by police when his plane landed in Lusaka, and was "forcefully" prevented from entering the country. The party has called the Zambian government's behavior "shameful" and has urged the South African government to lodge a diplomatic protest. Maimane has been vocal about his support for Hichilema, using social media to call for solidarity and awareness about the Zambian opposition leader's plight. He has argued that as a fellow African, he has a responsibility to speak out against oppression and stand in solidarity with those fighting for the rule of law. The Zambian government, however, has defended its decision to expel Maimane, saying that his presence in court would have undermined the independence of the judiciary. Zambia's top diplomat in South Africa, Emmanuel Mwamba, said that it was imperative that the due process of the law was respected without undue pressure or interference. The case against Hichilema is set to continue, with the magistrate's court ruling that his lawyers can seek a judicial review of the charges. If convicted, Hichilema faces a minimum jail term of 15 years and a maximum sentence of death. The international community is watching the case closely, with many calling for Hichilema's release and an end to the persecution of opposition leaders in Zambia.
Cyprus enjoys a free media landscape, with state-run and private operators competing, and unrestricted internet access for over 656,000 users, according to Freedom House.

A recent inspection at Queen's House, a private care home in Kelso, has highlighted concerns over staffing after a nurse was found to be working without suitable qualifications. The Care Inspectorate, which carried out the inspection, graded the facility's staffing as "weak", despite awarding excellent ratings in three other categories. The incident, which was described as an "isolated incident" by Queen's House chairman Alastair Turnbull, involved a member of staff who was appointed to a position without being suitably qualified. An investigation was launched, involving the police and Scottish Borders Council's social work department, and the staff member was subsequently dismissed. According to the Care Inspectorate, the issue was identified by the care service itself, which "acted swiftly and took the appropriate action". A spokesman for the inspectorate said that the safety, welfare, and dignity of service users were the top priority, and that they were satisfied that the well-being of residents was not affected. However, relatives of residents have expressed concerns over the fact that the woman was not a registered nurse. Inspector Lesley Smith, who carried out the inspection in January, noted that Queen's House had a recruitment policy in place, but that it had not been "strenuously followed" in this instance. Chairman Alastair Turnbull acknowledged that there had been an incident, but emphasized that it had been dealt with and that there was "no issue with care". He pointed out that the home had received excellent ratings in all other areas, and that the incident was an isolated one. Queen's House is a not-for-profit home that cares for 32 older people, and is run by a voluntary management committee. The Care Inspectorate has emphasized the importance of robust recruitment practices in care services, particularly when working with vulnerable individuals. The incident highlights the need for care homes to ensure that staff are properly qualified and vetted to provide the highest level of care.

High Court Hears Shocking Alleged Confession in Murder Trial A dramatic turn of events unfolded at the High Court in Glasgow as a key witness testified against Ronnie Coulter, the 48-year-old accused of murdering Surjit Singh Chhokar in 1998. Noreen McPolland, 54, took the stand and revealed a shocking alleged confession made by Coulter during a prison visit in 1998 or 1999. According to McPolland, Coulter made the startling admission while she and his sister, Margaret Chisholm, visited him at Barlinnie Prison. When asked by prosecutor Alex Prentice QC if Coulter had ever spoken about Chhokar's death, McPolland replied, "He said'I stabbed him'." She further testified that Coulter's sister had urged him to own up to his actions, prompting him to make the incriminating statement. McPolland, who was married to Coulter's brother Andrew for 15 years, described her reaction to the alleged confession as one of shock and disengagement. She claimed to have gotten up and gone to the canteen, not wanting to be involved in the conversation. However, she did recall another instance where Coulter allegedly spoke about the murder, this time during a visit to his brother's home just days after Chhokar's death. On that occasion, McPolland testified that her husband had asked Coulter if he had stabbed Chhokar, to which Coulter allegedly replied that he had. Coulter also reportedly mentioned that Chhokar was shouting for his partner, Liz Bryce, after being stabbed. The prosecution has alleged that Coulter, along with his nephew Andrew Coulter and David Montgomery, had gone to see Chhokar on the day of the murder over a dispute regarding a £100 Giro cheque. The trial has heard that Andrew Coulter admitted to hitting Chhokar with a homemade lead-filled bat but denied stabbing him. Montgomery has also denied any involvement in the stabbing. Pathologist Dr. Marjorie Turner previously testified that Chhokar suffered three stab wounds to the chest and died from massive blood loss. Notably, Ronnie Coulter was tried and acquitted of Chhokar's murder in 1999. However, the case was reopened, and Coulter now faces trial again, with a special defense blaming his nephew Andrew Coulter and David Montgomery for the crime. The trial, presided over by Judge Lord Matthews, continues, with the jury carefully considering the evidence presented. As the proceedings unfold, the court awaits further testimony and evidence that will ultimately determine Coulter's fate.

Bristol's homeless population is receiving support from two new initiatives. Keep Bristol Warm is collecting rucksacks filled with essential items at the city's Bearpit. Meanwhile, Pending Coffee has launched, allowing customers to buy extra cups for homeless individuals to claim. Organiser Gavyn Emery was inspired by a similar project in Edinburgh after seeing a man in need with his dog. With 74 people recorded as sleeping rough in Bristol, these projects aim to provide vital assistance. Emery's father described Pending Coffee as "people giving to people," highlighting the simple yet effective nature of the initiative.

A 27-year-old man from Kent is recovering after a lucky escape on Helvellyn. He fractured his ankle falling from Striding Edge, near Red Tarn, in "full-on winter conditions" on Thursday. The Patterdale Mountain Rescue Team responded, airlifting him to hospital in Carlisle with coastguard assistance. The four-hour rescue involved support from Penrith Mountain Rescue Team. Team leader Mike Blakey warned that Helvellyn is in full winter conditions, stressing the need for proper equipment, including ice axes and crampons, and knowledge of how to use them to enjoy the mountains safely.

A theme park playground incident has sparked a police appeal after two six-year-old girls were inappropriately touched by a man. The incident occurred on August 11 at Legoland in Windsor, Berkshire, in the pirate-themed Castaway Camp play area. One parent expressed surprise that an adult was inside the playground, stating she had not expected it and was more concerned about her child getting lost. The assaults happened between 12:15 and 12:30 BST, when approximately 14,200 people attended the theme park. Thames Valley Police have released an e-fit of the suspect and will air a reconstruction on BBC One's Crimewatch, followed by a police appeal. The mothers of the girls shared their concerns, with one saying the incident was a shock, as Legoland was a highlight of their summer holiday plans. A man in his 20s from Bracknell was arrested but released without charge on August 31. The police are now seeking the public's help to identify the suspect and bring him to justice. The incident has raised concerns about safety at the theme park.

Hershey, North America's largest chocolate maker, has revised its sales forecast downward due to macroeconomic challenges in China. The company now expects net sales to increase by 2.5%-3.5% this year, a significant decrease from its previous prediction of 4.5%-5.5%. To adapt to changing consumer behavior, Hershey plans to cut 300 jobs and shift its focus to smaller format stores. The company will also prioritize brands with high returns. While sales in China have been slow, Hershey's North America confectionery business is thriving, driven by solid gross margin expansion. The company is on track to meet its 2015 financial objectives at home. Shares in Hershey fell over 2.5% in New York trading following the announcement. Despite this, the company remains a major player in the industry, producing iconic brands like Hershey chocolate bars and Reese's Peanut Butter Cups.

US Regulators Demand Improved "Living Will" Plans from Major Banks The US Federal Reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp (FDIC) have issued a stern warning to three major banks, including HSBC, Royal Bank of Scotland (RBS), and French bank BNP Paribas. The regulators have deemed the banks' "living wills" - plans outlining how they would be wound up in the event of a catastrophic shock - as inadequate and in need of significant improvement. The plans, which were submitted as part of the 2010 Dodd Frank Act, failed to meet the required standards, with the FDIC describing them as "not credible". The regulators have called for the banks to make considerable changes, including improving derivative contracts to allow for quick termination in the event of bankruptcy. Additionally, the banks must ensure that critical functions can continue to operate during a crisis and that they can produce reliable information rapidly. The warning comes as part of a broader effort to prevent a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis, where taxpayer funds were used to bail out struggling banks. The Dodd Frank Act requires banks to draw up living wills to demonstrate how they can navigate ordinary bankruptcy without relying on government assistance. The US Fed and FDIC have the power to shut down or split up the operations of a US bank or subsidiary of a foreign bank if their plans are deemed insufficient. This is not the first time regulators have criticized banks for their living wills, with 11 banks, including JP Morgan Chase and Deutsche Bank, being censured last year.

A 19-year-old man has been jailed for six months for religiously aggravated harassment of four Orthodox Jews, including a 13-year-old boy. Patrick Delaney, from Twin Oaks Caravan Park in Essex, admitted to the offense, which occurred on January 6, 2016, at Tottenham Hale retail park. Delaney, who was under the influence of nitrous oxide, yelled "Hitler" at the victims and threw gas canisters. One victim and her son took shelter in a nearby supermarket. Judge John Dodd QC condemned Delaney's actions as unacceptable in "any civilised society". The sentencing comes amid rising anti-Semitic hate incidents in the UK, with recent figures reaching record levels. Delaney's actions were widely condemned, highlighting the need for greater tolerance and respect for all communities.
An inventor has created a road-making method using recycled plastic to replace bitumen, combining it with rocks and sand for a sustainable alternative.

A 26-year-old man has been fined and ordered to pay court costs after stealing a pink beret from comedian Eddie Izzard during a Brexit march in London. David Czerwonko, of Clitherow Road, Brentford, appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court where he pleaded guilty to the offense. The court heard that Izzard was leading the march down Whitehall when a group of masked men blocked the path with a large Brexit campaign banner. Izzard responded by condemning the group, calling them "the face of Brexit, masked and dangerous." Czerwonko, who did not recognize the comedian, then snatched Izzard's beret, which had sentimental value due to its UK and EU badges. However, Izzard quickly chased after him and reclaimed the hat with the help of police. Czerwonko's defense argued that the act was an "instinctive and silly reaction" and not a premeditated attempt to cause trouble. The court acknowledged that the incident was spontaneous and that the beret was recovered. Czerwonko was fined £185 and ordered to pay £85 in court costs, as well as a £30 victim surcharge. The incident has raised questions about the police's response to the incident, with Green Party peer Jenny Jones suggesting that Izzard's fame may have influenced the swift reaction and sentencing. Jones stated that it would be "fantastic" if all small crimes were treated with the same level of seriousness. The march was one of several rallies held across the country on the anniversary of the outbreak of World War II, calling for a pause in the Brexit process.

Gocompare Founder Hayley Parsons to Step Down in £190m Deal In a significant development, Gocompare's founder and chief executive, Hayley Parsons, will be standing down from her position as part of a £190m deal. The company, which was started by Ms Parsons eight years ago, will continue to operate from its current headquarters in Newport. The deal, which requires regulatory approval, values Ms Parsons' remaining 23% stake at almost £44m. Esure, which already owns 50% of Gocompare after investing in the company in 2010, will now take full control. Ms Parsons expressed her pride in the company's achievements, stating that it has become a leading price comparison business in the UK. She attributed this success to the hard work of her team in Newport. Gocompare gained widespread recognition for its advertising campaigns featuring the fictional Italian tenor, Gio Compario. Ms Parsons, 41, has had a distinguished career in the insurance industry, having spent 14 years at Admiral insurance in Cardiff before setting up Gocompare in 2006. She has won several awards for her entrepreneurial achievements, including an OBE for services to the economy in 2012. The deal marks a significant milestone for Gocompare, which has grown rapidly since its inception. Ms Parsons' decision to step down will likely have a significant impact on the company's future direction. However, with Esure at the helm, Gocompare is expected to continue its growth trajectory and remain a major player in the UK's price comparison market. The regulatory approval process is expected to be completed in the coming months, paving the way for a new era at Gocompare.

A Dundee University student is shedding light on the potential knee injuries faced by curlers, particularly those using the toe-sliding technique. Iona Robertson, who is studying applied orthopaedic technology, has been collecting data from members of the men's British curling team that competed in the 2014 Winter Olympics. The research sessions, held at The Peak sports village in Stirling, involved Olympians David Murdoch, Scott Andrews, and Michael Goodfellow. As part of the study, the team members delivered 12 stones, with six from a flat foot slide position and six from a toe slide, while wearing in-shoe pressure measurement insoles. Robertson also recorded video footage of the deliveries to measure the knee angles of the players. Her preliminary findings suggest that toe-sliding may indeed be more likely to cause knee injuries, with significantly higher joint forces in the knee compared to flat-footed slides. Although the final results are not yet complete, Robertson is optimistic about the promising data collected so far. The study aims to understand and establish the differences in knee force between the two delivery techniques, providing valuable insights for curlers and coaches to minimize the risk of injury.

Whether you've captured a stunning sunset, a bustling city scene, or a peaceful landscape, we want to see it. To submit your photo, simply email us at england@bbc.co.uk, post it on our Facebook page, or tweet it to @BBCEngland. By sharing your photo, you grant the BBC a royalty-free, non-exclusive licence to publish and use the material in any way we want. However, you still retain the copyright to your work, and we will publish your name alongside your photo if it's selected for use. Remember to always follow safety guidelines and respect the law when taking photos. We look forward to seeing your contributions to England's Big Picture.

Former Thai Monk Arrives in Bangkok to Face Charges Wirapol Sukphol, a former Thai monk, has arrived in Bangkok to face charges of child molestation, child abduction, money laundering, and fraud. Sukphol, who was once known as Nen Kham, gained notoriety in 2013 after a YouTube video showed him on a private jet with luxury items. He was later accused of having sex with an underage girl and fled to the US, where he resisted extradition efforts. Sukphol, who was expelled from the monkhood, arrived in Bangkok on Wednesday wearing clerical garments. He is expected to strongly contest the charges against him. The case has drawn attention to the scandals plaguing the Thai monkhood, which is a cornerstone of Thai society. The military, which has been in power since 2014, is under pressure to address the alleged excesses of the monkhood. The charges against Sukphol include the discovery of millions of dollars in assets in his name. His case is one of several high-profile scandals involving the monkhood, including that of influential abbot Phra Dhammajayo, who is wanted on money laundering charges. The arrival of Sukphol in Bangkok marks a significant development in the case, and his trial is expected to be closely watched. The outcome may have implications for the reputation of the Thai monkhood and the military's efforts to reform it.

Turing Pharmaceuticals to Lower Price of Daraprim After Public Outcry Following widespread criticism and outrage, Martin Shkreli, the CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, has announced that the company will lower the price of Daraprim, a life-saving medication used to treat a parasitic infection. The decision comes after Turing Pharmaceuticals raised the cost of the drug from $13.50 to $750 in August, sparking accusations of price-gouging. Shkreli initially defended the price hike, stating that the increased revenue would be used to fund research and development of new treatments. However, the move was met with fierce criticism from medical groups, with one organization describing the price increase as "unjustifiable." The pharmaceutical industry's main lobbying group, PhRMA, also distanced itself from Turing, tweeting that the company "does not represent the values of PhRMA member companies." In an interview with ABC News, Shkreli announced that the company would reduce the price of Daraprim to a more affordable level, allowing the company to make a "very small profit." While the exact price reduction has not been disclosed, the move is seen as a significant concession in the face of public pressure. The controversy surrounding Daraprim highlights the complex and often contentious issue of drug pricing. In the US, prices are determined by a market-driven system, where private insurance companies and government programs such as Medicare and Medicaid negotiate with pharmaceutical companies. This can lead to significant price fluctuations, with some medications becoming prohibitively expensive for patients. The debate over fair pricing for life-saving medications is likely to continue, with many arguing that profits should not come at the expense of patient access to essential treatments.

Small Energy Providers Fear CMA Rule Change Will Stifle Competition A group of six smaller energy providers has expressed deep concern over proposed new rules by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), which they believe will favor the "Big Six" energy companies and discourage competition in the market. The CMA's proposals, which follow its energy market review earlier this year, suggest that price comparison websites will no longer be required to show all available energy deals, but rather only those from companies that have paid them a commission or fee. The smaller providers, including GB Energy Supply, COOP Energy, Go Effortless Energy, Bulb, So Energy, and Zog Energy, have written to Energy Secretary Amber Rudd, warning that this move will lead to a lack of transparency and create an unfair market. They argue that consumers use price comparison websites believing they will be shown the cheapest prices available, but under the new rules, these websites will only show deals from the Big Six suppliers who have paid for advertising. "This will mean that millions of people will be misled into thinking they are getting the best deal, when in fact they are only being shown a limited selection of options," the providers said in their letter. "We are deeply worried about the serious ramifications of this proposal and urge the Government to think again." The CMA's investigation into the energy market found that price comparison websites often allowed consumers to switch energy suppliers immediately, but it was not always clear that they only showed options from firms that had paid a commission or fee. The watchdog believes that allowing price comparison websites to prioritize certain deals will lead to increased competition and lower prices, as sites will be incentivized to compete for exclusive deals with suppliers. However, the smaller providers disagree, arguing that this will only serve to strengthen the dominance of the Big Six energy companies. They point out that these companies already have a significant market share and will be able to pay more for advertising, making it even harder for smaller providers to compete. Uswitch, the UK's third-largest price comparison website, has disagreed with the smaller providers' analysis. A spokesperson for the site said that price comparison websites offer a cost-effective way for energy suppliers to advertise their products and acquire customers. "The CMA's package of proposals will incentivise sites to compete for exclusive deals with suppliers, boost competition and lower energy prices for consumers," they said. The Government has said that it wants a "competitive and effective energy market" that works for consumers. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy said that the number of energy suppliers has increased significantly since 2010, with over 40 providers now operating in the market, and smaller firms making up 15% of the dual fuel market. The CMA is set to publish its final recommendations on remedies for the energy sector before the end of June. The smaller providers will be hoping that their concerns are taken into account and that the Government will reconsider the proposed rule change. If not, they fear that the energy market will become even more dominated by the Big Six, and consumers will lose out as a result.

Former Tory Chief Whip Andrew Mitchell has spoken out about the media storm that led to his resignation, claiming that his treatment by the press was "completely wrong". In an interview with Channel 4's Dispatches programme, Mr Mitchell denied allegations that he called Downing Street police officers "plebs" and insisted that he did not lose his temper during the incident on September 19 last year. The altercation, which took place when a police officer refused to let Mr Mitchell exit through the main Downing Street gate with his bicycle, sparked a wave of media criticism and demands for his resignation. However, Mr Mitchell claims that the coverage was unfair and that he was "caught between the pincers of the police on the one hand and the media on the other". CCTV footage of the incident has cast doubt on the original police accounts, and four people have been arrested in an investigation into their handling and reporting of the episode. Mr Mitchell's denial of the allegations has been supported by some, including Steve White, vice-chairman of the Police Federation, who attempted to distance the national organisation from the criticism of Mr Mitchell. Despite this, Prime Minister David Cameron has repeated his desire for a "thorough" inquiry into the incident, and a Downing Street spokesman has said that the prime minister takes full responsibility for the way the case was handled. Mr Mitchell has also criticised Number 10's handling of the situation, claiming that they did not do enough to support him in the days following the incident. The incident has raised questions about the relationship between the police and the media, and the impact of media pressure on public figures. Mr Mitchell's comments come as the Leveson Inquiry into media standards has highlighted the need for greater accountability and transparency in the way that the media reports on public figures. In the interview, Mr Mitchell expressed his frustration with the way that the incident was handled, saying that it was "completely wrong" and that it led to his demise. He also argued that the media coverage made it appear that the Leveson Inquiry had never taken place, and that the principles of fairness and accuracy that it established had been ignored. The Dispatches programme, which is due to be broadcast on Monday night, will provide a detailed examination of the incident and the surrounding controversy. It is likely to add to the ongoing debate about the relationship between the police, the media, and public figures, and the need for greater accountability and transparency in the way that the media reports on those in power.

England Rugby Coach Excited About Sam Burgess's Code-Switching Move In a move that has sent shockwaves through the rugby world, Sam Burgess, the 25-year-old Australian rugby league star, has completed his highly-anticipated switch to rugby union. The former South Sydney Rabbitohs player has joined Bath Rugby Club, and England coach Stuart Lancaster has expressed his excitement about the prospect of Burgess representing England in the 2015 World Cup. Lancaster praised Burgess's leadership qualities, mental strength, and ability as a player, saying, "He's got the ability as a player, but also as a leader. I think he's got great mental strength." The England coach cited Burgess's man-of-the-match performance in the NRL grand final, where he played on despite breaking a cheekbone in the opening minute, as evidence of his ability to adapt to the 15-a-side game. Bath head coach Mike Ford echoed Lancaster's comments, saying that Burgess's mentality can take him "all the way to the top, to international rugby." However, Ford noted that it is still unclear which position Burgess will play in for the Aviva Premiership side, with options including the centres and back row. "He's gone out to Australia and actually been the best player in the competition, and that takes some mental strength to do that," Ford said. Despite the excitement surrounding Burgess's move, not everyone is convinced that he can make a seamless transition to rugby union. Former England captain Martin Corry expressed his doubts about Burgess's credentials as a potential World Cup star, saying, "Sam has to come out and prove himself. The timeframe does scare me - can someone be fast-tracked so quickly?" Corry urged caution, saying that he doesn't want to get "caught up in the hype" surrounding Burgess's code-switching move. Burgess, who is still recovering from the injury he suffered in October's grand final, is unsure when he will make his Bath debut. However, with Lancaster and Ford backing him to succeed, the young player is likely to be given every opportunity to prove himself in the rugby union arena. As Lancaster noted, "He's in a competitive position and he'll have to earn the right to get into our [England] team. But if he gets in our squad I'm sure he'll make an impact." Only time will tell if Burgess can live up to the hype and become a star player for England in the 2015 World Cup.

BBC Launches Digital Store with Over 60 Years of Content The BBC has launched a new digital service, allowing the public to purchase and download over 60 years of its iconic shows. The BBC Store, available through bbcstore.com and the iPlayer, offers a vast library of content, including cult comedies, popular dramas, and even some previously banned programs. The store boasts an impressive collection of BBC programmes, with prices starting at £1.89 per episode. Series can be purchased for £6.99, with prices clearly marked on the site. According to Marcus Arthur of BBC Worldwide, the prices are "broadly competitive" and offer a convenient way for fans to own their favorite shows. Among the notable titles available are the 1976 Dennis Potter drama Brimstone and Treacle and the 1965 documentary The War Game, which depicts the impact of a nuclear war in Britain. Classic comedies such as Morecambe & Wise and Dad's Army can also be purchased digitally for the first time, along with legendary interviews conducted by David Frost. In addition to its extensive archive, the BBC Store will offer exclusive content, including a series of Top Gear clips fronted by Matt LeBlanc. The store will also feature a "Best Of" collection from the popular car show. Furthermore, popular dramas like EastEnders and Holby City can be bought just a day after transmission. The BBC plans to expand its service over time, offering "value added material" to shows, such as behind-the-scenes footage or cast interviews. The store's initial focus is on drama, comedy, and factual entertainment, including a collection of Sir David Attenborough's most memorable documentaries. However, the BBC hopes to include more content for children and music programming in the future. The launch of the BBC Store marks a significant shift in the way the corporation makes its content available to the public. While consumers can still access BBC shows through subscription services like Netflix, the BBC Store provides a unique opportunity for fans to own and download their favorite programmes. The BBC iPlayer will continue to offer a free catch-up service for 30 days after shows have aired. With its vast library and competitive pricing, the BBC Store is set to revolutionize the way we consume and engage with BBC content.

Colombian Rebel Group Farc Urges Dissenters to Abandon Violent Path The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) has issued a statement urging a group of rebel commanders to abandon their plans to continue the armed struggle. The call comes as the country prepares to implement a historic peace accord, which will see the Farc transform into a political party and lay down their arms. The statement, released by the Farc, condemned the actions of five commanders who have allegedly refused to adhere to the peace agreement. The commanders, identified as Gentil Duarte, Euclides Mora, John Cuarenta, Giovanny Chuspas, and Julian Chollo, were based in a jungle area in south-east Colombia and had been part of the Farc's command structure until recently. According to reports, the commanders may have left their base with a group of fighters, money, and arms, and are no longer following orders from the Farc central command. The Farc has warned that their actions could jeopardize the peace process, which has been years in the making. The peace accord, signed last month by Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos and Farc leader Timoleon Jimenez, aims to bring an end to the country's 52-year conflict, which has claimed the lives of at least 220,000 people. The agreement has been the result of four years of negotiations in Havana, and its implementation is seen as a crucial step towards lasting peace in Colombia. However, there are concerns that some Farc members may be reluctant to give up their involvement in the lucrative cocaine smuggling business, which has been a key source of funding for the rebel group. The Farc has urged its members to abandon this "futureless path" and to work towards a peaceful and democratic future. As the country moves forward with the implementation of the peace accord, there are still challenges to be overcome. Opponents of the deal, led by former President Alvaro Uribe, have expressed concerns that the agreement is too lenient on Farc leaders, and that it does not do enough to address the issue of impunity for those who have committed crimes during the conflict. Despite these challenges, the Farc's call for its members to abandon violence and work towards peace is a significant step towards a more peaceful and stable future for Colombia.

Spanish authorities have rescued two migrants from Guinea who were found hidden in a car during a customs check near the Moroccan border. The incident occurred late on Sunday at El Tarajal, a border crossing in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. The two men, identified as TD and AB from Guinea Conakry, were discovered suffering from a lack of oxygen and were given first aid by Spain's Guardia Civil police. The migrants were found in a Mercedes 300 with false number plates, and two Moroccan men who were in the car at the time were detained by police. One of the migrants was hiding in the engine compartment, where he had been inhaling noxious fumes. The length of time he was exposed to the fumes is unclear. The migrants, who did not have any papers, are now under official investigation. This incident highlights the desperate measures some migrants take to enter the EU through Ceuta and Melilla, tiny Spanish enclaves on the North African coast.

Bali Nine Leaders Set to be Executed in Indonesia, Lawyers to File Constitutional Court Challenge The leaders of the "Bali Nine" group of heroin smugglers, Andrew Chan and Myuran Sukumaran, are one step closer to being executed in Indonesia after a court ruled that they cannot challenge the president's decision to refuse them clemency. However, their lawyers have vowed to take the case to the constitutional court, arguing that the president has an obligation to properly consider their exceptional rehabilitation. Chan and Sukumaran, both Australians, were arrested in Bali in 2005 while attempting to smuggle heroin to Australia. They were found to be the organizers of a nine-member smuggling operation and have been on death row ever since. Despite their initial sentences, the two men have undergone significant rehabilitation, with many arguing that they have reformed and should be shown mercy. The Indonesian President, Joko Widodo, has a policy of denying clemency to drug offenders, citing the huge damage that the drug trade has caused to Indonesia. Earlier this year, he rejected the clemency appeals of Chan and Sukumaran, paving the way for their potential execution. In January, he authorized the executions of six drug offenders, including five foreigners, and the two Australians are part of a second group of 10 foreign nationals who are set to be put to death. However, their lawyers argue that the president's decision to reject their clemency appeals was not properly considered, and that their rehabilitation was not taken into account. "We believe that these men over the last 10 years have rehabilitated themselves and we are very concerned that that fact has not been properly and genuinely considered by the Indonesian authorities and the Indonesian legal system," said Michael O'Connell, one of the lawyers representing the men. The case will now go to the constitutional court, where Chan and Sukumaran's lawyers will argue that the president has an obligation to properly consider their clemency appeals. The application is expected to be filed this week, with a preliminary hearing to follow in the coming weeks. The news has sparked a passionate response from the Australian government, with Foreign Minister Julie Bishop stating that it is "important that all legal processes are allowed to run their course." The Australian government has mounted a diplomatic campaign on behalf of the two men, arguing that they have reformed and should be shown mercy. Indonesia has faced criticism from other countries whose nationals are facing execution, including Brazil, France, Nigeria, and the Philippines. The executions have sparked a debate about the use of the death penalty, with many arguing that it is an inhumane and ineffective deterrent. As the case continues to unfold, the fate of Chan and Sukumaran remains uncertain. While the Indonesian authorities have stated that they are waiting for all legal avenues to be exhausted before carrying out the executions, the two men's lawyers remain hopeful that their clients will be given a chance to have their clemency appeals properly heard. The world waits with bated breath as the story of the Bali Nine continues to unfold, a stark reminder of the complexities and challenges of the international justice system.

A revolutionary new treatment for heart attacks is being trialled at the Essex Cardiothoracic Centre, with a 50-year-old man becoming one of the first to benefit from the innovative procedure. Steve Jaggers, a maintenance worker at a care home, was rushed to Basildon Hospital in Essex last month after suffering a heart attack. In a bid to minimise damage to his heart, doctors used a pioneering technique known as "therapeutic hypothermia" to cool his body temperature from the inside. The procedure involves inserting a catheter with a balloon into the main vein, which is then filled with a cool liquid to bring the body's temperature down. According to Dr Thomas Keeble, a consultant cardiologist, the goal is to cool the patient quickly while keeping their outside warm, much like a "baked Alaska". This helps to protect the heart muscle from further damage when the blocked artery is opened. Mr Jaggers was fully conscious during the procedure, which he described as a "strange sensation". To prevent shivering, a common side effect of cooling, doctors used blankets to keep him warm. A stent was also inserted into his heart to keep the artery open. After the procedure, Mr Jaggers' body was slowly warmed up in recovery, a feeling he likened to being abroad in the sun. Remarkably, he now feels "completely fine", with no lingering effects from the heart attack. The Essex Cardiothoracic Centre is the only site in the UK currently trialling this groundbreaking technology, which has the potential to significantly reduce heart damage in patients suffering from heart attacks.

Crystal Palace manager Alan Pardew has confirmed that Yannick Bolasie is close to joining Premier League rivals Everton. The 27-year-old winger, who came on as a substitute in Palace's 1-0 home loss to West Brom, is expected to complete a move to Goodison Park. Pardew revealed that a "big offer" has been made for Bolasie and the deal is nearing completion. Although no medical has taken place, Pardew has given his blessing for the transfer to go ahead. Bolasie, a DR Congo international, has been with Palace since 2012 and was warmly applauded by the home crowd when he came on during Saturday's match. Pardew praised Bolasie's commitment, saying it showed his love for the club. The manager acknowledged that Palace will miss Bolasie if he leaves, but wishes him well. The transfer is expected to be finalized soon.

A Southampton school has reversed its decision to let pupils finish early to watch the England v Wales football match, following accusations of "hypocrisy" from term-time holiday campaigners. Oasis Academy Lord's Hill had initially planned to finish at lunchtime on June 16, allowing students to watch the Euro 2016 game. However, principal Ian Golding has since stated that it is "more appropriate" for pupils to stay in class, with the game being screened during school time instead. The initial decision had been met with criticism from campaigners, including Jon Platt, who recently won a High Court ruling after refusing to pay a fine for taking his daughter on an unauthorised term-time holiday. Platt argued that the school's decision was hypocritical, given that they have fined parents in the past for taking their children out of school for holidays. "I understand that there is a little bit of hypocrisy here," he said. "This school has fined parents in the past for taking their kids out of school for holidays, so they are going to come in for a bit of stick." In a statement, principal Golding said that the school takes attendance "extremely seriously" and that sporting events like the Euro 2016 match are "a cause for celebration and enjoyment" that can be experienced by pupils during school time. He announced that the game would be shown during the last hour of school time for those who wish to watch it, allowing students to enjoy the event together.
