The reversal of the decision has been seen as a victory for campaigners, who argue that schools should be consistent in their approach to attendance and term-time holidays.

A landmark ruling has been made in the High Court, deeming Westminster City Council's decision to ban a mother-of-three from re-applying for social housing in the borough for 12 months as unlawful. The woman, known as "Ms A", lost her home in March 2014 when her housing benefit was cut, leaving her unable to afford the rent. The council temporarily relocated her to north London and offered her temporary accommodation in Enfield, but also imposed a 12-month ban on applying for social housing in Westminster. The family's lawyers argued that this ban breached the 1996 Housing Act, which requires councils to give homeless families "reasonable preference" for social housing. Judge Peter Blair QC agreed, stating that the ban was unlawful. Jayesh Kunwardia, the family's solicitor, welcomed the ruling, saying it makes clear that homeless people have the right to bid for social housing from the time they secure a full housing duty from a local authority. The ruling highlights the significant challenges faced by those in need of social housing in Westminster, where demand far outstrips supply. Judge Blair noted that the waiting lists are "so vast" that applicants can expect a seven to 10-year wait before being allocated a permanent council home. The case has significant implications for local authorities and their treatment of homeless families, and is likely to have far-reaching consequences for social housing policy.

Yemen's Humanitarian Crisis Worsens as Two Million People Face Emergency Food Aid Shortage The humanitarian situation in Yemen has reached catastrophic levels, with two million people in dire need of emergency food aid to survive, according to the United Nations. The warning comes as child malnutrition has risen by a staggering 63% in just one year, with a child under the age of five dying every 10 minutes from preventable causes. The crisis is attributed to a combination of factors, including severe poverty, war damage, and a naval embargo imposed by the Saudi-led coalition. The blockade has had a devastating impact on food security, with approximately 14 million people currently facing food insecurity, including 2.2 million children who are acutely malnourished and nearly 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition. Stephen O'Brien, the UN's emergency relief coordinator, has urged the Saudi-led coalition to lift its no-fly zone and reopen Sanaa airport, citing the "disproportionate impact" of the blockade on civilians. The closure of the airport has prevented life-saving medication from being flown in and has denied 20,000 Yemenis access to specialist medical treatment abroad. The situation on the ground is dire, with Jamie McGoldrick, the UN's humanitarian coordinator in Yemen, describing the desperation of the population. "Everywhere you go, you see people begging in the streets in bigger numbers, you see people rummaging through rubbish to survive," he said. "You hear catastrophic stories of children dying because they can't get to health centers. People dying of malnutrition, people dying of preventable diseases." The economic situation in Yemen is also in shambles, with the banking sector barely functioning and 1.25 million civil servants not receiving regular salaries. Widows, orphans, the disabled, and elderly are no longer receiving a monthly allowance from the government, leaving them without a safety net. The conflict in Yemen, which has been raging for nearly two years, has destroyed half of the country's medical facilities, with some being bombed by the Saudi-led coalition and others struggling with funding shortages. The naval embargo has also crippled the country's ability to import food, with Yemen previously reliant on imports for 90% of its staple food. Despite the gravity of the situation, Yemen's humanitarian crisis remains overlooked by donors and the international community, with the conflict attracting less attention than those in Syria and Iraq. The lack of media coverage has been attributed to the difficulty of accessing the country, with only UN flights allowed to land at Sanaa airport and Saudi Arabia restricting journalist access. As the situation continues to deteriorate, the international community is being urged to take action to address the crisis. The UN is calling for an immediate lifting of the blockade and for increased funding to support humanitarian efforts. With wheat supplies expected to last only an estimated three more months, the clock is ticking for the people of Yemen, and urgent action is needed to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe.

A fatal car crash occurred in Irlam on Tuesday. A Daewoo Matiz collided with a Volkswagen Tiguan at the junction of Cadishead Way and Fairhills Road. The driver, a woman, and her 15-year-old passenger were trapped. They were freed by emergency services. The woman was airlifted to Wythenshawe hospital, where she died. The teenager was taken to Manchester Royal Children's Hospital. The Volkswagen driver, 52, is being treated for injuries at Salford Royal Hospital. Police are appealing for witnesses to come forward and contact Greater Manchester Police.

Kettering General Hospital has been criticized by the Care Quality Commission (CQC) for failing to provide adequate care and support to its patients. The CQC visited the hospital in June and found that "people did not always experience care, treatment and support that met their needs". This is the second damning report in just a few months, with the hospital being told to raise its quality and safety standards in May. Despite making some significant improvements in areas such as cleanliness and infection control, the hospital was found to be lacking in its care and welfare of patients. Inspectors discovered that daily care plans were often brief and lacked important patient information, and in some cases, there were no instructions for staff to follow. The hospital was also found to have staffing issues, particularly at weekends, and was not providing enough specialist attention to children in Accident & Emergency. The CQC has taken enforcement action against the hospital trust and has outlined a number of improvements that need to be made. The hospital's director of nursing, Clare Culpin, has stated that the hospital is "absolutely committed" to improving safety and the patient experience, and that action plans are in place to tackle the problems. The trust is acting on all issues raised by inspectors and is working to implement systematic changes to address the concerns.

Residents of Orchard Village in Rainham are at their wit's end as they continue to deal with a plethora of problems, including raw sewage, mice infestations, and gas leaks. The estate, which was opened in 2014, was built using £31m of public money as part of an £80m project to replace the notorious Mardyke housing estate. Despite its promising beginnings, the estate has been plagued by issues, leaving residents to suffer. One resident, Colin Nickless, has had to endure a nightmare situation. He moved into the estate in 2015 to be near a special school for his daughter, who has cystic fibrosis. However, his family has been beset by problems, including wastewater leaks, roof leaks, and mould growth. His daughter has been hospitalized with a bacterial infection, while his son has been admitted with breathing difficulties. Nickless has dubbed the situation the "Orchard Village Sickness" or "Orchard Village Flu," highlighting the widespread nature of the issues. The association managing the estate, Clarion Housing, has acknowledged the situation is "unacceptable" and has offered to buy back 58 of the 387 homes. However, some residents and local officials are calling for more drastic action. Havering UKIP councillor Phil Martin has suggested that the entire estate be demolished, citing the severity of the problems and the plummeting property values. "We've had residents living on sewer-soaked carpets for days before anything was done about it," he said. "The only solution is to start again from scratch." Clarion Housing has stated that it is taking concerns seriously and has instructed specialists to conduct rigorous scientific tests to address the build defects. The organization's dedicated project team has already made significant progress, according to a spokesperson. Nevertheless, residents remain frustrated and concerned about their living conditions, and it remains to be seen whether Clarion's efforts will be enough to resolve the issues plaguing Orchard Village.

The Great British Bake Off returned to BBC One on Wednesday, attracting a massive audience of 10 million viewers at its peak. The popular baking competition, hosted by Sue Perkins and Mel Giedroyc, saw 12 amateur bakers embark on their journey to be crowned the latest winner. The show's premiere did not disappoint, with musician Stuart Henshall becoming the first contestant to leave after his bakes failed to impress judges Mary Berry and Paul Hollywood. The episode was filled with drama, including a signature bake that completely collapsed after the contestant's chocolate mousse did not set. Dorret Conway's sunken gateau brought on the first tears of the series, setting the tone for what promises to be an exciting competition. The judges were tough but fair, providing constructive feedback to the contestants as they navigated the challenges of the first episode. Sue Perkins made a triumphant return to Twitter ahead of the premiere, joking about a fictional "Swimwear Round" replacing the Showstopper Challenge. Her return to social media came after a four-month sabbatical, during which she faced a barrage of hateful tweets. Perkins and Giedroyc are a major part of the show's appeal, bringing their unique blend of humor and warmth to the hosting duties. The show's massive audience and popularity have also sparked controversy, with Ladbrokes suspending betting on the show due to a flurry of suspicious wagers. The bookmaker reported a "run of bets" placed on one contestant, many of which were made in shops in the Ipswich area, leading to fears that the winner's name may have been leaked. Despite the controversy, The Great British Bake Off remains one of the most popular shows on British television, with its unique blend of baking, humor, and competition continuing to captivate audiences.

Hillary Clinton Set to Announce Presidential Bid, Eyes Democratic Nomination In a move that has been widely anticipated, Hillary Clinton is expected to announce her candidacy for the 2016 presidential election on social media. The 67-year-old former First Lady and Secretary of State will then embark on a trip to Iowa and New Hampshire, two crucial early primary contests in the Democratic nomination process. This will mark Clinton's second attempt at the presidency, having previously run in 2008. Clinton's decision to announce her candidacy on social media, rather than with a large, formal speech, is seen as a strategic move to connect with a wider audience and build momentum for her campaign. She is expected to release a video outlining her campaign themes, which will provide insight into her vision for the country and the issues she intends to prioritize. As one of the most recognizable and experienced candidates in the Democratic field, Clinton is already considered a strong contender for the nomination. Her previous bid for the presidency in 2008 ultimately fell short, as she was defeated by then-Senator Barack Obama in the Democratic primaries. However, she has since gained valuable experience as Secretary of State under Obama, serving from 2009 to 2013. Despite her impressive resume, Clinton's campaign is not without its challenges. She has recently faced criticism over her use of a private email address to conduct official business as Secretary of State, as well as her handling of public records. These controversies have raised questions about her transparency and accountability, which she will need to address in order to win over skeptical voters. The Democratic field is currently relatively narrow, with Clinton as the clear frontrunner. However, she may still face challenges from other candidates, including former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley and possibly Vice-President Joe Biden. Some on the left-wing of the party are also urging Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren to enter the race, although she has repeatedly stated that she is not running. On the Republican side, two major candidates, Ted Cruz and Rand Paul, have already formally announced their campaigns. Several other high-profile Republicans, including former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, are also expected to enter the race. A Clinton-Bush matchup would revive the debate about powerful political dynasties in the US, with the Bush and Clinton families having produced three presidents between them. As Clinton embarks on her campaign, she will need to demonstrate what she has learned from her past mistakes and how she plans to connect with voters. With a long and grueling campaign season ahead, Clinton will need to prove that she is ready to lead the country and that voters are ready for her. Only time will tell if she has what it takes to succeed where she fell short in 2008.

The search for a new bishop of Southwell and Nottingham is underway, with candidates being interviewed on Tuesday and Wednesday. For the first time, applications from women are being considered for the vacancy, following the Church of England's decision to allow women to become bishops. The move, which was formally adopted in November, marks a significant shift for the Church, which has previously restricted women from taking on senior roles. After the interviews, a preferred candidate and a second preference will be put forward. However, no announcements will be made until 2015, as the appointment needs to be approved by the Queen on the recommendation of the prime minister. The vacancy arose after Bishop Paul Butler left to become the Bishop of Durham in January. The appointment is being closely watched, as it could potentially see one of the first women bishops in the Church of England.

Former Peterborough United player, Joe Gormley, has parted ways with the club due to a serious knee injury. Gormley, who joined Posh in 2015, became "disillusioned with football" after struggling to recover. He has returned to Northern Ireland and is seeking to return to part-time football. Director of football, Barry Fry, confirmed that all parties have written to Fifa for special dispensation to cancel his contract by mutual consent outside the January window. Gormley had previously broken records for goals scored at Cliftonville, but failed to score after turning full-time.

Catherine Coulson, the beloved actress best known for her iconic role as the Log Lady in the cult TV series Twin Peaks, has passed away. Her agent and friend, Mary Dangerfield, confirmed the news to The Hollywood Reporter, stating that the family has not yet disclosed the cause of death. Dangerfield expressed the profound sadness felt by all who knew Coulson, saying, "We are all deeply sad - she meant so much to so many." Director David Lynch, who created Twin Peaks with Mark Frost, released a heartfelt statement mourning the loss of his dear friend. He praised Coulson's unwavering dedication to her work, her great sense of humor, and her spiritual nature. Lynch fondly remembered Coulson as "solid gold" and "a long-time meditator" who was always there for her friends and family. Coulson's collaboration with Lynch began in the 1970s, when she appeared in his short film The Amputee and worked as an assistant director on his debut feature film Eraserhead. The idea for the Log Lady character was born on the set of Eraserhead, and Coulson brought the character to life in Twin Peaks, as well as in the prequel film Twin Peaks: Fire Walk With Me. Despite describing her character as the "only normal person on the show," Coulson noted that the Log Lady had experienced trauma and formed a deep bond with her iconic log. Twin Peaks, which premiered in the early 1990s, was a groundbreaking series that won three Golden Globe awards in 1991. The show's influence can still be seen in modern TV dramas, and its legacy continues to endure. A sequel series, directed by Lynch, is set to air on Showtime next year. Coulson's passing is a significant loss for the Twin Peaks community, and she will be deeply missed by her friends, family, and fans around the world.

Valtteri Bottas edged out fellow Finn Kimi Raikkonen to top the timesheets in the final practice session for the Grand Prix, with Mercedes teammate Lewis Hamilton finishing third. Bottas' fastest lap was 0.095 seconds quicker than Raikkonen, while Hamilton was 0.416 seconds off the pace. The session was a mixed bag for the championship contenders, with Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel struggling with a suspected water leak that limited him to just one quick lap. As a result, he finished 12th fastest, which will be a concern given his 12-point lead over Hamilton in the standings. Hamilton, on the other hand, will be encouraged by his performance after a difficult Friday. He had struggled with tyre temperature and traffic, but was able to record a more representative lap in the final session. However, the margin to Bottas will still be a concern, and some of the deficit may be attributed to the fact that Bottas secured a slipstream from Red Bull's Max Verstappen on both his best laps. Verstappen was looking strong before his engine cut out about 10 minutes before the end of the session, and he ended up sixth. His teammate Daniel Ricciardo finished fourth, 0.545 seconds off the pace, while the impressive Esteban Ocon in the Force India was fifth. Williams' Felipe Massa finished seventh, ahead of rookie teammate Lance Stroll, who continues to show improved confidence after scoring his first points in Canada two weeks ago. Stroll's session ended with a trip into the escape road at Turn Two after overshooting his braking. McLaren's Fernando Alonso finished 14th, but will start from the back of the grid due to a total of 40 places of grid penalties for using too many engine parts. Renault's Jolyon Palmer had another difficult session, pulling off early with flames and smoke pouring from the back of his car after crashing on Friday. Overall, the final practice session set the stage for an intriguing qualifying session, with the championship contenders looking to gain an edge ahead of the Grand Prix.

A 42-year-old man, Mohammed Khalil, was found seriously injured at his Sheffield home and later died in hospital. South Yorkshire Police have made four arrests in connection with the killing. Two 20-year-old men are in custody on suspicion of murder. A 26-year-old man, also detained on suspicion of murder, remains in custody. A 46-year-old man, arrested on suspicion of murder and possession of a weapon, has been released on bail as the investigation continues.

The Independent Monitoring Board (IMB) for the city centre jail is seeking to expand its membership from eight to 15 volunteers. The board ensures fairness and decency for all prisoners, and members are responsible for checking on inmates in solitary confinement and evaluating cell conditions. New members will receive training to prepare them for their duties. According to Steve Cocks, chairman of the Cardiff IMB, the board is looking to diversify its membership, particularly seeking ethnic minority representation and younger individuals. Currently, the board consists of mostly white British members. Cocks described the role as "challenging but rewarding," with members having complete access to the prison as official representatives of the justice minister. As part of their duties, members sample food, visit education facilities, and monitor the admission of new prisoners. They also attend disciplinary hearings and investigate serious incidents within the prison. The IMB plays a crucial role in ensuring the well-being of prisoners and bringing any concerns to the attention of those responsible.

A former hospital worker has been jailed for 16 months for stealing from semi-conscious patients at Morriston Hospital in Swansea. Jacqueline Perry, 49, from Morriston, pleaded guilty to nine counts of theft and was sentenced at Swansea Crown Court on Friday. Perry's colleagues became suspicious about items disappearing and reported their concerns to the authorities, leading to a sting operation being set up by police. Marked bank notes were placed around Ward G, and when one disappeared, officers searched staff and found it in Perry's possession. It was revealed that Perry had stolen a total of £2,739, including three gold rings worth £1,800 from an 89-year-old patient. The court heard that the thefts had a major impact on Perry's colleagues, with lead nurse Tina Smith stating that morale was affected as staff were all under suspicion. The patients targeted by Perry were described as "quite sick and quite vulnerable". Perry's defense team claimed that the offenses were motivated by financial hardship, rather than greed, and that she had stolen the money to pay for alcohol for her husband. However, Recorder Christopher Clee QC described her actions as "a despicable offense" and said he had no good reason to suspend the sentence. Perry will serve half of her sentence in prison and half on licence. Abertawe Bro Morgannwg University Health Board has apologized to the victims and stated that the sentence should "act as a deterrent" to others. The board emphasized that theft from patients or staff is a serious criminal offense and a severe breach of trust that will not be tolerated. Perry's actions have caused significant distress to her victims and former colleagues, and a disciplinary hearing will follow the court proceedings, which is expected to result in her losing her job.

Principals from 15 schools in Comber and Newtownards have joined forces to warn parents about the devastating impact of spending cuts on education. In a joint letter, the principals urged parents to contact local authorities, including MLAs, the Department of Education, and the Education Authority, to express their concerns about the issue. The letter stated that the cuts would result in fewer teachers and resources, larger classes, and ultimately, worse education outcomes for students. The principals emphasized that every school in the area is facing a financial crisis, regardless of its size or enrollment numbers. They pointed out that over the past five years, the funding per child has only increased by 0.9%, while costs have risen by approximately 14.5%. This significant shortfall is having a "real, urgent, and disastrous" impact on schools. In response to the letter, a spokesperson for the Department of Education claimed that providing financial assistance to schools has been a priority for Education Minister Peter Weir. The spokesperson highlighted that Mr. Weir had reallocated over £7m of new funding to the 2016-17 schools budget. However, the principals' letter suggests that this measure is insufficient to address the scale of the problem. In fact, Mr. Weir himself has stated that schools need an extra £240m over the next three years just to maintain spending at 2015/16 levels. The principals are calling on parents to take action and make their voices heard to prevent further damage to the education system.

A year-long project aimed at reducing patient frustration and aggression in NHS accident and emergency departments has yielded promising results. The initiative, commissioned by the Department of Health, sought to identify simple and cost-effective solutions to ease tensions in A&E units. With the help of psychologists, designers identified key factors that contribute to patient violence, including inhospitable environments and lack of communication. The project's findings come at a time when attacks on NHS staff are on the rise. According to recent figures, there were 57,830 physical assaults on NHS staff in England in 2010-11, resulting in significant costs to the healthcare system. It is estimated that these attacks cost at least £69m a year, primarily due to staff taking time off work and legal costs associated with pursuing cases. To address this issue, the Design Council worked with experts to develop practical solutions that can be easily implemented in A&E departments. One key strategy involves improving communication with patients, including a new approach to greeting them upon arrival and providing clear answers to their questions. Additionally, the use of clearer signs and maps can help patients understand the different stages of treatment, reducing confusion and frustration. Other suggestions include the use of screens to provide live updates on the number of cases being handled by staff, as well as guidance on lighting, decor, and seating for hospital managers planning refurbishments. These solutions can be implemented at a relatively low cost, with estimates suggesting that hospitals can install the system for around £60,000. Three hospitals in Chesterfield, Southampton, and London are set to test these ideas, with the goal of reducing patient aggression and creating a calmer environment. According to David Kester, head of the Design Council, "This is design at its best - solving a long-standing, high-cost problem through creativity, simplicity, and collaboration." Health Minister Simon Burns echoed this sentiment, stating that "difficult situations can be diffused by simply giving patients more information." Dr. John Heyworth, a consultant in the emergency department at Southampton General Hospital, emphasized the importance of addressing this issue. "Violence and aggression towards staff and other patients in the emergency department is a major nationwide issue," he said. "While there will always be a small minority intent on causing trouble, there are others who can resort to aggressive behavior because they don't feel they have been communicated with effectively and they don't know what to expect." By implementing these simple yet effective solutions, hospitals can take a significant step towards reducing patient aggression and creating a more positive experience for both patients and staff. As the project moves forward, it is hoped that these innovations will be adopted by hospitals across the country, ultimately leading to a safer and more compassionate healthcare system.

Microsoft's Focus on Cloud Computing Pays Off, While eBay's Profits Take a Hit Microsoft has reported a significant increase in revenue and profits, thanks to its focus on cloud computing. The tech giant's revenue rose to $23.3 billion in the quarter, up from $20.6 billion in the prior year, while profits jumped to $5.3 billion, up from $3 billion the year before. The company's emphasis on cloud-based software, storage, and services has paid off, with executives citing strong sales and renewals. Chief Executive Satya Nadella said, "Overall, the approach we have taken for multiple years now is to transform everything that we do. We've now got very good customer momentum." The company's share price climbed more than 3% in after-market trading, beating analyst expectations. In contrast, eBay's profits took a hit, dropping 94% in the three months that ended in June. The e-commerce firm recorded an income tax provision of more than $400 million, which included a $311 million tax charge related to a reorganization since it split from PayPal in 2015. eBay's stock dropped almost 4% in after-hours trade, as its profit forecast largely fell below estimates. Despite the drop in profits, eBay's quarterly revenue increased 4% year-on-year to $2.3 billion, with two million new buyers turning to its platforms. However, the company's US StubHub business suffered without major events such as Hamilton and the Copa America football tournament to drive buyers. eBay has been working to move beyond its identity as an auction site, spending on marketing and updating its websites. The company is looking to reinvent itself and become more competitive in the e-commerce market.

Brazil's volleyball team secured their seventh gold medal in Rio, defeating their opponents 3-0. The win came in a lively atmosphere at Maracanazinho arena, where Neymar was in attendance. The victory made up for their 2012 loss to Russia, and the USA took bronze with a comeback win over Russia.

Chelsea captain John Terry has praised the return of Didier Drogba to Stamford Bridge, stating that the Ivory Coast striker is still a "nightmare" to play against in training. Drogba, 36, signed a one-year deal with the club last month, marking his second spell with the Blues. The striker scored 157 goals in 342 games during his initial eight-year stint with the team. Terry, 33, expressed his admiration for Drogba's enduring skills, saying, "He's still strong, sharp, and hungry." The Chelsea captain believes that Drogba's presence will have a positive impact on the team's younger players, such as Kurt Zouma, by instilling a winning mentality. This summer, Chelsea has made several high-profile signings, including Diego Costa, Cesc Fabregas, and Filipe Luis, at a combined cost of £75m. Terry is impressed with the new additions, saying, "If I was a Chelsea fan, I'd be impressed from what I have seen so far." However, he admits it feels strange to see former teammates Frank Lampard and Ashley Cole playing for other clubs, with Lampard joining Manchester City and Cole signing with Roma. Terry noted, "It just doesn't seem right to see them in different shirts." With Drogba's return and the influx of new talent, Chelsea is poised for a successful season.

Serbia's Capital Belgrade Sees Daily Protests Against Vucic's Victory For the past several weeks, the streets of Belgrade have been filled with the sounds of whistling, chanting, and drum-beating protesters, as thousands of people gather daily to express their discontent with the outcome of the presidential election. The vote, which took place on April 2, saw Prime Minister Aleksandar Vucic win an overwhelming majority, securing over 50% of the vote and avoiding a second-round runoff. However, rather than accepting the results, many of Vucic's detractors have taken to the streets to voice their concerns about the direction of the country. The protests, which have been largely peaceful, have become a daily routine, with demonstrators gathering in front of key landmarks such as the National Assembly, Republic Square, and the headquarters of state broadcaster RTS. The protesters, many of whom are university students, have been vocal about their opposition to Vucic's government, which they claim is becoming increasingly authoritarian. They have also expressed frustration with the lack of media freedom in the country, with many outlets being heavily biased towards the ruling Progressive Party (SNS). According to an analysis, over half of the pre-election media coverage focused on Vucic, with that figure rising to over 90% when reporting on his activities as prime minister was included. This has raised concerns about self-censorship and government interference, with many protesters accusing the media of being too cozy with the government. In response, protesters have taken to buying and carrying copies of Danas, a newspaper critical of the government, which has been struggling to attract advertisers. "The people voted like this because nobody had access to the media," said Stefan, a protester. "We want to show that there are alternative voices in this country, and that we will not be silenced." Despite the protests, Vucic has remained unperturbed, stating that everyone has the right to be unhappy with the election results as long as the demonstrations remain peaceful. So far, the police have shown a light touch, and the protesters have also been restrained, with some even displaying a sense of humor, carrying placards that read "Wenger Out" and "No to Salty Plazma," a reference to a controversial savory variant of a popular Yugoslav biscuit. As the protests continue, it remains to be seen how long they will last and what impact they will have on the government. However, for now, the demonstrators show no signs of letting up, with their daily chants of "see you tomorrow" becoming a familiar refrain in the streets of Belgrade. With a sense of humor and determination, the protesters are determined to make their voices heard and bring about change in Serbia.

Scotland's transportation landscape has undergone significant changes over the past decade, with mixed results. According to the updated National Transport Strategy, the overall use of public transportation has declined by 6% since 2006. This decline is attributed to a 12% decrease in bus passengers and a 7% decrease in ferry passengers. However, ScotRail has bucked this trend, with a remarkable 29% increase in passengers. Despite the decline in public transportation use, the Scottish government has invested heavily in the sector. Transport Minister Derek Mackay noted that progress has been made in key areas, including a significant reduction in road deaths. The number of fatalities on Scotland's roads has decreased by 36%, from 314 in 2006 to 200 in 2014. However, not everyone is pleased with the progress made. Colin Howden, Director of Transform Scotland, described the lack of progress in moving people from cars to public transportation as "tragic." He pointed out that while public transportation use has declined, traffic on the country's roads has increased by 2% over the same period. On the other hand, Mr. Mackay highlighted the successes in the rail sector, citing the newly opened Borders Railway as a major factor in the 29% increase in ScotRail passengers. The Scottish government has committed £5 billion to transforming Scotland's rail network, including a £475 million train improvement program. This investment is expected to result in a 10% increase in trains for the ScotRail fleet, providing 23% extra seats for passengers. Transport Scotland acknowledged that more work needs to be done, particularly in improving bus patronage figures. A review is planned for the next parliament to explore these issues in more depth. Despite the challenges, the updated National Transport Strategy provides a roadmap for future investment and development in Scotland's transportation sector. As the country continues to grow and evolve, it is likely that transportation will remain a key priority for the Scottish government.

A leap second will be added to clocks worldwide at the end of June. This adjustment is made to keep pace with the Earth's rotation, which can vary in speed. Atomic clocks, which measure atomic vibrations for precise timekeeping, are used to determine when a leap second is needed. Since their introduction in 1972, 25 leap seconds have been added, including one in 2012. While not everyone agrees with the practice, scientists argue that it prevents significant inaccuracies over time. Without leap seconds, clocks could drift away from actual time, causing problems in navigation and other fields that rely on precise timing.

UK MPs Reveal Lavish Freebies in Latest Register Update The latest update to the UK Parliament's register of members' financial interests has revealed a slew of lavish freebies received by MPs. Speaker John Bercow, a self-proclaimed tennis enthusiast, topped the list with two Royal Box tickets to Wimbledon, valued at a staggering £8,590. Labour deputy leader Tom Watson also received two Wimbledon tickets, although at a significantly lower price point. Meanwhile, Conservative MPs Damian Collins and Nigel Adams declared tickets to the iconic Glastonbury music festival. Collins, chairman of the Commons Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee, and Adams, a committee member, did not disclose the value of their tickets. Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn, who addressed the crowds at Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage, had previously declared two tickets worth £476, which he claimed were given to a family member. Other notable freebies included two tickets to the England v South Africa test match at Lords for Defence Secretary Sir Michael Fallon, and two tickets to the Grand Prix at Silverstone for Labour's Richard Burden. Conservative Mims Davies received a ticket to Royal Ascot, while Labour's Stephen Doughty and Tory John Howell got tickets to the Royal International Air Tattoo. In addition to event tickets, several MPs declared significant payments for various endeavors. Former Labour leader Ed Miliband is set to receive £2,500 for hosting Jeremy Vine's BBC Radio 2 show for a week, while Conservative backbencher Nadine Dorries declared a £50,000 signing fee for a new book deal. Under parliamentary rules, MPs are required to declare any financial interest that could be seen as influencing their actions or words within 28 days. The register update provides a glimpse into the perks and privileges enjoyed by UK lawmakers, with Prime Minister Theresa May also registering a discount card from luxury shoe retailer Russell & Bromley. The value of the discount card, valid from January 2017 to January 2018, was not disclosed.

A Scottish family is growing increasingly concerned that their loved one, Kausar Uddin, is being left to languish in a Saudi Arabian prison despite serving his 35-day sentence. The 47-year-old taxi driver from Sighthill was arrested during a pilgrimage to Mecca in February after allegedly assaulting a policeman. However, his family claims that the incident was a misunderstanding, and that Uddin was only trying to steady himself in a crowded area. According to his 17-year-old daughter, Kaulsom Uddin, her father lost his balance and grabbed onto the nearest person, who happened to be a police officer. The officer allegedly misinterpreted the situation and began punching Uddin, who attempted to leave the scene to avoid further conflict. Despite his sentence being completed, Uddin remains in prison, awaiting a decision from a Saudi court on his future. The family is now fearing that Uddin's case is in danger of being forgotten. Kaulsom Uddin expressed her frustration with the Foreign Office, stating that she does not feel they are doing enough to secure her father's release. "We were hoping ideally that he would be out before his sentence finishes, but even after his sentence has finished, they still haven't got him out," she said. The Foreign Office has confirmed that they are providing assistance to Uddin and his family, and will remain in contact with local authorities. However, for the Uddin family, time is of the essence, and they are urging the authorities to take swift action to bring Kausar Uddin home.

Share Your England: Join the Big Picture Project The BBC is inviting the public to share their stunning images and videos of England as part of the England's Big Picture project. Whether you're a professional photographer or an amateur snapper, we want to see your best shots of the country's landscapes, cities, and landmarks. To submit your pictures, simply email them to england@bbc.co.uk, post them on our Facebook page, or tweet them to @BBCEngland. You can also share your images on Instagram using the hashtag #englandsbigpicture. A selection of the best photos will be featured on our Pinterest board and may even be used on the BBC website or social media channels. When submitting your photos, please include your name and any relevant details about the image. Please note that we prioritize photos taken in the past week, and by submitting your image, you agree to grant the BBC a royalty-free licence to use it. Don't worry, you'll still own the copyright, and we'll make sure to credit your name if your photo is used. So, grab your camera or phone and start snapping – we can't wait to see your England!

Wolverhampton Wanderers secured a thrilling 3-1 comeback victory over local rivals Birmingham City, earning their second league win of the season. Despite trailing to Che Adams' opener, Wolves' manager Walter Zenga's side rallied in the second half, with Iceland striker Jon Dadi Bodvarsson scoring one of three goals to seal the win. Zenga attributed the success to his experienced starting XI, which featured 10 players from last season's squad. "They're good players and they only need a warm up," he said. "They understood what is the spirit of Wolves and what they have to do to create enthusiasm." The Italian manager emphasized the importance of dedication and focus in training, stating that his team's style is to "give 100% all the time" and concentrate on daily tasks. With this win, Wolves continue to build momentum, but Zenga remains calm and focused, choosing not to dwell on the team's current standing in the table.

Cambridge University Hospitals has faced significant challenges with its new online patient record system. The system, designed by US firm Epic, was launched in October and allows staff to access and update records on hand-held devices and 7,000 computers. However, the system has failed in key areas, prompting Epic to send in expert staff and doctors from California to provide assistance. Local GPs have raised concerns about the system, citing issues such as complex patient reporting and the inability of computers to communicate with other devices like printers. Medical director Dr Jag Ahluwalia has acknowledged these concerns and announced an urgent meeting to address "communication" issues. The problems have had significant consequences, including ambulances being rerouted away from Addenbrooke's accident and emergency department in early November. According to Cambridgeshire Clinical Commissioning Group, the department's performance has fallen by 20% since the system's launch. Hospital staff are working to resolve these issues to ensure patient safety and efficient care.

BBC Disputes Rwanda's Claim of Biased Documentary The BBC has expressed extreme disappointment over the findings of an inquiry led by Martin Ngoga, which claims that a documentary about the 1994 Rwandan genocide failed to meet the broadcaster's own editorial standards. The documentary, titled "Rwanda, The Untold Story," was aired in October 2014 and included interviews with researchers and former aides of President Paul Kagame, who accused him of plotting to shoot down the presidential plane that triggered the genocide. The Rwandan government has been critical of the documentary, claiming that it attempts to revise the history and facts of the genocide and disrespects the memory of those who died. In response, the BBC has strongly rejected any suggestion that the documentary constitutes genocide denial. The broadcaster argued that it has a duty to investigate difficult and challenging subjects and believes that the program was a valuable contribution to the understanding of the tragic history of the country and the region. The inquiry's findings have led to Rwanda suspending broadcasts by the BBC's Kinyarwanda language service. The BBC has stated that it stands by its right to produce independent journalism, which has made it the world's most trusted news source. The broadcaster's editorial complaints process is still ongoing, but provisional findings suggest that the documentary does not breach the BBC's editorial standards. The genocide, which occurred over a 100-day period in 1994, resulted in the deaths of at least 800,000 people, mostly from the minority ethnic Tutsi group and Hutus opposed to the mass slaughter. The documentary's claims that most of those killed may have been Hutus, killed by members of the then-rebel Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), have been met with criticism from the Rwandan government and some survivors of the genocide. The BBC has attempted to get the Rwandan government to respond to the allegations made in the documentary, but these attempts have been unsuccessful. Despite the controversy surrounding the documentary, the BBC remains committed to independent journalism and will continue to investigate challenging subjects, including the complex and tragic history of the Rwandan genocide. The broadcaster's commitment to editorial standards and independence has made it a trusted source of news and information around the world.

Rangers Search for New Manager After Warburton's Departure The Scottish football world is abuzz with speculation as Rangers Football Club searches for a new manager following the departure of Mark Warburton. The 53-year-old Englishman left the club on Friday, along with his assistant David Weir and head of recruitment Frank McParland. As the club navigates this transition period, former players and coaches are weighing in on potential candidates to take the reins. One name that has been mentioned is Billy Davies, a 52-year-old veteran coach with a proven track record in the English Championship. Davies has been out of coaching for nearly three years since his second stint at Nottingham Forest came to an end. However, his impressive resume and ability to drive results have caught the attention of many, including former Rangers striker Kris Boyd. Boyd, who spent time on loan at Nottingham Forest during Davies' first stint, sang the praises of his former coach. "He'll do anything to win," Boyd told BBC Scotland. "It's a results-driven world, and for me, there's not a better man." Boyd, who had a prolific spell at Rangers from 2006 to 2010, credited Davies with helping him regain his scoring form during a difficult period at Middlesbrough. "He got me back scoring goals inside a week," Boyd recalled. "That didn't happen by coincidence." Davies' ability to motivate players and drive results is well-documented. During his time at Motherwell, he took the club from relegation candidates to European contenders. His tenure at Derby and Preston also yielded impressive results, with Boyd noting that "a lot of the good work he's done in England has gone unnoticed up here." Another name in the running is Alex McLeish, a former Rangers manager and player. McLeish, 58, has expressed interest in returning to the club, and former Rangers captain Barry Ferguson believes he would be an excellent choice. "He knows what the club is all about, he knows the traditions and what is expected," Ferguson said. "He assembled a good team at Rangers, and we had a real togetherness. He wanted us to work hard and play attacking football." Ferguson, who played under McLeish for Scotland, Rangers, and Birmingham, believes that McLeish's experience and knowledge of the club make him an ideal candidate for the short-term solution that Rangers are seeking. "He has more experience now, and if they are looking for someone to take over until the end of the season, he's a serious contender," Ferguson said. As Rangers continues their search for a new manager, one thing is certain – the club needs a leader who can drive results and restore the team's former glory. With the Scottish Cup win over Morton on Sunday, the team has shown glimpses of their potential, but it will be up to the new manager to harness that energy and propel the team forward. Whether it's Billy Davies, Alex McLeish, or another candidate, the Rangers faithful will be watching with bated breath as the club navigates this critical period in their history.

Colombia's Historic Step Towards Peace: Farc Rebels Decommission 60% of Registered Weapons In a significant milestone towards achieving lasting peace, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc) have decommissioned 60% of their registered weapons, marking a crucial step in the implementation of the peace agreement signed with the government. The gesture has been welcomed by President Juan Manuel Santos, who described it as a "historic day" in the country's journey towards peace. The decommissioning ceremony took place in the south-western Cauca region, where Farc leaders and UN officials gathered at La Elvira, one of several transition zones designated for the rebels to gather before reintegrating into civilian life. Although President Santos was unable to attend the ceremony due to bad weather, he expressed his commitment to the peace process, stating that "peace will be built little by little, like a cathedral, which you build brick by brick." The Farc has agreed to give up more than five decades of armed struggle under the terms of the accord, which was signed after four years of negotiations in Cuba. The peace deal was initially rejected in a referendum last October but was reworked and approved by Congress a month later. As part of the agreement, the rebels have until June 20 to hand over the remaining weapons, a deadline that was extended from the original date of May 30. The decommissioned weapons, including rifles, RPGs, and pistols, are being stored at 26 locations around the country under the supervision of UN observers. The images of the weapons being checked and stored have been released, providing visual evidence of the Farc's commitment to the peace process. While some may have expected more dramatic images of fighters handing over their rifles, the Farc insists that such a display would be perceived as a sign of defeat, rather than a voluntary decision to lay down arms. Farc leader Pablo Catatumbo emphasized the group's commitment to peace, stating, "We are totally committed to peace and will do all we can to help build this country we dream of." The decommissioning of weapons is a critical step towards the Farc's transformation into a political party, a process that is expected to be completed once all registered weapons have been handed over. President Santos's efforts to reach a peace agreement with the Farc earned him the Nobel Peace Prize last year. The successful implementation of the peace deal is seen as a major achievement for the country, which has been plagued by conflict for over five decades. As Colombia continues on its path towards peace, the international community remains hopeful that the country will finally be able to put its troubled past behind it and build a brighter future for its citizens.

In a surprising turn of events, Malik Obama, the half-brother of President Barack Obama, has expressed his support for Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump. In an interview with the BBC, Malik Obama, a Muslim with both Kenyan and US citizenship, stated that Trump's proposal for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the US was "common sense". This statement comes despite the widespread condemnation of Trump's plan, which has been touted as a security measure. Malik Obama also criticized his half-brother, President Obama, for allegedly turning his back on their family. He noted that it was "disappointing" and "hypocritical" that no representatives from the Obama family in Kenya were attending the Democratic convention in Philadelphia. The president has often spoken proudly of his heritage, but Malik Obama feels that he has not been supportive of their family. As an aspiring politician in Kenya, Malik Obama has decided to vote for Trump in the upcoming election, marking a shift in his allegiance from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party. This unexpected endorsement has sparked interest in the presidential race, with Trump facing off against Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton in November.

Geert Wilders, the leader of the Freedom Party in the Netherlands, has once again sparked controversy with his latest comments on Moroccan immigrants. Speaking to his supporters in the ethnically diverse area of Spijkenisse, near Rotterdam, Wilders vowed to crack down on what he termed "Moroccan scum" who make the streets of Holland unsafe. This comes just two months after he was convicted in a hate speech trial over his promise to reduce the number of Moroccans in the country. Wilders, who is currently topping opinion polls ahead of the 15 March parliamentary vote, addressed his supporters on Saturday amid tight security. He emphasized that not all Moroccans are a problem, but his words were met with concern and outrage from many. According to the 2011 census, there are over 167,000 Moroccan-born residents of the Netherlands, making up the third-largest group of non-EU residents. This figure does not take into account second or third-generation Moroccans, who are also likely to be affected by Wilders' policies. The Freedom Party leader has vowed to ban Muslim immigration and shut mosques if he wins the election. His comments have been met with widespread criticism, with many accusing him of promoting hate speech and discrimination. A small group of demonstrators turned up to protest against Wilders' comments, with one protester, Emma Smeets, telling the Associated Press that she was "very, very scared" of what Wilders might do if he comes to power. Despite his lead in the polls, Wilders' support appears to be waning in recent weeks. His nearest rival, right-wing Prime Minister Mark Rutte, has narrowed the gap, and many Dutch voters are increasingly concerned about the impact of Wilders' policies on the country's stability and reputation. The BBC's Anna Holligan, reporting from The Hague, notes that Wilders' championing of US President Donald Trump's policies appears to be backfiring, with many voters believing that Trump is bad for global stability. Wilders' three-week trial last year was triggered by his comments during a municipal election campaign in The Hague, in which he asked supporters whether they wanted "fewer or more Moroccans in your city and in the Netherlands". The crowd's response of "Fewer! Fewer!" was met with a smiling Wilders, who said "We're going to take care of that". At the trial, prosecutors took testimony from Dutch-Moroccans who said Wilders' comments made them feel like "third-rate citizens". He was ultimately convicted of insulting a group and inciting discrimination. Even if Wilders wins the election, he may struggle to put together a coalition, as leading parties have said they would not work with him. The Freedom Party currently holds 12 of the 150 seats in the lower house of Parliament, and it remains to be seen whether Wilders will be able to translate his popularity into a workable government. As the election approaches, Dutch voters will be closely watching Wilders' next moves, and weighing the potential consequences of his policies on the country's future.

Researchers at the University of Dundee have made a groundbreaking discovery that could potentially lead to new treatments for fertility issues in women. A study analyzing medical records from over half a million British women found that those who had their tonsils and appendix removed were more likely to become pregnant. The findings, published in Fertility and Sterility, suggest that the removal of these organs may have a direct impact on fertility or be linked to behavioral factors. According to the study, for every 100 pregnancies in women who had no surgical procedures, there were significantly more pregnancies in women who had undergone tonsillectomy or appendectomy. Dr. Sami Shimi, one of the researchers, noted that the findings dispel the common myth that having an appendix removed damages fertility. In fact, the study found that removing inflamed or potentially inflamed organs, such as the appendix and tonsils, may actually improve a woman's chances of becoming pregnant. The exact explanation for these findings is still unclear, and more research is needed to determine the underlying causes. One possibility is that chronic inflammation in the body, caused by infected tonsils or appendixes, may affect the ovaries and womb, making it more difficult to conceive. Alternatively, the researchers suggest that behavioral factors, such as increased sexual activity, may be at play. Women who are more likely to engage in liberal sexual activity may also be more likely to have pelvic inflammatory disease, which could lead to the removal of the appendix. While the study's findings are promising, experts caution against drawing premature conclusions. Prof. Allan Pacey, from the University of Sheffield, noted that the study is "interesting" but more research is needed to fully understand the relationship between organ removal and fertility. He advised against suggesting that infertile women undergo unnecessary surgery, such as tonsillectomy or appendectomy, as a means of improving their fertility. Instead, the study may ultimately lead to the development of new treatments or therapies that can enhance women's fertility. As the research continues to unfold, one thing is clear: this study has opened up new avenues for exploration and may potentially lead to breakthroughs in the field of fertility medicine.

Bombardier has secured a significant deal with Malaysian airline Flymojo, worth approximately $3 billion. The airline has signed a letter of intent to purchase 20 CS100 aircraft, with the option to buy 20 more. The wings of the CSeries will be manufactured by Bombardier in Belfast. Despite years of delays and cost overruns, the CSeries is set to enter service later this year. Michael Ryan, VP and GM of Bombardier Belfast, expressed his pleasure with the deal, citing it as an endorsement of the aircraft's credentials. This brings Bombardier's total orders and commitments for the CSeries to 603 aircraft, marking a major milestone for the company.

Leicestershire police have introduced a unique initiative to prevent gold necklace thefts in the Belgrave area. Scarves have been designed to cover up valuable gold chains, particularly popular among Asian women. The garments were made by individuals on the Community Payback scheme using donated fabric from local businesses. Following a spike in thefts in previous summers, officers have been visiting community centres and temples to distribute the scarves and raise awareness about the issue. In 2014, 72 chain snatches were reported in the area, prompting police to take proactive measures to combat the problem. So far, this year has seen no incidents, thanks to the efforts of the police and community.

A groundbreaking investigation is set to take place in a Moray cave where human remains from the Late Bronze Age were previously discovered. Michelle Walker, a graduate of the University of the Highlands and Islands (UHI), will lead the research, which aims to explore the acoustic properties of Sculptors Cave. The cave is believed to have been used by prehistoric people for burial rituals, which involved beating a drum. As part of the study, Ms Walker plans to beat a drum in the cave, replicating the ancient rituals. Volunteers will be asked to complete a questionnaire, recording their thoughts and feelings during the two-minute drumming session. The research, known as archaeoacoustics, has previously shed light on the behavior of sound in Neolithic temples in England and Ireland. The UHI has been at the forefront of uncovering clues to life in prehistoric Scotland. Recently, archaeologists from the university discovered a significant complex of Bronze Age buildings at Tresness in Sanday, which were buried by sand dunes over 3,000 years ago. Additionally, the remains of 8,000-year-old hazelnut shells were found at a dig on the island of Skye, providing insight into the lives of Mesolithic hunter-gatherers. The new investigation in Sculptors Cave is expected to further our understanding of the lives and rituals of Scotland's ancient inhabitants.

US Missile Mistakenly Sent to Cuba, Sparking Diplomatic Efforts A highly sensitive US missile was inadvertently shipped to Cuba, sparking a diplomatic effort to retrieve the advanced weaponry. The AGM 114 Hellfire missile, which did not contain explosives, was originally sent to Spain for a NATO training exercise before being routed to Germany and eventually to Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris. However, instead of being sent to its intended destination in Florida, the missile was loaded onto an Air France flight to Havana. The incident has been deemed a serious mistake, with US officials expressing concern that Cuba could share the missile's advanced technology with countries such as North Korea, China, or Russia. The Cuban government has stated that the missile arrived in the country "by mistake or mishandling in the country of origin" and has cooperated with US efforts to retrieve the missile. The US and Cuba, which restored diplomatic relations last year after more than 50 years, are working to resolve the issue. The incident is an embarrassment for the US, which has had to request the return of its own military technology. Despite the setback, the two countries are expected to announce the reinstatement of commercial flights between US cities and Havana on Tuesday, marking a significant step forward in their efforts to rebuild economic and trade ties.

Cardiff Blues prop Anton Peikrishvili has been handed a five-week ban for biting an opponent. The 29-year-old Georgian was sent off during a game against Ospreys after biting back-rower Rob McCusker. Peikrishvili's ban has been back-dated to November 22, making him eligible to play again from January 2, 2017. He joined the Blues on a short-term contract and featured in two games, including a debut against Exeter Chiefs. The Rugby Football Union oversaw the case, as the competition falls under their jurisdiction. Meanwhile, Scarlets' Jack Condy was also banned for punching in a separate match. Peikrishvili previously played for Ulster on a short-term contract but did not make an appearance for the province. His suspension will keep him sidelined until the new year.

Concerns have been raised by the Northern Ireland Police Federation regarding the potential impact of physical border posts on officer safety and community relations. Mark Lindsay, chair of the federation, expressed his concerns that enforcing border controls would put officers at risk and have a negative effect on PSNI resources. The government has repeatedly stated its desire to avoid recreating the "borders of the past," instead suggesting the use of technological solutions to manage the border. However, Mr. Lindsay believes that regardless of the type of border implemented, the police will be required to enforce new post-Brexit regulations. This, he argues, would create a security threat and necessitate police protection for customs agencies, putting officers in the line of fire. The predictable patterns of police patrols would make them an easy target for terrorist attacks. The comments come as Prime Minister Theresa May announced plans for the UK to leave the European Customs Union, a move that Sinn Féin claims would result in a "hard border" on the island of Ireland and undermine the Good Friday Agreement. Mr. Lindsay warned that enforcing a hard border would be a "step backwards" for community policing, as it would require significant additional resources and potentially disrupt communities that straddle the border. The PSNI currently lacks the resources to effectively manage a hard border, highlighting the need for alternative solutions to be explored.

A major breakthrough has been made in the 35-year-old murder case of Lorraine McCausland, with police preparing a file for the Public Prosecution Service. The 23-year-old's body was found beside a stream in Forthriver in 1987. She was last seen alive in a loyalist club at Tyndale, where police believe she was raped and "savagely beaten" before her body was dumped. Recently, several arrests were made in connection with the case, including a 54-year-old and a 56-year-old in Belfast, and two men aged 53 and 59 in Antrim. Additional arrests were made in Scotland and England, bringing the total number of suspects to seven. The original investigation in 1987 resulted in 14 arrests, but no charges were filed. Lorraine's son, Craig, who was just two when she was killed, was tragically murdered 18 years later in a separate incident. The case has sent shockwaves through the community, and police are hopeful that justice will finally be served for Lorraine and her family. Detectives have conducted extensive searches and gathered over 100 witness statements, bringing them closer to resolving the case.

In a significant victory for multinational corporations operating in India, the Bombay High Court has ruled in favor of Shell's Indian unit in a long-standing tax dispute. The court dismissed allegations that the company had under-priced shares transferred to its parent firm by $2.5 billion in 2013, which would have resulted in a substantial tax bill. The Indian tax authorities had claimed that the company should pay tax on the interest that would have been earned if the shares had been transferred at a higher price. However, the court ruled that the stock transfers were exempt from taxation under the country's share transfer provisions. Shell's India lawyer, Mukesh Butani, welcomed the decision, stating that the tax department had "clearly exceeded its jurisdiction". This ruling is a major boost for Shell and other international companies operating in India, which have been targeted in a series of high-profile tax disputes in recent years. Companies such as IBM, Nokia, HSBC, and AT&T have all been embroiled in tax battles with Indian authorities, which has damaged the country's reputation as a destination for foreign investment. The Indian government, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has pledged to end the "tax terrorism" that has been scaring companies away. The court's decision in the Shell case, combined with a similar ruling in favor of Vodafone in October, will be closely watched by other multinationals involved in similar disputes. The outcome is seen as a positive step towards improving India's investment climate and attracting much-needed overseas investment. The ruling is also expected to provide a boost to India's efforts to attract foreign investment, which is crucial for the country's economic growth. With the government's initiatives to improve the business environment and reduce bureaucratic hurdles, this decision is likely to send a positive signal to international companies considering investing in India. As the country continues to navigate its complex tax landscape, this victory for Shell is a significant step in the right direction.

In the city of El Alto, Bolivia, a burst of color has emerged in the form of vibrant, ostentatious mansions designed by local architect Freddy Mamani. Dubbed "cholets," a combination of the words "chalet" and "chola," meaning indigenous woman, these structures are a stark contrast to the city's predominantly unpainted brick houses, many of which remain unfinished. Mamani's creations have not only transformed the cityscape but have also become a status symbol for the wealthy Aymara indigenous community. Mamani's inspiration stems from indigenous Andean iconography, drawing from the geometric patterns found in the pre-Incan ruins of Tiwanaku, located near Lake Titicaca. By incorporating these traditional designs into his buildings, Mamani aims to celebrate the cultural heritage of Bolivia's indigenous people. The result is a unique blend of modern architecture and ancient cultural influences. The cholets, which can cost anywhere from $150,000 to $300,000, feature elaborate designs, including penthouses, shops, and party halls. These spaces can be rented out, providing a lucrative source of income for the owners. The party halls, in particular, have become a popular venue for weddings and other celebrations within the Aymara community. Mamani's work has gained widespread recognition, with 70 of his cholets already constructed in El Alto and many more orders pouring in daily. His designs have also inspired a new generation of architects and builders, some of whom have attempted to replicate his style. However, according to Mamani, what sets his work apart is the essence and language that underlies his creations. "Mine have an identity, a language that can be described," he explains. As one drives through El Alto with Mamani, it becomes apparent that his influence extends beyond his own designs. The city is dotted with colorful buildings, many of which bear a resemblance to Mamani's signature style. While some may be copies, Mamani remains unfazed, acknowledging that his work has inspired a new wave of creativity in the city. With his cholets continuing to leave a lasting impression on El Alto's landscape, Mamani's contribution to the city's cultural and architectural heritage is undeniable.

A shocking discovery was made at Hull Royal Infirmary when a mouse was spotted sticking its head out from under a door. Julie Saunders, a visitor to the hospital, alerted staff after her son made the unsettling observation. "It was a bit of a shock really, you don't expect mice in a hospital," she expressed. In response, staff took immediate action, placing blankets along the bottom of the door to prevent the rodents from entering. Saunders and her son reported seeing two mice, while other patients claimed to have seen four. The Hull and East Yorkshire Hospitals NHS Trust quickly called in a pest control team to address the issue. The team is currently working to minimize disruption and reopen the affected unit as soon as possible. The incident has raised concerns about the hospital's pest control measures.

Tragedy Strikes in Dalgety Bay: Twin Toddlers Found Dead in Garden Tank A devastating incident occurred in Dalgety Bay on Saturday, leaving a family and community in shock. Two-year-old twins, Rhys and Shaun Scott, were discovered in a garden tank at their rented home at approximately 08:20. Despite being rushed to the hospital by ambulance, the twins were pronounced dead upon arrival. The rented property, formerly used as a business selling ornamental koi carp, had been granted planning permission by Fife Council in 2012 for the installation of a fish tank and enclosure, valued at £25,000. The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is currently liaising with the police to investigate the circumstances surrounding the twins' deaths. The twins' parents, Mervyn Scott and Sarah Aitken, have released a heart-wrenching statement, describing their children as "miracle babies" who were "full of love, happiness, fun, and cheek." They expressed their devastation and shock at the loss, stating that the twins had touched the lives of everyone they met and would be "forever missed and loved." Police Scotland is continuing to investigate the incident, with a specialist family liaison officer providing support to the grieving family. The HSE may compile reports for prosecutors if it is found that the landlords had put tenants in danger. The community is left to mourn the tragic loss of two young lives, taken far too soon in a freak accident.

The National Trust property in Enniskillen, Castle Coole, is set to host the prestigious Last Night of the Proms event on September 9. Approximately 6,000 people are expected to attend the classical music show, which will feature internationally acclaimed musicians performing alongside the Ulster Orchestra, led by conductor David Brophy. This year's event marks the 16th year of the Northern Ireland Proms, with previous years seeing major outside broadcasts in Hillsborough, Carrickfergus, and Bangor. The BBC Proms is the world's largest classical music festival, boasting over 90 concerts and events across the UK over eight weeks. According to BBC Northern Ireland director Peter Johnston, audiences can expect "a very special evening" with "the very best in music-making" from the Castle Coole show. The concert will be hosted by Claire McCollum and Noel Thompson, with key moments broadcast live on BBC television and a highlights programme shown at a later date. The show will also be live on BBC Radio Ulster. Robert Gibson of Fermanagh and Omagh District Council praised Castle Coole as an "inspired choice" to mark the Last Night of the Proms, promising an unforgettable experience for attendees.

Papua New Guinea Toughens Penalties for Violence, Repeals Sorcery Act In a move aimed at addressing the country's high levels of violence, Papua New Guinea's parliament has passed legislation that repeals the 1971 Sorcery Act and introduces tougher penalties for various crimes. The new laws make killings linked to allegations of witchcraft punishable as murder, with the death penalty applicable in such cases. The decision has been met with mixed reactions, with human rights groups condemning the introduction of stricter penalties. The repeal of the Sorcery Act is seen as a significant step forward in protecting women from violence, as accusations of sorcery are often used to justify brutal attacks on women. In recent years, several high-profile cases of sorcery-related killings have made headlines, including the burning alive of a 20-year-old mother in a village market and the beheading of a woman accused of black magic. Under the new laws, such killings will be treated as murder, and perpetrators will face the death penalty. However, the introduction of stricter penalties for other crimes, including rape and armed robbery, has been criticized by human rights groups. Amnesty International has condemned the move, stating that Papua New Guinea has "taken one step forward in protecting women from violence, but several giant steps back by moving closer to executions." The organization's deputy director for the Asia-Pacific, Isabelle Arradon, accused the government of "attempting to end one form of violence by perpetrating state-sanctioned violence." The new laws also prescribe longer jail terms for kidnapping, theft, and white-collar crime, and introduce several methods of execution, including hanging, lethal injection, firing squad, and electrocution. Justice and Attorney General Kerenga Kua defended the tough new laws, stating that they reflect the country's high crime levels and community demands. Prime Minister Peter O'Neil has announced plans to begin implementing the death penalty and increasing prison sentences for violent crimes, citing the need for "draconian" measures to address the country's crime problem. Despite the introduction of the death penalty for murder in 1991, Papua New Guinea has not carried out an execution since 1954. At least 10 people are currently on death row, according to Amnesty International. The introduction of stricter penalties has sparked concerns about the country's human rights record and the potential for miscarriages of justice. As Papua New Guinea continues to grapple with high levels of violence, the effectiveness of the new laws in addressing the root causes of crime remains to be seen.

A young entrepreneur, Ms Kgatlhanye, has won $50,000 to launch her innovative business. She creates bags with built-in solar lights, allowing school children without electricity to study after dark. With her prize money, she invested in machinery and staff, employing 20 people. The company plans to expand production, introducing new lines. Her success story is part of the BBC's "Women of Africa" series, highlighting inspiring female entrepreneurs across the continent. Kgatlhanye's initiative is making a difference in her community, providing a sustainable solution for children to continue their education after dark.

New Evidence Emerges in Hillsborough Disaster Inquests The ongoing inquests into the 1989 Hillsborough disaster have heard new evidence regarding the final moments of two of the 96 fans who lost their lives in the tragic event. The court, sitting in Warrington, Cheshire, was presented with witness statements and video footage detailing the desperate attempts to save Ian Glover, 20, and Christopher Edwards, 29, who were both fatally injured in the crush on the Leppings Lane terrace during the Liverpool versus Nottingham Forest FA Cup semi-final. Ian Glover, from Walton in Liverpool, had attended the match with his brother Joseph and two friends. According to a witness statement given by Joseph in 1989, the brothers were thrown forward by a crowd surge, and while Joseph managed to escape through a gate in the perimeter fence, Ian was left trapped. Joseph described how he watched in horror as his brother's face turned blue, and his voice grew quieter as he shouted for help. Despite attempting to give his brother mouth-to-mouth resuscitation when his body was brought onto the pitch, Ian sadly did not survive. The court heard that Ian Edwards, a Liverpool supporter who had been in the North Stand, helped to carry Ian Glover on a makeshift stretcher to a nearby gymnasium where casualties had been taken. Along with a police officer, Edwards performed CPR on Glover, and at one point, he believed he saw a "flicker of the eyes," suggesting that Glover may have shown signs of life. However, despite their best efforts, there were no further signs of life, and Edwards realized that Glover had sadly passed away. The inquests also heard about the final movements of Christopher Edwards, who had traveled to the game with a friend and his son. Video footage shown to the court depicted fans and police attempting to carry Edwards out of pen three on the Leppings Lane terrace, over 20 minutes after the game had been stopped. Former police sergeant Martin Hemingway, who was treating another victim in the central pens, stated that he believed Edwards was still breathing when he was first alerted to his condition. However, upon reaching the pitch, there were no signs of life, and Edwards was later pronounced dead by a doctor in the gymnasium. The difficulties in accessing medical assistance at the time of the disaster were also highlighted during the inquests. The court heard that the lack of adequate medical care and the chaos on the pitch made it challenging for those attempting to save the lives of the injured fans. The inquests, which are expected to resume on Wednesday, continue to shed new light on the tragic events of that day and the devastating consequences for the families of the 96 victims. As the inquests progress, the families of those who lost their lives in the Hillsborough disaster remain hopeful that the truth will finally be revealed, and justice will be served. The tragedy, which occurred on April 15, 1989, remains one of the darkest days in British sporting history, and the ongoing inquests serve as a poignant reminder of the importance of ensuring that such a disaster never happens again.

UK leaders weigh in on the upcoming election, each making their case for why they should hold the balance of power. Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg stated that his party, along with UKIP's Nigel Farage or the SNP's Alex Salmond, could be the deciding factor on May 8. Farage emphasized UKIP's plan to improve the lives of working people through a "low tax revolution." Meanwhile, Labour leader Ed Miliband remained unfazed by media scrutiny, saying he would be overwhelmed if he reacted to every story. As the campaign heats up, the BBC Election 2015 newsletter offers a daily round-up of the latest news, available in your inbox every weekday afternoon. With just days to go, the UK's political landscape is poised for a significant shift, and each leader is making a strong pitch to voters. The election's outcome remains uncertain.

Swansea's Kingsway road is set to undergo significant changes as part of a plan to improve safety and reduce accidents. The road will be converted into a full one-way system, following a series of tragic incidents, including the deaths of two people. In recent months, the road has been the scene of numerous accidents, prompting concerns over its safety.
