The current traffic system, which allows two lanes of traffic to travel west on one side and two lanes of public transport to travel in both directions on the other, has been criticized for its "serious design issues". A coroner's investigation into the death of Daniel Foss, 37, who was hit by a bus, called for urgent action to address these issues. In response, Swansea council installed barriers along the carriageway to prevent pedestrians from crossing. However, council leader Rob Stewart has stated that any further changes, including the possibility of introducing a two-way traffic system, will depend on the outcome of plans to regenerate the Kingsway into a business district. Work on this project is set to begin in October, with the demolition of the former Oceana building. The site is being considered as a potential new home for the council. Mr Stewart has promised that necessary changes will be made to the road, but a final decision on its layout will be made once the master plan for the Kingsway is finalized.

A collection of belongings from the late actress Lauren Bacall has been sold at auction, exceeding expectations. A hand-coloured etching of an American white pelican by John James Audubon sold for $173,000, three times its predicted value. Additionally, a granite games table from her Los Angeles home, which she shared with Humphrey Bogart, fetched $26,250. The auction, held by Bonhams, featured other unique items, including a Tiffany necklace, a brass Japanese tea set, and sculptures by Henry Moore. The proceeds will benefit Bacall's three children. The sale showcases Bacall's eclectic taste and collecting sense, according to Bonhams' vice president Jon King. The actress passed away in August at 89, and her New York home is currently on the market for $26m. The auction highlights the enduring legacy of the Hollywood star and her distinctive style.

Scotland Sees Significant Reduction in Single-Use Bag Usage A recent report has revealed that Scotland has witnessed a substantial decrease in the use of single-use bags, with a reduction of 129 million bags in the final quarter of 2014. This decline came after the introduction of a 5p levy on single-use bags, which was implemented for the last 11 weeks of the year. The statistics, released by the Scottish government, demonstrate the effectiveness of the charge in reducing the number of bags used by shoppers. Environment Secretary Richard Lochhead described the figures as "astounding" and highlighted the country's commitment to tackling litter and reducing waste. He expressed his hope that the public will continue to reuse their bags and that more retailers will donate money to good causes when bags are necessary. Lochhead emphasized that small changes can make a significant difference, and the reduction in single-use bag usage is a testament to this. In contrast, England saw an increase of 200 million single-use bags in 2014, with supermarkets distributing over 7.6 billion bags, according to research by waste reduction body Wrap. However, from October, large retailers in England will be required to charge a minimum of 5p for single-use bags, bringing the country in line with Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland has seen a significant reduction in single-use bag usage, with a 42.6% decrease in 2014, following a 71% drop after the introduction of a carrier bag charge in 2013. Wales, on the other hand, experienced a 5.2% increase in single-use bag usage last year, although the number of bags handed out has fallen by 78.2% since 2010. The Scottish government aims to reduce the use of single-use bags by 80% in the first full year of the charge, a target that has been achieved by Wales and Northern Ireland in their respective campaigns. The reduction in single-use bag usage is a step towards minimizing litter and waste, and the Scottish government's efforts are expected to have a positive impact on the environment. As the rest of the UK follows suit, it is likely that the country will see a significant decrease in single-use bag usage, contributing to a more sustainable future.

Rangers' Under-20s coach Graeme Murty has been handed a significant boost after his side secured a thrilling 3-2 victory over St Johnstone at Ibrox. The win, which marked Murty's first Premiership triumph in charge, has been hailed by the players as a testament to his exceptional leadership and coaching skills. Midfielder Emerson Hyndman, who scored the late winner against the Saints, praised Murty's ability to establish a clear vision for the team despite the challenges he faced as an interim manager. "He's been brilliant," Hyndman said. "It's always a tough position, but he's come in and established what he wants us to do, and the boys have gotten behind him." Hyndman's sentiments were echoed by fellow loan player Jon Toral, who joined Rangers from Arsenal in January. "It was massive for Graeme on Wednesday," Toral said. "He has put a lot of effort into the other games as well, and for us to give him that first league win was crucial." The victory has reignited hope for Rangers, who are now just six points behind second-placed Aberdeen in the Premiership table. With a Scottish Cup quarter-final against Hamilton Academical on the horizon, Hyndman believes there is still plenty to play for this season. "Of course, there is," he said. "We need to get ourselves right, and I think we took our first step against Saints. It was about the three points, not about how we got it." Despite the expected appointment of a new head coach next week, the players are focused on the task at hand. "At the minute, we are just thinking about the cup tie on Saturday, and then whatever happens, happens," Toral said. With Murty's interim tenure potentially coming to an end, the players are eager to give him a strong finish to his spell in charge. As Hyndman noted, "It was nice to give him that positive feeling on Wednesday night."

Tobacco Giants Take EU to Court Over New Packaging Rules In a significant move, major tobacco companies, including Philip Morris, British American Tobacco (BAT), and Imperial Tobacco, have joined forces to challenge the European Union's (EU) new tobacco regulations. The case, which was heard in London's High Court on Monday, has been referred to the EU's Court of Justice. The tobacco companies are contesting the EU's Tobacco Products Directive, which requires health warnings to cover 65% of the front and back of cigarette packaging. The EU's highest court will now be tasked with determining whether the EU has overstepped its authority in introducing the new rules and whether they are proportionate. The court must also decide if the directive complies with European guarantees on fundamental rights and the principle of subsidiarity, which dictates that decisions should be made at the national or regional level whenever possible. The tobacco companies argue that the new rules disrupt the balance between the EU and its member states, and raise concerns about the free movement of goods and competition within the EU. Philip Morris senior vice president Marc Firestone stated that while the company agrees that tobacco products should be strictly regulated, "measures must honour the EU treaties." The review by the Court of Justice is expected to take up to two years, and its ruling will have significant implications for the tobacco industry and public health policies in the EU.

Pakistan Heatwave Claims Hundreds of Lives in Karachi A severe heatwave has gripped the city of Karachi, Pakistan, resulting in the deaths of hundreds of people, mostly elderly individuals, over the past few days. The city has been experiencing temperatures as high as 45C (113F), with power cuts exacerbating the situation due to increased demand for electricity. The power outages have been particularly problematic during the holy month of Ramadan, when Muslims fast during daylight hours and rely on air conditioning to cope with the heat. According to provincial health secretary Saeed Mangnejo, hundreds of patients are being treated at government hospitals for heat-related illnesses, including fever, dehydration, and gastric problems. The Edhi morgue in Sohrab Goth has reported a significant increase in the number of bodies received, with over 150 bodies taken in since Saturday, compared to the usual daily average of 20. The heatwave has sparked angry protests in parts of the city, with some residents blaming the government and the city's main power utility, K-Electric, for failing to prevent the deaths. "In our area, there is no electricity since morning. We have complained several times, but there is no response from K-Electric," said Karachi resident Iqbal, who added that his family has been unable to go outside to work due to the extreme heat. The prolonged power outages have made it difficult for people to access basic necessities like cool water and air conditioning, which are essential for survival in such extreme temperatures. The human body is not equipped to handle temperatures above 40C, and prolonged exposure can lead to heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and even multiple organ failure. Experts warn that heatstroke can occur at any temperature over 40C and requires immediate medical attention. In extreme heat, the body's normal cooling mechanisms, such as sweating, can fail, leading to a rapid deterioration in health. To mitigate the effects of the heatwave, residents are advised to stay indoors, stay hydrated, and avoid strenuous activities during the hottest part of the day. The Pakistan Meteorological Office has forecast that the hot and humid weather is likely to continue on Monday, but cooler temperatures are expected from Tuesday. The all-time record temperature in Karachi is 47C (117F), recorded in 1979. The current heatwave has drawn comparisons to a similar heatwave in neighboring India last month, which claimed the lives of nearly 1,700 people. As the city struggles to cope with the heatwave, authorities are under pressure to provide relief to affected residents and prevent further deaths. The government has been criticized for its handling of the situation, and there are growing calls for increased investment in the city's infrastructure, including its power grid, to prevent such disasters in the future.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has issued a mixed assessment of Japan's economic outlook, citing a "modest recovery" but warning that bold structural reforms are needed to sustain growth and achieve financial consolidation. The IMF's latest annual report comes as Tokyo's reform package, known as Abenomics, marks its tenth year since its introduction in 2012. According to the IMF, Japan's growth is expected to stabilize at around 0.7% over the medium term, with inflation projected to reach 1.5%, still below the Bank of Japan's target of 2%. While the decline of the yen has been beneficial for Japan's exports sector, the outlook remains negative due to weak domestic demand and incomplete policies, particularly with regards to fiscal consolidation and structural reforms. The IMF has cautioned against relying too heavily on yen depreciation and has called for Abenomics to be "reloaded" to address policy shortcomings. The next round of reforms should focus on increasing labor supply and reducing labor market flexibility, as well as continuing deregulation of the agricultural and services sectors. The financial sector should also be leveraged as a driver of reforms. Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's reform package has achieved short-term growth, but the government has struggled to deregulate the job market and open up protected industry sectors. The IMF's report serves as a reminder that more needs to be done to ensure Japan's long-term economic prosperity. With the right reforms in place, Japan can unlock its growth potential and achieve sustainable economic recovery.

Welsh Government Introduces New Measures to Hold Health Boards Accountable The Welsh government has announced new arrangements to strengthen the inspection and regulation of health boards in Wales, following a damning report into the mismanagement of the Betsi Cadwaladr Health Board in north Wales. The new measures, which come into effect next month, are designed to provide clarity on the roles and responsibilities of the Welsh government, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales (HIW), and the Auditor General Wales in dealing with potential problems. Under the new arrangements, the Welsh government will have the power to suspend a health board's board or ask another body to run the service in cases of severe mismanagement. Less drastic options, such as "enhanced monitoring" and "targeted intervention", will also be available. These measures are intended to ensure that health boards are held accountable for poor performance and that patients receive the best possible care. The need for a stronger inspection and regulation regime emerged from last year's joint HIW and Wales Audit Office (WAO) report into governance arrangements at Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board. The report found that the board had delayed operations and allowed waiting lists to grow to avoid financial problems, and that "significant management failings" had risked patient safety by under-reporting infections. Health Minister Mark Drakeford said that the new arrangements would provide a clear set of processes for dealing with issues that give rise to concern. "I am confident that, where issues do emerge which give rise to concern, we now have a clear set of arrangements for all to understand how such matters will be systematically dealt with, to ensure proportionate and timely action," he said. The Conservatives have welcomed the changes, saying that the situation at Betsi Cadwaladr health board had been "allowed to fester for far too long" and that the previous processes were "far too murky and needed to change". Shadow Health Minister Darren Millar said that patients and their families need to have confidence that health boards will be held to account for poor performance, and that these changes should go some way to ensuring that this is the case. The new arrangements are expected to provide greater transparency and accountability in the Welsh healthcare system, and to ensure that patients receive the best possible care. With Wales already having one of the most closely inspected healthcare systems in the UK, these changes are intended to build on this foundation and provide a robust quality assurance system.

Daily flights from the Isle of Man to Glasgow will resume on May 2, operated by Eastern Airways. The route was previously cancelled when Citywing went into liquidation in March. Eastern Airways has already taken over services to Belfast and Newcastle. The renewed link is "very important" according to Isle of Man Airport's Director of Ports, Ann Reynolds. The airline prioritized protecting vital routes before reinstating the Glasgow service. The new daily flights will operate from Ronaldsway to Glasgow, reestablishing a crucial connection between the island and the UK city.

Welsh First Minister Criticizes UK Government's "Laggardly" Response to Refugee Crisis During the first First Minister's Questions session after the summer recess, Welsh First Minister Carwyn Jones slammed UK Prime Minister David Cameron's response to the ongoing refugee crisis as "laggardly". The criticism came as opposition parties called for a full debate on the crisis in the Welsh Assembly. Jones' comments were in response to a question from Plaid Cymru leader Leanne Wood, in which he expressed his support for a quota system for each nation to handle the influx of refugees. The Welsh Tory leader, Andrew RT Davies, had earlier emphasized the need for a "substantial package of integration" for migrants, rather than just "tokenism". Meanwhile, Deputy Plaid leader Elin Jones expressed disappointment and surprise at the lack of a Welsh government response to an urgent question on the crisis. Despite no scheduled statement on the refugee crisis, several Assembly Members raised the issue during the session. Jones announced that he would be calling a summit on the crisis for Thursday, inviting charities and local councils to send representatives to coordinate the Welsh response. The summit aims to develop a coordinated Wales-wide response to the crisis, which will be the start of a government-led action that will continue throughout the autumn. The UK government has pledged to accept up to 20,000 refugees from camps surrounding Syria, with priority given to vulnerable children. The Welsh Refugee Council estimates that Wales could provide sanctuary to around 1,600 Syrians. However, local councils have expressed concerns about meeting the costs, highlighting the need for support from the government. The First Minister's criticism of the UK government's response reflects the growing concern among Welsh politicians and charities about the need for a more effective and coordinated approach to addressing the refugee crisis. As the situation continues to unfold, the Welsh government's summit on Thursday is expected to play a crucial role in shaping the country's response to this humanitarian crisis.

Rare'Floating Gold' Worth £40,000 Found by Young Boy on Beach A young boy from Christchurch has stumbled upon a rare and valuable treasure while exploring the shores of Hengistbury Head in Bournemouth. Charlie Naysmith, with the help of his father Alex, discovered a 600g lump of ambergris, a natural substance produced by sperm whales, hidden among a patch of seaweed. Initially, Charlie thought he had found a "normal stone," but after researching online, they realized the significance of their discovery. Ambergris, often referred to as "floating gold," is a rare and highly sought-after material used in perfumes and some medicines. It is produced by sperm whales as a digestion aid and can float on the ocean for years before washing ashore. The lump found by Charlie is estimated to be around 20 years old and could be worth up to £40,000. Charlie's father, Alex Naysmith, expressed his excitement and surprise at the discovery, stating, "It's very rare. You don't hear of it coming around very often, and it's only found in small amounts usually." He added that while the value of ambergris may have decreased over time, the family is hopeful that they can sell it for a significant amount. Charlie has already made plans for what he will do with the money if they are able to sell the ambergris. The young boy wants to use the funds to create a nature reserve for animals in the UK, showcasing his passion for wildlife conservation. Ambergris has been mythologized for thousands of years, with its unique properties and rarity making it a highly prized material. However, its association with whaling and the vulnerable status of sperm whales have led many perfume makers to opt for synthetic alternatives. Despite this, the discovery of ambergris remains a significant find, and Charlie's luck has sparked excitement among scientists and treasure hunters alike. As the family waits to determine the authenticity and value of their discovery, Charlie's find has already made waves in the scientific community and beyond.

Canberra Ranked as Best City to Live in the World, Australia Tops Country Rankings The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has released its latest survey, ranking 362 regions across its 34 member nations based on nine measures of well-being. The results show that Canberra, the capital city of Australia, is the best place to live in the world, with Australia also leading the country rankings. Norway follows closely behind in the country rankings. The OECD's survey takes into account various factors such as income, education, jobs, safety, health, and environment to determine the quality of life in each region. The top 10 regional rankings feature five Australian cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, and Perth, in addition to Canberra. Other high-scoring regions include the states of New Hampshire and Minnesota in the US. On the other hand, Mexican states occupy all 10 of the bottom regional rankings, with Mexico, Turkey, Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia being ranked as the hardest places to live at a country level. The OECD's findings have been met with a mix of pride and surprise in Australian media outlets. While some have hailed Canberra as the best city in the world, others have expressed skepticism, with one headline reading "Is Canberra really the world's best city? More like capital punishment". Despite its reputation for being dull and devoid of soul, Canberra has been defended by its residents and some media outlets. The Canberra Times has said that the rankings "yet again confirmed what many Canberrans have long known; that our city is the best place to live in the world". An opinion piece on news.com.au has also come to the city's defense, describing it as a great place to live and work. The OECD study highlights the importance of considering a range of factors beyond economic statistics when evaluating the quality of life in different regions. As the OECD notes, "recent years have seen an increasing awareness that macroeconomic statistics, such as GDP, do not provide policy-makers with a sufficiently detailed picture of the living conditions that ordinary people experience". The organization's survey is one of the few to analyze the quality of life in countries, making it a valuable resource for policymakers and individuals alike. Overall, the OECD's rankings provide a unique insight into the quality of life in different regions around the world. While there may be some debate about the merits of Canberra as the best city to live in, the fact that Australia tops the country rankings is a testament to the country's high standard of living and strong economy. As the world continues to urbanize and populations grow, understanding what makes a city or region a great place to live will become increasingly important.

Sun European Partners, a subsidiary of Sun Capital, has acquired O&S Holdings, a business established in 1988 by Peter O'Donnell. The company employs over 360 people and has shown significant financial growth, with a pre-tax profit of £6m on a turnover of £32m in 2014. Chris Carney, vice president at Sun European Partners, praised O&S for its exceptional customer service and product quality. The acquisition is expected to increase market share and build upon valuable customer relationships. Peter O'Donnell believes the deal will help develop the company and strengthen its offerings. O&S was advised by PwC Corporate Finance during the acquisition process. With Sun European Partners' support, O&S is poised for further growth and expansion, leveraging its strong reputation and financial foundation. The acquisition marks a new chapter for the company, with exciting opportunities ahead.

Surrey County Council Leader David Hodge has issued a stark warning that the authority may be unable to guarantee school places for children from 2015 unless it receives additional funding from the government. The council is facing a significant shortfall in its budget, which would require it to borrow £200m over the next five years to meet the rising demand for school places. According to Hodge, the council has been forced to borrow tens of millions of pounds to fund the expansion of schools, but this cannot continue. The borrowing would leave the council with a significant debt that would take 40 years to pay off, placing a substantial burden on Surrey taxpayers. Hodge expressed his frustration, stating that despite repeated requests, the government has failed to guarantee the necessary funding to meet the growing need for school places. The issue of school places in Surrey has been a longstanding concern, with the council struggling to keep up with the rising demand due to an unanticipated increase in the birth rate over the past decade. In October, Hodge warned that the council had only managed to find places for every child "by the skin of our teeth." The council has been working to provide additional spaces, including 4,100 extra places in September 2014, but the problem persists. The Conservative-controlled council has been critical of the government's funding allocation, arguing that Surrey contributes more in tax than any region outside the City of London but receives less money than the average county council. The Department for Education (DoE) has responded by stating that Surrey will have received £104m for new school places between 2011-2015, compared to £24m allocated by the previous government over an equivalent period. Additionally, the government has announced that Surrey County Council will receive a further £60m to spend on new school places in 2015-17. The DoE has also pointed to the opening of two free schools in the county, with another due to open in September, which will provide over 1,800 extra places. However, Hodge and the council remain unconvinced, arguing that the funding is insufficient to meet the growing demand for school places. The opposition councillors have criticized the council's "failures" in forecasting and planning for schools, but Hodge's warning has highlighted the urgent need for a solution to the school places crisis in Surrey. As the council awaits the government's response to its funding request, parents and children in the county remain anxious about the future of their education. The situation is a stark reminder of the challenges facing local authorities in providing essential services, and the need for a fair and sustainable funding settlement to ensure that every child has access to a quality education.

Everton is on the verge of signing Malaga's Sandro, a 21-year-old striker who had a remarkable season in La Liga, scoring 14 goals. The young player has a £5.2m buy-out clause, which has caught the attention of several top-tier clubs, including Atletico Madrid. However, due to Atletico's transfer ban, Everton manager Ronald Koeman has seized the opportunity to bring Sandro to Goodison Park. Sandro's potential signing is seen as an addition to Everton's striking resources, rather than a replacement for Romelu Lukaku, who has been linked with a return to Chelsea. Koeman is also keen on signing Ajax captain Davy Klaassen, a 24-year-old midfielder who played against Manchester United in the Europa League Final. The Netherlands international has attracted interest from other clubs, including Inter Milan and Napoli, but Everton is reportedly in talks with Ajax to secure his signature. Meanwhile, Everton remains in pursuit of Burnley defender Michael Keane and Sunderland goalkeeper Jordan Pickford. However, the future of midfielder Ross Barkley remains uncertain, as he continues to refuse a new contract. With several key signings on the horizon, Koeman is shaping up his squad for a strong season ahead.

Aurimas Butkys, 25, escaped Boston Police Station in Lincolnshire on Thursday. He was detained on an extradition warrant for a Lithuanian assault. Lincolnshire Police called the incident "embarrassing" and are investigating. Butkys had just entered the station before fleeing, prompting a search effort.

A charity auction of 64 snowdog sculptures has raised a significant amount for St Oswald's Hospice. The public art trail featured colourful designs, including some with North East themes. According to Jane Hogan, the response was "beyond anything we imagined". The event's success has led to plans for a similar initiative in autumn 2019. St Oswald's provides care for those with incurable conditions and relies on £7m in annual donations. The auction and subsequent donations will help support the charity's vital work in the North East, caring for adults, young people, and children.

Scotstown Edges Trillick to Reach Provincial Final In a thrilling match at Brewster Park, Scotstown secured a spot in the provincial final with a 1-9 to 2-6 victory over Trillick. Darren Hughes stole the show, scoring two goals and adding two points to lead the Monaghan team to their first provincial final since 1989. Trillick's Daniel McDonnell opened the scoring, but Hughes' first goal helped Scotstown take a 1-5 to 1-4 lead at halftime. Hughes completed his double, and Niall Gormley's goal brought Trillick within a point. However, points from Orin Heaphy and Rory Beggan sealed the win for Scotstown. Trillick, led by All Star Mattie Donnelly, squandered several opportunities in the second half, ultimately costing them the game. Scotstown will face Crossmaglen, who defeated Kilcoo by four points, on November 29. Joint-manager Mattie McGleenan praised his team's performance, saying they were "outstanding" in difficult conditions. McGleenan expressed pride in his team and vowed to give Crossmaglen a good game, despite acknowledging their opponents' strength.

A Damning Report: Health Board Failed to Protect Patient from Avoidable Stroke A scathing report by the Public Services Ombudsman has revealed that Cwm Taf health board failed to properly protect Margaret Harries, a patient from Porth, Rhondda Cynon Taff, from an avoidable stroke in 2012. The report, which upheld the family's complaint, found that the health board failed to assess and treat Mrs. Harries' symptoms promptly and effectively, leading to a devastating second stroke. Mrs. Harries was admitted to the Royal Glamorgan Hospital in Llantrisant on March 24, 2012, with symptoms of diarrhea and vomiting. However, despite her family's repeated requests for medical attention, she was not seen by a doctor for over six hours after suffering her first stroke on April 4, 2012. Tragically, she suffered a further significant stroke overnight while sleeping. The ombudsman's report identified several failings in Mrs. Harries' care, including a delay in her being seen by a suitably trained clinician and in transferring her to an acute stroke unit. The report's findings have left Mrs. Harries' family feeling angry and upset. Her son, Ceri Harries, expressed his dissatisfaction with the way the complaint was handled by the health board, stating, "I still feel angry about it. Just reading the report now is quite upsetting." In response to the report, Cwm Taf University Health Board has apologized for the failings and agreed to pay £5,500 in compensation. Allison Williams, the chief executive of the health board, said, "We reiterate our sincere apologies to Mrs. M's family following her treatment in April 2012, and apologize for the distress caused as a result of the failings identified within the report." The health board has also committed to implementing the report's recommendations to prevent similar incidents in the future. Mrs. Harries was transferred to another hospital for rehabilitation a week after her stroke and was later discharged to a nursing home in February 2013. Sadly, she passed away in November 2014. The report's findings serve as a stark reminder of the importance of prompt and effective medical care, and the devastating consequences that can occur when this standard is not met. The Harries family hopes that their mother's case will lead to improvements in patient care and prevent similar tragedies from occurring in the future.

Egyptian Military Strikes Down Top Jihadist Leader in Sinai The Egyptian military has announced the death of Abu Duaa al-Ansari, a key leader of the Sinai Province jihadist group, in a series of air strikes near the town of El-Arish. The raids, which targeted strongholds of the group, also known as Ansar Beit al-Maqdis, resulted in the deaths of over 45 terrorists and injured dozens more. Several arms caches were also destroyed in the operation. According to Brig-Gen Mohammed Samir, the military operation was guided by "accurate intelligence" and led to the killing of Ansari. The air strikes were carried out in southern and south-western areas of El-Arish, the largest town in northern Sinai. The Sinai Province group has been active in the region since 2011 and has been linked to numerous deadly attacks in Sinai and Cairo. The group's activities have increased since the army deposed President Mohammed Morsi in 2013, with a recent survey showing that they carried out over 31 attacks in a two-week period in March 2016. The Egyptian military has been actively targeting the group, and this latest operation is a significant blow to their leadership. The Sinai Province group has not commented on Ansari's death, but a recent video from the group issued a rare direct threat to Israel, warning that they would soon "pay a high price".

Cracks Discovered in Windsor Park Stadium, But Euro 2016 Qualifier to Proceed as Planned Despite the recent discovery of cracks in the East Stand of Windsor Park stadium, the Irish Football Association (IFA) has confirmed that the crucial Euro 2016 qualifier against Romania will go ahead as scheduled on June 13. The decision was announced by Patrick Nelson, who addressed Stormont's Culture, Arts and Leisure committee, reassuring fans that the necessary repairs will be made to ensure the stadium's safety. The cracks were first discovered last month, after a match between Northern Ireland and Finland, which drew a crowd of 4,000 spectators to the stand. Following a structural engineer's report, the IFA board has decided to demolish the stand, with work set to begin immediately. According to Nelson, the demolition is necessary to make the stand safe, and investigations into the cause of the damage are ongoing. In the meantime, the IFA has accelerated work on the East Stand, South East Quadrant, and South Stand to ensure that the stadium's 10,000 capacity is met for the upcoming match against Romania. The Irish Cup Final, which was originally scheduled to take place at Windsor Park, has been relocated to the Oval in east Belfast, with the IFA working closely with Belfast City Council, the clubs, and the ground to accommodate as many fans as possible. Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill has expressed his confidence in the plan, stating that he was impressed by the attention to detail and is looking forward to the match against Romania. Martin Lennon, of the construction firm O'Hare & McGovern, which is redeveloping Windsor Park, has assured that the company is committed to carrying out the IFA's instructions and has plans in place for the controlled demolition of the stand. Gary McAllister, of the Amalgamation of Northern Ireland Supporters Clubs, has welcomed the IFA's statement, believing that fans will be reassured by the plans for the stadium and the upcoming match. With the Euro 2016 qualifier just weeks away, the IFA and its partners are working tirelessly to ensure that the stadium is safe and ready for the big match. As the football community comes together to support the team, fans can rest assured that everything is being done to make the event a success.

Defending Masters Champion Danny Willett Returns to Augusta with High Hopes It's been a year since Danny Willett shocked the golf world with his maiden major win at the Augusta Masters. The Englishman's impressive five-under-par 67 in the final round, combined with Jordan Spieth's dramatic collapse, earned him the coveted Green Jacket and a career-high ninth spot in the world rankings. However, since his historic victory, Willett has struggled to replicate his form, dropping to 17th in the world rankings. As Willett returns to Augusta as the defending champion, he admits that the experience has given him a newfound spring in his step. Nevertheless, he acknowledges that his game remains unchanged, and the pressure to perform has mounted. "You do have a spring in your step coming back as champion, but you can't change your game like that," he said. Despite his inconsistent form, Willett remains optimistic about his chances at this year's Masters. He has had some notable performances, including a third-place finish at the PGA Championship and a second-place finish at the Italian Open, following his Masters win. However, a dip in form ahead of his Ryder Cup debut in October, where he failed to win a single point, raised concerns about his ability to perform under pressure. Willett attributes the pressure to his own high expectations, rather than external factors. "The pressure has been more from myself. It's not a nice feeling to not hit good golf shots when you know what you can do," he said. The 29-year-old Yorkshireman has only managed one top-10 finish so far in 2017, blowing a three-shot lead to finish fifth at the Maybank Championship in February. As part of his defending champion duties, Willett has chosen the menu for the annual Masters champions' dinner on Tuesday. The 34 former winners in attendance will be treated to a traditional British feast, featuring cottage pie, roast beef with Yorkshire pudding, and apple crumble. Willett is eager to share a taste of his hometown, Sheffield, with his fellow champions, and has warned Augusta's chef to get the Yorkshire puddings just right. With the Masters tournament just around the corner, Willett is focused on rediscovering his winning form. Despite the challenges he has faced over the past year, he remains confident in his abilities and is determined to make a strong defense of his title. As he prepares to tee off at Augusta, Willett will be drawing on the experience and knowledge he gained from his historic win last year, hoping to once again don the Green Jacket and prove himself as a major champion.

Liberal Democrat MP Mr George has expressed concerns over the upcoming axing of the helicopter service to the Isles of Scilly. Following a meeting with Transport Minister Norman Baker, Mr George stated that he is in discussions with various companies to find a replacement service to commence next year. The current service, operated by British International Helicopters (BIH), will cease on October 31 due to financial difficulties. Mr Baker announced plans to invest millions of pounds in improving St Mary's Airport, as well as the harbours on the islands and in Penzance. However, locals are calling for a reliable and affordable transport link, particularly during the winter months when the Scillonian ferry is not in operation and the Skybus service is weather-dependent. Marion Bennett, from Friends of Isles of Scilly Transport (FRIST), highlighted the significant costs involved in establishing a new helicopter service from scratch. She is scheduled to meet with Mr Baker later this month to reiterate the need for a transport service that meets the criteria of being affordable, all year round, and reliable. Mr George has been advocating for improved transport links to the Isles of Scilly for over 15 years, drawing comparisons with the subsidized ferry and air services in the Scottish islands.

At 109 years old, John McLarnon has witnessed a multitude of significant historical events, including two world wars and the creation of the Irish Free State. Born in 1914, he has lived in the same house in Largy, near Portglenone, his entire life. John's childhood was marked by simplicity, with he and his peers often going to school barefoot. However, the invention of the bicycle brought about a significant improvement in his life, providing a means of transportation and freedom. John's secret to longevity is a life of moderation. He neither smokes nor drinks, but does have a weakness for sweets, despite having all his own teeth. He gave up driving at the age of 100, citing the increasing speed of cars as a concern. John credits his good health as the greatest gift of all and is thankful for his ability to remain active. As part of a BBC NI appeal for Age NI, John is sharing his wisdom on living a long and healthy life. His advice is simple yet profound: "Take care of your health, because if you lose your health it never comes back," and "Don't put off tomorrow what you can do today." John's experiences and insights are invaluable, and his participation in the "Playing Our Part" appeal highlights the significant contributions older people make to society. Through his story, John serves as an inspiration to people of all ages, demonstrating the importance of living a balanced and active life.

The south of Scotland is gearing up for a spectacular 10-day celebration, running from January 20 to 29 next year. The event promises "something for everybody" with a diverse lineup of acts, including Peatbog Faeries, Skerryvore, and Dervish. Previously announced performers include The Ukulele Orchestra of Great Britain, Charlie Landsborough, Seth Lakeman, and Hackney Colliery Band. One of the highlights of the event is a carnival on January 22, themed around Tam O' Shanter, which will feature over 2,000 participants. The popular Le Haggis cabaret show will also return for its fourth edition. A special Burns Night Live event on January 25 will be hosted by local folk artist Emily Smith. This year's event will also feature a new community development project, Transform Dumfries, which aims to encourage local participation. Eight neighbourhood "hubs" will present 35 different events across various locations, including Lochside, Lincluden, and the town centre. According to Executive Producer Graham Main, the project is about putting audiences at the centre of the celebration and inviting more people to join in. The event is expected to re-energise Dumfries as a cultural winter destination, with parties and events happening throughout the town.

Wales' Rugby Team Prepares for Summer Tour with Young Squad Wales' national rugby team is gearing up for their summer tour, which kicks off on June 17 against Tonga, followed by a match against Samoa on June 24. The team, led by coach Robin McBryde, features 12 uncapped players, making for a exciting and unpredictable series of matches. According to McBryde, the team is well aware of the challenges that lie ahead. "It's going to be a huge test for us," he said. "The boys are pretty switched on and have been exceptional in their preparation." The team warmed up for the tour with an impressive 88-14 win over Welsh Premiership side RGC 1404 in Colwyn Bay. The summer tour will be a significant step up in intensity for the young squad, with the first match against Tonga at Eden Park in Auckland promising to be a thrilling encounter. The team will then face Samoa on their home turf, just a week after the Samoans take on the All Blacks. McBryde acknowledges that this will be a tough test, but is confident that the more experienced members of the squad will help guide the younger players. Injury setbacks have forced Exeter full-back Phil Dollman and Scarlets prop Samson Lee to pull out of the tour, but they have been replaced by Scarlets fly-half Rhys Patchell and Ospreys prop Rhodri Jones. With a mix of youth and experience, Wales' rugby team is ready to take on the challenges of the summer tour.

The Welsh Government has revised its proposal to rename the National Assembly for Wales, following a postponement of the original vote. The motion, which was due to be voted on by Assembly Members (AMs) on Tuesday, has been re-tabled for next week with significant changes. The term "Welsh Parliament" has been dropped, and instead, the motion calls for the assembly to change its name to reflect its constitutional status as a national parliament. The revised motion, tabled by Labour's chief whip Jane Hutt, invites the Presiding Officer, Elin Jones, and the Assembly Commission to consider the implications of the name change and how to implement it. This move has been seen as a compromise, with the Welsh Government working closely with the Presiding Officer to agree on the new motion. The proposal to rename the assembly has been debated for several years, with many arguing that the current name does not accurately reflect the institution's powers and responsibilities. Welsh Conservative leader Andrew RT Davies has previously stated that the assembly is a parliament "in all but name." However, the Welsh Tories have criticized the government for "overestimating its influence" in the matter, suggesting that the original motion was too prescriptive. Plaid Cymru AM Bethan Jenkins plans to amend the motion to propose that the Welsh language word "Senedd" be used to refer to the institution itself, rather than just the building that houses the assembly chamber. The word "Senedd" is currently used to refer to the UK Parliament in Welsh. The Welsh Government and the assembly have stated that they are happy to work together on the wording of the motion, with the Presiding Officer playing a key role in defending the autonomy of the assembly. The proposal will require a majority vote from AMs to proceed. The Welsh Conservatives have welcomed the revised motion and the involvement of the Presiding Officer, stating that they look forward to the proposal being taken forward if it secures the necessary support. The vote is now scheduled to take place next Tuesday.

A wild tiger that wandered into the Nandankanan Zoological Park in Orissa, India, has sparked debate among wildlife officials and zookeepers. The big cat, estimated to be around seven years old, entered the zoo on Monday night and has been roaming around the enclosure of a female tigress named Sara, indicating its desire to mate. The tiger had been causing panic in the adjacent safari park for several months, prompting officials to open the emergency gates and allow it to enter the zoo. The tiger's movement is being closely monitored with high-resolution cameras, and officials are now discussing whether to release it back into the wild or keep it in the zoo. Orissa's chief wildlife warden, JD Sharma, suggests that putting a radio collar on the tiger would enable them to track its movement and monitor its activity if it is released. However, senior zoo officials and wildlife activists argue that keeping the tiger in the zoo would be beneficial for the conservation and breeding program. The zoo currently has 24 tigers, all of which are descendants of a single male tiger brought to the park in 1965. Keeping the new tiger would introduce new genes and infuse fresh blood into the program, according to wildlife activist Subhendu Mallick. India's tiger population has been declining alarmingly due to poaching, with numbers shrinking from an estimated 100,000 a century ago to just 1,700 in the wild, according to a 2011 census. The decision on the tiger's fate is still pending, with officials weighing the pros and cons of releasing it back into the wild or keeping it in the zoo.

UK Minister Tobias Ellwood has warned that air drops of food and medical supplies to Aleppo could be "hugely complicated" and put British forces "in harm's way". The statement came in response to an urgent question in the Commons, where over 120 MPs have urged the government to authorize aid drops to the besieged city. Labour's Alison McGovern reiterated the demands, reading out a statement from the Syrian Civil Defence, which described Aleppo as being "in a state of emergency" with 279,000 people under siege for 94 days. Ellwood cautioned that aid drops could land in the wrong place or fall into the wrong hands, and emphasized that negotiating safe passage for land vehicles was a more viable option. He also highlighted the enormous scale of aid required, stating that the number of aid drops needed would be staggering. When challenged by shadow foreign secretary Emily Thornberry, Ellwood warned that British aircraft carrying out aid drops could be shot down, putting air personnel at risk. Thornberry argued that despite the complexity and risks involved, air drops were a necessary measure to prevent thousands of deaths. She emphasized that with no alternative solutions, the government must be prepared to take these risks. Ellwood, however, maintained that any such action would require the full support of Parliament. The debate comes as the humanitarian crisis in Aleppo continues to worsen, with the international community facing mounting pressure to take action. The UK government is under increasing scrutiny to explore all possible options to alleviate the suffering of civilians trapped in the city. As the situation remains dire, the government must weigh the risks and complexities of air drops against the urgent need for humanitarian aid.

Scottish club Edinburgh is set to lose one of its key players, Sam Beard, as the 25-year-old has announced that he will be joining Welsh region Dragons at the end of the season. Beard's contract with Edinburgh expires in the summer, and he has opted to make the move to Wales, where he also holds qualification. Beard, who has played 41 times for Edinburgh, including 24 starts, has expressed his gratitude to the Scottish club for the opportunities he has had. "My time at Edinburgh has been really good," he said. "We've been heading in the right direction and it's good to have been a part of it." Despite only making five appearances this season, Beard is hopeful of getting some decent game-time before the end of the season to finish his time at the club on a high. Dragons director of rugby Lyn Jones is thrilled to have secured Beard's services, saying: "Sam has played exceptionally well for Edinburgh and starred against us. He's a talented individual and we look forward to him joining the region." Edinburgh head coach Alan Solomons has also praised Beard, wishing him all the best in his new challenge and describing him as a "first-class bloke and a good team man." Beard's move to Dragons is seen as a significant boost to the Welsh region, and he is expected to make a big impact when he joins the team.

Wales Air Ambulance Unveils New State-of-the-Art Helicopter The Wales Air Ambulance (WAA) has taken a significant step towards providing 24-hour emergency services with the launch of its new H145 aircraft. The custom-built helicopter, based in Llanelli, will serve south Wales and is the first of three new aircraft to be introduced by the charity this year. The new helicopter is equipped with night vision technology, weather radar, and additional lighting, enabling it to operate effectively in the dark. According to WAA chief executive Angela Hughes, the new aircraft brings the charity closer to its goal of providing round-the-clock services. "With continued fundraising, this new aircraft will support our aim to progress to a 24-hour operation, so we can help anyone in their most difficult hour," she said. The H145 replaces the older EC135 model and boasts a top speed of 150mph, extra room for treatments, and a longer flying range without refuelling. The new helicopter also features a high-speed internet connection, allowing crews to transmit vital medical information directly to hospitals while en route. Operations manager Mark Winter praised the new aircraft, saying it is "a significantly more advanced machine" that will enable the team to provide better care to those in need. The WAA hopes to utilize the new helicopter to respond to time-critical missions more efficiently, staying within the crucial "golden hour" that can mean the difference between life and death.

A goalless draw was the outcome as Woking hosted Guiseley, with both teams creating scoring opportunities but failing to capitalize. Guiseley's Jordan Preston had an early chance, but his header sailed over the bar. Jake Cassidy came close to breaking the deadlock just before half-time, hitting the post with a well-struck shot. After the restart, Guiseley continued to dominate, with Michael Rankine's shot saved by Woking's busy goalkeeper, Brandon Hall. Hall's best save came in the 68th minute, when he repelled Cassidy's long-range effort. Despite multiple substitutions and yellow cards issued to Simon Walton, Connor Brown, and Fabio Saraiva, neither team could find the back of the net. The match ended 0-0, with Woking and Guiseley sharing the points. The draw highlights the closely contested nature of the match, with both teams demonstrating strong defensive performances.

Herefordshire Voters Express Diverse Views Ahead of General Election As the general election approaches, voters in Herefordshire are making their voices heard, expressing a wide range of opinions and concerns. The county, which shifted from Liberal Democrat to Conservative control in 2010, is now seeing a rise in independent candidates, with many residents skeptical of national political parties. At a recent market stall, residents shared their thoughts on the upcoming election, with many citing the National Health Service (NHS) as a top priority. The NHS has been a consistent concern among voters in the area, with many expressing worries about its future. Other issues, such as the potential impact of a European Union exit on farmers and the need to encourage tourism in the area, were also raised. Some residents, like Dorian from Hereford, advocated for a reduction in government spending and taxation, suggesting that the focus should be on essential services like the police, military, and court systems. Others, like Sue, emphasized the importance of increasing the number of women in government, believing that they would do a better job running the country. Young people, like Joe from north Herefordshire, are concerned about the lack of opportunities and affordable housing. Joe suggested that building more houses should be a priority, citing the struggles of young people facing high house prices and the prospect of renting until they are 50 or older. The diverse views expressed by Herefordshire voters reflect the county's independent streak, with many residents looking beyond traditional party lines for solutions. As the election approaches, it remains to be seen how these concerns will be addressed by the candidates. Voters will have a choice between the Conservative, Liberal Democrat, Labour, UKIP, and Green parties, but the presence of independent candidates on the local ballot paper may indicate a desire for alternative voices to be heard. For a comprehensive guide to the general election in Herefordshire and Worcestershire, including videos and interviews with candidates, visit our website. The election takes place on May 7, and residents are encouraged to make their voices heard by casting their ballots.

A trial is underway for a man accused of murdering a book dealer in his Oxford home. Michael Danaher, 50, denies stabbing Adrian Greenwood, 42, to death in April. The court has heard testimony from several individuals who knew the victim and the defendant, painting a picture of two men with troubled pasts. Evelyn Altemeyer, Mr. Greenwood's ex-girlfriend, described him as "often in fights" and "could be really aggressive." She stated that he had been blacklisted by a post office after attacking a postman and had a history of heavy drinking. Despite this, she said he was never physically violent towards her. Ms. Altemeyer also revealed that Mr. Greenwood had been taking anti-depressants in 2011 and had held a man hostage during a dispute over a washing machine installation. A friend of Mr. Greenwood's, Martha Stewart, who attended Christ Church College with him, described him as "defensive and aggressive, like a cross little boy." On the other hand, Mr. Danaher's estranged wife, Elaine Danaher, testified that her husband had admitted to having a temper when he was younger. The couple was married for 12 years before splitting in 2012 and have two sons together. The prosecution alleges that Mr. Danaher's motive for the stabbing was to steal a valuable first edition of Wind in the Willows, worth £50,000, which Mr. Greenwood had listed on eBay for £2,000. A spreadsheet found on Mr. Danaher's computer contained a list of "people of means" he intended to steal from or kidnap, including high-profile individuals like Kate Moss and Jeffrey Archer. A witness, Michael Gillnagh, who has known Mr. Danaher since childhood, visited him in prison after his arrest. According to Mr. Gillnagh, Mr. Danaher claimed that Mr. Greenwood had come at him with a knife, and he had acted in self-defense. Mr. Danaher reportedly became tearful during their conversation. The trial is ongoing, with the jury continuing to hear evidence in the case.

A march and rally were held in west London to demonstrate unity and condemn the rise of racist incidents in the area. The event was organized by the local council in response to the discovery of "racist" graffiti scrawled on a Polish Cultural centre in Hammersmith, which occurred in the aftermath of the European referendum. The centre, a beloved local institution for 50 years, was vandalized with hateful messages, prompting widespread outrage and concern. Hammersmith MP Andy Slaughter expressed his support for the protest, stating that it was a necessary response to the "terrible racist attack" on the Polish centre. He noted that the incident reflects a broader concern that the EU referendum and Brexit have emboldened a small minority of people to express offensive and racist opinions. Slaughter emphasized that the protest and rally were a testament to the community's commitment to unity and inclusivity. Residents from the area attended the march, including Michael Roach, who felt it was his "duty" to participate. Roach stressed the importance of coming together as a community, stating that "we need to come together as just one family, one world family." He also highlighted the need for solidarity with other marginalized groups, saying "black lives matter" and expressing his concern for the future of his children and grandchildren. The Metropolitan Police reported a significant increase in racial and religious hate crimes, with 771 incidents reported between June 24 and July 5. While exact statistics for the period before the referendum are not available, reports of hate crimes had risen 13% in the 12 months leading up to May. The community's response to the incident serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of standing together against hate and promoting a culture of inclusivity and respect.

Fresh from her Strictly Come Dancing win, Joanne Clifton is set to take the stage as a lead dancer in the musical'Thoroughly Modern Millie'. Over 13 million viewers watched her lift the glitterball trophy with partner Ore Oduba just before Christmas. Rather than taking a break, Joanne has been busy in rehearsals, preparing for her new role as a New York dancer. This has been a childhood dream for Joanne, who will need to adapt to acting and singing in addition to dancing. She draws parallels between herself and the character Millie, who moves to New York to pursue her dreams, much like Joanne's own move to Italy at 16 to join a dance school. Cast in the musical last summer, Joanne's Strictly commitments delayed her start in rehearsals. She hopes to return to the show later this year to defend her title.

Plans for the North East's first directly elected mayor have been abandoned after four out of seven local councils voted to halt the proposal. The decision was made due to concerns over funding from the government following the UK's decision to leave the European Union. Sunderland, Durham, Gateshead, and South Tyneside councils expressed dissatisfaction with the reassurances provided, prompting them to reject the devolution deal. The Communities Secretary, Sajid Javid, expressed his disappointment at the decision, stating that the region would miss out on over £1 billion in investment as a result. The deal would have brought significant powers and funding to the area, including £30 million annually for 30 years, as well as control over transport, skills, and training. Newcastle, North Tyneside, and Northumberland councils, however, remain committed to the plan. Mr. Javid has announced that the government will now focus on securing a new agreement with these councils to progress with devolution. The North East Combined Authority chairman, Paul Watson, described the government's decision to end discussions as "very disappointing," emphasizing that all council leaders were committed to devolution, but a majority agreement could not be reached. The scrapped plans were part of the government's Northern Powerhouse program, which aims to decentralize power and promote economic growth in the north of England. Elections for directly elected mayors are still scheduled to take place in other areas of England in May 2017. Meanwhile, the Department for Communities and Local Government has confirmed that work is ongoing to secure a devolution deal for the Tees Valley.

Liam Laverick, 25, appeared at Hull Crown Court regarding the death of Tommy Lee Laverick-Whitworth. The charge will be altered to murder at his next appearance in September. Laverick was remanded in custody and is due back in court on September 11. The victim died in hospital on September 25 after an ambulance call to Anlaby Road, Hull, two days prior.

Renowned Bhutanese filmmaker Tshering Wangyel has passed away, leaving the nation's movie industry in shock. The Bhutan Film Association announced his death, stating that he was hospitalized last month with pneumonia while shooting his latest movie. With a career spanning over two decades, Wangyel made 40 films that uniquely blended Bollywood with Buddhist themes. He played a pivotal role in developing Bhutan's film industry, providing opportunities for countless actors and actresses. According to Yeshi Dorji, executive director of the Bhutan Film Association, Wangyel's contributions were immense, creating jobs and launching careers. His first film, "Rawa," was released in 1999, and he went on to transport screens and projectors to villages, bringing cinema to the people. Wangyel's legacy will be deeply felt in the Bhutanese film community. His death is a huge loss, and he will be remembered for his dedication to Bhutanese cinema.

New Study Reveals Nine Key Risk Factors for Dementia, Emphasizes Importance of Lifestyle Changes A groundbreaking study presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference in London has identified nine key risk factors for dementia, including lack of education, hearing loss, smoking, and physical inactivity. The research, which combines the work of 24 international experts, suggests that lifestyle factors can play a significant role in increasing or reducing an individual's dementia risk, with modifiable risk factors accounting for 35% of the total risk. The study, led by Professor Gill Livingston from University College London, emphasizes the importance of acting now to reduce the risk of dementia, which is projected to affect 131 million people globally by 2050. Currently, there are an estimated 47 million people living with the condition. "Although dementia is diagnosed in later life, the brain changes usually begin to develop years before," said Prof Livingston. "Acting now will vastly improve life for people with dementia and their families and, in doing so, will transform the future of society." The report highlights the benefits of building a "cognitive reserve," which involves strengthening the brain's networks to enable it to function effectively in later life despite damage. Failure to complete secondary education is identified as a major risk factor, while continuing to learn throughout life can help build additional brain reserves. Hearing loss in middle age is also a significant risk factor, as it can lead to social isolation and depression, which are among other modifiable risk factors for dementia. The study also emphasizes the importance of maintaining a healthy lifestyle, with factors such as not smoking, exercising regularly, and keeping a healthy weight all contributing to a reduced risk of dementia. Treating high blood pressure and diabetes is also crucial, as these conditions can increase the risk of dementia, as well as cardiovascular disease and cancer. While the researchers did not have enough data to include dietary factors or alcohol in their calculations, they believe that these could also be important factors in reducing the risk of dementia. Dr Doug Brown, director of research at Alzheimer's Society, said: "Though it's not inevitable, dementia is currently set to be the 21st Century's biggest killer. We all need to be aware of the risks and start making positive lifestyle changes." Dr David Reynolds, chief scientific officer at Alzheimer's Research UK, added: "Alongside prevention research, we must continue to invest in research to find a life-changing treatment for people with this devastating condition." By making informed lifestyle choices and taking steps to reduce our risk of dementia, we can help create a healthier and more supportive society for all.

A new record high temperature for November has been set in the UK, with the mercury reaching 22.4C (72.3F) in Trawsgoed, Ceredigion, on Sunday afternoon. This surpasses the previous record of 21.7C (71.1F) set in Prestatyn, Wales, in 1946. According to BBC Weather's Helen Willetts, the record-breaking temperature is due to mild southerly winds and humid air. However, fog in many areas brought temperatures down, with some flights cancelled at Heathrow. Despite the fog, areas without it experienced temperatures in the high teens. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for fog, effective from Sunday evening to Monday midday, covering much of England and parts of eastern Wales. The warning advises of potential travel disruptions due to poor visibility. More warm air is forecast for Monday, but showers are expected on Wednesday and Thursday. Willetts noted that the record could potentially be broken again on Monday, highlighting the unusual warmth for this time of year. The average UK temperature for November is typically around 10-15C (50-59F), making this warm spell a notable exception.

Body Image Concerns Plaguing UK Teenagers, Says New Report A shocking new report has revealed that almost a third of UK teenagers are avoiding activities such as physical education due to fears about their appearance. The Be Real Campaign, which conducted a survey of 2,000 UK teenagers, found that 52% of 11 to 16-year-olds regularly worry about their looks, with 60% of girls and 43% of boys affected. One teenager, Josh from Renfrew near Glasgow, has spoken out about his own struggles with body image. The teenager, who has already had to leave one school due to bullying related to his weight, says he feels pressure to conform to a certain physical ideal. "I genuinely don't know one big male model," he said, highlighting the lack of diversity in the fashion industry. Josh also admitted to photoshopping all of his online profile pictures, spending up to 25 minutes editing out imperfections such as spots and double chins. The report warns that fears about appearance are having a "profoundly negative effect" on young people, with many suffering in silence due to fear of sharing their insecurities. The Be Real Campaign is calling on schools to play a key role in combating body anxiety, and has launched a toolkit to help teachers promote positive body image in the classroom. Denise Hatton, YMCA chief executive for England and Wales, said: "Evidence shows that schools are uniquely placed to support young people to hold positive discussions around body image with their peers and help reduce the negative impact low body confidence can have." Julie Hunter, assistant head teacher at Bradon Forest School in Wiltshire, welcomed the toolkit, saying it would help teachers to use "accurate language" when discussing body image and make students more aware of the issue. The report's findings are a stark reminder of the need for greater support and education around body image in UK schools. By working together, teachers, parents, and young people can help to promote positive body confidence and reduce the negative impact of low self-esteem. As Josh's story highlights, the pressure to conform to unrealistic beauty standards can have serious consequences for young people's mental health and wellbeing. It is time for schools and society as a whole to take action and promote a more inclusive and accepting definition of beauty.

BNP Launches Campaign, Vows to Outdo UKIP on Immigration and EU Withdrawal The British National Party (BNP) has officially launched its campaign for the upcoming European and local elections, with leader Nick Griffin asserting that his party's policies on immigration and EU withdrawal are more robust than those of its rival, UKIP. Speaking to the BBC, Griffin claimed that the BNP has been instrumental in bringing the debates on cutting immigration and leaving the EU to the forefront of public discourse. Despite the party's declining opinion poll ratings and internal feuding, which has led to the loss of members, including one of its MEPs, Andrew Brons, Griffin remains confident that the BNP's stance on immigration and EU withdrawal will resonate with voters. The party won almost a million votes in the 2009 European elections, securing two seats in the European Parliament, including Griffin's own seat in North West England. Griffin took aim at UKIP, accusing the party of being soft on immigration. While UKIP advocates for tighter border controls, the BNP is calling for a total halt to immigration, citing Britain's already strained resources. "We are the only party that, when we say'Stop immigration,' we actually mean it," Griffin said. "UKIP is saying 50,000 net, but that would actually mean 300,000 Africans and Asians coming in every year under their plans. Our position is very simple: Britain's full, and we should shut the doors." The BNP leader also reiterated his party's commitment to British withdrawal from the EU, dismissing the idea of a referendum as a potential "rigged" process. Instead, Griffin argues that Britain should withdraw from the EU immediately, without hesitation or further debate. This stance is in contrast to UKIP, which has called for a referendum on EU membership. Griffin's comments come as the BNP faces increased competition from UKIP, which has gained significant traction in recent years. However, Griffin remains undeterred, citing his party's unique approach to politics and his own reputation as a known quantity among voters. "A lot of people are going to be fooled into voting for UKIP, but we really don't need that many voters to get me back in the North West," he said. "A lot of people want to have an MEP where they actually know who he is. The others are all faceless. I'm a character." The European and local elections are scheduled to take place on May 22, with the BNP fielding a full slate of 70 candidates. Despite the party's current low opinion poll ratings, Griffin is confident that his party can make a significant impact, particularly in the North West region, where he has a strong base of support. As the campaign heats up, it remains to be seen whether the BNP's uncompromising stance on immigration and EU withdrawal will resonate with voters, or if the party will continue to struggle in the face of increased competition from UKIP.

Motorists who slowed down to gawk at a three-lorry collision in Thurrock on Thursday are being issued court summonses by Essex Police. The incident, which occurred at 04:40 BST, resulted in one lorry driver being trapped in his cabin, although his injuries were not serious. However, the real concern for authorities was the behavior of other drivers on the scene. As police and emergency services worked to free the trapped driver and clear the damaged vehicles, many motorists on the opposite carriageway were caught "rubber-necking," or slowing down to look at the crash scene. Some were even using their mobile phones to film the incident, putting themselves and others at risk of further accidents. Charges will include careless driving and using a mobile phone while driving. The anti-clockwise carriageway was closed until 14:00, resulting in tailbacks of up to 12 miles. Adam Pipe, casualty reduction manager for Essex Police, expressed his disappointment at the behavior of these drivers, stating that it showed a lack of respect for the casualties and emergency services. He also warned that sharing crash footage on social media can lead to families of victims finding out about the incident before being officially notified by police.

Belfast Airport Targets New European Routes with Government Aid Belfast Airport is in talks with the government to explore potential aid for establishing new routes to major European cities. Brian Ambrose, the airport's representative, has identified Frankfurt, Munich, and Brussels as key targets for expansion. Although a timeline for these new services is uncertain, Ambrose expressed optimism about the prospects. The news comes as Vueling announces its entry into the Northern Irish market with flights from George Best Belfast City airport to Barcelona. Meanwhile, Belfast International has unveiled ten new routes, including a service to Iceland. A report on air connectivity is forthcoming from Stormont, which may pave the way for a new air development fund. This initiative would be similar to a previous £4m fund that successfully attracted routes such as New York in 2003. Ambrose confirmed that the government is open to supporting route development, provided a state-aid compliant solution can be found.

In a groundbreaking move, Scotland and Iceland have signed a historic agreement that brings together all snowsports areas in both countries. The deal, announced at the North Atlantic Ski Areas' Association conference, is believed to be a world first. Five Scottish ski centres, including CairnGorm Mountain, Glencoe Mountain, Glenshee, Nevis Range, and The Lecht, have joined forces with all nine of Iceland's snowsports centres. This innovative partnership aims to share information, advice, and best practices on quality development, sustainability, and other key areas. The agreement is an extension of the memorandum of understanding signed earlier this month between VisitScotland and the Icelandic Tourist Board. According to Heather Negus, chairwoman of Ski-Scotland, this deal is unique in that it includes every lift at every resort in both countries, making it a comprehensive and exciting collaboration. With daily flights connecting Glasgow, Aberdeen, and Edinburgh to Reykjavik, skiers and snowboarders from both countries can now explore new terrain and experience the culture of a new country. Malcolm Roughead, chief executive of VisitScotland, highlighted the strong relationship between the two countries, saying that both Scotland and Iceland "punch well above their weight on the global tourism stage." This partnership is expected to boost tourism and promote the sharing of expertise, ultimately enhancing the snowsports experience for visitors to both countries. The collaboration is a significant step forward for the snowsports industry and is set to bring numerous benefits to both Scotland and Iceland.

A 33-year-old man who reversed his car at speed and struck his mother, causing her serious injury, has had his prison sentence reduced on appeal. Abdul Abbasi, of Thorndale, Hull, was initially jailed for two years and four months for causing serious injury by dangerous driving. However, at a Court of Appeal hearing, his sentence was reduced to 16 months. The incident occurred in October on Redmire Close, Hull, where Abbasi reversed into his 65-year-old mother, Rehana Abassi, after a disagreement. He then crashed into a parked car and drove off with his mother still under the vehicle. Mrs Abassi suffered serious injuries, including broken ribs, and spent two weeks in hospital. Despite the severity of the incident, the court heard that Mrs Abassi has forgiven her son. The jury at Abbasi's trial had cleared him of attempted murder and causing grievous bodily harm, as they were "not satisfied" that he knew his mother was behind the car when he reversed into her. The Court of Appeal judges, Sir Andrew Smith and Geoffrey Marson QC, took into account Abbasi's previously good character and mental wellbeing when reducing his sentence. Abbasi, a taxi driver with no previous convictions, was described as "mentally fragile" and a "decent man who lost control under pressure". His six-year driving ban was also cut to two years.

Austrian police have seized medical equipment, products, and mobile phones from the Kazakhstan biathlon team's accommodation. The raid was conducted in collaboration with Austria's anti-doping authority, which also collected blood and urine samples. The International Biathlon Union (IBU) has stated that Kazakhstan can still participate in Thursday's mixed relay event in Hochfilzen. According to Manas Ussenov of the Kazak biathlon federation, the seized medical equipment was found in the team doctor's room, but they have all necessary documentation for the medicines. The raid was prompted by the discovery of a cardboard box containing used medical equipment and notes suggesting doping activity at a nearby petrol station last month. Meanwhile, French biathlete Martin Fourcade protested against Russian athletes by walking off the podium during the medal ceremony. Fourcade, a two-time Olympic champion, has been vocal about the need for the IBU to take a stronger stance against doping. The incident occurred during the mixed relay event, which was the first competition since Russian athlete Alexander Loginov's return from a doping ban. The Russian team refused to shake hands with Fourcade, who eventually rejoined his team on stage.

A major fire at Bakers Quay in Gloucester has been brought under control by the Gloucestershire Fire and Rescue Service. The blaze was reported at 18:47 BST, and two 19-year-old men have been arrested on suspicion of arson. The historic 19th Century building is now structurally unsafe, with a section having collapsed. Fortunately, nearby rugby fans watching the England v Australia match were not at risk and did not need to be evacuated. The fire service will remain on site, and engineers will assess the building's safety. The cause of the fire is being investigated, with the two suspects currently in police custody.

A Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) worker had a harrowing experience when he was confronted by a swarm of angry honey bees while checking a meter box at a house in Belleeks. The bees had built a nest around the meter, and the worker was stung up to 10 times on his face and neck before he managed to escape to safety. Fortunately, the worker did not have a bee sting allergy, which could have made the incident much more serious. According to NIE's meter reading manager, Cormac McCamphill, the company's priority was the safety of their staff member, but they also wanted to avoid destroying the bees. Instead, they called in an expert from the Ulster Beekeepers' Association, Darren Nugent, to safely relocate the bees. Nugent used a homemade suction device to remove the bees from the meter box and transferred them to a hive at his home in Kilkeel, County Down. The operation was a success, and the bees have settled into their new home. Nugent even managed to harvest half a dozen jars of honey from the nest, which he shared with the farmer who owned the house. The incident was a first for NIE staff, who sometimes encounter animal hazards like livestock and dogs, but never bees in a meter box. The bees are believed to have been in the box for around eight weeks and were thriving in their unusual location. As Nugent noted, "They were doing well in there. In fact, they were doing better than some of the bees in the hives outside my house." The successful relocation of the bees is a testament to the importance of preserving these vital pollinators and finding humane solutions to unexpected problems.
