Broughty Ferry lifeboat station responded to the same number of calls in 2016 as 2015, launching 92 times. The crew rescued 29 people, a 45% increase from 2015, making it the UK's 11th busiest station.

A former council leader has referred himself to the standards committee for investigation, following reports that council officers failed to act quickly enough on claims made against a councillor before the 2015 elections. The councillor in question, Simon Carter, later admitted to 16 charges of making indecent images of children. The move comes after an independent review found that former chief executive Mike Owen and head of children's services Mark Carriline had "inexplicably" and "deliberately" delayed implementing safeguarding procedures when allegations about Carter first came to light in 2015. The review suggested that the pair had done so to help the council's ruling Labour group before the 2015 election and protect the then-leader, Mr. Connolly, from public scrutiny. Mr. Connolly, who quit as leader last year, has apologized for giving Carter a written reference on council-headed notepaper ahead of his sentencing, describing him as "trustworthy, honest and reliable". He has stated that he wants to be "open and transparent" and has cooperated fully with the independent review. He will also cooperate fully with the standards committee investigation. The disciplinary reports have been published, and the council has agreed to carry out a further investigation into councillors' conduct. Current council leader Rishi Shori has said that Mr. Connolly has apologized for writing the reference and accepts that it was a "terrible error of judgement". Any necessary action will be taken once the investigation is complete. The leader of the Conservative group, James Daly, has expressed his sadness and disappointment at the events, stating that the political fortunes of a party should never trump the responsibility to look after vulnerable children. Mr. Shori has also emphasized that no child was put at risk in relation to these proceedings and that he acted decisively when he received information from a member of the public. The council's decision to publish the reports and carry out a further investigation is a step towards transparency and accountability. The investigation will aim to determine the extent of the failures and whether any further action is needed to prevent similar incidents in the future. The people of Bury deserve to know that their council is committed to protecting the most vulnerable members of their community.

Dilwyn Williams of Caerphilly died in a collision on the A4058 Trehafod bypass. His family remembered him as a "loveable local character." Two women driving other cars were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries. Williams' family said he "never missed an opportunity," leaving a lasting impact on those who knew him.

Kim Jong-nam, the Half-Brother of North Korea's Leader, Killed in Malaysia Airport In a shocking turn of events, Kim Jong-nam, the half-brother of North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un, was killed at Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia on Monday. The 45-year-old was waiting to board a flight to Macau when he was allegedly poisoned by two women, who were later arrested along with a man. The incident has sparked widespread speculation and concern, with many questions still unanswered. According to Indonesian national police chief Tito Karnavian, one of the women, Siti Aisyah, claimed to have been paid to perform what she thought was a prank. She allegedly told authorities that she and another woman had previously performed the prank on other men, convincing them to close their eyes before spraying them with water. However, on this occasion, the sprayer allegedly contained a poisonous substance that was sprayed into Kim Jong-nam's face. Karnavian said that Aisyah had been given a few dollars for each prank and was unaware that the latest incident was an assassination attempt by alleged foreign agents. A grainy image broadcast in South Korea and Malaysia showed a woman, believed to be Aisyah, running in the airport wearing a white T-shirt with the letters "LOL" written on the front. Aisyah's family and former neighbors in Indonesia have expressed shock and surprise at her arrest. Her former father-in-law, Tjia Liang Kiong, told the Associated Press that she had moved to Malaysia in 2011 with her then-husband to find work after their garment-making business went bust. Hundreds of thousands of Indonesian migrants work in Malaysia, where incomes are much higher. Meanwhile, North Korea has demanded that Malaysia immediately release the body of Kim Jong-nam. The North Korean ambassador to Malaysia, Kang Chol, said that his country had not consented to the post-mortem already carried out and would categorically reject its findings. He urged Malaysia not to be "entangled with the political plot" by forces hostile to North Korea and to release the body without condition. However, Malaysia has refused to release the body until it receives a DNA sample from Kim Jong-nam's next-of-kin. The Malaysian authorities are still investigating the incident and have arrested several individuals in connection with the murder. South Korea's intelligence agency has accused North Korea of assassinating Kim Jong-nam, saying that Pyongyang had wanted to kill him for years but that he was being protected by China. Kim Jong-nam was largely estranged from his family after being passed over for the North Korean leadership in favor of his younger half-brother. He spent most of his time overseas in Macau, mainland China, and Singapore, and had spoken out in the past against his family's dynastic control of North Korea. The incident has sparked widespread concern and speculation, with many questions still unanswered. The investigation is ongoing, and it remains to be seen what further developments will emerge in the coming days. One thing is certain, however: the death of Kim Jong-nam has sent shockwaves around the world and has raised concerns about the safety and security of individuals who are seen as threats to the North Korean regime.

A charity football match is set to take place on Thursday, with the current Glenavon squad facing off against a Derry team comprised mainly of former teammates of Mark Farren, a former Derry City player. The match aims to raise funds for Farren, who is battling a brain tumour. Farren, 33, recently underwent his third operation to remove the tumour, with surgeons successfully removing over 80% of it. However, the tumour has been found to be highly aggressive, and Farren's speech and mobility have been affected. The football community has rallied around Farren, with his former teammate James McClean pledging £1,000 to the fund. Farren's family has appealed for financial help to raise around £25,000, which will enable him to undergo treatment at a specialist cancer centre in Germany. Glenavon manager Gary Hamilton has urged fans to support the match, saying, "I'm sure all the good people around the club will come out and support Mark in this very serious situation in his life." Farren, a Greencastle native, had a successful career with Derry City, becoming the club's record goal-scorer in 2012. He was initially diagnosed with a benign brain tumour in 2008 but continued to play until 2009. After undergoing surgery, he returned to the pitch in 2011 and broke the club's scoring record a year later. Farren joined Glenavon in 2013 and was named the Irish League's player of the month in April of that year. The charity match on Thursday is expected to feature former Derry City players such as Barry Molloy, Ciaran Martyn, and Ruaidhri Higgins, all of whom will be playing in support of their former teammate.

A lesbian student in China has spoken out against the Guangdong University of Foreign Studies after she was initially refused her diploma following a public proposal from her girlfriend at their graduation ceremony. Xiaoyu Wang, a 23-year-old translation student, said that the university told the couple that their act had "violated regulations" and that they should "keep our homosexuality to ourselves." The proposal, which took place on campus, was a romantic gesture that aimed to express the couple's feelings and raise awareness about LGBT issues. However, it was met with backlash from university officials, who reportedly told the couple that they would "face punishment" after pictures of them kissing went viral on social media. One official even accused Ms. Wang of spreading vulgar content and misbehaving in public, despite previous warnings from the university. Ms. Wang said that the university's actions caused her significant emotional harm, and that the experience turned what was supposed to be a joyful day into a "nightmare." She took to social media to express her feelings, writing, "I'm devastated and humiliated, but I'm fighting back and need your help." The university has since given Ms. Wang her diploma, but the incident has sparked widespread outrage and calls for greater support and protection for LGBT students on campus. The incident has also drawn attention to the broader issue of discrimination against LGBT individuals in China. A 2012 poll by the Aibai Centre, an LGBT organization, found that 77% of gay students reported being subjected to bullying on campus because of their sexual orientation or gender identity. Ms. Wang's case is not an isolated one, and she hopes that by speaking out, she can help spark change and bring an end to discrimination against LGBT individuals. The LGBT group All Out has called on the university to apologize publicly to the two students and to take comprehensive measures to prevent discrimination and homophobic harassment on campus. Supporters have delivered a statement to the university headmaster, who said he would look into the matter. Ms. Wang's girlfriend, Jean Ouyang, who proposed to her at the graduation ceremony, told Chinese media that the "mental and emotional harm" caused by the university's actions could not be erased. Ms. Wang's experience has also had a personal cost, as university officials reportedly outed her to her parents by asking them to come and collect her diploma together. An official even sent a video of the marriage proposal to Ms. Wang's mother, causing tension and stress for the family. Ms. Wang said that her biggest headache now is mending her relationship with her parents, who were hurt by the incident. As Ms. Wang fights for justice and equality, she remains determined to speak out against discrimination and to advocate for the rights of LGBT individuals. "I'm sick of staying silent," she wrote. "No school should intimidate students for who they are or who they love. My case is just one in many, but it could spark a change." Her courage and resilience have inspired many, and her story serves as a reminder of the importance of promoting inclusivity, acceptance, and support for all individuals, regardless of their sexual orientation or gender identity.

Brazilian Judge Orders Immediate Reinstatement of WhatsApp Service In a dramatic turn of events, a Brazilian judge has ordered the immediate reinstatement of the WhatsApp messaging service, which was suspended for 48 hours on Thursday. The suspension, which was imposed due to the company's failure to comply with a court order, had sparked widespread outrage and frustration among the app's millions of users in Brazil. Judge Xavier de Souza ruled that the suspension was unreasonable and that it was not fair to punish millions of users for the company's inertia. The court had ordered WhatsApp to provide investigators with information related to a criminal court case, but the company failed to comply, leading to the suspension. The suspension of WhatsApp had a significant impact on Brazilians, who rely heavily on the app to communicate with family, friends, and colleagues both inside and outside the country. According to the TechCrunch website, a staggering 93% of Brazil's internet population uses WhatsApp, making it an essential tool for communication. Many Brazilians took to social media to express their frustration and disappointment, with the hashtag #Nessas48HorasEuVou (#Inthese48hoursIwill) trending on Twitter. The hashtag was used to joke about all the things people would do during the suspension, from reading books to taking long walks. The suspension also had significant implications for expats living in Brazil, who rely on WhatsApp to keep in touch with loved ones back home. With mobile providers charging high rates for monthly plans and international calls, WhatsApp's free text message and internet telephone service is a lifeline for many. Facebook, which owns WhatsApp, also weighed in on the issue, with CEO Mark Zuckerberg expressing his shock and disappointment at the suspension. "I am stunned that our efforts to protect people's data would result in such an extreme decision by a single judge to punish every person in Brazil who uses WhatsApp," he wrote in a post on Facebook. The suspension was ordered after WhatsApp failed to comply with a court order related to a criminal case. According to Brazilian media, the company was asked to provide details of communication by a suspected gang member who allegedly used WhatsApp to organize illegal activity. The incident has also highlighted the ongoing tensions between WhatsApp and Brazilian phone companies, which have urged the government to restrict the use of free voice-over-internet services offered through the app. The phone companies argue that the rise of WhatsApp has damaged their businesses, and have been seeking to limit its use. Meanwhile, other messaging services have reported a surge in new users since the suspension was imposed. Telegram, a rival messaging app, reported that over 1.5 million Brazilian users had joined its platform since the court order was handed down. With the reinstatement of WhatsApp, Brazilians can once again communicate freely with each other and with the rest of the world. The incident has highlighted the importance of WhatsApp in Brazilian life and the need for the company to comply with court orders to avoid similar disruptions in the future.
A body was found near a Haddington plant in East Lothian on Monday at 06:00. Police are treating the death as unexplained, with forensic officers investigating the scene.

Australian Police Rescue Stranded Sailors in Treacherous Seas In a daring rescue operation, Australian police saved two stranded sailors, Irishman Nick Dwyer, 55, and Frenchwoman Barbara Heftman, 44, who were battling turbulent seas 210 nautical miles off Sydney. The couple, on a 10-year circumnavigation of the globe, had activated an emergency beacon on Tuesday after their rudder broke three days earlier. The sailors described the conditions as "enormous seas, waves the size of buildings" and gale-force winds that made it impossible to stand up. Their 40ft yacht "rolled" on Tuesday, prompting them to issue a distress call. "We weren't sure whether we were going to be rolled again, and each time a wave hit, we thought,'is this the one that's going to take us?'" Mr. Dwyer said. The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) responded to the distress call by sending a jet to the remote location, followed by a request for police assistance. The New South Wales Police rescue boat took over 13 hours to reach the pair amid "treacherous conditions." Mr. Dwyer expressed his gratitude, saying, "It was truly amazing, to think that somebody had to come that far to save us..... I owe them my life. We owe them our lives." The couple will remain in Sydney while deciding their next move. Despite losing their yacht, they are relieved to be alive. "Our home's gone, we're alive, I expect to live a little bit longer, and that'll be okay," Mr. Dwyer said. The rescue operation is a testament to the bravery and dedication of the Australian police and maritime authorities, who risked their lives to save the stranded sailors in the treacherous seas.

SNP Calls for Abolition of House of Lords Amid Reform Resistance The Scottish National Party (SNP) has renewed its calls for the abolition of the House of Lords, citing the chamber's lack of democratic legitimacy and recent scandals. The comments come after Lord Sewel resigned from the House of Lords following allegations of taking drugs with prostitutes. Pete Wishart, MP for Perth and North Perthshire, argued that the unelected chamber has no place in modern society, and that its reputation has been further tarnished by the recent scandal. Wishart criticized the House of Lords as a "repository for the cronies and donors of the UK parties," and expressed concern over the increasing costs of maintaining the parliament. He also highlighted the hypocrisy of the government considering reducing the number of elected members while planning to appoint more Conservative peers to the Lords. The SNP has long refused to take seats in the House of Lords on principle, and Wishart reiterated the party's commitment to democratic reform. Despite growing calls for wider reforms, Prime Minister David Cameron is resisting pressure from other parties to address the issue. A recent report suggested that Cameron intends to press ahead with plans to appoint more Conservative peers, which would further entrench the party's dominance in the chamber. The current composition of the House of Lords stands at 226 Tory peers, 212 Labour, 101 Liberal Democrats, and 179 crossbenchers. In response to the criticism, Lord Hill defended the House of Lords, arguing that the actions of a few individuals should not tarnish the reputation of the entire chamber. He claimed that the House of Lords remains an effective revising chamber, despite its flaws. However, Wishart remained unconvinced, stating that the current House of Lords is "beyond reform" and must be abolished and reconstituted on democratic principles. The debate is set to continue, with the SNP and other parties pushing for meaningful reform and the government resisting calls for change.

Gillingham Avoid Points Deduction Despite Fielding Ineligible Player Gillingham Football Club has escaped a points deduction after midfielder Emmanuel Osadebe played in their 4-0 win over Sheffield United on August 8 without proper clearance. The 19-year-old, who joined the club from Tottenham's youth development program last August, was found to have been registered with the Football League but not the Football Association due to an error in his documentation. Osadebe's previous registration was with Irish side Dundalk, and he required international clearance to play for Gillingham. However, the Football Association failed to process his registration ahead of the 2015-16 season. A football disciplinary commission has fined the club, but the penalty will only be enforced if Gillingham fields another ineligible player within the next 12 months. The Football League acknowledged that Gillingham had admitted to the mistake, but also noted that the FA should have identified the issue earlier. As a result, the commission ruled that a points deduction would be unfair, given the exceptional circumstances of the case. Gillingham currently sits third in the League One table, just one point off the automatic promotion places. The decision is a welcome relief for the club, which can now focus on maintaining its strong start to the season.

Tranmere Rovers striker Andy Mangan has made a surprise return to Shrewsbury Town, just six months after leaving the club. The 29-year-old joined Rovers on a one-year deal in July, but has struggled to regain his starting place after an injury. Mangan expressed his desire to play regular 90-minute matches, which Tranmere manager Gary Brabin could not guarantee. Shrewsbury, currently 20th in League One, offered Mangan an 18-month contract, and he has opted to rejoin his former club. Mangan denied any rumors of a fallout with Brabin, stating that they had a lengthy discussion and the manager agreed not to stand in his way. Shrewsbury boss Micky Mellon is undergoing a mid-season overhaul, having already seen two strikers leave the club. James Collins has joined Northampton Town on loan, while Tyrone Barnett has moved to Southend United. Mellon emphasized the need for his team to score more goals, particularly from the front line. In addition to Mangan's signing, Shrewsbury has also re-signed defender Jack Grimmer from Fulham and is in advanced talks with another League One side to bring in a striker. The deal is expected to be completed within the next 24 hours. With these new additions, Shrewsbury hopes to improve their position in the league and avoid relegation. Mangan's return is seen as a significant boost to the team, and fans will be eager to see him back in action.

Essex County Cricket Club has announced the signing of Pakistani left-arm bowler Mohammad Amir. The 24-year-old will join the team following his international commitments and will be available for all formats of the game. Amir's signing is a significant coup for Essex, who won the Division Two title this summer and will play in Division One of the County Championship in 2017. Amir has played 20 Tests for Pakistan, including four against England this summer. His career was put on hold in 2010 when he was banned from cricket for five years after being convicted of spot-fixing in a Lord's Test. He served three months in prison and was cleared to play domestic cricket in Pakistan in January last year. Essex head coach Chris Silverwood expressed his delight at the signing, stating that Amir showed a "real desire" to join the club. Silverwood praised Amir's talent, noting that he has already proven himself at international level despite being only 24 years old. Amir's addition to the team is expected to strengthen Essex's chances in the upcoming season.

Golf Action Resumes After Thunderstorm Delay The Golf Club of Houston in Humble, Texas, played host to a busy Saturday morning as 27 players, including Ryder Cup player Jamie Donaldson, returned to complete their second rounds. Friday's play was delayed by 90 minutes due to thunderstorms, and bad light eventually curtailed the action. Donaldson, 40, had three holes to finish and returned a 68, but dropped a shot in the process. Charley Hoffman currently leads the pack at 10 under, closely followed by Jamie Lovemark at 9 under. Donaldson's impressive seven birdies in 15 holes on Friday propelled him up the leaderboard by 29 places. However, a dropped shot on Saturday saw him slip back slightly. Scotland's Martin Laird also dropped a shot to finish at 5 under, while world number two Jordan Spieth trails behind at 6 shots back. The cut was made at level par, resulting in the elimination of players such as Englishman Greg Owen and three-time major winner Padraig Harrington.

A pedestrian was fatally struck in Hilton, Derbyshire, on Tuesday at approximately 16:50 BST. The incident occurred on Main Street after a police pursuit was initiated. A Vauxhall Astra, signaled to stop by a marked Derbyshire Police vehicle near the A38, failed to comply, prompting a chase. Although the pursuit was eventually abandoned, the Astra later collided with two vehicles and a pedestrian. Matthew Luke Hogg, 24, has been remanded in custody and is set to appear at Derby Crown Court next month. The Independent Police Complaints Commission is investigating the "tragic incident" to determine if police policies and procedures were followed. The incident has raised questions about the events leading up to the crash, and the IPCC's findings will be crucial in providing answers. The community is awaiting the outcome of the investigation.

A widow's tragic death from asbestos-related cancer has sparked a legal investigation into the safety protocols of a former Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ) site. Jayne Eustace, 48, passed away in March after a battle with pericardial mesothelioma, an aggressive form of cancer caused by exposure to asbestos dust. Her husband, Andy, has instructed lawyers to pursue whether GCHQ provided adequate protection against asbestos dust during her time at the ex-Oakley base in Cheltenham. Mrs. Eustace worked at the Oakley site from 1983 to 1990, where demolition work was carried out, releasing asbestos fibers into the air. According to her recollection, a wrecking ball was used to demolish buildings near her workspace, and her car was often dusty from the demolition work. Despite this, she and her colleagues were not provided with protective clothing or equipment. A post-mortem examination revealed alarming levels of asbestos fibers in Mrs. Eustace's lungs, with 4,200 fibers per gram of dried tissue. Her husband is concerned that other workers may have been similarly affected. A GCHQ spokesman stated that they cannot comment on individual staff members but will "deal appropriately with any legal correspondence received." The case highlights the importance of proper safety measures in workplaces where asbestos is present, and an investigation is ongoing to determine whether GCHQ failed to provide adequate protection for its employees.

A Newport man faces charges including vehicle theft and drunk driving after a fatal crash on Usk Way. Xana Doyle, 19, died when a Toyota Avensis overturned. A 15-year-old girl was injured. The man will appear in court Monday. A 21-year-old arrested in connection with the incident was released without further action, according to Gwent Police.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is facing a formal investigation by the federal ethics commissioner over his recent winter vacation to the Bahamas. The trip, which took place over the New Year's holiday, has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest due to Trudeau's acceptance of hospitality from the Aga Khan, a wealthy businessman and spiritual leader. Trudeau, his family, and several Liberal Party officials, including MP Seamus O'Reagan and Party President Anna Gainey, were guests at the Aga Khan's private island home. The Aga Khan Foundation has received significant funding from the Canadian government over the years, totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. This has led to concerns that Trudeau's trip may have violated Canadian conflict of interest laws, which prohibit ministers from accepting gifts, including free travel. The ethics commissioner, Mary Dawson, launched a preliminary inquiry into the matter last week and has since announced that she will conduct a formal investigation. Trudeau has stated that he is "more than happy" to answer any questions and is working with the commissioner's office to set up a meeting. He has characterized the trip as a "personal family vacation" and noted that the Aga Khan is a close family friend. The Aga Khan, also known as Prince Karim Aga Khan, is a prominent figure in the Ismaili Muslim community and has a long history of philanthropic work. He is also one of the wealthiest royals in the world, with an estimated net worth of $1 billion. Trudeau's father, Pierre, had a close relationship with the Aga Khan, who served as an honorary pallbearer at his funeral. If the ethics commissioner finds that Trudeau breached conflict of interest rules, he could face a fine of up to $500 per penalty. While no Canadian prime minister has been found in breach of a federal statute to date, the fallout from this investigation could potentially damage Trudeau's reputation and popularity. Analysts suggest that the scandal could hurt Trudeau's image as an accessible and transparent leader, which has been a key factor in his popularity with the voting public. As the investigation continues, Trudeau will likely face ongoing questions and scrutiny over his decision to accept the Aga Khan's hospitality.

HSBC Reports 5% Rise in Pre-Tax Profit, Announces $2bn Share Buyback Europe's largest bank, HSBC, has reported a 5% increase in pre-tax profit to $10.2 billion (£7.8 billion) for the first six months of 2017, exceeding expectations by approximately $500 million. The bank has also announced plans to buy back up to $2 billion worth of shares, which it expects to complete by the end of the year. This news sent HSBC shares soaring by 3% initially, although they later fell back. However, the bank's share price has rallied over the past year, largely due to the weak pound, which has made profits earned abroad more valuable when repatriated to the UK. The share buyback is part of HSBC's ongoing efforts to return value to shareholders. Since the 2008 financial crisis, the bank has been streamlining its operations, cutting jobs, and selling assets to boost profitability while maintaining dividend payments to shareholders. According to HSBC's chief executive, Stuart Gulliver, the bank has paid out more in dividends than any other European or American bank over the past 12 months and has returned $3.5 billion to shareholders through share buybacks. The latest announcement brings the total value of HSBC's share buybacks since the second half of 2016 to $5.5 billion. While HSBC's headline numbers were encouraging, the bank's results also highlighted the ongoing challenges it faces in the aftermath of the financial crisis. The bank is still grappling with pending litigation from investors, ongoing investigations by US and UK authorities, and the significant costs associated with meeting new financial regulations. In the UK, one of the major regulatory requirements is the "ring-fence," which aims to separate retail and investment banking operations by 2019. HSBC has already spent nearly £400 million on this project, which involves setting up a new Birmingham headquarters for its retail arm. The ring-fencing process has been a complex and costly exercise, employing up to 2,000 people at its peak, according to HSBC chairman Douglas Flint. The bank has spent around $500 million on splitting its retail and investment banking arms, describing it as "one of the largest projects ever undertaken by the group." The new Birmingham headquarters for HSBC's UK retail business is expected to begin operating in July 2018. Experts believe that the ring-fencing requirement is a significant expense that is creating uncertainty for banks. "The ring-fence is a big expense creating lots of uncertainty," said Peter Hahn of the London Institute of Banking and Finance. "It's not just the headquarters, it's separating lots of the systems in the bank." HSBC also took a charge of £228 million ($300 million) during the reporting period for PPI claims, primarily due to a recent increase in complaint volumes. The bank has set aside £3.3 billion to date to deal with claims related to mis-sold mortgage payment protection, a issue that continues to cast a long shadow over the balance sheets of UK banks. Overall, HSBC's results demonstrate the bank's progress in recovering from the financial crisis, but also highlight the ongoing challenges it faces in navigating the complex regulatory landscape. As the bank continues to streamline its operations and return value to shareholders, it must also contend with the significant costs and uncertainties associated with meeting new regulatory requirements.

Manchester United midfielder Juan Mata is confident that the club will return to winning major trophies in the near future. Despite not claiming any significant silverware since Sir Alex Ferguson's retirement in 2013, Mata believes that the Red Devils have the mentality and talent to compete for titles. The Spanish international's comments come ahead of the FA Cup final against Crystal Palace on Saturday, where United have the opportunity to end the season with a trophy. Mata acknowledged that failing to qualify for the Champions League next season was a disappointment, but highlighted the emergence of young players such as Marcus Rashford and the form of Anthony Martial as positives from the current campaign. Rashford, who has scored eight goals in 17 appearances, and Martial, who has impressed since his £36m signing, have been standout performers for United. Mata praised the pair, stating that they are "exciting players" who have shown their talent to the world. The 28-year-old also emphasized the importance of Rashford's Manchester roots, saying that he has "known the club since he was a kid." As United prepare to face Crystal Palace, Mata is hopeful that the team can bring home the FA Cup and end the season on a high note. With the club's rich history of success, Mata is convinced that they will be "fighting for titles" again soon. Fans can also have their say on who should start the FA Cup final by using the team selector tool to pick their ideal XI.

Hanna Sabic, missing since Monday, has been found in Edinburgh. Police had expressed concern for her welfare after she failed to arrive at work. She was last seen at Falkirk Grahamston Station. Police Scotland thanked the public and media for their help in tracing her, located at 13:45 on Tuesday.

Australian snooker player Neil Robertson has vowed to change his approach to the game after a disappointing loss in the World Championship second round. The 35-year-old was beaten 13-11 by Marco Fu on Tuesday, and he was scathing in his assessment of his own performance, labeling it "garbage". Robertson's loss was marked by a dramatic turn of events, as he celebrated going 11-10 up by shouting and punching the table, only to lose the next three frames. The Cambridgeshire-based player acknowledged that his emotions got the better of him, but he believes that playing with passion is essential to his success. "I've tried to play within myself, but I need adrenaline and need to be pumped up to play well," Robertson said. "Otherwise, you'll see snoring snooker like that." He added that he will not be holding back his emotions in the future, saying "I won't be giving it a fist pump every frame, but I will be showing my emotion when I feel like it." Robertson's struggles this season have been well-documented, with his only major success coming in the Riga Open. He was knocked out in the first round of the UK Championship and lost in the quarterfinals of the Masters. The 12-time ranking event winner believes that a change in tactics will benefit not only himself but also the sport as a whole. "At the moment, there are probably only three or four players in the world worth watching, and I am not one of them," Robertson said. "I need to play a lot more aggressively and with a lot more freedom. I will not be running around the table taking 15 seconds a shot, but I will be playing with a lot more passion and emotion." Robertson cited players like Ronnie O'Sullivan and Judd Trump as examples of the kind of exciting, attacking snooker that he wants to play. He believes that this style of play is essential to bringing more fans to the sport, saying "as soon as Ronnie goes out, a large interest from the general public goes from a tournament - Judd as well." With a renewed focus on playing with passion and aggression, Robertson will be looking to bounce back from his disappointing loss and make a stronger impact in the world of snooker.

The 2015 Rugby World Cup is expected to bring a significant economic boost to England and Wales, according to a report by accountancy firm EY. The tournament, which will be hosted in 11 cities across the two countries, is predicted to attract 466,000 visitors who will spend up to £869m. This makes it one of the most lucrative sporting events in the world, second only to the football World Cup in terms of paid spectators. Visitors are expected to spend £32m on food and drink, and a further £13m in "fanzones" - city centre attractions with a Rugby World Cup theme. The report also highlights the benefits of improved infrastructure, including investment in transport and stadia. England Rugby 2015 chief Debbie Jevans said the tournament will create economic opportunities across many sectors, supporting jobs and generating revenue in host cities and beyond.

US Researchers Discover Hidden Fat in Bones of Overweight Individuals A groundbreaking study conducted by researchers at Harvard Medical School in Boston has revealed that some overweight individuals may be harboring hidden fat inside their bones, making them more susceptible to weakness and fractures. The study, published in the journal Radiology, involved body scans of 106 obese but healthy men and women. The scans showed that some participants carried fat in unexpected areas, including their liver, muscles, and bone marrow, in addition to their belly, hips, or thighs. Dr. Miriam Bredella, who led the research, notes that individuals with an apple-shaped body, who tend to carry weight around their waist, may be at greatest risk. The discovery is significant, as bone marrow is responsible for producing osteoblast cells, which are essential for new bone formation. When fat cells take over the marrow, it can weaken the bones, making them more prone to fractures. Dr. Bredella warns that having a spine filled with fat can compromise its strength. The findings challenge the long-held assumption that obesity is protective against bone loss. With almost three million people in the UK estimated to have osteoporosis, the researchers emphasize the importance of maintaining a healthy weight to prevent bone-related issues.

In a groundbreaking effort to preserve the native species of South Georgia, a team of conservationists has embarked on a three-month mission to eradicate brown rats from the island. The rodents, which have been a menace to the island's ecosystem since the 18th century, will be targeted with 100 million poisonous pellets dropped from three former air ambulance helicopters. The project, led by Prof Tony Martin from the University of Dundee, aims to clear more than half of the remaining area of brown rats, building on the success of the first phase in 2011, which saw the extermination of the rodents from a smaller portion of the island. The brown rats, with no natural predators on the island, have thrived since their arrival as stowaways on sealing ships, posing a significant threat to ground-nesting birds such as the South Georgia pipit and pintail. The helicopters will employ mathematical precision to distribute the bait pellets, covering every square meter of the island. According to Prof Martin, the mission's success hinges on eradicating every single rat, as "killing 99.999% is a failure." The team's goal is to eradicate, not control, the invasive species, and the unique terrain of South Georgia, with its glaciers separating rat colonies into isolated pockets, makes this ambitious project feasible. Despite facing challenging weather conditions, including gale-force winds and blizzards, the team is poised to resume the largest-ever species eradication project. Time is of the essence, as the retreating glaciers threaten to allow the separate colonies to mingle, making eradication much more difficult. With the weather improving, the team is ready to tackle this critical phase of the four-year project, ultimately aiming to safeguard the future of South Georgia's native species.

Hull FC Snatch Victory Over St Helens with Sneyd's Stunning Kick In a game marred by bad weather, Hull FC managed to secure a hard-fought win over St Helens, thanks to a brilliant 50-meter penalty kick from Marc Sneyd. The match, which saw few clear-cut chances, was decided by Sneyd's solo effort, which sailed over the bar to give Hull FC a narrow victory. The game got off to a flying start, with Saints winger Regan Grace opening the scoring inside four minutes with an acrobatic finish. However, Sneyd leveled the scores just before the half-time break, converting his own solo effort. Despite having few openings, Sneyd's kick proved to be the difference-maker, securing a crucial win for Hull FC. Grace will rue the chances he had to extend his team's lead, having knocked on 20 meters out and later dropping a pass from Theo Fages in open space. The win keeps Hull FC in third place in the Super 8s table, while St Helens remain in fifth, one point behind fourth-placed Wakefield Trinity. Hull FC head coach Lee Radford hailed the win as one of the team's most significant of the season, saying, "We had to win ugly and I was pleased when the heavens opened up because then I knew they were going to play with a bar of soap." St Helens head coach Justin Holbrook, on the other hand, described the game as "one of the worst games of rugby league I have been involved in," citing the poor weather conditions and numerous errors from both teams. Despite the disappointing performance, Holbrook acknowledged that the game was closely contested, with Sneyd's penalty kick ultimately proving to be the decisive factor.

Legendary Actress Julie Harris Passes Away at 87 The theater world is mourning the loss of Julie Harris, a renowned actress who jointly holds the record for the most Tony Award wins. Harris passed away at her home in Massachusetts due to congestive heart failure, according to family friend and actress Francesca James. She was 87 years old. Harris' illustrious career spanned over six decades, with her breakthrough role coming in 1950 with the hit play "The Member of the Wedding." Her portrayal of the lonely 12-year-old Frankie earned her critical acclaim and paved the way for her future success. She went on to win her first Tony Award in 1952 for her role as Sally Bowles in "I Am a Camera," which was later adapted into the iconic musical "Cabaret." Throughout her career, Harris won a total of five competitive Tony Awards, with her final win coming in 1977 for her one-woman show "The Belle of Amherst." She also received a special lifetime achievement Tony in 2002 and holds the record for the most nominated performer in the awards' history. Harris is joined by Angela Lansbury and Audra McDonald as the only performers to have won five competitive Tonys. In addition to her theater work, Harris appeared in over 30 films, including the 1955 classic "East of Eden" alongside James Dean. She also had a successful television career, winning three Emmy Awards and starring in the popular soap opera "Knot's Landing" in the 1980s. Harris' health had been declining in recent years, with her suffering two strokes in 2001 and 2010. Despite her health issues, she remained a beloved figure in the entertainment industry, and her passing has sent shockwaves throughout the theater and film communities. She will be deeply missed by her fans and fellow performers, who remember her as a talented and dedicated actress who left an indelible mark on the world of entertainment.

A major infrastructure project is underway in Glasgow with the construction of the Shieldhall Tunnel, a 3.1-mile sewer tunnel that will run from Craigton to Queen's Park. The tunnel, which will be capable of handling sewage and excess rainfall, is set to be one of the largest in Scotland and will play a crucial role in protecting the environment and reducing the risk of flooding. Scottish Water is investing over £100m in the project, which is part of a larger £250m, five-year programme to improve the waste water network in the Glasgow area. The tunnel will be big enough to fit a double-decker bus inside and will stretch for over five times the length of the Clyde Tunnel. A 1,000 tonne, 180 metre-long tunnel boring machine is set to arrive on site in the coming weeks, marking a major milestone in the project. The machine will be used to construct the tunnel, which will follow a route from Craigton industrial estate to Queen's Park, passing under several parks and roads along the way. According to Scottish Water chief executive Douglas Millican, the project is the biggest investment in waste water infrastructure in Glasgow for over a century. "The modernisation of the system and construction of new underground assets, such as the Shieldhall Tunnel, will protect the natural environment, reduce the risk of flooding and meet the needs of growth, economic development and regeneration," he said. The tunnel is expected to be completed by 2018.

Colombian President Juan Manuel Santos has expressed his enthusiasm for a potential free trade agreement with the UK, suggesting it could surpass the country's current deal with the EU. In an interview with the BBC's Andrew Marr Show, Santos emphasized the opportunities for increased trade between the UK and emerging markets, particularly with the Pacific Alliance bloc comprising Colombia, Chile, Peru, and Mexico. During his recent state visit to the UK, Santos held talks with Prime Minister Theresa May at Downing Street, where he highlighted the "huge opportunity for British business" in the region. He proposed a free trade agreement with the UK, offering "the same conditions or even improved" terms as the current EU deal. However, Santos clarified that negotiations would only commence once the UK's economic relationship with the EU is finalized. The UK and Colombia's trading relationship is already valued at £1 billion, with a new oil and gas partnership announced during Santos' visit. Prime Minister May has also encouraged Colombian businesses to view the UK as a leading hub for finance, innovation, and research. With the UK's departure from the EU looming, Santos' comments suggest a potential boost to trade relations between the two nations.

Blades defender McGahey to join Rochdale on July 1, after his contract expires. The 20-year-old made 34 appearances over two seasons, but started only nine games last season, leading to his release under new manager Chris Wilder.

Carers Scotland Sounds Alarm on Financial Burden of Unpaid Caregivers A shocking new report from Carers Scotland has highlighted the devastating financial impact of unpaid caregiving on families across the UK. The charity's year-long investigation, known as the Caring & Family Finances Inquiry, reveals that vast numbers of carers are struggling with unmanageable debt, with one in six owing more than £10,000. The findings have prompted Carers Scotland to call for urgent reform of the financial help available to carers and a commitment from the UK and Scottish governments to ensure that future policy does not leave carers worse off. The research paints a stark picture of the challenges faced by those caring for loved ones who may be old, disabled, or seriously ill. Almost half (47%) of carers are in debt as a result of their caregiving responsibilities, with a fifth relying on overdrafts or credit cards to make ends meet. A staggering third of carers are said to be more than £20,000 worse off as a result of caring, while 44% have been forced to cut back on essentials like food. Furthermore, 59% of carers are living in fuel poverty, highlighting the desperate need for support. Simon Hodgson, director of Carers Scotland, emphasized the importance of recognizing the vital role that carers play in society. "Those caring, unpaid, for loved ones save society vast sums, but at huge personal cost – a cost this inquiry shows is pushing families to the brink," he said. Hodgson argued that the current system is unsustainable and that government cuts to support are leaving carers across the UK facing a £1bn cut. In response to the report, the UK government claimed that it is spending around £2bn this year on carer's allowance, with even more allocated for future years. A Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) spokeswoman acknowledged the invaluable service provided by carers and highlighted the government's commitment to supporting them. However, Carers Scotland argues that this funding is insufficient to address the scale of the problem. The Scottish government has announced an additional £9.2m for the Scottish Welfare Fund, which it claims will help alleviate the burden of poverty on carers. A Scottish government spokesman acknowledged the difficulties faced by full-time carers and emphasized the need to ensure they receive the support they deserve. However, the charity argues that more needs to be done to address the root causes of the financial struggles faced by carers. Carers Scotland is urging the UK and Scottish governments to implement a "carer test" for future benefits and social care proposals, ensuring that carers are not left worse off by policy changes. The charity's director, Simon Hodgson, warned that the current situation is unacceptable and unsustainable, with the ageing population set to increase the number of people caring for loved ones. As the charity's report makes clear, it is time for urgent action to support the unsung heroes of unpaid caregiving.

UK Government to Match Donations to Aid Gaza Crisis as Ceasefire Enters Final Day The Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) has issued a dire warning that hundreds of thousands of people in Gaza are in desperate need of food, water, shelter, and medical care following four weeks of intense conflict between Israeli forces and Hamas militants. In response, the UK government has pledged to match donations to the DEC, effectively doubling the impact of public generosity. International Development Secretary Justine Greening emphasized the urgency of the situation, stating that the British people have consistently shown immense kindness in times of crisis. "The UK government will help that generosity go twice as far," she said. "For people wanting to help civilians in Gaza caught up in this crisis, giving now means every pound they donate will buy twice as many food parcels, provide twice as many blankets, and help twice as many people to get through this crisis." The UK government has committed £2 million to the DEC appeal, bringing its total support for the people of Gaza since the start of the crisis to £17 million. Saleh Saeed, chief executive of the DEC, described this as a "vital moment" for Gaza, where hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced and are struggling to access basic necessities like food and water. The healthcare system, he warned, is on the verge of collapse. As a three-day ceasefire in Gaza enters its final day, indirect talks are ongoing in Cairo to negotiate a long-term truce. While Israeli officials have expressed willingness to extend the ceasefire, Hamas has stated that there is no agreement and significant gaps remain between the two sides' positions. The conflict has claimed over 1,900 lives, including at least 1,875 Palestinians and 64 Israeli soldiers. The DEC, an umbrella organization representing 13 UK aid charities, is scaling up its relief efforts as the ceasefire continues to hold. However, the organization urgently needs funds to support its work. With the UK government's matching commitment, donations to the DEC will have twice the impact, providing vital assistance to those affected by the crisis in Gaza.

A 2nd Century sculpture depicting Buddha's footprints has been returned to Pakistan after being smuggled into the US. The piece, which features religious symbols, was taken from the Swat Valley and eventually made its way to New York, where it was expected to sell for $1 million at auction. However, the sale was intercepted by authorities, and a Japanese antiques dealer, Tatsuzo Kaku, pleaded guilty to possessing stolen property in April. At a ceremony on Wednesday, New York prosecutors returned the sculpture to Pakistan's Deputy Chief of Mission, Rizwan Saeed Sheikh. Sheikh described the piece as "an important element of the cultural history of Pakistan" and said it would likely be kept in New York for the short term, possibly going on display. Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus R Vance Jr emphasized the significance of the sculpture, stating it was "so much more than a piece of property" and a vital part of Pakistan's cultural heritage. Kaku was fined $5,000 and left the country voluntarily after serving his sentence. Experts have dismissed Kaku's claim that he was motivated by a desire to protect Pakistan's artefacts, citing the country's existing structures for preservation.

The Football Association of Malawi (FAM) has announced that it will continue its search for a foreign coach, despite appointing former international striker, Phiri, as the new head coach of the national team. Phiri's first task will be to lead the team in the Africa Nations Championship (CHAN) qualifier against Madagascar in April. Phiri, who will be assisted by Deklerk Msakakuona, has acknowledged the challenge ahead, stating that the team needs to come up with a winning system. FAM General Secretary, Alfred Gunda, clarified that Phiri and his assistant will sign one-year contracts, but the association is still looking for an expatriate coach to join the team. Phiri, who will turn 49 next month, previously led the team as a caretaker in a friendly match against Guangzhou FC in January. He replaces Ernest Mtawali, who was fired in June 2016, following a poor performance at the Cosafa Cup. The team will begin a training camp on April 2, ahead of their CHAN game in Madagascar on April 22. A friendly match against Kenya is also scheduled for April 18. FAM is expected to announce the appointment of a foreign coach once the selection process is complete.

A fire broke out at a disused building in Leicester, causing significant structural damage. The blaze started at 03:00 GMT on the corner of Littleton Street and Bradgate Street. Firefighters arrived to find the building "well alight" but managed to contain the fire. An attached chimney remained stable. Nearby units suffered minor damage, and surrounding roads were closed. The fire service is working with police to trace the owners of the affected units. Firefighters will remain on site throughout Thursday to dampen down the area, ensuring the fire is fully extinguished. An investigation into the cause is ongoing.

A 32-year-old pregnant woman, Sarah Keegan, has been sentenced to prison for her role in supplying heroin in a Scottish caravan park. Keegan, who is due to give birth in June, pleaded guilty to the offense, which took place in April last year at the Moffat Manor Country Park in Beattock. Despite her defense counsel's plea for a non-custodial sentence, Judge Lord Boyd deemed the crime too serious and sentenced her to prison. The court heard that Keegan had been arrested alongside her co-accused, Jason Jolley, 45, following a police operation codenamed Operation Boswell. The operation uncovered a significant heroin supply ring, with Jolley and Keegan believed to be flooding the Dumfries area with the drug. Police recovered heroin and cutting agent worth a potential £65,000 from the caravan, as well as drugs paraphernalia, including scales and knotted bags of heroin. Keegan's defense counsel, Susan Duff, argued that her client had been a heroin addict at the time of the offense but had since overcome her addiction and was determined to be a "role model" for her unborn child. Duff pleaded with the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, citing Keegan's pregnancy and her desire to be with her baby when it is born. However, Lord Boyd was unmoved, stating that Keegan's involvement in the crime, although lesser than Jolley's, was still significant. The court was told that Keegan's DNA and fingerprints were found on various items in the caravan, and a small amount of heroin was discovered in her underwear during a strip search. While Lord Boyd acknowledged that Jolley was the "moving force" behind the operation, he emphasized that Keegan's involvement was still a serious offense. "You have yourself been an addict," he said. "You should know the misery that drugs bring to people and the communities blighted by it." Jolley, who was jailed for five years, was found to be directly supplying others and had local dealers working for him. The police operation that led to their arrest was the result of intelligence suggesting that Jolley and Keegan were organizing deliveries of heroin from the caravan park into Dumfries and the surrounding area. The recovery of the significant quantity of heroin and paraphernalia from the caravan highlighted the scale of the operation and the seriousness of the offense. In sentencing Keegan, Lord Boyd made it clear that he could not ignore the severity of the crime, despite her pregnancy and desire to be with her baby. The case serves as a reminder of the devastating impact of drug supply and addiction on individuals and communities, and the need for robust law enforcement to combat these issues.

Students at Delhi's Ghandi Memorial Public School investigated air pollution's effects on children's health. They measured air quality, finding high pollution levels due to heavy traffic, posing health risks to young residents in the city.

A plane crash in Ecuador's eastern province of Pastaza has resulted in no survivors. The Israeli-built Arava plane carried 19 Ecuadoran soldiers, two pilots, and a mechanic. President Rafael Correa expressed solidarity with the families and armed forces, calling it a "tragedy." The cause of the crash, which occurred at 14:30 local time, is unknown. Defence Minister Ricardo Patino and rescue teams are en route to the area to investigate.

Barrow's loan spell for 24-year-old Parry has ended. The player, who can play in defense and midfield, had previously played for Altrincham. Bluebirds boss Paul Cox hopes to make another signing soon. Nearby, Luton's transfer activity is expected to be quiet, having already signed Alan Sheehan and Joe Pigott, with Luke Guttridge and Luke Wilkinson leaving for other clubs.

Former Tottenham defender Gary Mabbutt, 55, has been released from Kings College Hospital in London. He was admitted last Monday with chest pains and breathing issues. Mabbutt, who won the 1991 FA Cup, will recover at home. He thanked hospital staff, the cardiac team, and Spurs fans for their support and get-well messages. The Tottenham legend played over 600 games for the club.

Sri Lankan cricketer Kusal Perera faces a doping ban after failing an out-of-competition test. The sports minister is backing him, citing a possible "conspiracy" to keep him out of the T20 World Cup, and will provide legal representation to appeal the decision.

Yeovil Town has signed MK Dons striker Kabongo Tshimanga on loan. The 20-year-old impressed Glovers manager Darren Way, who noted his threat behind the back four and eye for goal. Tshimanga came through the Stadium MK academy and previously played for Nuneaton Town. He has played 12 games for MK Dons this season, including a Football League Trophy match against Yeovil. Tshimanga is Yeovil's fifth January signing, joining Shayon Harrison and Andre Wright on loan at the club.

A man has taken to living in a tree to protest a 225-bedroom hotel development in Edinburgh. The project, led by developer Andy Jansons, includes a bar, restaurant, and retail units, and involves historic buildings. The man, who wishes to remain anonymous, has been in the tree for a week. Jansons is seeking an eviction notice from Edinburgh Sheriff Court. Work on the site was set to begin on Monday, but the protester's actions have caused a delay, sparking a showdown over the redevelopment of the derelict site. A court decision is expected soon.

A teenager has been charged after an incident at a Blackheath supermarket. Armed officers responded on Saturday, closing several roads. The boy, now in custody, faces charges including making an explosive substance and possessing a bladed article. No one was hurt, and road closures have been lifted, according to West Midlands Police.

A fatal car accident occurred on Plodder Lane in Bolton early Thursday morning, claiming the life of Latham Schofield. He was one of four people in a silver Renault Megane when the incident happened. Schofield's family remembered him as "cheeky and silly sometimes," but loved him even more for it. Another 17-year-old boy was hospitalized and remains in serious but stable condition. An 18-year-old from Bolton has been charged with various offenses, including causing serious injury by dangerous driving. He is set to appear in Bolton Crown Court on March 11. A 19-year-old man who was also arrested has been released without charge, pending further investigation.
The 23-year-old midfielder rejoined Marseille on loan, scoring twice in 14 games, after making just 16 appearances for Newcastle following a £12m summer transfer.

A 40-year-old woman has been charged with the murder of her 82-year-old neighbour in Leven. Sandra Weir appeared at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court, facing five charges including murder, theft, and attempting to pervert the course of justice. Mary Logie, 82, was found dead in her Green Gates home on January 5. Weir made no plea and was fully committed for trial. Additional charges were added to the initial murder charge. Her solicitor, David Fitzpatrick, did not request bail, and she was remanded in custody. Weir will now await trial for the alleged crimes. The case has shocked the local community.

Blues have signed defender Ryan Shotton on a deal until 2019 for an undisclosed fee. The 27-year-old, who played for the team earlier this year, becomes their second summer signing. Shotton previously played for Stoke City, Wigan, and Barnsley, and scored one goal in nine appearances for Blues. He joins midfielder Robert Tesche as the club's new additions ahead of the upcoming season.

A search operation is underway for Josh Winsper, a man from Cornwall who went missing in Milford Haven. The captain of a vessel alerted authorities on Saturday morning after crew members realized he was missing. Police divers and HM Coastguard are involved in the search. Winsper was last seen at Astoria nightclub at 02:30 BST on Saturday. His family has posted a plea on social media, with his aunt saying they are "holding out for a miracle." The family has praised the support from the local community and the Welsh police, who are working to locate Winsper.

Local TV stations feature home-grown comedies and Spanish soaps, while cable TV offers multichannel options and radio plays popular formats like news and Spanish pop music, with 1.8 million internet users reported.

In Copenhagen, thousands created the world's largest chalk pavement painting, breaking the US record. Over a kilometre of pavement was covered in flags, flowers, and artwork within hours. The new record spans 18,598 square metres, exceeding the 2008 record of 8,361 square metres by over 10,000 square metres.

Nominations have closed for the May 4 by-election to replace late MP Sir Gerald Kaufman. The poll coincides with Greater Manchester's mayoral election, marking a significant day in local politics. Candidates are set to contest the seat left vacant by Sir Gerald's passing in February.

Glamorgan made a strong start on the first day of their match, despite losing Jacques Rudolph early on for 17 runs. James Kettleborough and Colin Ingram formed a solid partnership, adding 71 runs for the second wicket. Kettleborough went on to score 81, putting on a further 66 runs with Aneurin Donald before being caught off David Payne's bowling. Donald, just 18 years old, continued to impress, scoring an unbeaten 91 and surpassing his previous best of 67. Chris Cooke also made a significant contribution, hitting a quickfire 65 as the team reached 315-4 before rain brought an early close to the day's play. A total of 19 overs were lost due to the bad weather, which could have seen Glamorgan's score even higher. Kettleborough expressed satisfaction with his performance, and praised Donald and Cooke for their impressive batting. He also voiced his support for Donald to become Glamorgan's youngest Championship centurion.

Australia's hopes of winning the mixed 4x100m relay were dashed after a disqualification due to a botched handover between Jack Hale and Fabrice Lapierre. The team's mistake in the change from the second to the third leg resulted in a score of -10, ultimately leading to their downfall. Usain Bolt's All-Stars took advantage of the error, winning the relay and securing a total of 930 points to Australia's 895. Initially, a refereeing error awarded Australia the top ranking, but this was quickly corrected after Bolt threatened to protest. The eight-time Olympic champion, competing in his farewell season, has been selective with his events, only participating in the relays on the first two nights of the series. However, he may make an appearance in the 150m on Saturday, depending on the meeting's progression. Bolt's All-Stars have now claimed their second victory in the three-event series, with England currently sitting in fourth place, ahead of New Zealand and Japan. The Nitro Athletics series has been praised by IAAF president Lord Coe, who believes it will "revolutionise" the sport. Despite the disappointment, Australia will look to bounce back in the remaining events, while Bolt's team will aim to continue their dominance.

Subah Amini, a member of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Youth Association, was among 350 volunteers who aided flood victims in Cumbria and Yorkshire. After a near-fatal fall in 2014, Amini spent 10 months in hospitals in London, Wakefield, and China. Grateful to be alive, he now dedicates his life to helping others. Volunteers assisted with transportation, sandbag organization, and emotional support. Amini noted that the efforts brought the community together, making them feel more connected to Christmas than ever before. The flooding, which hit parts of Yorkshire and Lancashire on December 26, was met with a strong response from volunteers like Amini.

Bath's new signing will debut on Thursday in the Premiership Rugby Sevens at Kingsholm. The 27-year-old back-rower expressed excitement to join Bath, eager to start his career. With experience playing sevens for Samoa and a nomination for IRB International Sevens Player of the Year, he's well-suited for the competition. He previously played for Toulouse and Bristol, bringing valuable experience to his new team.

A 43-year-old man, John Parker, was found injured in Hedderley Walk, St Ann's, on Sunday and later died in hospital. Jonathan Jones, 39, has been charged with murder and is set to appear before magistrates. Another 39-year-old man is being held for questioning in connection with the incident. A 14-year-old boy, arrested for suspected involvement, has been released without charge. A 35-year-old woman, arrested for GBH related to an earlier incident involving the victim, has been bailed. Police are seeking the occupants of a silver Ford Focus seen in the area, as they may have information about the incident. The occupants are not believed to be involved, but detectives hope they can provide valuable insights to aid the investigation. The community is urged to come forward with any information that may help the police.

A 17-year-old motorcyclist, Jack Mander, was killed in a collision with a heavy goods vehicle in Strood, Kent. The incident occurred on Anthony's Way, and Jack died at the scene. His family described him as a careful rider. The lorry driver, 44, was released on bail. Kent Police are investigating and appealing for witnesses to come forward. The collision happened on Thursday at 21:00 BST.

Ireland's bid to become a full member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) has taken a significant step forward. Following Wednesday's ICC meeting, Cricket Ireland's application will now be reviewed by a newly-created membership committee. The committee will assess whether Ireland meets the necessary criteria, including governance, finance, national team performance, and development programs. Cricket Ireland chief executive Warren Deutrom expressed cautious optimism about the application, stating that while there are some uncertainties surrounding the financial criteria, Ireland appears to be in a strong position. Deutrom emphasized the importance of respecting the opinions of ICC members, whose decision is ultimate. The ICC's board agreed on the new membership process at a meeting in Dubai, marking a change from the previous system where teams required a proposal and seconding from full member nations. Ireland and Afghanistan are currently seeking to upgrade from associate member status to full membership, joining the current 10 full member countries. A decision on their applications is expected to be made after the membership committee's review.

A hot air balloon made an unexpected landing in Northampton on Friday evening. Matt Rate brought the balloon down in Hilldrop Road, citing a sudden wind drop. Resident Ian Callaghan captured the landing on film. The quick thinking ensured a safe landing, avoiding a potential descent over the town centre.

A record-breaking attempt in Yangzhou, east China, has ended in controversy. The city cooked 4,192kg of fried rice, surpassing Turkey's previous record. However, celebrations were short-lived as photos showed the rice being loaded into waste lorries. Guinness World Records has disqualified the attempt, stating that the food was not consumed by humans. Event organizers claimed the rice would be donated to local canteens, but the tourism bureau revealed that 150kg of "inedible" rice was sent to pig farms. Guinness World Records has clarified that it will not accept claims for large food items if they are inedible or unfit for consumption. Yangzhou's signature dish, fried rice, typically combines rice, eggs, chicken, and vegetables. The city's attempt to showcase its culinary pride has ultimately ended in disappointment. The incident highlights the importance of ensuring that record-breaking attempts are both impressive and responsible.

A fatal collision occurred on the highway between junctions 46 and 45 on Friday. A Peugeot Partner van passenger suffered fatal injuries, while the driver was taken to Morriston Hospital. The road has reopened, easing traffic queues that stretched up to six miles. South Wales Police have launched an investigation into the incident's cause. Motorists are advised to check for updates to avoid disruptions to their journey. The incident occurred after 06:10 GMT, causing significant morning traffic congestion.

An inquest has concluded that an 18-day-old baby, James Rawlings, died due to a lack of oxygen and sepsis. James was born at Ipswich Hospital and passed away at home in May last year. The hearing revealed that despite concerns from a midwife and James' mother, Jo Rawlings, a Caesarean delivery was delayed by Dr. Lovelina Das. The hospital trust admitted that an earlier delivery would have likely saved James' life. Dr. Das is no longer employed at the hospital and is believed to be working abroad. The coroner, Peter Dean, stated that the evidence shows James would not have died if delivered earlier. James' parents, who now have a new son, Joshua, praised the midwife for her support during a difficult time. The hospital trust has acknowledged its mistakes and is taking steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.

Jersey's cricket team is gearing up to compete in the fourth tier of the global tournament for the third time, seeking to break their relegation curse. Having won Division Five in May, the island side is confident of making a strong showing in the 2016 event. Coach Neil MacRae expressed his team's optimism, stating that they have a young squad with a lot of experience and are eager to take on the challenge. The team's previous appearances in the fourth tier, in 2008 and 2014, ended in relegation. However, they go into this tournament on a high note, having won the World League Five final in May. Their first opponents will be Oman, a team they defeated in the final earlier this summer. MacRae believes that his team's two-year gain in experience will make a significant difference in their performance. Jersey has been an international cricket nation since 2005 and has made significant strides in recent years, including qualifying for the World Twenty20 global qualifiers in 2015. With their sights set on promotion to the highest level they've ever played at, the team is excited and motivated. MacRae is looking forward to the challenge, citing his team's exceptional performance in tough conditions during their previous tournament in Singapore. With their recent win and added experience, Jersey's cricket team is ready to take on the best in the world.

A police officer was struck by a silver Honda Estate in Evesham on Tuesday at 13:20 GMT. The officer suffered minor leg and head injuries. The vehicle was found unoccupied in Warwickshire and the driver is being sought. Witnesses are urged to come forward to aid the investigation into the incident at the junction of Chapel Street and Oat Street.

Michael Kightly joins Southend after leaving Burnley. The 31-year-old made 88 appearances for Burnley and had a loan stint at Burton Albion. Kightly previously played for Southend from 2003 to 2005, featuring in 19 games. He is the team's second summer signing, following Stephen Hendrie's arrival.

Nigerian Authorities Seize $43.4m in Cash from Lagos Flat In a shocking discovery, Nigerian authorities have seized a massive stash of cash from a flat in Lagos's affluent Ikoyi area. The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) revealed that investigators found US notes worth $43.4m, along with nearly £27,800 and 23m naira ($75,000), in a four-bedroom flat on the seventh floor of a building. The cash was neatly arranged in sealed wrappers and stashed in wardrobes and cabinets. The raid was carried out after a tip-off about a "haggard-looking" woman in "dirty clothes" taking bags in and out of the flat. Guards at the building reported that no one lived in the flat, but a source claimed that the woman would often appear with Ghana Must Go bags, sparking suspicion. The EFCC believes the money may be from unlawful activity, but no arrests have been made yet. This is the latest in a series of raids that have uncovered large amounts of cash in Nigeria, Africa's biggest economy.

A heartwarming reunion has taken place in Beijing after a blind man's beloved dog, Qiaoqiao, was abducted by a group of men on Monday. The seven-year-old Labrador was taken while being walked outside, leaving her owner Tian Fengbo in a state of distress. Mr. Tian, who relies on Qiaoqiao for companionship, said he was unable to eat or sleep after her disappearance. The incident sparked widespread outrage among Chinese netizens, with many taking to social media to condemn the actions of the dog thieves. Residents in the area reported a series of recent dog thefts, fueling speculation that Qiaoqiao may have been targeted for sale to meat markets. Fortunately, Qiaoqiao was found on Tuesday with a letter attached to her collar, reading "We were wrong..... we beg pardon." The motive behind Qiaoqiao's abduction remains unclear, but the incident has highlighted the growing concern over dog theft in China. Many have called for harsher punishment for those involved in the trade, with some expressing frustration over the lack of protection for pets. As one netizen remarked, "Dogs are man's best friend, not food." The case has sparked a national conversation, with many celebrating the safe return of Qiaoqiao and calling for greater action to prevent similar incidents in the future. Mr. Tian has been reunited with his beloved dog, and the community is breathing a sigh of relief.

Proposals for a statue commemorating the birthplace of football on Parker's Piece are now on display at the Grand Arcade. The public is invited to view the four shortlisted designs, submitted by artists Neville Gabie, Alan Ward, Kenny Hunter, Nayan Kulkarni, and Mark Titchner, and provide their feedback until December 5. The statue aims to celebrate the city centre green as the spot where students developed the original rules of football in 1848. A plaque already exists at the park, acknowledging the "Cambridge Rules" as a defining influence on the 1863 Football Association rules. However, the Football Association notes that while elements of the Cambridge Rules were incorporated, there are significant differences between the two sets of rules. City councillor Carina O'Reilly believes the statue could become a "significant landmark" for the city. The proposed designs include a granite slab with the rules inscribed in multiple languages, a mirror-like design with a bench, a life-size bronze of a female referee, and a word sculpture. The chosen design will be selected by city councillors on January 15, with the project costing up to £115,000, funded by public art money from developers. The public's opinions will play a crucial role in determining which sculpture will be brought to life.

A rare and historic book has been stolen from St Oswald's Church in Grasmere, Cumbria. The book, dated 1835, was on display in a glass cabinet and was taken between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning. Church warden Sonia Rickman described the book as "irreplaceable" and believes the thieves knew what they were looking for. The book holds significant value due to its connection to William Wordsworth, who lived and prayed in Grasmere and is buried in the churchyard. The church was open at the time of the theft, and the discovery was made when a caller reported smashed glass. Cumbria Police is appealing for information and urging antique dealers to be vigilant for anyone attempting to sell the stolen book. The loss is felt deeply by the community, who come to visit Wordsworth's grave and the church where he worshiped.

RWE Npower has announced plans to demolish the remaining structure of the boiler house at the Didcot A plant, where a partial collapse in February resulted in the deaths of four men. Despite ongoing protests from the families of the three men whose bodies are yet to be recovered, the energy company has begun preparations for a controlled explosive demolition. Residents living near the site have been informed of the plans through letters, which stated that the exact timing of the demolition would be made public 48 hours in advance. The letter warned that the explosion may be heard off-site and could generate airborne dust, although this is not expected to be harmful. To minimize noise and dust disturbance, residents are advised to keep their doors and windows closed. The plans are currently being finalized and will be submitted to a multi-agency strategy team, including the Health and Safety Executive. The recovery of the men's bodies, including Christopher Huxtable, Ken Cresswell, and John Shaw, has been halted due to safety concerns, with contractors unable to access the area within the 50m exclusion zone. The delay has been criticized by family members and Labour MP Sarah Champion, who has branded it a "national scandal." The incident has also incurred significant costs, with Oxfordshire Fire and Rescue Service spending £300,000 on attendance and search operations.

Scotland's rugby team has been dealt a blow with the news that centre Duncan Taylor will miss the second Test against Japan due to a hamstring injury. The 26-year-old Saracens player picked up the injury in last weekend's 26-13 win over Japan in Toyota City and has failed to recover in time for the upcoming match. Despite the loss, Scotland has ample cover in midfield, with Peter Horne, Matt Scott, and uncapped Huw Jones all available for selection. Additionally, winger Sean Lamont has experience playing Test rugby at centre, providing coach Vern Cotter with a range of options. The team, which will be announced on Thursday, is expected to show several changes from the first Test. One player who will definitely start is 23-year-old Rory Sutherland, who will make his debut at loose-head prop in place of the injured Alasdair Dickinson.
