Sutherland will be joined by Gordon Reid, who was called up to the squad as a replacement for Dickinson and had his first full training session with the team on Tuesday. Reid, who was enjoying a day on the beach with his family when he received the call-up, joked that he had brought the Scottish weather with him to Tokyo, as the team trained in persistent rain. The Glasgow Warriors forward is likely to feature in the upcoming match, along with back-row forward Josh Strauss, who was not in the squad for the first Test. However, there are some injury concerns for Scotland, with flanker John Barclay carrying an injury and props WP Nel and Ryan Wilson also nursing slight injuries. Despite these concerns, Cotter is expected to give all of his players game time on tour, as he seeks to build depth and experience within the squad.

Former Nigerian President Goodluck Jonathan has expressed concerns that his allies may face corruption investigations under the new administration of General Muhammadu Buhari. In a church service held on Sunday, Mr. Jonathan stated that his friends and former ministers may be "persecuted" as a result of his decision to concede defeat in the March elections. This move was widely praised for preventing a potential crisis in the country. General Buhari, who is set to be inaugurated on May 29, has pledged to tackle corruption in Nigeria, Africa's largest oil producer. Many Nigerians are eagerly awaiting his administration to investigate numerous corruption scandals that plagued Mr. Jonathan's government. Mr. Jonathan became president in 2010 after the death of President Umaru Musa Yar'Adua and made history by being the first Nigerian leader to relinquish power after losing an election. The former president's comments suggest that he fears his allies may be targeted in corruption probes, and he has urged them to be prepared for potential persecution. Despite his concerns, Mr. Jonathan's decision to accept defeat has been hailed as a significant step towards consolidating democracy in Nigeria. As General Buhari prepares to take office, Nigerians are watching closely to see if he will deliver on his promise to tackle corruption and bring about positive change to the country.

Mysterious Skulls Discovered in Totnes, Devon In a bizarre incident, two human skulls were discovered in Totnes, Devon, on Monday. The first skull was found by workmen behind an empty shop on Fore Street at 12:15 BST, while the second skull was later discovered on the banks of the River Dart, approximately half a mile away. According to Devon and Cornwall Police, the discoveries are not being treated as a criminal investigation at present. The police revealed that the "owner" of the first skull came forward and informed them about the presence of another skull in the area, which is frequently visited by homeless people. Upon examination, it was determined that one skull belonged to a male and the other to a female, both of whom were over 21 years old at the time of death. Notably, the female skull was better preserved, with traces of hair still present, suggesting it had been kept in a crypt-like environment. Specialist officers have dated the skulls to be over 100 years old, with further forensic analysis to be conducted to determine a more accurate date. The skulls will be sent to the Centre for Anatomy and Human Identification at the University of Dundee, where experts will attempt to calculate the time since death, potentially using radiocarbon dating. While the discoveries are not currently being treated as a criminal investigation, Totnes Police's Criminal Investigation Department is making further enquiries to uncover the origins of the mysterious skulls.

Brentford Crush Fulham 4-1 to Move Up to Fifth in the Table Brentford secured a convincing 4-1 victory over Fulham at Griffin Park, moving up to fifth in the table and leaving their opponents seven points above the relegation zone. The win marked a significant boost for the Bees, who began the day in seventh place, and has kept their promotion hopes alive. The game got off to a flying start, with Dallas scoring a fine low shot from 20 yards out in the 24th minute, beating Fulham keeper Marcus Bettinelli. The home side had earlier created a chance, with Alex Kacaniklic forcing a good save from Brentford keeper David Button. However, it was Brentford who took the lead, and they doubled their advantage in the second half through Dallas's stunning 25-yard strike into the top corner. Fulham pushed hard for an equalizer, with Cauley Woodrow forcing a save from Button with a low 25-yard strike. However, their efforts were in vain, and Brentford should have wrapped up the game shortly after the hour mark when Andre Gray fired over from close range with the goal gaping. The Cottagers were given a lifeline when Toumani Diagouraga was adjudged to have tripped James Husband in the box, and Ross McCormack scored from the spot in the 67th minute. Fulham pressed for the equalizer, with Kacaniklic's free-kick going off target, but it was Brentford who ultimately sealed the victory. In the last minute of the game, Judge curled a stunning free-kick into the top corner via the underside of the crossbar, giving Brentford a 3-1 lead. And to add insult to injury, Jota converted a pass across the box on the half-volley from 12 yards out in injury time, securing a 4-1 win for the Bees. Brentford manager Mark Warburton expressed his delight at the result, saying, "I'm really pleased. After that 15-minute spell, I thought we were very good. It keeps us going. We are in contention, be that for top or the play-offs, we are still in with a chance." Warburton also emphasized the importance of focusing on his own team's performance, rather than worrying about other teams. Fulham manager Kit Symons, on the other hand, was left to rue his team's mistakes, saying, "Ultimately, people just look at the scoreline at the end of the game, and 4-1 looks like a hammering. But the actual fact of the matter is that it wasn't. We were well in the game, but obviously, we didn't get anything out of it. We shot ourselves in the foot for the first two goals." The defeat leaves Fulham with just one win from their past six games, and Symons acknowledged that his team has work to do to avoid relegation trouble. "We are not out of it," he said. "We have work to do, especially with Millwall winning today." The Cottagers will need to regroup and refocus if they are to climb away from danger and secure their place in the league.

California has taken a significant step towards introducing driverless autonomous vehicles on its roadways. The state's Department of Motor Vehicles has proposed new rules to allow testing of autonomous vehicles without a human driver present. Currently, 27 manufacturers, including Google's Waymo, have permits to test autonomous vehicles, but a human must always be in the car. Waymo reported 124 human interventions in 636,000 miles driven in 2016, down from 341 in 2015. The proposed framework outlines testing procedures and requirements for manufacturers to make vehicles available outside of tests. The public can provide written feedback until April 24. According to Jean Shiomoto, director of the California DMV, this is a crucial step towards eventually allowing driverless vehicles on California roads.

Liverpool FC is set to announce the signing of Southampton midfielder Adam Lallana, 26, after the England international completes his medical and formalities this weekend. The Reds had initially seen two bids rejected for Lallana before the World Cup, but resumed talks upon his return from Brazil. Lallana will be joining former teammate Rickie Lambert at Anfield, following Lambert's move to the club earlier in the transfer window. The midfielder has spent 14 years at Southampton, joining the club at the age of 12 from Bournemouth, who will receive 25% of the transfer fee due to a sell-on clause. The sale of Lallana will bring Southampton's summer transfer earnings to £56m, following the departures of Luke Shaw to Manchester United for £27m and Rickie Lambert to Liverpool for £4m. Executive director Les Reed has assured that new manager Ronald Koeman will be able to reinvest the revenues generated from the transfers into the team. Liverpool has already secured the signing of Emre Can from Bayer Leverkusen, and is rumored to be targeting Sevilla left-back Alberto Moreno and Belgian forward Divock Origi. The arrival of Lallana is expected to strengthen the Reds' midfield, and his experience at the international level will be a valuable asset to the team.

Delhi Toddler Fighting for Life After Brutal Attack Raises Fresh Concerns Over Women's Safety A horrific attack on a toddler in the Indian capital has sparked fresh concerns over women's safety in Delhi. The two-year-old girl, who was found unconscious near her home in a poor neighborhood in north Delhi on Friday night, is currently in intensive care after undergoing surgery for extensive injuries. According to the family, the child was lured away by a group of men who offered her food or sweets. The deputy commissioner of police, Vijay Singh, told the BBC that no arrests have been made yet, and an investigation is underway. The Delhi commissioner for women, Swati Maliwal, who visited the child in hospital, described her injuries as "horrific" and called for swift action to bring the perpetrators to justice. The incident has raised disturbing questions about the safety of women and children in Delhi, a city that was shocked by the brutal gang rape and murder of a student in 2012. The attack led to widespread protests and the introduction of new anti-rape laws, but despite these efforts, brutal sexual attacks against women and children continue to be reported across the country. The family of the toddler lives in a small, cramped house near a railway track, where locals often relieve themselves due to a lack of proper toilets. Women in the area say they are afraid to let their children out of their sight, fearing they may be taken away by unknown men. The presence of liquor shops in the area is also a concern, as drunk men often tease and harass women who venture out to use the makeshift toilets. The attack on the toddler is just one of many cases of rape and sexual assault that have been reported in Delhi this year. According to police records, over 1,500 cases of rape have been recorded so far, but many more are believed to go unreported. In July, a man was arrested for confessing to sexually assaulting and murdering 30 children in and around Delhi, highlighting the need for greater vigilance and action to protect women and children. As the toddler fights for her life in hospital, her family and community are demanding justice and calling for greater efforts to ensure women's safety in Delhi. The incident is a stark reminder of the need for continued action to address the deep-seated social and cultural attitudes that perpetuate violence against women and children in India.

The Royal Air Force (RAF) has bid farewell to the Tornado, its key fast attack jet for nearly 40 years. A flypast and simulated ground attack marked the final formal sortie of 15 Squadron, the training unit for the Tornado. The squadron is the last of four to be disbanded as the aircraft is replaced by Eurofighter Typhoons. Based at Lossiemouth since the 1990s, the Tornado's distinctive noise will be missed in Moray's skies. The multi-role aircraft saw combat in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Libya. The Eurofighter Typhoons will now form the Quick Reaction Force, tasked with intercepting unidentified aircraft in British airspace. The Tornado's retirement marks the end of an era for the RAF, as it welcomes a new generation of fighter jets. The Typhoons will provide enhanced capabilities, ensuring the UK's airspace remains secure.

Violence Erupts on Turkish-Syrian Border as IS Militants Advance on Kobane The Turkish-Syrian border has descended into chaos as Islamic State (IS) militants continue their relentless advance on the strategic town of Kobane. The situation has become increasingly volatile, with clashes between Turkish security forces and Kurdish activists, as well as refugees, escalating into violent confrontations. The latest incident involved a team of journalists who were fired upon by police with tear gas canisters, one of which smashed into their vehicle, filling it with gas and starting a fire. The incident occurred near Kobane, where fierce fighting has been ongoing between IS militants and Syrian Kurds defending the town. The Kurdish community in Turkey is outraged at what they perceive as Turkish inaction in the face of the IS onslaught, and their anger boiled over into violent protests on the border. The Turkish authorities, attempting to maintain order, responded with a heavy-handed approach, using volleys of tear gas to disperse the crowds. As the situation spiralled out of control, a rocket landed in a house on the Turkish side of the border, prompting the authorities to evacuate the area. However, their methods were widely criticized as excessive, with Kurdish activists being pursued across fields by white clouds of tear gas. The violence showed no signs of abating, with angry Kurdish youths in the nearby town of Suruc blocking roads and brandishing stones, spoiling for a fight. Meanwhile, reports from the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights indicate that a female Kurdish fighter has carried out a suicide attack on IS positions in the east of Kobane, killing a number of jihadists. The US-led coalition has been conducting air strikes on IS positions in the area, which appear to have slowed the militants' advance. However, IS has captured part of a strategically important hill, which would give them a significant advantage in their bid to take the town. The fate of Kobane hangs in the balance, with over 160,000 Syrians, mainly Kurds, having fled across the border since the IS offensive began nearly three weeks ago. Capturing the town would give IS unbroken control of a long stretch of the Syrian-Turkish border, a prospect that has sparked widespread concern. Turkey, which has pledged to prevent Kobane from falling to the militants, has come under intense criticism for its perceived inaction. Its parliament has authorized military operations against militants in Iraq and Syria, but so far, no action has been taken to prevent the fighting. The reason for Turkey's reluctance to lend support to the Kurdish forces in Kobane is believed to be their alliance with the PKK, a banned terrorist organization in Turkey. The situation is complex and delicate, with Turkey walking a fine line between preventing the fall of Kobane and avoiding being drawn into a conflict with the IS militants. As the violence continues to escalate, it remains to be seen how the situation will unfold, but one thing is certain – the fate of Kobane and the stability of the region hang precariously in the balance.

A Scottish man named Steve Bannon has found himself at the center of a Twitter storm, as he's constantly being mistaken for Stephen Bannon, the former chief strategist to US President Donald Trump. To clear up the confusion, Steve, who lives in England, has updated his Twitter bio to "Nothing to do with US politics or running the White House" and changed his banner to "This is not the Steve Bannon you're looking for." Despite his phone being "melted" by the sheer volume of tweets, Steve has been patiently responding to messages intended for his American namesake. He's been directing people to "go after the other guy" and "get the right guy," and has even seen the humor in the situation. Steve, originally from East Kilbride, told BBC Scotland News that his younger girls think the attention from social media has been hilarious. This isn't the first time a Scot has been mistaken for someone involved in US politics. Last November, a Glasgow woman named Kellyanne Conway was confused with her US namesake, a Republican Party campaign manager who worked at Trump HQ. The Scottish Kellyanne received strange emails, including one thanking her for "boarding the Trump train!" and was forced to issue a disclaimer on her Facebook profile warning that she was the "wrong Kellyanne Conway!" Steve Bannon's experience serves as a reminder of the importance of verifying identities online, especially in the age of social media.

Myndtown Church in Shropshire has been awarded a significant grant from the Heritage Lottery Fund to undergo much-needed restoration work. The Grade II-listed building will receive £20,600 for the development phase, which is expected to last up to one year, and a further £202,500 for construction. This investment will enable the church to address essential repairs, including a new roof, stonework repairs, and re-rendering of interior and exterior walls, as well as the installation of underground drainage. Reverend Norman Morris, rector of Myndtown, expressed his delight at the news, highlighting the church's rich history and potential as a hub for walkers and cyclists. Despite having a small population, the church holds significant value to the community and beyond. Local fundraisers had already raised £8,000 towards the restoration scheme, demonstrating the community's commitment to preserving the historic building. John Burt, project organiser, thanked the Heritage Lottery Fund for their support, stating that without the grant, the church would likely have fallen into disrepair. He emphasized that the building's significance extends beyond its current usage, citing its largely untouched Victorian-era architecture as a unique feature. The restoration work will ensure the long-term preservation of this 800-year-old church, allowing future generations to appreciate its history and beauty.

Tragedy Strikes Swithens Farm as Young Boy Dies in Accident A devastating incident occurred at Swithens Farm in Rothwell on Friday morning, resulting in the death of a young boy. Harry Whitlam, from Wakefield, was injured at approximately 09:20 BST and airlifted to Leeds General Infirmary, where he underwent head surgery. Unfortunately, he succumbed to his injuries and passed away on Friday night. A 48-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of drinking and driving and causing death by dangerous driving. He has been bailed pending further investigations. The farm's owners have described the incident as a "tragic accident" that occurred on the working part of the farm. The community is in shock, with local MP Alec Shelbrooke expressing his condolences to the boy's family. "The community in Rothwell is very close and friendly, and these tragic events will have sent a shockwave through the local community," he said. Jim Reid, father of the farm's co-owner, added that everyone on the site is "very, very upset" and that their thoughts are with Harry's parents and family. West Yorkshire Police are continuing their investigation into the incident and appeal for anyone with information to come forward. Despite the tragedy, Swithens Farm remains open to visitors, with the owners confirming that the shop, open farm, cafe, and play barn are still operational.

G20 Summit Overshadowed by Paris Attacks, Syria Conflict The G20 summit in Turkey has been dominated by discussions on the recent Paris attacks and the ongoing conflict in Syria. European Council President Donald Tusk urged Russia to focus its efforts on combating Islamic State (IS) militants, rather than targeting moderate Syrian opposition groups. Tusk's comments come as Russia continues to carry out air strikes in Syria, which it claims are aimed at IS, but many in the West suspect are intended to prop up Moscow's ally, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad. The two-day summit in Antalya, primarily focused on economic matters, has been overshadowed by the deadly attacks in Paris, which left 129 people dead. IS has claimed responsibility for the assaults, and Tusk emphasized the need for cooperation between the US and Russia in their efforts to combat the militant group in Syria. "We need not only more cooperation, but also more good will, especially from Russian action on the ground in Syria," he said. US President Barack Obama also addressed the summit, condemning the Paris attacks as an "attack on the civilized world" and pledging to "redouble" efforts to bring an end to Syria's civil war. Obama met with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the summit, despite their differences on how to resolve the conflict. The US and its allies insist that Assad must step down as part of a political solution to the crisis. The conflict in Syria has contributed to a massive refugee crisis, with millions fleeing the country and seeking safety in Europe. Tusk warned that Russian operations in Syria could lead to a new wave of refugees, and expressed concern that this process may have already begun.

Raith Rovers have extended their unbeaten run to six games with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Morton at Cappielow. The decisive goal came early in the second half, courtesy of James Craigen's seventh strike of the season. The win sees Raith move 13 points clear of their opponents, who sit fifth in the Scottish Championship table with just five games remaining. The visitors started strongly, utilizing the long throw capabilities of Rory McKeown to cause problems for the Morton defence. Mark Stewart and Ross Callachan both had opportunities to open the scoring, but their efforts were thwarted by the home side's goalkeeping and defending. As the half progressed, Morton began to gain the upper hand, with Bobby Barr and Stefan McCluskey both having shots blocked by the Raith defence. The second half began with a bang, as Craigen pounced on a through pass from Callachan to give Raith the lead. The midfielder's shot went through the legs of advancing goalkeeper Derek Gaston, leaving the home side reeling. Morton pushed hard for a leveller, with McCluskey and Declan McManus both having efforts saved or deflected wide. The home side also had a penalty appeal turned down, as Craig Barr was deemed not to have handled the ball inside the box. Despite the pressure, Raith held firm to secure a valuable win. The result means that Rovers have beaten Morton in all four meetings this term, a impressive feat that will give them confidence heading into the final stretch of the season. With five games remaining, Raith will be looking to maintain their momentum and finish the season on a high note. For Morton, the defeat is a setback, but they will be determined to bounce back and secure a strong finish to the campaign.

Andy Murray's Struggles Continue as French Open Looms World number one Andy Murray is facing a crisis of form as the French Open approaches. The 30-year-old suffered a disappointing defeat to Fabio Fognini in Rome, losing 6-2 6-4. This latest setback means Murray has won only one title from eight events in 2017, a far cry from his impressive run of five consecutive victories at the end of last year. Murray's struggles on clay have been evident, with the Scot reaching only one semi-final in his last four events on the surface. His movement, which has been a key factor in his success in recent years, has been hindered, and he has found it difficult to create chances for himself. Against Fognini, ranked 29th in the world, Murray was unable to find his rhythm, suffering a fifth defeat in 10 matches. Despite his difficulties, Murray insists that the pressure of being world number one is not a contributing factor. However, he acknowledges that his form has been a long way from where he would like it to be. "I'm just not playing good tennis and need to try to work out how to turn it around," he said. "I believe I will." Murray's last title came in Dubai in February, and he will be looking to regain his momentum as he heads to Roland Garros, where he was runner-up to Novak Djokovic last year. Murray's coach, Ivan Lendl, will join the team later this week as they prepare for the grand slam event in Paris. The Scot will need to improve significantly if he is to mount a serious challenge for the title. With nearly 4000 points to defend at the French Open, The Queen's Club, and Wimbledon, Murray's ranking is under threat. His successful run at the end of last year means he has a significant number of points to defend, and a poor performance in the coming months could see him lose his position at the top of the rankings. BBC Sport tennis correspondent Russell Fuller believes that Murray will need to play exceptionally well to remain at the top of the rankings come the autumn. With the tennis ranking system calculated on an annual basis, Murray's recent losses in Madrid and Rome have already seen him shed a significant number of points. As the French Open approaches, Murray will be looking to turn his form around and regain his position as one of the dominant forces in men's tennis. The question is, can he do it? Only time will tell.

A nationwide strike is underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo, as opposition parties pressure President Joseph Kabila to revive a collapsed political deal. The deal, brokered by the Catholic church, aimed to create a transitional government and pave the way for a general election. However, the agreement fell apart over disagreements on power-sharing, including the appointment of a prime minister. President Kabila, whose term ended last November, has refused to step down, citing financial and logistical difficulties in organizing elections. The opposition coalition, Rassemblement, has called for the strike, blaming the government for the collapse of the deal. Security forces have been deployed to protect businesses that have chosen to remain open, despite the strike. The Catholic church has urged President Kabila to intervene and salvage the political process. The DR Congo has a history of instability and has never experienced a smooth transfer of power since gaining independence in 1960. The strike is the latest attempt by opposition parties to push for democratic reforms and a peaceful transition of power. The situation remains tense, with the opposition demanding that President Kabila honor the original agreement and step down to allow for free and fair elections.

British sprinter Darren Campbell has come out in support of a radical proposal to reset European athletics records in an effort to restore trust in the sport following a series of high-profile doping scandals. The plan, put forward by European Athletics, would see existing records reassessed against strict criteria, potentially resulting in the erasure of records set by athletes who have been implicated in doping. Campbell, who won Olympic silver in 2000 and gold in 2004, could potentially lose his 4x100m European record from 1999 if the proposal is implemented. However, he has stated that he is willing to "sacrifice whatever it takes" to save the sport and restore its credibility. "I've lost medals in the past due to team-mates being involved in doping scandals, and while it's tough to accept, I believe it's for the greater good," he told BBC Radio 5 live. Not all British athletes share Campbell's views, however. Paula Radcliffe, who faces losing her 2003 marathon world record, has spoken out against the proposal, stating that clean athletes like herself are being unfairly penalized for the actions of cheats. Colin Jackson, the 60m indoor hurdles record holder, has also expressed his opposition, arguing that clean athletes are still in the majority and should not be caught up in the fallout. Despite the controversy surrounding the proposal, Campbell believes that tough decisions need to be made to restore trust in the sport. "Records are there to be broken, and some of those records can't be broken unless you're taking drugs," he said. "The punishment has to fit the crime, and the level of pain these people have put us through - we have to do something." The proposal will be put to the world governing body, the IAAF, when its council meets in August. Campbell has called for the governing bodies to provide more details on how the proposal will be implemented and how it will help to save the sport. "We need to know how it's going to save the sport," he said. "We don't want to end up right back here in 20 years. It's radical, it's a recommendation, but tell me how it's going to save the sport? That's the important thing."

One Direction's surprise release of their new single "Drag Me Down" has taken the music world by storm. The track, which debuted on Friday, has already surpassed its closest competitor, Little Mix's "Black Magic", with more than double the sales. According to the Official Charts Company, "Drag Me Down" is dominating the charts, with an average of 3.11 million daily plays on Spotify. Industry experts estimate that the song is earning around $21,700 per day, which could translate to approximately $152,000 in its opening week. This impressive feat comes just two days after former band member Zayn Malik announced his solo record deal. The song's success is a significant milestone for the band, now a foursome, and showcases their enduring popularity. Meanwhile, the midweek chart has seen a re-entry from the late Cilla Black, with her classic hit "Anyone Who Had A Heart" climbing to number 91. The song is expected to rise further as the week progresses. In the album charts, The Maccabees are currently leading Lianne La Havas by a narrow margin of just over 300 copies. Fans can tune in to BBC Radio 1's Official Chart Show to stay up-to-date on the latest music rankings.

Horizon Nuclear Power has reached a significant milestone in its plans to build a new nuclear power plant at Wylfa on Anglesey, as the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) begins a 19-month assessment of the site. The £8bn project, owned by Hitachi Ltd, is a major step forward for the company, which hopes to have all necessary permissions in place by 2018. The ONR's assessment will evaluate the suitability of the site, the organization, and the reactor designs, ensuring that the project meets the highest safety standards. Horizon Nuclear's safety and licensing director, Anthony Webb, stated that the company is focused on providing the ONR with "confidence in our ability to safely deliver this crucial project." He added that the company has a proven technology, experienced leadership, and is rapidly building the necessary capability and organization to ensure success. The site licence application is one of several key consents required before the project can proceed. Horizon is also preparing for a final public consultation in the summer, followed by a Development Consent Order request to the UK Government's Planning Inspectorate. Additionally, the advance boiling water reactors planned for the new power plant are undergoing the final stage of a Generic Design Assessment, which is expected to be completed by the end of 2017. The ONR's deputy chief inspector, Mike Finnerty, noted that this is the first licence application for a new nuclear power station since 2011, and that the organization has been working closely with Horizon to ensure that the company meets the robust requirements expected of a nuclear site licensee. If all planning and safety regulations are approved, construction on the new site could begin as early as 2020, with the potential to generate significant economic benefits for the region.

Arsenal midfielder Aaron Ramsey is set to miss the next three weeks of action due to a hamstring injury. The 25-year-old international was forced off in the second half of Arsenal's opening Premier League defeat against Liverpool. According to Gunners boss Arsene Wenger, Ramsey will be sidelined until after the international break, ruling him out of league matches against Leicester and Watford. The injury is a blow to Wales manager Chris Coleman, who is already dealing with other fitness concerns ahead of the team's upcoming qualifiers. Crystal Palace midfielder Jonny Williams will miss the opening three qualifiers with an ankle injury, and is expected to be out for up to 10 weeks. Striker Hal Robson-Kanu, who scored twice in Euro 2016, is also a concern due to his current lack of match fitness, having been released by Reading and not played since the semi-final. Ramsey was a standout performer for Wales during their successful Euro 2016 campaign, earning a spot in Uefa's official team of the tournament. His absence will be felt, but Coleman will be hoping he can return to full fitness after the international break and help Wales in their upcoming qualifiers. With several key players struggling with injuries, Coleman faces a challenging task in preparing his team for the upcoming matches.

Lewis Hamilton Dominates First Practice Session at Hungaroring Amidst Drama The first practice session of the Hungarian Grand Prix got off to a dramatic start as Sergio Perez's car flipped and landed upside down after a rear suspension failure. The incident, which occurred at Turn 11 of the Hungaroring, sent shockwaves through the paddock, reminding everyone of the ever-present dangers involved in Formula 1. Thankfully, Perez emerged unscathed and was able to conduct media interviews just minutes after the crash. The Mexican driver's car suffered a rear suspension failure, causing him to spin out of control and hit the wall. The impact was severe, and the car flipped over, coming to rest upside down. Perez was quick to reassure his team that he was unhurt, and an investigation into the cause of the failure is currently underway. Despite the drama, the session continued, and it was Mercedes' Lewis Hamilton who dominated the proceedings. The world champion set a blistering pace, ending the 90-minute session 0.109 seconds ahead of his teammate Nico Rosberg. Hamilton's performance was impressive, and he was two seconds clear of the field after the first 20 minutes. Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen finished third, 0.671 seconds slower than Hamilton, while Red Bull's Daniel Ricciardo was fourth. The second Red Bull of Daniil Kvyat was sixth, ahead of Ferrari's Sebastian Vettel. Toro Rosso's Carlos Sainz, despite Perez's crash, finished eighth, while Williams's Valtteri Bottas and Toro Rosso's Max Verstappen completed the top 10. The session was not without its other incidents, as Raikkonen's front wing dropped off his car coming out of Turn 12, leaving debris on the track and puncturing the Ferrari's front tire. The incident brought out the red flag, but the session was restarted with just a few minutes to go, allowing some teams to sneak in a few extra laps. Lotus, who had earlier solved a financial dispute with tyre supplier Pirelli, had a limited outing, with Pastor Maldonado finishing 17th and reserve driver Jolyon Palmer 20th. At Manor, reserve driver Fabio Leimer had his first outing on a grand prix weekend, finishing 19th, about a second slower than teammate Will Stevens. The incident involving Perez was a stark reminder of the risks involved in F1, coming just three days after the funeral of Jules Bianchi, who died last week from injuries sustained in a crash at last October's Japanese Grand Prix. The teams and drivers are all carrying tributes to the Frenchman on their cars and helmets at this weekend's race. As the teams head into the second practice session, they will be looking to fine-tune their cars and make the necessary adjustments to challenge Hamilton and Mercedes. With the pace of the session being so intense, it promises to be an exciting weekend of racing at the Hungaroring.

Tragic Death of a Young Woman with a Dream to Become a Midwife On July 7, 2005, a devastating act of terrorism shook the city of London, claiming the lives of 52 innocent people. Among the victims was 24-year-old Emily Jenkins, a vibrant and caring young woman who had her whole life ahead of her. Emily's dream of becoming a midwife was tragically cut short when she boarded the southbound Piccadilly Line Tube at King's Cross station, heading towards Russell Square, where a bomb exploded. Born in Hammersmith, west London, Emily was the youngest of four children. From a young age, she showed signs of the compassionate and nurturing person she would become. At school, she would often befriend the quietest or most vulnerable members of her class, demonstrating a natural ability to care for others. Her love of dance led her to take ballet classes, which she continued until she was 18, passing all her exams with high grades. As she grew older, Emily's rebellious streak began to emerge, particularly during her A-levels. However, this spirit of adventure and independence also led her to take a gap year in South America, where she learned to speak Spanish and developed valuable life skills. Her travels took her to Salamanca in western Spain, where she spent a year, and later to Australia, where she lived with a group of self-sufficient individuals in Melbourne. Despite her love of travel and adventure, Emily eventually returned to the UK, settling in London and finding work at a project management company, AYH. She quickly became a valued member of the team, rising to the position of PA to her boss. Emily's family and friends remember her as a kind, sociable, and popular person, who adored her role as an aunt to her two nieces. Her parents, Sarah and Nick Jenkins, recalled her enthusiasm and deep passion for her family and friends, saying, "She had a love of life and a great ability to bring out the best in people." Emily's dream of becoming a midwife was a testament to her caring nature and desire to help others. Although she did not have the necessary qualifications, she was determined to pursue her goal. Her former classmate, Rachael Oliver-Redgate, remembered Emily as a lively and funny girl, always surrounded by friends, and extremely kind and caring. "She would have made a great midwife," Rachael said. The inquest into Emily's death heard from her parents, who described their daughter as a young woman on a path of fulfillment when her life was tragically cut short. Emily's story is a poignant reminder of the devastating consequences of terrorism and the importance of cherishing the time we have with loved ones. Her memory will live on through her family and friends, who will always remember her enthusiasm, kindness, and deep passion for life.

A stage adaptation of The Hunger Games is set to launch in a purpose-built theatre next to Wembley Stadium in London. The innovative production will be created by Robin de Levita, known for his work on a Dutch stage show about Anne Frank. The Hunger Games film franchise has taken in over $1.5 billion at the worldwide box office, with the latest installment, Mockingjay - Part 1, releasing this month. The stage show will bring to life the dystopian tales of Suzanne Collins, following heroine Katniss Everdeen. While details are scarce, Tim Phelan of Lionsgate promises a "uniquely immersive experience" for fans. De Levita adds that the theatre is an ideal medium to explore the depth of Collins' writing. The new theatre will be constructed specifically for the production, although further details have not been disclosed. The adaptation is expected to provide a new and exciting way for fans to experience the beloved series.

Police Investigation Underway into Possible Poisoning of 18-Year-Old Tennis Player An investigation is currently underway by Scotland Yard into the alleged poisoning of 18-year-old tennis player Gabriella Taylor, who spent four days in intensive care after being diagnosed with a rare strain of leptospirosis, known as Weil's disease. Taylor, from Southampton, was admitted to hospital after falling ill during her girls' quarter-final match at Wimbledon last month. According to her mother, Milena Taylor, it is "impossible" for her daughter to have simply become ill, given that she was staying in a "completely healthy environment". The police are investigating an allegation of poisoning with the "intent to endanger life" or cause grievous bodily harm. However, medical experts have expressed skepticism about the possibility of deliberate poisoning, citing the rarity of the disease and the difficulty of intentionally cultivating the bacteria. Dr. Anna Checkley, from the Hospital for Tropical Diseases, stated that she had "never heard of it being used as a poisoning agent". Leptospirosis is a bacteria that can be transmitted through rat urine, and people in the UK usually contract the infection after coming into contact with contaminated water. Dr. Checkley noted that the disease is "pretty unusual" in the UK, with only 50-100 cases reported per year, mostly among workers who come into contact with contaminated water or animals. Professor Elizabeth Wellington, an environmental microbiologist at the University of Warwick, also expressed doubts about the possibility of intentional poisoning, stating that it would require a high level of expertise to intentionally grow the bacteria. She described claims that the disease could be used to deliberately poison someone as "a bit laughable", suggesting that Taylor's illness was likely a case of bad luck, contracted through contaminated water. The police investigation is ongoing, with no arrests made yet. The incident is alleged to have taken place at an address in Wimbledon between July 1 and 10, and Taylor was taken ill on July 6. As the investigation continues, Taylor's mother has expressed concern about her daughter's health, stating that she is "still not 100%". The rare and serious nature of Weil's disease has raised concerns about the potential risks of contracting the disease, and the need for further awareness and education about the risks of leptospirosis.

Chancellor George Osborne is scrambling to find alternative ways to save £4 billion after the House of Lords rejected his plans to cut working tax credits. The move has sparked a heated debate within the government, with Treasury officials exploring options to increase penalties for claimants who take on extra work. However, Work and Pensions Secretary Iain Duncan Smith is said to be strongly opposed to such measures, which he believes would undermine the principles of Universal Credit. Universal Credit is a new benefit system designed to support people on low incomes or out of work, replacing six existing benefits. At its core is the principle that those who take on extra work should not see their benefits reduced disproportionately. Currently, for every extra pound earned over a set threshold, Universal Credit claimants lose 65p in benefits. However, Treasury officials are considering increasing this "taper rate" to 75p in the pound, which could raise £1.5 billion to £2 billion. But Work and Pensions officials argue that such an increase would have a devastating impact on the effectiveness of Universal Credit, which is intended to encourage people to take on work without fear of losing their benefits. They claim that increasing the taper rate would create a disincentive for people to work extra hours, undermining the very purpose of the benefit system. Shadow Chancellor John McDonnell has slammed the proposal, saying that it would create another "work penalty" for low- and middle-income families. He called for a full reversal of the Chancellor's plans to cut working tax credits, which would take £1,350 a year from over three million working families. "The reality is that it would simply create yet another work penalty for low and middle-paid families, which is what caused this huge cross-party calamity in the first place," he said. An ally of Mr. Duncan Smith, who did not want to be named, told the BBC that the Work and Pensions Secretary had made it clear that increasing the taper rate was not an acceptable solution. "Iain is clear that increasing the taper rate of Universal Credit from 65p to 75p for every pound earned over the limit is not where you should go to find the money that would have come from tax credit savings," the ally said. Instead, Mr. Duncan Smith is said to have suggested alternative options for finding savings, including a proposal put forward by Baroness Philippa Stroud, a former aide to the Work and Pensions Secretary. In a paper published this week for the Centre for Social Justice, Baroness Stroud argued that the Chancellor should not touch the Universal Credit taper rate if he is looking for savings. The Treasury has refused to comment on the proposals ahead of the Autumn Statement later this month. However, it is clear that the government is facing a major challenge in finding alternative ways to save £4 billion. With the House of Lords having rejected the original plans to cut working tax credits, the Chancellor must now find new ways to balance the books without undermining the principles of Universal Credit. The coming weeks will be crucial in determining the fate of the benefit system and the millions of families who rely on it.

Schapelle Corby, the Australian woman convicted of drug smuggling in 2005, has been granted parole after serving nine years of her 20-year prison sentence. The 36-year-old former beauty student was found with 4.1kg of marijuana in her bag at Denpasar airport in Bali in 2004, and has always maintained her innocence. The news of Corby's parole was announced by Indonesian Justice and Human Rights Minister Amir Syamsuddin at a press conference, where he revealed that Corby's application was one of 1,291 approved for parole. Syamsuddin emphasized that Corby had not been given special treatment, stating that "parole is not a matter of policy and not a minister's generosity. It's the right of inmates. We're a dignified country and we uphold the laws." Corby's case has generated intense interest in Australia, with many people debating her guilt or innocence and criticizing the length of her sentence. A poll in 2012 found that 43% of Australians believed she should be granted clemency, despite 60% agreeing that she was guilty as charged. The case has also led to criticism of Indonesia's tough stance on drug smuggling, with some arguing that Corby's sentence was too harsh. Corby's mental health is said to have deteriorated during her time in jail, and she will be required to serve out her parole period in Bali. She is expected to live with her sister, Mercedes, on the Indonesian island. However, she will not be able to return to Australia until 2017, as she is required to stay in Indonesia for an extra year after her sentence ends in 2016 to comply with her parole conditions. The news of Corby's parole has sparked a frenzy of media interest, with large numbers of Australian journalists gathered outside Kerobokan prison in Bali, where Corby has been held. There are reports that Australian media outlets are competing to pay for Corby's story following her release, with some offering significant sums of money for exclusive interviews. Not everyone is happy about Corby's release, however. Some Indonesian MPs have spoken out against her early parole, arguing that it is inconsistent with Jakarta's attempts to crack down on the drug trade. The MPs claim that Corby's release sends the wrong message and undermines the country's efforts to combat drug smuggling. Despite the controversy surrounding her case, Corby's release is seen as a significant development in a saga that has captivated Australia for over a decade. Since Lindy Chamberlain, who was jailed and eventually acquitted of killing her own daughter in 1980, there has not been a more divisive female Australian inmate, nor such a feast of lurid headlines and allegations. As Corby prepares to begin her new life in Bali, she will undoubtedly face intense scrutiny from the media and the public. However, for now, she will be focused on rebuilding her life and adjusting to freedom after nearly a decade behind bars. The prison governor has said that Corby could be released as early as Monday afternoon, once the correct paperwork is received, marking the beginning of a new chapter in her life.

Wakefield Council has secured a significant grant from the Heritage Lottery Fund to unlock previously inaccessible areas of Pontefract Castle. The £3.5m project will restore historic paths and platforms, allowing visitors to explore the Sally Port and Swillington Tower areas for the first time since the mid-1600s. This major restoration work could ultimately lead to the castle's removal from English Heritage's'at risk' register. The castle, built in the 11th Century, is steeped in history, having been a Lancastrian stronghold during the Wars of the Roses and the site of King Richard II's imprisonment and murder. The grant will also be used to extend the arts and crafts area, incorporating a new shop and café. Wakefield Council and English Heritage will provide additional funding to support the project. Councillor Peter Box, leader of the council, expressed his delight at the funding, stating that it will "put Pontefract on the map for tourists" and bring economic benefits to the town. The project aims to build on the castle's existing popularity, attracting more visitors and showcasing its rich history. With work underway, Pontefract Castle is set to become an even more compelling destination for history enthusiasts and tourists alike.

Lewis Hamilton has been forced to miss a tyre testing session due to a minor foot issue. The Mercedes driver was scheduled to test the 2017 Pirelli tyres on Wednesday, but team-mate Nico Rosberg took his place instead. Hamilton's reserve driver, Pascal Wehrlein, also replaced him for Thursday's test. According to Mercedes, Hamilton experienced discomfort in his foot after a training session on Tuesday. The team decided it was best for him to rest and undergo physiotherapy to ensure he is in top shape for the upcoming US Grand Prix in Austin on October 23. Hamilton is currently 33 points behind his team-mate Nico Rosberg in the world championship with four races remaining. Despite the setback, Mercedes has stated that there is "no concern" over Hamilton's availability for the Austin race. The three-time world champion will be looking to close the gap on Rosberg and get back on track after a tumultuous weekend in Japan.

FanDuel, the fantasy sports firm, has welcomed new legislation in New York that clarifies the legality of its activities. The company was forced to stop operating in the state in November after regulators deemed its operations to be illegal gambling. However, since January, eight US states have passed laws that recognize fantasy sports as a legitimate activity, paving the way for FanDuel's return to the New York market. The legislation is a significant victory for FanDuel, which claims to have six million registered users across the US and Canada. New York is one of the company's biggest markets, and its technology platform allows sports fans to pick fantasy teams from real players and follow their performances. FanDuel's chief executive, Nigel Eccles, praised the move, saying that sports fans in the state had played a crucial role in lobbying lawmakers to support the company's case. According to Eccles, over 110,000 letters and nearly 3,000 calls were made to lawmakers by fans backing FanDuel. The company's future had been uncertain due to legal hurdles in several states, with Eccles warning that it may not be able to continue as a going concern. However, the new legislation has provided a significant boost, and FanDuel is now poised to resume operations in New York. The company has also expanded its reach to the UK, launching a new one-day fantasy football platform focused on the English Premier League. With its headquarters in New York and offices in Edinburgh and Glasgow, FanDuel is well-positioned to capitalize on the growing demand for fantasy sports.

A devastating crash on the M1 in Leicestershire in 2014 has led to a stark warning about the dangers of using mobile phones while driving. Christy George, 38, from Hucknall, was jailed for five years and banned from driving for 10 years after her car crashed into a lorry, causing a horrific eight-vehicle pile-up. The collision resulted in the death of Murray Simpson, from London, and left Liese Bowers-Straw, from Nottinghamshire, with severe injuries, including a broken neck and brain damage. The incident occurred when George became distracted while using her phone, and her car collided with a lorry, which then crashed through to the opposite carriageway. The lorry's load of beer barrels spilled onto the road, and it crashed into a BMW traveling in the opposite direction. Bowers-Straw, who was involved in the crash, has spoken out about the traumatic experience, saying it has completely changed her life. She is now a "prisoner in her own home" and struggles to leave due to the severity of her injuries. The release of a warning film by Leicestershire Police, featuring the incident, comes as the government announces plans to double penalty points and fines for drivers caught using handheld mobile phones next year. Detective Constable Pete Davies, who investigated the collision, described it as the "largest collision site" he had ever seen, and emphasized the devastating consequences of George's actions, saying someone died and Bowers-Straw was left with "appalling injuries" due to her selfishness. The incident serves as a harrowing reminder of the dangers of using mobile phones while driving and the importance of staying focused on the road.

UK Sends Additional Aid to Nepal as Earthquake Death Toll Continues to Rise The UK government has announced plans to send nearly 20,000 more shelter kits to Nepal as part of its ongoing aid efforts in response to the devastating earthquake that struck the country on April 25. The move comes as aid agencies work tirelessly to deliver emergency supplies to the thousands of people displaced by the disaster. According to International Development Secretary Justine Greening, the majority of shelter kits were already in place before the earthquake hit, allowing for the rapid provision of temporary homes to thousands of people within 24 hours of the quake. Ms Greening praised the UK's search and rescue workers for their heroic efforts, saying they had "saved many lives" in the aftermath of the disaster. The 7.8-magnitude earthquake has had a catastrophic impact on Nepal, triggering avalanches and mudslides, and reducing entire villages to rubble. The death toll has now surpassed 7,500 and continues to climb, with at least one Briton confirmed to have died in the tragedy. The UN estimates that a staggering eight million people have been affected by the earthquake, with 2.8 million people displaced from their homes. Ms Greening emphasized the importance of providing shelter to those affected, particularly with the monsoon season approaching. "Our pre-positioned shelter kits meant that within 24 hours of the earthquake, British aid was reaching communities who had been hit hard and providing temporary homes to thousands of people across Nepal," she said. "Ahead of the monsoon season, we are delivering thousands more to help the Nepalese people cope as they recover from this tragic disaster." The UK's 60-strong international search and rescue team, which has been working tirelessly to locate people trapped in the rubble, is now returning home as the Nepalese government has announced the end of the search and rescue effort. The focus has shifted to providing aid to those left homeless, with a emphasis on delivering shelter, clean water, and food before the monsoon season arrives. The UK public has responded generously to the disaster, with a UK Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) public appeal raising over £33 million to date. The UK government has also committed £17.5 million in humanitarian aid. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office (FCO) is working to establish whether any other British nationals were among the dead, and has provided practical assistance to over 350 British nationals in Nepal, arranging flights out of the country for around 150. Among those still missing is 23-year-old architecture student Matt Carapiet, from Bearsted, Kent, who was trekking through Langtang Valley when the earthquake struck. His family and friends are enduring an agonizing wait for news, with family friend Rob Bailey describing the situation as "a horrible feeling." The only option now is to be patient and hope that Matt was not in the village at the time of the earthquake. The thoughts of the nation are with the people of Nepal and all those affected by this tragic disaster.

A unique exhibition showcasing the portraits of five prominent UK party leaders, created from tweets about them, is set to open in central London. Birmingham artist Annemarie Wright has drawn the portraits of David Cameron, Ed Miliband, Nick Clegg, Nigel Farage, and Natalie Bennett, using a collection of tweets that range from praise to criticism. The exhibition, titled "What do you think of?", aims to capture the public's opinion on the recent general election. Wright collected the tweets by setting up a Twitter account for each leader and following relevant hashtags between November 2014 and February 2015. She then spent 30-40 hours on each portrait, drawing the leaders before overlaying the tweets on top of the images. The result is a fascinating insight into the public's perception of each leader, with opinions ranging from "vaguely complimentary to absolute condemnation". The portraits will be on display at the Woolff Gallery from April 30 to May 15. Joining the party leaders will be life-sized portraits of the Queen, Baroness Thatcher, Winston Churchill, and Nelson Mandela, composed from their famous speeches. Wright's innovative approach to art has previously caught the attention of notable figures, including Sir Alex Ferguson and Adele, who have both commissioned portraits from her. The exhibition promises to be a thought-provoking commentary on the power of social media and public opinion.

Worcestershire's Tom Fell scored his fourth first-class century to help his team gain a strong foothold in their County Championship match against Middlesex. Resuming on 195-3, Fell's 228-ball knock of 114 not out took Worcestershire past the hosts' first innings total of 309. His mature display, which included 17 boundaries, was a crucial factor in the visitors' overall score of 385. Fell's innings was a testament to his growing reputation as a talented young batsman. At just 21 years old, he showed remarkable composure and concentration, even as wickets fell around him. His partnership with Jack Shantry, who contributed an unbeaten 41, was particularly impressive, and the two batsmen added 53 runs to the total before Shantry was dismissed. Middlesex's reply got off to a disastrous start, with Sam Robson edging Charlie Morris behind for his second duck of the game. Nick Compton, however, steadied the ship with a solid 47, and Paul Stirling and Joe Burns' unbroken stand of 67 took the hosts to 140-3 at stumps. Despite this, Worcestershire will be optimistic about their chances of securing a win, particularly if they can take early wickets on the final day. Fell was understandably pleased with his performance, and credited a pre-game chat with director of cricket Steve Rhodes for helping him to refocus his approach. "I've felt like I've had quite a few starts this season without really going on to get a big score, so it was nice to do it today," he said. "Actually, I had a chat with Steve Rhodes before this game and we spoke about going back to the plans I had in the first match of the season when I got a hundred against Yorkshire." The pitch, which is becoming increasingly worn, may yet play a significant role in the outcome of the match. With variable bounce and a hint of unevenness, it could prove challenging for Middlesex's batsmen to negotiate. As Fell noted, "it was never easy out there..... there's a little bit of up-and-down bounce which is obviously good for us." With the visitors still in with a chance of securing a win, the final day of the match promises to be an intriguing one.

Australian Transport Minister Warren Truss has announced the implementation of the "rule of two" for all domestic and international passenger planes carrying 50 people or more. This move comes in response to the recent Germanwings crash, where investigators believe the co-pilot deliberately crashed the aircraft, killing all 150 on board. The new rules, which take effect immediately, require two authorized personnel to be present in the cockpit at all times. The "rule of two" is already common in the US, where cabin crew members enter the cockpit when one of the pilots is absent. Recently, airlines in Canada and New Zealand have also adopted this rule. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) has also recommended its adoption. In Australia, carriers such as Qantas, Jetstar, and Virgin Australia will be affected by the new rules. Minister Truss expects the policy to be in place within hours on major airlines. The rules will be reviewed in 12 months. This change aims to enhance safety and prevent similar incidents in the future. The Germanwings crash has raised concerns about pilot mental health and cockpit security, and the "rule of two" is seen as a step towards addressing these issues.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has confirmed that the country will hold a snap election on November 1, after Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu failed to form a coalition government following the June polls. The election was announced by the head of the election board, Sadi Guven, and comes as a result of the AK Party's loss of its 12-year majority rule. The June elections saw the pro-Kurdish HDP party make significant gains, which led to the AK Party's loss of power. The HDP's success has been seen as a major factor in the AK Party's failure to form a coalition government. President Erdogan has now asked Prime Minister Davutoglu to serve as interim PM and oversee the upcoming elections. As part of his role, Davutoglu will be responsible for forming a cabinet within the next five days. However, the constitution states that all parties should be represented in the interim administration, which could prove to be a challenge. The leader of the Kurdish Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP), Selahattin Demirtas, has stated that his party would be willing to take part in the interim government, but the main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP) and Nationalist Movement Party (MHP) have refused to do so. The CHP had initially asked for a mandate to form a new government, but President Erdogan opted for a re-run of the elections instead. This decision has raised concerns that Erdogan may be attempting to undermine the coalition talks in order to force a new vote. The June election results had appeared to block Erdogan's plans to boost the powers of the presidency in Turkey, and the AKP will need to secure 60% of seats in the new election to be able to call a referendum on presidential powers. The political uncertainty in Turkey comes amid rising violence in the region, including the recent breakdown of a two-year ceasefire with the outlawed Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). Turkish forces have carried out attacks on militants from the so-called Islamic State in Syria and have bombed Kurdish PKK camps in northern Iraq. The army reported on Tuesday that it had carried out further strikes against PKK bases in northern Iraq, killing 34 PKK members. The situation is likely to remain volatile in the lead-up to the November elections.

New Study Reveals Fair-Skinned Individuals May Need Vitamin D Supplements A recent study funded by Cancer Research UK has found that individuals with pale skin may not be able to produce enough vitamin D, even with extensive sun exposure. The research, conducted by a team at the University of Leeds, suggests that fair-skinned individuals may need to consider taking vitamin D supplements to maintain optimal levels of the essential vitamin. Vitamin D is crucial for healthy bones and teeth, and deficiency can lead to a range of health problems. While most people can get enough vitamin D through short periods of sun exposure, the study found that those with fair skin may not be able to produce sufficient amounts, even with prolonged sun exposure. In fact, the researchers found that 730 out of 1,200 participants had lower than optimal vitamin D levels, with many of these individuals having very pale, freckled skin. The study's lead author, Professor Julia Newton-Bishop, explained that people with fair skin may be less able to make and process vitamin D in the body, regardless of how much time they spend in the sun. Additionally, those who burn easily are more likely to cover up and avoid the sun, further reducing their vitamin D production. The findings suggest that fair-skinned individuals should be added to the list of groups recommended to take vitamin D supplements, which currently includes people with dark skin, the elderly, young children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and those who avoid the sun. Hazel Nunn, of Cancer Research UK, emphasized the importance of striking a balance between the benefits and harms of sun exposure, particularly for people with fair skin who are at higher risk of developing skin cancer. While it is too soon to start recommending supplements for all fair-skinned individuals, the study's findings suggest that taking 10 micrograms of vitamin D per day may be a safe and effective way to maintain optimal levels. Nunn advised that individuals concerned about their vitamin D levels should consult their doctor, who may recommend a vitamin D test. The study's results highlight the complexities of vitamin D production and the need for personalized advice. As Professor Newton-Bishop noted, "It's very difficult to give easy advice that everyone can follow. There's no one-size-fits-all." However, by taking a targeted approach to vitamin D supplementation, fair-skinned individuals can help maintain optimal levels of this essential vitamin and reduce their risk of related health problems. As research continues to uncover the nuances of vitamin D production, it is clear that a comprehensive approach to sun exposure and supplementation will be crucial in promoting public health.

Delays in Iraq Inquiry Report Publication Spark Frustration and Calls for Action The long-awaited report from the Iraq Inquiry, led by Sir John Chilcot, has been delayed once again, sparking frustration and anger among the families of soldiers who lost their lives in the conflict. The inquiry, which began in 2009, has been plagued by delays, with Sir John citing the "Maxwellisation" process as the primary reason for the hold-up. This process allows individuals facing criticism in the report to respond and provide their side of the story. In a statement released on Wednesday, Sir John expressed his understanding of the "anguish" felt by the families of the bereaved and acknowledged the need for closure. However, he also revealed that some of the responses received during the Maxwellisation process had opened up new lines of inquiry, further complicating the already lengthy process. Lawyers representing the families of soldiers who died in Iraq have responded to Sir John's statement by announcing that they will take "further legal steps" to push for the publication of the report. Matthew Jury, of McCue and Partners, stated that Sir John had refused to impose a deadline on the Maxwellisation process, making it impossible to set a date for the report's publication. Reg Keys, whose son Tom died in Iraq in 2003, expressed his "bitter disappointment" at Sir John's explanation for the delay. Keys argued that witnesses should have been given a maximum of six months to respond to criticism and that the prolonged process had become a "farce." He emphasized the unbearable pain and suffering that the delay was causing for the families of the fallen. The Iraq Inquiry has faced intense criticism in recent weeks, with Prime Minister David Cameron expressing his frustration at the delays. Sir John has maintained that the inquiry has remained in control of its deadlines throughout the process, but critics argue that the Maxwellisation process is not the sole reason for the hold-up. Clare Short, a former international development secretary, has questioned the validity of Sir John's explanation, suggesting that the draft report may be poorly written and in need of significant revisions. Short, who is among those criticized in the report, believes that the inquiry team may be struggling to produce a coherent and comprehensive document. The Chairman of the Foreign Affairs Select Committee, Crispin Blunt, has weighed in on the debate, stating that Parliament cannot impose a deadline for the publication of the report as it would "wreck the inquiry." Blunt has called on Sir John to "bring clarity" to the process as soon as possible and hopes that the inquiry will conclude within six months. As the delay in the Iraq Inquiry report publication continues, the families of soldiers who lost their lives in the conflict remain in limbo, seeking answers and closure. The ongoing saga has sparked widespread frustration and calls for action, with many demanding that Sir John and his team provide a clear timeline for the report's publication. With the inquiry already spanning over a decade, it remains to be seen when the truth about the UK's involvement in the Iraq War will finally be revealed.

A significant proportion of women born in the 1970s may remain childless, according to a recent report by France's National Institute of Demographic Studies. The study reveals that more than a fifth of women from this generation may not have children, exceeding the average rates in northern and western Europe, which stand at 15% and 18%, respectively. The report attributes this trend to a combination of factors, including a precarious labor market and a lack of family-friendly work policies. These challenges have led to an increase in involuntary childlessness, as women are forced to postpone parenthood due to economic uncertainty and demanding careers. The study notes that very few women intentionally choose not to have children; instead, many end up delaying parenthood until it is too late. Interestingly, the report highlights that childlessness was also prevalent among women born in the early 20th century, with 17-25% remaining childless due to factors such as the loss of potential partners during World War I, emigration, and the Great Depression. Since then, the trend has formed a U-shape, with childlessness declining among women born in the 1930s and 1940s, who benefited from post-war prosperity and generous welfare systems. However, childlessness began to rise again among women born in the 1940s in western Europe and the 1960s in eastern Europe, driven by a complex interplay of personal and external factors. The report cites reliable contraception, delayed union formation and childbearing, and greater family fragility as contributing factors. Additionally, high unemployment, inadequate family policies, and persistent gender inequalities in domestic work and childcare have also played a significant role. The study concludes that childlessness is likely to continue rising in southern Europe, where up to a quarter of women born in the 1970s may remain childless. Similarly, central and eastern Europe are also expected to see an increase in childlessness. In contrast, western and northern Europe have seen a stabilization of childlessness rates. As the report notes, the economic and cultural trends of the last half-century have steered women and men away from having children, highlighting the need for policymakers to address these underlying factors and implement supportive family policies to mitigate the rise in involuntary childlessness.

Groundbreaking Research Raises Questions About Gray Whale Conservation Status A recent study published in Biology Letters has shed new light on the migratory patterns of gray whales, sparking concerns about their conservation status. The research, conducted by US and Russian biologists, reveals that a female gray whale made an astonishing 22,500 km (14,000 miles) round trip from the east coast of Russia to breeding grounds off Mexico and back. This remarkable journey, undertaken by a whale named Varvara, has significant implications for our understanding of gray whale populations. Until now, it was believed that there were two distinct groups of gray whales: the Eastern gray whale, found along the west coast of North America, and the critically-endangered Western gray whale, found along the coast of eastern Asia. However, the study suggests that these populations may be more closely linked than previously thought. In fact, three of seven whales tagged off Russia crossed the North Pacific to breeding grounds off Mexico, indicating that they may be part of the same population. The lead researcher, Prof Bruce Mate of Oregon State University Marine Mammal Institute, notes that the tagged whales were likely born in Mexico, which raises questions about the existence of a separate Western gray whale population. "If this small sample size is typical, it would suggest that [the two populations are one]," Prof Mate said. However, he also acknowledges that there may be an alternative explanation, suggesting that "true" Western gray whales may still exist, but in significantly lower numbers than previously thought. The gray whale was driven to the brink of extinction by whaling last century, but the Eastern population has since recovered to around 20,000 animals. In contrast, the Western gray whale population remains critically low, with only around 180 individuals left, according to the International Whaling Commission. The research, combined with genetic fingerprinting and photo-identification evidence, suggests that the two populations may be closely linked or even the same, which could mean that "true" Western gray whales are now extinct. The International Whaling Commission is currently conducting further research to determine whether the historic Western population still exists. Meanwhile, scientists have raised concerns about the threat of oil exploration in eastern Russia to gray whales in the area. As the conservation status of these majestic creatures continues to unfold, one thing is certain – further research is needed to ensure the long-term protection of gray whales.

Government's Plan to Convert All Schools to Academies by 2022 Raises Concerns The government's recent announcement to convert all schools in England to academies by 2022 has sparked concerns among educators and experts. The plan, outlined in the White Paper on schools, aims to empower teachers and leaders by giving them more autonomy to make decisions that benefit their students and communities. However, Fasna, a national forum for self-governing schools and academies, has questioned whether there is sufficient capacity to execute this policy effectively. According to Fasna chairman Tom Clark, the timeline for converting over 16,000 non-academy schools to academies is overly ambitious. "Given that there are 16,000 schools that are not academies, to get them to switch to that new structure on this timescale and for that to be effective is really quite challenging," he said. While Fasna supports the concept of autonomous schools and system leadership, Clark expressed surprise at the speed and timeline of the government's plan. The government's White Paper relies heavily on system leadership by schools, where successful schools support and assist underperforming ones. However, Clark pointed out that there is a "shallow pool" of schools capable of providing this kind of support, estimated to be around a third of the 24,000 schools in England. "System leadership needs time to mature to be effective," he explained. "It's a big ask of established system leaders – the ones who are most able to help and support schools – to provide that effectively." Moreover, Clark warned that the rapid expansion of multi-academy trusts could lead to difficulties in building supportive relationships between teachers and heads in different schools. This, he argued, is essential for successful collaboration and improvement. The Department for Education, however, remains confident in its plan, stating that the academy system "empowers great teachers and leaders and gives them the autonomy to make the decisions that are right for their community and their pupils." A spokesman for the department emphasized that full academisation will enable schools to address underperformance decisively and become part of a dynamic self-improving system. The government has given schools until 2020 to consider their options and until 2022 to convert to academies. Regional School Commissioners will play a key role in recruiting new sponsors to take on underperforming schools, and the government will invest in the necessary people and systems. Despite the government's reassurances, concerns about the feasibility of the plan persist. Fasna's concerns highlight the potential risks of rapid change and the need for careful planning and support to ensure that the conversion to academies is successful. As the education sector prepares for this significant transformation, it remains to be seen whether the government's ambitious timeline can be met without compromising the quality of education in England's schools.

Renowned War Hero's Medals and Logbooks Find New Home at Fleet Air Arm Museum The remarkable collection of medals and logbooks belonging to Captain Eric "Winkle" Brown, a legendary war hero and record-breaking pilot, has been acquired by The Fleet Air Arm Museum in Yeovilton, Somerset. The museum successfully purchased the items, which include Brown's Distinguished Service Cross and CBE, after they failed to sell at auction. The exact sum of the purchase remains undisclosed, but the medals were previously valued between £150,000 and £200,000. Captain Brown, who was born in Edinburgh's Leith area in 1919, passed away earlier this year at the age of 97. He left behind an incredible legacy as a pilot, having flown an unprecedented 487 different types of aircraft – a world record that is unlikely to be matched. During his illustrious career, Brown achieved numerous milestones, including the most aircraft carrier landings, with 2,407, and the most catapult launches, with 2,721. He also conducted some of the world's first helicopter tests and survived 11 plane crashes. The collection, which features Brown's Air Force Cross, awarded in 1947, and the Defence Medal with King's Commendation for Brave Conduct, was put up for auction at Bonhams in London by the pilot's family. However, thanks to the intervention of a generous donor, the museum was able to reach an agreement with the family and secure the items. The donor, who wishes to remain anonymous, played a crucial role in facilitating the purchase. The Fleet Air Arm Museum is thrilled to have acquired Brown's medals and logbooks, which date from 1942 to his final flights in 1970. A spokesman for the museum expressed their delight, stating, "Capt Brown was by many measures the Fleet Air Arm's most significant pilot of the post-war period, and we are thrilled and honoured to be able to class this collection as one of our own." The museum plans to preserve the record of innovation contained within Brown's logbooks, which includes previously untapped information, and display them for the public to see. John Millensted, Bonhams head of medals and coins, commented that Captain Brown's family had decided to sell the extraordinary archive "so that others might appreciate them."
