He added, "We are delighted that the medals are going to such an appropriate home where visitors will be able to learn about the achievements of this extraordinary man." Captain Brown's remarkable life and achievements will now be showcased at the museum, inspiring future generations of aviation enthusiasts and historians. His legacy continues to fascinate, with a career that included witnessing the liberation of the Bergen Belsen concentration camp and forming a close friendship with the first man to walk on the moon, Neil Armstrong.

Gambian President Yahya Jammeh has rejected the results of the country's recent election, citing "abnormalities" in the voting process. In a surprise move, Jammeh, who has been in power since 1994, appeared on state TV to announce his decision. He claimed that a thorough investigation had uncovered "serious and unacceptable abnormalities" and called for fresh elections to be held. Jammeh's defeat to opposition candidate Adama Barrow, a property developer, was seen as a major upset. Barrow won over 45% of the vote, securing his place as the country's next leader. However, Jammeh's rejection of the results has thrown the transition into uncertainty. Barrow is due to take office in late January, but it remains to be seen how Jammeh's announcement will affect the handover of power. Jammeh's 22-year rule has been marked by accusations of human rights abuses and suppression of opposition. Ahead of the election, Human Rights Watch accused him of using violence to silence critics, with reports of activists dying in custody and dozens being jailed without access to medical or legal help. The international community will be watching closely to see how the situation unfolds in the small West African nation.

Jose Mourinho has opened the door for Bastian Schweinsteiger to remain at Manchester United beyond the January transfer window. The 32-year-old midfielder made his first appearance of the season on Wednesday, coming on as a late substitute in the EFL Cup win over West Ham. Schweinsteiger had been training on his own earlier in the season, but has since worked his way back into contention. Despite being linked with a move to Major League Soccer side Chicago Fire, Mourinho insists that the decision is ultimately Schweinsteiger's. "Of course he can stay," said the United manager. "If you have a contract, you are the powerful one that can decide your future. In January, he is the powerful one - and with better feelings than before." Mourinho praised Schweinsteiger's dedication and work ethic, saying that "everybody was happy" to see him back on the pitch. Mourinho's comments come as he prepares his team to face Everton on Sunday. United are currently sixth in the Premier League table, and the manager has been told that funds are available to make signings in the January transfer window. One player who has been heavily linked with a move to Old Trafford is Benfica's Victor Lindelof, with Mourinho keen to strengthen his defence. The United manager has a large squad at his disposal, having used 24 outfield players so far this season. However, he insists that he is comfortable with the size of his squad, and that no player deserves to be pushed out. "I am comfortable having them all, and it hurts me not to select them because of the way they work," he said. Mourinho was speaking after serving a one-match ban for being sent off during the Premier League match against West Ham. He was fined £16,000 and banned from the dugout for kicking a water bottle in anger. The United manager accepted the punishment, but called for consistency in the way that managers are treated. "I kick a bottle of water. I cannot do it. I accept the suspension of one match, it's as simple as that. But it has to be the same for every manager," he said.

Trinity Mirror, the publisher of the Western Mail, Daily Post, and Wales Online, has announced a 24% rise in annual profit despite declining print circulation. CEO Simon Fox attributed the success to the company's growing online audience. In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Fox emphasized the importance of regional journalism, stating that local councils, schools, and police forces are no longer being adequately covered. As a result, Trinity Mirror's digital audiences in the regions are larger than ever. However, when asked about the closure of four local papers in England last October, Fox did not rule out further closures, suggesting that the company may shift its focus to online platforms. He noted that some titles, particularly free ones, may be closed, with more news being made available on mobile sites and websites. This shift reflects the changing media landscape.

A controversy is brewing at Llangennech school as some parents object to the council's plan to extend Welsh medium provision. A solicitor's letter has been sent to the council on behalf of a parent. The council aims to increase bilingualism, citing a decline in Welsh speakers. However, parents argue that replacing the current schools with a Welsh-medium primary would significantly impact children seeking an English-medium education, sparking a petition against the move. The council's decision has ignited a debate about language and education in the community. Parents are awaiting the council's response.

Fighting Erupts on Lebanon-Syria Border as Hezbollah Launches Offensive Against Militants A military operation launched by Hezbollah and Syrian forces against militant groups on the Lebanon-Syria border has raised concerns for the safety of thousands of Syrian refugees in the area. Pro-Hezbollah media reported that the forces are attacking the Jroud Arsal area and Qalamoun mountains from two directions, targeting around 1,000 militants affiliated with the Islamic State (IS) group and al-Qaeda's former affiliate, Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS). The operation began with Syrian forces and Hezbollah shelling the area, followed by an advance from Flita on the Syrian side of the border and from the south of Arsal, on the Lebanese side. Television footage showed columns of smoke rising as Hezbollah fired artillery towards hills where the militants are based. The Lebanese army has also announced plans to launch its own offensive against militants in the area, who have used Arsal's refugee camps as a safe haven. The influx of refugees from the war in Syria has heightened sectarian tensions in Lebanon, and the area around Arsal is home to tens of thousands of refugees. According to a Lebanese security source, hundreds of refugees are fleeing towards Arsal as the fighting intensifies. The situation is precarious, with many fearing for the safety of civilians caught in the crossfire. The offensive is expected to continue indefinitely, according to Hezbollah-affiliated media, which described the operation as a campaign to flush out "armed terrorists".

Seychelles: A Tropical Paradise with a Thriving Economy Located in the Indian Ocean, the archipelago of Seychelles is a haven of fine beaches, turquoise seas, and an array of wildlife, including giant tortoises and sea turtles. With a population of 87,400 and a land area of 455 square kilometers, this former British colony has transformed into a thriving economy, boasting a high per capita income, excellent healthcare, and education system. The country's economy is heavily reliant on the fishing industry and upmarket tourism, which attracts visitors from around the world to its stunning natural beauty. Much of the land is protected as part of nature reserves, preserving the unique biodiversity of the islands. The government has taken significant steps to conserve the environment, ensuring that the country's natural resources are utilized sustainably. In recent years, Seychelles has experienced a significant shift in its political landscape. In 2016, Danny Faure was sworn in as president, succeeding James Michel, who resigned after parliamentary elections saw the opposition coalition, Linyon Demokratik (LDS), take control of the legislature for the first time in the country's history. President Faure, a former finance minister and governor of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), has pledged to continue the country's economic growth and development. The media landscape in Seychelles is characterized by a mix of government-controlled and private outlets. While the government operates radio and TV stations, as well as the sole daily newspaper, private publications have been robust in their reporting, despite tough libel laws. However, steep licensing fees have discouraged the growth of private broadcast media. The internet has become increasingly popular, with around 50,000 users by the end of 2015, providing citizens with access to a wide range of information and news sources. Seychelles has a rich history, with French planters and their slaves settling in the islands in 1768. The country was later annexed by Britain in 1794 and became a separate British colony in 1903. Seychelles gained independence in 1976, with James Mancham as president and France Rene as prime minister. However, a coup in 1977 saw Rene become president, a position he held until 2004, when he was succeeded by James Michel. In recent years, Seychelles has faced challenges from Somali piracy, which has affected the country's fishing industry and tourism sector. However, with the help of international partners, including the US and the European Union, the country has been able to combat piracy and ensure the safety of its citizens and visitors. The EU has signed an anti-piracy agreement with Seychelles, allowing EU troops to be deployed on the islands, while the US has provided drone spy-planes to help fight piracy. Today, Seychelles is a thriving democracy, with a strong economy and a high standard of living. The country's stunning natural beauty, rich history, and vibrant culture make it a popular destination for tourists and a great place to live for its citizens. With its commitment to conservation, sustainable development, and good governance, Seychelles is well-placed to continue its growth and prosperity in the years to come.

Astronomers have captured a remarkable transformation in a young star's development, observing the formation of an elongated column of hot, ionized gas in just 18 years. The star, known as W75N(B)-VLA2, is located approximately 4,200 light-years from Earth and is surrounded by a doughnut-shaped cloud of dust. This cloud slows down the star's powerful wind, causing it to form a column perpendicular to the dusty ring. Using the Very Large Array (VLA) in New Mexico, a team of researchers compared data from 1996 and 2014, providing a unique "before and after" glimpse of the star's development. The results, published in the journal Science, show a compact, rounded wind in 1996 transforming into a distinctly elongated outflow by 2014. According to Carlos Carrasco-Gonzalez, the first author of the study, "The comparison is remarkable." W75N(B)-VLA2 is an infant star that is about 300 times brighter than the Sun. Its dramatic growing pains are being observed in real-time, providing scientists with a rare opportunity to study the formation of a massive star. Prof Huib van Langevelde from Leiden University in the Netherlands noted, "This object is providing us an exciting opportunity to watch the developments over the next few years, as this very young star develops the characteristic bipolar outflow morphology." The study also sheds light on the role of magnetism in the star's formation. Earlier research had shown that the large-scale magnetic field in the region is neatly aligned with the field surrounding the young star. The newly formed elongated outflow is also aligned with this magnetic field, suggesting that magnetism plays a crucial role in the star's development. The team hopes to continue monitoring W75N(B)-VLA2 as it undergoes further changes. Dr Gabriele Surcis, a co-author of the study, noted, "Our understanding of how massive young stars develop is much less complete than our understanding of how Sun-like stars develop." The opportunity to observe this protostar's turbulent development in real-time is expected to provide valuable insights into the formation of massive stars. As the star continues to evolve, scientists will be watching closely, eager to learn more about the complex processes that shape the early lives of these celestial bodies.

A shocking revelation has emerged in the ongoing Takata airbag saga, with five major carmakers admitting to temporarily replacing defective airbags with identical devices in Australia. Toyota, Mazda, Lexus, BMW, and Subaru have all confessed to using the same faulty airbags as a stopgap measure, sparking outrage from consumer advocacy group Choice. The organisation has slammed the carmakers, saying that people are being left to "drive ticking time-bombs". The defective airbags, made by Japanese manufacturer Takata, have been linked to at least 18 deaths worldwide, including one in Australia earlier this month. The airbags' faulty inflators can explode with too much force, spraying metal shrapnel and putting drivers' lives at risk. Choice's investigation found that around 70% of the 2.1 million cars recalled in Australia had not yet been refitted with safe airbags. Toyota has defended its actions, saying that the temporary replacements would be safe for several years, but ultimately need to be replaced again due to environmental exposure. The Australian government's consumer watchdog has announced that it will investigate the recall, following a recent road death in Sydney linked to a defective Takata airbag. The incident highlights the urgency of the situation, and the need for carmakers to take immediate action to ensure public safety.

UK Defence Budget Faces "Budget Black Hole" Due to Sterling's Fall The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) has warned that the UK's defence budget is facing a "budget black hole" due to the fall in sterling, which has made military equipment purchases from the US more expensive. The pound's decline to its lowest level against the dollar in over 30 years has resulted in increased costs for the Ministry of Defence (MoD), which buys much of its military equipment in US dollars. According to Prof Trevor Taylor, from the RUSI think tank, the extra costs could present a serious problem for the UK's defence stance. "The UK pays the US about $10 billion a year for defence products, and with the fall in sterling, this is going to become even more expensive," he said. The MoD has already committed to buying several high-profile defence products from the US, including nine P8 maritime patrol aircraft, 138 F-35B aircraft, and 50 Apache aircraft. The MoD will also have to buy spares and support services for their existing aircraft and defence systems, such as Chinook helicopters, Trident missiles, and the AWACS surveillance system. The UK has committed to spending 2% of its GDP on defence, a minimum set by NATO. However, with the UK's GDP potentially shrinking due to Brexit, this could result in a reduced spending figure. Lord West, the former head of the Royal Navy and a Labour peer, described the issue as a "perfect storm" for the MoD. "The government has delayed the purchase of frigates, which will push up their costs, and now we have the fall in sterling making our defence purchases more expensive," he said. A source with experience of the issue at a high level of government warned that the situation could push an already stretched budget "to breaking point". However, not everyone is alarmed by the situation. Another former insider, who did not wish to be named, argued that sterling could well recover and the issue was merely a "headache" for the MoD. Major Tim Cross, a retired British Army officer who supported the Leave campaign, called for time to be spent assessing the situation post-Brexit, rather than "running around like headless chickens". The chairman of the House of Commons defence select committee, Julian Lewis, a Brexit supporter, said defence had "fallen too far down the scale of national priorities". He argued that the 2% of GDP spent on defence was "nowhere near where we need to be spending" and that the figure should be more like 3%. The MoD has said it takes "appropriate financial precautions in all its procurement contracts" and "remains committed to the procurement set out in last year's defence review". Despite these reassurances, the situation remains a cause for concern. With the UK's defence budget already stretched, the extra costs resulting from the fall in sterling could have serious consequences for the country's defence capabilities. As Prof Taylor warned, "The UK's defence budget is facing a budget black hole, and it's not clear how it's going to be filled."

A primary school in Leyton has sparked controversy by advising parents that children will not be allowed to fast during Ramadan. Barclay Primary School cited concerns over student health and wellbeing, stating that some children had previously fallen ill or fainted while fasting. However, critics, including Imam Ajmal Masroor, have labeled the move as an "overreaction" and "stupidly foolish". Masroor argued that children, especially primary school age, are not expected to fast and that the issue could have been resolved through dialogue with parents. The school's decision has been seen as unnecessary and has drawn negative attention to the Muslim community. The school suggested that older children who wish to fast do so on weekends, citing a busy time of year with sports days and field trips, as well as a recent hot spell.

Residents of Lynton Avenue in Hull are up in arms after the government's Valuation Office Agency (VOA) raised their council tax bands from A to B, resulting in a £160 annual increase. The move has been met with widespread criticism, with many residents feeling that the decision is unfair and has been made without proper justification. The controversy began when one unidentified neighbour complained to the VOA that their rates were too high. Instead of reducing the complainant's tax, the VOA reviewed the tax banding of the entire street and decided to raise everyone else's tax. Residents are outraged, claiming that the decision is a classic case of penalizing the many for the perceived mistake of one. "All the houses on the street are identical, so we should all be paying the same rate," said one resident, who wished to remain anonymous. "One person on the street was paying a higher rate than everyone else, so they questioned it with the government, and I think they've been a bit cynical. Instead of admitting that this person has been overpaying all these years and giving them a refund, they have decided to put everyone else up. It's just so typical, if you ask me." The VOA sent letters to each house on the street, informing residents that their homes would be revalued. However, the increase in council tax was implemented without further notice, leaving many residents feeling blindsided. Council tax bands in England are calculated based on the value of the property in April 1991, with Band A being the cheapest and Band H being the most expensive. Accounts manager Kerry Wilson, who has lived on Lynton Avenue for 16 years, is leading the charge against the decision. "We have been in Band A as long as we've lived here," she said. "The move to Band B means our houses would have been valued at more than £40,000 in 1991, but there is no way that can be true. My husband has found all the house prices from that time, and none of them were more than that. It's caused a right rumpus, and we're making sure everyone in the street will send their letter of appeal in." The increase in council tax will have a significant impact on many residents, particularly pensioners like Pat Garrett, who has lived on the street for almost 40 years. "As a pensioner, my monthly income isn't going up anytime soon, and I'll definitely feel the pinch," she said. "The amount doesn't sound like much, but it makes a big difference when you consider everything else is going up in price too." A spokesman for the VOA defended the decision, stating that bands can change as a result of one person expressing concerns about the amount they were paying. "If a taxpayer contacts us with concerns about their council tax banding, we will review it free of charge," he said. "We might need to review the bands of similar neighbouring properties to ensure they are correct, which can lead to other properties' bands being changed. We alter council tax bands only if evidence indicates they are incorrect, or there has been a physical change to a property or its locality." Hull City Council has declined to comment on the row, stating that it acts on the instructions of the Valuation Office Agency. The decision has left residents feeling frustrated and angry, and many are determined to appeal against the increase. As the row continues to simmer, one thing is clear: the residents of Lynton Avenue will not go down without a fight.

British tennis star Johanna Konta is on the verge of making history as she prepares to face Russian opponent Ekaterina Makarova in the Australian Open. A win would see Konta match Jo Durie's feat of reaching the quarter-finals at a major, a milestone not achieved by a British female since 1984. Konta, 24, has a promising record against Makarova, having beaten her in their only previous meeting at Eastbourne in June. That victory marked a significant turning point in Konta's career, as it was her first win over a top-10 player and sparked her rise into the world's top 40. Since then, Konta has been in impressive form, defeating former world number one Venus Williams in the first round and taking down five top-20 players. Her win over Czech Denisa Allertova in the previous round made her the first British woman to reach the fourth round of the Australian Open since Jo Durie and Anne Hobbs in 1987. Despite the growing interest and pressure, Konta remains grounded and focused on her game. "It's as big as you make it, really, and it becomes as important as you want it to," she said. Konta, who moved to England with her family in 2005, is aware of the significance of her potential achievement but is determined to stay humble and prioritize her goals. A win against Makarova would be a major breakthrough for British tennis, and Konta is ready to seize the opportunity and make her mark on the sport.

Tributes have been pouring in for Dan Rooney, the former US Ambassador to Ireland and chairman of the Pittsburgh Steelers, who has left behind a legacy of peace, reconciliation, and philanthropy. Irish President Michael D Higgins led the tributes, praising Mr. Rooney's contributions to Ireland and the Irish people. "He was deeply committed to Ireland and the Irish people, and his contributions to peace and reconciliation have left a real and tangible legacy," said President Higgins. Mr. Rooney, who was born in Pittsburgh in 1932, was instrumental in setting up the Ireland Funds charity in 1976, which has since raised over $550 million for thousands of Irish organizations around the world. He co-founded the charity with Irish businessman Sir Anthony O'Reilly, with the aim of supporting and promoting peace efforts and Irish culture. Today, the charity is known as the Ireland Funds, and its work is a testament to Mr. Rooney's selfless dedication to the Irish people. John Fitzpatrick, chairman of the Ireland Funds, described Mr. Rooney as "an utter gentleman and utterly selfless." "The work of the Ireland Funds is his legacy, and Ireland is a better place because of him," said Mr. Fitzpatrick. "Thousands have benefited from his care and concern, and his impact will be felt for generations to come." Mr. Rooney's connection to Ireland ran deep, with his grandfather emigrating from County Down to the US in the 19th century. His family went on to found the Pittsburgh Steelers, which has won more Super Bowl titles than any other NFL team. Mr. Rooney was also instrumental in introducing the NFL's "Rooney Rule," which requires teams to interview at least one black or ethnic minority candidate for a head coach vacancy. In 2008, Mr. Rooney was awarded an honorary CBE for his contributions to peace and reconciliation in Northern Ireland. He served as the US Ambassador to Ireland from 2009 to 2012, appointed by then-US President Barack Obama, who described him as "an unwavering supporter of Irish peace, culture, and education." Mr. Rooney's legacy is a testament to his commitment to Ireland and its people, and he will be deeply missed by all who knew him.

The state of emergency in the Maldives has been lifted, according to Foreign Affairs Minister Dunya Maumoon. The emergency was declared on November 4 to aid security forces in investigating an alleged plot to assassinate President Abdulla Yameen. The president had narrowly escaped injury when a blast struck his boat last month. However, US investigators found no evidence to support the claim that the blast was an assassination attempt. During the state of emergency, police and armed forces were given wider powers to arrest suspects and restrict freedom of assembly and movement. The military patrolled the streets, and a planned protest by the opposition Maldivian Democratic Party was potentially disrupted. The Maldives has experienced political unrest in recent months, including the impeachment of Vice President Ahmed Adeeb, who is accused of high treason. The lifting of the state of emergency is seen as a step towards returning the country to normalcy. Minister Maumoon expressed satisfaction with the swift resolution of the matter, stating that the country is looking forward to getting back on track. The Maldives, a popular tourist destination, aims to regain stability and reassure visitors of their safety.

It's been 10 years since the passing of football legend Jeff Astle, a prolific goal-scorer who played for West Bromwich Albion during the 1960s and 1970s. Astle's death at the age of 59 was a tragic reminder of the potential risks associated with heading heavy leather footballs. A coroner's report concluded that Astle had suffered brain damage as a result of repeatedly heading the ball, leading to his untimely death. Despite the coroner's findings, the Football Association (FA) has been criticized for its response to Astle's death. His widow, Laraine Astle, claims that the FA has been reluctant to acknowledge the potential dangers of heading footballs, stating that "they don't want to hold their hands up and own up that the game that we loved proved to be a killer." Astle's family has been unsuccessful in their bid to win compensation from the FA, despite the coroner's report highlighting the link between heading footballs and brain damage. The FA has responded by stating that "there remain conflicting opinions on the possible effects of frequent heading of a football over time." While the organization acknowledges Astle's contributions to the sport, it has stopped short of accepting responsibility for his death. The FA has implemented standards for the size, weight, and pressure of footballs, and continues to work with FIFA on medical issues related to the sport. Jeff Astle's legacy extends far beyond his tragic death. He was a talented footballer who scored 137 goals in 292 league appearances for West Bromwich Albion, earning him a place as one of the club's greatest players. He also represented England in the 1970 World Cup and made memorable appearances on TV's Fantasy Football League in the 1990s. As the football community remembers Astle's achievements, his family continues to push for greater recognition of the potential risks associated with heading footballs, and for the FA to take greater responsibility for protecting the health and wellbeing of its players.

Jurors in the Hillsborough inquest visited the site of the 1989 disaster yesterday, walking through the tunnel where a crush led to the deaths of 96 Liverpool fans. The eleven jurors, accompanied by coroner Lord Justice Goldring, made their way down the tunnel of the Leppings Lane stand, where the fatal crush occurred. The visit was part of the inquest into the deaths of the fans, which was ordered after the accidental death verdicts were quashed. As they walked towards the stadium, Lord Justice Goldring pointed out key features, including the former location of exit gates and other areas that have changed since the disaster. The jurors carried photographs of the stadium in 1989 to help them visualize the old layout. They were also shown the police control box, which is now much larger than its 1989 counterpart, and the site of the former gymnasium, which was used as a temporary mortuary on the day of the disaster. The jury's visit to the stadium was part of a larger tour of locations relevant to the inquests. They also visited the White Horse Inn, a pub where some Liverpool fans went before the match, and Wadsley Bridge railway station, from which supporters were accompanied by police to the stadium. The coroner explained the significance of each location, highlighting the events that unfolded on the day of the disaster. In addition to the stadium and surrounding areas, the jurors visited the Northern General and Royal Hallamshire Hospitals, which both took casualties on the day. Lord Justice Goldring told the jury that the Northern General accepted 88 casualties, many of whom died, while 71 went to the Royal Hallamshire, where not all died. The visit was an important part of the inquest, allowing the jurors to gain a better understanding of the events that led to the tragedy. The inquests into the deaths of the 96 Liverpool fans have been ongoing, with the jury hearing a minute-by-minute countdown of how the disaster unfolded earlier this week. The hearing included rarely seen footage of the day, taken by police and BBC cameras, as well as stadium CCTV. The fresh inquests were ordered after a panel of three High Court judges quashed the accidental death verdicts, and are aimed at providing a more detailed understanding of the events surrounding the tragedy.

Scottish Economy Shows Signs of Slowing Down, Survey Reveals A recent survey conducted by the Scottish Chambers of Commerce (SCC) has indicated that the Scottish economy is experiencing a slowdown, with key sectors such as construction, tourism, and manufacturing showing disappointing results. The survey, which covered the three months to June 30, found that construction activity had decreased, while tourism performed "markedly" worse than the same period last year. Additionally, there was little sign of improvement in manufacturing, retail, and financial and business services. According to the SCC report, business performance across the Scottish economy was more consistent in the second quarter of 2016 compared to the first quarter, but both performance and optimism were lower than in the same period of 2015. The report's findings have raised concerns about the potential impact of the Brexit vote on Scotland's economy, with the SCC calling on the UK and Scottish governments to take measures to prevent a further slowdown. Neil Amner, chairman of the SCC economic advisory group, emphasized the need for clarity on the future of talented individuals working in Scotland, stating that everyone must have confidence in their ability to fulfill their long-term ambitions in the country. He also called on the government to reconsider policies that impose burdens on businesses and to use their powers to boost growth, suggesting measures such as a cut in business rates and an accelerated reduction in Air Passenger Duty. The SCC is urging the government to take proactive steps to support businesses and attract new investment and trading opportunities to Scotland. With the Brexit vote presenting both challenges and opportunities, the organization believes that it is essential for businesses to be at the forefront of driving growth and stability in the Scottish economy. As the UK and Scottish governments navigate the post-Brexit landscape, they will need to work closely with businesses to ensure that Scotland remains an attractive place to do business and invest.

The Royal British Legion is utilizing the social media platform Thunderclap to encourage Twitter and Facebook users to observe a two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday. At 09:00 GMT, thousands of users are expected to simultaneously send the message "I'll be remembering the fallen at 11 o'clock #2MinuteSilence #LestWeForget" to show their respect for those who have paid the ultimate sacrifice. This campaign aims to create the largest online show of remembrance, harnessing the power of social media to reach millions of Britons. The Royal British Legion hopes that the estimated 10 million Twitter and 33 million Facebook users in the UK will participate in the Two Minute Silence Thunderclap. Helen Hill, head of remembrance at The Royal British Legion, emphasized the importance of honoring the men and women who have given their lives in wars and conflicts. Thunderclap, a crowdspeaking platform, has been used by international charities and causes, including the UN to support World Humanitarian Day. The platform allows users to be heard by saying something together, amplifying their message and increasing its impact. By using Thunderclap, The Royal British Legion aims to remind the nation of the significance of the two-minute silence, which began in 1919 after the Armistice at the end of World War I. The Royal British Legion is the UK's leading armed forces charity, dedicated to ensuring that those who have made the ultimate sacrifice are remembered and honored.

A historic warship that sank off the Essex coast in 1665 has yielded a treasure trove of artefacts, including soles and insoles, during a series of dives. The London, a British warship, mysteriously exploded while en route to Gravesend, resulting in a significant loss of life. Recent excavations have uncovered evidence of cabins and hand-made glass windows, offering a glimpse into life on board during a pivotal period in British history. English Heritage has likened the discovery to the Mary Rose warship, suggesting it could be of similar scope and significance. The artefacts are expected to provide valuable insights into the daily lives of those on board, shedding light on Britain's emergence as a sea power during the 16th and 17th centuries. Following a review of the operation, the artefacts will undergo conservation and eventually be put on permanent display at Southend-on-Sea Borough Council's Museums Service, with further dives scheduled for next year.

Gerry Mallon has left Danske Bank to become Ulster Bank's CEO in the Republic of Ireland. Mallon, who led Danske in Belfast since 2008, will start his new role in June. His banking knowledge in Ireland is deemed "invaluable" by Ulster Bank's owner, Royal Bank of Scotland. Kevin Kingston, former deputy CEO, has replaced Mallon at Danske Bank, bringing his own experience as former president of the Northern Ireland Chamber of Commerce.

Ukraine Reconnects Electricity to Crimea After Talks with Activists One of the damaged power lines supplying electricity to Crimea has been reconnected, bringing some relief to the peninsula's two million residents who have been struggling with widespread blackouts. The Kakhovskyy-Titan power line was reestablished overnight after negotiations with activists who have been blocking energy supplies to the region. The Ukrainian authorities and Russian energy ministry confirmed the resumption of power supply. The move comes after unknown attackers damaged four power pylons on November 22, leaving Crimea without electricity. Anti-Russian activists were blamed for the incident, which highlighted the peninsula's reliance on Ukraine for power. With the four lines being the only source of electricity for Crimea, their damage plunged the territory into darkness, prompting the closure of schools and a state of emergency. The reconnection of one line is a positive development, but three lines remain down, and the situation remains fragile. Russia has begun constructing an undersea cable to bypass Ukraine and provide a more stable source of electricity to Crimea. The incident has also led to a reduction in coal supplies to Ukraine from Russia and rebel-held eastern Ukraine, exacerbating the energy crisis in the region.

Violence Continues to Plague Israeli-Palestinian Conflict A wave of violence between Israelis and Palestinians shows no signs of slowing down, with multiple incidents reported over the weekend. On Sunday, four Palestinians were killed in separate incidents, while a teenage girl was critically wounded in an attempted assault. No Israelis were hurt in any of the incidents. The first incident occurred near Jenin in the northern West Bank, where two 15-year-old boys were throwing rocks at passing cars. When an Israeli army patrol arrived, one of the boys opened fire with a rifle, prompting the soldiers to return fire and kill both teenagers. Later, at a checkpoint in Jerusalem, a 17-year-old Palestinian youth with a knife ran at officers and was shot and killed. In another incident, two Palestinians were killed after they opened fire on Israeli police with automatic weapons outside Jerusalem's Old City. Meanwhile, in Hebron, a 17-year-old woman who attempted to stab a policeman was shot and taken to hospital in critical condition. However, Palestinian media reported conflicting accounts of the incident, with some sources claiming that the girl had not attempted an attack and was shot six times while walking away from a military checkpoint with her sister. The violence is part of a larger wave of stabbing, shooting, and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians and Israeli Arabs that has resulted in the deaths of over 160 Palestinians and 26 Israelis since October 2015. The attacks have been sporadic but persistent, with correspondents noting that they show no sign of abating. The situation remains volatile, with tensions between Israelis and Palestinians continuing to run high. As the conflict drags on, concerns about the safety and well-being of civilians on both sides continue to grow.

Fairfield Energy has announced that production from all Dunlin cluster fields will be shut down in mid-June, marking the beginning of the decommissioning process. Despite the shutdown, Dunlin Alpha will remain fully manned and operational, continuing to export third-party oil into the Brent system pipeline. The decision to decommission the fields comes as a result of the depressed oil price and challenging operational conditions in the North Sea. The Dunlin field, located 300 miles north-east of Aberdeen in the East Shetland basin, has been in production since August 1978. At its peak, the field produced approximately 120,000 barrels of oil per day in 1979. Originally operated by Shell, the field was acquired by Fairfield in 2008, along with the Dunlin SW, Merlin, and Osprey fields. The decommissioning process, which is expected to cost around £400m, will require regulatory approvals and is anticipated to take several years to complete. Fairfield has stated that its subsidiaries, Fairfield Betula and Fairfield Fagus, along with joint venture partner MCX Dunlin, will lead the decommissioning program. The company has assured that high offshore activity levels will be maintained throughout the process. According to Fairfield's chief executive, David Peattie, the decision to decommission the Dunlin field is the most appropriate action, given the asset's lifecycle and the current market conditions. Peattie emphasized the company's commitment to delivering a safe and transparent decommissioning process, working closely with staff and stakeholders to achieve this goal. The decommissioning of the Dunlin field is part of a larger trend in the North Sea, where many oil and gas installations are nearing the end of their lifespan. The industry body Oil and Gas UK estimates that the decommissioning of oil and gas installations in the UK sector of the North Sea could cost up to £40bn over the next 35 years. There are currently 113 oil platforms and 189 gas platforms in the UK Continental Shelf, many of which will require decommissioning in the coming years. Environmental groups have welcomed the announcement, emphasizing the importance of protecting the marine environment during the decommissioning process. Lang Banks, director of WWF Scotland, stated that the oil industry has a responsibility to clean up its mess, having made significant profits over the years. Banks urged Fairfield to take all necessary steps to ensure the protection of the marine environment during the decommissioning process. As the North Sea oil and gas industry continues to evolve, the decommissioning of fields like Dunlin will become an increasingly important issue. With the potential cost of decommissioning reaching £40bn over the next 35 years, it is essential that companies like Fairfield prioritize safe and responsible decommissioning practices, minimizing the impact on the environment and ensuring a sustainable future for the industry.

UK Manufacturing Sector Sees Slowdown in Growth and Job Losses The UK manufacturing sector has experienced a slowdown in growth, with the purchasing managers' index (PMI) falling to 51.5 in August, down from 51.9 in July. Although the score remains above 50, indicating expansion, it is significantly lower than the average over the past two-and-a-half years. The sector has also seen a reduction in headcount for the first time in 26 months, marking the end of a two-year period of continuous job creation. According to Rob Dobson from Markit, the compiler of the PMI, the sector is currently in a "holding pattern" with production growth stagnating and marginal job losses reported. The main culprit behind this slowdown is the weakness in export orders, which has been impacted by the strong sterling exchange rate, weak sales growth to the eurozone, and the slowdown in China. Analysts have highlighted the weakness in exports as a major problem for UK manufacturers, with Howard Archer from IHS Global Insight stating that the sector is being "held back" by weak foreign orders. The strength of the pound, in particular, is making UK exports more expensive and less competitive in the global market. On a more positive note, the survey found a significant drop in input prices, which fell at one of the steepest rates seen in the past 16 years. This is due to lower oil and commodity prices, as well as the strong pound making imports cheaper. The news has had an immediate impact on the currency markets, with the pound slipping against the dollar and euro as investors bet that the weaker manufacturing figures will push back the timing of any interest rate rise by the Bank of England.

Tragedy at Leicester Royal Infirmary: Two Medical Professionals Found Guilty of Manslaughter by Gross Negligence A devastating case of medical negligence has come to a close, with two medical professionals being found guilty of manslaughter by gross negligence in the death of six-year-old Jack Adcock. Doctor Hadiza Bawa-Garba, 39, and nurse Isabel Amaro, 47, were both given a two-year suspended sentence for their roles in the tragic events that unfolded at Leicester Royal Infirmary in February 2011. Jack, who had Down's syndrome, was admitted to the hospital with vomiting and diarrhoea, but his condition rapidly deteriorated, and he died approximately 11 hours later due to cardiac arrest caused by sepsis. The court heard that both Bawa-Garba and Amaro failed to realize the severity of Jack's illness, with Bawa-Garba stopping CPR after incorrectly assuming that Jack had a do-not-resuscitate order in place. Amaro, on the other hand, was criticized for her inadequate monitoring of Jack's treatment and her failure to alert colleagues to his deteriorating condition. In his sentencing, Mr. Justice Nichol emphasized that the pair's medical careers "will come to an end" and stated that Jack's life was "cut short prematurely" due to their negligence. The judge acknowledged that neither Bawa-Garba nor Amaro had acted out of laziness or selfishness, but rather had failed to prioritize Jack's care amidst their other responsibilities. Bawa-Garba's sentence was influenced by her role as the sole carer for her five-year-old son, who has autism and behavioral problems, while Amaro's sentence took into account her psychiatric problems, which would be exacerbated by imprisonment. The case has had a profound impact on Jack's family, with his mother, Nicky, expressing her anger and grief in a powerful impact statement. "Jack was neglected from the moment he entered the Leicester Royal Infirmary Children's Assessment Unit," she said. "I will never forgive myself for taking him there. I could have cared and looked after him better than they ever did." Jack's father, Vic, also spoke out, saying, "I wish I could forgive them, but at the moment, I don't know if I ever can. To hear their excuses has been so hard to bear. I had to watch my little man laid to rest." In their defense, Bawa-Garba cited her exhausting 12-hour shift with no break and the miscommunication that occurred in the ward, while Amaro acknowledged that she had breached her duty of care but denied that her actions significantly contributed to Jack's death. Theresa Taylor, another nurse involved in Jack's care, was cleared of the same charge. The outcome of this case serves as a stark reminder of the importance of prioritizing patient care and the devastating consequences that can result from medical negligence. As the medical community reflects on this tragedy, it is essential that lessons are learned, and measures are taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future. For Jack's family, the sentence brings a measure of closure, but the pain of their loss will undoubtedly endure.

A 55-year-old man has been cleared of causing serious injury by dangerous driving after a collision with a lollipop lady in Kempston, near Bedford. Brian Wright was acquitted by a jury at Luton Crown Court, who accepted that he was blinded by the sun at the time of the incident. The collision occurred on December 19 last year, when Wright's VW Golf failed to stop at a pedestrian crossing outside Bedford Road Lower School. Sylvia Blackburn, 72, was on crossing patrol duty when the incident happened. She suffered serious head injuries, including a blow to the head that caused her to hit the pillar of the windscreen of Wright's car. Blackburn is still undergoing treatment at a care facility in Northampton, after initially being treated at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge. Her family has described her injuries as life-changing. The court heard that traffic coming from the opposite direction had stopped at the red light, and Blackburn was wearing a high-visibility coat at the time of the incident. Wright claimed he could not remember whether the traffic lights were green or red, but said he was "totally blinded by the sun" and only heard a bump. He expressed remorse for the incident, stating that he had thought of nothing else but Blackburn and her family since the collision. Despite his acquittal, Wright acknowledged that he had "turned their world upside down."

A South Korean man, identified by his surname Lee, has been arrested for allegedly posting a threat against the US Ambassador to South Korea, Mark Lippert, on the White House website. According to Yonhap, Lee was taken into custody on July 14 at the request of US authorities. A search of his laptop revealed draft copies of the threatening letter, as well as a screenshot of the post on the White House website. Ambassador Lippert has been the target of violence before, having been injured in a knife attack in Seoul last year. The attacker, Kim Ki-jong, is currently on trial for the incident. Lee denies any wrongdoing, but police believe he was acting alone. The US embassy has stated that the threat has not affected Ambassador Lippert's activities, and has praised the quick action of Korean authorities in identifying a suspect. The US is cooperating with South Korea on the investigation, with law enforcement agencies working together to gather more information. The details of the threatening letter have not been made public.

Scotland's Iconic Red Phone Boxes Get a New Lease on Life In 2003, Scotland was home to nearly 7,000 phone boxes, a ubiquitous sight on streets and in towns across the country. However, with the rise of mobile phones, the number of call boxes has been steadily declining. Today, there are fewer than 5,000 phone boxes in Scotland, with just over 1,000 of them being the iconic red phone boxes that were once a staple of British streets. As the demand for payphones continues to decrease, some communities are finding new and creative ways to repurpose these nostalgic structures. In the village of Comrie, a old phone box has been transformed into a life-saving device. The community has converted the phone box into a community access defibrillator site, complete with a defibrillator that can be used in emergency situations. The project was funded by locals in memory of Irene McCartney, who died in 2012. Her widower, Gordon, hopes that the defibrillator will make a real difference to someone in the future. According to Alan Moffat, the manager of the first response team in Comrie, the defibrillator is a vital piece of equipment that can greatly increase a person's chances of recovering from a cardiac arrest. In Portobello, another phone box has been given a new lease on life as an art exhibition space. The Porty Light Box, as it is known, is the brainchild of Steven Wheatley, who wanted to retain the phone box as a feature of the street scene. The small space is now home to a vibrant and constantly changing array of artwork, showcasing the talents of local artists. While these examples demonstrate the creativity and resourcefulness of Scottish communities, the question remains as to whether phone boxes will eventually disappear altogether. According to Brendan Dick, director of BT Scotland, the demand for payphones is indeed decreasing, but there is still a future for them in some areas. "In some urban parts, some of them are used very extensively, so there is a future for payphones in the broader sense," he said. BT currently operates 4,864 kiosks in Scotland, down from 6,962 in 2003. The company has also seen a significant decrease in the number of paid calls made from phone boxes, with 1,723 payphones, including 684 red boxes, receiving no paid calls in the last 12 months. In Alyth, Perthshire, another phone box is set to be transformed into a unique community resource. The Story Box, as it is known, will be a "time machine" that allows users to hear stories and histories from the town, both past and present. The project, which is being coordinated by Marian Bruce, will also involve young people in thinking about the future of Alyth and what the town will be like when they are grown up. As Scotland's phone boxes continue to decline in number, it is heartening to see communities finding new and innovative ways to breathe new life into these iconic structures. Whether as a life-saving device, an art exhibition space, or a community resource, the humble phone box is proving that it still has a vital role to play in Scottish life.

Israel's President Reuven Rivlin has called for urgent action to address the grievances of the country's Ethiopian minority, following violent clashes between police and protesters in Tel Aviv on Sunday night. The unrest was sparked by the emergence of a video showing an Ethiopian Israeli soldier, Damas Pakedeh, being beaten by two police officers in a suburb of Tel Aviv. The video, which was widely shared on social media, has fueled tensions and sparked widespread outrage, with many in the Ethiopian community feeling that it is just the latest example of systemic racism and discrimination. On Sunday, thousands of protesters took to the streets, blocking a busy road and marching through the city, before the demonstration turned violent as night fell. Police fired tear gas and stun grenades as protesters threw stones, bottles, and chairs, and tried to enter the municipality building. At least 46 police officers and seven protesters were injured, and dozens of protesters were arrested. President Rivlin condemned the violence, blaming a "handful of violent trouble-makers" for the unrest, but acknowledged that the protests had exposed "the pain of a community crying out over a sense of discrimination, racism, and of being unanswered." The Israeli government has been quick to respond to the crisis, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu meeting with Damas Pakedeh, the soldier who was beaten by police. Netanyahu praised Pakedeh and expressed his shock at the video, saying that it was "unacceptable" and that those responsible would be held accountable. One of the police officers involved has already been fired, and the other has been suspended, pending an investigation. The protests have highlighted the long-standing grievances of the Ethiopian community in Israel, who have struggled to integrate into Israeli society despite being airlifted to the country in secret operations in the 1980s and 1990s. Many have faced discrimination in jobs and education, and have lower incomes and limited opportunities compared to the general population. According to The Ethiopian National Project, a non-governmental organization that assists Ethiopian Jews in Israel, Ethiopian Jews are much more likely to face limited educational opportunities and to end up in prison. The Israeli government has acknowledged that more needs to be done to address these issues, and has pledged to take action to address the community's grievances. President Rivlin has called for a national conversation about racism and discrimination, and has urged Israelis to "look directly at this open wound" and to work towards a more inclusive and equal society. The crisis has also highlighted the complex and often fraught history of the Ethiopian community in Israel. The airlifts that brought tens of thousands of Ethiopian Jews to Israel were seen as a triumphant moment for Zionism, but the community has struggled to adjust to life in Israel. Many have felt that their treatment has not matched the generosity and imagination of the impulse that brought them to the country. As the investigation into the beating of Damas Pakedeh continues, and the government works to address the grievances of the Ethiopian community, it is clear that this is a critical moment for Israel. The country must confront its own racism and discrimination, and work towards a more inclusive and equal society for all its citizens. The Ethiopian community has been crying out for justice and equality for too long, and it is time for Israel to listen.

Momentum, the Labour-supporting group formed from Jeremy Corbyn's 2015 leadership campaign, has launched a new initiative to provide childcare services and engage children in politics. The program, called Momentum Kids, aims to facilitate "political engagement" for single parents and offer "fun, engaging and child-friendly" activities for youngsters. This move is part of the group's efforts to create a "mass movement for real transformative change" and secure general election success for Labour. Momentum Kids will provide a creche at the group's upcoming four-day festival, The World Transformed, in Liverpool, where Labour is holding its annual conference. The event will feature storytelling and workshops on campaigning, specifically designed for young people. Organisers hope to expand the program across Momentum's 150 local branches, creating a space for children to question, learn, and express themselves. The initiative also seeks to address the issue of women being "shut out of many political spaces" due to their disproportionate caring responsibilities. Jeremy Corbyn has previously spoken out against companies that discriminate against women by promoting after-work drinking, highlighting the need for more family-friendly policies. Children's author Alan Gibbons has expressed his support for the program, emphasizing the importance of creative activities in a child's development. "As young people grow, they need stories, poems, songs, drama and play to develop as complete human beings," he said. The launch of Momentum Kids comes as the Labour party prepares for its leadership election on Saturday, with Corbyn facing a challenge from Owen Smith. Despite the controversy surrounding his leadership, Corbyn remains committed to his vision for Labour, and Momentum Kids is just one example of the group's efforts to engage new audiences and build a more inclusive movement. With its focus on childcare and youth engagement, Momentum Kids has the potential to make a positive impact on the lives of families and young people across the country.

Chris Gayle Set to Return to Somerset Despite Recent Controversy West Indian cricket star Chris Gayle is set to return to Somerset for a six-game stint in the T20 Blast, despite recent controversy surrounding his behavior. Earlier this month, Gayle was fined £4,900 after asking a TV reporter for a date in a live interview while playing for Melbourne Renegades in Australia's Big Bash League. The incident sparked a backlash, with many criticizing Gayle's actions as unprofessional and disrespectful. However, Gayle has apologized for his actions, although he believes the reaction was "out of proportion." The 36-year-old is now looking forward to putting the controversy behind him and focusing on his cricket. He will join Somerset on June 1 and will play his first game against Sussex. His six-game stint will come to an end on June 19 against Hampshire. Gayle has a strong affinity for Somerset, having played for the club in 2015. During his previous stint, he scored 328 runs in just three appearances, making a significant impact on the team. The left-hander's impressive form included a 12-ball half-century, which equalled the record for the fastest fifty in Twenty20 cricket. Somerset's director of cricket, Matt Maynard, has described Gayle as "box office," suggesting that his presence was a major factor in the club selling out their seven T20 Blast games last year. Maynard has also backed Gayle despite recent criticism from the club's newly-appointed County Championship skipper, Chris Rogers. Rogers, who played alongside Gayle in the Big Bash League three years ago, has made it clear that he is not a fan of the West Indian's attitude and behavior. However, Maynard believes that Gayle got on well with everyone during his time with Somerset last summer and expects him to make a positive impact once again. Gayle's return to Somerset has been welcomed by the club's chief executive, Guy Lavender, who has hinted that the club may be able to bring him back to Taunton if they qualify from the group stage. With Gayle's impressive form and experience, Somerset will be hoping that he can help the club make it through to the later stages of the competition. Despite the controversy surrounding his recent behavior, Gayle remains a fan favorite, and his return to Somerset is likely to generate significant excitement among supporters. With his explosive batting style and charismatic personality, Gayle is sure to be a major draw for the club, and his presence will undoubtedly add to the excitement of the T20 Blast. Gayle's schedule with Somerset includes matches against Sussex, Essex, Surrey, Glamorgan, Gloucestershire, and Hampshire. With his first game just around the corner, fans will be eagerly awaiting his return to the pitch, hoping that he can recapture the form that made him such a success during his previous stint with the club. As one of the most talented and entertaining cricketers in the world, Chris Gayle is sure to make a significant impact on the T20 Blast, and his return to Somerset is a major coup for the club.

**Outrage in China as CCTV Footage Shows Woman Being Dragged Across Hotel Corridor** A disturbing video has sparked widespread outrage in China, showing a woman being grabbed and dragged across a hotel corridor in full view of bystanders. The incident, which occurred at the Yitel Hotel, has prompted millions of posts on social media, with the hashtag "Girl attacked at Yitei hotel" being used over two million times and viewed by two billion users. According to the victim, who uploaded the video on Sina Weibo under the username "Wanwan", the incident began when a man approached her in the hotel corridor and asked which room she was in. When she refused to answer, the man started to drag her away, clutching her neck and face, making it difficult for her to breathe. The woman attempted to run downstairs, but the man grabbed her by the hair and dragged her towards the stairway. The CCTV footage shows the staff member and other hotel guests watching the scuffle, but most did not intervene, assuming it was a couple's quarrel. It was only when a bystander appeared to help the woman leave the scene that the situation was brought under control. The incident has raised concerns about the lack of intervention from bystanders in China, where there have been several high-profile cases in recent years of people refusing to help those in need. In one notable case in 2011, a two-year-old girl was knocked over in a hit-and-run accident, and 18 people passed by before someone came to her rescue. She later died from her injuries. The Yitel Hotel's parent company, Homeinns, has issued an apology to the victim and the public, stating that the incident showed "insufficient security management and customer service". Beijing police are investigating the incident, and the hotel has promised to take steps to improve its security measures. The video has sparked a heated debate on social media, with many expressing their anger at the hotel and calling for greater awareness about the importance of intervening in such situations. Some have circulated a video campaign called "#WhoWillYouHelp", produced by the Ontario government last year to combat sexual harassment. Others have shared tips on self-defence for women, while some have urged people to stop turning a blind eye to such incidents. Weibo user Winston commented, "If people stop being indifferent and calling it a'domestic incident' when husbands/boyfriends beat, drag or abuse their wives/girlfriends in public, wouldn't there be fewer of these dangerous situations?" The incident has highlighted the need for greater awareness and education about the importance of intervening in situations where someone is in need of help. The reluctance of bystanders to intervene in China is often attributed to the fear of being blamed or sued by the injured person. However, this incident has sparked a renewed call for people to take action and help those in need, rather than standing by and doing nothing. As the investigation into the incident continues, it is hoped that it will lead to greater awareness and a change in attitude towards intervening in such situations.

A search operation for three missing climbers on New Zealand's Mt Cook has been suspended after aerial searches yielded no results. The climbers, Sydney doctor Michael Bishop, 53, German national Yohann Viellehner, 58, and his son Raphael, 27, were last seen on Monday as they attempted to reach the summit. The men, who were roped together, failed to return to their hut, prompting a search effort. Despite the suspension of the search, police say they will re-evaluate their plans if new information or sightings come to light. The families of the missing men, who are from Australia and Germany, are understandably upset but aware of the reasons behind the decision. Mt Cook, also known as Aoraki, is a challenging climb that has claimed over 230 lives since it was first conquered in 1894. The search team is disappointed with the outcome, and their thoughts are with the families of the missing climbers.

Birmingham's 21-year-old midfielder, Arthur, will leave the club at season's end. He made his debut in 2013 but hasn't featured since 2015. Arthur had a loan stint with Cheltenham, making seven appearances. Republic of Ireland's Noe Baba and goalkeeper Josh Tibbetts will also depart St Andrew's.

Outrage has erupted in Tunisia after a video emerged of a DJ playing a dance version of the Muslim call to prayer at a festival in the north-eastern town of Nabeul. The incident occurred on Friday at the Orbit Festival, where two European DJs were performing near the popular seaside resort of Hammamet. The footage, shared on social media on Sunday, sparked widespread outrage and condemnation. As a result, the governor of Nabeul, Mnaouar Ouertani, has announced that the nightclub where the incident took place will "remain closed" until further notice. An investigation has been launched, and the club's manager has been detained for "violation against good morals and public outrage against modesty." Governor Ouertani stated that the authorities "will not allow attacks against religious feelings and the sacred." The organisers of the Orbit Festival have since apologised on Facebook, although they claim not to accept responsibility for the playing of the offensive music. The DJ responsible, Dax J, has also offered his "sincere apologies" for any offense caused, stating that it was never his intention to upset or cause offense to anybody. The incident has highlighted the importance of cultural sensitivity and respect for religious traditions. The investigation is ongoing, and it remains to be seen what further action will be taken.

A fatal accident inquiry into the death of 12-year-old Keane Wallis-Bennett has begun, nearly nine years after she was killed when a modesty wall in her school's PE changing room collapsed on top of her. The incident occurred on April 1, 2014, at Liberton High School in Edinburgh, and a police investigation at the time found that no one would face criminal charges. The inquiry, which is expected to last for two weeks, aims to establish the full circumstances surrounding Keane's death. Sheriff Principal Mhairi Stephen, who is leading the inquiry, said that the hearing comes at a poignant time, as many of Keane's former classmates have recently been taking exams and are preparing to start their lives. The inquiry heard that pupils had been leaning on the wall while changing their shoes when it suddenly collapsed, trapping Keane underneath. Witnesses described the efforts of fellow pupils to lift the wall, but it was too heavy. Det Ch Insp Keith Hardie, who investigated the incident, told the inquiry that he still cannot say why the wall fell on that particular day. The court also heard statements from Keane's classmates, who described the moments leading up to the tragedy. One girl said that PE teacher Nicole Christie must have heard the bang as the wall fell and told the pupils to leave the area. Christie then went over to Keane and reassured her that an ambulance was on the way. Other witnesses described how pupils would often push or shove against the wall, and one girl said that she had seen a gap at the bottom of the wall on previous occasions. Another pupil said that she had seen a girl try to climb up the wall, but had stopped when she saw it move. The inquiry will focus on why the wall collapsed, why it collapsed when it did, and the property maintenance regime at the school. Sheriff Principal Stephen said that the whole community was shocked by Keane's death, and that school should be a safe place for all pupils. The inquiry will continue to hear evidence over the coming days, in an effort to provide answers for Keane's family and to prevent such a tragedy from happening again in the future.

New Study Reveals Bats as Primary Carriers of Potential Viral Threats to Humans A groundbreaking study conducted by the EcoHealth Alliance in New York has shed light on the mammals that pose the greatest risk of transmitting viruses to humans. The research, published in the journal Nature, analyzed 586 viruses known to infect 754 species of mammals, with a focus on identifying potential zoonotic infections that could make the jump from animals to people. The findings suggest that bats are the primary carriers of viral threats, with an estimated 17 zoonotic infections per species. The study's lead researcher, Dr. Kevin Olival, explained that the team used existing data to fill gaps in knowledge and estimate which species were likely to harbor viruses with the potential to infect humans. The results revealed that bats, primates, and rodents are among the top carriers of zoonotic infections, with bats posing the greatest threat. The researchers mapped the ranges of these species and the infections they carry, identifying global hotspots where the risk of viral transmission is highest. The study's findings have significant implications for global health, as some of the most devastating outbreaks in recent history, including Ebola and HIV, are believed to have originated from animals. Dr. Olival emphasized that the key to preventing future pandemics lies in minimizing human contact with wildlife, including through hunting and habitat destruction. "Our take-home message is that these diseases are emerging because of the human impact on the environment," he said. While the study's predictions are not intended to drive specific policy decisions, they can be used to prioritize research and viral surveillance efforts. James Lloyd-Smith, a researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles, noted that "although most pandemics are zoonoses, most zoonoses do not cause pandemics." The EcoHealth Alliance's next project will focus on birds, which are another significant source of zoonotic infections, including avian flu. The study's findings serve as a reminder of the importance of proactive measures to prevent the spread of viral diseases. By understanding the risks posed by different species and geographic regions, researchers and policymakers can work together to develop strategies for mitigating the threat of zoonotic infections and protecting global health. As Dr. Olival emphasized, "it's not the bat's fault" – rather, it is human activity that drives the emergence of these diseases. By taking a proactive and informed approach, we can reduce the risk of future pandemics and promote a healthier, more sustainable relationship between humans and the environment.

**Gorse Fires Continue to Ravage Northern Ireland, Fire Service Appeals for Public's Help** A staggering 498 gorse fires have been reported across Northern Ireland since the start of May, with the latest incident forcing the closure of the Cuilcagh Mountain trail in County Fermanagh. The Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service (NIFRS) has condemned the deliberate starting of these fires, warning that they put not only firefighters but also the public and property at risk. Group Commander Brian Stanfield of the NIFRS described the phenomenon as "complete madness" and "reckless anti-social behaviour". He appealed to the public to come forward with any information about individuals who may be starting these fires, urging them to report such incidents to the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI). "We're appealing to the public, if you do know people who are fire setting, let the PSNI know so we can put them through the courts because this is absolutely ridiculous," he said. Fire crews have been working tirelessly since Sunday to bring a massive gorse fire near Fivemiletown, County Tyrone, under control. The fire, which covers an extensive area at Mullaghfad forest on the Tyrone and Fermanagh border, has required the deployment of eight fire appliances and specialist equipment, including tanker lorries bringing water to the site. Dozens of personnel are involved in the effort, which has been ongoing for two days. The fire is believed to have started in multiple locations, and the NIFRS is working with the forestry service and the Southern fire service to bring it under control. The area is part of a large forest that includes Crocknagrally, Jenkin, and Fardross forests, and is located within a Special Protection Area for hen harriers and the Slieve Beagh Area of special scientific interest. The NIFRS has warned that gorse fires are "resource intensive" and that crews are prepared to deal with any further incidents this week. However, with the countryside being "like a tinder box", the service is concerned that its resources will be stretched to the limit if the fires continue at the current rate. Mr Stanfield cautioned that people are unaware of the personal risks they take when starting these fires, saying that "when the ground is that dry and there's a change in wind direction, the fire will move faster than the person can run, and it's only a matter of time until someone is seriously injured or killed at one of these fires". The public is urged to remain vigilant and to report any suspicious activity to the authorities. The NIFRS is moving its engines around the country to keep the public safe and is appealing for the public's help in preventing these devastating fires. As the situation continues to unfold, one thing is clear: the reckless starting of gorse fires must be stopped to prevent further damage to the environment and to protect the lives of those who live and work in the affected areas.

Last night's televised debate on The Good Friday Agreement Generation sparked a frenzy of discussion on social media, with the hashtag #GFAGen trending across the UK. The debate, which featured representatives from the DUP, Sinn Féin, Ulster Unionists, SDLP, and Alliance, among others, was watched by thousands and generated a significant amount of buzz on Twitter. The young audience members who posed questions to the panel were widely praised on social media for their thought-provoking queries and confident demeanor. In contrast, some of the politicians on the panel received criticism from viewers, who were unimpressed with their responses. Veteran political commentator Eamonn Mallie was among those who expressed his admiration for the young questioners, while also expressing his disappointment with some of the politicians' answers. The debate was attended by representatives from various parties, including Alastair Ross of the DUP, Chris Hazzard of Sinn Féin, and Naomi Long of the Alliance. Other parties, such as the TUV, Green Party, and UKIP, were also represented. As the election approaches on May 5, it remains to be seen whether the debate has swayed the opinions of first-time voters. The next major televised election debate will take place on May 3, when the BBC will host a leaders debate.

A teenager was attacked on Dunkeld Road near the Stagecoach building on Wednesday at 16:40. Two men, aged 20-25 and slim, were involved. One was 5ft 11in with brown hair, wearing a dark red tracksuit and blue jeans. The other was 5ft 9in with dark brown hair and dark clothes.

Tragedy Strikes at Disney: Body of Two-Year-Old Boy Found A devastating discovery was made in the search for Lane Graves, a two-year-old boy from Nebraska who was dragged into the water by an alligator at Disney's Seven Seas Lagoon. Divers found a body, believed to be Lane's, intact in the water on Wednesday. Orange County Sheriff Jerry Demings confirmed that the body has not been formally identified, but authorities are confident it is the missing boy. The incident occurred on Tuesday evening when Lane was wading in shallow water near the shore of the lagoon, despite a "no swimming" sign in the area. His father attempted to retrieve him, sustaining minor lacerations to his arm. A massive search effort ensued, with 50 people using sonar equipment to scour the lakes and ponds linked to the lagoon. Five alligators were seized and killed in the hopes of finding Lane's remains. The absence of warning signs about alligators in the area has raised questions, with a Disney spokesperson stating that the situation would be reviewed. The tragic incident has left the community in shock, and an investigation is underway to determine the circumstances surrounding Lane's death. The Graves family, from Elkhorn, Nebraska, was on vacation with their three children when the incident occurred.

Ravi Shastri, 55, has been named India's new cricket coach, replacing Anil Kumble. Shastri brings significant experience as a player and coach. Zaheer Khan and Rahul Dravid will support as bowling and overseas batting consultants, respectively. The change comes after Kumble's resignation due to an "untenable" partnership with captain Virat Kohli. Shastri previously served as India's team director before Kumble's appointment.

Princess Anne Reveals Wild Boar Attack on Her Farm A recent farming conference was shocked to hear that Princess Anne's farm had been visited by a wild boar, resulting in the death of one of her prized Gloucestershire Old Spot boars. The Princess Royal, who is patron of the Gloucestershire Old Spots Pig Breeders' Club, revealed the incident to delegates, stating that the wild boar had killed her boar after being introduced to her two sows in season. The princess, who lives at Gatcombe Park in Gloucestershire, has kept pigs for many years and is known for her passion for farming and conservation. She expressed her concerns about the origins of the wild boar and the potential for further incidents, saying "So far, we haven't found the origins of this particular invader and I'm hoping I'm not going to see him again for a bit." The incident has highlighted the growing issue of wild boar sightings in the area, with a large population of the animals living in the nearby Forest of Dean, just 17 miles away from Gatcombe Park. In a separate incident, a wild boar wandered onto the M4 in Wiltshire, causing a fatal crash that killed 47-year-old Raymond Green. The two incidents have prompted North Wiltshire MP James Gray to write to Natural England, expressing his concerns about the wild boar population and seeking advice on how to address the issue. Gray stated that his constituents are increasingly worried about the growing number of wild boar sightings, with recent spottings in Box and Corsham. The Gloucestershire Old Spot breed, which Princess Anne is so passionate about, is listed as a minority breed on the Rare Breeds Survival Trust watchlist, with only between 500 and 1,000 breeding females believed to be in the country. The princess's loss is not only a personal one but also a blow to the conservation efforts of this rare breed. As the issue of wild boar sightings continues to grow, it remains to be seen how authorities will address the problem and prevent further incidents.

Teachers in Belfast and Newtownabbey are set to go on strike on Wednesday, as part of a long-running dispute over pay. The NASUWT union, one of the largest teaching unions in Northern Ireland, has announced that its members in the two areas will be taking industrial action, with other areas to follow in the coming months. The strike is the first to be called by the NASUWT since 2011, and comes after all teaching unions in Northern Ireland rejected an offer that would have seen their pay frozen last year and a rise of 1% for 2016-17. While some schools have written to parents to inform them which classes will go ahead as normal on the day, the NASUWT has warned that this could potentially breach the Data Protection Act. The union claims that by revealing which classes will be affected, some schools may be inadvertently disclosing the identity of NASUWT members, which could be seen as intimidation.
