As a result, some principals have been warned that they could face legal action if they are found to be in breach of the law. In a letter to one principal, the NASUWT stated that there may be grounds for a complaint to the Information Commissioner and for seeking compensation for distress through the courts. However, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) has criticized the warnings, describing them as "shocking". Paul McClenaghan, the president of the NAHT in Northern Ireland, said that school leaders were being "threatened" for simply carrying out their duties and informing parents about the impact of the strike. He argued that school leaders have always put the needs of children first and supported their colleagues, often at a high personal cost. Justin McCamphill from the NASUWT defended the union's position, saying that it had a duty to ensure that the law was being upheld. He stated that it would be wrong for the union not to inform principals of potential breaches of the law, and that the warnings were simply a matter of informing them of their legal obligations. The strike is set to go ahead on Wednesday, with further action planned for January and February 2017. Other teaching unions are currently engaged in industrial action short of a strike, and it remains to be seen how the dispute will be resolved.

Bangladesh Vows to Stop Deadly Attacks as Opposition Accuses Government of Targeting Political Opponents Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to do whatever it takes to stop the wave of deadly attacks that have plagued the country in recent years. Her comments came a day after police launched a massive crackdown on Islamist militants, arresting over 3,000 people. However, the opposition has accused the government of using the operation to target political opponents, sparking concerns about the true motives behind the campaign. Speaking at a meeting of her ruling Awami League party on Saturday, Ms. Hasina said, "It may take time, but God willing, we will be able to bring [the perpetrators] under control. Where will the criminals hide? Each and every killer will be brought to book." The police campaign, which began on Friday, is set to last for a week and has been focused on arresting Islamist militants. However, critics argue that many ordinary criminals have been caught up in the sweep, and that the government is using the operation to silence opposition voices. Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, the leader of the opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party, claimed that "hundreds of opposition activists have been arrested in the police drive." He told the AFP news agency, "In the name of the crackdown against Islamist militants, many ordinary and innocent people are being detained." The government has denied targeting opposition activists, with Nadeem Qadir, a government spokesman at the Bangladesh High Commission in London, telling the BBC, "There's no targeted political elements in this case, it's an operation...to stop this targeted killing, it's as simple as that." The crackdown comes amid a surge in deadly attacks in Bangladesh, which have claimed the lives of over 40 people, including secular bloggers, academics, gay rights activists, and members of religious minorities. The latest victim was a Hindu monastery worker who was hacked to death in Pabna district on Friday. In the past week alone, a Hindu priest, a Christian grocer, and the wife of an anti-terror police officer were all killed in attacks by suspected Islamist militants. Analysts believe that the killing of a police officer's wife last Sunday may have triggered the crackdown. The attacks have been claimed by so-called Islamic State (IS) or al-Qaeda-linked groups, but the government has disputed these claims, with some members blaming opposition parties and local Islamist groups. Bangladesh's home minister has even suggested an Israeli link to the killings, describing an "international conspiracy" against Bangladesh. However, both the opposition and the Israeli government have denied any involvement, with Israel describing the accusations as "utter drivel." As the government struggles to contain the violence, it faces accusations of not doing enough to protect minorities in the Sunni-dominated nation. The killings have sparked widespread concern, both at home and abroad, and have raised questions about the rise of extremism in Bangladesh. The country has a long history of secularism, but in recent years, there has been a growing trend towards sectarianism and terrorism. Until the killings stop, the government will face mounting pressure to take decisive action to protect its citizens and restore stability to the country. With the police campaign underway, it remains to be seen whether the government's efforts will be enough to bring the perpetrators to justice and put an end to the bloodshed. One thing is certain, however: the people of Bangladesh deserve peace and security, and it is the government's responsibility to ensure that they receive it.

Belgian Minister Refuses to Back Down on Asylum Case, Despite Fines and Criticism A high-profile asylum case in Belgium has sparked a heated debate over the country's immigration policies, with the Minister for Asylum and Migration, Theo Francken, refusing to back down despite facing fines and criticism. The case involves a Syrian family of four, including two children aged five and eight, who have been granted visas by a Belgian tribunal but are being denied entry by Minister Francken. The family, who live in the war-torn city of Aleppo, have been offered food and lodging by friends in Namur, but Minister Francken argues that their links to Belgium are weak and that granting them asylum would open the door to "asylum chaos". The minister has refused to pay fines of €4,000 per day, which have now surpassed €30,000, and has even joked about seeking political asylum in the office of his colleague, Interior Minister Jan Jambon. In a dramatic turn of events, Minister Francken posted a picture of an empty party office on Facebook, claiming that bailiffs had seized the furniture. However, it later emerged that no furniture had been taken, although the threat still exists. The ministry is appealing against both the fine and the ruling, with a spokeswoman stating that they will continue to work despite the challenges. The Syrian family's lawyer, Mieke Van den Broeck, has accused Minister Francken of trampling on Belgium's separation of judicial and government powers, saying that he is "playing with our clients' lives and with Belgian tax money". The lawyer argues that the family's situation is exceptional and urgent, given the ongoing conflict in Aleppo and the fact that their home has been destroyed. Minister Francken, a member of the centre-right New Flemish Alliance, has countered that the family should have applied for refuge in Lebanon, where the father initially applied for asylum at the Belgian consulate. He argues that courts should not set asylum policy and that Belgium has already welcomed refugees, but cannot grant a home to every Syrian who applies. The case has sparked a wider debate over Belgium's asylum policies, with many criticizing Minister Francken's stance as inhumane and overly rigid. The Belgian family who have offered to support the Syrian family have promised to pay for all their costs, but Minister Francken remains unmoved, insisting that he is elected to serve the public interest and will continue to do so. As the case continues to unfold, it remains to be seen whether Minister Francken will ultimately be forced to back down and grant the family asylum, or whether he will continue to resist the pressure and criticism.

Judd Trump has claimed his seventh ranking title after a thrilling 10-8 victory over Marco Fu in the Llandudno final. The 27-year-old from Bristol staged an impressive comeback, making three centuries in four frames to turn the match around. Trump had found himself 5-2 down early on, but he responded with consecutive century breaks of 136 and 115 to close the gap. Trump's momentum continued into the final session, with further breaks of 110 and 76 putting him within reach of victory. Although Fu fought back to win the next two frames, Trump held his nerve to secure the title with a fourth century break of 102. Fu reduced the deficit to 9-8 with a 58, but Trump was able to hold on and atone for three defeats in finals this season. The victory sees Trump move up to second in the rankings, adding to his European Masters title won in October. Fu, who won the Scottish Open in December, had started strongly with runs of 67, 48, 39, and 83 to establish his early lead. However, Trump's superior form in the end proved too much for the world number nine, as he claimed a hard-fought victory. The win marks a significant milestone for Trump, who has now won seven ranking titles in his career.

Eagles of Death Metal Dropped from Festivals After Singer Reiterates Bataclan Attack Conspiracy Theories The rock band Eagles of Death Metal has been dropped from two French music festivals after lead singer Jesse Hughes repeated conspiracy theories surrounding the 2015 Bataclan attack. Ninety people were killed when gunmen opened fire during the band's set at the venue in November 2015. Hughes had previously suggested that some security guards may have known about the attack in advance, sparking outrage and condemnation from the Bataclan and others. Despite apologizing for his earlier remarks, Hughes reiterated his claims in a recent interview with Taki's Magazine, stating that the terrorists must have had inside help to carry out the attack. "There's no denying the terrorists were already inside, and they had to get in somehow," he said. "During the shooting I went outside and the backstage door was propped open. How did that happen?" These comments have been widely criticized, with many accusing Hughes of spreading baseless and hurtful conspiracy theories. The Bataclan venue has condemned Hughes' comments as "grave and defamatory," and has called for speculation about the tragedy to be kept to a minimum while a judicial investigation is underway. The venue has praised the professionalism and courage of the security agents who were on the ground during the attack, saying that hundreds of people were saved thanks to their intervention. As a result of Hughes' comments, the band has been dropped from the line-up of the Rock En Seine and Cabaret Vert festivals. Organizers of the festivals said they are "in total disagreement with Jesse Hughes' recent allegations" and do not want to be associated with his conspiracy theories. Hughes has apologized for his earlier comments, saying they were "unfounded and baseless" and expressing his "humble beg[ging] for forgiveness" from those hurt or offended by his words. However, it is unclear why Hughes has chosen to revisit these comments now, despite the harm and offense they have caused. The singer has said he is suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from the Bataclan tragedy, which also took the life of the band's merchandise manager Nick Alexander. An inquest into Alexander's death closed on Thursday, with the coroner ruling that he was unlawfully killed. The court heard that Alexander's former girlfriend tried to save him after he had been shot in the stomach and abdomen. The decision to drop Eagles of Death Metal from the festivals is a clear indication that Hughes' conspiracy theories will not be tolerated. The Bataclan and others are still trying to come to terms with the trauma and loss caused by the attack, and Hughes' comments have only served to reopen old wounds. As the judicial investigation into the attack continues, it is essential that speculation and conspiracy theories are kept to a minimum, and that those affected by the tragedy are treated with respect and dignity.

Rangers Sign Midfielder Ryan Jack on Three-Year Deal Rangers Football Club has announced the signing of midfielder Ryan Jack on a three-year deal under freedom of contract. The 25-year-old joins the team after leaving Aberdeen, where he spent seven years and became captain in 2015. Jack's signing is seen as a significant boost to Rangers' midfield, which has been weakened by the departure of loan players Jon Toral and Emerson Hyndman. St Johnstone defender Richard Foster, a former teammate of Jack's at Aberdeen, has praised the midfielder's skills, describing him as "very much underrated." Foster, who has also played for Rangers, told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound that Jack is a talented player who excels at tackling and winning the ball. He also believes that Jack has more quality on the ball than he was often given credit for during his time at Aberdeen. Rangers, who finished third in the 2016-17 Scottish Premiership, have been looking to strengthen their squad ahead of the new season. The signing of Jack, combined with the earlier acquisition of Portuguese defender Bruno Alves, suggests that the team is building a strong foundation for the upcoming campaign. Foster believes that Jack will provide much-needed protection for Rangers' center-backs, who were often under pressure last season due to the team's high-pressing style of play. With his experience and skills, Ryan Jack is expected to make a significant contribution to Rangers' success in the seasons to come.

A debate on granting Welsh Labour more autonomy from the UK party has sparked division at the party's conference. Matthew van Rooyen, a delegate from Bridgend, expressed frustration at attempts to delay a vote on the proposals, saying "We have got Jeremy Corbyn as leader, whether we like it or not." The plans include a seat on Labour's national executive committee, but supporters of Mr Corbyn want the Welsh representative to be elected by party members, rather than nominated by Welsh Labour leader Carwyn Jones. The conference chairman intervened, rebuking delegates for booing a speaker and urging them to be respectful. Mike Payne from GMB Wales called for an end to "prevarication" and for the party to "get on with it." Delegates will vote on the changes later on Tuesday, amid ongoing divisions within the party. The outcome is expected to shape the future of Welsh Labour's relationship with the UK party.

A 49-year-old man from Belfast has been granted bail after being charged with possessing cocaine with intent to supply. Hugh Brady, of Molyneaux Street, was stopped by police on the Sydenham bypass on Wednesday night, where officers seized 3kg of drugs from his car. According to the court, Brady had been driving around Bangor, County Down, for at least 90 minutes before giving up and heading back towards Belfast. During this time, he stopped at a garage to ask for directions and purchased a mobile phone from a Tesco store, but was unable to buy credit for it. A detective opposing bail told the court that Brady had alleged he was approached by individuals who he "couldn't say no to" and was asked to deliver a package to another location. However, Brady failed to find the intended address and eventually gave up, leading to his arrest. Brady's defence solicitor argued that he was at the "very bottom" of any operation to move the drugs and was simply following instructions. The lawyer said that Brady's inability to find the address and his decision to give up and drive back to Belfast demonstrated his ineptness and lack of involvement in the drugs gang. The detective acknowledged that Brady's actions suggested he was not a major player in the drugs trade, but rather someone who had been entrusted with a consignment due to his trusted position. Despite this, the judge granted Brady bail, ordering him and his wife to lodge a £3,000 cash surety, which represents their life savings. Brady is due to appear in court again on June 26. The case has raised questions about the involvement of ordinary citizens in the drugs trade and the extent to which they are coerced or intimidated into participating. Brady's apology and apparent remorse during interview suggest that he may have been a reluctant participant in the operation.

A mother has testified in court about the moment she discovered her son had traveled to Syria to join the so-called Islamic State. Sue Boyce told the Old Bailey that her son, Thomas Petty, had kept his plans a secret until after he had left their home in the summer of 2014. Tragically, Mr. Petty, 25, was killed in battle later that year. Ms. Boyce recounted how her son had converted to Islam at the age of 15, but she had no idea he was considering traveling to Syria to fight. She described how, in July 2014, Mr. Petty flew to Athens and then to Cairo, initially maintaining contact with his family before suddenly going quiet. It wasn't until late August that he called to inform his family that he was on the border of Syria and intended to enter the country as an aid worker. Ms. Boyce expressed her horror and concern, urging her son not to go through with his plans. However, Mr. Petty was resolute in his decision, sending an email to his family entitled "New Life" in which he explained his desire to live in a "proper Islamic state" where he could freely practice his faith. He wrote that he had been unhappy living in the UK since his conversion to Islam and felt compelled to join his "brothers and sisters" in Syria. The email also revealed that Mr. Petty had been training to become a "soldier" and believed it was necessary to defend himself in a world that was "uniting to destroy" Muslims. He emphasized that no one had brainwashed or tricked him into making this decision, but rather it was a choice he had made of his own free will. Ms. Boyce's testimony came during the trial of Lorna Moore and Ayman Shaukat, both from Walsall, who deny terror-related offenses. The court heard that Mr. Petty was one of a group of friends from Walsall who had left Britain in 2014 to join the Islamic State. Ms. Boyce eventually identified her son's body from video footage, which was shown to her by police 10 months after his death. The trial has also heard that others had sought to follow in Mr. Petty's footsteps, with some receiving assistance from Mr. Shaukat, 27. Trainee maths teacher Lorna Moore, 33, denies failing to disclose information about acts of terrorism, while Mr. Shaukat is accused of helping two men, Sajid Aslam and Alex Nash, on their way to Syria. He denies two counts of preparing for terrorist acts and one charge of possession of a terrorist document. The case highlights the complexities and challenges faced by families and authorities in preventing and responding to radicalization and terrorism. As the trial continues, it is likely to shed further light on the circumstances surrounding Mr. Petty's decision to join the Islamic State and the roles that others may have played in supporting or facilitating his actions.

US Faces Surge in Child Migrants, Seeks $1.4bn in Aid The United States is bracing for a massive influx of unaccompanied child migrants, with estimates suggesting up to 60,000 children will cross the border illegally this year. The majority of these children are from Central America and Mexico, fleeing domestic abuse, violent gangs, and poverty in their home countries. Many hope to reunite with parents or relatives already living in the US. In response to the crisis, the White House has requested an additional $1.4 billion from Congress to provide temporary housing and care for the children. Two military bases have been designated as temporary shelters. According to Cecilia Munoz, Director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, the number of children traveling alone has been increasing since 2009, with a notable rise in girls and children under 13. The situation is dire, with many children unaware of the dangers they face on their journey, including sexual assaults, forced labor, and hunger. The US government predicts that the number of unaccompanied child migrants could soar to nearly 130,000 next year. This represents a significant increase from previous years, with 24,668 children apprehended by border agents in 2013, nearly double the number from the previous year. The White House is urging Congress to act swiftly to address the crisis and provide the necessary resources to support these vulnerable children.

A 78-year-old man from west Belfast has appeared in court charged with aiding and abetting the murder of Jean McConville, a mother-of-10 who was abducted and killed by the IRA in 1972. Ivor Bell, of Ramoan Gardens, was charged in connection with the high-profile case, which has been adjourned several times since he was first charged in March 2014. Mrs McConville, 37, was taken from her flat in front of her children after being wrongly accused of being an informer. Her body was not recovered until 2003, when it was found on a beach in County Louth. The Public Prosecution Service had been given a final deadline to proceed with the case, and Bell's appearance at Belfast Magistrates Court was the last chance for the service to decide if the case would go ahead. Bell is also charged with membership of the IRA. He is due to return to court in six weeks, when a date will be set for a preliminary inquiry to determine if the case will proceed to trial in the Crown Court. Despite a call from the defence to discontinue the case, the prosecution is moving forward, seeking justice for the McConville family over 40 years after her tragic death.

Tensions Escalate in South China Sea as US and China Trade Accusations A recent incident in the South China Sea has sparked a war of words between the United States and China, with both nations accusing each other of engaging in reckless behavior. On May 17, a US maritime reconnaissance aircraft was carrying out a routine patrol in international airspace when it was intercepted by two Chinese aircraft. According to US officials, the Chinese planes engaged in "dangerous maneuvers," forcing the US pilot to descend approximately 200 feet to avoid a collision. However, China has vehemently denied these allegations, with a foreign ministry spokesperson, Hong Lei, stating that the US plane had flown too close to Hainan Island and that the Chinese aircraft had followed and monitored it at a safe distance. Lei claimed that the actions of the Chinese pilots were "completely professional and safe." The US Defense Department has addressed the issue through military and diplomatic channels, acknowledging that China has made improvements in its actions over the past year, flying in a safe and professional manner. The incident highlights the growing tensions in the South China Sea, a region rich in resources and claimed by several nations, including Taiwan, China, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Brunei. The US has accused China of militarizing the area, while China has criticized increased US naval patrols and exercises in Asia. The frictions between the two nations have sparked concern that the area is becoming a flashpoint with possible global consequences. As the situation continues to unfold, the US has reaffirmed its commitment to opposing restrictions on freedom of navigation and unlawful sovereignty claims by all sides.

India has successfully launched a record-breaking 20 satellites into space from its Sriharikota space centre off the east coast. The satellites belong to various countries including the United States, Canada, Germany, and Indonesia. This achievement marks a significant milestone for India's space program, solidifying its position as a major player in the multi-billion dollar space market. The launch, which was closely monitored by Indian scientists and government ministers, saw a rocket carrying the 20 satellites blast off from the launch facility in Andhra Pradesh state. The payload included a range of devices, from a 700kg Indian cartographic satellite to smaller satellites weighing as little as 1.5kg. Notably, 13 of the satellites were from the US, including one made by a Google-owned company. This launch surpasses the previous records held by the US space agency Nasa, which launched 29 satellites, and Russia, which holds the record for the most number of satellites launched in a single mission with 37 in 2014. According to the chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro), Kiran Kumar, launching multiple satellites in a single mission reduces costs and showcases India's capabilities as a low-cost operator in the international commercial space market. India's space program has recorded several achievements in recent years, including sending probes to the Moon and Mars. With this latest launch, India is poised to become a key player in the global space industry, offering affordable and efficient launch services to international customers. As Kumar aptly put it, "Each of these small objects that you are putting into space will carry out their own activity, which is independent of the other, and each of them will live a wonderful life for the finite period for which they have been designed."

Glencore Shares Plummet 30% as Analysts Warn of "Severe Problems" In a shocking turn of events, mining giant Glencore's shares dove 30% on Monday, sparking concerns over the company's financial stability. The drastic decline came after a note from analysts at Investec warned that Glencore's equity value could be "eliminated" if the company fails to cut its debt and commodity prices do not recover. According to Investec's Laura Lambie, Glencore faces "severe problems" due to its significant debt burden and the slump in commodity prices. "Miners grew hugely to meet the demand from China and they borrowed heavily to find it, and the cost of servicing that debt and the schedule of repayments are really putting companies such as Glencore under the spotlight," Lambie told the BBC. "The risk is if commodities don't recover, then companies like Glencore will be in trouble trying to repay its debt." Glencore's debt pile, which stands at approximately £20 billion, has been a major concern for investors. Despite efforts by chief executive Ivan Glasenberg to reduce debt through share sales, asset disposals, and dividend cancellations, the company's shares have continued to plummet. In recent weeks, Glencore has announced plans to sell its grains business, hoping to generate up to $12 billion to alleviate its debt burden. However, Investec has questioned the valuation of the agriculture division, citing the volatility of the business. The mining company's stock has fallen by a staggering 85% since its initial public offering in 2011, when shares were priced at £5.30. On Tuesday, Glencore's shares rallied, closing up nearly 17% at 80.24p, but the company still has a long way to go to recover its losses. Nigel Wilson, chief executive of Legal and General, a significant shareholder in Glencore, warned that the company is facing a "quasi-Lehman moment," referencing the collapse of the US investment bank during the 2008 financial crisis. Wilson called on Glencore's management to provide clarity on the company's viability to stem further stock declines. "There's a lot of noise, and there's not enough signaling. That lack of information causes a huge amount of uncertainty at Glencore, which is having a massive contagion effect across the world," Wilson said. In response to the concerns, a Glencore spokesperson assured that the company has no solvency issues. "Glencore has taken proactive steps to position our company to withstand current commodity market conditions," the spokesperson said. "Our business remains operationally and financially robust. We have positive cash flow, good liquidity, and absolutely no solvency issues." Not all analysts share the same pessimistic outlook, however. Citigroup analysts believe that the sell-off in Glencore shares has been overdone and that there is still value in the business. The firm even suggested that Glencore should consider going private via a management buyout if the market rout continues. "In the event the equity market continues to express its unwillingness to value the business fairly, the company management should take the company private, whereby restructuring measures can be taken easily and quickly," Citigroup said. As the commodity market continues to slump, Glencore's future remains uncertain. While some analysts warn of severe problems, others see value in the business. One thing is clear, however: Glencore must take drastic measures to address its debt burden and restore investor confidence to avoid a potentially catastrophic outcome.

Iranian Vice-President Eshaq Jahangiri has withdrawn from the country's presidential election, set to take place on Friday. The move was widely expected and is seen as a strategic decision to consolidate support for incumbent President Hassan Rouhani, who is seeking a second term. Jahangiri, a key ally of Rouhani, announced his withdrawal in a speech to thousands of people in the southern city of Shiraz, urging his supporters to back the president. The withdrawal of Jahangiri and Tehran's hardline mayor Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who dropped out of the race on Monday, has cleared the path for a showdown between Rouhani and conservative cleric Ebrahim Raisi. Raisi, a close ally of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, is now seen as the main threat to Rouhani's re-election bid. Recent polls have put support for Raisi and other hardliners at around 52%, with Rouhani trailing at 42%. Jahangiri played a crucial role in defending Rouhani's record during heated televised debates, criticizing his conservative rivals and highlighting the president's achievements. However, Rouhani's economic record has been a significant challenge, as the landmark nuclear deal he negotiated in 2015 has not triggered the expected economic recovery. Raisi, on the other hand, has promised to build a self-sufficient "resistance economy", create millions of jobs, and triple cash handouts to the poor. With four candidates remaining in the race, a run-off election may be necessary if none of them secure more than 50% of the vote. The outcome of the election will have significant implications for Iran's future, with Rouhani's re-election seen as crucial for the country's continued engagement with the international community. As Iranians head to the polls on Friday, the contest between Rouhani and Raisi is expected to be closely watched, both domestically and internationally.

Glamorgan Cricket Club has announced the signing of a new long-term contract with 21-year-old Ruaidhri Smith. The Glasgow-born bowler, who has come through the Welsh development system, expressed his delight at committing to the club he has supported since childhood. Despite missing much of the 2015 season due to injury and university studies, Smith has shown promise with a highest first-class score of 57 not out and best bowling figures of 3-23. Glamorgan chief executive Hugh Morris praised Smith as a "very talented young bowler" with real potential. The contract extension is part of the club's efforts to develop young talent, with Smith joining Andrew Salter and David Lloyd as emerging players. Salter recently signed a three-year contract extension, while Mark Wallace agreed to a one-year deal. Smith's signing is a positive move for the club, and fans will be eager to see him make an impact in the first team.

"Between Worlds", the latest English National Opera production at the Barbican in London, has garnered mixed reviews from critics. The opera, which reflects on the events of 11 September 2001, has been praised for its "awesome power" and "crazy courage" by some, with the Daily Telegraph's Ivan Hewett stating that it "tears at the heart". However, others have found it to be "not as affecting as it ought to be", with The Guardian's Andrew Clements noting a lack of "sheer chaotic terror" in the production. Despite this, composer Tansy Davies and librettist Nick Drake's work has been hailed as a "meditative lament on this human tragedy". The production, directed by Deborah Warner, has been criticized for its "lack of clarity" and "monochrome pace". "Between Worlds" is Davies' first opera and runs until April 25. As the second ENO production to be co-commissioned by the Barbican, it is a notable addition to the opera scene, and its success is being closely watched. With its thought-provoking themes and powerful music, "Between Worlds" is sure to spark important discussions and reflections on the tragic events that inspired it.

The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum has launched a Kickstarter campaign to raise $500,000 to preserve and display the iconic spacesuit worn by Neil Armstrong during the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. The suit, which has been in storage for nine years, is deteriorating due to the materials used in its construction, which were only intended for short-term use. According to Cathy Lewis, the museum's spacesuit curator, the suit is a complex machine made of 12 different types of textiles and fabrics. Preserving each material individually would be possible, but it would require taking the suit apart, which is not an option. Instead, the museum plans to build a climate-controlled display case to safeguard the suit and slow down its deterioration. The museum also plans to digitize the suit using 3D scanning technology. The goal is to have the suit ready for display by the 50th anniversary of the first lunar landing. Later, it will be the centerpiece of a new gallery called Destination Moon, set to open in 2020. The Kickstarter campaign aims to raise funds to support the conservation and display of this historic artifact, ensuring its preservation for future generations.

Tragedy struck on the football pitch in Omagh on Saturday when a player broke his leg in three places during a match. Mark O'Sullivan, a player for Omagh Hospitals, suffered the severe injury 40 minutes into the game against Glebe United. An ambulance was quickly called to the scene, which was located off Retreat Close near the Tyrone County Hospital. However, the emergency vehicle's response was hindered by the lack of a proper path or road to the pitch. The team's manager, Paul McCabe, has been vocal about the need for improved access to the field, citing the danger it poses to players and spectators. "People could end up having a life-threatening problem and an ambulance may not be able to reach them," he warned. McCabe expressed relief that the ambulance was able to reach the injured player without getting stuck, but emphasized that this was a lucky exception. He has been urging the council to install a path or road to ensure that emergency vehicles can reach the pitch quickly and safely. O'Sullivan was taken to Altnagelvin Hospital in Londonderry for treatment, and his team is hoping for a speedy recovery. The incident has highlighted the need for improved infrastructure at the football field to prevent similar incidents in the future.

Former UN Secretary General Kofi Annan has spoken out against the handling of the International Criminal Court (ICC) cases against Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and his deputy William Ruto. In an interview with the Financial Times, Annan stated that the two leaders should not have been allowed to remain free during their trials for crimes against humanity. The ICC ultimately dropped the charges against them, citing witness intimidation. The cases stemmed from the violent aftermath of Kenya's disputed 2007 elections, which left 1,500 people dead and 600,000 displaced. Annan, who mediated Kenya's post-election crisis in 2007-08, accused the Kenyan government of using state resources to undermine the ICC's efforts. He believes that Africans should seek justice abroad if they cannot get it domestically, and rejects accusations that the ICC is biased against Africa. Annan pointed to the successful prosecution of war crimes in the former Yugoslavia as evidence of the ICC's impartiality. He also praised the recent conviction of former Chadian President Hissene Habre, who was tried in an African Union-backed court in Senegal. The African Union has been critical of the ICC, with some member states threatening to withdraw from the court. Kenya has already announced its intention to withdraw from the ICC, a move that Annan's comments are likely to do little to reverse.

Tragedy struck in Kildysart village on Wednesday evening, resulting in the deaths of a 27-year-old woman and a 44-year-old man. Officers responding to the scene on Main St at approximately 19:30 local time found the injured woman and immediately called for emergency medical assistance. They also discovered an injured man at a nearby house. Despite efforts to save them, both individuals were pronounced dead at the scene by a local doctor. The Garda have sealed off the area for a technical examination and notified the state pathologist. Authorities have confirmed that they are not seeking any additional suspects in connection with the incident. The police are now appealing for witnesses, particularly those who were in the vicinity of Main St between 18:00 and 19:30 local time, to come forward and contact them. The investigation is ongoing, with the Garda working to determine the circumstances surrounding the tragic events.

UK Experiences Hottest Day of the Year as Heatwave Continues The UK has witnessed its hottest day of the year so far, with temperatures soaring to 30.2C (86.36F) in Teddington, south-west London, according to the Met Office. Forecaster Charles Powell has predicted that Sunday and Monday will be just as scorching, with "dry, sunny, warm, humid weather with high UV, high pollen" dominating the forecast. The high temperatures are attributed to warm, humid air from the tropical Atlantic, which is expected to bring highs of 32C (89.6F) on Sunday and 33C (91.4F) on Monday to the south and south-east of England and Greater London. This is approximately 10C (18F) above the average temperature for this time of year. However, northern parts of Scotland have experienced some respite from the heat, with rain falling on Sunday and more expected on Monday. The Met Office has warned that a "wedge of really hot air" will blow in from France on Thursday, pushing temperatures in eastern and southern England up to 34C. The UV strength in some areas has been recorded as high as that in Cyprus and Gibraltar, prompting Public Health England (PHE) to issue a heat health warning. Dr Thomas Waite, a spokesman for PHE, urged people to look out for vulnerable individuals, such as older people, those with underlying health conditions, and young children, who may be at risk from the heat. "The summer heat can bring real health risks, and we're urging everyone to keep an eye on those you know who may be at risk this summer," he said. Despite the heat, the weather is expected to remain dry in the lead-up to the Glastonbury Festival next weekend, with only a 20% chance of isolated showers on Wednesday and Thursday. However, the Met Office predicts cooler and fresher temperatures on Saturday and Sunday, with a mixture of sunny spells and showers. As the heatwave continues, people are advised to take necessary precautions to stay safe and healthy.

The Welsh Rugby Union's (WRU) senior player selection policy (SPSP) has sparked controversy, with former dual-code international Hadley labeling it "ridiculous". The policy, aimed at keeping top players in Wales, restricts the number of players who can be selected for the national team while playing outside of the country to just three. Hadley believes that Taulupe Faletau, George North, and Jamie Roberts will be the three wildcard selections, leaving Rhys Priestland facing the end of his Test career. Priestland, who plays for Bath, has been affected by the policy, which Hadley thinks will ultimately lead to his exclusion from the team. With Dan Biggar, Sam Davies, Rhys Patchell, and Gareth Anscombe all playing in Wales, Priestland's chances of selection appear slim. "Unless one of the others gets injured and cannot be picked, then there's a possibility he becomes the third wildcard choice," Hadley said. Priestland had previously taken an 18-month break from playing for Wales but reversed his decision in 2015. He has 48 caps for Wales and featured in all five games of the 2016 Six Nations. The WRU has revealed its seven-man list of players affected by the policy, including lock Dominic Day, flanker Nicky Thomas, and scrum-half Rhodri Williams. However, players who signed contracts with clubs outside Wales before the policy was introduced, such as Leigh Halfpenny and Tomas Francis, are exempt from the rule. Hadley argues that the policy should be scrapped, allowing the coach to pick the best players regardless of where they play their club rugby. "For Wales, you want to be playing your best players, whether they're playing in Wales or not," he said. "You want to try and keep them in Wales if you can, but if you can't, then surely you want them still playing for Wales." The policy has sparked debate, with many questioning its effectiveness in keeping top players in Wales.

Avram Grant has announced that he will be stepping down as the head coach of Ghana's national football team. The Israeli coach's contract is set to expire, and he revealed at the Africa Cup of Nations that he would not be renewing it. Grant informed Ghana FA president Kwesi Nyantakyi of his decision, stating that "the time is right for me to move on to a new challenge." During his tenure, Grant led Ghana to the Nations Cup final in 2015 and the semi-finals this year. Although he was unable to secure Ghana's fifth title, he successfully rebuilt the team after a tumultuous World Cup campaign in 2014. Grant took over the role in November 2014, when Ghana was still reeling from a disastrous World Cup performance. He expressed his gratitude for the experience, citing the passion and loyalty of the supporters as something he will always remember. Grant's departure marks the end of an era for Ghanaian football, and his legacy will be remembered as one of rebuilding and revitalization. His decision to move on has sparked speculation about his next coaching destination.

The FTSE 100 share index experienced a significant decline on Tuesday, dropping 106.72 points to 7,220.38 by the close of trading. The index was already trading lower, but the pound's sudden strengthening led to a further decline. A stronger pound has a negative impact on multinational firms listed on the FTSE 100, as it reduces the value of their overseas profits when converted back into sterling. The pound surged above the $1.23 mark following a speech by Prime Minister Theresa May, ending the day up nearly 2.9% against the dollar at $1.2392. It also gained 1.83% against the euro, closing at 1.157 euros. The currency's rally was driven by optimism about the UK's economic prospects. Despite the overall decline in the FTSE 100, some individual stocks performed well. Rolls-Royce shares jumped nearly 7% after the company agreed to pay £671m to settle bribery and corruption cases with UK and US authorities. However, the gain was later trimmed to 694.50p. Hargreaves Lansdown and Greggs also saw their shares rise, by 4% and 1.2% respectively. In contrast, British American Tobacco shares slipped 3.83% to £45.80 after the company announced a $49.4bn deal to acquire US rival Reynolds.

A brazen attempt to steal a statistics exam at a university took a dramatic turn when the instructor, John Cain, surprised two students, Henry Lynch II and Troy Kiphuth, in his office. The incident occurred at approximately 02:00 on Wednesday, according to university spokesman Jay Blanton. Lynch, a 21-year-old biosystems engineering student, had crawled through the campus building's ceiling ducts to gain access to Cain's office. Once inside, Lynch opened the door for his accomplice, Kiphuth, and the pair began searching for the exam while blocking the door. However, their plan was foiled when Cain returned to his office after a meal and found the door blocked. When Cain threatened to call the police, the two students fled the scene. Lynch later confessed to the crime, revealing that he had attempted to steal the exam earlier that day as well. This is not the first time Lynch has been involved in exam theft. He admitted to stealing an exam earlier in the semester, although he claimed not to have shared it with other students. The university has referred the matter to its internal discipline system, taking a strong stance against cheating and theft. "Cheating and theft of this kind is very serious in an academic institution," Blanton emphasized. Lynch and Kiphuth are set to appear before a judge next month to face charges related to the incident.

Chris Coleman, the renowned Welsh football manager, has been awarded the Freedom of the City of Swansea. The 46-year-old, who guided Wales to the semi-finals of Euro 2016, received the honour at a ceremony held at the city's Guildhall on Thursday. This prestigious award is a testament to Coleman's outstanding achievements in the world of football and his dedication to his home city. In an interview with BBC Wales, Coleman expressed his pride and gratitude, stating that it is "important" for him to remain connected to his roots in Swansea. He attributed his success to the values instilled in him from a young age, which have served him well throughout his career. Coleman also expressed his pride in being associated with the Welsh team and his pride in being a Welshman. The Lord Mayor of Swansea, David Hopkins, praised Coleman as a "proud Swansea boy" and a "terrific ambassador" for the city, making him a deserving recipient of the honour. Other notable individuals who have received the Freedom of the City include Prince Charles, President Jimmy Carter, and football legends John Charles and Mel Nurse. A celebration was held at Brangwyn Hall, featuring a performance by James Dean Bradfield of the Manic Street Preachers, to mark the occasion. Coleman's achievements have truly captured the hearts of the nation, and his legacy in Welsh football will be remembered for years to come.

A jury at the Old Bailey has delivered a verdict of not guilty in the case of a lorry driver accused of causing the death of a 26-year-old cyclist in London. Janina Gehlau, a German postgraduate student from Dusseldorf, was killed in October 2014 when the lorry turned left at Ludgate Circus, pulling her under its wheels. The driver, Vincent Doyle, 45, had overtaken Gehlau 200 meters before the junction and had waited at a red light for 23 seconds. However, he failed to spot her in the cycle lane, despite claiming to have made safety checks and looked in his mirrors "five or six times" before the green light. The court heard that if his mirrors had been correctly positioned, he would have had Gehlau in his sights for three to five seconds before the accident. Doyle told the jury that he never saw Gehlau waving her arms or heard her shouting before she fell under the lorry. He described how he felt a "bump" and looked in his mirror to see her head sticking out, and then held her hand and pleaded with her to "hold on" as he waited for the ambulance to arrive. Tragically, Gehlau died just as the paramedics got to the scene. The verdict has left Gehlau's family devastated, with her mother Andrea Tasic stating that they do not feel they have got justice for Janina. Tasic expressed her hope that her daughter's death would serve as a warning to others, saying "My only hope is that this makes people think twice before cycling in London." Doyle, who has been affected by the accident, revealed that he had a nervous breakdown last year and spent eight months in a psychiatric hospital. The case highlights the dangers of cycling in London and the importance of road safety awareness.

Supreme Court Rejects Appeal by Former MPs in Expenses Scandal The Supreme Court has rejected an appeal by three former Labour MPs, David Chaytor, Elliot Morley, and Jim Devine, who argued that their cases should be heard by Parliament rather than the courts. The three men, who deny theft by false accounting, will now face separate trials at Southwark Crown Court. The decision upholds a ruling by the Court of Appeal in July, which stated that the three were not protected by parliamentary privilege in relation to their expenses claims. Parliamentary privilege is an ancient right that protects MPs from legal action arising from proceedings in Parliament. However, the Court of Appeal ruled that this privilege had never been attached to allegations of "crimes of dishonesty" such as theft by false accounting. The three former MPs had argued that the expenses scheme was created and administered by Parliament, and therefore, any allegations related to it should be dealt with by Parliament. However, the Supreme Court disagreed, with President Lord Phillips stating that "each of these appeals is dismissed" and that the reasons for the decision would be given at a later date. The trials of the three men are expected to begin soon, with Mr. Morley's trial scheduled to start on November 22. All three men are on unconditional bail and have been barred by their party from standing again as Labour MPs. The charges against them followed a nine-month police investigation triggered by the leak of MPs' expenses claims to a national newspaper. The case has raised important questions about the accountability of MPs and the role of parliamentary privilege in protecting them from prosecution. The Supreme Court's decision is seen as a significant milestone in the ongoing expenses scandal, which has led to widespread criticism of MPs and calls for greater transparency and accountability. The trials of the three former MPs are expected to be closely watched, and the outcome will likely have significant implications for the future of parliamentary privilege and the regulation of MPs' expenses.

Game of Thrones star Maisie Williams has opened up about her own experiences with online bullying, revealing that she was subjected to cruel messages and harassment during her teenage years. The 17-year-old actress, who plays Arya Stark in the hit HBO series, said that she would often sit in her bedroom crying, with her brother attributing her mood to typical teenage behavior. However, Maisie explained that there was more to her emotional state than just adolescence. She felt unable to confide in anyone about the bullying, which led to feelings of isolation and sadness. The situation became so unbearable that she would scroll through hurtful messages on her phone, even when sitting next to her mother on the train, trying to hold back tears. The bullying eventually stopped when Maisie deleted her online profiles and left school, but she acknowledges that this is not a viable solution for most people. Instead, she advises young people to be mindful of their online behavior, urging them to think before posting anything that they wouldn't say or do in person. Maisie's experiences have given her a unique perspective on the issue of online bullying, and she is now speaking out to help others who may be going through similar struggles. Her story will be featured on Radio 1 Stories: Anti-Social Media on Tuesday night, and she hopes that by sharing her experiences, she can help raise awareness and provide support to those affected by online harassment.

UK Defence Secretary Sir Michael Fallon has announced the sale of three military sites in County Down as part of a long-term strategy to reduce costs and improve efficiency. The sites, which include Abercorn Barracks in Ballykinler, Kinnegar Logistics Base in Holywood, and the Volunteer Gliding School at Newtownards Airfield, are among 56 across the UK slated for sale. The move is expected to save the Ministry of Defence approximately £140m over the next decade, which will be reinvested in creating "areas of military expertise" across the country. The sale of these sites will also release enough land to build around 55,000 homes. However, not everyone is pleased with the decision. Strangford MP Jim Shannon has described the move as "backwards" and "illogical", particularly with regards to the potential demolition of 200 houses at Abercorn Barracks, which he believes could be used as social housing. The Kinnegar base is expected to relocate to nearby Palace Barracks, although it is unclear whether any jobs will be lost as a result. The decision to sell two hangars at Newtownards Airfield has also been met with criticism, with Shannon stating that there is no potential for housing development at the site and that the decision has not been well thought out, especially given recent funding for the air cadets. The sale of these sites is part of a larger effort to streamline the UK's military operations and reduce costs.

Saudi Arabia Cracks Down on Controversial Fatwas with Website Blocks In a move aimed at reducing the influence of ultra-conservative clerics, King Abdullah of Saudi Arabia has issued a decree restricting the right to issue fatwas to members of an officially approved council of Islamic scholars. The decree has resulted in the blocking of several websites that offered fatwas, which are religious edicts or advice. The decision comes after a series of controversial fatwas sparked embarrassment for the Saudi authorities. Some clerics have used fatwas to publicly oppose attempts to modernize and Westernize Saudi society, while others have issued bizarre and outdated rulings. For example, one fatwa suggested that a man could symbolically become a woman's child by sucking on her breast or drinking her breast milk, thereby circumventing the prohibition on mixing of the sexes. In response to the decree, the popular website Islam Today has closed its fatwa pages to avoid being shut down by the authorities. The website, which is run by influential cleric Salman al-Awdah, has a large following in Saudi Arabia and is known for its moderate interpretations of Islam. Al-Awdah, a former hardline cleric who was imprisoned in the 1990s, has reinvented himself as a moderate figure and has become a prominent voice in Saudi Arabia's religious landscape. The blocking of websites and restriction on fatwas is seen as an attempt by King Abdullah to promote reform and reduce the influence of conservative clerics. However, the move is likely to face opposition from some members of the Saudi ruling family and the religious establishment. As the Saudi government continues to navigate the complex balance between tradition and modernity, the issue of fatwas is likely to remain a contentious one.

US-based Liberty Media is set to finalize its purchase of a controlling interest in Formula 1 after receiving approval from the FIA, the sport's governing body. The deal, which will see Liberty take over from CVC Capital Partners, is expected to be completed within weeks. Liberty has already acquired 18% of Delta Topco, the holding company of the F1 Group, and will increase its stake to 35.3% in the coming weeks. The company has outlined its vision for the sport, including protecting historic European races and establishing new events in the USA and Latin America. Liberty also plans to grow the sport through digital media, expanding its global reach and fan base. The FIA has welcomed the partnership, believing it will "ensure the continued success and development" of F1. With regulatory hurdles cleared, Liberty's shareholders have approved the buy-out, paving the way for a new era in Formula 1.

Ukraine has secured a major investment deal with US-based Cargill and Ukraine's M.V. Cargo to build a grain terminal on the Black Sea. The terminal, expected to be completed by spring 2018, will enable Ukrainian farmers to export an additional five million tons of grain. This move is seen as a significant step in boosting the country's agricultural exports. Despite ongoing conflicts with Russia and corruption concerns, Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk believes this deal will demonstrate Ukraine's reliability as an investment destination. US Ambassador Geoffrey Pyatt echoed this sentiment, stating that Ukraine has the potential to become an "agricultural superpower." The investment is a notable vote of confidence in Ukraine's economy, with the country expecting to export a record 37 million tons of grain between July 2015 and June 2016. The new terminal will play a key role in achieving this goal, solidifying Ukraine's position as a major player in the global agricultural market.

Leicestershire County Cricket Club has announced the return of overseas players Umar Akmal and Kevin O'Brien. Akmal, 25, scored 133 T20 runs in four matches this season. O'Brien, 31, will participate in both the T20 Blast and One-Day Cup. According to chief executive Wasim Khan, both players had a positive influence on the club and are match-winners. They made an immediate impact, with O'Brien batting well at Lancashire and Akmal playing a standout innings at Nottinghamshire. The club is excited to welcome them back to Grace Road, and fans are eagerly anticipating their return.

Mexico's Popocatepetl volcano has prompted the closure of several nearby schools as a precautionary measure. The National Disaster Prevention Centre raised the alert to "yellow stage three," the third-highest level, due to increased activity. The 5,450m volcano, located 70km from Mexico City, has been rumbling, with locals reporting they can hear its roar and feel its force. Concepcion Perez, from the town of Xalitzintla, described the experience to Agence France-Presse. Evacuation shelters have been prepared, and officials warn the alert could remain in place for weeks or months. Popocatepetl, meaning "Smoking Mountain," is Mexico's second-highest peak and has a history of major eruptions, including one in 2000 that forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people. Residents are bracing for potential further activity.

Scotland's Six Nations Championship Hopes Dented by Injury to Key Player The Scottish rugby team has been dealt a significant blow ahead of the upcoming Six Nations Championship, with the news that prop forward WP Nel will miss the tournament due to a neck injury. The 30-year-old Edinburgh tight-head, who has won 15 caps for Scotland, suffered the injury during a Challenge Cup tie against Harlequins and a subsequent scan revealed damage to an intervertebral disc in his neck. Nel's injury is a devastating blow to Scotland's chances in the championship, which gets underway on February 4 when they host Ireland at Murrayfield. The Scots will then travel to France on February 12, before facing Wales, England, and Italy in the following weeks. Head coach Vern Cotter, who will be leading the team for the last time before taking charge of Montpellier, had included Nel in his 37-man squad for the tournament. The injury to Nel is not only a setback for Scotland, but also a personal blow to the player himself. The South Africa-born prop, who qualifies to play for Scotland on residency rules, was considered one of the country's few guaranteed Lions for the summer tour to New Zealand. However, with the uncertainty surrounding his neck injury, particularly serious for a prop forward, he must now be considered a major doubt for the Lions. Nel's absence will be felt by Scotland, who played well in the autumn without him but are undoubtedly a better team with him in the lineup. He brings experience and solidity to the scrum, as well as carrying hard in the loose, and his loss will be deeply felt. As BBC Scotland's Tom English noted, "This is devastating news..... Nel is a world-class tight-head and was, until this latest injury, one of Scotland's very few guaranteed Lions for the summer tour to New Zealand." The Scottish Rugby Union has announced that Nel will be assessed to determine whether he requires corrective surgery. In the meantime, Edinburgh, his club team, has stated that they have had "positive conversations" about keeping him in the Scottish capital, despite reported interest from French Top 14 sides Toulon and Clermont Auvergne. Scotland's squad for the Six Nations Championship includes a number of experienced players, including Greig Laidlaw, Richie Gray, and Stuart Hogg. However, the loss of Nel will undoubtedly be felt, and the team will need to regroup and refocus ahead of their opening match against Ireland. With the championship just around the corner, Scotland will be hoping that their other players can step up and fill the void left by Nel's injury.

Controversy Surrounds Indian Businessman Vijay Mallya's Whereabouts Speculation has risen regarding the whereabouts of Indian businessman Vijay Mallya, following a Supreme Court case involving unpaid debts of $1.4 billion. A consortium of banks and creditors had demanded that Mallya's passport be impounded and his $75 million severance pay from Diageo be blocked to repay debts. Although the payout was blocked, it emerged that Mallya had already left India, sparking an uproar among opposition MPs who accused the government of allowing him to flee. Mallya, known for his lavish lifestyle and dubbed "India's Richard Branson," has denied fleeing the country and criticized his "media trial." Reports suggest he is currently residing in London. Opposition MPs are now demanding that the government bring Mallya back to face the law. The businessman, who sold a significant portion of United Spirits to Diageo in 2014, was set to receive the $75 million payout after being ousted from the firm. Mallya also owns a stake in the Formula One team Force India. The Indian government is under pressure to take action and bring Mallya to justice.

Coleraine FC has announced the signing of Jordan Allan, a 21-year-old striker, on a loan deal until January. Allan joins the Bannsiders from Derry City, where he has been playing since December. Manager Oran Kearney expressed his delight at the new signing, stating that Allan "gives us another option up top and provides a bit more competition for places." Kearney praised Allan's ability to hold the ball, run behind defenses, and finish chances. Despite his young age, Allan has gained significant experience playing for various clubs, including Dundee United, Albion Rovers, and Montrose. He played a crucial role in helping Montrose avoid relegation in the 2014-15 season. Allan's addition to the Coleraine squad is expected to bolster their attacking lineup and provide a fresh challenge for the team. His loan deal is set to run until January, and fans are eagerly awaiting his debut.
